authors.name: Annie Besant
authors.nationality: English; the pamphlet, the secularist lecture and the socialist essay
authors.identity: Freethinker, socialist, trade-union organiser and later theosophist; one of the most effective radical orators and polemicists of the 1880s.
authors.biography: Born Annie Wood in London on 1 October 1847, the daughter of an Irish doctor; she married the clergyman Frank Besant in 1867 and separated from him in 1873 after refusing to continue in orthodox belief. She became a secularist lecturer, edited the National Reformer with Charles Bradlaugh, was prosecuted with him in 1877 for publishing a birth-control pamphlet, led the matchgirls' strike at Bryant and May in 1888 and was elected to the London School Board in 1888. She joined the Theosophical Society in 1889 and later settled in India, where she founded the Central Hindu College and became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress in 1917. She died at Adyar, Madras, on 20 September 1933.
authors.profile: Besant's early writing is the literature of freethought and of the new socialism: the pamphlet, the public lecture and the radical essay, written in a plain, forceful, argumentative prose designed to be read aloud and to convert. Her 1880s work on behalf of the matchgirls and the unemployed of the East End made her the most prominent woman radical in Britain, and her autobiography is a classic record of Victorian unbelief and self-making.
authors.style: Direct argument and plain diction; the platform address with its rhythm and repetition; the polemical pamphlet; the reasoned appeal to evidence against scripture; the first-person narrative of conversion and release.
authors.concerns: Freethought and biblical criticism; birth control and the position of women; poverty, sweated labour and the rights of the unskilled worker; socialism and the land; education; the spiritual and the occult.
authors.significance: Besant is one of the most important British radical writers of the 1870s-80s: her trial with Bradlaugh established the right to publish birth-control literature, she founded the matchgirls' union, and she was a central figure in the early British socialist movement before her later career in India and the Theosophical Society.

authors.name: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English peer and moralist whose Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times (1711) made politeness, wit and ridicule the tests of virtue and of religious sincerity.
authors.biography: Born in London on 26 February 1671 and named for his grandfather, the First Earl of Shaftesbury, he was educated privately under the supervision of John Locke and kept only a brief residence at Oxford. He sat in the Commons for Christchurch from 1695 until he succeeded to the earldom in 1699. A failing chest ended any political career, and from 1704 he travelled for his health in the Netherlands and in Italy, corresponding with Dutch and French heterodox writers. He revised the essays, letters and dialogues of those years into Characteristics (1711), which he superintended through the press himself and introduced with a Design'd Letter satirising bookmaking. He died at Consendula in Calabria on 4 February 1713, leaving a daughter; the earldom passed to a nephew.
authors.profile: A philosopher of polite conversation who wrote in genres - letter, dialogue, soliloquy, rhapsody - and treated the inspection of one's own heart as a moral exercise.
authors.style: Aphoristic, urbane and deliberately witty; sustained irony and theatrical self-examination; long periodic sentences pointed by sententious tags; argument conducted as banter.
authors.concerns: An innate moral sense and self-approval; enthusiasm, superstition and the ridicule of fanatics; the fitness of religion to common sense; politeness, reputation and the love of one's country.
authors.significance: He set the terms of eighteenth-century moral-sense theory and of the age's debate about enthusiasm, influencing Hutcheson, Hume, Adam Smith, Chesterfield, Voltaire and Kant, and making ridicule a standard weapon against priestcraft.
authors.uncertainty: Several pieces in Characteristics circulated in manuscript and in unauthorized copies, so the order of composition is still debated.

authors.name: Anthony Collins
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Barrister and freethinker whose Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and inquiry on human liberty (1717) made him the boldest English deist before Hume.
authors.biography: Born at Heston in Middlesex in 1676, he was educated at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge, and was called to the bar. He became the close friend and literary executor of John Locke, lived on a property in Lincolnshire, divided his years between Heston and Pall Mall, and gathered a club of free inquirers. His Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and the Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion (1707) drew a barrage of replies from churchmen, and the published correspondence with the Bishop of Winchester on the evidences of Christianity ran through 1708 and 1709. A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty (1717) denied the liberty of indifference, and The Scheme of Literal Prophecy Considered (1727) denied that Old Testament prophecy proved the gospel. He died in London on 13 December 1729, and a servant's tale that he defied the priests on his deathbed was long printed as a model of infidel constancy.
authors.profile: A lawyer's deism: courteous, relentlessly procedural argument that demands of revelation the same evidence it would require in court.
authors.style: Clear, dry and forensic; scholastic distinctions and long chains of consequence; courteous invective; a fondness for published correspondence and formal rejoinder.
authors.concerns: The boundaries of reason in religion; liberty, necessity and the will; the evidential value of miracle and prophecy; priestly authority and the rights of private judgement; tolerance as a civil necessity.
authors.significance: He moved deism from a defence of natural religion into a historical and philosophical critique of revelation, and defined the freethinking tradition that Bentley, Clarke and Butler were recruited to answer.
authors.uncertainty: The celebrated deathbed declaration is reported by a hostile servant and is generally doubted by modern scholars.

authors.name: Anthony Hope
authors.nationality: English; the Ruritanian romance and the adventure novel
authors.identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of The Prisoner of Zenda and the inventor of the Ruritanian romance.
authors.biography: Born Anthony Hope Hawkins in London on 9 February 1863, the son of a school headmaster; he was educated at Marlborough and Balliol College, Oxford, and practised as a barrister until the success of The Prisoner of Zenda (1894) allowed him to write full time. He wrote over thirty novels, served as a war correspondent in the First World War, and was knighted in 1918. He died at Walton-on-the-Hill, Surrey, on 8 July 1933.
authors.profile: Hope invented the Ruritanian romance: The Prisoner of Zenda created a fictional central Europe of small kingdoms, court intrigue and swordfights, and in doing so created a formula that has never left the popular imagination. He was also a considerable writer of the English social novel, and his best work — The Dolly Dialogues, Rupert of Hentzau — shows a light, ironic talent that the Zenda industry has obscured.
authors.style: Fast-moving adventure narrative with a first-person narrator; the fictional kingdom with its invented geography and protocol; the double and the impostor; swordplay and the set-piece escape; ironic comedy of manners in the social novels; the light, assured dialogue.
authors.concerns: Royalty, legitimacy and the impostor; courage, loyalty and the gentleman's code; court intrigue and the small kingdom; love and renunciation; the Englishman abroad; honour and the duel.
authors.significance: Hope created the Ruritanian romance, one of the most durable formulas in popular fiction: The Prisoner of Zenda has never been out of print, it gave the language the word 'Ruritanian', and it stands at the head of a tradition that runs through Graustark to The Prisoner of Zenda's many film versions.

authors.name: Anthony Trollope
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel, Barsetshire and Westminster
authors.identity: Novelist of the church, the civil service and Parliament; the most prolific and the most systematic of the great Victorian realists, with forty-seven novels, five travel books and two short-story collections.
authors.biography: Born in London on 24 April 1815, the fourth son of Thomas Anthony Trollope, a Chancery barrister whose practice failed, and Frances Milton Trollope, the novelist and travel writer. The family collapsed financially and moved to Harrow Weald and then to a farm near Bruges; Trollope was educated at Winchester and Harrow as a day boy and was miserable at both. He obtained a clerkship in the General Post Office in 1834 and was sent to Ireland as a surveyor's clerk in 1841, where he married Rose Heseltine in 1844 and wrote his first two novels. He invented the pillar box (1851-52) and rose to surveyor-general; from 1859 he lived in London and edited the Fortnightly Review (1865-67) and later Saint Pauls. He stood unsuccessfully for Parliament as a Liberal in 1868 and for a second time in 1874. The Warden (1855) began the Barsetshire series; The Last Chronicle of Barset closed it in 1867; the Palliser novels ran from Can You Forgive Her? (1864) to The Duke's Children (1879-80). He travelled constantly and died in London on 6 December 1882; his posthumously published Autobiography (1883) scandalised the age by stating exactly what he earned.
authors.profile: Trollope wrote fiction as a daily trade, 250 words every quarter of an hour before breakfast, and his art is built on that regularity: he produces a stable fictional world (the county of Barsetshire, the political London of the Pallisers) in which the same institutions — the bishop's palace, the county set, the Government office, the hunting field — recur, and in which character is established by habitual action and by conversation rather than by crisis. His plots are unashamedly about money, marriage and place, and he is the least sentimental of Victorian novelists about the marriage market, clerical ambition and political careerism. He is also an unusually explicit narrator, commenting on his own characters' motives in a tone of tolerant worldly wisdom.
authors.style: Multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention; a narrator who addresses the reader as a co-resident of the fictional county; exact notation of income, debts, preferment and social obligation; dialogue that carries class and profession; a refusal of violent incident; long-distance management of dozens of characters over decades.
authors.concerns: Ambition, preferment and the machinery of institutional life; the marriage market and the economics of the genteel poor; the Church of England as a career; the relation of private vice to public position; hunting, sport and the rituals of county society; the compromises of political liberalism.
authors.significance: Trollope mapped the professions of Victorian England as no other novelist did, and the Barsetshire and Palliser series are now read as the most complete single portrait of Victorian institutional life. His Autobiography, with its exact accounts of earnings and working method, made authorship a profession in the public eye. He was depreciated by Henry James and the aesthetes, rehabilitated by the twentieth-century critics, and has held a central place in the canon of the realist novel since.

authors.name: Aphra Behn
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: The first English woman to earn a living as a professional writer; a prolific playwright, poet, novelist, and (she claimed) secret agent, whose The Rover (1677) and the novella Oroonoko (1688) are landmarks of Restoration drama and of the early English novel.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640, probably at Canterbury; she claimed (in Oroonoko) to have lived as a girl in Surinam, though this is disputed. She may have served as a royalist intelligence agent in Antwerp (as 'Astrea') during the Second Dutch War, was imprisoned for debt in 1668, and from the 1670s supported herself by writing for the stage. She produced some nineteen plays — comedies including The Rover (1677, 1681), The Feign'd Curtizans (1679), and The Lucky Chance (1686), and the tragicomedies Oroonoko (adapted) and The Widow Ranter (1689) — as well as poetry, translations (from Fontenelle and La Rochefoucauld), and the prose fiction Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (1688), Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister, and The Fair Jilt. A staunch royalist and Tory, she wrote for James II's cause and died on 16 April 1689, buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The professional woman of letters who wrote with energy and commercial acumen across every genre, defending a woman's right to write and to pleasure while exposing the sexual and colonial politics of her age.
authors.style: Vigorous comic prose and verse; the rake and the resourceful heroine; bawdy wit and sexual frankness; narrative prose blending travel, romance, and reportage; and political and amorous verse.
authors.concerns: Women's authorship, sexuality, and economic independence; libertinism and the double standard; slavery, colonialism, and the 'noble slave'; royalist and Tory politics; and the professional writer's life.
authors.significance: Behn is the first Englishwoman to have lived by her pen and a founding figure of the English novel; Oroonoko is an early anti-slavery narrative, and her recovery by Virginia Woolf and feminist criticism has made her central to women's literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Behn's early life, her Surinam voyage, her marriage, and her espionage are all disputed or thinly documented; she freely fictionalised her own biography, making the factual record uncertain.

authors.name: Arnold Bennett
authors.nationality: British; the Five Towns novel, the realist chronicle and the professional writer's essay
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and journalist; the French-trained realist of the Staffordshire Potteries, the author of The Old Wives' Tale, and the period's most professional man of letters.
authors.biography: Born Enoch Arnold Bennett at Hanley, Staffordshire, on 27 May 1867, the son of a solicitor; he read law, worked as a solicitor's clerk in London and then as a journalist and editor of Woman magazine, and became famous with The Old Wives' Tale (1908). He wrote over eighty books, kept a yacht and a flat in Paris, and was ridiculed by Woolf in 'Mr Bennett and Mrs Brown' (1924) as the Edwardian materialist. He died of typhoid in London on 27 March 1931.
authors.profile: Bennett brought the French naturalist novel into English and made the industrial Potteries a literary country. The Old Wives' Tale is one of the great English novels of time, Clayhanger a great novel of provincial ambition, and his journalism made the professional writer a public figure. His quarrel with the modernists — over whether character is made by clothes, furniture and income — is the period's clearest statement of the realist case.
authors.style: Solid material specification — furniture, houses, incomes, the exact weight of a life; the long chronological sweep and the undramatic passage of years; the Five Towns idiom given in dialogue; the ironic narrator who knows more than his characters; the plain, unadorned sentence.
authors.concerns: The industrial Potteries and their chapels; provincial ambition and the escape from the town; time and the slow erosion of a life; money, thrift and respectability; women's work and women's endurance; the professional writer and the literary market.
authors.significance: Bennett is the period's principal realist and the literary historian of the industrial Midlands: The Old Wives' Tale and Clayhanger are permanent novels of provincial life, his Five Towns gave English fiction a new region, and his quarrel with Woolf is the defining debate about what the novel is for.

authors.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
authors.nationality: Scottish; the Victorian detective story and historical romance
authors.identity: Physician and writer; the creator of Sherlock Holmes and the founder of the modern detective story.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859 into an Irish Catholic family of artists; educated at Stonyhurst and the University of Edinburgh, where he qualified in medicine in 1881. He practised as a ship's surgeon and then in Southsea, and published A Study in Scarlet in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887; the Holmes stories were commissioned by the Strand Magazine from 1891, and the character became a national institution, which Doyle attempted to kill off in 1893 and was forced to revive in 1903. The historical novels Micah Clarke (1889), The White Company (1891), Rodney Stone (1896) and Sir Nigel (1906), the Brigadier Gerard stories and The Lost World (1912) show the range he claimed for himself. He served as a volunteer physician in the Boer War, wrote The Great Boer War (1900) and The War in South Africa (1902), and campaigned for spiritualism for the last twenty years of his life. He died at Crowborough, Sussex, on 7 July 1930.
authors.profile: Doyle invented the detective story as a modern genre: the Holmes stories are constructed as a problem and a solution, with a narrator who is intelligent but not deductive, and a detective whose method is observation combined with an encyclopedia of specialised knowledge. The stories are also a document of late-Victorian London — the hansom, the gaslight, the chemical laboratory, the colonial return, the country house and the bank — and their form (the short story sequence with a stable pair of characters) became the template of the modern series.
authors.style: The clue and the deduction; the Watson narrator as the reader's stand-in; the opening problem and the explanatory retrospect; the adventure story's energy and the historical novel's scholarship; the plain, lucid narrative prose; the repertory of characters and the mythical London.
authors.concerns: Rationality and method against mystery; crime, class and the colonial fortune; the imperial frontier and the war; honour, courage and the gentleman; the supernatural (in his later work) against the scientific; the professional man and his expertise.
authors.significance: Doyle created the most famous character in English fiction and the form of the modern detective story: Holmes and Watson are the origin of the mystery series, and the Holmes canon is a central document of Victorian London. His historical novels were considered by their author his best work, and The Lost World founded the modern science-fiction adventure.

authors.name: Arthur Golding
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: translator; Puritan gentleman
authors.biography: Born about 1536, half-brother of Margaret Golding, mother of the Earl of Oxford. Educated perhaps at Jesus College, Cambridge, he served in the household of Sir William Cecil and translated steadily through the 1560s and 1570s, chiefly from the classics and from Calvin. He died in May 1606.
authors.profile: The translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses — the first four books in 1565, the complete fifteen in 1567 — together with versions of Caesar, Justin, Seneca, and Calvin's sermons and treatises; his Ovid is 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
authors.style: Energetic fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets) that render Ovid with moralizing commentary and a homespun vividness; Puritan in gloss, pagan in gusto.
authors.concerns: The reconciliation of classical myth with Protestant morality; the edification of the common reader.
authors.significance: His Metamorphoses made Ovid an English book and fed Shakespeare, Spenser, and the entire mythological vocabulary of the Elizabethans.

authors.name: Arthur Hugh Clough
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period
authors.identity: Poet and educationalist; the most sceptical of the Victorian poets and the author of The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich and Amours de Voyage.
authors.biography: Born in Liverpool on 1 January 1819, son of a cotton merchant; brought up in Charleston, South Carolina, and educated at Rugby under Thomas Arnold and at Balliol College, Oxford. He resigned his Oxford fellowship in 1848 over the Thirty-Nine Articles, was principal of University Hall, London, in 1849-52 and an examiner in the Education Office from 1852; he travelled to America and Italy in 1849 and married Blanche Smith in 1854, a cousin of Florence Nightingale, whose biography he began. He died in Florence on 13 November 1861, and his poems were collected by his wife and by his friend Matthew Arnold, whose 'Thyrsis' is his elegy.
authors.profile: Clough wrote the Victorian long poem as a debate: The Bothie, in hexameters, is a holiday romance that turns into an argument about class, education and marriage, and Amours de Voyage is an epistolary novelette in verse whose hero's paralysis of will makes him a comic and painful ancestor of the modern anti-hero. His scepticism is not agonised but dry, ironic and unresolved, and he refuses the consolations that Tennyson and Arnold supply.
authors.style: Hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms; letters, journals and reported speech inside the poem; a self-mocking narrator; deliberate flatness of diction; the intrusion of contemporary politics (the Roman Republic of 1849, the Crimean War) into private love.
authors.concerns: Religious doubt and intellectual honesty; the relation of the educated Englishman to the working class; love and the fear of commitment; the 1848 revolutions and Italian independence; education and national life; the comic exposure of Victorian earnestness.
authors.significance: Clough is the poet in whom Victorian doubt becomes a modern, ironic intelligence rather than a crisis; his influence on Hopkins (who was his pupil at Oxford), on Arnold's elegy and on the twentieth-century long poem is out of proportion to his small output. He is now read as the missing link between the Romantic conversation poem and the modernist verse-novel.

authors.name: Arthur Koestler

authors.identity: Novelist and political writer; the author of Spanish Testament and Darkness at Noon.
authors.biography: Born Artúr Kösztler at Budapest on 5 September 1905; he worked as a journalist in Palestine and Berlin, joined the Communist Party in 1931, and was imprisoned by the Francoists in Spain, the experience of Spanish Testament (1937). Leaving the party, he wrote Darkness at Noon (1940), the great novel of the Moscow trials, in German and had it translated by Daphne Hardy; Arrival and Departure (1943) carried the war's refugees into the novel of the psychoanalysis. He took his own life in London on 1 March 1983.
authors.profile: Arthur Koestler is the novelist of the totalitarian century: Darkness at Noon made Rubashov's cell and its confession the definitive novel of the show trials, and Spanish Testament is the testimony of the party's disillusion in the decade of the Popular Front.
authors.style: The argument carried in the cell and the interrogation; the plain analytical prose of the political mind; the confession as the moral problem; the refugee's war in the psychoanalytic novel; the essay and the testament beside the fiction.
authors.concerns: Totalitarianism and the show trial; the party and the disillusion; the Spain of the Popular Front; the refugee and the war; the confession and the conscience of the revolutionary.
authors.significance: Arthur Koestler is the novelist of the totalitarian century: Darkness at Noon made the cell and its confession the definitive novel of the show trials, and Spanish Testament is the testimony of the party's disillusion.

authors.name: Arthur Machen
authors.nationality: Welsh; the tale of the pagan survival and the horror of the ancient world
authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and journalist; the great Welsh writer of supernatural horror and the author of 'The Great God Pan' and The Hill of Dreams.
authors.biography: Born Arthur Llewellyn Jones at Caerleon, Monmouthshire, on 3 March 1863; he failed to get into medicine, worked as a clerk, a tutor and a journalist, and published The Great God Pan and The Inmost Light in 1894 and The Three Impostors in 1895. The Hill of Dreams followed in 1907, The Bowmen — the story that created the Angel of Mons — in 1915, and a stream of essays, translations and memoirs thereafter. He died at Beaconsfield on 15 December 1947.
authors.profile: Machen is the great Welsh writer of supernatural horror: The Great God Pan is the most influential English horror story of the 1890s, The Hill of Dreams is one of the finest decadent novels in the language, and 'The White People' is the strangest story of its kind in English. His paganism and his Welsh landscape gave the ghost story a mythology, and Lovecraft and Stephen King both acknowledge him.
authors.style: The tale built on an ancient survival beneath the modern town; the Welsh landscape and the Roman ruins; the decadent novel of the artist's vision; the document and the hearsay that never quite resolve; the prose of ecstatic description; the horror that is never shown.
authors.concerns: The pagan survival and the ancient world beneath the modern; Wales, the Roman past and the Celtic inheritance; the artist's vision and its cost; the city (London) as a place of corruption; the body and the sexual secret; the occult and the esoteric.
authors.significance: Machen wrote the most influential English horror story of the 1890s and one of the finest decadent novels: The Great God Pan shaped the whole modern genre, The Hill of Dreams is a permanent novel of the artist, and 'The White People' is the strangest story in English. He gave the supernatural tale a mythology and a Welsh landscape.

authors.name: Arthur Morrison
authors.nationality: English; the slum novel and the detective story
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the chronicler of the East End and the creator of the first English professional private detective.
authors.biography: Born in the East End of London on 1 November 1863, the son of an engine fitter; he left school at sixteen and worked as a clerk at the People's Palace in Mile End, where he began writing and where his first sketches of East End life were composed. Tales of Mean Streets (1894) and A Child of the Jago (1896) made him the leading English writer of slum fiction; he later became a connoisseur and collector of Japanese art and wrote little fiction after 1911. He died at Chalfont St Peter, Buckinghamshire, on 4 December 1945.
authors.profile: Morrison wrote the East End from inside: his Jago is not an exotic hell but a precise topographical and economic reality, and his refusal to sentimentalise it made him controversial with both the philanthropists and the socialists. He is also, in Martin Hewitt, the inventor of the English professional private detective who works with the police rather than against them — a deliberate, bureaucratic answer to Sherlock Holmes.
authors.style: Cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care; topographical exactness (street names, courts, public houses); short, hard sentences; refusal of moral commentary; documentary detail of rents, trades and food.
authors.concerns: Poverty, criminality and environment; the 'street' as a social organism; philanthropy and its failures; the professional detective and the police; class and the East End; race and the Chinese and Jewish communities of the docks.
authors.significance: Morrison is the central English novelist of the East End slum in the 1890s and a key figure in the transition from the Victorian social-problem novel to the twentieth-century working-class novel. A Child of the Jago was the most discussed English novel of 1896, and Martin Hewitt is a foundational figure in the history of the English detective story.

authors.name: Arthur Ransome
authors.nationality: British; the sailing adventure of the Lake District and the Swallows series
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the creator of Swallows and Amazons and of the great sailing novels of English childhood.
authors.biography: Born Arthur Michell Ransome at Leeds on 18 January 1884, the son of a history professor; he read chemistry at Yorkshire College and went to London to write, publishing Bohemia in London (1907) and A History of Storytelling (1909), and serving as a foreign correspondent in Russia, where he witnessed the revolution and married Trotsky's secretary, Evgenia Shveliepina. From 1930 the sailing novels made him the most read writer of English childhood; he died at Manchester on 3 June 1967.
authors.profile: Arthur Ransome invented the sailing novel of English childhood: the Swallows and Amazons series took the practical detail of boats, camps, charts and weather and made it the whole substance of adventure, so that the children's own competence is the plot. His Russia books and his journalism are forgotten beside them, but the series remains the standard against which every English children's adventure of the open air is measured.
authors.style: The plain, exact, practical prose of the sailor; the chart, the knot, the meal and the weather reported as the adventure itself; the dialogue of children left competently alone; the absence of adults except as distant authorities; the Lake District and the Norfolk Broads rendered with a navigator's exactness.
authors.concerns: Childhood competence and the children's own republic; the boat, the camp and the chart as the instruments of imagination; the English lake and broad as the theatre of adventure; the Russian revolution witnessed at first hand; the quarrel between the journalist's eye and the novelist's loyalty.
authors.significance: Arthur Ransome's Swallows and Amazons series is the founding cycle of the English sailing novel for children: its practical exactness, its children's republic and its Lake District water made competence the substance of adventure and gave English childhood its classic open-air fiction.

authors.name: Arthur Symons
authors.nationality: English; the symbolist lyric, the criticism of decadence and the essay on the dance
authors.identity: Poet, critic and editor; the central impresario of the English Decadence and the first English critic of the Symbolist movement.
authors.biography: Born at Milford Haven on 28 February 1865; he was brought up in Devon and London, edited the Savoy with Aubrey Beardsley in 1896, and published Days and Nights (1889), London Nights (1895) and The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899), the book through which Yeats, Eliot and Pound learned about French poetry. He edited the seven-volume Collected Works of Dowson and the plays of Webster. A mental breakdown in 1908 ended his central period; he lived on in Cornwall and Kent and died at Wittersham on 22 January 1945.
authors.profile: Symons wrote the poetry of urban night and the prose of aesthetic criticism: his lyrics of the music hall, the ballet and the prostitute's room made the city a place of the senses, and his Symbolist book changed the course of English and American poetry by teaching a generation that literature is the expression of an invisible world through symbol. His criticism of the dance, of Beardsley, of Huysmans and of Wagner is the central body of English Decadent prose.
authors.style: The short lyric built on a single mood; the city at night; the dance rhythms of the music hall; musical repetition and refrain; the prose essay of aesthetic appreciation; the critical definition by evocation.
authors.concerns: The city and its pleasures; the dancer and the music hall; the prostitute and the outsider; sexual desire and its costs; the Symbolist theory of art; the relation of the arts; decadence and exhaustion.
authors.significance: Symons is the central English critic of the Decadence and the man who introduced Symbolism to the English-speaking world: The Symbolist Movement in Literature is one of the most influential critical books ever published in English, and his poetry and his Savoy editorship made him the impresario of the 1890s.

authors.name: Arthur Wing Pinero
authors.nationality: English; the well-made play, the problem drama and the social comedy
authors.identity: Dramatist; the master of the well-made play and the writer who brought the moral problem of the 1890s onto the English stage.
authors.biography: Born Arthur Wing Pinero in London on 24 May 1855, the son of a solicitor; he trained as an actor and joined the Lyceum company in 1876, then turned to playwriting, producing a long series of farces and comedies in the 1880s. The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) made him the most discussed dramatist in England; he wrote The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith, Trelawny of the 'Wells', The Gay Lord Quex and Mid-Channel, and was knighted in 1909. He died in London on 23 November 1934.
authors.profile: Pinero made the English stage serious: his farces gave the 1880s their comic idiom, and his problem plays of the 1890s — above all The Second Mrs Tanqueray — put the fallen woman, the double standard and the woman with a past at the centre of a drama built with the mechanical perfection of the well-made play. He was the professional playwright as craftsman, and his stagecraft was the technical foundation on which Shaw and Wilde built.
authors.style: The well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion; dialogue of London society with its clipped idiom; stage directions of meticulous precision; the problem stated and then followed to its social consequence; a comic subplot counterpointing the serious action.
authors.concerns: The woman with a past and the double standard; marriage, divorce and respectability; the theatre and its professional world; class, money and the marriage market; the New Woman and the claims of the individual; the provincial town and the London stage.
authors.significance: Pinero is the greatest English craftsman of the well-made play and the dramatist who made the Victorian stage confront the moral questions of the 1890s: The Second Mrs Tanqueray is the central English problem play before Shaw, Trelawny of the 'Wells' is a permanent classic of the theatrical comedy, and his technical example shaped the modern English theatre.

authors.concerns: The justification and celebration of Alfred's kingship; the union of learning with rule.

authors.name: Augusta Webster
authors.nationality: English; the dramatic poem, the sonnet and the woman's monologue
authors.identity: Poet, playwright, essayist and translator; the author of the finest Victorian dramatic monologues by a woman, and a campaigner for women's education and the vote.
authors.biography: Born Julia Augusta Davies at Poole on 30 January 1837, the daughter of a naval officer; she was educated at the Cambridge home of her grandfather and at the South Kensington art school, and married the solicitor and philologist Thomas Webster in 1863. She published four volumes of poetry, the verse dramas Theaus (1867) and Medea (1878), a translation of Euripides, and three novels, and she campaigned for women's suffrage and against the Contagious Diseases Acts. She died at Kensington on 5 September 1894.
authors.profile: Webster wrote the dramatic monologue as a woman's form: 'A Castaway' is the greatest Victorian poem spoken by a prostitute, and 'Circe', 'The Happiest Girl in the World' and the Medea translation adapt the classical and the contemporary to a woman's voice. She was a learned and technically ambitious poet — her verse is dense, allusive and often deliberately difficult — and her essays on poetry and on women are among the sharpest of the period.
authors.style: The dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker; classical and mythological subjects turned to modern use; dense, allusive, syntactically suspended verse; sonnet sequences; translation as interpretation.
authors.concerns: The position of women and the sexual double standard; the fallen woman and the prostitute's voice; marriage and the loss of self; classical myth as a vehicle for modern feeling; education and women's intellectual capacity; motherhood.
authors.significance: Webster is the most important woman writer of the Victorian dramatic monologue: 'A Castaway' is the classic Victorian poem on prostitution from the woman's own side, and her Medea is a landmark of nineteenth-century classical translation. Her work is now central to the recovery of Victorian women's poetry.

authors.biography: Born Emma Magdolna Rozalia Maria Jozefa Borbala Orczy in Hungary on 23 September 1865; her family moved to London in 1880, and she became a painter and writer. The Scarlet Pimpernel (1905), the play of 1903 and its many sequels made her famous. She died in Monte Carlo on 12 November 1947.
authors.profile: Baroness Orczy created the Scarlet Pimpernel, the first masked hero of modern fiction and the direct ancestor of Zorro, Batman and the superhero: her novel and play founded the double-life hero and the rescue narrative of the twentieth century.

authors.name: Beatrix Potter
authors.nationality: English; the picture book and the animal tale
authors.identity: Writer and illustrator; the creator of the modern English picture book and one of the most important children's authors of the twentieth century.
authors.biography: Born Helen Beatrix Potter in Kensington, London, on 28 July 1866 into a wealthy Unitarian family; she was educated at home by governesses and studied drawing and painting privately, becoming a skilled scientific illustrator and mycologist. She began making picture letters to the children of her former governess, and The Tale of Peter Rabbit was privately printed in 1901 and published by Warne in 1902. She bought Hill Top Farm in the Lake District in 1905 and became a sheep farmer and conservationist, leaving her land to the National Trust. She died at Near Sawrey on 22 December 1943.
authors.profile: Potter made the modern picture book: the small square format, the exact watercolour illustration on every spread, the plain and mischievous story in which animals behave like naughty children and are nearly eaten. Her scientific accuracy and her feeling for the Lake District landscape give the books a permanence that most Victorian children's fiction lacks, and her stories are among the first to treat the child reader as an intelligent equal.
authors.style: Simple, concrete sentences; the illustration as half the narrative; the animal protagonist as child; exact natural history; the comic chase; a very English sense of danger held within a safe frame.
authors.concerns: Childhood disobedience and its consequences; animals and the natural world; the English countryside and its seasonal work; property, trespass and the boundaries of the farm; the small-scale domestic economy.
authors.significance: Potter invented the modern picture book and became the first children's author to control the whole design of her books, including format, illustration and typography; her twenty-three tales have sold in the hundreds of millions and she is one of the most important figures in the history of English children's literature.

authors.name: Bede
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (Northumbrian)
authors.identity: historian; theologian; poet; scholar
authors.biography: Entered the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow as a child and remained there all his life, becoming priest and teacher; he never travelled beyond Northumbria yet became the most learned man of his age in western Europe. Died on Ascension Day, 26 May 735, dictating his last work.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (completed 731), the foundational history of the English people; De temporum ratione (725), which fixed the practice of dating from the Incarnation (AD); biblical commentaries on nearly every book of scripture; the metrical and prose lives of St Cuthbert; De natura rerum; the letter to Egbert (734); and school texts on orthography and metre.
authors.style: Clear, economical, carefully sourced Latin; narrative skill in the miracle stories of the Historia; scholarly exactitude in computus and chronology.
authors.concerns: The unity and orthodoxy of the English church; chronology and computus; the transmission of patristic exegesis; the moral formation of clergy.
authors.significance: 'The father of English history'; the Historia preserves the Cædmon story, the earliest extended Old English verse, and much else besides; his computus standardized European chronology.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertainty: the Historia's autobiographical colophon and Cuthbert's account of his death are reliable; birth year inferred from his own statements.

authors.name: Ben Jonson
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and critic; the first great English literary professional and the presiding classicist of the Jacobean stage, author of the comedies of humours, the masques, and 'To Penshurst'.
authors.biography: Born June 1572 in Westminster (posthumous son of a clergyman), educated at Westminster School under William Camden, and briefly a bricklayer (his stepfather's trade) before soldiering in Flanders. By 1597 he was acting and writing for Henslowe (imprisoned in 1598 for killing the actor Gabriel Spencer in a duel, escaping hanging by benefit of clergy); Every Man in His Humour (1598, with Shakespeare in the cast) made his name. The comedies Volpone (1606), Epicene (1609), The Alchemist (1610), and Bartholomew Fair (1614) and the tragedies Sejanus (1603) and Catiline (1611) followed, together with the masques written with Inigo Jones for the Jacobean court (1605–31). He published his Works in folio in 1616 — the first English playwright to do so — and died on 6 August 1637, buried upright in Westminster Abbey ('O rare Ben Jonson').
authors.profile: The laureate of the Stuart court and the legislator of classical taste: his comedies anatomize human folly through the theory of humours, his poems ('Drink to me only', the Cary–Morison ode, the epitaphs) set the standard of English neoclassical lyric, and his Timber is the period's major critical commonplace book.
authors.style: Classical discipline and satirical vigour; the humours theory of character; erudite, plain-style verse of great metrical skill; the masque's fusion of poetry, spectacle, and antimasque.
authors.concerns: The moral function of poetry and satire; the correction of folly and vice; classical imitation and the English claim to Augustan standing; patronage, fame, and the writer's craft.
authors.significance: The first English author to treat writing as a profession and the canon as a curated Works; his comedies and critical authority shaped English drama and letters for a century, and his 'tribe of Ben' founded the Cavalier lyric.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth (1572 or 1573) is inferred; the canon of his collaborations (with Chapman, Marston, and others) and the lost plays are matters of scholarly reconstruction.

authors.name: Benjamin Disraeli
authors.nationality: English; the political novel and the romance of Young England
authors.identity: Novelist and statesman; the creator of the English political novel and twice Prime Minister of Britain.
authors.biography: Born Benjamin D'Israeli in London on 21 December 1804, the son of a Jewish man of letters who had his children baptised; he was articled to a solicitor but made his name with Vivian Grey (1826) and travelled in the Levant in 1830-31. He entered Parliament in 1837 after four defeats and led the Young England group in the 1840s, publishing Coningsby (1844), Sybil (1845) and Tancred (1847); he became Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1852 and Prime Minister in 1868 and again in 1874-80, and died at Hughenden on 19 April 1881.
authors.profile: Disraeli created the English political novel: his trilogy of the 1840s uses the forms of romance and society comedy to argue that the aristocracy must recover its duty to the people, and Sybil is the first English novel to give the industrial working class a central place. He is also the great stylist of English political prose — his epigrams, his orientalising descriptions and his biting satirical portraits made him the most quotable novelist of the age, and his novels are the key documents of the Young England imagination.
authors.style: Epigrammatic dialogue and brilliant repartee; the satirical portrait of a real political world; the oriental and the exotic as counters in an argument about England; the romance plot with a concealed identity; the rhetorical set speech; the purple descriptive passage.
authors.concerns: The condition of England and the two nations; aristocracy, duty and the Young England ideal; political ambition and the machinery of party; race, religion and the Jewish question; the East and the English imagination; money and the purchase of power.
authors.significance: Disraeli is the founder of the English political novel and its greatest practitioner: the Young England trilogy is the central literary expression of Victorian Toryism, Sybil first brought the industrial poor into fiction as a national question, and his epigrammatic style shaped the political prose of the century.

authors.name: Benjamin Lundy
altNames: Benjamin Lundy of Mount Pleasant and Baltimore
authors.nationality: American; the Quaker frontier abolitionism of the old Northwest and the border states; editor and journalist of the formative periodical stage of American antislavery, between the gradualism of the 1820s and the immediatism of the 1830s
authors.identity: An editor, conducting 62 numbers and then hundreds more of a single sustained abolitionist sheet, and therefore chiefly a writer of leading articles, extracts, statistical tables, petitions, correspondence and prospectuses. His independent literary productions are a tract on the colonisation and emancipation questions, his circulars and annual registers of the manumitted, and an enormous body of letters. He invented the American abolitionist periodical as an institution: a monthly carried by agents, sustained by female subscribers, and dependent on the reprinting of British and foreign material.
authors.biography: He was born on 4 January 1789 at Hardwick in Sussex County, New Jersey, the son of Joseph and Eliza Lundy, and was raised in the plain speech and circuit ministry of the Society of Friends on the western frontier. He served an apprenticeship, learned the saddler's trade, and for many years financed his presswork with his own hands and with the proceeds of a small shop. He became an emancipationist through familiarity with the slave country of the border regions, began to contribute to the antislavery press about 1817, and in January 1821 established at Mount Pleasant in Jefferson County, Ohio, on the bank of the Ohio River and immediately opposite slave territory, the Genius of Universal Emancipation. Long afterwards held to have been the first American newspaper wholly devoted to emancipation, it was in fact preceded by Elisha Bates's short-lived Emancipator of Ohio, whose name and subscription lists Lundy bought and merged into his own sheet. He carried the paper to Jonesboro in Tennessee and then in 1824 to Baltimore, where it found its largest circulation and its most dangerous readership, and where for a decade he edited it, appointed agents, and supplied it with reprinted British parliamentary returns, slave-code extracts and accounts of manumission by will. In 1829 he engaged the young William Lloyd Garrison as a corresponding agent and contributor, gave him charge of the memoranda of the department called Plain Fact, and so provided the apprenticeship from which The Liberator issued in the following year. The two men parted over Garrison's immediatism and unconditional refusal of colonisation, Lundy holding to gradual measures, to emancipation financed by the sale of western land, and to the counsel of the Maryland Colonisation interest. He continued the Genius through the crisis years of the 1830s, travelling and publishing to the last, and died at Lowell, Illinois, on 22 August 1839.
authors.profile: His writing is the prose of an editor obliged to fill a sheet monthly at almost no cost: sober, argumentative, heavily indebted to quotation and to table. He worked by accumulation, re-printing British debates, legislative enactments, wills of manumission and Methodist and Quaker resolutions, and framing them with a leading article that stated the case for compensated and staged emancipation. The tone is exhortatory rather than prophetic, and it is characteristically addressed to slaveholders as erring neighbours rather than to the nation as a whole. His most effective prose is in the short factual paragraph, where a single returned fugitive, a shipload of the newly kidnapped or a price-current from a southern market carries its own argument.
authors.style: Plain unadorned Quaker diction; heavy use of extract, quotation and tabulated statement; a modest first-person editorial voice that reports his own journeys and receipts; moral argument conducted by enumeration of cases; long running titles and departmental headings; earnest, repetitive address to the conscience of the border-state reader; little irony except in the Plain Fact memoranda compiled by his sub-editor.
authors.concerns: The extension of slavery into the western states and its effect upon free labour; the education and moral elevation of the free coloured population; gradual emancipation, compensated manumission by will and the purchase of land for the settled freedom of the manumitted; the danger of the slave trade's renewal after the abolition of importation; the use of periodical publicity and female subscription as the engine of reform; the kinship of American and British emancipation, and the example of the West Indian apprenticeship debate.
authors.significance: He made American abolition a continuing organised press enterprise rather than an occasional address. For a dozen years the Genius was the movement's record and its correspondence network, and through it Lundy trained and launched William Lloyd Garrison, whose first abolitionist editorship was in Lundy's Baltimore office. His papers document the transition from the founding generation's gradualism to the immediatism of 1831 and later, and the disputes in which he was defeated, over colonisation, over the union of the churches and over the sinfulness of slaveholding, defined the programme of the movement that succeeded him. He is justly called the father of American organized abolition.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is disputed in popular account: the weight of authority places it at Hardwick or in Sussex County, New Jersey, while a minority of local and school tradition gives a Pennsylvania birth, and the family's settlement on the upper Ohio is variously dated. The exact chronology of the Genius is complicated by changes of title, place and frequency, and surviving runs are incomplete, so that particular numbers and their contents cannot always be tied to a fixed date. His share in the authorship of material printed under his editors name, as distinct from that contributed by Garrison and by corresponding agents, is not separable in every case.

authors.name: Bernard Mandeville
authors.nationality: Anglo-Dutch moralist writing in English
authors.identity: London physician and satirist whose Fable of the Bees (1714) argued that private vices, worked through vanity and emulation, produce public benefits.
authors.biography: Born at Rotterdam about 1670 into a medical family, he trained in medicine in the Dutch Republic, spent time in France, and from the 1690s practised as a physician in London. His Grumbling Hive (1705) was reissued in 1714 as The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits, with prose remarks on the paradox. A medical treatise on the hypochondriacal and hysterick passions (1715) and Free Thoughts on Religion, the Church and National Happiness (1720) established him as a sceptical physician-philosopher. The enlarged Fable of 1723, with its Essay on Charity and Charity-Schools, was presented by the Middlesex grand jury as a public nuisance and denounced from pulpits. He added a second part in 1729 and an anonymous enquiry into the original of honour in 1732, which broke with the moral-sense creed of the late Earl of Shaftesbury. He died at Hackney on 21 January 1733.
authors.profile: A clinical satirist of commercial society who turned the maxim tradition of the French moralists into an unsentimental analysis of appetite, flattery and trade.
authors.style: Tight Augustan couplets and deadpan prose paradox; fable, dialogue and case history; medical and commercial vocabulary; a sardonic refusal to moralise.
authors.concerns: Vice as the motor of prosperity; vanity, luxury and emulation; the hypocrisy of public benevolence; the origin of honour and shame; the self-deception of the virtuous.
authors.significance: The Fable became the century's most provocative thesis about commercial society, censured in its own day and recovered later by writers from Adam Smith to Keynes as a forerunner of the economics of unintended consequences.
authors.uncertainty: His birth is only fixed approximately, about 1670; his early training and the details of his practice are thinly documented, and the dating of some tracts varies.

authors.name: Booker T. Washington
authors.birthplace: Hale's Ford, Franklin County, Virginia, United States
authors.nationality: African-American; the autobiography, the address and the literature of uplift
authors.identity: Educator, orator and writer; the founder of Tuskegee Institute and the most powerful African-American voice of the generation after Reconstruction.
authors.biography: Born into slavery in Franklin County, Virginia, on 5 April 1856; he worked in the salt and coal mines of West Virginia after emancipation, studied at Hampton Institute from 1872, and in 1881 was chosen to head a new normal school at Tuskegee, Alabama, which he built into a major institution. His address at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition in 1895 made him the spokesman of black America; he advised presidents, founded the National Negro Business League in 1900, and died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915.
authors.profile: Washington wrote the literature of black self-help: his autobiography, Up from Slavery, is one of the classic American narratives of self-making, and his addresses construct a public philosophy of industrial education, economic advance and accommodation that dominated black American politics for a generation. He is also the central figure in the debate — with W. E. B. Du Bois — over what African-American freedom should mean, and his prose is a masterclass in the rhetoric of indirection.
authors.style: First-person narrative of struggle and institutional building; the anecdote as moral lesson; the plain, deliberate sentence; the oratorical cadence of the platform address; conciliation and the calculated omission.
authors.concerns: Education, industrial training and self-help; the legacy of slavery and the work of uplift; race relations and the politics of accommodation; the founding and building of institutions; the dignity of labour; the South and the American future.
authors.significance: Washington is the central African-American public figure of the generation after Reconstruction and Up from Slavery is one of the great American autobiographies: his programme built Tuskegee and the black business class, provoked the founding debate of modern black politics, and his autobiography is a permanent document of American self-making.

authors.name: Bram Stoker
authors.nationality: Irish; the Victorian Gothic and the fin-de-siècle
authors.identity: Novelist, theatre manager and short-story writer; the author of Dracula and the creator of the modern vampire.
authors.biography: Born in Clontarf, Dublin, on 8 November 1847; an invalid in childhood, he was educated at Trinity College Dublin, where he was a mathematician and athlete, and became a civil servant in Dublin Castle. He wrote the theatre column for the Dublin Evening Mail and in 1878 became the business manager of the Lyceum Theatre and Henry Irving's secretary, a post he held until Irving's death in 1905. The Snake's Pass (1890), Dracula (1897), The Jewel of Seven Stars (1903), The Man (1905) and The Lair of the White Worm (1911) followed, together with the stories of Under the Sunset (1881) and the memoir Personal Reminiscences of Henry Irving (1906). He died in London on 20 April 1912.
authors.profile: Stoker wrote the Gothic novel for the age of the typewriter and the medical case study: Dracula is assembled from diaries, letters, newspaper reports, telegrams and 'phonograph' transcripts, its narrative is a montage of documents in the manner Collins had established, and its monster is a figure of the new sciences — of blood transfusion, hypnosis, degeneration and sexual anxiety. The novel's geography runs from the Carpathians to Whitby, London and Transylvania again, and its organisation is that of a league of professional men and one exceptional woman who must hunt the undead.
authors.style: Epistolary and documentary collage; the journal and the newspaper report as narrative units; precise medical and legal notation; the eruption of the archaic into the modern city; the use of place and travel; sexual and religious symbolism at the edge of the speakable.
authors.concerns: Fear of the foreign and the imperial reverse; sexuality, repression and the Victorian double standard; science, medicine and the new technology; the family and the position of women; empire, race and degeneration; the past returning into the present; superstition against enlightenment.
authors.significance: Dracula is the most influential horror novel ever written and the origin of the modern vampire in literature, film and popular culture. Its documentary method shaped the twentieth-century horror and detective novel, and its figure of the vampire became a permanent instrument for thinking about sexuality, empire and the fear of otherness.

authors.name: Bret Harte
authors.nationality: American; the local-colour story of the mining camps
authors.identity: Poet and short-story writer; the inventor of the American western story and the founder of the local-colour movement.
authors.biography: Born in Albany, New York, on 25 August 1836; the family moved to California in 1854, and he worked as a miner, a teacher, a journalist and an editor of the Overland Monthly, in which 'The Luck of Roaring Camp' (1868) made him famous. He was professor of literature at Berkeley in 1871 and then lived in New York and Europe, serving as American consul at Crefeld and Glasgow. He died at Camberley, England, on 5 May 1902.
authors.profile: Harte invented the American western story: his mining-camp tales of California — the gambler, the dance-hall girl, the Chinese cook, the runaway — fixed the characters and the sentiment that would dominate the American imagination of the West. He was also the first editor to pay serious attention to regional writing, and the Overland Monthly under his editorship launched the local-colour movement that Twain, Jewett and Freeman would develop.
authors.style: The single dramatic scene with a surprise ending; sentiment about the outcast and the child; dialect and stock characters; precise description of the mining camp; verse with a strong narrative line.
authors.concerns: The California gold rush and the mining camp; the outcast, the gambler and the prostitute; the American West and its myth; the racial and ethnic margins of the frontier; death and sentiment; the clash of civilisation and wilderness.
authors.significance: Harte is the founder of the American western story and of the local-colour movement: 'The Luck of Roaring Camp', 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat' and 'Tennessee's Partner' are the founding texts of the American literature of the West, and his Overland Monthly created the market for regional writing in America.

authors.name: Bryan Waller Procter
authors.nationality: English; poet and essayist of the Romantic period writing under a pseudonym, and a lawyer who served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy
authors.identity: Lyric and dramatic poet of the Hunt school, who published as 'Barry Cornwall' to keep his professional reputation as a lawyer clear of his verse, and who became one of the most reprinted short-poem writers of mid-Victorian anthologies.
authors.biography: Born at Leeds on 21 November 1787, the only son of the circuit barrister and public orator Bryan Procter, he was educated in the north and in London, entered a solicitor's office, and was called to the bar, where he practised as a special pleader. He began to publish verses about 1815 and came under the notice of Leigh Hunt, whose papers gave him a first public; in 1819 he issued 'Dramatic Scenes, and Other Poems', and the volumes that followed established him as a writer of simple, musical lyric and of dramatic verse for the closet. He was on terms of close friendship with Charles Lamb, whose letters to him are among the happiest documents of Regency letters, and with Hunt, Hazlitt, and the circle about the Indicator and the London Journal. From 1832 to 1861 he served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy, an office which gave his career its public shape and which he held while continuing to publish poems, essays, and literary-critical prose. His collected poetical works were reissued repeatedly, his lyrics entered the school and gift-book canon, and his songs and dramatic monologues were praised by Robert Browning and by the editors of household anthologies. He died on 5 October 1874.
authors.profile: His work is mostly short: songs and lyrics of quiet domestic or melancholy turn, dramatic scenes and monologues in the Elizabethan manner, metrical tales and legends of Italy and of the Cavalier period, and a few closet tragedies and sacred dramas. He wrote also prose essays and literary reminiscence, including papers on the old drama and on his friends, and his volumes of 1819-23 gathered the pieces by which Hunt's circle hoped to be read next after Byron.
authors.style: Verse of deliberate plainness and song-like regularity: short lines, recurring refrains, and an affectation of old English and Cavalier music ('Cavalier Tones' is his best-known experiment in the manner). His dramatic poems take the monologue or the dialogue of two, with a prose-like directness of speech, and his prose is garrulous, affectionate, and anecdotal after Lamb.
authors.concerns: The persistence of the past in song and in domestic feeling; the pathos of private life and of the abandoned or betrayed woman; Elizabethan and Cavalier culture as an alternative to the high Romantic manner; the claims of professional respectability upon the literary life; madness, confinement, and the institutions charged with their care, which his official duties brought before him daily.
authors.significance: He marks the transmission of Hunt's 'new poets' programme into the mid-Victorian recital tradition: his lyrics and songs were staples of anthologies and of the household recitation that gave Romantic verse a popular afterlife. His friendships with Lamb, Hunt, and the Indicator circle make his work and papers a useful record of Regency literary society, and his career in the lunacy commission is a document of the professional Victorian man of letters.

authors.name: C. S. Lewis
authors.nationality: British; the Christian apologist, the space trilogy and the allegory of love
authors.identity: Critic, novelist and apologist; the author of The Allegory of Love, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters.
authors.biography: Born Clive Staples Lewis at Belfast on 29 November 1898; he served in the war, was wounded in 1918, and took the triple first at Oxford that began his fellowship at Magdalen College. The Allegory of Love (1936) made him a scholar of the first rank; his conversion of 1929-31 issued in The Pilgrim's Regress, The Problem of Pain and The Screwtape Letters, and the space trilogy carried the argument into fiction. He held the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance English from 1954 and died at Oxford on 22 November 1963.
authors.profile: C. S. Lewis is the central Christian writer of the English twentieth century and one of its great scholars: The Allegory of Love founded the modern study of the medieval allegorical imagination, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters turned the argument about belief into fiction of the first order, and his broadcasts made the case for Christianity the common property of the reading public.
authors.style: The lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer; the allegory built as a landscape to be crossed; the science fiction of the unfallen planet; the satire in the voice of the devil; the scholar's quotation worn lightly in the apologist's sentence.
authors.concerns: Allegory and the medieval imagination; belief and the argument from desire; the unfallen world and the fall of the will; the devil as bureaucrat; joy and the inconsolable longing; the quarrel with the scientific materialism of his own faculty.
authors.significance: C. S. Lewis is the central Christian writer of the English twentieth century: The Allegory of Love founded the modern study of medieval allegory, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters carried the argument about belief into fiction, and his apologetic prose remains the standard voice of the converted intellect.

authors.name: Caroline Norton
authors.birthplace: London, into the Sheridan theatrical and Whig-political family; her father was Thomas Sheridan, actor, soldier and later colonial secretary at the Cape of Good Hope, and her grandfather the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan
authors.nationality: English; the Byronic lyric and the literary-annual and periodical writing of the closing Romantic decades, together with the sentimental legal-reform pamphlet literature generated by the agitation over the civil disabilities of married women
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and annual-writer who became the most publicised campaigner in England for reform of the law of infant custody and of the property and divorce rights of married women
authors.biography: Caroline Elizabeth Sarah Sheridan was born in London on 22 March 1808, the second of three daughters of Thomas Sheridan and Caroline Henrietta Callander, herself a novelist; her grandfather was Richard Brinsley Sheridan. Thomas Sheridan died at the Cape of Good Hope in 1817 in the public service, leaving his widow nearly penniless, and the Duke of York obtained grace-and-favour apartments for the family at Hampton Court Palace. Caroline and her sisters Helen, afterwards Lady Dufferin, and Georgiana, afterwards Duchess of Somerset, were famous for beauty and wit, and she turned to writing to escape her feelings and because her family depended on her pen. On 30 June 1827 she married the Honourable George Chapple Norton, barrister and Member of Parliament for Guildford. The marriage was embittered by his violence and debts; she left him in 1836, and his criminal-conversation action against Melbourne, tried on 23 June 1836, collapsed but ruined her reputation. Under the law she lost all access to her three sons and the proceeds of her own books, and her second son William was killed by a fall from his pony in 1842. Out of that private catastrophe she made a public campaign, publishing the factory poem 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), 'The Separation of Mother and Child by the Law of "Custody of Infants" Considered' (1838) and her 'Plain Letter to the Lord Chancellor on the Infant Custody Bill' (1839), which helped carry the Custody of Infants Act of that year. She petitioned unsuccessfully for the laureateship after Southey's death in 1843, wrote socially purposeful verse in 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), and renewed her agitation in 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and her 'Letter to the Queen' (1855) before the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857. After George Norton's death in 1875 she married, on 1 March 1877, Sir William Stirling-Maxwell, an old friend; she died at her London home on 15 June 1877 and was buried in the Stirling-Maxwell vault at Lecropt church near Keir; she is now remembered as a founding figure of English marriage-law reform.
authors.profile: Norton's reputation rests on three bodies of writing. Her verse begins with 'The Sorrows of Rosalie: a Tale, with other Poems' (1829), warmly praised in 'Noctes Ambrosianae', continues with 'The Undying One and Other Poems' (1830), a romance on the Wandering Jew legend, 'The Dream and Other Poems' (1840), 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), 'Aunt Carry's Ballads for Children' (1847) and 'The Lady of La Garaye' (1862), the last thought her best by contemporaries; lyrics, ballads and metrical tales supplied the literary annuals in seasons when she is said to have earned fourteen hundred pounds. Her fiction includes 'The Wife, and Woman's Reward' (1835), 'Stuart of Dunleath' (1851), 'Lost and Saved' (1863) and 'Old Sir Douglas' (1867), the last appearing in Macmillan's Magazine. Third, and historically the most consequential, the reform prose: 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), the custody pamphlets of 1838-9, 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and the letters to the Queen and on Cranworth's divorce bill of 1855-7, with much anonymous literary and artistic criticism in her later years.
authors.style: Her manner is the Byronic one of the 1820s and 1830s: emphatic first-person remonstrance, pathos, passion, sonorous blank verse and closed couplets, and strong simple ballad stanzas for popular recitation. The Dictionary of National Biography recorded the judgement that 'she follows Byron as the dominant poet of her day', with sincere emotion but conventional expression, and that her best effects are passages of impassioned rhetoric embedded in the longer poems; 'The Lady of La Garaye' was thought to temper the Byronic note toward something like Thomas Campbell's dignity. Two lyrics, 'Joe Steel' and 'The Faded Beauty', show an arch Irish humour quite unlike her usual manner. The pamphlets are argumentative, autobiographical, pointedly domestic in their appeal to motherhood, and written to be quoted in Parliament.
authors.concerns: The legal non-existence of a married woman: the custody of children, the confiscation of a wife's earnings by her husband, the expense and sex-bias of the divorce court, and the exposure of a woman who defended herself in public. Her writing also holds the condition-of-England questions of the 1840s - factory labour, the education of the poor, the Prince of Wales as a national emblem - and shows her reading of Carlyle and Disraeli, while her famous refusal of the 'doctrine of equality' in 1838 marks her reform as maternal and sentimental rather than proto-feminist in the later sense. Personal grievance, evidence and petition are treated as literary instruments.
authors.significance: She converted a private scandal into a legislative campaign, and the Custody of Infants Act of 1839 gave married women for the first time a legally enforceable right to their children; her later pamphlets fed the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and she is often claimed for the Married Women's Property Act of 1870, though her part in that measure is disputed. Lord Melbourne's trial and her notoriety touched the politics of the early Victorian premiership, she supplied hints for Dickens's 'Bardell v. Pickwick', she modelled for Daniel Maclise's House of Lords fresco of 'Justice', and George Meredith used her as the basis of Diana of the Crossways (1885). Modern scholarship and legal history treat her as the emblematic case of the personal made political in Victorian reform agitation.
authors.uncertainty: Her own later assertions are sometimes unverifiable - including her claim to have taken part in the Tolpuddle Martyrs demonstration of 1834 - and biographers differ over how far her pamphlets caused the Acts of 1839 and 1857 and over any share in the Act of 1870; no fully satisfactory portrait of her survives.

authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and playwright; the author of The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter, written at twenty-three, and the youngest of the great Southern writers.
authors.biography: Born Lula Carson Smith in Columbus, Georgia, on 19 February 1917; she went to New York at seventeen to study music, worked in a variety of jobs, and published The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter in 1940 at the age of twenty-three. Reflections in a Golden Eye (1941), The Member of the Wedding (1946) and The Ballad of the Sad Café (1951) followed, together with the play The Square Root of Wonderful (1958); she suffered strokes and illness through her adult life and died at Nyack, New York, on 29 September 1967.
authors.profile: McCullers wrote the most haunting Southern novel of adolescence: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter made deafness, loneliness and the small Georgia mill town into a great American subject, and The Member of the Wedding is one of the finest American novels of a girl's growing up. Her Gothic of the solitary heart — the freak, the outsider, the unloved — is the period's distinctive contribution to the Southern tradition.
authors.style: The plain, bare, exactly observed sentence; the grotesque character rendered without condescension; the novel of adolescence and the single summer; the symbolic situation (the deaf mute, the wedding, the café); the loneliness that is never explained.

authors.significance: McCullers wrote the most haunting Southern novel of adolescence and one of the finest American novels of loneliness: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter, written at twenty-three, is a permanent American classic, The Member of the Wedding a great novel of growing up, and The Ballad of the Sad Café a perfect Gothic novella.

authors.name: Catharine Maria Sedgwick
authors.nationality: American; novelist and writer of the domestic and historical tale of New England, the most considerable American woman fiction-writer of the 1820s and 1830s and a chief practitioner of the Protestant moral tale
authors.identity: A writer of prose fiction, chiefly domestic, moral and historical novels and shorter tales, together with a body of religious and educational narrative, a memoir of a friend and occasional biographical and editorial work. She published her first two novels without her own name and wrote in the manner of the novel of character and conscience rather than of romance or sensation.
authors.biography: She was born at Stockbridge, Massachusetts, on 28 December 1789, the daughter of Theodore Sedgwick, a Federalist member of Congress from Massachusetts and later chief justice of the state, and of Pamela Dwight Sedgwick of the Stockbridge Dwight family. She grew up in the Stockbridge household, where a woman formerly held in slavery who had obtained her freedom by suit in the courts of the state served the family, and an early religious experience attached her to the Unitarian sympathy rather than to the strict Calvinism of her parents' world. Her own illness and convalescence in 1816, when she was nursed by a physician of the new school and read the novels she had been forbidden, decided her upon fiction as her work. A New-England Tale appeared anonymously in 1822, Redwood followed in the same concealment in 1824, and with Hope Leslie in 1827 her name first stood upon a title-page and her reputation as a writer of the national tale was made. Through the 1830s she published tales of New England and of colonial history, wrote for the annuals and for her friend's magazine, and supported her family by her pen; Elm Park, the Stockbridge house, became her home and a centre of the country's literary visiting. She remained unmarried by choice, corresponded widely with the men of letters of her generation, and after her brother's death wrote a memoir and an account of the household which had formed her. She died in 1867 at the age of seventy-seven, and by the end of her life was beginning to be read as the representative woman novelist of the early republic.
authors.profile: Her novels fall into a domestic and moral group, treating conscience, prejudice and the discipline of a young woman's judgment, and a historical group, treating the colonial and Indian border of New England; between them are shorter tales, religious and educational narratives and contributions to the literary annuals. Her habit is the novel of opinion and character, argued through a heroine's errors of judgment, with the sect, the party and the treatment of the Indian brought into the moral account. The memoir and the family narrative show the same concern with testimony, character and the reliability of a community's memory.
authors.style: A clear, straightforward and consciously unadorned narrative prose, with a firm control of the middle-length sentence and an economy of description; her force lies in the analysis of motive and in the dialogue of household and country society. She is careful of probability, dislikes the machinery of sensation, and closes her argument with a moral reckoning which she declines to dress up as providence.
authors.concerns: The duty and the right of private judgment against priest, party and neighbour; the education of a woman's mind and the claims of an unmarried woman's independence; the treatment of the Indian and the justice of the settlement; sectarian bitterness and the possibility of a reasonable religion; slavery, freedom and the memory of service in the household; the authority of prejudice in a small community; the obligations of the powerful to the dependent.
authors.significance: She established the woman's American novel on grounds of conscience and social argument rather than sentiment, and Hope Leslie gave the colonial and Indian material a critical treatment unmatched before her. For half a century she was the example by which the professional woman fiction-writer of the republic was understood, and recent scholarship has returned her to the history of the American novel and of the argument over removal.
authors.uncertainty: Accounts differ as to the place of her death, some putting it at Stockbridge and others at a relative's house in the neighbourhood of Boston; the exact share of the physician who superintended her convalescence in determining her career rests chiefly on her own autobiographical papers.
