authors.name: Catherine Parr
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: queen consort; devotional writer
authors.biography: Born about 1512; the sixth wife of Henry VIII, whom she married in 1543. A learned woman of reformist sympathies, she narrowly escaped arrest for heresy in 1546. Her Prayers or Meditations appeared in 1545, the first book printed under the name of an English queen, and The Lamentation of a Sinner in 1547 after the king's death. She died on 5 September 1548, shortly after marrying Thomas Seymour.
authors.profile: The first English queen in print. Prayers or Meditations (1545) adapts the Imitatio Christi into a personal devotional idiom, and The Lamentation of a Sinner (1547) is a conversion narrative and confession in the new evangelical mode, declaring the futility of works and the sufficiency of faith in Christ.
authors.style: Warm, first-person devotion; the language of interiority and the afflicted conscience; scriptural quotation woven into prayer.
authors.concerns: Personal faith and justification; the education of women (she oversaw the schooling of the young Elizabeth); the reform of devotion from within the court.
authors.significance: A pioneer of English women's devotional writing and a patron of the reformed cause; her example licensed the religious authorship of later English women.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1512); the extent of her direct influence on Elizabeth's education is documented but partly inferential.

authors.name: Charles Brockden Brown
authors.nationality: American; novelist, tale-writer and editor of the early republic, working in Philadelphia and New York; the first American writer of prose fiction to attempt a professional literary career
authors.identity: A writer of prose fiction and of periodical and editorial work: four gothic narratives published in 1798 and 1799, a domestic romance of 1801, tales and sketches for the magazines he edited, and moral, political and historical argument in essays, prefaces and reviews. He wrote no verse of consequence and no drama; his criticism lives in advertisements and periodical matter rather than in a treatise.
authors.biography: He was born in Philadelphia on 7 January 1771, the son of Elijah Brown, a Quaker merchant of English descent, and grew up within the discipline of the Society of Friends. The prosperity of his father's house broke up in the early 1790s, and the loss of a commercial fortune of his own while still in his twenties decided him upon the pen. He had already left the Friends after a religious crisis of opinion, and turned instead to the rational dissent he found in Godwin and in the English moralists. In 1796 he began Brown's Weekly Political Intelligencer and in 1797 the American Monthly Magazine, the first of several editorial ventures by which he tried to live by periodical writing in the United States. During 1798 and 1799 the Philadelphia publisher Mathew Carey issued his four novels in quick succession, and their reception, hostile at home and warmer in Britain, encouraged him to believe that an American romance of ideas was possible. He tried briefly and unsuccessfully to practise law after being admitted to practice, and for a season kept a country place in the New Jersey shore and in the Genesee region with no better result. From 1806 to 1811 he edited The American Register at New York and Philadelphia, a miscellany which reprinted British review criticism and American news and gave him the largest reading public he ever commanded. He died in Philadelphia in 1810, at the age of thirty-nine, leaving editorial and historical projects unfinished.
authors.profile: His fiction divides into the four gothic narratives of 1798 and 1799 and the later domestic romance of 1801, with tales and sketches scattered through the magazines he controlled. His non-fictional work is larger than his surviving novels and consists of prefaces, reviews, political intelligence, historical and biographical compilation and editorial matter of every kind. The whole of it is prose, and its most distinctive feature is the argumentative narrative: a plot of evidence, rumour and mistaken testimony carried by speakers who reason about their own case. He also wrote on the abolition of slavery and on the condition of the Indian countries, and his western tale draws upon captive narratives as well as upon romance.
authors.style: A plain, unadorned and deliberately rational diction applied to scenes of terror; long first-person confessions, letters within letters, and a preference for memoir and journal forms over the plot of the ordinary romance. Explanation is pushed so hard that it becomes an engine of doubt, and the tales end in contentions about what the evidence proves. Topographical and medical detail is used to give the marvellous an air of report, and the prefaces argue the moral purpose of the fiction before the fiction is allowed to speak.
authors.concerns: Godwinian inquiry into the power of opinion over conduct; enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination and its relation to religious and political credulity; the pathology of solitude and sleep; the credibility of testimony and the limits of evidence; the condition of women without fortune or protection; slavery, manumission and the meaning of republican equality; the interior frontier as a moral as well as a geographical zone; the education of a republic and the uses of periodical literature.
authors.significance: He created the American gothic and with it the first American prose fiction taken seriously by British reviewers, so that the history of the American novel cannot be written beginning anywhere else. His treatment of belief, sleep and pursued virtue opened lines of development that run through later American romance, and his editorial labours showed what a man of letters in the republic could actually do for a living. Twentieth-century scholarship, which at first set him aside as an oddity, restored the four novels to the canonical history of gothic and early American fiction.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his legal studies and his admission to practice is imperfectly settled; the religious crisis which ended his connection with the Friends is known only from his own allusions and from those of his family; and the cause of his death at thirty-nine, variously reported as consumption and as an acute fever, cannot be determined from the surviving accounts.

authors.name: Charles Dickens
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel
authors.identity: Novelist, editor, journalist and public reader; the central figure of the Victorian novel and the most widely read English novelist of the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born on 7 February 1812 at Landport, Portsmouth, the second child of John Dickens, a navy pay-office clerk, and Elizabeth Barrow. The family's move to London in 1822 and his father's imprisonment for debt in the Marshalsea in 1824 ended his schooling at twelve and put him to work pasting labels at Warren's blacking warehouse, an experience he concealed until late in life and drew on directly in David Copperfield. He was articled to a solicitor in 1827, learned shorthand, and from 1832 reported for the True Sun and the Morning Chronicle, where his Sketches by Boz began to appear in 1833-36. The Pickwick Papers (1836-37) made him famous within months; he married Catherine Hogarth on 2 April 1836, the same month the first number appeared. From 1836 to 1870 he wrote fifteen novels, edited Bentley's Miscellany (1836-39), Master Humphrey's Clock (1840-41), the Daily News (1846) and from 1850 Household Words, continued from 1859 as All the Year Round; he toured America in 1842 and 1867-68, Italy and Switzerland in 1844-45, and from 1858 to 1870 gave public readings of his own work that ruined his health. The separation from Catherine in 1858 and the long attachment to Ellen Ternan belong to the same years as Great Expectations and Our Mutual Friend. He died at Gad's Hill Place, Kent, on 9 June 1870, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished at the sixth of twelve projected numbers; he is buried in Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: Dickens made the serial novel the central literary institution of the Victorian period and gave it a double audience: the family reading aloud the monthly part and the crowded weekly number of Household Words. His plots are built on withheld identity, inheritance, legal chancery and the long orbit of a single city, and his prose moves between a reportorial exactness about institutions, a comic inventiveness of speech and name, and a rhetorical pathos that addresses the reader directly. He wrote as a reformer with specific targets — the workhouse, the Yorkshire schools, Chancery, the Circumlocution Office, the factory system, the prison and the criminal law — and the novels argue by caricature and by the multiplication of institutions into systems. From Bleak House (1852-53) onward the novels take a darker structure: a central secret which the narrative withholds from its protagonist, and a double narrative, first-person and third-person, that measures the cost of knowledge.
authors.style: Innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt); a syntax of accumulating clauses that builds comic or pathetic crescendos; the present-tense opening of Bleak House ("London. Michaelmas Term lately over") and the fog that states a legal system; recurring motifs that structure whole novels (the river in Our Mutual Friend, the dust-heaps, the fog, the Marshalsea); an unrivalled ear for the idiolects of class, trade and profession.
authors.concerns: The condition of England and the mutual obligations of the classes; childhood as a moral test of social arrangements; the law, the bureaucracy and the institution as machines for the destruction of persons; the criminal and the outcast as the mirror of respectable society; education as training or as repression; money, speculation and the corruption of the will; death, memory and the recovered parent; the city as an organism.
authors.significance: Dickens fixed the form of the English serial novel and its commercial economy, invented or consolidated the Christmas book and the public reading, and made novel-writing a platform for social investigation that led directly to reform (the Sanitary Act, the reformatory schools, the abolition of the Court of Chancery's abuses). His example shaped Gaskell, Collins, Reade, Dostoevsky, Kafka, and the whole tradition of the novel as an indictment. In the twentieth century his reputation was remade by Leavisite and later by post-structuralist criticism, and he is now read with Trollope as the double centre of the Victorian novel.

authors.name: Charles Eastman
authors.birthplace: Near Redwood Falls, Minnesota, United States
authors.nationality: Santee Dakota; the Native American autobiography and the literature of the assimilation debate
authors.identity: Physician, writer and activist; the first Native American to qualify in medicine in the United States and the most widely read Native American author of his generation.
authors.biography: Born Hakadah, later named Ohiyesa, near Redwood Falls, Minnesota, on 19 February 1858, of a Santee Dakota family that fled to Canada after the 1862 uprising; he was raised in the traditional way until his father sent for him at fifteen, and he then took the name Charles Alexander Eastman and studied at Dartmouth and Boston University, graduating in medicine in 1890. He was the physician at Pine Ridge during the Wounded Knee massacre, became a national spokesman for Native rights, and wrote eleven books. He died in Detroit on 8 January 1939.
authors.profile: Eastman wrote the Native American autobiography at its most readable: Indian Boyhood is the classic account of a traditional Dakota childhood, and its companion volumes — The Soul of the Indian, From the Deep Woods to Civilization — record the passage from one world to another with a dignity and a clarity that made them the most widely read Native American books of the period. He was also a central figure in the debate over assimilation, and his work presents the Native case to a white readership without bitterness.
authors.style: Clear, unhurried expository prose; the remembered detail of the traditional life; the comparative explanation of Dakota belief for a white audience; the narrative of the journey from the woods to the university; the appeal to a common humanity.
authors.concerns: Dakota childhood, hunting and the traditional education; the passage from the traditional world to white civilisation; the massacre at Wounded Knee and the betrayal of the treaties; Native religion and its relation to Christianity; the education of the Indian and the policy of assimilation.
authors.significance: Eastman is the most widely read Native American author of his generation and the central figure of the assimilation debate: Indian Boyhood is the classic Native American autobiography, The Soul of the Indian is the foundational account of Dakota religion in English, and his work made the Native American case known to a mass white readership.

authors.name: Charles Kingsley
authors.nationality: English; the social novel, the historical romance and children's fantasy
authors.identity: Clergyman, novelist and poet; the leading voice of Christian Socialism and of 'muscular Christianity'.
authors.biography: Born at Holne, Devon, on 12 June 1819, the son of a clergyman; educated at King's College London and Magdalene College, Cambridge. He was curate and then rector of Eversley, Hampshire, from 1844, and became a canon of Chester (1870) and Westminster (1873). He was a founder of the Christian Socialist movement with F. D. Maurice and J. M. Ludlow, wrote the social novels of the 1840s-50s, was a keen naturalist and sanitarian, and became Regius Professor of History at Cambridge in 1860. He died at Eversley on 23 January 1875.
authors.profile: Kingsley wrote the Victorian novel of social conscience as a Christian vocation: Yeast and Alton Locke exposed the condition of the agricultural labourer and the Chartist tailor, while Hypatia and Hereward the Wake made the historical romance a vehicle for a muscular, imperial Protestantism. He is also the author of The Water-Babies, one of the strangest and most inventive of English children's books, in which a chimney sweep's death becomes a fable of sanitation, evolution and redemption.
authors.style: Direct moral address; documentary detail of poverty and disease; vigorous narrative action; natural history as moral illustration; a romantic, rhetorical prose; poetry of the sea and of the Christian year.
authors.concerns: Christian socialism and the condition of England; sanitation and public health; Chartism and working-class education; the relation of science and faith; empire and the English character; childhood and education.
authors.significance: Kingsley was the most influential Christian Socialist writer of the 1850s and the origin of the 'muscular Christianity' that shaped the Victorian public school and the imperial romance. Alton Locke is a founding text of the English working-class novel, and The Water-Babies is a permanent classic of children's literature.

authors.name: Charles Lamb
authors.nationality: English; the familiar prose of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Essayist and letter-writer, a London clerk by profession, who wrote as Elia and became the most admired practitioner of familiar prose between the spectatorial essay and the Victorian essay.
authors.biography: Lamb was born in London into a family long in the service of the Inner Temple, the elder brother of Mary Lamb. He was educated at Christ's Hospital, where Samuel Taylor Coleridge was a schoolfellow and remained a friend for life, and in 1792 he was placed in the East India Company's accounts office at India House, where he worked as a clerk until his retirement in 1825. His early ambition was the stage, and the plays and verses of those years are lost. On 18 March 1796 Mary, in an attack of insanity, killed their mother, and Lamb thenceforward lived with her as her guardian and companion through recurring illness, quarrels and reconciliation. He contributed occasional verse, essays and theatrical criticism to the morning papers from the 1790s, published a selection of the old dramatists with observations in 1808, and worked with his sister on books for children. From 1820 the Elia papers began to appear in periodicals and were collected in 1823 and again in 1833; his letters, much imitated in the century after his death, were published in full only after him. He died at Edmonton in December 1842 of erysipelas and was buried in the churchyard there.
authors.profile: His work is almost wholly prose of a personal kind: the Elia essays and their sequel, a book of old-play specimens with commentary, an editorial and collaborative share in children's books, and a body of letters that he treated as a form of essay. He wrote occasional verse and dramatic criticism, and projected histories and scholarship that he never completed. The characteristic piece is a short meditative essay on a London or a country scene, on the theatre, on books, or on the poor, which wanders from anecdote to reflection and returns to the writer's own life. His subject is memory, friendship, the pleasures of the town, the ruined eighteenth-century house of his childhood, and the tender treatment of the failings of the mind.
authors.style: A colloquial yet elaborately allusive prose, full of half-quoted phrases from the old drama and from the Bible, with Latinate inversions, parenthetical self-correction, sudden tenderness under irony, and a persona that admits its own fictions. The sentences imitate the rhythms of talk and of the seventeenth-century writers together; the humour is self-deprecatory and the pathos is never separated from it.
authors.concerns: The essayist's persona as a moral and social mask; sympathy with the poor, the servants, the outcast and the insane; the value of the old plays as a school of imagination; the lost haunts and houses of childhood; the claims of duty and dependence within a family; the place of literature in an ordinary working life.
authors.significance: With Hazlitt he defined the Romantic prose essay, and Elia supplied the model of the familiar essayist that the Victorians inherited, most obviously in the essayists of the 1840s and in Stevenson's treatment of the essay voice. His edition and commentary helped establish the modern serious reading of the Jacobean and Caroline dramatists, and his letters form one of the principal records of London literary society between the 1790s and the 1840s.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of Mary Lamb's share in the children's books and in some of the papers printed over his name is debated; the plays and most of the early writings are lost and can only be dated approximately; and the part of the Elia voice that is a self-portrait and the part that is invention cannot be separated.

authors.name: Charles Reade
authors.nationality: English; the documentary and sensation novel
authors.identity: Novelist and dramatist; the Victorian pioneer of the documentary novel and of the fiction of social reform.
authors.biography: Born at Ipsden, Oxfordshire, on 8 June 1814, the son of a landowner; he was educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, where he held a fellowship from 1842, and was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1843. He wrote plays, beginning with The Ladies' Battle (1849) and Masks and Faces (with Tom Taylor, 1852), and turned to fiction with Peg Woffington (1853). He researched his novels by collecting newspaper cuttings, visiting prisons, workhouses and factories, and corresponding with experts, and he campaigned in fiction against private lunatic asylums and for prison reform. He died in London on 11 April 1884.
authors.profile: Reade is the inventor of the English documentary novel: he called his method 'fictional history' and built his books out of verified cases, newspaper reports, blue books and personal investigation. The result is a fiction of argument and exposure — the private asylum in Hard Cash, the prison system in It Is Never Too Late to Mend — combined with a melodramatic power that made him one of the most popular novelists of the 1860s. The Cloister and the Hearth is the finest English historical novel of the fifteenth century and a deliberate answer to the romance of Scott.
authors.style: The dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative; violent melodramatic climaxes; polemic and reformist anger; a huge, crowded canvas; dialogue in period and dialect; the alternation of comedy and outrage.
authors.concerns: The abuse of institutional power (asylums, prisons, factories); the law and its failures; the condition of England and the two nations; religious controversy and the Reformation; love against money and class; the ethics of the writer as investigator.
authors.significance: Reade is the founding figure of the English novel of documented fact and a major influence on Zola's naturalism and on the twentieth-century documentary novel: Hard Cash helped to expose the private asylum scandals and It Is Never Too Late to Mend the prison system. The Cloister and the Hearth remains the classic English historical novel of the Burgundian fifteenth century.

authors.name: Charles Robert Maturin
authors.nationality: Irish
authors.identity: Gothic novelist, Anglican clergyman, and dramatist
authors.biography: Charles Robert Maturin was born in Dublin of French Huguenot descent; his grandfather was the distinguished mathematician Lord Chief Baron Maturin. Educated at Trinity College Dublin, he took Anglican orders and served as rector of St Peter's, Dublin, attracting audiences with sermons that advanced controversial Calvinist doctrines. He published Gothic novels from 1812 to 1820, including The Milesian Chief, Bertram, Women, and Melmoth the Wanderer. He left the ministry under some cloud and turned to theatre management and ultimately emigrated to England, where he died in poverty in 1824. He was the maternal grandfather of Oscar Wilde.
authors.profile: Maturin is the pre-eminent Irish Gothic novelist of the Romantic period. His fiction explores theological terror — damnation, guilt, and the impossibility of redemption — through labyrinthine narrative structures. Melmoth the Wanderer is the last great Gothic novel of the 1790s tradition. His verse drama Bertram drew Byron's public praise.
authors.style: Elaborate recursive frame structures; prose of rhetorical intensity and theological solemnity; sustained Gothic imagery; embedded narratives across multiple centuries and nations; the double and the pursued self as recurring psychological motifs.
authors.concerns: Calvinist theology and the anxiety of election; Catholic-Protestant conflict in Ireland; colonial subjectivity and the politics of dispossession; the Gothic as spiritual allegory; narrative form as psychological and theological entrapment.
authors.significance: Maturin represents the Irish Gothic as a distinct tradition: the colonial subject's terror turned into theological drama. Melmoth influenced Balzac and Baudelaire; his work was central to the recovery of Gothic fiction by Victorian and modernist writers.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birth year (1780 or 1782) is uncertain; the circumstances of his departure from the Anglican ministry remain obscure.

authors.name: Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset

authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Courtier, patron, and occasional poet; as Lord Buckhurst he was a leading Restoration wit and rake, famed for his songs and satires, and later as Earl of Dorset a generous patron of Dryden, Prior, and the writers of the 1690s.
authors.biography: Born c. 1643 (baptised 24 January 1638 — the commonly cited birth year is 1643; records vary), styled Lord Buckhurst, educated at Westminster. He served at sea against the Dutch (reportedly writing the song 'To all you ladies now at land' the night before the Battle of Lowestoft, 1665), was a boon companion of Rochester and the court wits, and succeeded as Earl of Dorset and Middlesex in 1675. After the Revolution of 1688 he became Lord Chamberlain to William III and a key literary patron, supporting Dryden after his fall, and Prior, and Montagu. He died 19 January 1706.
authors.profile: The elegant, careless court versifier whose few surviving songs and satires were praised by contemporaries (Prior, Dryden) for their natural wit and ease, and whose chief literary role was patronage.
authors.style: Light, graceful songs and satires; an easy, natural wit; libertine and amorous subjects; and the occasional political satire.
authors.concerns: Love, pleasure, and court life; the passing of youth; loyalty and the politics of the Revolution; and the patronage of letters.
authors.significance: Dorset is remembered more as the ideal Restoration patron — Dryden dedicated works to him and mourned his circle — than for his slender but admired verse, which exemplifies Cavalier wit surviving into the 1690s.
authors.uncertainty: Dorset's birth year is variously given (1637–38 or 1643); his poetic canon is small and some attributions are uncertain, and much of his reputation rests on testimony rather than surviving verse.

He was killed by a sniper at Hulluch on 13 October 1915, and his Marlborough and Other Poems appeared in 1916.

authors.name: Charles W. Chesnutt
authors.nationality: African-American; the short story, the novel of the colour line and the plantation tradition revised
authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and lawyer; the first African-American writer of fiction to be published by a major American house, and the most important literary critic of the plantation tradition.
authors.biography: Born in Cleveland, Ohio, on 20 June 1858, but brought up in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where his parents had returned after the Civil War; he taught school, became principal of the State Normal School in Fayetteville, and in 1883 moved to Cleveland, where he studied law and passed the bar. The Conjure Woman (1899) and The Wife of His Youth (1899) were published by Houghton Mifflin; his novels followed, and after 1905 he devoted himself to law and business. He died in Cleveland on 15 November 1932.
authors.profile: Chesnutt wrote the literature of the colour line from inside: his conjure stories use the frame of the old plantation tale in order to undo it, and his novels — The Marrow of Tradition above all — give the first full fictional treatment of the white supremacist terror that ended Reconstruction. He was also the most incisive African-American critic of the plantation tradition and of the publishing industry's demand for minstrel comedy.
authors.style: Frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself; dialect used as a voice of authority rather than comedy; plot built on the legal and social machinery of segregation; satire and irony; exact documentation of the 1898 Wilmington coup in fiction.
authors.concerns: Race and the colour line; the legacy of slavery and the failure of Reconstruction; lynching, the Wilmington massacre and white terror; passing and mixed ancestry; the black professional class; the publishing market and the caricature of black life.
authors.significance: Chesnutt is the founding novelist of the African-American literary tradition after Douglass and the most important black American fiction writer before the Harlem Renaissance: The Marrow of Tradition is the first novel about the Wilmington coup of 1898, and The Conjure Woman permanently changed the American short story of race.

authors.name: Charles Wesley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican clergyman and the finest hymn-writer of the English revival, whose lyrics gave Methodism its voice and much of its theology.
authors.biography: Born at Epworth in 1707, one of the numerous children of Samuel and Susanna Wesley, he was sent on a scholarship to Westminster School and from there to Christ Church, Oxford, where he kept a journal of his religious progress and joined with his brother John and a few friends in the small society later mocked as methodists. Ordained and briefly in Georgia with John, he returned to an assured conversion recorded in his journal in 1738, and thereafter preached as an assistant revival preacher while labouring chiefly in verse. He married Sarah Gwynne in 1749, lived for years near the Methodist work at Bristol, where the Wesleyan school at Kingswood was founded, and settled in London later, remaining an Anglican priest who disliked several of his brother's concessions. His collections of hymns, published singly and with John, begin with Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739 and run through the following decades. He died in London in March 1788.
authors.profile: The lyric theologian of the revival, who put doctrine, penitence and joy into metres that congregations could carry away.
authors.style: Dense, tuneful, ecstatic lyrics in common and ballad measures; first-person plural address; paradox, tenderness and bodily feeling; a gift for the repeating clause that binds a singing congregation.
authors.concerns: Assurance, atonement and the witness of the Spirit; the praise of God by redeemed creatures; the holy year of nativity, passion and resurrection; the communion of the faithful and the terrors of judgement.
authors.significance: He is the century's most sung religious poet in English and the founder of Methodist hymnody; his texts still stand in most English-speaking hymnals and shaped the devotional language of revival Christianity.
authors.uncertainty: The number of hymns credited to him varies widely between early accounts and modern scholarship, and some of his texts were revised by others in transmission.

authors.name: Charlotte Brontë
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel, Yorkshire
authors.identity: Novelist and poet; the author of Jane Eyre and the first of the Brontë sisters to publish, and the one who turned the provincial parsonage into a literary subject.
authors.biography: Born at Thornton on 21 April 1816, the third daughter of Patrick Brontë, perpetual curate, and Maria Branwell; the family moved to Haworth in 1820, and her mother died in 1821. She and her sisters were sent in 1824 to the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, the model for Lowood in Jane Eyre, where her two elder sisters Maria and Elizabeth died in 1825. She taught at Roe Head (1835-38) and was twice a governess (1839, 1841); in 1842 she and Emily went to the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels to qualify to open a school of their own, and her unreturned attachment to Constantin Heger produced the letters she wrote to him in 1844-45. The school project failed. Poems by Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell (1846) sold two copies; Jane Eyre appeared on 16 October 1847 and was an immediate success. She nursed Emily and Anne through their deaths in 1848-49, published Shirley in 1849 and Villette in 1853, and married Arthur Bell Nicholls, her father's curate, on 29 June 1854. She died at Haworth on 31 March 1855, in the first year of her marriage; her first novel, The Professor, was published posthumously in 1857.
authors.profile: Charlotte Brontë wrote the first English novel whose heroine claims the right to feel and to speak in her own person, and Jane Eyre's first-person narrative gives the Victorian novel its most sustained study of the interior life of an unregarded woman. Her novels work by a strict first-person confinement: the reader knows only what the narrator has experienced and can articulate. She is a writer of Gothic intensity inside a realist frame, and her landscapes and weather are states of feeling. Shirley turns from the private to the historical (the Luddite risings of 1811-12), Villette to the isolation of the Englishwoman abroad, and the late novels deliberately refuse the marriage-plot consolations that Jane Eyre permits.
authors.style: Intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader; short, abrupt paragraphs and direct address; dream and vision sequences used as psychological evidence, not as supernatural event; dialect speech (Joseph, Emily Brontë's Yorkshire voices) used as a moral register; a symbolic use of weather and landscape; the plain hero and the plain heroine, both ugly by convention and both proud of it.
authors.concerns: The rights of the feeling subject against social and economic power; the governess and the class position of educated women without money; the relation of the passions to religious vocation; the struggle of the will (Rochester's, Paul Emanuel's, Lucy Snowe's) with love; madness, inheritance and the colonial fortune; the family as a closed and often destructive system.
authors.significance: Jane Eyre changed what an English novel could say about a woman's inner life, and the phrase 'the reader, I married him' style of direct address became a permanent resource of first-person fiction. Her example (with Emily's and Anne's) made the Brontë parsonage a central site of English literary history, and the twentieth-century feminist recovery of the Brontës made her work the starting point for the criticism of women's writing. Wide Sargasso Sea (1966), Jean Rhys's reply to Jane Eyre, is the most famous postcolonial rewriting of a Victorian novel.
authors.uncertainty: The authorship of the three 'Bell' novels was from 1846 concealed behind pseudonyms, and Charlotte's later editorial work on her sisters' texts (1850) altered Emily's poems; the early letters survive only in copies made by Ellen Nussey.

authors.name: Charlotte Dacre
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Gothic novelist, poet, and dramatist
authors.biography: Charlotte Dacre was born Charlotte Robinson, daughter of Lieutenant-Colonel George Augustus Robinson, known as the 'Chinese Officer' after years in India, and Anne Remee, said to be of part-African descent — a family history that gave rise to Dacre's persistent preoccupation with racial otherness and belonging. She began writing in the 1790s and published her first collection of poems, The Choice of the World, in 1797. Her novel Zofloya; or, The Moor (1806) made her reputation in the Gothic. She continued publishing fiction and verse into the 1820s; her exact date of death is not recorded.
authors.profile: Dacre's Gothic combines the sensational traditions of Lewis and Radcliffe with exploration of female agency, racial otherness, and the destructive power of desire. Zofloya is the great Gothic femme fatale novel of the period; her later verse and prose continued to examine fantasy, transgression, and the limits of sensibility.
authors.style: Lush, ornate prose; saturated Gothic imagery; psychological interiority from the perspective of transgressive women; embedded tales; dramatic dialogue in the verse works.
authors.concerns: Female desire and agency within the Gothic; the social construction of racial and cultural otherness; imagination and delusion; the dangers of unchecked sensibility; the subversion of patriarchal authority.
authors.significance: Dacre's Gothic represents the female appropriation of the sensational mode; Zofloya is a key text in the genealogy of the femme fatale. Her recovery as a major contribution to 1790s–1820s Gothic fiction is well established in modern criticism.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact birth year is debated — candidates include 1771, 1772, and 1777; the date and circumstances of her death are not precisely recorded.

authors.name: Charlotte Lennox
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Novelist, dramatist, and editor, a writer of Scottish parentage born in Gibraltar whose The Female Quixote made her one of the leading novelists of the mid-eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Charlotte Ramsay around 1729 or 1730, probably in Gibraltar, the daughter of a Scottish army officer, she came to London after family losses and made her way as a writer. Her novel The Female Quixote (1752), a parody of romance-reading, was admired by Samuel Johnson, who befriended her and contributed to the periodical The Adventurer, with which she was associated; a tale in that periodical concerning a romantic heroine has often been linked to her. She later published Henrietta (1758), the novel Shirley (1760), and edited the periodical The Lady's Museum (1760-61). She also wrote plays and historical and translated works. She died on 4 January 1804.
authors.profile: A writer of social and didactic fiction who critiqued the illusions of romance and the marriage market from a woman's perspective, and who moved comfortably among the literary circles of her age.
authors.style: Ironical, corrective realism; a light satirical touch on romance conventions; social comedy of manners; and an editorial, periodical-bred economy of narration; with a move toward more serious domestic plotting in later fiction.
authors.concerns: The dangers and pleasures of reading; female expectation and disillusion; romance versus reality; education and reason; and women's position in the marriage market.
authors.significance: A prominent woman novelist and editor of the Augustan and Johnsonian age, whose The Female Quixote is now studied as a key text in the debate over fiction and female readers and in the rise of women's writing.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact year of birth (1729 or 1730) and place (Gibraltar is probable but not certain) are uncertain, and the precise extent of her authorship of the periodical The Adventurer and of related tales remains a matter of scholarly debate.

authors.name: Charlotte M. Yonge
authors.nationality: English; the domestic chronicle and the High Church novel
authors.identity: Novelist and historian; the most influential writer of the Victorian High Church novel and the inventor of the family chronicle for girls.
authors.biography: Born Charlotte Mary Yonge at Otterbourne, Hampshire, on 11 August 1823, the daughter of a retired army officer; she was educated at home and never married, living all her life in the village where her father was patron of the living. Her first novel appeared in 1844, and The Heir of Redclyffe (1853) made her famous; she edited The Monthly Packet for nearly forty years and wrote over a hundred and fifty books, including the sequence of family chronicles known as the 'Dynasty'. She died at Otterbourne on 24 May 1901.
authors.profile: Yonge wrote the novel of church and family: her subject is the moral formation of a young person within the discipline of the family and the Anglican communion, and her enormous 'Dynasty' follows a group of intermarried families through the nineteenth century. She was more influential on the Victorian imagination than any novelist except Dickens — The Heir of Redclyffe was the favourite book of the young officers of the Crimean War — and her best work is a fine, dense picture of the ordinary life of the Victorian gentry.
authors.style: The large family chronicle with an enormous cast; the direct moral appeal; dialogue of the county and the vicarage; the historical novel of the English church; the deathbed scene; the use of the novel for teaching.
authors.concerns: Religious faith and church loyalty; the family and its moral discipline; the education of children; the history of the Church of England; class and the county gentry; renunciation and self-sacrifice.
authors.significance: Yonge was the most influential woman novelist of the mid-Victorian period and the founder of the family chronicle for girls: The Heir of Redclyffe shaped the Victorian ideal of the Christian gentleman, her historical novels taught a generation its church history, and her 'Dynasty' is one of the most ambitious fictional projects of the century.

authors.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
authors.nationality: American; the feminist treatise, the utopia and the short story
authors.identity: Writer, sociologist and feminist theorist; the author of 'The Yellow Wallpaper' and Women and Economics, and the most systematic American feminist thinker of the century.
authors.biography: Born Charlotte Anna Perkins in Hartford, Connecticut, on 3 July 1860, the great-niece of Harriet Beecher Stowe; she married the artist Charles Walter Stetson in 1884, suffered severe postpartum depression, and was treated by the rest cure of S. Weir Mitchell, which produced 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (1892). She divorced in 1894, supported herself by lecturing and writing, published Women and Economics in 1898, edited the Forerunner (1909-16), and married her cousin George Houghton Gilman in 1900. She died in Pasadena on 17 August 1935.
authors.profile: Gilman wrote the American feminist argument as social science: Women and Economics analyses the economic dependency of women as the root of their subjection, and 'The Yellow Wallpaper' turns the medical treatment of women into the greatest American story of the 1890s. Her utopian fiction — Herland and Moving the Mountain — is the first sustained American feminist utopia, and her cultural criticism is systematic, clear and often startlingly modern.
authors.style: Clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis; the first-person narrative of mental breakdown; satirical utopia and the reversed anthropology; the sociological essay with statistics and cross-cultural comparison; direct address and repetition.
authors.concerns: Women's economic dependency and the case for their paid work; the medical treatment of women and the rest cure; marriage, motherhood and the home as an institution; utopian alternatives; race and the 'woman problem'; work and human dignity.
authors.significance: Gilman is the central American feminist theorist of the nineteenth century after Fuller and a founding figure of the sociology of gender: Women and Economics was translated into seven languages, 'The Yellow Wallpaper' is one of the most studied American stories ever written, and Herland founded the American feminist utopia.

authors.biography: Born Charlotte Eliza Lawson Cowan at Carrickfergus, County Antrim, on 30 September 1832; she moved to London, married the widowed novelist J. H. Riddell, and supported the family by her pen after his death. George Geith of Fen Court (1864), The Race for Wealth (1866), Austin Friars (1870) and the ghost stories Weird Stories (1882) followed. She died at Ashford, Kent, on 24 September 1906.
authors.profile: Charlotte Riddell was the first English novelist of the City of London and one of the finest Victorian ghost-story writers: George Geith of Fen Court opened the City to fiction, her financial novels gave the Victorian reader the world of the counting-house, and Weird Stories contains some of the best ghost stories in English.
authors.style: The documentary detail of the counting-house and the ledger; the financial plot of speculation and ruin; the ghost story of the haunted house with its legal cause; the plain, businesslike prose; the sympathetic portrait of the working woman.

authors.name: Charlotte Smith
altNames: Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex
authors.birthplace: London, King Street, off St James's Square, born on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, and Anna (Towers) Turner
authors.nationality: English; the pre-Romantic and Romantic lyric tradition of the sensibility and the sonnet revival, joined to the radical and domestic novel of the 1790s and to the educational literature for young women produced by the London and provincial presses between the French Revolution and her death
authors.identity: Poet and novelist who revived the regular English sonnet in the 1780s and, from 1789 to 1806, supported herself by her pen through a series of epistolary and domestic novels, juvenile letters, a blank-verse poem on the French Revolution and a topographical poem of the Sussex coast
authors.biography: Charlotte Turner was born in King Street, off St James's Square, London, on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, a country gentleman, and Anna Turner. Her mother died early and, after her father's reckless speculation dissolved the family fortune, she was largely raised by an aunt and put to girls' schools at Chichester. On 23 February 1765, aged fifteen, she was given by her father in marriage to Benjamin Smith, a much older man of violent temper and ruinous debts whom she afterwards described as a species of sale; the marriage produced a large family, twelve children being counted, of whom six survived her. The couple lived successively on the Isle of Wight and in Hampshire and Sussex, and Smith filled her years of marriage with the duties of a gentleman's wife, French and Italian reading, drawing, music and the care of her children's education. Benjamin Smith squandered a considerable legacy and was committed to the King's Bench prison for debt in December 1783, where his wife stayed with him, and it was during these years of confinement and disgrace that she assembled Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (1784), the little volume which made her name and went through nine or more enlarged editions in her lifetime. On her separation from her husband she became, in effect, the first English woman of letters to live by professional authorship under the modern meaning of the word: she wrote a novel, a juvenile work or a volume of verse almost annually for the rest of her life, and her later title pages describe her as 'Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex'. From 1776 the disposition of a family inheritance worth nearly £36,000, settled on her by her uncle James Turner in preference to her brother George, was tied up in Chancery for almost forty years; the litigation, its costs and the failures of her solicitors absorbed her income and her attention until her death and long afterwards, and she dedicated much of her preface-writing to telling the story of it. She lived in consequence at Chichester, Brighton, Storrington, Bath, Exmouth, Weymouth, Oxford, London, Frant and Elstead, moving whenever her creditors or her health required it; at Brighton in 1791-3 she was in the company of English radicals, and her sympathy with the Revolution in France, openly declared in Desmond (1792) and The Banished Man (1794), cost her subscribers and publishers in the reaction of the late 1790s. She corresponded with Joseph Cooper Walker, with the Cadells and with Samuel Harper, and in her last years her health failed, one eye being lost and her chest disease advancing. Charlotte Smith died at Tilford in Surrey on 28 October 1806 and was buried at Stoke Church, Stoke Park, near Guildford, within sight of the downs she had celebrated; she was widely lamented, especially by other women writers, and left unfinished manuscripts which her daughter published afterwards.
authors.profile: Her poetry begins with Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (London, 1784), enlarged in successive editions (third edition 1786; fifth 1789; seventh 1795; eighth 1797; ninth 1800) by new sonnets, by translations and imitations from Petrarch and other originals, and by an increasingly explicit advertisement of the poet's own injuries. To it she appended the two-book blank-verse poem The Emigrants (1793), on the French royalist exiles of the Revolution, and her last and most assured volume, Beachy Head, and Other Poems (1807), published after her death and including shorter pieces such as 'Flora' and 'Studies by the Sea' which had first appeared in her juvenile books. Her fiction, when she resumed it after 1788, is at the centre of her modern reputation: Ethelinde, or, The Recluse of the Lake (1789), Celestina (1791), Desmond (1792), The Old Manor House (1793), The Wanderings of Warwick (1794), The Banished Man (1794), Montalbert (1795), Marchmont (1796) and The Young Philosopher (1798), with the tale-series The Letters of a Solitary Wanderer (1800). She also made a permanent parallel reputation as an educational writer, in The Rural Walks (1795), Rambles Farther (1796), Minor Morals (1798) and Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young (1804), and she printed A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports (1796) for the benefit of a survivor of the wreck. Her earlier books, the translation The Romance of Real Life (1787) and the revised edition of her first novel Emmeline (Cadell, 1788), belong to the eighteenth century; the collections and the comedy got up after 1806, including the Commonplace Book and the novel attributed to her as the Literary Don Quixote, extend the record but not the lifetime's work. Modern scholarship is served by Stuart Curran's edition of her Poems (Oxford University Press, 1993), by Judith Phillips Stanton's Collected Letters (Indiana University Press, 2003), by the Pickering and Chatto collected edition of her Works in a numbered series of volumes, and by the essay collection Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism edited by Jacqueline Labbe (2008).
authors.style: Her sonnets are written in the regular fourteen-line form she preferred, with an attention to turn and closure that she set against what she thought the license of the Pindaric and Della Cruscan modes; the diction is that of sensibility - elegiac, personal, topographically exact, frequently addressed to a river, a headland, an old tree or a remembered haunt, and closing on a pointed couplet or a turned sentence. She introduced into the lyric a documentary force, the poet's own history of injury and dependence appearing in prefatory prose beside the verses. Her novels are mostly epistolary and self-consciously empirical, opening with an advertisement or prefatory letter claiming that the events are drawn from real life and from her own observation, and dividing sympathy between an impoverished heroine, a disputed heir and an oppressive relative; Gothic machinery - the abbey, the castle, the secret of birth - is retained but explained by law, money and interest rather than by fate. The juvenile books put instruction into conversation and the familiar letter, with natural-history observation and short quoted poems as the method of teaching. Her late blank verse, in The Emigrants and Beachy Head, is descriptive and meditative, moving from panoramic landscape to local history and personal resignation in the same sentence.
authors.concerns: The condition of a woman compelled to make a living by writing, and the dependence, debt and litigation that governed her work; the justice of property, the rights of an disinherited heir and the operation of law and the equity courts upon families; the French Revolution followed at first hand and in its effects on exiles, on the poor and on the conscience of a sympathiser; the education of young women and the uses of conversation, natural history and poetry as teaching; the claims of sensibility and their limits; landscape as evidence of feeling and as a record of loss; the superstition and the suffering of Catholic and rural communities; and the dignity of the humble and the aged, especially women, in a poetry of place.
authors.significance: By reviving the legitimate sonnet in the 1780s and holding it open through nine editions she made the form available for the meditative and personal use that Wordsworth and his contemporaries afterwards made standard; Stuart Curran's judgement that she is 'the first poet in English whom in retrospect we would call Romantic' states the modern claim. Her novels supplied the model of empirical, socially realistic domestic fiction written by a woman for a professional living, and Desmond and The Old Manor House are now read as political fictions of the 1790s answering Godwin and arguing with the reaction; her juvenile books carried that realism into the education of girls. Her long Chancery suit and her prefaces made the economics of authorship part of her texts, and her recovery since the 1990s, through Curran's, Stanton's and the Pickering and Chatto editions, has made her the central case in scholarship on women's writing, the sonnet revival and Romantic print culture.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth is fixed at 4 May 1749 by the Dictionary of National Biography tradition and by modern accounts, but older reference works long hesitated over the year, and her own statements about her childhood differ; the day and year of several first editions remain disputed in the secondary literature, Desmond (1792 in the English Short Title Catalogue records inspected here) still often being cited as 1796, and the revised Emmeline as 1788 or 1789 according to the copy examined; the attribution of the anonymous comedy What Is She? (printed 1799) is accepted by some modern scholars and doubted by others; the number of her children and the details of her residence at Bignor Park are variously reported; and the date at which her Chancery suit ceased to be pending is usually given from her own letters rather than from the court records.

authors.name: Christina Rossetti
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period, Pre-Raphaelite circle
authors.identity: Poet; the finest English devotional lyric poet of the century and a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle.
authors.biography: Born in London on 5 December 1830, youngest child of Gabriele Rossetti, an Italian political exile and Dante scholar, and Frances Polidori; sister of Dante Gabriel and William Michael Rossetti. Devoutly Anglo-Catholic from adolescence, she broke two engagements on religious grounds, and lived a retired life of writing, devotional work and, from 1876, teaching at the St Mary Magdalene penitentiary at Highgate. Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) was illustrated by her brother; The Prince's Progress (1866), Sing-Song (1872) and A Pageant and Other Poems (1881) followed, and she wrote the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' for Scribner's Monthly in 1872. She died of cancer in London on 29 December 1894.
authors.profile: Rossetti's poetry is small in compass and absolute in control: short lyric forms, plain diction, a strict metrical discipline and an imagery that is simultaneously devotional, erotic and deathly. Goblin Market is her one long poem, a fairy-tale narrative of temptation and redemption that has been read as an allegory of the Eucharist, of sisterhood, of sexual knowledge and of the Victorian market. Her later work turns increasingly to the preparation for death, and the sonnets 'Remember' and 'A Birthday' are among the most anthologised poems in English.
authors.style: Simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme; refrain and repetition used as a devotional instrument; sensuous and often grotesque imagery of fruit, hair, jewels and flowers; a quiet, unemphatic voice; the deliberate bareness of the late devotional poems.
authors.concerns: Temptation, sacrifice and redemption; the sisterhood of women; the body and its dangers; death, the grave and the afterlife; the relation of earthly to divine love; the position of women within the Anglo-Catholic church.
authors.significance: Christina Rossetti is the central woman poet of Victorian England and the finest religious lyricist after Herbert. Goblin Market is a founding text for the modern criticism of Victorian sexuality and of women's writing, and her influence runs through the twentieth-century devotional lyric and through the feminist recovery of the 1970s and 1980s.

authors.identity: Critic and poet; the Marxist aesthete of Illusion and Reality and Studies in a Dying Culture.
authors.biography: Born Christopher St John Sprigg at Putney on 20 October 1907; he left school at fifteen, worked in Fleet Street and wrote aviation books and thrillers under the Sprigg name before joining the Communist Party in 1935 and becoming Christopher Caudwell. Illusion and Reality (1937), the Marxist study of the sources of poetry, appeared in his last year; he drove an ambulance in Spain and was killed at the Jarama in February 1937, leaving the essays of Studies in a Dying Culture (1938) to be published after his death.
authors.profile: Christopher Caudwell is the Marxist critic of the dying culture: Illusion and Reality made the sources of poetry a study of the economics of the imagination, and Studies in a Dying Culture carried the critique of the bourgeois culture to the freedom, the psychology and the law - all written before he was twenty-nine and killed at the Jarama.
authors.style: The essay of the argument in the plain Marxist prose; the poetry read through the economics of the society; the dying culture diagnosed in its institutions; the thriller's craft carried into the criticism; the speed of the young mind at work.
authors.concerns: Marxism and the aesthetics of the thirties; the poetry and its sources in the society; the dying culture and its institutions; Spain and the generation that went; the young critic killed at twenty-nine.

authors.name: Christopher Isherwood
authors.nationality: British-American; the Berlin novel, the documentary report and the autobiography of a generation
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and memoirist; the author of Goodbye to Berlin and Berlin Stories, the source of Cabaret, and the closest collaborator of Auden.
authors.biography: Born Christopher William Bradshaw-Isherwood at Disley, Cheshire, on 26 August 1904; he read at Cambridge, left without a degree, worked as a tutor and a secretary, and went to Berlin in 1929, where he taught English and wrote The Last of Mr Norris (1935) and Goodbye to Berlin (1939). He collaborated with Auden on three plays, emigrated to America in 1939, worked in Hollywood as a screenwriter, became a Hindu monk and the disciple of Swami Prabhavananda, translated the Bhagavad Gita, and wrote the autobiographical Lions and Shadows (1938) and Christopher and His Kind (1976). He died at Santa Monica on 4 January 1986.
authors.profile: Isherwood's Berlin novels are the finest English record of the Weimar Republic's last years: Goodbye to Berlin gave the period its image of the doomed city and its narrator's famous 'I am a camera', and the two Berlin books became the musical Cabaret. His documentaries — Journey to a War with Auden, The Condor and the Cows — and his frank autobiography made him the period's great witness and one of the first English writers to write openly about homosexuality.
authors.style: The camera-eye narration: the observer who records without comment; the flat, exact, unadorned sentence; the scene assembled from dialogue and detail; the documentary report with the novelist's eye; the self-deprecating autobiographical confidence.
authors.concerns: Berlin and the collapse of the Weimar Republic; the rise of the Nazis and the political emergency; the expatriate and the Englishman abroad; homosexuality and the double life; the documentary witness and the artist's responsibility; India, religion and the search for a teacher.
authors.significance: Isherwood wrote the definitive English book about Weimar Berlin and one of the great documentaries of the period: Goodbye to Berlin gave the thirties its image of the doomed city, the Berlin stories became Cabaret, and Christopher and His Kind made him a pioneer of gay autobiography.

authors.name: Christopher Marlowe
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and translator; the creator of the Elizabethan tragic stage and of the 'mighty line' of blank verse.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 February 1564 at Canterbury, son of a shoemaker; a King's Scholar at the King's School, Canterbury, and a Parker Scholar at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge (BA 1584, MA 1587, the latter after the Privy Council intervened over his absences, plausibly for government service). In London he wrote Tamburlaine (1587–88), Doctor Faustus (c. 1588–92), The Jew of Malta (c. 1589–90), Edward II (c. 1592), and The Massacre at Paris (c. 1592–93), and translated Ovid's Amores and Lucan's Pharsalia I. He was associated with Ralegh's circle and suspected of atheism (the 'Baines note'); on 30 May 1593 he was killed in a quarrel at a Deptford house by Ingram Frizer, the coroner recording the stabbing as self-defence in a dispute over the reckoning.
authors.profile: The founder of Elizabethan tragedy: Tamburlaine's conquering rhetoric, Faustus's aspiring intellect, Barabas's satanic wit, and Edward II's study of a king's fall created the overreacher and the tragic stage that Shakespeare inherited.
authors.style: The 'mighty line' — muscular, end-stopped blank verse of enormous rhetorical force; the set-piece oration; lyric interludes ('Come live with me'); ironic juxtaposition of grandeur and brutality.
authors.concerns: The limits of human aspiration — power, knowledge, wealth, desire; Machiavellian statecraft; religious scepticism and the fear of damnation; the collision of the individual will with the order of things.
authors.significance: The greatest dramatic innovator before Shakespeare: he made blank verse the language of the stage, created the Elizabethan history play and tragedy, and his life and death — poet, spy, atheist — became the legend of the Elizabethan imagination.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of the plays rest on publication and performance records (none of the plays was printed in his lifetime); the circumstances of his death, his alleged espionage, and the authorship of parts of his canon (Dido with Nashe, the Henry VI plays) remain debated.

authors.name: Christopher Smart
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet, scholar, and editor, a brilliant and erratic man of letters whose religious hymns, especially Song to David, make him a singular visionary voice.
authors.biography: Smart was born in Kent, educated at Cambridge, and took holy orders. A fine Hebrew and classical scholar, he lived in London as an editor, schoolmaster, and hack writer, and edited early plays and other texts. His great religious poem, Song to David (1763), was published amid a reputation for madness, and in 1763 he was confined in a private madhouse for some years, during which he wrote the wild private poem Jubilate Agno in a manuscript not printed until the twentieth century. Released in later life, he continued to write and edit and was eventually admitted to an institutional charity for the poor. He died in 1771 of exhaustion.
authors.profile: A poet of intense religious enthusiasm and metrical experiment, whose verse praises the created world and its Creator with an incantatory, cataloguing energy; he also edited, translated, and wrote in prose.
authors.style: Irregular, energetic metrical vitality; antiphonal and parallel religious praise; catalogues of creatures and things; Hebrew and liturgical influence; and a visionary, sometimes deranged sublimity of imagery.
authors.concerns: Divine praise through the natural world; enthusiasm, reason, and madness; the sanctity of language and naming; liberty and the animal creation; and the poet's suffering and consolation.
authors.significance: Long undervalued, Smart is now recognised as one of the most original religious and visionary poets of the century, a forerunner of Romantic interest in the irrational and a master of ecstatic hymnody.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1722 from baptismal records; the chronology of his confinement and the survival and dating of the Jubilate Agno manuscript are complex and partly reconstructed.

authors.name: Clara Reeve
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English novelist and critic of the tale of romance, known for The Old English Baron and for the critical Progress of Romance.
authors.biography: Born on 23 January 1729 at Ipswich, the daughter of an attorney, she grew up in a literary household and turned to writing and translation. Her Gothic novel first appeared as The Champion of Virtue (1777) and was soon republished and long known as The Old English Baron (1778), modeled on Walpole's The Castle of Otranto but more probability-bound. She also published other fiction and, in 1785, the critical history The Progress of Romance, an early survey of prose fiction. She died on 3 December 1807.
authors.profile: A writer of Gothic and sentimental romance and a pioneering critic of the prose tale, who sought to defend and historicize romance while making it more rational and morally restrained.
authors.style: A moderated, realistic Gothic that tempers marvel with probability; plain, earnest prose; epistolary and moralizing passages; and a self-conscious critical awareness of the conventions of romance.
authors.concerns: The legitimacy and history of romance and fiction; the balance of wonder and probability; female virtue and sensibility; and the moral and social uses of the tale.
authors.significance: A key transitional figure in the development of Gothic fiction and one of the earliest historians of the prose romance, whose Progress of Romance is an important document of eighteenth-century critical thought about fiction.
authors.uncertainty: Her broad life is documented, though details of her education and early writings are imperfectly recorded, and the dating of the first appearance of her Gothic novel has often been confused between 1777 and 1778.

authors.name: Claude McKay
authors.nationality: Jamaican-American; the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and the novel of Black labour
authors.identity: Poet and novelist; the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the author of 'If We Must Die' and Home to Harlem.
authors.biography: Born Festus Claudius McKay in Clarendon Parish, Jamaica, on 15 September 1889; he was apprenticed to a wheelwright and then served in the Jamaican constabulary, published Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads in 1912, and came to the United States to study at Tuskegee and Kansas State. He moved to Harlem in 1914, published 'If We Must Die' in 1919, Harlem Shadows in 1922, and the novels Home to Harlem (1928), Banjo (1929) and Banana Bottom (1933); he travelled to Russia and France, became a Catholic, and died in Chicago on 22 May 1948.
authors.profile: McKay is the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of the period's most famous protest poem: 'If We Must Die' — written during the Red Summer of 1919 and quoted by Churchill in 1940 — gave the movement its trumpet call, Harlem Shadows its first substantial book of verse, and Home to Harlem the first best-selling Black novel of the decade. His Jamaican dialect poems are the first body of West Indian verse in English.
authors.style: The sonnet and the ballad used for protest; the Jamaican dialect written phonetically; the blunt, direct, unornamented statement; the image of the body under threat; the travel narrative of the Black migrant worker.
authors.concerns: Race and the colour line; the Black worker and the colonial inheritance; the Jamaican folk and the peasantry; Harlem, the cabaret and the migrant's city; the body, desire and the police; the revolutionary and the exile.
authors.significance: McKay wrote the period's most famous protest poem and the first substantial body of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem of resistance, Harlem Shadows gave the movement its first book, and his Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.

authors.name: Colley Cibber
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Actor-manager, playwright, poet laureate, and autobiographer; his comedy Love's Last Shift (1696) inaugurated 'sentimental comedy', and his flamboyant An Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber (1740) is a vivid memoir of the Restoration stage — though Pope made him the hero of The Dunciad.
authors.biography: Born 6 November 1671 in London, son of the sculptor Caius Gabriel Cibber; educated at the Free School, Grantham. He joined the stage as an actor and wrote some twenty-five plays, beginning with Love's Last Shift (1696), whose reformed rake launched sentimental comedy; his adaptations of Shakespeare and Molière and farces like The Non-Juror were commercially astute. He became a leading actor-manager (patentee of Drury Lane, 1710), poet laureate (1730, a deeply unpopular appointment), and wrote his celebrated Apology (1740). He died on 12 December 1757.
authors.profile: The shrewd, vain, and gifted man of the theatre whose sentimental comedies and lively memoir shaped eighteenth-century drama and whose laureateship made him the byword for poetic dullness.
authors.style: Sentimental, moralising comedy; theatrical savvy and adaptation; a lively, self-promoting prose in the Apology; and occasional verse of modest quality.
authors.concerns: Moral reform and sentimental virtue; the business and life of the theatre; vanity and self-justification; and the reform of comedy toward feeling.
authors.significance: Cibber founded sentimental comedy and left in his Apology one of the most valuable first-hand accounts of the Restoration and early Georgian stage; his laureateship and feud with Pope secured his immortality as the 'king of dunces'.
authors.uncertainty: Cibber's Apology is candid but self-serving; details are embellished for effect, and his reputation was distorted by Pope's satire.
movements: Comedy of Manners

themes: Marriage and women's conduct

authors.name: Compton Mackenzie
authors.nationality: British; the comic novel and the Scottish island
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and nationalist; the author of Whisky Galore and Sinister Street, and a central figure of the Scottish Renaissance.
authors.biography: Born Edward Montague Compton Mackenzie at West Hartlepool on 17 January 1883; he was educated at Oxford, published Sinister Street (1913–14) and Youth's Encounter (1913), served in the Aegean in the First World War, and founded the Scottish National Party's predecessor. Whisky Galore (1947), The Monarch of the Glen (1941) and The Four Winds of Love followed, and he died in Edinburgh on 30 November 1972.
authors.profile: Compton Mackenzie was one of the great comic novelists of the century and a central figure of the Scottish Renaissance: Whisky Galore is the funniest Scottish novel ever written, Sinister Street made the novel of Oxford and London, and his Scottish nationalism gave the movement one of its founders.
authors.style: The comic novel of the island; the exact topography of the Hebrides; the dialogue of the islanders; the society comedy of the metropolis; the plain, warm, discursive prose.
authors.concerns: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the absurd, the void.
authors.significance: Compton Mackenzie was one of the great comic novelists of the century and a central figure of the Scottish Renaissance: Whisky Galore is the funniest Scottish novel ever written, Sinister Street made the novel of Oxford and London, and his nationalism gave the movement one of its founders.

authors.name: Constance Fenimore Woolson
authors.nationality: American; the Great Lakes story and the European exile
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and the close friend of Henry James.
authors.biography: Born Constance Fenimore Woolson at Claremont, New Hampshire, on 5 March 1840, a great-niece of James Fenimore Cooper; she grew up in Cleveland, published Castle Nowhere (1875) and Rodman the Keeper (1880), and lived in Europe from 1879. Anne (1882), For the Major (1883) and Jupiter Lights (1889) followed. She died in Venice on 24 January 1894.
authors.profile: Constance Fenimore Woolson was the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and the closest American friend of Henry James: her Great Lakes and Southern stories created the American regional tale at its most finished, and her European novels made the American woman abroad into a subject of the first importance.
authors.style: The regional sketch of the Great Lakes and the Sea Islands; the precise topography and the social detail; the American woman abroad; the ironic ending and the withheld marriage; the Jamesian point of view.
authors.concerns: Regional identity and the American sectional character; the woman alone and the limited estate; the American in Europe and the expatriate; the Reconstruction South; art and the woman artist.
authors.significance: Constance Fenimore Woolson was the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and Henry James's closest American friend: her Great Lakes and Southern stories created the American regional tale at its most finished, and her European novels made the American woman abroad a subject of the first importance.

authors.name: Constance Holme
authors.nationality: British; the Westmorland novelist of the fell farm and the dalesfolk
authors.identity: Novelist; the Westmorland writer of The Lonely Plough and Old Vicarage, Grantley.
authors.biography: Born Constance Holme in Lancashire on 2 December 1880, of a Westmorland farming family; she lived at Kendal and wrote the novels of the fell farm and the dalesfolk - The Lonely Plough (1920), Old Vicarage, Grantley (1921), The Trysting Place (1922), Green Harvest (1926) - in the prose of the fell weather and the farming year. Her books were reissued in the 1940s and she died at Kendal on 20 January 1955.
authors.profile: Constance Holme is the Westmorland novelist of the fell farm: The Lonely Plough and Old Vicarage, Grantley recorded the dalesfolk, the farming year and the fell weather in a prose of the place that made her the most exact of the regional novelists of the 1920s, and her recovery in the 1940s made her the test case of the neglected regional woman novelist.
authors.style: The prose of the fell weather, the farming year and the stone; the dialogue of the dalesfolk in the local speech; the household and the farm as the whole of the world; the slow season as the plot; the elegy of the last of the line.
authors.concerns: The Westmorland fell and the dalesfolk; the farming year and the stone of the wall; the last of the line and the inheritance of the farm; the woman of the farmhouse; the region as the world entire.
authors.significance: Constance Holme is the Westmorland novelist of the fell farm: The Lonely Plough and Old Vicarage, Grantley recorded the dalesfolk and the farming year in a prose of the place, and she remains the most exact of the regional novelists of the 1920s.

authors.name: Countee Cullen
authors.nationality: American; the lyric in the English tradition and the poetry of the colour line
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and anthologist; the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the movement's principal defender of the inherited English lyric.
authors.biography: Born Countee LeRoy Porter in New York on 30 May 1903 and raised in Harlem by the Reverend Frederick Asbury Cullen; he won prizes at high school and at New York University, published Color in 1925, graduated from Harvard in 1926, and edited Caroling Dusk (1927), the anthology of Black verse. He married Yolande Du Bois in 1928, taught in the New York schools, and published Copper Sun (1927), The Black Christ (1929), One Way to Heaven (1932) and The Medea and Some Poems (1935). He died in New York on 9 January 1946.
authors.profile: Cullen is the most formally gifted poet of the Harlem Renaissance: Color and Copper Sun contain the finest English lyrics written by an African American of the period, and 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and 'Incident' are permanent poems of the colour line. His editorship of Caroling Dusk gave the movement its anthology, and his insistence that a Black poet might use the whole English tradition was the counter-position to Hughes's folk programme.
authors.style: The strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave; the Keatsian and Housmanesque diction; the irony of a formal grace turned on a brutal subject; the refrain and the clanging rhyme; the poem that ends on a question.
authors.concerns: Race, the colour line and the burden of a 'double consciousness'; Africa and the ancestral inheritance; the lynch mob and the murdered child; the Christian faith and the Black church; love and the private life; the poet's quarrel with his own tradition.
authors.significance: Cullen is the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of some of its finest lyrics: Color and Copper Sun are permanent books of American verse, 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are central poems of the colour line, and Caroling Dusk is the movement's defining anthology.

authors.name: Coventry Patmore
authors.nationality: English; the domestic epic and Catholic devotional verse
authors.identity: Poet and essayist; the poet of Victorian marriage and domestic love, whose long poem The Angel in the House gave the age its image of the wife.
authors.biography: Born at Woodford, Essex, on 23 July 1823, the son of the writer Peter George Patmore; he was educated privately and at the British Museum, and worked for eighteen years in the printed books department of the Museum. He married Emily Andrews in 1847; her death in 1862 and his second marriage to Marianne Byles shaped his later verse. The Angel in the House (1854-62) made him famous and gave Victorian England its ideal of the domestic woman; after his conversion to Rome in 1864 his poetry became increasingly mystical, culminating in The Unknown Eros (1877). He died at Lymington on 26 November 1896.
authors.profile: Patmore is the poet of marriage as a sacrament: The Angel in the House is a long domestic epic, deliberately plain and conversational, which idealises the wife as the moral centre of the home and made the phrase 'the angel in the house' a permanent description of the Victorian ideal. His later odes in The Unknown Eros are among the most daringly irregular and mystical poems of the century, and his essay 'The Poetry of the Future' is a remarkable piece of prophetic criticism.
authors.style: Conversational narrative verse in the plain style; the domestic detail; the ode with irregular, long-breathed stanzas; mystical eroticism; the deliberately unpoetic vocabulary of hearth and household.
authors.concerns: Marriage and domestic love as a religious state; the wife as the angel of the home; the education of the affections; Catholic mysticism and the love of God; death, bereavement and the afterlife; the relation of the sexes.
authors.significance: The Angel in the House created the Victorian ideal of the domestic woman and is therefore one of the most historically important poems of the century, the text against which the whole feminist critique of Victorian marriage was written. The Unknown Eros is a major achievement in its own right, admired by Hopkins and by the modernists.
