authors.name: Cynewulf
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon
authors.identity: poet
authors.biography: Nothing is known of Cynewulf beyond his name, which he wove as a runic acrostic into the epilogues of four Old English poems: The Fates of the Apostles, Elene, Juliana, and Christ II. Candidates proposed for identification include a Cynewulf bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 783), but the question remains open.
authors.profile: The four signed poems form a coherent body of religious narrative and meditation; scholars have also attributed other poems (notably in the Exeter and Vercelli books) to his 'school' without consensus.
authors.style: Ornate, reflective religious narrative; typological reading of scripture and legend; runic signature passages that meditate on judgment and the last things.
authors.concerns: Salvation, judgment, and the vanity of the world; the apostolic and imperial foundations of the Church; the poet's own sinfulness.
authors.significance: The only named author of a substantial Old English poetic corpus besides Cædmon, and the first English poet to sign his work.
authors.uncertainty: Identity and dates entirely unknown; dating proposals range from the late eighth to the tenth century.

authors.name: Cyril Tourneur
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist; soldier; diplomat
authors.biography: Born about 1575, of obscure family. He served in military and diplomatic posts — in the Low Countries, and as secretary to the council of war in the Cadiz expedition of 1625. On the return voyage he fell ill and was put ashore at Kinsale, Ireland, where he died on 28 February 1626.
authors.profile: Certainly his are the morality-influenced tragedy The Atheist's Tragedy (1611) and the elegy A Grief on the Death of Prince Henry (1613); The Revenger's Tragedy (1606–07) was long printed under his name but is now generally assigned to Middleton.
authors.style: Senecan rhetoric pressed toward allegory and emblem; a satiric, almost allegorical handling of revenge and atheism.
authors.concerns: The punishment of atheism; the workings of providence; revenge and its ironic reversals.
authors.significance: His name remains attached to one of the masterpieces of Jacobean tragedy, even as scholarship has transferred the play itself to Middleton.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; the Revenger's Tragedy attribution is now disputed and generally given to Middleton.

authors.name: Cædmon
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (Northumbrian)
authors.identity: poet
authors.biography: The first named English poet. According to Bede's account (Historia ecclesiastica IV.24), Cædmon was an illiterate cowherd at the monastery of Whitby under Abbess Hild who received the gift of song in a dream; thereafter he turned biblical narrative into vernacular verse, becoming a monk and composing a large body of religious poetry, of which only the nine-line 'Hymn' survives in Old English.
authors.profile: Cædmon's Hymn, a praise of God the Creator, survives in Northumbrian and West Saxon versions copied into manuscripts of Bede's Historia. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English and the foundation of the English vernacular religious tradition.
authors.style: Alliterative verse in the traditional Germanic style applied to Christian subject matter; simple, dignified praise of creation.
authors.concerns: The rendering of scripture into the vernacular; creation as the work of God.
authors.significance: As narrated by Bede, Cædmon exemplifies the consecration of native poetic form to Christian content; his Hymn is the starting point of the English poetic record.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from Bede's account, which has legendary elements; dates approximate; no poetry beyond the Hymn is securely attributed to him.
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age
themes: Creation and cosmology

authors.name: D. H. Lawrence
authors.nationality: British; the novel of the body, the mining-country elegy and the poetry of free verse
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, essayist and painter; the greatest English writer of the mining Midlands, the prophet of the body and of instinct, and the most controversial author of the period.
authors.biography: Born David Herbert Lawrence at Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, on 11 September 1885, the son of a coal miner and a schoolteacher; he trained as a teacher, published The White Peacock in 1911, married Frieda von Richthofen in 1914, and was driven from England by the war, the censorship of The Rainbow (1915) and the hostility of the police. He travelled in Italy, Ceylon, Australia, Mexico and the south of France, writing Sons and Lovers (1913), Women in Love (1920), Kangaroo (1923), The Plumed Serpent (1926) and Lady Chatterley's Lover (1928, privately printed), and died of tuberculosis at Vence on 2 March 1930.
authors.profile: Lawrence made the body, the marriage and the industrial Midlands the great subjects of the English novel. Sons and Lovers is the first English novel of working-class childhood, The Rainbow and Women in Love are the period's most ambitious novels of love and consciousness, and Lady Chatterley's Lover — banned until 1960 — became the century's test case for literary censorship. As a poet he wrote the freest and most bodily free verse of the period, and as an essayist (Studies in Classic American Literature, 1923) he invented a whole idiom of criticism.
authors.style: The loose, repetitive, urgent sentence driven by the rhythm of feeling and breath; the free indirect style that dissolves into the character's body; the symbolic landscape (the colliery, the sea, the Mexican plain) charged with psychic force; free verse written in the rhythm of speech and desire; the polemical, vatic essay.
authors.concerns: Sex, the body, and the marriage of true minds; the mining village and the industrial ruin of England; class and the educated miner's son; the machine against the instinct; the mother and the son; travel and the search for a living civilisation; leadership, power and the male bond.
authors.significance: Lawrence is the period's most radical novelist and its greatest poet of the body: Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow and Women in Love remade the English novel, his free verse gave English poetry a new nakedness, and Studies in Classic American Literature remains one of the most influential critical books ever written in English. His censorship made him the period's symbol of the fight for literary freedom.

authors.nationality: English (Kent)
authors.identity: translator; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, who in 1340 completed the Ayenbite of Inwyt (Remorse of Conscience), a Kentish translation of the French Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens. He is the first known translator of that influential manual of vices and virtues into English.
authors.profile: Translator of the Ayenbite of Inwyt (1340), the most extensive surviving Kentish prose text and a mine of early fourteenth-century English vocabulary.
authors.style: Faithful, word-for-word translation preserving the structure of the French original; conservative Kentish dialect with extensive learned vocabulary.
authors.concerns: The moral instruction of the laity through the doctrine of vices, virtues, and the sacrament of penance.
authors.significance: The Ayenbite is a unique record of the Kentish dialect and a major document of lay religious instruction on the eve of the Black Death.

authors.name: Daniel Defoe
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English writer, journalist, and pamphleteer, long regarded as one of the founders of the English novel and among the most prolific and versatile prose authors of his age.
authors.biography: Born in London around 1660, the son of James Foe, a candlemaker and Dissenter, he was raised outside the Church of England and educated at a Dissenting academy. He engaged in trade, went bankrupt, and turned to political writing, publishing verse and hundreds of pamphlets, often courting danger from the authorities. He is best known for fiction written later in life, including Robinson Crusoe (1719), Moll Flanders (1722), and Roxana (1724). He was also associated with periodical and intelligence work under the government. He died in London on 24 April 1731.
authors.profile: A prolific author of fictional narrative, travel writing, conduct literature, and journalism, whose longest-lasting achievements are extended first-person fictions that treat crime, survival, and self-examination with realistic detail. His place as an early novelist rests on the vividness of that persona-based narration.
authors.style: Plain, direct, largely unornamented prose; an insistent first-person voice; accumulation of concrete and material detail; and a documentary, autobiographical surface that lends improbable stories an air of fact.
authors.concerns: Providence and self-preservation; sin, repentance, and material rising; credit, risk, and survival in a commercial world; political allegiance and religious nonconformity; and the fortunes of social outsiders.
authors.significance: One of the most widely read English prose writers of his generation and a central figure in the emergence of the novel, with Robinson Crusoe becoming one of the most influential narratives in English.
authors.uncertainty: His birth year (c. 1660) and exact birthplace are not firmly documented, and the authorship of a body of works attributed to him remains disputed.

authors.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period, Pre-Raphaelitism
authors.identity: Poet, painter and translator; the founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and the central figure of the aesthetic poetry of the 1860s-70s.
authors.biography: Born in London on 12 May 1828, son of Gabriele Rossetti; trained at Sass's academy and the Royal Academy Schools, and in 1848 founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood with Holman Hunt and Millais. He painted The Girlhood of Mary Virgin (1849) and Ecce Ancilla Domini (1850), wrote the Germ (1850), and after the death of his wife Elizabeth Siddal in 1862 buried his poems in her coffin, then exhumed them in 1869 to publish Poems (1870). The 1871 attack by Robert Buchanan ('The Fleshly School of Poetry') began a scandal that damaged his reputation; his health and eyesight failed, and he died at Birchington-on-Sea on 9 April 1882.
authors.profile: Rossetti's poetry is the literary counterpart of his painting: a sensuous, heavily jewelled and incantatory verse of visionary women, of the moment between life and death, and of a synaesthetic correspondence of sound, colour and scent. He translated the early Italian poets (Dante's Vita Nuova, the stilnovisti) and the ballad tradition, and he made the sonnet sequence The House of Life a record of love as both spiritual and physical. His late poems are simpler and more elegiac.
authors.style: Rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound; archaic and medievalising diction; the sonnet sequence; the ballad with supernatural machinery; pictorial description that catalogues jewels, hair and flowers; a pervasive atmosphere of dream and suspended time.
authors.concerns: Love as a religion, sacred and erotic; the dead beloved and the cult of Beatrice; the relation of the poet to the painter; time, mortality and the permanence of art; the body and the soul; Italy and the medieval past as an alternative to Victorian industrial England.
authors.significance: Rossetti founded Pre-Raphaelitism and gave the aesthetic movement its central images and its doctrine of art for beauty's sake; The House of Life is the major English sonnet sequence of the century after Barrett Browning, and the Buchanan controversy is the decisive episode in the Victorian debate over the morality of art. His influence on Swinburne, Morris, Pater, Wilde and Yeats is direct.

authors.name: David Hartley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Physician and Dissenting philosopher whose Observations on Man (1749) built a complete system of mind, morals and religion on the doctrine of association of ideas.
authors.biography: Baptised at Luddenden near Halifax in 1705, the son of a poor clergyman, he lost both parents early and was brought up by an uncle. Educated at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he took his degrees and later his MD, he abandoned a clerical career, studied medicine in London and at Cambridge and practised successively in the provinces, in London and at Bath. His early medical studies prepared his larger scheme, which reduced mental life to vibration, sensation and the association of ideas as Locke had described them. Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Anticipations (1749, two volumes) derived the whole of ethics, religion and hope from that mechanism, and its second part argued for a future state of universal happiness. He married and had several children, and died at Bath in 1757.
authors.profile: The architect of associationist psychology, who made the mechanical linking of ideas the explanation of character, virtue and religious expectation.
authors.style: Tight, numbered, propositional prose; long chains of deduction from a single principle; a physician's plainness and a dissenting divinity's earnestness of reference.
authors.concerns: Association as the law of mind; the physiological basis of thought; the derivation of moral sense from education and habit; the accumulation of desires and the scheme of future happiness; necessitation and prayer.
authors.significance: His Observations founded the associationist tradition that Priestley, Darwin, the Mills and the psychology of the next century developed, and made the link between mind and mechanism a standard explanatory programme.
authors.uncertainty: The date and exact place of his birth are uncertain; his son's memoir and later accounts disagree on the details.

authors.name: David Hume
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Philosopher, essayist and historian of the Scottish Enlightenment, the most rigorous sceptic in English prose, whose Treatise and Enquiries remade the theory of knowledge, morals and politics.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh in April 1711 into a small landowning family, he was educated at home and at the university, tried a merchant's life in Bristol, and then withdrew to France to write. The Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40) appeared to little acclaim, and he confessed his distress at its neglect; the moral and political essays of 1741 and the Enquiries of 1748 and 1751 restated the same philosophy in a public style. He was blocked from an Edinburgh professorship in 1745 by clerical opposition and was summoned before the presbytery of that city in 1756 without being censured; he earned his living as a private tutor, as keeper of the Advocates' Library and, from 1754, as a historian, and his History of England made him wealthy. He served in the embassy in Paris from 1763, briefly at the foreign office, and accompanied Rousseau to England in 1766 before their quarrel. He died in Edinburgh on 25 August 1776, having written his own short account of a life he called so little interrupted.
authors.profile: A sceptical humanist who reduced causation, induction, the self and moral obligation to habit, sentiment and custom, yet wrote with an urbanity that made disbelief amiable.
authors.style: Lucid, measured, ironized prose; the clean paragraph of the Enquiries; examples drawn from common life; dry humour and a refusal of technical jargon; historical narrative of stately balance.
authors.concerns: Custom as the guide of life; the limits of reason in belief and in morals; the passions and the rules of justice; natural religion, miracle and the design argument; the principles of taste, party and commerce.
authors.significance: He set the agenda of post-Kantian philosophy in the problem of induction and personal identity, founded the empirical study of religion and of politics, and gave classical liberalism its sceptical defence of convention.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his father's estate, his Bristol period and his Parisian secretarial work are patchy; his posthumous Dialogues were published in 1779 under his brother's editorship against his own instructions on timing.

authors.name: David Walker
authors.nationality: American; the abolitionist writing of the free Black communities of the northern seaports, of Black mutual-aid and Masonic civic life, and of the immediatist pamphlet agitation of the later 1820s
authors.identity: Boston clothes merchant, civic organizer and pamphleteer; the author of the first and most uncompromising American demand for immediate unconditional emancipation written by a Black American, and the founding polemicist of the immediatist agitation in the United States.
authors.biography: Walker was born in Wilmington, North Carolina, in or about 1796, and grew up free; his mother's condition and his father's status are reported differently in the sources, and under the law of the state his freedom or enslavement would have followed the condition of the mother. He appears in the record as a mariner's and then a merchant's man, with years in Charleston, South Carolina, before he settled in Boston by 1825. There he kept a clothing and second-hand goods business, joined the Prince Hall Masonic lodge and took an active part in the Black civic, mutual-aid, educational and religious networks of the city, whose print culture and subscription lists gave the abolitionist press its first readers and its earliest money. He was in sympathy with the colony scheme then advancing in the white press and became its most furious opponent, and his Appeal, issued in Boston on 28 September 1829, was printed at his own instance, smuggled into the Southern states through sailors and Black seaport channels, and reissued in three enlarged editions within a year. Its call to the enslaved to read, remember and act, and its prophecy of judgment on the republic, produced a legislative reaction in the Southern states, a bounty on his person announced in Georgia, and a permanent alarm in the slaveholding press. He died in Boston on 6 August 1830, at about thirty-four years of age, and was buried in what is now an unmarked grave; the cause of his death was never established, and from his own lifetime some suspected he had been murdered. The Liberator, founded the year after his death, printed his Appeal in full and treated it as the opening document of the movement.
authors.profile: His surviving literary work is a single pamphlet, and a work of sustained argument rather than narrative: Walker's Appeal, in four articles with a preamble, addressed in the first instance to the coloured citizens of the world and particularly of the United States. It mixes indictment, scriptural exegesis, historical parallel, statistical citation from encyclopaedias and the slave codes, and an appeal to the diaspora to educate, organise and remember itself; a supplementary appeal to the slaveholders follows in later editions. Its manner is sermon, courtroom remonstrance and open letter at once, and its four articles pass from the condition of free Black Americans, through the crimes of slavery and the rebuttal of racist pseudo-science, to a programme of self-help, schools and mutual inspection. He also wrote short public letters and minutes to the Black press of the later 1820s, and left a son of the same name who preserved the text.
authors.style: An amplified, prophetic and incantatory prose, built on apostrophe, anaphora, long cumulative sentences and repeated charges of hypocrisy; the irony of quotation turned against the quotations' authors, with the Declaration, the Bible and the language of Christianity cited to condemn the nation that uses them. The argument proceeds by indictment, evidence and threat rather than by politeness, and it deliberately abandons the petitioning manner of earlier reform writing.
authors.concerns: The standing of the enslaved as fully human and as citizens of the republic that professes their equality; the sin and political danger of slavery and of the colour line; the complicity of the churches and of the colonisation movement in American slavery; the duties of self-education, industry, temperance and organisation in the free Black community; the use of scripture and of founding documents as instruments of accusation; the right of the oppressed to speak for themselves and, under judgment, to act.
authors.significance: The Appeal marks the moment when American abolitionist writing turned from gradualist appeal and white benevolence to immediate unconditional demand voiced by the oppressed themselves, and it supplied the rhetorical model of the agitation of the 1830s. It was the first American pamphlet to make the condition of the enslaved a national rather than a charitable question in the language of self-assertion; it was read aloud, reprinted, smuggled and prosecuted, and the laws passed against Black literacy and importation of seditious press in the Southern states after 1829-30 were partly a reply to it. Garrison's paper made him its prophetic precursor, and later Black radical tradition has read him as its founding political writer.
authors.uncertainty: Almost all the facts of his life before Boston are uncertain. The year of his birth is given only approximately (c. 1796, sometimes 1797), and the date of 28 September in some accounts is borrowed from the anniversary of the Appeal's publication; the conditions of his parents, and therefore the basis of his own free status, are reported contradictorily, with one account making his mother free and his father enslaved and another the reverse. The story of his early life is derived largely from what he says of himself in the Appeal and from Southern newspaper reportage hostile to him. The cause of his death is unknown, and the poisoning theory belongs to contemporary suspicion and to later tradition rather than to evidence. No manuscript of the Appeal survives and the details of its printing and distribution are known from the editions themselves and from the reports of agents.

authors.identity: English novelist, playwright, and political satirist, one of the most prominent and scandalous female writers of the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born on the island of Jersey, the daughter of Sir Roger Manley, a military governor, she was raised within an aristocratic milieu and later turned to literary work to support herself. She wrote fiction, plays, and political journalism, and her satirical key to court and party figures, The New Atalantis (1709), brought her fame and a prosecution for libel. Her fictionalized account of her own career, The Adventures of Rivella, appeared in 1714, and other prose romances circulated under her name. She died in London on 24 July 1724.

authors.concerns: Party rivalry and court corruption; reputation, scandal, and the exposure of the powerful; the situation of the writing woman; and the interplay of sex, money, and political patronage.
authors.significance: A leading female author of early-eighteenth-century London letters and a key figure in the development of political satire and scandalous fiction, her work a central document of party-age writing.

authors.name: Dorothy L. Sayers
authors.nationality: British; the detective novel of character and the theological drama
authors.identity: Novelist, translator and dramatist; the finest stylist of the Golden Age detective novel, the creator of Lord Peter Wimsey and Harriet Vane, and the translator of Dante.
authors.biography: Born Dorothy Leigh Sayers in Oxford on 13 June 1893, the daughter of a clergyman and schoolmaster; she took a first in medieval literature at Somerville and worked in publishing and advertising. Whose Body? (1923) introduced Lord Peter Wimsey; Strong Poison (1930), The Nine Tailors (1934) and Gaudy Night (1935) are the finest English detective novels of the period. She gave up fiction in the late 1930s for theological drama (The Man Born to Be King, 1941) and her Penguin translation of Dante's Inferno (1949). She died at Witham, Essex, on 17 December 1957.
authors.profile: Sayers is the finest writer of the Golden Age detective novel: The Nine Tailors is the most perfectly constructed English mystery, Gaudy Night is the first detective novel built on the inner life of a woman intellectual, and her Lord Peter Wimsey — with Harriet Vane — is the most fully realised detective in English fiction. Her theological plays made Christian drama a popular form, and her Dante translation is still the standard Penguin edition.
authors.style: The fair-play plot carried by character rather than mechanism; the detective novel as a novel of manners; the donnish wit and the literary allusion; the English village, the bell-ringing and the ecclesiastical setting; the love plot developed across several volumes.
authors.concerns: Murder and the closed community; the English village, the church and the bell tower; money, marriage and the family; the woman intellectual and the price of her education; guilt, forgiveness and Christian doctrine; the detection as a search for truth.
authors.significance: Sayers is the finest stylist of the Golden Age and the period's most accomplished woman of letters: The Nine Tailors and Gaudy Night are the finest detective novels in English, her theological drama made Christian broadcasting a popular form, and her Dante is the standard modern English translation. She gave the genre its first fully realised woman intellectual.

authors.name: Dorothy Osborne
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Letter-writer; her Letters to Sir William Temple (1652–54), written during their protracted courtship against her family's opposition, are among the finest and most natural prose works of the century and a rare surviving woman's voice of the Interregnum.
authors.biography: Born 1627 at Chicksands Priory, Bedfordshire, daughter of a royalist family; she nursed her father during the Civil Wars and lost most of her siblings. Between 1652 and 1654 she conducted a secret correspondence with William Temple (later the diplomat and essayist), whom she married in 1654 against strong family pressure and other suitors. Her letters — witty, tender, shrewd, and critical of the romances and poetry of the day — survive in some seventy-seven; Temple preserved them and they were published in 1888. She lived as Lady Temple, accompanying her husband's career, and died in 1695.
authors.profile: The natural, intelligent letter-writer whose prose, free of artifice, offers a woman's candid view of love, family duty, books, and society in the 1650s, and a remarkable literary self-portrait.
authors.style: Easy, colloquial, unforced prose; wit and psychological insight; literary criticism and quotation; and an intimate epistolary voice of great spontaneity.
authors.concerns: Love, marriage, and family obligation; the position and intelligence of women; reading, romances, and poetry; society and character; and the conduct of the inner life.
authors.significance: Osborne's Letters are a masterpiece of informal English prose and one of the most important documents by a seventeenth-century woman, valued for their literary quality and as a witness to women's intellectual life and to the early career of Temple.
authors.uncertainty: Only Osborne's side of the correspondence survives in full; her later life is documented mainly through Temple's papers, and the letters' publication was long delayed.

authors.name: Dorothy Richardson
authors.nationality: British; the first English stream-of-consciousness novel and the woman's life in sequence
authors.identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of Pilgrimage, the first sustained English novel of consciousness and the finest fictional record of the independent woman writer of the period.
authors.biography: Born Dorothy Miller Richardson in Abingdon on 17 May 1873; her family's finances collapsed with her father's bankruptcy, and she left school at seventeen to teach, working in a Hanover school and in a London office. Pointed Roofs (1915) began Pilgrimage, a sequence of thirteen novels that she published over twenty years and never completed; she was associated with the Freewomen and with the modernist little magazines, married the artist Alan Odle in 1917, and died at Beckenham on 17 June 1957.
authors.profile: Richardson is the inventor of the English stream-of-consciousness novel: Pointed Roofs preceded Ulysses by seven years and gave the technique its first sustained English use, and Pilgrimage is the fullest fictional record of a woman's consciousness making itself in the period. Her sequence is the great alternative to Joyce and Woolf, and her essays on the woman novelist are among the period's sharpest feminist criticism.
authors.style: The interior monologue uninterrupted by an explaining narrator; the present tense of perception; the sentence that records rather than describes; the refusal of plot in favour of the texture of experience; the recurring image that surfaces across volumes.
authors.concerns: The woman's consciousness and the woman's work; the school, the office and the lodging house; poverty and the class of the shabby-genteel; friendship between women; the artist's formation; London and the rented room.
authors.significance: Richardson wrote the first English stream-of-consciousness novel and the longest fictional record of a woman's inner life in the period: Pointed Roofs opened the way for Joyce and Woolf, Pilgrimage is a central modernist sequence, and her work is the foundation of the English novel of female consciousness.

authors.name: Douglas Hyde
authors.nationality: Irish; the founder of the Gaelic League and the playwright of the Irish-language Abbey drama
authors.identity: Scholar, playwright and founder of the Gaelic League; 'An Craoibhín Aoibhinn', the first President of Ireland.
authors.biography: Born Douglas James Hyde at Castlerea, County Roscommon, on 17 January 1860, the son of a Church of Ireland rector; he grew up among the Irish speakers of Frenchpark and founded the Gaelic League in 1893. His one-act plays in Irish - Casadh an tSugáin (The Twisting of the Rope, 1901), The Marriage, The Lost Saint - opened the Irish-language drama of the Abbey, and his Religious Songs of Connacht (1906) is the great collection of the Irish religious lyric. He was elected the first President of Ireland in 1938 and died in Dublin on 12 July 1949.
authors.profile: Douglas Hyde is the founder of the Gaelic League and the first playwright of the Irish-language theatre: The Twisting of the Rope, played at the Abbey in October 1901, was the first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage, and his collections of the songs and religious lyrics of Connacht made the Irish-speaking west the source of the literary revival. As first President of Ireland he carried the revival into the state.
authors.style: The spoken Irish of Connacht carried into English by the translation of Lady Gregory; the one-act play of the cottage and the road; the religious lyric and the charm collected from the mouth of the singer; the scholar's exactness in the collector's note; the gaiety of the Irish idiom in the comic exchange.
authors.concerns: The Irish language and the de-Anglicising of Ireland; the songs, prayers and charms of Connacht; the cottage play and the Abbey stage; the scholar as the collector of the living speech; the revival as the recovery of a language rather than of a politics.
authors.significance: Douglas Hyde is the founder of the Gaelic League and the first playwright of the Irish-language theatre: The Twisting of the Rope was the first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage, and his collections of the songs of Connacht made the Irish-speaking west the source of the literary revival.

authors.name: Douglas William Jerrold
authors.nationality: English; the Regency and Victorian stage and the comic journalism of the metropolis
authors.identity: Dramatist, journalist and humorist; the most popular writer of domestic melodrama of the later 1820s and a defining voice of the metropolis's comic press
authors.biography: He was born in London into a poor family, was apprenticed as a boy, ran to sea in his early youth, and then took to the stage as an actor in the minor theatres. He turned to writing for those theatres, and his nautical domestic drama of a sailor's sweetheart, played south of the water in 1829, became the most performed and most pirated piece of the decade, acted with alterations all over the country and in America. He then lived by journalism, and his sketches of married life from a bedpost and his contributions to the great comic weekly made him one of the most widely read prose humorists of the 1840s. He edited a cheap daily paper of wide circulation, quarrelled with the managers of the patent theatres and campaigned publicly against their monopoly of legitimate drama, and wrote plays, essays and stories for the periodicals until his later years. His miscellaneous comic prose was collected in several series, and his after-dinner wit was reported throughout the period. He died in 1866, leaving a son who continued his father's theatrical and journalistic work.
authors.profile: A long list of dramas, melodramas and farces for the minor and patent theatres, of which the nautical domestic drama is the surviving piece; the bedpost sketches and the other collected humorous prose; essays, tales and journalistic writing on the metropolis and its poor. His characteristic method is the sentimental domestic situation treated with a comic, speech-reporting economy, in which the jokes of character and the pathos of the situation are delivered by the same lines.
authors.style: A plain, point-driven comic prose built on the epigram and on reported cockney and maritime speech; in the drama, workmanlike dialogue, effective stage business and a song placed exactly where the pathos of the situation needs relief. His humour is domestic and verbal rather than satirical in the philosophical manner.
authors.concerns: The virtue and the exposure of the poor. The sailor's condition, the press-gang and domestic waiting. The monopoly of the licensed theatres and the interests of the unlicensed stage. Marriage, its drudgery and its comedy, seen from the bedroom and the public house.
authors.significance: He is the central figure of the great decade of penny melodrama and of the agitation over theatrical monopoly which led to the patents reform of the 1840s; his comic journalism defined the voice of the mid-century metropolitan weekly. His best-known drama remains the standard example of nautical melodrama in criticism and theatre history.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his boyhood at sea and of his first acting engagements are given inconsistently in the memoirs written after his death.

authors.name: e e cummings
authors.nationality: American; the typographic lyric and the satire of the modern state
authors.identity: Poet and painter; the great experimenter of American typography, whose lower-case, punctuation-scattered lyrics made the printed page part of the poem.
authors.biography: Born Edward Estlin Cummings in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 14 October 1894, the son of a Harvard professor and minister; he took his degrees at Harvard, served in the First World War as an ambulance driver, was interned by the French in 1917 for three months — the subject of The Enormous Room (1922) — and published Tulips and Chimneys (1923), & (1925), XLI Poems (1925) and Is 5 (1926). He painted, travelled in the Soviet Union (Eimi, 1933), won the Bollingen Prize in 1958 and the National Book Award in 1960, and died in North Conway, New Hampshire, on 3 September 1962.
authors.profile: Cummings is the period's great typographic poet: he made the page itself a unit of composition — the word broken across the line, the parenthesis, the lowercase 'i', the space that carries the pause — and his love lyrics ('somewhere i have never travelled,gladly beyond', 'i carry your heart with me') are among the most popular American poems of the century. His satire of the state ('next to of course god america i', 'i sing of Olaf glad and big') is the sharpest political verse of the period.
authors.style: The typographic page as a compositional unit; the word broken and the parenthesis; the lowercase pronoun and the deliberate misspelling; the sonnet and the ballad re-shaped by spacing; the syntax that must be read aloud to be understood; the satire delivered in the voice of its victim.
authors.concerns: Love and the private erotic world; the individual against the state and the army; satire of patriotism and bureaucracy; spring, roses, the moon and the natural world; the city and the crowd; death and the fragility of the person.
authors.significance: Cummings is the most popular experimental poet in English of the century: he made typography a poetic instrument, wrote the most-quoted American love lyrics after Frost, and produced the sharpest anti-war satire of the period. His work changed how poems are printed.

authors.name: E. M. Forster
authors.nationality: British; the liberal novel of connection and the travel book of the East
authors.identity: Novelist, essayist and critic; the author of Howards End and A Passage to India, and the period's most exact liberal moralist.
authors.biography: Born Edward Morgan Forster in London on 1 January 1879, the son of an architect who died when he was a baby; he was raised by his mother and two aunts, read classics at King's College, Cambridge, where he joined the Apostles, and travelled in Italy and Greece. He published Where Angels Fear to Tread (1905), The Longest Journey (1907), A Room with a View (1908), Howards End (1910) and A Passage to India (1924), then wrote no more novels; he worked for the Red Cross in Egypt, broadcast on the BBC and became a Fellow of King's. He died at Coventry on 7 June 1970; Maurice, written in 1913–14, was published posthumously in 1971.
authors.profile: Forster is the great liberal novelist of the period: his five novels test the claims of the private life against the demands of class, empire and nation, and his famous imperative 'only connect' is the period's most quoted moral programme. Howards End is the definitive Edwardian condition-of-England novel and A Passage to India the greatest English novel about the empire; Aspects of the Novel (1927) is one of the century's most influential books of criticism.
authors.style: The plain, flexible, slightly ironic prose with the sudden lyric intensification; the symbolic motif (the house, the caves, the music) held inside a realistic plot; the round and the flat character; the narrator's confidential address; the comedy of manners crossed with the moral fable.
authors.concerns: Connection and the failure to connect; class, culture and the 'undeveloped heart'; England as a place of houses and motor roads; the empire and the Englishman in India; Italy and the Mediterranean as a release; homosexuality and the double life; music and the inner life.
authors.significance: Forster is the period's central liberal novelist and one of its finest critics: Howards End and A Passage to India are permanent novels, 'only connect' became the period's watchword, and Aspects of the Novel taught two generations how to read fiction. His posthumously published Maurice made him a pioneer of English gay literature.

authors.name: E. M. W. Tillyard
authors.nationality: British; the scholar of the Elizabethan world picture and of Milton
authors.identity: Scholar; the author of The Elizabethan World Picture and The Miltonic Setting.
authors.biography: Born Edgar Merion Wilson Tillyard at Cambridge on 24 March 1889; he took his degrees at Cambridge and held the chair of English at Durham and then the readership at Cambridge. The Miltonic Setting (1938) and The Elizabethan World Picture (1943) made the doctrine of the order and of the correspondence the common property of the readers of the period, and his Shakespeare's Last Plays (1938) and The Elizabethan World Picture fixed the terms of the study of the Renaissance imagination; he died at Newcastle on 12 December 1962.
authors.profile: E. M. W. Tillyard is the scholar who gave the twentieth century its account of the Elizabethan world picture: his books on the great chain of being, the correspondences and the order made the doctrine the common key to the reading of Shakespeare, Donne and Milton, and the famous debate with C. S. Lewis on the personal heresy fixed the method of the period study.
authors.style: The exposition of the doctrine in the plain ordered sentence; the diagram of the chain and the correspondence carried in the prose; the quotation from the schoolbooks and the sermons as the evidence of the common belief; the lecture manner of the scholar addressing the general reader.
authors.concerns: The great chain of being and the doctrine of order; the correspondences of the macrocosm and the microcosm; Milton and the Puritan imagination; the Elizabethan schoolbook and the common belief; the debate on the personal heresy in the reading of poetry.
authors.significance: E. M. W. Tillyard gave the twentieth century its account of the Elizabethan world picture: his books on the chain of being and the correspondences made the doctrine the common key to the reading of Shakespeare, Donne and Milton, and his Miltonic Setting remains the standard introduction to the Puritan imagination.

authors.name: E. W. Hornung
authors.nationality: British; the gentleman thief and the imperial adventure
authors.identity: Writer of fiction and verse; the creator of A. J. Raffles, the gentleman burglar, and the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle.
authors.biography: Born Ernest William Hornung at Middlesbrough on 7 June 1866; he was sent to Australia for his health in 1884 and returned to London in 1886, publishing Under Two Skies in 1892. The Amateur Cracksman (1899) introduced Raffles; The Shadow of the Rope (1902), Stingaree (1905) and The Crime Doctor (1914) followed. He married Constance Doyle in 1893, served in the First World War, and died at Saint-Jean-de-Luz, France, on 22 March 1921.
authors.profile: Hornung created A. J. Raffles, the first gentleman thief in English fiction and the direct ancestor of the modern heist story and the charming criminal, and he wrote the finest of the imperial adventure novels of the 1890s in The Shadow of the Rope. His work gave the detective story its mirror image and made the criminal into a hero of style.
authors.style: The first-person narrative by the admiring accomplice; the aristocratic criminal with a code of honour; the cricket match and the country house as settings for the crime; the epigrammatic dialogue of the club; the sudden violence under the surface of the gentleman's world.
authors.concerns: The gentleman and the criminal; the public school code and its corruption; the empire and the colonial return; money and the idle rich; loyalty between men.
authors.significance: E. W. Hornung created the first gentleman thief in English fiction and the ancestor of the modern heist story: Raffles gave the detective genre its mirror image, made the criminal into a hero of style, and opened the way for the moral ambiguity of the twentieth-century crime novel.

authors.name: Ebenezer Elliott
authors.nationality: British; the Corn Law rhymes and the poet of the poor
authors.identity: Iron-founder, poet and radical; the 'Corn Law Rhymer', the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era.
authors.biography: Born at Masbrough, near Rotherham, on 17 March 1781, the son of a radical iron-founder; he worked in the family ironworks, went bankrupt, and made his name with Corn Law Rhymes (1831). The Splendid Village (1833), The Ranter (1830) and his collected Poems followed. He died at Argyle Street, Hull, on 1 December 1849.
authors.profile: Ebenezer Elliott was the 'Corn Law Rhymer' and the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era: his Corn Law Rhymes gave the campaign for free trade its poetry, made him the best-known radical poet of the 1830s, and founded the tradition of the English political poem of the poor that Chartism inherited.
authors.style: The rhymed political attack on the landlords; the direct address and the refrain; the vivid image of the hungry poor; the hatred of the Corn Laws and the aristocracy; the plain, forcible, popular stanza.
authors.concerns: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; poverty and the price of bread; democracy and the Reform movement; the land and the landlord; the education of the poor.
authors.significance: Ebenezer Elliott was the 'Corn Law Rhymer' and the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era: his Corn Law Rhymes gave the campaign for free trade its poetry and founded the tradition of the English political poem of the poor.

authors.name: Edgar Allan Poe
authors.nationality: American; the Richmond, Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world, and the Southern and Mid-Atlantic review and magazine culture of the 1830s and 1840s
authors.identity: Poet, tale-writer, reviewer and editor; the most exacting and most combative American critic of his generation, the maker of the analytical and the tales of horror, and the poet of the pure musical lyric, who attempted to live wholly by the pen in a country that had not yet a paying market for it.
authors.biography: Poe was born Edgar Poe at Boston, the second of three children of travelling actors, and was left fatherless and motherless in early childhood: David Poe deserted the family, and his mother Elizabeth, an actress of Richmond, died there in 1811, after which he was taken into the household of John Allan, a wealthy Richmond tobacco merchant, from whom he took his middle name but who never adopted him. He went with the Allan family to England in 1815, was schooled in London and its neighbourhood, and returned to Richmond a boy formed on the Byron models and on the German tale then reaching America in translation. At the University of Virginia, which he entered in 1826 on Allan's terms, he contracted gambling debts that Allan refused to discharge; he broke with his foster father, removed to Boston, where his first slim volume of verse appeared without his name in 1827, served a short time in the United States army under an assumed name, and obtained through Allan's interest an appointment to the Military Academy at West Point, which he was deliberately dismissed from in the spring of 1831. Comes of age and without a fortune, he resolved to live by his pen, and the early 1830s found him contributing poems, tales and reviews to the annuals and magazines of the Southern and Middle States, with the collected volume of 1831, printed by subscription and prefaced by an attack upon the current American poets, as his profession of faith. He became editor of the Southern Literary Messenger at Richmond in 1835, and by his tales, his poems and his reviews made it the most widely circulated American monthly of its day; there followed the New York and Philadelphia years, employment on the magazines of those cities, and in 1840 the two-volume collection of his tales, which established the prose reputation that then carried him far beyond his verse. In 1836 he had married at Richmond his cousin Virginia Clemm, a child of thirteen, whose mother kept house with them; her long consumption and her death in 1847 left him, in his own account, without any tie. He edited a short-lived journal at New York in 1845, lectured on poetry and on the material universe, printed his prosimetrical cosmology in 1848, and projected a magazine of his own that was never funded. He was found in a state of insensibility at Baltimore in the first days of October 1849, on his way to remove to the city where his father's family lived, and died there on 7 October, aged forty; the circumstances of those last days have never been settled, and the friend who printed his works at length after him did so with a malicious preface which governed his reputation for a generation.
authors.profile: Within the range of this installment his work is the verse of three pamphlets and volumes - the first anonymous booklet, the longer poem of the star-island and the collected volume of 1831 with its short lyrics of classical beauty and its vision of the doomed city; afterwards came the tales, the poems of the later magazines, the criticism, the essay on the principle of composition and the prose of the cosmic argument. He wrote the analytical tale of ratiocination and the tale of nervous horror, the hoaxes and the marginal criticism of his own review work, and he projected, in his criticism of contemporary American books, the first serious American account of the poetical principle. His career as an editor is part of his work: the monthly, the annual, the magazine and the projected review are the forms in which he wrote.
authors.style: In verse an intense and deliberate music, with internal rhyme, refrain, repetition of key words and an incantatory regularity of stanza, a command of the short lyric of address and of the long meditative or narrative poem; in prose an analytical first person, a nervous precision of detail, an art of suspense and anticlimax, and a criticism of bludgeon irony - abrupt, technical, and personal in attack, with a habit of defining his own practice against that of the traffic in magazines.
authors.concerns: Beauty as the sole province of the poem, and its exaltation into the supernal; the death of a beautiful woman as the most poetical of topics; the unity of effect and the economy of means by which a work of art should be constructed; the reach and the limits of analysis and of the calculating intellect; the isolation of the imaginative individual in a commercial letterscape; the material unity of the universe and the theological consequences of drawing it together.
authors.significance: He invented the analytical or detective tale and practised before anyone in English the short tale of single psychological effect; his theory of the poem, of the unity of impression and of the music of verse, passed by his French interpreters into the symbolist movement and so into the modern poetry of Europe, and his criticism created the model of the professional American reviewer. His tales of horror and of analysis founded durable native genres, and his career, cut short by a struggle with the economics of American periodical writing, became the standard case of the unhoused artist in a commercial republic.
authors.uncertainty: The identity of the woman addressed in the lyrics of beauty, and the chronology of his engagement to Sarah Helen Whitman, are variously stated; the quarrel and money history with John Allan is known largely from the Allans' side and from Poe's own complaints; the causes of the insensibility in which he was found at Baltimore, and the company he kept in the two or three days before his death, remain unexplained, and the evidence is disputed between intemperance, bodily disorder and the political violence of the election week. The printed obituary and the first collected edition were prepared by a literary enemy, and many anecdotes of the early life rest on his own jesting and on later reminiscence.

authors.name: Edgar Wallace
authors.nationality: British; the thriller and the mass-market crime novel
authors.identity: Journalist, novelist and screenwriter; the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century.
authors.biography: Born Richard Horatio Edgar Wallace in Greenwich on 1 April 1875; he served in the army and as a war correspondent, and published The Four Just Men in 1905, followed by some 170 novels, including the Sanders of the River stories, The Ringer (1925) and The Door with Seven Locks (1926). He died in Hollywood on 10 February 1932.
authors.profile: Edgar Wallace was the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century: his some 170 novels created the modern thriller, the mass-market crime novel and the screen story, and his Four Just Men and The Ringer made him the founder of the British thriller industry.
authors.style: The rapid plot of pursuit and revelation; the grotesque villain and the comic detective; the colonial setting and the London underworld; the plain, breathless, serial prose; the twist in the last chapter.
authors.concerns: The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination.
authors.significance: Edgar Wallace was the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century: his some 170 novels created the modern thriller, the mass-market crime novel and the screen story, and his work made him the founder of the British thriller industry.

authors.name: Edith Nesbit
authors.nationality: English; the children's adventure story, the fantasy and the social tale
authors.identity: Writer and poet; the founder of the modern children's adventure story and one of the most influential children's writers in English.
authors.biography: Born Edith Bland in Kennington, London, on 15 August 1858; she was educated in boarding schools in England, France and Germany, and married Hubert Bland in 1880. She supported the family by writing, and with Bland was a founder of the Fabian Society in 1884. She published verse, novels and journalism for adults, and from 1899 a series of children's books that transformed the genre. After Bland's death she married Thomas Tucker in 1917 and died at New Romney, Kent, on 4 May 1924.
authors.profile: Nesbit wrote children as they are: quarrelsome, resourceful, greedy and brave, in families that are short of money and long on invention. Her great innovation was to put the magic in the middle of an ordinary suburban household and to let the children talk their way through it, and her time-travel and Psammead stories are the direct ancestors of the twentieth-century children's fantasy. She was also a socialist and a feminist whose adult fiction and verse are sharper than her reputation suggests.
authors.style: Conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader; comedy of family quarrels; magic treated as a practical problem; precise suburban interiors; rapid, episodic plotting.
authors.concerns: Childhood and the family; magic and the everyday; time travel and history; poverty and class; the position of women and girls; empire and the English abroad; the pleasures and dangers of wishes.
authors.significance: Nesbit invented the modern children's adventure story: The Story of the Treasure Seekers, Five Children and It and The Railway Children changed what children's fiction could be, and her influence on C. S. Lewis, Edward Eager and J. K. Rowling is direct and acknowledged.

authors.name: Edith Sitwell
authors.nationality: British; Façade, the modernist lyric and the Sitwell little magazines
authors.identity: Poet and critic; the editor of Wheels and the author of Façade, the most performed experiment of English verse.
authors.biography: Born Edith Louisa Sitwell at Scarborough on 7 September 1887, the eldest of the three poetic Sitwells; she edited the anthology Wheels against the Georgian anthologies and published The Mother and Other Poems (1915) and Clown's Houses (1916). Façade, the settings of her poems to William Walton's music, was first performed in 1923; Gold Coast Customs (1929) and Street Songs (1942), with 'Still Falls the Rain', mark her later, darker manner. She died in London on 9 December 1964.
authors.profile: Edith Sitwell is the central woman poet of English modernism before 1945: Façade made the sound of the poem its subject and remains the most performed experiment in English verse, the early lyrics gave the imagist and vorticist little magazines their most accomplished English contributor, and Street Songs carried the war elegy into the modernist idiom. Her criticism and her quarrels shaped the reception of the new poetry.
authors.style: The poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line; the baroque image of the harlequin, the sun and the clown; the later deepening into the elegiac and the religious; the prose of the critic, combative and exact; the reading voice as part of the instrument.
authors.concerns: Sound and the autonomy of the poem; the mask, the clown and the harlequinade; the family and the wound of the childhood; the war elegy and the crucifixion; the quarrel with the Georgian anthologists and with the reviewers; aristocracy and the artist.
authors.significance: Edith Sitwell is the central woman poet of English modernism before 1945: Façade made the sound of the poem its subject, the early lyrics gave the little magazines their most accomplished English voice, and Street Songs carried the war elegy into the modernist idiom.

authors.name: Edith Wharton
authors.nationality: American; the novel of manners, the social satire and the ghost story
authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and designer; the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the finest American novelist of manners.
authors.biography: Born Edith Newbold Jones in New York on 24 January 1862 into a family of the old Knickerbocker aristocracy; she was educated privately and in Europe, married Edward Wharton in 1885, and published The Decoration of Houses with Ogden Codman in 1897. The House of Mirth (1905) made her famous; she lived in Paris from 1907, divorced in 1913, and was decorated for her relief work in the First World War. She won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921 for The Age of Innocence and died at Saint-Brice-sous-Forêt, France, on 11 August 1937.
authors.profile: Wharton wrote the American novel of manners with a European severity: her subject is the New York aristocracy and the individual trapped by its codes, and her method is the ironic, beautifully built narrative in which the social surface is described with absolute precision and the moral cost is allowed to emerge without comment. She was also a superb writer of ghost stories and a serious critic of American culture, and no one has written better about the small cruelty of a society that has no visible power except opinion.
authors.style: Precise, ironic exposition of a social world; the withheld judgement; symbolic architecture and interiors; the tragic or near-tragic ending that the social code makes inevitable; dialogue that carries the pressure of what cannot be said; the elegant chapter ending.
authors.concerns: The New York aristocracy and its codes; marriage, divorce and the marriage market; money and the new rich against the old; the American and Europe; the woman of intelligence in a society that has no use for it; the ghost and the supernatural.
authors.significance: Wharton is the finest American novelist of manners and the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction: The Age of Innocence, The House of Mirth and The Custom of the Country are permanent classics, her ghost stories are among the best in the language, and her portrait of old New York is the essential record of the American upper class.

authors.name: Edmund Blunden
authors.nationality: British; the war memoir of the English countryside and the pastoral elegy
authors.identity: Poet, critic and memoirist; the author of Undertones of War, the most lyrical prose memoir of the First World War, and a great scholar of the English rural tradition.
authors.biography: Born Edmund Charles Blunden at Yalding, Kent, on 1 November 1896, the son of a schoolmaster; he went from Christ's Hospital to Queen's College, Oxford, but enlisted in 1915 and served on the Somme and at Ypres, winning the Military Cross. After the war he worked as a literary journalist in London and Tokyo, edited Leigh Hunt and John Clare, taught at Oxford (1931–43) and in Hong Kong (1953–64), and was professor of poetry at Oxford (1966–68). He died at Long Melford, Suffolk, on 20 January 1974.
authors.profile: Blunden wrote the most beautiful prose memoir of the war: Undertones of War (1928) records the Western Front through the eyes of a country poet, without protest and without rhetoric, and it stands with Blunden's own poems as the finest pastoral writing about the war. His scholarship on Clare, Hunt and the rural poets made him the period's great custodian of the English countryside tradition, and his poems are the best English rural verse between Thomas and Larkin.
authors.style: The pastoral lyric in traditional measure; the exact naming of plants, streams and villages; the prose that moves as a walk moves, with a poet's eye for weather; the elegy that consoles by remembering; the understatement that refuses protest.
authors.concerns: The English countryside and the Kentish and Suffolk landscape; the war remembered as an intrusion on the rural world; the passing of the agricultural labourer's England; cricket, the village and the seasons; friendship and the dead of the war.
authors.significance: Blunden wrote the finest lyrical memoir of the First World War and was the period's great poet-scholar of the English countryside: Undertones of War is the pastoral counterpart to Good-bye to All That, his edition of Clare recovered a major poet, and his own verse is the best English rural poetry between Edward Thomas and Philip Larkin.

authors.name: Edmund Burke
authors.nationality: Irish-born British; Anglo-Irish, and the Whig parliamentary oratory and the political and aesthetic prose of the later eighteenth century
authors.identity: Statesman, political writer and philosophical critic of the passions; the Rockingham Whig parliamentarian and manager of the Hastings impeachment, whose Reflections on the Revolution in France became the classic English argument against the French Revolution, and whose Enquiry of 1757 supplied the period's standard analysis of the sublime and the beautiful.
authors.biography: Burke was born in Dublin in 1729, the son of a solicitor who conformed to the church of Ireland and of Mary Nagle of a Cork Catholic family; brought up in his father's communion but kept on friendly terms with his Catholic kindred, he entered Trinity College Dublin, and removed to London and the Middle Temple about 1750, where he abandoned the law for letters. His first books made his name: A Vindication of Natural Society (1756), a sceptical exposure of civil government which many readers mistook for a grave attack on revelation, and the Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757). Through the publisher Robert Dodsley he founded the Annual Register and wrote its historical and critical survey of Europe for many years. He entered the Commons in 1761 as member for Wendover, was private secretary to Rockingham in the administration of 1765-66, and in the Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770) turned party connexion into a doctrine of organised principled opposition. Member for Bristol from 1774, he argued in his address of that year and in the Speech on Conciliation with America of 1775 that a representative owes his unbiased judgement to his constituents, not his obedience. He bought the estate of Gregories near Beaconsfield in 1768 and lived thereafter in permanent tension between country propriety and heavy borrowing. Paymaster of the Forces in the Rockingham ministry of 1782, he became the manager of the impeachment of Warren Hastings, which he opened in Westminster Hall in 1788 and which filled the rest of his public life. The French Revolution broke his long alliance with Charles James Fox; the Reflections on the Revolution in France of November 1790, the Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs of 1791 and the Letters on a Regicide Peace of 1795-97 made him the most read and most attacked political writer of the war years. He retired from the Commons in 1794 and died at Beaconsfield in 1797, buried at Gerrards Cross. The death of his only son Richard in 1794 darkened his last years, and unfinished pieces on the revolution and on Shakespeare were published after his death.
authors.profile: His writings form three connected bodies: the early philosophical treatise, the parliamentary speech and printed letter, and the great state paper of the impeachment. The Philosophical Enquiry states a theory of the sublime and the beautiful as passions rooted in self-preservation and in society, and its divisions on the passions, on the sublime, on the beautiful and on the effect of general and obscure notions became the received framework of aesthetic discussion in the 1790s. The Annual Register's annual historical and critical articles made it the standard English chronicle of European affairs for two generations. The Reflections is a letter of remonstrance and prophecy that mixes constitutional argument with the elevated lament; the speeches on America and on the conduct of the East India manager are oratory revised into printed state papers; the Letters on a Regicide Peace argue publicly and at great length against a settlement with revolutionary France.
authors.style: A prose of sustained periodic sentence in which abstraction is embodied in image and in moral feeling, and argument advances by concession, by historical instance and by the accumulating weight of clause upon clause. He can be plainly businesslike in a minute or a resolution, ironical in definition, and torrential in the rhetorical burst, of which the passage on the queen of France in the Reflections is the most quoted and most imitated specimen in English. The characteristic movement is nevertheless the long qualification and the appeal to prescriptive usage, the concrete enumeration of institutions and orders. In the treatise the manner is analytic and deliberately dry; in the speeches judicial and cumulative; in the late pamphlets urgent, and occasionally uneven with anger.
authors.concerns: Liberty as an inherited and prescriptive estate rather than an abstract speculable right; the moral limits of empire and the duties and accountability of power; party, connexion and principled opposition as the conditions of constitutional freedom; the dangers of an armed metaphysics and of geometric abstraction in politics; the civilising uses of prejudice, of religious establishment and of the learned and gentle orders; the passions of the sublime and of beauty, and the effect of obscurity and sympathy; the prudence and historical consequence that should govern imperial and foreign policy.
authors.significance: The Reflections created the durable language of modern political conservatism and supplied the founding text of the anti-Jacobin answer to 1789, at which Paine's Rights of Man and Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Men were aimed; the Enquiry fixed the terms of the debate on the sublime for two generations of artists and writers. His speeches and letters are the central English documents on the American and Indian questions, and his management of the impeachment established the doctrine of public accountability in colonial government. His account of party and of the independence of the representative remains the standard statement of eighteenth-century Whig parliamentary practice.
authors.uncertainty: His Dublin birthplace is not in question, though the street of his birth is variously identified and the day is usually given as 12 January 1729. The day of his death is reported now as the ninth and now as the end of July 1797 in different calendars, and his house is described sometimes at Beaconsfield and sometimes at Gregories in that parish. His matriculation and degree at Trinity College Dublin, the chronology of his removal to London and of his keeping in the Temple are set down with small variations in the biographies. The extent of his share in the earliest volumes of the Annual Register, and the responsibility for the anonymously printed pieces of the 1750s, remain matters of bibliographical inference rather than of documented fact.

authors.name: Edmund Gosse
authors.nationality: English; literary history, biography and the memoir
authors.identity: Poet, critic and biographer; the author of Father and Son, one of the greatest Victorian autobiographies, and the first English historian of modern literature.
authors.biography: Born in London on 21 September 1849, the son of Philip Henry Gosse, the naturalist and Plymouth Brother; he was brought up in a strict Evangelical household and left it in 1867, an experience recorded in Father and Son (1907). He worked in the Department of Printed Books at the British Museum, became a prolific reviewer and translator, and was Clark Lecturer at Cambridge (1889-1901) and librarian of the House of Lords (1904-14). He did more than any other critic to introduce Ibsen and the Scandinavians to England, and he was knighted in 1925, dying in London on 16 May 1928.
authors.profile: Gosse's Father and Son is the classic Victorian memoir of a religious upbringing: it is a study of a father's faith and a son's escape, written with a novelist's sense of scene and a scientist's precision. His critical writing — A History of Eighteenth Century Literature, the lives of Donne, Congreve, Ibsen and Swinburne — made him the great Victorianiser and publicist of the modern, and he was the first English critic to take Ibsen seriously.
authors.style: The scene-based memoir; ironic comedy of two incompatible minds; exact period detail; the critical survey with a clear narrative line; the biographical essay; translation from the Scandinavian and the French.
authors.concerns: Religious upbringing and the loss of faith; the conflict of generations; the history of English literature as a national narrative; the introduction of modern drama; biography as literary gossip and as scholarship; the Victorian literary world and its networks.
authors.significance: Gosse's Father and Son is one of the founding texts of the modern autobiography and the finest account we have of Victorian Evangelical family life; his critical histories and his promotion of Ibsen made him a central agent in the making of the modern English literary canon.

authors.name: Edmund Spenser
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet; colonial administrator in Ireland; the self-fashioned 'new poet' of the English Renaissance and its greatest non-dramatic poet.
authors.biography: Born in London c. 1552, the son of a journeyman clothmaker; educated at Merchant Taylors' School under Richard Mulcaster and at Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (BA 1573, MA 1576), where he associated with Gabriel Harvey. He entered the household of the Earl of Leicester, met Sidney and Dyer in the 'Areopagus' circle, and published The Shepheardes Calender (1579) to immediate fame. In 1580 he went to Ireland as secretary to Lord Grey de Wilton and spent most of his remaining life there as a planter and official (Kilcolman Castle, Co. Cork), publishing The Faerie Queene (1590, 1596), Complaints (1591), Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), Amoretti and Epithalamion (1595), and Prothalamion (1596). In 1598 Kilcolman was burned in Tyrone's rebellion; Spenser fled to London and died there on 13 January 1599, and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer.
authors.profile: The laureate of Elizabethan England, whose career was a deliberate imitation of Virgil's — from pastoral to epic — in the service of Protestant nationhood; he made the English language the vehicle of a full-scale national epic and a new poetic idiom (the Spenserian stanza).
authors.style: Archaizing diction ('the antique rolles'), the nine-line Spenserian stanza, elaborate allegory, musical fluency, and the fusion of Italian romance (Ariosto, Tasso), classical epic, and native English tradition (Chaucer, Langland).
authors.concerns: Protestant nationalism and the reform of the church; virtue and courtesy as the disciplines of the self; Ireland and the ethics of colonization; mutability, time, and the poet's immortal fame; love and marriage as sacramental.
authors.significance: The greatest non-dramatic poet of the English Renaissance: The Faerie Queene created the English national epic and shaped the language's poetic tradition from Milton to Keats ('the poet's poet'), while Amoretti and Epithalamion founded the English marriage poem.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth rests on the sonnet 'Amoretti' 60's allusion and the records of his schooling; the exact circumstances of his final flight from Ireland and his poverty at death are reported by Ben Jonson and William Camden.

authors.name: Edmund Waller
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Court poet and politician, credited with perfecting the smooth closed heroic couplet and the Cavalier lyric; a long-lived figure whose verse was admired for its polish, melody, and gallantry from Charles I's court to the Restoration.
authors.biography: Born 3 March 1606 at Coleshill, educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge. He entered Parliament and court society, celebrated Sacharissa (Lady Dorothy Sidney) in his lyrics, and was implicated in 'Waller's Plot' (1643) to secure London for the king, for which he was fined and banished. He returned under the Commonwealth, was elected to Parliament, and served through the Restoration with continued favour, revising his poems across a long career. He died 21 October 1687 at Beaconsfield.
authors.profile: The courtly lyricist whose 'smooth' verse and closed couplets became the model of elegant Restoration poetry; Dryden credited him with beginning 'the excellence of numbers' in English.
authors.style: Melodious, polished, and balanced verse; the closed heroic couplet; gallant compliment and Petrarchan conceit refined to ease; panegyric and occasional poetry of public grace.
authors.concerns: Love and courtly compliment; royalist loyalty; the praise of patrons and the nation; the value of poetic polish and decorum; and, in later poems, time and old age.
authors.significance: Waller's technical refinement of the couplet directly shaped Denham, Dryden, and the whole Augustan line; though his reputation declined after the seventeenth century, he was the acknowledged father of smooth Restoration verse.
authors.uncertainty: Waller's life is well recorded; the dating of individual lyrics and the identity of 'Sacharissa' are established, though many poems circulated in manuscript before print.

authors.biography: Born in Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts, on 26 March 1850; he studied law, turned to journalism, and published Six to One (1878), Dr Heidenhoff's Process (1880) and Miss Ludington's Sister (1884) before Looking Backward (1888) made him famous. authors.style: The sleeper-awakes frame; the guided tour of the future society; the documentary exposition of the new economy; the romance that crosses the centuries; the plain, expository, persuasive prose of the reformer.

authors.name: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
authors.nationality: English; the silver-fork novel, the historical romance and the domestic drama
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and politician; the most popular and most versatile English writer of the 1830s-40s, and the inventor of the 'silver-fork' fashion novel.
authors.biography: Born Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer at London on 25 May 1803, the son of a general; he published Falkland in 1828 and Pelham in 1828, made his name as a dandy novelist, sat in Parliament from 1831 and became a baronet in 1838, taking the name Bulwer-Lytton. He wrote historical romances (The Last Days of Pompeii, 1834; Rienzi, 1835; Harold, 1848), the occult romance Zanoni (1842), and the domestic drama The Lady of Lyons (1838), and served as Secretary for the Colonies in 1858-59. He died at Torquay on 18 January 1873.
authors.profile: Bulwer-Lytton was the dominant popular novelist of the 1830s: he invented the 'silver-fork' novel of fashionable life in Pelham, established the English historical romance of classical antiquity in The Last Days of Pompeii, founded the occult romance in Zanoni, and wrote the theatre's most durable domestic drama. He was the first English novelist to unite society comedy, historical scholarship, the criminal underworld and the occult in a single prolific career, and Dickens called him the most popular writer of the age.
authors.style: Fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue; the detailed description of dress, furniture and fashionable interiors; the historical set piece reconstructed from antiquarian reading; the sensational plot with a criminal secret; the rhetorical blank-verse declamation of the stage.
authors.concerns: Fashionable society and the pursuit of distinction; ambition, crime and the criminal underworld; the ancient world and its destruction; the occult and the will; politics and the reform of society; the artist and the adventurer.
authors.significance: Bulwer-Lytton is the missing link between Scott and Dickens: he created the fashionable novel, the classical historical romance and the occult novel, he wrote The Lady of Lyons, one of the most performed Victorian plays, and his influence on Dickens, Disraeli, Collins and the sensation novelists is direct. He is also, through the annual Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest, the most mocked novelist in English — a reputation that has obscured a genuinely inventive career.
