authors.name: Edward FitzGerald
authors.nationality: English; Victorian poetry and translation
authors.identity: Poet and translator; the author of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám and the greatest English translator of Persian verse.
authors.biography: Born at Bredfield on 31 March 1809 into an old Suffolk family of Irish descent; educated at Bury St Edmunds and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he met Thackeray and, through him, Tennyson, whose friend and correspondent he remained. He published Euphranor (1851), a dialogue on education, and Polonius (1852), a collection of aphorisms; he learned Spanish and translated Calderón, and in 1859 published the Rubáiyát anonymously in a paper wrapper, priced at one shilling. It was ignored until Rossetti and his circle found it in 1861; FitzGerald then revised it, and the fourth edition of 1879 made it famous. He translated the Agamemnon of Aeschylus (1865) and the Oedipus Tyrannus (1881) and lived the life of a solitary country reader and sailor, dying at Merton, Norfolk, on 14 June 1883.
authors.profile: The Rubáiyát is a free translation and rearrangement of the Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyám into English stanzas; FitzGerald made it a poem of Victorian melancholy — the potter, the sultan, the veiled figure, the wine, the 'Book of Verses underneath the Bough' — in which the pleasures of the present are the answer to a world without a future. His verse is quiet, exact and resigned, and his translations from the Greek are among the boldest and most successful of the century in rendering the feel of the original. The letters are the finest in Victorian English after those of Keats and Lamb.
authors.style: The Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain); a plain syntax and a complete absence of ornament; the personification of the potter, the pot and the cup; the refrain and the variation; a tone of amused resignation.
authors.concerns: The uncertainty of life and the brevity of pleasure; the mystery of creation and the futility of speculation; the potter and the clay as emblems of the soul; death, dust and resurrection; wine, love and the 'paradise enow' of the present.
authors.significance: The Rubáiyát is the most popular English poem of the later nineteenth century and the origin of the vogue for Persian literature in English; its philosophy of 'a jug of wine, a loaf of bread' shaped the aesthetic and the melancholy of the 1890s, and its stanzas were among the most quoted lines in the English-speaking world. FitzGerald's translations of Aeschylus are still read, and his letters are a permanent record of the Victorian circle of Tennyson and Thackeray.
authors.uncertainty: The Rubáiyát is a creative adaptation rather than a literal translation: FitzGerald reversed the order of the quatrains, invented some stanzas, and built a continuous poem out of material scattered in Omar's Persian. The fifth edition (1889) is the text usually reprinted.

authors.name: Edward Gibbon
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Historian of the decline and fall of the Roman Empire, whose six volumes (1776-1788) made the fate of ancient civilisation and of Christianity the central narrative of the age.
authors.biography: Born at Putney in 1737, a delicate child largely left to his own reading, he went up to Oxford in 1752, was converted to Rome there and was removed from the university, and spent several formative years at Lausanne under a Calvinist pastor. He returned to Protestantism, read widely in French and Latin, and served in the Hampshire militia during the Seven Years' War without seeing action. In 1764 he reached Rome, and among the ruins of the Capitoline resolved to write the history of its decline. The first volume of the Decline and Fall appeared in 1776, the second and third in 1781 and the last three in 1788; between them he sat in Parliament, took office at the board of trade, and endured a hostile controversy over his fifteenth and sixteenth chapters, which he answered in 1779. He fell with the North ministry in 1782, settled for years at Lausanne with his friend Deyverdun, and completed his history there before returning to London, where he died in January 1794.
authors.profile: A philosophic historian who explained empires by manners, superstition and circumstance, and whose irony gave religious narrative the poise of an autumn evening.
authors.style: A grand periodic style of balanced clauses and weighted antithesis; sustained irony that never declares itself; narrative panache in collapse and battle; a footnotes apparatus of learning used as concealed argument.
authors.concerns: The causes of the fall of the western empire; the relation of Christianity to the decline of civic and military virtue; superstition, enthusiasm and ecclesiastical history; national character, barbarism and the progress of society.
authors.significance: The Decline and Fall set the modern standard of source-based secular history and remains the model of historical narrative in English; its account of the triumph of the church has been argued over ever since.

authors.name: Edward Hall

authors.biography: Born in London about 1497; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and at Gray's Inn. A lawyer and MP, he compiled his great chronicle of the Wars of the Roses, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York, which Richard Grafton printed in 1548, the year after Hall's death.
authors.profile: Author of the chronicle that made the Tudor interpretation of history — the Wars of the Roses as God's judgement on rebellion, culminating in the providential union under the Tudors — the official story of England. Shakespeare drew the material of his English history plays, often nearly phrase by phrase, from Hall's Union through Holinshed.
authors.style: Ample, oratorical prose; set speeches composed for the great men of the action; the providential scheme applied to the narrative of faction and battle.
authors.concerns: The horror of civil war; the legitimacy and providence of the Tudor dynasty; history as the school of princes.
authors.significance: The principal historiographical source of Shakespeare's histories and of the Elizabethan understanding of the fifteenth century; his set speeches shaped the English historical imagination.

authors.name: Edward Jenner
authors.nationality: English; the provincial medical and scientific writing of the Gloucestershire country practitioners, and the empirical pamphlet literature of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries
authors.identity: Country physician and naturalist, and the founder of vaccination; a writer of short, plain, evidence-driven medical pamphlets whose Inquiry of 1798 is one of the most consequential scientific books in English, and whose published work sits beside a large unpublished record of observation on birds, geology and the natural history of the Severn vale.
authors.biography: Jenner was born at Berkeley in Gloucestershire on 17 May 1749, the son of the vicar of Berkeley, the Rev. Stephen Jenner, and lost his parents while still a child. He was put out at about thirteen to a neighbouring surgeon-apothecary at Sodbury, and served his apprenticeship in that practice before removing to London, where he lodged and studied, attended the lectures and the house practice at St George's Hospital, and worked under John Hunter, whose experimental method he adopted. Admitted a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1773, he returned to Berkeley and settled there in practice, in a country partnership which gave him the range of cases, and the leisured observation, on which his later work was built; he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1788. His inquiry into the cowpox of the Gloucestershire dairies grew out of the common belief of the dairy women, that infection with the cow's distemper protected against smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he inoculated with cowpox matter taken from the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid, James Phipps, the young son of his gardener, and afterwards tested the boy's immunity by variolous matter. The results were published in London in 1798 in a small self-printed volume, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, a Disease Discovered in Some of the Western Counties of England, Particularly Gloucestershire, and Known by the Name of the Cow Pox, which established the practice of vaccination and gave it its name. The book was attacked, ridiculed and answered in pamphlets, and was also adopted rapidly on the Continent and in the Americas; Jenner continued to publish the progress of the new practice, supplied vaccine matter gratuitously to inquirers and correspondents, and prosecuted his observations on the migration and habits of the swallow and on other natural-history questions. His wife Catherine died in 1815; his own health failed after a mild stroke in 1822, and he died at Berkeley on 26 January 1823, buried in the church there. The practice he founded became the basis of immunology and of the public vaccination programmes of the century.
authors.profile: His published medical writing is short, practical and cumulative rather than systematic: the Inquiry of 1798, a plain statement of cases arranged as evidence, with the history of the cow-pox, the account of the experiments on Phipps and on other persons, and the anatomical and clinical description of the vesicle; the Continuation of Facts and Observations relative to the Variolae Vaccinae of 1800; and The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation of 1801, a summary of the case against variolation. To these belong his introductory letters to correspondents, his papers to the Royal Society, and his observations on the natural history of the rook and the swallow, published separately and in the philosophical transactions of the day. He wrote also an account of his own inoculations and a pamphlet of popular instruction, and left the manuscripts and notebooks of a lifelong naturalist.
authors.style: A spare, unornamented and avowedly diffident prose of case, date and outcome, in which the claim is carried by the enumeration of instances and by the repetition of the same experiment on different persons, with a deliberate refusal of theory. He writes plainly and even homely, names his informants and their parishes, dates each case, and reserves his judgement to the shortest possible conclusion; the polemic against his opponents, when it appears, is cool, factual and occasionally wry. His natural-history writing shares the same habits of close observation of particular creatures in a particular country.
authors.concerns: The relation of cattle disease to human infection, and the specific protection given by one disease against another; the trial of an hypothesis by a single designed experiment and its repetition; the immunity produced by cow-pox and its duration; the comparison of vaccination with the dangerous practice of inserting smallpox matter; the safety and public diffusion of a cheap remedy; the honest reporting of failed and anomalous cases; the natural history, habits and migration of the birds and animals of the Gloucestershire vale.
authors.significance: The Inquiry of 1798 founded vaccination and gave preventive medicine its first rational procedure; within a few years the practice spread through Europe and the Americas, was adopted by governments and public institutions, and displaced the older variolation, preparing the way for the eradication of smallpox announced in the twentieth century. His method, an hypothesis tested by inoculation and by subsequent challenge with the dangerous matter, became a model of experimental medicine, and the derivation of that method from John Hunter's practice is the best-known instance in English of the country physician changing the practice of a whole society. He is also a figure of literary history, since the controversy over vaccination filled the pamphlet and cartoon literature of the Regency years.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his apprenticeship and of the Sodbury years, and the chronology of his London study with Hunter at St George's, are given with small variations in the memoirs, which depend heavily on his own notebooks and on the family Life written by his early biographer John Baron. The order of the first cowpox experiments is sometimes told so as to make the 1796 Phipps case the sole decisive instance, whereas his earlier local observations and the trial on his own children are variously dated; and the exact priority of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes's infection, and of the accounts of farmers and physicians who had practised something like vaccination before him, remains disputed. The day of his death is given as 26 January 1823.

authors.name: Edward Lear
authors.nationality: English; nonsense verse, the limerick and the landscape traveller
authors.identity: Poet, painter and illustrator; the inventor of the modern nonsense poem and the greatest English writer for children after Carroll.
authors.biography: Born in Highgate, London, on 12 May 1812, the twentieth child of a stockbroker; he was raised by his elder sister Ann and earned his living from the age of fifteen as an ornithological draughtsman, drawing the parrots for the Zoological Society. He published A Book of Nonsense in 1846 for the grandchildren of his patron the Earl of Derby, and spent the rest of his life travelling in Italy, Greece, Egypt and India, publishing illustrated journals of his journeys. He suffered from epilepsy and from loneliness all his life and died at San Remo on 29 January 1888.
authors.profile: Lear invented the modern nonsense poem: his limericks, his 'Nonsense Botany' and 'Nonsense Alphabets', and above all The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, create a world of pure verbal play in which melancholy and absurdity are inseparable. He was also a superb landscape painter and travel writer, and his nonsense is the other side of Victorian earnestness — a private, melancholy man making a world of impossible creatures who are nonetheless entirely at home in it.
authors.style: Closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity; invented words and impossible creatures; the perfect rhythmic and rhyming control of nonsense; the comic drawing integrated with the text; the melancholy undertow beneath the play; the topographical journal with comic illustrations.
authors.concerns: Nonsense, play and the liberation of language; travel, exile and the loneliness of the wanderer; childhood and the freedom of the imagination; the absurdity of social forms; landscape and the picturesque; melancholy and the consolations of art.
authors.significance: Lear is the founder of the modern nonsense tradition and one of the most beloved poets in English: his limericks established a form, The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies are among the most quoted poems in the language, and his nonsense gave twentieth-century poetry and children's literature their model of verbal freedom.

authors.name: Edward Moore
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English dramatist, poet, and periodical essayist, editor of the essay series The World and a writer of fables and plays.
authors.biography: Born on 22 March 1712 at Abingdon in Berkshire, the son of a Dissenting minister, he was educated at a Dissenting academy and turned to literary work in London. He wrote poems, including Fables for the Female Sex (1744), and stage works such as the tragedy The Trial of Selim the Persian (1748) and the adaptation Gil Blas (1751). He was editor of the periodical essay series The World (1753-56). He died on 1 March 1757.
authors.profile: A miscellaneous writer of the mid-century who moved between the stage, the periodical essay, and verse, best remembered as a compiler-editor of one of the more successful periodical collections of his decade.

authors.significance: A representative figure of mid-eighteenth-century periodical and theatrical writing, whose editorship of The World situates him within the age of the essay series that flourished after the Spectator.

authors.name: Edward Thomas
authors.nationality: British; the English rural lyric and the poetry of the threshold of war
authors.identity: Poet and essayist; the finest English nature poet of the century, who wrote almost all his poems in the last three years of his life and was killed at Arras.
authors.biography: Born Philip Edward Thomas in Lambeth on 3 March 1878 to a Welsh father and an English mother; he read history at Oxford, married Helen Noble in 1899, and spent fifteen years as a prolific hack writer of reviews, country books and biographies — The Woodland Life (1897), The South Country (1909), Wales (1905) — in chronic depression and poverty. Encouraged by Robert Frost, whom he met in 1913, he began writing poems in December 1914; he enlisted in 1915, went to France in 1917, and was killed by a shell at Arras on 9 April 1917.
authors.profile: Thomas wrote the greatest English poems of the First World War that are not about the war: in three years he produced some 140 poems of the English countryside, of the road, the hedge, the bird and the passing of a way of life, in a quiet, unemphatic, perfectly weighted verse. His war poems — 'Rain', 'Lights Out', 'The Trumpet' — are among the finest in the language, and his prose is the foundation of the English nature essay of the century.
authors.style: The plain, quiet, unrhymed or loosely rhymed line; the conversation held in the poem; the exact naming of plants, birds and places; the melancholy that never becomes rhetoric; the ending that simply stops; the prose of the country walk.
authors.concerns: England and the English countryside; the vanishing rural world and the coming of the road; solitude, depression and the burden of work; war, the soldier and the sense of doom; birds, weather and the seasons; the marriage and the unlived life.
authors.significance: Thomas is the finest English nature poet of the century and one of the great war poets: his 140 poems, written in three years, are among the permanent achievements of English verse, his prose founded the modern nature essay, and his death at Arras made him the period's symbol of the writer destroyed by the war he had enlisted to escape his own despair.

authors.name: Edward Young
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and essayist, Regius Professor of Civil Law at Oxford, whose meditative Night Thoughts and critical Conjectures made him a precursor of Romantic sensibility.
authors.biography: Young was born in Hampshire, educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and became a fellow, later holding the Regius Professorship of Civil Law. His early verse included a poem on Parliament, and he wrote occasional and festival verse before settling into his characteristic meditative mode. After years of relative quiet he published The Complainture, or Night Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality (1742-1745), which made his name through its meditations on grief after family bereavements. Later nine additional nights followed, together with plays and the prose critical treatise Conjectures on Original Composition (1759). In his last years he was tied to the Welwyn living through family connections. He died at Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1765.
authors.profile: A poet of melancholy, death, and immortality in blank verse, and a critic of genius and originality; his grave meditation and his theory of the creative self mark him as a bridge to Romanticism.
authors.style: Tumid, exclamatory blank verse of the night and the grave; rhetorical question, antithesis, and point; an introspective, brooding persona; and a taste for the sublime and the morbid.
authors.concerns: Death, grief, and the proof of immortality; the vanity of worldly ambition; the nature of poetic genius and originality; the self in solitude; and religious consolation against despair.
authors.significance: Night Thoughts dominated the graveyard and melancholy vogue of later eighteenth-century poetry, and his Conjectures shaped the Romantic cult of original genius and influenced writers abroad.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, commonly given as 1683 but sometimes earlier; the precise chronology of his Oxford preferment and family tragedies rests partly on his own partly fictionalised accounts.

authors.name: Edwin Arlington Robinson
authors.nationality: American; the dramatic lyric, the New England character poem and the modern narrative
authors.identity: Poet; the founder of modern American poetry in traditional forms, and the first American poet to make a whole town the subject of his art.
authors.biography: Born Edwin Arlington Robinson at Head Tide, Maine, on 22 December 1869 and raised in Gardiner, Maine; he studied at Harvard for two years, worked in New York in poverty, and published The Torrent and the Night Before (1896) and The Children of the Night (1897) at his own expense. Theodore Roosevelt gave him a government post in 1905; he won the Pulitzer Prize three times (1922, 1925, 1928) and died in New York on 6 April 1935.
authors.profile: Robinson wrote the modern American poetry of character: his Tilbury Town poems — portraits of failures, misers, drunkards and quiet desperate lives — are the first great American poems of the small town seen without sentiment, and his long narratives of Arthurian and modern life made him the finest American narrative poet of his age. He kept the traditional forms while the modernists broke them, and his plain, ironic style made him the bridge between Victorian and modern American poetry.
authors.style: The plain, colloquial line in traditional metre; the dramatic monologue and the character sketch; irony held under tight formal control; the sonnet and the quatrain; the long narrative in blank verse; the ending that withholds consolation.
authors.concerns: Failure, loneliness and quiet desperation; the small New England town and its outcasts; marriage and the unlived life; money, drink and decline; the Arthurian legend and the modern quest; the American individual and his illusions.
authors.significance: Robinson is the first major modern American poet and the founder of the American poetry of the small town: his Tilbury Town poems changed American poetry, he won the Pulitzer Prize three times, and his example made it possible for American poets to be both traditional and modern — the bridge from Dickinson and Hardy to Frost and the moderns.

authors.name: Edwin Muir
authors.nationality: Scottish; the mythic lyric and the autobiography of lost Eden
authors.identity: Poet, critic and translator; the great Orcadian lyric poet of the century and the author of The Story and the Fable, one of the finest Scottish autobiographies.
authors.biography: Born Edwin Muir on a farm at Deerness, Orkney, on 15 May 1887; the family moved to Glasgow in 1901 and was destroyed by the city's poverty, an experience that became the ground of all his poetry. He worked as a clerk in a bone factory and an office, married Willa Anderson in 1919, translated Kafka with her, wrote criticism for The Freeman, the New Age and The Listener, and published First Poems (1925), The Narrow Place (1943), The Voyage (1946) and One Foot in Eden (1956). He died at Swaffham Prior, Cambridgeshire, on 3 January 1959.
authors.profile: Muir is the great Scottish poet of the modern lyric: his poems of Eden, the fall, the journey and the lost childhood are among the finest in twentieth-century English, and The Story and the Fable (1940) is one of the great autobiographies of the period. With his wife Willa he translated Kafka's novels into English for the first time, an act of transmission as important as his own verse.
authors.style: The plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric; the dream image held in regular stanza; the archetype deployed without ornament; the child's vision and the adult's guilt; the prose of an autobiography that reads like a fable.
authors.concerns: Eden, the fall and the lost childhood; the city and the destruction of the family; the journey, the voyage and the dream; Scotland, Orkney and the inheritance of myth; time, dream and the archetypal image; the poet's vocation.
authors.significance: Muir is the finest Scottish lyric poet of the period and one of the great autobiographers: his mythic poems of Eden and the journey are permanent, The Story and the Fable is a central Scottish autobiography, and his translations of Kafka gave English the writer who remade the modern novel.

authors.name: Eliza Haywood

authors.identity: English novelist, playwright, and actress, one of the most prolific and popular writers of amatory fiction in the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born around 1693 (her birthplace is disputed, with Ireland traditionally but uncertainly given), she married a Welsh gentleman and, after his early death, turned to the stage and to writing. She first achieved fame with the long romance Love in Excess (1719), followed by shorter amatory fictions such as Fantomina (1724). She acted, wrote plays, and later published the novel The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless (1751), a more morally serious work. She also edited periodical and miscellaneous collections. She died in 1756.
authors.profile: A central author of the amatory-fiction vogue whose narratives explore desire, deception, and the vulnerability of women in a commercial marriage market, and whose range later extended toward conduct-adjacent domestic realism.
authors.style: Sensational, emotionally heightened prose; first-person and epistolary insertions within narrative; elaborate rhetoric of passion; tightly plotted intrigue centered on seduction; and a strong attention to the interior states of female characters.
authors.concerns: Desire and deception; the seduction and reputation of women; the economics of marriage; the perils and knowledge of the female heart; and the pleasures and dangers of reading romance.
authors.significance: A leading and widely read novelist of her day, once ranked alongside Richardson and Fielding, whose recovery by modern scholarship has made her central to the study of women's writing and the rise of the novel.

authors.name: Eliza Lynn Linton
authors.nationality: English; the periodical essay, the novel of the woman question and the satirical sketch
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the first woman to earn a regular salary on the London press, and the most notorious 'anti-feminist' essayist of the Victorian age.
authors.biography: Born Eliza Lynn at Keswick on 10 February 1822, the daughter of a clergyman; she went to London in 1845 and became the first woman employed on the staff of a London daily newspaper, the Morning Chronicle. She married the wood-engraver William Linton in 1858 and left him in 1867; she published twenty-five novels and a mass of journalism, and her essay 'The Girl of the Period' (1868) made her the most discussed woman writer in England after George Eliot. She died in London on 14 July 1898.
authors.profile: Linton wrote the essay that named the modern young woman: 'The Girl of the Period' is a satire on the fashionable girl who paints her face and thinks of nothing but dress, and it set the terms of the debate on the New Woman for twenty years. But her position was more complex than the label 'anti-feminist' allows: her novels attack the marriage law, her journalism defends women's right to work, and her autobiography is one of the frankest records of a woman's professional life in the century.
authors.style: The satirical periodical essay with a strong persona; the social sketch; the novel of the woman question with a harsh realism about money and sex; the ironic description of dress and manners; direct polemical address.
authors.concerns: The 'woman question' and the modern girl; marriage, work and female independence; dress, fashion and the body; class and the professions; the condition of women in the colonies; the vanity of the fashionable world.
authors.significance: Linton is the central figure in the Victorian debate on the 'Girl of the Period' and one of the first women to hold a salaried post on the London press: her journalism set the terms of the debate over the New Woman, and her autobiography and her best novels are key documents of Victorian women's professional life.

authors.identity: Playwright; the author of Chains and the realist dramas of the lower middle class.
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Baker in London on 20 August 1876; she worked as a typist while writing plays, and Chains (1909) - first performed at the Court Theatre and then in the Duke of York's repertory season - made the obscure office worker one of the most discussed playwrights in England. Her dozen produced plays kept to the clerks, the shopgirls and the suburban strivers - The Price of Thomas Scott (1913) at the Gaiety, Manchester, Partnership (1917) at the Court - and she continued her typing through the success; she died on 8 March 1962.
authors.profile: Elizabeth Baker is the playwright of the clerks' London: Chains, with its suburban couple, the dream of Australia and the return to the routine, is the landmark realist play of the lower middle class, and her repertory plays carried the typist's own knowledge of the office and the suburb onto the new drama's stage.
authors.style: The plain exact dialogue of the clerk and the shopgirl; the suburb, the office and the routine of the lower middle class; the moral dilemma in the small decision; the woman's knowledge of the typist's world; the new drama's realism without its propaganda.

authors.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period
authors.identity: Poet, translator and political writer; the most widely read English woman poet of the nineteenth century and the author of Sonnets from the Portuguese and Aurora Leigh.
authors.biography: Born on 6 March 1806, the eldest of twelve children of Edward Moulton-Barrett, a Jamaican plantation owner, she was educated at home and read Greek and Hebrew as a child. A spinal illness from 1821 and the death of her brother Edward in 1840 confined her at 50 Wimpole Street, where she wrote The Seraphim (1838), Poems (1844) and the sonnets that became Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850). Her correspondence with Robert Browning began in January 1845; they married secretly in September 1846 and left for Italy, living in Pisa and Florence, where their son Pen was born in 1849. Casa Guidi Windows (1851), Aurora Leigh (1856) and Poems before Congress (1860) belong to the Italian years of the Risorgimento. She died in Florence on 29 June 1861.
authors.profile: Barrett Browning made the woman poet a public intellectual. Her subjects are the political struggles of Italy, the condition of women, slavery, child labour and the vocation of the artist, and her forms are the sonnet sequence, the verse novel, the ballad and the polemical poem. Aurora Leigh is the first English verse novel written by a woman about a woman writer, and it argues explicitly for a woman's right to an independent vocation. Her style is dense, allusive and often colloquial, and the earlier poems show the influence of Greek tragedy and of the Hebrew prophets.
authors.style: Blank verse of sustained narrative drive; the sonnet sequence used as a single psychological document; a rhetoric of apostrophe and of political address; baroque imagery of Italy and of the Old Testament; a deliberate mixing of the domestic and the prophetic registers.
authors.concerns: The woman artist and the claims of vocation against marriage; Italian nationalism and the Risorgimento; slavery and the condition of the American South; child labour and social reform; religious doubt and the argument from human love; the relation of poetry to the age.
authors.significance: Barrett Browning was the most influential English woman writer of the century before George Eliot: Sonnets from the Portuguese made the amatory sonnet sequence a woman's form, and Aurora Leigh gave the nineteenth-century woman's movement its central literary text. Her Italian poems made her a figure of the Risorgimento, and her influence runs through Christina Rossetti, the Brontës and the twentieth-century feminist recovery of women's poetry.
authors.uncertainty: The family's income derived from Jamaican sugar plantations worked by enslaved people, a fact the family concealed and which modern scholarship (and Barrett Browning's own 'The Runaway Slave at Pilgrim's Point') addresses; the marriage was kept secret from her father, who never forgave it.

authors.name: Elizabeth Bowen
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish; the novel of consciousness and the Big House
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest Anglo-Irish novelist of the century and one of the great English novelists of the modern period.
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Dorothea Cole Bowen at 15 Herbert Place, Dublin, on 7 June 1899; she grew up at Bowen's Court in County Cork and in England, and published Encounters (1923), The Last September (1929), The House in Paris (1935) and The Death of the Heart (1938). authors.style: The image that carries the emotion; the dialogue that circles and evades; the child's eye and the adult's failure; the Big House and the empty room; the precise, sensuous, exact prose.

authors.name: Elizabeth Carter
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Scholar, poet, and translator, one of the most learned of the Bluestockings, famed for her Greek and her translation of Epictetus.
authors.biography: Born on 16 December 1717 at Deal in Kent, the daughter of the Reverend Nicholas Carter, a clergyman, she displayed an early aptitude for languages and largely educated herself in Greek and other tongues. She published poems in Gentleman's Magazine and other collections and moved in learned and Bluestocking circles, corresponding widely with Elizabeth Montagu. Her major work, a translation of the discourses of Epictetus, was published in 1758 and earned her high regard among scholars. She never married and continued literary work in later life. She died on 19 February 1806.
authors.profile: A classicist and writer whose translation of Epictetus and whose learned essays and poems made her a byword for female scholarship, and whose correspondence is a key document of Bluestocking culture.
authors.style: Learned, precise, and unadorned prose; measured, didactic verse; and a scholarly, self-effacing manner suited to translation, essay, and letter.
authors.concerns: Learning and the intellectual life of women; Stoic philosophy and virtue; religion and morality; and friendship and correspondence as a form of sociable culture.
authors.significance: One of the most accomplished of the eighteenth-century Bluestockings, celebrated as a female scholar of Greek and a moral writer, whose life expanded the accepted scope of women's learning.

authors.name: Elizabeth Gaskell
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel and social reportage
authors.identity: Novelist and biographer, born Elizabeth Cleghorn Stevenson; the great novelist of the industrial north and of the rural village, and the first biographer of Charlotte Brontë.
authors.biography: Born in Chelsea on 29 September 1810, the daughter of William Stevenson, a Unitarian minister turned government clerk, and Elizabeth Holland; her mother died a month after her birth, and she was brought up by an aunt at Knutsford in Cheshire, the Cranford of her fiction. In 1832 she married William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister in Manchester, where she spent the rest of her life and came to know the poverty of the mill districts at first hand. Her first son died in infancy in 1833 and she wrote her first novel, Mary Barton, in the aftermath of his death; it appeared anonymously in October 1848 and was attacked as a one-sided account of the Manchester strikes. Cranford was serialised in Household Words in 1851-53; North and South in 1854-55; The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857), commissioned by Patrick Brontë, was attacked by Mrs Brontë's friends and had to be revised. She died suddenly at Holybourne, Hampshire, on 12 November 1865, leaving Wives and Daughters unfinished; it was printed complete with the editor's note in the Cornhill in 1866.
authors.profile: Gaskell wrote from the two vantage points of the Manchester parsonage and the Cheshire village, and her novels hold industrial investigation and domestic comedy in a single frame. Mary Barton and North and South are condition-of-England novels that take the wage, the strike and the masters' blindness as central conflicts; Cranford and the shorter tales make a comic art out of small economies and the claims of gentlewomen without money; Ruth (1853) treats the seduced and abandoned woman without the punitive ending the convention required. Her prose is mobile and observational, she is a superb ventriloquist of different registers of speech, and she works best in the short and middle-length forms where incident accumulates rather than a single plot resolves.
authors.style: Concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid); rapid shifts between comedy and pathos within a chapter; a strong sense of the local speech of Lancashire and Cheshire; use of letters and reported conversation as the main instruments of character; an unobtrusive but steady moral commentary on social duty.
authors.concerns: The relation of masters and men in industrial conflict; the social position of women without money or protection; the ethics of sympathy across class; the claims of the past and of traditional community; religious conscience (Unitarian and Anglican) and its social expression; illness and death in the household.
authors.significance: Mary Barton was among the first English novels to describe the mill-worker's household and the strike from within, and it shaped the whole condition-of-England tradition from Dickens's Hard Times to the twentieth-century industrial novel. The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857) is the founding work of Victorian literary biography. Cranford has kept a permanent place as the finest English comic-idyllic fiction of the century, and the late Wives and Daughters is now read as one of the greatest of Victorian novels.
authors.uncertainty: 1 of the 6 works catalogued here carry a research status of 'partial' - Wives and Daughters: An Every-Day Story - and are reported only so far as the evidence allows. The attribution of Mary Barton: A Tale of Manchester Life rests on the publisher's records, the correspondence and the internal evidence rather than on a title page.

authors.name: Elizabeth Hamilton
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish and Scottish; the anti-philosophical novel and educational writing of the 1790s
authors.identity: Novelist and educational writer; the sharpest woman satirist of rational philosophy applied to domestic life
authors.biography: She was born in the north of Ireland in the middle years of the century, of a Scottish family settled there, and was left early dependent on her own abilities; she spent much of her life in Scotland and in the north of England, supporting herself and her household by writing. Her first book, a satire in the form of translated letters from an Indian envoy observing England, appeared in 1796 and was an immediate success, establishing her name in the Edinburgh and London reviews. The following years brought the great anti-philosophical novel of a family ruined by a system-maker, published in 1800 and much the most effective of the conservative answers to the fashion for speculative fiction. She then turned to education, publishing a long series of letters on the principles of teaching children which was widely used and reissued, together with tales and tracts on the conduct and instruction of young people and a work on the preferences and prejudices of nations. Her later writings mixed educational theory with political and religious argument, and she corresponded with the reviewers and moralists of the day. She died in 1816, leaving a body of fiction and educational prose which her nineteenth-century readers remembered chiefly as a defence of orthodoxy against the schools.
authors.profile: An epistolary oriental satire, a five-volume novel of philosophical delusion, an educational correspondence in several volumes, tales and tracts for young readers, and a work on national prejudice. Her fiction argues by exposure of consequences: an idea is placed in a household and observed until the household is undone. Her educational writing belongs to the Scottish tradition of instruction by development rather than by rote.
authors.style: A clear, argumentative and deliberately unimpassioned prose, strong on the reported dialogue of doctrinal talk and on the comic exposure of a speaker's inconsistency. Her satirical voice is more directly polemical than that of the contemporary English comedy of manners, and her educational writing is orderly, examples-driven and addressed to parents.
authors.concerns: The domestic consequences of speculative philosophy. The education and judgement of children and of young women. National prejudice, the character of nations and the British empire in India. Religious orthodoxy against infidelity. The duties and dependencies of household life.
authors.significance: Her novel of 1800 is the most effective single piece of fiction in the campaign against the philosophical schools and helped end the fashion it attacked; her educational letters were a standard work of the first decades of the century. She is now studied as a central figure of the conservative woman's novel and of writing on the British rule in India before the 1820s.
authors.uncertainty: The year and place of her birth are not securely documented, and the chronology of her residence in Scotland and the north of England, and of her family's circumstances, is known mainly from the prefaces and letters she published.

authors.name: Elizabeth Heyrick
authors.nationality: English; the Quaker plain-style remonstrance, the women's anti-slavery agitation of the Midlands, and British immediatism
authors.identity: Leicester banker's wife, plain-style Quaker and pamphleteer; the writer of the tract which broke the British movement's long gradualism and supplied the slogan and the logic of immediate emancipation.
authors.biography: Heyrick was born Elizabeth Coltman at Leicester on 4 December 1769, the daughter of John Coltman, a surgeon and apothecary of the town, and was educated in a family of dissenting and then Quaker connection. She married John Heyrick, a Leicester banker and businessman whose affairs miscarried, and after his death and the failure of the house she maintained herself and her daughters in the town by keeping a shop and by her writings, living a life of plain-living, careful dressing of the poor and strenuous correspondence. She joined the Society of Friends, and her Quaker habits of remonstrance, of the plain style and of personal testimony shaped everything she printed. She had long written against the slave trade and the colonies, sending tracts on the subject to Zachary Macaulay and to the friends of gradual measure, and in 1824 she threw a printed circular, Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition, upon the members of the London society, following it with an Apologia and with the arguments addressed to the conscience of the slave-holder and to the West India interest. The pamphlet was passed from hand to hand, reprinted, and made the turning-point of the agitation, furnishing the demand for unconditional and immediate emancipation which the new society of 1831 adopted and which the abolition act of 1833 carried. She was one of the first to urge the women's anti-slavery societies, the boycott of slave-grown sugar and the apprenticeship scheme's rejection, and she corresponded with American friends on the colonisation enterprise, denouncing the American Colonization Society in letters published after her death. She died at Leicester on 18 October 1831, within a few months of the foundation of the society which took her programme, and her posthumous volume of essays and letters on the colonies appeared in 1832.
authors.profile: Her writing is the short reform tract and the printed circular, argumentative, urgent and addressed to a named society or to the reader's conscience: the 1824 pamphlet states the case for the shortest, safest and most effectual means of getting rid of colonial slavery, and the Apologia of 1825 defends the principle against the gradualists of her own party. Her later letters on the colonisation system and her essays on the condition of the people, published in a volume after her death, extend the same method of plain appeal, arithmetic and moral demonstration. She wrote also on war and nonresistance, on the treatment of animals and on the education and dress of the labouring poor, in a literature of remonstrance rather than of system.
authors.style: The plain Quaker style of remonstrance: direct address, short declarative sentences, the pointed question, the enumeration of instances and the arithmetic of compensation turned against the claim it supports; an absence of ornament and of classical allusion, and a moral pressure carried by repetition and by the refusal of euphemism. The tone is neither petitioning nor declamatory but adjuring, and it is frequently startling because it will not concede the premises of its opponents.
authors.concerns: The sin of holding the enslaved and the impossibility of a just gradual measure; immediate emancipation without compensation to the holder; the duty of the consumer, and the boycott of the product of slave labour; the claims of women to take a public part in moral agitation; nonresistance, the cruelty of war and the treatment of animals and of the poor as one question of justice; the colonisation of free Black Americans as a scheme of expulsion rather than of liberation.
authors.significance: Her pamphlet is the pivot text of British immediatism, the document that shifted the agitations demand from apprenticeship and gradual measure to unconditional emancipation, and it directly shaped the programme of the society founded in 1831 and the argument over compensation before the legislation of 1833. She is also a founding figure of women's organised anti-slavery work in England, since her circulars and her example supplied the logic of the female societies and of the sugar boycott, and her colonisation letters carried into the American debate.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth and death dates are given in the parish and family records of Leicester but are omitted altogether, or printed wrongly, in many standard histories of the movement and in most nineteenth-century notices, and her place of birth is sometimes stated only as the town, sometimes as a village near it. The extent of her authorship of anonymous tracts and letters in the abolitionist press is uncertain, and the part she played in the founding of the Leicester ladies society and in the national immediate-abolition organisation of 1830-31 is known chiefly from the proceedings and the correspondence of those bodies.

authors.name: Elizabeth Montagu

authors.identity: Writer, critic, and hostess, the most prominent of the Bluestockings, long called the 'Queen of the Blues.'
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Robinson on 2 October 1718 in Yorkshire, she was largely self-educated through the library of her family's York home and moved to London, where she married her cousin Edward Montagu. A central figure in literary society, she hosted salons that gathered writers and scholars and corresponded with Elizabeth Carter, Hannah More, and others. Her critical work An Essay on the Genius and Writings of Shakespeare (1769) defended Shakespeare against neoclassical objections. Her many letters remain a major source for the period. She died on 25 September 1800.

authors.style: Vigorous, assertive critical prose; lively, witty, and discursive letters; a sociable, argumentative tone; and an emphasis on nature and original genius against rigid classical rule.

authors.significance: The presiding figure of the Bluestocking movement and an influential critic, whose salon and correspondence shaped literary culture and whose Essay helped to advance the reputation of Shakespeare.

authors.name: Elizabeth Rowe
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and prose writer, known as the 'Heavenly Singer,' a leading woman writer of pious verse and moral fiction in the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Singer on 11 September 1674 at Ilchester in Somerset, the daughter of a Nonconformist minister, she was educated at home and began writing verses and answering the Athenian Mercury's queries as a young woman. Her early poems appeared as Poems on Several Occasions, written by Philomela (1696). She later married the minister Thomas Rowe, after whose death she continued to write devotional and moral works, including the biblical poem The History of Joseph (1736). Posthumous collections of her letters and writings were published and widely read. She died on 11 February 1737.
authors.profile: A writer of religious, moral, and sentimental verse and prose whose pious tone and defense of female learning made her one of the most admired women authors of her day, read across the eighteenth century.
authors.style: Devotional and moralizing verse and prose; elevated, earnest diction; a plain, reflective Augustan manner; and an epistolary and meditative tone in her prose works.
authors.concerns: Piety and the virtuous life; female education and learning; friendship and moral duty; and the consolation and exemplarity of Scripture.
authors.significance: A highly esteemed woman writer whose posthumous reputation lasted well into the century, influencing ideals of pious womanly letters and serving as a model for later women writers.
authors.uncertainty: The outlines of her life are documented, though the composition and dating of some early poems and the extent of her early manuscript circulation are imperfectly recorded.

authors.name: Elizabeth Stuart Phelps
authors.nationality: American; the spiritualist novel, the woman's novel and the social story
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and feminist; the most popular American woman novelist of the 1870s and the author of The Gates Ajar.
authors.biography: Born Mary Gray Phelps in Andover, Massachusetts, on 31 August 1844, the daughter of a professor of sacred rhetoric and the writer Elizabeth Wooster Stuart Phelps; she took her mother's name after her death in 1852. The Gates Ajar (1868) made her famous at twenty-four; she wrote over fifty books, campaigned for women's education and dress reform, and was a leading opponent of vivisection. She taught at Boston University from 1883 and died in Newton, Massachusetts, on 28 January 1911.
authors.profile: Phelps wrote the American novel of the afterlife and of women's work: The Gates Ajar is the book in which Victorian American grief is answered by a domestic heaven, and it was the most consoling novel of the post-war decade. Her later fiction — The Story of Avis, Doctor Zay — is among the first American writing about women's professional ambition and the conflict between marriage and vocation.
authors.style: Domestic detail extended into the afterlife; the first-person letter narrative; sentiment controlled by irony; the professional woman's interior life; argument carried by dialogue; the reformist aside.
authors.concerns: Death, mourning and the afterlife; women's education and professional work; marriage versus vocation; vivisection and animal suffering; the Civil War and its bereaved; spiritualism and faith.
authors.significance: Phelps was the best-selling American woman novelist of the 1870s and a significant feminist thinker: The Gates Ajar shaped the American literature of mourning, The Story of Avis is a founding text of the American novel of the woman artist, and Doctor Zay is one of the first American novels with a woman physician as its heroine.

authors.name: Emily Brontë
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel and lyric poetry
authors.identity: Novelist and poet; the author of Wuthering Heights, and the most original and least documented of the Brontë sisters.
authors.biography: Born at Thornton on 30 July 1818, the fifth child of Patrick Brontë; she grew up at Haworth and, apart from a few months at Roe Head (1835) and the year at the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels (1842-43), never left the parsonage and the moors. She kept the Gondal chronicle, a verse and prose saga of an imaginary north Pacific kingdom, with Anne from childhood, and her poems and Anne's were included in the privately financed Poems by Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell (1846). Wuthering Heights was published in December 1847 in three volumes together with Anne's Agnes Grey; the reviewers were largely hostile or puzzled, and the novel sold poorly. Her health declined through the autumn of 1848, and she refused medical treatment, dying at Haworth on 19 December 1848. Her poems were edited with a memoir by Charlotte in 1850.
authors.profile: Emily Brontë wrote one novel and a body of lyric and Gondal poems, and no other English writer of comparable standing is so entirely without a biography. Wuthering Heights refuses the moral and formal conventions of the Victorian novel: it is narrated at two removes, by the outsider Lockwood and the servant Nelly Dean, whose accounts disagree; its structure is that of a chronicle extending over three generations; and the passion at its centre exceeds both narrators' comprehension. The poems are hard, short, stoical and impersonal, and the finest of them ('No coward soul is mine', 'The Prisoner', 'Remembrance') have the accent of the border ballad and of the hymn rather than of the Romantic lyric.
authors.style: A frame-within-a-frame narrative with two partial and unreliable narrators; a dialect voice (Joseph) used as a barrier to comprehension; violent abrupt transitions and a refusal of explanation; a prose that is spare in description and dense in the notation of weather, stone and animal life; in the poems, short ballad measure, abrupt syntax, and a deliberate coldness of tone even at the height of grief.
authors.concerns: The passion that exceeds social form; the relation of the self to place and to the dead; revenge and inheritance across two generations; the Calvinist inheritance and its alternatives (Nelly's moralism, Joseph's fanaticism, Catherine's dream of heaven); class and property in a moorland yeoman economy; the supernatural as a fact of psychology, not a device of plot.
authors.significance: Wuthering Heights is the one Victorian novel that has never settled into the Victorian canon, and each generation has remade it (as a Gothic romance, a Marxist study of property, a feminist account of the female will, a postcolonial reading of Heathcliff's origin). Its double narration is a permanent model for the unreliable frame, and the Gondal poems are a central document in the debate about poetic imagination as a private system.
authors.uncertainty: Almost nothing is documented of her life: no letters survive in her own hand except two notes, and the Gondal prose chronicles were lost. Charlotte's 1850 memoir and her editing of the poems are the source of most later accounts and are themselves contested; the standard evidence is Winifred Gérin's biography (1971) and the Clarendon edition of the poems.

authors.name: Emily Dickinson
authors.nationality: American; the lyric, the riddle and the poetry of the inner life
authors.identity: Poet; one of the two or three greatest lyric poets in English, and the central woman poet of the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born in Amherst, Massachusetts, on 10 December 1830, the daughter of a lawyer and congressman; she was educated at Amherst Academy and Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, which she left after a year. She lived almost entirely in her father's house, increasingly withdrawn after 1861, dressed in white, and conducted her closest relationships by letter. She wrote nearly 1,800 poems, sewn into fascicles, and published fewer than a dozen in her lifetime. She died in Amherst on 15 May 1886; the first collection appeared in 1890.
authors.profile: Dickinson wrote the lyric of extreme compression: her poems are short, usually rhymed in ballad or hymn stanzas, and organised around a single image or a riddle that the reader must solve. She writes about death, immortality, the mind, nature, love and fame with a wit and a metaphysical daring unmatched in American poetry, and her dashes, capitals and slant rhymes create a syntax of hesitation that is entirely her own.
authors.style: Hymn and ballad measures broken by slant rhyme and irregular stress; dashes in place of punctuation; capitalised nouns; riddling circumlocution for the central subject; paradox and irony; the poem as a single compressed argument.
authors.concerns: Death and immortality; the mind and its power; nature and the seasons; love, renunciation and absence; religious doubt and the Calvinist inheritance; fame, publication and the woman artist.
authors.significance: Dickinson is one of the greatest poets in English and the founder of a distinctively American lyric of the inward life: her influence on twentieth-century poetry is as large as Whitman's, and the recovery of her manuscripts has made her a central figure in the criticism of gender, religion and American poetics.

authors.identity: Novelist, historian and poet; the finest woman novelist of the Irish revival and the author of Hurrish and Grania.
authors.biography: Born the Hon. Emily Lawless at Lyons, County Kildare, on 17 June 1845, the daughter of the third Baron Cloncurry; she grew up in Kildare and in the Burren of County Clare. authors.style: The western landscape as the determining force; the Aran and Burren detail; the heroine divided between two men and two Irelands; the historical retrospect of the Jacobite wars; the plain, unsentimental prose.

authors.name: Emma Lazarus
authors.nationality: American; the lyric, the verse essay and the poetry of immigration
authors.identity: Poet and essayist; the author of 'The New Colossus', the sonnet inscribed on the Statue of Liberty, and the first American poet of the Jewish immigrant.
authors.biography: Born Emma Lazarus in New York on 22 July 1849 into a wealthy Sephardi Jewish family; she published her first book at seventeen and was encouraged by Emerson. In the 1880s the Russian pogroms turned her into a Zionist and a campaigner for the Jewish refugees, producing Songs of a Semite (1882) and The Dance to Death (1882), and 'The New Colossus' (1883) for the Bartholdi Pedestal Fund. She died in New York on 19 November 1887, aged thirty-eight.
authors.profile: Lazarus wrote the American poetry of immigration: 'The New Colossus' is the most quoted American sonnet and the founding poem of American immigration, and Songs of a Semite is the first English book of poetry to treat the Jewish people as a nation with a modern destiny. She was also a considerable critic and essayist, and her work marks the moment when American poetry began to speak for the immigrant and the exile.
authors.style: The classical sonnet and the verse drama in a formal, measured style; the prophetic and biblical idiom; the rhetoric of the verse address; the essay of cultural argument; the elegy for a persecuted people; the image that becomes a national symbol.
authors.concerns: Immigration, exile and the promised land; the Jewish people and the Zionist idea; slavery, persecution and emancipation; American national identity; the city and the harbour; women's education and the woman writer.
authors.significance: Emma Lazarus is the first American poet of immigration and the author of the most famous American sonnet: 'The New Colossus' is inscribed on the Statue of Liberty and has been read by millions, Songs of a Semite founded the literature of American Zionism, and her work made the immigrant experience a central subject of American poetry.

authors.name: Erasmus Darwin
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Physician, inventor and didactic poet of the Midlands Enlightenment, who put Linnaean botany, the chemistry of the senses and the transmutation of organs into heroic verse.
authors.biography: Born at Elston in Nottinghamshire in 1731, the seventh child of a small landowner, he was educated at a school in the neighbouring town and at St John's College, Cambridge, where he won a reputation as a Latin poet, and completed his medical training in the north. He settled as a physician at Nottingham and then at Derby from the mid-1750s, and built one of the widest provincial practices in England, visiting patients over the counties about him. At Derby he became the friend and neighbour of the manufacturers, potters and natural philosophers who met in the Lunar Society, helped to found the Derby Philosophical Society in 1783, and occupied himself with canals, drainage and agricultural machinery. His poems made the new science readable: the first published part of his projected Botanic Garden, The Loves of the Plants, appeared in 1789 with elaborate prose notes, and its companion The Economy of Vegetation followed in 1791. His prose speculations on life, Zoonomia (volume one in 1794), and the poem The Temple of Nature (1803), belong to the years after the period covered here; both scandalised the pious and anticipated debates about the derivation of species. He died at Derby in April 1802, the grandfather of Charles Darwin.
authors.profile: The poet of the senses and of machinery, who wrote physiology, botany and agriculture as a single animated system of pleasure and use.
authors.style: Couplet didactic verse of florid energy, with personified plants, sexual metaphor and an appeal to the five senses; long explanatory prose notes; exuberant, sometimes overreaching imagery.
authors.concerns: The Linnaean sexual system and the culture of plants; the chemistry of sensation, irritation and the motions of living bodies; the improvement of agriculture, machinery and public health; the derivation and progress of organic life; the rights of reason against priestcraft.
authors.significance: He carried the scientific Enlightenment into English verse and into provincial industry, and his speculations on life made him one of the ancestors of evolutionary biology as well as the grandfather of its founder.
authors.uncertainty: His early education and medical qualifications are imperfectly recorded, and the chronology of the parts of the Botanic Garden is complicated by pirated and revised printings.

authors.name: Ernest Dowson
authors.nationality: English; the Decadent lyric and the short story of exhaustion
authors.identity: Poet and short-story writer; the most pure and the most tragic of the English Decadent poets.
authors.biography: Born at Lee, Kent, on 2 August 1867; he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, but left without a degree, and worked in his father's failing dock business. He fell in love with the eleven-year-old daughter of the proprietor of a London Italian restaurant, and the hopeless passion of his life, together with the deaths of his parents and his own alcoholism, produced the verse of Verses (1896) and Decorations (1899). He died of tuberculosis at Catford on 23 February 1900, at thirty-two.
authors.profile: Dowson wrote the poetry of renunciation and exhaustion: his lyrics are short, perfectly made and obsessive, and their subject is the love that cannot be possessed, the wine that cannot console and the faith that has been lost. His prose, especially the stories collected in Dilemmas (1895) and the unfinished novel Madame de Vionnet, is the finest Decadent prose after Pater, and his influence on the modern lyric is out of all proportion to the smallness of his output.
authors.style: Short lyric metres of great smoothness; refrain and repetition; the Latin refrain ('non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae'); the exhausted cadence; imagery of wine, roses, twilight and the sea.
authors.concerns: Hopeless love and renunciation; the loss of faith; wine and exhaustion; the passing of youth; the city at evening; the memory of a happiness that never was.
authors.significance: Dowson is the purest of the English Decadent poets and the author of some of the most quoted lines in the language: 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae' and 'They are not long, the weeping and the laughter' are permanent parts of English poetry, and his small body of work has influenced Yeats, Eliot and the modern lyric of loss.

authors.name: Ernest Hemingway
authors.nationality: American; the hard-boiled sentence, the code hero and the modernist short story
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the revolutionary of American prose, the author of The Sun Also Rises and A Farewell to Arms, and the Nobel laureate of 1954.
authors.biography: Born Ernest Miller Hemingway in Oak Park, Illinois, on 21 July 1899; he worked as a reporter on the Kansas City Star, served as an ambulance driver on the Italian front in 1918 and was badly wounded, and covered the Greco-Turkish war for the Toronto Star. Three Stories and Ten Poems (1923) and In Our Time (1925) made his name, The Sun Also Rises (1926) made him the voice of the Lost Generation, A Farewell to Arms (1929), For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940) and The Old Man and the Sea (1952) followed. He won the Nobel Prize in 1954 and died at Ketchum, Idaho, on 2 July 1961.
authors.profile: Hemingway changed the American sentence: his prose, built on the concrete noun, the plain verb and the omission of everything that can be left out, invented a style that the century has never escaped. In Our Time made the modernist short story an American form, The Sun Also Rises defined a generation, and A Farewell to Arms is the finest American novel of the First World War. The iceberg theory — that meaning lies in what is omitted — is his permanent contribution to narrative art.
authors.style: The short declarative sentence; the concrete noun and the exact place-name; omission of the connective and the explanation; the dialogue that says less than it means; the repeated scene and the withheld emotion; the first-person narrator who does not comment.
authors.concerns: War, wounding and the code of endurance; the Lost Generation and the expatriate life; bullfighting, hunting and the mastery of fear; love and the loss of it; drink, Paris and the café; grace under pressure and the dignity of work.
authors.significance: Hemingway is the great revolutionary of American prose and the dominant American novelist of the period: his sentences changed how the century writes, In Our Time created the modern American short story, The Sun Also Rises and A Farewell to Arms are permanent, and the Nobel Prize confirmed his standing. He is the writer against whom every American stylist since has measured himself.

authors.name: Ernest Jones
authors.nationality: English; the Chartist poem, the ballad and the political novel
authors.identity: Chartist leader, poet and novelist; the most gifted poet of the Chartist movement and its most effective orator.
authors.biography: Born in Berlin on 25 January 1819, the son of a British diplomat; he was educated at London and Göttingen and came to England in 1844, where he joined the Chartist movement and edited the Northern Star and the Labourer. He was imprisoned for sedition in 1848-50, was elected to the Chartist National Assembly, and in 1852 tried to restructure the movement; he later practised as a barrister and stood unsuccessfully for parliament. He died in Manchester on 26 January 1869.
authors.profile: Jones wrote the poetry of political revolution: his Chartist songs and ballads were written for mass meetings and for the pages of the Northern Star, and 'The Song of the Lower Classes' and 'The Factory Slave' are among the most effective political poems in English. His novel The Gold Harp is a Chartist romance of the medieval peasant and the modern worker, and his poems are the most important body of working-class verse between Burns and Morris.
authors.style: Ballad and song forms with heavy refrain; the direct address of the platform orator; the vocabulary of the Rights of Man; the industrial imagery of mill, furnace and prison; a deliberately popular diction.
authors.concerns: The rights of labour and the Charter; the prison and the political prisoner; the factory and the mine; the solidarity of the workers; Ireland and the United Kingdom; the history of popular resistance.
authors.significance: Jones is the central poet of Chartism and the most important English political poet between Shelley and Morris: his songs were sung at mass meetings across Britain, and his verse is the essential literary record of the first mass working-class movement in history.

authors.name: Ethel Mannin
authors.nationality: British; the prolific popular novelist of the working woman and the anarchist's travel books
authors.identity: Novelist and travel writer; the author of Sounding Brass and Ragged Banners.
authors.biography: Born Ethel Edith Mannin in London on 6 October 1900, the daughter of a postal worker; she left school at fifteen, worked in a pension office and in advertising before Sounding Brass (1926) began a career of more than a hundred books - a novel and a non-fiction book a year. Her early novels of the working woman, her autobiography Confessions and Impressions (1930), her anarchism and her anti-fascism made her a popular and committed voice of the decades; she died at Teignmouth on 5 December 1984.
authors.profile: Ethel Mannin is the prolific popular novelist of the working woman: Sounding Brass and Children of the Earth carried the life of the working-class woman into the bestseller, Ragged Banners is her homage to the eccentrics, and Men Are Unwise brought her advanced ideas of marriage to the mountaineering novel of the thirties.
authors.style: The plain fast prose of the popular novelist; the working woman of the suburbs and the office; the eccentrics and the road; the anarchist's argument carried in the travel book; the two books a year of the professional writer.
authors.concerns: The working-class woman and her life; the suburb and the office; anarchism and anti-fascism; the road and the travel book; the eccentric and the ordinary.
authors.significance: Ethel Mannin is the prolific popular novelist of the working woman: her hundred books made the working woman, the road and the anarchist's argument the matter of the popular literature of the decades.

authors.name: Eudora Welty
authors.nationality: American; the comic-grotesque Southern story and the novel of the small town
authors.identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest comic writer of the Southern Renaissance and the author of A Curtain of Green and The Optimist's Daughter.
authors.biography: Born Eudora Alice Welty in Jackson, Mississippi, on 13 April 1909; she studied at Mississippi State College for Women, the University of Wisconsin and Columbia, worked as a publicity agent for the WPA in Mississippi in the 1930s — photographing the rural poor — and published A Curtain of Green in 1941. The Robber Bridegroom (1942), Delta Wedding (1946), The Ponder Heart (1954), The Optimist's Daughter (1972, Pulitzer Prize) and One Writer's Beginnings (1984) followed. She died in Jackson on 23 July 2001.
authors.profile: Welty wrote the finest comic fiction of the Southern Renaissance: her stories of the Mississippi small town and the rural poor — 'A Worn Path', 'Why I Live at the P.O.', 'Petrified Man' — made the grotesque funny without condescension, and her novels of the Mississippi family are the warmest in the Southern tradition. Her photographs of the Depression South are a documentary record of equal importance.
authors.style: The comic monologue and the first-person eccentric voice; the story built on a single comic situation; the precise rendering of dialect without caricature; the fairy-tale and folk-tale structure (The Robber Bridegroom); the lyric description of the Mississippi landscape.
authors.concerns: The Mississippi small town and its eccentrics; the family, the wedding and the funeral; race and the Southern social order; the rural poor and the Depression; the comic survival of the isolated woman; memory and the return home.
authors.significance: Welty is the great comic writer of the Southern Renaissance and the finest American short-story writer of her generation: A Curtain of Green and The Wide Net are permanent, The Optimist's Daughter won the Pulitzer Prize, and her photographs and memoir made her the period's most humane Southern witness.

authors.identity: Playwright; the founder of the modern American theatre and the Nobel laureate of 1936.
authors.biography: Born Eugene Gladstone O'Neill in a Broadway hotel in New York on 16 October 1888, the son of the actor James O'Neill; he went to sea, worked as a reporter, and made his name with Beyond the Horizon (1920, Pulitzer Prize). The Emperor Jones (1920), Anna Christie (1921), Desire Under the Elms (1924), Strange Interlude (1928), Mourning Becomes Electra (1931) and Long Day's Journey into Night (written 1940) followed. He died in Boston on 27 November 1953.
authors.profile: Eugene O'Neill founded the modern American theatre and was the first American playwright to win the Nobel Prize: his experimental plays brought expressionism, psychoanalysis and the classical tragedy into the American theatre, and he is the central figure of American drama in the century.
authors.style: The expressionist set and the mask; the long monologue and the aside spoken to the audience; the dialect of the sailor and the farmer; the classical tragedy in a New England house; the plain, insistent, repetitive speech of obsession.

authors.name: Evelyn Waugh
authors.nationality: British; the comic novel of the twenties, the Catholic novel and the war trilogy
authors.identity: Novelist, biographer and travel writer; the greatest English comic novelist of the century and the author of Decline and Fall, Brideshead Revisited and Sword of Honour.
authors.biography: Born Arthur Evelyn St John Waugh in London on 28 October 1903, the son of a publisher; he read at Oxford, failed to settle to anything, taught in Wales and travelled in the Mediterranean, and made his name with Decline and Fall (1928) and Vile Bodies (1930). He converted to Catholicism in 1930, published A Handful of Dust (1934), Scoop (1938), Brideshead Revisited (1945) and the Sword of Honour trilogy (1952–61), and wrote the finest English travel books of the period. He died at Combe Florey, Somerset, on 10 April 1966.
authors.profile: Waugh is the greatest English comic novelist of the century: Decline and Fall and Vile Bodies invented the twenties' comic manner, A Handful of Dust is one of the darkest novels in English, Brideshead Revisited is the period's great elegy for the Catholic aristocracy, and Sword of Honour is the finest English novel of the Second World War. His prose — exact, sonorous, merciless — is the period's most perfect comic instrument.
authors.style: The comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face; the sentence that ends in a catastrophe delivered as an aside; the catalogue of eccentric characters; the travel book's comic encounter; the Catholic novel's structure of grace and vocation; the elegy for the great house.
authors.concerns: The twenties' smart set and its empty pleasures; the English aristocracy and the great house; Catholicism, grace and the vocation; the Second World War and the comedy of the army; the empire and the English abroad; death, judgement and the failure of the world.
authors.significance: Waugh is the greatest English comic novelist of the century and the period's finest prose stylist: Decline and Fall and Vile Bodies made the comic novel modern, A Handful of Dust and Brideshead Revisited are permanent, and Sword of Honour is the finest English novel of the Second World War.

authors.name: Ezra Pound
authors.nationality: American; imagism, the modernist epic and the translation as form
authors.identity: Poet, critic and translator; the founder of Imagism and Vorticism, the editor of The Waste Land, and the author of the Cantos — the most influential and most contested American poet of the century.
authors.biography: Born Ezra Loomis Pound at Hailey, Idaho, on 30 October 1885; he studied at Hamilton College and the University of Pennsylvania, taught briefly, and left for Europe in 1908, settling in London (1908–20), Paris (1921–24) and Rapallo (1924–45). In London he founded Imagism (1912), edited Blast (1914), wrote Cathay (1915) and Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (1920), and cut The Waste Land down to its published form. He broadcast for Mussolini during the war, was indicted for treason, and was confined in St Elizabeths Hospital, Washington, from 1946 to 1958, where he completed Rock-Drill and Thrones. He died in Venice on 1 November 1972.
authors.profile: Pound is the single greatest force in the making of modern poetry in English. His manifesto of Imagism taught the century to write free verse; Cathay (1915) invented the modern translation-poem; Mauberley is the finest short sequence of the period; and the Cantos, begun in 1915 and left unfinished in 1972, are the period's attempt at the American epic. As editor, talent-spotter and controversialist he made the careers of Eliot, Joyce, Frost, H.D. and Hemingway possible.
authors.style: The image as the unit of the poem; the line composed by the musical phrase; the ideogram and the juxtaposition without connectives; translation as a mode of original composition; the collage of document, quotation and satire in the long poem; the vorticist economy of language.
authors.concerns: The modern city and the usura of the money economy; the American past and the epic of the republic; Confucius and the order of the state; art, patronage and the artist's place; love, desire and the troubadour inheritance; the betrayal of the intellect by the market.
authors.significance: Pound is the central maker of modernism: he taught the age to write free verse, edited The Waste Land into its permanent form, discovered and published the writers who changed the century, and spent fifty years on the Cantos. His politics were catastrophic and his influence was decisive; both facts are part of the record.

authors.name: F. R. Leavis
authors.nationality: British; the critic of the great tradition and the founder of the Cambridge school

authors.biography: Born Frank Raymond Leavis at Cambridge on 14 July 1895; he served in the war, took his degree at Cambridge and taught there, founding the journal Scrutiny in 1932. He held the readership at Cambridge until 1962 and died there on 14 April 1978.
authors.profile: F. R. authors.style: The polemical sentence of the moral urgency; the quotation examined word by word in the argument; the verdict delivered as a definition; the rejection of the historical and the sociological in favour of the valuation; the canon as the instrument of the discipline.
authors.concerns: The minority culture against the mass civilisation; the valuation and the canon; the great tradition of the English novel from Austen to James; the revaluation of the English poets; the discipline of English as a defence of the civilisation; the war and the loss of the organic community.

authors.biography: Born Frank Stuart Flint in London on 19 November 1885; he worked as a clerk and a journalist, founded the Poets' Club and the Secession Club, and with Ezra Pound and T. E.
