authors.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
authors.nationality: American; the jazz-age novel, the lyric of the American dream and the short story of the twenties
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the laureate of the Jazz Age and the author of The Great Gatsby, the most perfect American novel of the period.
authors.biography: Born Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on 24 September 1896; he read at Princeton without graduating, served in the army without seeing action, and made his name with This Side of Paradise in 1920, marrying Zelda Sayre a week after publication. The Beautiful and Damned (1922), The Great Gatsby (1925), Tender Is the Night (1934) and the unfinished The Last Tycoon followed, together with some 160 stories for the Saturday Evening Post. He died of a heart attack in Hollywood on 21 December 1940.
authors.profile: Fitzgerald is the essential novelist of the 1920s and the author of the most nearly perfect American novel: The Great Gatsby is a lyric study of the American dream's corruption, Tender Is the Night a study of money and marriage that is formally years ahead of its time, and the stories are the definitive record of the jazz age. His prose — the fresh, exact, romantic sentence — is the period's most influential style.
authors.style: The romantic lyric sentence held in tight structure; the image chosen for its glamour and its hollowness; the collapse of the narrator's sympathy into judgement; the time-shift and the retrospective frame (Gatsby, Tender Is the Night); the short story built on a single social scene.
authors.concerns: The American dream and the corruption of it; money, class and the careless rich; the jazz age, drink and the party; love, marriage and the illusions of the beautiful; the Midwest and the East; failure, decline and the grace of the second chance refused.
authors.significance: Fitzgerald wrote the most perfect American novel of the period and the definitive record of the 1920s: The Great Gatsby is a permanent classic, Tender Is the Night is one of the century's great studies of marriage and money, and his short stories made the jazz age a literary period. He is the period's great poet of the American dream and its failure.

authors.name: Felicia Hemans
authors.birthplace: 118 Duke Street, Liverpool, in a family of Welsh descent; raised from about the age of seven at Gwrych near Abergele in Denbighshire
authors.nationality: English by birth and Welsh by upbringing and self-identification; the popular lyric, metrical romance and devotional verse of the later Romantic period, and the literary annual and gift-book public that made it
authors.identity: The most extensively read and reprinted woman poet of the nineteenth century in Britain and America, and the first to build a complete professional authorship on the lyric of domestic affection; a contributor of verse and prose to every leading magazine and annual of her day, and the settled authority for a whole repertoire of women's feeling.
authors.biography: Hemans was born at Liverpool on 25 September 1793, the daughter of George Browne, a merchant whose affairs failed at the turn of the century, and of a mother whose father had held a foreign consular appointment in the same city; when the girl was about seven the family removed to Gwrych, near Abergele in the Welsh north, and the scenery and the Welsh claims of her childhood stay visible throughout her work and in her own account of herself. She was educated largely at home, an avid and early reader with an unusual memory for verse, and by about 1808 she was contributing poems to a popular monthly magazine; her first collected volume, declaring domestic affection as the durable ground of happiness, appeared in 1812. In that year she married an army officer of Welsh birth, Captain Hemans, a Peninsular-war survivor several years her senior, and within the next few years she bore him a family of sons; about 1818 her husband quitted England for the continent and did not return, and from her twenties until her death she maintained herself and her children wholly by her pen. The following decades made her the leading female poet of the day: volumes of lyric and occasional verse, translations and imitations from the Romance languages, metrical tales, and in 1825 the ambitious Spenserian romance of a child preserved within a monastic retreat. Records of Woman of 1828, whose title names a design rather than a poem, consolidated her authority over the history of women's feeling and drew a substantial notice in the Edinburgh review; Songs of the Affections followed in 1830, gathering the shorter manner of her last decade. Her homes moved from Wales to the neighbourhood of Liverpool, where she rented in the later years, and finally to Dublin, in which city she had lived at an earlier period of her married life; her income came from the annuals and the magazines, and from an American market which reprinted her faster than any copyright could follow. Her health, never robust, gave way under overwork, anxiety about her sons and private grief, and she died at her lodging in Dublin on 16 May 1835, in her forty-second year, and was buried in the vault of the Dublin church near her house. The collected editions, one of them with a memoir prepared by a member of her family, and the interminable reprints in gift-books, schoolbooks, hymnals and recitation collections, kept her lines before the English-speaking world for the rest of the century; her dismissal by high modernist taste as merely sentimental, and her recovery by later scholarship on women's writing, are both part of her recorded history.
authors.profile: Her canon runs to many separate volumes and includes the lyric meditation and song, the short dramatic address in a historical or imaginary woman's voice, the metrical tale and romance, the devotional hymn and sacred poem, the topographical and national piece, and translations or imitations from Spanish and Italian sources; her prose is slight beside her verse, and a great deal of that verse was made to order for the annuals, often written to accompany a specified engraving. Her characteristic single poem builds upon one emblem, one farewell or one grave, and develops it as a meditation; the longer narrative poems of the middle years, of which The Forest Sanctuary is the example, are her attempt to be read as a moral poet of sustained design. Posthumous collections gathered what the market had demanded, and the arrangement of her volumes by length and tone rather than by plan is itself evidence of her relation to her publishers.
authors.style: A deliberately vocal and singable smoothness, in common and short iambic measure with marked refrains, adapted to recitation and to musical setting; the closed heroic couplet used where feeling is to settle into maxim; personification, apostrophe and the address to an absent or dead beloved; an emblematic method in which a token, a lamp, a bracelet or a bird carries the whole argument; historical and Romance colouring softened to a domestic and moral use; and a pathos concentrated on a single situation, which contemporaries found overpowering and later critics found repetitive.
authors.concerns: Affection tried by separation, bereavement and time, and its survival as the ground of identity; the destinies, claims and education of women, and the mind set against the lot allowed it; constancy, forbearance and jealousy recorded as history; Providence, gratitude and vocation in the poem of preservation; consolation and the hope of reunion after death; exile and homelessness; Catholic and legendary Romance matter subdued to a plainly Protestant devotional temper; national memory, Wales and the scenery of childhood.
authors.significance: She made the woman poet a mass-market professional figure, and the idiom of her affectionate and mourning lyric became the ordinary language of Victorian domestic and devotional culture, quoted, paraphrased and set to music without attribution for generations. Her career is the clearest record of the economics of the literary annual before it reached its full height, and of the transatlantic circulation that could support a British writer's income. The design of Records of Woman gave the century a durable subject and a set of transferable female personae, and the sequence of her reputation - enormous fame, modernist dismissal, and recovery by feminist scholarship from the late twentieth century - is now a standard case in the history of canon formation and of the gendering of literary value.
authors.uncertainty: Her birthplace and her national identity are given variously in the authorities: the register evidence places her birth in Duke Street, Liverpool, in September 1793, while a strong Welsh tradition, resting on her upbringing and on her own identification, has claimed her as Welsh, and older handbook accounts sometimes misdate the month of her birth. The christian name of the officer she married is given by most modern sources as Alfred, though some catalogue traditions style her by the other name; the date and terms of the separation, and the number and survival of her sons, rest largely on family and later testimony; the nature of the illness that killed her is variously described; and how much editorial control she exercised over the posthumous collections, and what share her family's memoir has in shaping the record of her life, cannot be determined.

authors.name: Fitz-Greene Halleck
authors.nationality: American; New England and New York Knickerbocker letters
authors.identity: Poet and periodical essayist, the most widely read American verse-writer of the 1820s and 1830s and a mentor to the younger New York authors
authors.biography: Fitz-Greene Halleck was born at Guilford, Connecticut, on 8 July 1790, the son of a farmer of old New England stock, and was named after a family friend. His formal education was fragmentary: he attended Yale College as a teenager without taking a degree, and then earned his living for years as a clerk, working in a Virginia counting house before settling in New York City about 1811. There his friendship with Joseph Rodman Drake became a literary partnership. In 1819 the two contributed the "Croaker Papers", a series of Addisonian essays and satires on New York society, to the New York Evening Post and the National Advertiser; Drake's death in 1820 left Halleck the surviving partner and, later, the devoted compiler of Drake's Poetical Works (1835) with a memoir. Halleck's verse spread quickly through anthologies and newspapers: the humorous narrative "Fanny" appeared anonymously in December 1819, and his first collected volume, Alnwick Castle, with Other Poems (1827), made him nationally famous and, for a generation, the canonical American poet of the schoolroom recitation. Commercial failure of that volume and a large family kept him in salaried work; from 1832 he served in New York as private secretary and adviser to the philanthropist John Jacob Astor, a post that also involved him in the Astor family's quarrels and in the slanders that dogged his later reputation. He returned to Guilford, where he died on 19 November 1867, honoured in his lifetime as the "American Byron" and as the patron of emerging writers such as Junius Henri Wilson and the young Herman Melville's circle.
authors.profile: Halleck wrote occasional, descriptive and satirical verse in a deliberately polished public style: lyric and meditative poems on the American landscape ("Columbia", "The Western Worlds", "Robin Day"), humorous character sketches in verse ("Fanny"), and elegies and odes on national subjects. His essays in the Croaker series are urban comedy of manners. He published little fiction and no drama; his prose work is chiefly the biographical memoir prefixed to Drake's poems and a body of letters.
authors.style: Diction is elevated but plain, modelled on eighteenth-century sententiousness rather than on Romantic experiment. Blank verse and the eight-line stanza of Burns dominate; the couplet of Pope and the periodical essay of Addison shape his satirical voice. His effects rest on antithesis, apostrophe to America and nature, prosodic regularity designed for recitation, and a pathos that is sentimental rather than psychological. The humorous pieces rely on colloquial New England and New York speech and brisk narrative pacing.
authors.concerns: National identity and the possibility of an American literature; the poet's economic dependence on business employment; friendship, loss and posthumous reputation; the moral influence of landscape and home; Whig and Jacksonian-adjacent politics of the era; the education of a popular reading public through anthologised verse.
authors.significance: Halleck helped make professional authorship a visible American ambition and was the first United States poet to be read continuously in Britain after Byron's vogue. The Croaker Papers gave New York its first native periodical-essay school; Alnwick Castle circulated American themes in British editions for decades; his memoir of Drake fixed the enduring image of the two Knickerbocker poets. Long a staple of nineteenth-century elocution and school readers, his eclipse in the twentieth century is itself a document of changing American taste.
authors.uncertainty: The brief given for this project stated a 1777 birth and an 1819 Alnwick Castle volume; both are incorrect against the sources checked, which give 8 July 1790 for his Guilford birth and 1827 for Alnwick Castle, with the 1819 date belonging to the Croaker Papers and the anonymous "Fanny". The precise identity of his pre-Astor clerkships, including the stage-boat "hire office" employment recorded in older memoirs, is inconsistently reported.

authors.name: Ford Madox Ford
authors.nationality: British; the impressionist novel, the war tetralogy and the modern editor's craft
authors.identity: Novelist, editor and critic; the author of The Good Soldier and Parade's End, the editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review, and the great teacher of the modern novel.
authors.biography: Born Ford Hermann Hueffer at Merton, Surrey, on 17 December 1873, the son of a German-born music critic and the grandson of the Pre-Raphaelite painter Ford Madox Brown; he published his first book at eighteen, collaborated with Conrad on The Inheritors (1901) and Romance (1903), edited the English Review (1908–09) — discovering and publishing Hardy, James, Wells, Pound and Lawrence — and the transatlantic review (1924). The Good Soldier appeared in 1915, the Parade's End tetralogy in 1924–28. He changed his surname to Ford in 1919, taught at Olivet College, Michigan, in the 1930s, and died at Deauville on 26 June 1939.
authors.profile: Ford is the great teacher of the modern novel: The Good Soldier is the most perfect English novel of the period — a study of deception told by a narrator who is himself deceived — and Parade's End is the finest English novel of the First World War and the transition from Edwardian to modern England. As editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review he published the modern movement into existence, and his criticism (The March of Literature, 1938) taught a whole generation how to read.
authors.style: The impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in; the deliberate withholding of information ('this is the saddest story I have ever heard'); the long, loose, conversational sentence; the progression d'effet; the editorial preface as criticism.
authors.concerns: Marriage, adultery and the conventions that conceal them; the Edwardian ruling class and its code; the First World War and the end of the old England; the Catholic conscience and the protestant mind; the artist and the patron; time and the reconstruction of memory.
authors.significance: Ford wrote the finest English novel of the period in The Good Soldier and the finest English war novel in Parade's End, and as editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review he made modernism publishable. He is the period's great theorist and practitioner of the impressionist novel.

authors.name: Frances Burney
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Novelist and diarist, creator of the comedy of manners in early women's fiction and a keen observer of eighteenth-century society.
authors.biography: Born on 13 June 1752 at King's Lynn in Norfolk, the daughter of the music historian Charles Burney, she was raised in literary and musical circles and began writing early. Her first novel, Evelina (1778), published anonymously, was a success, followed by The Wanderer's precursor Cecilia (1782). She served at court as a lady of the bedchamber to Queen Charlotte and, after marriage to the French exile Alexandre d'Arblay, lived partly in France. Her diaries and letters, spanning decades, are a major social document, and she continued to write fiction and drama. She died in Bath on 6 January 1840.
authors.profile: The inventor of a graceful comedy of female sensibility and manners in Evelina, a precursor to Austen, and a memoirist whose diaries record the society and literary world of her age with wit and precision.
authors.style: Witty, observed comedy of manners in her fiction; epistolary and third-person narration; an acute ear for social speech; and lively, detailed, self-aware journal and letter prose.
authors.concerns: Female sensibility and the navigation of society; reputation and the marriage market; the manners of the court and the town; the position of the writing woman; and class and identity.
authors.significance: A pioneering woman novelist of manners whose Evelina shaped the school of social realism and proto-feminist comedy, and whose diaries and letters are indispensable to the history of late-eighteenth-century society and letters.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is abundantly documented through her own journals; the chief editorial question concerns the dating, abridgment, and revision of her diaries rather than any biographical crux.

authors.name: Frances E. W. Harper
authors.nationality: African-American; the poem of reform, the novel of the colour line and the lecture
authors.identity: Poet, novelist, essayist and lecturer; the most important African-American woman writer of the nineteenth century and the first black woman to publish a novel in the United States.
authors.biography: Born Frances Ellen Watkins in Baltimore on 24 September 1825, orphaned early and raised by an uncle who was a Methodist minister and abolitionist; she taught in Ohio and Pennsylvania, and in 1854 delivered her first antislavery lecture, becoming a paid agent of the Maine Anti-Slavery Society. She married Fenton Harper in 1860 and was widowed in 1864; she then worked for the freedpeople in the South, helped found the National Association of Colored Women, and died in Philadelphia on 22 February 1911.
authors.profile: Harper wrote the literature of black reform as poetry and fiction: her poems were recited at meetings and passed from hand to hand, and Iola Leroy (1892) is the first novel by an African-American woman, a story of passing, slavery and service that answers the plantation tradition and Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin at once. Her verse is direct, public and designed for the platform, and her prose records the interior life of a black woman of education and faith.
authors.style: Ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat; narrative verse of slavery and escape; the novel of the colour line with a didactic purpose; the lecture as literature; direct address and biblical allusion.
authors.concerns: Slavery, emancipation and the duty of the freedpeople; racial uplift and education; the position of black women; passing and the colour line; temperance and Christian duty; the American nation and its betrayal of its own ideals.
authors.significance: Harper is the founding mother of African-American women's writing and the first black woman to publish a novel in America: Iola Leroy and Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects are central texts of nineteenth-century black literature, and her career as a lecturer made her the most widely heard black woman of her generation.

authors.name: Frances Hodgson Burnett
authors.nationality: British-American; the children's classic and the sentimental novel
authors.identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Little Lord Fauntleroy, A Little Princess and The Secret Garden, and one of the most successful transatlantic writers of the period.
authors.biography: Born Frances Eliza Hodgson in Manchester on 24 November 1849; her father died in 1853 and the family emigrated to Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1865. That Lass o' Lowrie's (1877) and Haworth's (1879) made her name, and Little Lord Fauntleroy (1886) made her rich. A Little Princess (1905) and The Secret Garden (1911) followed. She lived between England and America, married twice, and died at Plandome, New York, on 29 October 1924.
authors.profile: Burnett wrote three of the permanent children's classics in English and was one of the first writers to make a fortune from both the book and the dramatisation. Her transatlantic career, her business acumen and her invention of the children's novel of inner life gave the genre The Secret Garden, which remains the most widely read children's book of the period after Alice.
authors.style: The child's-eye view of adult failure; the garden as a place of renewal; the orphan who remakes the household; the fairy-tale structure of loss and restoration; the plain, warm, direct prose of the story-teller.
authors.concerns: Childhood, illness and the recovery of the body; class and the servant problem as seen by a child; the healing power of place and cultivation; the orphan and the found family; the transatlantic crossing of manners.
authors.significance: Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote three permanent children's classics and was one of the first authors to make a fortune from both the book and the stage play: Little Lord Fauntleroy created the modern children's bestseller, and The Secret Garden became the most widely read children's book of the period after Alice in Wonderland.

authors.name: Frances Power Cobbe
authors.nationality: Irish-English; the periodical essay, polemic and social criticism
authors.identity: Essayist, feminist and animal-rights campaigner; one of the most important Victorian writers on the position of women and the founder of the English anti-vivisection movement.
authors.biography: Born near Dublin on 4 December 1822, the daughter of a landed Irish family; she was educated at home, left the family home after a quarrel over her refusal of orthodox religion, and worked as a governess before inheriting an income in 1857. She wrote for the Westminster Review, the Fortnightly and the Contemporary, campaigned for the Married Women's Property Acts and against the Contagious Diseases Acts, and in 1875 founded the Society for the Protection of Animals Liable to Vivisection. She lived for thirty-six years with the sculptor Mary Lloyd and died at Hengwrt, Wales, on 5 April 1904.
authors.profile: Cobbe wrote the Victorian essay as an instrument of political argument: she was the most important woman publicist between Martineau and Mill's circle, and her essays on 'Wife-Torture in England' (1878), 'The Final Cause of Woman' and 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' turned the periodical press into a feminist platform. Her later work on animal ethics made her the founder of English philosophical argument for animal rights.
authors.style: The documented essay with statistics and case evidence; the reasoned petition; vivid narrative case histories; a direct, forceful plain style; the moral appeal over the head of the specialism.
authors.concerns: The legal position of women and the married woman's property; wife-beating and the courts; the Contagious Diseases Acts and the double standard; education and women's paid work; animal suffering and the ethics of experimental science; religion and conscience.
authors.significance: Cobbe is a founding figure of English feminism and of the animal-rights movement: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' is one of the most effective pieces of Victorian feminist polemic, her evidence to the Royal Commission on wife-beating helped to change the law, and her anti-vivisection writing is the origin of the modern philosophical case against animal experimentation.

authors.name: Francis Bacon
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: philosopher; essayist; statesman; lawyer
authors.biography: Born 22 January 1561 at York House, London; son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, he rose under James I to Attorney General (1613), Lord Keeper (1617), Lord Chancellor (1618), and Viscount St Alban (1621), then fell in 1621 on charges of corruption, was fined and briefly imprisoned, and spent his last five years in philosophical retirement at Gorhambury. He died on 9 April 1626 of bronchitis contracted while stuffing a chicken with snow to test refrigeration.
authors.profile: The Essays (1597; enlarged 1612 and 1625), The Advancement of Learning (1605), Novum Organum (1620), the utopian New Atlantis (1626, published 1627), and the History of the Reign of King Henry VII (1622), together with a mass of legal, scientific, and political writings.
authors.style: Aphoristic compression, balanced antithesis, and the deliberate plainness of a mind committed to lucid exposition; his Essays made the form an English genre.
authors.concerns: The reform of learning; induction and the interpretation of nature; the uses of knowledge for power and charity; the conduct of public life.
authors.significance: The chief English spokesman of the new science and the maker of the English essay; his vision of organized inquiry shaped the Royal Society and the Enlightenment that followed.
authors.uncertainty: The circumstances of his fall are still debated by historians; the 'Baconian' claims about Shakespeare's works are rejected by scholarship.

authors.name: Francis Beaumont
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist; poet
authors.biography: Born in 1584 to a prominent Leicestershire legal family; his brother was the poet Sir John Beaumont. He entered Broadgates Hall, Oxford, in 1597 and the Inner Temple in 1600, but the law gave way to the theatre. From about 1606 to 1613 he collaborated with John Fletcher in one of the most celebrated partnerships in literary history, living with him in Bankside 'in the same house and bed'. He married an heiress in 1613, retired to Kent, and died on 6 March 1616; he is buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: With Fletcher he wrote Philaster (c. 1609–10), The Maid's Tragedy (c. 1610–11), A King and No King (1611), and The Knight of the Burning Pestle (c. 1607), the brilliant mock-romance that failed on its first production; his unaided works include the verse epistle to Jonson and the poems in the 1618 collection.
authors.style: Wit, metrical suppleness, and a taste for burlesque and self-conscious theatricality; the Beaumont–Fletcher canon is noted for its tragicomic design and its courtly polish.
authors.concerns: The ethics of honour and friendship; the conventions of romance and their parody; the relation of the stage to its audience.
authors.significance: Half of the partnership whose plays dominated the stage for fifty years after Shakespeare's death; Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy defined the Caroline and Restoration taste that followed.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of labour between Beaumont and Fletcher in each play is unknown and much debated.

authors.name: Francis Hutcheson
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish moral philosopher of the Scottish Presbyterian tradition
authors.identity: Seceding minister and first professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow, who founded the moral-sense school and taught the generation that carried natural rights into the Atlantic revolutions.
authors.biography: Born at Saintfield in County Down in 1694 into a Scottish Presbyterian family, he studied at Glasgow and was licensed by the Associate or Seceding ministry, though he soon gave up preaching for teaching. He kept a school in Dublin, and in 1730 was appointed to the newly founded chair of moral philosophy at Glasgow, which he held until his death. His Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue (1725), with its defence of a disinterested moral sense against Mandeville, and his Essay on the Passions (1728) established a new science of approval. His System of Moral Philosophy was published after his death in 1755 from his manuscripts and lectures. He died in Dublin on 8 August 1746.
authors.profile: The systematizer of sentiment as a moral faculty, who located virtue in benevolence toward the greatest number rather than in self-interest or in reason alone.
authors.style: Textbook plainness with a preacher's warmth; definitions, divisions and a running argument with opponents; a vocabulary of sense, taste, benevolence and approval.
authors.concerns: Moral sense and disinterested benevolence; the happiness of the greatest number; the distinction of natural and moral good; the right of resistance and limited government; the senses and the relish of beauty.
authors.significance: He founded the sentimental and utilitarian strands of eighteenth-century ethics, taught the generation that framed American natural-rights politics, and made benevolence a central term of moral philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his Dublin academy years is uncertain; his Irish and Ulster origins are documented but his university career was cut short by his early death.

authors.name: Francis Jeffrey
authors.nationality: Scottish; the Whig criticism of the Edinburgh Review and the Scottish legal and literary culture of the early nineteenth century
authors.identity: Advocate, critic and judge; the founder and long editor of the Edinburgh Review, the maker of the modern review article as an instrument of literary and political power, and the most feared English-language critic of the Romantic generation.
authors.biography: Jeffrey was born in Charles Street in Edinburgh on 23 October 1773, the son of a depute-keeper of the signet, and was educated at the Royal High School and at the University of Edinburgh, from which he was withdrawn at fourteen and sent to complete his studies at home in the classics. He studied law, was admitted to the Scottish bar in 1794, and passed the 1790s in a literary Edinburgh society in which the terrors of the French Revolution and the trials of the Scottish radicals had made liberal opinion cautious. With Sydney Smith, Horner and Brougham he projected a quarterly journal, and the Edinburgh Review began in October 1802 with his article on the peerage, which he wrote at once as a defence of the new undertaking and as a statement of its principles. He edited the journal to 1829, wrote the critical and review articles in enormous number, and practised at the English bar after 1815, taking silk in 1821. His reputation for severe and elegant judgement made him the arbiter of Romantic poetry: his treatment of Wordsworth, of Byron and of the Lake school established the review as a power in letters, and his name gave the enterprise the credibility that a Scotch and Whig quarterly needed in a loyal and Tory reading public. In 1830 he went to the bench as a lord of session and justiciary under the title Lord Jeffrey, from which office his death at London on 26 January 1850 relieved a career that had long been more legal than critical. His contributions to the later numbers of the Review were collected and reprinted, and his correspondence and the memoirs of his brother-in-law Lord Cockburn remain the chief record of the circle that founded the journal.
authors.profile: His literary form is the review article, and he practised it as a genre of its own: a discursive essay that reviews books as occasions for argument on constitution, finance, education, religion and taste, written in the first person plural of the journal and closing with an assessment of a nation's condition. His critical papers on the poets and novelists of the day, on the Scottish law schools and on the Whig historians, and his contributions on the French revolutionary and post-revolutionary writers, make up a continuous commentary on the literature of the first third of the century; his editorial and political articles on the peerage, on Catholic emancipation and on reform are documents of Whig argument.
authors.style: A polished, urban and deliberately moderate irony, in which severity of judgement is carried in the language of good-breeding; long circumstantial periods, understatement, the concession that precedes the demolition, and a marked use of the collective editorial voice. The prose is rhetorical rather than technical, and its effects depend on balance, on the well-placed aside, and on a self-conscious elegance which his opponents read as the arrogance of the critic.
authors.concerns: The authority of criticism and its relation to party and to patronage; the freedom of the press and of review against the quarterlies and the publishers; the Whig account of liberty, of the peerage and of reform; the taste and the standing of the new Romantic poetry, and the charge of egotism and of deliberate vulgarity brought against it; the place of Scottish letters within a British public; the relation of religion, education and political temper in a commercial society.
authors.significance: He made the Edinburgh Review the model of the literary-quarterly as a political institution and gave the review article its modern authority and its modern weapon, and for a generation English Romantic writing was read, priced and judged in relation to his verdicts. His editorship established the practice of the unsigned but personally identified critic, and his career from bar to bench is the central case of the union of letters and public office in nineteenth-century Britain. He also fixed the shape of the anti-Romantic reception, since the famous quarrel over the Lake poets began with his pages.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of individual unsigned articles in the early numbers of the Edinburgh Review is still in part a matter of inference from diary, correspondence and the ledgers of the journal, and the standard tables of attribution are not unanimous. His birth is given in some earlier biographical accounts at the family place of Argaty near Doune in Perthshire rather than in Edinburgh, though the Edinburgh parochial and school records support the city.

authors.name: Francis Quarles
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Emblem-book poet and devotional writer; author of Emblems (1635), the most popular book of verse in seventeenth-century England, whose combination of picture, biblical motto, and moral verse made religious meditation accessible to a vast readership.
authors.biography: Born 1592 at Romford, Essex, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge and Lincoln's Inn. He held minor offices under the crown, served as cupbearer to the Princess Elizabeth (the 'Winter Queen') at Heidelberg, and wrote a series of biblical paraphrases and religious poems (Esther, Job Militant, Divine Poems, 1620s–30s). His Emblems (1635) and Hieroglyphikes of the Life of Man (1638) were phenomenally popular. A royalist, he wrote pamphlets during the Civil Wars and died in London on 8 September 1644.
authors.profile: The master of the English emblem, whose illustrated moral verses blended Protestant devotion, common proverb, and baroque imagery for an enormous popular audience.
authors.style: Emblem structure (picture, motto, epigram, verse); biblical paraphrase; a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely wit; and a mixture of learned allusion and popular appeal.
authors.concerns: Protestant devotion and moral instruction; the vanity of the world and the soul's pilgrimage; scripture and its paraphrase; and the edification of a lay readership.
authors.significance: Quarles's Emblems was arguably the bestselling English poem-book of the century and shaped popular religious imagination; though later critics (and Pope's 'the mob of gentlemen who wrote with ease') mocked him, his influence on Bunyan, the emblem tradition, and devotional culture was profound.
authors.uncertainty: Quarles's life is documented in outline; his enormous popularity was later eclipsed by critical contempt, and the attribution of some anonymous emblem verses is uncertain.

authors.name: Francis Thompson
authors.nationality: English; the Catholic lyric, the ode and the poetry of the outcast
authors.identity: Poet and essayist; the author of 'The Hound of Heaven', the most famous religious poem of the English 1890s.
authors.biography: Born at Preston on 16 December 1859, the son of a doctor; he was educated at Stonyhurst and studied medicine at Owens College, Manchester, but failed his examinations and went to London in 1885, where he lived for three years as a destitute opium addict, selling matches and sleeping on the Embankment. Wilfrid and Alice Meynell rescued him in 1888 and published his work in Merry England; Poems appeared in 1893 and Sister Songs in 1895. He died of tuberculosis at St John's Wood on 13 November 1907.
authors.profile: Thompson wrote the poetry of guilt and pursuit: 'The Hound of Heaven' is the great English poem of the soul fleeing God, and its long, irregular, tormented lines gave English religious verse a new music. His imagery is drawn from the Catholic liturgy, from the seventeenth-century poets and from the streets of London, and his essays — especially the Shelley and the 'Health and Holiness' — are among the finest of the Catholic revival.
authors.style: Irregular odes with long, hovering lines; internal rhyme and alliteration; the imagery of blood, wings, fire and the city street; the baroque catalogue; the rhythm of the fugue.
authors.concerns: The pursuit of the soul by God; guilt and unworthiness; poverty and the outcast; the Eucharist and the Passion; childhood and lost innocence; London as purgatory.
authors.significance: Thompson is the finest Catholic poet of the English 1890s after Johnson and the author of the most famous religious poem of the period: 'The Hound of Heaven' reshaped English devotional poetry, and his essays and ballads made him a central figure of the Catholic literary revival.

authors.name: Frank Norris
authors.nationality: American; the naturalist epic and the romance of the West
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of McTeague and The Octopus and the leading American theorist of naturalism.
authors.biography: Born Benjamin Franklin Norris in Chicago on 5 March 1870; the family moved to San Francisco in 1884 and he studied art in Paris, then English at Berkeley and Harvard. He worked as a war correspondent in South Africa and Cuba, joined the San Francisco Wave and McClure's, and published McTeague in 1899 and The Octopus in 1901. He died of peritonitis in San Francisco on 25 October 1902, aged thirty-two, leaving the unfinished epic of which The Pit was the second volume.
authors.profile: Norris wrote the American naturalist epic: his subject is the great determining forces — greed, wheat, the railroad, the brute inheritance — and his method is the 'romance of the real', in which the individual is destroyed by powers larger than himself. The Octopus is the central American novel of the railroad and the wheat country, and McTeague is the first great American novel of the urban poor: his theoretical essays on naturalism defined the movement for his generation.
authors.style: Large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories; the documentary description of an industry; the recurring symbolic motif (the wheat, the tooth, the railroad); the sudden eruption of violence; the scientific and biological analysis of character; a romantic rhetoric at odds with naturalist doctrine.
authors.concerns: The railroad, the wheat and the agrarian revolt; greed, money and the ownership of land; the brute inheritance and the animal in man; the West and the city; the class war of the 1890s; the American empire in Cuba and the Philippines.
authors.significance: Norris is the theorist and the epic novelist of American naturalism: The Octopus is the greatest American novel of the railroad and one of the central documents of the populist revolt, McTeague founded the American novel of the urban poor, and his essays defined the movement that carried American fiction into the twentieth century.

authors.biography: Born Michael Francis O'Connor O'Donovan at Cork on 17 September 1903; he fought on the anti-Treaty side in the civil war and was interned, and published the stories of Guests of the Nation in 1931 and Bones of Contention in 1936. As librarian, teacher and critic - The Lonely Voice (1963) is the theory of the short story - and as translator of the Irish verse, he made the Irish short story one of the forms of the century; he died in Dublin on 10 March 1966.
authors.profile: Frank O'Connor is one of the two or three masters of the Irish short story: Guests of the Nation put the civil war and the ordinary decencies into the form, Bones of Contention carried the Cork of his childhood into the story, and The Lonely Voice gave the short story its theory of the submerged population.
authors.style: The short story of the single moral turn told in the spoken Irish-English; the Cork of the childhood and the civil war; the plain sentence of the teller who reports the decencies; the translation that carries the Irish verse into English; the criticism of the form as the art of the submerged.
authors.concerns: The civil war and the internment camp; the Irish short story and its submerged population; Cork and the childhood; the Irish verse and its translation; the ordinary decencies against the ideology.

authors.biography: Born Frederic Norton Manning in Sydney on 22 July 1882; he came to England with his family, worked in a solicitor's office and lived by his pen, publishing The Vigil of Brunhild (1907), Scenes and Portraits (1909) and Eidola (1917). He served in the Shropshire Light Infantry on the Somme and wrote The Middle Parts of Fortune (1929, published as Her Privates We in 1930). He died in London on 22 February 1935.

authors.style: The third-person narrative that stays with the ranks; the dialect speech of the soldiers; the unsparing detail of mud, hunger and fear; the absence of plot and rhetoric; the documentary exactness of the battalion.

authors.name: Frederick Douglass
authors.birthplace: Cordova, Talbot County, Maryland, United States
authors.nationality: African-American; the slave narrative, the oration and the political essay
authors.identity: Orator, editor and autobiographer; the greatest African-American writer of the nineteenth century and the most eloquent voice of the abolitionist movement.
authors.biography: Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818; he was enslaved until 1838, when he escaped to New York disguised as a sailor, and took the name Douglass. He spoke for the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society from 1841, published his Narrative in 1845, founded and edited the North Star in Rochester (1847-51), and after the Civil War held federal appointments in Haiti and Washington. He wrote three autobiographies and died in Washington on 20 February 1895.
authors.profile: Douglass wrote the American language of freedom: his Narrative is the classic slave narrative, built on the movement from ignorance to literacy to liberty, and his oratory — the Fourth of July address of 1852, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' — is the greatest American political speech of the century. His prose is lucid, cadenced and controlled, and it turns the language of the Declaration against the republic that betrayed it.
authors.style: First-person narrative of escape and self-making; direct oratorical address; biblical and constitutional quotation turned to indictment; irony and sarcasm; exact documentary detail of slavery's economy.
authors.concerns: Slavery and the destruction of the self; literacy and the awakening of freedom; the hypocrisy of American democracy; the Constitution and natural rights; Reconstruction and the failure of emancipation; the position of black women.
authors.significance: Douglass is the central African-American writer of the nineteenth century and one of the great prose writers in the language: his Narrative is the founding text of the African-American literary tradition, his Fourth of July oration is a permanent indictment of American hypocrisy, and his life made him the most photographed and most widely heard black man of his century.

authors.name: Frederick Goddard Tuckerman

authors.identity: Poet; the most original American sonneteer of the nineteenth century and the great neglected poet of the New England woods.
authors.biography: Born in Boston on 4 February 1821; he graduated from Harvard, studied law, and retired to Greenfield, Massachusetts, after the death of his wife, where he wrote the sonnets and lyrics collected in Poems (1860). He published little and died at Greenfield on 9 May 1873.

authors.style: The sonnet sequence on nature and grief; the minute observation of the New England woodland; the harsh, knotted syntax; the elegiac address to the dead wife; the refusal of the popular and the sentimental.
authors.concerns: Bereavement and the immortality of the dead; nature as the language of grief; solitude and the woods; the failure of fame; the relation of the poet to the community.
authors.significance: Frederick Goddard Tuckerman was the most original American sonneteer of the nineteenth century: his Poems of 1860, neglected in his lifetime, were rediscovered as a central text of American poetry and his influence runs through Frost and the American formal lyric.

authors.name: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Courtier, statesman, and poet; Sidney's closest friend and biographer, and the most philosophically austere of the Elizabethan sonneteers.
authors.biography: Born 3 October 1554 into a Warwickshire gentry family; educated at Shrewsbury (with Sidney) and Jesus College, Cambridge. He served Elizabeth as treasurer of the navy and of war, and James I as chancellor of the Exchequer (1614–21), being created Baron Brooke in 1621. His poetry — Caelica, the treatises on monarchy and religion, and Mustapha and Alaham — circulated in manuscript in his lifetime; he was murdered on 30 September 1628 by a servant he had omitted from his will, and was buried in St Mary's, Warwick. His Life of the Renowned Sir Philip Sidney (printed 1652) is the classic memoir of the period.
authors.profile: A philosophical poet of power and dark inwardness whose verse dramas and treatises anatomize the corruptions of monarchy and the vanity of earthly desire; his Caelica turns the sonnet sequence into a meditation on the failure of worldly love and the turn to God.
authors.style: Dense, aphoristic, and abstract diction; Senecan sententiae; a Calvinist suspicion of the world expressed in sinewy couplets and dramatic choruses.
authors.concerns: The corruption of power and the duties of counsel; the vanity of human wishes; predestination and divine grace; the memory and meaning of Sidney's life and death.
authors.significance: The intellectual centre of the Sidney circle after Sidney's death; his poems and treatises form the most searching Elizabethan anatomy of politics and the soul outside Shakespeare and Donne.
authors.uncertainty: His works were printed posthumously (1633, 1652) and the dating of Caelica's composition is approximate (c. 1580s–1610s).

authors.name: G. A. Henty
authors.nationality: British; the historical adventure of empire
authors.identity: Novelist and war correspondent; the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history.
authors.biography: Born George Alfred Henty at Trumpington on 9 December 1832; he served in the Crimean War and as a war correspondent in the Austro-Italian war, the Abyssinian expedition and the Ashanti war. After the success of Out on the Pampas (1871) he produced some eighty historical adventure novels, from The Young Buglers (1880) to With the Allies to Pekin (1904). He died on board his yacht in Weymouth harbour on 16 November 1902.
authors.profile: Henty was the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history: his eighty novels taught a generation the history of the British Empire as a series of campaigns in which a young man could take part, and they fixed the formula of the historical adventure novel that lasted until the Second World War.
authors.style: The young hero placed at the centre of a real historical campaign; the meticulous military and topographical detail; the episodic campaign narrative; the didactic preface and the imperial moral; the plain, reportorial prose of the correspondent.
authors.concerns: The empire and the imperial idea; war and the heroic code; the historical past as a school of manhood; race and the colonial encounter; the British character and its destiny.
authors.significance: G. A. Henty was the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history: his eighty novels taught a generation the history of the empire as a series of campaigns and fixed the formula of the historical adventure novel for the next fifty years.

authors.name: G. K. Chesterton
authors.nationality: British; the paradox, the detective and the distributist
authors.identity: Essayist, novelist, poet and critic; the most brilliant English controversialist of the century and the creator of Father Brown.
authors.biography: Born Gilbert Keith Chesterton in Kensington on 29 May 1874; he trained as an artist, reviewed for the press, and made his name with The Defendant (1901), Heretics (1905) and Orthodoxy (1908). The Man Who Was Thursday (1908), The Innocence of Father Brown (1911), The Napoleon of Notting Hill (1904) and his studies of Dickens and Chaucer followed. He was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1922 and died at Beaconsfield on 14 June 1936.
authors.profile: Chesterton was the most brilliant English controversialist of the century and the creator of Father Brown: his paradox and his jokes made orthodoxy exciting, the Father Brown stories created the metaphysical detective story, and The Man Who Was Thursday is the greatest English metaphysical thriller.
authors.style: The paradox turned inside out; the epigram that reverses the reader's expectation; the argument by image and joke; the ordinary man as hero; the detective story as a parable of the moral order.

authors.name: Gavin Douglas
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: poet; translator; bishop of Dunkeld
authors.biography: Born about 1474, third son of the Earl of Angus; educated at St Andrews and provost of St Giles, Edinburgh. His Palice of Honour (c. 1501) and the allegories King Hart and Conscience followed; his Eneados, the translation of Virgil's Aeneid completed on 22 July 1513, is the first complete rendering of the poem in any British language. Bishop of Dunkeld from 1515, he died in London of the plague in September 1522.
authors.profile: The last great poet of the Scottish Chaucerians and the first British translator of the Aeneid. The Palice of Honour is a courtly dream vision of dazzling learning; King Hart an allegory of the heart's court; and the Eneados — in vigorous Scots couplets, with a prologue to each book describing the Scottish seasons — ranks with Surrey's as one of the two great Tudor translations of Virgil.
authors.style: Aureate Chaucerians diction in the allegories; in the Eneados, a plain, energetic Scots that renders Virgil's gravitas in northern idiom; the seasonal prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots.
authors.concerns: The translation of classical epic into the vernacular; honour, fame, and the education of princes; the defence of poetry against its detractors.
authors.significance: Author of the first complete Aeneid in any form of English and the summit of the Scottish Chaucerians; his Eneados passed the classical inheritance to the northern Renaissance.

authors.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; courtier; civil servant; diplomat
authors.biography: Son of a London vintner; page in the household of the Countess of Ulster, soldier in France (captured 1359–60), and thereafter a royal servant — esquire of the king's household, controller of customs and of the wool subsidy, justice of the peace for Kent, clerk of the king's works, and member of parliament. His diplomatic missions took him to France and Italy (1372–73, 1378), where he encountered the poetry of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio. He died on 25 October 1400 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, founding what became Poets' Corner.
authors.profile: Author of the Book of the Duchess (c. 1368–72), the House of Fame (c. 1378–80), the Parliament of Fowls (c. 1380–82), Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1382–86), the Legend of Good Women (c. 1386–88), the Treatise on the Astrolabe (1391), and the unfinished Canterbury Tales (c. 1387–1400), together with Boece, the Romaunt of the Rose (disputed), and the short poems.
authors.style: The perfection of the decasyllabic line and rhyme royal in English; mastery of frame narrative, ironic personae, and dramatic monologue; the synthesis of French courtly forms, Italian narrative, and native English comedy into a new poetic language.
authors.concerns: Love in its courtly, comic, and philosophical dimensions; the ethics of storytelling; fortune, free will, and providence; the estates of society in pilgrimage and satire.
authors.significance: Universally regarded as the father of English poetry: he fixed the London dialect as the literary standard, naturalized the decasyllabic line, and created a body of work — above all the Canterbury Tales and Troilus — of the first European rank.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon and chronology of some minor works are debated; the Romaunt of the Rose attribution is disputed.

authors.name: George Berkeley
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish
authors.identity: Irish-born philosopher and Church of Ireland bishop whose immaterialism, theory of vision and Alciphron make him one of the two or three metaphysicians whom the century could not ignore.
authors.biography: Born at Thomastown in County Kilkenny in 1685, he went to Trinity College Dublin, where he became a fellow and a tutor, and in 1707 took his degree. In a single brilliant period of young manhood he published the Essay towards a New Theory of Vision (1709), the Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and the Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713), which reduced sensible qualities to ideas in a mind and made the existence of matter depend on being perceived. Ordained in the Church of Ireland and appointed dean of Derry in 1724, he married Esther Vanhomrigh in 1723 and spent a decade in America trying to fund a college in Bermuda. The failure of that scheme ended his hopes of a transatlantic church; from 1734 he lived as bishop of Cloyne, where he wrote Siris (1744) on tar-water as a remedy, and he died at Oxford on 14 January 1753.
authors.profile: A philosopher of perception and language who argued that mind, not matter, is the ground of the visible world, and who wrote his hardest metaphysics as lively dialogue.
authors.style: Sparse, precise, almost aphoristic argument; numbered propositions and sharp objection-and-reply; a sceptic's ingenuity in the service of a pastor's conclusions.
authors.concerns: The nature of ideas, perception and the external world; abstraction and the misuse of signs in language; the absolute space and time of the Newtonians; the reality of spirit and active agency; religious language and the minute philosopher.
authors.significance: He carried early modern empiricism to its sceptical limit, anticipated later work on vision and on language, and supplied Hume, Reid and the whole tradition of idealism with the problems they inherited.
authors.uncertainty: The details of the Bermuda college scheme and of his American years survive unevenly, and his motives for the enterprise are still argued.

authors.name: George Bernard Shaw
authors.nationality: Irish; the drama of ideas and the preface of the playwright
authors.identity: Dramatist, critic and socialist; the greatest English-language playwright of the modern age and the reformer of the Victorian stage.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin on 26 July 1856, the son of a drunken civil servant and a musical mother; he left school at fifteen, followed his mother to London in 1876, and spent nine years in poverty writing five unsuccessful novels. He became a music critic, then drama critic for the Saturday Review (1895-98), joined the Fabian Society in 1884, and published Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant in 1898. His plays — Mrs Warren's Profession, Arms and the Man, Candida, Man and Superman, Pygmalion, Saint Joan — made him the dominant dramatist of the century; he won the Nobel Prize in 1925 and died at Ayot St Lawrence on 2 November 1950.
authors.profile: Shaw reinvented the English stage: he replaced the well-made play with the drama of argument, put the discussion at the centre of the action, and wrote long, combative prefaces that made every play a pamphlet. His subject is the conflict of ideas — prostitution and capitalism, love and the Life Force, poverty and the Salvation Army, class and speech — and his method is the inversion of the sentimental expectation: the soldier is a coward, the hero is a fool, and the woman chooses the man who will be useful to her.
authors.style: Extended dialectical argument as dramatic action; the reversal of romantic and stage conventions; brilliant, epigrammatic and unflagging dialogue; the Shavian preface; the comic unmasking of the respectable; a prose that is colloquial, precise and rhetorically explosive.
authors.concerns: Poverty, prostitution and the economics of vice; socialism, the Fabian Society and the reform of society; marriage, the New Woman and the relations of the sexes; class and the ownership of language; war, heroism and the illusions of patriotism; the Life Force and creative evolution.
authors.significance: Shaw is the central English-language dramatist of the twentieth century and the decisive reformer of the Victorian stage: his prefaces and his plays made the theatre a place of argument, he created the modern drama of ideas, and plays from Pygmalion to Saint Joan have entered the permanent repertoire of the world.

authors.name: George Borrow
authors.nationality: English; the picaresque travel narrative and the literature of the road
authors.identity: Writer, linguist and Bible agent; the author of Lavengro and The Bible in Spain, and the great English writer of the open road.
authors.biography: Born George Henry Borrow at East Dereham, Norfolk, on 5 July 1803, the son of an army recruiting officer; he was articled to a solicitor, learned Welsh and Romany, and in 1833 became an agent of the British and Foreign Bible Society in Russia and Spain. The Bible in Spain (1843) made him famous; Lavengro (1851), The Romany Rye (1857) and Wild Wales (1862) followed. He died at Oulton Broad, Suffolk, on 26 July 1881.
authors.profile: Borrow wrote the English picaresque of the road: his books are not novels and not travel books but a unique mixture of autobiography, philology, adventure and dialogue with the outcast and the wanderer, and their sympathy with the Roma, the Welsh and the Spanish poor gives them a freedom no Victorian writer possessed. His style — plain, digressive, full of extraordinary conversation — made him a model for the English literature of vagabondage.
authors.style: Picaresque episodic narrative; long, vivid conversations with strangers and outcasts; the writer's own unapologetic opinions; the documentary record of languages and customs; the digression and the anecdote; the plain, vigorous English sentence.
authors.concerns: The open road and the wanderer; Roma life and language; Wales, Spain and Russia; the encounter with the poor and the outcast; philology and the love of languages; freedom and independence of spirit.
authors.significance: Borrow is the great English writer of the open road and the founder of the modern literature of vagabondage: Lavengro and The Bible in Spain are among the most original books of the century, his sympathy with the Roma was unique in Victorian writing, and his influence runs through the English travel book to Borrow's many admirers.

authors.name: George Cavendish
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: biographer; gentleman usher to Cardinal Wolsey
authors.biography: Born in Suffolk about 1497; entered the service of Cardinal Wolsey as gentleman usher about 1522 and attended him through his fall and death in 1530. Retiring to Suffolk, he wrote The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey between about 1554 and 1558 from his intimate knowledge of the Cardinal's household. The work circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1641. He died about 1562.
authors.profile: Author, with Roper's Life of More, of the twin masterpiece of Tudor biography. The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey — the rise, magnificence, and fall of the butcher's son who ruled England — is the classic of Tudor life-writing: eyewitness, circumstantial, and tragic, with the great scenes (Wolsey's fall at Cawood, his death at Leicester) rendered as drama. Shakespeare drew on it for Henry VIII.
authors.style: Ample, plain narrative prose; the usher's exact memory for gesture, word, and scene; tragic structure imposed on recent history.
authors.concerns: The fall of princes as moral example; the memory of Wolsey against his detractors; loyalty to the great house he had served.
authors.significance: With Roper, founded English secular biography; his portrait of Wolsey — and through it of Henry VIII's court — shaped the English historical imagination from Shakespeare onward.

authors.name: George Chapman
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; dramatist; translator of Homer
authors.biography: Born near Hitchin about 1559; studied at Oxford but left without a degree, then served in the Low Countries. He began writing for the theatre around 1594 and completed Marlowe's Hero and Leander in 1598. His great labour was the translation of Homer: the Iliad (1598–1611) and Odyssey (1614–15), which Keats would celebrate in the sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'. He died in London on 12 May 1634.
authors.profile: Plays include The Blind Beggar of Alexandria (1596), the two-part Bussy D'Ambois (c. 1604), The Conspiracy and Tragedy of Charles, Duke of Byron (1608), Eastward Ho (1605, with Jonson and Marston, which landed its authors in prison for satire of the Scots), and The Widow's Tears (c. 1605); his verse includes the philosophical poem The Shadow of Night (1594) and Ovid's Banquet of Sense (1595).
authors.style: A dense, oracular style — packed conceits, stoic sententiae, a 'dark' obscurity his contemporaries mocked but which carries his tragedies of heroic aspiration.
authors.concerns: Stoic virtue; the heroic individual against the court; Neoplatonic theories of inspiration and learning.
authors.significance: His Homer fixed the English reading of the epics for two centuries, and his tragedies of Bussy D'Ambois and Byron are the fullest English expression of the heroic, Senecan mode.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his claims of gentility and a university degree are unproven.

authors.name: George Douglas Brown
authors.nationality: British; the anti-kailyard novel
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of The House with the Green Shutters, the novel that destroyed the kailyard.
authors.biography: Born George Douglas Brown at Ochiltree, Ayrshire, on 26 January 1869, the illegitimate son of a farmer; he studied at Glasgow and Oxford, worked as a journalist in London, and published The House with the Green Shutters under the name George Douglas in 1901. He died of pneumonia in London on 28 August 1902, at thirty-three.
authors.profile: The House with the Green Shutters is the single most important Scottish novel of the period and the book that ended the kailyard: its unsparing portrait of a small-town tyrant, its refusal of sentiment and its tragic ending gave Scottish fiction its first modern novel and made it the founding text of the Scottish Renaissance.
authors.style: The objective, unsentimental narrative; the free indirect style that enters every mind in the town; the tragic structure of rise and fall; the grotesque and the violent detail; the Ayrshire vernacular in direct speech.
authors.concerns: The small town and its gossip; the tyranny of the father and the failure of the son; commercial ambition and bankruptcy; the provincial mind and the desire to escape; the death of the old Scotland.
authors.significance: The House with the Green Shutters is the most important Scottish novel of the period and the book that ended the kailyard school: its unsparing realism founded the modern Scottish novel and made it the direct ancestor of Lewis Grassic Gibbon and the Scottish Renaissance.

authors.name: George du Maurier
altNames: George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier
authors.nationality: French-born British; the comic illustration, the society novel and the psychological romance
authors.identity: Illustrator and novelist; the author of Trilby, the most popular novel of the 1890s, and the creator of Svengali.
authors.biography: Born George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier in Paris on 6 March 1834; he studied chemistry and then art, lost the sight of one eye, and settled in London in 1860, where he became the principal illustrator of Punch for thirty years. His social cartoons created the Victorian image of the aesthetic and the nouveau riche; Trilby (1894) sold in enormous numbers and gave the world Svengali. He died in London on 8 October 1896.
authors.profile: Du Maurier's Trilby is the great popular novel of the 1890s and one of the founding texts of modern mass culture: its story of the tone-deaf model hypnotised into a great singer by the sinister Svengali gave the language a word and a myth, and its bohemian Paris made the art student a permanent figure of the popular imagination. His Punch drawings are the definitive visual record of Victorian middle-class manners.
authors.style: Direct, confiding narration with comic digression; the bohemian studio and the Latin Quarter; the sinister hypnotist as villain; sentiment and the supernatural; comic illustrations integrated with the text; the society party and the fashionable salon.
authors.concerns: Bohemia and the artist's life; hypnotism and the manipulation of the will; love, beauty and the artist's model; the Englishman abroad and the Latin Quarter; class, manners and the nouveaux riches; the power of the manipulator.
authors.significance: Du Maurier is the central Victorian comic illustrator and the author of Trilby, one of the most popular novels of the century: it created Svengali and the idea of the hypnotic manipulator, it made bohemian Paris a popular literary subject, and his Punch drawings are the essential visual record of Victorian middle-class life.

authors.name: George Eliot
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel and periodical criticism
authors.identity: Novelist, translator, editor and critic, born Mary Ann Evans; the most philosophically ambitious of the Victorian novelists and the one who made realism a conscious literary programme.
authors.biography: Born on 22 November 1819 at South Farm, Arbury, the daughter of Robert Evans, agent to the Newdigate estate; she was educated at boarding schools in Attleborough and Coventry and was converted to evangelical religion in 1832 and away from it, under the influence of Charles and Cara Bray, by 1841. She translated Strauss's Das Leben Jesu (1846) and Feuerbach's Das Wesen des Christentums (1854), edited the Westminster Review from 1851 to 1854, and in 1854 left England with George Henry Lewes, who could not divorce his wife; their union, unlegalised, lasted until his death in 1878, and they lived as husband and wife in London and at The Priory, Regent's Park. Scenes of Clerical Life appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in 1857 under the pseudonym George Eliot; Adam Bede (1859) was an immediate success, and the pseudonym was dropped in 1860. She married John Walter Cross, twenty years her junior, in May 1880, and died in London on 22 December 1880.
authors.profile: Eliot brought to the English novel a philosophical seriousness formed by German idealism, Comtean positivism, Feuerbachian humanism and the new sciences of heredity and social causation. Her realism is not a technique of description but a moral position: the claim that ordinary lives and ordinary provincial places are worthy of art, and that judgement must be suspended while the web of circumstance and inheritance is shown. From Adam Bede through The Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner and Middlemarch to Daniel Deronda her novels widen from the parish to the nation, and their plots turn on the conflict between a vocation and the claims of ordinary happiness. She is the first English novelist to build a novel on the principle of multiple centres of consciousness, and the narratorial voice — ironic, aphoristic and compassionate — is her central instrument.
authors.style: Aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal; free indirect style used to enter many minds without losing critical distance; a 'web' of parallel and counterpointed plots; a careful notation of dialect, provincial speech and class position; a use of symbols that are natural rather than Gothic (the river, the loom, the stone pit, the portrait); chapter epigraphs.
authors.concerns: Sympathy as the basis of ethics; the pressure of the past and of inherited circumstance on the will; vocation and the claims of the affection; women's education and the waste of female intelligence; the movement of religious feeling into secular moral commitment; the individual's relation to the community; the limits of knowledge, in other minds and in history.
authors.significance: Middlemarch is generally taken as the greatest of the Victorian novels and the fullest statement of Victorian liberal realism; Eliot's translation and editorial work carried German thought into English intellectual life, and her criticism shaped the period's ideas of realism and of the novel's moral office. She set the terms for the twentieth-century novel of consciousness (James, Woolf, Proust all read her closely) and for the modern criticism of sympathy in fiction.
authors.uncertainty: The name George Eliot is a pseudonym, and the works published under it are attributed to George Eliot on the evidence of the publisher's records, the correspondence and the contemporary attribution. No work catalogued here carries a disputed, conjectural or shared attribution, and every one of them was published under the author's own name between 1858 and 1879.

authors.name: George Etherege
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Restoration wit and dramatist; the originator of the comedy of manners with The Comical Revenge (1664), She Would if She Could (1668), and especially The Man of Mode (1676), which created the ideal rake-hero Dorimant and set the pattern for Wycherley and Congreve.
authors.biography: Born c. 1635–36, probably in Berkshire; educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge and the Middle Temple, with time in France. His first play, The Comical Revenge (1664), mixed verse and prose; She Would if She Could (1668) was less successful; but The Man of Mode (1676), with its rake Dorimant (thought to caricature Rochester) and the witty Harriet, was the triumph of the age. Etherege led a dissolute court life, was knighted (1679), and served as diplomat at Regensburg (1685–89), where he famously neglected business for pleasure. He returned after the Revolution and died c. 1691–92, possibly in Paris.
authors.profile: The elegant, careless founder of the comedy of manners, whose plays established the prose of witty gallantry, the rake-hero, and the social world of the town that the genre would perfect.
authors.style: Sparkling prose repartee; the rake and the witty heroine; intrigue and sexual politics; a light, ironic tone; and a deliberate 'careless' elegance.
authors.concerns: Wit, gallantry, and libertinism; courtship and marriage as social negotiation; fashion, affectation, and the town; and the amoral play of desire.
authors.significance: The Man of Mode is the first great comedy of manners and defined its conventions; Etherege's rake-hero and social comedy directly shaped Wycherley, Congreve, and the whole tradition of English wit comedy.
authors.uncertainty: Etherege's birth and death dates are approximate, his diplomatic correspondence survives but his private life is thinly documented, and he has been confused with a namesake.

authors.name: George Farquhar
authors.nationality: English (Anglo-Irish)
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish Restoration-early Augustan dramatist; author of the lively, humane comedies The Constant Couple (1699), The Inconstant (1702), and his masterpiece The Beaux' Stratagem (1707), which infused the comedy of manners with warmth, Irish vigour, and social observation.
authors.biography: Born c. 1677–78 at Londonderry, educated at Trinity College, Dublin. He became an actor (stabbing a fellow-player in a stage duel), then a playwright with Love and a Bottle (1698) and The Constant Couple (1699), whose Sir Harry Wildair was hugely popular. He served briefly as an army officer and recruiting agent (the material for The Recruiting Officer, 1706). Despite success he died poor and young on 29 April 1707, weeks after The Beaux' Stratagem. His plays' gaiety and humanity mark the transition from Restoration wit to the gentler comedy of the eighteenth century.
authors.profile: The comic dramatist who softened Restoration intrigue with warmth, humour, and social realism, creating breezy, well-constructed comedies of love, roguery, and provincial life.
authors.style: Lively, humorous prose; brisk plotting; roguish, charming heroes; Irish and provincial colour; and a humane, genial comic tone.
authors.concerns: Love, courtship, and roguery; money and marriage; the world of the provinces and the recruiting office; and the good humour of human frailty.
authors.significance: The Beaux' Stratagem and The Recruiting Officer are among the most enduring comedies of the period, continuously performed and admired for their vitality; Farquhar bridged Restoration and Augustan comedy and influenced Goldsmith and Sheridan.
authors.uncertainty: Farquhar's birth year is uncertain (1677 or 1678) and details of his life are thin; the anecdotes of his stage-duel and poverty are traditional.

authors.biography: Born about 1539 at Cardington, Bedfordshire, into a landed family; educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. authors.name: George Gissing
authors.nationality: English; the realist novel of poverty and the literary profession
authors.identity: Novelist; the great English novelist of the struggling writer and of the urban poor of the 1880s-90s.
authors.biography: Born at Wakefield on 22 November 1857, the son of a chemist; he was a brilliant scholar at Owens College, Manchester, but was expelled and imprisoned for a month in 1876 after stealing money to help a young woman, Nell Harrison, whom he later married. He lived in London and then in the United States (1876-77), returned and married twice more, and supported himself by tutoring and by writing. He wrote twenty-three novels, of which New Grub Street (1891) and The Odd Women (1893) are the best known, and he died at Saint-Jean-de-Luz in France on 28 December 1903.
authors.profile: Gissing wrote the English novel of the failed intellectual: his subject is the educated man or woman without money, condemned to grind in the literary marketplace or in the genteel poverty of the lodging-house. He is a realist of a peculiarly bleak kind, precise about rents, wages, publishers' advances and the cost of respectability, and his best work is a permanent record of the London of the 1880s. He is also, in The Odd Women, one of the first English novelists to take the surplus of unmarried women seriously as a social problem rather than a joke.
authors.style: Grim documentary realism; exact accounting of money, food and rent; the interior monologue of disappointed intelligence; irony verging on despair; London fog, lodging-houses, reading-rooms and offices; a classical, fastidious prose set against sordid material.
authors.concerns: Poverty and the shame of the educated poor; the literary marketplace and the prostitution of talent; marriage as an economic transaction; the 'odd women' and female self-support; class, education and the failure of aspiration; the city as a machine of isolation.
authors.significance: Gissing is the finest English novelist of the literary profession and of lower-middle-class poverty in the 1880s: New Grub Street is the founding novel about the writer's market, and The Odd Women is a central text in the history of English feminism. His work influenced Orwell, who wrote an essay on him, and the twentieth-century novel of the unsuccessful writer.
