authors.name: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
authors.nationality: English; British peer, poet of the Romantic period, and a central figure of the European Romantic movement
authors.identity: Poet above all: writer of narrative and lyric verse, of metrical romances and tales, of verse satire in couplet and ottava rima, and of tragic poems designed for the reader rather than the playhouse; also the first modern literary celebrity, whose life was read as commentary on his work.
authors.biography: Born 22 January 1788 in London, son of Captain 'Mad Jack' Byron (d. 1791) and Catherine Gordon of Aberdeen, he spent part of his childhood in Aberdeen before returning to England. In 1798 he inherited the barony and the embarrassed estate of Newstead Abbey, Nottinghamshire, from his great-uncle the fifth baron. He was at Harrow from 1801, where he wrote and circulated a great deal of school verse, and matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1805, withdrawing in 1808 without a degree. 'Hours of Idleness' was privately printed in 1807, and the hostile Edinburgh Review notice of its enlarged London issue drew from him the reply-satire 'English Bards and Scotch Reviewers' (1809). A journey to Portugal, Spain, Albania, and Greece with his companion John Cam Hobhouse (1809-11) supplied the matter of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage', Cantos I-II, whose appearance in 1812 made his fame in a single season; he sat in the House of Lords, making his first speech against the Frame Bill in 1812. His marriage in January 1815 to Anneabella Milbanke ended in separation in January 1816 amid public scandal, and within months he left England for good, passing by Geneva and Lucerne to Venice (1816-19), Ravenna (1819-21), and Pisa and Genoa (1821-3), where he projected the monthly 'The Liberal' with Leigh Hunt and Percy Bysshe Shelley. In July 1823 he sailed to Greece for the war of independence, fell ill at Missolonghi in December, and died there on 19 April 1824 after repeated bloodletting; burial in Westminster Abbey being refused, he was laid in the Byron vault at Hucknall, Nottinghamshire.
authors.profile: His canon falls into three recognizable groups: the early satire and the romance tales in verse of 1813-16; the meditative-narrative 'Childe Harold' with the lyrics and short poems of the Italian exile; and the late work in which ottava rima and the tragic poem carry his most serious argument ('Beppo', 'Don Juan', 'Manfred', 'Cain', 'Heaven and Earth', the Venetian plays). He wrote no fiction of his own, no systematic criticism, and only prefatory and controversial prose, so his literary thought is best read in the poems, their advertisements and prefaces, and his letters and journals. His late verse tales and dramas in Greece and Italy were also the period's most spectacular commercial successes, and his letters and journals, edited after his death by Thomas Moore, became a foundational Romantic document.
authors.style: Two contrasting manners in one voice: a high, sonorous descriptive rhetoric (Alpine, Adriatic, and Trojan scenery, apostrophe, the proud solitary speaker) and an urban, colloquial, laughing irony learned from Pope and from Italian ottava rima. He rhymes with ease and often with designed anticlimax, interrupts his own narrative to address the reader or publisher, and blends autobiographical confession with romance plot. In the dramas he aimed at a plain, passion-driven declamation and famously refused the 'poetry of description' for the stage.
authors.concerns: Liberty against tyranny, political and domestic; the guilt and self-fashioning of the outlawed aristocrat; scepticism toward revealed religion and sympathy with Milton's rebellious intellect; fame measured against its machinery of publishers and reviewers; sexual love, constancy, and betrayal; the rise and fall of states and dynasties; the capacity of irony to speak truth in a corrupt public culture.
authors.significance: He made the Romantic poet a European public person: 'Byron mania' swept British fashion, imitative verse tales, and the stage, while his example governed the second generation (Shelley's 'Adonais' and 'Epipsychidion' answer him), Pushkin and Lermontov, Mickiewicz, and the French Romantics. 'Don Juan' is the last great English poem in the Augustan satirical line and one of the first modern irony-driven long poems; his tragic poems and the Greek cause for which he died made him a liberal icon deep into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The precise grounds of the 1816 separation and the rumours of incest with his half-sister Augusta Leigh were suppressed in the family settlement and remain a matter of disputed interpretation; the paternity of his daughter Allegra was doubted in contemporary gossip and cannot be settled from the surviving evidence.

authors.name: George Grossmith

authors.identity: Actor, singer and writer; the co-author of The Diary of a Nobody and the principal comedian of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas.
authors.biography: Born George Grossmith in London on 9 December 1847, the son of the entertainer George Grossmith; he created the patter roles in The Sorcerer, H.M.S. Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance, Patience, Iolanthe, Princess Ida, The Mikado, Ruddigore, The Yeomen of the Guard and The Gondoliers. With his brother Weedon he wrote The Diary of a Nobody (1892), first serialised in Punch; his comic lectures and his autobiography A Society Clown (1888) followed. He died in Folkestone on 1 March 1912.
authors.profile: George Grossmith was the greatest English comic performer of his age and, with his brother Weedon, the author of The Diary of a Nobody, the funniest English comic novel of the nineteenth century and the founding text of the suburban comedy of manners.
authors.style: The mock diary form with its deadpan self-importance; the suburban setting of brick and respectability; the running gag and the recurring minor character; the comic understatement of catastrophe; the parody of the Victorian diary and the memoir.
authors.concerns: The suburb and the lower middle class; respectability and its anxieties; social aspiration and its humiliation; the family and the domestic routine; the comic dignity of the ordinary man.
authors.significance: George Grossmith was the greatest English comic performer of his age and, with Weedon Grossmith, the author of The Diary of a Nobody: the funniest English comic novel of the century and the founding text of the suburban comedy of manners, which has never been out of print and which founded the comic suburb in English fiction.

authors.name: George Herbert
authors.nationality: English (Welsh-born)
authors.identity: Anglican priest and devotional poet; author of The Temple, the greatest work of English religious lyric, whose intricate forms enact the struggles and consolations of the soul in God's service.
authors.biography: Born 1593 at Montgomery into the distinguished Herbert family, brother of Lord Herbert of Cherbury; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge (Fellow 1609, MA 1616), where he became Public Orator (1620). Patronized by James I, he hoped for court preferment, but on the king's death turned to the church, taking holy orders (1626) and the poor country rectory of Bemerton near Salisbury (1630). He served as a devoted parish priest ('the holy Mr Herbert') until his death from consumption on 1 March 1633, aged 39. The Temple was published posthumously in 1633 by his friend Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding.
authors.profile: The poet of the parish and the conscience, who made the plain country church the setting for a demanding, intimate, and formally inventive poetry of devotion, doubt, and surrender.
authors.style: Metaphysical wit turned to religious use; shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'); emblematic simplicity; dramatic colloquy with God; puns, scriptural allusion, and a musical variety of stanza forms.
authors.concerns: The soul's relation to God; obedience, affliction, and consolation; the priesthood and pastoral care; the conflict between worldly ambition and spiritual calling; the discipline of prayer.
authors.significance: The Temple is the supreme achievement of English devotional verse, influencing Vaughan, Crashaw, Coleridge, and the twentieth-century religious poets; Herbert's marriage of metaphysical wit to Anglican humility made him the model of the priest-poet.
authors.uncertainty: Herbert's life is documented by Izaak Walton's Life (1670); the dating of individual poems in The Temple is largely inferential.

authors.name: George MacDonald
authors.nationality: Scottish; fantasy, the fairy tale and the Scottish novel
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and Congregational minister; the founding father of modern fantasy and the greatest Victorian writer of the fairy tale.
authors.biography: Born at Huntly, Aberdeenshire, on 10 December 1824, the son of a farmer; educated at King's College Aberdeen and at Highbury College, London, he was minister of a Congregational church at Arundel from 1850 until his unorthodox views on hell forced his resignation in 1853. He supported himself by writing and lecturing, moved to Manchester and then to London, and from 1872 made several reading tours of the United States. He wrote over fifty books, including the Scottish novels of the 1860s, the fairy romances and the adult fantasies Phantastes and Lilith. He died at Ashtead, Surrey, on 18 September 1905.
authors.profile: MacDonald wrote the fairy tale as a form of theology: his fantasies proceed from the premise that the imagination is the organ of spiritual knowledge, and his stories of death, resurrection and the journey of the soul are the direct ancestors of the modern fantasy. He is also the finest Scottish novelist of rural life after Scott, and his portrayal of the Calvinist peasantry in David Elginbrod, Robert Falconer and Sir Gibbie is unmatched.
authors.style: Dream-vision narrative; allegory carried by concrete imagery rather than abstraction; Scottish dialect speech; the kindly, unhurried narrator; the fairy-tale logic of transformation and redemption; a theology of universal love.
authors.concerns: The love of God and the possibility of universal salvation; death and the afterworld; the imagination as spiritual faculty; Scottish Calvinism and the peasant community; childhood and education; poverty and charity.
authors.significance: MacDonald is the founding figure of modern fantasy: C. S. Lewis called Phantastes the book that baptised his imagination, Tolkien and Chesterton acknowledged the debt, and Lilith and The Princess and the Goblin are permanent classics. His Scottish novels are a major achievement of nineteenth-century regional fiction, and his theology of universal love was one of the most original religious positions of the century.

authors.name: George Meredith
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel and poetry
authors.identity: Novelist and poet; the most intellectually demanding of the Victorian novelists and the author of Modern Love and The Egoist.
authors.biography: Born at Portsmouth on 12 February 1828, the grandson of a naval outfitter; his mother died when he was five and he was sent to a Moravian school in Germany at fourteen. He was articled to a solicitor in London in 1845, married Mary Ellen Nicolls — the widowed daughter of Thomas Love Peacock — in 1849, and was left by her in 1858 for the painter Henry Wallis; she died in 1861, and Modern Love (1862) is the record of the marriage. He worked as a publisher's reader for Chapman and Hall (the first reader of Far from the Madding Crowd) and as a journalist, and married Marie Vulliamy in 1864. The Ordeal of Richard Feverel (1859) began his career; Emilia in England (1864), Rhoda Fleming (1865), The Adventures of Harry Richmond (1871), Beauchamp's Career (1876), The Egoist (1879), Diana of the Crossways (1885), One of Our Conquerors (1891) and The Amazing Marriage (1895) followed. He received the Order of Merit in 1905 and died at Box Hill on 18 May 1909.
authors.profile: Meredith wrote the English novel of comedy in the high, philosophic sense: his subject is the ego and its illusions, and his method is a prose of metaphor, epigram and abrupt transition that demands a reader's alertness. Modern Love is a sequence of fifty sixteen-line sonnets that narrates the breakdown of a marriage in the third person, and it is the first English poem to treat sexual infidelity from inside both partners. His women — Diana Warwick, Clara Middleton, Carinthia Jane — are among the most intelligent in Victorian fiction, and his theory that comedy is the 'spirit of the social' and a test of conduct made him, for the next generation, the novelist's novelist.
authors.style: Epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor; dialogue that is a contest of wits; abrupt ironic transitions; the 'comic spirit' as a narrator who corrects the characters; a difficult, allusive syntax; the sonnet sequence with a narrative arc.
authors.concerns: Egoism and self-deception; marriage, constancy and the war of the sexes; the position of the educated woman; the gentleman as a moral problem; scientific evolution and its social implications; English politics and the aristocratic tradition; comedy as a moral instrument.
authors.significance: Meredith is the finest comic intelligence of Victorian fiction and the writer through whom the Victorian novel passed its most demanding test of intelligence: The Egoist is the classic English comedy of the ego, Modern Love the founding sequence of nineteenth-century poems on marriage, and his criticism of fiction shaped Hardy, Gissing and James. He was the first English novelist to be praised primarily for style, and the 1890s regarded him as their master.

authors.name: George Moore
authors.nationality: Irish; the naturalist novel, the memoir and the literature of the 1890s
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and autobiographer; the Irish writer who brought French naturalism into English fiction and the first great modern Irish prose writer.
authors.biography: Born George Augustus Moore at Ballyglass, County Mayo, on 24 February 1852, the son of a landowner and MP; he went to Paris in 1873 to study painting, met Manet, Zola and the Impressionists, and returned to London in 1880. A Modern Lover (1883), A Mummer's Wife (1885) and Esther Waters (1894) brought French naturalism into English; he helped found the Irish Literary Theatre in 1899 and wrote the memoir Hail and Farewell (1911-14). He died in London on 21 January 1933.
authors.profile: Moore wrote the English naturalist novel and the modern literary memoir: A Mummer's Wife and Esther Waters treat the lives of the working woman and the servant with a frankness about sex, money and drink that no English novelist had attempted, and Esther Waters is the finest English novel of domestic service. His later Irish books, The Untilled Field and Hail and Farewell, invented the modern Irish short story and the irreverent literary memoir.
authors.style: Flaubertian impersonality and exact detail; the plain record of work, wages and drink; the unsparing treatment of sexuality; the free indirect style; the colloquial Irish speech of the later stories; the anecdotal and malicious memoir.
authors.concerns: The working woman and domestic service; poverty, drink and the London streets; the Irish land and the Irish peasant; the artist and the literary world; religion and the Catholic childhood; the machinery of literary reputation.
authors.significance: Moore is the founder of English naturalism and the first modern Irish prose writer: Esther Waters is the classic English novel of the servant and one of the great novels of the 1890s, The Untilled Field made the modern Irish short story possible, and Hail and Farewell is the most entertaining literary memoir in the language.

authors.name: George Orwell
authors.nationality: British; the political essay, the documentary report and the dystopian novel
authors.identity: Novelist, essayist and journalist; the greatest English political writer of the century, the author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, and the master of the modern essay.
authors.biography: Born Eric Arthur Blair at Motihari, Bengal, on 25 June 1903, the son of an opium department official; he was educated at Eton, served in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma (1922–27), lived in poverty in London and Paris, and published Down and Out in Paris and London (1933), Burmese Days (1934), The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and Homage to Catalonia (1938). He fought in the Spanish Civil War and was shot through the throat; he wrote for the Tribune and the Observer, broadcast for the BBC, and published Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949). He died of tuberculosis in London on 21 January 1950.
authors.profile: Orwell is the greatest English political writer of the period: his essays ('Politics and the English Language', 'Shooting an Elephant', 'Why I Write') are the finest in the language, The Road to Wigan Pier is the great documentary of the Depression, Homage to Catalonia the finest English book on the Spanish war, and Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four the two most influential political fables ever written in English. He made plain prose a moral instrument.
authors.style: The plain declarative English sentence with no ornament; the essay built as an argument that turns on an example; the documentary detail and the transcribed testimony; the fable and the allegory (Animal Farm); the invented political vocabulary (Newspeak, doublethink); the honesty that records what it would rather not.
authors.concerns: Totalitarianism, propaganda and the corruption of language; poverty, unemployment and the English class system; empire and the colonial servant; the Spanish Civil War and the betrayal of the revolution; the individual against the state; the honest record against the lie.
authors.significance: Orwell is the greatest English political writer of the century and the period's central essayist: Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four are the most influential political fables in English, The Road to Wigan Pier and Homage to Catalonia are permanent documentaries, and his essays made plain prose a moral instrument. His vocabulary — Big Brother, doublethink, Newspeak, thoughtcrime — has entered the world's political language.
authors.uncertainty: Orwell published his books under the pen name George Orwell, first used for Down and Out in Paris and London (1933); his legal name remained Eric Arthur Blair, under which some early periodical writing appeared. Two questions remain open in the sources: how far 'Such, Such Were the Joys' is an accurate account of St Cyprian's, which contemporaries at the school and biographers have challenged, and whether the typescript of 'The Freedom of the Press' was found in 1971 or 1972.

authors.identity: dramatist; poet; pageant-maker
authors.biography: Baptized 25 July 1556; son of the clerk of Christ's Hospital. Educated at Christ's Hospital and Broadgates Hall (later Pembroke College), Oxford, where he took BA (1577) and MA (1579). He came to London in the early 1580s, wrote for the public stage and the City, and dissipated his talents and health; he was buried on 9 November 1596.
authors.profile: His pastoral-mythological court play The Arraignment of Paris (c. 1581–84) pleased Elizabeth; The Old Wives' Tale (c. 1591–93) is a folkloric comedy of enchantment; The Battle of Alcazar (c. 1588–89) and Edward I (c. 1590) are chronicle plays; he also wrote Lord Mayor's pageants and the biblical tragedy David and Bethsabe (c. 1594).
authors.style: Lyrical sweetness, Ovidian ornament, and a gift for pageantry and stage spectacle; the famous 'garden speech' in the anonymous play sometimes assigned to him shows his fluent, decorative blank verse.
authors.concerns: Court compliment and civic ceremony; classical myth reworked for English audiences.
authors.significance: A pioneer of the history play and of polished stage verse; traditionally credited with a share in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus.

authors.name: George Washington Cable
authors.nationality: American; the local-colour story of Louisiana and the literature of racial justice
authors.identity: Novelist and essayist; the first American writer to make New Orleans and the Creole South the subject of serious fiction, and a lifelong campaigner for racial equality.
authors.biography: Born in New Orleans on 12 October 1844, the son of a slaveholding family ruined by the Civil War; he served in the Confederate cavalry, and after the war worked as a clerk and surveyor before publishing Old Creole Days in 1879. He became the most outspoken white southern advocate of civil rights in the 1880s, moved to Massachusetts in 1885, and wrote a series of novels on Louisiana life and history. He died at St Petersburg, Florida, on 31 January 1925.
authors.profile: Cable invented the American local-colour story of the deep South: his Old Creole Days and The Grandissimes record the speech, the courtyards, the manners and the racial complexity of French Louisiana with a precision no northern writer could imitate, and his essays of the 1880s were the most courageous white southern defence of black civil rights in the period. He was also the first American novelist to treat the legacy of slavery and the mixing of the races as the central moral problem of southern life.
authors.style: Exact reproduction of Creole and black dialect; the vivid set piece of courtyard, market and street; the story told through a frame and a remembered voice; the sharp analysis of racial and class difference; the historical romance reconstructed from old New Orleans.
authors.concerns: Slavery, emancipation and the unfinished work of Reconstruction; the Creole inheritance and the mixing of races; New Orleans and the Mississippi; the corruption of the Reconstruction governments; the moral responsibility of the white southerner; the literature of regional memory.
authors.significance: Cable is the founder of the Southern local-colour school and the most important white southern literary voice for racial justice in the nineteenth century: Old Creole Days and The Grandissimes created the literary image of New Orleans, and his civil-rights essays cost him his southern audience while making him a central figure in the American literature of race.

authors.name: George Whitefield
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Calvinistic Methodist preacher of the Great Awakening, the first true celebrity of the Atlantic religious world, whose open-air sermons and journals moved crowds on two continents.
authors.biography: Born at Gloucester in 1714, the son of an innkeeper who died while he was a child, he worked as a servant at the town grammar school and went up to Oxford in 1735 as a humble self-paying student, where he joined the small religious society and experienced the conversion he never ceased to describe. Ordained in the Church of England, he began to preach in the fields about Bristol in 1739 and in London's Moorfields, since the pulpits were closed to him, and crossed the Atlantic repeatedly, preaching through the colonies in 1739-40 and again on great touring circuits. His Calvinism separated him from John Wesley in the early 1740s, and he devoted much of his later energy to fundraising for the Georgia orphan house he called Bethesda and for the preaching houses his converts built. His journals and his Narrative of God's Dealings with Him (1740) made his inner life public property, and Benjamin Franklin, who printed them, left the most admired contemporary account of his command of crowds. He died at Newburyport in Massachusetts in September 1770 and was buried there beneath the pulpit he had used.
authors.profile: A declaimer of irresistible voice and posture who turned conversion narrative and printed publicity into an engine of revival.
authors.style: Vocal, theatrical, extempore sermon style preserved imperfectly in print; vivid personal narrative; plain scriptural address with an actor's gesture; prolific printed circulars and journals.
authors.concerns: Election, new birth and the immediate call of the Spirit; the ministry of the word out of doors; the unity of the revival across the denominations; the religious education and charity of converts, and the problem of slavery in the colonies he loved.
authors.significance: He created the model of the transatlantic evangelist and gave the Great Awakening its public form, influencing American preaching, revivalism and the culture of religious celebrity.
authors.uncertainty: His early years at Oxford and the chronology of his ordination are recorded unevenly, and his journals were edited by friends and by himself.

authors.name: Gerald Massey
authors.nationality: British; the Chartist poet and the Egyptologist
authors.identity: Poet, lecturer and Egyptologist; one of the leading Chartist poets and a pioneer of the comparative study of myth.
authors.biography: Born at Tring, Hertfordshire, on 29 May 1828, the son of a canal boatman; he worked in a silk mill from the age of eight, published Voices of Freedom (1850) and The Ballad of Babe Christabel (1854), and became one of the most popular poets of the 1850s. authors.name: Gerald of Wales
authors.nationality: Welsh-Norman
authors.identity: chronicler; topographer; churchman
authors.biography: Grandson of Nest, the Welsh princess, and of a Norman baron; educated at Paris, he became archdeacon of Brecon and courtier of Henry II, accompanying Prince John to Ireland in 1185 and preaching the crusade through Wales with Archbishop Baldwin in 1188. He twice sought the see of St Davids and was twice refused; retired to Lincoln, he died c. 1223, still writing.
authors.profile: Author of the Topographia Hibernica (1188), Expugnatio Hibernica (1189), Itinerarium Cambriae (1191), Descriptio Cambriae (1194), and the autobiographical De Rebus a Se Gestis, among much else.
authors.style: Vivid, gossipy, self-promoting Latin; ethnography seasoned with marvel and prejudice; the love of a good story over strict accuracy; an unflagging attention to his own career.
authors.concerns: The Welsh church's independence; the conquest and description of Ireland; the character and customs of the Welsh and Irish peoples.
authors.significance: The Itinerarium and Descriptio are the classic medieval accounts of Wales, and the Expugnatio the principal narrative of the English conquest of Ireland; his works are foundational for both national historiographies.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his own writings, though copious, are self-serving.

authors.name: Geraldine Jewsbury
authors.nationality: British; the novel of the woman's vocation
authors.identity: Novelist, reviewer and correspondent; the author of The Half Sisters and one of the most influential literary women of the mid-Victorian period.
authors.biography: Born Geraldine Endsor Jewsbury at Measham, Derbyshire, on 22 August 1812; she moved to Manchester and then London, where she became the reader for Bentley's and a reviewer for the Athenaeum, and the intimate friend of Jane Welsh Carlyle. Zoe (1845), The Half Sisters (1848), Marian Withers (1851) and Constance Herbert (1855) followed. She died in London on 23 September 1880.
authors.profile: Geraldine Jewsbury wrote The Half Sisters, one of the most important English novels of the woman's vocation and a founding text of the novel of female independence: her Manchester setting, her professional heroine and her argument that a woman's work is her life made her the most radical of the pre-Braddon novelists and a model for the New Woman fiction.
authors.style: The double heroine divided between marriage and vocation; the Manchester commercial setting; the argument in dialogue; the reviewer's irony; the refusal of the conventional ending.
authors.concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.

authors.name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period
authors.identity: Poet and Jesuit priest; the great technical innovator of Victorian poetry, whose work was almost entirely unpublished in his lifetime.
authors.biography: Born on 28 July 1844 into a High Church family, educated at Highgate School and Balliol College, Oxford, where he was taught by Walter Pater and befriended by Robert Bridges. He became a Roman Catholic in 1866 and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868, burning his early poems; he was ordained in 1877, taught at Stonyhurst and in Lancashire, and held parish posts in London, Oxford, Glasgow and Liverpool, becoming Professor of Greek at the Royal University of Dublin in 1884. His poems were sent to Bridges and to Coventry Patmore but not published; the 'terrible' sonnets of 1885 and the Dublin poems record a crisis of desolation. He died of typhoid in Dublin on 8 June 1889, and Bridges edited the first edition in 1918.
authors.profile: Hopkins invented sprung rhythm — a metre based on stress rather than on the count of syllables, with a fixed number of stresses per line and any number of unstressed syllables between them — and inscape, the theory that every created thing has an individual pattern that the poet must perceive and render. His poetry is devotional in argument and radically modern in technique: dense alliteration, compound epithets, compressed syntax, and a rhythm that breaks the iambic habit of English verse.
authors.style: Sprung rhythm; heavy alliteration and internal rhyme; compound and coined words ('dapple-dawn-drawn', 'selfwrung'); exclamatory syntax and abrupt ellipsis; the sonnet form used with extreme variation; a diction that draws on Anglo-Saxon and on Welsh and Latin poetry.
authors.concerns: The glory of God in created particularity; the Jesuit discipline and the exercises of obedience; the beauty of nature and the industrial destruction of it ('Binsey Poplars', 'God's Grandeur'); personal desolation and the dark night of the soul; death, resurrection and the 'terrible' sonnets; Wales, Lancashire and Ireland.
authors.significance: Hopkins is the technical origin of free verse's stress-based metrics in English and the ancestor of the modernist line from Pound and Eliot to the confessional poets. The posthumous 1918 edition changed the course of English poetry, and the 'terrible' sonnets are among the most powerful religious poems in the language.
authors.uncertainty: Almost the whole corpus remained in manuscript and was published posthumously (1918, ed. Robert Bridges; the 4th edition of 1967 ed. Gardner and MacKenzie is standard). The dating of individual poems depends on autograph fair copies and on the letters to Bridges, Dixon and Patmore.

authors.name: Gerrard Winstanley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Digger (True Leveller) leader and radical pamphleteer; his tracts — The New Law of Righteousness (1649) and The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652) — argued for communal cultivation of the land and an agrarian communism grounded in reason and the inner light.
authors.biography: Born c. 1609 at Wigan, Lancashire, son of a merchant; he worked as a cloth merchant in London before being bankrupted by the Civil Wars. In 1649 he led the 'Diggers' in communally cultivating St George's Hill and other commons in Surrey, publishing pamphlets defending the action against landlords and the state. Suppressed by local opposition and the authorities, the movement collapsed by 1650. His fullest statement, The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652), dedicated to Cromwell, set out a communist commonwealth governed by reason and law. Little is known of his later life; he may have become a Quaker and died c. 1676.
authors.profile: The visionary radical whose prophetic, plain-style pamphlets argued that true freedom requires common ownership of the earth and the abolition of wage labour, grounding communism in reason, scripture, and the 'inner light'.
authors.style: Urgent, prophetic, plain-style pamphlet prose; scriptural and rationalist argument; dialogue and declaration; and a direct, popular address.
authors.concerns: Common ownership and agrarian communism; the rights of the poor and the commons; reason, the inner light, and true religion; the critique of private property, law, and clergy; and popular sovereignty.
authors.significance: Winstanley is the foremost theorist of the Diggers and an early exponent of agrarian socialism and communism; his tracts are foundational documents of English radicalism and have been central to Marxist and libertarian-socialist readings of the English Revolution.
authors.uncertainty: Winstanley's life after 1652 is very poorly documented; his birth and death dates are approximate and his later Quakerism is conjectural.

authors.name: Gertrude Stein
authors.nationality: American; the experimental prose, the portrait and the syntax of repetition
authors.identity: Writer and patron; the great American experimentalist of the period, the host of the Paris salon that made the Lost Generation, and the inventor of a prose without nouns.
authors.biography: Born Gertrude Stein in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, on 3 February 1874 into a wealthy German-Jewish family; she studied at Radcliffe under William James and at Johns Hopkins medicine, moved to Paris in 1903 with her brother Leo, and began collecting the paintings that made 27 rue de Fleurus the centre of modern art. Three Lives appeared in 1909, Tender Buttons in 1914, The Making of Americans in 1925 and The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas in 1933. She lived with Alice B. Toklas from 1907 and died at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 27 July 1946.
authors.profile: Stein is the great experimentalist of the period: her 'continuous present', her repetition, her abolition of the noun and her cubist portraits made a prose that dismantles the conventions of English syntax, and she taught a generation of American writers — Hemingway among them — how to write a sentence. The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is one of the period's most entertaining books, and her Paris salon was the social centre of modernism.
authors.style: The continuous present and the deliberate repetition; the abolition of the noun and the article; the portrait made of repeated traits; the cubist arrangement of phrases; the plain declarative sentence used against its own grammar; the memoir written as a joke and a history at once.
authors.concerns: The making of Americans and the American family; the ordinary object and the ordinary life; the Paris of the avant-garde; genius, patronage and the woman artist; the war and the occupation; language itself as a subject.
authors.significance: Stein is the central American experimental writer of the period: Three Lives and Tender Buttons changed the possibilities of English prose, her Paris salon made modernism a social fact, The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is a permanent memoir, and her influence on Hemingway, Anderson and the American sentence is beyond calculation.

authors.name: Gilbert Burnet
authors.nationality: English (Scottish-born; Church of England)
authors.identity: Scottish-born Anglican bishop, historian, and memoirist; author of the History of the Reformation of the Church of England (1679–1715) and the posthumous History of His Own Time, whose vivid, opinionated accounts are primary sources for the politics and religion of the era.
authors.biography: Born 2 September 1643 in Edinburgh, educated at the University of Aberdeen and in Holland; ordained in the Scottish church, he travelled and preached widely, becoming a moderate latitudinarian and a chaplain to Charles II. He fell from favour, went into exile after the accession of James II (1685), and supported William of Orange, becoming Bishop of Salisbury (1689) and a leading Whig churchman. His History of the Reformation (in parts, 1679–1715) won him fame (and a doctorate from Oxford); his memoir, History of His Own Time, was published posthumously (1724–34). He had attended the deathbed of the Earl of Rochester (1680), which he recorded. He died on 17 March 1715.
authors.profile: The busy, partisan, and readable bishop-historian whose histories and memoir give a vivid, if biased, first-hand account of the Reformation, the Restoration, and the Revolution.
authors.style: Lively, discursive, opinionated historical prose; memoir and eyewitness reportage; a plain, energetic style; and polemical digression.
authors.concerns: Church history and the Reformation; the politics and religion of Restoration and Revolution England; latitudinarianism and toleration; and the defence of the Protestant succession.
authors.significance: Burnet's History of the Reformation and History of His Own Time are indispensable (if partisan) sources for the period; his memoirs of Rochester's conversion and of the Whig churchmen illuminate the religious politics of the age.
authors.uncertainty: Burnet's life is well documented through his own writings; his histories are avowedly partisan and require critical use, and the History of His Own Time was edited and published posthumously.

authors.name: Gilbert White
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Selborne naturalist and clergyman whose Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne (1789), assembled from letters to correspondents, founded the English observation of the living world.
authors.biography: Born at Selborne in 1720 into a family of Hampshire clergymen and college men, he was educated at Winchester and at Oriel College, Oxford, took holy orders, and returned to the parish of his birth, of which he held the living. He never married and spent his income on his books and collections. For decades he kept registers of the weather and of the dates of flowering, bird arrival, nesting and hibernation, and he tested his questions by experiment, on the torpor of tortoises and bats, on the flight of swifts and swallows, on the insect world and on the habits of the field and the garden. His letters on these matters went to the Royal Society and to correspondents, above all to Daines Barrington and to the naturalist Thomas Pennant, whose questions and his own made the printed book. His book appeared at last in 1789, cast as a correspondence, and its two parts were quickly followed by a third volume of further letters. He died at Selborne in 1793.
authors.profile: The quiet observer of a single parish, whose method of numbered dates, experiment and plain statement made small facts carry weight.
authors.style: Epistolary, unhurried and exact prose; dated field entries and the language of experiment; a naturalist's precision joined to a countryman's affection and gentle humour.
authors.concerns: The seasonal movements and instincts of birds and beasts; the limits of the systems of the schools; local history, antiquities and the surface of an English parish; the evidence of patient observation against the authority of books.
authors.significance: His book became the most beloved of English natural histories and a model for field biology, phenology and the whole later literature of the countryside.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his observations and the relation between the manuscript journals and the printed letters have been re-examined by later editors.

authors.name: Grace King
authors.nationality: American; the Louisiana story and the Creole memory
authors.identity: Novelist and historian; the finest writer of the Louisiana local-colour story and the recorder of the Creole past.
authors.biography: Born Grace Elizabeth King in New Orleans on 29 November 1852; after the failure of her family's sugar plantation she turned to writing, and Balcony Stories (1893) made her reputation. Monsieur Motte (1888), Tales of a Time and Place (1892), New Orleans: The Place and the People (1895) and The Pleasant Ways of St Medard (1916) followed. She died in New Orleans on 14 January 1932.

authors.style: The balcony story told from above the street; the Creole French in direct speech; the elegiac frame of the lost regime; the ironic ending; the history folded into anecdote.

authors.name: Grant Allen
authors.nationality: Canadian-British; the scientific populariser, the sensation novel and the New Woman fiction
authors.identity: Writer and science populariser; the author of The Woman Who Did, the most scandalous New Woman novel of the 1890s, and one of the busiest men of letters of the age.
authors.biography: Born Charles Grant Blairfindie Allen at Kingston, Ontario, on 24 February 1848, the son of an Irish Protestant minister; he was educated in Canada, France and England, and taught at Brighton College and in Jamaica before turning to writing in 1876. He wrote over thirty books of popular science and evolution, then turned to fiction, and The Woman Who Did (1895) made him notorious. He died at Hindhead, Surrey, on 25 October 1899.
authors.profile: Allen wrote the science of his age for the general reader and then put the same evolutionary arguments into fiction: his 'Hill-Top Novels' and the New Woman stories dramatise the propositions of Darwinism, heredity and free love, and The Woman Who Did was the most radical feminist novel of the decade — its heroine refuses marriage because it degrades women and dies for her principles. His scientific journalism made evolution a common English possession.
authors.style: Clear, expository prose; the argument carried by a thesis-plot; the systematic application of evolutionary theory to social questions; the shocking set piece; the plain and deliberate refusal of literary ornament; the travel sketch of Sussex and the Riviera.
authors.concerns: Evolution, heredity and the science of society; marriage law and free union; the position of women and the 'woman question'; religion and the secular worldview; the English countryside and its natural history; the ethics of scientific progress.
authors.significance: Allen is the most influential scientific populariser of the late Victorian period and the author of the most radical New Woman novel: The Woman Who Did made him the most discussed novelist of 1895, his science writing reached an enormous public, and he is a central figure in the transmission of Darwinism into English literary culture.

authors.name: Granville Sharp
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: London merchant's apprentice turned jurist-divine, the first great legal strategist of British abolition, who made the condition of enslaved people in England a question of common law.
authors.biography: Born at Durham in 1735 into a large clerical family, he was apprenticed to a London draper at fifteen and, with the help of a legacy, kept himself free for study, mastering law, divinity, biblical languages, music and a remarkable range of authors. A beaten black servant, Jonathan Strong, whom his brother's hospital had discharged, drew him in the mid-1760s into the question of whether a man could be held as property in England, and he answered it by research and by litigation. He gave counsel and money to the test cases of the following years, and the cause of James Somerset, argued before Lord Mansfield in 1772, was pressed forward by his advice and reporting. He printed legal essays and letters maintaining that slavery had no footing in English law, corresponded with governors and colonists, promoted schemes for settling freed people in Africa, and was among the founders of the committee of 1787 for the abolition of the trade, in which Ottobah Cugoano lived and worked in his household. He wrote also on prophecy, on translation and on the affairs of the church, and died unmarried at Fulham on 6 July 1813, buried in the churchyard there.
authors.profile: A lay lawyer of immense industry who read texts, digested opinions and turned scholarship into an instrument for the deliverance of individuals.
authors.style: Dense, citational and dogged prose; folio-long footnotes of law, scripture and the fathers; argument built from authority pressed to a single conclusion; a devout and combative directness.
authors.concerns: The legal status of persons on English soil; the sin and the policy of the slave trade; the rights of the individual against magistrates and merchants; the interpretation of prophecy and of the languages of the Bible; the duty of public charity.
authors.significance: He made the Somerset judgment possible and founded the legal and organisational base of British abolition, standing beside Wilberforce and Equiano as an architect of the movement that ended the trade.
authors.uncertainty: The exact contribution of his advisers and of Cugoano to his papers and cases is difficult to separate, and his chronology of the earlier suits is debated.

authors.name: H. D. (Hilda Doolittle)
authors.nationality: American; the imagist lyric, the long poem and the modernist woman's epic
authors.identity: Poet and novelist; the finest poet of Imagism and the author of Trilogy, one of the great long poems of the Second World War.
authors.biography: Born Hilda Doolittle in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, on 10 September 1886 into a Moravian family; she studied at Bryn Mawr, travelled to Europe in 1911, and was named 'H. D., Imagiste' by Pound in 1912. She married Richard Aldington in 1913, published Sea Garden (1916), had a daughter by Cecil Gray in 1919, and began a long relationship with the novelist Bryher; she lived in Switzerland and London, was analysed by Freud in 1933–34, and wrote Trilogy during the London Blitz (published 1944–46) and Helen in Egypt (1961). She died in Zurich on 27 September 1961.
authors.profile: H. D. is the purest poet of Imagism and one of the most important women writers of the period. Sea Garden gave the movement its permanent texts; her later long poems — Trilogy, Helen in Egypt — turned the imagist fragment into a mythic epic of war, exile and female divinity, and her prose (HERmione, Tribute to Freud) is among the most experimental of the century. She is the poet through whom modernism becomes a woman's tradition.
authors.style: The single crystalline image; the short free-verse line broken at the phrase; the Greek mask and the mythic persona; the hard, mineral vocabulary of sea, stone and flower; the absence of the article and the connective; the ecstatic repetition of the late long poems.
authors.concerns: The sea, the shore and the mineral world; Greek myth and the female god; war, the Blitz and the ruined city; exile, expatriation and the woman artist; the body, illness and analysis; the mother and the daughter; the sacred and the occult.
authors.significance: H. D. is the finest poet of Imagism and the founder of the modernist woman's epic: Sea Garden gave free verse its purest examples, Trilogy is one of the great poems of the Second World War, and Helen in Egypt rewrote the epic tradition from a woman's point of view. Her recovery in the 1970s and 1980s made her central to the modernist canon.

authors.name: H. P. Lovecraft
authors.nationality: American; the weird tale's architect of the Cthulhu Mythos
authors.identity: Writer of the weird tale; the creator of the Cthulhu Mythos and of the cosmic horror.
authors.biography: Born Howard Phillips Lovecraft at Providence, Rhode Island, on 20 August 1890; he grew up in the antiquarian Providence of his grandfather's library, wrote for the amateur press, and from 1923 made the weird tale of the pulps - The Colour Out of Space (1927), The Call of Cthulhu (1928), At the Mountains of Madness (1936) and The Shadow over Innsmouth (1936) - into the cosmic horror of the indifferent universe. He died at Providence, in poverty, on 15 March 1937, and the mythos he built became the foundation of the modern weird tale.
authors.profile: H. P. Lovecraft is the architect of the modern weird tale: the Cthulhu Mythos made the horror of the cosmos - the indifferent universe, the buried gods, the degenerate town - the matter of the pulp tale, and his influence on the horror and the science fiction of the later century is unmatched by any writer of the pulps.
authors.style: The antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript; the adjectives of the unnameable and the geometry that is not Euclidean; the New England of the decayed port and the haunted hill; the cosmic indifference in place of the ghost's malice; the tale told as the document of the scholar.

authors.significance: H. P. Lovecraft is the architect of the modern weird tale: the Cthulhu Mythos made the cosmic horror of the indifferent universe the matter of the pulp tale, and his influence on the later horror is unmatched.

authors.name: H. Rider Haggard
authors.nationality: English; the imperial adventure romance and the lost-world story
authors.identity: Novelist and agricultural reformer; the author of King Solomon's Mines and She, and the founder of the modern adventure romance of Africa.
authors.biography: Born Henry Rider Haggard at Bradenham, Norfolk, on 22 June 1856; he went to South Africa in 1875 as secretary to the governor of Natal and served on the staff of Sir Theophilus Shepstone during the annexation of the Transvaal, returning to England in 1879. King Solomon's Mines (1885) made him famous at once, and he published over sixty books, including She (1887), Allan Quatermain (1887), Cleopatra (1889) and Eric Brighteyes (1891). He served on agricultural commissions in the 1890s and was knighted in 1912, dying in London on 14 May 1925.
authors.profile: Haggard wrote the adventure romance of the imperial world: his Africa is a place of lost civilisations, ancient treasure and supernatural women, and his narrative method — the plain testimony of the hunter, the discovered document, the framing editor — gave the fantastic a documentary authority that the modern adventure story has never lost. He was also a serious critic of the imperial project in his own way, and Ayesha is one of the great disturbing figures of English fiction.
authors.style: The first-person testimony of the practical man; the frame narrative and the discovered manuscript; the precise geographical and ethnographic detail; the ordeal and the escape; the archaic and the supernatural encountered as fact.
authors.concerns: Empire and the exploration of Africa; the lost civilisation and the ancient world; the supernatural woman and the limits of knowledge; courage, hunting and masculine virtue; reincarnation and immortality; race and the imperial imagination.
authors.significance: Haggard founded the modern adventure romance and the lost-world story: King Solomon's Mines and She created the formula of the imperial adventure that Conan Doyle, Kipling and the cinema would develop, and Ayesha is one of the most influential female figures in English popular fiction.

authors.name: Hall Caine
authors.nationality: British; the Manx romance and the three-decker bestseller
authors.identity: Novelist, dramatist and Manx patriot; the most popular serious novelist in the world in the 1890s, and the first English writer to sell in millions.
authors.biography: Born Thomas Henry Hall Caine at Runcorn on 13 May 1853 to a Manx father and an English mother; he was raised in Liverpool and on the Isle of Man, trained as an architect, and became a lecturer and critic before The Deemster (1887) made him famous. The Manxman (1894), The Christian (1897), The Eternal City (1901) and The Woman of Knockaloe (1923) followed. He was made a Companion of Honour in 1918 and died at Greeba Castle, Isle of Man, on 31 August 1931.
authors.profile: Caine wrote the most widely read serious novels of the 1890s and the first English bestsellers in the modern sense, selling in hundreds of thousands and being adapted for the stage and screen. He put the Isle of Man and its dialect into fiction, and his melodramas of conscience and renunciation set the pattern for the popular religious novel that dominated the circulating libraries at the end of the century.
authors.style: The three-decker architecture of climax and reunion; the Manx landscape and dialect as a moral setting; the melodrama of renunciation and sacrifice; the serious 'problem' theme carried by a popular plot; the plain, emphatic, declarative prose of the platform orator.
authors.concerns: The relation of religious faith to modern doubt; sexual temptation and the renunciation of desire; the island community against the individual conscience; the position of women under a double standard; the duty of the artist to the people.
authors.significance: Hall Caine was the most popular serious novelist in the world in the 1890s and the founding figure of the modern bestseller: The Deemster and The Manxman put the Isle of Man at the centre of English fiction, and his commercial success made the Victorian literary marketplace into a mass market.

authors.name: Hamlin Garland
authors.nationality: American; the Middle Border story and the literature of agrarian protest
authors.identity: Novelist, essayist and reformer; the founder of the American realistic story of the farm and the chronicler of the Middle Border.
authors.biography: Born Hannibal Hamlin Garland at West Salem, Wisconsin, on 14 September 1860, the son of a homesteader; he taught school, homesteaded in Dakota, and went to Boston in 1884 to study and lecture. Main-Travelled Roads (1891) made him the spokesman of the western farmer; he campaigned for the Populist Party, wrote the 'Middle Border' memoirs from 1917, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1922. He died in Hollywood on 4 March 1940.
authors.profile: Garland founded the American literature of the farm: Main-Travelled Roads is the first American story collection to tell the truth about the drudgery, debt and loneliness of midwestern farm life, and its revolt against the sentimental rural idyll made it the central literary document of the Populist movement. He was also the first American writer to theorise 'veritism', the doctrine that fiction should record the actual conditions of the ordinary life, and his Middle Border memoirs are a classic of American autobiography.
authors.style: Plain, documentary, unadorned prose; the single incident that reveals a life; dialect and the actual speech of the farm; the grey landscape and the unremitting labour; the political argument carried through the situation; the memoir of the ordinary family.
authors.concerns: The farm, debt and the single tax; the loneliness and drudgery of women on the prairie; Populism and the revolt of the farmer; the closing of the frontier; the Middle Border and the passing of the pioneer generation; the artist who escapes and the price of escape.
authors.significance: Garland is the founder of American agrarian realism and the central literary voice of the Populist revolt: Main-Travelled Roads changed the American picture of the farm for ever, his 'veritism' was the American version of naturalist doctrine, and his Middle Border books are among the great American memoirs of the westward movement.

authors.name: Hannah Cowley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Dramatist and poet, one of the most successful female playwrights of the late eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Hannah Parkhouse on 14 March 1743 at Tiverton in Devon, the daughter of a bookseller, she married Thomas Cowley and moved to London, where she supported herself by writing. Her poems circulated widely under the name Anna Matilda. Beginning in the later 1770s she became the most performed woman dramatist of her generation, writing comedies and sentimental drama for Drury Lane and Covent Garden, of which the best known is The Belle's Stratagem, with later successes including Which Is the Wife?. She retired from the theatre in the 1780s, returned to Devon after her husband's death, and continued to publish verse. She died at Tiverton on 11 March 1809.
authors.profile: A writer of sentimental and witty comedy and verse who became the most frequently performed woman dramatist of her era, her plays championing female constancy and cleverness within the comic and sentimental modes.
authors.style: Neat comic dialogue in the manner of sentimental comedy; well-made plots of courtship and testing; virtuous, articulate heroines; and conventional, polished eighteenth-century verse.
authors.concerns: Female constancy and virtue; wit and the testing of character in marriage; reputation and delicacy; and the social position of women within sentimental comedy.
authors.significance: The most successful female playwright of the 1770s and 1780s in London, whose comedies held the repertory and whose career is a landmark in the history of women's professional authorship in the theatre.
authors.uncertainty: Her year of birth has sometimes been given as 1742 or 1743, and her death date was long misreported in some older sources; modern scholarship, following the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, fixes it as 1809.

authors.name: Hannah More
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Writer, dramatist, and philanthropist, a Bluestocking and Evangelical who became one of the most influential moral and religious authors of her age.
authors.biography: Born on 2 February 1745 at Fishponds near Bristol, the daughter of a schoolmaster, she was educated partly at her father's schools and moved in Bath and London literary circles, where she was befriended by Joshua Reynolds and the Montagus and associated with the Bluestockings. She wrote plays and poems, including the popular tragedy Percy (1777), and conduct works. In later life she turned decisively to Evangelical and moral writing and philanthropy, becoming associated with abolition and popular religious tract work. She died at Clifton on 7 September 1833.
authors.profile: A versatile author of drama, conduct literature, and religious and moral writing who bridged the fashionable literary world of the 1770s and the Evangelical reform culture of the following decades.
authors.style: Polished sentimental drama and conduct prose in her early career; then a plain, persuasive, urgent moral and religious manner aimed at wide popular readership.
authors.concerns: Female education and conduct; religion, evangelism, and social duty; the abolition of slavery and moral reform; taste versus piety; and the responsibilities of the educated to the poor.
authors.significance: One of the most prolific and widely read women writers of her era, whose career traces the shift from Augustan literary society to Evangelical reform, and whose later tract work reshaped popular religious literature.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is extensively documented; some details of her early education and the precise dating of individual plays and tracts vary across sources.

Seth's Brother's Wife (1887), The Lawton Girl (1890), The Damnation of Theron Ware (1896) and ill-fated Gloria Mundi (1898) followed. He died in London on 19 October 1898.

authors.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
authors.nationality: American; the anti-slavery novel and the regional sketch
authors.identity: Novelist and abolitionist; the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, the most influential novel ever published in the United States.
authors.biography: Born at Litchfield, Connecticut, on 14 June 1811, the daughter of the evangelical reformer Lyman Beecher; she was educated at her sister Catharine's Hartford Female Seminary and moved with the family to Cincinnati in 1832, where she married the clergyman and biblical scholar Calvin Stowe in 1836 and lived for eighteen years on the border of the slave state of Kentucky. Uncle Tom's Cabin was serialised in 1851-52 and published as a book in 1852; she wrote some thirty more books and died at Hartford on 1 July 1896.
authors.profile: Stowe wrote the novel as a moral instrument: Uncle Tom's Cabin is built for conversion, moving from comic domesticity to scenes of almost unbearable suffering, and its sentimental method was the most effective political rhetoric of the century. She was also a superb regional writer, and her New England village sketches and her novels of Calvinist households are the finest fictional record of nineteenth-century New England domestic life.
authors.style: Sentimental tableaux designed to produce tears and conversion; dialect speech, black and Yankee; direct address to the reader; comic domestic dialogue; scriptural quotation and hymn; abrupt shifts of tone from comedy to martyrdom.
authors.concerns: Slavery and its destruction of families; Christian faith under persecution; the moral responsibility of the North; domesticity and the home as a moral unit; Calvinism and conversion; women's moral authority.
authors.significance: Uncle Tom's Cabin is the most influential novel in American history: it sold 300,000 copies in its first year in the United States and a million in Britain, was translated into more than sixty languages, and is credited by Lincoln's reported remark with starting the Civil War. It is a founding text of the American novel, of abolitionist literature and of the literature of human rights.

authors.name: Harriet E. Wilson
authors.nationality: African-American; the first African-American woman's novel
authors.identity: Novelist and seamstress; the author of Our Nig, the first novel published by an African-American woman in the United States.
authors.biography: Born Harriet E. Adams in Milford, New Hampshire, in 1825, apparently the daughter of a free black man and a white woman; she was indentured as a servant to a farm family after her father's death and was cruelly treated, then worked as a seamstress. She married Thomas Wilson, a fugitive slave and lecturer, who abandoned her, and she wrote Our Nig (1859) to raise money for herself and her son, who died young. She died in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1900.
authors.profile: Wilson wrote the first African-American woman's novel and the first American novel about the free black experience in the North: Our Nig is a fictional autobiography of a mixed-race indentured servant in a New Hampshire household, and it takes the form of a domestic sentimental novel in order to indict northern racism and the 'peculiar institution' of New England servitude. Its recovery in 1983 rewrote the chronology of African-American fiction.
authors.style: First-person and third-person autobiographical narrative; the sentimental domestic mode turned into protest; documentary detail of indentured labour; ironic addresses to the reader; the appeal for patronage printed with the text.
authors.concerns: Northern racism and 'slavery's shadows'; indentured servitude and child labour; the mixed-race woman and her vulnerability; Christian hypocrisy; the economics of the free black woman; motherhood and loss.
authors.significance: Our Nig is the founding novel of African-American women's literature and the first African-American novel to be published in the United States by a woman: its recovery in 1983 by Henry Louis Gates Jr pushed back the chronology of African-American fiction and made Wilson a central figure in American literary history.

authors.name: Harriet Jacobs
authors.nationality: African-American; the slave narrative and the literature of the fugitive woman
authors.identity: Writer and abolitionist; the author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, the first full-length slave narrative written by a woman.
authors.biography: Born into slavery in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813; she was taught to read by her mistress and, after her mother's death, was taken into the household of Dr James Norcom, whose sexual pursuit she escaped by hiding for seven years in a small garret above her grandmother's shed. She escaped to the North in 1842, was freed in 1852, worked as a nursemaid in New York and as a relief worker among the freedpeople in Virginia during and after the Civil War. She died in Washington in March 1897.
authors.profile: Jacobs wrote the slave narrative as a woman's testimony: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl tells what the male narratives could not — the sexual exploitation of enslaved women, the destruction of motherhood, and the cost of protecting a daughter's honour — and it does so in a controlled, ironic first person that addresses a white female readership directly. It is the founding text of African-American women's autobiography.
authors.style: First-person retrospective narrative with direct appeal to the reader; the concealment of the narrator's name and identity; scenes of domestic terror and comic endurance; the seven-year hiding as a central emblem; plain documentary prose with a strong ironic edge.
authors.concerns: Slavery and sexual exploitation; motherhood and the sale of children; the cult of true womanhood and its exclusion of black women; concealment, literacy and self-defence; the North and the Fugitive Slave Law; Christian hypocrisy.
authors.significance: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl is a founding text of African-American women's writing and of American autobiography: it is the first slave narrative to make the sexual abuse of enslaved women its central subject, and its account of the seven-year hiding is one of the most extraordinary documents in American literature. Long read as fiction, it was authenticated as autobiography in the 1980s and is now canonical.

authors.name: Harriet Martineau
authors.nationality: English; political economy, social analysis and the novel of ideas
authors.identity: Sociologist, political economist, journalist and novelist; the first woman to earn a living by the Victorian periodical press and the great populariser of political economy.
authors.biography: Born at Norwich on 12 June 1802 into a Unitarian family of manufacturers; she lost most of the family fortune in 1829 and began writing to support herself, publishing Illustrations of Political Economy (1832-34), which sold in enormous numbers. She travelled to America in 1834-36 and wrote Society in America (1837) and Retrospect of Western Travel (1838) after a tour of the slave states that made her an abolitionist. She wrote thirty-five books, translated Comte, edited a periodical, and after 1855 lived at Ambleside, where she wrote leaders for the Daily News while ill. She died at Ambleside on 27 June 1876.
authors.profile: Martineau invented the popular social-science essay and the sociological travel book. Her Illustrations of Political Economy are fictional case studies designed to teach the new science of political economy to ordinary readers; Society in America and its companion volume are among the founding texts of English sociology, and her Autobiography is one of the most exact self-portraits in the language. She wrote as an authority, not as a lady, and she made the position of women, the poor and the slave the test cases of social analysis.
authors.style: The exemplary narrative with a documented argument; the plain declarative sentence; the systematic division into topics; the use of statistics and first-hand observation; the leader and the review essay as forms of public education.
authors.concerns: Political economy and the condition of the working classes; slavery and abolition; the position of women and the marriage law; education; the comparative study of religions and of society; the authority of the woman writer.
authors.significance: Martineau is the founding English woman sociologist and one of the inventors of the modern profession of journalism: she made political economy a subject for the general reader, wrote the most important English book on American society before Tocqueville's readership was established, and helped to shape the feminist argument of the 1830s-50s. Her Autobiography is a classic of Victorian self-writing.

authors.name: Harriet Taylor Mill
authors.nationality: English; Victorian feminism, political economy and social thought
authors.identity: Philosopher and essayist; the intellectual partner of John Stuart Mill and a founding thinker of Victorian liberal feminism.
authors.biography: Born Harriet Hardy in London in October 1807 and married at eighteen to the wholesale druggist John Taylor, by whom she had three children. Her friendship with John Stuart Mill began in 1830, and the scandal of their attachment — she separated from Taylor but remained married to him until his death in 1849 — caused her exclusion from respectable society. She married Mill in April 1851. Between 1848 and 1858 she wrote a series of essays, chiefly on the position of women and on the moral character of the age; the most substantial is The Enfranchisement of Women (1851), published anonymously in the Westminster Review. She died of consumption at Avignon in November 1858, and Mill lived afterwards at Avignon to be near her grave.
authors.profile: Harriet Taylor Mill's writings are few and difficult to disentangle from Mill's: The Enfranchisement of Women argued for women's suffrage and for their admission to all the professions at a time when the public campaign had barely begun, and her essays on toleration and on the moral 'improvement' of society anticipate the argument of On Liberty. Mill states in the Autobiography that her influence was decisive for On Liberty and for The Subjection of Women, and recent scholarship has established her as an independent thinker rather than a mere collaborator.
authors.style: Polemical clarity and a command of the vocabulary of rights; the argument from the perversion of women's nature by constraint; an emphasis on the moral and intellectual benefits of equality to men; the use of concrete examples of the legal disabilities of married women.
authors.concerns: The legal and educational subordination of women; the moral consequences of the double standard; toleration and the limits of social opinion; the relation of personal freedom to social progress; the use of 'nature' as an instrument of custom.
authors.significance: Harriet Taylor Mill is a founding figure of the liberal feminist tradition and the intellectual origin of the two greatest works of Victorian feminism: On Liberty and The Subjection of Women. The Enfranchisement of Women is the first sustained English argument for women's suffrage, and her recovery in the later twentieth century (the Hayek edition of the Mill–Taylor correspondence, and the modern biographies) has changed the history of English political thought.
authors.uncertainty: Her authorship and her influence on Mill have been much disputed since the nineteenth century. The attribution of The Enfranchisement of Women is established by Mill's papers and by the Westminster Review's records; the extent of her share in On Liberty and The Subjection of Women is argued by Hayek, Rossi and Jacobs, and the honest position is that the exact division of labour cannot be documented.

authors.name: Hart Crane

authors.identity: Poet; the author of The Bridge, the most ambitious American long poem of the period and the great lyric poet of the American sublime.
authors.biography: Born Harold Hart Crane at Garrettsville, Ohio, on 21 July 1899, the son of a candy manufacturer; he left school without a diploma, worked in advertising in Cleveland and New York, and published White Buildings in 1926. The Bridge appeared in 1930 to mixed reviews; he spent a year in Mexico on a Guggenheim fellowship and drowned himself from the steamship Orizaba in the Caribbean on 27 April 1932, aged thirty-two.

His dense, prophetic style and his tragic death made him the emblem of the American poet destroyed by his own vision.
authors.style: The dense, prophetic, syntactically compressed lyric; the extended metaphor held across a whole poem; the imagery of the sea, the bridge and the machine; the metrical experiment inside traditional stanza; the rhetoric of the American sublime.
authors.concerns: America and the American myth; the machine and the modern city; the sea and the voyage; memory, love and the loss of the beloved; the poet's vision and its cost; Whitman's inheritance and Eliot's counter-example.
authors.significance: Crane wrote the great American long poem of the period after Paterson and the finest American lyric of the sublime: The Bridge answered The Waste Land with an American epic, 'Voyages' is one of the great love poems in American literature, and his death at thirty-two made him the period's emblem of the poet destroyed by his vision.

authors.name: Hartley Coleridge
authors.birthplace: On the Bristol side of the Severn at Kingsdown, Gloucestershire, according to modern authorities, though the Dictionary of National Biography gave Clevedon, Somerset; eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge
authors.nationality: English; the Lakeland and Wordsworth-Coleridge circle of British Romanticism inherited by the second generation, and the province of the magazine essay, of old-dramatist scholarship and of northern biographical compilation
authors.identity: A poet of sonnets and short occasional lyrics, an essayist and biographer of the early English dramatists, and a schoolmaster who never held a steady post; the most celebrated instance in English letters of brilliant promise unfulfilled, and by inheritance and by friendship the closest surviving link between Wordsworth, his father and the Victorian man of letters.
authors.biography: Hartley Coleridge was born on 19 September 1796, the eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge, and was named after David Hartley, the associationist philosopher of his father's early allegiance; he is the infant addressed in 'Frost at Midnight'. His childhood was passed mainly in the Lake District, where he was schooled at Ambleside and, after the Wordsworth family settled at Rydal Mount, enjoyed the unusual privilege of the use of Wordsworth's library; about the age of eight he and his brother Derwent invented the imaginary kingdom of Ejuxria, whose affairs he continued in later years to record and to regret. He went up to Oxford in 1815 and was elected to a fellowship at Oriel College, which he lost within a few years on the ground of intemperance; that loss determined the outline of the rest of his life. Two years in London as a journalistic writer were followed by a return to Ambleside, where an attempt to keep pupils was abandoned about 1830 and he was thrown upon the kindness of friends and of the publisher F. E. Bingley, under whose eye he compiled the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and printed the small volume of Poems of the same year. The Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire followed in 1836, and his scholarly work on the old drama issued in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford of the late 1830s and about 1840, while he wrote at intervals for Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine and the London Magazine and in 1837 and 1838 helped to manage Sedbergh grammar school. Dependency on alcohol, embarrassment of money and a constitutional indolence defeated every plan of steady work; he died of bronchitis on 6 January 1849 and was buried in Grasmere churchyard within sight of Wordsworth's grave. His brother Derwent Coleridge edited his Poems and his Essays and Marginalia, four volumes in all, in 1851, and his letters, an indispensable record of the Coleridgean household, were edited in the twentieth century, as modern reassessment has established the sonnets and the dramatic criticism as a considerable minor body of work.
authors.profile: His verse is small in bulk and almost all occasional: the Poems of 1833, enlarged in the two volumes of 1851, consist of sonnets on friendship, on the Lakeland landscape, on books and on his own defeat, together with ballad-measure pieces, translations and fragments such as the Prometheus; the longer narrative and dramatic projects remained unfinished. His prose divides between biographical compilation, in the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and the Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire of 1836, and dramatic scholarship and criticism, in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford and in the magazine essays which the posthumous Essays and Marginalia of 1851 gathered; his correspondence, published as Letters, is a third and perhaps the most valuable part of his work.
authors.style: A compressed, plain and deliberately unimpassioned manner of verse, in which the sonnet of ten or twelve lines carries the argument in a single sentence of argument and close with a sententious turn; a fondness for the abstract noun, for balance and antithesis, and for the colloquial idiom of cultivated speech, with an occasional Jonsonian point and an occasional Wordsworthian simplicity of diction. His prose is digressive, allusive and conversational, made of quotations, marginal notes and catalogues of names, and its virtue is rather its range of reading and its good sense than any sustained architecture.
authors.concerns: Associationist psychology and the formation of character, inherited from Hartley and argued over with his father; providence, prayer and the morality of a clergyman's family in an age of doubt; the claims of genius against indolence and appetite, and the ethics of self-knowledge; the dignity and the national use of the old English drama; the worthies tradition of regional biography, in which local fame is gathered as evidence of a nation's intellectual history; and the obligations of a son to a father's texts, which made him editor, witness and apologist.
authors.significance: He stands in the history of Romanticism as the living proof of its anxieties of inheritance, the child of the Lyrical Ballads generation whose failure was memorialised by his own father and by Wordsworth and afterwards read as the paradigm of unfulfilled promise. His essays and his edition of the old dramatists kept the Jacobean and Caroline stage before a Victorian public, his northern worthies volumes made regional biography an instrument of literary history, and his letters and conversations are a primary source for the Coleridge family and for Wordsworth at Rydal, giving him a durable, if subordinate, place in the documentation of the period.
authors.uncertainty: Reference works long antedating the modern calendars give his birth as 1791 and the Dictionary of National Biography gives Clevedon where later scholars give Kingsdown, while the year in which he held and lost the Oriel fellowship is reported variously as about 1819, 1820 and 1826; the long narrative poem 'Davysses', sometimes entered among his works in library catalogues, could not be traced in the printed bibliographies and should be treated as unverified.
