authors.name: Henry Adams
authors.nationality: American; the historical essay, the autobiography and the literature of the modern
authors.identity: Historian, essayist and memoirist; the author of The Education of Henry Adams and the most searching American writer on the meaning of modernity.
authors.biography: Born in Boston on 16 February 1838, the grandson and great-grandson of presidents; he graduated from Harvard in 1858, served as his father's secretary in the American legation in London during the Civil War, and taught medieval history at Harvard from 1870 to 1877. He wrote the nine-volume History of the United States during the Administrations of Jefferson and Madison (1889-91), the novels Democracy (1880) and Esther (1884), Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres (1904) and The Education of Henry Adams (1907, printed privately). He died in Washington on 27 March 1918.
authors.profile: Adams wrote the American literature of the modern crisis: The Education of Henry Adams is the great American autobiography and the central American meditation on the difference between the medieval world of unity and the modern world of the dynamo, and its third-person narrative of a failure to be educated invented a new form. His histories are the finest American historical writing of the century, and Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres is the classic American study of the medieval imagination.
authors.style: The third-person autobiography that treats the self as a scientific case; the ironic, epigrammatic sentence; the comparative analysis of epochs through a single symbol (the Virgin, the dynamo); the historical narrative of great scope; the aphorism as argument.
authors.concerns: History, progress and the meaning of modernity; the medieval world and the modern; power, technology and the dynamo; American politics and the corruption of democracy; education and the failure of education; science and the second law of thermodynamics.
authors.significance: Adams is the central American intellectual of the Gilded Age and the author of the greatest American autobiography: The Education of Henry Adams is a founding text of modern American thought, his histories remain the standard account of the Jefferson and Madison administrations, and his meditation on the dynamo and the Virgin is the origin of the modern American debate about technology.

authors.name: Henry Arthur Jones
authors.nationality: English; the melodrama, the problem play and the drama of the provinces
authors.identity: Dramatist; the most prolific serious playwright of the 1880s-90s and one of the first English dramatists to argue for a national theatre.
authors.biography: Born Henry Arthur Jones at Grandborough, Buckinghamshire, on 20 September 1851, the son of a farmer; he left school at twelve and worked as a draper's assistant and a commercial traveller before writing his first play in 1878. The Silver King (1882), with Henry Herman, made him rich; Saints and Sinners (1884), The Middleman (1889) and Mrs Dane's Defence (1900) established him as a serious dramatist. He campaigned for a national theatre and died in London on 7 January 1929.
authors.profile: Jones wrote the English melodrama and then the English problem play: The Silver King is the finest melodrama of the 1880s, and his later work — The Middleman, Mrs Dane's Defence, The Liars — treats industrial conflict, the double standard and the moral cowardice of society with a seriousness that prepared the way for Shaw. He was also the most articulate English advocate of a national theatre and a professional dramatic literature.
authors.style: The strong melodramatic situation with a moral core; the social problem dramatised through a family; dialogue of the manufacturing middle class; the cross-examination scene; the direct address to the audience on a question of the day.
authors.concerns: The double standard and the fallen woman; industrial capital and the middleman; religious hypocrisy and the Nonconformist conscience; class and the social ladder; marriage and respectability; the provinces and the metropolis.
authors.significance: Jones is the central English dramatist of the transition from melodrama to the problem play: The Silver King was the most successful melodrama of its decade, Mrs Dane's Defence is one of the finest English problem plays before Shaw, and his campaign for a national theatre made him the most important theatrical publicist of the period.

authors.name: Henry David Thoreau
authors.nationality: American; the nature essay, the journal and the political essay
authors.identity: Essayist, naturalist and surveyor; the author of Walden and 'Civil Disobedience', the two founding texts of American nature writing and of the literature of conscience.
authors.biography: Born at Concord, Massachusetts, on 12 July 1817; he was educated at Harvard and taught school, worked in his father's pencil factory, and from 1841 lived for periods in Emerson's household. He built his cabin at Walden Pond in 1845 and lived there two years, wrote 'Civil Disobedience' after spending a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax in 1846, and afterwards made several excursions to Maine, Cape Cod and Canada. He published A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) and Walden (1854), and died of tuberculosis at Concord on 6 May 1862.
authors.profile: Thoreau wrote the American sentence as a form of attention: his prose is exact, sinewy and full of puns, and his great subject is the disciplined perception of the natural world as a way of living rightly. Walden is at once a practical account of a two-year experiment in economy and a spiritual autobiography, and 'Civil Disobedience' is the founding modern argument that individual conscience outranks the state. His Journal, of over two million words, is the greatest American nature diary.
authors.style: Concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences; exact measurement and enumeration; pun, paradox and irony; the excursion narrative; the journal entry developed as an art form; quotations from classical and Eastern texts.
authors.concerns: Nature and the discipline of attention; simplicity and economic independence; civil disobedience and the individual against the state; slavery and the fugitive; the seasons and the local landscape; reading, the classics and self-culture.
authors.significance: Thoreau is the founding figure of American nature writing and of the literature of non-violent resistance: Walden shaped the modern environmental movement, 'Civil Disobedience' influenced Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King, and the Journal is one of the great unread works of the nineteenth century.

authors.name: Henry Fielding
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English novelist, dramatist, and magistrate, creator of the comic epic in prose and one of the most influential of the early English novelists.
authors.biography: Born on 22 April 1707 in Somerset into a gentry family, he was educated at Eton and studied briefly abroad and at law in London. He began as a playwright, producing political and theatrical satires in the early 1730s, and after the licensing censorship of 1737 turned to prose fiction. He published Joseph Andrews (1742), the burlesque Shamela in response to Pamela, the masterpiece The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749), and Amelia (1751). He also served as a Westminster and Bow Street magistrate and wrote on law and social reform. He died in Lisbon on 27 June 1754.
authors.profile: A novelist who defined the picaresque comic epic in prose, combining broad social panorama, irony, and authorial commentary, and who responded critically to the sentimental and epistolary modes of his contemporaries.
authors.style: Omniscient, intrusive narration with discursive chapter prefaces; irony and good-humoured satire; a picaresque, episodic plot; robust and colloquial diction; and careful structural balancing of character and design.
authors.concerns: Human nature and motive; hypocrisy versus goodness; class and the social order; justice, law, and authority; and the education of the individual within society.
authors.significance: A central founder of the English novel, whose theoretical prefaces and Tom Jones set the terms for realist narrative, and whose dramatic and legal careers left a major imprint on eighteenth-century culture and on the reform of the theatre and the law.
authors.uncertainty: The outlines of Fielding's life are well documented, though some dates of early writings and details of his authorship of particular pamphlets remain matters of scholarly attribution.

authors.name: Henry Home, Lord Kames
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Judge of the Court of Session and polymath of Edinburgh, the patron and publisher of the Scottish Enlightenment, whose Sketches of the History of Man tried to write the whole of society as natural history.
authors.biography: Born about 1696 at Kames House in Berwickshire and educated largely at home, he became an advocate and built a leading practice at the Scottish bar. He rose to the bench of the Court of Session in 1752 as Lord Kames and sat there until his death, taking a prominent part in the political and cultural life of Edinburgh. His Historical Law-Tracts (1732) read early law as evidence of early society; his Essays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion (1751), which grounded morals in instinct rather than in revelation, were censured by the church courts. Elements of Criticism (1762) analysed the passions and the effects of the beautiful and the sublime, and the four-volume Sketches of the History of Man (1774) surveyed races, languages, government and agriculture as a single natural history. He encouraged and published the younger writers around him, and died in Edinburgh on 27 December 1782.
authors.profile: A lawyer-naturalist of society who treated customs, laws and tastes as specimens to be classified rather than as doctrines to be defended.
authors.style: Miscellaneous, encyclopaedic and aphoristic; numbered propositions, cases and historical instances; a judge's love of definition combined with an amateur's appetite for generalisation.
authors.concerns: The historical development of law and property; the instincts underlying morality and religion; the physiology of the passions and the analysis of aesthetic effect; the comparative history of races and of the stages of society.
authors.significance: He gave the Scottish Enlightenment its institutional encouragement and its model of conjectural history, and his criticism of the passions shaped the aesthetic theory of his century.
authors.uncertainty: The year of his birth is only approximately fixed, and his authorship of some tracts and his role in the patronage of others are difficult to separate.

authors.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: nobleman; soldier; poet; translator
authors.biography: Born at Hunsdon about 1516, eldest son of the Duke of Norfolk; brought up with the Duke of Richmond (Henry VIII's illegitimate son) and educated in the humanist manner. A soldier and courtier — he served in the French wars of the 1540s and was wounded at the siege of Montreuil — he was arrested in December 1546 on largely fabricated charges of quartering the royal arms, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 19 January 1547, the last victim of Henry VIII's reign. His poems circulated in manuscript and were printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557); his translation of Aeneid II and IV was published in 1554 and 1557.
authors.profile: The refiner of the English sonnet: he gave the form the rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that became the 'English' or Shakespearean sonnet, and his smooth decasyllabic line pointed the way to the Elizabethan style. His translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the first English blank verse — created the unrhymed iambic pentameter that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
authors.style: Regular, musical decasyllables; elegant management of the Petrarchan materials; a grave, chivalric sensibility; in the Aeneid translation, a new plainness of diction answering Virgil's.
authors.concerns: Nobility and honour under tyranny; love, constancy, and the ruin of Troy as an image of English court politics; the translation of classical epic into English verse.
authors.significance: Inventor (with Wyatt) of the English sonnet form and of blank verse — the two technical foundations of Elizabethan poetry and drama; his life and death dramatized the fate of the old nobility under the Tudors.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year given as 1516 or 1517 in the records; some lyrics attributed to him in Tottel are of uncertain authorship.

authors.name: Henry James
authors.nationality: American-British; the novel of consciousness and the international theme
authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and critic; the greatest American novelist of the later nineteenth century and the master of the psychological novel.
authors.biography: Born in New York on 15 April 1843, the son of the philosopher Henry James Sr and the brother of William James; he was educated in New York, Geneva, London, Paris and Bonn and studied law briefly at Harvard. He settled in London in 1876 and in Rye, Sussex, in 1897, and became a British subject in 1915 in protest at American neutrality. He published Roderick Hudson (1875), The American (1877), The Portrait of a Lady (1881), The Bostonians (1886), The Princess Casamassima (1886), What Maisie Knew (1897), The Wings of the Dove (1902), The Ambassadors (1903) and The Golden Bowl (1904). He died in London on 28 February 1916.
authors.profile: James made the novel a study of consciousness: his late style follows the interior movement of a mind as it perceives, hesitates and revises, and his great subject is the American encounter with European civilisation — the innocent abroad, the heiress and the fortune-hunter, the moral cost of experience. He was also the finest English critic of fiction of the century, and his prefaces to the New York Edition are the founding documents of the modern theory of the novel.
authors.style: Long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification; the 'central consciousness' through which everything is filtered; dialogue that works by indirection and inference; the withheld fact; the elaborate metaphor drawn from architecture, painting or the theatre.
authors.concerns: The American and Europe; innocence, experience and the loss of illusions; marriage, money and the marriage market; the artist and society (above all in The Tragic Muse); the woman's consciousness and freedom; betrayal, renunciation and the conduct of life.
authors.significance: James is the central American novelist of the nineteenth century after Melville and the founder of the modern psychological novel: his late novels are the most technically ambitious in English, his criticism is the foundation of narrative theory, and his influence on Woolf, Proust, Conrad and the whole twentieth-century novel is decisive.

authors.name: Henry Lawson
authors.nationality: Australian; the bush story, the ballad and the Australian vernacular
authors.identity: Poet and short-story writer; the founding writer of Australian national literature in English, and the first great voice of the Australian working man.
authors.biography: Born Henry Archibald Hertzberg Lawson at Grenfell, New South Wales, on 17 June 1867, the son of a Norwegian seaman and a suffragist mother who took the family to Sydney in 1883. He published for the Bulletin, the radical Sydney weekly, from 1887, and in 1892 his mother sent him to Bourke, in the western back country, where a year in the drought gave him the material for the bush stories. He married Bertha Bredt in 1896 and travelled to England, where he published Joe Wilson and His Mates (1901). Alcoholism and deafness destroyed his later years, and he died in Sydney on 2 September 1922.
authors.profile: Lawson wrote the Australian outback as a place of terrible beauty and terrible loneliness: his stories are short, laconic, often anecdotal, and told in the voice of the man who has been there — the swagman, the selector, the shearer, the woman keeping house in a bark hut. His verse is the ballads of the Bulletin school, and 'The Drover's Wife' is the founding story of Australian literature.
authors.style: Terse, laconic, anecdotal prose; the dialect of the Australian working man written as it sounds; the subordination of plot to a single scene of endurance; sentiment restrained almost to the point of silence; ballad stanzas and refrains.
authors.concerns: The isolation of the bush and the rural woman's endurance; mateship and solidarity; poverty and the swagman's life; the Australian landscape of drought and flood; class and the squatter; alcoholism and defeat.
authors.significance: Lawson is the founding writer of modern Australian literature: 'The Drover's Wife' and the Joe Wilson stories created the Australian short story, his ballads became a national folklore, and his portrait of the bush made the landscape itself a national theme.

authors.name: Henry Medwall
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: playwright; chaplain to Cardinal Morton
authors.biography: Born about 1462; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and employed as chaplain and notary to Cardinal John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury. His Fulgens and Lucrece, played at Morton's household at Lambeth about 1497, is the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell about 1512–16. He died about 1502.
authors.profile: Author of the first secular English drama. Fulgens and Lucrece dramatizes a humanist debate — whether nobility lies in birth or in virtue — as a Roman comedy of courtship, complete with a subplot in which two servants, A and B, compete for the audience's employment; his Nature is a full-scale morality play of man's fall and amendment. Both were played in Morton's great hall, the seedbed of the Tudor interlude.
authors.style: Debate framed as drama; the interweaving of serious argument and servant comedy; the morality convention put to secular and humanist use.
authors.concerns: True nobility and the claims of virtue over birth; the reform of manners; the education of the great household through play.
authors.significance: Bridging medieval morality and humanist comedy, Fulgens and Lucrece begins the secular English stage tradition that runs to the Elizabethan theatre.

authors.name: Henry More
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: The leading Cambridge Platonist; a poet-philosopher who defended a rational, spiritual Christianity against materialism and atheism, and who corresponded with Descartes and Anne Conway while writing philosophical and mystical treatises in verse and prose.
authors.biography: Born 12 October 1614 at Grantham, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow (1639) and remained for life, declining preferment. He corresponded with Descartes (1648–49) and was the philosophical mentor of Anne Conway. His works include the Philosophical Poems (1647, including the 'Psychozoia' and 'Antipsychopannychia'), An Antidote Against Atheism (1653), Enthusiasmus Triumphatus (1656), and the Enchiridion Metaphysicum (1671), which argued against Cartesian mechanism and for the reality of spirit, extension, and the 'boniform faculty'. He defended belief in spirits and apparitions and died on 1 September 1687.
authors.profile: The Platonic philosopher-theologian who sought to reconcile reason, religion, and the new philosophy, opposing Hobbesian and Cartesian materialism with a spiritual, emanative metaphysics expressed in both verse and prose.
authors.style: Philosophical verse (Spenserian stanzas) and prose; Platonic and mystical argument; a serene, speculative, sometimes visionary style; and polemic against atheism and 'enthusiasm'.
authors.concerns: The existence and nature of spirit and God; reason and religion; the critique of materialism and of religious 'enthusiasm'; the immortality of the soul; and the relation of Descartes to Platonism.
authors.significance: More was the central figure of Cambridge Platonism, influencing Conway, Glanvill, and later Latitudinarian and Romantic thought; his correspondence with Descartes is a key document of seventeenth-century philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: More's life is documented through his works, correspondence, and a contemporary biography; his philosophical positions evolved and some attributions of influence are interpretive.

authors.name: Henry Newbolt
authors.nationality: English; the imperial ballad and the poetry of the public school
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and historian; the author of 'Vitaï Lampada' and the laureate of the Victorian public school and the imperial idea.
authors.biography: Born Henry John Newbolt at Bilston, Staffordshire, on 6 June 1862, the son of a vicar; he was educated at Clifton College and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, was called to the bar in 1887, and published Admirals All in 1897. His ballads of the navy and the public school made him the most popular poet of the imperial movement; he edited the Nelson classics and wrote the official history of the naval operations of the First World War. He was knighted in 1915 and died in London on 19 April 1938.
authors.profile: Newbolt wrote the poetry of the imperial ideal: 'Vitaï Lampada' is the most famous English poem about the playing fields of the public school as the training ground of empire, and his naval ballads gave the late-Victorian navy its literary image. He is also the key witness to the English ideal of the gentleman-sportsman, and his poems are the essential documents of the imperial imagination at its most confident.
authors.style: Ballad measure with a strong refrain; the schoolboy and the naval anecdote; the moral drawn from a game; the cadenced appeal to duty and tradition; the rhetoric of the imperial mission; the plain, memorable lines.
authors.concerns: The public school and the making of the English gentleman; duty, discipline and the imperial mission; the navy and the sea; sport, cricket and the ethos of fair play; the empire and the English race; the Great War and its commemoration.
authors.significance: Newbolt is the central poet of the English imperial ideal and the public school: 'Vitaï Lampada' is one of the most quoted and most parodied English poems, his naval ballads shaped the image of the navy, and his work is the indispensable document of the imperial imagination of the 1890s.

authors.name: Henry Vaughan
authors.nationality: English (Welsh, Anglo-Welsh)
authors.identity: Anglo-Welsh physician, royalist, and metaphysical devotional poet; author of Silex Scintillans, whose mystical nature-poetry and longing for eternity distinguish him among Herbert's followers.
authors.biography: Born 1621 (baptised 16 April) at Newton St Bridget, twin brother of the alchemist Thomas Vaughan; educated privately and at Jesus College, Oxford, then trained in medicine. A royalist during the Civil Wars, he retired to his native Breconshire, practised medicine, and published Olor Iscanus (1651) and Silex Scintillans (1650, expanded 1655), influenced by Herbert. He also wrote prose devotional and hermetic works (The Mount of Olives, 1652) and translations of Nolle and Boece. He lived quietly through the Restoration at Newton and Alway, dying 23 April 1695.
authors.profile: The 'Silurist' whose verse seeks God through the natural world and childhood memory, marked by a mystic's sense of eternity glimpsed behind the material world ('intimations' later echoed by Wordsworth).
authors.style: Luminous nature imagery; a mystical, visionary quality; Herbert's influence tempered by a wilder, more personal imagination; emblematic structure; and Welsh landscape as the locus of spiritual experience.
authors.concerns: Eternity and the soul's pre-existence; nature as the book of God; childhood innocence; royalism and religious loyalty; hermetic and alchemical philosophy; death and resurrection.
authors.significance: Long neglected, Vaughan was recovered in the nineteenth century and prized by the Romantics and T. S. Eliot as a visionary metaphysical poet; 'The Retreat' and 'The World' are among the great English mystical lyrics.
authors.uncertainty: Much of Vaughan's life is obscure; his exact birth date and many details of his royalist activities and medical practice rest on inference and local records.

authors.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

authors.identity: Poet, professor and translator; the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem.
authors.biography: Born in Portland, Maine, on 27 February 1807; he taught modern languages at Bowdoin and at Harvard, where he held the Smith chair from 1836 to 1854. Voices of the Night (1839), Evangeline (1847), The Song of Hiawatha (1855), The Courtship of Miles Standish (1858) and Tales of a Wayside Inn (1863) made him the most popular poet in the English-speaking world. He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 24 March 1882, the first American poet honoured with a bust in Poets' Corner.
authors.profile: Longfellow was the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem: Evangeline and Hiawatha gave American literature its epics of the Acadian exile and the Native American past, and his public poetry made the poet a national institution in a way no American writer had been before.
authors.style: The long narrative poem in regular tetrameter; the historical and legendary subject nationalised; the simile drawn from the natural world; the moral sentiment of the public poet; the plain, melodious, accessible line.
authors.concerns: The American past and the national memory; the Native American and the vanishing race; the Puritan inheritance; the sea and the New England coast; death and the consolation of fame.
authors.significance: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem: Evangeline and The Song of Hiawatha gave American literature its epics and made the poet a national institution, and his influence on the public poetry of the English-speaking world was unmatched.

authors.name: Herbert George Wells
authors.nationality: English; the scientific romance, the social novel and the popular history
authors.identity: Novelist, journalist and social prophet; the inventor of the modern scientific romance, the most widely read English writer of his generation, and the great populariser of science, history and the idea of the future.
authors.biography: Born at Bromley on 21 September 1866, the son of Joseph Wells, a shopkeeper and professional cricketer, and Sarah Neal, a former lady's maid; he was apprenticed to a draper, won a scholarship to the Normal School of Science in South Kensington in 1884 (he studied there until 1887), and was taught biology by T. H. Huxley, an experience that made him a lifelong evolutionist. He taught science and wrote for the Saturday Review before The Time Machine (1895) made him famous; The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896), The Invisible Man (1897), The War of the Worlds (1898), When the Sleeper Wakes (1899) and The First Men in the Moon (1901) followed, and from 1900 he turned to the social novels (Kipps, Tono-Bungay, The History of Mr Polly) and to the utopian and prophetic works (A Modern Utopia, The Outline of History, The Shape of Things to Come). He joined the Fabian Society in 1903 and quarrelled with the Webbs, produced a stream of novels, popular histories and world-state tracts for half a century, and died in London on 13 August 1946.
authors.profile: Wells took the evolutionary biology he had learned from Huxley and made it the basis of a new kind of fiction: the scientific romance, which uses an invention or a discovery as the premise for a realistic narrative of its social and psychological consequences. His early romances are single-conceit stories carried by a precise, journalistic specification of detail, and their subject is the fragility of the human species, the possibility of degeneration and the relative insignificance of man in time. After 1900 he wrote the 'novel of ideas' as social criticism, aiming to make fiction an instrument of reform; his Edwardian social novels (Kipps, Tono-Bungay, The History of Mr Polly) made lower-middle-class life a serious literary subject, and The Outline of History (1920) sold in millions and taught a mass readership its own past.
authors.style: The rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership; the single scientific premise developed to its consequences; precise technical and topographical detail; a first-person witness narrator; the sudden perspective change (the Martian view of England, the Eloi of the far future); the comic lower-middle-class idiolect (Kipps, Mr Polly); the documentary and polemical essay folded into fiction; the epigram and the Utopian debate in the later novels.
authors.concerns: Time, evolutionary deep time and the fate of the species; the machine and the alienation of labour; imperialism reversed (the Martians as colonisers); science, experiment and moral responsibility; class division, the shop and the small man's struggle (the Eloi and the Morlocks, Kipps); utopia, the world state and the possibility of catastrophe; education and self-improvement; war and the aeroplane; marriage and sexual reform.
authors.significance: Wells founded modern science fiction: The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds and The Island of Doctor Moreau are the foundational texts of the genre, and their images (the time traveller, the Martian cylinder, the Morlocks, the invisible man) became permanent English myths. With Shaw he was the most influential English public writer of the Edwardian and interwar years: Kipps and Tono-Bungay gave the lower middle class a literature, The Outline of History made him one of the most widely read writers in the world, and his influence on Huxley, Orwell, Stapledon and the whole twentieth-century literature of the future is direct.

authors.name: Herman Melville
authors.nationality: American; the epic romance, the sea narrative and the short story
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and short-story writer; the author of Moby-Dick and the greatest American writer of the sea.
authors.biography: Born in New York City on 1 August 1819; his father's bankruptcy and death in 1832 ended his schooling, and he went to sea in 1839 on a merchant ship and in 1841 on the whaler Acushnet, from which he deserted in the Marquesas in 1842. Typee (1846) and Omoo (1847) made him famous as a writer of the South Seas; Moby-Dick (1851) failed, Pierre (1852) scandalised, and after The Confidence-Man (1857) he wrote almost nothing but poetry and the posthumous Billy Budd. He worked as a customs inspector in New York from 1866 and died there on 28 September 1891.
authors.profile: Melville wrote the American epic against the American romance: Moby-Dick is at once a whaling narrative, an encyclopaedia of cetology, a tragedy of obsession and a metaphysical argument, and its prose is the most various in nineteenth-century American writing — Shakespearean soliloquy, comic catalogue, sermon, stage direction and lyric. His later work turns to the short story and to poetry, and 'Bartleby' and Billy Budd are among the most haunting things in the language.
authors.style: Encyclopaedic digression and catalogue; Shakespearean soliloquy and aside; multiple narrative genres inside one book; symbol and emblem pushed to the point of allegory; alliteration and blank-verse cadence in prose; irony and black comedy.
authors.concerns: The whale and the sea as metaphysical absolutes; obsession and the will; race, slavery and the crew of the Pequod; the failure of American democracy; the artist and a hostile market; innocence and the law ('Bartleby', Billy Budd); the Pacific and the colonial encounter.

authors.name: Hester Chapone

authors.identity: Moralist and essayist, a Bluestocking associated writer best known for her conduct work Letters on the Improvement of the Mind.
authors.biography: Born Hester Mulso on 27 October 1727 at Twywell in Northamptonshire, the daughter of a clergyman, she was educated largely at home and became known in learned society, corresponding with Elizabeth Carter and moving in Bluestocking circles before marrying the lawyer John Chapone. Her Letters on the Improvement of the Mind (1773), addressed to young women, went through many editions, and she published further conduct and moral works, including Miscellanies in Verse and Prose (1775). She continued to write for the education of women into later life. She died at Hampton in 1801.
authors.profile: A writer of conduct and educational literature whose Letters shaped thinking about women's rational and moral improvement, making her one of the most widely read female didactic authors of her period.
authors.style: Clear, warm, rational didactic prose in the letter form; an accessible, moralizing tone; and an easy blend of religious seriousness with practical advice.

authors.significance: An important conduct writer and Bluestocking figure whose Letters on the Improvement of the Mind circulated widely and influenced ideas about female education in the late eighteenth century.

authors.identity: Poet, essayist, historian and controversialist; the author of Cautionary Tales and one of the great English comic poets.
authors.biography: Born Joseph Hilaire Pierre Rene Belloc at La Celle-Saint-Cloud near Paris on 27 July 1870, the son of a French barrister and an English mother; he was educated at the Oratory and Balliol, and became a naturalised Briton in 1902. The Bad Child's Book of Beasts (1896), The Path to Rome (1902), Cautionary Tales for Children (1907) and his histories and polemics followed. He died at Guildford on 16 July 1953.
authors.profile: Belloc wrote the funniest children's verse in English and one of the great English travel books: Cautionary Tales made the comic moral poem a permanent form, The Path to Rome invented the modern walking book, and his polemics made him the most pugnacious Catholic man of letters of the century.

authors.name: Horace Walpole
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English man of letters, antiquary, and politician, creator of the first Gothic novel and one of the most celebrated letter-writers of the century.
authors.biography: Born on 24 September 1717 in London, the son of Sir Robert Walpole, the first Prime Minister, he was educated at Eton and Cambridge and entered Parliament as a Whig. A lifelong man of letters, he built the Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill and wrote on art and antiquities. He published the novel The Castle of Otranto (1764), at first presented as a translation, and later the tragedy The Mysterious Mother (1768). His extensive letters, on society, politics, and literature, are a major historical source. He died on 2 March 1797.
authors.profile: The author of the founding Gothic romance and a prolific writer of tales, plays, antiquarian histories, and correspondence, whose work fused taste, antiquarianism, and a cultivated horror of the medieval past.
authors.style: Elegant, urbane, witty prose; deliberate archaism and romance convention in Otranto; a gossipy, polished epistolary style; and an antiquarian's eye for the picturesque and the marvelous.
authors.concerns: The revival of interest in the Middle Ages and Gothic taste; ancestry, prophecy, and the supernatural; the interplay of romance and reason; sociability and political gossip; and the aesthetics of terror and the picturesque.
authors.significance: The originator of the Gothic novel with The Castle of Otranto and a defining figure of eighteenth-century taste, antiquarianism, and letter-writing, whose influence shaped Gothic fiction and the Gothic Revival.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well documented; the chief uncertainty concerns the framing and initial pseudonymous or 'translated' presentation of The Castle of Otranto rather than his biography.

authors.name: Hugh Blair
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Scottish Presbyterian minister, rhetorician, and literary critic of the Scottish Enlightenment, the first professor of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at Edinburgh.
authors.biography: Blair was born in Edinburgh, studied divinity there, and was ordained to a ministry in the Church of Scotland, rising to the leading Edinburgh congregations and becoming a prominent figure of the Moderate interest. He lectured on rhetoric and belles lettres and was appointed to the newly created chair of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at the University of Edinburgh in 1762. His best-known work, Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, was published in 1783, drawing on decades of teaching and becoming a standard text on taste, style, and criticism. He wrote influential sermons and critical essays, and his endorsements figured in the literary debates over Ossian and the ballad. He died in 1800.
authors.profile: A critic, rhetorician, and preacher who codified Enlightenment ideas of taste, style, and eloquence, defending polite letters, sensible religion, and the analysis of beautiful writing.
authors.style: A clear, measured, authoritative critical prose of definition, example, and classification of styles; a temperate homiletic voice in the sermons; and an emphasis on perspicuity, harmony, and decorum.
authors.concerns: The nature of taste, genius, and the sublime; rhetoric and the principles of eloquence; the history and criticism of style and genres; and the alliance of politeness with reasonable religion and morality.
authors.significance: A defining voice of the Moderate wing of the Scottish Enlightenment; his Lectures standardised rhetorical and literary-critical teaching for a century, and his judgments shaped taste in the Ossian and ballad debates.

authors.name: Hugh Henry Brackenridge
authors.nationality: American, born in Scotland; the letters of revolutionary Philadelphia and of the western Pennsylvania frontier, the first American writer of that interior
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, playwright, orator, lawyer, judge, schoolmaster and founder of colleges; the inventor of the American picaresque comic novel of politics and settlement, and the most considerable man of letters of the Pennsylvania west before the 1830s.
authors.biography: Brackenridge was born on the Kintyre peninsula near Campbeltown in Argyllshire, in the year 1748, of a Scottish family in straitened circumstances, and was carried by his parents to York County in Pennsylvania in the fifth year of his life. He grew up on the edge of the settlement, largely self-taught, herding cattle and picking up such learning as the country afforded until a neighbour recognized his capacity and helped him to books; he entered the college at Princeton, graduated in 1770, and gave himself afterwards to teaching, keeping a classical school and preparing young men for the college. He served the Revolutionary army as a chaplain, and about the same time began to publish verse, including a poem on the death of the general before Quebec which was recited and reprinted through the war years and gave him his first name in America. After the peace he removed to Philadelphia, read and practised law, wrote for the stage and the press, and about 1779 fixed himself in the western country, at first near Hannastown and afterwards about Pittsburgh, where the frontier supplied the society he satirized. There he founded an academy in 1787, the institution which became the university of the city, gave aid to the first newspaper of the west, and practised his profession before the county courts; he sat in the convention which framed the state constitution of the 1790s, and was made a judge of the courts of the western district. In the excise trouble of 1794 he rode with the militia, and tried at once to suppress the insurrection and to restrain the measures which had provoked it, and was reviled by the partisans of both sides; the controversy cost him his political standing and much of his professional business. His comic romance of Captain Farrago and his ragged Irish servant was put out in parts beginning in 1792, continued at intervals, and reissued in a revised and completed form shortly before his death; he wrote also a tragedy on the point of honour, sermons, orations and a quantity of controversial pamphlet matter, and he projected histories and plans of western education which he did not finish. His last years were clouded by the death of an elder son through intemperance, by his own increasing dependence on drink, by removed poverty and by quarrels with the neighbours among whom he had made his fortune, and he died on 25 June 1816 at Carlisle, whither he was journeying, and was buried there in the churchyard.
authors.profile: His central work is the long comic romance, begun in numbers and completed after more than twenty years, which follows a captain of militia and his servant through the elections, militias, speculations, sects and law circuits of the western republic, and which is the first American fiction to make popular politics and office-seeking its sustained subject. He wrote verse of the college and war occasion, including the funeral poem on the general at Quebec, a tragedy of honour and the duel, sermons and orations on education and on the diffusion of knowledge, and pamphlets on the insurrection and on the affairs of the west. Education was his lifelong scheme: the academy, the college, the school and the public library were for him the instruments by which a frontier country might be made a community, and his fiction is continuously an argument about learning, pretension and the uses of books.
authors.style: A robust and colloquially various prose, moving between the high-flown rhetoric of the speculators and politicians, the blunt sense of the servant and the ironied narration of the author, with proverbs, misquotations, Latin school phrases and the speech of the courts and the back settlements all set against one another; an episodic and unhurried picaresque structure, tolerant of digressions and of essays within the story; and in the verse and the orations a fluent eighteenth-century diction of couplet and periodic sentence.
authors.concerns: The dangers and the promise of a republic without ranks, which has only invented new ones; office-seeking, demagogy and the pretensions of the wilder democracy; education and learning as the only safe foundation of western settlement; sectarian zeal and enthusiasm measured against reason and decency; the law, the militia and the conduct of the frontier; the claims of chivalry, honour and duelling in a country of common men.
authors.significance: He is the founder of the literature of the American interior and the author of the first American comic novel of politics, a book which carries the eighteenth-century picaresque across the mountains and applies it to the elections, speculations and sects of the new settlements. His academy became a university and his fiction is the beginning of a native tradition of the frontier satirists; the modern recovery of his work has placed him at the head of the line which runs to the comic storytellers of the Mississippi, and his career documents the intellectual history of the American west in the generation after the Revolution.
authors.uncertainty: The year and place of his Scottish birth are given in the earliest memorials with small variations, the interval and conditions of his emigration rest on family narrative, and the chronology of the several parts and revised issues of his comic romance, and of the authorship of some pamphlets printed in his name, is still imperfectly settled.

authors.name: Hugh Kelly

authors.identity: Dramatist and poet, an Irish-born writer of sentimental comedy who became a prominent figure and government supporter on the London stage.
authors.biography: Born around 1739 in Ireland (his birthplace is given variously as Dublin or Killarney), the son of a publican, he worked as a staymaker and studied law before turning to the stage and journalism in London. Employed as a writer for government, he produced the successful sentimental comedy The False Delicacy (1768), followed by A Word to the Wise (1770), and wrote verse including the poem Thespis (1766). His rivalry with Oliver Goldsmith generated well-known theatrical and literary quarrels. He died in London on 3 February 1777.
authors.profile: A writer of sentimental and moral comedy and occasional verse, whose plays appealed to mid-century tastes for delicacy and virtue and who was a rival to Goldsmith in the competition for the comic stage.
authors.style: Sentimental comedy of delicate feeling and moral testing; neat comic plotting; conventional Augustan diction in his verse; and a polished, sometimes didactic tone.

authors.significance: A leading comic dramatist of the 1760s and 1770s and a memorable rival of Goldsmith, whose career illustrates the intertwining of the stage, government propaganda, and literary politics in the period.

authors.name: Hugh Latimer
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: preacher; bishop of Worcester; martyr
authors.biography: Born of a yeoman family at Thurcaston about 1485; educated at Cambridge, where he was converted from conservative orthodoxy to the reformed faith in the 1520s. A preacher of extraordinary popular power, he became bishop of Worcester in 1535, resigned in 1539 over the Six Articles, and preached through the Edwardian years, notably the Sermon of the Plough (1548) and the Lent sermons before Edward VI (1549). Under Mary he was imprisoned with Ridley and Cranmer and burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555, urging Ridley: 'we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.'
authors.profile: The greatest English preacher of the Reformation. His printed sermons — above all the Sermon of the Plough and the Sermons before King Edward VI — are the classics of Tudor homiletics: plain, concrete, homely in metaphor, and fearless in their attack on landlords, enclosers, and corrupt clergy.
authors.style: The plain style made dramatic: rural simile, proverb, anecdote, and direct address; a yeoman's concreteness yoked to scriptural authority.
authors.concerns: Preaching as the cure of the commonwealth; social justice against enclosure and greed; the duty of bishops and landlords; the Word before ceremony.
authors.significance: The model of English preaching for a century and a principal voice of the Reformation's social conscience; his sermons document the moral crisis of mid-Tudor England.

authors.name: Hugh MacDiarmid
authors.nationality: Scottish; the synthetic Scots lyric and the modernist long poem of national self-examination
authors.identity: Poet and polemicist; the founder of the Scottish Renaissance, the author of A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle, and the most important Scottish poet of the century.
authors.biography: Born Christopher Murray Grieve at Langholm, Dumfriesshire, on 11 August 1892, the son of a postman; he trained as a teacher, worked as a journalist in Montrose, founded the Scottish Chapbook (1922) and the Scottish Nation, and published Sangschaw (1925), Penny Wheep (1926) and A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle (1926) under the name Hugh MacDiarmid. He joined the Communist Party (1934), was expelled and rejoined, published the long poems To Circumjack Cencrastus (1930), In Memoriam James Joyce (1955) and The Kind of Poetry I Want (1961), and died in Edinburgh on 9 September 1978.
authors.profile: MacDiarmid founded the modern literature of Scotland: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is the century's greatest long poem in Scots and one of the great poems of national self-examination in any language, and his synthetic Scots — made from Jamieson's dictionary and the ballads — gave the language a modern poetic instrument. His later English long poems extended the same ambition into science, linguistics and world culture.
authors.style: The synthetic Scots lyric with its dictionary richness; the long poem built of lyric bursts and argument; the sudden shift from Scots to English and back; the manifesto, the pamphlet and the insult; the scientific and linguistic vocabulary carried into verse.
authors.concerns: Scotland, the Scots language and its loss; Calvinism and the Scottish psyche; the industrial city and the emptied glen; communism and the political poem; language itself as a national inheritance; the poet as a public scourge.
authors.significance: MacDiarmid is the central Scottish poet of the century and the founder of the Scottish Renaissance: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is a permanent long poem, his synthetic Scots restored the language as a poetic medium, and his polemics made Scottish literature a modern question. He is the period's great poet of national identity.

authors.name: Humphry Davy
authors.nationality: English (Cornish); the Regency science and literary culture of Bristol and the metropolitan institution
authors.identity: Chemist, lecturer and poet; the most brilliant public expositor of the new chemistry, the founder of electro-chemical investigation in Britain, and a representative figure of the union of science, literature and celebrity in the Romantic period.
authors.biography: Davy was born at Penzance in Cornwall on 17 December 1778, the second of eight children of a carpenter and portrait-painter of modest means, and was put out as an apprentice to his brother John, a Penzance surgeon, where the pharmacy and a chance of chemistry first attracted him. Removed to Bristol in 1798 by Thomas Beddoes, he worked at the Pneumatic Institution founded for the trial of the new gases in disease, and the experiments on nitrous oxide and on other aeriform fluids recorded in the Researches, Chemical and Philosophical of 1800 made his name. He came to London as assistant lecturer at the metropolitan institution and from 1802 delivered the annual course that made him the most attended scientific speaker in the kingdom, lecturing on agriculture, on the chemistry of combustion and respiration, and, before a mixed fashionable audience, on the powers of the new science. In 1807 and 1808, with the great battery of the institution, he decomposed the fixed alkalis and the earths and isolated the metals of potash and soda, and he established the electro-chemical doctrine of affinity; he was knighted in 1812, and the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of that year, the first part only of a projected treatise, gathered the new chemistry into a philosophy. Returned to Parliament for the Devon borough of Ashburton in 1812, he also took the professional care of mining safety that produced the safety lamp of 1815, the instrument for which he refused a patent. He was president of the Royal Society from 1820 until ill health compelled his resignation in 1827; his marriage of 1812 had ended in separation, and after leaving the presidency he set out on a last tour of the Continent, dying at Geneva on 29 May 1829 at the age of fifty, a figure of celebrity whom the literary public remembered as a poet and a moralist of science as well as a chemist.
authors.profile: His scientific writing is at once an experimental record and a public performance: the Bristol volume of 1800 is a narrative of inquiry, with the history of the compound, the account of the inhalations made on his own body and on his friends, and the physiological speculation about respiration and animal heat, while the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of 1812 states the doctrines of the elements, of the atomic theory and of electro-chemical affinity as a complete system, and closes with a celebrated prospectus of the power of chemical discovery. He left also lectures on agricultural chemistry, papers to the Royal Society, a set of early poems and dramatic attempts preserved in his notebooks, and a large correspondence.
authors.style: A lecture prose of great rhetorical command, in which the experimental narrative is arranged as discovery, with the sentence of wonder, the apostrophe to nature and the elevated close on the uses of science; the technical writing is clear, generalising and ambitious of system, and it self-consciously claims the imagination for the chemist. His early verse and the manuscripts of his youth show an accomplished Romantic diction of the school he read, and the two manner, the poetical and the philosophical, are continuous in the public lectures.
authors.concerns: The chemical constitution of bodies and the electrical origin of affinity; the decomposition of the earths and alkalis and the nature of the elements; the chemistry of respiration, of animal heat and of the effects of gases upon living bodies; the safety of the miner and the duty of the scientist to useful invention; the relation of physical enquiry to poetry, to religion and to public improvement; the limits of the atomic and the electro-chemical explanations.
authors.significance: He founded electro-chemistry as a branch of the science, established the list of the elements as it stood before the periodic scheme, and gave the Royal Institution its public character, making the scientific lecture a fashionable and literary event for the first time in England. His safety lamp, adopted with modifications after the inquiry into coal mining, was the first great instrument of industrial humanity produced by scientific method, and his presidency of the Royal Society and his teaching of Michael Faraday place him at the origin of the professional scientific culture of Victorian Britain.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his Cornish apprenticeship and of the removal to Bristol is given with small variations in the biographies, and the dating of his earliest verse and dramatic manuscripts is uncertain. The full extent of his authorship of anonymous reviews and of contributions to the fashionable literary and scientific journals of the 1800s has never been settled, and the records of the inhalation experiments at Bristol survive only as he and Beddoes reported them.

authors.biography: A monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow from boyhood who studied in Ireland in his youth and took the religious name Eusebius. authors.concerns: The encyclopedic ordering of knowledge; the riddling description of creation; the transmission of Aldhelmian learning in Northumbria.
authors.significance: His riddles, together with Tatwine's, carried the Aldhelmian riddle tradition into the Northumbrian Renaissance and stand behind the vernacular riddle collection of the Exeter Book.

authors.name: I. A. Richards
authors.nationality: British; the founder of Practical Criticism and of the semantics of the poem
authors.identity: Critic and rhetorician; the author of Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism.
authors.biography: Born Ivor Armstrong Richards at Sandgate, Kent, on 26 February 1893; he read philosophy and English at Cambridge and taught there from 1919, where the experiments of the classroom became Principles of Literary Criticism (1924), Science and Poetry (1926) and Practical Criticism (1929). Coleridge on Imagination (1934) and The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936) carried the argument into the theory of metaphor; his later work on Basic English took him to China and Harvard, where he died on 7 September 1979.
authors.profile: I. A. Richards founded the modern discipline of practical criticism: the experiments of Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism made the reading of the poem, rather than its history, the object of the discipline, and gave the New Criticism of England and America its method and its vocabulary of the pseudo-statement, the impulse and the stock response.
authors.style: The analytic prose of the psychologist of reading; the experiment and the protocol as the form of criticism; the definition and the distinction carried in the plain sentence; the rejection of the biographical and the historical in favour of the reading; the rhetoric of metaphor as the instrument of thought.
authors.concerns: The reading of the poem and the psychology of the reader; the pseudo-statement and the language of science; metaphor and the rhetoric of thought; Coleridge and the imagination; Basic English and the teaching of reading; the discipline of criticism as a science of the response.
authors.significance: I. A. Richards founded the modern discipline of practical criticism: Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism made the reading of the poem the object of the discipline and gave the New Criticism of England and America its method and its vocabulary.

authors.name: Ian Maclaren

authors.identity: Minister and novelist; the pseudonym of John Watson, whose Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s.
authors.biography: Born John Watson at Manningtree, Essex, on 3 November 1850 to Scottish parents; he was raised in Perthshire, studied at Edinburgh, and was minister of the Free Church at Logiealmond and then of Sefton Park Presbyterian Church, Liverpool. Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush (1894) sold in vast numbers; The Days of Auld Lang Syne (1895) and Kate Carnegie (1896) followed. He died at Mount Pleasant, Iowa, on 6 May 1907 while on a lecture tour.
authors.profile: Maclaren's Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s and the central text of the kailyard school: its sketches of the minister, the schoolmaster and the dying child created a sentimental image of the Scottish parish that dominated the popular imagination and provoked the reaction of George Douglas Brown and the Scottish Renaissance.
authors.style: The linked sketch rather than the plotted novel; the dialect of the parish in direct speech; the deathbed scene and the consoling anecdote; the minister as narrator and moral centre; the short, sententious paragraph.
authors.concerns: The Presbyterian parish and its discipline; death, consolation and the life to come; poverty and the pride of the Scottish poor; education as the ladder out of the parish; the rural community against the modern city.
authors.significance: Ian Maclaren's Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s and the central text of the kailyard school: its sentimental parish sketches shaped the popular image of Scotland for a generation and provoked the realist reaction of The House with the Green Shutters.

authors.name: Ida B. Wells
authors.nationality: African-American; the investigative pamphlet and the literature of anti-lynching
authors.identity: Journalist, editor and activist; the founder of the modern investigative journalism of racial terror and the central figure of the anti-lynching movement.
authors.biography: Born Ida Bell Wells in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on 16 July 1862, six months before emancipation; she was orphaned at sixteen and supported her siblings as a teacher, then moved to Memphis and edited the Free Speech and Headlight. After the lynching of three friends in 1892 she published Southern Horrors (1892) and was driven from Memphis; she toured Britain and the United States, married the lawyer Ferdinand Barnett in 1895, and was a founder of the NAACP in 1909. She died in Chicago on 25 March 1931.
authors.profile: Wells invented the modern documentary pamphlet: her anti-lynching reports collect statistics, court records, newspaper accounts and her own interviews, and they destroy the myth of the black rapist with evidence while naming the economic motive behind the terror. Her prose is controlled, factual and utterly fearless, and The Red Record is the founding text of American investigative journalism on race.
authors.style: Documented statistics; case by case narrative; the exposure of newspaper lies; direct indictment of named officials; irony and controlled anger; the pamphlet and the lecture as political instruments.
authors.concerns: Lynching and racial terror; the sexual politics of the myth of the black rapist; the economic competition behind the violence; the failure of the law and the churches; the black woman's testimony; the American South and the nation's silence.
authors.significance: Wells is the founding figure of anti-lynching journalism and one of the most important American writers of non-fiction: Southern Horrors and The Red Record created the documentary literature of racial terror, and her work is the direct ancestor of the civil rights journalism of the twentieth century.

authors.name: Isaac Rosenberg
authors.nationality: British; the war lyric of the Jewish East End and the poetry of the painted image
authors.identity: Poet and painter; the greatest of the soldier-poets after Owen, the first major English poet of the Jewish immigrant poor.
authors.biography: Born Isaac Rosenberg in Bristol on 25 November 1890, the son of Lithuanian Jewish immigrants, and brought up in the East End of London; he left school at fourteen to be an apprentice engraver, studied art at the Slade (1911–14) with Mark Gertler and David Bomberg, and published Night and Day (1912) and Youth (1915) at his own expense. He enlisted in 1915, served with the King's Own Royal Lancasters, and was killed at Fampoux on the Arras front on 1 April 1918; his Poems were collected in 1922.
authors.profile: Rosenberg is, with Owen, the greatest poet of the First World War and the first English poet to write out of the Jewish immigrant experience. 'Break of Day in the Trenches', 'Dead Man's Dump' and 'Returning, We Hear the Larks' are among the finest war poems in the language, and 'The Burning of the Temple' and the plays show a visionary ambition cut off at twenty-seven. He wrote from the ranks, not the officers' mess, and his poetry keeps the physical pity of the war without rhetoric.
authors.style: The image that comes from a painter's eye; the rough, uneven, spoken line; the sudden visionary or biblical image inside a trench poem; the unrhymed lyric; the exact weight and colour of the physical world; the deliberate awkwardness that refuses polish.
authors.concerns: The war and the dead body; the Jewish East End and the immigrant poor; the painter's vision and the biblical image; death, the grave and the unquiet spirit; comradeship and the ordinary soldier; the beauty of the visible world.
authors.significance: Rosenberg is the greatest soldier-poet after Owen and the first major English poet of the Jewish immigrant working class: 'Break of Day in the Trenches' and 'Dead Man's Dump' are permanent war poems, and his visionary fragments stand with the best poetry of the period. His work is the period's clearest evidence that the war's literature came from the ranks as much as from the officers.

authors.name: Isaac Watts
authors.nationality: English Dissenter
authors.identity: Independent minister, logician and the father of English hymnody, who taught Dissent to sing its own composed songs and wrote a textbook of reasoning used on both sides of the Atlantic.
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1674, the eldest of the children of a Southampton Nonconformist family whose father suffered imprisonment for religious meetings, he showed a remarkable gift for Latin as a child and was educated for the ministry under Dissenting tutors. He preached early and reluctantly, held a small charge in the country, and settled in London, where from the early 1690s he led the Independent assembly in Mark Lane and built one of the largest and most cultivated congregations in Dissent. His hymns and songs of worship began with the Horae Lyricae and the Hymns and Spiritual Songs of 1707, followed by Divine and Moral Songs for Children and by his bold paraphrases of the psalms, which provoked long disputes about whether congregations might sing anything not taken from the biblical psalter. His Logic, or the Art of Reasoning, his Improvement of the Mind and his theological and homiletic works made him a standard author for schools and preachers. Suspected by some of abandoning the Trinity, he was honoured with a doctorate and spent his last decades an invalid, still writing and visiting, until his death in November 1748; he was buried at Bunhill Fields.
authors.profile: The scholar-preacher of hymns and rules of thinking, who joined catechetical plainness to a lyricist's sense of meter and of congregational feeling.
authors.style: Clear, taught, unhurried prose in his logic and divinity; hymn verse in simple common measures with strong doctrinal structure and affective immediacy; a psalm paraphrase of dignified warmth.
authors.concerns: The signs, ideas and method of right reasoning; human composition in worship and the education of a singing people; the doctrine of the atonement and the disputed Trinity; childhood, catechism and the piety of the common Christian.
authors.significance: He invented the English congregation hymn and made it the vehicle of doctrine, and his Logic was a chief instrument of education for a century, used by Dissenters, Anglicans and the American colleges alike.
authors.uncertainty: The precise sequence of his early pastoral settlements is uncertain, and the authorship of a few works printed under his name has been debated.

authors.name: Israel Zangwill
authors.nationality: English-Jewish; the ghetto novel, the problem play and the literature of immigration
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and Zionist; the first English writer to make the Jewish immigrant experience the subject of major fiction.
authors.biography: Born in London on 21 February 1864, the son of Russian-Polish Jewish immigrants; he was educated at the Jews' Free School and at London University, became a teacher and then a journalist, and published The Children of the Ghetto in 1892, which made him famous as the 'Dickens of the Ghetto'. He wrote the play The Melting Pot (1908), was an early Zionist and later a territorialist, and campaigned for women's suffrage. He died at Midhurst, Sussex, on 1 August 1926.
authors.profile: Zangwill wrote the English novel of the immigrant: The Children of the Ghetto and its sequels are the first substantial English fiction about the Jewish East End, and they record the speech, the poverty, the religion and the humour of the immigrant community with exactness and affection. He was also the first English writer to make the ghetto the subject of serious literature, and The Melting Pot gave the language its phrase for the American assimilation of immigrants.
authors.style: Dialect speech transcribed with care; comic caricature with a documentary purpose; the large cast of a whole community; the essay and the sermon worked into the narrative; the problem play of ideas.
authors.concerns: Jewish immigration and the East End ghetto; assimilation and the loss of tradition; Zionism and the Jewish nation; poverty and sweated labour; the American melting pot; women's suffrage and the position of the Jewish woman.
authors.significance: Zangwill is the founding figure of English-Jewish literature: The Children of the Ghetto is the first major English book about the Jewish immigrant community, it made the East End ghetto a literary subject, and The Melting Pot gave the English language its most enduring metaphor for immigrant assimilation.

authors.name: Izaak Walton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican biographer and author of The Compleat Angler (1653), the beloved pastoral dialogue of fishing whose serene celebration of the contemplative country life made it one of the most reprinted books in English.
authors.biography: Born 9 August 1593 at Stafford; apprenticed to a linen-draper, he prospered as a haberdasher in London (Fleet Street and later Chancery Lane) and moved in literary circles. A devout royalist Anglican, he served the cause during the Civil Wars and at the Restoration. He wrote gentle biographies of John Donne (1640), Sir Henry Wotton, Richard Hooker, George Herbert (1670), and Robert Sanderson, collected as Walton's Lives. His masterpiece The Compleat Angler (1653), enlarged over five editions to 1676 (with Charles Cotton's second part on fly-fishing), became a classic. He retired to the country and died on 15 December 1683 at Winchester, aged 90.
authors.profile: The biographer of the devout and the angler of the contemplative life, whose unhurried, genial prose celebrates friendship, piety, and the pleasures of riverside retirement.
authors.style: Gentle, pastoral, conversational prose; dialogue form (Piscator, Venator, Auceps); a serene, pious tone; digressive quotation of verse and lore; and unpretentious charm.
authors.concerns: The contemplative and retired life; friendship and piety; the natural world of rivers and fish; Anglican devotion and modest virtue; and the celebration of simple pleasures.
authors.significance: The Compleat Angler has been continuously in print and is one of the most beloved of English books; Walton's Lives established a tradition of affectionate biographical portraiture and shaped the ideal of the Anglican 'holy life'.

authors.biography: Born John Burdon Sanderson Haldane at Oxford on 5 November 1892, the son of the physiologist J. S. authors.biography: Born John Collings Squire at Plymouth on 14 November 1884; he was literary editor of the New Statesman from 1913 and editor of the London Mercury from 1919 to 1934, the house journal of the Georgian poets. authors.name: J. M. Barrie
authors.nationality: Scottish; the children's fantasy and the sentimental Scottish comedy
authors.identity: Dramatist and novelist; the creator of Peter Pan and the most popular Scottish writer of the age.
authors.biography: Born James Matthew Barrie at Kirriemuir, Angus, on 9 May 1860, the ninth child of a hand-loom weaver; he was educated at Edinburgh University and worked as a journalist in Nottingham and London before his Scottish sketches, collected as Auld Licht Idylls (1888) and A Window in Thrums (1889), made him famous. His novels The Little Minister (1891) and Sentimental Tommy (1896) were best-sellers; he turned to the stage in 1897, and Peter Pan was first performed in 1904. He was made a baronet in 1913 and died in London on 19 June 1937.
authors.profile: Barrie wrote the English and Scottish sentimental comedy and the fantasy of childhood: his Peter Pan is the central myth of the modern imagination of childhood — the boy who will not grow up, the island of lost boys, the fairy and the pirate — and his plays and Scottish sketches are full of a delicate, ironic tenderness for small lives and lost mothers. His work is also one of the great Victorian and Edwardian studies of grief: the death of his brother David, on whom he modelled Peter, haunted everything he wrote.
authors.style: Kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect; whimsy and pathos held together by irony; stage directions of extraordinary detail; the child's point of view rendered without condescension; the fantasy that is also a study of loss.
authors.concerns: Childhood and the refusal to grow up; motherhood and the loss of the mother; Scotland, the village and the kailyard; fantasy and escape; time and memory; money, class and the small town.
authors.significance: Barrie is the most popular Scottish writer of his age and the creator of Peter Pan, the most influential children's myth of the twentieth century: the play gave the language a permanent figure, its royalties endowed Great Ormond Street Hospital, and its treatment of childhood and grief has made it a central text of modern children's literature and of Scottish writing.

authors.name: J. M. Synge
authors.nationality: Irish; the peasant drama, the Aran travel book and the poetic prose of the stage
authors.identity: Dramatist; the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival and the author of The Playboy of the Western World, Riders to the Sea and The Well of the Saints.
authors.biography: Born Edmund John Millington Synge at Rathfarnham, Dublin, on 16 April 1871 into an evangelical landowning family; he read at Trinity College Dublin, studied music and then literature in Germany and Paris, and was sent by Yeats to the Aran Islands in 1898. The Aran Islands (1907) records those visits; In the Shadow of the Glen (1903), Riders to the Sea (1904), The Well of the Saints (1905), The Playboy of the Western World (1907) and Deirdre of the Sorrows (1910) made the Abbey Theatre. He died of Hodgkin's disease in Dublin on 24 March 1909, aged thirty-seven.
authors.profile: Synge is the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival: he made the speech of the Aran and Wicklow people into a poetic prose of extraordinary density, and The Playboy of the Western World is the finest Irish play of the century and one of the great comedies in English. Riders to the Sea is a perfect one-act tragedy, Deirdre of the Sorrows a great verse-prose tragedy, and The Aran Islands one of the finest travel books in the language.
authors.style: A poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech; the single cottage set and the one-act compression; the folk tale and the wonder tale as structure; comedy that turns into tragedy without a join; the lyrical final speech.
authors.concerns: The Aran Islands and the western seaboard; the sea, drowning and the mother's grief; the peasant imagination and its stories; the wanderer, the tramp and the stranger; the woman, marriage and the arranged match; paganism and the priest; the national character and its myths.
authors.significance: Synge is the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival and one of the finest playwrights in English of the century: The Playboy of the Western World is a permanent comedy, Riders to the Sea a perfect tragedy, and his prose invention — Irish speech made into a literary language — gave modern drama a new music. The Playboy riots of 1907 made him the period's most controversial playwright.

authors.identity: Novelist, poet and philologist; the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings and the Merton Professor of English Language at Oxford.
authors.biography: Born John Ronald Reuel Tolkien at Bloemfontein on 3 January 1892; he was brought up in the West Midlands after his father's death, read English at Exeter College, Oxford, and served as a signals officer on the Somme in 1916. He held the Leeds chair of English Language and then the Rawlinson and Bosworth chair of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, and from 1945 the Merton professorship; The Hobbit appeared in 1937 and The Lord of the Rings in 1954-55. He died at Bournemouth on 2 September 1973.
authors.profile: J. R. R. Tolkien created the modern high fantasy and, with it, the most read fiction of the twentieth century: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings gave the invented world its grammar, its languages and its history, while 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' and On Fairy-Stories rewrote the theory of the northern epic and of faerie. His philology is the root of the fiction, and the fiction is the proof of his claim that a language grows a mythology.
authors.style: The invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it; the slow, layered, annalistic narrative that reports a history rather than a plot; the comic homeliness of the hobbit set against the high style of the elves; the elegiac north; the sentence built on the rhythms of the Old English prose he edited.
authors.concerns: Language and the mythology it generates; the north, the heroic and the elegiac; faerie and the recovery of the marvellous; the machine and the dominion of the will over creation; the Roman Catholic imagination under the invented world; the fellowship and the refusal of the ring.
authors.significance: J. R. R. Tolkien is the inventor of the modern high fantasy and the most read novelist of the twentieth century: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings gave the invented world its languages and its history, and his essays on Beowulf and on fairy-stories remain the founding criticism of the mode he created.

authors.name: Jack London
authors.nationality: American; the adventure romance, the socialist tract and the novel of the North
authors.identity: Novelist, journalist and socialist; the most widely read American writer of his time and the author of The Call of the Wild.
authors.biography: Born John Griffith Chaney in San Francisco on 12 January 1876, the illegitimate son of an astrologer and a spiritualist; he left school at thirteen and worked in a cannery, as an oyster pirate, a sailor and a tramp, and was jailed for vagrancy in 1894. He joined the Klondike gold rush in 1897 and began writing on his return; The Call of the Wild (1903) and The Sea-Wolf (1904) made him rich. He joined the Socialist Party, wrote The Iron Heel and Martin Eden, and died at Glen Ellen, California, on 22 November 1916.
authors.profile: London wrote the American adventure story as a vehicle of ideas: his Klondike tales are stories of survival at the limit of nature, and his novels carry a socialist and Darwinian argument about the struggle for existence and the class war. He was also the first American writer to make a fortune from the mass magazine market, and his best work — The Call of the Wild, 'To Build a Fire', Martin Eden — is unmatched in the American literature of the far north.
authors.style: Direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third; the ordeal narrative of survival; the animal's point of view; the documentary account of work at sea, in the mines and on the trail; the socialist argument carried by plot; the return to the primitive.
authors.concerns: Survival, the struggle for existence and the call of the wild; the Klondike and the frontier north; socialism and the class war; the sea and the working sailor; the artist and the market; the primitive and the civilised.
authors.significance: London is the most widely translated American writer of his era and a central figure in the American literature of naturalism and of socialism: The Call of the Wild has never been out of print, 'To Build a Fire' is the classic American story of the wilderness, and his Klondike fiction created the modern myth of the north.
