authors.name: Jedidiah Morse
authors.nationality: American; New England Congregational (Orthodox standing order) and early-national scientific writing
authors.identity: Congregational minister, geographer and publicist; the "father of American geography" whose school textbooks defined geographic education for a generation, and the chief orthodox polemicist against Unitarianism
authors.biography: Jedidiah Morse was born at Woodstock, Connecticut, on 23 August 1761, the son of a Congregational minister of modest means, and was educated at home and in the local schools before entering Yale College, from which he graduated in 1783. He studied divinity, was licensed and ordained in 1785-86, held a brief pastorate at Norwich, and in 1789 began the long pastorate of the First Church at Charlestown, Massachusetts, which he served until ill health and the controversies he had stirred forced his retirement to New Haven about 1820. From his student years he wrote for the classroom: Geography Made Easy (1784), the two-volume American Geography (1789) with its maps, The American Universal Geography (first edition in the early 1790s, repeatedly revised and reissued through the 1820s), and The American Gazetteer (1796) - the first American gazetteer - together with atlases, a Universal Geography for schools, and a series of enlargements that made him the standard authority on the physical and political geography of the new nation and a supplier of maps to Congress and to state governments. A convinced Federalist and opponent of the French Revolution, he kept politics inside his religion: he helped found Andover Theological Seminary in 1808 as an orthodox alternative to Harvard, backed foreign missions and the missionary printing that flowed through the Missionary Herald, and served as corresponding secretary of Massachusetts mission societies. In September 1822 he preached the annual sermon before the Association of Ministers of Massachusetts at Cambridge, an explicit challenge to Unitarian teaching and an argument that associations should examine orthodoxy before ordination; its publication, requested by the Association, detonated the Unitarian controversy in the standing order, producing replies from William Ellery Channing and others and years of pamphlet war. He died at New Haven on 9 June 1826 and was buried in Grove Street Cemetery, leaving sons - among them Samuel Finley Breese Morse - who carried his public prominence into art and invention.
authors.profile: Morse's output is essentially informational and polemical rather than imaginative: school geography and gazetteers, maps and their explanatory keys, a compendious New England history, sermons, election and missionary discourses, tracts on political character, and the 1822 Cambridge sermon. He writes as a compiler-didact, arranging observation under moral and providential headings; his prose exists to be learnt, recited and believed.
authors.style: Expository prose of tremendous compression: enumerative, topographical, and laden with statistics, distances and tables, yet framed by homiletic reflection on climate, character and providence. The schoolbooks are deliberately plain and question-driven. In the sermons and tracts the same clarity turns adversarial - syllogistic argument, pointed biblical inference, and an insistence on definitions, tests and confessions of faith.
authors.concerns: How a young republic might know its own space and produce its own textbooks instead of importing British ones; the relation of climate, geography and national character; the authority of scripture and of confessional standards in a changing New England; the danger of theological liberalism to social order; education, missions and print as instruments of civic and religious unity.
authors.significance: Morse established American geography as a school subject and a publishing industry, and his gazetteers and maps were the reference works of the early republic; his 1822 Cambridge sermon is conventionally taken as the opening gun of the Unitarian-Congregational split that remapped New England religion and led directly to the founding of Harvard Divinity's rival, Andover, and to the institutional separation of Unitarianism. As a Federalist churchman he also links partisan politics, missions and education in a single career.
authors.uncertainty: The exact first-publication year of The American Universal Geography varies in the sources consulted (the early 1790s; commonly 1793, with a two-volume edition of 1792 also cited), as does the end-date of his Charlestown pastorate (given as 1819 or 1820). The precise day of the 1822 Cambridge sermon is not fixed by the accounts checked, though its place before the Association of Ministers and its 1822 date are standard. His role as an Indian-trades agent and the later Texas-colonization accusation against him belong after this period and remain disputed.

authors.name: Jeremy Bentham
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Law reformer and moral philosopher, founder of classical utilitarianism, who measured institutions by pleasure and pain and subjected the common law, the church and the prison to the test of utility.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1748 into a wealthy family of attorneys, a child prodigy in Latin and French law books, he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1769, though he never practised and soon abandoned the profession to write on legislation. He inherited property and leisure, attached himself to no party, and passed his life in lodgings and in correspondence, drafting codes, inspecting prisons, and corresponding with rulers and reformers across Europe and America. Two long stays at the estates of his brother Samuel, the engineer in Russia, sharpened his ideas about inspection and the organisation of labour. He wrote against Blackstone in the 1760s, published the Fragment on Government anonymously in 1776, the Defence of Usury in 1787 and the Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. His Panopticon scheme and his writings on colonies and on judicial procedure belong to the 1790s; the coded works edited for him by Dumont appeared in the 1800s, and his attack on Blackstone's Commentaries remained in manuscript until the twentieth century. He died in London in 1832, having asked that his body be dissected and preserved as his auto-icon.
authors.profile: A jurist of facts and consequences, whose vocabulary of utility, felicity and the greatest number recast moral and legal argument as an arithmetic of interests.
authors.style: Technical, taxonomic, tireless prose; long definitions, enumerated situations and coined terms; polemic conducted through analysis rather than rhetoric; a satirist's dryness about lawyers and priests.
authors.concerns: The greatest happiness principle; the anatomy of law, sovereignty and obligation; punishment, deterrence and the inspection of the idle; the interests of women, of colonial subjects and of animals; the corruption of church, university and common law.
authors.significance: He founded utilitarian ethics and systematic law reform, shaped Victorian policing, education and welfare legislation, and made the critical test of institutions their consequences for the greatest number.
authors.uncertainty: The order of his vast unpublished manuscripts, much of it first printed by editors after his death, makes the dating of his ideas a continual problem.

authors.name: Jeremy Taylor
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican divine and devotional writer, called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'; his Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651) are the supreme prose achievements of Caroline Anglican piety, rich in imagery, learning, and moral casuistry.
authors.biography: Born August 1613 at Cambridge, son of a barber; educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (BA 1630, MA 1634) and All Souls, Oxford. Patronised by William Laud and Charles I, he became a royalist chaplain, was twice imprisoned during the Civil Wars, and was deprived of his living. In seclusion in Wales he wrote his great devotional manuals Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651), and the casuistical Ductor Dubitantium (1660). At the Restoration he was consecrated Bishop of Down and Connor (1661) and Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College, Dublin; he died on 13 August 1667 at Lisburn.
authors.profile: The eloquent Caroline divine whose devotional prose combines baroque imagery, immense learning, and tender moral guidance, treating the whole of life as a preparation for a holy death.
authors.style: Lush, metaphorical, Latinate prose; abundant simile and classical and scriptural allusion; casuistical moral reasoning; and a rich, musical rhythm.
authors.concerns: Holy living and dying; Christian virtue, patience, and repentance; liberty of conscience and toleration (The Liberty of Prophesying, 1647); moral casuistry; and Anglican devotion.
authors.significance: Holy Living and Holy Dying shaped English devotional prose and the Anglican ideal of the good life and good death for centuries; Taylor's eloquence and advocacy of toleration mark him as one of the greatest prose writers and most liberal-minded of the Caroline divines.
authors.uncertainty: Taylor's life is documented; his imprisoned royalist years and some details of his preferment rest on tradition and ecclesiastical records.

authors.name: Jerome K. Jerome
authors.nationality: English; the comic travel book and the farce
authors.identity: Humorist, novelist and playwright; the author of Three Men in a Boat, the most durable English comic book of the century.
authors.biography: Born Jerome Klapka Jerome at Walsall, Staffordshire, on 2 May 1859, the son of a coal-mine owner and lay preacher who died in poverty; he left school at fourteen and worked as a railway clerk, a schoolmaster, a journalist and an actor before Three Men in a Boat (1889) made him famous. He founded and edited The Idler (1892-97) and wrote many plays and essays; he died at Northampton on 14 June 1927.
authors.profile: Jerome wrote the modern comic travel book: Three Men in a Boat takes the Victorian vogue for the Thames excursion and turns it into a shaggy-dog narrative of three incompetent young men, a dog and a great deal of unnecessary luggage, in which the comedy lies in the gap between the heroic intention and the domestic disaster. He was also a considerable comic playwright and a gentle satirist of the late-Victorian office and suburb.
authors.style: Digressive, anecdotal first-person narration; the comic list and the escalating catalogue; deadpan reporting of absurdity; the mock-heroic treatment of trivial mishaps; self-deprecating irony; dialogue of three friends who talk past one another.
authors.concerns: Holiday, leisure and the English weekend; friendship and masculine companionship; the comic body, illness and medicine; the suburb and the office; the Thames and the English landscape; the gap between pretension and performance.
authors.significance: Jerome is the funniest English writer of the 1890s and Three Men in a Boat one of the small number of English comic classics: it has never been out of print, it made the comic travel book a genre, and its tone — self-mocking, humane, digressive — is the model for English comic writing from Wodehouse to Bryson.

authors.name: Joanna Baillie
authors.nationality: Scottish; the tragedy of the passions and the dramatic verse of the Romantic decade
authors.identity: Tragic dramatist and poet; the most serious English-language woman dramatist of the age and the theorist of the analysis of a single passion
authors.biography: She was the daughter of a Scottish university teacher of divinity and grew up in the Lanarkshire manse before the family removed to Glasgow and then to London, where her brother became one of the most distinguished physicians of the day. She was formed by a long private reading in the old drama and in Greek and modern tragedy rather than by the theatre itself, and she wrote from early womanhood with the plan of a series of plays each founded on one passion analysed in its progress. The first series appeared by subscription in 1798 and was praised by the most influential critic of the age as the work of a serious tragic mind; two further instalments of the series followed in the next fifteen years, and one tragedy of the number, of a man consumed by hatred, was acted at the patent theatre and held the stage with great success in the 1820s. She published a volume of dramatic and descriptive verse and a tragedy attempted at Drury Lane which failed in spite of management support, and she wrote much occasional and ballad verse for the annuals. She never married, lived with her brother and his family and afterwards in her own house in north London, and became the centre of a long literary circle of visitors and correspondents. She died in 1851 at Hampstead, leaving unpublished papers.
authors.profile: A planned series of plays on the passions, issued in several volumes over fourteen years, of which the tragedy of hatred is the enduring piece; a volume of metrical sketches and descriptive and occasional verse; a ballad and legend of the Scottish past; and an important preface and argument setting out the theory of the single-passion analysis. Her dramaturgy is analytic and rhetorical, built on soliloquy and on the progressive disclosure of one governing feeling rather than on incident.
authors.style: Correct and sustained blank verse, closer to the eighteenth-century school of tragedy than to the looser practice of her contemporaries, with a strong use of sententious generalisation and of the interrupted speech of self-examination. Her prose argument is plain and methodical, and her ballad and descriptive verse is quieter and more colloquial than her tragedy.
authors.concerns: The anatomy of the passions and their tyrannical progress. The obligations and injuries of family and benefaction. Revenge, hatred and their effect on the mind that harbours them. The responsibility of the dramatist to moral philosophy. Women's authority in the serious drama and the difficulty of the stage for a woman's writing.
authors.significance: She is the principal tragic poet of the Romantic period who was also a woman, and her series is the most systematic attempt of the age to unite the moral-philosophical analysis of the passions with regular drama. The successful revival of her best play by a famous actor of the 1820s gave her a place in the acting repertory, and her theoretical preface remains a key document of Romantic dramatic thought.
authors.uncertainty: The date at which the several plays of the series were composed is uncertain, since the published volumes were assembled from a much longer period of writing, and the extent of her brother's household's influence on her publication is imperfectly documented.

authors.name: Joel Barlow
authors.nationality: American; the New England letters of Hartford and New Haven in the 1780s, and the revolutionary and deist circle of Americans and French philosophes in the 1790s
authors.identity: Epic poet of the New World, didactic and mock-heroic verse writer, deist controversialist, farmer of America's first great poem on its own subject, and the American diplomat who ended his life on the retreat from Moscow; the most considerable and most compromised American poet of the generation before Bryant.
authors.biography: Barlow was born at Redding in Connecticut, of farming stock with a New England schoolmaster's ambition attached to it, and was put forward to Yale, where he graduated in 1778 of the class which gave the American republic some of its best-known scholars and writers. He served as a chaplain with the Continental forces for three years during the Revolution, was afterwards a tutor at Yale, and belonged in the 1780s to the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of wits who wrote the burlesque and satirical miscellany of the Federalist years, from which he parted company in religion and politics as the French Revolution divided American opinion. He removed to France, where he lived for the rest of his life with short absences, wrote and published the poem on Columbus which he had begun in America, and became an active friend of the American and French reformers; his marriage, his residence near Paris and his correspondence made him the centre of a small American colony in revolutionary France. He was employed by his government in the negotiation of the peace with the regency of Algiers, and was afterwards sent as minister to France; but he had taken French naturalization and had been chosen into the revolutionary legislature, the Directory declined to receive an American minister who was also a citizen of France, and his Federalist countrymen regarded him from that time as something little short of a renegade. He wrote the enlarged and sumptuously given epic of the New World which succeeded the Vision of Columbus, the mock-heroic poem on a New England dish which is still the most agreeable of his verse, and much pamphlet and controversial matter on the politics and the religion of the two countries between which his life was divided; he was also the friend and defender of the age's most infamous radical writer, whose last papers he had the handling of. He accompanied the French army into Russia in 1812 in a department of supply, and, worn out and sick, died at Zarnowiec on the retreat from Moscow on 26 December 1812, leaving a grave in a Polish village churchyard and an almost wholly forgotten epic.
authors.profile: His work is epic, didactic and occasional verse, a body of political and religious pamphlet writing, and a large correspondence: the Columbus poem first printed in 1787, recast and greatly enlarged as the national epic of 1807 with a train of illustrative notes and dissertations on the science, the history and the geography of the New World; the mock-heroic poem on a New England pudding, written abroad and the best-known of his shorter pieces; and prose arguments on deist and Unitarian theology, on education, on the slave trade and on the politics of the French Revolution. The epic was designed as a work of the American continent - its discovery, its colonization, its war and its future - and it is the largest attempt at a national poem made in America before the nineteenth century was well advanced.
authors.style: A command of the eighteenth-century heroic couplet, fluent, descriptive and argumentative, and a blanket ambition of scale in the epic which outruns the execution: enumeration, prophecy, apostrophe to the continent, and a didactic paraphrase of science and history in verse. The lower and better manner is the easy narrative and the joke - the mock-heroic exaltation of a country dish - and the prose is plain, urgent and often sarcastic, with the controversialist's habit of the numbered argument.
authors.concerns: The moral and providential destiny of America, and the use of the epic to a republic; the progress of knowledge, agriculture and civil society; deist and anti-Trinitarian religion against the creeds of New England Calvinism; the rights of man, representative government and the causes of the French Revolution; the slave trade and the condition of the poor; the education of a national taste and a national language.
authors.significance: He wrote the first ambitious American epic and the first American poem to take the whole continent and its history as its subject, and his attempt, ridiculed by the British review press and abandoned by American readers, defined the problem of the long American poem for the generation of Bryant and of the Knickerbocker writers. His diplomatic business with the Barbary regency belongs to the early foreign history of the republic, his religious and political writings carry American deism and republicanism into the European circle of the 1790s, and his career is the clearest case of the American man of letters divided between the revolution he celebrated and the country that distrusted him.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his marriages and of his first wife's death, and the chronology of the several recensions and issues of the Columbus poem, are imperfectly recorded; his acceptance of French naturalization and his election to the Council of Five Hundred are stated variously by hostile Federalist accounts and by the later defence of his family, which extenuated them; and the details of the journey of 1812 and of his death rest on the letters of his companions and on local tradition at Zarnowiec.

authors.name: Joel Chandler Harris
authors.nationality: American; the dialect tale and the framing of black oral narrative
authors.identity: Journalist and writer; the author of the Uncle Remus stories, the most influential collection of African-American folklore in the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born in Eatonton, Georgia, on 9 December 1848, the illegitimate son of an Irish day labourer; at thirteen he was apprenticed to a plantation newspaper, the Countryman, where he lived on the Turnwold plantation and heard the African-American animal tales from the enslaved workers. He worked for the Savannah Morning News and from 1876 for the Atlanta Constitution, where the Uncle Remus sketches appeared from 1878. Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings was published in 1880. He died in Atlanta on 3 July 1908.
authors.profile: Harris wrote the American dialect tale as a record of black oral narrative: the Brer Rabbit stories are African-American folk tales collected with real fidelity, and their trickster hero is one of the great creations of American literature. The frame of the kindly old freedman telling stories to a white boy is also a myth of the plantation that later black writers — Chesnutt above all — had to dismantle, and Harris's work must be read in both lights.
authors.style: Frame narrative in which the tale is told to a listener; phonetic dialect transcription of great care; the trickster plot of the weaker against the stronger; the comic ending; the plantation setting and its idealisation.
authors.concerns: African-American folklore and oral tradition; the trickster and the powerless; the plantation myth and its ideology; childhood and storytelling; the post-Reconstruction South; the relation of black and white Southerners.
authors.significance: Harris collected and preserved the most important body of African-American folklore of the nineteenth century and introduced Brer Rabbit to the world: his dialect transcription is a landmark of American dialect writing, and the Uncle Remus books are central — and contested — documents of American race and literature.

authors.name: John Addington Symonds
authors.nationality: English; criticism, the Renaissance history and the literature of desire
authors.identity: Critic, historian of the Renaissance and poet; the author of Renaissance in Italy and one of the founders of the modern literature of male same-sex desire.
authors.biography: Born at Bristol on 5 October 1840, the son of a physician; he was educated at Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford, where he fell in love with a Bristol chorister and wrote the sonnets that became part of his life's secret work. He married Janet North in 1864 and lived at Clifton and Davos, Switzerland, for his health. He wrote Renaissance in Italy (1875-86), biographies of Michelangelo and Ben Jonson, translations of Greek poetry and a large body of verse and prose on Greek love. He died at Rome on 19 April 1893.
authors.profile: Symonds wrote the history of the Renaissance as a history of feeling: his seven-volume Renaissance in Italy is the first full English account of the period as a whole, and his studies of Greek ethics, Walt Whitman and Michelangelo were the foundation of the modern study of same-sex desire in literature. He was a poet of considerable power and a prose writer of great range, and his private writings — the Memoirs and the 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' — are among the first sustained English arguments for the dignity of homosexual love.
authors.style: Historical narrative on a large scale; biography as psychological analysis; the sonnet and the elegy; scholarly prose with a personal urgency; the translation as an act of identification; private manuscript and careful publication.
authors.concerns: The Renaissance and its culture of the individual; Greek ethics and the love of men; the relation of art to sexuality; Whitman and democratic comradeship; Italy and the Alps as scenes of self-discovery; the ethics of concealment.
authors.significance: Symonds wrote the first comprehensive English history of the Italian Renaissance and was the most important English writer on same-sex desire before Wilde's trials: his 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' (privately printed, 1883) is a founding text of the modern discourse, and his influence on Pater, Gosse, Havelock Ellis and the 1890s is decisive.

authors.name: John Arbuthnot
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Aberdeenshire-born physician of Queen Anne, mathematician and wit, the inventor of John Bull and the author of the design argument that later natural theology reused.
authors.biography: Born at Marnoch in Aberdeenshire in 1667, the son of a Calvinist minister, he studied medicine at Aberdeen, took his degree in Scotland and removed to London, where he built a large and prosperous practice and was named one of the physicians to Queen Anne. He became the friend and adviser of Pope, Swift and Gay, and is held to have given the first impulse to the wits who met as the Scriblerus Club, while his own learned jokes about the arts and sciences supplied much of their matter. His essay on the usefulness of mathematical learning, published at the beginning of the century, put the argument from design in a form that was quoted for generations and that William Paley enlarged in his Natural Theology of 1802, long after the period covered here. In 1712 he wrote the History of John Bull, an allegory of the nation, its law and its trades, which gave English politics a permanent personification, and in the same year an essay on the art of political lying, an anatomy of party rhetoric. Pope addressed to him one of his most searching verses, and he died in London in February 1735.
authors.profile: A physician-mathematician who turned professional learning into political satire and moral argument, and whose allegory taught a nation to see itself as a character.
authors.style: Dry, learned, deadpan irony; the allegorical case history and the law suit as national portrait; precise definitions and enumerations; a populariser's clarity about mathematics and medicine.
authors.concerns: The evidence of design in nature and the uses of mathematical reasoning; the mechanics of party, credit and national interest; the character of the English constitution and its trades; the corruption of political language; the mixture of learning and quackery in the arts.
authors.significance: He gave Augustan politics its national allegory and its analysis of spin, carried the design argument into ordinary English prose, and stood at the centre of the circle that produced the greatest satires of the age.
authors.uncertainty: The ascription of individual pieces of Scriblerus work is unsettled, and the date of his London settlement and of his Scottish degree is variously reported.

authors.name: John Aubrey
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Antiquary, biographer, and gossip-collector; his Brief Lives — vivid, candid, anecdotal sketches of his famous contemporaries (Shakespeare, Hobbes, Donne, Bacon) — invented an intimate, factual mode of biography and preserved priceless literary history.
authors.biography: Born 12 March 1626 at Easton Piers, Wiltshire; educated at Trinity College, Oxford (no degree) and the Middle Temple. A gentleman antiquary and Fellow of the Royal Society (1663), he roamed the country recording monuments, folklore (Remains of Gentilisme and Judaisme), and the lives and sayings of learned men. A close friend of Hobbes (whose Life he wrote), he compiled his 'Minutes of Lives' — the Brief Lives — mostly in the 1660s–90s, not intended for publication. Ruined by lawsuits, he lived on others' charity and died in Oxford on 7 June 1697. His manuscripts, held by the Bodleian, were published in full only in the twentieth century.
authors.profile: The pioneer of intimate, empirical biography, whose frank, discursive, note-strewn 'Lives' capture the personalities, quirks, and scandals of the great with an unprecedented immediacy.
authors.style: Anecdotal, colloquial, note-form prose; candid reportage and quotation of others' testimony; digressive and unfinished quality; and an antiquarian accumulation of fact and folklore.
authors.concerns: Biography and personal character; antiquities, monuments, and folklore; the lives of the learned and of Hobbes; astrology and the supernatural; and the preservation of literary history.
authors.significance: Brief Lives is a unique and indispensable source for seventeenth-century literary and intellectual history and a founding work of modern, personal biography; Aubrey's methods anticipated the empirical, factual approach of later biographers.
authors.uncertainty: Aubrey's own life is documented through his manuscripts and correspondents; his Brief Lives are notes and gossip of varying reliability, requiring editorial caution.

authors.name: John Bale
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: playwright; polemicist; antiquary; bishop of Ossory
authors.biography: Born at Cove, Suffolk, on 21 November 1495; entered the Carmelite order at Norwich, then converted to the Reformation in the 1530s. He wrote King Johan (c. 1538), the first English history play and a weapon of Henrician propaganda; The Image of Both Churches (c. 1545), a running commentary on Revelation; and the Illustrium Maioris Britanniae Scriptorum Summarium (1548), the first bio-bibliography of British writers. Bishop of Ossory in Ireland in 1553, he fled abroad under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying at Canterbury in November 1563.
authors.profile: The founder of English literary history and of the Protestant history play. King Johan turned the chronicle matter of England into stage polemic, and the Summarium — enlarged at Basel in 1557–59 as the Scriptorum Illustrium Maioris Brytanniae Catalogus — preserved the names and titles on which later literary history rests.
authors.style: Furious polemical energy; the apocalyptic scheme of the two churches applied to history; catalogue and inventory as instruments of scholarship and propaganda alike.
authors.concerns: The identification of the pope with Antichrist; the English church and nation as God's elect; the record of British writers as proof of national dignity.
authors.significance: Inventor of the English history play and of English literary bibliography; his catalogues transmitted knowledge of the medieval English canon to the Renaissance.

authors.name: John Banim
authors.birthplace: Kilkenny city, county Kilkenny, on 3 April 1798, son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper of the Catholic middle class, and of Judith Banim (née Carroll); Banim is a Kilkenny-Tipperary variant of Bannon, and the brothers were long associated with Callan and with Windgap on the edge of the city
authors.nationality: Irish; the Catholic Irish tale of peasant life and of the national history which followed Maria Edgeworth and the Waverley model, and which the Banims published as 'the O'Hara Family'. Joint with his elder brother Michael: Tales by the O'Hara Family, first series (1825) and second series (1826), the songs of the Chaunt of the Cholera (1831), The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). Single-handed: The Celt's Paradise (1821), Damon and Pythias (1821), Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824), The Boyne Water (1826), The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828) and The Smuggler (1831)
authors.identity: Novelist, tale-writer, dramatist in blank verse, song-writer and essayist, and first an aspirant historical painter; with his brother Michael the founder of the Irish peasant tale written by an Irishman rather than by the Anglo-Irish ascendancy, and long known to English readers as the 'Scott of Ireland'.
authors.biography: John Banim was born in Kilkenny city on 3 April 1798, the son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper, and of Judith Carroll his wife, and grew up in the consciously Catholic middle-class world of the Midland townland, where the memory of 1798 and the penal grievance were matter of family fact. He showed early skill with the pencil, studied painting in the Kilkenny and Dublin circle of T. J. Mulvany, and failed to establish himself as a historical painter; his ambition then turned to verse and the stage, and in 1821 he published The Celt's Paradise, a poem in four duans professedly translated from the Irish, and the blank-verse classical tragedy Damon and Pythias, acted at Covent Garden with his friend Richard Lalor Sheil helping on the stage version. Removing to Dublin about 1820 and to London in the early 1820s, he knew poverty and journalism before the success of the first series of Tales by the O'Hara Family in 1825, under the invented name of an Irish family and welcomed for its humour, its landscape and its pathos; the second series of 1826, the anonymous essays of Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824) and the historical novel The Boyne Water (1826), on the settlement of 1690, established him as the chronicler of the Irish tenantry. The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828), The Denounced (1830) and The Smuggler (1831) followed, and his songs, among them 'Soggarth Aroon', passed into popular recitation. Broken health, failing sight and debt curtailed his later work; The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842), issued jointly with Michael, were his last books, a testimonial was raised for him by his readers, and he died at his cottage at Windgap near Kilkenny in August 1842, aged forty-four. His brother survived him thirty-two years, wrote the notice in The Nation, and helped P. J. Murray with the Life of John Banim of 1857, which fixed his legend as a neglected genius; collected editions kept the O'Hara stories in print through the century, before the twentieth century reduced him to a few anthologised pieces.
authors.profile: He wrote in four genres at once: verse and drama, with The Celt's Paradise (1821) and Damon and Pythias (1821) and a body of Irish song and lyric; the collaborative Irish tale, the two series of Tales by the O'Hara Family (1825, 1826), with 'Crohoore of the Billhook', 'The Fetches', 'John Doe', 'The Nowlans' and 'Peter of the Castle', and the later joint volumes The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842); the single-handed three-volume novel of Irish history and society, The Boyne Water (1826), The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828), The Denounced (1830) and The Smuggler (1831); and miscellaneous essay and sketch, Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824), reissued in 1845 as London and its Eccentricities in the Year 2023.
authors.style: A spoken Hibernian English carried by dialogue, in which the peasant's exuberance, proverb, liturgy and lament are transcribed at length and with evident delight, and the narration breaks into description of place, of weather and of the body's suffering; the comic and the afflictive are placed side by side without transition, and the frame-tale device of the O'Hara family lets a tale tell itself. The blank verse of Damon and Pythias is formal and classical, the songs simple and repetitive, and the essays colloquial, digressive and given to caricature.
authors.concerns: The character and the grievance of the Irish poor under the Protestant ascendancy and the penal inheritance; the tenantry, the hedge-school, the priest, the smuggler and the informant as social types; the memory and the judgement of 1798 and of the Williamite revolution; the authenticity of Irish bardic poetry and song; the reading of character by landscape and by weather; the fate of the artist and the man of letters in a country without a market; and the moral economy of debt, drink and patronage.
authors.significance: With his brother he made the Irish peasant tale a distinct branch of the nineteenth-century national tale, Irish in authorship, Catholic in sympathy and realist in observation, and gave the English reading public, which knew Ireland through Edgeworth and through Waverley imitation, its own chronicler; reviewers made him the 'Scott of Ireland' and his vogue prepared the way for Lever, for the fiction of the Nation and for the later Irish revival. His case is also central in the history of collaborative and pseudonymous publication, and his songs and his 'Fetches' ghost tale entered the repertory of Irish popular literature.
authors.uncertainty: He is called now the eldest and now the younger son of his father, the year of his removal to London is given as 1820 or 1822, the day of his death as 13, 30 or 31 August 1842, and the share of each brother in the O'Hara volumes, in the Chaunt of the Cholera songs and in such tales as 'Crohoore of the Billhook' and 'The Mayor of Windgap', remains disputed in the bibliographies.

authors.name: John Barbour
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: poet; chronicler; churchman
authors.biography: Archdeacon of Aberdeen and a clerk in the service of Robert II; he travelled repeatedly to England and France for study (Oxford and Paris) and royal business. His Brus, completed c. 1375, earned him a royal pension, and he died on 13 March 1395.
authors.profile: Author of The Brus (c. 1375), a verse chronicle of the wars of independence celebrating Robert Bruce and James Douglas; other works attributed to him (including a Troy book) are lost.
authors.style: Energetic octosyllabic couplets; vivid battle narrative and stirring speeches; the celebration of freedom ('A! Fredome is a noble thing!') within a providential frame.
authors.concerns: Scottish independence and national identity; the virtue of freedom against tyranny; chivalric loyalty.
authors.significance: The father of Scottish poetry and of Scottish national historical literature; the Brus is the first great work in Older Scots.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his other works are lost, so the canon rests on the Brus alone.

authors.name: John Boynton Priestley
authors.nationality: British; the time play, the condition-of-England essay and the popular theatre
authors.identity: Novelist, dramatist and essayist; the great middlebrow man of letters of the period, the author of Dangerous Corner, Time and the Conways and The Good Companions.
authors.biography: Born John Boynton Priestley at Bradford on 13 September 1894; he served in the infantry from 1914 and was wounded and gassed, took his degree at Cambridge after the war, and made his name with The Good Companions (1929) and Angel Pavement (1930). He wrote some fifty plays — Dangerous Corner (1932), Laburnum Grove (1933), Time and the Conways (1937), When We Are Married (1938), An Inspector Calls (1945) — and broadcast and wrote on English social questions for forty years. He died at Stratford-upon-Avon on 14 August 1984.
authors.profile: Priestley invented the modern English time play and brought the condition-of-England argument to the commercial stage: Dangerous Corner and Time and the Conways are the finest technical experiments in the interwar theatre, An Inspector Calls is the most performed English play after the war, and The Good Companions is the period's most popular English novel. His broadcasts of 1940–41 made him a national figure and nearly cost him his wartime career.
authors.style: The symmetrical three-act play with a single set and a small cast; the time-slip that reveals the present from the future (Time and the Conways); the detective structure used as social argument (An Inspector Calls); the comic picaresque of the English road (The Good Companions); the plain essayistic prose of the broadcast.
authors.concerns: The English class system and the condition of England; time, determinism and the possibility of change; the provincial town and the touring company; the First World War and the lost generation; money, business and the moral compromise; the ordinary English life.
authors.significance: Priestley invented the modern English time play, wrote the most popular English novel of the period in The Good Companions, and made the condition-of-England argument a form of popular theatre in An Inspector Calls. His wartime broadcasts made him the period's most trusted public voice.

authors.name: John Brown Russwurm
authors.birthplace: Port Antonio, Jamaica, then a British slaveholding colony, born on 1 October 1799 (some accounts give 1 May), the son of a white English father and an enslaved Black mother; he was sent to school in Quebec and in 1812 removed to Maine, where he attended the Hebron Academy
authors.nationality: African-American, Jamaican-born; the free-Black print culture of the early American republic and the emigrationist and colonisation writing it produced, passing into the literature of the Liberia settlements
authors.identity: Journalist, teacher and public officer; co-founder and after 1827 sole editor of Freedom's Journal, afterwards editor of the Liberia Herald and governor of the Maryland colony in Africa
authors.biography: John Brown Russwurm was born at Port Antonio in Jamaica on 1 October 1799, the son of an English father and a woman held in slavery, and was educated at a school in Quebec before passing to Maine in 1812 with his father, where he worked his way through the Hebron Academy. He entered Bowdoin College, graduated in 1826 as the first African American to take a degree there and, as the college itself records, is thought to be the third African American to graduate from an American college; he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa in September 1826. He taught at a school for African-American children in Boston, and in March 1827 he and the Reverend Samuel E. Cornish established Freedom's Journal in New York, the first African-American-owned newspaper in the United States, whose first number appeared on 16 March 1827. Cornish withdrew in September 1827 and Russwurm conducted the paper alone to its last number in 1829, during its final months openly advocating African colonisation, the position that divided him from his colleague and from the emerging immediatist abolitionists. In November 1829 he emigrated to Liberia, where he edited the Liberia Herald from 1830, served the colony as secretary and as agent of the Maryland State Colonization Society, took charge of its schools and education work, and from 1836 was governor of the Maryland colony in Africa, a post he held until his death at Harper on 9 June 1851. He married Sarah McGill and left children; his life and writings were edited and republished by Winston James as those of a pan-Africanist pioneer.
authors.profile: His writing divides into two careers. In New York and Boston it is the journalism of Freedom's Journal (1827-29): editorials on slavery and the slave trade, on the claims and capacities of the coloured people, addresses to African-American societies and churches, and the arguments for African emigration with which he brought the paper to a close; these numbers are the earliest substantial body of opinion printed by an African-American college graduate. In Liberia his work is that of a colonial editor and official - the numbers of the Liberia Herald from 1830, official reports and addresses of the Maryland colony, tracts and letters on the settlement's agriculture, schools and relations with the United States and with the American Colonization Society, and the case for the colony's absorption into Liberia which occupied him through the 1840s. Nothing of his Bowdoin exercise writing or of his Boston teaching survives in the accounts consulted here as a separate literary work.
authors.style: His prose is that of a classically trained rhetorician of the college exercise school: formal, periodic and heavily subordinate, with a moralist's apparatus of example and appeal to providential history. The Freedom's Journal editorials are argumentative and conciliatory at once, addressed to white as well as Black readers, and their diction is far nearer the Augustan essay than to the prophetic manner of the later abolitionist press; his letters as a colonisation official are administrative, evidential and self-justifying, pressed into the defence of an unpopular policy. Where Cornish writes as the pastor exhorting his flock, Russwurm writes as the editor-convinced of a scheme, and his later prose is increasingly that of the report and the minute.
authors.concerns: Whether the people of colour could hope for citizenship in the United States, and therefore whether separate national life in Africa was the prudent or the necessary course; the education and moral elevation of African Americans as the proof of capacity; the ownership and control of Black representation in print, which he shared with Cornish in founding the first Black newspaper; the character, government, agriculture and commerce of the Liberia settlements; the responsibility of the slaveholding colonies, Jamaica including, and the Atlantic world of plantation slavery out of which he came; and the relation of race, Christianity and civilisation in the missionary and colonisation literature of the 1830s and 1840s.
authors.significance: He was the first African American to graduate from an American college to enter journalism, and as co-founder and then sole editor of Freedom's Journal he helped create the Black press; as a Jamaican-born, US-educated emigrant he became the most prominent individual convert to organised colonisation, and his governorship of the Maryland colony made him the leading African-American public figure in Liberia, a standing which the American Colonization Society used in its propaganda and which the abolitionist press, from Freedom's Journal's successor papers onward, treated as a defection. Modern scholarship, helped by Winston James's collection of his life and writings, reads him as a pan-Africanist pioneer rather than a renegade, and his career is the central case study of the colonisation split in early Black American politics.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is given as 1 October 1799 by the Smithsonian portrait record and the usual modern accounts, with 1 May 1799 reported elsewhere, and his birth at Port Antonio rests on those modern accounts; his mother's name is not recorded in the sources consulted here, and his father's identity and standing are variously described. The end of Freedom's Journal is variously placed in February, March or December 1829, and his sole editorship is accordingly dated by different authorities. His Liberian offices are unevenly reported: modern accounts give him as editor of the Liberia Herald from 1830, as colonial secretary, as agent of the colonization society in the United States and as governor of the Maryland colony from 1836, but the exact sequence and the dates of the secretarial and agency years differ, and the founding of a school or institute at Cape Palmas attributed to him could not be verified here. His place of death is given as Harper and as Cape Palmas, and the number of his children as four or six. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty.

authors.name: John Buchan
authors.nationality: British; the adventure novel and the imperial romance
authors.identity: Novelist, historian and statesman; the author of The Thirty-Nine Steps and the greatest Scottish writer of adventure in the century.
authors.biography: Born in Perth on 26 August 1875, the son of a Free Church minister; he was educated at Glasgow and Oxford, worked in South Africa with Milner, and served as a war correspondent and in intelligence. The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915), Greenmantle (1916), The Three Hostages (1924), Sick Heart River (1941) and the histories followed, and he was Governor-General of Canada from 1935. He died in Montreal on 11 February 1940.
authors.profile: Buchan was the greatest Scottish writer of adventure in the century and the inventor of the modern political thriller: The Thirty-Nine Steps created the chase novel and the man-on-the-run, and Greenmantle and the Richard Hannay books gave the English adventure story its intelligence and its moral seriousness.
authors.style: The chase through landscape; the competent amateur hero; the topographical exactness; the political conspiracy at the heart of the ordinary; the plain, rapid, confident narrative.
authors.concerns: Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation.
authors.significance: John Buchan invented the modern political thriller: The Thirty-Nine Steps created the chase novel and the man-on-the-run, and the Hannay books gave the English adventure story its intelligence, its moral seriousness, and a permanent place in the century's fiction.

authors.name: John Bunyan
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Puritan preacher, nonconformist, and author of The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, 1684), the greatest allegory in English and one of the most widely read books ever written, born of his years of imprisonment for preaching without a licence.
authors.biography: Born November 1628 (baptised 30 November) at Elstow, Bedfordshire, son of a tinker; little educated, he served briefly in the Parliamentary army and followed his father's trade. After a profound spiritual crisis recounted in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666), he became a Baptist preacher at Bedford. Refusing to conform after the Restoration, he was imprisoned for twelve years (1660–72) and briefly again in 1675–76, during which he wrote and, likely, began The Pilgrim's Progress. Published in two parts (1678, 1684), it was an immediate and enduring popular success. He also wrote The Holy War (1682), The Life and Death of Mr Badman (1680), and much doctrinal and controversial prose. He died on 31 August 1688 in London after a stormy journey.
authors.profile: The tinker-preacher whose plain, biblical, vividly imaginative prose gave the Puritan pilgrimage of the soul an unforgettable narrative form, drawing its power from scripture, the vernacular, and his own tormented and triumphant experience.
authors.style: Allegory with concrete, homely, scriptural imagery; a plain, vigorous, rhythmic prose saturated with the Bible; vivid personification (Christian, Faithful, Apollyon, Mr Worldly Wiseman); and dream-frame narrative.
authors.concerns: Salvation, grace, and the pilgrim's journey; sin, despair, and assurance; the Christian life as warfare and pilgrimage; persecution and nonconformity; and the vanity of the world.
authors.significance: The Pilgrim's Progress is the supreme English allegory and a foundational text of Protestant spirituality, translated into hundreds of languages and influencing the novel, hymnody, and countless writers from Dickens to the present; Grace Abounding is a landmark of spiritual autobiography.
authors.uncertainty: Bunyan's life is documented through his own writings and Bedford church records; the exact circumstances and dates of his composition of The Pilgrim's Progress during imprisonment are traditional rather than certain.

authors.name: John Capgrave

authors.identity: hagiographer; chronicler; Augustinian friar
authors.biography: Born at Lynn on 21 April 1393, he studied at Cambridge, joined the Augustinian friars, and became prior of their house at Lynn; he travelled to Rome in 1450 and died on 12 August 1464. The most learned English writer of his generation, he composed in both Latin and English.
authors.profile: Author of the Life of St Katharine (c. 1445), the Life of St Norbert, the Abbreuiacion of Cronicles, the chronicle of England to 1417, the pilgrimage guide Ye Solace of Pilgrimes, and numerous Latin commentaries and lives.
authors.style: Learned, well-ordered prose and Lydgatean verse; the devout scholar's care for accuracy and orthodoxy; the blending of chronicle and hagiography.
authors.concerns: The cult of St Katharine and the defence of learning; English history in the Lancastrian interest; orthodox devotion against Lollardy.
authors.significance: The leading East Anglian man of letters of the mid-fifteenth century; his Katharine is a classic of the learned saint's life.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertain: his own works and the Lynn records document his career closely.

authors.biography: A knight of Richard II's household and lifelong companion of Sir William Neville, with whom he is buried at Constantinople, where both died in October 1391; their joint tomb, with its crossed swords, survives in Istanbul. authors.profile: Author of The Two Ways (c. 1391), a Lollard-leaning devotional prose tract, and of The Boke of Cupide (The Cuckoo and the Nightingale, c. 1386), a Chaucerian dream poem long attributed to Chaucer.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian verse in the dream poem; plain, scriptural prose in the devotional tract.
authors.concerns: The two ways of life and death; the reform of the church; courtly love within a Christian frame.
authors.significance: The Two Ways is a principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite, and the Boke of Cupide testifies to the immediate diffusion of Chaucerian poetry.

authors.name: John Clare
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Labouring-class or peasant poet, hedge-layer and day-labourer in husbandry, topographical and bird poet, and a systematic natural historian of one fen-edge parish; the central figure of English rural labouring poetry after Bloomfield.
authors.biography: John Clare was born on 13 July 1793 in West Street, Helpston, then in Northamptonshire and afterwards in the Soke of Peterborough, the eldest son of Parker Clare, a farm servant whose wages fell until he lived on parish relief, and of Ann Parker. He had little formal schooling, taught himself from a handful of borrowed books, and began verses in his teens. He worked as a shepherd boy and then as a hedge-paler and day-labourer, and the enclosure of the Helpston commons and sheep-walks in 1809 gave his earliest mature poems their subject of dispossession. In 1819 he put out a manuscript volume entitled The Shepherd's Calendar; it reached local patrons, came to the notice of the Rev. Brownlow North, Lord Radstock, and through the Stamford bookseller Edward Drury reached John Taylor of Fleet Street, who with Radstock organised the subscription. Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery, carrying on its title page the designation the Northamptonshire Peasant, was published in March 1820 for Taylor and Hessey and sold some four thousand copies within weeks, making Clare a metropolitan celebrity; Taylor took him to London, the subscribers' surplus provided him with a cottage at Helpston, and he married Patty Turner in August 1820, fathering a large family. The Village Minstrel and Other Poems followed in 1821 and sold far less well; The Shepherd's Calendar with Village Stories appeared in 1827 through John Taylor, and The Rural Muse in 1835 by subscription, both poorly received. Signs of mental illness appeared in the early 1830s, and in July 1837 Clare was admitted to the private asylum at High Beach in Epping Forest kept by Dr Matthew Allen, passing in 1841 into the same physician's Northamptonshire practice at Castle Eden and Highbeecote, where he remained above twenty years, was visited by Wordsworth in 1841, and was allowed regular returns to Helpston. In 1863 he was moved to the county institution, the Northampton General Lunatic Asylum, where he died on 20 May 1864 and was buried on 25 May in the churchyard at Helpston. Manuscript poetry of the confinement years, including the bird pieces, the autobiographical The Misanthropos, and the lyric I Am, was recovered only in the twentieth century.
authors.profile: His printed canon is small and heavily mediated by publishers, while the manuscript canon is enormous: memorandum volumes of the Helpston and confinement years, bird-nest registers, and records of weather, plants, and birds, alongside thousands of sonnets. The fourteen-line sonnet he developed on his own, without an accepted pattern, carries much of his best work. His poetry is at once topographical, encyclopaedic, and elegiac, holding precise field observation and the complaint against enclosure in a single line of thought, and his late lyrics on identity, memory, and derangement are the strongest part of his modern reputation.
authors.style: A close ear for the speech of the Northamptonshire and Soke fen-edge and for the names of birds, plants, and field tasks; a syntax that runs in parataxis after the sense rather than after grammatical rule; heavy use of the present participle and of demonstrative deictics; a rhyming ear that prefers the exact and homely word; and a fourteen-line sonnet in which octave and sestet turn on a single perceived image rather than on argument.
authors.concerns: Enclosure and the loss of common ground; the relation of local knowledge to printed authority; the rights of the labourer to leisure and to authorship; the observation of nature as a form of piety; selfhood, memory, and derangement; the tyranny of grammar, spelling, and editorial correction over a dialect voice; fame, patronage, and dependence.
authors.significance: He is the culminating figure of the eighteenth-century labouring-class poetic tradition and, in critical estimation from the 1960s onward, a major Romantic poet rather than a curiosity. His vogue of 1820 shows the mechanism of Romantic patronage and subscription at work on a peasant hand, and his printed text shows what that mechanism cost a dialect writer in revision. His posthumous manuscripts made him a central authority for twentieth-century nature writing and for the cultural history of the enclosure of the English commons.
authors.uncertainty: The printed texts of 1820 to 1835 were altered by John Taylor, by the patronal circle, and later by Robert Chambers, so the degree to which the published dialect represents Clare's practice is unsettled. His diagnosis has been argued variously as manic depression, epilepsy, porphyria, and the effects of alcohol, without consensus. Dates of many confinement poems rest on manuscript rather than documentary evidence, and the account of his second partnership at Helpston and of the burial of his heart there rests on family tradition. Two particulars are often mis-stated in secondary accounts: his birthplace is Helpston, though the poem and the early title pages print Helpstone, and his 1837 admission was to a private house in Essex, the Northampton county asylum following only in 1863; he died at Northampton and was buried at Helpston.

authors.name: John Colet
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: humanist; dean of St Paul's; founder of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born in London in 1467, son of a Lord Mayor; studied at Oxford and in Italy. His Oxford lectures on the epistles of St Paul (c. 1497–1505) broke with scholastic method and made him the father of English humanism; he became dean of St Paul's in 1505 and founded St Paul's School in 1509, appointing William Lily its first master. He died on 16 September 1519. His grammatical treatise, the Aeditio, was printed in 1527.
authors.profile: The founder of the Oxford reform that produced English humanism. His Paul's lectures, teaching scripture from the plain text rather than the glosses, converted a generation — including Erasmus, who called him the ideal of the Christian humanist — and his Aeditio contributed the English accidence to the standard school grammar.
authors.style: Expository clarity aimed at the unlearned; plain-text biblical exposition; the reformer's impatience with ceremonial and gloss.
authors.concerns: The primitive church as model; education as the reform of Christendom; the layman's access to scripture.
authors.significance: The inspirer of Erasmus and More and the founder of the English humanist movement; his school and his lectures set the intellectual course of the Tudor century.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Aeditio's precise date of composition is approximate.
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth

authors.name: John Davidson
authors.nationality: Scottish; the ballad of the city, the verse drama and the poetry of the will
authors.identity: Poet, playwright and essayist; the most original and the most neglected of the poets of the 1890s, and a forerunner of the modern poetry of the city.
authors.biography: Born at Barrhead, Renfrewshire, on 11 April 1857, the son of a minister; he taught in Glasgow and Greenock, and went to London in 1889, where he published In a Music-Hall (1891), Fleet Street Eclogues (1893), Ballads and Songs (1894) and the 'Testaments' of the late 1890s. His verse plays were never staged successfully, his health and his marriage failed, and he drowned himself at Penzance on 23 March 1909.
authors.profile: Davidson wrote the poetry of the modern city and the modern will: In a Music-Hall and its successors are the first English poems to find a tragic art in the music hall and the street, and his long 'Testaments' are an attempt at a new secular scripture of human self-creation. His blank-verse plays and his ballads of the Scottish town are equally original, and his insistence on the poet's right to be difficult and modern made him the bridge from the 1890s to the poetry of Hardy and the Georgians.
authors.style: The ballad and the dramatic monologue; the music-hall song and the street cry; colloquial diction and slang; long rhetorical blank verse; the 'testament' as a new form; a harsh, energetic rhythm.
authors.concerns: The modern city and its spectacles; the will and self-creation; poverty and the artist's degradation; Scottish town life; the loss of religious faith; the crowd and the individual.
authors.significance: Davidson is the most original poet of the 1890s and the first English poet of the modern city: his music-hall poems and his 'Testaments' anticipated the urban poetry of the twentieth century, and he is a central figure in the transition from Victorian to modern verse.
authors.uncertainty: 18 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text. No work catalogued here carries a disputed, conjectural or shared attribution, and every one of them was published under the author's own name between 1891 and 1901.

authors.name: John Dennis
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English critic, playwright, and controversialist, a passionate early theorist of the sublime and one of the most quarrelsome and perceptive literary minds of his age.
authors.biography: Dennis was educated at a grammar school in Hertford and, by some accounts, at Cambridge, before briefly joining the army and then devoting himself to letters and the stage. He wrote tragedies, including Appius and Virginia (1709), and many critical works, among them The Advancement and Reformation of Poetry and Music (1701), The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry (1704), and treatises on the sublime, the operas, and the stage. He anticipated the Romantic enthusiasm he preached, and his quarrels, notably with Addison over Cato and with Pope and Steele, made him a notorious figure. A Whig and a devoted student of French classical criticism and of Longinus, he championed enthusiastick poetry. He died in 1734, in poverty and mental distress.
authors.profile: An aggressive, original critic and theorist of poetry and religion who, drawing on Longinus and Boileau, argued for enthusiastic imagination and the sublime against cold neoclassical regularity.
authors.style: Vehement, hyperbolic, often ranting critical prose; a rhetoric of enthusiasm and transports; sharp personal invective; and an earnest, sometimes incoherent eagerness in praise of the sublime.
authors.concerns: The sublime and enthusiastic imagination against rule; the relation of poetry to religion and passion; the defence of modern learning and national drama; and the corruption of critical taste.
authors.significance: A major forerunner of eighteenth-century and Romantic theories of the sublime and enthusiastic imagination; his critical writings, despite his notoriety, influenced Addison and later aesthetic thought.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1657 from baptismal evidence, his exact birthplace is uncertain, and his claim to a university education rests on later testimony rather than firm records.

authors.name: John Donne
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet, preacher, and Dean of St Paul's; the greatest of the metaphysical poets, author of the Songs and Sonnets, the Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries, the Devotions, and the sermons.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1572 into a recusant Catholic family (his mother was a daughter of John Heywood, and his uncle Jasper Heywood led the Jesuits); educated at Hart Hall, Oxford, and possibly Cambridge, and at Lincoln's Inn. He sailed on the Cadiz (1596) and Islands (1597) expeditions and was secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton before his secret marriage to Egerton's niece Anne More in 1601 wrecked his secular career ('John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done'). After years of poverty and patronage-seeking, he took orders in 1615 at the king's urging, became Reader at Lincoln's Inn, Dean of St Paul's (1621), and the most famous preacher of the age. His poems circulated in manuscript in his lifetime (the Songs and Sonnets, Elegies, Satires, Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries of 1611–12 on Elizabeth Drury); the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions appeared in 1624; the poems were first collected in 1633. He died on 31 March 1631 after preaching his own funeral sermon, 'Death's Duel'.
authors.profile: The poet of wit and the preacher of love: the Songs and Sonnets and Elegies are the great secular lyrics of the period, the Holy Sonnets and 'Good Friday, 1613. Riding Westward' its great devotional poems, and the sermons the summit of English pulpit prose.
authors.style: The dramatic opening, the extended conceit, the colloquial vehemence of an argumentative line, paradox and hyperbole, and the union of the erotic and the divine; in the sermons, a baroque prose of enormous periodic energy.
authors.concerns: The inseparability of body and soul; constancy and inconstancy in love; death, judgement, and resurrection; the discovery of the new philosophy and the decay of the old cosmos; the self as microcosm.
authors.significance: The greatest English metaphysical poet and one of the supreme preachers: his poetry was rediscovered by Grierson (1912) and Eliot as the alternative tradition to Spenserian sweetness, and shaped twentieth-century poetry; his Devotions ('No man is an island') and sermons remain classics of prose.
authors.uncertainty: Nearly all the poems are undated and circulated in widely varying manuscripts; the canon and ordering of the Songs and Sonnets depend on the 1633 and 1635 editions; several elegies' attributions remain contested.

authors.name: John Dos Passos
authors.nationality: American; the collective novel, the newsreel collage and the documentary epic
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the great experimental novelist of American social history and the author of U.S.A., the most ambitious American novel of the period.
authors.biography: Born John Roderigo Dos Passos in Chicago on 14 January 1896; he read at Harvard, served in the Norton-Harjes ambulance corps and the American army in 1917–18, and published Three Soldiers (1921) and Manhattan Transfer (1925). The U.S.A. trilogy — The 42nd Parallel (1930), Nineteen Nineteen (1932) and The Big Money (1936) — was collected in 1938; he wrote over forty books of fiction, reportage and history, broke with the left after the Spanish Civil War, and died in Baltimore on 28 September 1970.
authors.profile: Dos Passos invented the collective novel: U.S.A. tells the history of America from 1900 to 1930 through twelve lives, interrupted by the Newsreel, the Camera Eye and the biographies of public figures — a technique of collage that gives the period its most complete social panorama. Manhattan Transfer is the first American novel of the modern city, and Three Soldiers one of the finest American novels of the war.
authors.style: The collage of narrative, newspaper headline (Newsreel), autobiographical prose poem (Camera Eye) and biography; the discontinuous montage of lives; the flat documentary sentence; the panoramic city novel with no central protagonist; the slang and the song of the period transcribed.
authors.concerns: America as a collective social machine; the city and the crowd; labour, capital and the class war; the First World War and its profiteers; the lost generation and the political betrayal; the individual swallowed by history.
authors.significance: Dos Passos wrote the most ambitious American novel of the period: U.S.A. invented the collective documentary novel and gives the fullest social panorama of America 1900–1930, Manhattan Transfer created the modern city novel, and his collage technique influenced the political novel for the rest of the century.

authors.name: John Dryden
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet laureate, dramatist, critic, and translator; the dominant literary figure of the Restoration, who perfected the heroic couplet, founded modern English criticism and verse satire, and moved between Puritan, royalist, and Catholic allegiances with the times.
authors.biography: Born 9 August 1631 at Aldwincle; educated at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1654). He supported Cromwell at his death (Heroic Stanzas, 1658) then hailed the Restoration (Astraea Redux, 1660). In London he married Lady Elizabeth Howard (1663), wrote heroic plays and comedies for the King's Company, became laureate and historiographer royal (1668), and defended the moderns and the English stage in An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668). His political satires Absalom and Achitophel (1681) and Mac Flecknoe (1682) and the religious poems Religio Laici (1682) and The Hind and the Panther (1687, after his conversion to Catholicism) mark his maturity. Deprived of his offices by the Protestant William III (1688), he turned to translation, producing the great Virgil (1697) and Fables Ancient and Modern (1700). He died 1 May 1700 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The versatile master of Restoration letters — playwright, laureate, critic, satirist, and translator — who established the heroic couplet as the standard medium of serious English poetry and created a durable critical vocabulary.
authors.style: The balanced, pointed heroic couplet; conversational yet elevated diction; satiric wit and character portraiture; a critical prose of clarity and good sense; and a translational idiom that naturalized the classics into contemporary English.
authors.concerns: The nature and decorum of drama and poetry; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; political legitimacy, party, and succession; religious faith and conversion; the craft of translation and the history of the language.
authors.significance: Dryden created the Augustan style that Pope and Johnson inherited, founded English literary criticism, and produced the greatest political verse satire of the century; his translations made the classics central to English literary culture.
authors.uncertainty: Dryden's life is well recorded; his religious and political shifts are documented in his own poems and prefaces, though their sincerity has been debated.

authors.name: John Duns Scotus
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: philosopher; theologian; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: The subtlest of the scholastic philosophers: he entered the Franciscans c. 1280, studied and taught at Oxford and Paris, and lectured on the Sentences at Oxford c. 1300–02 and Paris 1302–05; transferred to Cologne in 1307, he died there on 8 November 1308. His thought defined one of the two great schools of late medieval theology.
authors.profile: Author of the Ordinatio (his revision of the Oxford Sentences lectures, c. 1300–08), the Quaestiones Quodlibetales, and treatises on metaphysics, logic, and natural theology, including his famous proof of God's existence.
authors.style: Rigorous, compressed, terminologically innovative argument; the 'formal distinction' and the univocity of being; a dialectical subtlety that earned him the title Doctor Subtilis.
authors.concerns: The univocity of being and the nature of metaphysics; the freedom of God and of the will; the Immaculate Conception; individuation (haecceitas).
authors.significance: Founder of Scotism, which rivalled Thomism for centuries and shaped theology into the Reformation; among the most influential British philosophers of all time.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early life approximate; the authenticity of parts of the corpus remains disputed.
themes: The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion

authors.name: John Dyer
authors.nationality: Welsh
authors.identity: Welsh-born poet and painter, associated with Thomson and the descriptive school, author of Grongar Hill and the georgic The Fleece.
authors.biography: Dyer was a Welshman, born about 1700, who first trained for a profession connected with architecture and surveying before turning to painting and poetry in the artistic circle around James Thomson and the Burlington set. His topographical poem Grongar Hill (1726) celebrates a Welsh landscape in light-reflective blank verse. He travelled in Italy and, back in Wales, farmed and wrote, producing the georgic The Fleece (1757), a poem on the Welsh wool trade. Weak memory and modest means marked his later years. He died in 1758.
authors.profile: A poet of landscape and the visual, whose descriptive and georgic verse reflects a painter's eye for colour, distance, and light and a patriot's attachment to Welsh scenery and industry.
authors.style: Clear, pictorial blank verse of space and colour; a sense of the distance and depth of a prospect; ease in the topographical and georgic mode; and a calm, contemplative, sensuous eye.
authors.concerns: The perception of landscape, distance, and light; patriotic and economic interest in the Welsh wool trade; retirement and rural labour; and the interplay of painting and poetry.
authors.significance: Grongar Hill is an early, much-admired poem of the picturesque prospect and a precursor of Romantic nature perception; Dyer helped link Thomson's descriptive verse to a Welsh topographical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain, given only as about 1700; the details of his early training and his later farming and mental decline rest on fragmentary accounts.

authors.name: John Evelyn
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Diarist, author, horticulturist, and founding Fellow of the Royal Society; his long Diary (1641–1706) records the intellectual and public life of the age, and his Sylva (1664) — a plea for reforestation — was a pioneering work of natural history and one of the Society's first publications.
authors.biography: Born 31 October 1620 at Wotton, Surrey, educated at Balliol College, Oxford and the Middle Temple. He travelled Europe (1643–52), keeping a journal, and after the Restoration settled at Sayes Court, Deptford. A founder-member of the Royal Society (1662), he published Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees (1664), Fumifugium (1661, on air pollution), and works on engraving, numismatics, and horticulture, and translated Lucretius and others. His Diary, kept over six decades, is the great public counterpart to Pepys's private one. A devout Anglican and royalist, he died on 27 February 1706.
authors.profile: The cultivated gentleman-scholar and improver whose wide-ranging diary, essays, and horticultural writings document the new science, the arts, and public affairs with learned, pious, and practical curiosity.
authors.style: Learned, observant, sometimes formal prose; the discursive diary and treatise; antiquarian and scientific detail; and a pious, improving tone.
authors.concerns: Horticulture, forestry, and the improvement of the land; the new science and the Royal Society; art, architecture, and engraving; air pollution and the environment; religion and public affairs.
authors.significance: Sylva is a landmark of natural history and environmental writing and helped reforest England for the navy; Evelyn's Diary is an invaluable record of the intellectual and cultural life of the seventeenth century, complementing Pepys.
authors.uncertainty: Evelyn's life and writings are thoroughly documented through his diary, letters, and family papers; his works are numerous and some are translations.

authors.name: John Fisher
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: bishop of Rochester; theologian; cardinal; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born at Beverley in 1469; educated at Cambridge, where he became Master of Michaelhouse and chancellor of the university, and the patron of Erasmus and of Greek studies. Bishop of Rochester from 1504, he was the confessor of Lady Margaret Beaufort and the most respected preacher of his age. Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was made a cardinal by Paul III and executed on 22 June 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The great conservative preacher of the early Reformation. His sermons — against Luther (1521) and on the penitential psalms — are the classic statements of the old orthodoxy in the new age of print, and his commentary on the seven penitential psalms (1505, enlarged 1508) was the devotional bestseller of the early Tudor period.
authors.style: Scholastic learning in a plain, forceful pulpit style; the expository sermon built on the literal text; pastoral warmth under doctrinal rigour.
authors.concerns: The defence of the old faith; penance and the sacrament; the reform of the clergy from within; the university as the church's school.
authors.significance: The intellectual leader of English Catholicism in the crisis of the 1520s and 1530s; his life and death defined the conservative alternative to the Henrician settlement.
authors.uncertainty: None significant.
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
