authors.name: John Fletcher
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Baptized 20 December 1579 at Rye; son of Richard Fletcher, later Bishop of London. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and probably began writing for the stage about 1606. After his partnership with Beaumont he collaborated with Shakespeare (Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen) and with Massinger, and in 1616 succeeded Shakespeare as principal dramatist of the King's Men. He died of the plague in August 1625 and is buried in Southwark Cathedral.
authors.profile: Sole and collaborative canon of some fifty plays, including The Faithful Shepherdess (c. 1608), The Woman's Prize (c. 1611), The Island Princess (c. 1621), Rule a Wife and Have a Wife (1624), and, with Beaumont, Philaster, The Maid's Tragedy, and A King and No King.
authors.style: Supple, flowing blank verse with feminine endings; rapid plotting; a taste for surprise, disguise, and the reversals of tragicomedy.
authors.concerns: Honour, love, and friendship under pressure; the follies of tyranny; the pleasures of wit and gallantry.
authors.significance: His fluent verse and tragicomic plots set the pattern for Restoration drama; for the next half-century 'Beaumont and Fletcher' outran even Shakespeare at the box office.
authors.uncertainty: Shares in the fifty-play canon are often uncertain; the Beaumont–Fletcher division of labour remains debated.

authors.name: John Florio
authors.nationality: English (of Italian descent)
authors.identity: translator; lexicographer; language teacher
authors.biography: Born in London in 1553, son of Michelangelo Florio, an Italian Protestant exile. He taught Italian to the court and nobility, served in the household of the Earl of Southampton, became reader in Italian to Queen Anne (1604), and groom of the privy chamber (1619). A friend of Jonson and Samuel Daniel, he died of the plague at Fulham in October 1625.
authors.profile: His Italian–English dictionaries A World of Words (1598) and Queen Anna's New World of Words (1611), the dialogue manuals First Fruits (1578) and Second Fruits (1591), and above all the translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), one of the great translations in the language.
authors.style: A florid, expansive English that enlarges Montaigne's French into the idiom Shakespeare knew; a tireless coiner and collector of words.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Continental learning; language as national wealth; scepticism and the essay form.
authors.significance: His Montaigne gave English thought and letters — including Shakespeare's Tempest — direct access to the Essays, and his dictionaries record the Italian loan-words entering Elizabethan English.
authors.uncertainty: His role as possible editor for Southampton's circle remains a matter of speculation.

authors.name: John Ford
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Caroline tragedian; the most intense and morbidly introspective of the later Jacobean-Caroline dramatists, author of 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, The Broken Heart, and Love's Sacrifice, whose plays explore transgressive passion, melancholy, and divided conscience.
authors.biography: Born c. 1586 at Ilsington, Devon (baptised 17 April), educated at Exeter College, Oxford and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1620). He collaborated with Dekker, Rowley, and Webster on comedies and tragicomedies in the 1620s before writing his surviving solo tragedies in the early 1630s: Love's Sacrifice (1633), 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (1633), The Broken Heart (1633), and Perkin Warbeck (1634), with later comedies The Fancies Chaste and Noble (1638) and The Lady's Trial (1639). Little of his later life is recorded; he died c. 1639–40.
authors.profile: The tragedian of forbidden and self-destructive passion, whose plays probe incest, jealousy, and Stoic endurance with a melancholic, casuistical intensity and a detached moral ambiguity.
authors.style: Grave, formal blank verse; rhetorical lamentation and masque-like set pieces; a preoccupation with melancholy and Stoic self-mastery; and a disturbing moral neutrality toward transgression.
authors.concerns: Incestuous and forbidden desire; honour, jealousy, and reputation; melancholy and the divided self; Stoic endurance of suffering; and the ethics of passion versus social law.
authors.significance: Ford is the last great tragedian before the closing of the theatres; 'Tis Pity She's a Whore and The Broken Heart are central to the Caroline tragic canon and to modern interest in the psychology and transgression of Renaissance drama.
authors.uncertainty: Very little of Ford's biography is known; his birth and death dates are approximate, many of his works are lost, and his collaborations complicate attribution.

authors.name: John Foxe
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: martyrologist; church historian
authors.biography: Born at Boston, Lincolnshire, in 1516 or 1517. Educated at Brasenose and Magdalen College, Oxford, he resigned his fellowship over religious scruples, tutored in the households of the Protestant gentry, and fled to the Continent under Mary I, working at Basel as a proofreader for the printer Oporinus. He returned under Elizabeth and spent his later years as a preacher and writer in London, where he died on 8 April 1587.
authors.profile: Actes and Monuments of These Latter and Perilous Days — the 'Book of Martyrs' — first published in English in 1563 and greatly expanded in 1570, a vast church history built around the sufferings of Protestant martyrs from Wyclif to his own day.
authors.style: Massive documentary accumulation, vivid narrative set-pieces, and the rhetorical urgency of a man writing the history of his own cause.
authors.concerns: Providence in history; the true church against Antichrist; the testimony of the martyrs.
authors.significance: His book, ordered to be placed in every cathedral church, shaped English national and religious identity for three centuries and is a primary source for the Marian persecutions.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date uncertain (1516 or 1517).

authors.name: John Gabriel Stedman
altNames: Captain John Gabriel Stedman of the Scots Brigade
authors.birthplace: Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands (now Belgium); earlier authority gives Antigua
authors.nationality: Anglo-Dutch; an officer of the Scottish brigade in the service of the Dutch Republic writing in English; the colonial testimony and travel-narrative wing of abolitionism, and a forerunner of the Romantic documentary horror narrative
authors.identity: A journal-keeper and memoirist rather than a literary professional. His single great work is a first-person narrative of five years of forest warfare in Surinam, interleaved with natural history, plans for the reform of colonial government, verse inscriptions and a sustained indictment of plantation slavery. He also left projected religious and educational writings, and a body of drawings which were engraved to illustrate his own text.
authors.biography: He was born in 1744 at Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands, now in Belgium, the son of Robert Stedman, a Scotsman who held a commission in the service of the Dutch Republic; earlier biographers, finding him afterwards in English-speaking colonies, reported his birth at Antigua and the older story of a West Indian origin persists in some accounts. He followed the family profession into the Scots Brigade in Dutch service and in 1772 answered a call for volunteers to act against the revolted negroes of Surinam, the Bosjes or Boni maroons who had won territory in the interior from the plantation colony. He served seven campaigning seasons between 1772 and 1777 in forest and river warfare against these maroon settlements, and kept during them the journals from which his book was made. While at Paramaribo he lived with Joanna, an enslaved woman of mixed descent whom he had bought, loved and intended to emancipate; the record of her two public whippings for theft, the second of them inflicted with a halter and a bit, is the most terrible single passage in his narrative and is written in her defence and in his own condemnation. Broken in health and unable to complete the purchase of Joanna's freedom, he quitted the service and returned to Europe, where for nearly twenty years he lived in London in straitened circumstances, occupied with religious and educational projects and with the reduction of his Surinam journals to a fair copy. He wrote the narrative out in 1790 and sent the manuscript to Joseph Johnson, the London publisher. The Narrative of a Five Years' Expedition, against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam, in Guiana, on the Wild Coast of South America, from the Year 1772 to 1777 appeared in London in 1796 in stately volumes with a series of engraved and aquatint plates, and Stedman died on 7 March 1797, within a year of its publication, still grieved by the fate of Joanna and of the son he had succeeded in obtaining freedom for and educating in England.
authors.profile: The narrative alternates the campaigning journal, the natural-history survey and the abolitionist charge, and its peculiar power comes from the confession of an implicated insider. Stedman describes punishments he has witnessed, sanctioned or failed to prevent, with an eye for the technology of the scene, the number of lashes, the instruments and the speech of the victim. He draws the maroons as brave, articulate and politically able, and the planters and their managers as vain, lazy and cruel, an inversion that made the book a repository of argument for British abolitionists. The 1796 printed text was revised and abridged by an editor before and after the author's death, and the tone of the surviving manuscript, first transcribed entire in the twentieth century, is more frank, more religiously eccentric and more self-accusing than the printed version.
authors.style: Precise, dreadful enumeration of bodies, wounds and instruments; a journal's chronology of dates, marches and weather; apostrophic outburst and lament for Joanna; embedded verse epitaphs and inscriptions; natural-history nomenclature placed beside scenes of torture; an unconcealed first-person narrator who reports his own weakness; elaborate period punctuated by exclamation; drawing and engraving treated as evidence coequal with the written account.
authors.concerns: The morality of resistance by the enslaved and the character of maroon societies; the cruelty of colonial jurisprudence and of corporal punishment; the complicity of the officer, the witness and the owner; the relation of Christianity to plantation government; schemes for the amelioration and eventual emancipation of the colonial slave; the natural history and geography of tropical America; the fate of mixed unions and of the children of the enslaved.
authors.significance: His narrative of 1796 supplied British and continental abolitionism with some of its most effective evidence and some of its most circulated images, and its plates, designed by the author and engraved by William Blake and others, became standard antislavery illustrations. Read alongside the speeches and enquiries of the 1790s, it carried the case against Dutch and British colonial slavery into the drawing room and made the treatment of Joanna a canonical instance of the argument that slavery degrades the master. Its complicated textual history, from an edited and abridged 1796 print to the first transcription of the 1790 manuscript in the late twentieth century, is a central case study in how colonial testimony was shaped by abolitionist publishers.
authors.uncertainty: The place of his birth is unsettled: recent authority derives from Dutch and Belgian records and gives Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands, while older English accounts give Antigua, and his mother's family and his education remain ill documented. The extent and direction of editorial alteration in the 1796 printed text, and the identity and method of the friend who prepared the second volume from his papers, are disputed among the scholars of the manuscript. The dates of Joanna's life, her death and the success of Stedman's efforts to manumit her cannot be fixed from his own text alone, and the chronology of the return to Europe varies between accounts.

authors.name: John Galsworthy
authors.nationality: British; the family saga, the social-problem novel and the problem play
authors.identity: Novelist and playwright; the chronicler of the Forsytes and of the English propertied class, and the Nobel laureate of 1932.
authors.biography: Born John Galsworthy at Kingston upon Thames on 14 August 1867 into a family of shipowners and country gentlemen; he took a law degree at Oxford, travelled and met Joseph Conrad, and made his name with The Man of Property (1906), the first Forsyte novel. He wrote a long series of novels and plays on social questions — the law, the prison, the strike, the divorce court — served in the First World War as a hospital worker, and won the Nobel Prize in 1932. He died in London on 31 January 1933.
authors.profile: Galsworthy wrote the definitive English family saga and the period's most accomplished social-problem drama. The Forsyte Saga is a chronicle of property — houses, wives, pictures, reputations — that becomes a history of the English middle class between the 1880s and the 1920s, and his plays (Strife, Justice, The Silver Box) put the law, the prison and the strike on the commercial stage. He is the last great Victorian liberal in English fiction.
authors.style: The leisurely, orderly, ironic family chronicle; the recurring character across volumes; the social panorama held in a single family; the plain, correct, slightly cold English prose; the well-made problem play with a balanced case on both sides.
authors.concerns: Property, possession and the Forsyte instinct; the family and the generations; marriage, divorce and the law; the strike and the two nations; the prison and the penal system; beauty, art and the collecting instinct; the decline of the Victorian propertied order.
authors.significance: Galsworthy gave the English middle class its own epic in The Forsyte Saga, wrote the period's most effective social-problem plays, and won the Nobel Prize for a body of work that documents the transition from Victorian confidence to interwar uncertainty.

authors.name: John Galt
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Novelist, memoirist, and founder of colonial settlement schemes
authors.biography: John Galt was born in Irvine, Ayrshire, and educated at Greenock and the University of Glasgow, where he attended without taking a degree. As a boy he befriended the young Lord Byron. After a period in London as a writer and a brief career in Canadian administration, he returned to Scotland and became a promoter of the Canada Company, founding the settlement of Guelph in Upper Canada in 1827. His novelistic career began in 1820 with Annals of the Parish, published in the wake of Waverley's success. He continued to publish fiction and memoir until his declining health and the failure of his Canadian ventures forced him back to writing. He died in Greenock in 1839.
authors.profile: Galt invented the Scottish parish chronicle with Annals of the Parish and the provincial picaresque with The Ayrshire Legatees. His fiction records the transformation of rural Scotland under agricultural improvement with affectionate irony; his later novels turn to Covenanting history and to Canadian emigration. He is a major figure of the Scottish regional novel between Burns and Hardy.
authors.style: Dialect-rich first-person memoir; deadpan comic narration; digressive episodic structure; sympathetic but clear-eyed treatment of provincial worthies; Scots-inflected English prose.
authors.concerns: Agricultural improvement and the death of the old parish; religious dissent and the Covenanting inheritance; Scottish emigration and colonial settlement; provincial innocence versus metropolitan institutions.
authors.significance: Galt's parish chronicles founded the Kailyard tradition and influenced Hardy and the regional novel; his Canadian writings are early major documents of emigration literature; Scott ranked him among the finest Scottish novelists of his generation.

authors.name: John Gay
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and dramatist, friend of Pope and Swift, best known for the ballad opera The Beggar's Opera and his Fables.
authors.biography: Born in Devon and apprenticed to a silkseller in London, Gay attached himself to the Augustan literary circle, befriending Pope, Swift, and John Arbuthnot, and joining the Scriblerus Club. Early poems such as Rural Sports, also called Trivia (1716), won notice. He wrote for the theatre in various modes, including pastoral and burlesque tragedy. His The Beggar's Opera (1728), a ballad opera satirising politics and the stage, was a great success and provoked political controversy that helped block his sequel Polly. His Fables, first and second collections appearing in 1727 and posthumously in 1738, remain famous. He died in London in 1732.
authors.profile: A versatile versifier and dramatist working in georgic, pastoral, fable, and burlesque, whose enduring achievements are the satiric ballad opera and the morally pointed fable.
authors.style: Lucid, unambitious Augustan diction; ease in popular and borrowed airs; epigrammatic moralising in the fables; and a genial, often sly satire rather than Swiftian ferocity.
authors.concerns: The corruption beneath social polish; the economics of crime and respectability; the rivalry between Italian opera and native drama; and the conduct of ordinary life as illustrated by beast-fable.
authors.significance: Inventor of the ballad opera with The Beggar's Opera, a landmark that reshaped English musical theatre and literary satire of manners, and a leading fabulist of his generation.
authors.uncertainty: His exact year of birth is not recorded and is given as about 1685; the chronology of his early poems and plays rests partly on manuscript and dedicatory evidence.

authors.name: John Gower
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; moralist
authors.biography: A London poet of Kentish or Yorkshire gentry stock, connected with the court of Richard II and later a supporter of Henry IV; friend of Chaucer, who dedicated Troilus and Criseyde to him. He composed in three languages — French (Mirour de l'Omme, c. 1376–79), Latin (Vox Clamantis, c. 1377–81), and English (Confessio Amantis, c. 1386–90) — and spent his last years blind at St Mary Overey priory, Southwark, where his tomb with its effigy of the three books remains.
authors.profile: The Confessio Amantis, a collection of some 140 exemplary tales framed by the confession of the lover Amans to Genius, the priest of Venus, is the most substantial English poem of the century after Chaucer's; the Vox Clamantis allegorizes the Peasants' Revolt and the corruption of the estates.
authors.style: Smooth, correct octosyllabic couplets; a 'middle style' of plain moral discourse; the frame-narrative and exemplary tale as instruments of ethical teaching.
authors.concerns: Love as a school of virtue and self-knowledge; the corruption of the estates; good kingship and the common good.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Langland, one of the three great English poets of the Ricardian age; the Confessio is a principal monument of late medieval narrative art.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and family origins conjectural; the chronology of his three major poems is partly inferred.

authors.name: John Greenleaf Whittier
authors.nationality: American; the abolitionist poet and the New England idyll
authors.identity: Poet and abolitionist; the most important anti-slavery poet in America and the poet of the New England farm.
authors.biography: Born in Haverhill, Massachusetts, on 17 December 1807 to a Quaker farm family; he edited the Middlesex Standard and the abolitionist Pennsylvania Freeman, was mobbed for his views in 1835, and published Voices of Freedom (1846), Snow-Bound (1866) and The Tent on the Beach (1867). He was a founder of the Republican Party in Massachusetts and died at Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, on 7 September 1892.
authors.profile: Whittier was the most important anti-slavery poet in America and one of the two or three finest poets of the New England farm: Snow-Bound is the great American poem of the rural household, and his abolitionist verse gave the movement its hymns and its moral authority.
authors.style: The plain, ballad-like quatrain and the domestic idyll; the Quaker plainness of speech; the abolitionist appeal and the moral indignation; the New England landscape and the fireside; the dialect poem of the rural poor.
authors.concerns: Slavery and the abolitionist cause; the New England farm and the vanishing rural world; the Quaker conscience; death and the immortality of the household; poverty and the dignity of labour.
authors.significance: John Greenleaf Whittier was the most important anti-slavery poet in America: his abolitionist verse gave the movement its hymns and moral authority, and Snow-Bound is the great American poem of the rural household and the fireside.

authors.name: John Hamilton Reynolds
authors.nationality: English; poet, sketch-writer, and dramatist of the Romantic period, a member of the Hunt circle
authors.identity: Journalist-poet of the Examiner and the Indicator: writer of ballads, humorous tales in verse, sketches, and plays, and the friend to whom Keats addressed some of his most outgoing letters and verses.
authors.biography: Born 9 September 1794 at Shrewsbury, he came to London as a young man and lived by literary and journalistic work. Leigh Hunt brought him into the circle of the Examiner and the Indicator, and through Hunt he met John Keats in October 1816; the two became inseparable during the years in which Keats was deciding to give up medicine, and Reynolds was the friend of Keats's most companionable poems, his sonnets, epistles, and the 'Epistle to John Hamilton Reynolds, during his excursion to the Leigh Hunt's'. He was one of the young writers attacked under the name of the 'cockney school', published ballads and tales in verse from about 1814, and in 1819 issued the continuation of Wordsworth's 'Peter Bell' which drew from Shelley a third part of his own. He contributed prose sketches, parodies, and plays of the comic and melodramatic kind through the 1820s and 1830s, wrote for the annuals and the magazines, and died on 15 November 1852. His later career lay outside the Romantic moment for which his friends remembered him, and his connection with Keats has often been allowed to stand for a larger body of work now little read.
authors.profile: Reynolds wrote in the mixed prose-and-verse idiom of the Hunt papers: narrative ballad and humorous metrical tale, the descriptive sketch, parody of the great style, and stage farce and drama of the minor theatres. His 'Peter Bell the Second' (1819) is the clearest surviving instance of the circle's method of poet-to-poet reply, and his essays and sonnets supply much of the evidence for the society of the Indicator and for the last years of Keats's life.
authors.style: An easy, colloquial versifier of the Hunt school: ballad and anacreontic measures, pointed rhymes, a delight in parody of Wordsworthian and Byronic manner, and a prose of quick observation rather than argument. His sketches favour the first person, the anecdote, and the comic caricature of literary celebrities, and his dramatic pieces show the pull of the fashionable German-derived melodrama and of the Covent Garden and minor-theatre repertory.
authors.concerns: Friendship and companionship as the ground of literary life; the pleasures of the old English and Italian story told lightly; parody as a form of reading and of allegiance; the politics of the periodical press and the position of the unpatronised young writer; the theatre as a school of effect rather than of character.
authors.significance: His chief place in literary history is as the friend and interlocutor of Keats, whose letters to him (1817-21) are among the central documents of Romantic poetics and whose most companionable poems were written for or with him. His 'Peter Bell the Second' and Shelley's reply also map the circle's habit of competitive sequel-writing, and his journalism records the everyday texture of the Hunt papers between 1816 and 1822.
authors.uncertainty: Reynolds's education and early employment, the chronology of his contributions to the Examiner and the Indicator, and the dates of his several plays and collections are imperfectly documented, and his share in pieces written jointly with Keats in 1819 is still debated.

authors.name: John Henry Newman
authors.nationality: English; Victorian religious prose and the Oxford Movement
authors.identity: Clergyman, theologian, novelist, poet and cardinal; the leader of the Oxford Movement and the period's greatest religious autobiographer.
authors.biography: Born in London on 21 February 1801, son of a banker; educated at Ealing and Trinity College, Oxford, where he became a fellow of Oriel in 1822 and vicar of St Mary's in 1828. His Evangelical conversion at fifteen and his subsequent High Church convictions made him the intellectual leader of the Oxford Movement from Keble's assize sermon of 1833; he edited the Tracts for the Times and was the author of Tract 90 (1841), which sought to reconcile the Thirty-Nine Articles with Catholic doctrine. The storm that followed drove him out of Oxford to Littlemore, where he was received into the Roman Catholic Church in October 1845. He founded the Oratory at Birmingham, was a moving and much-loved preacher, wrote the Apologia Pro Vita Sua in 1864 in answer to Charles Kingsley's charge of dishonesty, and was made a cardinal by Pope Leo XIII in 1879. He died at Edgbaston on 11 August 1890.
authors.profile: Newman's prose is the finest of all Victorian religious writing: measured, cadenced, exact, and utterly without Carlyle's prophetic violence. His subject is the grounds of belief — conscience, probability, the convergence of independent evidence, the 'illative sense' — and his method is the autobiographical narrative that turns the history of a mind into an argument. The Apologia is the great Victorian spiritual autobiography and a masterpiece of self-defence; the sermons and the lectures on the Idea of a University are the foundation of modern thinking about the purpose of liberal education; the poem The Dream of Gerontius became, in Elgar's setting, a central work of the English musical and religious tradition.
authors.style: Ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax; a personal voice of great courtesy and precision; the careful accumulation of probability rather than the assertion of certainty; theological vocabulary handled with legal exactness; the use of letters and documents as the substance of argument.
authors.concerns: The authority of conscience; faith and the cumulative argument; development in doctrine; the relation of the university to the Church and to knowledge; the claims of Rome against the Church of England; death, judgment and the soul's journey; the education of the gentleman.
authors.significance: Newman is the intellectual centre of the Oxford Movement and one of the greatest of English prose writers: the Apologia created the modern religious autobiography, the Idea of a University defined the modern debate about liberal education, and Gerontius gave the English oratorio its greatest subject. His theory of the 'development' of doctrine changed Catholic theology, and his account of the illative sense is a permanent contribution to the theory of knowledge.
authors.uncertainty: Newman's Anglican and Catholic sources and his use of his own letters in the Apologia have been scrutinised since Kingsley's attack of 1864; the standard scholarly account is Ian Ker's biography (1988) and the Oxford Authors edition of the Apologia.

authors.name: John Heywood
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: playwright; epigrammatist; court entertainer
authors.biography: Born about 1497, probably in London; a singer, musician, and entertainer at the court of Henry VIII and the household of Princess Mary. He married Joan Rastell, the niece of Thomas More, and remained a Catholic: in 1564 he left England for Mechelen, where he died about 1580. His interludes were played at court and in the great households, and his collections of proverbs and epigrams were bestsellers for a century.
authors.profile: The master of the Tudor interlude. The Four PP, The Play of the Weather, and A Play of Love turn the debate form into comedy of ideas — the palmer, pardoner, pothecary, and pedlar disputing who can tell the greatest lie; Jupiter taking petitions on the weather. His A Dialogue Conteynyng the Nomber in Effect of All the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue (1546) collected the proverb wisdom of England, and The Spider and the Fly (1556) is the great allegorical poem of the Marian reaction.
authors.style: Deadpan comic logic, punning debate, and the proverb as structural unit; a style that teaches while it jokes, and jokes while it teaches.
authors.concerns: The comedy of opinion and authority; religious satire from within orthodoxy; the wisdom of proverb lore; the politics of the Reformation seen from the losing side.
authors.significance: The first English comic dramatist of the print era and the conduit by which the interlude became the comedy of the Elizabethan stage; his proverb collections fixed the common sayings of the language.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the dating of the interludes is largely inferential.

authors.name: John Home
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Scottish Church of Scotland minister and dramatist, author of the celebrated tragedy Douglas.
authors.biography: Born on 2 September 1722 at Leith, near Edinburgh, he was educated at Leith Grammar School and the University of Edinburgh, became a schoolteacher, and was licensed as a minister of the Church of Scotland, serving at Athelstaneford. His tragedy Douglas, first performed in Edinburgh in 1756, brought him fame and notoriety, drawing a hostile response from the clergy and prompting his move to London, where it was championed by David Hume and others. He later wrote on history, including an account of the Jacobite rebellion of 1745, and returned to the Scottish ministry. He died on 4 September 1808.
authors.profile: A clergyman-dramatist whose neoclassical tragedy Douglas became one of the most discussed Scottish plays of the century, and whose historical and literary writings made him a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment's literary circles.
authors.style: Dignified blank-verse tragedy in the neoclassical manner; rhetorical set pieces and heightened sentiment; and, in his prose history, a polished Augustan narrative style.
authors.concerns: Virtue, Providence, and the passions; the theatrical and moral legitimacy of tragedy; Scottish national identity and history; and the relation of the clergy to the theatre.
authors.significance: A central figure of the Scottish Enlightenment's literary world, whose Douglas both exemplified and provoked the eighteenth-century quarrel between the church and the stage and helped establish a native Scottish tragedy.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well documented; details of the composition and revision of his unpublished dramas and minor writings are less fully recorded.

authors.name: John Keats
authors.nationality: English; poet of the Romantic period, member of the Hunt circle and the target of the 'cockney school' label applied by the quarterly reviews
authors.identity: Poet only: sonneteer, writer of the long romance 'Endymion', of metrical tales, and of the great odes and 'Hyperion' poems of 1819; a medically trained man who gave up practice for verse, and a letter-writer whose phrases ('negative capability', 'soul-making') entered the period's documented criticism.
authors.biography: Born 31 October 1795 in London, eldest child of a livery-stable keeper, he was orphaned young: his father died of a fall from a horse in 1804 and his mother of consumption in 1810, leaving the children in the guardianship of the surgeon Richard Abbey. He was educated at John Clarke's school at Enfield, where he read Chapman's Homer, Spenser, and the modern histories with a schoolboy's appetite, was bound apprentice in 1810 to the surgeon-apothecary Thomas Hammond at Edmonton, and trained at Guy's Hospital from 1815, qualifying as an apothecary in 1816 before abandoning medicine the following year to live by verse. Leigh Hunt brought him into the circle of the Examiner and the Indicator in October 1816, introducing him to his brothers, to John Hamilton Reynolds, to Woodhouse, Haydon, and Shelley; 'O Solitude' was printed in the Examiner on 5 May 1816, and the Chapman sonnet in the same paper that December. The volume 'Poems' appeared on 3 March 1817 and 'Endymion: A Poetic Romance' in 1818, and the attacks on both in Blackwood's Magazine and the Quarterly Review fixed the 'cockney' warfare that shadowed his career. In 1818 he walked in the Lake District and with Reynolds in Scotland, nursed his brother Tom, who died of consumption that December, and fell in love with Fanny Brawne at Hampstead. At Wentworth Place in 1819 he wrote 'Isabella', 'The Eve of St. Agnes', 'Lamia', the Hyperion poems, and the spring odes; with health failing and marriage impossible he sailed for Italy with Joseph Severn in September 1820 and died near the Piazza di Spagna in Rome on 23 February 1821, aged twenty-five. He lies in the Protestant Cemetery at Rome under the stone he dictated, recording only that here lies one whose name was writ in water.
authors.profile: His output is short and dense: the early Spenserian and Homeric exercises, the 1816-18 sonnets, epistles, and 'Sleep and Poetry'; the four-book romance 'Endymion'; the metrical tales 'Isabella' and 'Lamia' and the romance 'The Eve of St. Agnes'; the two Hyperion poems; the odes of 1819 with 'To Autumn' and the late lyrics; and two unfinished attempts in tragedy and dramatic sketch. His prose letters - to Reynolds, to Woodhouse, to Bailey, to the Dilkes and Woodleys, and to Severn from Rome - carry his most quoted critical statements on negative capability, the poetical character's want of self, and the world as a vale of soul-making.
authors.style: Sensation rendered as texture: heavy sensory concreteness, compound epithets, synaesthesia, and a slow, vowel-weighted music; an insistence on the palpable image that stays before the senses instead of resolving into argument. He rebuilt the English ode in stanzas of his own devising, handled the Spenserian and Elizabethan stanza and the Italian romance stanza with a romantic ear, and turned the sonnet into a vehicle of high statement about poetry, mortality, and the imagination.
authors.concerns: Identity and the dissolution of the self in other existences (negative capability); the agonistic love of the old poets - Chapman, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton; beauty, truth, and the evidence of the imagination; early death, consumption, and the endurance of verse; the ethics of making in a reviewing market that punished ambition of humble origin; the Hellenic world as a school of form; the search for a theodicy without theology in the 'vale of Soul-making'.
authors.significance: Within a decade of his death he had become one of the most reprinted poets in English, and the 1819 ode sequence set the model for later aesthetic and sensualist traditions. His letters made him the Romantic period's most quoted theorist of imagination and selflessness; the 'cockney' attacks on him sharpened the class war in Romantic letters, and his death at twenty-five in Rome fixed the enduring myth of the early-martyred poet which Shelley's 'Adonais' first consecrated and which Hunt's and Woodhouse's papers afterwards preserved.
authors.uncertainty: The exact course of his last illness (consumption, with a fatal haemorrhage, aggravated by the treatment he received) and the weight of the hostile criticism in hastening his decline were argued from 1821 onward and remain matters of interpretation rather than record; the dates of his engagement to Fanny Brawne are better documented than the later legend that he died of a broken heart.

authors.name: John Keble
authors.nationality: English; Victorian religious poetry and the Oxford Movement
authors.identity: Poet, clergyman and professor; the devotional poet whose Christian Year was the most widely read poetry book of the Victorian age, and by tradition the first mover of the Oxford Movement.
authors.biography: Born at Fairford on 25 April 1792, son of a clergyman; educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1811 and won the Newdigate prize. The Christian Year, published anonymously in 1827, sold by the thousand and remained in print throughout the century. His assize sermon on 'National Apostasy' at Oxford in July 1833 is conventionally taken as the beginning of the Oxford Movement; he contributed Tracts for the Times and his life of Bishop Wilson. He was Professor of Poetry at Oxford (1831-41), and in 1836 became vicar of Hursley, Hampshire, where he lived in obscurity until his death on 29 March 1866, cared for by his wife Charlotte and his sister Anne.
authors.profile: The Christian Year is a cycle of poems for every Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer, designed as family devotion: each poem takes the Gospel and Epistle of the day and turns them into a meditative lyric of nature, remembered childhood and moral reflection. Keble's verse is plain and its music is unostentatious; its power is the power of the Prayer Book, and it gave the Tractarian movement its devotional idiom. His prose (the sermons, the Life of Bishop Wilson) is practical and unadorned. His most influential criticism is the Latin lecture on the 'primitive' and the modest claim that poetry is the indirect expression of wishes for what we cannot attain.
authors.style: Simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood; the structure of the liturgical year; the refraining phrase and the mild warning; the absence of any but the most conventional poetic ornament; the sustaining of a single tone of trusting sentiment through 109 poems.
authors.concerns: The Church, the sacraments and the liturgical year; nature as a sign of grace; childhood and death; providence and resignation; the beauty of holiness and the danger of reform.
authors.significance: The Christian Year was the most influential book of devotional poetry in nineteenth-century England and shaped the spirituality of the Oxford Movement; Keble's assize sermon is the formal opening of the Tractarian controversy, and his influence on Newman, Pusey and the devotional verse of Christina Rossetti is direct. Its later neglect is itself a document of the Victorian crisis of faith it so thoroughly ignored.

authors.name: John Leland
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: antiquary; poet; King's Antiquary
authors.biography: Born in London about 1503; educated at St Paul's School under William Lily and at Cambridge, Oxford, and Paris. Commissioned in 1533 as King's Antiquary, he travelled England and Wales in the 1530s and 1540s recording libraries, monuments, and topography, planning a vast description of Britain he never completed. He went mad in the late 1540s and died on 18 April 1552. His Itinerary remained in manuscript until the eighteenth century.
authors.profile: The father of English antiquarianism. His Itinerary notes preserve the record of monastic libraries on the eve of the Dissolution and remain a primary source for English topography; his Cygnea Cantio (1545), a Latin poem on the Thames, and his other Latin verse earned him a European reputation in his lifetime.
authors.style: The note-taking style of the field antiquary: inventories, measurements, and reports jotted on the road, without literary finish.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the description of the realm; the preservation of manuscripts and monuments against the destruction of the Dissolution.
authors.significance: Founded the study of British antiquities and preserved irreplaceable evidence of medieval England; his collections were quarried by every later antiquary from Bale to Camden.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Itinerary's exact itinerary chronology is editorial.
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

authors.name: John Lilburne
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Leveller leader and pamphleteer; 'Freeborn John', whose tracts and trials demanded popular sovereignty, extended suffrage, and the legal rights of the 'freeborn Englishman', making him a founding figure of English radical and constitutional argument.
authors.biography: Born c. 1614–15, probably at Greenwich, Kent; apprenticed to a London clothier and drawn to Puritan dissent. Imprisoned by Star Chamber (1638) for distributing unlicensed books, he was whipped and pilloried but defied the court, refusing to incriminate himself — a landmark for the right against self-incrimination. He fought for Parliament in the Civil Wars, then turned against the Grandees, co-authoring Leveller petitions and The Agreement of the People and repeatedly publishing tracts demanding legal rights and popular sovereignty. Repeatedly imprisoned by both Royalists and Parliament/Cromwell, he briefly became a Quaker before his death on 29 August 1657.
authors.profile: The tireless polemicist of the 'freeborn' rights of Englishmen, whose pamphlets and courtroom defiance advanced principles of due process, self-incrimination, and popular consent that echo in modern constitutional law.
authors.style: Forceful, plain, popular polemic; legal and scriptural argument; petitions, tracts, and declarations; and a combative, self-justifying, energetic prose.
authors.concerns: Popular sovereignty and suffrage; the rights of the freeborn Englishman; legal process, self-incrimination, and imprisonment; the Leveller programme; and resistance to arbitrary power.
authors.significance: Lilburne and the Levellers produced the earliest sustained English arguments for democracy and legal rights; his defence against self-incrimination influenced the development of due process and the Fifth Amendment, and his tracts are foundational to radical constitutionalism.
authors.uncertainty: Lilburne's birth year and birthplace are uncertain; his voluminous pamphlets and trials are well documented, though his shifting allegiances complicate his record.

authors.name: John Locke
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), the foundational text of British empiricism, and the Two Treatises of Government (1689), whose defence of natural rights, consent, and toleration shaped the Enlightenment and modern liberalism.
authors.biography: Born 29 August 1632 at Wrington, Somerset, educated at Westminster and Christ Church, Oxford, where he turned from scholasticism to medicine and the new science, associating with Boyle and Sydenham and joining the Royal Society (1668). He became physician and close adviser to Anthony Ashley Cooper (later Earl of Shaftesbury), was drawn into Whig politics and the Exclusion Crisis, and fled to Holland (1683–89). Returning with William of Orange after the Revolution, he published in 1689 the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the Two Treatises of Government, and A Letter Concerning Toleration, and later Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693) and The Reasonableness of Christianity (1695). He spent his last years at Oates in Essex in the Masham household, dying on 28 October 1704.
authors.profile: The empiricist who argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate furnished only by experience, and the liberal who grounded government in consent, natural rights, and the pursuit of happiness — a prose of patient, plain, argumentative clarity.
authors.style: Clear, methodical, argumentative prose; plain style as an ideal; careful definition and example; and a moderate, reasonable, conversational tone addressed to the 'underlabourer's' task.
authors.concerns: Knowledge, ideas, and empiricism; personal identity and the limits of understanding; natural rights, consent, and government; religious toleration; property and money; and education.
authors.significance: Locke founded British empiricism and modern liberal political theory, profoundly influencing Berkeley, Hume, the American and French revolutions, and all subsequent Western political thought; his Essays and Treatises are also classics of English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Locke's life is thoroughly documented through his correspondence and journals; the authorship of the Two Treatises (published anonymously) was long uncertain but is now securely his.

authors.name: John Lydgate
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; translator; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: Benedictine monk of the abbey of Bury St Edmunds, ordained priest in 1397, and educated (perhaps at Gloucester College, Oxford) before a career as the most prolific English poet of the fifteenth century. He enjoyed the patronage of Henry V, Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, and the London civic elite; late in life he received a royal pension, and he died c. 1449, buried at Bury.
authors.profile: Author of the Troy Book (1412–20), the Siege of Thebes (c. 1420–22), the Fall of Princes (1431–38), the Temple of Glas (c. 1400–05), the Life of Our Lady, and an immense output of mummings, pageants, saints' lives, and devotional and occasional verse — over 140,000 lines attributed to him.
authors.style: Chaucerian forms (rhyme royal, couplets) with aureate diction and rhetorical amplification; copious moralizing; the 'Lydgate line' (often headless pentameter) that became the standard of mid-century verse.
authors.concerns: The moral exemplarity of history (the falls of princes); the honour of England and its rulers; devotional and civic piety.
authors.significance: The dominant English poet between Chaucer and Skelton, read and imitated throughout the fifteenth century (and printed by Caxton and de Worde); his Fall of Princes shaped the Tudor mirror-for-magistrates tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the canon is so large that attributions remain in flux.

authors.name: John Lyly
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: prose writer; dramatist; courtier
authors.biography: Grandson of William Lily the grammarian; educated at Magdalen College, Oxford (BA 1573, MA 1575). His Euphues (1578) made him famous overnight. From 1583 he wrote court comedies for the Children of Paul's and the Children of the Chapel, and sat in Parliament four times. He spent years petitioning in vain for the post of Master of the Revels and died in relative poverty, buried 30 November 1606.
authors.profile: Inventor of Euphuism — the antithetical, allusion-laden prose style of Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578) and Euphues and His England (1580) — and author of the elegant court comedies Campaspe (1584), Sapho and Phao (1584), Gallathea (c. 1588), Endymion (1588), Midas (1589), Mother Bombie (c. 1590), and Love's Metamorphosis (c. 1590).
authors.style: Euphuism: balanced antitheses, elaborate similes drawn from the natural histories of Pliny, proverbial wisdom, and a polished, self-conscious wit carried into his prose-like dramatic dialogue.
authors.concerns: The education and conduct of the courtier; the claims of love against the claims of state; the language of power and persuasion.
authors.significance: His prose style dominated fashionable writing for a decade and his court comedies laid the foundation of high English comedy; Shakespeare parodied and absorbed him in equal measure.

authors.biography: Baptized 7 October 1576; son of a lawyer of the Middle Temple, where he himself was admitted in 1592. He took his BA at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1594. He wrote verse satires and plays for the boy companies, fought the war of the theatres with Jonson (who caricatured him in Poetaster), then abruptly left the stage in 1608, took holy orders in 1609, and spent his last years as rector of Christchurch, Hampshire. He resigned his living in 1631 and died in London on 25 June 1634.
authors.profile: Verse satires The Scourge of Villainy and The Metamorphosis of Pygmalion's Image (1598); plays include Antonio and Mellida (c. 1599–1600), Antonio's Revenge (c. 1600), The Malcontent (1604), The Dutch Courtesan (1605), and Eastward Ho (1605, with Chapman and Jonson).
authors.style: A deliberately harsh, snarling satiric style — neologism, paradox, and a bitter wit aimed at courtly vice and poetic affectation alike.
authors.concerns: The exposure of vice; malcontentedness as a moral stance; the corruption of the court and the law.
authors.significance: The malcontent he created in The Malcontent became one of the defining types of Jacobean drama and inspired Shakespeare's and Webster's handling of the figure.
authors.uncertainty: The reasons for his abrupt retirement from the theatre are unknown.

authors.name: John Masefield
authors.nationality: British; the sea ballad, the narrative poem and the Georgian public poem
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and dramatist; the Poet Laureate from 1930 to 1967, the author of 'Sea-Fever' and The Everlasting Mercy, and the most popular English narrative poet of the period.
authors.biography: Born John Edward Masefield at Ledbury, Herefordshire, on 1 June 1878; orphaned young, he went to sea at fifteen, deserted his ship in New York, worked in a Greenwich Village bar and a carpet factory, and returned to England to write. Salt-Water Ballads (1902) and Ballads and Poems (1910) made him famous, and The Everlasting Mercy (1911) caused a scandal by using the word 'bloody' in a narrative poem of country life. He served in the Red Cross in Gallipoli and France, became Poet Laureate in 1930, and died at Abingdon on 12 May 1967.
authors.profile: Masefield revived the English narrative poem and gave the period its most popular sea poetry: 'Sea-Fever' and 'Cargoes' are among the best-known short poems in the language, and The Everlasting Mercy and Dauber brought the country and the sea into the long poem as living speech and story. As Laureate for thirty-seven years he wrote the period's public poetry, and his adventure novels established the historical sea story.
authors.style: The rhymed ballad with a strong driving narrative; the sea chantey measure; colloquial and sometimes violent diction in the long narrative poem; the story told by a character in his own voice; the plain, muscular, image-based lyric.
authors.concerns: The sea, the ship and the sailor's life; the English countryside and the farming year; the fight, the fair and the boxing booth; the wasted artist (Dauber); England and the public occasion; youth, adventure and the call of the horizon.
authors.significance: Masefield is the period's most popular narrative poet and the Laureate of the Georgian age: 'Sea-Fever', 'Cargoes' and The Everlasting Mercy gave the period its most widely recited verse, his long narratives restored story to English poetry, and his Laureate poems defined the public voice of the period.

authors.name: John Millar
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Regius Professor of Civil Law at Glasgow, who turned the history of ranks and of property into an explanation of law, government and the condition of women.
authors.biography: Born at the manse of Kirk o'Shotts in 1735, the son of the parish minister, he was educated at Glasgow, where he sat under Adam Smith, and became an advocate. With the support of Adam Smith and of the Duke of Buccleuch he was appointed in 1761 to the Glasgow chair of civil law, which he held until his death. His Origin of the Distinction of Ranks (1771) explained subordination as the consequence of subsistence, marriage and property rather than of nature, and drew a friendly critique of its chapter on women from John Dalton, printed with later editions. His Historical View of the English Government from the Settlement of the Saxons to the Revolution of 1688 (1787) applied the same method to English liberty and to the growth of the commercial orders. A sympathiser with the French Revolution after 1789, he was harassed by the alarm of the 1790s. He died on 30 May 1801.
authors.profile: The most systematic of the Scottish historians of society, who wrote the equality of conditions as a question of law, labour and domestic authority.
authors.style: Clear, cumulative, lecture-hall prose; long historical sequences argued from causes; a lawyer's precision about ranks, tenures and rights; comparatively little ornament.
authors.concerns: The dependence of political authority on property; the origins of rank, servitude and gender subordination; the history of law as social history; the foundations of English liberty and of representative government.
authors.significance: He carried stadial conjectural history into the analysis of class and of the family, and became a chief source for later theories of social development, including the tradition that linked property to political power.
authors.uncertainty: His published works are only parts of a large lecture output, some of which survives in student notes of uncertain date.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
movements: The Scottish Enlightenment

authors.name: John Milton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet, polemicist, and Latin secretary to the Commonwealth; the author of Paradise Lost and the greatest English epic poet after Chaucer, whose career moved from lyric and masque through two decades of political prose to the late biblical epics and tragedies written in blindness.
authors.biography: Born 9 December 1608 in London, son of a scrivener and composer; educated at St Paul's School and Christ's College, Cambridge (BA 1629, MA 1632), where he wrote his early odes and masques. After six years of private study at Horton (1632–38) producing 'L'Allegro', 'Il Penseroso', 'Comus', and 'Lycidas', he travelled in Italy (1638–39), meeting Galileo. From 1641 he threw himself into the Puritan cause, writing anti-prelatical tracts, the divorce pamphlets, Areopagitica (1644), and, after the regicide, The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates (1649) and Eikonoklastes; he served as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth under Cromwell, defending the republic in Latin (Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano, 1651). Totally blind by 1652, widowed twice, and imprisoned briefly at the Restoration, he composed and dictated Paradise Lost (1667), Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes (1671). He died 8 November 1674 in London.
authors.profile: The poet who claimed to write with 'no middle flight' and to 'justify the ways of God to men'; his career is the most consciously ambitious in English literature, yoking classical and Hebrew learning, republican politics, and Protestant faith to a grand style of Latinate blank verse.
authors.style: Unrhymed blank verse of great sonority and extended periodic syntax; dense allusion to classical, biblical, and Renaissance sources; grand invocations and epic similes; a learned, muscular diction; and, in the prose, a fierce polemical vigour with sprawling, powerful sentences.
authors.concerns: Liberty of conscience, republicanism, and the defence of regicide; the problem of evil and free will; obedience and temptation; the fall and regeneration of mankind; the vocation of the poet as prophet and public teacher; marriage and divorce; the corruption of the church.
authors.significance: Paradise Lost is the supreme epic of the English language and reshaped English poetry and politics for three centuries; his prose tracts are foundational documents of free speech and republican theory, and his example defined the role of the poet as moral and political witness.
authors.uncertainty: Milton's life is exceptionally well documented (Edward Phillips's and John Aubrey's early lives); the dating of Paradise Lost's composition and the precise nature of his blindness remain matters of scholarship.

authors.name: John Mirk
authors.nationality: English (West Midlands)
authors.identity: homilist; Augustinian canon
authors.biography: An Augustinian canon and prior of Lilleshall Abbey, Shropshire, active in the 1380s and 1390s; he compiled the Festial, a cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, with a companion instructional work for parish priests (Instructions for Parish Priests).
authors.profile: Author of the Festial (c. 1380s) and Instructions for Parish Priests, among the most widely copied English sermon collections of the later Middle Ages.
authors.style: Plain, lively English sermons built on exempla, miracles, and verse tags; the vivid storytelling of popular piety adapted for parish preaching.
authors.concerns: The instruction of the laity in the feasts, sacraments, and moral duties of the church year.
authors.significance: The Festial is the classic collection of the English late medieval sermon and a principal witness to orthodox vernacular preaching in the age of Lollardy.

authors.name: John Neal
authors.nationality: American; the Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world and the aggressive New England literary nationalism that preceded the Young America movement
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, critic, editor and lecturer, the most combative and most influential American reviewer of the 1810s and 1820s, the chief American champion of Byron and of the new British and German poetry, and the boldest early claimant of an American literature independent of English judgment.
authors.biography: Neal was born at Portland in the district of Maine, then part of Massachusetts, of a family of small means; his father was a schoolmaster, the household fell into difficulty early, and the boy was put behind a shop counter instead of being sent to a college. Largely self-taught, he was bound to learn law and read it, went to Baltimore in 1816, was admitted to the bar there but practised little, and gave himself to the newspapers and the weekly literary journals of the city. He edited at Baltimore a short-lived review of arts and books called The Portico in 1818, and for a season a political paper; his poems of 1819 and 1820, his frontier tale of 1822 and his novel of the revolutionary year followed fast, and made him the most forward and most quarrelsome of the young American men of letters. His survey of American writing, contributed to a Scottish monthly from the winter of 1824 into 1825, was the first attempt to take the whole of the native literature as a single history and made him the most quoted critic of the decade. He passed to England in 1823 and remained in London and on the continent until 1827, knew the painters, publishers, reformers and periodical writers of the London literary world, contributed at length to the Edinburgh magazine which had taken him up, and in those years made the acquaintance of the young American poet of the Baltimore and Richmond periodicals whose cause he afterwards pleaded against his own former friends. His novels of the later 1820s, which turned to colonial history and to social and religious doctrine, sold poorly and one of them provoked a scandal of its own; he married in 1828, and after a return to Portland he gradually reinvented himself as the respected man of letters of his native city, writing history and biography for young readers, reminiscence and domestic papers, lecturing on American society, and taking part in civic, temperance and charitable work. He died at Portland on 20 June 1876, having long abandoned the aggressive manner that had made his name notorious, and leaving a body of criticism which the twentieth century reprinted as the founding document of American literary nationalism.
authors.profile: His work covers almost every province of the letters of his generation: verse in the Byronic and the descriptive manner, tales and novels of border adventure, society and doctrine, a large body of critical and programmatic prose, editorial miscellany, lectures, reminiscence and autobiography. His critical papers are the first sustained American argument for literary nationalism and for a realism of language and character, and they attacked at once the caution of American letters and its deference to Edinburgh and London. His fiction is experimental in scale and in manner, opening the Revolution and the western settlements to a colloquial, sensational and digressive narrative voice; the later books on the founders of independence, on Catholicism and on social questions belong to the respectable Victorian career that succeeded the earlier warfare.
authors.style: A deliberate vehemence and abruptness of style, with short paragraphs, exclamations, coined words, Americanisms and colloquialisms forced upon the page, and an incessant personal challenge to reader and opponent alike; in the fiction an expansive, digressive and sensational manner, with direct address, self-quotation, unfinished plots and a roughness of execution that later critics reclaimed as a native modernism. The criticism is aphoristic and combative, the autobiography garrulous and self-justifying.
authors.concerns: The independence of American letters from English judgment and imitation; the originality of the individual genius and the cowardice of the deferential critic; realism of language and the dignity of common speech; the claims of the new poetry and of the romance; national character, the Puritan inheritance and the duties of the American writer to his own public; the condition of women, Roman Catholicism, slavery and temperance in their American forms.
authors.significance: He was the first American critic of sustained force and a principal transmitter of the new British and German poetry to American readers, and his demand for an American literature of the present shaped the generation that followed, from the Young America writers to the romancers of the 1840s and 1850s. His survey of American writing supplied the first history of the whole native field and helped make the phrase American literature current; his advocacy was decisive for the American recognition of Edgar Allan Poe, whom he introduced to the Richmond and Philadelphia journals, and his irregular, open-form novels are now read as part of the native origin of American prose fiction.
authors.uncertainty: Much of his periodical writing of the Baltimore years appeared over shifting names and is still imperfectly identified; the names sometimes proposed for him in general reference works cannot be confirmed, and only the Byronic and Scottish-magazine pen name recorded in his own bibliography is secure; part of his early career is known chiefly from his own later reminiscences, which are self-serving and variously dated.

authors.name: John Newton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Former slave-ship captain turned Anglican minister and hymn-writer, whose Authentic Narrative (1764) and Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788) made a converted trader the most searched witness against the trade.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1725, the son of a sea captain, and left largely to his own devices after the early death of his mother in his seventh year, he ran to sea as a lad, was pressed into the navy, flogged for desertion and then carried on the slave ships between West Africa and the Americas, where for a time he was in effect the property of an African owner. A violent storm in 1748 opened a religious conversion that he never forgot, although he continued in the trade and rose to be the master of a slave ship before illness and conscience ended his sea service in the mid-1750s. He left the sea in the mid-1750s, held a minor shore appointment, married and studied for the ministry, and published in 1764 An Authentic Narrative, an account of his mercy and of his former occupation that was widely read. About the same time he was appointed curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where he became the friend and guide of William Cowper and gave the village its hymn book of 1779. Presented in 1780 to St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, he preached there for the rest of his life, consulted the parliamentary abolitionists and gave them Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788), a belated and unsparing self-accusation. He died in London in December 1807, having written the inscription for his own grave.
authors.profile: A pastor of the converted sinner who wrote his own career as a case of grace and then pressed that case into public argument against the trade that had made him.
authors.style: Plain, nautical and self-examining narrative prose; homely, concrete hymn verse in familiar metres; sermons built of plain doctrine pressed home; a letter-writer's intimacy and candour.
authors.concerns: Grace, remorse and the reality of change; the guilt of the slave trade and the complicity of churches and nations; providence in the lives of sailors; assurance, obedience and comfort for the afflicted.
authors.significance: His narrative and his 1788 tract supplied the abolitionist movement with its most credible first-hand testimony, and his hymns, written with Cowper, remain part of the ordinary worship of English-speaking Christianity.
authors.uncertainty: His early years and the details of his service in Africa are known chiefly from his own narrative, which shapes the facts to a providential design.
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

authors.name: John of Salisbury
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: philosopher; political theorist; bishop
authors.biography: Educated at Paris under the greatest masters of the twelfth-century schools — Abelard, William of Conches, Gilbert of Poitiers — he returned to England as secretary to Archbishop Theobald and then to Thomas Becket, whose exile he shared and whose murder he witnessed (1170). He became bishop of Chartres in 1176 and died there on 25 October 1180.
authors.profile: Author of the Policraticus (1159), the first great medieval treatise on political theory; the Metalogicon (1159), a defence of the trivium; the Historia Pontificalis; and a celebrated correspondence.
authors.style: Classical learning worn lightly and worn for moral ends; the organic metaphor of the body politic; satiric portraits of courtiers; the first medieval theory of tyrannicide.
authors.concerns: The limits of royal power; the education of the prince and the clerk; the relation of church and state; the value of humane letters.
authors.significance: The Policraticus is the most important political treatise between Augustine and Aquinas and the fountainhead of medieval constitutionalism; its organic state theory shaped political thought for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his Paris studies is reconstructed from the Metalogicon.

authors.name: John Ramsay McCulloch
authors.nationality: Scottish and British - a Romantic-period political economist, statistician and reviewer: an Edinburgh-trained Ricardian who made his career in London, and the genre-defining writer of the expository treatise, the review article and the statistical dictionary.
authors.identity: A publicist and systematiser of political economy rather than an original theorist - the man who made Ricardo a curriculum. His proper forms are the expository treatise, the review article, the pamphlet addressed to a parliamentary committee, and the statistical dictionary built from consular returns; his most lasting single performance is the Introductory Discourse prefixed to Adam Smith, where a science is given a history, a pedigree and a canon of texts.
authors.biography: John Ramsay McCulloch was born at Whithorn, Wigtownshire, on 1 March 1789, eldest son of Edward McCulloch, laird of Auchengool in the stewartry of Kirkcudbright, and Sarah Laing. His father died while he was a child and his grandfather taught him first; after his mother's remarriage he went to school at Kinross, then attended Edinburgh University without taking a degree, sitting with Sir John Leslie, who became his friend, and with Thomas Brown, from whom he learned to distrust metaphysics. He entered a writer to the signet's office and soon left it in disgust. His Essay on a Reduction of the Interest of the National Debt (1816) drew Ricardo's correspondence, and his Edinburgh Review essay on Ricardo's Principles of 1818 began twenty years of periodical writing, seventy-six articles in all by 1837. He helped to found The Scotsman in 1817, edited it from 1818 to 1820 and wrote its economic copy for a decade. In 1824 he delivered the Ricardo Memorial Lectures in London, which became A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824), the Britannica article on Political Economy, and The Principles of Political Economy with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825), the standard textbook until Mill's treatise of 1848. The Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826) gave the English-speaking world the wages-fund doctrine, and his edition of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations with an Introductory Discourse appeared in 1828, the year he took the unendowed chair of political economy at the new University of London. Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and his Dictionary of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832) were followed by the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837), the geographical dictionary of 1841, the Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System (1845), The Literature of Political Economy (1845), his edition of Ricardo's Works (1846) and the Political Economy Club's collections of scarce tracts (1856-59). Comptroller of the Stationery Office from 1838, he died there on 11 November 1864 and lies in Brompton Cemetery.
authors.profile: His work is systematic rather than imaginative, and divides into four bodies. Treatise and textbook: A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824) and The Principles of Political Economy, with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825; enlarged editions 1830, 1843, 1849), with the applied studies An Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826), the Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and the treatises on Taxation and the Funding System (1845) and on Succession to Property Vacant by Death (1848). Reference and statistics: the Dictionary, Practical, Theoretical and Historical, of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832), the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837) and the geographical dictionary of 1841. Editing and bibliography: Smith's Wealth of Nations (1828), Ricardo's Works (1846), The Literature of Political Economy (1845) and the tract collections edited for the Political Economy Club and for Lord Overstone (1856-59). Periodical prose: seventy-six Edinburgh Review articles (1818-37) and a decade of economic leading in The Scotsman.
authors.style: Bald, emphatic and expository: a prose of definition, enumeration and example, written to be taught from. He repeats himself across book, review and pamphlet until a doctrine becomes a commonplace, and his habitual move is to dispute an opponent's terms rather than his facts. Abstractions are handled concretely - the cask of new wine that gains five pounds in the cellar carries the whole question of profit - and his tables of prices, rents, colonies and population are themselves the evidence. Caricature caught the manner with the accent: Carlyle's McGroudy, Peacock's MacFungus, Christopher North's Stot and the Mordecai Mullion parody of 1826 all satirise a dogmatic, repetitive, plain-spoken Scot.
authors.concerns: The labour theory of value and the impossibility of an invariable measure of value; rent and the corn laws; the wages-fund and the condition of the labouring classes; profit, interest and whether time can of itself produce value; taxation, the funding system and the national debt; free trade, colonization and emigration; the statistical knowledge of a commercial state as the ground of legislation; the history, literature and right boundaries of political economy as a science; and the diffusion of economic orthodoxy by textbook, review, professorial chair and discussion class.
authors.significance: He was the leader of the Ricardian school after 1823 and the man who turned it into a teachable public doctrine: his Principles was the orthodoxy that Mill superseded, was translated into French, German and Italian, and made him the most quoted and most abused of economists in his own generation. His editions of Smith and of Ricardo fixed the canon of classical political economy, and their prefaces, with The Literature of Political Economy, founded the history and bibliography of the subject. The Dictionary of Commerce and the Statistical Account of the British Empire set the model of the official factual compendium, and his appointment in 1828 made him the first professor of political economy in the University of London.
authors.uncertainty: The dates are firm and agreed (born 1 March 1789, died 11 November 1864). The birthplace is given as Whithorn, Wigtownshire, by the Dictionary of National Biography and repeated by modern encyclopedias and by Wikipedia, but the family's standing is reported differently: the Dictionary of National Biography calls his father laird of Auchengool, while social-science encyclopedias describe a small landowner who lost his fortune, so the economics of McCulloch's childhood cannot be stated precisely. The end of his University College professorship is disputed: the Dictionary of National Biography and the Macmillan Encyclopedia of Economic History say he resigned the unendowed chair in 1832, while the History of Economic Thought archive has him holding it until 1837. He is sometimes described as an editor of the Edinburgh Review; the succession from Francis Jeffrey in October 1829 belongs to MacVey Napier, and his relation to the Review should be stated as contributor and its principal writer on political economy. His Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System is dated 1845 by the Dictionary of National Biography and by first-edition imprints, but appears under 1863 in some modern lists, presumably a later issue. The surname is printed both McCulloch and M'Culloch, and the count of seventy-six Review articles is the Dictionary of National Biography's estimate rather than a census.

authors.name: John Rastell
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: printer; lawyer; playwright
authors.biography: Born in London about 1475; a lawyer of the Middle Temple and the brother-in-law of Thomas More, whose circle he printed. His press issued More's early works and his own plays — The Four Elements (c. 1520) and the translation Calisto and Melebea (c. 1530) — and his chronicle The Pastime of People (c. 1529). His opposition to the clergy's exactions brought him imprisonment, and he died in prison in June or July 1536.
authors.profile: The first English printer-playwright. The Four Elements is a didactic interlude teaching cosmology and geography through drama, and The Pastime of People compresses the history of Britain into a popular chronicle; his press was the vehicle of the More circle and of the earliest English humanist drama.
authors.style: Instruction through entertainment; the interlude as lecture hall and theatre at once; plain prose and functional verse.
authors.concerns: Popular education in the new learning; the reform of clerical exactions; law, printing, and the spread of knowledge.
authors.significance: A founder of the English printing trade in its humanist phase; his interludes and chronicles made the new learning available to a popular audience.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the date of his death (1536) is established by legal records.

authors.name: John Redford
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: playwright; composer; master of the choristers at St Paul's
authors.biography: Born about 1486; almoner and master of the choristers at St Paul's Cathedral, where he trained the boys who performed his play Wit and Science (c. 1539). He was a noted composer and organist — John Heywood married his daughter — and died in 1547.
authors.profile: Author of Wit and Science, the most accomplished of the school moralities: the allegory of Wit's wooing of Lady Science, with the giant Tediousness, the Vice Idleness, and the comic conversion of the booby Ingnorance, written for boy actors with songs and dances. The play survives in a single manuscript with its music cues.
authors.style: The morality convention refreshed with music, dance, and schoolroom comedy; allegorical personification handled with theatrical tact.
authors.concerns: The marriage of wit and learning; the discipline of the school; the education of boys through play and music.
authors.significance: The finest of the school interludes and a direct ancestor of the academic drama and the court masque; his St Paul's boys became one of the great Elizabethan playing companies.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the play's date (c. 1539) is editorial.
