authors.name: John Ruskin
authors.nationality: English; Victorian art criticism and political economy
authors.identity: Art critic, draughtsman, and social critic; the greatest English writer on art and the Victorian critic who turned from pictures to the political economy of labour.
authors.biography: Born in London on 8 February 1819, the only child of a wealthy sherry merchant; educated privately and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate prize in 1839. His mother moved with him to Oxford and read the Bible with him daily; his father financed the publication of Modern Painters I (1843), which defended Turner against the critics. He married Euphemia Gray in 1848; the marriage was annulled in 1854 after a famous and unhappy failure. The Stones of Venice (1851-53) established his reputation for architectural history, and from Unto This Last (1860, in the Cornhill) he turned to political economy and to the critique of Victorian capitalism. He was Slade Professor of Fine Art at Oxford from 1869 to 1879 and again in 1883-85, founded the Guild of St George (1871), published Fors Clavigera as letters to working men from 1871 to 1884, and suffered repeated mental breakdowns. He died at Brantwood, Coniston, on 20 January 1900.
authors.profile: Ruskin changed the way the Victorian age looked at art. His criticism begins with the truth to nature of the Pre-Raphaelites and Turner, passes to the moral and social analysis of architecture (the Stones of Venice's chapter 'The Nature of Gothic' makes the labour of the craftsman the test of art), and ends in a complete indictment of industrial capitalism as a system of slavery and ugliness. His prose is the most magnificent of Victorian descriptive writing — simple declarative sentences in the early work, and a wilder, evangelical, exclamatory manner in the late letters — and his method is always the accumulation of observed detail followed by a moral judgement that is both aesthetic and economic.
authors.style: Precise, patient description of natural fact; the moral interpretation of ornament and building; direct address and personal confession; an apparently artless simplicity that carries a religious intensity; the letter form and the aphorism; the coined phrase ('the pathetic fallacy', 'the illth', 'There is no wealth but life').
authors.concerns: Truth to nature and the moral meaning of art; the relation of the artist's society to the art he makes; labour, craft and the dignity of the hand; the political economy of wealth and 'illth'; education and the reading of pictures; the destruction of the landscape by industry and tourism; the preservation of the past; the education of the working man.
authors.significance: Ruskin is the central English art critic and the origin of the idea that a society can be judged by its buildings. 'The Nature of Gothic' taught Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement that art was labour; Unto This Last gave the Labour movement and the founders of the British welfare state (Attlee and the Webbs) their moral vocabulary; the Pre-Raphaelites took their programme from him, and Pater, Wilde and the Aesthetic movement defined themselves by turning his moral criticism into an aesthetic one.
authors.uncertainty: 1 of the 6 works catalogued here carry a research status of 'partial' - Praeterita: Outlines of Scenes and Thoughts Perhaps Worthy of Memory in My Past Life - and are reported only so far as the evidence allows. 31 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text.

authors.name: John Skelton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; satirist; orator regius; tutor to Prince Henry
authors.biography: Educated at Cambridge and Oxford, where he was laureated (1488), and at Louvain (1492); he styled himself 'poet laureate'. Tutor to Prince Henry (the future Henry VIII) from about 1496 to 1502, he became rector of Diss in Norfolk (c. 1504) and 'orator regius' at court. His later career was a running satirical war with Cardinal Wolsey, whom he attacked in verse so freely that he took sanctuary at Westminster in 1523, where he died on 21 June 1529.
authors.profile: The dominant English poet of the early Tudor period and the inventor of the 'Skeltonic' line — short, breathless, rhymed couplets of irregular length. His canon runs from the dream-satire The Bowge of Courte (c. 1499) through the mock-elegy Philip Sparrow (c. 1505), the low-life tour de force The Tunning of Elinour Rumming (c. 1517), the morality play Magnificence (c. 1515–23), and the great anti-Wolsey satires Speke Parrot (1521), Colin Clout (c. 1522), and Why Come Ye Nat to Courte? (c. 1522–23), to the self-crowning dream vision The Garland of Laurel (1523).
authors.style: The Skeltonic: tumbling short lines, obsessive rhyme, macaronic Latin, colloquial diction, and a satirical voice that moves between learned allusion and street abuse; also a master of the aureate, 'laureate' high style.
authors.concerns: The corruption of the clergy and the court; the duties of kingship; the poet's laureate authority; the defence of the English language against Latinate pretension.
authors.significance: The first great English satirist of the print era and the bridge between the medieval and Renaissance poetries; his Skeltonics were imitated for a century and admired by the Elizabethans, who read him as the scourge of Wolsey.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace uncertain; some Skeltonic attributions among minor poems remain debated.
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry

authors.name: John Steinbeck
authors.nationality: American; the Depression novel and the California valley
authors.identity: Novelist; the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962.
authors.biography: Born John Ernst Steinbeck Jr in Salinas, California, on 27 February 1902; he worked as a labourer, fruit picker and journalist, and made his name with Tortilla Flat (1935). Of Mice and Men (1937), The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Cannery Row (1945) and East of Eden (1952) followed; he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1962 and died in New York on 20 December 1968.
authors.profile: Steinbeck was the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962: The Grapes of Wrath is the central American novel of the 1930s and Of Mice and Men one of the most performed plays and novels in the language, and his California valley gave American fiction a permanent landscape.
authors.style: The documentary detail of the migrant road; the flat, plain, biblical prose; the dialogue of the dispossessed; the intercalary chapter and the wide social view; the compassion without sentimentality.
authors.concerns: The Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; the closing of the American frontier; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.
authors.significance: Steinbeck was the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962: The Grapes of Wrath is the central American novel of the 1930s, Of Mice and Men one of the most performed works in the language, and his California valley gave American fiction a permanent landscape.

authors.name: John Stow
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: antiquarian; chronicler; tailor
authors.biography: Born in the parish of St Michael Cornhill, London, about 1525, son of a tallow-chandler. A tailor by trade, he gave up the craft for antiquarian study, publishing chronicles and surveys on which he spent his modest means. In old age he was licensed to beg, and he died in poverty on 6 April 1605; his monument stands in St Andrew Undershaft.
authors.profile: The Survey of London (1598; enlarged 1603), the loving topographical description of the city, and A Summary of English Chronicles (1565), the basis of his larger Annales (1580, 1592).
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, accumulative prose — the voice of a man walking his city street by street, ward by ward, remembering what was there before.
authors.concerns: The preservation of civic memory against Reformation destruction and urban change; the antiquity and honour of London.
authors.significance: The Survey is the foundation of London historiography and an irreplaceable record of the pre-Fire city.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

authors.name: John Stuart Mill
authors.nationality: English; Victorian philosophy, political economy and political thought
authors.identity: Philosopher, political economist, civil servant and feminist; the central liberal thinker of the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born in London on 20 May 1806, the eldest son of the Scottish philosopher James Mill, who educated him from the age of three with the rigour recorded in the Autobiography (1873): he read Greek at three, had mastered the whole of political economy by thirteen, and suffered a crisis at twenty from which he was saved by Wordsworth's poetry and by the love of Harriet Taylor, whom he married in 1851 after twenty years of attachment. He worked for the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, was elected to Parliament for Westminster in 1865, and moved the amendment that gave women the vote in 1867, defeating his own party. His books include the System of Logic (1843), Principles of Political Economy (1848), On Liberty (1859), Considerations on Representative Government (1861), Utilitarianism (1863), An Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy (1865) and The Subjection of Women (1869). He died at Avignon on 8 May 1873.
authors.profile: Mill refashioned Bentham's and his father's utilitarianism into a philosophy capable of defending individuality and liberty. His System of Logic established the methods of empirical science as the model of reasoning, and On Liberty set out the harm principle — the only ground for restricting a person's liberty is to prevent harm to others — which became the foundation of modern liberal thought. In political economy he distinguished the laws of production from the possible distribution of wealth, opening the way for a socialist and reformist economics; in The Subjection of Women he produced the most rigorous philosophical argument for women's equality in the nineteenth century.
authors.style: Lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose; the argument by distinction and by the counter-example; the use of a stated 'exception' to define a rule; the conversion of philosophical positions into historical narratives of their development; personal confession used as evidence (the Autobiography).
authors.concerns: Liberty of thought and expression; individuality and the tyranny of opinion; the subjection of women; the aim of utilitarian ethics and the quality of pleasures; representative government and the democratic danger of mediocrity; the logic of induction; the economics of distribution and the 'stationary state'.
authors.significance: Mill is the father of modern liberalism and the most rigorous exponent of the Victorian liberal mind: On Liberty, Utilitarianism, and The Subjection of Women are foundational documents of modern politics, and his amendment on women's suffrage began the parliamentary campaign that ended in 1918 and 1928. His System of Logic shaped the social sciences, and his Principles of Political Economy taught the century economics until Marshall superseded it.

authors.name: John Tillotson
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Latitudinarian divine and Archbishop of Canterbury; the most influential preacher of the late seventeenth century, whose clear, reasonable, moral sermons defined Anglican pulpit prose and the ideal of a tolerant, rational Christianity.
authors.biography: Born 1630 at Sowerby, Yorkshire, educated at Clare Hall, Cambridge (Fellow). A Puritan by upbringing, he conformed at the Restoration, held preferment, and became Dean of St Paul's (1664) and a leading latitudinarian preacher. He supported the Revolution of 1688, was made Archbishop of Canterbury (1691) under William III, and worked for comprehension and toleration. His sermons — reasonable, moral, and elegantly plain — were immensely popular and widely published (posthumous collected volumes 1695–1704). He died on 22 November 1694.
authors.profile: The model Latitudinarian preacher, whose sermons argued for a reasonable, benevolent, practical Christianity in a lucid, classical prose that set the standard for Augustan pulpit and essay style.
authors.style: Clear, plain, elegant, well-reasoned prose; the moral sermon of practical divinity; classical balance and lucidity; and an irenic, moderate tone.
authors.concerns: Reasonable religion and natural theology; morality and practical Christianity; toleration and comprehension; the relation of reason and revelation; and the church's public role.
authors.significance: Tillotson's sermons were among the most read prose of the age, shaping Anglican latitudinarianism, the plain prose style, and eighteenth-century moral and religious writing (admired by Addison, Swift, and Johnson).
authors.uncertainty: Tillotson's birth year is approximate; his life and sermons are well documented, and his posthumous publications were edited by others.
movements: The Anglican and Latitudinarian Divines
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

authors.name: John Toland
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish
authors.identity: Ulster-born freethinker, heterodox scholar and hard-line Whig pamphleteer, a founding figure of English deism after Christianity Not Mysterious (1696).
authors.biography: Born in 1670 on the Inishowen peninsula, of a Gaelic family whose name was anglicised from O'Tolian, he studied at Glasgow, at Edinburgh, where he took his MA, and at Leiden, acquiring an extraordinary range of languages. Christianity Not Mysterious (1696), arguing that the gospel holds nothing properly above reason, was ordered burned by civil and ecclesiastical authority and made him the most attacked writer of his generation. He moved in London Whig and commonwealth circles, edited Milton's prose, defended Lucan against his classical detractors, and wrote on party management, the Hanoverian succession and the Bible as history: Nazarenus (1718) recovered apocryphal gospel fragments, and Tetradymus (1720) gathered four sceptical treatises. His political work carried him between Dublin, London and the Hague, where he cultivated Leibniz and Berkeley; he died at Putney on 11 March 1722.
authors.profile: A combative polymath of letters, party and scripture, who treated the history of religion as a history of power and of priestly imposture.
authors.style: Dense, allusive and polemic; scholarly footnotes used as weapons; blunt deistical reasoning dressed in commonwealth rhetoric; a restless, digressive pamphlet energy.
authors.concerns: The reduction of mystery to evidence; tolerance and its clerical enemies; the political history of the biblical canon; pantheistic materialism and the eternity of matter; the management of parties and the secret history of states.
authors.significance: He fixed the agenda of deism and of the historical criticism of Scripture, gave the commonwealth Whigs a model of scholarship in the service of liberty, and provoked the century's long rearguard action of Christian apologetics.
authors.uncertainty: His degrees, employments and embassies are imperfectly documented and rest partly on his own claims; several works appeared anonymously.
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

authors.name: John Trevisa
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: translator; scholar; priest
authors.biography: Cornish-born scholar of Exeter College and Queen's College, Oxford, fellow of Queen's and later vicar of Berkeley, Gloucestershire, in the household of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, for whom he translated major Latin works into English prose.
authors.profile: Translator of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon (completed 1387, with his famous Dialogue on Translation between a Lord and a Clerk) and of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (1398); also translated works of religious instruction and political theory.
authors.style: Vigorous, expansive English prose; the confident handling of learned Latin vocabulary and its rendering into idiomatic English; a stated program of translation for the benefit of English readers.
authors.concerns: The provision of learning in English; the dignity of the vernacular; the duties of lordship and clergy.
authors.significance: With the Wycliffite translators, Trevisa helped create the learned English prose of the late fourteenth century; his Dialogue on Translation is a classic statement of vernacular self-consciousness.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his role in the Wycliffite Bible translation is debated.

authors.name: John Vanbrugh
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Restoration playwright and, later, the great baroque architect of Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard; his bawdy, energetic comedies The Relapse (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697) revived the Restoration comedy of manners at the turn of the century.
authors.biography: Born January 1664 (baptised 24 January) in London, of a Flemish merchant family; educated at Chester and briefly a soldier and an officer in the East India Company. Imprisoned in the Bastille (1690–92) on suspicion of espionage, he turned to the stage on his release, producing The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697), huge successes that scandalised the reformers. He also wrote The False Friend (1702) and farces. From about 1702 he became, astonishingly, a leading architect (Knighted 1714), designing Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard in the English baroque. He died on 26 March 1726.
authors.profile: The robust, good-humoured comic writer whose plays are broad, bawdy, and structurally bold, contrasting with Congreve's polish; his Lord Foppington and his treatment of marital misery are Restoration comedy at its most energetic.
authors.style: Broad farce and bawdy wit; energetic, colloquial prose; bold double plots; memorable comic types (Lord Foppington); and a genial, unsentimental view of vice.
authors.concerns: Sexual appetite and marriage; social pretension and foppery; virtue and its dangers; and the comedy of manners under moral attack.
authors.significance: Vanbrugh's comedies are the last great works of Restoration comic drama and a bridge to eighteenth-century comedy; his subsequent career as England's foremost baroque architect makes him a unique figure in the arts.
authors.uncertainty: Vanbrugh's early life (soldiering, Bastille) is documented but partly legendary; his birth date is approximate, and the transition to architecture is remarkable but well recorded.

The Restoration Theatre

authors.name: John Webster
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Son of a prosperous London coachmaker and member of the Merchant Taylors' Company; born about 1580. He entered the Middle Temple about 1598 and began collaborating with Dekker and others (Westward Ho, 1604; Northward Ho, 1605) before the independent tragedies that made his name. Nothing is known of his last years; he was dead by about 1634, when Heywood called him 'that worthy poet' in the past tense.
authors.profile: The White Devil (1612), The Duchess of Malfi (c. 1614), The Devil's Law Case (c. 1619), and Appius and Virginia (c. 1626, with Heywood); his famous character essays were appended to the 1615 Overbury collection.
authors.style: A poetry of darkness: lurid emblems, macabre wit, great set-piece dirges, and a sombre moral seriousness beneath the sensational surface.
authors.concerns: Corruption of courts; the abuse of women by rank and power; the gulf between appearance and worth; death as the great leveller.
authors.significance: With The Duchess of Malfi he wrote what many rank the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage; his heroines and villains shaped the Jacobean imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Both birth and death dates approximate; almost all personal details are inferred from records of the Coachmakers' Company and the Middle Temple.

authors.name: John Wesley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican priest, evangelist and organiser of the Methodists, whose sermons, journals, hymnals and rules of society made a religious revival into a permanent connection.
authors.biography: Born at Epworth in 1703, the fifteenth of the children of Samuel Wesley, a country rector, and of Susanna Wesley, who governed the household and its education, he was sent to the Charterhouse and then to Christ Church, Oxford, where he was elected a fellow and took his degrees. Ordained in the Church of England, he went with his brother Charles to Georgia as a missionary in the mid-1730s and came home a failure in his own judgement. At a meeting in Aldersgate Street in May 1738 he described the assurance of his pardon, and in the following year he began to preach out of doors in Bristol at Whitefield's example, since the churches would not open to him. For fifty years he travelled through Britain and Ireland on horseback, organising societies, classes and bands, training lay preachers and holding annual conferences, and he wrote and printed for the movement with tireless industry: sermons on several occasions, Notes upon the New Testament, a Journal, a Christian Library and the Collection of Hymns of 1780. He defended the salvation of slaves in Thoughts upon Slavery (1775) and in his last years encouraged the parliamentary agitation against the trade. He died in London in March 1791, having preached almost to the end, and was buried beside his chapel in City Road.
authors.profile: A preacher-writer of enormous practical energy, whose plain prose and vigorous verse carried a revived religion to colliers, miners and farm servants.
authors.style: Direct, urgent, colloquial sermon prose; rules, minutes and class lists shaped for use; a journal kept for the public; hymn and paraphrase verse of muscular, repetitive simplicity.
authors.concerns: Original sin and universal redemption; justification by faith and the witness of the Spirit; Christian perfection and the means of grace; free grace against Calvinist decree; Methodist discipline, education and the duty of saving souls.
authors.significance: He made Methodism, the largest religious movement of the century in the English-speaking world, and shaped the hymnody, revival practice and later social history of Britain and America.
authors.uncertainty: The tallies of his sermons and mileage are traditional estimates rather than records, and the editing of his Journal for publication was a work of self-presentation.
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

authors.name: John Wilkins
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Clergyman, natural philosopher, and organizer of science; the central figure of the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society, whose works on a universal philosophical language and on the plurality of worlds made him a pioneer of scientific communication.
authors.biography: Born 1614 (baptised 1 January 1614/15), probably at Fawsley, Northamptonshire; educated at New Inn Hall and Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as chaplain and, under the Commonwealth, as Warden of Wadham College, Oxford (1648), where he gathered the circle of experimental philosophers (including Boyle, Wren, and Hooke) that formed the nucleus of the Royal Society. He married Robina, sister of Oliver Cromwell (1656), was deprived at the Restoration but reconciled, became vicar of Polebrook and then Dean of Exeter. His works include The Discovery of a World in the Moone (1638) and An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (1668), a scheme for a universal language. He died on 19 November 1672.
authors.profile: The genial organizer and populariser of the new science, whose speculative works on the moon, cryptography, and a philosophical 'real character' promoted experimental learning and clear communication.
authors.style: Clear, expository, speculative prose; scientific and linguistic schemes; popularisation of the new philosophy; and an irenic, moderate clerical tone.
authors.concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institutions; a universal philosophical language; the plurality of worlds and astronomy; cryptography and communication; and religious latitude and toleration.
authors.significance: Wilkins was the practical founder of the Royal Society's collaborative ethos and a pioneer of the search for a universal language and of scientific popularisation; his Essay influenced later philosophers of language and utopian writers.
authors.uncertainty: Wilkins's birthplace and early life are uncertain; his career is documented through university, church, and Royal Society records.

authors.name: John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
altNames: John Wilmot, Second Earl of Rochester
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Libertine poet, courtier, and wit of Charles II's court; the greatest of the Restoration rakish versifiers, whose savage satires, bawdy lyrics, and bleak 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' combine intellectual rigour with scandalous candour.
authors.biography: Born 1 April 1647 at Ditchley, Oxfordshire; educated at Burford and Wadham College, Oxford, then travelling in France and Italy. He became a favourite of Charles II, distinguished himself in the Second Dutch War (1665–66), and lived a notorious life of debauchery, abduction (of the heiress Elizabeth Malet, whom he married), imprisonment, and wit. His verse circulated largely in manuscript among the court wits; he wrote for the stage (a version of Valentinian, 1685) and translated Lucretius and Seneca. After a profound deathbed conversion under the bishop Gilbert Burnet, he died at Woodstock on 26 July 1680, aged 33. His Poems on Several Occasions appeared posthumously (1680).
authors.profile: The libertine philosopher-poet whose work interrogates reason, appetite, and human pretension with a cynical honesty and formal skill that modern critics rank among the finest of the age.
authors.style: Biting satiric verse; the bawdy and obscene lyric; a philosophic bleakness and intellectual paradox; vigorous colloquial energy; and skilful use of the couplet and the song.
authors.concerns: Reason and appetite; the hypocrisy of civilization and court life; sexual libertinism; mortality and the vanity of human pride; and, at the last, repentance and faith.
authors.significance: Once dismissed as merely obscene, Rochester is now recognised as a serious and original satirist whose 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' is a major philosophic poem and whose influence extends to the modern revival of interest in Restoration libertinism.
authors.uncertainty: Rochester's canon is unstable because most poems circulated anonymously in manuscript; attribution of individual verses is often uncertain and disputed.

themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present

authors.name: John Wyclif
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: theologian; philosopher; reformer
authors.biography: Fellow and master of Balliol College, Oxford, and the dominant figure in the university's theological debates from the 1360s; doctor of theology c. 1372. From c. 1376 he developed the doctrines — dominion founded on grace, the primacy of scripture, and the rejection of transubstantiation — that were condemned by the Blackfriars council of 1382. Retired to his living at Lutterworth, Leicestershire, where he died on 31 December 1384; his remains were exhumed and burned as a heretic in 1428.
authors.profile: Author of an immense Latin corpus — De Civili Dominio (1375–76), De Veritate Sacrae Scripturae, De Officio Regis, the Trialogus, the Postilla, and many sermons — and traditionally credited (though modern scholarship dissents) with inspiring the English Wycliffite Bible.
authors.style: Relentlessly logical scholastic argument deployed for radical ends; a plain, urgent English style in the sermons attributed to him.
authors.concerns: The poverty of the church and the renunciation of temporal lordship; scripture as sole authority; the eucharist; the rights of kings against the papacy.
authors.significance: The intellectual founder of Lollardy and the most consequential English heretic: his movement produced the first English Bible and permanently altered the terms of English religious debate.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his personal role in the English Bible translation is disputed.
movements: Lollardy
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Lollardy and religious dissent

authors.name: Jonathan Swift
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish satirist, pamphleteer, and cleric, Dean of St Patrick's Dublin, widely regarded as the greatest prose satirist in English.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin, Swift was educated at Trinity College Dublin and took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He worked in London as secretary to Sir William Temple and later sought Anglican preferment, aligning with the Tories as editor of the Examiner. His political and literary writings include the Battle of the Books (1704), the Bickerstaff pamphlets, and A Tale of a Tub (1704). The Drapier's Letters (1724) made him a popular hero in Ireland for resisting Wood's halfpence. His masterpiece, Gulliver's Travels, appeared in 1726, followed by the Modest Proposal (1729). In his last years a probable illness impaired his speech and memory; he died in Dublin in 1745.
authors.profile: A prose satirist and moralist whose range runs from savage irony to learned parody and invective; he wrote fiction, pamphlets, sermons, journals, and verse, always in service of unmasking pride, folly, and abuse of power.
authors.style: The plain, concrete style he prized, with short clauses and deadpan seriousness; sustained irony and personation; grotesque and anatomical imagery; and a harsh, uncompromising satiric logic.
authors.concerns: The pride and rationalisation of humankind; the abuse of learning, religion, and language; English domination of Ireland and political corruption; and the tension between reason and the passions.
authors.significance: The foremost English-language satirist and a defining prose stylist; Gulliver's Travels and the Modest Proposal became touchstones of satire, and his Irish writings shaped modern Irish political consciousness.
authors.uncertainty: The diagnosis of his later mental and physical decline is uncertain and retrospectively labelled by modern physicians; his parentage and early years in Dublin are partly known only from contested accounts.

authors.name: Joseph Addison
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English essayist, poet, dramatist, and Whig politician who, with Richard Steele, created the periodical essay and shaped Augustan letters.
authors.biography: Born at Milston in Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman, Addison was educated at the Charterhouse and at Queen's College, Oxford, where he became a fellow. Early Latin and English verse won him patronage, and he travelled on the Continent before returning to public life. With Richard Steele he wrote for the Tatler and then founded the Spectator, which established the modern periodical essay. His blank-verse tragedy Cato (1713) was widely performed and admired. He held government posts, including a secretaryship of state, as a prominent Whig, and edited the Whig journal the Guardian. He died in London in 1719.
authors.profile: Best remembered as a moral essayist and critic of taste whose Spectator papers observe manners, commerce, reading, and sociability with urbanity and restraint. He also wrote neoclassical tragedy and didactic and occasional verse.
authors.style: Clear, balanced, conversational prose in the middle style; a temperate, courteous humour; aphoristic moral reflection; and a preference for good sense, decorum, and polished plainness over extravagance.
authors.concerns: Cultivation of polite sociability and taste; the moral duties of commercial and leisure classes; religion regulated by reason; classical learning made accessible; and the refinement of public manners through letters.
authors.significance: Co-creator of the periodical essay, a form that influenced eighteenth-century prose, journalism, and the idea of a reading public; Cato was a model of neoclassical English tragedy and a lasting political emblem.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is recorded, though the precise circumstances of his Oxford fellowship and his share of authorship in the joint periodicals with Steele remain debated by scholars.

authors.name: Joseph Butler
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican bishop and the most formidable Christian apologist of the century, author of the Analogy of Religion (1736) and of the sermons on human nature.
authors.biography: Born at Wantage in Berkshire in 1692 into a Presbyterian family, he was designed for the Dissent and educated under Dissenting tutors in London before turning to the Church of England and entering Oriel College, Oxford. His published correspondence with Samuel Clarke on the foundation of virtue and moral government (1716) gave him an early philosophical reputation, and he was chosen a fellow of his college. As preacher at the Rolls Chapel he delivered the sermons on human nature, conscience and self-love printed in 1726. The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature (1736), answering the deists of his day by arguing that the course of nature is as full of mystery and difficulty as revelation, made him the acknowledged champion of his church. Preferred by Queen Caroline, he was clerk of the closet, then bishop of Bristol, dean of St Paul's and, from 1750, bishop of Durham. He died at Bath on 16 June 1752.
authors.profile: A casuist of common sense who argued from probability, analogy and the structure of the mind rather than from demonstration.
authors.style: Balanced, deliberate, heavily qualified prose; a preacher's plainness sharpened by philosopher's distinctions; patient enumeration of cases and the famous weight given to probability.
authors.concerns: Conscience as supreme authority within the mind; selfishness and benevolence; the analogies between nature and revelation; theodicy and future punishment; the historical evidences of Christianity.
authors.significance: His Analogy set the terms of British natural theology for a century, and his account of conscience and of the plurality of motives shaped British moral philosophy and theology alike.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his academy years and his Oxford degrees is imperfectly documented.

authors.name: Joseph Conrad
authors.birthplace: Berdyczów, Podolia, Russian Empire (now Berdychiv, Ukraine)
authors.nationality: Polish-British; the sea tale, the political novel and the prose of moral extremity
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski, a Polish nobleman's son who went to sea at seventeen, became a British master mariner and wrote in his third language the greatest English novels of moral isolation.
authors.biography: Born 3 December 1857 at Berdyczów in the Russian Ukraine, the son of a Polish patriot exiled for conspiracy; orphaned by 1869 and raised by his uncle, he left for Marseille in 1874, served sixteen years in the British merchant marine and the Congo (1890), and took British nationality in 1886. He published Almayer's Folly in 1895, married Jessie George in 1896, and died at Bishopsbourne, Kent, on 3 August 1924. He declined a knighthood in 1914 and was buried at Canterbury.
authors.profile: Conrad remade the English novel of the sea into a novel of the mind and the political conscience. Heart of Darkness (1899) is the central European text about empire; Lord Jim, Nostromo, The Secret Agent and Under Western Eyes invented the political novel as a study of moral failure under pressure. His technical innovations — the framed narrator, the broken chronology, the delayed disclosure — gave the twentieth-century novel its characteristic means of withholding, and his prose, written in a third language, is among the most sonorous in English.
authors.style: The framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow); the broken and retrospective chronology; a Latinate, sonorous, deliberately foreign diction; the sea and the ship as closed moral worlds; irony that refuses moral summary; the image that recurs and swells across a book.
authors.concerns: The sea, the ship, and the men who fail her; empire, the Congo, and the idea of the civilising mission; the isolated individual and moral solitude; fidelity, honour, and the test of character; political conspiracy and the police state; memory, guilt, and the impossibility of full knowledge.
authors.significance: Conrad is the greatest English novelist of the period and one of the founders of the modern novel: Heart of Darkness is the indispensable text about the European empire, Nostromo and The Secret Agent created the political novel, and his technical experiments in narration changed what fiction could do. He is the bridge from the Victorian sea story to the modern novel of consciousness and politics.

authors.name: Joseph Glanvill
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Latitudinarian clergyman, philosopher, and apologist for the new science; his Scepsis Scientifica (1665) argued a constructive scepticism and the value of experimental enquiry, and his writings on witchcraft defended the reality of spirits against atheism.
authors.biography: Born c. 1636 at Plymouth, educated at Exeter College and Lincoln College, Oxford (MA 1658), where he came under the influence of the Platonic and latitudinarian circle. A Fellow of the Royal Society (1664), he published The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), revised as Scepsis Scientifica (1665), advocating a modest, probabilist scepticism and the new experimental philosophy, and Essays on Several Important Subjects (1670). As a clergyman (vicar of Frome and later a prebendary of Worcester) he wrote latitudinarian sermons and, famously, defended belief in witchcraft and spirits (Saducismus Triumphatus, 1681, posthumous) as a bulwark against atheism. He died on 4 November 1680.
authors.profile: The 'sceptical' apologist who turned doubt to the service of the new science and of religion, arguing for a plain, probabilist, experimental approach to knowledge in an influential, readable prose.
authors.style: Clear, persuasive, latitudinarian prose; philosophical scepticism turned constructive; advocacy of the Royal Society's plain style; and a reasoned, moderate argumentative manner.
authors.concerns: Scepticism and the limits of dogmatism; the new experimental philosophy; the defence of religion and of spirits against atheism; the reform of prose style; and religious toleration and latitude.
authors.significance: Glanvill was a leading populariser of the Royal Society's ideals and of latitudinarian theology; his Scepsis Scientifica influenced Locke and the plain-style movement, and his witchcraft writings reflect the period's contested boundary between science and superstition.
authors.uncertainty: Glanvill's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through his works and Royal Society records; his witchcraft defence has been much debated by historians.

authors.name: Joseph Lancaster
authors.nationality: English (Quaker); British and trans-Atlantic monitorial / Lancasterian education movement
authors.identity: Educational pioneer and popular writer on mass schooling; the demonstrator-organizer whose name attached to the undenominational "Lancasterian" system of mutual instruction
authors.biography: Joseph Lancaster, a Friend by birth and breeding, was born on 25 November 1778 in the Borough side of Southwark, London, the son of a working Quaker family; he was educated at a Friends' school and served twice as an assistant teacher before, in 1798 and at about nineteen, he gathered a handful of poor neighbourhood children into a borrowed room to teach them reading, writing and arithmetic on a plan of his own. His method - the school divided into classes each governed by a pupil monitor, taught from cards and slates, drilled by signals, rewarded by badges and regulated by emulation, so that one master might superintend hundreds at trivial cost - filled his room and then, in 1801, larger premises in Borough Road, where his Free School became the most visited educational spectacle in Europe. Merchants, Whigs and dissenters subscribed; the Prince of Wales and King George III were shown the school, and royal and parliamentary money followed. In 1803 he published Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community, a plain, boastful, persuasive tract that ran through many editions and translations and made "Lancasterian" schooling a movement in Britain, Ireland and the United States. From 1805 he was embroiled in the priority quarrel with Andrew Bell, whose Madras monitorial plan he had learned of and adopted, and whose supporters accused him of borrowing the system while his own patrons quarrelled over the money he raised; a Royal Lancasterian Institution was formed in 1808 with royal patronage, and after his dismissal in 1814 its rivals merged their efforts into the British and Foreign School Society of 1814, which carried the Lancasterian schools forward. His public career was ruined by the mismanagement of funds and by prosecution in 1813, and he spent his last two decades promoting his system abroad: invited to New York in 1815 by De Witt Clinton and the city's friends of education, where Lancasterian schools were established and he was paid for superintendence; then to Venezuela and New Granada, where Bolívar's government employed him to organize schooling; and later in British North America, where he continued to found schools. Returning to New York, he was killed in a street accident on 23 October 1838, trampled by a horse, still lecturing and planning schools. His writings are practical - the 1803 Improvements, its enlarged editions with instructions, lessons and accounts of the school, and a stream of letters, replies and appeals - a literature of demonstration rather than of argument.
authors.profile: Lancaster was an author of one sustained subject: how to teach numbers of poor children cheaply. Improvements in Education (1803, enlarged 1805 and 1807) mixes rules, lesson plans, prices, class returns and testimonials; his later pamphlets, letters and reports are appeals to subscription and to government, and his American writings adapt the plan to public schooling. Nothing in his output is imaginative, and the rhetorical power of the books comes from the visible school.
authors.style: Direct, unlearned and urgent, in the plain Quaker idiom of fact and testimony; long enumerations of apparatus, method and cost, punctuated by personal narrative and by effusive appeals to patrons and to the reader's philanthropy. The prose is procedural - rule following rule - but the argumentative move is always demonstration: the school itself as evidence.
authors.concerns: Cheap mass instruction as the remedy for poverty and ignorance; religious neutrality in state-supported schooling and the quarrel it provoked with the established Church; emulation, order and self-government as pedagogy; the education of the poor as a public and imperial duty; the management of charitable funds and the accountability of the reformer.
authors.significance: Lancaster made universal elementary schooling seem technically and financially possible and created the first international school movement: Lancasterian societies and schools spread through Britain, Ireland, the United States, Canada and Latin America, and the British and Foreign School Society descended from his work. His visit to New York in 1815 helped prepare the American public-school idea; his fall in 1813-14 and the Bell controversy also defined the denominational politics of English education for half a century.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given in the sources checked as Southwark, while some biographies place his family's origin at Rokeby in Westmorland; the day and month of his death are variously reported (23 October and 23 December 1838), with the Dictionary of Canadian Biography giving 23 October. The name of the 1798 premises ("Borstret House" in some accounts) could not be confirmed, and the details of his 1813 prosecution, conviction and sentence are reported inconsistently.

authors.name: Joseph Priestley
authors.nationality: English Dissenter
authors.identity: Unitarian minister, chemist and controversialist who isolated the gas he called dephlogisticated air and who argued that the same free enquiry applied to matter, to government and to Christian doctrine.
authors.biography: Born at Birstfield in Yorkshire in 1733, the son of a clothier and a dissenting mother, he was intended for the ministry, studied under Dissenting tutors, learned several languages and began to preach. He held small charges in Suffolk, taught for years at the academy in Warrington, and in the early 1760s began the electrical and chemical experiments that won him election to the Royal Society in 1766. Abandoning the doctrine of the Trinity, he served at Mill Hill in Leeds, acted as librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne on a continental tour, and settled in Birmingham in 1780 as minister of New Meeting, in the company of the natural philosophers and manufacturers of the Lunar Society circle. His Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air (1774-1777) made him famous; his Institutes of Natural and Revealed Religion, his Essay on a Doctrine of Scriptural Necessity and his histories of early Christian opinion attacked corruptions he believed priests had introduced. His defence of the French Revolution, printed in 1791, brought a mob to Birmingham, and he emigrated to Pennsylvania, where he died in 1804.
authors.profile: An investigator who refused the distinction between laboratory and pulpit, and whose prose kept the plain, earnest manner of the practical dissenting preacher.
authors.style: Clear, unadorned, accumulative expository prose; experiment described in reproducible detail; polemic conducted as historical evidence and close reading of texts; a controversialist's appetite for reply.
authors.concerns: The chemistry of the air and the phlogiston question; electricity, optics and the materialism of mind; the historical corruptions of Christianity and the rejection of the Trinity; political liberty, toleration and the progress of society.
authors.significance: He was a central figure of the Enlightenment's unite of science with radical religion and politics, a founder of modern gas chemistry, and the most feared Unitarian apologist of his day.
authors.uncertainty: Priority in the discovery of oxygen, and the chronology of his religious conversion, are still argued between his partisans and historians of chemistry.

authors.name: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu
authors.nationality: Irish; the Gothic and the tale of terror
authors.identity: Novelist, short-story writer and journalist; the finest Irish writer of the supernatural tale before Stoker.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin on 28 August 1814, the son of a Church of Ireland chaplain and the grand-nephew of Richard Brinsley Sheridan. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and called to the bar in 1839, but abandoned law for journalism; he owned and edited the Dublin University Magazine and later the Dublin Evening Mail, and after the death of his wife Susanna in 1858 he withdrew from society and wrote at night. He produced the sensation novels of the 1860s and the supernatural tales collected in In a Glass Darkly (1872). He died in Dublin on 7 February 1873.
authors.profile: Le Fanu is the great Irish master of the Gothic after Maturin: his subject is the return of the past into the respectable present, and his method is the slow accumulation of documentary detail — the case notes of Dr Hesselius, the old family papers, the remembered rumour — until the supernatural becomes unavoidable. He wrote ghost stories as a scholar of the occult, with a precise sense of the psychology of fear, and his women (Carmilla, Maud Ruthyn, Madame de la Rougierre) are among the most disturbing in Victorian fiction.
authors.style: The 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor; precise domestic detail followed by an irruption of the impossible; the haunted house, the old family, the revenant; a rich, deliberate prose; an oppressive sense of place, especially the Irish midlands and Dublin.
authors.concerns: The past returning on the present; ancestral guilt, secret marriages and disputed inheritance; the supernatural as psychological truth; the vulnerability of young women in a corrupt household; the Irish landscape and its folklore; religious dread and the Church of Ireland conscience.
authors.significance: Le Fanu is the central Irish Gothic novelist between Maturin and Stoker and the most important writer of the English supernatural tale before Henry James. 'Carmilla' (1872) is the founding text of the lesbian vampire narrative and a direct influence on Dracula; Uncle Silas is one of the great novels of suspense in English, and his work was admired by Yeats, M. R. James and Elizabeth Bowen.

authors.name: Joseph Skipsey
authors.nationality: English; the miner's lyric and the working-class ballad
authors.identity: Miner, poet and self-taught scholar; the finest of the Northumbrian pitmen poets and a remarkable example of working-class literary culture.
authors.biography: Born at Percy Main, Northumberland, on 17 March 1832, the son of a pitman who was killed in a mining accident when he was five; he went down the pit at seven and worked as a coal miner until 1882, when he became a caretaker at the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre in Stratford. He taught himself to read and write, published his first volume in 1859, and was supported by subscriptions from the literary world. He died at Gateshead on 1 September 1903.
authors.profile: Skipsey wrote the lyric of the pit: his poems of the mine, of the dead miner, of the poor house and of his own self-education are among the finest working-class poems in English, and his ballads of the Northumbrian coast have a spare, hard beauty. He was a genuine poet, not a curiosity, and his best work stands comparison with Clare and with the best Victorian minor verse.
authors.style: Plain ballad stanzas and simple lyric metres; the concrete detail of the pit and the cottage; the sobriety of a self-taught craftsman; a strong elegiac note; the absence of rhetoric and self-pity.
authors.concerns: Labour and the mine; death underground; poverty and the poor house; self-education and the love of Shakespeare; the Northumbrian landscape and sea; the dignity of the working life.
authors.significance: Skipsey is the best of the English miner poets and one of the most accomplished working-class writers of the century: his poems were admired by Rossetti, Ruskin and Oscar Wilde, and they remain the essential record of the literary culture of the northern coalfield.

authors.nationality: English; the pamphlet, the speech and the literature of social reform
authors.identity: Reformer and writer; the leader of the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts and one of the great Victorian prose writers of moral outrage.
authors.biography: Born at Milfield, Northumberland, on 13 April 1828, the daughter of a cousin of the Earl of Shaftesbury; she married the clergyman George Butler in 1852 and after the death of their daughter in 1864 turned to public work. From 1869 she led the Ladies' National Association for the Repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts, campaigned against the state regulation of prostitution, and after the Acts were suspended in 1883 and repealed in 1886 she campaigned against the traffic in women in Europe. She died at Wooler, Northumberland, on 30 December 1906.
authors.profile: Butler wrote the literature of moral agitation: speeches, pamphlets, letters and a remarkable body of periodical prose in which the language of Evangelical religion is turned into a weapon against the state. Her subject is the double standard made law — the Acts subjected women to examination and registration while leaving their clients untouched — and her argument is that a law which treats a woman as a thing cannot be accepted by any Christian or any citizen.
authors.style: Prophetic, impassioned oratory in print; the personal address and the appeal to conscience; the concrete case and the direct quotation; the use of religious language against legal authority; the pamphlet as a political instrument.
authors.concerns: The state regulation of prostitution and the double standard; the traffic in women; the rights of the subject under the law; Christian conscience against state policy; the position of women in public life; the Empire and the colonial extension of the Acts.
authors.significance: Butler is one of the most important British social reformers of the nineteenth century and a major writer of Victorian polemic: her campaign repealed the Contagious Diseases Acts (1886) and her international work shaped the first international conventions against the traffic in women. Her biography of Catherine of Siena and her pamphlets are read as classics of Victorian religious feminism.

authors.nationality: English

authors.biography: Born in Kent in 1563, son of a clothier. He was educated at King's School, Southampton, and worked as a merchant and secretary, spending much of his life on the Continent in the service of the Merchant Adventurers. He died at Middelburg in the Netherlands on 28 September 1618.
authors.profile: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works — his translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine, published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608 — the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.

authors.concerns: The creation and providential order of the world; sacred poetry as the highest calling; Protestant piety in verse.
authors.significance: His Du Bartas was a schoolbook of the seventeenth century and a formative influence on the young Milton.

authors.name: Julian Grenfell
authors.nationality: British; the Georgian war lyric of Into Battle
authors.identity: Poet and soldier; the officer-poet of 'Into Battle', the most argued-over lyric of the first year of the war.
authors.biography: Born Julian Henry Francis Grenfell in London on 30 March 1888, the son of Lord Desborough; he was educated at Eton and Balliol College, Oxford, and commissioned into the Royal Dragoons in 1910. He served in France from October 1914, was wounded in May 1915, and died of his wounds on 26 May 1915, days after 'Into Battle' appeared in The Times and in the second edition of his Poems. His letters and journals were published posthumously.
authors.profile: Julian Grenfell stands at the centre of the argument about the poetry of 1914-15: 'Into Battle', with its exultant acceptance of death in the open air, was taken by his generation's critics as the type of the lyric that the later war poetry had to answer, and it remains the test case in every account of how the Georgian lyric met the trench. His letters and journals, equally vivid, are the prose companion to the poem.
authors.style: The long, swelling, sunlit line of the Georgian lyric; the exultant apostrophe to death and to the body in the open; the exact observation of the French landscape from the saddle; the rhyme that carries the line rather than closes it; the prose of the letters, equally visual and equally unguarded.
authors.concerns: The body in the open air and the joy of physical life; the English and French countryside as the ground of the lyric; war as fulfilment rather than sacrifice; the officer's eye for the landscape and the horse; the elegy that refuses to be elegiac.
authors.significance: Julian Grenfell's 'Into Battle' is the most famous and most contested lyric of the war's first year: read by his contemporaries as the voice of the happy soldier and by the later war poets as the voice that had to be answered, it fixed the terms of the argument about 1914 and remains the type of the Georgian lyric turned to war.

authors.name: Julian of Norwich
authors.nationality: English (East Anglia)
authors.identity: mystic; theologian; anchoress
authors.biography: An anchoress of St Julian's church, Norwich, who at the age of thirty and a half, during a grave illness in May 1373, received sixteen revelations ('showings') of Christ's Passion; she spent the following decades meditating on their meaning and composed two versions of her account — the Short Text and the Long Text (the latter c. 1393). Her actual name is unknown; she is called Julian from her church.
authors.profile: Author of Revelations of Divine Love (the Book of Showings), the first surviving book in English known to have been written by a woman and one of the great theological works of the Middle Ages.
authors.style: A plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; the famous image of the hazelnut and of the world's littleness held in God's hand; paradoxical, affirmative theology expressed with homely simplicity.
authors.concerns: The love of God shown in the Passion; the motherhood of God ('Jesus as mother'); sin, suffering, and the final 'all shall be well'.
authors.significance: The first woman author in English whose major work survives; her theology of divine love and of the motherhood of Christ has made her a central figure in both medieval studies and modern spirituality.
authors.uncertainty: Almost everything about her life is conjectural; her name, family, and education are unknown.

authors.name: Juliana Horatia Ewing
authors.nationality: English; the children's story and the family chronicle
authors.identity: Writer for children; one of the finest Victorian authors of the domestic children's story and a central figure of the golden age of children's literature.
authors.biography: Born Juliana Horatia Gatty at Ecclesfield, Yorkshire, on 3 August 1841, the daughter of the clergyman and naturalist Alfred Gatty and the writer Margaret Gatty. She was educated at home and wrote stories for her mother's magazine, Aunt Judy's Magazine, which she later edited. She married Alexander Ewing, an army officer, in 1867 and travelled with him to Canada, Malta and India, writing her best stories in the intervals. She died at Bath on 13 May 1885.
authors.profile: Ewing wrote the children's story as a form of moral education without moralising: her children are real, quarrelsome, funny and often unhappy, and her plots turn on the ordinary crises of family life — a lost toy, a broken promise, a move to a new country. Her Canadian and Indian stories are among the first English children's books about the imperial experience, and her fairy tales and her novel The Story of a Short Life are still read.
authors.style: Domestic realism with a child's-eye view; dialect and family idiom; gentle comedy; practical detail of toys, games and housekeeping; the family chronicle; the story shaped around a single moral problem.
authors.concerns: Childhood, obedience and self-knowledge; family life and the sibling world; emigration and the imperial family; illness and death; the natural world and the country year; the education of the affections.
authors.significance: Ewing is one of the great Victorian writers for children: her stories were admired by Ruskin and by the next generation of children's writers, and her Canadian and Indian tales are founding texts of the imperial children's book. Aunt Judy's Magazine, which she edited, was one of the most important nurseries of Victorian children's literature.

authors.name: Kate Chopin
authors.nationality: American; the local-colour sketch and the novel of female awakening
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of The Awakening and the finest American writer of Louisiana Creole life.
authors.biography: Born Katherine O'Flaherty in St Louis on 8 February 1850, the daughter of an Irish merchant and a French-Creole mother; she was educated at the Sacred Heart convent and married Oscar Chopin, a cotton factor, in 1870, moving to New Orleans and then to a plantation in Natchitoches Parish. Widowed in 1882, she returned to St Louis and began writing in 1889. Bayou Folk (1894) and A Night in Acadie (1897) made her a successful local colourist; The Awakening (1899) was condemned and she wrote little afterwards. She died in St Louis on 22 August 1904.
authors.profile: Chopin wrote the American short story of sexual and social truth: her Louisiana stories are exact, unsentimental and often very funny about the arrangements between men and women, and The Awakening is the first American novel to treat a woman's sexual and spiritual awakening as its central subject without either condemning or sentimentalising it. Her prose is quiet, exact and entirely free of moralising, which is why it seemed so dangerous.
authors.style: Cool, exact, sensory prose; the withheld judgment; the Creole dialect of the Louisiana stories; the short lyric epiphany; the refusal of a moral conclusion; the symbolism of sea, sleep and music.
authors.concerns: Marriage and the position of women; female desire and selfhood; Creole and Cajun Louisiana and its racial order; motherhood as an institution rather than an instinct; suicide and freedom; the artist and the woman.
authors.significance: Chopin is the central American woman novelist of the 1890s and the author of the founding American novel of female emancipation: The Awakening was condemned in 1899 and rediscovered in the 1960s, and it is now the key text of American feminist literary criticism and one of the great novels of the century.

authors.biography: Born Kate O'Brien at Limerick on 23 July 1897; she worked as a governess and a journalist before Without My Cloak (1931) won the James Tait Black prize. authors.style: The prose of the family chronicle and the censored conscience; the Limerick middle class and the convent; the woman's desire stated plainly against the church and the state; the return to Ireland as the novel's occasion; the dialogue of the drawing room and the chapel.

authors.name: Katherine Anne Porter
authors.nationality: American; the short story as a perfected form and the Southern family of memory
authors.identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest American short-story writer of the period, the author of Flowering Judas and Ship of Fools.
authors.biography: Born Callie Russell Porter at Indian Creek, Texas, on 15 May 1890; she was raised by her grandmother in Texas and Louisiana, married young and divorced, worked as a journalist in Chicago, Denver and Mexico, and published her first stories in the 1920s. Flowering Judas appeared in 1930, Pale Horse, Pale Rider in 1939, The Leaning Tower in 1944 and the novel Ship of Fools in 1962, which became a best-seller and a film. She won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award in 1966 and died in Silver Spring, Maryland, on 18 September 1980.
authors.profile: Porter wrote the most perfectly finished American short stories of the period: 'Flowering Judas', 'The Jilting of Granny Weatherall', 'Noon Wine' and 'Pale Horse, Pale Rider' are the finest stories in American literature between Anderson and Cheever, and their compression, their exactness of detail and their moral seriousness made the story a form for grown-up art. Ship of Fools is the great American novel of the 1930s' political shipwreck.
authors.style: The story built on a single scene and a single revelation; the exact material detail (the food, the clothes, the room); the free indirect style that enters a mind without breaking; the retrospective frame of memory; the unemphatic, perfectly weighted ending.
authors.concerns: Memory and the lost Southern childhood; the family and the grandmother; love, betrayal and the jilting; illness, death and the influenza epidemic; Mexico and the revolutionary expatriate; the ship, the voyage and the political exile.
authors.significance: Porter wrote the finest American short stories of the period and the great American novel of the 1930s: Flowering Judas and Pale Horse, Pale Rider set the standard for the modern story, her childhood stories of Texas and Louisiana preserve a lost world, and Ship of Fools is a permanent record of the decade's political despair.

authors.name: Katherine Mansfield
authors.nationality: New Zealand-British; the modernist short story and the epiphany of the ordinary
authors.identity: Short-story writer; the finest English-language short-story writer of the period, the inventor of the modern story of the moment, and the central woman writer of English modernism after Woolf.
authors.biography: Born Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp in Wellington, New Zealand, on 14 October 1888 into a wealthy colonial family; she came to London in 1903, returned to New Zealand in 1906, and left for good in 1908. She married George Bowden (1909), met John Middleton Murry (1911), published In a German Pension (1911) and, after her brother Leslie's death in the war, the stories of Prelude (1918), Bliss (1920) and The Garden Party (1922). Tuberculosis was diagnosed in 1917; she died at Fontainebleau on 9 January 1923, aged thirty-four.
authors.profile: Mansfield made the modern short story: 'Prelude', 'The Daughters of the Late Colonel', 'At the Bay', 'The Garden Party' and 'The Fly' gave English prose a new compression and a new way of rendering the moment of perception. Her stories dissolve plot into the texture of ordinary life, and her use of the shifting point of view and the withheld conclusion is the model for the twentieth-century story. She is, with Woolf and Richardson, the central woman modernist of English prose.
authors.style: The story without a plot: a moment of perception, a family scene, a shift of light; the multiple point of view and the free indirect style; the exact rendering of a child's or a servant's consciousness; the detail that carries the emotion; the ending that simply closes.
authors.concerns: Childhood, the family and the New Zealand of her memory; the woman's life, marriage and solitude; illness, the sanatorium and death; the servant and the class below stairs; the ordinary moment and its hidden violence; exile and the lost home.
authors.significance: Mansfield is the greatest English-language short-story writer of the period and the central innovator of the modern story: 'Prelude', 'At the Bay' and 'The Garden Party' changed what a short story could do, her technique of the epiphany influenced every subsequent practitioner, and her letters and journals are among the finest autobiographical writing of the century.

authors.name: Katherine Philips
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and translator, the first Englishwoman to achieve a significant public literary reputation and to have a play performed on the professional stage; celebrated as 'the Matchless Orinda' for her verse on female friendship and royalist loyalty.
authors.biography: Born c. 1631–32 in London, daughter of a merchant; married the much older Philip Philips of Cardigan (1647) and lived at her estate of Owenia (Cardigan). There she formed a 'Society of Friendship', giving its members pastoral names (herself 'Orinda'), and wrote poems of idealised female friendship, love, and royalist politics. During the Interregnum she translated Corneille's Pompey and Horace, the first plays by a woman performed on the English public stage (1663). An unauthorised edition of her Poems appeared in 1664; she died of smallpox in London on 22 June 1664, and her collected Poems was published posthumously in 1667 to great acclaim.
authors.profile: The poet of virtuous female friendship and Cavalier loyalty, whose refined, platonic verse won her an unprecedented public reputation for a woman writer and made her a model for later women poets.
authors.style: Polished couplets and songs; a chaste, platonic idealism; the rhetoric of friendship; and translations of French neoclassical drama in vigorous verse.
authors.concerns: Female friendship and virtue; retirement and the country life; royalist politics; the role of the woman writer; and the idealisation of platonic love.
authors.significance: Philips was the first Englishwoman to gain wide literary fame, to have her work printed (though against her wishes) and plays staged, and to be memorialised by Dryden and others as 'the Matchless Orinda' — a founding figure of women's professional authorship.
authors.uncertainty: Philips's birth year is uncertain (1631 or 1632); the 1664 Poems was pirated and she disowned it, so the authoritative canon rests on the 1667 edition.

authors.name: Kenneth Grahame
authors.nationality: Scottish-English; the animal fantasy and the essay of childhood
authors.identity: Writer; the author of The Wind in the Willows and of the finest Victorian essays on childhood.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh on 8 March 1859; his mother died when he was five and he was brought up by his grandmother at Cookham Dean in Berkshire, the river landscape of his books. He could not afford Oxford and worked from 1879 at the Bank of England, rising to secretary in 1898. He published Pagan Papers (1893), The Golden Age (1895) and Dream Days (1898), and The Wind in the Willows in 1908. He retired from the Bank in 1908, and died at Pangbourne on 6 July 1932.
authors.profile: Grahame wrote the English river as a paradise: The Wind in the Willows is at once a children's book, an elegy for the Thames landscape and a comedy of English social types — Mole the suburban clerk, Rat the river poet, Toad the landed egotist, Badger the country magistrate. His earlier essays on childhood, narrated by children who have outgrown the nursery, are the most delicate English writing of the 1890s on the loss of the child's world.
authors.style: Lyrical descriptive prose; gentle irony and self-mockery; the animal fable as social comedy; the rhythm of the seasons and the river; dialogue that makes character through idiom and catch-phrase.
authors.concerns: The English landscape and the river; friendship and contentment; the loss of childhood; class and the English gentleman; the machine and the modern world (Toad's motor-car); escape and homecoming.
authors.significance: The Wind in the Willows is one of the permanent books of English childhood and one of the great English pastoral idylls; it has been read as a parable of English social life, of the loss of Eden and of the friendship of men, and it has never gone out of print. Grahame's essays on childhood are the finest prose of the aesthetic 1890s.

authors.name: Lady Caroline Lamb
authors.birthplace: London, in the Ponsonby circle of great Whig families; her father was Frederick Ponsonby, third earl of Bessborough, her mother Lady Henrietta Frances Spencer, daughter of John, first earl of Spencer, and her aunt by her mother's side Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire
authors.nationality: English; the society novel and roman a clef of the late Regency and its Byronic Gothic offshoot, written by an aristocratic salonnière who also moved in the Anglo-Irish society and politics of her father's and her husband's families
authors.identity: Novelist and occasional verse-writer of the Regency salons, remembered above all as the author of Glenarvon and as the woman who supplied the phrase and the scandal by which posterity has read Byron
authors.biography: Caroline Ponsonby, afterwards Lady Caroline Lamb, was born on 13 November 1785, the only daughter of Frederick Ponsonby, third earl of Bessborough, by Lady Henrietta Frances Spencer, younger daughter of John, first earl of Spencer; known till 1793 as the Honourable Caroline Ponsonby. Taken to Italy at the age of three and kept there six years, she was on her return educated with her cousins at Devonshire House and then entrusted to her grandmother Lady Spencer, who was so alarmed at her eccentricities that she consulted a physician about her state of mind. On 3 June 1805 she married the Honourable William Lamb, afterwards second Viscount Melbourne and prime minister; of their children only George Augustus Frederick Lamb, born in 1807, survived, and he grew up a hopeless invalid. Byron's introduction in 1812 produced the passionate infatuation entered in her diary as 'mad, bad, and dangerous to know', and his rupture with her in 1813 made her conduct so ungovernable that her husband reluctantly prepared a deed of separation; while the legal instruments were being made ready she wrote and sent to the press 'Glenarvon', which appeared anonymously in three volumes in 1816, weeks after Byron left England. A sudden reconciliation on the day fixed for signing the deed postponed, but did not prevent, a formal separation in 1825, and her caricatures of the ton had already cost her her vouchers at Almack's. In 1819 she published anonymously the Byron imitation 'A New Canto' and canvassed the Westminster electors for her brother-in-law George Lamb; 'Graham Hamilton', sent to Colburn in 1820 with an earnest injunction not to name the author, appeared anonymously in two volumes in 1822, and 'Ada Reis; a Tale' and 'Penruddock' followed in 1823. Meeting Byron's funeral procession in July 1824 shook her afresh, and she lived chiefly at Brocket with her father-in-law and her son. She died at Melbourne House, Whitehall, on 26 January 1828, in her forty-third year and in her husband's presence, and was buried at Hatfield, having predeceased the peerage by which her name is commonly recorded.
authors.profile: Her work is almost wholly fiction and occasional verse. 'Glenarvon: A Tale' (anon., 3 vols., 1816), reprinted in one volume in 1865 as 'The Fatal Passion', is a tale of Irish rebellion and fashionable society which carries the first Byronic hero outside Byron's own poems and a self-portrait of its author as lady Adeline; the narrative poem 'A New Canto' (anon., 1819) answers 'Don Juan' in its own free manner; 'Graham Hamilton' (anon., 2 vols., 1822), whose design was said to have been suggested by Ugo Foscolo, and 'Ada Reis; a Tale' (anon., 3 vols., 1823; Paris, 1824) develop the sentimental and religious problem-novel, while 'Penruddock' (1823) turns to provincial and political life. She also wrote poetry for the literary annuals, several of her pieces being set to music by Isaac Nathan, who republished some of her verses with letters and reminiscences in 1829. Eleven of her letters survive in Lady Morgan's 'Memoirs' and seven in Paul's 'William Godwin' (1876), and her novels and poems were collected and edited by Leigh Wetherall Dickson and Paul Douglass (Pickering and Chatto, 2009).
authors.style: Those who praised her conversation - 'full of wild originality', combining 'great and sudden contrasts' - found the same quality in her prose: rapid, rhapsodical and personal rather than crafted. The 'Monthly Review' called 'A New Canto' 'a rhapsody from beginning to end', and 'Glenarvon', which owed its brief success to its caricature portrait of Byron, was dismissed by most critics as pulp fiction while Goethe thought it worthy of serious consideration; its strength is the recognition scene and the self-dramatising heroine, its weakness unlocked emotion and a plot carried by scandal. The later fiction is more disciplined and moralised, written under Foscolo's admonition that women 'cannot afford to shock', and treats Ireland, Italy and the Catholic question as picturesque sympathy rather than argument. Salon dialogue, letter and diary aphorism remain her proper medium.
authors.concerns: Celebrity and its price; the power of a woman's self-portrayal in print when every character she draws is recognised; the guilt and fascination of Anglo-Irish aristocratic rule, worked out in Glenarvon's rebellion and in her own part in her husband's Irish connection; the Byronic temperament admired and reviled in the same breath; the sexual double standard of fashionable society, which excluded her after 1816 while consuming her book; and in the later novels religious faith, superstition, education and the fate of the erring woman.
authors.significance: She fixed one of the enduring images of Byron and, through 'Glenarvon', produced the first Byronic novel outside his own verse and an early and much-cited example of Irish Gothic fiction, while her roman a clef practice and her Almack's downfall made her the permanent emblem of Regency scandal. Her notoriety intersected the politics of her husband's career, and Lord Lytton, who fell briefly under her spell, used her as the original of Mrs Felix Lorraine in 'Vivian Grey' and of other of his heroines. Her diaries, letters and novels are standard sources for Byron and for the Holland House set, and modern scholarship, helped by the 2009 collected edition, has restored her from Byron anecdote to a novelist of the post-Waterloo salon and of the Irish question.
authors.uncertainty: The day of her birth is given by the Dictionary of National Biography and most modern accounts as 13 November 1785 but is sometimes stated as 13 January, and the day of her death variously as 25 and 26 January 1828; 'Penruddock' (1823) is attested by her modern biographer and by the collected edition but is absent from the older biographical accounts checked here; her reported attachment to the Duke of Wellington after Waterloo rests on modern biography alone; and the degree of mental illness, alcohol and laudanum dependence in her last years is judged differently by every biographer.
