authors.name: Lady Florence Dixie
authors.nationality: Scottish; the travel narrative, the war despatch and the feminist utopia
authors.identity: Traveller, war correspondent and feminist; the author of Across Patagonia and the suffrage utopia Gloriana.
authors.biography: Born Florence Caroline Douglas at Cummertrees, Dumfriesshire, on 24 May 1855, the daughter of the eighth Marquess of Queensberry and the twin sister of Lord James Douglas; after her father's death in 1858 her mother became a Roman Catholic and took the youngest children to France. She married Sir Alexander Beaumont Churchill Dixie in 1875, published the dramatic tragedy Abel Avenged in 1877, rode across southern Patagonia with her husband, two of her brothers and Julius Beerbohm in 1878-79 and described the journey in Across Patagonia (1880). In 1881 she reported the First Boer War and the aftermath of the Zulu War for the Morning Post and interviewed the captive Cetshwayo, writing In the Land of Misfortune (1882). She published the feminist utopia Gloriana (1890) and two Patagonian books for children, became president of the British Ladies' Football Club in 1895, and died of diphtheria at Glen Stuart, Dumfriesshire, on 7 November 1905.
authors.profile: Lady Florence Dixie was one of the most outspoken aristocratic feminists of the late Victorian press: Across Patagonia presented a woman riding, hunting and enduring on equal terms with the men of her party, her Morning Post despatches from South Africa made her one of the first women war correspondents, and Gloriana imagined a woman who wins the vote for her sex by passing as a man and governing as Prime Minister.
authors.style: The first-person narrative of travel, hunting and hardship in a wild landscape; the heroine who equals or outdoes the men around her; the polemical preface and the political fable; the melodramatic plot of disguise, trial and rescue; the direct appeal to the reader on behalf of women.
authors.concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; education and the professions opened to both sexes; the saddle, the hunting field and the open country; the Zulu kingdom and the war correspondent's conscience; Irish and Scottish Home Rule.
authors.significance: Lady Florence Dixie was one of the most outspoken aristocratic feminists of the late Victorian press: Across Patagonia, her South African despatches and the suffrage utopia Gloriana made her travel, her journalism and her fiction a single argument for the equality of the sexes.

authors.name: Lady Gregory
authors.nationality: Irish; the folk chronicle, the one-act comedy and the institutional making of the Abbey Theatre
authors.identity: Dramatist, folklorist and theatre director; the co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, the collector of Irish folklore and the author of some forty plays.
authors.biography: Born Isabella Augusta Persse at Roxborough, County Galway, on 15 March 1852; she married Sir William Gregory in 1880, was widowed in 1892, and met Yeats in 1896; with him and Edward Martyn she founded the Irish Literary Theatre (1899) and the Abbey Theatre (1904), for which she wrote comedies, tragedies and translations. Her collections — A Book of Saints and Wonders (1906), Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland (1920), Gods and Fighting Men (1904) — preserve the folk tradition, and her journals and memoirs are a central record of the revival. She died at Coole Park on 22 May 1932.
authors.profile: Lady Gregory is the practical founder of the Irish national theatre and the preserve of its folklore: without her money, her management and her plays there would have been no Abbey Theatre. Her one-act comedies (Spreading the News, The Rising of the Moon, The Workhouse Ward) are the finest of their kind in English, Gods and Fighting Men is the great popular compendium of Irish myth, and her translations of the Cuchulain cycle gave Yeats his material.
authors.style: The one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close; the Anglo-Irish dialect written phonetically; the folk tale transcribed and shaped for the stage; the plain prose of the collector who records rather than embellishes.
authors.concerns: Ireland and the Irish peasantry; the folklore, the fairies and the saints; the landlord and the tenant; the police, the prison and the law; the workhouse and the emigrant ship; the national past and the Cuchulain cycle.
authors.significance: Lady Gregory is the co-founder and practical manager of the Abbey Theatre and the period's great collector of Irish folklore: she wrote some forty plays, preserved the myths in Gods and Fighting Men, and her journals are the indispensable record of the revival. Without her there would be no Irish national theatre.

authors.name: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Aristocratic letter-writer and poet, celebrated for her Turkish Embassy Letters and her witty, independent verse.
authors.biography: Born Lady Mary Pierrepont on 15 May 1689 at Holme Pierrepont in Nottinghamshire, the daughter of Evelyn Pierrepont, later Duke of Kingston, she was largely self-educated and began writing verse and letters early. She eloped in 1712 to Edward Wortley Montagu, and accompanied him to Constantinople when he was ambassador, her account of that journey forming the basis of the letters published after her death. She championed smallpox inoculation in England, introducing the practice from the East. A prominent figure in Augustan society and letters, she died in London on 21 August 1762.
authors.profile: A writer of letters, occasional verse, and prose whose best-known work, the Turkish Embassy Letters, blends travel observation with wit and a critical eye on gender and culture, while her poems engage Augustan debate.
authors.style: Brisk, colloquial, sharply observant epistolary prose; witty and pointed heroic-couplet verse; a satirical, conversational tone; and an easy mixture of the personal and the polemical.
authors.concerns: Gender and the condition of women; custom and cultural comparison; learning versus fashionable prejudice; medicine and the body; and reputation and independence.
authors.significance: One of the most distinguished women writers of the Augustan age, remembered for her travel letters and for introducing smallpox inoculation to England, and a central figure in the literary and social circles of her time.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is well documented; the chief scholarly caution concerns the posthumous editing of the Turkish Embassy Letters and the precise dating and authority of some poems.

authors.biography: Born in 1587, eldest daughter of Robert Sidney of Penshurst and niece of Sir Philip Sidney and of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke. In 1604 she married Sir Robert Wroth of Loughton, Essex, who died in 1614 leaving her with debts and a small child. Her long affair with her cousin William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, was the scandal behind her fiction. She died about 1651 or 1653.
authors.profile: The Countess of Montgomery's Urania (1621) — the first prose romance by an Englishwoman, a continuation of her uncle's Arcadia — with its appended sonnet sequence Pamphilia to Amphilanthus, and the pastoral closet drama Love's Victory (c. 1620, circulated in manuscript).
authors.style: A Sidneyan inheritance — pastoral romance, interlaced plots, and sonnets of constancy — transformed by a woman's perspective on love's costs to women.
authors.concerns: Female constancy and male inconstancy; the politics of marriage; women's authorship and its risks.
authors.significance: The first Englishwoman to write a prose romance and a sonnet sequence; the outcry over Urania's court portraits shows the reach of her fiction.

authors.name: Langston Hughes
authors.nationality: American; the blues poem, the Harlem Renaissance lyric and the satire of the colour line
authors.identity: Poet, novelist, playwright and columnist; the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the first American to make the blues a literary form, and the most widely read Black writer of the century.
authors.biography: Born James Mercer Langston Hughes in Joplin, Missouri, on 1 February 1902; he was raised by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas, and his mother in Illinois and Ohio, spent a year at Columbia, worked as a ship's cook and a busboy, and was 'discovered' in a Washington restaurant by Vachel Lindsay in 1925. The Weary Blues appeared in 1926 and Fine Clothes to the Jew in 1927; he wrote the novel Not Without Laughter (1930), the play Mulatto (1935), the Jesse B. Semple stories and the Montage of a Dream Deferred (1951). He died in New York on 22 May 1967.
authors.profile: Hughes is the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the first American poet to make the blues and jazz a literary form: The Weary Blues put the blues on the printed page, 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'I, Too' and 'Harlem' are among the most quoted American poems, and his Jesse B. Semple columns made a Black vernacular voice a national institution. He wrote for the whole race, not for the salon, and that is the source of his permanence.
authors.style: The blues stanza and the jazz line; the plain vernacular speech of Harlem; the repetition-with-variation of the blues form; the short ironic lyric with a withheld pain; the comic monologue (Simple); the poem that asks a question instead of making a statement.
authors.concerns: Race, the colour line and the New Negro; Harlem and the Great Migration; the blues, jazz and the pleasure economy; the dream deferred and the American promise; the working Black man and the comic survivor (Semple); Africa, the South and the ancestral past.
authors.significance: Hughes is the central African American poet of the century and the founding figure of the Harlem Renaissance in verse: he made the blues a literary form, wrote the period's most quoted poems of Black America, created the Jesse B. Semple voice, and maintained a public Black poetry for four decades when almost no one else did.

authors.name: Laurence Sterne
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish-born Anglican clergyman and novelist, an experimental comic writer whose Tristram Shandy and A Sentimental Journey redefined narrative form.
authors.biography: Born on 24 November 1713 at Clonmel in Ireland into an Anglo-Irish military family, he was educated at Cambridge and took orders in the Church of England, settling as a curate in Yorkshire. In mid-life he published The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman (begun 1759 and completed over the following years), which made his name, followed by A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy (1768) and sermons and other writings. He traveled widely in Europe and was a sought-after figure in London literary society. He died in London on 18 March 1768.
authors.profile: A comic and experimental moralist whose fiction digresses endlessly, plays with the reader, and turns the telling of a life into an exploration of time, memory, and feeling, anticipating modern narrative techniques.
authors.style: Digressive, self-reflexive narration; typographic experimentation (blank pages, marbled pages, dashes); associative and comic logic; abrupt shifts between humor and sentiment; and a conversational, reader-addressing voice.
authors.concerns: The nature of time, memory, and selfhood; the difficulty of telling a story; sentiment and fellow-feeling; mortality; learning and its absurdities; and the workings of the mind through association.
authors.significance: A radical innovator in prose fiction, whose experiments in form make him a forerunner of modernist and postmodern narrative and a central figure in the sentimental tradition of the eighteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The outline of Sterne's life is well attested, but the chronology of the composition and publication of individual volumes of Tristram Shandy, and details of some relationships, remain debated.

authors.name: Leigh Hunt
authors.nationality: English; poet, essayist, editor, and critic of the Romantic period, the manager and chief theorist of the Hunt circle
authors.identity: Essayist and editor first, poet next: the conductor of the Examiner and the Indicator whose prose, criticism, and personal patronage made possible much of the verse of 1814-1822, and whose own romantic narratives and lyrical sketches were read as a manifesto of a poetry free from the neoclassical school.
authors.biography: Born 19 October 1784 in London, son of a Philadelphia-born lawyer of Puritan stock who had been disinherited for his Loyalism and of an English mother, he was put to work young and became a clerk in the Receiver General's office before turning to journalism. With his younger brother John he founded the Examiner in 1808, and through the Reflector (1810-11) and the weekly Indicator he built the paper into the organ of a literary as well as a political party. His prosecution for libel on the Prince Regent in 1812 and his two-year imprisonment made him a liberal martyr and drew to him Byron, Shelley, Keats, Hazlitt, and Reynolds; in prison and after it he wrote 'The Story of Rimini' (1816), which Hunt's circle took as the model of a new simplicity drawn from Boccaccio and the old English tales. He introduced Keats to Shelley, published the sonnets of 1816-17, and lent his name and his press to the poetry which the Quarterly and Edinburgh reviews afterwards grouped as the 'cockney school'. Invited by Byron to join the projected 'Liberal', he sailed for Italy in 1821, edited the magazine through its three numbers with Byron's poems and Shelley's, and remained abroad until 1825, enduring the collapse of the enterprise and the deaths and quarrels it had gathered. Back in London he revived his editorial career (the London Journal of 1828), published his controversial 'Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries' (1828), and wrote on drama, poetry, and the arts until his death on 28 August 1859; his 'Autobiography', published in 1850-56, became a primary document of the period he had helped to make.
authors.profile: His work divides into the light narrative and descriptive verse ('The Feast of the Poets', 'Rimini', the sonnets and sketches of the Indicator), the familiar prose of the periodical essay and of criticism on poetry and the theatre, and the memoir and biographical writing of the later years. He was also, practically, an editor and manager: the Examiner's literary page, the Indicator's papers on the old poets, and the 'Liberal' are literary works in the collective sense, and their policy of publishing young and unpopular verse shaped the period's canon.
authors.style: A prose of ease, intimacy, and apparent unpremeditation - short sentences, parentheses, the tone of a friend talking in a room - concealing a deliberate theory of 'spontaneity' and of the 'love of beauty for its own sake'. His verse prefers the easy narrative stanza, the familiar sonnet, and the descriptive sketch, with an Italian and Elizabethan secondhand music and a fondness for the tale of illicit tenderness; his criticism quotes rather than argues.
authors.concerns: The emancipation of poetry from neoclassical decorum and from party patronage; the literary public sphere and its economics of reviews and magazines; political libel and the price of a free press; Italian and old English literature as a school of romantic feeling; the fellowship of poets against the 'thundering' school; the biography and gossip of literary fame as evidence of character; sensibility and its enjoyment, defended against the charge of coarseness.
authors.significance: No single figure did more to create the institutional conditions of the second generation of English Romanticism: he discovered or advertised Keats, published and defended Shelley, supplied Byron with the tale of Rimini and with the Liberal, and with Hazlitt and Lamb defined the familiar critic's voice for the century's periodical writing. His imprisonment, the reviews' war on the 'cockney school', and the ruin of the Liberal enterprise are also the best documented case of politics and personality acting on Romantic literary reputation.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of his own responsibility for the Examiner's most provocative passages, and the fairness of his later charges against Byron and against Moore's editing of Byron, are contested; his account of his own precedence in the 'Rimini' quarrel and in the discovery of Keats must be read against the records of the reviews and of his brothers' papers.

authors.name: Leslie Stephen
authors.nationality: English; criticism, biography and the history of ideas
authors.identity: Critic, biographer and mountaineer; the first editor of the Dictionary of National Biography and the greatest Victorian critic of the eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born in London on 28 November 1832, the son of the Under-Secretary of the Colonial Office; he was educated at Eton and Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and in 1862 was ordained. He lost his faith and left the church in 1875, and supported himself by journalism and scholarship: he was editor of the Cornhill Magazine (1871-82) and of the Dictionary of National Biography (1882-91), for which he wrote 378 lives. He married Harriet Marion Thackeray in 1867 and, after her death, Julia Jackson Duckworth in 1878, becoming the father of Vanessa Bell and Virginia Woolf. He died in Kensington on 22 February 1904.
authors.profile: Stephen is the great Victorian critic of the English eighteenth century and the founder of the modern biographical dictionary. His History of English Thought in the Eighteenth Century (1876) is a systematic account of the deist controversy and the moral philosophy of the age; his Hours in a Library, The English Utilitarians and the essays on Pope, Johnson and Swift are the foundation of the scholarly criticism of Augustan literature, and his agnostic 'Essays on Freethinking and Plainspeaking' made him the most formidable of Victorian rationalists.
authors.style: The plain, exact critical prose; the biographical reconstruction of a writer's mind; the systematic history of ideas; the mountaineering essay; the short life in the Dictionary; irony without malice.
authors.concerns: The history of ideas and the growth of rationalism; eighteenth-century literature and society; agnosticism and the ethics of unbelief; biography as a form of criticism; the Alps and the physical life; the education of women.
authors.significance: Stephen founded the Dictionary of National Biography and wrote the founding modern study of English eighteenth-century thought: he is the ancestor of the scholarly biography and of the history of ideas in England, and his agnostic essays are the classic statement of Victorian unbelief as a moral position.

authors.name: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
authors.nationality: English; the metropolitan periodical and literary-annual public of the later Romantic period, and the verse romance and short lyric of the 1820s and 1830s
authors.identity: Poet, critic and novelist: the first English woman of letters to make a complete living by periodical verse and review, the controlling presence in the poetical pages of a leading weekly paper for well over a decade, and the creator of the persona of the gifted, wounded and professional woman poet that the annuals made canonical.
authors.biography: Landon was born at Hans Place in Chelsea on 14 August 1802, the daughter of John Landon, at that time a partner in an army agency house and a traveller in his youth to Africa and the West Indies, and of Catherine Jane Bishop; a precocious child, she was educated at home and by her own reading rather than by any regular schooling, and began to publish verse in the magazines about 1820. Her contributions to a widely circulated weekly literary paper, and above all the poetical notices and reviews which she wrote over her initials, gave her at once a name and a critical power unusual for a woman of her years; the first volume, issued in 1821 under her own name rather than over initials, announced the situations of her whole career, and the volume of 1824, named for its long poem on the Italian singer-poetess, made her famous. Her father's death in 1824 left the family relatively poor and she became its support, a responsibility she carried for the rest of her life; about the end of the decade losses sustained by the household through the impositions of an unscrupulous man, and the public trial that followed, exposed her to a gossip about her judgement and her conduct that never entirely subsided. Through the later 1820s and the 1830s she remained the annuals' most constant and most imitated poet, publishing a series of verse romances of which The Golden Violet and The Venetian Bracelet are examples, and turning increasingly to prose fiction, with three novels of romance and historical matter appearing between the early and the late 1830s, alongside a large quantity of magazine verse and review. Her position as a woman who judged other people's poetry, and who was paid for it, made her a target of personal attack in the periodical press of the 1830s, and soon after the volume of 1829 the house that had published her earlier romances closed its engagement with her; the reading of her verse as confession, which her market encouraged, turned her private affiliations and her broken engagements into public knowledge. In 1837, in her thirty-fifth year, she married George Maclean, a Scotsman in the service of the British settlement on the Gold Coast of West Africa, and she quitted England for that station in the summer of 1838. She died at Cape Coast Castle on 15 October 1838, aged thirty-six, having been in Africa only a few months, and was buried at the castle; an empty phial of prussic acid was found with her, and the verdict of the inquest, which took note of the medicine she had been taking, returned accidental self-poisoning, while report has never stopped arguing the case. Her collected verse appeared after her death with a memoir of her life, and her name stayed before readers through the middle decades of the century before a long eclipse from which modern scholarship and modern editions have brought her back.
authors.profile: Her work divides between the long verse romance in stanzas, drawing on chivalric, Italian and legendary matter and interrupted by personal comment; the short lyric and sonnet-like piece written for the annual and often in company with an engraving; the critical and descriptive prose on poetry and on the literature of the day; and the three novels of romance and historical fiction of the later years. She left also a large body of magazine verse, much of it first printed over her initials and gathered afterwards into volumes, and a correspondence which is a record of the professional writer's life. The characteristic structure is a situation of pledged and misread feeling worked out in a token or an emblem, and the characteristic persona is the woman of genius whose gift is at once her fame and her exposure.
authors.style: A stanzic iambic measure of rapid declamatory movement, much given to triple time, refrained closings and an enjambed talky ease, plainly tuned for recitation; compressed direct address and apostrophe in the shorter lyrics; an emblematic method in which a bracelet, a veil, a flower or a picture carries the argument and turns against the person who wears it; historical and local colour used as the scenery of feeling rather than as antiquarian display; and a sustained irony, usually unintended by its first readers, between the confessional voice and the commercial occasion that required it.
authors.concerns: The woman artist's vocation and its price; fame purchased by self-exposure; constancy, desertion and jealousy as social rather than private facts; the symbol that pledges love and then accuses; the inheritance of romance and chivalry converted into a grammar of feminine feeling; poverty, dependence and the economics of professional authorship for a woman with a family to maintain; exile, travel and the European south; early death and the mourning of poets.
authors.significance: She defined the possibility of a full-time women's literary career in the periodical market, at once the annuals' typical contributor and their most powerful editor of taste, and she supplied the nineteenth century with its most influential image of the woman poet as popular artist and victim, a figure reworked by later novelists and poets. Her practice fixed the short lyric of the keepsake as a serious form and made the emblematic token a lasting device of gift-book writing. Her death became at once a scandal and a literary event, and the recovery of her work by modern scholarship has made her central to the history of Romantic authorship, of women's professional writing and of the transatlantic book trade.
authors.uncertainty: The circumstances of her death remain genuinely disputed: the phial of prussic acid, the medicine she had been prescribed for illness, the verdict of accidental self-poisoning, the rumours of deliberate suicide and of despair over her marriage, and the possible share of other parties cannot be resolved on the surviving evidence, and the account given by her husband and by her friends is necessarily interested. Her childhood residences and the extent of her formal education are imperfectly recorded; the details of the family's financial losses in the later 1820s and of the trial that followed are reported with large inconsistencies; the story of her broken engagements rests on letters and on later memoir; and the division between her public persona and her private feelings, which her contemporaries read as one text, is the permanent difficulty of her biography.

authors.name: Lewis Carroll
authors.nationality: English; Victorian children's literature, nonsense and logic
authors.identity: Writer, logician, mathematician and photographer, born Charles Lutwidge Dodgson; the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and the greatest English writer of literary nonsense.
authors.biography: Born at Daresbury on 27 January 1832, son of a clergyman; educated at Rugby and Christ Church, Oxford, where he matriculated in 1851, became a student (fellow) in 1852 and remained until his death, lecturing in mathematics from 1855 to 1881. He was ordained deacon in 1861 and never proceeded to the priesthood. The Alice stories began as a tale told on 4 July 1862 to Alice Liddell and her sisters during a river excursion; Alice's Adventures in Wonderland appeared in 1865 with Tenniel's illustrations and Through the Looking-Glass in 1871. The Hunting of the Snark (1876), Sylvie and Bruno (1889, 1893) and the mathematical and logical works followed, under his own name. He died at Guildford on 14 January 1898.
authors.profile: Carroll made nonsense a serious literary form: the Alice books are built on the logic of dreams and of language, on puns that turn on the ambiguity of words, on parodies of the Victorian didactic poem, and on a mathematics of inverted rules. He is the first writer for children to treat his reader as an intellectual equal, and his nonsense is not decoration but argument — the reductio ad absurdum of Victorian pedagogy, of the legal system (the Knave's trial), of the schoolroom and the nursery. The later Sylvie and Bruno attempts a fairy tale with a mathematical and theological structure.
authors.style: Logical paradox, pun and wordplay; parody of the moralising children's poem; the dream frame and the abrupt transition; invented words (the portmanteau); dialogue driven by the literal reading of a metaphor; mathematical and diagrammatic structures (the chess game of Looking-Glass).
authors.concerns: Childhood and the adult world's irrationality; language and meaning; rules, games and justice; time, memory and identity; education and its absurdities; the logic of nonsense as a form of moral criticism.
authors.significance: Carroll is the founding figure of English nonsense literature and the most influential children's writer of the century: the Alice books changed what a children's book could be, gave the language 'chortle', 'galumphing' and 'portmanteau', and have been read as philosophy, as mathematics, as political satire and as psychoanalysis. Their influence on Joyce, Eliot, Nabokov and the modern fantastic is direct.
authors.uncertainty: The name Lewis Carroll is a pseudonym, and the works published under it are attributed to Lewis Carroll on the evidence of the publisher's records, the correspondence and the contemporary attribution. 11 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text. No work catalogued here carries a disputed, conjectural or shared attribution, and every one of them was published under the author's own name between 1865 and 1889.

authors.name: Lewis Grassic Gibbon
authors.birthplace: Hillhead of Segget, Auchterless, Aberdeenshire, Scotland
authors.nationality: Scottish; the agrarian novel of the Mearns and the Scots prose of the modern novel
authors.identity: Novelist; the author of Sunset Song and A Scots Quair, the finest Scottish novel of the century and the greatest English-language novel of rural dispossession.
authors.biography: Born James Leslie Mitchell at Hillhead of Segget, Aberdeenshire, on 13 February 1901; his family moved to the farming country of the Mearns, which became the 'Kinraddie' of his fiction. He left school at fourteen, worked as a journalist in Aberdeen, Glasgow and London, served in the Royal Army Service Corps in the Middle East, and wrote under the name Lewis Grassic Gibbon: Sunset Song (1932), Cloud Howe (1933) and Grey Granite (1934), collected as A Scots Quair, together with the historical and anthropological books of his last years. He died in Welwyn Garden City on 7 February 1935, aged thirty-three.
authors.profile: Gibbon wrote the greatest Scottish novel of the century: Sunset Song is the elegy of the crofting world destroyed by the war and the machine, and A Scots Quair is the most complete account in fiction of Scotland's passage from the land to the city in a single generation. His prose — a Scots-inflected English that moves between the parish voice and the modern narrative — is one of the period's great inventions.
authors.style: The Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness; the choric parish voice at the chapter's opening; the lyric description of landscape and weather; the historical sweep of a community rather than a life; the direct address of the tale-teller.
authors.concerns: The land, the croft and the vanishing rural Scotland; the First World War and its destruction of the parish; the industrial city and the class struggle; Calvinism and the Scottish mind; the woman's passage through three worlds (Chris Guthrie); progress and its cost.
authors.significance: Gibbon wrote the finest Scottish novel of the period and one of the great novels of rural dispossession in English: Sunset Song and A Scots Quair record the destruction of a whole way of life with lyric power, and his Scots prose gave the modern Scottish novel its language. He is the prose counterpart of MacDiarmid in the Scottish Renaissance.

authors.name: Lionel Johnson
authors.nationality: English; the Catholic lyric, the critical essay and the poetry of the Rhymers' Club
authors.identity: Poet, critic and essayist; the most learned and the most tormented of the English Decadent poets, and a founding member of the Rhymers' Club.
authors.biography: Born at Broadstairs on 15 March 1867, the son of a captain in the Royal Army Medical Corps; he was educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, where he became a Catholic in 1891 and took a first in classics. He was a founder of the Rhymers' Club with Yeats and Dowson, wrote Poems (1895) and Ireland and Other Poems (1897), and published the finest critical essays of his generation on Hardy, Pater and the Celtic revival. He drank himself to death in London on 4 October 1902.
authors.profile: Johnson wrote the poetry of faith and damnation: a Catholic convert who could not reconcile his religion with his desires, he produced lyrics of great technical finish and terrible interior tension, and his critical prose — collected in Post Liminium and Reviews and Critical Papers — is the most learned criticism of the 1890s. He was the scholar of the Decadence, and his essays on the Celtic literature of Ireland helped to make the Irish revival possible.
authors.style: Classical and medieval metres handled with learning; the stanza of Wyatt and the seventeenth century revived; the Catholic imagery of the Mass and the martyrs; the elegiac and penitential tone; the critical essay of close reading.
authors.concerns: Catholic faith and sin; the divided self and the impossibility of peace; Ireland and the Celtic past; the English literary tradition; friendship and loneliness; death and the last things.
authors.significance: Johnson is the finest Catholic poet of the English 1890s and one of the best critics of his generation: his essays on Hardy and Pater are standard, his Poems are the most formally accomplished of the Rhymers' Club volumes, and his influence on Yeats's criticism and on the Catholic literary revival was decisive.

authors.name: Lorraine Hansberry
authors.nationality: American; African American playwright, essayist and civil rights activist
authors.identity: Playwright and activist; author of A Raisin in the Sun (1959), the first play by an African American woman to be produced on Broadway.
authors.biography: Lorraine Vivian Hansberry was born in Chicago on 19 May 1930, the youngest child of a prominent African American family. When her father bought a house in the white neighbourhood of Woodlawn, the family faced a hostile reception and a legal battle over racially restrictive covenants that reached the United States Supreme Court, an experience that later shaped A Raisin in the Sun. She studied at the University of Wisconsin from 1948, left in 1950 for New York, and worked as a staff writer and then associate editor on Paul Robeson's newspaper Freedom (1951-53); in 1952 she represented Robeson at a peace congress in Montevideo. She married the songwriter and producer Robert Nemiroff in 1953; they divorced in 1964, though he remained her collaborator and literary executor. A Raisin in the Sun opened on Broadway in March 1959 and won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award. Her second play, The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window, opened in 1964. She was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 1963 and died in New York on 12 January 1965, aged thirty-four. Nemiroff later adapted To Be Young, Gifted and Black (1969) from her writings and completed and published her last plays.
authors.profile: Hansberry's few finished plays brought working-class African American family life to the centre of the American stage and joined it to a wider politics of civil rights, anti-colonialism, feminism and intellectual commitment.
authors.style: Realist family drama with naturalistic, humorous dialogue that carries political argument; vivid, many-sided characters; symbolic objects and gestures; in the later plays a move towards the drama of ideas and fable.
authors.concerns: Housing segregation and racial discrimination; the American Dream and its costs; the dignity of working-class Black families; African independence and colonialism; the responsibility of intellectuals to commit themselves; women's independence.
authors.significance: A Raisin in the Sun is ranked among the classics of American drama and opened Broadway to Black playwrights, directors and audiences; Hansberry's essays, letters and late plays have made her an important figure in the histories of the civil rights movement, Black feminism and lesbian writing.
authors.uncertainty: Her letters to the lesbian magazine The Ladder in the late 1950s were published anonymously and attributed to her later; the AmericanLiterature.com profile reports them, and the attribution is widely accepted.

authors.name: Louis MacNeice
authors.nationality: Irish-British; the thirties poem of the ordinary and the elegy of the modern city
authors.identity: Poet, dramatist and radio writer; the finest poet of the Auden generation after Auden, the author of Autumn Journal, and the period's great writer for radio.
authors.biography: Born Frederick Louis MacNeice in Belfast on 12 September 1907, the son of a clergyman; his mother died when he was six and he was sent to school in England, reading classics at Oxford and lecturing in classics at Birmingham and London. Blind Fireworks (1929), Poems (1935) and Autumn Journal (1939) made his name; he worked for the BBC from 1941 as a writer and producer of radio features, translated Aeschylus and Goethe, and died in London on 3 September 1963.
authors.profile: MacNeice is the most individual poet of the Auden generation: Autumn Journal — a long poem of the months from autumn 1938 to the spring of 1939 — is the finest poetic diary of the period, and 'Bagpipe Music', 'Snow' and 'The Sunlight on the Garden' are among the best-loved poems of the century. As a BBC writer he invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism (Modern Poetry, 1938) is the sharpest account of what the thirties were doing.
authors.style: The long conversational poem in sections; the rhyme that falls with comic exactness; the catalogue of ordinary things (the bicycle, the pub, the newspaper); the classical and the modern held side by side; the radio script's montage of voices and sound.
authors.concerns: The thirties and the coming war; Belfast, Ireland and the divided inheritance; the ordinary English life and the objects of the modern city; time, love and the transience of everything; the classics and the modern world; the provinces and the metropolis.
authors.significance: MacNeice wrote the finest long poem of the thirties in Autumn Journal and the best-loved lyrics of the Auden generation, invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism gives the period its clearest account of itself. He is the most individual and the most durable poet of his group.

authors.name: Louisa May Alcott
authors.nationality: American; the family novel, the sensational story and the children's book
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Little Women and, in her anonymous thrillers, one of the boldest American writers of the 1860s.
authors.biography: Born in Germantown, Pennsylvania, on 29 November 1832, the daughter of the Transcendentalist Amos Bronson Alcott; she grew up in Concord among Emerson, Thoreau and Hawthorne, and supported the family by sewing, teaching and writing. Hospital Sketches (1863) came from her service as a nurse in the Civil War, where she contracted typhoid; the anonymous sensation stories of the 1860s paid the bills, and Little Women (1868-69) made her rich and famous. She died in Boston on 6 March 1888.
authors.profile: Alcott wrote the American family novel as a woman's economic document: Little Women is a book about girls who must work, and its charm rests on the frankness with which it treats money, ambition and disappointment. Her anonymous thrillers — Behind a Mask, Pauline's Passion and Punishment — are among the most subversive American stories of the decade, and her children's books created the modern moral novel for girls without ever being merely pious.
authors.style: Domestic realism with a strong narrative voice; dialogue that individualises the sisters; comic episode; the sentimental climax undercut by irony; in the thrillers, the femme fatale and the revenge plot borrowed from the sensation novel.
authors.concerns: Women's work and the economics of the family; female ambition and the choice of vocation; sisterhood and rivalry; the Civil War and nursing; the Transcendentalist household and its ideals; poverty and respectability.
authors.significance: Alcott is the central American writer of the family novel and the creator of the most beloved girls' book in American literature: Little Women has never been out of print, and the recovery of her sensation fiction has established her as a far more daring writer than her reputation as a children's author suggested.

authors.name: Lucas Malet
authors.nationality: English; the novel of heredity, the religious problem novel and the decadent romance
authors.identity: Novelist; the pen name of Mary St Leger Kingsley, the daughter of Charles Kingsley, and one of the boldest English novelists of the 1890s.
authors.biography: Born Mary St Leger Kingsley at Eversley, Hampshire, on 4 June 1852, the daughter of Charles Kingsley; she married William Harrison in 1876 and took the pen name Lucas Malet in 1882. Her best novels — Colonel Enderby's Wife (1885), The Wages of Sin (1891), The History of Sir Richard Calmady (1901) and The Far Horizon (1906) — treat heredity, disability, Catholicism and sexual desire with a frankness that startled her father's admirers. She died at Tenby on 27 October 1931.
authors.profile: Malet wrote the English novel of heredity and physical disaster: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is the story of a man born with deformed legs, and it treats his body, his desires and his fate with a sympathy and a frankness that no English novelist had attempted. Her late novels move from the religious problem to a decadent Catholicism, and she was one of the few women of the 1890s to write about the male body and male desire without apology.
authors.style: Rich, elaborate, slightly archaic prose; the family chronicle organised around a physical or moral inheritance; the detailed analysis of religious and erotic experience; the set piece of a death or a conversion; the baroque description of place and interior.
authors.concerns: Heredity and the body; disability, difference and the right to love; the conflict of Catholicism and modernity; the burden of a family's past; desire and renunciation; the position of the artist and the aristocrat.
authors.significance: Malet is one of the boldest English novelists of the 1890s and the most important English woman writer on heredity and disability: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is a landmark of Victorian fiction, and her frank treatment of the body and of male desire made her a central figure in the transition from the Victorian to the modern novel.

authors.name: Lucy Hutchinson
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Translator, poet, and memoirist; the first person to translate the complete Lucretius into English (De Rerum Natura, c. 1650s), author of the Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson, and of the biblical epic Order and Disorder — a major, recently recovered woman writer of the Interregnum.
authors.biography: Born January 1620 in the Tower of London, where her father was Lieutenant; unusually well educated alongside her brothers, she showed precocious talent in languages. She married the Puritan Colonel John Hutchinson (1638), governor of Nottingham during the Civil Wars, and after his death in royalist captivity (1664) wrote his Memoirs — a classic of biography and of Civil War history. She also translated Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (presented to the Earl of Anglesey, c. 1675; she later repudiated it on religious grounds) and wrote the verse epic Order and Disorder (only a canto was published in 1679; the full text recovered from manuscript in the twentieth century), as well as theological and elegiac verse. She died in 1681 at Owthorpe, Nottinghamshire.
authors.profile: The learned Puritan woman writer whose biography, epic, and translation display remarkable erudition and literary ambition, and whose work offers a woman's republican and religious perspective on the Civil Wars.
authors.style: Eloquent biographical and historical prose; philosophical translation in verse; biblical epic; and elegiac and devotional poetry of intellectual depth.
authors.concerns: Puritan and republican politics; the Civil Wars and her husband's career; Lucretian atomism and its reconciliation with faith; biblical narrative and providence; and grief and memory.
authors.significance: Hutchinson's Memoirs are a primary source for the Civil Wars and a landmark of English biography; her Lucretius translation and Order and Disorder make her a major figure in the recovery of early modern women's writing and of the period's engagement with Epicureanism.
authors.uncertainty: Hutchinson's life is documented through her own writings and family papers; much of her work was unpublished in her lifetime and recovered from manuscript, so dating and textual questions remain.

authors.name: Lydia Howard Sigourney
authors.nationality: American; the Hartford literary establishment, and the religious and domestic verse and prose of the New England periodicals and annuals
authors.identity: Poet, essayist and moralist of Hartford, the most widely read American woman poet of the decades between the literary aftermath of the Revolution and the Civil War, and the first American woman to make a recognized professional livelihood by her pen.
authors.biography: Sigourney was born at Norwich in Connecticut, the only child of Ezekiel Huntley, a gardener and general workman of small means, and of Zerviah Wentworth Huntley, and she was named after her father's first wife. Her formal schooling was slight and she was largely self-taught, reading the moral essayists, the poets and the religious writers accessible in a New England household. She kept a little school for young children with a friend in her native town, and in her middle twenties removed to Hartford at the invitation of the painter Daniel Wadsworth to educate the girls of his family; there she opened and for some years conducted a school for young women until her marriage. About those years she began to send verses and moral sketches to the Hartford newspapers and to journals at Washington, Boston and Philadelphia, sometimes signing only her initials, and her occasional poems on bereavement and on public tragedy circulated widely before she had a book. On 16 June 1819 she married Charles Bartlett Sigourney, a printer, publisher and editor of the same city, whose reason gave way in the middle of the next decade and who survived as an invalid until 1831; the support of the household and of her sons thereafter rested on her writing. Her Moral Pieces in Prose and Verse, followed by the Poems of 1827 issued without her name and put forward as the work of the author of the earlier volume, made her at once the most widely read woman poet in the United States, and both books were reissued in enlarged and collected editions through the next thirty years. Letters to Young Ladies and Letters to a Mother, with books of maxims, of daily meditations and of scriptural and historical reading for families, gave her prose a circulation larger still, while her sketch-books of travel in Connecticut and in France, her verses on the murdered missionary family at the western settlement of the Sandusky affair, on Washington, on Napoleon and on the dead of the Mexican war made her the recorded feeling of the middle-class American household for a generation. She corresponded with men and women of letters on both sides of the Atlantic, contributed continuously to the gift-books and monthlies, was among the American correspondents of a household journal edited by Dickens, was honoured with portraits and with tribute volumes from her women readers, and was elected to historical societies. A stroke in her last years did not stop her writing; she died at Hartford on 10 June 1865 and was buried in the hill cemetery there, at her death the best-known American poetess and within two generations an author the schoolbooks had all but forgotten.
authors.profile: Her work divides between short lyrical, elegiac and reflective poems, largely on grief, death, remembrance and the consolation of faith, and prose of moral and domestic instruction: letters and manuals for young women and mothers, sketch-books of travel at home and in France, essays and tales in the manner of the annuals, and books of maxims and daily meditations. She wrote also the elegies and narrative poems on public tragedy and on missionary enterprise for which the women's societies of the day commissioned her, and she supplied the gift-books, the newspapers and the magazines with a steady stream of occasional verse. Her collected poetry appeared in successive enlarged editions and her prose in cheap religious reprints, and the moral earnestness of the pieces carries a social acuteness and a irony that later readers rediscovered.
authors.style: A decorous, hymn-like diction in the regular lyric stanza, with abstract and elevated nouns, apostrophe, and an antithetical balance of sorrow and consolation; a pointed, compressed and frequently epigrammatic prose manner, close to the maxim and the daily meditation, with domestic and social observation of character beneath the gravity of tone. Verse on public events becomes more narrative and more rhetorical, and the later pieces on the Civil War are more explicitly political.
authors.concerns: Bereavement, mortality and the faith that survives them; the moral agency and the education of women; the religious and charitable duties of the prosperous, including the missionary cause and the treatment of Native Americans; the temperate conduct of public and domestic life; the place of poetry as an instrument of piety, refinement and national memory.
authors.significance: She was the first American woman poet to command a national readership and a professional income, and for thirty years her name stood for the possibility of a female literary career in the United States. Her elegies and domestic verse set the tone of middle-class American mourning and devotion, her commissioning by missionary and charitable societies created the model of the woman writer as public moral servant, and her success prepared the ground for the women's writing of the 1840s and 1850s. Her reputation fell sharply after the century's turn; modern scholarship in American women's writing and in the culture of sentiment has restored her to the history of the period.

authors.name: Lydia Maria Child
authors.nationality: American; New England Unitarian letters turned to reform; the woman of letters who joined fiction, children's editing, domestic economy and abolitionist argument in a single career, and a founder of the American sentimental reform novel
authors.identity: An extraordinarily various writer: novelist of colonial Indian scenes, historian for children, editor of the first American periodical for the young, authoress of the standard American household manual, essayist, letter writer, poet of occasional verse and, after 1833, the most widely read white female advocate of immediate emancipation. She wrote for the nursery, the kitchen, the subscription list and the platform, and she regarded these as one province.
authors.biography: She was born Lydia Maria Francis at Medford, Massachusetts, on 11 February 1802, the youngest of the children of David Francis and Susannah Rand Francis, and she lost her mother while still a little girl. The household was of the middling trades and the formation of her mind was largely her own, aided by an elder brother who entered the Unitarian ministry and whose library and example gave her her first sense of a religious vocation in letters. She kept a school at Medford, and at twenty-two she published anonymously a short romance of the colonial period, Hobomok, which sold well and established her as a writer of Indian and frontier subject matter; it was followed in 1825 by The Rebels; or, Boston before the Revolution, a domestic history of the town on the eve of resistance to the crown. In 1826 she founded and conducted the Juvenile Miscellany, the first periodical printed in the United States for children, which she edited for several years and by which she was made known to families across the states. On 3 October 1828 she married David Lee Child, a lawyer of Massachusetts who afterwards turned to farming, and in 1829 she published The Frugal Housewife, afterwards known as The American Frugal Housewife and dedicated to those who are not ashamed of economy, the most successful of her books and for generations a standard of New England household management. The First Settlers of New-England, a history of the Pequot and Narraganset wars related by a father to his children, appeared in 1828. Her reading of the colonial and contemporary treatment of Native Americans prepared her for the great change of her life: An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans, published at Boston in 1833, cost her friends, subscribers and her children's readership, and made her a central figure of the new immediatism. She continued to write for the cause, edited the National Anti-Slavery Standard in the forties, advocated the rights of women and of the freedpeople, adopted a ward of the race she had befriended, and died at Wayland, Massachusetts, on 20 October 1880.
authors.profile: Her characteristic form is the address to a beginner: the child, the bride, the young reader of history, the conscience newly awakened. She writes with an assumption of intimacy and with a talent for the illustrative anecdote, and her historical fiction and her juvenile books alike proceed by homely detail, dated event and moral gloss rather than by plot of great force. Her abolitionist writing shifts the method of the household book into argument, accumulating evidence, precedent and appeal in orderly chapters, and her letters and memoirs carry the same plain unaffected manner. She is at her best where instruction and feeling are made one, and her worst where the moral takes the place of observation.
authors.style: Clear simple syntax with a conversational warmth; direct address to the reader, often as child or housekeeper; inventory and prescription, lists of economies and of facts; historical romance relieved by moral reflection; scriptural and providential cadence inherited from Unitarian preaching; sentiment restrained by practical good sense; a tendency to apostrophe and reproach in the polemic writing of the 1830s.
authors.concerns: The education and moral formation of children; the economy and dignity of household labour and the competence of women in domestic management; the writing of American history for the young and the justice owed to the first possessors of the land; slavery as a national sin and a question of immediate duty; the condition and capacity of women; the union of literary profession and reform; the character of republican nationhood tested by its treatment of subject races.
authors.significance: She created the American children's periodical, wrote the most widely used American domestic manual of her generation, and, by the Appeal of 1833, gave the immediatist movement in the United States its first comprehensive statement from a woman's pen and its most influential book among the reading public. Her career shows the passage of New England women's letters from fiction and instruction into political polemic, and the price paid by a woman who made that passage publicly. Later writings for the freedpeople and for women's rights place her at the opening of a reform tradition that ran to the civil war and beyond.
authors.uncertainty: The account of her father's trade and of her mother's death varies between biographies, and the dates and conduct of her schoolkeeping at Medford are slight in the record. The first edition of The Rebels is anonymous, and her authorship of material in the Juvenile Miscellany is not always separable from that of her contributors. Her titles were several times re-named in reissue, and the date of the first series of the Frugal Housewife and of the Miscellany's suspension is variously printed. The extent of her share in the editorial management of the Anti-Slavery Standard, and the details of her later religious and spiritualist readings, depend upon memoir rather than upon documents.

authors.name: Lytton Strachey
authors.nationality: British; the modern biography, the debunking essay and the Bloomsbury polemic
authors.identity: Biographer and critic; the author of Eminent Victorians, the founder of modern literary biography and the most brilliant English prose satirist of the period.
authors.biography: Born Giles Lytton Strachey in London on 1 March 1880 into an Anglo-Indian military family; he read at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he joined the Apostles, and lived in Bloomsbury from 1905. Landmarks in French Literature (1912) preceded Eminent Victorians (1918), which made him famous and transformed biography; Queen Victoria (1921) won the James Tait Black Prize, and Elizabeth and Essex (1928) was his last great work. He died at Ham Spray, Wiltshire, on 21 January 1932.
authors.profile: Strachey invented modern biography: Eminent Victorians took four Victorian sages — Manning, Florence Nightingale, Arnold and Gordon — and reduced them with irony, psychology and a novelist's sense of scene, and every literary biographer since has worked in its shadow. Queen Victoria is the most admired short life in English, and his prose — epigrammatic, witty, perfectly controlled — is the period's finest satirical style.
authors.style: The short, ironic, epigrammatic life; the revealing detail chosen for its absurdity; the sudden shift of tone from solemnity to bathos; the long periodic sentence with a sting in the tail; the narrative scene in which the subject is caught unawares.
authors.concerns: The Victorian age and its sages; the discrepancy between public reputation and private life; power, ambition and the will; religion and its functionaries; the biography as an art form and a moral instrument; the English ruling class and its illusions.
authors.significance: Strachey founded modern English biography: Eminent Victorians changed how lives are written, Queen Victoria remains the finest short life in English, and his prose gave the period its most brilliant irony. Every twentieth-century biographer who debunks or humanises a subject works in his debt.

authors.name: M. R. James
authors.nationality: British; the antiquarian ghost story and the scholarly supernatural tale
authors.identity: Medievalist, palaeographer and ghost-story writer; the greatest English writer of ghost stories and the Provost of Eton.
authors.biography: Born Montague Rhodes James at Goodnestone, Kent, on 1 August 1862; he was educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, where he spent his working life as a scholar of medieval manuscripts and became Provost of King's (1905) and then of Eton (1918). Ghost Stories of an Antiquary appeared in 1904, More Ghost Stories in 1911, A Thin Ghost in 1919 and A Warning to the Curious in 1925; his catalogue of the Cambridge manuscripts is a foundation of medieval scholarship. He died at Eton on 12 June 1936.
authors.profile: James invented the modern English ghost story: his four collections gave the genre its antiquarian form — the scholar, the document, the exact topography, the withheld apparition — and his stories ('Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad', 'Casting the Runes', 'A Warning to the Curious') are the finest in the language. He is also one of the great medieval scholars of the century, and the combination of the two is what makes his stories work.
authors.style: The antiquarian frame: the discovery of a document, an object or a manuscript; the dry, exact scholarly tone; the English landscape and the English county named precisely; the withheld apparition and the deliberately unexplained ending; the short story delivered on Christmas Eve.
authors.concerns: The unquiet dead and the violated grave; antiquity and the recovered object; the scholar's curiosity and its punishment; the English landscape as a place of buried history; the limits of knowledge; the horror of the ordinary and the domestic.
authors.significance: James is the greatest English writer of ghost stories and the founder of the modern supernatural tale: his four collections established the antiquarian form, 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and 'Casting the Runes' are the finest stories of their kind, and his scholarly authority gave the genre a seriousness it had lacked. He is the central figure of the movement recorded here.

authors.name: Malcolm Muggeridge
authors.nationality: British; the satirical journalist of the thirties and the Moscow correspondent
authors.identity: Journalist, satirist and novelist; the author of Winter in Moscow and The Thirties.
authors.biography: Born Thomas Malcolm Muggeridge at Sanderstead, Surrey, on 24 March 1903, the son of the Labour politician H. T. Muggeridge; he grew up in Croydon, read natural sciences at Selwyn College, Cambridge, taught English literature at Union Christian College in the Kingdom of Cochin, India, and then in Egypt, where Arthur Ransome recommended him to the Manchester Guardian. He went to Moscow for the paper in 1932; his reports of the famine in Ukraine were printed anonymously in March 1933, and his novel Picture Palace, drawn from his years at the Guardian, was published in 1934 but not distributed for fear of libel. Winter in Moscow (1934), The Earnest Atheist (1936), a study of Samuel Butler, In a Valley of This Restless Mind (1938) and The Thirties (1940) followed. He served as a soldier and intelligence officer in East Africa and Paris during the Second World War, was deputy editor of the Daily Telegraph (1950-53), converted to Christianity under the influence of Hugh Kingsmill and later became a Roman Catholic, and died in Hastings on 14 November 1990.
authors.profile: Malcolm Muggeridge was a satirical journalist of the thirties: his anonymous Manchester Guardian reports of March 1933 were, with Gareth Jones's, among the accounts that confirmed the extent of the famine in Ukraine, and Winter in Moscow satirised the Western journalists who took an uncritical view of the Soviet regime.
authors.style: The satirical sentence of the journalist with the moralist's edge; the Moscow satire; the social survey of the decade in The Thirties; the broadcast voice of the later years; the ridicule carried by the Christian conscience.
authors.concerns: The Soviet regime and its Western admirers; the famine and its reporting; the newspaper world; the social history of the thirties; the pilgrim's road of the later conversion.
authors.significance: Malcolm Muggeridge was a satirical journalist of the thirties: his famine reports of 1933 and Winter in Moscow (1934) set him against the uncritical Western reporting of the Soviet regime, and his later career ran from the Daily Telegraph and Punch to religious broadcasting.

authors.biography: Born Marcus Mosiah Garvey in Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica, on 17 August 1887; he worked as a printer, travelled in Central America and London, and founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica in 1914, moving it to Harlem in 1916. The Negro World, the Black Star Line and his speeches made him a world figure; he was convicted of mail fraud in 1923 and died in London on 10 June 1940.

authors.name: Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Prolific and original author of philosophy, science, poetry, drama, and prose fiction; the first woman to write science fiction (The Description of a New World, Called The Blazing World, 1666) and the first woman admitted to a meeting of the Royal Society (1667).
authors.biography: Born c. 1623 at Colchester, daughter of Sir Charles Lucas; she became a maid of honour to Queen Henrietta Maria and followed her into exile in Paris (1644), where she married William Cavendish, Marquis (later Duke) of Newcastle. She published prolifically from 1653 — Poems and Fancies, Philosophical Fancies, Orations, plays, and The Blazing World (1666), appended to her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (a critique of the Royal Society and of Hooke's microscopy). Eccentric, ambitious, and ridiculed as 'Mad Madge', she nevertheless defended women's education and imagination and visited the Royal Society in 1667. She died on 15 December 1673 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The bold, self-taught natural philosopher and imaginative writer who, across genres, developed a vitalist materialism and gave it narrative form in a utopian romance, while asserting a woman's right to knowledge and fame.
authors.style: Speculative, energetic, sometimes digressive prose and verse; philosophical dialogue and treatise; utopian romance and imaginary voyage; and a defiantly personal, self-promoting voice.

authors.significance: Cavendish is a pioneering woman of letters and of science, an early critic of the new experimental philosophy, and the author of the first English science-fiction narrative; feminist and history-of-science scholarship has restored her as a major, original figure.
authors.uncertainty: Cavendish's life is documented through her own (self-dramatising) memoirs and her husband's biography; her birth year is approximate and her reception was distorted by contemporary mockery.

authors.name: Margaret Fuller
authors.nationality: American; the Transcendentalist essay, criticism and the feminist treatise
authors.identity: Critic, editor and feminist; the first woman to work as a professional literary critic in the United States and the author of Woman in the Nineteenth Century.
authors.biography: Born Sarah Margaret Fuller at Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, on 23 May 1810, and educated by her father in the classics. She taught at Bronson Alcott's school, edited The Dial (1840-42), translated Goethe, and wrote for Horace Greeley's New-York Tribune from 1844, becoming the paper's first woman correspondent. In Europe she met Mazzini and aroused the admiration of the young Emerson circle; she married the Italian revolutionary Giovanni Angelo Ossoli in 1847 and supported the Roman Republic in 1849. She drowned with her husband and son when the ship carrying them to America was wrecked off Fire Island on 19 July 1850.
authors.profile: Fuller wrote the most important American feminist argument before the Civil War: Woman in the Nineteenth Century turns the 'woman question' into a question of the self's right to develop, and it made her the first woman in America to command the authority of a public intellectual. Her criticism is the first substantial American body of writing on literature by a professional critic, and her dispatches from Italy are among the finest American war reportage of the century.
authors.style: Conversational, digressive and allusive prose; the critical survey; the dialogue and the 'Conversation' as form; quotation and translation; the impassioned direct address of the feminist argument.
authors.concerns: The right of women to self-development and to intellectual life; democracy and the 'greatness' of the modern era; American literature and national culture; European revolutions and Italian freedom; the dignity of the woman artist; Transcendentalist religion.
authors.significance: Fuller is the founding figure of American feminism and the first professional woman of letters in the United States: Woman in the Nineteenth Century gave the American women's movement its first intellectual charter, and her Tribune criticism made literary journalism a serious American form. Her death off Fire Island made her a permanent figure of American legend.

authors.name: Margaret Oliphant
authors.nationality: Scottish; the chronicle novel and the literary life
authors.identity: Novelist, biographer and critic; the most prolific serious novelist of the Victorian age and the author of the Carlingford chronicles.
authors.biography: Born Margaret Wilson at Wallyford, Midlothian, on 4 April 1828; the family moved to Liverpool and she began writing to support them. She married her cousin Frank Oliphant in 1852; he died in 1859, and she supported three children, a brother and two nieces by her pen for the rest of her life, losing two sons and a daughter. She published over a hundred books, including the Carlingford series (1861-76), Miss Marjoribanks (1866), Hester (1883) and Kirsteen (1890), wrote for Blackwood's for forty years, and died at Wimbledon on 25 June 1897.
authors.profile: Oliphant wrote the Victorian novel of the ordinary life: her subject is the woman without money, the family in decline, the provincial town and the small ambitions that make up a life, and her method is the long, easy, ironical chronicle in which nothing much happens and everything is at stake. She was also the finest woman of letters of her generation — the biographer of Edward Irving and Laurence Oliphant, the historian of the publishing house of Blackwood, and the reviewer whose essays on women, fiction and religion were read across Britain.
authors.style: The leisurely chronicle with a large cast; free indirect style and ironic commentary; dialogue that catches provincial idiom; the comedy of the ordinary; the long view of a family across generations; a plain, flexible prose.
authors.concerns: Women's work and the economics of the genteel poor; marriage and the unmarried woman; provincial society and its hierarchies; family decline and inheritance; the literary profession and its costs; Scotland and the Scottish past.
authors.significance: Oliphant is the most underestimated Victorian novelist and the finest chronicler of ordinary women's lives in the century: Miss Marjoribanks and Hester are among the great English novels, her Carlingford series is the equal of Trollope's Barsetshire, and her autobiography is one of the most moving documents of Victorian literary life.

authors.nationality: English (East Anglia)
authors.identity: mystic; autobiographer; pilgrim
authors.biography: Daughter of John Brunham, mayor of Lynn, and wife of the merchant John Kempe, with whom she had fourteen children. After a post-natal crisis and a vision of Christ, she adopted a life of intense devotion — weeping uncontrollably at the thought of the Passion, wearing white, and travelling as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela, and through northern Europe — while repeatedly examined for heresy and vindicated. She dictated her Book to scribes in the late 1430s.
authors.profile: The Book of Margery Kempe (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English, records her spiritual life, pilgrimages, and trials in vigorous third-person prose.
authors.style: Direct, colloquial, vivid narrative; the blending of mystical experience with the detail of everyday mercantile and domestic life; a startling frankness about body, tears, and social conflict.
authors.concerns: The imitation of Christ's Passion; the legitimacy of lay, female, married spirituality; the discernment of her own calling against clerical suspicion.
authors.significance: Her Book is a unique document of female lay piety and of the social world of fifteenth-century East Anglia, and a foundational text of women's writing in English.
authors.uncertainty: Known almost entirely from her Book; dates approximate; the scribe's mediation complicates the text's authorship.

authors.name: Maria Edgeworth
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish; the Irish tale and the fiction of national character, and the educational writing of the Edgeworthstown household
authors.identity: Novelist of Anglo-Irish society and writer for children; the founder of the Irish national tale and of the realist provincial novel in English, and with her father the author of the period's great treatise of educational practice.
authors.biography: Edgeworth was born at Black Bourton in Oxfordshire, the estate of her mother's family, on 1 January 1768, the eldest daughter and third child of Richard Lovell Edgeworth and of Honora Sneyd, his second wife, and she was brought up in the large household of Edgeworthstown in the county of Longford, where her father's scheme of practical education was tried upon his children and where she learned languages, science, pottery-work and the management of an estate. Her mother died in 1776 and her father married her sister Elizabeth, and the education of the household continued unchanged; from her teens she wrote tales, translations and plays for the family theatre and for the instruction of the younger children. She began to publish to increase the income of a property embarrassed by her father's speculations and by his fourth marriage, and the two volumes of Practical Education, written with him and issued in 1798, were the first substantial work of her household to reach the public. Castle Rackrent, printed anonymously in 1800, gave the English novel its first Irish family history told by the steward of three successive masters, and the Irish tales of the Popular Tales of 1804 extended the same analysis of the tenantry, the absentee and the ascendancy; Ennui, The Absentee of 1812 and Patronage of 1814 made her the most read novelist of the Irish question, and the Tales of a Grandfather, begun in 1810, supplied the standard English history written for young readers. She moved in the literary and political society of London and Paris, was visited and corresponded with by the chief writers of the day, and observed with a close and anxious eye the operation of the union, of the Catholic question and of distress in her own county. She edited and printed her father's Memoirs in 1820 and 1821, continued to publish tales and juvenile books through the 1820s, never married, and after her father's death governed the household and the estate. She died at Edgeworthstown on 22 May 1849, the first Irish novelist of consequence in English and one of the most quoted writers on education and on national character.
authors.profile: Her work divides between the Irish tale of national and provincial character, the novel of opinion and of the educated family, the history and story written for children and young readers, and the educational, political and personal letters. Castle Rackrent introduced the framing of an Irish narrative by an oral servant voice and the comic use of a family history to expose a class, and the Popular Tales, Ennui, The Absentee and Patronage carry the same analysis of Anglo-Irish society into other forms. Practical Education, written with her father, reports the experiments of a cultivated household and argues from the principles of the philosophy of the mind to the practice of the nursery, and her tales for young readers, with the later family and literary correspondence, make a substantial prose work of instruction and of observation.
authors.style: A plain, rapid and conversational prose of dialogue, of circumstance and of the telling small fact, with the didactic manner always in view of the reader's pleasure; in the Irish tales the voice is deliberately oral, digressive, full of the proverb, the aside and the understatement of the servant-narrator, and the irony is carried by the speaker's own innocence. The educational and letters writing is exact, dry and unpretentious, and the tales for children give the same concrete method to the instruction of the young.
authors.concerns: The character and the government of Ireland, the absentee system, the tenantry and the politics of the union; the education of the infant and child mind, the association of ideas and the discipline of the natural consequence; the morals of opinion, of patronage and of the man of science in a family and a county; the condition and the employment of women and of the governess; the making of national history for the young, and the ethics of how a conquest is remembered.
authors.significance: She founded the Irish national tale and the realist novel of provincial and national character in English, and the framing and the oral irony of Castle Rackrent made it the starting point of the modern Irish novel and a model for the historical fiction of the following generation. Practical Education carried associationist psychology into nursery and schoolroom practice and set the terms of the family literature of instruction, and her tales and histories for children were standard reading in English-speaking schoolrooms for a century; as an observer of the Irish ascendancy she is also a primary witness of the society that the union changed.
authors.uncertainty: The division of labour between father and daughter in Practical Education, and in the household experiments which that book reports, is not wholly separable, and the account of her education and of the family theatrics rests largely on her own recollections and on the Memoirs of her father which she edited. The dating of her early unpublished tales and translations, and the extent of her share in the joint educational volumes issued under her father's name and hers, are variously stated in the biographies.
