authors.name: Maria Graham
authors.nationality: British - a Romantic-period writer of travel journals, art history, scientific observation and school books, born in Cumberland into a Scottish naval family and at home in the Edinburgh publishing world, the London review circles, the Geological Society and the Royal Academy.
authors.identity: Travel writer and children's author, with art history, translation and geological observation on either side: the first woman to publish an article in the Transactions of the Geological Society, and the author of the most durable school history of the mid-nineteenth century. Her proper form is the journal of residence - daily observation, measured, documented and drawn by her own hand - and the instructed child's book built upon it.
authors.biography: Maria Dundas was born at Papcastle, near Cockermouth, Cumberland, on 19 July 1785, eldest child of George Dundas (1756-1814), a Royal Navy officer who rose to rear-admiral. She met Samuel Rogers and Thomas Campbell at her uncle Sir David Dundas's Richmond house. In December 1808 she sailed with her father to Bombay; on 9 December 1809 she married a fellow passenger, Captain Thomas Graham, R.N., and travelled in India, returning to England in June 1811. Her Journal of a Residence in India appeared in 1812, Letters on India in 1814 and her translation of Rocca's Memoirs of the War of the French in Spain in 1815-16. Italy in 1819 yielded Three Months Passed in the Mountains East of Rome and the Memoirs of the Life of Nicholas Poussin, both of 1820. Sailing for the Pacific in HMS Doris in 1821, she was widowed off Cape Horn in April 1822 and passed the next year at Valparaiso, where she observed the great earthquake of November 1822; her account of the raised seabed, printed in the Transactions of the Geological Society in 1824, was the first article by a woman in that series, entered Lyell's Principles of Geology in 1830, was ridiculed by Greenough and vindicated by Darwin's Chilean evidence. Her Chile and Brazil journals appeared in 1824, and after teaching the young Donna Maria da Gloria at Rio she reached England in 1825. The Voyage of the H.M.S. Blonde to the Sandwich Islands, compiled from official papers and the Bloxams' journals, came in 1826; on 20 February 1827 she married the painter Augustus Wall Callcott, R.A., and her A Short History of Spain followed in 1828. A ruptured blood vessel in 1831 confined her to the desk: Giotto's chapel at Padua and Little Arthur's History of England in 1835, the Histoire de France du petit Louis in 1836, Essays towards the History of Painting in 1836-38, The Little Bracken-Burners in 1841 and A Scripture Herbal in 1842. Callcott was knighted in 1837 and she became Lady Callcott; she died at the Kensington Gravel Pits and lies in Kensal Green Cemetery.
authors.profile: Her work divides into four streams. The travel journals: Journal of a Residence in India (1812), Letters on India, with Etchings and a Map (1814), Three Months Passed in the Mountains East of Rome (1820), Journal of a Residence in Chile during the year 1822 and a Voyage from Chile to Brazil in 1823 (1824), Journal of a Voyage to Brazil (1824), and the compiled Voyage of the H.M.S. Blonde to the Sandwich Islands (1826). Art history and translation: Rocca's Memoirs of the War of the French in Spain (1815-16), Memoirs of the Life of Nicholas Poussin (1820), the Description of the Chapel of the Annunziata dell'Arena, or Giotto's Chapel in Padua (1835), and Essays towards the History of Painting (1836-38). Books for children and the nursery: Little Arthur's History of England (1835), its French pendant Histoire de France du petit Louis (1836), and The Little Bracken-Burners with Little Mary's Four Saturdays (1841). Devotional natural history: A Scripture Herbal (1842). She etched plates for her own books, and her geological letters form a separate printed body.
authors.style: A plain, exact and deliberately unadorned prose of observation, strong in measurement, level, date and named informant, and modest about itself. She attributes knowledge readily - to her father's naval and Orientalist books, to interpreters, to the Bloxams' journals - and yet keeps a distinct first-person presence. Botanical and geological detail is given in the technical language of her authorities, drawn as well as written, her etchings and sketches carrying part of the argument. Controversy sharpens her: her reply to Greenough is combative and closely quoted. In Little Arthur the manner changes to the catechetical and conversational, an uncle telling English chronology to a child reader, with moral and patriotic point made plainly and the sentences shortened for the nursery.
authors.concerns: The authority of the eyewitness against the authority of sex and office; the uplift of coasts, the record of earthquakes and the reading of the earth's changes; the instruction of children as the making of citizens, and patriotic history taught in the nursery; the religious content of natural history, pursued in A Scripture Herbal; the appreciation and classification of painting, from Poussin to Giotto and the Paduan frescoes; the duties of a European in India, Chile and the court of Brazil, and the value of accurate account of native peoples, Parsi worship and Sanskrit learning; the education of princesses and the political uses of tutoring.
authors.significance: She was among the most successful women travel writers of the Romantic generation and the chief English eyewitness of the 1822 Chilean earthquakes: her letter to Henry Warburton, printed in the Transactions of the Geological Society in 1824, is the first article by a woman in that series, and her observation of coastal elevation passed into Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830), was mocked by Greenough and later supported by Darwin's evidence. Her Poussin memoir of 1820 gave English readers their first sustained life of the painter; her journals remain primary authority on Chilean independence and on the Brazilian court of Pedro I; the Blonde volume is a chief source for that voyage. Little Arthur's History of England remained a standard child's history for three quarters of a century, and Chile honours her as an early friend of its nationhood.
authors.uncertainty: The years are firm (born 19 July 1785; died 1842), but the day of death is given as 28 November 1842 by the Dictionary of National Biography and as 21 November 1842 by most modern accounts; her burial in Kensal Green Cemetery is documented. The birthplace is given by the Dictionary of National Biography and by the British Travel Writing project as Papcastle near Cockermouth, Cumberland, though Wikipedia words it as 'near Cockermouth', and no parish register has been checked here. The batch brief assigns her The History of Little Henry and his Bearer (1814): that tale is attributed in the Dictionary of National Biography, in the standard children's-literature scholarship (M. N. Cutt), in library catalogues and in the Hockliffe Collection to Mary Martha Sherwood, who composed it anonymously in India; no contemporary impression connects it with Maria Graham, whose own books for children begin with Little Arthur in 1835, and the attribution is therefore not accepted in this record. Her Brazilian teaching service is variously dated: the Dictionary of National Biography has her instructress to Donna Maria from 22 November 1822 to January 1823, while later accounts place the court engagement after her 1824 return to Rio, and her unpublished 'Memoir of the Life of Don Pedro' survives only in manuscript. The share of the Blonde volume that is her own composition, the volume having been made from official papers and the journals of the chaplain R. Rowland Bloxam and the naturalist Andrew Bloxam, is open to judgement.

authors.name: Maria W. Stewart
authors.nationality: American; the Black sermon and public-address tradition of the Northern free communities; the Garrisonian press of the 1830s and the religious oratory of the African Methodist and Baptist circles of Boston
authors.identity: A preacher-speaker and essayist whose literary unit is the address. Her canon is small and of a single piece: a tract of religious and racial counsel, four public lectures delivered in Boston, a collected volume of meditations and essays, and the later contributions to the Black press. She writes in the idiom of the sermon, with scripture, reproach, prophecy and appeal, but she is also the earliest American woman to argue in print for the education, the economic improvement and the public voice of her own sex and colour.
authors.biography: She was born Maria Miller at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1803, in the free Black community of the town; orphaned in childhood and bound out as a servant in a clergyman's household, she had such schooling as the Sabbath schools of Hartford afforded and taught herself to read and write with diligence. She worked in service from her earliest years and passed some years in New York City, and on 10 August 1826, in Boston, she married James W. Stewart, a Black shipping agent who had served in the United States navy during the war of 1812. His death three years later left her a widow without the property her husband's will was intended to secure for her, defrauded by white claimants and dependent again upon teaching and housework. In Boston she joined the religious and mutual-aid circles of the free Black community, was moved by a conversion experience to labour for the elevation of her people, and came under the notice of William Lloyd Garrison, who printed her first written address, Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality, the Sure Foundation on Which We Must Build, in the columns of The Liberator and in tract form, commonly dated 1831. She then began the public career for which she is remembered, addressing the African American Female Intelligence Society on 28 April 1832, delivering at Franklin Hall on 21 September 1832 the lecture known as Why Sit Ye Here and Die, and speaking twice more in 1833, all before mixed audiences of women and men. The addresses, with a sermon and meditations, were gathered in 1833 as Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart, printed for her by Garrison's friends. The criticism passed upon a woman who spoke in public determined her to withdraw from the platform; she continued to teach, contributed prose to the press of her own community in later decades, lived finally in the capital, and died at Freedmen's Hospital, Washington, on 17 December 1879.
authors.profile: Her prose is oral by design and religious by premise. The sermon form supplies her structure, an exposition of text, an application to the audience's condition and a closing summons, and she fills it with statistical and historical instance, with the examples of biblical women and with pointed reproach to men who permit their wives and daughters to sit unlettered. The rhetorical question and the apostrophe carry her argument, and her most powerful writing turns upon the shame of inaction rather than upon description of injury. The volume of 1833 shows her range, passing from exhortation to enterprise, to education, to patience under wrong, and its prefatory matter explains and defends her own public speech.
authors.style: Preaching rhythms with a woman's first-person authority; dense scriptural quotation and typology; sustained interrogative address, why sit ye here and die; direct rebuke of the audience's sloth joined to tenderness for its suffering; parallelism and triadic emphasis; moral analogy drawn from nature, from the classical and sacred past and from the everyday economy of Northern Black life; a print style shaped by oral delivery and by the Liberator's columns.
authors.concerns: The religious duty of self-improvement and of public speech; the education of Black women and children as the foundation of racial elevation; the moral and economic uplift of the free coloured community; the complicity of the North with slavery and the shame of passive waiting; Providence, race and national destiny in the American republic; the rights and obligations of women as teachers, writers and speakers; temperance, industry and the dignity of labour.
authors.significance: She was the first American-born woman known to lecture on political, racial and religious subjects to mixed audiences of women and men, and one of the first to publish such writing, and her pamphlet and addresses of 1831 to 1833 open the literature of Black women's reform in the United States. Her public career marks the entrance of African American women into Garrisonian abolitionism, and her defence of her own voice supplies the founding argument of a tradition running through the anti-lynching and suffrage oratory of later decades. The recovery of her texts in modern scholarship has established her as a central figure of American religious and feminist letters.
authors.uncertainty: The month of her birth at Hartford, the free or enslaved condition of her parents before her own birth, and the exact chronology of her childhood servitude are variously reported. The pamphlet of Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality is dated 1831 by some authorities and 1832 by others, and its first printing, in the Liberator or in tract form, cannot always be sequenced. The date of her husband's death, the details of the litigation over his estate, and the years of her teaching in New York and Baltimore are imperfectly documented, and the record of her last decades in Washington rests mainly on institutional notice.

authors.name: Marianne Moore
authors.nationality: American; the syllabic poem, the accurate eye and the modernist menagerie
authors.identity: Poet, critic and editor; the great American poet of exact observation, the editor of The Dial, and the inventor of the syllabic stanza.
authors.biography: Born Marianne Craig Moore in Kirkwood, Missouri, on 15 November 1887 and raised in Carlisle, Pennsylvania; she studied biology at Bryn Mawr, taught stenography and worked in a library before editing The Dial from 1925 to 1929. Poems (1921) was published by H.D. and Bryher without her knowledge; Observations followed in 1924, Selected Poems (with an introduction by Eliot) in 1935, and the Collected Poems in 1951, which won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the Bollingen Prize. She died in New York on 5 February 1972.
authors.profile: Moore is the great American poet of exact observation and of the moral weight of the precise word: her syllabic stanzas, her quotations embedded in her own text, her animals and baseball and armadillos, made a poetry of fact that is also a poetry of judgement. 'Poetry', 'The Fish', 'A Grave' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts, and her editorship of The Dial made her the period's most influential American editor.
authors.style: The syllabic stanza counted by syllables and not by stress; the rhyme that falls inside the line; the quotation folded into the syntax; the exact zoological and botanical naming; the indented line and the elaborate stanza shape; the prose sentence broken into verse.
authors.concerns: Exact observation and the moral weight of fact; animals and the natural world; America, baseball and the ordinary hero; the sea and the shore; the poet's duty to be 'literal for the purposes of being allegorical'; modesty and self-deprecation.
authors.significance: Moore is one of the central American modernists: her syllabic stanza gave American poetry a new measure, her exact and quoted verse made fact a poetic value, and her fifteen years at The Dial made her the period's most important American editor. 'Poetry', 'The Fish' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts.

authors.name: Marie Corelli
authors.nationality: British; the romance of the occult and the bestseller of the 1890s
authors.identity: Novelist; the most popular woman writer in England in the 1890s and the great populariser of the occult romance.
authors.biography: Born Mary Mackay in London on 1 May 1855, the illegitimate daughter of the journalist Charles Mackay; she trained as a musician and took the name Marie Corelli, publishing A Romance of Two Worlds in 1886. The Sorrows of Satan (1895), The Mighty Atom (1896), The Murder of Delicia (1896) and The Master-Christian (1900) followed. She lived at Stratford-upon-Avon from 1899, where she campaigned for the Shakespeare memorial, and died there on 21 April 1924.
authors.profile: Corelli was the best-selling novelist in England in the 1890s and the first woman writer to outsell her male contemporaries by an enormous margin, with The Sorrows of Satan breaking every record of the trade. She gave the popular novel its taste for the occult, the oriental and the sensational, and her attacks on the literary establishment made her the first celebrity author in the modern sense.
authors.style: The occult machinery of the romance — electricity, reincarnation, the astral body; the direct address to the reader and the authorial lecture; the sensational contrast of luxury and poverty; the florid, exclamatory, moralising prose; the melodramatic set-piece of the temptation.
authors.concerns: The reality of the soul and the survival of personality; the corruption of wealth and the metropolis; the hypocrisy of the churches; the position of the woman artist; the moral responsibility of fiction.
authors.significance: Marie Corelli was the most popular woman writer in England in the 1890s and the great populariser of the occult romance: The Sorrows of Satan broke the sales records of the trade, and her mixture of spiritualism, social protest and melodrama created the mass-market fiction of the twentieth century.

authors.name: Mark Akenside
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and physician, author of the philosophical poem The Pleasures of Imagination, an early statement of associationist aesthetics.
authors.biography: Akenside was born at Newcastle, the son of a butcher of Dissenting inclinations, and was educated at a Dissenting academy and then at the University of Edinburgh and Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and turned to medicine. He practised in various English towns and at length in London. His three-book philosophical poem The Pleasures of Imagination appeared in 1744 and was revised in 1763, making his reputation. He also wrote odes and medical and political verse. A Fellow of the Royal Society, he took a medical degree at Leiden late in life. He died in 1770.
authors.profile: A didactic poet of taste and the mind who treats the imagination philosophically, drawing on associationist psychology, Shaftesburian moral sense, and the language of the sublime and the beautiful.
authors.style: Miltonic blank verse of stately length; philosophical paraphrase and abstraction; personification of mental powers; and an elevated, rhapsodic, sometimes diffuse didactic manner.
authors.concerns: The nature and training of taste; the association of ideas; beauty, sublimity, and the pleasures of the mind; moral sense and virtue; and the relation of imagination to truth and feeling.
authors.significance: The Pleasures of Imagination is a key early work of eighteenth-century aesthetic theory in verse, transmitting Shaftesbury, Addison, and associationism to a poetic audience and influencing later aesthetic thought.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1721 but sometimes 1722; the details of his medical practice and his London hospital connections are only partly documented.

authors.name: Mark Twain
authors.nationality: American; the vernacular novel, the travel book and the tall tale
authors.identity: Novelist, humorist and travel writer; the author of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and the founder of the American vernacular prose style.
authors.biography: Born Samuel Langhorne Clemens in Florida, Missouri, on 30 November 1835 and brought up in Hannibal on the Mississippi; he was apprenticed to a printer, worked as a riverboat pilot until the Civil War closed the river, served briefly in a Confederate militia, and went west to Nevada and California in 1861. 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' (1865) made him famous; The Innocents Abroad (1869), Roughing It (1872), Tom Sawyer (1876) and Huckleberry Finn (1884-85) followed. He married Olivia Langdon in 1870, lost a fortune in the Paige typesetter, and made a world lecture tour in 1895-96. He died at Redding, Connecticut, on 21 April 1910.
authors.profile: Twain wrote American English as it was spoken: his great innovation is the first-person vernacular narrator whose idiom, irony and moral hesitation carry the whole book, and Huckleberry Finn is the founding text of the American novel of voice. He is also the great American satirist of pretension, of the South's romance of itself, and of the 'damned human race', and his late work is one of the darkest bodies of writing in American literature.
authors.style: First-person vernacular narration; deadpan comic exaggeration; the tall tale and the shaggy-dog story; ironic understatement; dialect rendered phonetically; the abrupt turn from comedy to horror.
authors.concerns: Slavery and the moral conscience of a boy; the Mississippi and the American frontier; the romance of the South and its self-deception; money, speculation and the Gilded Age; imperialism and the Philippine war; death, determinism and the dark side of providence.
authors.significance: Twain is the central American humorist and the founding novelist of American vernacular prose: Huckleberry Finn is the book from which, in Hemingway's phrase, all modern American literature comes, and his influence on American comedy, on the short story and on the literature of race is foundational.

authors.name: Mary Astell
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Philosopher, polemicist, and early feminist; her A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (1694, 1697) argued for a women's educational institution and her Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700) exposed the double standard, making her a founder of English feminist argument.
authors.biography: Born 12 November 1666 at Newcastle upon Tyne, daughter of a coal merchant; deprived of formal education and a dowry by her father's early death, she moved to London (c. 1688) and, supported by a circle of aristocratic women patrons, became a prolific writer. A High Church Tory and intellectual correspondent of John Norris and George Hickes, she published A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (Part I 1694, Part II 1697), advocating a Protestant 'monastery' or academy for women's education, and Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700). She also wrote philosophical and theological works (The Christian Religion, 1705) and controversial pamphlets, and ran a charity school for girls in Chelsea in retirement. She died on 9 May 1731.
authors.profile: The rigorous female philosopher and polemicist who used Cartesian method and High Church theology to argue that women are rational souls entitled to education and to critique the inequalities of marriage and custom.
authors.style: Argumentative, ironic, and polemical prose; rhetorical questions and wit; philosophical reasoning applied to women's condition; and an earnest, hortatory tone.
authors.concerns: Women's education and rational capacity; marriage and the double standard; female friendship and community; religion and reason; and political and theological controversy.
authors.significance: Astell is a pioneering English feminist philosopher whose proposals for women's education and her critique of marriage anticipate later feminist thought; her recovery has made her central to the history of women's writing and of the Enlightenment debate on women.
authors.uncertainty: Astell's life is documented through her works, correspondence, and patrons; details of her early life and her Chelsea charity school rest on records and tradition.

authors.name: Mary Augusta Ward
authors.nationality: English; the novel of faith and the social-problem novel
authors.identity: Novelist; the best-selling serious novelist of the 1880s-1900s and the author of Robert Elsmere, the central Victorian novel of the loss of faith.
authors.biography: Born Mary Augusta Arnold at Hobart, Tasmania, on 11 June 1851, the granddaughter of Thomas Arnold and niece of Matthew Arnold; the family returned to England in 1856 and she was educated at Oxford and in London. She married the historian Thomas Humphry Ward in 1872, wrote for the Times and Macmillan's, and published Robert Elsmere in 1888; she founded the Passmore Edwards Settlement in 1897 and worked for women's education. She led the anti-suffrage movement from 1908 and died in London on 24 March 1920.
authors.profile: Ward wrote the novel of the Victorian crisis of faith: Robert Elsmere is the book in which the Broad Church conscience, the higher criticism and the social gospel meet, and its account of a clergyman who loses his belief and finds a religion of social service was the most discussed English novel of the decade. Her later novels — Marcella, Sir George Tressady, Helbeck of Bannisdale — treat the woman question, politics and Catholicism with the same seriousness, and her biography of her father is a fine piece of Victorian life-writing.
authors.style: The long novel of ideas with a large social canvas; dialogue that argues a theological or political case; the domestic interior as the stage of moral crisis; the set-piece description of a landscape or an institution; a plain and dignified prose.
authors.concerns: Religious doubt and the social gospel; the Broad Church and the higher criticism; the woman question and women's education; politics and the political conscience; Catholicism and the modern world; the university and the settlement house.
authors.significance: Ward was the most widely read serious novelist of her generation and Robert Elsmere the central English novel of the Victorian religious crisis: it sold in hundreds of thousands and was discussed from every pulpit, and its picture of the transition from faith to social service made it the representative novel of the 1880s.

authors.name: Mary Brunton
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Philosophical and Gothic novelist
authors.biography: Mary Brunton was born in Orkney, the daughter of the minister Thomas Balfour. Educated largely at home, she was recognised as a prodigy in her youth and read widely in philosophy and theology. She published Self-Control (1811) to immediate success and Walter Scott's public praise. In 1812 she married the minister John Brunton and continued to write after marriage, publishing Emmeline, a verse narrative, and Discipline (1814), her second novel. She died in childbirth in 1818 at Biggar.
authors.profile: Brunton fused Gothic narrative with philosophical argument in the Godwinian tradition, though her moral framework was Calvinist and her treatment of sensibility more critical than Godwin's. Her Scottish and Canadian settings in Self-Control and her theological drama in Discipline made her one of the most distinctive novelists of the 1810s.
authors.style: Measured prose with philosophical digressions; controlled Gothic suspense; interiority of moral reasoning; a distinctive blend of Scottish Calvinism and Enlightenment philosophical discourse.
authors.concerns: Self-control versus passion; the moral education of women; Calvinist theology and the doctrine of election; the Scottish philosophical tradition; the Gothic captivity plot as moral and spiritual test.
authors.significance: Brunton's novels represent the intersection of Gothic sensation and Scottish moral philosophy in the Romantic period. Her praise by Scott and her influence on later Scottish women novelists, including Susan Ferrier, establish her as a significant transitional figure between Godwinian philosophy and Victorian moral fiction.

authors.biography: Born Mary Lee in August 1656 at Wonford near Exeter in Devon, the daughter of a Devon gentleman, she was largely self-educated through wide reading and correspondence. Her prose defense of women, An Essay to Defend the Womens Cause, circulated in manuscript and was printed in 1701, and her Poems on Several Occasions appeared in 1703, including verse on the soul, learning, and friendship. She moved in dissenting and learned circles. She was buried on 15 December 1710.

authors.name: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
authors.nationality: American; the New England village story and the literature of women's lives
authors.identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest American regionalist of the New England village and the great chronicler of unmarried and widowed women.
authors.biography: Born Mary Eleanor Wilkins at Randolph, Massachusetts, on 31 October 1852, into a strict Congregational family that lost its money; she attended Mount Holyoke Female Seminary for a year and began writing to support herself and her family. A Humble Romance (1887) and A New England Nun (1891) made her reputation; she married Dr Charles Freeman in 1902 and moved to New Jersey, where she wrote the novels and plays of her later years. She won the William Dean Howells Medal in 1926 and died at Metuchen, New Jersey, on 13 March 1930.
authors.profile: Freeman wrote the American story of the village woman: her subject is the unmarried daughter, the widow, the woman who keeps house for a man who does not notice her, and her method is the small, exact, almost cruel narrative in which a whole life is settled in a single afternoon. A New England Nun is one of the great American stories, and her novels Pembroke and The Shoulders of Atlas extend her vision to the whole village economy of New England.
authors.style: Small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn; exact rendering of New England dialect and domestic detail; the withheld epiphany; ironic comedy that edges into tragedy; the interior of the village house; the dignity and the narrowness of women's lives.
authors.concerns: Unmarried women, spinsterhood and the economics of the village household; marriage and the marriage market; women's work and women's property; the decay of rural New England; poverty and pride; the small cruelties of community.
authors.significance: Freeman is the finest American regionalist of the New England village and one of the great American writers of women's lives: A New England Nun is a permanent classic, her portrait of the unmarried woman is unique in nineteenth-century American fiction, and her work has become central to the feminist criticism of American literature.

authors.name: Mary Elizabeth Braddon
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian sensation novel
authors.identity: Novelist, editor and the most commercially successful of the sensation novelists.
authors.biography: Born in London on 4 October 1835, the daughter of a solicitor's clerk whose family broke up when she was young. She went on the stage in 1856 and acted with Edmund Falconer's company until 1860, when she turned to fiction. Lady Audley's Secret, serialised in Robin Goodfellow and then in the Sixpenny Magazine in 1861-62, made her famous; she founded and edited Belgravia (1866-76) and ran a large household at Richmond with her publisher John Maxwell, whose five children she raised before marrying him in 1874. She wrote more than eighty novels and died at Richmond on 4 February 1915.
authors.profile: Braddon took the machinery of the sensation novel — the secret, the grave, the locked room, the woman with a past — and made it the vehicle of a sustained argument about the position of women under the marriage law. Lady Audley is not a monster but a woman with no legal existence of her own, and the novel's famous question (is she mad, or only poor?) is answered by the Victorian asylum. Braddon wrote at speed and to a market, but her best books are technically adroit and socially sharp: she invented the professional woman writer as a commercial operator and made the sensation novel a woman's genre.
authors.style: Rapid, incident-packed serial plotting; the big secret withheld to the last chapter; the ordinary domestic interior hiding a crime; a cool, ironic narrating voice; comedy of manners beside melodrama; the woman's viewpoint on marriage, money and the law.
authors.concerns: Marriage, bigamy and the legal non-existence of wives; madness and the asylum as instruments of family control; class, governesses and the genteel poor; money and the marriage market; theatricality and self-invention; the professional woman writer.
authors.significance: Braddon was the most widely read novelist in Britain in the 1860s and the central figure of the sensation vogue after Collins: she made the genre a woman's form, ran a magazine, and built a career independent of any male protector. Feminist criticism from the 1970s onward recovered Lady Audley's Secret as a serious analysis of the legal position of women, and Braddon is now canonical in Victorian fiction studies.

authors.name: Mary Lamb
authors.nationality: English; children's and educational writing of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Writer of books for children and of educational and religious works for young readers, and the collaborator with her brother in the retelling of Shakespeare that became a standard of nineteenth-century childhood.
authors.biography: Lamb was born in London, the younger sister of Charles Lamb, and was largely self-taught in a household in her brother's keeping. She began to publish for a juvenile market in the early years of the century, contributing a biography of the dramatists to a children's history series and writing verse and prose for the juvenile libraries. With her brother she retold the plays in a volume published in 1807, and she afterwards continued to work for children and to take part in the family's collaborative books. She suffered recurrent attacks of insanity, of which the deadliest was that of 18 March 1796, when she killed her mother; the illness governed the terms of her life and her brother's, and she was in and out of care for the rest of it. She died at Edmonton in May 1847 and was buried there beside her brother.
authors.profile: Her writing is chiefly didactic and for the young: retold fiction, a history of the dramatists written for juvenile readers, and other educational pieces, alongside the share in the collaborative tales and in the joint children's books that were printed over one or both names. The manner of the retellings is plain, brisk and moral, addressed to a child's capacity rather than to a child's fancy, and it carries an unusual weight of quotation from the original plays.
authors.style: A clear, unornamented narrative prose, close paraphrasing of dramatic speech, an economical moral framing, and a directness of address to the young reader; where her work is joint with her brother's, the plainer narrative manner is the distinguishable element.
authors.concerns: The education and moral formation of children; the transmission of Shakespeare to readers too young for the plays; the conduct of a life constrained by illness; dependence, duty and secrecy within a family.
authors.significance: The retellings she made with her brother became the standard introduction to Shakespeare for Victorian childhoods and are still in print, and her case has become central to the modern reassessment of authorship, collaboration and mental illness in Romantic-era writing, which has restored her name to works long printed under one author alone.
authors.uncertainty: The division of the plays between her and her brother in the volume of 1807 rests on later testimony and is variously reported, several of her works are printed without a name or over a shared title-page, and the intervals and severity of her illness are recorded only in the letters and reminiscences of the family.

authors.name: Mary Louisa Molesworth
authors.nationality: English; the children's novel and the family story
authors.identity: Writer for children; the most popular English author of the family story in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Mary Louisa Stewart in Rotterdam on 29 May 1839, where her father was a merchant; she was brought up in Manchester and educated privately in Switzerland and London. She married Major Richard Molesworth in 1861 and, after an unhappy marriage ended in separation, supported herself and her children by writing. She published her first children's book in 1877 and produced over a hundred books, including the Carrots and The Cuckoo Clock series. She died in London on 20 July 1921.
authors.profile: Molesworth wrote the children's novel of everyday family life: her children are neither angels nor monsters, her nurseries are full of real furniture and real quarrels, and her stories teach by example and affection rather than by sermon. Her fairy tales, especially The Cuckoo Clock, are among the finest Victorian fairy stories, and her portraits of the English nursery and its governesses are a permanent record of middle-class Victorian childhood.
authors.style: Plain, unhurried narrative; realistic dialogue, including the speech of servants and nurses; the small domestic incident as plot; gentle fantasy accepted as ordinary; a kindly, ironic narrator.
authors.concerns: Childhood and the nursery; the family and the household; education and the governess; illness; the fairy tale as a form of consolation; the relation of the middle-class child to servants and to the poor.
authors.significance: Molesworth was the most widely read children's writer in England between 1877 and 1900, and her books formed the taste of a whole generation: The Cuckoo Clock and The Tapestry Room are classics of the Victorian fairy tale, and her domestic stories are a key source for the history of Victorian childhood.

authors.name: Mary Martha Sherwood
authors.nationality: English; evangelical children's literature and missionary-education writing
authors.identity: Prolific evangelical children's author and educationist, the dominant English supplier of juvenile religious fiction between the Cheap Repository and the 1850s
authors.biography: Mary Martha Butt was born at Stanford, Worcestershire, on 6 May 1775, the elder daughter and second child of the Rev. Dr. George Butt, a clergyman and classical scholar whose death in 1795 left the family dependent; her mother had died when she was an infant, and she was raised partly under the discipline of a strict stepmother. An early ambition to write was formed on a French-themed novel and on the pious books of her childhood, and a conversion experience in the 1790s fixed the evangelical purpose of her work. On 30 June 1803 she married the Rev. Henry Watson Sherwood, an ordained chaplain of the East India Company who had been converted under Thomas Charles's influence and who later rose to be archdeacon of Agra. She followed him to India in 1804-05, living at Calcutta and in the North-Western Provinces at Cawnpore and Agra until 1816, keeping a school, superintending the education of Indian and Eurasian children, and absorbing the missionary world of the Baptists at Serampore and of the clergymen Hoby Martyn and Claudius Buchanan; the death in 1811 of little Henry, the Indian Christian servant or bearer who attended Captain (later Colonel) Barry St Leger and died of fever while waiting on him, supplied the incident she turned into The History of Little Henry and his Bearer (1814), written at Cawnpore from a missionary account of the boy's piety and instantly a best-seller, reaching its twenty-second edition by 1825 and its thirty-seventh by 1850. Her The History of the Fairchild Family; or, the Child's Manual (1818, first part; further parts in 1842 and 1847) made her name in England, and she followed it with The Lady of the Manor (1825-29), hundreds of tract-sized tales, verse, and textbooks, more than four hundred works in all, many of them written to maintain a household income and to fund the schools and missions she supported. After widowhood and declining health she lived quietly in England, still writing until her death on 20 September 1851.
authors.profile: Sherwood's canon is didactic fiction in every available juvenile form: the Indian tale and martyrdom story (Little Henry and his Bearer; The Indian Pilgrim; The Nun), the domestic family manual (The Fairchild Family), the village and squire-tale (The Lady of the Manor), verse and catechetical dialogues, alphabet books, travel narratives for children, and a stream of Cheap-Repository-style tracts. She also wrote journals and letters of missionary life and edited a family magazine.
authors.style: Unmistakably tract-style: brisk, plain, unornamented narrative built from incident, deathbed and moral reckoning, with dialogue serving doctrine. Her pathos is physical and specific - fever, dirt, the corpse, the saved child - and her terror is pedagogical, the famous death-of-Henry scenes designed to make salvation visible to a reader of six. Repetition, chapter-headings of proof-texts, and an unapologetic authorial intrusion mark the prose.
authors.concerns: The education of the child as the instrument of national and missionary future; the immortality of the soul as the only useful knowledge; caste, culture and Christianity in India; the duties and authority of mothers, governesses and clergy; providence in domestic economics; the moral economy of print and charity.
authors.significance: Sherwood virtually invented the Anglo-Indian children's book and made the missionary narrative a staple of the English nursery; Little Henry and his Bearer shaped British ideas of India and of Christian sacrifice for decades, and The Fairchild Family is the most influential English work of evangelical childhood before the 1850s, a decisive presence in the history of children's literature and of the missionary imagination that her books also made embarrassing to later readers. As a woman earning her living by the pen across empire, she marks the mass market of juvenile religious publishing.
authors.uncertainty: The day of her death is given variously as 20 and 22 September 1851; the year she sailed for India is reported as 1804 or 1805 depending on the account. Attributions within her huge and rapidly reprinted canon are unstable - The Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar (1818) is credited to her by library catalogues and the Hockliffe Collection but appeared in an uncertain trade context, and many of her four hundred titles survive only in re-issued or anonymous form.

authors.name: Mary Noailles Murfree
authors.nationality: American; the Southern mountaineer story
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature.
authors.biography: Born Mary Noailles Murfree at Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on 24 January 1850; lame from childhood, she spent her summers in the mountains of east Tennessee and published In the Tennessee Mountains under the name Charles Egbert Craddock in 1884. The Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains (1885), The Despot of Broomsedge Cove (1889) and The Frontiersmen (1904) followed. She died at Murfreesboro on 31 July 1922.
authors.profile: Mary Noailles Murfree was the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature: her Tennessee mountain stories of 1884 created the genre, and her dialect, her landscape and her feud narratives prepared the way for the Southern Renaissance and for the Appalachian novel.
authors.style: The mountain dialect rendered phonetically; the landscape of the Great Smokies as a character; the feud and the clan; the frame of the outsider visitor; the tragic ending without consolation.
authors.concerns: Regional identity and the American sectional character; the mountain poor and the feud; isolation and the closed community; the closing of the American frontier; the Southern past.
authors.significance: Mary Noailles Murfree was the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature: her Tennessee mountain stories created the genre, and her dialect, landscape and feud narratives prepared the way for the Southern Renaissance.

authors.name: Mary Prince
authors.nationality: Bermudian and Antiguan by enslavement, published in London; the first enslaved Black woman to give her testimony to the press in Britain, and a founding text of the women's slave narrative and of British immediatist agitation
authors.identity: An oral narrator rather than a writer. Her text was spoken and transcribed by Susanna Strickland and arranged and annotated by Thomas Pringle, and it appears in print as a first-person testimony with an editor's supplement, an appendix of documents and the appended narrative of Asa-Asa. Her literary form is the witness statement: a continuous account of hire, labour, punishment and endurance addressed to a public assumed to be ignorant and required to be convinced.
authors.biography: She was born in Bermuda about 1 October 1788, of enslaved parents, and she grew up in the hired-out childhoods of the island's poor, passed from holder to holder and put to domestic, field and out-of-door labour as a child. She describes with exactness the punishments inflicted for small faults, the injuries which left her permanently damaged in one eye and in her limbs, and the sequence of sales and bequests by which she came finally into the property of John Adams Wood, an Antiguan mariner, on whose Antigua estate and in whose household she worked for many years. When Wood travelled with his family to London in 1828 she found herself in a country where the law did not compel the service of the enslaved, left his household, maintained herself in the capital and came under the protection of antislavery friends there. Through the introduction of those friends she reached Thomas Pringle, the secretary of the London Anti-Slavery Society, who arranged that Susanna Strickland should take down her account, and The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave. Related by Herself, with a Supplement by the Editor, was published in London in 1831 at the charge of the Society, priced within the reach of the local auxiliary societies and of the women's subscriptions. Three editions were printed in that year and its evidence of flogging, of the punishment of expectant women and of the exposure of the sick in the field was attacked with fury by proslavery writers in Edinburgh and London. In 1833 Pringle recovered damages for libel, and Wood at once brought his own action against him, which the editor could not effectively answer because West Indian witnesses were unattainable; the threat of further suits stopped a projected fourth edition, and Pringle and his associates worked to secure Prince's freedom and her support. She disappears from the record after 1833, and the place and date of her death are unknown.
authors.profile: The History is built as testimony and its eloquence is that of exact statement. She names places, holders, overseers, instruments and numbers of lashes, and she dates her sufferings by the hurricanes, the droughts and the deaths that marked them. Where argument seems required she does not argue but reports, so that the reader supplies the verdict, and where grief seems required she turns at once to the condition of other women, to the mothers parted from their children and to the workers killed by over-exertion. The book is frankly devotional, holding to the hope of heaven and refusing to let Christian profession excuse the plantation, and its closing appeal to the mothers and women of England is among the most effectual passages of abolitionist prose.
authors.style: First-person witness narration, direct and unhedged; naming and numbering as the principal rhetorical device; short declarative sentences broken by exclamations of appeal; biblical cadence and lament; recurring address to the pity and conscience of the reader; an unsentimental register for bodily injury; editorial frames, notes and documents interposed around a voice that remains recognisably individual.
authors.concerns: Slavery as property in the body, in women's labour and in children; the exposure of tropical field and household service to metropolitan readers; the failure of Christian masters and the authority of an enslaved woman's own word; marriage, motherhood and the insecurity of the enslaved family; the freedom obtained in England and the legal doubts attending it; the complicity of a public that buys slave-grown produce and reads attacks on the narrative.
authors.significance: Her book of 1831 was the first narrative of a woman's experience of slavery published in Britain and one of the most effective pieces of evidence produced by the immediatist campaign before the abolition act of 1833; three editions appeared in its first year, it was reviewed and reprinted transatlantically, and it carried the condition of colonial slavery into ordinary reading. The litigation of 1833 which followed it laid bare the legal vulnerability of abolitionist publication, cost Pringle his position and suppressed a projected edition. Her text is now a foundational work of Caribbean and feminist literary history, a national text in Bermuda, and the earliest canonical instance of the enslaved woman's voice in English.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth is given as 1788 in Bermuda by the weight of modern authority, the day fixed to about the first of October by the narrative's own statement of her age, while a few accounts print 1787. Nothing certain is known of her death or of her whereabouts after 1833, and whether she remained in Britain or returned to the West Indies; no contemporary likeness of her survives. The succession of her early holders is variously reported, and the degree to which Pringle and Strickland shaped her dictated words is disputed, the text being testimony taken down rather than writing composed by its subject.

authors.name: Mary Robinson
authors.birthplace: Bristol, daughter of Nicholas Darby, a captain in the navy who deserted his family; the register of St Augustine's Church, Bristol records her baptism on 19 July 1757 with a memorandum that she was born on 27 November 1756, while she herself in her memoirs gave 1758 and the day as 27 November
authors.nationality: English; the Della Cruscan and newspaper verse of the 1780s and 1790s, the Romantic sonnet revival, the Gothic and domestic novel of the revolutionary decade, and the feminist prose controversy about the education and civil condition of women
authors.identity: Actress, poet, novelist, dramatist and feminist controversialist, famous first as the king's mistress 'Perdita' and afterwards as 'the English Sappho', who turned her celebrity into a professional literary career after her withdrawal from the stage
authors.biography: Mary Darby was born in Bristol, in the winter of 1756 or 1757 by the parish register and 1758 by her own account, the daughter of Nicholas Darby, a naval captain who deserted the family, and of a mother who took in sewing and kept the household with difficulty. Fond of poetry from childhood and precociously reading her Shakespeare, she was put to work as a teacher at fourteen and, having attracted the notice of actors and writers in Bristol, was married in 1772 to Thomas Robinson, a barrister's clerk and afterwards a soldier and actor of her own family's acquaintance. She appeared on the stage at Drury Lane as Juliet in 1776 and made her lasting reputation in December 1779 as Perdita in The Winter's Tale, a performance so admired that the young Prince of Wales, afterwards George IV, paid her an assiduous court; she is generally recorded as his first public mistress, the negotiation included an offer of £20,000 to relieve her husband's debts and to settle her allowance, and the connexion ended in 1781 in a public and humiliating rupture. The birth of her daughter Maria, who became an actress and then the wife of the painter Thomas Hoppner and was widely said to be the Prince's child, did not save her marriage; she was separated from her husband, and for some years in the 1780s lived on the Continent in France and Germany, partly to remove her from scandal and partly from debt. Returning to London she recovered her position by her pen: from 1788 she wrote society and occasional verse for the newspapers, joining the fashionable Della Cruscan circle associated with Robert Merry and answering his 'Della Crusca' numbers in The World under the name of Laura, and she was celebrated as 'the English Sappho'. In the 1790s she published collected Poems (1791, with a second volume in 1793), single-issue political and occasional verse including the Monody on the late Queen of France (1793), the sonnet sequence Sappho and Phaon (1796), a volume of Lyrical Tales (1800), eight novels beginning with Vancenza (1792) and including Walsingham (1797) and The Natural Daughter (1799), three plays, and feminist prose, most confidently her Letter to the Women of England on the Injustice of Mental Subordination (1799). Like Mary Wollstonecraft she argued for the rights and education of women and was an ardent supporter of the Revolution, though her poetry also mourned its victims. Consumption, a lingering and disfiguring illness, the loss of her favour and constant money troubles marked her last years; she retired to Surrey, and died in poverty at Englefield Cottage, Englefield Green, on 26 December 1800, aged by her own register entry forty-three. Her unfinished Memoirs, written by herself, were published posthumously in 1801 in London for Richard Phillips, with simultaneous New York and later Philadelphia editions; administration of her estate was granted to her estranged husband Thomas Robinson, who in 1803 unexpectedly inherited a substantial fortune from his half-brother William.
authors.profile: Her work divides into four bodies. Her poetry, gathered from newspaper and annual verse into Poems (two volumes, the first 1791, the second 1793) and reissued as a New Edition in 1795, includes the separately printed Monody on the Queen of France (1793), sight-poems such as 'Sight, the Cavern of Woe, and Solitude' (1793) and 'Modern Manners' (1793), and the odes issued at Manchester in 1797 and 1800; its centre is Sappho and Phaon, in a Series of Legitimate Sonnets, with Other Poems, and a Ballad (1796), the self-conscious classicising of her sonnet practice and her monument of her relation with Robert Merry, and its last achievement is Lyrical Tales (1800), a volume of ballads and metrical tales which answers Wordsworth and Coleridge poem by poem. Her novels, counted as seven or eight in the surviving record, comprise Vancenza; or, The Dangers of Credulity (1792), The Widow (1794), Angelina (1796), Hubert de Sevrac (1796), Walsingham; or, The Pupil of Nature (1797), The False Friend (1799) and The Natural Daughter (1799), are epistolary and Gothic or domestic tales of credulity, seduction, concealed parentage and contested inheritance, mostly printed for herself and sold by Hookham, or issued in four volumes for Longman, and paid for at prices she had to negotiate against her declining sales. Her dramas include the opera The Lucky Escape (1778), the comedy Nobody (1794), the opera Kate of Aberdeen (withdrawn 1793) and the tragedy The Sicilian Lover (1796). Her prose of argument includes Impartial Reflections (1791), the Letter to the Women of England (1799), Thoughts on the Condition of Women (1799), a translation of the Picture of Palermo (1800) and the Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson, Written by Herself (1801); her posthumous Poetical Works appeared from Richard Phillips in 1806 and again in 1824. The standard scholarly text is The Works of Mary Robinson, 8 volumes, general editor William D. Brewer (Pickering and Chatto, 2010), with Paula Byrne's biography Perdita: The Life of Mary Robinson (2004) as the usual biographical apparatus.
authors.style: Her early verse is the ornamental, allusive manner of the Della Cruscans, which she afterwards deliberately restrained; the sonnets of Sappho and Phaon claim the 'legitimate' form against the license of contemporary experiment, with a compressed diction, an archaeological interest in Sappho's fragments and a persistent identification of the poet-lover with the ancient Lesbian. Her later lyrics and Lyrical Tales take up ballad and popular stanza, plain speech and humble speakers, and the topography of the Wye and of the revolutionary wars. The novels are written in letters or as a series of tales within a frame, mixing Gothic excitement - convents, castles, ghosts, imprisonment - with an argument about belief: Vancenza is expressly a warning against the dangers of credulity, and Walsingham turns the fashionable 'pupil of nature' into a satirised self-justifying lover. Her polemic prose is personal, indignant and closely argued, addressing women directly and using her own injuries as evidence, and the Memoirs conduct the same defence in narrative, presenting her life as a history of male seduction and female dependence. Byron's dismissal of her in English Bards and Scotch Reviewers fixed the older view of her as a decorative poet, which modern editions have overturned.
authors.concerns: The injustice of women's mental and civil subordination and the claims of genius and education; the double standard by which a woman's sexual history destroys her credit while making her famous; the dependence of the woman writer on subscription, patronage and the booksellers; the dangers of credulity, superstition and Gothic belief against reason and evidence; the French Revolution, its promises, its terror and its victims, mourned in the Monody on the Queen of France and celebrated elsewhere; exile, travel and the condition of the refugee; seduction, concealed parentage and the fate of the illegitimate child; and the possibility of recovering a self and a reputation in print.
authors.significance: She is one of the most published and most reviewed women poets of the 1790s and a central figure in the Romantic sonnet revival, whose Sappho and Phaon reworked the Petrarchan sequence as the record of a woman's own desire and loss, and whose Lyrical Tales (1800), printed by Longman and Rees in the same year as the second edition of Lyrical Ballads, is the most sustained contemporary poetic answer to Wordsworth and Coleridge. Her novels carried the Gothic of the 1790s into a self-conscious critique of belief and of the marriage market, and her Letter to the Women of England is a staple text of the feminist controversy of the revolutionary decade, now standard in anthologies of the period. As Perdita she became a permanent figure of the royal scandal of the Prince Regency, and her posthumous Memoirs made the actress-courtesan-author into a model of autobiographical self-defence. Recent scholarship - Brewer's eight-volume edition, Byrne's life, Ashley Cross's study of her relation to Romantic literary history and the ongoing work on the Della Cruscans - has restored her from anecdote to a writer whose career defines the possibilities and the costs of female professional authorship between 1788 and 1800.
authors.uncertainty: Her year of birth is irreducibly uncertain: the Bristol register entry inspected by modern editors records her baptism on 19 July 1757 with a memorandum of birth on 27 November 1756, she herself gave 27 November 1758 in the Memoirs, and reference works have variously printed 1756, 1757 and 1758, while the Gentleman's Magazine obituary and some catalogues enter 1758. The terms of the Prince of Wales's settlement, including the sum of £20,000, rest on her own account and on report rather than on surviving documents; the paternity of her daughter Maria is asserted in tradition but not established; the date of her marriage to Thomas Robinson and of her separation are variously given; the number and dating of her plays and novels differ between the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry, the English Short Title Catalogue and her modern editors, and the separately printed odes of 1797 and 1800 exist in issues whose contents are not identical.

authors.name: Mary Russell Mitford
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Essayist, dramatist, and poet
authors.biography: Mary Russell Mitford was born in Alresford, Hampshire, and lived most of her adult life at Three Ponds near Reading, Berkshire, in genteel poverty after her grandfather's bankruptcy. Her father was a physician whose declining health made her the family's main earner. She began publishing verse and prose in 1811; Our Village (1824) brought her sudden popularity and a steady income. She wrote a series of historical dramas including Julian (1835) and Foscari (1826), the latter performed at Covent Garden. She corresponded extensively with the literary figures of her age and was a pioneer of the women's letter as literary form. She died in 1855 in Swallowfield.
authors.profile: Mitford is best known for Our Village, the supreme rural sketch sequence of the Romantic period, which created an influential model of intimate, affectionate, and gently humorous observation of village life. Her poetry and plays are now largely forgotten but were taken seriously in her lifetime; her letters are a major document of literary life in the early nineteenth century.
authors.style: Conversational essay prose; first-person persona of the gentlewoman observer; natural-history description; affectionate irony; a prose lyricism that brings landscape and character into a single observational mode.
authors.concerns: Rural community and its observances; the natural history of the English countryside; women's independence through professional writing; genteel poverty and its constraints; the village and the county as England.
authors.significance: Our Village founded the tradition of the English rural sketch book and remains a landmark of the Romantic prose of place; her model of the essayist persona influenced later writers from Charles Jefferies to the county writers of the Edwardian period.
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

authors.name: Mary Seacole
authors.nationality: Jamaican-Scottish; the travel narrative and the memoir of the Crimean War
authors.identity: Nurse, traveller and memoirist; the author of Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, one of the great Victorian autobiographies of travel and war.
authors.biography: Born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, the daughter of a Scottish army officer and a free black Jamaican woman who kept a boarding house; she learned nursing and doctoring from her mother and travelled to England, the Bahamas, Haiti and Cuba. She went to the Crimean War in 1855 after being refused by the official nursing service, ran the British Hotel behind the lines at Balaklava, and was present at the siege of Sevastopol. Her autobiography was published in 1857; she died in London on 14 May 1881.
authors.profile: Seacole wrote the memoir of a black woman's professional life in the British Empire: her narrative is comic, sharp, practical and unsentimental, and it records a journey through the colonial world — Jamaica, Panama, the Crimea — from a position that no other Victorian writer occupied. She writes as a businesswoman and a healer, claims her place at the front as a matter of right, and gives one of the very few first-hand accounts of the Crimean War by a woman of colour.
authors.style: First-person comic narrative with direct address to the reader; anecdotes of travel and medicine; the commercial traveller's eye for trade and provisions; self-deprecating irony that carries a serious claim to recognition.
authors.concerns: Race and the black subject of the British Empire; nursing and the professional woman; travel and the colonial world; the Crimean War and the army; commerce and self-making; the claim to belong.
authors.significance: Seacole is the most remarkable black British woman writer of the Victorian period: her memoir is a founding text of black British autobiography, a central account of the Crimean War and a permanent record of a black woman's professional life in the empire. Her exclusion from the official nursing service, and her presence at the front as an independent businesswoman, have made her a central figure in the history of race and medicine.

authors.name: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Translator, poet, and literary patron; the sister of Sir Philip Sidney and the most important female literary figure of the Elizabethan period after the queen.
authors.biography: Born 27 October 1561, daughter of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at home in French, Italian, and music. In 1577 she married Henry Herbert, second Earl of Pembroke, and made Wilton House a centre of letters; after her brother's death in 1586 she became his literary executrix, completing his verse translation of the Psalms (the Sidney Psalter) and supervising the publication of the Arcadia (1593). She translated Robert Garnier's Marc Antoine (1592) and Philippe de Mornay's Discours de la vie et de la mort (1592), wrote the pastoral dialogue for the queen's visit to Wilton (c. 1599), and patronized Spenser, Daniel, and Donne. She died of smallpox on 25 September 1621.
authors.profile: The presiding female patron of the Sidney circle, whose own translations — above all the 107 psalms of the Sidney Psalter — constitute one of the major poetic achievements of the period, uniting Reformed piety with the most sophisticated metrical experimentation in English.
authors.style: Metrical virtuosity (the Psalter uses over 120 different verse forms), learned paraphrase, and a devotional voice of disciplined intensity.
authors.concerns: The Protestant poetics of the psalm tradition; the consolation of mortality; the continuation of her brother's literary and religious legacy; female authorship within the bounds of aristocratic propriety.
authors.significance: The first English woman to sustain a major literary career as patron, editor, translator, and poet; the Sidney Psalter influenced Donne and Herbert and stands as the great English monument of the Genevan psalm tradition.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of her contribution to the Psalter (as against her brother's) is secure for Psalms 44–150; the degree of her editorial intervention in the 1593 Arcadia is debated.

authors.name: Mary Webb
authors.nationality: British; the Shropshire novelist of Precious Bane and the nature romance
authors.identity: Novelist; the Shropshire writer of Precious Bane and Gone to Earth.
authors.biography: Born Mary Gladys Meredith at Leighton, Shropshire, on 25 March 1881; she lived in the Shropshire hills and wrote the novels of the county - The Golden Arrow (1916), Gone to Earth (1917), The House in Dorset (1920), Seven for a Secret (1922) - until Precious Bane (1924), with its harelipped narrator and its bargain for the land, won the Femina prize and, after Stanley Baldwin's praise in 1928, a national public. She died at St Leonards-on-Sea on 8 October 1927.
authors.profile: Mary Webb is the Shropshire novelist of the English nature romance: Precious Bane, with its harelipped narrator Prue Sarn and its bargain for the land, is the most read provincial novel of the 1920s, and Gone to Earth carried the nature romance into the tragedy of the hunted creature. Her prose of the hills, the weather and the soul made the county a world.
authors.style: The charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather; the first-person narrator of the county speech; the bargain, the curse and the chapel set against the hill and the mere; the image drawn from the farm, the loom and the storm; the elegy of the hunted creature.
authors.concerns: The Shropshire hills and the mere; the bargain for the land and the price of the soul; the nonconformist chapel and the old religion of the hills; the woman and the hunted creature; nature as the moral weather of the novel.
authors.significance: Mary Webb is the Shropshire novelist of the English nature romance: Precious Bane, with its harelipped narrator and its bargain for the land, is the most read provincial novel of the 1920s, and her prose of the hills and the soul made the county a world.

authors.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Writer and philosopher and the most influential advocate of women's rational education of her generation.
authors.biography: Born on 27 April 1759 at Spitalfields in London into a family of limited means, she escaped an unhappy home, worked as a teacher and companion, and turned to letters in London, becoming associated with the publisher Joseph Johnson and radical intellectual circles. She published Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787) and the novel Mary (1788), alongside other works in the 1780s and early 1790s. Her famous Vindication of the Rights of Men appeared in 1790 and A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792. After years abroad and a relationship with Gilbert Imlay and later marriage to William Godwin, she died on 10 September 1797 shortly after the birth of her daughter, the future Mary Shelley.
authors.profile: A polemicist, novelist, and essayist whose arguments for women's reason and education and whose accounts of feeling and society mark her as a founder of modern feminist thought and a distinctive Romantic-era writer.
authors.style: Passionate, argumentative prose combining Enlightenment rationalism with the language of sentiment; direct, urgent polemic; and a morally intense, self-conscious narrative voice in her fiction.
authors.concerns: The rational education and moral standing of women; virtue, independence, and citizenship; the critique of Custom and prejudice; feeling and reason; and the rights and duties of the individual in society.
authors.significance: One of the most important and enduring writers in the history of feminist argument, whose works in the 1790s shaped debates about rights, gender, and education and whose reputation has grown steadily since her own time.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is well documented, largely through Godwin's Memoirs, whose candid detail was itself contested; the precise dating and reception of some minor writings remain matters of editorial reconstruction.

authors.name: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
authors.nationality: English; radical Romanticism and the philosophical and Gothic novel of the 1810s and 1820s
authors.identity: Novelist, biographer and editor; the creator of modern scientific romance and the chief prose fiction writer of the second generation of Romantic radicalism
authors.biography: She was the daughter of the philosophical writer on political justice and of the author of the vindication of the rights of woman, who died shortly after her birth; she was named for her mother and grew up in the father's house under the care of a stepmother whom she did not love. Her education was the extraordinary one of the Godwin library and circle, and in her teens she was visited by the poet who was to become her husband; in 1814 she left England with him, and the years of poverty, travel and the deaths of two children followed. In 1816, on the shore of a Swiss lake with other writers, a company of ghost-telling produced the first sketch of her tale of the made creature, which she enlarged into her first novel, published anonymously in 1818. Her husband drowned in Italy in 1822, leaving her with a young son and the task of editing and establishing his reputation, on which she worked for the rest of her life. She returned to England in 1823, wrote novels of historical and domestic calamity through the 1820s and 1830s, revised her first tale with a new preface in 1831 under her own name, and contributed tales, travel writing, biographical articles for a cabinet cyclopaedia and the memoranda to her husband's poems. She died in London in 1851, having spent her later years as a literary executrix of the Romantic movement.
authors.profile: Four completed novels of increasing historical and domestic reach, from the tale of the made creature to the plague ending of the last man, the romance of a pretended plantagenet prince and the study of a failed marriage; an unfinished novel; collections of tales and travel; and a lifetime's editorial work on the poetry and prose of her husband. Her fiction consistently places an ambitious solitary intellect in a world of family and obligation, and treats creation, pursuit and abandonment as moral problems rather than as machinery.
authors.style: A framed, embedded and epistolary narration which withholds the central disclosure until the last pages of its first books. A prose of lucid, restrained emotional report, with a powerful command of landscape as moral state. A tendency to argue by situation rather than by dialogue. And in the late fiction a plain, domestic realism quite unlike the Gothic opening.
authors.concerns: The responsibility of the maker; the claims and the desertion of family. The education of the sensitive being by society; ambition, guilt and the pursuit that follows. Epidemic and the end of political order; historical injustice and the rights of the disinherited. Women's confinement and choice.
authors.significance: Her first novel founded science fiction and remains the most endlessly adapted and quoted prose fiction of the Romantic period; her last man is the origin of the modern plague and post-apocalypse narrative. Her editorial and biographical work determined the shape in which the second generation of Romantics was transmitted to the nineteenth century, and her fiction is now central to study of the period's science, philosophy and gender.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of her husband's hand in the first draft of her earliest tale, and the dating of the 1816 sketch and the 1817 enlargement, are contested; her own journals and family papers have been edited and, in some accounts, altered.

authors.name: Mason Locke Weems
authors.birthplace: Anne Arundel County, Maryland, United States (near Herring Bay)
authors.nationality: American; early-national evangelical and juvenile-biography tradition
authors.identity: Episcopal clergyman, itinerant book agent and myth-making biographer whose Life of Washington became the standard American children's biography for generations
authors.biography: Mason Locke Weems was born on 11 October 1759 in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, near Herring Bay, of humble parentage; he is traditionally said to have owed the forenames "Mason" and "Locke" to the family that befriended his mother, and he himself cultivated the homely signature "Parson Weems". He was ordained a deacon and priest of the Episcopal Church in 1784, served Maryland parishes including All Hallows in Anne Arundel County, and supplemented a small stipend by teaching and by farming at his Bel Air plantation. The Revolution's debts and the collapse of Maryland's established church pushed him out of the pulpit and into the book trade: from the 1790s he became the most successful travelling book agent in the new republic, selling subscriptions for Philadelphia publishers, above all Mathew Carey, and peddling divinity, geography, schoolbooks and his own pamphlets through the Southern states with a packhorse and a printed advertisement. He first met George Washington in 1792 and, after Washington's death in 1799, compiled The Life of Washington, with Curious Anecdotes, Equally Honourable to Himself and Exemplary to His Young Countrymen (1800), an abridgement of David Ramsay's and John Marshall's lives reshaped into anecdote for young readers. It sold continuously, was reissued in edition after edition, in abridgements, in newspaper serialisation and in numerous unauthorized piracies through the nineteenth century, and it was into this book, in editions published after 1800, that Weems inserted the cherry-tree confession - "I cannot tell a lie" - which became the national parable of Washington's character, along with the little white-fence and snake stories. He later wrote lives of General Mercer (1810) and General Gates (1820) and religious tracts for children. He died while on a book tour at Beaufort, South Carolina, on 23 May 1825 and was buried at his Bel Air home in Maryland.
authors.profile: Weems is a maker of popular biography rather than a historian: his books fuse abridgement, sermon and anecdote, addressed to "young countrymen" and to family reading. Alongside The Life of Washington he produced military lives, devotional children's titles such as God's Ways Made Clear to Man, and a stream of prefaces, advertisements and promotional leaflets that are themselves a primitive American marketing literature.
authors.style: Plain, colloquial, garrulous and directly hortatory; short chapters of incident capped by moral application. The prose relies on dialogue, vernacular detail (the hatchet, the fence, the colt), apostrophe to the reader and a deliberate affect of guilelessness that lets invention pass as recalled anecdote. Repetition across editions was aggressive: passages were re-titled, expanded and re-combined to open new markets.
authors.concerns: Character formation of the republican child; the union of Protestant piety and civic virtue; the availability of fame and moral example as merchandise; the tension between pious fiction and historical truth; the diffusion of books into regions no publisher could reach.
authors.significance: Weems created the vernacular Washington - the honest boy, the farmer, the Christian patriarch - and thereby the dominant American origin-story of the nineteenth century and the template for the juvenile life-story industry. As Carey's agent he was a decisive figure in the commercial expansion of American publishing into the South and West, an author-businessman who showed that a book could be sold from the saddle. The cherry tree, long mistaken for documented history, is a case study in how legend enters a national curriculum.
authors.uncertainty: The project brief gave a Virginia birth; the sources checked (Wikipedia, Founders Online, the South Carolina Historical Society) place his birth in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, though he spent much of his career south of the Potomac and Virginia is often named in older accounts. The exact edition and year in which the cherry-tree anecdote first appears is variously reported (commonly after 1800, often given as the 1806 or 1809-10 expansions); the total count of editions and pirated reprintings is not firmly established. His parental history and the origin of his forenames are legendary.
