authors.name: Mathilde Blind
authors.nationality: German-born English; the long poem, the lyric and women's biography
authors.identity: Poet, biographer and translator; a leading woman of letters of the 1870s-90s and the first English biographer of George Eliot.
authors.biography: Born Mathilde Cohen in Mannheim on 21 March 1841; her mother remarried the revolutionary Karl Blind and the family settled in London in 1852 as political exiles. She was educated at a private school in London and became a freethinker, a feminist and an admirer of Mazzini and Shelley. She published The Prophecy of Saint Oran (1881), The Ascent of Man (1889) — a long evolutionary epic in blank verse — and a biography of George Eliot (1883), the first full life of the novelist. She died in London on 26 November 1896.
authors.profile: Blind wrote the poetry of evolution and of women's intellectual ambition: The Ascent of Man is a Victorian epic of Darwinian progress, and her lyrics and sonnets are among the most technically accomplished by a woman poet of the period. She was also a substantial critic and translator, and her life of George Eliot remains one of the most perceptive early accounts of the novelist.
authors.style: Blank-verse narrative epic; the sonnet and the lyric; scientific and evolutionary imagery; rhetorical and oratorical periods; translation from the German and the French; the biography as critical study.
authors.concerns: Evolution and the ascent of humanity; freedom and political exile; women's intellectual life and the right to love freely; Greek myth and the tragic; death and the natural world; the European revolutionary tradition.
authors.significance: Blind was one of the most ambitious women poets of the century: her Darwinian epic is unique in Victorian verse, her biography of George Eliot is a founding work of the feminist criticism of the novel, and her translations and essays made German and French literature available to English readers.

authors.name: Matthew Arnold
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period
authors.identity: Poet, school inspector and critic; the founder of English cultural criticism and the century's most influential theorist of the function of criticism.
authors.biography: Born on 24 December 1822, the son of Thomas Arnold, headmaster of Rugby; he was educated at Rugby and Balliol College, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate in 1843 and was elected to a fellowship in 1845. He became private secretary to Lord Lansdowne, travelled in Europe, and was appointed an inspector of schools in 1851, a post he held for thirty-five years. In 1851 he married Frances Lucy Wightman; the death of his father in 1842 and of his son in 1868 shape the elegiac poems. The Strayed Reveller (1849), Empedocles on Etna (1852), Poems (1853) and New Poems (1867) contain the verse; from 1857 he was Professor of Poetry at Oxford, and Essays in Criticism (1865), Culture and Anarchy (1869) and Literature and Dogma (1873) made him the central Victorian critic. He died suddenly in Liverpool on 15 April 1888.
authors.profile: Arnold's criticism defines the modern idea of culture as 'the best that has been thought and said' and of criticism as 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world'. His poetry is elegiac and classical, written in a restrained, slightly flat and deeply melancholic voice, and its subject is the loss of faith and the impossibility of action after the Romantics. From 1853 he deliberately suppressed Empedocles on Aetna because it dramatised a 'dialogue of the mind with itself' rather than offering a remedy, and the critical prose takes up the work the poetry could not do.
authors.style: Classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary; elegiac stanzas and blank-verse meditation; the use of a mask or a historical figure as a screen for personal feeling; in the prose, irony, urbanity, quotation and a taste for the telling phrase ('sweetness and light', 'Philistines', 'Barbarians', 'the archery of the intellect').
authors.concerns: The loss of religion and the consolations of culture; the conflict of Hellenism and Hebraism; the state, the aristocracy and the middle class as objects of satire; education and the national school system; the function of criticism in a commercial age; the sea of faith and the retreat of the supernatural.
authors.significance: Arnold invented the vocabulary of English cultural criticism: 'culture', 'Philistine', 'Barbarian', 'sweetness and light', 'the best that has been thought and said' all entered the language from his prose. Culture and Anarchy is the founding text of the English critique of industrial modernity, and its argument shaped Leavis, Eliot, Raymond Williams and the whole institutional history of English studies.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems; The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems rests on the publisher's records, the correspondence and the internal evidence rather than on a title page. 17 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text.

authors.name: Matthew Gregory Lewis
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Gothic novelist, dramatist, and translator of German Romantic drama
authors.biography: Matthew Gregory Lewis was born in London into a family of literary and diplomatic connections; his father was a critic and diplomat. Educated at Christ Church, Oxford, he entered Parliament briefly before devoting himself to writing. The Monk (1796) made him notorious at twenty-one and defined the English Gothic. He became a playwright and theatre manager at Covent Garden, staging Gothic melodramas and translations of Schiller. He travelled extensively, became a West Indian plantation owner attempting to reform his slaves' conditions, and died at sea returning from Jamaica, aged forty-two. The circumstances of his death — whether illness or suicide — remain debated.
authors.profile: Lewis specialised in the Gothic romance and its stage adaptations. His fiction exploited conventions of terror, sexual transgression, and Catholic imagery with deliberate sensationalism; his dramas translated those conventions into Regency popular theatre. He was a significant translator of Schiller, helping introduce German Romantic drama to England.
authors.style: Fast-paced, lurid prose saturated with Gothic imagery — dungeons, convents, demons; dialogue mixing colloquial realism with heightened declamation; embedded narratives and tales-within-tales drawn from the European romance tradition.
authors.concerns: The psychology of obsession and transgression; the corruption of religious authority; the boundary between terror and desire; the commercial possibilities of sensation in fiction and theatre; German Romantic drama and its relationship to the Gothic.
authors.significance: Lewis defined the English Gothic in the 1790s; The Monk established the genre's template for supernatural terror and sexual excess and shaped its commercial potential. His translations from Schiller anticipated later Romantic interest in German literature; his theatre work shaped Regency Gothic melodrama.
authors.uncertainty: The cause of his death at sea in 1818 is debated: some sources attribute it to fever, others to suicide.

authors.name: Matthew Paris
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: chronicler; cartographer; artist; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A monk of St Albans from 1217, he succeeded Roger Wendover as the abbey's chronicler in 1236 and made St Albans the foremost centre of English historical writing; friend and correspondent of Henry III, he travelled to Norway (1248) and died in 1259. He wrote, copied, and illuminated his own manuscripts with maps and drawings of exceptional skill.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronica Majora (begun c. 1240, continued to 1259), the greatest English chronicle of the thirteenth century; also the Historia Anglorum (abbreviation), the lives of the two Offas and of St Alban, and the Gesta Abbatum.
authors.style: Vivid, opinionated, encyclopedic narrative; fierce criticism of the king, the papacy, and the friars; the integration of maps, itineraries, and marginal drawings into the historical record.
authors.concerns: The liberties of the English church and kingdom against papal and royal encroachment; the moral judgement of rulers; the recording of contemporary events from documents and eyewitnesses.
authors.significance: The Chronica Majora is the indispensable narrative source for the reign of Henry III and a landmark of medieval book art as well as of historiography.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; his surname may reflect continental training.

authors.name: Matthew Prior
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and diplomat; a master of light verse, the burlesque, and the occasional poem, whose career under the patronage of Dorset and his diplomatic service produced the witty, polished poetry of the transition from Dryden to Pope.
authors.biography: Born 21 July 1664 in London, educated at Westminster School (where, per legend, the Earl of Dorset discovered him reciting Horace) and St John's College, Cambridge. Patronised by Dorset, he entered diplomacy and government service under the Earls of Portland and the Tories, serving at the negotiations of the treaties of Ryswick (1697) and Utrecht (1713) and as a Commissioner of Customs. He wrote the burlesque 'The City Mouse and Country Mouse' (with Montagu, 1687), Solomon on the Vanity of the World (1718), Alma, and many songs, tales, and epistles. He died on 18 September 1721.
authors.profile: The poet of urbane lightness, whose easy, witty verse and translations made him one of the most popular poets between Dryden and Pope and a model for the familiar style.
authors.style: Graceful octosyllabics and couplets; wit, irony, and colloquial ease; burlesque and mock-heroic; fable and tale; and a polished, Horatian lightness.
authors.concerns: Love and gallantry; the vanity of worldly ambition; politics and diplomacy; friendship and patronage; and moral philosophy in a light, Horatian key.
authors.significance: Prior's Poems on Several Occasions (1709) and later works were immensely popular; his light verse and translations helped form the Augustan taste and influenced Pope, who both admired and satirised him.
authors.uncertainty: Prior's life is well documented, though the anecdotes of his discovery by Dorset are partly legendary; his diplomatic career is recorded in state papers.

authors.name: Matthew Tindal
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Civil lawyer and deist, author of Rights of the Christian Church (1706) and of Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), the creed-book of eighteenth-century deism.
authors.biography: Born at Bere Ferrers in Devon, probably in 1657, the son of a clergyman, he went up to Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln and Exeter and became a fellow of All Souls. He conformed to Rome during the reign of James II and returned to the Church of England after the Revolution, an episode that sharpened his lifelong interest in church authority. The Rights of the Christian Church (1706) argued for a national establishment controlled by the state and answered his High Church critics; Vindiciae Judaeorum (1707) defended the Jewish nation against slanders. Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), published anonymously as the work of a person of the Church of England, reduced the gospel to a republication of the religion of nature and provoked dozens of answers within a year. He died on 16 August 1733.
authors.profile: The systematiser of deism, who read Christianity as a moral institution whose truth must be measurable by a reason common to all nations.
authors.style: Arid, lawyerly, definitional prose; axioms and corollaries and exhaustive division of terms; a polemical coolness that invites reply rather than assent.
authors.concerns: The reasonableness and universality of natural religion; the civil rights of churches and the reach of state supremacy; priestcraft, mystery and the commerce of God with man; the interests of Israel and of toleration.
authors.significance: Christianity as Old as the Creation gave deism its mature form and forced the apologetic literature of the 1730s into a defensive debate about reason, revelation and the political power of clergy.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is only approximately fixed, and his principal works were issued anonymously, complicating attribution.

authors.name: Max Beerbohm
authors.nationality: British; the essay, the parody and the caricature
authors.identity: Essayist, parodist and caricaturist; the wittiest writer of the 1890s and the finest parodist in English.
authors.biography: Born Henry Maximilian Beerbohm in Kensington on 24 August 1872; he went from Charterhouse to Oxford, published The Works of Max Beerbohm in 1896 and became the drama critic of the Saturday Review in 1898. Zuleika Dobson (1911), Seven Men (1919) and A Christmas Garland (1912), the greatest book of parodies in English, followed. He lived in Rapallo from 1910 and died there on 20 May 1956.

authors.style: The parody that catches the style exactly; the essay of elegant nonsense; the caricature in prose; the period detail of the 1890s; the epigram and the exquisite, measured sentence.

authors.significance: Max Beerbohm was the wittiest writer of the 1890s and the finest parodist in English: Zuleika Dobson is the only great English comic novel about Oxford, and A Christmas Garland perfected and thereby ended the art of parody.

authors.name: Michael Banim
authors.birthplace: Kilkenny city, county Kilkenny, on 5 August 1796, elder brother of John Banim and son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper, and of Judith Banim (née Carroll)
authors.nationality: Irish; the Catholic Irish tale of the peasantry and of 1798, written in partnership with his brother John under the persona of 'the O'Hara Family'. Joint with John: Tales by the O'Hara Family, first series (1825) and second series (1826), the songs of the Chaunt of the Cholera (1831), The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). Single-handed, and usually the graver and more historical half of the partnership: The Croppy (1828), The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833), The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835), Clough Fionn (1852) and The Town of the Cascades (1864)
authors.identity: Novelist and tale-writer, the quieter and longer-lived of the two Kilkenny brothers, who carried most of the joint Irish tales after John's fame had begun to fail, added a rebellion novel and a ghost story of his own, and spent his later years as a public servant in his native city and as the custodian of his brother's reputation and papers.
authors.biography: Michael Banim was born in Kilkenny city on 5 August 1796, the elder brother of John Banim, and son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper; he was bred in the same Catholic, schoolmaster-ridden, remembrance-obsessed world of Midland Kilkenny that supplied the matter of the O'Hara tales. He was intended for the law, was entered briefly as a student and abandoned it to help in his father's business, and so stayed at home and in Ireland while John tried painting in Dublin and journalism in London. The partnership that made the brothers' name was formed at a distance: he supplied the local knowledge, the Irish speech and much of the substance of the first series of Tales by the O'Hara Family in 1825 and of the second in 1826, and he contributed to the tales afterwards reissued as 'John Doe' and 'The Fetches' while John's share was more widely advertised. After the brothers' quarrels with fortune he published on his own account The Croppy, a tale of 1798, in 1828, the ghost story The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833), the country-politics comedy The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835), and with John the joint volumes The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). On his brother's death in 1842 he became the family's literary executor and its public historian, writing the notice in The Nation and furnishing P. J. Murray with the materials and recollections of the Life of John Banim of 1857. He took a prominent place in the civic and political life of his native city, serving as postmaster of Kilkenny through the 1850s and 1860s and as mayor, and he published late fiction of Irish landscape and tradition, Clough Fionn in 1852 and The Town of the Cascades in 1864. He retired to Booterstown near Dublin, where he died on 30 August 1874, outliving by a generation the fame which had been shared and which the histories of the Irish novel have only lately tried to divide between the brothers again.
authors.profile: His work is narrative and largely Irish in subject: the collaborative peasant and national tale of the two O'Hara series (1825, 1826) and of the later joint books, to which his contributions of local custom, Shrove Tuesday and country-wedding description are considerable; the rebellion novel The Croppy (1828), which made 1798 a matter of sympathy rather of caricature; the supernatural tale The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833); the comic country-politics novel The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835); and the late romances of Irish place and tradition, Clough Fionn (1852) and The Town of the Cascades (1864). He also wrote verse and song with his brother and left memoir and editorial matter on which all later biography of the pair depends.
authors.style: A plainly told, oral and dialogic narrative in Irish English, transcribing peasant speech at length, with a strong eye for custom, ceremony and the texture of country business; a heavier and more directly historical seriousness than John's, since the rebellion and the priesthood are handled as public events rather than as picaresque matter; and a fondness for the ghost story's machinery of fetches, warnings and death-beds, where the sentences shorten and the description is repeated for effect. His comedy is of electioneering, of the public house and of the ambitious farmer, and the later prose is more deliberate, more explanatory and more antiquarian.
authors.concerns: The justice and the meaning of 1798 and of secret society oathing in Ireland; the priesthood, the Mass-place and the moral order of a penal peasantry; death, haunting and the credibility of the supernatural in a Catholic country; the effect of the union, of electioneering and of the relief and dispensary system upon rural society; the authenticity of Irish names, topography and tradition; the ethics and the economics of joint authorship, and the duty of a brother to a brother's fame.
authors.significance: As the joint author of the Tales by the O'Hara Family he helped to transfer the representation of the Irish peasant from Anglo-Irish management to Irish, Catholic and self-respecting narration, a move that matters in the line running to the fiction of the Nation, to Lever and to the Irish revival; The Croppy is one of the earliest sympathetic Irish novels of the 1798 rebellion, and his ghost and country tales are documents of supernatural and popular-culture writing in the 1830s. He also preserved the record of the partnership, and the uncertainty over which brother wrote what makes him a central instance of the collaborative, pseudonymous production of the early Victorian literary market.
authors.uncertainty: His birth year is given now as 1796 and now as 1800 in older catalogues, and the elder or younger rank of the brothers is reversed in different sources; attribution between them of the O'Hara tales, of 'Crohoore of the Billhook', 'The Mayor of Windgap' and the Chaunt of the Cholera songs is still disputed, the personae 'Abel' and 'Barnes' O'Hara are assigned inconsistently, and the volume sometimes cited for him as 'The Ghost Book and Other Pictures' could not be traced in the printed bibliographies, which give The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833).

authors.name: Michael Drayton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet; the author of Idea, Poly-Olbion, and 'Since there's no help', the most prolific and professionally dedicated of the Elizabethan poets.
authors.biography: Born 1563 at Hartshill, Warwickshire, where he served as a page in the household of Sir Henry Goodere; possibly at Oxford for a time. He settled in London in the 1590s as a professional writer, publishing the sonnet sequence Idea (1594, revised to 1619), the historical legends (Mortimeriados 1596, revised as The Barons' Wars 1603; England's Heroical Epistles 1597), the pastoral Endimion and Phoebe (1595), and the vast topographical poem Poly-Olbion (1612, 1622), before the late odes and elegies of his Poems (1619) and The Muses Elizium (1630). He died in London on 23 December 1631 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The period's most devoted professional poet, who ranged across every genre — sonnets, epistles, odes, pastorals, topography, satire, and the 'nymphidia' fairy verse — and revised his canon continuously across five decades.
authors.style: Varied and capable rather than intense; the elegant sonnet, the sinewy epistle, the ambitious chorographical couplet of Poly-Olbion, and a late lyric grace ('Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part').
authors.concerns: English topography and the nation's antiquities; the historical memory of the Wars of the Roses; the poet's fame and the patronage system; love's vicissitudes.
authors.significance: The most complete professional man of letters of the age; Poly-Olbion is the great topographical poem of England, and his sonnets and odes remained in the anthologies that formed later English taste.
authors.uncertainty: Details of his early life and of his alleged service to the Goodere family rest on late testimony; much of his early work survives only in his own revisions.

authors.name: Michael Field
authors.nationality: English; the dramatic monologue, the lesbian lyric and the verse of the aesthetic movement
authors.identity: Poets and diarists; the pseudonymous partnership of Katharine Bradley and her niece Edith Cooper, whose joint work is the greatest body of English love poetry written by two women.
authors.biography: Michael Field was the pen name of Katharine Harris Bradley (1846-1914) and her niece and lover Edith Emma Cooper (1862-1913), who lived together from 1878 and wrote poems, plays and travel books as a single author. They were friends of Robert Browning, Ruskin and the Pater circle, published The Long Ago (1881), Underneath the Bough (1893) and Wild Honey from Various Thyme (1908), converted to Catholicism in 1907, and died within nine months of one another at Richmond. The rediscovery of their 9,000-page journal in the twentieth century made them central to the history of English lesbian literature.
authors.profile: Michael Field wrote the poetry of a shared life: their lyrics of love between women, written in the forms of the Elizabethan and the Celtic revival, are the most sustained English poetry of female desire in the nineteenth century. They were also considerable classical scholars, and their verse dramas and their journals are an extraordinary record of the aesthetic movement, of Victorian travel and of a lifelong partnership.
authors.style: The sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric; classical and mythological subjects; the lyric of intimacy and secrecy; the diary as a literary form; travel writing; devotional poetry after the conversion.
authors.concerns: Love between women and the secrecy of the shared life; classical myth and Sappho; art, poetry and the religion of beauty; travel and the European landscape; Catholic conversion and the saints; the passing of time.
authors.significance: Michael Field is the greatest and most neglected body of English love poetry written by two women: the authorship of two women in one voice, the lyrics of intimacy and the extraordinary journal have made the pair central to the recovery of Victorian women's writing and of the history of sexuality.
authors.uncertainty: A joint pseudonym: Katharine Harris Bradley (1846-1914) and Edith Emma Cooper (1862-1913) published as one author; the birth and death dates here span the two lives.

authors.name: Miles Coverdale
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Bible translator; bishop of Exeter
authors.biography: Born about 1488 in the North Riding of Yorkshire; educated at Cambridge and an Augustinian friar before converting to the Reformation. Working in Antwerp, he produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, and he edited the Great Bible of 1539, which was ordered to be read in every parish church. Bishop of Exeter in 1551, he went into exile under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying on 20 January 1569.
authors.profile: The translator of the first complete printed English Bible. The Coverdale Bible (1535), translating chiefly from German and Latin versions, gave the English church its Psalter — still sung as Coverdale's version in the Book of Common Prayer — and the Great Bible (1539) put an English Bible in every parish church, its wording (largely Tyndale's) forming the base of the Authorized Version.
authors.style: A flowing, musical prose less angular than Tyndale's; mastery of the cadence of the Psalms; the dignity of liturgical English.
authors.concerns: The complete vernacular Bible; the Psalter in English worship; the reform of the church through the Word.
authors.significance: Completed the English Bible and fixed the English Psalter; the Coverdale Psalms remain in liturgical use into the twenty-first century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate; the exact place of printing of the 1535 Bible (Antwerp or Cologne) is debated.

authors.biography: Born Mary Nesta Skrine at Newbridge, County Kildare, on 20 July 1904, the daughter of the poet Moira O'Neill; she published eight novels as M. J. Farrell from The Knight of Cheerful Countenance (1926) to The Rising Tide (1937), with the comedy Spring Meeting (1938, with John Perry) beside them, and returned after the war as Molly Keane with Good Behaviour (1949) and the late masterpieces. She died at Ardmore, County Waterford, on 22 April 1996.
authors.profile: Molly Keane is the satirist of the Anglo-Irish big house: the Farrell novels of the 1920s and 1930s dissected the vicious snobbery of her own class with the affection of the insider, and the return as Molly Keane made the big-house novel one of the forms of the Irish twentieth century.
authors.style: The satirical sentence of the insider; the big house, the hunt and the drawing room of the Anglo-Irish; the dialogue of the class that cannot see itself; the comedy of manners turned to the elegy of the house; the later first-person of the unloved daughter.
authors.concerns: The Anglo-Irish big house and its decay; the snobbery and the genteel racism of the class; the hunt, the dinner and the drawing room; the woman of the house and the unloved daughter; the comedy of manners as the elegy of a class.

authors.name: Mona Caird
authors.nationality: English; the feminist essay and the New Woman novel
authors.identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of 'Marriage', the essay that provoked the greatest debate on marriage in Victorian England.
authors.biography: Born Alice Mona Alison at Ryde, Isle of Wight, on 24 May 1854; she married James Henry Caird in 1877 and published her first novel, Whom Nature Leadeth, in 1883. Her essay 'Marriage' appeared in the Westminster Review in 1888 and provoked over 27,000 replies in the periodical press; she wrote seven novels, including The Daughters of Danaus (1894), and campaigned for women's suffrage and against vivisection. She died at Rye, Sussex, on 4 February 1932.
authors.profile: Caird wrote the most radical English feminist argument of the 1880s: 'Marriage' attacks the indissoluble marriage as a form of legalised slavery and calls for divorce on the grounds of incompatibility, and the storm it caused made the marriage question unavoidable. Her novels — especially The Daughters of Danaus — are the most intellectually ambitious of the New Woman fictions, and they test the feminist case against the actual lives of women.
authors.style: The polemical essay with a plain and logical argument; the thesis novel with a wide social canvas; the analysis of the marriage law; the satirical portrait of the anti-feminist; the tragic ending refused by the conventional novel.
authors.concerns: Marriage and divorce law; the woman artist and the sacrifice of vocation; maternity and the 'maternal instinct'; the economic position of the married woman; the double standard; the ethics of heredity and vivisection.
authors.significance: Caird is the most radical English feminist theorist of the 1880s and the author of the essay that created the Victorian marriage debate: 'Marriage' is a founding document of English feminism, and The Daughters of Danaus is one of the most important New Woman novels.

authors.name: Mrs Henry Wood
authors.nationality: English; the sensation novel and the domestic serial
authors.identity: Novelist; the author of East Lynne, the most successful sensation novel of the 1860s and one of the most performed plays of the century.
authors.biography: Born Ellen Price at Worcester on 17 January 1814, the daughter of a glove manufacturer; she married Henry Wood in 1836 and lived in France before returning to England in 1856. East Lynne (1861) made her famous and was reprinted eight times in its first year; she edited the Argosy from 1867 and wrote over thirty novels. She died in London on 10 February 1887.
authors.profile: Mrs Henry Wood wrote the Victorian domestic sensation novel with a moral seriousness that her rivals lacked: East Lynne is the story of a wife who elopes, loses her child, returns as a governess and dies of remorse, and its combination of adultery, retribution and maternal grief made it the century's most successful example of the form. Her novels are the finest record of the Victorian middle-class home under threat.
authors.style: Direct, urgent narrative address; the domestic interior rendered in detail; the moral catastrophe that follows a single error; the deathbed scene; the author's commentary and warning; the serial cliff-hanger.
authors.concerns: Marriage, adultery and the fallen woman; the family and its destruction; class, inheritance and legitimate birth; mothers and children; the law and the courtship plot; the middle-class home and its secrets.
authors.significance: Mrs Henry Wood is the most successful woman novelist of the sensation school and East Lynne one of the central novels of the 1860s: it sold in hundreds of thousands, was dramatised all over the world for fifty years, and its portrait of the erring wife and the lost child made it the definitive Victorian sensation novel.

authors.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
authors.nationality: American; the romance, the tale and the literature of the Puritan past
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the first great American novelist and the master of the American romance.
authors.biography: Born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804, into a family descended from a judge of the 1692 witch trials; he was educated at Bowdoin College, where his friends were Longfellow and Franklin Pierce. He published Twice-Told Tales in 1837 after twelve years of solitary apprenticeship, worked in the Boston customs house and the Salem custom house, and published The Scarlet Letter in 1850, followed by The House of the Seven Gables (1851), The Blithedale Romance (1852) and The Marble Faun (1860). He was American consul at Liverpool in 1853-57 and died at Plymouth, New Hampshire, on 19 May 1864.
authors.profile: Hawthorne wrote the American romance as an enquiry into guilt: his subject is the inward consequence of sin, the secret life of the respectable, and the relation of the present to a Puritan past that will not let it go. His method is allegory handled with great psychological delicacy — the scarlet letter, the birthmark, the house of seven gables — and his prose is a cool, deliberate, faintly ironic instrument for the analysis of conscience.
authors.style: Allegory with psychological depth; the single emblem around which a story is built; the romance of the 'neutral territory' between the real and the imaginary; the narrator's ironic commentary; the long retrospective sentence; the New England past as a haunting.
authors.concerns: Sin, guilt and the conscience; the Puritan inheritance and the witch trials; secrecy and the divided life; the artist and the community; adultery and the position of women; the American past and the failure of utopia.
authors.significance: Hawthorne is the first major American novelist and the central writer of the American romance: The Scarlet Letter is the founding novel of American literature, his tales created the American short story of moral mystery, and his influence runs through Melville, James, Faulkner and O'Connor.

authors.name: Nathaniel Lee
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Restoration tragedian; the leading exponent of heroic drama after Dryden, whose bombastic but powerful The Rival Queens (1677) held the stage for two centuries, and who collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus and The Duke of Guise.
authors.biography: Born c. 1653 at Waltham Abbey, Essex, son of a clergyman; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge. He turned from brief attempts at law and teaching to the stage, writing heroic plays and tragedies including The Tragedy of Nero (1674), Sophonisba (1675), Gloriana (1676), and his great success The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great (1677). He collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus (1679) and The Duke of Guise (1682). Suffering from mental illness and alcoholism, he was confined in Bedlam (1684–88); released after the Revolution, he wrote The Princess of Cleve (1689) and died in poverty on 6 May 1692.
authors.profile: The passionate, sometimes ranting tragedian of the Restoration, whose heroic and blank-verse tragedies of overwhelming emotion and elevated rhetoric were enormously popular and long-lived on the stage.
authors.style: Elevated, bombastic rhetoric; heroic couplets and blank verse; scenes of violent passion and grandiose declamation; and, at best, real pathos and poetic power.
authors.concerns: Heroic passion, love, and glory; political conspiracy and tyranny; madness and the extremes of emotion; and the fate of great figures.
authors.significance: The Rival Queens was one of the most frequently performed plays from the Restoration into the nineteenth century; Lee's heroic tragedy carried the mode to its popular peak and influenced the acting style of the age.
authors.uncertainty: Lee's birth year is approximate and his biography, including his madness and Bedlam confinement, is documented but partly anecdotal.

authors.name: Nicholas Rowe
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English dramatist, poet, and editor, appointed Poet Laureate in 1715, celebrated for sentimental tragedy and an early scholarly edition of Shakespeare.
authors.biography: Rowe was educated at the Middle Temple and turned early to the stage. His first play, The Ambitious Statesman (1697), was followed by Jane Shore (1700) and The Fair Penitent (1703), the latter containing the villain Lothaire and often considered his finest. He wrote several further tragedies, including a Lucius Junius Brutus and a Lady Jane Grey. In 1709 he published an edition of Shakespeare, an early largely scholarly attempt to edit the plays and to give accounts of the actors, drawing on earlier sources and issued through the publisher Jacob Tonson. A Whig, he succeeded Thomas Tate as Poet Laureate in 1715 and died unexpectedly in London at the end of 1718.
authors.profile: A playwright of domestic and sentimental tragedy and a literary editor; his dramas turn on female virtue, seduction, and penitence, and his Shakespeare edition began the formal text-critical study of the plays.
authors.style: Smooth, decorous blank verse; moralising pathos; well-made tragic situations; and an editorial method marked by conjectural emendation and a taste for regularity and probability.
authors.concerns: Virtue under assault and the ethics of penitence; domestic and feminine suffering; national literary heritage and the canonisation of Shakespeare; and Whig political virtue.
authors.significance: His 1709 Shakespeare is a founding document of English literary scholarship and editing, and as laureate and dramatist he shaped early eighteenth-century taste in tragedy and commemorative verse.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is not securely recorded; Rowe is associated with places in Buckinghamshire and the south, and the precise location of his birth remains uncertain.

authors.name: Nicholas Udall
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: playwright; schoolmaster; translator
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1504; educated at Winchester and Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Headmaster of Eton from 1534 (dismissed in 1541) and later of Westminster, he was a reformer who prospered under Edward VI and Mary alike. His Ralph Roister Doister, written about 1552, was printed about 1566. He died on 23 December 1556.
authors.profile: Author of the first English comedy. Ralph Roister Doister — five acts of Roman comedy built on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, with the braggart soldier, the parasitic Merrygreek, and the London widow Dame Christian Custance — transplanted classical comic structure into English life and English verse, establishing the pattern the Elizabethan comedians followed.
authors.style: Doggerel couplets of deliberate comic roughness; the miles gloriosus and the cunning servant in English dress; songs and jigs built into the action.
authors.concerns: The imitation of Roman comedy; school drama as moral and rhetorical training; the comic punishment of vanity and presumption.
authors.significance: Wrote the first English comedy on the classical model, the direct ancestor of the Elizabethan stage comedy; his school drama linked the interlude tradition to the professional theatre.
authors.uncertainty: The precise date and first printing of Roister Doister are uncertain (c. 1552–53, printed c. 1566).

authors.name: Noah Webster
authors.nationality: American; the New England Federalist letters of Hartford and New Haven, and the national project of an American language, an American spelling and an American education
authors.identity: Lexicographer, grammarian, orthoepist, schoolbook maker, political pamphleteer and newspaper editor; the man who gave American English its spelling, its schoolbook and its dictionary, and who argued that a republic must have its own language as well as its own government.
authors.biography: Webster was born at West Hartford in Connecticut, of a family of farmers and deacons with a strong notion of learning in it, and was put forward to Yale, whose courses were interrupted by the war, graduating in 1778. He studied law, was admitted to the bar, and found that the law in a new country would not maintain him; for some years he kept schools and taught in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York while he collected materials for a system of English education suited to the United States. The first part of his Grammatical Institute, the spelling book which Americans carried in their satchels for a century, appeared in 1783, and he travelled through the states to introduce it and to persuade the legislatures and the congress to secure to authors and printers a property in their books. He took part in the great argument over the frame of government with an examination of the leading principles of the Constitution, which was among the earliest and most widely read expositions of the new instrument, and he wrote afterward against slavery, against the political and religious consequences of infidelity, and for the measures by which a republic might preserve its character. In 1793 he established at New York the first daily newspaper of that city, a Federalist journal which he conducted for some years and in which he wrote most of its columns himself; he removed to New Haven about 1798 and gave the rest of his life to language, education and religion. His Compendious Dictionary of 1806 was the first considerable dictionary published in the United States, and the two-volume American Dictionary which followed in 1828, prepared with interruptions over more than two decades, with a tour of Europe for the study of the kindred languages and with an enormous correspondence, gave the country its standard of authority in words, its enlarged vocabulary of the arts and of the new republic, and its practical settlement of spelling. He wrote grammars, readers and treatises on the language, revised and corrected the text of the Bible for household reading, took a constant part in the schools, the public affairs and the religious and moral societies of Connecticut, and was a strenuous and sometimes unattractive controversialist on orthography, copyright, education and the temperance of the age. He died at New Haven on 28 May 1843, in possession of a fame which Americans already understood as their own, and was buried in the cemetery there; the property in his dictionary passed into other hands and became, through revision, the great American lexicographical work of the later century.
authors.profile: His writings are a system rather than a set of separate books: the spelling book, grammar and reader which made his name in the schools; the dictionaries of 1806 and 1828, the second built on a great enlarged vocabulary, with illustrations of use and with a preface arguing that language grows from the people who speak it; the political pamphlets of the ratification and of the 1790s; the newspaper columns, letters and dissertations on the language, on the origin of words, on the effects of slavery and on the education of the young; and the religious tracts and Bible revision of his old age. He was also a traveller and a collector of the statistics of the country, and his journals and records amount to an unmatched acquaintance with the speaking and the schooling of the United States.
authors.style: In the schoolbooks an economy and practicality of method - the syllabary, the exponent, the table and the lesson - which sets the tone of American instruction and is spare, direct and often bluntly moral; in the prefaces and dissertations a long, argumentative and accumulative prose, full of etymological matter, of tables of pronunciation and of national argument; in the journals of the 1790s a dense, urgent and combative Federalist style; and in the dictionary definitions a precision of generalizing which is the best of his writing.
authors.concerns: The relation of a national language to national independence and national character; the reform and fixing of spelling, pronunciation and usage; the education of a republican people and the morals of the common school; copyright and the property of authors; the principles of the Constitution, the danger of French revolutionary opinion, and the sin of slavery; the divine authority and the right reading of the Bible, and the duty of a Christian lexicography.
authors.significance: He made American English a self-respecting standard, and his spelling book and dictionary together gave the United States the orthography and the reference book which still distinguish it from Britain; no single writer did more to create a national medium of instruction, and his argument that language is a national institution passed into the mainstream of American educational and political thought. His dictionary is the foundation of the great American lexicographical tradition, his advocacy helped secure the first American system of protection for authors and printers, and his editorial and political work belongs to the making of the Federalist party and of the American public sphere of the 1790s.
authors.uncertainty: The exact periods and places of his schoolkeeping and of his law study are unsettled, and the chronology of the several parts, issues and pirated editions of the spelling book is complicated and variously told; the dates of his European journeys and the extent to which his later dictionaries drew on the collections of his correspondents cannot be precisely measured.

authors.name: Noel Coward
authors.nationality: British; the comedy of manners, the revue and the popular song
authors.identity: Playwright, composer, actor and director; the most performed English dramatist of the period and the definitive voice of interwar sophistication.
authors.biography: Born Noël Pierce Coward at Teddington on 16 December 1899; he went on the stage as a child, wrote his first play at eleven and served in the army in the First World War. The Young Idea (1923), The Vortex (1924), Hay Fever (1925), Bitter Sweet (1929), Private Lives (1930), Cavalcade (1931), Design for Living (1933), Blithe Spirit (1941) and Brief Encounter (1945) made him the most successful playwright of his time; he wrote the songs, composed the music and directed and starred in the productions. He was knighted in 1970 and died in Jamaica on 26 March 1973.
authors.profile: Coward is the most performed English dramatist of the period and the definitive voice of interwar sophistication: Private Lives and Hay Fever are the finest English comedies of manners of the century, Blithe Spirit is the best English comedy of the supernatural, and Brief Encounter (from his one-act Still Life) is one of the great English films. His songs — 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen', 'Mad About the Boy', 'Someday I'll Find You' — are the period's lyric poetry of the drawing room.
authors.style: The epigram and the witty exchange; the symmetrical three-act construction; the single drawing-room set; the sophisticated, amoral, unillusioned tone; the song written into the action; the revue's sketch structure and the musical's integration of song and scene.
authors.concerns: Love, marriage and infidelity among the leisured; the country house weekend and the Riviera hotel; the pursuit of pleasure and the fear of boredom; the changing position of women; class, money and the nouveaux riches; the English abroad.
authors.significance: Coward is the most performed English dramatist of the period: Private Lives and Hay Fever are the finest comedies of manners of the century, Blithe Spirit and Brief Encounter are permanent, and his songs and revues made him the voice of interwar England. He is the period's definitive comic dramatist.

authors.name: Olaf Stapledon
authors.nationality: British; the future history, the cosmic romance and the philosophy of the species
authors.identity: Philosopher and novelist; the most ambitious writer of the scientific romance, the author of Last and First Men and Star Maker, and the inventor of the cosmic future history.
authors.biography: Born William Olaf Stapledon at Seacombe, Wallasey, on 10 May 1886; he read modern history at Oxford, worked in a shipping office in Liverpool and with the Friends' Ambulance Unit in the First World War, took a PhD in philosophy at Liverpool, and taught at West Kirby. Last and First Men (1930), Last Men in London (1932), Odd John (1935), Star Maker (1937) and Sirius (1944) followed; he lectured and wrote on ethics and politics until his death at Caldy on 6 September 1950.
authors.profile: Stapledon wrote the most ambitious scientific romances in English: Last and First Men tells the history of eighteen future human species over two billion years, Star Maker the history of the universe and its creator, and Odd John and Sirius the first serious studies of the superman and the animal mind. He gave science fiction its cosmic scale and its philosophical seriousness, and no writer of the genre has since attempted what he did.
authors.style: The future history narrated by a species rather than a character; the immense time-scale and the biological transformation; the philosophical essay folded into narrative; the invented terminology and the imagined religion; the plain, lucid, unornamented prose of the philosopher.
authors.concerns: The future of the species and of the universe; evolution, biology and the transformation of the mind; the superman and the next step; war, civilisation and the possibility of peace; God, the stars and the spiritual life; the individual life against the cosmic scale.
authors.significance: Stapledon wrote the most ambitious scientific romances in English and gave science fiction its cosmic scale: Last and First Men and Star Maker are unique in the genre, Odd John and Sirius founded the serious treatment of the superman and the animal mind, and his philosophical seriousness has never been matched.

authors.name: Olaudah Equiano
authors.birthplace: Essaka, in the interior of what is now Nigeria (contested; a birth in South Carolina has also been argued)
authors.nationality: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
authors.identity: Formerly enslaved mariner and author of The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African (1789), the founding text of the English-speaking slave narrative and of abolitionist argument.
authors.biography: Born about 1745, he recorded his childhood in the village of Essaka, in the interior of what is now southern Nigeria; the archival work of Vincent Carretta has raised the alternative that he was born in South Carolina, and the question is still debated. Brought into the trade as a child and carried to the West Indies, he was purchased by a naval officer, taken to England, christened and given the name by which he published, and afterwards served at sea in North America and the West Indies. In 1766 he bought his own freedom, worked as a mariner and merchant, went north with an Arctic voyage in 1773, settling in London, where he joined Methodist and abolitionist circles and made a living by his pen and his lectures. His Interesting Narrative appeared in 1789 by subscription, ran into several editions in his lifetime and was translated into several languages, and it became the standard account of the horrors of the middle passage. In 1791, after the period covered here, he was appointed to office in the Sierra Leone enterprise; he married an Englishwoman in 1792 and had children. He died in London in March 1797.
authors.profile: An autobiographer who combined the captive's narrative, the Methodist conversion account and the commercial self-assessment to make a claim on the reader's reason and pity.
authors.style: Clear, orderly, controlled first-person narrative; catalogues of ship, cargo, price and place used as evidence; horror reported without rant; a scriptural and civic vocabulary of liberty, brotherhood and redress.
authors.concerns: The evil and the economics of the slave trade; the capacity and the humanity of Africans; the religion of the converted captive; the rights of British subjects regardless of colour; the moral danger of colonial luxury to the metropole.
authors.significance: His Narrative was a decisive instrument of the abolitionist campaign and the earliest and most influential of the Atlantic slave narratives, still read as a foundation text of African-diaspora writing.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace, date of birth and the details of his early captivity remain contested, since the archival record does not confirm the account he printed of himself.

authors.name: Olive Schreiner
authors.nationality: South African; the colonial novel, the allegory and the feminist treatise
authors.identity: Novelist, allegorist and feminist theorist; the first major writer of the British colonial world in southern Africa and the author of the founding feminist novel of the 1880s.
authors.biography: Born Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner on 24 March 1855 at the Wittebergen mission station in the Cape Colony, the daughter of a German missionary and an English mother. She worked as a governess in the Karoo from 1874, wrote The Story of an African Farm there, and went to England in 1881 to study medicine; ill health ended her medical training and she became a writer instead. She was a friend of Havelock Ellis, Eleanor Marx and Edward Carpenter, wrote Woman and Labour (1911), and returned to South Africa in 1899, where she campaigned against the war and against racial injustice. She died in Cape Town on 11 December 1920.
authors.profile: Schreiner wrote the colonial world from inside the colonial subject: The Story of an African Farm is the first novel to make the South African interior its own place rather than a backdrop, and its three children — Waldo, Em and Lyndall — are among the first fully realised colonial characters in English. She is also the great English allegorist of the 1890s and the first theorist of what she called 'labour' as a problem of women's economic dependency.
authors.style: Landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary; allegory and dream-visual inserted into realistic narrative; a plain, passionate prose; the first-person confession; the woman's argument against marriage as an economic institution.
authors.concerns: The position of women and the economics of marriage; the colonial childhood and the empty interior; religion, freethought and the loss of faith; the labour question; race and the native population; empire and the South African war.
authors.significance: Schreiner is the founding figure of South African literature in English and one of the most important feminist writers of the century: The Story of an African Farm is the first colonial novel of the interior, Woman and Labour is a central text of the suffrage movement, and her allegories made her a legend of the 1890s.

authors.name: Oliver Goldsmith
authors.nationality: Irish
authors.identity: Irish-born poet, essayist, novelist, and dramatist, a central figure of the London literary world, author of The Deserted Village, The Vicar of Wakefield, and She Stoops to Conquer.
authors.biography: Goldsmith was born in rural Ireland, the son of a clergyman, and studied medicine, spending time at Edinburgh and at a continental university before taking his degree; much of his student career is legendary. He went to London to live by his pen, working as an apothecary's assistant, a hack-writer, and a tutor, and became part of the group that founded The Club with Samuel Johnson and others. He wrote and edited widely, including the cosmopolitan essays The Citizen of the World (1760-1761). His poem The Traveller (1764), his novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), and the longer The Deserted Village (1770) established his fame, and his comedy She Stoops to Conquer (1773) revived laughter on the stage. He also wrote histories and natural histories. He died in London in 1774.
authors.profile: A writer of pastoral poetry, sentimental fiction, and laughing comedy who idealises rural abundance, childhood, and Christian innocence, and who attacks luxury, depopulation, and fashionable sentimental comedy on the stage.
authors.style: Clear, mellifluous heroic couplets in the pastoral poems; a warm, simple, often self-mocking prose; and easy, generous, laughing dramatic dialogue.
authors.concerns: Rural depopulation, luxury, and empire; the virtues of childhood and Christian simplicity; the rivalry between laughing and sentimental comedy; and the cosmopolitan comparison of nations and manners.
authors.significance: One of the most widely read writers of the later eighteenth century, in poetry, novel, and comedy alike; The Deserted Village became a touchstone of anti-commercial nostalgia, and his comedy redirected the English stage.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, given as 1728 or 1730, and his exact Irish birthplace and his scattered university career are partly mythologised by later accounts, especially by his friend and biographer Johnson.

authors.name: Osbert Sitwell
authors.nationality: British; the satirical novelist and memoirist of the Sitwell autobiography
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and memoirist; the satirist of the English upper class and the author of the five-volume autobiography.
authors.biography: Born Osbert Sitwell in London on 6 December 1892, the middle of the three poetic Sitwells; he served in the Grenadier Guards in the war and turned to satire in the verse of Argent and Azure and the prose of Discursions. The novels A Place of One's Own (1940) and The Man Who Lost Himself (1941) and the five volumes of autobiography from Left Hand, Right Hand (1945) made him the memoirist of his class; he died at Montegufoni, Italy, on 4 May 1969.
authors.profile: Osbert Sitwell is the satirical memoirist of the English upper class between the wars: the five volumes of his autobiography are the most sustained portrait of an aristocratic family in English letters, and the novels of the war years, with their ghosts and their lost selves, carried the satire into fiction. His verse and his editing of Wheels placed him at the centre of the modernist coterie.
authors.style: The polished satirical sentence of the man of the world; the portrait of the family and the house as an institution; the ghost and the lost self as the instruments of satire; the memoir that accumulates the portrait rather than the plot; the verse of the drawing room turned to the trench.
authors.concerns: The aristocratic family and its decay; the house and the collection as the memory of a class; the war and the loss of the self; Italy and the Tuscan villa as the place of retreat; the quarrel with the reviewers and with the Georgian anthologists.
authors.significance: Osbert Sitwell is the satirical memoirist of the English upper class between the wars: his five volumes of autobiography are the most sustained portrait of an aristocratic family in English letters, and the novels of the war years carried the satire into fiction of the ghost and the lost self.

authors.name: Oscar Wilde
authors.nationality: Irish; the Victorian period, aestheticism and the 1890s
authors.identity: Poet, playwright, novelist, essayist and wit; the central figure of the English aesthetic movement and the greatest comic dramatist of the nineteenth century.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin on 16 October 1854, son of Sir William Wilde, surgeon and antiquary, and Jane Francesca Elgee, poet and nationalist. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate prize in 1878 and became a disciple of Pater and Ruskin. After London and a lecture tour of America in 1882 he married Constance Lloyd in 1884 and edited Woman's World (1887-89). The Happy Prince (1888), The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890-91), Lady Windermere's Fan (1892), A Woman of No Importance (1893), An Ideal Husband (1895) and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) followed. His relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas led to his prosecution at Douglas's father's instigation, the trials of April-May 1895 and a sentence of two years' hard labour; he wrote De Profundis in Reading Gaol and The Ballad of Reading Gaol after his release in 1897. He died in Paris on 30 November 1900.
authors.profile: Wilde made the epigram the central English literary form of the 1890s: his comedies are constructed entirely of witty exchanges in which the conventional moral sentence is inverted, and their subject is the hypocrisy of late-Victorian society in matters of marriage, class and reputation. The Picture of Dorian Gray turns the aesthetic doctrine of Pater into a fable of the cost of living for beauty, and De Profundis is the most remarkable Victorian prison letter. His fairy tales and his criticism ('The Decay of Lying', 'The Critic as Artist') argue that art is not a copy of life but the source of it — the most radical statement of the autonomy of art in English.
authors.style: The inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram; the comedy of manners with a sudden access of seriousness; the symbolist set-piece and the decorative catalogue; a rhythmic, cadenced prose; the mask and the alias (Bunbury, Ernest); the self-justifying critical dialogue.
authors.concerns: Art and its autonomy from morality; appearance and reality; the double life and the secret; marriage and the marriage market; class, manners and the English gentleman; the prison and the outcast; love and its shame; Ireland and the Anglo-Irish position.
authors.significance: Wilde is the central figure of the English aesthetic movement and the greatest writer of comedy after Congreve: The Importance of Being Earnest is the most perfect English farce, Dorian Gray the most perfect English decadent novel, and De Profundis the period's most searching act of self-analysis. His trials made him the Victorian type of the persecuted artist, and his arguments shaped the modern defence of the autonomy of art and the modern gay literary tradition.
authors.uncertainty: The trials of 1895 are documented in the official record and the newspaper reports; Wilde's own accounts (De Profundis, the letters) are self-interested. The standard biographies are Richard Ellmann (1987) and the Oxford edition of the letters (2000).

authors.name: Ottobah Cugoano
authors.birthplace: the Gold Coast (the Fante coastal region of present-day Ghana; the town is given variously)
authors.nationality: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
authors.identity: Formerly enslaved writer and campaigner in London, author of Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species (1787), the century's most radical English abolitionist argument.
authors.biography: Born on the Gold Coast in the 1750s, he was kidnapped as a child, sold among the coastal forts and carried to Grenada, from which he was brought to England in the early 1770s. Named John Stuart in service, he remained in England a free man and joined the small circle of free Black Londoners clustered about Granville Sharp, for whom he acted as an intermediary and whose legal cases he helped to press. His Thoughts and Sentiments, published in 1787 and reprinted in the following years, argued from natural rights, scripture and the law of nations that the trade and slaveholding were crimes requiring restitution, and it demanded an end to the commerce rather than amelioration of it. He addressed the British public, the legislature and the slaveholders directly, and urged the commercial and religious advantages of an intercourse with Africa. He witnessed and advised in the campaigns of the later 1780s, and a shortened version of his book appeared in 1791. Nothing certain is known of him afterwards; he is usually supposed to have died about 1791.
authors.profile: A philosopher of natural rights from inside the experience of enslavement, who reasoned from first principles to restitution and to the equality of all mankind.
authors.style: Earnest, tightly argued prose of principle; scriptural and legal citation pressed into a single moral case; direct address to monarchs, merchants and slaves; a dignity that refuses apology.
authors.concerns: Natural liberty and the sin of man-stealing; the rights of Africans and the duties of Britain; restitution and compensation; the abolition of the trade rather than the reform of slavery; the religious and commercial future of Africa.
authors.significance: He supplied the abolitionist movement with its most uncompromising theoretical case and the first English book by a formerly enslaved writer to argue for total abolition, and his work stands beside Equiano's as a founding document of African-diaspora writing.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is approximate, the town of his birth is variously reported, and the date of his death is unknown; no record of him is certainly identified after 1791.

authors.name: Ouida
authors.nationality: English; the three-decker romance and the novel of high life
authors.identity: Novelist; the most extravagant and widely read romance writer of the 1870s-80s, and a genuine critic of Victorian smugness.
authors.biography: Born Marie Louise Ramé at Bury St Edmunds on 1 January 1839, the daughter of a French father and an English mother; she adopted the pen name Ouida from her childish pronunciation of 'Louisa'. She lived from the 1860s in London and after 1874 mostly in Italy, at Florence and Lucca, surrounding herself with dogs and writing in bed. Under Two Flags (1867) made her the highest-paid novelist of her day; her later books attacked vivisection, the English treatment of Italy, and the vanity of the aristocratic world, and she died poor at Viareggio on 25 January 1908.
authors.profile: Ouida wrote the romance of excess: guardsmen, Italian patriots, aristocratic women, horses and dogs, all rendered in a shimmering, extravagant prose that her admirers called poetry and her critics called nonsense. But the extravagance is a critique as well as an indulgence: her novels attack the marriage market, the cruelty of the English ruling class and (in the animal books) vivisection, and she was one of the very few popular novelists of the period to write seriously about animals as moral subjects.
authors.style: Highly coloured, rhythmic prose; the gorgeous inventory of dress, furniture and landscape; heroic and often doomed heroes; the glamour of the foreign and the aristocratic; interpolated moral tirades; sentiment about animals, especially dogs.
authors.concerns: Love against social convention; aristocratic honour and its decay; Italy and the English abroad; the position of women in the marriage market; animal suffering and vivisection; the morality of the beautiful.
authors.significance: Ouida was the most popular English novelist of the 1870s and one of the most influential stylists of the romance for the next generation; her animal novels were a real force in the anti-vivisection movement, and her Italian stories shaped the English image of the Risorgimento. Her reputation collapsed in the twentieth century, but she is now read again as a writer about gender, nationality and animal ethics.

authors.name: P. G. Wodehouse
authors.nationality: British-American; the comic invention and the language of the absurd
authors.identity: Humorist and novelist; the creator of Jeeves and Bertie Wooster, and the finest comic prose writer in English.
authors.biography: Born Pelham Grenville Wodehouse at Guildford on 15 October 1881; he worked in a bank and then as a comic writer for the London magazines, creating Psmith in 1903 and publishing My Man Jeeves in 1919. authors.style: The elaborate comic plot of farce and coincidence; the invented slang and the classical allusion side by side; the perfectly timed subordinate clause; the running cast of aunts, valets and peers; the refusal of any shadow of real harm.

authors.significance: P. G. Wodehouse was the finest comic prose writer in English and the greatest inventor of comic plots of the century: Jeeves and Wooster gave the language a mythology of its own, and his prose style is the most admired in English comedy since Dickens.

authors.style: The spoken Irish idiom carried into English dialogue; the peasant scene built on the land question and the emigrant ship; the tale retold in the plain narrative sentence of the storyteller; the lyric of the road, the fair and the leaving; the comic exchange set against the elegiac set speech.
authors.concerns: The land and the small farmer; emigration and the ship; the Irish tale and the Greek tale as the inheritance of childhood; the Abbey and the peasant play; exile in America and the remembered Ireland.

authors.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar
authors.nationality: African-American; the dialect poem, the standard English lyric and the short story
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and short-story writer; the first African-American poet to achieve national fame and the central black poet of the 1890s.
authors.biography: Born in Dayton, Ohio, on 27 June 1872, the son of former slaves from Kentucky; he was the only black student at his Dayton high school, where he edited the school paper with Orville Wright, and worked as an elevator operator while publishing his first poems. Majors and Minors (1895) was praised by William Dean Howells, and Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896) made him famous; he toured England, worked at the Library of Congress, married Alice Moore in 1898, and died of tuberculosis in Dayton on 9 February 1906.
authors.profile: Dunbar wrote in two registers and the tension between them is the heart of his achievement: the dialect poems gave his white audience the plantation nostalgia it wanted, while the standard English poems and the novels speak in the voice of an educated black American who knows exactly what the dialect trade costs. His best work — 'We Wear the Mask', 'Sympathy', The Sport of the Gods — is among the most important American writing about race at the turn of the century.
authors.style: Dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill; standard English lyrics of great technical finish; the mask and the double voice; short stories of black urban and rural life; the novel of the colour line.
authors.concerns: Race and the mask of accommodation; the legacy of slavery; the black artist and the market; love, loss and mortality; the city and the migration north; the cost of the dialect tradition to black self-representation.
authors.significance: Dunbar is the first African-American poet of national reputation and the central black writer of the 1890s: 'We Wear the Mask' is one of the most quoted American poems, his dialect verse permanently shaped the black literary tradition, and his double register made him the key figure in the debate over African-American representation that runs from Chesnutt to Du Bois.

authors.nationality: English; poet and prose polemicist of the Romantic period, the most systematically radical of the major Romantic writers
authors.identity: Poet of philosophical narrative poems, of the lyric and ode, and of verse drama written for the reader rather than the manager; also an essayist on poetry, atheism, diet, and reform whose polemic is inseparable from his verse.
authors.biography: Born 4 August 1792 at Field Place in Sussex, eldest son of Timothy Shelley (later second baronet) and Elizabeth Pilfold, he was educated at Syon House, at Eton (1804-10), where he wrote the gothic romances 'Zastrozzi' (1810) and 'St. Irvyne' (1811), and at University College, Oxford, from 1810. In March 1811 he and Thomas Jefferson Hogg were expelled for refusing to answer for the pamphlet 'The Necessity of Atheism', and in the same year he ran off to Scotland with the sixteen-year-old Harriet Westbrook, whom he married. He intervened in Irish agitation in 1812, privately printed 'Queen Mab' in 1813, and in July 1814 eloped to the Continent with Mary Godwin, daughter of William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft. The 1816 summer at the Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva, with Byron and Claire Clairmont, produced 'Hymn to Intellectual Beauty' and 'Mont Blanc' and the germ of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Harriet Shelley's suicide in December 1816 cleared the way for his marriage to Mary, but their position in England became untenable and the family moved to Italy in March 1818; the deaths of the children Clara (1818) and William (1819) and the loss of the guardianship suit over Percy Florence deepen the grief of the great years 1819-20, which yielded 'Prometheus Unbound', 'The Cenci', the west wind and skylark odes, and 'Peter Bell the Third'. At Pisa in 1821 he wrote 'Adonais' for Keats, and his alliance with Leigh Hunt brought out the monthly 'The Liberal' (1822). He was drowned on 8 July 1822 when his boat 'Bolivar' went down in a storm in the Gulf of La Spezia on the return from Livorno; his ashes lie in the Protestant Cemetery at Rome beside Keats.
authors.profile: His work moves from schoolboy gothic prose to the long philosophical poem ('Queen Mab', 'Alastor', 'Laon and Cythna'), and then to the mature compact of lyric, elegy, and drama in Italy ('Prometheus Unbound', the odes of 1820, 'Adonais', 'Epipsychidion', 'Hellas', 'The Triumph of Life'). A parallel prose body - 'A Defence of Poetry', 'The Necessity of Atheism', 'A Philosophical View of Reform', 'A Vindication of Natural Diet', the 'Letter to Maria Gisborne' and the letters from Italy - states the doctrine that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. Much of it went unpublished or appeared piratically in his lifetime, and his canon was largely made posthumous by Mary Shelley's editions of 1824 and after.
authors.style: An eloquence of transference: abstractions personified, natural agencies made emblems of mind, and verse periods that lengthen and recur within intricate stanzas ('The Cloud', 'Ode to the West Wind'). He adapts Italian and English forms with self-conscious formal experiment - terza rima, the Spenserian-like stanzas of 'Laon and Cythna', the complex stanzette of 'Adonais', the tailless lyric stanza of 'To a Skylark' - and his prose is argumentative, lucid, and frequently turns into manifesto.
authors.concerns: Necessity and the ethics of reform; atheism, freethought, and the critique of revealed religion; sexual love, free marriage, and the equal claim of women; diet, medicine, and the perfectibility of the body; imagination as a way of knowing and poetry as the engine of moral change; the tyranny of priest, king, and established opinion, tested against the French revolution, Greek freedom, and Italian despotism; death, mourning, and the survival of the poet's thought.
authors.significance: He bequeathed to later radicals and aesthetes a single powerful idea - that poetry reforms the mind which law cannot reach - which made him the hero of Chartists, of the freethought press of the 1820s-1890s, and of twentieth-century radical literary history. 'Prometheus Unbound' and the Italian lyrics rewrote the Miltonic and Wordsworthian inheritance, and 'A Defence of Poetry' remains a founding document of the autonomous-poetry tradition.

authors.name: Philip Doddridge
authors.nationality: English Dissenter
authors.identity: Congregational minister and the principal teacher of his generation of Dissenting pastors, whose Family Expositor and Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul joined practical divinity to a wide philosophical charity.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1702, the youngest of twenty children, of whom only he and one sister reached adulthood, he was briefly apprenticed, then educated largely by his own reading with the help of neighbouring ministers, and began to preach as a teenager. He held a country charge at Kibworth Harborough and settled at Northampton, where he led a large congregation and kept the academy that educated many Dissenting ministers of the following generation. His writings were at once devotional, instructional and practical: the Family Expositor, a commentary for household reading issued in parts from 1739, the Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul (1745), sermons, letters and a psalmody, with posthumous collections of his lectures and hymns. His courtesy, his stress on the inward work of grace and his readiness to commend experimental religion across party lines made him the best-loved of the Dissenting divines; his works were read by Edwards and by the American revivalists, and his academy trained preachers for England and the colonies. A failing chest sent him south for the winter of 1750, and he died at Lisbon in October 1751.
authors.profile: A pastoral writer of method and tenderness who brought the academy, the family desk and the congregation into one plan of religious education.
authors.style: Warm, lucid, closely organised prose; commentary arranged for reading aloud in the family; case-divinity addressed to the conscience; a temperate ecumenical charity of phrase.
authors.concerns: The conduct and progress of religion in the soul; scripture read with the help of the learned and the critical; Dissenting education and the qualifications of the ministry; the duties of family worship; the friendship of Christians across parties.
authors.significance: He gave English Nonconformity its most influential programme of piety and ministerial training, and his books on the inner history of conversion shaped evangelical spirituality in Britain and America.
authors.uncertainty: Several of his works were assembled and edited after his death from sermons and lectures, so their dates and completeness are uncertain.

authors.name: Philip Larkin
authors.nationality: English; British poet, novelist, jazz critic and university librarian
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and librarian; the most widely read English poet of the post-war decades and the central poet of the Movement of the 1950s.
authors.biography: Philip Arthur Larkin was born in Coventry on 9 August 1922 and read English at St John's College, Oxford, where he began a lifelong friendship with Kingsley Amis. He became a librarian, first at Wellington in Shropshire, then as assistant librarian at University College, Leicester, from 1946, sub-librarian at Queen's University, Belfast, from 1950, and from March 1955 Librarian of the University of Hull, the post he held for the rest of his life. His first book of poems, The North Ship (1945), was followed by two novels, Jill (1946) and A Girl in Winter (1947). After a privately printed pamphlet, XX Poems (1951), The Less Deceived (1955) made his reputation, and The Whitsun Weddings (1964) and High Windows (1974) confirmed him as the leading English poet of his generation. He reviewed jazz records for the Daily Telegraph, edited The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973) and chaired the Booker Prize judges in 1977. He died of cancer in Hull on 2 December 1985. His Collected Poems (1988), Selected Letters (1992) and Andrew Motion's biography (1993) transformed his posthumous reputation.
authors.profile: Larkin's reputation rests on three mature collections of formally exact, colloquial and ironic poems about ordinary lives, love, ageing and death, together with two early novels, jazz criticism and a small body of essays.
authors.style: Traditional stanzas and rhyme handled with conversational ease; plain, precise diction that rises in closing lines to lyrical or visionary images; irony, self-deprecation and bleak comedy; the persona of an unillusioned provincial observer.
authors.concerns: Mortality and the fear of death; the gap between expectation and experience; love, marriage and solitude; time and ageing; English towns, landscape and customs; the decline of religious belief and what might replace it.
authors.significance: Larkin is widely regarded as the foremost English poet of the second half of the twentieth century. His rejection of modernist difficulty in favour of a tradition descending from Thomas Hardy shaped the Movement and much later British poetry, while the posthumous letters and biography opened a lasting debate about his views on race and women.
