authors.name: Philip Massinger
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Baptized 24 November 1583 at Salisbury; son of a gentleman servant to the Herbert family. He studied at St Alban Hall, Oxford (1602–06), then went to London and collaborated with Fletcher, Dekker, and Field. After Fletcher's death in 1625 he became chief dramatist of the King's Men. He died suddenly on 17 March 1640 at his house on the Bankside and was buried in Fletcher's grave in Southwark Cathedral.
authors.profile: Some thirty plays survive, including The Roman Actor (1626), The City Madam (c. 1632), A New Way to Pay Old Debts (c. 1625), and The Bondman (1623); he completed Fletcher's unfinished work and wrote many plays in partnership.
authors.style: Careful construction, political earnestness, and a moral seriousness that made his comedies satires on greed and his tragedies studies of tyranny.
authors.concerns: The abuse of power; the corruption of wealth; justice and mercy in the state.
authors.significance: The last major dramatist of the pre-Civil War stage; his Sir Giles Overreach in A New Way to Pay Old Debts became one of the great actor's roles of the English repertoire.
authors.uncertainty: A period of obscurity and possible religious conversion (he was reputed a Catholic) in the 1610s is poorly documented.

authors.biography: Born Phyllis Eleanor Bentley at Halifax, Yorkshire, on 19 November 1894, the daughter of a partner in a woollen mill; she taught after war work in munitions and published from 1922 with Gollancz. Inheritance (1932), the chronicle of the Oldroyd family and of the woollen trade across the century, made her the Yorkshire novelist of the industrial family; A Modern Tragedy (1934) and the later Oldroyd books followed; she died at Halifax on 27 June 1977.
authors.profile: Phyllis Bentley is the Yorkshire novelist of the woollen chronicle: Inheritance, the saga of the Oldroyd family and of the mill across the nineteenth century, made the industrial family the matter of the regional novel and was the most read of the Yorkshire sagas of the 1930s.
authors.style: The chronicle of the family and the mill across the generations; the woollen trade and its machinery reported from the partner's daughter's eye; the Halifax of the west riding as the world; the plain narrative sentence of the saga; the industrial town and its owners.

authors.biography: Born Quesie Dorothy Roth at London on 14 September 1906; she read English at Cambridge, married F. R. Leavis in 1929, and published Fiction and the Reading Public in 1932, the study of the bestseller and the reading habit that founded the sociology of English reading. Her essays in Scrutiny and her editions of the Victorian novelists, with her study of the country house novel, made her the historian of the popular fiction of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; she died at Cambridge on 17 August 1981.
authors.profile: Q. D. Leavis founded the sociology of English reading: Fiction and the Reading Public traced the division of the reading public into the highbrow, the middlebrow and the lowbrow and made the bestseller and the circulating library the objects of criticism, and her essays on the Victorian and the country house novel recovered the popular fiction of the nineteenth century for the discipline.
authors.style: The sociological survey carried in the critical sentence; the bestseller and the library catalogue as the evidence; the division of the reading public stated as a diagnosis; the quotation from the popular novel read against the canon; the polemic of the standard.

authors.name: Queen Elizabeth I
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: monarch; poet; translator; orator
authors.biography: Born 7 September 1533 at Greenwich, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Educated by Roger Ascham and others in the new humanist curriculum, she became queen in 1558 and reigned until her death on 24 March 1603 at Richmond Palace. Her learning, her speeches, and her poems made her one of the most literate monarchs in English history.
authors.profile: Poems including 'The Doubt of Future Foes' (c. 1571), 'On Monsieur's Departure' (c. 1582), and 'When I Was Fair and Young'; translations from Boethius, Horace, and Plutarch made in her youth; prayers and meditations; and the great public orations — the speech at Tilbury (1588) and the 'Golden Speech' to Parliament (1601).
authors.style: A pointed, antithetical, proverbial style in verse and a commanding rhetorical art in her speeches, learned and plain by turns.
authors.concerns: Kingship and its burdens; marriage, succession, and the body politic; divine protection and personal constancy.
authors.significance: Her speeches and poems made the queen herself a literary presence; the cult of Elizabeth pervades Spenser, Shakespeare, and the entire literature of her reign.
authors.uncertainty: A few poems are assigned to her by tradition rather than manuscript authority.

authors.identity: Playwright and screenwriter; the author of Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War.
authors.biography: Born Robert Cedric Sherriff at Kingston upon Thames on 6 June 1896; he worked in insurance, served as a captain in the East Surrey Regiment on the Western Front, and wrote Journey's End from his own experience; it was produced in 1928 and became the great success of the London stage. authors.profile: Sherriff wrote Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War and the central dramatic text of the war: its dugout, its officers and its ordinary courage made the war visible to the theatre audience of 1928 and it remains the most performed war play in English.
authors.style: The single dugout set and the unbroken real time; the ordinary speech of the officers; the raid and the waiting; the class hierarchy inside the platoon; the tragic ending without rhetoric.
authors.concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
authors.significance: R. C. Sherriff wrote Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War: its dugout, its officers and its ordinary courage made the war visible to the theatre audience of 1928, and it remains the most performed war play in English.

authors.identity: Writer for boys; the author of The Coral Island, one of the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire.
authors.biography: Born Robert Michael Ballantyne in Edinburgh on 24 April 1825, the son of the printer and novelist James Ballantyne; he went to Canada as a clerk with the Hudson's Bay Company at sixteen, returned to Scotland in 1847, and made his name with The Coral Island (1858). Hudson Bay (1848), Martin Rattler (1858), The Dog Crusoe (1860), The Gorilla Hunters (1861) and dozens more followed. He died in Rome on 8 February 1894.
authors.profile: Ballantyne wrote the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire: The Coral Island invented the desert-island adventure for boys, and his Canadian and African tales created the formula of the young hero, the wilderness and the trial of manhood that Rider Haggard, Stevenson and Kipling all inherited.
authors.style: The documentary detail drawn from first-hand experience; the episodic adventure of the voyage and the island; the direct address to the boy reader; the moral lesson folded into the action; the plain, energetic, instructive prose.
authors.concerns: The wilderness and the frontier; the empire and the fur trade; the boy's initiation into manhood; race and the encounter with the native; natural history and the observation of the world.
authors.significance: R. M. Ballantyne wrote the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire: The Coral Island invented the desert-island adventure for boys and it was the book that Stevenson, Haggard and Kipling all read as children, making it the origin of the imperial adventure novel.

authors.identity: Cambridge Platonist philosopher and theologian; his vast True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678) argued against atheism and materialism for a rational, divinely ordered cosmos and an innate moral sense, a major work of seventeenth-century philosophy.
authors.biography: Born 1617 at Aller, Somerset, educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where he became Master (1654) and a leading figure of the Platonic circle. He served as Regius Professor of Hebrew, held livings, and was a correspondent of Temple's and an influential university figure (he tutored William Temple). His magnum opus, The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), the first part of a projected larger work, refuted 'atheism' through erudite argument and posited 'plastic natures' and innate moral ideas. Posthumous treatises on morality (A Treatise Concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality, 1731) were published later. He died on 26 February 1688.
authors.profile: The learned metaphysician whose encyclopaedic, erudite arguments for a rational, moral, divinely ordered universe represent the philosophical summit of Cambridge Platonism.
authors.style: Dense, erudite, argumentative prose; massive learning and citation; philosophical and theological reasoning; and a systematic, cumulative method.
authors.concerns: The existence of God and the refutation of atheism; the true intellectual system of the universe; innate moral ideas and eternal morality; free will; and 'plastic natures' as a middle principle.
authors.significance: Cudworth's True Intellectual System was a major philosophical work that influenced later thinkers (including Shaftesbury and the moral-sense school) and stands as the most systematic statement of Cambridge Platonist metaphysics and ethics.
authors.uncertainty: Cudworth's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through university and church records; much of his planned oeuvre was left unfinished or published posthumously.

authors.name: Ralph Ellison
authors.nationality: American; African American novelist, essayist and critic of jazz and American culture
authors.identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of Invisible Man (1952), the most honoured American novel of the post-war decades, and of two collections of essays on literature, music and American identity.
authors.biography: Ralph Waldo Ellison was born in Oklahoma City on 1 March 1913 and named after Ralph Waldo Emerson. He studied music at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama from 1933, left for New York in 1936, and there met Langston Hughes and Richard Wright, who encouraged him to write reviews and stories; he worked for the Federal Writers' Project and served in the merchant marine during the Second World War. Invisible Man, begun in 1945 and published by Random House in 1952, won the National Book Award in 1953. He held a fellowship at the American Academy in Rome in the mid-1950s, published the essays of Shadow and Act in 1964, taught at Bard, Rutgers and Yale, and held the Albert Schweitzer Chair in the Humanities at New York University from 1970 to 1979. He received the National Medal of Arts in 1985 and published a second collection, Going to the Territory, in 1986. He worked for some forty years on a second novel that he never finished. He died of pancreatic cancer in New York on 16 April 1994; his literary executor John F. Callahan edited his essays (1995), stories (1996) and the novel Juneteenth (1999) from his papers.
authors.profile: Ralph Ellison's reputation rests on one finished novel and two books of essays: Invisible Man fused the African American folk and blues tradition with the techniques of modernist fiction, and the essays argued that Black American culture is central to, not separate from, American culture as a whole.
authors.style: A densely allusive, comic and lyrical prose that shifts between registers, from sermon, folk tale and blues to surrealist nightmare; a first-person narrator who reflects on his own telling; essays that move from personal reminiscence to cultural argument, often through jazz.
authors.concerns: Race and visibility in American democracy; identity as improvisation; the folk and vernacular sources of art; jazz and the blues as models of discipline and freedom; the American nation as a mixed, unfinished culture.
authors.significance: Ellison stands with Richard Wright and James Baldwin among the defining African American writers of the mid-twentieth century; Invisible Man was voted the most important American novel since the Second World War in a 1965 Book Week poll, and his essays shaped later arguments about the relation between Black culture and American identity.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year: Wikipedia and the New World Encyclopedia give 1 March 1913; the Gale entries reproduced by Encyclopedia.com give 1914, the year found in many older references. 1913 is recorded here.

authors.name: Ralph Fox

authors.identity: Critic, journalist and novelist; the Communist writer of Storm over England and The Novel and the People.
authors.biography: Born Ralph Winston Fox at Leeds in 1900; he read modern languages at Oxford, worked as a journalist and for the Comintern, and wrote for the Daily Worker through the thirties. Storm over England (1935) told the three centuries of the English class war, The Colonial Policy of British Imperialism (1933) made the Marxist case against the empire, and The Novel and the People (1937) was published after he was killed fighting in Spain in the winter of 1936-7.
authors.profile: Ralph Fox is the Communist critic of the people's novel: The Novel and the People made the case for the novel as the literature of the people and against the dying bourgeois form, and his death in Spain made him, with Caudwell and Cornford, one of the martyrs of the thirties left.
authors.style: The plain argumentative prose of the Communist journalist; the class war told as the history of the people; the novel judged by its service to the people; the colonial critique of the empire; the pamphlet's speed and conviction.
authors.concerns: The class war and the English history; the empire and its colonial policy; the novel and the people; Spain and the thirties left; the martyrdom of the Communist writers.

authors.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
authors.nationality: American; Transcendentalist essay, lecture and poetry
authors.identity: Essayist, lecturer and poet; the central figure of American Transcendentalism and the first American writer to make a philosophy of self-reliance a national literature.
authors.biography: Born in Boston on 25 May 1803, the son of a Unitarian minister; he was educated at Harvard and at the Divinity School, was ordained in 1829, and resigned his Boston pastorate in 1832 over his refusal to administer the Lord's Supper. He travelled in Europe in 1833, met Carlyle, Coleridge and Wordsworth, and settled at Concord. Nature appeared anonymously in 1836; the Divinity School Address of 1838 made him notorious, and the Essays (1841, 1844) made him famous. He edited The Dial (1840-44), lectured across the northern states for forty years, and died at Concord on 27 April 1882.
authors.profile: Emerson invented the American essay: informal, oracular, built of separate paragraphs that circle a subject rather than argue it through, and addressed to the individual reader's own intuitions. His subject is the divinity of the self and of nature, the rejection of institutions and the authority of the present moment, and the call to original work. He was the intellectual centre of the Concord circle and the man who made American writing independent of Europe.
authors.style: The aphoristic paragraph; abrupt transitions and serial assertion; the lecture as literary form; symbolic uses of nature; the first-person plural of address; images drawn from science, Plato and the Orient.
authors.concerns: Self-reliance and the divinity of the individual; nature as revelation; the rejection of institutional religion; the American scholar and the nation's intellectual independence; representative men and the uses of great persons; fate, compensation and the moral law.
authors.significance: Emerson is the founding philosopher of American literature: 'Nature', 'Self-Reliance', 'The American Scholar' and the Divinity School Address created the vocabulary of American individualism, and his influence runs through Thoreau, Whitman, Dickinson, Nietzsche, William James and the whole tradition of American pragmatism.

authors.name: Ranulf Higden
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: chronicler; encyclopedist; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Werburgh's abbey, Chester, where he spent his whole career, dying on 12 March 1364; his Polychronicon, a universal history and geography compiled from earlier writers, became the standard history of England, translated into English by John Trevisa in 1387 and printed by Caxton in 1482.
authors.profile: Author of the Polychronicon (completed c. 1327, continued to 1352), with its celebrated first book describing the geography of the world and of Britain, and of the Ars Componendi Sermones and other didactic works.
authors.style: The industrious compiler's art: orderly encyclopedic arrangement, clear Latin, and a moralizing attention to the marvellous; the Polychronicon's world-description was a favourite of later chroniclers and cartographers.
authors.concerns: The unity of sacred and secular history; the description of the world and of Britain; the moral instruction of the clergy.
authors.significance: The Polychronicon dominated English historical writing for two centuries and, in Trevisa's translation, became one of the great monuments of fourteenth-century English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his continuations of the Polychronicon are hard to separate from those of his successors.

authors.name: Rebecca Harding Davis
authors.nationality: American; the industrial sketch and the social-problem novel
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of 'Life in the Iron-Mills', the founding text of American literary realism and of the American industrial novel.
authors.biography: Born Rebecca Blaine Harding in Washington, Pennsylvania, on 24 June 1831; she was educated at the Washington Female Seminary and taught school, then moved to Wheeling, Virginia, where she observed the iron mills and wrote 'Life in the Iron-Mills' for the Atlantic Monthly in 1861. She married the journalist Lemen Clark Davis in 1863 and wrote over five hundred stories, essays and serial novels for the periodical press, while raising a family in Philadelphia. She died in Mount Kisco, New York, on 29 September 1910.
authors.profile: Davis wrote the industrial novel before Howells or Garland: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' is the first American work of fiction to treat industrial labour as a subject of high literary art, and its portrait of the Welsh puddler Hugh Wolfe and his hunger for beauty is one of the founding scenes of American realism. Her war journalism of 1862 and her later essays on women's work are equally important, and her best fiction unites documentary observation with a symbolic intensity then unknown in American writing.
authors.style: Documentary detail of mill work and company housing; the symbolic image (the korl sculpture, the river, the fire); direct address to the reader; the narrator's moral urgency; dialect and immigrant speech; the short story as social argument.
authors.concerns: Industrial labour and the American working class; poverty, wages and the mill town; the artist born in the wrong class; women's work and the 'woman question'; the Civil War and the hospital; immigration and the Welsh, Irish and German workers.
authors.significance: Davis is the founding figure of American literary realism and of the American industrial novel: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' anticipated Howells, Garland and Dreiser by thirty years, and her recovery in the 1970s made her a central figure in the canon of American women's writing and of the literature of labour.

authors.name: Reginald Pecock
authors.nationality: English (Welsh-born)
authors.identity: theologian; apologist; bishop
authors.biography: Fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, and successively bishop of St Asaph (1444) and Chichester (1450). The outstanding orthodox theologian of fifteenth-century England, he wrote in English to answer Lollardy by reason rather than force; his rejection of the church's reliance on authority and his defence of preaching earned him trial for heresy in 1457, public abjuration, and imprisonment at Thorney Abbey, where he died c. 1461.
authors.profile: Author of the Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy (c. 1449–55), The Book of Faith (1456), the Donet, the Folewer to the Donet, and other works of vernacular theology, most of them condemned and burned with him.
authors.style: A remarkable plain English of argument, invented vocabulary (e.g., 'unbileve' for infidelity), and dialectical method applied to vernacular controversy.
authors.concerns: The rational defence of orthodoxy; the 'doom of reason' against mere authority; the instruction of the laity.
authors.significance: The most original English theologian between Wyclif and the Reformation and a pioneer of philosophical prose in English; his condemnation dramatizes the fifteenth-century church's fear of vernacular theology.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; much of his corpus survives only in fragments or in his own summaries.

authors.name: Rhoda Broughton
authors.nationality: English; the sensation and marriage-question novel
authors.identity: Novelist; a best-selling 'daring' writer of the 1860s whose later fiction became a sharp comedy of manners.
authors.biography: Born at Denbigh, north Wales, on 29 November 1840, the daughter of a clergyman and the niece of Sheridan Le Fanu, who encouraged her first stories. Her first novel, Cometh Up as a Flower (1867), was a sensation: a frank, first-person narrative of a woman's love and death that made her famous and notorious. She wrote twenty-six novels over more than forty years and lived latterly at Oxford, where she was a friend of Henry James and a celebrated talker. She died at Headington Hill, Oxford, on 5 June 1920.
authors.profile: Broughton began as a 'fast' novelist for the circulating libraries — her heroines desire, speak their minds and die of love — and became, in her later books, a cool and witty observer of the English marriage market. She was one of the first women novelists to write in the first person about female sexual feeling, and her best work combines the sensation plot with a genuinely modern irony about courtship and money.
authors.style: First-person female narration with direct address to the reader; sentimental climax and ironic deflation; lively dialogue; the marriage market as a comic and cruel spectacle; a vein of self-mockery about the novelist's own trade.
authors.concerns: Marriage, courtship and the position of women; female desire and its punishment; money and the gentry; the contrast between provincial and London society; ageing, widowhood and the comedy of the older generation.
authors.significance: Broughton was one of the most popular and controversial woman novelists of the 1860s and a bridge from the sensation novel to the New Woman fiction of the 1890s: her frankness about women's desire opened ground that later writers could occupy, and her late novels were admired by Henry James and by the writers of the 1890s.

authors.identity: Poet, novelist and biographer; one of the founders of Imagism and the author of Death of a Hero.
authors.biography: Born Edward Godfree Aldington at Portsmouth on 8 July 1892; he was at University College London, became one of the founders of Imagism with Pound and H.D. (whom he married in 1913), and served on the Western Front from 1916. Images of War (1919), Death of a Hero (1929), the biography of Lawrence of Arabia (1955) and his later novels followed. He died at Sury-en-Vaux, France, on 27 July 1962.

authors.style: The Imagist image without ornament; the free verse line of the early poems; the savage satire and the documentary detail of the novel; the first-person outburst; the refusal of consolation or rhetoric.
authors.concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; sexuality, the new psychology; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.

authors.name: Richard Blackmore
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English physician and ambitious religious epic poet, remembered chiefly as a target of Pope's satire in the Dunciad.
authors.biography: Blackmore was born in the west of England about 1654 and studied medicine at Exeter College, Oxford, taking his medical degree there and becoming a fellow of the College of Physicians. He practised as a physician in the west country and then in London, and was physician to William III. He published a long sacred epic, Creation (1712), a paraphrase of Job, and a sequel Paradise Regain'd (1718), together with poems on the mind and nature and medical and philosophical writings. His grand but heavily moralising verse drew ridicule from his rivals, and Pope mocked him in the Dunciad. He died in 1729.
authors.profile: A writer of didactic and religious epic who sought to render Miltonic verse into sober Protestant instruction; his ambition was greater than his reception.
authors.style: Weighty, moralising blank verse; elaborate scientific and theological paraphrase; a plain earnestness and diffuseness that contemporaries found tedious; and an addiction to poetic machinery of the mind.
authors.concerns: Providence, creation, and sacred history; the relation of medicine, body, and soul; natural philosophy and vitalism; and the defence of a pious, learned verse against the wit of the age.
authors.significance: A representative of the earnest sacred-epic and physico-theological tradition that his Augustan rivals displaced; his treatment in the Dunciad helped fix his posterity as a cautionary figure of misapplied ambition.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given only as about 1654, and his exact birthplace in the west of England is not firmly established; the chronology of his medical career and publications is partly reconstructed.

authors.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
authors.nationality: Irish-born English
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and Whig politician, the leading comic dramatist of the late eighteenth century and long owner and manager of Drury Lane.
authors.biography: Born on 30 October 1751 in Dublin, raised partly in England, and educated there, he entered the stage and politics through literary talent and marriage connections. His first play, The Rivals (1775), was an immediate success, followed by the comic opera The Duenna (1775) and his masterpiece The School for Scandal (1777). He became manager and part-owner of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and sat as a Whig Member of Parliament, a friend of Charles James Fox. Later comedies included The Critic (1797). Financial and political difficulties attended his last years. He died in London on 7 July 1816.
authors.profile: The foremost writer of Restoration-style comedy of manners in his age, whose witty, well-made comedies satirize hypocrisy, slander, and the manners of fashionable society.
authors.style: Brilliant, epigrammatic dialogue; the comedy-of-manners plot of masks and revelations; witty character types such as the malcontent and the rake; and a skilled balancing of sentiment and satire.
authors.concerns: Reputation, slander, and hypocrisy; wit and the manners of the fashionable world; sincerity versus affectation; and the politics of patronage and public life.
authors.significance: The most successful comic dramatist between Congreve and Wilde, whose School for Scandal and Rivals remain central to the repertory and to the study of eighteenth-century comedy.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well recorded, though the details of his education and early years and the precise chronology of some later political and financial events are sometimes variously given.

authors.name: Richard Brome
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Caroline comic dramatist and former servant and protégé of Ben Jonson; author of robust, satirical city comedies such as The Antipodes, A Jovial Crew, and The Sparagus Garden, prized for their low-life energy and social observation.
authors.biography: Born c. 1590 (records are sparse); he served Ben Jonson as a menial and became his literary protégé ('my man', Jonson called him). From 1629 he wrote some fifteen comedies for the Salisbury Court, Queen Henrietta's, and other companies, including The Northern Lass (1629), Bartholomew Fair-ish city comedies, The Antipodes (1638), and A Jovial Crew (1641), the last major play before the theatres closed. He signed a notorious contract with the Salisbury Court theatre (1635–40). He survived into the Interregnum, dependent and impoverished, dying in 1652.
authors.profile: The most Jonsonian of the Caroline comic writers, whose satirical, energetic comedies of London low life, country gentry, and humours anticipate the social breadth of Restoration comedy.
authors.style: Vigorous prose and verse comedy; satire of humours and social types; realistic London and rustic settings; bawdy energy; and intricate farcical plotting.
authors.concerns: Social satire and the manners of town and country; wit, folly, and pretension; the world of beggars, players, and gallants; and the comic correction of humours.
authors.significance: Brome is the most important comic dramatist of the 1630s after Jonson's decline; his plays offer an unparalleled social portrait of Caroline London and directly influenced Restoration comedy, and A Jovial Crew was long popular in adaptation.
authors.uncertainty: Brome's life is very poorly documented; his birth date is conjectural, and the dating and company attribution of several plays are uncertain.

authors.name: Richard Church
authors.nationality: British; the Georgian lyric of the country and the critic of the modern poets
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and critic; the Georgian lyricist of the country and the author of Eight for Immortality.
authors.biography: Born Richard Thomas Church at Battersea on 26 March 1893; he worked as a civil servant until 1933, publishing verse from 1917 in the Clarion and the periodicals, and made his name with the lyrics of A Glance Backward (1930), News from the Mountain (1932) and The Solitary Man (1941), with the novels Oliver's Daughter (1930) and High Summer (1931) beside them. His criticism of the modern poets in Eight for Immortality (1941) and his three volumes of autobiography, from Over the Bridge (1955), closed the career; he died on 4 March 1972.
authors.profile: Richard Church is the last and one of the finest of the Georgian lyricists: his lyrics of the country, the mountain and the solitary man carried the plain observed lyric through the modernist decades, his novels of the English village held the realist manner of the 1930s, and Eight for Immortality is a key document of the reception of the modern poets by their Georgian contemporaries.
authors.style: The plain observed lyric of the country and the season; the narrative poem of the village; the novel of the English village in the realist manner; the criticism that reads the modern poets through the Georgian ear; the autobiography of the enchanted ordinary.
authors.concerns: The country and the vanishing rural world; the solitary man and the life of the lyric; the English village and its church; the reception of the modern poets by their contemporaries; the enchantment of the ordinary as the subject of autobiography.

authors.name: Richard Crashaw
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Metaphysical religious poet and Catholic convert; author of Steps to the Temple and Carmen Deo Nostro, whose ecstatic, sensuous, and baroque devotional verse — especially to St Teresa and the Virgin — is unique in English.
authors.biography: Born c. 1613 in London, son of a Puritan preacher; educated at Charterhouse and Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (Fellow of Peterhouse). A Laudian Anglican, he was ejected during the Civil Wars, converted to Roman Catholicism, and went into exile, first to Paris and then to Italy. He became a client of Cardinal Palotta and, in 1649, a canon of the Holy House of Loreto, where he died in July 1649. His Steps to the Temple (1646) was published in England; the Catholic Carmen Deo Nostro appeared in Paris in 1652.
authors.profile: The English poet most at home in the continental baroque, whose fervent Catholic imagination rendered the mystical ecstasy of the saints in lush, sensuous, and sometimes startlingly physical conceits.
authors.style: Baroque extravagance; sensuous and paradoxical imagery; the epigram and the witticism turned to devotion; musical repetition; and a Catholic and Counter-Reformation intensity alien to the Protestant mainstream.
authors.concerns: Mystical union and ecstasy; the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalene, and St Teresa; martyrdom and the wounds of Christ; the conversion of the soul; the sensuous apprehension of the divine.
authors.significance: Crashaw is the principal English representative of continental baroque religious poetry; his 'Hymn to St Teresa' and his epigrams were admired by Cowley and, later, by the decadents and modern critics as the most sensuously daring of the metaphysicals.
authors.uncertainty: Crashaw's birth year (1612 or 1613) and the details of his conversion and exile are uncertain; his biography rests on scattered records and the testimony of Abraham Cowley.

authors.biography: Born on 24 January 1287, he became tutor to the future Edward III, and thereafter the king's trusted servant: keeper of the privy seal, chancellor (1334–35), and bishop of Durham from 1333. authors.concerns: The preservation and circulation of learning; the duties of clergy and princes to books; the reform of the universities.
authors.significance: The Philobiblon is the foundational text of English bibliophilia and a precious record of fourteenth-century book culture; de Bury's library fed Durham's later collections.
authors.uncertainty: The precise authorship of the Philobiblon (de Bury or his chaplain Robert Holcot) is debated.

authors.biography: Born at Longworth, Berkshire, on 9 June 1825 and raised in Devon; he was educated at Blundell's and Exeter College, Oxford, trained as a barrister, and gave up the law for market gardening in Teddington. authors.significance: R. D. Blackmore wrote the most popular West Country romance in English: Lorna Doone has never been out of print since 1869, and its Exmoor landscape and dialect narrative created the regional historical novel that Hardy inherited.

authors.name: Richard Henry Dana
authors.nationality: American; poet, critic, essayist and lawyer of Boston and Cambridge, the elder Richard Henry Dana, father of Richard Henry Dana the younger (1815-1882) the writer of the seagoing narrative Two Years Before the Mast, to which this record does not belong
authors.identity: A writer of romantic narrative verse, of a few short lyrics, of a prose romance fragment and of criticism and editorial matter, joined to a long career as a lawyer and as a man of letters. This record covers the father: the poet and critic of 1815 to 1840 and the conservative man of letters of the later Cambridge years. His son, of the same name, wrote the prose narrative of the California coast and the legal and political works of the 1860s and 1870s, and the two are constantly confounded in short accounts and in library catalogues.
authors.biography: He was born at Cambridge in Massachusetts on 15 November 1787 into the old Dana family of that town, descended from the Cambridge settler of 1640 and allied to the leading families of the coast, a connection which gave him its manners and its politics. He was entered at Harvard as a boy, studied there through several terms and quitted the College in 1807 without a degree, removing to the law, in which he was admitted and in which he afterwards practised at Boston with fair success and with small appetite for the work. About 1815 he was one of the young men who founded the North American Review, the quarterly which gave Boston the command of American criticism for a generation, and to which he contributed some of the earliest and most discussed of its papers. In 1821 and 1822 he conducted The Idle Man, a monthly of sketches and essays in the manner of the Spectator which ran to six numbers and which he chiefly wrote; it was the most notable of the many rivals of Irving's Sketch Book, and the failure of its subscriptions taught him the narrowness of the American book trade. In 1827 he published the volume of Poems which contained his reputation and the long narrative The Buccaneer, a tale of the sea and of the rover of the Spanish main, with the prose romance Paul Felton and other pieces of his earlier years; the poem was praised in Edinburgh by the critic who wrote as Christopher North, and gave him the place of the accomplished and melancholy poet of the Boston school. Through the following decades he wrote little and published less, living at Cambridge as a lawyer, a critic and a consulted man of letters, an unrepentant conservative in politics and in taste, and an authority upon the older literature of New England. He survived his generation, his friends and his reputation, and died at his house in Boston on 2 February 1879 in his ninety-second year; his son had preceded him into print with the book that has since kept the name of Dana before readers, and the two are still so constantly confounded that the elder's verse is seldom read without a correction of the biography.
authors.profile: His printed work is small and was collected late: the Poems of 1827, which gathered the narrative verse and the lyrics written from his student years onward, the prose fragment Paul Felton, the sketches and essays of The Idle Man of 1821 and 1822, and the reviews and articles contributed to the North American Review and to the magazines of the 1810s and 1820s. The verse is romantic and narrative in the English manner, dealing with the sea, with guilt and with the return to settlement, and the shorter pieces, of which The Little Beach Bird is the best known, are lyric in the eighteenth-century sense rather than in the Wordsworthian. His prose criticism, and the essays of the Idle Man, are the part of his work which the history of the American essay has kept.
authors.style: A dignified, deliberate and deliberately old-fashioned blank verse, sound in ear but not various, with long descriptive sweeps of sea and coast and a moral weight laid upon the closing lines; in the prose an eighteenth-century periodic sentence, ironic, restrained and formal, carrying the manner of the periodical essay into American subject. He is at home in the narrative of guilt and retribution and in the elevated description, and uneasy in rapid dialogue and in comedy; his diction keeps the vocabulary of the older English poetry and avoids the colloquial.
authors.concerns: The guilt and the retribution of the passionate and solitary man; the sea as a scene of moral discipline and of doom; the culture of the mind and the refinement of taste as the end of letters; the claims of the old conservative order in a democratic country; the dignity and the perils of the literary profession in America, where the magazine and the subscription list governed what could be written; the distinction of masculine and feminine powers in writing, which he argued; the duty of criticism and the memory of the New England past.
authors.significance: He was one of the founders of the North American Review, the organ through which Boston dominated American criticism for a generation, and the editor and chief writer of The Idle Man, the most accomplished American attempt at the periodical essay of the 1820s. The Buccaneer gave American romantic narrative verse one of its serious specimens and won him a British notice of consequence, and his essays and reviews set the standard of taste against which the native subject of the sea and of the New England town was judged. He is also of consequence as the father of the author of Two Years Before the Mast and as the instance most cited of the elder generation of Boston men of letters who could live by the law and by criticism but not by poetry alone.
authors.uncertainty: The day and month of his death are reported variously in the printed records, one archive finding aid placing it in July 1879 while the biographical accounts give 2 February of that year; the extent of his share in the founding and in the early numbers of the North American Review, and the division of authorship among the several conductors of that journal, have never been settled. The reason for his withdrawal from Harvard without a degree is reported from family and later biographical accounts rather than from the College record, and the claim that he supplied the preface to his son's narrative of 1840 rests upon the memoirs of the family rather than upon a documented statement of authorship.

authors.name: Richard Hurrell Froude
authors.nationality: English; the Oxford Movement and Victorian religious prose
authors.identity: Priest, fellow of Oriel and Tractarian controversialist; the ascetic and fiery early influence of the Oxford Movement, whose Remains became the scandal and the manifesto of the Tracts.
authors.biography: Born at Dartington on 25 March 1803, son of the archdeacon of Totnes; educated at Eton and Oriel College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1826 and met Newman and Keble. He wrote some of the first Tracts for the Times, travelled with Newman in the Mediterranean in 1832-33 (where the poems of Lyra Apostolica were written), and was perpetually ill; he was ordained in 1829 and appointed archdeacon of Totnes in 1830. He died of tuberculosis at Dartington on 28 February 1836, aged thirty-two. Newman published his Remains in 1838-39, and their extreme opinions on the Reformation caused a controversy that helped both to define and to divide the Oxford Movement.
authors.profile: Froude supplied the Oxford Movement with its ascetic ideal and its historical theory: he was a High Churchman who believed the Church of England had been corrupted at the Reformation, and his biography of Becket set the martyr and the king in the pattern that his successors repeated. The Remains, with their journals and letters, present a personality of radical earnestness and self-mortification, and their publication was the moment at which the movement's extreme wing became visible.
authors.style: Personal journals and letters as devotional documents; unqualified assertion and the polemical aside; a historical argument that treats the Reformation as a national apostasy; the aphorism and the ascetic self-examination.
authors.concerns: The authority of the Church against the state; apostolic succession and the eucharistic sacrifice; asceticism, fasting and celibacy; the corruption of the sixteenth-century settlement; the relation of the Anglican Church to Rome.
authors.significance: Froude's Remains made the Oxford Movement visible as a party and provoked the critical reaction that produced the 1841 Tract 90 crisis and, finally, Newman's secession. He is the movement's intimate historian, and his influence on Newman, Keble and Pusey was the decisive personal influence of its first decade.

authors.name: Richard Jefferies
authors.nationality: English; the nature essay, the rural chronicle and the autobiographical fantasy
authors.identity: Nature writer, novelist and essayist; the greatest English prose writer on the countryside and the author of After London.
authors.biography: Born John Richard Jefferies at Coate, Wiltshire, on 6 November 1848, the son of a struggling farmer; he became a newspaper reporter at seventeen and sold his first essay to the Pall Mall Gazette in 1877. Tuberculosis drove him to London and then to the Sussex coast, where he wrote the essays collected as The Amateur Poacher (1879), Round About a Great Estate (1880), Nature Near London (1883) and The Life of the Fields (1884), and the novels Bevis (1882) and After London (1885). He died at Goring, Sussex, on 14 August 1887, aged thirty-eight.
authors.profile: Jefferies wrote the English countryside from inside the experience of labour and observation: his essays record the field, the hedge, the poacher and the farm worker with an exactness and a rapture that no other Victorian nature writer matched, and his late work — The Story of My Heart — turns nature writing into a mystical autobiography. After London is the first great English post-apocalyptic novel, and Bevis is the finest English children's book of the rural world.
authors.style: Precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals; the essay built on observation and memory; the child's outdoor world rendered without sentiment; the visionary rhapsody; the rural dialect and the speech of the labourer.
authors.concerns: The English countryside and its seasons; the rural poor and agricultural decline; childhood, freedom and the outdoor world; the mystical apprehension of nature; the collapse of civilisation and the return of the wild; the unity of the self with the natural world.
authors.significance: Jefferies is the greatest English nature writer of the nineteenth century and a major figure in the literature of the rural world: his essays are unmatched in their precision and their passion, After London invented the English post-apocalyptic novel, and The Story of My Heart is one of the central texts of English nature mysticism.

authors.name: Richard Lovelace

authors.identity: Cavalier poet, courtier, and soldier; the archetype of the gallant royalist gentleman whose lyrics of love, honour, and imprisonment — 'To Althea, from Prison' and 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars' — became the defining verse of the Cavalier cause.
authors.biography: Born 1616 (baptised 10 December at St Bride's, London), educated at Charterhouse and Gloucester Hall, Oxford, and a favourite of the court of Charles I. He served in the Bishops' Wars and, in 1642, presented the Kentish petition for the restoration of episcopacy, for which he was imprisoned in the Gatehouse; a second imprisonment (1648–49) followed his loyalty after the Civil War, during which he prepared his collection Lucasta (1649). He spent his later years in poverty in London, publishing Lucasta: Posthume Poems (1659 was posthumous; actually published 1660). He died in 1657, reportedly in great poverty.
authors.profile: The Cavalier gentleman-poet whose code of honour made 'I could not love thee, dear, so much, / Loved I not honour more' the motto of royalist gallantry.
authors.style: Elegant, musical lyrics; the argumentative conceit of love and honour; a gallant, dignified tone; and occasional metaphysical wit in the service of courtly feeling.
authors.concerns: Love and honour; loyalty to the king and the Cavalier cause; freedom of the spirit in imprisonment; friendship; and the consolation of poetry in defeat.
authors.significance: Lovelace's Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; his lyrics epitomise the royalist gentleman's ethos and remain among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Lovelace's later life and the date and circumstances of his death are poorly documented; his reputation for a ruined, impoverished end rests partly on later tradition.

authors.name: Richard Lovell Edgeworth
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish; the provincial improvement and educational writing of the later eighteenth century, and the natural-philosophical and inventive culture of the Midlands and of Ireland
authors.identity: Landowner, inventor, engineer and educational theorist; the Irish country gentleman of the Lunar Society circle who made the government of a great family and the training of infant minds an experiment, and whose Practical Education and household tales, written with his daughter Maria, form one of the most original pedagogic enterprises of the 1790s.
authors.biography: Edgeworth was born at Bath in 1744, the son of an Anglo-Irish family with estates in Longford, and was educated afterwards at Trinity College Dublin and for a short time at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He came into the family estate at Edgeworthstown in Longford and spent the rest of his life as an Irish country landlord, engineer and improver. He married four times, the wives being Anna Maria Elers, Honora Sneyd, Honora's sister Elizabeth Sneyd, and, in 1798, Frances Ann Beaufort; by them he left a very large family, many of whom died young, and among his surviving children the eldest was Maria, afterwards the novelist. He belonged to the Birmingham circle afterwards known as the Lunar Society, and worked and corresponded with James Watt, Joseph Priestley, Erasmus Darwin and Matthew Boulton. His inventions, which he recorded at length, were serious rather than fortunate: a copying and measuring machine, a steam-carriage and road-making scheme he described as a cart carrying its own road, a telegraph, a method of teaching the deaf, and improvements in the roads and drains of Ireland. He was employed on canal and harbour surveys, and published a treatise on road-making and a plan for teaching arithmetic by self-instruction. In politics he was a reforming Irish Protestant who urged concession to the Catholics and a limited parliamentary reform, and who opposed the Act of Union of 1800. After the death of his second wife he undertook the education of his children as an experiment in the training of the understanding, conducted at Edgeworthstown with Maria as his closest collaborator. The method was printed in Practical Education of 1798, stated on its title page as the work of Miss Edgeworth and her father, and followed by the Essays on Professional Education of 1809 and by Readings on Poetry of 1816; the household stories out of which it grew were published as The Parent's Assistant in 1796 in his daughter's name, and the plan of instruction for the youngest children appeared afterwards as Early Lessons. He wrote his own Memoirs, which Maria completed and published in 1820, and he died at Edgeworthstown on 13 June 1817.
authors.profile: His books are practical and experimental: the educational treatises, the scientific and engineering papers, the political pamphlets on Irish affairs, and the household narratives. Practical Education, in two volumes, argues from the history of his own children's teaching that the powers of the mind are formed by association and use, and its chapters on reading, writing, grammar, natural philosophy and the classics are illustrated with the small facts of a family experiment; the Essays on Professional Education carry the same method into the training of the professions, and Readings on Poetry applies it to literary teaching. The Memoirs are an autobiography of inventions, friendships and family, written without reserve and finished by his daughter. To these belong his account of road-making, his papers on the copying and telegraph machines, and the plans for the instruction of the deaf and for teaching arithmetic.
authors.style: A plain, quick, argumentative prose of the laboratory and the estate, full of named instances, of the small concrete cases from which a principle is drawn, and of a self-conscious candour about his own failures; the educational writing is conversational and domestic, addressed to parents, and it turns the anecdote into evidence. The Memoirs add a garrulous and impatient first-person manner, in which invention, friendship and family grief are told in one breath; the scientific and political pamphlets are drier, more technical, and given to numbered proposals and to the estimate of cost.
authors.concerns: The formation of the infant understanding by association, use and self-instruction rather than by memory and fear; the education of judgement for the professions and for public life; the invention and practical application of machines, and the useful arts of road, canal and harbour making; the improvement and government of an Irish estate and of a largely Catholic tenantry; the claims of religious toleration and parliamentary reform in Ireland; the uses of emulation, of conversation and of the child's own curiosity in teaching; the relation of scientific friendship to literary work.
authors.significance: He gave the English education of the nineteenth century one of its founding ideas, that the mind is to be studied in the actual child and trained by the management of association, and Practical Education, whatever the share of his daughter in its authorship, made that idea widely known and was read and answered through the century. His household tales founded the realistic domestic story for children, and the long Memoirs are an indispensable record of the Lunar Society, of Watt and the midlands philosophers, and of Irish improvement and politics between the American and the French wars.
authors.uncertainty: The number of his children is variously given in the accounts, and the names and dates of his four marriages are recorded with small differences, the usual order being Anna Maria Elers, Honora Sneyd, Elizabeth Sneyd and Frances Ann Beaufort. The dating and the division of work between father and daughter in The Parent's Assistant and in Practical Education remain the subject of scholarship rather than of settled record, since the books appeared under his daughter's name or under a joint designation; and the value of his own account of his inventions, and of his share in the inventions attributed to Watt and to others, cannot be measured independently of the Memoirs, which are necessarily self-reporting. The chronology of his college years at Durham, Dublin and Oxford is imperfectly documented.

authors.name: Richard Price
authors.nationality: English Dissenter
authors.identity: Unitarian minister at Newington Green and one of the century's most influential moral philosophers, whose sermons on liberty made him a European authority on the rights of man.
authors.biography: Born at Bristol in 1723 and apprenticed to a glover, he found his vocation in the Dissent, studied mathematics, philosophy and a range of languages, and in the late 1750s became the minister of a small congregation at Newington Green, where he lived for the rest of his life. His Review of the Principal Questions in Morals (1769), a rigorous attack on sentiment and self-love as the foundation of right, gave him a philosophical rank beside Butler and Reid. Mathematical and demographic papers on annuities, life assurance and the value of marriage and mortality tables made him a Fellow of the Royal Society and an adviser to government on the funding of life. His sermons and tracts on the American Revolution, on the love of one's country, on toleration and on the corruptions of civil and ecclesiastical liberty were read, reviewed and answered across Britain, France and America. He died at Newington Green in June 1791, having refused richer preferment and stayed with his small meeting.
authors.profile: A moralist of reason and rights, who held that right and wrong are as fixed as the relations of number and that government exists only by the trust of the governed.
authors.style: Austere, tightly argued plainness; definitions and divisions carried into pulpit oratory; arithmetic and actuarial precision applied to human affairs; a sermonist's solemnity of appeal.
authors.concerns: Objective moral obligation against sentiment and interest; the reasonableness and corruptions of Christianity; the rights of individuals and the accountability of rulers; the valuation of life, annuities and population; the sin of the slave trade.
authors.significance: He supplied the rationalist morality and the doctrine of popular consent that made dissenting England a school of radical politics, and his actuarial work founded the mathematics of life assurance.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his early conversion to Unitarian beliefs is loose, and the full text of several sermons survives only in reports made from shorthand.

authors.name: Richard Rolle
authors.nationality: English (Yorkshire)
authors.identity: mystic; devotional writer; hermit
authors.biography: Studied briefly at Oxford, then withdrew c. 1321 to become a hermit, finally settling near the Cistercian nunnery of Hampole in south Yorkshire, where he died in the Black Death (1349). The most widely read English spiritual writer of the fourteenth century, he was venerated as a saint, though never canonized.
authors.profile: Author of Latin treatises (Incendium Amoris, Emendatio Vitae, Melos Amoris) and English epistles (Ego Dormio, The Commandment, The Form of Living, addressed to the anchoress Margaret Kirkby) and of English psalm commentaries; his writings survive in hundreds of manuscripts.
authors.style: A highly personal, affective style built on the experience of 'fire, sweetness, and song' (calor, dulcor, canor); rhythmic prose with alliterative cadence; scriptural commentary fused with autobiography.
authors.concerns: The love of God as experienced warmth and song; the solitary life; the guidance of contemplatives, especially women recluses.
authors.significance: The father of the English mystical tradition: his affective spirituality shaped Rolle-influenced devotional prose for two centuries, and his English epistles are the earliest surviving writings of their kind.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his writings is debated; the medieval cult attributed miracles to him.

authors.name: Richard Steele
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish-born essayist, dramatist, and Whig publicist who founded the Tatler and co-founded the Spectator with Joseph Addison.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin and raised partly in England, Steele was educated at the Charterhouse and entered the army, buying a commission. He turned to writing and in 1709 founded the Tatler, a daily periodical of essays and news, soon joined by Addison. In 1711 the two launched the Spectator, to which Steele also contributed essays of feeling and reform. He wrote sentimental comedy, most successfully The Conscious Lovers (1722), and several political journals. A Whig member of Parliament, he fell into debt and estrangement from Addison in later life. After illness he retired to Wales, where he died in 1729.
authors.profile: A writer of familiar prose and sentimental drama, more impulsive and emotionally warm than Addison, who used the periodical to promote benevolence, fashion reform, and domestic feeling.
authors.style: Open, affectionate, sometimes hurried prose; a strong appeal to the heart rather than to judgement; lively character sketches; and an earnest, confessing moral voice.
authors.concerns: Reform of manners and duelling; benevolence and filial duty; Whig politics and religious toleration; and the sentimental education of the middle-class reader.
authors.significance: Inventor of the periodical essay through the Tatler and joint founder of the Spectator; a pioneer of sentimental comedy whose The Conscious Lovers dominated early eighteenth-century stage reform.
authors.uncertainty: His year and circumstances of birth are uncertain and commonly given only as about 1672; the precise division of labour between him and Addison in the Tatler and Spectator is still disputed.

Christ's Company (1861), Historical Odes (1864) and the five-volume History of the Church of England followed; he became a canon of Carlisle. He died at Warkworth on 23 January 1900.

authors.concerns: The medieval and Reformation past; the Church and the Oxford Movement; the fall of the monasteries and the old faith; the English landscape and the cathedral close; art versus life.
authors.significance: Richard Watson Dixon was the most learned of the Pre-Raphaelite poets and one of the finest historical poets of the century: his Historical Odes and his History of the Church of England made him the central historian of the Oxford Movement.

authors.identity: Novelist and memoirist; the author of Native Son and Black Boy, the central Black American writer of the 1940s.
authors.biography: Born Richard Nathaniel Wright on the Rucker plantation near Roxie, Mississippi, on 4 September 1908; he grew up in poverty in Mississippi, Memphis and Chicago, joined the Communist Party, and published Uncle Tom's Children (1938), Native Son (1940) and Black Boy (1945). He moved to Paris in 1946 and died there on 28 November 1960.

authors.style: The naturalist accumulation of detail; the protest and the documentary; the bigger Thomas and the courtroom; the first-person memoir of hunger and violence; the plain, hard, urgent prose.

authors.name: Robert Blair
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Scottish Church of Scotland minister and poet, author of the meditative grave-poem The Grave, a landmark of the graveyard school.
authors.biography: Blair was born about 1699 and was ordained a minister of the Church of Scotland, where he became associated with the more liberal, Moderate interest in the kirk. He is remembered above all for his blank-verse poem The Grave (1743), a somber meditation on death and the resurrection that went through many editions and influenced the grave poetry that followed. He published sermons and devotional writings, but The Grave was his only poem of lasting note. He died in 1746.
authors.profile: A minister-poet whose single enduring work, The Grave, gives the eighteenth-century meditation on mortality an elevated, didactic, and pictorial blank-verse form.
authors.style: Grave, sonorous blank verse; accumulated images of burial, decay, and resurrection; sermon-like urgency; and a sustained mood of solemn meditation rather than narrative or wit.
authors.concerns: Death, the grave, and the hope of resurrection; the vanity of worldly distinctions before death; the equality of all in the tomb; and Christian consolation and judgement.
authors.significance: The Grave is a defining text of the graveyard school, alongside Young's Night Thoughts, shaping the later-eighteenth-century poetics of melancholy and mortality; Blair also belongs to the Moderate current of the Scottish kirk.
authors.uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain and variously recorded; details of his Scottish charges and of the early illustration history of The Grave are imperfectly established.

authors.name: Robert Bloomfield
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Journeyman shoemaker and rural poet, the first labouring-class writer in England to reach a mass reading public, and the author of the seasonal countryside poem that created the market into which Clare and the mechanic poets of the 1810s were afterwards launched.
authors.biography: Robert Bloomfield was born on 3 December 1766 at Honington in Suffolk, the son of George Bloomfield, a tailor whose trade failed, and of Elizabeth Bloomfield, a village schoolteacher who gave him his earliest lessons. Removed from school to work while still a boy, he earned his living in country service and then in London as a journeyman shoemaker, working at his trade among Cheap-side houses, and he composed verse in garret lodgings after hours of hand labour, describing the poet's whole domain of that period as a garret. The Farmer's Boy, a rural poem in four parts following the working year of a farm household from spring ploughing to the winter fire-side, was published in 1800, printed for Vernor and Hood of London, and its success was immediate and sustained: it ran through many editions and reached a cumulative circulation put at some twenty-five thousand copies, the largest for a single poem of the labouring-class tradition. The book made him the most famous working man of letters of his generation and drew patrons about him, among them the Duke of Grafton, whose support included a small annuity, and it established the model of the discovered and edited peasant poet on which every later case was formed. Prosperity was repeatedly undone by the size of his family, by the hard terms on which his copyright and his labour were bought, and by the poor sale of his later books, which returned to the same seasonal and domestic material in ballad and easy descriptive measure. His last years were spent in Bedfordshire, where he lived in reduced circumstances at Shefford, and he died there on 19 August 1823, being buried in the churchyard at Campton near Shefford, where his grave has been the site of commemorations by the society that bears his name. His correspondence, which records the working of subscription, patronage, and provincial bookselling around a journeyman hand, survives in modern scholarly edition, and his family papers and letters are the chief evidence for the circle of labouring writers that gathered about him.
authors.profile: His career is almost identical with one book. The Farmer's Boy adapts the Thomsonian seasonal estate poem to the working calendar of an East Anglian and Midland household, keeping the closed couplet of the eighteenth-century didactic manner but filling it with the tool, animal, sound, and task vocabulary of actual husbandry; the accompanying poems, tales, and lyric numbers rework the same material in the popular stanzas of the period. The volume that carried his name was framed by prefixed matter and by illustrations, making him an early instance of a labouring poet whose text was shaped as a commodity for a genteel subscribing market.
authors.style: Closed iambic heroic couplets of the plain rural school, with a low and concrete vocabulary of field tasks, weather, animals, and domestic economy; frequent apostrophe to personified abstractions held decorously; a strong sense of the working day rather than of incident; provincial Suffolk and Bedfordshire household speech; and a sentimentality of pathos carried by detail rather than by rhetoric.
authors.concerns: The dignity and the exhaustion of regular labour; the rural year as an ordered world; depopulation, low wages, and the distress of the labouring parish in the dear years of the 1790s; patronage, copyright, and the economics of authorship for a working man; temperance, dependence, and self-respect; the education of a reader's eye through the seasons.
authors.significance: He created the reading market that afterwards received the mechanic and peasant poets of the 1810s and 1820s, and he established the labouring-class countryside poem as a publishable form. His career documents both the possibility and the limits of patronage and subscription for working-class authors, and the garret-to-popularity plot he supplied was repeated and resisted by later labouring poets, Clare chief among them, whose first volume was built on the model his sales had made fashionable.
authors.uncertainty: The cumulative sales of The Farmer's Boy and the size of its earliest print runs vary between accounts, and the twenty-five thousand figure is an approximation from bibliographical rather than from trade records. The publisher of the first edition is recorded in bookseller descriptions as Vernor and Hood, while later editions passed through other hands. Three particulars long attached to his career were not confirmed from primary titles during this review and should be checked against the copies themselves: the hand-coloured plate editions associated with Rudolph Ackermann and with the drawings of William Henry Pyne, a medal or premium from the Society of Arts, and a burial grant or permission connected with Westminster Abbey. The attribution of the prefixed account of the author to John Aikin, and the dating and imprint of a two-volume collection of 1813, are likewise matters on which secondary accounts disagree.

authors.name: Robert Boyle
authors.nationality: English (Anglo-Irish)
authors.identity: Natural philosopher and chemist, a founder of the Royal Society; his The Sceptical Chymist (1661) championed the new experimental method and corpuscular philosophy, and his pious writings defended Christianity as compatible with science.
authors.biography: Born 25 January 1627 at Lismore Castle, County Waterford, the youngest son of Richard Boyle, first Earl of Cork (the richest man in Britain); educated at Eton and in Europe (Geneva, Florence, where he read Galileo). Settling in England, he joined the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society (chartered 1662), conducted experiments with his assistant Robert Hooke (inventor of the air pump), and formulated Boyle's law of gases. A devout Anglican, he wrote prolifically on both science and religion — The Sceptical Chymist (1661), Some Physico-Theological Considerations (1665), and works defending the faith — and endowed the Boyle Lectures. He died on 31 December 1691.
authors.profile: The experimental philosopher who separated chemistry from alchemy and medicine, argued for the corpuscular (mechanical) philosophy, and reconciled scientific enquiry with Christian piety in a clear, plain prose.
authors.style: Plain, experimental, methodical prose; detailed reports of apparatus and results; dialogic form (The Sceptical Chymist); and a pious, reasoned apologetic style.
authors.concerns: Experimental method and the corpuscular philosophy; chemistry, gases, and the air pump; the reconciliation of science and religion; the plain style of the new science; and natural theology.
authors.significance: Boyle is a founder of modern chemistry and of the experimental method, and his advocacy of the plain style and of physico-theology shaped both scientific writing and the religious defence of science; the Boyle Lectures continued his apologetic project for generations.
authors.uncertainty: Boyle's life and works are thoroughly documented; his scientific and religious writings are extensive and partly published posthumously.

authors.name: Robert Bridges
authors.nationality: English; the classical lyric, the metrical experiment and the poet laureate
authors.identity: Poet and physician; the Poet Laureate from 1913 and the finest English technical poet of his generation.
authors.biography: Born Robert Seymour Bridges at Walmer, Kent, on 23 October 1844; he studied medicine at Oxford, where he met Gerard Manley Hopkins, and practised at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London until 1882, when he retired to Yattendon, Berkshire, to write. He published The Growth of Love (1876), Shorter Poems (1890) and The Testament of Beauty (1929); he edited Hopkins's poems in 1918 and was Poet Laureate from 1913. He died at Boar's Hill, Oxford, on 21 April 1930.
authors.profile: Bridges wrote the classical English lyric with a perfection of technique unmatched in his generation except by Housman: his short poems of love, nature and mortality are models of form, and his long metrical experiments — the sonnet sequence, the quantitative hexameters, the 'loose Alexandrines' of The Testament of Beauty — make him the most technically inventive English poet of his age. He is also the editor who made Hopkins known to the world.
authors.style: Exquisite metrical control in received forms; classical smoothness and restraint; a private, unfashionable lyric quietness; experiment in quantitative and accentual metre; the long philosophical poem in a new metre; the poem of English landscape and rural peace.
authors.concerns: Love, beauty and the passing of the seasons; mortality and the consolations of nature; the English countryside and rural peace; religion and the modern world; the art of poetry itself; time and the permanence of beauty.
authors.significance: Bridges is the finest English technical poet of his generation and the editor who preserved Hopkins for the language: The Testament of Beauty was a best-seller in 1929 and made him a public figure, his lyrics are models of form, and his edition of Hopkins changed the course of English poetry.

authors.name: Robert Browning
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian period
authors.identity: Poet and dramatist; the master of the dramatic monologue and the poet who made the difficult, allusive, spoken voice the instrument of Victorian psychology.
authors.biography: Born in Camberwell on 7 May 1812, the son of a Bank of England clerk with a large library; he was educated privately and at University College London, which he left without a degree. Pauline (1833) was published anonymously at his own expense; Paracelsus (1835) and Sordello (1840) followed, the latter's obscurity becoming a byword. Strafford was staged at Covent Garden in 1837 with Macready, and the plays of 1841-46 were collected as Bells and Pomegranates. He married Elizabeth Barrett in September 1846 and lived in Florence and Rome until her death in 1861; Men and Women appeared in 1855, Dramatis Personae in 1864, and The Ring and the Book in four volumes in 1868-69 made him famous. He returned to England in 1861 and died in Venice on 12 December 1889; he is buried in Poets' Corner.
authors.profile: Browning's central invention is the dramatic monologue as an instrument of self-betrayal: a speaker, usually at a moment of crisis, addresses an imagined listener, and the poem's meaning lies in what the speech reveals against the speaker's intention. He wrote in a deliberately rough, colloquial, parenthetical syntax and in rhymed forms whose rhymes are often grotesque, and he set the poem in the Renaissance, in the medical lecture room or in the modern drawing room indifferently. His religion of human love and of the value of the imperfect, stated most fully in the epilogue to Men and Women and in The Ring and the Book, is the intellectual centre of the work.
authors.style: Dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice; abrupt openings; colloquial parenthesis and asyndeton; elaborate and often comic rhyme; the use of historical documents and trial records as raw material; the casuistical argument conducted in verse.
authors.concerns: The psychology of self-justification; the relation of art to moral action (Fra Lippo Lippi, Andrea del Sarto, A Grammarian's Funeral); religion, doubt and the value of imperfect faith (Bishop Blougram, Caliban upon Setebos); marriage and the claims of the flesh; the Renaissance as a mirror of the Victorian present; the problem of evil and the justice of God.
authors.significance: Browning made the dramatic monologue the central Victorian poetic form, and with Tennyson he dominated the poetry of the age. His influence on Pound, Eliot and the modernist long poem is direct, and The Ring and the Book is the fullest Victorian attempt to write a truth by the multiplication of partial perspectives.

authors.name: Robert Burns
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Scottish poet in English and in the Scots dialect, celebrated for songs, narrative, and lyric, and honoured as the national poet of Scotland.
authors.biography: Burns was born in Ayrshire to a poor tenant farmer and was largely educated at home and by informal tutoring, working the land from childhood. His Kilmarnock edition, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (1786), was an immediate success and took him to Edinburgh, where he moved among literary and aristocratic circles. Later he settled as an officer of excise and continued to collect and adapt Scottish songs, contributing to James Johnson's Musical Museum and to George Thomson's collections. His lyrics and songs, and his narrative and satiric poems, such as Tam o' Shanter (1790) and Holy Willie's Prayer, display a range of humour, sentiment, and radical sympathy. He died in Dumfries in 1796, aged thirty-seven.
authors.profile: A poet and songwriter of the common tongue, equally at home in tender lyric, bawdy, comic narrative, and democratic or religious satire, drawing on the native Scottish song and vernacular tradition.
authors.style: Vivid Scots vernacular diction and idiom; song-measures of great melodic fluency; direct, passionate, and often humorous address; and a blend of rustic naturalness with refined lyric sensibility.
authors.concerns: Common humanity and democratic fellow-feeling; the critique of religious hypocrisy and cant; the value of nature and vernacular song; nationality, friendship, and the dignity of the ordinary.
authors.significance: The national poet of Scotland and a seminal figure of the Romantic age and of vernacular and song literature; he elevated Scottish dialect poetry and became a global emblem of popular, egalitarian feeling.
authors.uncertainty: The authorship and dating of individual songs are often complicated by his free borrowing, adaptation, and reconstruction of traditional texts; some details of his political sympathies are disputed.

authors.name: Robert Burton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: scholar; clergyman; prose writer
authors.biography: Born 8 February 1577 at Lindley, Leicestershire. Educated at Brasenose and Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent his life as student, tutor, librarian of Christ Church, and vicar of St Thomas's. A recluse among books, he died on 25 January 1640, having predicted his own death by horoscope; he is buried in Christ Church Cathedral.
authors.profile: The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621; five expanded editions in his lifetime, with a sixth posthumous in 1651), the vast encyclopedic treatise-disguised-as-self-cure written under the name 'Democritus Junior'.

authors.concerns: Melancholy in all its causes and cures; the vanity of learning; love, religion, and the passions as diseases of the mind.
authors.significance: A summa of Renaissance psychology and a fountainhead for Sterne, Lamb, and the whole tradition of English digressive prose.

authors.name: Robert Fabyan
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: chronicler; draper; alderman
authors.biography: A London draper, alderman, and sheriff (1493–94), Fabyan retired from civic life about 1502 and compiled his chronicle of England and France, which he finished by 1504 (with continuations to 1509). He died in London in 1513, and the work was printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France.
authors.profile: Author of the standard London chronicle of the early Tudor period. Organized annalistically around the mayors and sheriffs of London, Fabyan's chronicle supplied Shakespeare and the Tudor historians with the matter of English history from Brutus to Henry VII, and its verse interjections ('L'envoy') give it a distinctly civic literary character.
authors.style: The annalist's plain record, organized by civic year; occasional moralizing verse; a Londoner's eye for pageant, execution, and civic ceremony.
authors.concerns: The history of England and France as moral example; the dignity and record of the city of London.
authors.significance: The principal vernacular chronicle between the Brut tradition and Hall; a chief source of Tudor historical consciousness and of Shakespeare's history plays at second hand.
