authors.name: Robert Frost
authors.nationality: American; the New England dramatic lyric and the poem of the speaking voice
authors.identity: Poet; the greatest American poet of the period, the master of the New England dramatic lyric, and the only poet to win the Pulitzer Prize four times.
authors.biography: Born Robert Lee Frost in San Francisco on 26 March 1874; after his father's death in 1885 the family returned to New England, and he farmed in Derry, New Hampshire, taught, and published A Boy's Will (1913) and North of Boston (1914) in England, where Pound and Edward Thomas championed him. He returned to America in 1915, became the most honoured poet in the country — four Pulitzer Prizes (1924, 1931, 1937, 1943), the Congressional Gold Medal, the position of poetry consultant to the Library of Congress — and read 'The Gift Outright' at Kennedy's inauguration in 1961. He died in Boston on 29 January 1963.
authors.profile: Frost is the great American poet of the speaking voice and of the dark under the commonplace. His blank-verse dialogues of New England farm life — 'The Death of the Hired Man', 'Home Burial', 'The Wood-Pile' — brought the sound of actual speech into poetry, while his short lyrics ('Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay', 'Fire and Ice') are the most widely known American poems of the century. He is the period's central poet of the American landscape and the American loneliness.
authors.style: The sound of speech in strict iambic measure; the dramatic dialogue and the narrative poem; the plain word chosen for its weight; the metaphor that is a whole poem and not an ornament; the ending that turns the poem over; the New England landscape used as a moral instrument.
authors.concerns: The New England farm and the empty house; isolation, marriage and the failure of speech; the woods, the snow and the dark; work, and the dignity of the unglamorous; the American past and the American individual; the fear that lives under the ordinary.
authors.significance: Frost is the most honoured and most widely read American poet of the century: his New England dialogues gave American poetry the sound of speech, his lyrics are the most quoted in the language, and his four Pulitzer Prizes and the inauguration reading made him the national poet. He is the period's great poet of the ordinary and the terrible.

authors.name: Robert Graves
authors.nationality: British; the war memoir, the historical novel and the mythographic essay
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and mythographer; the author of Good-bye to All That, I, Claudius and The White Goddess, and the most productive English man of letters of the century.
authors.biography: Born Robert von Ranke Graves in Wimbledon on 24 July 1895, of Irish and German descent; he went from Charterhouse to the Royal Welch Fusiliers in 1914, was so badly wounded at the Somme in 1916 that he was reported dead, and published Over the Brazier (1916) and Fairies and Fusiliers (1917). He read at Oxford after the war, lived with Laura Riding in Majorca from 1929, wrote Good-bye to All That (1929), I, Claudius (1934), Claudius the God (1934) and The White Goddess (1948), held the chair of poetry at Oxford (1961–66) and died at Deià, Majorca, on 7 December 1985.
authors.profile: Graves is the period's most versatile writer: Good-bye to All That is one of the great memoirs of the war, I, Claudius and Claudius the God are the finest English historical novels of the century and became a landmark of television, and The White Goddess is one of the period's most influential — and most disputed — works of mythography. As a poet he wrote the best English love lyric of the period and kept a formal, lucid, unfashionable style through every modernist vogue.
authors.style: The plain, lucid, formal lyric in the eighteenth-century manner; the prose of the professional storyteller — swift, exact, unadorned; the first-person historical narration (Claudius); the argumentative, provocative essay of mythological speculation; the epigram and the satire.
authors.concerns: War and the waste of a generation; love, the beloved and the muse; the classical world and the Roman Empire; myth, the goddess and the poetic imagination; England and the English tradition; literary quarrels and the war between poet and critic.
authors.significance: Graves wrote one of the great war memoirs, the two finest English historical novels of the century, and one of the period's most influential books of mythography: Good-bye to All That changed the writing of autobiography, I, Claudius made imperial Rome a modern subject, and The White Goddess gave the period its idea of the poetic muse. He is the period's most productive and least categorisable writer.

authors.name: Robert Greene
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist; prose romancer; pamphleteer
authors.biography: Baptized 11 July 1558 in Norwich; took his BA at St John's College, Cambridge (1580) and MA from Clare Hall (1583), and was incorporated at Oxford. He came to London to live by the pen, married, abandoned his wife, and died in poverty on 3 September 1592 after a banquet of Rhenish wine and pickled herring, leaving the deathbed pamphlet Greene's Groatsworth of Wit, which contains the notorious 'upstart Crow' attack on Shakespeare.
authors.profile: The most prolific of the University Wits: plays include Alphonsus, King of Aragon (c. 1588), Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (c. 1589), James IV (c. 1590), and Orlando Furioso (1591); romances include Pandosto (1588), the source of The Winter's Tale, and Menaphon (1589); pamphlets include the cony-catching series (1591–92) exposing the tricks of London's underworld.
authors.style: Euphuistic prose, romantic plotting, pastoral charm, and a pamphlet style of vivid, confessional journalism.
authors.concerns: The moral and financial perils of authorship; repentance; the underworld of London; the rivalries of the professional stage.
authors.significance: A central University Wit whose romantic comedy and prose fiction fed Shakespeare directly; his cony-catching pamphlets are landmarks of English prose realism and rogue literature.
authors.uncertainty: His repentances were staged for the press; the Groatsworth attribution is generally accepted though its circumstances are murky.

authors.biography: A university graduate ('Master') who served as schoolmaster of the grammar school of Dunfermline and as a notary public; his name appears in the records of Dunfermline Abbey in 1478. authors.significance: Universally ranked with Dunbar as the greatest of the makars; his Testament of Cresseid is the most powerful continuation of Chaucer ever written, and his Fabillis the summit of the European fable tradition in the vernacular.

authors.name: Robert Herrick
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Cavalier poet and country parson; author of Hesperides (1648), a vast collection that joins pagan festivity, erotic lyrics, and devotional verse to a staunch Anglican and royalist piety rooted in rural Devon.
authors.biography: Born August 1591 in London (baptised at St Vedast), educated at St John's College, Cambridge (BA 1617, then transferred). A 'Son of Ben' in the London wit circles, he took orders and was presented to the living of Dean Prior in Devon (1629), where he served — grumbling at the rustic parishioners — until ejected by Parliament in 1647 as a royalist. He returned to London, published Hesperides (1648) and the religious Noble Numbers, then was restored to Dean Prior in 1662 after the Restoration and lived there until his death in October 1674.
authors.profile: The poet of 'gather ye rosebuds while ye may', whose Hesperides celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of the English countryside with a classical gaiety shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith.
authors.style: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics; classical and rustic imagery; a light, mellifluous metrical variety; and the pairing of pagan 'Hesperides' with the Christian 'Noble Numbers'.
authors.concerns: Carpe diem and mutability; rural festivity and custom; erotic love and marriage; Anglican ceremony and royalist loyalty; death and the consolations of faith.
authors.significance: Herrick is the greatest of the Cavalier lyricists in range and charm; Hesperides preserved the folklore and ceremonial culture of the English countryside and his lyrics have remained continuously popular.
authors.uncertainty: Herrick's life is documented mainly through his own poems and parish records; his exact attitudes and the arrangement of Hesperides remain matters of interpretation.

authors.name: Robert Hooke
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Natural philosopher, inventor, and microscopist; his Micrographia (1665), with its spectacular engravings of the flea, the louse, and plant cells (he coined the word 'cell'), was a landmark of scientific illustration and of the literature of discovery.
authors.biography: Born 18 July 1635 at Freshwater, Isle of Wight; educated at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became assistant to Boyle (building the air pump) and later Professor of Geometry. A founder-member and Curator of Experiments to the Royal Society, he published Micrographia (1665), a sensational success, and made contributions across physics (Hooke's law of elasticity), astronomy, geology, and architecture (as Surveyor to the City of London after the Great Fire, working with Wren). He disputed priority with Newton over optics and gravitation. He died on 3 March 1703; no certain portrait of him survives.
authors.profile: The brilliant experimentalist and observer whose Micrographia opened an invisible world to readers through its prose descriptions and magnificent engravings, inspiring wonder and the new empirical vision.
authors.style: Descriptive, observational scientific prose; detailed accounts of apparatus and experiments; spectacular engraving and visual rhetoric; and a plain, empirical style.
authors.concerns: Microscopy and the structure of matter; experimental method and instrumentation; elasticity, light, and mechanics; geology and fossils; and architecture and rebuilding.
authors.significance: Micrographia is a founding work of microscopy and scientific illustration and influenced the literature and imagination of the new science (Pepys called it 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'); Hooke's wide contributions made him a central figure of the Royal Society.
authors.uncertainty: Hooke's life is documented through Royal Society records and his diary; the destruction of his papers and the absence of a portrait have left his appearance and some achievements obscure.

authors.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
authors.nationality: Scottish; the Victorian adventure romance and the short story
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer; the great revivalist of the adventure romance and one of the finest English essayists of the century.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh on 13 November 1850, the only child of Thomas Stevenson, a lighthouse engineer. He was educated at Edinburgh Academy and the University of Edinburgh, read law and was called to the bar in 1875, though he never practised. Tuberculosis drove him to travel in search of health: France (1876-79), California (1879-80), where he married Fanny Osbourne in 1880, then Switzerland, the Riviera and Bournemouth. Treasure Island (1883), The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Kidnapped (1886), The Black Arrow (1888), The Master of Ballantrae (1889) and Catriona (1893) made him famous. In 1888 he sailed for the Pacific and settled at Vailima, Samoa, in 1890, where he took the Samoan name Tusitala and intervened in the politics of the islands. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage at Vailima on 3 December 1894 and is buried on Mount Vaea.
authors.profile: Stevenson wrote against the Victorian realist novel: he defended romance, the tale of adventure and the story as craft, and he made the Short Story a serious form in English. His prose is the most perfectly finished of the period — lucid, rhythmic and exact — and his essays on 'A Humble Remonstrance' and 'The Art of Fiction' set out a theory of fiction as a pattern of events rather than a transcript of life. Jekyll and Hyde is his one great myth, a fable of the divided self that became the nineteenth century's most enduring image of the unconscious.
authors.style: Classical purity and economy of prose; the carefully planted detail and the withheld explanation; a plot that turns on a single discovery; the Scottish historical novel's vernacular speech; the short story as a designed artefact; the essay as conversation.
authors.concerns: The divided self and the beast in man; the romance of adventure and of the boy's initiation; Scottish history, Jacobitism and the Union; travel, exile and the South Seas; honour, loyalty and courage; disease, death and the will to live; the craft of writing.
authors.significance: Stevenson made the adventure romance respectable again after the realists had rejected it, and Jekyll and Hyde is the founding text of modern psychological horror and of the literature of the double. His essays established the short story as a designed form, his South Sea writings are a central document in the critique of imperialism, and his influence on Conrad, Kipling, Borges and the modern story is continuous.

authors.name: Robert Nichols
authors.nationality: British; the Georgian war poet
authors.identity: Poet and playwright; one of the Georgian war poets and the author of Ardours and Endurances.
authors.biography: Born Robert Malise Bowyer Nichols on the Isle of Wight on 6 September 1893; he served in the Royal Field Artillery on the Western Front, was invalided out with shell shock, and published Invocation (1915) and Ardours and Endurances (1917), which made him famous as a war poet. He taught at Tokyo and wrote plays and broadcasts, and died at Cambridge on 17 December 1944.

authors.name: Robert Owen
authors.nationality: Welsh-born British; the Owenite and cooperative writing of the early industrial decades, and the Welsh-English prose of social reform, report and autobiography
authors.identity: Cotton manufacturer, manager of New Lanark and social reformer; the writer who turned the government of a manufacturing community into a published argument for character, education and cooperation, and whose pamphlets, reports and autobiography founded the Owenite movement of the 1830s and 1840s.
authors.biography: Owen was born at Newtown in Montgomeryshire on 14 May 1771, the son of a saddler and ironmonger, and was apprenticed as a draper in London in early youth. He bought his way out of service, took a share in a Manchester manufacturing business, and taught himself the theory and practice of cotton spinning. In 1799 or 1800 he became a partner in, and manager of, the cotton works at New Lanark on the Clyde, founded by David Dale whose daughter he had married, and there for a quarter of a century he carried out the experiment that made his name: a shortened working day, the refusal to take children under ten into the mills, an infant school and schools for the older children, company shops, housing, saving banks and insurance, and the deliberate government of the population as a moral and educational concern. New Lanark was visited by foreign observers and by statistical inquirers, and Owen published his practice in A New View of Society of 1813, which was widely translated. His success in manufacture he now turned against the system of competition. At the request of the magistrates and clergy of his adopted county he drew up the Report to the County of Lanark, printed at Glasgow in 1821, which argued from the distress and surplus labour of the post-war years for villages of cooperation and mutual interest to be raised by parishes, counties and the state, and which offered his famous national plan of education and production to Parliament. Disappointed in Britain, he bought the settlement of New Harmony in Indiana and removed thither in 1825 with his sons and a company of friends; the experiment failed in a few years and left him heavy losses and an unpopularity he never wholly overcame. He returned to Britain, settled in London, and spent the rest of his life as a public teacher of cooperation, lecturing, printing and organising, and giving his countenance to cooperative communities and to the trade unions of 1834. His Book of the New Moral World gathered his later teaching; his Autobiography, revised by his son, was published in the 1850s. He died at Newtown, where he had been born, on 17 November 1858, and was buried there.
authors.profile: His writings are those of a reformer and a manager rather than a literary artist: the New View of Society of 1813, a series of short argumentative essays on the formation of character, on the vice of the existing system and on the means of its remedial change; the Report to the County of Lanark of 1821, a statistical and practical proposal of villages of cooperation, written for a county meeting and printed with the returns of population and distress; a great body of addresses, letters, open letters to ministers and to governments, and evidence before committees; the Book of the New Moral World, in which his later teaching on society, production and religion was systematically set out; and the Autobiography, the plainest and most readable of his books, which records his boyhood, his apprenticeship and his management of New Lanark.
authors.style: A plain, urgent, unprefaced prose of proposition and proof, written in short numbered paragraphs and in the vocabulary of fact, of experience and of common sense; he reasons from the case of his own mills, uses figures and returns of population, wages and product, and is confident to the point of dogma, with a marked habit of addressing parliaments, counties and nations directly. The Autobiography is conversational, unaffected and anecdotal, with a dissenting plainness of statement; his later polemical writing grows repetitive, abstract and missionary.
authors.concerns: The formation of character by circumstance, education and example, and therefore the irresponsibility of punishing the vices produced by bad institutions; the moral government and education of a manufacturing population, and the infant school as the key to social change; the waste, cruelty and instability of competition and of the cheap-labour system; the village or community of cooperation and mutual interest as the unit of reorganised production; the surplus labour and distress of the peace; the public duty of the state, the parish and the rich in education and in the relief of the poor; the relation of religion, of marriage and of property to social improvement.
authors.significance: He made New Lanark the best-known example in Europe of the manufacturer's management of his people, and his Formation of Character and his Report to the County of Lanark set the terms on which education, the relief of distress and model communities were argued in the 1820s; his name gave the cooperative movement its most powerful English organising impulse, and the villages of cooperation he proposed were the parent of the Owenite communities of the 1820s and 1830s in Britain and America. His teaching, his lectures and his sponsorship of the trade union and cooperative enterprises of 1834 stand between the philanthropic paternalism of the eighteenth century and the organised labour and cooperative movement of the nineteenth, and the Autobiography remains a founding text of the working-man's own record of industrial life.
authors.uncertainty: The year in which he became a partner at New Lanark is given as 1799 and as 1800, the difference turning on the date of the written agreement and of his taking up the management. His first publication, the New View of Society, is generally dated from the private printing of 1812 and the public edition of 1813, and the Report to the County of Lanark is described both as composed for the county meeting of 1820 and as printed in 1821. The numbers he gives of the New Lanark population, of his returns and of the losses at New Harmony are his own report and cannot be independently verified, and the extent to which his later writings were drafted or revised by his sons and by his secretary is not settled.

authors.name: Robert Southey
authors.birthplace: Bath, Somerset, in a family of Bristol merchants and dissenters
authors.nationality: English; poet, prose-writer and historian, of the Lake school and of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Poet of the Eastern and national epic, historian and biographer, and the most prolific and most various of the three Lake writers of the first generation, whose long career carried him from the radicalism of the 1790s to the laureateship and the establishment letters of the 1820s and 1830s.
authors.biography: Southey was born at Bath into a Bristol family, was educated largely at Bristol grammar school and entered Balliol College, Oxford in 1792, where he made the acquaintance that led to the American communitarian scheme; he was intended for the church but abandoned the design of orders, and after a short stay in Scotland and an attempt at the law he lived by his pen. He married in 1795 the elder of the two sisters whose sister his friend of the scheme had first married, and after years in the west he settled in 1802 at Greta Hall in Keswick, where the lake country gave the group its name. The epics of the first decade, with the Welsh romance and the Hindu tale, made him the most conspicuous narrative poet of the day, and his later work was chiefly historical and biographical: a history of Brazil, a history of the Peninsular war, lives of the admiral of Trafalgar and of the founder of Methodism, a miscellaneous prose series and a vast correspondence. He accepted the laureateship in 1813 along with a government recognition of his studies, married a second time in 1829 to a writer of the north, and in March 1843 a fire at Greta Hall destroyed part of his library and hastened his death.
authors.profile: His poetry runs from the republican epic of the Maid of Orleans through the Eastern tales and the Welsh legend of the discoverer to the later romance and the national and religious verse of the laureate years; his prose includes biography, history, letters of travel, controversy and miscellany. The ambition of a national epic and of a national history governed his life, and he was the busy centre of the literary and publishing business of the Lakes. His present reputation rests on the prose life of the admiral, on the letters, and on the record of the radical writings of his youth.
authors.style: In verse a fluent and stately blank verse and a deliberate experiment in an accentual and reiterated stanza, with narrative plainness and a wealth of descriptive matter; in prose a clear, brisk and often witty style of narrative and argument, direct in the letters and comprehensive in the historical and biographical books.
authors.concerns: The epic, the national poem and the machinery of the Eastern religions; Providence, law and obedience in the moral government of the world; the history, character and settlement of nations; the condition of the church and of letters as a profession; the duties of the writer to the state and to the public.
authors.significance: As the prolific narrative poet of the 1800s he made the Eastern and national romance in verse a leading form of the day, and as historian, biographer, letter-writer and editor he was an institutional centre of Romantic letters; his life of the admiral became the standard English biography of the national hero. His early radical writings and his later establishment were used by rivals to define the politics of the Lake school, and the long review controversy over his epic career is a permanent chapter of Romantic literary history.

authors.name: Robert Tressell
authors.nationality: British; the proletarian novelist of The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists
authors.identity: Painter and novelist; the author of The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists.
authors.biography: Born Robert Phillipe Noonan at Dublin on 18 April 1870; he worked as a house painter in Cape Town and Hastings and wrote The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists, the novel of the painters of the town of Mugsborough, in the years before his death. He died of tuberculosis at Liverpool on 3 February 1911, and the book was published, cut, in 1914, with the full text only in 1955.
authors.profile: Robert Tressell is the proletarian novelist of the English working class: The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists, the novel of the painters of Mugsborough and of the tearing of the bread, is the founding text of the working-class novel in England and the book of the labour movement's own canon.
authors.style: The plain angry prose of the painter's argument; the job, the tool and the wet wall reported from the ladder; the lecture in the novel, the economics in the dialogue; the satire of the charity and the philanthropy; the working speech of the shop and the street.
authors.concerns: The working class and the tearing of the bread; the charity, the philanthropy and the ragged trousers; the economics of the job and the profit; the religion of the church and the religion of the worker; the dying painter and the book he leaves.

authors.name: Robert Whittington
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: grammarian
authors.biography: Born at Lichfield about 1480; studied at Oxford, where he was laureated for grammar. He taught in London and wrote a series of grammatical and rhetorical textbooks, of which the Vulgaria (1520) — model sentences in Latin and English for schoolboys — is the most famous. He died about 1553.
authors.profile: The most successful school grammarian of the generation before Lily's Grammar was standardized. The Vulgaria's paired Latin and English sentences, drawn from everyday school and city life, are at once a textbook and a vivid picture of early Tudor London, and its jibes at Lily made it a document of the grammar wars of the 1520s.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's sentence-builder; colloquial English paired with schoolboy Latin; combative prefaces addressed to rival grammarians.
authors.concerns: The teaching of Latin through the vernacular; the rivalries of the grammar schools; the manners and language of London boys.
authors.significance: A principal maker of the Tudor school curriculum; the Vulgaria is a unique record of the spoken English of the early sixteenth century.

authors.name: Rodney Ackland
authors.nationality: British; the West End dramatist of The Dark River
authors.identity: Playwright and screenwriter; the author of Strange Orchestra and The Dark River.
authors.biography: Born Norman Ackland Bernstein at Westcliff-on-Sea in 1908, the son of the musical comedy star Ada Rodney; he trained at the Central School of Speech Training and wrote his first play, Improper People, at fifteen - it was staged at the Arts Theatre in 1929. Strange Orchestra (1932) was Gielgud's first contemporary play in the West End, After October (1936) is his most autobiographical, and The Dark River (1937), with Peggy Ashcroft, was called on its revival the one indisputably great play of the half-century; he also wrote screenplays with Rattigan; he died on 6 December 1991.
authors.profile: Rodney Ackland is the neglected master of the between-wars West End: The Dark River set the idle household of the Thames backwater against the Spanish war and the coming of fascism with a Chekhovian exactness, and its revivals have made him the rediscovered dramatist of the thirties stage.
authors.style: The drawing-room dialogue of the West End with the politics of the decade beneath it; the household cut off in the English countryside; the bohemian family of After October; the film script's pace; the contrast of the frivolous and the responsible in the same scene.
authors.concerns: The coming war and the household that ignores it; the English countryside as the refuge and the trap; the bohemian life of the writer; the West End stage and the repertory; the rediscovery of the neglected play.
authors.significance: Rodney Ackland is the neglected master of the between-wars West End: The Dark River set the idle household against the Spanish war with a Chekhovian exactness, and its revivals made him the rediscovered dramatist of the thirties stage.

authors.name: Roger Ascham
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: humanist; tutor to Elizabeth I; Latin secretary
authors.biography: Born at Kirby Wiske about 1515; educated at St John's College, Cambridge, where he taught Greek and reformed the pronunciation of it. Tutor to Princess Elizabeth from 1548 to 1550, he served as Latin secretary under Mary and Elizabeth. His Toxophilus (1545), a dialogue in praise of archery, won him a royal pension, and The Schoolmaster, begun about 1563, was published posthumously in 1570 by his widow. He died on 30 December 1568.
authors.profile: The most readable of the English humanist educators. Toxophilus is the first English treatise on a sport and a model of the plain style; The Schoolmaster — built around the instruction of the young Elizabeth — attacks Italianate corruption, prescribes the double translation of Latin, and records the educational practice of the age in the finest English prose between More and Hooker.
authors.style: The plain style refined into art: concrete, anecdotal, sinewy English that he explicitly opposed to the inkhorn inflation of his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The education of the English governing class; the discipline of imitation and translation; the morality of travel; archery and bodily training as parts of the curriculum.
authors.significance: Tutor and intellectual model of Elizabeth I; The Schoolmaster governed English pedagogical theory for two centuries and remains the classic defence of the vernacular for learning.

authors.name: Roger Bacon
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: philosopher; scientist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: Educated at Oxford and Paris, where he lectured on Aristotle, he joined the Franciscans c. 1257 and, frustrated by the neglect of experimental science, sought the patronage of Pope Clement IV, for whom he composed the Opus Maius, Opus Minus, and Opus Tertium in 1267–68. He was condemned by his order c. 1278 and imprisoned, and died c. 1292.
authors.profile: Author of the Opus Maius (1267), a programmatic encyclopedia of the sciences — mathematics, optics, experimental science, moral philosophy, and the reform of learning — together with works on grammar, astronomy, alchemy, and the calendar.
authors.style: Urgent, polemical, encyclopedic prose; the advocacy of mathematics and experiment ('scientia experimentalis') as the foundation of knowledge; prophetic visions of technology (ships, cars, flying machines).
authors.concerns: The reform of the universities and of the church through science; the study of languages and texts; the practical power of knowledge.
authors.significance: The greatest scientific mind of the medieval West before the fourteenth-century natural philosophers; his experimental program made him the patron figure of early modern science in England (and the hero of Victorian legend).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and the chronology of his Oxford years approximate; the circumstances of his condemnation are unclear.

authors.name: Roger Fry
authors.nationality: British; the art criticism of the Post-Impressionists and the formalist essay
authors.identity: Painter, critic and curator; the man who brought Post-Impressionism to England, the founder of the Omega Workshops, and one of the period's most influential art writers.
authors.biography: Born Roger Eliot Fry in London on 14 December 1866 into a Quaker family; he studied natural sciences at Cambridge and painting in Paris and Italy, worked as a critic for the Athenaeum and the Burlington Magazine, and organised the two Post-Impressionist exhibitions in London (1910 and 1912) that changed English painting. He founded the Omega Workshops in 1913, became Slade Professor at Cambridge in 1933, and died in London on 9 September 1934; Virginia Woolf's biography of him appeared in 1940.
authors.profile: Fry is the great English art critic of the period: the 1910 exhibition introduced Cézanne, Gauguin, Van Gogh and Matisse to England, and his formalist criticism — Vision and Design (1920), Transformations (1926), Cézanne (1927) — gave English writing about art a new vocabulary and a new seriousness. The Omega Workshops made modern design a Bloomsbury enterprise.
authors.style: The formalist description of a picture — line, mass, colour and the organisation of the surface; the conversational lecture; the polemical review; the plain, exact, unmystical prose of the working painter.
authors.concerns: The formal qualities of art and the independence of the aesthetic; Post-Impressionism and the modern movement; the decorative and the applied arts; Italian painting and the classical tradition; criticism as a profession.
authors.significance: Fry made modern art visible in England: the Post-Impressionist exhibitions of 1910 and 1912 introduced the century's painting to a British public, his criticism established formalism as a method, and the Omega Workshops made modern design practical. He is the period's central art writer.

authors.name: Rosamond Lehmann
authors.nationality: British; the novel of the young woman's consciousness
authors.identity: Novelist; the author of Dusty Answer and The Weather in the Streets, and one of the finest English novelists of the 1930s.
authors.biography: Born Rosamond Nina Lehmann at Bourne End, Buckinghamshire, on 3 February 1901; she read at Girton College, Cambridge, and published Dusty Answer in 1927, which made her famous. authors.name: Rudyard Kipling
authors.nationality: English-Indian; the imperial tale, the ballad and the children's book
authors.identity: Poet, short-story writer and novelist; the greatest English writer of the imperial experience and the youngest winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
authors.biography: Born in Bombay on 30 December 1865; he was brought to England at five and boarded with a family in Southsea whose cruelty he later recorded in 'Baa Baa, Black Sheep', then went to the United Services College at Westward Ho. He returned to India in 1882 and worked as a journalist in Lahore and Allahabad, publishing Departmental Ditties (1886) and Plain Tales from the Hills (1888). He lived in London and Vermont from 1889, married Carrie Balestier in 1892, and wrote the Indian and English stories, the Jungle Books, Kim and the Just So Stories. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1907 and died in London on 18 January 1936.
authors.profile: Kipling made the Empire a literary subject: his Indian stories are written from inside the working of the Anglo-Indian administration, with an exactness about native speech, bureaucracy and violence that no other English writer of the period achieved. His verse — Barrack-Room Ballads, The Seven Seas, Recessional — gave the imperial project its songs and, in 'Recessional' and 'The White Man's Burden', its most troubling self-criticism. His children's books are formal masterpieces, and Kim is the finest English novel of India.
authors.style: Terse, concrete narrative; technical and dialect vocabulary; the story as a single hard incident; ballads with a driving refrain; the epigram and the gnomic utterance; a narrator who assumes a community of knowledge with the reader.
authors.concerns: Empire and the work of administration; the English in India and the native soldier; machinery, engineering and the modern world; courage, endurance and the code of the man at work; childhood and the loss of India; the supernatural and the uncanny.
authors.significance: Kipling is the central writer of the British Empire and one of the most technically accomplished poets and story-writers in English: Kim, the Jungle Books and the Just So Stories are permanent classics, the Barrack-Room Ballads changed English poetry, and his stories of India are the foundation of the literature of the British in Asia. His politics have made him a contested figure, but his formal mastery is beyond question.

authors.name: Rupert Brooke
authors.nationality: British; the Georgian lyric and the 1914 war sonnet
authors.identity: Poet; the golden boy of the Georgian anthology and the author of the 1914 sonnets, the most famous English poems of the war's first year.
authors.biography: Born Rupert Chawner Brooke at Rugby on 3 August 1887, the son of a schoolmaster at Rugby School; he read at King's College, Cambridge, where he acted, wrote and became an Apostle, travelled in Germany, America and the Pacific, and published Poems (1911) and the Georgian Poetry volume of 1912. He joined the Royal Naval Division in 1914, saw action at Antwerp, and died of septicaemia from an infected mosquito bite aboard a French hospital ship off Skyros on 23 April 1915; he was buried on the island that evening, and 'The Soldier' was read from St Paul's the following Sunday.
authors.profile: Brooke is the period's emblem of the lost generation and the author of the most famous English war poems: the five 1914 sonnets — 'Peace', 'Safety', 'The Dead', 'The Dead', 'The Soldier' — gave the war its rhetoric of sacrifice, and his death made him a national myth. His earlier poetry is the best of the Georgian lyric, and his letters and travel prose are among the finest of the period.
authors.style: The Georgian sonnet and the rhymed lyric; the exact English landscape and the names of places; the speaking voice held in strict form; the rhetoric of the last line; the travel letter and the Pacific sketch.
authors.concerns: England, home and the English dead; the war as a summons and a purification; the Pacific and the South Seas idyll; friendship, love and the Cambridge years; the body and the swimming sea.
authors.significance: Brooke is the most famous English poet of the war's first year and the emblem of the Georgian generation: the 1914 sonnets gave the war its language of sacrifice, 'The Soldier' is one of the best-known English poems, and his death on Skyros became the period's defining national myth — the poem and the myth are the record of a generation's illusions.

authors.name: Saki (H. H. Munro)
authors.nationality: British; the short comic story and the satire of Edwardian society
authors.identity: Short-story writer; the greatest English writer of the comic short story, the master of the surprise ending, and a satirist of Edwardian society more savage than any of his contemporaries.
authors.biography: Born Hector Hugh Munro at Akyab, Burma, on 18 December 1870; he was brought up in Devon by his aunts after his mother's death, served in the Burma police (1893–95), and worked as a journalist in London and as a foreign correspondent in the Balkans and Russia. Reginald (1904), Reginald in Russia (1910), The Chronicles of Clovis (1911) and Beasts and Super-Beasts (1914) made his name; he enlisted in 1914 at forty-three, refused a commission, and was killed by a sniper at Beaumont-Hamel on 14 November 1916.
authors.profile: Saki is the greatest English writer of the comic short story: his Reginald and Clovis stories are the most perfect examples of the surprise ending in the language, and their satire of Edwardian society — the aunts, the house parties, the hunting, the children — is far more savage than the surface gaiety suggests. 'Sredni Vashtar', 'Tobermory' and 'The Open Window' are permanent anthology pieces, and his death in the war cut off one of the period's most distinctive comic talents.
authors.style: The short story built on a single surprise; the epigram and the outrageous aside; the child's revenge on the adult world; the animal as agent of retribution; the comedy of the English house party; the ending that turns the whole story over in a line.
authors.concerns: Edwardian society and its aunts; childhood, cruelty and the revenge of the child; the English house party and the hunting field; animals as moral agents; the supernatural played for comedy; the war and the end of the Edwardian idyll.
authors.significance: Saki is the greatest English writer of the comic short story and the finest satirist of Edwardian society: 'Sredni Vashtar', 'Tobermory' and 'The Open Window' are permanent, his surprise endings taught a whole century how a short story works, and his death in the war made him the period's most poignant casualty among the comic writers.

authors.identity: Novelist, poet and critic; the author of More Pricks Than Kicks, Echo's Bones and Murphy before the war.

authors.significance: Samuel Beckett is the central writer of the twentieth century: the English books of the 1930s - the Joyce essay, More Pricks Than Kicks, Echo's Bones and Murphy - are the first act of the career that the French trilogy and the plays would complete.

authors.name: Samuel Butler
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Satirist and poet; author of Hudibras, the brilliant mock-heroic burlesque of Puritan hypocrisy that became one of the most quoted poems of the Restoration and defined English comic satire for a century.
authors.biography: Born c. 1612–13 at Strensham, Worcestershire; educated at the free school of Worcester and possibly Cambridge. He served in Puritan and royalist households, acted as steward to the royalist Sir William Waller, and after the Restoration held posts including secretary to the Lord President of the Marches at Ludlow. He published Hudibras in three parts (1663, 1664, 1678), a huge success celebrated by the court but poorly rewarded; he left a mass of unpublished 'characters' and notes (printed posthumously as Miscellaneous Thoughts, 1759, and The Genuine Remains, 1694). He died in poverty on 25 September 1680.
authors.profile: The scourge of Puritan cant, whose Hudibras attacked the hypocrisy of the Presbyterian Independents in rollicking doggerel and proverbial wit, coining countless phrases still in use.
authors.style: Comic octosyllabic couplets with absurd rhymes; mock-heroic and burlesque; a dense store of proverbs, puns, and learned-satiric allusion; and terse, epigrammatic 'characters' in prose.
authors.concerns: Hypocrisy, fanaticism, and false learning; royalist and Anglican loyalty; human folly and self-interest; and the satire of sectarian politics.
authors.significance: Hudibras was the most popular satire of the Restoration, a favourite of Charles II, and its mock-heroic technique directly influenced Dryden, Swift, and Pope's Dunciad.

authors.name: Samuel Butler (1835-1902)
authors.nationality: English; Victorian satire, fiction and Darwinian controversy
authors.identity: Novelist, satirist, translator and controversialist; the most anti-Victorian of the Victorians, and the author of Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh.
authors.biography: Born at Bingham on 4 December 1835, son of a clergyman and grandson of the headmaster of Shrewsbury; he was educated at Shrewsbury under his grandfather and at St John's College, Cambridge, and ran away to Canterbury, New Zealand, in 1859 rather than take orders, where he made money as a sheep farmer. He returned to London in 1864 and became a painter, musician and writer. Erewhon appeared anonymously in 1872, The Fair Haven in 1873, Life and Habit in 1877, Evolution Old and New in 1879, Unconscious Memory in 1880 and his prose translations of the Iliad (1898) and Odyssey (1900). The Way of All Flesh was written in 1873-84 and published posthumously in 1903; he died in London on 18 June 1902, leaving his money to found a controversy on the authorship of the Odyssey.
authors.profile: Butler wrote against the grain of Victorian belief: against the literalism of the Christian creed, against the Darwinism of Darwin himself (he argued for the inherited memory of habit and attacked the mechanism of natural selection), against the family, the school, and the cult of money. Erewhon is a Swiftian imaginary country whose institutions invert English ones — criminals are treated as invalids, illness is punished — and whose 'Book of the Machines' is the first serious English account of the possibility of machine consciousness. The Way of All Flesh is a satirical family chronicle of four generations of clergymen, and it became one of the defining attacks on Victorian patriarchy.
authors.style: Swiftian inversion and the invented institution; a plain, sceptical, argumentative prose in the essays; in the fiction, the ironic narrator and the family chronicle; the use of the imaginary society to test the real one; epigram and the deliberately flat conclusion.
authors.concerns: The mechanical and the purposive in evolution; the machine and its possible consciousness; the tyranny of the Victorian family and the clergy; hypocrisy, money and respectability; the authorship of the Odyssey; religion as a provisional hypothesis.
authors.significance: Butler is the great anti-Victorian satirist and the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century 'strangers to the Victorian age': The Way of All Flesh was a central influence on Butler's admirers, on Shaw, and on Samuel Butler studies at the beginning of modern English literature; Erewhon's Book of the Machines is a foundational text of the literature of artificial intelligence, and his Homeric translations remain among the most readable in English.

authors.biography: Samuel Eli Cornish was born in 1795 in Sussex County, Delaware, of free parents, and grew up to be one of the most influential African-American men of letters in New York before 1860. The Presbytery of Philadelphia launched his ministry in 1819 and he was ordained in 1822, afterwards preaching in New York City and gathering the first African Presbyterian church there, whose pastorate he held for years. In March 1827 he and John Brown Russwurm, a Bowdoin College graduate then teaching school in Boston, founded Freedom's Journal in New York, recognised by the Library of Congress as the first African-American-owned and -edited newspaper in the United States; it began weekly publication on 16 March 1827 and Cornish served as its senior editor. He withdrew in September 1827 over the colonisation question, which he opposed while his colleague came to advocate removal to Africa, and the paper, in its last months under Russwurm alone, endorsed the colonisation societies before ceasing publication in 1829. Cornish answered with The Rights of All, launched in the spring of 1829, which lived less than a year, and from 1837 to 1839 he edited with Philip A. Bell and Charles B. Ray the Colored American, which had begun as the Weekly Advocate in January 1837 and took its known name on 4 March 1837. He continued to preach, to publish and to plead for the moral, educational and economic betterment of the coloured people of New York until his death at Brooklyn on 6 November 1858; he had married Jane Livingston and left children.
authors.profile: His surviving writing is occasional and editorial rather than bookish. The numbers of Freedom's Journal (16 March 1827 onward) carry his opening claim that the people of colour must be able to speak for themselves and no longer need anyone to define them, together with editorials on slavery and the slave trade, on the pretensions of the colonisation societies, on education, temperance and industry, and letters, statistics and notices of African-American churches, schools and achievements drawn from the Black communities of the Atlantic states. The Rights of All (1829-30) was his own weekly reply to Russwurm's emigrationism, and the Colored American (1837-9) gave him a larger organ for the same programme of self-help, denominational news and antislavery argument; his name also appears as a contributor to that paper's numbers after his editorial connection ended, and a speech or address of his is recorded in the abolitionist archive for October 1839. No independent volume of sermons or treatises by him survives in the accounts consulted here.
authors.style: His manner is that of the coloured pulpit turned to editorial use: earnest, declarative, and built on the first-person plural, with the balanced period of the moral essay and the cadence of scripture. The argument is usually from conceded premises to a demand for recognition rather than from statistical detail, and the tone shifts between remonstrance with white patronage, exhortation to his own community, and irony at the colonisation societies. Self-representation is his governing device: the paper's independence is itself the claim, and his editorials treat the act of printing as evidence of capacity.
authors.concerns: The right and duty of the oppressed to speak in their own voice in print; the moral and economic elevation of the free Black population through churches, schools, temperance and skilled labour; the colonisation controversy and the claim that removal to Africa could solve the problem of American slavery and prejudice; the relation between the abolitionist cause and white benevolent societies; citizenship, nativity and belonging in a republic that denied both; and the education and self-government of the coloured ministry.
authors.significance: As first editor of Freedom's Journal he broke the white monopoly on the public representation of African Americans and founded the Black press tradition that ran through the Colored American and the later abolitionist newspapers; his resignation of 1827 and the success of The Rights of All mark the opening of the quarrel between abolitionist immediatism and colonisation emigrationism, a division that shaped Black politics for two decades. The New York coloured Presbyterian church he gathered is a landmark in African-American religious history, and his career is the standard case in histories of the Black press of the minister-editor who makes a newspaper an instrument of communal self-definition.
authors.uncertainty: Only the year of his birth is settled, and it is given as 1795 with the day and month unknown, some genealogical and encyclopedic accounts printing 'about 1795' or '1795?'; his birth in Sussex County, Delaware, rests on the account of his life in the BlackPast and New-York Historical Society sketches. The date at which he founded or took the pastorate of the first African Presbyterian church in New York is variously given as 1821, 1822 and 1829, and the order of his licences and settlements cannot be established from the sources consulted. The opening of The Rights of All is dated April 1829 by some accounts and May 1829 by others, and its end is reported as 'less than a year' and as 1829-30. His editorial connection with the Colored American is given as 1837-9 while the paper ran to 1842. His death is usually given as 6 November 1858 at Brooklyn, but another modern account places it in August 1858. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty.

authors.name: Samuel Daniel
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and historian; the author of Delia, one of the first of the 1590s sonnet sequences, and of the long poem The Civil Wars, tutor to Lady Anne Clifford.
authors.biography: Born c. 1562 near Taunton, the son of a music master; educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as tutor to William Herbert, later Earl of Pembroke, and travelled in Italy; his sonnet sequence Delia appeared in 1591–92 (appended to Astrophel and Stella in its first edition), followed by The Complaint of Rosamond (1592) and the tragedies Cleopatra (1594) and Philotas (1605). He was tutor to Lady Anne Clifford and groom of the chamber to Queen Anne; his Civil Wars (1595, revised to 1609) chronicled the Wars of the Roses. He died in October 1619 at Beckington, Somerset.
authors.profile: A laureate of moderate, musical verse — 'well-languaged Daniel' — whose sonnets, epistles, and philosophical poems (Musophilus, 1599) exemplify the Elizabethan ideal of learned eloquence in the service of moral reflection.
authors.style: Smooth, balanced, sententious verse; the plain-style reaction against Petrarchan conceit; an Augustan moderation of diction and rhythm that anticipates the seventeenth century.
authors.concerns: The uses of history as moral example; the fortunes of kings and the instability of power; poetry as the civilizing art; constancy in love and in the self.
authors.significance: A principal shaper of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and of the verse-epistle and historical poem; his influence ran to Milton and the Augustans, and his Delia's 'Care-charmer Sleep' remains a classic.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth (1562 or 1563) is uncertain; the extent of his rewriting of The Civil Wars across editions makes the poem's textual history complex.
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
themes: Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress

authors.name: Samuel Ferguson
authors.birthplace: Belfast, born on 10 March 1810 in the house of his maternal grandparents, the Knoxes, in High Street; his father, John Ferguson of Collon House, co. Antrim, had wasted a competence, and the family lived successively at Cider Court near Crumlin, at The Throne near Belfast and at Collon in Glenwhirry
authors.nationality: Irish; the Ulster Protestant and antiquarian strand of Irish Romantic writing, which made the Old Irish sagas, the Latin texts of St Patrick and the Irish song tradition the matter of a national poetry, and which looked to Scott, Burns and the metrical romance rather than to the English lake poets
authors.identity: Poet, satirist, adapter of Irish saga and song, and antiquary; a barrister who became the first Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland, was knighted, and presided over the Royal Irish Academy
authors.biography: Samuel Ferguson, third son of John Ferguson of Collon House, co. Antrim, by Agnes Knox, was born in Belfast on 10 March 1810 in his maternal grandparents' house and grew up at Collon in Glenwhirry, where he received those impressions of nature and romance which governed his taste. His mother read aloud to the children Shakespeare, Scott, Milton, Burns, Byron, Shelley and Keats, and his father's declining means obliged him to support himself by his pen. Educated at the Belfast Academical Institution and at Trinity College Dublin, which he left, as he said, before graduation, he was called to the Irish bar in 1838, practised on the north-eastern circuit and took silk in 1859. 'The Forging of the Anchor' appeared in Blackwood's in 1832, when he was twenty-one, and was read by Professor Wilson in the 'Noctes Ambrosianae'; 'The Wet Wooing' followed, and from 1833 he was a constant contributor to the Dublin University Magazine, where 'Hibernian Nights' Entertainments' ran beside his metrical versions of Irish sagas and his 1834 attack on Hardiman's 'Irish Minstrelsy'. He versified the quarrels of the forties in 'Dublin' and 'Inheritor and Economist' (1849), and his lament for Thomas Davis, written in 1845, entered Duffy's 'Ballad Poetry of Ireland'. A founding member of Butt's Protestant Repeal Association in 1848, which he quickly left over its Young Ireland connexions, he served on the defence in John Mitchel's treason-felony trial, and on 16 August 1848 married Mary Catharine Guinness, whose North Great George's Street house drew every Dubliner who cared for letters, music or art. 'Lays of the Western Gael' (1865), 'Congal' (1872) and 'Poems' (1880), with his blank-verse 'Confession of St. Patrick' (1885), established his claim to be Ireland's national poet. First Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland from 1867, knighted in 1878 and president of the Royal Irish Academy from 1882, he died at Strand Lodge, Howth, on 9 August 1886 and was buried at Donegore; his widow's posthumous 'Ogham Inscriptions' (1887) and 'Lays of the Red Branch' (1897) fixed his standing as the forerunner of the Irish literary revival.
authors.profile: His verse, first dispersed in Blackwood's and the Dublin University Magazine, gathers the Gaelic and ecclesiastical matter of Ireland into metrical tale, lament and song: 'The Forging of the Anchor' and 'The Wet Wooing' (1832), the versions of 'O'Byrne's Bard', the 'Lament over the Ruins of Timoleague Abbey', 'The Fair Hills of Holy Ireland' and 'The Forester's Complaint' (1834), 'The Fairy Thorn' and 'Willy Gilliland' (1836), 'The Cromlech on Howth' (1841), the elegy on Thomas Davis, 'Lays of the Western Gael' (1865), 'Congal: a Poem in Five Books' (1872) on the Ulster cycle, 'Deirdre: a One-Act Drama of Old Irish Story' (1880), 'Poems' (1880), and the St Patrick translations of 1885 and 1888. In prose he wrote the mixed verse-and-tale series 'Hibernian Nights' Entertainments' (magazines 1833-6; collected 1887), the satires 'Father Tom and the Pope' (1865), 'Dublin' and 'Inheritor and Economist' (1849), and antiquarian work in the Royal Irish Academy Transactions, 'Ireland's Claims to an Adequate Parliamentary Representation of Learning' (1847), 'Our Architecture' (1867), 'Shakespearean Breviates' (1882) and the posthumous 'Ogham Inscriptions in Ireland, Wales, and Scotland' (1887).
authors.style: Ferguson's instrument is the strong closed and heroic line of the Scottish and Augustan school, reinforced by Moore's melody and the Irish song stave, and by blank verse for saga and translation. His best effects are narrative energy and topographical exactness - the forge, the lough, the rath - rather than reflection; the ballads are plain and direct, the satires witty, colloquial and merciless, the 'Hibernian Nights' mixing prose and verse after the manner of Cowley's essays. His long versions of Irish sagas were praised by Whitley Stokes and by Judge O'Hagan, while the Dictionary of National Biography judged that, not perfectly acquainted with Irish, he sometimes gave the stories more beauties than he took away and missed something of the reality of ancient life. The poems are usually annotated, and the notes carry the antiquarian argument.
authors.concerns: Whether a modern Irish poetry could be built out of the Old Irish tales, the saints and the record itself, and by an Ulster Protestant voice; the ownership of Ireland's antiquities and their defence against the British Museum; the authenticity of Ossianic and fabricated Gaelic verse, tested against genuine saga and Ogham monument; the education, church and land questions of 1840s Ireland, attacked in the satires; home colonisation, industry and the dignity of labour in 'The Forging of the Anchor'; the Union, repeal and the loyalty of Protestant Ireland; and the antiquary's demand for evidence, cast, transcript and precise locality.
authors.significance: He created, before the revival, the repertory of Irish subject-matter that Yeats and Synge inherited; Yeats called him the greatest poet Ireland has produced, because the most central and most Celtic, and Lady Gregory's circle used his 'Congal' and 'Deirdre'. As first Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland he organised a department whose contents scholars had formerly misdescribed, and his Ogham corpus, published after his death with the help of Ingram, Anderson and Whitley Stokes, remained the standard collection. 'The Coolin' and 'The Lark in the Clear Air', from Gaelic originals, entered the Irish song repertory; his knighthood of 1878, his presidency of the Royal Irish Academy and his house in North Great George's Street made him the centre of Dublin literary and antiquarian life.
authors.uncertainty: The title 'Ballads of the Fathers', named in the commission for this record, could not be found in the Dictionary of National Biography, in Lady Ferguson's biography of 1896, in the Ricorso checklists, or in the library catalogues searched, and it is therefore not listed among his works. His university career is differently reported - the Dictionary of National Biography gives him B.A. 1826, M.A. 1832 and honorary LL.D. 1864, while he himself said that he left Trinity College before graduating; 'The Forging of the Anchor' is placed in February and in May 1832 by different accounts; 'Lays of the Western Gael' was announced in November 1864 but carries the date 1865 on its title page; and 'Father Tom and the Pope', whose authorship Lady Ferguson attested, was ascribed by Yeats to William Maginn.

authors.name: Samuel Johnson
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet, essayist, lexicographer, and critic, the dominant man of letters of later-eighteenth-century England.
authors.biography: Johnson was born at Lichfield, studied at Pembroke College, Oxford, and after a brief schoolmastership returned to the Midlands before going to London to live by his pen. He wrote for the Gentleman's Magazine, and as editor produced the dictionary that defined English for a century, A Dictionary of the English Language (1755). Between 1750 and 1752 he wrote the moral weekly The Rambler, and later contributed to other periodicals including The Idler; the philosophical tale The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia appeared in 1759. His poetry includes London (1738) and The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). A devoted Tory and Anglican and a founding member of The Club, he edited Shakespeare (1765) and wrote the Journey to the Western Islands (1775) and the Lives of the English Poets (1779-1781). He died in London in 1784.
authors.profile: A moralist, critic, and lexicographer of immense range, who practised the periodical essay, didactic verse, dictionary-making, textual editing, and biography, always subordinating fancy to judgement and common sense.
authors.style: Latinate, balanced, periodic prose of antithesis and generalisation; the weighty heroic couplet of his moral verse; a sententious, authoritative, common-sense tone; and a preference for truth over ornament.
authors.concerns: The regulation of the passions and the vanity of worldly hopes; the stability and authority of language; the criticism of literature by general nature; religion, duty, and mortality; and the common life.
authors.significance: The most authoritative English literary voice of his age, whose dictionary standardised the language and whose criticism set the terms for assessing poetry and the canon well into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: A probable congenital condition and an uncertain recovery from scrofula are described in accounts that mix fact with family legend; the dating of his early marriage and his first London writings is imperfect.

authors.name: Samuel Pepys
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Naval administrator and diarist; his Diary (1660–69), kept in shorthand and published only in the nineteenth century, is the most famous diary in English — a candid, vivid record of the Restoration, the Great Plague, and the Great Fire, and of his own private life.
authors.biography: Born 23 February 1633 in Salisbury Court, London, educated at St Paul's School and Magdalene College, Cambridge (BA 1654). Through the patronage of his cousin Edward Montagu (later Earl of Sandwich) he entered the Navy Office as Clerk of the Acts (1660), becoming an able administrator and later Secretary to the Admiralty. From January 1660 to May 1669 he kept a meticulous private diary in shorthand covering public affairs (the coronation, the Dutch Wars, the Plague of 1665, the Fire of 1666) and his own finances, ambitions, affairs, and domestic life. Failing eyesight ended the diary in 1669; he served as MP and President of the Royal Society (1684–86) but lost office after the Revolution. He died on 26 May 1703.
authors.profile: The incomparable diarist whose immediacy, curiosity, and unembarrassed self-revelation — of work, pleasure, money, sex, music, and public catastrophe — create an unrivalled portrait of Restoration England and of a single vivid personality.
authors.style: Spontaneous, detailed, colloquial prose in shorthand; a diary's day-by-day immediacy; candid self-scrutiny; vivid reportage of events; and an eye for the telling particular.
authors.concerns: Public affairs and naval administration; ambition, money, and social climbing; pleasure, music, theatre, and women; the Plague and the Fire; and the private conscience.
authors.significance: The Diary is a primary historical source of the first importance for the 1660s and a literary classic; its frankness and observational brilliance established the diary as a major form and Pepys as one of the most beloved figures in English letters.
authors.uncertainty: Pepys's Diary and letters are richly documented; the diary was deciphered only in the nineteenth century, and some shorthand passages remain uncertain in reading.

authors.name: Samuel Purchas
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: clergyman; compiler of travel narratives
authors.biography: Born at Thaxted, Essex, about 1577. Educated at St John's College, Cambridge, he took orders and served as chaplain and rector, most notably of St Martin Ludgate, London. He inherited Richard Hakluyt's unpublished papers and made them the core of his great collection. He died in 1626, probably in London.
authors.profile: Purchas His Pilgrimage (1613) and Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes (1625), the four-volume folio that continued and crowned Hakluyt's work of collecting the world's voyages.
authors.style: Compilatory and devout: he arranges others' narratives within a providential frame, adding moral reflection and apology for his 'pilgrimage' through the world's records.
authors.concerns: The spread of the Gospel and of English trade; the world as theatre of providence; the preservation of voyages from oblivion.
authors.significance: His Pilgrimes preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and helped form the English colonial imagination in the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

authors.name: Samuel Richardson
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English printer and novelist, the master of the epistolary novel and one of the founders of the English novel tradition.
authors.biography: Born in 1689 (the year is accepted but not precisely documented, and details of his birthplace are uncertain), the son of a joiner, he was apprenticed to a printer and rose to become one of London's leading master printers and printer to the House of Commons. Late in life he turned to authorship, publishing the epistolary novel Pamela (1740), followed by the much longer Clarissa (1748) and Sir Charles Grandison (1753). His fiction drew on his experience of letter-writing and conduct material. He died on 1 July 1761.
authors.profile: The great eighteenth-century writer of the novel in letters, whose extended fictions dramatize the inner moral lives of their characters, especially women, and probe seduction, conscience, and social constraint through the unfolding present tense of correspondence.
authors.style: Epistolary form; intense psychological realism; an immediate, deliberating narrative voice; elaborate moral and sentimental rhetoric; and structural suspense built from letters that advance scene by scene.
authors.concerns: Virtue under pressure; female autonomy and vulnerability; conscience, duty, and temptation; the perils of the libertine; religion and morality; and the ethics of reading and sympathy.
authors.significance: One of the pivotal figures in the rise of the English novel, whose Pamela and Clarissa set new standards for psychological depth and whose epistolary method influenced writers across Europe for generations.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birth year and birthplace are not fully documented, and parts of his early life rest on inference from later records.

authors.name: Samuel Rogers
authors.birthplace: Newington Green, Middlesex, on the northern edge of London (some authorities say the adjacent Stoke Newington), in a prosperous Unitarian family
authors.nationality: English; the eighteenth-century didactic and topographical tradition carried on within the Romantic period, and the polite London letters of the Regency and post-Regency decades
authors.identity: Banker by profession and poet by vocation: the most honoured of those Romantic-era verse-writers who stood outside the Lake and Byronic schools, the last great practitioner of the reflective heroic couplet, and the host of the most celebrated breakfast table in the literary history of London.
authors.biography: Rogers was born at Newington Green on 30 July 1763, the third son of a Unitarian family of large means, and was educated at dissenting schools in the neighbourhood of London rather than at a university. He was put early into business and became a partner in a London house, and on his father's death he inherited enough to withdraw from active trade and to live in London as a man of letters, a collector and a patron. His first considerable poem, an essay on the pleasures of recollection, appeared in 1792 and went through many editions, while the verse of his student years was quietly suppressed. For decades he was the centre of a famous weekly breakfast table at his house in St James's Place, where statesmen, actors, painters, publishers and poets of every party sat together, and where the conversation which was reported after his death as his Table Talk took shape. He twice travelled in Italy after the Napoleonic wars reopened the continent to English visitors, and those journeys supplied the matter of the topographical poem published anonymously in part in 1822 and completed under his own name in the later 1820s; an early disappointed attachment and the deaths of friends return through it as the loss which reflective verse attempts to console. He lived unmarried, on terms of closeness with his sister and with a small circle of friends, and passed his last years between London and the continent, taking a formal part in the affairs of the national collection of painting, of which he was a trustee from 1834 until his death. When the laureateship fell at the death of the elder poet of the Lakes in 1850 he was approached, refused the honour on the ground of his years, and named a younger successor who accepted it. His collected Poems of 1827, revised and re-set from the separate issues of 1792, 1819 and 1822, gave him at last the single authoritative form in which he was read for the rest of the century; he died in London on 18 December 1855, aged ninety-two, and the record of his talk and of his generosity to poorer writers and to imprisoned Italian liberals was published by his friends in the years immediately following.
authors.profile: His printed work is deliberately small and elaborately made: two long reflective poems on common life and on Italy, a shorter earlier poem on memory, and a company of lyrics, ballads, hymn-like pieces, romances and translations, many of them intercalated into the longer structures or first sold to the keepsake and magazine market. He wrote no prose book of his own; his prose remains is the reported table-talk and the letters, and his serious editorship was exercised on his own texts, of which he left several substantially different states. The characteristic poem is a meditative progress in couplets, interrupted by a song, in which an observed scene or a remembered person is raised to a general reflection on ordinary experience.
authors.style: Closed and heavily pointed heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, descended from the eighteenth-century schools rather than from the blank verse of his contemporaries; a diction of polish, reticence and understatement, avoiding archaism, technical vocabulary and experiment; epigrammatic and sententious closure, balanced antithesis, and a strong sense of the audible line for recitation; contrasted with these, in the intercalated songs and ballads, a light and genuinely tuneful lyrical measure which was widely set and widely imitated. Revision is the visible method: the printed text is the residue of many cancelled draft states, and the reticence of the surface is the product of labour rather than of ease.
authors.concerns: The dignity of ordinary and domestic life as a subject for serious verse; memory, attachment and the consolation of the bereaved; taste, decorum and the rules of an inherited metre; religion of a liberal and anti-sectarian kind, with a sympathetic but unconverted interest in Catholic ceremony; exile, political imprisonment and the claims of liberty on the poet's purse; the moral uses of painting and of the Italian landscape; the poet's duty to a reading public that buys the annual rather than the subscription volume.
authors.significance: For half a century he was the standard instance of a poet who could be ranked with the first generation of the Romantic school without belonging to it, and his refusal of the exotic and the heroic was a live alternative to Wordsworthian simplicity and to Byronic rhetoric. His Italy was for much of the nineteenth century the usual English poem about Italy, and the illustrated editions that paired it with engraved landscape vignettes made it a defining object of the gift-book market. His breakfast table and the Table Talk reported from it are a primary record of the social life of Romantic letters and an indispensable source of anecdote about the greater poets of the age; and the rise and disappearance of his reputation is a standing case study in Victorian and modern canon formation.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is reported variously as Newington Green and as Stoke Newington, and the boundary between the two makes the difference one of naming rather than of fact; the details of his schooling and of his years in the banking house are thinly documented; and the identity and chronology of the early attachment that lies behind the mournful passages of his Italian poem rest largely on the recollection of friends.

authors.name: Samuel Rutherford Crockett
authors.nationality: British; the Galloway kailyard romance
authors.identity: Novelist and minister; the most prolific of the kailyard writers and the author of The Stickit Minister.
authors.biography: Born at Duchrae, Balmaghie, in Galloway on 24 September 1859; he studied at Edinburgh University and the Free Church divinity hall, was ordained in 1886, and gave up the ministry for writing after The Stickit Minister (1893) became a bestseller. The Raiders (1894), The Lilac Sunbonnet (1894), Men of the Moss-Hags (1895) and a long series of Galloway romances followed. He died at Tarascon, France, on 16 April 1914.
authors.profile: Crockett was the most prolific of the kailyard writers and the one who gave the movement its historical dimension: his Galloway romances of the Covenanters, the gypsies and the smuggling trade carried the Scottish vernacular novel into the bestseller lists and made the south-west of Scotland a literary country.
authors.style: The Galloway dialect in direct speech; the historical adventure of the Covenanting wars; the comic and pathetic minor characters; the rapid serial plot; the landscape of the Solway shore and the moor.
authors.concerns: Scottish national identity and the Covenanting past; the rural community and its oral culture; the relation of the minister to his people; poverty and the pride of the small farmer; emigration and the empty glen.
authors.significance: S. R. Crockett was the most prolific of the kailyard novelists and gave the movement its historical dimension: his Galloway romances of the Covenanters and the smugglers made the south-west of Scotland a literary country and carried the Scottish vernacular novel into the bestseller lists.
