authors.name: Samuel Selvon
authors.nationality: Trinidadian; Indo-Trinidadian Caribbean (West Indian) novelist, short-story writer and playwright writing in English, of Indian and Scottish-Indian descent, in England from 1950 to 1978 and in Canada from 1978
authors.identity: Trinidad-born novelist whose The Lonely Londoners (1956), narrated as well as spoken in Trinidadian creole, founded the fiction of Caribbean migrant London, and whose novels of Indo-Trinidadian village life, from A Brighter Sun (1952) to The Plains of Caroni (1970), trace the meeting of Indian and Creole Trinidad.
authors.biography: Samuel Dickson Selvon, known as Sam Selvon, was born on 20 May 1923 in San Fernando, in the south of Trinidad, the sixth of seven children. His father, Bertwyn Fraser Selvon, was a Christian of Madrasi Indian descent who managed a dry-goods store; his mother, Daisy Irene Dickson, was the daughter of a Scotsman and of Keasoo, a woman of South Asian origin. Peepal Tree Press, drawing on his own accounts, describes a creolised household with little part in Hindu ritual, and a boy formed by the American films at the local cinemas. He left Naparima College at fifteen and from 1940 to 1945 was a wireless operator with the Trinidad branch of the Royal Naval Reserve (Dawes calls him a telegraph operator), the post that brought him into contact with the wartime American presence. From 1945 (1946 in Britannica) to 1950 he worked for the Trinidad Guardian as a reporter and on its literary page, South Asian Britain says as literary editor of the Sunday Guardian, publishing stories and sketches under the names Michael Wentworth, Esses, Ack-Ack and Big Buffer. He married Draupadi Persaud in 1947. In 1950 he moved to London, where he lived first in a hostel near Earl's Court, took menial jobs and became a clerk at the Indian Embassy, while reading for the BBC's Caribbean Voices and placing stories and poems in the London Magazine, the New Statesman and The Nation. Guggenheim Fellowships (1955 and 1968 in Wikipedia; 1954 and 1968 in Dawes), a Society of Authors travelling scholarship (1958) and Arts Council grants (1960) supported his work, and in 1969 Trinidad and Tobago awarded him the Hummingbird Medal (Gold). He wrote more than twenty radio plays and several television scripts for the BBC, scripted Horace Ové's Pressure (1976), the first full-length Black British feature film, and in the late 1960s took part in the Caribbean Artists Movement. In 1963 he married Althea Daroux. After a creative writing fellowship at the University of Dundee (1975-77) he moved in 1978 to Canada and settled in Calgary, Alberta; he taught creative writing as a visiting professor at the University of Victoria, worked for some months as a janitor at the University of Calgary and then became its writer-in-residence, and Dawes adds residencies at Alberta and Winnipeg. The University of the West Indies (1985) and Warwick (1989) gave him honorary doctorates. He died of respiratory failure on 16 April 1994 during a visit to Trinidad, at Piarco International Airport according to Wikipedia (Britannica says Port of Spain), and received the Chaconia Medal (Gold) posthumously that year.
authors.profile: Selvon published ten novels between 1952 and 1983 (Peepal Tree and Dawes count eleven), one collection of stories, two books of plays and a selection of prose. Six of the novels are set in Trinidad, mostly among Indo-Trinidadians: A Brighter Sun (1952) and its sequel Turn Again Tiger (1958), An Island Is a World (1955), I Hear Thunder (1963), The Plains of Caroni (1970) and Those Who Eat the Cascadura (1972). The others follow West Indians in London: The Lonely Londoners (1956), The Housing Lark (1965) and the two later Moses novels, Moses Ascending (1975) and Moses Migrating (1983); the stories of Ways of Sunlight (1957) move between the two settings. Much of his drama was written for the BBC, and two collections, Eldorado West One (1988) and Highway in the Sun (1991), preserve some of it; Foreday Morning (1989) gathers prose from 1946 onwards.
authors.style: In The Lonely Londoners Selvon used creolised English, or 'nation language', for narration as well as dialogue, an innovation Wikipedia calls groundbreaking; he explained that the novel 'just shot along' once he wrote both in dialect. Dawes praises folk idioms of 'sophistication and sheer virtuosity', a rare union of empathy and humour, and a Lonely Londoners told like a 'ballad' or calypso. Schwarz finds in Selvon's London an exact geography and an echo of Eliot's 'unreal' city, and Britannica singles out the 'extensive and striking use of dialect' in Turn Again Tiger.
authors.concerns: Creolisation and the relations of Indian and African Trinidadians; the peasant culture of the cane fields and its passing under mechanisation; manhood, marriage and domestic violence; migration to Britain, racism, poverty and the improvised community of 'the boys'; return, Anglophilia and the divided loyalties of the migrant; Carnival as a fleeting image of a society beyond race.
authors.significance: Selvon came to attention in the 1950s with other Caribbean writers, Naipaul among them (Britannica), and is a founder of Caribbean migrant fiction in Britain. The Lonely Londoners, his most widely known book, is read as a forerunner of Zadie Smith's White Teeth and Hanif Kureishi's The Buddha of Suburbia, and Dawes finds his influence 'consistently apparent' in the many fiction writers who followed him. Britannica judged A Brighter Sun the first book in which an East Indian author wrote 'with such quiet authority and simple charm' about Indo-Trinidadian life, and it was long a set text on the Caribbean Examinations Council syllabus.

authors.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
authors.nationality: English; poet, critic and thinker of the Romantic period, of the Lake school and of the Unitarian and German-influenced tradition of ideas
authors.identity: Poet of the supernatural ballad and of the visionary fragment, founder-critic of the Romantic theory of imagination, and moral and religious writer whose prose affected nineteenth-century thought more widely than that of any contemporary except one essayist.
authors.biography: Coleridge was the youngest but one of the ten children of a Devonshire clergyman who kept a grammar school, and after his father's death he was placed at Christ's Hospital in London, where one of his schoolfellows became the essayist of the familiar style. At Jesus College, Cambridge he formed the acquaintance that led to the communitarian scheme for a settlement on the American frontier, and in 1795, having left the university without a degree, he married one of the Fricker sisters, whose sister had married his friend of the scheme. The west-country years of 1795-98 produced the conversation poems, the ballad volume and the two great unfinished romances, and a season at Göttingen in 1799-1800 brought him into contact with German philosophy and criticism. There followed public lectures on government and on the drama, the conduct of a weekly literary sheet at his own charge, a secretaryship in the British service at Malta, and a short government post that ended in quarrel with his patrons. From 1816 he lived in the north of England and then in London and its neighbourhood, at last in the house of a medical friend at Highgate, where he died in 1834. His long dependence on opium and laudanum, his estrangement from his family and his hopeless attachment to his wife's sister belong to the record of a nature of extraordinary intellectual appetite and imperfect execution.
authors.profile: His verse is small in bulk and central in influence: the supernatural ballad, the two unfinished romances, the vision of the pleasure-dome, and the conversation poems and odes of 1795-1802. His prose divides between critical and philosophical works, of which the literary autobiography is the chief, the essays of his weekly sheet, the treatise on the faculties of the mind, the sermons and charges on church and state, and the table-talk reported by friends and edited after his death. He is the originator of the Romantic distinction between fancy and imagination and of much of the vocabulary in which English criticism discusses symbol, organic form and belief.
authors.style: In verse a command of several distinct mannerisms - the archaic reiteration of the ballad, the reiterated stress and internal music of the fragment, the soft suspended blank verse of the meditation and the exclamatory syntax of the ode; in prose a learned, abstract and often hortatory style, full of coined terms, of long definitions and of quotation from the moralists of the seventeenth century and of Germany.
authors.concerns: The imagination as a way of knowing and as the agent of all perception; the relation of philosophy to religion, and the distinction between reason and understanding; guilt, penance and the moral government of the universe; the education of the will, and the duties of the state and the clergy; the nature of poetic language and the faults of the substituted vocabulary of the eighteenth-century schools.
authors.significance: As poet he created the English supernatural ballad and the visionary fragment, and with the friend of the ballad volume he founded the Romantic poetry of imagination and of humble life; as critic and philosopher he transmitted the idealist philosophy to the nineteenth century and supplied the terms in which Romantic poetics has since been stated. His conversation, his printed lectures and his prose made him a governing presence in Victorian intellectual life, and his career remains the standard case of Romantic promise interrupted.
authors.uncertainty: The date of composition of the vision of the pleasure-dome, and the chronology and extent of his opium use, are matters of continuing argument between biographers and textual scholars.

authors.name: Sarah Fielding
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English novelist and children's writer, best known for David Simple and the pioneering children's novel The Governess.
authors.biography: Born on 8 November 1710 at East Stour in Dorset, the sister of Henry Fielding, she was educated in the family circle and remained close to her brother. She published The Adventures of David Simple (1744), later issuing sequels and contributing to the periodical contest and miscellany writing of the day. In 1749 she published The Governess; or, The Little Female Academy, often described as the first novel in English written expressly for children. She also translated and edited. She died on 9 April 1768 at Bath.
authors.profile: A novelist and moralist of a quieter, more reflective cast than her brother, whose fiction emphasizes sensibility, friendship, and female education, and who helped to create a native tradition of the story written for young readers.
authors.style: Sentimental and didactic prose; a simpler, more domestic realism than the picaresque; dialogic and moralizing structure; and a plainly addressed, instructive narrative voice suited to didactic and children's writing.
authors.concerns: Friendship, benevolence, and the education of the character; the situation and instruction of women and girls; sincerity versus worldly artifice; and the moral development of the young.
authors.significance: An important early woman novelist and a landmark figure in the history of children's literature in English, whose David Simple circulated widely and rivaled some of her brother's fiction in its day.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact birth and death dates are usually given but her life is unevenly documented, and parts of her early education and unpublished work remain imperfectly recorded.

authors.name: Sarah Grand
authors.nationality: Irish-English; the New Woman novel and the literature of marriage reform
authors.identity: Novelist and feminist; the writer who coined the phrase 'the New Woman' and the most influential woman novelist of the 1890s.
authors.biography: Born Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke at Donaghadee, County Down, on 10 June 1854, the daughter of a naval officer; she married a widowed army surgeon in 1870 and lived in India and Malta before settling in England in 1878. The Heavenly Twins (1893) made her famous and gave the 1890s the term 'New Woman'; she lectured for women's suffrage and against the Contagious Diseases Acts, became a Poor Law guardian in Tunbridge Wells, and died at Calne, Wiltshire, on 12 May 1943.
authors.profile: Grand wrote the New Woman novel as a weapon of social reform: her subject is the double standard, the sexual ignorance of girls and the marriage market, and her method is the long, argumentative, deliberately shocking novel that puts the case in the mouths of her heroines. The Heavenly Twins is the central English novel of the 1890s on marriage and sexual knowledge, and its popularity made the New Woman a national figure.
authors.style: The long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays; the comic satire of the marriage market; the shocking set-piece; the idealised New Woman heroine; direct address to the reader.
authors.concerns: The sexual double standard and marriage reform; girls' education and sexual knowledge; venereal disease and the Contagious Diseases Acts; the New Woman and her enemies; the position of women in the professions; mothering and child welfare.
authors.significance: Grand is the central English novelist of the New Woman and the coiner of the phrase that names her: The Heavenly Twins was the most discussed novel of 1893, it made the marriage question a national debate, and Grand's work is the founding text of the English novel of female sexual education.

authors.name: Sarah Josepha Hale
authors.nationality: American; New England domestic and women's-periodical tradition
authors.identity: Poet, novelist, children's verse-writer and editor; the first American woman to edit a national magazine and the chief architect of the mid-century lady's-book tradition
authors.biography: Sarah Josepha Buell Hale was born on 24 October 1788 at Newport, New Hampshire, the youngest child of Gordon Buell, a Revolutionary veteran and innkeeper who kept the local school, and Martha Whittlesey Buell; she was largely self-taught in a household of books and received almost no formal schooling. She married the lawyer David Hale on 23 October 1813 and when he died in 1822 she was left a widow with five young children and small means, which forced her into writing as paid work. Her first book, The Genius of Oblivion and Other Original Poems (Concord, New Hampshire, 1823), appeared with subscriptions raised partly through her late husband's Masonic lodge; Sketches of American Character (1825) and the domestic novel Northwood; or, A Tale of the East and West (1827) followed. In 1828 she founded in Boston the monthly Ladies' Magazine, usually called the American Ladies' Magazine, the first United States periodical projected and edited by a woman, and she conducted it until 1837, when Louis A. Godey attached her to Godey's Lady's Book in Philadelphia as its editor. She held that editorship until December 1877, turning the monthly into the most widely circulated American magazine of the century and a national institution of letters: she promoted American authors, historic sites and domestic science, and used her columns as a platform for sustained campaigns. Her Poems for Our Children (1830) collected the verse pieces, including "Mary's Lamb", that entered American nursery culture. She lobbied presidents for nearly two decades until Lincoln's 1863 proclamation made Thanksgiving a national holiday; she raised money for the restoration of the Bunker Hill Monument, pressed for higher education for women and for medical training for women, and assisted the founding of Vassar College. She died at her home at 1413 Locust Street, Philadelphia, on 30 April 1879 and was buried in Laurel Hill Cemetery there.
authors.profile: Hale wrote across three genres at once: occasional and moral verse (The Genius of Oblivion, 1823; Poems for Our Children, 1830), didactic prose sketches and tales of national character (Sketches of American Character, 1825), and the regional domestic novel (Northwood, 1827; Pleasant Personal Narratives, the late anti-slavery novel Mary Preston, 1852-55). Her longest-lived compositions are the nursery lyrics and the editor's voice itself, a prose of advice, review, and petition. She also compiled anthologies and textbooks, including The Book of Flowers and the Sketches of American Women / Woman's Record biographies.
authors.style: A diction of plain feeling: sentimental, quotable and deliberately unlearned, with hymn-like meters and the common-measure and nursery-rhyme rhythms that made her children's verse memorable. Her prose is hortatory, domestic in register, addressed to a collective "we" of American readers, and organised by anecdote, contrast of North and South, and moral application rather than by plot or argument. Revision was pragmatic, aimed at magazine serialization and at recitation and schoolroom use.
authors.concerns: Women's intellectual capacity and education as civic duty; the moral authority of mothers; national union and the making of an American calendar and heritage; the tensions of sectionalism, slavery and colonization in her fiction; the professionalisation of authorship and editing by a woman; piety, charity and domestic economy as public policy.
authors.significance: Hale created the model of the woman editor as a national cultural power and, through Godey's Lady's Book, standardized a trans-Atlantic reading public of households. Her Thanksgiving campaign is one of the few successful single-issue reforms of antebellum letters; her preservation of the Bunker Hill monument and support for Vassar shaped American heritage and women's higher education. "Mary's Lamb" remains the best-known nursery verse by an American woman of the period, and her career marks the entry of women into the periodical economy inside the Romantic era.
authors.uncertainty: Sources differ on the date she began editing Godey's Lady's Book: most literary histories give 1837 (after the merger of her own magazine), while the National Park Service and some bibliographies give 1841; her Boston monthly also appears under shifting titles (Ladies' / American Ladies' / Ladies' American Magazine). The project brief's attribution of a "Liberator" editorship to her could not be verified in the sources consulted and conflicts with Garrison's Boston Liberator. The nursery rhyme's original printing is titled "Mary's Lamb" in her Poems for Our Children, and a rival authorship claim for the prose anecdote (John Roulstone / Mary Oliver Soule) persists in folklore.

authors.name: Sarah Orne Jewett
authors.nationality: American; the regional sketch and the novel of women's friendship
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest American regionalist of the nineteenth century and the author of The Country of the Pointed Firs.
authors.biography: Born Theodora Sarah Orne Jewett at South Berwick, Maine, on 3 September 1849, the daughter of a country doctor whose rounds gave her the material for her fiction. She published her first story in the Atlantic Monthly in 1869, and Deephaven (1877) established her as a writer of Maine coastal life; she travelled in Europe, was a close friend of Annie Fields, and received an honorary degree from Bowdoin in 1901. She died at South Berwick on 24 June 1909 after a carriage accident.
authors.profile: Jewett wrote the American regional story as a form of delicate social history: her subject is the small Maine port towns after the decline of the shipping trade, and her method is the sketch, the remembered voice and the quiet epiphany rather than plot. Her masterpiece, The Country of the Pointed Firs, has almost no story and yet is one of the most perfectly constructed books in American literature; her treatment of the friendship of women and of the life of unmarried women is unique in her period.
authors.style: Episodic sketch structure held together by a visiting narrator; exact rendering of dialect and of old people's speech; precise, unfussy description of coastal houses, herbs and weather; irony and tenderness in balance; the epiphany at the level of a shared silence.
authors.concerns: The decay of the New England port towns; the lives of unmarried and elderly women; friendship and community; the sea and the coastal landscape; memory and the local past; the contrast between the summer visitor and the settled inhabitant.
authors.significance: Jewett is the finest American regionalist writer of the century and the most important woman writer of New England after Stowe: The Country of the Pointed Firs is a permanent classic, and its treatment of women's friendships and of the dignity of ordinary lives made her a central figure for the feminist criticism of American literature.

authors.name: Sean O'Casey
authors.nationality: Irish; the Dublin tenement tragedy and the politicised tragi-comedy
authors.identity: Dramatist and autobiographer; the great working-class playwright of Dublin, the author of the Abbey Theatre's three great tenement plays, and the finest Irish memoirist of the century.
authors.biography: Born John Casey in a Dublin tenement on 30 March 1880 into a poor Protestant family; he worked as a labourer, a railwayman and a docker, joined the Gaelic League and the Irish Citizen Army, and took part in the 1916 Rising's periphery. The Shadow of a Gunman (1923), Juno and the Paycock (1924) and The Plough and the Stars (1926) made him the Abbey's greatest discovery; the riot that greeted The Plough drove him to England in 1926, where he wrote The Silver Tassie (1929), Within the Gates (1934), Red Roses for Me (1942) and the six-volume autobiography. He died at Torquay on 18 September 1964.
authors.profile: O'Casey wrote the greatest working-class tragedy in English: Juno and the Paycock and The Plough and the Stars made the Dublin tenement and the Easter Rising the subjects of a tragic art, and his tragi-comic idiom — the rhetoric of 'the patter of the blows' — is one of the period's great inventions. The Silver Tassie, with its expressionist second act, opened the Irish theatre to European experiment, and his autobiography is the finest Irish prose of the century.
authors.style: The tragi-comedy that turns from farce to tragedy in a single scene; the tenement speech of Dublin rendered phonetically; the choric commentators (Juno, Bessie Burgess); the expressionist act inserted into a realistic play; the ballad and the song as structural device.
authors.concerns: The Dublin tenement and the Dublin poor; the Easter Rising and the war of independence; poverty, drink and the pawnshop; the mother's grief and the son's death; the Church, the Union and the Citizen Army; the emigrant and the emptied city.
authors.significance: O'Casey is the greatest working-class dramatist in English and the central Irish playwright after Synge: the three Abbey plays are permanent, The Silver Tassie brought expressionism to the Irish stage, and his autobiography is the period's finest Irish prose. The riots against his plays are the period's clearest evidence of the writer's collision with nationalism.

authors.identity: Short-story writer, novelist, critic and editor; the founder of The Bell and the biographer of the revival.
authors.biography: Born Sean Proinsias O Faolain at Cork on 22 February 1900; he fought in the IRA and the civil war, and published Midsummer Night Madness (1932), The Saint and Mary Kate (1932) and Bird Alone (1936). As editor of The Bell from 1940 and as critic and biographer of the revival he shaped Irish letters for two decades; he died at Dublin on 20 April 1991.
authors.profile: Sean O'Faolain is the central figure of Irish letters between the war and the republic: Midsummer Night Madness and Bird Alone made the short story and the novel of the civil war and the censorship, The Bell gave Irish writing its magazine for the 1940s, and his criticism of the revival fixed the terms of the national question in literature.
authors.style: The short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence; the novel of the young man against the church and the state; the criticism of the revival as the argument with the fathers; the editor's prose of the standard and the quarrel; the biography of the national leader as the study of the myth.
authors.concerns: The civil war and the republic that followed; the censorship and the church; the Irish short story and its magazine; the revival and the argument with the fathers; the national question as the question of the writer.
authors.significance: Sean O'Faolain is the central figure of Irish letters between the war and the republic: Bird Alone and Midsummer Night Madness made the fiction of the civil war and the censorship, and The Bell gave Irish writing its magazine of the 1940s.

authors.name: Sherwood Anderson
authors.nationality: American; the small-town story and the American grotesque
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Winesburg, Ohio, the book that gave American fiction its modern small-town story and its term for the inarticulate outsider.
authors.biography: Born Sherwood Anderson in Camden, Ohio, on 13 September 1876; he left school at fourteen, served in the Spanish-American War, ran a paint factory in Elyria, Ohio, and in 1912 walked out of it in a nervous collapse to become a writer. Windy McPherson's Son (1916) and Marching Men (1917) preceded Winesburg, Ohio (1919), which made his name; he published many novels and stories, edited two little magazines, and died in Panama on 8 March 1941.
authors.profile: Anderson wrote the book that made the modern American short story possible: Winesburg, Ohio gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden loneliness — the 'grotesques' whose truth is not told — and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner, Wolfe and Carver. He was the first American writer to make the inarticulate the subject of the form.
authors.style: The plain, bare, repetitive sentence; the story without plot, built on a single moment of longing; the recurring town and the recurring characters; the framed sequence of stories as a novel; the voice of a man who cannot say what he means.
authors.concerns: The small town and its hidden lives; loneliness and the failure of speech; sex, adolescence and the fear of the body; the industrial town against the old agrarian America; the artist and the escape from the town; the grotesque and the truth of the outsider.
authors.significance: Anderson wrote the founding book of the modern American short story: Winesburg, Ohio changed what an American story could be about, gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden lives, and was acknowledged by Hemingway, Faulkner and Wolfe as the source of their generation's prose.

authors.name: Sidney Lanier
authors.nationality: American; the Southern lyric, the poetry of music and the critical essay
authors.identity: Poet, musician and critic; the finest Southern poet of the postwar generation and the founder of the scientific criticism of English verse.
authors.biography: Born Sidney Clopton Lanier in Macon, Georgia, on 3 February 1842; he served in the Confederate army, was captured and imprisoned at Point Lookout, where he contracted tuberculosis, and after the war taught, played the flute professionally and wrote poetry. He published Poems (1877), The Science of English Verse (1880) and The English Novel (1883), and died at Lynn, North Carolina, on 7 September 1881, aged thirty-nine.
authors.profile: Lanier wrote the Southern lyric after the war: his poems of the Georgia marshes, the Chattahoochee and the sea are the finest American poetry of nature written between Whitman and Frost, and his theory of verse as a form of music — The Science of English Verse — is the founding work of American prosody. He is the central literary figure of the post-war South, and his 'Marshes of Glynn' is one of the great American poems.
authors.style: Long, musical, rhythmically inventive lines; the cataloguing of natural detail; the orchestral repetition and the symphonic structure; the fusion of music and metre; the Southern landscape and the memory of the war.
authors.concerns: Nature, the marsh and the sea; music and the theory of verse; the South after the war and the memory of the Confederacy; mortality and the shortness of life; the trade of poetry and the struggle for a living; God and the natural world.
authors.significance: Lanier is the finest Southern poet of his generation and the founder of the scientific study of English versification: 'The Marshes of Glynn' and 'The Symphony' are permanent American poems, The Science of English Verse changed the study of prosody, and his example made the post-war South a place where poetry could be written again.

authors.name: Siegfried Sassoon
authors.nationality: British; the war poem of protest and the prose memoir of the trenches
authors.identity: Poet and memoirist; the war poet of anger and protest, and the author of the Sherston trilogy, the finest English prose memoir of the First World War.
authors.biography: Born Siegfried Lorraine Sassoon at Matfield, Kent, on 8 September 1886 into a wealthy Anglo-Jewish family; he read history at Cambridge, hunted, played cricket and published privately financed verse before 1914. He served with the Royal Welch Fusiliers from 1915, was decorated, and in July 1917 threw his Military Cross into the Mersey and published 'A Soldier's Declaration' against the war; he was sent to Craiglockhart, where he met Wilfred Owen. He wrote the Sherston trilogy (1928–36), became a Catholic in 1957, and died at Heytesbury on 1 September 1967.
authors.profile: Sassoon is the great poet of protest of the First World War: his satirical war poems — 'They', 'Base Details', 'The General', 'Aftermath' — gave the anti-war movement its most quotable lines, and his meeting with Owen at Craiglockhart in 1917 changed the course of English war poetry. The Sherston trilogy is the finest prose memoir of the war and one of the great English autobiographies of the century.
authors.style: The short satirical poem with a savage last line; colloquial speech and the officer's drawl; the sudden shift from anecdote to indictment; the rhyming couplet used as a weapon; the long prose memoir written with a novelist's eye for scene and a poet's ear for speech.
authors.concerns: War, protest, and the incompetence of the staff; the soldier and the rhetoric of sacrifice; courage, cowardice and the Military Cross; the English county families and the hunting field; memory and the reconstruction of a lost boyhood; pacifism and the conscience of the individual.
authors.significance: Sassoon is the central poet of protest of the First World War and one of its finest memoirists: his satirical poems made the anti-war case in the language of the mess and the trench, the Sherston trilogy is the great English war memoir, and his friendship with Owen made the greatest of the war poets possible.

authors.name: Silas K. Hocking
authors.nationality: British; the Methodist popular novel
authors.identity: Methodist minister and novelist; the author of Her Benny, one of the most popular religious novels of the Victorian age.
authors.biography: Born Silas Kitto Hocking at St Stephen-in-Brannel, Cornwall, on 24 March 1850; he was a Methodist minister in Liverpool and Manchester, and Her Benny (1879), the story of two Liverpool waifs, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Alec Green (1881), Dick's Fairy (1883), The Strange Adventures of Israel Pendray (1899) and a long series of temperance and religious novels followed. He died at Southport on 16 September 1935.
authors.profile: Hocking wrote the most widely read Methodist popular novels of the Victorian age and Her Benny was one of the great bestsellers of the religious press, selling in the hundreds of thousands on both sides of the Atlantic. His temperance and waif narratives carried the evangelical novel into the mass market and gave the Victorian reader the sentimental street arab that Dickens had made respectable.
authors.style: The waif narrative of the street and the workhouse; the deathbed scene of the pious child; the temperance plot of the drunkard's progress; the direct appeal to the reader's sympathy; the plain, emphatic, hortatory prose.
authors.concerns: Poverty and the street child; drink and the temperance cause; the Christian conversion and the good death; the city slum and the rural emigrant; the reward of virtue in this world and the next.
authors.significance: Silas Hocking wrote the most widely read Methodist popular novels of the Victorian age: Her Benny sold in the hundreds of thousands, carried the evangelical novel into the mass market, and gave the temperance movement its most effective piece of fiction.

authors.name: Sinclair Lewis
authors.nationality: American; the satire of the American small town
authors.identity: Novelist; the first American to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, and the great satirist of the American small town and the business culture.
authors.biography: Born Harry Sinclair Lewis in Sauk Centre, Minnesota, on 7 February 1885; he worked as a journalist and editor, and made his name with Main Street (1920). Babbitt (1922), Arrowsmith (1925), Elmer Gantry (1927) and It Can't Happen Here (1935) followed; he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1930 and died in Rome on 10 January 1951.

authors.style: The documentary accumulation of detail; the satirical caricature with a name that becomes a type; the dialogue of the booster and the salesman; the wide social panorama; the plain, energetic, journalistic prose.
authors.concerns: The American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; regional identity and the American sectional character; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; industrial wealth, accumulation, and the gospel of accumulation.

authors.name: Sir David Lindsay
altNames: Sir David Lindsay of the Mount
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: poet; playwright; herald; Lyon King of Arms
authors.biography: Born about 1486 at the Mount in Fife; attached to the court of James IV and the companion and usher of the young James V, whom he exhorted in The Dreme (1528). Lyon King of Arms from 1542 and a lord of session, he was the leading advocate of the reformed cause in Scottish letters. His Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis was played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552. He died about April 1555.
authors.profile: The major Scottish poet of the Reformation. The Dreme (1528) instructs the young king in a dream vision; The Testament of the Papyngo (1530) is a dying parrot's satire of court and clergy; and Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis — the great morality of the Scottish Reformation — stages the trial of the estates before King Humanitie, with John the Common-Weill the plaintiff and the vices of the church in the dock.
authors.style: Direct satirical address in fluent Scots; the dream vision and the testament turned to political use; the morality play expanded to a national parliament.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the Scottish church; the education of the king; the common weal against the estates; justice for the poor.
authors.significance: The poet of the Scottish Reformation and the author of its greatest dramatic work; the Satyre is the summit of Scots drama and was played and reprinted for generations.

authors.name: Sir John Davies
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Lawyer, statesman, and poet; author of Orchestra and Nosce Teipsum, the most accomplished philosophical poems of the Elizabethan period, and later attorney-general for Ireland.
authors.biography: Born in 1569 in Wiltshire; educated at Winchester and the Queen's College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1595). His Orchestra, or A Poem of Dancing was published in 1596, and Nosce Teipsum in 1599, both dedicated to Queen Elizabeth; he was disbarred in 1598 for striking Richard Martin in the Middle Temple hall, restored in 1601, and sat in the parliaments of James I. As solicitor-general (1603) and attorney-general (1606) for Ireland he administered the Ulster plantation and became speaker of the Irish parliament (1613); he returned to England as a judge in 1619, was lord chief justice briefly in 1626, and died on 8 December 1626.
authors.profile: A philosophical poet of unusual lucidity who turned the hardest questions of the soul into polished quatrains; Nosce Teipsum ('Know thyself') was celebrated by contemporaries as the proof that English verse could reason.
authors.style: The decasyllabic quatrain used with argumentative precision; elegant metaphysical wit without obscurity; the marriage of law, philosophy, and verse.
authors.concerns: The immortality of the soul and the nature of knowledge; the cosmic order expressed in the dance (Orchestra); the union of poetry and philosophy; the reform of Ireland and the duties of the magistrate.
authors.significance: The finest English philosophical poet before the metaphysicals, whose Nosce Teipsum was admired by Coleridge and remains the classic Elizabethan poem of self-knowledge.
authors.uncertainty: The poems' dates are approximate; the attribution of several epigrams between Sir John Davies and John Davies of Hereford has been a source of confusion since the seventeenth century.

authors.name: Sir John Denham
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and royalist administrator; author of Cooper's Hill (1642), the first great English topographical and reflective poem, whose balanced couplets established the model for Augustan nature-and-meditation verse.
authors.biography: Born 1615 (baptised at St Andrew Holborn), educated at Trinity College, Oxford, and Lincoln's Inn. His tragedy The Sophy (1642) and Cooper's Hill (1642) won him immediate fame. A moderate royalist, he served Charles I and Charles II on diplomatic missions and as Surveyor of the King's Works (1660, after Inigo Jones), was knighted in 1660, and suffered a much-publicised bout of madness in 1666. He died in March 1669 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The poet of the meditative landscape, whose view of the Thames from Cooper's Hill yoked topography, history, and moral reflection in the balanced couplet that Pope praised as 'strong sense ... most correctly writ'.
authors.style: The smooth, balanced closed couplet; topographical description as moral and political meditation; classical allusion; and a grave, sententious tone.
authors.concerns: Nature and order; the Thames, trade, and the English constitution; moderation and the 'golden mean'; royalist politics; and the relation of landscape to history and morality.
authors.significance: Cooper's Hill founded the English topographical and estate-mediation tradition that runs through Marvell, Pope ('Windsor-Forest'), and Thomson's Seasons, and its couplets shaped Augustan versification.
authors.uncertainty: Denham's life is well documented, including his madness and the scandal of his wife's death; the dating of Cooper's Hill's revisions (1642, 1650, 1655, 1668) is established.

authors.name: Sir John Suckling
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Cavalier wit, courtier, and poet-playwright; famous for his rakish elegance, his sprightly songs, and his role as a dashing but ultimately tragic royalist, whose suicide in exile at thirty-three made him a legend of the Cavalier generation.
authors.biography: Born February 1609 at Whitton, educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He inherited a large fortune, travelled Europe, served in the Bishops' Wars (raising a troop at his own expense), and became a celebrated figure of the court wits around the Earl of Holland and Thomas Hobbes. He wrote plays (Aglaura, 1638; The Goblins, 1638) and lyrics, and was knighted in 1630. He took part in the First Army Plot (1641) to rescue the Earl of Strafford, fled to Paris, and died there in June 1642, reportedly by his own hand after a servant's insult. His Fragmenta Aurea was published in 1646.
authors.profile: The most fashionable Cavalier wit, whose careless grace and easy songs ('Why so pale and wan, fond lover?') embodied the rakish elegance of Charles I's court.
authors.style: Light, witty, conversational songs; a deliberately 'careless' aristocratic ease; satiric and bawdy verse; and dramatic prose and blank verse in his plays.
authors.concerns: Love and gallantry; wit and courtly fashion; royalist loyalty; sceptical libertinism; and the vanity of romantic pretence.
authors.significance: Suckling's lyrics and his legend as a doomed Cavalier made him an emblem of the Caroline court; his plays influenced Restoration comedy, and 'A Ballad upon a Wedding' is a lively social satire.
authors.uncertainty: The exact circumstances of Suckling's death (suicide or accident) are uncertain and were debated even by contemporaries.

authors.name: Sir Philip Sidney
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Courtier, soldier, diplomat, and poet; the model of the Renaissance man whose posthumously published works founded the English sonnet sequence and the critical defence of poetry.
authors.biography: Born 30 November 1554 at Penshurst, eldest son of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at Shrewsbury School and Christ Church, Oxford, then travelled the continent (1572–75), witnessing the St Bartholomew's Day massacre and meeting continental humanists. At court he was a favourite of Elizabeth's diplomacy and a patron of letters (dedicatee of Spenser's Calender); his quarrel with the Earl of Oxford (1579) and his 'Letter to Queen Elizabeth' against the Anjou match (1579–80) marked his temporary rustication to Wilton, where he wrote the Arcadia. He served in Parliament, was knighted in 1583, and in 1585 was appointed governor of Flushing; he died on 17 October 1586 of a thigh wound received at Zutphen (famously giving his water to a dying soldier), and was mourned as the flower of English chivalry.
authors.profile: The courtier-poet who practised poetry as an aristocratic accomplishment rather than a profession — 'look in thy heart, and write'; his Defence of Poesy remains the period's central statement of the moral and cultural claims of literature, and Astrophel and Stella set the sonnet vogue of the 1590s in motion.
authors.style: Elegant courtly wit, the first sustained English sonnet sequence with a narrative of courtship, the mingling of prose romance and eclogue in the Arcadia, and a critical prose of luminous argument.
authors.concerns: The defence of poetry against Puritan attack; the education of the aristocrat in virtue and action; the psychology of desire and self-knowledge; Protestant politics and the duties of the public man.
authors.significance: The posthumous publication of his works (Arcadia 1590, Astrophel and Stella 1591, The Defence of Poesy 1595) made him the tutelary genius of the 1590s literary generation and the English type of the poet-hero.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his major works rests on inference (the Arcadia is usually assigned to c. 1577–80, the Defence to c. 1579–81); none of his major works was printed in his lifetime by his own act.

authors.name: Sir Thomas Browne
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Physician, antiquary, and prose stylist; author of Religio Medici (1643), Hydriotaphia (Urn Burial, 1658), and The Garden of Cyrus (1658), whose majestic, digressive, Latinate prose is among the richest in English and fuses faith, scepticism, and learned curiosity.
authors.biography: Born 19 October 1605 in London, educated at Winchester and Pembroke College, Oxford (BA 1626, MA 1629), then studying medicine at Montpellier, Padua, and Leiden (MD 1633). He settled as a physician in Norwich (1637), where he lived for the rest of his life, marrying Dorothy Mileham (1641) and fathering twelve children. Religio Medici, circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent (1643), made his name; he answered critics and published Pseudodoxia Epidemica (1646–72), a vast enquiry into 'vulgar errors', and the twin treatises Hydriotaphia and The Garden of Cyrus (1658). Knighted by Charles II in 1671, he corresponded with the Royal Society and died on 19 October 1682.
authors.profile: The physician-essayist who meditated on belief, death, and the wonders of the natural world in a grand, allusive prose, holding faith and sceptical enquiry in a richly personal balance.
authors.style: Sonorous, Latinate, digressive prose; paradox and learned allusion; a baroque richness of phrase; antiquarian and scientific curiosity; and a meditative, tolerant tone.
authors.concerns: Faith and reason; death, burial, and the resurrection; the errors of popular belief; nature, plants, and antiquities; the mystery of the self; and Christian tolerance.
authors.significance: Browne is one of the supreme English prose stylists, influencing Johnson, De Quincey, Lamb, and Woolf; Religio Medici created a new genre of personal, tolerant religious autobiography, and Urn Burial remains a masterpiece of meditative antiquarianism.
authors.uncertainty: Browne's life is well documented through his letters and Norwich records; the publication history of Religio Medici (pirated editions before his authorised text) is complex.

authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: humanist; diplomat; lexicographer; political theorist
authors.biography: Born about 1490 into a family of west-country lawyers; he served Wolsey as clerk and became a diplomat and clerk of the king's council. Falling from favour in the 1530s, he devoted himself to letters: The Boke Named the Governour (1531), dedicated to Henry VIII, The Castle of Health (1534), and the first Latin–English dictionary (1538). He died on 26 March 1546.
authors.profile: The principal English theorist of humanist education and the gentleman magistrate. The Governour — drawing on Castiglione, Erasmus, and the Italian humanists — defined the curriculum, the virtues, and the physical training of the ruling class, and it introduced scores of classical commonplaces into English prose. His Dictionary (1538) founded English lexicography.
authors.style: Earnest, copious Ciceronian prose; the deliberate enrichment of English vocabulary from Latin; a moralist's directness beneath the classical apparatus.
authors.concerns: The education of princes and magistrates; the union of learning and virtue in the ruling class; the health of body and commonwealth; the capacities of the English language.
authors.significance: Author of the classic statement of the Tudor educational ideal, read by every Elizabethan schoolmaster, and of the dictionary that began the English lexicographical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
The education of princes and magistrates

authors.name: Sir Thomas More
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: humanist; lawyer; statesman; Lord Chancellor; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born in Milk Street, London, on 7 February 1478, the son of a judge; page to Cardinal Morton; studied at Oxford and the Inns of Court. A friend of Erasmus from 1499, he translated Lucian with him, wrote the Latin epigrams, and published Utopia at Louvain in 1516. Entered royal service in 1517; undersheriff of London, speaker of the Commons (1523), chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Lord Chancellor (1529–32). Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534 and beheaded on 6 July 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The presiding genius of English humanism. Utopia (1516) invented the fictional commonwealth; The History of King Richard III (c. 1513–18), written in both Latin and English, is the first great work of English historical prose and the source of Shakespeare's Richard III; the controversial dialogues of 1529–33 (A Dialogue Concerning Heresies, The Supplication of Souls, The Confutation of Tyndale's Answer) are the summit of Reformation polemic; and A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (1534), written in the Tower, is a masterpiece of devotional prose.
authors.style: Irony, wit, and the dramatic management of dialogue; the plain English style of the later controversial works; Latinity of European standard in the epigrams and Utopia.
authors.concerns: The reform of Christendom and the commonwealth; the claims of conscience against the state; property, enclosure, and social justice; the defence of the old church against the new theology.
authors.significance: Author of the founding text of utopian fiction, the first classic of English historiography, and one of the great prose styles of the language; his life and death made him the exemplary conscience of the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the dating of Richard III's composition remains approximate.
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth

authors.name: Sir Thomas North
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: translator; soldier; justice of the peace
authors.biography: Born 28 May 1535 in London, younger son of Edward North, 1st Baron North. Educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn, he saw military service in Ireland and the Low Countries and later sat as a justice in Cambridgeshire. He died about 1603.
authors.profile: The Dial of Princes (1557, from Guevara via French) and the Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579) — his translation of Plutarch from Jacques Amyot's French, which became the single most important non-dramatic source for Shakespeare's Roman and Greek plays.
authors.style: A full, energetic, idiomatic English prose of remarkable dramatic vividness; Shakespeare followed it so closely that whole passages of the plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
authors.concerns: The exemplary lives of great men; counsel and conduct; the translation of classical wisdom for English readers.
authors.significance: North's Plutarch is the most consequential translation of the English Renaissance, the quarry of Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate; the records of his last years are scanty.

authors.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: courtier; diplomat; poet
authors.biography: Born at Allington Castle, Kent, in 1503; educated at St John's College, Cambridge. A courtier and diplomat for Henry VIII — he was esquire of the body, ambassador in France, Italy, and Spain, and knighted in 1535 — he was twice imprisoned in the Tower: in 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn, and in 1541 on charges of treasonable correspondence. Released through the influence of Catherine Howard, he died of fever at Sherborne, Dorset, on 11 October 1542. His poems circulated in manuscript during his life; 96 were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
authors.profile: The founder of the English lyric tradition. He introduced the Petrarchan sonnet into English (translating and imitating the Rime sparse with rugged, deliberate roughness), wrote the great courtly lyrics ('They flee from me', 'Whoso list to hunt', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness'), the three verse epistles known as the Satires (c. 1536), and a paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms composed after his 1536 imprisonment.
authors.style: A difficult, compressed, colloquial style — enjambment against the rhyme, metrical irregularity used for dramatic emphasis, and the plain speech of the courtier set against Petrarchan convention.
authors.concerns: The dangers of court life under an absolute prince; the claims of truth against flattery; love, honour, and the unstable self; the psalmist's repentance as a model for the Tudor subject.
authors.significance: With Surrey, he established the sonnet, the courtly lyric, and the verse satire in English, providing the formal foundations of the Elizabethan poetic achievement; Tottel's printing of his verse made him the first modern English poet of the anthologies.
authors.uncertainty: The canon rests on manuscript attributions (principally the Egerton MS); the extent of his relationship with Anne Boleyn is conjectural.
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal

authors.name: Sir Walter Ralegh
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: courtier; explorer; poet; historian
authors.biography: Born about 1554 at Hayes Barton, Devon. He fought in France and Ireland, rose at court through the favour of Elizabeth I, and was knighted in 1585. He organized the attempted Roanoke colony and expeditions to Guiana. After Elizabeth's death he was convicted of treason on flimsy evidence and imprisoned in the Tower (1603–16), where he wrote his History of the World. Released for the disastrous Guiana voyage of 1617, he was executed on 29 October 1618 on the old sentence.
authors.profile: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana (1596), the History of the World (1614), the Cynthia poems ('The Ocean to Cynthia' fragments), and lyrics such as 'The Lie', 'The Passionate Man's Pilgrimage', and the poem written the night before his death.
authors.style: A grave, plain, sententious style in prose; in verse, an introspective melancholy unusual in the Elizabethan court lyric.
authors.concerns: Fortune and the fall of greatness; colonial wealth and its moral cost; providence and the vanity of human glory.
authors.significance: The embodiment of the Elizabethan adventurer-intellectual; his History of the World was read for its stoic grandeur, and his myth has haunted English literature ever since.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon of his shorter poems rests on early anthologies and is partly uncertain.

authors.name: Sir Walter Scott
authors.nationality: Scottish; the ballad revival and the historical novel
authors.identity: Poet, editor, novelist and lawyer; the defining figure of Scottish Romantic writing and the creator of the modern historical novel
authors.biography: He was born in Edinburgh, the son of a Writer to the Signet, and a childhood attack of paralysis left him permanently lame and given to reading and to the oral traditions of the household and of the Borders. He was admitted to the Scottish bar and served for many years as sheriff-deputy of Midlothian, a post that paid for the life at Abbotsford he built up from 1811. In youth he gathered Border ballads, made translations from German romance and ballad sources, and printed the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, which established his reputation as an editor of native poetry. Narrative poems beginning with the lay of the border minstrel made him the most widely read English-language poet of the wartime decade until the prose romance appeared to occupy the ground his poetry had won. The publishing catastrophe of 1826, in which the firm in which he was involved failed, obliged him to pay the creditors by writing fiction at enormous rate under the pseudonym of the editor of the Waverley romance, and the later novels were produced to that public debt. He travelled in France and on the continent in his last years, was created a baronet in 1820, and died at Abbotsford shortly after returning from Italy, leaving his journals and his debt discharged by the novels.
authors.profile: An editorial career in ballad and Scottish historical printing; a decade of narrative poetry in romance measures; and the series of prose romances from the Jacobite tale of sixty years since to the tales of the Crusades, the Commonwealth and the Scottish Reformation, with late works in the contemporary and Scottish legal novel. He also wrote drama, a life of Napoleon, a history of Scotland, letters on witchcraft and demonology, and an enormous correspondence. His fiction is organised around the collision of a private, domestic, commercial Scotland and England with public event - rising, trial, succession, religious persecution - and its heroes are typically competent, unexceptional young men carried through history by others.
authors.style: Long narrative momentum carried by dialogue and by the dialect speech of a fully realised social lower world. The ballad measure and the romance stanza in the poems, with a striking command of the popular fourteener and the couplet. A habit of editorial framing, dedication, preface and note that makes the fiction talk about its own sources. And a moral vocabulary of honour, interest and duty expressed through concrete material detail rather than philosophy.
authors.concerns: The mechanics of historical change and the price of improvement; the passing of clan, Covenant and border society into commercial Britain. The legitimacy of the '45 and the problem of loyalty; ballad, tradition and national memory as evidence. Superstition, witchcraft and the limits of explanation; the economics of authorship, patronage and debt.
authors.significance: He made the historical novel the dominant prose form of nineteenth-century Europe and set the terms on which nations wrote their pasts as fiction; his ballad editing shaped the Romantic revival of popular poetry, and his poetry and romances defined the British reading of Scotland for a generation. His account of the interaction of material life and event was the direct ancestor of the historical fiction of the later century, and his career as an anonymous, debt-driven professional author is the period's central case study in the literary market.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of his anonymous publishing, the share of his printing house's work in the Ballantyne failure, and the date of some early editorial work remain matters of documentary argument; his own posthumous journals were edited and partly suppressed by his biographer, so that the personal record is available only through that mediation.

authors.name: Sir William Davenant
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet, playwright, and impresario; the crucial bridge between the Caroline and Restoration stages, who kept drama alive during the Interregnum with 'entertainments' and the proto-opera The Siege of Rhodes, held one of the two Restoration theatre patents, and introduced women players and scenery to the English stage.
authors.biography: Born February 1606 in Oxford, son of a vintner (legend, fostered by Davenant, claimed Shakespeare as his father and godfather). He wrote masques and plays for the Caroline court, succeeded Jonson as poet laureate (1638), and was knighted (1651) for royalist service. During the Commonwealth he produced The Siege of Rhodes (1656) at Rutland House — often called the first English opera — evading the ban on plays as 'moral representations'. Imprisoned and pardoned for his part in royalist plots, he survived to hold, with Thomas Killigrew, the royal patent of 1660 that reopened the theatres; his Duke's Company introduced moveable scenery and, in 1660, the first professional actresses. He adapted Shakespeare (with Dryden, The Tempest, 1667) and died on 7 April 1668, buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The impresario-poet who modernised the English stage, blending masque, opera, and neoclassical drama, and whose Gondibert (1651) experimented with a new quatrain epic form praised by Hobbes.
authors.style: Masque and spectacle; the experimental four-line stanza of Gondibert; neoclassical dramatic theory; heroic and operatic forms; and a verse of public, philosophical ambition.
authors.concerns: The reform and moral justification of drama; Platonic and heroic virtue (Gondibert); the integration of music, scenery, and spectacle; royalist loyalty; and the new stagecraft.
authors.significance: Davenant founded the institutional and technical shape of the Restoration theatre — its patents, scenery, women players, and operatic ambitions — and mentored the young Dryden; without him the continuity of English drama across the Interregnum would have been broken.
authors.uncertainty: The claim that Davenant was Shakespeare's biological son is legend, not fact; his biography is otherwise well documented through theatre records and state papers.

authors.name: Sir William Temple
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Diplomat, statesman, and essayist; author of Observations upon the United Provinces (1673) and the elegant miscellaneous essays Of Gardens (1685) and Of Poetry, whose polished, urbane prose and patronage of Swift made him a central figure of late-century letters.
authors.biography: Born 25 April 1628 in London, son of Sir John Temple; educated at Bishop's Stortford and Emmanuel College, Cambridge (under Ralph Cudworth), travelling widely in Europe. He served as ambassador and negotiator (the Triple Alliance, 1668; the treaties of Nijmegen), and as Secretary of State (1679), before retiring to Moor Park, Surrey. There he wrote his Observations upon the United Provinces (1673), his Miscellanea (1680, 1690), and essays including 'Upon the Gardens of Epicurus' (1685), and employed the young Jonathan Swift as his secretary (1689–99). His 'Essay upon the Ancient and Modern Learning' (1690) provoked the Battle of the Books. He died on 27 January 1699.
authors.profile: The cultivated statesman-essayist whose clear, graceful, conversational prose exemplifies the polite ideal of the late seventeenth century and who introduced the Chinese garden and a cosmopolitan urbane taste to English letters.
authors.style: Polished, lucid, urbane prose; the short, balanced sentence; conversational ease; digressive reflection; and a Horatian ideal of retirement.
authors.concerns: Politics, diplomacy, and the Dutch republic; gardens, retirement, and the Epicurean ideal; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; poetry and wit; and the conduct of public and private life.
authors.significance: Temple's essays shaped Augustan prose style and the taste for retirement and gardening; his patronage launched Swift, and his 'Ancient and Modern Learning' essay ignited the Battle of the Books that Swift and Wotton fought out.
authors.uncertainty: Temple's diplomatic career is well documented in state papers; his private life and the details of his relationship with Swift and his household are known through correspondence and memoirs.

authors.name: St John Ervine
authors.nationality: Irish; the Ulster playwright of John Ferguson and the Abbey's manager
authors.identity: Playwright, novelist and critic; the Ulster dramatist of Jane Clegg and John Ferguson.
authors.biography: Born St John Ervine at Belfast on 1 February 1883; he worked in London insurance and journalism before the plays of Jane Clegg (1913) and John Ferguson (1915) made him the Ulster dramatist of the new drama, and the novel Mrs. Martin's Man (1914) carried the same country into the fiction. He managed the Abbey Theatre in 1915-16, served in the war and was wounded on the Somme, became the Observer's dramatic critic and one of the century's most combative reviewers, and wrote the great life of his friend Bernard Shaw; he died at Oxfordshire on 14 June 1971.
authors.profile: St John Ervine is the Ulster playwright of the new drama: John Ferguson, with its Bible on the table and its avenger from America, is the classic play of the Ulster conscience, Jane Clegg made the deserted wife a figure of the suffrage stage, and his Abbey management and his criticism carried the same combative conscience into the institutions.
authors.style: The plain Ulster dialogue of the farmhouse and the chapel; the conscience and its scripture in the dramatic argument; the critic's combative sentence; the Shaw of the biography; the moral passion of the new drama without its subtlety.
authors.concerns: Ulster and its conscience; the scripture and the revenge; the deserted wife and the suffrage stage; the Abbey and its management; Shaw and the friendship of the biography.
authors.significance: St John Ervine is the Ulster playwright of the new drama: John Ferguson is the classic play of the Ulster conscience and Jane Clegg made the deserted wife a figure of the suffrage stage.

authors.identity: Historian, journalist and novelist; the writer who reintroduced the Irish heroic sagas to the nineteenth century and inspired the Irish Literary Revival.
authors.biography: Born at Castletown Berehaven, County Cork, on 18 September 1846; he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and practised law before History of Ireland: Heroic Period (1878) made him the herald of the Irish revival. Cuculain and His Contemporaries (1880), The Story of Ireland (1894) and The Bog of Stars (1893) followed. He died on the Isle of Wight on 18 May 1928.

authors.style: The retelling of the saga in Victorian prose; the heroic epithet and the set speech; the landscape of the Irish epic; the historian's narrative frame; the romantic nationalism of the address.
authors.concerns: National identity and the heroic code; the Irish past and the recovery of the native tradition; heroism and the warrior elite; the relation of the poet to the nation; the Celtic periphery.

authors.biography: Born Stanley Houghton at Ashton-under-Lyne on 19 February 1881; he worked in the Manchester textile trade and wrote for the Manchester Guardian before the repertory of Annie Horniman's Gaiety Theatre produced his plays. authors.profile: Stanley Houghton is the Manchester School's greatest playwright: Hindle Wakes - Fanny Hawthorn, the mill-owner's son and the holiday week - made the Lancashire working woman's refusal of the respectable marriage one of the new drama's most famous scenes, and the play's revivals have kept it on the stage for a century.
authors.style: The plain Lancashire dialogue of the mill and the terrace; the working woman's independence in the holiday week; the generational conflict of the factory family; the Manchester repertory's realism; the comedy carried by the dialect and the moral.
authors.concerns: The Lancashire mill town and its classes; the working woman and the refusal of marriage; the younger generation against the old; the holiday week and the pleasure resort; the Manchester School and the repertory.

authors.style: The parody of the rural novel and its dialect; the comic catalogue of the gloomy farm; the sensible heroine against the romantic tradition; the footnote and the pastiche; the light, dry, exact prose.

authors.name: Stephen Crane
authors.nationality: American; the naturalist novel, the war report and the ironist of the city
authors.identity: Novelist, poet and war correspondent; the author of The Red Badge of Courage and the founder of American literary naturalism.
authors.biography: Born in Newark, New Jersey, on 1 November 1871, the fourteenth child of a Methodist minister; he was educated at Lafayette College and Syracuse University without taking a degree, and worked as a journalist in New York, where he wrote Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893) at his own expense. The Red Badge of Courage (1895) made him internationally famous; he went to the war in Cuba in 1896-97, was shipwrecked on the Commodore, and died of tuberculosis at Badenweiler, Germany, on 5 June 1900, aged twenty-eight.
authors.profile: Crane invented American naturalism: Maggie and The Red Badge of Courage take the poor of the Bowery and the soldier in battle and record them without moralising, in a prose of brilliant colour and cold distance. He was also the first great American war correspondent, and his best stories — 'The Open Boat', 'The Blue Hotel' — are among the finest in the language: his irony, his imagery and his refusal of consolation changed what American fiction could do.
authors.style: Impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation; the ironic narrator who withholds judgement; the short sentence and the stark scene; dialogue in dialect from the street; the refusal of a moral or a comforting ending; the image that becomes the story's meaning.
authors.concerns: Poverty, drink and the urban poor; war, fear and the illusions of courage; the indifference of nature; the city and the slum; the individual against a determining environment; the failure of the American promise.
authors.significance: Crane is the father of American naturalism and the most influential American prose stylist of the 1890s: The Red Badge of Courage changed the literature of war, 'The Open Boat' is one of the great American stories, and his example made possible Norris, London, Dreiser and Hemingway.

authors.name: Stephen Hawes

authors.biography: Born about 1474, probably in Suffolk; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became groom of the chamber to Henry VII. His Pastime of Pleasure was printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509 and The Example of Virtue about 1504; he died about 1523, the last significant poet of the Chaucerian-Lydgatian school.
authors.profile: The last of the medieval allegorists and a favourite of the early Tudor court. The Pastime of Pleasure recounts the education, courtship, and knightly career of the hero Graunde Amoure in rhyme royal and couplets, an allegorical summa of chivalric and learned ideals; The Example of Virtue traces the soul's progress through Youth to Age and Eternity.
authors.style: Aureate diction in the Lydgatian manner; rhyme royal handled with fluency; allegorical machinery of pilgrimage, tower, and tournament.
authors.concerns: The seven liberal arts; chivalric education and courtly love; the soul's moral progress; the poet's role as teacher of princes.
authors.significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical tradition and Tudor court poetry; Spenser read him, and The Pastime of Pleasure kept the dream-allegory alive into the Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; little is known of his life beyond his court service.

authors.name: Stephen of Ripon
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (Northumbrian)
authors.identity: hagiographer; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: A priest of Ripon and member of Bishop Wilfrid's household, conventionally identified with the Æddi Stephanus whom Bede says Wilfrid brought back from Kent as a singing-master (fl. c. 670-720). He accompanied Wilfrid on his journeys and wrote the Vita Sancti Wilfridi (c. 712-714) at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. Nothing else is known of his life, and even his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' rests on a plausible but unproven equation.
authors.profile: The earliest identifiable Anglo-Latin biographer after the anonymous Lindisfarne life of Cuthbert. His Vita Wilfridi is a partisan defence of his hero against the charges of Wilfrid's enemies, cast in the conventions of late-antique hagiography.
authors.style: Vigorous, episodic narrative with a strong authorial voice; vivid set-piece scenes (Wilfrid's shipwreck, his Roman appeals, his deathbed); simpler and more direct Latin than Aldhelm's, with a notable absence of the hermeneutic manner.
authors.concerns: Episcopal authority and the primacy of Rome; the sanctity of a controversial political bishop; the deeds of the apostolic missionary as evidence of holiness.
authors.significance: His Vita Wilfridi is the earliest surviving biography written in England about a contemporary English churchman, and a principal source for the history of the seventh-century Northumbrian church and Wilfrid's career.
authors.uncertainty: Identification with Bede's Æddi Stephanus is traditional, not proven. Birth and death dates unknown; floruit c. 670-720.

authors.identity: Poet, essayist and editor; one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the editor of Horizon and Encounter.
authors.biography: Born Stephen Harold Spender in London on 28 February 1909, the son of a journalist; he read at University College, Oxford, where he printed Auden's first book, and published Twenty Poems (1930), Poems (1933), Vienna (1934) and The Still Centre (1939). He joined the Communist Party briefly in 1937, served in the National Fire Service in the war, edited Horizon with Cyril Connolly (1939–41) and Encounter (1953–67), taught at American universities, and died in London on 16 July 1995.
authors.profile: Spender is the lyric poet of the Auden generation: 'The Pylons', 'The Express', 'Not Palaces' and 'I Think Continually of Those Who Were Truly Great' are the finest poems of the thirties' public manner, and his Spanish Civil War poems gave the decade its conscience. As editor of Horizon and Encounter he made the period's literary conversation, and his autobiography World Within World is one of the great English memoirs of the century.
authors.style: The lyric line held in traditional stanza; the aeroplane, the pylon and the machine as symbols of the future; the political statement made in the first person; the elegy for the dead of Spain; the autobiographical prose of a generation.
authors.concerns: The thirties and the coming war; the Spanish Civil War; the machine, the pylon and the modern landscape; love, homosexuality and the private life; the artist's politics and the betrayal of the cause; memory and the lost generation.
authors.significance: Spender is one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the period's great editor: 'The Pylons' and 'Not Palaces' are the finest poems of the thirties' public style, his Spanish war poems gave the decade its conscience, and Horizon and Encounter made him the period's principal literary editor.

authors.name: Sui Sin Far
authors.nationality: Chinese-British-American; the Chinese-American short story and the literature of the immigrant
authors.identity: Journalist and short-story writer; the first Chinese-American writer of fiction in English and the great chronicler of Chinese immigrant life in America.
authors.biography: Born Edith Maude Eaton at Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 15 March 1865, the daughter of an English silk merchant and a Chinese mother; the family emigrated to Montreal in 1872, and she worked as a stenographer and journalist, moving to San Francisco in 1898 and to Boston in 1912. She published stories under the name Sui Sin Far from 1890, collected in Mrs Spring Fragrance (1912), and died in Montreal on 7 May 1914.
authors.profile: Sui Sin Far wrote the first fiction in English about the Chinese in America: her stories of San Francisco's Chinatown and of the Chinese-American household record the immigrant experience from inside, with sympathy for both the Chinese and the white characters, and refuse the stereotypes of the yellow-peril press. Mrs Spring Fragrance is the founding text of Asian-American literature, and her journalism and essays make her the first important Asian-American literary voice.
authors.style: The short story with a domestic interior and a small crisis; realistic dialogue across languages; the mixed-race perspective of a narrator who belongs to both worlds; gentle irony at the expense of white misunderstanding; the precise material detail of immigrant life.
authors.concerns: Chinese immigration and exclusion; the Chinese-American family and the arranged marriage; race, law and the immigrant; the encounter of East and West; mothering and childhood across cultures; the prejudice of the American press.
authors.significance: Sui Sin Far is the first Chinese-American writer of fiction and the founder of Asian-American literature: Mrs Spring Fragrance introduced the Chinese immigrant to American fiction as a human being rather than a stereotype, and her work is now recognised as a foundational text of Asian-American and multiracial American literature.

authors.name: Susan Ferrier
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Novelist of manners and Scottish social comedy
authors.biography: Susan Ferrier was born in Edinburgh, daughter of William Ferrier, a writer to the signet, and niece of James Ferrier, a close friend of Walter Scott. After her father's death reduced the family to genteel poverty she turned to fiction with Scott's active encouragement. Marriage (1818) was a critical success; The Inheritance (1824) consolidated her reputation as Scotland's finest living novelist. A brief marriage in 1825 to James Ferrier's son was unhappy and ended in early separation. She continued to write, publishing the novel The Dangerfield Confessions in 1843, but her later works did not match her early triumphs. She died in Edinburgh in 1854.
authors.profile: Ferrier is the principal Scottish novelist of manners of the Romantic generation. Her fiction examines the economics of the marriage market, the pretensions of rank, and the moral education of women in genteel poverty with a brisk irony directly comparable to Austen. Her use of Scottish dialect and her attention to legal and clerical society distinguish her from the English novel of manners.
authors.style: Brisk, ironic dialogue; satirical portraits of mercenary gentility; dialect passages for Scottish servants and lairds; three-volume social comedy with a double-plot structure contrasting rival heroines.
authors.concerns: The economics of marriage for women without fortune; Scottish gentility and class mobility; moral worth versus social rank; the limited professions available to genteel women.
authors.significance: Ferrier established the Scottish novel of manners in the Waverley era and is now recognised as a central figure in the genealogy connecting Burney and Edgeworth to Austen and to later Victorian social fiction; her recovery in modern criticism corrected a long underestimation.

authors.identity: English playwright, poet, and actress, widely considered the most successful female dramatist of the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Susanna Freeman, though her maiden name is disputed, in Lincolnshire and baptized there around 1669, she was said to have been largely self-educated and to have entered the theatre early. She acted briefly and then turned to playwriting, becoming a dominant presence on the London stage in the reign of Queen Anne. Her best-known comedies include The Busie Body (1709), The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret (1714), and A Bold Stroke for a Wife (1718). She also wrote a prologue and other occasional verse and was associated with Whig political circles. She died in London on 1 December 1723.
authors.profile: A prolific writer of city and manners comedies who specialized in brisk plots of mistaken identity, female cunning, and marriage intrigue, and whose plays remained a staple of the repertory long after her death.
authors.style: Sprightly, witty comic dialogue; well-made intrigue plots; stock and humours characters; clever, spirited heroines; and prose comedy designed for effective stage performance.
authors.concerns: Marriage, money, and social mobility; wit and the cunning of clever women; busybody culture and the manners of the town; and party and public life in Augustan London.
authors.significance: The most frequently performed woman playwright of her era in Britain, whose comedies helped shape the early-eighteenth-century stage and were revived and adapted throughout the century.
