authors.name: Susanna Moodie
authors.nationality: English-Canadian; the emigrant memoir and the colonial sketch
authors.identity: Writer and settler; the author of Roughing It in the Bush, the classic English memoir of Canadian settlement.
authors.biography: Born Susanna Strickland at Bungay, Suffolk, on 6 December 1803, the sister of Agnes Strickland and Catharine Parr Traill; she was an abolitionist and an early contributor to the anti-slavery album of 1826. She married the half-pay officer John Wedderburn Dunbar Moodie in 1831 and emigrated to Upper Canada in 1832, settling first in the bush near Peterborough and later at Belleville. She wrote for the Literary Garland and the Montreal newspapers, and published Roughing It in the Bush (1852), Life in the Clearings (1853) and her novel Mark Hurdlestone. She died in Toronto on 8 April 1885.
authors.profile: Moodie wrote the emigrant experience as a woman's ordeal: Roughing It in the Bush is a series of sketches of settlement in the backwoods of Upper Canada, in which the genteel Englishwoman confronts hunger, childbirth, fire, drinking neighbours and the loss of everything her class had taught her to value. It is the finest English account of the Canadian frontier and one of the most important documents of nineteenth-century emigration.
authors.style: Episodic sketch narrative in the manner of the periodical; the first-person testimony of the gentlewoman turned settler; comic and grim anecdote; the description of the bush as an alien and hostile world; the poem embedded in the prose.
authors.concerns: Emigration and the settler's ordeal; the colonial woman and her household; class and gentility in the bush; the Canadian winter and the wilderness; drink and violence; religion and consolation.
authors.significance: Roughing It in the Bush is the central English memoir of Canadian settlement and one of the great Victorian accounts of emigration: it shaped the English image of Canada and is a foundational text of Canadian literature, of the literature of the frontier and of women's settler writing.

authors.name: Sydney Owenson
authors.nationality: Irish; the national tale and the literature of Irish identity
authors.identity: Novelist, travel writer and celebrity author; the creator of the Irish national tale and its most public exponent
authors.biography: She was the daughter of a Dublin medical man and of a family with theatrical and literary connections, and grew up in the Irish capital in the years of the volunteer movement and of the debates on the parliament's future. She began to write for the press and the stage in her teens and early twenties, publishing verse and tales and acting in private performances in the houses of the Irish nobility, where she was admired for her recitation and her presence. Her first national tale, of an Englishman converted to admiration of an ancient Irish house, appeared anonymously in 1806 and made her famous on both sides of the channel; a second, of the Irish Rebellion of the seventeenth century, followed in 1814, and tales of contemporary Irish and Scottish society in the years after the union. She married a physician in 1812 and became, on his baronetcy, the lady of the title by which she was afterwards known; her accounts of France, of Italy and of Spain, written after long residence abroad, were widely read. Her last Irish novels were bitterly attacked in the English press and her reputation declined, though she continued to write and to entertain at her house in London until her death in 1845. Her papers and her autobiography were printed after her death and have been much reissued.
authors.profile: A series of Irish national tales, a historical romance of the seventeenth-century confederate war, novels of contemporary society in Ireland, Scotland and Wales, three books of travel and commentary on France, Italy and Spain, and a volume of verse and of contributions to annuals. Her plot is habitually the marriage of an English interest to an Irish inheritance, figured as the settlement of a national wrong, and her narration is interrupted by songs, legends and told tales which carry the native tradition inside the English book.
authors.style: An impassioned, rhetorical and highly demonstrative prose, with long apostrophe, exclamation and editorial pleading on behalf of the injured nation. Her lyrics and simulated translations from the Irish are formal and musical, and her later travel writing is brisk, conversational and self-referential by comparison.
authors.concerns: The justice due to a conquered nation and the property confiscated from it. The value and survival of native song, legend and hospitality. The condition of women as the measure of a nation's civility. Toleration, catholic relief and the union settlement. The education of the English reader about Ireland.
authors.significance: She invented the national tale as a form and set the pattern that the historical novelists of the next generation followed in Ireland and Scotland; her public career is the century's most conspicuous example of the woman of letters as a national advocate. Her representation of the marriage plot as political allegory is a founding text of Irish-studies readings of the Romantic novel.
authors.uncertainty: The year of her birth is variously given and her early education is described differently in the family and later biographical accounts; the details of her theatrical and private performances in Ireland rest on memoir written to serve her reputation.

authors.biography: Born Sylvia Nora Townsend Warner at Harpenden on 6 December 1893; she edited the ten-volume Tudor Church Music and published Lolly Willowes in 1926, followed by Mr Fortune's Maggot (1927), The True Heart (1929), Summer Will Show (1936) and After the Death of Don Juan (1938). She lived with the poet Valentine Ackland, wrote the Kingdoms of Elfin stories, and died at Maiden Newton, Dorset, on 1 May 1978.
authors.profile: Sylvia Townsend Warner wrote Lolly Willowes, one of the most original English novels of the century and the founding text of the modern feminist fantasy: her story of the spinster who becomes a witch made a permanent argument for the woman's freedom, and her historical novels and Elfin stories made her one of the great English fantasists.
authors.style: The fantasy that begins as realism; the exact and sensuous description; the spinster and the devil; the historical past rendered in present detail; the dry, precise, unsentimental prose.

authors.name: T. E. Lawrence
authors.nationality: British; the desert memoir and the prose of the Arab Revolt
authors.identity: Soldier, archaeologist and writer; the author of Seven Pillars of Wisdom, the finest English prose account of the First World War in the Middle East.
authors.biography: Born Thomas Edward Lawrence at Tremadog, Wales, on 16 August 1888; he read history at Oxford, worked as an archaeologist at Carchemish in Syria (1911–14), and served in the Arab Bureau in Cairo and with the Arab forces under Feisal from 1916 to 1918. He wrote Seven Pillars of Wisdom (privately printed 1926, published 1935), abridged it as Revolt in the Desert (1927), and translated Homer and Forestier; he enlisted in the RAF under an assumed name, and died of injuries from a motorcycle accident at Bovington Camp, Dorset, on 19 May 1935.
authors.profile: Lawrence wrote the finest English prose account of the war in the Middle East: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is a great memoir, a study of a national revolt and the confession of a man who believed he had betrayed the cause he served. Its prose — sonorous, exact, self-lacerating — is among the finest in twentieth-century English, and it is the only soldier's book of the period to rank with Blunden's and Sassoon's.
authors.style: The memoir written as a confession and a history at once; the exact topography of the desert; the prose that swells into the biblical and the epic; the self-examination that turns against the narrator; the ethnographic observation of the Arab tribes.
authors.concerns: The Arab Revolt and the making of the modern Middle East; empire, betrayal and the promises of 1916; the desert and the Arab people; the individual and the historical role; guilt, self-punishment and the divided self; the machine (the aeroplane, the motor bike) and the archaic world.
authors.significance: Lawrence wrote the finest English memoir of the First World War in the Middle East and one of the great English prose works of the century: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is a permanent classic, its account of the Arab Revolt remains the essential literary record of the making of the modern Middle East, and its self-lacerating honesty makes it unique among the war books.

authors.name: T. S. Eliot
authors.nationality: American-British; the modernist long poem, the verse drama and the criticism of tradition
authors.identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the author of The Waste Land and Four Quartets, the most influential poet-critic of the century, and the Nobel laureate of 1948.
authors.biography: Born Thomas Stearns Eliot in St Louis, Missouri, on 26 September 1888 into a Unitarian family of New England descent; he studied at Harvard, Paris and Oxford, settled in London in 1915, married Vivienne Haigh-Wood in 1915, worked in Lloyds Bank (1917–25) and edited The Criterion (1922–39). Prufrock and Other Observations appeared in 1917, The Waste Land in 1922, The Hollow Men in 1925; he became a British subject and an Anglo-Catholic in 1927, published Ash-Wednesday in 1930, Murder in the Cathedral in 1935, Four Quartets in 1943 and won the Nobel Prize in 1948. He died in London on 4 January 1965.
authors.profile: Eliot changed the language of English poetry. The Waste Land made the fragment, the quotation and the mythic parallel the instruments of modern verse; Four Quartets is the period's great religious poem; and his criticism — 'Tradition and the Individual Talent', 'The Metaphysical Poets', 'Ulysses, Order, and Myth' — invented the vocabulary in which modern literature has been discussed ever since. As editor of The Criterion and as a director of Faber and Faber he shaped what modernism published.
authors.style: The abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations; the objective correlative and the avoidance of direct statement; free verse organised by the musical phrase; the dramatic monologue and the dramatic lyric; the allusion that carries the argument; the flat conversational tone broken by sudden lyric intensity.
authors.concerns: The waste land and the decline of the West; time, memory, and the moment of incarnation; doubt, faith, and the via negativa; the modern city and the crowd; sex without love and the failure of desire; tradition and the individual talent; the theatre and the ritual of the church.
authors.significance: Eliot is the central poet and critic of the period: The Waste Land is the defining poem of modernism, Four Quartets its great religious meditation, and his criticism set the canon and the vocabulary of the twentieth century. He is the only writer of the period who is equally decisive as poet, critic, editor and dramatist.

authors.name: Tatwine
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (Mercian)
authors.identity: Latin riddler and theologian; grammarian
authors.biography: A Mercian by birth who became a monk at Breedon-on-the-Hill in Leicestershire, a house with Northumbrian connections. He was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 731, succeeding Berhtwald, and died in office in 734. Bede records his consecration in the Historia ecclesiastica.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata, forty Latin riddles with a preface, on theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects, and of a Latin grammar (Ars Tatuini) based on Donatus. His riddles are the first Latin riddle collection composed in England to survive complete.
authors.style: Compact hexameter riddles in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm, but with doctrine rather than natural history as their usual subject; the verse is plain and schoolmasterly rather than hermeneutic.
authors.concerns: The union of grammatical learning with theology; the encyclopedic description of creation through the riddle form; Christian teaching for the schoolroom.
authors.significance: With Aldhelm and Hwætberht he established the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that fed into the vernacular Exeter Book Riddles; his grammar helped transmit the Insular grammatical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and place uncertain (Mercia by tradition); the attribution of the riddles and grammar to him is secure.

authors.name: Terence Rattigan
authors.nationality: British; the well-made play, the restraint of feeling and the English middle-class drama
authors.identity: Dramatist; the finest English writer of the well-made play, the author of The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables.
authors.biography: Born Terence Mervyn Rattigan in London on 10 June 1911; he read at Trinity College, Oxford, and made his name with French Without Tears (1936), After the Dance (1939), The Winslow Boy (1946), The Browning Version (1948), The Deep Blue Sea (1952) and Separate Tables (1954). The arrival of Look Back in Anger in 1956 made him unfashionable for a decade; he was reassessed before his death at Hamilton, Bermuda, on 30 November 1977, and his centenary in 2011 restored him to the centre of the English theatre.
authors.profile: Rattigan is the finest English writer of the well-made play: The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables are the most accomplished plays in the English language of their kind, and their restraint — the emotion held under the surface of the dialogue — is a technique the English theatre has never excelled. He wrote the period's great plays about the price of respectability, and the reaction against him in 1956 is one of the period's revealing literary scandals.
authors.style: The tight three-act construction with a single set and a small cast; the dialogue that never states the feeling; the understated curtain line; the public-school and the service officer as material; the social comedy that becomes a tragedy without a change of tone.
authors.concerns: The English middle class and its code of restraint; respectability and its price; the law, the newspaper and the ruined reputation (The Winslow Boy); the unhappy marriage and the loveless life; the officer and the schoolmaster; homosexuality in a society that punished it.
authors.significance: Rattigan wrote the finest English well-made plays of the century: The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables are permanent, his restraint is a technique of great sophistication, and his fall and recovery is the period's clearest example of how literary reputations are made.

authors.name: Theodore Dreiser
authors.nationality: American; the naturalist novel of the city and the literature of American desire
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of Sister Carrie and An American Tragedy, and the most thoroughgoing American naturalist.
authors.biography: Born Herman Theodore Dreiser in Terre Haute, Indiana, on 27 August 1871, the ninth child of a devout German Catholic immigrant family; he was a newspaper reporter in Chicago, St Louis and Pittsburgh in the 1890s, and Sister Carrie was published in 1900 only after the publisher's wife objected to it. He worked as an editor of women's magazines until 1910, published Jennie Gerhardt and The Financier in 1911-12, and became the leading figure of American naturalism. He joined the Communist Party in 1945 and died in Hollywood on 28 December 1945.
authors.profile: Dreiser wrote the American naturalist novel of desire: Sister Carrie follows a young woman's rise in the city through the men who desire her, and An American Tragedy follows a young man's fall, both with a patient accumulation of detail and an absence of moral judgement that was new in American fiction. He was a clumsy stylist and a great novelist, and his refusal to condemn his characters made him the central American writer of the naturalist tradition and the model for the American novel of the twentieth century.
authors.style: Slow accumulation of documentary detail; the flat, unhurried sentence; the interior of the city street, the hotel and the factory; the analysis of motive in biological and social terms; the refusal of authorial judgement; the long novel of a whole life.
authors.concerns: Desire, money and the American city; the woman who rises and the man who falls; poverty and the fear of poverty; the class system and the machinery of success; crime, guilt and the law; the determinism of heredity and environment.
authors.significance: Dreiser is the central American naturalist and one of the founders of modern American fiction: Sister Carrie and An American Tragedy are permanent classics, his refusal of moral judgement changed the American novel, and his influence on Fitzgerald, Faulkner, Richard Wright and the whole twentieth-century American novel is decisive.

authors.name: Theodore of Tarsus
authors.nationality: Greek-speaking Cilician; Archbishop of Canterbury (668-690)
authors.identity: exegete, canonist, and teacher; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Tarsus in 602 and educated in the Greek East (probably at Antioch and Constantinople), he was living as a monk in Rome when Pope Vitalian consecrated him archbishop of Canterbury in 668, with Hadrian the African as his companion and adviser. Together they toured England, reformed the English church, and founded the school of Canterbury, where Greek and Latin learning, canon law, and biblical exegesis were taught. He died on 19 September 690.
authors.profile: The Laterculus Malalianus, a Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, is attributed to him (written at Canterbury in the 670s); the biblical commentaries from the Canterbury school preserve his and Hadrian's teaching; the penitential that circulates under his name is traditionally attributed to him. His school produced Aldhelm and the earliest English manuscript culture.
authors.style: In the Laterculus Malalianus, dense and sometimes idiosyncratic Latin shaped by Syriac and Greek exegetical sources, with a chronological apparatus; the Canterbury commentaries preserve an unusual blend of Greek and Latin patristic learning.
authors.concerns: The chronology and exegesis of the life of Christ; the union of Greek and Latin Christian learning; church order and penance; the education of an English clergy.
authors.significance: As organizer of the Canterbury school he is the founder of Anglo-Saxon Latin learning; his church reforms and synods (Hertford 672, Hatfield 679) unified the English church, and his teaching reached Bede's Northumbria through his pupils.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Laterculus Malalianus and the Penitential to him is traditional and widely accepted, but not beyond dispute. Birth and death dates are recorded by Bede.

authors.name: Thomas Babington Macaulay
authors.nationality: English; the Whig historical and essayistic prose of the mid-nineteenth century
authors.identity: Essayist, narrative historian, poet of the ballad revival and Whig parliamentarian; the most widely read English prose stylist of his generation and the representative voice of liberal historical optimism.
authors.biography: Macaulay was born at Rothley Temple in Leicestershire on 25 October 1800, the eldest son of Zachary Macaulay, the Scottish evangelist and abolitionist who had been governor of Sierra Leone, and of Selina Mills, the daughter of a Quaker banker; the family's abolitionist and Clapham connections shaped his earliest convictions. A precocious reader, he wrote an epic-poem plan as a schoolboy at the Hill House school in Huntingdon and won prizes at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he joined the Cambridge discussers and won the Chancellors medal for an English essay on Milton. Called to the bar in 1826, he abandoned practice for letters and politics, and his essay on Milton in the Edinburgh Review in 1825 began a career of review-writing that made him the acknowledged master of the Whig essay. Elected to Parliament for Cambridge in 1830, he served in the Grey ministry as Paymaster of the Forces, took a leading part in the reform bill debates, and went to India in 1834 as a member of the governors council, where his Minute on Education of 1835 argued for English-language instruction and had lasting consequences for Indian policy. He returned to England in 1838, declined office for a decade, and published in 1842 the Lays of Ancient Rome, his most popular verse. The first two volumes of the History of England from the Accession of James the Second appeared in 1848 to extraordinary success, and he held office again as Secretary at War and then as Foreign Secretary in the Crimea ministry before failing to return to Parliament in 1856 and accepting a peerage as Baron Macaulay of Rothley. He died in London on 28 December 1859 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, leaving the History unfinished at the peace of Ryswick and a great body of posthumous essays, letters and diary.
authors.profile: His work is chiefly the review essay and the narrative history: the essays on English statesmen, poets and historians, collected from the Edinburgh and Foreign Reviews, which made a public philosophy of Whig progress, and the History of England, a continuous narrative of the reigns of James the Second and William the Third built out of parliamentary, memoir and newspaper sources. The Lays of Ancient Rome are ballad-like narrative poems rendered out of Roman history and designed to imitate the popular strain of ancient song, and his occasional verse, translations and schoolboy romances belong to the same accomplished literary game. The posthumous Critical and Historical Works, edited with the famous Life and Letters by his younger sister, gathered the essays, stories, and speeches that had appeared separately.
authors.style: The most imitated English prose style of the mid-century: a rhetoric of parallelism, tricolon and balanced clauses, of emphatic negatives and self-answerings, of the abrupt short sentence after a long period, and of a confident enumeration of instances. The narrative movement is rapid and visual, the judgement always pronounced, the irony directed at opponents rather than at his own side, and the effect is oratorical, the essay being written as if from a parliamentary bench.
authors.concerns: The Whig account of the revolution settlement of 1688 as the source of modern liberty; the growth of wealth, of population and of letters under constitutional government; the relation of religious persecution to political power; the uses of literature as national instruction, and of English in the government of India; the character and limits of party; the place of great men and of measures in history; the confidence in improvement and its subsequent interrogation.
authors.significance: The History of England fixed for generations the popular English narrative of the seventeenth century and became one of the best-selling works of non-fiction of the century; his essays set the standard of the review article as a vehicle of political and literary argument, and the Lays supplied a schoolroom canon of narrative verse. As an educational legislator in India and as a parliamentarian of reform he influenced policy directly, and his confident Protestant Whiggery has been the chief target of the later revisionist histories it provoked.
authors.uncertainty: His Indian minutes and despatches are numerous and were published posthumously in edited form, and the extent of his responsibility for anonymous review and magazine matter before 1830 is not wholly settled. The account of his schoolboy writings and of the Cambridge years depends largely on family memoir and on his own recollections, and the editors of the Letters and Life made deliberate omissions.

authors.name: Thomas Campbell
authors.birthplace: Glasgow, in the house in the High Street of a merchant family which claimed Argyllshire descent
authors.nationality: Scottish, working within a British public; popular narrative and lyric verse of the war decades and of the Regency, and the Edinburgh-and-London publishing world that connected them
authors.identity: Poet, anthologist and literary manager: the Scottish contributor to the popular Romantic bestseller list, a maker of nationally remembered lyrics and metrical romances, the editor whose selections taught a century its own poetic history, and one of the promoters of the metropolitan university founded in the 1820s.
authors.biography: Campbell was born in Glasgow on 27 July 1777, the youngest of the eleven children of Alexander Campbell, a merchant whose fortunes were destroyed by the losses of the American war, and his childhood was shaped by a ruined family's shift to modest dependence in the west of Scotland. He was educated at school in Glasgow and for a time at the university there, was placed young in a counting house, and then earned his living as a private tutor, with a period of service in the Highlands, before he gave himself wholly to letters; a few schoolboy verses were printed before he was twenty. The Pleasures of Hope appeared in 1799, when its author was twenty-two, and made his reputation at once and at large; enlarged editions, with the shorter poems that were soon recited everywhere, followed through the next two decades. He removed to London in 1801, endured several years of pressing poverty, and then established himself as a professed man of letters by his pen, by his friendships with the leading writers of the day and by his management of his own publishing interests. Gertrude of Wyoming in 1809 made him the most widely read narrator of romantic verse before the vogue of the metrical tales of his senior friends, and his lyrics of the war years passed into ordinary recitation and into schoolbooks. His Specimens of the British Poets of 1819, a work of selection rather than of scholarship, gave him a second career as the period's popular historian of English verse, and he was at once a proprietor and conductor of one of the leading monthlies and the busiest of the poets in the London book trade. Later recognition came from several directions: government acknowledgement of his standing, wide subscription support for his collected verse, and a share, vigorously promoted in print and at public meetings, in the foundation of the metropolitan university. He was a friend and correspondent of the leading Scottish and English writers of his generation, a habitual visitor to the continent, and an unremitting worker for funds for distressed authors and their families; he died away from home, at Boulogne, on 15 June 1844, and was buried in Westminster Abbey among the poets, his funeral attended by friends and by foreign admirers of his poems of national liberty.
authors.profile: His work falls into four recognisable groups: the didactic and reflective poem in couplets, of which The Pleasures of Hope is the example; the metrical romance or tale, of which Gertrude of Wyoming is the most successful; the short patriotic, maritime and elegiac lyric intended for recitation and for the singing clubs; and the editorial and critical prose of the Specimens and its separately circulated biographical notices. He wrote steadily for magazines and annuals, conducted correspondence on literary business on a large scale, and left a considerable body of letters. Sustained ambition to a larger epic design was a permanent and unfulfilled part of his career, and his later volumes repeat and vary the situations of the earlier ones.
authors.style: An instinct for the line that can be heard, quoted and sung, worked out in common and short measure stanzas with marked refrains and an easy command of ballad movement; the inherited heroic couplet of the eighteenth-century didactic poem used with spirit in the longer argumentative work; Spenserian stanzas for romance, with an archaising dignity that reviewers debated; a plain, earnest and frequently rhetorical diction, relying on a single strong situation of pathos rather than on subtlety of thought, and much given to the sententious closing line that passes into proverb.
authors.concerns: Hope, moral progress and the education of the species; national liberty and the fate of small and injured peoples, Poland and Ireland among them; the claims of Scotland and its scenery within a British literature; domestic affection tested by violence and death; the transatlantic frontier and the fate of its first inhabitants thought in the sentimental vocabulary of the age; the formation of a national poetic canon and the material condition of the writer who lives by it.
authors.significance: He showed that the couplet didactic poem of the previous century could still be an immediate bestseller in the 1790s, and that a Scottish poet of the Romantic generation could reach the widest popular audience of all by combining revolutionary hope with domestic romance. Gertrude of Wyoming carried popular verse from border matter to American colonial subject and was reprinted across the United States, and his lyrics and songs long held a place in recitation, in the schoolbook and in the national memory of the war years. As editor of the Specimens he was for two generations the ordinary introduction to the earlier English and Scottish poets, and as a public worker he helped to make the writer's trade respectable and institutional. The subsequent eclipse of his reputation is itself a much-cited instance of Romantic canon formation and its later revisions.
authors.uncertainty: The family's claimed Argyllshire descent rests largely on the poet's own account and on the memoir made after his death; the dates of his university attendance and of his employment as clerk and as tutor are unevenly recorded; the year of his final settlement in London is variously given as 1800 or 1801; and the sums and dates of the subscription income and of official financial recognition differ between the biographies.

authors.name: Thomas Campion
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet, composer, and physician; the supreme English writer of the lute song, author of the airs and of the treatise on English metre Observations in the Art of English Poesy.
authors.biography: Born 12 February 1567 in London; educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, and took his medical degree at the University of Caen (1605), practising medicine in London. He published the Latin Poemata (1595), Observations in the Art of English Poesy (1602), the masque for Lord Hayes (1607), and above all the songbooks A Book of Airs (1601, with Philip Rosseter) and the Two, Third, and Fourth Books of Airs (c. 1613–17), for which he wrote both words and music. He died in London on 1 March 1620.
authors.profile: The one English poet-composer of the first rank: his airs — 'When to her lute Corinna sings', 'Rose-cheeked Laura', 'Never weather-beaten sail' — wed the Elizabethan lyric to the continental lute song with a musical economy unmatched in the language.
authors.style: Quantitative experiments in Latin and English; short-lined, song-like verse of classical restraint; an anti-rhyming polemic in the Observations belied by his own masterly rhymes.
authors.concerns: The union of music and poetry; classical prosody and the reform of English metre; the pleasures and deceits of love; moral and religious consolation.
authors.significance: The summit of the English lute-song tradition and a major figure in the history of English prosody; his airs remained in performance and shaped the lyric taste of the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of several poems between Campion and his collaborators (notably Rosseter) is partly editorial; the dates of the later songbooks are inferred.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Time, death, and immortality through verse

authors.name: Thomas Carew
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Cavalier lyric poet and courtier of Charles I's household; admired by his contemporaries as perhaps the finest of the Caroline wits, he combined Jonsonian polish with Donnean wit in short, intense love poems.
authors.biography: Born c. 1595 at West Wickham, Kent, educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple. After a dissolute youth and service abroad (in the household of the ambassador at The Hague, from which he was dismissed for 'scurrility'), he became a server-in-ordinary to Charles I and moved in the court literary circle. His elegy 'An Elegy upon the Death of the Dean of Paul's, Dr John Donne' (1633) is a key document of the metaphysical transition. His Coelum Britannicum (masque, 1634) and his Poems were published in 1640, shortly before his death in 1639/40.
authors.profile: The consummate Caroline court lyricist, whose poems fuse sensual elegance with intellectual wit in a manner Clarendon called the 'muses' most delicate son'.
authors.style: Polished, musical short lyrics; Donnean argument and conceit softened by Cavalier grace; sensuous wit; and a masterly control of the octosyllabic couplet.
authors.concerns: Love and desire; the pleasures and pains of courtship; poetry and immortality; the critique of Petrarchan convention; and courtly virtue.
authors.significance: Carew was ranked by contemporaries above most Cavalier poets; his synthesis of Donne and Jonson and his elegy on Donne make him central to understanding the metaphysical-to-Cavalier transition.
authors.uncertainty: Carew's birth and death dates are approximate and his life poorly documented; most of his poems were printed posthumously in 1640.

authors.name: Thomas Carlyle
authors.nationality: Scottish; Victorian prose, historiography and social criticism
authors.identity: Essayist, historian, translator and social prophet; the great Victorian prose stylist and the moralist against whom the age measured itself.
authors.biography: Born on 4 December 1795, son of a stonemason and Calvinist farmer; educated at Annan Academy and Edinburgh University, where he trained for the ministry and abandoned it. He translated Goethe's Wilhelm Meister (1824) and wrote the Life of Schiller (1825) before his marriage in 1826 to Jane Baillie Welsh, whose letters became one of the great documents of the age. Sartor Resartus appeared in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34, The French Revolution in 1837, Chartism in 1840, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History in 1841, Past and Present in 1843, Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches in 1845 and the History of Friedrich II of Prussia in six volumes (1858-65). He gave the lectures that made him famous in 1837-40, refused all honours including the offer of the laureateship, and after Jane's death in 1866 wrote little; he died in Chelsea on 5 February 1881.
authors.profile: Carlyle invented the Victorian prose of prophecy: a style built on capitalised abstractions, apostrophe, Hebraic parallelism, exclamation and a ferocious irony, which he used to indict utilitarianism, laissez-faire political economy, parliamentary talk and the 'cash nexus'. His method in history is to make a document speak — the French Revolution as a 'terrible purification', Cromwell's letters as the voice of a man of God — and his theory of the hero, stated in 1841, was the most influential Victorian account of history as the work of great men. He turned German idealism and Goethe's aesthetics into the common currency of English thought.
authors.style: Incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences; invented compounds and archaisms; abrupt transitions between the prophetic, the comic and the documentary; direct address to the reader and a self-dramatising narrator; the quotation of primary documents in extenso; the use of symbols (the clothes philosophy, the 'everlasting Yea').
authors.concerns: The spiritual condition of the age and the loss of faith; work, the gospel of labour and the dignity of the manual worker; hero-worship and the great man in history; the French Revolution as judgment; the 'cash nexus' and the failure of political economy; silence, sincerity and the contempt of talk; the state and the aristocracy of talent.
authors.significance: Carlyle was the most influential prose writer in Victorian Britain: his French Revolution changed the writing of history, On Heroes supplied the century's theory of leadership, Past and Present its critique of industrialism, and Sartor Resartus its spiritual autobiography. He shaped Ruskin, Arnold, Dickens (to whom he lent the French Revolution while Hard Times was being written), Froude, Kingsley, George Eliot's early criticism and the American Transcendentalists; the twentieth-century reaction against his authoritarianism has not diminished his formal influence on English prose.
authors.uncertainty: 9 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text. No work catalogued here carries a disputed, conjectural or shared attribution, and every one of them was published under the author's own name between 1836 and 1858.

authors.name: Thomas Chalmers
authors.nationality: Scottish; the Church of Scotland and Scottish moral philosophy, political economy and natural theology of the early nineteenth century
authors.identity: Presbyterian preacher, evangelist, political economist and professor of moral philosophy and then of theology; the most powerful Scottish religious orator of his generation and the leader of the party that formed the Free Church of Scotland in 1843.
authors.biography: Chalmers was born at Anstruther in Fife on 17 March 1780, the sixth of the fourteen children of a shipowner and general merchant, and was put to the parish school before entering the University of St Andrews at about twelve years of age. He graduated M.A. in 1797, was licensed to preach by the clergymen of the neighbouring parishes, and served as a colleague minister at Anstruther and then at Kelvin near Glasgow, where his mathematical and astronomical abilities were already known. The years 1811-12 brought a conversion from the easy deism of his early reading to an evangelical Trinitarianism, and in 1815 he was translated to the large Trinity Church parish in Glasgow, where he threw himself into the religious and social government of a manufacturing population. There he carried out the district scheme of visiting, schooling, savings banks and poor-law administration that he reported in the discourses on the Christian and civic economy of large towns, and there also he argued, in the controversy over slavery, for immediate improvement rather than for the measures the abolitionist societies demanded, a position later used against him. He became professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow in 1823, published the first Bridgewater Treatise on the design of the inanimate world, and in the same year moved to St John's, West Edinburgh, where his preaching drew audiences far beyond the congregation. He was translated to the chair of theology at Edinburgh in 1828, took a leading part in the Ten Years' Conflict over spiritual independence and patronage, and after the Disruption of 1843 was the first moderator of the Free Church of Scotland, dying at Edinburgh on 31 May 1847 while still organising colleges, churches and missions for the new body.
authors.profile: His works divide between the sermon and the discourse, the argumentative treatise and the piece of applied social enquiry. The Bridgewater Treatise of 1823 restates the design argument from the inorganic creation for an age of expanding physical science, and the discourses on the Christian and civic economy of large towns of 1821 apply the same method to the city, arguing that a church without territorial organisation cannot govern or relieve a population that has no local ties. He wrote also astronomical and mathematical papers, articles on political economy and on the colonies for the Encyclopaedia Britannica and the Edinburgh Encyclopaedia, in which he handled the Malthusian and Ricardoian doctrines as a moralist, and a great body of popular religious and missionary tracts, sermons and letters.
authors.style: A spoken and periodic style of great command, in which the argument is built up in balanced clauses, in the cumulative arrangement of instances and in an appeal to the imagination of the reader; the printed sermon retains the rhetorical accent, the direct address and the long swell of the pulpit. In the economic and theological treatises the manner becomes cooler, more definitional and more scholastic, and in the tracts it is homely, concrete and full of named cases from the district.
authors.concerns: The evidence of design in the inanimate creation and its relation to the advances of physical science; the moral government of great towns, the failure of centralised administration, and the district as the unit of church, school and relief; the adequacy of the voluntary and established systems for a manufacturing population; the duties of the state toward religion and education; the relation of political economy to morality and to Christian obligation; the claims of foreign missions and of colonial Protestantism.
authors.significance: He gave the natural-theology tradition of Paley its most ambitious nineteenth-century statement and made the Bridgewater series a landmark of the argument from design in a scientific age, and his district experiment in Glasgow supplied the model on which later Scottish and English territorial church and school administration was rebuilt. His writings on political economy carried the Malthusian and Ricardian debates into moral and religious argument for a wide audience, and his leadership of the Disruption made him the central figure of Victorian Scottish religious history.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given as Anstruther in most modern accounts and as Couper (Cowper) in some earlier biographies and archival calendars, the family having connections in both Fife towns; the day of his death is given as 30 or 31 May 1847. The extent of his responsibility for the anonymous and joint contributions in the Glasgow religious tract movement of his ministry is not fully established.

authors.name: Thomas Chatterton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and forger, the marvellous boy, whose fabricated medieval Rowley poems and tragic early death made him a Romantic legend.
authors.biography: Chatterton was born in Bristol into a poor musical family and, as a boy connected with the church of St Mary Redcliffe, he discovered old manuscript documents he claimed were the work of a fifteenth-century monk, Thomas Rowley. From these he forged an entire pseudo-antique body of verse in a convincing archaic diction. He moved to London in 1770 to seek patronage and made a precarious living as a reporter and hack, also writing learned essays and poetry. Neglected and despairing, he died in London in 1770 by arsenic poisoning, aged seventeen. His story and the Rowley poems were taken up by Horace Walpole and later by the Romantics.
authors.profile: A poet of astonishing early gift who invented a medieval voice and persona; the Rowley pieces mix archaic pastiche with genuine lyric feeling, and his own later verse anticipates the grave and melancholy modes.
authors.style: Ingenious Rowley archaism of invented Middle-English diction; ballad and hymn measures; and in his modern verse a meditative, often melancholy descriptive and personifying style.
authors.concerns: The authenticity and romance of the literary past; imitation and forgery; the neglected genius and the cruelty of patronage; mortality and despair; and national poetic origins.
authors.significance: The Rowley forgeries stimulated the antiquarian revival of old English poetry and helped shape the Romantic cult of the doomed child-genius; his legend, told by Wordsworth, Keats, and others, became a literary myth.
authors.uncertainty: The circumstances and even the date of his death by suicide are partly legendary; the exact nature of the parish documents behind the Rowley forgeries is known chiefly from Chatterton's own unreliable accounts.

authors.name: Thomas Chestre
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: romance poet; translator
authors.biography: A late fourteenth-century English poet known only from his works, which name him 'Thomas Chestre' in their final lines; he flourished c. 1380–1400. Nothing else is recorded of his life.
authors.profile: Author of Sir Launfal (an English adaptation of Marie de France's Lanval), the romance Libeaus Desconus (from Renaud de Beaujeu's Le Bel Inconnu), and the romance Octavian; some scholarship also attributes The Isle of Ladies to him.
authors.style: Energetic tail-rhyme stanzas; brisk narrative compression of French sources; a fondness for the supernatural generosity of fairy mistresses and the rewards of loyalty.
authors.concerns: The adaptation of French courtly romance for English popular audiences; the claims of loyalty, love, and largesse.
authors.significance: A representative figure of the late Middle English tail-rhyme romance; his Sir Launfal is the fullest English treatment of the Lanval story and a staple of the Breton lay tradition in England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates and circumstances wholly unknown; the attributions rest on the poems' self-naming.

authors.name: Thomas Clarkson
altNames: The founder of the abolition committee
authors.nationality: English; the abolitionist movement and its literature, and the reform writing of the Atlantic world
authors.identity: Scholar, investigator, organiser and historian of the abolition movement; the man who turned a college essay question into a quarter-century of evidence-gathering, travel and publication, and who wrote the movement's first and greatest documentary history.
authors.biography: Clarkson was born at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire on 28 March 1760, the son of the headmaster of the free grammar school of the town, a clergyman who died while Thomas was still a child, and he was brought up in a family of some letters and small means. He went to St John's College, Cambridge, took his degrees, won the university's Latin prize in 1785 for an essay on the slavery and commerce of the human species, and found in the reading of that essay the conviction that fixed his life. He removed to London, where the Latin essay, translated and published in 1786, brought him into acquaintance with the Quaker friends of the cause and with Granville Sharp, and in 1787 he was a founding member of the committee of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. For the next twenty years he made the movement's evidence: he travelled some thirty-five thousand miles to the seaports and the great trading towns, collected the ships' papers, the cargoes, the surgeons' depositions and the testimony of sailors and of the enslaved themselves, drew up the plans and the sections of a slave ship which became the movement's most famous image, and wrote the pamphlets, the summaries and the appeals that carried the case to the counties and to Parliament. He was the chief labourer of a campaign in which others spoke in the House, and he saw the abolition of the trade carried in 1807. He settled in 1816 at Playford in Suffolk, where he passed his last years in retired literary, religious and agricultural work; the great History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade by the British Parliament appeared in 1808, followed later by a portrait of the system of colonial slavery and by tracts on moral and religious improvement; his own life, begun for publication, was finished after his death by his daughter. He died at Playford on 26 September 1846, the last survivor of the founding committee, and was buried in the churchyard there, with a commemoration in Westminster Abbey raised by the subscribers of the cause.
authors.profile: His writings form a deliberate literature of evidence and of argument: the Latin dissertation and its English translation state the moral and classical case against slavery; the Essay on the Slave Trade, the Summary View and the addresses to the people of England, to the legislators and to the merchants press the argument by fact; the History of 1808, in two volumes, is at once a personal narrative of the agitation, a documentary record of the trade and an argumentative history of a quarter-century of public work. He wrote also on the African commerce and the colonies, on the condition of the enslaved in the colonies, on rural economy and on his own parish, and his letters and his unfinished autobiography belong to the same body of reform life-writing.
authors.style: A plain, earnest and cumulative prose of enquiry, in which the argument is carried by enumeration, by the deposition and by the specification of fact rather than by rhetoric, and by a persistent moral address to the reader's humanity; the long sentence of the eighteenth-century argumentative style, with little ornament and a frequent appeal to scripture, to law and to common observation. In the History the manner becomes at once judicial and personal, the investigator's record interwoven with the narrative of his own journeys and labour.
authors.concerns: The evidence for the cruelty and the waste of the trade, and the duty of enquiry and of publication; the relation of testimony, document and image to moral argument; the obligations of the Christian and commercial nation to its own conduct; the education and the improvement of the labouring poor and of the African; the claims of humanity toward animals and toward the colonised; the history and the morality of a successful agitation, and the example it offers to future reform.
authors.significance: He made the British abolition movement into an organised public enquiry, and the evidence he gathered, the plans he caused to be drawn and the pamphlets he wrote gave the cause the documents on which its parliamentary success depended; the act of 1807 was in great part the result of his labour. His History of 1808 is the foundational documentary history of the movement and one of the largest works of argumentative prose in the reform literature of the period, and his method of accumulated testimony became the model on which later agitations, American as well as British, were conducted.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his collections and of the priority of the several plans, images and depots of evidence used by the society are difficult to disentangle, since the committee's papers and its published accounts do not always mark authorship; the date and place of his retirement residence are given variously before his settlement at Playford, and the text of his autobiography, begun by himself and completed and edited after his death by his daughter, cannot be wholly separated from her hand.

authors.name: Thomas Cranmer
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: archbishop of Canterbury; liturgist; theologian; martyr
authors.biography: Born at Aslockton on 2 July 1489; fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge. His suggestion that the universities should judge the validity of Henry VIII's marriage brought him to the king's notice; he became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1533 and presided over the annulment, the royal supremacy, and the dissolution. Under Edward VI he produced the two Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552), the Book of Homilies (1547), and the Forty-Two Articles (1553). Under Mary he was tried, degraded, and — after recanting and then withdrawing his recantations — burned at Oxford on 21 March 1556, thrusting the hand that had signed the recantations first into the fire.
authors.profile: The architect of the English liturgy. The Book of Common Prayer is his monument: collects, services, and the prose of worship that fixed the devotional language of English for four centuries ('ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). He was the principal author of the first Book of Homilies (1547) and of the doctrinal statement of the Edwardian church.
authors.style: Ritual prose of unmatched gravity and compression: parallel phrasing, scriptural cadence, and the direct address of congregation by priest; a style built for the voice.
authors.concerns: Worship in the vernacular; the simplification of the liturgy on scriptural principles; royal supremacy and the reform of doctrine; the unity of the English church.
authors.significance: Author of the defining text of Anglican worship, still in daily use; the Prayer Book's prose ranks with Tyndale's Bible as the foundation of modern English devotional language.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the division of authorship within the 1547 Homilies is partly editorial.

authors.name: Thomas Crofton Croker
authors.birthplace: Buckingham Square, Cork, Ireland, born on 15 January 1798, the only son of Major Thomas Croker; he was bound apprentice to merchants in Cork and Lisbon before removing to London, where his official and literary life was passed
authors.nationality: Irish; the antiquarian folk-collecting strand of Irish Romanticism, which gathered fairy legends, keens and popular song from the south of Ireland and set them beside the metrical romance and the national tale; an Irish writer working in the London book and periodical trade
authors.identity: Antiquary and folklorist, collector and editor of Irish fairy legends, songs and traditions; the first substantial English-language collector of southern Irish folk narrative, and a London clerk of letters
authors.biography: Thomas Crofton Croker was born in Cork on 15 January 1798, the only son of Major Thomas Croker, and was apprenticed to merchants in Cork and Lisbon before settling in London, where from about 1818 until his retirement in February 1850 he was a clerk in the Admiralty, augmenting a modest salary with literary work and serving from 1837 as registrar of the Royal Literary Fund. His rambles through the south of Ireland between 1812 and 1816 had yielded folk songs, keens and fairy traditions, and a collection of orally transmitted poems brought him in 1818 into touch with Thomas Moore. Researches in the South of Ireland (1824) laid this spoil before the public, and the Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, beginning in 1825 with later series to 1828, made his name; it went out with no author's name on the title page, because Croker had lost his originals and let passages be rewritten by friends, among them William Maginn. Legends of the Lakes, or Sayings and Doings at Killarney (1829), illustrated by William Maclise, followed, and The Popular Songs of Ireland (1839) gathered his life's collecting. On 30 March 1830 he married at Barnes, Surrey, Marianne Nicholson, only daughter of the watercolour painter Francis Nicholson (1792-1854); their only son, Thomas Francis Dillon Croker, born 26 August 1831, became an antiquary and edited his father's papers. Croker died at Old Brompton, London, on 8 August 1854, and his wife survived him only a short time.
authors.profile: His books are collections rather than compositions, and their art is that of the frame, the selection and the note. Researches in the South of Ireland (1824) mixes topographical narrative, legend and translated verse from the southern counties; the Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland (series of the later 1820s, reissued in new editions with illustrations, one of them dated 1844) gathers the fairy and ghost tale of Cork and Kerry, its best-known piece the Legend of O'Donoghue of the Killarney lakes, and its later arrangements class the Irish folk beings as sheerie, cluricaune, banshee, phouka, merrow, dullahan and fir darrig; Legends of the Lakes, or Sayings and Doings at Killarney (1829) applies the same method to lake legend with Maclise's designs; and The Popular Songs of Ireland (1839), with its companion treatment of the keen, prints the airs and verses he had transcribed since 1812. The Dictionary of National Biography also lists an early piece called 'The Talisman' (1820) among his works, and his son reported that other books, among them 'The Adventures of Barney Mahoney', belonged to other hands.
authors.style: His prose is that of the conversational antiquary: brisk, garrulous and first-person, framing each tale as something heard from a named narrator at a named place, then annotating it with parallels from other European collections. The retellings are deliberately comic and vernacular, softening what the tradition gives bluntly, and that humour is the ground on which Yeats afterwards reproached him for sentimentalising Irish tale-telling. Scholarship travels in the notes and appended songs rather than in argument, and he prints the keens and laments as seriously as the fairy romance. His manner belongs to the Scottish popular-antiquarian vogue of the post-Waverley decade and to the song-editing practice of Moore's Irish Melodies, both of which he knew at first hand.
authors.concerns: Whether Ireland possessed a vernacular mythology worth recovering before it disappeared under the pressures of the 1820s and the famine years that followed; the relation of Irish folk narrative to the German, Scandinavian and Celtic corpora, with which his work was compared and into whose circulation it passed; the evidential value of legend, place-name and song for history and topography; the authenticity of a retelling, made a live question by his own unsigned and collaboratively rewritten title pages; and the antiquary's civic loyalties, where official record work, patronage and the Royal Literary Fund meet.
authors.significance: He created the first permanent repertory of Irish folk narrative in English, and the Fairy Legends made that repertory part of European Romantic folklore: the book was praised by Sir Walter Scott, was translated into German in the later 1820s and entered the orbit of the Brothers Grimm, whose own influence on Irish collecting his case exemplifies. His songs, keens and legends were a storehouse for writers of the Irish literary revival, which used them even while W. B. Yeats blamed him for humourising the tales; his son's editions and the learned societies he joined kept his record work in use. As an instance of the anonymous, collaborative and partly rewoven condition of early folk collecting, his texts are now standard evidence in the history of folklore studies.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of the Fairy Legends is unsettled - the Dictionary of National Biography gives 1825, 1827 and 1834 for the successive issues while modern accounts speak of three series from 1825 to 1828, and the year of the German translation is given as 1826 by the Dictionary of Irish Biography and variously elsewhere. Authorship is disputed at several points: the first series went out anonymously because Croker had lost his manuscripts and let Maginn and other friends rewrite parts; 'The Adventures of Barney Mahoney' is dated 1832 by Ricorso and 1852 by the Dictionary of National Biography, and Ricorso and his son's testimony would give it to his wife Marianne Nicholson Croker; and 'The Talisman' (1820) rests on the Dictionary of National Biography alone. His mother's name and fortunes, and the share in his collections of Richard Sainthill and of the manuscripts of R. Adolphus Lynch, are variously reported. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty: Scott's praise and Moore's acquaintance are relations of reception and friendship, not documented influence.

authors.name: Thomas De Quincey
authors.nationality: English; the confessional and analytical prose of the later Romantic period
authors.identity: Essayist, confessor and magazine writer, the most deliberate artist of prose rhythm among the Romantics and the first English writer to make the opium habit and the divided mind the sustained subject of a book.
authors.biography: De Quincey was born at Manchester, the son of a merchant, and was educated at Manchester Grammar School, at boarding schools near London and at Bristol Grammar School. A rebellious adolescence took him away from his guardians and, by his own later account, into a period of wandering and destitution; he entered the University of Oxford in 1803 and left without a degree. Reading the poetry of the day led him to the Lake District, where in the years after 1808 he lived near the poets he admired, at one time in the cottage their family had quitted, and where he began the habit of opium that he described as governing his life. He settled in London as a contributor to the magazines, and his narrative of an opium eater, printed in a metropolitan periodical in 1821 and in book form the following year, made his name. From the middle of the decade he was a steady contributor to a leading Edinburgh magazine, publishing essays on literature, on German writing, on logic, on postage and on murder as a subject of taste, together with a long autobiographical sequel and a narrative of the mail-coach mail service. His later years were spent largely in Scotland, and he died at Edinburgh in December 1859, shortly after a fire at his lodgings had destroyed his papers and the stores of opium that had long been in his keeping.
authors.profile: His proper field is prose of a highly elaborated kind: the autobiographical confession and its sequel, the literary and political essay, the tale of murder and its parody of forensic reasoning, and a large body of periodical writing on books, on German literature and on the questions of the day. He published no volume of poetry and planned a vast history of literature and a learned dictionary that were never executed; his output was chiefly written for magazines and collected, often revised and often incompletely, after publication. His characteristic manner is the digressive essay that returns upon itself, with a passionate elaboration of the periodic sentence and a fondness for the nightmare image.
authors.style: Prose built on long cadenced periods, balanced clauses, repeated keywords and sudden shifts from the ironic to the terrible, self-consciously modelled on the rhythms of Latin and English biblical prose; a irony that is carried by elaborate courtesy of tone; and a imagery of dreams, palaces, seas and pursuers that he himself discussed as the rhetoric of the opium vision.
authors.concerns: The divided and self-observing mind under stimulation; guilt, pursuit and the logic of crime as a pleasure of the intellect; literature as a power of expansion rather than of instruction; the machinery of the mind as studied by the metaphysicians; the social economy of letters and the condition of the magazine writer; the sublime and the pathetic as the two modes of great writing.
authors.significance: He created the modern literary confession of addiction and the literature of dream psychology, and his analytic tale of murder invented a form that the detective story later inherited; his essays on prose style, on the literature of knowledge and on the laws of rhetorical composition were among the most influential statements of the nineteenth century, and through them his work reaches the symbolists and the twentieth-century prose imaginations.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology and quantity of his opium use rest almost entirely on his own statements, which he allowed to be rhetorical; the dates and incidents of his wanderings in Wales as a boy, and of his first residence in the Lake District, cannot be verified independently and are differently reported in the biographies.

authors.name: Thomas Dekker
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist; pamphleteer
authors.biography: Born in London about 1572, probably of Dutch descent. He began writing for Henslowe's companies in 1598 and was imprisoned for debt in the Poultry Counter (1598–99). He collaborated with nearly every dramatist of the age — Jonson, Marston, Webster, Middleton, Ford, Massinger — and wrote some of the period's most vivid plague pamphlets. He died on 25 August 1632, still in debt.
authors.profile: Plays include The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), Old Fortunatus (1599), Satiromastix (1601, with Marston, in the war of the theatres against Jonson), The Honest Whore (1604–05, with Middleton), and The Witch of Edmonton (1621, with Ford and Rowley); prose includes The Wonderful Year (1603) and The Gull's Hornbook (1609).
authors.style: Warmth, sentiment, and a Londoner's ear for the trades and cries of the city; his best scenes have a lyrical realism unmatched by his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The dignity of citizens and craftsmen; plague and providence; the cheerful endurance of poverty.
authors.significance: The great celebrant of London's citizens; The Shoemaker's Holiday remains the most performed city comedy of its generation, and his pamphlets are major documents of urban life.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; little is known of his family and education.

authors.name: Thomas Deloney
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: balladeer; prose fiction writer; silk weaver
authors.biography: A silk weaver by trade, probably born in Norwich about 1560. He became the most popular ballad-maker of his generation; several of his broadsides offended the authorities, and he was briefly in trouble over a ballad on the scarcity of grain in 1596. He died in 1600, apparently in poverty, leaving the fiction on which his later fame rests.
authors.profile: The prose narratives Jack of Newbury (1597), The Gentle Craft (c. 1597–98), and Thomas of Reading (c. 1600), which turned the lives of English craftsmen and merchants into popular fiction, together with hundreds of ballads of which a handful survive.
authors.style: Plain, vigorous, humorous prose full of proverbs, workman's lore, and the speech of shop and street; a bourgeois realism new to English fiction.
authors.concerns: The dignity and prosperity of trade; the pleasures of the middling sort; charity, industry, and honest dealing.
authors.significance: The first English novelist of the working people; his fictions reached a readership far below the court and founded the tradition of popular prose romance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate; his surviving ballad canon is a fraction of a much larger lost output.

authors.name: Thomas Fuller
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Anglican clergyman, historian, and wit; author of The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), a compendium of characters and maxims, and The History of the Worthies of England (1662), a pioneering biographical-topographical survey written in an energetic, proverbial style.
authors.biography: Born 1608 at Aldwincle, Northamptonshire (the same parish as Dryden); a prodigy educated at Queens' College, Cambridge (BA 1624/25) and Sidney Sussex College. He held various livings, served as a royalist chaplain during the Civil Wars, and was known for his preaching, memory, and wit. His major works include The Holy State (1642), Good Thoughts in Bad Times (1645), The Church-History of Britain (1655), and the posthumous Worthies of England (1662). A moderate during the Interregnum, he was restored at the Restoration and died on 16 August 1661 in London.
authors.profile: The learned, witty compiler and historian whose pithy, proverbial, digressive style and love of anecdotes and characters made him one of the most readable prose writers of the century.
authors.style: Terse, epigrammatic, proverbial prose; the 'character' sketch; abundant anecdote, pun, and quotation; a genial, learned wit; and a digressive, associative method.
authors.concerns: Moral and religious instruction; English history, biography, and topography; the virtues of the 'holy state' and the vices of the 'profane'; wit and wisdom; and moderation in the church.
authors.significance: Fuller's Worthies is a foundational work of English local history and biography, and his Church-History a pioneering ecclesiastical history; his prose style, full of quotable maxims, was widely admired and influential.
authors.uncertainty: Fuller's life is documented; the accuracy of some of his historical and biographical anecdotes was questioned even in his day and he himself admitted a love of a good story.

authors.name: Thomas Gray
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and scholar, Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is among the most quoted poems in the language.
authors.biography: Gray was born in London and educated at Eton and at Peterhouse, Cambridge, where he later returned as a scholar and, from 1768, held the Professorship of Modern History. A careful, slow writer of small output, he published little in his lifetime, including the Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College and the Hymn to Adversity. His finest Pindaric odes, The Progress of Poesy and The Bard, appeared in 1757. His Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) brought him fame. He declined the laureateship and lived a studious, largely private life, close to a circle that included Horace Walpole. He died at Cambridge in 1771.
authors.profile: A poet of the graveyard, the meditative ode, and antiquarian romance; he combined neoclassical polish with a new interest in melancholy, the common dead, and the music and history of earlier English and Welsh verse.
authors.style: Exquisite diction and sonorous, Latinate word order; a restrained, melancholy dignity; Pindaric and Norse-influenced ode experiments; and an antiquarian taste for the ballad and the picturesque.
authors.concerns: Unfulfilled potential and the fate of obscure lives; death, memory, and the moral lesson of the grave; the history and progress of poetry; and the aesthetics of melancholy and the sublime.
authors.significance: The Elegy became the landmark of the graveyard school and a touchstone of sensibility, while his odes and editorial interests in old poetry helped open the way to Romantic and antiquarian taste.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1716, but some records support 1717; the dating of the Elegy's composition, long associated with the churchyard at Stoke Poges, is debated.

authors.name: Thomas Hardy
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian and Edwardian novel and poetry
authors.identity: Novelist and poet; the last great Victorian novelist and one of the most important English poets of the twentieth century.
authors.biography: Born on 2 June 1840 at Higher Bockhampton, Dorset, son of a builder and stonemason; he was apprenticed to an architect in Dorchester at sixteen and worked in London as an architect's assistant from 1862 to 1867, when ill health returned him to Dorset. Desperate Remedies (1871) began his career; Under the Greenwood Tree (1872), A Pair of Blue Eyes (1873) and Far from the Madding Crowd (1874) established him, and Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895) made him notorious, the latter's reception causing him to abandon fiction for poetry. He married Emma Lavinia Gifford in 1874, and after her death in 1912 made the pilgrimage that produced the 1912-13 poems; he married Florence Dugdale in 1914 and received the Order of Merit in 1910. He died at Max Gate, Dorchester, on 11 January 1928; his heart was buried at Stinsford and his ashes in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: Hardy's novels are set in 'Wessex', a mapped region of the English southwest, and their action is governed by an indifferent universe, by the accidents of time and place, and by the social codes of the rural and small-town world. His method is scenic and ironic: he stages the crucial moments as tableaux, describes landscape and weather with the eye of a painter and the knowledge of a countryman, and observes his characters from a distance that is compassionate and judicial at once. After 1895 he wrote poetry almost exclusively, and the poems — tight, metrically formal, elegiac, often bleak, sometimes bitterly ironic — are among the greatest of the twentieth century, and the 1912-13 poems on his first wife are the central English sequence of grief after In Memoriam.
authors.style: Regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs; the vivid static scene and the dramatic tableau; a narrator's commentary that is ironic and philosophical; chance, coincidence and mis-timed communication as plot machinery; a formal, often archaic diction in the verse; a poetic line that holds tension between the formal measure and the plain statement.
authors.concerns: Fate, chance and the indifference of nature; the decline of the rural community; the position of women within marriage and at law; class, ambition and education; desire and its prohibitions; memory and mourning; religion in decline and the persistence of its rituals; the old village and the modern world.
authors.significance: Hardy is the last of the great Victorian novelists and the first great modern English poet of the rural world: Tess and Jude carried Victorian fiction to the edge of the permissible and made him the crucial English novelist of tragedy, and the poems shaped the twentieth-century poetry of landscape, memory and unbelief (Auden, Larkin, Hill all acknowledge him). His Wessex maps made a literary region a permanent imaginative possession, and his influence on the English novel of place is unmatched.
authors.uncertainty: 2 of the 9 works catalogued here carry a research status of 'partial' - Jude the Obscure; Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented - and are reported only so far as the evidence allows. 18 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text.

authors.name: Thomas Heywood
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: dramatist; poet; prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Lincolnshire about 1573; studied at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He was acting and writing for Henslowe's companies by 1598 and claimed to have had 'an entire hand, or at least a main finger' in 220 plays. He wrote pageants, translations, and compendious works of history and mythology, and died in Clerkenwell on 16 August 1641, one of the last survivors of the great Jacobean generation.
authors.profile: A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603), the domestic tragedy The English Traveller (c. 1627), the four-part Ages cycle (1611–32), The Fair Maid of the West (c. 1600), and the prose An Apology for Actors (1612), the period's chief defence of the stage.
authors.style: Plain, humane, middle-style verse; domestic settings; moral plots of patience and repentance that avoid the lurid excesses of his rivals.
authors.concerns: The dignity of the ordinary household; marital betrayal and forgiveness; the moral legitimacy of the theatre.
authors.significance: His domestic tragedy founded a genre that runs through Lillo to Ibsen; An Apology for Actors is the classic defence of the English stage.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the vast collaborative canon makes his exact share in many plays uncertain.

authors.name: Thomas Hobbes
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of Leviathan (1649), the founding text of modern political philosophy, whose materialist, mechanistic system and prose of austere clarity transformed English thought and letters.
authors.biography: Born 5 April 1588 at Westport, Wiltshire (the year of the Armada — 'fear and I were born twins', he joked); educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served for decades as tutor and secretary to the Cavendish family (Earls of Devonshire), travelling Europe and meeting Mersenne, Gassendi, Descartes, and Galileo. Alarmed by the political crisis, he went into exile in Paris (1640–51), publishing De Cive (1642) and, in 1651, Leviathan, whose defence of absolute sovereignty and its Erastianism offended both royalists and Parliamentarians. He returned to England, was distrusted by the restored court, and, after the Clarendon attack and the 1666 parliamentary scrutiny of 'atheism', published little more political philosophy. His later works include Behemoth (1668–70) and an autobiography in verse. He died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick.
authors.profile: The philosopher who derived the state from a contract among self-interested individuals in a 'war of every man against every man', and who wrote with a logical, powerful, and lucid prose that made philosophy English literature.
authors.style: Rigorous, deductive argument; a clear, forceful, sometimes ironic prose; striking metaphors (the state as 'Leviathan', life as 'nasty, brutish, and short'); and a materialist, mechanistic vocabulary.
authors.concerns: Sovereignty, the social contract, and the state of nature; materialism and mechanism; human nature, appetite, and reason; religion and its political control; and the philosophy of language and knowledge.
authors.significance: Leviathan founded modern political philosophy and social contract theory, profoundly influencing Locke, Rousseau, and all subsequent thought; Hobbes's materialism and prose style also made him a central, if feared, figure in English intellectual and literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Hobbes's life is well documented (including his own prose and verse autobiographies and Aubrey's Life); the sincerity of his religious professions remains debated.

authors.name: Thomas Hoccleve
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: poet; clerk
authors.biography: A clerk of the Privy Seal office in Westminster from c. 1387 for some thirty-five years, he knew Chaucer personally and called himself his disciple; his poems — above all the autobiographical passages of the Series — record his anxiety, his 'maladie' of 1416, and the precarious life of a married office-holder. He died in 1426.
authors.profile: Author of the Regiment of Princes (1411), the classic English mirror-for-princes addressed to the future Henry V; the Series (c. 1419–21), a linked set of tales and complaints containing the first English poetic autobiography; and shorter poems including the Male Regle.
authors.style: Correct Chaucerian verse with a plain, personal voice; rueful self-portraiture; the adaptation of courtly and didactic forms to the experience of bureaucracy and illness.
authors.concerns: Good governance and the duties of princes; poverty, patronage, and the ethics of office; his own mental suffering and its consolation.
authors.significance: The first English poet to write extensively about his own life and illness; the Regiment is a principal document of Lancastrian political literature and of the Chaucerian inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the cause of his 1416 'maladie' remains debated.
movements: Fifteenth-Century Chaucerians
