authors.name: Virginia Woolf
authors.nationality: British; the novel of consciousness, the modernist essay and the feminist polemic
authors.identity: Novelist, essayist and publisher; the central English modernist prose writer, the theorist of the novel of consciousness, and the author of A Room of One's Own.
authors.biography: Born Adeline Virginia Stephen in London on 25 January 1882, the daughter of Sir Leslie Stephen, the editor of the Dictionary of National Biography; she was educated at home in her father's library, suffered the first of her mental breakdowns after her mother's death in 1895, moved with her siblings to Bloomsbury after her father's death in 1904, married Leonard Woolf in 1912 and founded the Hogarth Press with him in 1917. The Voyage Out appeared in 1915, Jacob's Room in 1922, Mrs Dalloway in 1925, To the Lighthouse in 1927, Orlando in 1928 and The Waves in 1931. She drowned herself in the River Ouse at Rodmell on 28 March 1941.
authors.profile: Woolf remade the English novel as an instrument of consciousness: her lyric, luminous prose renders the flow of thought, the sudden 'moment of being', and the way a life is made of ordinary days. Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse are the central English modernist novels, The Waves its most radical experiment, Orlando its wittiest, and A Room of One's Own (1929) and Three Guineas (1938) are the founding texts of modern feminist criticism. As publisher, essayist and diarist she is the period's most complete literary intelligence.
authors.style: The lyric stream of consciousness and the interior monologue; free indirect style carried to the limit of dissolution; the recurrent image and the symbolic motif; the single day or the single house as a structure; the parenthesis and the semicolon; the essayistic, conversational critical voice.
authors.concerns: Time, memory, and the duration of consciousness; the woman artist and the conditions of women's work; the family and the Victorian father; war, shell shock and the post-war ruin; class and the servant; the ordinary mind on an ordinary day; the moment of vision and its loss.
authors.significance: Woolf is the greatest English prose writer of the period and the central figure of English modernism: Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and The Waves changed the form of the novel, A Room of One's Own founded modern feminist criticism, and the Hogarth Press made modernism publishable in England. She is the period's indispensable writer.

authors.name: W. B. Yeats
authors.nationality: Irish; the symbolist lyric, the verse play and the poetry of the national revival
authors.identity: Poet and dramatist; the founder of the Irish Literary Revival, the greatest poet in English of the period's first half, and the Nobel laureate of 1923.
authors.biography: Born William Butler Yeats in Sandymount, Dublin, on 13 June 1865, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats; he was brought up between Dublin, London and Sligo, studied painting and then poetry, founded the Irish Literary Society (1892) and the Abbey Theatre (1904) with Lady Gregory, and made his name with The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), The Wind Among the Reeds (1899) and The Green Helmet (1910). He married George Hyde-Lees in 1917, served as a Senator of the Irish Free State (1922–28), won the Nobel Prize in 1923, and died at Roquebrune in the south of France on 28 January 1939, reburied at Drumcliff in 1948.
authors.profile: Yeats is the greatest poet in English of the first half of the twentieth century. He began as a symbolist of the Celtic twilight, made the Abbey Theatre a national institution, and then remade his style three times — into the public, colloquial, bitter poetry of Responsibilities (1914) and The Wild Swans at Coole (1917), the mythic system of A Vision (1925) and the late, bare, terrifying poems of The Tower (1928) and Last Poems. He is the only poet of the period who is equally important as a lyric poet, a dramatist, a prose writer and a public figure.
authors.style: The symbolist image and the esoteric system; the rhymed stanza and the refrain refined into bareness; the antithetical rhetoric ('That is no country for old men'); the dramatic mask and the anti-self; the public poem in the grand manner; the prose of a great talker.
authors.concerns: Ireland, nationality, and the national question; the heroic past and the mythic cycle; love, the beloved and the ageing body; the occult, the séance, and the system of the gyres; violence, revolution, and the Easter Rising; age, death, and the fury of the old man.
authors.significance: Yeats is the central poet of the period and the founder of the Irish national literature: he created the Abbey Theatre, made Irish myth a modern poetic resource, and wrote the greatest body of lyric poetry in English in the twentieth century. His late poems are among the summit achievements of the language.

authors.name: W. E. Henley
authors.nationality: English; the hospital poem, the imperial ode and the editor's magazine
authors.identity: Poet, critic and editor; the author of 'Invictus' and the most influential literary editor of the 1890s.
authors.biography: Born William Ernest Henley in Gloucester on 23 August 1849, the son of a bookseller; tuberculosis of the bone led to the amputation of his leg in 1873-75 at the Edinburgh Infirmary, where he wrote the poems of In Hospital. He edited the Magazine of Art, the Scots Observer and the National Observer, discovered Kipling and was a friend of Stevenson, who modelled Long John Silver on him. He died in Woking on 11 July 1903.
authors.profile: Henley wrote the English poetry of endurance and of the imperial idea: 'Invictus' became one of the most quoted poems in the language, and the hospital poems of In Hospital are the first English poems to treat a patient's experience with clinical realism. As an editor he shaped the literature of the 1890s more than any other single figure, and his magazine published the early work of Kipling, Yeats and Wells.
authors.style: Short, hard, rhymed verse in the ballad and the song measure; the hospital poem of exact physical detail; the imperial ode with its rhetorical refrain; the critical essay that discovers and defines a new writer; the editorial anthology of the new movement.
authors.concerns: Illness, surgery and the body; courage, endurance and the unconquerable will; the sea, the hospital and the city; empire, the English race and the imperial destiny; friendship and the literary life; the new poetry of the 1890s.
authors.significance: Henley is the central English literary editor of the 1890s and the author of 'Invictus', one of the most quoted poems in the language: his National Observer was the nursery of the literature of the decade, In Hospital is a landmark of English poetry about illness, and his influence on Kipling, Yeats and the whole 'new poetry' was decisive.

authors.name: W. H. Auden
authors.nationality: British-American; the thirties public poem, the elegy and the poetry of the modern city
authors.identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the central English poet of the 1930s, the leader of the Auden generation, and one of the great public poets of the century.
authors.biography: Born Wystan Hugh Auden in York on 21 February 1907, the son of a physician; he read at Christ Church, Oxford, where his Poems (1928, privately printed by Spender) and Poems (1930) made him the leader of his generation. The Orators (1932), Look, Stranger! (1936), the plays with Isherwood (The Dog Beneath the Skin, 1935; The Ascent of F6, 1936; On the Frontier, 1938) and Journey to a War (1939) made him the voice of the decade; he emigrated to America in 1939, became an American citizen in 1946, and returned to Oxford as professor of poetry (1956–61). He died in Vienna on 29 September 1973.
authors.profile: Auden is the central English poet of the 1930s and one of the great poets of the century: he gave the decade its public voice — the clipped, journalistic line, the parable, the political fable — and then, in America, wrote the great religious and meditative poems ('In Memory of W. B. Yeats', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'September 1, 1939', the Christmas oratorio For the Time Being). His technical range — ballad, sonnet, sestina, haiku, libretto, light verse — is unmatched in modern English poetry.
authors.style: The clipped journalistic line with the flat technical vocabulary; the rhymed parable and the nursery-rhyme turned political; the catalogue of places and machines; the public elegy; the sudden turn from satire to tenderness; the colloquial idiom held in strict form.
authors.concerns: Totalitarianism and the coming war; class, the public school and the English ruling order; love, anxiety and the divided self; the modern city, the aeroplane and the machine; faith, the Church and the possibility of belief; history and the individual's place in it.
authors.significance: Auden is the central English poet of the period after Eliot: he gave the thirties its public voice, invented the political poem as a modern form, wrote the great elegies and meditations of the century, and his technical range made him the model for every English poet since. He is the period's most influential poet after Eliot and Yeats.

authors.name: W. H. Davies
authors.nationality: Welsh; the tramp poet of Leisure and the Georgian lyric
authors.identity: Poet and autobiographer; the super-tramp of the Georgian anthologies and of 'Leisure'.
authors.biography: Born William Henry Davies at Newport, Monmouthshire, on 3 July 1871; he lost a foot jumping a freight train in Ontario in 1899 and lived as a tramp and cattle-drover in Wales, England and North America until The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp (1908), with its introduction by George Bernard Shaw, made him a writer. The Georgian anthologies and 'Leisure' made him a household poet; he died at Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, on 26 September 1940.
authors.profile: W. H. Davies is the tramp poet of the Georgian lyric: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp is the classic English account of the road, and 'Leisure' - 'What is this life if, full of care, we have no time to stand and stare' - is one of the most quoted short poems in the language. His plain, unadorned lyric of the roadside and the hedge gave the Georgian anthology its voice from below.
authors.style: The plain short line and the plain word; the lyric of the roadside, the hedge and the open sky; the absence of the literary allusion and of the learned metaphor; the tramp's eye for weather, food and shelter; the quiet, unforced moral at the close of the lyric.
authors.concerns: The road and the life of the tramp; poverty, begging and the charity of the countryside; nature observed from the hedge rather than from the garden; the body's want and the sky's plenty; Wales and the Welsh border as the remembered home.
authors.significance: W. H. Davies is the tramp poet of the Georgian lyric: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp is the classic English account of the road, and 'Leisure' is among the most quoted short poems in the language, the voice of the roadside in the anthology of the garden.

authors.identity: Writer for boys; the most prolific author of naval and colonial adventure stories in the mid-Victorian period.
authors.biography: Born William Henry Giles Kingston in London on 28 February 1814; he spent some years in Portugal in the wine trade, and after the success of Peter the Whaler (1851) and The Three Midshipmen (1873) he devoted himself to writing for boys, producing well over a hundred books. authors.profile: Kingston was the most prolific writer of boys' sea stories in the mid-Victorian period and did more than anyone to establish the naval adventure as a genre: his midshipmen, his storms and his sea battles gave the boy reader the Navy as a moral institution and shaped the sea story that Marryat and Conrad both worked in.
authors.style: The voyage as the organising structure; the technical language of sail and seamanship; the storm and the sea battle; the moral improvement of the young officer; the patriotic digression and the improving address.
authors.concerns: The Navy and the empire; duty, discipline and the chain of command; the sea as a test of character; the contact with the colonial world; the Christian mission.
authors.significance: W. H. G. Kingston was the most prolific writer of boys' sea stories in the mid-Victorian period and the writer who made the naval adventure into a genre: his midshipmen and his sea battles gave the boy reader the Navy as a moral institution and shaped the sea story that Conrad inherited.

authors.name: W. H. Hudson
authors.nationality: Argentine-British; the nature romance, the travel narrative and the English rural chronicle
authors.identity: Writer and naturalist; the author of Green Mansions and the finest English prose writer on the South American pampas and the English countryside.
authors.biography: Born William Henry Hudson at Quilmes, near Buenos Aires, on 4 August 1841, to American parents of English descent; he grew up on the pampas, collected birds for the Smithsonian, and settled in England in 1874 in poverty and ill health. He published The Purple Land in 1885, The Naturalist in La Plata in 1892, Green Mansions in 1904, and the English country books Far Away and Long Ago (1918) and A Shepherd's Life (1910). He was granted a civil-list pension in 1900 and died in London on 18 August 1922.
authors.profile: Hudson wrote the romance of the natural world: Green Mansions is the great English novel of the tropical forest and its vanishing people, and his South American books are unmatched in their evocation of the pampas and the jungle. In England he became the finest writer of rural memory in the language: Far Away and Long Ago and A Shepherd's Life record a world of shepherds, birds and unmechanised labour with a tenderness and a precision that make them classics of English nature writing.
authors.style: Lyrical, unhurried descriptive prose; the remembered landscape rendered with an ornithologist's eye; the romance of the untouched natural world; the plain record of rural labour and speech; the elegy for a vanished England.
authors.concerns: Nature and the untouched world; the pampas and the tropical forest; the English countryside and its vanishing rural life; childhood and the natural world; the clash of civilisation and the wild; memory and the lost home.
authors.significance: Hudson is one of the greatest English writers of the natural world and Green Mansions is the central English romance of the tropical forest: his South American books created the English literary image of the pampas, his English rural books are classics of nature writing, and he is the finest prose stylist of the English countryside between Jefferies and Edward Thomas.

authors.name: W. S. Gilbert
authors.nationality: English; the comic opera, the burlesque and the comic verse
authors.identity: Dramatist and librettist; the author of the Savoy operas and one of the greatest comic writers in English.
authors.biography: Born William Schwenck Gilbert in London on 18 November 1836; he served as a militia officer, was called to the bar in 1864, and made his name with the Bab Ballads (1869) and the burlesques. His collaboration with Arthur Sullivan began with Thespis in 1871 and produced fourteen operas, from Trial by Jury (1875) to The Gondoliers (1889), staged by Richard D'Oyly Carte at the Savoy. He was knighted in 1907 and died at Grim's Dyke, Harrow, on 29 May 1911.
authors.profile: Gilbert wrote the English comic opera, and in doing so he wrote the English comic tradition of the late century: his librettos unite the topsy-turveydom of the burlesque with a satire of the professional and legal classes, and their verbal dexterity — the patter song, the logical absurdity, the inverted proverb — is unmatched. His early Bab Ballads are the finest comic verse of the period after Lear, and his stagecraft made the Savoy opera the most successful theatrical enterprise of the age.
authors.style: Inverted logic carried to absurdity; the patter song with accelerating syllable count; rhyming of impossible words; satire of the law, the army, the peerage and the aesthetic movement; the chorus of the conventional and the individual who defies it; comic verse with illustrations.
authors.concerns: The law, the state and the professions; class and the peerage; aestheticism and the 'greenery-yallery' pose; love, marriage and the war of the sexes; duty, duty and the parody of duty; the Englishman abroad and the satire of national character.
authors.significance: Gilbert is the greatest English librettist and one of the greatest comic writers in the language: the Savoy operas are the most successful theatrical works ever produced in Britain, they created a permanent repertory and a national comic idiom, and the Bab Ballads are a classic of English nonsense verse.

authors.name: W. Somerset Maugham
authors.nationality: British; the narrative craft and the colonial short story
authors.identity: Novelist, playwright and short-story writer; the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century and the master of the plain narrative.
authors.biography: Born William Somerset Maugham at the British embassy in Paris on 25 January 1874; orphaned young, he trained as a doctor at St Thomas's and drew on the slums for Liza of Lambeth (1897). Of Human Bondage (1915), The Moon and Sixpence (1919), the plays that made him rich in the 1900s, Cakes and Ale (1930), The Razor's Edge (1944) and the stories of The Trembling of a Leaf (1921) followed. He worked in intelligence in the First World War and died at Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat on 16 December 1965.
authors.profile: Maugham was the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century and the master of the plain narrative: Of Human Bondage gave the English novel its great study of obsession, The Moon and Sixpence and Cakes and Ale its satires of the artist, and the colonial stories of The Trembling of a Leaf created the modern short story of the tropics.
authors.style: The first-person narrator who listens rather than judges; the plain, unadorned, perfectly paced sentence; the story told at a club or on a verandah; the ironic ending withheld to the last line; the refusal of rhetoric and of experiment.
authors.concerns: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist; sexuality, the new psychology; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation.
authors.significance: Maugham was the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century: Of Human Bondage is the great English novel of obsession, Cakes and Ale the finest satire of the literary life, and the colonial stories of The Trembling of a Leaf created the modern short story of the tropics and made the plain narrative the dominant English prose style of the century.

authors.name: W. W. Jacobs
authors.nationality: English; the comic short story and the tale of terror
authors.identity: Short-story writer and dramatist; the author of 'The Monkey's Paw' and the finest English comic writer of the sea and the riverside.
authors.biography: Born William Wymark Jacobs in Wapping, London, on 8 September 1863, the son of a wharf manager; he worked as a clerk in the savings-bank department of the Post Office while writing stories of the London docks, and his first collection, Many Cargoes, appeared in 1896. He published over twenty collections and the play The Monkey's Paw (1907, with Louis N. Parker); he died in London on 1 September 1943.
authors.profile: Jacobs wrote the English comic short story at its most consummate: his tales of bargees, night watchmen, sailors and henpecked husbands are models of construction, with a twist at the end that is never merely mechanical, and his dialogue is the most exact rendering of London working-class speech in the period. 'The Monkey's Paw' is one of the most famous horror stories in English, and its cold economy shows the same technical mastery as the comedies.
authors.style: The tightly constructed story with a final turn; comic dialogue in London vernacular; the domestic interior of the riverside household; the unspoken and the withheld; the horror that is implied rather than shown; a narrative voice of complete deadpan calm.
authors.concerns: The sea, the docks and the riverside; marriage and the henpecked husband; poverty, luck and the small windfall; superstition and the supernatural; class and the working man's world; fear and the inexplicable.
authors.significance: Jacobs is the finest English comic short-story writer of his generation and the author of one of the most famous horror stories in the language: 'The Monkey's Paw' has been adapted, anthologised and imitated for a century, and his comic stories are the technical model for the English short story from Wodehouse to Saki.

authors.name: Wallace Stevens
authors.nationality: American; the philosophical lyric and the poetry of the imagination
authors.identity: Poet; the great American philosophical poet of the century, an insurance executive who wrote the most sumptuous and abstract verse of the period.
authors.biography: Born Wallace Stevens in Reading, Pennsylvania, on 2 October 1879; he studied at Harvard for three years and then at New York Law School, worked as a journalist and a lawyer, and joined the Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company in 1916, where he became vice-president in 1934 and remained until his death. Harmonium appeared in 1923, Ideas of Order in 1935, The Auroras of Autumn in 1950, and The Collected Poems in 1954; he won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award in 1955 and died in Hartford on 2 August 1955.
authors.profile: Stevens is the great American poet of the imagination: his poems ask, in the most sensuous language, what it means to make a world with the mind when the gods have gone. 'Sunday Morning', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'The Idea of Order at Key West' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' are the central texts of American philosophical poetry, and his late long poems are among the most ambitious in the language.
authors.style: The exotic and sumptuous vocabulary; the abstract argument carried by sensuous image; the blank verse paragraph and the unrhymed tercet; the single-colour image (blue, green, white) held until it becomes an idea; the aphorism and the late long poem.
authors.concerns: The imagination and reality; the death of God and the poetry that replaces religion; order, art and the made thing; the American landscape and the Florida sun; the body, desire and the weather; the ordinary and the supreme fiction.
authors.significance: Stevens is the central American philosophical poet of the century: Harmonium gave American poetry its most gorgeous surface, 'Sunday Morning' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' established the imagination as the period's great subject, and his Collected Poems won every honour the country has. He is the period's most influential American poet after Eliot.

authors.name: Walt Whitman
authors.birthplace: West Hills, Long Island, New York, United States
authors.nationality: American; the free-verse epic and the democratic lyric
authors.identity: Poet, journalist and essayist; the inventor of American free verse and the poet of American democracy.
authors.biography: Born at West Hills, Long Island, on 31 May 1819; he left school at eleven, worked as a printer's devil, a schoolmaster and a journalist, and edited the Brooklyn Eagle (1846-48) and the New Orleans Crescent (1848). He set the type for the first edition of Leaves of Grass himself in 1855; Emerson's letter of praise made him known. During the Civil War he nursed wounded soldiers in Washington hospitals, and after a stroke in 1873 he lived in Camden, New Jersey. He died there on 26 March 1892.
authors.profile: Whitman invented a poetry for the American continent: long unrhymed lines generated by the breath and by the catalogue, an inclusive vocabulary that admits the technical, the vulgar and the democratic, and a first-person speaker who is at once an individual body and a national 'I'. Leaves of Grass grew through nine editions in his lifetime and is the founding book of modern American poetry.
authors.style: Free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora; catalogue and inventory; the long breath-line; first-person address to the reader; colloquial and technical diction; the poem as a growing organism revised across a lifetime.
authors.concerns: Democracy, equality and 'the common man'; the body, sex and physical life; death and immortality; the Civil War and Lincoln; comradeship and the love of men; America as the future of the race; the poet as national voice.
authors.significance: Whitman is the founder of modern American poetry and one of the most influential poets in the world: Leaves of Grass changed the possibilities of verse in English, his Civil War poems are the finest written by an American, and his influence runs through Hopkins, Crane, Hart Crane, Neruda, Ginsberg and the Beat generation.

authors.name: Walter Bagehot
authors.nationality: English; Victorian political science, economics and criticism
authors.identity: Economist, political journalist and critic; the founder of the modern study of the English constitution and one of the finest Victorian essayists.
authors.biography: Born at Langport on 3 February 1826, son of a Unitarian banker; educated at Bristol and University College London, where he took a degree in mathematics. He read for the bar, joined his father's bank, and in 1857 became a partner and married Eliza Wilson, daughter of the founder of the Economist; from 1861 to his death he was the editor of the Economist, shaping it into the leading journal of liberal economics. The English Constitution (1867) is his masterpiece; Physics and Politics (1872) applied the new ideas of evolution to the development of nations, and Lombard Street (1873) is a classic account of the money market. He published Literary Studies (1879) and Economic Studies (1880) posthumously and died of pneumonia at Langport on 24 March 1877.
authors.profile: Bagehot's method is the description of an institution as it actually works rather than as it is described by its official theory. The English Constitution distinguishes the 'dignified' from the 'efficient' parts of the constitution — the monarchy and the Lords as the symbols that make the system acceptable, the cabinet as the real executive — and that distinction became the essential tool of political science. His style is the best of Victorian journalism: concrete, epigrammatic, faintly mocking, and capable of large generalisations resting on a single vivid case. He is also an acute literary critic who wrote on Shakespeare, Arnold, Tennyson and the Victorian novel.
authors.style: Epigram and paradox; the concrete example used to test a large proposition; the distinction of the nominal from the real; the ironic understatement; a domesticate vocabulary for technical subjects; the long essay as the vehicle of ideas.
authors.concerns: The working of representative government; the relation of the Crown, the Lords and the Commons; the psychology of a free people and of an hereditary monarchy; evolution and social progress; the money market and the crises of credit; character and literature.
authors.significance: The English Constitution is the founding work of modern political science in Britain, and its distinction between the 'dignified' and 'efficient' constitution is still the standard analysis of the British system. Lombard Street is the origin of the modern theory of central banking and the lender of last resort, and Physics and Politics introduced evolutionary theory into the study of nations.

authors.name: Walter de la Mare
authors.nationality: British; the ghost story, the children's poem and the lyric of the other world
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and short-story writer; the master of the English supernatural lyric and the finest writer of ghost stories of the period after M. R. James.
authors.biography: Born Walter John de la Mare at Charlton, Kent, on 25 April 1873, of Huguenot descent; he worked for twenty years in the counting house of the Anglo-American Oil Company and wrote in the evenings, publishing Songs of Childhood (1902) under the pseudonym Walter Ramal and The Listeners (1912), which made him famous. He edited Come Hither (1923) and won the Order of Merit in 1953. He died at Twickenham on 22 June 1956.
authors.profile: De la Mare wrote the best English supernatural lyric of the century and the best children's poems in the language: 'The Listeners' is the most famous English ghost poem, 'Silver' and 'The Song of the Mad Prince' are permanent anthology pieces, and his stories (The Riddle, 1923; The Connoisseur, 1926) are among the finest ghost stories in English. His anthology Come Hither shaped the reading of two generations of children.
authors.style: The lyric of the half-heard and the unseen; the trochaic and anapaestic measure that walks rather than sings; the exact naming of the domestic and the natural; the refrain and the refrain that changes; the story in which nothing is explained and everything is felt.
authors.concerns: The other world and the unquiet dead; the child's imagination and the hidden world; the house, the empty room, the moonlit road; the sea and the voyage; memory and the vanished past; the double and the self that watches.
authors.significance: De la Mare is the defining poet of the English supernatural lyric: 'The Listeners' is the era's most famous ghost poem, his stories stand with M. R. James's, and his children's verse and his anthology Come Hither formed the taste of generations. He is the period's great poet of the unseen.

authors.name: Walter Greenwood
authors.nationality: British; the working-class novel of the Depression and the documentary of the dole
authors.identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Love on the Dole, the most influential English working-class novel of the 1930s.
authors.biography: Born Walter Greenwood in Salford on 17 December 1903, the son of a barber's assistant; he left school at thirteen and worked in a warehouse, a pawnbroker's office and an engineering works before writing Love on the Dole (1933) in the Salford public library while unemployed. The novel was dramatised in 1934 and filmed in 1941, and he remained a professional writer, publishing His Worship the Mayor (1934), Standing Room Only (1936) and the autobiographical There Was a Time (1967). He died at Adlington, Lancashire, on 13 September 1974.
authors.profile: Greenwood wrote the definitive English novel of the Depression: Love on the Dole sold over 70,000 copies in its first year, was banned in some libraries, and became the most performed English play of the thirties. It is the period's clearest literary record of the means test, the dole and the pawnshop, and it made a working-class writer from a Salford warehouse a national figure.
authors.style: The plain, documentary, unadorned prose; the transcribed Lancashire speech; the working-class family as the unit of the story; the specific detail of wages, rents and the pawnshop; the political argument carried by incident and not by speech.
authors.concerns: The Depression and unemployment; the dole, the means test and the pawnshop; the Salford working class and the industrial town; the position of women and the marriage market of poverty; the class solidarity and the betrayal of the Labour movement; respectability and shame.
authors.significance: Greenwood wrote the definitive English novel of the Depression and the most performed English play of the 1930s: Love on the Dole changed the terms in which poverty could be described, gave the working class a literature of its own and remains the period's most direct record of the dole.

authors.biography: Probably educated at Cambridge and trained in canon law before becoming an Augustinian canon of Thurgarton Priory, Nottinghamshire; he died on 24 March 1396. His writings circulated widely and were printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1494.

authors.concerns: The reformation of the soul in the image of God; the relation of active and contemplative lives; the discernment of spirits.
authors.significance: The classic systematizer of English mysticism; the Scale of Perfection remained a standard of English devotional reading into the seventeenth century (used by Augustine Baker and his circle).

authors.nationality: English; aesthetic criticism and the prose of art
authors.identity: Essayist and critic; the founder of English aesthetic criticism and the master of the Victorian prose of sensation.
authors.biography: Born at Stepney on 4 August 1839, the son of a surgeon; he was educated at King's School, Canterbury, and at Queen's College, Oxford, where he took a second class in 1862 and remained as a fellow of Brasenose from 1864. He published Studies in the History of the Renaissance in 1873, the book that gave the aesthetic movement its creed; Marius the Epicurean (1885) was his only completed novel, and he published Imaginary Portraits (1887), Appreciations (1889), Plato and Platonism (1893) and the posthumous Greek Studies (1895). He lived quietly at Oxford, a legend among undergraduates, and died there on 30 July 1894.
authors.profile: Pater's prose is the most musical and the most deliberate in Victorian criticism: he wrote to convey the sensation of a work of art rather than a judgment on it, and his famous 'Conclusion' to The Renaissance — that we are to burn always with a hard, gem-like flame and that art gives the highest quality to our moments as they pass — became the manifesto of the 1890s. His criticism is historical and psychological at once, and his fiction invents the imaginary portrait, the exemplary life rendered as a study in feeling.
authors.style: Rhythmical, suspended sentences; the cadenced clause and the carefully withheld verb; sensuous and exact description of art; the essay as a meditation; the imaginary portrait and the imagined life; a refusal of moral summary.
authors.concerns: The transience of experience and the value of the moment; art and sensation; Hellenism and the pagan sensibility against Christian asceticism; the Renaissance as a rebirth of the senses; the education of the soul; style as a form of knowledge.
authors.significance: Pater is the founder of English aesthetic criticism and the prose writer who shaped Wilde, Yeats, Proust's reading of English prose and the whole literature of the 1890s. The Renaissance is one of the most influential books of Victorian England, and Marius the Epicurean is the finest English novel of ideas of the century.

authors.name: Walter Savage Landor
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Poet and prose writer, principally a writer of Latin-English lyric and of imaginary dialogue; one of the great English prose stylists, and a Jacobean-reviving romantic classicist rather than a participant in the Lake or Cockney schools.
authors.biography: Landor was born in 1775 at Ipswich into a prosperous Warwickshire family, the eldest son of a doctor and a mother who died while he was young. He was sent to Rugby and then to University College, Oxford, where he was rusticated for firing a gun in his rooms and for the quarrels that followed, and where he wrote the verse that became Gebir. His marriage in 1797 to Julia Guadagni, daughter of a Florentine nobleman, brought wealth and a long domestic estrangement which ended in separation in Italy in 1819 and in the loss of access to his children, a wound he never stopped writing about. He lived chiefly in Italy, at Como, Bagni di Lucca, and above all at Bath and then at the Villa Fiesole and in Florence, with a long residence at Bath in the 1830s. In 1836 he quarrelled with his friend and patron Robert Forster, whose family he had attacked, and the resulting scandal and the loss of a share of his income shadowed his last decades. He published steadily but poorly from the 1820s, with Imaginary Conversations in 1824, Pericles and Aspasia in 1836, and the last volumes of verse in the 1860s, and he died at Florence in 1864, aged eighty-nine, leaving a large posthumous prose and verse collection.
authors.profile: His canon is small for its length of years and almost wholly made up of short or modular forms: the Spenserian romance of Gebir, the anonymous epic of The Battle of Hastings, the compact elegies, and above all the prose conversations, which he kept revising and regrouping for half a century. He wrote in a double register, English and Latin, and thought of style as the chief moral possession of a writer. His reputation rests less on any single large work than on the intensity and compression of the whole manner, and on a handful of short poems which stand outside the main currents of romanticism.
authors.style: Austere, epigrammatic, and archaising: periods of balanced subordination, monosyllabic emphasis at the close of a passage, and a habitual refusal of transition and explanation. His dialogue dispenses with stage direction and narration, letting character appear wholly through speech, and his lyric reduces diction to the barest nouns and verbs. He is capable of extreme tenderness in the shortest space and of sustained invective in the same syntax.
authors.concerns: Liberty of private judgement against priest, king, and party; the claims of the affections against the family and the law; style as an ethical achievement; the study of Greek, Latin, and Italian literature as a living constitution; the moral history of tyranny and exile, and the dignity of the cultivated individual in a degraded public life.
authors.significance: He stands outside the metropolitan schools of romanticism and supplies its classical and archaising counter-tradition, handing on to later writers the imaginary conversation as a form of criticism and the short elegy as a model of condensation; his life and quarrels also document the economics and the family politics of the professional man of letters in the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of the poems of the 1790s, including the elegies addressed to Rose Aylmer, rests on manuscript evidence and on later recollection rather than on a settled chronology, and the first printing of several short pieces is imperfectly recorded.

authors.name: Washington Irving
authors.nationality: American; essayist, tale-writer, sketch-writer, biographer and historian of the early republic, the central figure of the Knickerbocker group and the first American author of prose to obtain a wide British and European reputation
authors.identity: A writer of prose in several related modes: the comic antiquarian history, the periodical paper and character sketch, the legend and ghost tale of the Dutch country, the familiar essay of English scene and society, and later the romantic history and biography of the Spanish and American past. He wrote no poetry and no fiction of the systematic novel kind; his characteristic form is the sketch, in which observation, memory, humorous invention and moral reflection are left unwelded.
authors.biography: He was born in New York City on 3 April 1783, the youngest but one of eleven children of a Scotch settling family, and was named, it was said, in honour of the recent declaration of independence. He was apprenticed to a law firm, was admitted to practice without ever taking much interest in the bar, and from about 1802 began to write for the New York papers with his brothers. In 1807 and 1808 he shared with his friend James Kirke Paulding the periodical Salmagundi, and in 1809 he brought out at New York the burlesque history which established the persona of Diedrich Knickerbocker. Business disaster in the family importing house sent him to England on its affairs from 1815 to 1823, and there he wrote the English and American sketches of The Sketch Book, issued in parts from 1819 to 1820 and making his name on both sides of the Atlantic. He published miscellaneous histories and sketches of the British and Spanish field through the middle 1820s, travelled in the American prairies in 1832, and in 1835 settled at Sunnyside on the Hudson, where he built up a reputation as the senior man of letters of the country. He served as United States minister at Madrid from 1842 to 1846, wrote the life of Washington in five volumes at Sunnyside, and died there on 28 November 1859, a few weeks after finishing the last volume.
authors.profile: His work falls into a humorous historical group, a group of essays and tales in the manner of the periodical sketch, and a late group of biography, history and travel; between them he compiled lives of western and Spanish personages and a great deal of occasional address and preface. The History of New York and the Salmagundi papers are the native and comic beginning; The Sketch Book, with its two companion collections of 1822 and 1824, is the characteristic body of his work and the source of the American short tale. His later prose is antiquarian and diplomatic in tone, and his Spanish histories and biographies of Columbus and of the conquerors of Granada belong to the romantic treatment of national past rather than to scholarly history.
authors.style: A smooth, old-fashioned, consciously literary English, shaded from easy irony into sentiment without the reader being warned of the turn. He is an excellent describer of quiet scenery and of ruined places, a droll narrator in the personating vein, and a writer who prefers the half-light of the legend and the sketch to the resolved plot; his humour is generated by persona, by the assumption of a naive or pompous voice, and by the pedantic accumulation of invented authority.
authors.concerns: The making of an American literary past out of Dutch, Indian and revolutionary materials; the depreciation and the admiration of the old country by a colonial writer; the value of tradition, holiday and legend to a calculating republic; the commerce of the nations and the fate of the settled and displaced peoples of America; the education of taste through English scene and architecture; the dignity of the man of letters in a country of lawyers and merchants.
authors.significance: He gave the American short prose tale its first durable models and the sketch essay its American manner, and by his success with British publishers and readers he established that American writing could be a European commodity. Diedrich Knickerbocker named a school, a city's mythology and a literature's self-image, and The Sketch Book was the most widely read American book of its generation. His late life of Washington and his prairie travel also fixed the sentimental and legendary treatment of the national story for a century.
authors.uncertainty: The story of his naming in honour of the declaration of independence is family tradition rather than documented fact; the precise extent of Paulding's and of his brother's share in the Salmagundi papers has never been settled to general satisfaction.

authors.name: Wilfred Owen
authors.nationality: British; the trench lyric of pity and the pararhyme
authors.identity: Poet; the greatest of the First World War poets, killed a week before the armistice, whose poems became the central English statement about the pity of war.
authors.biography: Born Wilfred Edward Salter Owen at Plas Wilmot, Oswestry, Shropshire, on 18 March 1893, the son of a railway clerk; he read at London University without taking a degree, taught English in Bordeaux (1913–15), and enlisted in the Artists' Rifles in 1915. He was commissioned in the Manchester Regiment, served on the Somme and at Serre, was blown up and spent 1917 in Craiglockhart, where Sassoon encouraged him; he returned to France in 1918, won the Military Cross, and was killed on the Sambre canal on 4 November 1918, a week before the armistice. His mother received the telegram as the bells were ringing.
authors.profile: Owen is the greatest poet of the First World War: in some two dozen finished poems he made the pity of war the subject of a lyric poetry that refuses both patriotism and despair. His technical invention — pararhyme, the half-comic half-horrified colloquialism, the long vowel held across an impossible rhyme — gave English poetry a new instrument, and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting' are among the small number of poems every English reader knows by heart.
authors.style: Pararhyme (graves/groves, killed/cold) as a structural device; the colloquial voice that can turn to prophecy; the exact and terrible physical detail; the sonnet and the irregular ode adapted to the trench; the pre-Raphaelite richness put to anti-heroic use; the ellipsis and the unfinished line.
authors.concerns: The pity of war and the waste of the young; the gas attack and the drowning man; the dead brother and the enemy met in hell; the church, the funeral and the mockery of the liturgy; the home front and the lie of the old rhetoric; comradeship and the doomed generation.
authors.significance: Owen is the greatest poet of the First World War and one of the most important English poets of the century: his two dozen finished poems changed the language of war poetry, his pararhyme gave modern verse a new technique, and 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting' are permanent national texts. His preface — 'the Poetry is in the pity' — is the period's definitive statement about the poet's duty.

authors.name: Wilkie Collins
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian sensation novel
authors.identity: Novelist and playwright; the inventor of the English sensation novel and of the modern detective story.
authors.biography: Born in London on 8 January 1824, son of the landscape painter William Collins. He was educated privately in Italy and at Lincoln's Inn, where he was called to the bar in 1851 but never practised. He met Dickens in 1851 and became his friend, collaborator and contributor to Household Words and All the Year Round. Antonina (1850) was his first novel; The Woman in White (serialised 1859-60) made him famous and The Moonstone (1868) invented the English detective novel. From the 1860s he suffered from rheumatic gout and became dependent on laudanum, and he lived with two households, a wife and a mistress, in a domestic arrangement that Victorian society did not acknowledge. He died in London on 23 September 1889.
authors.profile: Collins took the Gothic machinery of the 1790s — the asylum, the forged will, the substituted identity, the secret in the family — and moved it into contemporary England and English law. His great innovation is the multiple-narrator method: the story is told in turn by the witnesses and participants, each with a limited and interested view, and the reader must assemble the truth from their testimony. He wrote as a lawyer's son about the legal position of women (the woman in white has no name, no property and no credibility), and as a professional novelist about the new class of doctors, clerks and detectives.
authors.style: Documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements; the withholding of information by a narrator with a reason to withhold it; precise legal and medical detail; doubles, substituted identities and mistaken names; a plot built on the exact sequence of evidence; short chapters and serial climaxes.
authors.concerns: Identity and the legal person; marriage, coverture and the property of women; madness, confinement and the asylum; class and the professional middle class; empire and the colonial secret; crime and the limits of the law; the double life of the respectable Victorian.
authors.significance: Collins invented the English sensation novel and, with The Moonstone, the English detective novel; his multiple-narrator method is the model for the whole modern literature of testimony, from Conrad to the contemporary crime novel. His treatment of women's legal non-existence helped to make the Married Women's Property Acts arguable, and his novels are now read as the central case of Victorian popular fiction.

authors.name: William Baldwin
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: satirist; editor; corrector of printing
authors.biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
authors.profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
authors.style: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
authors.concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
authors.significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.

authors.biography: Born on 29 September 1760 in London, the son of William Beckford, twice Lord Mayor of London and a West Indian planter and politician, he inherited great wealth and entered public life as a Member of Parliament and briefly a sheriff. As a young man he wrote the Oriental romance Vathek, originally composed in French and published in English in 1786. He built the eccentric country house at Fonthill Abbey and pursued collecting and writing. He died on 2 May 1844.
authors.profile: The author of Vathek, a tale of oriental magnificence and forbidden knowledge that fused Gothic luxury with the Arabian Nights tradition and helped define the decadent and exotic strain in Romantic-era fiction.
authors.style: Ornate, sensational, orientalizing prose; lavish descriptive excess; a framing of wonder and magic; and a deliberate artificiality and luxury of detail inherited from the Arabian Nights vogue.
authors.concerns: Curiosity, power, and transgression; the pursuit of forbidden knowledge; orientalism and exotic magnificence; pleasure and damnation; and aesthetic luxury.
authors.significance: A distinctive and influential author of Gothic-Oriental fiction, whose Vathek became a landmark of the supernatural tale and an important source for later decadent and fantasy writing.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is well attested; some details of the composition and translation history of Vathek, and of the dating of his writings, remain subjects of scholarly note rather than of real dispute.

authors.name: William Black
authors.nationality: British; the Scottish landscape romance
authors.identity: Novelist and journalist; the most popular Scottish novelist of the 1870s and 1880s, and the inventor of the holiday romance of the Highlands and the sea.
authors.biography: Born in Glasgow on 9 November 1841, the son of a manufacturer; he trained as a painter, turned to journalism, and made his name with A Daughter of Heth (1871). The Strange Adventures of a Phaeton (1872), The Princess of Thule (1873), Macleod of Dare (1878) and White Wings (1880) followed. He travelled constantly and died at Brighton on 10 December 1898.
authors.profile: Black wrote the most popular Scottish landscape romances of the 1870s and 1880s and invented the holiday novel in which the scenery of the Highlands and the Hebrides is itself the subject. His picture of the yacht, the hotel and the shooting lodge gave the Victorian reader the touring romance that Stevenson refined and that the twentieth-century Scottish novel inherited.
authors.style: The touring narrative — coach, yacht, walking tour; the set-piece description of loch and mountain; the contrast of English visitor and Highland community; the light comedy of manners; the sentimental heroine of the islands.
authors.concerns: The Highlands and the clearances; the relation of the visitor to the native community; the place of women in a landscape romance; the commercialisation of scenery; the Celtic periphery and the English centre.
authors.significance: William Black was the most popular Scottish novelist of the 1870s and 1880s: his Highland and Hebridean romances invented the touring novel, made the scenery of the west of Scotland a literary property, and prepared the ground for the Scottish Renaissance.

authors.name: William Blackstone
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Oxford don, serjeant at law, judge and Tory MP, whose four-volume Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-1769) made English law a readable rational system.
authors.biography: Born in Cheapside in London in 1723, the posthumous son of a City merchant, he was educated at a London grammar school and at Pembroke College, Oxford, with the help of relations, and was elected a fellow of All Souls. Called to the bench of the Middle Temple and practising on the Oxford and home circuits, he won fame by a book on gavelkind and by lecturing on English law, which led to his appointment as the first Vinerian professor in 1758. His Analysis of the Laws of England (1756) and his Discourse on the Study of the Law (1765) prepared the Commentaries, published in four parts between 1765 and 1769 and immediately made his name. He sat in the Commons, was appointed to the bench of the Common Pleas and knighted in 1770, and was transferred to the King's Bench in 1779, where his rigorous, sometimes unpopular judgments tested his own theory of law. He died in London on 14 February 1780.
authors.profile: The great systematiser and apologist of the common law, who presented its intricacies as an ordered, decent and largely admirable inheritance.
authors.style: Clear, stately, judicious prose that explains difficulty without hiding it; balanced periods and a scholar's courtesy; historical narrative used to legitimate existing doctrine.
authors.concerns: The reasonableness and continuity of the common law; the rights of persons and of things; the nature of law, sovereignty and the reach of parliamentary authority; the legal condition of servants, women, children and colonial subjects; the relation of law to religion and morality.
authors.significance: The Commentaries became the standard education of English-speaking lawyers for two centuries and, with their American reprints, one of the chief sources of early American legal and political vocabulary; Bentham's attack on them opened the age of law reform.
authors.uncertainty: The order and dating of his lectures and of the several editions of the Commentaries, which he revised to his death, are complex and disputed.

authors.name: William Blake
authors.birthplace: London, in the Golden Square quarter, of a dissenting shopkeeping family
authors.nationality: English; poet, engraver and visionary painter of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Poet-engraver who made his books by his own hands, the creator of a private prophetic mythology, and the most uncompromising visionary writer of the English Romantic generation.
authors.biography: Blake was born in London, the son of a hosier, and showed from early childhood a disposition to drawing and an familiarity with visions; he was not sent to school but was bound apprentice to an engraver at about fourteen, served the seven years, and then entered the schools of the Royal Academy, where the academic manner of the presidents offended him. He set up as an engraver and print-seller, married in 1782 a woman whom he taught to read and to work at his printing, and produced the illuminated books by a method of etching and relief-printing of his own invention, colouring the plates by hand and selling them in numbers far below their merit. He knew and was friendly with the painter of the Nightmare and with the publishers and dissenting writers of the revolutionary decade, visited France in 1792, and wrote and engraved the prophetic books of the years of hope and reaction. From 1800 to 1803 he worked under the patronage of a poet of the earlier school at Felpham in Sussex, where a soldier's complaint brought him before a magistrates' court and an acquittal; the last decades brought commissions for illustrations to a book of scripture and to the vision of the Italian poet, a small circle of devoted younger painters, a display of his own designs at his own price, and death in 1827 in lodging in the Strand, his wife beside him and his funeral attended by friends of both his arts.
authors.profile: His writing divides between the songs and shorter lyrics of the two illuminated collections, the prophetic books in verse and prose, and the mass of annotations, memoranda, letters and designs; his mythology of the four powers of the human mind, of the fallen reason and of the labouring imagination is the most systematic private system in English. He was also a designer and engraver whose plates carry his poems, so that text and image must be read as one, and a painter in water-colour and in tempera who executed a series of large designs and illustrations.
authors.style: Lyric verse of great simplicity in song measures, with reiterated lines and a balance of innocent and terrible images; prophetic verse of stern and rapid accentual lines, filled with proclamation, question and catalogue; prose of aphoristic vehemence, with the rhetoric of the angel and the devil and a continuous war of contraries.
authors.concerns: The contraries by which the soul progresses, and the falseness of a morality of patience and restraint; imagination as the divine body in man and the enemy of single reason; the guilt of law, priesthood and empire, and the bondage of the slave, the child and the inhibited lover; the redemption of the divided giant and the building of a city of vision in England.
authors.significance: He anticipated by a decade the ballad revolt against polished verse, and he left the only fully developed personal mythology in English. His illuminated books are the foundation of the art of the printed page in which poem and design are one object, and his prophecy of a redeemed imagination, with his phrases for the dark satanic mills and for the child and the sweep, has entered the language of literature, of religious radicalism and of national song.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of the first issue of several illuminated books and the order in which the plates were executed and sold are disputed, and the account of his visions rests almost wholly on his own statements and on those of his wife and his friends.

authors.name: William Camden
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: antiquarian; historian; herald; schoolmaster
authors.biography: Born 2 May 1551 in the Old Bailey, London. Educated at Christ's Hospital and St Paul's School, then at Magdalen and Christ Church, Oxford. He taught at Westminster School (1575–97), where his pupils included Ben Jonson, and ended his career as Clarenceux King of Arms (1597). He died on 9 November 1623 at Chislehurst, Kent.
authors.profile: Britannia (1586, in Latin; English translation by Philemon Holland, 1610), the chorographical description of Britain, and the Annales of the reign of Elizabeth I (1615–25).
authors.style: Exact, methodical, elegant Latin and an English style of grave plainness; the scholar's impartiality joined to patriotic purpose.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the writing of sober, documented history against legend; national identity through the past.
authors.significance: The father of English antiquarianism; his Britannia launched the great tradition of county and national history that runs through the seventeenth century and beyond.
authors.uncertainty: The accuracy of the Annales on some episodes is disputed by later historians.

authors.name: William Carlos Williams
authors.nationality: American; the objectivist lyric, the American idiom and the long poem of place
authors.identity: Poet and physician; the inventor of the American objectivist line and the author of Paterson, the great American long poem of place.
authors.biography: Born William Carlos Williams in Rutherford, New Jersey, on 17 September 1883 of an English father and a Puerto Rican mother; he studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, where he met Pound and H. D., took his degree in 1906, and practised as a pediatrician in Rutherford for forty years while writing. He published Poems (1909), Al Que Quiere! (1917), Spring and All (1923), The Red Wheelbarrow (1923), An Early Martyr (1935), the first book of Paterson in 1946, and Pictures from Brueghel (1962), which won the Pulitzer Prize. He died in Rutherford on 4 March 1963.
authors.profile: Williams is the great American poet of the thing itself and of the spoken American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' is the period's most influential poetic programme. His short poems — 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'This Is Just to Say', 'Danse Russe' — are among the most imitated in the language, Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period, and Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land.
authors.style: The line measured by the breath and broken by speech; the plain American word; the image without metaphor; the variable foot and the triadic stanza; the poem as a field of perception; the prose-and-verse collage of Spring and All and Paterson.
authors.concerns: The American place and the American idiom; the object and the thing seen without metaphor; the local city (Paterson, Rutherford); the body and desire; the immigrant and the working town; the poet as doctor and witness.
authors.significance: Williams is the founder of the American objectivist tradition and the great poet of the American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' changed American poetry, his short poems are the most imitated of the century, Spring and All is a foundational modernist text, and Paterson is the period's great American long poem. He is the poet through whom American poetry escaped the English line.

authors.name: William Caxton
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: printer; translator; merchant
authors.biography: A Kentish mercer who spent three decades in the Low Countries, rising to governor of the English merchants at Bruges, where he learned printing at Cologne and produced the first book printed in English, his own Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–74). In 1476 he set up the first English press at Westminster, printing some hundred books — Chaucer, Malory, Gower, Lydgate, the Golden Legend, and his own translations — before his death c. 1491.
authors.profile: Printer and translator: the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (c. 1473–74), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), the History of Reynard the Fox (1481), the Golden Legend (1483), and numerous prologues and epilogues that constitute a body of critical prose.
authors.style: Lucid, idiomatic translation from French sources; a merchant's plain style enriched by courtly vocabulary; the prologues' genial self-presentation as servant of the 'comyn wele'.
authors.concerns: The provision of good books in English; the standardization of the language ('ouer rude termes' and the dialect of Kent); the moral and chivalric education of the nobility and gentry.
authors.significance: The introducer of printing to England: his press fixed the form of the English classics, began the standardization of written English, and made the fifteenth century's literature the sixteenth century's inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the exact site and date of his first printing remain debated.

authors.name: William Cobbett
altNames: Peter Porcupine (as used in his American writing)
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Journalist, polemicist, farmer, and political historian; the greatest writer of English plebeian radical prose, and the founder of the weekly political journal as an instrument of class argument.
authors.biography: Cobbett was born in 1763 at Goodwood near Chichester, the son of a farm bailiff, and grew up with field work, book learning, and the grammar schools within reach but not taken. He ran to sea at nineteen, married an Irish servant girl, Anne Reid, in 1791, and after a period as a clerk and a soldier, set himself up as a writer. He went to America in 1792, made his name in Philadelphia as Peter Porcupine, editor of a fiercely loyalist newspaper and of a series of pamphlets, and returned to England in 1800 disillusioned with the republic. In 1802 he founded the Political Register, which he edited almost without interruption until 1835. His imprisonment in 1810 for an attack on flogging earned him a popular martyrdom, and from the end of the war he turned his agrarianism into a systematic attack on paper credit, the funds, the taxes, and the corn laws. He fought the six Acts, defended the reformers, was repeatedly prosecuted, and in 1832 was elected to parliament for Oldham, where he spoke briefly against poor-law policy before his death at Kensington in 1835.
authors.profile: His work is at once journalistic, agricultural, historical, and autobiographical, and it was written overwhelmingly for a weekly serial audience of mechanics, small traders, and farm labourers. The Rural Rides, the currency letters, the grammar, and the polemic against the Protestant Reformation share one method: concrete observation, a documented grievance, and an appeal to the reader's own experience against 'the system'. He also wrote extensively on husbandry, on timber and planting, on style, and on education, and he was a serious editor of documents.
authors.style: Plain, Anglo-Saxon, rhythmic, and spoken: short words, direct address, repetition, and an idiom built from the workshop and the field. His prose carries invective and endearment in the same sentence, uses figures drawn from farming and from money, and treats the familiar noun as an argument in itself. He is the great English example of writing that refuses gentility without becoming colloquially vague.
authors.concerns: The political economy of paper money, taxation, and the national debt; the property confiscations of the Reformation as the origin of modern pauperism; the dignity and the wages of agricultural and artisanal labour; representation and corruption; the education of the labouring child in the standard language; and the defence of the small producer against both aristocracy and manufactured capital.
authors.significance: He created the popular weekly journal in England, shaped the language in which reform was argued before and after 1832, and made the condition of the labouring poor a subject of literary as well as political analysis; the documentary force of his prose is one of the two or three foundations of the social history of the romantic period.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his childhood schooling and of the farm where he was born are variously reported, and the extent to which the Parliamentary History and other compilations was composed by others working for him was disputed in his lifetime and remains so.

authors.name: William Collins
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English lyric poet of the Odes, associated with Gray and with the rise of imaginative, impassioned, and personified poetry.
authors.biography: Collins was born at Chichester, the son of an insurer, and studied at Winchester College and at Queen's College, Oxford. A volume of odes appeared in 1746 but sold poorly and was effectively withdrawn, and the pieces came to be prized chiefly after his death. Later poems such as Ode on the Poetical Character and his oriental and Persian imitations mark his range. Mental illness and early death cut short his career; he was tended in his last years by his lifelong friend the painter Joseph Hammell, and he died at Chichester in 1759. Gray, who admired him, did much to secure his posthumous reputation.
authors.profile: A short-lived lyric poet whose best work casts abstract qualities as personified figures in an atmosphere of imaginative reverie, enthusiasm, and melancholy; he stands between the Augustans and the pre-Romantics.
authors.style: Rich, sustained personification; lyric and ode measures of great musicality; elevated, sometimes archaic diction; and an intoxicating, enthusiastic imaginative tone distinct from Pope's point.
authors.concerns: The power of imagination and poetic enthusiasm; the personified emotions and qualities of the mind; the appeal of the exotic, the supernatural, and melancholy; and the poet's isolation.
authors.significance: One of the most important lyric poets between Pope and the Romantics; his odes were championed by Samuel Johnson and later admired for prefiguring Romantic imagination and sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: The number and publication history of his odes are complicated by the suppression of his 1746 volume and later editorial reconstruction; the nature and onset of his mental illness are imperfectly documented.

authors.name: William Congreve
authors.nationality: English (Anglo-Irish upbringing)
authors.identity: The greatest master of the comedy of manners; author of The Way of the World (1700), Love for Love (1695), and the tragedy The Mourning Bride (1697), whose flawless comic prose and brilliant repartee represent the summit of English wit comedy.
authors.biography: Born 24 January 1670 at Bardsey, Yorkshire, son of an army officer; raised in Ireland and educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin. He came to London, studied law at the Middle Temple, and astonished the town with The Old Bachelor (1693), followed by The Double Dealer (1693), Love for Love (1695), and The Mourning Bride (1697, the most successful tragedy of the decade). His masterwork The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received, and, sensitive to criticism and enjoying a comfortable government sinecure and the friendship of the Whig Junto (and a long liaison with Henrietta Godolphin, Duchess of Marlborough), he wrote little after 1700. He died on 19 January 1729 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The consummate artist of comic prose, whose plays achieve a perfection of wit, structure, and tone — 'the prose Shakespeare' — treating the negotiation of love, marriage, and money in a society of manners with ironic elegance.
authors.style: Brilliantly epigrammatic prose; the 'proviso' scene of negotiated marriage; balanced, ironic repartee; elegant plotting; and, in The Mourning Bride, sonorous blank-verse declamation.
authors.concerns: Wit and true wit; love, marriage, and money; hypocrisy, affectation, and scandal; the social code of the town; and the relation of art and manners.
authors.significance: The Way of the World is universally regarded as the finest comedy of manners in English; Congreve defined the genre, influenced Sheridan and Wilde, and his tragic lines ('Musick has charms to soothe a savage breast') became proverbial.
authors.uncertainty: Congreve's life is well documented; his early retirement from writing is explained by his finances, health, and sensitivity to criticism, though the reasons remain partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Cowper
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and hymn-writer of the evangelical and sentimental age, whose Task and Olney Hymns opened a new nature poetry and whose life was marked by depression and religious terror.
authors.biography: Cowper was born in Hertfordshire, the son of a clergyman, was called to the bar, and after a breakdown and an attempt at self-destruction found a measure of religious assurance in evangelical Christianity. He lived much of his life in retirement under the shelter of the Hill family, at Olney and later in Norfolk. With John Newton he contributed to the Olney Hymns (1779), writing such hymns as God Moves in a Mysterious Way. His long conversational poem The Task (1785) established his fame, followed by translations of Homer and shorter poems including The Castaway and an account of his despair. Plagued all his life by melancholy and by a recurring conviction of reprobation, he died in 1800.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, domestic life, nature, and religious feeling, who combined the descriptive, meditative, and comic-familiar modes and wrote with startling honesty of depression and faith.
authors.style: Smooth, conversational blank verse of the familiar line; descriptive tenderness and homely humour; a passionate, troubled religious lyricism; and a gift for hymn and melancholy song.
authors.concerns: Providence, evangelical assurance, and despair; the consolation of rural and domestic life; anti-slavery and humane feeling; nature, retirement, and melancholy; and the critique of luxury and city life.
authors.significance: A leading poet of sensibility and the evangelical revival and one of the most influential nature poets before the Romantics, admired by Wordsworth and Coleridge for the honesty and feeling of his verse.
authors.uncertainty: A lifelong fear of eternal reprobation makes his own accounts of his religious states hard to date precisely; the chronology of his breakdowns and his late poem on despair is partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Cullen Bryant
authors.nationality: American; poet, political editor, critic and translator, the first American poet of the nineteenth century to command an international audience and the founder of the American nature lyric in the Wordsworthian manner
authors.identity: A poet of short and middle-length meditative and descriptive pieces and of a few longer topographical poems, together with an enormous body of editorial, critical and political prose. His verse is predominantly blank verse and the didactic or descriptive stanza; his later work included the prose retelling of the Latin tale, a national poem of the Revolution's memory and the blank verse translation of Homer which completed his career. As editor of a New York daily for near half a century he was also a principal political writer of his time.
authors.biography: He was born at Cummington, in the hill country of western Massachusetts, on 3 November 1794, the second son of Peter Bryant, a physician and occasional writer of the neighbourhood, and he learned his first Latin and Greek at his father's table. He went to Williams College in 1810 and left in the following year without a degree, then studied law, was admitted to the bar and for a short season practised in the same western counties. In 1811 he married his cousin Frances Fairchild, and about these same years he wrote the pieces which first made his name, including the brief satirical poem on national policy which he gave out under a disguise to spare his father's Federalist connections. His early meditative poem was printed in a Boston review in 1817 and was for long treated as the beginning of his reputation, and the volume of 1821 established him as a poet of the American scene. Finding no support for literature in Massachusetts, he removed to New York in 1825, took a share in the editing of periodicals, and from 1829 until his death was the leading spirit of a great daily newspaper, in which he wrote the political and literary argument of a generation of New York conservatives and reformers. He lectured on the national literature, edited a poetical and prose anthology, wrote the long poem on the American prairies at the end of his active work, and in the last years completed his blank verse Homer. He died in New York in June 1878, having been for half a century the most public of American men of letters.
authors.profile: His verse is small in bulk compared with his prose and is built around a few durable meditations, a group of short lyrics on waterfowl, flowers, death and the seasons, and two long descriptive poems of the prairie and of American history. His editorial and critical work fills an enormous file of newspaper columns and a course of lectures and addresses, and his translations, Latin fables, Homer and the prose romance retelling, occupy a large part of his later labour. The theory he held of poetry as moral and serious thought in elevated numbers gave the American nature lyric its first sustained practice, and he was the acknowledged centre of the New York literary world for thirty years.
authors.style: A grave, sustained and deliberately elevated diction in blank verse of great smoothness, with long sentences, frequent inversion, apostrophe and a moral close; in the shorter lyrics a plain descriptive accuracy which passes into meditation. He is a poet of twilight, winter, water and the death of the year, and his strength is the slow descriptive paragraph in verse rather than the quick stroke of passion or the comic vein, which he rarely attempted.
authors.concerns: Death, immortality and the consoling proof drawn from the order of nature; the soul's instruction by landscape and solitude; the transience of earthly glory and the permanence of moral truth; the dignity and the destiny of the republic and of its western wilderness; the religion of a reasonableness hostile to sect and to fanaticism; the education of a nation's taste by criticism and by the daily press.
authors.significance: He fixed the American nature meditation in the blank verse and the diction of the English eighteenth century, and through a long editorial career he gave poetry and criticism a recognised place in American public life. His shortest poems entered the schoolbook and the recitation as no American verse had done, and his Homer remained for a generation the standard English rendering. As a political editor he also shaped the antislavery and reform opinion of the North, so that his literary and his public authority were exercised in one continuous career.
authors.uncertainty: The first printing of his earliest printed poem, and the exact relation between the 1811 and later texts, are imperfectly documented; the long dispute over how much of the meditative poem was his own work and how far his father's papers have been counted in it remains only partially settled.
