authors.name: William Dean Howells
authors.nationality: American; the realist novel and the criticism of fiction
authors.identity: Novelist, critic and editor; the theorist and chief practitioner of American literary realism.
authors.biography: Born at Martins Ferry, Ohio, on 1 March 1837, the son of a printer and newspaper editor; he taught himself the trade and languages, wrote a campaign life of Lincoln in 1860, and was American consul at Venice in 1861-65. He was assistant editor (1866-71) and then editor (1871-81) of the Atlantic Monthly, and from 1886 wrote the 'Editor's Study' for Harper's Monthly, the most influential critical column in America. He wrote some forty novels, including A Modern Instance (1882), The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885) and A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890). He died in New York on 11 May 1920.
authors.profile: Howells made realism the official programme of American fiction: he argued that the novel should concern itself with the ordinary, contemporary and 'smiling aspects' of American life, and his own best novels — the Boston of The Rise of Silas Lapham, the New York of A Hazard of New Fortunes — give the most exact picture we have of the American middle class in the Gilded Age. He was also the most generous and consequential literary editor of his time, the first American champion of Tolstoy, Ibsen and Zola, and the defender of the Haymarket defendants.
authors.style: Plain, unobtrusive narrative prose; dialogue that reproduces the hesitations of educated American speech; the detailed interior of the middle-class home; the drama of business and marriage; irony so dry it can be missed; the broad social canvas organised around a single family.
authors.concerns: The ethics of business and the making of an American fortune; marriage, divorce and the position of women; the city and the suburban home; class and the immigrant poor; the literary marketplace; socialism and the American conscience after Haymarket.
authors.significance: Howells is the founding theorist of American realism and a major novelist in his own right: his editorial and critical work created the climate in which Twain, James, Crane and Wharton wrote, and The Rise of Silas Lapham and A Hazard of New Fortunes are the central American novels of business and of the Gilded Age city.

authors.name: William Dunbar
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: poet; courtier; priest
authors.biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
authors.profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
authors.style: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
authors.concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
authors.significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.

authors.name: William Edmondstoune Aytoun
authors.nationality: British; the Scottish ballad and the parody of the spasmodic
authors.identity: Poet, translator and Professor of Rhetoric; the author of Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers and the wittiest parodist of the Victorian poet.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh on 21 June 1813; he practised law, wrote for Blackwood's, and became Professor of Rhetoric at Edinburgh in 1845. Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers (1849), Firmilian (1854) and the History of the Scottish Cavaliers followed, and with Theodore Martin he wrote the Bon Gaultier Ballads (1845). He died at Blackhills, near Elgin, on 4 August 1865.
authors.profile: Aytoun wrote Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers, the most popular Scottish historical poem of the century, and the Firmilian, the wittiest parody of the spasmodic poetry of the 1850s: his ballads gave the Scottish past its permanent popular form, and his parodies ended the fashion they mocked.
authors.style: The stirring historical ballad with a refrain; the Jacobite and Covenanting matter; the martial rhetoric and the dying speech; the parody of the contemporary poet; the plain, vigorous, regular stanza.
authors.concerns: Scottish national identity and the Jacobite past; heroism and the lost cause; the ballad and the oral tradition; the war of the seventeenth century; the vanity of literary fashion.
authors.significance: Aytoun wrote Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers, the most popular Scottish historical poem of the century, and Firmilian, the wittiest parody of the spasmodic poetry of the 1850s: his ballads gave the Scottish past its permanent popular form.

authors.name: William Ellery Channing
authors.nationality: American; the Unitarian Boston circle of Federal Street and the review writers about Harvard and the Connecticut Valley, and the liberal preaching of New England in the 1820s and 1830s
authors.identity: Preacher and moralist, the most influential religious writer and the most quoted preacher of New England in his generation, the chief expounder of American Unitarianism, and the centre of the Boston circle from which the liberal religion and the liberal literature of New England together proceeded.
authors.biography: Channing was born at Newport in Rhode Island, of a family connected with the commerce and the revolutionary leadership of the State, and was marked early for the professions by a precocity of reading joined to a diffidence of manner. He went to Harvard, graduated in 1798, and earned his living for some years as a tutor in the families of Virginia, where the leisure of the country house gave him his formative reading in the rational dissenting divinity and where, after a season of religious depression and moral struggle, he ceased to believe the doctrines of the Trinity and of the Calvinist scheme of salvation. He was licensed to preach, and in 1803 was settled over the Federal Street congregation at Boston, a church of merchants, physicians, lawyers and scholars, which he served for the rest of his life and which he kept at the centre of the intellectual and charitable affairs of the city. For years he avoided the doctrinal controversy into which his position carried him, preaching instead the moral and religious themes of duty, culture, self-denial and the likeness of man to God, until the occasion of an ordination at Baltimore in May 1819 drew from him the sermon which gave the liberal party its public confession of faith and its answer to the charge of unbelief. From that time he was the most quoted and most attacked divine in the United States; his sermons, discourses and reviews built up a body of practical theology which made the nature of God, the credibility of revelation, the dignity of the human mind and the duties of the Christian the ordinary subjects of American religious discourse. His writings on the character and the treatment of the slave, called out by the violence of the antislavery controversy of the middle and later 1830s, made him an authority on the abolition question and an outlaw in the Southern states, and he was at once a friend, a patron and at last a problem to the younger writers who went beyond him. He was an adviser of education and reform movements, a constant contributor to the American and the British journals, and a preacher whose discourses on public occasions were taken as moral events; the most famous of them gave its name and its programme to a religious party. Failing health sent him in search of strength out of Boston in his last years; he died at Old Bennington in Vermont on 2 October 1842, and was buried in the cemetery at Cambridge, leaving a congregation, a denomination and a generation of preachers formed on his manner.
authors.profile: His works are almost wholly the sermon, the discourse and the review article: the confession of faith of 1819 and the subsequent defences of the Unitarian position against the charges of the Orthodox review press; practical and theological discourses on the attributes of God, on the likeness of the human soul to God, on self-denial, on the culture of the mind, on the union of religious profession with common life, and on the duties of a Christian people; the letters and treatise on slavery; remarks on education, on the character of the age and on the religion of a republic; and a considerable body of review writing on books of theology, history and biography. He projected greater works of history and of doctrinal argument which he never executed, and the journals, letters and conversations of his later years were printed by his family and friends after his death.
authors.style: A prose of deliberate, candid and moral argument: the long qualifying sentence, the repeated appeal to reason and to the sentiments, an evident diffidence carrying itself into authority, and a preaching manner that expounds rather than terrifies; the sermon constructed as an essay, with numbered propositions, illustrations from common life and an unction of benevolence; and the review article written with the same courtesy and the same weight of moral assertion.
authors.concerns: The unitary being and the moral attributes of God, and the wrong done to them by a creed which divides or debases them; the dignity and capacity of the human soul and its likeness to God as the ground both of religion and of education; the credibility of revelation judged by reason and by the conscience; the duties of self-culture and of the Christian in society; slavery as a national sin and as a trial of character; the union of churches and of the States, and the obligations of the citizen in a republic.
authors.significance: His sermon of 1819 is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a distinct religious body, and through him Boston became the capital of a liberal Protestantism which supplied the clergy, editors and professors of New England for two generations. His writings on the mind, on culture and on the divine humanity prepared the language which the Transcendentalists inherited and reacted against; his public letters on slavery gave the moderate conscience of the North a text; and his preaching remains the standard example of the moral and reasonable sermon in American religious history.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his Virginia tutoring and of the changes of his father's fortunes are given variously, and the exact course of his religious conversion is known chiefly from his own memoranda and from the recastings of his biographers; the chronology of his unpublished projections, and the extent of his share in the journals for which he wrote, are imperfectly reported, and opinions attributed to him on abolition in his last months rest on letters and conversations of doubtful authority.

authors.name: William Empson
authors.nationality: British; the critic of ambiguity and the poet of the argumentative lyric
authors.identity: Critic and poet; the author of Seven Types of Ambiguity and Some Versions of Pastoral.
authors.biography: Born William Empson at Yokefleet, Yorkshire, on 27 September 1906; he read mathematics and then English at Cambridge under I. A. Richards, and published Seven Types of Ambiguity in 1930, Some Versions of Pastoral in 1935 and his Poems in the same year. He taught in Japan and China through the war years and at Sheffield after them; his later criticism, from The Structure of Complex Words (1951), and his verse of the argumentative lyric made him the most original critic-poet of his generation. He died in London on 15 April 1984.
authors.profile: William Empson is the most original critic-poet of the English twentieth century: Seven Types of Ambiguity made the analysis of verbal ambiguity the instrument of the close reading that the century took as its method, Some Versions of Pastoral read the whole range of English literature as versions of the pastoral irony, and his poems are the argumentative lyric of the scientific intellect.
authors.style: The close reading that unfolds every sense of the word; the argumentative lyric of the compressed syntax and the irony; the pastoral read as the social irony of the degree; the wit of the parenthesis and the aside; the prose that thinks in the sentence rather than in the paragraph.
authors.concerns: Ambiguity and the plurality of sense; the pastoral and the social irony; the complexity of the key word; Buddhism and the argument of the self; the mathematics and the poem; the quarrel with the doctrine of the unified response.
authors.significance: William Empson is the most original critic-poet of the English twentieth century: Seven Types of Ambiguity made verbal ambiguity the instrument of the close reading the century took as its method, Some Versions of Pastoral read English literature as versions of the pastoral irony, and his poems are the argumentative lyric of the scientific intellect.

authors.name: William Faulkner
authors.nationality: American; the Southern Gothic, the mythical county and the novel of history's weight
authors.identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the greatest American novelist of the century, the creator of Yoknapatawpha County, and the Nobel laureate of 1949.
authors.biography: Born William Cuthbert Falkner in New Albany, Mississippi, on 25 September 1897 and raised in Oxford, Mississippi; he served in the Canadian Royal Air Force in 1918 without seeing combat, worked briefly in New York and New Orleans, and published Soldiers' Pay (1926) and Mosquitoes (1927). Sartoris (1929), The Sound and the Fury (1929), As I Lay Dying (1930), Sanctuary (1931), Light in August (1932) and Absalom, Absalom! (1936) built the county of Yoknapatawpha; he worked in Hollywood, won the Nobel Prize in 1949 and the Pulitzer Prize twice, and died in Oxford, Mississippi, on 6 July 1962.
authors.profile: Faulkner is the greatest American novelist of the period: The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom! are among the most formally daring novels of the century, and the invention of Yoknapatawpha gave American literature a complete imaginative world to set beside Balzac's Paris or Hardy's Wessex. He made the burden of Southern history — slavery, defeat, guilt, the land — the matter of a great tragic art, and his late novels and stories extend the county to the edge of the modern world.
authors.style: The long retrospective sentence with its parentheses and its piled-up subordinate clauses; the broken chronology and the multiple narrators; the interior monologue that renders illiteracy and idiocy; the Gothic grotesque and the violent scene; the county map and the family genealogy as apparatus; the rhetoric of the Southern pulpit.
authors.concerns: The Southern past and the burden of history; race, slavery and the guilt of the owning family; the family, the decaying house and the doomed line; the land and the wilderness; violence, sexuality and the honour code; endurance and the human capacity to prevail.
authors.significance: Faulkner is the greatest American novelist of the period and one of the great novelists of the century: The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom! changed the form of the novel, Yoknapatawpha is American literature's most complete imaginative world, and the Nobel speech is the period's most quoted statement of the writer's duty. He is the centre of the Southern Renaissance.

authors.name: William Godwin
authors.nationality: English; Rationalist dissenting and radical philosophical prose of the 1790s
authors.identity: Dissenting minister turned philosopher, essayist and novelist; the systematic exponent of justice, private judgement and the indefinite perfectibility of the mind, and the era's most influential builder of a rational anarchism.
authors.biography: Godwin was born at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire on 3 March 1756, the son of a Strict Baptist minister, and was intended for the dissenting ministry. He was trained at Hoxton Academy and served as an independent pastor at Ware and then at St Alphage's, Canary Street, in London, where he began to move from Calvinism towards Socinian and philosophical opinions. Publicly avowing deist and anti-monarchical views, he resigned his pulpit around 1783 and lived thereafter by his pen, befriending Samuel Holcroft, Thomas Holcroft and the circle of the radical book-seller and reform. An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793) made his name overnight; his second edition, rewritten while the printers waited, already softened the strictest conclusions. In 1797 he married Mary Wollstonecraft, whose Rights of Men and Vindication of the Rights of Woman he had long admired and whose Memoirs of the Author of a Vindication of the Rights of Woman he published in 1798 to general disgust; their daughter Mary, later Mary Shelley, was born a few months before Wollstonecraft's death in childbed. The reopening of the Baker Street lecture rooms after the Gagging Acts, his campaign against the war with France, the essays of the Political Register and the Friend of the People, and the Enquiry's revised third edition of 1798 kept him at the centre of a shrinking radical public. His later career was long and increasingly domestic and literary: the novels and romances of the 1800s, the Life of Chatham, histories of England and of Commonwealth, a Life of Marat and the Essays; and the Courtauld lectures on necromancy. He was by then regarded as a venerable rather than a dangerous figure, died in London on 7 April 1836, and was buried beside Wollstonecraft in Bunhill Fields.
authors.profile: His work is a continuous prose project rather than a body of separate genres: a philosophical treatise on justice and government, a series of novels that test the same principles in the passions, and a large occaional literature of biography, history, political pamphlet and review essay. Enquiry Concerning Political Justice states the system in three parts on political justice, its application to government and punishment, and the morals and opinions that a rational institution would produce; the Dissertation on First Principles of Government of 1795 reissued the political portions as a shorter, more practical argument. Caleb Williams (1794) is at once a gothic narrative and an illustration of how institutional power and curiosity destroy an individual. His late prose turned to the history of ideas, to literature and to elaborate accounts of opinion, superstition and civilisation, in a manner closer to learned essay than to polemic.
authors.style: A severe, unhurried argumentative prose of long balanced periods, abstract nouns and repeated key terms, in which a proposition is stated, qualified and restated until its consequences are exhausted; occasional polemic sharpened by irony and by plain contempt for argument from authority. In the novels and romances the same analytical habit appears as an insistence on motives, causes and the chain of reasoning that betrays a character, and the narrative voice is frequently intrusive and explanatory. Late work is digressive, bookish and cumulative rather than epigrammatic.
authors.concerns: Private judgement and the duty to follow the evidence of one's own reason; the opposition of justice to institution, and of general utility to promise, contract and allegiance; the critique of government, of coercion, of property held by inheritance and of marriage as an exclusive compact; the perfectibility of the mind and the gradual withering of political authority; the relation of opinion to virtue, and of literature and narrative to moral improvement; the morality of publication and the duty to tell truth.
authors.significance: Godwin supplied the first fully reasoned anarchism in English and gave radical thought of the 1790s its most systematic text; the Enquiry became a recognised authority for reformers, and its fame was such that it was read widely, answered in the press and cited in Parliament. He shaped, more than any single writer, the philosophical temper of the Romantic generation that grew up under the reputation of his principles, and his domestic history, as Wollstonecraft's husband and Mary Shelley's father, places him at the source of Frankenstein. His novels established the analytical, socially-caused English narrative; his Essays and histories kept the eighteenth-century argument about superstition, opinion and civilisation alive into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his education at Hoxton Academy and the precise dating of his early pastorates at Ware and in Canary Street are variously given in the biographies; the full account of his marriage and of Wollstonecraft's death depends on his own Memoirs, published in 1798 and immediately contested by readers as injudicious.

authors.name: William Harrison Ainsworth
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Popular historical and romance novelist; editor of Bentley's Miscellany
authors.biography: William Harrison Ainsworth was born in Manchester, the son of a lawyer, and was educated at Manchester Grammar School. He was called to the bar but abandoned law for writing and moved to London. His early work included the novel Rookwood (1831-32), which established his reputation with its mixture of Gothic and highwayman romance. He succeeded Dickens as editor of Bentley's Miscellany and contributed to it his most famous novel, Jack Sheppard (1839), which provoked controversy over its glorification of a criminal. He went on to publish a long series of historical and Newgate romances, including Old St. Paul's, Windsor Castle, and The Lancashire Witches, which appeared well beyond the Romantic period.
authors.profile: Ainsworth is the popular novelist who bridged the late Gothic of the Romantic period and the Victorian romance of criminal history and topography. His subjects are real places and historical events populated with legendary and criminal figures; his mode is melodramatic, fast-paced, and strongly visual.
authors.style: Melodramatic prose; strong sense of place and topography; embedded illustrations (often by George Cruikshank); serial structure with cliff-hangers; the Newgate Calendar as source and model.
authors.concerns: London's criminal and historical past; the legend of the highwayman and the apprentice; the Gothic survival in popular narrative; the visual dimension of fiction and illustration; the moral boundaries of popular entertainment.
authors.significance: Rookwood fixed the modern Dick Turpin legend and inaugurated Ainsworth's long career as the most prolific popular novelist of early Victorian London; his serial novels represent a transitional form between Romantic Gothic and Victorian sensation fiction.

authors.name: William Hazlitt
authors.nationality: English; Radical criticism and the periodical essay of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Critic, essayist and polemicist, the leading English reviewer of his generation and the most forceful writer of character-sketches in prose, who also held an office in the Excise and tried for a while to earn his living as a painter.
authors.biography: Hazlitt was born at Maidstone, the son of a Unitarian minister who took the family to America during the Revolutionary war and returned to England in the middle of the 1780s. He was educated for his father's profession at the Warrington Academy, where the new philosophical theology was taught, and for a short time afterwards attended lectures in Scotland; he never took holy orders. He tried painting, working as a portrait painter and as an engraver of portraits, and he held a salaried post in the Excise, which for years made his literary work possible. From about 1813 he wrote theatrical and political criticism for the liberal journals of the day, most importantly for Leigh Hunt's Examiner, and he contributed essays and reviews to other periodicals until his death. He lectured on poetry and on the drama in London in 1818, 1819 and 1820, and his published lectures, his characters of the dramatists and his series of contemporary portraits made him the most discussed critic of the period. A long attachment, exposed in a printed confession in 1822, coincided with the breach of his marriage and with years of quarrel, debt and ill health; his books were sold to meet his obligations, and he died in Frith Street, Soho, in September 1830, in the poor circumstances his own essays had often described.
authors.profile: His work divides between criticism, philosophical writing and the essay. He edited and annotated the English poets, wrote continuously on the stage, and practised in his magazines and lectures the character-writing that he defined as the critic's proper task; his earliest and most ambitious book was a treatise on the human mind in its action, which he long considered the foundation of all his other work. His prose subjects are the theatre and the poets, the painting of Italy, the political conflict of his own decade, and the temper of the ages he read. He is at his strongest in the short analytical sketch, where a single quality of a writer or a public figure is followed out to its consequences.
authors.style: An assertive, colloquial and heavily accented prose, built on balance, contrast and blunt verdict, with a sustained rhetorical momentum in the paragraphs of the essays; a habit of opening with a general proposition and closing with a personal one; imagery drawn from painting, from the theatre and from the landscape, and an unapologetic first person that turns criticism into a form of autobiography.
authors.concerns: The association of ideas as the ground of mind and of taste; liberty of thought and the hatred of tyranny, in politics as in the theatre; the distinction between power and genius; imagination as the faculty that enlarges sympathy; the prejudice and self-interest of the established orders; the relation of the age to its writers.
authors.significance: He is the principal English critic between Johnson and the Victorians, and his method of describing the dominant faculty of a writer set the pattern for later character-writing; his Shakespearean and Jacobean criticism, his account of the poets of his own age, and his essays on the principles of the mind together form the most complete body of Romantic critical prose outside German idealism, and his political writing is a primary record of English Radicalism in the years of repression.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his student years in Scotland and of his first contributions to the periodicals are not exactly settled, and the chronology and the details of the attachment described in the printed confession of 1822 are known chiefly from his own account, which is a literary representation rather than a record.

authors.name: William Langland
authors.birthplace: probably Cleobury Mortimer, Shropshire, or the Malvern Hills area
authors.nationality: English (West Midlands)
authors.identity: poet; satirist; allegorist
authors.biography: Almost everything known of him is inferred from Piers Plowman, whose dreamer 'Will' is a long-clothed clerk of the Malvern country, married, and living in London in poverty among the Cornhill folk; the poem's A-text (c. 1367–70), B-text (c. 1377–79), and C-text (c. 1386–88) show a career of continuous revision. He is commonly identified with the William Langland recorded at Oxford and in London in the 1390s, though the identification is uncertain.
authors.profile: Author of Piers Plowman, the greatest English allegorical poem: a sequence of dream visions in which Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest amid the estates of fourteenth-century England.
authors.style: Unrhymed alliterative long lines of extraordinary range — satiric, homiletic, apocalyptic, tender; the allegorical dream vision fused with estates satire and biblical exegesis; the personification of abstract virtues with concrete social observation.
authors.concerns: The reform of society and church through penance and truth; the theology of grace and merit; poverty, labour, and the social order.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Gower, the third summit of Ricardian poetry; Piers Plowman became the rallying text of reformist and radical traditions (it was read by the rebels of 1381 and printed by the Tudor reformers) and one of the most studied poems in English.
authors.uncertainty: Biography almost entirely conjectural; the attribution of the poem rests on manuscript rubrics and internal evidence.

authors.name: William Law
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Nonjuring clergyman and devotional writer, author of A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1728) and of the Christian perfection tracts that shaped Methodist and Anglo-Catholic piety.
authors.biography: Born at King's Cliffe in Northamptonshire in 1686, he was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and held a fellowship there. He refused the oaths to the Hanoverian succession in 1715, lost his fellowship and spent the following decade as a schoolmaster in London. Retiring to his birthplace in 1727, he lived there, writing and governing his household, until his death in 1761. In 1726 he entered the stage controversy with an attack on theatrical entertainment as a snare of Satan; in 1728 A Serious Call applied the rules of devotion to the ordinary hours of a gentleman's or a lady's day. From the 1730s his letters on the spirit of prayer and on the spirit of faith set him against Bishop Warburton; with the help of the lawyer William Bryan he edited and translated Jacob Boehme and printed a selection of Boehme's works in 1745.
authors.profile: A practical diviner of the daily closet, whose prose makes the whole of life, and not its religious intervals, an offering.
authors.style: Plain, urgent, exact devotional prose; moral portraiture and example; a rule-of-life cadence of precept, reproof and prayer; later a mystical exuberance of type and figure.
authors.concerns: The universality of devotion; Christian perfection and the death of self-will; church, oath and civil obedience; the stage, dress and the amusements of the world; the hidden God of Boehmean mysticism.
authors.significance: The Serious Call made him the most read English devotional writer between Bunyan and the Tractarians; it formed the religious imagination of Samuel Johnson and of the Oxford movement, and his mystical writings fed Methodist and Anglo-Catholic holiness.
authors.uncertainty: His reasons for conforming outwardly after 1727 are debated, and the serial publication of his letters makes their chronology awkward.

authors.name: William Lecky
authors.nationality: Irish; the history of morals and the rationalist historian
authors.identity: Historian and philosopher; the author of History of European Morals, the great rationalist history of the Victorian age.
authors.biography: Born William Edward Hartpole Lecky near Dublin on 26 March 1838; he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and made his name with The Leaders of Religious Opinion in Ireland (1861), A History of the Rise and Influence of the Spirit of Rationalism in Europe (1865) and A History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne (1869). He sat as an MP for Dublin University from 1895 and died in London on 22 October 1903.
authors.profile: William Lecky wrote the great rationalist histories of the Victorian age: A History of European Morals and The Spirit of Rationalism in Europe made him the central historian of the rise of modern unbelief and the most influential Irish historian of the century.
authors.style: The historical survey of opinion and morals; the rationalist argument by narrative; the candid treatment of persecution and fanaticism; the plain, dignified, historical prose; the liberal moral judgement.

authors.name: William Lily
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
authors.profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
authors.concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
authors.significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.

authors.name: William Lloyd Garrison
authors.nationality: American; the Garrisonian reform press of Boston and the immediatist abolitionist movement
authors.identity: Journalist, editor and agitator; the founder and editor of The Liberator and the chief architect of American immediate-emancipation doctrine, of the reform newspaper as an instrument of mass moral agitation, and of the moral-suasion wing of the movement.
authors.biography: Garrison was born at Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 10 December 1805, the son of a sailing captain of difficult circumstances who emigrated to Europe and died abroad, and he grew up in partial want. He was apprenticed as a boy to a Newburyport printer, worked in Boston composing rooms, and by his early twenties was printing and editing on his own account; he took up the temperance cause, protested the treatment of seamen, and was at first friendly to the colonisation enterprise. He became agent for the American Colonization Society in 1828, but the friendship of Benjamin Lundy and his growing conviction that the society was a plan for expelling rather than freeing the enslaved turned him to immediate emancipation. On 1 January 1831 he began The Liberator in Boston with the famous resolution not to equivocate, not to retreat and to be heard, and it ran weekly for thirty-four years to 1865. The New England Anti-Slavery Society followed in 1832, the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833, and the movement's mail, its meeting-house and its agent's lives were attacked: a mob tried to seize him in 1835 and the post office excluded abolitionist matter from Southern delivery. His principles widened into a general reform programme of nonresistance, women's rights and moral suasion, and he broke with the political abolitionists and with most of his former allies in 1840 over the participation of women and over his refusal of voting and office-holding as support for a slaveholding constitution. The disunion slogan of the 1840s and his public burning of the Fugitive Slave Law and of a pro-slavery sermon in the 1850s expressed the same logic; the Thirteenth Amendment and the end of slavery in 1865 allowed him to close the Liberator. He lived his last years in Boston, engaged in women's suffrage, education and prison and labour reform, and died in New York on 24 May 1879 at his daughter's house. He left behind the movement he founded and the model of the reform editor who makes a weekly paper into a book of argument.
authors.profile: His literary medium was the periodical: four thousand weekly numbers of The Liberator, with its leading articles, its reprinted testimony, its correspondence, its poetry and its documentary appendix, together with the open letters to public men, the remonstrances to legislatures, the 1832 tract on the colonisation society, and the speeches of his two lecture tours in Britain. He wrote also pamphlets of doctrine on the character of the federal compact as an agreement with slavery, and a large body of correspondence which is itself part of the movement's literature. His editorial practice is itself a literary achievement: he built a paper out of letters, testimony, and reprinting, and made the aggregate of documents into argument.
authors.style: A plain New England prose of high moral pressure, in which short declarative sentences and anaphora of resolution give way to long periods of indictment; directness deliberately courted, with the plain style of Quaker remonstrance fused to the jeremiad and to the revival address. The prose shifts between the editorial we, the first-person vow and the second-person arraigning of the reader, and it is unreservedly figurative, turning on the language of blood, compact, altar and judgment.
authors.concerns: Immediate and unconditional emancipation without compensation; the Constitution and the churches as compacts with slavery; moral suasion as the means of reform against political and clerical management; the identity of the slave's cause with the freedom of speech and of the press; the rights of women as inseparable from the rights of the enslaved; nonresistance, pacifism and the refusal of oaths and office; the brotherhood of humanity and the sin of colonisation and of prejudice.
authors.significance: Garrison converted American abolition from a charitable and gradualist project into a mass movement with its own vocabulary, its own press and its own full-time agents, and The Liberator remains the model of the reform periodical that makes an agitation. His intransigent rhetoric, and his willingness to be hated, made slavery a national question of conscience rather than of policy, and his quarrels over politics, women and the Constitution shaped the party and clerical lines of the movement for thirty years. He is the central figure of the sectional literature of the 1830s and 1840s and a defining instance of the Romantic reform writer whose paper is his book.
authors.uncertainty: The day of his birth is given as 10 December 1805 in most accounts and as 12 December in some official biographical notes. The details of his apprenticeships and of the first years of his own printing and editing are recorded mainly from his own later reminiscence and from the memories of associates, and the chronology of his conversion from colonisation agency to immediatism in 1828-29 is variously assigned between the influence of Lundy, his own reading and his quarrel with society managers. His authorship of unsigned leading articles in his own paper is a matter of editorial convention rather than of itemised record.

authors.name: William Makepeace Thackeray
authors.nationality: English; the Victorian novel and periodical satire
authors.identity: Novelist, satirist, travel writer and periodical essayist; the great comic-satirical novelist of the 1840s and 1850s and Dickens's chief rival in the monthly-part market.
authors.biography: Born in Calcutta on 18 July 1811, the only child of Richmond Thackeray, a revenue official of the East India Company, and Anne Becher; he was sent to England in 1817 and educated at Charterhouse and Trinity College, Cambridge, which he left without a degree in 1830. An inheritance from his father was lost in part through the failure of two Indian banks (1834) and in part through his own gambling and the collapse of a newspaper he had financed; he read law at the Middle Temple, and in 1836 married Isabella Shawe, after which he turned to journalism to support a growing family. He was Paris correspondent and then part-owner of the Constitutional, and from 1837 contributed to Fraser's Magazine, the New Monthly Magazine and Punch (from 1842), where the Yellowplush Papers, The Book of Snobs (1846-47) and the Snob Papers established the persona of a moralizing dandy. Vanity Fair appeared in monthly parts in 1847-48 and made him famous; from 1851 he lectured in England and in America on the English humourists and the Georges. He stood unsuccessfully for Parliament in 1857 and edited the Cornhill Magazine from 1860, where his last completed novels were serialised. He died in London on 24 December 1863.
authors.profile: Thackeray wrote the Victorian novel against the Victorian novel: his narrators are intrusive, worldly, digressive and self-accusing, and they refuse the consolations that Dickens's plots allow. His subject is the machinery of social self-presentation — the snob, the adventuress, the place-seeker, the respectable man who has quietly ruined himself — and his method is a cool retrospective narration that knows the ending from the first page and passes judgement while withholding it. He is a historian of manners by instinct: Esmond and The Virginians reconstruct the eighteenth century from its newspapers, its memoirs and its genealogies, and Henry Esmond is the first English novel to be narrated throughout in the first person by a man of a past age in that age's own idiom.
authors.style: Retrospective narration and the extended aside; irony so even that sympathy and contempt are deliberately indistinguishable; chapter titles and epigraphs that moralise in miniature; an exact notation of small social transactions (a bow, a dinner, a debt); the rejection of coincidence and of the heroic climax; a prose that carries the rhythms of the eighteenth-century essayists.
authors.concerns: Snobbery and the fear of social shame; vanity and the market in reputation; marriage as a commercial transaction; the gentleman as a problem in morals rather than in birth; the illusions of family history; the corruption of politics and of the press; the vanity of human wishes, in a register nearer Ecclesiastes than to satire.
authors.significance: Vanity Fair is the most complete English novel of the 1840s about the 1840s, and the phrase itself passed into the language as the name of the world of display. With Dickens he established the monthly-part novel as the dominant cultural form of the decade. His historical novels taught the nineteenth century how to imagine the eighteenth, and his lectures and Cornhill editorship made him an arbiter of the literary profession. Trollope, Meredith, Wilde and the whole line of the novel of manners descend from him.

authors.name: William Mason
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet, dramatist, and garden theorist, author of blank-verse tragedy and essays on poetry and gardening, associated with pre-Romantic sensibility.
authors.biography: Mason, sometimes called the younger to distinguish him from a kinsman of the same name, was educated at Westminster School and Queen's College, Oxford, and inherited an estate at Nuthall in Nottinghamshire. His Poems (1754) won immediate attention, and he followed with elegiac and didactic verse, including essays on eclogues and on garden design. He turned to blank-verse historical tragedy with Elfrida (1763) and Caractacus (1769), and he wrote a Life of his friend Thomas Gray. A keen gardener and man of letters, he corresponded widely within the literary circles of the age. He died at Nuthall in 1797.
authors.profile: A poet, dramatist, and man of letters whose work spans the sentimental elegy, the garden essay, and declamatory blank-verse tragedy, reflecting the movement from Augustan taste toward pre-Romantic feeling.
authors.style: Correct, elevated blank verse; didactic ease in the essay poem; mournful sensibility in the elegy; and a rhetorical, declamatory grandeur in the tragedies, with a cultivated taste for the picturesque garden.
authors.concerns: Taste and the design of gardens; moral and heroic virtue in historical drama; friendship, biography, and literary memory; melancholy, retirement, and religious consolation.
authors.significance: A transitional figure of later-eighteenth-century letters whose garden writings and blank-verse tragedy reflect the spread of picturesque taste and pre-Romantic sensibility; his Life of Gray is an important literary document.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given variously in biographical accounts; the precise chronology of his poems and essays, and his relation to the older William Mason of the same family, require careful distinction.

authors.name: William Morris
authors.nationality: English; the narrative poem, the socialist romance and the literature of design
authors.identity: Poet, designer, translator and socialist; the author of The Earthly Paradise and News from Nowhere, and the most complete artist of the Victorian age.
authors.biography: Born at Walthamstow on 24 March 1834, the son of a financier; he was educated at Marlborough and Exeter College, Oxford, where he met Edward Burne-Jones and was drawn to the Pre-Raphaelites. He founded the firm of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co in 1861, masterminded the Kelmscott Press in 1891, and wrote The Defence of Guenevere (1858), The Life and Death of Jason (1867), The Earthly Paradise (1868-70), Sigurd the Volsung (1876) and News from Nowhere (1890). He was a founder of the Socialist League in 1884 and died at Hammersmith on 3 October 1896.
authors.profile: Morris wrote the great narrative poetry of the Victorian age: his subject is the heroic and the mythic past, and his method is the long, fluent, objective narrative in which the story carries the emotion. He was also the first English writer to make the utopian romance a serious political form, and his work on design, printing and the decorative arts made him the central figure of the English arts and crafts movement.
authors.style: Long, even, unrhymed or heroic-couplet narrative; the archaic and the Norse-Teutonic vocabulary; the objective storytelling with little psychological commentary; the catalogue of the decorative and the natural; the dream-vision frame.
authors.concerns: The heroic past and the death of the hero; love and fate; the Norse and classical myths; labour, craft and the dignity of work; socialism and the utopian future; the natural world and the decorative art.
authors.significance: Morris is the central figure of the English arts and crafts movement and one of the great narrative poets of the century: The Earthly Paradise and Sigurd the Volsung restored the long poem to English literature, News from Nowhere is the classic English socialist utopia, and his designs, printing and prose romances shaped the modern book and the modern fantasy.

authors.biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
authors.profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
authors.concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
authors.significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.

authors.name: William of Ockham
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
authors.profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
authors.style: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
authors.concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
authors.significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.

authors.name: William Paley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Archdeacon of Carlisle and the century's master of utilitarian divinity, whose Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) made happiness and obedience the whole of duty.
authors.biography: Born at Peterborough in July 1743, the son of a clergyman who later became headmaster of the free school at Giggleswick, he was educated at that school and at Christ's College, Cambridge, where an idle first year was retrieved by hard reading, a fellowship and a tutorship that made him the most successful coach of his university. He took orders in the Church of England, held a succession of northern livings at Musgrave, Dalston and Appleby, and was made archdeacon of Carlisle in 1782. His Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) soon became a standard university text and the target of reviewers who thought it reduced virtue to expedience. His argument for the undesigned coincidence of the apostolic letters appeared in the Horae Paulinae of 1790, and his Evidences of Christianity (1794) and Natural Theology (1802), both later than the period covered here, long stood as textbooks in the schools of theology. He was installed at Bishopwearmouth in his last years and died on 25 May 1805.
authors.profile: A clear-eyed churchman who wrote the morality of obedience and the evidences of belief for a reading public that wanted argument in plain terms.
authors.style: Conversational, concrete and unornamented; cases and common-life examples carried through a single rule; the plainness of a good tutor, with a polemicist's patience in reply.
authors.concerns: Utility as the measure of duty; the obligations imposed by civil government and by the established church; the evidences of revelation and the credibility of miracle; design in nature and the relation of pleasure to virtue.
authors.significance: He gave utilitarian ethics its first systematic ecclesiastical form and supplied the teleological argument in the version Mill and Darwin had to answer; his textbooks governed English theological education for a generation.
authors.uncertainty: The order in which his preferments and lecture texts were produced is complicated by posthumous edition and by his own revisions.

authors.name: William Robertson
authors.nationality: Scottish
authors.identity: Minister of the Church of Scotland, principal of Edinburgh and royal historiographer, whose History of America (1777) made philosophical history a professional discipline in Britain.
authors.biography: Born at Borthwick near Langholm in 1721, the son of a country clergyman, he was educated at Edinburgh, entered the ministry and served a southern parish before he removed to Edinburgh and became one of the city's most fashionable preachers. The History of Scotland (1759) established him as the leading historian of his generation, and the great work on the reign of Charles V (1769) displayed his command of archives and of the European sixteenth century. Appointed principal of the University of Edinburgh in 1762 and royal historiographer, he at last produced the History of America (1777), three volumes of sources, geography, conquest and character which were translated across Europe, and the History of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth (1787). His disquisition on the ancients' knowledge of India came in 1791, after the period with which this record deals. He was a leader of the moderate interest in the church, a friend of Hume, Smith, Ferguson and Home, and died in 1793.
authors.profile: The historian of states and religions who wrote narrative as instructed enquiry, combining Scottish church politics with the sources of the Spanish and Italian archives.
authors.style: Dignified, lucid, well-paced narrative; disquisitions and notes carrying the argument; a preacher's moral seriousness and an editor's restraint; balance of character, cause and consequence.
authors.concerns: The origins of American civilisation and conquest; the political and religious history of Europe in the age of Charles V; feudal law, ranks and the rise of the commons; the character of Queen Elizabeth and of the Reformation.
authors.significance: He professionalised historical writing in Britain, gave the English-speaking world its standard account of America's discovery and conquest, and set the model of philosophic narrative that Gibbon and the nineteenth century inherited.
authors.uncertainty: His early parish years are documented thinly, and his use of other men's manuscripts and collections has been re-assessed by later scholarship.

authors.name: William Roper
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: biographer; lawyer; More's son-in-law
authors.biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
authors.profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
authors.concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
authors.significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.

authors.name: William Roscoe
authors.nationality: English; the commercial, dissenting and abolitionist culture of Liverpool, and the Whig historical scholarship of the revolutionary decade
authors.identity: Merchant, banker, lawyer, historian of Renaissance Italy, abolitionist poet and patron of arts and botany; the first considerable English historian of the Medici and one of the earliest and most consistent English poet-critics of the slave trade.
authors.biography: Roscoe was born at Liverpool on 8 March 1753, the only surviving son of a small trader in the market-garden and bowling-green line, and was educated at the dissenting and proprietary schools of the town before being bound apprentice to a Liverpool merchant house. Called upon to support a widowed mother and young sisters, he studied law, was admitted an attorney, and in the years of the town's enormous prosperity built up a mercantile and banking business of large reputation, at the same time pursuing scholarship, botany and the collection of pictures and books with a single-mindedness unusual in a tradesman. The Wrongs of Africa, a poem, published in two parts in 1787 and 1788 for the cause of the abolition committee, made him at once known beyond Liverpool and marked him permanently in his own town, where the slave-trade interest was powerful and where he was afterwards burnt in effigy. His two great historical works, the Life of Lorenzo de' Medici called the Magnificent of 1796, with its introductory view of Italian history, and the Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth of 1805, were built partly out of manuscripts which he obtained in Italy at his own cost, and gave the English reading public its first scholarly account of the age in which the revival of letters and the Reformation met. Elected in 1806 one of the first two members for the newly enfranchised town, he sat a single session, voting against the trade and against the party that had returned him, and withdrew from Parliament with his banking interests already embarrassed. The commercial crash of the post-war years ruined his firm about 1814-1815, and the sale of his library, his garden and his pictures, which included the sculptures and the collection of prints he had gathered with so much care, was a public event in the town. He gave his remaining years to letters, to botanical and artistic patronage and to the small poems and fables for children of which The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast is the survivor, and he died at Liverpool on 27 June 1831, leaving a reputation as the scholar-tradesman of the great trading community and a family of sons, one of whom wrote his Life.
authors.profile: His work runs in three unrelated veins, all of them considerable. The abolitionist poem The Wrongs of Africa, in two parts, puts the whole progress of the trade, from the coast of Africa through the voyage to the colonies, into the heroic line of the moral plea. The Italian histories are scholarly narrative biography on the model of the eighteenth-century life, prefaced by disquisitions on the state of Italy and of the papacy and resting on printed authorities and on transcripts gathered in Italian libraries. The nursery verse, of which the insect masquerade is the most durable, belongs to the new small-book trade of the years after 1800, and he wrote also fables, translations from the Italian, botanical and historical essays, and the manuscripts on painting and on his own collection which his son printed after his death.
authors.style: A decorous and deliberate eighteenth-century prose, grave in the histories, heavily qualified in the argumentative prefatory disquisitions, and circumstantial in the narrative of courts and councils; the abolition verse is in a stately heroic line of moral appeal, addressed to the conscience of a nation, with the enumeration of instances doing the rhetorical work. The nursery pieces are light, quick and plain, in short common metres of the child's ear, and show the same gift of concrete description that marks his botanical writing.
authors.concerns: The sin and the national interest of the slave trade, and the duty of a trading community to examine its own gains; the civilisation of Renaissance Italy, the papacy, and the fate of Italian liberty; the study of the age of the Medici as a case in the relation of letters, power and church; the encouragement of the fine arts and of botany in a commercial town; the instruction and the innocent fancy of very young children; the education and patronage of a manufacturing community.
authors.significance: The Wrongs of Africa was the first of the great abolition poems and gave the movement its earliest sustained verse indictment, published by the friends of the cause in the year of the first petition to Parliament; his Italian biographies founded the scholarly English study of the Renaissance and long stood as the standard accounts of Lorenzo and of Leo the Tenth. As a banker, collector and civic patron he made Liverpool a provincial centre of art and learning, and his ruin and the sale of his collections became the cautionary case of the merchant-scholar; his nursery poem passed into the childhood of two continents.
authors.uncertainty: A few older biographical accounts place his birth in London rather than Liverpool, and the day of his death is given as the 27th or the 30th of June 1831. The extent of his responsibility for anonymous pamphlets on the trade and on the affairs of the town is not settled, and the account of his Italian manuscript researches depends largely on the prefaces to the two lives and on the family Life edited by his son, which is a defence as well as a record.

authors.name: William Shakespeare
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and actor; the central figure of English literature, author of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and two narrative poems.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 April 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, son of the glover and alderman John Shakespeare; educated at the Stratford grammar school. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582 (children Susanna, and the twins Hamnet and Judith), and by 1592 was established in the London theatre (Greene's 'upstart crow' attack). He wrote for the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from 1594) and its successor the King's Men (from 1603), was a sharer in the Globe (1599) and Blackfriars, and prospered as actor, playwright, and investor, buying New Place in Stratford in 1597. The narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594) were his first printed works; the Sonnets appeared in 1609. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there on 23 April 1616; the First Folio of his plays was published by Heminges and Condell in 1623.
authors.profile: The supreme dramatist of the language and its greatest poet of the human interior: his histories, comedies, tragedies, and romances transformed every genre they touched, and his sonnets reinvented the Petrarchan sequence as a meditation on love, time, and art.
authors.style: Unmatched range of register — from the euphuistic wit and sonneteering of the early plays to the metaphysical density of the great tragedies and the late romances' verse of reconciliation; mastery of blank verse, prose, and song; the invention of character through soliloquy.
authors.concerns: Kingship, legitimacy, and the body politic; love, jealousy, and self-deception; time, mortality, and the immortality of art; the theatre itself as the mirror of nature; conscience and the divided self.
authors.significance: The measure of English literature: his works constitute the largest single achievement of the language's canon, translated into every tongue and performed continuously since the 1590s.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of the plays rests on printed dates, records of performance, and stylistic evidence; the authorship of several plays (Titus Andronicus, Pericles, Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen, Edward III, Sir Thomas More) is collaborative, and the biographical record between 1585 and 1592 is a blank.

authors.name: William Shenstone
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: English poet and gardener, of the Leasowes, a pastoral writer and letter-writer whose ornamental garden became an eighteenth-century landmark of taste.
authors.biography: Shenstone was born into the Worcestershire gentry, educated at Halesowen and at Pembroke College, Cambridge, and succeeded to the family estate, the Leasowes, which he laid out as a celebrated ornamental farm. He wrote the pastoral poem The Schoolmistress (1742) and other pastorals, songs, and epistles, publishing his Poetical Works in a collected form in 1763. His letters and his critical and horticultural writings circulated among friends and were partly printed after his death, notably his account of the Leasowes and his essays on taste and gardening. He died unmarried at the Leasowes in 1763.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, rural sympathy, and sensibility, and a practised maker of landscapes; his verse and his garden together embody the cult of the picturesque and the ornamented farm.
authors.style: Gentle, conversational pastoral and occasional verse; Spenserian and Thomsonian descriptive influence; a warm, familiar, sometimes digressive epistolary prose; and an aesthetic of artless variety.
authors.concerns: Rural life and the education of rustic minds; taste, the picturesque, and the design of landscapes; retirement, friendship, and benevolence; and the integration of art and nature.
authors.significance: A central figure in the development of the English landscape garden and picturesque taste, and a respected pastoral and epistolary writer linking Thomson's nature poetry to later sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birthplace is given variously in accounts of the Worcestershire parish; the precise dating of his garden improvements and of the circulation of his letters and essays remains partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Tyndale
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Bible translator; reformer; martyr
authors.biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
authors.profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
authors.style: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
authors.concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
authors.significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.

authors.name: William Wells Brown
authors.nationality: African-American; the slave narrative, the travel narrative, the novel and the drama
authors.identity: Writer, historian, playwright and abolitionist; the first African-American novelist and the first African-American playwright.
authors.biography: Born into slavery near Lexington, Kentucky, in 1814; he escaped in 1834, took the name of a Quaker helper, and worked as a steam-boat steward on Lake Erie, where he assisted other fugitives across to Canada. He lectured for the American Anti-Slavery Society from 1843, travelled to Britain in 1849 and stayed five years, and wrote the first African-American novel (Clotel, 1853), the first African-American travel book, and a pioneering history of black Americans. He settled in Boston and died there on 6 November 1884.
authors.profile: Brown wrote the whole range of African-American literature for the first time: the narrative, the travel book, the novel, the play and the history. Clotel is the first African-American novel, and it takes the story of Thomas Jefferson's black daughter as the vehicle for an indictment of the founding father and the slave system; his travel writing and his histories invented a black public prose in America.
authors.style: First-person testimony with documentary documents; the multiple plot of separated slave families; the travel narrative with statistics and anecdote; the historical compilation; the melodramatic scene of sale and escape.
authors.concerns: Slavery and the hypocrisy of the American republic; the founding fathers and race; the black family destroyed by sale; the North and the fugitive; Britain and Europe as places of relative freedom; the history of black achievement.
authors.significance: Brown is the first African-American novelist, playwright and travel writer and one of the founders of black American literature: Clotel is the first novel by an African-American, The Escape the first play, and his histories the first substantial black historiography in the United States.
authors.uncertainty: 4 further writings are documented on this author's record but are not given separate work records here, because no description of them can be supported from a surviving text. No work catalogued here carries a disputed, conjectural or shared attribution, and every one of them was published under the author's own name between 1847 and 1867.

authors.name: William Wordsworth
authors.nationality: English; the Lake school of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Poet and theorist of poetry of the Lake District, the maker of the lyrical ballad and of the Romantic blank-verse meditation, and the most authoritative English voice on nature, memory and the growing mind.
authors.biography: Wordsworth was born at Cockermouth in Cumberland, the second of five children of an estate agent, and was educated at Hawkshead grammar school and at St John's College, Cambridge. He walked the mountains in his student holidays, and stayed in France in 1790 and again in 1791-95, when the early promise of the Revolution made a lasting impression on him and a daughter, Caroline, was born there. Settling with his sister Dorothy first at Racedown and then at Alfoxden in the west, he began in 1797-98 the collaboration that produced the anonymous ballad volume; in 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson, and after the Keswick years he settled at Allan Bank and then at Rydal Mount, where he lived until his death. The later decades brought public employment as Distributor of Stamps for Westmorland, an unfinished scheme of a philosophical poem, the volumes of 1807, The Excursion of 1814, the Ecclesiastical Sketches of 1822, and a national fame marked by a civil pension and by the laureateship accepted in 1843. The autobiographical poem on the growth of a poet's mind, long revised and never published by its author, appeared after his death in 1850. His politics moved from revolutionary sympathy to a conservative attachment to church, state and the rural order, a change much used against him by later critics.
authors.profile: His work divides between the lyrical ballads and short lyrics of humble life, the blank-verse meditations and sonnets, and the long philosophical and autobiographical poem planned as The Recluse, of which only The Excursion was published in his lifetime. He wrote also a prose guide to his own country and a large body of letters and memoranda, and his Preface to Lyrical Ballads is the period's most quoted theory of poetry. His subjects are the mountain landscape, the labouring poor, children, grief and endurance, and the education of the imagination, and his characteristic form is the poem that passes from an observed scene to a history of the mind that remembers it.
authors.style: A deliberate plainness of diction drawn from ordinary speech, rising in the blank verse to great weight of syntax; long suspensive periods, apostrophe, repetition and an insistent use of general nouns; in the lyrics a song-like regularity of stanza and refrain, and in the sonnets a compressed and Latinate turn. The manner changes markedly between the deliberate roughness of the experimental ballads and the serenity of the later lyrics.
authors.concerns: The mind's intercourse with nature and the shaping power of landscape; memory and the pleasure re-created in tranquillity; the imagination as a moral and perceptual faculty; childhood as the season of vision; the loss of revolutionary hope and its consolation in duty, the church and the permanences of rural life; the proper language and audience of poetry.
authors.significance: With the collaborators of the ballad volume he opened the English Romantic period and supplied its most durable account of how poems are made; his blank-verse meditation and his autobiographical poem founded the modern poetry of the self's education, and his sonnets helped revive the English sonnet. His practice and his theory together changed the subject and the diction of English verse, and his later career remains the central case in the long argument about the relation between Romantic poetry and political allegiance.
authors.uncertainty: The sequence of his French sojourns of the early 1790s and the circumstances of his daughter Caroline's parentage and upbringing are recorded imperfectly and are variously stated in the biographies.

authors.name: William Wycherley
authors.nationality: English
authors.identity: Restoration dramatist; author of the two fiercest comedies of manners, The Country Wife (1675) and The Plain Dealer (1676), whose savage wit and moral seriousness about lust, hypocrisy, and jealousy set him apart from his more elegant contemporaries.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640–41 at Clive, Shropshire, educated at Queen's College, Oxford, the Middle Temple, and in France (where he briefly became a Catholic before reverting). He served at sea in the Second Dutch War and moved in court circles. His plays — Love in a Wood (1671), The Gentleman Dancing-Master (1672), The Country Wife (1675), and The Plain Dealer (1676) — won him fame but little money. A secret marriage to the Countess of Drogheda ruined him; he spent seven years in the Fleet for debt, was briefly reconciled to his father, and lived in obscurity and poverty until, in old age, he married a young heiress days before his death on 1 January 1716, leaving his manuscripts to the young Alexander Pope.
authors.profile: The most savage and morally earnest of the Restoration comic writers, whose comedies expose sexual appetite, jealousy, and hypocrisy with a harsh, near-Jacobean intensity beneath the manners-comedy surface.
authors.style: Biting, energetic dialogue; intrigue plotting drawn from Molière and the Spanish; sexual frankness and dark comedy; and a moral seriousness unusual in the comedy of manners.
authors.concerns: Lust, jealousy, and cuckoldry; social and sexual hypocrisy; the corruption of town and country; misanthropy and plain dealing; and the vanity of pretence.
authors.significance: The Country Wife and The Plain Dealer are among the greatest English comedies; Wycherley's moral ferocity influenced Congreve and later satirists, and his late-life friendship with Pope linked Restoration and Augustan letters.
authors.uncertainty: Wycherley's birth year is uncertain (c. 1640–41) and much of his biography, especially his marriages and debts, is recorded only in anecdotal sources.

authors.name: Wulfstan
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (West Saxon/Mercian)
authors.identity: homilist; lawgiver; archbishop
authors.biography: Bishop of London 996–1002, bishop of Worcester 1002–1016, and archbishop of York 1002–1023; the principal counselor and draftsman of law under kings Æthelred II and Cnut.
authors.profile: Author of the Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014), the most famous Old English sermon, preached in the crisis of the Danish invasions; the Institutes of Polity (a treatise on the orders of Christian society); the Canons of Edgar; the law codes of Æthelred and Cnut; and a series of eschatological homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis) warning of the approaching end.
authors.style: A distinctive, urgent rhythm built on two-stress phrases, alliteration, intensifying repetition, and cumulative word-pairs; the most recognizable idiolect in Old English prose.
authors.concerns: National repentance; social order and the duties of each estate; the coming of Antichrist; the law of God as the foundation of earthly law.
authors.significance: With Ælfric, the last great writer of Old English prose; his homilies and law codes shaped the response of the English church and state to the conquest of 1016.

authors.name: Zitkala-Sa
authors.birthplace: Yankton Reservation, Dakota Territory, United States
authors.nationality: Yankton Dakota; the Native American autobiography, the short story and the essay of Indian policy
authors.identity: Writer, musician and activist; the first Native American woman to write and publish her own life story, and a leading campaigner for Native American citizenship.
authors.biography: Born Gertrude Simmons on the Yankton Reservation in Dakota Territory on 22 February 1876; she was educated at White's Manual Labor Institute in Indiana and Earlham College, taught at Carlisle Indian School, and published her stories and essays in the Atlantic Monthly and Harper's from 1900. She co-founded the Society of American Indians in 1911, edited American Indian Magazine, and campaigned for the citizenship act of 1924. She died in Washington on 26 January 1938.
authors.profile: Zitkala-Sa wrote the first Native American autobiography by a woman and the founding texts of modern Native American literature: her 'Impressions of an Indian Childhood' and 'The School Days of an Indian Girl' record the trauma of assimilation with a controlled anger that no white writer of the period could match, and Old Indian Legends is the first collection of Dakota stories by a Native author. She was also a formidable political writer, and her essays on the land, citizenship and the Bureau of Indian Affairs shaped federal policy.
authors.style: Autobiographical narrative in a clear, restrained first person; the remembered detail of Dakota life; the ironic contrast between Dakota and white values; the spoken cadence of the oral tradition in the legends; the direct political essay.
authors.concerns: Assimilation, boarding school and the loss of language; Dakota culture, legend and kinship; land, allotment and the destruction of the reservation; citizenship and the rights of Native people; the memory of childhood and the mother.
authors.significance: Zitkala-Sa is the first Native American woman to publish her own life story and the founder of modern Native American literature: her autobiographical essays are the central Native American texts of the period, Old Indian Legends is the first Native-authored collection of Dakota tales, and her activism made her a leading figure in the struggle for Native American citizenship.
