authors.name: Zora Neale Hurston
authors.nationality: American; the folk novel, the anthropology of the Black South and the woman's voice
authors.identity: Novelist, folklorist and anthropologist; the great recorder of Black Southern folk culture and the author of Their Eyes Were Watching God, the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance.
authors.biography: Born in Notasulga, Alabama, on 7 January 1891 and raised in Eatonville, Florida, the first incorporated Black town in America; she worked as a maid, a waitress and a manicurist, studied at Howard and at Barnard under Franz Boas, and did fieldwork in Florida, New Orleans and Haiti. Jonah's Gourd Vine (1934), Mules and Men (1935), Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Tell My Horse (1938) and Moses, Man of the Mountain (1939) followed; she died in poverty at Fort Pierce, Florida, on 28 January 1960, and her work was recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s.
authors.profile: Hurston wrote the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and the great record of Black Southern folk culture: Their Eyes Were Watching God made a Black woman's voice and a Black woman's desire the centre of an American novel, and Mules and Men preserved a body of folklore that would otherwise have been lost. Her prose — the free indirect rendering of Eatonville speech — is one of the period's great achievements.
authors.style: Free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension; the frame of the tale-teller and the 'lying' session; the folk idiom transcribed as literature; the metaphor drawn from the natural world; the novel structured by a woman's marriages.
authors.concerns: Race, the Black South and the folk community; the Black woman's desire and self-making; marriage, work and independence; the Eatonville town and its 'lying' culture; the hurricane, nature and God; the migration north and the return south.
authors.significance: Hurston wrote the finest African American novel of the period and the greatest record of Black Southern folklore: Their Eyes Were Watching God is a permanent American novel, Mules and Men preserved a whole oral culture, and her recovery in the 1970s made her the central woman writer of the Harlem Renaissance.

authors.name: Ælfric Bata
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon
authors.identity: Latin colloquy writer; schoolmaster
authors.biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
authors.style: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
authors.concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
authors.significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.

authors.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (West Saxon)
authors.identity: homilist; hagiographer; grammarian; translator
authors.biography: Educated at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold, the leading figure of the Benedictine Reform; monk and mass-priest at Cerne Abbas (c. 987–1005); first abbot of Eynsham (1005–c. 1010). The greatest and most prolific writer of Old English prose.
authors.profile: Author of the two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints (c. 993–998), the Grammar and Glossary (the first Latin grammar in a European vernacular), the Colloquy, translations of Genesis and other Old Testament books (the Old English Hexateuch), De temporibus anni, pastoral letters, and numerous shorter homilies and treatises.
authors.style: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of extraordinary clarity and control — a deliberately plain style designed to be read aloud and understood; careful avoidance of apocryphal excess.
authors.concerns: Orthodox teaching for clergy and laity; the dignity and capacity of the English language; the education of the young; resistance to superstition and error.
authors.significance: The culmination of the Old English prose tradition; his works circulated more widely than any other vernacular prose of the period and influenced English religious writing for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; several works are attributed to him on stylistic grounds.

authors.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
authors.nationality: Anglo-Saxon (West Saxon)
authors.identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
authors.biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
authors.profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
authors.style: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
authors.concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
authors.significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.

works.title: 'A Castaway'
works.description: Published in the collection Portraits in 1870 and the greatest Victorian poem spoken by a prostitute: the monologue of a woman of the town who has become rich and respectable and finds her life hollow.
works.plot: The speaker, the courtesan Eulalie, reads the prim diary of her girlhood and confronts her present self in the mirror, recalling the steps by which she fell and setting her trade beside the hypocrisies of a society that buys and sells women in marriage, and refuses the sentimental alternatives of repentance or death.
works.significance: 'A Castaway' is the most important Victorian poem about prostitution and one of the finest dramatic monologues of the century: it gives the woman her own voice and refuses both the sentimental and the punitive ending, and it is a central text of Victorian feminist poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is the dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker.

works.title: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge'
works.form: Short story; war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: Published in 1890 and the most famous American short story of the nineteenth century: a Confederate planter's escape from execution exists only in the final moment of his life. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Ambrose Bierce; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Peyton Farquhar stands on a bridge over Owl Creek with a rope round his neck; the rope breaks, he falls into the water, escapes the bullets, swims downstream, and walks all night to his home and his wife — and then the story returns to the bridge, where his body hangs, and the escape is revealed as the last thought of a dying man.
works.significance: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' is the most anthologised American short story of the century and one of the foundations of the modern short story: its manipulation of time and its revelation of the escape as a dying illusion influenced writers from O. Henry to Borges, and it remains the model of the ironic American story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the common soldier: the plain first-person account, the exact vocabulary of the trench, the ration, the march and the casualty, and the understatement that carries the horror. The author's characteristic manner is the short, precisely engineered story with a reversed or delayed ending.
works.context: 1862 and 1890: the Union occupation of northern Alabama, the laws of war, the American cult of the planter-hero, and the 1890s vogue for the trick story. The record dates the work as composed in 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Peyton Farquhar; his wife; the Federal scout disguised as a Confederate soldier; the soldiers of the hanging party
works.structure: A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: 'Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street'
works.description: Published in Putnam's Monthly in 1853 and the greatest American short story: the account of a Wall Street lawyer's clerk who answers every request with the words 'I would prefer not to'. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The narrator, a lawyer, hires Bartleby as a copyist; Bartleby copies perfectly for a while and then refuses, without explanation, to do anything but copy — and finally to do anything at all; he is removed to the Tombs, where he dies of self-starvation against the wall.
works.significance: 'Bartleby' is one of the most analysed stories in world literature and the founding text of the modern literature of the office: its phrase 'I would prefer not to' has become the central modern statement of passive resistance, and it stands at the origin of Kafka, Beckett and the literature of the absurd.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The 1850s, Wall Street and the new commercial office, the American economy of speculation, and the growth of the bureaucratic city. The record dates the work as composed in 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; realist novel of common life.

A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: 'Because I could not stop for Death'
works.form: Lyric poem; pastoral elegy, first issued in 1890
works.description: Written about 1863 and first published in 1890: the single most famous American poem, in which Death comes as a gentleman caller and the speaker rides with him toward eternity. It is a verse work of 1890 by Emily Dickinson; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The speaker is collected by Death and Immortality in a carriage; they pass the school, the fields and the setting sun, and arrive at a house that is a grave, and the poem ends with the recognition that the journey has lasted centuries.
works.significance: 'Because I could not stop for Death' is the central poem of American literature and one of the greatest lyrics in English: its domestic allegory of death and its final image of eternity have made it the most anthologised American poem.
works.meter: Six four-line ballad stanzas, mostly iambic tetrameter and trimeter, with slant rhyme.

works.title: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors': Is the Classification Sound?
works.description: Published in Fraser's Magazine in December 1868 and the most effective single piece of Victorian feminist polemic: an argument against the legal classification of married women with criminals, idiots and minors.
works.plot: Cobbe takes the legal doctrine of coverture and reads it literally: the married woman can make no contract, hold no property, sue no one and be sued by no one, exactly like the lunatic and the infant; she demonstrates the consequences through cases of deserted and abused wives and demands the reform of the law.
works.significance: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' is one of the founding documents of English feminism and gave the campaign for the Married Women's Property Acts its most memorable argument; the essay is still the standard short statement of the legal position of the Victorian wife.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
works.context: The 1868 debate on the Married Women's Property Bill, the doctrine of coverture, and the case of the deserted wife. The record dates the work as composed in 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

works.title: 'I heard a Fly buzz — when I died —'
works.form: Lyric poem; pastoral elegy, first issued in 1896
works.description: Written about 1862 and first published in 1896: the deathbed scene in which the mourners wait for the King and the room is filled with the sound of a fly. It is a verse work of 1896 by Emily Dickinson; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The speaker lies dying, the watchers have gathered, the wills and the keepsakes are divided, and at the moment of expectation — 'the Windows failed' — the fly intervenes and the poem ends in the blank light.
works.significance: 'I heard a Fly buzz' is one of the greatest short poems in American literature and the central text of Dickinson's ironic theology: its refusal of consolation, and the fly that fills the place of God, make it a permanent challenge to the religious poetry of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is hymn and ballad measures broken by slant rhyme and irregular stress.
works.context: The 1860s, the New England deathbed, the Calvinist expectation of salvation, and the American essay on death. The record dates the work as composed in 1862 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: 'Invictus'
works.description: Written in 1875 and published in 1888: the most quoted English poem of heroic defiance, the stoic's answer to fate. It is a verse work of 1875 by W. E. Henley; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The speaker, in the darkness of a fate that has beaten him, thanks whatever gods may be for his unconquerable soul; under the bludgeonings of chance his head is bloody but unbowed, and he declares himself the master of his fate and the captain of his soul.
works.significance: 'Invictus' is one of the most quoted poems in English and the central Victorian poem of stoic defiance: it gave the language its great statement of self-mastery, it has been cited by statesmen and prisoners across the world, and it is the poem by which Henley is permanently known.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is short, hard, rhymed verse in the ballad and the song measure.
works.context: 1875: the Victorian crisis of faith, the stoicism of the age of Darwin, and Henley's own experience of illness and amputation. The record dates the work as composed in 1875 and first published in 1875 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: 'Leaves from the Mental Portfolio of an Eurasian'
works.description: Published in 1909 and the founding Asian-American autobiography: a Eurasian writer's account of her divided inheritance and her decision to speak for the Chinese. It is a prose work of 1909 by Sui Sin Far; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Eaton recounts her English childhood, her Chinese mother, the prejudice she met in Montreal and San Francisco, her work as a journalist, and the moment when she chose to identify herself publicly as Chinese rather than pass as white, in order to write on behalf of the immigrant community.
works.significance: 'Leaves from the Mental Portfolio of an Eurasian' is the first Asian-American autobiography and a central document of American multiracial identity: its account of the choice to claim a stigmatised ancestry made it a founding text of Asian-American literature and of the American literature of passing.

works.title: 'Life in the Iron-Mills'
works.description: Published in the Atlantic Monthly in April 1861, the month the Civil War began, and the founding text of American literary realism: a night in the life of an iron mill town. It is a prose fiction work of 1861 by Rebecca Harding Davis; it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Hugh Wolfe, a Welsh puddler, sculpts a figure of a woman out of the mill's waste korl and is accused of theft by his employer's son; his cousin Deborah takes the blame, and Hugh dies in prison, while the mill owner's daughter looks at the sculpture and understands nothing.
works.significance: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' is the first great American work of industrial fiction and the founding text of American realism: it preceded Howells, Garland and Dreiser by a generation, and its portrait of the worker's hunger for beauty is one of the permanent scenes of American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is documentary detail of mill work and company housing.
works.context: The 1850s-60s: the iron mills of Wheeling, the immigrant Welsh and Irish workers, and the American industrial revolution before the war. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1861 and first published in 1861 and it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Hugh Wolfe; Deborah Wolfe; Janey; Kirby; Doctor May; Mitchell
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.

works.title: 'Marriage' (1888)
works.description: Published in August 1888 and the essay that provoked the greatest marriage debate of the century: an argument against the indissolubility of marriage. It is a prose work of 1888 by Mona Caird; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: 'Marriage' argues that the legal indissolubility of marriage makes the wife a chattel, that the double standard is enforced by law, that many marriages are legalised prostitution, and that women must be free to leave intolerable unions; the essay calls for equal divorce, for the economic independence of wives and for a single moral standard.
works.significance: 'Marriage' is a founding document of English feminism and the most radical Victorian argument on marriage: it drew over 27,000 replies in the periodical press, it made Caird the most notorious woman in England, and it set the agenda of the New Woman novel for the next decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical essay with a plain and logical argument.

works.title: 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae'
works.form: Lyric poem (in The Second Book of the Rhymers' Club, 1894)
works.description: Published in the Second Book of the Rhymers' Club in 1894 and the most famous English Decadent lyric: the poem of the lover who has betrayed his beloved and cannot forget her. It is a verse work of 1894 by Ernest Dowson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The speaker recounts the nights of wine and roses and the women he has held, and after each stanza returns to the refrain 'I am desolate and sick of an old passion, / Yea, hungry for the lips of my desire: / I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion.'
works.significance: 'Non sum qualis eram' is the central English Decadent poem and one of the most quoted lyrics in the language: its refrain entered common speech, and its fusion of classical Latin and modern self-disgust made it the model for the modern poem of sexual betrayal.
works.meter: Five five-line stanzas of iambic metre, with the Latin epigraph from Horace and the refrain drawn from Catullus.
works.context: 1894: the Rhymers' Club, the London of the music hall and the restaurant, and the Latin poetry of Catullus and Propertius. works.title: 'Resistance to Civil Government' ('Civil Disobedience')
works.description: Published in Aesthetic Papers in 1849 after Thoreau's night in the Concord jail in 1846: the founding modern argument for the primacy of individual conscience over the state. It is a prose work of 1849 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Thoreau argues that a government that permits slavery and wages an unjust war forfeits the citizen's obedience; he describes his refusal to pay the poll tax, his imprisonment, and the principle that the individual must withdraw cooperation from injustice even at the cost of punishment.
works.significance: 'Civil Disobedience' is the founding text of the modern theory of non-violent resistance: it shaped Tolstoy, Gandhi, Martin Luther King and the whole tradition of conscientious objection, and it is one of the most influential essays in the language.

works.title: 'Richard Cory'
works.description: Published in 1897 and one of the most anthologised American poems ever written: the rich gentleman who is envied by the whole town and shoots himself. It is a verse work of 1897 by Edwin Arlington Robinson; it belongs to The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem describes Richard Cory, the gentleman who is admired and envied by the people of the town, and then ends in two lines: 'And Richard Cory, one calm summer night, / Went home and put a bullet through his head.'
works.significance: 'Richard Cory' is one of the most famous American poems of the century: its two-line reversal and its study of the gap between appearance and reality made it a permanent part of the American canon, it has been set to music and adapted many times, and it is the poem by which Robinson is most widely known.

works.title: 'Self-Reliance'
works.description: Published in Essays: First Series in 1841 and the most influential essay in American literature: the argument that the individual must trust his own thought against the whole weight of society, custom and history.
works.plot: Emerson denounces conformity, consistency, philanthropy and travel as escapes from the self, and insists that 'whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist'; the essay builds an ethic of self-trust from the doctrine that the soul in each person is the same universal soul.
works.significance: 'Self-Reliance' is the central statement of American individualism and one of the most quoted essays in the language: it has shaped American ideas of the self, of originality and of dissent from Emerson's own day to the present.

works.title: 'Slavery in Massachusetts'
works.description: Delivered at Framingham on 4 July 1854 and published in the Liberator: Thoreau's furious response to the rendition of the fugitive slave Anthony Burns from Boston. works.title: 'Song of Myself'
works.form: Long poem (section of Leaves of Grass)
works.description: The central poem of Leaves of Grass: fifty-two sections in which the poet identifies himself with all American life — the child, the runaway slave, the trapper, the prostitute and the reader. It is a verse work of 1855 by Walt Whitman; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem begins with 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself', moves through the grass as the flag of the soul, the body and the senses, the catalogue of American occupations and persons, and ends with the poet's death and his continuing presence in the reader's hands.
works.significance: 'Song of Myself' is the central poem of American literature and the greatest American statement of democratic identity: it made the long free-verse poem possible and its first lines are perhaps the most famous in American poetry.

The author's characteristic manner is free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora.

works.title: 'Tennessee's Partner'
works.description: Published in 1869 and the finest of Harte's stories of male friendship: the tale of Tennessee and his partner in a California mining camp. It is a prose fiction work of 1869 by Bret Harte; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch.
works.plot: Tennessee, a gambler who once ran off with his partner's wife, is tried by an impromptu court of miners for robbery; his partner offers the court all his gold for Tennessee's life and is refused, and after the hanging he carts the body home and buries it, then wastes away and dies with a vision of Tennessee coming to meet him, while the narrator records the camp's belated recognition of his loyalty.
works.significance: 'Tennessee's Partner' is one of the founding American stories of male friendship and a key text in the literature of the American West: its irony and its sentiment made it the model for the western story of loyalty and violence.

works.title: 'The Hound of Heaven'
works.description: Written in 1889 and published in Poems in 1893: the most famous English religious poem of the century, and the record of the soul's flight from the God who pursues it. It is a verse work of 1893 by Francis Thompson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The speaker describes his flight from the 'Hound of Heaven' through the worlds of nature, art, love and human companionship, and ends with the voice of God: 'All things betray thee, who betrayest Me' and 'I am He Whom thou seekest! / Thou dravest love from thee, who dravest Me.'

works.title: 'The Marshes of Glynn'
works.description: Published in 1878 and the greatest American nature poem of the South: the poet's vision of the Georgia marshes at dawn. It is a verse work of 1878 by Sidney Lanier; it belongs to The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poet goes out among the marshes of Glynn at dawn and feels himself dissolved into the ocean of light and air; the poem moves from the description of the marsh to a vision of the infinite, in which the self is lost and found in the divine unity of the natural world.
works.significance: 'The Marshes of Glynn' is the finest American nature poem between Whitman and Frost and the central poem of the Southern landscape: its musical structure and its mystical vision made it a landmark, and it is the poem in which Lanier's theory of verse as music is most completely realized.

works.title: 'The Monkey's Paw'
works.form: Short story; ghost story, first issued in 1902
works.description: Published in 1902 and the most famous English horror story of the century: a mummified paw grants three wishes, and the third is made in terror. works.title: 'The Yellow Wallpaper'
works.description: Published in the New England Magazine in 1892 and the greatest American story of the 1890s: the diary of a woman confined by her doctor husband for a 'nervous condition', and of the wallpaper she comes to see as alive.
works.plot: The narrator is taken to a colonial mansion for a rest cure and forbidden to write; she becomes obsessed with the yellow wallpaper in her room, sees a woman behind its pattern, and at the end tears it off to release her, crawling round the room while her husband faints.
works.significance: 'The Yellow Wallpaper' is the central American text on the medical treatment of women and one of the most important stories ever written about mental illness: it is read as a feminist indictment of the rest cure, as a Gothic study of confinement, and as a permanent challenge to the medical profession.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
works.context: The 1890s: the rest cure of S. Weir Mitchell, the medical treatment of women's mental illness, and the American woman's movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the narrator; John, her physician husband; Jennie, his sister; the woman behind the wallpaper
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: 'Thirty Bob a Week'
works.description: Published in Ballads and Songs in 1894 and the first great English poem about the office worker: the monologue of a clerk living on thirty shillings a week. It is a verse work of 1894 by John Davidson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance.
works.plot: The clerk describes his life of work, marriage, children and debt, and insists, against the moralists and the socialists, that his narrow life is his own and not to be pitied, ending with the image of men who 'fall, face forward, fighting, on the deck'.
works.significance: 'Thirty Bob a Week' is the founding English poem of the white-collar worker and one of the most technically original poems of the century: its colloquial voice and its refusal of melodrama made it a model for the modern dramatic monologue, and Eliot named it as an influence.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The stanza is the ballad stanza, the four-stress and three-stress lines rhyming on the even lines. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the dramatic monologue.
works.context: 1890s: the London clerk, the new white-collar class and the monthly salary, and the socialist critique of the 'black-coated proletariat'. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.characters: the clerk, the speaker; his wife; his children
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

works.title: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore
works.description: John Ford's notorious tragedy of incestuous love between the siblings Giovanni and Annabella in Parma, and of Giovanni's murder of his sister and his entrance bearing her heart on his dagger.
works.plot: Governing himself by passion rather than religion, Giovanni declares his love to his sister Annabella; she yields, marries the noble Soranzo to conceal her pregnancy, is discovered, and is killed by Giovanni, who then dies fighting Soranzo's followers.
works.significance: The most powerful and most discussed Caroline tragedy; it pushed the theatre's moral limits further than any contemporary play and remains a central text in the study of early modern incest and tragic passion.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained lyric intensity, with Ford's characteristic repetition and lament.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix in Drury Lane, probably c. 1629-33, and published in 1633 with a remarkable author's dedication defending the play's seriousness.

works.structure: Five acts of a single, tightly driven tragic action with subordinate comic plots, ending in the public catastrophe at the cardinal's feast.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

works.title: 'To Build a Fire'
works.form: Short story; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1908 in the revised version and the greatest American story of the wilderness: a man freezes to death in the Yukon because he has built his fire in the wrong place. It is a prose fiction work of 1908 by Jack London; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A cheechako travels alone through the Yukon at seventy-five below zero, against the advice of an old-timer; he breaks through the ice, soaks his feet, builds a fire under a spruce tree, and the snow from the tree falls and extinguishes it, after which he cannot light another, and the story ends with the dog watching him die.
works.significance: 'To Build a Fire' is the purest American naturalist story and one of the most perfect short stories in English: its reduction of a human life to the failure of a single fire is the naturalist thesis in narrative form, and it is the most anthologised American wilderness story ever written.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third.
works.context: 1902-08: the Klondike trail, the science of hypothermia, the American naturalist view of nature as indifferent, and the fashion for the survival story. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.
works.characters: the man, a newcomer to the Yukon; his dog; the old-timer from Sulphur Creek
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider.

works.title: 'Vitaï Lampada'
works.form: Lyric poem; political verse, first issued in 1892
works.description: Published in 1892 and the most famous English poem about the public school: the cricket field as the training ground for the empire. It is a verse work of 1892 by Henry Newbolt; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poem moves from a school cricket match, where a boy holds the game while the fate of the school hangs on the last ball, to a battle in the desert where the same schoolboy, now a soldier, rallies the broken ranks with the cry his captain once gave him, 'Play up! play up! and play the game!'
works.significance: 'Vitaï Lampada' is the most quoted and most parodied poem of the imperial ideal: it fixed the English equation between sport and empire, it became the classic text of the public school ethos, and it is the indispensable document of the mindset that went to war in 1914.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The author's characteristic manner is ballad measure with a strong refrain.
works.context: 1892: the English public school cult of games, the imperial campaigns of the 1890s, and the debate on the moral value of sport. The record dates the work as composed in 1892 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the schoolboy batsman, later the soldier; his captain
works.structure: A single poem, read as one continuous whole from its opening to its close.

works.title: 'Walking'
works.description: Published in the Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, a month after Thoreau's death: the great essay on walking, wilderness and the preservation of nature. It is a prose work of 1862 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Thoreau argues that walking is a religious exercise, that the west and the wild are the true America, and that 'in wildness is the preservation of the world'; he calls for the protection of the forests and the creation of public parks.
works.significance: 'Walking' is the founding text of the American conservation movement and one of the most important essays on the natural world: its call to preserve the wilderness led to the national park system and to the modern environmental essay.

Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences.
works.context: The 1850s, the settlement of the American west, the railroad, and the early conservation movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; nature essay and the rural observation.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.

works.title: 'We Wear the Mask'
works.form: Lyric poem (in Majors and Minors, 1895; Lyrics of Lowly Life, 1896)
works.description: Written in 1895 and published in Majors and Minors and then in Lyrics of Lowly Life: the central American poem of the mask, in which the black speaker addresses a deceitful world. works.significance: 'We Wear the Mask' is the central American poem about race and concealment and one of the most quoted poems in English: its image of the mask has become the key term of African-American literary criticism, and it is the founding text of the literature of double consciousness.
works.meter: Three five-line stanzas of iambic tetrameter and trimeter, rhymed aabba, with a refrain.

works.title: 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'
works.description: Delivered at Rochester on 5 July 1852 and published the same year: the greatest American political speech of the nineteenth century, and the most complete indictment of American hypocrisy. It is a prose work of 1852 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Douglass tells his audience that the Fourth of July is not his, that the slave's wrongs are shared by every American, and that the republic's professions of liberty are mocked by the slave market in the capital; he ends with a call to abolish slavery and to make the Declaration true.
works.significance: The Fourth of July address is the central American oration and the founding text of the black critique of American democracy: its phrases have entered the language, and it remains the most powerful statement of the gap between American ideals and American practice.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
works.context: The year 1852, the Fugitive Slave Law, the abolitionist movement, and the American celebration of the Fourth of July. The record dates the work as composed in 1852 and first published in 1852 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.title: 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'
works.description: Published in Sequel to Drum-Taps in 1865 and the greatest American elegy: a lament for Abraham Lincoln built on the lilac, the western star and the hermit thrush. It is a verse work of 1865 by Walt Whitman; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poet brings the lilac bloom to the coffin of the president, follows the funeral train across the country, listens to the hermit thrush sing in the swamp, and comes to accept death as part of the cycle of the natural year.
works.significance: The 'Lilacs' elegy is the central American poem of mourning and one of the great elegies in English: its three symbols and its free-verse structure made the public elegy possible in the modern idiom, and it is the founding text of the American poetry of grief.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The poem is elegiac, the mourning stanza repeated through the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora.
works.context: The year 1865, Lincoln's assassination and funeral train, the end of the Civil War, and the elegiac tradition from Milton and Shelley. The record dates the work as composed in 1865 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.

works.title: 'Why I Am a Pagan'
works.description: Published in 1902 and the most important Native American essay of the period: a defence of Dakota religion against Christian conversion. It is a prose work of 1902 by Zitkala-Sa; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.

works.title: 'Wife-Torture in England'
works.description: Published in the Contemporary Review in 1878 and the most important Victorian essay on domestic violence: a documented account of wife-beating in England, with cases from the police courts and the assizes.

works.title: 1914 and Other Poems
works.description: The five 1914 sonnets and the Georgian lyrics of the poet who became the emblem of the war's first year. It is a verse work of 1915 by Rupert Brooke; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric; Trench Lyric and the War Poem.
works.plot: The collection contains the five war sonnets of 1914 — 'Peace', 'Safety', 'The Dead' (two), 'The Soldier' — together with the earlier Georgian lyrics, 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester', 'The Great Lover' and the South Seas poems.
works.significance: 1914 and Other Poems gave the war its rhetoric of sacrifice: 'The Soldier' — 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England' — is one of the most famous English poems of the century, and the book's posthumous publication made Brooke the myth of the golden generation.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Georgian sonnet and the rhymed lyric.

works.form: Novella; ghost story, first issued in 1880
works.description: Published in 1880 and Oliphant's strange masterpiece of the supernatural: a French cathedral town is besieged by invisible forces after its dead return. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Margaret Oliphant; it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The small town of Semur is suddenly evacuated, as its inhabitants find themselves driven out by the presence of the dead; the mayor Martin Dupin, the aristocrat M. de Bois-Sombre, the visionary Paul Lecamus, who alone stays within the walls, and the women of the mayor's household each narrate their account of the visitation, and the town is left changed by the experience of a reality beyond the visible.
works.significance: A Beleaguered City is one of the finest Victorian supernatural tales and a profound meditation on grief and belief: Oliphant turns the ghost story into a theological fiction about the communion of the dead, and it has been recognised as a forerunner of the modern uncanny story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1880: the Victorian interest in spiritualism, the French provincial setting, and Oliphant's own bereavements of the 1870s. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Martin Dupin, the mayor; Agnès Dupin, his wife; Madame Dupin, his mother; Paul Lecamus; M. de Bois-Sombre; Jacques Richard; the Curé
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Margaret Oliphant Wilson Oliphant. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Bold Stroke for a Wife
altTitles: A Bold Stroke for a Wife: A Comedy
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The author's best-known comedy, a comic campaign in which a clever lover wins an heiress by personating the several guardians who have been charged with keeping her from him. It is a sustained satire on religious and political cant, each guardian standing for a species of enthusiasm.
works.plot: A colonel loves a young woman whose fortune is controlled by four guardians, a Quaker, a nun, a Whig knight and a Tory general, each pledged to keep her from him. He and his friends disguise themselves as a Quaker preacher, a confessor and a petitioning politician, and by playing each guardian's own cant against him they obtain her consent. The exposure of the tricks reconciles the guardians and the lovers marry.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comedy about enthusiasm as a social language, and a central text for the study of the woman dramatist in the Augustan theatre; its personation structure was a model for later comedy of disguise.
works.meter: Predominantly prose dialogue with verse epilogue, the humour carried by the stylised cant of each guardian - Quaker plainness, Romish casistry, party phraseology.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1718, in the season of the Whig split and the Jacobite scare, and held a repertory place through the century; its portraits of Quaker and papist enthusiasts draw on the controversy comedy of the previous age.
works.characters: Colonel Fainwell; Miss Lovely; Obadiah Prim the Quaker; the nun Perpetua; Sir Simon Affection; the Tory general
works.structure: Five-act comedy built on a single conceit of successive personation, with an epilogue and prologue addressing the party divisions of the house; the disguise scenes are arranged as set pieces of mimicry.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name, though the pirated acting editions of the century alter its lines.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Marriage and women's conduct
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
The city and urban life
movements: Comedy of Manners
The Restoration Theatre

works.title: A Book of Airs
works.description: The songbook of 1601 by Thomas Campion (words and music) and Philip Rosseter (music): twenty-one lute songs and one masque song, including 'My sweetest Lesbia', 'Follow thy fair sun', 'When to her lute Corinna sings', and 'I care not for these ladies' — the volume that made Campion the supreme English lyricist of the lute-song golden age.
works.plot: No plot: the airs set the commonplaces of love — carpe diem, the lady's beauty, the lover's complaint, the joys of country over court — each song a perfected miniature in the courtly lyric tradition.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan lute-song tradition — poetry and music fused as nowhere else in the language, and a touchstone for every later English lyricist.
works.meter: Short-line lyric stanzas of exquisite finish — trochees, iambs, and the quantitative experiments of Campion's 'observations' — composed for music and printed with tablature.
works.context: Published 1601 in the first great decade of the English ayre, alongside Dowland's and Jones's books; Campion's preface defends the new union of English verse and music against the metrical pedants.
works.characters: the singer-lover; Lesbia; Corinna; the beloved ladies
works.structure: A printed songbook of twenty-one airs plus the masque song, arranged for voice and lute (some also for viol consort), in the standard format of the English ayre books.
works.attributionNotes: Words by Campion throughout, with one masque song; music by Campion for half the airs and by Rosseter for the rest.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: A Book of Miscellaneous Lyrics
works.description: Published in 1878 and Skipsey's major collection of lyrics: poems of the Northumbrian countryside, the sea, the cottage and the pit. It is a verse work of 1878 by Joseph Skipsey; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem.
works.plot: The volume contains 'The Haymakers', 'The Cranes', 'The Wreck', 'The Starling' and 'The Old Church', and moves between the natural world and the industrial one.
works.significance: A Book of Miscellaneous Lyrics contains some of the finest minor English poetry of the century and shows the range of working-class literary culture in the 1870s.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is plain ballad stanzas and simple lyric metres.
works.context: The 1870s, the Northumbrian landscape, and the Victorian taste for the rural lyric. The record dates the work as composed between 1860s and 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Book of Nonsense
works.description: Published in 1846 and the first collection of English nonsense verse: seventy limericks written for the children of the Earl of Derby. It is a verse work of 1846 by Edward Lear; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
works.plot: Each page presents a limerick about a person of a place — a man of the hills, a lady of Wales, a young person of Dee — whose odd behaviour or physical peculiarity produces a comic catastrophe, with a drawing that completes the joke and a final line that repeats or echoes the first.
works.significance: A Book of Nonsense invented the modern limerick and the modern nonsense book: it established the five-line form, it made nonsense a respectable genre for children, and it was the model for the whole tradition of comic verse from Lear's own later books to the nonsense of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity.
works.context: 1846: the Victorian nursery and its books, the vogue for the comic illustrated book, and the amateur theatricals of the Knowsley household. The record dates the work as composed in 1846 and first published in 1846 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Lear's nonsense. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Brighter Sun
works.description: Selvon's first novel, published in London by Allan Wingate in 1952, follows Tiger, a sixteen-year-old Indo-Trinidadian married off to the still younger Urmilla, through his first years of adult life in the suburban village of Barataria during the Second World War. Britannica summarises its subject as East Indians and Creoles in Trinidad, their prejudices and mutual distrust, and the effect of that animosity on a young man; Wikipedia notes that the building of the Churchill-Roosevelt Highway is seen through Tiger's eyes.
works.summary: Tiger's first years of marriage, set against the war and the American presence in Trinidad: the move from the cane district of Chaguanas to Barataria, friendship with Creole neighbours, work on the highway the Americans build, a crisis in Urmilla's pregnancy and Tiger's resolve to build a better house.
works.plot: At sixteen Tiger is married by his family to Urmilla and sent from the sugar-cane district of Chaguanas to Barataria, where the couple begin life in a mud hut and Tiger farms. Away from their parents' influence they make friends with their Afro-Creole neighbours, Joe and Rita, whose brick house, with electricity and running water, Tiger envies. The couple have a daughter, and Tiger longs for a son. When the American military arrives to build a highway through the farmland, Tiger does not protest but takes work on the construction, and he tries to learn better English in order to rise. Anxious to prove himself a man, he invites his American bosses to dinner, gets drunk and beats the pregnant Urmilla. She falls ill; an Indian doctor and a Creole doctor both refuse to treat her, and an English doctor agrees to. The son Tiger wanted is stillborn. Chastened and more mature, Tiger begins to build a new house with the help of friends and neighbours.
works.significance: Wikipedia notes that it was a popular choice on the Caribbean Examinations Council's English literature syllabus for many years. It began Selvon's fiction of Indo-Trinidadian life, which Turn Again Tiger (1958) continues, and Selvon later adapted its story of Tiger and Urmilla's first year of marriage as the play Highway in the Sun (published 1991).
works.meter: Britannica found in it, for the first time, an East Indian author writing 'with such quiet authority and simple charm' about Indo-Trinidadian life; Dawes credits Selvon's work in general with an innovative use of folk idiom.
works.context: Selvon wrote it in London after 1950, looking back to the years when he served as a wireless operator and, as Peepal Tree's author profile puts it, was closely involved with the wartime American presence that provides the novel's backdrop: American bases and the highway built to serve them.
works.characters: Tiger, a young Indo-Trinidadian; Urmilla, his wife; Joe and Rita, their Afro-Creole neighbours; American supervisors on the highway; an English doctor
works.structure: A chronological narrative that follows Tiger from his wedding through the war years to the start of the new house; Dawes describes it as a novel of maturation set in a rural Indian community.
themes: Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
Class, labour and social mobility
Family, marriage and domestic life
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: A Bronzeville Mother Loiters in Mississippi. Meanwhile, a Mississippi Mother Burns Bacon
altTitles: A Bronzeville Mother Loiters in Mississippi
works.form: Poem (long narrative and dramatic poem in free verse)
works.description: A long poem by Gwendolyn Brooks on the murder of Emmett Till, published in The Bean Eaters (1960). It is told through the consciousness of a white woman modelled on Carolyn Bryant, whose husband was one of the men accused of killing the fourteen-year-old Chicago boy in Mississippi in 1955, as she makes breakfast in her kitchen after the acquittal.
works.summary: The young wife's reflections on the ballad she had imagined herself in, on the 'Dark Villain' who turned out to be a child, on her husband and her own children, and on the boy's mother; her growing revulsion from her husband.
works.plot: From childhood the woman has imagined life as a ballad, with herself as the milk-white maid, a Dark Villain and a Fine Prince who rescues her. Now, in her kitchen, burning the bacon as she makes breakfast after the trial, she finds the story will not fit: the villain was a child of fourteen, his eyes and his mother's grief haunt her, and the prince is her husband, who has killed and been acquitted. When he slaps one of their small children across the face, the blood she has been imagining seems to rise in the room, and as he embraces her she can think only of the killing. She does not scream, but a hatred for him bursts into glorious flower, bigger than all magnolias. The poem ends by pointing to the last bleak news of the ballad: 'The last quatrain.'
works.significance: Brooks's most ambitious poem in The Bean Eaters and one of the major literary responses to the Till case, unusual in imagining it through the white wife.
works.meter: Interior monologue in the third person, mixing fairy-tale and ballad diction with domestic realism and newspaper fact; recurrent imagery of red, blood and magnolias.
works.context: Emmett Till, a black Chicago teenager visiting relatives, was murdered in August 1955 after being accused of whistling at Carolyn Bryant; his mother's open-casket funeral and the acquittal of the killers made the case a catalyst of the civil rights movement. Brooks, a mother in Chicago, published the poem five years later.
works.structure: Long free-verse paragraphs of varying line length following the woman's thoughts through a single morning, with the ballad as a frame she keeps testing; the title's full stop divides it into two headline-like sentences, and the last line hands over to 'The Last Quatrain of the Ballad of Emmett Till'.
themes: Family, marriage and domestic life
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
Violence, crime and justice
movements: Postwar African American Writing: Protest and Its Critics

works.title: A Century of Dishonor
works.description: The founding book of the American Indian rights movement: seven tribes and the record of broken treaties. It is a prose work of 1881 by Helen Hunt Jackson; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Jackson documents the history of the government's dealings with seven tribes — the Delawares, the Cheyennes, the Nez Perces, the Sioux, the Poncas, the Winnebagoes and the Cherokees — through the treaties, the massacres and the broken promises, with an appendix of the Indian Rights Association's documents.
works.significance: A Century of Dishonor is the founding book of the American Indian rights movement: it was sent to every member of Congress, it changed the debate about Indian policy, and it prepared the way for the Dawes Act; as a documentary indictment it has no equal in American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary record of treaties and massacres.
works.context: The United States in 1881, the reservation system and the campaign for Indian citizenship and land title. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; lecture and popular address.
works.characters: the Seven Tribes; the commissioners; the settlers; Jackson as advocate
works.structure: A documentary record in chapters by tribe, with appendix of documents. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Helen Maria Hunt Jackson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside
works.description: Middleton's comedy of London's sexual economy: the goldsmith Yellowhammer's daughter Moll, betrothed by her parents to the decadent knight Sir Walter Whorehound, loves the poor Touchwood Junior; the city's trades in food, sex, and legitimacy — the Allwits' household, the promoters, the puritans feasting at a christening — fill the play, until Sir Walter's ruin and Moll's mock-death restore the lovers.
works.plot: Sir Walter finances the Allwits and fathers their 'children' while courting Moll; Touchwood Senior's fertility and his brother's love-plot run through the middle acts; the christening feast and the arrest of the gallants expose the city's corruptions; and the final scene, with Moll's pretended death and revival, joins the lovers and topples the knight.
works.significance: The sharpest of the Jacobean city comedies — a play that makes money, sex, and religion a single system of exchange.
works.meter: Prose and verse of Middleton's quickest, cruellest wit, with the christening scene's hypocritical feasting as its summit.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Swan in 1613 and printed in 1630; its satire of the Jacobean marriage market and puritan hypocrisy is the most scathing of the age.
works.characters: Moll Yellowhammer; Touchwood Junior; Touchwood Senior; Sir Walter Whorehound; Yellowhammer; Maudlin Yellowhammer; the Allwits; the Kixes; the promoters; the wench; the puritans
works.structure: A five-act cross-section of Cheapside — multiple households joined by Sir Walter's purse — in Middleton's most populous and corrosive comic design.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: A Child of the Jago
works.description: Published in 1896 and the most famous English slum novel of the 1890s: the childhood and death of Dicky Perrott in the Old Jago, a handful of courts in Bethnal Green. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Dicky Perrott grows up in the Jago, steals, is sent to prison, tries to go straight, and is killed by a gang at the age of seventeen; the novel's exact record of the rents, trades, shops and fights of the district is its argument.
works.significance: A Child of the Jago is the central English slum novel of the 1890s and the most influential text in the transition from the Victorian social-problem novel to modern working-class fiction; its controversy over heredity and environment made it a reference point for the sociology of poverty.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
works.context: The 1890s, the East End of London, the closing of the Old Nichol slum in 1891-95 (the model for the Jago), and the debate between philanthropy and environmental determinism. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Dicky Perrott; Old Perrott; Hannah Perrott; Josh Perrott; Father Sturt; Bill Rann; Aaron Weech; Sally Green; Looey
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Child's Garden of Verses
works.description: Published in 1885 and the most influential English children's poetry collection of the century: sixty-four poems of childhood, illness, imagination and the country house, written from the memory of Stevenson's own sickly Edinburgh childhood.
works.plot: The poems move from 'The Land of Counterpane' and the sickroom to the garden, 'The Land of Nod', 'My Shadow', the 'Swing' and 'Foreign Lands', and end with the child's view of the adult world in 'The Unseen Playmate' and 'Happy Thought'.
works.significance: A Child's Garden of Verses created the modern poetry of childhood: its child's-eye perspective and its unpatronising tone mark the break between Victorian didactic verse for children and the twentieth-century tradition of children's poetry.
works.meter: Mostly four-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter or trimeter, with a few longer lyrical forms.
works.context: The 1880s, the Victorian invention of childhood as a separate imaginative world, and the Stevenson family's Edinburgh houses. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.

works.title: A Child-World
works.description: Published in 1896 and Riley's most sustained work: a sequence of poems on a single Indiana childhood and the town that surrounded it. It is a verse work of 1896 by James Whitcomb Riley; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The sequence follows a boy and a girl through the seasons of a small-town childhood — the school, the church, the circus, the illness and death of a child, the first love and the departure — and ends with the town remembered by the grown man who has left it.
works.significance: A Child-World is Riley's most ambitious and most unified book: its sequence form and its elegiac tone made it something more than a collection of recitation pieces, and it is the finest American verse narrative of small-town childhood before Edgar Lee Masters.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse with exact phonetic spelling.
works.context: 1895-96: the Indiana of the 1850s, the American small town before the railway and the factory, and the market for the nostalgic verse narrative. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

works.title: A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
altTitles: Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
works.description: Published on 19 December 1843, the first of the five Christmas books, and the one that fixed the Victorian Christmas and the modern image of Scrooge; it sold 6,000 copies in a week and has never been out of print.
works.plot: Ebenezer Scrooge, the miser of a counting-house, is visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his partner Jacob Marley and then by the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, who show him his own childhood, the Cratchit family and the death of Tiny Tim, and his own unmourned death. He wakes on Christmas morning transformed, sends a turkey to the Cratchits, and becomes 'as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew'.
works.significance: A Christmas Carol created the modern Christmas story and the secular morality of Christmas giving, and it was Dickens's most effective single act of social persuasion. It is also the founding text of the English ghost story as a vehicle of moral argument.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
