works.title: A Clergyman's Daughter
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1935
works.description: Orwell's second novel and third book, published by Victor Gollancz on 11 March 1935. Dorothy Hare, the overworked daughter of an East Anglian rector, loses her memory and passes through vagrancy, hop-picking, a night in Trafalgar Square and a private school before returning home without her faith. It is his most formally experimental novel, with one chapter written entirely as drama, and the one he most disowned.
works.plot: Dorothy keeps house for her disagreeable widowed father, the Rector of Knype Hill, fending off his creditors, visiting parishioners, making costumes for church events and mortifying her flesh to keep her faith. After dinner with Mr Warburton, the town's disreputable atheist bachelor, she is seen in his forced embrace by the gossip Mrs Semprill. She next finds herself on the New Kent Road in London with no memory and eight days unaccounted for; she joins the vagrant Nobby and two friends, who take her last half-crown and lead her to the Kent hop fields, while Mrs Semprill's story that she has eloped with Warburton fills the newspapers. After Nobby's arrest for theft she returns to London, is turned away from respectable hotels, sleeps rough in Trafalgar Square among tramps, including the defrocked clergyman Mr Tallboys, and is arrested for vagrancy. Her father's cousin, Sir Thomas Hare, has her found, and his solicitor places her as a teacher at Mrs Creevy's fourth-rate girls' school, where her attempts at a more liberal education clash with parents who want only handwriting and arithmetic; she is dismissed without notice. Warburton arrives to say that Mrs Semprill has been sued for libel and takes her home; she refuses his proposal of marriage, though he argues that without her faith her life will be meaningless, and resumes her old routine without the self-mortification.
works.significance: Orwell called the novel 'tripe' except for the Trafalgar Square chapter, prevented its reprinting during his lifetime and left instructions that it should not be reprinted after his death, though he allowed cheap editions that might bring in money for his heirs. The Trafalgar Square night, written under the influence of the 'Nighttown' episode of Joyce's Ulysses, is the most experimental passage in his fiction. Reviewing the American edition in 1936, Vincent McHugh placed the book in the tradition of Dickens and Gissing, and the novel's social criticism falls on the hop-picking wage system and on a private school run for its fees ('It's the fees I'm after'). Richard Smyer read it as a picture of England's 'spiritual dryness'.
works.meter: Third-person narrative prose whose manner changes with the setting; the third chapter, the night in Trafalgar Square, is set out entirely as dramatic dialogue, written under the influence of the 'Nighttown' episode of Joyce's Ulysses.
works.context: Orwell used his parents' house at Southwold, on the Suffolk coast, as his base from December 1929. The hop-picking chapters draw on the journal he kept in the Kent hop fields in August and September 1931, and the school chapter on his teaching at a small private school in Hayes, West London, in 1932-33. He wrote the novel between mid-January and 3 October 1934, and Gollancz made last-minute alterations to it for fear of libel.
works.characters: Dorothy Hare; the Reverend Charles Hare; Mr Victor Warburton; Mrs Evelina Semprill; Nobby; Mr Tallboys; Sir Thomas Hare; Mrs Creevy
works.structure: Five chapters: a day at Knype Hill; amnesia, the road and the hop fields; a night in Trafalgar Square written wholly as dramatic dialogue; the school; and the return home.

works.title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
works.description: John Wesley's canonical hymnal, gathered from the brothers' earlier collections into some five hundred and twenty-five hymns, his last great editorial act and the book Methodism long sang from. He meant it as a compact scripture of heart and doctrine, its order teaching the whole Methodist way of salvation in verse.
works.plot: The collection orders the Christian and Methodist life from general hymns of praise through the acts and sufferings of Christ, the operations of the Spirit, the states of the believer, the means of grace, the sacraments, and the seasons of the year, a walk through divinity in song. Its nucleus is Charles Wesley's lyric theology, with the best of Watts, Doddridge, and the older hymnists admitted beside John's own translations and paraphrases. The editor pruned, altered, and regularized the texts of forty revival years into a single honest compass of experimental religion. Its preface states the design plainly: that the people called Methodists should own the whole of their religion and hope in one small book they could sing.
works.significance: It is the parent of almost all later Methodist hymnals and one of the most influential hymn books in the language, fixing the canon of Charles Wesley's lyrics in the worship of the whole communion.
works.meter: The common, long, short, and varied eight-line hymn metres of Augustan psalmody, the texts regularized in diction and measure by the editor.
works.context: Published in 1780 as the societies entered the last decade under John Wesley's sole governance, it deliberately canonized the revival's song against the multiplicity of earlier collections and became the standard of Methodist worship.
works.structure: An ordered hymnal in heads following the course of divinity and the church year, with preface and indices by subject and first line.
works.attributionNotes: Edited throughout by John Wesley; the majority of hymns are Charles Wesley's, with others by Watts, Doddridge, and earlier hands.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Evangelical experience and assurance
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: A Collection of Psalms and Hymns
works.description: The Wesleys' first London hymn collection, issued in 1738 for the society they met with and drawing on the psalter versions and hymns then in use among the Oxford and London methodists. It carries the earliest printed fruits of Charles Wesley's hymnwriting alongside metrical psalms and the brothers' translations.
works.plot: The collection sets David's psalms in metrical version beside hymns for the chief seasons and doctrines: Advent, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, repentance, faith, and the last things. Its prefatory address pleads the conscience of the writers in choosing and mending the old versions, and its hymns already display Charles's gift for first-person assurance and tender doctrine. The volume thus forms a bridge from the Psalm-singing of the Church of England to the full Methodist hymnody of the Bristol collections.
works.significance: It marks the moment the Wesleyan movement began to sing in print, the first public shape of the revival's lyric theology and the ancestor of the great Methodist collections.
works.meter: Common, long, and short metre psalm stanzas and hymn measures of iambic lines; the language plain and singable, after the style of the earlier methodist psalmody.
works.context: Published in London in 1738 in the months of Aldersgate and the societies' forming, after the Oxford Psalm and Hymn pocket book of 1733 and before the Bristol Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739.
works.characters: the London society
works.structure: A dual collection, psalms in metre followed by hymns arranged by seasons and subjects, with preface and occasional doxologies.
works.attributionNotes: Prepared by John and Charles Wesley; Charles is the author of the new hymns, the psalter versions being collaborative and largely rehandled from earlier hands.

works.title: A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language
works.form: Lexicography and philological writing; school and usage dictionary
works.description: The first considerable dictionary published in the United States, a single-volume compendium intended to fix American spelling, pronunciation and usage. It gathers the common English vocabulary with the new words of the republic and adds a grammatical and orthographical preface. It is the working ancestor of the great dictionary of 1828.
works.plot: The work defines the ordinary vocabulary of the language, marking parts of speech and offering usage notes rather than literary quotation. It sets out the American preferences in spelling that its author had long argued for, and it appends tables of words pronounced and spelled alike but differently written. Its front matter states the case for a national language independent of British decision. The whole is designed for the schoolroom and the counting house rather than for the scholar.
works.significance: It established the authority of the American dictionary and made the lexicon a question of national policy. Its spellings passed generally into American use. It is the necessary predecessor of the 1828 work and a document of the linguistic nationalism of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1806 after two decades of the author's spelling books and political pamphlets on language, and in the season of the American argument that a republic needed its own dictionary. Its spelling reforms answered the Federalist and nationalist claim that language is an instrument of national character. It drew on Johnson and on the technical vocabulary then entering American speech.
works.structure: Alphabetical dictionary with a doctrinal preface and appended tables; no narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.description: Published in 1884 and Jewett's most directly feminist novel: the story of a young woman who chooses medicine over marriage, and of the cost of that choice. works.title: A Defence of Poetry
works.form: Critical treatise and occasional essay of the Romantic theory of imagination; a polemical defence written in the manner of the reply pamphlet and enriched by aphoristic prose rhythm.
works.description: The period's most influential essay of poetic theory, written in a few weeks as a reply to a friend's prose argument that poetry must inculcate moral truth. It defines poetry as the expression of the imagination, morality as the calculation of the relations of action to effect, and argues that a man who is good must love the beautiful, so that the poet who only creates is the unacknowledged legislator of the world. Its aphoristic manner and its argument for the utility of the useless have made it the centre of the Romantic theory of imagination.
works.plot: The essay opens by accepting that poetry is a branch of the art whose end is pleasure, and then distinguishes reasoning, which tabulates the relations of what is known, from imagination, which represents action as it is affected by the qualities of the mind that contemplates it. It argues that poetry is connected with the principles of our nature by the same ties as language and that the reasoning and the imaginative faculties are as the measure and the harmony of composition. It passes to a history of the civilizing power of poetry, from the ballad and the drama to the great works of the age it lives in, and defends the modern poets against the charge of indifference to moral instruction. Its close asserts that the influence of the poet is all-sufficient, that poetry is the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds, and that the world's moral regeneration is the work of imagination.
works.significance: It is the most compact statement of the Romantic doctrine of imagination and, with its companion essay on the same occasion, the standard text of the defence of poetry's utility against a utilitarian age. Its definition of reason and imagination, and its claim for the poet as an unacknowledged legislator, have governed most later discussion of the social function of literature.
works.meter: Prose; a highly rhythmic periodic style, built on balanced clause, reiteration and the sententious closing member, much quoted as prose aphorism.
works.context: Written at Bagni di Lucca and at Pisa between February and March 1821 in reply to a prose essay, published in a review by a friend, on the demand that poetry should inculcate moral truth, and at a moment when the poet was defending his own longest and most philosophical drama against the charge of irrelevance. It was not printed in the author's lifetime; it first appeared posthumously in a collection of his prose edited by his widow, and its fame belongs to the reprints of the later century.
works.structure: A continuous occasional essay in twenty numbered sections, opening with the concession to the opponent's definition, proceeding by distinction, example and historical survey, and closing with the aphorisms on the legislator and on the happiness of the imaginative mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the essay was unfinished, the closing section fragmentary, and the printed text rests on a copy made by a friend of the author in the last year of his life.

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
altTitles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
works.description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
works.plot: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
works.structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.

works.form: antiquarian description and catalogue of a collection
works.description: A room-by-room account of the author's Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill, its collections, its chapels and its libraries, written for the guidance of visitors and printed at his own instance. It is the founding document of the Gothic revival house as a literary and antiquarian artefact.
works.plot: The description leads the visitor through the exterior and the several apartments, reporting the arrangements of the Gothic chambers, the painted glass, the armour, the books and the relics with their provenances. It explains the taste and the scholarship that assembled them, and defends the villa's imitations of the old styles as faithful and instructive. The account of the collection ends with the library and the collections of prints and drawings, the whole forming a theory of antiquarian pleasure.
works.significance: It established the model of the described Gothic house and is the primary source for the taste, the antiquarian methods and the humour of the century's most famous literary residence.
works.meter: A plain descriptive prose of measurement, provenance and modest comment, with the epigraphic and heraldic phrases of the antiquarian tradition.
works.context: Printed in 1784 in the season of the vogue for Strawberry Hill and of the author's late quarrels over the authenticity of the relics he displayed; the villa itself, built and altered over some thirty years, is the work the book describes.
works.structure: A topographical and inventory description ordered by the plan of the house, with inserted catalogues and historical notes on individual pieces; there is no argument beyond the tour.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was printed by the owner's direction, and the later editions were enlarged by other hands after his death.

works.title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
altTitles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
works.description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
works.plot: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
works.significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
works.characters: Thomas More (as speaker); The Messenger
works.structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
The English Reformation

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
works.description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
works.plot: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
works.characters: Anthony (the uncle); Vincent (the nephew)
works.structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
The English Reformation

works.title: A Dictionary of the English Language
altTitles: A Dictionary of the English Language, in Which the Words are Derived from the Originals, and Illustrated in Their Different Significations by Examples from the Best Writers (first edition title)
works.form: two-volume folio dictionary with a prefixed grammar and prospectus; lexicographical and philological writing
works.description: The two folio volumes that settled the lexicography of English for half a century and remained the standard authority until the Oxford English Dictionary. Johnson gave some 42,773 words and illustrated their senses with a vast body of literary quotations, treating the language as a national literature rather than as a set of logical terms. The work was performed largely by Johnson's own labour, assisted by a small body of clerks, on the booksellers' contract signed in 1747.
works.plot: Each entry gives the orthography, the etymology where it can be traced, the parts of speech and the senses arranged from the primary to the derived, each authenticated by a quotation from an approved writer. Johnson's discussions of the difficulty of fixing a living language, of the limits of etymology and of the treatment of low or indecent words are recorded in the Grammar and the Plan prefixed to the volumes, and the illustrative citations - Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden, Pope and hundreds more - amount to an anthology of English writing.
works.significance: It established quotation-as-evidence, the historical treatment of senses and the idea that a dictionary is a record of a literature, all of which passed into later lexicons; it also created the modern image of the independent professional writer. Its definitions remain a literary document, and the work is a central text for eighteenth-century theories of language, usage and national letters.
works.meter: Prose of extreme compression in the definitions, with the illustrative quotations supplying the rhythm and the authority; the Grammar is written in the same periodic style as the Plan.
works.context: Produced in the decade after Chesterfield's indifference to projects for an English academy and in the same years as the Rambler papers; the booksellers' share system, the labour of the six copying clerks and Johnson's lodging in Gough Square provide the physical conditions of the work, and the Seven Years' War had already begun when it was published.
works.structure: A reference work: an alphabetical macrostructure, preceded by the Plan and a Grammar of the English tongue; no narrative order, but a strict microstructure of word, etymology, senses, examples.
works.attributionNotes: Johnson is the author of the whole design and of the definitions; the clerks and later bibliographers assisted the execution, and the etymologies relied on the philology then available, including Junius, Skinner and Tooke's predecessors.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The English vernacular and national letters
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: A Disciple
works.description: The Abbey play of the disciple and the critique of the rural Ireland. It is a dramatic work of 1931 by Teresa Deevy; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement.
works.plot: A Disciple - later retitled In Search of Valour - sets the young woman's discipleship to the ideals of the rural Ireland against the household that confines her, in the Abbey dialogue that drew the criticism of the revival's audience for its edge.
works.significance: A Disciple is Deevy's critique of the rural Ireland's ideals: its heroine's confinement by the custom and the pulpit made it the first of her plays to measure the distance between the revival's Ireland and the woman's life.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the Abbey dialogue of the rural Ireland with the woman's confinement at its centre.
works.context: The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, 1931. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1931 and first performed in The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, 1931 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.
works.characters: the disciple; the household; the idealists of the town
works.structure: A three-act Abbey play of the disciple and the household. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Teresa Deevy. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion
works.description: Collins's historical-critical pamphlet, treating Christianity as a this-worldly political phenomenon whose grounds lie in Jewish messianic expectation and whose reasons for assent are those of the Jewish religion it answered. Published amid the Woolston trials, it provoked a swarm of replies and a parliamentary outrage.
works.plot: Collins argues that the Jews expected a temporal Messiah, and that the first preachers addressed purely political hopes shaped by that expectation. On this account Christianity's rise is explained by causes within history: a deluded expectation later corrected by an allegorical reading after the failure of the temporal kingdom. The spiritualizing interpretation, he suggests, is a shift that saved the sect from extinction and made prophecy serve whatever happened. He closes with a proposal: the true Messiah remains to come, and the grounds of Christian assent, being historical and political, are weaker than those of the Jewish religion they displaced.
works.significance: It is the most political of the deist attacks, turning the evidences inside out by explaining religion from the interests it served, and a decisive provocation for the historical and moral apologetics of the following decades.
works.meter: Level, deadpan argumentative prose, with startling conclusions reached through a series of apparently neutral historical enquiries.
works.context: Published in 1724, the same year as Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation and in the shadow of Woolston's libel trial; the House of Commons resolved to prosecute the author, making it a cause celebre of the deist decade.
works.structure: A compact single discourse moving from the political state of the Jews, through the causes of Christianity's rise, to the allegorizing solution and a concluding query about the true Messiah.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country
altTitles: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country, on a Review of the Revolution of 1688
works.description: Price's sermon to the Revolution Society on the centenary of the Glorious Revolution, delivered two months after the fall of the Bastille and read as a blessing upon the French Revolution. It defined true love of country as attachment to liberty and to the rights of mankind, not to soil, state, or church establishment, and it provoked Burke's Reflections directly.
works.plot: Price argues that the love of our country, rightly understood, is a moral attachment to the commonwealth of free people, not a jealous patriotism set against the rest of the world. He reviews the English Revolution of 1688 as a real assertion of the rights of mankind, and insists that the same principles authorize the French people's resistance to tyranny; the glory of Britain lies in having taught the lesson, not in reserving it. He warns that churches and courts which turn religion into an engine of state betray both, and closes with a universalist prayer for the progress of liberty, knowledge, and virtue among all nations. The discourse was answered by loyal addresses, by clerical replies, and above all by Burke.
works.significance: It is the great text of cosmopolitan British radicalism and the book that called Burke into print, defining the argument about the rights of nations and the love of country that ran through the revolutionary decade.
works.meter: Sermonic prose of grave, sustained warmth, the periods built by parallel and antithesis, its rhetoric deliberately pacific and universal.
works.context: Delivered on 4 November 1789 to the Revolution Society at the Old Jewry in the first fever of the French Revolution, printed by the author's appointment and reprinted within the year; it was the immediate occasion of Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France.
works.structure: A single commemorative sermon, the centenary meditation opening into a universal theory of liberty and its love.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: A Dog of Flanders
works.form: Novella (in the collection A Leaf in the Storm, 1872)
works.description: Published in 1872 and one of the most beloved animal stories in the world: the tale of Nello, a poor Flemish boy, and his dog Patrasche, who dream of seeing Rubens's triptych in Antwerp cathedral. It is a prose fiction work of 1872 by Ouida; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Nello and Patrasche live with the old man Jehan Daas, haul milk to Antwerp, and are accused of a crime they did not commit; on Christmas Eve the boy and the dog walk to the cathedral, find it closed, and are found dead before the Rubens the next morning.
works.significance: A Dog of Flanders is one of the most widely translated animal stories ever written and the finest thing Ouida wrote: its fusion of art, poverty and animal devotion made it a permanent children's classic, and it is a key text in the Victorian literature of animals.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is highly coloured, rhythmic prose.
works.context: The 1870s, the Flemish peasant economy, the cult of Rubens, and the Victorian vogue for animal stories after Black Beauty. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Nello; Patrasche; Jehan Daas, his grandfather; Alois Cogez; Baas Cogez, the miller
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Marie Louise Ramé. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Drama in Muslin
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1886
works.description: Published in 1886 and Moore's Irish novel of the marriage market: a group of girls brought out in Dublin to find husbands. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by George Moore; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Alice Barton and her friends are brought from their convent school to the Dublin season of balls and garden parties, where the girls are sold to the highest bidder; Alice, plain and clever, escapes into a marriage with a Dublin doctor and a life of social conscience, while her beautiful sister Olive is driven through the market by their ambitious mother and her crippled friend Cecilia Cullen retreats into a convent.
works.significance: A Drama in Muslin is the strongest Irish novel of the 1880s and one of the most astringent treatments of the marriage market in English: its picture of the Dublin season and of the destruction of women by the marriage system made it a key text of the New Woman debate and it was banned by the circulating libraries.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is flaubertian impersonality and exact detail.
works.context: 1885-86: the Irish landed class in decline, the Dublin Castle season, the Land League agitation, and the Victorian debate on women's education. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Alice Barton; Olive Barton; Mrs Barton; Arthur Barton; Cecilia Cullen; May Gould; Violet Scully; Lord Kilcarney; Dr Edward Reed; Captain Hibbert
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: A Dream of John Ball
works.description: Serialised in the Commonweal in 1886-87 and published in 1888: a time-travel fantasy of the Peasants' Revolt, in which the narrator joins the rebels of 1381. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by William Morris; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Lecture and Popular Address and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The narrator, a nineteenth-century socialist, dreams himself into a Kentish village in 1381, joins the archer Will Green and the men of the rising, hears John Ball's sermon on the equality of men at the village cross, sees the knights' attack beaten off, and spends the night in the church talking with Ball about the long struggle for freedom that will continue to the dreamer's own day.
works.significance: A Dream of John Ball is the finest English historical fantasy of the century and a founding text of the socialist historical novel: its sermon on equality and its vision of the long revolution made it a central text of the English labour movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is long, even, unrhymed or heroic-couplet narrative.
works.context: 1381: the Peasants' Revolt, the preaching of John Ball, the socialism of the 1880s, and the Victorian socialist revival of the medieval past. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; lecture and popular address.
works.characters: the dreamer, the narrator; John Ball; Will Green, the archer; the men of the rising
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Morris (designer and poet). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle
altTitles: Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle
works.description: The greatest long poem in Scots: a drunk man's night on a hillside with a thistle, and the whole condition of Scotland. It is a verse work of 1926 by Hugh MacDiarmid; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The speaker, drunk, lies on a hillside beside a thistle and holds a night-long argument with it: about Scotland, Calvinism, the Scots language, love, drink, the industrial city, communism, the universe and his own soul, in a sequence of lyric passages and dramatic monologues that moves between Scots and English.
works.significance: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is the greatest long poem in Scots and the founding work of the Scottish Renaissance: it restored Scots as a modern literary language, made the condition of Scotland the subject of a great poem, and is one of the permanent long poems of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the synthetic Scots lyric with its dictionary richness.
works.context: The Scotland of the 1920s: the industrial depression, the loss of the Scots language, the Calvinist inheritance, and the nationalist revival of the Scottish Renaissance. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.characters: The drunk man; the thistle
works.structure: A night-long sequence of lyric and dramatic passages in Scots and English. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

works.title: A Fable for Critics
works.description: The wittiest review of the American writers ever written: a fable of the critics and their authors. It is a verse work of 1848 by James Russell Lowell; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Phoebus, the god of poetry, complains that the critics have taken over; he commissions a review of the American poets and writers, and Lowell delivers a series of brilliant verse portraits of Emerson, Hawthorne, Whittier, Cooper, Poe, Longfellow, Holmes and the rest.
works.significance: A Fable for Critics invented the verse review of contemporaries and is the wittiest treatment of the American literary world ever written: its portraits of Emerson, Poe and the rest are still quoted, and it made literary criticism into a comic art.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is the Yankee dialect of Hosea Biglow.
works.context: The American literary world of the 1840s and the new national literature. The record dates the work as composed between 1847 and 1848 and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric; Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Phoebus; Emerson; Hawthorne; Whittier; Cooper; Poe; Longfellow; Holmes; Lowell as critic
works.structure: A verse satire in dialogue, with portraits of the contemporary writers. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.

works.title: A Farewell to Arms
works.form: Novel; war memoir, first issued in 1929
works.description: The finest American novel of the First World War: an ambulance driver, the retreat from Caporetto and a love affair that ends in loss. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Ernest Hemingway; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Frederic Henry, an American ambulance lieutenant in the Italian army, falls in love with Catherine Barkley, a British nurse; he is wounded at the front, recovers in Milan, returns to the retreat from Caporetto, deserts after the battle police shoot his comrades, and escapes with Catherine to Switzerland, where she dies in childbirth with the baby.
works.significance: A Farewell to Arms is the finest American novel of the First World War and the book that made Hemingway a major writer: its prose, its love story and its ending — 'the world breaks everyone' — made it one of the permanent American novels of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the short declarative sentence.
works.context: The Italian front of 1915–18, the retreat from Caporetto, Milan in wartime, and the armistice. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; jazz-age novel and the expatriate romance.
works.characters: Frederic Henry; Catherine Barkley; Rinaldi; the priest; Helen Ferguson; Miss Van Campen
works.structure: Five books with a coda, in a first-person narrative. A novel in chapters of the pleasure and the retrospect, the party scene and the elegiac judgement held in the same short paragraphs.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ernest Miller Hemingway. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Flat Iron for a Farthing
works.description: Published in 1872 and the best of Ewing's longer family stories: the childhood of a boy remembered by himself, and the household of servants, aunts and cousins that made him. It is a prose fiction work of 1872 by Juliana Horatia Ewing; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: The narrator recalls his childhood in a large country house, his father's absence in India, his aunt's rule, the servants who care for him, and the small events — a flat iron, a pony, a Christmas — that shape his character.
works.significance: A Flat Iron for a Farthing is one of the finest Victorian children's novels of English family life and a key text in the literature of childhood memory; its picture of the child's world among servants is unmatched in the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a child's-eye view.
works.context: The 1840s-50s, the English country house and its servants, and the Victorian literature of childhood recollection. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Juliana Horatia Gatty. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Fragment on Government
altTitles: A Fragment on Government; or, A Comment on the Commentaries
works.description: Bentham's anonymous first book, a savage critique of Blackstone's Commentaries that made the greatest legal oracle of the age the enemy of rational law. Its preface planted the principle of utility - the greatest happiness of the greatest number - at the foundation of legislation, and its commentary exposed fiction, prescription, and mystery as the armour of misrule.
works.plot: Against Blackstone's account of original contract and passive obedience, Bentham argues that government rests on the obedience actually rendered, and that the test of institutions is their utility, not their antiquity or the lawyer's applause. He dissects the Commentaries passage by passage: the state of nature fable, the fictional contract, the praise of English law's mystery and its trifling with the people's interest under the name of ease. The celebrated passages expose Blackstone's apology for the equity of the judges, the vagueness of natural law, and the treason-law's tyranny, until the famous declaration that the standard of right and wrong is the greatest happiness of the greatest number. The fragment thus turns a commentary into a manifesto for radical reform.
works.significance: It founded utilitarian radicalism and the critique of the common-law mystique, gave the English reform movement its watchword and its method, and made its author, unknown for years, the legislator of the reforming century.
works.meter: Ferocious, vivid, quotational prose, the polemical repetition of an opponent's own phrases turned against him by emphasis and scorn.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1776, the year of the Wealth of Nations and Common Sense, after Bentham's youthful revolt in the Temple from Blackstone's lectures; its first public detection as Blackstone's critic scandalized the profession.
works.structure: A double work: a preface of principle and then a running paragraph-by-paragraph commentary on selected sections of Blackstone.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, with only the advertisement's clues; authorship known within the circle of Bentham's friends and declared openly in later years.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
The education of princes and magistrates
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: A General History of the Pyrates
altTitles: A General History of the Pyrates, From Their First Rise and Settlement in the Island of Providence
works.form: collective biography and historical narrative in prose
works.description: The chief narrative source for the lives of the great pirates of the American station, compiled and dramatised as a history of the profligate colony of the Bahamas. Its first volume is a continuous series of captains' lives, and its style is a hybrid of the criminal biography, the sea narrative and the moralising tale.
works.plot: The work traces the rise of pyrating after the peace discharged the privateers, describes the settlement at New Providence under Hornigold and the seizures made by the new confederacy, and then gives the careers, customs, articles, trials and deaths of the principal captains. It dwells on Roberts's articles and discipline, on the terrors of Teach, and on the female pirates' disguise and capture. It moralises throughout on the inevitable end of the pyrating course, so that even the successful captains are reported into the gallows or the desert.
works.significance: It is the sourcebook of the modern image of piracy, the black flag, the articles and the ship's democracy, and one of the most influential of the Newgate-derived prose series; its uncertain authorship makes it a test case for the attribution of hack history.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose of the criminal life, with sea-cant, trial reportage and the abrupt sentences of the hanging report; the inserted documents preserve official and notarial styles.
works.context: Published in London between 1724 and 1728 in the wave of public interest following the vice-admiralty trials of the pirates, and drawing on the court records, the colonial news sheets and the captains' own depositions.
works.characters: Henry Every; Blackbeard; Bartholomew Roberts; Henry Jennings; Charles Vane; Anne Bonny; Mary Read
works.structure: A serial of biographical lives inside a short historical introduction, with inserted documents such as articles and trial reports; a second volume extends the series with a more evidently inventive manner.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution disputed: the first volume was entered in the name of Captain Charles Johnson, a pseudonym many scholars have identified with the novelist and pamphleteer of the same publishing circle, while others deny the identification and question the second volume; the record is held for that disputed ascription and the pseudonym alone is named in the text.

works.title: A Girl in Winter
works.description: A Girl in Winter is Philip Larkin's second and last published novel, issued by Faber and Faber in 1947: a quiet, lyrical study of Katherine Lind, a young foreign woman working as a library assistant in an English provincial town during the war.
works.summary: One winter day in Katherine's present life, framing a long middle section that recalls the summer six years earlier when, as a schoolgirl, she stayed with her English pen-friend Robin Fennel and his sister Jane.
works.plot: On a cold wartime Saturday Katherine endures her bullying superior, Mr. Anstey, and takes a colleague suffering from toothache to a dentist and then home, a small act that draws her into the lives of strangers. The middle part returns to her adolescent visit to the Fennels' comfortable house, where her romantic hopes of Robin were disappointed in a summer of boating, tennis and misunderstanding. In the final part, back in the snowbound present, Robin, now a soldier, unexpectedly seeks her out; they spend the night together without love, and she accepts that neither the past nor romance can rescue her from her solitude.
works.significance: Admired for its control and atmosphere, it marked the end of Larkin's ambitions as a novelist; he abandoned a third novel and turned to poetry.
works.meter: Slow, precise, imagistic prose whose descriptions of frost, light and weather carry much of the emotional meaning; critics have called it a prose poem.
works.context: Larkin finished the novel in 1945, while working as a librarian; it drew on his experience of provincial libraries and his own sense of isolation in wartime England.
works.characters: Katherine Lind; Robin Fennel; Jane Fennel; Mr. Anstey; Miss Green
works.structure: A three-part, symmetrical design in which a remembered summer is enclosed by a single winter day.
themes: Alienation, absurdity and existential freedom
Love, intimacy and loss
Migration, exile and diaspora

works.title: A Glance Backward
works.description: The collection that made Church's name: the plain observed lyric of the country. It is a verse work of 1930 by Richard Church; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: A Glance Backward gathers Church's lyrics of the country, the season and the backward glance of the title poem, in the plain observed line of the Georgian lyric carried into the 1930s.
works.significance: A Glance Backward made Richard Church's name as the last of the Georgian lyricists: its plain observed lyric of the country carried the manner of Thomas and Davies through the modernist decades.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain observed lyric of the country and the season.
works.context: England in 1930, and the Georgian lyric after the modernist revolution. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
works.structure: A collection of short observed lyrics, ordered by the seasons. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Richard Thomas Church. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Grammar of the English Language
works.form: Grammar and didactic prose, a schoolbook consciously written as an instrument of popular education rather than as scholarship.
works.description: The author's grammar, first written for his son at school in America and then issued as a book for the English labouring classes. It teaches parts of speech, syntax, prosody and composition through sentences drawn from ordinary speech and from the best writers, and it is candidly polemical against Latin and French derived rules. The volume also carries his famous account of the 'Saxon' idiom and his insistence that clear writing is a moral as well as a civic accomplishment.
works.plot: The rules are set out in question-and-answer form, with parsing exercises on sentences of farm, shop and workshop, and with corrections of faulty examples. The writer argues that English is a language of short Saxon words which should be preferred to long derived ones, and that the grammar of the tongue is learned by use and imitation rather than by translation from Latin. He gives instructions on spelling, on the choice of words, and on writing plain prose, and adds advice on reading the best English authors. The later part addresses composition, punctuation and versification, and argues that a labourer's child properly taught has the same access to the language as a gentleman's.
works.significance: One of the most widely read English grammar books of the nineteenth century, long a standard school text in Britain and America, and a key document of the period's belief that control of the standard language was a route to political enfranchisement.
works.meter: Prose, with illustrative verse passages on prosody.
works.context: Written after its author's American exile and his son's schooling at Bristol, and issued cheaply as part of the series of useful knowledge for mechanics and labourers that flourished in the later 1810s alongside the Lancasterian schools and the mechanics' institutes.
works.structure: Didactic treatise in progressive lessons with exercises and examples, addressed in a first-person voice to a pupil and to his parent; prefaced by an account of the book's origin in correspondence with the author's son.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
The English vernacular and national letters

works.title: A Handful of Dust
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1934
works.description: Waugh's darkest novel: the end of a marriage and the collapse of a civilisation, ending in a South American jungle. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Evelyn Waugh; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tony Last, the owner of Hetton Abbey, is devoted to his house and his illusions; his wife Brenda takes a lover, and their divorce is engineered — until the death of their son destroys every calculation. Tony escapes to Brazil, is captured by a madman who keeps him to read Dickens aloud, and ends his life in the jungle.
works.significance: A Handful of Dust is Waugh's darkest and most perfect novel: its movement from comedy to desolation and its portrait of the country house as a religion made it one of the great English novels of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face.
works.context: The English country house between the wars, the London of the Bright Young Things, and the Amazonian exploration narratives of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Tony Last; Brenda Last; John Beaver; John Andrew Last; Mrs Beaver; Todd
works.structure: Five parts, from Hetton Abbey to London to the Brazilian jungle. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.

works.title: A Hazard of New Fortunes
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1890 and Howells's masterpiece: a panorama of New York in the Gilded Age, built around the founding of a literary magazine and the streetcar strike of 1889. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by William Dean Howells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Basil March moves from Boston to New York to edit a new magazine financed by the rich and capricious Dryfoos; the magazine's staff, the Dryfoos family, the old socialist Lindau and the artist Beaton are drawn into the streetcar strike, in which Dryfoos's gentle son Conrad is shot dead and Lindau mortally injured, and the novel ends with the broken Dryfoos selling the magazine to March and Fulkerson and taking his family to Europe.
works.significance: A Hazard of New Fortunes is the central American novel of the Gilded Age city and the finest American social novel of the nineteenth century: its panoramic method and its treatment of class, labour and immigration made it the model for the American urban novel from Dreiser to Dos Passos.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unobtrusive narrative prose.
works.context: The 1889-90: the New York streetcar strike, the Haymarket aftermath, the new mass magazines, and the socialist movement in America. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Basil March; Isabel March; Fulkerson; Jacob Dryfoos; Conrad Dryfoos; Christine and Mela Dryfoos; Berthold Lindau; Angus Beaton; Alma Leighton; Margaret Vance; Colonel Woodburn
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: A History of Brazil
works.form: National and colonial history on the model of Robertson, with an antiquarian's apparatus and a moralist's commentary.
works.description: The author's great work of documentary history, the first comprehensive account in English of Portuguese Brazil from the earliest discoveries to the expulsion of the Dutch. It rests on a mass of Portuguese and Spanish printed sources and manuscript material assembled during the years of the Iberian letters and the Cid. The three volumes set out to write colonial history as a moral subject: conquest, plantation, slavery and missionary enterprise are all weighed and judged.
works.plot: The first volume narrates the discovery and the plantation of the coast, the captaincy system, and the long war with the French interlopers, with a substantial natural history of the country. The second covers the Dutch invasion and the quarter-century of Nassau's rule in Pernambuco, the sugar economy, and the religious and racial politics of the colony. The third brings the story to the restoration of Portuguese authority and to the mature colonial society of the eighteenth century. Throughout the author documents the treatment of the Indians, the Jesuit missions, and the slave trade, and repeatedly condemns the avarice of settlers and administrators.
works.significance: The standard English history of colonial Brazil for most of the nineteenth century and a major document of romantic-era imperial scholarship, evidencing how a poet of the Lyrical Ballads generation became an archivist of the Atlantic world; its treatment of slavery and of the Indians is central to the period's moral debate on empire.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Published while the Peninsular War made Portugal a British ally and while the Brazilian court had removed to Rio de Janeiro, so that its subject was a matter of current imperial policy; its abolitionist passages answer the campaigns of the same decade.
works.structure: Formal annalistic history in three volumes, chronological and documentary, with long digressive chapters on natural history, ethnography, and colonial administration and heavy citation of printed sources in the notes.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Mission, conversion, and the Church
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world

works.title: A History of Eighteenth Century Literature
works.description: Published in 1889 and the standard Victorian history of eighteenth-century English literature: a survey from Dryden to the Romantics, written for the general reader. It is a prose work of 1889 by Edmund Gosse; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Gosse traces the poetry, drama, prose and criticism of the age in a continuous narrative, with chapters on Pope, Swift, Addison, Johnson, Gray, Goldsmith, Cowper and the novelists, and gives the century a coherent literary shape.
works.significance: Gosse's history was the standard account of eighteenth-century English literature for a generation and helped to establish the academic study of the period; it is a key document in the making of the English literary canon.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
works.context: The 1880s, the growth of English studies in the universities, and the demand for a national literary history. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: A History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne
altTitles: History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne
works.description: The great rationalist history of the Victorian age: the rise of morals and the decline of superstition. It is a prose work of 1869 by William Lecky; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lecky traces the moral history of Europe from the Roman Empire to Charlemagne: the pagan virtues, the rise of Christianity, the monastic ideal, the treatment of women and slaves, and the growth of the moral sense, in a history written from a rationalist and liberal standpoint.
works.significance: A History of European Morals was the great rationalist history of the Victorian age: it made Lecky the central historian of modern unbelief, influenced Mill, Stephen and the whole liberal intelligentsia, and remains the founding text of the secular history of morals.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the historical survey of opinion and morals.

works.title: A History of New York from the Beginning of the World to the End of the Dutch Dynasty
works.form: Burlesque pseudo-history and comic chronicle; mock-epic prose narrative with essays and digressions
works.description: A mock-historical account of Manhattan under its Dutch governors, written in the invented voice of a deceased New England antiquary. It parodies annalistic history while inventing the colonial past as comic legend. The book supplied the etymology of Knickerbocker and the template for the American burlesque of origins.
works.plot: The fictional historian begins with the creation and the discovery of the New World, then narrates the planting of New Amsterdam and the succession of Dutch directors in a style of inflated solemnity that turns every event into absurdity. A long digression on the arts of thinking and on the privileges of idlers sets out the book's burlesque philosophy of history. The reign of Peter Stuyvesant occupies the later books, with his quarrels, his wooden leg and his surrender of the province to the English. The history ends where legend begins, leaving the reader to decide whether the colonial past is a usable inheritance or a joke.
works.significance: It created the founding myth of New York's Dutch past and gave the city the nickname Knickerbocker. Its method, comic scholarship in a ventriloquized voice, became the model for the American burlesque of history. It is the first American comic masterpiece to reach a British public.
works.meter: Prose, with interspersed verse quotations and songs
works.context: Published anonymously in 1809 in the nick of a Federalist-Democratic-Republican quarrel in New York, and dedicated to a historical society in the manner of antiquarian works. Its jokes about Dutch inheritance answered the era's obsession with founding and lineage. The fabricated title-page, announcing the manuscript as the remains of a deceased antiquarian, was a knowing bibliographic fiction.
works.characters: Diedrich Knickerbocker; Peter Stuyvesant; the Dutch governors of New Amsterdam
works.structure: Mock-annalistic history in nine books, framed by a publisher's advertisement, an essay on the historian and long ironic digressions; chronological narrative is constantly interrupted by disquisition.
works.attributionNotes: Published under a fictitious antiquarian author, Diedrich Knickerbocker, whose biography is invented in the front matter; the work is nonetheless unitary in composition.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
The city and urban life
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters
The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch

works.title: A History of Nineteenth Century Literature
works.description: The central academic history of Victorian literature: the survey and the judgement. It is a prose work of 1896 by George Saintsbury; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Saintsbury surveys the literature of the nineteenth century from the Romantic poets to the Victorians, with chapters on the novel, the drama, the essay and the historians, and with judgements that made and unmade reputations.
works.significance: A History of Nineteenth Century Literature is the central academic history of Victorian literature and the book that established English literature as a university subject: Saintsbury's survey and his judgements made him the most influential critic of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the survey history with its judgements.
works.context: Britain in the 1890s, the new academic study of English literature and the literary establishment. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Saintsbury as critic; the poets; the novelists; the historians
works.structure: A literary history in chapters by genre and author. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Edward Bateman Saintsbury. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A History of the Protestant "Reformation" in England and Ireland
altTitles: History of the Protestant Reformation in England and Ireland
works.form: Polemic ecclesiastical history and controversy, in the tradition of Reformation and counter-Reformation writing turned to a radical agrarian argument.
works.description: The author's polemic history of the English and Irish Reformation, issued in parts and in two volumes, which reads the dissolution of the monasteries as the origin of the modern confiscation of the poor. Its notorious device is the scare quotes around 'Reformation', a word the author uses to mean robbery dressed in Protestant language. The book is at once a work of documentary history and the most sustained religious attack of his later career.
works.plot: The narrative begins with the state of religion and learning before the break with Rome, and then documents the visitations, the surrenders, and the partition of monastic lands among the new purchasers. It argues that the Reformation's real business was the extinction of the hospitals, alms, and schools maintained out of church property, and that the poorer classes were made destitute at the same stroke. Irish chapters carry the argument further, treating the plantations and the persecution of the Irish peasantry as the same confiscation applied to another people. Throughout, the historian quotes the reformers themselves, especially Foxe, to make them witnesses against their own cause.
works.significance: The most influential nineteenth-century popular account of the Reformation as an act of class confiscation, and a primary document in the history of the Catholic-and-radical reading of English religion; it fixed the phrase 'the Protestant Reformation' in its ironic modern use.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the Corn Law depression and on the eve of the Irish and Reform agitations, when the property of the dissolved monasteries and the tithe were live legislative questions; the book's attack on the church-endowed state helped make its author a hostile figure to the moderate reformers.
works.characters: Henry the Eighth; Thomas Cromwell; Archbishop Cranmer; Queen Elizabeth; the monks and abbots of the dissolved houses; the Irish of the plantations
works.structure: Chronological documentary history in two volumes, with long verbatim extracts from primers, chronicles, acts of parliament and Foxe's Acts and Monuments, framed by an uninterrupted editorial harangue.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Monasticism and the religious life
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: The English Reformation

works.title: A House and Its Head
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1935
works.description: Compton-Burnett's masterpiece of the family: a tyrannical father, a murder and a marriage. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Ivy Compton-Burnett; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Duncan Edgeworth, a bullying father, dominates his household; his wife dies, his daughter is married off, and the family's secrets are exposed in a novel of Victorian family tyranny told entirely in the dialogue of the dinner table.
works.significance: A House and Its Head is Compton-Burnett's masterpiece and the central text of the dialogue novel: its portrait of the tyrannical father and its comedy of the family made it one of the finest English novels of the period and the model of the modern novel of the household.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the novel composed almost entirely of dialogue.
works.context: An English country house at the end of the nineteenth century. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1935 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Duncan Edgeworth; Ellen Edgeworth; Nance; Sibyl; Grant; Ursula
works.structure: A novel in dialogue, following the household through death and marriage. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Ivy Compton-Burnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A House of Women
works.description: The novel of the household of women and the man who enters it. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by H. E. Bates; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: A House of Women sets the household of women - the mother, the daughters and the servants of the house - against the man who enters it, and the novel follows the quarrel of the house and the intruder through the seasons of the 1930s.
works.significance: A House of Women is Bates's novel of the household of women and one of the finest of the decade: its house, its women and its intruder made the domestic novel a study of the woman's world between the wars.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the field, the season and the weather, charged but never purple.
works.context: England in the mid-1930s, and the household of women. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the mother; the daughters; the servants; the man who enters
works.structure: A novel of the household in chapters of the seasons. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herbert Ernest Bates. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
