works.title: A Humble Romance and Other Stories
works.description: Published in 1887 and Freeman's first collection: twenty-eight stories of the poor and the obscure in the New England villages. It is a prose fiction work of 1887 by Mary E. Wilkins Freeman; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The stories follow the pedlars, the hired girls, the poor relations and the old women of the Massachusetts hill towns through courtships, deaths and disappointments, each rendered in the plain speech of the village and each ending with a small, unremarked tragedy or a moment of unexpected dignity.
works.significance: A Humble Romance established Freeman as the finest American writer of the village poor and made her reputation as a regionalist: its stories of hired girls and pedlars are among the earliest American fictions of working-class women, and it prepared the way for the masterpiece of 1891.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn.
works.context: 1884-87: the rural poverty of post-war New England, the decline of the hill farms, and the American local-colour market of Harper's and the Century. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1887 and first published in 1887 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Sally and the tin-peddler Jake Russell ('A Humble Romance'); David Emmons and Maria Brewster ('Two Old Lovers'); Harriet and Charlotte Shattuck ('A Mistaken Charity'); Martha Patch ('An Honest Soul'); Old Lady Pingree
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary Eleanor Wilkins Freeman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
altTitles: The Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
works.form: travel journal and personal narrative in prose
works.description: The account of a dying man's sea passage, written by an author who sailed for Lisbon in the hope of health and died on the way home. It mixes the journal of the voyage, the complaint of the ship's company and a serious meditation on the conduct of a physician and the resignation of a man who expects to die.
works.plot: The traveller, broken by illness and obliged to leave England, describes his departure, the passage and his sufferings on board, with the behaviour of his own family and of the other passengers under the same trial. He reports the quarrels, the sickness, the crew and the treatment of the sick by the ship's surgeon, arriving at Lisbon in a condition little amended. The journal closes with the return homeward and the traveller's death, which the publishers' advertisement disclosed.
works.significance: It is the most affecting of the century's dying autobiographies and a crucial companion to the fiction, its candid account of the body and of domestic weakness confirming the argument of the last novel.
works.meter: A plain diary prose of the daily entry, with the heightened periodic manner reserved for the closing meditations on death.
works.context: Written in the autumn of 1754 and published a few months after the author's death in Lisbon in October of that year, in the season of his retirement from the office and of the controversy over his conduct as a magistrate.
works.characters: the travelling author; his wife and attendants; the ship's company and the surgeon; the fellow passengers of the Lisbon packet
works.structure: A dated prose journal of a single crossing, continuous in its observation and rising to a set of reflective conclusions on sickness, death and the duties of those who attend them.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published posthumously from the writer's own journal, with a prefatorial advertisement of the circumstances of his death.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Medicine, healing, and the body
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Sea voyage and seafaring
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
movements: The Spectator and Periodical Journalism

works.title: A Journal of the Plague Year
altTitles: The Journal of the Plague Year
A Journal of the Plague Year: Being Observations or Memorials, of the Most Remarkable Occurrences
works.description: A week-by-week history of the London visitation of 1665, compiled as a journal by a surviving citizen and published in 1722. It is neither a memoir nor an invention but a deliberately documentary fiction, assembled from bills of mortality, medical broadsides and the city's own alarm.
works.plot: H.F., a stay-and-watch baker, follows the sickness from its first appearance in parishes north of the river through the closing of houses, the weekly bills, the heaps of dead, the flight of the court and the greed of doctors and officers. He reports the Aldgate burying-ground, the mad people, the poor, and the French church; he records his own narrow escapes, his visit to a doctor's house, and the disorder of the streets. The journal ends as the mortality falls with the cold weather and the city recovers.
works.significance: It is the model of empirical urban narrative in English fiction and a foundational text for the history of the epidemic as a literary form, its mixture of statistic and fear defining how the disaster city is later fictionalised.
works.meter: Austere prose of numeration and specification, with bills, tables and parish totals quoted as authority; the rhetorical heightening is confined to the passages of remonstrance with the city's wickedness.
works.context: Written nearly sixty years after the event during a period of continental plague scares, and built on the bills of mortality, visitation archives and printed accounts of 1665; its publication coincided with a wider antiquarian revival of interest in the city's catastrophe.
works.characters: H.F. the baker; his brother the physician; the watchmen, searchers and buryers of the parishes; the doctors and the mountebanks
works.structure: A dated and partly weekly serial journal, impersonal and statistical in the outer parts and anxiously first-person in the visits and wanderings; the observing 'I' stands inside an impersonal civic record.
works.attributionNotes: The text was inscribed with the initials 'H.F.' and long read as a genuine memoir; attribution to the author of the 1719-22 fiction is now generally accepted on stylistic and bibliographical grounds and is here recorded as single authorship.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel

works.title: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794, through Holland and along the Eastern Frontier of France; in a Series of Letters. With Observations on the Sublime and Beautiful, as They Appear in the Works of Nature, and the Arts
altTitles: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794
A Journey through Holland and along the Eastern Frontier of France
works.form: Travel writing in a series of letters with appended aesthetic observations; topographical and descriptive prose
works.description: Ann Radcliffe's book of travel, the record of the continental journey of the summer of 1794, written as the tour proceeded and published in 1795 under her own name. In a series of letters she keeps the road through Holland, along the Rhine and the eastern frontier of France, and by the way of Switzerland and the Netherlands, describing cities, ruins, mining countries and mountain scenery with the eye of the novelist of Udolpho, weighing the effect of landscape on the feeling mind, and appending remarks on the sublime and the beautiful and on picturesque beauty that bring her theory of Gothic scene-setting before the reader of fact. It is the only book of her own composition on travel, the companion to the romances that its scenery explains, and one of the Romantic period's documents of the woman tourist's eye.
works.plot: No argument in the strict sense: the letters report the progress of the tour, the company kept, the towns and passes seen, with continuous observation of the effect of scenery, an account of a mining party near the Laerboom and Falck, an excursion up the Rhine, and reflections on the picturesque, on the conduct of tourists, and on the effect of great landscape on the mind; the closing remarks on the sublime and beautiful draw the aesthetic theory out of the journey.
works.significance: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794 is the primary document of Radcliffe's aesthetics of landscape outside the fiction, the evidence by which her scenes of terror are read as picturesque science, and an early book-length example of a English woman's published tour; it remains the standard witness for the scenery of the Rhine and the eastern frontier in the revolutionary war years and for the theory of the sublime and beautiful current in Romantic prose.
works.meter: Prose; no verse. The style is the measured descriptive manner of the picturesque writers, with the balanced sentence of aesthetic essay in the closing remarks.
works.context: Written on the tour of the summer of 1794, the year of Udolpho's publication and of the war that made the Rhine and the frontier of France a theatre of campaign, and published in 1795 in the full tide of the picturesque vogue that Gilpin, the tour books and the Lake and Alpine journals had created; Radcliffe's own 1794 excursions, the Lakes tour of that summer and the continental journey here recorded, belonged to the married freedom she had won a few years before.
works.characters: the lady travellers and their party, including Radcliffe herself as observing narrator; guides, post-horses and country people met on the road
works.structure: A tour in letter form, sequential by road and date, framed by general observations on taste and scenery; the design is associative rather than argumentative, with descriptive set-pieces and a final aesthetic essay.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name, Ann Radcliffe; authorship undisputed.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
National identity and Englishness
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: A Journey Through France and Italy
altTitles: A Journey Through France and Italy, in a Series of Letters
works.description: A book of travels in letters from an English invalid travelling with his family through France into the north of Italy, written during a residence abroad and published some years after the writer's death. It mixes the guidebook, the medical complaint and the moral essay, and is one of the most readable of the century's continental tours.
works.plot: The traveller conducts his family from Dover through France, complains of the posts, the inns, the cooks and the beggars, and praises the laws and the politeness that make travelling easy. He enters Italy by Genoa and passes to Pisa and Livorno, where the climate and the medical advice are weighed; the letters report the companies, the opera and the antiquities. The final part recommends the Italian residence to consumptive English patients and judges the nations by their accommodation of the sick.
works.significance: It stands with the great travel books of the century as a document of the continental tour and of the medical geography of exile, and it supplies the circumstances of the author's last years.
works.meter: A testy and idiomatic epistolary prose, with the enumerative energy of the complaint and the balanced manner of the political observation.
works.context: Composed during the author's residence at Nice in the years after the peace of 1763, and published posthumously in 1776 in the season of the vogue for the Italian tour and the health-travel of the English.
works.characters: the travelling invalid and his family; the physicians and the innkeepers; the companies of the waters and of the opera
works.structure: A continuous series of letters arranged by route, with digressions on commerce, government, medicine and taste; the itinerary supplies the order and the invalid's temper the unity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after his death from his own letters and papers.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: A Jovial Crew
altTitles: A Jovial Crew; or, The Merry Beggars
works.description: Brome's most admired comedy, in which three gentlewomen run away to join a band of strolling beggars, and their idyll of freedom is tested by hunger, lust, and the law before they return home.
works.plot: Rachel, Amy, and the widow Springlove's daughters abandon their comfortable homes for the beggars' life; the beggar community is ruled by the mysterious Patrico, and the experiment ends with marriage and the reintegration of the runaways.
works.significance: Brome's masterpiece and the most substantial dramatic treatment of English beggar life in the period; it is a key text for Caroline social history and for the development of comic realism.
works.meter: Prose dominant, with songs and verses.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1641, just before the theatres closed; the play was popular again after the Restoration and inspired several adaptations, including the ballad opera The Jovial Crew (1731).
works.characters: Rachel; Amy; Meriel; Oldrents; Hilliard; Springlove; Patrico; Randall; Vincent; Martin
works.structure: Five acts, alternating between the gentleman's houses and the beggars' barn, with an unusually detailed portrait of vagrant society.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Brome; authorship undisputed.

Loyalty and the comitatus bond

works.title: A Jubilate Agno
works.form: Devotional and encyclopaedic poem in responsive measure, related to the litany, to the psalms and to the hymn; surviving in author's manuscript and unprinted for two centuries.
works.description: Christopher Smart's immense poem of universal rejoicing, written during his years of confinement and retirement and not printed in his lifetime. It is structured as a responsive sequence of pairs, each joining some creature, object or abstraction to another in the duty of praising God, and it expands from the animal kingdom to the alphabet, to the languages of the world, to the poet's own person and history. Its mixture of theology, natural history, philology and autobiography is without analogue in English verse.
works.plot: There is no narrative, only an enormous act of doxology. The poem proceeds in responsive pairs, in which a member of creation is set to rejoice with another, and it passes through cats, dogs, birds, insects, the elements, the parts of the body, the letters, the tongues ancient and modern, and the institutions and professions of men. The governing argument is that all being is under an obligation to praise, and that the poet, whose own case and wrongs are repeatedly pleaded in the middle of the doxology, stands as an example of the created thing that refuses or is unable to complete its part. The effect is at once encyclopaedic and intensely personal, and the poem's logic is that of a litany rather than of a discourse.
works.significance: It is one of the few entirely original large forms created in English religious poetry, and its recovery established Smart as a central rather than eccentric figure of Augustan letters; its prosody, its catalogue method and its fusion of natural history with praise anticipate much later poetry. It is also the principal document of the age's quarrel between enthusiasm and reason.
works.meter: The pair-verse of the poem: a long line divided by a caesura into two responding parts, with the reiterated formulas 'for' and 'let ... rejoice with ...', producing a prosody of parallelism and accumulation closer to Hebrew and to chant than to any Augustan measure.
works.context: It was composed during the poet's confinement, the same period that produced the 'Song to David' and the other poems of the retirement, and it belongs to the culture of enthusiasm, religious melancholy and psalm-praise which the Augustan public found so difficult to classify. Its survival in manuscript made it a twentieth-century discovery, and its publication changed the terms of Smart's reputation.
works.characters: The Creator addressed and praised; the whole catalogue of creatures, letters and languages; the poet's own self, 'for I' clauses of defence and complaint
works.structure: A continuous responsive sequence in paired half-lines, with the response of the priest and the people marked, broken into sections by the change of subject and by the poet's intrusive personal passages; no closure was supplied by the author.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Smart is unquestioned; the difficulty is bibliographical, not authorial. The poem survived only in his manuscript and was not printed in the eighteenth century, so no publication year can be recorded and the field is left null; the composition years are given as the span of the confinement, which is the accepted but not precisely dated account.

works.title: A Letter Concerning Toleration
works.description: Locke's argument for religious toleration, written in Latin in Holland in 1685 and published anonymously in 1689 in William Popple's English translation; it separates the ends of civil government from the care of souls.
works.plot: The magistrate's power extends only to civil interests — life, liberty, health, and property; the care of souls belongs to no one but God, and persecution cannot produce sincere belief; therefore the state must tolerate all religions that do not threaten civil peace.
works.significance: The classic statement of the case for religious toleration and a foundational text of liberal pluralism; three further letters followed in 1690, 1692, and 1704.
works.meter: Clear Latin prose, widely read in Popple's English translation.
works.context: Written in 1685 after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, in correspondence with Philip van Limborch; published in 1689 at Gouda in the same year as the Revolution settlement.
works.structure: A single continuous letter addressed to an unnamed friend.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as Epistola de Tolerantia; the English translation was by William Popple; Locke's authorship was suspected but not acknowledged.

works.title: A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly
altTitles: Letter to a Member of the National Assembly
works.form: open letter and political pamphlet; short polemical epistle
works.description: A short open letter published as a pendant to the constitutional polemic of the two previous years, answering a French correspondent who pressed the claim that the Revolution had given France a right to dictate the terms of opinion to its neighbours. It is compressed and angry, and it states the case against revolutionary propaganda in Europe more plainly than the longer book of 1790.
works.plot: The letter grants that a people may reform its own government, but denies that any nation has a right to oblige its neighbours to accept a change of constitution as a model, and it treats the doctrine of a crusading Revolution as a menace to the settled order of Europe. It argues that the French assemblies have substituted the will of the moment for law, and that a government resting on such a basis must depend ultimately on force. Its most memorable claim is that a system founded on the destruction of all ancient institutions can end only in military rule, because nothing else remains to hold it together. The letter closes on the prospect of a Europe armed against a gospel of untried rights.
works.significance: It supplies the earliest clear statement of the argument against revolutionary war and against the international propagation of constitutional change by doctrine, later to be argued at length in the letters on a regicide peace. Its diagnosis of a Revolution that must become expansionist or militarise at home became a stock of nineteenth-century commentary on the Revolutionary settlement.
works.meter: Tight, satirical epistolary prose, more sententious and less ornamental than the Reflections, with the abrupt courtesy of a debater dismissing an opponent's premise.
works.context: It appeared after the festival and oath of the Federation, when the French constitution seemed temporarily settled and when British societies of the friends of Revolution were urging address and imitation, and the author's alarm had turned from domestic party quarrel to the foreign policy of a propagandist state. It was written in the months before the declaration of war by France in the following spring.
works.structure: A single unbroken epistolary argument, opening with the correspondent's plea, passing through the denial of the right of propagation, and ending in prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author and its correspondence occasion is recorded by the author himself.

Revolutionary hope and its disappointment

works.title: A Letter to a Noble Lord
works.form: open letter and personal vindication; political invective with historical digression
works.description: A vindication of himself and of the reward he had received from the Crown, written in answer to a peer's attack on pensions in a debate on the civil list. It is at once a personal apology, a history of the author's public services, and one of the great invectives against the new wealth of the war and against the aristocracy that flattered it.
works.plot: The letter first pleads the modesty of a bounty granted for long service, and argues that a public reward conferred on a man who had served without profit is a praise of public spirit rather than a job. It then turns on the nobility, whose ancient wealth and station, it urges, were planted by wise statesmen and nursed by good princes for the shade of the commonwealth, and which now, having married its land to its ruin, sits in judgment on a single pension while it applauds the vast fortunes of the war. The anatomy of the new moneyed interest, with its influence upon the funds and its dependence upon the minister of the day, is the most quoted part of the book. The letter closes on the writer's own approaching death and on his refusal to be made an example by a party that wanted a precedent.
works.significance: It is the classic statement of the older critique of a moneyed interest by a servant of the landed constitution, and its passage on the 'great oaks' became the most quoted image of organic conservatism. As apology it is also the most autobiographical of the political writings, and it is the source most often read for the author's sense of service, poverty, and ingratitude.
works.meter: Sustained, indignant periodic prose, rich in metaphor of growth and decay, of trees and blight; the style of the late ornamental parliamentary manner at its fullest stretch.
works.context: It was provoked by a debate in the House of Lords early in 1796, in which a duke moved for a committee on civil-list expenditure and attacked the pensions granted at the close of the American war, and by the attacks of a pamphleteer retained against the author. The book belongs to the scarcity and war-finance politics of 1796, when the fortunes made upon the funds had become a subject of moral argument.
works.structure: A single long letter in three movements: personal vindication, historical and constitutional digression on the great oaks of the aristocracy, and the invective against paper fortune; the personal frame returns at the end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, though it is the most occasional and personal of them.

works.title: A Letter to the Women of England, on the Injustice of Mental Subordination
altTitles: A Letter to the Women of England
works.form: Polemic, Pamphlet, and Open Letter; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
works.description: Mary Robinson's most sustained feminist prose argument, a published letter to the women of England urging them to refuse the mental subordination that their education and their laws impose on them. Addressed to women rather than to their husbands, it complains of the denial of education, of the double standard of sexual conduct, of the confinement of wives to domestic dependence, and of the emptiness of accomplishments, and it calls on its readers to think and to write for themselves. It stands with the writing of Wollstonecraft as one of the sharp feminist statements of the 1790s.
works.plot: The letter argues that women are made inferior by treatment rather than by nature: they are educated for display and not for judgement, denied the means of subsistence by the law of marriage, judged by a harsher rule than men in conduct, and encouraged to submit their minds to husbands, fathers, and opinion; Robinson answers each of these injustices with an appeal to female reason, independence, and mutual instruction, and closes by exhorting her readers to claim intellectual freedom as their birthright.
works.significance: The Letter is one of the canonical feminist polemics of the Revolutionary era and is now standard reading in the history of women's writing; its insistence that subordination is mental before it is legal, and its address to women as rational agents, make it an essential companion text to the fiction with which it is now usually anthologized.
works.meter: Plain declamatory prose in the manner of the published letter, with balanced periods and direct address; no metrical design.
works.context: Published in 1799, in the final years of Robinson's life, when she was ill, impoverished, and dependent on her pen, and in the decade that produced the most concentrated English debate on the condition of women; the intellectual climate of Wollstonecraft's feminism and her own experience of scandal, separation, and financial precarity give the letter's complaints about law, reputation, and dependence a directly personal ground.
works.characters: the women of England as the addressed reader; husbands, fathers, and tutors as the imposed authorities; the professed advocates of female inferiority
works.structure: A single continuous open letter in prose, developed as a sequence of grievances and refutations rather than as a narrative, with direct apostrophe to the women of England throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer

Women's education and intellectual friendship

works.title: A Life for a Life
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1859
works.description: Published in 1859 and Craik's most daring novel: a doctor's love for the woman whose brother he killed. It is a prose fiction work of 1859 by Dinah Mulock Craik; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Dr Max Urquhart, an army surgeon, falls in love with Dora, the sister of a man he shot in a duel; the novel follows his concealment of the fact, the revelation that destroys their happiness, and the slow expiation of the guilt through years of service and suffering.
works.significance: A Life for a Life is one of the boldest English novels of the 1850s: it treats duelling, guilt and sexual love with an intensity that anticipates the sensation novel, and it shows Craik's readiness to put a moral problem rather than a courtship at the centre of her fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is plain, warm narrative prose.
works.context: 1859: the Victorian duel and its disgrace, the Crimean War, the ethics of medical confession, and the sensation market of the late 1850s. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; realist novel of common life.
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: A Little Princess
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1905
works.description: The greatest English school story: a rich girl reduced to a servant in her own boarding school. It is a prose fiction work of 1905 by Frances Hodgson Burnett; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Sara Crewe, the daughter of a wealthy English officer, is the show pupil of Miss Minchin's school until her father is ruined and dies; she is set to work as a servant, and her courage and imagination sustain her until the lost fortune is restored.
works.significance: A Little Princess is the greatest of the English school stories and the finest of Burnett's novels: its portrait of Sara Crewe's imagination under humiliation made it a permanent children's classic, and it established the moral seriousness of the children's novel of school life.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the child's-eye view of adult failure.
works.context: London at the turn of the century, the girls' boarding school and the imperial wealth of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1905 and first published in 1905 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Sara Crewe; Miss Minchin; Becky; Ermengarde; Lottie; Captain Crewe; Ram Dass
works.structure: A novel in nineteen chapters, from the school's show pupil to the servant in the attic. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: A London Plane-Tree and Other Verse
works.description: Published in 1889, the year of her death, and Levy's last collection: urban lyrics of London, the British Museum, the omnibus, the Thames and the plane trees. It is a verse work of 1889 by Amy Levy; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: The poems include 'A London Plane-Tree', 'Ballade of an Omnibus', 'The Street' and 'A March Day in London', and move between the city's anonymity and the wistfulness of the observer who loves it.
works.significance: A London Plane-Tree is one of the founding collections of English urban poetry: Levy's London is the modern city of strangers, and her city poems prepared the way for the 1890s poetry of Davidson, Symons and Johnson.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is metrical accomplishment in traditional forms (sonnet, ballad, dramatic monologue).
works.context: The 1880s, the London poetry of the 1890s, the aesthetic interest in the city, and the vogue for the French forms of the ballade. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: A Mad World, My Masters
works.description: Middleton's early city comedy of tricks: the rake Follywit, disguised as a lord and then as a player, gulls his rich grandfather Sir Bounteous Progress; the courtesan Frank Gullman is passed off as a virgin; and the bawdy plot of Penitent Brothel and the Harebrain household runs alongside — the whole a 'mad world' of disguises whose final scene dissolves into the play-within-the-play of The Slip.
works.plot: Follywit robs his grandfather three times over in three disguises; the gullings of the 'virgin' Gullman and the jealousy comedy of Harebrain interweave; the final robbery turns into the play performed before Sir Bounteous, who is robbed as he watches — the trick revealed only in the last lines, when Follywit marries Gullman with his grandfather's blessing.
works.significance: The wittiest of Middleton's early comedies — a laboratory of the trick-plot and the play-within-the-play he would perfect.
works.meter: Prose and verse in Middleton's swift, sardonic mix, with the mock-tragedy of the players as its final parody.
works.context: Performed by the Children of Paul's in 1605 and printed in 1608; its frank bawdry answered the fashion of the private-theatre comedies.

works.structure: A five-act intrigue of triple disguise built on the trick-play device, with the play-within-the-play as its climactic joke on the audience as well as the gull.

works.title: A Man Lay Dead

works.plot: At a weekend party at Frantock, a game of murder turns into a real killing when Sir Hubert Handesley's guest is found stabbed in the passage, and Inspector Roderick Alleyn of Scotland Yard investigates a house full of suspects.

works.title: A Man's a Man for A' That
altTitles: For A' That, and A' That
works.form: song lyric and political hymn in the Scottish vernacular, in the radical verse tradition of the 1790s
works.description: Burns's democratic anthem, which asserts that rank, ribbons and titles are nothing against the worth of the honest man, and that the true aristocracy is that of virtue and character. The song gathers the language of the 1790s radical argument about precedence and desert into a strophic hymn of equality, closing with the prophecy of a day when the brotherhood of man shall be more than a phrase. It is the most quoted of all verses on human equality in Scottish.
works.plot: The speaker catalogues the marks of worldly distinction - the coat of arms, the livery, the belt and the star, the flattery of menials - and insists that none of them makes the man better than his poor neighbour. The independent mind, poor and unpatented, is declared the true nobility, and the external rendings of rank are set against the worth of the upright heart. The final stanza looks forward to the coming time when man shall be a brother to man for a' that, turning the song's invective into a promise.
works.significance: It has become the standard lyrical statement of human equality in the language, quoted at inaugurations, funerals and political meetings, and a touchstone for the history of democratic sentiment. Its union of vernacular song with a political proposition makes it a central text of the literature of the nations in the 1790s.
works.meter: Four-beat Scots stanzas with the burden-like return of the phrase a man's a man for a' that, adapted to an air; the diction is colloquial, abrupt and full of monosyllables.
works.context: Written in the later Dumfries years, when the repressive measures following the French war and the agitation over parliamentary reform sharpened the language of rank and desert in Scotland; the song belongs to the same 1790s argument as the Address to the Deil and Tam o' Shanter in its contempt for precedence and for the trappings of nobility.
works.characters: The upright poor man; the hireling and slave of rank; the 'rulers' and 'wrigglers' of precedence
works.structure: A strophic argument in the manner of a song, each verse restating and intensifying the proposition of the refrain, ending with the prophetic closing stanza.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is variously assigned by the biographers within the last years of Burns's life, and the song was not printed in his lifetime, so the composition range entered here is deliberately broad and publication_date is left null.

works.title: A Mere Chance
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1882
works.description: Published in 1882 and the first of Cambridge's colonial novels: the story of a young woman's first season in Melbourne, and of the chances and choices that decide her life. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Ada Cambridge; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Rachel Fetherstonhaugh, a poor relation, comes to Melbourne to stay with her wealthy aunt Mrs Hardy and is courted by two men, the rich Mr Kingston among them; her choice is shaped by the expectations of her family and by the accidents of colonial life.
works.significance: A Mere Chance is an early and perceptive Australian novel of the marriage market and a key text in the development of the colonial novel of manners.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a strong narrative voice.
works.context: The 1880s, colonial Melbourne society, the 'season' in the new city, and the position of the poor relation. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Rachel Fetherstonhaugh; Mrs Hardy, her wealthy aunt; Mr Kingston
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
works.description: Shakespeare's fairy comedy of lovers, artisans, and the dream-wood: four Athenian lovers flee into the forest, the fairy king and queen quarrel over an Indian boy, Puck's love-juice scrambles every affection, and the 'rude mechanicals' rehearse the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe — the whole resolved at dawn into Theseus's wedding feast and the play-within-the-play.
works.plot: Hermia must marry Demetrius or die; she flees with Lysander, pursued by Demetrius and Helena; Oberon's magic makes both men love Helena; Titania, enchanted, dotes on Bottom the weaver in his ass's head; all is set right by dawn, and the mechanicals' catastrophic performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' crowns the triple wedding.
works.significance: The most perfect English comedy of the supernatural, and the play through which most of the world first meets Shakespeare.
works.meter: Lyric blank verse for the lovers and fairies, prose for the mechanicals, with the songs and charms of the fairy scenes.
works.context: Probably written for an aristocratic wedding about 1595–96; its 'rude mechanicals' satirize the artisan theatre culture of Elizabethan London.
works.characters: Theseus; Hippolyta; Lysander; Demetrius; Hermia; Helena; Oberon; Titania; Puck (Robin Goodfellow); Nick Bottom; Peter Quince; Francis Flute; Egeus
works.structure: Four interwoven plots — court, lovers, fairies, artisans — braided through the night and united in the final act's play-within-the-play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
The public theatre and the players' world

works.title: A Minor Poet and Other Verse
works.description: Published in 1884 and Levy's second collection: dramatic monologues spoken by the marginal and the defeated — a minor poet, a magician, a fallen woman, a suicide. It is a verse work of 1884 by Amy Levy; it belongs to The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The title poem is the monologue of a poet who has failed and is about to die; the volume also contains 'Xantippe' (spoken by Socrates' wife), 'A Greek Girl', 'Christopher Found' and the elegiac lyrics of the city.
works.significance: A Minor Poet is the finest English collection of dramatic monologues by a woman of the century: Levy takes the Browningesque form and turns it to the voices of the excluded, and the title poem is a classic statement of the artist's failure.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is metrical accomplishment in traditional forms (sonnet, ballad, dramatic monologue).
works.context: The 1880s, the Browning vogue for the dramatic monologue, the woman's poetry of the 1880s, and the London literary world. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the minor poet of the title monologue; Xantippe; Socrates; Plato and the disciples ('Xantippe'); the Greek girl; the Christopher of 'Christopher Found'
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: A Mirror for Magistrates
works.description: The great Elizabethan collection of 'complaints', planned by Thomas Sackville and others as a continuation of Lydgate's Fall of Princes: the ghosts of England's fallen rulers and nobles — from Albanact and Cordila to Richard III and the Duke of Buckingham — rise before the poets and tell their tragedies, warning magistrates against ambition, flattery, and misrule; Sackville's own 'Induction' and 'Complaint of Buckingham' crown the 1563 edition.
works.plot: In Sackville's Induction, the poet descends with Sorrow into the underworld and meets the train of the fallen; each ghost then speaks his or her complaint — the causes of the fall anatomized in de casibus form — in poems by Sackville, Baldwin, Ferrers, Churchyard, and others across the successive editions.
works.significance: The great poetic quarry of Elizabethan tragedy — the book Shakespeare, Marlowe, and the chroniclers all mined for their falls of princes.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and varied stanzas, with Sackville's Induction in his stateliest blank verse and rhyme.
works.context: The first edition (1559) was suppressed for its treatment of living magnates; the fuller editions of 1563 and later became the storehouse of plots and moral themes for the Elizabethan history play.
works.characters: Sorrow; the poet; the ghosts of Richard III, the Duke of Buckingham, Jane Shore, Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Hastings, the Black Prince, and many others
works.structure: A frame (the poets meeting to continue Lydgate) enclosing a series of dramatic monologues by the ghosts of the great, in the medieval de casibus tradition revived for Tudor statecraft.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, planned by Sackville and written chiefly by William Baldwin and George Ferrers, with Sackville's Induction and Buckingham; individual attributions follow the early editions.
themes: Fortune and mutability
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: A Modern Instance
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1882 and the first American novel to treat divorce as a serious subject: the marriage and separation of Marcia Gaylord and Bartley Hubbard. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by William Dean Howells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Bartley Hubbard, a charming and unscrupulous journalist, marries Marcia Gaylord and moves from Maine to Boston; his gambling and infidelity destroy the marriage, Marcia takes their child and leaves him, and the novel ends with Bartley's death in a western mining town and Marcia's return to her family.
works.significance: A Modern Instance is the founding American novel of divorce and a key text in the American literature of marriage: its portrait of an unhappy marriage and its treatment of the legal and social consequences made it a landmark of American realism.

works.context: The 1870s-80s: the American divorce law, the new journalism, and the Boston of the 1870s. works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. works.title: A Modern Tragedy
works.description: The modern tragedy of the embezzler and the woollen town. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Phyllis Bentley; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Naturalist and Determinist Novel.
works.plot: A Modern Tragedy follows Leonard Tasburgh, the failing woollen manufacturer, from the temptation of the accounts through the embezzlement and the murder to the trial, in the Yorkshire novel that carries the industrial chronicle into the crime of the depressed town.
works.significance: A Modern Tragedy is Bentley's novel of the Depression's crime: its manufacturer-embezzler joined the Yorkshire chronicle to the tragedy of the failing trade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the chronicle of the family and the mill across the generations.
works.context: The Halifax woollen district in the Depression of the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; naturalist and determinist novel.

A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes. works.title: A Modest Defence of Publick Stews
altTitles: A Modest Defence of a Publick Stew
A Modest Defence of Publick Stews; or, An Essay Upon Whoring
works.description: Mandeville's notorious polemical pamphlet proposing licensed public brothels ('stews') as a remedy for the social miseries of clandestine prostitution, seduction, and venereal disease. Its calm institutional logic, applied to the most censurable subject, makes it both a piece of social planning and an experiment in the rhetoric of Mandevillian paradox.
works.plot: The essay first states the problem in terms of the failure of law and morality to suppress private prostitution, which spreads disease and ruins women and families unseen. It then proposes regulated stews, arguing by analogy with the management of the poor, the army, and the taxes that what cannot be prevented can be supervised, taxed, and made innocent of its worst harms. Objections from religion, modesty, and policy are enumerated and answered one by one with the pamphlet's signature deflating arithmetic of consequences. The conclusion holds that a legislature which consults 'the Nature of the Beast' rather than its ideals will secure public health and quiet where sermons have failed.
works.significance: It remains Mandeville's boldest test of whether public policy should reason from things as they are rather than as piety wishes them, and a key document of eighteenth-century debates about prostitution, regulation, and the language of projects.
works.meter: Plain, reasoningly colloquial prose,ironically modelled on the tones of a modest proposal, with lists of objections and answers driving its rhythm.
works.context: Published in London in 1724 with a letter to the Grand Jury of Middlesex, in the immediate aftermath of the Fable's prosecution and of the 'Mauduit' affair; it engages the same licensed-immorality debate that the Reformation of Manners societies and the Gin Age produced.
works.structure: A single sustained argumentative pamphlet: statement of the mischief, proposal, systematic confutation of objections, and practical peroration.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed without serious doubt to Mandeville, who signed related material and defended the pamphlet's premises within his own system; the imprint does not name him.

works.title: A Modest Proposal
altTitles: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country
works.description: Swift's ironical project for Ireland, in which a compassionate calculator proposes that the children of the poor be fattened and sold as food, and computes the profit to the landlord, the shopkeeper and the kingdom.
works.plot: The projector states the misery of the breeders in Dublin, dismisses the expedients of others, then lays down the arithmetic of the infants' carcases, their skins and their use for the tables of the rich, and closes by listing the objections he has already answered.
works.significance: It is the most quoted single satire in English and the permanent example of what the ironised first person can do to a society's moral arithmetic, especially its calculation of human bodies as commerce.
works.meter: The smooth arithmetical prose of political arithmetic, with the parenthesis of tender feeling and the exact figures of the computation.
works.context: Printed in the depth of the Irish distress after the failure of the linen trade and the abortive schemes for the kingdom, when the pamphlets of political economy were proposing population and export as the remedy for poverty.
works.characters: the projector; the knowing American of his acquaintance; the poor breeders and their children; the landlords and the shopkeepers
works.structure: A single short tract in the form of a disinterested proposal, moving from the statement of the pressure, through the computation, to the catalogue of the scheme's additional advantages.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the tract appeared anonymously with a fabricated Irish imprint in its first issue.

works.title: A Mummer's Wife
works.description: Published in 1885 and the first English naturalist novel: the destruction of a Midland draper's wife by the theatre, drink and desire. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by George Moore; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Kate Ede, the wife of a consumptive draper in Hanley, falls in love with a travelling actor, leaves her husband and joins the touring company; the novel follows her years on the road, her husband's death, her decline into drink and her death in a London lodging-house, recorded with clinical flatness.
works.significance: A Mummer's Wife is the first English naturalist novel and a landmark of English fiction: its unsparing record of a woman's decline and its refusal to moralise or console introduced the Zola method into English and prepared the way for Gissing, Hardy and Moore's own Esther Waters.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is flaubertian impersonality and exact detail.
works.context: 1884-85: the French naturalism of Zola and the Goncourts, the provincial theatre and the touring companies, and the circulating-library censorship of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; sensation novel.
works.characters: Kate Ede; Ralph Ede; Mrs Ede, Ralph's mother; Dick Lennox
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture, a Native of Africa: But resident above sixty years in the United States of America. Related by Himself
altTitles: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture, a Native of Africa
works.form: Slave narrative and abolitionist testimony in its earliest American form: a related-by-himself life story with a documentary and economic precision unusual in the genre, framed by an editor's prefacing note.
works.description: An Afro-American autobiography dictated by a man born in West Africa, kidnapped and sold, and eventually able to buy his own freedom and that of family members. It is the earliest secular slave narrative printed in the United States and is remarkable for its matter-of-fact economic detail: prices paid, wages earned, debts and lawsuits. The African sections, including the succession politics of his father's country and the manner of his own capture, give it an ethnographic value rare in the genre. Its closing pages recount his legal attempts to recover his wife, illegally sold out of the state, and the family settlements that made him a respected property-holder in Connecticut.
works.plot: The narrative opens with an account of his African birth, name and rank, and of the customs, religion and commerce of his country before describing the treachery by which he was betrayed to European traders. It follows the Middle Passage and sale in the West Indies and then to a New England master, whose service he buys out of over two decades of labour at a fixed wage. It details his successive purchases of his children and wife, the sea and land work by which he accumulated property, and the loss through the law of his second wife's freedom when she was sold despite an earlier purchase. The conclusion states his present condition, his earnings and his religious hopes, together with a note on the size and strength that gave him his reputation.
works.significance: It is the foundational text of the American slave narrative tradition before the religious model hardened, and one of the strongest surviving first-person accounts of African origins, the Middle Passage and the West Indian slave market. Its insistence on wages, contracts and property makes it an early argument that slavery is an economic crime, a line later abolitionist writing developed fully.
works.meter: Plain declarative prose in the oral manner of the narrator, with long sequences of dates, sums and place names.
works.context: Published in New London, Connecticut, in the decade when a free Black population was growing in the northern states and when the first American slave narratives were appearing, most of them religious confessions. Its appearance precedes by a decade the closing of the African trade to American ports, and it records the lived experience of the middle phase of the trade. The legal pursuit of an illegally sold wife registers the weak protection that northern law offered to Black families.
works.characters: Venture; his African father and his brother; the African woman who betrayed him to the traders; his first master in New England; his wives and the children whose freedom he purchased; the minister who wrote down the narrative
works.structure: Linear first-person autobiography in one continuous movement, from African childhood through enslavement, self-purchase and family restoration, with an appended explanatory note by the person who took down the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: The narrative is attributed to the narrator himself as related by him and taken down by a local minister who disclaimed editorial shaping; modern editions treat the account as his, mediated in the recording.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Exile and homelessness
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports
altTitles: Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports
works.form: Prose; Polemic, Pamphlet, and Open Letter
works.description: A short prose narrative by Charlotte Smith recording the loss of the transport vessels Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont, drawn up, as its title page states, from information taken on the spot, and published to raise money for a survivor of the wrecks and her infant child. It is a work of emergency charity writing in which accurate maritime detail, distress, and the appeal to the reader's benevolence are combined, and it shows Smith turning her name and her style to immediate practical use.
works.plot: The narrative reconstructs the departure, the storm, the loss of the three transports, and the sufferings and escapes of those on board, naming the circumstances of the wreck and of survival with the particularity of report rather than of romance; the account closes with the case of the surviving woman and her child, for whose benefit the whole profit of the pamphlet was assigned.
works.significance: The narrative matters as a document of Smith's professional method and of the maritime and charitable writing of the 1790s: it shows the same writer who made wreck and exile the matter of verse and fiction turning the real disaster of the transports into a factual appeal, and it is cited in the history of women's philanthropic publication.
works.meter: Plain prose of report and address, in the syntax of the printed letter or pamphlet appeal; no metrical design.
works.context: Published in a year of heavy maritime loss along the English coast and of convoy disaster, and at a moment when Smith's own earnings were irregular and her family dependant on her; the volume belongs to the philanthropic pamphlet literature of the 1790s, in which a known author's name was used to convert distress into subscription.
works.characters: the passengers and crews of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont; the unfortunate survivor and her infant child for whom the book was published
works.structure: A single continuous prose narrative without chapters of art, moving from the voyage to the disaster and then to the condition of the survivors, with the appeal for subscriptions framed as the occasion of publication.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; the work is occasionally listed among Smith's minor prose rather than among her fiction, but its attribution to her is not disputed.

Sea voyage and seafaring

works.title: A New England Nun and Other Stories
altTitles: New England Nun and Other Stories
works.description: Published in 1891 and the finest American collection of New England village stories: the small, exact lives of unmarried and widowed women. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by Mary E. Wilkins Freeman; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The title story follows Louisa Ellis, who has waited fourteen years to marry Joe Dagget and realises, when he returns, that she prefers her quiet house and her little dog; the other stories present the village widow, the woman who keeps house for a man who does not notice her, and the girl who is left behind, each settled in a single afternoon.
works.significance: A New England Nun is the central American book of the unmarried woman and one of the finest story collections of the nineteenth century: its title story is a permanent classic, and Freeman's exact, unsentimental portraits of village women made her the most important American regionalist after Jewett and a founding figure for the feminist criticism of American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn.
works.context: 1887-91: the declining rural villages of Massachusetts and Vermont, the surplus of unmarried women in New England, and the local-colour movement after Jewett. works.title: A New View of Society
altTitles: A New View of Society; or, Essays on the Principle of the Formation of the Human Character
works.form: social and educational treatise; the essays on the formation of character with the report of the practical experiment
works.description: The founding book of English Socialism, four essays published anonymously by the manager of the greatest cotton works in the kingdom, laying down the principle that the character of every human being is formed for and not by him, and arguing from that doctrine that the vices and the misery of the labouring population are the necessary product of their early training and circumstances, and may be changed with them.
works.plot: The first essay states the principle of the formation of character: that every individual, from the cradle, is made such as he is by the circumstances which have surrounded him, by the opinions that have been placed before him, and by the training he has received, none of which he could control; so that selfishness, crime, and misery are to be pitied and remedied rather than punished, and no man is properly the author either of his own vices or of his own merit. The following essays apply the doctrine in order to the established religion and the divisions of the churches, to the existing arrangements of private property and of the relations of the sexes, and to the practice of government, arguing that the institutions of the country, the punishments of the law, and the rival sects of religion are themselves products of the old system of formation and must give way when the conditions of the people are changed. The practical proof is drawn from the management of the manufacturing population under the writer's own care, where the children were received into the infant school, the reading, writing, and arithmetic and the habits of cleanly and orderly life were taught without the rod, the dwellings, the shops, and the hours of the village were amended, and the general intelligence and good behaviour of the working people were thereby increased together with the profit of the concern; and the closing appeal is to the legislature and to the magistrates to provide a national education as the first measure for the cure of the distress and the demoralisation of the labouring classes.
works.significance: The central text of the English literature of education, of character, and of social regeneration, and the book from which the co-operative movement, the writers of the communities, and much of the later reforming writing of the century took their doctrine that circumstances make the man and that the circumstances may be made; its influence ran through the factory reform, the school-boards, the co-operative movement, and the American communities of the 1840s, and as a document of the self-made reformer's faith in his own principle it holds a first place in the prose of argument of the period.
works.meter: Plain, earnest, declaratory prose of the practical projector, with the long affirmative period, the perpetual appeal to fact and to twenty years' experience, and the serene confidence of a writer who reasons as if his whole question were settled by the stating of it; the style carries conviction by its air of benevolence and command rather than by wit or subtlety.
works.context: Written in the years of the writer's management of the Lanarkshire cotton works, when the machinery of the manufacturing system, the distress of the labouring classes after the peace, the infant-school movement, and the projects of the education societies were all before the public, and published in 1813 anonymously, the copies being sent to statesmen, to philosophers, and to the princes of the blood, and the work being announced to a London dinner of the friends of the reform. It belongs to the harvest of the doctrine of circumstances which came from the French writers of the eighteenth century and from the English associationist psychology, and it was the immediate provocation of the long literature of the communities and of the co-operative schools of the following two decades.
works.structure: Four essays in a single argument, the first stating the principle and the rest applying it successively to religion, to the social institutions, and to practice; the plain statement of the doctrine, the illustration from the existing system, and the evidence of the experience of the works, with the appended accounts of the establishment and the letters of the visitors, the whole being enlarged by the added essays of the later editions.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, the copies being given out without the writer's name, and the later editions and the collected issues of the writings carry the authorship openly; the essays were enlarged and re-stated in the several editions, and the appended practical accounts vary between the issues, so that the text is best cited from the edition with the writer's own annotations.

works.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
works.description: Massinger's comedy of the extortioner's fall: Sir Giles Overreach, who has swallowed the estates of his neighbours through mortgage and fraud, plots the marriage of his daughter Margaret to the young Lord Lovell; the conspiracy of the just — Welborne's recovery of his lands, Lady Allworth's pretended favour, and the servants' evidence — brings Overreach to the mad scene in which he is dragged off 'in a frenzy', his schemes destroyed and his daughter married to the man she loves.
works.plot: Welborne, ruined by Overreach, is raised by Lady Allworth's courtesy and wins his lands back through Overreach's own greed; Overreach forces Margaret toward Lovell, who instead promotes her marriage to Allworth; the double exposure — the deeds and the daughter's defiance — breaks the extortioner; and the final scene's madness ('The devil has left his shape') closes the comedy on the ruin of the usurer.
works.significance: The last great comedy of the pre-Civil War stage — and the vehicle of one of the English theatre's most durable villains.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose in Massinger's careful, moral style, with Overreach's mad scene as the great actor's moment it became.
works.context: Written about 1625 and printed in 1633; Overreach was modelled on the notorious extortioner Sir Giles Mompesson; the role became the property of the great actors from the Restoration to the twentieth century.
works.characters: Sir Giles Overreach; Frank Welborne; Margaret Overreach; Tom Allworth; Lady Allworth; Lord Lovell; Justice Greedy; Marrall; Will-do; the parson; the servants
works.structure: A five-act city comedy of the Jonsonian school, built on the double plot of Welborne's restoration and Margaret's marriage, with Overreach's fall as its moral engine.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A New-England Tale
altTitles: A New-England Tale; or, Sketches of New-England Character
works.form: Sentimental and domestic novel; tract-derived tale of religious bigotry with sketches of manners
works.description: The first novel by a New England woman to reach a wide American audience, and a direct attack on clerical bigotry and Calvinist discipline. It grew out of a religious tract and became a domestic tale of a girl rescued from an enthusiast's household. Its subject is the power of a hard teaching over a sensitive conscience.
works.plot: A gentle and imaginative girl is thrown into the charge of a severe Calvinist minister and his household, where her scruples are tormented by a doctrine of election she cannot answer. She is protected by neighbours of liberal and rational religious opinion, and is finally delivered from spiritual tyranny by their countenance and by marriage. The tale interposes sketches of New England village life, of the free school and of the clergy as a class. Its argument is that a sect's discipline can damage a child's mind, and that toleration and education repair the injury.
works.significance: It opened the tradition of the American domestic novel of religious persecution and of the woman writer's critique of the clergy. It established the model of the New England tale in which community and conscience are the real antagonists. It is an early example of fiction used as a party instrument in the Unitarian controversy.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published anonymously in 1822, in the decade in which Unitarian and Calvinist parties in New England were contesting churches and colleges. Its author was the daughter of a Federalist congressman and had been converted under the influence of a Universalist preacher. The novel's satire of clerical authority is a document of the denominational quarrels of the 1820s.
works.structure: Third-person domestic novel with inserted tales and sketches; a didactic plot of spiritual oppression and deliverance framed by character portraits of clergy and neighbours.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; attribution established from the author's own later acknowledgement and from contemporary correspondence about the tract from which the novel grew.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.description: Published in 1897 and the second collection of Chopin's Louisiana stories: twenty-one tales, more openly concerned with sex and marriage than the first. works.title: A Nocturnal Reverie
works.description: Anne Finch's celebrated night-piece, in which the poet describes the peace and beauty of the natural world by moonlight and the freedom of the imagination in solitude, until daylight and the world's cares return — a poem Wordsworth praised as the finest nature poem between Milton and himself.
works.plot: In a night of perfect calm the speaker contemplates the sleeping landscape, the freedom of the birds and her own fancy, and the liberty of the night, until 'a rude voice' and the approaching day break the spell and recall her to the world.
works.significance: A precursor of Romantic nature poetry, admired by Wordsworth, and one of the finest descriptive lyrics by a woman of the period.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of quiet, sensuous description with a contemplative, almost Romantic tone.
works.context: Composed in the 1680s–90s and circulated in manuscript among Finch's literary circle; published in her Poems on Several Occasions (1713).
works.characters: the poet; nature; Ardelia (her pastoral name)
works.structure: A single meditative blank-verse-couplet reflection on a night scene, framed by the return of day.

works.title: A Pageant and Other Poems
works.form: Poetry collection, including the sonnet sequence 'Monna Innominata'
works.description: Published in 1881, containing 'A Pageant', 'Monna Innominata: A Sonnet of Sonnets', 'The Key-Note' and the devotional and elegiac lyrics of her later manner: the volume in which she turns fully to the preparation for death.
works.plot: 'Monna Innominata' is a sequence of fourteen sonnets in which a woman speaks the unspoken love of the great Tuscan poets, prefaced by an argument that the Lady of the sonnet tradition has never spoken for herself; 'A Pageant' is a series of visionary poems on the months and on mortality.
works.significance: A Pageant and Other Poems contains the most formally perfect sonnet sequence of the Victorian period by a woman and the one that most directly challenges the male tradition. Its preface to Monna Innominata is a founding text for the feminist criticism of the sonnet tradition, and the volume's death poems are among the greatest English devotional lyrics.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
works.context: The 1880s, her increasing illness (Graves' disease diagnosed in 1871), the devotional life at Highgate, and the aesthetic movement's cult of the sonnet. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christina Georgina Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Paper Against Gold
works.form: Political economy and commercial writing in the form of open letters and polemic pamphlet.
works.description: The author's great currency pamphlet, made out of the letters on paper credit which had appeared in the Political Register during and after the Restriction period. It argues that paper money and the national debt together transfer the substance of the country from producers to fundholders, and that the return to cash payments would restore honest measure. The book is the clearest statement of his 'distance' theory of political economy and the most quoted of his economic writing.
works.plot: The letters define gold and paper as measures of value and show how a debased measure raises nominal prices while lowering the real reward of labour. They trace the national debt from its origins in the funds to the sinking-fund and tax machinery that served it, and name the classes that gained by the system: contractors, jobbers, and the great monied interest. The post-war depression, the fall of agricultural prices and the distress of 1815-16 are offered as proof that the system works against the producer. The remedy proposed is a return to coin, the reduction of the debt and of the civil and military establishments, and the repeal of the corn laws, with an appeal to the labourer to understand the mechanism that robs him.
works.significance: The most influential popular exposition of the case against paper credit and the funded debt in the period, and a source for all later radical-economic accounts of the transition from a Saxon to a moneyed England; E. P. Thompson treated it as the hinge of its author's conversion to the labouring poor.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written at the moment of the resumption of cash payments and the agricultural distress after Waterloo, in the same debate that produced the Bullion Report and the Corn Law of 1815; it gave the currency argument a popular vocabulary and cost its author much of his earlier supporting readership.
works.structure: A sequence of numbered letters forming a continuous argument, written for the Register and gathered into a single pamphlet volume, with the reasoning advancing from definition to history to remedy.

works.title: A Paraphrase upon Part of the Book of Job
altTitles: A Paraphrase on Part of the Book of Job
