works.description: Young's late blank-verse paraphrase of Job, which turns the patriarch's trial into a further Night Thought on affliction, the silence of providence and the immortality of the sufferer.
works.plot: The paraphrase follows the argument of Job and his friends, the adversary's license and the calamities of the righteous man, and reads the poem as a proof of patience and of a life to come, ending in the restoration and the moral application.
works.significance: It is the last great English verse paraphrase of Job before the century's end, and it completes the meditation on affliction and immortality which the Complaint had opened.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic and Youngian manner, with the inflated period and the apostrophic interruption.
works.context: Published in the closing years of Young's life, in the season of the argument from the suffering of the righteous, of the Job revivals in devotional poetry and of his own quarrel with the critics of the Complaint.
works.characters: Job; the friends of Job; the adversary; the voice out of the whirlwind

works.title: A Parliamentary History of England, from the earliest Period to the Year 1803
altTitles: Parliamentary History of England, from the earliest period to the year 1803
works.form: Documentary compilation and record of parliamentary proceedings, with editorial history and polemic; a reference work built as an instrument of popular politics.
works.description: The author's great publishing enterprise: a cheap complete record of English parliaments, from the earliest period to 1803, continued by the Debates of his own time, issued in parts and gathered into thirty-six volumes. It was a working man's edition of the constitution, putting the record of what parliaments had said and done within reach of the reading public. Its author used it to supply the documentary basis for his own history of taxation, monopoly, and corruption.
works.plot: The series reprints and continues the earlier collections of parliamentary history and state trials, adds the debates of the reigns from George the First onwards, and covers the sessions of the author's own day. It records the business of the two houses, the petitions and the remonstrances, and the division lobbies, with editorial prefaces that interpret the record for the reader. The editor's purpose is polemical as well as archival: to show by documents how the revolution of property, the funding system, and the corruption of the representation had been legislated into existence, and to give the labouring reader evidence he can use for himself.
works.significance: The standard cheap repository of parliamentary record for the nineteenth century and still a cited source for debates not otherwise reported, and the material foundation of its author's whole political economy of the 'system'; it made documentary evidence a popular possession.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Begun in the years after the Act of Union and the failure of parliamentary reform, and issued in weekly and monthly parts at prices deliberately set for mechanics and farm labourers; the enterprise was also a commercial and personal quarrel, since others claimed the labour of its composition.
works.structure: Multi-volume serial compilation arranged by parliament and by session, with prefatory and connecting editorial matter; the order of the record is chronological, and the argument emerges cumulatively across the whole.
works.attributionNotes: The series reprints and continues earlier collections, and the question of how much of the composition was done by others, and under whose claim, was disputed in its author's lifetime and since; it is recorded here as his publication and editorial undertaking.

works.title: A Passage to India
works.description: The great English novel about the empire: an Englishwoman in Chandrapore, the Marabar Caves, and the impossibility of friendship between ruler and ruled. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by E. M. Forster; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Adela Quested arrives in British India to consider marrying Ronny Heaslop, the city magistrate. She befriends Dr Aziz, who arranges an expedition to the Marabar Caves; in the caves Adela is overcome by a hallucination or an assault and accuses Aziz of attacking her. The trial divides the British and Indian communities, Adela withdraws the charge, and Aziz is acquitted — but the friendships are destroyed, and the novel ends with the two men riding through the Mau jungle and agreeing that they cannot be friends yet, not until the English have been driven out.
works.significance: A Passage to India is the greatest English novel about the empire and the last great English novel of the liberal tradition: its three-part structure (Mosque, Caves, Temple), its handling of the unrepresentable in the caves, and its ending — 'not yet' — make it the most complete fictional treatment of the colonial situation in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, flexible, slightly ironic prose with the sudden lyric intensification.
works.context: British India after the Amritsar Massacre (1919) and under the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms; the Anglo-Indian community and the beginnings of the nationalist movement. Forster's own two journeys in India (1912–13, 1921) supplied the material.
works.characters: Dr Aziz; Cyril Fielding; Adela Quested; Mrs Moore; Ronny Heaslop; Professor Godbole; Mrs Turton; Nawab Bahadur
works.structure: Three titled parts (Mosque, Caves, Temple) over two seasons and two locations. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Morgan Forster. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty
works.description: Anthony Collins's libertarian manifesto, the first sustained English argument that liberty is a power of acting according to the determination of the will, and that necessity so understood is compatible with, indeed the condition of, freedom. It attacks the doctrine of liberty of indifference as unintelligible and self-contradictory.
works.plot: Collins defines liberty as a power of acting according to the will's determination, and argues that every act of the will is determined by its object or by preceding causes. The liberty of indifference, a power to choose either way without preponderating motive, he shows to be unintelligible, since an undetermined choice would be mere chance and not agency. He then presses the moral and theological consequences: a determined will can still be free in the only sense that matters for praise, blame, and law. The closing chapters answer the objection that necessity destroys religion and morality, and defend the compatibility scheme against its clerical opponents.
works.significance: It fixed the vocabulary of the liberty-necessity debate in English for half a century, providing the hard libertarian position against which Hutcheson, Hume, and Reid defined their own schemes.
works.meter: Clear, terse argumentative prose with scholastic distinctions handled lightly; the chapters close on sharp either/or dilemmas.
works.context: Published in 1717 during the noise made by Collins's earlier Essay on the Use of Reason and his dispute with Clarke, and part of the freethinking campaign that Hume's later writings on liberty and necessity would answer.
works.structure: A short treatise in ten chapters: definitions, the history of the controversy, the confutation of indifference, the affirmative argument, and replies to moral and religious objections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: A Pin to See the Peepshow
works.form: Novel (the woman on trial); detective novel
works.description: The fictional treatment of the Thompson-Bywaters case. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by F. Tennyson Jesse; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: A Pin to See the Peepshow follows Julia Almond - the shopgirl of the romantic letters and the murder of the husband - from the suburb childhood through the affair and the crime to the trial and the gallows, in the fictional treatment of the Thompson-Bywaters case that makes the woman on trial the century's question.
works.significance: A Pin to See the Peepshow is the classic novel of the woman on trial: its Julia, its letters and its gallows turned the Thompson-Bywaters case into the moral novel of the press, the sex and the law, and its revivals have made it Jesse's enduring book.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact prose of the criminologist.
works.context: England of the early 1930s, remembering the case of 1922. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Julia Almond; the husband; the young lover; the press and the court
works.structure: A trial novel from the suburb childhood to the gallows. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Wynifried Margaret Jesse. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Place of One's Own
works.description: The ghost novel of the house: the Berridge couple and the old lady of the room. It is a prose fiction work of 1940 by Osbert Sitwell; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind.
works.plot: The Berridges, a retired couple of the middle class, buy the house in the country and discover that the upper room is held by the ghost of the old lady who lived and died in it; the novel carries the haunting as the satire of the class that keeps its place after death.
works.significance: A Place of One's Own is the finest ghost novel of the English twentieth century: its old lady of the upper room made the haunting a satire of the class and the house, and it remains the standard text of the modern ghost story of character.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the polished satirical sentence of the man of the world.
works.context: England between the wars, and the haunted house of the middle class. The record dates the work as composed in 1939 and first published in 1940 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Mr and Mrs Berridge; the ghost of the old lady; the agent; the servants
works.structure: A ghost novel in chapters, from the purchase of the house to the last night in the room. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Osbert Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
altTitles: Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language, Humbly Submitted to the Publick by Samuel Johnson
The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
works.form: printed prospectus and critical dissertation in formal balanced prose
works.description: The prospectus and manifesto issued to launch the Dictionary, addressed nominally to the Earl of Chesterfield and the nine other booksellers who subscribed for the work. It sets out the method, the historical scope and the philosophy of a dictionary of an untreated, unauthorised modern language, and distinguishes an orthoepist, a grammatist and a critic. It is at once a working proposal, a piece of self-justification, and one of the finest occasional prose performances of the century.
works.plot: Johnson argues that English has never been settled by a national academy, and that the attempt to fix a living language is in itself vain: words and meanings change with the commerce and literature of a nation. He proposes to register rather than to regulate, to collect the vocabulary from the best writers within a limited historical period, and to illustrate each word with quotations that both authenticate the sense and preserve the literary record. The Plan reviews previous English and Continental lexicons, defends the division of labour he has contracted for with the booksellers, and closes with a frank claim to have carried the work through without patronal assistance.
works.significance: The Plan is the foundational statement of English philological self-consciousness, replacing the dream of an academy with the authority of usage and the evidence of quotations, a practice that still governs historical lexicons. Its frank account of the economics of authorship makes it a key document for the professionalisation of letters, and its closing pages were long read as the manifesto of independent labour.
works.meter: Prose; periodic sentences of Latinate weight, tricolon and balanced clause, in the manner of the attached dedication; no verse.
works.context: Issued in 1747 after the booksellers of London had contracted with Johnson for a dictionary on the model of the French Academy's, in the same decade as the repeated but failed projects for an English academy and the debate over ascertaining the language that Swift had opened in 1712. The subscription and copyright economy of the trade, and the example of the French and Italian lexicons, set the terms of the proposal.
works.structure: A continuous epistolary essay: dedication to Chesterfield, historical account of previous dictionaries and of the absence of an English academy, statement of method and of the three provinces of the lexicographer, and a personal peroration on the conditions of authorship.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the Plan was written under contract and in the shadow of a booksellers' subscription list; the coolness of Chesterfield, which Johnson recorded in the letter of 1755, belongs to the later correspondence rather than to this document.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The English vernacular and national letters
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: A Play of Love
works.description: John Heywood's debate interlude on the pains and pleasures of love, printed by William Rastell in 1534; the first English play devoted wholly to the analysis of courtship.
works.plot: A man loved but not loving pleads his case against a man loving but not loved, each claiming the sharper pain; their debate is referred to a woman neither loving nor loved, who judges between them; the argument moves through the paradoxes of desire to a reconciliation in which the four parties pair off, demonstrating that love's pleasures and pains are inseparable.
works.significance: The first sustained dramatic treatment of love in English and the purest example of the debate-interlude form; it links medieval love-casuistry to the Renaissance comedy of courtship.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic lyric interludes
works.context: Printed in 1534, the year of the Act of Supremacy; the play belongs to the courtly debate tradition of the early Tudor household, drawing on the amatory casuistry of the medieval demande d'amour and anticipating the love-debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.characters: Lover Not Loved; Loved Not Loving; Neither Lover Nor Loved; Both Lover and Loved
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Vice 'Neither-lover-nor-loved' as referee and a concluding judgement that resolves the debate into mutual pairing.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: A Political Romance
works.form: allegorical prose satire and political squib
works.description: A short squib on the politics of the northern church, in which the possessions and dignities of a see are represented as a family estate disputed by greedy relations. It was printed privately and suppressed almost at once, and its suppression is the best-documented quarrel of the author's Yorkshire years.
works.plot: The affairs of an ancient manor and its offices are thrown into confusion by the designs of a steward and a faction of dependants, who would divide the profits and dispose of the lady of the house. The several parties plead their rights in a style of mock-legal and romantic gallantry, until the whole scheme is exposed as a traffic in dignities. The tale ends in the defeat of the project and in an ironical apology to the offended readers.
works.significance: It is the earliest publication of the author and the key to the personal and ecclesiastical material that later surfaces in the fiction, and its suppression is a case study in the practical limits of Augustan libel.
works.meter: A dense parodic prose of the romantic and the conveyancing styles, with the personated legal phrases of the real quarrel reproduced for effect.
works.context: Written in 1759 in the heat of the dispute over the York diocesan offices and the family interests of the author's own circle, and withdrawn by the printer after threats of an action for scandal; the affair is recorded in the letters of the year.
works.characters: the personated dignitaries of the northern church; the scheming steward and his faction; the lady of the manor and her dependants
works.structure: A brief continuous allegorical tale in the romantic and lawyerly manner, the persons standing transparently for the parties of the diocese; the design is a single sustained joke of personation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; printed without the author's name and identified in his correspondence and by the parties attacked.

works.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
altTitles: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
works.description: The novel of the artist's formation: Stephen Dedalus from infancy to exile, and the definitive novel of the aesthetic consciousness. It is a prose fiction work of 1916 by James Joyce; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Stephen Dedalus grows up in Dublin: the Jesuit school of Clongowes, the family's decline, the sexual awakening, the retreat and the sermon on hell, the aesthetic revelation by the sea, and the university years in which he formulates his theory of art and decides to leave Ireland, 'to forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race'.
works.significance: A Portrait is the founding novel of the modern artist's self-making: its stream of consciousness, its development of style along with the mind it renders, and its theory of the epiphany made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of education.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the epiphany and the open ending (Dubliners).
works.context: Dublin at the turn of the century, Irish Catholic education, the Parnell controversy, the revival and its nationalism, and the aesthetics of Aquinas and Aristotle. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1914 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Stephen Dedalus; Simon Dedalus; Mr Casey; Cranly; Emma Clery; Father Arnall
works.structure: Five chapters, each a stage of Stephen's life, with the prose developing alongside his consciousness.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Augustine Aloysius Joyce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Priest to the Temple
works.description: Herbert's prose manual of pastoral practice, written for the guidance of country clergy; in short chapters it describes the parson's character, duties, preaching, catechising, visiting, and conduct, presenting the ideal of the devoted, humble, and practical parish priest.
works.plot: Each chapter ('The Parson's Character', 'The Parson Preaching', 'The Parson in Circuits', etc.) offers practical and spiritual counsel, arguing that the parson must know and love his flock, teach plainly, and sanctify every part of life.
works.significance: A classic of Anglican pastoral literature, valued for its humane wisdom and its influence on Izaak Walton's Life of Herbert and on the ideal of the country parson in English letters.
works.meter: Plain, homely, wise prose with occasional proverbial turns and scriptural allusion.
works.context: Written c. 1632 at Bemerton and circulated in manuscript; published in 1652 as part of Herbert's Remains, it reflects the Laudian and practical devotional ideals of the Caroline church.
works.characters: the country parson; his parishioners
works.structure: A series of short prose chapters forming a complete guide to the pastoral office.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A Problem in Greek Ethics
works.description: Printed privately in an edition of ten copies in 1883 and the first sustained English argument for the dignity of same-sex love: a study of the Greek institution of male love and its ethical justification.
works.plot: Symonds examines the Greek ideal of paiderastia in Homer, the Dorian institutions, Plato's Symposium and Phaedrus, and the Greek poets, and argues that the love of men was a recognised ethical institution in the ancient world, distinct from the vice condemned by modern law.
works.significance: A Problem in Greek Ethics is a founding text of the modern discourse on homosexuality: it was the first English work to treat same-sex love as an ethical and historical subject, and it circulated secretly through the circle of Pater, Wilde and Havelock Ellis, shaping the modern gay identity.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is historical narrative on a large scale.
works.context: The 1880s, the Labouchere Amendment of 1885, the English reception of Greek homosexuality, and the private circulation of sexual knowledge. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. A. Symonds. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Project for the Advancement of Learning
altTitles: A Project for the Advancement of Learning, and an Discourse of the Mechanical Operation of the Spirit
works.description: Swift's mock-project pamphlet, spoken by the same mad author of the Tale, which proposes that all learning may be bought at a shop and dispatched by mechanical means, and that the spirit of the age may be operated upon by instruments.
works.plot: The projector offers the universities a compendium of the whole corpus of knowledge, abridged to a single pocket volume, together with the machinery of memorising, speaking and writing by art, and reports the cold reception of such projects by the learned.
works.significance: It is the period's most economical exposure of the idea that knowledge can be mechanised, and it supplies the link between the Tale and the Laputa of the third book of Gulliver.
works.meter: The officious prose of the projector, full of article, offer and specification, broken by the narrator's self-pity.
works.context: Written in the wake of the Tale and printed with the miscellaneous Swift pieces of 1711, in the season of the Royal Society's projects, the abridgement vogue and the new market for the mechanical digressions of learning.
works.characters: the projector narrator; the universities and the learned societies; the mechanical authors
works.structure: A continuous ironical proposal, in the manner of the machine pamphlets, with the narrator's narrative of his own failure appended.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Swift's; the piece belongs to the narrator of the Tale, so that the projected voice is a fiction rather than a statement of Swift's own educational program.

works.title: A Proposal for Correcting, Improving and Ascertaining the English Tongue
altTitles: A Proposal for Correcting the English Tongue
works.description: Swift's plea for the regulation of English by public authority: a historical account of the language's corruption, a proposal for an academy of six or twelve persons to compile a dictionary, refine the tongue and ascertain its settled use.
works.plot: The letter traces English from its Teutonick and Norman stocks, complains of the corruption introduced at the court of the late reign and by the politeness and the trade of the age, then argues that the language wants the authority of an academy, and offers a sketch of its rules and of the composition of a dictionary.
works.significance: It is the century's most influential statement of the desire to ascertain the language, and the direct provocation to the lexical and Augustan work which Johnson later performed without an academy.
works.meter: Swift's plain prose of the argument, with the historical enumeration and the abstract of the proposed rules.
works.context: Written in the season of Addison's and Steele's attempt to polish English for the tea-table and to fix the idiom by authority, and addressed to the minister, in the years when the Royal Society's linguistic schemes and the project of an English academy were live topics.
works.structure: A single letter, dividing into the historical complaint and the project, with the closing enumeration of the academy's methods.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A Raisin in the Sun
works.description: A Raisin in the Sun is Lorraine Hansberry's first play, which opened at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre in New York on 11 March 1959: the first play by an African American woman produced on Broadway. A realist drama about a working-class Black family on Chicago's South Side, it turns on what the family will do with a life-insurance payment and on their decision to move into a white neighbourhood. Its title comes from Langston Hughes's poem "Harlem": 'What happens to a dream deferred?... Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?'
works.summary: Three acts set in the Youngers' cramped apartment: the arrival of the insurance cheque after the father's death and the family's conflicting plans for it; Mama's purchase of a house in the white suburb of Clybourne Park and Walter Lee's loss of the remaining money; and the visit of a white neighbourhood representative offering to buy them out, which ends with the family's decision to move.
works.plot:
The Younger family, three generations sharing a small, run-down apartment, awaits a cheque for ten thousand dollars from the life insurance of Walter Younger senior, who worked himself to death. His widow, Lena, known as Mama, is the head of the household. Her son, Walter Lee, a chauffeur in his thirties who feels humiliated by his job, wants to invest the money in a liquor store with two friends. Walter's wife, Ruth, worn down by work and poverty, discovers she is pregnant and considers an abortion rather than bring another child into their crowded rooms. Walter's sister, Beneatha, a college student, intends to become a doctor and is courted by two men who represent opposed ideas of Black identity: George Murchison, the wealthy and assimilated son of a successful family, and Joseph Asagai, a Nigerian student who encourages her interest in Africa.

Mama refuses to use the money for a liquor store. Instead she makes a down payment on a house with a garden in Clybourne Park, a white neighbourhood, because it is the only decent house the family can afford. Seeing Walter's despair, she then entrusts him with the rest of the money, asking him to bank part of it for Beneatha's medical education. Walter gives all of it to his friend Willy Harris, who disappears with it, and their associate Bobo brings the news. Beneatha's future and Walter's dream collapse at once.

Meanwhile Karl Lindner, a mild-mannered representative of the Clybourne Park Improvement Association, has visited to offer to buy the house back at a profit, explaining that the community does not want Black neighbours. The family had sent him away, but after the loss of the money Walter telephones him, intending to accept the offer and to perform the humiliation the white world expects. When Lindner arrives, however, Walter, standing before his son Travis and his mother, cannot go through with it: he tells Lindner that the family is proud, that his father earned the house, and that they will move in. As the movers carry out the furniture, Mama goes back for her small, struggling houseplant, the symbol of her care for the family, and follows the others to the new house.
works.significance: The play ran for 530 performances and won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award for 1959, over new plays by Eugene O'Neill, Tennessee Williams and Archibald MacLeish; Hansberry was the youngest American and the first Black dramatist to receive it. The 1961 film, for which she wrote the screenplay, received a special award at the Cannes Film Festival. It is ranked with Death of a Salesman and The Glass Menagerie among the classics of the American theatre and opened Broadway to Black writers, actors and audiences; James Baldwin wrote that he had never in his life seen so many Black people in the theatre.
works.meter: Naturalistic dialogue rich in humour, African American speech and family argument; carefully balanced characters, each with a credible point of view; symbolic objects such as the cheque, the plant and Beneatha's Nigerian robes; moments of heightened, almost musical speech in Walter's monologues.
works.context: Hansberry wrote the play in 1956-57 in New York, drawing on her family's experience of moving into a white Chicago neighbourhood in the late 1930s and on the restrictive-covenant litigation that followed. It reached Broadway in 1959, five years after Brown v. Board of Education and during the rise of the civil rights movement, after try-outs in New Haven, Philadelphia and Chicago, directed by Lloyd Richards, the first African American to direct a Broadway play in decades.
works.characters: Lena Younger (Mama); Walter Lee Younger; Ruth Younger; Beneatha Younger; Travis Younger; Joseph Asagai; George Murchison; Karl Lindner; Bobo; Mrs. Johnson
works.structure: Three acts and a single realistic interior set, observing near-unity of place and a compressed time scheme; each act ends on a turning point (the cheque, the loss of the money, the decision to move), and the climax places Walter's choice before his son.

works.title: A Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
altTitles: Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
works.description: Published in 1895 and the most complete documentary record of American lynching produced in the nineteenth century: the statistics for 1892-94, case by case. It is a prose work of 1895 by Ida B. Wells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Wells tabulates the lynchings, the alleged causes, the states, the races and the circumstances; she demonstrates that the charge of rape was invented after the fact and that the real causes were economic competition and political intimidation, and she names the officials who permitted the murders.
works.significance: A Red Record is the founding text of American statistical journalism on race and the most important documentary record of lynching: its method and its findings made it the basis of all later anti-lynching work, and it is a permanent indictment of American justice.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass.
works.context: The 1892-95: the black exodus from the South, the founding of the NAACP, and the American and British anti-lynching campaigns. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ida Bell Wells-Barnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Red, Red Rose
altTitles: O my Luve's like a red, red rose
works.form: song lyric written for a Scottish air, in the collecting and adapting practice of the Scots Musical Museum
works.description: Burns's song of enduring affection, two brief stanzas of departure and of the vow to return, which became the most familiar love lyric in Scottish and one of the most set, translated and quoted poems in English. Its opening compares the beloved to the red rose and the melody, and its closing pledge of return across the widest distance gives the whole its pathos. Burns entered it among the songs he was collecting and reworking for Johnson's musical collection.
works.plot: The speaker likens his love to the newly blown rose and to the tune that strikes the ear, states the certainty of love beyond measure, and then faces the distance of parting. The second stanza pledges the return across the farthest seas and mountains till all the world be changed, closing with the image of the rivers and the sea that makes the promise seem at once impossible and certain.
works.significance: It is the most widely known of Burns's songs in English translation and setting, and a standard instance of how the antiquarian song-collecting of the 1790s produced original lyric. Its treatment of love and distance supplied a repertoire of phrase and image that passed into popular song generally.
works.meter: Short ballad-like song stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines, adapted to the air's phrasing, with simple diction and a single sustained simile.
works.context: Composed in the mid-1790s during Burns's last years in Dumfries, while he was contributing hundreds of songs and notes to Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, and drawing on traditional Scottish openings of the 'rose' and 'melodie' type. The song belongs to the great project of recovery and reissue of Scottish song that made the 1790s a decade of national anthology.
works.characters: The loving speaker; the absent beloved
works.structure: Two short stanzas of song, the first of comparison and present joy, the second of parting and the vow of return, with no narrative development beyond the single address.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns's song reworks and re-voices older traditional material, as he himself recorded in the notes to the collection, so the record of authorship should be read together with his practice of collecting and adaptation.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian
Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: A Report to the County of Lanark
altTitles: A Report to the County of Lanark; of a Plan for Relieving Public Distress and Removing Discontent, by Giving Permanent Productive Employment to the Great Mass of Skill Labour
Report to the County of Lanark
works.form: social report and project; political economy of public distress with the plan of the home colony
works.description: The most concrete and the most radical of the great plans of social regeneration of its age, drawn up as a paper for the meeting of the freeholders and householders of the county of Lanark and given to the public as a report of the managers of the manufacturing village: a proposal for home colonies of agriculture and manufacture which should employ the ruined labour of the country and educate the people into a new character.
works.plot: The report begins with the experience of twenty years' management of a manufacturing population, and with the demonstration that the habits, the health, the intelligence, and the productiveness of the same people may be raised together by a changed arrangement of their schooling, their dwellings, and their labour. It then states the cause of the public distress of the years after the peace: that the productive power of the country, increased infinitely by machinery and by skill, has produced far more than the consumers who are paid wages can consume, so that the plenty of the country and the poverty of its makers exist together, and the labourer is unemployed because he cannot be paid in the old way. From this he argues, not for relief by gifts, but for a permanent plan: the establishment throughout the kingdom of villages or home colonies of from five hundred to two thousand persons, upon grounds of a thousand to two thousand acres, each colony laid out with the dwellings, the schools, the kitchens, the workshops, and the gardens in one square of good building, the agriculture and the manufactures joined in the same body, the children educated at the common cost from the earliest years, and all the labour lightened by machinery and by combination. The expense he computes, and proposes to meet it from the parochial and county funds and from the poor-rate already raised, the colonies being managed by committee of the persons interested; and he pleads that the plan saves the country, the law, and the morals of the people at once, and removes both the distress and the discontent of which the county meeting had sat.
works.significance: The chief document of the proposal for regeneration by the village of united and mutual co-operation, and one of the most influential of English plans of social building: the home colony described in it governed the co-operative and the community writing of the 1820s and 1830s, was pleaded before the poor-law commissioners and the boards of health of the following generation, and anticipated the modern literature of the model village, the garden city, and the planned community; its analysis of distress as the product of excessive productive power joined to deficient means of consumption is one of the notable economic arguments of its time.
works.meter: The flat, fluent, statistic prose of the manager addressing his county, with the long periodic sentence, the confident enumeration of numbers, acres, and pounds, and the perpetual appeal to the experience of twenty years; a style of proposal which persuades by the weight of its particulars and by its benevolence rather than by analysis or wit.
works.context: Drawn up after the meeting of the freeholders and inhabitants of the county of Lanark at Hamilton in the closing months of 1820, in the depth of the distress of the manufacturing and agricultural labourers which followed the bad harvests, the returning officer's accounts of the poor-rates, the pressure of the restrictive and corn laws, and the agitation of the great meeting of the metropolis for reform; and it belongs to the decade of the plans, the county meetings, and the parliamentary inquiry which made the condition of the labouring population the first question of the day.
works.structure: A report and address in the form of the county paper: the statement of the experience, the analysis of the causes of the distress, the plan of the home colony in its detail of numbers, ground, building, and education, the estimate of the expense and of the returns, and the closing appeal to the county and to the legislature, with the resolutions of the meeting and the several letters appended.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; the report is given out in the name of the managers of the establishment in the first issue, and the writer's own authorship is stated in the collected editions; the several reprints of the plan, the letters to the counties, and the reports of the co-operative bodies restate the proposal with alterations of detail.

Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer

works.title: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery; or, of Admitting the Least Claim of Private Property in the Persons of Men, in England
altTitles: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery
works.form: Polemical and legal-religious treatise addressed as a public representation
works.description: The founding document of Granville Sharp's anti-slavery campaign, addressed to the merchants and planters of Great Britain and printed in London in 1769. Sharp, a clerk in the York Office and a self-taught Hebraist and grammarian, brings together biblical, legal and moral evidence that no master can hold a Christian as property, and warns that tolerating slavery corrupts English law and religion alike. Its learning, heat and long appendices of evidence made it the reference text of the British abolitionist case before Somersett's case of 1772.
works.plot: Sharp argues first from scripture that the Old Testament's servitude laws are not the modern form of chattel slavery, and that the gospel, which forbids men to rule over conscience, condemns holding human beings as goods and chattels. He then reviews English law and the earlier decisions against villeinage and imported servitude, urging that no custom or statute within England can authorise property in the persons of men. He next examines the planters' pleas of commerce, necessity and colonial prescription, treating them as interests against justice; and closes with a plain remonstrance to slave-owners, inviting them to manumit voluntarily before the law or divine judgment compels them. The volume appends testimony about the treatment of slaves in the colonies and a grammatical and critical disquisition much of which concerns the Hebrew and Greek terms for servitude.
works.significance: It supplied the legal and scriptural brief on which later abolitionists built, and its philological appendix anticipated the modern debate over the Bible's servitude texts. As the first substantial English attack on slavery written by a lay patron of the enslaved rather than by a Quaker or a cleric in the colonies, it marks the entry of the question into English public argument about law and conscience.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, lawyerly and scriptural register
works.context: Written in the decade of the Somersett litigation and of Sharp's patronage and education of enslaved people in England, it belongs to the evangelical and legalistic attack on the trade, to Sharp's own work as a patron and teacher of freed and abandoned enslaved people in London, and to the wider British argument about personal liberty that ran from the Wilkes controversies to the American dispute.
works.structure: Single sustained address in numbered argumentative divisions, followed by appended evidence, testimony and philological notes.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Granville Sharp is established and undisputed.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: A Romance of Two Worlds
works.description: The founding text of the occult bestseller: a dying woman is cured by electricity and travels through the spheres. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by Marie Corelli; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: A young woman, ill and suicidal, is treated by a mysterious physician, Heliobas, who uses electricity to release her spirit from her body; she travels through the solar system in the company of spirits and returns with the assurance of immortality.
works.significance: A Romance of Two Worlds was Corelli's first novel and the founding text of the occult bestseller: it made the mixture of electricity, reincarnation and Christian mysticism into a mass-market formula and created the audience for Theosophy in England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the occult machinery of the romance — electricity, reincarnation, the astral body.
works.context: The 1880s, the vogue for spiritualism and theosophy, and the new electrical science. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the narrator; Heliobas; Zara; Azul; the spirits of the spheres
works.structure: A first-person narrative in four books, from the sickroom to the spheres. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary Mackay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: A Satire Against Reason and Mankind
altTitles: A Satyr Against Reason and Mankind
works.description: Rochester's most substantial philosophical poem, a libertine dialogue between a satirist who would rather be a dog than a man and a clergyman who defends reason, in which 'right reason' is reduced to the guidance of appetite.
works.plot: The poet attacks the pride and falsity of human reason; the bishop replies in defence of reason as the light of God; the poet answers by distinguishing true reason, which serves the senses, from speculative reason, which is mere fear and fancy.
works.significance: The most intellectually serious poem of Restoration libertinism and a central text for understanding Rochester's rehabilitation in the late twentieth century.
works.meter: Irregular pentameter couplets, colloquial and argumentative.
works.context: Composed c. 1674-5 and circulated in manuscript in the court coterie; Rochester's Hobbesian scepticism answers the Cambridge Platonists and the new natural philosophy.
works.characters: the speaker; the bishop (Thomas Sprat, according to tradition)
works.structure: A dramatic dialogue in two unequal parts, closing with the poet's self-portrait of the man of sense and pleasure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Rochester in contemporary manuscript witnesses; authorship accepted, though individual lines vary between witnesses.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Wit, libertinism, and the rake

works.title: A Scots Quair
works.description: The great Scottish trilogy: the land, the town and the city in one woman's life, and the passage of Scotland into the modern world. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Lewis Grassic Gibbon; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The trilogy — Sunset Song (1932), Cloud Howe (1933) and Grey Granite (1934) — follows Chris Guthrie from the Mearns croft through her marriage to a minister in the small town of Segget and her son Ewan's life as a communist agitator in the industrial city of Duncairn.
works.significance: A Scots Quair is the most complete account in fiction of Scotland's passage from the land to the city in a single generation: its three volumes, its Scots prose and its historical sweep made it the central work of the Scottish Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness.
works.context: Scotland from 1911 to the Depression of the 1930s: the farming Mearns, the small town, and the industrial city. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1934 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Chris Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Robert Colquohoun; Ewan Colquohoun; Ellen Johns
works.structure: Three volumes, each with its own setting and its choric openings. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Leslie Mitchell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Select Collection of Original Scottish Airs for the Voice
altTitles: A Select Collection of Original Scotish Airs for the Voice
Select Collection of Original Scottish Airs
works.form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of Scottish song with musical arrangements; ballad and popular song written for publication in a polite album series
works.description: George Thomson's rival song collection, issued in five volumes from 1793 to 1818 and marketed as a polite as well as a national repertory: Scottish airs furnished with instrumental introductions and closings and with keyboard and string accompaniments written or adapted by Ignaz Pleyel, Leopold Koželuch and Joseph Haydn, and supplied with characteristic verses in Scots and, for the English market, with added English translations of the songs. Thomson, an Edinburgh writer to the signet and collector of music, made the series a commercial enterprise on a larger scale than James Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, and from 1793 he secured the labour of Robert Burns, whose songs and revisions for it were advertised on the title pages themselves as upwards of one hundred new songs. The collection is the scene of Burns's most sustained quarrel with an editor: Thomson wanted the dialect smoothed and the airs dressed for drawing-room sale, Burns insisted on the old words and on the singable economy of the stanza, and the resulting letters form the most systematic body of Romantic criticism of song-making.
works.plot: As a repertory the work presents air after air with its text and its arrangement: Scottish melodies, many traditional, set with symphonies and accompaniments in the current keyboard style and fitted with verses in the Scottish dialect together with English rendering. The songs gathered or commissioned by Thomson cover love, absence and fidelity, drinking and fellowship, landscape and the rural round, and patriotic and border themes; Burns supplied new lyrics, restored or trimmed traditional texts, and proposed alternatives where he judged the existing words unworthy of the air. His correspondence with Thomson states the poetics behind the entries: that the poet must be the servant of the music, that old songs should be preserved with their imperfections, and that a single offending word can spoil a stanza sung to a favourite tune.
works.significance: The collection preserves the second and more commercially ambitious half of Burns's late song work, and its title-page claim to Burns's new songs made the poet's labour for a music publisher a public feature of the book. The Burns-Thomson correspondence called out by it is the chief Romantic document on the making of songs, on the authority of the tune over the text, and on the editorial handling of a national vernacular repertory. As a publishing object the series is the standard test case for the argument that the Romantic ballad revival was as much a commercial and musical enterprise as a literary one.
works.meter: Song stanzas measured to pre-existing airs, so that line length, stanza shape and refrain are dictated by the musical period; Burns's texts for Thomson move between common and short measure ballad stanzas, four-line and six-line song stanzas with tags, and the irregular stanzaic patterns he adopted for particular airs. The accompanying prose notes and letters show the working principle: syllable for syllable fitting to the notes, with elision in the Scots dialect used to keep the singer's phrase intact.
works.context: Thomson's series appeared in the competitive Edinburgh music trade of the 1790s and after, when the demand for national airs among Scottish and English subscribers supported a cottage industry of collection, arrangement and subscription publishing. The first volumes relied on Pleyel and Koželuch; from the end of the century Haydn was engaged to arrange Scottish songs, which set the collection at the centre of a transnational exchange between Viennese classicism and Scottish tradition. Burns, who had known Thomson since the Edinburgh years of 1787, agreed in 1793 to supply verses; his contributions continued until his death in 1796, and the later volumes, with their added English verses, realised Thomson's programme of making Scots song saleable to a polite and English-speaking market.
works.characters: the lovers, absent friends and false hearts of the song texts; the shepherds, reapers and harvest figures of the pastoral numbers; the honest drunkards and vagrants of the comic songs; George Thomson as editor-proprietor, Robert Burns as supplying poet, and the arrangers Pleyel, Koželuch and Haydn as the collection's other makers
works.structure: A serial publication in five volumes of independent songs with musical settings, ordered by Thomson's commercial and musical scheme rather than by any argument; the volumes were issued successively between 1793 and 1818 with variant Edinburgh and London imprints, and the Burns material belongs chiefly to the numbers published during and just after his lifetime, the later volumes continuing without him.
works.attributionNotes: This is Thomson's publication and Thomson's editorial conception, with musical arrangements by Pleyel, Koželuch and Haydn and verses by several hands; Robert Burns is not its author. Burns is named here only as the contributing poet whose songs the volumes advertise and whose dialect verses Thomson revised or replaced. The number of his contributions is variously stated in the scholarship (around one hundred songs is the common estimate, and the contemporary title pages claim upwards of one hundred new songs), and individual songs exist in more than one state because of Thomson's editorial interference, so each attribution within the series must be checked against the scholarly edition of Burns's songs for Thomson rather than taken from the printed volumes alone.

works.title: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy
altTitles: The Sentimental Journey through France and Italy
works.description: The journal of a clergyman travelling in France and Italy with nothing but his feelings for an equipment, a book of episodes in which the encounter, not the place, is the subject. It gave the century the word sentimental in its modern sense and made the traveller's sympathetic alarm a literary form.
works.plot: Yorick sets out alone, unprovided, and falls into a succession of small encounters - the monk of Calais, the fair grisette, the imprisoned French volunteer, the orphan girl at the convent gate, the dying lover at Lyons. Each meeting asks of him a feeling he is not always equal to, and his own vanity and desire are reported with the same candour as his tenderness. The journey ends with the lady of the last part unpossessed, the traveller's resolutions defeated and renewed.
works.significance: It is the defining text of literary sentimentalism and one of the most imitated prose styles of the century, and its treatment of sympathy as a precarious, sexual and self-interested feeling shaped the later novel of feeling.
works.meter: An interrupted, breathless prose of half-sentences, dashes and exclamations, with the apostrophe to the heart as its characteristic cadence.
works.context: Published in 1768 after the author's continental tour of the previous years and the death of his father, in the season of the cult of feeling, the sensibility controversy and the Anglo-French travel of the peace; it was answered at once by a rival's travels.
works.characters: Mr. Yorick; the monk of Calais; the poor grisette; Maria, the orphan at the convent; the captive of the war and the company of the road
works.structure: A loose first-person journal of episodes without continuous plot, arranged in short titled sequences; the movement is emotional rather than geographical, and the reader supplies the connections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the persona of the sermons retained.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel

Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
altTitles: The Practical Series of a Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
works.description: William Law's great devotional conduct book, teaching a rule of universal devotion by which every common action, business, and hour of the day is turned into prayer. It argues that religion is not a set of duties but the whole temper of a life resigned to God's will.
works.plot: Law first grounds devotion in the Gospel's own rules for ordinary conduct, then shows how the daily offices, work, meals, social hours, sleep, and sickness may each be sanctified by a fixed temper of resignation. Through portraits of worldly wise men, women of quality, the miser, the politician, and the clergyman, he proves that everything admirable in politeness is a poor counterfeit of devotion. The second movement directs the inward life: the love of God as the sole motive, the renunciation of self-will, and the sacramental use of the world. It closes with the famous counsel that a man must be a saint or wretch, and a moving description of the devout life as one hour of continuous offering.
works.significance: The most influential English devotional prose of the century between Ken and the tractarians, a standard of Anglican spiritual direction and a school of style for Samuel Johnson and many readers of the evangelical revival.
works.meter: A grave, rhythmic, iteratively clause-balanced prose, built on scriptural paraphrase and moral paradox; its solemn cadences were much admired and much parodied.
works.context: Written in the quiet of Kings Clipston after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment over the nonjurors' question, and published in 1729 when deist controversy had made practical Christianity a contested idea; Johnson, Wesley, and later Newman counted it formative.
works.structure: Two-part conduct treatise: doctrinal direction and rule of life, interwoven with a gallery of moral characters and closing meditations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
The contemplative life

works.title: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of Their True and Greatest Interest
altTitles: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies
works.description: Mary Astell's feminist treatise proposing a Protestant monastery or religious retirement where women could pursue education and the life of the mind free from marriage and male authority.
works.plot: Part I (1694) argues that women's intellectual inferiority is the product of defective education and proposes a religious community for their instruction; part II (1697) supplies a method for the improvement of women's minds based on Cartesian clear and distinct ideas.
works.significance: The first systematic argument for women's education in English and a founding text of English feminism; its proposal for a female intellectual community anticipates later educational reform.
works.meter: Vigorous, ironic, and rhetorically accomplished prose.
works.context: Part I published anonymously in 1694, part II in 1697; the proposal attracted the attention of Princess Anne of Denmark and provoked the suspicion that Astell was a crypto-Catholic.
works.structure: Two parts, each a continuous argument with a prefatory dedication.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as 'A Lover of Her Sex'; attribution to Astell is established.

works.form: Collection of translations from French poetry
works.description: Published in 1876 and the first book by an Indian writer of translations from French poetry: versions of Hugo, Lamartine, Chénier, Béranger and a hundred other French poets. works.title: A Short Account of God's Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield

works.description: Whitefield's spiritual autobiography, first printed in Philadelphia and enlarged in a Dublin edition of 1740 with a preface by John Wesley. It told the story of the conversion of an orphaned tallow-chandler's apprentice into the field preacher of three continents, the most read conversion narrative of the evangelical revival.
works.plot: Whitefield recounts his boyhood at the Bell Inn in Gloucester, the Oxford years with the Wesleys and the Holy Club, and the methodist disciplines of fasting, communion, and service in the prisons. He tells of his conversion through a book on the meritorious blood and righteousness of Christ, the moment he knew himself a child of God, and the fervour that followed into ordination and the sermon at Cincinnati? no: into his first American journey and the open-air field. The narrative weighs each experience against scripture, giving the Word as the evidence of every inward turn, and closes on the providence that carried the preacher from closed pulpits to the multitudes of the fields.
works.significance: It gave the evangelical revival its canonical conversion plot and made the autobiography of grace a mass genre; it remains the primary source for the Holy Club and the origins of Methodism in open air.
works.meter: Earnest, plain, exclamatory autobiographical prose, biblical quotation as the measure and sanction of every stated feeling.
works.context: Published in the first Atlantic season of the revival, 1739-40, as Whitefield's field preaching and his American journey made him the transatlantic evangelist; its printing by Franklin in Philadelphia? use: its American printing in 1739 and Wesley's Dublin preface in 1740 secured its wide circulation.

works.title: A Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy
altTitles: Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy, in Three Books
works.description: Hutcheson's mature summary of his ethical system in three books, written as a student vade mecum: the moral sense and its determinations, self-love and benevolence in their due proportions, and the obligations of the natural, social, and divine life. Its final maxim made the greatest happiness of the greatest numbers the sole rule of duty.
works.plot: Book I grounds virtue in the moral sense, showing that this sense determines us to approve benevolent affections and that the laws of nature are intelligible only through it. Book II analyses self-love and its vanity when made the end, and benevolence as the happiness of the agent as well as of the species. Book III deduces the duties to God, to ourselves, and to our neighbours from the dictates of right reason joined to benevolence, and closes on the famous formula that the action is best which procures the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers. The whole is compressed into aphoristic numbered sections for classroom use.
works.significance: It transmitted utilitarian's first canonical formula and the moral-sense system to the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and the American founding, becoming the most-copied ethics textbook of the colonies.
works.meter: Bare, sententious, heavily numbered textbook prose, almost a series of theses, with occasional passages of the older warmth.
works.context: Published in 1747, distilling Hutcheson's forty years of Glasgow teaching into a classroom manual read by the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and by students at Harvard and Princeton.
works.structure: Three books of numbered propositions in catechetic order, each doctrine placed under its heads and their moral.

works.title: A Shropshire Lad
works.description: Published in 1896 at the author's expense and the most popular sequence of English lyrics of its age: poems of the Shropshire countryside, of young men dying and of the brevity of life. It is a verse work of 1896 by A. E. Housman; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet.
works.plot: The sequence moves through the Shropshire landscape from spring to winter: the lad who must leave for London, the soldier who dies in battle, the lovers who are parted, the hanged man and the suicide, all set in a countryside that is beautiful and completely indifferent to the fate of the people in it.
works.significance: A Shropshire Lad is the most influential English poetry collection of the 1890s: it made the short lyric the dominant form of English verse, it became a talisman for the generation of 1914 (whose soldiers carried it in their packs), and its poems have been set to music by Vaughan Williams, Butterworth, Gurney and dozens of composers. It is also the central English text of unavowed homosexuality.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the song measure in quatrains.
works.context: 1896: the agricultural depression, the decay of the rural counties, the imperial wars of the 1890s, and Housman's own silence about his love for a fellow student. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: The work is in 63 poems. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.description: Published in 1880 and the most brilliant critical book of the Victorian age: a study of Shakespeare's development through the metre of his plays. works.title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
altTitles: System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
works.description: Published in 1843 and the foundational work of English empiricist philosophy of science: an account of the methods of induction, of the logic of the moral sciences, and of the errors of the a priori school.
works.plot: The six books treat names and propositions, reasoning, induction, the operations subsidiary to induction, the fallacies, and the logic of the moral sciences. The central contribution is the formulation of the 'methods of experimental inquiry' — agreement, difference, residues and concomitant variations — and the argument that the moral sciences must be deductive in method but cannot predict individual conduct.
works.significance: The System of Logic established the empiricist philosophy of science in English and gave the social sciences their methodological foundation; its 'methods of inquiry' are still the standard formulation, and its sixth book founded the modern logic of the social sciences.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
works.context: The 1830s-40s, the Scottish philosophy of Thomas Brown and Dugald Stewart, Whewell's and Herschel's philosophy of science, and the controversy with the intuitionist school of Coleridge and Hamilton. The record dates the work as composed between 1830 and 1843 and first published in 1843 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: A Tale of a Tub
altTitles: A Tale of a Tub: Written for the Universal Improvement of Mankind
works.description: Swift's first great prose satire: the ironised digressions of a mad Grub Street author, within which the parable of the three brothers and their coats exposes the corruptions of the Christian churches, and which ends in the celestial voyage and the tower of Fame.
works.plot: Three brothers, Peter, Martin and Jack, receive coats and a will from their father; Peter enlarges his coat with additions of his own, breaks the will and expels his brothers, so that Martin reforms and Jack splits into sects; the narrator's account of his own mechanical digressions and of the voyage to the island of the Aeolians surrounds the parable with a anatomy of enthusiasm, criticism and learning.
works.significance: It founded the Swiftian method of complete impersonation of a deranged narrator and remains the century's most radical analysis of religious zeal, textual corruption and the pathology of printed learning.
works.meter: Prose that passes from the nakedness of the plain style to the inflated cadences of the enthusiasm and the projectors, the satire carried by the register rather than by verse.
works.context: Composed in the aftermath of the 1690s quarrel of the ancients and moderns and of the Toleration debate, and printed in 1704 with The Battle of the Books; its anticlerical edge long obstructed Swift's preferment, and he disowned its authorship when the volume was reissued at the height of the party war.
works.characters: Peter; Martin; Jack; the digressive narrator; the father; the mob of Grub Street
works.structure: A framed and digressive prose satire: the allegorical history of the brothers set within the narrator's self-revealing preface, digressions, mechanical project and voyage, with no continuous sequence of action.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Swift on the evidence of his friends and of the volume's later apparatus; Swift himself for long refused to own the book, and the ascription of individual passages of the appended pieces to his hand is debated.

works.title: A Tale of Paraguay
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: a domestic romantic narrative in the line of his earlier tales, reduced in scope and raised in moral seriousness.
works.description: The author's last completed long narrative poem, a romance of the Jesuit reductions of Paraguay, published in the volume that also contained his Vision of Judgement and other short pieces. It deliberately abandons the machinery and the exotic theatres of the earlier metrical tales for a quieter, domestic and more humane story of love across the boundaries of race and creed. The poem is a summary of its author's late romantic practice: courteous, elegiac, and sceptical of conquest.
works.plot: The tale is laid in the Guarani mission towns of Paraguay and turns on the affection of a Spanish settler for a daughter of the converted Indians, and on the trial their union undergoes from the greed of the colonists and from the slave-hunting raids of the Paulistas upon the reductions. The poem gives the missions a social reality - their agriculture, their music, their government by the Jesuit fathers - and sets against it the avarice of those who would divide the Indians among themselves. Persecution, displacement and separation test the lovers, and a providential close restores what rapacity had nearly destroyed. Interpolated songs and lyric apostrophes mark the crises of the story, and the poet's comment on the usage of the Indians grows plainer as the narrative proceeds.
works.significance: The most admired of its author's later poems in his own lifetime and the one Victorian readers valued most; it is an early English Romantic example of anti-colonial sympathy expressed through the domestic romance form.
works.meter: Chiefly blank verse with rhymed stanzas and interpolated lyric songs; a softer, more conversational movement than the earlier metrical tales.
works.context: Written after its author's accession to the laureateship in 1813 and during his residence at Green Hill, Wimbledon, when he was engaged on the History of Brazil and increasingly interested in the treatment of Indians under Spanish and Jesuit rule.
works.structure: Continuous narrative poem in cantos, interrupted by inserted songs and lyric addresses and by a first-person editorial comment that grows stronger as the tale approaches its close.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Mission, conversion, and the Church
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets
