works.title: An Island Is a World
works.description: Selvon's second novel, published by Allan Wingate in London in 1955, is set in Trinidad after the Second World War. Its present publisher calls it a novel of personal and intellectual quest; the Anthurium special issue on Selvon (2025) reports Ramabai Espinet's case for reconsidering its place in his work.
works.summary: Two brothers leave post-war Trinidad, one for England and one for the United States, while their elders think of returning to India.
works.plot: In the post-war colony, as an earlier generation thinks of returning to India, the young Foster goes to England and his brother Rufus leaves for the United States, each in search of himself and his world. Mawenzi House's description, the only account of the plot consulted, presents the book as a moving story of personal and intellectual quest told with Selvon's humour and vivid sense of place.
works.significance: One of Selvon's least discussed novels, though Espinet argues for its importance; it was reissued in Toronto by TSAR (1993) and Mawenzi House (2019).
works.meter: The Globe and Mail, quoted by the publisher, praised Selvon's evocative description, affectionate humour and subtle use of folklore.
works.context: Published between A Brighter Sun and The Lonely Londoners; Nalini Mohabir, in the Anthurium issue, reads it with Selvon's 1955 essay 'The West Indian Patchwork' and his BBC play Home Sweet India as part of his thinking about return.
works.structure: Built, in the publisher's account, on the parallel quests of two brothers; the arrangement of the narrative was not examined.

works.title: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
works.form: Poetry collection (posthumous, with a memoir by Edmund Gosse)
works.description: Published posthumously in 1882 and the first English retelling of the Indian epics by an Indian writer: ballads drawn from the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and the Puranas. It is a verse work of 1882 by Toru Dutt; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume contains 'Savitri', the story of the wife who wins back her husband from Death; 'Lakshman', from the Ramayana; 'Jogadhya Uma'; 'The Royal Ascetic and the Hind'; 'Dhruva'; 'Buttoo'; and 'Sindhu', among others.
works.significance: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan is the founding work of Indian-English poetry: it is the first collection in which an Indian writer retells the national epics in English verse, and its ballads made the Sanskrit stories available to English readers in a form they could recognise.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and lyric metres with a French and English formal discipline.
works.context: The 1870s, the Bengal Renaissance, the Sanskrit epics in English translation, and the colonial education of the Indian elite. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1877 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Tarulatta Datta. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Ancrene Wisse
works.form: rule and devotional treatise in prose
works.description: A rule of life for three anchoresses, written in the West Midlands 'AB language' c. 1225–40: eight parts treating the devotional routine, the custody of the senses, temptation, confession, penance, love, and the inner life. It is the greatest prose work of early Middle English, celebrated for its psychological acuity, its homely and exact imagery, and its humane severity.
works.plot: Addressing the anchoresses as a loving director, the author regulates their prayers and reading, anatomizes the temptations of the solitary life (with the famous allegory of the royal wooing of the soul), teaches the art of confession, and unfolds the degrees of love culminating in union with Christ.
works.significance: The masterpiece of early Middle English prose and the supreme English contribution to the literature of the solitary life; its influence reaches the Cloud-author and beyond.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of great art; concrete domestic metaphor (the anchorhold as house, the heart as its lady).
works.context: Written in Herefordshire or the Welsh Marches for three sisters enclosed near a church, in the milieu that produced the Katherine Group; revised and translated into French and Latin, and copied into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the three anchoresses (addressees); Christ as lover-king (allegorical)
works.structure: Eight books moving from outer rule (devotions, senses) to inner rule (heart, conscience) and love; interlaced with exemplary tales and allegories.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus (the author is sometimes speculatively identified with a Dominican or Augustinian director).
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Penance, confession, and sin
The contemplative life
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)

works.title: And Then There Were None
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1939
works.description: The most perfectly constructed detective novel in English: ten strangers on an island, and a nursery rhyme that kills them. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Agatha Christie; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ten people, each guilty of a death the law could not punish, are lured to an island off the Devon coast by a mysterious host; they die one by one in the manner of the nursery rhyme 'Ten Little Soldier Boys', and the solution is revealed in a manuscript by the murderer, the judge Lawrence Wargrave.
works.significance: And Then There Were None is the most perfectly constructed detective novel in English: its mathematical elegance, its nursery-rhyme structure and its impossible solution made it Christie's masterpiece and the best-selling mystery novel of all time.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play plot with its clues planted in plain sight.
works.context: The Devon coast of the 1930s, the closed island setting, and the pre-war atmosphere of approaching catastrophe. The record dates the work as composed in 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire.
works.characters: Justice Wargrave; Vera Claythorne; Philip Lombard; Emily Brent; General Macarthur; Dr Armstrong; Mr Blore
works.structure: Ten victims in the order of the nursery rhyme, with a final manuscript explaining the plot. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Agatha Mary Clarissa Christie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Andreas
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 1,722 lines on the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew, sailing incognito with Christ himself as his helmsman, voyages to the cannibal city of Mermedonia to rescue his fellow apostle Matthew. The poem recasts the apostle as a heroic seafarer in the manner of Beowulf, with some of the corpus's most vivid voyage imagery.
works.plot: Christ, disguised as a ship's captain, ferries the reluctant Andrew over the stormy sea, hearing his preaching on the way; in Mermedonia, Andrew is seized, tortured, and imprisoned, but a flood released from a stone pillar drowns his tormentors and revives them, converting the city; Andrew establishes a church and departs, leaving the poem's didactic epilogue.
works.significance: The fullest Old English saint's life in verse and a celebrated example of the heroic adaptation of hagiography.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in the classical heroic manner.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 29v-52v); based on a Latin version of the apocryphal Acts, itself known in Old English prose from the Blickling manuscript.
works.characters: Andrew; Christ (the helmsman); Matthew; the Mermedonians
works.structure: A sea-voyage frame enclosing the martyrdom-and-conversion narrative, with speeches, miracles, and a flood scene modelled on Exodus; the poem borrows formulaic lines directly from Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Beowulf borrowings are stylistic, not evidence of authorship.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Sea voyage and seafaring
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
altTitles: The Satire of the Three Estates
works.description: Lindsay's great morality drama of the Scottish Reformation: King Humanitie, seduced by Sensualitie and the vices, is recalled to virtue by Divine Correction, and summons a parliament of the three estates — Spirituality, Temporalitie, Merchant — where John the Common-Weill indicts the church's abuses and the vices are tried and hanged. Played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552.
works.plot: Rex Humanitas falls under the rule of Wantonness, Placebo, and Solace; Divine Correction reforms him; the estates meet in parliament, hear John the Common-Weill's complaint, and pass the acts of reform, the play closing with the sermon of Folly.
works.significance: The greatest Scottish play and the dramatic summa of the northern Reformation; its parliament scene made drama an instrument of national reform and remained a living text into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Scots couplets of great stage energy; songs, interludes, and the sermon of Folly closing the action.
works.context: First played before James V at Linlithgow in 1540; the enlarged Cupar performance (1552) addressed the eve of the Scottish Reformation, and the play remained in performance for a century.
works.characters: Rex Humanitas; Divine Correction; Sensualitie; Flatterie; Falset; Dissait; John the Common-Weill; Spirituality; Temporalitie; Merchant
works.structure: A two-part morality expanded to a national parliament: the king's moral fall and recovery (Part I) and the public trial and reformation of the estates (Part II).
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Angel Pavement
works.description: Priestley's London novel: a City firm, a mysterious stranger and the lives of the clerks. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by John Boynton Priestley; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: In the offices of Twigg and Dersingham, a firm of veneer merchants in the City, the arrival of the mysterious Mr Golspie transforms the business and the lives of the clerks — the ambitious Mr Dersingham, the clerk Mr Smeeth and the typist Turgis — before the crash and the disappearance.
works.significance: Angel Pavement is Priestley's London novel and his finest: its portrait of the City, its sympathy for the clerks and its picture of the slump made it one of the great English novels of the Depression.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the symmetrical three-act play with a single set and a small cast.
works.context: The City of London in 1930, the Depression and the lives of the lower middle class. The record dates the work as composed in 1930 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.

works.structure: A novel of the office and the City, following several lives through a year. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.

works.title: Animal Farm
works.form: Novella (beast fable; first edition subtitled 'A Fairy Story')
works.description: Orwell's beast fable of a revolution betrayed: the animals of Manor Farm drive out their drunken farmer and found a commonwealth of equals, which the pigs turn step by step into a tyranny indistinguishable from the one it replaced. Written in 1943-44 as an allegory of the Russian Revolution and the Stalin era, it was refused by several publishers while the Soviet Union was Britain's ally and became Orwell's first great success.
works.plot: Old Major, a prize boar, tells the animals of Manor Farm of his dream of a world without men and teaches them the song 'Beasts of England'. After his death the pigs Snowball and Napoleon lead a rising that drives out the farmer Mr Jones; the farm is renamed Animal Farm and governed by the Seven Commandments of Animalism, summed up in 'All animals are equal'. Snowball teaches the animals to read, plans a windmill and leads the defence in the Battle of the Cowshed, but Napoleon, who has reared a litter of puppies in secret, uses them as an armed guard to chase Snowball off the farm and takes sole power. The pig Squealer explains away every privilege the pigs award themselves; the windmill, built by the animals' labour and above all by the devoted cart-horse Boxer, collapses and is blamed on Snowball; animals confess to imaginary plots and are killed by the dogs, and the commandments are secretly rewritten. After the neighbouring farmer Frederick blows up the rebuilt windmill, the worn-out Boxer is sold to the knacker while the pigs buy whisky with the proceeds. Years later the pigs walk on two legs and carry whips, the commandments have become the single maxim 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others', and the animals watching a card game between the pigs and the neighbouring farmers can no longer tell pig from man.
works.significance: Animal Farm is the most widely read political fable in English and the book that made Orwell famous: its allegory of the Russian Revolution (Old Major as Marx and Lenin, Napoleon as Stalin, Snowball as Trotsky, Squealer as the official press) gave the age of totalitarianism a form a child can follow, and 'some animals are more equal than others' entered the language. In 'Why I Write' Orwell called it the first book in which he tried, with full consciousness of what he was doing, to fuse political purpose and artistic purpose into one whole; it prepared the way for Nineteen Eighty-Four.
works.meter: The level, simple sentences of a children's fable, told by an unobtrusive narrator who reports what the animals see and believe; the irony lies in the gap between their understanding and the reader's, and in the slogans ('Four legs good, two legs bad') and commandments that are altered as the story proceeds.
works.context: Written between November 1943 and February 1944, when Britain was allied with the Soviet Union and Stalin was widely admired by the British intelligentsia; Orwell's hostility to Stalinism had been formed by the Communist suppression of the POUM in Barcelona in 1937. The manuscript was refused by several British and American publishers, including Gollancz, and Orwell's unused preface records that one publisher withdrew after consulting the Ministry of Information. By the time it appeared, in August 1945, the wartime alliance was giving way to the Cold War.
works.characters: Old Major; Napoleon; Snowball; Squealer; Boxer; Clover; Benjamin; Mollie; Moses the raven; Mr Jones; Mr Frederick; Mr Pilkington; Mr Whymper
works.structure: Ten chapters of plain third-person narrative, moving from the rebellion through Snowball's expulsion, the purges and the building of the windmill to the final scene at the farmhouse window.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Annals of the American Revolution
altTitles: Annals of the American Revolution; or, A Record of the Causes and Events which Produced, and Terminated in the Establishment and Independence of the American Republic
works.form: History and chronicle with documentary editing; the national annalistic record
works.description: A year-by-year record of the war of independence, compiled from documents, state papers and the published histories, and issued with a documentary apparatus. It treats the Revolution as a providential national history and arranges its matter chronologically for reference. It belongs to the wave of centennial-era preservation of founding records.
works.plot: The annals follow the progress of the war from its political origins through the campaigns, the councils, the correspondence and the treaties, entering each year's principal events in order. They interweave the operations in the northern and southern states and at sea, and record the civil measures of the states and of Congress. Documents and letters are printed at length or abstracted, with notes identifying their sources. The work ends with the peace and with the establishment of the government it treats as the fruit of the contest.
works.significance: It is an early American attempt to fix the chronology of the Revolution from sources rather than from memory, and it stands beside the editorial work of the same generation. Its providential reading of national history was characteristic of the clerical nationalism of New England. It supplies a reference frame for the historical fiction of the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at Hartford in 1824, in the decade of the fiftieth-anniversary celebrations, the tours of Lafayette and the first great editorial enterprises for the founding records. Its compiler was a Congregational minister and geographer who read the Revolution as a religious as well as a political event. The book anticipates the documentary series edited by the historical societies of the following decade.
works.structure: Chronological annals with entries arranged by year and campaign, supported by printed documents and editorial notes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the volume also contains edited documentary papers relating to the war.
themes: Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
Warfare and battle
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Annals of the Parish; or, The Chronicle of Dalmailing
works.description: the author's first and most celebrated novel, the affectionate memoir of the Rev. John Halcyon Balwhidell, minister of a west-of-Scotland parish, chronicling nearly fifty years of rural transformation. A foundational text of the Scottish regional novel, it records agricultural improvement, Methodism, and the French wars from inside the old kirk.
works.plot: The minister Balwhidell narrates the history of his parish from his settlement in 1758 through to 1805. He records the coming of agricultural improvement, the disputes between the old and new husbandry, the inroads of Methodism and secession churches, the enthusiasm and disillusion of the French wars, and the quiet passing of the patriarchal laird system. The narrative's gentle irony arises from the gap between Balwhidell's complacent self-satisfaction and the reader's perception of the world passing him by.
works.significance: Annals of the Parish invented the Scottish parish chronicle and is a direct ancestor of Kailyard fiction and of Hardy's Wessex; its dialect realism and ironic memoir form make it one of the major experiments in voice in Romantic fiction.
works.context: Written by the author, an Ayrshire-born friend of Byron and admirer of Ferguson and Burns, and published in 1821 as the Waverley vogue opened the market for regional Scottish fiction. Its subject — the death of the old parish under improvement — reflects the author's own experience of rapid social change in southwest Scotland.
works.characters: The Rev. John Halcyon Balwhidell; Bailie Blair; Mr. McCorkindale; Andy Glovers; Miss Broun; Robert Lang; Gavin Mossgiel
works.structure: First-person memoir covering 1758-1805; episodic and digressive, organised by ecclesiastical and agricultural events rather than plot; the unreliable but lovable narrator generates the novel's irony.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside

works.title: Anne
works.form: Novel; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1882
works.description: Woolson's Mackinac novel: a young woman, an island and the choice between two men. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Constance Fenimore Woolson; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.

works.significance: Anne was Woolson's first novel and the book that established the Great Lakes as an American literary landscape: its island setting and its study of a woman's choice made it one of the finest American novels of the 1880s and the model for the regional novel of the lakes.

works.context: Mackinac Island and the Great Lakes in the 1870s, and the meeting of the frontier and the Eastern seaboard. works.characters: Anne Douglas; the father; the frontiersman; the Eastern visitor
works.structure: A novel in three parts set on Mackinac Island. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: Annus Mirabilis
altTitles: Annus Mirabilis: The Year of Wonders 1666
works.description: Dryden's long historical poem on the two disasters of 1666 — the Second Anglo-Dutch War and the Great Fire of London — written from Charlton in Wiltshire, offering the nation an optimistic, providential reading of catastrophe.
works.plot: The poem narrates the naval victories over the Dutch, then the Fire, and concludes with a prophecy of London's rebirth as a greater commercial empire under Charles II.
works.significance: The major English public poem of the 1660s; it demonstrates Dryden's ability to turn current events into national myth and anticipates the scientific imagery of his later verse.
works.meter: Quatrains (alternately rhymed iambic pentameter, ABAB), deliberately chosen over couplets to imitate the stateliness of history writing.
works.context: Composed while Dryden was absent from plague-stricken London; dedicated to the City of London in the year of the Great Fire, and closely engaged with the Royal Society's new empiricism.
works.structure: A two-part public narrative (war, fire) framed by dedication and prophetic conclusion, with episodic set-pieces for individual battles.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.
themes: Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
The New Science and experimental philosophy
The city and urban life

works.title: Another Time
works.description: The last collection of Auden's English years: 'September 1, 1939', 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' and the farewell to England. It is a verse work of 1940 by W. H. Auden; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Thirties Political Lyric and the Auden Generation and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats', 'September 1, 1939', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'The Unknown Citizen', 'Refugee Blues' and 'Law Like Love' — the great public poems of 1939 and the farewell to the England he was leaving.
works.significance: Another Time contains the two most quoted poems of 1939 and the definitive elegy of the period: 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' — 'poetry makes nothing happen' — and 'September 1, 1939' gave the outbreak of the war its permanent lines.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the clipped journalistic line with the flat technical vocabulary.
works.context: The Munich crisis, the fall of Czechoslovakia, the outbreak of the Second World War, and Auden's emigration to America in January 1939. The record dates the work as composed between 1938 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under thirties political lyric and the auden generation.

works.structure: Fifty-two poems in varied forms. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.

works.title: Antonius
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: Mary Sidney Herbert's translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy Marc-Antoine (1578), the first English version of a French classical tragedy: a closet drama in which Mark Antony, after Actium, debates his ruin with his friends and Cleopatra, and falls on his sword.
works.plot: Antony, defeated and despairing, rejects the counsel of his followers, is reproached and forgiven by Cleopatra, and kills himself; the play closes with the chorus's meditation on Fortune and with Cleopatra's grief and resolve.
works.significance: The bridge by which French neoclassical tragedy entered English, and the first English tragedy of Cleopatra.
works.meter: Blank verse with rhyming choruses, matching Garnier's French alexandrines with English iambic pentameter.
works.context: Published in 1592, amid the English vogue for Senecan tragedy and the Pembroke circle's literary patronage; it anticipated the Antony plays of Shakespeare and Daniel.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Charmian; Philostratus; Lucilius; the Chorus of Egyptians
works.structure: Five acts of Senecan structure with choruses, designed for reading rather than performance.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Mary Sidney Herbert from Robert Garnier's Marc-Antoine (1578); uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Antony and Cleopatra
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of empire and desire: the ageing Antony, caught between Rome and Egypt, duty and Cleopatra, loses the world at Actium and, hearing the false report of her death, falls on his sword; Cleopatra, refusing Octavius's triumph, dies by the asp, and the play ends with the lovers' deaths transfigured into myth.
works.plot: Antony's dalliance in Alexandria draws him back to Rome and the marriage to Octavia; the breach with Caesar sends him back to Cleopatra; the sea-fight at Actium is lost when she flies and he follows; his rage, her feigned death, his botched suicide, and her staged one complete the tragedy — 'I am fire and air' — with Caesar left to bury them side by side.
works.significance: The greatest English poem of erotic grandeur — the tragedy in which the lovers outgrow tragedy itself.
works.meter: A hyperbolic, sensuous verse of superlatives — Enobarbus's barge speech its summit — with the prose of Egypt's court as the foil to Roman plainness.
works.context: Written about 1606–07 from North's Plutarch, whose phrasing Shakespeare follows at the barge and the death scenes; the play's imperial themes shadow the Jacobean debate over empire and union.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Octavius Caesar; Enobarbus; Octavia; Charmian; Iras; Lepidus; Pompey; Alexas; Eros; Dolabella; the Clown
works.structure: A tragedy of scenes, not acts — forty-two rapid movements between Rome and Alexandria — in which the lovers' deaths are deliberately drawn out across the final acts as ceremony and apotheosis.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Apollonius of Tyre
works.form: prose romance in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English prose translation of the Historia Apollonii regis Tyri — the story of the shipwrecked prince Apollonius, his lost wife and daughter, and their final reunion: the first prose romance in English and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Pericles and of the Apollonius tradition that runs through Gower and the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Apollonius of Tyre, having solved the riddle of the incestuous king Antiochus, flees by sea; shipwrecked at Pentapolis, he wins the king's daughter in marriage; at sea their daughter is born and the queen, apparently dead, is cast overboard in a sealed coffin; the daughter, raised at Mytilene, is sold to a brothel-keeper but preserves her honour by her wisdom; the story ends in the great recognition scene, when the family is reunited at Ephesus and Mytilene.
works.significance: The first English prose romance; the bridge between the classical romance tradition and the Middle English romances and Shakespeare's Pericles.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated c. 1000-1050 from the Latin Historia Apollonii (a late antique romance); the unique manuscript is Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201, which also contains Wulfstan's homilies.
works.characters: Apollonius; Antiochus; Arcestrates of Pentapolis; the queen; the daughter (Thasia); Athenagoras of Mytilene
works.structure: A continuous romance narrative of adventure, loss, and recognition, in the incest-riddle frame of the Latin source.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translator.
themes: Sea voyage and seafaring
Women's experience and the feminine voice
Wyrd (fate) and providence

works.title: Apologia Pro Vita Sua
altTitles: Apologia Pro Vita Sua: Being a History of His Religious Opinions
works.form: Spiritual autobiography (in seven parts, with a supplementary chapter)
works.description: Published in eight parts in 1864-65 in answer to Charles Kingsley's charge that he had taught that truth need not be kept with heretics: the greatest Victorian religious autobiography, and the book that restored Newman's reputation and made his name.
works.plot: The Apologia narrates the development of Newman's religious opinions from his Evangelical childhood through the Oxford Movement, the Tracts for the Times, Tract 90, the move to Rome and the Oratory; the argument is that his changes were not inconsistencies but a coherent development under an authority he could not resist.
works.significance: The Apologia created the modern spiritual autobiography and is the most persuasive account in English of the grounds of religious belief; it is also the central historical document of the Oxford Movement, and its prose is the standard against which Victorian religious writing is measured.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
works.context: The 1864 controversy with Kingsley and the pages of Macmillan's and the Birmingham Oratory's pamphlet, the Oxford Movement's memory, and the position of Catholics in Victorian England after the restoration of the hierarchy in 1850.
works.characters: John Henry Newman; Charles Kingsley, his accuser; John Keble; Richard Hurrell Froude; Edward Pusey; Richard Whately
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self

works.title: Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber
works.form: Autobiographical memoir and theatrical history in prose.
works.description: An autobiographical memoir published in 1740 after the writer's retirement from the stage, at once a defence of a career and the richest contemporary account of the London patent theatre in its first brilliant half-century. Written in a garrulous, self-admiring prose that rarely distinguishes vanity from evidence, it reviews the author's own plays and acting, the quarrels and collapses of the companies he helped to manage, and the attacks of his enemies, the most formidable of which had long since enthroned him as the emperor of dullness.
works.plot: The narrative runs from a boyhood in the theatre world and a first sight of a play to management at Drury Lane, feuds with rival companies and with the poets who succeeded, and final retirement; it is interrupted by set defences of the author's treatment of the Shakespearean text, of his own dramatic writings, and of the actors and actresses he employed. Passages of portraiture of players, managers and their noble patrons are worked up from memory and were repeatedly borrowed by later historians of the stage. The memoir prints or paraphrases the prologues, epilogues and occasional verses by which its author had advertised himself, and quotes the insults levelled at him at length so as to return them with good humour.
works.significance: It is the principal source-book for the company history, repertory and acting style of the London stage between the 1680s and the 1730s, and the standard illustration of how a manager turned autobiography into reply. Historians use its testimony with caution because self-love governs its dates and its judgments, and its apology for adapting the national dramatist to modern taste is the fullest contemporary defence of that practice.
works.context: The memoir was put together in the years of the author's retirement, when the theatre he described had been reconstituted by new managers and licences, and when the satire that had made his name a byword for dullness was still in circulation. It belongs to the flourishing of theatrical memoir and anecdote that also produced the biographical prefaces of the play collections of the 1730s and 1740s, and it is a specimen of the Augustan practice of answering lampoon with autobiography.
works.characters: the author himself as boy, actor, manager and old man; the players and actresses of the two patent houses; the booksellers and rivals with whom he quarrelled; the noble patrons and box-keepers of the theatre
works.structure: Continuous first-person prose narrative running in one line from youth to old age, with documentary matter - verses, letters, the published records of quarrels - embedded in it and with digressive chapters on the drama and on editorial dealings with the national dramatist.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

The Restoration Theatre

works.title: Appius and Virginia
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: Dennis's blank-verse Roman tragedy, drawn from the decemviral history of Livy, in which the lust of the mighty magistrate for a plebeian maid and the father's pious murder of her become a study of corrupt power, chastity and republican fury. Severe in its moral register and unstinted in its invective against the decemvirs, it is the dramatic illustration of the theories of enthusiasm and of the terrors of virtue set out in the treatises of 1701 and 1704. Its failure at the playhouse and the quarrel over its re-use by other authors made it also the most famous case in the century of the professional writer's grievance.
works.plot: Appius, one of the decemvirs, designs to get Virginia, the betrothed of Icilius, by a judicial fiction of sale, and uses his authority to defeat her advocates in the forum; Virginius, her father, rather than yield her to the tyrant's power, kills her in the street with a sentence that at once frees and destroys her; the outraged commons secede, the decemviral yoke is attacked, and Appius, stripped of office and abandoned by his patrons, dies in captivity. The play thus moves from the corruption of law into tyranny, to private catastrophe, and then to the restoration of public liberty.
works.significance: Its severity and its political indignation made it a permanent exemplum of the neglected Augustan tragedian, and the anecdote attached to it entered the common lore of authorial property in dramatic texts; it also survives as the practical test case of a critical theory that demanded terror, enthusiasm and moral gravity in the same play.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, declamatory and heavily sententious, with long impassioned periods and a deliberate accumulation of terror-words proper to Dennis's account of poetical enthusiasm.
works.context: First acted in London in 1709, in a season when the theatre was contested ground for Whig and Tory interpretations of Roman liberty; it held the stage for only a very short run, and the later revival of its scenes in another company's play provoked Dennis's well-known public protest against the appropriation of his work.
works.characters: Appius Claudius; Virginia; Virginius; Icilius; the seceding commons of Rome
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy in the neoclassical manner, with a public forum action, a central recognition and killing, and an offstage political resolution; the catastrophe is reported rather than represented, and the political action closes the design.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's ownership of the text is documented by his own publication and by the anecdote of the reclaimed scenes.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Revenge and justice
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Appreciations, with an Essay on Style
works.description: Published in 1889 and Pater's central statement of critical theory: essays on Wordworth, Coleridge, Charles Lamb, Sir Thomas Browne, Shakespeare's English kings, Rossetti and Mérimée, with the great essay 'Style'.
works.plot: 'Style' argues that literature is a matter of the exact correspondence of form and meaning, that the writer's business is to give pleasure, and that prose has its own music; the essays on the English writers are studies of temperament rather than judgment.
works.significance: Appreciations is the classic English argument for style as a form of knowledge and the founding text of the modern criticism of prose; its essay on style is still the best short defence of the artistic integrity of English prose.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is rhythmical, suspended sentences.
works.context: The 1880s, the debate on criticism after Arnold, and the new paganism of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1880 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: Arcadia
works.description: Sidney's prose romance written for his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke: the 'Old Arcadia' (c. 1577–80, complete in five books or acts) is a tragicomic tale of two princes in disguise among the shepherds of Arcadia; the unfinished 'New Arcadia' (c. 1584–86) reworks the first books into a heroic romance of chivalric adventure; the composite edition of 1593 joined the revised books to the old ending.
works.plot: Princes Musidorus and Pyrocles, in love with the princesses Pamela and Philoclea, disguise themselves as a shepherd and an Amazon to gain access to the secluded royal household; their courtships, the rebellion of the commons, the trial of the princes for the supposed death of King Basilius, and the oracles that haunt the plot drive the action of the Old Arcadia, while the New Arcadia expands it with the wars of the rebel Amphialus and the captivity episodes.
works.significance: The most influential prose fiction of the English Renaissance — the model for a century of romances and the direct ancestor of Wroth's Urania and of Shakespeare's borrowed plots.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate periodic balance, with verse eclogues in many stanza forms at the act divisions.
works.context: Written in retirement at Wilton after Sidney's withdrawal from court (1579) and revised in the mid-1580s; printed after his death in 1590 and, with his sister's composite arrangement, in 1593.
works.characters: Pyrocles; Musidorus; Philoclea; Pamela; Basilius, King of Arcadia; Gynecia; Euarchus; Amphialus; the shepherds Dorus and Strephon
works.structure: An interlaced romance in prose with verse eclogues between the books, deliberately organized by Sidney into 'five acts' on the model of drama.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the 1593 composite text was assembled by Mary Sidney Herbert.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Kingship and good rule
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Arden of Faversham
altTitles: The Lamentable and True Tragedy of Master Arden of Faversham
works.description: The anonymous domestic tragedy of the real murder of Thomas Arden of Faversham in 1551: his wife Alice and her lover Mosby hire a succession of bungling assassins — Black Will and Shakebag among them — whose attempts fail comically until the murder is done in Arden's own house; the killers are caught, and the play ends with the executions and Alice's burning, 'the sin of murder' its homiletic close.
works.plot: Alice's adultery and Arden's blindness to it set the plot; the hired murders fail through fog, chance, and cowardice; the final ambush in the parlour succeeds; the discovery of the body, the flight of the murderers, and the punishment of all — including Alice, who dies 'bewailed' only by her guilt — complete the tragedy's documentary arc.
works.significance: The founding text of English domestic tragedy — the first play to make an English household and an English murder the matter of tragedy.
works.meter: A plain, powerful verse (and prose) of the provincial scene — the play's very anonymity has invited attribution to Shakespeare, Kyd, and others.
works.context: Printed in 1592 and performed by the Admiral's Men; based on the notorious Faversham murder of 1551 as told in Holinshed; it is the first English play of a real, recent, and domestic crime.
works.characters: Thomas Arden; Alice Arden; Mosby; Black Will; Shakebag; Greene; Michael; Franklin; the Mayor of Faversham; Susan; Clarke the painter
works.structure: A five-act tragedy built directly on Holinshed's account of the real 1551 murder, with the comic failures of the assassins as its counterpoint to the horror.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributions to Kyd, Shakespeare, and others have been proposed but none is proven.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Ardours and Endurances
works.description: The Georgian war poetry that made Nichols famous: the artillery, the attack and the pity. It is a verse work of 1917 by Robert Nichols; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The collection gathers Nichols's war poems — 'The Assault', 'The Day's March', 'Battery Moving Up to a New Position', 'Comrades' — in which the artillery and the attack are rendered in long, rhetorical, declamatory verse.
works.significance: Ardours and Endurances was one of the most popular war books of 1917 and made Nichols famous: its long rhetorical poems of the artillery and the attack were read aloud to vast audiences and its reception shows how the war was made into public poetry in the middle of the conflict.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the long rhetorical war poem for recitation.
works.context: The Western Front in 1916–17, and the poetry-reading culture of wartime England. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1917 and first published in 1917 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War; Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem; georgian anthology lyric.
works.characters: the gunner; the battery; the infantry; the poet as witness
works.structure: A collection of long war poems in the Georgian manner. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.

works.title: Areopagitica
altTitles: Areopagitica: A Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc'd Printing
works.description: Milton's prose speech to Parliament (24 November 1644) against the Licensing Order of 1643, arguing that prior censorship of books destroys learning, virtue, and truth, and that a free people must be trusted to choose good over evil — the classic English defence of freedom of the press.
works.plot: Milton traces the history of licensing from the Inquisition, argues that books contain the 'life-blood of a master spirit', distinguishes the testing of virtue from its seclusion, and contends that truth will prevail in a free and open encounter.
works.significance: One of the foundational texts of the argument for free speech and a free press, still quoted in constitutional and press-freedom debates, and a masterpiece of English prose.
works.meter: Eloquent, Latinate prose with a powerful oratorical rhythm and dense classical allusion.
works.context: Published during the Civil War against Parliament's 1643 licensing order; it drew on Milton's own experience of unlicensed publication and the collapse of censorship.
works.structure: A classical oration in prose, modeled on Isocrates's Areopagiticus, moving through historical example, argument, and eloquent peroration.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration

Wisdom and learning

works.title: Armadale
works.description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from November 1864 to June 1866: the most complex of Collins's plots, built on a dream, a shipwreck and two generations of the Armadale name. It is a prose fiction work of 1866 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Allan Armadale is warned in a dream by a German doctor that he will meet a man who will be his fate and a woman who will be his ruin. He meets Ozias Midwinter, the son of the first Allan's victim, and Lydia Gwilt, a governess, forger and adventuress, who marries Midwinter in order to murder Armadale; the plot turns on a letter, a sanatorium and a poison, and ends with Lydia's death and Midwinter's survival.
works.significance: Armadale is the most technically daring of the sensation novels and the one most concerned with the psychology of the adventuress: Lydia Gwilt is one of the great villainesses of Victorian fiction, and the novel's use of the dream and the hereditary curse links it to the Gothic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1860s, the law of the shipwreck and the insurance fraud, the private asylum, and the Victorian fascination with mesmerism and hereditary destiny. The record dates the work as composed between 1864 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.

works.title: Arms and the Man
works.description: First performed in 1894 and Shaw's first great commercial success: a romantic young woman's illusions about war and love are destroyed by a practical Swiss soldier. It is a dramatic work of 1894 by George Bernard Shaw; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Raina Petkoff, a Bulgarian officer's daughter engaged to the heroic Sergius, shelters a Swiss mercenary, Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolates instead of cartridges; the war ends, Bluntschli returns to recover his coat, and the play ends with Raina engaged to him and her romantic ideals entirely dismantled.
works.significance: Arms and the Man is the play that made Shaw's reputation and the founding English anti-war comedy: its destruction of the romantic hero and its argument that the soldier's real business is survival had an enormous influence on the English theatre, and it remains one of the most performed of his plays.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1894: the Serbo-Bulgarian war of 1885, the vogue of the heroic war play, and the New Woman's criticism of romantic love. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and first performed in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.

works.structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Army Life in a Black Regiment
works.form: Prose (regimental memoir); war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: The finest firsthand record of the Black soldier in the Civil War, written by his colonel. It is a prose work of 1870 by Thomas Wentworth Higginson; it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Higginson records the formation and service of the 1st South Carolina Volunteers: the drill, the raids up the rivers, the camp life, the spirituals and the soldiers' letters, and his own conversion to the conviction of Black capacity.
works.significance: Army Life in a Black Regiment is the finest firsthand record of the Black soldier in the Civil War and one of the great American memoirs: its transcription of the spirituals preserved the earliest written record of the Black American religious song, and it is the central documentary text of emancipation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the common soldier: the plain first-person account, the exact vocabulary of the trench, the ration, the march and the casualty, and the understatement that carries the horror. The author's characteristic manner is the regimental memoir of the camp and the march.
works.context: The Sea Islands of South Carolina in 1862–64 and the emancipation of the enslaved population. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: Arrival and Departure
works.description: The war novel of the refugee and the psychoanalysis of the motive. works.significance: Arrival and Departure is Koestler's refugee novel: its Slavek, its analysis and its fallen Europe carried the politics of Darkness at Noon into the war's displaced lives and the new psychology.

works.title: Arrowsmith

works.description: The American novel of science: a doctor, a plague and the integrity of research. It is a prose fiction work of 1925 by Sinclair Lewis; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Martin Arrowsmith, a small-town doctor, becomes a medical researcher; the novel follows his career, his marriage and his work on a plague in the West Indies, where he insists on the controlled experiment against the interests of the commercial institute that employs him.
works.significance: Arrowsmith won the Pulitzer Prize (which Lewis refused) and is the great American novel of science: its portrait of the researcher and its argument for the integrity of science made it the founding text of the American scientific novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. works.title: Arthur Mervyn; or, Memoirs of the Year 1793
works.form: Picaresque journey novel and city documentary; epidemic narrative with an embedded historical appendix
works.description: A picaresque and documentary novel built around the yellow-fever epidemic that emptied Philadelphia in the summer of 1793. The first part follows an impressionable young draughtsman through the disease-ridden city; the second part pursues the thieves and shipboard villains who exploited the crisis. It is the first major American fiction to treat epidemic and commerce as historical forces.
works.plot: An apprentice from a Pennsylvania village comes to Philadelphia and falls under the influence of a cultivated but amoral stranger who robs the sick and dying. As the fever turns the city into a place of flight, speculation and burial carts, the hero is himself exposed to contagion, quarantine and the collapse of the household that shelters him. An appendix of memoranda documents the mortality, the physicians' disputes and the benevolent committees with a historian's precision. Later the same villain resurfaces aboard ship and in the West Indies, and the hero's pursuit of him exposes the traffic in stolen goods and forged identities that the epidemic made possible.
works.significance: It gave American fiction its first sustained treatment of an epidemic and of the city as an epidemiological space. The inserted memoranda anticipate the documentary realist mode. Its moral anatomy of profiteering in crisis has made it a persistent subject for histories of medicine and of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: The epidemic of 1793 struck the temporary national capital during the Jeffersonian contest over French and British allegiance, and its relief efforts were organized by voluntary committees. The novel draws on contemporary medical bulletins and on the public's argument about contagion and quarantine. Its second part reflects the anxious commerce of the 1790s Atlantic, including the slave trade and the flight of planters from Saint-Domingue.
works.characters: Arthur Mervyn; Hawksfield
works.structure: Two-part memoir by a first-person narrator, the first book closed by an inserted statistical and medical appendix; the second part continues the same voice in a wider geographic field.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the first part was issued serially and then collected.

works.title: As I Lay Dying
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1930
works.description: The Bundren family's journey to bury Addie: fifty-nine monologues, and the blackest comedy in American fiction. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by William Faulkner; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Addie Bundren dies and her husband Anse and five children set out to carry her body to Jefferson for burial; the journey takes nine days, the coffin is nearly lost in a flooded river and a fire, and each member of the family narrates in turn, revealing their own motives and the family's terrible poverty.
works.significance: As I Lay Dying is the blackest comedy in American fiction and one of the great experimental novels of the century: its fifty-nine monologues and its journey structure made it the most formally perfect of Faulkner's novels.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the long retrospective sentence with its parentheses and its piled-up subordinate clauses.
works.context: The rural Mississippi of the 1920s, the poor white farming family, and the funeral customs of the South. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.

works.title: As You Like It
works.description: Shakespeare's pastoral comedy, adapted from Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde: Duke Senior, exiled to the Forest of Arden, is joined by his daughter Rosalind (disguised as the boy Ganymede), her cousin Celia, the clown Touchstone, and eventually the melancholy Jaques and the reformed usurper — while Orlando's love-verses to Rosalind hang on every tree.
works.plot: Orlando, robbed of his birthright, flees to Arden; Rosalind, banished, tutors him in love while disguised as Ganymede; the usurping Duke is converted on the forest's edge; and the play ends with four weddings and the god Hymen's masque, followed by Rosalind's epilogue.
works.significance: The definitive English pastoral comedy and the vehicle of Shakespeare's greatest comic heroine.
works.meter: Alternating prose and blank verse — Rosalind's prose wit against Orlando's verses — with the songs 'Under the greenwood tree' and 'It was a lover and his lass'.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe's opening, from Lodge's Rosalynde (1590); the forest reimagines the Ardennes through Warwickshire memory.
works.characters: Rosalind; Orlando; Celia; Touchstone; Jaques; Duke Senior; Duke Frederick; Oliver; Adam; Silvius; Phebe; Audrey; William; Corin; Charles the wrestler
works.structure: A movement from court to forest and back, built on the contrast of the two worlds and on the play's chain of love-dialogues, with the 'Seven Ages of Man' speech and the songs of Amiens as set pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Ash-Wednesday
works.description: Eliot's conversion poem: the turn from despair to faith, and the most penitential poem in modern English. It is a verse work of 1930 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The sequence moves from the speaker's refusal of hope and his ascent of the purgatorial stairs, through the vision of the lady and the yew trees, to the prayer for intercession that closes it.
works.significance: Ash-Wednesday is the great poem of Eliot's conversion and one of the central religious poems of the century: it is the bridge between The Waste Land and Four Quartets.

works.title: Astraea Redux
altTitles: Astraea Redux: A Poem on the Happy Restoration & Return of His Sacred Majesty Charles the Second
works.description: Dryden's first public poem, celebrating the Restoration of Charles II in May 1660 and announcing the young poet's allegiance to the returning monarchy; it recasts the civil wars as a national illness now cured by the king's return.
works.plot: The poem traces the disorder of the Interregnum, praises General Monck's role, and celebrates Charles II as the providential healer of the nation, drawing on biblical and classical typology.
works.significance: Established Dryden's public reputation and set the tone for the political panegyric of the Restoration; a benchmark for his later development.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in closed iambic pentameter, with occasional alexandrines; one of the earliest displays of Dryden's mature couplet.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's landing at Dover on 25 May 1660 and published in the same year.
works.structure: A panegyric in three movements: the diagnosis of national disorder, the mechanism of restoration, and the prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden on the title page of the 1660 quarto; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Astrophel and Stella
works.description: The first great English sonnet sequence: 108 sonnets and eleven songs tracing the love of Astrophel (the star-lover) for Stella (the star) — widely read as Sidney's love for Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich — from first sight through desire, frustration, and the lady's marriage to another, to the renunciation of the last sonnets.
works.plot: Astrophel falls in love with Stella at first sight; he pleads, she rebuffs; she marries Lord Rich; the poems anatomize every phase of the love — reason versus desire, sleep and dreams, the stolen kiss, jealousy, absence — until the final sonnets turn from the vain suit.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue: Spenser, Daniel, Drayton, and Shakespeare all wrote in its wake.
works.meter: The English (Shakespearean-type) sonnet form of Sidney's own stamp — abab abab cdcd ee — with hexameter final lines in several sonnets.
works.context: Composed about 1581–82 in the circle of the Earl of Oxford's and Sidney's London; printed posthumously in 1591 by Thomas Newman in an unauthorized edition, which launched the vogue of the sonnet sequence.
works.characters: Astrophel; Stella; Lord Rich (alluded to); Cupid; Reason; Virtue
works.structure: A sequence with a genuine plot — courtship, crisis, renunciation — varied by the eleven songs inserted at points of dramatic action.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the biographical reading as Sidney and Penelope Devereux is a later interpretation, not a fact in the text.

works.title: At Swim-Two-Birds
works.form: Experimental novel (the author and his characters)
works.description: The experimental novel of the author, his characters and his characters' characters. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Flann O'Brien; it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: At Swim-Two-Birds sets the student-narrator writing a novel of three beginnings, in which his characters rebel against their author and write their own book, in the comic experiment of the novel of the author and his characters.
works.significance: At Swim-Two-Birds is the great experimental comic novel of Ireland: its three beginnings and its rebel characters made the novel of the author and his characters the form of the Irish modernism and the book Joyce praised.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. works.title: At the Back of the North Wind
works.form: Children's fantasy novel, first issued in 1871
works.description: Published in 1871 and the most beautiful of MacDonald's fairy tales: the story of Diamond, a London cab-horse boy, and his journeys with the North Wind. It is a prose fiction work of 1871 by George MacDonald; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Diamond meets the North Wind, who appears to him as a beautiful woman, and travels with her through the sky; he is taken to the country at her back, where the river runs through the land, and the novel ends with his early death into that country.
works.significance: At the Back of the North Wind is the greatest Victorian children's book about death and the most important influence on C. S. Lewis after Phantastes: its portrait of the dying child and its allegory of the country beyond the wind are among the finest things in English children's literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain.
works.context: The 1870s, the London of the cab trade and the overcrowded poor, and the Victorian allegorical fairy tale after Bunyan. works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: At the Mountains of Madness
works.description: The Antarctic novella of the elder things and the buried city. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by H. P. Lovecraft; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: At the Mountains of Madness tells, through the geologist Lake's expedition and the survivor Dyer, of the elder things' city beyond the mountains of the title, their history of the earth before man and the shoggoth, in the long scientific novella that joins the weird tale to the antarctic exploration and the evolutionary epic.
works.significance: At the Mountains of Madness is Lovecraft's longest and most scientific tale: its elder things, its buried city and its deep time made the cosmic horror a history of the earth and joined the weird tale to the science fiction of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript.
works.context: The Antarctic plateau of the Miskatonic expedition. works.structure: A novella of the expedition and the buried city's history. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.

works.title: Atalanta in Calydon
works.description: Published in 1865 and Swinburne's first great success: a Greek tragedy in the manner of Aeschylus and Euripides on the hunting of the Calydonian boar. It is a dramatic work of 1865 by Algernon Charles Swinburne; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Meleager leads the hunt for the boar sent by Artemis, kills it, gives the spoil to Atalanta, and is destroyed by his mother Althaea, who burns the brand on which his life depends when he kills his uncles in a quarrel over the prize.
works.significance: Atalanta in Calydon is the greatest English classical drama of the century and contains 'When the hounds of spring', the most famous chorus in Victorian poetry: it made Swinburne's name and established the Victorian taste for the Greek closet drama.

works.title: Athelston
works.description: A dark romance of kingship and treason, unique in the canon: the king Athelston, swayed by the traitor Wymond, puts his sworn brother and his family to the ordeal of fire, and is saved from tyranny only by the intervention of the archbishop and the test of the fire itself. Its grim political realism makes it unlike any other English romance.
works.plot: Four messengers become sworn brothers; Athelston becomes king, and the envious Wymond persuades him that Earl Egeland plots treason; Athelston's violence against the earl's pregnant wife and children is halted when the archbishop curses him and the ordeal of fire acquits the innocent, exposing Wymond and restoring the fellowship.
works.significance: The most politically serious of the English romances — a study of tyranny, sanctuary, and the ordeal — and a favourite text for the romance's engagement with law and kingship.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, often grimly emphatic.
works.context: Composed c. 1355–80 in the East Midlands, drawing on the legend of St Edmund and on baronial and ecclesiastical politics; preserved uniquely in Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 175.
works.characters: Athelston; Wymond; Egeland; Edyff; the archbishop
works.structure: A compact tragedy of misrule in three movements (oath, slander, ordeal), with the archbishop's excommunication as its pivot.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

Kingship and good rule

works.title: Aubade
works.description: Aubade is Philip Larkin's last major poem, first published in the Christmas issue of The Times Literary Supplement on 23 December 1977 and not collected in any of his books during his lifetime. An aubade is traditionally a lovers' dawn song; Larkin's is a meditation on the fear of death at four in the morning.
works.summary: Five rhymed ten-line stanzas in which the speaker, awake before dawn, contemplates his inevitable death, rejects the consolations of religion and philosophy, and watches the ordinary day begin.
works.plot: Waking at four in the morning, the speaker sees the certainty of his own extinction with complete clarity: not remorse or wasted chances, but the total emptiness of being dead. He dismisses religion as a vast, moth-eaten musical brocade created to pretend we never die, and the argument that it is irrational to fear what we will not feel, since that is exactly what terrifies him. Courage, he says, is no help; it simply means not scaring others. As light comes, the room takes shape, telephones prepare to ring, and the world resumes its work; the poem ends with postmen going from house to house like doctors.
works.significance: It is widely considered one of the greatest English poems on mortality and the culmination of Larkin's lifelong preoccupation with death.
works.meter: Plain, conversational statement of extreme feeling, set within a strict rhymed stanza; famous aphoristic lines balanced by concrete images of the room and the street.
works.context: Begun in 1974 and completed on 29 November 1977, when Larkin was writing very little poetry, it was the last substantial lyric he wrote; it was first collected in the posthumous Collected Poems (1988).
works.structure: Five stanzas of ten lines, mainly in iambic pentameter with a shorter line, moving from night to dawn.
themes: Death, illness and mourning
Faith, doubt and the sacred

works.title: Auld Lang Syne
works.form: song lyric in the Scottish vernacular, collected and reworked from traditional material for a musical anthology
works.description: The song of old acquaintance and of remembrance, in which the pairs of friends who have run the world together ask whether the times of 'auld lang syne' shall be forgotten. Burns presented it to Johnson as a recovered old song rather than as an invention, and his own stanzas gave the traditional phrase its enduring form. It has since become the most performed commemorative song in the English-speaking world.
works.plot: The speaker proposes that the partners in former merriness should drink a cup of kindness yet for the sake of the old days, recalling the runs over the braes and the talks before they were parted by years and distance. The refrain insists on the phrase itself, converting a drinking song's occasion into a general meditation on memory, friendship and the passage of time, and closing with the pledge of remembrance.
works.significance: It is the most widely performed and most universally recognised song in the language, and the exemplar of the way Burns's collecting practice could make an old phrase into a new poem. It also stands as a document of the 1790s effort to define a national song repertory against imported opera and English popular air.
works.meter: Ballad stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a refrain, set to the air Burns associated with the words; the diction is plain and the syntax colloquial.
works.context: Sent by Burns to Johnson in 1793 with a letter describing it as taken down from an old man's recitation and as belonging to the store of ancient Scottish song; the phrase and title had already been used by Allan Ramsay, and Burns's work is an act of recovery and revision within the collecting culture of the Scottish Musical Museum.
works.characters: The speaker and the old friend or friends toasted
works.structure: A strophic song with a fixed refrain, each verse adding a remembered scene to the toast, the argument carried by the return of the phrase auld lang syne.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Burns is uncontested for the familiar text, but the song is expressly a recovery and reworking of earlier traditional verse, and the standard editions record the anterior phrase and Ramsay's use of the title; the composition date follows Burns's letter to Johnson.

works.title: Aureng-zebe; or, The Great Mogul
works.description: Dryden's heroic play on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb's succession struggle, notable for its more restrained hero and for Dryden's prefatory doubt about the value of rhyme.
works.plot: The aged emperor Shah Abbas is suspected of loving his son Aureng-zebe's mistress Indamora; the prince's constancy and filial duty survive a rebellion by his brother Morat, and order is restored.
works.significance: The last of Dryden's heroic plays and the point at which he turned away from rhyme toward blank verse in All for Love; it marks the end of the heroic drama's ascendancy.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets, with a looser and more conversational movement than in The Conquest of Granada.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676, dedicated to the Earl of Mulgrave; the prologue's complaint about 'the dull duties of a poet's trade' reflects Dryden's growing disenchantment with rhyme.

works.structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single main action and a rival brother subplot.
