works.title: Aurora Floyd
works.description: Published in 1863 and Braddon's second great sensation novel: the story of an heiress with a violent temper, a secret marriage and a husband who may return at any moment. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Aurora Floyd, the daughter of a banker, secretly marries the groom James Conyers and pays him to disappear; she later marries the landowner John Mellish, and Conyers's return leads to his murder, the trial of Mellish, and the eventual discovery that the killer is Aurora's cousin's husband.
works.significance: Aurora Floyd is the fullest sensation treatment of the woman with a secret past and one of the earliest English novels to give a heroine an aggressive, physical energy — riding, hunting, fighting — that the period associated with men.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.

works.title: Aurora Leigh
works.form: Verse novel in nine books, in blank verse
works.description: Published in November 1856 and the great Victorian poem on the woman artist: the autobiography of a poet, Aurora Leigh, from her childhood in Italy to her mature work and love, and a sustained argument for women's access to art and to meaning.
works.plot: Aurora, orphaned in Florence, is brought up in England by her Puritan aunt, refuses the proposal of her cousin Romney Leigh (who is to be a social reformer), goes to London to write, and publishes her book; Romney's socialist schemes at Leigh Hall fail (the burning of the hall and the death of the people in it), he is blinded, and the novel ends with their marriage on the basis of her art and his repentance.
works.significance: Aurora Leigh is the first English verse novel by a woman and the central literary argument of the Victorian feminist movement; its heroine is a professional artist, its plot refuses the marriage-ending until the woman has become the equal partner, and its treatment of the social problems of the 1840s (prostitution, poverty, the reformer's failure) is unusually direct. Virginia Woolf's account of it in Second Common Reader (1925) is the standard critical point of departure.
works.meter: Blank verse, with a median line of eleven or twelve syllables and an unusually free handling of the iambic base, suited to narrative and argument.
works.context: The 1850s: the woman question, the 'surplus women' census of 1851, the reforming philanthropies of the 1840s, the position of the woman writer in a market dominated by men, and the Italian exiles of London and Florence.
works.characters: Aurora Leigh; Romney Leigh; Marian Erle; Lady Waldemar; the aunt; Vincent Carrington; Lord Howe
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.

works.title: Autobiography
works.description: Written in the 1850s and revised in the 1860s, and published posthumously by Mill's stepdaughter Helen Taylor in 1873: the most discussed autobiography of the Victorian period, and the record of the education that produced its author and of the crisis that nearly destroyed him.
works.plot: The chapters follow Mill's extraordinary education by his father, his work at the East India Company, the mental crisis of 1826-27 and his recovery through poetry (Wordsworth, particularly), his discovery of Harriet Taylor, his political and philosophical development, his parliamentary career, and his estimate of the age.
works.significance: The Autobiography is a central document of Victorian intellectual history and of the theory of education: its account of the 'crisis' in which a man educated only in analysis finds himself with no feeling left is the classic case of the dangers of a purely rational education, and its portrait of Harriet Taylor made her a figure in the history of English feminism.

works.description: Written from the 1850s and published after her death in 1877, with a memorial by Maria Weston Chapman: one of the greatest Victorian autobiographies, and a completely unsentimental account of a working literary life.

works.title: Autumn
works.description: The fourth of Thomson's seasonal poems, on the harvest, the gleaning, the vine and the melancholy of the closing year, with the celebrated account of the poet's own love and the meditation on the season of the mind.
works.plot: The poem follows the year to its ripening and its ingathering, the harvest field, the orchard and the vineyard, the mists and the melancholy of the evening, and ends with the tale of Cynia and the poet's retreat to contemplation and to the hymn of the season.
works.significance: It gave English verse its enduring imagery of autumn, harvest and melancholy evening, and its meditation on the seasons of the mind is the direct ancestor of the mid-century night and graveyard poem.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of the most sustained richness in the sequence, with the long evening period and the inserted lyric ode.
works.context: Issued at the close of the first publication of the four seasons, when the poem of the harvest and of melancholy was the most fashionable species of descriptive writing.
works.characters: the reapers and the gleaners of the harvest field; the maid of the inset tale; the contemplative poet
works.structure: A descriptive progression through the operations of the harvest, with the inset love tale and the closing meditative retreat.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Autumn Journal
works.description: The finest long poem of the thirties: a poetic diary from the autumn of 1938 to the spring of 1939. works.plot: The poem records the months from October 1938 to the spring of 1939: the Munich crisis, the fear of war, a journey to Spain and Ireland, the death of MacNeice's mother, and the ordinary life of London — in a conversational, rhymed, sectioned meditation.
works.significance: Autumn Journal is the finest long poem of the thirties and one of the great poems of the period: its conversational tone, its rhyme and its record of the last months of peace made it the definitive poetic diary of the decade.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the long conversational poem in sections.

works.title: Azarias
altTitles: The Canticle of the Three Youths
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem with embedded canticle
works.description: A poem on the ordeal of the three youths — Azarias, Ananias, and Misael — in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, based on Daniel 3 and on the canticle of praise they sing from the flames. The poem shares a substantial passage with the Junius manuscript poem Daniel.
works.plot: The three youths refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and are cast into the furnace; protected by the angel of God, they walk unharmed amid the flames and sing a canticle of praise in which all creation is summoned to bless the Lord, from the heavens and waters to the beasts and the sons of men.
works.significance: Together with Daniel it shows how Old English poets rendered the canticles of the liturgy in the native heroic idiom, turning scriptural praise into alliterative poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the canticle's catalogues of creation are carried by parallel alliterative phrases in the liturgical style.
works.context: The story of the three youths was read typologically in Anglo-Saxon England: the furnace prefigured both the Incarnation (the fire that does not burn) and the Church's endurance under persecution. The poem is closely related to Daniel in the Junius manuscript.
works.characters: Azarias, Ananias, Misael, Nebuchadnezzar
works.structure: A bipartite structure: a brief narrative of the ordeal followed by the long canticle of praise, a liturgical catalogue of creation in the manner of the Benedicite.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The relationship with Daniel (shared lines) is a standing crux of Old English scholarship; the two poems may derive from a common source or one from the other.

works.title: Babbitt

works.plot: George F. Babbitt, a real-estate broker in the city of Zenith, is prosperous, conformist and restless; his attempt to break free into bohemian life and liberal opinion ends in social ostracism and his return to the fold.
works.significance: Babbitt gave the English language the word for the conformist businessman and is the central satire of American business civilisation: its portrait of Zenith and George F. Babbitt made it one of the defining American novels of the century.

works.title: Balcony Stories
works.description: The finest Louisiana story collection of the century: the Creole past told from a balcony above the street. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by Grace King; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.

works.significance: Balcony Stories is the finest Louisiana story collection of the century and Grace King's masterpiece: its balconies, its old narrators and its elegiac comedy made the Creole past into a literary world and gave the Southern local-colour story its most finished form.

works.title: Bald's Leechbook
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.D.xvii (mid-tenth century, Winchester)
works.description: The most ambitious medical work in any early medieval vernacular: a systematic Old English leechbook in three books, compiled at Winchester in the mid-tenth century and named for Bald and Cild, the physicians named in its metrical colophon. It organizes hundreds of remedies for ailments from head to foot, drawing on Latin medical learning translated into English.
works.plot: Book I treats external ailments (head to toe), Book II internal diseases, and Book III a miscellany of surgical procedures, with remedies drawn from Greek, Latin, and native traditions; the work instructs the physician in diagnosis, pharmacy, bloodletting, and surgery, and includes charms as well as herbal and mineral preparations.
works.significance: The earliest substantial medical treatise in any western European vernacular, invaluable for the history of medicine and of Old English scientific prose, and a demonstration of the vernacular's capacity for technical writing.
works.context: Compiled in the Winchester milieu on the eve of the Benedictine Reform, the Leechbook shows the court's patronage of practical learning and the translation of Mediterranean medicine into English; it is the ancestor of the Middle English medical manuscript tradition.
works.structure: A systematic reference work organized by ailment and body-part (a capite ad calcem), with numbered remedies under each heading; the third book is looser, mixing surgery, obstetrics, and charms.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the colophon names Bald as owner and Cild as writer, not as authors of the medical content.
themes: Medicine, healing, and the body

works.title: Balder
works.description: The great poem of the spasmodic school: a Norwegian warrior's madness and the vision of the soul. It is a verse work of 1854 by Sydney Dobell; it belongs to The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: Balder, a Norwegian warrior, is driven mad by the death of his love and by the guilt of his own violence; the poem follows his wanderings, his visions and his final redemption in a dramatic poem of the tormented soul.
works.significance: Balder was the great poem of the spasmodic school and one of the most original long poems of the 1850s: its madness, its visions and its dramatic structure made it the central text of the movement and a major influence on the poetry of the 1860s.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is the spasmodic long poem of the tormented soul.
works.context: Norway in the Viking age, and the crisis of Victorian religious faith in the 1850s. The record dates the work as composed between 1852 and 1854 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Balder; the mother; the ghost; the Norwegian warriors
works.structure: A dramatic poem in three parts, from the madness to the redemption. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Ballads and Songs
works.description: Published in 1894 and the best selection of Davidson's shorter poems: the ballads of the city, the dramatic monologues and the lyrics of love and poverty. works.title: Ballads and Sonnets
works.description: Published in 1881, the year before his death, and containing the completed House of Life in its final order, together with 'The White Ship', 'The King's Tragedy', 'Rose Mary' and the late sonnets. It is a verse work of 1881 by Dante Gabriel Rossetti; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The ballads are supernatural narratives of doom — the loss of the White Ship, the murder of James I of Scotland, the crystal ball of Rose Mary — and the sonnets complete the sequence of love, loss and the memorial image.
works.significance: Ballads and Sonnets is the final form of Rossetti's poetic testament, and The House of Life in its 1881 order is the definitive English sonnet sequence of the aesthetic movement; the volume's influence on Yeats and on the 1890s is direct.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound.
works.context: The 1880s, Rossetti's last years at Kelmscott and Cheyne Walk, his addiction to chloral and his failing sight, and the aesthetic movement at its height. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.

works.title: Barchester Towers
works.description: Published in 1857, the most celebrated of the Barsetshire novels and the fullest comedy of ecclesiastical politics in English: the struggle for the bishopric and the wardenship at Barchester between the High Church party of the archdeacon and the new Low Church bishop and his wife.
works.plot: Bishop Proudie dies and is succeeded by Dr Proudie, whose wife and chaplain Mr Slope dominate him; Slope schemes to become warden of Hiram's Hospital and to marry Eleanor Harding, and is defeated in both by the arrival of the Stanhope family and by the comic catastrophe of the bishop's tea party. Mr Arabin becomes the new warden, and Eleanor marries him.
works.significance: Barchester Towers is the classic English novel of ecclesiastical intrigue and one of the funniest novels of the nineteenth century; its narrator's constant commentary and its slow rotation of sympathy set the manner for the whole of Trollope's later work and for the Victorian novel of institutional life.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.

works.title: Barnaby Rudge: A Tale of the Riots of 'Eighty
works.form: Historical novel (Master Humphrey's Clock, weekly parts)
works.description: Dickens's first historical novel, serialised in Master Humphrey's Clock in 1841 and set in 1775-80, with the Gordon Riots of June 1780 as its centrepiece. It is a prose fiction work of 1841 by Charles Dickens; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The novel braids three plots: the murder of Reuben Haredale and the false accusation of his gardener, the disappearance of Emma Haredale's brother and the villainy of Sir John Chester, and the domestic tragedy of the locksmith Gabriel Varden and his apprentice Sim Tappertit. Barnaby Rudge, an 'innocent' with a pet raven, is swept up in the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots, which the novel narrates as an anatomy of mob violence; the riots end with the storming of Newgate and the burning of the distillery, and the plots are unravelled by Lord George Gordon's trial and Chester's death.
works.significance: Barnaby Rudge is the first English novel to treat the urban crowd as an organised political phenomenon, and its account of the Gordon Riots is the most sustained piece of crowd-writing in Victorian fiction before A Tale of Two Cities. It is also Dickens's fullest study of the 'idiot' figure whose innocence is at the mercy of public violence.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Gordon Riots of 1780, the anti-Catholic agitation that followed the Relief Act of 1778, and the memory of mob violence revived for a Chartist-era readership by the Newport rising of 1839; Dickens drew on the contemporary pamphlet and trial literature for the crowd scenes.
works.characters: Barnaby Rudge; Gabriel Varden; Dolly Varden; Sim Tappertit; Sir John Chester; Edward Chester; Emma Haredale; Geoffrey Haredale; Lord George Gordon; Hugh; Grip the raven
works.structure: Double historical plot (private murder and public riot) braided across five years, narrated in weekly installments that culminate in the riot sequence.

works.title: Barrack-Room Ballads
works.description: Published in 1892 and the volume that changed English poetry: ballads in the voice of the ordinary British soldier in India, sung in dialect and slang, with a rhythm learned from the music hall. It is a verse work of 1892 by Rudyard Kipling; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: 'Danny Deever' opens with the hanging of a soldier; 'Tommy' defends the private against the civilian's contempt; 'For to Admire' and 'Mandalay' celebrate and regret the East; 'Gunga Din' honours the native water-carrier; 'The Widow at Windsor' and 'Screw-Guns' record the soldier's view of the imperial machine.
works.significance: Barrack-Room Ballads broke the Victorian poetic diction and made the private soldier a subject of lyric poetry; its influence on the language of popular verse, on Hardy, on the First World War poets and on the modern ballad is incalculable, and it remains the central poetic document of the British Empire.
works.meter: Ballad stanzas and music-hall metres, with heavy anaphora and refrain; mimetic dialect and soldiers' slang.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, the British army in India and Egypt, the music hall and the new popular press, and the imperial jingoism of the Jubilee years. works.title: Bartholomew Fair
works.description: Jonson's comedy of the fair: on St Bartholomew's Day, the whole of London pours into Smithfield — the justice Adam Overdo in disguise, the hot Puritan Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, the gallants Winwife and Quarlous, the pig-woman Ursula and her booth, the puppet-show of Hero and Leander — in a play whose carnival world exposes every pretension, and whose induction mocks its own audience's 'warrant' for the satire.
works.plot: Overdo patrols the fair to 'enormities' in disguise; Busy denounces the fleshpots and falls to the pig; the gallants win the rich widow and the ward through the fair's games; the cutpurse Edgeworth and the bawd Whit ply their trades; and the last act's puppet trial before Overdo ends with the puppets' own argument and the universal pardon of the fair.
works.significance: The greatest carnival play in English — a comedy that swallows its own satire and leaves the audience judged along with the fair.
works.meter: Almost wholly prose — the most populous and idiomatic prose of Jonson's career — with the puppets' verse as the final parody.
works.context: First performed at the Hope theatre on 31 October 1614, before James I; printed 1631; its 'enormities' satire answers the puritan attacks on the stage Jonson had answered in his own person.
works.characters: Adam Overdo; Dame Overdo; Zeal-of-the-Land Busy; Winwife; Quarlous; Bartholomew Cokes; Grace Wellborn; Wasp; Ursula the pig-woman; Leatherhead (Lantern); Joan Trash; Edgeworth; Whit; Justice Trouble-All; the Puppets
works.structure: A deliberately sprawling carnival structure — no single plot, but a cross-section of the fair in five acts, with Overdo's exposures as the running joke and the puppet trial as the finale.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
The public theatre and the players' world
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War
works.form: Poetry collection; war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: Published in 1866 and the greatest book of American Civil War poetry by a participant: seventy-two poems on the battles, the leaders and the moral meaning of the war. It is a verse work of 1866 by Herman Melville; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poems move from 'The Portent' (John Brown) through 'Shiloh', 'The March into Virginia', 'A Utilitarian View of the Monitor's Fight' and 'The Armies of the Wilderness' to the elegy for Lincoln and the prose 'Supplement' on Reconstruction.
works.significance: Battle-Pieces is the central American poetic record of the Civil War and the finest body of war poetry written by an American: its refusal of triumphalism and its sympathy for the defeated make it a permanent rebuke to the patriotic verse of the period.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The years 1861-65, the American Civil War, the assassination of Lincoln, and the debate on Reconstruction. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Melvill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Bayou Folk
works.form: Collection of short stories; local-colour sketch
works.description: Published in 1894 and the collection that made Chopin's reputation: twenty-three stories of the Creoles, Acadians and freedpeople of Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Kate Chopin; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The stories include 'Désirée's Baby', the terrible tale of a mother and her child of mixed ancestry; 'A No-Account Creole'; 'In and Out of Old Natchitoches'; 'La Belle Zoraïde'; and the comic dialect tales of the Acadian farmers.
works.significance: Bayou Folk is the finest American local-colour collection of the 1890s and the founding text of the literature of Louisiana: its treatment of race in 'Désirée's Baby' is one of the most powerful short stories in American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is cool, exact, sensory prose.
works.context: The 1890s: the Louisiana plantation and bayou country, the Creole and Acadian communities, and the new American local-colour market. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Désirée, Armand Aubigny and Madame Valmondé ('Désirée's Baby'); Placide Santien, Euphrasie and Wallace Offdean ('A No-Account Creole'); Alphonse Laballière and Suzanne St Denys Godolph ('In and Out of Old Natchitoches'); Zoraïde and Mézor ('La Belle Zoraïde'); La Folle ('Beyond the Bayou')
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katherine Chopin. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Beachy Head, and Other Poems
works.form: Topographical and Descriptive Poetry; Nature Lyric and Meditation; Romantic Sonnet Revival
works.description: Charlotte Smith's last and greatest volume of verse, published after her death at her own expense from copies she had prepared: the long topographical-descriptive poem Beachy Head, together with sonnets and shorter lyrics. From the cliff of the Sussex headland the poem takes in geology, natural history, the fishing and wrecking of the coast, the fate of the poor, and the poet's own age, dependence, and approaching death, in a blank verse of unusual range that opens with one of the great cosmological panoramas of Romantic poetry.
works.plot: The title poem rises from the view from Beachy Head to the turning earth and the remoter planets, returns to the chalk cliff, its ruined chapel and its tradition of hermits and outcasts, and passes through the fishing, wrecking, and poverty of the Sussex coast to a meditation on the poet's own exhaustion, bereavement, and death; the accompanying sonnets and shorter lyrics repeat the same repertoire of melancholy, natural observation, and consolation, several of them written and published earlier in her life.
works.significance: Beachy Head is now recognized as one of the major long poems of the Romantic period and as the most powerful statement of a women's topographical and scientific imagination between the Revolution and its disappointment; its combination of the sublime, natural history, and the politics of poverty has made it central to the recovery of Smith and to the redefinition of Romantic landscape poetry.
works.meter: Beachy Head is written in decasyllabic blank verse of long, suspended periods, with elaborate descriptive enumeration and apostrophe; the remainder of the volume supplies Petrarchan and hybrid sonnets and shorter lyrics in varied stanzaic and metrical patterns.
works.context: Prepared during Smith's last years of increasing illness, poverty, and anxiety for her children, and issued in 1807, a year after her death, printed for the author and sold by her long-time publisher; its coastal setting is the country of her own residences, and its treatment of geological deep time, natural history, and the suffering of the poor responds to the scientific and topographical writing of the 1790s and 1800s.
works.characters: the poet on the headland; the hermit and the outcast of the cliff tradition; the fishermen, wreckers, and poor of the Sussex coast; the mourner of the shorter poems
works.structure: A volume dominated by one long descriptive-meditative poem in the manner of Thomson and Cowper, whose movement is associational and from which the shorter poems and sonnets form a second, lyric division.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name from manuscripts she prepared; attribution is undisputed, though the volume was posthumous and its final arrangement was made by others.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Natural history, science, and the poetic eye
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Topographical and Estate Poetry

works.title: Beasts and Super-Beasts
works.description: Saki's finest collection: 'The Open Window', 'Sredni Vashtar' and the revenge of the young. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by Saki (H. H. Munro); it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Open Window', 'Sredni Vashtar', 'The Schartz-Metterklume Method', 'The Story-Teller', 'Tobermory' and 'The Interlopers', in which children, animals and practical jokers overturn the certainties of their elders.
works.significance: Beasts and Super-Beasts is Saki's finest collection and the central text of the English comic short story: it contains 'The Open Window' and 'Sredni Vashtar', two of the most anthologised stories in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story built on a single surprise.
works.context: Edwardian England and the country-house world of the years before the First World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1913 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: Vera; Conradin; Mrs Sappleton; Clovis Sangrail; Tobermory
works.structure: Thirty-six stories in a single collection. The work is in 36 stories. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hector Hugh Munro. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Beat to Quarters
works.description: The first Hornblower novel: the frigate of the Napoleonic wars. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by C. S. Forester; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Beat to Quarters - published in England as The Happy Return - follows Captain Horatio Hornblower of HMS Lydia on the Pacific station, the capture of the Spanish galleon and the diplomacy of the Central American coast, in the exact professional prose of the ship, the gun and the wind that made the series.
works.significance: Beat to Quarters began the Hornblower series: its Lydia, its captain and its exact professional prose made the naval novel of the Napoleonic wars the most read serial fiction of the middle century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact prose of the professional.
works.context: The Pacific coast in the Napoleonic wars. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1937 and first published in 1937 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Horatio Hornblower; the crew of the Lydia; the Spanish and the Central American powers
works.structure: A naval novel in the chapters of the station, the capture and the diplomacy. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cecil Scott Forester. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Beau Geste
works.form: Novel; historical novel, first issued in 1924
works.description: The greatest Foreign Legion novel: the fort, the jewel and the brothers. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by P. C. Wren; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Three brothers — Michael, Digby and John Geste — join the French Foreign Legion after a theft at their aunt's house, and defend the desert fort of Zinderneuf against an Arab siege, in a novel that begins with the mystery of the dead men propped at the walls.
works.significance: Beau Geste is the greatest French Foreign Legion novel ever written and one of the great adventure stories of the century: its desert fort, its mysterious theft and its brothers made it a permanent popular classic and the founding text of the Legion romance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the desert fort and the siege.
works.context: England, Algeria and the Sahara in the early twentieth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Michael Geste; Digby Geste; John Geste; Sergeant Lejaune; Lady Brandon; the Touareg
works.structure: An adventure novel in the Legion, framed by the mystery of the fort. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Percival Christopher Wren. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Beauchamp's Career
works.form: Novel in three volumes; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1875-76 and the most political of Meredith's novels: the story of Nevil Beauchamp, a Radical naval officer who stands for Parliament and is destroyed by his own honesty. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by George Meredith; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Beauchamp campaigns for the Radical cause in a Tory constituency, is rejected by the aristocratic Cecilia Halkett, is drawn back to Renée de Croisnel, the Frenchwoman he loved in his youth, now unhappily married to an old marquis, and, after Cecilia marries the Tory Blackburn Tuckham, marries Jenny Denham, ward of the old Radical Dr Shrapnel, only to drown saving a poor boy from the water; the novel's argument is that his integrity is both his glory and his ruin.
works.significance: Beauchamp's Career is among the finest English political novels of the nineteenth century and the most direct treatment of Radical politics by a major novelist.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
works.context: The 1867-74 electoral politics, the first Gladstone ministry, the Franco-Prussian war of 1870, and the Victorian debate on the aristocratic versus the democratic principle. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Nevil Beauchamp; Cecilia Halkett; Renée de Croisnel; Jenny Denham; Dr Shrapnel; Everard Romfrey; Rosamund Culling; Colonel Halkett; Blackburn Tuckham
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Becket
works.form: Verse tragedy (five acts); victorian verse drama
works.description: Published in 1884 and performed at the Lyceum Theatre by Henry Irving on 6 February 1884: Tennyson's most successful play, on the conflict of Henry II and Thomas Becket. It is a dramatic work of 1884 by Alfred Tennyson; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Becket, the king's chancellor turned archbishop, resists Henry's attempt to subject the Church to the royal courts; the conflict over criminous clerks, the exile in France, the return and the murder in the cathedral of 29 December 1170 form the play's structure, and Becket's death is presented as a martyrdom accepted in advance.
works.significance: Becket is the best of Tennyson's late plays and one of the few Victorian verse tragedies to hold the stage; it revived the historical verse drama in England and prepared the way for the poetic theatre of the 1890s and of Yeats.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.
works.context: The 1880s and the disestablishment question, the Oxford Movement's legacy, and the Victorian stage's revival of verse drama under Irving and Ellen Terry. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Thomas Becket; Henry II; Queen Eleanor; Rosamund de Clifford; John of Salisbury; Herbert of Bosham; Gilbert Foliot; Roger of York; Reginald Fitzurse; Margery
works.structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Bede's Death Song
works.manuscriptDate: St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek 254 (ninth century or earlier); Northumbrian version in Cambridge, University Library Kk.5.16 (the Moore Bede, c. 737)
works.description: A five-line alliterative poem, the last words of the dying Bede, recorded in the Epistola Cuthberti de obitu Bedae. The poet meditates on the soul's necessary journey out of the body and the judgment each man must face for his deeds. It is the earliest datable Old English poem.
works.plot: Bede, near death, reflects that no man's wisdom can outrun his need to consider, before departing, what judgment his soul will receive for the good and evil he has done.
works.significance: The earliest datable poem in English, and a uniquely documented case of vernacular verse preserved with its author, date, and occasion of composition.
works.meter: Five lines of classic alliterative verse in the Northumbrian dialect, preserved with Latin paraphrase; the earliest securely datable example of English poetry.
works.context: Recorded by Bede's pupil Cuthbert in the letter describing the master's death on 26 May 735; the poem circulated in two dialect versions and in many manuscripts of the Historia ecclesiastica, often with a Latin translation.
works.characters: Bede (speaker)
works.structure: Five alliterative long lines in two movements: the inevitability of the soul's departure, and the reckoning of deeds before the judge.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bede in the Epistola Cuthberti, composed, according to the letter, on his deathbed; the attribution is accepted by modern scholarship, though the poem circulated anonymously in some manuscripts.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Wisdom and learning
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Behemoth; or, The Long Parliament
works.description: Hobbes's history of the English civil wars in the form of a dialogue, written in old age as a companion to Leviathan and suppressed by Charles II, but printed without authority in 1679 and after Hobbes's death in 1682.
works.plot: In four dialogues between A and B, Hobbes explains the causes of the civil wars as the spread of seditious doctrines from the Presbyterians, the Independents, and the universities, and the ambition of the parliamentary leaders.
works.significance: Hobbes's own interpretation of the events that produced Leviathan and a key text for understanding his theory of sedition and the role of universities and clergy in politics.
works.meter: Conversational prose dialogue.
works.context: Written c. 1668-70; Charles II refused permission to publish it, and it appeared in an unauthorised edition in 1679 and an authorised edition in 1682.
works.characters: A (the narrator); B (the questioner); Charles I; Cromwell; the Long Parliament
works.structure: Four dialogues covering 1640 to 1660.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; the 1679 edition was unauthorised and Hobbes complained of its errors.

Ecclesiastical reform and criticism

works.title: Behind a Mask; or, A Woman's Power
works.form: Novella (published anonymously as A. M. Barnard)
works.description: Published anonymously in 1866 as by A. M. Barnard and the most subversive of Alcott's thrillers: the story of a governess who is not what she seems. It is a prose fiction work of 1866 by Louisa May Alcott; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Jean Muir, a thirty-year-old actress, passes herself off as a nineteen-year-old governess in an aristocratic English family and systematically ensnares the Coventry men — the younger son Edward, the indolent heir Gerald and finally their uncle Sir John Coventry, whom she marries just before the letters exposing her past are read to a family that must now accept her as Lady Coventry.
works.significance: Behind a Mask is one of the boldest American stories of the 1860s and the key text in the recovery of Alcott's sensation fiction: its femme fatale heroine and its attack on the English aristocracy have made it central to the feminist reading of Alcott.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a strong narrative voice.
works.context: The 1860s: the sensation vogue, the governess question, and the American market for anonymous thrillers. The record dates the work as composed in 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel.
works.characters: Jean Muir; Gerald Coventry; Edward Coventry; Bella Coventry; Mrs Coventry; Sir John Coventry; Lucia Beaufort; Dean, Lucia's maid
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: It was first published anonymously and the authorship was established afterwards from the publisher's records and the correspondence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Believe as You List
works.description: Massinger's political tragedy on the false Sebastian of Portugal, suppressed by the Master of the Revels for its treatment of a recent alliance and then rewritten; it survives in the author's manuscript with Sir Henry Herbert's annotations.
works.plot: A young man claiming to be the lost King Sebastian of Portugal is recognised by many, pursued by Spain, and finally exposed as an impostor; the play explores the politics of belief and dynastic legitimacy.
works.significance: The most important surviving manuscript of a Caroline play, documenting the workings of censorship; it is also Massinger's most serious political tragedy.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: First drafted in 1631 and banned by Herbert as seditious because of its allusion to the Anglo-Spanish alliance; Massinger recast the story in a Roman setting and the revised version was licensed on 6 May 1631.
works.characters: Antiochus (the false Sebastian); Titus Flaminius; the Roman Senate; Marcella; Sulpitius
works.structure: Five acts following the pretender's rise, recognition, and exposure.
works.attributionNotes: The authorial manuscript is signed 'P.M.' and is universally accepted as Massinger's holograph.

works.title: Belinda
altTitles: Belinda. By Maria Edgeworth. In Three Volumes
works.form: novel of manners and of marriage negotiation in the third person; conversational and didactic comedy
works.description: The novel of manners which its author's reputation has most consistently rested upon her, and the plainest proof that the Irish tale-writer of Castle Rackrent was also a searchingly English comic novelist. Belinda Portman, a young woman of good family and no fortune, comes to London under the protection of her early friend Lady Anne Manwarring and is drawn at once into two societies: the elegant and intellectually vain circle of the widow Lady Delacour, and the newer, merrier and more assertive household formed by her friend's husband's marrying relation. The book follows the negotiation of Belinda's marriage - between the suit of a serious foreign banker who wants a wife of domestic habits and the importunities of a fashionable foreign lover - with a steadiness of irony which keeps the heroine's thoughts in view while allowing the reader to see further than she does.
works.plot: Belinda, generous and uninstructed, accepts the protection of Lady Anne and passes under the care of Lady Delacour, a brilliant, unquiet widow whose household is governed by her friendship with a pretender to literary eminences, and whose son is left to the devices of a projecting educator. The domestic peace of the Manwarrings is destroyed by the arrival of a young wife of the new fashion, who brings with her an attached child from the West Indies, a Black girl whose grateful affection for the children of the house she has served supplies one of the most quietly moving episodes in the book. Against this society Belinda's constancy, and the plain good sense which her friends call want of genius, are tested by the perseverance of an admirer of foreign manners and by the jealousy and mismanagement of those who profess to guide her. Her friend Lady Anne is driven into apparent delinquency by a jealous and tyrannical husband, and the novel's most discussed sequence follows the attempts of Belinda and Lady Delacour to relieve her from the confinement into which his authority over her person and her fortune had cast her. The argument, carried by example rather than assertion, is that a woman's independence is a question of law, money and reputation, not of sentiment; that the fashionable reformers of education and of society are charlatans of a mild kind; and that marriage, fairly looked at, is an estate question as much as a matter of the heart.
works.significance: It is the book by which Maria Edgeworth takes her place in the history of the novel of manners between Fanny Burney and Jane Austen, and it has been the most continuously re-edited and most critically discussed of her fictions, both for its handling of the marriage market and the condition of women and for its treatment of the West Indian child, of affectionate service, and of marriage between the planter and the lady of colour. Its plain style and its refusal of the sentimental crisis were read by later novelists as a lesson in the possible seriousness of comedy, and its last chapter, which leaves its heroine's happiness uncompleted, has long been a test case for the interpretation of her art.
works.meter: Prose. The style is the plain, quick, unornamented manner its author described as the natural language of a mind in motion: short declarative sentences, the reported exclamation, the abrupt moral aside, and a command of dialogue which carries argument and character at the same moment; the effect is of irony delivered by silence rather than by comment.
works.context: Published in London in 1801 in three volumes, after Castle Rackrent (1800) had been issued anonymously, and at the moment when the Anglo-Irish Ascendancy, its.absentees and its schemes of education and improvement were the subject of daily argument; the book's quarrel with projectors, with the literary lady and with the fashionable wife belongs to the controversy over female conduct and education carried on by its author's family, and its West Indian child and its planter marriages bring the question of slavery and of the colonial estate into the drawing-room novel.
works.characters: Belinda Portman; Lady Anne Manwarring; Mr Manwarring; the fashionable young mistress of the house; Lady Delacour; her son; the attached West Indian child; the serious foreign admirer; the foreign lover of fashion
works.structure: A single continuous third-person narrative in short chapters, with the letter and the printed extract introduced where they serve the argument; the action is compressed into a London season and its country excursion, and the plot turns upon two paired crises in the situations of Belinda and of her friend.
works.attributionNotes: There has been no dispute as to its authorship: the title page names Maria Edgeworth, whose initials and family position were already known to the book's public from Practical Education and Castle Rackrent, and the novel's composition and publication are documented in the family correspondence which she herself edited.

Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world

works.title: Belinda. A Novel
works.description: Published in 1883 and the novel that made Broughton a satirist: the story of a young woman whose reticence loses her the man she loves and who marries in despair an elderly pedant, Broughton's portrait of Mark Pattison.
works.plot: In Dresden Belinda Churchill falls in love with the young David Rivers, but her shyness reads as coldness and their understanding is left unspoken; when he is called home and never writes, she marries in despair the elderly, humourless Professor Forth, her sister Sarah's discarded fiancé, and three days after the wedding receives the letter that shows her mistake. The rest of the novel tests her loyalty to a loveless marriage.
works.significance: Belinda marks Broughton's turn from sensation to social comedy and is one of the first English novels to make the mother, rather than the daughter, the comic protagonist of the marriage plot.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is first-person female narration with direct address to the reader.
works.context: The 1880s, the 'marriage market' and the peerage, the entry of women into university education, and the spread of divorce. The record dates the work as composed in 1883 and first published in 1883 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Belinda Churchill; Sarah Churchill, her sister; Professor Forth; David Rivers; their grandmother; Miss Watson
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Benito Cereno
works.description: Published in Putnam's Monthly in 1855 and the most disturbing American story about slavery: the account of an American sea captain who boards a Spanish slave ship and fails to see the truth. It is a prose fiction work of 1855 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Captain Amasa Delano of the Bachelor's Delight finds the San Dominick off the coast of Chile, with its captain Don Benito Cereno and the faithful slave Babo; the truth — that the Africans have seized the ship and are forcing the Spaniards to sail to Africa — is concealed from Delano until Babo's final attack, and the story ends with Cereno's death and Babo's execution.
works.significance: Benito Cereno is the central American literary treatment of slavery and of the failure of American perception: its study of Delano's inability to see the truth of the ship has made it the foundation of the criticism of race in American literature, and it is the greatest novella in American writing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The year 1799, the Spanish slave trade, the Haitian revolution, and the American debate on slavery after the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850. The record dates the work as composed in 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Captain Amasa Delano; Don Benito Cereno; Babo; Atufal; Don Alexandro Aranda
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Melvill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale
themes: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction
movements: Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance

works.title: Beowulf
works.description: The greatest surviving poem in Old English: a heroic epic of 3,182 alliterative lines recounting the deeds of the Geatish hero Beowulf against the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, fifty years later, a dragon. It combines the legendary history of Scandinavia with a profound Christian meditation on heroism, mortality, and the limits of earthly glory.
works.plot: The young hero Beowulf sails from Geatland to Denmark to rid King Hrothgar's hall Heorot of the man-eating monster Grendel, whom he defeats in a night combat; he then tracks Grendel's mother to her underwater lair and slays her. Rewarded and honoured, he returns home and eventually rules the Geats for fifty years, until a dragon, enraged by the theft of a cup from its hoard, ravages his kingdom; the aged king kills the dragon but dies of his wounds, and the poem ends with his funeral pyre and the foreboding of his people's doom.
works.significance: The foundational epic of English literature; the first extended poetic masterpiece in any Germanic vernacular; a touchstone for subsequent English poetry (Tolkien, Auden, Heaney) and for the study of Germanic legend.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre: four stresses per line divided by a caesura; formulaic diction, kennings, and variation throughout.
works.context: Composed somewhere between the age of Bede and the eve of the Conquest, and copied c. 1000 in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv); its heroes belong to sixth-century Scandinavia (Hygelac's raid on Frisia, c. 521, is historical), while its audience was Christian Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: Beowulf, Hrothgar, Grendel, Grendel's mother, the dragon, Wiglaf, Hygelac, Unferth, Wealhtheow, Scyld Scefing
works.structure: A bipartite structure (youthful Danish adventures; old age and the dragon) framed by the funerals of Scyld Scefing and Beowulf; interlaced with digressions — the Finnsburh episode, the Sigmund lay, the Swedish-Geatish wars, and the 'Lay of the Last Survivor' — that mirror and darken the main action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus. Ascribed to no known poet.
themes: Christian-pagan synthesis
Heroism and the heroic code
Kingship and good rule
Loyalty and the comitatus bond
Monsters and the marvellous
Treasure, gift-giving, and reciprocity
Wyrd (fate) and providence
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics
works.form: Lecture and essay (British Academy, Sir Israel Gollancz Memorial)
works.description: The lecture that made the monsters the centre of Beowulf and rewrote the study of the poem. It is a prose work of 1936 by J. R. R. Tolkien; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tolkien argues that the monsters - Grendel, his mother and the dragon - are not the flaws of the poem but its centre, that the poem is an elegy and not an epic of the tribe, and that the critic must read the verse as verse; the lecture turned Beowulf studies from the sources to the poetry.
works.significance: 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' is the most influential lecture in the history of Old English studies: it made the monsters the centre of the poem and the elegiac tone the key to its structure, and it remains the starting point of every modern reading of Beowulf.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is the invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it.
works.context: The British Academy lecture of 25 November 1936, and the state of Beowulf scholarship. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; critical essay and the modern review.
works.structure: A lecture in sections: the state of the criticism, the monsters, the elegy and the verse. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Ronald Reuel Tolkien. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Beppo
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Romantic narrative romance in ottava rima; the conversational verse tale and mock-romance, in deliberate opposition to the serious oriental tale of the same authorship.
works.description: A light narrative poem in ottava rima, founded on an anecdote the author had heard in Venice, which tells how a long-absent husband returns to find his wife established with a lover and, instead of the expected tragedy, gives them both dinner. Its irony, its digressions on Carnival, the opera, the Pope and English manners, and its refusal of the sensational ending made it a new kind of popular poem. It is the first full exercise of the conversational, laughing manner that the later romance of Spain and England was to carry to its limit.
works.plot: The Genoese captain, pressed into pirate service, has been absent fourteen years, and his young wife has consoled herself with the lord of the house next door; the Carnival supplies the mask and the opera the occasion of their happiness. The captain returns unlooked for at the very moment when a knife has been produced in jealousy, and after a scene of astonishment the three sup together, and the poet reports the neighbours' verdict on the adventure. The argument, carried by constant digression, is that life is more comic than romantic, that the expected catastrophe of the tale of jealousy is a convention of books rather than of Venice, and that the reader's appetite for sensation is part of the subject.
works.significance: It introduced ottava rima and the ironized narrator into English Romantic narrative, and supplied the technical means for the later digressive romance; its handling of the marriage plot as comedy rather than tragedy of jealousy widened the range of the verse tale. It also showed the reading public that the maker of the outlaw hero could write conversationally and laugh at his own reputation.
works.meter: Ottava rima, seven iambic pentameter lines rhyming abababcc, with the closing couplet used for point and aside; the manner is easy, colloquial and heavily dependent on enjambment and the abrupt rhyming turn.
works.context: Written in October 1817 during the Venetian sojourn and issued early in 1818 by a publisher who printed it from a sent manuscript without waiting for the author's final consent, the poem appeared between the serious pilgrimage canto and the great romance of Spain. Its defence of the Carnival, the opera and the domestic arrangements of Italy against northern censoriousness was a deliberate provocation to the quarterly review public, and the preface's apology for its levity became a document of the controversy over a poet's duty to be serious.
works.characters: the Genoese captain; his wife; her lover, the master of the house; the friend who tells the story; the neighbours and Carnival crowd
works.structure: A single continuous narrative of sixty stanzas, interrupted at every turn by the poet's own digressive address on the theatre, the Carnival, the Pope, and the habits of the English, so that the frame of comment is larger than the tale it suspends.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the printing history is unusual rather than disputed, the first issue being produced by the publisher without the author's final approval.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: Bertram; or, The Castle of St. Aldobrand
works.description: the author's Gothic blank-verse tragedy set in a medieval Italian castle, in which Bertram, a soldier of fortune, confronts his own secret incestuous desires and the crimes committed by his father. Lord Byron praised it highly in the British Press in 1816, connecting it to the Byronic revolt tradition. It represents the intersection of Gothic and Byronic modes in Romantic verse drama.
works.plot: Bertram, a wanderer seeking refuge, arrives at the Castle of St. Aldobrand and falls in love with Imelda, believing her to be of noble birth. He discovers that his father, the late Count, committed atrocities of usurpation and murder to secure the estate. The recognition that Imelda is his own sister precipitates Bertram's despairing confrontation with his father's ghost. The drama ends in his curse and self-destructive resolve.
works.significance: Bertram connects the Gothic novel tradition to Byronic verse drama; its incest theme prefigures Manfred. the author's verse shows the Gothic mode's migration from prose to dramatic poetry in the 1810s.
works.meter: Blank verse, iambic pentameter
works.context: Written in the same period as Byron's Manfred and The Prisoner of Chillon; it drew on the Italian romance tradition and the Gothic stage tradition of the 1790s. Byron's enthusiastic review helped secure its Dublin and London publication.
works.characters: Bertram; Imelda; Count Albert; the ghost of Count St. Aldobrand; Marcella; the Hermit
works.structure: Five-act dramatic structure in blank verse; unified in place and time; the ghost of Count St. Aldobrand drives the recognition scene.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Revenge and justice

works.title: Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush
works.description: The most popular Scottish book of the 1890s: a parish minister, a schoolmaster and the deaths of the good. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Ian Maclaren; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: A sequence of sketches of the parish of Drumtochty: the minister and the dying scholar Lachlan Campbell, the schoolmaster, the doctor and the return of the emigrant, ending in the death of the minister's wife and the consolation of the parish.
works.significance: Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s and the central text of the kailyard school: it sold in the hundreds of thousands, created the sentimental image of the Scottish parish, and provoked the realist reaction of The House with the Green Shutters.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the linked sketch rather than the plotted novel.
works.context: The Scottish parish of the 1890s and the Free Church ministry in the countryside. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the minister of Drumtochty; Lachlan Campbell; the schoolmaster; Marget; the doctor
works.structure: A sequence of linked sketches with a parish frame. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Watson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Bevis of Hampton
works.description: One of the most popular of all Middle English romances: the adventures of Bevis of Southampton, sold into heathen lands by his mother's treachery, who wins the Saracen princess Josian, fights dragons and giants, and at last reclaims his English inheritance. Its vigorous, episodic narrative survived in verse, prose, and print into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: Bevis's mother plots his father's murder and marries the murderer; the boy is sold overseas, but wins fame and the love of Josian; after adventures in Armenia, Cologne, and England — including his defeat of the dragon of Cologne and his final siege of Southampton — he regains his lands and ends his days as a monk with Josian.
works.significance: The archetypal popular romance: its immense circulation (Chaucer's Sir Thopas parodies its tail-rhyme form) makes it central to the history of English popular reading.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, later rewritten in tail-rhyme in some manuscripts.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman original (Boeve de Haumtoun); preserved in six manuscripts, the Auchinleck (c. 1330) foremost, and repeatedly printed from c. 1500 to the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Bevis; Josian; Ascopard the giant; Saber; the dragon of Cologne; King Ermin
works.structure: A sprawling episodic quest in the Auchinleck manner, with exile, conversion, combat, and restoration as its repeating units.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
National identity and Englishness
Warfare and battle

works.title: Bevis: The Story of a Boy
works.description: Published in 1882 and the finest English children's book of the outdoor world: two boys' summer of sailing, camping and adventure on a Wiltshire lake. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Richard Jefferies; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Bevis and his friend Mark spend a summer on the island in the lake near their farm, sailing, fishing, camping, building a hut and fighting imaginary battles with the village boys, while the natural world around them is recorded in exact and loving detail.
works.significance: Bevis is the greatest English children's book about the outdoor world and the finest of Jefferies's books for young readers: its combination of exact natural history and the freedom of childhood made it a model for the English adventure story, and it is the English equivalent of Tom Sawyer in its picture of a boy's summer.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals.
works.context: 1882: the Victorian country childhood, the vogue of the boys' adventure book after Treasure Island's precursors, and the natural history of the Wiltshire downs. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Bevis; Mark, his friend; Pan, the spaniel; the village boys of the mock battles
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Richard Jefferies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Beware the Cat
altTitles: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
works.description: William Baldwin's anti-Catholic prose satire of 1552–53, in which a company of men swap stories proving that cats can speak and understand; printed posthumously in 1561 and often claimed as the first English novel.
works.plot: The narrator, Master Streamer, overhears a conversation among the household of John Young while lodged at the printing house; the talk turns to cats, and Gregory Streamer relates how, having eaten a cat, he gained the power to understand animal speech, recounting the trial of Mouse-slayer before the cat parliament and the bawdy doings of cats and priests — a satire on Catholic superstition, oral tradition, and the credulity of tale-collectors.
works.significance: Claimed as the first English novel for its sustained prose fiction and self-conscious narrative framing; it is also a sophisticated satire on storytelling, tradition, and the authority of print, anticipating the narrative experiments of the Elizabethan period.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in 1552–53 at the press of John Day, where Baldwin worked; its satire of Catholic ritual (the cat's mass) fitted the Edwardian Reformation moment, and by its printing in 1561 (with a prefatory epistle to John Young) the political climate had changed again.
works.characters: Master Streamer (narrator); Gregory Streamer; Mouse-slayer; Grimalkin; John Young (the printer)
works.structure: A framed narrative in three orations, with inset stories (the cat's life of Grimalkin, the trial of Mouse-slayer) and a self-conscious apparatus of marginal glosses and running commentary on the reliability of oral report.
works.attributionNotes: Printed anonymously in 1561 with initials 'G. B.'; the attribution to William Baldwin rests on the prefatory matter and the internal evidence of the printing-house setting, and is accepted by modern scholarship.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
