works.title: Beyond the Horizon
works.description: O'Neill's first Pulitzer Prize: two brothers and the farm they should have traded. It is a dramatic work of 1920 by Eugene O'Neill; it belongs to The American Theatre and the Modern Stage and it is catalogued here under Domestic and Sentimental Tragedy; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Andrew Mayo stays on the farm while his brother Robert goes to sea, but Robert marries Andrew's girl and stays, and Andrew goes to sea; the play follows the failure of the farm and the death of Robert in a tragedy of the wrong choices.
works.significance: Beyond the Horizon was O'Neill's first Pulitzer Prize and the play that made the modern American theatre: its tragic structure and its portrait of the farm made him the central American playwright of the century.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the expressionist set and the mask.
works.context: A New England farm in the 1910s, and the American rural world at the turn of the century. The record dates the work as composed between 1918 and 1920 and first published in 1920 and first performed in 1920 and the corpus places it within The American Theatre and the Modern Stage, it is catalogued under domestic and sentimental tragedy; problem play and well-made drama.

works.structure: Three acts, from the farm to the death. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Billy Budd, Sailor (An Inside Narrative)
works.description: Written in the last years of Melville's life and left unfinished at his death in 1891: the story of a beautiful sailor, a false accusation and a summary execution at sea in 1797. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Billy Budd, the Handsome Sailor, is impressed into the Bellipotent, where the master-at-arms Claggart accuses him of mutiny; Billy, unable to speak, strikes Claggart dead, and Captain Vere convenes a drumhead court-martial and hangs him.
works.significance: Billy Budd is the last great work of American prose and one of the most debated: its treatment of innocence, law and the inside narrative has made it central to the literature of justice, and its unfinished state has produced a century of textual scholarship.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The year 1797, the Spithead and Nore mutinies, the Napoleonic wars, and the American debate on law and justice at the end of the century. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1891 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Billy Budd; John Claggart; Captain Edward Fairfax Vere; the Dansker
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Left unfinished at Melville's death in 1891; the text was reconstructed and first published in 1924, and the scholarly editions of 1962 and 2017 differ substantially.

works.title: Binsey Poplars
works.description: Written in March 1879 after the felling of the poplar trees along the Isis at Binsey, near Oxford: the most quoted English poem of ecological mourning and one of the clearest statements of Hopkins's doctrine of inscape.
works.plot: The poem records the felling of the aspens 'that dandled a sandalled shadow', laments that the 'sweet especial rural scene' can never be restored, and ends with the warning that 'ten or twelve' strokes of the axe 'unselve' the countryside.
works.significance: 'Binsey Poplars' is the founding poem of English ecological literature and the key text for Hopkins's theory of inscape as the individual signature of a place; its coinage 'unselve' has become a permanent English word for environmental destruction.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free.
works.context: The felling of the Binsey poplars in 1879 and the Victorian destruction of rural landscape by industry and agriculture, which Hopkins addressed in several poems and letters. The record dates the work as composed in 1879 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.

works.title: Biographia Literaria
altTitles: Biographia Literaria; or, Biographical Notices of my Literary Life and Opinions
works.form: Critical treatise and literary autobiography, in the line of the formal miscellany of the period; it combines memoir, philosophical psychology and practical criticism in a single discursive work.
works.description: The central work of English Romantic literary criticism and theory, published in two volumes in 1817 and made up of the author's literary autobiography, his history of his own opinions, and a sustained analysis of imagination, fancy and symbol. It is famously miscellaneous, interrupting its own narrative with translations, psychological disquisition and quarrels, and it contains both the classic account of the Romantic theory of the imagination and the most searching criticism of the poems and the prefatory theory of the collaborator who had supplied the ballad volume's shorter pieces.
works.plot: The book moves between three kinds of matter. First, a memoir of the author's education, his communitarian scheme on the American frontier, his residence in Germany and his first lectures, which supplies the account of a mind formed by books and by disappointment. Second, a philosophical criticism which distinguishes fancy from imagination, describes the primary imagination as the living power and prime agent of all human perception, repeats the echo of that infinite act in every finite mind, and gives the secondary imagination as an echo of the former, coalescing with the objects of its contemplation and dissolving, diffusing and re-creating in order to idealise; symbol is defined as that which partakes of the reality of the thing it conveys. Third, a critical history of the ballad volume, in which the prose romances of the author's own hand are said to aim at the willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith, and in which the theory and the practice of the collaborator's verse are examined with admiration and with reproach, the famous chapters on the philosophy of the mind being at once an exposition and a quarrel.
works.significance: The most quoted body of theory in English Romantic criticism, and the source of the standard distinctions between fancy and imagination, of the definition of symbol, and of the phrase for the willing suspension of disbelief. Its account of perception and creation has governed later reading of Romantic poetry, and its mixture of memoir, philosophy and polemic defines the Romantic critical book.
works.meter: Prose of great density and range, passing from the plain autobiographical sentence to the Latinate periods of the philosophical chapters; the style of the book, with its coinages and its vocabulary of perception, became itself a model for English critical writing.
works.context: Written out of the author's London lecturing years and his residence in Germany, where he had read the transcendental philosophy, and published in the year of his collected poems, when the reputation of the Lake school was being made and attacked in the reviews; the book's history of the ballad volume is also a defence of his own share in it, and one of its chapters was withdrawn when its dependence on a German source was challenged.
works.characters: The author as the memoirist of his own opinions; the friend and collaborator whose theory and verse are examined; the German philosophers and the English critics whose texts and doctrines are translated, quoted or answered
works.structure: A two-volume miscellany following no single order: autobiography, translation, philosophical dissertation and practical criticism alternate, and the book repeatedly breaks off its own story, the author's apology for its desultory plan forming part of its design; whole chapters were withdrawn or recast in the reprintings.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; questions of the book's obligation to German and to English writers, and the dates of its chapters, have been much studied, and the withdrawal of one chapter in later issues is documented in the author's own correspondence.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Bird Alone
works.form: Novel (the young man against the church and the state)
works.description: The novel of the young man against the church and the state, banned in Ireland. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Sean O'Faolain; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bird Alone follows Corney Cassidy from the civil war to the Dublin of the censorship, against the church, the state and the family, in the first person of the young man alone; the book was banned in Ireland in the year of its publication.
works.significance: Bird Alone is O'Faolain's masterpiece and one of the great censored books of Ireland: its Corney Cassidy alone against the church and the state made the novel of the republic a national text and its banning a national scandal.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence.
works.context: Ireland from the civil war to the 1930s, and the censored book. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Corney Cassidy; the family; the priests; the women of the city
works.structure: A novel in the first person, in chapters from the civil war to the alone. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

works.description: The dystopian thriller of the revolution in England. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Dennis Wheatley; it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Imperial Adventure Romance.

works.title: Black No More
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1931
works.description: The funniest Black satire of the century: a machine that turns Black Americans white. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by George S. works.title: Black Thunder
works.description: The finest American novel of the slave rebellion: Gabriel Prosser and the rising of 1800. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Arna Bontemps; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Gabriel Prosser, a slave blacksmith in Richmond, Virginia, organises a rebellion of the slaves for August 1800; the rising is betrayed by a storm and by informers, and Gabriel and his men are hanged in a novel of the slave South and its failed revolution.
works.significance: Black Thunder is the finest American novel of the slave rebellion and Bontemps's masterpiece: its portrait of Gabriel Prosser made the slave revolutionary into a tragic hero, and it is the central novel of Black historical fiction in America.

Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is the historical novel of the slave South.

works.title: Black-Eyed Susan; or, All in the Downs
works.form: Drama; nautical and domestic melodrama with songs
works.description: A domestic nautical drama in which a sailor's sweetheart waits two years at a Deal inn for the man pressed into the service, and is menaced by the shipmate who ruined her brother. The play's celebrity rests on its domestic pathos, its sea-life detail and its final shipboard recognition and trial, with a famous song given to the heroine. It ran for an unprecedented number of performances at a Surrey theatre and was pirated, adapted and re-acted across the country and in America within months. It is the classic example of the Regency domestic melodrama at the height of its commercial power.
works.plot: The sailor William is pressed from the Downs and leaves Susan, the black-eyed barmaid of an inn at Deal, where her father keeps house and her brother's death at the hands of a shipmate is still unatoned. Tom Hatchet, the villain of the same watch, persecutes Susan and prospers by treachery at sea; an American merchant and his suit are interwoven with the lovers' trials. Three years later the ship returns, Hatchet is charged with mutiny and worse, and the courtroom and quarter-deck scenes expose his guilt; William is restored, the villain is condemned, and Susan's fidelity is rewarded with her sailor's hand.
works.significance: The most performed and most copied melodrama of its decade and the standard case study for the nautical drama, for theatrical piracy, and for the sentimental heroine recast as a working woman. Its combination of domestic injury and professional sea detail made it the model for later maritime sensation and remains the touchstone of melodrama criticism.
works.meter: Chiefly prose dialogue with set songs and a moral in verse; the lyric numbers are in popular stanzas
works.context: First played in June 1829 at a theatre south of the water that was building its reputation on maritime spectacle and working-class domestic pathos, at a time when impressment, naval discipline and the sailors' condition were live public questions. Its success shows the commercial ascendancy of melodrama over legitimate drama in the later 1820s, and its unlicensed touring and American revivals illustrate the absence of effective copyright protection before the 1830s.
works.characters: Susan, the black-eyed innkeeper's daughter; William, the pressed sailor; Tom Hatchet, his shipmate and her brother's destroyer; Susan's father, the publican; an American merchant; the ship's captain and officers
works.structure: Domestic drama in three acts moving between a Kentish inn and a ship's deck; the plot is built on separation, persecution and public proof, with the recognition and trial scenes as its designed climaxes and a sententious moral spoken at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Performed and published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship, though the many pirated and altered country and American versions circulated under other arrangements and titles.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Sea voyage and seafaring
The public theatre and the players' world

works.title: Bleak House
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from March 1852 to September 1853, the first of the great 'dark' novels, and the most technically ambitious: two narrators alternate, Esther Summerson in the first person and an unnamed third-person narrator in the present tense, and the Court of Chancery presides over both.
works.plot: Jarndyce and Jarndyce, a Chancery suit over a contested will, has consumed generations of litigants; its costs finally consume the whole estate at the close. Esther Summerson, raised by the harsh Mrs Rachael and sent for by John Jarndyce as companion to his young cousins Richard Carstone and Ada Clare, discovers in the course of the novel that she is the illegitimate daughter of Lady Dedlock, whose secret the lawyer Tulkinghorn discovers and is murdered for; the murder is solved by Inspector Bucket, the first police detective in English fiction. Lady Dedlock dies at the pauper graveyard where her lover is buried, Richard dies of the Chancery suit, and Esther marries Woodcourt.
works.significance: Bleak House is the most complete Victorian indictment of institutional England and the technical masterpiece of the Victorian multiplot novel; it brought the detective into English fiction and the public-health question into the novel. Its double narration is a permanent model for the novel of contested knowledge, and the opening fog paragraph is among the most analysed passages in English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Court of Chancery and the legal profession in the 1840s-50s, the sanitary reform campaign that followed the 1848 cholera epidemic (the death of Jo the crossing-sweeper is the novel's political centre), the metropolitan police detective branch, and the railway and the new suburb.
works.characters: Esther Summerson; Lady Dedlock; Sir Leicester Dedlock; John Jarndyce; Harold Skimpole; Richard Carstone; Ada Clare; Inspector Bucket; Tulkinghorn; Mr Guppy; Jo; Krook; Smallweed; Allan Woodcourt; Caddy Jellyby; Mrs Jellyby
works.structure: Alternating first-person (Esther) and third-person present-tense narration, with the Chancery suit as the master plot and the Dedlock secret as the withheld centre.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot

works.title: Blickling Homilies
works.description: A collection of eighteen anonymous Old English homilies for the church year, preserved in the Princeton Blickling manuscript: the earliest substantial vernacular sermon collection, contemporary with the first series of Ælfric's Catholic Homilies but plainer and more popular in style. Contains the famous vision of hell and of the places of the souls ('the three utterances of the soul').
works.plot: The homilies treat the major feasts — Annunciation, Palm Sunday, Easter (with the harrowing of hell), Rogationtide, Ascension, Pentecost, the Assumption, and the feasts of the apostles — expounding the gospel readings with vivid narrative expansions: the descent into hell, the soul's journey after death, and the architecture of the otherworld.
works.significance: The principal witness to the pre-Ælfrician homiletic tradition and to vernacular eschatological imagery.
works.meter: Old English prose; occasional rhythmical passages.
works.context: Copied c. 971, probably in Mercia or East Anglia; the manuscript (Princeton, Scheide Library, MS 71) is closely contemporary with the Beowulf manuscript's milieu.
works.characters: the evangelists' figures (Christ, the apostles, Mary, the blessed and the damned)
works.structure: Eighteen independent homilies in calendar order, each built on a gospel pericope with exegetical and exemplary digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Benedictine Reform
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Blithe Spirit
works.description: The longest-running comedy in the English theatre: a séance brings back a novelist's first wife. It is a dramatic work of 1941 by Noel Coward; it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Charles Condomine, a novelist, invites the medium Madame Arcati to a séance to gather material; the ghost of his first wife Elvira appears, visible only to him, and sets out to destroy his second marriage — until a second accident brings Ruth back as well.
works.significance: Blithe Spirit was written in six days in 1941 and became the longest-running comedy in the English theatre: its technical brilliance and its portrait of the haunted household made it Coward's most popular play.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the epigram and the witty exchange.
works.context: An English country house during the Second World War, and the vogue for spiritualism between the wars. The record dates the work as composed in 1941 and first published in 1941 and first performed in 1941 and it is catalogued under comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage; ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: Charles Condomine; Elvira; Ruth; Madame Arcati; Dr Bradman; Mrs Bradman; Edith
works.structure: Three acts, in the Condomines' living room. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A comedy in acts, the scene built as a succession of entrances, revelations and exits, with the social convention breached and restored.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Noël Pierce Coward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage
Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
Death, elegy, and the modern funeral
Love, constancy, and betrayal
The absurd, the void, and the failure of meaning

works.title: Boece
works.description: Chaucer's prose translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the work that above all others shaped his thought: the dialogue between the imprisoned Boethius and Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, providence, and the sovereign good. Made c. 1380–86 with the aid of the commentary tradition, it is the foundation of the Boethian strain that runs through all his poetry.
works.plot: Boethius, imprisoned and awaiting death, laments his fall until Lady Philosophy appears and, through a graduated argument in prose and verse (the metres), cures him: showing that fortune is mutable by nature, that true happiness lies in God, that evil men are punished by their own wickedness, and that providence and free will are compatible.
works.significance: The most consequential translation Chaucer made: through it, the Consolation became English literature's native philosophical idiom, from Chaucer to Elizabeth I's translation and beyond.
works.meter: Prose translation of the whole, metres included, dense with the philosophical vocabulary Chaucer coined or naturalized.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–86, drawing on the Latin text and the commentary of Nicholas Trevet; its influence pervades Chaucer's mature poems (Troilus, the Knight's Tale, the ballades) and the whole English Boethian tradition.
works.characters: Boethius; Lady Philosophy
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and metrical sections, in the Menippean form of the original; Chaucer renders the metres in prose, with explanatory glosses from the commentaries.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the Retraction).
themes: Consolation and endurance
Fortune and mutability
Wyrd (fate) and providence

works.title: Bogle Corbet; or, The Emigrants
works.description: the author's great Canadian novel, an epic of Scottish emigration and settlement in Upper Canada, drawn directly from the author's own experience as founder of Guelph and manager of the Canada Company. It is the foundational work of Canadian emigration literature and the author's most politically urgent fiction.
works.plot: Bogle Corbet, the son of a ruined Scottish tenant, leads a company of emigrants from Ayrshire to the wilderness of Upper Canada. The novel follows the clearing of the settlement, the hostility of the colonial bureaucracy, the failures and deaths of the pioneers, and Corbet's eventual return to Scotland broken in health but undefeated in principle. The second half chronicles the colony's struggle for survival and independence from the corrupt Canada Company. the author's argument is that principled colonisation can transform individuals and nations.
works.significance: Bogle Corbet is the first major literary treatment of Scottish emigration to Canada and a central text in transatlantic Romantic literature; it records with unmatched immediacy the social transformation produced by post-war displacement.
works.context: Published in 1831, as mass Scottish emigration to British North America accelerated and the author's own Canada Company venture was under attack; the novel is both a practical guide to emigration and a political argument for the colonization scheme.
works.characters: Bogle Corbet; Major Morroch; Bellenden; Mrs. Corbet; the emigrant community
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative in two broad movements — Scotland and Canada; the settlement chronicle structure; the novel's autobiographical core is fictionalised through Corbet as the active founder.
themes: Exile and homelessness
Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Bohoursky
works.form: war elegy and occasional meditative poem, in the Ossianising manner of the late century
works.description: Cowper's late war elegy on a Russian general killed in the storming of Ochakov, a short poem that turns a printed notice of a stranger's death into a meditation on honour, pity and the cost of arms. It mourns the fallen commander as a brave and humane soldier and sets the horrors of a stormed town against the praise of the man who died in the breach. It is characteristic of Cowper's last decade in its mixture of northern romantic colour and Christian regret.
works.plot: The poem recalls the general's conduct and courage, the storm of the place and his death in the attack, and then asks what glory can mean for a Christian who must count the slain. It dwells on the spectacle of the field and the breach, on the pity that survives the battlefield, and on the uncertainty of fame, closing with the sense that the warrior's reward is a mourned name rather than a triumph.
works.significance: It is the best of Cowper's short war poems and a useful instance of how the 1790s made a remote general's death an occasion of Christian pity, an argument later central to the literature of war. Its handling of printed report into reflection shows the late topographical voice turned to contemporary history.
works.meter: Stanzaic iambic verse of Cowper's late manner, with a solemn slow movement and much monosyllabic weight.
works.context: Written in 1789 on the printed accounts of the Russo-Turkish war and the storming of Ochakov, at the close of a decade in which Cowper was deeply interested in the news of Europe and in the morality of war; his late poems on the Russian campaigns and on the French Revolution belong to the same journalistic and providential imagination.
works.characters: The Russian general Bohoursky; the assailants and defenders of the town; the mediating poet
works.structure: A brief epitaphic meditation in continuous stanzas, moving from the notice of the death to the description of the assault and to the reflection on honour and pity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem's occasion is the printed account of the Russian general's death in the Russo-Turkish war, and its date rests on the printing of 1789.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Warfare and battle
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian
The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation

works.title: Bones of Contention
works.form: Short-story collection (the Cork of the childhood)
works.description: The collection of the Cork of the childhood and the quarrel. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Frank O'Connor; it belongs to The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bones of Contention gathers the stories of the Cork of O'Connor's childhood - the pub, the chapel, the quarrel of the families - in the spoken Irish-English of the teller who reports the decencies.
works.significance: Bones of Contention carried the Irish short story from the civil war into the city of the childhood: its Cork is the standard text of O'Connor's submerged population.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the single moral turn told in the spoken Irish-English.
works.context: Cork in the 1920s and 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: the publicans; the priests; the families of the quarrel
works.structure: A collection of city stories of the childhood. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Frank O'Connor, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Frank O'Connor is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Boniface's Letters
works.description: The correspondence of the missionary Boniface and his circle — some 150 letters exchanged with popes, kings, and above all the English friends and pupils who sustained his mission (Eadburga, Bugga, Leoba, Lull, Egbert of York): the most vivid documentary record of the Anglo-Saxon missions to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters carry the whole business of the German mission: requests for books and prayers, reports of synods and conversions, the felling of the sacred oak at Geismar, appeals for English nuns and scholars, consolations, and the last letters before the martyrdom at Dokkum (754); several are verse epistles with riddles for the nuns of Wessex.
works.significance: The richest source for the Anglo-Saxon missionary movement and for the literary culture of its female religious correspondents.
works.meter: Latin prose with verse epistles.
works.context: Written 716-754 from the mission field in Frisia and Germany; edited by M. Tangl, MGH Epistolae Selectae I (1916).
works.characters: Boniface; Lull; Leoba; Eadburga of Minster-in-Thanet; Bugga; Egbert of York; Daniel of Winchester; Pope Gregory II and III
works.structure: A correspondence of c. 150 letters, including letters addressed to Boniface.
works.attributionNotes: The core letters are Boniface's own; the collection includes his correspondents.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Boy
works.form: Novel; proletarian novel, first issued in 1931
works.description: The most brutal English novel of the thirties: a Liverpool boy, a ship and the sea. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by James Hanley; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Thirteen-year-old Francis Ferris is taken from his brutal father and sent to sea as a cabin boy; the voyage of the SS Trevithick through the Suez Canal to the Far East becomes an ordeal of beatings, hunger and sexual exploitation, and the novel ends with his death in a dockside brothel.
works.significance: Boy is the most brutal English novel of the thirties: its unsparing prose and its treatment of the working-class child at sea made it a landmark of the proletarian novel, and it was banned and prosecuted on publication.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, harsh, unadorned prose.
works.context: Liverpool and the merchant navy in the late 1920s, and the poverty of the English working class. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Francis Ferris; Mr Ferris; the captain; the crew of the SS Trevithick
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from Liverpool to the sea and the brothel. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Joseph Hanley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form
Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction

Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Sexuality, the new psychology, and the Freudian century
The Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march

works.title: Brave New World
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1932
works.description: The most influential English dystopia: a World State of engineered happiness, and the savage who cannot live in it. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Aldous Huxley; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In the World State of AF 632, human beings are bred in hatcheries and conditioned into five castes; pain, art, religion and family have been abolished, and happiness is administered in doses of 'soma'. Bernard Marx and Lenina Crowne bring back John the Savage from New Mexico, and he cannot accept the engineered happiness of the new world and is destroyed by it.
works.significance: Brave New World is the most influential English dystopia and one of the permanent books of the century: it invented the vocabulary — soma, conditioning, the feelies, the castes — in which the debate about technology and happiness is still conducted.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of ideas with a large cast and competing arguments.
works.context: Fordism and mass production, the eugenics movement, the psychology of conditioning, the Soviet Five-Year Plans, and the hedonism of the late 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; scientific romance and the utopian tale.
works.characters: Bernard Marx; Lenina Crowne; John the Savage; Linda; Mustapha Mond; Helmholtz Watson
works.structure: Eighteen chapters in three parts, from the World State to the Reservation and back. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Aldous Leonard Huxley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Brideshead Revisited: The Sacred and Profane Memories of Captain Charles Ryder
works.description: The great English elegy for the Catholic aristocracy: Charles Ryder, the Flyte family and Brideshead Castle. It is a prose fiction work of 1945 by Evelyn Waugh; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Charles Ryder, an officer in the Second World War, is billeted at Brideshead Castle and remembers his youth: his friendship with Sebastian Flyte at Oxford, his love for Sebastian's sister Julia, the decline of the Marquess of Marchmain and the family's Catholicism, and the slow return of grace that ends with the chapel lamp relit.
works.significance: Brideshead Revisited is the period's great elegy for the English Catholic aristocracy and one of the most loved novels in English: its portrait of Oxford, of the great house and of the workings of grace made it the century's most popular Catholic novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face.
works.context: Oxford in the 1920s, the English Catholic aristocracy, the country house, the 1930s and the Second World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1943 and 1944 and first published in 1945 and it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Charles Ryder; Sebastian Flyte; Julia Flyte; Lady Marchmain; Lord Marchmain; Cordelia Flyte; Anthony Blanche; Nanny Hawkins
works.structure: Book One (Et in Arcadia Ego) and Book Two (A Twitch upon the Thread), framed by a wartime prologue and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Evelyn St John Waugh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Brief Lives
works.description: John Aubrey's vast collection of biographical memoranda on the notable men of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — Bacon, Hobbes, Shakespeare, Donne, Milton, Harvey, and hundreds more — compiled as notes for Anthony Wood's Athenae Oxonienses and never published in his lifetime.
works.plot: The entries are informal, gossipy, and anecdotal, recording physical appearance, habits, sayings, and eccentricities alongside dates and facts, in Aubrey's own hurried hand with gaps and marginal queries.
works.significance: The most vivid and most human biographical source for seventeenth-century England; Aubrey's method of personal recollection and physical detail anticipates modern biography, and the Lives have been continuously read since their publication.
works.meter: Informal, hurried, anecdotal prose, often in note form.
works.context: Compiled chiefly between 1669 and 1696, partly for Anthony Wood; the manuscripts passed to the Bodleian and were first printed in part in 1813.
works.characters: Thomas Hobbes; William Shakespeare; John Milton; Francis Bacon; John Donne; William Harvey; Sir Walter Raleigh
works.structure: An alphabetical collection of biographical memoranda, many incomplete, with Aubrey's characteristic asterisks and queries.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Aubrey; the manuscripts are in his own hand.
themes: Melancholy and self-analysis
Patronage and the literary marketplace
The New Science and experimental philosophy
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Britannia
works.description: William Camden's chorographical description of Britain, published in Latin in 1586 and enlarged through six editions (the English translation by Philemon Holland appearing in 1610): the island's name, peoples, counties, towns, and antiquities — Roman, Saxon, and medieval — surveyed county by county in the work that founded English antiquarianism and taught the nation its own past.
works.plot: The book proceeds from the general description of Britain and its inhabitants through the counties of England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland: each county's etymology, history, noble families, and antiquities set down with the new documentary scholarship of the age.
works.significance: The founding work of British antiquarianism — the book that made the island's past a subject of systematic knowledge.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical elegance (translated by Holland into the full Elizabethan English of 1610).
works.context: First edition 1586, dedicated to Burghley; Camden's Britannia launched the great tradition of county histories and the Society of Antiquaries' programme, and its 1610 English version made the past accessible to the nation.
works.characters: Britain itself; the Britons, Romans, Saxons, and Normans; the noble families and antiquaries
works.structure: A chorography in the classical tradition (Ptolemy, Pausanias), organized geographically by county, with the apparatus of sources and the author's correspondence as its scholarly frame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the English translation of 1610 is Philemon Holland's.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Britannia (Thomson)
works.description: Thomson's patriotic poem, calling on the national spirit and the naval force of the island and urging that Britain's safety lies in the command of the sea and in the virtue of a free people.
works.plot: The poem summons the genius of the country, remembers its ancient and modern deliverances, and argues that the naval and commercial power of Britain is the instrument of her liberty against the ambition of the continent.
works.significance: It is one of the founding texts of the British naval-patriotic lyric, the immediate context of the odes on the rule of the ocean which the following years made national.
works.meter: The martial and anthem-like measures of the national ode, with the short stirring line and the recurring summons; the precise stanzaic scheme of the first issue is not asserted here.
works.context: Written in the years of the disputes over the navy and the commercial system that preceded the war of the Spanish succession, when the government's pacific economy was being attacked by the patriot writers in the language of the island's sea power.
works.characters: the genius of Britannia; the navy and the merchant; the threatened nation
works.structure: A continuous patriotic argument in the ode-like measures of the anthem, with the historical recollection and the direct address to the nation.
works.attributionNotes: Disambiguated in the title from Camden's LATIN Britannia already in this database; the poem here is Thomson's.

works.title: Brother Jonathan
works.form: Historical novel of the Revolutionary period; provincial comedy in romantic machinery
works.description: A historical novel of the Revolutionary war and of the Connecticut Yankee, published in Edinburgh at the height of its author's engagement with British romantic fiction. It takes the popular figure of the shrewd New Englander and puts him in the machinery of war, intrigue and border adventure. The book is an early study of provincial character as national character.
works.plot: Through the campaigns and privations of the war, a company of New Englanders and their British and Loyalist antagonists are drawn into a succession of surprises, disguises and escapes. The Yankee of the title turns his homely craft to the business of intelligence and survival, and the narrative treats his shrewdness at once as comedy and as a national capacity. Private feuds and family claims run under the public history until the war resolves them. The tale ends with the peace established and its characters changed by what the contest made them.
works.significance: It is the most elaborate of the antebellum novels to build a nation's character out of a provincial type. Its treatment of the Yankee as a form of knowledge anticipates later American comic realism. It documents the dependence of the American historical novel on Edinburgh.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1825 by the Edinburgh house that also issued the author's criticism, in the decade when British publishers took charge of American reputations. Its use of the Yankee type answers the English interest in American character after the war of 1812. The book belongs to the same burst of historical fiction as the author's other native romances.
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, episodic and heavily dependent on reported speech, interweaving military history with private intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature

works.title: Bucolic Comedies
works.description: The pastoral comedies of the chanted line after Façade. It is a verse work of 1923 by Edith Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bucolic Comedies carries the sound-pattern of Façade into the pastoral: the clown, the shepherd, the sun and the fountain of the baroque garden are the matter of the comic lyric, in the line of the spoken poem.
works.significance: Bucolic Comedies is the pastoral of the Façade manner and the proof that the chanted line could carry the comic set piece; it is the bridge between the early lyrics and the elegies of the 1930s.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
works.context: England in 1923, and the modernist pastoral. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.structure: A collection of comic pastorals in the chanted line. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Edith Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Burmese Days
works.description: Orwell's first novel and the great English novel of the empire: a colonial club in Burma and the rot at its heart. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by George Orwell; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: John Flory, a timber merchant in a small Burmese town, is a lonely, liberal Englishman with a Burmese mistress and a birthmark; he befriends the Indian doctor Veraswami and tries to prevent the elevation of the corrupt U Po Kyin to the club, but is destroyed by the racism, gossip and hypocrisy of the colonial community.
works.significance: Burmese Days is the great English novel of the empire and the finest thing Orwell wrote before his nonfiction: its portrait of the colonial club and its diagnosis of imperial racism made it the most honest English novel about the empire before A Passage to India's successors.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the plain declarative English sentence with no ornament.
works.context: British Burma in the 1920s, the colonial club, the timber trade, and the racial hierarchy of the empire. The record dates the work as composed in 1933 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: John Flory; Elizabeth Lackersteen; Veraswami; U Po Kyin; Ma Hla May; Mr Lackersteen
works.structure: Chronological third-person narrative in twenty-five chapters. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Bussy D'Ambois
works.description: Chapman's tragedy of heroic virtue at court: the poor gentleman Bussy d'Ambois, raised by the Duke of Anjou to the French court, defies the great, wins the love of the married Tamyra, and is destroyed by her husband Montsurry's trap — dying on his feet, propped against the wall, 'like a Roman' whose spirit cannot be killed.
works.plot: Bussy arrives at court in poverty and virtue, quarrels and triumphs with the courtiers, and is loved by Tamyra; the friar's conjuring reveals the affair to Montsurry; the revenge plot — the summoned spirits, the forced confession, the ambush — kills the friar and corners Bussy; his death speech turns defeat into apotheosis, and Tamyra's final letters close the tragedy.
works.significance: The great English tragedy of heroic self-assertion — the play in which the Renaissance individual asserts himself against the court and the stars.
works.meter: Chapman's dense, oracular blank verse — packed with stoic sententiae — reaching its height in Bussy's death speech.
works.context: Based on the historical Bussy (d. 1579) as reported in French chronicles; performed about 1604 and printed in 1607, with a revised text in 1641.
works.characters: Bussy d'Ambois; Tamyra; Montsurry; the Duke of Anjou (Monsieur); the King of France; the Guise; the Friar; Pero; Behemoth and the spirits
works.structure: A five-act Senecan tragedy of the heroic mode, with the friar's necromancy and the spirits (Behemoth and the rest) as its supernatural machinery.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher

works.title: Butcher's Broom
works.description: The historical novel of the Sutherland clearances. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Neil Gunn; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle.
works.plot: Butcher's Broom tells the clearances of Sutherland from the crofting township - the burning of the houses, the removal of the people, the sheep and the broom of the title - through the eyes of Mairi and the families of the strath, in the historical prose of the Scottish Renaissance at its most committed.
works.significance: Butcher's Broom is the Scottish Renaissance's novel of the clearances: it made the removal of the Gaelic people the central trauma of the modern Scottish novel and the standard against which the later clearance fiction is read.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain.
works.context: Sutherland in the years of the clearances, remembered from the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Mairi; the people of the strath; the factors and the improvers
works.structure: A historical novel of the clearances in the chapters of the township and the burning. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Neil Miller Gunn. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Cadences
works.description: The collection of the imagist years: the window, the street and the evening. It is a verse work of 1915 by F. S. Flint; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line.
works.plot: Cadences gathers Flint's imagist lyrics of the window, the street, the evening and the river, in the unrhymed cadence of the manifesto years, with the translations of the French poets beside the original poems.
works.significance: Cadences is the collection of Flint's imagist years and the record of the doctrine's first practice: its window, its street and its evening are the standard text of the English vers libre of 1915.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short unrhymed cadence of the French vers libre.
works.context: London in the war years, and the imagist little magazine. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.
works.structure: A collection of imagist lyrics and translations. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frank Stuart Flint. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Caelica
works.description: Fulke Greville's sequence of 109 short poems, written over some three decades: it begins as a Petrarchan sequence to 'Caelica' and 'Myra', then turns through political and philosophical verse to the great religious poems of renunciation ('Down in the depth of mine iniquity', 'Sion lies waste') with which it ends.
works.plot: The lover's courtship of Caelica gives way to meditations on the fall of princes, the vanity of earthly love, and the corruption of the will, until the final poems renounce the world for God.
works.significance: The bridge between the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and the metaphysical and devotional poetry of the next generation; its late religious poems rank with the greatest of the century.
works.meter: Varied short forms — songs, sonnets, and stanzaic meditations — in Greville's characteristically compressed, gnomic style.
works.context: Composed from the 1580s onward by the friend and biographer of Sidney, who served Elizabeth and James in high office; printed posthumously in the 1633 volume Certain Learned and Elegant Works.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Caelica; Myra; Cynthia
works.structure: A sequence in three movements — love, politics, religion — recording a lifelong spiritual itinerary.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Caesar's Column: A Story of the Twentieth Century
works.description: The great American dystopia of the 1890s: the class war and the coming tyranny. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Ignatius L. Donnelly; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Naturalist and Determinist Novel.
works.plot: Gabriel Weltstein, a European visitor, arrives in New York in 1988 to find a city of two nations in which a handful of plutocrats own everything and the rest live in the depths; the class war destroys the city and the Brotherhood of Destruction builds a column of bodies, before the survivors found a better order in Africa.
works.significance: Caesar's Column is the great American dystopia of the 1890s and the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century anti-utopia: its vision of class war, the modern metropolis and the totalitarian mob made it a populist bestseller and a central text of the American protest novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the future history narrated from a later age.
works.context: The United States of the Gilded Age, the labour wars of 1886 and 1892, and the populist movement of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Gabriel Weltstein; Caesar Lomellini; the Brotherhood of Destruction; the Prince
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the arrival to the fall of the city and the return. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ignatius Donnelly. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Cain
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Closet drama and mystery in blank verse; the biblical re-visioning of the school of the older visionary drama, with the chorus and the spectacular ascent of the older religious play.
works.description: A dramatic mystery in two acts which rewrites the first murder as a story of knowledge and disobedience rather than of jealousy. The spirit of the day-star, Lucifer, takes the first ploughman to the spaces beyond the earth and shows him the eternity of the world and the emptiness of the worship demanded of his family; when the accepted offering is refused and the brother slain, Cain is marked and sent out over the eastern land. The poem was read as an attack on providence and became one of the most denounced texts of its year.
works.plot: The family of the first parents, driven from the garden and labouring under a law of offering, are divided in their temper, the elder impatient of a worship whose violence he cannot praise. Lucifer, who refuses adoration and is therefore exiled, teaches him the history of the earth's former ages and the procession of spirits, and shows that the deity who claims his brother's fleece is one among powers, not the maker of all. The offering of the fruit is despised and the favored brother killed at the altar of stone; Cain, questioned by the voice from the cherubim, replies that he is his brother's keeper only in the sense the murderer is, and is marked and condemned to wander, while his wife is promised that the fruit of her womb shall not be cut off. The argument is that obedience to a demanded sacrifice, not the act of murder, is the origin of the world's guilt.
works.significance: It is the Romantic period's most influential rewriting of the Cain story and a central document of the poetry of secular questioning, the text by which the charge of a Satanic school was made concrete for a generation of readers. Its elevation of disobedient knowledge over demanded sacrifice was answered by the devout poets of the later century and its machinery, and its two-act design became a model for the modern closet mystery.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines for the dialogue, with lyric hymns and choruses in short measures; the manner is deliberately plain and close to the speech of the English version of scripture.
works.context: Written at Ravenna between January and May 1821, in the season of the Neapolitan and Piedmontese uprisings and their suppression and of the quarrels over the theology of the age, and published in the same December in a single volume with two other dramatic poems. Its treatment of the fall and of the acceptability of sacrifice was taken as a defence of infidelity by the quarterly and religious press, and the volume's own preface, in which the poet affected to be astonished at the offense, deepened the attack.
works.characters: the first ploughman; his sacrificed brother; their mother; Lucifer, the spirit of the day-star; the archangel of the flaming sword; the chosen bride of the wanderer
works.structure: Two acts of dramatic dialogue with chorus, opened by an address to the morning star and closed by a vision of the coming race; the scene shifts from the tent and altar to the high place of the world and back.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume containing it appeared without its author's own preface of advice, and the text was lightly revised in the collected editions.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: Cakes and Ale
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1930
works.description: The finest English satire of the literary life: the truth about a great novelist and his two wives. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by W. Somerset Maugham; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The narrator, a writer named Ashenden, is asked to write a memoir of the recently dead novelist Edward Driffield; he remembers the provincial boy, the barmaid Rosie who was Driffield's first wife, and the literary establishment that has made him a monument.
works.significance: Cakes and Ale is the finest English satire of the literary life and Maugham's own favourite among his novels: its portrait of Rosie Driffield and its demolition of literary reputation made it a permanent comedy of the writer's world and a scandal on publication.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrator who listens rather than judges.
works.context: London and the Kent and Essex coast in the 1880s and 1920s, and the English literary establishment. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Ashenden; Edward Driffield; Rosie Driffield; Amy Driffield; Alroy Kear; George Kemp
works.structure: A first-person memoir in six chapters, moving between the 1880s and the present. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Somerset Maugham. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Calisto and Melebea
altTitles: A New Comedy in English in Manner of an Interlude
works.description: An anonymous English adaptation of the first four acts of Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, printed by John Rastell c. 1525–30; the first English version of the Spanish classic.
works.plot: Calisto, rejected by Melibea, seeks the help of the old bawd Celestina, who wins the lady for him by her arts; the fragment (the play survives incomplete) follows the first movement of Rojas's tragicomedy through the lovers' meeting, ending before the deaths that close the original.
works.significance: The first English adaptation of the Celestina and an early witness to Anglo-Spanish literary exchange; it extends the range of the interlude to tragicomic romance and anticipates the Elizabethan stage's use of continental fiction.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1525–30, probably by John Rastell, whose press had connections to the Spanish trade through the More circle (More's daughter married into the Rastell family, and Vives was in England); the Celestina, the great Spanish masterpiece of 1499, was thus introduced to English readers a generation before Mabbe's full translation.
works.characters: Calisto; Melibea; Celestina; Sempronio; Parmeno
works.structure: A scene-by-scene dramatization of the opening of the Celestina, compressed into interlude form, with the bawd's character preserved in translation.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named; the play has been attributed to John Rastell on the evidence of the press and the More circle's Spanish connections, but the attribution is conjectural.

works.title: Campaspe
works.description: Lyly's court comedy of the painter's triumph: Alexander the Great, in love with his captive Campaspe, commissions her portrait from the painter Apelles — who falls in love with her himself; the emperor, discovering the mutual love, renounces her and gives the couple his blessing, proving himself 'Alexander' in magnanimity as in conquest.
works.plot: Alexander's philosophers (Diogenes in his tub, Plato, Aristotle) and generals debate around the love affair; Apelles paints and conceals his love; the courtiers' plots to part the lovers fail; and the play ends with Alexander's renunciation and the painter's marriage, the emperor's 'discipline' the play's moral.
works.significance: The first English high comedy of the court — the play that founded the elegant, debating tradition Jonson and the Restoration inherited.
works.meter: Prose throughout — the Euphuistic manner transferred to the stage — with the songs of the finale.
works.context: Performed before Elizabeth I by the Children of Paul's and the Chapel children on the same day (1 January 1584) in the 'battle of the theatres' between the two boy companies; printed the same year.
works.characters: Alexander; Campaspe; Apelles; Diogenes; Plato; Aristotle; Hephestion; Parmenio; Manes; Psyllus; the pages
works.structure: A five-act classical comedy on the Italian model, built of debate scenes — the philosophers' wit, the generals' counsel — with the painter's studio as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Can Such Things Be?
works.description: Published in 1893 and the best American collection of supernatural tales of the century: twenty-four stories of ghosts, revenants and inexplicable events. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by Ambrose Bierce; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories include 'The Damned Thing', in which an invisible creature kills a man in the California hills, 'The Death of Halpin Frayser', in which a man is murdered by his mother's corpse, and 'The Moonlit Road', in which a murder is narrated three times from three points of view.
works.significance: Can Such Things Be? is the finest American supernatural collection of the period and the central book of American weird fiction before Lovecraft: its invisible monster, its corpse-bride and its multiple narration made it a founding text of the American weird tale, and Lovecraft named Bierce as one of his masters.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. works.title: Candida
works.description: Written in 1894 and performed in 1897: the most accomplished of Shaw's early plays, a comedy about a wife, a clergyman and the poet who loves her. It is a dramatic work of 1894 by George Bernard Shaw; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Candida Morell, the wife of a Christian Socialist clergyman, is loved by the young poet Eugene Marchbanks; she is forced to choose between them and chooses her husband, not out of weakness but because he is the weaker of the two and needs her, while the poet is left to go alone.
works.significance: Candida is the finest of Shaw's early comedies and one of the great English plays about marriage: its treatment of the wife as the strongest person in the house and its rejection of both the romantic and the sentimental view of love made it a classic of the modern stage.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1894: the Christian Socialist movement, the New Woman debate, and the cult of the poet as the superior being. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and first performed in 1897 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Candida Morell; the Reverend James Mavor Morell; Eugene Marchbanks; Proserpine Garnett ('Prossy'); Mr Burgess, Candida's father; the Reverend Alexander Mill ('Lexy')
works.structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Cane
works.description: The most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance: a collage of the Black South and the urban North. It is a prose fiction work of 1923 by Jean Toomer; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cane moves from the Georgia cane fields — 'Karintha', 'Fern', 'Esther', 'Blood-Burning Moon' — through the poems and prose of the migration north to Washington and Chicago, and ends with 'Kabnis', a play of a Northern Black teacher in the South.
works.significance: Cane is the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts: its collage of story, poem and drama, its lyric prose and its structure from South to North made it the only major book of the movement as formally advanced as Ulysses or The Waste Land.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the collage of genres (story, poem, drama) in a single book.
works.context: Sparta, Georgia, where Toomer taught in 1921, and the Black migration to Washington and Chicago; the Harlem Renaissance and the new modernist art. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.

works.structure: Three parts: the Georgia South, the urban North, and the play 'Kabnis'. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: Cannery Row
works.form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1945
works.description: Steinbeck's pastoral of the Depression: the Monterey street and its community of the poor. It is a prose fiction work of 1945 by John Steinbeck; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The novel follows the inhabitants of Cannery Row in Monterey — Doc, the marine biologist, Mack and the boys, Dora Flood and the Bear Flag Restaurant — through a series of episodes that make a community out of the poor and the odd.
works.significance: Cannery Row is Steinbeck's pastoral of the Depression and one of his finest books: its community of the poor, its comedy and its tenderness made it the great American novel of the marginal community and the source of the modern Californian literary landscape.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail of the migrant road.
works.context: Monterey, California, in the 1930s, and the cannery district of the Depression. The record dates the work as composed between 1944 and 1945 and first published in 1945 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; comic novel and the satire of manners.
