works.title: Captain Blood
works.form: Novel; historical novel, first issued in 1922
works.description: The greatest pirate novel: a doctor transported to slavery becomes a buccaneer. It is a prose fiction work of 1922 by Rafael Sabatini; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Peter Blood, an Irish physician in England, is condemned to slavery in Barbados for treating a rebel, escapes with the other slaves, and becomes the most famous buccaneer of the Caribbean, in the greatest pirate novel ever written.
works.significance: Captain Blood is the greatest pirate novel ever written: its doctor-turned-buccaneer, its sea fights and its romance made Sabatini's reputation and created the modern pirate hero, and it has never been out of print.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the swashbuckling hero and the duel.
works.context: England and the Caribbean in the 1680s. The record dates the work as composed between 1921 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Peter Blood; Arabella Bishop; Lord Willoughby; Levasseur; Jeremy Pitt
works.structure: A sea novel of slavery, escape and buccaneering in the Caribbean. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rafael Sabatini (Scaramouche). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Caractacus: A Dramatic Poem
works.form: Dramatic poem / closet tragedy with a strong lyrical and descriptive element; regular acts; printed with prefatory and dedicatory matter and with the author's account of the subject's sources.
works.description: Mason's most admired tragedy, and a work he labelled a 'dramatic poem' rather than a play, partly because it was written for a circle of subscribers and for the reader's theatre as much as for the pit. Its subject is the British chief Caractacus, defeated by Rome, carried in chains to Italy and displayed in triumph before the emperor, and there outdoing his captors in the dignity with which he speaks of liberty and of his country. The machinery of Druids and of British superstition gives the poem its religious and sublimer colour.
works.plot: The action is built on the collision between Roman imperial splendour and captive British virtue. Caractacus, having lost his kingdom in the field, keeps his sovereignty in the language he uses at Rome, refusing the concessions that would make his captivity comfortable. Around him the poem arranges the expected attachments of love and friendship, and the Druidic element supplies prophecy, sacred grove and solemn rite, all of which Mason treats as a national priesthood of great moral elevation. The dramatic interest is thereby concentrated not in the plot but in the set-piece of the conquered man before the conqueror, where the language of liberty is spoken with a force the contemporary reader recognised as the sublimity of unrhymed verse achieved.
works.significance: For decades it was the standard example of modern English blank verse and of the patriotic 'British' subject treated in elevated measure, and it was praised for exactly that by later critics of the poetical revival. It also became a schoolroom and elocutionary text, and its Druidical machinery is a notable stage in the eighteenth-century imaginative recovery of the Celtic past.
works.meter: Blank verse of a carefully modulated kind, with short sententious lines for declamation and longer, more rhythmic periods for the Druidical and descriptive passages; Mason's practice here was commonly cited by later editors of the blank-verse controversy as evidence that unrhymed measure could be made 'musical'.
works.context: Published in the year after the fall of Quebec, when British patriotic feeling and the cult of ancient 'British' liberty were unusually available to a poet, and in the middle of the critical debate about dramatic measure. Mason composed it largely in private and issued it by subscription, a publishing route that let a clergyman-poet keep the dignity of the work independent of theatrical managers.
works.characters: Caractacus; the Druids of the British grove; the court of the emperor Claudius at Rome
works.structure: A five-act dramatic poem whose movement is episodic rather than tightly plotted, rising to the Roman triumph and the audience with the emperor as its rhetorical centre.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem carries Mason's name in the first edition and its making is documented in his correspondence and in his later collected edition. Its first stage representation, whenever it came, is not asserted here.

works.title: Carew's Poems
works.description: The posthumous collection of Thomas Carew's lyrics (1640), including 'A Song: Ask Me No More', 'The Spring', 'The Primrose', and the celebrated elegy 'Upon the Death of the Dean of Paul's, Dr John Donne', which praised Donne for purging poetry of 'th'hyperboles' and is a key document of the metaphysical transition.

works.context: Published in 1640, shortly after Carew's death, by his friend Thomas Walkley; it established his reputation as the finest of the Caroline wits.

works.title: Carmilla
works.description: Published in the collection In a Glass Darkly in 1872 and the founding text of the lesbian vampire narrative: the story of a young woman in Styria who is visited by a beautiful guest who is not alive.
works.plot: Laura, the daughter of a retired Austrian officer, is visited as a child and then as a young woman by Carmilla, who is in fact the revenant of the Countess Mircalla Karnstein; Laura weakens, a peasant girl dies, and Baron Vordenburg traces the vampire to the ruined chapel of Karnstein, where she is destroyed.
works.significance: Carmilla is the most influential vampire story before Dracula and the origin of the female vampire in English literature; its treatment of an intense attachment between two women has made it the founding text of the queer Gothic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is the 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor.
works.context: The 1870s, the Austrian frontier and its folklore, the Gothic tradition of the vampire from Polidori, and the Victorian medical discourse on hysteria. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. works.title: Caroling Dusk
works.description: The defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance: thirty-eight Black poets, from Dunbar to the young writers of the 1920s. It is a verse work of 1927 by Countee Cullen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cullen's anthology gathers thirty-eight African American poets — Paul Laurence Dunbar, James Weldon Johnson, Claude McKay, Langston Hughes, Jean Toomer, Arna Bontemps, Georgia Douglas Johnson, Angelina Weld Grimké and others — with a preface defending the use of the inherited English forms.
works.significance: Caroling Dusk is the defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance and the book that fixed its canon: Cullen's preface made the case for the English tradition against Hughes's folk programme, and the anthology remains the essential collection of the movement's poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is an anthology, the pieces ordered by the editor. The author's characteristic manner is the strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave.
works.context: The Harlem Renaissance of 1925–27 and the debate over whether Black poetry should use the folk tradition or the English lyric. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem; critical essay and the modern review.
works.structure: An anthology of thirty-eight poets with biographical notes. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.

works.title: Carols from the Coal-Fields
works.description: Published in 1886 and the best selection of Skipsey's poems: lyrics of the pit, elegies for the killed miners, songs of the Northumbrian coast, and the ballads of poverty and self-education. It is a verse work of 1886 by Joseph Skipsey; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection includes 'The Collier's Lad', 'The Dead Miner', 'The Old Pitman', 'Golden Hair', 'The Lonely Death' and 'A Memory', and its subjects are the pit, the cottage, the sea and the dead.
works.significance: Carols from the Coal-Fields is the finest single volume of English miner poetry and a key text in the literature of the working class: it preserves the voice of the Northumbrian pitman and the elegy for the dead miner in a way that no middle-class writer could.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is plain ballad stanzas and simple lyric metres.
works.context: The 1880s, the northern coalfield, the mining disasters of the 1860s-80s, and the self-taught literary culture of the miners' institutes. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Carrots: Just a Little Boy
works.description: Published in 1876 and Molesworth's first great success: the story of a small boy in a large family, his nursery, his sisters and his small adventures. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by Mary Louisa Molesworth; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
works.plot: Carrots, the youngest of a family of children, is often overlooked and often naughty; the novel follows his games, his illnesses and his relations with his sisters and the servants, and ends with his growing up into a schoolboy.
works.significance: Carrots established Molesworth as the leading children's writer of realistic family fiction and is a key source for the social history of the Victorian nursery; its child's-eye realism was a decisive break with the moral tale of the earlier century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unhurried narrative.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian middle-class nursery, and the vogue for realistic family stories after Ewing. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Carrots; Floss, his sister
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: Casa Guidi Windows
works.form: Two-part political poem in blank verse
works.description: Published in 1851 and written in the apartment in Florence whose windows look on the streets of the 1847-49 revolution: a poem in two parts on Italian liberty, the failure of the 1848-49 risings and the continued hope of the Risorgimento.
works.plot: Part I records the civic festivals of 1847 and the hopes of an Italian nation; Part II, written after the defeat of the Roman Republic and the flight of the Grand Duke, refuses despair and calls on the Italian people to renew the struggle.
works.significance: Casa Guidi Windows is the finest English poem of the Italian Risorgimento and a major political statement by a woman poet; it broke with the Victorian convention that women's poetry should be domestic and established the public, prophetic voice that Murat and the later poets of liberation emulated.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
works.context: The 1847-49 Italian revolutions, the flight of Grand Duke Leopold II from Florence, the fall of the Roman Republic in 1849, and the English liberal sympathy for Italy that shaped the Brownings' Florentine years.
works.structure: A single poem, read as one continuous whole from its opening to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Castle Rackrent
works.form: Comic chronicle-novel and character tale; the first of the national tales, an estate history told in servant's Hibernian-English.
works.description: The first Irish national novel and one of the earliest great uses of an unreliable vernacular narrator: the hereditary steward of a long-descended family tells, with unshakable loyalty, the history of the four or five squires who wasted his master's estate. It is a comic chronicle of absenteeism, gaming, lawyers, electioneering and imprudent improvement, closing on the Act of Union. Its prefatory memoir and its explanatory glossary of Hibernian terms, both supplied by an editor, place the tale at a deliberate historical distance from its readers.
works.plot: Thady Quirk, born on the estate and servant to four generations, reports the successive squires: the easy first squire, who quarrelled with his brother and died; the next, whose extravagance and whose family's intrigue over an heiress and an elopement brought in lawyers; the lawyer squire, a devout bigot who worried his tenants with process; the dissolute absentee; and finally the improving and popular last squire, whose well-meant schemes of cultivation, his marriage to an Englishwoman, and the machinations of Thady's own son about the deeds, consume the property. The family's representative votes for Union, the estate passes out of the name, and the steward dies unprosperous but content.
works.significance: Founded the national tale and the Big House novel, and set the pattern of the loyal partisan narrator whose testimony the reader must reconstruct. It is the earliest extended use of Irish vernacular speech as the governing medium of an English novel, and a standard document for the history of the absentee estate. Its framing apparatus made it a model for the edited and annotated tale.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a sustained Irish vernacular voice, with proverb, biblical tag and law-phrase, and an explanatory glossary of Hibernian-English.
works.context: Written in the years after the 1798 rising and published in the year of the Act of Union, its subject is the Irish Ascendancy's management of land, law and loyalty. The tale's distance from contemporary politics is itself political: it treats the misgovernment of Ireland as a social comedy of manners and tenures. Its authorship grew out of household education and of the publisher's demand for improvement literature, and it was read as an explanation of the Union to an English public.
works.characters: Thady Quirk, the steward-narrator; the successive squires of Castle Rackrent, from the first squire to the improving last; Constantia, an injured heiress of the family; Kit Corry, her eloping lover; Myrtle, the English wife of the last squire; the Editor of the memoir
works.structure: First-person memoir by the steward, edited and annotated by a scholarly 'Editor' who supplies a family memoir before and a note after the narrative; chronological by squire, with dialect glosses and documentary intrusions (leases, bills, an oath).
works.attributionNotes: The first edition carried the attribution to the author of an earlier pedagogical work rather than a name; authorship has never been in doubt.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales

works.title: Cathay
works.description: The most influential translation-poem of the century: versions of Chinese poetry made through the Fenollosa notebooks. It is a verse work of 1915 by Ezra Pound; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Pound's nineteen poems — 'The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter', 'The Jewel Stairs' Grievance', 'Lament of the Frontier Guard', 'South-Folk in Cold Country' — translate classical Chinese poetry through the notes of Ernest Fenollosa, creating a new English lyric of dramatic situation, precise image and withheld feeling.
works.significance: Cathay invented the modern translation-poem and gave English poetry a new idiom: its clean lines and dramatic situations made it the model for twentieth-century translation, and 'The River-Merchant's Wife' is one of the great English poems of the period.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the image as the unit of the poem.
works.context: The Fenollosa notebooks, the Chinese poetry that had reached the West through the Imagist movement, and the First World War, during which the poems were written. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.
works.characters: The river-merchant's wife; the frontier guard
works.structure: Nineteen poems translated from the Chinese, in free verse. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ezra Loomis Pound. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Catherine of Siena
works.form: Biography; review essay, first issued in 1879
works.description: Published in 1879 and Butler's best-known book after the campaign pamphlets: a life of the fourteenth-century Dominican tertiary who intervened in the politics of the papacy and the Italian city-states.
works.plot: The biography follows Catherine Benincasa from her childhood visions in Siena through her work among the plague-stricken, her letters to popes and princes, her campaign for the return of the papacy from Avignon to Rome, and her death in 1380.
works.significance: Butler's Catherine of Siena made the medieval woman mystic a model for the Victorian woman reformer and is one of the most influential Victorian lives of a woman saint; it showed the suffrage movement that the public woman had a long history.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is prophetic, impassioned oratory in print.
works.context: The 1870s, the Catholic revival, the new interest in medieval mysticism, and the women's movement's search for a female tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.characters: Catherine Benincasa (St Catherine of Siena); Pope Gregory XI; Pope Urban VI; Raymond of Capua; Niccolò di Toldo
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Josephine Elizabeth Butler. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Catholic Homilies
altTitles: Ælfric's Catholic Homilies, First and Second Series
works.description: Ælfric's two series of forty sermons for the church year (c. 989-995), the masterpiece of Old English prose: orthodox, elegantly plain expositions of the gospel readings, written in the rhythmical alliterative style and prefaced by a Latin preface deploring the doctrinal errors of the anonymous homiletic tradition. The most widely copied vernacular preaching text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: Each homily expounds the pericope of the day with patristic learning made lucid for the laity — the feasts of Christ and the saints, the parables, the miracles — carefully distinguishing orthodox doctrine from apocryphal excess; the two series together provide a complete homiletic cycle for the year in the order of the liturgical calendar.
works.significance: The summit of the Old English homiletic tradition and the foundation of standard literary Old English.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of Ælfric's mature 'plain style'.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 989-995 at the request of the ealdorman Æthelweard and his son Æthelmær; over thirty manuscripts and fragments survive.
works.characters: Christ; the saints of the calendar
works.structure: Two series of forty homilies each, organized by the church year; each homily opens with the gospel text in English and proceeds by exegesis, exemplum, and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Benedictine Reform

works.title: Cato
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: Addison's serious tragedy of the last days of Cato of Utica, written as a demonstration that regular neoclassical drama in blank verse could teach Stoic virtue and resignation to providence. It was the most acted, read and imitated English tragedy of the first half of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: After Thapsus the defeated Cato refuses Caesar's clemency and holds Utica; his friend Lucilius dies by poison in a scene of Stoic obedience, the treachery of Sempronius is exposed, and Juba's suit for Marcia fails; Cato secures the safety of those about him, reconciles public liberty with resignation to providence, and kills himself, the catastrophe being reported rather than shown.
works.significance: It fixed for a generation the model of the rational moral tragedy and made Roman liberty and Christian resignation a national schoolroom exemplum, admired across party lines, imitated on the stage and in the closet, and answered by the later tragedy of feeling.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat blank verse of the moderated post-Dryden line, with balanced antithetical periods and sententious closures; the speeches are built as declamatory rhetorical units.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in the spring of 1713, during the party struggle over the peace settlement, when the theatre was an arena of political interpretation; the play was praised in The Tatler in the season of its first performance, and the rival Whig and Tory press each claimed it.
works.characters: Cato; Caesar; Lucilius; Sempronius; Marcia; Juba
works.structure: Five-act regular tragedy closely observing the unities of time, place and action, moving from the council at Utica through the discovery of the conspiracy to the protagonist's suicide and its reportage.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Addison's authorship is documented by his own publication and by contemporary correspondence.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: Cautionary Tales for Children
works.description: The funniest children's verse in English: Jim, Matilda and the consequences of bad behaviour. It is a verse work of 1907 by Hilaire Belloc; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Belloc's verses tell the fates of children who disobey: Jim, who is eaten by a lion, Matilda, who tells lies and is burned to death, Henry King, who chews string, and Rebecca, who slams doors, each with an illustration by Basil Blackwood.
works.significance: Cautionary Tales for Children made the comic moral poem a permanent English form and is the funniest children's verse in English: its deadpan catastrophes and its perfect couplets gave the language 'Matilda' and 'Jim' and have never been bettered.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the comic moral tale in regular verse.
works.context: Edwardian England and the nursery of the period. The record dates the work as composed in 1907 and first published in 1907 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; children's fantasy and the golden-age tale.
works.characters: Jim; Matilda; Henry King; Rebecca; George; Algernon
works.structure: A collection of comic cautionary verses with illustrations. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hilaire Pierre Rene Belloc. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Cavalcade
works.description: Coward's pageant of English life from the Boer War to 1930: the Marryot family and the century. It is a dramatic work of 1931 by Noel Coward; it is catalogued here under Melodrama and Nautical Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The play follows the Marryot family and their servants, the Bridges, from New Year's Eve 1899 to New Year's Eve 1929, through the Boer War, the Titanic, the First World War and the General Strike, ending with a vision of England's future.
works.significance: Cavalcade was the greatest popular success of the thirties' theatre and the period's most ambitious attempt to put the national experience on the stage: its film version won the Academy Award for Best Picture, and its final scene remains one of the most famous in English drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose or verse: the dialogue carries the whole, and the text is written for performance. The author's characteristic manner is the epigram and the witty exchange.
works.context: The Boer War, the Titanic, the First World War, the General Strike and the Depression, seen from a single London household. The record dates the work as composed in 1930 and first published in 1931 and first performed in 1931 and it is catalogued under melodrama and nautical drama.
works.characters: Jane Marryot; Robert Marryot; Alfred Bridges; Ellen Bridges; Fanny Bridges; Joe Marryot; Edward Marryot
works.structure: Two parts, twenty-two scenes, from 1899 to 1929. The play is divided into acts and scenes, the dialogue carrying the whole of the action.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Noël Pierce Coward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Cecil
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The silver-fork novel at its most expert: a dandy, a fortune and the fashionable world. It is a prose fiction work of 1841 by Catherine Gore; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cecil Danby, a beautiful and heartless young man of fashion, makes his way through London society in pursuit of an heiress, in a novel of drawing rooms, epigrams and the precise observation of the aristocracy.
works.significance: Cecil was the most popular of Gore's silver-fork novels and the finest English comedy of fashionable life of the 1830s: its dandy, its epigrams and its precise observation of the aristocracy made it the model of the fashionable novel and a direct ancestor of Thackeray.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the fashionable assembly and the great house.
works.context: London in the 1830s, the fashionable world of the Reform era and the fashionable novel. The record dates the work as composed between 1840 and 1841 and first published in 1841 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; sensation novel.
works.characters: Cecil Danby; the heiress; the dowager; the dandy's friends
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, following the dandy through society. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Catherine Grace Frances Gore. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Cecilia; or, Memoirs of an Heiress
works.form: novel of manners and of the marriage market
works.description: The history of an heiress whose fortune makes her the property of everyone who desires it, and who is worn between the claims of several marriages and the demands of a society that cannot conceive of a woman with money acting for herself. It is the broadest and most public of the author's novels, ending in a catastrophe the century's readers thought severe.
works.plot: Cecilia Beverley, left an estate on condition that her husband take the name, is courted by a lawyer of merit and by a young fellow of fashion, while her guardians consult their own interest in the choice. She is carried to Bristol and into the companies of the town, is drawn into a friend's distress and loses money at the card table through the artifice of a designing relation. She at last accepts the suit of the man she had undervalued, and his death from a wound received in defence of her reputation exposes the world that destroyed him. The novel closes on her renunciation of society and her retirement, the heiress having purchased her independence at the price of every attachment.
works.significance: It is the most complete analysis of the position of the propertied woman in the fiction of the century before the age of its author's rivals, and its argument about independence shaped the later novel of women's circumstance.
works.meter: An ample, reflective third-person prose with the free indirect report of the heroine's opinion, and the epistolary and conversational set pieces of the earlier novel retained in modified form.
works.context: Published by subscription in 1782, in the season of the debates on women's property, the law of marriage and the influence of the fashionable circle; its author was by then a recognised novelist and a member of the Bluestocking society.
works.characters: Cecilia Beverley; Mr. Belfield; the young man of fashion; her guardians and their families; Madame de Burgh; the friends of the town and of Bristol
works.structure: Third-person narration in five or six volumes, with the heroine's consciousness reported rather than voiced, and a public plot of debts, assemblies and the law; the conclusion is a retirement rather than a marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the anonymous first novel, the issue by subscription being recorded in its own lists.

works.title: Celestina
works.form: Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
works.description: Charlotte Smith's third published novel, following Emmeline and Ethelinde, and the first of the fictions she wrote after her husband's imprisonment and her life apart from him had made her the family's breadwinner; it appeared in four volumes in 1791. It follows a young woman raised and disposed of by guardians who are not her parents, and traces the discovery of her true birth, her education in sensibility and principle, and her marriage, against a social analysis of inherited property, paternal authority, and the limited options of women. Its Alpine scenery and its portrait of an aristocratic French household on the eve of 1789 give the domestic plot a political breadth unusual in fiction of the moment.
works.plot: Celestina, a young woman brought up in a household not her own and made the object of other people's financial and social calculations, is kept from knowing her parents and from choosing her own marriage; the novel recounts her long separation from the man she loves, the exposure of the interests that govern her fortune, and the eventual recovery of a lawful birth and of the marriage her inclinations had always marked out. The action is continuously interrupted by argument on the injustice of disposing of wards and heiresses in marriage, on the abuse of guardianship and of paternal authority, and on the idleness and corruption of great wealth, with set-piece passages among the Alps and in France before and after 1789.
works.significance: Celestina established Smith as a novelist of property and feeling whose domestic plots conduct explicit argument about coverture, guardianship, and the marriage market; it opened the sequence of her fictions that later criticism reads as a sustained analysis of women's economic dependence, and its Alpine and pre-revolutionary French settings anticipated the political geography of her later novels.
works.meter: Prose romance in regular paragraphing; no metrical design is present, though the narrative's address to the reader and its set-piece descriptions of mountain scenery are shaped by the cadences of Smith's own sonnet prose.
works.context: Written and published in the years of Smith's separation from Benjamin Smith and of her increasing reliance on the press, and in the immediate aftermath of 1789, when French aristocratic society was being reinterpreted in Britain as a system of abuse. Its treatment of guardianship and of the disposition of an heiress draws on the family litigations and Chancery dependency that had consumed Smith's adulthood.
works.characters: Celestina; the heroine's guardian and the interests that control her fortune; the man she loves and is long denied; the French aristocratic household of the Alpine and Parisian episodes
works.structure: A four-volume novel of formation in the third person, organized around the slow revelation of the heroine's parentage, with embedded letters and tale-within-tale passages, and a double setting that carries the plot from England and the Savoyard and Alpine country to France on the eve of the Revolution.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name on the title page; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Cely Letters
works.description: The business correspondence of the Cely family, London wool merchants of the Staple of Calais, 1472–88: some 250 letters and papers recording the wool trade, shipping, politics, and daily life of a merchant family in the age of Edward IV and Richard III. The most vivid surviving record of English commercial life in the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The letters pass between the brothers Robert, Richard, and George Cely in London and Calais and their factors, recording the buying and shipping of wool, prices and freights, news of the wars in France and at home (including the fall of Richard III), and the family's hunting, hawking, and domestic affairs.
works.significance: The classic document of fifteenth-century English commerce and the merchant's English, complementing the Paston archive's gentry perspective.
works.meter: Prose: brisk, practical mercantile English, of great linguistic value.
works.context: Written 1472–88, when the Celys' Calais staple stood at the centre of England's wool economy; discovered in 1860 among the family's papers and edited by H. E. Malden (1900).
works.characters: George Cely; Richard Cely the elder and younger; William Maryon; the Calais factors
works.structure: A documentary archive of business correspondence, chronological in arrangement, spanning sixteen years.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (family and factors); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.

works.title: Centuries of Thankfulness
works.description: Thomas Traherne's great mystical prose meditations — four 'centuries' of numbered paragraphs celebrating God's goodness, the soul's felicity, and the wonder of creation as apprehended by an innocent eye — unpublished in his lifetime and discovered and printed only in the early twentieth century.
works.plot: The Centuries argue that true happiness consists in rightly valuing and enjoying God's creation, recover the infant soul's vision of infinity, and exhort gratitude and thanksgiving as the path to felicity.
works.significance: The Centuries are a unique achievement in English mystical prose, anticipating Romantic celebrations of childhood vision and influencing later spiritual and literary writers.
works.meter: Rhapsodic, cumulative, rhythmic prose of wonder, with visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood.
works.context: Written in the early 1670s and left in manuscript; misattributed to Henry Vaughan until Bertram Dobell acquired and published them in 1908, revealing a major unknown mystic.
works.characters: the soul; God; the self in childhood
works.structure: Four 'centuries' of 100 numbered meditative paragraphs each (partly incomplete), forming a cumulative rhapsody of wonder and thanksgiving.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested once Dobell established Traherne's authorship; the manuscripts were long misattributed to Vaughan.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Creation and cosmology
Divine love and holy desire

works.title: Chains
works.description: The landmark realist play of the lower middle class. It is a dramatic work of 1909 by Elizabeth Baker; it belongs to Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre and it is catalogued here under Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: A clerk and his wife, living in the suburb in the chains of the office and the marriage, dream of Australia and escape; the play that made the obscure office typist one of the most discussed playwrights in England and remains the landmark realist drama of the lower middle class.
works.significance: Chains is Baker's landmark realist play of the lower middle class: its suburb, its clerk and its dream of Australia made the office typist one of the most discussed playwrights in England.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact dialogue of the clerk and the shopgirl.
works.context: The London suburb and the clerk's office in 1909. The record dates the work as composed between 1908 and 1909 and first published in 1909 and first performed in 1909 and the corpus places it within Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre, it is catalogued under suffrage play and the woman's drama; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Charlie Wilson; Ethel Wilson; their children; the office
works.structure: Three acts, in the suburban house and its chains. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Baker. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Chamber Music
works.description: Joyce's early lyric sequence: Elizabethan-style songs of love and loss, written before the great prose. It is a verse work of 1907 by James Joyce; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The thirty-six poems follow a loose sequence of love, courtship, parting and loss in the manner of the Elizabethan songbook and the Irish lyric — the work of the young poet who would presently dismantle the lyric altogether.
works.significance: Chamber Music is the foundation of Joyce's art and one of the purest bodies of lyric verse in modern English: several of its songs were set to music, and the collection shows the traditional discipline out of which the experimental prose came.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the epiphany and the open ending (Dubliners).
works.context: The Dublin and Paris of the 1900s, the Irish lyric tradition and the fin-de-siècle aesthetic of the young Joyce. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1904 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.
works.structure: Thirty-six short lyrics in rhymed stanza, loosely sequenced. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Augustine Aloysius Joyce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
altTitles: Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.form: collected philosophical essays, treatises, dialogue, and maxims
works.description: Shaftesbury's collected philosophical miscellany, binding together his earlier treatises on virtue, enthusiasm, wit, and the moral sense with meditations, maxims, and letters. It set out the argument that moral approval rests on a natural sentiment rather than on divine law or self-interest, and that ridicule is the test of a healthy, sociable mind.
works.plot: The volume assembles several distinct essays: an inquiry showing virtue to consist in the balance of social affections, an enquiry into the nature of enthusiasm and superstition, a defence of wit and freedom of thought, a rhapsodic dialogue on the moralists, and meditations on the self and on human life. Shaftesbury argues that every creature's affections divide into natural, social, and selfish, and that virtue is the right system of these when guided by reflection. A 'test or sieve' of ridicule is offered for opinions about religion, since what can bear being ill-used is likely true. The miscellaneous thoughts and maxims draw the portrait of the accomplished 'gentleman' whose virtue, wit, and taste are one politeness. The whole is presented not as a system but as a character of the author's own mind, inviting free censure and examination.
works.significance: It supplied the eighteenth century's vocabulary of moral sense, politeness, wit, and enthusiasm and shaped Hutcheson, Hume, and the British aesthetic tradition; its theory of ridicule and its ideal of the accomplished character are central documents of the English Enlightenment.
works.meter: Prose of epigrammatic density, mixing periodic balance with abrupt sententious brevity; the maxims compress moral observation into pointed, often antithetical sentences.
works.context: Published in London in 1711 as the party war over the Sacramental Tests made toleration and enthusiasm live issues, and self-published by its author without a dedicated patron. It gathered the separately printed works of 1699-1710 and at once became a focus of the controversy over natural theology that Toland, Collins, and their opponents were conducting.
works.structure: An artfully ordered miscellany rather than a single argument: treatises of different dates are framed by advertisements, letters, and a self-memoir, so that the reader encounters one continuing intelligence under several genres.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct

Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: Characters of Shakespeare's Plays
works.form: Character-writing and practical criticism of the drama, in the line of the Elizabethan book of characters and of the periodical essay, applied to a repertory of plays and to the theory of imaginative sympathy.
works.description: The first of the author's books of criticism, published in 1817, a series of essays on the principal plays which is at once a defence of poetry and imagination against abstract morality and the most influential English book of Shakespearean character-criticism of its century. Its method is to read each play as a succession of minds, argued from the speeches themselves and from the effect of the plays on the stage and in the imagination, and its governing claim is that the dramatist's poetry is a poetry of character and feeling rather than of plot or of instruction.
works.plot: The opening essay states the principle that the author's characters are not specimens of a class but individual creations, and that to judge the plays by rules of criticism or by a moral account is to miss the reason they please. Successive papers take the tragedies and the comedies in turn: the doubting and self-analysing prince of the Danish court, whose hesitation is a disease of the reflective mind and not a defect of the plot; the Moor, whose jealousy is a jealous and credulous nature wrought upon by art; the king divided between his daughters and the flatterers about him; the Macbeth hurried to guilt by a will that is at once his own and another's, with the queen who unmakes her sex; and the comedies, with their fools, their persons of pomp and their women of spirit, and the sentimental and the cynical characters of the earlier plays. The argument throughout is that the poet's gift was an imaginative sympathy which entered into every mind and was nothing exclusively itself, and that criticism of the plays should be a report of the passion and the character as they are felt.
works.significance: The foundation of modern character-based Shakespeare criticism and the book by which the plays were read by the nineteenth century for their minds rather than for their scheme; its essays on the great tragedies are still quoted as the classic statements of the imaginative and sympathetic method. It also fixed the reputation of its author as the first critic of the Romantic period.
works.meter: Prose of the most forceful and compressed kind, full of pointed antithesis, of short sentences of assertion and of long periods of accumulation, with quotation woven into the argument; the style itself is a model of English critical prose.
works.context: Published in 1817, when the old drama was being revived on the London stage and when the poet's contemporaries, the lecturers and the editors, were making a new profession of literary criticism; the book grew out of papers contributed to periodicals and was written in the years of the author's work as a reporter and as a reviewer for the leading journals.
works.characters: The figures of the plays discussed - the Danish prince, the Moor of Venice, the learned king and his daughters, thane and lady of the Scottish play, the women of the comedies, the fools, the persons of state and the men of fancy
works.structure: A series of free-standing essays, one to each of some twenty plays, with a general introduction and a concluding paper on the plays of the earlier and later manner; there is no historical or chronological design, and the order is that of the critic's own argument about the faculties of the poet.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world

works.title: Chartism
works.description: Published in December 1839 at the height of the Chartist agitation and the most important contemporary analysis of it by an intellectual: an essay that takes the Charter seriously as a symptom of a deeper condition rather than as a programme.
works.plot: Carlyle asks 'what the condition of England really is' and answers that Chartism is the symptom of the 'dyspepsia' of a society in which the working man has no voice, no leader and no hope; the remedy is not the ballot but the recognition of the duties of the governing class and the right of the worker to work.
works.significance: Chartism invented the phrase 'the condition of England question' and set the terms of the Victorian social novel: Disraeli's Sybil, Gaskell's Mary Barton and Dickens's Hard Times all answer Carlyle's diagnosis, and it is the founding document of the critique of Victorian industrialism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: The Chartist petition of 1839, the Newport rising of November 1839, the Poor Law and the factory question; Carlyle's argument was delivered as the agitation reached its height. The record dates the work as composed in 1839 and first published in 1840 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Chaucer's Short Poems
altTitles: The Minor Poems of Geoffrey Chaucer
works.description: The corpus of Chaucer's shorter poems: the philosophical ballades (Fortune, Truth, Gentilesse, Lak of Stedfastnesse), the complaints (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars, the Complaint unto Pity, A Complaint to his Lady), the envoy to Scogan, the ABC to the Virgin, and the love lyrics. Together they show the courtly poet at work across every register, from the rueful 'Flee fro the prees' to the burlesque of Sir Thopas's kin.
works.plot: The poems range from the lover's complaints of Mars and Anelida (with its paired verse of great formal ambition) through the moral ballades on truth and steadfastness — 'Flee fro the prees, and dwelle with sothfastnesse' — to the devotional ABC and the comic self-portraits of the envoys.
works.significance: The ballade of Truth and its kin made Chaucer the English master of the short moral poem; the corpus preserves the courtly occasions and formal experiments of his art.
works.meter: Ballades, roundels, rhyme royal, and experimental stanzas; the ABC is an alphabetical acrostic in translation from Deguileville.
works.context: Composed across Chaucer's career (c. 1370–1400), many for courtly occasions and patrons (John of Gaunt, the king's circle); preserved in the manuscript anthologies of the fifteenth century and collected by Thynne (1532).
works.characters: the speakers of the complaints and ballades; Mars; Venus; Anelida; Arcite
works.structure: A corpus of independent lyrics and complaints, several (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars) with substantial narrative frames.

works.title: Chester Mystery Plays
works.description: The Chester cycle of twenty-four plays, from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed at Whitsun by the guilds of Chester from the early fifteenth century (with later tradition dating its origin to the fourteenth) until 1575, the last of the great cycles to be suppressed. Its eight-line stanza, its Expositor figure, and its homiletic restraint give it a distinctive ceremonial gravity.
works.plot: The cycle dramatizes salvation history in twenty-four pageants — the Creation and fall, Noah's flood (with the famous drinking-song of Noah's wife), Abraham and Isaac, the Prophets, the Nativity, the ministry, the Passion, the Harrowing of Hell, and the Last Judgement — with the Expositor commenting on the action's prophetic meaning.
works.significance: The last surviving performance tradition of the English cycles (revived at Chester from 1951), and a classic of English civic theatre.
works.meter: The characteristic Chester stanza (aaabcccb, with internal rhyme) and the Expositor's couplets.
works.context: Performed at Whitsun in Chester from at least the early fifteenth century (a fourteenth-century origin is traditional), revised in the early sixteenth century, and performed until 1575; preserved in five manuscripts and printed in 1607.
works.characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah and his wife; Abraham and Isaac; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Antichrist; the Expositor
works.structure: Twenty-four pageants on the Corpus Christi model, with the Expositor's speeches linking the Old Testament type to its New Testament fulfilment.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the tradition attributing the cycle's origin to the monk Ranulph Higden is legendary.

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Fourth
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Romantic travel poem and topographical meditation in the Spenserian stanza; the ruins poem and the philosophy-of-history ode in narrative measure.
works.description: The last and most finished canto of the pilgrimage poem, and the one in which the travelling hero disappears altogether, leaving the poet alone with the ruins of northern and central Italy and with Rome. It passes from the Venetian lagoon through Padua, Ferrara, Bologna, Florence and Pisa to the city of the dead and the living papal capital, and ends on the Adriatic shore with an address to the ocean. It is the period's most sustained verse argument about the transience of glory and the survival of the mind among ruins.
works.plot: The canto opens on Venice, the Arsenal and the wasted palaces, and mourns a republic drowned by its own oligarchy and by the foreign yoke; it then runs through the memorials of the literary and princely dead at Padua, Ferrara and the Este court, the tombs and exiles of Florence, and the Pisan sands, before reaching Rome. There the ruins, the pope's city, the buried emperors and poets, the dying gladiator and the petrified Niobe supply the argument that earthly power is a spent coin while the mind and the verse that recorded it endure. The pilgrim is finally detached as a figure of the past, and the close turns to the sea, whose restless permanence offers a reason for endurance that no city can.
works.significance: It is the summit of the period's ruins meditation and gave English verse its most quoted lyrics on transience, the sea and the endurance of the mind; the canto's treatment of Italy became the template for the century's verse on Italian places. Its withdrawal of the fictional pilgrim also marked a decisive shift from Romantic narrative to Romantic meditation, and its measure was imitated by the long poems of travel that followed.
works.meter: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, handled with the greatest regularity and command of the four measures in the series; the final stanzas of the ocean stretch the last line for weight.
works.context: Written largely during the Venetian and Roman residence of 1817-18 under Austrian restoration rule, in a Italy whose principalities had been rearranged by the congress settlement and whose papal government was the subject of daily liberal complaint; the canto's mourning for a lost Venetian liberty and its treatment of the living pope were read as political statements. It was published separately in 1818, the first canto to appear without the earlier ones, and its reviews were drawn into the quarrel over the poet's character.
works.characters: the poet-speaker; Childe Harold, who withdraws early; the personified cities of Venice and Rome; the dead of Ferrarese and Florentine history; the ocean of the close
works.structure: A single topographical progression from lagoon to city to shore, organised as a sequence of meditative set pieces on named places, with the apostrophe and the personified address carrying the argument in place of incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the canto was revised for the collected editions, and the manuscript and first issue differ in a number of passages bearing on contemporary persons.

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Third
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Romantic travel poem and lyric meditation in the Spenserian stanza, with the sublime scenery essay and the confession of the divided mind.
works.description: The first canto written after the poet's separation and departure from England, and the point at which the travel poem becomes a soliloquy. Harold reappears at Waterloo and on the Rhine, but the canto's centre is the Lake of Geneva, where the scenery of glacier, lake and mountain draws out a confession of guilt, endurance and self-forgetting. The scheme of the fictional pilgrim is all but abandoned in favour of the poet's own voice, and the water and ice of the Alps are treated as the only language adequate to a mind under public judgment.
works.plot: The pilgrim arrives at the field of Waterloo, where the recent battle supplies the theme of imperial rise and wreck, and moves down the Rhine among the castles and vineyards of the German romantic past. On the Lake of Geneva the travel scheme gives way to meditation on the glacier, the depth and velocity of the lake, and the mountains, and to the poet's own history of a marriage collapsed and a name made notorious. At the valley of Chamounix the canto reaches its argument that the soul has a kindred in the abyss of ice and water, and that solitude is at once loss and liberation; it closes with the pilgrim turning again toward the south. The suppressed stanzas, removed from the first text, made the domestic reference explicit and were restored only long afterward.
works.significance: It turned the Byronic travel poem into the Romantic meditation on water, mountain and self-forgetting, and became the rival within the poetry of exile of the great lake school's own nature meditations. Its quotations formed a popular vocabulary of solitude, and its history of suppression made it the standard example of the Victorian bowdlerization of a famous text.
works.meter: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with a closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc; the canto's characteristic movement is a long descriptive period resolved by the twelfth line, with frequent apostrophe and personification.
works.context: Written in the year of the poet's permanent exile, at the lake where he had stayed with his party in the summer of 1816 and where the glacier journey was made, and published late in that year at a moment of intense public curiosity about his domestic history. Waterloo and the Rhine gave the canto its political frame in the first months of the second restoration, and its treatment of marriage, guilt and the world's judgment was read as autobiography by every reviewer.
works.characters: Childe Harold; the poet-speaker; the presiding spirit of Geneva; the waters of the lake and glacier, addressed as companions
works.structure: A single canto of progressive meditation, loosely held by the traveler's route, in which the pilgrim recedes and the poet-speaker takes over; it ends in a farewell to the lake and an apostrophe to the mountain scenery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the first issue differs from the manuscript in the removal of several stanzas bearing on the poet's marriage, and the erased lines survive in a fair copy and were printed in the collected scholarly editions.

themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn

The sublime, terror, and the ruin

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Cantos I and II
altTitles: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the First and Second
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Romantic travel poem and verse romance of exile in the Spenserian stanza, combining the topographical meditation, the domestic tale and the personal effusion; its model of the melancholy, secretive outlaw became a stock of the century.
works.description: The poem that made its author famous overnight: a narrative of travel and refusal in Spenserian stanzas, following an imagined young nobleman through Iberia and the Greek lands while the poet speaks in his own person in the interpolated stanzas and appended epistles. It converts a two-year tour in the Mediterranean into a meditation on national character, on the wreck of the Napoleonic wars, and on the weariness of a sinner who leaves his own country. The hero is at once a portrait of the fashionable outlaw and a mask the poet can step behind, and the mixture of journal, description and confession proved irresistibly quotable.
works.plot: Harold, sated with pleasure, dissipation and some unconfessed guilt, leaves his native country and travels as a spectator and volunteer through the Iberian peninsula, where the poem surveys the sufferings of Portugal and Spain under French invasion and the character of their people. He passes to Greece and the archipelago, where the ruins of Athens, the plain of Troy, the Albanian shore and the living customs of Greek, Slav and Turk supply meditation on liberty, decay and the transience of fame. An affectionate episode and the death of a companion interrupt the journey, and the cantos close with the pilgrim's withdrawal from society and the poet's farewell to the scenes he has described. The governing argument is that the ruined and war-torn south reflects and satisfies a mind already estranged from its own country, and that the poet's own guilt can be displayed only when disguised as another man's.
works.significance: It created the Byronic hero in narrative form, and fixed the Romantic association of southern landscape, political oppression and imaginative exile; its Spenserian measure was widely imitated in long poems of travel and reflection through the nineteenth century. Its blend of description, note and self-quotation also made it a central exhibit in the contemporary argument between a poetry of sensation and a poetry of description.
works.meter: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with a closing alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc, taken from the romance and meditation tradition and used for sustained description, with a strong caesura, rhetorical apostrophe and an habitual turn of the last line.
works.context: The cantos were written from the notebooks of a tour made between 1809 and 1811, through Portugal and Spain at the height of the Peninsular war and into Albania and Greece under Ali Pasha, and published in 1812 during the last years of the struggle against Napoleon. The poem's sympathy with Spanish and Greek resistance, and its contempt for the northern journals, addressed a public that had followed the war in the reviews and prints. Its instant fame, quoted in the fashionable and the radical press alike, made the poet's biography a public commodity from the first week of sale.
works.characters: Childe Harold; the poet-speaker who overtakes his own character; the lady of Canto I; the companion who dies on the journey; the Spanish peasant and his daughter; the guides and boatmen of the Greek waters
works.structure: Two cantos of traveling meditation, loosely progressive and episodic, with the pilgrim's story told in outline and the lyric effusions, apostrophes and appended epistles carrying the emotional argument; explanatory notes by the poet document the places and translate the passages of foreign speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text exists in several authorially revised issues of the 1810s, with cancelled stanzas on the poet's private history suppressed from the first text and restored only by modern editors.

works.title: Children of the Earth
works.description: The novel of the working-class childhood and the earth. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Ethel Mannin; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Children of the Earth follows the working-class children of the London streets through the seasons of the childhood and the poverty, in the plain prose of Mannin's sympathetic realism of the decade's turn.
works.significance: Children of the Earth is Mannin's novel of the working-class childhood: its streets, its children and its poverty carried the life of the poor into the popular novel at the decade's turn.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain fast prose of the popular novelist.
works.context: London in the year of the Depression's beginning. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the children of the streets; the families; the London of the poor
works.structure: A childhood novel in the seasons of the streets. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ethel Edith Mannin. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Children of the Ghetto
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1892 and the first great English novel of the Jewish East End: a year in the life of the immigrant community of London. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by Israel Zangwill; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The novel follows the Ansell family and their neighbours through the synagogue, the workshop, the Board School and the pawnshop: the clever Esther Ansell grows up in poverty and rises into the West End, Reb Shemuel's daughter Hannah is torn between her father's Law and her love for David Brandon, and the community's poverty, piety and humour are recorded in a series of connected scenes.
works.significance: Children of the Ghetto was the first English novel to give the Jewish immigrant community a full literary existence: it made Zangwill famous as the 'Dickens of the Ghetto', it recorded the speech and customs of the East End before they vanished, and it stands at the head of the English-Jewish tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is dialect speech transcribed with care.
works.context: 1891-92: the mass immigration of Russian and Polish Jews after 1881, the Whitechapel ghetto, the Jews' Free School, and the debate on anglicisation. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Esther Ansell; Moses Ansell; Benjamin Ansell; Reb Shemuel; Hannah Jacobs, Reb Shemuel's daughter; Levi Jacobs; Sam Levine; David Brandon; Raphael Leon; Melchitsedek Pinchas
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Chrestomathia
works.form: educational treatise and institutional plan; didactic prose with a curriculum scheme
works.description: A plan of day-education for the middle and working classes, printed with a coined title word for the 'useful learning' it proposed, and one of the most original of the period's educational books. It sets out a curriculum of positive knowledge, an economical organisation of teaching, and a withering criticism of the monopoly of classical learning and of the boarding-school.
works.plot: The treatise first defines the chrestomathic method as the instruction of youth in that portion of stock of ideas which is useful to the individual and to the community, and charges the existing system with spending the years of the young upon a branch of knowledge that few ever turn to use. It then lays out the plan of the school: a day-school for the neighbourhood, with a graded series of classes, the period of instruction divided by the clock into short parcels, the mutual instruction of the pupils, and the government of the house by a code of detailed rules for the teacher, the assistant, and the registrar. The curriculum, the largest part of the book, enumerates the useful branches: the mother tongue, the modern and ancient languages, the mathematical and physical knowledge, the logic and analysis of the human mind, the moral and political branches, the arts and employments, and the matter of taste, each with its subdivisions and its relative value. The argument throughout is economic as well as pedagogic, measuring the cost of instruction against the quantity of use produced, and treating the classical monopoly as a job in the market of education.
works.significance: It is one of the founding documents of the secular and utilitarian critique of classical education, anticipating the long nineteenth-century argument for scientific and modern education and for the day-school, and it supplied the analytical vocabulary of curriculum and of school management. Its influence on the educational writings of the reforming school, and on the later debate over the value of the classics, was considerable, though the school it planned was short-lived.
works.meter: Technical, enumerating, expository prose of the jurist applied to the schoolroom: coined terms, numbered divisions, and an relentless arithmetic of time and utility, with occasional dry sallies against the established system.
works.context: Published in the year of the controversy over the monitorial schools and of the quarrel between the rival national systems of education, and designed to be embodied in a school actually opened in London a few years later on the day principle. Its utilitarian measurement of knowledge belongs to the same school of legislative reform that in the same years was remapping the law, the prison, and the poor-law.
works.structure: A single treatise in numbered parts: the statement and defence of the chrestomathic name and plan, the details of the school and of its management, and the enumeration of the branches of useful knowledge with their several precepts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose manuscripts and correspondence record the long delay between the plan's conception and its printing.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Wisdom and learning
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle
