works.title: Christ and Satan
works.form: religious narrative poetry in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 729 lines in three parts, closing the Junius manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, the harrowing of hell and the Resurrection, and the temptation of Christ in the wilderness. Its long speeches of Satan and the fallen host are the most extended 'infernal' passages in Old English.
works.plot: Part I: Satan and his angels bewail their fall and their exile from the light of heaven, in a series of remorseful laments. Part II: the harrowing of hell — Christ's descent to liberate the patriarchs — is narrated together with the Resurrection and Ascension. Part III: the devil tempts the fasting Christ in the desert, and is answered and routed; the poem ends with the Last Judgment.
works.significance: The fullest English treatment of the fallen angels before Milton; its harrowing-of-hell narrative is the classic vernacular statement of the theme.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the style varies sharply between sections, suggesting composite authorship.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 213-229); the three parts may be independent poems of different dates gathered by the compiler.
works.characters: Satan; the fallen angels; Christ; the devils of the temptation; Eve (in retrospect)
works.structure: Three loosely joined narrative sections on a cosmic theme — fall, redemption, and the final victory — unified by the figure of Satan's defeat.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; possibly composite.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Typology and biblical interpretation
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Christ I (The Advent Lyrics)
works.description: The first part of the Exeter Book 'Christ' trilogy: twelve Advent lyrics (439 lines) elaborating the 'O' antiphons of the Christmas liturgy, hailing Christ under his liturgical titles — key of David, cornerstone, dayspring, Emmanuel. The eleventh lyric's 'Eala Earendel' inspired Tolkien's mythology of Eärendil.
works.plot: The lyrics, addressed to Christ or spoken in his voice, celebrate the mystery of the Incarnation: the closed door of the Virgin, the cornerstone rejected by builders, the light rising in darkness, the bridegroom come to Zion. Each lyric meditates on a title or antiphonal image and prays for the coming of the Lord.
works.significance: The great Advent poetry of the period; source of the 'Earendel' passage that founded Tolkien's legendarium.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; lyric intensity rather than narrative continuity.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book as the opening of the composite poem 'Christ' (fols. 8a-14a); the antiphons are those sung at vespers in the week before Christmas.
works.characters: Christ; Mary; the faithful of Zion
works.structure: A lyric sequence of twelve meditations on the antiphons, framed by the liturgical season of Advent.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; once attributed to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy, but the Advent lyrics are now regarded as separate and unsigned.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Typology and biblical interpretation
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Christ II (The Ascension)
works.description: The middle section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (427 lines), signed by Cynewulf: a meditation on the Ascension based on Gregory the Great's homily, celebrating Christ's 'leaps' — from heaven to earth, into the womb, onto the cross, into the tomb and hell, and back to the throne of glory.
works.plot: The poet meditates on the Ascension as the climax of Christ's career of 'leaps' (from the Song of Songs image of the beloved leaping upon the mountains), recounts the apostles' grief and the angel's promise of return, interprets the 'gifts of men' of Psalm 67 (the talents of wisdom and craft distributed to mankind), and closes with a vision of the Last Judgment and Cynewulf's runic signature and prayer.
works.significance: The classic Old English treatment of the Ascension; its gifts-of-men passage inspired The Gifts of Men and Fortunes of Men.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is elaborately wrought.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 14a-20b) between the Advent lyrics and Christ III; based on Gregory the Great's Homily 29 on the Gospels.
works.characters: Christ; the apostles; the angel
works.structure: A homiletic meditation in verse: Gregory's leaps, the ascension narrative, the catalogue of gifts, eschatological conclusion, and runic signature.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.
themes: Judgment Day and eschatology
Typology and biblical interpretation
Wisdom and learning
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Christ III (The Judgment)
works.form: religious narrative (eschatological vision) in alliterative verse
works.description: The final section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (798 lines): the grandest poetic vision of the Last Judgment in Old English, in which Christ appears on the cross at doomsday, the elements dissolve, the sinners and the blessed speak their laments and thanks, and the poem closes on the joys of heaven.
works.plot: The poem opens with the sudden coming of the Judge, the blast of trumpets, and the conflagration of the world — the sea, the stars, the mountains consumed; Christ, still bearing the wounds and the cross, separates the blessed and the damned, who speak in antiphonal choruses (the damned reproaching their sins, the blessed thanking Christ for the 'thirst on the cross'); the poem ends with the blessed entering the heavenly city.
works.significance: The summit of Old English eschatological poetry; a major source for later medieval judgment literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of sustained grandeur; celebrated descriptions of the dissolving cosmos.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 20b-32a); the judgment scenes draw on patristic and homiletic eschatology.
works.characters: Christ the Judge; the blessed; the damned
works.structure: A visionary sequence: theophany, cosmic dissolution, the dialogue of blessed and damned, and the entry into heaven; the speeches are organized in paired laments and thanksgivings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; formerly assigned to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Christ's Tears over Jerusalem
works.description: Nashe's plague-year pamphlet: Christ's prophecy of Jerusalem's fall becomes a sermon on London's sins — usury, pride, and the city's feasting amid the plague — with the famous address to the 'adulterous and sinful' city and the appended 'Tears over London'; the book that made Nashe feared as a prophet and jailed for its satire.
works.plot: The opening visions of Jerusalem's destruction give way to the anatomy of London's sins: the merchants' frauds, the gallants' pride, the women's painting; the closing 'Tears' plead for repentance before the plague's judgment, with the whole framed as Christ's lament applied to the present city.
works.significance: The great plague literature of the 1590s — the pamphlet that turned the biblical lament into an instrument of urban satire.
works.meter: Prose of pulpit rhetoric crossed with the pamphlet's street energy — the style that made Nashe the most imitated and most dangerous writer of the plague years.
works.context: Published 1593, in the worst plague year of the decade, when the theatres were closed and the authorities edgy; the satire on the city's magistrates landed Nashe in the Fleet prison.
works.characters: Christ (as speaker); Jerusalem; London; the personified sins
works.structure: A sermon-pamphlet in the complaint tradition — biblical exegesis turned urban satire, with the visionary frame and the moral application.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Christabel
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, combining the supernatural ballad, the Gothic tale of the enchanted woman and the romance of the castle and its rites.
works.description: A long metrical romance in two incomplete parts, long circulated in manuscript and published in 1816, which tells how a knight's daughter walking alone at midnight in the woods about her father's castle meets a strange maiden, and how the household is changed by the stranger's presence. Its machinery belongs to the supernatural ballad and to the Gothic tale of enchantment, and its interest lies in an atmosphere of guilt, spell and dread rather than in an explained plot.
works.plot: Christabel, unable to sleep, goes out at midnight to the terrace and the forest and meets a stranger who names herself Geraldine and says that she has been forced from her home and dragged through the wood by those who would compel her to a hated marriage; she asks shelter, and Christabel, bound by a spell that forbids her to question or to name the stranger's errand, leads her through the hall and to her own chamber. The intermediate lay, sung by the minstrel Bard Brice, tells how a dove, guarding a nest, was killed by a serpent that coiled about the shrub, and is heard as an omen of the wrong done in the castle. The second part brings the return of Lord Leoline, who had been absent on a border errand, the greeting of his hound, and the strange new affection that the stranger excites in him, while Christabel sees and may not tell what sits about the form she has brought within doors. The poem breaks off with the spell unbroken and the story unfinished, the promised conclusion never having been written.
works.significance: One of the most imitated unfinished poems in English and a standard instance of the Romantic use of enchantment, guilt and suspense without explanation; its metre influenced the later lyricists of the period, and its fragmentary state has made it a permanent subject of textual and psychoanalytical reading.
works.meter: A deliberately irregular accentual metre of lines of unequal beat, whose pattern is regulated by the number of accents rather than of syllables, with recurring rhyme-schemes that vary with the emotional register of each scene; the verse was cited by later critics as the first modern English example of accentual measurement.
works.context: Begun in the years of the western collaboration and the ballad volume, the first part composed in the late 1790s and the second about 1800; its long circulation in manuscript made its reputation among the poet's friends before publication, and its appearance in print in 1816 coincided with a renewed public interest in tales of border and of enchantment.
works.characters: Christabel, the knight's daughter; Geraldine, the stranger maiden under a spell; Lord Leoline, her father; Bard Brice, the minstrel who sings the ominous lay; the mastiff of the hall
works.structure: An unfinished romance in parts, organised as a series of set pieces rather than as continuous narrative: the midnight meeting, the chamber scene, the interpolated lay of the dove and the serpent, and the return of the father; the promised third part was never executed, and the poem's meaning has been much discussed as an enchantment of the household by a seducing power.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author's own later accounts assign the parts to different years of composition, and the dating of the promised conclusion remains a matter of inference.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Penance, confession, and sin
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Christian Morals
works.description: Browne's posthumously published manual of Christian conduct in three parts, a series of terse aphorisms and exhortations on the duties of the Christian life.

works.meter: Compressed, gnomic prose.
works.context: Written in Browne's later years and left in manuscript at his death in 1682; first printed in 1716 with a life by John Whitefoot.

works.title: Christianity as Old as the Creation
altTitles: The Gospel a Republication of the Law of Nature
works.description: Tindal's mature deist statement, the fullest argument that true religion is nothing but the law of nature and must therefore be as old and as universal as creation. Its ironical appendix, the Character of a Low-Church Deist, turned the controversy into a satire on party divinity.
works.plot: Tindal argues that God's religion, being designed for all rational creatures, must be uniform, intelligible, and proportioned to the nature He gave them; therefore the moral law written at creation is the whole gospel. What is called revelation can only republication and commentary: nature's religion, known by the equal light of reason, is the touchstone of every pretence to supernatural religion. The duties of the law of nature, justice, benevolence, sobriety, and piety, are the only terms of acceptance, and no positive institution can add to them. The appended Dialogue of the Dead and Character of the Low-Church Deist satirize the clergy's treatment of mystery, authority, and party.
works.significance: It is the summation of English deism, the text from which the movement's later critics and its American heirs alike took their definitions, and the standing provocation to every theology of supernatural religion in the century.
works.meter: Amplified argumentative prose, heavily periodic and repetitive for emphasis; the appendices take the lighter manner of dialogue and character writing.
works.context: Published in the deist flush of 1729-32, the year after Berkeley's Alciphron and in the teeth of the Convocation controversy over blasphemy; it drew more than a hundred replies, Butler's Analogy among the most considered.
works.structure: A single systematic treatise followed by burlesque dialogues and a character sketch, so that serious natural religion closes in comic warfare.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: Christianity Not Mysterious
altTitles: Christianity Not Mysterioues; or, A Treatise Shewing, That there is nothing in the Gospel contrary to Reason, or above it
works.description: Toland's founding tract of the deist controversy, arguing that the gospel contains nothing contrary to reason or above it and that mystery in religion is a clerical invention imported from neoplatonism and popery. It insists that what is not universally knowable is not universally necessary, and so strips the Christian scheme of its esoteric hierarchy of truths.
works.plot: Toland first defines the terms of religious language and shows Scripture to address all rational capacities, containing nothing contradictory and nothing whose knowledge is required but withheld. He then traces the mystery system to the neoplatonic and Roman corruption of primitive Christianity, in which priests reserved hidden meanings to themselves. Against the plea of divine condescension to human weakness, he argues that a revelation for all mankind must be intelligible to all. Reason is made the ground of assent even to revealed propositions, since the evidence of miracles must itself be rationally weighed. The conclusion is that Christianity is a reasonable, plain institution whose mysteries are only things not yet understood.
works.significance: It set the agenda of the English deist controversy for a generation and made the intelligibility of revelation the central question of natural and revealed religion; its rationalist criterion became the foil for Butler's Analogy.
works.meter: Lean, polemical prose of sustained syllogistic pressure, divided into numbered propositions and scholastic distinctions in ironic contrast to their content.
works.context: Published the year after Locke's Reasonableness of Christianity and drawing on his unitarian temper, it was ordered burnt by the hangman and denounced in the Irish House of Lords, where Toland sat; it opened the chain of deist claims that Collins, Tindal, and Morgan would extend.
works.structure: A single argumentative treatise in two discourses with a preliminary defence of its propositions, advancing by definition, historical confutation, and theological conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: Chronica Majora
works.description: Matthew Paris's universal and English chronicle, revised and expanded from Roger of Wendover's Flores Historiarum and continued by Matthew with his own annals down to 1259; the greatest historical work of thirteenth-century England, illustrated with Matthew's own marginal drawings.
works.summary: Beginning with the creation, the Chronica Majora concentrates on English and European affairs from the Norman Conquest onward, becoming a detailed contemporary record for the reign of Henry III: the conflicts with the barons, the campaigns in Wales and Gascony, the affairs of the friars and the universities, and the author's outspoken criticisms of king and pope.
works.significance: The fullest and most vivid narrative source for thirteenth-century England, and a landmark of English book production through its author's maps and marginal illustrations.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Kingship and good rule

works.title: Chronicon
works.form: history and chronicle in Latin prose
works.description: The Latin chronicle of Ealdorman Æthelweard, descendant of King Æthelred I and patron of Ælfric: a translation and adaptation of a lost version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, dedicated to his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen. Its prologue contains the celebrated eulogy of King Alfred.
works.plot: The chronicle retells the annals from the creation and the Saxon settlement through the West Saxon and English kings to Edgar's death (975), in four books of deliberately archaic, 'hermeneutic' Latin studded with Grecisms; the prologue to Matilda praises Alfred — 'the unshakeable pillar of the western people' — and explains the work's purpose.
works.significance: A major witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin culture among the late Anglo-Saxon aristocracy.
works.meter: Dense hermeneutic Latin prose.
works.context: Composed c. 978-988 by the ealdorman Æthelweard, 'the historian' of the Æthelweard-Ælfric circle; the unique manuscript (Cotton MS Otho A.x) was destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731, and the text rests on Savile's 1596 edition.
works.characters: Matilda of Essen (addressee); Alfred; the West Saxon kings
works.structure: Four books of annals in translation, with a dedicatory prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Æthelweard's authorship is stated in the prologue.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle

works.title: Church Going
works.description: Church Going is a poem by Philip Larkin, written in 1954 and first published in his collection The Less Deceived (Marvell Press, 1955). An agnostic cyclist stops at an empty country church and, half mocking his own awkward reverence, asks what churches will become when belief has gone and why such buildings still draw him. It is generally regarded as one of his masterpieces.
works.summary: The speaker's visit to an empty church: his inventory of its furnishings, the words he reads aloud from the lectern, the Irish sixpence he leaves; his speculation about what the building will become when no one uses it; and his conclusion that it remains 'a serious house on serious earth'.
works.plot: Making sure nothing is going on inside, the speaker lets the door close behind him and takes off his cycle-clips in awkward reverence. He notes the flowers, the brass and the organ, runs a hand over the font, mounts the lectern and reads a few verses, ending 'Here endeth' much more loudly than he meant, signs the book and donates an Irish sixpence, deciding the place was not worth stopping for. Yet he did stop, as he often does, and he wonders what he is looking for. When churches fall out of use, will they be kept as museums, left to the rain and sheep, or visited by women with children for luck and cures? Who will be the last to seek the place for what it was: a scholar of rood-lofts, a lover of ruins, a Christmas-addict, or someone like himself, bored and uninformed but drawn to the spot where marriage, birth and death were solemnised? The final stanza answers with a tone of settled conviction: the building's air holds all our compulsions, recognised and robed as destinies, and someone will always discover in himself a hunger to be more serious and gravitate to this ground, which he once heard was proper to grow wise in, if only because so many dead lie round.
works.significance: One of the best-known English poems of the century, and the poem that fixed the image of Larkin as the cycle-clipped, unillusioned observer; it is among his most anthologised and studied works.
works.meter: Colloquial, self-deprecating narration ('brass and stuff / Up at the holy end') that rises into formal, almost liturgical cadence at the close; precise physical detail and comic deflation.
works.context: Drafted from April 1954 through some twenty-one pages, abandoned and resumed, and finished in July 1954 while Larkin was sub-librarian at Queen's University, Belfast; The Less Deceived made his reputation the following year.
works.structure: Seven nine-line stanzas in iambic pentameter, rhymed, moving from anecdote to speculation and to a closing stanza of grave statement.
themes: Death, illness and mourning
Faith, doubt and the sacred

works.title: Clarel: A Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land
works.description: Published in 1876 at the author's expense and the longest American poem of the century: the pilgrimage of a young divinity student through Palestine and the debate on faith among his companions. It is a verse work of 1876 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Clarel, a young American divinity student in Jerusalem, falls in love with Ruth, the daughter of an American convert to Judaism, and, barred from her by the rites of mourning for her murdered father, joins a pilgrimage to the Jordan, the Dead Sea and Bethlehem with Rolfe, Vine, the Anglican Derwent, the zealot Nehemiah, the Jewish geologist Margoth and the embittered ex-Confederate Ungar, among others; their arguments on religion, science, history and doubt fill the poem, Clarel returns to find Ruth dead, and the epilogue holds out only the hope that death may prove to rout life into victory.
works.significance: Clarel is the most ambitious American poem of the nineteenth century and the great American poem of religious doubt: its length, its intellectual range and its honesty make it the missing link between the American Renaissance and the modern religious poetry of Eliot and Stevens.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The 1857 journey, the American crisis of faith after Darwin, the religious diversity of the Ottoman empire, and the American reception of the higher criticism. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1875 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.characters: Clarel; Ruth; Nathan, her father; Agar, her mother; Rolfe; Vine; Derwent; Nehemiah; Mortmain; Ungar; Margoth; Celio; Djalea, the Druze guide
works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Melvill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady
altTitles: Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady. Written by a Fellow-Citizen to His Family
The History of Miss Clarissa Harlowe
works.description: The history of a young woman forced by her family toward an unloved husband, betrayed by the libertine she trusts and destroyed by his final outrage, written in a correspondence between the principals, their confidants and their gaolers. It is the longest and most ambitious English novel of the century and the supreme achievement of the epistolary form.
works.plot: Clarissa Harlowe, courted by her brother's enemy Solmes under family compulsion, accepts the protection of Lovelace, who carries her to London and confines her in a house of ill fame. Her letters to Anna Howe tell of stratagem after stratagem, her flight from house to house, and at last of rape and poisoned resolution. She refuses to marry her ravisher, declines to plead to the world, and dies by a long and prepared consumption; Lovelace is killed in a duel abroad, and the family's avarice is left exposed.
works.significance: It is the central tragedy of the English novel and the chief literary argument of the eighteenth century about female consent, family authority and the sovereignty of the individual conscience; its afterlife in the paintings, abridgements and imitations of the following fifty years is unmatched.
works.meter: An elastic prose capable of many registers, from the quick colloquial idiom of Lovelace to the Latinate gravity of Clarissa's meditations; the letters' periodic syntax enacts the self-examination of the writers.
works.context: Written over four years and published between 1747 and 1748, in the decade of the new divorce and seduction debate and of the printing of the author's own conduct and parliamentary work; the novel's legal detail assumes the property and marriage law of the period.
works.characters: Clarissa Harlowe; Robert Lovelace; Anna Howe; James Harlowe; the brother and sisters of the family; Solmes; Mrs. Sinclair; the physicians and the alms-house of the ending
works.structure: A correspondence of several hands arranged and edited by the surviving friend, with the narrator's interpolations; the plot is advanced by the uneven timing of letters, so that the reader is placed inside the delays of the post.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the correspondence fiction of the preface is the author's own device and the composition is documented in his letters of the 1740s.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Marriage and women's conduct
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: Clayhanger
works.description: A printer's son in the Potteries struggles against his father and the provincial world, in the finest English novel of the autodidact. It is a prose fiction work of 1910 by Arnold Bennett; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama.
works.plot: Edwin Clayhanger, the shy, intelligent son of a tyrannical printer in Bursley, is taken from school at thirteen to work in the family business. The novel follows his long struggle with his father, his thwarted love for the architect's daughter Hilda Lessways, his education and his slow assumption of the business — a study of provincial ambition that ends with him poised to become the prosperous man his father was.
works.significance: Clayhanger is Bennett's most personal novel and the finest English study of the provincial autodidact: it made the Potteries a literary country and gave the nineteenth-century novel of education a modern, ironic form. With Hilda Lessways and These Twain it forms one of the great English family chronicles.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is solid material specification — furniture, houses, incomes, the exact weight of a life.
works.context: The Potteries printing trade of the 1870s–90s, the Methodist chapel, the mechanics' institute, and the social ascent of the provincial middle class. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1910 and first published in 1910 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Edwin Clayhanger; Darius Clayhanger; Hilda Lessways; Janet Orgreave; Osmond Orgreave; Big James
works.structure: Chronological third-person narrative in five parts over some twenty years. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Cleanness
works.description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 1,812 alliterative lines on purity ('clannesse'): expanding the gospel parable of the wedding feast, it retells the Flood, the destruction of Sodom, and Belshazzar's feast as three great exemplary narratives of God's vengeance on filth and pride, culminating in the writing on the wall. The most rhetorically powerful of the Cotton Nero poems.
works.plot: From the parable of the guest without a wedding garment, the poet unfolds the doctrine of the clean heart; Noah's Flood shows God's cleansing of the world's filth; the destruction of Sodom his vengeance on unnatural lust; and Belshazzar's feast — with its vessels stolen from the Temple, its drunken blasphemy, and the mysterious hand writing Mene, Tekel, Peres — his judgement on sacrilege and pride.
works.significance: The most powerful homiletic poem of the alliterative revival; its Belshazzar episode is among the greatest descriptive set-pieces in Middle English poetry.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most sumptuous, with elaborate descriptive passages (the Flood, the feast, the Temple vessels).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The poem's courtly castigation of 'fylþe of þe flesch' speaks to the Ricardian culture of courtly and clerical reform.
works.characters: Noah; Abraham; Lot; Belshazzar; Daniel; the Queen; God
works.structure: A homiletic frame (the beatitude 'blessed are the clean of heart' and the wedding parable) enclosing three parallel biblical exempla of increasing elaboration, each a set-piece of alliterative description.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: Cleopatra
works.description: Published in 1889 and Haggard's great historical romance of the ancient world: the love of the Greek scholar Harmachis for the last queen of Egypt. It is a prose fiction work of 1889 by H. Rider Haggard; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Harmachis, the heir of the priests and the destined liberator of Egypt, is sent into the palace at Alexandria to destroy Cleopatra, but falls under her spell; her handmaiden Charmion, jealous of his love for the queen, betrays the conspiracy, he escapes to the desert, and returns years later to see the queen die by the asp before he dies himself.
works.significance: Cleopatra is the finest of Haggard's historical romances and one of the great Victorian recreations of antiquity: its narrative of an Egyptian priest destroyed by the power of a queen made it a best-seller and it remains a landmark of the imperial historical romance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person testimony of the practical man.
works.context: 1889: the Victorian fascination with Cleopatra, the archaeology of Egypt, and the imperial analogy between Rome and Britain. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Harmachis, the narrator; Cleopatra; Charmion, her handmaiden; Sepa, his uncle; Mark Antony
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Rider Haggard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story
themes: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
movements: Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire

works.title: Clotel; or, The President's Daughter
works.description: Published in London in 1853 and the first novel by an African-American: the story of Thomas Jefferson's enslaved daughter and of the sale of his family. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by William Wells Brown; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Currer, Jefferson's enslaved mistress, and their daughters Clotel and Althesa are sold at his death; the novel follows Clotel's life as a servant in Richmond, her escape disguised as a man, her reunion with her husband and her death in the Potomac, and the fates of her sister's children.
works.significance: Clotel is the first novel by an African-American and the founding text of African-American fiction: its use of the story of Jefferson's daughter makes it the most direct indictment of the American founding in the literature, and its themes of passing, sale and family destruction set the agenda for the whole black novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is first-person testimony with documentary documents.
works.context: The 1800-53: the Jefferson household, the domestic slave trade, the market in the capital, and the British abolitionist audience of 1853. The record dates the work as composed in 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Currer; Clotel; Thomas Jefferson; Horatio Green; Althesa; Henry; Mary; George Green; Nat Turner
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wells Brown (self-chosen name). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Clown's Houses
works.description: The second collection: the harlequinade and the houses of the clown. It is a verse work of 1916 by Edith Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Clown's Houses carries the baroque lyric of the first book into the harlequinade: the clown, the puppet, the sun and the room are the furniture of the poem, in the line built on assonance and consonant-chime rather than on the sense.
works.significance: Clown's Houses confirmed Edith Sitwell as the most original technical innovator of the English lyric of the war years: its harlequinade and its sound-pattern are the workshop of Façade.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
works.context: London in the war years, and the modernist little magazine. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.structure: A collection of lyrics in the chanted line, the harlequinade as the ordering figure. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Edith Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Coelum Britannicum
works.description: Thomas Carew's masque, performed at Whitehall on Shrove Tuesday 1634 before Charles I and Henrietta Maria and printed in 1640, in which Mercury reforms the heavens by purging them of the stars of obsolete heroes, celebrating Caroline court virtue and Platonic love.
works.plot: Mercury descends to announce that the reformed British court has earned the heavens' admiration and that the constellations of degenerate heroes will be replaced by the virtuous figures of Caroline courtiers.
works.significance: The most admired masque of the Caroline court, valued for its poetry and its articulation of Caroline Platonic and political ideals, and a high point of Carew's work.
works.meter: Verse and song in a polished, courtly style with classical allusion.
works.context: Performed at the Caroline court in 1634, reflecting its Platonic and ceremonial ideals; Carew was a server-in-ordinary to the king and a leading court wit.
works.characters: Mercury; Momus; the masquers; Charles I and Henrietta Maria (represented)
works.structure: A court masque with songs, dances, and speeches, framed by Mercury's reform of the celestial sphere.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; Carew wrote it, possibly with Inigo Jones's designs.

works.title: Cold Comfort Farm
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1932
works.description: The funniest English novel of the 1930s: Flora Poste and the gloom of the Starkadder farm. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Stella Gibbons; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Flora Poste, a resourceful young woman left with a small income, goes to live with her relatives at Cold Comfort Farm in Sussex, where the Starkadders brood over the sins of the past; she sets about tidying their lives, with results that are comic and entirely sensible.
works.significance: Cold Comfort Farm is the funniest English novel of the 1930s and the perfect parody of the rural novel: its heroine and her campaign of common sense against the gloom of the farm made it a permanent classic and the definitive satire of the Hardy-Lawrence tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the parody of the rural novel and its dialect.
works.context: Sussex in the early 1930s, and the rural novel of Hardy, Lawrence and Mary Webb. The record dates the work as composed in 1932 and first published in 1932 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Flora Poste; Ada Doom; Judith Starkadder; Seth Starkadder; Amos Starkadder; Elfine; Mr Mybug
works.structure: A comic novel in fifteen chapters, from London to the farm. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stella Dorothea Gibbons. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Coleridge on Imagination
works.description: The study of Coleridge's imagination as the theory of the poetic mind. It is a prose work of 1934 by I. A. Richards; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Biography and the Modern Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Coleridge on Imagination reads the Biographia and the notebooks as the theory of the poetic mind: the primary and secondary imagination, the fancy and the esemplastic power are stated in the semantics of the new criticism, and Coleridge is made the founder of the discipline.
works.significance: Coleridge on Imagination made Coleridge the founder of the modern theory of the poetic mind: its reading of the imagination through the new semantics fixed the account of the Biographia for a generation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the analytic prose of the psychologist of reading.
works.context: Cambridge in the 1930s, and the recovery of Coleridge. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1933 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; biography and the modern life.
works.characters: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
works.structure: A study in chapters of the imagination, the fancy and the esemplastic power. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ivor Armstrong Richards. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Colin Clout
works.description: Skelton's longest satire: the plain countryman Colin Clout — a persona borrowed from the shepherd-poets, which Spenser later took up — reports what the commons say of the clergy: their pomp, their ignorance, their neglect of preaching, and the corruption of the bishops, all in the voice of 'the people's' plain truth.
works.plot: Colin sets out to speak 'of the spiritual estate'; the poem catalogues the clergy's abuses through the reported speech of the commons, answers the expected objections of the bishops, and ends with an appeal to the lay powers for reform.
works.significance: The great English anticlerical satire of its age and the direct ancestor of Spenser's Colin Clout; its plain-man persona became a convention of English satire.
works.meter: Sustained Skeltonics over 1,200 lines; the metre's repetitiveness enacts the commons' insistent complaint.
works.context: Written as the Reformation crisis gathered, about 1522; the poem voices the anticlericalism of the laity without committing itself to the Lutheran programme.
works.characters: Colin Clout; the clergy (collectively)
works.structure: A long single-voiced complaint organized as report ('the commons say...') with interposed answers to clerical objections; the plain man's persona licenses the satire.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: Colin Clouts Come Home Againe
works.description: A pastoral allegory in which the shepherd Colin Clout (Spenser) recounts to his Irish fellow-shepherds his voyage to 'Cynthia's' court — England and Queen Elizabeth — praising the Queen and the court poets, and then turning a satirical eye on the court's vices.
works.plot: Returned from England, Colin describes the sea journey, the splendour of Cynthia and her ladies, the poets he met (thinly veiled portraits of Sidney's circle and of Shakespeare's and Daniel's generation), and contrasts the court's falsehood with the simplicity of the shepherds' life.
works.significance: The fullest contemporary map of the Elizabethan literary scene and the classic English poem of the court-versus-country debate.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter couplets, in the plain pastoral style of the Calender.
works.context: Written in 1591 after Spenser's visit to England in 1589–91, during which The Faerie Queene was presented to the Queen; it records his meetings with Ralegh and the London literary world.
works.characters: Colin Clout; Cynthia (Queen Elizabeth); the Shepherd of the Ocean (Sir Walter Ralegh); Hobbinol; the assembled shepherds
works.structure: A single pastoral dialogue: Colin's long reported narrative of the voyage and the court, framed by the shepherds' questions and a concluding debate on love.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Collected Parodies
works.form: Parody collection (the manners of the poets)
works.description: The collected parodies: the manners of the poets turned one degree. It is a verse work of 1921 by J. C. Squire; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: Collected Parodies gathers Squire's parodies of the poets of his day - the Georgians, the moderns and the Victorians behind them - each manner reproduced exactly and turned one degree, in the most accomplished parodies of the between-wars years.
works.significance: Collected Parodies remains among the most accomplished parody collections in English: its reproductions of the manners of the poets are criticism by the degree and the standard text of the parodist's art.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the polished Georgian lyric of the landscape and the season.
works.context: London in 1921, and the literary journalism of the quarterlies. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1920 and first published in 1921 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; georgian anthology lyric.
works.structure: A collection of parodies, one manner to a piece. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Solomon Eagle, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to J. C. Squire is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Collected Poems
works.description: Collected Poems is the posthumous edition of Philip Larkin's poetry edited by his friend and literary executor Anthony Thwaite and published jointly by the Marvell Press and Faber and Faber in 1988, three years after the poet's death.
works.summary: All the poems of Larkin's published collections together with many poems that were unpublished or uncollected during his lifetime, including "Aubade" and much early and unfinished work.
works.plot: By printing a large body of previously unknown poems beside the published collections, the edition revealed how much Larkin had written and withheld, and showed the private, often bleaker workshop behind the four books. Thwaite arranged the poems in order of composition rather than by the original volumes; the 2003 edition reversed this, restoring the four books and placing the other poems in appendices. Among the poems first collected here were "Aubade" and other late pieces written after High Windows, so that the volume completes the record of Larkin's final decade.
works.significance: It became a best-seller and the standard text of Larkin's poetry for fifteen years, and the newly published poems significantly enlarged understanding of his work.
works.meter: Includes the whole stylistic evolution from early neo-Romantic lyric to mature colloquial formalism.
works.context: Published in 1988, when Larkin's reputation was at its height and before the Selected Letters changed public perceptions of him.
works.structure: A chronological arrangement by date of composition, drawn from Larkin's workbooks and manuscripts.
themes: Death, illness and mourning
Love, intimacy and loss

works.title: Collected Poems of W. H. Davies (1916)
altTitles: Collected Poems of W. H. Davies
works.description: The collected poems that fixed the tramp poet's place in the Georgian lyric. It is a verse work of 1916 by W. H. Davies; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The volume gathers the lyrics of the road, the hedge and the sky from the earlier collections, with the war lyrics of 1914-16, and fixed Davies's place among the Georgian poets as the plain voice of the open air.
works.significance: The 1916 Collected Poems fixed Davies's canon and his reputation: its lyrics of the roadside and the sky are the standard text of the tramp poet and the measure of the Georgian lyric from below.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain short line and the plain word.
works.context: England in the war years, and the Georgian anthologies. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
works.structure: A collected edition of the lyrics, ordered by collection and by subject. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Davies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Colloquia (Ælfric Bata)
works.manuscriptDate: Oxford, St John's College MS 154 (eleventh century), alongside Ælfric's Colloquy
works.description: A pair of Latin conversation manuals by Ælfric Bata, a pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham: the Colloquia and the harder Colloquia difficiliora. Modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy, they dramatize the daily life of the monastic school with boisterous, hyperbolic dialogues about food, drink, beatings, theft, and the relations of master and pupil.
works.plot: The dialogues stage conversations among schoolboys and between pupils and master: bargaining for food, complaining of hunger, confessing petty theft, enduring (and threatening) beatings, and practising the vocabulary of daily life in the monastery — shoes, clothes, bedding, the refectory, the infirmary, and the latrine.
works.significance: The most vivid surviving picture of eleventh-century English school life, and evidence of the living tradition of spoken Latin that the Benedictine Reform established in English monasteries.
works.context: Composed in the generation after Ælfric's Colloquy (c. 998), the dialogues show the continuity of the reform's vernacular-Latin classroom tradition into the eleventh century, and their earthy realism is a deliberate antidote to the classicizing curriculum.
works.characters: Ælfric Bata (speaker), his pupils, stock schoolboys and masters
works.structure: A loose sequence of dramatic dialogues without sustained plot, each built to drill vocabulary through exchange; the speakers are stock schoolboys and masters, and the humour is deliberately exaggerated.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric Bata, who names himself in the texts and addresses Ælfric of Eynsham as his master; the attribution is conventional and generally accepted, though the texts are transmitted anonymously in their manuscript.
themes: Wisdom and learning
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Colloquy
works.form: grammar and didactic prose (dialogue) in Latin with Old English gloss
works.description: A school dialogue between a master and his pupils who impersonate the trades — ploughman, shepherd, oxherd, hunter, fisherman, merchant, shoemaker, smith, cook — composed by Ælfric for the teaching of Latin conversation, with an Old English interlinear gloss added later by a teacher (Ælfric Bata). The liveliest classroom text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The master questions each boy about his craft: the ploughman feeds the oxen, the hunter takes deer and boar for the king, the fisherman risks the sea for his catch, the merchant crosses the sea to sell and buy; each defends the dignity of his work, and the dialogue ends with the master's advice on industry and good counsel.
works.significance: The most vivid picture of Anglo-Saxon daily life and trades in the period's literature.
works.meter: Latin prose with interlinear Old English gloss.
works.context: Composed c. 998-1005 at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century).
works.characters: the Master; the pupils (ploughman, shepherd, hunter, fisherman, fowler, merchant, shoemaker, salter, baker, cook, and others)
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue of some 75 exchanges, each trade a set piece.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric on stylistic grounds; the Old English gloss is by another hand (Ælfric Bata).
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Benedictine Reform
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Colonel Enderby's Wife
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1885
works.description: Published in 1885 and Malet's first major novel: the disastrous marriage of a young woman to a man of her father's generation. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by Lucas Malet; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Philip Enderby, an officer of nearly fifty with a chivalrous, idealising nature, marries Jessie, the pretty young ward of Mrs Pierce-Dawnay; the novel, an English story touched by Italian surroundings, follows the slow failure of a marriage built on his idealisation of a wife who cannot return his devotion.
works.significance: Colonel Enderby's Wife is one of the strongest English novels of the unhappy marriage before the New Woman fiction of the 1890s: its analysis of a marriage made without love and its refusal of the conventional ending made it a landmark of the Victorian novel of marriage, and it established the themes that Malet would develop for the rest of her career.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is rich, elaborate, slightly archaic prose.
works.context: 1885: the debate on the age of consent and the marriage law, the New Woman controversy before its name, and the Victorian novel of the unhappy marriage. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Philip Enderby; Jessie, his young wife; Mrs Pierce-Dawnay, her guardian
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary St Leger Kingsley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Colonel Jack
altTitles: The Life and Unexpected Fortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
The Fortunes and Misfortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
works.description: The life of a boy taken from a Newgate-connected childhood into a career of theft, transportation, soldiering and finally plantation ownership. It is the third and most openly autobiographical of the 1722 criminal narratives, with a narrator whose self-examination is obsessive and whose social climbing is a study in the making of a gentleman.
works.plot: Jack, the son of a widowed mother left in want, is apprenticed to a dancing master, runs away to London, and is drawn into a gang of child thieves drilled by an old pickpocket. He is tried and transported, escapes in America, and after a series of raids and duels becomes a planter; he raises horse in the wars in Flanders, takes the title in the army, and returns to England to marry. Throughout, the narrative pauses to audit his own motives and to count his shifts from honour to criminality and back.
works.significance: It is the most candid analysis in early fiction of class mobility and of the moral vocabulary of repentance as a social credential, and its child-thief episodes are a primary source for the history of London street life.
works.meter: Colloquial, garrulous first-person prose heavy with cant terms of the flash languages and with the accounting idiom of estates; the repentance sections adopt the periodic syntax of the serious address.
works.context: Published in the same current of Newgate biography as the criminal lives of 1722, and drawing on the post-1718 transportation trade and on the war in the Low Countries, which supplies the military career of the title.
works.characters: Colonel Jack; his mother and sister; the dancing master; the old pickpocket and the child gang; the Virginia and Carolina landlords; his several wives
works.structure: First-person autobiography in two parts closing in a conversion narrative, moving from picaresque episode to moral accounting; the narrator repeatedly interrupts himself to examine his own designs.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested in modern scholarship; the first part's title-page attributes the work to the author of Moll Flanders.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Colonial enterprise and the New World
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Penance, confession, and sin
The city and urban life
movements: The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: Color
works.description: The most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and the English lyric. It is a verse work of 1925 by Countee Cullen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage', 'Incident', 'Tableau', 'From the Dark Tower' and the love lyrics that made Cullen the movement's most elegant poet.
works.significance: Color is the most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: its English lyric grace and its poems of the colour line made Cullen the movement's counterweight to Hughes, and 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are permanent poems.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave.
works.context: Harlem and New York in the 1920s, the Black church and the English lyric tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1925 and first published in 1925 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.

works.structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and quatrains. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Countee LeRoy Porter. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Cometh Up as a Flower
works.description: Published in 1867 and Broughton's sensational first novel: a first-person narrative of a woman who loves one man, marries another for money, and dies of the consequences. It is a prose fiction work of 1867 by Rhoda Broughton; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Nell Lestrange, the daughter of an impoverished old family, falls in love with Dick M'Gregor, a penniless army officer; her scheming sister Dolly intercepts and forges their letters and drives her into marriage with the wealthy Sir Hugh Lancaster to save their father from ruin; Dick returns, the deception is discovered too late, and Nell, dying of consumption, tells her own story to the end.
works.significance: Cometh Up as a Flower is one of the founding texts of the 1860s 'fast' novel: its heroine's unashamed desire and its refusal of a moral ending made it scandalous and made Broughton famous, and it is a key document in the pre-history of the New Woman novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is first-person female narration with direct address to the reader.
works.context: The 1860s, the marriage market, the 'Girl of the Period' controversy, and the circulating-library censorship of frank heroines. The record dates the work as composed between 1866 and 1867 and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Nell Lestrange (the narrator); Dick M'Gregor; Sir Hugh Lancaster; Dolly Lestrange, her sister; their father
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: Comin' thro' the Rye
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1875
works.description: The runaway bestseller of the 1870s: a tomboy heroine, a Scottish estate and a misunderstanding. It is a prose fiction work of 1875 by Helen Mathers; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: The heroine, brought up as a boy on a Scottish estate, falls in love with the heir and is separated from him by a misunderstanding; the novel follows her adventures in London and her eventual reunion in a story of high spirits and sentiment.
works.significance: Comin' thro' the Rye was one of the great bestsellers of the 1870s, selling in the hundreds of thousands: it made the tomboy heroine a popular type and shows the romantic novel at the height of its commercial power.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the lively, slangy first-person heroine.
works.context: Scotland and London in the 1870s, and the romantic fiction of the circulating library. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1875 and first published in 1875 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the heroine; the heir; the guardian; the London friends
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, from the Scottish estate to the reunion. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Coming Up for Air
works.description: Orwell's finest novel: an insurance salesman returns to the childhood fishing pool and finds it built over. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by George Orwell; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: George Bowling, a fat, forty-five-year-old insurance salesman, wins seventeen pounds on a horse and returns to the Thames Valley town of his childhood to fish in a secret pool — only to find the town swallowed by the suburbs and the pool become a rubbish tip. The novel ends with his realization that the war is coming.
works.significance: Coming Up for Air is Orwell's finest novel and the great English novel about the destruction of the countryside: its portrait of the suburb and the motor road, and its elegy for the Edwardian childhood, made it the period's most moving book about the loss of England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the plain declarative English sentence with no ornament.
works.context: The English suburbs of 1939, the motor road and the new housing estates, and the outbreak of the Second World War. The record dates the work as composed in 1938 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: George Bowling; Hilda Bowling; Porteous; Old Porteous; Elsie
works.structure: First-person narrative moving between 1938 and the childhood of 1900. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Commentaries on the Laws of England
altTitles: Commentaries on the Laws of England, in Four Volumes
works.description: Blackstone's four-volume systematization of the common law, grown from his Oxford Vinerian lectures of 1753 onward: rights of persons, rights of things, private wrongs, and public wrongs. It made English law a teachable rational science and became the most influential legal book of the English-speaking world.
works.plot: Volume I narrates the rise of the laws, the kingdom's constitutional structure, and the rights of persons, from royal prerogative and parliamentary independence to domestic relations. Volume II reduces property, tenure, inheritance, and title to an intelligible historical grammar. Volume III treats civil wrongs and remedies, wrongs to things, and the law of actions. Volume IV defines crimes, their justifications and extenuations, and the machinery of public justice from arrest to pardon. Throughout, Blackstone presents the common law as a repository of collective wisdom, mild in its proportion of punishments and jealous of liberty, though later reformers found its apologetic tone and its fictions indefensible.
works.significance: It fixed the vocabulary in which English and Americans spoke of law, liberty, and property; Bentham's attack on it founded philosophical radicalism, while its account of the balanced constitution entered the Federal Convention's debates.
works.meter: Elevated,periodic expository prose deliberately written for gentlemen as well as lawyers, with set-piece characterizations of the constitution and frequent literary allusion.
works.context: Published by Clarendon Press at Oxford and W. Strahan in London between 1765 and 1769 after the lectures of the 1750s, it appeared in the age of Mansfield, of American rights rhetoric, and of Bentham's first Fragment; American lawyers before 1800 read it as a declaration of inherited liberty.
works.structure: A four-part systematic exposition ordered by the analytical divisions of the law, each volume a continuous argument from history to institution to remedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Common Sense
altTitles: Common Sense; Addressed to the Inhabitants of America
works.description: Paine's pamphlet of January 1776, written in a plain man's vernacular to carry the American colonists from grievance to independence. It sold by the hundred thousand, renamed the war's cause, and became the model of the revolutionary pamphlet as an instrument of mass politics.
works.plot: Paine opens by separating society from government, society a blessing produced by our wants and government a necessary evil produced by our wickedness, and then strikes at the royal constitution as an absurdity of hereditary succession in which a brutish herd of kings succeeds over a nation of cattle. He argues from common sense, scripture, and the natural order that a remote island ruling a continent is an inversion, that the true interest of America is independence, trade, and foreign alliance, and that the hour of separation has arrived while the colonies are armed and united. The closing parts on the present ability of America and on a continental frame of government turn the pamphlet into a practical argument for declaring war in the name of a new era.
works.significance: It is the most influential pamphlet in American history and a world-historical specimen of the plain style in politics, establishing the rhetoric of rights, republican modernity, and a new era that Paine's later writing extended.
works.meter: The new demotic: short declarative sentences, biblical cadences, single-word emphatic closes, the pulpit and the tavern fused into a political style.
works.context: Written in Philadelphia in late 1775 with Franklin's countenance and published anonymously in January 1776, sold in every colony and read aloud in the camps, it made independence thinkable within weeks and was cited by Washington and delegates as the turn of the crisis.
works.structure: A short pamphlet in numbered sections: of the origin of government, of monarchy and hereditary succession, of the present American dispute, of present ability, and of thoughts on a form of government, with preface, appendix, and a postscript added in later issues.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, by 'AN OLD Englishman'; Paine's authorship was acknowledged in the colonies within months and he became its known author in Europe after the Rights of Man.

works.title: Company Parade
works.description: The first of the Mirror in Darkness: the woman writer in the thirties. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Storm Jameson; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama.
works.plot: Company Parade follows Hervey Russell from the Yorkshire marriage through the separation and the London of the literary work to the writing of her first novel, in the trilogy of the woman's career that made Jameson's name.
works.significance: Company Parade opened the Mirror in Darkness and made Jameson the novelist of the woman's career in the decade: its Hervey Russell is one of the great working women of the thirties novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of the woman's career in the prose of the decade.
works.context: London and Yorkshire in the early 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Hervey Russell; the husband; the son; the London literary world
works.structure: The first of a trilogy: the marriage, the separation and the first novel. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.

works.title: Complaints
altTitles: Complaints: Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie
works.description: A volume of shorter poems on the vanity of worldly things, gathering The Ruines of Time, The Teares of the Muses, Virgils Gnat, Prosopopoia (or Mother Hubberds Tale), The Ruines of Rome (from du Bellay), Muiopotmos (or The Fate of the Butterflie), and Visions of the Worlds Vanitie.
works.plot: The poems vary from the beast-fable of Mother Hubberds Tale — the Fox and the Ape swindling their way to courtly power — to the mock-heroic tragedy of the butterfly Clarion in Muiopotmos, and the elegiac ruins meditations translated and adapted from du Bellay.
works.significance: The chief English monument of the Renaissance 'ruins of time' tradition and the home of the most influential Elizabethan beast satire.
works.meter: Varied: rhyme royal, ottava rima, and the Spenserian experiments of the translations from du Bellay.
works.context: Printed in 1591 while Spenser was in Ireland; Mother Hubberds Tale was long read as a satire on Burghley's court, and the volume was among the works attacked by the authorities in the 1599 satires ban.
works.characters: The Fox; the Ape (Mother Hubberds Tale); Clarion the butterfly; Aragnoll the spider (Muiopotmos)
works.structure: A miscellany of independent poems unified by the complaint-and-vanity theme, in varied forms from fable to vision.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
