works.title: Days and Nights
works.description: Published in 1889 and Symons's first collection of verse: the poems of the aesthete's sensations, the theatre, the sea and the passing of pleasure. It is a verse work of 1889 by Arthur Symons; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: Symons's first collection, dedicated to Pater, is made up largely of dramatic monologues and narrative studies in the manner of Browning, of outcasts, invalids and the poor, among them 'The Opium-Smoker', with only hints of the impressionist lyric of Silhouettes and London Nights.
works.significance: Days and Nights founded the English Decadent lyric of the 1890s and established the tone that Dowson, Johnson and the Rhymers' Club would develop.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short lyric built on a single mood.
works.context: 1889: the Rhymers' Club, the English reception of Pater, and the aesthetic culture of the late 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: De Cive
altTitles: Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society
works.description: Hobbes's first published statement of his political theory, the third part of his philosophical system, which argues from the state of nature to the necessity of an absolute sovereign and was published in Latin in Paris in 1642.
works.plot: In three parts — Libertas (the state of nature), Imperium (the establishment of government), and Religio (the kingdom of God) — Hobbes derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the natural right of self-preservation.
works.significance: The prototype of Leviathan and the first full modern statement of social contract theory; its influence on seventeenth-century political thought was immediate and enormous.
works.meter: Latin philosophical prose; translated into English as Philosophical Rudiments in 1651.
works.context: Published at Paris in April 1642, on the eve of the English civil wars, which Hobbes said determined his subject; expanded edition 1647.
works.structure: Eighteen chapters in three sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Order and degree: the body politic
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Commonwealth and Interregnum Literature

works.title: De Civili Dominio
works.description: John Wyclif's most explosive treatise (1375–76), expounding his doctrine of dominion: lordship is founded on grace, so that the sinful clergy — the pope included — forfeit their right to temporal possessions, and kings may and must strip the church of its wealth. The book that made Wyclif the theorist of disendowment and the target of papal condemnation.
works.plot: Wyclif argues that all dominion derives from God and is held only by the righteous; the reprobate hold possessions unjustly; the clergy's endowment was conditional on their holiness and may be revoked by lay lords; and the English king, as God's vicar in his realm, is bound to reform and disendow the delinquent church.
works.significance: The theoretical charter of Lollardy's attack on ecclesiastical wealth and the most consequential political theology written in medieval England.
works.meter: Latin prose in the Oxford scholastic manner, relentlessly syllogistic.
works.context: Composed at Oxford and Lutterworth in 1375–76, when the papal-imperial politics of the Great Schism's prelude and the English crown's anti-papal statutes (Provisors, Praemunire) gave Wyclif's theories immediate political force; nineteen propositions from it were condemned by Gregory XI in 1377.
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Three books of scholastic argument, from the metaphysics of dominion through its application to the church to the duties of the king.
works.attributionNotes: Wyclif's authorship secure.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Lollardy and religious dissent
movements: Lollardy
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis
altTitles: On the Correct Structure of Latin Prose
works.description: Thomas Linacre's treatise on Latin syntax, published in London by Richard Pynson in 1524; the first systematic Latin grammar composed by an Englishman and a landmark of the humanist reform of grammar.
works.plot: The work analyses Latin construction in six books, replacing the medieval speculative grammars with a descriptive account of syntax based on the usage of Cicero and the best classical authors, illustrated with abundant quotations.
works.significance: A founding document of English classical scholarship; its descriptive method influenced the whole European tradition of Latin grammar, and it secured Linacre's European reputation among humanists.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Linacre, physician to Henry VIII and the foremost English Greek scholar of his generation, composed the work over 1512–24 after his return from Italy; it was printed by Pynson and used in the schools alongside the authorized grammar.
works.structure: Six books of systematic grammatical exposition with a preface to Prince Arthur's tutor and a dedication to the grammar-school masters.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Wisdom and learning
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: De excidio et conquestu Britanniae
altTitles: On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain
works.description: Gildas's jeremiad against the sins of the British kings and clergy, opening with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon. The principal source for post-Roman Britain and the foundation of the providential reading of British history that Bede adopted.
works.plot: Part I narrates the Roman occupation, the coming of the proud Saxons as mercenaries, their revolt, and the British resistance culminating in Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mount Badon. Parts II and III denounce the five tyrant kings (Constantine, Aurelius Caninus, Vortipor, Cuneglas, and Maglocunus) and the corrupt British clergy in the manner of the Old Testament prophets.
works.significance: The indispensable (if tendentious) source for the adventus Saxonum and for the moral theology of national disaster.
works.meter: Rhetorical Latin prose saturated with biblical allusion.
works.context: Composed in Britain, traditionally c. 540s, a generation after Mount Badon; the earliest surviving extended insular text after the Roman period.
works.characters: Ambrosius Aurelianus; the five tyrant kings; the Saxon mercenaries
works.structure: A tripartite sermon-polemic: historical prologue, royal denunciations, clerical denunciations — history entirely subordinated to moral exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Gildas's authorship is traditional and generally accepted; the dating rests on inference.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Warfare and battle
Wyrd (fate) and providence
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: De Monfort
works.form: Drama; domestic and analytic tragedy of a single passion; closet-originated stage tragedy
works.description: A domestic tragedy in blank verse founded, in the author's own account, on the passion of hatred. De Monfort, raised by a benefactress and in love with her daughter, discovers that the man he has befriended is the son of his father's destroyer, and his settled hatred overmastering every other feeling drives him to kill him in a duel and confesses his hatred publicly. The play's power comes from the analysis of a single passion held up against softer domestic affection, and from its heroine's horrified discovery that the man she loves is an avenger. It was the most performed Romantic tragedy by a woman and a repertory piece for leading actors into the 1820s.
works.plot: De Monfort, adopted in childhood after his father's ruin and death, is beloved by Jane, the daughter of his benefactress, and is bound as well by a warm friendship with the amiable count, whose wife Rezenza had been De Monfort's own earlier attachment. When he learns that this friend is the son of the man whose prosecution destroyed his father, he resolves on revenge yet cannot extinguish his affection, and the strain of the two passions is dissected in long soliloquies. At a public entertainment Rezenza is accidentally shot by De Monfort's hand while he aims at the count, and she dies in a scene of terrified innocence. De Monfort then denounces the count before the company, abandons his love, and gives himself up to justice and despair.
works.significance: The most influential verse tragedy written by a woman in the Romantic period and a central text for study of the analysis-of-the-passions drama, of the debate between closet and acting texts, and of the nineteenth-century repertory's revival history. Its treatment of hatred as a self-consuming passion has been read as a case study in Romantic psychological determinism.
works.meter: Blank verse throughout, with a few rhymed passages for heightened effect; the idiom is conversational and argumentative rather than declamatory
works.context: Published in 1798 as the second volume of a series designed to delineate the stronger passions, and first played at Drury Lane in the spring of 1800 in a season when regulation domestic tragedy was competing with Gothic melodrama and with Shakespeare revivals. Its psychological method belongs to the late-eighteenth-century analysis of the passions carried on from the moral-philosophical tradition, and its female-authored domestic tragedy responded to the period's debate about women's access to the stage. A celebrated revival with a famous performer in the title role in the early 1820s re-established it in the repertory.
works.characters: De Monfort; Jane, the daughter of his benefactress and his beloved; the Count Montaigue, his friend and his father's son; Rezenza, his friend's wife and his early attachment; his old attendant and household dependants
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy with a single ruling passion as its organising principle; dialogue and soliloquy carry the psychological analysis, and the catastrophe depends on a public scene of accidental death and open denunciation.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name in the series title page; no dispute. The play's prefatory argument naming the governing passion is the author's own critical statement.
themes: Blood-feud, vengeance, and kinship
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Revenge and justice
movements: The Regency Stage and Popular Drama

works.title: De Nugis Curialium
works.description: Walter Map's miscellany of court gossip, satire, Welsh legend, ghost story, and moral anecdote, assembled piecemeal during his service at the court of Henry II; 'a jest book and a jest at the same time', as one editor put it, and the only certain work by one of the wittiest Latin writers of the age.
works.summary: Five distinctiones gather tales of the court of Henry II, satirical portraits of monks and courtiers, the legend of Sadius and Galo, the story of the Welsh king Herla and the fairy bride, and the earliest surviving connected account of the birth of Lancelot; Map's dissuasio to his friend Ruffinus against marriage closes the work.
works.significance: A unique window onto the oral culture and court life of Henry II's England, an early witness to Arthurian material, and a masterpiece of twelfth-century Latin satire and narrative.
themes: Arthurian legend
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The Twelfth-Century Renaissance

works.title: De Profundis
works.form: Epistolary essay (letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, written in Reading Gaol)
works.description: Written in Reading Gaol in early 1897 as a letter to Lord Alfred Douglas and published posthumously in 1905 in an abridged form; the complete text appeared in 1962. It is Wilde's confession, his defence and his most sustained work of prose.
works.plot: The letter recounts the intimacy with Douglas, the quarrel and separation, the catastrophe of the trials, and the prison discipline of suffering; it ends with the resolution to accept the past and to return to art.
works.significance: De Profundis is the finest English prison narrative since the seventeenth century and the fullest statement of Wilde's late philosophy: that suffering is not to be escaped but understood, and that the artist's subject is his own life.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1895-97 imprisonment, the prison reform debates, and the aesthetic philosophy under the pressure of disgrace. The record dates the work as composed in 1897 and first published in 1905 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: De temporum ratione
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin
works.description: Bede's treatise on time and its reckoning, the standard medieval textbook of computus: the calculation of Easter, the solar and lunar cycles, the ages of the world, and — decisively — the practice of dating years from the Incarnation of Christ (annus Domini), which the work made universal in western Europe.
works.plot: The treatise proceeds from the smallest units of time (moments, hours, days) through the calendar, the lunar cycles, and the Easter tables to the great divisions of world history — the six ages of the world and the seventh age of rest — closing with a chronicle of the world's six ages down to 725.
works.significance: The most influential computistical work of the Middle Ages; the origin of the BC/AD dating convention in general use.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Composed at Jarrow in 725 for the monks' instruction; a revision and expansion of Bede's earlier De temporibus (703).
works.characters: none
works.structure: A systematic didactic treatise in 71 chapters, concluding with the world chronicle (chapter 66) as the practical demonstration of its chronology.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Wisdom and learning
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: De virginitate (prose and verse)
works.form: didactic treatise in Latin prose and hexameter verse
works.description: Aldhelm's double treatise in praise of virginity, composed in both prose and verse: a celebration of chastity sustained by a vast catalogue of exemplars — biblical heroes, virgin martyrs, and ascetics — in the ornate 'hermeneutic' Latin that made Aldhelm the model of insular style.
works.plot: The prose treatise (addressed to the nuns of Barking, headed by Hildelith) argues the superiority of virginity over marriage and the other states of life, adducing the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, and virgins as witnesses; the accompanying Carmen de virginitate recasts the argument in hexameters with a culminating allegorical battle of the vices and virtues.
works.significance: The founding text of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition and of its characteristic learned style.
works.meter: Ornate hermeneutic Latin prose; the Carmen is in dactylic hexameters.
works.context: Composed for the double monastery of Barking, probably c. 675-705; the prose was praised by Bede and widely imitated.
works.characters: Hildelith and the nuns of Barking (addressees); the exemplars: Elijah, Daniel, the Maccabees, Agnes, Cecilia, and others
works.structure: A thematic treatise built from scriptural and hagiographical exempla, concluded by the allegorical psychomachia of the verse version.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Death and Doctor Hornbook
works.form: debate poem and personal satire in the popular 'Death and the Doctor' dialogue tradition
works.description: Burns's rollicking dialogue-poem of Death and the parish schoolmaster-doctor, a personal pamphlet against Peter Buchan, the Tarbolton excisier and poet who had insulted him in print. Death comes to drag the quack Hornbook to his trial, and the schoolmaster protests his useful ignorance of theology till the summons is served. The poem converts a local quarrel into a full-scale comic debate of the Death and the Doctor type, and a satire on pedantic presumption.
works.plot: Death, in the homeliest terms, rouses the doctor from his bed to answer for his misdeeds, and the schoolmaster protests that he was never taught to fear such visitors and that his learning has been of the bookish and useless kind. The two dispute the merits of learning, of practice and of preparation for the hour of death, with the doctor's excuses running out as Death presses the account. The dialogue ends with the parson's discomfiture and with an author's appeal to common sense against the pretensions of the professional neighbour.
works.significance: It is the best example of Burns's power to turn private pique into durable poetry, and one of the liveliest surviving instances of the Death-and-doctor debate in British verse. Its portrait of the schoolmaster-poaster has become a standard document for the history of the parish school and of rural self-education.
works.meter: Stanzaic Scots in the rambling six-line measures of the old Scottish comic narrative, with colloquial idiom, internal rhyme and a running dialogue of matched speeches.
works.context: Written in 1784 as a reply to Buchan's The Farmer's Ingle, which had caricatured Burns and his friends, and thus belongs to the local literary quarrels of Tarbolton and Mauchline; at the same time it works in a folk tradition of Death-dialogues and in the eighteenth-century contempt for the quack and the small pedant.
works.characters: Death; Doctor Hornbook (a portrait of Peter Buchan); the poet-speaker of the argument
works.structure: A two-voice debate poem in continuous dialogue, opening with Death's arrival, sustaining the exchange of summons and excuse, and closing with a direct address of the poet to his adversary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the quarrel with Buchan and the poem's occasion are documented by Burns's correspondence and by the rival pamphlets, and the identification of Hornbook with Buchan is accepted in the standard editions.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation

works.title: Death Comes for the Archbishop
works.form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1927
works.description: Cather's great novel of the American Southwest: two French priests and the desert. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Willa Cather; it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In 1851 the French missionary Bishop Latour arrives in New Mexico with his friend Father Vaillant to establish the Catholic Church in a vast and hostile territory; the novel follows their lives, the landscape and the people over forty years to the death of the archbishop.
works.significance: Death Comes for the Archbishop is one of the great American novels of the century and Cather's most perfect work: its prose, its desert landscape and its portrait of the two priests made it the finest American novel of the religious life.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact, unhurried sentence.
works.context: New Mexico in the second half of the nineteenth century, the Mexican and Native communities and the American annexation. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Bishop Latour; Father Vaillant; Magdalena; Kit Carson; Father Martinez
works.structure: A novel in nine books, without a conventional plot, over forty years. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Wilella Sibert Cather. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Death in a White Tie
works.description: Marsh's finest novel of the London season: a blackmailer among the debutantes. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by Ngaio Marsh; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Lord Robert Gospell, Alleyn's old friend, is murdered while investigating a blackmailer preying on the debutantes of the London season, and Alleyn must find a killer hidden in the drawing rooms of Mayfair.
works.significance: Death in a White Tie is Ngaio Marsh's finest novel of the London season and one of the great Golden Age detective stories: its portrait of the debutante world, its pathos and its exact detection made it the book that established Marsh as a novelist and not only a plotter.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the theatre and the country house as the setting of murder.
works.context: London in the late 1930s, and the world of the Season and the coming-out ball. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Inspector Alleyn; Lord Robert Gospell; Troy; Lady Carrados; Bridget O'Brien; Dimitri
works.structure: A London detective novel of the Season. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edith Ngaio Marsh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Death of a Hero
works.form: Novel; war memoir, first issued in 1929
works.description: The most bitterly anti-war novel of the 1929 flood: a young artist destroyed by the war and the society that made it. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Richard Aldington; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: George Winterbourne, an artist of the pre-war generation, escapes his stifling family, marries badly, and goes to France; the novel follows him through the war to his death from a sniper's bullet, blaming the war on the society and the elders who made it.
works.significance: Death of a Hero is the most bitterly anti-war novel of the 1929 flood and Aldington's masterpiece: its savagery, its documentary detail and its indictment of the pre-war society made it the central English novel of the war as generational tragedy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the Imagist image without ornament.
works.context: England and the Western Front in 1914–18, and the 1920s reckoning with the war. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: George Winterbourne; Elizabeth; Isabel; Mr and Mrs Winterbourne; the officers

The author's characteristic manner is the plain unadorned prose of the committee room and the laboratory.
works.context: The Mediterranean in the early 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery.

works.structure: A detective novel of the cruise and the investigation. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.

works.title: Death's Jest-Book; or, The Fool's Tragedy
works.description: The author's last and greatest drama, begun in 1825, carried through to completion about 1829, and revised against the manuscript until his death; it was printed posthumously in 1850 with a memoir by the friend who inherited the papers. A tragedy of a court fool who murders his duke, it turns the jest-book of death into a metaphysical drama of immortality, revenge, and the visible world's contempt for the soul. Its lyrics, including the dirge of a dead child and the song of the swallow, are among the finest short verse of the period.
works.plot: The play is founded on the chronicle story of a Silesian duke of Münsterberg stabbed by his court fool, and it builds from that nucleus a drama in which the fool undertakes the duty of revenge for a wronged household. The Duke and his courtiers pass through scenes of hunting, drinking, and instruction in which the fool's licensed speech conceals a settled purpose, and the murdered man's family, with a child whose dirge is sung, furnish the tragedy's pathos. Death appears as the only serious character, and the jest with which the fool's hand completes the killing is at once a trick and a sacrament. The play closes in the dissolution of nearly every figure who moves in it, and its imagery of the body, the grave, and the surviving spirit is continuous to the end.
works.significance: Death's Jest-Book is the supreme English closet tragedy of the later Romantic period and the source of the author's modern reputation, much quoted by later symbolists and decadents and by twentieth-century detective and gothic writers. Its treatment of mortality, laughter, and revenge has made it a central text for the study of Romantic pessimism and of the Gothic dramatist.
works.meter: Blank verse of great density and compression, full of compound epithet, broken syntax, and riddling address, varied by songs, a dirge, and nursery rhyme; the prosody is deliberately difficult and shifts between declamation and lyric intensity.
works.context: Begun at Oxford and completed during the author's years of travel and medical study on the continent, where he pursued the hope of physical evidence for a surviving human spirit; the play's debt to the German romance of the fool and to the Jacobean revenge drama is constant. It was never offered to the stage, and it passed from manuscript to print through the editorship of a literary friend after the author's death in 1849.
works.characters: Isbrand, the court fool and avenger; the Duke of Münsterberg, whom he kills; the wronged household whose cause he undertakes; the child whose dirge is sung in the second act
works.structure: A five-act tragedy with a prologue, constructed in short scenes of confrontation, song, and dumb-show rather than in a steady plot; multiple revisions left the text uneven, and the printed version reflects the editor's reading of a lifetime of manuscript change.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship, but the text printed in 1850 is an editor's reading of manuscripts revised over more than twenty years, and the several states of the drama make the printed play an editorial reconstruction rather than a final authorising impression.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Judgment Day and eschatology
Revenge and justice

works.title: Decline and Fall

works.title: Decorations
works.description: Published in 1899 and Dowson's second collection: the poems written in the last years of his life, when he had renounced the world and returned to the Catholic faith of his childhood. It is a verse work of 1899 by Ernest Dowson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume contains 'The Dead Child', 'Benedictio Domini', 'A Last Word', 'Vesperal' and the poems of renunciation and prayer; its subject is the exhaustion of pleasure and the turning to God.
works.significance: Decorations is the finest religious poetry of the English Decadence and the record of a deathbed conversion: it completes the arc from the paganism of Swinburne to the Catholicism of Thompson and Johnson, and it is one of the great small volumes of English verse.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short lyric metres of great smoothness.

The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano
works.description: Milton's Latin defence of the English Commonwealth and the regicide, answering the Defensio Regia of Claudius Salmasius; written for a European audience in his capacity as Latin Secretary, it vindicates popular sovereignty and the English people against royalist propaganda abroad.
works.plot: Milton refutes Salmasius's defence of monarchy and attack on the regicide point by point, arguing that kings are accountable to the people, that tyrants may be judged, and that the English republic is lawful and honourable.

works.meter: Eloquent, erudite Latin prose with powerful oratorical and satirical force.
works.context: Commissioned by the Council of State in 1650 and published in 1651; Milton's exertion on it (while already losing his sight) is said to have hastened his total blindness, and it earned him European fame.
works.structure: A learned Latin polemic of sustained argument, structured as a rebuttal of Salmasius's treatise.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: Dejection: An Ode
works.form: Romantic ode and meditation in the conversation manner, combining the eighteenth-century irregular ode with the letter of apology and the poem of psychological analysis.
works.description: An occasional ode of the spring of 1802, written over some days in a season of despair over a love that could not be answered and over the poet's own loss of imaginative power, and addressed to a woman named in an earlier version of the text. It is the most explicit verse statement of the Romantic theory of perception, since its argument is that the passion we bring to a scene is the source of its worth, and that a mind which cannot feel gives nothing to what it sees. The storm that gathers outside the window, watched without emotion, is the emblem of the speaker's condition.
works.plot: The opening invokes the evening wind, the last leaves that fall from the tree, and the storm gathering over the sea, and the speaker reports how he looks upon the face of the world with no sense of joy and no fear of loss, able neither to weep nor to sleep for want of feeling. Turning to the addressee, he says that grief without the imaginative power is a dumb and shapeless misery, and recalls that there was a time when the beauty of the world was attended by a holy light and by a joy too keen not to be painful. The central assertion is then laid down plainly: what we seem to receive from outward things is given and borrowed from ourselves, and the passion and the intelligence of the mind are the wedding garments of the world it beholds; a creature without imagination has no power to create or to enjoy. The closing stanzas return to the storm and to the prayer that the listener, whose life is bound to a household and to a child, may keep the fancy and the feeling that make the world fair, while the speaker accepts his own duller fate and asks only to be left to his silence and his penance.
works.significance: The classic Romantic poem on the failure of the imaginative faculty and one of the plainest statements of the mind-dependent view of perception; its claim that the mind supplies what it seems to receive from the world became a central tenet of Romantic theory. It remains a touchstone for readings of the relation between biography, intoxication and the Romantic ode.
works.meter: Irregular ode stanzas of unequal line-length with a complex rhyme scheme and persistent exclamatory and interrogatory periods; the alternation of long storm lines and shorter reflective lines marks the alternation of feeling and argument.
works.context: Written in April 1802, in a season of estrangement from his family, of increasing dependence on laudanum, and of hopeless attachment to a member of his wife's family; it belongs to the years in which his public lectures and his periodical were in difficulty, and its theory of the imagination was restated in prose in his critical work of 1817.
works.characters: The speaker beneath the storm in his room; the addressee, a woman loved and unattainable, whose household is named in the poem; the wind, the clouds and the sinking moon of the opening
works.structure: An irregular ode in eight sections, moving from the description of the storm, through the confession of impotence, to the philosophical assertion about the mind's agency, and back to the address to the listener; the design is that of a passionate self-analysis rather than of a close argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the identity of the addressee is a matter of biographical inference and does not affect the question of authorship.

works.title: Delia

works.title: Democracy: An American Novel

works.meter: Prose. works.title: Deor
works.description: A poem of 42 lines spoken by a displaced court poet, Deor, who consoles himself with a catalogue of legendary woes — Weland's captivity, Beadohild's pregnancy, Mæðhild's grief, Theodoric's exile, Eormanric's tyranny — each closed by the refrain 'Þæs ofereode, þisses swa mæg' ('That passed over, so may this').
works.plot: Deor, supplanted in his lord's favour by a rival scop named Heorrenda, lists the legendary sorrows that came to an end and applies the refrain to his own case, ending with a brief, ambiguous self-identification as the once-favoured poet of the Heodenings.
works.significance: A rare glimpse of the court poet's self-consciousness and of the consolation-structure that underlies the Old English elegies.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with a six-part strophic structure marked by the refrain.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its allusions are the earliest English witnesses to the legends of Weland the smith and Eormanric the Goth.
works.characters: Deor (speaker); Weland; Beadohild; Mæðhild; Theodoric; Eormanric; Heorrenda
works.structure: Five legendary exempla framed by the refrain, followed by the poet's personal application; the refrain is the earliest in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's name is part of the fiction.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Exile and homelessness
Wyrd (fate) and providence
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: Design for Living
works.description: The most scandalous comedy of the thirties: a woman, a painter and a playwright who cannot choose between them. It is a dramatic work of 1933 by Noel Coward; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Gilda, an interior decorator, lives with the painter Otto and the playwright Leo in turn and at once; the three travel from Paris to London to New York, and the play ends with all three together, a ménage à trois presented as the only honest arrangement.
works.significance: Design for Living was the most scandalous comedy of the thirties and Coward's most daring treatment of sexual freedom: its wit and its refusal to moralise made it the definitive play of the period's sexual politics.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the epigram and the witty exchange.
works.context: Paris, London and New York in the early 1930s, and the sexual politics of the smart set. The record dates the work as composed in 1932 and first published in 1933 and first performed in 1933 and the corpus places it within The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners, it is catalogued under comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Gilda; Otto; Leo; Ernest Friedman; Grace Torrence; Helen Carver
works.structure: Three acts (Paris, London, New York). The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A comedy in acts, the scene built as a succession of entrances, revelations and exits, with the social convention breached and restored.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Noël Pierce Coward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Desire Under the Elms
works.description: O'Neill's New England tragedy: a farm, a father and the wife who loves the son. It is a dramatic work of 1924 by Eugene O'Neill; it belongs to The American Theatre and the Modern Stage and it is catalogued here under Domestic and Sentimental Tragedy; Revenge Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ephraim Cabot brings his young third wife Abbie to the family farm; she seduces his son Eben to secure the farm for her own child, and the play ends in infanticide, confession and the mutual punishment of the lovers.
works.significance: Desire Under the Elms is O'Neill's great New England tragedy and one of the central American plays of the century: its combination of Greek tragedy and Puritan New England made it the finest American verse-free tragedy and a landmark of the modern theatre.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose or verse: the dialogue carries the whole, and the text is written for performance. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the expressionist set and the mask.
works.context: A New England farm in 1850, and the Puritan inheritance of the American rural world. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and first performed in 1924 and the corpus places it within The American Theatre and the Modern Stage, it is catalogued under domestic and sentimental tragedy; revenge tragedy.
works.characters: Ephraim Cabot; Abbie Putnam; Eben Cabot; Simeon Cabot; Peter Cabot
works.structure: Three acts in the Cabot farmhouse. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eugene Gladstone O'Neill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Desmond
works.form: Epistolary Fiction; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
works.description: Charlotte Smith's fourth published novel and the most openly radical of her fictions, written in letters and published at the height of the British controversy over the French Revolution. A young man of principle, Lionel Desmond, narrates his own education, his friendship with the political exile Verney, his unfortunate first marriage, arranged by interest, and his love for Geraldine Verney, while the book argues in favour of popular liberty, against hereditary government, and for the right of a wife to escape a marriage without affection. Its enthusiasm for the French cause made it a byword for Jacobin fiction in the 1790s.
works.plot: Desmond's letters describe a country upbringing, an early and uncongenial marriage arranged by interest, the protection of the political exile Verney and his daughter Geraldine, and the long legal and familial obstruction that keeps the woman he loves out of his reach; interleaved with the story are debates on the French Revolution, the rights of men, standing armies, and the condition of women in marriage, so that the resolution of the private plot is made to depend on the same principles that the public argument defends.
works.significance: Desmond is one of the boldest English novels of the 1790s to take the French Revolution side-by-side with the marriage question, and it is central to the recovered history of radical women's writing; its insistence that the oppression of women and of subjects are one argument made it a key text for the study of philosophical fiction, and its epistolary method showed how doctrinaire debate could be fictionalized without allegory.
works.meter: Prose correspondence in letters of varying length; the style moves between colloquial argument and declamatory political rhetoric, and verse quotations are interspersed as sententious comment.
works.context: Published in 1792, the year of the greatest vogue and alarm for revolutionary argument in England, in the circle of writing shaped by Godwin's political philosophy and by the dispute between Wollstonecraft's defenders and her attackers; Smith's own dependence on the proceeds of the book, and her separation from her husband, made its plea for the release of wives and for professional independence a personal as well as a political statement.
works.characters: Lionel Desmond; Geraldine Verney; Mr. Bethel, Desmond's friend; Verney, the political exile and father of Geraldine; the family interests that arrange Desmond's first marriage
works.structure: A largely epistolary novel: the correspondence of Desmond, of Geraldine Verney, and of the exiled Verney carries both plot and argument, and the exchange of letters is used to place competing readings of the French Revolution inside one fictional society.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed. Earlier scholarship confused its publication year, and the 1792 date is now settled by the contemporary imprint and reviews.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Devoted Ladies
works.form: Novel (the devoted ladies of the big house, as M. J. Farrell)
works.description: The Farrell novel of the two devoted ladies and the cruelty of devotion. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Molly Keane; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Novel of Manners and Fashion.
works.plot: Devoted Ladies follows the two devoted ladies of the big house, whose devotion is a cruelty, in the satirical sentence of the insider that dissected the class from within.
works.significance: Devoted Ladies is the Farrell novel of the cruelty of devotion: its two ladies made the big-house satire a study of the love that destroys and remain among the sharpest of Keane's pages.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of manners: the dialogue of the social world, the exact vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built on the breach or the observance of a convention. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical sentence of the insider.
works.context: The Anglo-Irish big house in the early 1930s. The record dates the work as composed in 1933 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; novel of manners and fashion.

works.title: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions
works.description: Donne's prose-and-prayer record of the near-fatal 'spotted fever' he suffered in December 1623, while Dean of St Paul's: twenty-three 'devotions', each in three parts — a Meditation on his sickness and the soul's, an Expostulation with God, and a Prayer — including the seventeenth, whose Meditation contains the most famous passage of his prose: 'No man is an island... for whom the bell tolls'.
works.plot: The book follows the stages of the illness — its first seizure, the physicians' consultations, the crisis, the convalescence — each stage becoming an emblem of the soul's disease and God's physic, from the opening meditation on man's miserable condition to the closing prayer of thankfulness.
works.significance: The classic of English devotional prose, whose 'No man is an island' meditation and 'for whom the bell tolls' have passed into the common language of mortality.
works.meter: Prose of the pulpit raised to art — the long periodic sentences, antitheses, and paradoxes of Donne's sermons compressed into the private page.
works.context: Written after the illness of late 1623 and published early in 1624; its great theme — sickness as the soul's education — belongs to Donne's last decade as Dean of St Paul's and the great plague years of Jacobean London.
works.characters: the sick man (Donne); God; the Physicians; the bell
works.structure: Twenty-three numbered devotions in strict tripartite form (Meditation, Expostulation, Prayer), each anchored to a moment of the illness — the tolling bell of the seventeenth marking the imagined death and burial.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Divine love and holy desire
Medicine, healing, and the body
movements: Metaphysical Poetry

works.title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
works.description: Hume's posthumous dialogue on natural theology, held between Cleanthes the empiricist design-theorist, Demea the sceptical orthodox, and Philo the ironic destructor of the argument from design. Left in manuscript at his death and published in 1779 by his friends at his request, it is the most famous English statement of the problem of natural religion.
works.plot: Cleanthes proposes the argument from design as an a posteriori analogy: the order of the world proves an intelligent cause proportioned to its effects. Philo, by turns playful and devastating, presses the weaknesses of the analogy: design is but one hypothesis among many, the world may be a crude embryo of a better system, an imperfect author, or the work of a plurality of gods, and from the mixture of good and ill in nature no perfection of the cause can be inferred. Demea then argues from the misery and vanity of human life toward a mystical, unknowable deity, which Philo's closing sceptical piety hardly distinguishes from atheism. The dialogue ends on the question whether the true religion can be defended by human reason at all, without resolving it.
works.significance: It remains the standard literary and philosophical presentation of the design argument and its critics, a touchstone for the philosophy of religion from nineteenth-century editions to contemporary debates.
works.meter: Measured dialogic prose of courtesy and retort in the classical manner, Philo's demolitions shaded beneath urbane periods and long rhetorical cadences.
works.context: Composed in fragments from the early 1750s and revised through the 1770s, it was withheld in Hume's lifetime and published posthumously in 1779 at his written desire, amid the public controversy over his dying scepticism reported by Boswell and others.
works.characters: Cleanthes; Demea; Philo
works.structure: Twelve parts of continuous dialogue in the classical manner, the argument rising through analogy, scepticism, and theodicy to an unresolved conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Published posthumously under Hume's direction; the date and extent of composition (1750-1776) are matters of scholarly inference from manuscripts and letters.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: Diana of the Crossways
works.form: Novel in three volumes; new woman
works.description: Published in 1885 and modelled on the life of Caroline Norton: the story of Diana Warwick, a brilliant Irishwoman trapped in a loveless marriage, whose social ruin and financial self-making made the novel a founding text of the New Woman debate.
works.plot: Diana Merion marries the cold Augustus Warwick in haste, partly to escape the advances of her friend Emma's husband, Sir Lukin Dunstane; separated from him after his divorce action fails, she supports herself by writing novels, falls in love with the rising politician Percy Dacier, and, in need of money, sells to the editor Tonans the cabinet secret Dacier has confided to her, which loses her Dacier. After Warwick's death she finally accepts the love of Thomas Redworth.
works.significance: Diana of the Crossways is the most important English novel of the 1880s on the position of the separated woman and the earning of a living by writing; its heroine is a self-made professional and a central text of late-Victorian feminism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
works.context: The 1880s, the Married Women's Property Act of 1882, the position of the separated woman, the law of libel and the political press. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Diana Merion (Mrs Warwick); Augustus Warwick; Percy Dacier; Thomas Redworth; Lady Emma Dunstane; Sir Lukin Dunstane; Lord Dannisburgh; Arthur Rhodes; Mr Tonans, the editor
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Dido, Queen of Carthage
works.description: Marlowe's earliest surviving play, written with Thomas Nashe, from Virgil's Aeneid: Aeneas, shipwrecked at Carthage, tells Dido the tale of Troy's fall; she loves him, he is commanded away by Jove, and her suicide on the pyre ends the play — a tragedy of love's rhetoric and the gods' indifference, performed by the Children of the Chapel.
works.plot: Venus disguises herself to guide Aeneas ashore; the courtship in the cave, the rivalry with Iarbas, and the recital of Priam's fall fill the middle acts; the false Ascanius (Cupid) kindles Dido's passion; the gods recall Aeneas; and Dido, abandoned, mounts the pyre with his gifts and dies cursing him.
works.significance: The seed of English classical tragedy — Marlowe's and Nashe's schoolroom Virgil become a stage poem of love and abandonment.
works.meter: Blank verse of a chamber-music delicacy suited to the children's company, with the speeches of Dido's grief as its lyric summit.
works.context: Probably written at Cambridge in the mid-1580s and revised for the Children of the Chapel; printed in 1594 with both names on the title page.
works.characters: Dido; Aeneas; Anna; Iarbas; Achates; Venus; Juno; Jupiter; Cupid (as Ascanius); the Nurse
works.structure: A five-act tragedy for boy players, structured on the Virgilian books I–IV, with the great set piece of Aeneas's narration of Troy at its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Title page assigns the play to Marlowe and Nashe jointly; the division of scenes is uncertain.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Digby Mary Magdalene
altTitles: The Digby Play of Mary Magdalene
works.description: The most ambitious of the English saints' plays (c. 1480–1500, 2,139 lines): the life of Mary Magdalene from her worldly grandeur and conversion through her apostolate in Marseilles to her thirty years as a desert hermit fed by angels. Its multiple locations, ship voyages, and spectacular effects make it the fullest surviving English drama of a female saint.
works.plot: Mary, the proud lady of Magdalene castle, falls into lechery; Christ's grace converts her, and after the Passion she sails to Marseilles, converts the king and queen, raises the queen from death, and converts the pagan priest; retiring to the wilderness, she is fed by angels, receives the last rites, and her soul is borne to heaven.
works.significance: The fullest English female saint's play and the most elaborately staged of the East Anglian dramas; its conversion and travel plot is a summit of the miracle play tradition.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with macaronic Latin in the liturgical scenes.
works.context: Composed c. 1480–1500 in East Anglia, in the flourishing of the Mary Magdalene cult; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 133 (c. 1512), with The Conversion of St Paul and the morality Wisdom.
works.characters: Mary Magdalene; Christ; the King and Queen of Marseilles; the pagan priest; the angels; the devils
works.structure: A multi-location saint's play in the continental manner, moving between Jerusalem, Marseilles, and the wilderness, with ships, temple, and heaven's scaffolds.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Dilemmas: Studies in Sentiment
works.form: Collection of short stories; modern short story
works.description: Published in 1895 and Dowson's finest prose: a collection of stories of moral and emotional exhaustion, in the manner of Pater and Huysmans. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Ernest Dowson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale.
works.plot: The stories include 'A Case of Conscience', 'The Diary of a Successful Man', 'An Orchestral Violin' and 'The Statute of Limitations', and each turns on a moment of recognition in which the protagonist sees the emptiness of his life.
works.significance: Dilemmas is the finest collection of English Decadent short stories and the prose counterpart to Dowson's verse: its study of emotional exhaustion made it a key text of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short lyric metres of great smoothness.

The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.

works.title: Dipsychus
works.form: Dramatic poem in blank verse and lyrics (posthumous)
works.description: Written in Venice in 1850 and published posthumously in 1865: a dramatic poem in which the earnest, divided Dipsychus is tempted by the cynical Spirit of the world through the streets, canals and churches of Venice.
works.plot: Dipsychus, an idealist, is accompanied by a Spirit who argues for pleasure, compromise and the acceptance of the world as it is; the poem moves through Venice's carnival, a ball, a church and the lagoon, and ends without resolving the argument, in a chorus of resignation.
works.significance: Dipsychus is the most sophisticated Victorian treatment of the divided self in dramatic form, and its Spirit is the ancestor of the ironic tempter in modern verse drama; its uncompleted state and its refusal of a moral answer make it a key document of Victorian scepticism.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms.
works.context: Venice in 1850 under Austrian rule, the Victorian debate between earnestness and worldliness, and the 'spirit of the age' as a literary commonplace of the 1840s-50s. The record dates the work as composed in 1850 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Dipsychus; the Spirit
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: Discipline
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's second novel, a philosophical Gothic romance set in the Tyrol and Italy, in which the heroine Rosalie endures a protracted spiritual discipline that tests Calvinist conviction against Catholic ecclesiastical authority. More ambitious and theologically complex than Self-Control, it treats the soul's education as a Gothic ordeal.
works.plot: Rosalie, daughter of the Marchese di Saxe-Roseneck, is subjected from childhood to a harsh regimen intended to break her pride and inculcate submission. Her education moves through Catholic institutions where Protestant conscience clashes with ecclesiastical authority; she suffers poverty, proselytising pressure, and romantic entanglement with the Marchese di Breme. Her spiritual discipline culminates not in the passive endurance of her father's plan but in a hard-won, reasoned faith. The novel treats the progress from enforced submission to chosen belief as the true work of grace.
works.significance: Discipline is the most theologically serious of the author's fictions and one of the finest Scottish novels of the 1810s; its argument about the education of conscience through suffering anticipated Victorian religious fiction and remains central to reassessments of Romantic-era women's philosophical writing.
works.context: Published in 1814 as the Napoleonic wars were ending and British readers' interest in Catholic Europe was intense. the author's treatment of Protestant conscience under Catholic authority draws on Scottish Calvinist polemic and on the post-Godwin philosophical novel; its theology has been read as an implicit critique of Godwinian perfectibility.
works.characters: Rosalie di Saxe-Roseneck; the Marchese di Saxe-Roseneck; the Marchese di Breme; Madame d'Albinea
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative tracing the heroine's spiritual education through successive trials; the sequence of Gothic ordeals (confinement, forced marriage, proselytism) is unified by the governing metaphor of discipline.

themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning

works.title: Disquisitions relating to Matter and Spirit
works.form: Philosophical and theological disquisition in polemic form
works.description: The philosophical statement of Joseph Priestley's unitarian materialism, published in London in 1777 and gathering his earlier controversy with the Scottish common-sense school into a positive doctrine. Priestley argues that mind is a property of organised matter, that the soul is not naturally immortal, and that the Christian hope is resurrection rather than an intermediate state of separate spirits. Its combination of physiology, necessity and biblical criticism made it, in contemporary judgment, the most dangerous of his writings.
works.plot: Priestley first examines the evidence of consciousness and of physiology, and concludes that thought, memory and desire are inseparable from the brain, so that an immaterial thinking substance is an unintelligible hypothesis. He then defends philosophical necessity, arguing that the will is determined by the strongest motive and that virtue and happiness advance by the same mechanism of association which Hartley had described. Against Reid, Beattie and Oswald he denies innate ideas and the authority of common sense in metaphysics, insisting that all belief is built on experience and testimony. Finally he turns to Scripture and shows that the hope of the Bible is a resurrection of the body, that the wicked are destroyed rather than tormented for ever, and that the popular philosophy of the soul supports a corrupt religion of selfishness.
works.significance: It is the boldest English attempt to found a religion on matter, necessity and association, and it set the terms of the nineteenth-century debate over the soul in which its opponents were obliged to answer its physiology as well as its exegesis. Its defence of the mortalist reading of Scripture remains a reference point in the history of heterodox theology, and its psychology influenced the associationist and utilitarian tradition.
works.meter: Prose only, in a blunt, businesslike, argumentative Nonconformist style
works.context: Written in the Birmingham circle's long controversy with the Scottish school and with the Evangelical Revival, and in the aftermath of Priestley's Hartleian physiology and his founding of unitarian theology, it belongs to the materialist and necessitarian current of the English Enlightenment and to the Dissenting attack on the popular doctrine of hell.
works.structure: Composite treatise of disquisitions and reprinted controversy, advancing from physiology and the will through the critique of common-sense metaphysics to a scriptural theology of resurrection.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Joseph Priestley is established and undisputed.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The New Science and experimental philosophy
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: Dissertation on First Principles of Government
altTitles: Dissertation on the First Principles of Government
works.form: political treatise in pamphlet form; first-principles argument and constitution theory
works.description: A compressed summary of the author's political philosophy, first printed in an American newspaper and soon reissued as a tract in Britain, arguing that the rights of man are the only foundation of a lawful constitution and that hereditary government is a usurpation over the living. It is the plainest and most catechetical of the revolutionary writings, and it was used for a century as a schoolbook of democracy.
works.plot: The dissertation states first that the only moral bond of society is the interest of the living, and that no generation has authority over another; from this it follows that a nation has a right to frame and to alter its constitution at its will, and that the constitutions of men may be as various as the circumstances of men. It then distinguishes the rights of man from the powers of government, holds that all power improperly delegated is the origin of abuse, and treats hereditary succession as a fraud against the consent of the governed and a source of war. Representation is advanced as the true and simple device by which a nation acts, in place of the person of a king, and the argument ends with the claim that a government of this kind must be pacific at home and confederate abroad, so that the rights of nations and the rights of men are one system.
works.significance: It distils the natural-rights case into its shortest and most quotable form, and it supplied the vocabulary of nineteenth-century democratic and republican movements in both hemispheres. Its insistence that constitutions are ordinary social devices rather than inheritances is the plainest statement of the doctrine the romantic critics of abstraction were later to attack from the other side.
works.meter: Aphoristic, declaratory prose, largely free of ornament and built out of reiterated definitions; the manner of the public lecture and of the catechism.
works.context: Published in the year of the author's release from imprisonment and of the controversy over the constitution of the French Republic, and printed first in Philadelphia and then as a separate tract in London, where it entered the circulating libraries with the rest of the revolutionary literature. It was prosecuted in England along with the earlier political writings.
works.structure: A short dissertation in continuous sections without numbered chapters, moving from first principles to the criticism of hereditary government, then to representation, and closing on the prospect of a pacific system of nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its first newspaper publication and subsequent separate issues are recorded in the contemporary accounts.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Dives and Pauper
works.description: An anonymous prose treatise of c. 1405–10 in dialogue form on the Ten Commandments, in which the rich man Dives asks and the poor man Pauper answers — a vast compendium of moral theology, canon law, and social commentary, notable for its defence of poverty, its discussion of images and tithes, and its sympathy with reformist positions short of heresy. The great popular summa of fifteenth-century English orthodoxy.
works.plot: Dives, the wealthy layman, poses the hard questions of Christian practice — the worship of images, oaths, tithes, usury, the duties of the rich to the poor — and Pauper, the poor and learned clerk, answers each with doctrine, law, and exemplum, through all ten commandments.
works.significance: The most comprehensive vernacular treatment of the Decalogue in medieval England and a central witness to the social teaching of the late medieval church on wealth, poverty, and images.
works.meter: Plain, copious prose with Latin quotations translated for the lay reader.
works.context: Composed c. 1405–10, in the aftermath of Arundel's Constitutions (1409), by a learned clerk conversant with both orthodox and reformist positions; printed by Pynson (1493) and read into the Reformation.
works.characters: Dives; Pauper
works.structure: A sustained catechetical dialogue in ten commandments, with the social argument between rich and poor as its dramatic engine.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; a Franciscan authorship has been conjectured.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: Divine and Moral Songs for the Use of Children
altTitles: Divine and Moral Songs for Children
works.description: Watts's hymnal for children, the first English collection written in and for the childhood of the Christian family, divided into divine songs for children of the first and second degree and moral songs on duties and gentlenesses of life. It made childhood a subject and an audience of evangelical literature.
works.plot: The divine songs bring doctrine home to little capacities: God's glory seen in the world, the Saviour as friend of children, repentance, prayer before and after sleep, and the care of the season of youth. The moral songs teach temperance, cleanliness, truth, kindness to beasts and servants, the use of time, and the government of the tongue. Watts writes with the double voice of tenderness and fear, the child's own speech joined to a warn? use: joined to parental awe. The collection became the ordinary prayer-and-praise book of Victorian nurseries and the model of all child-evangelical verse.
works.significance: It founded the literature of childhood in English Nonconformity and gave the nursery its first canon of hymns; its influence runs through every later children's religious book to the Victorian period.
works.meter: Short iambic common and short measures of nursery simplicity, direct address and little rhymes of the most lucid Augustan plain style.
works.context: Published in London in 1715, the fruit of Watts's catechetical teaching in his congregations and of the new dissenting attention to children's education, a decade before the century's child-literature boom.
works.structure: A graduated collection in two main classes, divine and moral songs, subdivided by the age of the child, each poem one lesson of heart or conduct.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
Wisdom and learning
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Divinity School Address
works.description: Delivered on 15 July 1838 and the most controversial religious address in American history: an attack on the historical Christianity of the churches in the name of the soul's immediate access to God. It is a prose work of 1838 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Emerson tells the graduating ministers that the church has made Jesus a historical idol, that the miracles and the scriptures have replaced the inward revelation, and that the preacher must speak from his own experience of the divine or not at all.
works.significance: The Divinity School Address is the founding text of American religious liberalism: it scandalised the Unitarian establishment, cost Emerson his Harvard invitations for thirty years, and gave American Transcendentalism its theology of the soul.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered.
works.context: The year 1838, the Unitarian controversy, the Transcendentalist revolt against Boston Unitarianism, and the American revival of the 1830s. The record dates the work as composed in 1838 and first published in 1838 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
Science, religion, and the question of design
movements: Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum

works.title: Divorce
works.description: The American society drama: a divorce case and the double standard. It is a dramatic work of 1871 by Augustin Daly; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage.
works.plot: A fashionable wife discovers her husband's infidelity and sues for divorce; the play follows the case, the scandal and the reconciliation through the drawing rooms and the courtroom, in the most successful American society drama of the 1870s.
works.significance: Divorce was the most successful American society drama of the 1870s: its treatment of the double standard made it a scandal and a success, and it established Daly as the leading manager of the American stage.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made adaptation of the European play.
works.context: New York in the 1870s, the fashionable world and the American divorce courts. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: the wife; the husband; the lover; the lawyer; the fashionable world
works.structure: Five acts, from the discovery to the trial and the reconciliation. The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Augustin Daly. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage
