works.title: Doctor Faustus
altTitles: The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor Faustus
works.description: Marlowe's tragedy of the scholar who sells his soul: Wittenberg's Faustus, sated with all knowledge, signs away his soul to Lucifer for twenty-four years of Mephistopheles' service — and spends them on empty marvels, pageants of the seven deadly sins, and the phantom Helen, whose kiss is the play's summit ('the face that launched a thousand ships') — until the last hour's soliloquy and the devils' claim.
works.plot: Faustus conjures Mephistopheles, signs the bond in blood, and debates theology with the demon; the good and evil angels contend for him through the middle acts of farce and magic; his repentance is always deferred — 'I'll burn my books' never said in time — and the midnight soliloquy ends with the Scholars finding his 'mangled limbs'.
works.significance: The founding myth of modern damnation drama — the play that gave Goethe, and the world, the figure of Faust.
works.meter: The mighty line at its most lyrical — the apostrophe to Helen and the final soliloquy are the touchstones of Elizabethan blank verse.
works.context: Based on the German Faustbuch in its English translation (c. 1592); the play exists in two texts (the A-text of 1604 and the expanded B-text of 1616), and its conjuring scenes were blamed for real devils in the audience.
works.characters: Doctor Faustus; Mephistopheles; Wagner; Lucifer; the Good Angel; the Evil Angel; the Old Man; Valdes; Cornelius; the Horse-Courser; Robin; Rafe; Helen of Troy; the Scholars
works.structure: A morality play inverted: the psychomachy of the angels, the pageant of sins, and the Old Man's pleas all fail against the irreversible bond, in a structure whose comic middle scenes are partly the work of collaborators.
works.attributionNotes: Marlowe's authorship of the core is uncontested; the comic scenes include the hand of collaborators (probably Samuel Rowley and William Bird).
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Penance, confession, and sin
Wisdom and learning
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Doctor Thorne
works.description: Published in 1858: the Barsetshire novel most openly about money, in which the illegitimate niece of a country doctor turns out to be the heiress of the railway fortune of the Scatcherd family. It is a prose fiction work of 1858 by Anthony Trollope; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Dr Thorne's niece Mary, the daughter of his dissolute brother and of a Scatcherd, is loved by Frank Gresham, the heir of a ruined squire; Frank's family demands a wealthy marriage, and the novel follows their opposition until Mary's inheritance is established and the estate is saved by her fortune.
works.significance: Doctor Thorne is Trollope's most direct study of the marriage market and of the relation between landed and industrial wealth, and the novel is the best single guide to the economics of Victorian courtship. Its treatment of illegitimacy is unusually free of moralising for its date.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The railway contractors and the new industrial wealth of the 1840s-50s, the landowning gentry's debt, and the marriage market as the mechanism by which estates were preserved. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Dr Thorne; Mary Thorne; Frank Gresham; Squire Gresham; Lady Arabella Gresham; Beatrice Gresham; Roger Scatcherd; Louis Scatcherd; Augusta Gresham; Mr Moffat
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Doctor Zay
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1882
works.description: Published in 1882 and one of the first American novels with a woman physician as its heroine: the story of a doctor and her patient, and of the man who must learn to accept her profession. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Waldo Yorke, a wealthy young Bostonian injured in an accident in rural Maine, is treated by Dr Zay, a woman physician of independent means and professional authority; he falls in love with her and must come to terms with a wife who will not give up her practice.
works.significance: Doctor Zay is the founding American novel of the woman doctor and a key text in the history of American women's professionalisation: its treatment of the marriage of equals makes it one of the most advanced feminist novels of the 1880s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is domestic detail extended into the afterlife.
works.context: The 1880s: the first generation of American women doctors, the women's medical colleges, and the debate on women's professional work. The record dates the work as composed in 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Waldo Yorke; Dr Zay Lloyd; the people of her country practice in Maine
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Dombey and Son
altTitles: Dealings with the Firm of Dombey and Son
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from October 1846 to April 1848, the first novel of Dickens's maturity and the first in which the railway enters as a structural and symbolic force. It is a prose fiction work of 1848 by Charles Dickens; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mr Dombey, of the shipping house Dombey and Son, despises his daughter Florence and invests all his pride in his son Paul, who dies at Dr Blimber's school. Dombey's second marriage, to the proud Edith Granger, collapses when she elopes with his manager Carker, who is killed by a train at the novel's climax; Dombey is ruined by Carker's speculations, and is restored only by Florence's return with her husband Walter Gay and her child.
works.significance: Dombey and Son marks the turn from the comic picaresque of the early novels to the symbolic structure of the later ones, and its treatment of the father-daughter relation is the first full statement of Dickens's great subject — the damage done by the failure to love. The railway in the novel became a permanent feature of Victorian literary iconography.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The railway mania of 1845-47 and the collapse of speculative finance, the shipping house and the counting-house, and the new professional schools and nursing of the 1840s; the novel's railway death is the first great literary use of the train as an instrument of fate.
works.characters: Mr Dombey; Florence Dombey; Paul Dombey; Edith Granger; Carker; Walter Gay; Solomon Gills; Captain Cuttle; Susan Nipper; Major Bagstock; Dr Blimber; Polly Toodle
works.structure: Monthly-part narrative organised around the firm of Dombey and Son, with a double movement of loss (Paul, Florence) and recovery, and the railway as the machine of retribution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Don Juan
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Romantic verse romance and mock-epic satire in ottava rima; the libertine tale retold as a comedy of convention, with the digressive narrator of the familiar essay inside the romance.
works.description: The unfinished romance in sixteen cantos that rewrote the libertine legend as a story of a young man who is pursued rather than pursuing, and who is carried by shipwreck, captivity, war and court life through the whole geography of contemporary Europe. Its narrator laughs at every convention it passes, the sentimental, the romantic, the heroic and the fashionable, and its ottava rima gives the digression the same dignity as the incident. It is the largest comic poem in English between the mock-heroic age and the Victorian period.
works.plot: Removed from his school and shipped from Cadiz after an exposure in his mother's house, Juan is cast on a Greek island, loved and lost at sea, rescued by a pirate chief's daughter, sold into a harem in the south, and delivered at last to the camp before a besieged black-sea town, where his bravery wins the favour of an empress. She sends him on a mission to the capital, from which he escapes to the English fleet and reaches an England of country houses, drawing rooms and cant; the last cantos observe the great, their marriages, their duels and their dinners. Throughout, the poet quarrels with his own public, with the review press, with the fashion of sorrow and with the poets who succeeded to the laurel, and the dedication opens the poem with an insult that the publishers feared to print.
works.significance: It is the period's supreme achievement in comic narrative verse and the fullest Romantic critique of Romanticism's own postures, and its measure and digressive freedom were taken up by every later English poet attempting ironic romance. Its treatment of the slave trade, of war, of the harem and of the English country house made it a resource for the century's arguments about empire, gender and fashion, and its unfinished state has been a permanent challenge to editors and critics.
works.meter: Ottava rima, seven iambic pentameter lines rhyming abababcc, carried at a speed rare in the measure, with the closing couplet used for irony, for sententious aside and for the suspension of the story.
works.context: Begun at Venice in the late summer of 1818 and continued at Ravenna, Pisa and Genoa until the author's death in 1824, the poem answers the fashionable sentimental novel, the quarterly moral criticism of the previous tales, and the laureate school's providential verse. Its first two cantos appeared anonymously in 1819, the next three in 1821, and cantos six to sixteen were issued by a different house from 1823 to 1824, the main publisher having withdrawn; the notoriety of the author's domestic history made every canto a political event, and the poem was widely pirated and suppressed in lending libraries.
works.characters: Juan, a Spanish youth; the lady of the Seville intrigue; the pirate's daughter of the island; the southern harem lady; the empress of the northern court; the English lord and his fashionable circle; the narrator who appears as a character
works.structure: Sixteen cantos in continuous ottava rima, episodically progressive and held together by the narrator's voice; the first canto and its dedicatory preface state the poem's principles, and the later cantos break off in the middle of an address as the author's death ended the work.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the posthumous cantos were printed from manuscripts and fair copies, and the editors of the collected editions record the author's own cancellations, several of which were suppressed in the first issues for legal caution.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
The marriage market and the limited estate
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: Don Sebastian, King of Portugal
works.description: Dryden's last great tragedy, written after the Revolution of 1688, on the Portuguese king captured at Alcazarquivir, his enslavement in Morocco, and the discovery that the woman he loves is his own daughter.
works.plot: Don Sebastian, presumed dead, is enslaved to the Mufti Moluch; he loves Almeyda, who is revealed as his sister's daughter and thus his own child; both renounce the world and retire to a monastery and a convent.
works.significance: Dryden's most complex late tragedy and a veiled meditation on fallen kingship and the legitimacy of allegiance; the character Dorax, a Portuguese renegade, is his finest creation after Almanzor.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1689 and published in 1690, after James II's flight and Dryden's loss of the laureateship for refusing the oaths to William and Mary.

works.title: Donovan
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1882
works.description: The religious problem novel of the 1880s: a man's loss of faith and the woman who saves him. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Edna Lyall; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Donovan, a young man of strong feelings, loses his faith and is driven to despair; the novel follows his struggle with doubt, his love for a woman of simple faith, and his final reconciliation with life and with God.
works.significance: Donovan was one of the most popular religious problem novels of the 1880s: its treatment of doubt and its argument for unselfishness made it a bestseller and established Lyall as the central novelist of the liberal religious conscience.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the problem novel of doubt and conscience.
works.context: England in the 1880s, the controversy over Darwinism and the Broad Church conscience. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Donovan; the woman of faith; the sceptical friend; the mentor
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, from the loss of faith to the reconciliation. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: Douglas
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A Scottish tragedy of hidden birth, maternal love and fatal revenge, written by a minister of the Kirk and first seen in private performance at Edinburgh before its London production. It was the most celebrated and most attacked new tragedy of the mid-century, and its pathos was held to have regenerated the national stage.
works.plot: Douglas, a youth of unknown parentage nurtured in the house of Lady Randolph, loves her ward and is beloved in return, while the Dane Norval presses his suit upon the lady. Norval is discovered to be the destroyer of Randolph, the lady's first husband, and Douglas kills him in the revenge he does not understand. The recognition of Douglas as the lady's long-lost son comes too late, and he dies in her arms after the fatal discovery.
works.significance: It established the model of the highland and national tragedy for the following generation, was the vehicle of the age's most admired acting, and carried the argument about the theatre's moral authority into Scotland.
works.meter: Plain and elevated blank verse of the school of the older English tragedy, with the short sententious line and the apostrophes of maternal grief as its characteristic effects.
works.context: Seen privately at Edinburgh in 1756 and first played in London at Covent Garden in April 1757, in the season of the debate over the stage's morality and of the new Scottish literary confidence; its clerical author was attacked from the pulpit and defended in the press.
works.characters: Douglas; Lady Randolph; Norval the Dane; the ward who loves Douglas; the attendants and retainers of the Scottish house
works.structure: Five-act regular tragedy of recognition and revenge, the delay of the discovery providing the suspense and the closing recognition the catastrophe; the language is deliberately simple and grave.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in the accounts of the first London performance.

works.title: Dover Beach
works.description: Probably written in 1851 on the honeymoon at Dover and published in the New Poems of 1867: the most famous short poem of Victorian doubt, spoken by a lover to his beloved at the window of a house on the strait.
works.plot: The speaker describes the calm sea, the cliffs and the moonlit strait, and hears in the tide the 'eternal note of sadness'; he recalls Sophocles hearing the same note on the Aegean, and the poem turns to the 'Sea of Faith' that was once full and is now retreating, leaving the world a 'darkling plain' of ignorant armies clashing by night.
works.significance: 'Dover Beach' is the most quoted Victorian poem and the definitive lyric of the retreat of faith; its 'darkling plain' and 'ignorant armies' have become permanent English images, and the poem's structure of a private love scene carrying a public argument is the model for the modern meditative lyric.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The 1851 honeymoon, the geological and biblical criticism of the 1850s-60s, and the publication of the poem at a moment (1867) when the doubt it articulates had become a public controversy after Essays and Reviews (1860) and the Colenso affair.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Down and Out in Paris and London
works.description: Orwell's first book, published by Victor Gollancz in London in January 1933 under the pen name George Orwell, used here for the first time: a memoir in two parts of poverty in two prosperous cities, the first an account of destitution and casual work in the restaurant kitchens of Paris, the second of life on the road among the tramps, casual wards and lodging houses of London.
works.plot: In Paris the narrator's savings are stolen and his English lessons come to an end; he pawns his clothes, goes two days without food and looks for work with Boris, a Russian waiter, before becoming a plongeur, or dishwasher, at the Hotel X near the Place de la Concorde, whose caste system of managers, cooks, waiters and plongeurs and whose dirt behind the service doors he describes. He and Boris leave for a new Russian-run restaurant, the Auberge de Jehan Cottard, where he is unpaid for ten days and then works seventeen and a half hours a day; worn out, he asks a friend in London for work and is offered the care of a 'congenital imbecile'. In London the employers have gone abroad, and until they return he lives as a tramp, moving between lodging houses, Salvation Army shelters and the casual wards, or spikes, which a vagrant may not enter more than once a month, in the company of the Irish tramp Paddy and Bozo, a pavement artist with a literary education. The book ends with a catalogue of the lodgings open to the destitute and the narrator's conclusions: he has seen only the fringe of poverty, but will never again think all tramps drunken scoundrels or expect a beggar to be grateful.
works.significance: Reviewed favourably by C. Day Lewis, W. H. Davies, Compton Mackenzie and J. B. Priestley, who called it 'a valuable social document', the book sold slowly until Penguin printed 55,000 copies at sixpence in December 1940. Orwell maintained that he had 'exaggerated nothing except in so far as all writers exaggerate by selecting', and wrote in The Road to Wigan Pier that 'nearly all the incidents described there actually happened, though they have been re-arranged'; his introduction to the French edition calls the characters 'representative types'. Cyril Connolly later called the book no more than 'agreeable journalism', a judgement Orwell accepted.
works.meter: Plain first-person narrative, often tragi-comic in its account of the descent into poverty, broken by anecdotes told by other characters (Valenti, Charlie, Bozo) and by chapters of general reflection, such as the one on the plongeur as 'one of the slaves of the modern world'.
works.context: Orwell drew on his own experience after he gave up his post as a policeman in Burma to become a writer. He made tramping expeditions in and around London from the end of 1927, lived in the Latin Quarter of Paris in 1928-29, where he fell ill, was robbed and worked as a dishwasher, and on his return made further expeditions, ending with hop-picking in Kent in 1931. A first version using only the Paris material, 'A Scullion's Diary', was completed in October 1930 and rejected by Jonathan Cape; an enlarged typescript with the London chapters was rejected by Faber, where T. S. Eliot found it 'of very great interest' but not 'possible as a publishing venture', before the agent Leonard Moore placed it with Gollancz.
works.characters: the narrator; Boris, a Russian waiter; Valenti, an Italian waiter; Charlie; the patron of the Auberge de Jehan Cottard; Paddy, an Irish tramp; Bozo, a pavement artist
works.structure: Thirty-eight chapters in two parts, chapters 1-23 in Paris and 24-38 in London, ending with a catalogue of cheap lodgings and the narrator's general conclusions.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Dracula
works.description: Published on 26 May 1897 and the most influential horror novel ever written: the story of the Transylvanian Count who comes to England to found a new empire of the undead, and of the small company that hunts him down.
works.plot: Jonathan Harker visits Count Dracula in Transylvania and escapes; the Count ships to Whitby, where Lucy Westenra is drained and dies, and Mina Harker is bitten; Van Helsing, Seward, Holmwood and Morris pursue the Count back to Transylvania and destroy him at his castle.
works.significance: Dracula is the founding modern vampire novel and one of the most analysed texts in English literature: its treatment of empire, gender, sexuality and science made it the central text of Gothic studies in the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is epistolary and documentary collage.
works.context: The 1890s, the British Empire and the fear of reverse colonisation, the new science of blood transfusion and hypnosis, and the literary vampire from Polidori to Le Fanu. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; sensation novel.

works.structure: Epistolary collage of journals, letters, telegrams and newspaper cuttings, with Mina's typescript as the organising document.

works.title: Dramatic Lyrics
works.description: Published in 1842 as the third Bells and Pomegranates pamphlet and containing 'My Last Duchess', 'Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister', 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'Johannes Agricola in Meditation': the founding collection of the English dramatic monologue.
works.plot: Each poem is spoken by a dramatic character at a moment of revelation: the Duke of Ferrara exhibits his last duchess's portrait and reveals that he had her killed; the Spanish monk reveals his hatred in the very cadence of his prayer; Porphyria's lover strangles her and is sure God has not said a word.
works.significance: Dramatic Lyrics is the collection in which the English dramatic monologue became a distinct genre; 'My Last Duchess' is the most anthologised English poem of the century, and the collection's technique of letting a speaker condemn himself by his own rhetoric is the foundation of the modern poetic exploitation of dramatic voice.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The 1842 pamphlet market, the Victorian fascination with the Italian Renaissance, and the religious revival and its pathologies (the 'madhouse cells' of the two first poems). The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1842 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.characters: the Duke of Ferrara ('My Last Duchess'); the monk ('Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister'); Porphyria's lover; the Pied Piper of Hamelin; Count Gismond; Waring
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.

works.title: Dramatic Scenes, and Other Poems
works.form: Dramatic lyric and soliloquy gathered in a miscellaneous volume; poems of feeling in the manner of the period's humanitarian verse
works.description: The first published volume of the barrister-poet who wrote under the name Barry Cornwall, issued anonymously in 1819 and made up of short dramatic monologues and lyric pieces spoken by imagined persons in moments of strong feeling. The Dramatic Scenes give voice to lovers, mothers, outcasts, and historical or legendary figures in a single sustained utterance, while the Other Poems add songs and meditations on nature, memory, and death. The volume established the quiet, sympathetic, and deliberately unobtrusive manner that made Cornwall one of the most reprinted poets of the 1820s and 1830s.
works.plot: The volume has no continuous plot; it presents a gallery of soliloquies and lyrics. In the dramatic pieces a speaker addresses an absent or present listener at the crisis of a passion: a lover pleading or mourning, a parent sorrowing for a child, a rejected or exile figure declaring inner pain. The lyrics turn on recollection, the consolation of natural scenery, the pity aroused by human suffering, and the peace found in resignation. Recurring situations are patient endurance of wrong, the sanctity of tender feeling, and sympathy with the lowly and the erring.
works.significance: The volume announced Barry Cornwall as a leading voice of the gentle, sympathetic current in Romantic verse, and its dramatic soliloquies look forward to the Victorian dramatic monologue. Its reprints and its praise by contemporaries, including the pre-Raphaelites, kept humanitarian lyric of feeling before the reading public through the century.
works.meter: Chiefly regular lyric stanzas and blank-verse meditations in iambic pentameter, with some sonnets; the diction is simple, musical, and deliberately free of obscurity, and the prosody is smooth and end-stopped rather than experimental.
works.context: Published in the post-Waterloo decade when a humane, sympathetic verse of feeling circulated alongside the more radical and the more sublime modes of Romanticism. The author, a bench lawyer, wrote in the circle of Charles Lamb and of the Ollier publishing house that also issued the works of Keats and of Leigh Hunt; the volume appeared anonymously in an age when a poet of feeling could win readers without a famous name.
works.characters: lover-speakers lamenting parted or lost affection; a mourning parent; an outcast or exile pleading his cause; the meditative lyric speaker contemplating nature, memory, and death
works.structure: A collection ordered loosely by kind, the dramatic soliloquies occupying the opening and the shorter lyrics and sonnets following; each poem is a self-contained utterance with no framing narrative linking the numbers, so the progression is thematic rather than sequential.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1819; the authorship by Bryan Waller Procter under the literary name Barry Cornwall is established by later collected editions and by the author's own acknowledgement.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics

works.title: Dramatis Personae
works.description: Published in May 1864 and the volume that reversed Browning's neglect, selling 1,700 copies in the first year: containing 'Rabbi Ben Ezra', 'Caliban upon Setebos', 'Mr Sludge, The Medium', 'Abt Vogler', 'Prospice' and 'James Lee's Wife'.
works.plot: The poems range from Caliban's grotesque theology to the spiritualist medium Mr Sludge's self-exposure, from the Rabbi's affirmation of age and love to the widower's defiance of death in 'Prospice'; the collection is organized around the theme of the soul's relation to God and to the beloved.
works.significance: Dramatis Personae made Browning famous in his own lifetime and contains the poems by which the Victorian religious sensibility is best known; 'Caliban upon Setebos' is the great Victorian poetic treatment of natural theology, and 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' the age's most quoted defence of the imperfect life.
works.meter: Verse. works.title: Dream Days
works.description: Published in 1898 and the sequel to The Golden Age, containing 'The Reluctant Dragon' and 'The Olympians'. It is a prose work of 1898 by Kenneth Grahame; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume includes the famous tale of the boy who befriends a poetry-loving dragon and negotiates a deal with St George, and the elegiac essays on the end of childhood and the departure of the Olympians.
works.significance: Dream Days contains 'The Reluctant Dragon', one of the most perfect short stories in English for children, and its essays on the loss of childhood are the finest in the language between Lamb and the modern memoir.

works.title: Dreamers of the Ghetto
works.description: Published in 1898 and Zangwill's gallery of Jewish lives: a series of imagined portraits of figures from Spinoza to Heine. It is a prose work of 1898 by Israel Zangwill; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The volume presents episodes in the lives of Spinoza, Sabbatai Zevi, Uriel Acosta, Heine, Lassalle, and a company of modern dreamers, each caught at the moment when the vision of the ghetto meets the world outside it.
works.significance: Dreamers of the Ghetto is the most ambitious of Zangwill's books and a key text of the early Zionist imagination: its portraits of the great Jewish heretics and dreamers gave the movement a gallery of heroic ancestors and it remains a striking experiment in the historical portrait.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: Dreams
works.description: Published in 1890 and the finest of Schreiner's allegories: a series of dream-visions on hunters, strangers, women and death, written in a plain prose that has the quality of the Old Testament. It is a verse work of 1890 by Olive Schreiner; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Fable and Apologue.
works.plot: In 'The Hunter' a man glimpses the reflection of the white bird of Truth, leaves the valley of superstition to seek her, and spends his life cutting steps into the mountains, dying with a single silver feather in his hand; in 'Three Dreams in a Desert' the history of women is unfolded in images of a woman bound to the earth beside a sleeping man, and of a woman who crosses the river of suffering towards the Land of Freedom on a track worn by the feet of those who went before.
works.significance: Dreams is the finest body of English allegory after Bunyan and the most original work of the 1890s: its prose poems were read as scripture by the feminist movement, and they anticipate the dream-visions of the modern short story.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
works.context: The 1890s, the vogue for the prose poem, the English reception of the Symbolists, and the allegorical tradition of Bunyan. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under fable and apologue.

works.title: Dred: A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp
works.description: Published in 1856 and Stowe's second anti-slavery novel, and the more radical of the two: the story of a fugitive insurrectionary in the Great Dismal Swamp and of the southern families he haunts. It is a prose fiction work of 1856 by Harriet Beecher Stowe; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Dred, the son of the rebel Denmark Vesey, lives as a fugitive in the swamp and preaches a coming judgement on slavery; the novel follows the decline of the Peyton family, the villainy of the lawyer Jekyl and of Tom Gordon, and the fates of the enslaved families who are separated and sold.
works.significance: Dred is the central American novel of slave rebellion and the most radical of Stowe's books: it is the first American novel to make an insurrectionary black hero the centre of its moral vision, and it is a key text in the literature of slavery and resistance.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: Drum-Taps
works.form: Poetry collection; war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: Published in 1865 and the finest body of American war poetry: the poems written from Whitman's experience nursing the wounded in the Washington hospitals. It is a verse work of 1865 by Walt Whitman; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The sequence moves from the recruiting and the march through the battles, the field hospitals and the dead, to the assassination of Lincoln in the 'Lilacs' elegy, and ends with the reconciliation of 'Reconciliation'.
works.significance: Drum-Taps is the central American war poetry and the finest poetic response to the Civil War: its plain record of suffering and its sequence of mourning made it the model for the modern war poem, and the 'Lilacs' elegy is the greatest American elegy.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora.
works.context: The years 1861-65, the Civil War, the Washington hospitals, the assassination of Lincoln, and the American debate on the meaning of the war. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1865 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works
works.description: Joshua Sylvester's translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine: the creation of the world in the 'Divine Weeks', with the vast encyclopedic digressions on natural history, astronomy, and the wonders of the creation — published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608, the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.
works.plot: The first Week narrates the seven days of creation with their cosmic and natural digressions; the second Week (incomplete in du Bartas) follows the history of the world from Eden toward the redemption; Sylvester's translation renders the whole with a copiousness and inventiveness that made the poem a schoolbook.
works.significance: The sacred epic of the English Renaissance — a formative book of the young Milton and the chief English poem of creation before Paradise Lost.
works.meter: Rhymed verse of extraordinary lexical invention — Sylvester's coinages and compounds feeding the word-hoard of the next generation.
works.context: Published in parts from 1592, complete in 1608; du Bartas's poem answered the Huguenot wars with cosmic piety, and Sylvester's version made it the English Protestants' epic, read by the young Milton.
works.characters: God the Creator; Adam; Eve; the patriarchs; the personified Creation
works.structure: The 'Weeks' of the hexameral tradition — creation and history in epic form, with the translator's dedications and apparatus.

works.title: Dubliners
works.description: The founding book of the modern short story: fifteen stories of Dublin paralysis, and the epiphany as narrative technique. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by James Joyce; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.significance: Dubliners invented the modern short-story sequence and the technique of the epiphany: its fifteen stories, written in what Joyce called a style of 'scrupulous meanness', gave the short story its modern discipline, and 'The Dead' is the greatest short story in English of the century.

works.title: Dusty Answer
works.description: Lehmann's first novel and the great novel of first love: Judith Earle and the Fyfe cousins. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Rosamond Lehmann; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Judith Earle, an only child, grows up next door to the four Fyfe cousins and falls in love with each of them in turn; the novel follows her through Cambridge and London and the loss of her illusions, in a study of first love and its aftermath.
works.significance: Dusty Answer was Lehmann's first novel and made her famous overnight: its portrait of Judith Earle made the modern English novel of the young woman's consciousness, and it remains the great novel of first love in English.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the interior monologue of the young woman.
works.context: England in the 1910s and 1920s, and Cambridge in the years after the war. works.title: East Lynne
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1861
works.description: Published in 1861 and the most successful sensation novel of the century: a wife who elopes, loses her child, returns as a governess and dies of remorse. It is a prose fiction work of 1861 by Mrs Henry Wood; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Isabel Vane marries the lawyer Archibald Carlyle, is neglected by him, and is seduced away by the villainous Sir Francis Levison; she leaves her children, is disowned, loses her son in a railway accident, returns disguised as a governess to her own former home, and dies of grief and illness after seeing her daughter.
works.significance: East Lynne was the most successful sensation novel of the century and one of the most performed plays in English: it fixed the pattern of the domestic sensation plot, its portrait of the erring wife and the lost child made it a permanent Victorian myth, and its sales and stage adaptations made Mrs Henry Wood one of the most popular novelists in the world.

works.title: Eastward Ho
works.description: The city comedy of 1605 by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston: the goldsmith's virtuous apprentice Golding prospers while the prodigal Quicksilver and the usurer Security speculate their way toward Virginia; Quicksilver's voyage ends in shipwreck on the Isle of Dogs and the counter, and the play ends with the prodigal's repentance — though not before its satire of the Scots landed the authors in prison.
works.plot: Touchstone the goldsmith divides his world between the good apprentice and the bad; Quicksilver drinks, cheats, and embarks for Virginia; the storms, the shipwreck, and the counter follow; Golding marries Touchstone's daughter and prospers; and the final scene distributes justice, mercy, and the play's famous verdicts on London's vices.
works.significance: The great satire of Jacobean London's money-madness and colonial fever — a collaboration of the age's three sharpest pens.
works.meter: Prose and blank verse in the collaborative mix, with Quicksilver's repentant ballad in the counter as its remembered set piece.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605; its gibes at the new Scots courtiers offended James I, and Chapman and Jonson were imprisoned for it — Marston escaping arrest — the most famous censorship case of the Jacobean stage.
works.characters: Touchstone; Golding; Quicksilver; Security; Mistress Touchstone; Gertrude; Mildred; Sir Petronel Flash; Winifred; Sindefy; the Captain; the Scrivener
works.structure: A five-act city comedy on the Jonsonian model, with the Virginia voyage as its satirical engine and the last act's trial-and-pardon as its resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston, as stated in the stationers' records; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.

works.title: Edgar Huntly; or, Memoirs of a Sleep-Walker
works.form: Gothic sleep-walking tale and frontier captivity narrative in epistolary form
works.description: The author's most violently imaginative tale and the first American fiction to make the western forest a theatre of the unconscious. A sleep-walker pursues a murderer through the Pennsylvania wilderness and wakes to find himself the agent of the violence he thought he was investigating. It fuses the frontier captivity narrative with the German source-stories of somnambulism.
works.plot: Edgar Huntly, living in a remote settlement with his friend Clitheroe, falls asleep while keeping a night-watch and, walking in his sleep, is attacked by a panther. Clitheroe, an English emigrant haunted by the accidental killing of a patron's son and by a love he believes he has forfeited, disappears into the woods after a night of somnambulism. Huntly follows him across the frontier, is captured by a party of Delaware warriors, escapes, and in a nocturnal trance kills sleeping men whom he takes for his enemies. The story ends with Clitheroe confessing from a prison cell, while Huntly's own responsibility for the deaths remains agonizingly unresolved.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the American wilderness as a figure for divided mind, anticipating later tales of sleepwalking, murder and pursuit. Its use of Indian capture reversed the older captivity formula by making the hero's own violence the real horror. It is central to the reputation of the American Gothic of the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written on the edge of the Pennsylvania and Virginia frontiers where settler and Indian violence was a daily report in the newspapers. It borrows its medical framing from the new literature on somnambulism and dream. The political subtext concerns the displaced Delaware and the failure of treaty obligations in the trans-Allegheny west.
works.characters: Edgar Huntly; Clitheroe
works.structure: Epistolary memoir in three parts, addressed successively to a female friend and to the imprisoned confessor, so that testimony, dream and confession are all filtered through letters.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Charles Brockden Brown and the American Gothic

works.title: Edward II
altTitles: The Troublesome Reign and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second
works.description: Marlowe's history play of a king undone by favouritism: Edward's dotage on Gaveston and then on the Spensers alienates his queen Isabella and the barons; rebellion, deposition, and the murder at Berkeley Castle follow — the famous stage direction of Lightborn's red-hot spit — in the first great English tragedy of state and private passion.
works.plot: Edward recalls Gaveston from exile; the barons capture and kill him; the king's grief turns to the Spensers and to revenge on Lancaster and Warwick; Isabella and Mortimer invade, the favourites fall, and Edward is deposed, imprisoned, and murdered by Lightborn, while the play ends with young Edward III's execution of Mortimer and the lament over his father's bier.
works.significance: The first fully achieved English history tragedy of psychology and state, and the direct model for Shakespeare's second tetralogy.
works.meter: A blank verse newly capable of the political and the intimate — the abdication scene and the prison soliloquy are its heights — which taught Shakespeare the form of Richard II.
works.context: Written about 1592 from Holinshed; printed 1594; its deposition scenes and its treatment of favouritism and sodomy made it the riskiest of the chronicle plays.
works.characters: King Edward II; Gaveston; Queen Isabella; Mortimer the younger; the Earl of Lancaster; the Earl of Warwick; the Spensers (father and son); Edmund of Woodstock, Earl of Kent; Lightborn; Prince Edward (Edward III)
works.structure: A chronicle tragedy of rise, fall, and retribution in the de casibus pattern, notable for the equal weight given to the king's grief and the barons' politics.

works.title: Edwin and Morcar, the Earls of Mercia and Northumberland
works.form: Tragedy for the London stage, printed in the ordinary acting edition format with dramatis personae; regular acts; sustained blank verse dialogue with sententious declamation.
works.description: William Mason's first tragedy, written while he was still a young man in the north and played in London in the spring of his debut season. Its claim on literary history is less its plot than its metre: it is one of the first English tragedies of the mid century to be written throughout in blank (unrhymed) verse, at a time when the critics of the 'just rules' still treated rhyme as the polite default of the stage. The subject is drawn from the period of the Danish conquest of England, and the two titular earls are offered as native, Saxon virtue under pressure from a foreign invader.
works.plot: The action turns on the Danish invasion of England and on the obligation of the great northern and midland earls to resist it while maintaining their honour at a hostile court. Edwin and Morcar are placed between the demands of patriotic resistance and the private ties of affection and friendship, so that the political crisis tests personal loyalty as much as it tests arms. As befits an early work by a poet more thoughtful than clever, the intrigue is relatively plain and the interest is carried by declarations of virtue, of friendship and of national spirit. The play's real argument is made in its preface and in its practice: that English tragedy should recover the 'native and sublime' dignity of unrhymed measure rather than submit to the tunnery of couplets.
works.significance: It is a landmark in the reinstatement of blank verse on the English stage, a development that runs from this play through Mason's Caractacus and the Shakespeare revivals of the 1740s and 1760s to the tragedies of the following generation. Its Saxon-patriotic matter also feeds the mid-century vogue for a native, 'British' antiquity as a source of moral and theatrical sublimity.
works.meter: Blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter, end-stopped and carefully accented, in the deliberate, 'meditated' manner Mason preferred, without the running enjambment of the later Shakespearean revivals.
works.context: It belongs to the 1740s efflorescence of British and Saxon subjects on the stage and to the contemporaneous quarrel over rhyme in dramatic verse, in which Joseph Warton and the editors of periodical reviews pressed the case for blank measure while neoclassical judges thought it harsh. Mason, a country clergyman and then a tutor, wrote as an amateur in the respectable sense, and his success encouraged the same blank-verse tragic experiment he pursued again in Caractacus.
works.characters: Edwin, Earl of Mercia; Morcar, Earl of Northumberland
works.structure: A regular five-act tragedy in the neo-classical arrangement, with the political and amatory plots running in parallel and resolved by the close; the printed edition is preceded by dedication and prefatory matter in which the author defends his choice of measure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with Mason's name and its authorship was never in doubt. The date of composition is not fixed by the surviving evidence and is left null rather than estimated.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
National identity and Englishness
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: Ego Dormio
altTitles: Ego Dormio et Cor Meum Vigilat
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle on the three degrees of love, written c. 1340 for a nun of Yedingham (or a recluse of his circle): a lyrical meditation, interspersed with the lyric 'My king that water grette', on the ascent from the love of God's creatures through the love of Christ's humanity to the highest love, which he describes as 'wonderful' — the experience he had felt at Hampole.
works.plot: Taking its text from the Song of Songs ('I sleep and my heart wakes'), the epistle teaches the recipient the three degrees of love — insuperable, inseparable, singular — describes Rolle's own experience of heavenly song, and closes with the Passion meditation and the lyric of Christ's weeping for man's sin.
works.significance: The classic statement of Rolle's three degrees of love and a key text of the early English mystical epistles.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose with the lyric 'My king' in rhymed stanzas.

works.title: Eight for Immortality
works.description: The study of eight modern poets by their Georgian contemporary. It is a prose work of 1941 by Richard Church; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: Eight for Immortality reads eight contemporary poets in the ear of the Georgian lyricist, and states the case for their immortality in the plain critical sentence of the poet-critic.
works.significance: Eight for Immortality is a key document of the reception of the modern poets by their Georgian contemporaries: its eight readings state the case of the traditional ear before the modernist verse and remain a witness of the quarrel of the two poetries.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The author's characteristic manner is the plain observed lyric of the country and the season.
works.context: England in 1941, and the reception of the modern poets by their contemporaries. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1941 and first published in 1941 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A critical study in eight chapters, one poet to a chapter. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Richard Thomas Church. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Eikonoklastes

works.description: Milton's point-by-point rebuttal of the Eikon Basilike, the hugely popular devotional memoir attributed to the martyred Charles I; as 'the image-breaker' (eikonoklastes), Milton dismantles the royalist cult of the king's suffering and exposes the book's political purposes.
works.plot: Following the chapters of the Eikon Basilike, Milton answers each pious self-portrait of the king with argument, scriptural counter-example, and political critique, denying Charles the status of martyr and the book its authority.
works.significance: A central text of the Eikon Basilike controversy and of Civil War print propaganda, important for understanding the battle over Charles I's image and the culture of polemic.
works.meter: Sustained, ironic, and forceful argumentative prose.
works.context: Commissioned by the Commonwealth in 1649 to counter the immense popularity of the Eikon Basilike; it forms part of Milton's official defence of the regicide alongside The Tenure.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter refutation in prose, mirroring and dismantling the structure of the royalist book it answers.

works.description: Seven one-act plays, published by Peepal Tree Press in Leeds in 1988 and edited with an introduction and notes by Susheila Nasta. Selvon turned several of his novels and stories into scripts for the BBC, and these plays bring to dramatic life characters first seen in The Lonely Londoners and Moses Ascending.
works.summary: Seven one-act radio plays about Moses Aloetta and his friends Sir Galahad, Cap and Harris in London.
works.plot: The publisher's description asks whether Moses Aloetta, after long hard years in 'the Old Brit'n', will ever save enough money to go home to Trinidad, and answers that he will not if 'those damn vagabonds and reprobates', Sir Galahad, Cap and Harris, his so-called friends, have anything to do with it. The plays stage dreams and schemes, summer gaiety and winter disappointments, the experience of the parents and grandparents of today's Black British children, with Selvon's humour and poignancy.
works.significance: One of two books that preserve some of Selvon's work for radio, of which South Asian Britain counts more than twenty plays.
works.meter: Louis James, reviewing the book in Wasafiri, called them vivid radio plays that teachers wishing to dramatise Selvon's colourful stories would welcome.
works.context: Wikipedia dates Selvon's conversion of novels and stories into BBC radio scripts to the 1960s and 1970s; the collection appeared in 1988, ten years after he left Britain.

works.title: Eleanor
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1900
works.description: Published in 1900 and Ward's most controversial novel: an American girl in Rome, torn between a career of religious scepticism and a Catholic lover. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Mary Augusta Ward; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Eleanor Burgoyne, a delicate and clever English widow, helps her cousin Edward Manisty, a brilliant, unstable politician, write a book defending the Papacy at a villa above Rome, and loves him; when Lucy Foster, a young New England girl of Puritan upbringing, joins the household, Manisty falls in love with her, and Eleanor, after a long struggle with jealousy, gives him up and, dying, brings the two together.
works.significance: Eleanor was Ward's most discussed late novel and one of the most intelligent treatments of religious choice in English fiction: it dramatises the conflict between the aesthetic appeal of Catholicism and the claims of intellectual freedom, and it shows her at the height of her powers as a novelist of ideas.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of ideas with a large social canvas.
works.context: 1900: the American colony in Rome, the modernist crisis in the Catholic Church, and the debate over religious authority at the turn of the century. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Eleanor Burgoyne; Edward Manisty, her cousin; Lucy Foster
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems
works.form: Romantic Sonnet Revival; Sonnet Sequence; Elegy
works.description: Charlotte Smith's first book and the volume that made her name: a collection of sonnets and shorter lyrics from the pen of a wife and mother turned professional writer. The poems give voice to a woman dispossessed of home and expectation, addressing the seaside, the night, melancholy, lost hope, and the ruins of her family's property claims. Reissued throughout the 1780s and 1790s in enlarged editions that added new sonnets, it established the sonnet as a vehicle of female distress and made Smith the most imitated poetic voice of her decade.
works.plot: The volume gathers self-contained lyric meditations rather than a narrative. Sonnets complain of fortune, of a love fixed on an unattainable or departed object, of exile from home and from a paternal inheritance, and of the consolation offered by landscape, solitude, and the contemplation of death; poems addressed to the sea, to the moon, to melancholy, and to deceased friends carry the argument that sensibility and poverty are the true education of the poet. Later issues added new sonnets and prose matter, enlarging the same repertory of complaint and consolation.
works.significance: Elegiac Sonnets is the founding book of the 1780s-1790s vogue for the sensibility sonnet and one of the most influential volumes of the preromantic and Romantic period; its identification of the sonnet with a feminine voice of bereavement and financial dependence shaped the form's revival by Smith's contemporaries and successors, including the writers of the Lyrical Ballads generation, and it created the public persona on which all her later fiction and poetry depended.
works.meter: Fourteen-line sonnets and shorter lyrics in iambic pentameter, with Smith's characteristic blend of Italian-style octave-and-sestet patterns and English closing couplets, and frequent exclamatory, apostrophic address; the diction is deliberately plaintive and musical, in the manner later reviewers credited her with helping to refashion for the 1780s and 1790s.
works.context: Published while Smith was legally dependent on her husband Benjamin Smith and fighting the generations-long Chancery suit over the inheritance she had brought into the marriage; her imprisonment-adjacent poverty and the King's Bench confinement of her husband in late 1783 belong to the same decade of crisis that the book's rhetoric of sorrow converts into publication. The sonnet, then a scarce and somewhat antiquated form, was being revived by a group of writers, and Smith's volume, repeatedly enlarged and reissued, became its best-known vehicle.
works.characters: the poet-speaker of the sonnets; an idealised absent beloved; departed friends and relations remembered in the elegies; personified Melancholy, Hope, and Fortune
works.structure: A collection, not a sequence with a plot: numbered sonnets and lyrics follow one another in an arrangement that stresses variety of mood rather than progression, so that the reader assembles a persona from repeated situations of mourning, seaside reverie, and disappointed hope.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; no serious dispute attaches to the volume, though the number and ordering of poems change between issues, so citations should specify the edition used.

works.title: Elegies
works.description: Donne's love elegies, modelled on Ovid's Amores: some twenty poems in which the speaker moves through the bedrooms, streets, and jealous households of an erotic London — 'The Perfume', 'The Anagram', 'To His Mistress Going to Bed', 'The Change' — with a frankness and irony that scandalized and defined the genre in English.
works.plot: The elegies dramatize an erotic career: seduction, jealousy, constancy debated, the farewell, the anatomy of love's changes — each poem an argumentative scene in the Ovidian manner, from the perfumed lover detected to the mistress commanded 'License my roving hands'.
works.significance: The most powerful English answer to Ovid's Amores and the seedbed of the Restoration's libertine couplet.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of colloquial force — Ovid's couplet crossed with the speech of the Inns of Court — with enjambment and parenthesis as the instruments of wit.
works.context: Written in the 1590s, the decade of the English Ovidian vogue and of the 1599 ban that burned Marlowe's and Marston's elegiac verse; Donne's elegies circulated in manuscript and were printed in 1633.
works.characters: the poet-lover; the mistresses; the rival; the husband; the father (in 'The Perfume')
works.structure: A group of poems in the classical elegy form, not a sequence, gathered posthumously; individual poems circulated widely in manuscript from the mid-1590s.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the canon and order of the elegies vary among the early manuscripts.

works.title: Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard
altTitles: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
works.description: Gray's meditation on the humble dead of a village churchyard, which reads the close of the day and the unremembered rustics as the proof that poverty hides merit, that the great die unknown to the poor, and that the tomb keeps its deposit without distinction.
works.plot: The curfew and the closing light leave the thoughtful man among the mounds; he pictures the lives the villagers were denied, the unbeached and unpraised worth and beauty that lie there, and prays that the neglected poor may find in his own low verse a memorial; the meditation turns at last upon a fellow mourner cut short of his years, and the poem closes with an epitaph.
works.significance: It is the most quoted and most imitated English poem of the century, the central document of the culture of feeling and of the thought of the obscure dead, and the schoolroom text by which several generations learned the elegiac temper.
works.meter: Quatrains of iambic five-beat lines in the Latin elegiac manner of the century's translation of the classics, with the balanced close, the postponed adjective and the hush of the evening stanza.
works.context: Printed in the middle years of the century's quarrel over the gloomy and the descriptive lyric, in the circle of the graveyard taste and of the antiquarian interest in the churchyard monument, and after the publication of the Eton ode had made the meditative stanza Gray's own.
works.characters: the dead of the churchyard; the rustic forefathers and the unnoticed women of the village; the neglected talent and the mute monument; the youth of the epitaph
works.structure: A continuous stanced meditation from the landscape of the evening through the general reflection to the wish for the poet's own memorial and the closing epitaph
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Elements of Chemical Philosophy
works.form: scientific treatise; systematic philosophy of chemistry with experimental evidence
works.description: The first attempt of the new chemistry to state itself as a complete philosophy, made out of the matter of its author's lectures by its most brilliant expositor; only the first part of the projected treatise appeared. It gathers the doctrines of the elements, of the atomic theory, and of electro-chemical affinity into a systematic account of the science, and it closes with the most quoted prospectus of the power of chemical discovery over the arts of life.
works.plot: The work begins with a statement of the objects and methods of chemical inquiry, of the distinction between the elements and the compounds, and of the evidence by which a substance is proved simple or compound, and it then enumerates the simple bodies known to the science with their sensible and measured characters. It proceeds to the doctrine of combination: the laws of definite proportions and the theory of the atoms, the nature of chemical affinity, and the order of the compounds, are stated as a system in which the philosophy of the science is separated from its technique. The middle divisions handle the chemistry of the gases, of the acids and the bases, of the metallic earths and alkalis, and of the saline and organic bodies, in a sequence of classes and of their mutual relations. The largest and most original part is the electro-chemical doctrine: that the attractions of chemistry are of the same nature as the electricity of the machine and of the great battery, that combination is a case of the union of the opposite electricities, and that the decomposition of the fixed alkalis and of the earths by the battery is the proof. The treatise ends with the application of the science to the arts, to manufactures, and to agriculture, and with the confident peroration that the day will come when the forces of nature shall be called to the service of man.
works.significance: It is the founding systematic text of the new chemistry in English, the book by which the electro-chemical dualism and the atomic doctrine were set before the British student, and a landmark in the literature of science as rhetoric: its closing passage on the command of the forces of nature became one of the most quoted sentences of the industrial age. Its influence on chemical teaching and on the practical chemists of the following decades is recorded in its many editions and translations, and its pages remain the best document of the imaginative habit of the science at the moment of its greatest expansion.
works.meter: Elevated and imaginative scientific prose, technical precision joined to a rhetoric of power, attraction, and life; the lecture manner of the greatest talker of the schools, with its enthusiasm kept within the definition.
works.context: Published in the year of its author's knighthood and at the height of his chemical work, out of the discoveries of the preceding decade, the decomposition of the fixed alkalis and of the earths, the arguments on the hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acids, and the great battery of the metropolitan institution; it belongs to the moment when the revolution in chemical nomenclature and the electrical researches of the author's own school had made a new statement of the whole science possible.
works.structure: A single large volume in numbered sections: the objects and elements of the science, the laws of combination and the atomic theory, the classification of the compounds, the electro-chemical theory, and the applications; the projected second part never appeared.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume is the first only of the treatise its author planned, and the matter of the unfinished second part appears in his separate papers and in the posthumous collections of his scientific writing.

works.title: Elements of Criticism
works.description: Henry Home, Lord Kames's systematic rhetoric and aesthetics of literary taste, grounded in the moral-sense psychology he shared with Hutcheson: the criticism of a work proceeds from the principles of the human mind which its beauties and faults act upon. It was the most used English handbook of criticism for half a century, on both sides of the Atlantic.
works.plot: Kames first establishes that the fine arts operate on the mind through emotion and the perception of beauty and deformity, not through instruction alone, and derives a grammar of the passions and of taste. He then analyses the province of criticism: the distinction of the just from the false in judgment, the characters of style, sublimity and beauty, the emotions excited by composition, and the theory of figurative language. The treatise proceeds through the species of writing, the drama, epic and lyric poetry, and wit, every rule referred to experience of the mind's operative principles. The critic's office is thus to trace the effect of every artifice by the anatomy of the human understanding, and the book closes on the unity of taste grounded in a common mental structure.
works.significance: It defined the taste curriculum of the English-speaking eighteenth century and is the standard source for the century's rhetoric of the sublime, the beautiful, and the pathetic, the working manual of British criticism between Addison and the Romantic era.
works.meter: Neat, sententious, aphoristic prose of a judge's bench-cleanness, numbered propositions and compressed definitions, occasionally warmed by rhetorical passages.
works.context: Published at Edinburgh and London in 1758, naturalizing the French aesthetic tradition of Du Bos and the academy into Scottish moral-sense theory after Shaftesbury and Hutcheson; its authority is proved by its long use in schools and colleges on both sides of the Atlantic.
works.structure: A continuous series of short numbered chapters arranged as an anatomy of the mental principles exercised by literature, followed by the rules of the several species of composition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Elements of Political Economy
works.form: treatise of political economy; textbook of the abstract method
works.description: The compactest textbook of the Ricardian school, written to make the science of wealth teachable and to settle the controversies of the day by a few rigorous definitions. It states the doctrine of value, of wages, of profit, and of rent in the shortest and hardest form, and it argues that political economy is not the art of making a nation rich but the exposition of the laws according to which wealth is produced and divided.
works.plot: The elements first define wealth as the things useful and agreeable which are the objects of desire and the subjects of production, and political economy as the science of those phases of human conduct which arise from wealth; they then distinguish productive from unproductive labour, and show that the produce of a country is made up of rent, profits, and wages, divided among the three classes of proprietors, capitalists, and labourers. The doctrine of value is settled by labour, and the celebrated argument on demand proves that demand is not the creator of production but only the rule by which the quantities of the several commodities are adjusted to the wishes of the consumers, so that the notion that public or charitable expenditure can enrich a nation by stimulating demand is exposed as a fallacy. Wages are determined by the proportion of population to capital, profits by the cost of maintaining labour and by the fertility of the marginal land, and rent is the excess of the produce of the better lands, which rises with the progress of population and falls with its relief from foreign supply. The closing chapters apply these principles to the corn laws, to taxes, to colonies, and to the currency, and argue that every device for the protection of one class at the cost of the whole is a mistake in science as well as an injustice.
works.significance: It became the standard elementary text of the classical political economy, the book by which a generation was first taught the science, and the source of the 'elements' style of exposition which the abstract method made dominant. Its wages-fund doctrine, its treatment of value by labour, and its argument against the demand fallacy remained points of controversy for the hundred years of the science.
works.meter: Taut, catechising, axiomatic prose, without illustration or apology: definition, proposition, and consequence, with a plain contempt for the fallacies of popular reasoning.
works.context: Published in the year of the Ricardian ascendancy and of the quarrel over the corn bill, in a cheap series designed to carry the science to the educated general reader, and written by a man whose history of the empire had just established his official reputation. Its most quoted doctrine, that demand does not regulate production, was aimed at the current arguments for public spending and for the protection of agriculture.
works.structure: A short treatise in numbered sections, opening with the definitions and divisions of the science, proceeding through production, value, wages, profit, and rent, and closing with the applications to legislation, in the order of a syllabus for the lecture room and the examining board.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the later editions, one of which received notes and an appendix from the author's son, are the ground of the only bibliographical question, which concerns the edition and not the writing.
