works.title: Elene
altTitles: The Finding of the True Cross
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's longest signed poem (1,321 lines), on the legend of the Finding of the True Cross: the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, journeys to Jerusalem, compels the Jews to reveal the site of the Crucifixion, and recovers the cross. The poem is a masterpiece of typological narrative, casting Helena as a heroic queen and the cross as the sign of victory.
works.plot: Constantine, granted a vision of the cross before battle, sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem; her search, the interrogation of the Jew Judas (who resists, is imprisoned, converted by a sign, and baptized as Cyriacus), the miraculous finding of the three crosses, the proof by resurrection of a dead youth, the conversion of the Jews, and Helena's building of churches; the epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature and his meditation on judgment and poetry.
works.significance: The richest treatment in early English poetry of the cross as sign of victory; the locus classicus of Cynewulf's typological art.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is among the most ornate in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 121v-133v); based on the Latin Acta Cyriaci tradition of the Inventio crucis legend.

works.title: Eloisa to Abelard
works.description: Pope's verse epistle from Heloise to Abelard, written in the Ovidian manner as a confession of a love that the convent cannot extinguish; the poem analyses the passion of religious and erotic love confused in one mind.
works.plot: Eloisa, abbess in the cloister, writes to the man who has abandoned her to her vows: she recounts her education and their love, argues with her own guilt, and resolves finally to preserve his fame by her silence and her unhappiness.
works.significance: It gave English poetry its most quoted study of a woman's divided consciousness, and it became the standard model for the poetic epistle of feeling for half a century.
works.meter: Heroic couplets made nervous by exclamation, apostrophe and broken syntax, the periodic closure repeatedly delayed by the passion it describes.
works.context: Written after the letters of Abelard and Heloise had been made English and adapted by the early-eighteenth-century theatre, and in the same season as the controversy over female desire and the convent in the Gothic and sentimental tale.
works.characters: Eloisa; Abelard
works.structure: A single letter in verse, progressing from address to narrative memory, to self-examination and passion's quarrel with duty, to a closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Melancholy and self-analysis
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules
Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: Elsie Venner: A Romance of Destiny
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1861
works.description: The first American medical novel: a girl poisoned before birth by a snakebite. It is a prose fiction work of 1861 by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Naturalist and Determinist Novel.
works.plot: Elsie Venner, whose mother was bitten by a rattlesnake while pregnant, is born with a serpent nature; the young doctor who loves her tries to cure her, and the novel ends with her death and the moral question of inherited sin.
works.significance: Elsie Venner was the first American medical novel and one of the first novels in English to make heredity its subject: it anticipates the naturalist novel and the psychological case study, and it conducted the argument over original sin in fictional form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the discursive table-talk of the breakfast room.
works.context: New England in the 1850s, the Calvinist doctrine of original sin and the new science of heredity. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1861 and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Elsie Venner; Dr Bernard Langdon; Helen Darley; the Rev. Mr Fairweather
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the school to the diagnosis and the death. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oliver Wendell Holmes. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
Science, religion, and the question of design
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
movements: Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance

works.title: Emaré
works.description: A Breton lay on the Constance legend: the princess Emaré, cast out by her incestuous father, drifts across the sea in a boat with her child, and through the marvellous cloth she weaves and the recognitions it brings, is restored to her husband and kingdom. The legend Chaucer used for the Man of Law's Tale, told as a fairy-tale of patient suffering.
works.plot: Emaré, given a magic cloth by the emperor, refuses her father's marriage proposal and is set adrift; she marries the king of Galys, is slandered by her wicked mother-in-law and cast out again with her son Segramour; after years in Rome, her husband finds her and all are reconciled.
works.significance: The most artful English version of the Constance story and a central text for the romance's treatment of incest, exile, and female patience.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, from the Constance legend (ultimately Trivet's chronicle, as in Chaucer); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Emaré; her father the emperor; the king of Galys; the wicked mother-in-law; Segramour
works.structure: A double exile-and-return plot organized by the magic cloth and the repeated sea voyages, in the Constance tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Marriage and women's conduct
sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: Emblems
works.description: Francis Quarles's emblem book (1635), the most popular work of verse in seventeenth-century England, in which each of five books pairs an engraved emblem with a biblical motto, epigram, and moral verse, making religious meditation vivid and accessible to a mass readership.
works.plot: Each emblem presents a picture and motto drawn from scripture (largely the Song of Songs, Job, and Hosea) followed by meditative verse that moralises the image for the reader's devotion.
works.significance: Emblems shaped the popular religious imagination of the period and influenced Bunyan's allegory; it is the classic English emblem book and a key text of devotional culture.
works.meter: Varied verse forms (quatrains, couplets) accompanying engraved emblems, in a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely style.
works.context: Published in 1635 and reprinted constantly through the century and beyond; it was read by the devout and by Bunyan, and was both hugely popular and later critically scorned.
works.characters: the soul; Christ; biblical figures
works.structure: Five books of emblem-and-verse units, adapted from the Jesuit emblem books of Hugo Pia and others.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Penance, confession, and sin
The contemplative life
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: Commonwealth and Interregnum Literature
The Caroline Theatre

works.title: Eminent Victorians
works.description: The book that invented modern biography: Manning, Florence Nightingale, Arnold and General Gordon, reduced to human size. It is a prose work of 1918 by Lytton Strachey; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Biography and the Modern Life; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Strachey's four short lives — Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold of Rugby and General Gordon — use irony, psychology and the revealing scene to dismantle the Victorian ideal of the great man, and the book ends with Gordon's death at Khartoum.
works.significance: Eminent Victorians invented modern biography: its irony, its psychological penetration and its use of the revealing detail changed how lives are written, and every twentieth-century biographer who debunks or humanises a subject works in its debt.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. The author's characteristic manner is the short, ironic, epigrammatic life.
works.context: The First World War, which had destroyed the Victorian world the book dismantles, and the Bloomsbury reaction against Victorian earnestness. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1918 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under biography and the modern life; critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: Cardinal Manning; Florence Nightingale; Thomas Arnold; General Gordon
works.structure: Four separate lives, each with a preface and a short bibliography. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Giles Lytton Strachey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Critical Essay and the Modern Review
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents
Religion, doubt, and the post-war faith

works.title: Emma
works.form: Comedy of manners and novel of moral education; an inversion of the conduct-plot in which the heroine's imagination, not her circumstances, is the obstacle.
works.description: A comic novel of a self-sufficient young gentlewoman who mistakes her own discernment for a right to arrange other people's lives, written in a deliberately narrower style than its predecessors: 'three or four families in a country village'. The plot is a slow education of the imagination in which every act of matchmaking is a misreading, and the discovery of the heroine's own feeling for Mr. Knightley arrives as surprise to her and to the reader. It is the most technically self-conscious of the Regency novels of manners.
works.plot: Emma Woodhouse, having persuaded her former governess to marry and resolved to continue as an amateur of destinies, takes the pretentious Harriet Smith as her project, discourages her from a respectable farmer's suit, and imagines her fit for the vain vicar Mr. Elton. The vicar's unexpected advance on Emma herself explodes the scheme, and the arrival of the lively, mysterious Frank Churchill, long linked by rumour to Jane Fairfax, generates a second set of false readings until the secret engagement of the two is disclosed. A botched picnic at Box Hill exposes Emma's cruelty to the dependent Miss Bates and draws from Mr. Knightley the rebuke that becomes the novel's moral centre; Harriet's alarming encounter with gypsies confirms Emma in her errors, and Knightley's jealousy of Churchill reveals the attachment Emma has never perceived in herself. Harriet is redirected to a suitable partner, Jane Fairfax married in secret no longer, and Emma united to Knightley with her father accommodated in the two families' shared household.
works.significance: The most complete realisation of the technique of ironic free indirect discourse, and a decisive model for the later novel of limited consciousness. Its treatment of a woman's imagination as a moral problem, and of marriage as a settlement of class as well as feeling, has made it central to feminist and historicist criticism. It is also the period's most explicit theorising of the novel of ordinary life in its own metacommentary about length and attention.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; dry, clipped sentence rhythms, with irony largely produced by reported thought rather than narrator comment.
works.context: Written in the last years of the Napoleonic Wars and published after Waterloo, its village of Highbury is an image of an England insulated from the continent; the elopement of Harriet with the gypsy band, which never happened, is a parody of Gothic plots still circulating in the periodical fiction of the 1810s. Its social anxieties about the Gentleman's class, the genteel spinster and the professional dentist belong to the expanding Regency middle rank. It was dedicated, at a command performance of sorts, to the Prince Regent's circle through the intervention of his librarian.
works.characters: Emma Woodhouse; Mr. Knightley; Harriet Smith; Mr. Woodhouse; Frank Churchill; Jane Fairfax; Mr. Elton; Mrs. Elton; Miss Bates; Mrs. Weston; Colonel and Mrs. Campbell
works.structure: Free indirect discourse carried further than in any earlier novel, so that the narration is coloured by Emma's errors and the reader shares her limited knowledge; long set-piece scenes (the ball, Box Hill) supply the plot's turning points.
works.attributionNotes: Published as 'By the author of Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, &c.'; authorship undisputed.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The marriage market and the limited estate
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems
works.description: Published anonymously in 1852 with 'Tristram and Iseult', 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (added in 1853), 'Memorial Versions' and the 'Switzerland' lyrics, including 'To Marguerite'. The title poem was withdrawn by Arnold from the 1853 collection.
works.plot: Empedocles, the Sicilian philosopher, has lost the power to think and act; he converses with Pausanias and with Callicles, whose songs celebrate the world he can no longer enter, and climbs Etna to throw himself into the crater. The lyrics 'Tristram and Iseult', 'The Buried Life' and 'To Marguerite' dramatise the same estrangement in modern English terms.
works.significance: Empedocles on Etna is the central English poem of Victorian unbelief and the work in which Arnold's classical method and his modern melancholy meet; the Preface to the 1853 Poems, in which he explained its withdrawal, is one of the founding documents of modern criticism, and the poem's portrait of the intellectual's isolation is the direct ancestor of the modernist long poem of the divided mind.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The 1850s and the Victorian crisis of faith; the Greek philosopher's suicide as an image of the modern intellectual's despair; the poem's withdrawal from the 1853 Poems because it offered no remedy, only a 'dialogue of the mind with itself'.
works.characters: Empedocles; Pausanias; Callicles; Tristram and the two Iseults ('Tristram and Iseult')
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: It was first published anonymously and the authorship was established afterwards from the publisher's records and the correspondence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: Enchiridion
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin and Old English
works.description: Byrhtferth of Ramsey's bilingual manual of computus and the related sciences (c. 1011), written in alternating Latin and English: the fullest surviving treatise on the Anglo-Saxon science of time — the calendar, the lunar cycles, number symbolism, and the harmony of the cosmos — composed for the instruction of the young monks of Ramsey.
works.plot: The manual explains the computation of Easter, the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac, the elements, the ages of the world and of man, the symbolic meanings of numbers, and the figures of grammar and rhetoric, all ordered to the liturgical year and the contemplation of the world's design.
works.significance: The richest surviving witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Bilingual prose with verse passages.
works.context: Composed 1011 at Ramsey Abbey by Byrhtferth, pupil of Abbo of Fleury; unique manuscript: Oxford, Bodleian Library, Ashmole 328.
works.characters: the young monks of Ramsey (addressees)
works.structure: Four books of didactic exposition, alternating between Latin and English, with diagrams and tables.
works.attributionNotes: Byrhtferth's authorship is certain (he names himself).
themes: Creation and cosmology
Wisdom and learning
movements: Benedictine Reform

works.title: Endymion
altTitles: Endymion, the Man in the Moon
works.description: Lyly's allegorical court comedy: Endymion's hopeless love for the moon-goddess Cynthia casts him into a forty-year sleep from which only her kiss can wake him; the intrigues of the sorceress Dipsas and the braggart Sir Tophas complicate the court, and the play ends with Endymion's awakening and the famous reading of Cynthia as the Queen whose 'virtue' the play mirrors.
works.plot: Endymion renounces Tellus for Cynthia; Tellus's jealousy and Dipsas's enchantment cast him asleep; his friend Eumenides quests for the cure, and the riddle of the fountain directs him to the kiss; the sub-plot of Sir Tophas's mock-chivalry and the pages' comedy runs alongside; Cynthia's kiss wakes the sleeper, and the play closes on the praises of her constancy.
works.significance: The most influential of the Elizabethan court allegories — the model of the dream-play of royal favour and disfavour.
works.meter: Prose for the court scenes, verse for the enchantments and the finale, with the songs of the fairies.
works.context: Performed at court in 1588 and printed in 1591; the play's veiled allusions to Leicester's fall and the Queen's favour have kept its allegory a critical puzzle for four centuries.
works.characters: Endymion; Cynthia; Tellus; Eumenides; Semele; Dipsas; Sir Tophas; Geron; Corsites; the Fairies; the pages (Epiton, Samias, Dares)
works.structure: A five-act court allegory with a fairy-tale centre (the sleep, the quest, the cure) and a burlesque chivalric sub-plot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Endymion (Disraeli)
works.form: Novel (political); realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1880 and Disraeli's last completed novel: the rise of a young man of no family in London politics. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Benjamin Disraeli; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Endymion Ferrars, the son of a ruined politician, begins as a clerk at Somerset House and is carried to the highest office by the women who believe in him: his ambitious twin sister Myra, who marries first the Foreign Secretary Lord Roehampton and then King Florestan, and the political hostess Lady Montfort, whom he marries; the novel follows his rise through the drawing rooms, the clubs and the press of the 1830s and 1840s to the prime ministership.
works.significance: Endymion is the most finished of Disraeli's political novels and the best picture of the London political world of the 1870s: its portrait of a young man's rise through society is a masterly study of the relation between politics and the drawing room, and it forms a pair with Lothair as his testament to his own world.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is epigrammatic dialogue and brilliant repartee.
works.context: 1880: the London of the Reform Club and the great political hostesses, the Eastern crisis of 1876-78, and the world of the 'social politics' of the 1870s. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Endymion Ferrars; Myra Ferrars, his twin sister; William Pitt Ferrars, his father; Lady Montfort; Lord Roehampton; Prince Florestan; Zenobia; Job Thornberry; Nigel Penruddock; Adriana Neuchatel; Sidney Wilton; St Barbe
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Benjamin D'Israeli. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story
themes: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital

works.title: Endymion: A Poetic Romance
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the elastic Spenserian romances of the older school and the episodic tale poem, with the interpolated song and the allegorical vision.
works.description: The author's first long poem, a four-book romance of the shepherd who loves the moon and must learn that the love of an immortal and of a mortal are one thing. Its opening sentence, that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever, states the poem's creed of endurance, and the fable of pursuit, despair and discovery is laid out in a succession of epodes, songs, cavils and visions. The book was written in haste and in the country, in the hope of making a living by verse, and its reception in the Scottish and metropolitan journals the same year was one of the mortal injuries of the poet's short life.
works.plot: Endymion, who has won the prize of a contest by the mountain and is loved for it, burns for the sight of the moon and abandons the company of shepherds to follow her shadow over hill, dale and sea. He descends in the second book to an under-water palace, where he is told of a rival's constancy and of his own trial, and in the third is led through a desert and shown the procession of Fancy's children before being warned by a voice that his quest is hopeless. The fourth book sets him in the power of Glory and of the tempter of the earth, from which the love of a woman, who has been given him as a shadow of the immortal, delivers him, and at the last the moon herself accepts him. The argument is that the love of beauty passes through earthly love and that endurance and sympathy are the education of the soul.
works.significance: It is the richest and most ungoverned of the period's romances in verse, and its creed of the enduringness of beauty became one of the most quoted moral positions of later aestheticism. Its failure in the reviews fixed the biography of the persecuted young poet in the popular imagination, while its diction, its songs and its under-water and desert visions mark the point from which the greater lyrics of 1819 were written.
works.meter: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter of a very flowing and often enfeebled kind, with songs in popular measures and an epode of longer lines; the line's movement is deliberately luxuriant and unargumentative.
works.context: Written mainly between the spring of 1817 and the January of 1818, at the house of a friend in the country and at the seaside, in the season of the poet's decision to give up the hospital apothecary's profession and live by his pen; it was published in the same year by the firm which had taken him on from the first publisher. Its attack in a Scottish journal and in the metropolitan critical reviews, which treated its luxurious diction as the fault of a school of London cockneys, was the beginning of the public war that the later lyrics and the hyperion poems were written to answer.
works.characters: Endymion, the shepherd in love with the moon; Cynthia, the moon goddess; the woman who is her shadow; the rival shepherd of the palace; Arethusa and the ocean powers; Fancy's children in the procession
works.structure: Four books of continuous romance, each opened by an epode or address and diversified by songs, a dream-vision, an under-water scene and a contest in the desert, with a long lyrical epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the drafts and fair copies, several in the hand of a friend, survive, and the poem was revised only slightly for the collections.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Early death and the mourning of poets
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Imagination as a way of knowing
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: Eneados
works.description: Douglas's complete translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots couplets, completed on 22 July 1513 — the first full translation of the poem in any British language — with a thirteenth book from Mapheus Vegius, and a prologue to each book in which the translator speaks of the Scottish seasons, his art, and his critics. Printed at London in 1553.
works.plot: Virgil's epic entire: Aeneas's flight from Troy, the wanderings, the tragedy of Dido, the descent to the underworld, and the wars in Italy — with Vegius's supplement completing the hero's apotheosis.
works.significance: The first complete British Aeneid and the summit of Scots humanist translation; its prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots, and the translation passed Virgil to the northern Renaissance.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in vigorous Scots; the prologues alternate aureate and plain registers with seasonal description.
works.context: Completed in the year of Flodden (1513), when the Scottish court and much of its nobility were destroyed; Douglas's translation of the epic of exile and foundation speaks to a nation in crisis.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Venus; Juno
works.structure: Twelve books of the Aeneid plus the thirteenth book of Vegius; each book preceded by a prologue, of which the seasonal prologues (VII, XII, XIII) are the most celebrated.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
The English vernacular and national letters

works.title: England in Time of War
works.description: The finest English poetry of the Crimean War: the soldier, the nurse and the home front. It is a verse work of 1856 by Sydney Dobell; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Dobell's Crimean War poems — 'A Shaft from the Battle', 'The Wounded', 'The Death of the Soldier', 'The Army Surgeon' — in which the war, the hospital and the bereaved home are rendered in vivid, contemporary verse.
works.significance: England in Time of War is the finest English poetry of the Crimean War: its vivid battle and hospital poems gave the war its most immediate verse record and anticipated the poetry of the First World War.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the spasmodic long poem of the tormented soul.
works.context: The Crimean War of 1854–56, the hospital at Scutari and the first war reporting. The record dates the work as composed between 1855 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: the soldier; the nurse; the surgeon; the bereaved mother
works.structure: A collection of lyric and narrative war poems. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sydney Thompson Dobell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: England's Birth-Right Justified
altTitles: England's Birth-Right Justified Against All Arbitrary Usurpation
works.description: John Lilburne's principal Leveller pamphlet, in which he claims that the free-born people of England possess an inalienable birth-right of liberty that no parliament or king may take away.
works.plot: Lilburne argues that arbitrary imprisonment, taxation without consent, the monopoly of the law, and the power of the great are all violations of the birth-right of every free-born Englishman, and that the people's representatives must be accountable.
works.significance: A foundational text of English radicalism and of the doctrine of popular sovereignty; its language of birth-right influenced the Leveller Agreements and, through them, later democratic theory.
works.meter: Fierce, urgent, colloquial prose of the pamphlet wars.
works.context: Published in October 1645 during the civil wars, while Lilburne was serving in the parliamentary army; it laid the intellectual foundations of the Leveller movement.
works.structure: A single polemical tract with a dedicatory epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lilburne; authorship undisputed.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Kingship and good rule
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: English Bards and Scotch Reviewers
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Augustan verse satire and personal catalogue; mock-heroic invective in the restored couplet, with the prosopopoeia and the retreating apostrophe of the didactic poem.
works.description: A verse satire in heroic couplets, issued anonymously in 1809, which answers the review journals and the living poets of the day in the manner of the Augustan satires of dulness. It moves from a general complaint about the decay of letters to a roll-call of named contemporaries, then to an attack on the critical ascendancy of the northern journals and on the booksellers who pay for reputation. The personal notes of the earlier volume's reception give the whole its motive of insulted honour. It was greatly enlarged in successive issues and then disowned, so that the poet's own collected editions ceased to print it.
works.plot: The satire opens on the degraded state of English letters and passes to a catalogue of the living poets, the lake school and its 'cast-off devotional' followers, the complacency of the laureate, the opium and unfulfilled promises of a distinguished critic-poet, and the merely popular singers, each disposed of in a couplet or two. It then turns on the reviewers of the northern journals, on the booksellers and their patronage, and on the Scottish critical dominance that had judged the first book. A passage of bitter prospect, of exile and of the writer's loneliness, gives way in later issues to an enlarged attack on the neoclassical school of the quietist critics and on the poetasters of the day. The argument is not systematic but cumulative: taste, money and criticism are shown to have corrupted each other, and the satirist claims the right to answer insult in kind.
works.significance: It showed that a poet of twenty-one could master the closed couplet of the age of Pope, and it installed the satiric personae that the later narrative and romantic irony of the Don Juan period would wear again. Its roll-call is one of the most quoted documents of contemporary reputation, and its history of enlargement and suppression is a case study in the revision of youthful malice by a famous author. It also fixed the quarrel with the northern journals that the pilgrim poem was to convert into a politics of exile.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, closed and antithetical, with triplets, alexandrines and a frequent satiric use of the name dropped into the line; the handling is consciously that of the late seventeenth and eighteenth century couplet school.
works.context: Published in the interval between the reviews of the first volume and the fame of the pilgrimage poem, it belongs to the rowdy Regency book trade in which anonymous personal satire was both a commercial and a legal risk. Its targets were the Edinburgh and Critical journals, the quarterly reviewers, and the lake poets, then at the height of their reputation, and its charge of northern usurpation voiced a real anxiety about metropolitan literary control. Its later suppression, at the point when the author's relations with the trade and with his former opponents were repaired, made the poem a notorious crux of self-censorship.
works.characters: the satirist-speaker; the personified Muse of England; the avenging figure of Cursery at the close
works.structure: A single continuous satire in the epistle manner of the Dunciad and the Art of Criticism, moving from general complaint to enumerated personal attack, with interpolated apostrophes, an argument in verse prefixed to the second issue, and notes added in the enlarged editions.
works.attributionNotes: Issued anonymously; attribution rests on the author's own later acknowledgement to a friend and on the revision history recorded in the manuscript and letters, and is uncontested in scholarship.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: English Songs, and Other Small Poems
works.form: Lyric song-book: short stanzic poems written to be sung or recited, in the popular English-song tradition revived by Romantic poets
works.description: A volume of short lyric songs and small poems by Barry Cornwall, issued in 1832 and gathering the compact, singable pieces for which the poet was best remembered by later Victorian readers. The songs treat love, parting, home, childhood, and the consolation of nature in an artless, melodious style that courts the air of the traditional English song. It is the clearest statement of Cornwall's gift for the brief lyric and the volume from which several of his songs passed into nineteenth-century anthologies and into recitation.
works.plot: The book has no argument; it is a sequence of independent lyrics. Individual songs address a beloved, lament absent or lost love, welcome sleep or the evening, recall the pleasures of childhood and home, or draw a gentle moral from a natural scene such as the falling of leaves or the sound of bells. The tone throughout is tender, melancholy, and resigned, with feeling kept within the limits of the simple song rather than carried to meditation or narrative.
works.significance: The volume preserved the short Romantic song as a living form and supplied later anthologies and reciters with some of Cornwall's most quoted lyrics; its emphasis on melody, simplicity, and sympathetic feeling anticipates the Victorian lyric song and shaped his reception as a poet of the heart rather than of the intellect.
works.meter: Chiefly regular song stanzas in common and short measure with simple recurring rhyme schemes, framed for melody and repetition; the lines are short, the accents even, and the diction deliberately plain and musical so as to imitate and renew the old English song.
works.context: Published at the close of the Romantic period, when the anthology and the recited song were reaching a wide middle-class readership and when Romantic lyricists were returning to the brief, singable lyric as a counterpoise to the long meditative poem. Cornwall's songs belong to this current of humane, melodic verse, and the volume appeared as his reputation as a poet of feeling was being consolidated by the collected editions.
works.characters: the lover who sings of presence and absence; the mourner of lost love or youth; the child or the voice recalling home; the speaker who draws comfort from evening, sleep, and natural scenes
works.structure: A miscellaneous collection of separate short songs and poems with no ordering principle or framing narrative; the reader moves from one self-contained lyric to the next, with variety supplied by changes of speaker, occasion, and mood rather than by sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name as Barry Cornwall; the volume's authorship by Bryan Waller Procter is established and undisputed.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: English Traits
works.description: Published in 1856 and the most acute American book on England: a series of chapters on the English race, land, aristocracy, universities, religion, literature and character, drawn from three visits. It is a prose work of 1856 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Emerson describes the English as a nation of shopkeepers with an instinct for the sea, a genius for the practical, and a brutal class system; his portraits of the aristocracy, the Toryism of the English mind and the English Sunday are comic, exact and unsentimental.
works.significance: English Traits is the best portrait of the English national character by an American and a key text in the literature of national character; it shaped the American image of England for a generation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
works.context: The 1850s, the Anglo-American literary relations of the period, the Great Exhibition of 1851, and the American debate on English institutions. The record dates the work as composed between 1847 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Ralph Waldo Emerson, the narrator; Coleridge, Wordsworth, Landor and Carlyle, whom he visits
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait

works.title: Ennui
works.form: National tale and domestic romance; a frame narrative of the post-Union Irish estate novel.
works.description: The most searching of the Irish tales of the post-Union decade, a story of an English-raised young nobleman whose listlessness is broken by the discovery that his Irish tenancy and his very title rest on a suppressed claim. It is a tale of identity, of the consequences of concealed evidence, and of what the writer calls ennui as a social as well as a moral disease. Its framing documents - letters and a deposition - make it a central instance of the period's edited Irish fiction.
works.plot: The hero, a young man of wealth and no occupation, wastes his time in England among friends who flatter him, and returns to his Irish estate where the claims of an old dependant family begin to interrupt his possessions. An attached narrative, put in the mouth of a half-witted Irish retainer whose shrewdness is the tale's engine, discloses the history of the exchanged child and of the evidence that would ruin him. The woman of the family who has loved him dies; his rival in claim recovers his own place; and the reformed hero, stripped of his assumed name, must build a life out of the loss. The tale ends in a marriage and in a hard-won purpose.
works.significance: One of the most subtle fictional analyses of Anglo-Irish property and identity before the famine novel, and a key document of the national tale after the first and best-known example of the form. Its use of an Irish oral narrator inside an English frame has been much studied. It supplies the period's fullest fictional account of boredom as a social condition.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; alternation of polite English narration with Hibernian-English oral storytelling.
works.context: Written in the years after the Union, when the settlement of the Irish Ascendancy's estates, the question of concealed title, and the education of a landlord class were pressing public matters. Its diagnosis of ennui is a diagnosis of a class with property and no function. The author's household background in law, estate management and educational writing supplies the tale's technical knowledge of evidence and claim.
works.characters: The young English-raised nobleman of the title; the Irish dependant whose claim displaces him; the faithful half-witted retainer who tells the family history; the Irish woman whose fate his idleness touches
works.structure: Framed and documentary: a main third-person narrative interrupted by an embedded Irish oral narration and by letters and papers; the embedded teller's voice carries the revelation that changes the plot.
works.attributionNotes: First published under a designation referring to an earlier tale rather than under the author's name; authorship undisputed. Certain details of the frame and of the naming of the principal characters are not asserted here.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Fortune and mutability
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography
The Cambridge Companion to British Romanticism

works.title: Enoch Arden, and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1864 and sold 17,000 copies on the day of publication: the story of a fisherman cast away for ten years who returns to find his wife remarried, together with 'The Northern Farmer' dialect poems and 'Aylmer's Field'.
works.plot: Enoch Arden is shipwrecked and lives alone on a desert island for more than ten years; rescued, he returns to find his wife Annie married to his rival Philip, and, unwilling to destroy their happiness, keeps his secret until on his deathbed he confides it to his landlady Miriam Lane. The volume also includes 'The Northern Farmer, Old Style' and 'New Style', dialect monologues, and 'Aylmer's Field', a narrative of avarice and vengeance.
works.significance: Enoch Arden was the most popular narrative poem of the century and the type of the Victorian verse tale read aloud in the home; it also contains the dialect poems that make Tennyson one of the earliest serious users of regional English speech in verse, a technique taken up by William Barnes and by the twentieth-century regional poets.
works.meter: Blank verse for Enoch Arden; the Lincolnshire dialect poems in rhymed couplets and rural measures.
works.context: The 1860s, the Victorian taste for the narrative poem as family reading, the Lincolnshire dialect of Tennyson's boyhood, and the emigration and shipwreck narratives of the period. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.characters: Enoch Arden; Annie Lee; Philip Ray; Miriam Lane; the Northern Farmer, Old Style and New Style; Edith Aylmer, Leolin Averill and Sir Aylmer Aylmer ('Aylmer's Field')
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm
works.description: Henry More's influential analysis of religious enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination, published in his Collection of Several Philosophical Writings and directed against the sectarian excesses of the Commonwealth.
works.plot: More identifies enthusiasm with the disturbance of the animal spirits, with melancholy, with ignorance, and with the pride of private revelation, and proposes reason, self-examination, and the discipline of the church as its cure.
works.significance: The standard seventeenth-century treatment of enthusiasm and a key text in the history of the psychology of religion; it influenced Shaftesbury, Swift's Tale of a Tub, and the eighteenth-century debate on fanaticism.
works.meter: Learned, argumentative prose.
works.context: Published in 1656 during the Commonwealth, when the sects proliferated; More was a Cambridge Platonist concerned to defend a rational Christianity against both enthusiasm and materialism.
works.structure: A single treatise in sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Henry More; authorship undisputed.
themes: Melancholy and self-analysis
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: The Cambridge Platonists

works.title: Epicene
works.description: Jonson's comedy of noise and silence: Morose, who cannot bear sound, marries the 'silent woman' Epicene to disinherit his nephew Dauphine — only to find his bride a torrent of talk, his house invaded by the collegiate ladies and the barber Cutbeard, and the play's last trick the revelation that Epicene is a boy, Dauphine's instrument, and the marriage void.
works.plot: Dauphine plots to break his uncle's will: the silent bride, the mock divorce consultation, and the siege of Morose's house by the Otiers' collegiates drive the old man to any terms; the contract signed, Dauphine strips the boy of his disguise and the play ends on the audience's own exposure to satire.
works.significance: The most audacious of Jonson's comedies of sex and gender — the play Restoration comedy learned its tricks from.
works.meter: Predominantly prose — Jonson's most assured comic prose — with the wit-duels of Truewit as its set pieces.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels at Whitefriars, 1609; its boy-bride was played by a boy, doubling the play's game with gender; printed in the 1616 Folio.
works.characters: Morose; Dauphine; Epicene; Truewit; Clerimont; Sir John Daw; Sir Amorous La Foole; Captain Otter; Mistress Otter; Cutbeard; Mavis; the collegiates
works.structure: A five-act farce of escalating noise and counter-plot, with the collegiate ladies' scenes as a satire of female learning and the divorce farce as its centrepiece.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: Epigrammata
altTitles: Epigrammata clarissimi disertissimique viri Thomae Mori
works.description: More's collected Latin epigrams, printed together with his Utopia in 1518, including translations from the Greek Anthology, satirical and courtly verse, and the poems on his own fortune and on kingship.
works.plot: The collection has no single argument; it ranges from verse translations of Greek epigrams made with William Lily, through witty satires on astrologers and courtiers, to the programmatic 'Progymnasmata' and poems celebrating the accession of Henry VIII.
works.significance: The finest Latin verse written by an Englishman of the early Renaissance and a showcase of the Erasmian revival of classical epigram; the coronation poems mark the beginnings of English Renaissance panegyric.
works.meter: Elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, and other classical metres
works.context: Composed across More's humanist career from the late 1490s; the Progymnasmata with Lily (an exercise translating Greek epigrams) dates from c. 1503–04; the collection was printed by Froben at Basel in 1518 together with the third edition of Utopia.
works.structure: A printed miscellany grouped by type: translations from the Greek Anthology, original epigrams, and the coronation poems of 1509.
themes: Wisdom and learning
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: Epigrams
works.description: Jonson's collection of 133 epigrams, printed in the 1616 Folio of his Works: poems of praise to the great and good of his acquaintance (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; the Sidneys; Donne; Shakespeare), and poems of satiric castigation to the vicious — 'On Court-Worm', 'On Gut', 'On My First Son', and the epitaphs on his children among them — the classical epigram remade as a moral instrument.
works.plot: No plot: the collection alternates poems of praise and blame, with the commendatory poems to patrons and fellow poets balancing the satires of fools and knaves, and the personal elegies (on his son, on his first daughter) at the collection's heart.
works.significance: The foundation of the English epigram tradition and the seedbed of the Augustan moral couplet.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of lapidary finish — the model for the Augustan couplet of the next century.
works.context: Written across Jonson's career and collected for the 1616 Works, the first folio of an English playwright's own canon; 'To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author, Mr. William Shakespeare' appeared separately in the 1623 Folio.
works.characters: the poet; the named patrons and poets (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; Donne; Shakespeare; the Sidneys); the satirized types (Court-Worm, Gut, Poet-Ape)
works.structure: A book of 133 short poems in the Martial tradition, arranged as a gallery of virtues and vices, prefaced by Jonson's defence of the genre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Epipsychidion
works.form: Romantic lyric meditation and poem of idealized love, with the autobiographical retrospect of the greater odes and the marriage argument of the prose of the same season.
works.description: A long lyric poem of ideal love, written for a young Italian woman confined by her father in a convent and addressed to her as the visible type of a beauty the poet had sought all his life. It passes from the portrait of the lady to an autobiography of the poet's own successive ideals, to a proposal of a life together on a boat in the Archipelago, and ends in a protest that the poem has mistaken its subject. Its frankness about plural desire and its theory of the mingled soul made it notorious at once and long uneditable.
works.plot: The poem opens with the portrait of Emily, the winter prisoner of the convent, whose coming has awakened the poet's long-seated passion, and proceeds to an account of an ideal shape of beauty pursued in dream and missed in every mortal form. The middle sections argue that love divides itself into a community of kindred minds, and the poet proposes that the three of them, himself, his wife and the lady, should live together on a small vessel in the southern islands. The close turns against the poem itself, calling it an error and a trespass, and ends with an address to the poet's own verse and to the friends who are to judge it. The argument is that the soul seeks its own type in another and that the union of spirits is not violated by plurality.
works.significance: It is the period's most candid analysis of idealizing love and of the plurality of desire, and a central exhibit in the argument about the poet's relations, domestic arrangements and the ethics of the mind. Its phrase for the mingled soul became a permanent possession of later love poetry, and its history of private printing and friends' remonstrance is a document of the Romantic handling of autobiographical matter.
works.meter: Predominantly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with frequent triple rhymes, alexandrines and irregular lyric runs; the movement is hurried and the rhymes often strain for the sense.
works.context: Written at Pisa in the spring of 1821, in the months following the poet's friendship with the liberal circle of the Tuscan city and the visit of the young lady confined by her father, and published in London in 1822 in a separate issue without the author's name. Its account of a three-fold union and its treatment of conventual restraint were at once read as a scandal of private life, and the poet's own friends counselled suppression of the poem; it was reprinted among the posthumous volumes in the following decade.
works.characters: the imprisoned lady of the poem's occasion; the poet-speaker; the wife addressed as the second and gentler spirit; the father and the convent that keep the lady
works.structure: A continuous lyric argument of some four hundred and thirty lines, divided by shifts of address, the portrait, the autobiography of ideals, the proposal of the island life and the penitential close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the first issue was anonymous, and the poem's dedication and accompanying advertisement, which named the occasion, were cancelled before publication.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Idealized love and the lost beloved
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: Epistle on the Mixed Life
works.description: Walter Hilton's epistle addressed to a wealthy layman, probably a lord, teaching the 'mixed life' — the life that joins the active works of mercy and the duties of estate with the inner practice of contemplation. It is the classic English statement that contemplation is not the preserve of monks: lay people in the world may and should live the contemplative life in their degree.
works.plot: Hilton distinguishes three lives — active, contemplative, and mixed — and argues that the mixed life, combining works of charity and governance with prayer and meditation, is the life of prelates and devout lay lords; he then teaches his addressee the practice of this life in his daily affairs.
works.significance: The founding text of the 'mixed life' tradition that legitimized lay contemplation and shaped the spirituality of the fifteenth-century gentry.
works.meter: Plain, authoritative prose of the Hilton school.
works.context: Composed c. 1385, when the growth of lay piety and the demand for vernacular guidance was transforming English religious life; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the Scale of Perfection.
works.characters: Hilton (writer); the devout layman (addressee)

works.title: Epsom Wells
works.description: Thomas Shadwell's most popular comedy, set at the Epsom mineral wells, in which the fashionable world of gallants, cits, and country justices is exposed in a series of comic intrigues.

works.title: Erewhon Revisited Twenty Years Later, Both by the Original Discoverer of the Country and by His Son
works.form: Satirical utopian novel; early scientific romance
works.description: Published in 1901, the year before Butler's death, and his own sequel to Erewhon: Higgs's own return, twenty years on, to the country where his escape by balloon has become a religion, told by his English son.
works.plot: Higgs, the original discoverer, returns to Erewhon twenty years after his escape by balloon and finds that his ascent has become the basis of a new religion, 'Sunchildism', administered by the scheming Professors Hanky and Panky; he meets his Erewhonian son George, the child of Yram, his attempt to tell the truth is suppressed by the professors, and the story is told by his English son John.
works.significance: Erewhon Revisited is the classic English satire on the origin of religions and on the priestcraft that preserves them: it anticipates the modern sociology of religion and the fictional treatment of the historical Jesus, and its portrait of a belief system founded on a misunderstanding is among the most sophisticated in Victorian satire.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
works.context: The 1890s, the comparative study of religion and the 'higher criticism' of the Bible, the growth of the Victorian imperial cult, and Butler's interest in the 'historical Jesus' controversy. works.title: Erewhon: or, Over the Range
works.form: Satirical utopian novel; early scientific romance
works.description: Published anonymously in 1872 and one of the most original satires in English: the account of an imaginary country discovered beyond a mountain range, whose institutions invert those of Victorian England.
works.plot: Higgs, a sheep farmer, crosses the range into Erewhon, where he finds a society in which sickness is a crime and crime is treated as illness, where the churches are 'Musical Banks', where 'hypothetical' language is forbidden, and where the 'Book of the Machines' records the debate on whether machines might become conscious and should be abolished. He falls in love with Arowhena and escapes with her in a balloon.
works.significance: Erewhon is the first English novel to treat the possibility of machine consciousness seriously (its 'Book of the Machines' anticipates the literature of artificial intelligence) and one of the sharpest satires on Victorian institutions; 'Erewhon' (nowhere) and 'Erewhonian' entered the language, and the book influenced Huxley, Orwell and the modern dystopia.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.

The record dates the work as composed in 1871 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.title: Eric Brighteyes
works.description: Published in 1891 and Haggard's saga of the Viking age: the heroic life and death of an Icelandic warrior and his love for Gudruda the Fair. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by H. Rider Haggard; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier.
works.plot: Eric Brighteyes, the strongest and most generous of the Icelandic heroes, loves Gudruda the Fair, but her half-sister Swanhild, a witch's daughter who loves him herself, works against them: married off to the old Earl Atli of Orkney, she wrecks Eric's ship by sorcery; outlawed for his feud with his rival Ospakar Blacktooth, Eric serves King Edmund in England, returns to kill Ospakar at the wedding feast, and loses Gudruda, slain on her bridal night by Ospakar's son Gizur at Swanhild's bidding; he dies with the berserk Skallagrim, carrying Gizur with him over a precipice, and Swanhild sails out to sea with the dead.
works.significance: Eric Brighteyes is the best of Haggard's historical novels and a remarkable English imitation of the Icelandic saga: its stern style and heroic fatalism made it a favourite of the saga revival and it stands at the head of the English tradition of Northern historical fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person testimony of the practical man.
works.context: 1890-91: the Victorian enthusiasm for the Icelandic sagas, William Morris's and Eiríkur Magnússon's translations, and the imperial cult of northern courage. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Eric Brighteyes; Gudruda the Fair; Swanhild the Fatherless, her half-sister; Skallagrim Lambstail, the baresark; Ospakar Blacktooth; Gizur, Ospakar's son; Asmund the Priest; Atli the Good, Earl of Orkney; Groa, Swanhild's mother; Saevuna, Eric's mother; Koll the Half-witted
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Rider Haggard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
altTitles: An Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
works.description: Parnell's short verse essay on the styles proper to the several kinds of poetry, arguing that the numbers of verse must be chosen for the subject and that the harmony of the line is a matter of judgment rather than of rule.
works.plot: The essay distinguishes the lofty, the smooth and the loose measures, censures the affectation of harmony for its own sake, and commends the poet who suits his stiles to his design.
works.significance: It is one of the earliest and most readable English poems on style and numbers, and it stands beside the Essay on Criticism for its account of imitation in verse.
works.meter: Heroic couplet, with the illustrative lines deliberately imitating the measures under discussion.
works.context: Published in the years of the quarrel over rhyme, blank verse and the harmony of the couplet, when the periodical essay, Dennis's criticism and Pope's Essay on Criticism were making versification a public argument.
works.structure: A continuous argument in verse, opening with the occasion and closing in a character of the finished poet.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the printing history of the piece is obscure and it survives chiefly in the collected editions of Parnell's poems.

works.title: Essays and Poems
works.description: The transcendentalist martyr's book: the ecstatic sonnets of 1838 and the essays on the divine life. It is a prose work of 1839 by Jones Very; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Emerson's edition of Very's work gathers the sonnets written during his crisis of 1838 — 'The Hand and the Foot', 'The Living Temple', 'The Prayer', 'The Dead' — with essays on the indwelling of the Holy Spirit and the annihilation of the self.
works.significance: Essays and Poems is the central document of the American ecstatic and the book that made Very the martyr of transcendentalism: published by Emerson after Very's confinement, it is the purest expression of the movement's religious intensity.
works.meter: Prose. Prose: the argument or the account is carried in continuous prose, divided into sections or chapters. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet as ecstatic utterance.
works.context: The Transcendentalist movement of the late 1830s and the religious revival that produced the crisis at Harvard. The record dates the work as composed between 1838 and 1839 and first published in 1839 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.

works.structure: A collection of essays and sonnets. Continuous prose in sections or chapters, the argument or the account advanced from its statement to its conclusion.

works.title: Essays in Criticism
works.description: The first series of 1865 collects the essays that established Arnold as the leading critic of the age — 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time', 'The Literary Influence of Academies', 'Maurice de Guérin', 'Eugénie de Guérin', 'Heine', 'Joubert', 'Spinoza and the Bible', 'Marcus Aurelius' — and the second series of 1888 adds the essays on Wordsworth, Byron, Shelley, Gray, Keats and Tolstoy.
works.plot: The central argument, stated in 'The Function of Criticism', is that criticism must be disinterested: it must 'learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world' and must resist the practical, party and personal considerations that make English criticism provincial. The essays on French and German writers are examples of that disinterestedness applied to English culture.
works.significance: Essays in Criticism is the founding work of modern English criticism: its definition of criticism as disinterested and its demand that English culture learn from the continent set the terms for the discipline into which English studies later grew, and its second series shaped the Victorian and modern estimate of the Romantic poets.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The 1860s: the periodical culture of the Cornhill and the Fortnightly, the Victorian ignorance of continental literature, and the crisis of religious belief that Arnold addressed in the same years. The record dates the work as composed between 1863 and 1888 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.context: Written after Cowley's retirement to Chertsey following the Restoration and published posthumously in 1668; 'Of Plants' is an Englishing of his Latin De Plantis and engages the new science.
works.structure: A collection of familiar essays, some with verse interspersed, on moral and philosophical subjects.

works.title: Essays Moral and Political
altTitles: Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary (1741-42 volumes)
Essays Moral and Political, Vol. I
works.description: Hume's first popular publications, two volumes of essays (1741-42) on taste, passion, the stoics, the jealousy of trade, party, and the balance of power, which established his literary reputation where the Treatise had failed. They introduced the essay as an instrument of the new psychology of refinement and modern politics.
works.plot: The moral essays argue that refinement of the age softens the man rather than enervates him, that a true delicacy of taste depends on a sound sense joined to passion, and that the ancient stoic ideal of extirpating the passions is an enthusiastic self-deception; the modern essayist counsels the regulation rather than the destruction of feeling. The political essays analyse the vices of party, the jealousy of trade as a groundless zero-sum fear, the blessings of industry, civility, and refinements, and the delicate balance of authority and liberty in a modern commonwealth. Essays on the first principles of government ground political obligation in convention and utility rather than an original contract. Together they sketch the 'taste and temperament' of commercial modernity the later writings would theorize.
works.significance: They made Hume a man of letters before he was a philosopher, fixed the classic essays on taste and the jealousy of trade, and supplied the humane public philosophy that the Enquiries and History later carried.
works.meter: The clear, balanced middle style of the polite essay, periodic where meditative, pointed where polemical, with its signature generalizations in short declaratives.
works.context: Volume I appeared in Edinburgh in 1741 and Volume II in 1742, during Hume's failed embassy and clergymen's uproar over the Treatise, and after the pattern of the Spectator papers was already worn; Hume's essays reinvented the form as moral philosophy in undress.
works.structure: A miscellany of independent essays in two volumes, ordered moral then political and historical, with no sustained argument across papers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Essays of Elia
altTitles: The First Series of the Essays of Elia
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch in the revived line of the Elizabethan and of the eighteenth-century paper, written with the deliberate archaism and the personal digression that distinguish the Romantic essay from the Spectator manner.
works.description: A volume of familiar essays collected in 1823 from papers contributed to a London magazine over the preceding years under an assumed name, and comprising some of the most loved prose of the century. The persona of the essays is a gentle, retired, half-humble town writer who remembers his childhood, his brothers and sisters, the offices in which he worked, the plays and the books he has read, and the poor and the odd characters of the metropolis. Its manner is allusive, digressive and affectionate, and its best pieces, among them the reverie of the dream children and the dissertation upon roast pig, have never been out of print.
works.plot: The essays have no plot but a succession of meditations and portraits. Some turn on the writer's own life: the counting-house and the India Office with their clerks, their pensioners and their usages, the decayed relations and the old country house, the reverie in which two children, invented as his own, are found to be the children of another, and the remembrance of the sister from whom a long and painful interval separates him. Others take up a class or a custom - the stage and the players of the old theatres, the chimney-sweepers and the beggars of the holiday streets, the roast pig of China and its inventors, the punsters and the poor relations, the actors of the great and little towns. A third group are studies of books and characters: the old drama and its heroes, a distant cousin of the family, and the meditations on the mercy of the rich and on the use of riches. The argument throughout is that the imaginative and tender reading of common life, in an age of hurry and of money-getting, is the truest wisdom available to a private man.
works.significance: The volume that defined the English familiar essay of the nineteenth century and made its persona a model for later writers of the personal paper; its pieces on the old plays, on the children of the dream and on the beggars of the metropolis are standard texts of the prose anthologies. It also fixed the writer's reputation as the chief link between the Elizabethan essayists and the prose of the Victorian period.
works.meter: Prose of extraordinary flexibility, mixing the short sentence of gossip with the long periodic sentence charged with half-remembered quotation, the rhythm of the older English writers being imitated and transformed; the style is the essay's chief instrument of feeling.
works.context: Written during the years in which the essayist, a London clerk by profession, contributed to the magazines of the day, and collected in 1823; the papers belong to the flourishing of the familiar essay in the 1820s and to the revival of interest in the old drama and its actors, and they are written out of a family history that included the calamity of 1796, in which his mother was killed and the surviving sister became the partner of his whole after-life.
works.characters: Elia, the retired and imaginative essayist; his sister; the children of the dream reverie; the clerks and pensioners of the counting-houses; the old actors and the odd characters of the London streets
works.structure: A collection of free-standing essays, with no continuous scheme, arranged in an order that alternates the autobiographical, the character-sketch and the literary-critical pieces; the unity is that of the persona, whose memory and temperament connect all the subjects.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the essays were written under an assumed name, and a small number of magazine contributions of these years, printed elsewhere under other heads, are distinguished from the Elia papers in the collected editions.

works.title: Essays on the Active Powers of Man
works.form: Analytical treatise in moral philosophy, essay by essay
works.description: The second half of Thomas Reid's planned division of the human mind, published in Edinburgh in 1788 after the Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Its seven essays analyse what a person does rather than what a person knows: agency, will, motive and freedom, conscience, the moral power, and the authority of the understanding over conduct. It is the mature statement of the common-sense school's philosophy of action and of its defence of liberty against Hume and Hartley.
works.plot: Reid begins by distinguishing active power from mere event, arguing that the very notion of cause is drawn from our consciousness of our own agency. He then examines the will, motive and the relation of volition to desire, and maintains that a free agent is an efficient cause whose choices are determined by neither necessity nor the strongest motive. The following essays treat moral agency, the conscience as a judge pronouncing upon character and not only upon actions, and the principles of action in brute animals and in human art and science. Finally Reid argues that sound judgment, or common sense, governs practice as much as belief, so that the same original principles which direct the understanding direct conduct.
works.significance: It is the principal eighteenth-century defence of human liberty and of the moral sense against sceptical analysis, and the source of Reid's influential account of conscience as a judicial faculty. Its philosophy of action, largely neglected in its own century, has been recovered by recent work on agency and free will, and it completes the Common-Sense programme that shaped Reid's American disciples.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, patient, lecture-derived analytical style
works.context: Written in the last Aberdeen and Edinburgh decades of Reid's life, after the Intellectual Powers and amid the controversy over Humean necessity and Priestley's materialism, it belongs to the Scottish Enlightenment's systematic reconstruction of the faculties and to the Common-Sense school's debate with the physiology of Hartley.
works.structure: Seven sequential essays of analytical moral psychology, advancing from the analysis of agency to the will, moral obligation, conscience and the governance of common sense in action.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Thomas Reid is established and undisputed.
