works.title: Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man
works.form: philosophical essays on the mental powers
works.description: Reid's mature encyclopaedia of the mind, the Glasgow lectures of the 1770s? keep general: the mature summing-up of common-sense philosophy, eight essays on the powers of perception, memory, consciousness, conception, judgment, reasoning, and taste. It is the fullest statement of the anatomy of the human understanding after Locke and the companion to its successor volume on the active powers.
works.plot: The first essays analyse the power of perception in its original and acquired forms, the perceptions that make a landscape readable to the eye, and the roles of memory and consciousness as the direct testimony of the mind. Conception, the conceptions of primary and secondary qualities, and the general conceptions by which language works, are then distinguished from the principles of judgment, the self-evident first principles of common sense which the sceptic must borrow before he can argue. The closing essays examine the power of reasoning and the province of taste and criticism. Throughout, Reid answers the sceptical account of belief and the geometry of probabilities, reasserting that the natural faculties are, and must be, the measure of their own trustworthiness.
works.significance: It consolidated the school of common-sense philosophy into the century's great alternative account of the mind and remains the standard text of the non-sceptical Scottish epistemology that shaped the American common-sense tradition through Reid's Scottish pupils and their descendants.
works.meter: The plain, cumulative, exemplum-rich prose of the lecture-room, with long definitions and numbered first principles delivered in a tone of candid remonstrance.
works.context: Published in 1785 after years of Glasgow lectures and amid the running Scottish response to Hume and to Beattie's Essay on Truth, it preceded the companion volume on the active powers and was widely reviewed and soon translated on the continent.
works.structure: Eight essays in the manner of the Glasgow lectures, each on one intellectual power, arranged from perception through judgment to reasoning and criticism.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
movements: The Scottish Enlightenment

works.title: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse
altTitles: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse. By the Author of Sensibility
works.description: A collection of occasional essays, tales and verses gathered from the author's papers of the previous five years and published in the same season as her first tragedy. It shows the range of her early moral and sociable writing, from the character and the familiar letter to the short tale of feeling.
works.plot: The volume passes from the essay on manners and on the duties of the heart to the narrative illustrations of the same themes, the tales exhibiting the errors of a good-nature ungoverned by principle. Its verses address friends and occasions, and its closing pieces turn from the world of the tea-table to the claims of religion and of seriousness. The design throughout is to recommend an active and disciplined virtue over the passive refinement of the age.
works.significance: It fixed her early reputation as a moral essayist and is the base from which her later conduct writing and her religious work were developed; several of the pieces were reprinted separately through the decade.
works.meter: Argumentative prose of the mid-century essay for the discursive pieces, and heroic couplets and lyrical stanzas for the verse, the two being kept in the polite middle register.
works.context: Published in 1777 in the season of the author's establishment in the London and Bath circles and of her first successes on the stage, in the same years as the quarrel between the sensibility writers and their moral critics.
works.structure: A miscellany of prose essays, inset tales and occasional verse, arranged with the longer argumentative pieces first and the shorter pieces following; no continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the advertisement of the previous poem.

works.title: Esther Waters
works.description: Published in 1894 and the finest English novel of domestic service: the life of a servant girl who bears an illegitimate child and fights to keep him. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by George Moore; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Esther Waters, a kitchenmaid in a racing household, is seduced by the footman William Latch, loses her place when she is pregnant, and raises her son alone through years of service in London and the south coast; she gives up the respectable Fred Parsons to marry the returned William, who keeps a public house and makes a book on the races until gambling and illness ruin him, and the novel ends with Esther back at Woodview with her old mistress, Mrs Barfield, and her son grown into a soldier.
works.significance: Esther Waters is the classic English novel of the servant and one of the greatest novels of the 1890s: its patient, unsentimental record of a working woman's life has been recognised as the English masterpiece of naturalism, and it remains the finest fictional account of domestic service in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is flaubertian impersonality and exact detail.
works.context: 1894: the servant question, the racing world, the workhouse and the lying-in hospital, and the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Esther Waters; William Latch; Mrs Barfield; Mr Barfield; Fred Parsons; Jackie, Esther's son; Mrs Latch; Sarah Tucker; Margaret Gale
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Augustus Moore. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Ethan Frome
works.form: Novella; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1911 and the most concentrated American tragedy of the period: three people trapped in a New England farmhouse and a hopeless love. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Edith Wharton; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ethan Frome, a poor farmer in the hill town of Starkfield, Massachusetts, is married to the sickly and tyrannical Zeena and in love with her young cousin Mattie; when Zeena determines to send Mattie away, Ethan and Mattie attempt a double suicide by sledding into a tree, and the novel ends years later with both crippled and living in the Frome house under Zeena's care.
works.significance: Ethan Frome is the most perfect short novel in American literature and Wharton's masterpiece of tragic inevitability: its use of the New England landscape, its framing narrator and its terrible ending make it a classic, and it is the finest American example of the regional tragedy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is precise, ironic exposition of a social world.
works.context: 1911: the declining hill farms of western Massachusetts, the New England winter, the rural poor, and the American regionalist tradition of Jewett and Freeman. The record dates the work as composed in 1911 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Ethan Frome; Zeena Frome; Mattie Silver; the narrator; Harmon Gow; Mrs Hale
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edith Newbold Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Euphorion
works.form: Studies of the Renaissance in Italy
works.description: Published in 1884 and Vernon Lee's masterpiece of aesthetic criticism: studies of the Renaissance in Italy and the psychology of its art. It is a prose work of 1884 by Vernon Lee; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The essays examine the Italian Renaissance through its painting, its music, its poetry and its religion: Botticelli's spring, the Florence of the Medici, the sacred music of Palestrina, the figure of the Renaissance tyrant, and the relation of art to the society that produced it.
works.significance: Euphorion is the central English work of aesthetic criticism of the 1880s and the finest study of the Italian Renaissance in the language: its psychological account of art and its analysis of the relation between art and society made it a landmark of English criticism and a key influence on the modern study of the Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, analytical prose that moves between description and argument.
works.context: 1884: the Victorian enthusiasm for the Italian Renaissance, the aesthetic criticism of Pater, the new professional study of art history, and the English colony in Florence. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Violet Paget. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Euphranor: A Dialogue on Youth
works.description: Published in 1851, a Socratic dialogue on education set in the Cambridge of the 1830s and modelled on Plato: a discussion of what a young man should be taught and how. It is a prose work of 1851 by Edward FitzGerald; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Euphranor and his friends debate the aims of education, the value of mathematics and the classics, the influence of the tutor and of the family, and the formation of character; the dialogue ends without a dogmatic conclusion.
works.significance: Euphranor is one of the best Victorian imitations of the Platonic dialogue and a significant document for the history of English educational thought; its conviction that education is the formation of a person rather than the transmission of information is the standard Victorian humanist position.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).
works.context: The 1850s debates on education, the Cambridge of FitzGerald's youth, and the Victorian taste for the Platonic dialogue (Arnold's and Helps's essays). The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward FitzGerald. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Euphues and His England
works.description: Lyly's sequel: Euphues and his friend Philautus sail for England, where the courtship of the ladies — Camilla, Surius's sister, and the rest — and the praises of Elizabeth I, the English court, and English women fill the book, in the second and final installment of the Euphuistic diptych.
works.plot: The voyage, the arrival in Dover, and the tour of England's marvels frame the main action: Philautus courts the ladies, Euphues plays the counsellor, and the long debate on love, beauty, and constancy ends with the famous 'glass for Europe' — the encomium of Queen Elizabeth that closes the book.
works.significance: The completion of the Euphuistic diptych and a founding text of English literary nationalism.
works.meter: The Euphuistic prose at its ripest, with the encomium of Elizabeth as its set piece.
works.context: Published in 1580, the year of Drake's circumnavigation and the Jesuit mission's arrival; its celebration of England answered the national mood and fixed Euphues as the English style's patron.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Camilla; Lady Flavia; Surius; Fidus; Psellus; Queen Elizabeth (praised in the encomium)
works.structure: A travel frame enclosing the courtship debates, letters, and the concluding praise of England, mirroring the first book's structure.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit
works.description: Lyly's first Euphues book and the fountain of Euphuism: the young Athenian Euphues comes to Naples, where the friendship with Philautus, the love of Lucilla, and her inconstancy teach him the anatomy of wit — the whole told in the balanced, antithetical, simile-laden prose that took England by storm and gave the decade its style.
works.plot: Euphues wins Philautus's friendship and then Lucilla's love, betraying his friend; Lucilla's fickleness (she turns to Curio) punishes the traitor; the debate on love, the letters of counsel, and Euphues's departure close the book with the moral anatomy — 'wit' dissected into its deceits and remedies.
works.significance: The most influential prose style of the English Renaissance — the book that taught a generation to write, and to think in balances.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate Euphuistic balance — antithesis, isocolon, and the zoological similes of Pliny's natural history.
works.context: Published in 1578 and reprinted a dozen times by 1600; the style it founded was imitated by Greene, Lodge, and the court, and parodied by Shakespeare and Nashe within the decade.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Lucilla; Curio; the old gentleman of Naples; the ladies of Naples
works.structure: A moral romance in the manner of the Italian questioni d'amore: narrative framed by debate, letters, and the concluding 'Cooling Card' against love.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Europe a Prophecy
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a political vision of the European reaction following the American revolution, written in the same prophetic manner as its predecessor.
works.description: The second of the illuminated prophecies of the revolutionary decade, etched and printed in 1794 and written as a vision of Europe sunk in a long night of kings, priests and built walls, from which a spirit of revolt at last breaks forth. The American act of the preceding prophecy is here followed by the European reaction, and the poem's argument is that the old continent, watched by its cyclops builders and its grey priests, is delivered not by counsel but by the fires of a new imagination.
works.plot: The poem opens with the night of the fallen church and of the kings of Europe, and with the sleep of Albion's daughters; the powers of the dead king's mother, the grey priest and the builders of the golden walls, who measure and fortify the continent against the voice of the people, hold the hour of darkness. A female power, bound and weeping, is watched over by the cycle of years, and the grey daughters of the old state are summoned to the sound of a trumpet. The central action is the coming of the youth of fire, who, urged by the female spirit of the west, descends upon the cities of Europe, and the closing plates give the fall of the built and measured order, the breaking of the seals of the grey books, and the voice of the awakened earth, the poem ending with the announcement that the hour is accomplished and that the morning is come for the nations of the old world.
works.significance: The completest statement of the poet's early revolutionary myth and, with its companion prophecy, the foundation of his later system of the four continents and their binding powers; its images of the measured and fortressed Europe are a permanent part of Romantic writing about the old order, and the book's argument that imagination rather than reform delivers the nations shaped all his later work.
works.meter: Blank verse of solemn and reiterated movement, with short chorus-lines and the flourish of the closing proclamation; the poet's own note on the verse, added when the book was reissued, explains the design of the lines.
works.context: Etched and published in London in 1794, in the year of the Terror, of the war and of the repression of the English societies, and of the author's own most openly revolutionary printing; the poem's picture of a continent walled by priests and builders is a comment on the reaction that had overtaken the hopes of the previous five years.
works.characters: The grey priest and the builders of the golden walls; the female powers of the old continent, watchful and bound; the youth of fire who descends upon Europe; the spirit of the west; the grey daughters of the old state, summoned to the trumpet
works.structure: A prophecy in two movements, a long night-piece of the sleeping and fortified continent and a short catastrophe of fire and trumpet, with an elaborate machinery of kings, priests, builders and bound female powers; the verse carries the argument by vision and proclamation rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the dating of the issue and the relation of the several copies' plate order are matters of bibliography rather than of authorship.

themes: Exile and homelessness
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Warfare and battle
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: Evangeline: A Tale of Acadie
works.description: The American epic of the Acadian exile: Evangeline's search for Gabriel across a continent. It is a verse work of 1847 by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Evangeline Bellefontaine and Gabriel Lajeunesse are separated on their wedding day when the Acadians are expelled by the British in 1755; Evangeline searches for him across America for the rest of her life and finds him dying in a Philadelphia hospital.
works.significance: Evangeline gave American literature its first enduring epic of exile and one of its permanent love stories: its dactylic hexameter, its Acadian heroine and its landscape of the American continent made it a national poem and the founding text of the literature of the Acadian diaspora.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The line is the English hexameter, the unrhymed six-stress line of the classical experiment. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the long narrative poem in regular tetrameter.
works.context: The Acadian expulsion of 1755, the exile of the French settlers of Nova Scotia, and the Louisiana and American landscape of the 1840s. The record dates the work as composed between 1846 and 1847 and first published in 1847 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Evangeline Bellefontaine; Gabriel Lajeunesse; Benedict Bellefontaine; Father Felician
works.structure: A narrative poem in dactylic hexameter and two parts, from Acadie to Philadelphia. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. W. Longfellow. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Evelina; or, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
altTitles: Evelina, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
works.description: The history of a young woman of unknown birth introduced by her guardian's family into London and Bristol society, told in her letters home to the grandfather she has never known. Its publication was anonymous and its immediate success surprised its author, who had thrown it out as a juvenile exercise.
works.plot: Evelina Anville, the daughter of a private and disobliged marriage, is taken by her grandfather Lady Howard's connection into the company of the Mirvan family. She is annoyed by Madame Duval, her mother's relation, insulted and compromised in the gardens and at the assemblies, and carried through the theatre, the balls and the rackets of the town. At Bristol she is robbed and rescued, and in London her conduct under continual provocation is vindicated; the discovery of her birth and her grandfather's consent prepare the marriage with the man she has deserved.
works.significance: It created the comedy-of-manners novel written by a woman and is the standard account of the initiation of a girl into the sexual and social grammar of polite London; its influence on the later novel of observation is very large.
works.meter: A carefully graded epistolary prose, the heroine's letters polite, naive and increasingly articulate, the comic letters of Captain Mirvan and of Madame Duval carrying the broad humour; the style of the reporting letters is the book's chief instrument.
works.context: Published in London in 1778 by a young woman writing from the household of the musical family of the Drury Lane manager, in the season of the new attention to the manners of the town, the assemblies and the public gardens, and of the quarrel over women's novels.
works.characters: Evelina Anville; Mr. Villars; Lady Howard; Mrs. and Miss Mirvan; Captain Mirvan; Madame Duval; Lord Ormont; the servants and the assistants of the town
works.structure: A novel in a series of letters, principally from Evelina to Mr. Villars, with the letters of others supplying the report of her conduct; the sequence of public amusements forms the social anatomy of the book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; issued anonymously as by a lady in the first edition, its authorship being declared by the writer in the second and later editions and established by her papers.

works.title: Every Man in His Humour
works.description: Jonson's first great comedy of humours, performed by the Lord Chamberlain's Men with Shakespeare in the cast: the jealous merchant Kitely, the braggart Captain Bobadill, the town gull Matthew, and the poetaster's crew are all 'humorous' — each ruled by an obsession — until the exposure of the final act lets the sane (Clement, Wellbred) judge the fools, in a London whose names Jonson later anglicized from the Italian setting.
works.plot: Old Knowell worries over his son's London dissipations; Kitely suspects his wife; Bobadill boasts and fights by words only; the gulls and their plots collide at Cob's house, and Justice Clement's court of the final scene administers the comic verdicts — including the purging of the humours by the 'vent' of exposure.
works.significance: The foundation of Jonson's comic method and of the English comedy of character — the template for Restoration and eighteenth-century comedy alike.
works.meter: Mostly prose in the 1616 Folio revision, with the verse of the earlier Italian version smoothed away — the first great prose comedy of the English stage.
works.context: Performed 1598 at the Curtain by the Chamberlain's Men (Shakespeare played Old Knowell); Jonson revised the play, resetting it in London, for the 1616 Folio of his Works.
works.characters: Kitely; Dame Kitely; Captain Bobadill; Edward Knowell; Brainworm; Wellbred; Stephen; Matthew; Justice Clement; Downright; Bridget; Cob; Tib
works.structure: A unified-plot comedy on the classical model — one city, one day, one action — built on the humours theory announced in the Induction and resolved in the judgment scene.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: Everyman
works.description: The most famous of the English moralities, translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) around 1500: Everyman, summoned by Death to render his account, finds that Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, and even his own Strength and Beauty desert him, and that only Good Deeds — and Knowledge, Confession, and the priesthood — go with him into the grave. Its stark allegory of death has kept it on the stage for five centuries.
works.plot: God, seeing mankind sunk in worldly love, sends Death to Everyman with the summons to his reckoning; one by one his companions refuse the journey — Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, Goods — until Good Deeds, weakened by his neglect, sends him to Knowledge, who leads him through Confession and penance to the sacraments; at the grave, Strength, Discretion, Beauty, and the Five Wits desert him in turn, and only Good Deeds descends with him, as the angels receive his soul.
works.significance: The classic English play of death and the reckoning: its allegory has made it the most performed medieval English drama in the modern world.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, plain and weighty, with the Dutch original's structure faithfully kept.
works.context: Translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) c. 1500 and printed by Richard Pynson and John Skot c. 1510–1535; continuously performed since, including modern productions (Hofmannsthal's Jedermann at Salzburg descends from it).
works.characters: Everyman; Death; God; Fellowship; Kindred; Cousin; Goods; Good Deeds; Knowledge; Confession; Strength; Discretion; Beauty; the Five Wits; the Angel; the Doctor
works.structure: A single-movement morality of the final journey, with the successive desertions of the companions as its pitiless rhythm and the doctrine of the reckoning as its frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; translated from the Dutch, whose authorship is likewise disputed.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: Vernacular Religious Drama

works.title: Exodus
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 590 lines on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea, from the Junius manuscript: a bravura reworking of Exodus 13-14 in which Moses becomes a heroic leader and the crossing a nautical epic, prefiguring the Christian's passage through the waters of baptism and the harrowing of hell.
works.plot: After a prologue on Moses and the law, the poem narrates the pursuit of the Israelites by Pharaoh's host, the pillar of cloud and fire, the parting of the waters, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the Israelites' division of spoils on the far shore; it closes with an allegorical exegesis of the crossing (the 'keys of the deep', the 'spiritual meanings') and allusions to Noah, Abraham, Solomon's temple, and the end of the world.
works.significance: The most stylistically daring of the Old Testament poems; its sea imagery is a high point of Old English diction.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of unusual density; famous kennings for the sea ('the whale's road', 'the swan's riding-place').
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 143-171); the poem is often linked with the Cædmonian school of biblical paraphrase mentioned by Bede.
works.characters: Moses; Pharaoh; the Israelites; Abraham; Noah
works.structure: Narrative epic with an extended typological epilogue; the abrupt shifts of scene (Noah, Abraham, the temple) have prompted theories of textual disruption.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Cædmonian attribution is traditional only.
themes: Sea voyage and seafaring
Typology and biblical interpretation
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air
altTitles: Experiments upon Different Kinds of Air
works.description: Priestley's founding reports of pneumatic chemistry, the first volume published in 1774 and the series extended through the 1780s, in which he isolated and named the airs, fixed air, dephlogisticated air and the rest, and made the study of gases a science. The work established his European fame and transformed the chemistry of the atmosphere.
works.plot: Priestley describes his method of collecting airs over water and quicksilver, and reports the generation of fixed air from fermentation, chalk, and living mice, showing its abundance in ordinary processes. He proves that common air is indefinitely alterable, that mice and flame consume and corrupt it, and that dephlogisticated air, obtained by heat from mercurial calcine and niter, is air purified beyond compare, in which a candle burns with unparalleled lustre and animal life is prolonged. He then trials nitrous, phlogisticated, and alkaline airs, the composition and the respirability of each, the later volumes extending these discoveries through the 1780s. The narrative insists that the airs are chemical individuals, not modifications of a single element.
works.significance: It created the chemistry of gases and is one of the foundational experimental records of modern chemistry; its discovery of oxygen, however interpreted within the phlogiston scheme, stands among the turning points of the science.
works.meter: Homely, exact laboratory prose: operation, observation, inference, with occasional rhapsody at the wonders disclosed.
works.context: Begun at Leeds and Birmingham after the Electricity history, amid the phlogiston controversies and Priestley's nonconformist ministry; the first volume appeared in 1774, and the series was soon rebuilt by Lavoisier into the oxygen chemistry and answered by the British phlogistonists.
works.structure: Serial volumes of reported experiments, each a chain of trials with the apparatus described, the observation, and the inference, the later volumes answering critics.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Medicine, healing, and the body
The New Science and experimental philosophy
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy
The New Science and the Royal Society

works.title: Explanatory Notes Upon the New Testament
altTitles: Wesley's Explanatory Notes on the New Testament
works.description: John Wesley's one-volume commentary on the New Testament, verse by verse, the most widely circulating English exegesis of Methodism and a deliberate distillation of Bengelius, Grotius, Lightfoot, and the practical writers. It gave the preachers and a lay readership a complete working interpretation of the text in English.
works.plot: Wesley prints the received English text in sense paragraphs and follows each verse with notes that paraphrase, clear the idiom, weigh the sense against other translators, and press the practical and experimental meaning. The notes are strongest on justification by faith, assurance, inward sanctification, and Christian perfection, doctrines he reads through the whole of the epistles and Gospels; he handles prophecy, the church, and the sacraments with a return to primitive antiquity. Difficulties of gospel chronology and the Pauline argument receive plain, workmanlike solutions. The whole is a manual of the New Testament made for preachers on horseback and pious families.
works.significance: It became the working New Testament of early Methodism on both sides of the Atlantic and remains the fullest witness to Wesley's exegetical mind and his doctrine of experimental religion.
works.meter: Condensed, abbreviated note prose of marginal shorthand made discursive, its sentences pared to the practical point.
works.context: Produced in the thick of Wesley's preaching ministry and the society's growth, published in 1754 for the use of the Methodists, it gathered earlier continental and English annotation into a standard of Methodist scriptural reason joined to heart-religion.
works.structure: A continuous verse commentary on the books of the New Testament in canonical order, paragraph by paragraph.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Expugnatio Hibernica
works.description: Gerald of Wales's history of the Anglo-Norman invasion and conquest of Ireland (1169–85), framed as a panegyric of Henry II and of Gerald's own relatives among the conquerors, the Geraldines; composed from 1188 and read publicly at Oxford in 1188 or 1189.
works.summary: Gerald recounts the coming of the Normans under Strongbow and the campaigns that established English lordship in Ireland, devoting special attention to the deeds of the FitzGeralds, to the character of the Irish, and to the prophecies and prodigies attending the conquest.
works.significance: The foundational narrative of the English presence in Ireland, shaped by family partisanship but indispensable as the earliest extended account of the conquest; a model of twelfth-century historical rhetoric.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle
movements: The Twelfth-Century Renaissance

works.title: Eyeless in Gaza
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1936
works.description: Huxley's most experimental novel: a life told in fragments, and the search for a mysticism that will hold. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Aldous Huxley; it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The novel tells the life of Anthony Beavis in a collage of dated fragments, from his Edwardian childhood through the First World War, his affairs and his political disillusion to his discovery of a pacifist mysticism in Mexico.
works.significance: Eyeless in Gaza is Huxley's most experimental novel and the record of his turn from satire to mysticism: its fragmentary chronology made it the most formally ambitious English novel of ideas of the decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of ideas with a large cast and competing arguments.
works.context: The First World War, the 1920s and 1930s, the rise of fascism, and Huxley's own turn toward pacifism and mysticism. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Anthony Beavis; Helen Amberley; Mark Staithes; Brian Foxe; Joan Thursley; Dr Miller
works.structure: A collage of dated fragments over forty years, moving backwards and forwards. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Aldous Leonard Huxley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form
Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind
themes: Religion, doubt, and the post-war faith
Sexuality, the new psychology, and the Freudian century
Time, memory, and the duration of consciousness
Totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel

works.title: Fables (First Collection)
altTitles: Fables by John Gay, Part the First
works.description: Gay's first collection of the beast fables, cast in the manner of the Eastern and classical apologue and applied, in the dedication and the moral, to the court, the city, the stage and the marriage market of his own country.
works.plot: A succession of short tales of beasts, birds and insects, each closing with an application: on credulity and the guide who leads the rash, on the great and their favourites, on the tyrant and his courtiers, on the traveller and the city, and on the marriage market.
works.significance: It restored the fable to the English canon as a form of social and political realism, and it long stood in the schoolroom beside Aesop and later with the century's own collection of the short moral tale.
works.meter: Heroic couplet in the plainest narrative use, with the short sententious close that carries the moral.
works.context: Published by subscription in the year of the Beggar's Opera's first run, when the vogue for eastern tales and for La Fontaine's imitators had made the apologue a vehicle of national comment; the dedication commends the instruction of a princess of the House of Hanover.
works.characters: the beasts and birds of the apologues; the court, the city and the theatre they figure
works.structure: A collection in numbered books of independent fables, each with its own narrative and appended application, unified only by the dedicator's frame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the collection reworks earlier apologue material, and Gay acknowledges his Eastern and classical obligations.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: Fables (Second Collection)
altTitles: Fables by John Gay, Part the Second
works.description: Gay's second and last collection of fables, prepared for publication shortly before his death and more openly personal and political than the first, with the poet's own retirement and independence as its recurring subject.
works.plot: Independent apologues of beasts, plants and the domesticks of the world, each with its application, several of them taking the fortunes of court friendship, the poet's patron and the dangers of the great.
works.significance: It completes the most considerable English fable sequence of the century and preserves the image of the poet's protected retirement which the age attached to Gay's memory.
works.meter: Heroic couplet, more reflective and sometimes more broken than in the first collection, with the lyric insertion in the closing fable.
works.context: Composed across the 1730s, after the suppression of Polly and the withdrawal of the theatre patronage, and published in the year of Gay's death in the subscription manner he had used for the first collection.
works.characters: the beasts and trees of the apologues; the court friend and the poet
works.structure: A collection in books of separate fables with their morals, framed by the poet's retirement among his books and closing with the fable of the old apple-tree.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Fables Ancient and Modern
works.description: Dryden's last volume, a collection of verse translations and adaptations from Homer, Ovid, Boccaccio, and Chaucer, dedicated to the Duke of Ormond and prefaced by his famous account of translation.
works.plot: The volume contains, among others, Palamon and Arcite (from Boccaccio's Teseida), The Cock and the Fox (from Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale), The Wife of Bath Her Tale, Theodore and Honoria, Cymon and Iphigenia, and the twelfth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses.
works.significance: The greatest achievement of Dryden's late career and a founding document of English translation theory; Palamon and Arcite and the preface are canonical texts in the history of Chaucer reception.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout, including the celebrated octosyllabic-free Chaucerian adaptations rendered in five-beat lines.
works.context: Published in March 1700, two months before Dryden's death, by subscription after he had been stripped of the laureateship in 1689.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emily; Chaunticlere; Pertelote; Reynard; Theodore; Honoria; Cymon; Iphigenia; the Wife of Bath
works.structure: A miscellany of narrative poems unified by the preface's theory of translation as the art of conveying a dead author's spirit in the living language.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.
themes: Fortune and mutability
The English vernacular and national letters
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Façade
works.form: Verse suite for speaking voice with Walton's music (first performed 1923)
works.description: The settings of the poems to Walton's music: the most performed experiment of English verse. It is a verse work of 1922 by Edith Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Façade sets Edith Sitwell's poems - the horn, the polka, the waltz, the yodelling song - to be spoken through the Sengerphone to William Walton's instrumental music, so that the sound of the poem is the poem; the first performance of 1923 made it the most argued-over experiment of English verse.
works.significance: Façade is the most performed experiment in the history of English verse: its settings made the sound of the poem its subject and gave English modernism its most original collaboration, and the suite remains the test case of the poem as music.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
works.context: London in 1922-23, and the modernist experiment of the spoken poem. The record dates the work as composed between 1920 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and first performed in 1923 and it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Sir Beelzebub; Old Sir Faulk; Black Mrs Behemoth; Daisy and Lily ('Waltz'); Lily O'Grady ('Popular Song'); Mr Wagg ('Polka'); Jumbo ('Lullaby for Jumbo'); the Man from a Far Countree; the reciting voice behind the curtain
works.structure: A suite of settings for speaking voice and instrumental music, in numbers. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Edith Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom
Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule

works.title: Fair Stood the Wind for France
works.description: The novel of the airman shot down in occupied France and the farm that hides him. It is a prose fiction work of 1944 by H. E. Bates; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The bomber of the RAF is shot down over occupied France and the crew is hidden by the farm of the girl Françoise; the novel follows the escape through the France of the occupation, the farm and the line, in the prose of the airman and the field.
works.significance: Fair Stood the Wind for France is the most read novel of the airman behind the lines: its France of the farm and the occupation made the escape story a novel of the occupied country and gave the war its most popular English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the field, the season and the weather, charged but never purple.
works.context: Occupied France in the war years. The record dates the work as composed between 1942 and 1943 and first published in 1944 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Franklin; Françoise; the crew; the farmers of the occupation
works.structure: A novel of escape in chapters, from the crash to the line. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herbert Ernest Bates. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Falkner
works.form: Prose fiction; domestic novel of conscience and renunciation; the novel of education
works.description: The last completed novel, a study of a man haunted by an accidental death and of the education of a girl committed to his charge. Falkner, whose prosperity rests on an inheritance obtained after the death of a benefactor whom he unwittingly caused, places his ward under the protection of a family of high character and loves her in silence, while the secret of his conscience presses on him until disclosure. The book is quiet, domestic and almost entirely free of the machinery of its author's earliest fiction, and its interest is the patience of guilt and the cost of renunciation. It closes a series of novels on maker's responsibility and desertion.
works.plot: A gentleman of broken fortune, carrying the secret of an accidental death which gave him his ward, educates the girl he has injured and loves, and watches her attract a suitor of her own class. A rival's malice, a mother's disappointment and a marriage made against inclination try the household, and Falkner keeps his secret until his health and hope fail. The confession, the marriage and the death of the woman he loved and of the man who loved her bring the tale to its close, with the surviving child the only promise of repair.
works.significance: Important as the closing novel of a career that founded two prose traditions, and as evidence of a movement from Gothic and philosophical romance to domestic realism. It is studied for its treatment of concealed guilt and for the relation it sets up between its author's earliest and latest fiction.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain, reflective and unornamented narrative style, with quoted lyric at the chapter heads
works.context: Published in 1835, in the decade of reform and of the new poor-law and factory debates, it belongs to the author's long later career of editing, biographical writing and domestic fiction. Its subject of conscience, guardianship and the education of a dependent girl reflects the period's literature of moral responsibility, and its quiet realism marks the distance from the philosophical romance of the 1810s in which the series began.
works.characters: Falkner, the man of the secret; Margaret, the daughter of the family whose death he caused and his own ward; her mother; a suitor of her own rank and his family; a rival of malice and interest
works.structure: Third-person domestic novel in three volumes, narrated with a restrained, reflective economy and a single concealed cause running beneath the household surface; it opens with a brief history of the hero's earlier life.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Marriage and women's conduct
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Fall of Princes
works.description: John Lydgate's monumental translation (over 36,000 lines) of Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, commissioned by Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and completed in 1438: a procession of the falls of princes from Adam to King John of France, moralized by the ghostly narrator Boccaccio himself. The encyclopedic English 'tragedy' of fortune, and the ancestor of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.plot: The poet, in a Boethian frame, receives the sorrowing Boccaccio, who recounts example after example of greatness overthrown — Nimrod, Saul, Priam, Alexander, Caesar, Nero, Arthur, and the modern princes — each tale closing with the moral of fortune's wheel; the work ends with the falls of the French and English kings and a defense of poetry itself.
works.significance: The great English poem of the falls of princes and the conduit by which Boccaccio's tragic vision became the Tudor theory of tragedy; its influence on the Elizabethan stage is direct.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with prose links, aureate and copious.
works.context: Commissioned by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1431 and completed in 1438, during the wars in France and the king's minority; printed by Pynson (1494) and continuously read; the Mirror for Magistrates (1559) descends directly from it.
works.characters: Lydgate (dreamer); Boccaccio (narrator); the fallen princes of history
works.structure: Nine books of exemplary falls within the dream-vision frame, with the envoy to Duke Humphrey as its patronage climax.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.
themes: Fortune and mutability
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)

works.title: False Delicacy
works.form: sentimental comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A sentimental comedy of a young woman who loses the man she loves by an over-scrupulous reserve, written to prove that virtue itself may err by excess of refinement. It was the successful rival of a kindred play of the same season and took the argument for sentimental reformation of the stage.
works.plot: A lady of exalted principles conceals her affection from the lover she has promised, from a false notion of modesty, and by her silence gives his family the opening for another match. A second pair, less refined and more frank, carry the underplot of honest inclination, and the friends and guardians divide the counsel of the world. The exposure of the mistake restores the first lovers, the comedy closing on the argument that a delicacy which costs a woman her happiness is false.
works.significance: It is the standard example of the sentimental comedy in its hour of triumph, and the season's pamphlets on the two species of comedy make it a fixed point in the history of the century's genre quarrel.
works.meter: A smooth prose dialogue of delicate refinement and sententious argument, the emotional moments raised into short declamations of principle.
works.context: First performed at Covent Garden in January 1766 in the same season and on the same bill as the rival comedy of the same quarrel, the contest being made the occasion of a public debate on the laughing and the sentimental comedy by the authors of both sides.
works.characters: the lady of the false delicacy of the title; the lover lost by her reserve; the guardian and the friends who misadvise; the frank pair of the underplot
works.structure: Five-act comedy of concealed feeling and mistaken counsel, with the underplot of the frank pair set against the main plot of scruple; the moral case is argued directly in the dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the prefatory argument on the design.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Fame Is the Spur
works.description: The political novel of the radical career and its price. It is a prose fiction work of 1940 by Howard Spring; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Fame Is the Spur follows Hamer Shawcross from the Welsh radical beginnings through the Liberal career and the betrayals of the ideal to the peerage and the ruin of the son, in the political prose of the career novel that reads the decade's politics through one man's rise.
works.significance: Fame Is the Spur is Spring's political novel: its Shawcross - the radical made lord - is the classic study of the corrupted ideal in the popular political fiction of the war years.

Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the Welsh pulpit and the household of the preacher.
works.context: Wales and Westminster from the 1890s to the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Hamer Shawcross, the radical; the wife; the son; the party
works.structure: A career novel in the chapters of the rise and the price. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Fantastic Fables
works.description: Published in 1899 and Bierce's American version of Aesop: short, savage political fables about politicians, journalists and the human animal. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Ambrose Bierce; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Fable and Apologue and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The fables take the form of the classical apologue but turn it into political satire: a statesman is shown to be a thief, a journalist to be a liar, a reformer to be a fool, and the moral is invariably the opposite of the official one.
works.significance: Fantastic Fables is the most concentrated American political satire of the period and the best American imitation of Aesop: its savage reduction of public life to animal behaviour made it a permanent text of American political cynicism, and it is the model for the modern American political fable.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short, precisely engineered story with a reversed or delayed ending.
works.context: 1899: the American politics of the Gilded Age, the Spanish-American War and the imperial debate, the Hearst press, and the tradition of the political fable from Swift to Twain. The record dates the work as composed in 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under fable and apologue.
works.structure: A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ambrose Gwinnett Bierce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze
altTitles: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze. By a Fine Lady
works.description: A short amatory tale in which a young woman, pursued no longer than she chooses to be, pursues a young officer by successive disguises, inventing for him one fictional person after another. It is the most praised of its author's fictions, a compact study of the masquerade of identity and of the economics of the sexual chase.
works.plot: Seeing a young officer at a public exhibition, a lady of quality resolves to be enjoyed by him on her own terms; she lodges near him as a poor woman, is bought and resold by him, and then personates a wanton, a neighbour and finally a man to keep his desire alive. Each invention is exhausted and replaced by another until the last disguise, that of a rival male, forces him to flee the town; she then appears in her own person and renews the pursuit from the beginning.
works.significance: It has been recovered as a masterpiece of early feminist narrative, its serial personation being read as an analysis of gender as performance and of the novel's own dependence on disguise.
works.meter: Lucid, ironic prose with the free-indirect reporting of the heroine's calculations, and a rhetorical heightening borrowed from romantic diction but turned to comedy.
works.context: Published in 1725 in a collected volume of the author's short fictions, in the season of the revival of the masquerade operas and of the controversy over the novel of intrigue; its own tale of disguise is a commentary on the theatre of the town.
works.structure: A single continuous third-person tale with a close ring composition: the last scene restores the first, so that the maze of the title is formally completed; the disguise episodes are arranged in escalating irony.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published as by 'a fine lady' and gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction.

themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning

works.title: Far Away and Long Ago
works.description: Published in 1918 and the greatest English book of childhood in the natural world: Hudson's own boyhood on the Argentine pampas. It is a prose work of 1918 by W. H. Hudson; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Hudson remembers his childhood on the pampas in the 1840s: the great plains and their birds, the gauchos and the cattle, the house and its people, the snakes and the storms, and the natural world that was for him the first and greatest of all companions.
works.significance: Far Away and Long Ago is one of the great English autobiographies and the finest book about a childhood in the natural world: its prose and its freshness made it a classic, it is the source of much of the English literary image of the pampas, and it is the best loved of Hudson's books.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, unhurried descriptive prose.
works.context: 1840s and 1918: the Argentine pampas before the railway, the English settler families of South America, and the Edwardian fashion for the rural memoir. The record dates the work as composed between 1917 and 1918 and first published in 1918 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: Far from the Madding Crowd
altTitles: Far from the Madding Crowd: A Pastoral Romance
works.description: Serialised anonymously in the Cornhill Magazine in 1874 and published in two volumes: the novel that made Hardy famous and the first of the Wessex novels to be set in the fully realised rural world of his invention.
works.plot: Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm at Weatherbury and is courted by the shepherd Gabriel Oak, the prosperous farmer William Boldwood and the soldier Frank Troy; she marries Troy, who is killed by Boldwood, and after years of widowhood and the ruin of Boldwood she marries Oak.
works.significance: Far from the Madding Crowd established the Wessex novel and made Hardy a major novelist; its integration of rural labour, landscape and the marriage plot is the model for the English regional novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.

works.title: Farmer Giles of Ham
works.form: Comic tale (mock-heroic, with maps and glossary)
works.description: The farmer, the dragon Chrysophylax and the comic kingdom of the Middle Ages. It is a prose fiction work of 1949 by J. R. R. Tolkien; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Farmer Giles of Ham, an unwilling hero of the medieval English countryside, turns the dragon Chrysophylax Dives from his farm with a blunderbuss, is sent by the king to bargain with the dragon, and returns with the dragon's oath, the treasure and the little kingdom of his own.
works.significance: Farmer Giles of Ham is Tolkien's comic masterpiece and the proof that his invented England could carry the mock-heroic: its farmer, its dragon and its parody of the court made the tale a classic of English comic prose beside the high fantasy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The author's characteristic manner is the invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it.
works.context: An invented medieval England, 'in the days of King Augustus Bonifacius Ambrosius Aurelianus Antoninus'. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1949 and first published in 1949 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.

works.structure: A comic tale in chapters, with a mock-scholarly frame, maps and glossary. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. works.title: Father and Son: A Study of Two Temperaments
works.description: Published anonymously in 1907 and one of the greatest English autobiographies: the record of a childhood under the religious tyranny of a Plymouth Brother and of the son's slow escape into the modern world.
works.plot: Gosse recalls his mother's death in the London house at Islington, the move with his widowed father to the Devon coast, the father's obsession with the literal truth of the Bible, the family prayers and the anathemas, and the boy's discovery of science, poetry and the world — culminating in his departure to the British Museum at seventeen.
works.significance: Father and Son is the classic account of the Victorian conflict between Evangelical religion and modern thought, and one of the founding works of the modern autobiography: its portrait of a father destroyed by his own faith has no equal in English.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. works.form: Comedy (the Abbey play of the TD and the devil)
works.description: The Abbey comedy of the TD who out-bargains the devil. It is a dramatic work of 1943 by Flann O'Brien; it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage; Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.title: Felix Holt, the Radical
works.description: Published in 1866, set in the Midlands at the time of the first Reform Bill (1832), and the novel in which Eliot confronted electoral politics most directly: a study of radicalism, inheritance and class loyalty in the town of Treby Magna.
works.plot: Felix Holt, a watchmaker and Radical, and Harold Transome, the heir of Transome Court who returns from the East to stand as a Radical, are rivals for the hand of Esther Lyon, who is revealed to be the true heir of the Transome estate; the election riot, the trial of Felix for manslaughter, and the family secret of the Transome inheritance resolve into Esther's renunciation of her claim and her marriage to Felix.
works.significance: Felix Holt is the most direct Victorian novel about parliamentary reform and the most serious attempt by a major novelist to represent working-class political conviction; its analysis of the transference of estates and of the rhetoric of the hustings is a valuable document for the social history of 1832, and its heroine's choice is one of Eliot's most carefully argued moral conclusions.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The General Election of 1832 and the Reform Act, the decline of the landed estate, the money of the East India trade, and the religious Dissent of the provincial town. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.

works.title: Festial
works.description: John Mirk's cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, composed c. 1380s at Lilleshall Abbey: lively, exemplum-rich homilies designed for parish priests to read to their congregations, from Advent through the temporale and sanctorale to the dedication of the church. works.title: Fingal
works.form: Ancient epic in the restored or reconstructed manner, in books, with argument or analysis prefixed to each book and with introductory and explanatory dissertation; accompanied by a group of shorter songs and laments.
works.description: Macpherson's first long Ossianic poem, offered as an ancient epic in six books on the deeds of Fingal, the Caledonian hero, together with several shorter translated poems. It greatly enlarges the manner of the 'Fragments' into a narrative machine of invasions, single combats, ghosts and bardic recitation. Its publication, with a prefacial dissertation, provoked both enthusiasm in Europe and attack at home.
works.plot: The epic frame is a war in which the forces of the north and of Ireland contend, and Fingal, aged, venerable and supreme in judgement as well as in arms, leads his Caledonians to the relief of the distressed. The action is interrupted and deepened by the recursive method of the poems: bards sing the past, heroes recount their own sorrows, and the ghosts of the departed appear to hasten or to lament a death. Love, friendship and the observance of hospitality are the governing virtues, and the great motive power is grief, expressed in lamentation over the slain and over fallen greatness. The shorter poems appended are mostly laments and narratives of private calamity, and they supply the tenderness the epic's battles refuse.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the Ossianic vogue in its full epic form, and one of the most widely translated and imitated poems of the later eighteenth century in Europe; its machinery of grief, mist, ghosts and heroic moderation supplied preromantic poetry with a whole repertoire. Its claim to have supplied Britain with an ancient epic of its own remains the centre of the authentication controversy.
works.meter: Unrhymed cadenced verse of great uniformity and weight, with inversion, accumulation of epithets, and long rolling periods; the measure is deliberately unlike heroick couplet or blank verse of the Augustan school, and was admired as a recovery of ancient harmonious barbaric numbers.
works.context: Published in 1762, in the war years, when Scottish and English readers were being offered national epics on every side, and when the dissertation on ancient poetry prefixed to the work was itself a contribution to the criticism of taste and sublimity. The volume's success established Macpherson's position and his claim to have recovered a Homeric-age literature from the Gaelic.
works.characters: Fingal; his sons and warriors; the heroes and heroines of the appended poems; the spirits of the dead and the reciting bards
works.structure: An epic in six books with a strongly episodic and recursive organisation: the present action is repeatedly suspended by songs, recitations and visions of the past, so that the temporal structure is that of an ancient tradition recollected by bards rather than of a continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Recorded as disputed because Macpherson published the work as a translation of an ancient epic and contemporaries, and many since, have held that the ancient original is largely or wholly his own composition, made from such Gaelic tradition as he genuinely gathered. The ascription to 'Ossian' and to the ancient bards is not verifiable; Macpherson's own responsibility for the printed text is undisputed.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Warfare and battle
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: Finnegans Wake
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1939
works.description: The most radical prose work in English: the dream of a Dublin publican, in a language made of every language. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by James Joyce; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Finnegan, a Dublin builder, is laid out for his wake; he becomes Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, the publican of Chapelizod, his wife Anna Livia Plurabelle, and their children Shem, Shaun and Issy. The seventeen chapters are the dream of Earwicker through a single night, in a language of portmanteau words, puns in dozens of languages, quotations and riddles, circling back to its own opening word.
works.significance: Finnegans Wake is the most radical work of prose in any language: it dissolved English into a dream language of portmanteau words, absorbed the whole history of the world into a Dublin night, and set the outer limit of the experimental novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the epiphany and the open ending (Dubliners).
works.context: The history of Ireland, the Catholic Church, the Viking invasions, the fall of Parnell and the First World War, dissolved into the dream language of a Dublin family. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker (HCE); Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP); Shem the Penman; Shaun the Post; Issy
works.structure: Four books of seventeen chapters, structured by Vico's cycles and the dream of a single night. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Augustine Aloysius Joyce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind

works.title: Firmilian: A Spasmodic Tragedy
works.description: The wittiest parody of the Victorian poet: the spasmodic school destroyed in one tragedy. It is a verse work of 1854 by William Edmondstoune Aytoun; it belongs to The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice and it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy.
works.plot: Aytoun, writing as 'T. Percy Jones', parodies the spasmodic poets in a tragedy of Firmilian, a poet of intense sensibility who stabs his wife, his friend and himself in a series of impossible scenes, ending with the famous stage direction 'The whole of the dramatis personae here sit down upon the ground and howl'.
works.significance: Firmilian is the wittiest parody of the Victorian poet and the book that ended the spasmodic fashion: its impossible tragedy made the movement ridiculous overnight and it remains one of the funniest poems in English.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is the stirring historical ballad with a refrain.
works.context: Edinburgh and London in 1854, and the fashion for the spasmodic poets. The record dates the work as composed in 1854 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; victorian verse drama and revived tragedy.
works.characters: Firmilian; his wife; his friend; the dramatis personae
works.structure: A parody tragedy in several acts. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. E. Aytoun. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
