works.title: Gertrude of Wyoming
altTitles: Gertrude of Wyoming; A Pennsylvanian Tale, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: an sentimental frontier narrative in the revived Spenserian stanza, drawing on the ballad revival and on the poetry of domestic pathos.
works.description: A narrative poem in Spenserian stanzas set on the frontiers of Pennsylvania during the American Revolutionary war, and the most successful romance in verse of its decade. It tells of Gertrude, bride of a colonial settler, whose household is destroyed in an attack on the Wyoming valley, and who dies in her husband's arms. The volume also contains shorter tales and lyrics which helped fix the poet's popular reputation.
works.plot: The poem opens on a settler household in the Wyoming valley and on the marriage of its heroine, and it dwells on the friendly compact between the colonists and the neighbouring Native Americans before that compact is broken by war. The settlement is surprised and destroyed, parents perish, and the heroine dies in the arms of those she loves, while an infant survivor is carried to safety. A wandering bard, who has himself lost family in the same catastrophe, recovers the child and transmits the story, so that the tale reaches the reader as a remembered and recited romance. The massacre of 1778 in the Wyoming valley supplies the historical kernel, and the poem's emotional argument turns on conjugal and filial fidelity tested by frontier violence. Spenserian stanzas lend the tale an archaising dignity that contemporary reviewers thought at once its ornament and its limitation.
works.significance: It supplied the nineteenth century with its most widely read verse account of the American frontier and helped legitimate sentimental domestic tragedy in heroic-measure romance. Its fame travelled to the United States, where the Wyoming story was already national myth, and it was attacked and praised chiefly for the archaism of its stanza. Later historians of the ballad revival treat it as the moment when popular Romantic narrative verse turned from Scottish border matter to transatlantic colonial subject.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine.
works.context: Written when British readers were avid for American frontier material and when the Wyoming massacre of 1778 had already become a transatlantic cause celebre. Its publication coincides with the vogue for historical romance in verse that the leading Scottish poet-novelist of the generation soon dominated, and its treatment of Native Americans recycles the enlightened vocabulary of the noble savage current after the Scottish Enlightenment's theories of society. The poem was repeatedly reprinted, pirated in America, and used by its author as the anchor of his collected edition.
works.structure: A framed romantic narrative in six cantos: an idyllic settlement, a betrayed compact, a catastrophe, and a survival carried into a reciting frame by a bard who has himself been bereaved by the same violence.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
Warfare and battle
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
altTitles: Deeds of the Kings of the English
works.description: William of Malmesbury's history of the English kings from the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons (449) to the twenty-eighth year of Henry I (1127–28), the most learned English history of the twelfth century, deliberately modelled on Bede and written with a polished Latinity that set a new standard for English historiography.
works.summary: Five books carry the narrative from the adventus Saxonum through the kings of Wessex and the Norman Conquest to Henry I; the work combines narrative history with biography, anecdote, and documentary research, drawing on a library of sources now partly lost and on William's own travels and enquiries.
works.significance: The outstanding English historical work between Bede and the later twelfth century; a model of critical method and style, cited and pillaged by later chroniclers, and a primary witness to Anglo-Saxon history after the Conquest.

National identity and Englishness

works.title: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary
works.description: The founding book of the modern English ghost story: 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and the antiquarian terror. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by M. R. James; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Canon Alberic's Scrap-Book', 'Lost Hearts', 'The Mezzotint', 'The Ash-tree', 'Number 13', 'Count Magnus', 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and 'The Treasure of Abbot Thomas' — stories of scholars, manuscripts and things that should not be disturbed.
works.significance: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary founded the modern English ghost story: its antiquarian frame, its exact topography and its withheld apparitions made it the model for the genre, and 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' is the most famous ghost story in English.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian frame: the discovery of a document, an object or a manuscript.
works.context: The English cathedral towns and country houses of the 1890s, the antiquarian scholarship of the period, and the Christmas ghost-story tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1903 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: Professor Parkins; Canon Alberic; Count Magnus; Mr Williams; Stephen Elliott
works.structure: Eight stories, each framed by a document, a manuscript or a scholarly discovery. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.

works.title: Gloria I and II
altTitles: The Greater and Lesser Doxology Poems
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two short Old English versifications of the liturgical Gloria: Gloria I (57 lines) paraphrases the Greater Doxology sung at Mass, praising the Trinity and Christ the Lamb of God; Gloria II (20 lines) is a brief rendering of the doxology of praise to Father, Son, and Spirit.
works.plot: Gloria I moves from the angels' song of praise through the attributes of the persons of the Trinity to Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, ending with a prayer for mercy. Gloria II offers a compact doxology in verse.
works.significance: Evidence of the Old English church's project of rendering the central texts of the liturgy into the vernacular poetic idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the balanced parallelism appropriate to liturgical praise; the shorter poem is notably compact.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's devotion to the liturgy gave new prominence to the sung ordinary of the Mass; vernacular paraphrases like these made its texts accessible to those whose Latin was limited.
works.structure: Both poems are direct liturgical paraphrases; Gloria I is organized by the successive clauses of the Gloria in excelsis, closing with the Agnus Dei petitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are separate compositions.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Mission, conversion, and the Church

works.title: Gloriana; or, The Revolution of 1900
works.description: A feminist utopian novel in which a woman, disguised as a man, becomes Prime Minister and wins the vote for women. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Lady Florence Dixie; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: As a girl Gloria de Lara vows to free her sex; disguised as Hector D'Estrange she passes through Eton and Oxford, founds institutions where women learn to ride, shoot and swim, and enters the House of Commons, where her campaign makes women's suffrage law and, at twenty-eight, wins her the premiership. Lord Westray, the man who had wronged her mother, hides himself so that D'Estrange is tried for his murder; at the trial D'Estrange confesses that he is a woman, Gloria de Lara, and is sentenced, but Flora Desmond and her White Guards rescue her and she escapes her pursuers. The disclosure wins many waverers to her side, a general election returns her party with a majority over all the others, and a closing chapter set in 1999 describes a prosperous and peaceful Britain transformed by women's share in its government.
works.significance: Gloriana turned the suffrage argument into utopian romance: its heroine wins the vote for women by passing as a man and governing as Prime Minister, is vindicated when her sex is revealed, and is surrounded by women who drive the plot, so that the novel joins the feminist utopia to romance, trial melodrama and detective plotting.
works.meter: Prose: a declamatory present-tense narrative of melodrama and political oratory, with set-piece speeches in Parliament and the courtroom and occasional verse.
works.context: Published by Henry and Co. in 1890, while women's suffrage bills were repeatedly failing in the Commons; Dixie's preface argues not only for the vote but for educating the sexes together and opening every profession and position to women.
works.characters: Gloria de Lara (Hector D'Estrange); Mrs de Lara, her mother; Captain Kintore, her father; Lord Westray; Flora Desmond and her White Guards; Colonel Delamere
works.structure: A polemical preface followed by a novel in three books of short chapters, narrated largely in the present tense and ending in a chapter set in 1999.

works.title: Go Down, Moses
works.description: The McCaslin family across a century: slavery, the land and the bear, and Faulkner's most moving book. It is a prose fiction work of 1942 by William Faulkner; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The seven stories follow the McCaslin and Beauchamp families from the 1850s to the 1940s — the hunting of the great bear Old Ben, the discovery of the family's slave heritage, the death of the old hunter Sam Fathers, and the return of Lucas Beauchamp's grandson — in a book about the land, race and inheritance.
works.significance: Go Down, Moses is Faulkner's most moving book and the finest treatment of race and inheritance in American fiction: 'The Bear' is one of the great American stories, and the book's century-long family chronicle made the McCaslins the equal of the Compsons.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the long retrospective sentence with its parentheses and its piled-up subordinate clauses.
works.context: The Mississippi wilderness and its destruction by the lumber companies, the legacy of slavery, and the Southern hunting tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1941 and first published in 1942 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; modern short story and the magazine tale.

works.title: Goblin Market and Other Poems
works.form: Poetry collection; title poem in irregular rhymed couplets
works.description: Published in 1862 with illustrations by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and the volume that made her reputation: Goblin Market, 'Remember', 'A Birthday', 'After Death', 'The Convent Threshold', 'Up-Hill' and 'An Apple Gathering'.
works.plot: In Goblin Market, Laura buys and eats the goblins' fruit and begins to waste away, calling for 'more'; her sister Lizzie resists the merchants' assault and returns with the juice of the fruit on her face, which restores Laura; the poem ends with the two as wives and mothers telling the story to their children.
works.significance: Goblin Market is the most discussed Victorian poem by a woman and a central text of modern feminist criticism, read as an allegory of consumerism, of sexual knowledge, of sisterhood and of the Eucharist; its fairy tale surface and its theological depth made it the model for the fantastic moral tale from MacDonald and Kingsley to the modern fantasy.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The verse runs in rhymed couplets. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
works.context: The 1860s, the Pre-Raphaelite circle and its treatment of the fallen woman, the Victorian debate on sensual temptation and the spiritual reading of fairy tale, and the penitentiary work at Highgate where Christina Rossetti taught from 1876.
works.characters: Laura; Lizzie; the goblin men; Jeanie
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.

works.plot: Little Augie, a jockey of extraordinary talent, rides the Southern race tracks, loves the wrong women and drinks too much, in a picaresque novel of Black sporting life that ends in California with Augie penniless and alone.

works.title: God's Grandeur
works.description: Written in 1877: a sonnet on the grandeur of God in the world and the human refusal to see it — 'the world is charged with the grandeur of God' — and one of the founding texts of modern nature poetry.
works.plot: The octave states the presence of God's grandeur in the world and the way 'generations have trod, have trod, have trod' until the ground is seared; the sestet turns to the renewal of the world by the Holy Ghost, whose brooding over the bent world makes it 'warm with the grandeur of God' again.
works.significance: 'God's Grandeur' is the most quoted Victorian religious sonnet and the central poem of Hopkins's sacramental nature poetry; its combination of industrial imagery with the doctrine of the Holy Ghost has made it a permanent text for the criticism of Victorian religion and of modern ecology.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
works.context: The industrial England of the 1870s, the Jesuit training in Lancashire and Wales, and the 1877 sermons on the created world as the manifestation of God. The record dates the work as composed in 1877 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: God's Trombones: Seven Negro Sermons in Verse
works.description: The great poem of the Black folk sermon: the creation, the flood and the judgement. works.title: Godfrey of Bulloigne
works.description: Edward Fairfax's translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1581), under the title Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600): the crusaders' siege and taking of Jerusalem — Godfrey's command, Rinaldo's enchantment in Armida's garden, Tancred and Clorinda's tragedy — in English ottava rima of grave and musical fidelity, the translation Dryden ranked with the originals.
works.plot: The Christian army besieges Jerusalem; the pagan enchantments of Armida and Ismeno delay the victory; Rinaldo is rescued from the garden of Armida; the duel of Tancred and Clorinda, the battles, and the final assault take the city; and the poem ends with Godfrey's worship at the Sepulchre.
works.significance: The great English Tasso — the version through which the Italian romantic epic entered English poetry, and a landmark of translation as an art.
works.meter: Ottava rima (abababcc) of sustained dignity and sweetness — the metre Fairfax naturalized for English heroic verse.
works.context: Published 1600, in the decade of the English epic translations (Harington's Ariosto, Sylvester's Du Bartas); Fairfax's Tasso was read by the Spenserians and praised by Dryden as the model of translation.
works.characters: Godfrey of Bouillon; Rinaldo; Armida; Tancred; Clorinda; Erminia; Peter the Hermit; Ismeno; Solyman; Argantes
works.structure: Twenty cantos of ottava rima following Tasso's order, with Fairfax's 'Allegory of the Poem' appended as the moral key.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Fairfax; uncontested.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Warfare and battle

works.title: Godly Queen Hester
altTitles: A New Interlude Drawn out of the Holy Scripture of Godly Queen Hester
works.description: An anonymous interlude on the biblical story of Esther, printed in 1561 but composed c. 1525–29; a political allegory in which the virtuous queen and her wise counsellor save the realm from the wicked minister.
works.plot: King Ahasuerus, misled by the proud Aman, signs a decree against the Jews; Queen Hester, advised by the wise Mardocheus, intercedes with the king at the risk of her life, exposes Aman's malice, and obtains his overthrow and the deliverance of her people — with the collop-eating scene of Aman's gluttony played as comic Vice-business.
works.significance: The first surviving English dramatization of the Esther story and a striking example of the interlude as political counsel; it shows biblical drama absorbing the new humanist debate on counsel and tyranny.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1525–29, almost certainly for a noble household: the story of Esther had long served as an allegory of good counsel and royal deliverance, and the play has been read (by Greg Walker and others) as a veiled commentary on the fall of Wolsey, in which the virtuous queen intercedes against an overmighty minister.
works.characters: King Ahasuerus; Queen Hester; Mardocheus; Aman; Ardion (Aman's servant); Hardydardy; Pride; Adulation; Ambition
works.structure: A continuous interlude alternating the counsel scenes of Hester and Mardocheus with the comic scenes of Aman and his servants, ending in judgement and the elevation of Mardocheus.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Religious persecution and martyrdom
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: Going to the Territory
works.description: Going to the Territory is Ralph Ellison's second collection of essays, published by Random House in 1986: seventeen essays, speeches and reminiscences from the 1960s to the 1980s on American culture, literature and music.
works.summary: Pieces on William Faulkner and on Ellison's friend Richard Wright, an homage to Duke Ellington, reminiscences of his Oklahoma childhood, and lectures on the contribution of African Americans to American national identity, including the title address and "The Little Man at Chehaw Station".
works.plot: The essays extend the argument of Shadow and Act into a broader theory of American culture as a democratic, improvised mixture in which African Americans have been central creators. Ellison imagines an ideal listener, the 'little man' who may turn up anywhere and judge an artist's work, as a figure for America's unpredictable democratic audience; he recalls the Oklahoma 'territory' of his youth as a frontier of possibility; and he pays tribute to Ellington and Wright as artists who made American culture.
works.significance: It confirmed Ellison's standing as a cultural critic and offered his fullest account of American culture as a vernacular, mixed democracy; "The Little Man at Chehaw Station" is among his most cited essays.
works.meter: Expansive, digressive and anecdotal, the prose of a public lecturer and memoirist, more relaxed than the polemics of the earlier book.
works.context: Published in 1986, more than twenty years after Shadow and Act, when Ellison's long-promised second novel had still not appeared and multiculturalism was reshaping debates about American culture.
works.structure: Seventeen essays, addresses and interviews arranged by theme, ranging from reminiscence to formal lecture.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Nationhood and national identity
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: Going, Going
works.description: Going, Going is a poem by Philip Larkin commissioned by the Department of the Environment and first printed in its working party report on the human habitat, How Do You Want to Live? (1972), then collected in High Windows (1974). It foresees the English countryside lost to development and profit.
works.summary: The speaker's former confidence that the fields would last his time; the demands for more houses, parking and caravan sites; the business pages and takeover bids; and the prophecy that England will be gone, leaving concrete and tyres.
works.plot: The speaker had thought the sense of fields and farms beyond the town would last his time, and that the earth would always recover however it was abused. Now he doubts it, or perhaps is only getting old: the young crowd in the motorway cafe want more houses, more parking, more caravan sites, more pay, and the business pages approve takeovers that move industry into the unspoilt dales. Before he dies, he thinks, the whole country will be bricked in except for the tourist parts, the first slum of Europe; and that will be England gone, the shadows, meadows, lanes, guildhalls and carved choirs surviving only in books and galleries. Most things are never meant, he ends, but the greeds and garbage are too thick-strewn to be swept up now: he thinks it will happen soon.
works.significance: Larkin's best-known public poem and an early literary statement of environmental anxiety in Britain, often quoted in debates about planning and the countryside.
works.meter: Conversational, sardonic and plain, with lists of modern clutter set against a lyrical inventory of the England being lost.
works.context: Completed on 25 January 1972 for the report of a Department of the Environment working party; Her Majesty's Stationery Office gave permission for its inclusion in High Windows.
works.structure: Nine six-line stanzas, rhymed, moving from memory through satire of the present to prophecy.
themes: Land, place and regional belonging
Nationhood and national identity
Nature, ecology and environmental crisis
movements: The Movement

works.title: Gold Coast Customs
works.form: Long poem (the satire of the London season)
works.description: The great satire of the London season and the waste land of the west. It is a verse work of 1929 by Edith Sitwell; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Gold Coast Customs sets the cannibal feasts of the Gold Coast against the dinners of the London season, in the long chanted line of the drum and the jazz band, and carries the satire of the rich into the elegy of the civilisation that eats its own.
works.significance: Gold Coast Customs is Edith Sitwell's greatest poem before the war elegies: its drum, its jazz and its cannibal feast made the satire of the rich a poem of the waste land and gave English modernism its most sustained indictment of the pleasure economy.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
works.context: London at the end of the 1920s, and the satire of the waste land. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
works.characters: Lady Bamburgher
works.structure: A long poem in chanted sections, the feast and the season in counterpoint. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Edith Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Gondal Poems
works.form: Poems of a private imaginary chronicle
works.description: The body of verse written by Emily (and, in part, Anne) Brontë from about 1836 into the 1840s, set in the imaginary island kingdom of Gondal in the North Pacific and concerned with its queens, its prisoners and its wars; a substantial part of it was printed in the 1846 volume, and the prose chronicles that framed it were lost.
works.plot: The poems are dramatic fragments rather than a continuous narrative: 'A. G. Rochelle' is a prisoner's song of endurance, 'The Death of A. G. Rochelle' and the Queen Augusta poems dramatise the politics of Gondal, and the elegiac and love poems register the passions of its royal houses. The recovering of the Gondal story from the poems has been a long scholarly exercise.
works.significance: The Gondal poems are the private laboratory of Emily Brontë's art and a central document for the study of the imaginative life of the Brontë household; they are the clearest English example of a nineteenth-century writer maintaining a complete secondary world across two decades.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is a frame-within-a-frame narrative with two partial and unreliable narrators.
works.context: A childhood and adolescent imaginative project shared with Anne Brontë from 1827 onwards, descended from the Brontës' reading of Scott, Byron and Blackwood's, and conducted in manuscript notebooks (the 'Gondal poems' are preserved in the Ashley and Bonnell collections).
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution of individual Gondal poems between Emily and Anne Brontë rests on manuscript evidence and on Charlotte's 1850 editing; a number remain uncertain, and the prose chronicles are lost.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: Gone to Earth
works.form: Novel (the nature romance of the hunted creature)
works.description: The tragedy of Hazel and the hunted creature: the chapel, the squire and the hounds. It is a prose fiction work of 1917 by Mary Webb; it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Gone to Earth follows Hazel Woodus, the child of the hills and the old religion, between the chapel of her husband the minister and the desire of the squire, until the hunt that closes the novel takes her with the hunted creature she loved.
works.significance: Gone to Earth is Mary Webb's tragedy of the hunted creature: its Hazel, its chapel and its hunt carried the nature romance into tragedy and made her name among the novelists of the province.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is the charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather.
works.context: Shropshire in the years of the war. The record dates the work as composed in 1916 and first published in 1917 and it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Hazel Woodus; Edward Marston; Jack Reddin; the hunted creature; the hounds
works.structure: A tragedy in chapters of the hills, the chapel and the hunt. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary Gladys Meredith. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle

works.title: Good Morning, Midnight
works.description: Rhys's great novel of the woman alone in Paris: Sasha Jansen and the bars of the Left Bank. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Jean Rhys; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Sasha Jansen, a middle-aged Englishwoman, returns to Paris with money from a friend and drifts through the bars and hotels of her youth, in a first-person narrative of drink, memory and the search for a room of her own.
works.significance: Good Morning, Midnight is Rhys's greatest novel and one of the finest English novels of the 1930s: its first-person narrative of drink and memory made the modern novel of the woman alone, and its reputation has grown to make it a central text of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrative of the woman without money.
works.context: Paris in the late 1930s, and the expatriate world of the Left Bank. The record dates the work as composed between 1938 and 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Sasha Jansen; Rene; the young man; the hotel keeper
works.structure: A first-person narrative in four parts, in the Paris bars and hotels. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ella Gwendolen Rees Williams. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form
Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind

Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict

works.title: Good-bye to All That
works.form: Autobiography; war memoir, first issued in 1929
works.description: The great English war memoir: Charterhouse, the trenches, the wound that was reported as death, and the flight from England. It is a prose work of 1929 by Robert Graves; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Graves recounts his childhood and public school, his enlistment in 1914, the trenches of the Royal Welch Fusiliers, the Somme and the wound of 1916 that was reported as his death, the shell shock of his recovery, and his post-war Oxford and marriage — and ends with his departure for Majorca and his farewell to England.
works.significance: Good-bye to All That is one of the two great English memoirs of the First World War and the book that changed the writing of autobiography: its irony, its detail and its refusal of consolation made it the model for the war books boom of 1929.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, lucid, formal lyric in the eighteenth-century manner.
works.context: The First World War and its aftermath, Charterhouse and the English public-school system, and the literary London of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Robert Graves; his family; Siegfried Sassoon; the Royal Welch Fusiliers
works.structure: Chronological autobiography in chapters, from childhood to the departure for Majorca. A memoir in episodic chapters organised by posting or battle, the later self reflecting on the earlier experience. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert von Ranke Graves. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Goodbye to Berlin
works.description: The definitive English book about Weimar Berlin, and the source of Cabaret: 'I am a camera'. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Christopher Isherwood; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The narrator, an English writer in Berlin from 1930 to 1933, records the boarding house of Fräulein Schroeder, the cabaret singer Sally Bowles, the Jewish family Landauer, the working-class Nowaks and the rise of the Nazis — and leaves as Hitler comes to power.
works.significance: Goodbye to Berlin is the definitive English book about Weimar Berlin and one of the great documentaries of the period: its camera-eye narration, its portrait of Sally Bowles and its record of the Nazi rise became the source of Cabaret and the century's image of the doomed city.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The author's characteristic manner is the camera-eye narration: the observer who records without comment.
works.context: Berlin from 1930 to 1933, the last years of the Weimar Republic, the cabaret and the boarding house, and the Nazi seizure of power. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: The narrator; Sally Bowles; Fräulein Schroeder; Natalia Landauer; Bernhard Landauer; Otto Nowak
works.structure: Six linked stories narrated by an English observer, from 1930 to 1933. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christopher William Bradshaw-Isherwood. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Goostly Psalmes and Spirituall Songes
works.description: Miles Coverdale's collection of metrical psalms, hymns, and carols translated from the German (chiefly Luther), printed c. 1535; the first English hymn book, intended for congregational singing.
works.plot: Forty-one pieces — metrical versions of the psalms, Luther's hymns (including 'Ein feste Burg' as 'Our God is a defence and tower'), the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and canticles — each with its tune indicated, prefaced by an epistle on the right use of psalmody in church and home.
works.significance: The first English hymn book and the beginning of English congregational song; its psalms anticipate the metrical psalters of Sternhold and Hopkins, and its translation of 'Ein feste Burg' entered the English hymnic tradition.
works.meter: Metrical stanzas in ballad and hymn metres, set to German tunes
works.context: Printed c. 1535 during Coverdale's continental exile, drawing on the Wittenberg hymn books; Henry VIII's 1546 proclamation against 'ballads, rhymes, and lewd songs' included it among the books to be burned, and only one complete copy survives (Queen's College, Oxford).
works.structure: A hymn book arranged by liturgical use, with a preface on singing and notes of the tunes to which the pieces are set.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The English Reformation
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

works.title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
works.description: Bunyan's spiritual autobiography, written in Bedford Gaol during his twelve-year imprisonment for preaching without a licence, which records his agonising struggle with doubt, temptation, and the assurance of salvation.
works.plot: Bunyan traces his life from a childhood of swearing and bell-ringing through his conversion under John Gifford, his long torments of doubt and despair, his reading of Luther's Commentary on Galatians, and his final assurance of grace; the narrative is organised around biblical typology rather than chronology.
works.significance: The greatest spiritual autobiography in English and a foundational text of the Protestant confessional tradition; it supplied the raw material of inner experience that Bunyan transformed into the allegory of The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Vigorous, colloquial prose saturated with biblical language, especially the Psalms, Paul, and Hebrews.
works.context: Written in 1666 during Bunyan's first long imprisonment (1660-72) and published in the same year with a preface addressed to his Bedford congregation; a seventh edition appeared before his death.
works.characters: John Bunyan (the narrator); John Gifford; his first wife; his second wife Elizabeth; the Bedford congregation
works.structure: A first-person retrospective narrative in numbered paragraphs, with scriptural glosses on the margins, following the pattern of the Pauline conversion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Melancholy and self-analysis
Penance, confession, and sin
Religious persecution and martyrdom

works.title: Graham Hamilton
altTitles: Graham Hamilton; a Tale of the Old School
works.description: A two-volume historical novel of Scottish covenanting and border material, written after the author's notorious first romance and issued anonymously with the publisher's explanation that the manuscript had been placed in his hands two years earlier with an earnest injunction neither to name the writer nor to publish it at that time. It is the novel in which the author tried the plan of writing a book that would offend nobody. The tale takes the form of a family history set in the old Scottish school of persecution and covenant.
works.plot: Graham Hamilton grows up under the instruction of a stern covenanting household, is bound to an unequal love, and is drawn into the troubles of the Scottish southwest, where the old covenanters' feud with the civil and ecclesiastical authority supplies the machinery of the plot. The narrative moves between the house, the moor, and the field of arms, and the hero's education in honour and enthusiasm is tested by the disasters of his family's cause. A tale of the older religion and of the lovers divided by it, the novel ends with the destruction of the generation it has followed. The romance is deliberately gentler than the author's first book in its handling of society and of persons.
works.significance: The novel marks the attempt of a woman author of scandalous celebrity to convert the Waverley model into a decorous covenanting romance, and it records the pressure of anonymity on the women's fiction market of the 1820s. Its publication history, with the manuscript held back two years at the writer's request, is a document of authorial anxiety in the period.
works.context: Written in the early 1820s when the Scottish historical novel had become the dominant form of fiction and when its author, having published a violent personal roman a clef in 1816 and a verse satire in 1819, was advised by an exile poet friend to write a book that would offend nobody. It appeared from a Conduit Street publisher in two small volumes in 1822, anonymously, the delay and the anonymity being stated in the publisher's own note.
works.characters: Graham Hamilton; the covenanting elder of his household; the woman he loves and cannot marry; the soldiers and preachers of the southwest rising
works.structure: A conventional multi-volume historical novel of education and persecution, with a continuous third-person narrative interrupted by letters and by explanatory notes on the covenanting period.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1822; the publisher's note records the request for concealment, and the authorship rests on contemporary knowledge of the writer and on the collected editions.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Religious persecution and martyrdom
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Grammar and Glossary
works.form: grammar and didactic prose in Old English
works.description: Ælfric's Latin grammar written in English — the first grammar of Latin composed in any European vernacular — with its companion glossary of Latin words arranged by subject. A landmark in the history of education and of the vernacular as an instrument of learning.
works.plot: The Grammar adapts the Excerptiones de Prisciano to teach the parts of speech, declensions, and conjugations entirely through the medium of English, explaining Latin forms with English equivalents; the Glossary lists vocabulary by topics (the body, kinship, the church, tools, birds, beasts) in Latin with English glosses.
works.significance: The first vernacular Latin grammar in Europe; a milestone in the history of English education.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Composed c. 998, when Ælfric was at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; at least fifteen manuscripts survive, evidence of its use in schools into the twelfth century.
works.characters: the schoolboys of Eynsham (addressees)
works.structure: A systematic school grammar in sections on the eight parts of speech, followed by the thematic glossary.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Wisdom and learning
movements: Benedictine Reform
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Grania: The Story of an Island
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Lawless's masterpiece: two sisters on the Aran Islands and the sea that takes them. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by Emily Lawless; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Grania and Honor O'Malley live alone on Inishmaan in the Aran Islands; Grania loves a man who loves her sister, and the novel follows the two women through a winter of storms, illness and renunciation, ending with Honor's death and Grania's survival on the island.
works.significance: Grania is Emily Lawless's masterpiece and the finest novel ever written about the Aran Islands: its portrait of the two sisters, its storms and its limestone landscape made it a classic of Irish regional fiction and a central text of the Irish revival.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the western landscape as the determining force.
works.context: The Aran Islands in the 1880s, the Congested Districts and the isolation of the western seaboard. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Grania O'Malley; Honor O'Malley; Murdough Blake; the islanders
works.structure: A novel in three parts, following the sisters through the seasons. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hon. Emily Lawless. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
themes: Regional identity and the American sectional character
The closing of the American frontier
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Great Expectations
works.form: Novel in weekly parts (All the Year Round); three volumes 1861
works.description: Serialised weekly in All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861 and published in three volumes in July 1861; the second great first-person novel and the one in which Dickens rewrote the Bildungsroman as a story of moral education by disillusion.
works.plot: Philip Pirrip, 'Pip', is brought up by his sister and her husband Joe Gargery, the village blacksmith; he is summoned to play at the house of Miss Havisham, who has stopped her clocks at the hour of her desertion and raised the beautiful Estella to break men's hearts. Pip becomes convinced that Miss Havisham is his benefactor and that Estella is intended for him; the arrival of the convict Magwitch reveals that his great expectations have come from a transported felon, and the novel turns into a study of Pip's shame, of Magwitch's devotion, and of the loss of the fortune. The original ending leaves Pip and Estella parted; the published ending gives them a tentative reunion.
works.significance: Great Expectations is the most perfectly constructed of Dickens's novels and the central English novel about class and shame; its treatment of Pip's gentlemanly self-invention and of Magwitch's colonial fortune made it a foundational text for later postcolonial and class criticism, and its two endings are a permanent case study in narrative authority.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The 1810s-20s of the novel's setting and the 1860s of its composition: the convict hulks and transportation to Australia, the gentleman's education and the idle 'expectations' of the gentry, the counting-house and the trading house, and the working of the criminal law.
works.characters: Philip Pirrip (Pip); Joe Gargery; Mrs Joe; Magwitch (Provis); Miss Havisham; Estella; Herbert Pocket; Mr Jaggers; Wemmick; Mr Pumblechook; Biddy; Orlick; Compeyson; Clara Barley
works.structure: First-person retrospective narrative in three stages of expectation, revelation and correction, with the convict plot displacing the fairy-tale plot at the centre.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story

Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination

works.title: Green Mansions: A Romance of the Tropical Forest
works.description: Published in 1904 and the great English romance of the tropical forest: a traveller's love for the bird-girl Rima in the forests of Venezuela. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by W. H. Hudson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Abel, a young Venezuelan, flees into the forest after a political murder and finds a wild girl, Rima, who lives among the birds and speaks their language; he loves her, takes her to his own people for protection, and she is killed by the Indians who fear her, leaving Abel to wander the forest for the rest of his life.
works.significance: Green Mansions is the central English romance of the tropical forest and one of the most influential novels of the natural world: Rima became one of the great mythic figures of English fiction, the novel was a best-seller on both sides of the Atlantic, and it made Hudson's name as a writer as well as a naturalist.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, unhurried descriptive prose.
works.context: 1904: the South American travel literature of the nineteenth century, the Victorian romance revival, and the English fascination with the untouched tropical world. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Abel; Rima; Nuflo; Cla-cla; Runi; the Indians of the forest
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Hudson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Science, religion, and the question of design
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: Greenfield Hill
altTitles: Greenfield Hill: A Poem, in Seven Parts
works.form: Topographical and descriptive poetry with didactic and historical argument; the estate and township poem transferred to America
works.description: A topographical, historical and didactic poem on a hill settlement in New Haven county, and the most ambitious verse of the early American republic before the 1820s. Its seven parts pass from the scene of the grove to the history of the country, its institutions, its commerce, its religion and its morals. It gives the American township as a subject for the Thomsonian and Goldsmithian descriptive manner.
works.plot: The poem opens on the grove and the vale of Greenfield Hill and its seasons, and then retells the settlement of the country from the first planting of the colony. It passes to the survey of the neighbouring towns, to the character of the people, to the pleasures of study and to the claims of religion and of public duty. Admonitions against intemperance, gambling and irreligion are woven through the descriptive passages. The close commends the hill, its church and its schools to the reader as a model of a republican community.
works.significance: It is the largest American poem of the 1790s and the standard example of the transplanted British topographical manner. Its social survey makes it a primary document for the cultural history of Connecticut. Its reputation stood high through the nineteenth century as the work of the president of Yale.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with occasional longer stanzas
works.context: Published in 1794 at New York, in the president's second decade, and written from the author's settled life at Greenfield Hill in Connecticut. Its models were Thomson, Goldsmith and the British descriptive school, and its subject was the newly confident Congregational township. Its political passages reflect the 1790s quarrel over French revolutionary principles and over the fate of religion in a republic.
works.structure: Descriptive and didactic poem in seven parts, moving from local scene to colonial history to moral and religious instruction, with long topographical and catalogue passages.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Greenland, and Other Poems
works.form: Descriptive and elegiac poem in the Thomsonian and mission-inspired mode, gathered with shorter lyrics in a miscellaneous volume
works.description: A volume of poems by James Montgomery of Sheffield, published in 1819, whose title piece is a melancholy meditation on the vanished Norwegian colony of Greenland. The volume mixes the descriptive and missionary imagination with lyric and moral pieces, reflecting Montgomery's double life as a radical editor and a hymn-writer. Greenland itself, the chief poem, imagines the lost settlements of the Norse in the frozen north and the extinguished Christian community that once flourished there, turning topography into an elegy for a perished people.
works.plot: The title poem traces the rise and disappearance of the old Norse settlements in Greenland: the faith and labour of the colonists, their isolation and gradual extinction, and the modern traveller who finds only ruins, ice, and the Inhabitant where a Christian people had been. The companion poems of the volume move among moral, descriptive, and sentimental subjects, several touched by Montgomery's interest in missions, distant lands, and the transience of human establishments.
works.significance: The volume is the principal example of Montgomery's Romantic descriptive verse and of his poetry of vanished peoples and missionary sympathy; Greenland gave the lost Norse colony its best-known English poetic treatment of the period and helped fix the vanished-settlement theme in Romantic literature of the North.
works.meter: Greenland is written in smooth iambic pentameter couplets suited to swelling description and moral reflection; the accompanying lyrics use regular song and hymn stanzas with simple rhyme, the whole marked by Montgomery's clear, tuneful, and unforced prosody.
works.context: Published in 1819, when the Arctic, the vanished Norse settlements, and the great missionary societies were vivid topics for a reading public fascinated by lost civilisations and distant heathendom. Montgomery, editor of the Sheffield Register and a committed Evangelical, wrote within a current that joined Romantic topographical melancholy to a missionary and humanitarian interest in perished and un evangelised peoples.
works.characters: the lost Norse colonists of Greenland; the extinguished Christian settlement; the modern traveller or speaker who surveys the ruins; the Inuit inhabitant met in the emptied land
works.structure: A miscellaneous volume dominated by the single long descriptive-elegiac poem Greenland, with shorter lyric and moral pieces grouped after it; there is no continuous plot across the volume, and Greenland itself proceeds as a historical meditation from settlement to ruin rather than as a story with characters in action.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; Montgomery's authorship of the volume and of Greenland is undisputed.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)

works.title: Greenmantle
works.description: Buchan's greatest adventure: four men and a holy war in the East. It is a prose fiction work of 1916 by John Buchan; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Richard Hannay, Peter Pienaar, Sandy Arbuthnot and the American John Blenkiron travel through wartime Germany and Turkey to find the secret of Greenmantle, the prophet who is to raise the East against the Allies.
works.significance: Greenmantle was Buchan's own favourite among his novels and the greatest of the Hannay adventures: its four companions, its wartime journey and its vision of the East made it the finest English adventure novel of the First World War.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the chase through landscape.
works.context: Europe and the Middle East in 1915–16, the First World War and the German attempt to raise the Islamic world. The record dates the work as composed in 1916 and first published in 1916 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Richard Hannay; Sandy Arbuthnot; Peter Pienaar; John Blenkiron; Hilda von Einem
works.structure: A first-person adventure narrative in twenty chapters. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as 1st Baron Tweedsmuir. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents
Exile, expatriation, and the lost generation
The First World War and the myth of sacrifice
Totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel

works.title: Guests of the Nation
works.description: The collection of the civil war: the title story of the prisoners and the decencies. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by Frank O'Connor; it belongs to The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Guests of the Nation gathers the stories of the civil war and the internment, among them the title story in which the IRA men guard the English prisoners who become their guests and then must shoot them, in the spoken Irish-English of the teller.
works.significance: Guests of the Nation is the founding collection of the Irish short story of the civil war: its title story put the ordinary decencies against the ideology in the form and made O'Connor one of the masters of the story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the single moral turn told in the spoken Irish-English.
works.context: Ireland in the civil war and after, published 1931. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1930 and first published in 1931 and the corpus places it within The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Bonaparte; Noble; the English prisoners; the old woman of the cottage
works.structure: A collection of civil-war stories, each with its single moral turn. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Frank O'Connor, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Frank O'Connor is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale
War Narrative of the Common Soldier
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question
The First World War and the myth of sacrifice

works.title: Gulliver's Travels
altTitles: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
works.description: Swift's four-part voyage satire, narrated by the surgeon and captain Lemuel Gulliver, which reduces the scale of mankind to Lilliput, enlarges it in Brobdingnag, sends him to the flying island and the projectors of the Academy, and ends among the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos.
works.plot: Gulliver is cast away and reaches a nation of six-inch men whose politics, war and parties are a miniature of Europe; then a land of giants where his own species is judged; then the projects of the mechanicks and the shades of the dead; and finally a country of rational horses whose human brutes, the Yahoos, force him to see his own kind as vermin, till his return and his disgust.
works.significance: It is the century's largest satiric fiction, converting the travellers' tale into an anatomy of human pride, and it founded the tradition of the constructed utopian and satirical voyage that runs to the nineteenth century.
works.meter: The deliberately unadorned prose of the navigator's log, with the exact measurement, the enumeration of customs and the flat statement of the most outrageous conclusion.
works.context: Written in the years between the fall of the Harley ministry and Swift's retirement to Dublin, and published anonymously in 1726 at a moment when the travel narrative and the new fiction of Defoe were making the invented first person respectable; the contemporary key identified nearly every personage of the first part.
works.characters: Lemuel Gulliver; the court and army of Lilliput; the farmer and the queen of Brobdingnag; the sages of the flying island; the Houyhnhnms; the Yahoos
works.structure: Four independent voyages in the first person, in the plain manner of the travel relation, each with its own ascent from curiosity to judgment; the sequence tightens from the political satire of the first two to the philosophical conclusion of the fourth.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of Lemuel Gulliver, initially a surgeon and lately a captain, with the printer's pretence of an unauthorised copy; Swift's authorship was understood at once and is uncontested.

Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history

Wisdom and learning

works.title: Guthlac A
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 818 lines on the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland: his arrival in the fenland retreat, his battles with the demons who tempt and torment him, and his vindication by the apostle Bartholomew. Based on Felix's Latin Vita, the poem turns the saint's spiritual warfare into heroic combat in the native manner.
works.plot: The young Mercian warrior Guthlac, renouncing war, takes up the solitary life in the fens of Crowland; demons assault his cell, carry him to the gates of hell, and accuse him of pride; the apostle Bartholomew commands his release and the devils obey; Guthlac returns victorious, and the poem closes with his death and the angels' reception of his soul.
works.significance: The classic vernacular treatment of the hermit-warrior and of the fenland as spiritual battlefield.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with the diction of heroic combat applied to spiritual warfare.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 32b-44b); source: Felix of Crowland's Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730-740).
works.characters: Guthlac; the demons; Bartholomew; the angels
works.structure: A hagiographical epic in the heroic mode: renunciation, the demonic wars (a psychomachia in narrative form), heavenly vindication, and death; speeches dominate the central combat scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Solitude and the hall community
Warfare and battle
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Guthlac B
works.description: A poem of 561 lines on the death of St Guthlac of Crowland, from the Exeter Book: the saint's illness, his last conversation with his servant Beccel, and the ascent of his soul, which flies like a bird to heaven. Distinct from Guthlac A in style and emphasis, it is one of the most tender poems in the corpus.
works.plot: Stricken with his final illness, Guthlac instructs his disciple Beccel, foretelling his own death on the seventh day; his soul departs like a bird to the heavenly home, and a light shines over the fen; Beccel, instructed to tell his sister Pega, buries him and the poem closes with a prayer. The poet's meditation on death — 'death is no man's friend' — frames the narrative.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on the death of a saint; its bird-image for the soul's flight is among the period's most memorable figures.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; gentler and more meditative than Guthlac A.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 44b-52b); source: Felix's Vita Sancti Guthlaci.
works.characters: Guthlac; Beccel; Pega; the angels
works.structure: A single, intimate deathbed narrative: prophecy, farewell dialogue, and the ascent of the soul, framed by prologue and prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; distinct authorship from Guthlac A is generally accepted.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer
works.form: Historical novel and romance of Border society with a strong comic and dialect component; the mystery of identity gives it an early detection plot.
works.description: The second tale of the new school of Scottish fiction, a romance of Borders gentry, smuggling and legal fraud in which the fortunes of a family are read in advance by an astrological prediction. A colonel from India, quartered at a Border inn, becomes the witness and friend of the heir who had been carried off in childhood, and the tale's curiosity is sustained by the concealment of that identity. Its portraits of a sour landlady, a starved pedant and a terrier-fancier became some of the most reproduced types of Scottish popular fiction.
works.plot: Colonel Mannering, seeking a lodging in the south of Scotland, is warned by an astrologer's figure of the child then missing from the neighbouring house; the infant heir Bertram had been abstracted in his mother's chamber years before, and his kinsman Glossin, the heir presumptive, had profited by the loss. Bertram returns unknown to himself, takes a farm under another name, and is entangled with the smuggler Hatteraick and with the treachery of Glossin's factor. Meg Dods, the innkeeper who loves him spitefully, Dominie Sampson, the scholar whom a marriage would starve, and Dandie Dinmont, whose puppies end the quarrels of the county, carry the novel's comedy. Detection, a trial at the circuit court and a recovery of name and estate bring the prediction to its fulfilment.
works.significance: Established the second, comic-native mode of the historical novel and supplied the period's stock of Scottish character types. Its treatment of stolen inheritance and legal title made it a source for later sensation and detection plotting. Its dialect comedy was widely imitated and remains a document of Scots speech at the Union.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; heavy use of Scots speech for the servant and border characters, with songs and ballad tags interpolated.
works.context: Written in the same season as the author's antiquarian work on Border legends, and dependent on the record of smuggling along the Solway coast and of the civil law of entail and hypothec then being modernised. The East India interest represented by the colonel reflects the returns of Anglo-Indian wealth into Scottish land. Its publication, within months of the former tale, created the commercial pattern of the anonymous national series.
works.characters: Colonel Guy Mannering; Henry Bertram, the lost heir; Glossin, the heir presumptive; Hatteraick the smuggler; Dominie Sampson; Meg Dods; Dandie Dinmont; Julia Mannering; the astrologer
works.structure: Third-person narrative with Colonel Mannering as the chief intelligence-gathering witness; a large cast observed through dialect talk; a concluding assembly of evidence in court supplies the discovery of the lost heir.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the Author of Waverley; attribution undisputed.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Guy of Warwick
altTitles: The Romance of Guy of Warwick
works.form: romance in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas
works.description: The longest and one of the most widely read of the English romances, in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas: the career of Guy, earl of Warwick, who wins the lady Felice by feats of arms, then renounces the world to fight as God's champion and die as a hermit. Its hero was England's favourite romance champion for three centuries.
works.plot: Guy, a steward's son, wins Felice through tournaments and foreign wars; struck by remorse, he leaves her to do penance as a pilgrim, returning in disguise to defend England against the giant Colbrond at Winchester; recognized only at his death, he is buried by Felice, who follows him in holiness.
works.significance: The romance of Guy fixed the image of the penitent knight in English culture and remained a bestseller until the Civil War; it is central to the study of romance readership.
works.meter: Couplets in the Auchinleck version; tail-rhyme stanzas in later copies.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from Anglo-Norman sources, drawing on Warwick legend and the cult of Guy; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript and many later copies and prints, into the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Guy; Felice; Colbrond the giant; Reinbrun (their son); Herhaud
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric career, then penitential career — with the Colbrond episode and the deathbed recognition as climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Penance, confession, and sin
sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: H.M.S. Pinafore; or, The Lass That Loved a Sailor
works.description: First performed in 1878 and the first great Savoy opera: a captain's daughter loves a common sailor, and a forgotten baby-swap makes everything right. It is a dramatic work of 1878 by W. S. Gilbert; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Josephine Corcoran, the captain's daughter, loves the sailor Ralph Rackstraw but refuses him because of the difference in class; the bumboat woman Little Buttercup reveals that she had years ago swapped the babies of Captain Corcoran and Ralph, so that the captain is really the lowly sailor and Ralph the gentleman, and the lovers are united while the class order is restored in reverse.
works.significance: H.M.S. Pinafore was the first English opera to conquer America and the founding work of the Savoy operas: its satire of class and the navy made it a national institution, it established the Gilbert and Sullivan partnership as the most successful in theatrical history, and it is a permanent part of the English comic repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is inverted logic carried to absurdity.
works.context: 1878: the Royal Navy of the 1870s, the English class system, the American copyright wars of the 1870s, and the commercial theatre of Richard D'Oyly Carte. The record dates the work as composed in 1878 and first published in 1878 and first performed in 1878 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Captain Corcoran; Josephine Corcoran; Ralph Rackstraw; Little Buttercup; Sir Joseph Porter; Dick Deadeye
works.structure: The action is divided into two acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Schwenck Gilbert. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule
themes: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

The Norton Anthology of English Literature, Vol. E: The Victorian Age (1830–1901), 11th edn

works.title: Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes
works.description: Samuel Purchas's four-volume continuation of Hakluyt's collections: the voyage narratives and geographical documents left unpublished at Hakluyt's death — the travels of the East and West Indies, the relations of China and Japan, the Arctic voyages, and the Virginia enterprises — gathered and framed in Purchas's 'pilgrimage' of the world's records, the great Jacobean storehouse of travel literature.
works.plot: No single plot: the Pilgrimes arranges its hundreds of narratives by region and voyage — Purchas's own summaries and moral reflections interlacing the documents — from the voyages of the ancients to the discoveries of his own day.
works.significance: The great Jacobean continuation of Hakluyt — the book that carried the age of discovery's records into the age of colonization.
works.meter: Prose of many hands within Purchas's devout editorial frame.
works.context: Published 1625, the year of Purchas's death and of the Virginia Company's dissolution; the collection preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and fed the English imagination of empire for two centuries.
works.characters: the voyagers and travellers (Hudson, Baffin, Cavendish, and hundreds of others)
works.structure: Four folio volumes of documentary compilation, with Purchas's prefaces, indices, and the running apparatus of his editorial 'pilgrimage'.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled and edited by Purchas from Hakluyt's papers and other sources; uncontested.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Sea voyage and seafaring
