works.title: Hali Meiðhad
works.description: An alliterative prose epistle in praise of virginity, addressed to young women contemplating the religious life, in the AB language of the Katherine Group. It contrasts the blessedness of the virgin bride of Christ with the miseries of married life, in a rhetorical tradition going back to patristic treatises on virginity.
works.plot: The author extols virginity as the highest estate, describes the joys of the heavenly bridegroom, and — in famously vivid passages — details the pains and humiliations of marriage and childbearing to urge his readers to choose the better part.
works.significance: The classic Middle English statement of the virginity ideal, and a prime exhibit of the period's energetic anti-matrimonial rhetoric (the counterpart of the Wife of Bath's prologue).
works.meter: Rhythmical, heavily alliterative prose of the AB language group.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, in the circle of Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: the virgin reader (addressee); Christ as bridegroom
works.structure: A single sustained exhortation moving from praise of virginity through satiric anatomy of marriage to the rewards of the heavenly marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
The contemplative life
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: Hamlet
altTitles: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of revenge and consciousness: the ghost of Hamlet's father charges him to avenge his murder by Claudius, who now wears the crown and the queen; Hamlet's feigned madness, the play-within-the-play ('The Mousetrap'), the deaths of Polonius and Ophelia, and the final duel — poisoned rapier and cup — in which the stage is cleared of the whole royal house.
works.plot: Hamlet tests the ghost's word by staging a murder-play before the king; Claudius's guilt is exposed; Hamlet spares the praying king, kills Polonius, is sent to England with a death warrant he reverses; Ophelia drowns; Laertes returns for revenge; and the poisoned duel at Elsinore kills Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius, and Hamlet himself, with Fortinbras inheriting Denmark.
works.significance: The most famous play ever written — the tragedy of modern consciousness itself, and the summit of the English language's claim on world literature.
works.meter: The widest range in Shakespeare — soliloquy, prose, song, the Player's speech, the graveyard quibbles — with 'To be or not to be' at its centre.
works.context: Written about 1600–01 in the wake of the lost ur-Hamlet and of the death of Shakespeare's son Hamnet; the three texts (Q1 1603, Q2 1604–05, F 1623) present the classic problem of Shakespearean textual scholarship.
works.characters: Hamlet; Claudius; Gertrude; the Ghost; Polonius; Ophelia; Laertes; Horatio; Rosencrantz; Guildenstern; Fortinbras; Osric; the First Gravedigger
works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy infinitely deferred and interiorized — soliloquies, plays, and feigned madness displacing action — until the catastrophe of Act 5.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the relationship of the three early texts remains the central problem of its bibliography.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Melancholy and self-analysis
Revenge and justice
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Handlyng Synne
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's English verse adaptation (begun 1303) of the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington: a manual of penance in some 12,000 lines expounding the commandments, the deadly sins, the sacraments, and the art of confession, illustrated with scores of exemplary tales. It is the classic Middle English penitential handbook.
works.plot: The poem moves systematically through the commandments and sins, each doctrine illustrated by cautionary exempla — the dancing carolers cursed by a priest, the usurer, the witch of Ely — and concludes with instruction on confession, contrition, and satisfaction.
works.significance: The principal English treatment of penance between the thirteenth-century homilies and Chaucer's Parson's Tale (which draws on related material), and a treasury of the exemplum tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of plain, efficient didactic verse in the Lincolnshire dialect.
works.context: Begun in 1303 by the Gilbertine canon Robert Mannyng at Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, translating Wadington's manual for an English lay audience; preserved in the Vernon and Bodleian Digby manuscripts among others.
works.characters: the exemplary sinners and saints of the tales
works.structure: A didactic sequence organized by commandment, sin, and sacrament, with narrative exempla inset throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed by the author's own preface to 'Robert of Brunne'.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Penance, confession, and sin
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: Hangover Square
works.description: The great English novel of the London pub: George Harvey Bone and the murder in the blackout. It is a prose fiction work of 1941 by Patrick Hamilton; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: George Harvey Bone, a failed musician with a drink problem, is obsessed with Netta, who exploits him; the novel follows him through the pubs and boarding houses of Earl's Court until, in a state of dissociation, he kills her during the blackout.
works.significance: Hangover Square is one of the finest English novels of the period and the great novel of the London pub: its portrait of George Harvey Bone, its pubs and its blackout murder made it a central text of English fiction and the definitive novel of the drinking man.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the pub and the boarding house.
works.context: Earl's Court and the London pubs in 1939, on the eve of the war. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1941 and first published in 1941 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: George Harvey Bone; Netta; Peter; John; Maud; Bob
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the pub to the blackout murder. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Hamilton (Hangover Square). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
Sexuality, the new psychology, and the Freudian century
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital

works.title: Hard Cash: A Matter-of-Fact Romance
works.description: Published in 1863 and the most polemical of Reade's novels: a sensation plot built on the private lunatic asylum and on a stolen fortune, designed to expose the abuses of the English asylum trade. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Charles Reade; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Alfred Hardie, an Oxford undergraduate in love with Julia Dodd, is confined in a private asylum by his father, the banker Richard Hardie, who has embezzled the fourteen thousand pounds of 'hard cash' that Julia's father, Captain David Dodd, brought home from India, while the Captain, driven mad by the loss, is himself shut up; Alfred endures and exposes the abuses of the asylum trade, escapes, recovers the money and marries Julia.
works.significance: Hard Cash is the central English novel of the private asylum scandal and the model of the documentary social novel: its evidence was drawn from parliamentary papers and court cases, and its publication helped to shape the public campaign against wrongful confinement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative.
works.context: The 1850s-60s, the private madhouse scandals, the Lunacy Commission, and the debate on wrongful confinement that produced the Lunacy Act of 1890. The record dates the work as composed in 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Alfred Hardie; Julia Dodd; Captain David Dodd; Mrs Lucy Dodd; Edward Dodd; Richard Hardie, Alfred's father; Jane Hardie; Noah Skinner, the clerk; Dr Sampson; Dr Wycherley
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey
themes: Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations

works.title: Hard Times. For These Times
works.form: Novel in weekly parts (Household Words); single volume 1854
works.description: Serialised in Household Words from 1 April to 12 August 1854 and published in one volume the same year: the shortest of the major novels and the most concentrated attack on utilitarianism in English fiction.
works.plot: In the cotton town of Coketown, Thomas Gradgrind educates his children Louisa and Tom on 'facts'; Louisa marries the manufacturer Josiah Bounderby, the self-made 'Humbug' of the novel, and nearly elopes with the political adventurer James Harthouse before returning to her father's house broken. Tom robs the bank and is exposed by the circus girl Sissy Jupe's circle; Stephen Blackpool, the hand-loom weaver, is falsely accused, refuses to join the union, and dies down a mine shaft; Rachael nurses him, and the circus, with its horse-riding and its 'fancy', stands against the school of fact.
works.significance: Hard Times is the classic Victorian novel of industrial capitalism and the definitive literary critique of utilitarianism; it is the shortest and most taught of Dickens's novels and has been central to the criticism of Victorian ideology from Leavis to the Marxist and postcolonial readings of our own time.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Preston strike of 1853-54, which Dickens reported for Household Words, the 1840s-50s factory system and the Ten Hours agitation, and the utilitarian education of the Mechanics' Institutes and the monitorial schools.
works.characters: Thomas Gradgrind; Louisa Gradgrind; Tom Gradgrind; Josiah Bounderby; Stephen Blackpool; Rachael; James Harthouse; Sissy Jupe; Mrs Sparsit; Bitzer
works.structure: Three-book structure (Sowing, Reaping, Garnering) with a narrow cast and a plot built on the contrast of two systems of education and two philosophies of life.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations

works.title: Harlem Shadows
works.description: The first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and Harlem. It is a verse work of 1922 by Claude McKay; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'If We Must Die', 'The Lynching', 'America', 'The Harlem Dancer', 'Tropics in New York' and the Jamaican dialect poems — the first body of West Indian verse in English.
works.significance: Harlem Shadows is the first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance and the collection that made the protest sonnet a modern form: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem, and the Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet and the ballad used for protest.
works.context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Red Summer of 1919, and the Jamaica of McKay's childhood. The record dates the work as composed between 1917 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.
works.structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and dialect poems. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Festus Claudius McKay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem
themes: Exile, expatriation, and the lost generation
Race, the colour line, and the New Negro
The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road
movements: The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro

works.title: Harmonium
works.description: The most gorgeous first book in American poetry: 'Sunday Morning', the Florida sun and the imagination making its world. It is a verse work of 1923 by Wallace Stevens; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Sunday Morning', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'Peter Quince at the Clavier', 'Le Monocle de Mon Oncle', 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird' and 'The Comedian as the Letter C' — poems of the imagination, the body, the weather and the made thing.
works.significance: Harmonium is the greatest first book in American poetry and the founding collection of the American philosophical lyric: 'Sunday Morning' and 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird' are permanent, and its sumptuous surface established the imagination as the century's great poetic subject.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the exotic and sumptuous vocabulary.
works.context: The imagination's response to the death of the gods, the Florida landscape of Stevens's travels, and the aesthetics of the 1910s. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1922 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.characters: Crispin ('The Comedian as the Letter C'); Peter Quince, Susanna and the elders ('Peter Quince at the Clavier'); the woman of 'Sunday Morning'; the speaker of 'Le Monocle de Mon Oncle'
works.structure: Sixty-seven poems in free and blank verse, from epigrams to long meditations. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Sexuality, the new psychology, and the Freudian century

works.title: Harrington
works.form: Prose fiction; novel of education and moral reformation; the autobiographical child-narrator novel
works.description: A novel of the education of a spoiled only child, and the writer's most serious study of the formation and the unlearning of prejudice. The boy is made irrational by indulgence and by a tyrannical schoolmaster, and the book then shows how the habits of a generous nature are recovered through shame, friendship and the example of suffering. Its central and most discussed passage is an embedded tale of an injured Jewish family, which converts the boy's unreasoned contempt into a lesson on the persecution he has himself helped to inflict. It was the last of the writer's major novels and is the most explicitly moral in purpose.
works.plot: An only child of a weak father and an indulgent mother is tortured at school by a brute master whom his family will not believe against, and his character is warped by sympathy denied and by flattery accepted. He is rescued and educated by a plain-spoken friend of his father, whose method of honour and reason restores his judgement. The middle of the book is taken up with the history of a money-lender of the wronged faith and of his daughter, whose injuries at the hands of the boy's own family expose the cruelty of a prejudice inherited and never examined. The young man's life is then governed by reparation, by a friendship tested in illness, and by the choice of a wife whose worth he is at last able to recognise.
works.significance: A founding text of the English novel of childhood and of the literary argument against religious prejudice, and the writer's last important fiction. Its embedded tale is a standard document for study of writing about Jews in the Romantic period, and its first-person education design anticipates the nineteenth-century novel of development.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain, reflective first-person style, changing from the speech of an injured child to the measured idiom of an examining adult
works.context: Published in 1817, it belongs to the post-war debate on the civil condition of Jews in Britain, to the controversy over classical schooling and the punishment of children, and to the writer's long engagement with the education of judgement begun in the family's educational books. Its plea for the recognition of a persecuted minority is a direct answer to the treatment of Jewish characters in contemporary romance, and its school chapters draw on the reports of English academies of the period.
works.structure: First-person autobiographical fiction in three volumes, looking back on a boyhood and young manhood; the embedded tale of the injured family interrupts the forward movement and reframes the whole education as an argument about prejudice.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel
The Bluestockings and Women's Letters

works.title: Hauntings
works.description: Published in 1890 and the most sophisticated English collection of ghost stories: four tales in which the supernatural is a fact of place, art and psychology. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Vernon Lee; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: 'Amour Dure' follows a German historian in Italy who falls in love with a Renaissance murderess; 'Dionea' presents a child of Venus who destroys the men who love her; 'Oke of Okehurst' tells of a woman who becomes the double of her husband's ancestress; 'A Wicked Voice' is the confession of a composer haunted by an eighteenth-century castrato.
works.significance: Hauntings is the finest English collection of ghost stories after Henry James and the central text of the aesthetic supernatural: its ghosts are always psychological and artistic facts, and its theory of the haunted place made it a founding text of the modern psychological ghost story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, analytical prose that moves between description and argument.
works.context: 1887-90: the aesthetic movement, the Italian Renaissance revival, the new psychology of the Society for Psychical Research, and the vogue for the supernatural tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Spiridion Trepka and Medea da Carpi ('Amour Dure'); Dionea ('Dionea'); Alice and William Oke ('Oke of Okehurst'); Magnus, the composer, and the castrato Zaffirino ('A Wicked Voice')
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Violet Paget. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Havelok the Dane
altTitles: The Lay of Havelok the Dane
works.description: A Lincolnshire romance of some 3,000 lines on the dispossessed prince Havelok, brought up as a kitchen-boy at Grimsby, whose royal birthmark, strength, and marriage to the princess Goldeboru lead to the recovery of the thrones of Denmark and England. Its sympathetic depiction of labouring life and its Lincolnshire topography make it unique among the romances.
works.plot: The orphaned Havelok is saved from the usurper Godard by the fisherman Grim, who flees with him to England; in disguise he serves as a kitchen hand at Lincoln, where the usurper Godrich marries the princess Goldeboru to him in mockery; Havelok's revealed royalty, his defeat of the usurpers, and his double coronation conclude the poem.
works.significance: One of the finest English romances: its realism about work and poverty, and its fusion of folk-tale, dynastic, and hagiographical elements, make it a classic of the genre.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with marked northern (East Midland/Lincolnshire) dialect features.
works.context: Composed c. 1280–90 in Lincolnshire, drawing on local legend (Grimsby's foundation) and Anglo-Norman sources (Lai d'Haveloc, Gaimar); preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108.
works.characters: Havelok; Goldeboru; Grim the fisherman; Godard; Godrich; Ubbe
works.structure: A double exile-and-restoration plot (Havelok and Goldeboru in parallel), with an interpolated miracle episode and a long climactic battle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Kingship and good rule
National identity and Englishness
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Hawthorn and Lavender, with Other Verses
works.description: Published in 1901 and Henley's last collection: love poems, hospital memories and the imperial songs of his final years. It is a verse work of 1901 by W. E. Henley; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem.
works.plot: The title sequence follows a love affair through the seasons, with the hawthorn of spring and the lavender of summer standing for the phases of passion; the other poems return to the hospital, to the city, and to the imperial themes of the 1890s.
works.significance: Hawthorn and Lavender is Henley's most sustained love sequence and the finest of his later work: it shows the lyric gift that his admirers valued above the imperial rhetoric, and it is the collection in which his two themes — the body and desire — are most completely joined.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short, hard, rhymed verse in the ballad and the song measure.
works.context: 1898-1901: the imperial enthusiasm of the Boer War, the London literary world of the National Observer, and Henley's last illness. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Ernest Henley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Hay Fever
works.description: Coward's first great comedy: the Bliss family and their four weekend guests. It is a dramatic work of 1925 by Noel Coward; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Judith Bliss, a retired actress, and her novelist husband David, their children Simon and Sorel, and the writer Myra Arundel entertain four weekend guests at their country house, each of whom has been invited by a different member of the family; by Sunday lunchtime all four guests have fled.
works.significance: Hay Fever is Coward's first great comedy and one of the funniest plays in English: its portrait of the self-absorbed theatrical family made it a permanent part of the repertory and established Coward's style.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the epigram and the witty exchange.
works.context: The English country house of the 1920s and the theatrical family at its centre. The record dates the work as composed in 1924 and first published in 1925 and first performed in 1925 and the corpus places it within The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners, it is catalogued under comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Judith Bliss; David Bliss; Sorel Bliss; Simon Bliss; Myra Arundel; Richard Greatham; Jackie Coryton; Sandy Tyrell
works.structure: Three acts, a Saturday evening, Sunday morning and Sunday afternoon. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A comedy in acts, the scene built as a succession of entrances, revelations and exits, with the social convention breached and restored.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Noël Pierce Coward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Headlong Hall
works.description: the author's first novel, a short comic dialogue novel in which seven guests of opposite intellectual temperaments are locked in a country house and talk past each other until a marriage plot resolves the chaos. It is the earliest of the author's novel-length satires of Romantic-era thought.
works.plot: Sir Arkandale Silkworm, a wealthy patron, gathers at Headlong Hall seven guests representing incompatible intellectual positions — a phrenologist, a metaphysician, an historian, a political economist, a beautist, a linguist, and others — each with a theory of human perfectibility. Their interminable argument is punctuated by practical jokes and forced to resolve by Sir Arkandale's arrangement of advantageous marriages among them. The novel's comedy is entirely conversational; the plot is a device for the clash of ideas.
works.significance: Headlong Hall established the 'novel of ideas' form in which the novelist became the century's master; its dialogue comedy influenced Huxley and the later campus novel. It is a key document of the reception of Romantic intellectual culture by its wittiest sceptical observer.
works.context: Published in 1816, the annus mirabilis of English Romanticism, in the immediate wake of Scott's Waverley novels; the author satirises the specialist intellectual vocabularies — phrenology, political economy, historicism — fashionable in Regency drawing rooms.
works.characters: Mr. Glossop; Mr. Floggington; Mr. Pammacassus; Miss Bellomyst; Sir Arkandale Silkworm; Mr. Skellet; Mr. Mavis; Mr. Fustifier
works.structure: Single setting, almost wholly dialogue-driven; the 'conversation piece' structure replaces conventional plot; intellectual types clash and are comically reconciled.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Heart and Science: A Story of the Present Time
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1883
works.description: Published in 1883 and Collins's most direct attack on the ethics of experimental science: the story of a vivisectionist who schemes to marry his ward for her money and to use her in his experiments. It is a prose fiction work of 1883 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ovid Vere, a gifted young surgeon, falls in love with his orphaned cousin Carmina Graywell; while he travels abroad for his health, his mother, the cold, science-worshipping Mrs Gallilee, persecutes the girl for the sake of her fortune until Carmina collapses into a nervous illness, which the vivisector Dr Benjulia watches as an experiment rather than treat; Ovid returns with a cure learned from a dead doctor's manuscript, and Benjulia, forestalled, sets fire to his laboratory and dies in it, carrying the novel's argument against vivisection.
works.significance: Heart and Science is the central English novel of the anti-vivisection controversy and one of the earliest fictional treatments of the ethics of scientific experiment.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1870s-80s, the English anti-vivisection movement and the 1876 Cruelty to Animals Act. The record dates the work as composed in 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Ovid Vere; Carmina Graywell; Mrs Maria Gallilee; Dr Nathan Benjulia; Mr Gallilee; Teresa, Carmina's nurse; Miss Minerva, the governess; Mr Mool, the lawyer
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: Heart of Darkness
works.form: Novella (three-part serial, Blackwood's Magazine 1899; book form in Youth, 1902)
works.description: Marlow's night journey up an African river to find the ivory agent Kurtz: the central European text about empire, and one of the great English novellas. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Joseph Conrad; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Marlow, a riverboat captain, sits on the deck of the Nellie on the Thames and tells the story of a journey up the Congo to fetch Kurtz, the company's most successful agent, who has installed himself as a god among the local people and has gone mad. Marlow finds him dying and hears his last words — 'The horror! The horror!' — and returns to Europe carrying his memory.
works.significance: Heart of Darkness is the indispensable European text about empire and one of the founding works of modern fiction: it invented the colonial journey narrative that the century would find endless uses for, gave the language 'the horror', and its technique — the framed narrator, the delayed disclosure, the symbolic river — made Marlow the model for the modern unreliable narrator. Chinua Achebe's attack on it in 1977 made it the centre of the debate about the colonial canon, which is itself part of its record.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
works.context: The Congo Free State of Leopold II, where Conrad himself served as a river captain in 1890 and saw the rubber and ivory system at first hand; the book appeared in the year of the Boer War, at the height of the imperial confidence it dismantles.
works.characters: Charles Marlow; Mr Kurtz; the Intended; the Manager; the Harlequin; the Accountant
works.structure: Three-part serial narrative framed by Marlow's narration aboard the Nellie; a journey structure with a descent into the interior.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Helbeck of Bannisdale
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1898 and Ward's most concentrated tragedy: the love of an old Catholic squire and a young woman of the modern world, destroyed by their beliefs. It is a prose fiction work of 1898 by Mary Augusta Ward; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Alan Helbeck, the last of an ancient recusant family, falls in love with Laura Fountain, the daughter of a Cambridge sceptic; their love is destroyed by the conflict between his Catholicism and her inherited unbelief, and Laura drowns herself in the river rather than submit to a faith she cannot accept.
works.significance: Helbeck of Bannisdale is the finest of Ward's novels and one of the great English tragedies of religious difference: its portrait of an old Catholic family and its unsparing ending made it a critical favourite and it remains the most accomplished of her works.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of ideas with a large social canvas.
works.context: 1896-98: the Catholic revival in the north of England, the Victorian debate on education and dogma, and the position of the old Catholic gentry. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Alan Helbeck; Laura Fountain; Augustina Fountain, Helbeck's sister and Laura's stepmother; Father Bowles; Hubert Mason; Polly Mason; Dr Friedland
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Hellas
works.form: Closet drama and lyrical drama in the classical masked form, with the chorus of the older Attic tragedy; a political ode cast as a scene.
works.description: A short lyrical drama written in a few weeks to celebrate the Greek rising against the Ottoman power, and built on the poet's own statement in its preface that its scenery and machinery are drawn from the hills and gulf of the modern Morea. A phantom of the ancient glory of Hellas appears to a worshipper by the sea at Lepanto and shows the regeneration of the race, while the chorus of captive women doubts and the despairing old men answer with the prophecy of a new age. It is the most purely political of the author's dramas and the shortest of his serious verse plays.
works.plot: A devotee of the ancient muse keeps the vigil of the year at Sunium and by the Gulf of Lepanto, mourning that Greece has no voice left, and the phantom of her buried glory rises upon the waters to promise a coming day of deliverance. The chorus of captive women and the despairing chiefs of the race dispute the promise, and the vision passes to the triumph of a regenerated people, the tyrant's power broken and the altars of the free rebuilt. The close retracts the certainty, the poet's own voice acknowledges the doubt of the human heart, and the drama ends with the invocation of the immortal spirit of the scene. The argument is that a nation's ancient memory is the warrant of its political resurrection.
works.significance: It became the lyrical testament of philhellenism and one of the most recited and quoted political lyrics of the following century, its stanzas used in the cause of Greek and of Italian freedom. Its preface is also a document of the author's late theory of poetry and of his disillusionment with the immediate effect of verse, and its treatment of national memory as a political force shaped the later poetry of liberation movements.
works.meter: A variety of lyric measures, free iambic and trochaic lines for the dialogue and short responsive strophes for the chorus, with the anapestic movement of the prophetic passages.
works.context: Composed at Pisa between October and December 1821, in the months of the outbreak of the Greek revolution, the rise of the eastern question in European politics and the execution of the patriarch, and published in London in 1822 with a prose preface on the poet's design and his own account of the poem's failure to sell. The dedication to the friends who had fought and died in the cause made it a public act of subscription to a foreign war of liberation.
works.characters: the devotee of the ancient glory; the phantom of Hellas; the chorus of captive women; the despairing chief of the race; the tyrant of the East as the power denounced
works.structure: A dramatic scene of some four hundred lines with choral entry and exit, opened by the devotee's soliloquy, the vision and its questioning in the middle and the retracting close; the movement is entirely lyric and prophetic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's lifetime and its text is stable, with minor revisions in the posthumous collections.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: Helpstone
altTitles: Helpstone. A Local Scenery on the Banks of the Welland
works.form: Topographical and Descriptive Poetry; Nature Lyric and Meditation
works.description: A sequence of eleven fourteen-line sonnets addressed to the author's native village on the Welland in the Northamptonshire fens, and the opening poem of his first published volume. The sequence moves from affectionate greeting of an unlettered place to mourning over the loss of common grazing, of sheep-walks and of the neighbours who knew them. It is the founding statement of a labouring-class poetry in which local topography becomes the evidence of dispossession.
works.plot: The first sonnets hail Helpstone as a village unknown to fame, where humble genius tries to rise above the vulgar, and recall the sports, birds, and seasons of childhood. The middle numbers name specific losses: the trees felled, the bushes cleared, the banks and waters changed by new husbandry. One sonnet curses Wealth as the cause that levels every tree and takes away labour and bread, and complains that the impounding and cutting of the Welland destroyed the sheep-herds' feeding grounds. Later numbers turn to the aged and dead who are gone, to the poet's own dependence and infirmity, and finally to the spot itself as a comfort in life's decline.
works.significance: The sequence made the author the most famous of labouring-class poets and gave the enclosure controversy its most quoted verse complaint, in which the loss of common grazing is stated as a loss of memory, pleasure, and personal identity. It established the local-poem convention later poets of rural labour imitated, and it remains the touchstone for discussions of a plebeian Romanticism distinct from the Lake school.
works.meter: Eleven sonnets of fourteen lines in iambic pentameter rhymed in running couplets (aa bb cc dd ee ff gg), the sequence closing each number on a pointed rather than a turned couplet; the diction is plain, with frequent enjambment. Verified from the first-edition text, where the sequence occupies pages 1 to 11.
works.context: Written when the author was a day-labourer in husbandry whose father had fallen to parish relief, in a village whose commons and sheep-walks were being destroyed by enclosure, drainage, and the cut of a river navigation. The poems were gathered for publication after a Stamford bookseller and a London publisher took up a manuscript of a labouring poet, and the volume appeared with an introduction stressing that the poems were the genuine productions of a young peasant.
works.characters: the poet-speaker of Helpstone; the shepherd and sheep-heard of the Welland banks; the father on parish relief; the dead and absent village neighbours; Wealth, personified as the agent of destruction
works.structure: A linked sonnet sequence without plot, each fourteen-line number a self-contained meditation that repeats the heading HELPSTONE in the volume; the progression is associative, from salutation through complaint and recollection to resignation.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name on the title page of the first volume; no dispute attaches to the sequence.

works.title: Henrietta
works.form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction
works.description: A novel of a portionless young woman, a poor relation in a great house, whose virtue is tried by presumption, by a fraudulent seduction and by the world's readiness to believe the worst of a woman alone. It is darker and more analytical than the author's earlier fiction and much concerned with the opinion of the world as a tribunal.
works.plot: Henrietta, dependent on relations of consequence, is pursued by a man of fortune who offers protection rather than marriage, and later by one whose design is outright seduction. She defends herself with spirit, is compromised in appearance, and must bear the verdict of society while the men who injured her are spared. Her constancy and the exposure of her persecutors prepare a marriage on equal terms, the narrative arguing that a woman's reputation is a social construction.
works.significance: It is one of the most acute mid-century analyses of the sexual double standard in fiction and a key text in the development of the novel of the unprotected woman.
works.meter: An argentine prose of reflection and reported conversation, with the narrator's essays on female dependency interrupting the narrative.
works.context: Published in 1758, in the decade of the mid-century novel's turn to the analysis of reputation and dependency, and after the author's critical work on the drama had fixed her place in letters.
works.characters: Henrietta; her protectress and the great family; the two pursuers, one coarse and one designing; the suitor who finally offers equality
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes with a strong current of moral essay; the plot turns on the difference between Henrietta's conduct and the world's report of it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.

works.title: Henrik Ibsen
works.description: Published in 1907 and Gosse's life of the Norwegian dramatist whose work he had done more than anyone to introduce to England. works.significance: Gosse's Ibsen is the book through which the English literary world understood the dramatist, and Gosse himself was the decisive agent in the English reception of modern European drama; the volume is a central document of the making of the modern English theatre.

works.title: Henry IV, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The first play of the Henriad proper: Prince Hal's education between the tavern of Falstaff and the field of Shrewsbury, where he kills the rebel Hotspur and redeems his reputation — the comedy of Eastcheap and the tragedy of the Percys joined in the greatest of the English history plays.
works.plot: Hotspur and the Percys rebel against the king they helped make; Hal plays truant with Falstaff until the crisis calls him to arms; at Shrewsbury he saves his father, kills Hotspur, and leaves Falstaff to counterfeit death and claim the honour — a claim the prince allows, 'for my part, if a lie may do thee grace, I'll gild it with the happiest terms I have'.
works.significance: Contains Shakespeare's greatest comic creation in Falstaff, and his profoundest study of a prince's education in power.
works.meter: The fullest range of Shakespeare's early style: Hotspur's verse, Falstaff's prose, Hal's movement between them, and Glendower's Welsh lyricism.
works.context: Written about 1596–97 from Holinshed and the anonymous Famous Victories of Henry V; Oldcastle's name was changed to Falstaff after protest from the Cobham family.
works.characters: Prince Hal (Henry, Prince of Wales); Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; Hotspur (Henry Percy); the Earl of Worcester; the Earl of Northumberland; Owen Glendower; the Earl of Douglas; Poins; Bardolph; Mistress Quickly; Lady Percy
works.structure: A double plot of court/camp and tavern braided by Hal's movement between the two worlds, with the Gadshill robbery as hinge and the battle as convergence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Henry IV, Part 2
altTitles: The Second Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The darker sequel: rebellion flickers out at Gaultree Forest, the king sickens under the weight of his usurped crown, Falstaff conscripts the rag-tag army of Gloucestershire and runs up his tavern score, and the play ends with the new king's public rejection of his old companion — 'I know thee not, old man' — and Falstaff's ruin.
works.plot: Northumberland's rebellion collapses; Prince John tricks the rebels into disbanding; the dying king and Hal are reconciled; Henry V's coronation is followed by the rejection of Falstaff and the justice's promise of the new reign.
works.significance: The most sombre of the histories — a study of the costs of power whose rejection scene is among the most painful in the canon.
works.meter: Prose dominates the Falstaff scenes and verse the court; the play's elegiac music belongs to its age and sickness.
works.context: Written about 1597–98; its Epilogue promises the further adventures of Falstaff, fulfilled instead in The Merry Wives of Windsor.
works.characters: Prince Hal; Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; the Lord Chief Justice; Prince John of Lancaster; the Earl of Northumberland; the Archbishop of York; Justice Shallow; Justice Silence; Pistol; Doll Tearsheet; Mistress Quickly; Bardolph; Poins; Lady Percy
works.structure: A chronicle of endings — of rebellion, of reign, of friendship — built on scenes of age, disease, and memory, with the Gloucestershire justices and the tavern as the comic underworld.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Kingship and good rule
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Henry V
altTitles: The Life of Henry the Fifth
works.description: The climax of the second tetralogy: the Chorus's apology for the 'wooden O' frames the epic of Agincourt — Henry's claim to France, the traitors at Southampton, Harfleur's breach, the night before battle, and the victory of the 'band of brothers' — followed by the comic peace of the wooing of Katherine.
works.plot: Henry, urged by the church and provoked by the Dauphin's tennis balls, invades France; the campaign moves through Harfleur to Agincourt, where the outnumbered English win; the play closes with the treaty of Troyes and the king's rough wooing of the French princess.
works.significance: The national epic of the English stage — and, in its ambivalences, the most debated of the histories in every age of war.
works.meter: The great set speeches — 'Once more unto the breach', the Crispin's Day oration — in verse, against the prose of the soldiers and the dialect comedy of the captains.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe and of Essex's Irish expedition (to which the Chorus looks forward); the play made Agincourt the founding myth of English arms.
works.characters: King Henry V; the Chorus; the Duke of Exeter; Fluellen; Pistol; Bardolph; Nym; Mistress Quickly; the Dauphin; the Constable of France; Katherine; Princess of France; Alice; Montjoy; Williams; the King of France
works.structure: A choric five-act epic, each act introduced by the Chorus, alternating the high rhetoric of war with the low comedy of the tavern remnants (Bardolph, Pistol, Fluellen) and ending in the romance of the wooing scene.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Kingship and good rule
National identity and Englishness
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Henry VI, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Sixth
works.description: The first play of Shakespeare's earliest tetralogy, probably written in collaboration: the loss of France, the rise and burning of Joan la Pucelle (Joan of Arc), the quarrels of Gloucester and Winchester, and the white rose and the red plucked in the Temple Garden that plant the Wars of the Roses.
works.plot: Henry V's funeral opens the play; the French recover their towns through Joan's victories; Talbot, the English Achilles, dies at Bordeaux; the factions of York and Lancaster form in England; and the play ends with Suffolk's capture of Margaret of Anjou as Henry's bride — and his own instrument.
works.significance: The foundation of the English history-play cycle, and the apprenticeship of its greatest master.
works.meter: Early blank verse, often stiff and end-stopped, with the play's documentary sweep compensating for its poetic unevenness.
works.context: The Talbot scenes were celebrated by Nashe in 1592; the play is the first in the sequence that runs through Richard III.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; the Bishop of Winchester; Richard, Duke of York; the Earl of Warwick; Talbot; Joan la Pucelle; Charles the Dauphin; the Duke of Suffolk; Margaret of Anjou; Edmund Mortimer
works.structure: An episodic chronicle alternating English and French scenes, unified by Talbot's tragedy and the growth of the court factions.
works.attributionNotes: Generally regarded as collaborative (the shares of Nashe and others are debated); assigned to Shakespeare by the Folio.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle

works.title: Henry VI, Part 2
altTitles: The First Part of the Contention
The Contention of the Two Famous Houses of York and Lancaster
works.description: The second play of the tetralogy: the fall of Duke Humphrey of Gloucester, the rebellion of Jack Cade, and the rise of Richard, Duke of York, through the disintegration of Henry VI's England toward the first battle of St Albans.
works.plot: The court faction destroys Gloucester; York exploits the Cade rebellion to test his claim; the play's great set pieces — Gloucester's murder, the miracle at St Albans, Cade's insurrection — carry England from anarchy to open war, with Margaret and Suffolk's fall along the way.
works.significance: The first English play to put the whole commonwealth — commons, court, and crown — on stage together.
works.meter: Blank verse growing more assured, with the prose of the Cade scenes as the first great crowd-comedy in English drama.
works.context: The Cade rebellion scenes dramatize the 1450 rising through Elizabethan anxieties about the commons; printed in 1594 as The First Part of the Contention.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; Eleanor Cobham; the Duke of Suffolk; the Duke of York; Jack Cade; the Earl of Warwick; the Cardinal (Beaufort); Lord Say; Dick the butcher
works.structure: A chronicle of successive falls (Gloucester, Suffolk, Cade) leading to York's armed claim, in the de casibus pattern of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative with Marlowe or Nashe in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Henry VI, Part 3
altTitles: The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York
works.description: The third play of the tetralogy: the Wars of the Roses in full blood — York's death on the molehill at Wakefield, Margaret's taunting of him with the paper crown, the slaughter of young Rutland, and the rise of Richard of Gloucester through the battles of Towton, Barnet, and Tewkesbury to his soliloquized ambitions at the play's end.
works.plot: York breaks his oath and claims the crown; the wars swing between Lancaster and York; Edward IV wins the throne and marries Elizabeth Woodville; Warwick changes sides and dies at Barnet; and Richard murders Henry VI in the Tower, then turns to the audience to announce his design on the crown.
works.significance: The bridge from the Henry VI plays to Richard III — and the first sketch of Shakespeare's greatest villain.
works.meter: Blank verse of mounting power, culminating in Richard's first great soliloquy.
works.context: Written about 1590–91, the play's cycles of revenge answered the Senecan fashion while its national matter spoke to the post-Armada moment.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Richard, Duke of York; Edward IV; George, Duke of Clarence; Richard, Duke of Gloucester; the Earl of Warwick; Lady Grey (Elizabeth Woodville); the Duke of Exeter; Rutland; Clifford
works.structure: A rapid battle-chronicle built on reversals of fortune, with Richard's emergence as the play's climactic revelation.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.
themes: Blood-feud, vengeance, and kinship
Kingship and good rule

works.title: Henry VIII
altTitles: The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth
works.description: The last of the history plays, written with John Fletcher: the pageant-like fall of Buckingham, the trial and divorce of Katherine of Aragon, the rise of Anne Bullen and of Cranmer, and the christening of the infant Elizabeth — ending in Cranmer's prophecy of the golden age to come under the 'maiden phoenix'.
works.plot: Buckingham falls to Wolsey's faction; the king's conscience turns against his marriage; Katherine defends herself at the legatine trial; Wolsey's fall follows; Anne is crowned and Elizabeth christened, with Cranmer's prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.significance: The Stuart court's official version of the Reformation, and the last flowering of the history play Shakespeare had invented.
works.meter: Verse of late-Shakespearean looseness with Fletcherian run-on lines; the trial scene of Katherine is its moral and poetic summit.
works.context: First performed 29 June 1613 at the Globe, when the firing of the chambers set the theatre alight and burned it down — the play's alternate title, All Is True, is the one recorded at that performance.
works.characters: King Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey; Queen Katherine of Aragon; Anne Bullen; the Duke of Buckingham; Thomas Cranmer; the Duke of Norfolk; the Duke of Suffolk; Gardiner; Cromwell; the Old Lady
works.structure: A series of state show-scenes — trials, coronations, christenings — in the masque-like mode of late Jacobean spectacle, structured as successive falls and risings.
works.attributionNotes: Collaboration with John Fletcher established by stylistic and metrical evidence; the Folio assigns the play to Shakespeare alone.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Kingship and good rule
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Her Benny
works.description: The great waif bestseller of the Victorian religious press: two Liverpool children and the streets. It is a prose fiction work of 1879 by Silas K. Hocking; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Benny and Nell Bates, two orphaned Liverpool children, survive by selling matches and crossing-sweeping; Benny's honesty wins him a place in a merchant's office, and Nell dies of consumption after a deathbed scene that made the book one of the most popular of the century.
works.significance: Her Benny was one of the great bestsellers of the Victorian religious press, selling in the hundreds of thousands on both sides of the Atlantic and dramatised for the stage. It made the Liverpool street child into a national symbol and gave the temperance movement its most effective piece of fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is the waif narrative of the street and the workhouse.
works.context: Liverpool in the 1870s, the street trades, the workhouse and the temperance movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; sensation novel.
works.characters: Benny Bates; Nell Bates; Mr Lawrence; Mrs Bates; Granny Binks
works.structure: A novel in thirty-one chapters, from the street to the deathbed. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Silas Kitto Hocking. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations

works.title: Hereward the Wake: 'Last of the English'
works.description: Published in 1866 and the last of Kingsley's historical novels: the story of the Fenland outlaw who resisted William the Conqueror after 1066. It is a prose fiction work of 1866 by Charles Kingsley; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Hereward, outlawed by his own family, returns from exile to find his lands seized, joins the resistance of the Isle of Ely, fights the Normans, and after the fall of Ely escapes and lives as an outlaw, dying in a last fight against Norman knights.
works.significance: Hereward the Wake is the founding English novel of the Anglo-Saxon resistance and a key text of Victorian racial and national mythology; its Fenland landscape and its hero made the story of 1066 a central English national legend.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1066-71 years, the Norman Conquest, the Fenland geography and the legend of Hereward in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the medieval romances. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Hereward; Torfrida, his wife; Lady Godiva, his mother; Martin Lightfoot; Alftruda; Ivo Taillebois; William the Conqueror
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Regional identity and the American sectional character
movements: Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire

works.title: Herland
works.description: Published in the Forerunner in 1915 and the first sustained American feminist utopia: the discovery of a country inhabited entirely by women and the consequences for three male explorers. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Charlotte Perkins Gilman; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Three American men find Herland, a country without men where the women reproduce parthenogenetically, have built a harmonious civilisation of gardens and education, and have no war, poverty or crime; the three men marry Herland women, and the novel ends with Terry's expulsion after he tries to force himself on his wife Alima, Jeff staying behind with the pregnant Celis, and the narrator, Van, leaving with his wife Ellador to show her the outside world.
works.significance: Herland is the founding American feminist utopia and the most influential work of its kind before the 1970s: its vision of a society organised by women has shaped feminist science fiction from Marge Piercy to Ursula Le Guin.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
works.context: The 1910s: the American suffrage movement, the First World War, and the utopian tradition of Bellamy and Morris. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Vandyck Jennings (Van), the narrator; Terry O. Nicholson; Jeff Margrave; Ellador; Alima; Celis; Somel; Zava; Moadine
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Perkins Stetson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

themes: Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
Science, religion, and the question of design

works.title: Hero and Leander
works.description: Marlowe's unfinished Ovidian epyllion, left at the lovers' first night and completed by George Chapman in 1598: the priestess Hero of Sestos and the youth Leander of Abydos meet at Venus's festival and fall in love; Leander swims the Hellespont nightly, and the poem breaks off with the consummation — 'Love is not full of pity, as men say' — before Hero's death in the familiar myth.
works.plot: Leander, 'amorous Leander, beautiful and young', woos Hero at the feast of Adonis; her vows to Venus yield to his eloquence; the first swim, the first embrace, and the lovers' debate with the dawn occupy the completed portion, with Neptune's dalliance with the swimming Leander as its most celebrated episode.
works.significance: The masterpiece of the Elizabethan epyllion and the direct ancestor of the Restoration erotic couplet — the poem Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis answered and vied with.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of extraordinary wit and sensuousness — the poem that defined the English erotic couplet for the next two centuries.
works.context: Written in 1593, the year of Marlowe's death; printed first by Edward Blount in 1598 and again the same year with Chapman's continuation ('Hero and Leander: Begun by Christopher Marloe; and finished by George Chapman').
works.characters: Hero; Leander; Neptune; Venus; Cupid; the Nurse (Chapman's continuation)
works.structure: Two completed sestiads (Marlowe's) followed by Chapman's four, the whole framed as a narrative of seduction and delay in the epyllion manner.
works.attributionNotes: Marlowe's two sestiads are uncontested; the continuation is Chapman's.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Hesperides
altTitles: Hesperides; or, The Works Both Humane and Divine of Robert Herrick
works.description: Robert Herrick's vast collection of some 1,400 poems (1648), divided into the pagan 'Hesperides' and the Christian 'Noble Numbers', which celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of rural Devon and the pleasures of the present, shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith — including 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' ('Gather ye rosebuds while ye may').
works.plot: The poems range over love, wine, flowers, country customs, kings and loyalty, and devotion, urging carpe diem while acknowledging death, and pairing classical festivity with Christian piety.
works.significance: Hesperides is the most varied and charming of Cavalier collections, a treasury of English rural folklore and lyric, and 'Gather ye rosebuds' the most famous carpe diem poem in English.
works.meter: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics in a great variety of meters with a light, mellifluous touch.
works.context: Written largely during Herrick's years as vicar of Dean Prior (1629–47) and published in 1647/48 after his ejection by Parliament as a royalist; it preserves the ceremonial culture of the English countryside.
works.characters: the poet; Julia and other mistresses; the rural folk
works.structure: A large collection of short lyrics, epigrams, and songs in two parts, loosely grouped by theme.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Country retirement and the estate poem

Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Hester
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1883 and Oliphant's great novel of the woman of business: the conflict between the old banking family of the Vernonys and the capable young woman who saves it. It is a prose fiction work of 1883 by Margaret Oliphant; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Hester Vernon, the proud daughter of the man whose failure once nearly wrecked the family bank, lives with her mother as a dependant of the formidable old Catherine Vernon, who saved it; Catherine's favourite and heir, Edward Vernon, courts Hester while secretly speculating with the bank's money, and the crisis that follows brings the two proud women, so alike and so mutually hostile, to the edge of ruin together.
works.significance: Hester is Oliphant's finest single novel and one of the great Victorian novels of a woman's professional life: it treats money, work and female independence with a clear-eyed realism that makes it a bridge between the Victorian novel and the New Woman fiction of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1880s: the provincial banking town, the South Sea Bubble speculation and its aftermath, and the Victorian debate on women's work. The record dates the work as composed between 1882 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Hester Vernon; Catherine Vernon; Edward Vernon; Hester's mother; the dependent cousins of the Vernonry
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Margaret Oliphant Wilson Oliphant. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Hickscorner
works.description: An anonymous early morality interlude of the conversion of three rogues — Freewill, Imagination, and the Vice Hickscorner — printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1513–15.
works.plot: Freewill and Imagination, fallen into idleness and vice, meet the hardened rogue Hickscorner, who boasts of his crimes and rails at virtue; Pity and Contemplation reprove them, and the three rogues are brought to repentance, confess their sins, and set out on pilgrimage, with the play ending in a vision of the joys of heaven.
works.significance: One of the earliest printed English moralities and the first to centre on the conversion of rogues; its Vice, Hickscorner, is a landmark in the development of the stage devil's comic heir, and its tavern realism anticipates the rogue literature of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Printed c. 1513–15 by Wynkyn de Worde, in the generation after Everyman; the play's tavern scenes and rogue-cant document the underworld of early Tudor London, and its popularity carried it through editions to the 1560s.
works.characters: Freewill; Imagination; Hickscorner; Pity; Contemplation; Perseverance
works.structure: A continuous morality play in two movements — the rogues' boasting fellowship and their conversion — with the Vice Hickscorner as the play's comic engine.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: High Summer
works.description: The village novel of the season: the harvest, the chapel and the quarrel. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by Richard Church; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: High Summer sets the harvest, the chapel and the quarrel of the village in the single season of the title, in the realist manner of the country novel of the 1930s.
works.significance: High Summer is the season novel of Church's village fiction: its harvest and its chapel quarrel made the farming year the plot of the realist country novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain observed lyric of the country and the season.
works.context: The English village in the summer of 1931. The record dates the work as composed between 1930 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: the farmer; the chapel folk; the village; the harvest crew
works.structure: A novel of the season in chapters of the harvest year. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Richard Thomas Church. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
