works.title: High Windows
works.description: High Windows is Philip Larkin's fourth and last collection, published by Faber and Faber in 1974. It sold six thousand copies in its first three weeks. Darker, coarser and more formally varied than his earlier books, it confronts old age, death, sexual freedom and the decline of England, and it persuaded many critics, for the first time, to take Larkin as a major poet.
works.summary: Poems written between 1965 and 1974, opening with "To the Sea" and closing with "The Explosion", including "The Trees", "Livings", "High Windows", "The Old Fools", "Going, Going", "The Card-Players", "The Building", "Posterity", "Homage to a Government", "This Be The Verse", "Sad Steps", "Annus Mirabilis", "Vers de Société", "Show Saturday" and "Cut Grass".
works.plot:
The book opens with seaside holidays in "To the Sea", where the poet sees an old custom of ordinary happiness still being kept up, and moves through the three monologues of "Livings", glimpses of other lives in a hotel, a lighthouse and a Cambridge college. The title poem watches a young couple and supposes that they enjoy a sexual freedom he never had; he then recalls that older people must once have envied his own generation's freedom from religion, and the poem rises from crude speech to the thought of high windows: 'the sun-comprehending glass, / And beyond it, the deep blue air, that shows / Nothing, and is nowhere, and is endless.' "Annus Mirabilis" gives the same theme a comic turn, dating the start of sexual intercourse to 1963, between the end of the Chatterley ban and the Beatles' first LP.

Mortality dominates the central poems. "The Old Fools" looks with horror and pity at the senile, asking what they think is happening and recognising that the same end awaits everyone. "The Building" presents a hospital as a modern cathedral, full of patients waiting in a kind of faith for a cure that cannot finally be given. "Sad Steps" contrasts the moon's romantic associations with the poet's ageing body, and "Vers de Société" weighs a tedious party invitation against the worse prospect of being alone with one's thoughts.

Other poems turn to England and its politics. "Going, Going" fears that the countryside will be covered by motorways and estates, so that 'that will be England gone'. "Homage to a Government" mocks the withdrawal of British troops from overseas for financial reasons, and "Show Saturday" celebrates an agricultural show as a ritual that renews community. The collection ends with "The Explosion", in which miners walk to work one morning, a pit explosion kills them, and their wives in chapel see them for a moment alive and gold, carrying lark's eggs unbroken.
works.significance: High Windows confirmed Larkin as the most important English poet of his time and, according to the Sogang University study, first won him the serious attention of critics. Poems such as "High Windows", "The Old Fools", "The Building" and "This Be The Verse" are among the most widely quoted in modern English poetry.
works.meter: A sharper juxtaposition than before of obscenity and lyricism, colloquial bluntness and exalted imagery; masterly control of rhyme and rhythm; frequent shifts within a poem from satire to vision.
works.context: The poems were written in Hull between 1965 and 1974, years of sexual liberation, economic decline, the end of Britain's military role east of Suez and the spread of motorways and new towns; "Going, Going" was commissioned for a government report on the environment.
works.structure: Lyrics of widely varying length and form, from quatrains and sonnet-like poems to long, intricately rhymed stanzas and unrhymed trochaic verse in "The Explosion", arranged so that poems of crude statement and visionary endings alternate.
themes: Death, illness and mourning
Faith, doubt and the sacred
Nature, ecology and environmental crisis
Sexuality, desire and the closet

works.title: High Windows (poem)
works.description: High Windows is the title poem of Philip Larkin's last collection, High Windows (Faber, 1974), completed in February 1967. An older man watching a young couple imagines their sexual freedom as the paradise his generation dreamed of, wonders whether his own freedom from religion once looked like paradise to his elders, and ends not in words but in an image of high windows and endless blue air.
works.summary: The speaker's coarse imagining of a young couple's sex life; the reflection that every generation envies the next its freedom, and that his own youth was free of God and hell; and the final image of sun-filled glass and empty sky.
works.plot: Seeing a couple of kids, the speaker guesses that the boy is sleeping with the girl and that she takes the pill or wears a diaphragm, and he knows this is the paradise everyone old has dreamed of, with bonds and gestures pushed aside like an outdated combine harvester and the young sliding endlessly down to happiness. He wonders whether anyone looked at him forty years earlier and thought the same: no God any more, no sweating in the dark about hell, no hiding what you think of the priest, who will go down the long slide too, like free bloody birds. Then, rather than words, comes the thought of high windows: the sun-comprehending glass and, beyond it, the deep blue air that shows nothing, and is nowhere, and is endless.
works.significance: One of Larkin's most celebrated and discussed poems, and the title piece of the collection Clive James called 'despair made beautiful'.
works.meter: Obscenity and slang in the opening lines set against the lyrical abstraction of the close, a contrast characteristic of late Larkin.
works.context: Completed on 12 February 1967, the year of the Sexual Offences Act and of rapidly changing sexual mores, while Larkin lived in the top flat of 32 Pearson Park, Hull, whose windows are widely believed to have suggested the image.
works.structure: Five four-line stanzas, loosely rhymed, with a turn at the last stanza from argument to image.
themes: Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
Faith, doubt and the sacred
Sexuality, desire and the closet

works.title: Highland River
works.description: The river novel of the boy's north and the scientist's return. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by Neil Gunn; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation.
works.plot: Highland River follows Kenn, the boy of the Caithness river, from the salmon of his childhood through the trenches of the war to the scientific career of the south, and brings him back to the river at the novel's close, in the prose of water and memory that won Gunn the fiction prize of the year.
works.significance: Highland River is Gunn's most finished novel: it carries the river of the north through the war and the laboratory, and makes the return to the water the moral of the Scottish Renaissance's fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain.
works.context: Caithness, the war, and the scientific London of the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1937 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; nature essay and the rural observation.
works.characters: Kenn, the boy of the river; the scientist of the south; the people of the strath
works.structure: A novel of the river in three parts: the boyhood, the war and the career, the return. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Neil Miller Gunn. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Highway in the Sun and Other Plays
works.form: Plays (four plays first broadcast by the BBC)
works.description: Four plays that Selvon wrote for BBC broadcast in the 1970s, published by Peepal Tree Press in Leeds in December 1991. The publisher presents them as his most focused treatment of the choice Indians in the Caribbean must make between tradition and creolisation; three adapt his Trinidad novels.
works.summary: Highway in the Sun, Home Sweet India, Turn Again Tiger and Harvest in Wilderness.
works.plot: Highway in the Sun tells of Tiger and Urmilla's first year of marriage away from their extended family and of their dealings with Joe and Rita, their Afro-Creole neighbours, the matter of A Brighter Sun. In Home Sweet India Johnny, dismayed by his family's loss of culture, plans to return to India. In Turn Again Tiger, Tiger learns that he cannot turn his back on the Indian past if he is to lay its ghosts to rest and face the future whole. In Harvest in Wilderness the traditional cane-cutting world of Balgobin confronts the new technology of his creolised nephew Romesh, the conflict of The Plains of Caroni, 'but the past continues to spring surprises'.
works.significance: It gathers Selvon's drama of Indo-Trinidadian life as Eldorado West One gathers his London plays; Dawes cites it as the compilation of his dramatic works.
works.meter: Written for broadcast by the BBC, according to the publisher; their language and dramatic form were not examined.
works.context: The Anthurium special issue dates the BBC production of Home Sweet India to 1970, and Wikipedia and South Asian Britain list it among Selvon's television scripts; the book appeared in 1991, when he lived in Calgary.
works.structure: Four separate plays; three adapt the novels A Brighter Sun, Turn Again Tiger and The Plains of Caroni, while Home Sweet India has no novel behind it in the sources consulted.
themes: Family, marriage and domestic life
Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Migration, exile and diaspora
movements: Caribbean Literature in English

works.title: Hilda Wade
works.description: Published posthumously in 1900 and Allen's detective novel: a lady doctor's scientific pursuit of the man who murdered her father. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Grant Allen; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Hilda Wade, a nurse of uncanny intuition at a great London hospital, is secretly the daughter of Dr Yorke-Bannerman, who died under suspicion of poisoning, and has entered the hospital to watch the eminent Professor Sebastian, the man truly responsible; narrated by the young doctor Hubert Cumberledge, who loves her, the episodes follow her duel with Sebastian from London to Rhodesia and India until he is unmasked, the last of them completed after Allen's death by Arthur Conan Doyle.
works.significance: Hilda Wade is one of the earliest detective novels with a female scientific detective and a landmark of the woman-detective tradition: its heroine's medical expertise and her intellectual superiority to the men around her made it a forerunner of the modern female detective story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas.
works.context: 1900: the entry of women into medicine, the imperial exploration of Africa, and the detective-fiction boom after Sherlock Holmes. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Hilda Wade; Dr Hubert Cumberledge, the narrator; Professor Sebastian; Dr Yorke-Bannerman, her father
works.structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Hindle Wakes
works.description: The Manchester School's greatest play: the working woman's refusal of marriage. It is a dramatic work of 1912 by Stanley Houghton; it belongs to Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Fanny Hawthorn, a mill worker, spends the holiday week with the mill-owner's son and refuses to marry him; the play that made Houghton the Manchester School's greatest playwright and remains one of the most famous scenes of the new drama.
works.significance: Hindle Wakes is Houghton's great play of the Lancashire working woman: its holiday week, its mill-owner's son and its refusal of marriage made it the Manchester School's most famous play and a permanent part of the repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain Lancashire dialogue of the mill and the terrace.
works.context: The Lancashire mill town of Hindle in 1912. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and first performed in 1912 and the corpus places it within Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; suffrage play and the woman's drama.
works.characters: Fanny Hawthorn; Alan Jeffcoate; Jenny Hawthorn; Mrs. Hawthorn; the mill-owner
works.structure: Three acts, in the mill town and its holiday week. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stanley Houghton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Historia Anglorum
works.description: Henry of Huntingdon's history of England from the earliest times to the accession of Henry II in 1154, notable for its vivid battle narratives, its interest in the English past as national history, and the substantial body of original verse — including the political poems addressed to Henry I — embedded in the prose.
works.summary: Ten books (the latest recension) move from Roman and Anglo-Saxon Britain through the Norman kings to the anarchy of Stephen's reign; the work incorporates earlier sources (Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) while supplying independent contemporary witness for the twelfth century, including the famous account of the Battle of Lincoln.
works.significance: A principal narrative source for the reign of Stephen, and a central text of twelfth-century English national historiography; its verse makes it a bridge between Anglo-Latin and vernacular literary traditions.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Warfare and battle
movements: The Twelfth-Century Renaissance

works.title: Historia Brittonum
works.form: history and chronicle (composite) in Latin prose
works.description: A composite history of the Britons compiled in Wales in 829/30 and traditionally attributed to Nennius: genealogies, origin legends (the Trojan descent of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
works.plot: The work assembles disparate materials on the age of the world, the Trojan origins of the Britons, the Roman occupation, Vortigern and the coming of the Saxons, the boy-prophet Ambrosius, the wars of Arthur ('dux bellorum'), the genealogies of the Saxon and Welsh kings, and the 'wonders of Britain' — an anthology of British historical memory rather than a continuous history.
works.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature; the principal quarry of later Welsh and English Arthurian history (Geoffrey of Monmouth).
works.meter: Latin prose of varying registers.
works.context: Compiled in Gwynedd c. 829/30 during the Mercian ascendancy in Wales; preserved in some forty manuscripts in Welsh, English, and continental recensions.
works.characters: Vortigern; Ambrosius; Arthur; Patrick; Germanus; Hengist and Horsa
works.structure: Compilatory: a sequence of heterogeneous sections of varying provenance, several marked as the work of 'Nennius the disciple of Elvodugus'.
works.attributionNotes: The prologue attributes the compilation to Nennius, but not all manuscripts carry it; the work is demonstrably composite.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle

works.title: Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum
altTitles: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
works.form: history and chronicle (ecclesiastical history) in Latin prose
works.description: Bede's masterpiece, completed in 731: the history of the English church and people from Caesar's invasions to 731, in five books. It is the primary narrative source for early Anglo-Saxon history, the origin of the AD dating system's general use, and the conduit through which Cædmon's Hymn and much else survives.
works.plot: The five books trace the conversion of the English kingdoms — the mission of Augustine to Kent (597), the Northumbrian mission of Paulinus and Aidan, the Synod of Whitby (664) — interspersed with saints' lives (Cuthbert, Æthelthryth), miracles, letters, and the famous account of the poet Cædmon; the work closes with a summary of Britain's ecclesiastical state and Bede's autobiographical colophon.
works.significance: 'The father of English history'; the indispensable source for the first three centuries of English Christianity and for the early vernacular poetic record.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical clarity; contains the earliest recorded English verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in paraphrase.
works.context: Composed at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow from earlier annals, lives, and documents; dedicated to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria.
works.characters: Augustine of Canterbury; Æthelberht; Edwin; Oswald; Aidan; Hild; Cuthbert; Cædmon; Theodore; Wilfrid
works.structure: Annalistic-chronological within each book, organized by kingdom and diocese; documentary (letters, synods) and hagiographical materials are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain (his own colophon).
themes: Kingship and good rule
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Historia Regum Britanniae
altTitles: The History of the Kings of Britain
works.description: Pseudohistorical chronicle tracing the kings of Britain from the legendary Brutus of Troy to the Saxon conquest, the principal source of the Arthurian legend in England. Geoffrey claims to translate 'a certain very ancient book in the British tongue' given him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford; its authority was attacked by William of Newburgh and Gerald of Wales but it decisively shaped medieval British historiography.
works.summary: Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates the foundation of Britain by Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, and proceeds through the reigns of the legendary kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests extend over much of Europe — to the Saxon domination and the prophecies of Merlin (the Prophetiae Merlini, later incorporated as Book VII). The work made Arthur a pan-European figure and provided the framework for Wace, Layamon, and the later chronicle tradition.
works.significance: The single most influential piece of British historical writing of the Middle Ages: over 200 manuscripts survive, and it furnished the matter of Britain for romance, chronicle, and national myth from Wace's Roman de Brut to Malory and beyond.
themes: Arthurian legend
Kingship and good rule
National identity and Englishness

works.title: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
altTitles: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
Doubts on the History of Richard III
works.description: A controversial historical argument that the standard history of Richard III is a fabrication of the victorious house, the evidence being examined point by point against the chroniclers. It is an early and influential piece of critical historical method, and its defence of the king's reputation provoked a long pamphlet war.
works.plot: The work reviews the charges against Richard - the murder of the princes, the death of his wife, the tyranny and the usurpation - and finds in each case either no contemporary evidence or evidence contradicting the received story. It argues that the chronicles were composed under the new dynasty and that the most damning particulars were invented after the event. The conclusion leaves the king's guilt undemonstrated and his character to be reformed by the reader.
works.significance: It founded the modern defence tradition of Richard's reign and is a landmark in the application of evidential scepticism to English history, anticipating the source criticism of the following century.
works.meter: A cool, ironical and closely reasoned prose of the case and the query, with the rhetorical understatement used as a weapon against authority.
works.context: Published in 1768 in the season of the antiquarian revival and of the new criticism of the chronicles, and answered by several hostile pieces before the century's end; its composition coincided with the author's own historical and edition work.
works.characters: King Richard the Third; the princes in the Tower; the chroniclers and their patrons; the historians of the Tudor age
works.structure: A dissertation in numbered particulars, each charge stated, its authorities compared and its improbability urged; the argument is juridical and accumulative rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at first and acknowledged by the author, the dispute with the answerers being documented in his letters.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: Historical Odes and Other Poems
works.description: The Pre-Raphaelite historian's odes: the medieval past and the fall of the monasteries. It is a verse work of 1864 by Richard Watson Dixon; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet.
works.plot: The collection gathers Dixon's historical odes — 'The Death of Marlowe', 'The Fall of the Monasteries', 'The Plague of London', 'The Tournament' — in which the English past is rendered in grave, learned, Pre-Raphaelite verse.
works.significance: Historical Odes and Other Poems is the finest historical poetry of the Pre-Raphaelite circle: its odes of the monasteries and the plague made Dixon the central poet of the Oxford Movement's medievalism.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ode in the historical manner.
works.context: England in the 1860s, and the Oxford Movement's recovery of the medieval and Reformation past. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.characters: Marlowe; the monks; the plague dead; the knights
works.structure: A collection of historical odes and lyrics. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as R. W. Dixon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: History of English Thought in the Eighteenth Century
works.form: History of ideas in two volumes
works.description: Published in 1876 and the founding modern study of English eighteenth-century thought: a systematic account of the deist controversy, the moral philosophers, the political economists and the historians of the age.
works.plot: Stephen traces the rise of rationalism from Locke through the deists, Shaftesbury, Mandeville, Butler, Hume and Adam Smith, and argues that eighteenth-century England was a society working out the consequences of the new science and of the new commercial order.
works.significance: The History of English Thought is the founding work of the history of ideas in England and the model for the modern intellectual history of the eighteenth century; it is also the clearest statement of the rationalist case against Christian orthodoxy in Victorian England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact critical prose.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian debate on Darwin and religion, the new academic history of philosophy, and the crisis of faith among the Victorian intellectual class. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Leslie Stephen. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: History of Friedrich II of Prussia, called Frederick the Great
works.description: Published in six volumes between 1858 and 1865, the last and longest of Carlyle's works, and the most ambitious Victorian attempt to write the history of an age through the biography of a king. It is a prose work of 1858 by Thomas Carlyle; it belongs to Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The history follows Frederick from his brutal upbringing under Frederick William I through the Silesian wars, the Seven Years' War and the partition of Poland to his death in 1786, with long digressions on the German princes, the Prussian army and the diplomacy of the eighteenth century.
works.significance: Frederick the Great is Carlyle's masterpiece of narrative history and one of the great monuments of Victorian prose; it made the eighteenth century live for English readers and established the narrative-history method that Macaulay and Froude practised, and its admiration for Prussian order shaped Victorian and later attitudes to Germany.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. works.title: History of Ireland: Heroic Period
works.description: The book that brought the Ulster cycle back into modern literature and started the Irish revival. It is a prose work of 1878 by Standish James O'Grady; it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.

works.description: Published in nine volumes from 1889 to 1891 and the greatest American historical work of the century: the United States from 1800 to 1817. works.significance: The History is the greatest American historical narrative of the nineteenth century: its research, its irony and its analysis of the growth of American nationality made it the model of American historical writing, and it remains the standard account of the Jefferson and Madison administrations.

works.title: Holy Sonnets
works.description: Donne's nineteen divine sonnets — 'Batter my heart, three-personed God', 'Death be not proud', 'At the round earth's imagined corners', 'Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt' — in which the erotic and argumentative energies of the love poems are turned on God, sin, death, and the soul's terror of damnation.
works.plot: The sonnets dramatize the soul's wrestling with God: pleas for violent grace, meditations on death and judgment, griefs of bereavement, and the final sonnets' fear and love of a God who must be wooed with the poet's whole art.
works.significance: The supreme English devotional sonnets — the bridge from the Elizabethan love sonnet to the sacred poetry of Herbert, Crashaw, and Hopkins.
works.meter: The Italian and English sonnet forms strained to the breaking point — spondaic openings, abrupt turns, and the metaphysical conceit turned to devotion.
works.context: Composed chiefly between 1609 and 1619, the years of Donne's ordination (1615) and of his wife's death (1617); the poems circulated in manuscript and were printed posthumously in 1633.
works.characters: the speaker; God (as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit); Death; the soul; the angels
works.structure: A cycle of nineteen sonnets (in the standard canon; twelve in the earliest manuscript group, with the later 'Westmoreland' sequence adding the rest), not a plotted sequence but a linked series of meditations.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the canon of nineteen and the ordering are the work of later editors, from the manuscript groups.

works.title: Homage to a Government
works.description: Homage to a Government is an ironic poem by Philip Larkin about the British withdrawal of its forces from east of Suez because the country could no longer pay for them. Completed in January 1969, it first appeared in The Sunday Times and was collected in High Windows (1974).
works.summary: The announcement that the soldiers are to come home for lack of money; the repeated assurance that this is all right; and the picture of a country whose statues stand unchanged while it has become a different country.
works.plot: Next year, the poem begins, we are to bring the soldiers home for lack of money, and it is all right: the places they guarded must guard themselves, and we want the money for ourselves at home instead of working. It is hard to say who wanted it, but nobody minds; the places are far off, and from what we hear the soldiers only made trouble. Next year we shall live in a country that brought its soldiers home for lack of money; the statues will stand in the same tree-muffled squares, our children will not know it is a different country, and all we can hope to leave them now is money.
works.significance: Larkin's most explicitly political poem, often cited in discussions of his conservatism and of the literature of Britain's imperial decline.
works.meter: Deadpan irony, the government's own reassuring idiom turned against it.
works.context: Written after the Labour government's decision, announced in January 1968, to withdraw British forces from east of Suez by 1971; a commentator quotes Larkin calling the withdrawal for reasons of cost 'a dreadful humiliation'.
works.structure: Three six-line stanzas whose line endings repeat key words (home, right, orderly, money), giving the poem the sound of a flat, repeated excuse.
themes: Decolonisation, the end of empire and the new nation
Nationhood and national identity

works.title: Homage to Catalonia
works.description: Orwell's Spain: the Barcelona militias, the betrayal of the revolution and a bullet through the throat. It is a prose work of 1938 by George Orwell; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Orwell goes to Spain in 1936 to fight for the Republic, joins the POUM militia on the Aragon front, and experiences the revolutionary Barcelona of the first months; in May 1937 he is caught in the street fighting between the Communists and the anarchists, and later shot through the neck. The book ends with his escape from Spain and his anger at the left's complicity in the suppression of the revolution.
works.significance: Homage to Catalonia is the finest English book on the Spanish Civil War and the founding text of Orwell's political honesty: its account of revolutionary Barcelona and of the left's betrayal of its own cause is unmatched.

works.title: Home to Harlem
works.form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1928
works.description: The first best-selling Black novel of the decade: Jake Brown's Harlem, the cabarets and the return from the war. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Claude McKay; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance.
works.plot: Jake Brown, a Black soldier who has deserted from the army in France, returns to Harlem and lives through its cabarets, rent parties and love affairs, and goes looking for his friend Ray, a Haitian intellectual, in a novel of the Black migrant city.

works.title: Homiletic Fragment I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), late tenth century
works.description: Two homiletic poems in the Vercelli Book. Homiletic Fragment I (47 lines) is a meditation on deceitful friendship, comparing the false friend to the bee whose honey is sweet but whose sting is deadly. Homiletic Fragment II (20 lines) laments man's hardness of heart amid the world's sorrows.
works.plot: Fragment I warns against the friend who speaks fair but plots evil, elaborating the image of the bee through biblical and proverbial wisdom. Fragment II meditates on grief and the human failure to heed the truth, in a fragmentary surviving text.
works.significance: Witnesses to the close relationship between Old English homiletic prose and verse, and to the moral psychology of the late Anglo-Saxon church.
works.meter: Alliterative long line in the homiletic manner of the Vercelli Book's prose sermons; both texts are imperfectly preserved.
works.context: The Vercelli Book pairs these poems with its collection of doomsday homilies and with The Dream of the Rood, Elene, and Andreas; the fragments belong to the same culture of vernacular preaching and moral verse.
works.structure: Fragment I develops a single governing simile (the treacherous friend as bee) with proverbial expansions; Fragment II is a broken meditation on sorrow and heedlessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two fragments are distinct poems.
themes: Judgment Day and eschatology
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Hope Leslie
works.form: Historical novel and romance of the colonial period, with domestic and frontier plotting
works.description: The most ambitious early American historical novel by a woman, set in the Massachusetts Bay colony of the 1630s and 1640s. It makes the Pequot war, the treatment of Indians and the position of women in a theocratic commonwealth its joint subjects. Its famous argument is that the children of a Puritan generation may dissent from its creed and still be loyal.
works.plot: Two sisters, one spirited and one gentle, are left in the care of a severe Puritan governor after their father is ruined by a quarrel with him. The younger elopes with a young Indian of the Pequot nation and passes out of the colony's world, while the elder is bound to an accomplished English youth whose loyalty to the settlement is tried by her obstinacy. The narrative passes to the Pequot war, to the burning of the fort at Mystic, and to the death of the sister whom the colony has lost. It closes by asking whether justice between cultures is possible in a country founded on conquest.
works.significance: It is the central fiction of the Puritan inheritance by a woman writer and one of the earliest American novels to make Indian dispossession its explicit moral subject. Its sister-plot supplies the structural model for later domestic historical fiction. It has been recovered as a canonical text of early American women's writing.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1827, in the year of the removal debate, and written from the author's family recollections of New England colonial history. Its use of the Indian war answers the contemporary argument over the rights of the Cherokee and the conduct of the state. Its treatment of the cavalier and the roundhead inherits the Scottish historical romance.
works.characters: Hope Leslie; Faith Leslie; Everell Whittingham; Governor Winthrop
works.structure: Third-person historical romance alternating between domestic plot and public history, with a frame of chronicle and legend and a closing appendix of historical documents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal

works.title: Horae Paulinae
altTitles: Horae Paulinae; or, New Confirmed Evidences of the Divine Authority of the Holy Scriptures
works.form: critical dissertation and biblical commentary in the evidential manner
works.description: A critical-apologetical experiment, comparing the letters of the apostle Paul with the narrative of the Acts and with one another, and finding in their accidental agreements a proof of authenticity no forger could have produced. It is a work of scholarship used as evidence, and its method of undesigned coincidence became one of the most copied arguments in the defence of the scriptures.
works.plot: The treatise first states its rule: if two writers, writing independently and for different purposes, touch upon the same place, person, or incident in ways neither intended nor adverted to, and yet without contradiction, their concurrence is evidence that both were dealing with real transactions. It then applies the rule, setting the letters of the Thessalonians and of the Corinthians beside the narrative of the missionary journeys, and showing that the history and the epistles supply each other's omissions, that the characters, fortunes, and fellow-labourers agree without apparent study, and that the notices of the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem fall into place only when the two records are read together. A second line of comparison is drawn between the epistles themselves, whose differences of tone, of phrase, and of circumstance are shown to be marks of genuine correspondence rather than of a designed uniformity. The conclusion is that these writings are neither forged nor colluded, and that the same method may be extended to the rest of the canon.
works.significance: It created a permanent instrument of scriptural apologetic, the argument from undesigned coincidence, which passed into commentaries, into the popular evidential manuals, and into the literary criticism of the next century, where the same test was used to date and to authenticate documents. As criticism it anticipates the modern treatment of a correspondence as historical evidence, and as rhetoric it is the neatest example of the period's habit of arguing religion from the rules of proof.
works.meter: Quiet, patient, expository prose of the close reader: parallel text, minute comparison, and the restrained exultation of a reasoner who believes he has found a new class of proof.
works.context: Published in the year of the counter-revolutionary pamphlets and of the quarrel over infidelity, out of the same school of evidential divinity that produced a popular view of the Christian proof, and built upon a method its author had already worked out in private study before the sceptical crisis made such arguments a public need.
works.structure: Parts, each pairing one epistle or group of epistles with the corresponding portion of the narrative, and closing with general remarks on the extent and force of the concurrence; the argument proceeds by accumulated particulars rather than by deduction.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, who afterwards re-cast and enlarged portions of it in the collected editions of his theological works.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
Typology and biblical interpretation

works.title: Hospital Sketches
works.form: Collection of letters (first published in the Commonwealth, 1863)
works.description: Published in 1863 and based on Alcott's service as a nurse at the Union Hotel Hospital in Georgetown: the first great American book of the Civil War from a woman's point of view. It is a prose work of 1863 by Louisa May Alcott; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: Tribulation Periwinkle, the narrator, travels to Washington, takes up her duties among the wounded, and records the deaths, the jokes and the ordinariness of the hospital, ending with her own illness and return home.
works.significance: Hospital Sketches is the founding American narrative of the Civil War hospital and one of the first American books to treat nursing as a profession; its unsentimental record of death and its comic voice made it a model for the American literature of war and medicine.
works.meter: Prose. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a strong narrative voice.

works.title: Hours in a Library
works.description: Published in three series between 1874 and 1879: essays on the English writers of the past, from Defoe, Richardson, Fielding and Smollett to Johnson, Gibbon, Cowper, Wordsworth and Scott. It is a prose work of 1874 by Leslie Stephen; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Each essay takes a writer or a book and reads it with the combination of biography, history and appreciation that Stephen made his own; the essays on the eighteenth-century novelists are still among the best short accounts of their art.
works.significance: Hours in a Library is the classic Victorian collection of literary essays and one of the books through which the eighteenth-century English novel entered the modern canon; its critical method — historical, biographical and unsentimental — shaped the Cambridge criticism of the next generation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact critical prose.
works.context: The 1870s, the Cornhill readership, and the Victorian formation of the English literary canon. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1879 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

works.title: Hours of Idleness
altTitles: Hours of Idleness; Original and Translated
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Juvenile verse miscellany: pre-Romantic sensibility lyric and verse epistle in the manner of the 1790s school of sensibility, with Augustan translation and imitation as its display of education.
works.description: The first book of verse by a noble minor, gathered from school exercises, imitations and occasional poems written between the Harrow years and the coming of age. It mixes lyric meditations, verse epistles to friends and relations, elegies on the dead, descriptive pieces on Newstead Abbey and translations from the classics and from French. The prevailing manner is that of the sentimental school of the 1790s: a sensitive young poet, estranged from his schoolfellows, consoling himself with memory, friendship and the pleasure of verse. Its hostile review in 1808, and the satirical reply it provoked, turned a private printed book into the opening quarrel of the poet's public career.
works.plot: The volume has no sustained argument but is arranged as a miscellany, opening with odes and lyric meditations and passing through epistles, elegies on friends and dead kinsfolk, and descriptive verse on the abbey and the Harrow playing-field. Its recurring subjects are the loss of schoolfellows, the isolation of a boy among boys, the deaths of maternal relatives in Scotland, and a claim to feeling refined by misfortune. Several pieces address the poet's half-sister directly, and a group of epistles is written to Harrow friends, among them a schoolmate who became a lifelong companion. The close turns on the poet's own prospects and on the consolation of verse, in a diction borrowed from the Scottish school of Beattie and from Campbell. The imitation of prior poets, ancient and modern, is not concealed but presented as the honest exercise of an undeclared hand.
works.significance: It is the documentary starting point of a career that became the most famous in European poetry within five years, and the evidence that the later manner was an argument with the school of sensibility rather than an inheritance from it. Its reviews fixed the posture of the insulted young nobleman that the satire of 1809 exploited and that the pilgrimage poem later dramatized. It also preserves the private mythology of family, home and loss on which the public pose of the tale poems was built.
works.meter: Chiefly iambic pentameter couplets and quatrains, with irregular ode stanzas, an imitation of the walk-verse of the country poem, and a few lyric measures in the manner of song; the handling is competent and heavily modelled rather than inventive.
works.context: Printed at a provincial press in 1807 at the author's cost for private circulation, the book was refused by the publisher whom its dedicatee had served, and its augmented London issue of 1808 drew the severe Edinburgh Review notice of April of that year, which treated a noble minor's private verses as public folly. The attack, and the satirical answer it produced, exemplify the new power of the review journals to make or wound a career, and the sensitivity of class, patronage and the booksellers' market in the years of the anti-Jacobin settlement.
works.characters: the poet-speaker; the half-sister addressed in several poems; the Harrow schoolfellows of the epistles; the dead kinswomen of the elegies; the ghost of the abbey in its descriptive piece
works.structure: A miscellany in three loose groups, odes and lyric meditations, then epistles and elegies, then translations and imitations; the ordering is by mood and manner rather than theme, and the 1808 issue added prose argument in the form of a prefatory advertisement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume appeared over the author's peerage title and initials, and pieces from it were reused and revised in the collected editions.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: Howards End
works.description: Three families and a house: the definitive Edwardian condition-of-England novel and the source of 'only connect'. It is a prose fiction work of 1910 by E. M. Forster; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The estate of Howards End passes from the Wilcoxes to the Schlegel sisters and back. Margaret Schlegel, the elder sister, marries Henry Wilcox, the philistine businessman, and tries to hold together the world of 'telegrams and anger' and the world of 'books and music'; her sister Helen has an affair with the impoverished clerk Leonard Bast, who dies by a falling bookcase, and the novel ends with the house, a baby, and the possibility of connection.
works.significance: Howards End is the definitive Edwardian novel and one of the permanent English novels of the century: 'only connect' became the period's moral watchword, its analysis of class and the 'undeveloped heart' has never been bettered, and its portrait of England as a house to be inherited is the finest thing Forster wrote.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, flexible, slightly ironic prose with the sudden lyric intensification.
works.context: The Edwardian middle class and its property, the motor car's destruction of the countryside, the new class of clerks, the imperial business in Africa (the Wilcoxes' Imperial and West African Rubber Company), and the suffrage movement on its margins.
works.characters: Margaret Schlegel; Helen Schlegel; Henry Wilcox; Ruth Wilcox; Leonard Bast; Charles Wilcox; Tibby Schlegel
works.structure: Four-part novel with dated chapters; the house as the symbolic centre and the inheritance plot as the mechanism.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Morgan Forster. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Hudibras
works.description: Samuel Butler's mock-heroic satire in three parts on Presbyterian and Independent hypocrisy, following the knight-errant Hudibras and his squire Ralpho through a series of absurd adventures in the wake of the Restoration.
works.plot: Hudibras, a Puritan knight of absurd learning and courage, sets out with his squire Ralpho to suppress bear-baiting, is beaten by the widow's champion Trulla, is rescued by the astrologer Sidrophel, and courts the wealthy widow; each part satirises a different aspect of sectary enthusiasm.
works.significance: The most popular poem of the Restoration — Charles II carried a copy in his pocket — and the principal English model of low mock-heroic, influencing Swift, Pope's Dunciad, and the whole tradition of comic verse satire.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with grotesque double and triple rhymes, deliberately anti-heroic; the 'Hudibrastic' verse.
works.context: Part I published 1663, Part II 1664, Part III 1678; written from Butler's experience as secretary to the Presbyterian Sir Samuel Luke during the civil wars.
works.characters: Sir Hudibras; Ralpho; Trulla; Magnano; Cerdon; Sidrophel; Whachum; the Widow; Talgol; Orsin
works.structure: Three parts in eight cantos each, a picaresque sequence of digressive episodes with extensive marginal notes and a prose epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Part I published anonymously but immediately ascribed to Butler; authorship undisputed.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley
works.form: Poetry sequence (two parts, thirteen and five poems)
works.description: Pound's farewell to London and the finest short sequence of the period: the artist in a commercial civilisation. It is a verse work of 1920 by Ezra Pound; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The sequence follows 'E.P.' — a poet modelled on Pound himself — through the aesthetic movements of the pre-war years, the War and the post-war literary market, and then 'Mauberley', the aesthete destroyed by the world he refuses; it closes with the vision of the poet as a failed fountain.
works.significance: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley is the finest short sequence of the period and Pound's most perfectly achieved poem: its satire of the literary market, its elegy for the war dead and its self-portrait of the artist made it the model for the modernist sequence.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the image as the unit of the poem.
works.context: London in the 1910s, the First World War, the deaths of Gaudier-Brzeska and Henry James, and the commercial literary world Pound was leaving for Paris. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1920 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.characters: E.P.; Mauberley; Lady Valentine; Brennbaum
works.structure: Two parts: thirteen poems on 'E.P.' and five on Mauberley. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ezra Loomis Pound. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Human Life
works.form: Didactic and meditative poem in the eighteenth-century descriptive tradition, descended from the 'Pleasures' poems of the earlier century and from the school of pastoral and domestic moral verse.
works.description: A reflective poem on the ordinary cycle of domestic and civic life, treating the common-place as the proper subject of serious verse. Its speaker moves through the daily round of labour, rest, friendship, illness and death, arguing that a quiet, moral and sociable existence yields more genuine poetry than romance or heroics. It was published as a single long poem in three books and was re-issued with additional pieces in 1821 and in the collected edition of 1827.
works.plot: The poem's argument is that human life, in its homeliest and most recurring features, is at once the surest subject and the severest test of verse. It passes from the morning and labouring round of a community to the consolations of friendship, religion and domestic affection, and then to sickness and mortality, refusing to resolve these into a grand narrative. Episodic pictures of the poor, of the town at work and of the sickroom carry the moral reasoning. The closing books widen the scope to history and to the poet's own station, ending in a meditation on the small services a verse of observation can render. Its plainness of subject, earned by elaboration of revision, was the poem's provocation to a age of the exotic and the heroic.
works.significance: It established the model of the deliberately undramatic Romantic meditative poem, and its insistence on the ordinary as poetic material was praised by later poets who wanted a via media between Lake-school simplicity and Byronic rhetoric. Victorian school anthologies fixed a phrase from its closing lines as a definition of the practical value of poetry. Its reputation now rests less on argument than on the example it gives of revision as a poetic method.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with sententious closures and frequent apostrophe.
works.context: Written across the war years and published just after peace, when the vocabulary of 'human life' was being contested by radical, evangelical and Wordsworthian writers alike. Its celebration of ordinary labour and polite sociability belongs to the Regency book trade's well-fed middle-class readership, and its anti-romantic plainness was a deliberate contrast with the Oriental romances then selling widely. The poet's Unitarian family background and his position in London finance and patronage inform its quiet moral didacticism.
works.structure: A continuous reflective argument in numbered books, held together by a single meditating voice and by episodic tableau rather than by plot.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Hungarian Traductions
altTitles: Hungarian Traductions, from the Best Latin and Other Historians
works.language: English (translated from Latin and other languages)
works.form: Translation and editorial compilation in prose, of historical and antiquarian material, with notes and prefatory argument; a work of national history in the translated-compiler manner of the period.
works.description: Percy's earliest book-length publication as a translator and compiler: a volume of renderings from the Latin and other historians of Hungary, offering the English reader an account of the Hungarians and of the long frontier warfare of eastern Europe with the Ottoman powers. It is a work of the same antiquarian-historical imagination that produced the 'Reliques', applied to the origins and fortunes of a nation rather than to its poetry.
works.plot: The volume has no plot but an assembling argument: that the history of Hungary, its people, their migrations, their institutions and their struggles, can be recovered for English readers from the foreign historians and made intelligible as a single narrative of national fortune. Its substance is the rise and the trials of a nation placed on the border of empires, with the incursions of eastern peoples, the contests with the Turks, and the revolutions of its own dynasties treated as a lesson in the mutability of states. Percy's editorial interest shows itself in the choice and arrangement of the pieces and in the notes, which pursue the origin, manners and antiquities of the nations described. The implicit argument is that national character, like national poetry, is a proper object of study and of sympathetic curiosity.
works.significance: It is the lesser-known but revealing foundation of Percy's career, showing that the editor of the 'Reliques' began as a translator of national history, and that his project throughout was the recovery of the particular character of nations. It is a useful document of the eighteenth-century habit of making other countries' histories available through compiled translation.
works.context: It was published a year before the 'Reliques', when Percy was establishing himself as a compiler-antiquary supported by noble patronage, and when the history and present condition of the eastern European frontier was of live interest to a British reading public following Habsburg and Ottoman affairs. It belongs to the same antiquarian temper as his ballad collection, an interest in the origins and character of nations.
works.characters: The Hungarian nation as collective subject; the kings and commanders of the translated histories; the Ottoman and neighbouring powers
works.structure: A compiled and translated historical miscellany: independent rendered pieces and extracts arranged to give a continuous account of the nation and its wars, with editorial notes and prefatory matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Percy as translator and compiler is uncontested; the underlying historians are of course several and are named in the volume. The dates of the original pieces and of Percy's work upon them are not fixed here, so the composition fields are left null.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Warfare and battle

works.title: Hurrish
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The finest novel of the Irish land war: a Burren farmer, his mother, and the murder of a landlord. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by Emily Lawless; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Hurrish O'Brien, a Burren farmer, is caught between the Land League and the police when a landlord is murdered; his mother drives him to inform, and the novel ends in the violence that neither side can control, set against the limestone landscape of County Clare.
works.significance: Hurrish is the finest novel of the Irish land war and the founding text of the realistic Irish regional novel: its Burren landscape, its peasant characters and its refusal of romance made it the book that showed what the Irish novel could do, and it was admired by Gladstone and by Yeats.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the western landscape as the determining force.
works.context: County Clare in the 1880s, the Land War and the agrarian violence of the west of Ireland. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Hurrish O'Brien; his mother; the landlord; the police; the priest
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the land dispute to the murder. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hon. Emily Lawless. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Hwomely Rhymes
works.description: Barnes's second Dorset collection: the home, the child and the cottage. It is a verse work of 1859 by William Barnes; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers the domestic Dorset poems — 'The Wife a-Lost', 'The Child's Pity', 'The Broken Heart', 'The Turnstile' — in which the cottage, the family and the bereaved husband are rendered in the dialect with an extraordinary plainness.
works.significance: Hwomely Rhymes contains 'The Wife a-Lost', one of the greatest English elegies of the century, and it is the fullest expression of Barnes's art: the domestic Dorset poem in which ordinary grief is rendered in the plainest possible language.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The spelling and syntax carry a spoken dialect. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Dorset dialect in its full grammar.
works.context: Dorset in the 1850s, and the rural household of the mid-Victorian period. The record dates the work as composed between 1856 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.characters: the bereaved husband; the child; the wife; the village neighbours
works.structure: A collection of domestic eclogues in the Dorset dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Barnes (poet). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.description: Shirley's comedy of fashionable London society, set on the day of the horse races in Hyde Park, in which the wooing contests of the gentry, the tricks of a returned 'dead' husband, and the rivalry of suitors are resolved in a multiple marriage.

works.title: Hydriotaphia; or, Urn-Burial
works.description: Browne's treatise on the burial of the dead, occasioned by the discovery of Roman urns in Norfolk, which moves from antiquarian description to the great meditation on mortality and oblivion that is its famous second half.
works.plot: Chapters I-III survey the burial customs of the ancient world; chapter IV reflects on the vanity of funerary monuments; chapter V, the peroration, meditates on the certainty of oblivion and the Christian hope of resurrection.
works.significance: The supreme English meditation on death and oblivion; it has influenced writers from Johnson and De Quincey to W. G. Sebald, and its phrases ('that vulgar arithmetic of antiquity', 'to be ignorant of evil') are part of the language.
works.meter: The most magnificent prose of the seventeenth century; the closing paragraphs of chapter V are among the most quoted passages in English.
works.context: Published in 1658, in the same year as The Garden of Cyrus and the death of Cromwell; it was written during the Commonwealth when Browne was living quietly at Norwich.
works.structure: Five chapters of increasing rhetorical intensity, ending in the celebrated chapter V.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Hymn to Adversity
altTitles: Hymn to Adversity: Written on the Approach of Winter
works.description: Gray's short hymn addressed to Adversity as the grim daughter of Power and Wisdom, which thanks the harsh teacher for the discipline of sorrow and for the humanising effect of misfortune.
works.plot: The hymn invokes Adversity, attends her from the throne of the supreme, and shows how her stern schooling teaches compassion, self-knowledge and the value of the fleeting good, closing with the prayer that her discipline may not be in vain.
works.significance: It is the most perfect English short hymn of the school of feeling, converting the stoic and Christian argument of affliction into a regular lyric.
works.meter: Regular short stanzas of the hymn measure in the manner of the Horatian ode, with the clear close and the balanced personification.
works.context: Written in the same year as the Eton ode, in the circle of the poet's college retirement and of the Horatian revival, and long read as a companion to the century's discipline of sorrow.
works.characters: Adversity addressed as a power; the parent powers of Wisdom and of the chastening will
works.structure: A regular stanced hymn of invocation, argument and prayer, following the order of the Horatian and the church hymn.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Hymns and Sacred Poems
altTitles: A Collection of Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739)
works.description: The first hymn book of the Wesleyan revival, published at Bristol in 1739 by the two brothers and containing Charles Wesley's earliest great hymns. Its preface marked the break with the Church of England and gave Methodism its programme of 'Scripture, Reason, and Experience' in worship.
works.plot: The volume gathers hymns for the seasons, sacraments, and occasions of Christian experience: the nativity and passion, the resurrection and ascension, justification, assurance, prayer, and the close of the year. Its poems move from the 'little flock' of the societies through calls to repentance to the triumphant hark of the wedding hymn and the self-dedicating 'Leave all thy self behind'. The preface defends extempore singing in the field assemblies, answers the charges of enthusiasm, and sets out the Wesleyan reading of salvation by faith. The collection establishes the pattern of the Methodist hymn book: experience sung in the first person plural.
works.significance: It founded Methodist hymnody and introduced Charles Wesley's lyric voice, the most prolific and enduring hymn writer in English, into worship that spread through the Atlantic world.
works.meter: Chiefly common and long metre hymn stanzas of four and six lines in iambic measures, with the brothers' varied tunes indicated; the diction is deliberately plain and homiletic.
works.context: Published at Bristol in 1739 in the first open-air season of the revival, after the Aldersgate year and the brothers' American voyage, as the field preaching needed its own songbook against the established psalmody.
works.characters: the singing society; the Wesley family
works.structure: An ordered hymn collection with prefatory defence, the hymns arranged by Christian seasons and doctrinal heads rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Joint collection of John and Charles Wesley; individual hymns are generally assignable, with Charles as author of the great majority.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Evangelical experience and assurance
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Hymns and Spiritual Songs
altTitles: Hymns and Spiritual Songs, in Three Books
works.description: Isaac Watts's first hymn collection, three books of Scriptural, moral, and devotional songs, the foundation of English hymnody as a literate genre. Its preface argued the duty and privilege of singing 'new songs under the gospel dispensation' and freed nonconformist worship from the exclusive metrical psalter.
works.plot: Book I sings selected Scriptures into verse, psalm and canticle paraphrase with didactic edges; Book II offers moral and divine subjects, the temper of the soul, death, judgment, and grace; Book III gathers divine songs of a more spiritual and affectionate cast, the longest and most quoted. Watts moves the hymn from catechism to meditation, making the first person plural of the church the voice of the awakened individual. Its best texts, from the drowsy falling sleep of the slumbering Jesus to the cross, the throne, and the coming of the Lord, became staples of every later collection. The whole carries the Puritan sermon into tuneful, rationally ordered praise.
works.significance: Watts is 'the father of English hymnody' and this book the charter document, the collection from which the English-speaking churches have most drawn their songs of worship through three centuries.
works.meter: Chiefly common, short, and long metre iambic stanzas of Augustan psalmody, plain diction, strong syntax, and the memorable simple phrase.
works.context: Published in London in 1707 with the author's early independent-ministry years at Bury and London behind it, in the reforming decade when dissent began to sing hymns of modern composition beside Sternhold and Hopkins.
works.structure: Three books arranged by source and subject, the later books progressively more experimental, with preface defending gospel hymnody.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Evangelical experience and assurance
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Hymns for the Feasts of the Church
works.form: Hymn-cycle for the liturgical year, in the tradition of the paraphrase and of the church-meter hymn, with the poet's characteristic Hebraic and typological diction; the pieces are short, strophic and singable.
works.description: Smart's devotional hymns for the seasons and principal feasts of the Christian year, belonging to the liturgical side of his work and to the same religious imagination as the 'Song to David' and 'Jubilate Agno'. They were written for the uses of the church calendar rather than for the poetical market, and they survive outside any lifetime collection of his verse.
works.plot: The hymns take the anniversaries and offices of the church year as their occasions, and each is built upon the scriptural and typological material proper to its feast. Their argument is not doctrinal but doxological: the year is presented as a sequence of mercies and manifestations, and the worshipper is taught to rejoice in each in its order. As in the longer poems, the concrete and the created world is pressed into service as the imagery of praise, and the personal voice of the poet is subdued to the demands of a congregation's utterance.
works.significance: They complete the picture of Smart as a poet of the prayer book and the psalms rather than of the magazine, and they are the least Augustan of his verse in their intention to be sung by a congregation. Their survival outside print in his lifetime is part of the history of his neglect.
works.meter: Hymn measures of the common and long metre types, with the plain, accented and heavily parallelist phrasing Smart used for devotional verse; the stanzas are regular, in contrast with the experimental measures of his odes.
works.context: They belong to the religious culture of Smart's later years, in which hymn-writing for the church year was a work of party and of devotion, between the Latitudinarian and the evangelical and High-Church traditions. The same decade saw the great flowering of English hymnody by Watts, Doddridge and the Wesleys, against which Smart's church-year hymns assert an older and more liturgical model.
works.characters: The worshipping church addressed and instructing itself; the persons and events of scripture invoked at each feast
works.structure: A cycle of independent liturgical hymns arranged by the feasts and seasons of the church year, with no continuous narrative and with the calendar supplying the order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Smart is not contested; what cannot be settled here is their chronology and their first publication, since the cycle was not issued as a book in his lifetime and the separate hymns have complicated reprinting histories. The year fields are therefore left null rather than estimated.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Evangelical experience and assurance
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
movements: The Anglican and Latitudinarian Divines
The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Hymns for the Nativity
works.description: Charles Wesley's season collection for Advent and Christmas, published at Bristol in 1745 and the turning-point in which his nativity hymns took their permanent forms, including the text of Hark! the Herald Angels Sing after the 1739 Harks! how the joyful voices sound. It is the most nearly complete single-occasion volume of eighteenth-century English hymnody.
works.plot: The hymns run the Christian year's opening: the anticipation of the messiah, the forerunner, the annunciation, the birth in David's town, the shepherds, the wise men, the circumcision, and the presentation, closing with the childhood at Nazareth. Charles turns each scene into doctrine sung as experience, the little child and the mighty God joined in paradoxes of incarnation, and the season's joy poured out in invitation and praise. The volume's revision of the earlier wedding-hymn text set the pattern of Charles's practice of rewriting his own hymns toward their best forms. Its short songs for families and social worship make the Christmas narrative a domestic liturgy.
works.significance: It gave the English-speaking churches their Christmas hymnody, the source of the most sung nativity text in the language, and remains the central exhibit of Charles Wesley's lyrical theology.
works.meter: Varied hymn measures, chiefly common metre and the eight-line 8s with refrain patterns, in tight iambic lines with Charles's characteristic internal rhyme and exclamatory openings.
works.context: Published at Bristol in 1745, in the season of Charles Wesley's marriage and mature Bristol hymnwriting and the brothers' separate but parallel collections, when the revival's songbook was becoming a literature.
works.structure: A cycle of hymns following the gospel events of the nativity in seasonal order, with invitation, praise, and close-of-season pieces attached.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Evangelical experience and assurance
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing
