works.title: Hymns in Prose for Children
works.form: prose hymn and devotional writing for children, in the dissenting hymn tradition renewed in prose
works.description: Barbauld's devotional prose for the young, published in 1781 and designed to teach a child to address the Deity through the visible world. Each hymn takes some part of creation - the morning, the seasons, the insect and the elements, the breath of life - and turns its observation into praise, so that natural knowledge becomes the school of piety. The book is the most original religious writing of its author's middle period and one of the enduring children's texts of the century.
works.plot: The hymns proceed by address and by observation of nature, leading the child from the creature and the scene to the attributes of the Creator, and from the gifts of the earth to the duties of gratitude, gentleness and truth. They insist that the Divine presence is to be found in every part of the world, and that praise is the proper employment of a mind that has learned to look. Their moral teaching is of benevolence extended to animals and to other men, and their religious temper is a reasoned and affectionate deism rather than a doctrine of terror.
works.significance: It created the model of nature as a book of praise for the child reader and influenced both religious instruction and the nature-writing tradition of the nineteenth century. Its combination of sensibility, natural history and devotion makes it a central document of the culture of feeling applied to education.
works.meter: Rhythmed prose of short clauses and balanced address, pitched for recitation, with the cadences of prayer and of the hymn preserved without verse.
works.context: Published in 1781 alongside the elementary books that had made Barbauld's name in education, in a period when the hymn and the prose devotional were being addressed to children as never before, and within a Unitarian and dissenting culture that preferred rational piety to the language of dread.
works.characters: The child addressed; the speaking instructor; the creatures and elements of the meditations
works.structure: A series of short prose hymns, each a single meditation on an aspect of creation followed by ascription and petition, arranged for reading aloud with a child.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was published under the author's name as the writer of her elementary books, and the date of composition is not separately fixed, so the composition start is left null.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Creation and cosmology
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Hypatia; or, New Foes with an Old Face
works.description: Published in 1853 and Kingsley's greatest historical novel: Alexandria in the fifth century, the pagan philosopher Hypatia, and the conflict of Christianity, Judaism and the dying classical world. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by Charles Kingsley; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Philammon, a young Egyptian monk, comes to Alexandria and is caught between the pagan school of Hypatia, the Jewish community of the city and the Christian patriarch Cyril; Hypatia is murdered by the mob, the city is torn apart, and the novel argues for a Christian humanism that can inherit the best of the classical world.
works.significance: Hypatia is the finest English historical novel of late antiquity and a central text in the Victorian debate on the relation of Hellenism and Christianity; its picture of Hypatia shaped the modern legend of the philosopher-martyr.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence.
works.context: The 410s-420s, Alexandria under the Roman Empire, the murder of Hypatia in 415, and the Victorian controversy over the relation of Christianity to classical culture. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Philammon; Hypatia; Cyril, the patriarch; Orestes, the prefect; Raphael Aben-Ezra; Miriam; Pelagia; Arsenius; Peter the Reader; Wulf and the Goths
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Hyperion: A Fragment
works.form: Heroic epic of the Miltonic school, projected as a theogony and left a fragment; the Titanomachy matter of the classical epic in English blank verse.
works.description: The author's attempt at a Miltonic epic on the fall of the elder gods, abandoned in the autumn of 1819 and published as a fragment of two books in the volume of that year's poems. The deposed Saturn mourns in the caverns of the old sea, the Titaness urges him to rise, and the ocean-god argues that the elder powers have yielded by a law of gradation to a younger and fairer rule. The second book brings the messenger of the new reign and the assembly of the Titans, and the poem breaks off before the battle and the fall.
works.plot: Saturn, dethroned and hidden in the deep caverns by the mouth of the ocean, laments his lost empire, and the earth-goddess who has kept his company reproaches him for his unmanly grief. The elders debate their condition, and Oceanus answers that no throne is kept for ever, that the elder gods have fallen by gradation from the Titans to the Olympian rule, and that the new order is more beautiful; the voice is answered by the Titan of the east, who refuses the argument. The second book opens on the mourning of the fallen race and brings the rainbow-messenger from the seat of the new god, whose look of settled splendence overthrows the counsel of resistance; the gods deliberate whether to rise, and the fragment ends.
works.significance: It is the period's most impressive attempt at a non-religious epic and the standard case in the argument about whether the epic could be written after Milton, a question the fragment's own incompleteness answers. Its account of the gradation by which orders of the mind succeed one another became a permanent text for the philosophy of cultural progress, and its diction marks the point where the poet's rich sensuous style begins to be disciplined.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, loaded with compound epithets, Latinate inversion and a sustained end-stopped dignity designed to imitate the older epic's stateliness; it is the author's only considerable effort in pure epic measure.
works.context: Begun in the summer of 1818, in the months of the poet's northern tour and of his brother's fatal illness, and worked at through the winter, the poem's argument of the inevitable succession of powers was written in the season of the Italian and Spanish revolutions and their suppression; abandoned late in 1819, its books were published in 1820 in the volume of the later poems with an explicit mark of incompleteness. The poet's own letters on the causes of its abandonment, which turn on the failure of its diction and the impossibility of its Miltonic mask, are among the most searched documents of Romantic composition.
works.characters: Saturn, the deposed elder god; the earth-goddess his mate and reprover; Oceanus, the arguer of gradation; the eastern Titan of the last line; the rainbow-messenger of the new reign
works.structure: Two books of continuous epic narrative in blank verse, the first a council and argument in the caverns, the second the arrival of the messenger and the debate; a sketch for a third book and a projected theogony survive in the drafts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the two published books and the surviving drafts, with the alternative dream-version of the same argument, are all in the poet's hand and are printed together in the standard edition.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: I Hear Thunder
works.description: A novel of the Trinidadian middle class, published by MacGibbon & Kee in London in 1963 (1962 in Britannica), built on one young man's vow of chastity, in which Carnival stands for a society without racial barriers.
works.summary: Adrian's year-long vow of celibacy, his temptation by his best friend's white wife, and Carnival.
works.plot: Adrian, a middle-class Indo-Trinidadian 'fete-boy' disgusted by the sexual looseness around him, vows to remain chaste for a year, and is tempted by the white wife of his best friend, Mark (Caribbean Beat; Northern Arizona University essay). Carnival, in the essay's reading, is Selvon's image of a society without racial barriers, 'Black, white, brown and yellow, rich and poor ... all were out on the streets jumping up in the bands', but one that cannot last: an exhausted Mark is determined to carry on to the 'Last Lap'.
works.significance: One of the least discussed of Selvon's novels; Britannica lists it among his later works.
works.meter: Caribbean Beat calls it a story of middle-class foibles; the Northern Arizona University essay finds it more cynical than compassionate.
works.context: Published in 1963, the year after Trinidad and Tobago's independence; with Those Who Eat the Cascadura it brings Selvon's concern with race back to Trinidad, in the essay's account.
works.characters: Adrian; Mark, his best friend; Mark's white wife
works.structure: Built around the year of Adrian's vow, with an episode of Carnival.

Nationhood and national identity
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
works.form: Nature lyric and lyrical ballad of the collected manner; a short meditative lyric that makes the process of remembering its explicit subject.
works.description: A lyric of four stanzas comparing the poet to a lone cloud floating over a valley, who comes upon a host of golden daffodils beside the lake and beneath the trees. Written two years after the walk that suggested it, and revised after its first publication, it is the period's most familiar poem and a working model of its own poetic theory: an accidental sight, remembered at leisure, becomes a source of repeated pleasure. Its first printed form bore the title The Daffodils.
works.plot: The speaker, wandering solitary as a cloud, sees suddenly a long belt of daffodils stretching along the bay, tossing their heads in a sprightly dance, countlessly many as the stars that line the Milky Way. He at first gives the sight no value, gazing without thinking of the wealth the show had brought him; the second part of the poem transfers the scene to the mind, where, on a couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the flowers flash upon the inward eye which is the bliss of solitude, and the heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils. The argument is thus a demonstration that the richest gifts of nature are received afterwards, in recollection, and that the imagination stores sensible forms as a permanent possession.
works.significance: The most anthologised and most parodied lyric of the English Romantic period, and the shortest complete illustration of the theory of emotion recollected in tranquillity. Its image of the inward eye became a common property of Victorian and later discussion of imaginative memory.
works.meter: Four stanzas of six iambic lines, the first four of four beats and the last two of a shorter beat, with a strongly marked rhyme pattern; the regularity and the repeated gestures of the stanza give the poem the quality of an air.
works.context: Suggested by an afternoon walk by Ullswater in April 1802, recorded in the same words by the poet's companion in her journal of the tour, and composed in 1804 for the collection of short lyrics published in 1807. The revised text, with its second stanza added and its phrasing heightened, belongs to the edition of 1815.
works.characters: The solitary speaker, figured as a cloud; the host of daffodils; the lake, the trees and the breezy bay
works.structure: Two-part movement within a single lyric: the outward scene of 1802 told as an event in the past tense, then the inward scene of later hours, with the turn signalled by the contrast between the thoughtless gaze and the pleasure recollected.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the suggested wording and the incident were shared with the companion named in the journal, but the poem is uniformly assigned to the writer.
themes: Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Idea
works.description: Michael Drayton's sonnet sequence, first published as Ideas Mirrour (1594) and revised across five editions into its final 63-sonnet form as Idea (1619): a sequence of farewells — to the lady, to the sonnet form itself, and to love — crowned by the great sonnet 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part'.
works.plot: The lover's suit to the lady moves through adoration and complaint to the sequence's famous gesture of renunciation — a farewell to love that is also a virtuoso leave-taking of the sonnet convention.
works.significance: Home of the most famous valedictory sonnet in the language and a case study in the Elizabethan sequence as revisable form.
works.meter: The English sonnet, in Drayton's plain-spoken, muscular style.
works.context: Drayton revised the sequence continuously from 1594 to 1619, mirroring the rise and self-conscious decline of the sonnet vogue he had helped create.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Idea (the beloved)
works.structure: A sequence revised over twenty-five years, ending in the 1619 form with its valedictory design.

works.title: Ideala
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1888
works.description: Published in 1888 and the first of Grand's novels of the woman question: the spiritual history of a wife who cannot accept the double standard. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Sarah Grand; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Ideala, a beautiful and spiritual woman unhappily married to a dull and selfish husband, travels through Europe in search of faith and freedom, refuses the love of a good man rather than break the marriage law, and finds at last a vocation of social work among the poor.
works.significance: Ideala was the first of the New Woman novels and a founding text of the genre: its heroine's refusal of the double standard and her search for a life of her own made it a book that Victorian women read as a manifesto.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays.
works.context: 1887-88: the Victorian debate on marriage and divorce, the higher education of women, and the spiritual crisis of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Ideala; Lord Dawne, the narrator; Lorrimer, the doctor who loves her; her husband
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Idylls of the King
works.form: Arthurian epic in twelve idylls, in blank verse
works.description: Tennyson's Arthurian epic, published in instalments over twenty-six years — 'Enid' and 'Elaine' (as 'Enid and Nimue') in 1859, 'The Holy Grail' in 1869, 'Gareth and Lynette' and 'The Last Tournament' in 1872, 'Balin and Balan' in 1885 — and dedicated to the memory of Prince Albert.
works.plot: The twelve idylls trace the rise and fall of Arthur's order: the coming of Arthur and the founding of the Round Table; the individual knights' vows and failures (Gareth, Balin, Geraint and Enid, Lancelot, Percivale); the quest of the Holy Grail, which breaks the fellowship; the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere; the rebellion of Mordred and the last battle; and Arthur's passing to Avilion.
works.significance: The Idylls are the Victorian age's central myth of empire and of its corruption from within. They made Malory's Arthur a national possession and provided the moral vocabulary of Victorian chivalry, while the poem's increasingly pessimistic later books gave the twentieth century its image of the Victorian imperial self-doubt.
works.meter: Blank verse in the idyll form; each idyll a self-contained narrative episode with its own moral.
works.context: The Victorian revival of Arthurian matter (the 1839 Eglinton Tournament, the Pre-Raphaelite Arthurian paintings, Malory reprinted in 1817), the empire and its moral mission, and the death of Prince Albert in 1861, which gave the poem a national resonance.
works.characters: Arthur; Guinevere; Lancelot; Elaine; Enid; Geraint; Vivien; Merlin; Mordred; Percivale; Galahad; Balin; Balan; Gareth; Lynette; Bedivere
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Illusion and Reality
works.description: The Marxist study of the sources of poetry. It is a prose work of 1937 by Christopher Caudwell; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Illusion and Reality reads the poetry from the economics of the society - the ritual, the labour, the class and the illusion of the bourgeois culture - and makes the history of the English poetry a chapter of the history of the productive relations, in the brilliant compressed prose of the young Marxist aesthete.
works.significance: Illusion and Reality is the founding text of the Marxist aesthetics in English: its sources of poetry, written by a twenty-nine-year-old who was killed at the Jarama months after its publication, shaped the criticism of the left for two generations.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the essay of the argument in the plain Marxist prose.
works.context: England in 1937, in the year of the author's death in Spain. The record dates the work as composed between 1935 and 1936 and first published in 1937 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: the poet and the tribe; the bourgeois culture; the sources of the illusion
works.structure: A critical study of the poetry and the economics of the society. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.

works.title: Illustrations of Political Economy
works.form: Series of twenty-five tales in monthly parts
works.description: Published monthly from February 1832 to 1834 and Martineau's first great success: twenty-five fictional case studies designed to teach the principles of political economy to ordinary readers through stories of wages, prices, population and the poor law.
works.plot: Each tale takes a single economic principle and shows its working in the life of a family or a village: 'The Hill and the Valley' on capital and labour, 'A Manchester Strike' on combinations, 'Weal and Woe in Garveloch' on population, 'Cousin Marshall' on the poor laws.
works.significance: The Illustrations made political economy a popular literature: they sold tens of thousands of copies, were translated across Europe, and invented the fictional case study as a form of public education — the direct ancestor of the social-problem novel and of the documentary tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.

works.title: Images of War

works.title: Imaginary Conversations
altTitles: Imaginary Conversations of Literary Men and Statesmen
works.form: Literary dialogue and dramatic prose conversation: a Neoclassical revival of the humanist dialogue, distinguished by the absence of stage direction and by epigrammatic compression.
works.description: The author's masterpiece of prose and the first series of conversations in which two historical personages talk together about art, power, religion, and death. The dialogue form is stripped of narration: almost nothing but speech, with the characters' tempers doing the work of plot. The series ranges from Greek and Roman pairs to Italian, Spanish, and modern authors, and it established its author's reputation as the finest English prose stylist of his generation.
works.plot: Each conversation places two figures in a single situation and lets their disagreement disclose character: Plato with Aristarchus on the worth of poetry, Dante with Beatrice on the price of knowledge, Pope with the Earl of Oxford, or Thrasylachus with Amycus on tyranny. There is no developing action across the volume, but within each piece pressure rises as one speaker is driven to say what he has never said before. The political conversations test whether a good man can serve a bad cause, and the literary ones argue for style as a moral rather than a decorative achievement. Recurring presences are the dignity of the private mind against public power, and the consolation of letters at the end of life.
works.significance: The most important English prose style since the seventeenth-century worthies, and the origin of the modern imaginary dialogue; it shaped how later writers from Stevenson to Eliot thought about the ethics of style and the use of historical speech as argument.
works.meter: Prose, in a deliberately punctilious and Latinate idiom of balanced periods and short retorts.
works.context: Issued while its author was settled in Italy and after the Bath and Pisa years, when his quarrels with publishers and with his family had made him a professional man of letters; the series appeared while the review journals were the chief organ of literary authority, and it was received first coolly and then reverently.
works.characters: Plato; Aristarchus; Dante; Beatrice; Alexander; Thrasylachus; Pope; the Earl of Oxford; Joanna of Naples
works.structure: A series of self-contained prose dialogues without framing narrative, each with its own speakers, setting, and turn; the volume's unity is tonal and moral rather than sequential.

works.title: Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition; or, An Inquiry into the Shortest, Safest and Most Effectual Means of Getting Rid of West Indian Slavery
works.form: Abolitionist polemic pamphlet in the form of an inquiry or analysis: reasoned, scriptural, addressed to a British public, and built on the countersuggestion that the opposing party's own premises prove the immediate case.
works.description: A short London pamphlet that broke with the gradualist strategy of the older British abolition movement by arguing that immediate emancipation was at once morally obligatory and practically the shortest, safest and cheapest policy. It circulated first as a printed circular and then as a pamphlet, and it supplied the slogan and the logic for the new organisation founded in 1831. Its tone is that of the Quaker plain-style remonstrance, addressed to the conscience of the slave-holder and to the West India interest.
works.plot: The argument runs on three levels. On principle, the writer holds that the slave-holder has no right to the labour of other human beings, so that postponing emancipation is continuing a crime; justice cannot be gradual. On interest, she claims that free labour would be more productive than coerced labour and that the planter's ruin is the product of his own system, not of emancipation. On safety, she answers the standard fear that liberation brings massacre by contending that patience and religion have preserved the enslaved so far, and that injustice itself, not emancipation, is the provocation. The pamphlet closes by urging the abolitionists to drop compensation to slave-holders and to appeal directly to public opinion, and it recommends a plain remedy for the transitional difficulty: apprenticeship of the emancipated under contract, with wages.
works.significance: It is the pivot text of British immediatism, the pamphlet that shifted the movement's demand from gradual apprenticeship to unconditional emancipation, and it directly shaped the programme of the society founded in 1831 and the debate over compensation before the abolition legislation of 1833. It is also an early example of a woman's political pamphlet setting the terms of a national agitation.
works.meter: Plain prose, lucid and unhedged; emphasis by antithesis and by direct question rather than ornament.
works.context: Written in the long debate that followed the British abolition of the trade in 1807, when the West India planters were urging amelioration and Parliament was moving cautiously toward measures to improve the condition of the enslaved. Its appearance coincides with the emergence of women as organisers of anti-slavery agitation, including the female anti-slavery societies and the sugar-boycott campaigns of the later 1820s.
works.structure: Continuous argument in a single movement: statement of the question, argument from principle, argument from interest, argument from safety, practical plan, closing appeal.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to its author is certain; it was signed by her in later editions and was well known to contemporaries as her work.

works.title: Impressions of Theophrastus Such
works.form: Essays in the person of a fictional essayist
works.description: Published in 1879, the last book Eliot published in her lifetime: eighteen essays and character sketches written in the person of Theophrastus Such, a bachelor of independent means, on vanity, on the Jewish intellect, on the 'modern Hep! works.plot: There is no continuous narrative: the essays are the observations of a fictional essayist on his contemporaries, and the volume's interest is in the construction of the persona — a dry, self-aware, slightly ridiculous man — and in the essay on the Jews that anticipates the themes of Daniel Deronda.

works.title: Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community
works.form: educational report and treatise; the school statement with the plan for the education of the labouring classes
works.description: The published account of the school at Southwark by its Quaker founder, the book which brought the monitorial method before the public of the metropolis and made the mutual system a party, a subscription, and in time a national institution; a report of an experiment like the Madras statement, but written for the town and its subscribers rather than for the Company's settlement.
works.plot: The work describes the school of the author's opening in Southwark, in which a great number of children of the labouring classes were taught by one another under his single superintendence at an expense of a few shillings for each child in the year, and it sets out the machinery by which this was done: the classes, the monitors, the patrol of the yard, the slate, the sand, the wall for the first lessons, the marks of merit and of demerit, the register of the progress, the rewards of the badge and the public inspection, the arrangement of the hour of study, and the moral and religious teaching delivered to all without the doctrine of any party. It argues that the poor may thus be taught numerously, cheerfully, and at a price which makes the education of the industrious classes a subject for the subscription of the public, and it urges the political uses of the method, the obedience, the cleanliness, the habit, and the knowledge which it gives being the securities of the order of the country. The several parts are supported by the account of the expenses, the examination of the visitors, and the evidence of the masters of other schools.
works.significance: With the Madras statement of 1797 it is the foundation text of the monitorial system, and through the British and Foreign School Society, the free schools, and the model normal schools of the nineteenth century its machinery became the working form of popular education in Britain, America, and the colonies; its claim to teach the children of the poor cheaply, in numbers, and without sectarian doctrine is one of the governing ideas of English social reform, and the book itself is a primary document of the history of the elementary school.
works.meter: Plain, businesslike, persuasive prose of the schoolmaster addressing his subscribers, with the minute enumeration of the arrangements, the repetition of the figures of cost and numbers, and the frank appeal to the feelings of the reader for the children of the poor; less technical and more hortatory than the Indian statement of the same method.
works.context: Published in 1803, after five years of the school at Southwark which he had opened for the children of the labouring poor under the inspection of a friendly society of subscribers, in the season of the anxiety about the discipline of the manufacturing population, of the Sunday-school movement, and of the project of a national education; the book won the subscriptions and the visits of the great, including at length the countenance of the court, and it set forward the rival claim of priority to the Indian system which the same method had already obtained, the two parties dividing the public and the religious aid of the following generation.
works.structure: A report in the manner of the second edition of the educational statement: the account of the school, the description of the method in its order of proceeding, the evidence of the proficiency made, the estimate of the expense, the replies to the objections, and the appeal to the public, with the papers of the inspecting society and the certificates appended.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; the title is variously abridged in the many editions, and the enlarged later issues, given out in parts and with the memoir of the author prefixed, contain matter not in the first; the long priority controversy with the promulgator of the Indian system obliges the careful citation of the edition.

works.title: In a Music-Hall and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1891 and the most original book of English poetry of its year: the poems of the music hall, the street and the working city that founded the urban poetry of the twentieth century. It is a verse work of 1891 by John Davidson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume opens with the sequence 'In a Music-Hall', monologues spoken by the performers of a Glasgow music-hall, and gathers lyrics and early ballads in which the city is seen as a spectacle and a prison; the famous 'Thirty Bob a Week' and 'A Ballad of a Nun' came later, in Ballads and Songs (1894).
works.significance: In a Music-Hall is the founding book of English urban poetry and 'Thirty Bob a Week' is the first great English poem of the white-collar worker: Davidson's music-hall poems changed the subject matter of English verse and influenced Eliot's early poetry directly.
works.meter: Verse. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the dramatic monologue.

The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

works.title: In Flanders Fields and Other Poems
works.description: The poem of the poppy and the dead: the most widely read war poem in English. It is a verse work of 1919 by John McCrae; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers McCrae's poems, with 'In Flanders Fields' at its centre: the dead speak from the poppy fields of Flanders, asking the living to take up their quarrel, in a rondeau that became the symbol of remembrance.
works.significance: In Flanders Fields and Other Poems contains the most widely read poem of the First World War: it made the poppy the symbol of remembrance across the English-speaking world and remains the single most influential piece of writing to come out of the war.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the rondeau with its refrain.
works.context: Flanders in 1915, and the Canadian army at Ypres. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1918 and first published in 1919 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the dead of Flanders; the lark; the poppies; the living
works.structure: A posthumous collection with a memoir. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: In Hospital
works.description: Published in Poems (1898/1900) and the first English poetic sequence about surgery and hospital life: the poems written after Henley's amputation at the Edinburgh Infirmary. It is a verse work of 1900 by W. E. Henley; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The sequence follows the poet through the ward: the clinical examinations, the operations, the ether, the sleepless nights, the dying patient in the next bed, the nurses, the visitors and the slow return of the sense of the body, in poems of exact physical detail and hard, unsentimental rhythm.
works.significance: In Hospital is a landmark of English poetry about illness and the body: it was the first sustained English poem to treat surgery and hospital life with clinical realism, and its influence on the war poetry of the twentieth century and on modern poetry of illness is direct and acknowledged.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is short, hard, rhymed verse in the ballad and the song measure.
works.context: 1873-75: the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary and Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery, the Victorian hospital ward, and the poetic realism of the 1870s. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1875 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.

works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. works.title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
works.form: Elegiac sequence in 131 sections and a prologue and epilogue; 'A. H. H.' = Arthur Henry Hallam
works.description: The great elegy of the nineteenth century, begun on the death of Arthur Henry Hallam in Vienna on 15 September 1833 and printed privately in 1849 and published in May 1850: 131 lyric sections in a single stanza, moving from raw grief through the geological and religious crisis of the mid-1840s to a hard-won faith in the 'one far-off divine event'.
works.plot: The sequence is not narrative but seasonal and argumentative: it opens with the yew tree and the funeral, moves through the first Christmas, the springs and winters of the following years, the night reading of the dead friend's letters, the vision of nature as 'red in tooth and claw', the vision of Hallam as a type of the perfected man, and ends with the marriage of Tennyson's sister Cecilia and Edmund Lushington and a benediction on the child to come.
works.significance: In Memoriam is the central poem of Victorian doubt and the one work in which the age's scientific and religious crisis is dramatised at full length. It gave the language 'nature, red in tooth and claw' and 'the ringing grooves of change', and its stanza (the 'In Memoriam stanza', abba) became the standard elegiac form of the century. Queen Victoria told Tennyson it was her consolation after the death of Prince Albert.
works.meter: The In Memoriam stanza: iambic tetrameter rhymed abba, a closed, echoing quatrain that became the standard English elegiac measure.
works.context: The 1830s-40s: the Oxford Movement, the geology of Lyell and the 'Vestiges' controversy, the crisis of faith, and the private world of the Tennyson family at Somersby and High Beach; the poem's theology is Broad Church and its science is the new geology.
works.characters: the elegist; Arthur Henry Hallam (A. H. H.); Cecilia Tennyson and Edmund Lushington, the bride and groom of the epilogue
works.structure: 131 numbered sections of three or four stanzas, grouped by the anniversaries of Hallam's death and by the seasons; a prologue and an epilogue (the marriage of Cecilia Tennyson).

works.title: In Our Time
works.description: The book that made the modern American short story: 'Indian Camp', 'Big Two-Hearted River' and the ice-fishing interludes. It is a prose fiction work of 1925 by Ernest Hemingway; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection alternates between short stories — 'Indian Camp', 'The Doctor and the Doctor's Wife', 'The End of Something', 'The Three-Day Blow', 'Soldier's Home', 'Cat in the Rain' and 'Big Two-Hearted River' — and brief prose vignettes of war, bullfighting and crime.
works.significance: In Our Time created the modern American short story: its iceberg theory — the meaning withheld from the surface — its prose and its structure of stories and interludes made it the founding collection of the American short story in the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short declarative sentence.

works.title: In Parenthesis
works.form: Poem (prose and verse epic); war memoir
works.description: The greatest English poem of the First World War: the infantry, the trench and the myth behind it. It is a verse work of 1937 by David Jones; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem follows Private John Ball and his company from their training in England to the attack on Mametz Wood on the Somme in July 1916, mixing prose and verse, the soldiers' speech, Welsh and Latin allusion and the liturgy in a single continuous texture.
works.significance: In Parenthesis is the greatest English poem of the First World War: its combination of prose and verse, its Welsh and Catholic mythology and its exact record of the infantry experience made it a unique achievement, and it stands with The Waste Land as the central English modernist long poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the mixed form of prose and verse.
works.context: The Western Front in 1915–16, and the Welsh and Catholic traditions that the soldiers carried with them. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1937 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; modernist long poem and the mythical method.

works.structure: Seven parts in mixed prose and verse, from the training to the attack. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.

works.title: In Praise of Limestone
works.form: Poem (meditative and topographical, in long and short unrhymed lines)
works.description: A poem by W. H. Auden, written on Ischia in May 1948, the first he wrote in Italy, and published in Horizon in July 1948 before its collection in Nones (1951). A meditation on the Mediterranean limestone landscape as the one human landscape, it is regarded as central to his canon and one of his finest poems.
works.summary: A description of a limestone landscape and of the people it forms, set against the granite, clay and ocean that tempt saints, tyrants and romantic solitaries, and ending in a vision of faultless love and the life to come as a limestone landscape.
works.plot: If there is one landscape that 'we, the inconstant ones' are consistently homesick for, the poem begins, it is because limestone dissolves in water: its rounded hills, caves, springs and short distances shape a people who are local, sensual, quarrelsome and unable to imagine a god of rage. The best and worst never stayed there long but sought immoderate soils: granite wastes for the saints-to-be, clays and gravels for the would-be tyrants, who left slamming the door, and the oceanic whisper for the really reckless: 'I am the solitude that asks and promises nothing'. The speaker admits that the landscape seems historically unimportant, and that the poet, admired for calling the sun the sun, is made uneasy by it. Yet it makes a further point: in a world where sins can be forgiven and bodies rise from the dead, the blessed will not care from what angle they are seen, having nothing to hide. Dear, he ends, I know nothing of either, but when I try to imagine a faultless love or the life to come, what I hear is the murmur of underground streams, what I see is a limestone landscape.
works.significance: Called sui generis and even the first postmodern pastoral, it is one of the most studied of Auden's later poems and a central text for his post-war turn to the body, the ordinary and Christian belief.
works.meter: Conversational, discursive and witty, with long sentences and a relaxed, unrhymed line; a mixture of plain speech and theological vocabulary.
works.context: Auden, who had moved to the United States in 1939 and returned to Christianity, spent the spring and summer of 1948 on Ischia with Chester Kallman; the poem opens the Italian phase of his work. He revised it from 1958 and gave it a prominent place in Collected Shorter Poems, 1922-1957 (1966).
works.structure: A single long verse paragraph moving from description through the catalogue of other soils and the poet's unease to the theological turn and the closing confession.
themes: Faith, doubt and the sacred
Land, place and regional belonging
Love, intimacy and loss

works.title: In the Days When the World Was Wide
works.description: Published in 1896 and the most popular volume of Australian verse of the period: ballads of the bush and the road, the selector and the swagman, and the famous 'The Teams'. It is a verse work of 1896 by Henry Lawson; it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The volume includes 'The Teams', 'The Fire at Ross's Farm', 'Middleton's Rouseabout', 'The Ballad of the Drover', 'Up the Country' and the title poem, all in the direct ballad metres of the Bulletin school.
works.significance: In the Days When the World Was Wide is the most important volume of Australian poetry of the century and the central text of the nationalist ballad: it made the bushman and the swagman the heroes of Australian verse.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, laconic, anecdotal prose.

works.title: In the Net of the Stars
works.form: Poetry collection (the vers libre of the French school)
works.description: The first English collection in the manner of the French vers libristes. It is a verse work of 1909 by F. S. Flint; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line.
works.plot: In the Net of the Stars gathers Flint's first poems in the unrhymed cadence of the French vers libre, with the translations and imitations of the symbolists, and announced the new manner in English two years before the imagist manifesto.
works.significance: In the Net of the Stars is the first English collection in the manner of the French vers libristes and the workshop of the imagist doctrine: its unrhymed cadence gave the English lyric the model the 1913 manifesto would state.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short unrhymed cadence of the French vers libre.
works.context: London in 1909, and the French vers libriste school. The record dates the work as composed between 1908 and 1909 and first published in 1909 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.
works.structure: A collection of vers libre lyrics and translations. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.

works.title: In the Tennessee Mountains
works.description: The founding book of the Southern mountain story: the Tennessee mountaineer and the feud. It is a prose fiction work of 1884 by Mary Noailles Murfree; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Eight stories of the Tennessee mountains — 'The Dancin' Party at Harrison's Cove', 'The Star in the Valley', 'Electioneerin' on Big Injun Mounting', 'The Romance of Sunrise Rock' and others — told in mountain dialect by a narrator who is a visitor from the valley.
works.significance: In the Tennessee Mountains founded the Southern mountain story and was the first book to make the Appalachian mountaineer a subject of American literature: its dialect, its feud narratives and its landscape made the genre and prepared the way for the Southern Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. works.title: In the Year of Jubilee
works.description: Published in 1894 and Gissing's most ambitious study of the new generation of women: the story of Nancy Lord, a Camberwell girl of the Jubilee year whose secret marriage tests the new freedoms of her generation.
works.plot: Nancy Lord, the half-educated daughter of a Camberwell piano dealer, is courted by the vulgar, energetic advertising speculator Luckworth Crewe but falls in love with the idle Lionel Tarrant, whom she marries secretly because her father's will would disinherit her if she married young; deserted while Tarrant is abroad, she bears his child alone, and the novel ends with the two reconciled to an unconventional marriage in which they live apart.
works.significance: In the Year of Jubilee is the sharpest English novel about the suburban girl of the 1890s and the most critical of the New Woman's pleasures; it is a key text for the study of gender, consumption and the city.

works.description: The sequel to The Garden That I Love: another year in the Kentish garden. works.title: Incendium Amoris
works.description: Richard Rolle's principal Latin treatise (c. 1340–43), an autobiographical and doctrinal account of the contemplative life as he himself had experienced it: the warmth of divine love (calor), its sweetness (dulcor), and its song (canor), with instruction on prayer, meditation, and the discernment of spirits. The founding text of the English mystical tradition.
works.plot: Rolle recounts his own conversion and his experience of the three degrees of love — fire, sweetness, and heavenly song — defends the contemplative life against its critics, and teaches the reader to progress from reading through prayer to the 'fire of love' that unites the soul to God.
works.significance: The first major work of the English mystical tradition and the fountainhead of its characteristic language of warmth, sweetness, and song.
works.meter: Latin prose, rhetorical and warm, with the psalm commentary woven in.
works.context: Composed c. 1340–43 in the north of England, early in Rolle's hermit career, and later translated into Middle English (the Fire of Love); among the most widely read Latin spiritual works of the English fourteenth century.
works.characters: Rolle (as witness and teacher)
works.structure: A prologue and forty-two chapters mixing autobiography, doctrine, and scriptural commentary, with the author's own experience as the organizing proof.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.

works.title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
works.form: Autobiography (slave narrative; published as Linda Brent, edited by Lydia Maria Child)
works.description: Published in 1861 under the pseudonym Linda Brent and the first full-length slave narrative by a woman: the account of Harriet Jacobs's life in slavery and of her seven years hiding in a garret. It is a prose work of 1861 by Harriet Jacobs; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Linda Brent is pursued by her master Dr Flint, becomes the mother of two children by a white lawyer, hides for seven years in a tiny garret above her grandmother's shed, escapes to the North, and after the Fugitive Slave Law is forced to hide again; she is finally freed and works as a nurse.
works.significance: Incidents is a founding text of African-American women's writing and of American autobiography: it is the first slave narrative to make the sexual exploitation of enslaved women its central subject, and its seven-year hiding is one of the most extraordinary acts of resistance in American history.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is first-person retrospective narrative with direct appeal to the reader.

works.title: Indian Boyhood
works.description: Published in 1902 and the classic Native American account of a traditional childhood: a Dakota boy's life on the plains and in the woods of Canada. It is a prose work of 1902 by Charles Eastman; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Ohiyesa remembers his Dakota boyhood: the games that trained him to hunt and to endure, the stories of the old people, the first buffalo hunt, the snowshoe journeys, the ceremonies and the moral education of a warrior, before he was taken at fifteen to be educated as a white man.
works.significance: Indian Boyhood is the classic Native American autobiography and one of the most widely read Native American books ever written: its account of a traditional Dakota childhood preserved a way of life that was disappearing, and it made Eastman the best-known Native American writer of his generation.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: Indian Summer
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1886 and the wittiest of Howells's comedies of manners: a middle-aged American bachelor in Florence is tempted by a beautiful young woman and consoled by a woman of his own age. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by William Dean Howells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Theodore Colville, a Chicago journalist burnt out at forty, returns to Florence where he had loved as a young man; he becomes engaged to the dazzling young Imogene Graham, discovers the impossibility of the match, and marries the widowed Mrs Bowen, whose good sense and irony have been the novel's chorus.
works.significance: Indian Summer is the finest of Howells's light comedies and one of the best American novels of the 1880s: its portrait of a man growing old among the monuments of Europe is a masterpiece of American irony, and it shows Howells at his most Jamesian in the international setting.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unobtrusive narrative prose.
works.context: The 1885-86: the American colony in Florence, the international theme of the American abroad, and the Howellsian comedy of ordinary life. works.title: Infants of the Spring
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1932
works.description: The definitive satire of the Harlem Renaissance, written from inside it. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Wallace Thurman; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: At a Harlem apartment house called Niggerati Manor, a group of young Black artists argue, drink and fail to produce their work, while the movement around them is commercialised and betrayed, in a satire of the Harlem Renaissance by one of its own.
works.significance: Infants of the Spring is the definitive satire of the Harlem Renaissance, written from inside it: its portrait of the movement's artists and its argument about the commercialisation of Black art made it the most honest book to come out of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the satire of the movement from inside.

works.title: Inheritance
works.description: The chronicle of the Oldroyd family and the mill across the century. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Phyllis Bentley; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Inheritance follows the Oldroyd family and the Stanhope Mill through the nineteenth century - the Luddite years, the machinery, the marriages, the strikes and the inheritance of the trade - in the Yorkshire saga that made Bentley the most read of the regional chroniclers of the 1930s.
works.significance: Inheritance is Bentley's masterpiece: its Oldroyds and its mill made the industrial family across the generations the classic form of the Yorkshire novel, and it was the most read of the regional sagas of the decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the chronicle of the family and the mill across the generations.
works.context: The Halifax woollen district from the Luddite years to the late nineteenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.

works.title: Inside the Whale and Other Essays
works.description: Orwell's first collection of essays, published by Victor Gollancz on 11 March 1940 in an edition of 1,100 copies, some of which were later destroyed in German bombing. It has three long essays: 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies' and the title essay, 'Inside the Whale', a review of Henry Miller's Tropic of Cancer that becomes a survey of English writing between the wars.
works.plot: 'Inside the Whale', in three parts, begins as a review of Tropic of Cancer (1934). Orwell values Miller less for his 'unprintable words' than for his writing about the ordinary man, which he compares with Joyce's in Ulysses, and he likens Miller to Whitman as a writer of acceptance rather than of a struggle to change life. He then surveys English writing since the First World War: Housman's nostalgic, adolescent pessimism; the pessimistic, unpolitical writers of the 1920s (Joyce, Eliot, Pound, Lawrence, Wyndham Lewis, Huxley and Strachey); and the serious, left-wing group of the 1930s around Auden and Spender, whose shared public-school and university background and sheltered English lives he blames for their attraction to Communism as a substitute faith, and whose phrase 'necessary murder', in Auden's 'Spain', he says could be written only by someone to whom murder is a word. Finally he takes up Miller's image of Jonah in the whale for a passive acceptance of experience, the last stage of irresponsibility, predicts the break-up of laissez-faire capitalism and liberal-Christian culture, and suggests that any novel worth reading will have to follow Miller's lines. The other two essays, 'Charles Dickens' and 'Boys' Weeklies', were reprinted in Critical Essays (1946), whose record describes them.
works.significance: Orwell's first book of criticism. The title essay sets literature against the politics of the 1930s, judges the Auden generation as a writer who had himself fought in Spain, and gives its name to the image of the writer inside the whale, passively accepting experience. The collection's other two essays opened Critical Essays (1946), the book that established him as a critic.
works.meter: Discursive critical prose that moves from the review of a single book to a survey of a literary generation and a political argument, quoting Housman and Auden among others and turning on a single governing image, Jonah inside the whale.
works.context: Orwell had lived in Paris in 1928-29, the city of Miller's book, and dined with Miller there in December 1936 on his way to the Spanish Civil War; Miller thought his going to Spain 'the act of an idiot'. The title essay was finished as the Second World War began: 'While I have been writing this book another European war has broken out.'
works.structure: Three essays: 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies' and 'Inside the Whale', the last in three parts.

works.title: Institutes of Polity
altTitles: Institutes of Polity, Civil and Ecclesiastical
works.form: didactic treatise (political theology) in Old English prose
works.description: Wulfstan's treatise on the orders of Christian society: the duties of the king, the bishops, the clergy, the nobles, and the people in a rightly ordered realm — 'eight columns that support the kingdom'. The clearest statement of Anglo-Saxon political theology and the seedbed of Wulfstan's law codes.

works.significance: The fullest Anglo-Saxon statement of the theory of the Christian commonwealth.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1008-1020 in the crisis of Æthelred's reign and revised under Cnut; preserved in later eleventh-century manuscripts, chiefly Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.characters: the Christian king; the bishops; the estates of the realm
works.structure: A systematic treatise in chapters on the estates of the realm, from the heavenly king down through the earthly orders.

works.title: Intentions
works.form: Collection of critical dialogues and essays
works.description: Published in 1891 and collecting 'The Decay of Lying', 'Pen, Pencil and Poison', 'The Critic as Artist' and 'The Truth of Masks': the manifesto of English aesthetic criticism. It is a prose work of 1891 by Oscar Wilde; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: 'The Decay of Lying' argues that life imitates art and that nature is a bad model; 'The Critic as Artist' makes criticism itself an art and the critic a creator; 'Pen, Pencil and Poison' treats the murderer Thomas Griffiths Wainewright as an artist in crime.
works.significance: Intentions is the central text of English aesthetic criticism and the most brilliant polemic in Victorian criticism; its paradoxes about art and life shaped the theory of the modern novel and of the criticism of culture.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the English reception of Pater, Ruskin and the French symbolists, and the periodical culture of the Fortnightly and the Nineteenth Century. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: Intercepted Letters; or, the Two-Penny Post-Bag
works.form: Verse epistle and periodical-style social satire in the Horatian-Butlerian familiar line, with a pseudonymous paratext of the kind used for Regency lampoon.
works.description: A sequence of satirical verse epistles published under a pseudonymous Irish correspondent's name, affecting to have been stopped in the post. The letters report the manners, fashions and quarrels of Regency London society, its theatres, its politicians and its literary parties, in a light familiar rhyme. The prefatory apparatus treats the supposed author as a young provincial introduced to the metropolitan world.
works.plot: The volume advances no plot but a progression of observations: a country relation arrives in London and reports, letter by letter, the spectacle of a society organised around card tables, the opera, the playhouse, the publisher's table and the political club. Persons of rank and letters are characterised through gossip and through the writer's professed simplicity, so that the satire works by apparent naivety. The closing letters widen from social portraiture to comment on war-time politics and on the vanity of public fame. The machinery of interception is itself part of the argument, since it justifies both the freedom of the attack and the pose of accidental disclosure.
works.significance: It established the satiric persona on which the author's later and more successful lampoons were built, and it is an unusually full poetic record of Regency high society and its literary economy. Contemporary readers treated its portraits as identifiable, which makes it useful evidence for the social history of the period. It marks the survival of Augustan verse epistle technique inside Romantic print culture.
works.meter: Heroic and octosyllabic couplets, iambic, with familiar conversational pauses and occasional lyric interpolations.
works.context: Written at the height of Regency society journalism, when the quarterly reviews, the fashionable publishers and the theatres formed a single contested public, and when Catholic emancipation and Irish representation were live issues. Its pseudonymous disguise answers the risk of libel and reflects the period's enthusiasm for detected and private correspondence. The author was already a known contributor to newspapers and to the music trade, and his Irish position sharpens the outsider's eye.
works.characters: The pseudonymous young Irish correspondent; his country family; the London society of politicians, actors, critics and fashionable hostesses he reports upon
works.structure: An epistolary sequence in verse, loosely progressive from arrival to disenchantment, unified by a single pseudonymous writing voice and by the fiction of intercepted correspondence.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the pseudonym of a young Irish correspondent, with prefatory matter affectedly assigned to a different hand; authorship has never been in doubt.
themes: The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: Interlude of Youth
works.description: An anonymous morality interlude of the fall and repentance of Youth, composed c. 1513–14 and printed c. 1530–35; a compact dramatization of the prodigal's return.
works.plot: Youth, flattered by Riot, Pride, and Lechery, abandons Charity and Humility for the tavern and the stews; Charity and Humility lament and warn him, and Youth, brought low, repents and returns to virtue, ending with a prayer for the king and the audience's amendment.
works.significance: A compact and influential example of the early Tudor morality, dramatizing the prodigal theme that would run through the century to the Elizabethan stage; it survives as a witness to the interlude's household origins.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1513–14, probably for a noble household (the prayer for the king suggests courtly performance), and printed c. 1530–35; it belongs to the same early Tudor wave as Hickscorner and Magnificence, in which the morality play becomes a vehicle for aristocratic moral counsel.
works.characters: Youth; Charity; Humility; Riot; Pride; Lechery
works.structure: A short two-part morality play of temptation and return, with the Vices' songs and taunts alternating with Charity's warnings.

works.title: Intimations of Immortality
altTitles: Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood
works.form: Romantic ode in the reflective and meditative manner, drawing on the English Pindaric and on Platonic and Christian ideas of the soul, and on the period's taste for the philosophical meditation in verse.
works.description: The poet's greatest ode and the central Romantic poem about the loss and recovery of imaginative vision, begun in the spring months of the early 1800s, completed in stages, and printed in 1807. Its speaker finds that the glory and the dream of childhood sight have fled, and seeks a reason for the decay that shall also console him; the answer is a Platonising myth that the soul comes to us from God and hither trails clouds of glory, so that the child is finest in the vision which the adult increasingly loses.
works.plot: The opening stanzas complain that a glory has passed away from the earth, and that the same flowers and the same sight of the heavens bring to the grown man none of the rapture they gave the child, for whom a cloud or a tale could fill the eye with tears. The central stanzas set out the myth of pre-existence: our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting, the soul that is our life's star has had its setting elsewhere and comes from afar, trailing clouds of glory from God who is our home, so that the infant, newest come from that country of light, sees most, and the growing boy sees least, until the shades of the prison-house begin to show upon him and the man is bound to the light of common day. The later stanzas recover the loss: the visionary gleam is gone, but the poet may still draw power from what remains behind, may read in the meanest flower that blows thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears, and may thank the human heart, with its tenderness, its joys and its fears, for the pity and the endurance that make the sober year of mature life richer than the rapturous first hours of childhood.
works.significance: The most ambitious Romantic statement of the relation between childhood, memory and loss, and the poem from which the language of the child as father of the man and of the glory that has passed away entered general use. It set the terms for later Victorian and modern discussions of imaginative decay, and it is the touchstone for readings of the poet's philosophy of the mind.
works.meter: Stanzas of irregular length and varied line, running from four to six beats, with an elaborate recurring rhyme pattern and refrains; the later ode stanzas lengthen and slow, so that metre is used to mark the difference between the child's quick vision and the adult's meditative periods.
works.context: Begun in 1802, in the months of the poet's engagement and of the sonnets on liberty and on public subjects, continued in 1803-04, and completed in 1806; the poem's philosophy of pre-existence and its account of the child drew on the Platonism current among the poets and critics of the day and on the associationist psychology then standard in education.
works.characters: The adult speaker; the child, infant, boy and youth whose successive stages are traced; Nature, personified as the nurse and guide of the child's days
works.structure: An irregular Romantic ode in stanzas of unequal length, moving from a general complaint about the loss of vision, through the pictures of the infant, the boy and the youth, to the philosophical myth and then to the turn of consolation; the design follows the movement of feeling rather than a logical argument, and the later stanzas lengthen and slow as reflection displaces description.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Into Battle
works.form: Lyric (in The Times, 28 May 1915, and in Poems)
works.description: The exultant war lyric of May 1915: the soldier who takes death as part of the open air. It is a verse work of 1915 by Julian Grenfell; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poem speaks in the voice of the soldier going into battle as into the open country: the body, the sun, the trees and the birds are taken into the act of fighting, and death is accepted as the completion of the life in the open, 'to stake the whole on the last throw' of the battle.
works.significance: 'Into Battle' is the most famous and most contested lyric of the war's first year: taken by his own generation as the voice of the happy soldier and by the later war poets as the voice that had to be answered, it fixed the terms of the argument about 1914 and remains the type of the Georgian lyric turned to war.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The author's characteristic manner is the long, swelling, sunlit line of the Georgian lyric.
works.context: The Western Front in the spring of 1915, and the Georgian lyric of the open air turned to war. The record dates the work as composed in 1915 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem.
works.structure: A single lyric in rhymed stanzas of irregular length, spoken by the soldier. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Julian Henry Francis Grenfell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
