works.title: Invisible Man
works.description: Invisible Man is Ralph Ellison's only completed novel, published by Random House in 1952: a first-person picaresque Bildungsroman in which an unnamed young Black man travels from the segregated South to Harlem and discovers that the people and institutions he trusts see him only as a role. It combines realist social observation with surrealism, satire, folklore and the blues, and it is framed by a prologue and epilogue spoken from an underground hiding place.
works.summary: A prologue in which the narrator, living secretly in a basement lit by 1,369 stolen light bulbs, announces that he is invisible; twenty-five chapters that tell, in retrospect, his expulsion from a Southern Black college, his work in a New York paint factory, his recruitment as a Harlem speaker for a political organisation called the Brotherhood, and a riot; and an epilogue in which he resolves to come out of hiding.
works.plot:
In the prologue the narrator explains that he is invisible because others refuse to see him. He lives rent-free in a forgotten basement of a whites-only building, steals electricity from Monopolated Light & Power to burn 1,369 bulbs, and listens to Louis Armstrong's recording of "(What Did I Do to Be So) Black and Blue".

The story proper begins in the South. On his deathbed the narrator's grandfather urges his family to "overcome 'em with yeses, undermine 'em with grins". As a promising high-school graduate the narrator is invited to give his speech to the town's white leaders, but first he must fight blindfolded with other Black boys in a "battle royal" and scramble for coins on an electrified rug; he is rewarded with a briefcase and a scholarship to the state college for Black students. There, assigned to drive the white trustee Mr. Norton, he takes him to the cabin of the sharecropper Jim Trueblood, who tells of fathering a child with his own daughter, and then to the Golden Day, a bar full of shell-shocked Black veterans, where Norton collapses. The college president, Dr. Bledsoe, expels the narrator and sends him to New York with sealed letters of recommendation to the trustees.

In New York the letters fail to open any door, until the son of a trustee, young Emerson, shows him that they instruct their readers to keep him running. He finds work at Liberty Paints, whose famous Optic White is made by adding drops of black, and is injured in a boiler-room explosion caused by his quarrel with the old Black engineer Lucius Brockway; in the factory hospital he undergoes electric-shock treatment that strips him of his name and past. Taken in by the kindly Mary Rambo, he makes an impromptu speech at the eviction of an elderly Harlem couple and is recruited by Brother Jack into the Brotherhood, which trains him as its Harlem spokesman.

His success brings him into conflict with the Black nationalist Ras the Exhorter and, eventually, with the Brotherhood itself, which moves him downtown and then changes its policy towards Harlem. His friend Tod Clifton, a gifted youth leader, leaves the organisation and is found selling dancing paper Sambo dolls on the street; a policeman shoots him dead. The narrator's funeral oration for Clifton earns a rebuke from the committee, and during the confrontation Brother Jack's glass eye falls out. Hiding behind dark glasses and a hat, the narrator is mistaken for Rinehart, a protean preacher, lover, numbers runner and hustler, and realises how fluid identity can be.

A riot breaks out in Harlem, which the narrator comes to believe the Brotherhood has allowed to happen; Ras, now the Destroyer, rides through the streets on horseback with a spear. Fleeing, the narrator falls through an open manhole into a coal cellar and burns the papers in his briefcase, his diploma, Clifton's doll and an anonymous warning note written in Brother Jack's hand, to make light. In the epilogue, after months underground, he concludes that he must emerge and play a socially responsible role, ending with the question "Who knows but that, on the lower frequencies, I speak for you?"
works.significance: Invisible Man won the National Book Award for Fiction in 1953, and a Book Week poll of some two hundred critics, writers and editors in 1965 named it the most important American novel published since the Second World War. It moved African American fiction beyond Wright's naturalist protest by joining Black folk and musical forms to the methods of modernism, and it became a central text of post-war American literature, studied as a novel about American democracy as much as about race.
works.meter: Ellison varies the style with the narrator's development, moving from naturalistic description in the Southern chapters to expressionist and surrealist distortion in the factory hospital and the riot; the prose absorbs the cadences of the sermon, the folk tale, the blues and jazz improvisation, uses dense symbolism and allusion (Dostoevsky's underground man, Emerson, T. S. Eliot), and is often comic and satirical.
works.context: Ellison began the novel in 1945, after wartime service in the merchant marine, and wrote it in New York through the late 1940s, when the Great Migration had made Harlem the capital of Black America and the Communist Party's appeal to Black intellectuals of the 1930s had turned to disillusion. It appeared in 1952, two years before Brown v. Board of Education, when Richard Wright's protest naturalism was the dominant model for Black fiction.
works.characters: The narrator (unnamed); his grandfather; Mr. Norton; Jim Trueblood; Dr. A. Hebert Bledsoe; Homer A. Barbee; young Emerson; Lucius Brockway; Mary Rambo; Brother Jack; Tod Clifton; Ras the Exhorter (the Destroyer); Rinehart (reported); Sybil
works.structure: A frame of prologue and epilogue, set after the events, encloses twenty-five chapters told in retrospective first-person narration; the action follows the episodic, journey-based pattern of the picaresque and the Bildungsroman, with each episode exposing a new institution and a new illusion, and recurring objects (the briefcase, the letters, the coin bank) binding the episodes together.
themes: Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Power, the state and surveillance
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
The city, the suburb and modern space
movements: Postwar African American Writing: Protest and Its Critics

works.title: Iola Leroy; or, Shadows Uplifted
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1892
works.description: Published in 1892 and the first novel by an African-American woman: the story of a beautiful mixed-race woman who is sold into slavery and of her life after emancipation. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by Frances E. W. Harper; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Iola Leroy, raised as white and educated in the North, is kidnapped and sold as a slave when her father's death reveals her mother's ancestry; she is rescued during the war, works as a nurse, searches for her scattered family, and dedicates her life to the education and uplift of her people.
works.significance: Iola Leroy is the first novel by an African-American woman and the founding text of African-American women's fiction: its treatment of passing, its picture of black life in slavery and freedom, and its argument for racial loyalty make it a central document of American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat.
works.context: 1892: the post-Reconstruction South, the black women's club movement, and the debate on passing and racial loyalty. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under sensation novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Iola Leroy; Eugene Leroy, her father; Marie Leroy, her mother; Harry Leroy, her brother; Robert Johnson, her uncle; Dr Frank Latimer; Dr Gresham; Aunt Linda; Uncle Daniel; Tom Anderson; Lucille Delany
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Ellen Watkins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Ireland, with Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1897 and the collection that made Johnson a figure in the Irish revival: the poems on Ireland, its saints and its martyrs, together with the odes and lyrics of his last years. It is a verse work of 1897 by Lionel Johnson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume contains 'Ireland', 'The Dark Angel' (in a revised version), 'Parnell', 'The Abbey of Saint Mary' and the poems of friendship and loneliness; its subject is the Catholic and Celtic past of Ireland and the poet's relation to it.
works.significance: Ireland is the finest English-language poetry of the Irish revival by a poet outside Ireland: its poems of the Irish past made Johnson an honorary figure of the movement and influenced Yeats's own early poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is classical and medieval metres handled with learning.
works.context: 1897: the Irish Literary Revival, the fall of Parnell, and the English Catholic revival. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the poet; Ireland, mourned and invoked; Charles Stewart Parnell; the Dark Angel; Ireland's dead and her martyrs
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Lionel Pigot Johnson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Irish Melodies
altTitles: Irish Melodies, with Accompaniments and Songs
works.form: Lyric and song cycle for voice with piano arrangement: a national-air setting sequence in the ballad and song tradition, with editorial prefaces arguing for the recovery of Irish music.
works.description: A series of lyric settings written to recovered Irish airs, issued in numbered parts over more than two decades and later gathered into complete volumes. The verse supplies new English words to traditional melodies, and the accompanying prefaces and advertisements argue the case for an Irish national music rescued from neglect. Its songs move between tenderness, Jacobite and patriotic grief, and witty accommodation with the English market that bought them.
works.plot: There is no continuous argument: each lyric takes a single air and builds a short dramatic situation around it, often a rejected lover, an exile, a minstrel, or a mourner for a lost national cause. Recurrent patterns of loss and memory give the series a political colouring, since the fallen glories of Ireland are figured as abandoned harps, broken thrones and forgotten friends. Several songs turn on the figure of the bard whose instrument is the nation's last surviving voice, and others quietly rework the language of union and emancipation current after 1800. The accompanying prose notes defend the antiquity of the music and the author's fidelity to Irish tradition, while the lyrics themselves often avoid direct polemic in favour of sentimental indirection.
works.significance: It was the most widely circulated body of Irish verse of the nineteenth century and fixed the Victorian and later image of Irish national song, exercised influence on popular music, and made the recovered air a model for other national lyrical revivals. It also generated lasting critical debate about the compromise between cultural nationalism and the metropolitan literary market. Its best-known lyrics remained standard recital pieces long after the surrounding politics had faded.
works.meter: Stanzaic lyric measures strictly adapted to the pre-existing airs, chiefly ballad and song metres with regular rhyme schemes and repeating refrains.
works.context: It appeared after the failure of the 1798 rising and after the Act of Union, when Irish national identity was being renegotiated in cultural rather than political terms, and when the collection and setting of national airs was a fashionable European enterprise. Its publication was shaped by Dublin and London music publishers and by the demand of the drawing-room market, and its author was simultaneously an emancipation advocate and a London celebrity. The series continued to grow through the 1820s and into the 1830s, so that its politics shift with the agitation for Catholic emancipation.
works.structure: A serial anthology of short lyrics organised by numbered publication rather than by any narrative plan, with paratextual notes on the airs; unity is musical and national rather than sequential.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
altTitles: Isabella, or the Pot of Basil
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the Italian novella in English ottava rima, with the gothic and the ballad's treatment of devoted female grief.
works.description: A short romance in ottava rima taken from a novellieri's tale of the fourteenth century, in which a merchant's sister, married by a trick to a young man of her own choosing, is robbed of her lover by her brothers, who murder him while he sleeps in the woods. The lady finds the body, carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, and waters it with her tears until the basil withers and her brothers take it from her. It is the most concentrated of the author's narrative poems and a study of jealous wealth against devoted grief.
works.plot: Isabella, the daughter of a wealthy family of Messina, loves a young clerk of her brothers' house, and by an artifice obtains her marriage to him; the brothers, ashamed of the match and anxious for their fortune, take their brother on a journey and kill him in a forest. The girl, told in a dream where her lover lies, goes to the spot, digs up the body, and carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, which she tends and waters, never leaving it, so that the plant grows strangely and the neighbours marvel. Her brothers at last steal the pot from her, and she pines and dies praying that her tomb may hold what they have taken; the pot was never afterwards found. The argument is that a mercantile family's honour can murder love, and that the devotion of grief is a thing which money cannot seize.
works.significance: It gave the English ottava rima one of its most finished narrative poems and made the pot of basil a permanent image of a grief that tends its own loss; the tale was repeatedly reprinted in the annuals and retold on the stage of the later century. Its handling of a woman's devotion against familial avarice became a touchstone for the discussion of the author's narrative sympathy.
works.meter: Ottava rima, seven-line iambic pentameter stanzas rhyming abababcc, used here with great fluency and a frequent closing couplet of sentiment; the song of the pot is set apart in shorter lyric measure.
works.context: Composed at the house of a friend's family in the north of London in the February of 1819, in the weeks after the death of the poet's younger brother and during the same season which produced the Belle Dame ballad and the beginning of the titan poem, and published in the 1820 volume. Its choice of an old Italian tale and its scorn for a mercantile brothers' world belong to the same argument about the poetry of sensation as the longer romance of the moon.
works.characters: Isabella, the merchant's daughter; her lover, the clerk of the house; her three brothers of the merchant's honour; the old nurse of the household; the people and priests of Messina
works.structure: A continuous narrative in some sixty ottava-rima stanzas, the exposition of the family and the love, the murder reported, the dream and the discovery of the grave, and the long middle of the basil's tending, closing on the lady's death and the lost pot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is dated by the letters of its composition and exists in a fair copy in another hand made for the printer.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Revenge and justice
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: It Is Never Too Late to Mend: A Matter-of-Fact Romance
altTitles: It Is Never Too Late to Mend
works.description: Published in 1856 and Reade's first documentary novel: a triple narrative of the English prison system, the Australian goldfields and a rural rivalry in love, designed to expose the cruelty of the separate system.
works.plot: George Fielding, a struggling Berkshire farmer, goes to the Australian goldfields to make the fortune that will let him marry Susan Merton, while the thief Tom Robinson passes through the brutal regime of a county gaol under the governor Hawes until the chaplain Eden reforms it; the prison chapters record, with documentary fidelity, the treadmill, the crank and the separate system. Transported to Australia, Robinson becomes George's partner on the diggings, and the two return to defeat the scheming Meadows, George's rival for Susan.
works.significance: It Is Never Too Late to Mend is the most influential English novel of prison reform: its prison chapters were read as evidence in the contemporary debate and helped to end the separate system, and it established the method of documentary fiction that Reade and Zola would develop.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative.
works.context: The 1850s, the separate system of prison discipline, the transportation system, and the Australian gold rush of 1851. The record dates the work as composed between 1855 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: George Fielding; Susan Merton; Tom Robinson; John Meadows; Isaac Levi; the Reverend Francis Eden; Hawes, the gaol governor; Josephs; Jacky; William Fielding
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Italy
works.form: Topographical and descriptive poem in the line of eighteenth-century Italian travel verse, inflected by the Romantic meditation on art, Catholicism and exile.
works.description: A topographical and historical meditation on Italy, written by a poet who had travelled there twice but who refused the conventions of the travel poem. The Italian scene is treated as a series of moral, artistic and personal reminders: ruins, pictures, monasteries and mountain villages prompt reflections on exile, faith, art and lost affection. Short songs, ballads and romances are intercalated in the reflective texture, so that the volume alternates between argument and lyric.
works.plot: The poem proceeds from place to place, letting each site draw out a meditation rather than narrating a journey with a fixed itinerary. It returns repeatedly to a personal history of disappointment and to the fate of the exiles and outlaws among whom the poet numbers himself, and it treats Roman Catholic ceremony and Italian banditti romance as objects of sympathetic curiosity rather than of antiquarian display. Painters, poets and historical sufferers appear as companions in the landscape, and several passages take the form of embedded tales or songs. The result is a poem whose real subject is the mind of the traveller meeting a country already overloaded with association. Its closing movements draw the reflection back from Italy to the poet's own loss and to the consolation of verse.
works.significance: For much of the nineteenth century it was the standard English poem about Italy, quoted by tourists and taught in schools, and its intercalation of songs inside a reflective structure was widely imitated in the annuals. It preserves a version of Romantic travel writing that is suspicious of the sublime and attentive to painting, ritual and social observation. Modern accounts of second-generation Romanticism treat it as the chief alternative to Byronic and Wordsworthian models of the topographical poem.
works.meter: Chiefly rhymed five-beat couplet lines in the descriptive tradition, broken by songs and ballad-measure lyrics of irregular stanzaic length.
works.context: Written after the Napoleonic wars reopened Italy to English tourists, at the height of the fashionable Italian sojourn and of the English debate over Catholic emancipation which the poem's treatment of monastic and ritual life inevitably touched. Its first part was published anonymously and the second under the author's name, a publishing history typical of a poet who cultivated reticence. Later editions supplied with engraved plates after the drawings of a famous landscape painter turned the poem into one of the century's most successful gift books.
works.structure: A loosely sequential meditation on places, interrupted by intercalated lyrics, romances and songs; no continuous plot, and a strong lyrical undertone running beneath the descriptive argument.
works.attributionNotes: The first part was issued anonymously in 1822; the second part appeared under the author's name, and the whole was revised and enlarged across several editions.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Itinerarium Cambriae
works.description: Gerald of Wales's account of the preaching tour of Wales undertaken in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury to recruit for the Third Crusade, combining topographical description, ethnography of the Welsh, anecdote, and vigorous self-promotion; the companion work to the Descriptio Cambriae (1194).

works.significance: One of the finest works of twelfth-century travel and ethnographic writing, a primary source for medieval Wales, and a major witness to the Latin literary culture of the Welsh marches.

works.title: Ivanhoe
works.form: Historical romance and adventure novel of chivalry, with comedy of the lower Saxon characters and a tragedy of the outsider.
works.description: The romance of twelfth-century England that moved the historical novel away from Scotland and supplied the nineteenth century with its image of medieval chivalry, tournament and Jewry. Its disowned Saxon heir, returned in secret, and its two opposed heroines - the disinherited Rebecca and the Saxon Rowena - carry an argument about tolerance, race and national fusion. The author's dedicated account of the change of subject in the introductory 'Dedicatory Epistle' is itself a famous piece of theory.
works.plot: Wilfred of Ivanhoe, disinherited for following King Richard abroad, appears incognito at the Saxon house of Cedric of Rotherwood, who plans to marry his ward Rowena to a rival claimant of the blood royal. The tourney at Ashby of the Tor, the insults of Prince John's party, and the abduction of the guests at Torquilstone leave the field to outlaws and to the medicine and charity of Rebecca, the Jewess, whom the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert pursues to the accusation of trial by combat. Richard returns in disguise, the baronial plot against John is broken, Bois-Guilbert falls dead in the lists, Rebecca is driven out of England by her own people, and Ivanhoe marries Rowena while the disinherited Saxon patrimony is restored.
works.significance: Fixed the popular image of medieval England and made the tournament, the castle and the outlaw band the standard equipment of romance; it also made the suffering Jewess one of the century's most discussed fictional creations. Its explicit theory of how a modern writer may fabricate a past has been continuously cited. Its influence on the medieval revival, in fiction, stage design and costume, is extensive.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; minstrel songs, brindisi and a Jewish hymn are interpolated; the dialogue is keyed to rank, from Norman French-inflected speech to Saxon plainness.
works.context: Written in the years of the post-Waterloo reaction, when medievalism, national theatre and the question of the civil status of minorities were in the air, and when the author's antiquarian studies had produced a command of the cast, armour and law of the middle ages. The treatment of the Templars and of the Jews draws on a long tradition of English prejudice and on the records of persecution. The book's instant commercial success changed the terms on which historical fiction was commissioned.
works.characters: Wilfred of Ivanhoe; Cedric of Rotherwood; Rowena; Rebecca; Brian de Bois-Guilbert; Front-de-Boeuf; Isaac of York; King Richard I; Prince John; Athelstan; Wamba; Gurth; the Prior Aymer; Ulrica
works.structure: Third-person romance in nineteen sections with a 'Dedicatory Epistle' and a 'Letter Prefixed to the Second Edition' on the composition of medieval fiction; the plot is episodic and set-piece driven, with the tournament, the feast and the trial as its pivots.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; authorship undisputed.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
National identity and Englishness
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Jack of Newbury
altTitles: The Pleasant History of John Winchcomb
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the clothier's golden age: John Winchcomb of Newbury rises from apprentice to the greatest clothier in England, his hundred looms employing hundreds, his wealth commanding kings, and his virtue (he feeds the poor, arms his men for Flodden, refuses a knighthood) making him the hero of England's craftsmen — the first English novel of the working world.
works.plot: Jack's rise, his marriage to his late master's widow, the great household of the looms, the visit of Queen Katherine, the expedition to Flodden, and the pranks of the courtiers against the honest clothier fill the episodic narrative, which closes on his death and the praise of his charity.
works.significance: The first great novel of English working life — the book that gave the artisan class its own literature, and the ancestor of the industrial novel.
works.meter: Plain, vigorous prose with interpolated songs and ballads, in the speech of shop and street.
works.context: Published 1597, in the decade of the cloth trade's crisis and the apprentices' unrest; its celebration of the clothier's charity answered the dearth and the poor laws with fiction.
works.characters: Jack (John Winchcomb); his wife (the widow); Queen Katherine; King Henry VIII; the courtiers; the clothiers of England
works.structure: An episodic biography in the jest-book and chronicle manner, built of set pieces — the banquet, the expedition, the courtiers' gulling — in the popular prose Deloney perfected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: Jacob and Esau
altTitles: A New Mery and Wittie Comedie or Enterlude, Newely Imprinted, Treating upon the Historie of Jacob and Esau
works.description: An anonymous Protestant biblical interlude on the story of Jacob and Esau from Genesis, printed in 1568; one of the liveliest mid-century dramatizations of the doctrine of election.
works.plot: The play follows Genesis 25–27: the differing natures of the twins Jacob and Esau, the sale of the birthright for a pottage, Isaac's blessing of Jacob obtained through Rebecca's counsel, and Esau's rage and reconciliation; the serious matter of election is framed by the comic servants of the household (Ragan, Mido, and the boy Abra) whose tricks and misadventures mirror the plot.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the mid-century biblical interludes and an important document of Protestant dramatic theory; its comic subplot anticipates the structure of Elizabethan biblical and history plays.
works.meter: Couplets and 'rhyming fourteeners'
works.context: Composed c. 1550–58 in the Edwardian and Marian years, when the doctrine of predestination was at the centre of English religious debate; the play's prologue makes the case for the godly theatre, and it was printed in 1568 for the Elizabethan market.
works.characters: Isaac; Rebecca; Jacob; Esau; Ragan; Mido; Abra; Deborah; Hanan
works.structure: Five acts with act and scene divisions, alternating the biblical action with a fully developed comic subplot, and a prologue arguing that election is the play's theme.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: Early Tudor Drama
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

works.title: James Burnham and the Managerial Revolution
works.description: Orwell's critique of the American political theorist James Burnham, first published as 'Second Thoughts on James Burnham' in Polemic (No. 3, May 1946) and issued under this title as a pamphlet by the Socialist Book Centre in the summer of 1946.
works.summary: An exposition of Burnham's The Managerial Revolution (1941) and The Machiavellians (1943), which predicted that capitalism would give way not to socialism but to a centralised society ruled by a managerial elite, followed by a test of Burnham's forecasts against events.
works.plot: Orwell grants that the drift of the age has almost certainly been towards oligarchy and the concentration of industrial and financial power, and notes that a servile post-capitalist society had already been foreseen by Belloc, Wells, Zamyatin and Huxley. He then lists Burnham's failed prophecies of 1940-41 (that Germany would win the war and that the USSR would be defeated) and traces them to power-worship: Burnham assumes that whatever is winning will go on winning, admiring Nazi Germany while it prospered and transferring his admiration to Stalin by 1944. Orwell predicts instead that the Russian regime, like Nazism, will destroy itself, and that Burnham's 'huge, invincible, everlasting slave empire' will not be established or will not endure.
works.significance: The clearest statement of the ideas about managerial oligarchy and rival superstates that Orwell dramatised in Nineteen Eighty-Four; Michael Shelden saw Burnham's work and Orwell's analysis as an influence on the novel, Christopher Hitchens noted how much the critique nettled Burnham, and Robert Conquest read it as an early prediction of Soviet collapse.
works.meter: Plain polemical exposition that quotes Burnham at length and then turns his own words against him.
works.context: Written in the first year of peace, when Burnham's theories were widely discussed in Britain and the United States, and in the year Orwell moved to Jura and began drafting Nineteen Eighty-Four.
works.structure: A single argued essay: exposition of Burnham's thesis, a catalogue of his mistaken predictions, a diagnosis of their cause and Orwell's own counter-forecast.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past
Power, the state and surveillance
sources: George Orwell bibliography (Wikipedia)
Second Thoughts on James Burnham (Wikipedia)

works.title: James IV
altTitles: The Scottish History of James the Fourth
works.description: Greene's Scottish romance-play: King James IV of Scotland, married to Dorothea, falls in love with the English lady Ida and plots his queen's murder; Dorothea escapes in disguise, is saved by the English knight Sir Eustace and nursed back to health, and the play ends with the king's repentance, the recognition scene, and the reunion — a history play turned romance, framed by the chorus of Oberon and the fairies.
works.plot: James, corrupted by the flatterer Ateukin, orders Dorothea's death; the honest lords refuse and the queen flees in disguise; wounded, she is healed by Lady Anderson; the wars with England and the king's remorse lead to the final scene, where the disguised queen reveals herself and all is forgiven in the play's comedy of errors and recognitions.
works.significance: The bridge between the chronicle play and Shakespearean romance — the play in which Greene's pastoral art and the history vogue met.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the comic scenes, and the fairies' songs in the induction.
works.context: Printed in 1598 and performed about 1590; its Scottish matter predates James VI's accession to the English throne, and its 'history' is romance from the first.
works.characters: King James IV of Scotland; Queen Dorothea; Ida; Sir Eustace; Ateukin; Lady Anderson; Sir Cuthbert Anderson; the Bishop of St Andrews; Oberon; the fairies
works.structure: A five-act romance on a chronicle frame, with the fairy induction and interludes of Oberon, and the Anderson sub-plot as the comic engine of the recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Jan of the Windmill
works.description: Published in 1876 and Ewing's finest novel: the story of a foundling brought up by a miller, who turns out to have a gift for painting and is torn between the mill and the wider world. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by Juliana Horatia Ewing; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Jan, an abandoned child, is raised by the miller Abel Lake and his wife; he shows an early talent for drawing, is taken up by a local artist, is sent to London to study, and returns to the mill to reconcile art with the life that made him.
works.significance: Jan of the Windmill is the best English children's novel about the artist's vocation and a key text in the Victorian literature of class and education; its picture of the rural craftsman's world is exact and unsentimental.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a child's-eye view.
works.context: The 1850s-60s, the English windmill economy, the Victorian art world, and the debate on the education of the artist. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Jan; Abel Lake, the miller; Mrs Lake
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Juliana Horatia Gatty. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Jane Clegg
works.description: The play of the deserted wife and the suffrage generation. It is a dramatic work of 1913 by St John Ervine; it belongs to Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre and it is catalogued here under Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: Jane Clegg, a wife deserted by her husband, tries to support herself and her children in Belfast while he drifts through England; the play that made Ervine the Ulster dramatist of the new drama and put the woman's question on the stage.
works.significance: Jane Clegg is Ervine's play of the deserted wife: its Belfast household and its woman's work made him the Ulster dramatist of the new drama and a figure of the suffrage stage.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain Ulster dialogue of the farmhouse and the chapel.
works.context: Belfast and England in the early 1910s, the suffrage generation and the new drama. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1913 and first performed in 1913 and the corpus places it within Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre, it is catalogued under suffrage play and the woman's drama; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Jane Clegg; her husband; her children; the neighbours
works.structure: Three acts, in a Belfast household and its aftermath. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as St. John Ervine. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography
works.form: Novel in three volumes, first person ('edited by Currer Bell')
works.description: Published on 16 October 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell, and the novel that changed the position of the first-person heroine in English fiction: an autobiography of a plain, poor, passionate woman who insists on speaking in her own voice.
works.plot: Jane Eyre, orphaned and abused at Gateshead by her aunt Mrs Reed, is sent to Lowood school, where she survives the regime of Mr Brocklehurst and the death of her friend Helen Burns. She becomes governess at Thornfield Hall, falls in love with her employer Edward Rochester, and on their wedding day discovers his mad wife Bertha Mason, kept in the attic. She flees, is taken in by the Rivers family, inherits a fortune from her uncle, refuses St John Rivers's proposal of a missionary marriage, and returns to find Rochester blinded and maimed by the fire that killed Bertha, to marry him as an equal.
works.significance: Jane Eyre is the founding text of the English feminist novel and one of the two or three most influential novels in the language; its first-person heroine who claims the right to feel, its treatment of colonial wealth at the centre of the English house, and its Gothic machinery inside a realist frame have made it a permanent subject of criticism, from the Brontës' contemporaries to Gilbert and Gubar's madwoman and Spivak's postcolonial reading.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
works.context: The 1830s-40s: the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, the governess's anomalous class position, the colonial fortune of the West Indies (Bertha Mason's family and Rochester's Jamaican estate), and the legal doctrine of coverture that made a wife's property her husband's.
works.characters: Jane Eyre; Edward Fairfax Rochester; Bertha Mason; Mrs Reed; Mr Brocklehurst; Helen Burns; Miss Temple; St John Rivers; Diana and Mary Rivers; Adèle Varens; Grace Poole; Blanche Ingram
works.structure: First-person retrospective autobiography in three volumes, each organised around a household (Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Marsh End, Ferndean) and each ending in expulsion or flight.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Jane Shore
works.description: Rowe's tragedy of the mistress of Edward the Fourth, reduced from her court favour to penance and poverty: the most persistent example of the fallen woman's tragedy on the eighteenth-century stage.
works.plot: Jane Shore, cast off with the king's death and pursued by the malice of Gloucester, abandons her riches, does public penance in the streets of London and dies in the humility of her own repentance, while the politics of the court and the fate of Hastings carry the action.
works.significance: It fixed the penitent courtesan as a permanent figure of English moral drama and, with The Fair Penitent, established the female calamity plot that Richardson and the sentimental drama later inherited.
works.meter: Blank verse of a deliberate plainness, with the prose of the lower stations and the sententious couplet at the scene's close.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the last months of the reign and the season of the succession, when the mirror of princes and the fate of the king's mistress were transparently political subjects.
works.characters: Jane Shore; King Edward the Fourth; Hastings; Gloucester; Alicia
works.structure: Five acts of court history and private fall, with the public penance and the closing deathbed scene as the two calculated crises.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Jennie Gerhardt
works.description: Published in 1911 and Dreiser's most sympathetic novel: a poor German girl's life of sacrifice for her family and the men who love her. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Theodore Dreiser; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Jennie Gerhardt, the daughter of a poor Ohio family, is seduced by the senator Brander and then becomes the mistress of Lester Kane, a rich manufacturer; she gives up Kane when his family and his ambitions demand it, raises her daughter, and ends the novel in quiet poverty, having been generous to everyone who used her.
works.significance: Jennie Gerhardt is the most humane American naturalist novel and the finest American portrait of a woman's lifelong self-sacrifice: its refusal to condemn Jennie made it a landmark of American fiction, and it is the book in which Dreiser's sympathy and his determinism are most completely reconciled.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is slow accumulation of documentary detail.
works.context: 1911: the German immigrant poor of the Midwest, the class system of the 1880s-1900s, the double standard, and the American debate on the 'fallen woman'. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Jennie Gerhardt; Lester Kane; William Gerhardt; Senator Brander; Robert Kane; Letty Pace; Vesta
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Theodore Dreiser. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Jenny
works.description: Written in 1848-70 and published in the 1870 Poems: a dramatic monologue spoken by a young man over the sleeping figure of a London prostitute, in which his aesthetic and sentimental reflections are gradually exposed as a failure of moral imagination.
works.plot: The speaker sits with the sleeping Jenny, compares her to his cousin Nell and to the women of society, reflects on her history and on the 'double standard' that condemns her while excusing him, and at last leaves gold coins in her hair and goes, having reached no decision and no action.
works.significance: 'Jenny' is the most direct Victorian poetic treatment of prostitution and the double standard, and its technique — a speaker whose cultivated sensibility becomes evidence against him — is the most sophisticated use of the dramatic monologue for social criticism in the period. Modern criticism has made it a central text in the study of Victorian gender and sexuality.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The verse runs in rhymed couplets. The author's characteristic manner is rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound.
works.context: The 1848-70 debate on prostitution (the Contagious Diseases Acts of 1864-69), the Victorian 'social evil' literature, and the Pre-Raphaelite fascination with the fallen woman. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1870 and first published in 1870 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: the speaker; Jenny; Nell, his cousin
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gabriel Charles Dante Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Jerusalem
altTitles: Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, the sum of the poet's myth, and a national prophecy in the form of a scripture of the imagination.
works.description: The last and largest of the illuminated books, begun in the year of the poet's settlement at Felpham and completed in plates over many years of work, which gathers the whole of his earlier myth into a single vision of the awakening of a giant and the rebuilding of a city in England. It is written in two kinds of verse, a measured line for the narrative of Albion and a long blazing line for the prophecies, and it opens with a prose preface that states the poet's duty to build a system of his own rather than to be governed by another's.
works.plot: The prose preface declares the poet's cause as vision and the defence of imagination against the men of single reason, and ends by invoking a new Jerusalem to be built in England's green and pleasant land among those dark satanic mills. The poem then tells how Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind, lies fallen and divided into the four Zoas or states of the soul, and how, in the night of his sleep, his emanation and the powers of loss and of error hold him in chains; the books trace the labours of the prophetic and creative power who works in the furnaces of the world to bring him back to unity. The argument passes through the histories of the daughters of Albion, of the priests of the law of one, and of the cities built in the name of measurement, and closes with the awakening of Albion, the reconciliation of the divided powers, and the vision of the Emanation gathered to the Man, the last plates declaring that the hour is come and that all the nations shall see the mercy of the Divine Humanity.
works.significance: The most ambitious illuminated book and the final shape of the poet's prophetic system, and, through the lyric placed in its preface, the source of a poem that became one of the most sung of all English verses. Its claim that a city of imagination is to be built in the midst of a labouring nation is a permanent text both of Romantic theory and of later writing about England.
works.meter: Two metres are used throughout: a measured and stately accentual line for the narrative and songs, and a long, reiterated and vehement line for the prophetic books, the verses being printed as part of the illuminated plates; the opening lyric and the closing hymn-like lines are among the most set to music in English.
works.context: Begun at Felpham in Sussex in 1804, in the years of the poet's quarrel with his patron and of his return to London, and worked at in plates until the last decade of his life, when copies were issued by himself and by his wife; its imagery of the fallen giant and of the dark mills answers the industrial and national condition of England during and after the long war with France.
works.characters: Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind; Los, the prophetic and creative power who labour in the furnaces; Enitharmon, his emanation; the four states or Zoas into which Albion is divided; Rahab and the powers of loss; the priests of the law of one and the builders of the cities of measurement
works.structure: A great illuminated book of over a hundred plates, divided into its own internal books and chapters, mixing narrative prophecy, song and dramatic dialogue, with the two metres and the two orders of argument alternating; the design is a single movement from the sleep of Albion to his awakening.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of completion and of the several issues of the plates, and the order in which the parts were executed, are matters of scholarship rather than of authorship.

themes: Creation and cosmology
Exile and homelessness
Imagination as a way of knowing
National identity and Englishness
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: Jill
works.description: Jill is Philip Larkin's first novel, published by the Fortune Press in 1946. It follows John Kemp, a shy scholarship boy from a northern industrial town, through his first term at wartime Oxford, where he invents an imaginary girl to hold his own among wealthier undergraduates.
works.summary: Kemp's arrival at Oxford and his uneasy dependence on his careless, public-school roommate Christopher Warner; his invention of 'Jill', a younger sister described in letters, a diary and a story; his infatuation with Gillian, a real schoolgirl who seems to be Jill made flesh; news that his home town has been bombed; and a party at which his hopes collapse.
works.plot: Lonely and out of place, Kemp tries to win Warner's approval by lending him money and running errands, and is mocked for his provincial background. To give himself a secret life he invents Jill, an idealised younger sister, writing her letters and a long story about her school. When he sees Gillian, a fifteen-year-old cousin of Elizabeth Dowling, a friend of Warner's, he believes he has found Jill and pursues her clumsily. An air raid on his home town sends him home, where he finds his parents safe but his former self strange to him. Back in Oxford, drunk at a party, he kisses Gillian, is roughly handled by Warner's friends and falls ill; the novel ends with his fantasy destroyed and his understanding of himself only beginning.
works.significance: A precursor of the provincial, anti-romantic fiction of the 1950s, including Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim, and an early statement of Larkin's lifelong concerns.
works.meter: Restrained, observant realism, with comic social detail and a poet's attention to atmosphere and weather.
works.context: Written in 1943-44 out of Larkin's own wartime years at St John's College, Oxford, when rationing and conscription had emptied and changed the university; the Fortune Press was a small publisher with which Larkin had placed The North Ship.
works.characters: John Kemp; Christopher Warner; Gillian; Elizabeth Dowling
works.structure: A linear third-person narrative of one term, with Kemp's invented letters, diary and story embedded in the text.
themes: Class, labour and social mobility
Education, institutions and the academy
Identity, authenticity and the divided self

works.title: Joan of Arc
altTitles: Joan of Arc, an Epic Poem
works.form: National epic in the heroic manner, on the model of the Christian epics of the older poems and of the war epic then being revived; its politics and its machinery mark it as a poem of the revolutionary decade.
works.description: An epic poem in twelve books on the Maid of Orleans, written in the first fervour of the author's republican enthusiasm and published in 1796 when he was barely over twenty, by subscription and through a Bristol printer, with a prefatory address that announced the plan of a national epic on a subject of Christian chivalry. It is a war epic and a poem of prophetic voices: the French shepherdess who hears the saints and leads an army, is rejected at the court and at the siege, and is finally taken and burnt, is the subject of a poem that gives its supernatural machinery a serious moral function.
works.plot: The poem opens in the civil war of France and England and in the divinely warned dream of the maid, who is sent to relieve Orleans and to lead the Dauphin to his coronation. Books of council and of battle follow, in which the English commanders take counsel with dark powers and the maid's visions and prayers counter the machinery of her enemies; the field-worship of the French is raised above the war-craft of the invaders in a series of sieges, single combats and nights of watch, and the poem closes with the Maid taken at the last, condemned and committed to the fire, the epic ending in martyrdom rather than in triumph. The argument is at once patriotic and moral, making the virtue of an untaught peasant girl the measure of the kingdoms about her and the promise of deliverance the ground of her authority.
works.significance: The earliest ambitious English epic of the Romantic generation and the document of a radical young poet's attempt to found a national poem on the subject of a martyred maiden; its reputation rests mainly on its history and on the contrast between its politics and its author's later years, and its subject was a standing point of reference in the controversy over the epic in English.
works.meter: Blank verse, iambic pentameter, sustained through the twelve books with an unrhymed flow and occasional apostrophical excursions, in a style imitating the epics of the previous century rather than the polished diction of recent narrative verse.
works.context: Composed during the author's undergraduate years at Oxford, in the first years of the French Revolution and of the English debating societies, and in the company of the communitarian scheme on the American frontier which occupied the same circle; its republican sympathy with France against England put it squarely in the radical poetry of the 1790s, from which the writer's later career was a long retreat.
works.characters: Joan, the Maid of Orleans; the Dauphin, afterwards Charles the Seventh; the shepherds and the parents of the maid; the English commanders and their counsellors of the dark power; the saints who visit and encourage the heroine
works.structure: An epic in twelve books with a continuous war narrative, framed by invocations, councils of gods and powers, prophetic dream and prophetic speech, and by long episodes of battle and siege; the machinery is distributed between the celestial guardians of the heroine and the dark advisers of her enemies.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Religious persecution and martyrdom
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Warfare and battle
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Joe Wilson and His Mates
works.description: Published in 1901 and the most autobiographical of Lawson's books: the stories of Joe Wilson, a bushman, and of his courtship, marriage and the death of his child. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Henry Lawson; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: 'The Author's Farewell to the Bushmen' introduces the cycle; 'Joe Wilson's Courtship', 'Brighten's Sister-in-Law', 'A Double Buggy at Lahey's Creek' and 'Water Them Geraniums' follow Joe from youth to marriage, through his small son Jim's illness and the hard years on a selection at Lahey's Creek, and the endurance of his wife Mary.
works.significance: Joe Wilson and His Mates is the finest single volume of Australian fiction of the nineteenth century and the book in which the Australian short story became an art: its story of a marriage in the bush is the most moving thing Lawson wrote.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, laconic, anecdotal prose.
works.context: The 1890s, the New South Wales bush, the selectors and the small farmers, and the Bulletin's version of the Australian character. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Joe Wilson, the narrator; Mary, his wife; Jim, their son; Jack Barnes, his mate; Brighten's sister-in-law; Mrs Spicer ('Water Them Geraniums')
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Archibald Hertzberg Lawson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Novel of Development and the Growth Story
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Regional identity and the American sectional character
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations

works.title: Johan Johan
altTitles: A Mery Play between Johan Johan the Husbande, Tyb his Wyfe, and Syr Jhan the Preest
works.description: John Heywood's one-act farce of a cuckolded husband sent on errands by his wife and her lover the priest; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Johan Johan, suspecting his wife Tyb of entertaining Sir John the priest, is dispatched by her on a series of errands — to mend a pail, to fetch wax — while she dines with the priest; returning to find them feasting on a pie he was sent away from, Johan at last drives the priest out with blows, and the play ends with the husband's triumphant threat to beat Tyb too.
works.significance: The first English farce on the theme of the cuckolded husband and the anticlerical triangle that would recur through the century; its rapid domestic action makes it the most theatrically economical of Heywood's plays.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed in 1533 by Rastell, the year that saw the first parliamentary attacks on clerical marriage jurisdiction and mortuary fees; the play's satire of the lecherous parish priest draws on the fabliau tradition of Chaucer's Miller's Tale and the popular anticlerical jest.
works.characters: Johan Johan; Tyb (his wife); Sir John (the priest)
works.structure: A single-scene farce of errands and discovery, ending in a cudgel-fight; the play is a dramatization of the anti-clerical fabliau of the priest, the wife, and the credulous husband.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Early Tudor Drama
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

works.title: John Bull
works.form: Political allegory and character tract in epistolary form
works.description: A political allegory in three letters, published anonymously in 1712 in support of the Harley ministry's peace policy and instantly the most effective piece of war-time argument of its decade. Dr John Arbuthnot turns the Grand Alliance into a family law suit in which John Bull, the plain honest Englishman, has been brought to ruin by trustees, lawyers and a foreign partner. Its homely, low-comic manner made the figure of John Bull the standing personification of the English nation.
works.plot: John Bull, a freeholder of old family, puts his estate in the hands of trustees who hire a foreign partner, Lewis Baboon, and a crew of lawyers and projectors who out-spend the rents, mortgage the land and make John fight to keep what he no longer owns. When John falls into the power of the court of Chancery and the law's bottomless pit, his old servants and neighbours conspire to recover the estate, and the allegory urges the removal of the trustees, the ending of the war and the settlement of the account. Arbuthnot's point is that a people may be enslaved by debt, law and management while believing themselves free.
works.significance: It created the national personification that British cartoon and political language used for two centuries, and it is the purest surviving example of Scriblerian political satire in the Augustan public sphere. Its diagnosis of a nation captured by creditors, lawyers and standing armies became a durable idiom for constitutional argument.
works.meter: Prose only, in a colloquial, proverb-laden, bunyanesque-narrative register
works.context: Written during the negotiation of the Preliminaries of the Peace of Utrecht by a physician-close to the Tory ministry and to the Scriblerus circle, it belongs to the ministerial journalism of the Examiner and the Memorials of 1711-12, and to the Scriblerian strategy of using low humour and popular form against the Whig moneyed interest.
works.characters: John Bull; Lewis Baboon
works.structure: Three letters forming a continuous comic allegory, later expanded into a four-part version, with the argument carried by incident and legal farce rather than by direct declamation.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Arbuthnot's authorship was established by his friends' testimony and by the Scriblerus correspondence, and is not now disputed. The later parts and reprints include additions of uncertain extent.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Order and degree: the body politic
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

works.title: John Ferguson
works.description: The classic Ulster play of conscience, scripture and the avenger. It is a dramatic work of 1915 by St John Ervine; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: John Ferguson, a man of the Ulster Bible, awaits the arrival of his son from America to settle the family score; the play that made Ervine the Ulster dramatist of the new drama and remains the classic play of the Ulster conscience.
works.significance: John Ferguson is Ervine's classic play of the Ulster conscience: its Bible on the table and its avenger from America made it the defining play of the Ulster new drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain Ulster dialogue of the farmhouse and the chapel.
works.context: Ulster in the early 1910s, the nonconformist household and the Bible. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and first performed in 1915 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: John Ferguson; Ruth; David; Mrs. Ferguson; the son from America
works.structure: Three acts, in the Ulster farmhouse and its aftermath. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as St. John Ervine. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement
themes: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question

works.title: John Halifax, Gentleman
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1856
works.description: Published in 1856 and the classic Victorian novel of self-help: the rise of a poor boy to wealth and honour as a manufacturer in a west-country town. It is a prose fiction work of 1856 by Dinah Mulock Craik; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: John Halifax, an orphan of unknown parentage, is befriended by Phineas Fletcher, the invalid son of a tanner, and works his way from mill-boy to master; the novel follows his marriage to Ursula March, his business struggles during the Napoleonic wars, the death of his children and his own death as a revered citizen.
works.significance: John Halifax, Gentleman was one of the most popular novels of the century and the central Victorian fiction of self-help: its hero became the model of the self-made Christian businessman, and the book's combination of business realism and domestic sentiment made it a standard text of Victorian values.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is plain, warm narrative prose.
works.context: 1850s: the industrial west country, the Victorian gospel of work and self-help, and the Quaker and Unitarian culture of the manufacturing towns. The record dates the work as composed between 1855 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: John Halifax; Phineas Fletcher, the narrator; Abel Fletcher; Ursula March; Guy, Edwin, Walter, Maud and Muriel Halifax; Lord Ravenel; Richard Brithwood; Lady Caroline Brithwood; Jael
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dinah Maria Mulock. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Johnny Ludlow
works.description: Published from 1867 in the Argosy and collected from 1874: the finest English series of domestic mystery stories, told by a Worcestershire schoolboy. It is a prose fiction work of 1874 by Mrs Henry Wood; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Johnny Ludlow, a boy of a Worcestershire county family, recounts the mysteries and disasters of his neighbourhood — a missing will, a poisoning, a ghost, a wrongful accusation, a lost child — in a series of quietly narrated stories in which the ordinary life of the English county is disturbed by crime and the supernatural.
works.significance: Johnny Ludlow is the best English series of domestic mystery stories of the century and the finest thing Wood wrote: its quiet narration, its county setting and its use of a boy's point of view made it a model for the English village mystery, and it is the point at which the sensation novel turns into the detective story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is direct, urgent narrative address.
works.context: 1867-79: the English county family, the Worcestershire countryside, the periodical market of the Argosy, and the vogue of the domestic detective story. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1879 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: Johnny Ludlow; Mrs Todhetley; Mr Todhetley; the Squire; the schoolmaster; the villagers of Dyke Manor
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ellen Wood. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Joseph Andrews
altTitles: The History of the Adventures of Joseph Andrews, and of His Friend Mr. Abraham Adams
works.form: comic novel in prose, described as a comic epic poem
works.description: A comic history of the road, the first English novel to announce itself as a comic epic poem in prose, following a footman and a poor scholar on their journeys out of and back into their master's house. Its prefatorial essay on the ridiculous supplied the age with its most used comic theory.
works.plot: Joseph, a footman who keeps his chastity against his mistress's importunity, is turned out of the house and sets out to find his beloved Fanny. With his friend Mr. Adams, an absent but good-hearted parson, he travels by stage-coach, foot and waggon through a sequence of inns, beggars, gypsies, justices and physicians. Affection, hypocrisy and the affectation of virtue are exposed on the way, and the discovery that Joseph is Adams's future son-in-law by birth removes the last obstacle to the marriage.
works.significance: It created the self-conscious comic novel in English and set the terms of the century's debate about humour, affectation and the ridiculous, from its own prefatory essay to its later critics.
works.meter: A narrative prose of high comedy with the periodic digression of the critical chapters; the style takes up and exaggerates the diction of the romance and dramatic writers it holds up to burlesque.
works.context: Written and published between the two Pamela-answer volumes of 1741-2, in the season of the war of the theatre and the new copyright debates; its theory of the ridiculous answers both the sentimental and the licentious vogue.
works.characters: Joseph Andrews; Mr. Abraham Adams; Fanny Goodwill; Lady Booby; Mrs. Slipslop; the various innkeepers, justices and physicians of the road
works.structure: Third-person picaresque narration in book form with an intrusive narrator, digressory critical chapters and a discovery plot; the road supplies the sequence, the digressions the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the first volume appeared in the author's name, and the prefatory essays are signed by the design of the work.

works.title: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides
altTitles: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, with Samuel Johnson
works.form: travel journal and autobiographical narrative, in the daily-notebook manner of Boswell's habit of recording
works.description: Boswell's account of the 1773 journey with Johnson to the western islands of Scotland, kept as a day-by-day journal and withheld from print for twelve years. It records the conversation, the arguments on Jacobite memory, religion, slavery and the worth of an island life, and the scenery of Skye and Mull, together with Boswell's own admiration and impatience. It is the companion to Johnson's own account of the same tour and one of the founding texts of the literature of Scottish travel.
works.plot: The journal follows the party from Edinburgh through St Andrews and Aberdeen to Inveraray, across to Skye and Mull and back by the west coast, noting what they saw and what Johnson said. The great subjects are the memory of the '45 and of the clan chiefs, the condition of the islanders, the debate over the Union and over the poverty of the islands, and Johnson's moral observations on the people he met, many of them at odds with Boswell's warmer sympathy. Boswell's own part - his devotion to Johnson, his flirtations, his pride in Scotland - is recorded as frankly as his companion's.
works.significance: It is one of the most reliable documents of Johnson's spoken mind and one of the classic travel narratives of Scotland, and its representation of Highland and island life belongs to the literature of the nations in the age of Ossian and of the romantic tour. It also shows how the journal of a single tour became a mode of autobiographical realism.
works.meter: Prose; plain, rapid and colloquial, with long passages of reported conversation and short topographical and antiquarian comment.
works.context: Written in the season of the Highlands' touring vogue opened by Pennant and others, when the aftermath of the '45, the cleared estates and the debate over the Union made the western islands an argument about national character; publication in 1785 followed Johnson's own Journey of 1775 and the long delay caused by the political and personal delicacy of the material.
works.characters: James Boswell; Samuel Johnson; the chiefs and families of the islands; the old Jacobites of the West
works.structure: A chronological day-by-day journal of a single tour, with continuous dialogue reported in the first person and no retrospectively imposed plot; the text prepared for 1785 retains the diary form.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the journal was kept by Boswell in 1773 and revised for the press, and the date of the tour and the date of first publication are both firmly documented.
