works.title: Journey's End
works.description: The greatest play of the First World War: a dugout, a raid and the waiting for the attack. It is a dramatic work of 1928 by R. C. Sherriff; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: In a dugout on the Western Front in March 1918, Captain Stanhope and his officers wait for the German offensive; Raleigh, a new subaltern who idolised Stanhope at school, joins them, the raid ordered by the staff destroys Osborne and a prisoner, and the play ends with the attack beginning and Raleigh dying.
works.significance: Journey's End is the greatest play of the First World War and one of the most important plays in English: its dugout, its officers and its ordinary courage made the war visible to the theatre audience of 1928, and it remains the most performed war play in the language.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the single dugout set and the unbroken real time.
works.context: The Western Front in March 1918, during the German spring offensive, and the mood of 1928 when the play was produced. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and first performed in 1929 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War; The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Captain Stanhope; Osborne; Raleigh; Trotter; Hibbert; Mason
works.structure: Three acts in a single dugout, over four days. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Cedric Sherriff. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Jude the Obscure
altTitles: Jude the Obscure: A Straightforward Novel
works.description: Published in 1895 and Hardy's last novel: the story of Jude Fawley, a stonemason refused admission to Christminster university, and of his cousin Sue Bridehead, whose intellectual freedom and sexual fear make her one of the most complex women in Victorian fiction.
works.plot: Jude Fawley studies the classics in a village and is tricked into marriage with Arabella Donn; he goes to Christminster, meets Sue Bridehead, and lives with her unmarried after she leaves her husband Phillotson; their children are killed in a murder-suicide that Jude interprets as a judgement, Sue returns to Phillotson in penance, and Jude dies in the rain at the Remembrance Day celebrations.
works.significance: Jude the Obscure is the most radical of the Victorian novels on class, education and marriage, and the novel whose reception ended Hardy's career as a novelist. Its critique of the university made it a founding text of the literature of class exclusion, and it stands at the exact boundary between Victorian and modern fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The 1890s, the university question and the exclusion of the working class, the marriage law, the 'New Woman' debate, and the publication crisis that followed the novel's reception. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Jude Fawley; Sue Bridehead; Arabella Donn; Richard Phillotson; Little Father Time; Mrs Edlin; Uncle Drusilla Fawley
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: The serial in Harper's Monthly (1894-95) was heavily cut; the 1895 one-volume edition restored the text and provoked the attack that led Hardy to abandon fiction.

works.title: Judith
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 349 lines (the opening is lost) retelling the apocryphal Book of Judith: the Hebrew heroine beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent and rouses her people to victory. The poem recasts the biblical heroine as a figure of the heroic tradition — a maiden of God wielding the sword against the enemies of her people.
works.plot: Judith, beautiful and wise, is brought to the drunken Holofernes's tent; praying for aid, she seizes his sword and strikes off his head in two blows, then carries the head back to Bethulia in a food-bag. At dawn she shows the head to her people and delivers a speech of triumph; the Hebrews attack the leaderless Assyrians, who flee; Judith receives the spoils of Holofernes as her reward, and the poem ends with praise of God.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on a female biblical hero; a masterly fusion of heroic style and devotional purpose.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with vigorous battle diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv) immediately after Beowulf; the biblical book of Judith was known to the Anglo-Saxons through the Vulgate and Ælfric's later prose homily on the same subject.
works.characters: Judith; Holofernes; the Bethulians
works.structure: Dramatic narrative in the heroic manner: the tent scene, the return, the battle, and the distribution of spoils; the heroine's speeches drive the action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Typology and biblical interpretation
Warfare and battle
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: Juliana
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's signed poem of 731 lines on the passion of St Juliana of Nicomedia: the virgin martyr who withstands her pagan suitor, defeats a demon sent to tempt her, and endures torture and death. The poem contains the most extended debate between saint and demon in Old English.
works.plot: Juliana refuses to marry the prefect Eleusius unless he converts; denounced by her father, she is beaten, hung by the hair, and thrown in prison, where a demon disguised as an angel urges her to yield; she seizes him and forces him to confess his works, then is subjected to fire and a boiling cauldron, and finally beheaded — her soul received into heaven, her persecutors drowned at sea. The epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature.
works.significance: The classic Old English virgin-martyr poem and the fullest statement of the saint-demon debate.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 65b-76v); based on a Latin passio of Juliana.
works.characters: Juliana; Eleusius; Africanus (her father); the demon; the angel
works.structure: A debate-driven passio: successive confrontations (suitor, father, demon, judge) leading to martyrdom, framed by the demon's confession of the history of evil and the poet's runic prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Mission, conversion, and the Church
Women's experience and the feminine voice
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Julius Caesar
works.description: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy of the republic's death: Brutus, honour's fool, joins the conspiracy against Caesar for Rome's sake; Caesar falls at the Capitol; Antony's funeral oration turns the crowd; and the play moves through the proscriptions and the quarrel of the conspirators to Philippi, where Brutus and Cassius die on their own swords.
works.plot: Cassius seduces Brutus into the conspiracy; Caesar, warned by the soothsayer and Calpurnia's dream, goes to the Senate and is murdered; Antony's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' speech swings the mob to vengeance; the triumvirate proscribes its enemies; and the battles of Philippi complete the tragedy of Brutus, the noblest Roman of them all.
works.significance: The schoolroom tragedy of the English-speaking world — the standard by which political drama, and political oratory, have been measured ever since.
works.meter: A restrained, 'Roman' verse — no rhyme — with the prose of the plebeians and the two great orations as the peaks of its rhetoric.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of Essex's fall, from North's Plutarch; its anatomy of mob, coup, and civil war spoke to a court obsessed with succession and rebellion.
works.characters: Julius Caesar; Brutus; Cassius; Mark Antony; Portia; Calpurnia; Casca; Octavius Caesar; Cicero; Decius Brutus; the Soothsayer; Cinna the poet
works.structure: A two-part structure of conspiracy and war hinged on the assassination, with the funeral orations as the pivot of the play's rhetoric and the ghost of Caesar as its revenant.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Kingship and good rule
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Juneteenth
works.description: Juneteenth is the novel edited from Ralph Ellison's unfinished second book and published posthumously by Random House in 1999. His literary executor John F. Callahan condensed it from the more than two thousand pages Ellison wrote over some forty years into a single narrative of about 350 pages.
works.summary: The deathbed conversation between a race-baiting New England senator, shot on the floor of the Senate, and the elderly Black preacher who raised him, interleaved with their memories of the boy's childhood in the Black revival circuit and of his later flight into a white identity.
works.plot: In 1955 Senator Adam Sunraider, notorious for his attacks on Black Americans, is shot while speaking in the Senate. Dying in hospital, he asks for the Reverend Alonzo Hickman, a former jazz trombonist turned Baptist preacher, who arrives with a group of Black church members. Through their memories and dialogue the novel reveals that Sunraider was once Bliss, a child of indeterminate race whom Hickman raised and made the star of his revival meetings, in which the boy rose from a small coffin to preach. Their recollections return to a great Juneteenth celebration, the commemoration of emancipation, at which Hickman preached on the Word and on the meaning of Black survival. Bliss later ran away, drifted through jobs including making films, and remade himself as a white politician who disowned his past.
works.significance: The publication made public the main narrative of Ellison's long-awaited second novel; a fuller scholarly edition of the manuscripts appeared later as Three Days Before the Shooting... (2010).
works.meter: Incantatory, sermon-based prose and extended interior monologue that draws heavily on the cadences of the Black church and of jazz.
works.context: Ellison worked on the novel from the early 1950s until his death; a fire at his summer house in 1967 destroyed part of the manuscript, and he published only excerpts in magazines during his lifetime.
works.structure: Alternating present-tense hospital scenes and long remembered passages, many in Hickman's sermonising voice, assembled by the editor from a much larger manuscript.
themes: Faith, doubt and the sacred
Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: Juno and the Paycock
works.form: Play in three acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 3 March 1924)
works.description: The great Dublin tenement tragedy: the Boyle family inherits a fortune that never arrives and is destroyed by the Civil War. It is a dramatic work of 1924 by Sean O'Casey; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Boyles — the boasting 'Captain' Boyle, his long-suffering wife Juno, their daughter Mary and their son Johnny — are told they have inherited a fortune. They furnish on credit; the inheritance collapses; Mary is pregnant and abandoned; and Johnny, who has betrayed a comrade, is shot and dragged away. The play ends with Juno taking her daughter away and Boyle left alone with his drunken friend Joxer.
works.significance: Juno and the Paycock is the greatest Irish tragedy of the century after Synge: its movement from farce to catastrophe, its musical working-class speech and Juno's final dignity make it a permanent play.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the tragi-comedy that turns from farce to tragedy in a single scene.
works.context: The Irish Civil War (1922–23), the Dublin tenements, the irregular IRA and the official executions, and the class pretensions of the Dublin poor. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and first performed in 1924 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Juno Boyle; 'Captain' Jack Boyle; Joxer Daly; Mary Boyle; Johnny Boyle; Maisie Madigan; Bentham
works.structure: Three acts in a single tenement room, moving from comedy to tragedy. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Casey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Just So Stories for Little Children
works.form: Collection of twelve tales (with the author's own illustrations)
works.description: Published in 1902 and Kipling's book for his own children: twelve 'just so' stories of how the animals acquired their distinguishing features, told as comic fables of the earliest world. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Rudyard Kipling; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection gives the whale his throat, the camel his hump, the rhinoceros his skin, the leopard his spots, the elephant his trunk, the kangaroo his legs and the alphabet its letters, and ends with 'The Butterfly That Stamped'.
works.significance: Just So Stories is one of the most inventive and beloved books in English and the finest comic prose Kipling wrote for children: its invented language, its nonsense logic and its invented cosmogonies made it a permanent nursery classic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
works.context: The 1890s, the Victorian and Edwardian nursery, the evolutionary fable, and the Brer Rabbit tradition of the animal tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Katie Roche
works.description: The three-act play of Katie Roche, the serving girl. It is a dramatic work of 1936 by Teresa Deevy; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Katie Roche follows the serving girl of the title from the kitchen of the provincial house through the marriage that promises an escape to the disquieting close that refuses it, in the three acts that made it the most popular of Deevy's Abbey plays.
works.significance: Katie Roche is Deevy's masterpiece: its serving girl, her marriage and its unsettling ending put the woman's life in the new Ireland on the Abbey stage with a directness the theatre did not forgive, and its recovery made her the rediscovered dramatist of the century.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the Abbey dialogue of the rural Ireland with the woman's confinement at its centre.

The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1936 and first performed in The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, March 1936 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.

works.title: Keep the Aspidistra Flying
works.description: Orwell's novel of the bookshop and the money-god: a poet's war against respectability. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by George Orwell; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Gordon Comstock, a would-be poet from a respectable family, gives up a good job to work in a bookshop and wage war on the 'money god'; he sinks into poverty, loses his girlfriend Rosemary and nearly destroys himself, and the novel ends with his surrender to marriage, a job and the aspidistra in the window.
works.significance: Keep the Aspidistra Flying is Orwell's finest novel of the 1930s and the great English novel about money: its portrait of the genteel poor and its analysis of the money-god made it the period's sharpest study of class and respectability.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the plain declarative English sentence with no ornament.
works.context: London in the 1930s, the book trade, the genteel poor and the cult of respectability. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Gordon Comstock; Rosemary Waterlow; Philip Ravelston; Julia Comstock; Mr Cheeseman
works.structure: Chronological narrative in the third person, ending in compromise. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Kenilworth
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of court and domestic tragedy
works.description: A historical romance of the Elizabethan court, built on the tradition that the favourite of a queen secretly married an English heiress and that her death removed the obstacle to his ambition. The novel gives that gossip a fully imagined domestic and political history: a young woman of noble expectations, married in secret and then deserted, is destroyed by the machinery of her husband's design while the court celebrates the queen's progress to a Warwickshire castle. The public magnificence of the entertainment and the private concealment of a imprisoned wife are cut against each other throughout. It is the most purely tragic of the later romances of this series.
works.plot: An English heiress of an old family, persuaded into a secret marriage by an ambitious courtier, finds herself concealed in a distant house and abandoned as her husband's chances at court improve. The queen's progress to the Midlands brings festivals, pageants and reconciliations, while the deserted wife, tended by a faithful dependant, wastes in confinement and is terrorised by an hired agent of her husband's design. Her death, arranged in secret, removes the impediment to the favourite's suit for the queen's own hand, and the closing disclosures expose the instrument of the murder while leaving the courtier's ambition unpunished. The narrative also follows a boy's flight, a pursuivant's hunt, and the old servants of the wronged house.
works.significance: The standard example in English fiction of the Elizabethan court romance, and the most quoted treatment of the rumoured murder of a secret wife; its progress and pageant chapters are a much-studied instance of the historical novel's use of ceremonial spectacle. Its reconstruction of a domestic tragedy inside a court history made it a source for later plays, ballads and pictorial treatments of the legend.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a courtly and ceremonial diction for the progress scenes, contrasted with homely Scots and west-country speech in the domestic chapters
works.context: Published in 1821 and founded on the Elizabethan gossip and chronology surrounding a famous favourite, the queen's progress, and the mystery of a gentlewoman's death, material then being reworked by historians and antiquaries. The romance belongs to the second great phase of the series which had remained anonymous, issued when its author's public fame was established but his name still withheld, and written in the depressed years immediately after the war with France.
works.characters: The favourite of the queen and secret husband; Amy Robsart, his concealed wife; Queen Elizabeth; the agent of his secret business; a faithful retainer of the wronged house; a runaway boy and the pursuivant set to take him
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes; a public court plot and a private domestic plot are conducted in parallel and meet in the last volume, with pageant, festivity and lower-class by-plot used to release and to comment on the central tragedy.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of the author of the Waverley romances, whose name was still withheld; the attribution is undisputed.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Keynotes
works.description: The most scandalous book of the 1890s: women's desire in a new prose. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by George Egerton; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Egerton's stories — 'A Cross Line', 'Now Spring Has Come', 'The Spell of the White Elf', 'Under Northern Sky' — in which women speak their sexual and emotional experience directly, without plot or moral, in an impressionistic prose.
works.significance: Keynotes was the most scandalous book of the 1890s and the founding text of the feminist short story in English: its direct treatment of women's desire and its impressionistic prose made it a landmark of the New Woman movement and of the modern short story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short impressionistic story without plot.
works.context: London and Norway in the early 1890s, and the New Woman controversy of the decade. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; sensation novel.
works.characters: the women of the stories; the husbands; the lovers; the singers
works.structure: A collection of impressionistic stories without conventional plots. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. works.title: Kidnapped: Being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751
works.form: Historical adventure novel (serialised in Young Folks, 1886)
works.description: Published in 1886 and set in the Highlands after the Jacobite rising of 1745: the story of David Balfour, cheated of his inheritance, kidnapped, shipwrecked, and thrown into the company of the Jacobite swordsman Alan Breck Stewart.
works.plot: David Balfour is kidnapped on his uncle's orders, shipwrecked off Mull, joins Alan Breck in the escape from the brig Covenant, is accused of the murder of the Red Fox at Appin, and flees with Alan across the Highlands to Edinburgh, where he recovers his estate.
works.significance: Kidnapped is the finest English historical adventure novel of the century and the fullest literary account of the Jacobite Highlands; its friendship of David and Alan is one of the great double acts of English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. works.title: Kim
works.description: Published in 1901 and the finest English novel of India: the story of Kimball O'Hara, an Irish orphan in Lahore, and of his wanderings with a Tibetan lama and his education as a spy in the Great Game.
works.plot: Kim, the orphaned son of an Irish soldier, meets a Tibetan lama on a pilgrimage and becomes his chela; he is taken up by the British intelligence service, is educated at St Xavier's school, and travels the Grand Trunk Road gathering intelligence, until he finds the lama again and chooses the world.
works.significance: Kim is the finest English novel of India and one of the great novels of the twentieth century: its picture of the road, its double education of the boy and the lama, and its fusion of imperial intelligence work with Buddhist pilgrimage make it the central English text on the relation of East and West.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, the British Raj, the Indian railways and the Grand Trunk Road, the Great Game with Russia in Central Asia, and the lama's Buddhism. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.

works.title: King Arthur; or, The British Worthy
works.description: The Dryden-Purcell dramatic opera in five acts, celebrating Arthur's wars against the Saxons and his love for the blind Emmeline; it was originally conceived as a political allegory for the Exclusion Crisis and revived in the 1690s.
works.plot: Arthur pursues the Saxon Oswald, who has stolen Emmeline; through enchantment, battles, and the restoration of Emmeline's sight, Arthur defeats the Saxons and unites Britain.
works.significance: The greatest of the English semi-operas and the finest collaboration between a poet and a composer in the period; Purcell's score (including 'Fairest Isle' and the Frost Scene) is a landmark of English music.
works.meter: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
works.context: Drafted in the 1680s as a Whig allegory of the Exclusion Crisis and rewritten for performance by the United Company at the Queen's Theatre, Dorset Garden, in June 1691 with music by Henry Purcell.
works.characters: King Arthur; Emmeline; Oswald; Merlin; Osmond; Philidel; Grimbald; Conon; Aurelius
works.structure: Five acts with extensive music, masque episodes, and spectacular machinery; the spoken roles are limited to the principal characters.
works.attributionNotes: The text is by Dryden, the music by Purcell; the 1691 quarto names Dryden.

works.title: King Hart
works.description: Douglas's allegory of the life of man: King Hart rules his castle of the body with the five senses as his servants until Dame Pleasance and her court — Youthheid, Fresche Delyte, Wantonness — enter and corrupt him; age, sickness, and death storm the castle, and the soul departs. The great Scots allegory of the body politic and the body natural.
works.plot: King Hart, counselled by Ressoun, admits Dame Pleasance and her court; the castle falls into riot; Conscience, Ressoun, and Wisdome are driven out; Age besieges and takes the castle, and Hart dies, leaving his soul to God's judgement.
works.significance: The finest Scots allegory of the body's rule and a bridge between the moralities and the Renaissance anatomy of the self; admired by the later Scots poets.
works.meter: Stanzaic verse in the Chaucerian tradition; vigorous personification allegory.
works.context: Written in Douglas's maturity, perhaps after the death of James IV at Flodden (1513); the castle's fall shadows the fall of the king's court.
works.characters: King Hart; Dame Pleasance; Youthheid; Fresche Delyte; Ressoun; Conscience; Age; Decrepitness
works.structure: A sustained allegory of the besieged castle in the morality tradition, moving from the entrance of pleasure through riot to death and judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Douglas on manuscript authority; the attribution is generally accepted.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: The Scottish Renaissance

works.title: King Horn
works.description: The earliest surviving Middle English romance, some 1,500 short couplet lines telling the exile, adventures, and restoration of Horn, son of the murdered king of Suddene, who wins the love of Rymenhild, defeats the Saracen invaders, and regains his kingdom. Its spare, ballad-like narrative makes it the classic of the 'ancestral romance' of exile and return.
works.plot: Horn, cast adrift by the invaders who killed his father, grows up at the court of King Aylmar, where Rymenhild loves him; exiled through the envy of Fikenhild, he proves himself in Ireland, rescues Rymenhild from a forced marriage in disguise as a beggar, and returns to avenge his father and reclaim Suddene.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the English romance tradition and the earliest witness to the exile-and-return plot that governs the genre.
works.meter: Short rhyming couplets, often of three stresses, with formulaic diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1225 in the south of England from an Anglo-Norman source (the Romance of Horn of Thomas); preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27 (c. 1300) and two later manuscripts.
works.characters: Horn; Rymenhild; Fikenhild; King Aylmar; Athulf; the Saracen invaders
works.structure: A tripartite exile-and-return plot with disguise, recognition, and wedding scenes; narrated in terse couplets with abrupt transitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Courtly love and fin'amor
Exile and homelessness

works.title: King Johan
works.description: John Bale's historical morality play of King John, composed c. 1538 and surviving in a single manuscript revised in the 1550s; regarded as the first English history play.
works.plot: King John, the champion of England's ancient liberties against the papal usurpation, is beset by the allegorical forces of Rome — Sedition, Dissimulation, Usurped Power, Private Wealth — and the clergy, who stir rebellion and bring about his poisoning by Dissimulation disguised as a monk; Widow England and her allies Verity and Imperial Majesty restore the true succession, and the play ends with John vindicated as a proto-Protestant martyr and the papal power expelled.
works.significance: The first English history play: its fusion of the morality tradition with national history and its anti-papal reading of King John set the pattern for the Elizabethan history play, directly anticipating Shakespeare's King John.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1538 during Bale's Protestant exile/activity under Cromwell's patronage, at the moment when Henry VIII's break with Rome made King John a usable hero; Bale revised the play for Elizabeth (the manuscript addresses her), aligning it with the Elizabethan settlement's anti-papal politics.
works.characters: King John; Widow England; Sedition; Dissimulation; Usurped Power; Private Wealth; Verity; Imperial Majesty; Nobility; Clergy; Civil Order; Stephen Langton; Pope Innocent III
works.structure: A two-part play mixing historical persons (John, Stephen Langton, the Pope) with morality personifications, revised by Bale to address Elizabeth I; the structure alternates the king's historical action with the Vices' comic plotting.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Religious persecution and martyrdom

works.title: King John
altTitles: The Life and Death of King John
works.description: Shakespeare's stand-alone history play of the Angevin crisis: King John's disputed title, the Bastard Faulconbridge's satirical commentary, the struggle with the papal legate Pandulph, and the play's terrible centre — the blinding of the boy Arthur and the grief of his mother Constance — ending in John's poisoning at Swinstead and the Bastard's closing appeal to England's unity.
works.plot: John defies Rome, battles France, captures Arthur, and orders his death; Hubert cannot blind the boy, but Arthur dies in his leap from the walls; the French invasion, the defection of the nobles, and John's poisoning follow, until the Bastard's loyalty and the Dauphin's withdrawal restore the kingdom.
works.significance: Shakespeare's boldest experiment in the history genre — a play without heroes, held together by the Bastard's irony and England's idea of itself.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong rhetorical sweep, with Constance's grief and the Bastard's 'commodity' soliloquy as the peaks.
works.context: Probably written 1595–96 in the anxious interval over the succession; its resistance to papal and foreign power spoke to Reformation England.
works.characters: King John; the Bastard (Philip Faulconbridge); Queen Elinor; Constance; Prince Arthur; Hubert; Cardinal Pandulph; King Philip of France; Lewis the Dauphin; Salisbury; Pembroke
works.structure: An episodic chronicle held together by the Bastard's choric commentary and by the Arthur tragedy at its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: King Lear
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of divided kingdom and broken nature: Lear abdicates, dividing Britain between the daughters who flatter him and disinheriting the one who loves him; cast out by Goneril and Regan, he goes mad on the heath in the storm with his Fool and the disguised Edgar, while the parallel plot of Gloucester and his sons runs to the blinding at Cornwall's hands — and the end brings Cordelia's death and Lear's over her body.
works.plot: Lear's love-test sets the tragedy in motion; Goneril and Regan strip him of his hundred knights; he rages into the storm, meets 'poor Tom' (Edgar), and is saved by Cordelia's French army; Gloucester, betrayed by Edmund and blinded, is led by Edgar to Dover; the battle is lost, Cordelia is hanged, and Lear dies of grief, leaving Edgar and Albany to close the play with its bleakest lines.
works.significance: By common consent the greatest tragedy in the language — the play that tests the limits of what tragedy can say about nature, justice, and the gods.
works.meter: A verse pushed to the edge of its resources — the storm scenes, Lear's curses, Edgar's mad speech, and the spare final lines — with prose for madness and the Fool's riddles.
works.context: Performed at court, 26 December 1606; the play draws on the old Leir play, Holinshed, and Sidney's Arcadia, and its two early texts (Quarto 1608 and Folio 1623) differ substantially.
works.characters: King Lear; Goneril; Regan; Cordelia; the Fool; the Earl of Gloucester; Edgar (Poor Tom); Edmund; the Duke of Albany; the Duke of Cornwall; Kent (Caius); Oswald; the King of France
works.structure: A double plot of Lear and Gloucester mirroring each other, built on the medieval morality pattern inverted — the trial of the daughters, the hovel, the cliff — and ending in the catastrophe that refuses consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Quarto/Folio textual divergence is the play's standing editorial problem.

works.title: King Solomon's Mines
works.description: Published in 1885 and the first great English adventure romance of Africa: Allan Quatermain's expedition into the interior in search of a lost civilisation and a legendary diamond mine. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by H. Rider Haggard; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Allan Quatermain, the hunter, is engaged by Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good to find Curtis's lost brother and the diamond mines of Solomon; the expedition crosses the desert, survives the mountains of Sheba, and reaches the lost Kukuana kingdom, where an Englishman is taken for a god and a civil war is fought before the treasure is found.
works.significance: King Solomon's Mines invented the modern adventure novel of Africa: its combination of documentary travel detail, a treasure hunt and an encounter with a lost civilisation set the formula for a century of imperial romance, and it made Haggard the most popular storyteller in England.

works.title: Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1905 and the first of Wells's great comic novels of class: the story of Arthur Kipps, draper's assistant, who inherits a fortune and discovers that money cannot buy the manners, taste or confidence of the English middle class.
works.plot: Kipps inherits a legacy and is propelled into the genteel leisure class he cannot inhabit; he is humiliated at a literary society, lost among builders and servants, and finally rescued by his marriage to his childhood sweetheart Ann, and the novel ends with the small happiness of a man who has stopped trying to be something else.
works.significance: Kipps is the finest English novel of the modest man made rich and the funniest of Wells's books; its treatment of class as a matter of accent, taste and competence is a permanent contribution to the sociology of English manners.
works.meter: Prose. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.

works.title: Kirsteen
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1890
works.description: Published in 1890 and Oliphant's last great novel: a Highland girl who leaves home to make her own way in the world rather than marry as her family insists. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Margaret Oliphant; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Kirsteen Douglas, the daughter of an impoverished and tyrannical Highland laird, refuses the marriage he has arranged with the elderly Glendochart, keeping faith with Ronald Drummond, who has gone to India, and runs away to London, where she prospers as a dressmaker and businesswoman, returning home only when her father is dying and she has made her own fortune.
works.significance: Kirsteen is the fullest Victorian novel of a woman's independent working life before the New Woman novels of the 1890s: its Scottish heroine, its hard realism about money and its refusal of a conventional marriage plot make it a key text of the Victorian woman's movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1890: the Scottish Highlands and the Clearances' aftermath, the London trade in journals and prints, and the New Woman debate on work and marriage. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: Kubla Khan
altTitles: Kubla Khan: A Vision in a Dream. A Fragment.
works.form: Visionary lyric and metrical romance in verse; a dream-poem in the line of the medieval vision, written as a study in the power of sound to carry what the argument cannot complete.
works.description: A short visionary fragment published in 1816 with a prose account of its origin in a sleep induced by an anodyne on a west-country tour, when the poem is said to have risen entire in the dreamer's mind and to have been lost, except for a few hundred lines, through interruption by a person on business from the village. The poem sets the pleasure-dome of the Mongol emperor against the image of a poet able to recreate such a place in song, and ends in terror at the power of the inspired man.
works.plot: The first movement decrees the stately pleasure-dome of Kubla Khan, with its gardens bright and its walls and towers, and the rivers that run with swift ecstatic friction through forests and measureless caverns to a sunless sea. The second movement turns to the deep romantic chasm that slanted down the green hill athwart a cedarn cover, wild with the woman wailing for her demon-lover, and to the fountain that rises in suspense, flinging up half-intermitted blocks and throwing logs and kottles into the labouring cavern, until the dome and the cavern-wonders are mingled in one hearing of the thunder of the waters. The closing movement abandons the description for the poet himself: could he revive within him the hollow and inspiring song of the Abyssinian maid, he would rebuild that dome and those caves of wonder, and his hearers, seeing the gleam and hearing the music, would fear and cry aloud at the sight; for the poet has fed on the paradise of the vision and drunk the milk of its divine woman. The argument is thus an image of the imaginative act, of the palace built in the air by the poet and of the terror that attends such power.
works.significance: The most celebrated fragment in English and a central text for all later writing on dream, intoxication and imaginative creation; its pleasure-dome and its caverns of measureless depth entered the language of literary and general discourse. It is also the most quoted example of the Romantic poem that makes the interruption of vision and the failure of memory its subject.
works.meter: Irregular accentual verse of exceptional richness, with lines running from two to six beats in a scheme of recurring rhyme, internal echo and repeated words, and a marked difference of pace between the flowing opening, the agitation of the chasm and the terror of the closing lines.
works.context: Composed, on the author's own later account, in the years of the western collaboration and of the opium experiments that followed; the date has been debated on the evidence of the manuscript and of contemporaries who heard the poem read before the turn of the century, and it was printed at last in 1816 at the instance of a brother-poet then abroad.
works.characters: Kubla Khan, the emperor who decrees the dome; the poet-speaker who would recreate the vision in song; the woman wailing for her demon-lover; the Abyssinian maid with her stringed instrument
works.structure: A fragment in three movements of unequal length and without a completed argument: the scene of the dome, the chasm and its supernatural music, and the poet's visionary ambition, the transitions being made by sound and by image rather than by exposition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date and circumstances of composition are debated, reliance falling on the author's own 1816 preface and on the evidence of readers who heard the poem before 1800.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind

works.title: L'Allegro and Il Penseroso
works.description: A pair of companion poems contrasting two temperaments and ways of life: L'Allegro celebrates the active, social, cheerful mirth of the day and the countryside, while Il Penseroso praises the contemplative, melancholic, studious and religious delights of night and solitude.
works.plot: L'Allegro banishes melancholy and summons Mirth, tracing a day of rustic and urban pleasures culminating in music and masque; Il Penseroso banishes vain deluding joys and invokes 'pensive Nun', tracing a life of study, woodland meditation, church music, and a hoped-for prophetic vision.
works.significance: Among the most admired of Milton's shorter poems, they established his command of the English lyric and became models for eighteenth-century descriptive and meditative verse.
works.meter: Mixed tetrameter and pentameter couplets with varied lyric effects; the two poems mirror each other in structure.
works.context: Written during Milton's years of private study at Horton (c. 1632), published in the 1645 Poems; they reflect the Renaissance contrast of the active and contemplative lives.
works.characters: the poet; Mirth (Euphrosyne); Melancholy; the pensive Nun (Contemplation)
works.structure: Two matched lyrics in alternating tetrameter and pentameter couplets, structured as a balanced debate between the active and contemplative lives.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
Melancholy and self-analysis
The contemplative life

works.title: L'Attitude de la France à l'égard de l'esclavage
works.description: Published in 1925 and Cooper's doctoral dissertation at the Sorbonne: a study of French attitudes to slavery during the Enlightenment and the Revolution. It is a prose work of 1925 by Anna Julia Cooper; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Cooper examines the French philosophes, the revolutionary legislation and the colonial interest in slavery, and shows how the French Enlightenment's commitment to liberty co-existed with its investment in the slave economy.
works.significance: Cooper's thesis made her the fourth African-American woman to receive a doctorate and the first to write a doctoral study of French slavery; it is a significant work of black Atlantic scholarship and a key text in the history of African-American intellectual life.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is formal essay with extensive quotation.
works.context: 1925: the Sorbonne, the French colonial empire, and the emerging field of black Atlantic studies. The record dates the work as composed between 1924 and 1925 and first published in 1925 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anna Julia Haywood. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Lacnunga
works.form: medical manual and charm collection (Old English prose and verse)
works.description: A less orderly but more eclectic collection of remedies, charms, and prayers than Bald's Leechbook, compiled in the early eleventh century. It is best known for preserving the pagan-tinged metrical charms — above all the Nine Herbs Charm — alongside Christian prayers and learned Latin-derived recipes.
works.plot: The collection gathers remedies for wounds, fevers, eye and ear complaints, and childbirth, mixing herbal preparations with spoken charms and ritual instructions; its metrical charms invoke Woden and the herbs' powers while concluding with Christian formulas, in a characteristic fusion of traditions.
works.significance: The richest source of Old English charms, including the great Nine Herbs Charm, and a unique window onto the interface of learned medicine, popular healing, and pagan survival in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: The embedded charms are in alliterative verse (the Nine Herbs Charm, the Journey Charm); the surrounding recipes are plain instructional prose.
works.context: The manuscript belongs to the late Old English period's flourishing of vernacular medicine, when remedies circulated in monastic and lay households; the charms preserve elements of Germanic pre-Christian ritual under a Christian surface, a central document of the 'Christian-pagan synthesis'.
works.structure: A compilation in no strict order, grouping remedies by source rather than ailment; the metrical charms stand out from the surrounding prose as the collection's literary high points.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the name 'Lacnunga' ('Remedies') is editorial, from the first remedy's heading.
themes: Christian-pagan synthesis
Medicine, healing, and the body

works.title: Lady Audley's Secret
works.form: Sensation novel (serialised in Robin Goodfellow and the Sixpenny Magazine, 1861-62; three volumes 1862)
works.description: Serialised in 1861-62 and published in three volumes: the most successful of all English sensation novels, and the one that made the beauties of the genre into a serious argument about the law. It is a prose fiction work of 1862 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Robert Audley investigates the disappearance of his friend George Talboys and comes to suspect that his uncle's beautiful young wife, Lady Audley, is George's supposedly dead wife Helen; he pursues her through a series of disguises to a private asylum in Belgium, and the novel ends with her confession and her retirement to a maison de sante, and with Robert's marriage to Clara Talboys.
works.significance: Lady Audley's Secret is the central English sensation novel and one of the most important Victorian novels about the legal and social position of women: its heroine's crime is the logical response to a world in which a poor woman has no legal existence of her own, and the novel's use of the asylum to silence her is a direct indictment of Victorian psychiatry.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.
works.context: The 1860s, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, the private lunatic asylum trade, and the circulating-library market for three-volume fiction. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: Lady Audley (Helen Talboys); Robert Audley; George Talboys; Sir Michael Audley; Alicia Audley; Clara Talboys; Luke Marks; Phoebe Marks; Dr Mosgrave
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as M. E. Braddon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Detective Story and the Tale of Detection

Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Lady Chatterley's Lover
works.description: The gamekeeper and the lady: the most famous banned novel of the century and Lawrence's last major work. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by D. H. Lawrence; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Constance Chatterley, married to Sir Clifford, a paralysed mine-owner, begins an affair with Oliver Mellors, the gamekeeper on the estate. Through the affair she recovers her body and her sense of life, while Clifford becomes a machine-man of the industrial world; the novel ends with Mellors working on a farm and writing to her of their future.
works.significance: Lady Chatterley's Lover is the most famous banned novel of the century and the book that ended literary censorship in Britain: the 1960 Penguin trial, which acquitted it, was the decisive moment in the modern history of English publishing, and the novel itself is Lawrence's final statement about the body, the machine and the death of England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the loose, repetitive, urgent sentence driven by the rhythm of feeling and breath.
works.context: The post-war English Midlands, the coal industry, the crippled aristocracy and the new class of the technically educated industrial manager; the censorship battles that kept the book out of Britain until 1960.
works.characters: Lady Constance Chatterley; Oliver Mellors; Sir Clifford Chatterley; Mrs Bolton; Hilda Reid; Michaelis
works.structure: Nineteen chapters in the third-person, with the affair structured in fourteen numbered encounters; three versions exist.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Herbert Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Lady Susan
works.form: Epistolary novel of conduct and dissembling, inheriting the eighteenth-century letter-novel and turning it against the sentimental use of the form.
works.description: A short novel entirely in letters, dominated by a beautiful, penniless and unscrupulous widow who secures a home with her estranged in-laws, attaches their brother-in-law to herself, and markets her daughter to the richest suitor she can trap. It is the most ruthless and least reconciliatory of the early epistolary fictions of the period, and the only completed novel of its school to give the whole stage to a heroine-villain. The fair-copy manuscript in the author's hand survives.
works.plot: Lady Susan Vernon, having compromised herself in London by an intimacy with the married Mr. Manwaring, retreats to the country house of her late husband's brother, Mr. Vernon, where she flatters and plunders the credulous Sir James Martin and captivates his young kinsman Reginald De Courcy. Her daughter, the gentle Catherine, whom she means to foist upon Sir James for a dowry, is taken into the family's protection and forms friendships that defeat her mother's plan. When Manwaring's jealous husband exposes the correspondence, Lady Susan abandons Reginald, extorts a settlement for herself, and at the end marries the elderly Mr. Vernon, whose estate she will command.
works.significance: An important document of the transition from epistolary to narrated fiction, and one of the very few early nineteenth-century novels wholly controlled by a manipulative female protagonist. Its unfinished, unrepentant ending makes it a constant subject of editorial and feminist discussion. The survival of the fair-copy manuscript gives it exceptional value for the study of the period's composing habits.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; the style differentiates characters by their letters, from Lady Susan's studied blandishment to the blunt remonstrance of the country gentry.
works.context: Written in the years of the author's earliest maturity, when the letter-novel was being displaced by narrated realism and when the dependence of widows and unmarried women on male property was the dominant plot problem of women's fiction. Its cynicism about the marriage market belongs to the 1790s reaction against the doctrine of sensibility. The work remained in family hands for three quarters of a century and reached print only as an appendix to a biographical memoir.
works.characters: Lady Susan Vernon; Frederica Vernon; Reginald De Courcy; Mr. Vernon; Mrs. Johnson; Sir James Martin; Mr. Manwaring; Mrs. Manwaring; Alice Woodford
works.structure: Complete epistolary form: letters, notes and memoranda exchanged among Lady Susan, her confidante Mrs. Johnson, Catherine, De Courcy and the Manwarings, with the reader largely at the mercy of a manipulative correspondent; a brief documentary conclusion rounds the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship established by the manuscript and family tradition; no serious dispute.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Marriage and women's conduct
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Lady Windermere's Fan: A Play About a Good Woman
works.form: Play in four acts; problem play
works.description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 20 February 1892, Wilde's first great social comedy and the play that made his name in the theatre: the story of a young wife's jealousy, a mother's sacrifice and a fan left in the wrong room.
works.plot: Lady Windermere is about to leave her husband for Lord Darlington when Mrs Erlynne, a woman of doubtful reputation, intervenes; Mrs Erlynne is in fact Lady Windermere's mother, who left her husband and child twenty years before, and she sacrifices her own chance of respectability to save her daughter's marriage.
works.significance: Lady Windermere's Fan brought the moral question of the fallen woman onto the fashionable stage in a new key and established the formula of Wilde's social comedy: the society epigram enclosing a serious argument about forgiveness.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the doctrine of the 'woman with a past', the double standard, and the conventions of the well-made play. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and first performed in St James's Theatre, London, 20 February 1892 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Lady Windermere; Lord Windermere; Mrs Erlynne; Lord Darlington; the Duchess of Berwick; Lord Augustus Lorton; Cecil Graham; Lady Agatha Carlisle
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Lalla Rookh
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: a framed oriental romance sequence in the line of the Arabian tales and of eighteenth-century oriental fiction.
works.description: An oriental romance in verse in which a princess of Cashmere, travelling to her betrothed, is diverted by four tales told by an attendant poet. The frame gives the four separate romances - of the Paradise and the Peri, of the veiled prophet of Khorassan, of the fire-worshippers, and of the city of the Sultan - their common situation and their lyrical ease. It was the most financially successful poem of its decade and the volume that confirmed the poet's European fame.
works.plot: The frame follows the princess's journey towards her bridegroom's court, with the poet who rides beside her supplying tales that modulate from celestial love to religious imposture, to forbidden love under conquest, and to the magnificence and cruelty of an eastern city. Each embedded romance has its own plot: a peri's quest for acceptance into Paradise through a martyr's love; a prophet's veil and the exposure of his imposture by a detected lover; the amours of a captive prince and a fire-worshipper maid under Muslim conquest; a Sultan's clemency and a slave's self-sacrifice. The frame's own history turns on the discovery that the teller of the tales is the woman the princess is destined to love, so that romance and narrative machinery close together. The volume is unified by its treatment of love, faith and religious jealousy as the motives of eastern history. Its lyrical effusiveness and its scenery were held by later readers to exemplify both the attraction and the superficiality of Oriental romance.
works.significance: It was the best-selling English poem of its years, secured the author's international reputation, and supplied the Victorian stage and the school anthology with their stock image of the poetic East. Its framing of tale within tale was one of the most widely imitated structures of Romantic narrative verse. Later criticism treats it as the term against which a more exacting Orientalism, and a more severe lyric practice, defined themselves.
works.meter: Highly varied lyrical stanzas, including anapestic and mixed measures with frequent refrains, adapted to each embedded tale.
works.context: Published when eastern scenery, translated Arabian tales and the Oriental narratives of the period's most famous living poet had made the form a staple of the fashionable market, and when British interests in India and Persia were being extended. The poem's religious subjects engage a period fascinated and uneasy about zeal, imposture and fanaticism. Its huge advance from the publisher was itself a celebrated incident in the literary marketplace, and the volume was quickly translated across Europe.
works.characters: Lalla Rookh, princess of Cashmere; the poet who accompanies her as her guide and tale-teller; the Peri; the veiled Prophet of Khorassan; the fire-worshippers of Ispahan; the Sultan of the city
works.structure: A framed tale: a journey narrative containing four independent metrical romances, with the frame returning at the end to reveal the relation between teller and hearer.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Monsters and the marvellous
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Lament for the Makaris
works.description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
works.plot: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
works.significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
works.meter: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
works.context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
works.characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
works.structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: The Scottish Makars

works.title: Lamia
altTitles: Lamia. Isabella. The Eve of St. Agnes. Ode to a Nightingale. Ode on a Grecian Urn. To Autumn, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the fable of the enchantment and the exposure, in the couplet manner of the older romance translation, with the philosophical argument carried by the second part.
works.description: A two-part narrative poem of a serpent-woman who, having been given a human form by the magic of her lover's devotion, is destroyed at a banquet by the cold eye of a philosopher who will not let an illusion stand. It is the author's most polished couplet poem and the subtlest of his statements of the quarrel between the imaginative and the analytic life. Its first part tells the love of Lamia and a young knight of Corinth, its second the banquet and the exposure, and the moral is left unresolved.
works.plot: A serpent of golden grain, who is in truth a woman and who has been seen by a youth of Corinth in the shape of a serpent, is granted her human form by the power of the love she wakes in him, and she builds a palace of cloud and shadow for their dwelling. The pair pass into Corinth as bride and lord of a house, and the lover's friends and the whole city are drawn to the splendour of the feast, while the philosopher Apollonius, asked to the banquet by the lovers, fixes his eye upon the bride and discovers the phantom nature of the palace. At his word the illusions fall away, the bride is seen as the serpent of the field, and the lover dies of the loss; the philosopher goes on his way rebuked. The argument is that the loveliness which the imagination creates may be the only truth by which a human life can be sustained, and that the analytic knowledge which exposes it is not innocent.
works.significance: It is the most complete of the period's couplet romances and the source of the enduring formula for the sacrifice of the world's loveliness to a philosophy of cold analysis. Its two-part design, the enchantment and its exposure, became a model for later poems of the destructive intellect, and its couplets are the standard instance of the poet's mastery of a measure he was accused of not possessing.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of iambic pentameter, handled with extraordinary fluency and a sustained use of the closed line, with short interpolated lyric passages and the famous lines of the exordium in a looser movement.
works.context: Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the season which produced the great lyrics and the two titan poems, and published in the volume of July 1820 which was his last in his lifetime. Its attack on the analytic coldness of the philosopher was read at once as a squib on the metaphysics of the day, and its treatment of an illusion which knowledge destroys gave it a permanent place in the argument about the value of the imagination.
works.characters: Lamia, the serpent-woman of the field; the young knight of Corinth her lover; Apollonius the philosopher; the guests and friends of the banquet; the mother of Lamia named in the exordium
works.structure: Two parts, the first of some hundred and forty couplets on the metamorphosis and the building of the palace, the second of the banquet and the exposure, with the second part carrying the poem's reflection on the philosopher's office.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was kept for the volume of July 1820 rather than given to the periodical press, and the manuscript and the printer's copy are the basis of the modern text.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
works.plot: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
works.significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
works.characters: Lancelot; Arthur; Guinevere; Galiot
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Arthurian legend
Courtly love and fin'amor
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Last and First Men
works.description: The most ambitious future history ever written: the eighteen species of humanity over two billion years. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Olaf Stapledon; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale; Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: An unnamed narrator of the last human species tells the history of humanity from the twentieth century to the end of the solar system: the First Men destroy themselves, the Second Men rise in Patagonia, the Martian invasion, the Great Brains, the Flying Men and the Last Men on Neptune, and finally the death of the sun.
works.significance: Last and First Men is the most ambitious future history ever written and the founding text of the cosmic novel: its scale and its philosophical seriousness gave science fiction a literature it had never had.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the future history narrated by a species rather than a character.
works.context: The astronomy and biology of 1930, the aftermath of the First World War, and the philosophy of the species. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under scientific romance and the utopian tale; dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire.
works.characters: The narrator; the First Men; the Second Men; the Martians; the Last Men
works.structure: A future history in sixteen chapters, narrated from the last age of humanity. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Olaf Stapledon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Last Poems
works.description: Published in 1922 and Housman's second and last collection, written over the previous twenty-six years and published at the urging of his friends. It is a verse work of 1922 by A. E. Housman; it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: The poems return to the themes of the earlier book — the soldier, the condemned man, the indifferent landscape, the love that cannot be spoken — and add a new hardness and economy, ending with the famous 'Epitaph on an Army of Mercenaries' and a final group of poems on death.
works.significance: Last Poems shows Housman's mastery at its most concentrated and his work at its most influential: its publication in 1922 made him the most admired English lyric poet after Hardy, and its poems carried his reputation into the twentieth century as the last great Victorian classicist.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the song measure in quatrains.
works.context: 1922: the aftermath of the First World War, the publication of The Waste Land, and Housman's fame as the poet of the war generation. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: The work is in 41 poems. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred Edward Housman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
