works.title: Liberty
altTitles: Liberty, a Poem, in Three Parts
works.description: Thomson's didactic poem on civil and moral liberty, in three parts: the ancient and modern history of free states, the constitution of Britain, and the relation of liberty to the arts, commerce and the sentiments of the individual.
works.plot: The poet invokes Liberty and traces her causes and effects in commonwealths and in the British constitution, argues that trade and independence are the guardians of the state, and passes in the last part to the culture of the mind, the fine arts and the virtue which alone can preserve a free people.
works.significance: It is the century's most ambitious attempt to make the history of free government the subject of a serious didactic poem, and it supplied the vocabulary of liberty later used by the American and the British radical traditions.
works.meter: Blank verse of the seasonal manner, more declamatory and more sententious than the descriptive poems, with the apostrophic invocation.
works.context: Published in the years of the patriot-Whig opposition to the Walpole administration, when the country language of liberty, independent property and the standing army was being renewed in poetry and in the journals.
works.characters: the goddess Liberty invoked; the patriot and the statesman; the free commonwealths of the example
works.structure: Three separately issued parts, each an argument of history, reflection and apostrophe, with the inserted episodes of the Swiss and Dutch deliverers and of the patriot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society

works.title: Life and Habit
works.description: Published in 1877, the first and most important of Butler's books against Darwin: an argument that heredity is a form of memory, that the embryo 'remembers' the habits of its ancestors, and that life is a series of unconscious recollections.
works.plot: Butler argues that personal identity is continuous through the generations, that the development of the embryo is an act of memory, and that the 'variations' on which natural selection depends are themselves the result of effort and habit rather than random accident.
works.significance: Life and Habit is the founding text of the modern idea of the 'selfish gene' era's opposite — inherited memory and unconscious habit: Butler's theory influenced Bergson, the early twentieth-century biology of Hering and Semon, and the modern discussion of epigenetics and the inheritance of acquired characteristics. It is the central English contribution to the anti-Darwinian argument of the nineteenth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
works.context: The 1870s, the Darwinian controversy, the 'provisional' theory of pangenesis, and the debate on instinct and inheritance in the new biology. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1877 and first published in 1877 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Samuel Butler. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience

works.title: Life of King Alfred
works.description: Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893 by the Welsh bishop of Sherborne: the principal contemporary portrait of the king — his childhood, illnesses, wars against the Vikings, piety, and program of learning — and the main source for the Alfredian Renaissance.

works.title: Lily's Grammar
works.description: The authorized Latin grammar of the English schools, compiled from the grammars of William Lily and John Colet, edited and revised by Erasmus, and imposed by royal proclamation of Henry VIII in 1540 as the single grammar to be used in all schools.
works.plot: A textbook in two parts: the English 'Introduction of the Eight Parts of Speech' (the Accidence) and the Latin 'Brevissima Institutio' (syntax and prosody), with the famous prefatory poem 'Carmen de Moribus' on schoolboy manners.
works.significance: The most influential textbook in the history of English education: in use (as the 'Eton Grammar') for three centuries, it shaped the Latinity of every educated English writer from Shakespeare to Johnson, and its jingling rules became proverbial.

works.context: The grammar grew out of Colet's statutes for St Paul's School (c. 1509), Lily's part in its composition, and Erasmus's revisions; after Lily's death (1522) it was printed in various forms until the royal proclamation of 1540 and the authorized edition of 1549 standardized it, making it the one book every grammar-school boy knew.
works.structure: Two-part pedagogical manual, with rules, paradigms, and examples arranged for memorization.
works.attributionNotes: A collaborative compilation traditionally credited to William Lily as first high master of St Paul's; Colet and Erasmus contributed substantially, and the standard attribution to Lily is conventional rather than strictly authorial.

works.context: Translated c. 1517–23 after Linacre's Greek studies under Chalcondyles and Politian in Italy; Pynson printed the treatises in 1521–23, and they were reprinted on the continent, remaining the standard Latin Galen for over a century.

works.title: Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey
altTitles: Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey, on Revisiting the Banks of the Wye during a Tour, July 13, 1798
works.form: Nature lyric and meditation in meditative blank verse; it transforms the eighteenth-century topographical and estate poem into an inward history of perception, retaining the local naming but abandoning the picturesque tour's habits of description.
works.description: The great blank-verse meditation of the early Romantic period, written at the close of a walking tour of the Wye valley and printed as the closing poem of the 1800 edition of the ballad volume. The speaker revisits a stretch of river-bank and steep woodland after five years and asks what the remembered landscape has actually done for his mind. The poem therefore moves from precise description to a history of three successive relations to nature, and ends as an address to his companion.
works.plot: The speaker names the scene - the steep woods, the pastoral cliffs, the hedgerows, the winding river and the dwelling-places of hermits and of cottages - and insists that he sees them again as a living presence, not merely as a picture. He then reports what has happened in the interval: in earlier boyhood the delights of the landscape were animal and unthinking; in a later period they passed into trances in which the senses seemed half created to their proper office and the eye was lost in the hearing; and now, at a mature stage, there is added a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused in the light of settings suns, the deep ocean, the air and the sky, which presses into the heart of man and moves all things that think and move. From this he learns to look on nature not as in the hour of thoughtless youth but hearing, sometimes, the still sad music of humanity, and finding in it a reward for former ceaseless wanderings. The poem closes by turning to his companion, in whom he sees what he once was, and praying that she will find the same binding influence in her future life, because nature never did betray the heart that loved her; she is addressed as the anchor of his purest thoughts and the guardian of his heart.
works.significance: The central text of the Romantic meditation and the canonical instance of the idea that landscape is given to the mind in stages, so that later readers have quoted it as the period's fullest account of how nature is known. Its phrases for the music of humanity and for nature's faithfulness are among the most quoted in English, and it is the standard test case for readings of memory, loss and the growing mind.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in a single continuous flow of 159 lines; the verse is built on the sentence rather than the stanza, with elastic syntax, delayed predicates and a heavy use of semicolon and colon, and lines of the most varied pause-pattern to imitate the movement of recollected thought.
works.context: Composed in July 1798 at the end of a tour of the Wye valley, in the months before the poet's marriage and his settlement in the north-west, when the ruined abbey and its wooded valley were already a standard object of the picturesque tour. Its account of a philosophic mind formed by landscape answers both the picturesque verse of the previous generation and the associationist psychology then current.
works.characters: The meditating speaker; his sister, walking with him on the bank; the absent companions of his former wanderings in the same valley
works.structure: A single continuous meditation in one voice, organised as a movement from present perception through remembered stages of the mind to a benediction addressed to another person; the topographical frame - the naming of the place, the date, the companion - is abandoned as the argument deepens and resumed in the closing lines.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is printed from the working manuscript draft and from the 1800 text, and its title varies in the manuscript tradition, which is recorded in modern editions.

works.title: Lions and Shadows: An Education in the Twenties
works.description: Isherwood's account of his Cambridge and Berlin years, and the most entertaining memoir of the twenties. It is a prose work of 1938 by Christopher Isherwood; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Autobiography and the Modern Memoir; Biography and the Modern Life.
works.plot: Isherwood recounts his childhood, his years at Cambridge, his medical studies, his time as a tutor and his first journey to Berlin, and sketches the friends and masters who made his education — with a lightly disguised portrait of Auden, 'Hugh Weston'.
works.significance: Lions and Shadows is the most entertaining memoir of the twenties and one of the finest English autobiographies of education: its portrait of the young Auden and its comic account of the formation of a writer made it a period classic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of autobiography: the first-person narrative of the life, the set-piece of the formative scene, the quotation from letters and diaries, and the reflection on the formation of a self. works.title: Literature and Dogma: An Essay towards a Better Apprehension of the Bible
works.description: Published in 1873 and the central work of Arnold's later religious criticism: an attempt to save the Bible and the Christian moral tradition from both the dogmatic theologians and the scientific sceptics by treating the biblical language as 'literature' and 'poetry' rather than as metaphysics.
works.plot: Arnold argues that the word 'God' in the Bible is used as a term of 'the Eternal, not ourselves, that makes for righteousness', not as the name of a metaphysical person; the book examines the language of the Bible, the meaning of miracles and prophecy, and the 'Aberglaube' (extra-belief) that has overlaid the original 'verifiable' experience of righteousness.
works.significance: Literature and Dogma is the classic Victorian attempt to preserve religious experience after the collapse of dogmatic belief, and it invented the modern idea of the Bible as literature; its influence on Pater, on the modernist theology of the twentieth century and on the study of the Bible in English departments has been continuous.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: Darwin's Origin (1859) and Descent (1871), Essays and Reviews (1860), the Colenso controversy and the new biblical criticism, and the Victorian debate on the disestablishment of the Irish Church (1869).
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: Little Dorrit
works.description: Published in nineteen monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, the most sombre of the novels and the one that converts the bureaucratic inertia of the 1850s into a whole imaginative system: the Circumlocution Office, the Marshalsea debtor's prison, and the 'Nobody's Fault' of the Merdle speculation.
works.plot: Arthur Clennam returns from twenty years in China to find his mother's house inhabited by the seamstress Amy Dorrit, whose father William Dorrit has been imprisoned in the Marshalsea for twenty-three years. The Dorrits are discovered to be heirs to a fortune and leave the prison only to be destroyed by it mentally; the fortune is lost in the collapse of Merdle's bank, and Clennam is imprisoned in the same Marshalsea for debt. The novel resolves through the collapse of the house of Clennam's secret and the marriage of Arthur and Amy.
works.significance: Little Dorrit is the great Victorian novel of bureaucracy and of debt, and its Circumlocution Office entered the language as the name of institutional obstruction. Its analysis of the 'Merdle' collapse precedes the financial crises of the later century, and the prison as a metaphor of society is carried further here than anywhere else in Dickens.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Crimean War and the administrative scandals it exposed, the 'Circumlocution Office' of the permanent civil service, the bankruptcy law and the Marshalsea, and the speculative mania of the 1850s that culminated in the failure of the Royal British Bank in 1856.

works.structure: Two interlocked plots — the Dorrit inheritance and the Clennam secret — mediated by the institutional spaces of the Marshalsea and the Circumlocution Office; monthly-part structure with a late revelation.

works.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy
works.form: Novel; children's fantasy, first issued in 1886
works.description: The children's bestseller of the century: a New York street boy becomes the heir to an English earldom. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by Frances Hodgson Burnett; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Cedric Errol, a seven-year-old American boy living with his widowed mother in New York, is discovered to be the heir to the earldom of Dorincourt; he comes to England, wins over his bitter grandfather, and reforms the estate by his innocence.
works.significance: Little Lord Fauntleroy was the children's bestseller of the 1880s and the first children's book to be a transatlantic mass-market phenomenon, selling in hundreds of thousands and being dramatised all over the world. It created the modern children's classic and the image of the velvet-suited boy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The author's characteristic manner is the child's-eye view of adult failure.
works.context: New York and England in the 1880s, the transatlantic aristocracy and the American democratic faith. works.description: Published in 1871 and the sequel to Little Women: the school for boys that Jo and Professor Bhaer establish at Plumfield. works.title: Little Women
works.description: Published in two parts in 1868 and 1869 and the most beloved American family novel: the lives of the four March sisters from adolescence to marriage. works.significance: Little Women is the central American family novel and the most widely read girls' book in the world: its portrait of four sisters, its treatment of work and ambition, and its frankness about money and death made it the model for the American novel of growing up.

works.title: Lives (Walton)
altTitles: The Lives of Doctor John Donne, Sir Henry Wotton, Mr Richard Hooker, Doctor George Herbert, and Doctor Robert Sanderson
works.description: Walton's five biographies of Donne (1640), Wotton (1651), Hooker (1665), Herbert (1670), and Sanderson (1678), collected in 1670 and revised until his death in 1683; they created the modern English literary biography and the hagiographic ideal of the Anglican divine.
works.plot: Each life presents its subject as a model of Christian virtue: Donne the penitent preacher, Wotton the courtier-diplomat, Hooker the learned divine, Herbert the country parson, Sanderson the casuist.
works.significance: The Lives established Walton as the founder of English biographical prose and shaped the Anglican devotional ideal of the holy life; modern scholarship has shown their factual liberties, but their literary influence is immense.
works.meter: A deceptively simple, warm prose of anecdote and character.
works.context: Written across the civil wars, Commonwealth, and Restoration; the Life of Donne was based on Walton's personal knowledge and on Donne's own papers.

works.title: Lives of Saints
works.form: hagiography (saints' lives) in Old English prose
works.description: Ælfric's collection of saints' lives, passions, and legends (c. 993-998), composed for his patron Æthelweard: the largest vernacular hagiographical collection of the Anglo-Saxon period — virgins, martyrs, kings, and hermits of the universal church, told in Ælfric's rhythmical prose with his characteristic doctrinal care.

works.significance: The fullest vernacular hagiography of the period; the principal vehicle of the saints' cults in late Anglo-Saxon England.

works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 993-998; the principal manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Julius E.vii.

works.title: Lodore
works.form: Domestic and educational novel; a character tale of family dissolution and female formation.
works.description: A domestic novel of education and of the consequences of a father's neglect, following a soldier's son from a romantic youth through an ill-advised marriage and through the separate formation of his daughter. Its running argument is that desire is never satisfied and that character is made by accident unless it is made by principle. It belongs to the moral domestic novel of the 1830s and is one of the last long fictions its author published.
works.plot: Harcourt Lodore, rescued from a wild and dependent childhood, is educated by a kinsman, runs to sea, and at a watering-place is won by the arts of a beautiful woman without fortune or principle, whom he marries against every warning. The marriage, founded on vanity and on deception, dissolves; the daughter is left to the hazard of chance instruction, partly governed by a stern and portionless governess and partly spoiled by indulgent relatives. The middle of the book disperses the family across Europe, and the close gathers the daughter's corrected character, the deaths of the guilty and the marriage of the innocent, into a quiet settlement.
works.significance: Closes the fiction of its author's career with the period's most sustained account of the hazards of female education and of the father's failure of duty. It is a significant document of the transition from Romantic domestic romance to the Victorian novel of character formation. Its reading has grown with the recovery of the author's later work.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain moral narrative with quoted maxim and reflective aside.
works.context: Written across the years of the author's professional dependence on periodical and novel contracts, and published in the decade of the reform crisis, when the education of an heiress, the custody of children and the law of marriage were matters of active controversy. Its domestic analysis continues the didactic fiction of the preceding generation while abandoning its tale of terror. The unfinished state of its author's papers shaped the text as it appeared.
works.characters: Harcourt Lodore; his wife; their daughter; Hester, the portionless governess; the kinsman who directs the boy's education
works.structure: Third-person narrative in three volumes, alternating between the education of father and daughter; held together by interpolated reflection, letter and maxim rather than by a single plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. One personal name in the family group is not asserted here.

works.title: Logan
works.form: Frontier and Indian tragedy in prose; the border tale treated as a moral and political indictment
works.description: The first in a rapid series of American romances by the era's most combative critic, and an early and violent treatment of the Indian question as a grievance rather than a picturesque. It locates its story in the Susquehannah valley and in the border warfare of the western settlements. The book announces its author's programme of an unrivalled and undecorous native style.
works.plot: A tale of the western valleys in which an Indian war and the ruin of a household are bound together by a single provocation. The narrative dwells on the injustice that converts a people's patience into revenge, and on the fate of those caught between the settlement and the forest. Its characters speak in a bold, compressed style that refuses the decorum of the ordinary frontier tale. The action ends in death and retribution rather than in reconciliation.
works.significance: It is the boldest of the pre-removal Indian novels and the first American attempt to write border tragedy as indictment. Its style, abrupt and rhetorical, was the provocation its author later theorized in his criticism. It anchors the argument for the originality of American frontier fiction before the genre settled into a single dominant hand.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at Philadelphia in 1822, the earliest of the author's native romances and the first of a rapid series. Its treatment of Indian grievance belongs to the last years before the removal crisis of 1830. The book appeared while its author was still identified with Baltimore journalism rather than with the settled literary establishment.
works.structure: Third-person border narrative of great compression, with long rhetorical passages and abrupt shifts between settlement and forest scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the standard dating of the first edition is 1822, though some handbook accounts give 1823.

works.title: Lolly Willowes; or, The Loving Huntsman

works.title: Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market
works.description: Published in 1873 and the classic English account of the money market: a description of how the Bank of England, the bill brokers and the joint-stock banks actually worked, and an argument for the Bank's responsibility as the holder of the ultimate reserve.

works.title: London
altTitles: London: A Poem in Imitation of the Second Satire of Juvenal
works.form: verse satire in the Juvenalian manner, an Augustan 'imitation' rather than a literal translation
works.description: Johnson's first published poem, a vigorous translation-of-argument of Juvenal's third satire that replaces the ancient Rome with the London of George II. The speaker Thales retires to a remote country village rather than endure the corruption, insecurity and snobbery of the capital, while Johnson's own indignation at the treatment of the poor, the Scotch immigrant and the dependent writer breaks through the Roman mask. It is the founding document of Johnson's literary career and of his lifelong quarrel with metropolitan patronage and moneyed pride.
works.plot: Thales, disgusted with London, resolves to leave it and persuade his friend to join him in a rational rural retirement. The poem then catalogues the evils of the city: the insecurity of property, the tyranny of the rich over the poor, the degeneracy of the great house and its flattered heir, the corruption of the law, the theatre and the court, and the insolence of wealth in high life. Scottish poverty and the waves of immigration south are given a famous passage of indignation, and the embers of Roman jealousy of foreign arts are turned on the fashionable importation of Italian opera and Continental taste. The conclusion returns to the defence of honest poverty, the pleasures of study and the hope that verse may preserve virtue from contagion.
works.significance: The poem announced Johnson as the leading satiric voice of the generation after Pope and established the moral vocabulary - independence, dependence, the dignity of poverty, suspicion of commercial splendour - that informs Rasselas and the periodical essays. Its handling of the Scottish immigrant makes it a central text for eighteenth-century writing about the nations, and its couplet practice widened the Augustan line for later moral poets.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with a heavy, polysyllabic and Latinate diction, occasional triple and dactylic rhymes, and long periodic sentences running across several couplets.
works.context: Written after Johnson's failed schoolmastership at Market Bosworth and his London literary apprenticeship, and published in the politically charged years of Walpole's ministry, when the excise scheme of 1737 and the growing quarrel with Spain had made the rhetoric of national corruption and ministerial influence a everyday subject of debate. Its attack on corrupt wealth and on the treatment of dependents addressed the anxieties of the newly professional Grub Street letters that Pope and Swift had already mapped.
works.characters: Thales; Astrella; Licentia; Corydon; the unnamed friend and addressee
works.structure: A single sustained argument in two loosely joined movements, the invective against London and the praise of retirement, framed as a dialogue between Thales and an unnamed friend and closed by an address to the muse; the Juvenalian progression is interrupted by strongly personal passages.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship is documented by his own publication and by later bibliographical and copyright evidence.

works.title: London Nights
works.description: Published in 1895 and the central collection of English Decadent city poetry: the poems of the music hall, the ballet, the prostitute's room and the London night. It is a verse work of 1895 by Arthur Symons; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.

works.significance: London Nights is the founding book of English urban Decadence and one of the first English collections to make the music hall and the streetwalker the subjects of serious lyric: its poetry of the city night made possible the urban poetry of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short lyric built on a single mood.

works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.description: The poetry of the Victorian poor: the outcast, the magdalen and the London night. works.title: Looking Backward: 2000-1887
works.description: The most influential American utopia ever written: a Bostonian wakes in the year 2000. works.title: Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries
altTitles: Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries; with Recollections of the Author's Life, and of His Visit to Italy
works.form: A prose memoir and work of literary criticism in the Romantic biographical tradition, close to the character-writing of Hazlitt and to the personal memoir, and built around the review-essay. Its constituent genres are biography, autobiography, personal sketch and the long examination of a single poem, and it belongs to the literature of the periodical even where it is not periodical in form, since its criticism is occasional, argumentative and addressed to a subscribing public interested in living reputations.
works.description: Hunt's memoir of Byron and record of their years in Italy, published in London in 1828 in two volumes with recollections of his own life and of the southern sojourn of 1821 to 1825. It is at once a defence of Byron's character, an account of the circle at Pisa and Genoa, a piece of autobiographical exposure and, in its long examination of Don Juan, one of the most ambitious critical essays of the decade. The book gave Hunt his most damaging quarrel with the powerful, because it mixed admiration for his dead friend with frank statement of his own opinions on living authors, and because its candour about its own period made it an authority and a scandal in the same breath.
works.plot: The work sets out to vindicate Byron against the calumnies of his publishers and reviewers, to describe the Italy in which he lived and died, and to give an honest account of Hunt's own dealings with him. Its argumentative core is the Examen of Don Juan, a long critical examination that insists on the poem's seriousness and moral intention against the consensus that it was a degradation of Byron's powers. Between these essays come sketches of contemporaries, recollections of the Hunt brothers and of the Examiner years, and narratives of the journey to Italy, of the society of the Pisan circle and of Byron's last plans. The book's purpose, as its title suggests, is to place Byron within a living literature rather than to bury him in anecdote.
works.significance: It is the principal contemporary witness to Byron's last years from inside his circle, and one of the earliest and most substantial critical defences of Don Juan, a claim for the poem's gravity that later readers have largely accepted. As autobiography it is the fullest account Hunt left of the Examiner years, of the imprisonment and of the London literary world that formed Keats and Shelley, and its sketches of contemporaries are still quarried by biographers. As criticism it marks the moment at which the familiar essay of sympathy was turned on the largest Romantic poem of the age, and it is central to the history of how the Romantics judged one another.
works.meter: Prose, in Hunt's familiar manner: open, conversational, digressive and unforced, with the sententious brevity of the essayist alternating with the longer amble of reminiscence. Verse is quoted throughout for evidence, especially from Don Juan, and the critical passages are shaped by the rhythm of spoken argument rather than by periodic art. There is no metrical composition in the work itself; its prosody is that of prose rhythm and of the quoted lines it is written to defend.
works.context: Published three years after Byron's death and after Hunt's return from Italy, the book enters the crowded field of Byron memoirs produced since 1823, when publishers, relations and friends competed to define the poet's memory against the attacks of the quarterly press. It also belongs to the history of British literary exile in Italy, to the Pisa circle of Shelley, Byron and their acquaintances, and to the campaign of reputation in which Hunt, now dependent on his pen and on subscription, attempted to speak for a generation. Its reception shows how dangerous such candour was: reviewers of the established journals received it as an act of Cockney presumption, and it deepened the quarrels that had already cost Hunt friends.
works.characters: Leigh Hunt; Lord Byron; the Pisan and Genoa circle of 1821-1825; contemporary authors discussed and characterised
works.structure: Two volumes arranged as memoir, recollection and critical essay rather than as a continuous narrative: the biographical account of Byron is interrupted by general criticism, by episodes from Hunt's own life and by portraits of other writers, and the Examen of Don Juan forms the largest single block of sustained argument. There is no chronological spine strong enough to hold the whole together; the ordering principle is the sequence of Hunt's memories and his cases. The result is a mixed form, part memoir, part criticism, part apology, in which the recollecting self is as prominent as the subject.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Hunt is certain and appears on the title page of the first issue; the work is, however, a mixed compilation in method, resting heavily on his letters, diaries and personal recollection, and its truth as testimony has long been qualified by reviewers who found its self-interest and its errors of fact irrepressible. There is no dispute about by whom it was written, only about how far it can be trusted as evidence, and much of its later history lies in the corrections and rejoinders it provoked from Byron's friends and from the quarterly press.

works.title: Lord Jim
works.description: The story of a young first mate who abandons a sinking ship and spends the rest of his life trying to recover his honour. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Joseph Conrad; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Jim, the chief mate of the Patna, jumps from the ship with the officers when it seems certain to sink with 800 pilgrims aboard; the ship does not sink, and Jim is publicly disgraced at the inquiry. He moves from port to port, and finally to Patusan, a remote Malayan settlement, where he becomes 'Tuan Jim' and the trusted ruler of the people — until the pirate Gentleman Brown's raid and the death of Dain Waris destroy him, and he goes to his death willingly.
works.significance: Lord Jim is Conrad's greatest novel and one of the finest studies of moral failure in English: it made 'one of us' a permanent phrase, invented the technique of the multiple retrospective narration (Marlow collecting Jim's story from others), and gave the twentieth-century novel its central subject — the man who fails his own code and cannot be forgiven. It is the bridge between the Victorian sea story and the modern psychological novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
works.context: The age of sail's last years and the Malay Archipelago of the 1880s; the code of the sea, the merchant marine inquiry and the imperial adventurer. Conrad's own experience as a master mariner and his reading of the East gave the novel its exact detail.
works.characters: Jim; Charles Marlow; Captain Brierly; Doramin; Dain Waris; Jewel; Gentleman Brown

works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1698 and published in 1699; Farquhar was a young Irish actor turned playwright after a stage accident.
works.characters: Roebuck; Lucinda; Leanwell; Clear; Sabina; Mrs Gainall; Lyrick
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Farquhar; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Love and Freindship
works.form: Juvenilia burlesque and epistolary parody of the novel of sensibility.
works.description: A burlesque epistolary tale of juvenile sensibility, written for family entertainment and headed 'Written at the Age of 14', in which every convention of the sentimental novel is pushed to absurdity. Its heroine narrates her own trials in a style of exhausted rapture, collapsing, eloping, disinheriting and weeping through a series of improbabilities. The surviving notebook copy preserves the author's original spelling of the title.
works.plot: Laura, an orphan left with an unkind guardian, falls in love with Edward, his son, and is banished; her friend Marianne, rich and self-dramatising, alternately supports and abandons her. Patrons, elopements and revivals of fortune succeed one another without pause, and feeling itself is treated as a physical malady producing fainting, delirium, loss of property and rapid recovery. The tale closes in marriages and a general reconciliation of the sentimental plot machinery, with the correspondents comfortably supplied with income.
works.significance: The earliest substantial evidence of a school of ironic treatment of sensibility that would mature into the regulated irony of the published novels. As a manuscript culture document it is much cited in studies of juvenile writing, family circulation and women's reading in the 1790s. Its survival lets scholars trace the making of a mature narrative voice from parody.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; deliberately over-wrought sentimental diction with mock-heroic exaggeration, the notebooks also preserving accompanying verse fragments.
works.context: Composed in the family reading circle of the late 1780s and early 1790s, when circulating-library fiction of feeling was at its height and parody of it was a household amusement. The manuscript belonged to a set of exercise and tale notebooks circulated among siblings and copied out for entertainment. It was not offered for publication and remained in private hands.
works.characters: Laura, the self-dramatising heroine-narrator; Marianne, her friend and correspondent; Edward, her guardian's son; Sir Edward, a rival suitor of sentimental rhetoric
works.structure: A novel in a series of letters, with abrupt recapitulations and a self-conscious narrator who comments on the speed of her own sufferings; the parody depends on the gap between the letter-writer's rhetoric and the triviality of the events reported.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship established by the manuscript notebooks; no dispute.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Love and Honour
works.description: Davenant's tragi-comedy of love tested by honour, in which a noble lady disguises herself as a poor servant to try the constancy of her lover before the war separates them.
works.plot: Evadne, beloved of the noble Prothall, disguises herself to test his faith; a series of misunderstandings, a supposed death, and a battlefield reunion resolve the conflict between love and honour.
works.significance: Davenant's first major success and a key example of Caroline tragicomedy; it also shows the beginnings of his interest in music and spectacle that would produce The Siege of Rhodes.
works.meter: Blank verse with songs.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1634 and published in Davenant's collected Plays of 1639.
works.characters: Evadne; Prothall; Alphonso; Melora; the Duke; Aurelio
works.structure: Five acts with a disguise-testing plot and a final recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling
altTitles: A Hymn for the Inner Room
works.description: Charles Wesley's great hymn of sanctifying love, a short lyric in which the soul prays to be bound to its Lord and made all the love it beholds. It stands among the most admired hymns in English and among the highest achievements of Charles Wesley's later Bristol period.
works.plot: The hymn opens on the captive soul's address to divine love, fixed and bound by the bands of its own choosing, and moves through petition for the lamp of pure flame and anticipation of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Its central desire is entire consecration, that the heart be fixed, abiding, and cleaving to its God, and the closing stanzas ask the loss of self in God, the soul dyed with the love of Christ, and a close in praise. The argument is Methodist perfectionism turned into lyric yearning, doctrine as amorous address. Each stanza advances the surrender one degree farther toward the wish to be all love.
works.significance: A summit of English hymnody and of the lyric of religious desire, anthologized universally and the model of the Methodist sanctification hymn; its imagery shaped later devotional verse and hymn-tune pairing.
works.meter: Stanzas of the eight-syllable trochaic seven-line measure known in hymnals as 7.7.7.7.7.7.7, with paired internal rhymes that give the verse its urgency; the received text runs to six stanzas and is now sung to tunes such as HYFRYDOL and NICAEA.
works.context: Composed at Bristol in 1762, in Charles Wesley's mature season of hymns for the societies' social worship and the inner room, the year of his wife's death and of some of his deepest lyrics, though the hymn's own first appearance is disputed among the small collections of these years.
works.structure: A single continuous lyric in six stanzas, from captivity and petition to union and doxology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Evangelical experience and assurance
The contemplative life
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Love for Love
works.description: Congreve's most popular comedy, in which the improvident Valentine, disinherited by his father and pressed by his creditors, feigns madness to escape a forced marriage and finally wins Angelica.
works.plot: Valentine signs away his inheritance to Trapland and Forester; his father Sir Sampson Legend tries to marry him to Miss Prue; the scheming Angelica and the mad prophet Tattle are entangled until the plot resolves in Valentine's recovery and marriage.
works.significance: The most frequently revived of Congreve's comedies in his own lifetime and a principal model for eighteenth-century comedy; its treatment of debt and disinheritance is unusually sharp social commentary.
works.meter: Prose of great variety, from high wit to coarse farce.
works.context: First performed at the new Lincoln's Inn Fields Theatre on 30 April 1695, the opening of the breakaway actors' company under Betterton, and published the same year.
works.characters: Valentine; Angelica; Sir Sampson Legend; Ben Legend; Tattle; Mrs Frail; Miss Prue; Foresight; Jeremy; Trapland; Buckram; Scandal
works.structure: Five acts with a rich comic subplot of the nurse, the astrologer Foresight, and the country Miss Prue.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park
works.description: Wycherley's first comedy, a sprawling intrigue play set in St James's Park, in which masked gallants and ladies pursue one another through a series of night adventures.
works.plot: Several couples are entangled in the fashionable world of the Park and the Exchange; disguises, duels, and betrayals are resolved in a set of marriages, with the virtuous Dapperwit exposed as a wit.
works.significance: An early and uneven but energetic comedy that anticipates Wycherley's later severity; its portrait of the Park is a valuable document of Restoration London.
works.meter: Prose dominant with some verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1671 and published in 1672, dedicated to the Duchess of Cleveland.
works.characters: Ranger; Vincent; Lydia; Martha; Dapperwit; Mrs Crossbite; Alderman Gripe; Simon
works.structure: Five acts with multiple plots and a low comic subplot of the city.

works.title: Love in Excess; or, The Fatal Enquiry
altTitles: Love in Excess: Or, The Fatal Enquiry
works.form: prose romance; amatory novel in several parts
works.description: The first and most ambitious of the amatory novels of its period, issued in parts over several years and built as a chain of interlaced histories of passion, seduction and betrayal. It sets the pattern of the long romance of the erring lover that its author afterwards dominated, and its tales of ruined women are narrated with a rhetoric of pity.
works.plot: A young gentleman of fortune pursues an heiress and meets refusals, while in the tales within the narrative other lovers are tried by seduction, discovery and revenge. Brothers and rivals abduct, disguise and betray; women of condition are ruined by inquiry into their past, and the several histories converge through letters and unexpected recognitions. The closing parts resolve the errors by revelation of birth and the forgiveness of the offended.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the amatory novel as a long form and the work that made its author the central female prose fiction-writer of the 1720s; its treatment of female complicity and male constancy shaped the genre down to the novelists of the 1740s.
works.meter: High romantic prose of apostrophe, exclamation and elaborated syntax, with letters and reported speeches; the style is consciously ornamented and emotionally intensified.
works.context: Published in parts between 1719 and 1722 in the efflorescence of the three-volume romance, succeeding the translation-based fashion and competing directly with the scandalous fiction of the same booksellers.
works.structure: A serial multi-volume romance with embedded tales and a frame of continuous narration; the interlacing of stories is deliberate and the sequence of parts extends the suspense over years of publication.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the parts were published with the author's name after the success of the early issues, and she reissued the whole in revised form in the following decade.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: Love in Idleness
works.description: Rattigan's comedy of the returning son: the mother, the tycoon and the young communist. It is a dramatic work of 1944 by Terence Rattigan; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: Olivia Marlowe has lived for years with a rich industrialist, Sir John Fletcher; her son Michael returns from the war a convinced communist, refuses to accept his mother's position or her protector's money, and the comedy runs through the quarrel between mother and son until Michael accepts that love is not a matter of ideology.
works.significance: Love in Idleness is Rattigan's comedy of the war years and the first of his post-war successes: its quarrel between the mother and the returned son, its politics and its sentiment made it one of the most popular plays of 1944 and the bridge between the drawing-room comedies of the thirties and the serious plays of The Browning Version and The Winslow Boy.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the tight three-act construction with a single set and a small cast.
works.context: England in the closing years of the Second World War, and the household of the rich man and the returned soldier. The record dates the work as composed between 1943 and 1944 and first published in 1944 and first performed in 1944 and the corpus places it within The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners, it is catalogued under comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Olivia Marlowe; Sir John Fletcher; Michael Marlowe; Mrs Barlow
works.structure: A comedy in three acts. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A comedy in acts, the scene built as a succession of entrances, revelations and exits, with the social convention breached and restored.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Terence Mervyn Rattigan. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Love on the Dole
works.form: Novel; proletarian novel, first issued in 1933
works.description: The great novel of the Depression: Salford, unemployment and the destruction of a family. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by Walter Greenwood; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Harry Hardcastle leaves school in 1926 and finds no work but the dole; his father is crippled in the mill, his sister is driven to the streets, and the family is broken by unemployment in a Salford slum in the years of the Depression.
works.significance: Love on the Dole is the great English novel of the Depression and the finest proletarian novel of the period: its documentary accuracy and its anger made it the most influential book of the 1930s and it was banned by the BBC and adapted into a celebrated play.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, documentary, unadorned prose.
works.context: Salford and the industrial North in the Depression of the early 1930s, and the means test. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1933 and first published in 1933 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Harry Hardcastle; Sally Hardcastle; Mr Hardcastle; Mrs Hardcastle; Larry Meath; Helen
works.structure: A novel in four parts, following the family through the Depression. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Love Won
works.description: The second of the Mirror in Darkness: the career and the marriage. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Storm Jameson; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama.
works.plot: Love Won continues Hervey Russell's story through the success of the first novel, the second marriage and the work of the decade, in the middle book of the trilogy.
works.significance: Love Won carries the trilogy's woman writer through the career and the second marriage, and keeps the decade's politics at the edge of the domestic novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of the woman's career in the prose of the decade.
works.context: London and Europe in the mid-1930s. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Hervey Russell; the second husband; the literary and political London
works.structure: The second of a trilogy: the success and the second marriage. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Margaret Storm Jameson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Love's Labour's Lost
works.description: Shakespeare's most verbally extravagant comedy: the King of Navarre and his three lords swear a three-year vow of study, fasting, and no women — a vow broken at once by the arrival of the Princess of France and her ladies, whose wit outmatches the men's until the play's astonishing turn: news of the Princess's father's death converts the comedy into a year of penance and a set of unfinished songs.
works.plot: The lords woo the ladies in disguise and are exposed; the pedants Holofernes and Nathaniel stage the pageant of the Nine Worthies and are mocked; and just as the marriages are to be concluded, Marcade enters with the news of the French king's death, and the ladies impose their year-long conditions on the suitors.
works.significance: The summit of Elizabethan verbal comedy and the play in which Shakespeare's lyric genius first runs free.
works.meter: The highest proportion of rhyme in Shakespeare, with sonnets, songs, and the prose of the pedants' Latinity.
works.context: Written about 1594–95 amid the French succession crisis and the Euphuistic wordplay fashion it both satirizes and surpasses; first printed in quarto, 1598.
works.characters: Ferdinand, King of Navarre; Berowne; Longaville; Dumaine; the Princess of France; Rosaline; Maria; Katherine; Boyet; Don Armado; Holofernes; Nathaniel; Costard; Jaquenetta; Moth
works.structure: A plotless, tournament-like comedy of wit built on symmetrical scenes of courtship, masque, and pageant, ending in the deliberately anti-comic 'dialogue' of Spring and Winter songs.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Wisdom and learning
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Love's Last Shift; or, The Fool in Fashion
works.description: Colley Cibber's first comedy, in which the rake Loveless is reformed by his long-suffering wife Amanda; the play's famous double structure — libertine comedy in the first half, moral reform in the second — provoked Vanbrugh's answer in The Relapse.
works.plot: Loveless, believing Amanda a stranger, seduces her in disguise; she reveals herself and he is reformed; the comic subplot of Sir Novelty Fashion satirises the fashionable fop.
works.significance: Usually cited as the first sentimental comedy in English and the pivot between Restoration libertinism and eighteenth-century moral reform; Cibber's career as actor-manager of Drury Lane shaped the Georgian stage.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in January 1696 with Cibber himself as Sir Novelty Fashion; the role made him famous and the play was a great success.
works.characters: Loveless; Amanda; Sir Novelty Fashion; Young Worthy; Snap; Narcissa; Flareit
works.structure: Five acts with a sharp generic shift at the centre that critics have called the origin of sentimental comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cibber; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Love's Sacrifice
works.description: Ford's tragedy of unwarranted jealousy, in which the Duke of Pavy, persuaded by his secretary Nibrassa, believes his duchess Bianca unfaithful to him with his friend Fernando, and kills her before learning the truth.

works.title: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
works.description: Behn's epistolary novel in three parts, based on the real scandal of Lord Grey of Warke's elopement with his wife's sister, in which Philander seduces Silvia and she descends through a series of lovers into prostitution and political intrigue.
works.plot: Philander writes to Silvia, his sister-in-law; they elope; he tires of her and takes another mistress; Silvia responds by seducing and abandoning a series of men, becoming a courtesan and finally a political agent of Monmouth's rebellion.
works.significance: The first major English epistolary novel and a decisive step toward the eighteenth-century novel of Richardson and Laclos; its portrayal of a woman's sexual and political agency was unprecedented.
works.meter: Prose with interpolated verse.
works.context: Published in three parts between 1684 and 1687, at the time of the Monmouth Rebellion; it is a roman à clef on the Grey-Sisters scandal.
works.characters: Philander; Silvia; Calista; Octavio; Don Alonzo; Cesario; the Countess
works.structure: Three parts (1684, 1685, 1687) of letters with narrative interludes, the first substantial English epistolary fiction.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in parts; attribution to Behn is long-established and undisputed.

works.title: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated
altTitles: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated into English Verse
works.description: Rowe's verse translation of Lucan's civil-war epic, the work by which the English reader of the early century knew the wars of Caesar and Pompey and the Stoic Cato.
works.plot: The translation follows Lucan's argument of the breach between Caesar and Pompey, the flight from Rome, Pharsalia and the suicide of Cato, with the poet's own reflections on the loss of Roman liberty running through the narrative.
works.significance: It was the standard English Lucan of the first half of the century, and its translator was later made the point of a satiric joke about the rendering that outdoes its original.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of the regular Augustan kind, straining to carry Lucan's declamation and his apostrophes.
works.context: Published in the years when the republicanism and the liberty of the Roman commonwealth were being read into the quarrels of the British constitution, and when the translation of the classics had become a profession's work.
works.characters: Caesar; Pompey; Cato; Lucan as the translated author
works.structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the ten books of the Pharsalia, with the preface, the arguments and the explanatory notes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the volume's later issues were revised and part of the prefatory matter has been assigned to another hand.

works.title: Lucasta
works.description: Richard Lovelace's collection of Cavalier verse (1649), named for his mistress Lucy Sacheverell ('Lucasta'), containing his most famous lyrics — 'To Althea, from Prison', 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars', and 'The Grasshopper' — which made the code of love and honour the motto of the royalist gentleman.
works.plot: The poems celebrate love, friendship, loyalty, and liberty of spirit even in prison and defeat, arguing that honour and constancy survive political ruin ('Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage').
works.significance: Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; 'To Althea' and 'To Lucasta' are among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century and define royalist gallantry.
works.meter: Musical, dignified lyrics in varied meters with argumentative conceits of love and honour.
works.context: Lovelace prepared the collection during his imprisonment in the Gatehouse (1648–49) for his royalist loyalty; it was published in 1649, the year of the regicide.
works.characters: the poet; Lucasta; Althea; fellow Cavaliers
works.structure: A collection of songs, odes, elegies, and occasional verse unified by the Cavalier ethos and the figure of Lucasta.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; a posthumous second part appeared in 1659/60.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Loyalty and the comitatus bond

works.title: Lucius Junius Brutus, Father of His Country
works.description: Lee's republican tragedy on the expulsion of the Tarquins and the founding of the Roman republic, banned by the Lord Chamberlain in 1680 for its allegedly republican politics.
works.plot: Brutus feigns idiocy under the tyrant Tarquin; after the rape of Lucretia he leads the revolt, and sacrifices his own sons for treason rather than betray the new republic.
works.significance: An important document of Whig political sentiment in the drama and a forerunner of the eighteenth-century republican tragedies of Addison and Thomson; its suppression is a classic case of Restoration censorship.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Prohibited from performance in 1680 by the Lord Chamberlain on the ground that it contained 'very scandalous expressions and reflections upon monarchical government'; printed in 1681 during the Exclusion Crisis.
works.characters: Lucius Junius Brutus; Tarquin; Lucretia; Teraminta; Titus; Tiberius; Collatinus; Herminius
works.structure: Five acts of political tragedy culminating in the hero's filial sacrifice.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lee; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Lusty Juventus
works.description: A Protestant morality interlude of the youth Juventus, tempted by Hypocrisy and the devil but restored by Good Counsel and God's Merciful Promises; printed c. 1550 with the author's name given as R. Wever.
works.plot: Juventus (Youth), fresh from his conversion, is tempted by the devil's instruments — Hypocrisy, Fellowship, and Abominable Living — who draw him into sin and despair; Good Counsel and Knowledge recall him, God's Merciful Promises assures him of forgiveness through Christ, and the play ends with Juventus's restoration and a call to the audience to follow his example.
works.significance: The most explicitly doctrinal of the Edwardian moralities and a prime example of the interlude as Reformation propaganda; its title character became the proverbial type of the reformed youth.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed in the early years of the Edwardian Reformation (c. 1547–53) and printed c. 1550; its polemic against hypocrisy and works-righteousness and its emphasis on justification by faith make it a direct dramatic expression of Protestant doctrine for a young audience.
works.characters: Juventus; Good Counsel; Knowledge; God's Merciful Promises; The Devil; Hypocrisy; Fellowship; Abominable Living
works.structure: A continuous morality play of temptation, fall, and restoration, with the devil and Hypocrisy as the comic Vices and a concluding address to the young.
works.attributionNotes: The title page names 'R. Wever' as author; nothing further is known of him, and the ascription cannot be independently confirmed.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: Lycidas
works.description: Milton's pastoral elegy for Edward King, a Cambridge contemporary drowned off the Irish coast in 1637, written for the memorial volume Justa Edouardo King; it mourns the young poet's death, indicts the corrupt clergy, and consoles with the promise of resurrection and fame in heaven.
works.plot: The shepherd-poet mourns Lycidas, questions divine justice, invokes the Muse and St Peter (who denounces the 'blind mouths' of the corrupt church), hears the tale of Lycidas's drowning and apotheosis, and finds consolation in the belief that he is 'sunk low, but mounted high' as the genius of the shore.
works.significance: Widely regarded as the greatest pastoral elegy in English, Lycidas combines personal grief, political and religious satire, and visionary consolation in a uniquely wrought form.
works.meter: A varied and intricately rhymed pastoral stanza of irregular line lengths, with carefully placed short lines and refrains.
works.context: Written in 1637 for the collection Justa Edouardo King Naufrago (1638); it draws on the pastoral elegiac tradition from Theocritus and Virgil to Spenser, transfigured by Milton's Puritan faith and anticlerical anger.
works.characters: the uncouth swain (Milton); Lycidas (Edward King); St Peter; the Muse; Jove
works.structure: A pastoral elegy in irregular verse, moving from grief and doubt through the prophetic denunciation by St Peter to Christian consolation and the poet's turn to 'pastures new'.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; signed 'J.M.' in the 1638 volume and included in the 1645 Poems.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Religious persecution and martyrdom
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Lyra Apostolica
works.form: Poetry collection (contributions with Newman and Froude)
works.description: Published in the British Magazine in 1833-36 and as a collection in 1836, with contributions by Keble, Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude: the poetry of the Oxford Movement's first generation, and the verse that gave the Tractarians their militant and penitential tone.
works.plot: The poems are short lyrics and sonnets on the Church, the sacraments, the power of the priesthood and the corruption of the age, many of them written on the Continental tour of Newman and Froude in 1832-33.
works.significance: Lyra Apostolica is the primary poetic document of the Oxford Movement and the source of much of the devotional language of Victorian Anglo-Catholicism; its sonnets are among the earliest Victorian examples of the devotional sequence.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood.
works.context: The 1833 assize sermon and the founding of the Tracts, the Oxford Movement's early militancy, and the Romantic inheritance of Wordsworth and Scott in religious verse. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1836 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: The work is recorded as a joint undertaking with John Henry Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude, the contribution of each being stated in the work-author relationship. Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience

works.title: Lyrical Ballads
altTitles: Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems
works.form: Lyrical ballad and popular-stanza narrative, together with the conversation poem and the dramatic dialogue; the volume draws on the revived antiquarian ballad tradition of the 1790s while abandoning its artificial diction.
works.description: A small anonymous volume of twenty-three poems issued in the autumn of 1798 by two friends then living in the southwest of England. The supernatural narrative ballad that opens the book is by one hand and most of the shorter lyrics, tale-poems and conversation pieces by the other, so that the volume is an experiment in two related manners rather than a single voice. Its programme - later stated in the Preface of 1800 - was to treat incidents and situations from humble and common life in language really used by men, with a colouring of imagination that would give the appearance of novelty to familiar things.
works.plot: The poems fall into three loose kinds. Long narrative ballads of guilt and penance supply the volume's emblem: a mariner kills an albatross gratuitously, is struck by a curse that leaves him the only survivor of his ship's company, and is condemned to tell his tale to each stranger he meets until the pain of the telling passes into love for all created things. Shorter tale-poems observe madness, destitution and superstition without moralising, letting an unreliable or agitated speaker make the story as he reports it. A third group of brief conversation lyrics and dialogues - a child who insists she is still seven although two of her siblings are dead, an old soldier and his solitary labour, a mother and her infant in the woods - locate moral instruction in the voice and the situation rather than in the poet's comment. The organising principle is therefore not plot but a stated policy of subject and diction.
works.significance: Conventionally taken as the opening act of the English Romantic period, and the practical demonstration of a poetics of ordinary speech, humble life and imaginative colouring. Its ballads made the supernatural tale and the rustic conversation poem central to Romantic verse, and its theory of feeling recollected in tranquillity became the most quoted account of how poems are made.
works.meter: Principally the common metre and short ballad stanza of nursery and popular song, sometimes deliberately roughened and sometimes irregularly truncated; the long ballad uses an archaic eight- and nine-line stanza with a repeating refrain-word, the dialogue poems use plain blank verse or couplet-adjacent quatrains, and the meditative pieces are in unrhymed iambic pentameter.
works.context: Composed in the years following the disappointment of the English hope raised by the French Revolution, during a retirement on Exmoor and in the Welsh and western borders, when an antiquarian ballad revival had already made popular stanza forms respectable again. The anonymous first edition was reviewed as the work of a single author and attacked for its meanness of subject and its prosaic diction, which drew out the explicit apology of the next edition's Preface.
works.characters: The Ancient Mariner; the Wedding-Guest; the Pilot and his son; Martha Ray of the thorn; the Mad Mother and her infant; the child who maintains that she is seven; Simon Lee and his young neighbour; Goody Blake and Harry Gill
works.structure: An anonymous collection rather than a designed sequence, with no frame narrative; the arrangement is rhetorical, opening on the long Romantic ballad, passing through tale-poems and dramatic dialogues, and closing on short meditative lyrics. Individual structures carry the diversity: the Mariner's tale-within-a-tale with its marginal gloss, monologues addressed to an overhearer, and single-voice conversation poems.
works.attributionNotes: Issued anonymously and at first reviewed as a single author's work; the division of poems between the two contributors is settled by their later collected editions, in one of which the Mariner's ballad was placed under a separate head with its own explanatory note.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse

Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The supernatural ballad and willed belief

works.title: Lyrical Tales
works.form: Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza; Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Lyric
works.description: Mary Robinson's last and most remarkable volume of poetry, a collection of narrative and lyrical tales published in 1800 and designed as a direct answer to the Lyrical Ballads of Wordsworth and Coleridge. Its ballads, metrical tales, and lyrics take as their subjects the outcast, the imprisoned, the abandoned woman, the emigrant, and the poor, in a deliberately popular stanzaic style; the volume asserts against the Lake poets an alternative theory of poetic subject, diction, and feeling, and it is now recognized as one of the central poetical books of its decade.
works.plot: The poems tell short stories of distress and endurance: women betrayed and cast off, prisoners and exiles, old and destitute figures of the street and the coast, and lovers separated by fortune or death; each tale converts a situation of suffering into an appeal to sympathy, and several reflect on the poet's own exposure, dependence, and fame, so that the volume's argument is at once political, moral, and personal.
works.significance: Lyrical Tales is the most complete attempt by a contemporary of Wordsworth to write an alternative book of Lyrical Ballads, and its recovery has changed the account of English verse around 1800; it shows the ballad and the metrical tale being used by a woman poet for a social argument about poverty, seduction, and exile, and it stands as one of the founding documents of popular Romanticism.
works.meter: Ballad and popular stanzaic measures - octosyllabic and alternately rhymed quatrains, lyric stanzas, and simple repeated refrains - with a deliberately plain diction that imitates and answers the theory of Lyrical Ballads while keeping the music of her earlier verse.
works.context: Published after the Lyrical Ballads of 1798 had made the tale of humble distress a school of poetry, and in the year of Robinson's final illness and death; printed for Longman and Rees by a Bristol firm and paid for at a sum recorded in the publisher's books, the volume compresses her whole career's concern with reputation, dependence, and the suffering of women into a popular form.
works.characters: the betrayed and abandoned heroines of the tales; prisoners, exiles, and emigrants; the aged and destitute figures of the street and coastal ballads; the poet's own speaker of the reflective numbers
works.structure: A collection of separate lyrical tales and ballads, some in dialogue and some in continuous narrative, arranged so that the popular stanzaic tales and the more reflective lyrics balance one another; there is no single organizing plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Lyrics of Lowly Life
works.form: Poetry collection (with an introduction by William Dean Howells)
works.description: Published in 1896 with an introduction by William Dean Howells and the book that made Dunbar famous: the dialect poems of the old plantation and the standard English lyrics of love, grief and race. It is a verse work of 1896 by Paul Laurence Dunbar; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection includes 'The Old Cabin', 'A Banjo Song', 'When Malindy Sings', 'Sympathy' ('I know what the caged bird feels'), 'We Wear the Mask', and the elegy 'Frederick Douglass'.
works.significance: Lyrics of Lowly Life is the founding book of African-American poetry and the volume through which Dunbar became the first black American poet of national reputation: 'We Wear the Mask' and 'Sympathy' are among the most important poems in American literature.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill.
works.context: 1896: the American plantation tradition, the Chicago World's Fair of 1893, and the black literary market of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Paul Dunbar. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
