works.title: Mac Flecknoe
altTitles: Mac Flecknoe: A Satire upon the True-blew-Protestant Poet, T. S.
works.description: Dryden's short mock-heroic satire on Thomas Shadwell, imagining the dull poet Richard Flecknoe abdicating his empire of nonsense and choosing Shadwell as his heir.
works.plot: Flecknoe, monarch of the realm of dullness, delivers a coronation speech naming Shadwell as his successor; Shadwell is crowned amid burlesque pomp and vanishes through a trapdoor.
works.significance: The first sustained mock-heroic in English and the direct model for Pope's The Dunciad; it established the 'empire of dullness' conceit that dominated Augustan satire.
works.meter: Heroic couplets used to comic effect by sustaining an epic register throughout.
works.context: Written between about 1678 and 1682, circulated in manuscript, and printed without Dryden's name in 1682; it arises from the quarrel over dramatic criticism that began with The Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
works.characters: Richard Flecknoe; Thomas Shadwell (Sh—-); Henry VIII's ghost; Arion
works.structure: A single continuous mock-coronation scene in elevated epic diction, ending with the sudden comic collapse of the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1682 and ascribed to Dryden by contemporaries; attribution undisputed.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: Macbeth
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, of ambition and the supernatural: the Scottish general Macbeth, told by the Weird Sisters that he shall be king, murders Duncan in his sleep and enters a reign of blood — Banquo's murder, the apparitions' riddling prophecies, the slaughter of Macduff's family — until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane and the tyrant falls to the man 'not of woman born'.
works.plot: The prophecies kindle Macbeth's ambition and Lady Macbeth steels him to the murder; the crown brings only sleeplessness and escalating violence; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking confession and death precede the final battle, where the equivocations of the witches are fulfilled and Macduff beheads the tyrant.
works.significance: The supreme English tragedy of evil's self-entrapment — the shortest road to the heart of darkness the stage has ever built.
works.meter: The densest verse in Shakespeare — image packed and accelerated — with the witches' tetrameter charms and the Porter's prose as deliberate descents.
works.context: Written 1606 for the new king, James I, the patron of the company and the author of Daemonologie; the play's Scottish matter, witchcraft, and Banquo's royal line all court the Stuart interest.
works.characters: Macbeth; Lady Macbeth; Banquo; the Weird Sisters; Duncan; Macduff; Lady Macduff; Malcolm; Donalbain; Ross; Lennox; the Porter; Fleance
works.structure: A single-line tragedy of mounting speed, structured by the three prophecies and their ironic fulfilments, with the banquet scene as its turning point and the sleepwalking scene as its moral climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Hecate scenes may be later interpolations (possibly by Middleton).
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Conscience and moral self-examination

works.title: Madame Delphine
works.description: Published in 1881 and Cable's most concentrated story of race and love in old New Orleans: a quadroon woman's sacrifice for her daughter's future. It is a prose fiction work of 1881 by George Washington Cable; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Madame Delphine, a free woman of colour who has kept her past secret, discovers that her daughter Olive is loved by a young white Creole; knowing that the match is impossible unless her own history is hidden, she swears falsely that Olive is not her child but a white woman's, so that the marriage may go ahead, and then dies in the confessional of Père Jerome after confessing the lie.
works.significance: Madame Delphine is the most concentrated American story of the colour line before Chesnutt: its portrait of a mother's sacrifice and its unflinching analysis of the racial law made it one of the most discussed American stories of 1881 and it remains a central text of the American literature of race.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is exact reproduction of Creole and black dialect.
works.context: 1881: the racial codes of New Orleans, the position of the free people of colour, and the American debate on interracial marriage. The record dates the work as composed in 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; sensation novel.
works.characters: Madame Delphine Carraze; Olive, her daughter; Ursin Lemaitre-Vignevielle; Père Jerome
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George W. Cable. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Madoc
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, and a national or founding epic of the discoverer type, combining Welsh legend, the voyage narrative and the imaginary history of an American settlement.
works.description: A long metrical romance on the Welsh legend of the twelfth-century prince who sailed westward and is reported to have reached and settled in America, published in 1805 after many years of revision. The poem joins the machinery and the civil war of medieval Wales to a voyage of discovery and a settlement in the western ocean, and its argument, openly stated in its closing invocation, is that the tale of a Welsh colony in America should serve as a bond of kindred between the two nations.
works.plot: The young princes Madoc and his brother are estranged by a quarrel of succession and a crime that is charged on the one and denied; Madoc, sailing west with a small company in search of a new home, is driven by storms past the islands of the Atlantic to a coast of a green and abundant country, where he encounters nations of people at war one with another, their customs and their superstitions drawn at length. Madoc and his Welsh companies assist one nation against its enemies, the prince's skill in war and in council winning the good opinion of his new allies, and the settlement is at last secured by a marriage, while the brother's expedition across the ocean brings a like fate to a southern region and the two Welsh colonies are said to flourish apart from the Old World. The argument thus moves from civil war in Wales to the founding of an American commonwealth, and the poem closes by anticipating a time when the descendants of the colonies shall be one people with their parent nation.
works.significance: The most ambitious English romance of the Welsh-America legend and a document of the period's habit of inventing a genealogy for the New World out of the Celtic west; its subject was much imitated in later British and American verse and its claim of a shared descent is a standing instance of Romantic transatlantic imagining.
works.meter: Blank verse in a rapid and unelaborated movement, with occasional shorter stanzas for the songs and the lyrical interpolations; the versification was revised repeatedly, the earlier radical manner being smoothed in the printings of the nineteenth century.
works.context: Begun in the years of the French Revolution and of the communitarian projects, when the author and his friends hoped for an asylum in the new world, and revised and at last published in 1805, in the decade of the transatlantic republic and of the renewed English interest in the discoverer legends; its plea of a Welsh blood-tie with America belongs to the poet's design of a literature serving an Atlantic kinship.
works.characters: Madoc, the Welsh prince; his brother, the rival claimant to the succession; their father, the aged king; the chiefs and warriors of the nations of the western coast; the companions and counsellors of the settlement
works.structure: A metrical romance in twenty-two books, in two parallel histories - the Welsh expedition under the prince and the later voyage of his brother - with long episodes of council, battle, shipwreck and description of the American coast and its peoples; the two threads are brought together only in the closing argument of the poet.

works.title: Mador of the Moor
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
works.description: the author's long narrative romance poem, published as the centrepiece of The Morning Lay of Clan-Alpin (1816), a metrical tale of Highland chivalry, exile, and romantic quest. It is his most ambitious narrative poem and part of his bid to establish himself as a Scottish Romantic poet rival to Scott.
works.plot: Mador, a Highland warrior, is exiled from his clan lands and undertakes a quest that carries him through enchanted and wild Scottish landscapes, encounters with rival chieftains, and a love for a lady of an adverse clan. The poem traces his sufferings, supernatural trials, and eventual restoration. Its structure and imagery draw on the metrical romance and border ballad traditions, recast in Scott's example.
works.significance: Mador of the Moor is the author's most sustained poetic narrative and a significant example of the verse metrical romance in Scottish Romanticism; it illustrates the continuing power of the oral ballad tradition within high literary Romanticism.
works.meter: Rhymed stanzas of varying length in a romance measure; predominantly iambic tetrameter and trimeter in ballad-derived patterns
works.context: Published in 1816, the year of Scott's Old Mortality and Byron's Siege of Corinth, in the midst of the vogue for metrical romance; the author was competing directly with Scott's model and asserting the living ballad tradition against the Waverley prose romance.
works.characters: Mador; his beloved; clan rivals
works.structure: Single long narrative poem in cantos; linear quest structure combining chivalric adventure with romantic sentiment; the Highland landscape functions as a Gothic setting.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Exile and homelessness
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
works.description: Published privately in 1893 and the first American naturalist novel: the destruction of a Bowery girl by poverty, drink and the city. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by Stephen Crane; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Maggie Johnson grows up in a violent tenement family in the Bowery; she falls in love with Pete, a bartender, is seduced and abandoned, is cast out by her mother and brother, and is driven to the street, where she dies, unnamed, at the end of the novel while her mother is comforted by a neighbourhood missionary.
works.significance: Maggie is the founding text of American naturalism and one of the first American novels to treat the slum without sentiment or moralising: its refusal of a redemptive ending and its ironic use of the mission worker made it a scandal, and it opened the way for Norris, London and Dreiser.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation.
works.context: 1893: the Bowery slums of New York, the saloon and the tenement, the temperance and mission movements, and the American discovery of the urban poor. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Maggie Johnson; Jimmie Johnson; Mary Johnson; Pete; Nellie; the missionary
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Magnificence
works.description: Skelton's morality play: Prince Magnificence, a figure of the good ruler (and transparently of Henry VIII), is seduced by the courtly vices — Fansy, Counterfeit Countenance, Cloaked Collusion, Courtly Abusion — into riot and misrule, stripped of his wealth and driven to despair, and finally restored by Good Hope, Perseverance, and Measure.
works.plot: Liberty and Measure advise the Prince against Fansy; Magnificence follows the vices, is robbed and reduced to suicidal despair by Adversity, and is rescued by Good Hope, Redress, and Perseverance, who restore him to the rule of Measure.
works.significance: The first English morality play with a political programme and the bridge between the medieval moralities and the Tudor interludes; it established the genre of the king-as-everyman that Bale and the Elizabethans inherited.
works.meter: Couplets and short stanzas of functional verse, with Skeltonic flourishes in the Vice speeches.
works.context: Written in the years of Wolsey's ascendancy, when Skelton watched the young king's government with alarm; the play reads as a warning to Henry VIII against misrule and extravagance.
works.characters: Magnificence; Fansy; Counterfeit Countenance; Cloaked Collusion; Courtly Abusion; Adversity; Good Hope; Perseverance; Measure
works.structure: A full-scale morality in the tradition of Everyman, with a political allegory of the prince's fall and amendment; the Vice roles carry the comic weight.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Kingship and good rule

works.title: Maid Marian
works.description: the author's lyrical romance in prose and verse, a retelling of the Robin Hood legend centred on Maid Marian and her love for the outlaw, distinguished by its celebration of the forest, its songs, and its idealisation of youthful love. It shows the author at his most lyrical and least satirical.
works.plot: The young lovers Fulke and Marian, separated by the politics of the Angevin court and the outlawry of the hero, are reunited in the greenwood, where the forest provides a pastoral refuge from courtly corruption. The narrative moves between prose and lyric verse, with Marian as the ideal object of courtly and pastoral love; the plot is simple and its appeal lies in the songs and the evocation of the forest as a world of natural joy.
works.significance: Maid Marian shows a lyrical and idealising side of the novelist that broadens his reputation as a comic satirist; it is the most significant of the Romantic-era reinventions of the Marian legend and a notable example of the prose-and-verse romance.
works.meter: Lyric songs in varied popular measures interspersed within prose; the verse is metrically and stanzaically diverse, drawn from the English song tradition
works.context: Published in 1822, during the great vogue for Robin Hood romances following Scott's Ivanhoe; the author's treatment is a lyrical counter to Scott's historical novel and an assertion of the pastoral and song traditions.
works.characters: Maid Marian; the outlaw hero; the Earl of Huntingdon; Little John
works.structure: Prose romance interspersed with lyric songs; episodic movement between court and forest; the songs are the principal expressive mode.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind

works.title: Main Street
works.form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1920
works.description: The great American satire of the small town: Carol Kennicott and Gopher Prairie. It is a prose fiction work of 1920 by Sinclair Lewis; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Carol Milford marries the country doctor Will Kennicott and goes to live in Gopher Prairie, Minnesota, where her attempts to bring culture and beauty to the town are met with suspicion and hostility, and she leaves and returns to a compromise.
works.significance: Main Street created the American novel of the provincial town and made Sinclair Lewis famous: its satire of the booster, the village and the woman who tries to change it made it one of the most discussed American novels of the century.

works.context: The small towns of Minnesota in the 1910s, and the American provincial culture of the period. works.title: Main-Travelled Roads
works.description: Published in 1891 and the founding American book of the farm: six stories of the drudgery, debt and loneliness of the Middle Border. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by Hamlin Garland; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories follow the farmers of Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota: the successful actor who comes home to find his brother embittered by toil and his mother worn out ('Up the Coulé'), the tenant whose labour only raises the price his landlord asks ('Under the Lion's Paw'), the Union soldier walking home from the war ('The Return of a Private'), and the lover who returns to take away the woman a bad marriage has broken ('A Branch Road') — each shown without romance and without pity.
works.significance: Main-Travelled Roads is the founding text of American agrarian realism and the central literary document of the Populist movement: its portraits of the farm wife and the mortgaged farmer destroyed the sentimental picture of American rural life and made Garland the most influential American short-story writer of the 1890s after Crane.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is plain, documentary, unadorned prose.
works.context: 1887-91: the agricultural depression of the 1880s, the Populist movement, the single-tax agitation of Henry George, and the American revolt against the rural idyll. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Major Barbara
works.description: First performed in 1905 and the greatest of Shaw's plays about poverty: a Salvation Army major and her millionaire munitions-making father contest the right way to save souls. It is a dramatic work of 1905 by George Bernard Shaw; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Major Barbara Undershaft, an officer of the Salvation Army, is confronted by her father Andrew Undershaft, the armaments magnate who owns the souls of the town of Perivale St Andrews; the Army accepts his money, Barbara loses her faith in its methods, and she goes to the model town to convert the well-fed workers of the armaments factory.
works.significance: Major Barbara is the most complete of Shaw's social plays and one of the greatest English plays of the century: its argument that poverty is the worst of crimes and that the soul cannot be saved on an empty stomach made it a landmark of modern drama, and its first-act meeting of Barbara and Undershaft is one of the great scenes of English comedy.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1905: the Salvation Army, the Boer War and the armaments industry, the Fabian campaign against poverty, and the ethics of the 'tainted money' debate. The record dates the work as composed in 1905 and first published in 1905 and first performed in 1905 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; industrial and condition-of-england novel.

works.structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Majors and Minors
works.description: Published in 1895 and the volume that brought Dunbar to Howells's attention: the first collection to mix the dialect poems ('majors') with the standard English lyrics ('minors'). It is a verse work of 1895 by Paul Laurence Dunbar; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The collection contains 'We Wear the Mask', 'Sympathy', 'The Path', 'A Summer's Night' and the dialect pieces that had made Dunbar popular in the Midwest, and its division between the two registers is the central fact of his career.
works.significance: Majors and Minors is the book that established Dunbar and the clearest statement of the double register of African-American poetry at the end of the nineteenth century; it is a central document in the history of black literary representation.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill.
works.context: 1895: the black literary market, the Chicago of the World's Fair, and the American debate on dialect poetry. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Man and Superman
works.form: Play (four acts, with 'Don Juan in Hell' interlude)
works.description: Published in 1903 and Shaw's masterpiece of ideas: the pursuit of a fugitive man by a woman determined to marry him, and the dream of Don Juan in hell. It is a dramatic work of 1903 by George Bernard Shaw; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Jack Tanner, a wealthy political theorist, is made guardian to Ann Whitefield, who decides to marry him; he flees to Spain with her and her mother in pursuit, is captured by brigands, dreams the third-act 'Don Juan in Hell' in which the Life Force is debated by Don Juan, the Devil and Doña Ana, and wakes to accept his destiny as Ann's husband.
works.significance: Man and Superman is the fullest statement of Shaw's philosophy and the central English play of ideas: its preface on the philosophic man, its dream interlude and its invention of the Shavian 'Life Force' made it one of the most influential plays of the twentieth century, and it brought the discussion play to its highest point.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1903: the Fabian Society, the Nietzschean philosophy of the superman, the debate on eugenics and the Life Force, and the New Woman's sexuality. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; early scientific romance and utopian speculation.

works.title: Mandeville
works.form: Historical novel and philosophical autobiography; a tale of the civil wars with a framing essay on enthusiasm.
works.description: The last of the great philosophical tales and the most explicitly historical, a narrative of the Wars of the Roses written by a Lancashire gentleman at the close of the Elizabethan age. Its subject is enthusiasm - religious, romantic and political - and its argument, delivered at length in the narrator's reflections, is that the human understanding is corrupted by the temper of the age in which it is trained. The book also conducts a late quarrel: its author had long been accused of impiety, and the tale defends the imaginative temper while satirising its excesses.
works.plot: Charles Mandeville, of a family impoverished by the part its father took in the rival cause, is bound as page to a noble household, is driven by a youthful attachment into the opposing camp, and is thrown by chance into the society of a band of outlaws and of a wandering scholar of mock philosophy. He passes through the great events of the period, is captured, escapes, and returns to a love he has been taught to distrust. The framing narrator, old and solitary under Elizabeth, revises his judgments on fortune, on religious zeal and on the claims of romance, and ends with a defence of enthusiasm of the mind against the merely cautious understanding.
works.significance: The most sustained attempt of the philosophical school to fuse history, romance and argument in a single narrative, and an important document of the late debate over enthusiasm and the imagination. Its historical machinery belongs to the same current of antiquarian research that produced the rival school of romance. It is now chiefly studied as the term of an experiment begun a quarter of a century before.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; an archaising, sententious periodic style with deliberate antiquarian colouring.
works.context: Composed during the last war with France and published at the moment when romance and history were being made into a national industry; its treatment of civil war, superstition and fanaticism answers both the historical romances of the day and the long dispute about enthusiasm in the author's earlier essays. Its Elizabethan framing allows a double historical perspective on the fifteenth century. The novel sold poorly and marks the end of its author's career as a fiction-writer.
works.characters: Mandeville, the narrating Lancashire gentleman; the household to which he is a dependant; the outlaw company; the wandering scholar he befriends
works.structure: Autobiographical manuscript of an old man, written in the later sixteenth century about the earlier fifteenth, with long reflective digressions; recollection interrupted by direct address and by quoted documents.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.

themes: Melancholy and self-analysis
Religious persecution and martyrdom
The sublime, terror, and the ruin

works.title: Mandeville's Travels
altTitles: The Voyage and Travels of Sir John Mandeville
works.description: The Book of Sir John Mandeville, the most popular travel book of the Middle Ages: a compilation, originally in French (c. 1357), of pilgrimage routes to Jerusalem, the marvels of Asia, the lands of Prester John, and the wonders of the East, framed by the persona of an English knight of St Albans whose travels are largely fictive. Its Middle English versions (from c. 1375) circulated more widely than any other travel narrative.
works.plot: The narrator describes the way to Jerusalem and the holy places, then the farther East — Egypt, India, Cathay, the isles of the East — collecting marvels (the vegetable lamb, the phoenix, the fountain of youth), the palace of Prester John, and the customs of strange peoples, in a geography poised between pilgrimage, wonder, and imperial fantasy.
works.significance: The great medieval bestseller of travel and wonder, and a foundational text of the European imagination of the East — read by explorers into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose: plain, fluent, and endlessly translatable; the English versions descend from the French via Latin.
works.context: Composed in French c. 1357, probably by a clerk in Liège or northern France using genuine itineraries and encyclopedias; translated into English from c. 1375 in several versions (the 'Defective' version foremost); printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1496); Columbus and Raleigh read it.
works.characters: Sir John Mandeville (persona); Prester John; the Great Khan
works.structure: An itinerary organized by regions and routes, with the pilgrimage to Jerusalem as its centre and the marvels of the East as its circumference.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the 'Sir John Mandeville' persona is generally regarded as fictional.

works.title: Manfred
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Closet drama and Romantic mystery in blank verse, with the lyric hymn, the choral invocation and the supernatural machinery of the older drama turned to a psychological end.
works.description: A closet drama in three acts, styled by its author a dramatic poem and set in the high Alps about a lord of the Simplon who has a past he will not name. Summoning the spirits of earth and water and the lord of the underworld, he learns that he is beyond their reach because his guilt is of his own knowing; the deaths of a beloved spirit and of the woman he loved bring the poem to his own resolute and unassisted end. It is the most exact statement of the school the quarterly critics called Satanic, and its preface defends the poem's unfitness for the stage.
works.plot: Manfred, alone in the tower over the glacier gorge, calls the seven spirits of nature and then the power that rules them, and is told that his secret sin is already forgiven by a being he will not address. He refuses penitence, summons the demon of the place, and is mocked by the witch of the Alps, who loves him and is powerless. News comes of the death of the spirit he has loved, and then of the woman whose loss made him what he is; the last act brings the hermit of St Bernard and a deputation of the country, and Manfred dies refusing the rites they offer, mastering his terror by an act of will. The argument is that a self-conscious guilt can be expiated only by the mind that bore it, and that the imagination of powers greater than the soul may be a disease of knowledge.
works.significance: It is the period's central dramatic study of the overreaching, self-condemned mind, and its model of a hero who refuses both forgiveness and despair was inherited by the later dramatic poems of the decade and by the century's treatment of guilt. Its lyric hymns and invocations, set to music later in the century, entered the concert repertoire, and its preface remains a standard text on the Romantic renunciation of the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines for the dialogue, with irregular lyric measures, refrains and choral songs for the incantations; the versification is deliberately colloquial and weighty, after the manner of the elder English drama.
works.context: Chiefly written on the tour through the Bernese Alps in September 1816, the year of the poet's separation and exile, with the third act rewritten in early 1817; its treatment of an unpardonable and unnamed offence was read at once as autobiography, and the quarterly press used it as the specimen of a school of poetry it denounced as impious. The preface's claim that the poem was unfit for representation made it an early document of the Romantic closet drama's quarrel with the Regency theatre.
works.characters: Manfred, lord of the Simplon; the seven spirits of nature; Arimanes and the herald of the underworld; the witch of the Alps; the lost beloved; the hermit of the Great St Bernard; Lionello, a tenant of the valley
works.structure: Three acts of scenically arranged soliloquy, invocation and dialogue, each opening with an incantation or chorus; the action is minimal and the poem advances by visions, addresses and the arrival of messengers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text was lightly revised in the collected editions, and the author's own notes on the machinery are printed with it.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: Manhattan Transfer
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1925
works.description: The first great American novel of the modern city: New York in the 1920s, in a montage of lives, newsreels and songs. It is a prose fiction work of 1925 by John Dos Passos; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The novel follows a large cast through New York in the first decades of the century — Ellen Thatcher, Jimmy Herf, George Baldwin, Congo Jake — in a montage of narrative, newspaper headlines and song lyrics, moving from the immigrant arrival to the boom of the 1920s.
works.significance: Manhattan Transfer is the first great American novel of the modern city and the direct forerunner of U.S.A.: its montage of lives, headlines and songs invented the American collective novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the collage of narrative, newspaper headline (Newsreel), autobiographical prose poem (Camera Eye) and biography.
works.context: New York in the 1900s–20s, the immigrant city, the boom and the new mass culture of the movies, the tabloids and the advertising. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1925 and first published in 1925 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel; American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
works.characters: Ellen Thatcher; Jimmy Herf; George Baldwin; Congo Jake; Anna Cohen
works.structure: A montage of many lives in five parts, interspersed with newspaper headlines and songs. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Roderigo Dos Passos. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Mankind
works.description: The liveliest of the English moralities (c. 1465–70): the comedy of Mankind, the East Anglian farmer, tempted from his spade and his beads by Mischief, New Guise, Nowadays, and Nought, and the devil Titivillus, whose whispered discouragements drive him to despair — until Mercy reclaims him. Famous for its scatological comedy and its collection of money from the audience, it shows the morality in its most theatrical form.
works.plot: Mercy instructs Mankind in labour and prayer; the vice-companions tempt him to idleness and lechery; the devil Titivillus, appearing under the stage, whispers despair and steals his devotion; Mankind falls, is saved from suicide by Mercy's return, and repents, beating off the vices with his spade.
works.significance: The most theatrical of the moralities and a key witness to professional playing in the fifteenth century; its Titivillus and audience games bridge medieval and Tudor comedy.
works.meter: Couplets, stanza forms, and the macaronic dog-Latin of the vices, with remarkable metrical variety.
works.context: Composed c. 1465–70 in East Anglia (Cambridgeshire/Norfolk), for performance by a travelling company; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354).
works.characters: Mankind; Mercy; Mischief; New Guise; Nowadays; Nought; Titivillus
works.structure: A compact morality of temptation, fall, and mercy, in the alternating mode of sermon and farce, with direct address and the audience collection ('Now gostly to our purpose') as its signature.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Vernacular Religious Drama

works.title: Mansfield Park
works.form: Domestic and sentimental novel of manners with a static moral centre; a country-house plot combined with didactic debate about acting, clergy and improvement.
works.description: The most morally severe of the early nineteenth-century English novels of manners, following Fanny Price, a poor relation boarded in her uncle's baronetcy, from the Portsmouth slums to a West Indian estate and back. The novel tests principle against charm, and makes the theatre, the improvement of grounds and the question of colonial wealth matters of explicit argument. Its quiet heroine's steadfastness has made it the most debated of her works.
works.plot: Fanny Price, sent at twelve to live with her wealthy relatives at Mansfield Park, loves her cousin Edmund and is loved in return by her uncle's circle, but is dispatched home to her disorderly Portsmouth family when her aunt hopes to marry her off. The arrival of the charismatic Crawfords breaks the household's decorum: brother and sister both court Fanny while pursuing her cousins, and a private theatricals scheme is only halted by her uncle's return. Fanny refuses the importunate Henry Crawford on principle; his elopement with Maria Rushworth exposes the corruption she had distrusted, and Edmund's settlement on a living, with a slow marriage to Fanny, closes the tale. The final paragraphs remark that the colonies were the source of the family's income and that its management was not in sympathetic hands.
works.significance: The most serious attempt in the school of manners to make moral principle, rather than wit, the subject of a novel, and the source of the long critical quarrel about whether Fanny's passivity is virtue or self-suppression. Its treatment of colonial income makes it a focal text for postcolonial readings of the Regency novel. Its influence on the later domestic novel of conscience is extensive.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a more formal, latinate diction than the earlier novels, with heavy use of reported speech and moral tag.
works.context: Written during the Peninsular War, when the Antiguan slavery and sugar interests that fund the Bertram estate were a live parliamentary issue and when the abolitionist cause was dividing families of the kind depicted. The campaign against private theatricals reflects the evangelical and clerical scrutiny of the stage then reshaping polite amusement. The novel's language of 'improvements' and 'living' belongs to the agrarian and clerical debates of the Regency decade.
works.characters: Fanny Price; Edmund Bertram; Sir Thomas Bertram; Lady Bertram; Tom Bertram; Maria Bertram; Julia Bertram; Henry Crawford; Mary Crawford; Mrs. Norris; Mr. Rushworth; Susan Price
works.structure: Third-person narration tightly focalised through Fanny, whose limited access and prolonged silence generate the novel's suspense; framed by a summarising conclusion that reports the later lives of the characters.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the author of the preceding novels; authorship undisputed.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The marriage market and the limited estate
Women's education and intellectual friendship
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Many Cargoes
works.description: Published in 1896 and Jacobs's first collection: comic stories of the London docks, the barges and the riverside. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by W. W. Jacobs; it is catalogued here under Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories follow the bargees, the night watchmen, the sailors and their wives through the small disasters of working life — a cargo lost, a wife deceived, a windfall squandered, a ghost that turns out to be a fellow — each told in the exact speech of the London riverside and each with a twist at the end.
works.significance: Many Cargoes established Jacobs as the finest English comic short-story writer of his generation: its dialogue and its construction are models of the form, and it founded the series of collections that made him the most popular humorous writer of the early twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the tall tale: the frame of the literate narrator and the vernacular teller, the dialect spelling, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan, and the punch that turns on the outsider's credulity. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the tightly constructed story with a final turn.
works.context: 1896: the London docks and the Thames barges, the working-class household of the 1890s, and the magazine market for the short comic story. The record dates the work as composed in 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under tall tale and south-western humour sketch; realist novel of common life.
works.structure: A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wymark Jacobs. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Marcella
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1894
works.description: Published in 1894 and Ward's great novel of the New Woman and the land question: an heiress who refuses her class and must learn to work within it. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Mary Augusta Ward; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel.
works.plot: Marcella Boyce, brought up by a Radical father and educated as an artist, returns to the decaying family estate and falls in love with Aldous Raeburn, the heir of the neighbouring Tory landowner; she breaks off the engagement over a poaching case, trains as a nurse, and finally marries him to work for housing and rural reform from within.
works.significance: Marcella is one of the most substantial New Woman novels and the finest English novel of the land question: its heroine's conversion from romantic Radicalism to practical social work made it a central text of the 1890s and it was read across the political spectrum.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of ideas with a large social canvas.
works.context: 1894: the agricultural depression and the land question, the London poor law and nursing reform, and the New Woman debate at its height. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Marcella Boyce; Aldous Raeburn; Richard Boyce; Mrs Boyce; Lord Maxwell; Harry Wharton; Jim Hurd; Minta Hurd; Edward Hallin
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Humphry Ward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Marchmont
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
works.description: Charlotte Smith's novel of the law and of Gothic injustice, published in four volumes in the same year as her wreck narrative and her collected poems. Althea Dacres, a young woman of fortune and principle, finds herself the prey of legal contrivance and of the interests of those set over her, while the character Marchmont, bound to her by an early attachment, pursues his own ruinous career. The book turns the machinery of conveyancing, custody, and suit into an exposure of a society in which property can be stolen by procedure, and it uses castle and mountain scenery to give that exposure a Gothic emphasis.
works.plot: The novel follows Althea Dacres through the attempts of guardians, lawyers, and kinsmen to intercept her fortune and control her marriage, and follows Marchmont, whose passionate nature and misplaced loyalty destroy his prospects, until the fraud practised on the heroine is unmasked and her birth and rights established; the two histories meet in a resolution that is made possible only by the failure of the legal schemes that had seemed invincible.
works.significance: Marchmont is Smith's sharpest indictment of the law of property and of the exposure of women to guardianship and procedure, and it is valued for the way it fuses Gothic romance with economic and legal realism; it is now read as an important document of the 1790s critique of inheritance, and as a link between the Gothic of the 1790s and the later fiction of legal dispossession.
works.meter: Prose romance; the scenery passages of the Gothic episodes are written in a descriptive manner continuous with Smith's topographical verse, and verse quotations point the moral of the action.
works.context: Written while Smith's own family cause in Chancery, the suit over the inheritance she had brought into her marriage, had been pending in the Court of Chancery since the 1770s and had consumed the income it was meant to secure; the novel's treatment of law as an instrument of depredation, and of a woman's inability to command her own property, transcribes her professional and personal experience of litigation into fiction.
works.characters: Althea Dacres; Marchmont; the lawyers, guardians, and interested kinsmen who scheme against the heroine's fortune
works.structure: A four-volume third-person narrative with two converging careers, a heroine's story of custody and contrivance and a young man's story of self-destructive attachment; legal explanation and Gothic scenery alternate with sentimental analysis.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Margaret Ogilvy
works.description: Published in 1896 and Barrie's memoir of his mother, the book in which the grief that produced Peter Pan is recorded. It is a prose work of 1896 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Barrie recalls his mother's life in the weaving town of Kirriemuir, her love for her dead son David, her influence on his childhood and her old age, and the strange, half-mourning, half-comic relation between the small boy and the woman who never recovered from the loss of a favourite child.
works.significance: Margaret Ogilvy is one of the most moving Victorian memoirs and the key to all of Barrie's work: its portrait of a mother who preferred a dead son to her living children explains the origins of Peter Pan, and it is a central document of Scottish childhood and of Victorian family grief.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect.
works.context: 1896: the Scottish weaving town of the 1860s, the Victorian cult of the mother, and Barrie's own childhood grief after his brother's death. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Margaret Ogilvy, his mother; J. M. Barrie, the narrator; David, his dead brother; Jane Ann, his sister
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: Margret Howth: A Story of To-Day
works.description: Published in 1862 and the first American novel of the industrial working woman: the story of a mill town and of the woman who keeps her family alive by her labour. It is a prose fiction work of 1862 by Rebecca Harding Davis; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Margret Howth keeps the books in a woollen mill to support her blind father and her mother; Stephen Holmes, the mill-owner she loves, means to marry the heiress Miss Herne for her money, and the reformer Dr Knowles, a part-owner of the mill, wants Margret for his refuge for the outcast. When Joe Yare, a released convict, burns the mill, his crippled daughter Lois saves Holmes and dies of the fumes; Holmes, humbled, marries Margret, and the discovery of oil on the Howth farm ends the family's poverty, the happy ending that the Atlantic's editor had asked for.
works.significance: Margret Howth is the first American novel with a working woman as its heroine and one of the founding texts of the American literature of labour: its treatment of the economics of the single woman's life is unmatched in its period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is documentary detail of mill work and company housing.
works.context: The 1861-62: the American mill town, the first generation of women clerks, and the outbreak of the Civil War. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Margret Howth; Stephen Holmes; Dr Knowles; Lois Yare; Joe Yare, her father; Miss Herne; Margret's blind father and her mother
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.

works.title: Mari Magno
works.description: Clough's last long poem, written on his final voyage and published posthumously in 1862: five tales told by passengers on a transatlantic steamer, on love, marriage, money and death. It is a verse work of 1862 by Arthur Hugh Clough; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: A group of travellers crossing the Atlantic, the young narrator, a lawyer, a clergyman and the ship's mate among them, tell tales of love and marriage to pass the voyage, and the frame and the tales together make an argument about chance, duty and the moral luck of love.
works.significance: Mari Magno is the most humane and least known of Clough's long poems, and its frame-narrative of travellers' tales gives the Victorian debate on marriage a genuinely popular form; it is the best introduction to the late Clough.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms.
works.context: The transatlantic passage of 1861 and the emigrant culture of the period, the Victorian debate on marriage and money, and Clough's own failing health. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1861 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: the narrator; the lawyer; the clergyman; the mate
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: Marino Faliero
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Historical tragedy in the classical unities, with the preface as a statement of dramatic theory; the Venetian conspiracy drama of the republican tradition.
works.description: A five-act historical tragedy in blank verse on the doge of Venice who, after an insult to his wife is punished by the oligarchy with a merely facial sentence, joins a conspiracy against the ruling council and is himself tried and beheaded. It was written to obey the classical unities of time, place and action, and its preface argues for that restraint as a principle of dramatic truth. The result is a tragedy of private honour set against public justice, the most disciplined of the period's historical dramas.
works.plot: A young patrician writes a satire on the aged doge's elevation, and the council of ten, to which the offender belongs, condemns the writing and not the writer; the insult to the princess his wife drives Faliero to join a plot whose real motive is his own wrong rather than the people's grievance. His fellow conspirators are betrayed by one of their number, the state arrests them in the courtyard, and the doge is tried by the very body he meant to destroy and condemned to die on the palace stairs. The argument is that a private passion cannot be made the engine of a public revolution and that the state's law, which survives all its magistrates, executes even the head it placed. The closing scenes give the doge his composure and the survivor's wife her pardon.
works.significance: It is the period's most exact attempt to write a modern tragedy on classical formal terms and a key text in the argument between the closet drama and the regulated Regency stage. Its treatment of a head of state executed by his own institutions was influential in the later historical drama of the century, and its prefaced letter became an anthology piece of Romantic dramatic theory.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, close and speech-like, with an unusual proportion of stichomythia and no songs or supernatural machinery.
works.context: Composed between April and July 1820 at Ravenna and Venice from the chronicles of the fourteenth-century doge's conspiracy and execution, and published in 1821 in an issue accompanied by a letter to the publisher on the unity of time, place and action. It reached the London stage within months of publication, at a theatre then under pressure of regulation, and its failure there was used by the review press as evidence that the poet's dramas were unreadable on the stage it had condemned.
works.characters: Marino Faliero, doge of Venice; his wife, the princess; the patrician writer of the libel; the leader of the conspiracy; the informer; the councillors of the ten and the advocate of the state
works.structure: Five acts observed with a strict unity of place and continuous time, the exposure of the insult early, the plot's betrayal in the fourth act, and the sentence and death in the fifth; the action is carried by dialogue and not by spectacle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the printed text varies from the manuscript in passages of the constitutional debate, and the theatrical versions altered the ending for the stage.
themes: Revenge and justice

works.title: Marius the Epicurean: His Sensations and Ideas
works.description: Published in 1885 and Pater's only completed novel: the education of a young Roman of the second century as he passes from Epicureanism through the cult of Cybele to the Christian church. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by Walter Pater; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Marius, a thoughtful Roman boy of the age of the Antonines, passes from the old household religion of his family's villa and the healing temple of Aesculapius, through the Cyrenaic philosophy of sensation shared with his friend Flavian, to the Stoicism of Marcus Aurelius's court; drawn by the Christian soldier Cornelius and the household of the saintly Cecilia, he gives himself up in his friend's place when Christians are arrested, and dies of fever among them, honoured as a martyr though never baptised.
works.significance: Marius is the finest English novel of ideas of the century and the model for the modern philosophical novel: it made the history of the soul a subject for fiction and shaped Proust, Wilde and the twentieth-century novel of consciousness.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is rhythmical, suspended sentences.
works.context: The 160s AD, the reign of Marcus Aurelius, the Antonine plague, and the second-century encounter of philosophy and Christianity; behind it, the 1880s and the Oxford debate on belief. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1884 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.description: Published in 1853 and Moodie's most ambitious novel: the story of a miser and his family in the English countryside, written in the sensation manner of the 1850s. works.significance: Mark Hurdlestone is a significant Canadian novel of the 1850s and a key example of the colonial adaptation of the sensation mode; its picture of the gold worshipper anticipates the money novels of the later century.

works.title: Marlborough and Other Poems
works.description: The finest poetry of the war by a poet killed in it: the sonnets of 1915. It is a verse work of 1916 by Charles Sorley; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Sorley's poems — 'All the Hills and Vales Along', 'When You See Millions of the Mouthless Dead', 'To Germany', 'The Song of the Ungirt Runners' — written at school and in the trenches before his death at twenty.
works.significance: Marlborough and Other Poems is the finest poetry of the First World War by a poet killed in it: Sorley's sonnets and his 'When You See Millions of the Mouthless Dead' destroyed the rhetoric of the war before it began, and he stands with Owen and Rosenberg as one of the great poets of the war.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet written in the trench.
works.context: Marlborough, Oxford and the Western Front in 1914–15. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem.

works.structure: A posthumous collection with a memoir by his parents. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.

works.title: Marmion
altTitles: Marmion: A Tale of Flodden Field
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, combining historical battle poem, legal thriller and convent gothic.
works.description: The second and greater metrical romance, a tale of the Scottish border on the eve of Flodden in which a subtle and unscrupulous courtier forges a false appeal of treason against the lover of the woman he desires. Its argument is carried by a villain of the law rather than by a hero, and its prefaced epistle to a friend on the difference between prose romance and metrical romance is one of the period's key statements of theory. The battle, the doom and the convent scenes gave the poem its immense popularity.
works.plot: Marmion, lord of Fontenelle and captain of Norham, loves the Lady Clara de Clare, who is betrothed to Sir Ralph de Wilton; to clear the way he procures a counterfeit appeal of treason against Wilton, and the trial at the bar of the king's bench is fought out with perjured evidence. Clara and her sister Constance, who has been wronged by Marmion and kept in a convent, die of the ruin he brings on them; Wilton escapes to the north. Marmion, abandoned by every claim he had made, rides against Scotland, and at Flodden, unhorsed and desperate, challenges Wilton alone; he dies of his wounds, having first confessed his fraud, while the Scottish king and his host are cut up in the field.
works.significance: Carried the metrical romance to its highest commercial pitch and supplied the century's best-known verses on battle and on national feeling. Its prefaced essay on romance, probability and the machinery of verse was much imitated and much discussed. The figure of the accomplished, amoral courtier gave the school of romantic narrative one of its permanent villains.
works.meter: Principally iambic tetrameter couplets in the short 'hitching' measure of the earlier poem, with ballad stanzas, hymn and lyric interpolation.
works.context: Written between the war with France and the renewal of national anxiety about invasion, and built on the records of the 1513 campaign and on the antiquarian collections of the border. Its depiction of early Tudor law, of the appeal of treason and of the bar reflects the author's own professional familiarity with the courts of Edinburgh. The poem's dedication and epistles were shaped by the contemporary review debate over romance and probability.
works.characters: Marmion; Clara de Clare; Sir Ralph de Wilton; Constance de Beverley; James IV of Scotland
works.structure: Six cantos preceded by an 'Epistle to William Erskine' on the writing of romance and interspersed with ballad, song and the independent 'Death of Constance' episode; the frame loosens as the poem moves from narrative to set piece.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Chivalry and knighthood
Warfare and battle
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Marriage
works.description: the author's first novel, a comedy of Scottish society centered on two young women of contrasting temperaments whose rival paths through the marriage market expose the economics of rank, fortune, and feeling in Regency Scotland. Published anonymously with Walter Scott's encouragement, it was widely read as the Scottish companion to Austen's novels of manners.
works.plot: The novel contrasts the fates of Mary Marlowe, modest, principled, and impecunious, and her cousin Marianne Carmichael, beautiful, proud, and determined to marry for rank. Marianne's pursuit of a titled match leads her into humiliating negotiation and social exposure; Mary's integrity is rewarded with a marriage of genuine affection. The narrative moves between Edinburgh and the Borders, satirising the mercenary calculation that governs genteel poverty and the limited expectations available to women without fortune.
works.significance: Marriage established the novelist as the leading Scottish novelist of manners of her generation; its ironic treatment of the economics of marriage makes it a central text in the genealogy connecting Burney and Edgeworth to Austen and to later Victorian social fiction.
works.context: Written in the wake of Scott's Waverley triumph, which created a market for Scottish fiction, and during a period of acute anxiety about gentility, debt, and the marriage market in post-war Scotland. The author drew on her own observation of Edinburgh society after the collapse of the family's fortunes.
works.characters: Mary Marlowe; Marianne Carmichael; Sir William Hamley; Mrs. Barfield; Lady Mary MacFarlane
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative in three volumes; the double-plot of the two cousins provides the novel's comparative structure; social satire is carried by dialogue and letters.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; the author's authorship was an open secret within Scott's circle and confirmed in her lifetime.
themes: Sensibility, feeling, and its critics

Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Marriage à la Mode
works.description: Dryden's tragicomedy, dedicated to the Earl of Rochester, which joins a high heroic plot of usurpation and concealed royalty with a low prose comedy of cuckoldry and gallantry.

works.title: Marriage, as It Was, as It Is, and as It Should Be
works.description: Published in 1878 to be sold for a penny and the most notorious of Besant's secularist pamphlets: a short, blunt argument that the English law of marriage treats a wife as the property of her husband.
works.plot: Besant sets out the legal position of the married woman under the existing statutes, contrasts it with the ideal of marriage as a partnership of equals, and proposes the abolition of the legal disabilities — property, custody, the grounds of divorce — in a series of propositions.
works.significance: Marriage, as It Was is one of the most effective popular feminist pamphlets of the century: sold in hundreds of thousands of copies, it carried the legal argument of the property campaign to a mass readership and helped to make the Married Women's Property Act of 1882 possible.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The author's characteristic manner is direct argument and plain diction.

works.title: Martin Chuzzlewit
altTitles: The Life and Adventures of Martin Chuzzlewit
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from January 1843 to July 1844; sales fell so sharply that Dickens's publishers renegotiated his contract, and Dickens responded by sending his hero to America, using the novel to settle scores from his 1842 American tour.
works.plot: Old Martin Chuzzlewit, convinced that his relatives are waiting for his money, has taken in the orphan Mary Graham as a companion; his grandson Martin is disinherited for falling in love with her. Martin is articled to the architect Seth Pecksniff, whose hypocrisy and whose daughters Cherry and Merry drive the plot of self-interest, and he leaves for America with Mark Tapley, where the Eden land-scheme swindle and the comic Americans (Colonel Diver, Mrs Hominy, Hannibal Chollop) expose a fraudulent democracy. The novel's darker plot is the murder of Montague Tigg by Jonas Chuzzlewit, and the resolution restores the repentant Martin to his grandfather's favour.
works.significance: Martin Chuzzlewit contains the most famous English satire of the United States before the twentieth century — the Eden swindle, Mrs Hominy and the 'Chuzzlewit' contempt for American manners — and it produced one of Dickens's great comic inventions in Pecksniff and Sairey Gamp, the nurse whose name became a byword for the drunken professional.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The American tour of 1842 and the copyright agitation, the land speculation of the western boom, the architectural profession and the 'restoration' of churches, and the insolvency and insurance fraud of the early 1840s.

works.title: Martin Eden

works.description: Published in 1909 and London's most personal novel: the self-education of a sailor into a writer, and his destruction by the success he achieves. works.title: Martin Hewitt, Investigator
works.description: Published in 1894 and the second great English detective series of the 1890s: the cases of Martin Hewitt, a professional investigator who works with Scotland Yard rather than against it. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Hewitt, a stout, genial former lawyer's clerk with an office off the Strand, chronicled by his journalist neighbour Brett, solves cases of stolen documents, disguised swindlers, a case of mistaken identity and a locked-room problem, and the solutions turn on close observation and institutional knowledge rather than genius.

works.title: Mary Barton: A Tale of Manchester Life
works.description: Published anonymously in October 1848, and the first English novel to take the Manchester mill-worker's household as its subject: written after the death of Gaskell's infant son and after years of parish visiting among the poor of Manchester.
works.plot: John Barton, a mill-hand and Chartist, and his daughter Mary live through the trade depression of the late 1830s and the Chartist petition of 1839; Mary is courted by the mill-owner's son Harry Carson and by the sailor Jem Wilson, and when Carson is murdered John Barton, in his capacity as the union's delegate, is the killer. Mary clears Jem of the charge and her father's confession and death close the novel, which ends with the masters persuaded to listen to the men.
works.significance: Mary Barton opened the condition-of-England novel and made the industrial poor the subject of serious English fiction for the first time; Dickens, Kingsley, Disraeli and Engels's readership all took note, and the novel is now the founding text of the criticism of Victorian industrial fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
works.context: The Manchester cotton industry in the depression of 1837-42, the Chartist petition and the Plug Plot riots of 1842, the new poor law, and the epidemic fever of the 1840s; the novel's account of the Barton household's hunger is drawn from Gaskell's own visiting.

works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1848; the authorship was soon known, and Gaskell's name appeared on the title page of the second edition.

works.title: Mary Broome
works.description: The servant's play of the class and the woman's emancipation. It is a dramatic work of 1911 by Allan Monkhouse; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: Mary Broome, a servant, and the household that holds her; the one-act play that made Monkhouse the critic-playwright of the Manchester School and put the class question and the woman's emancipation on the stage.
works.significance: Mary Broome is Monkhouse's play of the servant and the class question: its household and its woman's emancipation made him the critic-playwright of the Manchester School.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the plain dialogue of the servant's hall and the drawing room.
works.context: The Manchester servant's hall and the Edwardian household in 1911. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and first performed in 1911 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Mary Broome; the Watsons; the servant's hall
works.structure: A single act, in the servant's hall. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Allan Monkhouse. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
