works.title: Mary Lavelle
works.form: Novel (the convent-bred woman and the forbidden love)
works.description: The novel of the governess in Spain and the forbidden love, banned in Ireland. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Kate O'Brien; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mary Lavelle follows the convent-bred governess from Ireland to the Spanish house of her charge, where the forbidden love of the man and of the woman of the house carries her out of the Ireland of the church; the book was banned in Ireland.
works.significance: Mary Lavelle is Kate O'Brien's censored masterpiece: its governess in Spain and its forbidden love carried the woman's desire into the Irish canon and made the banning of the book a national scandal.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the family chronicle and the censored conscience.
works.context: Spain and Ireland in the 1930s, and the censored book. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; novel of manners and fashion.
works.characters: Mary Lavelle; the Spanish house; the man; the woman of the house
works.structure: A novel of the exile in chapters, from the convent to Spain and back. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters of the social world, the scenes built on the breach or the observance of a convention.

works.title: Mary's Lamb
works.form: Juvenile lyric narrative in the common-school manner; songlike stanzaic poem
works.description: A short lyric narrative for children about a lamb that follows its keeper to school, and the most memorized American poem of the nineteenth century. Its stanzas treat the animal's fidelity as a lesson in affection and in the proprieties of the schoolroom. It became the standard specimen of the juvenile verse of the common school.
works.plot: A little girl owns a lamb that follows her wherever she goes and waits at the school door. Its appearance in the schoolroom provokes laughter and study among the pupils, and the teacher's attempt to exclude it fails. The lamb's constancy is made the poem's moral, and the child's attachment its feeling. The poem closes on the picture of the animal waiting, faithful and patient, after the lesson is over.
works.significance: It is the best-known American poem for children before the war and a permanent item of the national memory. Its transmission shows how a poem of occasional authorship becomes folk property. It is the standard example of the sentimental juvenile lyric.
works.meter: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter quatrains with simple rhyme
works.context: Printed in 1830, in the season of the new juvenile magazines and the common-school readers that created a national market for children's verse. Its subject, a child and an animal, is the characteristic material of the juvenile annual. It was set to music and carried into the schoolroom by the readers and by the author's own periodical work.
works.characters: Mary; the lamb; the schoolmaster and the pupils
works.structure: Narrative lyric in several quatrains, progressing from statement of the fact to the schoolroom incident and to the closing image of fidelity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long established, though the poem's currency in song and reader has encouraged legend about its origin; the incident is generally reported as domestic rather than invented.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Mary's Meadow
works.form: Children's story (published posthumously in Aunt Judy's Magazine)
works.description: Published posthumously in 1886 and Ewing's most charming late story: the tale of a child's hedgerow garden, a neighbours' feud over a meadow, and the game of the 'Earthly Paradise' that inspired the real Parkinson Society.
works.plot: Mary, the eldest girl of a large family, reads with her brothers in John Parkinson's seventeenth-century herbal Paradisi in Sole Paradisus Terrestris and plays at the 'Earthly Paradise', planting old-fashioned flowers in the hedgerows of Mary's Meadow, which belongs to the crotchety Old Squire, with whom her father is at law over a footpath; her friendship with the Squire's chained dog Saxon and her care for the old man himself end the feud.
works.significance: Mary's Meadow is one of the most beloved Victorian children's stories and a founding text of the English garden literature of childhood; its combination of horticulture, family history and rural community is unique in the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a child's-eye view.
works.context: The 1870s-80s, the rural parish, the Victorian flower garden, and the cult of the old-fashioned garden after Ruskin and William Morris. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Mary (the narrator); her brothers Arthur, Harry and Christopher; Father and Mother; the Old Squire; Saxon, the Squire's dog; the Weeding Woman; Lady Catherine
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Juliana Horatia Gatty. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Mary: A Fiction
works.form: novel; fiction of sensibility and female education
works.description: The first novel of a writer then unknown to the reading public, the history of a young woman of ardent imagination and sensibility, married without affection and ruined by the loss of those she loves. It is the most openly romantic of its author's works and a deliberate exposure of the education of feeling.
works.plot: Mary, the daughter of an affectation of religion and a mother of sensibility, is educated in romance and forms attachments of extravagant intensity, first to a schoolfellow and then to a friend of her childhood. Her father's convenience marries her to a man she does not love, and the births and deaths of her children, the failure of her friends and her own wandering complete the trial. She ends in a state of grief and religious doubt, her sensibility having been given her as a substitute for an education of the mind.
works.significance: It is the founding fiction of its author's career and a key text for the analysis of sensibility as a female education, anticipating the later argument about the reason and the situation of women.
works.meter: An impassioned and exclamatory prose of the culture of feeling, with the abstract noun of sensibility carrying much of the argument; the sentences rise to the apostrophe and the apostasy.
works.context: Published in 1788, in the season of the novel of sensibility's crisis and of the author's own first engagements with the publishers and the philosophical circle, its design answering the conduct literature she had recently written.
works.characters: Mary; her mother and father; the friend of her childhood; the husband of her parents' convenience; her children
works.structure: Third-person narration of a single life in short chapters, organised as the history of an education in feeling; the episodes are sequenced by attachment and loss rather than by intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously with a prefatory advertisement, its authorship established by the publisher's records and by the later issues.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Marriage and women's conduct
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind

Women's education and intellectual friendship

works.title: Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture
works.form: Critical pamphlet (the defence of the minority culture)
works.description: The pamphlet that made the defence of the minority culture the task of criticism. It is a prose work of 1930 by F. R. Leavis; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture argues that the civilisation of the machine and the mass media has broken the continuity of the culture, that the minority of the capable readers carries the standard, and that the defence of the culture is the task of criticism and of the discipline of English.
works.significance: Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture is the founding pamphlet of the Leavisite criticism: its minority culture against the mass civilisation made the defence of the standard the task of the discipline and gave the Scrutiny school its programme.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical sentence of the moral urgency.
works.context: England in 1930, and the polemic of the depression. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A pamphlet in sections: the mass civilisation, the minority, the task of criticism. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frank Raymond Leavis. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Maud, and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1855 and Tennyson's own favourite among his long poems: a monodrama in a variety of metres spoken by a young man driven to madness and murder by his father's ruin, the love of Maud, and the Crimean War.
works.plot: The speaker, ruined by a fraudulent lawsuit against his father, falls in love with Maud, the daughter of his father's enemy; her brother opposes the match, the lovers are discovered, the speaker kills Maud's brother in a duel, and goes mad, imagining himself dead; the poem ends with his recovery and his departure for the Crimean War.
works.significance: Maud is the most modern and the most disturbing of Tennyson's long poems: its unstable speaker, its abrupt metrical shifts and its treatment of sexual hysteria and financial ruin make it a key text for the study of Victorian masculinity, and its war ending gave the poem its contemporary scandal. Modern criticism has made it the most discussed of the poems after In Memoriam.
works.meter: Eleven sections in varied metres, from lyric tetrameters to a prose-like dramatic speech, with refrains and song fragments.
works.context: The 1850s: the financial fraud of the period, the 'Maud mania' of the poem's reception, and above all the Crimean War (1853-56), which the poem's ending consecrates as a national redemption. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: the unnamed speaker; Maud; Maud's brother; Maud's father; the speaker's father
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Maxims I and II
works.form: wisdom poetry (gnomic verse) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two collections of gnomic verse — Maxims I in the Exeter Book (204 lines, in three sections) and Maxims II in British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i (66 lines) — assembling traditional wisdom about the order of the world: what befits a king, a warrior, a woman, a tree, frost, the sea, and the road; 'wyrd goes as it shall'.
works.plot: The maxims proceed by association through the natural and social orders: the king belongs in the hall, the sword in battle, the hawk on the glove, the frost to the earth, the mind to wisdom; each thing is 'in its place' — a poetic articulation of the period's sense of a world arranged by custom and providence.
works.significance: The fullest repository of Old English gnomic wisdom and of the period's sense of natural and social order.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in short, proverb-like units.
works.context: Maxims I: Exeter Book (fols. 88b-92b); Maxims II: London, British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius B.i (with the Menologium, c. 1050).
works.characters: none
works.structure: Catalogue structure: strings of 'X shall be / belongs to' gnomes, organized by loose association rather than narrative.

works.title: Mazeppa
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the wild-ride and outcast-founding legend, with the framed recitation and the northern or eastern ballad subject.
works.description: A Cossack tale of the wild ride in couplets, told by an old hetman to a young page: as a passionate courtier of a Polish magnate's household he was punished for an intrigue with the lady of the house by being bound naked to the mane of her own steed and set loose over the Ukraine steppe. The horse's headlong ride, in which the rider's wild hair and his own nails tear him, ends with the fallen pair in the woods of the Dnieper, and the tale passes from punishment to flight to the rise of its hero to the headship of his nation. Its energy, its treatment of shame and endurance, and its landscape of the wild ride made it one of the most reprinted of the tales.
works.plot: The hetman explains why his grey hair and scarred brow are not the marks of years but of a single night's punishment, and describes the noble household, his own youth, and the love that was discovered. The lady's husband sentences him to be fastened upon her own horse, the swiftest and fiercest of her studs, and the animal bears him away across the steppe, over rivers and through forests, while the riders give up the pursuit and the sun burns and the wolves follow. The exhausted horse falls at last in the wilds of the Ukraine, and the Cossacks of the Zaporozhian camp nurse the outcast back to life, so that the punished lover becomes the chief of his people and the ally or enemy of czars. The argument is that suffering can be converted into renown, and that the passions that destroy a man in a drawing room can make a leader in the field.
works.significance: It gave the century its most vivid narrative of pursuit and endurance, and its image of the rider bound to the speeding horse became a stock of painting, music and popular recitation. Along with the earlier tales it fixed the outlaw's elevation from shame to power as a Romantic plot, and its couplets are the most sustained example of the serious use of the heroic measure in the 1819 phase of the verse tale.
works.meter: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with a fast running line and anapestic substitution in the ride; the interpolated song of the ride is in short popular measure.
works.context: Written during the Venetian residence of 1818 and published in the summer of 1819, in the year of the first cantos of the great romance of Spain and of a European vogue for Cossack and Ukrainian material drawn from the history of Charles the Twelfth. Its subject of a punishment inflicted by a jealous husband on a nobleman, and its treatment of a free horse-nation's camp, spoke directly to a public fascinated by the politics of the eastern Europe, and its fame produced prose and stage versions within a decade.
works.characters: the aged Cossack hetman; the Polish magnate; the lady of the house; the wild steed of the Ukraine; the Zaporozhian Cossacks who tend the outcast
works.structure: A framed narrative, the tale told by the aged hero to his page in three movements, the household exposure, the ride, and the recovery and elevation, with the opening and closing stanzas of the frame returning to the camp.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the tale is dated in the poet's own memorandum prefixed to the text, and the first issue was made up with a separate lyric ode on the same authorship's Italian city.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Exile and homelessness
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: MCMXIV
works.form: Poem (four eight-line stanzas forming one sentence)
works.description: MCMXIV, the year 1914 in Roman numerals as on a war memorial, is a poem by Philip Larkin completed in May 1960 and first published in The Whitsun Weddings (Faber, 1964). A single sentence over four stanzas, without a main verb, it looks at what seems a photograph of volunteers queuing to enlist in August 1914 and at the England around them, and ends: 'Never such innocence again'.
works.summary: The long queues of men outside the recruiting offices; the shut shops, the coins and advertisements, the children named after kings and queens; the countryside and the great houses with their servants; and the closing lament for an innocence that changed into the past without a word.
works.plot: The poem opens on the lines of men standing patiently as if outside a cricket or football ground, their moustached, archaic faces grinning as if the war were an August Bank Holiday lark. It widens to the streets behind them, with shops shut and blinds drawn, farthings and sovereigns, children at play called after kings and queens, tin advertisements for cocoa and twist and pubs open all day, and then to the countryside, where the place names are hidden under the summer grass and the servants live in tiny rooms in huge houses. The last stanza turns to judgement: never such innocence before or since, which became the past without a word, with the men leaving the gardens tidy and the thousands of marriages lasting a little while longer. The war that ended this world is never described; the poem knows, as its people cannot, what is about to happen to them.
works.significance: One of the best-known English poems about the First World War written after it, often taught beside the poems of the war poets; its closing line has become proverbial.
works.meter: Rhymed short lines, a catalogue of period detail and a restrained, elegiac cadence, with the Roman-numeral title recalling the inscriptions on war memorials.
works.context: Completed on 17 May 1960; collected in The Whitsun Weddings, published by Faber on 28 February 1964, the book that established Larkin with a wider public.
works.structure: Four eight-line stanzas forming one sentence with no main verb, built of noun phrases, so that the scene stays suspended in time until the closing lines.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past

War, combat and its aftermath

works.title: McTeague: A Story of San Francisco
works.description: Published in 1899 and the first great American naturalist novel: the slow degradation of a San Francisco dentist and his wife by greed and the brute inheritance. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Frank Norris; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: McTeague, a huge, slow-witted dentist, marries Trina, the miserly woman whose teeth he has repaired; their life is destroyed by her hoarding of a lottery fortune, his drinking and violence, and the novel ends in the California desert, where McTeague, having murdered Trina for the money, is handcuffed to the corpse of his enemy and dies in Death Valley.
works.significance: McTeague is the founding American naturalist novel and the first American novel of the urban poor: its theory of the brute inheritance, its documentary detail and its terrible desert ending made it the model for American naturalism, and it is the source of the American tradition of the novel of violence and compulsion.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories.
works.context: 1899: the San Francisco working class of the 1890s, the unlicensed dentistry of the period, the gold-mining country of the Sierra, and the American reception of Zola. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: McTeague; Trina Sieppe; Marcus Schouler; Zerkow; Maria Macapa; Old Grannis; Miss Baker
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Benjamin Franklin Norris. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Measure for Measure
works.description: Shakespeare's great comedy of justice and mercy: the Duke of Vienna, disguised as a friar, leaves the puritanical Angelo to enforce the city's neglected laws; Angelo condemns Claudio to death for fornication, then offers to spare him if his sister Isabella will yield her virginity — a bargain exposed in the final judgment scene, where the Duke returns to measure all by their own measure.
works.plot: Angelo revives the death penalty for lechery; Claudio's sister Isabella pleads for him; Angelo's blackmail and the bed-trick with the jilted Mariana preserve Isabella and expose Angelo; the Duke's staged return conducts the play's long trial-and-pardon finale, ending with his abrupt proposal to Isabella.
works.significance: Shakespeare's deepest study of law, sex, and power — a play that has grown darker and more central with every century.
works.meter: A grave, economical blank verse, with the prose of the Vienna underworld (Pompey, Lucio) as corrosive chorus.
works.context: Performed at court, 26 December 1604; the play's Vienna shadows Jacobean London's anxieties over plague, puritanism, and the royal exercise of mercy.
works.characters: Duke Vincentio; Angelo; Isabella; Claudio; Mariana; Lucio; Escalus; Pompey; Mistress Overdone; Elbow; the Provost; Barnardine
works.structure: A legal fable on the title's biblical text, built on the Duke's disguised supervision and resolved in the massed judgment scene of Act 5.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; minor passages possibly revised by Middleton.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning

works.title: Medea of Euripides
works.description: Published in 1878 and the standard Victorian English translation of Euripides's Medea: a version in blank verse that made the Greek tragedy a modern play about marriage and revenge. It is a verse work of 1878 by Augusta Webster; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: Medea, betrayed by Jason, takes her revenge by killing his new bride and her own children, and escapes in the chariot of the sun; Webster's version emphasises the legal position of the foreign wife and the cold logic of the revenge.
works.significance: Webster's Medea is the finest Victorian translation of a Greek tragedy and the one that made Medea a central text for the feminist reading of classical drama; it remains one of the standard English versions.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is the dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian Greek revival, the position of the married woman under English law, and the debate on divorce. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Medea; Jason; Creon; Aegeus; the Nurse; the Chorus of Corinthian women
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Julia Augusta Webster. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Meditations among the Tombs
altTitles: Meditations and Devotions (collection including the Tombs meditation)
works.description: James Hervey's graveyard meditation, first printed in a London newspaper in 1746 and among the earliest classics of the graveyard school in prose. It passes from the dead to the living, from bones and monuments to faith, hope, and the resurrection.
works.plot: The meditant walks the churchyard at twilight, addressing the tombs, the ashes, and the names of the buried, and moralizing on the levelling vanity of rank and beauty. The scene turns from desolation to consolation: the believer reads the graves as pledges of the resurrection and the dust of the fathers as sleep, and the meditation rises through hope of immortality to a triumphant close on the day when death is swallowed up in victory. Hervey alternates the gloom of the night-piece with the rapture of gospel assurance, the fear and the feast of a funeral sermon turned into essay.
works.significance: It became the prose exemplar of the graveyard meditation, widely reprinted and praised by Johnson for its music, the bridge between the funeral sermon and preromantic grave-yard poetry.
works.meter: Solemn, periodic, rhapsodic prose of the preromantic manner, long cadences of gloom broken by exclamatory uplift and hymn-like fragments.
works.context: First printed in the General Evening Post in 1746 amid the vogue of the melancholy meditation and the grave-yard poetry of the decade, within the religious world the evangelical revival and the churchyard school shared.
works.structure: A single continuous meditation moving from dusk to hope through the stations of the churchyard.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)

works.title: Melmoth the Wanderer
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's last and most ambitious Gothic novel, a labyrinthine narrative of the ancient Melmoth who has sold his soul for extended life and must find another to inherit his damnation. It is the supreme achievement of Irish Gothic fiction and one of the most structurally experimental novels of the Romantic period. Its theological terror and recursive narrative form represent the final great flowering of the 1790s Gothic tradition.
works.plot: John Melmoth, a young heir, discovers papers relating to his ancestor Melmoth the Wanderer, who bargained for supernatural longevity but must persuade another to accept his curse. Within the text five embedded narratives illustrate Melmoth's appearances across centuries and nations: the tale of Alonzo in the Spanish Inquisition; Stanislaus among Jesuits in India; Margaret MT in Ireland; the tale of Monod in France; and a Dutch narrative. Each illustrates an extremity of suffering where Melmoth appears as the personification of temptation and despair. The outer narrator finally encounters Melmoth on an island and watches him depart still damned, having failed to secure a substitute.
works.significance: Regarded as the last major Gothic novel of the Romantic period and one of the most formally experimental fictions of the era. Its influence extends to Balzac, Baudelaire who made Melmoth the protagonist of his own myth, and the modern vampire fiction tradition; it is central to any genealogy of the Gothic.
works.context: Written amid the final phase of the Gothic novel tradition after Walter Scott's triumphs had redirected fiction toward historical romance; the author sought to outdo his predecessors in narrative complexity and theological terror. The novel engages Catholic-Protestant conflict in Ireland, the Inquisition, and colonial violence in the East Indies.
works.characters: Melmoth the Wanderer; John Melmoth; Alonzo; Imee; Stanislaus; Margaret MT; Monod; the woman of the island; Maitre Ibrahim
works.structure: Multi-layered frame narrative with five embedded tales set across Spain, India, Ireland, France, and the Netherlands; an outer frame featuring the narrator and John Melmoth; the recursive structure enacts the novel's theme of entrapment and inescapable guilt.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Exile and homelessness
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man
works.description: Sassoon's finest prose: a country childhood in the hunting field, told as a novel, before the war arrives. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Siegfried Sassoon; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: George Sherston grows up in the Kent and Sussex countryside before 1914: the hunting field, the point-to-point, the groom Dixon, the cricket and the county society — and the memoir ends with the outbreak of the war, which will take him to the trenches in the two following volumes.
works.significance: Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man is the finest English prose memoir of the war and one of the great English books about a lost world: its country childhood is the equal of any in English, and its structure — the idyll before the war — made it the model for the war books of 1929.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the short satirical poem with a savage last line.
works.context: The English county families and the hunting field before 1914, and the war that ended them. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: George Sherston; Dixon; Aunt Evelyn; Denis Milden; Stephen Colwood
works.structure: A first-person memoir-novel in two parts: the country childhood and the coming of the war. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Siegfried Lorraine Sassoon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Memoirs of Modern Philosophers
works.form: Prose fiction; novel of ideas and domestic satire; anti-philosophical comedy
works.description: A satirical novel in five volumes which attacks the application of rational philosophy to domestic life, following a family deluded by a philosopher who proposes to live by first principles and ends in ruin. Its target is not abstract argument but its social practice: a father persuaded out of religion and property, daughters reasoning themselves out of decorum, and a community of apostles exploiting the theory for money and seduction. The book was one of the most effective conservative fictions of the turn of the century and helped turn the fashion for philosophical romance against itself. Its comedy is institutional, conducted through clubs, periodicals and boarding-house argument.
works.plot: An easy Scottish laird is converted by a speculative philosopher, whose system of free inquiry removes his scruples about disinheriting his children and about the arrangements of marriage, and who designs a match between his own disciple and the family property. The daughters variously accept and resist the reasoning; a seduction and a flight follow, and the philosopher's party is revealed as a set of interests disguised as principles. The final volumes expose the fraud through a competing clergyman's counter-intrigue, and the restoration of orthodoxy and property is effected by force of ridicule rather than argument.
works.significance: A central text of the anti-philosophical novel and one of the most effective fictions of the 1790s campaign against rational dissent; its portraits of a philosopher's household supplied language later used to describe the schools, and it is now studied as a woman-authored conservative novel that helped end the fashion for the speculative romance.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a colloquial argumentative style carrying technical vocabulary of the system under satire
works.context: Published in 1800, at the height of the vogue for rational philosophy in fiction after the famous novel of justice and after the controversy over the conduct of the philosophical schools. The book draws on Scottish ecclesiastical and Jacobin debate, on the periodical culture of the 1790s, and on conservative alarm at the domestic consequences of infidelity following the French Revolution. It appeared under the author's name and was reviewed as a party work.
works.characters: The speculative philosopher and his disciple; the laird he persuades; his disinherited children and their suitor relations; an apostate clergyman and his family; a boarding-house and periodical-writing circle
works.structure: Third-person omniscient satire in five volumes, with long dialogues of argument, letters from disciples, and an intrusive narrator who glosses each doctrine; the plot of domestic delusion is sustained over a deliberately slow, encyclopaedic middle.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. The philosopher and his party are satirical personae, and the identification of individual portraits with living writers remains unproven.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Memoirs of My Life
altTitles: A Short Statement of the Incidents of My Life from the Earliest Period to the Present Hour
Memoirs of the Life of Edward Gibbon
works.description: Gibbon's autobiographical memoirs, drafted in several passes after the completion of the Decline and Fall and revised into his last years. A model of Enlightenment self-analysis, they tell the story of a sickly child, an inverted convert, a historian's vocation, and a life ordered by study and friendship at Lausanne.
works.plot: Gibbon recounts his fragile childhood, the mother he barely knew and the aunts who governed his education, and the schoolboy and Oxford experiments in reading which ended with his conversion to Rome and his removal from Magdalen. He traces the Swiss tour that reformed him under Pavillard, the militia years and the Parliament interlude, the loss of his father's fortune, and then the decisive return to study and the Roman revelation. The later drafts tell the friendships of Paris and Lausanne, the slow labour of the History, the deaths of those he loved, and the philosophic calm with which he faced the end. The self-portrait is rendered with ironical candour, its governing vanity the love of application and the choice of an independent life.
works.significance: It is the classic Enlightenment memoir of a historian's vocation, a founding text of modern autobiographical self-scrutiny and the principal source for the life behind the Decline and Fall.
works.meter: The Gibbon manner turned inward: balanced periods of reticence and rueful parenthesis, self-pity disciplined by irony and the syntax of understatement.
works.context: Composed between the completion of the History and his last years amid the wars that dissolved the Old World of Lausanne; Gibbon left no finished autobiography, and the memoirs were published after his death by friends and literary executors.
works.characters: the autobiographer; his aunts and tutors; Pavillard; the friends of Lausanne
works.structure: An incomplete series of memoir drafts and revisions written at intervals after 1789, the earliest short statement forming the core of the posthumous text.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer

works.title: Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson, Written by Herself
altTitles: Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson
works.description: Mary Robinson's autobiographical prose, published within months of her death and written in her own hand and voice: the story of a poor Bristol childhood, a child marriage, the years on the stage, the connexion with the Prince of Wales and the name of Perdita, estrangement, and the long effort to maintain herself and her daughter by her pen. It is at once a self-defence, a history of a woman's exposure to public report, and one of the earliest English autobiographies written by a woman for publication as a means of subsistence.
works.plot: The memoirs recount the author's girlhood in Bristol and her early teaching, her marriage, her years of poverty and dependence, her appearance before the public and the royal connexion that made her name notorious, the separation and the loss of reputation that followed, and her later life devoted to writing and to her daughter; the narrative conducts a continuous argument about the price paid by a woman for the protection she was given and for the independence she claimed, and it carries her story only part of the way through her own career.
works.significance: The Memoirs are a foundational text for the study of Robinson, of the Perdita story, and of women's self-writing in the 1790s, and they supplied the biographical shape of her reputation for two centuries; as an autobiography that converts a notorious life into a case against the conditions of women's existence they remain one of the most quoted prose documents of Romantic-period writing.
works.meter: Conversational prose autobiography, moving between narrative, reflection, and quoted letter; no metrical design.
works.context: Written as Robinson's means failed and her health gave way, and published in 1801, the winter after her death at Englefield Green, in the tradition of the female apology and the professional memoir; its printing and its immediate republication in America belong to the same bookselling network that had printed her poems and novels, and its frankness about royal favour, separation, and dependence made it a scandal as well as a book.
works.characters: the author as narrator of her own life; her family and early acquaintances at Bristol; the public and court figures of the Perdita years; her daughter
works.structure: A first-person continuous prose autobiography, and chronological in design, with letters and personal papers interspersed; the text breaks off before the events of the author's final years and was completed for the press after her death.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Robinson herself, as the title page asserted; the closing portion and the editorial matter added after her death are by others, and quotations from the Memoirs should observe that boundary.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Female authorship and the woman writer
Patronage and the literary marketplace
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's biography of her husband, the regicide Colonel John Hutchinson, written in the 1670s as a vindication of his honour and of the parliamentary cause, and the most important work of prose by a woman of the seventeenth century.

works.context: Written in the 1670s for her children and not published until 1806; it is a rare first-hand account of the parliamentary side by a woman of the gentry.

works.title: Men and Women
works.form: Poetry collection in two volumes (51 poems)
works.description: Published in two volumes in 1855 and a commercial failure — thirteen months after publication 244 copies had been sold — and now regarded as the greatest single volume of Victorian poetry: containing 'Fra Lippo Lippi', 'Andrea del Sarto', 'Bishop Blougram's Apology', 'Cleon', 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came', 'A Toccata of Galuppi's' and 'Love Among the Ruins'.
works.plot: The poems are a gallery of speakers — Renaissance painters, a Greek philosopher, an Elizabethan lover, a bishop, a Roman patrician, a Venetian musician's listener — each caught at the moment when his view of life is revealed as inadequate or heroic. 'Fra Lippo Lippi' defends the flesh against asceticism, 'Andrea del Sarto' is the painter who could do everything but the one thing, 'Bishop Blougram' is the worldly churchman who argues that doubt is a luxury only the faithful can afford.
works.significance: Men and Women is the central volume of Victorian poetry after In Memoriam: it invented the modern poetic anthology piece, and its speakers' arguments about art, faith and the flesh are the source of the Victorian poetic drama of ideas. Pound, Eliot and the modernist dramatic lyric are inconceivable without it.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The Florence of the 1850s and the Brownings' Italian life, the Victorian crisis of faith and its Catholic and sceptical answers, and the art criticism of the period (Vasari's Lives newly available to English readers).

works.structure: The work is in 51 poems. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: Men Are Unwise
works.description: The mountaineering novel of the advanced ideas of marriage. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Ethel Mannin; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Men Are Unwise sets the mountaineering party of the Alps against the marriage question and the free relation, in the novel that carries Mannin's advanced social ideas of the thirties into the popular fiction.
works.significance: Men Are Unwise is Mannin's novel of the marriage question: its climbers, its free relations and its argument made the advanced ideas of the decade the matter of the bestseller.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the plain fast prose of the popular novelist.
works.context: The Alps and England in the mid-1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.

A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. works.title: Menaphon
works.description: Greene's pastoral romance: the shepherd Menaphon, the disguised princess Sephestia and her son, and the rival suitors of Arcadia play out the loves, riddles, and recognitions of the pastoral world, with the inserted eclogues and the story of the treacherous Samela — the whole prefaced by Thomas Nashe's address 'To the Gentlemen Students', with its famous survey of the English poets.
works.plot: Sephestia, shipwrecked and disguised as Samela, is wooed by the shepherd Menaphon, the courtier Melicertus (her own husband in disguise), and the tyrant Democles; the oracles, the riddles of parentage, and the final recognitions restore the royal family, with the eclogues and debates of the shepherds as interludes.
works.significance: The best of Greene's Arcadian romances and the vehicle of Nashe's manifesto — the first public statement of the new Elizabethan literary generation.
works.meter: Prose of the pastoral mode with interpolated verse, in Greene's most polished Arcadian style.
works.context: Published 1589, in the wake of Sidney's Arcadia's manuscript fame; Nashe's preface praises Sidney, Spenser, and the new poetry and dismisses the 'deep read grammarians' — a manifesto of the 1590s avant-garde.
works.characters: Menaphon; Sephestia (Samela); Melicertus (Maximius); Democles; the child Pleusidippus; Doron; Carmela
works.structure: A prose romance with verse eclogues in the Sidneyan manner, prefaced by Nashe's critical epistle — one of the key documents of Elizabethan literary self-consciousness.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; Nashe's preface is his own.

works.title: Metrical Legends of Exalted Characters
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
works.description: A volume of narrative and descriptive poems on heroic subjects, published in 1821, whose preface insists that the word legend is used not for fictitious stories but for pieces built on the memory of great names. The book gathers a Scottish patriot poem, a poem on the discoverer of the New World, a legend of the author's own ancestry, and pieces on earlier Highland and border worthies. It is the volume in which the dramatist of the passions turned to national and heroic subject-matter.
works.plot: Wallace recounts the guardian of Scottish independence from the killing of his bride to the failure of the comital cause and the execution in London, with the poetry of remembrance framing the military narrative. Columbus presents the voyage and the disgrace of the discoverer, the poem turning on the ingratitude of the court that used and cast him out. The legend of the author's own great-grandmother and the pieces on Malcolm's heir and on a Scottish lord of the East bring the method home to family and border record. The argument of the volume throughout is the exposure of exalted character to envy, fortune, and the forgetfulness of those served.
works.significance: The book is the main poetic monument of a dramatist otherwise known for the series of plays, and it documents the transfer of closet-drama energy into the national metrical legend of the 1820s. Its treatment of the discoverer of the New World as a figure of ingratitude belongs to the period's persistent questioning of colonial enterprise.
works.meter: A measured rhymed narrative line of the descriptive school, with the Scottish pieces using ballad and border stave where the subject allows and with sustained meditative passages on the surviving landscape; the rhythm is closer to the eighteenth-century moral poem than to the loose Romantic tale.
works.context: Composed after a visit to Scotland in 1820, when the ballad revival, the national metrical tale, and the market for Scottish historical subject matter were at their height, and published in London by the house that then issued the leading serious poetry of the decade. The volume reflects the wider Romantic investment in patriot and discoverer legends as material for a moral rather than a patriotic poetry.
works.characters: Wallace; Columbus and his patrons; Lady Griselda Baillie; Malcolm's heir; the Scottish lord of the eastern commission
works.structure: A collection of independent long poems, each with its own argument and often with a frame of remembrance or of the surviving site; no organising fiction unites the volume.

works.title: Michael
works.form: Metrical tale and pastoral poem in blank verse; the eighteenth-century theme of rural depopulation and the deserted village is converted into a domestic tragedy of entailed land and of the covenant between a father and son.
works.description: A pastoral poem in blank verse, the longest narrative admitted to the ballad volume after 1798, which redefines pastoral as the serious representation of a yeoman family and its attachment to an inheritance of land. Michael, an upland shepherd, his wife and their only son are bound to the family holding by labour, duty and love; the boy is sent to service in a distant town to raise money to redeem a mortgage, is lost through a single act of dishonesty and shame, and Michael, dispossessed, is left to build a sheepfold of stones for the shepherd who will never use it. It is at once a domestic tragedy of inheritance and an argument for the moral dignity of peasant life.
works.plot: Michael's little inheritance lies under a mortgage contracted to relieve a kinsman's distress, and his infant son Luke is the heir of his labour, trained in the shepherds' duties from childhood and given a stated covenant and a stone to set at the building of the fold. To redeem the land the boy is sent to service with a relative in London, where he falls into dissipation and forfeits money entrusted to him; ashamed, he flees, and news reaches the valley only that he has died in prison or vanished. The old man's grief is silent, his wife's is passionate and reproachful, and the land passes out of the family's hands. Michael nevertheless lays out and builds the sheepfold on the rising ground above his cottage, stone by stone, in the expectation of a use that will never come, and the poem ends on the unfinished work and the fold that remains as a memorial of faithful love.
works.significance: The strongest single poem of the Lake group's claim that humble domestic life is a proper subject for serious verse, and a lasting example of tragedy without catastrophe, in which an unfinished act of love carries the pathos. Later readers have made it central to arguments about property, inheritance and the rural order, and it remains standard evidence for the practice implied by the Preface.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter with a deliberate weight and slowness of period and frequent enjambment; the diction avoids poetical ornament and is modelled on plain speech, an achievement the poem's first readers singled out in commendation.
works.context: Composed largely in the winter of 1799-1800, after the poet's settlement in the north-west, in a decade of enclosure, agricultural distress and renewed debate over the decay of the independent yeomanry inherited from Goldsmith. Its theory of land as a school of moral attachment answers both the sentimental peasant of the 1790s and the political economy of the same years.
works.characters: Michael, the shepherd; Isabel, his wife; Luke, their only son; the kinsman whose distress brings the mortgage on the land; the relative in the town with whom Luke is placed
works.structure: A single continuous narrative in blank verse, opened by the poet's address to the valley and to the old man, followed by slow domestic exposition, one turn of fortune in the city episode, and a closing scene of unfinished labour that serves as the poem's moral image.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

themes: Consolation and endurance
Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Micrographia: or, Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses
works.form: scientific treatise; natural history; illustrated book
works.description: Robert Hooke's account of his observations through the compound microscope, published by the Royal Society in 1665 with fifty-seven magnificent engraved plates, in which he first used the word 'cell' for the units of plant tissue.
works.plot: Hooke describes and illustrates the point of a needle, the edge of a razor, silk, cork, charcoal, moss, nettles, insects including the fly's eye and the flea, the moon, and the stars, arguing that microscopy reveals a hidden order in nature.
works.significance: The founding work of microscopy and of cell biology; the word 'cell' originates here, and its plates created the visual language of modern science.
works.meter: Precise descriptive prose; the plates by Hooke himself are among the finest scientific illustrations ever made.
works.context: Published in September 1665 by the Royal Society; it was the first major publication of the Society and a sensation at court, where Pepys recorded it as 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'.
works.structure: A series of numbered observations, each with an engraved plate and a commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hooke; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Middle English Religious Lyrics
works.description: The devotional strand of the Middle English lyric corpus: meditations on the Passion ('I syng of a myden', 'Lullay, myn lykyng'), laments of the Virgin at the cross (the planctus Mariae), prayers to Christ and the saints, and poems on death and judgement. These lyrics carry the affective piety of the period into verse of great formal variety and emotional power.
works.plot: The poems stage the central scenes of late medieval devotion — the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Crucifixion as witnessed by Mary, the soul's dialogue with the crucified Christ, the memento mori — in first-person, lyric form.
works.significance: The most intimate record of late medieval English piety; together with the mystery plays, the religious lyrics are the principal vernacular vehicle of Passion and Marian devotion.
works.meter: Carol form, tail-rhyme, rhyme royal, and macaronic verse, often with musical settings implied by burdens and refrains.
works.context: The lyrics were copied into preaching and devotional manuscripts (the Vernon manuscript, Digby 102, Sloane 2593) and printed in early sixteenth-century carol collections; many served Franciscan and parochial devotion.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the soul (speaker)
works.structure: A corpus of independent lyrics; the characteristic movements are invocation, meditation, and petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; a few poems are attributed to known devotional writers.
themes: The Passion of Christ
The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion

The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life
works.form: Novel in eight monthly parts (1871-72); four volumes 1872
works.description: Published in eight parts from December 1871 to December 1872, set in the provincial town of Middlemarch in the years of the first Reform Bill, and generally regarded as the greatest of Victorian novels: a study of four intersecting lives in a community, constructed on the principle that no single centre of consciousness can see the whole.
works.plot: Dorothea Brooke marries the pedantic scholar Edward Casaubon in the hope of sharing a great work, and is widowed into freedom and a second marriage with Will Ladislaw; the young doctor Tertius Lydgate comes to Middlemarch with plans for hospital reform and a new pathology, marries the beautiful and expensive Rosamond Vincy, and is destroyed by debt and provincial opinion; the banker Bulstrode's buried past returns to ruin him; and Fred Vincy is saved by Mary Garth's refusal to marry a man without a vocation.
works.significance: Middlemarch is the central novel of the English nineteenth century: it brought the multiplot novel to its highest point, made the study of ordinary lives an instrument of moral philosophy, and produced the period's most quoted statement of the ethics of sympathy ('the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts'). Its influence on the modern novel of consciousness and on the criticism of realism has been continuous since its publication.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The late 1820s and the first Reform Bill, the new medical science of the 1820s, the coming of the railway to the Midlands, the death of George IV and the hopes of reform, and the provincial town's government by the 'Middlemarch' oligarchy of the landowning and professional families.
works.characters: Dorothea Brooke; Edward Casaubon; Will Ladislaw; Tertius Lydgate; Rosamond Vincy; Nicholas Bulstrode; Fred Vincy; Mary Garth; Caleb Garth; Mr Brooke; Celia Brooke; Sir James Chettam; Peter Featherstone; Mr Farebrother; John Raffles
works.structure: Four interwoven plots across eight monthly parts, with a Prelude and a Finale and a narration that moves freely among the consciousnesses of the town.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Midsummer Night Madness
works.form: Short-story collection (the civil war and the big house)
works.description: The first collection: the civil war, the big house and the midsummer night. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Sean O'Faolain; it belongs to The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Midsummer Night Madness gathers O'Faolain's first stories of the civil war and of the Anglo-Irish big house in its madness and its decay, in the plain ironic sentence of the new Irish story.
works.significance: Midsummer Night Madness is the founding collection of O'Faolain's short story: its civil war and its big house made the fiction of the republic and of the decayed Ascendancy one of the forms of Irish letters.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence.
works.context: Ireland in the civil war and after, published 1932. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1931 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: the fighters of the civil war; the big-house folk; the priests
works.structure: A collection of civil-war and big-house stories. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sean Proinsias O Faolain. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Milton's Sonnets
works.description: Milton's twenty-four English and five Italian sonnets, written over some thirty years: a sequence of public and private meditations including 'How soon hath Time', 'On His Blindness' ('When I consider how my light is spent'), the political sonnets 'On the Late Massacre at Piemont' and 'To the Lord General Cromwell', and the dream-elegy 'Methought I saw my late espoused saint'.
works.plot: Rather than a love sequence, the sonnets treat vocation, blindness, public service, religious persecution, friendship, and loss, each an argument or meditation resolved in the closing lines.
works.significance: Milton restored the sonnet to serious public and moral use, breaking from the Elizabethan love sequence and influencing Wordsworth and the modern sonnet ('Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour').
works.meter: The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet with Miltonic enjambment and a grand, sonorous syntax that overflows the traditional divisions.
works.context: Composed from about 1630 to the 1650s–60s; most were published in the 1673 Poems, and they record Milton's engagement with the Civil Wars, the Commonwealth, his blindness, and personal bereavement.
works.characters: the poet; Patience (in 'On His Blindness'); various dedicatees (Cromwell, Vane, Fairfax)
works.structure: A non-sequential collection of occasional and meditative sonnets, unified by Milton's concern with duty, faith, and his poetic calling.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Kingship and good rule
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: Mine Eyes Have Seen
works.form: One-act play; problem play, first issued in 1918
works.description: Published in 1918 and the only play by Dunbar-Nelson: a black soldier's family waits for news on the eve of his departure for France. It is a dramatic work of 1918 by Alice Dunbar-Nelson; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Chris, the youngest of three orphaned siblings whose father was killed by a white mob in the South, is drafted and asks why he should fight for a country that denies his people justice; his crippled brother Dan, his sister Lucy and their Irish and Jewish neighbours argue the question, and, as a band plays 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic' outside, he resolves to go.
works.significance: Mine Eyes Have Seen is one of the earliest published plays by an African-American woman and the central black American dramatic text of the First World War: its argument about citizenship, service and the colour line made it a landmark of African-American drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is dialect and French-inflected Creole speech.
works.context: 1918: the First World War, the Great Migration, the hopes of black soldiers in 1917-18, and the American debate on 'making the world safe for democracy'. The record dates the work as composed in 1918 and first published in 1918 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Chris; Dan, his crippled brother; Lucy, his sister; Mrs O'Neill; Jake; Bill Harvey; Julia; Cornelia Lewis
works.structure: The action is divided into acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alice Ruth Moore. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border
altTitles: Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, in Three Volumes
works.form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of popular balladry, with attached critical dissertation; the verse proper belongs to lyrical ballad and popular stanza.
works.description: The great editorial work that supplied the raw material and the theory for the border romances: traditional ballads of the South, gathered from recitation and from printed and manuscript copies, with an introduction historical and traditional, explanatory notes, and essays on chivalry and on romantic poetry. It preserves 'Sir Patrick Spens', 'Thomas the Rhymer', 'The Battle of Otterbourne' and a large body of Border narrative verse, and it prints in its later volumes imitations and pieces composed by the editor himself. Its methods of conjectural restoration and of making up defective copies became a central case in the history of ballad editing.
works.plot: The collection is organised historically rather than narratively: a preliminary account of the border minstrels and of the conditions of their production; then the ballads of real or alleged history, arranged in chronological order with their traditions, from the fourteenth century to the Union; then the romantic and fantastical tales of the same region; and, in the volumes of imitations, pieces written in the ancient manner. The notes record authorities, variants and the circumstances of recitation, and the dissolving legend of Robin Hood receives an early essay.
works.significance: The foundation of modern Scottish ballad studies and a decisive model for the scholarly editing of popular verse; it also furnished plots, characters and phrases for the metrical romances and for the historical novels that followed. Its editorial licence - conjecture, restoration and interpolation - provoked the longest controversy in ballad scholarship. Its historical introduction remains a classic account of the social conditions of oral poetry.
works.meter: The ballad stanzas of the Scottish and Border popular tradition (common-measure and 'Marginal' four-line stanzas, often with refrain), with alliterative and Chronicle-verse residues; the editor's own imitations follow the same stanzas.
works.context: Gathered in the 1790s from oral reciters, from the manuscript collections of the Borders and from the printed sheets, at the moment when the old border recitation was ceasing and when the great mid-century anthologies of ancient national verse had made balladry a national property. Its publication coincided with the war years' appetite for native antiquity. The editor was a lawyer and an antiquary, and the collection's standards of evidence are those of the Scottish historical profession of the 1790s.
works.structure: Editorial anthology: framing dissertation, texts in sequence, and scholarly commentary; no single plot. Individual ballads supply their own narrative structures, from the abrupt scene-ballad to the metrical chronicle and the lyrical lament.
works.attributionNotes: The editor's own imitations and pieces are distinguished in the collection from the traditional texts; no dispute over the editorship.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Primitive genius and national poetry
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Miscellanies in Verse and Prose
works.form: collected miscellany of verse and critical prose
works.description: John Dennis's first collected volume, a miscellany of occasional verse, translations and short critical and philosophical papers assembled at the close of the stage controversy and the battle of the books. It carries his early essay of a critical personality: ambitious native verse, a partisan defence of the new English prosody, and a habit of turning quarrels into theory. The volume antedates the nominal scope of this installment, but is entered here because Dennis's critical importance belongs wholly to the Augustan age that followed.
works.plot: The volume mixes modes without pretending a single argument: poems of mourning, praise and compliment sit beside prose pieces on the drama, on learning and on the manners of the time, and all are informed by two convictions that Dennis spent the next forty years elaborating. These are, first, that modern poetry in the living languages has genuinely advanced upon the ancient model, and secondly, that its advance is purchased at a moral cost which the critic, not the player, must police. The miscellany's pose is therefore that of the corrective censor who is also a practising poet.
works.significance: It marks the appearance in English letters of the professional critic as a public character with a theory of his own, and it gathers the first drafts of the ideas of enthusiasm, magnificence and native poetical advancement that the great treatises of 1701 and 1704 would systematise.
works.meter: Occasional verse chiefly in the heroic couplet and in the looser stanzaic forms of the commendatory and elegiac tradition; prose of the heightened, syntactically straining Augustan critical style Dennis made his own.
works.context: Published in the immediate aftermath of the 1690s quarrel over the stage and of the ancient-modern dispute, when a hard-up writer could turn a miscellany into a manifesto and a subscription pitch; Dennis's later career as a professed critic, dependent on patrons and on the book trade, begins here.
works.structure: A printed miscellany of independent pieces, sequenced by the editor's sense of proportion rather than by argument, with verse and prose interleaved and each item carrying its own dedication or occasion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume carries Dennis's name. The dating of individual pieces within it is not fixed here.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Miss Brown
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1884
works.description: Published in 1884 and the most controversial English novel about the aesthetic movement: a poet's attempt to make a young woman into a work of art. It is a prose fiction work of 1884 by Vernon Lee; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Walter Hamlin, a wealthy Pre-Raphaelite poet, takes up Anne Brown, a poor and beautiful orphan, and sets out to educate her into his aesthetic ideal; she resists, develops her own mind and conscience, and finally rejects both the poet and the society that has used her, in a novel that attacks the aesthetic movement from inside.
works.significance: Miss Brown is the most important English novel about the aesthetic movement and the sharpest contemporary critique of it: its portrait of the aesthete as a self-absorbed exploiter made it a scandal in 1884, it drew an angry response from Whistler and the Pre-Raphaelites, and it is a central text of the Victorian debate on art and morality.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, analytical prose that moves between description and argument.
works.context: 1884: the Pre-Raphaelite circle, the aesthetic movement of the 1880s, the debate on the education of women, and Vernon Lee's own quarrel with the aesthetes. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Anne Brown; Walter Hamlin; Lady Blanche; Edmund Darnley; Mrs Brown; Sacha
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Miss Cayley's Adventures
works.form: Novel (episodic); new woman, first issued in 1899
works.description: Published in 1899 and the most entertaining of Allen's New Woman books: a penniless, clever woman makes her way round the world and solves a mystery on the way. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Grant Allen; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lois Cayley, a Girton graduate left alone in the world with twopence by her stepfather's death, sets out to live by her wits: she becomes companion to the crusty Lady Georgina in Germany, wins a bicycle race and sells bicycles in Switzerland, opens a typing business in Italy with her friend Elsie, writes travel letters on the Nile and is feted by a maharajah in India; refusing Lady Georgina's nephew Harold Tillington rather than cost him his inheritance, she turns detective when he is accused of forging his uncle's will, and exposes the plot of Lord Southminster.
works.significance: Miss Cayley's Adventures is one of the most enjoyable New Woman novels of the decade and an early female detective narrative: its heroine's professional adventures made it a model for the twentieth-century woman's travel novel, and it shows Allen's feminism in its most attractive form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature.
works.context: 1898-99: the new employment of women, the tourist route to Italy and India, the imperial world of the 1890s, and the demand for the female detective story after Sherlock Holmes. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Lois Cayley; Lady Georgina; Harold Tillington, her nephew; Elsie, Lois's friend; Lord Southminster
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
