works.title: Miss Lonelyhearts
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1933
works.description: The great American black comedy of the Depression: the agony columnist and his correspondents. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by Nathanael West; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A young newspaperman is assigned the agony column and is destroyed by the suffering of his correspondents; his attempts to find meaning in sex, religion and violence end with his death at the hands of a cripple he has tried to help.
works.significance: Miss Lonelyhearts is one of the finest American novels of the 1930s and the great black comedy of the Depression: its short, hard chapters and its vision of suffering made it a central text of American modernism and one of the most admired short novels in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the grotesque image and the surreal scene.
works.context: New York in the early 1930s, and the Depression city of the desperate. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1933 and first published in 1933 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; proletarian novel and the working-class fiction.
works.characters: Miss Lonelyhearts; Betty; Shrike; the cripple; the correspondents
works.structure: A novel in fifteen short chapters, from the assignment to the death. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor.

works.title: Miss Marjoribanks
works.description: Published in 1866 and the masterpiece of the Carlingford series: the comic history of Lucilla Marjoribanks, who returns from school to her provincial town determined to be its social centre. It is a prose fiction work of 1866 by Margaret Oliphant; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lucilla Marjoribanks comes home to Carlingford to keep her widowed father's house, and sets about reorganising the town's society with the serene confidence of a natural ruler; the novel follows her dinners, her campaigns, her refusal of several eligible men and her eventual marriage to the one man who understands her management.
works.significance: Miss Marjoribanks is one of the great comic novels of the century and the finest study of a woman's exercise of power within the narrow sphere allowed her: Lucilla is a complete original, and the novel's irony makes it a quiet masterpiece of English realism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1860s: the provincial town of the English midlands, the social economy of the dinner party, and the serial publication of the Carlingford chronicles in Blackwood's Magazine. works.title: Miss Mole
works.form: Novel; provincial novel, first issued in 1930
works.description: The finest English provincial novel of the period: a governess, a household and a secret. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by E. H. Young; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Hannah Mole, a woman of forty with a sense of humour and a secret in her past, becomes housekeeper to the Reverend Corder and his household in Bristol, and transforms their lives while keeping her own.
works.significance: Miss Mole won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and is one of the finest English provincial novels of the period: its portrait of Hannah Mole made a permanent heroine of the unmarried woman and made Young the great novelist of the provincial family.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the provincial household and its comedy.
works.context: Bristol in the late 1920s, and the provincial middle class of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; comic novel and the satire of manners.

works.title: Miss Toosey's Mission
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1878
works.description: The anonymous sentimental bestseller: a spinster's mission and a child's salvation. It is a prose fiction work of 1878 by Evelyn Whitaker; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Miss Toosey, a plain and pious spinster, undertakes the rescue of a neglected child and, through her patient love, transforms the household and brings about the conversion of its master.
works.significance: Miss Toosey's Mission was one of the most popular sentimental books of the 1870s: its anonymous authorship, its waif heroine and its religious consolation made it a phenomenon of the trade and a central text of the Victorian sentimental novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the sentimental plot of the waif and the rescuer.
works.context: England in the 1870s and the Evangelical philanthropy of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.

A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: Missee Lee
works.form: Children's novel (sea adventure in the China seas)
works.description: The South China Sea and the pirate captain Missee Lee of the Three Islands. It is a prose fiction work of 1941 by Arthur Ransome; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance.
works.plot: The Swallows and Amazons, sailing round the world with Captain Flint and the Callums, are taken by the pirates of the Three Islands in the South China Sea, where the pirate captain Missee Lee, the daughter of a Cambridge don, sets the crews' fate on the shooting of the sparrows with her pistols.
works.significance: Missee Lee is the sea book of the series and its most romantic invention: the pirate captain of the Three Islands carried the children's republic into the China seas and gave the sailing adventure its greatest antagonist and its most memorable set piece.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact, practical prose of the sailor.
works.context: The South China Sea in the 1930s, and the world voyage of the two crews. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1941 and first published in 1941 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; imperial adventure romance.

A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. works.title: Mob Rule in New Orleans
works.form: Pamphlet; social inquiry, first issued in 1900
works.description: Published in 1900 and Wells's study of the New Orleans race riot of 1900, and of the lynching of Robert Charles. It is a prose work of 1900 by Ida B. Wells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: Wells reconstructs the killing of Robert Charles and the subsequent massacre of black citizens by the police and the mob, documents the failure of the courts, and argues that the rule of law has collapsed in the American South.
works.significance: Mob Rule in New Orleans is a central document of the American literature of racial violence and a model of investigative reporting; it records one of the most serious episodes of racial terror in American history.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass.
works.context: 1900: the New Orleans race riot, the Louisiana disenfranchisement, and the national debate on lynching. The record dates the work as composed in 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale
works.description: Published in 1851 and the greatest American novel: the voyage of the whaler Pequod under Captain Ahab in pursuit of the white whale that took his leg, and the encyclopaedic and metaphysical work that contains it.
works.plot: Ishmael, the narrator, ships on the Pequod with the harpooneer Queequeg; Ahab nails a doubloon to the mast and declares the hunt for Moby Dick, the crew is drawn into his obsession, the Pequod meets the ships of the world, and the whale destroys the ship at the end, leaving Ishmael to float on Queequeg's coffin.
works.significance: Moby-Dick is the central work of American literature and one of the greatest novels ever written: its fusion of Shakespearean tragedy, cetological encyclopaedia, democratic epic and metaphysical speculation has made it the foundation of American studies, and its whiteness and its Ahab remain permanent symbols of the modern world.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The 1840s-50s, the Nantucket and New Bedford whaling industry, the American exploration of the Pacific, the debate on slavery, and the Romantic philosophy of the absolute. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1851 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance; Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; naturalist and determinist novel.

works.title: Modern Chivalry
altTitles: Modern Chivalry: Containing the Adventures of Captain John Farrago, and Teague O'Regan, His Servant
works.form: Picaresque and journey novel; comic satire of the republic, in the fielding manner
works.description: A picaresque comic novel of the western Pennsylvania republic, published in parts across more than twenty years, and the earliest American fiction to make popular politics and office-seeking its sustained subject. Its captain and his Irish servant travel a country of elections, militias, speculators and sectarians. The book is a satire on the pretensions of a society that has abolished ranks but invented new ones.
works.plot: Captain John Farrago, a half-learned frontier lawyer, sets out with his servant Teague O'Regan, an illiterate Irish adventurer, through the settlements and camps of the western districts. Teague, emboldened by flattery, aspires to every office in turn, from legislator to bishop, and each ambition ends in exposure and humiliation. The narrative interposes the captain's long discourses on chivalry, law, religion and government, and a company of Germans, Quakers, Methodists and speculators. The novel closes with the follies punished and the captain wiser than his servant.
works.significance: It is the first major American comic novel and the earliest native analysis of popular office-seeking as a social comedy. Its western setting makes it a founding text of the frontier tradition in prose. Its long publication history is a document of the instability of the early American literary marketplace.
works.meter: Prose, with interspersed verse and song
works.context: The first volumes appeared in 1792, with further volumes in the following decade and the completed work issued in its final form in 1815. Its scene is the western Pennsylvania of the Whiskey excise troubles, land speculation and rapid settlement. The author was a Princeton graduate, a teacher and a judge of the western circuits, and the book's politics are those of a skeptical republican lawyer.
works.characters: Captain John Farrago; Teague O'Regan; the candidates and office-seekers of the western districts
works.structure: Episodic picaresque in a succession of separately published volumes, with discursive chapters, embedded tales and a running argument between master and servant.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the novel was published in parts, and the several volumes carry different title-page dating.

works.title: Modern Love
works.form: Sonnet sequence of fifty sixteen-line poems
works.description: Published in 1862 and the record of the breakdown of the poet's marriage: fifty sixteen-line poems that narrate, in the third person, a husband's discovery of his wife's infidelity and the slow death of their marriage.
works.plot: The sequence follows a husband and wife through the night of the wife's confession, the husband's attempt at generosity, the wife's suicide and the husband's grief; the poems are spoken by a narrator who is neither the husband nor entirely outside him.
works.significance: Modern Love is the first English sonnet sequence to treat a marriage from inside and to make the wife's infidelity the subject; it broke the Petrarchan convention of the sequence as idealising worship and made the form available for psychological narrative.
works.meter: Fifty sixteen-line sonnets (four quatrains and a couplet), rhymed abba cddc effe gg, with considerable freedom of stress.
works.context: The 1861 death of Mary Ellen Meredith, the legal position of a wife under coverture, and the divorce law of 1857. The record dates the work as composed in 1861 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Modern Painters
altTitles: Modern Painters: Their Superiority in the Art of Landscape Painting
works.description: Begun in 1843 as a defence of J. M. W. Turner under the anonymous title 'by a Graduate of Oxford' and completed in 1860 in five volumes: the most ambitious work of art criticism in English, moving from the truth of landscape painting to a complete theory of the imagination and of the relation of art to religion.
works.plot: Volume I defends Turner's truth to nature against the critics; Volume II (1846) develops the theory of the beautiful and the 'pathetic fallacy' and the classification of the 'theoretic' and 'imaginative' faculties; Volumes III-V (1856-60) treat the symbolism of landscape, the Renaissance and the relation of art to the moral and religious state of the artist's age.
works.significance: Modern Painters established Ruskin as the leading art critic of the century and made Turner a national painter; it introduced the 'pathetic fallacy' into criticism, gave the Pre-Raphaelites their critical defence, and turned art criticism into a branch of moral philosophy that Pater and Wilde had to answer.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The 1840s and the Turner controversy, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of 1848 (which Ruskin defended in 1851), the growth of the Victorian art market, and Ruskin's own travels in Italy and Switzerland.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Moll Flanders
altTitles: The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders
The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders, Who Was Born in Newgate
works.form: novel; picaresque and confessional prose fiction
works.description: The confessions of a woman born in Newgate and traded through a lifetime of marriages, thefts, transportation and, at the end, repentance. It is the century's most sustained novel of the marriage market seen as an economy, in which the heroine's calculations of fortune and status are rendered with an unashamed precision.
works.plot: Raised from a gypsy boarding to a servant's place, Moll contracts successively to a brother-in-law, to a landlord, to a brewer, to a banker and to a jelly husband, each match measured in money and each ending in loss. She takes to theft in Bristol and London, is captured, tried and transported to Virginia, and there marries a planter, discovering only afterwards that the marriage was incestuous. She returns enriched, and the narrative closes with a professed reformation and a prospect of an estate.
works.significance: It is the central text for the study of early-eighteenth-century ideas of marriage, money and female dependency, and its moral ambivalence - a heroine whose virtue is her prudence - marked the distance between the amatory novel and the later novel of conduct.
works.meter: Businesslike first-person prose in which figures, dates and inventories carry the moral weight; the repentance passages adopt the cadences of the penitential tract, and the irony depends on the gap between the two registers.
works.context: Appeared in the same season as printed Newgate calendars and criminal life series, and in the decade of the 1718 Transportation Act, which made the American plantations the destination of the convicted; its marriage plots assume the property anxieties of a credit economy.
works.characters: Moll Flanders; her Newgate mother; the Lancashire landlord; the banker husband; the jelly husband; the Virginia planter husband; the Newgate gaoler
works.structure: First-person confessional retrospect with a preface commending the work to readers; chronology is continuous and picaresque but tied to a recurring economic arithmetic and to a late moral frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution rests on the writer's own later acknowledgment of the work and on stylistic and bibliographical continuity with the other volumes of 1722; no contemporary external evidence survives, and the fiction of an edited memoir is retained in the preface.

works.title: Monody to the Memory of the Late Queen of France
works.form: Elegy; Political and Revolutionary Verse; Lyric
works.description: Mary Robinson's public lament for Marie Antoinette, issued as a separate poem within months of the execution of the French queen and one of the most conspicuous political lyrics of 1793. Casting the death as the matter of a formal monody, it transforms an executed queen into the emblem of civilized suffering under revolutionary terror, and it declared Robinson's royalist and humane politics at a moment when the British debate about France was being closed by war and repression.
works.plot: The poet mourns the fate of the queen of France, traces her fall from splendour to the tribunal and the scaffold, sets domestic and conjugal virtue against public violence, and answers the spectacle of the Revolution with indignation at its proceedings and with consolation drawn from the endurance of those who mourn; the poem makes the private grief of the lament the ground of a public political judgment.
works.significance: The Monody is a document of the sudden English royalist elegy of 1793 and of the part women poets took in the revolution debate, and it is often cited as evidence that Robinson's politics cannot be assimilated to the radicalism of her friends; the poem's use of landscape mourning for a political end is characteristic of the decade's verse.
works.meter: A monody in the manner of the formal lament: sustained decasyllabic meditative verse in the elevated diction of the occasional elegy, with apostrophe and exclamatio governing the movement of the lines.
works.context: Published in the year of the execution of Louis XVI and of the British declaration of war on France, when sympathy for the queen was a politically charged act and when Robinson, like her contemporaries, was writing revolution controversy for immediate sale; the poem was admired by contemporaries and quickly became one of her most reprinted occasional pieces.
works.characters: the mourning poet; Marie Antoinette, the late queen of France; the actors and spectators of the revolutionary trial and execution
works.structure: A single continuous monody in the convention of the formal lament, moving from apostrophe through historical recapitulation and denunciation to consolation, without division into books.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Time, death, and immortality through verse
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Monsieur Motte
works.form: Novel; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1888
works.description: King's first book: a New Orleans school, a proud orphan and the secret of her birth. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Grace King; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Marie Modeste, a proud orphan at a New Orleans school, is supported by a mysterious benefactor; the novel uncovers the secret of her parentage and the position of the free woman of colour in Creole society, and ends in renunciation.
works.significance: Monsieur Motte was Grace King's first book and one of the first American novels to treat the free woman of colour and the Creole racial order with any complexity: it made her reputation and opened the way for Balcony Stories.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is the balcony story told from above the street.
works.context: New Orleans before and after the Civil War, and the complex racial order of Creole society. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; sensation novel.
works.characters: Marie Modeste; Monsieur Motte; the schoolmistress; the Creole family
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the school to the revelation. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Grace Elizabeth King. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Mont Blanc
altTitles: Mont Blanc: Lines Written Near the Source of the Arve
works.form: Nature lyric and meditation in blank verse; the sublime scenery poem of the philosophical kind, with an account of the imagination's share in the landscape drawn from the Geneva school of sensation.
works.description: The period's great poem of the high mountain and of the power it exercises over a mind that has abandoned the religious account of the world. Written in a few days beside the glaciers of the Arve, it makes the mountain the emblem of an impersonal power, 'the wilderness of death', and asks what the dreaming mind contributes to the landscape it beholds. Its argument is carried by a series of reiterations and revisions rather than by a progression, and its closing question about the voice of the unseen power is the century's most quoted statement of secular awe.
works.plot: The poem begins at the source of the Arve, where the ravine and the icy summit overhang the poet, and passes to the meditation that the same power which dwells in the mountain speaks also through the human mind, so that the scene is the joint creation of nature and imagination. The middle sections picture the avalanche, the glacier, the dead sea of ice and the small creeping things of the valley, and argue that what seems a wilderness of death is a harmony to the power that perceives it, while to the human sense the same spectacle is annihilation. The close addresses the mountain as the type of an enduring power, and asks what the vale, the heaven and the lake of the poet's own mind have to do with the dream he must be content to have dreamed. The argument is that the sublime is an encounter with a power that the mind can neither deny nor personify.
works.significance: It is the central English poem of the secular sublime and the period's most exact account of the mind's share in making the landscape it admires, and its argument has been the starting point of most later discussion of Romantic imagination theory. Its treatment of a power without personality or mercy answered directly the lake school's own great meditation on the same region, and gave the century its alternative to a providential reading of the mountain.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, with a heavy use of repetition, assonance and the re-entering phrase, and a famous slackening of the measure in the passages of the avalanche and of the wandering clouds.
works.context: Composed in a few days of the July of 1816 during the Alpine tour made with a small party on the Lake of Geneva, in the year of the iceless summer that followed the Tambora eruption and of the poet's own separation from his first wife's family circle; it first appeared in print attached to a narrative of the tour published the following year. Its philosophy of the power behind nature was formed in the same months as the essays on necessity and the translation of the classical dialogues.
works.characters: the poet-speaker beneath the mountain; the personified Power that dwells in the wilderness of snow; the Arve, the glacier and the avalanche as agents; the eternal quiet of the mountain
works.structure: A continuous meditation in five unequal movements, from the source of the Arve to the summit and back to the poet's own valley, proceeding by restatement and self-correction rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was first printed inside a travel narrative written jointly with the poet's companion, and its text varies between that issue and the posthumous collected volumes.
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres
works.description: Privately printed in 1904 and published in 1913: Adams's study of the medieval imagination, the companion to The Education. It is a prose work of 1904 by Henry Adams; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Adams reads the architecture, the glass, the sculpture and the poetry of twelfth- and thirteenth-century France — Mont-Saint-Michel, Chartres, the Song of Roland, the troubadours, the cult of the Virgin — as the expression of a unity of feeling and belief that the modern world has lost.
works.significance: Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres is one of the great American works of cultural criticism and the essential companion to The Education of Henry Adams: its reading of the medieval world as a unity of faith and art made it a founding text of American medieval studies and the source of Adams's central metaphor of the Virgin and the dynamo.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the third-person autobiography that treats the self as a scientific case.
works.context: 1900-04: the medieval revival of the 1890s, the Catholic aesthetics of the period, and the American study of the Middle Ages after Ruskin. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Brooks Adams. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience

works.title: Moonfleet
works.form: Novel; historical novel, first issued in 1898
works.description: The great English smuggling romance: a boy, a diamond and the church vault. It is a prose fiction work of 1898 by John Meade Falkner; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: John Trenchard, an orphan in the Dorset village of Moonfleet, discovers the secret of the smugglers and the missing diamond of Mohune, and is drawn into the smuggling trade, the church vault and a voyage to fight the French.
works.significance: Moonfleet is one of the great English adventure novels and the finest smuggling romance in the language: its Dorset, its vault and its boy hero made it a permanent classic of English fiction and one of the best-loved novels of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person Dorset narrative of the boy smuggler.
works.context: Dorset in the mid-eighteenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: John Trenchard; Elzevir Block; Grace Maskew; Ratsey; Mohune
works.structure: A first-person narrative of smuggling and adventure in Dorset. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. Meade Falkner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy

works.title: Moral Essays
works.description: Pope's sequence of verse epistles on the characters of men and of women, on taste and on the use of riches: a social anatomy conducted in the manner of Theophrastus and of the periodical character writing.
works.plot: Successive epistles examine the masks of the world, the inconstancy of female character, the false and the right use of wealth and the taste of the patron, and conclude that the science of life is the knowledge of ourselves.
works.significance: It carries the periodical essay's moral taxonomy into verse and preserves the century's shrewdest and most contested analysis of character, wealth and national taste.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of epigrammatic compression, with the rapid named portrait and the antithetical clause.
works.context: Issued in the same years as the Essay on Man and the Horace imitations, when the character of women had become a pamphlet subject and when the language of taste and of the arts of the patron was being argued over Burlington's building and gardening.
works.characters: the poet-observer; the man of the world; the woman of fashion; the patron of taste; the rich man and his steward
works.structure: Four independent epistles, each opening on a general proposition, running through a gallery of portraits and closing with a moral reflection.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the satiric portraits are drawn from living persons whose identification has never been settled.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem

works.title: More Pricks Than Kicks
works.form: Short-story sequence (the comic elegy of Belacqua)
works.description: The sequence of the comic elegy: Belacqua from birth to death. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Samuel Beckett; it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: More Pricks Than Kicks follows Belacqua Shuah, the Dublin student of the Dante, from the first love to the last accident, in the comic elegiac sentence of the learned allusion and the bodily joke.
works.significance: More Pricks Than Kicks is Beckett's first book of fiction and the comic elegy of Belacqua: its learned allusion and its bodily joke announced the prose that the later books would dissolve.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The poem is elegiac, the mourning stanza repeated through the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is the comic elegiac sentence of the learned allusion and the bodily joke.
works.context: Dublin in the early 1930s, and the Joyce circle. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1933 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Belacqua Shuah; the women of Dublin; the Dante
works.structure: A sequence of stories from the birth to the death of Belacqua. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Samuel Barclay Beckett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Moses Ascending
works.description: The second novel of the Moses trilogy, published in London by Davis Poynter in 1975, returns to Moses Aloetta of The Lonely Londoners, now the owner of a ramshackle house in Shepherd's Bush who means to write his memoirs while his handyman does the work. Wikipedia names it, with The Lonely Londoners, as the book for which Selvon is best known.
works.summary: A comedy of Moses' rise from tenant to landlord and would-be memoirist, set in a house that fills with the politics and people of 1970s black London.
works.plot: Moses, once a poor Caribbean immigrant, has become the proud landlord of a ramshackle house in Shepherd's Bush. He sees himself as master of his own domain, writing his memoirs while his trusty sidekick and handyman, Bob, does all the work. His troubles are far from over. A Black Power group takes over the basement, headed by the indomitable Brenda; an illegal people-smuggling ring is discovered upstairs (an AbeBooks description of the first edition says Moses shelters Pakistani immigrants); and there is harassment by racist police, sheep-slaughtering in the back yard and a Black Panther on the loose. The publisher's description asks whether Moses' 'elaborately constructed castle in the air' will be demolished by these unruly forces, and presents the book as following the fortunes of characters from The Lonely Londoners.
works.significance: After The Lonely Londoners the best known of Selvon's books (Wikipedia). It continues the Moses saga, which Dawes takes as Selvon's most telling treatment of identity and belonging, and its characters reappear in the radio plays of Eldorado West One (1988). It has been reissued by Heinemann (1984) and Penguin (2008, and in Penguin Modern Classics).
works.meter: Dawes counts the three Moses novels as a comic trilogy, and the publisher calls the book a hilarious and telling depiction of 1970s Britain.
works.context: Its Black Power group, people-smuggling and police harassment place it in the London of the early 1970s. It appeared in 1975, the year Selvon took up his fellowship at Dundee, three years before he left Britain for Canada.
works.characters: Moses Aloetta, landlord and would-be memoirist; Bob, his handyman; Brenda, leader of the Black Power group
works.structure: Set largely in Moses' house, from the basement taken by the Black Power group to the upper floor where the smuggled immigrants are found; the episodes arise from its tenants and visitors.

works.title: Moses Migrating
works.description: The last of the Moses novels, published by Longman in Harlow in 1983, five years after Selvon moved to Canada. It won the Georges Bugnet Award for the novel at the Alberta Literary Awards in 1984.
works.summary: Moses, more than twenty-five years after The Lonely Londoners, goes back from London to Trinidad.
works.plot: More than twenty-five years after he became one of the 'Lonely Londoners', Moses Aloetta, though an avowed Anglophile, hankers for Trinidad, for sunshine, Carnival and rum punch, and the novel tells of his re-encounter with his native land (Lynne Rienner synopsis). In Dawes's account he at last musters the courage to return and must cope with recognising that he has become thoroughly and yet peculiarly English in his values, his sense of the world and his perception of himself.
works.significance: Georges Bugnet Award (1984). Reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, in 2009 with an introduction by Susheila Nasta.
works.meter: The publisher speaks of Selvon's characteristic irony and delicacy of touch; Dawes includes it in the comic trilogy.
works.context: Published in 1983, after Selvon himself had left London for Calgary; the trilogy's homecoming came from a writer who had already left Britain for Canada.
works.characters: Moses Aloetta
works.structure: Framed by the return journey; the events in Trinidad are not described in the sources consulted.

works.title: Moses: A Story of the Nile
works.description: Published in 1869 and Harper's most ambitious poem: a blank-verse life of Moses, written as an allegory of the emancipation of the slaves. It is a verse work of 1869 by Frances E. W. Harper; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem.
works.plot: The poem follows Moses from his rescue in the bulrushes through his exile in Midian and the call at the burning bush to the exodus, the giving of the law and his death on Mount Nebo, and it reads the story of Israel as the story of the African-American people.
works.significance: Moses is one of the most ambitious American poems of the century and a founding text of the African-American literary use of the Bible: its identification of the black American with the enslaved Israel made the Exodus the central myth of black American religion and literature.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat.
works.context: 1869: the Reconstruction of the South, the black church, and the use of the Exodus narrative in African-American culture. The record dates the work as composed between 1868 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: Moses; Charmian, Pharaoh's daughter; Jochebed, his mother; Miriam; Aaron; Pharaoh
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Ellen Watkins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Mother and Daughter: An Uncompleted Sonnet Sequence
works.description: Published after her death in 1895: an unfinished sonnet sequence on the relation of a mother and a daughter, and the last thing Webster wrote. It is a verse work of 1895 by Augusta Webster; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The sequence follows the daughter from infancy through childhood to the threshold of adult life, and the mother's apprehension of loss, change and the approach of her own death.
works.significance: Mother and Daughter is one of the first sustained English poems on the mother-daughter bond and a landmark of Victorian women's poetry; its unfinished state has made it a text of particular interest to modern criticism.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is the dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker.
works.context: The 1890s, the Victorian sonnet revival, the poetry of family life, and the mother-daughter relation in Victorian writing. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Julia Augusta Webster. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Moths
works.description: Published in 1880 and the most notorious of Ouida's society novels: the story of a beautiful, bored aristocrat married to a man she does not love, and of the cosmopolitan world that destroys her. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Ouida; it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Vere Herbert, an innocent girl of seventeen, is married off by her worldly mother, Lady Dolly, to the brutal Russian Prince Zouroff; she loves the great tenor Corrèze but stays faithful through years of a degrading marriage among the 'moths' of fashionable society in London and Paris, until Zouroff divorces her and she goes to Corrèze, whose voice has been destroyed.
works.significance: Moths was the most scandalous novel of 1880 and the clearest English example of the society novel as a critique of the aristocracy; its 'daring' was debated in the press and it shaped the picture of the 1870s haut monde for later readers.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is highly coloured, rhythmic prose.
works.context: The 1870s, the 'fast' aristocratic set, the Prince of Wales's circle, and the circulating-library wars over the moral tone of fiction. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Vere Herbert; Lady Dolly, her mother; Prince Zouroff; Corrèze, the tenor
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Marie Louise Ramé. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Mountain Interval
works.description: The collection that gave America its most quoted poem: 'The Road Not Taken' and the New England hill farm. It is a verse work of 1916 by Robert Frost; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric; Nature Lyric and Meditation and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Road Not Taken', 'Birches', 'An Old Man's Winter Night', 'A Time to Talk', 'In the Home Stretch' and 'The Sound of the Trees' — lyrics and dialogues of rural New England.
works.significance: Mountain Interval gave American poetry its most quoted poem and Frost his popular fame: 'The Road Not Taken' has been misread as a celebration of individual choice for a century, and 'Birches' is one of the best-loved lyrics in the language.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sound of speech in strict iambic measure.
works.context: The New England hill farms, the First World War, and Frost's return to America in 1915. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric; nature lyric and meditation.
works.characters: the boy of 'Out, Out—'; the Hill Wife; Brother Meserve and Fred and Helen Cole ('Snow'); the old man of 'An Old Man's Winter Night'; the couple of 'In the Home Stretch'
works.structure: Twenty poems, several of them blank-verse dialogues. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Lee Frost. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Mourning Becomes Electra
works.description: O'Neill's American Oresteia: the Mannons, the Civil War and the return of the avenger. It is a dramatic work of 1932 by Eugene O'Neill; it belongs to The American Theatre and the Modern Stage and it is catalogued here under Domestic and Sentimental Tragedy; Revenge Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The trilogy — Homecoming, The Hunted and The Haunted — retells the Oresteia in a New England mansion after the Civil War: Lavinia and Orin Mannon destroy their mother's lover and their mother, and are destroyed in turn, ending with Lavinia's self-imprisonment.
works.significance: Mourning Becomes Electra is O'Neill's American Oresteia and the greatest American tragic trilogy: its combination of Greek tragedy and New England Puritanism made it the central American play of the century and one of the great theatrical achievements of modern drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose or verse: the dialogue carries the whole, and the text is written for performance. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the expressionist set and the mask.
works.context: New England after the Civil War, and the Puritan inheritance of the American family. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1931 and first published in 1932 and first performed in 1932 and the corpus places it within The American Theatre and the Modern Stage, it is catalogued under domestic and sentimental tragedy; revenge tragedy.
works.characters: Lavinia Mannon; Orin Mannon; Christine Mannon; Ezra Mannon; Adam Brant; Peter Niles
works.structure: A trilogy of three plays, from the homecoming to the haunted house. The play is divided into acts and scenes, the dialogue carrying the whole of the action.

works.title: Moving the Mountain
works.description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's first utopia: the return of an American who has been lost for thirty years to a country transformed by feminism and social reform. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Charlotte Perkins Gilman; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation.
works.plot: John Robertson, presumed dead, returns to America in 1940 to find a country without poverty, with professionalised housework and childcare, communal kitchens, a rational education and full equality for women, and he is gradually converted to the new order.
works.significance: Moving the Mountain is one of the founding American feminist utopias and the most detailed picture of Gilman's social programme; it is a key text in the history of American utopian fiction and of the Progressive movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
works.context: The 1910s: the Progressive era and the American utopian tradition of Bellamy's Looking Backward. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
works.characters: John Robertson (the narrator); his sister Nellie (Ellen), now a university president; the citizens of the transformed America of 1940
works.structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.

works.title: Mr Fortune's Maggot
works.description: Warner's second novel: a missionary alone on a Pacific island and the failure of his faith. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Sylvia Townsend Warner; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Timothy Fortune, a missionary, is left alone on a small Pacific island with the boy Lueli; his attempts to convert the island and to love the boy end in the loss of his faith and the destruction of the boy's god.
works.significance: Mr Fortune's Maggot is Warner's finest novel and one of the great English novels of the failure of faith: its Pacific island, its missionary and its tender, unsentimental prose made it a central text of the literature of the colonial encounter and of the loss of belief.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the fantasy that begins as realism.
works.context: A small island in the Pacific in the 1920s, and the missionary enterprise of the period. The record dates the work as composed in 1927 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Timothy Fortune; Lueli; the islanders
works.structure: A novel in four parts, from the arrival to the departure. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sylvia Nora Townsend Warner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Mr Weston's Good Wine
works.description: The great English allegory of the century: God comes to a Dorset village as a wine merchant. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by T. F. Powys; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Mr Weston, a wine merchant, arrives in the village of Folly Down with his van and his assistant Michael; he sells his good wine and his bad, and the village is visited by death and love in a parable of the divine judgement and mercy.
works.significance: Mr Weston's Good Wine is the great English allegory of the century and Powys's masterpiece: its parable of the divine wine merchant made it one of the strangest and finest novels of the period and the central text of English allegorical fiction between Bunyan and the moderns.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the allegory in a village setting.
works.context: A Dorset village in the 1920s, and the Puritan inheritance of the English countryside. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Mr Weston; Michael; Luke Bird; Mr Grunter; Tamar; the villagers
works.structure: A novel in nineteen chapters, one day in the village. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

works.title: Mrs Dalloway
works.description: A single June day in London in 1923: Clarissa Dalloway prepares a party while a shell-shocked veteran spirals toward death. It is a prose fiction work of 1925 by Virginia Woolf; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Clarissa Dalloway, fifty-two, walks through Westminster buying flowers for the party she is giving that evening. In counterpoint, Septimus Warren Smith, a war veteran with shell shock, walks through the same streets with his Italian wife Lucrezia and is taken to a psychiatrist. The novel moves through the minds of both and of a dozen others by interior monologue and free indirect style, and ends with the party, the news of Septimus's suicide, and Clarissa's recognition of a kinship with him.
works.significance: Mrs Dalloway is the central English modernist novel and the finest novel of a single day in the language: it perfected the interior monologue in English, made the ordinary consciousness — the party, the flowers, the memory — the matter of high art, and its treatment of shell shock gave the war's aftermath its most exact literary record.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric stream of consciousness and the interior monologue.
works.context: London on a June day in 1923, after the First World War; the suffrage generation's daughters, the Harley Street psychiatrists, the Empire's administrators at luncheon, and the new world of the motor car and the aeroplane writing letters in the sky.
works.characters: Clarissa Dalloway; Richard Dalloway; Elizabeth Dalloway; Peter Walsh; Sally Seton; Septimus Warren Smith; Lucrezia Warren Smith; Sir William Bradshaw; Miss Kilman
works.structure: Telescoped single day, alternating between Clarissa's and Septimus's consciousness, with free indirect narration and memory as the main movement.

works.title: Mrs Dane's Defence
works.description: First performed in 1900 and the finest English problem play before Shaw: a woman with a past is cross-examined before the man she is to marry. It is a dramatic work of 1900 by Henry Arthur Jones; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Mrs Dane, a widow engaged to a young man of good family, is confronted with her former life by Sir Daniel Carteret, a barrister and the young man's guardian; the third act is a cross-examination in which she is trapped into confessing, and the play ends with her leaving the house and the family's respectability preserved at the cost of their humanity.
works.significance: Mrs Dane's Defence is the most accomplished English problem play of the period and one of the finest in the language: its third act is the strongest scene of cross-examination written for the English stage, and it is the play in which the Victorian drama of the fallen woman reached its highest point.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the strong melodramatic situation with a moral core.
works.context: 1900: the Victorian double standard, the law of divorce, the censorship of the stage, and the vogue of the problem play at the end of the century. The record dates the work as composed in 1900 and first published in 1900 and first performed in 1900 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; new woman and marriage-question novel.

works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Mrs Spring Fragrance and Other Writings
works.description: Published in 1912 and the first book of fiction about Chinese America: stories of San Francisco's Chinatown and the Chinese-American household. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by Sui Sin Far; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories follow Mrs Spring Fragrance and her husband in their San Francisco flat, the Chinese merchant and his Americanised son, the white woman who marries a Chinese man, and the children of the Chinatown schools, presenting the immigrant world from the inside and the misunderstandings of the white world from outside.
works.significance: Mrs Spring Fragrance is the founding text of Asian-American literature: it was the first book of fiction in English to present Chinese immigrants as human beings rather than as the 'yellow peril' of the newspapers, and its mixed-race perspective made it a unique document in the American literature of immigration.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story with a domestic interior and a small crisis.
works.context: 1890-1912: the Chinese Exclusion Act, the San Francisco Chinatown, the anti-Chinese agitation of the 1890s, and the American debate on immigration and race. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edith Maude Eaton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Mrs Warren's Profession
works.description: Written in 1893 and the most notorious of Shaw's 'unpleasant' plays: a Cambridge graduate discovers that her mother's fortune comes from the brothels of Europe. It is a dramatic work of 1893 by George Bernard Shaw; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Vivie Warren, a brilliant young woman of the new generation, learns that her mother Kitty has made her money as a brothel-keeper, and that the elegant Sir George Crofts, who proposes to her, is her mother's partner in a chain of Continental brothels; she refuses to be shocked, refuses to be sentimental, breaks with both Crofts and the young idler Frank Gardner, and leaves for her actuarial work in London, while her mother defends the choice as the only one open to a poor woman.
works.significance: Mrs Warren's Profession was banned by the censor and not performed in public in Britain until 1925, and it remains the most powerful English play about prostitution: its argument that vice is an economic institution, not a moral failing, made it a founding text of modern social drama and the most radical of Shaw's early plays.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1893: the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, the debates over prostitution and the 'social evil', and the censorship of the Lord Chamberlain. The record dates the work as composed in 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.

works.title: Mucedorus
altTitles: A Most Pleasant Comedy of Mucedorus, the King's Son of Valentia
works.description: The anonymous romance-comedy that became the best-selling play of the age: Mucedorus, prince of Valentia, disguises himself as a shepherd to woo the princess Amadine of Aragon; the wild man Bremo, the bear, and the clown Mouse fill the forest adventures; and the play ends with the lovers' marriage, Bremo's defeat, and — in the 1610 revision — the added scenes of the bear's death and the king's feast.
works.plot: Mucedorus leaves court in disguise; Amadine, fleeing the wild man Bremo, meets the shepherd; the courtship, the clown Mouse's cowardice, and the fight with Bremo follow; the play moves to the recognition and the wedding, with the 1610 additions (attributed to Shakespeare in the printed text) supplying the bear scene and the final entertainment.
works.significance: The most popular play of the early Stuart stage — the romance-comedy that travelled England with the strolling players.
works.meter: Loose blank verse and prose, with the clown's jests and the Induction's debate of Envy and Comedy.
works.context: Probably written about 1590, printed in 1598, and revised in 1610 with additions 'newly set forth'; it went through more editions before 1642 than any other play, its Shakespearian ascription a bookseller's later device.
works.characters: Mucedorus; Amadine; Bremo the wild man; Mouse the clown; the King of Aragon; Segasto; Envy, Comedy (the Induction); the bear; the King of Valentia
works.structure: A five-act romance-comedy in the old-fashioned mode — disguised prince, wild man, clown — that its very simplicity made immortal in the provinces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the 1610 additions were claimed for Shakespeare by the publisher, an ascription now generally rejected.

works.title: Much Ado About Nothing
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of wit and slander: the 'merry war' of Beatrice and Benedick is tricked into love by their friends, while the villain Don John's plot makes Claudio believe his bride Hero unfaithful — a lie that kills her (apparently) at the altar, until the watch's comic detective work exposes the plot and Hero returns from the dead.
works.plot: Don Pedro's court at Messina: Claudio and Hero are betrothed; Beatrice and Benedick are gulled into confessing love by overheard conversations; Don John stages the scene of Hero's infidelity with Margaret; Hero is denounced and shammed dead; Dogberry and the Watch stumble on the truth, and the double wedding concludes the play.
works.significance: The model of the comedy of wit, whose sparring lovers founded a tradition running through Restoration comedy to the screwball film.
works.meter: Prose for the wit-combats, blank verse for the romantic crises, with the songs of Balthasar.
works.context: Written about 1598–99 from Bandello via Ariosto; printed in quarto, 1600; among the first plays staged after the reopening of the theatres under James I.
works.characters: Beatrice; Benedick; Claudio; Hero; Don Pedro; Don John; Leonato; Dogberry; Verges; Margaret; Borachio; Conrade; Friar Francis
works.structure: Twin plots of courtship — the gulling of Beatrice and Benedick, and the destruction and restoration of Hero — joined by the watch's comic inquest.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Mules and Men
works.description: The great record of Black Southern folklore: the lying sessions, the work songs and the Hoodoo of Florida and New Orleans. It is a prose work of 1935 by Zora Neale Hurston; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Hurston records the folklore she collected in Eatonville, Polk County and New Orleans: the 'lying' sessions, the animal tales of Brer Rabbit and Sis Cat, the work songs, the sermons, the conjure and the Hoodoo doctors, in the voices of the men and women who told them.
works.significance: Mules and Men is the greatest record of Black Southern folklore and the founding text of African American anthropology: its transcription of the voices of the rural Black South preserved a culture that was disappearing, and it made Hurston the first Black woman to publish a book of anthropology.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension.
works.context: The Black rural South of the 1920s, the turpentine camps and the sawmills, and the Hoodoo tradition of New Orleans. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: Hurston herself; the storytellers of Eatonville and Polk County
works.structure: Two parts (Florida and New Orleans), with the folk tales transcribed in dialect. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Zora Hurston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book

works.title: Murder & Its Motives

works.title: Murder as a Fine Art
altTitles: On Murder Considered with Reference to its Pleasures
works.form: Ironical critical essay and prose satire, applying the vocabulary of aesthetic taste to a subject from which it is repulsive, in the manner of the ironical project and of the club oration.
works.description: A prose essay published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1827, which treats the pleasures of murder as a branch of aesthetic criticism and is one of the most quoted pieces of English ironic prose. Under cover of a paper read to a club of connoisseurs, the writer argues that murder, duly considered as a fine art, has its rules, its pleasures and its properly aesthetic critics, and he reviews the celebrated cases of the day in the manner of a connoisseur discussing a picture. The leisurely ironic argument is its machinery, and the exposure of the reader's appetite for the dreadful is the point of the performance.
works.plot: The essay opens with the complaint that, whatever has been written on the agreeable, the beautiful and the sublime, murder has been left out of the catalogue of the fine arts, and proposes to supply the deficiency. A paper is therefore read before a club of amateurs, which distinguishes the kinds and the circumstances of murder, requires the true critic to read the case with the feelings of a connoisseur, and rebukes the public that will not attend to the pleasure of the thing. The body of the essay is a review of recent notorious cases and of their trials and reporting, in which the narrator criticises the paragraph writers and the jurymen, complains that the murders of the metropolis are unattended by taste and that the age has lost the relish for the art, and lays down the proper method for the future conduct of a murder, including the choice of subject, of season and of place and the arrangement for the amusement of the reader. The argument closes with a promise of a second paper, and its effect is a satire on the readers of the new police reporting and on the aesthetic criticism of the agreeable.
works.significance: The most famous essay in English on the aesthetic treatment of horror and a permanent source of the phrase and the notion it parodies; it established the model of the ironical critical sketch that later writers of prose virtuosity have imitated. It remains a standard text for the study of Romantic irony, of the literature of crime and of the periodical press, and its title was adopted for the collected edition of the author's papers on the subject.
works.meter: Prose of the urbane and deliberate kind, with long periods, parenthesis, the language of the club and of the pulpit, and an unfailing courtesy of tone that carries the irony.
works.context: Published in the same Edinburgh monthly that had first printed the author's confessions of an intoxication, in a season of popular interest in criminal trial and in the reporting of the new police; the piece belongs to the London journalism of the later 1820s and to the controversy about the taste and the morals of the periodical press.
works.characters: The narrator, a connoisseur and member of the club of amateurs; the members of the club who hear the paper; the reporters, the jurymen and the public of the metropolis whose taste is criticised; the sufferers and the criminals of the notorious cases reviewed
works.structure: A single free-standing essay in the form of a paper read to a club, with an opening statement of principles, a review of the cases and a closing promise of a sequel; the irony is sustained by the perfect good humour of the narrator, who never breaks the character of the connoisseur.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a second paper of the same design followed in a later year and is printed with this one in the collected edition from which the title used here is taken.

works.title: Murder in the Cathedral

works.form: Verse play (first performed in Canterbury Cathedral, 1935)
works.description: Eliot's verse drama of the martyrdom of Thomas Becket: the great modern verse play in English. It is a dramatic work of 1935 by T. S. works.plot: The Chorus of the Women of Canterbury, the three priests and the four tempters prepare for the archbishop's return; Becket refuses the tempters' offers of power, pleasure, political action and martyrdom itself, preaches his Christmas sermon on the paradox of the martyr, and is murdered in the cathedral by the four knights, who then address the audience directly.
works.significance: Murder in the Cathedral is the great verse play of the period and the founding work of the modern revival of poetic drama: its chorus, ritual structure and analysis of the will made it a permanent work of the English stage.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama: the poetic line, blank verse or a regular stanza, carries the dialogue, and the play alternates the verse speech with lyric and choral passages. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
works.context: The murder of Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170, and the political crisis of the 1930s, which made the play an allegory of the church against the totalitarian state.
