works.title: Murder on the Orient Express
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1934
works.description: The most famous closed-circle mystery in the genre: a murder on a snowbound train and twelve passengers with a secret. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Agatha Christie; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Hercule Poirot, travelling on the Orient Express from Istanbul, is snowbound in Yugoslavia when the American tycoon Ratchett is stabbed twelve times in his compartment; every passenger has an alibi, and Poirot's solution — that they all did it — is one of the most famous in detective fiction.
works.significance: Murder on the Orient Express is the most famous closed-circle mystery in the genre: its solution and its snowbound setting made it the definitive detective novel of the 1930s, and it remains the most widely adapted of all Christie's books.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play plot with its clues planted in plain sight.
works.context: The Orient Express of the 1930s, the Balkans, and the aftermath of a famous American kidnapping case. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery.

works.structure: A closed-circle investigation on a snowbound train, with Poirot's final reconstruction. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.

works.description: The novel of Murphy's mind and body: the chair, the biscuits and the little world. works.plot: Murphy sits in the chair of the little world of the mind against the big world of the body, in the London of the miss and of the hospital of the mind, until the accident of the kite and the biscuits ends the argument.

works.title: My Bondage and My Freedom

works.title: My Own Life
altTitles: The Life of David Hume (1777 autobiographical sketch)
works.description: Hume's short, serene autobiography, written in April 1776 and read to the club in Edinburgh in that year; published in 1777 as the preface to the fourth volume of the edition of his works. It became one of the most quoted self-characters in English, a model of the philosophic autobiography of a mind surveying its own impartiality.
works.plot: Hume recounts his birth and family, his studious childhood, the writing of the Treatise in France, its being still-born from the press, and the gradual success of the Essays, the Political Discourses, and above all the History of England. He tells of his Edinburgh offices, the embassy in France, and the quarrel with Rousseau, which he narrates as a notable incident of the malady of self-love in a mind he pitied rather than resented. His return to Scotland produced the Natural History of Religion, the Dialogues, and the revised editions of his works. He sums up his character as mild, candid, cheerful, and sociable, a lover of pleasure more than of ambition, and closes on his own philosophy in the face of death without hope of a future life.
works.significance: A founding document of the secular autobiography and of the Enlightenment's self-image of the philosophic mind, constantly quoted for its account of the still-born Treatise and its closing serenity.
works.meter: The clearest, coolest middle prose, self-portraiture in declaratives, every judgment of others balanced by an appeal to the testimony of enemies and friends.
works.context: Written in the spring of 1776 as Hume faced the cancer that killed him in August, it was intended to control the story of his life and death against Boswell's evangelizing and the churchmen's scandal over his dying composure.
works.characters: David Hume as narrator and subject
works.structure: A continuous compact autobiography in short paragraphs, chronological from birth to the year of writing.

works.title: N-Town Plays
works.description: A cycle of forty-two plays compiled in East Anglia in the second half of the fifteenth century, so called because its banns announce performance 'in N-town' — the name to be supplied by whatever town staged it. Its distinctive compilation includes a Passion play of great elaboration (the Mary Play tradition), the Parliament of Heaven, and the trial of Joseph and Mary, with a strong Marian and doctrinal emphasis.
works.plot: From the Parliament of Heaven and the fall of Lucifer, the cycle moves through the Old Testament, the life of the Virgin (her conception, presentation, and betrothal, the trial of Joseph and Mary), the Nativity, the ministry and Passion — with its long two-part Passion sequence — to the Resurrection, the Assumption, and the Last Judgement.
works.significance: The most learned and Mariological of the cycles, and the principal witness to the East Anglian Passion play tradition; its compilation shows the cycle form in the making.
works.meter: Thirteen-line and eight-line stanza forms, with the rime couée of the incorporated plays.
works.context: Compiled c. 1468–1500 in East Anglia (perhaps at Bury St Edmunds or Thetford), in the devotional culture that produced Bokenham and Capgrave; preserved in BL Cotton MS Vespasian D.viii.
works.characters: God; the Virgin Mary; Joseph; Christ; Pilate; Satan; the Prolocutor
works.structure: A compilation cycle: some pageants written for the cycle, others (the Mary Play, the Passion Play) incorporated from self-standing East Anglian dramas, under a general prologue claiming the N-town staging.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (compilational); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.

works.title: Nada the Lily
works.description: Published in 1892 and Haggard's Zulu epic: the rise of a Zulu warrior in the time of Chaka and the tragedy of his love for Nada the Lily. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by H. works.title: Naked Warriors
works.description: The Imagist war poems of a serving officer: the attack, the corpse and the landscape. It is a verse work of 1919 by Herbert Read; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line and the record grades it as major canon.

works.significance: Naked Warriors is the Imagist war poetry of a serving officer and one of the finest collections of the war: its exact images and its formal modernity made it a model for the poetry of the war and a central text of the Imagist movement.

works.title: Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno
altTitles: The Metrical Life of St Swithun
works.form: hagiography (saint's life) in Latin hexameter verse
works.description: Wulfstan the Cantor's verse life of St Swithun, bishop of Winchester (d. 862), composed c. 996 for the translation of the saint's relics into the rebuilt Old Minster: a Latin epic in the classical revival manner of the Benedictine Reform, with a prose preface (a letter to Bishop Ælfheah) describing the rebuilding of the cathedral and its monuments.
works.plot: The poem narrates Swithun's life and episcopate, his humility, his miracles (the broken eggs restored, the bridge-mending saint), and the translation of 971, when the reluctant saint consented at last to be moved indoors; the preface details the new tower, crypt, organ, and bells of Æthelwold's Old Minster — a unique architectural record.
works.significance: The principal Latin poem of the late Old English period and a major source for Winchester's architecture and liturgy.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters in the tenth-century classical manner.
works.context: Composed c. 996 at the Old Minster, Winchester, following the translation of Swithun's relics (971) and Æthelwold's building campaign; unique manuscript: British Library, Royal MS 15 C.vii.
works.characters: Swithun; Æthelwold; Ælfheah (dedicatee); Edgar
works.structure: A verse vita in two books framed by the prose dedicatory epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan the Cantor's authorship is certain (he names himself in the prose preface).

works.title: Narrative of a Five Years' Expedition, against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam, in Guiana, on the Wild Coast of South America; from the Year 1772 to 1777
altTitles: Narrative of a Five Years' Expedition against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam
works.form: Travel and campaign narrative with sentimental memoir and abolitionist polemic: a first-person military history in letters-and-episodes form, supplied with engraved plates and with an argument about the morality of colonial slavery.
works.description: A two-volume military and autobiographical narrative by a Scottish-born officer of Dutch service who was sent to suppress the maroon revolt in the plantation colony of Surinam, and who ended by indicting the slavery he had been hired to defend. Its matter is an eyewitness account of campaign life in the forest and, far more lastingly, of the punishments inflicted on the enslaved, recorded with a horror that the author repeatedly turns against his own complicity. The volumes were illustrated with a remarkable series of plates, several hand-coloured, which made the book an image-text of the slave trade unlike anything else of the decade. It became a standard quarry of abolitionist quotation and of later radical reading.
works.plot: The narrative opens with the author's enlistment and voyage, and with the society of Paramaribo: its dances, its duels, its treatment of the free people of colour and its economy of torture. The expeditionary chapters follow the pursuit of the maroon settlements through forest and river country, the desertions and deaths of the white troops, and the reliance on enslaved and Native fighters whose loyalty was bought with promises of freedom. Interwoven is the love story with a coloured woman, mother of his child, whose death is recounted with a grief that becomes the book's moral centre. Against these run the accumulations of judicial and private cruelty, the punishments described in exact detail, and an explicit argument that the planter's Christianity is a lie and that the enslaved have a right of resistance. The close sees the author's disillusionment complete and his departure from the colony.
works.significance: It is one of the most important documents of the Black Atlantic literary archive, and a founding text of the literature of colonial bad conscience: an insider's account that converts military report into abolitionist accusation. Its imagery shaped later representations of the enslaved, and its blend of sentimental intimacy with documentary horror makes it a central instance of the period's crossing of travel writing, memoir and polemic.
works.meter: Prose, moving between plain reportage, elevated lament and satirical invective; interpolated verse and song-fragments appear among the sentimental passages.
works.context: Written from journals kept during the 1772-1777 maroon war and prepared for publication in the 1790s, when British abolitionists were assembling evidence against the trade and when the French revolutionary crisis made colonial disorder a metropolitan topic. The book appeared in the same years as the great abolition enquiries and its plates were reused as anti-slavery imagery. Its publication history is complicated by editorial revision of the author's manuscript before and after his death.
works.characters: The officer-narrator; the coloured woman he loved and lost; their son; the planter families of Paramaribo; the maroon fighters; the Native and enslaved soldiers of the expedition; the commanding officer who shared his tent
works.structure: Mixed forms: a chronological campaign narrative with embedded sentimental episodes, letters, natural-history observation and explicit polemical digression, ending in a fragmentary continuation.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship is certain, though the printed text was substantially edited and partly bowdlerised by others before publication, and the manuscript recovered in the twentieth century differs from the printed version; the record here is of the 1796 printed edition.

Love, constancy, and betrayal
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition

works.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
works.description: Published in 1845 in Boston and the founding text of the African-American literary tradition: the account of Douglass's life from his birth in slavery to his escape and his first years of freedom. works.title: National Tales
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; The Sketch and Character Tale
works.description: Two volumes of short prose tales in the manner of the Italian novella, published in the same year as the author's serious verse. The subjects are drawn from Spanish, Italian, and legend-hungry Catholic Europe: treachery, convent intrigue, poisoned cups, sleeping saints, and lovers destroyed by honour. Together they form a domestic comic-Gothic counterpart to the fashionable historical romance of the later 1820s.
works.plot: The series runs from The Spanish Tragedy, a tale of Mantuan and Spanish court revenge, through The Miracle of the Holy Hermit, The Widow of Galicia, and The Golden Cup and the Dish of Silver to The Tragedy of Seville, The Lady in Love with Romance, The Eighth Sleeper of Ephesus, Madeline, and Masetto and his Mare. Each number compresses a single violent situation into a short narrative close to the Italian novella scheme of a tested love, a betrayed trust, or a providential exposure. The tone alternates between the terror and pity of the novella and a self-aware lightness that keeps the machinery from hardening into parody.
works.significance: The volumes document the range of a writer remembered chiefly for comic verse, and they show how the Romantic-period tale market absorbed the Italian novella and the legend of the saints into short commercial form. Their mixture of terror and lightness is a useful instance of the transition from Gothic romance to the Victorian sensation tale.
works.meter: Prose, with ballad and song stanzas interposed at several points; the sentence-rhythm is rhetorical and deliberate, imitating the translated novella rather than the colloquial manner of contemporary prose fiction.
works.context: Published in London in 1827 by a young publisher's list, in a season when the historical novel, the German tale translated into English, and the annual miscellany were competing for the same readers, and when the author's own serious poems appeared from one of the great houses. The collection belongs to the vogue for Catholic-Southern legend material that the Gothic novel had opened and that the tale-of-the-period market continued.
works.characters: the widow of Galicia; the lovers of Seville; the lady in love with romance; the eight sleepers of Ephesus; Masetto and his mare; the hermit of the miracle; the poisoned guests of the golden cup
works.structure: A framed collection of independent short tales without a continuous plot; each tale is single-incident and closes on recognition, death, or deliverance, with the occasional ballad stanza quoted inside the prose.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; no part of the collection has been claimed for the occasional collaborators of the author's magazine years.

works.title: Native Son
works.description: The central Black American novel of the 1940s: Bigger Thomas, Chicago and the crime. It is a prose fiction work of 1940 by Richard Wright; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.title: Natural Theology
altTitles: Natural Theology; or, Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity
works.form: natural theology; teleological treatise built on anatomical and natural-history evidence
works.description: The classic statement of the argument from design, opening with the famous supposition of a watch found upon a heath and proceeding to argue that what the watch is to a watchmaker, the structure of animals and plants is to a Deity. It gathers the contrivances of the organic world, eye, joint, bone, leaf, instinct, and the mutual relations of species, into a single cumulative case, and it remains the plainest and most seductive English form of the natural theology of design.
works.plot: The treatise begins by showing that a complex instrument found in a field forces the inference of an intelligence that made and placed it, and that the inference is not weakened by the ignorance of the finder as to its use. It then carries the analogy into the organic world: the jointed frame, the muscles, the circulation, the secretion, and above all the eye, with its lens, its humours, and its adaptation to distances, present the same relation of parts to a purpose which in any other case we refer to design. Following parts examine the contrivances of the sexes, of the provision for the young, of the structure of plants and seeds, of the instincts, of the relations of animals to their elements and to one another, and of the great balance by which the increase of each species is restrained. The closing argument turns from contrivance to the attributes, meets the difficulty of the suffering found in organic nature, and urges that the goodness as well as the power of the maker is to be collected from the preponderance of enjoyment in the system.
works.significance: It is the received text of the argument from design in English, the book against which the later nineteenth century measured its own revolution in biology, and one of the most widely read and most quoted works of natural theology of any period. Its influence is also a literary influence: the analogy of the watch, and the habit of reasoning from contrivance, entered the common stock of the period's writing on nature and remain the standard form the teleological argument still takes in popular discussion.
works.meter: Plain, homely, convincingly orderly prose, with the concrete instance always at hand and the analogy pressed home by repetition; the manner of the excellent teacher who distrusts ornament.
works.context: Published at the close of the century of natural history and of the anatomical schools, when the accumulated detail of the organic world offered itself as evidence, and when the sceptical handling of the design argument in the previous generation had made a restatement of it a duty of the pulpit; the author's own medical and anatomical reading, and the natural-history literature of the day, supply the whole texture of the book.
works.structure: A continuous treatise in numbered chapters without parts or volumes, rising from the single analogy of the instrument through the anatomy of contrivance to the inquiry after the attributes of the designer and the problem of organic suffering.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose long delay in publishing it is recorded by his family and by his biographers.

works.title: Natural Theology (Bridgewater Treatise)
works.form: natural theology; teleological treatise in the Bridgewater series
works.description: The first of the treatises founded by a ducal bequest for the demonstration of the power, wisdom, and goodness of God in the creation, and the most ambitious restatement of the design argument of its generation. Its plan is to show that the inorganic world is fitted to man before man is fitted to it, and that no advance of physical explanation touches the inference from contrivance to a contriving intelligence.
works.plot: The treatise distinguishes two branches of the argument, the physical, which inquires how things are done, and the metaphysical, which inquires why they are done and by whose choice; the one, it urges, can go for ever without ever superseding the other, because a law of nature names a regularity and never an agency. It then examines the properties of matter, the atmosphere, the relations of heat and light, the water cycle, and the constitution of the globe, and reads them as a series of anticipations of human need, so that the world appears prepared for its inhabitant before the inhabitant exists. From the inorganic it passes to the organic, to the structure of plants and animals, to the instincts, and to the mutual restraints by which the increase of every species is bounded. The closing argument collects the attributes: unity of counsel displayed in the mutual adjustment of separate contrivances, intelligence, power, and beneficence; and it meets the difficulties from animal suffering and from apparent waste by insisting upon the preponderance of enjoyment and upon the ignorance of the whole plan.
works.significance: It is the last great English attempt to make the argument from design secure against mechanism by dividing the two inquiries into different questions, a move that has remained the standard theistic reply to scientific explanation; and its treatment of the fitness of the environment to life set the agenda for the later 'adaptation' theologies of the Victorian crisis of faith. As rhetoric it is the finest single performance of the popular theological style of its author, and it was read across the Atlantic as well as in Britain.
works.meter: Diffusive, animated, preacher-like prose of great range: cumulative enumeration, abrupt address to the sceptic, and a rhetorical exultation in the vastness of the evidence, held together by the distinction between how and why.
works.context: Written for a series founded by the will of a noble testator and endowed for the express purpose of a nineteenth-century statement of creation's evidence, at a moment when the physical sciences were making their largest claims and when the evidence from geology and from anatomy had begun to disturb the older teleologies. Its author, at that time a Glasgow professor and the most powerful preacher of the evangelical party in the Church of Scotland, was chosen for the series on the strength of that reputation.
works.structure: Two volumes in numbered discourse-chapters: the distinction of the physical and metaphysical branches, the evidence from inorganic nature, the evidence from organic nature, and the collection of the attributes with the answer to the accompanying difficulties.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the treatise is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author and holds its allotted place in the endowment series.

works.title: Nature
altTitles: Nature, a goodly interlude of Nature
works.description: Henry Medwall's morality play of the fall and reformation of Man, the earliest surviving full-scale English morality written for a noble household; printed c. 1530–34 by William Rastell.
works.plot: Nature creates Man and sets Reason and Sensuality over him; Man follows Sensuality into the tavern and the arms of Pride, and the seven deadly sins strip him of his goods; Age and Shamefacedness bring him to repentance, and Reason restores him to grace. The play dramatizes the cycle of innocence, sin, and penitential return.
works.significance: The earliest surviving English morality play composed for a secular household audience and the first full example of the genre after Everyman; it documents the adaptation of the morality tradition to Renaissance taste and anticipates the moral interludes of the 1560s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets
works.context: Written in the late 1490s, probably for Morton's household like Fulgens and Lucrece; it draws on the tradition of The Castle of Perseverance and Everyman while giving new prominence to worldly temptation, and William Rastell's printing (c. 1530–34) secured its influence on the mid-century interludes.
works.characters: Nature; Man; Reason; Sensuality; Pride; World; Age; Shamefacedness; Innocence

works.title: Nature (1836)
works.description: Published anonymously in 1836 and the founding document of American Transcendentalism: a short book arguing that nature is the visible manifestation of spirit and that the individual may know God directly through it.
works.plot: Emerson divides the essay into Nature, Commodity, Beauty, Language, Discipline, Idealism, Spirit and Prospects, and argues in each that the natural world is a symbol of the mind's own laws and that 'the kingdom of man over nature' is available to anyone who will look with fresh eyes.
works.significance: Nature is the founding text of American Transcendentalism and of the American literature of nature: its call to look at the world with new eyes set the agenda for Thoreau, Whitman and the whole tradition of American nature writing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards.
works.context: The 1830s, the American Unitarian crisis, the German idealism of Kant and Coleridge, and the new science of natural history. The record dates the work as composed between 1835 and 1836 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: It was first published anonymously and the authorship was established afterwards from the publisher's records and the correspondence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Nellie's Memories
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1868
works.description: The founding domestic novel for girls: a large family, a governess and cheerful sacrifice. It is a prose fiction work of 1868 by Rosa Nouchette Carey; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Nellie, the eldest daughter of a large and improvident family, becomes a governess to support her brothers and sisters; the novel follows her household, her charges and her cheerful endurance through illness, poverty and the reward of goodness.
works.significance: Nellie's Memories was the founding domestic novel for girls and made Carey the most popular writer of the genre: its large family, its governess and its cheerful sacrifice shaped the girls' reading of a generation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the domestic chronicle of the large family.
works.context: England in the 1860s, the large middle-class family and the profession of governess. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: New Atlantis
works.description: Bacon's unfinished utopian fable, published posthumously with Sylva Sylvarum: a ship lost in the Pacific reaches the unknown island of Bensalem, where the narrator is received into a society organized around Salomon's House — the college of the 'Merchants of Light' whose institutes of experiment and invention anticipate the modern research laboratory.
works.plot: The sailors' arrival, the quarantine, and the Feast of the Family occupy the early pages; the governor's account of Bensalem's Christian origins and its concealment from the world follows; and the narrative climaxes in the Father of Salomon's House describing the college's 'preparations and instruments' — the prolongation of life, the making of new species, the knowledge of causes and secret motions of things.
works.significance: The great English utopia of science — the blueprint of the modern research institution and the ancestor of the scientific romance.
works.meter: Prose of ceremonial dignity, with the Father's discourse as the work's set piece.
works.context: Written about 1624, in Bacon's last years at Gorhambury, and published by William Rawley in 1627; its Bensalem answered More's Utopia and anticipated the Royal Society, which took Salomon's House as its inspiration.
works.characters: the narrator; the Governor of the Strangers' House; the Father of Salomon's House; Joabin; the sailors
works.structure: A utopian narrative in the Platonic and Morean tradition, unfinished, ending on the Father's promise that the narrator shall receive 'a relation of the true state of Salomon's House'.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: New Bearings in English Poetry

works.plot: New Bearings in English Poetry revalues the modern poets - Hopkins, Eliot and Pound against the Georgians and the verse of the quarterlies - and states the case for the new poetry as the necessary idiom of the civilisation.

works.title: New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air
works.description: Boyle's report of his experiments with the air-pump built for him by Robert Hooke, in which he demonstrated the elastic 'spring' of air, its necessity for respiration and sound, and stated the inverse relation between pressure and volume now known as Boyle's Law.
works.plot: Forty-three experiments establish the properties of the air and answer the objections of Hobbes and the Peripatetics; the famous Experiment 41 shows that a sound cannot be heard in an evacuated vessel.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern experimental physics and chemistry; it established the experimental report as a literary form and Boyle's Law as the first quantitative gas law.
works.meter: Detailed experimental prose; Boyle's practice of reporting full particulars became the model for the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions.
works.context: Published in 1660 at Oxford, where Boyle worked with Hooke; the second edition of 1662 added the Defence of the Doctrine Touching the Spring and Weight of the Air, containing the pressure-volume relation.
works.structure: A series of numbered experiments with descriptions of apparatus, results, and objections answered.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Boyle; Hooke built the apparatus and is credited in the text.

works.title: New Grub Street
works.form: Novel (three volumes); realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1891 and the central English novel about the literary profession: the parallel stories of a scholar who cannot sell his work and a journalist who can sell anything. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by George Gissing; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Harold Biffen and Edwin Reardon struggle in the London of Grub Street: Reardon's serious novels fail, his marriage breaks down, and he dies in poverty, while Jasper Milvain, who writes for the market, prospers and marries Reardon's wife's friend. Biffen's realistic slum novel, Mr Bailey, Grocer, is published to no effect.
works.significance: New Grub Street is the founding English novel about the writer's market and one of the most exact records of literary life in the nineteenth century: its account of the economics of authorship has been the starting point for every subsequent discussion of the literary marketplace.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1880s, the collapse of the three-volume novel, the rise of the literary agent, the new mass periodicals, and the professionalisation of authorship. works.title: News from Nowhere; or, An Epoch of Rest
works.description: Serialised in the Socialist League's Commonweal in 1890 and Morris's most influential prose work: the dream of a socialist England of the twenty-first century. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by William Morris; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.title: Nice Wanton
altTitles: A Preaty Interlude Called Nice Wanton
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality interlude of the divergent fates of three children, printed in 1560; a dramatization of godly education and its neglect.
works.plot: Xantippe's three children grow up under her indulgence: Ishmael and Dalila fall into idleness, gambling, and prostitution, and come to the gallows; the godly Barnabas, who studies scripture, is spared and comforts his repentant mother and sister; the Vice Iniquity frames the action, and the epilogue draws the moral of education and the rod.
works.significance: A representative Protestant morality whose twin plots of the saved and the damned child dramatize the educational programme of the Reformation; it marks the absorption of humanist pedagogy into the morality tradition.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1547–53, in the years of the Edwardian Reformation, when the godly education of children became a central Protestant theme; printed in 1560 for the Elizabethan market, with a title-page woodcut of the flogging schoolmaster.

works.title: Nicholas Nickleby
altTitles: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from March 1838 to October 1839, and the novel with which Dickens attacked the Yorkshire 'cheap schools' — the subject of his journey to Yorkshire with Hablot Browne in January-February 1838 in the company of the schoolmaster's son who had exposed them.
works.plot: After the failure of his father's speculation, Nicholas is placed as usher at Dotheboys Hall under Wackford Squeers, rescues the abused boy Smike, and flees with him to London; the two fall in with the theatrical manager Vincent Crummles and his company, and then with the Cheeryble brothers, whose charity sets Nicholas up in business. The subplot of Kate Nickleby's persecution by Sir Mulberry Hawk and of Ralph Nickleby's financial villainy is resolved when Ralph's ruin and suicide follow the revelation of Smike's parentage and the collapse of his schemes.
works.significance: Nicholas Nickleby ended the cheap boarding-school and did more than any single book to make the treatment of children a public question; the Crummles chapters are the fullest account in Victorian fiction of the provincial theatre, and the novel consolidated Dickens's comic and melodramatic range.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Yorkshire schools, the theatrical touring company of the 1830s, the counting-house and the speculative economy of the late 1830s; the novel appeared during the Chartist agitation and the Anti-Corn Law League's first campaigns.
works.characters: Nicholas Nickleby; Smike; Wackford Squeers; Ralph Nickleby; Kate Nickleby; Vincent Crummles; Newman Noggs; the Cheeryble brothers; Sir Mulberry Hawk
works.structure: Monthly-part narrative moving between three milieux — the school, the theatre and the City — with a subplot of female persecution and a resolved inheritance plot.

works.title: Night Watches
works.description: Published in 1914 and the last of Jacobs's great collections: the night watchman and the riverside household in the years before the war. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by W. W. Jacobs; it is catalogued here under Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The stories are told by or around a night watchman at the docks, and follow the small comedies of the working household: the lodger, the wife's relations, the legacy, the misunderstanding, the ghost that is only a fellow-worker in a white sheet.
works.significance: Night Watches is the finest of Jacobs's later collections and the culmination of his comic art: its dialogue and its construction are as precise as ever, and it is the collection in which the English riverside comedy reaches its fullest expression.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the tall tale: the frame of the literate narrator and the vernacular teller, the dialect spelling, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan, and the punch that turns on the outsider's credulity. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the tightly constructed story with a final turn.
works.context: 1914: the London docks before the First World War, the working-class household of the 1900s, and the last years of the comic magazine. The record dates the work as composed in 1914 and first published in 1914 and it is catalogued under tall tale and south-western humour sketch; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the night-watchman, the narrator; Ginger Dick, Peter Russet and Sam Small
works.structure: A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wymark Jacobs. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Nightmare Abbey
works.description: the author's second and most popular novel, a sparkling comedy satirising the epidemic of fashionable melancholy among the Regency intelligentsia. The house of Nightmare Abbey, presided over by the despairing Mr. Scythrop, becomes the stage for a parade of Romantic poses and their deflating exposure.
works.plot: Mr. Glowry, a hypochondriac widower, retreats to Nightmare Abbey with his son Scythrop, a Byronic poet who is in love with the unattainable Cellinara and despairing of the world. A succession of visitors — the optimist Mr. Jade, the mesmerist, the followers of various fashionable doctrines — arrive, complicating Scythrop's romantic plans. The novel culminates in a fire, a false death, and the comic exposure of every Romantic pose, as Scythrop is finally united with a worthy partner.
works.significance: Nightmare Abbey is the author's most widely read novel and a definitive satire of the Byronic pose; its portrait of Mr. Listless, exhausted by reading fashionable novels, remains one of the great comic passages of the Romantic period. It has influenced every subsequent campus novel.
works.context: Published in 1818, at the height of Byronic fashion and Gothic melodrama; The author, personally connected to Shelley and Byron, satirises the cult of sensitivity with intimate knowledge of its practitioners. The novel's 'misery' is the direct target of its comedy.
works.characters: Mr. Glowry; Scythrop; Marionette O'Carrol; Cellinara; Mr. Subtle; Mr. Listless; Mr. Fumflower
works.structure: Single-country-house setting; episodic sequence of visitor-arrivals each representing a philosophical or literary fashion; the fire and resolution provide a conventional comic climax.
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners
Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: Nights with Uncle Remus
works.description: Published in 1883 and the richest of the Uncle Remus volumes: seventy-one tales, including the great cycle of Brer Rabbit's adventures and the animal fables of the old plantation. It is a prose fiction work of 1883 by Joel Chandler Harris; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Uncle Remus continues his stories to the little boy, and the volume adds new tellers, the Gullah-speaking Daddy Jack, Aunt Tempy and the housemaid 'Tildy, whose rival versions of the tales of Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Tarrypin and Brer Wolf compete for the little boy's attention.
works.significance: Nights with Uncle Remus is the fullest record of African-American animal folklore in the nineteenth century and one of the most important books in the study of American folklore; its tales are among the great creations of American oral literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative in which the tale is told to a listener.

The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: Nightwood
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1936
works.description: The great modernist novel of expatriate Paris: Robin Vote and the obsession she leaves behind. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Djuna Barnes; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The novel follows Robin Vote, an American woman in Paris and Vienna, and the people who love her — her husband Felix, her lover Nora, the doctor Matthew O'Connor and the Baronin Jenny — through a series of nocturnal scenes that dissolve narrative into monologue.
works.significance: Nightwood is one of the great modernist novels in English and the finest novel of the expatriate lesbian Paris: its baroque prose, its portrait of Robin Vote and its exploration of sexual obsession made it a central text of modernism, introduced by T. S. Eliot.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the baroque, incantatory prose.
works.context: Paris and Vienna in the 1920s and 1930s, and the expatriate avant-garde of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1930 and 1936 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Robin Vote; Nora Flood; Felix Volkbein; Dr Matthew O'Connor; Baronin Jenny Petherbridge
works.structure: A novel in eight chapters, organised by scene and monologue rather than plot. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Djuna Chappell Barnes. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
works.description: Orwell's last novel and the defining English dystopia: a satire, set in a London that has become Airstrip One, a province of the totalitarian superstate Oceania, on a state that rules through perpetual war, total surveillance, the falsification of the past and the deliberate impoverishment of language. Drafted on the Hebridean island of Jura between 1946 and 1948 under the working title The Last Man in Europe, while Orwell was dying of tuberculosis, it was published by Secker and Warburg on 8 June 1949, seven months before his death, and in New York by Harcourt, Brace on 13 June 1949.
works.summary: The novel is in three parts and an appendix. Part One follows Winston Smith, a thirty-nine-year-old member of the Outer Party who rewrites old newspaper records at the Ministry of Truth, as he begins a forbidden diary. Part Two follows his affair with Julia and his approach to O'Brien, an Inner Party official whom he believes to belong to the underground Brotherhood, and gives long extracts from 'The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism', a book ascribed to the Party's enemy Emmanuel Goldstein. Part Three takes place in the Ministry of Love, where O'Brien breaks Winston. The appendix, 'The Principles of Newspeak', describes the official language as if from a later time.
works.plot:
On a bright cold day in April 1984, as he believes the year to be, Winston Smith returns to his flat in Victory Mansions, beneath the poster captioned BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU, and begins a diary in a corner hidden from the two-way telescreen, an act punishable by death. Oceania, one of three superstates permanently at war with one another, is ruled by the Party under the doctrine of Ingsoc; its slogans are WAR IS PEACE, FREEDOM IS SLAVERY, IGNORANCE IS STRENGTH, its Thought Police detect deviation, and its four ministries of Truth, Peace, Love and Plenty do the opposite of what their names declare. Winston's job at the Ministry of Truth is to alter back numbers of The Times so that the record always agrees with the Party's latest statement, consigning the originals to the 'memory holes'; people who fall from favour become 'unpersons' whose existence is erased. He has fragmentary memories of his mother and sister, who vanished in the turmoil of the 1950s, and of his estranged wife Katharine, and he believes that if there is hope it lies with the proles, the impoverished majority left outside politics; but an old man in a prole pub can remember nothing of use. From Mr Charrington, who keeps a junk shop, he buys a glass paperweight with a fragment of coral at its heart.

Julia, a young woman from the Fiction Department whom Winston has suspected of being a spy, slips him a note that says 'I love you'. They meet in the country and then in a room above Mr Charrington's shop, which they believe to be unwatched; Julia's rebellion is a matter of private pleasure rather than political conviction. Winston risks approaching O'Brien, a member of the Inner Party whom he has long believed to share his heresy. O'Brien receives them in his flat, enrols them in the Brotherhood, the conspiracy said to be led by Emmanuel Goldstein, and arranges for Winston to receive Goldstein's book. In the middle of Hate Week the enemy changes from Eurasia to Eastasia, and Winston works for days rewriting the records. Reading the book in the room above the shop, he learns how perpetual war consumes surplus production and keeps the hierarchy stable, and how doublethink lets Party members hold contradictory beliefs at once; but before he reaches the explanation of why the Party wants power, a voice from behind a picture tells them that they are the dead. Mr Charrington is an officer of the Thought Police, and the room has been watched throughout.

In the windowless cells of the Ministry of Love Winston is beaten and interrogated for months. O'Brien, who says he helped to write Goldstein's book, conducts his re-education: by torture he makes Winston see five fingers when four are held up, and he explains that the Party seeks power entirely for its own sake, offering as the image of the future a boot stamping on a human face for ever. Winston holds on only to his love for Julia, until in Room 101 he is confronted with what he fears most, rats, and begs for them to be set on Julia instead. Released, he meets Julia once more; each admits to having betrayed the other, and nothing remains between them. Sitting in the Chestnut Tree Café as the telescreen announces a great victory in Africa, Winston looks up at the face of Big Brother, and the novel ends with the sentence 'He loved Big Brother.'
works.significance: Few novels have had so great an effect on political language: 'Big Brother', 'doublethink', 'thoughtcrime', 'Newspeak', 'Room 101', '2 + 2 = 5' and the adjective 'Orwellian' became the common vocabulary in which totalitarianism, propaganda and mass surveillance are discussed. Nineteen Eighty-Four established the modern dystopia as a form of political argument and shaped the literature of the Cold War; it is on Time's list of the hundred best English-language novels of 1923-2005 and the Modern Library's list of the hundred best novels, and it came eighth in the BBC's Big Read poll of 2003.
works.meter: Plain, exact and unornamented prose that renders physical discomfort (Victory Gin, Winston's varicose ulcer, the smell of boiled cabbage, the grey of a bombed city) with documentary precision. Orwell invents a political vocabulary (Big Brother, doublethink, thoughtcrime, unperson, Newspeak, Room 101) by plain English compounding, and gives the Party's language its own parodic syntax in the slogans and in the specimens of Newspeak. The satire works by flat statement rather than exaggeration, so that the monstrous is reported as ordinary.
works.context: Orwell drafted the novel on Jura from 1946, finished a second draft in November 1948, retyped much of it himself while seriously ill, and sent the manuscript to Secker and Warburg on 4 December 1948. Its world draws on the Stalinist purges and show trials, on wartime propaganda and censorship, on James Burnham's forecast of a world divided among managerial superstates, which Orwell had analysed in 1946, and on the austerity of post-war Britain; Zamyatin's We and Huxley's Brave New World, which Orwell named among earlier pictures of a servile future society, are its predecessors.
works.characters: Winston Smith; Julia; O'Brien; Big Brother (never seen); Emmanuel Goldstein (never seen); Mr Charrington; Parsons; Syme; Katharine Smith
works.structure: Three parts of eight, ten and six chapters, followed by the appendix 'The Principles of Newspeak'. The close third-person narration is confined to Winston's perceptions, so that the reader knows no more than he does about O'Brien, the Brotherhood or the truth of the war; the long extracts from Goldstein's book in Part Two interrupt the story with political theory, and Part Three becomes a dialogue of interrogation. The appendix, written as if from a later period, frames the whole story as a historical document.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past
Language, writing and the limits of representation
Love, intimacy and loss
Power, the state and surveillance
Utopia, dystopia and imagined futures

works.title: No Name
works.form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1862; three volumes 1862)
works.description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1862: the story of Magdalen Vanstone, left illegitimate and penniless by the discovery that her parents' marriage was invalid, who sets out to recover her fortune by disguise and intrigue.
works.plot: Magdalen and Norah Vanstone lose their name, inheritance and social position when their father's marriage is found void; Magdalen trains as an actress, adopts a series of disguises, pursues the heir Noel Vanstone and his housekeeper Mrs Lecount, marries him, and loses him to death and the will; the novel ends with her illness, her sister's marriage and her own quiet recovery.
works.significance: No Name is the most direct Victorian novel about the legal construction of identity: Magdalen's loss of her name is a loss of her legal person, and the novel's argument for the reform of the law of legitimacy is as explicit as anything in the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1857 Matrimonial Causes Act and the law of legitimacy, the position of the illegitimate child, and the Victorian theatre. The record dates the work as composed in 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Magdalen Vanstone; Norah Vanstone; Captain Wragge; Noel Vanstone; Mrs Lecount; George Bartram; Admiral Bartram; Mr Pendril
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: None Turn Again
works.description: The close of the Mirror in Darkness: the decade at the war's edge. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Storm Jameson; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama.
works.plot: None Turn Again closes the trilogy with Hervey Russell in the Spain of the civil war and the England of the late thirties, in the final book that carries the woman's career to the edge of the second war.
works.significance: None Turn Again completed the Mirror in Darkness: its Spain and its closing decade made the trilogy one of the fullest novel records of the thirties.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of the woman's career in the prose of the decade.
works.context: England and Spain in the late 1930s. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Hervey Russell; the Spain of the war; the England of the decade's close
works.structure: The third of a trilogy: the war's edge and the career's close. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.

works.title: Nonsense Songs, Stories, Botany, and Alphabets
works.description: Published in 1871 and the collection that contains Lear's greatest nonsense poems: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', 'The Jumblies', 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' and the Nonsense Botany. It is a verse work of 1871 by Edward Lear; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
works.plot: The Owl and the Pussy-cat sail away and marry by the light of the moon; the Jumblies go to sea in a sieve and return in triumph; the Duck rides round the world on the Kangaroo's tail, and the Daddy Long-legs and the Fly sail away to the great Gromboolian plain; the botanical plates present absurd plants with mock-scientific names.
works.significance: This is the central book of English nonsense and the source of its best-loved poems: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', 'The Jumblies' and 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' are among the most quoted poems in English, and the collection established the nonsense poem as a form capable of holding genuine feeling and grief beneath its absurdity.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity.
works.context: 1871: the Victorian illustration boom, the children's book market after Alice, and Lear's own exile and loneliness in Italy. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.

works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.

works.title: North and South
works.form: Novel in weekly parts (Household Words); two volumes 1855
works.description: Serialised in Household Words from September 1854 to January 1855 (the last number after Dickens and Gaskell disputed the ending) and published in two volumes: the great novel of the industrial north seen through a southern woman's eyes.
works.plot: Margaret Hale, whose father has left the Church of England over a matter of conscience, moves with her family from the rural south to the cotton town of Milton, where she comes to know the mill-owner John Thornton and the striking workers Nicholas and Bessy Higgins. A strike and a riot, the death of her parents, her inherited wealth, and Thornton's business failure bring the two together in a marriage of mutual respect and of reconciled regions.
works.significance: North and South is the central English novel of the regional and class division of the nation, and its marriage plot is one of the period's most successful attempts to make a social reconciliation come true in the form of a personal one; it is a permanent counterpart to Hard Times, and its heroine is one of the most fully realised women of Victorian fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
works.context: The 1850s cotton industry and the Preston strike, the master-and-man conflict of the 1840s-50s, the contrast of the rural south and the industrial north, and the disruption of the Oxford Movement and the secessions to Rome.

works.title: North of Boston
works.description: The book that made Frost: blank-verse dialogues of New England farm life, and the sound of actual speech in American poetry. It is a verse work of 1914 by Robert Frost; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection opens with 'Mending Wall' and contains 'The Death of the Hired Man', 'Home Burial', 'After Apple-Picking', 'The Wood-Pile' and 'A Servant to Servants' — dramatic dialogues and narratives of New England farm life, in which the speakers reveal more than they know.
works.significance: North of Boston is the book that made Frost and the founding collection of the American dramatic lyric: its blank-verse dialogues brought the sound of actual speech into American poetry, and 'The Death of the Hired Man' and 'Home Burial' are among the greatest narrative poems in the language.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sound of speech in strict iambic measure.
works.context: The New Hampshire and Massachusetts farmland of Frost's years at Derry, and the England of 1912–15 where the book was first published. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1914 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric; American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.

works.title: Northanger Abbey
works.form: Comic novel of manners and parody of the Gothic romance of terror; a bildungsroman of reading.
works.description: A comic satire on the Gothic novel and on the heroine formed by reading it, drafted in the late 1798-99 as Susan and revised a few years before its posthumous appearance. Its heroine, Catherine Morland, goes from a Bristol pump-room to a Wiltshire abbey and invents a mystery of murder and concealment where there is only a plain domestic history. The work contains the period's most quoted defence of the novel as a form and a sustained parody of the conventions of terror.
works.plot: Catherine Morland, a plain and lively girl, is taken into fashionable Bath society by the well-meaning Mrs. Allen, learns to dance, and is encouraged in her hopes by the agreeable son of the master of Northanger Abbey. Reading the novels of the gothic school on the way to the Abbey, she transmutes a locked drawer, a blank manuscript and a curt question into evidence of a murdered wife and a concealed crime; the discovery that her reading has misled her is the novel's turning point, though General Tilney's pride and avarice prove all too real when he turns her from the house. The betrayal of her friend Isabella, who jilts Catherine's brother for a wealthy baronet and is then discarded, exposes the corruptions that Gothic plot-work disguises, and the concluding reconciliation with Henry Tilney arrives with an unromantic irony about the hero's prospects.
works.significance: The most sustained novelised critique of Gothic reading in English, and one of the earliest defences of the novel as an art; its parody of the pursued-heroine plot helped to end that plot's reign. It is also a key document for the history of women's reading and of circulating-library culture. Its posthumous publication made its author a named presence in the early nineteenth-century canon.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; light, rapid sentences, with parody pitched at the long trailing syntax of romance.
works.context: Conceived when the gothic bestseller and the circulating library had made terror a staple, and revised at the end of the period when that staple was being superseded; its Bath sections record the etiquette of the water-cure crowd and its ending a war-office patronage and a marriage into the naval interest. The novel's sale to a publisher in 1803 and its non-appearance for fourteen years is a documented instance of the period's unstable copyright trade.
works.characters: Catherine Morland; Henry Tilney; General Tilney; Eleanor Tilney; Isabella Thorpe; John Thorpe; James Thorpe; Mrs. Allen; Mr. Allen; Mr. Morland; Mrs. Morland
works.structure: Third-person narration with a self-conscious, addressing narrator, including an apologia for the novel in the opening book; a double structure of Bath society comedy and abbey parody, joined by Catherine's misreadings.
works.attributionNotes: Published posthumously with a biographical notice by a relative; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Nosce Teipsum
works.description: Sir John Davies's philosophical poem on the immortality of the soul: 'Know thyself' — the soul's nature, its faculties, its independence from the body, and the proofs of its immortality — argued in some 2,000 lines of didactic couplets, the poem that made Davies famous overnight and earned him the favour of James I.
works.plot: The poem proceeds from the Delphic command through the soul's definition, its powers of sense, fancy, and reason, the distinction of soul and body, the refutation of the soul's mortality, and the closing proof of its divine origin and destiny — a scholastic summa rendered in verse.
works.significance: The most accomplished English philosophical poem of its generation and a direct ancestor of the Augustan poetry of statement.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter couplets of a clear, dry, argumentative elegance — the manner that would become the Augustan couplet's parent.
works.context: Published 1599, in the same years as Donne's satires and the philosophical poems of the Inns of Court; Davies, a lawyer who became Attorney General for Ireland, dedicated it to Elizabeth I, and its success made his reputation at both courts.
works.characters: the poet as philosopher; the Soul; Reason; the Body
works.structure: Two books of sustained didactic argument, each section a step in the proof, with the famous passage on the soul's 'infinity of desire' as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard
works.description: The great political novel of South America: a silver mine, a revolution and the corruption of every ideal in the imaginary republic of Costaguana. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by Joseph Conrad; it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In the fictional South American republic of Costaguana, Charles Gould inherits the San Tomé silver mine and devotes his life to making it productive. When a revolution threatens, the silver is sent to sea with Nostromo, the Italian foreman of the dockers, who is trusted by everyone; he saves the silver, hides it, and is slowly destroyed by the secret of it, while the mine's wealth corrupts the whole society around him and the country passes from one dictator to another.
works.significance: Nostromo is the greatest political novel in English of the period: it invented the fictional republic as a model of the whole of politics, its structure of parallel and intersecting lives over decades is one of the most ambitious in the novel, and its analysis of how wealth and foreign capital corrupt every revolutionary ideal has never been surpassed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
works.context: The Central American and South American republics of the late nineteenth century, their cycles of revolution and foreign debt, and the imperial economics of the silver mine — Conrad drew on his knowledge of the Latin American revolutions and on the history of the American-financed mines.
works.characters: Nostromo; Charles Gould; Emilia Gould; Martin Decoud; Dr Monygham; Antonia Avellanos; Don José Avellanos
works.structure: Five-part structure moving backward and forward in time, with a large cast whose lives intersect around the mine and the silver.

works.title: Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction
works.description: Stevens's greatest long poem: it must be abstract, it must change, it must give pleasure. It is a verse work of 1942 by Wallace Stevens; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem's three parts — 'It Must Be Abstract', 'It Must Change' and 'It Must Give Pleasure' — argue for a poetry that replaces the dead gods with a fiction adequate to the modern world, and the sequence closes with the 'fat girl' and the 'ephebe' in the sun.
works.significance: Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction is Stevens's greatest long poem and the central American philosophical poem of the century: its three propositions make the case for the imagination as the modern equivalent of belief.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the exotic and sumptuous vocabulary.
works.context: The war years of 1941–42, the death of the gods, and Stevens's mature aesthetic philosophy. The record dates the work as composed in 1942 and first published in 1942 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.

works.title: Notions of the Americans, Picked Up by a Travelling Bachelor
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch combined with political dissertation; a book of national commentary
works.description: A book of sketches and dissertations by a travelling bachelor who observes American politics, society, literature and manners with an irony often mistaken for approval. It is at once a defence and an indictment of the republic's institutions, directed as much against British prejudice as against American self-satisfaction. Its chapter on the conditions of a national literature is a founding document of American literary criticism.
works.plot: The bachelor reports on elections, on the press, on banking and on the manners of the west and south, and on the diffusions of a commercial society. He then turns to the arts and to the question whether a country of equals can produce a literature, arguing that the American relation to English models is one of dependence rather than of inferiority. Its most discussed passages analyse the mechanics of party politics, and the notorious conclusion warns that the same public which destroys its dependencies will destroy its artists. The tone shifts from jest to prophecy without warning.
works.significance: It is the most acute American analysis of the dangers of popular power before Tocqueville. Its account of the material conditions of authorship anticipated the sociology of the literary marketplace. It supplies the context for the romances of the same decade and for the author's later attacks on the American press.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1828, the year of Jackson's election, out of the author's residence in Europe and his renewed quarrel with British reviewers. Its politics were shaped by the Anti-Masonic and nullification agitation then beginning. Its argument about literary dependence repeats the terms of the periodical controversy over American letters carried on in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine.
works.characters: The travelling bachelor; the political and literary society of the United States as observed by him
works.structure: Loose sequence of dissertations and reported observations under a single persona, framed by a preface that explains the licence of the travelling bachelor.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature

works.title: Novum Organum
works.description: Bacon's second part of the Instauratio Magna, published in Latin: the 'New Instrument' of science, in which the old logic of Aristotle is replaced by the new method of induction — the doctrine of the idols (of the tribe, cave, marketplace, and theatre), the tables of presence and absence, and the 'prerogative instances' that guide the interpretation of nature.
works.plot: Book I clears the ground: the idols that beset the mind, the signs of philosophy's failure, and the hope of a new beginning; Book II lays out the method — the tables of instances, the first vintage, and the ascending ladder of axioms that ends in the knowledge of forms and the power over nature ('knowledge and human power are synonymous').
works.significance: The founding document of the scientific method — the text that named the idols and invented induction as the modern world understands it.
works.meter: Latin aphorisms of epigrammatic force, with the prefatory matter framing the work as the 'second part' of the Instauratio.
works.context: Published in 1620, the year of the Mayflower, as the manifesto of the new experimental science; Bacon's idols doctrine became the common vocabulary of seventeenth-century epistemology.
works.structure: Two books of aphorisms, deliberately fragmentary, in the oracular style Bacon devised for his philosophical testament.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: O'Donnell
works.form: Prose fiction; historical national tale; romance of restoration and exile
works.description: A historical national tale built around the recovery of an Irish chieftain's name and fortunes, which moves between Confederate Ireland, the continental Irish brigades and the Scotland of the exiled court. Romance and family injury carry the argument: the dispossession of the Gaelic aristocracy is treated as a wrong whose remedy is honour rather than agrarian improvement. The book is the most openly political of the author's Irish fictions, written in the years when Catholic claims and the union settlement were under active debate. Its use of an early-seventeenth-century setting to speak to present questions is characteristic of the national-tale mode.
works.plot: The son of a dispossessed Irish house, serving in a continental brigade, returns towards his inheritance under the protection of an Irish-born commander, while an English relation and a court faction obstruct his claims and those of the woman he loves. Kidnapping, disguise, a journey through Scotland and the Irish Sea, and a duel bring the injury to public notice, and the closing settlement restores the family name while leaving the larger fate of the nation unresolved.
works.significance: Important as the most explicitly historical of the author's national tales and as a case study in the Romantic novel's use of seventeenth-century Ireland for contemporary political argument; its frame of exile and Restoration influenced the later historical fiction of the Irish national-tale tradition.
works.meter: Prose narrative with interpolated Irish lyrics and ballad stanzas
works.context: Published in 1814, at the end of the Napoleonic war and in a decade of contention over Catholic relief, the Irish lord-lieutenancy and the memory of the 1641 and Cromwellian settlements. Its treatment of the Irish brigades and of the exiled Stuarts reflects current antiquarian interest in Confederate Ireland. Contemporary reviewers read the book's pleas for justice to a dispossessed elite as commentary on the union settlement.
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with double dating: an early-seventeenth-century main action and a later frame of family tradition; embedded tales and songs interrupt the linear plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. The historic chief of the title is a vehicle for the plot rather than a biographical study.

works.title: Observations Concerning the Distinction of Ranks in Society
altTitles: Observations Concerning the Distinction of Ranks in Society, Vol. I
works.description: John Millar's pioneering social history of ranks, gender, and law, the first full application of the Scottish theory of society to the changing relations of masters and servants, sexes, ages, and conditions. It argued that the manner of subsistence shapes the laws, manners, and domestic relations of a people.
works.plot: Millar traces the distinctions of rank from the ranks of the savage and pastoral states, through the slavery and villeinage of agricultural societies, to the graded dependencies of commercial life. He shows the legal condition of servants, tenants, and slaves to vary with the species of industry and the balance of power between the rich and the state. A celebrated sequence treats the rank of the female sex in each stage, arguing that civilisation softens domestic authority and raises women's consideration, and other chapters follow the relations of parents and children, ages, and professions. The printed book, the fruit of the Glasgow lectures, ends unfinished in its design, its completed first volumes carrying the argument from dependence to the domestic and sexual orders of polished society.
works.significance: It founded the history of social ranks and of gender as a scholarly subject, supplied the stage-consciousness that ran into the nineteenth century through Comte and historical sociology, and remains a classic of Enlightenment thought about society and women.
works.meter: Cool, comparative, case-rich prose of the jurisprudential lecturer, long historical illustrations drawn to a general law of social development.
works.context: Published in 1771 from Millar's Glasgow lectures, in the decade of the stage-theory efflorescence and after Smith's and Ferguson's accounts of society; the volume carried only the designed first half, the remaining volumes issuing in the 1780s and 1790s from lectures revised against the French Revolution.
works.structure: A continuous analytical history in successive chapters on each relation of rank, each stage compared across nations and epochs.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
