works.title: Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Expectations
altTitles: Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Expectations. Part I
works.description: David Hartley's associationist philosophy of the mind and religion, published in two parts in 1749: a 'Frame' deducing all mental life from vibration and association, and 'Duty and Expectations' grounding morality and revealed religion in that same mechanism. It became the foundation of the British associationist tradition.
works.plot: Part I, on the Frame, proposes that outward objects produce vibrations in the sensory nerves and brain, which leave 'vibruncles', or permanent dispositions, the physical seats of memory and habit; from simple sensations the mind builds its whole world by association, so that tastes, motives, and even abstract ideas are compounded experiences. Part II argues that pleasures rise by association from the bodily to the moral and religious, that virtue is the attainment of the greatest happiness of the whole system of beings, and that providence's dispensations, including future punishment, are vindicated by their tendency to universal good. Hartley closes with a theodicy reading history and scripture as one curriculum of association toward eternal happiness.
works.significance: It founded the associationist psychology that Priestley, Darwin, and Mill inherited, gave the century its most influential account of the mechanism of taste and moral feeling, and shaped evangelical theories of character and atonement.
works.meter: Uneven, intense, digressive prose of a thinker writing his scheme under pressure, with numbered propositions and long self-interrupting parentheses.
works.context: Long maturing from the 1730s among the Hartley Circle and the Cambridge moralists' disputes, published in 1749 and noticed chiefly in the periodical reviews of the 1750s; its medical and Newtonian vocabulary places it between the New Science and the evangelical revival.
works.structure: Two-part treatise: a physiological-metaphysical analysis of the Frame, followed by moral, religious, and eschatological applications.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Observations on the Faerie Queene of Spenser
altTitles: Observations on the Faerie Queene of the Glorious Poet Ed. Spenser
works.form: scholarly annotation and critical dissertation; editorial commentary on a native classic
works.description: Warton's scholarly edition of and commentary on Spenser's poem, the work that revived the heroic allegory in the age of the rules and made Spenser a classic again. Its observations explain the obsolete language, the allegory, the sources and the romances that Spenser used, and its preliminary dissertation argues for the historical dignity of the native tradition of chivalric poem. The book is a foundation of English literary scholarship and of the Gothic revival.
works.plot: The commentary expounds the allegorical persons and the moral and political design of Spenser's fable, traces his imitation of earlier romance and of the Italian poets, and glosses the archaic vocabulary with the help of the old writers. The prefatory matter argues that the genius of Spenser belongs to a national tradition of allegory and chivalry which the false taste of later ages had neglected, and that the poet's allegory must be read historically as well as morally. Together the observations establish the method of editing a native classic by the evidence of its own age.
works.significance: It created the modern scholarly study of Spenser and supplied the model of historical annotation for English poets, influencing the editorial practice of the later eighteenth century. Its defence of allegory and romance is a central document of the Gothic and antiquarian revival and of the transfer of taste from the rules to national literary history.
works.meter: Prose of the notes and dissertation, the Spenserian stanza of the edited poem being the object of the historical account of metre.
works.context: Published in 1754, in the season of the revived esteem for Spenser among the Oxford and London wits and of the debate about the allegorical romance, and alongside the antiquarian work on chivalry and the British poetic tradition that Warton's own History of English Poetry later completed.
works.characters: Spenser; the allegorical persons of the Faerie Queene; the romancers and Italian poets named as sources
works.structure: An edition with preliminary dissertation and continuous annotation, the commentary arranged by book and stanza of the poem it illustrates rather than as a free-standing argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is Thomas Warton's, and the date of its composition before publication is not fixed for every part, so the composition start is left null.

works.title: Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution, and the Means of Making It a Blessing to the Nations of Britain
altTitles: Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution
works.description: Richard Price's dissenting sermon on the newly settled American peace, arguing that the Revolution could be a blessing only if Britain learned its lessons: parliamentary economy, religious liberty, and the end of the crown's unconstitutional influence. Its prosecution made Price a celebrated martyr of free speech.
works.plot: Price first praises the American event as the just resistance of a people oppressed by taxation without representation, then draws its moral for Britain. He argues that the expensive consolidated state, the crown's patronage and its placemen, and a standing revenue independent of the people are the true enemies of the constitution, and that economy, annual parliaments, and the extension of toleration are the means of making the American example a blessing. He urges the improvement of the peace by free trade with the new states and warns that corruption, not arms, undoes empires. The sermon closes with an appeal to the Christian and civil spirit of the nation to reform before a harsher lesson is taught.
works.significance: It became a charter text of English radicalism and dissenting whiggery, reprinted through the reform agitations and read in the American and French revolutionary circles that claimed Price as their prophet.
works.meter: Earnest, accumulative sermon prose, the argument driven by resolute reiteration and a plain arithmetic of public expense.
works.context: Preached and published in 1784 after the settlement of the American peace, in the first years of the movement for parliamentary economy and reform; Price, his printer, and his distributor were prosecuted in a King's Bench information that made the pamphlet a landmark of free-speech history.
works.structure: A single sermon with appended considerations, moving from the historical occasion to the political anatomy and the programme of reform.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty, the Principles of Government, and the Justice and Policy of the Mother Country, respecting the Colonies
altTitles: Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty
works.form: Political pamphlet and treatise on liberty and empire
works.description: The pamphlet that made the Unitarian minister Richard Price the most read political writer of the American crisis. Issued in London in early 1776 and running through many editions within months, it argues from the first principles of civil liberty that the colonies cannot lawfully be taxed without consent, and that a free people's relation to the mother country must be that of voluntary allegiance, not of subordinate taxation. Its cool arithmetic of empire and its appeal to the reason of the reader made it more influential in America than most American writing of the same year.
works.plot: Price first defines civil liberty as the right of a people to make their own laws, and asserts that this cannot be delegated or lost, so that no legislature may bind those it does not represent. He examines the constitutional history of the colonies, their charters and their practice of self-taxation, and concludes that Parliament's claim to legislate for them in all cases whatsoever is an assumption never consented to. He then weighs the policy of the mother country, arguing that trade and affection, not force, hold an empire together, and that an overgrown state tends toward despotism. Finally he urges accommodation, warning that coercion will produce the very independence it seeks and that Britain's true interest lies in justice.
works.significance: It supplied the most rigorous British statement of the colonial case and helped convert the argument from taxation into one about representation and the nature of consent, anticipating Paine and shaping American reading of the Declaration. As the work of a London Dissenting minister it also shows the transmission of the British radical tradition into revolutionary America, and its warning about overgrown states became a permanent element of Anglo-American republican language.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, reasoned, sermon-clean style of short paragraphs and rhetorical questions
works.context: Written between the Olive Branch Petition and the Declaration of Independence amid the British debate over American policy, it belongs to the Dissenting commonwealth tradition, to the Whig opposition of Rockingham and Chatham, and to the print boom of the crisis, when pamphlets were reprinted across the Atlantic within weeks.
works.structure: Continuous argumentative pamphlet in numbered sections moving from principles to constitutional case, commercial policy and counsel of accommodation.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Richard Price is established and undisputed, though early editions circulated under the cover of anonymity while his name was common knowledge.

works.title: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy
altTitles: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, to Which is Added The Description of a New Blazing World
works.description: Cavendish's philosophical critique of the new experimental philosophy, attacking the Royal Society's microscopy, Hooke's Micrographia, and the corpuscular theories of Hobbes, Descartes, and Boyle, and proposing her own vitalist materialism.
works.plot: Cavendish argues that matter is self-moving, sentient, and rational; she rejects the mechanical philosophy's reliance on instruments, which she thought distorted nature, and asserts a holistic, animistic view of the natural world.
works.significance: The most substantial philosophical work by an English woman of the seventeenth century and an important early critique of instrumental science; it has been revalued as a serious contribution to natural philosophy.
works.meter: Argumentative prose of remarkable originality and density.
works.context: Published in 1666; Cavendish was one of the few women to engage directly with the Royal Society, and her critique of Hooke's microscopy was a direct response to Micrographia (1665).
works.structure: A systematic critique in chapters, followed by the appendix The Blazing World.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cavendish; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Observations upon the United Provinces of the Netherlands
works.description: Temple's political and social analysis of the Dutch Republic, written after his years as English ambassador at The Hague, and one of the most influential English works of political observation of the period.
works.plot: Temple describes the constitution, government, religion, military strength, trade, and character of the United Provinces, and analyses why a small republic could rival the great monarchies of Europe.
works.significance: A classic of early modern political analysis and a model of plain prose; it influenced Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws and the English debate on republicanism.
works.meter: Clear, urbane prose in the new plain style.
works.context: Written in 1672-3 during the Franco-Dutch War and published in 1673; Temple was a leading Whig diplomat and a patron of Swift.
works.structure: A series of short chapters on the several aspects of Dutch government and society.

works.title: Odd John: A Story Between Jest and Earnest
works.form: Novel; scientific romance, first issued in 1935
works.description: The first serious study of the superman: a boy with a mind beyond the human, and the colony he founds. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Olaf Stapledon; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: John Wainwright, born to ordinary parents, is a mutant with an intelligence beyond the human; the narrator, a writer, becomes his friend and biographer as John gathers other mutants, founds a colony on an island, and finally confronts the human race.
works.significance: Odd John is the first serious study of the superman in English fiction: it gave the theme its moral seriousness and its tragedy, and it remains the finest treatment of the mutant in the genre.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the future history narrated by a species rather than a character.
works.context: The 1930s, the eugenics debate, and the philosophy of the superman. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under scientific romance and the utopian tale; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: John Wainwright; the narrator; Pax; the mutants of the island
works.structure: A biography by the narrator, in twenty-one chapters. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Olaf Stapledon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Ode for Music
works.description: Pope's irregular ode written for musical setting, an attempt to carry the English Pindaric of Dryden into a theory of music's powers over the passions and over the elements.
works.plot: The poem calls on music to descend and to rule the heart, traces its effects through the passions from terror to pity and love, and ends by claiming that the composer's art can remake the hearer's soul.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished of the early eighteenth-century odes written for composition and a document of the period's attempt to refound the sublime on music rather than on versification.
works.meter: A Pindaric stanza of long and short five-beat and four-beat lines with a varied rhyme scheme, written to be set; the verse imitates the progressions of the music it praises.
works.context: Composed in the same year as Windsor-Forest, when English odes were being written for Handel's London season and for the theatre's incidental music, and when the powers of music were a standard subject of the periodical essay.
works.structure: A strophic irregular ode, each stanza taking one power of music, with an invocation opening and a panegyric close.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College
works.description: Gray's ode written at Cambridge and looking over the playing fields of his old school, where the sports of the boys become the image of a life of unremembered cares and of the manhood that awaits them.
works.plot: The poet watches the boys at their games from the far side of the river, asks them to be happy while they are ignorant of their years, reviews the passions and the miseries of after life, and ends by committing the ignorant and the unhappy to Forgetfulness.
works.significance: It gave English poetry its durable image of childhood seen from without, and its stanza and its turn of reflection are the direct preparation for the Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard.
works.meter: Quatrains of iambic five-beat lines with the alternate rhyme, the stanza form Gray carried to perfection in the Elegy; the diction is plain and the cadence restrained.
works.context: Written in the year of the Elegy's beginnings and of Gray's residence at Cambridge, in the season when the schoolboy poem, the meditation on childhood and the reflection on future ill were becoming the topics of the descriptive lyric.
works.characters: the boys of Eton at their games; the personified passions and powers of the closing stanzas; the poet as spectator
works.structure: A stanced reflective ode progressing from the prospect and the apostrophe to the generalisation of human misery and the closing address to Forgetfulness.

works.title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
works.form: Romantic ode and ekphrasis of the school of the great odes of 1819; the poem on a piece of ancient art turned to a meditation on the permanence of the work against the passing of the beholder.
works.description: The companion ode of the same season to that of the nightingale, and the period's most searched poem on the relation of art to life. Addressed to a marble frieze of the old Greek world, the bride of silence, it asks what tale the shapes pursue, and answers itself that the figures, being fixed in art, shall love for ever and shall never be parted, while the lover for ever pines and for ever burns. Its closing sentences, on beauty and truth, have made it a centre of the argument about the poet's creed.
works.plot: The ode begins with the address to the foster-child of silence and slow time, and asks what legend of the old men and maidens, of Thessalian or Arcadian passion, the pictured tale pursues; the shapes cannot be told, and the speaker answers that the far-heard melodies are for the other sense, and that the boughs which never shed their leaves and the for ever singing love are happier than the winning of the heart. The middle stanzas pass to the Sacrificer going to his altar, the green little town which for ever is silent and hollows its streets, and to the beauty which draws the eye and the mind, till the last stanza names the urn Attic and the marble breeding friend of the human race, whose message to a generation like this, being beauty and being truth, is the whole of what it needs to know. The argument is that art's stillness is a truer condition than life's passing, and that the lesson of beauty is the only knowledge given to the troubled age.
works.significance: It is the period's supreme poem on the silent speech of the visual arts and the source of the most quoted and most analysed closing lines in English Romantic writing. Its treatment of art as a condition at once enviable and inhuman set the terms of much later discussion of aesthetic doctrine, and its stanza has been the standard model of the English ode in the century after.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in ten-line stanzas, the first four lines alternating and the sestet varied, with the shortened line of the second half of the stanza used for check; the diction is compressed and the questions of the opening give the poem its movement.
works.context: Written in the spring of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the same season as the ode of the nightingale and the two titan poems, and published in the volume of July 1820. Its subject was drawn from the old Greek marbles then a possession of the metropolis and from the engravings of the classical vase, and its identification of beauty with truth was at once, and has remained, the most quoted and most disputed statement of the poet's creed.
works.characters: the urn, addressed as bride, foster-child of silence and Attic shape; the lover and the beloved of the frieze; the priest and the Sacrificer of the heifer; the little town for ever silent
works.structure: Five stanzas of ten lines, the opening questions, the answer on the unattained love and the for ever burning fever, the vision of the sacrifice and the emptied town, and the close on the urn's message to the aging generation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in the drafts of the season and in the transcript of the volume, and its disputed sense has never been a question of authorship.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: Ode on the Poetical Character
works.description: Collins's ode on what the true poet is and how his imagination is made, arguing that the poetic character depends on a gift of fancy and on the union of learning, passion and sensibility.
works.plot: The ode asks by what power the poet raises his scene above the world, reviews the ancient makers as the company of the chosen, and concludes that the imaginative faculty and the ear of the poet are the conditions of his office.
works.significance: It is one of the century's shortest and most concentrated definitions of the imaginative poet, and its account of fancy was a source for the later theory of the secondary imagination.
works.meter: Varied lyric stanzas in the Collinsian manner, with the long winding line of the imaginative passage and the sententious close.
works.context: Written in the years of the argument over genius, imitation and the faculty of the poet, when the theory of fancy and imagination was being formed out of the Addisonian account of the pleasures of the imagination.
works.characters: the poet of the character; Fancy and the imaginative powers; the ancient bards of the review
works.structure: A continuous stanced argument with the invocation, the review of the ancient poets and the closing definition.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Ode on the Spring
works.description: Gray's reflective ode on the returning year, in which the music and the gladness of the spring become an occasion for the examination of the poet's own cold and disordered mind.
works.plot: The bird, the breeze and the opening year awake the senses and the fancy of every creature but the poet, who finds himself incapable of the spring's gladness, and turns the season to the argument that Wisdom's precepts leave the heart untaught while the social affections are allowed their play.
works.significance: It is Gray's earliest complete statement of the argument that feeling, not rule, is the life of virtue, and it stands between Thomson's seasons and the meditative lyrics of the following decade.
works.meter: Stanzaic lyric ode in the smooth measures of the descriptive school, with the short line of the bird passage and the longer period of the reflection.
works.context: Printed with the Eton ode in the first collected issue of Gray's poems, in the years when the description of the seasons and the philosophy of the affections were joining in the lyric.
works.characters: the creatures of the spring in their gladness; the poet as the exception; the personified powers of the moral argument
works.structure: A stanced description passing into self-examination and a closing moral address, in the order of the descriptive ode.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Ode to a Nightingale
works.form: Romantic ode of the school of the great odes of 1819, combining the elemental hymn, the meditation on death and the transport of the imagination in a single strict stanza.
works.description: The greatest of the author's odes of 1819 and one of the two or three most perfect lyrics in the language, written in the spring at the house of a friend's family in the north of London, after the singing of a nightingale in the garden. It passes from the wish for the draught of vintage that might let the speaker fade away with the bird, through a refusal of the drug of forgetfulness and an argument with the thought of death, to the vision of the bird's immortal song heard by emperor and clown in the old world and in the sea of the biblical past. Its close, waking from the fancy with the question whether the bird was a phantom or a living thing, is the period's most exact statement of divided belief.
works.plot: The poem opens in a numbness of heart as though of hemlock and of Lethe, and the speaker, hearing the full-throated ease of the bird in the dark woodland, asks for a draught that he may dissolve away from the world where palsy shakes a few pale silent nerves and where youth fades and the spectre of illness sits. He will use no chariot of the poet but the viewless wings of Poesy, and in the dark he is with the bird, knowing the flowers and the season by scent and by the fancy of the mother-ward green, and admires the ease of a death in such an hour. But the bird's immortal strain, heard in the old days and on the windows of the hostile camp of the biblical story, is not for the weary hearer, and at the word forlorn the fancy cannot cheat so well as she is famed, so the speaker wakes to his own solitary song and asks whether it was wake or dream. The argument is that the imaginative transport is at once real and insufficient, and that beauty which does not die only measures the pain of what dies.
works.significance: It established the Romantic ode at its highest and remains the standard example of a lyric whose form enacts its argument, the transport and its collapse being carried by the stanza's own structure. Its account of the bird's song as immortal, heard by the emperors and the clowns of the old world, became one of the most quoted passages of the period, and its division at the close is the classic statement of the Romantic quarrel with the sufficiency of imagination.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in ten-line stanzas rhyming abab, the sestet varied with a shortened fourth line of the second half, the structure giving the stanza both its weight and its check; the music of the vowel and the repetition are the poem's argument.
works.context: Composed in the spring of 1819 at the house in Hampstead grounds where the poet was living with a friend, in the year after the death of his younger brother of consumption and in the season of his own first symptoms and of his love for the woman of the neighbouring house; the nightingale's song in the garden is the reported occasion. It appeared in the volume of July 1820, the last of the poet's lifetime, and its treatment of the thought of death as a release and of the beauty of the immortal bird gave the century its model of the serious lyric.
works.characters: the nightingale of the wood, addressed as a bird and as a voice; the speaker who would fade away; the fancy which cannot cheat so well as she is famed
works.structure: Eight stanzas of ten lines, the movement from the numbness of the opening, through the invocation to the bird and the dark transport, to the immortal strain and the awakening; the argument advances by a succession of acts of attention rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in the drafts of the season and in the transcript made for the volume, and the textual questions concern only small readings.
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Imagination as a way of knowing
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: Ode to the West Wind
works.form: Romantic ode in the revived lyric form, combining the elemental hymn of the school of the earlier odes with the personal prayer of the meditation; an ode of vocation.
works.description: A five-part ode addressed to the autumn wind, which at once destroys the year's leaves and carries the seed to its springing, and which the poet asks to make the instrument of his own regenerative power. Written in the woods beside a river in a stormy October, it converts the description of air, water and earth into an argument about the poet's function. Its closing prayer, that the dead thought may quicken a new birth, is one of the most quoted passages of English lyric, and the terza rima sonnet structure of its parts is a technical monument.
works.plot: The ode addresses the wind first as the destroyer of the leaves and the carrier of the dead seeds to their winter graves, then as the spirit in the air, in the waves of the sea which it rouses and in the forest whose loose hairs it shakes. The poet then asks to be made one with the wind, a leaf, a wave and a cloud, and to be scattered like the ashes and sparks from an unextinguished hearth among mankind. The final part turns the prayer to speech itself, an exhortation that the blasts of the dead thought may wake the sleeping earth, and the poem ends with the promise of the returning spring. The argument is that the poet's power is not his own but the wind's, and that the same force which buries the year also germinates it.
works.significance: It is the period's most influential elemental hymn and the standard example of how a Romantic ode can fuse description, argument and prayer in a single strict form. Its closing figure of the dead thought scattered to quicken a new birth gave later revolutionary and educational poetry its most portable image of the intellectual's function.
works.meter: Fourteen-line sections built of four tercets and a closing couplet in the third-rhyme measure of the older Italian sequence, iambic pentameter, a structure that binds the argument tightly and forces the close into a couplet.
works.context: Composed in the Arno woods in the October of 1820, in the year of the poet's settlement near Pisa, of his failing health and of the Neapolitan rising and its crushing by the Austrian arms; the season's storm over the river is reported as the occasion. It appeared in the 1820 volume of the shorter poems and drew little attention there, its fame belonging to the later anthologies.
works.characters: the wind addressed as spirit; the dead leaves and the winged seeds; the waves of the Atlantic and the sea-mosses; the poet who asks to be the wind's lyre
works.structure: Five sections of fourteen lines each, the first three describing the wind's action on earth, air and water, the fourth and fifth passing to the poet's own prayer; the movement is from cosmology to vocation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the ode was printed in the author's lifetime and has been reedited from the manuscript with the interleaved corrections noted.
themes: Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: Odes and Addresses to Great People
altTitles: Odes and Addresses to Great People, by the Same Authors
works.form: Burlesque and mock-heroic verse of the recurrent kind, in the specific form of the ode and the address. It works within the Pindaric and Wordsworthian ode as Reynolds's earlier Peter Bell had worked within the lyrical ballad, and it belongs to the tradition of verse that lives on the periodical and the show rather than to the serious romantic narrative; the collaborative character of the volume gives it the texture of a double act.
works.description: A joint volume of comic odes and burlesque addresses by John Hamilton Reynolds and Thomas Hood, published in London in 1825 and reissued in a third edition as early as 1826. The book applies to the elevated Romantic ode, and to the public celebrities and wonders of the moment, exactly the kind of deflating treatment that Reynolds had earlier given to Wordsworth's Peter Bell: its pieces are addressed to great people, to machines, to curiosities exhibited for money and to the fashionable sentiments of the day. It was Hood's first book and one of the last of Reynolds's publications that reached a wide readership, and its success was such that it was still being described, in later accounts of Hood, as the joint beginning of a career.
works.plot: The volume has no continuous argument; its case is made piece by piece against the solemnity of the Romantic ode and against the cult of celebrity. Each address takes a grand form and directs it to an unworthy or absurd subject, so that the rhapsodic manner is exposed by being used where it does not belong; several of the pieces continue the parody of Wordsworthian diction and subject, and one at least, an ode on the aeronaut Graham, is recorded as a parody of Peter Bell. Together the odes and addresses make a comic argument about the difference between real and assumed enthusiasm.
works.significance: It is the principal record of Reynolds's last years as a published poet and the founding volume of Hood's career, and it is one of the most sustained examples of the Romantic-period burlesque of the ode. As a joint production it documents the collaboration and friendship that shaped much Cockney writing, and as parody it preserves, in comic form, the manners of Wordsworthian and Hunt-style verse for later students of the period.
works.meter: A deliberate imitation of elevated Romantic metres, used for comic ends: stanzas borrowed from the solemn ode and the pathetic ballad, with their diction and inversions preserved and their subjects replaced, together with the lighter anapaestic and songs measure at which Hood in particular excelled. The success of the writing depends on accuracy of mimicry, and the volume is therefore a useful record of the metrical habits of the generation it laughs at.
works.context: The book appeared in the later 1820s, when the great decade of Romantic experimentation was being consolidated, imitated and sold, and when parody had become a regular part of the periodical press. Reynolds brought to it the experience of the Examiner and Champion and of the Wordsworth parodies of 1819; Hood was a young contributor whose first book it was. Its reissue by Henry Colburn in 1826, and its survival in the bibliographies of both writers, show how quickly it became a recognised production of the metropolitan literary market.
works.characters: The celebrities, wonders and personified abstractions addressed in the separate pieces; the two comic poets' assumed public voices
works.structure: A miscellany of short separate poems arranged as a sequence of odes and addresses, without plot or sustained progression; the unity is that of a single comic method applied repeatedly to different occasions, persons and exhibits. Individual pieces are self-contained, and the volume reads as a joint notebook of effects rather than as a work with an order of development.
works.attributionNotes: The volume is a collaboration between Reynolds and Hood and is catalogued under both names; the individual pieces were not consistently signed, and the exact distribution of the contents between the two writers rests on later testimony and on the separate bibliographies of Hood and Reynolds rather than on the book itself. The third edition of 1826, which appeared with a different publisher, is described as the work of the same authors, so that the collaboration is documented from the first year of publication.

movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.description: Akenside's volume of odes, raising the Pindaric and the lyrical experiment of the decade into a book: the hymns, the lyrical addresses and the imitations of the ancient measures with the short essay on the odical composition.

works.title: Of Ancient and Modern Learning
altTitles: Essay upon the Original and Nature of Poetry (included)
works.description: Temple's essay defending the ancients against the moderns, written in reply to Fontenelle and the French Académie, and containing the famous praise of the Epistles of Phalaris; it opened the English Quarrel of the Books.
works.plot: Temple argues that the ancients surpassed the moderns in poetry, oratory, and philosophy, cites the Epistles of Phalaris as the oldest and best of the ancient letters, and dismisses modern learning as pedantic.
works.significance: The opening salvo of the English Battle of the Books, which Swift satirised in The Battle of the Books (1704); it is a key text in the history of the quarrel between the ancients and the moderns.
works.meter: Plain, urbane prose.
works.context: Published in 1692 in Temple's Miscellanea; it provoked Wotton's Reflections upon Ancient and Modern Learning (1694) and Bentley's demonstration that the Epistles of Phalaris were a later forgery, in which the young Swift served as Temple's amanuensis.
works.structure: A single continuous essay.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Temple; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Of Education
works.description: A letter to the educational reformer Samuel Hartlib proposing a complete humanist and practical curriculum for young gentlemen, combining classical languages, science, physical training, and moral and religious formation to fit them for public and private service.
works.plot: Milton sets out the ends of education ('to repair the ruins of our first parents by regaining to know God aright'), then details a graded curriculum from languages through literature, science, ethics, and rhetoric, with exercises, travel, and music.
works.significance: A key document of seventeenth-century educational reform, combining Renaissance humanism with the new practical and scientific emphasis, and influential in the history of pedagogy.
works.meter: Clear, argumentative prose with an idealistic and practical tone.
works.context: Written in 1644 for Samuel Hartlib's circle of educational reformers, reflecting Comenian and humanist ideals and Milton's own experience as a schoolmaster and private tutor.
works.structure: A short prose tract addressed as a letter, moving from first principles to a detailed syllabus.

works.title: Of Human Bondage
works.description: The great English novel of obsession: Philip Carey, Mildred, and the long education of a young man. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by W. Somerset Maugham; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Philip Carey, born with a club foot, is orphaned and raised by his uncle, the vicar of Blackstable; he studies in Germany, fails as an accountant and a painter, qualifies as a doctor in London, and destroys himself for the waitress Mildred Rogers before he finds his own life.
works.significance: Of Human Bondage is the great English novel of obsession and one of the central autobiographical novels of the century: its portrait of Philip Carey's long education and his bondage to Mildred made it a permanent study of human weakness.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrator who listens rather than judges.
works.context: England, Germany and Paris at the turn of the century, and the medical student's London of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Philip Carey; Mildred Rogers; Sally Athelny; Cronshaw; Hayward; Griffiths; Emma
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the orphanage to the medical practice and the marriage. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Somerset Maugham. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Of Mice and Men
works.description: The great American novella of the Depression: George, Lennie and the dream of the farm. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by John Steinbeck; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: George Milton and Lennie Small, two migrant workers, travel through California with the dream of a farm of their own; on a ranch they meet the old Swamper, the lonely wife of the boss's son and the vicious Curley, and the story ends with George's mercy killing of Lennie.
works.significance: Of Mice and Men is one of the most performed works in the American theatre and one of the great American novellas: its dialogue, its structure and its portrait of loneliness made it a permanent classic and Steinbeck's most widely read work.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail of the migrant road.
works.context: The ranches of the Salinas Valley in the 1930s, and the migrant labour of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1937 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.

works.title: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity
works.description: Hooker's great defence of the Elizabethan church: Books I–IV (1593) and Book V (1597) of the eight-book treatise answer the Puritan platform by grounding church order in the law of reason and nature — the famous account of law's hierarchy from God through angels and man to the laws ecclesiastical — in the prose that founded Anglican theology.
works.plot: Book I derives the kinds of law (eternal, celestial, natural, human, divine) and the necessity of law for the good life; Books II–IV refute the Puritan claim of scriptural exclusivity; Book V, the longest, defends the Prayer Book's liturgy, sacraments, and discipline against the Admonition controversies; the posthumous Books VI–VIII treat jurisdiction, episcopacy, and royal supremacy.
works.significance: The intellectual foundation of Anglicanism and of the English theory of law and consent — a book Locke and the constitutional tradition built upon.
works.meter: Prose of unrivalled dignity and clarity — the 'judicious' style that Izaak Walton celebrated and that set the standard for English theological writing.
works.context: Written through the 1590s against the Admonition controversy and the Presbyterian challenge; the completed books were printed in 1593 and 1597, with the later books posthumous and textually vexed.
works.structure: Eight books of systematic theological argument, each built on the scholastic method of position, objection, and answer, in the majestic periodic prose Hooker perfected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the posthumous books VI–VIII survive in imperfect texts.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: Of Time and the River
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1935
works.description: Wolfe's second novel: Eugene Gant at Harvard, in New York and in Europe, and the hunger that cannot be satisfied. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Thomas Wolfe; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Eugene Gant goes to Harvard to study playwriting, teaches in New York, travels to England and France, falls in love with Esther Jack, and returns to America — in a torrent of memory, hunger and loss that continues the story begun in Look Homeward, Angel.
works.significance: Of Time and the River is the great American novel of hunger and the most expansive autobiographical novel in American literature: its torrent of prose made Wolfe the most discussed young novelist of the 1930s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the long catalogue of names, objects and sensations.
works.context: Harvard in the 1920s, New York, the expatriate Europe of the period, and the American hunger for experience. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Eugene Gant; Esther Jack; Francis Starwick; Joel Pierce; Robert Weaver
works.structure: A long autobiographical narrative in many chapters, continuing Look Homeward, Angel. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Clayton Wolfe. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form
Novel of Development and the Growth Story
themes: Childhood, the nursery, and the Edwardian idyll
Exile, expatriation, and the lost generation
The absurd, the void, and the failure of meaning
Time, memory, and the duration of consciousness
movements: The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel

works.title: Old Creole Days
works.description: Published in 1879 and the founding American book of New Orleans: eight stories of Creole life in the old French quarter. It is a prose fiction work of 1879 by George Washington Cable; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories present the courtyards and the codes of the old Creole families — the ruined aristocrat, the quadroon woman, the young man who marries beneath him, the usurer and the orphan — in a series of gentle, exact narratives that end in renunciation or in a quiet disappointment.
works.significance: Old Creole Days created the literary image of New Orleans: it was the first American book to record the speech, architecture and manners of French Louisiana, it founded the southern local-colour school, and it remains the source of the American idea of the Creole city.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is exact reproduction of Creole and black dialect.
works.context: 1873-79: the post-war New Orleans, the decline of the Creole aristocracy, the mixed-race society of the French quarter, and the American local-colour movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Jean-ah Poquelin; 'Tite Poulette, Madame John and Kristian Koppig; 'Sieur George; Colonel De Charleu and Injin Charlie ('Belles Demoiselles Plantation'); Posson Jone' and Jules St-Ange; Madame Délicieuse and Dr Mossy
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George W. Cable. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
themes: Race, voice, and the dialect of freedom
Regional identity and the American sectional character
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
movements: American Realism and the Howells Program
Local Colour and the Regionalist School

works.title: Old English Bede
works.form: translation (ecclesiastical history) in Old English prose
works.description: The anonymous Old English translation of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica, produced in the Alfredian circle: the earliest vernacular rendering of a major historical work in England and a primary witness to the text of Bede. It preserves the Old English text of Cædmon's Hymn in the West Saxon dialect.
works.plot: The translation follows Bede's five books closely, rendering the history of the conversion and the saints of the early English church into fluent West Saxon prose, with the Hymn of Cædmon given in a West Saxon verse translation rather than in the original Northumbrian form.
works.significance: The standard vernacular text of Bede in late Anglo-Saxon England and a monument of the Alfredian translation program.
works.meter: Old English prose; contains alliterative verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in translation.
works.context: Translated c. 890-930, probably in Mercia within the Alfredian orbit; principal manuscripts: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 41, and Oxford, Bodleian Library, Tanner 10.
works.characters: Bede (author); the saints and kings of the Historia
works.structure: Five books of translated ecclesiastical history.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; no evidence for the older attribution to Alfred himself.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Boethius (with the Meters of Boethius)
altTitles: The Old English Consolation of Philosophy
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose and verse
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the most important philosophical work of the period in English: Boethius's dialogue with Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, and providence, transformed by the translator into the idiom of the Germanic heroic world (Wyrd becomes a goddess of fate under God's governance). An alliterative verse rendering of the work's songs, the Meters of Boethius, accompanies the prose.
works.plot: The imprisoned Boethius, lamenting his fall, is visited by Philosophy (Wisdom), who teaches him that true happiness lies not in wealth, power, or fame but in God; the dialogue moves through the problem of evil to the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human freedom — the translator's expansions turning Philosophy's arguments into vivid vernacular images (the wheel of fate, the tyrant's empty power, the 'tool' of kingship).
works.significance: The first English philosophical classic; the Meters are the largest surviving corpus of Alfredian verse.
works.meter: Old English prose; the Meters of Boethius are in alliterative verse.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899 from the Latin of Boethius with the help of a commentary tradition; preserved in Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 180 (prose, mid-tenth century) and British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.vi (meters, burned 1731, transcript).
works.characters: Boethius (the Mind); Wisdom (Philosophy); Wyrd (Fate)
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and verse (the metra), the prose translated freely, the verse rendered both in prose and, in a separate version, in alliterative verse.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred himself; modern scholarship sees his close direction with the possibility of personal composition.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Wisdom and learning
Wyrd (fate) and providence
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Dialogues of Gregory
works.form: translation (hagiographical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: Bishop Werferth of Worcester's translation of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, the collection of Italian saints' lives and miracle stories that was among the most popular books of the Middle Ages, including the life of St Benedict. Commissioned by King Alfred, it is the only Alfredian translation securely assigned to a named scholar other than the king.
works.plot: Gregory, in dialogue with his deacon Peter, recounts the lives and miracles of the holy men of Italy in four books: Benedict and his monks, the visionary saints, the raising of the dead, and the fate of souls after death — the work that fixed Benedict's cult in the west and fed the homiletic imagination of Anglo-Saxon England (its 'Vision of Fursey' and soul-journey stories echo through the Blickling and Vercelli homilies).
works.significance: The earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic work and the conduit of Gregory's hagiography into the vernacular.
works.meter: Old English prose, close and literal in style.
works.context: Translated by Werferth, bishop of Worcester (c. 872-915), at Alfred's request c. 890s; principal manuscripts: British Library, Cotton MS Otho C.i (fragmentary) and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 322.
works.characters: Gregory the Great; Peter the deacon; Benedict of Nursia; the Italian saints
works.structure: Four books of dialogue, each a collection of miracle narratives framed by Gregory's conversation with Peter.
works.attributionNotes: Werferth's authorship rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Hexateuch
works.description: The Old English translation of the first six books of the Bible (Genesis through Joshua), composed principally by Ælfric (who translated Genesis with his own preface) and completed by an anonymous translator: the earliest substantial rendering of the Bible into English and the most lavishly illustrated vernacular manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The Hexateuch renders Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua into English — the patriarchal narratives, the exodus and the law, the conquest of Canaan — in Ælfric's lucid prose for the first portion and a more literal style thereafter; the preface explains Ælfric's reluctance to translate scripture, lest the unlearned mistake its plain sense.
works.significance: The first English Bible translation of scale and a monument of late Anglo-Saxon book art.
works.meter: Old English prose; rhythmical in the Ælfrician portions.
works.context: Ælfric's Genesis and preface c. 1000; the whole compiled with the remaining books by the mid-eleventh century; principal manuscript: British Library, Cotton MS Claudius B.iv, with over 390 illustrations.
works.characters: Adam, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, and the biblical patriarchs
works.structure: Six biblical books in translation, prefaced by Ælfric's preface to Genesis.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship of Genesis (and the preface) is certain; the other books are by an anonymous contemporary.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: Benedictine Reform
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Martyrology
works.description: An anonymous ninth-century calendar of saints, the earliest substantial martyrology in any European vernacular: entries for each day of the year recording the feasts, passions, and wonders of the saints, compiled from Latin sources and full of exotic geographical and zoological lore.
works.plot: The martyrology proceeds day by day through the calendar year, each entry briefly narrating the saint's life or passion — apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins of east and west — with digressions on the places and creatures mentioned (the phoenix, the whale, the peoples of India).
works.significance: The earliest vernacular martyrology of Europe and a major source for Anglo-Saxon hagiography and geography.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Compiled in Mercia in the ninth century, probably before the Viking wars; survives in six fragmentary manuscripts, none complete.
works.characters: the saints of the universal church
works.structure: A calendar-ordered compendium of short hagiographical notices.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Mission, conversion, and the Church
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Orosius
altTitles: The Old English History of the World
works.form: translation (universal history) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Orosius's Seven Books of History against the Pagans, the standard ancient universal history, expanded with original accounts of the geography of northern Europe and the voyages of the Norwegian Ohthere and the Dane Wulfstan — the first travel literature in English.
works.plot: Orosius's history narrates the calamities of the world from creation to his own day (c. 417) to prove that the pagan past was more wretched than the Christian present; the translator condenses and adapts the narrative, and prefaces it with a geographical survey of the world that includes the famous reports of Ohthere's voyage around the North Cape into the White Sea and Wulfstan's voyage into the Baltic, told to King Alfred by the travellers themselves.
works.significance: The first universal history in English and the earliest English travel narrative (the Ohthere and Wulfstan passages).
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the principal manuscript is British Library, Additional MS 47967 (the Lauderdale or Tollemache Orosius, early tenth century).
works.characters: Ohthere; Wulfstan; Alfred (as recipient of the voyage accounts); the rulers of world history
works.structure: Seven books of world history, preceded by the translator's original geographical preface.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of the Alfredian circle.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Pastoral Care (with Alfred's Preface)
altTitles: Gregory's Pastoral Care in Old English
works.form: translation (didactic treatise) in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's translation of Gregory the Great's Regula pastoralis, the handbook of episcopal duties, prefaced by Alfred's own letter on the decay of learning and his program of translation — the founding document of English prose. Copies were sent to every bishopric, and the surviving manuscripts are the earliest extensive works of Old English prose.
works.plot: Gregory's treatise instructs the pastor in the office of the soul's physician — how the teacher must adapt his speech to each condition of his flock, the virtues required of rulers of souls, and the discipline of preaching; Alfred's Preface recounts how learning had decayed in England ('so clean fallen away'), and how he therefore resolved to translate into English the books most needful for all men to know.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the Alfredian program and of the entire Old English prose tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose of the early Alfredian style.
works.context: Translated c. 890-899 with the help of Plegmund, Asser, Grimbald, and John; the earliest manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Hatton 20, c. 890-897) was sent to Bishop Werferth of Worcester.
works.characters: Alfred (preface); Gregory the Great (text)
works.structure: Preface (prose letter) followed by the four books of the translation, with Alfred's characteristic expansions of Gregory's images.
works.attributionNotes: The Preface is Alfred's own; the translation was executed by his circle under his direction.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume A: The Middle Ages

works.title: Old English Soliloquies
altTitles: The Old English Soliloquies of Augustine
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Augustine's Soliloquies — a dialogue between Augustine and his Reason on God and the immortality of the soul — with additions from Augustine's other works and the translator's own reflections, including the famous image of gathering timber in the forest to build a fair dwelling (the book as a house of wisdom).
works.plot: Reason leads Augustine (the translator's 'Mind') through the argument for the soul's immortality: from the desire for knowledge to the certainty of one's own existence ('I know that I am'), the nature of truth, and the vision of God after death; the work closes with the image of the king's woodcutters gathering timber for the house of the mind, where each man may rest and live.
works.significance: The first English rendering of Augustine and a central text of the Alfredian philosophic program.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 4-59 (mid-twelfth century), copied with the same manuscript tradition as Beowulf.
works.characters: the Mind (Augustine/Alfred); Reason
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue in the Boethian manner, with the translator's expansions (the ship and anchor, the lord's favourite, the timber image) added to Augustine's text.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred; the attribution rests on the Preface of the work and the conventions of the Alfredian canon.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Wisdom and learning
movements: Alfredian Renaissance
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Old Fashioned Flowers
works.form: Prose of the garden (the flower and the memory of a civilisation)
works.description: The book of the old flowers: the garden as the memory of a civilisation. It is a prose work of 1939 by Sacheverell Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Nature Essay and the Rural Observation; Critical Essay and the Modern Review.
works.plot: Old Fashioned Flowers describes the old garden flowers - the auricula, the carnation, the rose and the lily - with their history, their breeders and their names, in the prose of the connoisseur, and made the book of the garden a literary genre.
works.significance: Old Fashioned Flowers is the classic of the English garden book: its flowers with their history and their breeders made the garden a subject of the prose of the arts and remains the standard text of the flower book.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is the long, loaded, alliterative line of the baroque lyric.
works.context: The English garden in the 1930s, and the history of the flower. The record dates the work as composed in 1938 and first published in 1939 and it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation; critical essay and the modern review.
works.structure: A book of the garden in chapters of the flower, each with its history. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Sacheverell Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Critical Essay and the Modern Review
Nature Essay and the Rural Observation
themes: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road
Time, memory, and the duration of consciousness

works.title: Old Indian Days
works.description: Published in 1907 and Eastman's finest collection of stories: the warrior life of the Dakota before the reservation. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Charles Eastman; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories follow the young Dakota men and women of the old life: the warrior who counts coup, the woman who follows the camp, the hunter, the medicine man and the lover, in narratives that record the code of honour and the daily life of the plains before the treaties.
works.significance: Old Indian Days is the finest collection of Native American short stories of the period: its narratives of the warrior code and the daily life of the plains made it a classic, and it is one of the few Native-authored accounts of the old life written by someone who had lived it.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is clear, unhurried expository prose.
works.context: 1904-07: the last years of the free Dakota life, the reservation system, and the American market for the 'vanishing race' story. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ohiyesa. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch
themes: Race, voice, and the dialect of freedom
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
The American wilderness and the myth of the forest
movements: American Realism and the Howells Program
Local Colour and the Regionalist School

works.title: Old Indian Legends
works.description: Published in 1901 and the first collection of Native American legends by a Native American author: fourteen Dakota stories of the trickster Iktomi and the great deeds of the old world. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Zitkala-Sa; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection retells the Dakota stories of Iktomi the spider-trickster and his schemes, of the buffalo and the prairie, of the great hunter and the sky, in versions taken from the oral tradition and retold for an English-reading audience while keeping the cadence of the original.
works.significance: Old Indian Legends is the first collection of Native American legends by a Native American author and the founding text of Native American literary translation: its versions of the Iktomi stories preserved the oral tradition at the moment of its destruction, and it established the model for all later Native American retellings.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is autobiographical narrative in a clear, restrained first person.
works.context: 1901: the American vogue for the Indian legend after Longfellow and Schoolcraft, the boarding-school experience, and the ethnographic collection of Native oral literature. The record dates the work as composed in 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gertrude Simmons Bonnin. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale
Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Race, voice, and the dialect of freedom

works.title: Old Myddelton's Money
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1874
works.description: The sensation novel of the lost inheritance: a double life and a stolen will. It is a prose fiction work of 1874 by Mary Cecil Hay; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection.
works.plot: A young woman is left penniless by the disappearance of her father and the loss of the Myddelton inheritance; the novel follows the double life of the villain, the discovery of the will and the restoration of the fortune, in a plot of concealed identity and legal suspense.
works.significance: Old Myddelton's Money was one of the most popular sensation novels of the 1870s: its plot of the lost will and the double life made it a circulating-library favourite and it shows the sensation formula at its most expert.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the sensational plot of the lost will and the double identity.
works.context: London and the English provinces in the 1870s, the Court of Chancery and the circulating library. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1874 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: the heiress; the villain; the lawyer; the lost father
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, from the loss to the restoration. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as M. C. Hay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Detective Story and the Tale of Detection
themes: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
movements: Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot

works.title: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
works.description: Eliot's book of cat poems: light verse of the highest order, and the source of the musical Cats. It is a verse work of 1939 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Fifteen poems introduce the cats of the tribe — Growltiger, the Rum Tum Tugger, Mr Mistoffelees, Macavity, Old Deuteronomy, Gus, Skimbleshanks and the rest — in nonsense verse of great technical accomplishment.
works.significance: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats is the finest book of children's verse of the period after the Alice books: its technical virtuosity in light verse is unmatched, and the poems became the basis of one of the longest-running musicals in history.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
works.context: The Eliot household's cats, the letters Eliot wrote to his godchildren, and the English light verse tradition of Lear and Carroll. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Growltiger; Rum Tum Tugger; Mr Mistoffelees; Macavity; Old Deuteronomy; Gus; Skimbleshanks
works.structure: Fifteen poems in varied stanza forms, with a mock-biological title. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Old Vicarage, Grantley
works.description: The vicarage novel: the household, the dalesfolk and the inheritance. It is a prose fiction work of 1921 by Constance Holme; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Old Vicarage, Grantley follows the household of the old vicarage and its quarrel with the dalesfolk and the inheritance, in the prose of the fell weather and the farming year.
works.significance: Old Vicarage, Grantley is Constance Holme's finest novel: its vicarage, its household and its dalesfolk made the Westmorland village a world and remain the standard text of the regional novel of the 1920s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the fell weather, the farming year and the stone.
works.context: Westmorland in the early 1920s. The record dates the work as composed in 1920 and first published in 1921 and it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the vicar's household; the dalesfolk; the inheritor; the village
works.structure: A novel of the household in chapters of the village year. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Constance Holme. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
