works.title: Oldtown Folks
works.form: Novel; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1869
works.description: Published in 1869 and Stowe's most autobiographical novel: the childhood of two orphans in a Massachusetts village, and a portrait of New England life after the Revolution. It is a prose fiction work of 1869 by Harriet Beecher Stowe; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Horace Holyoke and his cousins grow up in the village of Oldtown among ministers, deacons, farmers and spinsters, and the novel records the customs, the theology and the humour of the New England of Stowe's own childhood.
works.significance: Oldtown Folks is the finest American regional novel of New England and the great fictional record of the New England village culture that produced both Stowe and the American Renaissance; its portrait of the Calvinist community is a central document of American social history.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is sentimental tableaux designed to produce tears and conversion.
works.context: The 1790s-1800s, post-Revolutionary New England, the Congregational ministry, and the American village in the early republic. The record dates the work as composed between 1868 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Horace Holyoke (the narrator); Harry Percival; Tina Percival; Ellery Davenport; Grandmother Badger; Sam Lawson; Miss Asphyxia Smith; Esther Avery; Parson Lothrop
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Harriet Elizabeth Beecher Stowe. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Olive
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1850
works.description: Published in 1850 and Craik's first major novel: the story of a girl born with a deformity and her struggle for love and work. It is a prose fiction work of 1850 by Dinah Mulock Craik; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Olive Rothesay is born with a curved spine, hidden from her absent father by her beautiful, ashamed mother and coldly received by him on his return; after his death she supports her mother as a painter under the misogynist artist Michael Vanbrugh, whose proposal she refuses, discovers that the troubled orphan Christal Manners is her father's illegitimate daughter, and finally marries the doubting clergyman Harold Gwynne, widower of her childhood friend Sara, restoring his faith and mothering his child.
works.significance: Olive is one of the first English novels to make a disabled woman its heroine and one of the earliest to treat women's art as a vocation: it is a bold forerunner of the Victorian novel of the woman artist and a landmark in the representation of disability.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is plain, warm narrative prose.
works.context: 1850: the Victorian cult of female beauty, the position of disabled women, and the emergence of the woman artist as a fictional subject. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.
works.characters: Olive Rothesay; Captain Angus Rothesay, her father; Sybilla Rothesay, her mother; Harold Gwynne; Sara, Olive's friend and Gwynne's first wife; Christal Manners; Michael Vanbrugh
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dinah Maria Mulock. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches: with Elucidations
works.description: Published in 1845, and the work that rehabilitated Cromwell in the English historical imagination: the letters and speeches, edited with a commentary that presents Cromwell as the sincere Puritan hero and the founder of English liberty.
works.plot: Carlyle arranges the documents chronologically from the 1620s to Cromwell's death in 1658, with 'elucidations' that supply narrative and argument; the effect is a first-person portrait of the man in his own words, from the fen drainage and the Irish campaign to the Protectorate and the deathbed.
works.significance: Cromwell's Letters and Speeches made Cromwell a Victorian hero and established the documentary edition as a form of historical writing; it shaped Froude's and Gardiner's histories and the modern scholarly edition, and it is the classic example of Carlyle's method of letting a man speak for himself.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: The 1840s and the Victorian interest in the Puritan past, the edition of the letters by Carlyle's friend Thomas Carlyle and the earlier editions of the Thurloe papers, and the 1841-42 controversy over Cromwell's statue.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy's Progress
works.description: Dickens's second novel and the first English novel to make the workhouse child its hero, serialised in Bentley's Miscellany from February 1837 (while Pickwick was still running) and published in three volumes in November 1838, with illustrations by George Cruikshank.
works.plot: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse, spends his infancy in a branch workhouse under Mrs Mann, and at nine is returned to the main house, where he asks for more gruel and is apprenticed to an undertaker. He runs away to London, is taken up by the Artful Dodger and Fagin, is briefly in the hands of the burglar Bill Sikes and his dog, is shot and sheltered by the Maylies, and is then kidnapped back by Fagin and Nancy; Nancy's warning to Mr Brownlow and her murder by Sikes lead to the exposure of the plot of Monks, Oliver's half-brother, and to Oliver's restoration to his inheritance.
works.significance: Oliver Twist made the workhouse and the criminal child national subjects and established the 'condition-of-England' subject matter that Dickens, Gaskell, Kingsley and Disraeli developed through the 1840s. Its serialisation in a magazine alongside its author's other novel pioneered the double market of the Victorian writer.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, the workhouse system and the reportage of the Poor Law Commissioners, the criminal underworld of Field Lane and Saffron Hill, and the antisemitic conventions of the stage Jew which the character of Fagin reproduces and to which Dickens later responded in Our Mutual Friend.
works.characters: Oliver Twist; Fagin; Nancy; Bill Sikes; the Artful Dodger; Mr Bumble; Mr Brownlow; Rose Maylie; Monks; Mr Grimwig
works.structure: Third-person narrative with a double plot — the parish boy's progress and the exposure of Monks's conspiracy — organised as a series of institutions (workhouse, undertaker's, thieves' kitchen, Maylie household) through which the hero passes.

works.title: Oliver's Daughter
works.form: Novel (the village and the growth of the daughter)
works.description: The first novel: the village, the church and the daughter's growth. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Richard Church; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Oliver's Daughter follows the daughter of the village through the church, the school and the first love in the English village of the 1920s, in the realist manner of the country novel.
works.significance: Oliver's Daughter is Church's first novel and the founding text of his village fiction: its church, its school and its daughter's growth carried the realist manner of the country novel into the 1930s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the plain observed lyric of the country and the season.
works.context: The English village in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1930 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: Olney Hymns
works.form: congregational hymnal and devotional verse collection with scriptural and doxological headings
works.description: The hymn-book prepared jointly by William Cowper and John Newton for the Olney congregation, Newton supplying the public devotional verse and Cowper the poems of inward experience. Its several divisions serve social worship, private worship and the dispensations of providence, and its most lasting contribution is Cowper's sequence of hymns of fear, desertion and assurance. The volume stands beside Watts and the Wesleys as a foundation text of Evangelical and Nonconformist hymnody.
works.plot: The hymns move through the ordinary apparatus of Evangelical worship - praise, confession, prayer for grace, the conflicts of conscience, the comforts of providence and the hope of heaven - with the division devoted to private spiritual trial much of which Cowper left unfinished. His best hymns in the book, including God of my life, to thee I call and O for a closer walk with God, give the collection its enduring power, while Newton's contributions carry its narrative of redemption and mercy.
works.significance: It is one of the standard sources of English hymnody and the first public proof of Cowper's devotional gift, anticipating the religious passages of the Task. Its treatment of spiritual trial and assurance makes it a primary document of Evangelical religious feeling in the later eighteenth century.
works.meter: The common, proper and long measures of English hymn metre, mostly alternating four- and three-beat iambic lines with simple rhyme, written to be sung to current tunes.
works.context: Prepared during Cowper's residence at Olney under Newton's curacy and after his own conversion, in the household of the Morants; the book belongs to the Evangelical revival's programme of hymn-making for ordinary congregations and to the Olney custom of a full service of prayer and praise.
works.structure: A hymnal in several divisions ordered by the occasions of worship rather than by continuous argument, the parts assigned between the two authors and the whole framed by their Olney practice.
works.attributionNotes: The volume is expressly a joint work of Cowper and Newton and the divisions are assigned between them in the standard accounts; the printing history of individual hymns, including that usually identified as Amazing Grace, has been variously stated, so no particular first printing is asserted here.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Evangelical experience and assurance
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Olor Iscanus
altTitles: Olor Iscanus: The Swan of Usk
works.description: A collection of Vaughan's earlier secular and occasional verse, published by his brother William in 1651 against the poet's wish, including love poems, elegies, satires, epigrams, and translations of Boethius, The Distichs of Cato, and Casimire Sarbiewski.
works.plot: The volume gathers Vaughan's pre-conversion and secular work — amatory and elegiac poems, versions of Ovid and Ausonius, the satirical 'Time' poems, and pious translations — representing the literary range before his mystical turn.
works.significance: Important for understanding Vaughan's development and his classical and secular range, and as a document of royalist literary culture during the Interregnum.
works.meter: Varied lyric meters; translation in verse; a more worldly, sometimes uneven, manner than Silex Scintillans.
works.context: Composed largely in the 1640s; Vaughan suppressed it, but his twin brother Thomas's death and William's initiative led to its publication in 1651, dedicated with the 'swan of Usk' emblem of the river on which Vaughan lived.
works.structure: A miscellaneous collection of secular lyrics, translations, and epigrams without a unifying sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published by Vaughan's brother against his expressed preference.

works.title: Omniana
altTitles: Omniana; or, Results and Suggestions of Literature, and of Opinions in Politics, Economics, and Religion
works.form: Literary miscellany and commonplace-book prose: anecdote, quotation and short essay after the manner of the eighteenth-century analecta.
works.description: A two-volume miscellany of anecdotes, quotations, and short disquisitions on literature, politics, economy and religion, gathered from commonplace books and printed out of a professed indifference to system. Its manner - erudite, Tory, sententious, and full of unacknowledged quotation - is that of the author of Letters from England, and it was published anonymously. It is the least-annotated of its author's prose works and the one whose authorship is least settled.
works.plot: The items pass from Elizabethan drama and forgotten pamphlets to the corn trade, the poor laws, and the practice of abstracting books, with long transcriptions from scarce writers. Political entries defend prescription, order, and the settled constitution, and attack the speculators and paper-mongers of the war years. Several pieces argue for a national literature governed by the church and the universities. The miscellany closes on moral and religious reflection, with the compiler's own opinion always withheld or delivered in another's words.
works.significance: It preserves much rare material from books now hard to trace and is a document of the romantic-era habit of quotation; its editorship also bears on the dating and authentication of several short poems and sayings otherwise unrecorded.
works.meter: Prose, with verse quotations.
works.context: Compiled in the war years of high prices and paper currency, when its author was consolidating his editorial and antijacobin career and contributing to the Quarterly Review; its Tory economics and its antiquarian reading answer the period's expansion of literary history and periodical culture.
works.structure: Miscellany of numbered items of very unequal length with no arrangement by subject; the reader's sequence is that of the compiler's commonplace book rather than an argument.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1812 and attributed on the strength of publisher's accounts and contemporary evidence; the share of a collaborating friend has been raised in the bibliographical literature, so the attribution to a single author is not universally conceded, and part of the compilation may be by another hand.
themes: Order and degree: the body politic
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review
The Spectator and Periodical Journalism

works.title: On Fairy-Stories
works.form: Essay (Andrew Lang lecture, St Andrews, 1939; in Essays Presented to Charles Williams)
works.description: The theory of faerie: sub-creation, recovery, escape and the eucatastrophe. It is a prose work of 1947 by J. R. R. Tolkien; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tolkien defines fairy-story as the story of Faerie rather than of the fairies, and argues that the making of the secondary world is sub-creation, that its gifts are recovery, escape and consolation, and that its highest turn is the eucatastrophe, the sudden joyous turn that denies universal defeat.
works.significance: On Fairy-Stories is the founding theory of the modern fantasy: its sub-creation, its recovery and its eucatastrophe gave the mode its vocabulary and its defence, and it remains the essay against which every account of fantasy is measured.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is the invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it.
works.context: The Andrew Lang lecture of 1939 and the wartime theory of fantasy. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1947 and first published in 1947 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A lecture-essay in sections: the definition, the origins, the children, the making and the eucatastrophe.

works.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
altTitles: On First Looking to Chapman's Homer
works.form: Romantic sonnet of the revived school; the occasional lyric of literary experience, in the manner of the Leigh-Hunt circle's own sonnets on the arts.
works.description: The most famous sonnet of its author's first season and the document of his poetic awakening: written the morning after an evening spent reading an Elizabethan translation of Homer, and printed a few days later in the weekly journal of the circle that had just discovered him. It declares that the poet had travelled in imagination through the whole library of recognized poetry without finding its Homeric breadth, and that Chapman's version gave him the pure common air of the epics. Its two closing similes, the astronomer and the Spanish observer of the Pacific, made it the standard figure of the moment of literary discovery.
works.plot: The opening quartet reports a borrowed pilgrimage through the regions of art, the western islands of Homer, the bright leagues of Elizabethan romance and the courts and roads of the older poets, all visited in fancy and none of them penetrated. The first tercet names the instant of arrival, the sense of a new heaven and a fine gown of the old eagle, and the closing couplet turns to the two figures of astonishment, the astronomer watching a new planet swim into his ken, and the eagle-eyed stargazer, and the Spanish chief on the peak of Darien looking at the Pacific with a still stare while all his men gaze at one another and look solemn. The argument is that real reading is a discovery of a country, and that the great translation can give a modern reader more of the original's strength than a scholar's fidelity.
works.significance: It became the period's definitive statement that the reading of the classics is a discovery rather than a duty, and its final image of the astronomer and the conqueror is still the common property of the language for the moment of recognition. It also established the author's reputation among his contemporaries before any volume of his appeared, and fixed the relation of the revived English sonnet to the argument about translation and imaginative strength.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in the revived Italian form, the octave closed on two rhymes and the sestet turning through three; the manner is Latinate and plain in the diction of the Elizabethan reading, and the closing sentences are long and cumulative.
works.context: Composed in October 1816, the fortnight after the poet was introduced to the editor of the Examiner by a friend of the same circle and read an Elizabethan Homer with a schoolfellow in the evening, and printed in that journal on the first day of the following month. Its appearance belongs to the moment when the Hunt circle was making a new poetry of sensation against the review establishment, and the sonnet was at once taken as that circle's programme in miniature.
works.characters: the poet as imaginary traveller; the astronomer descrying a new planet; the conqueror on the Darien peak and his men
works.structure: A single fourteen-line argument in the revived Italian form, the two quatrains setting the general proposition of the prior wanderings, the first tercet the crisis of the new sight, and the close running to the twin similes of discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the sonnet is dated by the accounts of the writer's friends, and it entered the printed text from the journal in which it first appeared.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Primitive genius and national poetry
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
works.description: Six lectures delivered in London in May 1840 and published in 1841: the most influential Victorian statement of the theory that history is the biography of great men, organised as six types of hero — the divinity (Odin), the prophet (Muhammad), the poet (Dante, Shakespeare), the priest (Luther, Knox), the man of letters (Johnson, Rousseau, Burns) and the king (Cromwell, Napoleon).
works.plot: Each lecture presents its hero as the 'sincere' man who perceives the truth of his age and embodies it in action, and the sequence is an argument that the modern age, having lost its faith, finds its heroes in literature and in the 'man of letters'.
works.significance: On Heroes made hero-worship a central Victorian idea and supplied the age's theory of leadership; it shaped Carlyle's own Cromwell and Frederick, and Emerson's Representative Men, and its account of the man of letters as the modern priest gave Victorian authorship its sense of vocation. The twentieth century's reaction against its authoritarian implications made it the classic text for the critique of Victorian political thought.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: The 1840 lecture season, the Chartist agitation of 1839-40, and the Victorian search for authority after the collapse of the old order; the lectures were attended by Dickens, Mill and the intellectual public of London.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: On Liberty
works.description: Published in 1859 with the dedication to Harriet Taylor Mill, and the single most influential defence of individual freedom in the English language: the argument that the only justification for coercing an individual is to prevent harm to others.
works.plot: The five chapters treat the history of liberty and the tyranny of opinion, the liberty of thought and discussion, individuality as one of the elements of well-being, the limits of the authority of society over the individual, and applications of the doctrine to education and the state.
works.significance: On Liberty gave liberalism its central principle and its most quoted defence of free speech ('If all mankind minus one were of one opinion...'); it is a foundation text of modern democratic theory and civil liberties law, and it remains the reference point for the debate on the limits of state action.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
works.context: The 1850s, the growth of Victorian public opinion and the 'despotism of custom', the temperance and sabbatarian legislation, and Mill's own collaboration with Harriet Taylor. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: On Monsieur's Departure
works.description: Queen Elizabeth I's lyric on the departure of François, Duke of Anjou, her last serious suitor, about 1582: the queen's grief at parting, her public duty's compulsion to conceal it, and the paradox of a heart that cannot show what it feels — 'I grieve and dare not show my discontent' — the most personal of her surviving poems.
works.plot: The poem moves through the queen's private grief to the public impossibility of expressing it: love, duty, and statecraft in the single voice of the sovereign, with the refrain of the divided self as its burden.
works.significance: The queen's most intimate poem — the lyric in which the sovereign's two bodies, private and public, speak in one voice.
works.meter: Short-lined lyric stanzas with refrain, in the manner of the court's song-poetry.
works.context: Written about 1582, at the collapse of the French marriage negotiations that had divided the court for a decade; the poem survives only in manuscript, its attribution resting on the queen's circle's testimony.
works.characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); the departing Monsieur (François, Duke of Anjou)
works.structure: A single lyric of three movements — grief, concealment, resignation — in the courtly complaint mode.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Elizabeth I by manuscript tradition; the attribution is generally accepted.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: On Not Shooting Sitting Birds
works.description: A short story by Jean Rhys, collected in Sleep It Off Lady (1976), her last collection, after an earlier printing in The New Yorker: a young West Indian woman in London recalls an evening with an Englishman that goes wrong over a story about shooting birds.
works.summary: An evening out between a young woman from the Caribbean and an Englishman she hopes to impress, and the remark about shooting birds at home that ends his interest in her.
works.plot: The narrator, a young woman from the West Indies living in London, goes out with an Englishman she wants to please. Trying to interest him, she talks about her island and about going out shooting there; when he gathers that she has shot sitting birds, the one thing his sporting code forbids, he is put off, the evening falls flat and he drops her for good.
works.significance: One of the late stories that confirmed Rhys's revival after Wide Sargasso Sea; Norton pairs it with "The Day They Burned the Books".
works.meter: Spare, understated prose and dialogue in which the comedy of manners is barely distinguished from humiliation.
works.context: Sleep It Off Lady, published by André Deutsch in October 1976, arranges sixteen stories chronologically from the Dominica of the 1890s to the old age of its last heroines; Rhys died in 1979.
works.structure: A brief first-person reminiscence, one of the stories of Sleep It Off Lady that follow a Caribbean heroine from girlhood through Edwardian London.
themes: Gender, feminism and women's lives

works.title: On the Importance of Religious Opinions
altTitles: On the Importance of Religious Opinions. Translated from the French of Necker
works.form: translation of a religious argument, with prefatory essay
works.description: A translation of the French devotional and argumentative work of a statesman-writer of the preceding generation, undertaken by a young author then defining her own religious position. The version was issued with the translator's own prefatory reflection on the temper of the age.
works.plot: The work argues that the opinion a man holds on religious questions is of the first consequence to his conduct and happiness, and examines the duties of the inquirer after truth. It distinguishes between the forms of belief and their effects on the heart, presses the necessity of seriousness and charity, and answers those who profess indifference. The translator's preface urges the same argument on the readers of her own country.
works.significance: It records the religious thinking of a writer whose later work on the mind and on women's education rests on this period of enquiry, and its preface is one of her earliest published prose statements.
works.meter: A plain earnest prose of the devotional argument, its periods and divisions following the French original, the prefatory matter being in the writer's own idiom.
works.context: Published in 1788 in the season of the author's own religious enquiry, when translations of continental devotional work were a regular part of the dissenting book trade, and when the question of religious opinion was a live matter of public argument.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative treatise in short chapters, with the translator's prefixed discourse standing as an independent essay.
works.attributionNotes: The translation is attributed to the writer here recorded without dispute; the original remains the work of another hand, and the prefatory discourse is her own.

works.title: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
works.description: Milton's first major poem, written at twenty-one: a hymn celebrating the Incarnation, in which the birth of Christ brings universal peace and harmony, silencing the oracles and the pagan gods and summoning a heavenly music that the poet longs to join.
works.plot: A prologue in four stanzas asks whether the poet's verse may be laid in the manger before the Magi; the Hymn then describes the peaceful night, the music of the spheres, and the flight of the pagan deities (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon) before the true God.
works.significance: A precocious masterpiece of the early English baroque, it announces Milton's ambition to Christian epic and his fusion of classical and biblical learning.
works.meter: Prologue in rhyme royal; the Hymn in a complex varied stanza (aabbcccddedeeff) that Milton devised for the occasion.
works.context: Composed in December 1629, the year Milton took his MA at Cambridge; published in his Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645), where it leads the collection as his claim to a great poetic vocation.
works.characters: the poet; the infant Christ; Nature; Peace; the pagan gods (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon)
works.structure: A four-stanza prologue followed by an irregular Pindaric-style Hymn in varied stanza form, moving from celebration to the rout of the old gods.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; dated by Milton himself in the 1645 volume.
themes: Judgment Day and eschatology

works.title: On the Properties of Things
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (On the Properties of Things), the great medieval encyclopedia of nature, man, and the cosmos, completed c. 1398–99: nineteen books from God and the angels through the elements, animals, and plants to the human body and soul. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1495, it was the standard English encyclopedia for two centuries.
works.plot: The work proceeds systematically through the orders of creation — God, angels, the soul, the elements, the heavens, birds, beasts, herbs, and the arts and sciences — describing each thing's properties and their moral and medical meanings, in a summa of medieval natural knowledge.
works.significance: The great English encyclopedia of the Middle Ages and the principal channel by which medieval natural science entered English prose.
works.meter: Prose: Trevisa's learned yet idiomatic English, rich in technical vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1398–99 at Berkeley, dedicated to Thomas, Lord Berkeley; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (c. 1495), when it served the medical and scientific reading of the Tudor period; Shakespeare drew on it.
works.characters: none (encyclopedia)
works.structure: Nineteen books of encyclopedic description, each subdivided by topic, in the tradition of Isidore and the thirteenth-century encyclopedists.
works.attributionNotes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the text).

works.title: On the Study of Celtic Literature
works.description: Four lectures delivered as Professor of Poetry at Oxford in 1865-66 and published in 1867: the founding English study of Celtic literature, and the text in which Arnold set out his influential and contested theory of the Celtic 'genius'.
works.plot: Arnold surveys the Welsh, Irish and Gaelic literary remains, argues that English literature owes to Celtic a quality of 'natural magic' and sentiment which it needs, and calls for the study of Celtic at Oxford; the argument is conducted with Arnold's characteristic mixture of sympathy and condescension toward the 'Celtic race'.
works.significance: On the Study of Celtic Literature founded the academic study of Celtic literature in English and introduced the 'Celtic note' into English criticism; it is also a central text for the modern critique of nineteenth-century racial thinking, and it gave the Irish and Welsh revivals of the 1890s their critical vocabulary.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The 1860s Celtic revival, the Welsh Sunday Closing agitation and the Irish land question, and the new philology of the 1860s. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

works.title: Opus Maius
works.description: Roger Bacon's encyclopedic proposal for the reform of learning, written c. 1267 at the request of Pope Clement IV and sent to him with the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium; its seventh part on moral philosophy and its treatment of optics, experimental science, and the applications of mathematics to theology make it a landmark of thirteenth-century thought.
works.summary: Bacon surveys the causes of error, the relation of philosophy to scripture, the utility of grammar and of the learned languages (Hebrew, Greek, Arabic), mathematics and its uses (including calendar reform and geography), the science of perspective, experimental science, and moral philosophy — arguing throughout that the sciences are necessary instruments for the understanding and defence of the faith.
works.significance: The fullest medieval statement of an experimental and mathematically grounded program of learning; a foundation text for the later reputation of Bacon and a principal witness to thirteenth-century optics and natural philosophy.
themes: Creation and cosmology

works.title: Order and Disorder; or, The World Made and Undone
works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's biblical epic on Genesis, of which only canto V was published in her lifetime and the complete text survives in manuscript; it is the first epic poem in English by a woman and a direct answer to Milton's Paradise Lost.
works.plot: The poem retells the story of creation, the fall, and the expulsion, interpreting Genesis through a Calvinist theology and a republican politics that laments the Restoration of monarchy.
works.significance: The first English epic by a woman and an important early response to Paradise Lost; its republicanism and its female epic voice have made it a canonical text of seventeenth-century women's writing.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
works.context: Written after the Restoration, when Hutchinson, a widow and a Puritan, was reflecting on the failure of the republican cause; it engages directly with Milton's epic.
works.characters: Adam; Eve; God; Satan; the angels
works.structure: Twenty cantos in heroic couplets, of which only canto V was printed in 1679.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand and was first published complete in 2001.

works.title: Ordinatio
works.description: Duns Scotus's great revision of his Oxford lectures on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, left unfinished at his death; the Ordinatio sets out the subtle doctor's metaphysics of univocity, his formal distinction, his defence of the Immaculate Conception, and his voluntarist ethics, and became the authoritative alternative to Thomism in late medieval theology.
works.summary: In four books following the structure of the Sentences, Scotus develops a systematic theology distinguished by its precise use of logic: the univocal concept of being, the formal distinction, the primacy of the will, the demonstration of God's existence through the concept of infinite being, and the case for Mary's immaculate conception — arguments that set the agenda for fourteenth-century scholasticism.
works.significance: One of the most demanding and influential works of medieval philosophy and theology; the foundation of the Scotist school, taught in the universities into the seventeenth century and beyond.

works.title: Original Poems for Infant Minds
altTitles: Original Poems, for Infant Minds, by Several Young Persons
works.form: juvenile verse of the nursery lyric and the moral lesson-poem
works.description: The first successful collection of verse written for very young children as children, issued in two volumes in 1804 and 1805, and made by two sisters with the contributions of other hands. It set the pattern of the nursery lyric: the short poem of the common object, the animal, and the duty, put into the mouth of the child and meant to be repeated by him.
works.plot: The collection is a series of short lyrics, dialogues, and little narratives for the infant reader, arranged without a general argument but with a definite moral intention: the lesson of kindness to animals, of duty to parents and to the poor, of truthfulness, of the observation of the works of nature, and of the gratitude owed to the giver of all. Its poems teach by the concrete instance, the sheep, the dog, the bird's nest, the sick neighbour, the little reader's own hour and his own play, and they carry the child through a graduated range of feeling from the mere naming of the thing to the reflection upon death, upon duty, and upon the Creator. Alongside the moral pieces run the poems of simple observation and of the fancy, the description of the seasons and of the trades of the country, which give the collection its hold upon the notice of the child rather than upon his fears.
works.significance: It is the beginning of the English nursery lyric proper, and the book from which the poem of the common object and the small moral duty took its form; it trained several generations of children in their first recitations, and its manner, at once simple, didactic, and observant, is the source of the popular verse which has since been repeated to and by very young children.
works.meter: The simple stanzas of infant recitation: common measure and short lyric lines, hymn-like quatrains, and the dialogue in the smallest possible compass, with the reiterated moral close.
works.context: Issued from the juvenile trade of the metropolis in the years when the educational market for children's books was newly formed, out of the commission of a publisher who wanted verse of a class and a price for the very young, and read in the families and in the Sunday and day schools of the century that followed. The chief hands in the collection were two unmarried sisters of a dissenting family, one of them afterwards a known writer and painter, the other the more famous verse-maker of the pair.
works.characters: The infant speaker and the children of the several little narratives; the animals and the common objects about the nursery and the village
works.structure: Two volumes of independent short poems, graded in difficulty and length for the reading and recitation of very young children, with the preface and the advertisements of the publishers of the juvenile line; the units are single lyrics and dialogue-poems.
works.attributionNotes: The collection is a joint venture published under a collective designation, and contains matter by several hands besides the two sisters who wrote most of it; the distribution of the individual poems between the several contributors is settled by the memoranda and by the later family editions, and the sisters are the authors recorded here.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Natural history, science, and the poetic eye
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Original Stories from Real Life
altTitles: Original Stories from Real Life. With Reflections, Calculated to the Early Formation of the Mind on Principles of Truth and Benevolence
works.form: children's didactic fiction in framed tales
works.description: A book of tales for children, framed as the instruction given by a governess to two girls, each story being worked up into a reflection on truth, benevolence, industry and justice. Its first edition was designed and engraved by an artist then young, and its rational morality marks a stage in the history of children's reading.
works.plot: The governess of the household leads her little charges through the observation of the world about them - the poor, the animal creation, the labouring family, the proud and the falsehood-teller - and out of each case draws a lesson of duty. The children's own questions and faults carry the narrative, and the stories of the people they meet supply the illustration. The book closes on the principle that the imagination of a child must be governed by reason and by sympathy with the suffering.
works.significance: It is an important document of the eighteenth-century education of childhood and of the moral use of sympathy, and it shows the author's pedagogy before the argument of her later works on women.
works.meter: A clear and argumentative prose of conversation adapted to juvenile readers, with the reflective summing-up in a sententious cadence.
works.context: Published in 1788 after the author's first work on female education and among the new rational children's books of the period, in the circle of the dissenting publisher who also issued the scientific and educational works of the day.
works.characters: the governess who instructs; the two girls of her charge; the poor families and the servants of the inset tales; the animals and the objects of the children's curiosity

works.title: Orlando: A Biography
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1928
works.description: A biography across four centuries in which the poet-hero changes sex: the wittiest of the modernist novels and a love letter to Vita Sackville-West. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Virginia Woolf; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Orlando, a young Elizabethan nobleman, begins as a courtier of Queen Elizabeth I, has an affair with a Russian princess, becomes an ambassador to Constantinople, and falls asleep during a revolution and wakes as a woman. She lives through the eighteenth, nineteenth and twentieth centuries, publishes 'The Oak Tree', marries a sea captain, and arrives in the present with a car and a film contract.
works.significance: Orlando is the wittiest and most playful of the modernist novels and the first great English novel of gender as performance: its hero-heroine's change of sex is a philosophical joke that has become a founding text of queer and feminist criticism, and its panorama of English literary history is one of the funniest things Woolf wrote.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric stream of consciousness and the interior monologue.
works.context: English literary and social history from the Elizabethan age to 1928; the Sackville family and Knole, the great house that could not be inherited by a woman; the lesbian relationship with Vita Sackville-West that the novel celebrates.
works.characters: Orlando; Sasha; Marmaduke Bonthrop Shelmerdine; Nick Greene; Queen Elizabeth; Archduchess Harriet
works.structure: Six chapters by century, with mock-biographical documentation (prefaces, illustrations, dates).
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Adeline Virginia Woolf. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Ormond; or, The Secret Witness
works.form: Philosophical and moral tale in the Godwinian manner, inflected by Gothic suspense and by the domestic novel of conduct
works.description: The second of the author's experimental tales and the most explicitly philosophical of them, built around a set argument about the power of character over conduct. A self-sufficient republican heroine is pursued by a misanthropic European sage who believes that human beings are the puppets of circumstance and of fascination. Its dialogue on liberty, dependence and female virtue makes it a novel of ideas as much as a tale of terror.
works.plot: A young American woman of independent means and fixed principles forms an intimate friendship with a wealthy bachelor's sister and becomes the object of two very different suitors. One is a frank planter; the other is Ormond, a solitary thinker who denies the reality of virtue and resolves to prove that he can bend any will by art and fascination. He pursues her through disguise, surveillance and an appeal to her pity, and the crisis arrives when she must act without evidence on the character of the men around her. The ending leaves her security restored but the argument only partly answered, since Ormond's own conversion is reported at a distance.
works.significance: It is the earliest American novel to make female self-sufficiency, rather than courtship, its central ethical problem. Its figure of the manipulating sage supplied a template for the American seducer-villain. It remains the clearest link between the Godwinian circle and the native Gothic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published within a year of the author's first tale, during a brief American season of metaphysical fiction. The debate with which it engages was contemporary: whether a republic of equals could produce virtue without dependence, and whether female independence was defensible. Its European villain embodies Federalist anxieties about aristocratic artifice imported across the Atlantic.
works.structure: Third-person tale organized around a debate, with long set speeches and letters that interrupt the action; the secret witness of the title gives the plot its delayed revelations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Charles Brockden Brown and the American Gothic

works.title: Oroonoko (Southerne's adaptation)
works.description: Southerne's stage version of Behn's novella, which added a comic subplot of two London ladies and made Oroonoko the standard tragic role of the eighteenth century.

works.title: Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (Behn)
works.description: Behn's short novel, narrated by a female traveller in the English colony of Surinam, on the African prince Oroonoko, who is sold into slavery, leads a failed revolt, and is barbarously executed; it is the founding text of English anti-slavery fiction.
works.plot: Oroonoko, grandson of the king of Coramantien, loves Imoinda; both are sold into slavery and reunited in Surinam; he leads an unsuccessful rebellion, is captured, promises peace, is whipped and dismembered, and kills his pregnant wife before his own execution.
works.significance: The most influential prose fiction of the Restoration; it established the 'noble savage' trope, initiated the English anti-slavery literary tradition, and has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing and of postcolonial criticism. Thomas Southerne's 1695 stage adaptation held the stage for over a century.
works.meter: Elegant Restoration prose combining travel description with tragic narrative.
works.context: Published in 1688, the year of the Revolution and of Behn's death; it draws on her claimed residence in Surinam in 1663-4.
works.characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the narrator; Caesar; Trefry; Byam; Banister; the Indian lovers
works.structure: A first-person frame narrative with the narrator's eyewitness account, digressions on Surinam's flora, fauna, and indigenous people, and a sustained portrait of Oroonoko as a European-style hero.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; the narrator's identity is a literary persona, though the Surinam material is generally accepted as drawing on her experience.

works.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
works.description: Robert Henryson's retelling of the Orpheus myth (c. 1480, 633 lines): the harper-king's descent to the underworld to reclaim Eurydice, his fatal backward look, and — in Henryson's distinctive addition — a long moralitas allegorizing Orpheus as the intellect, Eurydice as the appetite, and the harrowing journey as the soul's quest for its lost harmony. The most learned of the makars' classical poems.
works.plot: Orpheus, whose harping masters the beasts and the spheres, loses Eurydice to the serpent's bite and follows her to the underworld, where his music wins her release on the one condition; his backward look loses her forever, and the poet's moralitas expounds the fable as the story of reason seeking the soul's lost good.
works.significance: The classic Scottish treatment of the Orpheus myth and a landmark in the allegorical reading of classical poetry that runs from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the moralitas in Henryson's plainest expository verse.
works.context: Composed c. 1480, drawing on Boethius's Consolation (the standard medieval source for the myth) and the commentary tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508), the first printed Scots poem.
works.characters: Orpheus; Eurydice; Pluto; Proserpina; the Furies; the narrator
works.structure: A bipartite poem: the classical narrative (with its celebrated catalogue of the underworld's inhabitants) followed by the allegorical moralitas.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure.
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
movements: The Scottish Makars

works.title: Orthodoxy
works.description: The wittiest defence of Christian orthodoxy in English: the paradox at the heart of the modern world. It is a prose work of 1908 by G. K. Chesterton; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Chesterton answers the charge that his optimism is merely sentiment by arguing that the Christian faith is the only system that accounts for the world's strangeness: the book ranges from the fairy tale to the suicide of the materialist, from the madman to the martyr, in a series of brilliant paradoxes.
works.significance: Orthodoxy is the wittiest defence of Christian orthodoxy in English and the book that made Chesterton a world figure: its paradoxes and its argument made it one of the most influential religious books of the century and the founding text of the modern Christian apologetic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the paradox turned inside out.
works.context: England in the 1900s, and the debate between materialism, agnosticism and the new orthodoxy. The record dates the work as composed between 1907 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Chesterton as author; the materialist; the madman; the martyr
works.structure: Nine chapters of argument by image and paradox. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.

works.title: Othello
altTitles: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of jealousy: the Moorish general Othello, married secretly to Desdemona, is undone by his ensign Iago — 'honest Iago' — whose insinuations about Cassio and the handkerchief persuade him of his wife's infidelity, until the murder in the marriage bed and the discovery of Iago's villainy leave Othello to execute judgment on himself.
works.plot: Iago, denied promotion, plots against Othello: he makes Cassio drunk and cashiered, then uses the dropped handkerchief to 'prove' Desdemona's adultery; Othello's jealousy mounts through the eavesdropping scene to the murder of Desdemona; Emilia exposes Iago, who kills her and is taken for torture; Othello, recognizing what he has destroyed, stabs himself on the bed.
works.significance: The definitive study of jealousy and of the will to destroy — the most painful, because the most intimate, of the great tragedies.
works.meter: Othello's 'Othello music' — the great periodic verse of the senate speech and the farewell to the 'Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war' — against Iago's prose of reduction.
works.context: Performed at court, 1 November 1604; its sources are Cinthio's novella of the Moor and the Venetian setting of the Cyprus wars; its treatment of race has made it the most urgently debated of the tragedies.
works.characters: Othello; Desdemona; Iago; Emilia; Cassio; Roderigo; Brabantio; Bianca; the Duke of Venice; Lodovico; Montano
works.structure: The most tightly constructed of the tragedies — a single plot of insinuation compressed into some thirty-six hours, with Iago's soliloquies as its engine.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning

works.title: Otherworld: Cadences
works.description: The later collection: the otherworld of the cadence after the war. It is a verse work of 1920 by F. S. Flint; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line.
works.plot: Otherworld gathers Flint's later cadences, the lyrics of the otherworld and of the London evening after the war, in the unrhymed line of the mature manner, and closed the imagist chapter of his verse.
works.significance: Otherworld: Cadences closed the imagist chapter of Flint's verse and remains the record of the doctrine's later practice, the lyric of the otherworld after the war.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short unrhymed cadence of the French vers libre.

works.structure: A collection of later cadences, ordered as a single otherworld. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.

works.title: Our Irish Theatre: A Chapter of Autobiography
works.description: Lady Gregory's account of the founding of the Abbey Theatre and the fight for an Irish drama. It is a prose work of 1913 by Lady Gregory; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Autobiography and the Modern Memoir and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lady Gregory tells the history of the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey from the inside: the first productions, the riots over The Playboy, the tours to America, and the arguments with the Castle and the Church over censorship.
works.significance: Our Irish Theatre is the essential memoir of the Irish dramatic revival and the only full account written from inside the movement: it recorded the founding of the Abbey and the battle over The Playboy, and it remains the primary source for the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The author's characteristic manner is the one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close.
works.context: Dublin in the years 1899 to 1913, the Irish literary revival and the controversy over Synge's plays. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1913 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; autobiography and the modern memoir.
works.characters: Lady Gregory; W. B. Yeats; J. M. Synge; Edward Martyn; the Abbey company
works.structure: A memoir in chapters, from the first productions to the American tours. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. works.title: Our Mutual Friend
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from May 1864 to November 1865, the last completed novel and the darkest of the London books: its dust-heaps, its river and its schoolmaster's 'whosoever' frame a satire on inheritance, money and the new finance.
works.plot: Old Harmon, a dust-contractor, leaves his fortune to his son John on condition that he marry Bella Wilfer, a girl he has never met; the son is reported drowned, and the will's legacy passes to the Boffins, the old servant and his wife. John Harmon returns under the name John Rokesmith as Boffin's secretary, tests Bella's character by pretending to miserliness, and reveals himself at the close. The other plots are the murder of the waterman Hexam by Bradley Headstone, the love of Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam, and the satirical career of the Veneerings and the Podsnaps.
works.significance: Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last complete statement on money, class and the river, and it contains his most sustained satire of the nouveaux riches and of the education system; its imagery of dust and water has been central to the modern critical reading of Dickens, and it is the novel in which his late style reaches its most elliptical.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The Thames as the city's sewer and its source of wealth, the dust-contractors and the new money of the 1860s, the spread of the joint-stock company and the limited liability of the Companies Act (1862), and the school system of the pupil-teacher and the training college.
works.characters: John Harmon (John Rokesmith); Bella Wilfer; Nicodemus Boffin; Mrs Boffin; Silas Wegg; Mr Venus; Lizzie Hexam; Charley Hexam; Gaffer Hexam; Eugene Wrayburn; Bradley Headstone; Mortimer Lightwood; Mr Podsnap; the Veneerings; Jenny Wren; Riah; Fledgeby
works.structure: Multiplot monthly-part narrative organised by the river and the dust-heap as its two governing images, with the Harmon inheritance as the master plot.

works.title: Our Nig; or, Sketches from the Life of a Free Black
works.form: Novel (autobiographical; published at the author's expense in Boston)
works.description: Published in Boston in 1859 at the author's expense and the first novel by an African-American woman: a fictionalised autobiography of a mixed-race indentured servant in New Hampshire. It is a prose fiction work of 1859 by Harriet E. Wilson; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Alfrado, the daughter of a black man and a white woman, is abandoned at six and bound out to a New England family who treat her with systematic cruelty; she grows up in servitude, is prevented from attending school, has a child by a fugitive slave who abandons her, and writes her book to support herself and her son.
works.significance: Our Nig is the first American novel by an African-American woman and the first African-American novel to depict slavery's northern analogue in indentured servitude: its recovery in 1983 rewrote the history of African-American fiction and made Wilson a founding figure of the tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is first-person and third-person autobiographical narrative.
works.context: The 1840s-50s: the free black population of the North, the indentured child servant, and the abolitionist market of the 1850s. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.

works.title: Our Town
works.description: The most performed American play: Grover's Corners, the Stage Manager and the ordinary life. It is a dramatic work of 1938 by Thornton Wilder; it belongs to The American Theatre and the Modern Stage and it is catalogued here under Expressionist and Epic Drama; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Stage Manager narrates the life of the small town of Grover's Corners, New Hampshire, from 1901 to 1913: the childhood of Emily Webb and George Gibbs, their marriage and Emily's death in childbirth, and her return to relive one ordinary day.
works.significance: Our Town won the Pulitzer Prize and is the most performed American play: its bare stage, its Stage Manager and its meditation on ordinary life created the modern American theatre and made it the central American play of the century.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose and verse of the non-realistic stage: the numbered or titled scenes, the chant and the direct address, the split self and the narrating figure who stands outside the action, and the bare platform in place of the furnished room. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the bare stage and the Stage Manager.
works.context: Grover's Corners, New Hampshire, in 1901–13, and the American small town of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and first performed in 1938 and the corpus places it within The American Theatre and the Modern Stage, it is catalogued under expressionist and epic drama; problem play and well-made drama.

works.title: Our Village
works.description: the author's celebrated sequence of rural sketches, a series of character pieces, natural history observations, and village tales drawn from her life at Three Ponds near Reading. The first series appeared in 1824 and made her one of the most widely read prose writers of the Romantic period.
works.plot: The sketches observe the village and its inhabitants with a gentle, humorous intimacy: the gipsy family, the village wedding, the old nurse, the schoolmaster, the country walks and their natural-history incidents. There is no sustained plot; the organising principle is the observer's eye moving from household to landscape and back. The series creates an idealised but affectionately detailed portrait of rural English community life in the agricultural depression.
works.significance: Our Village is the supreme example of the Romantic rural sketch sequence and a foundational text of the county and village tradition in English prose; it influenced Charles Lamb's contemporaries and later writers from Jefferies to the Edwardian county books.
works.context: Written from the Lady's Magazine sketches of 1824 and published separately the same year; the series appeared amid the rural distress of the post-war agricultural depression and the vogue for natural-history writing; the author's own genteel poverty made the sketches a practical income.
works.characters: The persona of the sketcher; the villagers of Three Ponds; the gipsy family; the old nurse; the schoolmaster
works.structure: Loose sequence of independent sketches; first-person essayistic persona; the village and its landscape replace narrative as organising structure.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind

works.title: Out of the Silent Planet
works.form: Scientific romance (the first of the space trilogy)
works.description: Ransom, Mars and the unfallen world: the first voyage of the space trilogy. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by C. S. Lewis; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The philologist Elwin Ransom is carried by the physicist Weston and the adventurer Devine to Malacandra, the unfallen Mars, where the three races of the planet and the Oyarsa who governs it teach him the meaning of the silent planet - the fallen Earth - and of the bent eldil of his own world.
works.significance: Out of the Silent Planet is the first book of the space trilogy and the founding text of the Christian science fiction: its unfallen Mars and its bent Earth turned the planetary romance into the argument about the fall and the dominion of the will, and it made the scientific romance a theological mode.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer.
works.context: The solar system of the 1930s, and the argument against the scientific materialism. The record dates the work as composed in 1937 and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under scientific romance and the utopian tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Elwin Ransom; Weston; Devine; the Oyarsa; Hyoi; Augray; the hrossa, sorns and pfifltriggi
works.structure: A planetary romance in chapters, from the abduction to the return and the frame of the editor. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Clive Hamilton, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to C. S. Lewis is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
altTitles: The XV Books of P. Ovidius Naso, Entitled Metamorphosis
works.description: Arthur Golding's complete translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses (the first four books in 1565, all fifteen in 1567): the myths of transformation — Daphne, Actaeon, Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Medea, and the rest — rendered in rollicking rhymed fourteeners with a Puritan's moralizing commentary, the version that was 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
works.plot: The fifteen books run from the Creation through the myths of gods and mortals, metamorphosis by metamorphosis, to the apotheosis of Caesar; Golding's translation adds the epistle and preface that turn the pagan fables into allegories of divine and moral truth.
works.significance: The English Ovid — the book through which the Renaissance knew its mythology, and the source of a thousand plots, images, and lines.
works.meter: Rhymed fourteeners (seven-stress couplets) of tremendous gusto — the metre the Elizabethans read aloud and imitated.
works.context: The four-book version of 1565 was completed in 1567, in the decade of the Ovidian revival; Shakespeare's allusions to the Metamorphoses — in Midsummer Night's Dream, Titus, and The Tempest — run through this translation.
works.characters: Jupiter; Apollo; Daphne; Actaeon; Narcissus; Echo; Pyramus; Thisbe; Medea; Orpheus; and the hundreds of Ovid's figures
works.structure: The fifteen books of Ovid in order, with Golding's prefatory apparatus (the epistle to Leicester and the preface to the reader) framing the whole.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Golding; uncontested.
themes: Creation and cosmology

works.title: Pale Horse, Pale Rider
works.description: Porter's finest book: the influenza epidemic, the South of her childhood, and 'Noon Wine'. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Katherine Anne Porter; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Old Mortality', 'Noon Wine' and the title novella 'Pale Horse, Pale Rider', in which Miranda, a young newspaperwoman in Denver in 1918, falls in love with a soldier and nearly dies of influenza in the epidemic that killed more Americans than the war.
works.significance: Pale Horse, Pale Rider is Porter's finest book and one of the great American novellas of the century: its title story is the definitive literary record of the 1918 influenza, and 'Noon Wine' is one of the finest American stories ever written.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the story built on a single scene and a single revelation.
works.context: The influenza epidemic of 1918, the American South of Porter's childhood, and the Texas farm of 'Noon Wine'. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1938 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Miranda; Adam Barclay; Mr Thompson; Mr Helton; Mr Hatch; Amy
works.structure: Three novellas in different settings, from the South to the Texas farm to Denver in 1918. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

works.title: Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded
altTitles: Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded. In a Series of Familiar Letters
works.description: A novel in letters and papers by a servant girl who defends her chastity against her young master and is finally rewarded with marriage into the gentry. It was written rapidly as a conduct example for servants and became the most discussed English prose fiction of the 1740s, generating answers, abridgements and imitations within months.
works.plot: Pamela Andrews, fifteen and in service, is pursued by her master with escalating importunity, from trickery and surprise to attempted rape and imprisonment at his country house. She writes to her parents at every stage, resists the instruments of his design, escapes to her home and is recovered by him. After his reformation, effected by her rejection and by his own shame, he marries her; the second part reports her conduct as a wife and lady of the family.
works.significance: It founded the epistolary novel of sexual danger and moral triumph in English and set the terms of the century's argument about fiction's instruction, from the critics of its detail to the defenders of its reward.
works.meter: A deliberately plain and idiomatic servant's prose, with the self-corrections of the writer-in-the-moment and a scriptural and proverbial tag; the elevated passages are reserved for the moral reflections.
works.context: Composed in the winter of 1739-40 and published in the season that also saw the new Licensing Act, the novelist's own printer's shop supplying the material conditions of the book; its immediate imitations included a celebrated burlesque and a rival continuation.
works.characters: Pamela Andrews; Mr. B; Mrs. Jervis; Mrs. Jewkes; Mr. Williams; the parson and the squire's mother; Jonathan
works.structure: Epistolary and journal form, the letters written in the heat of the event and revised by the editor-narrator; the second part shifts to a retrospective domestic narrative with letters and papers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the design stated in the preface and defended by the author in the postscript and the following year's writing.
