works.title: Pandosto
works.description: Greene's romance of jealousy and recognition, subtitled 'The Triumph of Time': King Pandosto of Bohemia, seized by groundless jealousy of his queen Bellaria and his friend King Egistus, destroys his family; the lost daughter Fawnia grows up a shepherd's daughter, is wooed by Egistus's son Dorastus, and the final recognitions restore her — though Pandosto's own suicide shadows the happy ending; the direct source of Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
works.plot: Pandosto's jealousy kills Bellaria and exposes the infant Fawnia; the shepherds raise her; Dorastus loves her despite his father's opposition; the lovers flee to Bohemia, where the recognition scene discloses Fawnia's birth; the marriages are made — and Pandosto, overcome, kills himself, the 'triumph of time' his epitaph.
works.significance: The romance that became The Winter's Tale — the most consequential of the Elizabethan prose fictions by its afterlife.
works.meter: Prose of Greene's pastoral sweetness, with the euphuistic balance softened into narrative flow.
works.context: Published 1588; it went through many editions as 'Pandosto' and 'Dorastus and Fawnia', and supplied Shakespeare with the plot, names, and even phrases of The Winter's Tale.
works.characters: Pandosto; Bellaria; Egistus; Fawnia; Dorastus; the shepherd Porrus; Capnio
works.structure: A prose romance in the Greek manner — jealousy, exposure, pastoral, recognition — with the oracles and storms as its machinery.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Papers on Literature and Art
works.description: Published in 1846 and the first collection of literary criticism by an American: essays on British, French and American literature and on the art of the American landscape. It is a prose work of 1846 by Margaret Fuller; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Fuller writes on Emerson, Hawthorne, Byron, Goethe, George Sand, the American poets and the question of whether there is an American literature; the volume includes the essays from the Dial and the Tribune.
works.significance: Papers on Literature and Art is the first substantial body of American literary criticism and a key text in the formation of the American canon; Fuller's estimate of Hawthorne and her advocacy of Goethe and Sand shaped the American reception of European literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, digressive and allusive prose.
works.context: The year 1846, the New York literary world, the American magazine culture of the 1840s, and the debate on national literature. The record dates the work as composed between 1844 and 1846 and first published in 1846 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: Parables, in Two Parts
works.form: Allegorical prose fiction; a pair of devotional and political parables in the visionary conference manner.
works.description: Two allegorical prose fictions published together in 1705, in which the distempers of church and nation are represented under the veil of a vision. The borrowed form, a conference of personified claims reported by an observer, lets its writer say in parable what a sermon or an occasional tract could less well maintain. The style is ornate, rhythmic and charged with scriptural cadence, and the argument is as much devotional as political.
works.plot: The reader is admitted to a sequence of personified conferences in which the complaints of the age are tried as in a vision: the claims of conscience against the claims of authority, the flatteries of the world against the discipline of a rule of life, and the divisions of a nation against the unity it is called to maintain. The argument running through both parts is that a people which relaxes its religion in order to compound with its politics will lose both, and that the private Christian's remedy is a settled conduct founded on the teaching of the church. The allegory is transparent enough to be read as church and party commentary and plain enough to serve as devotional counsel. The observer reports, applies and exhorts, and the two parts close in the same remonstrance with the conscience of the age.
works.significance: The parables show the range of her prose from the systematic treatise to visionary allegory, and are the best evidence of how a woman of letters used the fable form for church and party argument after the censorial assumptions of the 1690s had broken down. Their ornate rhythmic sentence is a marked instance of the scriptural manner in women's prose before the century's sermon style settled.
works.context: It was printed in 1705, the year after the occasional conformity measure had divided the parties and while the long war still governed the nation's politics and its church politics together. High-church writers of the period were trying allegorical and visionary forms for the language of the church in danger, and this pair of tracts belongs to that experiment rather than to the systematic prose of its author's earlier books. Its publication by the same bookseller as her other tracts kept it inside the circle of her occasional readers.
works.characters: the observing narrator; the personified claims of conscience, of authority and of the world
works.structure: Two parables in two parts, each a framed vision or conference with personified speakers, with the application attached to the figure; the sequence is argumentative rather than narrative.

works.title: Paracelsus
works.form: Verse drama in eleven scenes (closet drama)
works.description: Published in 1835 and praised by Wordsworth, Hazlitt and the actor Macready; a dramatic poem on the Renaissance alchemist Paracelsus, whose pursuit of knowledge is set against the claims of love and of common life.
works.plot: Paracelsus seeks universal knowledge and neglects his friends Festus and Michal; he achieves fame as a healer, is denounced, fails, and dies acknowledging that he has missed the truth by seeking it apart from human love, in a death scene of reconciliation.
works.significance: Paracelsus made Browning's name among the critics and established the Renaissance as his imaginative territory; its theme of the knowledge-seeker who fails through pride is the matrix of the later monologues from 'A Grammarian's Funeral' to 'Andrea del Sarto'.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The 1830s vogue for the Renaissance (Bulwer's novels, Carlyle's lectures), the Victorian debate about the claims of knowledge against feeling, and Browning's own ambition to be a poet of the intellectual life.
works.characters: Paracelsus; Festus; Michal; Aprile
works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.

works.title: Parade's End
works.description: The greatest English novel of the First World War: Tietjens, the trenches and the end of the old England, in four volumes. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The tetralogy — Some Do Not… (1924), No More Parades (1925), A Man Could Stand Up (1926) and The Last Post (1928) — follows Christopher Tietjens through the collapse of his marriage, his service on the Western Front, his love for Valentine Wannop, and his post-war life in the Sussex countryside, and ends with the birth of his child and the death of his brother Mark.
works.significance: Parade's End is the greatest English novel of the First World War and the finest study of the transition from Edwardian to modern England: its technical innovation, its portrait of Tietjens as the last gentleman and its movement from the war to the peace made it a permanent work.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.
works.context: The First World War and the Edwardian world it destroyed, from the golf links of Rye to the mud of the Somme and the peace of a Sussex farm. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1928 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.

works.title: Paradise Lost
works.description: Milton's epic of the Fall of Man in blank verse: Satan's rebellion and expulsion from heaven, his voyage to the new world to corrupt God's creatures, the temptation of Adam and Eve, and their expulsion from Eden — 'to justify the ways of God to men'. Published in ten books (1667) and reissued in twelve (1674).
works.plot: Satan, cast into hell, rallies the fallen angels, volunteers to explore the new world, seduces Eve through the serpent, and Adam falls with her through love; the Son pronounces judgment, Michael shows Adam the future of mankind, and the pair leave Paradise 'hand in hand' with providence their guide.
works.significance: The greatest epic in the English language and a central work of world literature; it shaped English poetry, theology, and political imagination for centuries and inspired responses from Blake and Shelley to modern criticism.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter (blank verse), with Milton's 'sense variously drawn out from one verse into another' and a Latinate grandeur of diction and syntax.
works.context: Composed chiefly after the Restoration (c. 1658–65), when Milton was blind, politically defeated, and in danger; dictated to amanuenses and published in 1667, it transposes the failed republican cause into a theodicy of obedience, liberty, and inner paradise.
works.characters: Satan; Adam; Eve; God the Father; the Son; Raphael; Michael; Beelzebub; Sin and Death
works.structure: An epic in twelve books with invocations, in medias res opening, councils in heaven and hell, extended similes, and a vast temporal and cosmic scope, drawing on classical epic and biblical narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: Paradise Regained
works.description: Milton's 'brief epic' in four books, retelling the temptation of Christ in the wilderness (Luke 4): Jesus resists Satan's offers of bread, wealth, empire, and classical learning through patient faith and reasoned constancy, thereby regaining Paradise lost through Adam.
works.plot: Satan, disguised, tempts the fasting Christ first with hunger, then with the kingdoms of the world and the glory of Athens; Christ refuses each, exposing Satan's false values, and stands unshaken on the pinnacle of the temple, whereupon Satan is confounded and angels minister to him.
works.significance: A deliberately quiet, intellectual counterpart to Paradise Lost that redefines the epic hero as the patient, obedient Christ; long undervalued, it is now admired for its severity and argumentative power.
works.meter: Blank verse, more austere and restrained than Paradise Lost, suited to the patient heroism of 'the better fortitude / Of patience and heroic martyrdom'.
works.context: Composed after Paradise Lost and published with Samson Agonistes in 1671; it reflects Milton's post-Restoration meditation on true heroism as inner, spiritual constancy rather than martial glory.
works.characters: Jesus (the Son); Satan; the disciples; Mary
works.structure: A dialogue-driven brief epic in blank verse, structured as a series of debates and temptations rather than action, with an austere, argumentative style.

works.title: Parochial and Plain Sermons
works.description: The sermons preached at St Mary's, Oxford, between 1828 and 1843 and published in eight volumes: the most influential body of Anglican preaching in the nineteenth century and the spiritual foundation of the Oxford Movement.
works.plot: The sermons are single-argument meditations on the creed, the sacraments, sin, conscience and the unseen world, delivered to an academic congregation and designed to awaken a sense of the reality of God; the most famous, 'The Second Spring' (1852), belongs to the later Catholic collection.
works.significance: The Parochial and Plain Sermons created the devotional literature of the Oxford Movement and are the finest English sermons of the century: their doctrine of the 'invisible world' and their appeal to conscience shaped Victorian religious feeling and gave the Tractarians their popular voice.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
works.context: The 1830s at Oxford, the Noetics and the Oriel common room, the Evangelical revival and the High Church reaction that became the Oxford Movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1828 and 1843 and first published in 1834 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Pasquin
works.form: comic drama with inserted tragedy, written for the stage
works.description: A comedy in two scenes with a play within it, subtitled a hermophrodite piece because it is at once comedy and tragedy. Its declared design is to show that the stage may correct the age, and its target is the corruption of a court and a ministry by flattery and place-taking.
works.plot: In the frame, a young lover of integrity is pressed by his friends to take a court position, and a wicked minister's designs on office and on the heroine are exposed. The inserted tragedy of the fair Virginia shows a virtuous subject destroyed by a tyranny, and its performance converts the spectators of the frame. The two plots together argue that the stage teaches by example, and the good are rewarded when the court's agents are unmasked.
works.significance: It is the most explicit statement in dramatic form of the century's argument for the stage as a school of public virtue, and a central document of the quarrel that produced the Licensing Act of 1737.
works.meter: Prose in the frame and verse in the inserted tragedy, the two styles being contrasted to make the critical point about the genres' different powers.
works.context: First performed at the little theatre in the Haymarket in March 1736, in the height of the Walpolean debate over the playhouse and the theatre's capacity for party attack, three months before the Lord Chamberlain's new censorship of 1737; the writer's theatre was among the institutions affected by it.
works.characters: the honest young lover of the frame; the corrupt courtier and his dependants; the spectators of the inserted tragedy; the heroine of the inserted drama
works.structure: A frame comedy of two parts enclosing a short serious drama, the inserted play's moral function being explicitly argued in the dialogue; the structure is essayistic rather than intrigue-driven.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and advertised with a preface on the design of the piece.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

works.title: Passing
works.description: Larsen's masterpiece: two women who look white, and one who chooses to pass. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Nella Larsen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Clare Kendry, who has passed for white and married a racist, meets her old friend Irene Redfield in Chicago; the novel follows their dangerous friendship in Harlem until Clare's fall from a window, in a study of race, desire and deception.
works.significance: Passing is the central novel of the American literature of racial passing and Larsen's masterpiece: its portrait of Clare and Irene, its ambiguity and its ending made it one of the great novels of the Harlem Renaissance and a permanent text of American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the short novel of the interior life.
works.context: Chicago and New York in the late 1920s, and the world of the Black bourgeoisie. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Clare Kendry; Irene Redfield; Brian Redfield; John Bellew; Hugh Wentworth
works.structure: A novel in four parts, from the Chicago meeting to the fall. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Nella Marian Larsen. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind

works.title: Passio Sancti Eadmundi
altTitles: Life of St Edmund, King and Martyr
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.ii; also transmitted through Ælfric's Old English adaptation
works.description: The earliest Latin life of Edmund, king of East Anglia, killed by the Viking Great Army in 869 and venerated as a martyr at Bury St Edmunds. Abbo of Fleury wrote it at Ramsey Abbey (985-987) from the eyewitness testimony of the aged Dunstan, who had heard the story from Edmund's own sword-bearer, and dedicated the work to Dunstan.
works.plot: The Danish army of Ingwar and Ubba invades East Anglia and demands Edmund's submission; the king, a model Christian ruler, refuses to deny Christ or rule as a viking's vassal, and is beaten, shot with arrows, and beheaded. A wolf guards the severed head until the faithful find it; the head rejoins the body, and Edmund is buried and venerated as a martyr whose body remains incorrupt.
works.significance: The founding text of the cult of St Edmund, England's royal patron saint, and the direct source of Ælfric's Old English life; an important link between continental hagiography and the English Benedictine Reform.
works.context: Written in the 980s when England again faced Danish attacks and when the cults of royal martyrs were being cultivated by the reformers; Abbo's Ramsey sojourn made the text a channel of continental learning into the English reform, and its story became the foundation of Bury St Edmunds' great cult.
works.characters: Edmund of East Anglia, Ingwar, Ubba, Bishop Theodred, Dunstan (as source)
works.structure: A classic passio in three movements: the invasion and the tyrant's demands, the martyrdom itself with its arrow-martyrdom patterned on St Sebastian, and the discovery and incorruption of the body, framed by Abbo's prefatory letter to Dunstan.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Abbo of Fleury, who dedicates the work to Dunstan and describes its composition at Ramsey.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Kingship and good rule
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Benedictine Reform

works.title: Past and Present
works.description: Written in seven weeks in 1843 and the most concentrated of Carlyle's social criticisms: a comparison of the twelfth-century monastery of Bury St Edmunds, recovered from the chronicle of Jocelin of Brakelond, with the 'condition of England' in the Hungry Forties.
works.plot: Book I, 'Proem', states the diagnosis of a society without a soul; Book II, 'The Ancient Monk', narrates Abbot Samson's governance of the monastery as a model of work and order; Book III, 'The Modern Worker', presents the 'Manchester insurrection', the 'Gospel of Work' and the parson and the priest of the modern world; Book IV, 'Horoscope', prophesies the consequences of the neglect of the poor.
works.significance: Past and Present is the founding text of Victorian social criticism and the source of much of the vocabulary of the later Labour movement; its 'Gospel of Work', its attack on the 'cash nexus' and its demand for a governing aristocracy of talent shaped Ruskin, Dickens, Kingsley, Morris and the Christian socialists, and it remains the classic English indictment of industrial capitalism from the right.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: The Chartist riots of 1839-42, the 'Hungry Forties', the New Poor Law and the factory system, and the Victorian debate between laissez-faire and the duty of the state. The record dates the work as composed in 1843 and first published in 1843 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture

works.title: Paston Letters
works.description: The correspondence and papers of the Paston family of Norfolk, spanning 1422–1509: over a thousand letters, wills, and memoranda recording the family's rise from yeoman stock to gentry status, their lawsuits (above all the struggle for Caister Castle), their marriages, and the texture of fifteenth-century provincial life. The richest surviving archive of medieval English family letters.
works.plot: The letters move among the three generations of Pastons — the judge William, his sons John I and John II, their wives Margaret and Margery — and their circle: the siege of Caister, John II's life at court, Margery's secret marriage, the boys' schooling, and the daily business of land, law, and loyalty in East Anglia.
works.significance: The first great English family letter collection: a unique window on the language, law, and life of fifteenth-century England, and the ancestor of the English epistolary tradition.
works.meter: Prose: the varied, idiomatic English of a literate gentry family, from Margaret's dictated letters to John II's courtier prose.
works.context: Written 1422–1509 by the Norfolk Pastons, whose archive passed to the Earl of Yarmouth and was edited by John Fenn (1787); it documents the Wars of the Roses from the perspective of a gentry family and is a primary source for the period's social history.
works.characters: William Paston; Margaret Paston; John Paston I; John Paston II; Margery Paston; the family's servants and opponents
works.structure: An epistolary archive, not a composed work: its order is chronological and documentary, spanning the reigns of Henry VI, Edward IV, and Henry VII.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (many family members and correspondents); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: Pastorals
works.description: Pope's four seasonal pastorals, printed when he was barely twenty and presented by him as the exercise of his earliest years: a Virgilian and Spenserian apprenticeship poem which nevertheless displays the couplet manner, the panegyric structure and the critical self-fashioning of his mature work.
works.plot: Shepherd speakers answer one another through spring, summer, autumn and winter, each season drawing its own song, lament or tribute; the sequence carries Pope's early commendation of Addison and of the military glory of the recent war inside the conventional eclogue.
works.significance: It announced the couplet style and the doctrine of imitation on which Pope's whole career depended, and it supplied the Dunciad with one of its longest-lived personal grievances.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets, lengthened and made melodious by Spenserian and Miltonic example, with shorter lyric stanzas for the embedded songs.
works.context: Printed in the sixth part of Tonson's Poetical Miscellanies in 1709, in the same years as Ambrose Philips's own pastorals; the ensuing dispute about priority, about the proper diction of shepherds and about the value of Spenser made the pastorals the opening battle of the century's quarrel over rules and genius.
works.characters: the shepherd speakers of the four seasons; the presiding Muse
works.structure: Four separately titled eclogues in dialogue, arranged as a year and each closing with a song or a panegyric passage.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though Pope's claim to have written the poems as a boy is supported partly by his own later testimony rather than by independent evidence.

works.title: Pastors and Masters
works.description: Compton-Burnett's second novel and the first in her mature manner of clipped, precise dialogue: a comedy of literary theft among the staff of a boys' preparatory school and the dons of a neighbouring college, in which two elderly men each pass off the same old manuscript as a new novel of their own.
works.plot: Nicholas Herrick, the seventy-year-old, self-absorbed proprietor of a boys' preparatory school in an old university town, lives with his half-sister Emily, who praises him sarcastically in public and despises him in private; the school is really run by the senior master, Mr Merry, whose talent is for presenting it in a falsely favourable light to parents. Herrick has always wanted to be a 'real author'. Clearing the room of Crabbe, a don who has just died, he finds the typescript of a short novel, takes it, and announces a sudden inspiration. At the same time the don Richard Bumpus announces a new novel, a rewriting of the book he wrote as a young man and had buried in a friend's grave, without admitting that his typescript, left in Crabbe's room, has vanished. When both men give readings, Bumpus's old friend William Masson reveals that he kept and read the youthful manuscript, and the identical first sentences show that neither man has written anything new: the only novel is Bumpus's early one. The book ends with a dinner party staged to impress the autocratic Reverend Henry Bentley, a parent with two sons at the school.
works.significance: Pastors and Masters established the method that made Compton-Burnett unique, the novel carried almost entirely by mordantly witty, precise dialogue, which she went on to turn on tyranny and power in secluded late-Victorian households; the New Statesman called it 'like nothing else in the world' and 'a work of genius'.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the novel composed almost entirely of dialogue.
works.context: England in the 1920s: a small boys' preparatory school in an old university town and the fellows of the college nearby. It appeared fourteen years after Compton-Burnett's apprentice novel Dolores (1911), which she never listed among her publications.
works.characters: Nicholas Herrick; Emily Herrick; Mr and Mrs Merry; Miss Basden; Mr Burgess; Richard Bumpus; William Masson; the Reverend Peter Fletcher and Teresa Fletcher; Lydia Fletcher; the Reverend Henry Bentley
works.structure: A short novel (126 pages in the first edition) told almost entirely in dialogue: a character study of the school and its circle, the two readings at which the theft is exposed, and a closing dinner party.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dame Ivy Compton-Burnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Paterson
works.description: The great American long poem of place: a New Jersey city, a doctor, and the search for a language in which things can be said. It is a verse work of 1946 by William Carlos Williams; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem follows the city of Paterson and its river, its falls and its people, and the figure of the doctor-poet who walks it; it assembles letters, documents, newspaper cuttings and lyric passages into a single work about the American place and the American idiom.
works.significance: Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land and the founding work of the American objectivist epic: it made a single American city the subject of a modernist long poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the line measured by the breath and broken by speech.
works.context: The industrial city of Paterson, New Jersey, and its history; the America of the 1940s and 1950s; and Williams's own medical practice among its people. The record dates the work as composed between 1944 and 1958 and first published in 1946 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
works.characters: The doctor; Paterson; the river; the falls
works.structure: Five books, each in three parts, mixing lyric, letter and document. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Patience
works.description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 531 lines on the prophet Jonah, expounding the beatitude 'blessed are the patient' through the comic drama of the reluctant prophet, the storm, the whale, and the withered woodbine. Patience, the poem argues, is the virtue God himself practises with sinners — and the one Jonah must learn.
works.plot: Jonah, fleeing God's command to preach at Nineveh, boards ship for Tarshish; the storm God raises forces the sailors to cast him overboard, and he is swallowed by the whale, in whose belly he prays his psalm of thanksgiving; delivered, he preaches at Nineveh, whose repentance God accepts — to Jonah's fury, which the parable of the woodbine answers: if Jonah pities a plant, shall not God pity a city of a hundred and twenty thousand?
works.significance: The liveliest biblical poem of the alliterative revival and the most sustained Middle English treatment of patience; its comic sympathy with the reluctant prophet is without parallel in the period.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, handled with colloquial vigour.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The Jonah story had a special medieval resonance through its typological link to the Resurrection.
works.characters: Jonah; God; the sailors; the Ninevites
works.structure: A homiletic prologue on the eight beatitudes, then a three-movement biblical narrative (flight and storm; whale and prayer; Nineveh and the woodbine), with the parable as the poem's doctrinal climax.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: Patience; or, Bunthorne's Bride
works.description: First performed in 1881 and the definitive Victorian satire of the aesthetic movement: a village of love-sick maidens adores two rival poets. It is a dramatic work of 1881 by W. S. Gilbert; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The twenty lovesick maidens of Castle Bunthorne abandon their soldier lovers for the aesthetic poet Bunthorne and his rival Grosvenor; Patience, the simple milkmaid, is the only one immune to aesthetics, and the opera ends with the poets renouncing poetry for the simple life and the maidens returning to their redcoats.
works.significance: Patience is the definitive satire of the aesthetic movement and one of the most important documents of Victorian cultural history: Wilde's tour of America as part of the opera's promotion made him famous, the opera fixed the popular image of the aesthete for ever, and it is the funniest treatment of the art-for-art's-sake movement in English.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is inverted logic carried to absurdity.
works.context: 1881: the aesthetic movement of the 1870s-80s, the Grosvenor Gallery, Oscar Wilde's early public image, and the vogue of the 'greenery-yallery' pose. The record dates the work as composed in 1881 and first published in 1881 and first performed in 1881 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Reginald Bunthorne; Archibald Grosvenor; Patience; Lady Jane; Lady Angela; Colonel Calverley; the Duke of Dunstable
works.structure: The action is divided into two acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Schwenck Gilbert. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Patronage
works.form: Prose fiction; novel of manners and institutional comedy; the county novel of opinion
works.description: A novel of church and state patronage, following three young men who must be provided for in a world where office, living and rank are distributed by interest rather than by merit. Its argument is institutional: it examines the machinery by which preferment is given, and measures the corruption it produces in families and in the professions. The plot turns on an illegitimate son's claims and on a father's anxiety for the education of dependants for public life. It is the most programmatic of the writer's English county novels.
works.plot: A man of family interest undertakes to advance his dependants and his natural son by means of patronage, and the three several careers of church, law and the army are tried against each other and against the demand for principle. Marriages of interest, a concealed relationship, and the discovery of a family claim disturb the plan, and the preferment sought by interest is in the end awarded on a different footing. The closing settlement defends the reformed use of patronage while exposing its abuses, and the education of the young men is the true subject of the book.
works.significance: An important early novel on the machinery of patronage as a social system, and a document of the reform argument that the century's institutional novels continued. It is read chiefly for its analysis of professional advancement and of education for public life, and it stands beside the author's Irish tales in the history of the novel of social institution.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain didactic style, with speech patterns marking church, law, army and trade
works.context: Published in 1814, during the last years of the war with France and at a moment of vigorous controversy over church patronage, pluralities and the sale of offices. Its county and metropolitan scenes reflect the post-war competition for professional advancement, and its treatment of a natural son's claim belongs to the period's debate on family obligation and property. The writer's own experience of the Irish estate and of London literary society supplies both its practical knowledge and its reforming purpose.
works.structure: Third-person omniscient novel of institutions in three volumes, with paired household plots, long explanatory dialogue, and an openly argumentative narrator; the design is illustrative rather than suspenseful.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.

works.title: Pauline: A Fragment of a Confession
works.description: Published anonymously at the author's expense in 1833 when he was twenty-one, and withdrawn by him in later life: the confession of a young poet to the woman he loves, tracing his search for a faith through Shelleyan idealism, nature and art.
works.plot: The speaker addresses Pauline across a blank-verse monologue in which he recounts his childhood, his worship of Shelley, his loss of faith, and his discovery that love for her gives him a centre; the poem ends with a vow of fidelity.
works.significance: Pauline is the earliest fully developed dramatic monologue in English in Browning's hand, and its confessional method — a speaker who reveals more than he knows — is the prototype of all his later work.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The 1830s, the Shelley cult, Byron's death and the decline of the 'Satanic' school, and the young Browning's reading of Shelley, Keats and the French memoirists. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1833 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the speaker; Pauline; the Sun-treader (Shelley)
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Payment Deferred
works.description: The novel of the poisoner of the suburbs. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by C. S. Forester; it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Payment Deferred follows William Marble, the cashiered clerk, from the poisoning of the nephew who brings the money to the speculation, the rise and the payment of the title, in the inverted crime novel whose criminal the reader watches from the first page.
works.significance: Payment Deferred is the first novel of Forester's career and a classic of the inverted detective story: its Marble belongs with the great amoral climbers of the between-wars crime novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact prose of the professional.
works.context: The London suburbs of the mid-1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: William Marble, the clerk; the nephew; the wife and the household
works.structure: An inverted crime novel in the chapters of the murder, the rise and the payment. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cecil Scott Forester. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Peacock Pie
works.description: The finest book of children's verse of the century: 'The Quince Tree', 'Off the Ground' and the world seen from a child's height. It is a verse work of 1913 by Walter de la Mare; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale; Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The collection's poems — 'The Horseman', 'Off the Ground', 'The Cupboard', 'The Quartette', 'Some One', 'The Ruin', 'The Window' — are songs and riddles of the nursery, the farmyard, the ghost and the dream, written with a perfect ear for the child's cadence.
works.significance: Peacock Pie is the finest book of children's verse of the period and one of the permanent children's books in English: its songs, riddles and ghosts have been read to children for a century, and it is the equal in its kind of the Alice books.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric of the half-heard and the unseen.
works.context: The Edwardian nursery, the English countryside, and the golden age of the illustrated children's book. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1913 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; georgian anthology lyric.
works.characters: Jim Jay; the Huntsmen; Old Shellover; the Mad Prince ('The Song of the Mad Prince'); Miss T.; the Horseman
works.structure: Over eighty short poems and songs for children. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Walter John de la Mare. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Pearl
works.description: The great elegiac dream vision of the Gawain-poet: 1,212 lines in 101 twelve-line stanzas linked by concatenation, in which a grieving father, mourning a lost 'pearl' (his infant daughter), dreams of her transfigured among the blessed, debates with her the theology of grace, and glimpses the heavenly Jerusalem. The most perfectly wrought poem of the Alliterative Revival.
works.plot: In an arbour where his pearl slipped from his hand, the dreamer falls asleep and finds himself by a crystal stream; across it stands a maiden crowned with pearls, whom he recognizes as his lost child grown in heaven. Their dialogue unfolds the parable of the vineyard — the justice of the penny's wage, the grace that admits the innocent and the repentant alike — and culminates in his vision of the New Jerusalem and the Lamb, before his waking returns him to the earth where the pearl is buried.
works.significance: The greatest English religious elegy and the most technically brilliant poem of the Middle English period; its theology of grace and its jewelled art have made it the centre of a vast critical literature.
works.meter: Twelve-line alliterative stanzas rhyming ababababbcbc, with concatenatio linking stanza to stanza.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet in the north-west Midlands, in the Ricardian flowering of the dream vision; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x with Sir Gawain, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: the Dreamer (father); the Pearl-maiden; the Lamb; St John
works.structure: Twenty sections of five stanzas each, the last line of each stanza echoed by the first of the next, and the poem's final line repeating its first; the stream divides the poem into the two worlds of earth and heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
The contemplative life
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: Pelham; or, The Adventures of a Gentleman
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1828
works.description: Published in 1828 and the founding English 'silver-fork' novel: the education of a fashionable young gentleman in the world of London society. It is a prose fiction work of 1828 by Edward Bulwer-Lytton; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Henry Pelham, a rich and elegant young man about town, polishes his dandyism in Paris, becomes entangled in the murder of the gambler Sir John Tyrrell, of which his friend Sir Reginald Glanville is suspected, clears Glanville by his own courage and intelligence, and settles down to marry Glanville's sister Ellen and to take up the political career that his fashionable idleness had postponed.
works.significance: Pelham created the fashionable novel and the dandy hero of the 1830s: its picture of London society, its epigrams and its elegant, self-conscious narrator made it the model for Disraeli's novels and for Thackeray's satire, and its portrait of the gentleman as a man of style rather than birth was a decisive innovation in English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue.
works.context: 1828: the London season, the dandy culture of the 1820s, the new gentleman's clubs, and the vogue for the fashionable novel after Scott. The record dates the work as composed between 1827 and 1828 and first published in 1828 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.
works.characters: Henry Pelham, the narrator; Sir Reginald Glanville; Ellen Glanville; Lady Frances Pelham, his mother; Lord Vincent; Sir John Tyrrell; Thornton; Job Jonson; Lady Roseville; Lord Guloseton
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Bulwer-Lytton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Pembroke: A Novel
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1894 and Freeman's finest novel: two New England families divided by pride and a broken engagement. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Mary E. Wilkins Freeman; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Barnabas Thayer breaks his engagement to Charlotte Barnard because of wounded pride, and the two families — the Thayers and the Barnards — are set against one another for years; the novel follows Charlotte's long fidelity, Barnabas's decline into drink and illness, and the slow reconciliation that comes only at the end.
works.significance: Pembroke is Freeman's masterpiece and one of the finest American regional novels of the century: its portrait of a community governed by pride and its study of a woman's long patience made it the fullest expression of her vision, and it is the equal of Jewett's best work.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn.
works.context: 1894: the Massachusetts village of the 1890s, the stern Congregational culture of the New England interior, and the American regional novel of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Barnabas Thayer; Charlotte Barnard; Deborah Thayer; Rebecca Thayer; Ephraim Thayer; Cephas Barnard; Sylvia Crane; Richard Alger; William Berry
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Percy
works.form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
works.description: A domestic tragedy founded on an old English ballad and on the stories of the heroic age of the north, in which a noble seducer and the ruined wife of his dependant are brought to a discovery and a catastrophe of feeling. It held the stage for many years after its author's religious conversion took her from the theatre.
works.plot: A lord of high family and little principle makes an artful attack upon the wife of an officer of his household, whose tenderness and duty expose her the more. The ruin of the family, the struggles of the injured husband and the terrors of the wife carry the action to its catastrophe. The closing scenes bring the seducer to remorse and the innocent to suffering, the play arguing that passion without virtue destroys a house.
works.significance: It is a notable instance of the ballad revival's contribution to serious drama and of a woman's command of the tragic repertory at Drury Lane; its later history bears on the quarrel between the stage and its author's religious principles.
works.meter: Blank verse of the mid-century school, elevated and pathetic, with the short broken line of the distress scenes and the set speeches of remonstrance.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1777 with success, in the season of the vogue for the ballad-derived domestic tragedy and before the author's withdrawal from the stage; it remained in the repertory into the following century.
works.structure: A regular tragedy in five acts of the school of sentimental domestic drama, the scenes built about the several attacks and the last discovery; the catastrophe is affective rather than violent.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and recorded in the theatre books of the season.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Marriage and women's conduct
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Garrick and the Regenerated London Theatre

works.title: Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
altTitles: Peri Bathous: Or the Art of Sinking in Poetry
works.description: The Scribleran mock-technical treatise burlesquing the pseudo-Longinian essay on the sublime by codifying the art of the bathos: rules, instances and cautions for lowering the dignity of verse, with a chapter on the deeper and higher dulness.
works.plot: An index of the figures and diseases of dull writing, delivered as a formal treatise with rules and examples: how to sink from sublimity, how to confound metaphor, and how the greater and lesser depths of bathos are to be measured.
works.significance: It supplied the century's word for the anticlimax of style and turned the technology of the treatise into a weapon, defining the sublime by its parody.
works.meter: Prose of the academic index, with the definition, the division and the quoted example; the illustrations are verse specimens of failure.
works.context: Circulated in the Scriblerus club papers of the second decade of the century and printed for the first time with the Dunciad Variorum, in the argument about taste, sublimity and the decline of poetry then being fought over Milton, over the unities and over the opera.
works.structure: A mock-dissertation in numbered chapters and rules, prefixed to and commenting on the Dunciad's account of degenerate taste.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative and disputed: a Scribleran compound circulated among Pope, Swift, Arbuthnot, Parnell and Atterbury, of which no separate contemporary edition exists and whose shares cannot be assigned; Pope printed it among his own apparatus without claiming its whole composition.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: Pericles and Aspasia; a Series of Dialogues, Letters, and Epitaphs
works.form: Prose romance in epistolary and dialogue form, with lyric and funerary inscriptions; a philosophical and antiquarian fiction in the line of the author's own dialogues.
works.description: The author's late romance of fifth-century Athens, built up out of dialogues, letters, songs and epitaphs among Pericles, Aspasia and the intellectual society of the Periclean age. It is at once a philhellenic ideal picture and a marriage manual in classical dress, and its deliberate archaisms carry its author's prose style to its most condensed and most artificial perfection. It lies at the very end of the period covered by this installment.
works.plot: The book traces Aspasia's arrival at Miletus and her influence over Pericles through the years of the Samian war, the building of the Parthenon, and the quarrels with Sparta, until the plague, the loss of friends, and the approach of the war exhaust the Periclean circle. Around the two figures move Anaxagoras, Socrates, Protagoras, Phidias, Sophocles and Thais, arguing about art, religion, and the education of women. Aspasia herself is drawn as the practical moral centre, capable of governing both a household and a statesman. The epitaphs and songs gather the civic religion of the piece, ending with the deaths of Pericles and his family.
works.significance: The most complete statement of its author's ideal of style as a form of moral architecture, and one of the last Victorian-adjacent English books to make classical Athens a usable model for marriage, friendship, and public taste; it sealed his late reputation with the aestheticists.
works.meter: Chiefly prose, with interpolated verse songs and epitaphs in English imitations of Greek lyric and sepulchral measure.
works.context: Composed in Bath and Florence in the last years before its author's final settlement in Italy, when Greek independence had made Hellenism a live political as well as an aesthetic question; its idealisation of Periclean Athens also answers the Reform-era debate about democracy, women's education, and the claims of art to public utility.
works.characters: Pericles; Aspasia; Anaxagoras; Socrates; Phidias; Sophocles
works.structure: Composite prose-and-verse sequence of letters, dialogues, fragments, songs and epitaphs, arranged chronologically but without continuous narration; the reader assembles the story from documents.
works.attributionNotes: Belongs to the extreme end of the Romantic period's working edges; recorded here with its date plainly stated because it postdates 1832 and overlaps the early Victorian age.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Women's education and intellectual friendship

works.title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
works.description: The first of the late romances, written with George Wilkins: the wanderings of Pericles, who flees Antiochus's riddle, wins Thaisa at Pentapolis, loses her in childbirth at sea, leaves their daughter Marina at Tarsus, and — after shipwreck, brothel, and the years of grief — is reunited with both in the recognition scenes at Mytilene and Diana's temple at Ephesus.
works.plot: Pericles solves the incest riddle and flees; he wins Thaisa in the tournament; Thaisa 'dies' at sea and is revived at Ephesus; Marina is raised at Tarsus and saved from murder by pirates; the brothel scenes test her virtue; and the double recognition — father and daughter, then husband and wife — restores the family under Diana's guidance.
works.significance: The gateway to the late romances — the play in which Shakespeare turned from tragedy to the art of restoration.
works.meter: Gower's tetrameter choruses frame a prose-and-verse play of variable texture, reflecting its joint authorship.
works.context: Based on the Apollonius of Tyre story via Gower's Confessio Amantis and Lawrence Twine's prose version; the play was a popular success, printed in 1609 and omitted from the First Folio.
works.characters: Pericles; Thaisa; Marina; Gower (the Chorus); Antiochus; Cleon; Dionyza; Simonides; Lysimachus; Cerimon; the Bawd; Boult; Diana
works.structure: An episodic sea-romance narrated and moralized by the poet Gower, who returns as chorus, in a deliberately archaic structure of storms, riddles, and reunions.
works.attributionNotes: Collaboration with George Wilkins for the first two acts is now generally accepted; the Folio omitted the play, which entered the canon in the Third Folio (1664).
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Sea voyage and seafaring

works.title: Perkin Warbeck

works.title: Persian Eclogues
works.form: eclogue pair after the eastern manner
works.description: Collins's earliest published verses: two short eclogues after the Persian, in which the oriental scene of the garden, the cup and the beloved carries the lover's complaint and the picture of the poet's own retirement.
works.plot: The eclogues set a lover's lament and the description of the Eastern season against the soft music of the pipe and the garden, with the poet's own wish for a like solitude and an unnoticed death.
works.significance: They show the formation of Collins's lyric manner out of the oriental fashion, and they prepared the softer and more melancholy measures of the odes of the following decade.

works.title: Personae: The Collected Poems of Ezra Pound
works.description: Pound's collected shorter poems to 1926: the troubadour translations, the imagist lyrics and the satires. It is a verse work of 1926 by Ezra Pound; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line; Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume gathers Pound's shorter poems from 1908 to 1926: the Provençal and Italian translations, the imagist lyrics of Ripostes and Lustra, the Chinese versions of Cathay, the satires and the Mauberley sequence.
works.significance: Personae is the essential single volume of Pound's shorter poetry: it made the case for translation as original composition and gathered the imagist lyrics that taught the century to write free verse.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the image as the unit of the poem.
works.context: The London and Paris of the 1910s and 1920s, and the whole range of Pound's early experiments in translation and form. The record dates the work as composed between 1908 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line; modernist lyric and the new idiom.

works.title: Personal Reminiscences of a Great Crusade
works.form: Memoir of the campaign; review essay
works.description: Published in 1896 and Butler's own account of the twenty-year campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, written after the final repeal in 1886. It is a prose work of 1896 by Josephine Butler; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Butler records the founding of the Ladies' National Association, the heckling and violence of the public meetings, the parliamentary campaigns of 1870-86, and the extension of the work to the international traffic in women.
works.significance: The Reminiscences are the central primary source for the history of Victorian feminist agitation and one of the great Victorian memoirs of a public campaign.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is prophetic, impassioned oratory in print.
works.context: The 1869-86 repeal campaign, the General Election of 1874, and the Brussels conference of 1899 against the white slave trade. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Josephine Butler, the narrator; George Butler, her husband; James Stansfeld
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Josephine Elizabeth Butler. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Persuasion
works.form: Novel of manners with elegiac and romantic inflection; an early example of the second-chance love plot treated as moral history.
works.description: The last completed novel, a mature and lyrical story of a woman who was persuaded nearly nine years before to break off her engagement to a poor naval lieutenant, now rich and successful, and who must decide whether his wounded pride can be forgiven. Its baronet and admiral world, its impaired gentry and its rising naval wealth make it the most historically explicit of the early nineteenth-century novels of manners. The prose is more relaxed, more feeling-led, and more openly autobiographical in its predicament than anything in the earlier work.
works.plot: Sir Walter Elliot, extravagant and vain, is persuaded by his steward's arithmetic to retrench and to let Kellynch Hall to Admiral Croft, whose wife is the sister of the very captain now returned from war. Anne Elliot, who nine years earlier gave way to Lady Russell's warning against the impecunious young Frederick Wentworth, is drawn back into his society at Uppercross and at Lyme, where Louisa Musgrove's fall from the Cobb throws the family into confusion and opens Wentworth's admiration for the lively, injured girl. The baronet's grasping cousin Mr. Elliott, who courts Anne only as a possible heiress, is exposed and banished; Louisa recovers to be betrothed to the mourning Captain Benwick; and at Bath a design to attach Wentworth to the fashionable Lady Dalrymple miscarries. Anne's overheared speech on the constancy of women, followed by the interrupted conversation at the Bell, produces Wentworth's letter, and a private marriage against the wishes of her family.
works.significance: Regarded as the most moving and least schematic of the early nineteenth-century comedies of manners, and the fullest period expression of the ideology of constancy in female feeling. Its treatment of age, regret and the second chance opened a line of later realist fiction. The surviving double version of the ending is one of the most studied documents of the period's novel-writing process.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; longer, more suspended periods than the earlier novels, with the quoted verse of the period (a ballad of the constancy theme) embedded in the text.
works.context: Written in the immediate aftermath of Waterloo, when the naval officers who had made fortunes and reputations were entering the landed families by marriage, and the old baronetcy was visibly losing its social monopoly. Its Lyme, Bath and country-seat geography maps the post-war circulation of naval capital. It was published with a companion volume after the author's death, prefaced by a family memoir.
works.characters: Anne Elliot; Captain Frederick Wentworth; Sir Walter Elliot; Elizabeth Elliot; Lady Dalrymple; Mrs. Clay; Admiral Croft; Mrs. Croft; Lady Russell; Mr. Musgrove; Mrs. Musgrove; Louisa Musgrove; Captain Benwick; Captain Harville; Charles Hayter; Mr. Elliott
works.structure: Third-person narration centred on Anne Elliot, with a double movement of stillness and delayed disclosure; reported conversation, overheard speech and a central letter carry the crisis; an abandoned earlier version ('Volume the First') of the same tale survives.
works.attributionNotes: Published posthumously; authorship undisputed.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Sea voyage and seafaring
The marriage market and the limited estate
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Peter Bell. A Lyrical Ballad
works.form: Verse burlesque and parody in the form of the lyrical ballad, written to be read against a well-known original by its own title and measure. As a piece of periodical-school polemics it is nearer to the occasional and satirical verse of the Regency press than to the romantic narrative Reynolds afterwards attempted, and its stanza is borrowed rather than invented.
works.description: A separate burlesque ballad by John Hamilton Reynolds, published in London in 1819 and running through several editions in that year. Reynolds takes up the title and the manner of the Wordsworthian lyrical ballad and turns them against the school they represented, offering a vagrant hero, a homely moral emergency and a mock-solemn narrative voice in the measure that the Lake school had made famous. It belongs to the lively quarrel over Wordsworth's diction carried on by Hunt's circle in the Examiner and the Champion, and it was one of the pieces that gave the young Reynolds a public name before his association with Keats was remembered.
works.plot: The poem follows the external form of its model: a rough and degraded wanderer, Peter Bell, is led through a series of low adventures to the crisis of feeling at which the original affected to reform him. Reynolds keeps the situation and the humble idiom but lets the rhetoric run over, so that the pathetic and the ludicrous occupy the same stanza, and the moral catastrophe is made to appear as the artifact of a method rather than of an experience. The argument of the piece is critical as well as comic: that the tenderness of the school-poetry could be produced at will by its machinery of diction and metre.
works.significance: The piece is the best surviving evidence of Reynolds's own weight in the literary quarrels of 1819, and of the extent to which the lyrical ballad had become a manner that could be worn, mocked and sold. Its bibliographical history, several editions in a single year, shows that parody of the school-poetry was a commercial form as well as a critical one, and its influence on the practice of Hunt's circle can be traced in the verse and criticism of the years that followed.
works.meter: The ballad stanza of the Wordsworthian model, in common measure with simple rhyme, sustained through a short narrative; Reynolds's point is made by exactness of imitation, so that the prosody is deliberately that of the original and the humour arises from its application.
works.context: The poem appeared in 1819, the year in which the contest between the Lake school and its younger critics was at its fiercest, and was one of the parodies that followed hard upon Wordsworth's own Peter Bell, bibliographical evidence suggesting that Reynolds's version was in print at about the same moment as the original. It was issued by Taylor and Hessey, Hunt's and Keats's publishers, and belongs with Reynolds's pieces in the Examiner and the Champion to the campaign of the Cockney press against what it took to be the assumptions of the established poets.
works.characters: Peter Bell, the vagrant hero of the parody
works.structure: A single short ballad narrative in continuous order, with no frame, no digression and no editorial intrusion except the mock-dedicatory manner of its title page. The movement is that of the lyrical ballad it parodies, an humble hero carried by successive episodes to a moment of change, and its unity is one of imitated form rather than of plot.
works.attributionNotes: There is no doubt of authorship; the poem is entered in the standard bibliographies of Romantic poetry under John Hamilton Reynolds's name and is recorded in library catalogues as a parody of Wordsworth. It must be distinguished from the poem of the same title which it imitates, and the repetition of the title in the book-catalogues of 1819 has occasionally confused the two.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Peter Ibbetson
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1891
works.description: Published in 1891 and du Maurier's strange, haunting first novel: a man in prison dreams his way into a shared world with the woman he has loved since childhood. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by George du Maurier; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Peter Ibbetson, an architect imprisoned for murder, discovers that he can enter the dreams of the Duchess of Towers, his childhood love, and that in the dream world the two of them can live an entire life together, until the dream becomes more real than the prison and death becomes the final reunion.
works.significance: Peter Ibbetson is the most original English novel of the 1890s and the founding text of the modern dream-romance: its invention of a shared dream-world made it a source for the twentieth-century fantastic novel, and its combination of Victorian sentiment and oneiric invention has never been imitated successfully.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is direct, confiding narration with comic digression.
works.context: 1891: the Society for Psychical Research and the new study of dreams, the Victorian interest in telepathy, and the aesthetic cult of the childhood romance. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under sensation novel; early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
works.characters: Peter Ibbetson; the Duchess of Towers; Mr Ibbetson; Mrs Ibbetson; Colonel Ibbetson; Griffiths; Mrs Glynne
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation
themes: Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
