works.title: Peter Pan; or, The Boy Who Would Not Grow Up
works.description: First performed in 1904 and the most influential children's myth of the modern world: the boy who flies to Never Land and refuses to grow up. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: Peter Pan returns to the nursery of the Darling family to find his shadow, takes Wendy and her brothers to Never Land to be his mother, and leads the Lost Boys against Captain Hook and his pirates; Wendy eventually returns home and grows up, while Peter remains a child for ever.
works.significance: Peter Pan is the central children's myth of the twentieth century: the play gave the language a permanent character, it made the 'shadow' and the 'second star to the right' part of the common imagination, and its treatment of childhood, motherhood and loss made it one of the most discussed texts in children's literature. Its royalties endowed Great Ormond Street Hospital.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect.
works.context: 1904: the London stage of the Edwardian period, the cult of childhood, the Boer War in the background, and the theatre of the spectacular transformation scene. The record dates the work as composed in 1904 and first published in 1904 and first performed in 1904 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Peter Pan; Wendy Darling; John and Michael Darling; Mr and Mrs Darling; Nana; Tinker Bell; Captain Hook; Smee; Tiger Lily; the Lost Boys
works.structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Matthew Barrie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Peter the Whaler
works.description: Kingston's first great success: a boy shanghaied to the Arctic and the Greenland whaling fleet. It is a prose fiction work of 1851 by W. H. G. Kingston; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Peter Lefroy, a clergyman's son, is kidnapped and sent to sea in a whaler, survives the ice and the mutiny of the crew, is rescued by a Greenland ship and returns to England a man.
works.significance: Peter the Whaler was Kingston's first great success and the book that made the Arctic whale fishery a subject for boys' fiction: its ice, its storms and its brutal shipboard life gave the sea story its documentary authority.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the voyage as the organising structure.
works.context: The Arctic whaling fleet of the 1840s and the Greenland and Davis Strait fisheries. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1851 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Peter Lefroy; Captain Soper; the harpooner; the mutineers
works.structure: A first-person narrative in three parts, from the English parsonage to the Arctic. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Giles Kingston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as minor canon.

works.title: Phantasmagoria and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1869 and Carroll's first collection of verse, including the title poem 'Phantasmagoria' — a comic dialogue between a ghost and the man he haunts — and 'The Sea-Bathing' and 'A Sea Dirge'.
works.plot: 'Phantasmagoria' stages a conversation between a spectre and an unimpressed householder about the rules of haunting, the etiquette of ghosts and the tedium of the profession; the shorter poems move between parody, sentiment and logical joke.
works.significance: Phantasmagoria is the best comic ghost poem in English and shows Carroll's method at its most characteristic: the application of strict logic to an impossible premise.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is logical paradox, pun and wordplay.
works.context: The 1860s, the Victorian vogue for spiritualism and the ghost story, and the Punch tradition of comic verse. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule

works.title: Phantastes: A Faerie Romance for Men and Women
works.description: Published in 1858 and the founding work of modern fantasy: the dream-journey of Anodos through a fairy land, in search of the ideal of beauty and of his own shadow. It is a prose fiction work of 1858 by George MacDonald; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Anodos, a young man, wakes to find a fairy land in his bedroom and wanders through it, meeting the marble lady, the evil ash-tree, the knight Percivale, and his own shadow; he is destroyed by the shadow and reborn, learning that the ideal he sought was to be found in the ordinary world.
works.significance: Phantastes is the founding text of modern fantasy: it gave the genre its dream-journey structure, its symbolic landscape and its theology of the imagination, and it was the book that converted C. S. Lewis's imagination. It is also a central text of the Victorian revival of the fairy tale for adults.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting.
works.context: The 1850s, German Romanticism, the fairy painting of the Pre-Raphaelites, and the Victorian interest in dreams and the imagination. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: Anodos; the marble lady; Percivale; Cosmo von Wehrstahl; the ash-tree; the shadow
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Macdonald. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Pharaoh
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative fragment in alliterative verse
works.description: An eight-line fragment on the drowning of Pharaoh's host in the Red Sea, dramatizing the moment when the returning waters destroy the pursuing Egyptians. Probably a fragment of a longer Exodus poem or a brief independent composition.
works.plot: Pharaoh's army, pursuing the Israelites across the sea-bed, is engulfed when the waters return; the poem emphasizes the totality of the destruction and the might of the God who saved his people.
works.significance: A witness to the popularity of the Exodus story in Old English verse beyond the Junius manuscript, and to the heroic idiom's capacity to render scriptural battle scenes.
works.meter: Eight alliterative long lines of heroic density; the diction of battle and the sea is that of the heroic tradition applied to scriptural warfare.
works.context: The Exodus was the type of baptism and of the Church's deliverance throughout Anglo-Saxon literature, most elaborately in the Junius manuscript Exodus.
works.characters: Pharaoh
works.structure: A single dramatic scene in eight lines, culminating in the overwhelming of the Egyptian host.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The fragment's relationship to the Junius Exodus is uncertain.
themes: Typology and biblical interpretation
Warfare and battle
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

works.title: Philaster
works.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragicomedy of the rightful heir: Philaster, prince of Sicily displaced by the usurper, loves the usurper's daughter Arethusa; his page Bellario (really the girl Euphrasia in disguise) is accused of adultery with her; and the play moves through the forest scenes, the attempted murders, and the double wounding to the final scene, where the king's lust is exposed, the lovers reconciled, and the kingdom restored to its prince.
works.plot: Arethusa is betrothed to the boorish Pharamond but loves Philaster; the page Bellario's devotion and the court's slanders complicate the love; the hunting scene's wounds — Philaster stabbing Arethusa and himself — lead to the trial; the king's attempt on Bellario reveals Euphrasia's disguise; and the final act restores all, with the rebellious citizens of Sicily as the deus ex machina of justice.
works.significance: The play that founded the Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy — the mode that would rule the English stage for the next fifty years.
works.meter: The supple Beaumont–Fletcher blank verse — run-on, conversational, and swift — that set the style of the Caroline stage.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1609–10 and printed in 1620; its popularity (it was the company's signature new play) made the partnership's name and the tragicomic genre's fortune.
works.characters: Philaster; Arethusa; Bellario (Euphrasia); the King of Sicily; Pharamond; Megra; Dion; Cleremont; Thrasiline; the citizens
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy in the new Fletcherian mode — suffering, apparent death, and restoration — with the page's disguise and the citizens' rising as its hinges.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is broadly agreed though not certain.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Women, chastity, and constancy

works.title: Philip Sparrow
works.description: A mock-elegy of some 1,400 Skeltonic lines in which Jane Scrope, a young gentlewoman of the household at Carrow Abbey, laments her pet sparrow Philip, killed by the cat Gib — the lament swelling into a virtuoso parody of the Latin Office of the Dead, with a commendation of Jane and a digressive defense of women.
works.plot: Jane Scrope mourns her sparrow; the poem moves from tender elegy through liturgical parody (Placebo, Dirige) to the praise of Jane's beauty and virtue, ending with an envoy sending the book to her.
works.significance: The classic of the English mock-elegy and a touchstone of Skelton's art; its play with the liturgy and its defense of women made it one of the most read poems of the century.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most supple: short lines of two or three stresses, tumbling rhymes, and Latin tags woven into English.
works.context: Written for the household of Sir Philip Calthorpe's widow at Carrow; the text's allusions to Jane Scrope's family place it about 1505.
works.characters: Jane Scrope; Philip (the sparrow); Gib (the cat)
works.structure: A single-voiced lament that repeatedly breaks its frame: elegy, liturgical parody, blazon, and envoy succeed one another by association.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Philobiblon
works.description: Richard de Bury's treatise in praise of books and of the love of learning, completed on his birthday, 24 January 1345 (i.e., 1344 by modern reckoning), while he was bishop of Durham; the work draws on his experience assembling one of the great private libraries of medieval England.
works.summary: In twenty chapters the Philobiblon celebrates the wisdom preserved in books, argues that they should be shared with scholars rather than hoarded, defends the clergy against the charge of neglecting their books, and prescribes the care, repair, and circulation of manuscripts; it closes with provisions for the dispersal of the author's own library to the scholars of Oxford.
works.significance: The most famous medieval book about books, a primary witness to the book culture of fourteenth-century England, and a key document for the history of libraries and of Oxford scholarship.
themes: Wisdom and learning

works.title: Phineas Finn, the Irish Member
works.form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers); two volumes 1869 (Palliser, 2)
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts in 1867-69: the first of the political novels of the Palliser series, and the first full English novel of the working of Parliament seen from the back benches. It is a prose fiction work of 1869 by Anthony Trollope; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Serial and Monthly-Part Novel.
works.plot: Phineas Finn, an Irish barrister's son without money or connections, enters Parliament for an Irish borough and rises through two ministries; he is tried for the murder of a political rival and acquitted, and the novel follows his courtship of three women — the rich and sensible Madame Goesler, the aristocratic Laura Standish, and the Irish Mary Flood Jones.
works.significance: Phineas Finn is the founding novel of parliamentary life in English and the best account in fiction of how a Victorian political career was actually made. Its Irish hero makes it a central text for the study of the Union, and the figure of Madame Goesler is among Trollope's finest portraits of the independent woman.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The Reform Bill of 1867 and the parliamentary session of the 1860s, the Irish question, the party whips and the lobby, and the expense of standing for Parliament. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; serial and monthly-part novel.
works.characters: Phineas Finn; Madame Max Goesler; Laura Standish; Mr Kennedy; Violet Effingham; Lord Chiltern; Mary Flood Jones; Mr Monk; Lord Cantrip; the Duke of Omnium; Barrington Erle; Mr Daubeny
works.structure: The work is in 20 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Physics and Politics; or, Thoughts on the Application of the Principles of 'Natural Selection' and 'Inheritance' to Political Society
works.description: Published in 1872 and first given as essays in the Fortnightly Review: the founding English work of social evolutionism, and an early attempt to apply Darwinian theory to the development of nations and to the question of why some societies progress and others do not.
works.plot: Bagehot argues that progress depends on the 'cake of custom' being broken by a 'preliminary age of discussion', that the 'nation-making' period precedes the 'nation-keeping' one, and that the 'verifiable progress' of modern societies depends on the spread of the 'discussion' that only free institutions permit.
works.significance: Physics and Politics founded the evolutionary study of politics and introduced the idea of the 'age of discussion' as the mechanism of progress; it is a key text for the history of social Darwinism and for the modern critique of the Victorian idea of progress, and it influenced the sociology of Spencer, Maine and the American social scientists.

works.title: Physiological Aesthetics
works.form: Treatise; review essay, first issued in 1877
works.description: Published in 1877 and Allen's first book and the founding English work of scientific aesthetics: an attempt to explain the experience of beauty in physiological terms. It is a prose work of 1877 by Grant Allen; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Allen argues that the pleasure of beauty is the pleasure of an easy and healthy exercise of the nervous system: that the beautiful is what the eye and the brain can take in without strain, and that the arts must therefore be understood as the deliberate production of that physiological state.
works.significance: Physiological Aesthetics is the founding work of evolutionary aesthetics in English and one of the first scientific accounts of aesthetic experience: it anticipated the modern psychology of art by a century, it influenced Vernon Lee and the whole tradition of physiological criticism, and it is a landmark of Victorian scientific thought.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
works.context: 1877: the new physiology of Helmholtz and Grant Allen's own science teaching, the aesthetics of Ruskin and Pater, and the Victorian attempt to found a science of the mind. works.title: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil
works.description: Nashe's first great pamphlet: Pierce Penniless, a scholar out of money and patience, writes his supplication to the devil, anatomizing the seven deadly sins as the diseases of London — greed, drunkenness, pride, and the rest — with the famous digression on the 'upstart' playwrights and the defence of poetry, in the fastest prose of the decade.
works.plot: Pierce, penniless, petitions the devil through the knight of the post; his catalogue of sins prosecutes each vice with its London specimens — the usurer, the drunkard, the proud courtier — and the digressions on players and poets mount the first defence of the professional writer's trade.
works.significance: The great satirical pamphlet of the 1590s — the prose in which the Elizabethan town found its voice and its conscience.
works.meter: Prose of furious energy — colloquial, learned, and comic by turns — with the famous passage on the theatre's power.
works.context: Published 1592 in the plague year; its satire of the sins and its praise of the stage (the passage on Talbot in Henry VI) made it the talk of London and fixed Nashe's reputation.
works.characters: Pierce Penniless; the Devil; the Knight of the Post; the personified sins; the poet and the player (in the digression)
works.structure: A mock-oration in the complaint tradition — the supplication as satirical frame — with the sin-catalogue and the digressions as its bravura set pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.form: allegorical dream vision in alliterative verse
works.description: William Langland's visionary masterpiece, surviving in three authorial versions (the A-text c. 1367–70, B-text c. 1377–79, C-text c. 1386–88): a sequence of ten dream visions in which the dreamer Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the estates of fourteenth-century England — the fair field full of folk, the pilgrimage of the seven deadly sins, the Tree of Charity, and the harrowing of hell. The greatest English poem of social and spiritual reform.
works.plot: Will falls asleep on the Malvern Hills and sees a field full of folk between the Tower of Truth and the Dungeon of Wrong; the quest for St Truth becomes the ploughing of the half-acre under Piers the Plowman; the later visions pursue Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the confession of the sins, the feast of Patience, the Tree of Charity, the Passion and harrowing of hell, and the founding of Holy Church, which the final vision shows besieged from within by Antichrist and the friars.
works.significance: With the Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain, one of the three summits of Ricardian literature: its blend of estates satire, theological vision, and vernacular prophecy made it the rallying text of reform for two centuries, from the rebels of 1381 to the Tudor reformers who printed it.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, ranging from colloquial satire to liturgical sublimity.
works.context: Composed and revised c. 1367–88, probably in London, against the background of plague, labour legislation, the Peasants' Revolt (1381), and Wycliffite controversy — all refracted in the poem's satire; preserved in over fifty manuscripts, more than any English poem except the Prick of Conscience.
works.characters: Will (the dreamer); Piers the Plowman; Holy Church; Lady Meed; Conscience; Patience; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Samaritan; Christ; Antichrist
works.structure: A series of ten (or eight) dream visions within dreams, progressing from social satire through theological allegory to apocalyptic vision, with Will's own spiritual biography as the connective thread; the B-text adds the great inner dreams of the C-text's revisions.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to William Langland by manuscript evidence and internal acrostic signatures; the three texts represent the author's own revisions.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Ricardian Poetry

works.title: Piers the Plowman's Creed
works.description: A Lollard-leaning alliterative satire of some 850 lines in imitation of Piers Plowman: a simple man, seeking to learn his creed, questions the four orders of friars in turn and finds only greed, sophistry, and pride — until the ploughman Piers teaches him the creed in the plain words of charity and labour. The fiercest of the Piers Plowman imitations.
works.plot: The narrator, who cannot say his creed, applies to the friars; each order's answer is a satiric portrait — their fine houses, their begging, their hatred of the ploughman's tithes — until Piers and his family, labouring in poverty, recite the creed and denounce the friars with apocalyptic anger.
works.significance: The most important literary offspring of Piers Plowman and the principal verse monument of Lollard satire; its Tudor printing made 'Piers Plowman' a name for English reform.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line with rhyme incorporated in places.
works.context: Composed c. 1395 in the orbit of the Lollard movement, satirizing the friars' wealth in the spirit of FitzRalph and Wyclif; preserved in BL Royal MS 18 B.xvii and printed by the Tudor reformers (1553).
works.characters: the narrator; the four friars; Piers the Plowman; his wife and children
works.structure: A quest-satire in the Piers tradition: four failed consultations with the friars, resolved by the ploughman's plain teaching.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; formerly attributed to the author of the Plowman's Tale.

works.title: Pigeon Post
works.description: The drought summer of 1934: the mine on the fell, the pigeon post and the moor fire. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Arthur Ransome; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The drought of 1934 empties the lake and turns the children to the old mine on the fell, where the search for gold, the pigeon post between the camps and the great moor fire at the close carry the summer's campaign; the book won the first Carnegie Medal.
works.significance: Pigeon Post won the first Carnegie Medal and is the series' most plotted book: its mine, its pigeon post and its moor fire carried the children's republic from the water to the fell and proved the adventure novel of competence at its height.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact, practical prose of the sailor.
works.context: The Lake District fells in the drought summer of 1934. The record dates the work as composed between 1935 and 1936 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: Pillars of the House
works.description: Published in 1873 and Yonge's longest and most ambitious family chronicle: the thirteen Underwood children left poor by their father's death. It is a prose fiction work of 1873 by Charlotte M. Yonge; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The Underwood family is left in genteel poverty when their father dies, and the novel follows the thirteen children over twenty years as they make their way through school, the church, the army, medicine and marriage, with the eldest son Felix, who gives up his hopes of Oxford to work in a bookseller's shop, and the lame artist Geraldine at the centre of the household.
works.significance: Pillars of the House is the fullest expression of Yonge's ideal of the Christian family and her largest single work of social portraiture: it is the Victorian chronicle novel at its most comprehensive and the best introduction to the 'Dynasty' that occupied her for half a century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the large family chronicle with an enormous cast.

works.title: Pindarique Odes
works.description: The odes in Cowley's Poems (1656) that established the loose, irregular 'Pindaric' form in English — ambitious, varied-line odes on great subjects, including 'The Muse', 'To Mr Hobs' (Thomas Hobbes), and 'The Plagues of Egypt' — which became a major vehicle for Restoration and Augustan poetry.
works.plot: The odes treat poetry and its critics, philosophy, biblical and heroic subjects, and public occasions in an elevated, digressive manner, claiming the liberty of Pindaric inspiration.
works.significance: Cowley's odes created the English Pindaric, used by Dryden ('Alexander's Feast'), Congreve, and the eighteenth-century ode-writers, and important in the history of the ode.
works.meter: Irregular line lengths and stanzas, giving the effect of inspired freedom — the 'Pindaric' that Dryden and others adopted.
works.context: Published in Poems (1656); Cowley mistook Pindar's regular triadic form for inspired irregularity, but his 'Pindaric' became a fashionable English form for grand subjects.
works.structure: A group of irregular odes with varied line lengths and stanza forms, loosely modeled on (a mistaken idea of) Pindar's structure.

works.title: Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury
works.form: Prose sketches with verse; tall tale
works.description: Published in 1889 and Riley's prose masterpiece: sketches of the Indiana town of Zekesbury and its characters. It is a prose fiction work of 1889 by James Whitcomb Riley; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The sketches present the inhabitants of a small Indiana town — the old soldier, the village doctor, the travelling salesman, the revivalist, the boy and the schoolteacher — in dialect narratives that are comic, affectionate and occasionally bitter, and that record a whole community.
works.significance: Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury is the finest American small-town sketchbook after Twain: its portraits and its dialect made it a landmark of the local-colour movement, and it is the book in which Riley's prose and his poetry are most completely united.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the tall tale: the frame of the literate narrator and the vernacular teller, the dialect spelling, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan, and the punch that turns on the outsider's credulity. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse with exact phonetic spelling.

works.title: Pippa Passes
works.form: Verse drama (dramatic poem with four episodes)
works.description: The first of the Bells and Pomegranates pamphlets, published in 1841: a dramatic poem in four episodes, in which the silk-winder Pippa's songs, overheard by the people of Asolo, change the course of their lives.
works.plot: Pippa, a poor girl of Asolo, is given one holiday a year; her innocent songs, sung as she passes, wake remorse in the adulterous murderers Ottima and Sebald, save the sculptor Jules's marriage to the girl he was tricked into wedding, send the young patriot Luigi to his mission, and move the Monsignor to foil a plot to sell Pippa herself into prostitution. The four episodes follow her through one New Year's Day, from morning to night.
works.significance: Pippa Passes is the most lyrical of Browning's early works and the one in which his faith in the power of art and undesigning goodness is stated most directly; 'The year's at the spring' became one of the best-known Victorian lyrics, and the structure of overheard song influencing action is a technical invention of lasting interest.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The 1840s and the Victorian idealisation of the pure redeeming woman; the Italian town of Asolo; and the pamphlet form of Bells and Pomegranates, sold cheaply to reach a new public. works.title: Plain Tales from the Hills
works.form: Collection of forty stories; local-colour sketch
works.description: Published in Calcutta in 1888 and Kipling's first collection of prose: forty short stories of Anglo-Indian life, written for the Civil and Military Gazette and the Pioneer, which made him famous at twenty-two.
works.plot: The stories move through the stations and hill towns of British India — Simla, Lahore, Dalhousie — and record the marriages, adulteries, careers and disasters of the English, told in a hard, laconic voice and with an unerring sense of the small incident that reveals a life.

works.title: Plato and Platonism: A Series of Lectures
works.description: Published in 1893 and Pater's last book: a series of Oxford lectures on Plato, the Platonic doctrine of ideas and the relation of Greek philosophy to the aesthetic life. works.description: Cavendish's collection of dramatic works, written in exile and never performed, including comedies, tragicomedies, and closet plays that experiment with genre and defend female authorship.

works.title: Plum Bun: A Novel Without a Moral
works.description: Fauset's finest novel: a Black woman passes for white to become a painter. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Jessie Redmon Fauset; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Angela Murray, a talented Black girl from Philadelphia, comes to New York, passes for white to study art in Paris, and returns to Harlem to choose her own life and her own man, in a novel with no moral but the truth of a woman's ambition.
works.significance: Plum Bun is Fauset's finest novel and one of the great Black American novels of the period: its subtitle, 'A Novel Without a Moral', made it the most modern of the Harlem Renaissance novels, and its portrait of a Black woman artist made the case for the Black woman's ambition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of the Black middle class.
works.context: New York, Paris and Harlem in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Angela Murray; Virginia Murray; Jinny; Roger Fielding; Anthony Cross; Miss Powell
works.structure: A novel in five parts, from Philadelphia to Paris and Harlem. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
altTitles: The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
works.description: Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, made from Jacques Amyot's French (1559): the paired biographies of the Greek and Roman great — Theseus and Romulus, Alexander and Caesar, Coriolanus and Alcibiades, Antony and Demetrius, and the rest — in the full, energetic English prose that became Shakespeare's quarry for Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
works.plot: Each pair of lives narrates its heroes' births, deeds, and deaths with the parallel moral comparisons; the collection as a whole is a gallery of virtue and vice in action — the school of statesmen and the storehouse of tragedy.
works.significance: The most consequential translation of the English Renaissance — the book through which Plutarch's heroes became Shakespeare's Romans.
works.meter: Prose of dramatic vividness and copiousness — Shakespeare followed its phrasing so closely that whole speeches of the Roman plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
works.context: Published 1579, in the decade of the English Plutarch vogue; it went through editions in 1595, 1603, and beyond, and was the most-read secular book of the Elizabethan age after the chronicles.
works.characters: Theseus; Romulus; Alexander; Julius Caesar; Coriolanus; Alcibiades; Mark Antony; Demetrius; the Greek and Roman worthies
works.structure: The paired lives in the Amyot order, with the comparisons of the pairs and North's dedication to Queen Elizabeth.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by North from Amyot's French; uncontested.

works.title: Poema Morale
works.description: A sermon in verse of some 400 lines on the conduct of life and the last things, often called the earliest Middle English poem of any consequence: the aged speaker meditates on a misspent youth, the brevity of life, and the terrors and joys of judgement, urging repentance before death.
works.plot: The speaker reviews the stages of life, the certainty of death and judgement, the pains of hell and the bliss of heaven, and counsels amendment of life while time remains.
works.significance: A touchstone of early Middle English: its popularity (seven manuscripts) and its homiletic style anticipate the great penitential literature of the thirteenth century.
works.meter: The loose fourteener (septenarius) couplet of the earliest Middle English homiletic verse.
works.context: Composed in the south of England c. 1170, in the Kentish or south-western dialect; preserved in seven manuscripts, the earliest in the Lambeth and Trinity homily collections of c. 1200.
works.characters: the aged speaker
works.structure: A monologic homily moving from personal confession through doctrinal exposition (death, judgement, heaven, hell) to exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's self-description as old is a homiletic persona.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Poems
works.form: Poetry collection, including The House of Life
works.description: Published in 1870 after the exhumation of the manuscript buried with Elizabeth Siddal in 1869: the collection that made Rossetti famous and provoked Robert Buchanan's attack on the 'Fleshly School of Poetry' in the Contemporary Review in October 1871.

works.significance: Poems of 1870 is the central volume of English aesthetic poetry and the work that made 'the fleshly school' a public controversy; The House of Life is the major English sonnet sequence of the century after Barrett Browning's, and Buchanan's attack became the defining document in the Victorian debate about the autonomy of art.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound.

works.title: Poems (1827)
works.form: Collected edition of Romantic-era verse: an Augustan-descended body of didactic and topographical poetry in closed couplets, framed as a single-author 'Poems' volume of the kind that defined a poet's public standing.
works.description: The first collected edition of the shorter and longer verse of a poet who had hitherto been known almost only through separately issued volumes. It gathers 'Human Life' and 'Italy' with the occasional and lyrical pieces that had appeared in magazines and in the gift-book market, and it presented the author for the first time as a complete rather than a fragmentary poet. The two-volume format, the wide margins and the print quality were designed for the drawing-room library rather than the study.
works.plot: The collection opens with the meditative poems on ordinary life and on Italy, whose arguments are reflective rather than narrative, and closes with lyrical pieces, ballads and translations. Its overall movement is from moral reflection on daily domestic experience to topographical and historical meditation, and finally to short occasional lyrics. Because most of the contents had appeared separately, the volume's real argument is editorial: it asserts that a small, reticent and severely revised body of verse can constitute a complete poetical reputation. The grouping also makes visible the poet's habit of intercalating songs and ballad-measure lyrics inside longer reflective structures.
works.significance: The collection consolidated a reputation that contemporaries rated close to the first rank of Romantic verse and that later Victorian readers kept alive through school and gift-book anthologies. It preserves the model of the deliberately small, elaborately revised volume that other second-generation Romantics found enviable, and it gave 'Italy' and 'Human Life' the fixed shape in which they were read for the rest of the century. Its afterlife in school extracts and keepsake reprints makes it a useful document of Victorian canon formation.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in the longer poems; interspersed songs, ballad stanzas and light lyrical measures among the shorter pieces.
works.context: Published in the later 1820s, when the quarterly reviews were arbitrating Romantic reputations and when collected editions were a recognised form of canon-making. The volume appeared in the same period as the illustrated editions of the Italian poem, which used engravers' work derived from a famous painter's drawings to reach a gift-book audience. Its polite, revisionist classicism ran counter to the growing prestige of Wordsworthian and Byronic models, and the poet's own dinner-table was a centre of the London literary world that the book's reputation depended upon.
works.structure: A two-volume collected edition ordered by scale and kind: the longer meditative and topographical poems first, then miscellaneous lyrics, ballads and translations. There is no frame narrative; unity is that of a single revised voice.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Poems (1832)
works.description: The 1832 volume (dated 1833) containing 'The Lady of Shalott', 'The Palace of Art', 'Oenone', 'The Lotos-Eaters' and 'A Dream of Fair Women' — the volume attacked by John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review in 1833, and the one whose ten years of revision produced the 1842 Poems.
works.plot: The poems are symbolic narratives: the Lady of Shalott weaves a mirror-image of the world until the curse falls on her; the Palace of Art is a soul's self-built retreat which decays; the Lotos-Eaters turn Homeric episode into a moral argument for withdrawal and oblivion; Oenone speaks the wrongs of Helen from the mountain.
works.significance: This is the volume that gave the Victorian age its central myths: the enclosed lady, the palace of art and the island of the lotos-eaters became permanent figures for the artist's relation to the world, and the 1832 text's 'obscurity' became the test case for the Victorian debate about difficulty in poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.
works.context: The 1830s, the Quarterly Review's hostility to the 'Cockney' school and to Tennyson as an example of poetic obscurity, and the deaths that darkened the decade (Hallam in 1833, Tennyson's brother Charles's family troubles).
works.characters: the Lady of Shalott; Sir Lancelot; Oenone and Paris; the soul of 'The Palace of Art'; the Lotos-eaters, Ulysses' mariners; the Miller's Daughter; the May Queen; Fair Rosamond, Cleopatra and Iphigenia (in 'A Dream of Fair Women')
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Poems (1833)
works.form: Romantic Sonnet Revival; Nature Lyric and Meditation
works.description: The only collected volume of verse published in its author's lifetime, a small octavo of sonnets, lyrics, and narrative pieces gathered from fifteen years of magazine and anonymous contribution. Its most prominent number is a metrical tale of Dutch settler life reprinted from a leading Scottish periodical, and the sonnet group gives the volume its weight. The book is the monument of a Lakeland poet who never took orders, never held a profession, and published little of what he wrote.
works.plot: The sonnets move between the poet's own housekeeping and solitude, the portraits of neighbours and of the dead, and meditations on time, mortality, and the surviving mind; several are written on the condition of a single man in a family neighbourhood and on the loss of early affection. The longer narrative piece tells of a settler family in a Dutch colony, of a betrothed girl, of the voyage and the wreck, and of a love that outlives misfortune, and it was the poem that had already made its way in print. Smaller lyrics and imitations supply the volume's variety, and its tone throughout is retrospective, moral, and quietly despondent.
works.significance: The book preserves the sonnet practice of the second generation of the Lake school and is the sole public record of a poet whose reputation has rested since on fragments and on his family position. Its narrative tale is one of the period's verse colonial subjects, and its sonnets on solitude and dependence supply the evidence for the poet's later elevation among readers of the minor Romantic verse.
works.meter: Sonnets of the legitimate school in iambic pentameter with a Latinate and compressed diction derived from the older divines and essayists, and a metrical tale in a plain rhymed narrative stanza; the lyrics use common measure and the epigrammatic closing line.
works.context: Published in 1833 by a contributor long identified with a Lakeland household and with the magazines of the previous generation, after his removal from a college fellowship and his years of provincial schoolteaching and clerical work had left his manuscript verse almost unpublished; several numbers had appeared in the Edinburgh and London periodicals of the 1820s. The volume belongs to the late phase of the Lake circle rather than to the annual market.
works.characters: the speaker of the sonnets, a solitary man among neighbours; the lovers of the colonial tale; the wrecked and absent betrothed
works.structure: A collection arranged with the sonnet group and the longer narrative tale given prominence; no frame unites the volume, and the order follows the convention of the lifetime selection rather than a design.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the volume was published with the author's initials and name and contains pieces of several dates, some first printed in magazines.

works.description: Published in 1895 and the finest single volume of the Rhymers' Club poets: the lyrics of faith, sin and the English literary past. works.title: Poems (Bryant)
works.form: Lyric and meditative collection; the first American volume of the nature lyric
works.description: The author's first collected volume, the book that made the American nature lyric a publishable career. It gathers the meditative blank-verse pieces, the shorter lyrics of natural observation and the juvenile political and classical verse. Its appearance with a British reprint in the same year marked the moment at which American poetry was accepted for import.
works.plot: The volume collects the long meditation on death and the shorter lyrics addressed to a waterfowl, to a flower and to the fragments of the moralist's table. It includes translations and paraphrases from the classics and from Hebrew, a couplet satire, and the inscriptional verse written for a woodland walk. Its organizing principle is the alternation of large blank-verse meditation with small stanzaed observation. The effect is to present a single mind, retired from business, conversing with nature in the country it inhabits.
works.significance: It established the American poetry of nature as an institution and gave the lyric meditation on death and the landscape its canonical form. Its reception in the British review shaped the transatlantic terms of the argument for a national literature. It remained the reference point for later American meditative verse.
works.meter: Blank verse for the longer meditations; iambic tetrameter and trimeter stanzas for the shorter lyrics; heroic couplets for the political pieces
works.context: Published at New York in 1821 after the poems had circulated in review and newspaper, and reissued in London in the same year, a rare transatlantic honour. Its appearance coincided with the first confident claims for a national literature after the peace of 1815. The volume's blank verse made its claim on the authority of Wordsworth and of the British review tradition.
works.structure: Collected volume of separate poems arranged by length and form rather than by sequence; later enlarged editions reorganized the contents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.description: Cowper's first collected volume, published in 1782 after long years of religious depression, retirement at Olney and work on the hymn-book, and the book that established his reputation. It gathers the didactic and meditative essays in verse, the addresses and reflections, the short elegies and the two familiar pieces Conversation and Retirement. The volume announces the temper of all his later work: reliance on providence, the praise of home, and the honesty of an unpatronised writer.
works.plot: The poems argue in turn against the errors of the world and on the claims of hope, moderation and charity, and record the writer's religious experience, his mourning for the dead and his contentment in domestic retirement. works.significance: The volume created Cowper's standing and made the Task possible, and its criticism of fashionable conversation and its praise of rural retirement fixed the themes for which he is read. It is a central text of the culture of feeling and of the religious verse of the Evangelical revival.
works.meter: Heroic couplets heavier and more Latinate than Pope's, together with meditative blank verse of the Thomson school in the two familiar pieces.
works.context: Published in the year that closes Cowper's first period of composition and opens his partnership with the Unwin household, after the Olney hymn project and in a season of revived interest in Thomson. Its appearance belongs to the retail book trade of the 1780s rather than to patronage.

works.title: Poems (Poe)
works.form: Lyric and romance-in-verse collection; the first American example of a poet's self-canonization by revision
works.description: The author's first collected volume of poetry and the most contentious of his early books, printed while he was a cadet at West Point. It gathers the two long poems, revises them heavily, and adds the shorter lyrics that became his permanent repertoire. Its prefatory prose letter denounces the current state of American poetry with a boldness that cost him readers.
works.plot: The volume reprints Tamerlane and Al Aaraaf in shortened and recast form, the latter reduced from a two-part cosmological poem to its descriptive core. It then presents the shorter lyrics: an address to a classical beauty, a lament for the dead, a song of the valley of unrest, a hymn of the intellect and a meditation on a doomed city. The prefatory letter argues that American verse is made by imitators who flatter their public, and that the true critic must be willing to be hated. The book as a whole is a claim to professional standing rather than a miscellany.
works.significance: It fixes the author's poetic canon in its first public form and shows his method of revision at work from the outset. Its prefatory letter is an early American statement of the doctrine of the critic against the public. The volume is the source of the lyrics, including the address to Helen and the city of the sinking towers, that later critics treated as his characteristic mode.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter and mixed lyric stanzas, with a marked experiment in long-line melody
works.context: Published at New York in 1831 and subscribed for by a small circle, while its author was an artillery cadet; the volume's attack on living reviewers provoked a newspaper response. It belongs to the period in which American poets were negotiating the terms of a professional literary career. Its revision of the earlier poems reflects the working practice of a writer who reissued his verse throughout his life.
works.structure: Collected volume with a prose letter at the head, followed by two revised long poems and a group of shorter lyrics arranged without a stated principle.

works.title: Poems (Sigourney)
altTitles: Poems; by the Author of Moral Pieces in Prose and Verse
works.form: Lyric and elegiac collection in the sentimental and meditative tradition; occasional and devotional verse
works.description: The first collected volume by the Hartford poet, issued without her name, and the book that made her the most widely read woman poet in America before the war. Its pieces take the occasions of mourning, the domestic round and the moral reflection of a Calvinist-minded but emotionally liberal piety. The volume established the native feminine verse of the annual and the gift-book.
works.plot: The poems move through elegy on the dead, meditation on bereavement and the consolations of nature, moral reflections on female duties and on the trials of life, and descriptive pieces on American and Italian scenery. Several poems address the deaths of children and of friends, and others treat poverty, old age and the obligations of the survivor. The volume's argument is that feeling rightly disciplined is a form of knowledge. Its closing pieces turn from private mourning to public and religious duty.
works.significance: It founded the American tradition of feminine occasional and elegiac verse, and its poems became the standard copy for the mourning and gift-book market. It shows the economics of anonymous women's publishing at the moment of its success. Its range of moral and domestic topics defines the feminine voice in American letters before 1850.
works.meter: Iambic stanzas of common and church metre, with longer meditative passages in pentameter
works.context: Published at Boston and Hartford in 1827, and issued anonymously in a season when women's authorship was commonly disguised. Its success was secured by the review press and by the new monthlies and annuals that needed poetry. Its religious manner belongs to the post-Calvinist piety of Connecticut and western Massachusetts.
works.structure: Collected volume arranged by class of subject, with elegy, meditation and descriptive poem as the organizing forms; no narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Issued anonymously; the author's identity was established within a few years and her name was prefixed to later editions, which were enlarged and reorganized.
themes: Consolation and endurance

works.title: Poems (Tuckerman, 1860)
works.description: The great neglected American sonnet sequence: the New England woods, the dead wife and the sorrow of the survivor. It is a verse work of 1860 by Frederick Goddard Tuckerman; it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The collection gathers Tuckerman's sonnets on the woods of Greenfield and the death of his wife, together with the lyrics 'The Cricket', 'The Stranger' and the long 'Sonnets, First Series' in a poetry of minute observation and unconsoled grief.
works.significance: Tuckerman's Poems is the finest American sonnet sequence of the nineteenth century and one of the great neglected books of American literature: rediscovered in the twentieth century, it is now recognised as a central text of American formal poetry and a major influence on Frost.

works.title: Poems and Ballads

works.title: Poems and Letters of Harriet Wilson
works.description: Scattered poems, letters and religious verses composed from the 1850s onward and recovered by modern scholarship: the small surviving body of Wilson's occasional writing. It is a verse work of 1850 by Harriet E. Wilson; it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: The poems are hymns and religious verses of consolation and reproach; the letters describe her work as a seamstress, her health and her appeals for patronage, and they are the only record of her life after the publication of Our Nig.

works.title: Poems before Congress

works.description: The finest English dialect poetry of the century: the Dorset farm in its own speech. It is a verse work of 1844 by William Barnes; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Barnes's Dorset eclogues — 'The Rustic's Talk', 'A Zong of the Harvest', 'The Maiden's Praise', 'The Shepherd's Wife' — in which the farm, the village and the seasons are rendered in the complete grammar of the Dorset dialect.
works.significance: Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect is the finest English dialect poetry of the century: it recorded the Dorset farm in its own complete grammar, made Barnes a model for Hardy, and remains the fullest literary record of the English rural vernacular.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The spelling and syntax carry a spoken dialect. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Dorset dialect in its full grammar.
works.context: Dorset in the 1830s and 1840s, and the rural world before the railway and the enclosure. The record dates the work as composed between 1840 and 1844 and first published in 1844 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: the Dorset farmer; the shepherd; the wife; the village choir
works.structure: A collection of eclogues and lyrics in the Dorset dialect. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Barnes (poet). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects
works.form: Poetry collection (with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison)
works.description: Published in 1854 with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison and the first book by an African-American woman poet: poems of slavery, freedom and Christian duty, written for the antislavery platform. It is a verse work of 1854 by Frances E. W. Harper; it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume contains 'The Slave Mother', 'Eliza Harris', 'The Slave Auction', 'Bury Me in a Free Land', 'A Mother's Heroism' and 'The Prodigal's Return', and its subjects are the sale of families, the fugitive's flight and the duty of the free North.
works.significance: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects is the founding book of African-American women's poetry: 'Bury Me in a Free Land' is one of the great American abolitionist poems, and Harper's recitation of these verses made her one of the most important black voices of the 1850s.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat.
works.context: 1854: the Fugitive Slave Law, the antislavery lecture circuit, and the free black community of the northern states. The record dates the work as composed between 1853 and 1854 and first published in 1854 and it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the slave mother and her child; Eliza Harris crossing the ice; the families of 'The Slave Auction'; the speaker of 'Bury Me in a Free Land'; the prodigal and his father
works.structure: A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Ellen Watkins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Barbauld)
altTitles: The Poems on Several Occasions of Anna Letitia Barbauld
works.form: collected odes, hymns, elegies and familiar verse epistles in the school of feeling
works.description: Anna Laetitia Barbauld's first volume of verse, published in 1773 when she was still Anna Aikin and the book that opened one of the most considerable literary careers of the later century. It contains the early odes, hymns and elegies, the familiar epistles to friends, and the pieces on retirement, on the pleasures of the imagination and on the duties of feeling. Its manner unites the eighteenth-century ode tradition with a new intimacy of domestic and moral observation.
works.plot: The poems argue for a poetry of sensibility and of religious feeling, addressing friendship, solitude, the death of the young and the consolation of the mind in retirement. The epistles cultivate the conversational line of the native school, praising a circle of friends and the pleasures of study and home, while the odes and hymns attempt the higher imaginative forms after the manner of the age. Throughout, the volume claims for women's writing a serious place in the moral and devotional registers.
works.significance: The volume established the voice that later made Barbauld the central writer for children and one of the most formidable critics and pamphleteers of the 1790s. Its handling of sensibility, devotion and friendship makes it a key text of women's writing in the culture of feeling and of the dissenting poetic tradition.
works.meter: The irregular ode and hymn stanzas of the eighteenth-century manner, with smooth heroic couplets and four-beat elegiac measures in the familiar pieces.
works.context: Published in 1773 in the circle of the Newington Green and Worcester nonconformist intelligentsia surrounding her father the Rev. John Aikin and her husband the Rev. John Aikin Barbauld, and in the years when the ode, the hymn and the domestic epistle were the living forms of dissenting and sentimental verse.
works.characters: The friends and correspondents of the epistles; the mourner and the child of the elegies; the personified pleasures and powers of the odes
works.structure: A collected volume of separate poems ordered by class, with the odes and hymns, the elegies and the familiar epistles distributed through the book; later editions were enlarged.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the early volume is entered in the standard bibliographies under her maiden and married names, and the pieces were composed across the years before publication, so the composition range is approximate.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
Women's education and intellectual friendship
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
The Bluestockings and Women's Letters

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Gay)
works.description: Gay's collected poems, gathered by subscription and bringing together Trivia, the Shepherd's Week and the occasional verse, epistles and burlesques of his first years in town.
works.plot: The volume passes from the town's shows and the village week to the verse epistles to his friends, the lyric and the theatrical prologue, without sustained narrative argument.
works.significance: It fixed Gay's public reputation before the Beggar's Opera and shows the full range of the minor Augustan verse, from urban description to the fable and the epistle.
works.meter: Heroic couplet for the didactic and epistolary pieces, and the lyric and mock-Spenserian stanzas for the shorter poems.
works.context: Issued by subscription at the opening of the decade, when the country seat and the patron's list were the means by which a professional poet financed a volume; the subscription itself included the great names of the new architecture and of the court.
works.characters: the poet and his friends; the town and the country of the earlier poems
works.structure: A collected miscellany arranged by piece rather than by design, with the dedication and the advertisements ordering the contents.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the collection reprints pieces first issued separately or in miscellanies, and the ordering is the author's.

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Prior)
works.description: The collected poems of the diplomatist and wit, gathering the tales, the songs, the epistles, the translations and the grave meditations that made him the most imitated familiar verse-writer between the two greater poets who admired and censured him. The collection settled his reputation and his place in the school of English light verse.
works.plot: The volume brings together the narrative tales in the manner of the old romance and of the fabliau, the songs and catch-poems of the club, the familiar epistles to friends and patrons, the paraphrases from the psalms and the translations of the ancients and of the moderns. Its compass runs from the professed gallantry of the love-poems to the moral gravity of the meditative pieces. The arrangement is that of the author's career rather than of a design.
works.significance: It fixed the familiar and narrative style that the following generation learned from it, and the collection's tales and songs are a principal source of the century's idea of the easy verse between Dryden and Pope.
works.meter: The full range of the easy Augustan manner: the flowing couplet of the tale and epistle, the lyric measures of the songs, and the longer stanzas of the meditative poems, all marked by an affectation of negligence that is the poet's most studied art.
works.context: Gathered in the years of the poet's employment and disappointment, in the season of the miscellany and of the collected volume as the instrument of a literary reputation, and before the long dispute between his friends and the next generation of versifiers.
works.characters: the several persons of the tales and epistles; the friends and patrons of the dedications; the lovers and the companions of the songs
works.structure: A collected miscellaneous volume ordered by species - tales, songs, epistles, translations and serious verse - with no overarching plot or argument beyond the range of the manner.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the collected volume carries the author's name, and the several pieces have a separate history in the pamphlets and miscellanies of the preceding years.

Exile and homelessness

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Rochester)
works.description: The collected verse of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester, issued in the year of his death, containing the satires, songs, and obscene verses that made him the most notorious poet of the Restoration court.
works.plot: The volume gathers Rochester's satires on the court and on Charles II ('I dreamt last night, though not designed to do so'), his songs including 'The Disabled Debauchee' and 'To a Lady in a Letter', his versified letters, and the bawdy lampoons.
works.significance: Rochester is now recognised as the most original English poet between Milton and Pope; his combination of Horatian ease with Hobbesian materialism anticipates the eighteenth century and the modern lyric of disillusion.
works.meter: Varied: heroic couplets in the satires, song stanzas and octosyllables in the lyrics.
works.context: Rochester's verse circulated mainly in manuscript within the court coterie; the 1680 edition was pirated and unauthorised, and the canon has been established only by modern editorial work on the manuscripts.
works.structure: A miscellany of satires, songs, epistles, and lampoons; the 1680 edition includes the prose speech on the death of Colonel Blood.
works.attributionNotes: The 1680 and 1716 printed collections contain pieces of doubtful authenticity; Vieth's 1968 edition establishes the canon from manuscript witnesses.

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Warton)
altTitles: The Poems on Several Occasions of Thomas Warton
works.form: collected odes, lyrics, translations and occasional verse, in the Pindaric and preromantic manner
works.description: Thomas Warton's first volume, published while he was still at Oxford and the book that announced the revival of the English ode and of the imaginative romance tradition. It gathers the Pindaric odes, the translations, the lyric and descriptive pieces and the pieces in the old romantic measures, together with the early critical essay on Pope's genius. The volume is the opening statement of the Warton programme: a history of English taste joined to the practice of imaginative verse.
works.plot: The odes attempt the irregular Pindaric forms on subjects of contemplation, fancy and moral description, while the lyric pieces cultivate melancholy, retirement and the observation of landscape. The critical essay measures Pope's art against the older English poets and argues for a wider and more historical sense of poetical excellence. The whole volume moves between imitation of the ancients, experiment in the native measures, and antiquarian curiosity about the romance tradition.
works.significance: The volume is one of the founding documents of the preromantic and Gothic revival in English verse, and its Pindaric experiments, with those of Mason and Gray, prepared the way for the Romantic ode. Its mixture of verse and literary-historical criticism marks the movement from Augustan taste to the history of taste.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas of long and short lines after the manner of Dryden and Oldham, together with smooth heroic couplets for the descriptive and critical pieces.
works.context: Published in 1746 from Oxford, in the season of the ode vogue and of the revival of interest in Spenser and in the old English romance, and in the intellectual circle of his brother Joseph Warton and of the Oxford critics who were revaluing imaginative poetry against Augustan rule.
works.characters: The personified Fancy and Melancholy of the odes; the contemplative speakers of the descriptive pieces; Pope, as the subject of the critical essay
works.structure: A collected volume of separate poems ordered by class, with the odes, the translations and the descriptive pieces distributed across the book and the critical essay printed as an early separate performance gathered into it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume belongs to Thomas Warton the younger, poet laureate from 1785, and must be distinguished from the poems of Joseph Warton and from the later collected editions in which pieces were added and withdrawn.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation

works.title: Poems on Slavery
works.description: Longfellow's abolitionist poems: the slave ship, the fugitive and the warning to the master. It is a verse work of 1842 by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Eight poems — 'The Witnesses', 'The Quadroon Girl', 'The Slave Singing at Midnight', 'The Slave in the Dismal Swamp', 'The Good Part', 'The Warning' and others — written after Longfellow heard the abolitionist lecturers and published as a pamphlet for the Anti-Slavery Society.
works.significance: Poems on Slavery was the most widely circulated abolitionist poetry by a major American poet and it marks the moment when the national poet put his reputation behind the anti-slavery cause: its pamphlet form and its direct address made it a document of the movement.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The author's characteristic manner is the long narrative poem in regular tetrameter.
works.context: The abolitionist movement of the early 1840s and the American controversy over slavery. The record dates the work as composed in 1842 and first published in 1842 and it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the slave; the quadroon girl; the master; the witnesses
works.structure: Eight short poems in a pamphlet for the Anti-Slavery Society. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. W. Longfellow. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.description: Behn's collected verse, including her celebrated lyric 'The Disappointment', the Pindaric odes to political occasions, and the translation of Fontenelle's Voyage to the Island of Love.
works.plot: The volume gathers court odes, love lyrics, songs, elegies, and political verse, including the Whig odes to Monmouth and the Tory poems of the 1680s.
works.significance: The most important collection of poetry by an English woman before the eighteenth century; 'The Disappointment' is a canonical treatment of female sexual experience and its failure.
works.meter: Varied: Pindaric odes, heroic couplets, song stanzas.
works.context: Published in 1684 by Tonson, establishing Behn as the first English woman to earn a living by her pen; a second volume appeared posthumously in 1701.
works.structure: A poetical miscellany with an appended translation of Fontenelle.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect
works.form: collected poems: Scots tales, fables, verse epistles, elegies, addresses and songs, with prefatory advertisement and glossary
works.description: Burns's first volume, printed by subscription at Kilmarnock in 1786 and the event that made him at once the most talked-of poet in Scotland. It gathers the tales and dramatic pieces, the elegies and addresses, the verse epistles to friends and brothers, and the songs, most of them in the Scottish dialect and in the stanzaic tradition inherited from Ramsay and Fergusson. The volume is a self-consciously provincial and labouring man's book, furnished with an advertisement to the subscriber and a glossary of Scots words.
works.plot: The collection moves between the Ayrshire world of ploughing, courtship, tavern and communion field, and the moral and elegiac registers of the addresses and laments. Its satirical pieces expose Presbyterian hypocrisy, rural quackery and the arrogance of rank, while the epistles build a community of friends, brothers and patrons about the poet. Throughout, the volume pleads for the dignity of the Scottish vernacular and of untaught genius, a claim made explicitly in the advertisement and in the poems on national character and song.
works.significance: The Kilmarnock volume is the foundation text of modern Scottish literature and the moment at which the vernacular revival of Ramsay and Fergusson was converted into a national poetry of observation, sympathy and satire. Its publication created the literary cult of Burns and remains a classic instance of subscription authorship in the provincial book trade.
works.meter: Chiefly stanzaic Scots in the six-line Habbie and rambling measures inherited from Ramsay, with songs to current airs, ballad stanzas, and a few pieces in conventional English prosody.
works.context: Produced while Burns was preparing to emigrate to a overseer's post in Jamaica after the failure of his Nithsdale farming scheme, and the success of the volume rescued him from that plan; it stands in the line of Allan Ramsay's The Ever Green and the Tea-Table Miscellany, of Fergusson's Edinburgh poems, and of Herd's collections of Scottish songs, and appeared in the full tide of the Scottish Enlightenment's institutional life in Edinburgh and Glasgow.
works.characters: Luath and Caesar; the cotter's family; Death and Doctor Hornbook; the ploughman-speaker of the addresses; the friends and brothers of the epistles
works.structure: A subscription volume ordered by the author into classes of piece - tales, addresses, elegies, epistles, songs - with an advertisement, a list of subscribers and a glossary of Scots terms, rather than a single sequential design.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns controlled the volume, its advertisement and its glossary, though several pieces adapt earlier printed and manuscript sources, a practice he recorded in his later musical and poetic collections.
