works.title: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical
works.description: Tennyson's first solo collection, published in 1830 when he was twenty, and the volume that announced an art of pure sensation: 'Claribel', 'Mariana', 'The Kraken', 'The Poet' and the elegiac 'Ode to Memory' are the poems by which it is known.
works.plot: The volume's poems are lyric and meditative rather than narrative: 'Mariana' fixes a woman in a moated grange in a single endlessly repeated condition; 'The Kraken' sleeps in the abysm of the deep; 'The Poet' describes the poet's mind as a world; 'Recollections of the Arabian Nights' builds a dream palace from pure sound.
works.significance: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical introduced the 'Tennysonian' manner that dominated English verse for the next sixty years: the picture of a state of mind held in a landscape, and the perfection of sound. It is also the volume in which the Cambridge circle of the Apostles found its poet.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.
works.context: The 1830 volume appeared in the year of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway and of the July Revolution; it was reviewed by Arthur Henry Hallam in the Englishman's Magazine as the work of a new school of poetry whose interest lay in the 'originality' of its feeling for nature and its 'descriptive' power.
works.characters: Mariana; Claribel; Isabel; Lilian; Adeline; the Kraken; the Merman and the Mermaid; Haroun Alraschid (in 'Recollections of the Arabian Nights'); the poet
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Poems, Second Series
works.description: Published in 1891 and the second posthumous selection: 166 poems, including 'I felt a Funeral, in my Brain', 'A narrow Fellow in the Grass' and 'The Brain — is wider than the Sky'. It is a verse work of 1891 by Emily Dickinson; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume continues the arrangement of the first series and adds the poems of the inner life, of the snakes and the birds of Amherst, and of the mind's power, which are among the most metaphysical in American poetry.
works.significance: Poems, Second Series deepened the first collection and made Dickinson's intellectual ambition unmistakable; together the two volumes established her as a major poet and set the terms of the critical debate that continues today.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is hymn and ballad measures broken by slant rhyme and irregular stress.
works.context: The year 1891, the first reception of Dickinson, the American debate on her metre, and the Victorian editing of her texts. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1886 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.

works.title: Poems. By Mrs. M. Robinson. In Two Volumes
works.description: Mary Robinson's first collected volume of verse, the book by which she converted the notoriety of the Perdita episode into a literary career. Gathering her lyric and occasional poetry, some of it already circulated in the periodical press, it presents an accomplished occasional and elegiac poet - addresses to the moment, meditations on loss, and sonnet-like numbers drawn from her own history - and consolidates the persona of the English Sappho she had been building since her Della Cruscan prominence. Its second volume appeared two years later with different publishers, evidence of the unstable bookselling arrangements under which she worked.
works.plot: The volume is a collection rather than an argument: its poems mourn lost children and lost love, describe retirement, autumn, and the seaside, complain of the cruelty of fame and of the price of a woman's reputation, and offer sententious reflection on mutability and endurance; several numbers turn on the disparity between the public notoriety of the narrator and the private sufferings she records.
works.significance: The volume established Robinson as a professional poet of the 1790s and is the basis of her reputation as one of the principal agents of the sonnet revival and of the lyrical vogue that preceded the Lyrical Ballads; it documents the making of a public female poetic identity out of scandal, and it is now read as an essential part of the popular Romanticism that Wordsworthian scholarship long effaced.
works.meter: Conventionally regular decasyllabic and octosyllabic lines in lyric stanzas and in sonnet forms, with a musical, complaint-driven diction inherited from the Della Cruscan and sentimental traditions and frequent apostrophe.
works.context: Published after Robinson's separation from Thomas Robinson, her ruin in the public eye following the rupture with the Prince of Wales in the early 1780s, and her years on the Continent, and at the moment when her association with Robert Merry and the Della Cruscan vogue was making her the most talked-about female poet in London; like Charlotte Smith she turned legal and financial dependence into a publishing career, and her first volume was a deliberate opening of that campaign.
works.characters: the poet-speaker of the volumes; the lost beloved and the dead children of the elegies; Fame and Misfortune as apostrophised powers
works.structure: Two volumes of separate lyrics and short descriptive poems, arranged without sustained sequence, the two volumes appearing years apart; the reader assembles an autobiographical persona from repeated situations of mourning, exposure, and complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name as Mrs. M. Robinson; attribution is undisputed, though the two volumes were issued separately and bibliographical statements that treat the collection as a single 1791 event are inaccurate.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Fortune and mutability
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Melancholy and self-analysis
Patronage and the literary marketplace
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: Poems: Third Series
works.description: Published in Boston in 1896, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd with a preface by T. W. Higginson: the third of the posthumous volumes that first gave Dickinson to the world. It is a verse work of 1896 by Emily Dickinson; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume gathers the poems of nature, death and the inner life that Todd and Higginson selected from the manuscripts, arranged in four parts on the pattern of the first two series, with the regularised punctuation and the titles supplied by the editors.
works.significance: Poems: Third Series completed the posthumous publication that made Dickinson an American poet and kept her before the reading public until the manuscript editions of the twentieth century; it remains the last of the nineteenth-century volumes and a document of the Victorian editing of her texts.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is hymn and ballad measures broken by slant rhyme and irregular stress.
works.context: The year 1896, the ten years after the two earlier volumes, and the first settled reputation of Dickinson as an American poet. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1886 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Posthumous edition by Todd with a preface by Higginson; the editors regularised the punctuation and supplied titles that the manuscripts do not carry.

works.title: Poganuc People: Their Loves and Lives
works.form: Novel; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1878
works.description: Published in 1878 and Stowe's last New England novel: the life of a Connecticut village and of the clergyman's daughter Dolly, drawn closely from her own childhood at Litchfield. It is a prose fiction work of 1878 by Harriet Beecher Stowe; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Dolly, the daughter of the minister of Poganuc, grows up among the parties, the sleigh rides, the revivals and the social distinctions of a small Connecticut town, and the novel ends with her coming of age and the departure of the old order.
works.significance: Poganuc People is the most charming of Stowe's New England books and a key text in the American literature of the village; its record of the religious revivals and the social life of the 1830s is a primary document of American culture.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is sentimental tableaux designed to produce tears and conversion.
works.context: The 1830s, Connecticut Congregationalism, the Second Great Awakening, and the American village before the railroad. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Dolly Cushing; Dr Cushing, her father, the minister; Mrs Cushing; Zeph Higgins; Nabby Higgins; Hiel Jones
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Harriet Elizabeth Beecher Stowe. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Point Counter Point
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1928
works.description: The great English novel of ideas of the twenties: a dozen characters in musical counterpoint around love, science and the failure of belief. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Aldous Huxley; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The novel alternates among a large cast — the novelist Philip Quarles, the scientist Lord Edward Tantamount, the sensualist Walter Bidlake, the fascist Spandrell, the painter Mark Rampion — and builds a contrapuntal argument about the life of the mind against the life of the body.
works.significance: Point Counter Point is the finest English novel of ideas of the period: its contrapuntal construction and its argument about the life of the body made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of debate.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of ideas with a large cast and competing arguments.
works.context: London in the 1920s, the intellectual set, the new science and the cult of the primitive, and the post-war loss of faith. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Philip Quarles; Mark Rampion; Lord Edward Tantamount; Walter Bidlake; Spandrell; Lucy Tantamount
works.structure: Contrapuntal structure alternating among a large cast, with Quarles's notebook as commentary. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Aldous Leonard Huxley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Pointed Roofs
works.form: Novel (first of Pilgrimage); novel of consciousness
works.description: The first English stream-of-consciousness novel: a young woman goes to Germany to teach and the world is rendered from inside her mind. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Dorothy Richardson; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form.
works.plot: Miriam Henderson, a shabby-genteel English girl of seventeen, goes to a German finishing school to teach English. The novel records her impressions — the school, the town, the other teachers, the music, the humiliation and the freedom — entirely through her consciousness, in the continuous present of perception.
works.significance: Pointed Roofs is the first English stream-of-consciousness novel, preceding Ulysses by seven years: it gave English fiction the sustained interior monologue, and it is the founding text of the novel of female consciousness that Woolf and Mansfield would develop.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the interior monologue uninterrupted by an explaining narrator.
works.context: The English and German boarding schools of the 1890s, and the restricted life of the educated but poor woman of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1914 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Miriam Henderson; the Fräulein; the school; the German town
works.structure: Continuous present-tense interior monologue in thirteen chapters. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dorothy Miller Richardson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Policraticus
altTitles: Policraticus: Of the Frivolities of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers
works.description: John of Salisbury's treatise on politics, court life, and philosophy in eight books, completed in 1159 and dedicated to Thomas Becket; the first full work of medieval political theory, famous for its organic metaphor of the body politic and its defence of tyrannicide.
works.summary: The Policraticus satirizes the frivolities of courtiers, expounds the duties of prince and magistrate under the image of the body politic (the prince as head, the clergy as soul), argues that the tyrant is a public enemy whose killing may be lawful, and ends with a survey of ancient philosophy and the true happiness of the contemplative life.
works.significance: The most important political treatise written in twelfth-century Europe, a conduit of classical political thought into the Middle Ages, and a standard authority cited into the seventeenth century.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Political Discourses
works.description: Hume's essays on money, trade, credit, population, and the sinews of public power, published in London in 1752 and instantly the most discussed economic writing of the decade. They argued that commercial growth is self-sustaining, that the balance of trade doctrines are sophistry, and that public credit is the Achilles heel of modern states.
works.plot: The discourses trace how industry, knowledge, and refinement spread from a cultivated court and city to the whole state, so that trade, not hoarded bullion, constitutes a nation's real opulence. Hume demolishes the jealousy of trade and mercantilist balances, shows money to be a veil over labour, and works out the price-specie-flow logic by which trade surpluses self-correct through rising prices. He then analyses interest as the price of the scarcity of lent capital, taxes, credit, paper money, colonies, and population, closing with gloomy reflections on the perpetual tendency of public credit to subvert modern government. The political discourses on the parties of antiquity and of England and on the limits of human policy frame the whole.
works.significance: It was Adam Smith's declared predecessor in commercial theory and one of the most reprinted, translated, and quoted economic texts of the century, the bridge from the mercantilists to classical political economy.
works.meter: Plain, rapid argumentative prose of the practised essayist, with numbers used as rhetoric and abrupt generalizing closers.
works.context: Published in 1752 amid the decade's debates over paper credit, population, and the balance of trade; its opening discourse grew out of Hume's celebrated statistical controversy with the Chevalier d'Eon over the comparative greatness of France and England.
works.structure: Fourteen connected discourses in a loose sequence from growth and trade to money, interest, credit, taxes, and the balance of parties.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history

works.title: Politics and the English Language
works.description: Politics and the English Language is an essay by George Orwell, first published in the April 1946 issue of the monthly Horizon and collected in Shooting an Elephant and Other Essays (1950). It argues that the English of its time was ugly and inaccurate, that slovenly language and foolish thought reinforce each other, and that political language in particular is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable. It closes with six rules for clear writing, and has become one of the most reprinted essays in English.
works.summary: Five specimen passages of bad contemporary prose; a catalogue of faults (dying metaphors, verbal false limbs, pretentious diction, meaningless words); a parody of a verse of Ecclesiastes in modern officialese; the analysis of political euphemism; the argument that insincerity is the great enemy of clear language; and six rules, with the claim that the decline of the language is reversible.
works.plot: Orwell begins by rejecting the view that the decline of English is a natural, irreversible process. Language becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but its slovenliness makes it easier to have foolish thoughts, as a man may drink because he feels a failure and then fail the more completely because he drinks; the process can be reversed by people willing to take the trouble. He quotes five passages, by Harold Laski, Lancelot Hogben, an essay on psychology in the American magazine Politics, a communist pamphlet and a letter to Tribune, and draws from them a catalogue of swindles and perversions: dying metaphors used without thought of their meaning, 'operators or verbal false limbs' that pad sentences with phrases instead of verbs, pretentious diction that dresses up bias as impartial and scientific, and meaningless words, common in art and literary criticism and in political terms such as democracy and fascism. Modern prose, he says, consists less of words chosen for their meaning than of phrases tacked together like the sections of a prefabricated henhouse, and he demonstrates it by translating a verse of Ecclesiastes ('the race is not to the swift') into modern English of the worst sort. Political speech and writing are largely the defence of the indefensible: the bombing of defenceless villages is called pacification, the expulsion of peasants transfer of population, imprisonment without trial elimination of unreliable elements. Orthodoxy demands a lifeless, imitative style, and the great enemy of clear language is insincerity: when there is a gap between real and declared aims, one turns to long words and exhausted idioms like a cuttlefish spurting out ink. Ready-made phrases think for the writer and can even conceal his meaning from himself. Orwell proposes that a writer should let the meaning choose the words, and offers six rules: never use a figure of speech you are used to seeing in print; never use a long word where a short one will do; cut every word you can; never use the passive where you can use the active; never use a foreign phrase, scientific word or jargon if there is an everyday English equivalent; and break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. He concedes that his own essay commits the faults it attacks, insists that he is concerned with language as an instrument for expressing thought, not with its literary use, and ends that political language is designed to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind, and that one can at least send some worn-out phrase into the dustbin where it belongs.
works.significance: One of the most influential essays in English on style and on political language. Lynn Z. Bloom found it reprinted 118 times in 325 editions of 58 composition readers published between 1946 and 1996, and it remains a staple of writing courses; its phrases about making lies sound truthful and murder respectable are constantly quoted in discussion of political rhetoric.
works.meter: Plain, concrete and vigorous prose, rich in homely analogies (the drinker, the cuttlefish, the prefabricated henhouse, the packet of aspirins at one's elbow), quoting its examples and parodying them; Orwell admits that the essay itself breaks some of its rules.
works.context: Written in late 1945, when Orwell's payment book records it on 11 December, after the success of Animal Farm and the death of his wife; it was meant for George Weidenfeld's Contact, which turned it down, and appeared in Horizon almost at the same time as 'The Prevention of Literature', which shares its concern with truth and language under political pressure.
works.structure: An argumentative essay that moves from a general claim, through quoted specimens and a classified catalogue of faults, to the political analysis and the practical rules, ending with qualifications and a short peroration.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past
Language, writing and the limits of representation
Power, the state and surveillance

works.title: Polly
altTitles: Polly: A Sequel to the Beggar's Opera
works.description: Gay's sequel to the Beggar's Opera, in which the reprieved Macheath, transported and escaped, pursues Polly to a plantation in the southern colonies, where she is disguised as a man and the slaves Cato and Lucida enact a tragedy of conjugal constancy.
works.plot: Macheath, having cheated the gallows, is banished, escapes his creditors and the governor, and reaches the American planter's household; Polly follows in a man's dress, is assaulted in the dark by her own husband and by the land-jobber Mordecai's intrigue, and the play closes with the exposures of the lovers' fidelity, the refusal of the transport and the Beggar's renunciation of the sequel.
works.significance: It turns the burlesque of the first opera into a sharper analysis of credit, marriage, transport and slavery, and its suppression made it the century's standard instance of the political censorship of the stage.
works.meter: Air-songs in ballad and sentimental stanzas with borrowed tunes, and the elegiac measures of the inserted slave scenes.
works.context: Written immediately after the success of the Beggar's Opera and forbidden by the Lord Chamberlain in the season of the administration's quarrel with the theatre, so that it reached the reading public in print rather than the stage; its colonial setting answers the plantation and transport literature of the same years.
works.characters: Polly; Macheath; Lucy Lockit; Mordecai the land-jobber; Cato and Lucida, slaves on the plantation; the governor of the province; the Beggar
works.structure: Three acts of ballad opera with the plantation scenes and the inserted slave tragedy, framed by the Beggar's dispute with the writer of the sequel.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the licence refused by the Lord Chamberlain is documented, and the sequel's later stage history is complex and is not asserted here.

works.title: Polychronicon (Trevisa's translation)
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, the universal history that dominated English historical reading: the world's geography, the history of Britain from the Britons to the fourteenth century, and the wonders of the world, in Trevisa's fluent, expansive prose, completed in 1387 for Thomas, Lord Berkeley. works.significance: The principal English universal history of the later Middle Ages and, with its Dialogue on Translation, a classic text of vernacular self-consciousness.
works.meter: Prose: fluent, idiomatic, and expansive — a landmark of fourteenth-century English prose style.
works.context: Completed in 1387 by Trevisa, chaplain of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, at Berkeley Castle; printed by Caxton (1482, with his continuation to 1460) and read into the sixteenth century.

works.context: Written during Philips's stay in Dublin (1662–63) and performed at the Theatre Royal, Smock Alley; it broke new ground for women in the professional theatre.

works.title: Popular Tales
works.form: Juvenile and domestic tale collection; character-writing and moral experiment in short prose fiction.
works.description: A three-volume collection of short tales for young readers and their families, the most internationally influential children's and domestic fiction of its decade. It mixes Irish, English and colonial settings, and turns the practical problems of temper, vanity, falsehood and fortune into close-analysed children's actions. Its title marks a deliberate theory of popularity: instruction designed to be read for pleasure.
works.plot: The collection proceeds by separate tales rather than a continuous plot: a child's stubbornness and its correction; a boy's vanity about his birth and a father's silence; a slave's return of a stolen estate in a West Indian insurrection; the deceptions of a child who cannot tell a lie from a fiction; and tales of trade, of Irish tenantry and of school emulation. Each closes with a plainly stated moral consequence rather than with marriage or inheritance.
works.significance: Set the standard for the analysed juvenile action in English fiction and shaped the pedagogical novel of the nineteenth century; it was translated widely and praised by contemporary critics and reviewers of the higher literature. Its handling of colonial and Irish material makes it a focal text for the study of the period's domestic ideology. Its editorial practice - prefacing tales with arguments on their use - is a document of period literary theory.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; plain conversational style with deliberately differentiated speech for children and for Irish and colonial characters.
works.context: Produced in a household devoted to educational experiment and to the publishing of children's books, and aimed at the expanding middle-class market for family reading after the pedagogical controversies of the 1790s. Its West Indian tale engages directly with the plantation insurrection of 1760 and with contemporary abolitionist argument. Its Irish tales assume the post-Union question of how the tenant might be represented to an English reader.
works.structure: Discrete short tales in three volumes, each with a self-contained crisis and an explicit moral resolution; a plain, explanatory narration with frequent dialogue and written documents such as letters and accounts.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education

works.title: Portraits
works.description: Published in 1870 and the collection that established Webster as the leading woman poet of the dramatic monologue: studies of women's lives in their own voices. It is a verse work of 1870 by Augusta Webster; it belongs to The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume contains 'A Castaway', 'Medea in Athens', 'Circe', 'The Happiest Girl in the World', 'Sister Annunciata' and 'Tired', each a portrait of a woman at a moment of crisis.
works.significance: Portraits is the central English collection of woman's dramatic monologues and one of the most important volumes of Victorian women's poetry; its range — from the classical witch to the London prostitute — is unmatched in the period.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker.
works.context: The 1860s, the Browning vogue, the woman's poetry of the 1860s-70s, and the debate on the 'woman question'. The record dates the work as composed between 1866 and 1870 and first published in 1870 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Eulalie ('A Castaway'); Medea ('Medea in Athens'); Circe; the happiest girl in the world; Sister Annunciata
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.description: The essays that made the modern science literary for the general reader. It is a prose work of 1927 by J. B. S. Haldane; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.significance: Possible Worlds is the classic essay collection of the modern science: its title essay and its On Being the Right Size made the laboratory's discoveries the literature of the general reader and set the form of the popular science essay.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. works.description: Published posthumously in 1911 and the best collection of Johnson's critical prose: essays on Hardy, Pater, the Celtic literature, the English poets and the Catholic writers. works.significance: Post Liminium contains some of the finest critical prose of the 1890s and is the best record of Johnson's learning and his sympathy; it is a key text in the history of English criticism and of the Catholic literary revival.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is classical and medieval metres handled with learning.

works.title: Practical Criticism
works.form: Critical study (the experiments of the reading)
works.description: The study of the protocols: the readers, the poems without names and the record of misreading. It is a prose work of 1929 by I. A. Richards; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Practical Criticism reports the Cambridge experiment in which students read thirteen poems without names or dates and records their protocols: the stock responses, the sentimentality, the irrelevance and the confusion are classified, and the reading of the poem is made an experimental discipline.
works.significance: Practical Criticism founded the discipline of the close reading: its protocols of misreading made the reading of the unnamed poem the object of criticism and gave the teaching of English its central exercise for half a century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the analytic prose of the psychologist of reading.
works.context: Cambridge in the later 1920s, and the classroom experiment. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1928 and first published in 1929 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A study in chapters: the experiment, the protocols, the classification of the faults, the theory.

works.title: Practical Education
altTitles: Practical Education, Inferred from the Principles of Philosophy
works.form: conduct and educational treatise; the practical philosophy of the mind applied to the nursery and the school
works.description: The great English treatise of educational practice of the turn of the century, written in two volumes by two hands of one household, a father and his daughter, and profounded in the title to be inferred from the principles of philosophy. It carries the science of the mind from the lecture-room into the nursery and the schoolroom, and it reports, in the plainest of all such books, the experiments of a large and cultivated family upon the powers of children.
works.plot: The work reasons from the principles of human nature, as they had been settled by the philosophy of the preceding century and by the modern enquiry into the powers of the mind, to the practice of education, and it treats in the successive chapters of the management of the infant from the cradle, of the principles of human nature as they appear in children, of the education of the feelings and the passions, of attention, of association, of the love of distinction and of sympathy, of early prejudice and of the learning of languages, of memory and of amusement, of the studies proper to the several ages, and of the moral discipline of the young. Its governing conclusions are that the child should be governed by the natural consequences of his actions and by the desire of approbation rather than by the task, the rote, and the rod; that whatever is to be known should be learned from the thing and the experiment rather than from the description in the book; that the powers of the mind are earned by practice in the affairs that interest them; and that the greatest error of the existing method is the teaching of words instead of ideas. The illustrations are drawn for the most part from the anecdotes of the children of the household and of the pupils of the family, and the argument is everywhere carried by the reported instance.
works.significance: One of the most influential books of educational practice in the English language, and the point at which the doctrine of association of ideas was turned into a method of teaching; it changed the practice of the nursery and of the better schools of both countries for two generations, supplied the vocabulary of the education controversy of the nineteenth century, and stands at once as a document of the history of childhood, of the philosophy of mind, and of the literary work of a family, being the first published fruit of one of the most remarkable pens of the following age of fiction.
works.meter: Clear, brisk, familiar argumentative prose, the style of the experimenting household: the principle stated plainly, the instance told as a little story with warmth and humour, and the rule deduced without ornament. Its characteristic manner is the anecdote used as evidence, and its sentence is short, unacademic, and addressed to parents rather than to schoolmen.
works.context: Published in 1798, the year of the treatise on population and of the strictures on the modern system of female education, in the season of the dissenting academy, of the educational projects of the philosophical radicals, and of the new attention to the infant mind which came from the philosophy of the preceding age and from the Continental book on the education of the child. The household from which the instances were drawn was itself a school of experiment, and the book was the first public product of a partnership of parent and child which continued in the juvenile stories and the letters of the following decades.
works.structure: A treatise in chapters, in two consecutively paginated volumes, each chapter a separate branch of the subject built of the philosophical principle, the familiar instance from the nursery or the school, and the practical rule; no continuous narrative runs through the work, but the several chapters are bound together by the reiterated appeal to the same domestic experience.
works.attributionNotes: The shares of the two hands of the household are not distinguishable in the first edition, which was given out without the names of the writers, and the division of the volumes between them has been variously guessed by the editors and the biographers, the daughter's hand being claimed for the more of the illustrative matter and the father's for the metaphysical statement, without decisive evidence. The work is therefore entered as collaborative, and the several chapters have been attributed now to the one and now to the other writer.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Practical Piety
altTitles: Practical Piety; or, the Influence of the Power of Godliness on the Felicity of this Life and of Eternity
works.form: practical divinity and devotional prose; religious conduct treatise
works.description: A long devotional and practical work addressed to persons of rank and fortune, urging that true religion is not a form but a power governing the actual hours and business of the world. It belongs to the author's later religious writings, in which the evangelic argument is turned from the poor to the rich, and happiness itself is pleaded as the reward of godliness.
works.plot: The work distinguishes the form of godliness from its power, and charges the religious world of leisure with a piety of seasons and of duties rather than of the heart, a religion of the closet and the Sunday which leaves the closet and the week unaltered. It then examines the practical influence of genuine religion upon the felicity of this life: upon time, which the religious person redeems from trifling and from the tyranny of engagement; upon the temper, upon the affections, upon the use of wealth and of hospitality, and upon the society of the world, where it claims that a sober and obliging piety is more amiable and more successful than the manners it condemns. The later parts turn to the trials of life, sickness, loss, disappointment, and the death of those beloved, and argue that a religion which does not meet these has not been tried. The conclusion urges the eternal motive: that the same principle which makes the present life happy is the only security for the happiness of another.
works.significance: It is one of the most widely circulated of the later practical-divinity books, and a key text of the religion of sensibility turned to use: its claim that piety and present happiness are the same thing was one of the strongest answers of the evangelical party to the charge that religion is ascetic and antisocial. Its portraiture of the religious world of fashion, in its mixture of counsel and satire, preserves the manners of its class with unusual exactness.
works.meter: Warm, persuasive, particularised prose of the experienced religious writer: direct address to the person of rank, the vivid little case from real life, the balanced period, and an unembarrassed use of the motive of happiness.
works.context: Written in the author's later period, after the tract enterprise and the Mendip school labours had turned her argument from the religion of the poor to the responsibility of the rich, and in the season of the evangelical and dissenting controversy over experimental religion. Its appeal to the leisured classes of the metropolis and the county belonged to the same movement that produced the society and the charity-school literature of the war years.
works.structure: A continuous practical-divinity argument in books or volumes of headed chapters, each unit a distinct branch of the influence examined, with scriptural text and practical application throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author.

works.title: Praeterita: Outlines of Scenes and Thoughts Perhaps Worthy of Memory in My Past Life
works.description: Ruskin's autobiography, serialised in the magazine of the same name in twenty-four parts from 1885 and left unfinished in 1889: the most beautiful of Victorian autobiographies, and the retrospective re-creation of a childhood, a family and a Europe before the railway.
works.plot: The narrative moves from the London house of his childhood and the sherry business of his father to the Continental tours of 1833-1845, his mother and father, his boyish passion for Adèle Domecq (his marriage to Effie Gray is passed over in silence), his work on Modern Painters and the Stones of Venice, and the death of his parents; the last chapters are fragmentary and haunted.
works.significance: Praeterita is the finest Victorian autobiography after Mill's and the model for the twentieth-century literary memoir; its reconstruction of childhood perception and its refusal of the conventional pieties made it a central text for Pater, Proust and the modern autobiography, and its unfinished condition is itself a document of the age.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The 1880s, Ruskin's failing mind and the death of his parents, and the Victorian vogue for autobiography (Mill, Darwin, Trollope, Newman). The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Unfinished: Ruskin wrote twenty-four chapters of a projected longer work and abandoned it in 1889 as his mental health failed; the published text is what he left.

works.title: Prayer for those on the Staff
works.description: The officer's wry prayer for the staff, written from the front in the spring of 1915. It is a verse work of 1915 by Julian Grenfell; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem.
works.plot: The poem prays, with the officer's irony, for the safety of the staff behind the line, and turns the prayer into the soldier's account of the distance between the headquarters and the trench, in the rhymed stanza of the war lyric.
works.significance: 'Prayer for those on the Staff' is the companion piece to 'Into Battle' and the proof that Grenfell's lyric could carry the officer's irony as well as his exultation; it is among the most quoted of the 1915 lyrics.
works.meter: Verse. The author's characteristic manner is the long, swelling, sunlit line of the Georgian lyric.
works.context: The Western Front in the spring of 1915, and the officer's view of the war's administration. The record dates the work as composed in 1915 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem.
works.structure: A short lyric in rhymed stanzas, cast as a prayer. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.

works.title: Prayers or Meditations
altTitles: Prayers Stirring the Mind unto Heavenly Meditations
works.description: Catherine Parr's book of devotional prayers and meditations, published in 1545; the first book published by an English queen under her own name, which ran through nineteen editions by 1600.
works.plot: The book adapts the third book of Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ into a sequence of prayers, meditations on the passion, and exhortations to penitence, faith, and the amendment of life, addressed to the reader in the queen's own voice as a fellow sinner seeking grace.
works.significance: The first printed book by an English queen and a landmark in the history of women's devotional writing; its combination of à Kempis's piety with Reformation emphasis on faith made it the century's most popular royal book.

works.context: Published in 1545 by Thomas Berthelet with the queen's name on the title page, in the months when Parr's evangelical household (including Askew's associates) was under suspicion; the book's success established the royal devotional voice that Elizabeth I and others would imitate.
works.structure: A devotional manual of prayers and meditations arranged by spiritual states — contrition, faith, thanksgiving — with scriptural centos and personal application.

works.title: Precepts
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which a wise father addresses ten counsels to his son, one by one: to avoid anger and envy, choose wise companions, keep faith, practise generosity, and fear God. Each counsel is introduced by a repeated formula of address.
works.plot: The father, speaking 'many winters' of experience, delivers ten distinct precepts to his son on the conduct of a good life — on anger, friendship, wisdom, speech, generosity, and the fear of the Lord — closing with an exhortation to remember the counsels always.

works.context: The father-son instruction poem has biblical and classical roots (Proverbs, the Disticha Catonis) and was a recognized genre in Anglo-Saxon England, as the Old English translation of the Distichs shows.

works.title: Precious Bane
works.description: The harelipped narrator, the bargain for the land and the price of the soul. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Mary Webb; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Precious Bane is told by Prue Sarn, the harelipped narrator of the Shropshire mere, and follows her brother Gideon's bargain for the land - the weaving, the wizard's pact and the price of the soul - until the water takes him and the love of the weaver Kester takes her.
works.significance: Precious Bane is Mary Webb's masterpiece and the most read provincial novel of the 1920s: its harelipped narrator, its bargain for the land and its mere made the Shropshire romance a national text after Stanley Baldwin's praise of 1928.

Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is the charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather.
works.context: Shropshire in the nineteenth century, remembered in the prose of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed in 1923 and first published in 1924 and it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Prue Sarn; Gideon Sarn; Kester Woodseaves; the wizard; the mere
works.structure: A novel in the first person of the narrator, in chapters of the bargain and the mere. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.

works.title: Preface to Lyrical Ballads
altTitles: Preface to the Second Edition of Lyrical Ballads
works.form: Prefatory literary commentary and theoretical essay in the tradition of the apologia dedicated to a published collection; it functions as a manifesto because it names the errors it intends to correct and proposes subjects and a style in their place.
works.description: The critical essay prefixed to the second edition of the ballad volume, greatly enlarged for the edition of 1802, and reprinted ever since as the founding document of English Romantic poetics. It defends a deliberate choice of humble and rustic life and of the language really used by such men, defines poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings originating in emotion recollected in tranquillity, and argues that the poet's distinguishing faculty is imagination rather than a conventional vocabulary of ornament. The essay also gives a polemical sketch of the diction of much eighteenth-century verse and a critical account of metre.
works.plot: The argument moves from the choice of subject to the choice of language, then to a psychology of composition, a definition of the poet, and a polemic against poetic diction. Humble life is preferred because its feelings are simpler, more permanent and better understood by the people who speak them, so that ordinary speech is more philosophical than the substituted vocabulary of abstractions and personifications which passes for poetry; the poet, though a man speaking to men, is described as endowed with more lively sensibility and a larger knowledge of human nature. Composition is then analysed as recollection: the poem begins in emotion remembered, is contemplated until the mind creates in itself an analogous feeling, and is delivered over to metre, which supplies a proportioned part of pleasure and acts as a restraint on the pain of passionate subjects. The closing sections defend the experiments of the volume, rebuke the reader's appetite for trite ornament, and claim that the most valuable poet is he who gives most pleasure to the most people.
works.significance: The most influential English statement of Romantic literary theory and the source of two of the period's most quoted formulas for the origin of poetry and for the poet's character. Its insistence that ordinary speech can be the medium of serious verse licensed the diction of later nineteenth-century poetry, and its account of imaginative perception remains the standard starting point for discussion of Romantic theories of the mind.
works.meter: Prose in long argumentative periods, deliberately free of ornament and of the Latinate manner of eighteenth-century critical prose, though the essay analyses verse closely and its own rhythm is that of earnest exposition.
works.context: Written in response to hostile reviews of the anonymous 1798 volume and to the taste for polished diction inherited from the later eighteenth century; the enlarged text of 1802 absorbed the criticisms of the experiments. Its ideas were inseparable from the collaboration and later disagreement with the co-author of the volume, whose own literary autobiography and criticism are in part a reply to it.
works.structure: A continuous discursive essay rather than a sequence of aphorisms: a statement of purpose, an argument for rustic subject and plain language, an account of the mental process of composition, a definition of the poet, and a polemic against current diction, with illustrative reference to particular poems in the volume and to Greek, Elizabethan and eighteenth-century practice.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is uncontested to the essayist of the volume's senior hand, with an acknowledged share for the co-author in the paragraphs on poetic metre; the texts of 1800 and 1802 differ, and scholarly editions print both.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art

works.title: Preface to Shakespeare
altTitles: Preface, containing an Account of the Observations and Corrections of the Editor
works.form: critical preface and dissertation attached to a scholarly edition; prefatory commentary and literary criticism
works.description: The general preface to Johnson's eight-volume edition of Shakespeare, the most influential piece of dramatic criticism of the eighteenth century. It defends Shakespeare as the poet of nature against the neoclassical rules, answers the charge of violating the unities, and grounds the pleasure of tragedy in the audience's real rather than imaginary credulity. The critical essay is attached to an editor's account of his own method and of his predecessors.
works.plot: Johnson first justifies the editorial work, defending his emendations and censuring the laxity or rash conjecture of earlier editors. He then argues that Shakespeare's primary merit is his just representation of universal nature and of individual human character, so that his dramas serve as a mirror of life. Against the rules he urges that the unities of time and place are not required by nature but by an arbitrary conception of the spectator's belief, since the audience knows it is in a theatre and is moved by real passions excited by fictitious events. He catalogues Shakespeare's faults - far-fetched language, quibbles, the mixture of tragic and comic scenes, inattention to moral teaching - and concludes that even his errors proceed from the abundance of his observations of life.
works.significance: The Preface is the decisive transfer of Shakespeare from the charge of barbaric irregularity to the defence of nature and general truth, and its analysis of theatrical belief remains a starting point for the aesthetics of drama. It established the model of the critical preface to a scholarly edition, and much later argument about character, plot and the rules has been conducted in the terms it set.
works.meter: Prose; the plainest and most direct of Johnson's styles, still periodic and balanced but without the Rambler's weight, with a famous sententious cadence in the closing paragraphs.
works.context: Written for the edition contracted after the Dictionary and the Rambler, in the same years as Garrick's regenerated Shakespearean performances at Drury Lane and the antiquarian editorial labours of Theobald, Warburton and Pope; the debate over the unities and over Shakespeare's regularity had filled English criticism since Rymer and Dennis.
works.characters: Shakespeare; Rymer; Theobald; Pope; Warburton; Thomas Otway; Addison
works.structure: A two-part preface: an editorial defence of the method used in the edition, followed by a critical essay on Shakespeare's excellences, the rules and the unities, the faults, and the closing assessment, the argument built through cases and instances rather than by system.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the edition was a collaborative book: the editorial assistance of Thomas Tyrwhitt, and Johnson's own account of that help, are documented in later letters.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world

works.title: Present Laughter
works.description: Coward's self-portrait: a matinee idol besieged by his admirers on the eve of a world tour. works.title: Pride and Prejudice
works.form: Comedy of manners and novel of character; two-plot comic structure in which the marriage plot is also a moral education.
works.description: The most widely read English novel of the marriage market: a comedy of misjudgement in which the quick-witted Elizabeth Bennet and the proud landowner Fitzwilliam Darcy must each revise their first readings of the other. Drafted rapidly in the mid-1790s as First Impressions and revised a dozen years later, it perfects the ironic narration of a heroine learning to distrust her own sagacity. Its social field is the country town and the county assembly, where rank, fortune and accomplishment are endlessly weighed.
works.plot: The arrival of the wealthy bachelor Bingley at Netherfield sets the five Bennet sisters in motion; Jane draws his attachment while Elizabeth forms an unfavourable judgement of his friend Darcy, reinforced by the handsome officer George Wickham. Darcy proposes despite his objections to her family and is refused with fury; his written vindication of himself, and his secret interference on her family's behalf after Lydia's elopement, reverse her opinion. Elizabeth rejects the obsequious clergyman Mr. Collins and the proud offer of her cousin's patronage, and accepts Darcy after the regaining of Lydia and the reconciliation of the two households.
works.significance: Established the model of the novel of manners with a first-rate ironic intelligence at its centre, and the most continuously imitated plot pattern in English fiction. Its account of self-knowledge through social humiliation made it a touchstone for later realist and feminist criticism. It is the standard example of the 1790s experimental juvenile novel matured into nineteenth-century form.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; epigrammatic balanced sentences ('It is a truth universally acknowledged'), colloquial dialogue, and quoted letters in a more formal register.
works.context: Composed in the decade of the French Wars and revised after 1811, when paper, copyright and the triple-decker system had made the novel a substantial commercial property. Its militia encampments, its anxiety about female dependence, and its estate arithmetic of four and ten thousand a year reflect the specific insecurities of the propertied classes under prolonged war. The absence of overt political reference is itself a historical effect of a novelist writing for a readership suspicious of Jacobin fiction.
works.characters: Elizabeth Bennet; Fitzwilliam Darcy; Jane Bennet; Charles Bingley; Mr. Bennet; Mrs. Bennet; Mr. Collins; Charlotte Lucas; George Wickham; Lydia Bennet; Lady Catherine de Bourgh; Mrs. Gardiner
works.structure: Third-person ironic narration focalised chiefly through Elizabeth, with strategic restriction of information; letters (Darcy's long letter, Mrs. Gardiner's accounts) act as the machinery of revelation; symmetrical proposal scenes form the structural hinge.
works.attributionNotes: Advertised as 'By the author of Sense and Sensibility'; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
The marriage market and the limited estate
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Principles of Literary Criticism
works.form: Critical treatise (the psychology of the reading)
works.description: The treatise that founded the semantics of the poem and the psychology of the reading. It is a prose work of 1924 by I. A. Richards; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Richards states the theory of the poem as the instrument of the experience: the impulse, the stock response, the pseudo-statement and the orders of the response are defined against the psychology of the reader, and the criticism of the poem is made a discipline of the reading rather than of the history.
works.significance: Principles of Literary Criticism founded the semantics of the poem and the psychology of the reading: its pseudo-statement, its impulse and its stock response gave the New Criticism of England and America its method and its vocabulary.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the analytic prose of the psychologist of reading.

works.title: Principles of Political Economy, with Some of Their Applications to Social Philosophy
works.description: Published in 1848 and the standard English economics text for a generation: a systematic restatement of the classical political economy that opened the way for reform by distinguishing the laws of production from the arrangements of distribution.
works.plot: The five books treat production, distribution (property, wages, profits, rent), exchange (value, money, international trade), the progress of society, and the influence of government, including the case for the taxation of unearned increments, the reform of land tenure, and the stationary state as a possible good rather than a disaster.
works.significance: The Principles taught political economy to the English-speaking world (the first edition sold out in a year) and made the distinction between production and distribution the basis of the reformist economics that led to the welfare state; Mill's discussion of the stationary state and the environment is the founding text of ecological economics.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
works.context: The 1847 crisis and the Irish famine, the Chartist and cooperative movements, the land question, and the socialist criticisms of Louis Blanc and the English Owenites. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1848 and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Private Lives
works.description: The wittiest comedy of the period: divorced lovers on adjacent honeymoons in the south of France. It is a dramatic work of 1930 by Noel Coward; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.

works.title: Progress and Poverty
works.description: The most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century: why poverty grows with progress. It is a prose work of 1879 by Henry George; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: George states the paradox that as wealth increases so does poverty, surveys the history of wages, rent and interest, and argues that the root of the problem is the private ownership of land, proposing a single tax on land value that would abolish poverty without confiscating capital.
works.significance: Progress and Poverty made the single tax a world movement and was translated into every major language: it shaped the progressive and labour politics of Britain, America and Australia for a generation and is the most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, forceful argument addressed to the common reader.
works.context: The United States and Britain after the depression of 1873, the land question of Ireland and the emerging labour movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; lecture and popular address.
works.characters: Henry George as author; the landowning class; the labouring poor
works.structure: Ten books of economic argument, from the paradox to the remedy. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry George (economist). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Prometheus Unbound
altTitles: Prometheus Unbound: A Lyric Drama in Four Acts
works.form: Closet drama and lyrical drama in the classical mask form, with the choral hymn, the epilogue and the philosophical prefatory essay; a re-visioning of the older Promethean tragedy.
works.description: The author's masterpiece, a four-act lyrical drama which rewrites the old myth of the stolen fire as a history of the mind's deliverance from fear. The titan, tormented on the Caucasus and sustained by hatred of the tyrant heaven, is taught by the spirit of the earth and by an oceanic vision of the future, and the act of renouncing his curse releases the power that ends the reign of the king of the gods. Its preface states a theory of poetry as the record of an imagination in action, and its fourth act is a pure choral cosmology.
works.plot: Prometheus, chained and fed by the ocean nymphs, refuses to reveal the secret that would save or ruin heaven's king, and his furies of hate are soothed by a vision of a coming love. Demogorgon, born of the hour and sitting in the cave of eternity, declares the law of change, and the titan, learning that his victim's suffering was not his triumph, withdraws his curses and is thereby free. The tyrant is swept from his throne by the hours, Hercules releases the eagle-wasted prisoner at the sound of the earth's rejoicing choirs, and Asia and Prometheus are crowned in the caves of the atoms, from which the last act sends the regeneration of the world abroad.
works.significance: It is the period's great poem of liberation from the theology of fear and its most ambitious fusion of dramatic, lyric and philosophical form; its fourth act supplied the template for the poetry of elemental process. Its preface and its practice together define the theory of imagination as a way of knowing, and its politics of non-violent renunciation has been a permanent resource for later radical readings.
works.meter: A vast range of measures, regular blank verse for the titan's speeches, and lyric stanzaic forms, cantos of short lines, triple rhymes and refrains for the spirits and choirs; the fourth act is almost entirely song.
works.context: Begun at Naples in the winter of 1818-19 in a house by the bay, and completed in 1819 during the poet's stays at Rome and in the Tuscan baths, in the months of his exile among the ruins of the papal states and of the European reaction after the risings in Italy and Spain were suppressed. It was published in 1820 with the short poems of that season and received almost no notice; its own preface, an answer to a critic's charge that poetry must inculcate moral feeling, became part of the work's argument.
works.characters: Prometheus, the titan of the stolen fire; Asia, his love and the type of the awakened mind; Jupiter, the tyrant of heaven; Demogorgon, the power born of the hour; the spirit of the earth, the ocean waves and the hours; Panthea and Ione and the satyrs
works.structure: Four acts, the first two of dialogue and prophecy, the third of the catastrophe and the crown of the heroes, the fourth an epilogue of choral cosmology; the argument advances by address, hymn and vision rather than by action.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; an earlier and shorter draft of the first act, begun before the final design, survives and is printed as a fragment in the standard edition.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Prothalamion
works.description: A wedding song ('spousal verse') written for the double marriage of the daughters of the Earl of Worcester, Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset, celebrated at Essex House on the Thames in 1596; the poem follows the bridal procession along the river and closes with the refrain 'Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song'.

works.title: Prufrock and Other Observations
works.form: Poetry collection (published by the Egoist Press)
works.description: The first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady' and the urban lyric. It is a verse work of 1917 by T. S. Eliot; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady', 'Preludes', 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night', 'Aunt Helen' and 'The Boston Evening Transcript' — the poems of the modern city, the anti-heroic voice and the ironic quotation that founded English modernism.
works.significance: Prufrock and Other Observations is the first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' made the anti-heroic voice the central instrument of modern poetry, and 'Preludes' and 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night' invented the modern urban lyric.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
works.context: The Boston and London of the 1910s, the drawing rooms of the American aesthete, and the new urban consciousness of the modern city. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1915 and first published in 1917 and it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.

works.structure: Twelve poems in free verse and irregular rhyme. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica; or, Enquiries into Very Many Received Tenets

works.context: Published in 1646, in the midst of the civil wars; it belongs to the new empirical spirit that would found the Royal Society, though Browne's method is as much scholarly as experimental.
works.structure: Seven books of learned enquiry organised by subject, each entry stating the received opinion and Browne's correction.

works.title: Pudd'nhead Wilson
altTitles: The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson and the Comedy of Those Extraordinary Twins
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1894
works.description: Published in 1894 and the darkest of Twain's novels: the story of a slave woman who switches her son with her master's heir, and of the lawyer who solves the case by fingerprints. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Mark Twain; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Roxy, a slave who is one-sixteenth black, exchanges her son Chambers with the master's son Tom; the false Tom grows up as a vicious white gentleman and the true heir as a slave, and the lawyer Wilson, the 'pudd'nhead' of the town, proves the exchange by fingerprints at the trial for murder.
works.significance: Pudd'nhead Wilson is the central American novel of racial passing and one of the first detective novels in American literature: its use of fingerprints and its treatment of slavery as a system of identity-theft make it a key text for the study of race in America.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is first-person vernacular narration.

works.title: Put Out More Flags
works.form: Novel (comic); comic novel, first issued in 1942
works.description: Waugh's wartime comedy: Basil Seal and the intelligence corps. It is a prose fiction work of 1942 by Evelyn Waugh; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Basil Seal, the ruined man of Vile Bodies and Black Mischief, is called up and finds his way into the intelligence corps, the War Office and the county regiment, where he makes a career of incompetence, blackmail and charm, in the comic novel of the phoney war and the Home Guard.
works.significance: Put Out More Flags is Waugh's comic novel of the war and the return of Basil Seal, the most amoral of his creations: its portrait of the phoney war, the intelligence corps and the county regiment made it the funniest English novel of the war years and the bridge between the comedies of the thirties and Brideshead Revisited.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face.
works.context: England in the years of the Second World War, and the army and the civil service of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1941 and 1942 and first published in 1942 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; realist novel of common life.
