works.title: Pygmalion
works.description: Written in 1912 and first performed in 1914: the flower-girl taught to speak like a duchess, and the professor of phonetics who cannot see what he has done. It is a dramatic work of 1913 by George Bernard Shaw; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Henry Higgins, a phonetician, bets Colonel Pickering that he can pass the Covent Garden flower-seller Eliza Doolittle off as a duchess in six months; she learns the accent and the manners, wins the ambassador's ball, and then confronts Higgins with the fact that he has made her a lady with no means of being one.
works.significance: Pygmalion is Shaw's most popular play and one of the great English comedies: its use of phonetics to expose the class system, its ambiguous ending and its portrait of Eliza made it a permanent part of the repertoire, and its adaptation into My Fair Lady carried it to a world audience.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1912-14: the phonetic science of Henry Sweet, the class system of English speech, and the campaign for women's suffrage. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1913 and first performed in 1914 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.

works.structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Quartet
works.form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1928
works.description: Rhys's first novel: the chorus girl, the prison and the patron who pays for her release. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Jean Rhys; it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Marya Stephanovski, a chorus girl, is left penniless in Paris when her husband is imprisoned for dealing in stolen pictures; the Heidlers, an English couple who take an interest in her, house her, feed her and use her, and Marya drifts between the prison visits, the hotel rooms and the Heidler marriage until she has nothing left to sell.
works.significance: Quartet is Rhys's first novel and the founding text of her method: the chorus girl adrift in Paris, the patron and the patron's wife, the hotel room and the prison, and the prose of exact humiliation made the modern novel of the dependent woman and established the voice of Voyage in the Dark, After Leaving Mr Mackenzie and Good Morning, Midnight.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrative of the woman without money.
works.context: Paris and London in the mid-1920s, and the expatriate world of the Left Bank. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1928 and it is catalogued under jazz-age novel and the expatriate romance; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Marya Stephanovski; H. J. Heidler; Lois Heidler; Stephanovski; Madame Hautchamp; Pierre
works.structure: A novel in short chapters, moving between the prison, the hotel and the Heidlers' flat. A novel in chapters of the pleasure and the retrospect, the party scene and the elegiac judgement held in the same short paragraphs. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

works.title: Queen Mab
works.form: Romantic philosophical vision-poem and didactic romance in the Spenserian stanza, with the annotated programme poem of the radical school.
works.description: A philosophical poem in nine cantos, privately printed in the author's twenty-first year and withheld from the trade during his lifetime, in which the spirit of the elvish queen of dreams carries a lover's soul through the past, present and future of the world. It shows the rise and wreck of religions and dynasties, the corruption of commercial society, and a coming age without priests, kings or gold. Its elaborate notes on necessity, on the vegetable system and on the ancient world are part of the work's design, and its fate as a pirated cheap classic of the movement press made it the most politically famous poem of the century.
works.plot: Under the influence of the poppy-drawn dream and the visitation of the fairy queen, Ianthe's soul is borne above the earth and shown the history of its governments and faiths, the procession of dead monarchs and the tyrants of the present. The middle cantos attack the marriage law, the priests and the merchants, and the moral economy of a society that makes hunger a crime, before the vision passes to a future revolution that restores nature to humankind. A closing canto on the distant stars and the eternity of mind brings the vision to an address to the poet's own land and to the youth who are to inherit the change. The argument is that the world's evils are the work of institutions and not of nature, and that a reasoned hope is a duty.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the author's radical vision and, through its nineteenth-century cheap reprints, one of the most widely read poems of the labour and freethought movements, exercising an influence on popular politics out of all proportion to its literary standing. Its union of a theory of necessity, a critique of institutional marriage and religion, and a millenarian history gave the later revolutionary odes their shape.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas of nine iambic pentameter lines with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, used for rapid visionary enumeration; the notes are prose, occasionally elevated to rhetorical periodicity.
works.context: Written largely in the spring of 1813, in the year of the author's flight to Ireland and his connection with the circle of the old dissenting philosophers, and printed in a small private run of some 250 copies that the author distributed at cost. It reached print properly only after his death, when a pirate issued it in a cheap edition alongside a companion tract on diet, an event that brought a prosecution against the publisher and made the poem the touchstone of the republican press through the mid-century.
works.characters: the fairy queen of dreams; Ianthe, the lover visited by the vision; the ghosts of kings and priests; the spirit of nature; the poet's own address to his country
works.structure: Nine cantos of visionary travel, opened and closed by the framework of the dream and the waking, with a sustained apparatus of prose notes that carries much of the philosophical argument independently of the verse.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author disowned the poem in later years in a letter, and the text exists in the private first issue and in the pirated and collected editions of the 1820s and 1830s, with substantial differences.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment

movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: Queen Victoria
works.description: The finest short life in English: Victoria, Albert, Melbourne and Disraeli, and the private life behind the public monument. It is a prose work of 1921 by Lytton Strachey; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Biography and the Modern Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Strachey follows Victoria from a lonely childhood through the accession, the domination of Lord Melbourne, the marriage to Albert, the widowhood of forty years, the highland servant John Brown, the Indian secretary Disraeli and the Diamond Jubilee, ending with her death in 1901.
works.significance: Queen Victoria is the most admired short life in English and won the James Tait Black Prize: it made the Victorian age intelligible as a private life and established the modern literary biography as an art.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. works.title: Quicksand
works.description: Larsen's first novel: a mixed-race woman's search for a place and a self. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Nella Larsen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Helga Crane, the daughter of a Danish mother and a Black father, leaves her teaching post in the South, moves to Harlem, to Denmark and back again, searching for a home and a self, and ends in a disastrous marriage and childbirth in the rural South.
works.significance: Quicksand is one of the great novels of the Harlem Renaissance and the finest novel of the mixed-race woman's search for a self: its portrait of Helga Crane made Larsen the central novelist of the movement and the book the founding text of the literature of racial ambiguity.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the short novel of the interior life.
works.context: The United States, Harlem and Denmark in the 1920s. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: Rachel Dyer
altTitles: Rachel Dyer: A North American Story
works.form: American Gothic tale and historical romance of the colonial period
works.description: The most notorious of the author's early romances and the one he defended as a declaration of literary independence in a prefatory manifesto. It is a Gothic tale of colonial North America, moving between the province, the sea and the Indian country. Its style of violent compression and its refusal of moral decorum made it a scandal and a landmark.
works.plot: A young woman of the province is bound by affection and by circumstance to men whose loyalties are divided between settlement, sea and war, and the narrative pursues her through capture, disguise and catastrophe. The colonial Indian war supplies the machinery of pursuit and reprisal by which the characters are tested. A tale of the ocean runs alongside the provincial story, giving the book its sense of a continent in motion. The action closes in death and in exposure of the hypocrisy that caused it.
works.significance: It is the central text of the author's programme of literary independence and the boldest American Gothic of the 1820s. Its theory of style, delivered in its prefatory argument, anticipated later American experimental prose. Its treatment of colonial violence gives it a place in the history of the Indian romance.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at Portland, Maine, in 1828, in the season of the removal debate and of the American Gothic's return after its 1790s vogue. Its prefatory manifesto answers the British review criticism with which its author had been engaged for four years. The book is the earliest of the American romances to treat colonial war as Gothic matter.
works.structure: Third-person Gothic romance with alternating provincial, maritime and Indian-war lines of action, introduced by an ironical unpublished preface that states the author's programme.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.title: Ralph Roister Doister
works.description: Nicholas Udall's five-act comedy of the braggart Ralph Roister Doister, written c. 1552–54 and printed c. 1566–67; generally regarded as the first English comedy.
works.plot: Ralph Roister Doister, a vainglorious suitor encouraged by the parasite Merrygreek, woos Dame Christian Custance, who is betrothed to the merchant Gawin Goodluck; his letters and verses are read to her as insults, and his siege of her house ends in a comic battle with her maids, the braggart routed by a broom; the play closes with the lovers reunited and Roister Doister invited to dinner — folly corrected without malice.
works.significance: The first English comedy: it transplants the Roman braggart soldier and parasite into a London setting, joins classical form to native farce, and inaugurates the line that runs through Gammer Gurton's Needle to Shakespeare and Jonson.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with songs
works.context: Written c. 1552–54, probably for performance by the boys of Westminster School (Udall was headmaster there from 1555, earlier at Eton); drawing on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus and Terence's Eunuchus, it belongs to the academic revival of Roman comedy that would produce Gammer Gurton's Needle and the school drama of the 1560s.
works.characters: Ralph Roister Doister; Matthew Merrygreek; Dame Christian Custance; Gawin Goodluck; Tristram Trusty; Madge Mumblecrust; Tibet Talkapace; Annot Alyface
works.structure: Five acts modelled on the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence, with a braggart soldier, a parasite, and a reunion plot; the action is domestic and the verse a rollicking doggerel.

works.title: Ramona
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1884
works.description: The most widely read American novel about the Native American: a California romance of injustice. It is a prose fiction work of 1884 by Helen Hunt Jackson; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ramona, the orphaned daughter of a Scottish sailor and an Indian woman, is raised in the Moreno household in Southern California; she marries the Indian Alessandro, and the couple are driven from place to place by the seizure of Indian lands, ending in Alessandro's death and Ramona's marriage to the rancher Felipe.
works.significance: Ramona is the most widely read American novel about the Native American and the founding text of the California romance: it created the tourist literature of Southern California, it was adapted for film four times, and it did more than any other book to make the Indian cause visible to the American public.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary record of treaties and massacres.
works.context: Southern California in the 1870s, the missions, the Mexican ranchos and the seizure of Indian lands. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under sensation novel; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: Rationale of Judicial Evidence
works.form: legal and analytical treatise; jurisprudence of evidence with procedural reform
works.description: The great analytical assault on the rules of evidence as then administered, printed in five volumes at the close of the author's life from long-accumulated manuscripts. Its principle is that evidence is the arm of justice and that every rule which excludes true evidence, upon a presumption of untrustworthiness, sacrifices real justice to a fiction of law.
works.plot: The work begins by defining judicial evidence as the species of address by which the persuasion of the existence or non-existence of a fact is produced in the mind of the judge, and by distinguishing the substantial from the adjective, or the course of procedure by which it is conveyed. It then attacks the exclusionary system: the rules that shut out the testimony of interest, of parties, of convicts, of the unbelieving and of children, are shown to be at once illogical, since interest does not always corrupt veracity, and mischievous, since their operation is to defeat the just cause and to enrich the profession by the delay they cause. The positive part analyses the several classes of evidence, direct and circumstantial, real and personal, original and transmitted, with their several degrees of probative force, and it examines the arts of trustworthiness, the sanctions of oath and of punishment, and the securities of publicity, of oral examination, and of the free minutes of the judge. The closing argument is constitutional as well as forensic: that a system of evidence built for the benefit of the judges and of the fee-fund is incompatible with the greatest happiness of the community, and that the substitute must be the simple method of a natural procedure before a single judge with full publicity.
works.significance: It is one of the founders of the analytic study of evidence and of procedure, the book which first subjected the exclusionary rules to a systematic test of their consequences, and an ancestor of the nineteenth-century reform of pleading, of the witness rules, and of the modern law of evidence. As a style it is the extreme example of the legislative analytical manner, and its exposure of the 'fictions' and fee-interests of the law stands among the most sustained pieces of argumentative invective of the period.
works.meter: Pitiless, voluminous, satirical analysis: the endless subdivision, the reductio ad absurdum carried on for pages, the inventories of absurdity, and a comic indignation that treats the law as a system of organised delusion.
works.context: Printed in the year of the author's death and of the beginning of the great procedural reforms, out of manuscripts composed over decades in the interval of the parliamentary and law-reform agitation, and addressed to a public already trained by the review journals to expect a utilitarian criticism of the institutions of the common law. Its matter had appeared in part through a foreign recension before the English original was published.
works.structure: Five volumes in numbered books and chapters: the definition and division of evidence, the exhibition of the exclusionary rules with their exposed absurdities, the analysis of the several kinds and their probative tendencies, the securities for trustworthiness, and the plan of a non-exclusionary procedure.
works.attributionNotes: The substance is securely the author's; the printed arrangement was made from his manuscripts by another hand, and the relation between the English recension and the earlier foreign edition leaves the order of the published volumes partly an editorial construction.

works.title: Records of Woman
works.form: Collected volume of lyrics and short dramatic poems unified by a title design; the governing genres are the dramatic lyric in a woman's voice and the meditative address.
works.description: A volume taking its title from a design - to record the feelings and fortunes of womankind across history, romance and everyday life - and gathering the shorter poems that illustrate it. It consolidates its author's command of the woman's voice in a series of dramatic and meditative lyrics.
works.plot: Rather than narrate, the volume accumulates cases: poems that place a woman's constancy, jealousy, mourning or forbearance in specific historical and imaginary settings, from court to cottage. The title concept treats female feeling as a document with a history, and the individual poems serve as its entries. Several pieces urge the claims of the mind against the limited destinies allowed to women, while others rehearse the virtues of endurance and attachment in the language of affection. The volume closes with shorter occasional and devotional lyrics that soften the argument into resignation.
works.significance: Records of Woman gave the period one of its most borrowed series of female personae and fixed the association of its author's name with the anatomy of women's feeling. Its design licensed a generation of gift-book verse on woman's phases and destinies. The volume is also a test case for the recent reassessment of a reputation long dismissed as merely sentimental.
works.meter: Chiefly iambic lyrics in varied stanzas - common measure, eight-line speakers and refrained songs - with a freer, more spoken cadence in the dramatic pieces; the closed couplet is used where an argument settles as maxim.
works.context: The volume appeared in the same years in which its author's fame was being made by the annual and the magazine, and it drew a notable notice in the Edinburgh Review that treated its design as evidence of a distinct poetical class. It also entered the transatlantic market at once, in an American edition carrying editorial notes. Its subject matter answers the decade's argument about female education and moral agency without adopting the vocabulary of polemic.
works.structure: A sequence without a governing plot, organised as a series of records or cases each complete in itself, and distributed among lyrics, short dramatic addresses and reflective pieces; the title design supplies the principle of order.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Marriage and women's conduct
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
altTitles: The Recuyell of the Histories of Troy
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Raoul Lefèvre's French Recueil des histoires de Troyes, begun in Bruges in 1468 and completed in Cologne in 1471, and printed by Caxton at Bruges in 1473–74 as the first book printed in English. A courtly Troy compilation made for the Burgundian duchess Margaret of York, it inaugurated both Caxton's career and the English printed book.
works.plot: The compilation recounts the deeds of Hercules and the first destruction of Troy, then the rebuilding of the city under Priam and the second war — the rape of Helen, the battles before Troy, the deaths of Hector and Achilles, and the fall of the city through the wooden horse.
works.significance: The first book printed in English and the founding text of the English print tradition; its Troy matter carried the medieval romance of antiquity into the print era.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's early style, French-inflected and courtly, before his London plainness matured.
works.context: Begun in Bruges in 1468 for Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, and printed at Bruges c. 1473–74 — the first English printed book; Caxton's famous prologue records his despair over the labour of translation and the duchess's command to finish.
works.characters: Hercules; Jason; Priam; Hector; Achilles; Paris; Helen; Ulysses
works.structure: Three books in Lefèvre's arrangement, translated in full, with Caxton's prologue and epilogue recording the circumstances of its making.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's authorship of the translation and printing is documented in his own prologue and epilogue.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Warfare and battle

works.title: Red as a Rose Is She
works.description: Published in 1870 and the best of Broughton's early novels: the story of a high-spirited girl of small means whose passionate, quarrelsome love for a richer man survives pride, separation and a near-fatal illness.
works.plot: Esther Craye, a high-spirited girl of small means, meets St John Gerard on a country-house visit and falls passionately in love, though he is expected to marry the cold beauty Constance Blessington; quarrels, pride and Esther's poverty part them, she goes out to earn her own living, and only a near-fatal illness brings the lovers to marriage.
works.significance: Red as a Rose Is She is Broughton's sharpest study of the costs of feminine pride, and one of the first English novels to analyse the convention that a woman must not declare her love.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is first-person female narration with direct address to the reader.
works.context: The 1860s, the marriage market of the country house, and the code of feminine reticence that forbids a woman to speak first. The record dates the work as composed between 1869 and 1870 and first published in 1870 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Esther Craye; St John Gerard; Constance Blessington; Lady Gerard; St John's father
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Redemption
works.description: Blackmore's last large religious poem, a sacred epic of the redemption of mankind which carries the Miltonic measure of Creation into the history of the fall and the work of the Saviour.
works.plot: The poem reviews the fall of man and the promise of redemption, the training of the Old Testament and the coming, teaching and passion of Christ, and closes on the application of the saving work to the conscience of the reader.
works.significance: It completes the series by which the physico-theological and the sacred epic were attempted in Miltonic blank verse, and it documents the isolation of a once fashionable poet from the taste that had superseded him.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic manner, sustained through the longest of Blackmore's religious poems.
works.context: Published in the closing years of the century's first great quarrel over the poem of religion, when Blackmore's verse had long been the target of the Scribleran burlesque of the art of sinking.
works.characters: the poet; the redeeming Saviour; Satan; the figures of the Old and New Testament narrative
works.structure: A continuous sacred narrative in numbered books, with the theological reflection interposed in the poet's own voice.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey

works.title: Redwood
works.form: Sentimental and domestic novel; frontier tale of orphan discovery and recognition
works.description: A tale of an orphan girl brought from the wilds of the New Jersey forest into society, and the author's second novel. It combines the frontier story with the novel of sensibility and with an argument about inheritance and mistaken identity. Its forest scenes were among the first by a New England woman writer.
works.plot: A young woman brought up in the seclusion of the New Jersey pine barrens is thought strange and proud by the settlement around her, and her ignorance of her own parentage is the source of the story's distress. Neighbours and incomers try in turn to explain her, and her exposure to the wider world of cultivation and kindred tests her temper and her principles. The recovery of the family history that gives her a place is delayed by disclosures withheld until the later books. Recognition and marriage close the tale, and the wilderness is left behind.
works.significance: It consolidated the position of the New England domestic novel of the 1820s and gave the woman-made frontier tale its earliest form. Its contrast between forest society and polite society is a genuine contribution to the wilderness theme. Its London reprint is evidence of the transatlantic market the author later helped to build.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1824 in two volumes at New York and reprinted in London, part of the first wave of American fiction that found British publishers. Its New Jersey setting reflects the settlement and land disputes of the pine barrens. Its treatment of female independence continues the argument of the author's first novel.
works.structure: Third-person novel of education and recognition, with a wilderness first section and a social second section; letters and disclosures carry the argument of inheritance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed in later editions.
themes: Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
works.form: political pamphlet in the form of a letter; polemic with historical and constitutional argument
works.description: The most powerful and most quoted attack on the French Revolution, thrown out as a long private letter made public within weeks of its writing. It refuses to try any constitution by the abstract rights of man, and pleads instead for prescription, for the inherited liberties of England, and for the moral institutions through which a nation ages gracefully. Its lament for the queen of France and its prophecy of a military adventurer sitting in judgment upon a nation made the book the founding text of modern conservative thought.
works.plot: The argument opens by declining to congratulate the French on their new constitution, on the ground that the gift of abstract liberty to an unprepared people is a curse rather than a benefit. Against the rights of man it sets the rights of Englishmen, derived from an immemorial and prescriptive inheritance rather than from speculation, and it reads the Revolution of 1688 as a settlement of ancient law, not as the assertion of primitive freedom. Church, nobility, chivalry, and the landed interest are defended as the pillars that temper power and make subordination amiable; the confiscation of Church lands and the reduction of the clergy to a stipend are attacked as robbery dressed as reform. Where the abstractions triumph, the book predicts, the age of chivalry is gone, its successors a race of sophisters, economists, and calculators, and a degenerate democracy ends in the domination of an armed leader. The conclusion is an appeal to prejudice as a reasonable and social being, to the habitual sentiments that make a people warm to what the understanding alone could never make binding.
works.significance: It established the vocabulary and the stock arguments of counter-Revolutionary thought, and it is the source of the enduring ideas of prescriptive liberty, of society as a partnership between the living, the dead, and the unborn, and of the claim that a state built on abstract political geometry dissolves the local attachments through which liberty is actually felt. Its influence runs through nineteenth-century conservatism and through the romantic dislike of abstraction; its critics, from the vindicators of natural rights to the pamphleteers of the 1790s, framed the whole British debate over Revolution.
works.meter: Large periodic prose of the parliamentary and pulpit schools, Latinate balance, apostrophe, and indignant interrogation, with a sustained rhetorical range from dry legal analysis to elegiac lament.
works.context: Written in the spring and summer of 1790 in answer to a young correspondent's request for the author's sentiments, it broke with the Whig party and with the Society for Constitutional Information, and provoked an immediate swarm of replies, of which the most famous was the vindication of the rights of man published the next year. The celebration of the anniversary of the Bastille by a London dissenting congregation, whose sermon argued the right of a people to choose and to expel its rulers, supplied the occasion and the target of the whole book.
works.structure: A single sustained epistolary argument in no numbered divisions, rising from constitutional reasoning to prophecy, invective, and elegy; the set pieces on the queen of France and on the 'little platoons' of local attachment are structural climaxes rather than ornaments.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its manuscript and printing history is well attested by contemporary correspondence and by the publisher's records.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Order and degree: the body politic
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: Regularis Concordia
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century) and Cotton Faustina B.iii
works.description: The customary drawn up at the Council of Winchester (c. 970) under Æthelwold of Winchester to unify the observance of all English monasteries: a national supplement to the Rule of St Benedict, adapting continental customaries from Fleury and Ghent to English conditions and binding the reformed houses together under royal protection.
works.plot: The Concordia sets out the daily, weekly, and yearly round of the monastic life — the hours of prayer, the psalms and canticles, the ceremonies of the great feasts, the commemoration of the king and queen, and the dramatic rites of Holy Week, including the earliest recorded Visitatio Sepulchri (the 'Quem quaeritis' dialogue) in England.
works.significance: The founding document of the unified English monasticism of the late tenth century, and the source of the earliest English dramatic text (the Visitatio Sepulchri), making it a landmark in the history of English theatre as well as of monasticism.
works.context: Produced at the high point of the Benedictine Reform under King Edgar (959-975), the Concordia institutionalized the alliance of crown and monastery: the king and queen are commemorated in the daily office, and the text was issued with royal authority for all houses.
works.structure: A prologue addressed to King Edgar, followed by a systematic customary organized by the liturgical day and year; the prescriptions culminate in the elaborated rites of the Triduum, with the dialogue of the three Marys and the angel at the Easter sepulchre.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Æthelwold of Winchester, who names himself as the compiler; the text is securely attributed.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Mission, conversion, and the Church
Monasticism and the religious life
movements: Benedictine Reform

works.title: Religio Laici
altTitles: Religio Laici: or, A Layman's Faith
works.description: Dryden's philosophical poem defending the Anglican via media against both Catholic tradition and Protestant private judgement, written while he was still a conforming member of the Church of England.
works.plot: The poem argues that Scripture is the sole rule of faith but is obscure in places, that private interpretation leads to chaos, and that the established church's tradition supplies the necessary authority.
works.significance: A key text in the history of English apologetics and the immediate predecessor of Pope's Essay on Man; it also marks the religious position Dryden abandoned when he converted to Catholicism in 1685-6.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, deliberately roughened, with frequent alexandrines and triplets.
works.context: Published in November 1682, after Dryden's translation of Simon's Criticial History; it responds to the Deist and Socinian challenge to revelation.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative poem with a prose preface defending its 'fugitive' method and rough verse.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Religio Medici
altTitles: Religio Medici: Its Author's Name is Thomas Browne
works.description: Sir Thomas Browne's meditative confession of faith, written privately in the 1630s and pirated in 1642 before Browne issued his own authorised text in 1643; it is the founding work of English introspective prose.
works.plot: In two parts Browne sets out his religious faith and his moral philosophy: the first defends his adherence to the Church of England against the charges of atheism and scepticism, the second explores charity and the duty to one's neighbour.
works.significance: The most influential work of English prose of the seventeenth century after the Authorised Bible; it created the genre of the personal religious meditation in prose and influenced Montaigne's English readers, Coleridge, Lamb, and Virginia Woolf.
works.meter: A richly Latinate, periodic prose with a strong personal cadence; Browne's style became the model of English 'character' writing.
works.context: Written while Browne was practising medicine, probably in the late 1630s; circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent in 1642, then authorised in 1643 with his own preface.
works.structure: Two parts of continuous meditative prose without formal division into chapters in the first edition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; he authorised the 1643 edition after the pirated 1642 printing.

works.title: Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality, the Sure Foundation on Which We Must Build
altTitles: Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality
works.form: Religious polemic and sermon-lecture in pamphlet form: the address to a community, blending the jeremiad, the reform programme and the testimony of personal experience.
works.description: A twelve-page Boston pamphlet, the first published work by the woman who became the first American Black woman to speak publicly to a mixed audience of men and women. It fuses the sermon, the address to a community and the abolitionist complaint into a single urgent appeal for self-improvement, education, industry and religious sincerity among free Black Americans. Its argument turns on the claim that prejudice against Black people will abate only when the community's own conduct, learning and piety refute it. It closes with a prophecy of racial justice that borrows the cadences of the Jeremiah style.
works.plot: The address opens by defining true religion as inseparable from pure morality, and insists that profession without practice is worthless before God. It then indicts the conditions of the free Black community: ignorance, dissipation, disrespect among spouses and the failure to send children to school, while counting against it the poverty and prejudice that made such failures predictable. Against the colonisation argument that Black Americans should leave the United States, it asserts their birthright in the country and their claim to its promises, and it praises Black industry, seafaring and the churches already built. It urges the founding of schools, a moral reform society and a savings institution, and it defends the right of women to speak and write in public as a religious duty. The conclusion declares that the day of deliverance is coming and that the oppressed must prepare themselves for it morally and intellectually.
works.significance: It is the founding text of African American women's political writing, the first published work by a Black American woman to argue at once against slavery, against racial prejudice and against the exclusion of women from public speech. Its blending of the jeremiad with a practical reform programme set a pattern for the agitation literature of the 1830s and 1840s, and its frank defence of women's right to speak anticipates the feminism of the abolitionist movement.
works.meter: Elevated vernacular prose with strong biblical rhythm, parallelism and direct apostrophe; no verse.
works.context: Published in Boston in 1831, the year of a great slave insurrection in Virginia and of intensified repression of Black meeting and literacy in the states, and in a city where a free Black community supported abolitionist societies, churches, schools and a weekly press. The pamphlet circulated through abolitionist channels and was the author's opening move in a season of public lectures that followed in 1832 and 1833, after which she retired from the platform under attack.
works.structure: Continuous exhortation in one movement: scriptural opening, indictment of the community, answer to prejudice and colonisation, practical programme of schools and moral reform, prophetic close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is certain; the pamphlet was published over the author's name and has been repeatedly reprinted in modern editions of her speeches and writings.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Religious persecution and martyrdom
The slave trade and abolition
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry
works.form: Anthology of editorial collection: ballads, songs, romances and fragments, printed with preface, essays, arguments, annotations and glossary; the founding model of the scholarly-popular national anthology.
works.description: Thomas Percy's three-volume collection of early English ballads, songs and other poetical remains, with prefatory essays, historical and critical notes and a life of several of the old poets: the book that made the native ballad tradition available to the polite reader and turned it into a subject of criticism. It drew on a recovered manuscript folio of ballads and on printed copies, and it presented the material in a carefully arranged historical order. Its editorial practice, modernising and repairing the old texts, was at once its popular strength and the ground of the quarrel about it.
works.plot: As a collection its argument is a history of English poetry told in specimens: that the native tradition, from the minstrelsy of the north through the ballad and the romance, possessed a genuine pathos, harmony and strength of description which the later 'polite' age undervalued. The volumes interleave heroic songs, ballads of love and chivalry, fragments of old romance, and pieces of lyric and devotional poetry, with critical remarks on each and with the famous defence of the 'antient' poets in the prefacial essay on minstrelsy. Percy also let the reader see the editorial hand: texts were amended, completed from other copies, and in places composed or interpolated where the original was judged defective, in the belief that he was restoring an ancient author's meaning. The collection thus argues two things at once, that English poetry has an ancient native inheritance, and that a modern editor of taste is its rightful guardian.
works.significance: It is the single most influential book of old English poetry of the century: it formed the taste of the Romantic poets for the ballad, revived the native tradition as a source of poetical pleasure, and established the anthology-with-notes as a critical genre. Both its method and its materials were answered and extended by later collectors, and its influence on the ballad revivals of the 1780s and 1790s is direct.
works.meter: The whole range of early English verse as Percy understood it: ballad stanzas of common and of long measure, the stanzaic forms of the native romance, and the several kinds of old English verse he set out to distinguish; the printed texts are smoothed toward modern regularity.
works.context: It appears at the centre of the 1760s revival of interest in national antiquity, alongside Chatterton's Rowley forgeries, Macpherson's Ossian and the debates over primitive genius, and it was edited by a clergyman-antiquary with patrons in the great houses, later himself a bishop in Ireland. Its appearance also coincides with the quarrel over editorial fidelity, in which Percy was attacked for modernising and for pretending to restore what he had in fact rewritten.
works.characters: The anonymous and named old poets and 'minstrels' whose songs are collected; the editors and printers whose copies are collated; Percy himself as the arranging and annotating voice
works.structure: A chronological and thematic anthology in three volumes, each book of specimens preceded or followed by historical and critical observation, with a preliminary essay and with notes, glossaries and life accounts attached to individual pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Percy is the editor and the responsibility for the arrangement, essays and the amended texts is his; the individual poems are of course anonymous and attributed within the volumes with varying degrees of confidence. Some pieces were printed from the folio manuscript he recovered, others from broadsides and earlier copies, and a number were repaired or completed by the editor, which is the notorious part of the book's attribution history.

Primitive genius and national poetry

works.title: Remarks on Several Parts of Paradise Lost
works.description: Addison's serial criticism of Milton's epic, first conducted as papers in The Spectator: it reads Paradise Lost as a work of sublime original genius disciplined by scriptural and classical learning, and defends its machinery, its diction and its allegory against the objections of the French neoclassical rules.
works.plot: Successive remarks take the fable, the characters, the machinery of angels, the episodes of limbo and of Pandemonium, the similes and the versification, arguing that Milton's faults are those of a genius and that his subject gives him a sublimity the classical epics could not reach.
works.significance: It established the Augustan rehabilitation of Milton and, through its account of the sublime and of allegorical machinery, supplied the vocabulary that later eighteenth-century criticism and the graveyard poets inherited.
works.meter: Prose of exemplary periodic balance, continuously reinforced by quoted hexameter and couplet passages from Milton and the ancients.
works.context: Delivered in the year of the quarrel over the unities and over the value of blank verse, when Tonson's cheap Milton and Dennis's and Bentley's rival criticisms made the national epic a contested property.
works.structure: A linked sequence of short critical dissertations, one per paper, each opening on a passage and closing with a general rule of taste.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested Addison; a single passage's share has occasionally been queried by bibliographers of the joint paper.

Wisdom and learning

works.title: Renaissance in Italy
works.form: Historical and critical study in seven volumes
works.description: Published in seven volumes between 1875 and 1886 and the first comprehensive English history of the Italian Renaissance: the age of the despots, the revival of learning, the fine arts, Italian literature, and the Catholic reaction.
works.plot: Symonds traces the Renaissance from the city-states of the fourteenth century through the recovery of the classics to the arts and literature of the sixteenth, and ends with the Counter-Reformation and the extinction of the Renaissance spirit in Italy.
works.significance: Renaissance in Italy made the Renaissance an English literary subject and shaped the aesthetic movement's image of Italy; it was the standard English account for half a century and the direct inspiration for Pater, Wilde and the whole 1890s cult of the Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is historical narrative on a large scale.
works.context: The 1870s-80s, the Victorian cult of the Renaissance, the unification of Italy, and the new German scholarship of Burckhardt. The record dates the work as composed between 1872 and 1886 and first published in 1875 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature; Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. A. Symonds. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Representative Men
works.description: Published in 1850 and the fullest statement of Emerson's theory of great men: studies of Plato, Swedenborg, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Napoleon and Goethe. It is a prose work of 1850 by Ralph Waldo Emerson; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Emerson argues that each great man is a 'representative' of a faculty or an idea — the philosopher, the mystic, the sceptic, the poet, the man of the world, the writer — and that the study of great persons is the study of what the age needed and produced.
works.significance: Representative Men is the central American statement of the philosophy of great men and a key text in the American reception of European culture; its essays on Montaigne and Shakespeare are among the best short criticism of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address.
works.context: The 1840s, the American lecture circuit, the Carlylean cult of the hero, and the democratic objection to hero-worship. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Waldo Emerson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Required Writing: Miscellaneous Pieces 1955-1982
works.description: Required Writing collects Philip Larkin's prose from 1955 to 1982: reviews, essays, introductions, statements on his own poetry and interviews, published by Faber and Faber in 1983.
works.summary: Autobiographical pieces such as "Not the Place's Fault", about his Coventry childhood; statements of poetics including "The Pleasure Principle"; reviews and essays on Thomas Hardy, John Betjeman, W. H. Auden, Wilfred Owen and Barbara Pym; and interviews, among them the Paris Review interview of 1982.
works.plot: The pieces set out the convictions behind Larkin's poetry: that a poem must give pleasure, that it begins in an emotion the poet wants to preserve, and that modernism severed art from its audience. His reviews champion Hardy's poetry and Betjeman's, regret the decline of the later Auden in "What's Become of Wystan?", and help revive the reputation of the novelist Barbara Pym. The interviews present the poet's carefully guarded public persona, ironic and self-deprecating.
works.significance: The main source for Larkin's poetics and critical opinions; the New World Encyclopedia singles it out as the most nuanced expression of his scepticism about modernism.
works.meter: Lucid, witty and direct prose, marked by the same irony and comic timing as the poems.
works.context: Published in the last years of Larkin's life, when he was writing very little poetry and was treated as an unofficial laureate.
works.structure: Pieces grouped by kind, with autobiographical essays and interviews alongside reviews and introductions.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Nationhood and national identity

works.title: Researches in the South of Ireland
altTitles: Researches in the South of Ireland, Illustrative of the Scenery, Character, Popular Remains, and Traditions of the County Cork
works.form: Local Guide and Topographical Prose; Travel and Wonders Literature
works.description: A quarto record of excursions made through the south of Ireland between 1812 and 1822, published in 1824 with plates and with an advertisement stating the humble pretensions of a book that is little more than an arrangement of note-books. It collects scenery, cabin life, the remains of the old churches and round towers, the fishery, the fairs and patterns, and the songs and legends taken down from speakers. The book is the foundation of its author's reputation as the gatherer of southern Irish tradition.
works.plot: The work moves through the counties of the south in a series of topographical and antiquarian excursions, describing the coast, the castle, the abbey, and the cabin with equal attention, and transcribing the songs, the coronach or lament, and the stories that the tours collected. Its most discussed material is the living peasant tradition: the fairy and churchyard tales, the wandering musicians, the hedge-school, the pattern, and the practice of the fishery. The author's method is accumulative and illustrative rather than argumentative, and his notes supply the evidence that his later legends were rewritten into.
works.significance: The Researches is the principal English-language record of south-Irish traditional culture made before the Famine and the source-book for the author's subsequent fairy legends; it established the model of the illustrated folklorist tour and supplied a body of material that the Celtic revivals of the later century drew upon. Its transcriptions of lament and song are early examples of field collection in Ireland.
works.context: Grown out of collecting journeys begun before the author took a clerkship in a government office, and published in the decade of the picturesque tour, of the society antiquarian movement, and of the first serious attention to Irish peasant song after the collections of the earlier century. The volume's illustrations were drawn by an artist who afterwards became the author's wife.
works.structure: A travel-and-antiquarian survey organised by excursion and by subject rather than by continuous narrative, with plates, transcribed songs, and appended notes on local remains.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the illustrations and a portion of the topographical matter are the work of cooperating artists and friends, as the advertisement allows.
themes: Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Researches, Chemical and Philosophical
altTitles: Researches, Chemical and Philosophical; Chiefly Concerning Nitrous Oxide, or Gaseous Oxide of Nitrogen
works.form: experimental reports and scientific treatise; medical and chemical writing with self-observation
works.description: The early volume of experiments which made its author's reputation, gathered from the work of a Bristol institution founded for the medical use of the new air, and chiefly concerning the gaseous oxide of nitrogen. It records the inhalations made upon the author's own body and upon his friends, the history of the compound and of its elements, and the observations on respiration and on animal heat which were the beginning of his chemical philosophy.
works.plot: The researches first state the composition and the properties of nitrous oxide, the proportions of its elements and the proofs of its nature, and then give an account of the machine and the method by which the gas was prepared and administered at the institution. The largest part is the record of the inhalations: the sensations produced, the elevation of the imagination, the vivid pleasure, the loss of the sense of time and of place, and the different effects upon different constitutions, all set down with a frankness of self-observation unusual in scientific writing. From these the author draws the practical inference that the power of the gas over sensation may be turned to the relief of pain, and the note that it may perhaps be used with advantage in surgical operations is the most quoted sentence in the book. The closing papers extend the inquiry to respiration, to the source of animal heat, and to the union of the gases with oxygen, and they state the general doctrine, afterwards to be the frame of his chemistry, that the changes of bodies are the result of the attractions of their parts and of the electrical powers of their elements.
works.significance: It is at once a founding document of electro-chemistry and of the physiology of respiration, and one of the most remarkable books of the age for its frank registration of altered consciousness; the suggestion of anaesthesia in its pages became one of the great unfinished chapters of medical history, and its accounts of the visions and the elevated feeling of the gas have made it a standing document in the history of the romantic interest in the alternations of the mind.
works.meter: A curious mixture of the technical memorandum and the lyrical report of sensation: plain experimental prose interrupted by passages of rapturous self-analysis, in the language of the philosophy of feeling as well as of the laboratory.
works.context: Issued at Bristol from the Pneumatic Institution founded by a physician for the trial of the new gases in disease, and written during the years when the author, a young apprentice to the trade, was making the experiments that carried him to the metropolitan lectureship. Its subject lay on the border of chemistry, medicine, and the psychology of sensation, and its publication fixed the reputation of the school of the new air.
works.structure: A single volume of separate papers and memorandum-records: the chemical history of the gas, the series of inhalations with their reported sensations, the concluding medical and physiological observations, and the appendix of the experimental details.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the records of the inhalations were partly kept with the help of the institution's assistants, and the clinical cases reported were in part those of other practitioners, as the volume itself states.
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Medicine, healing, and the body
The New Science and experimental philosophy
movements: The New Science and the Royal Society

works.title: Resignation
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A first-person penitential prayer in which the speaker, an exile and outcast from his lord's favour, submits himself wholly to God's will and prays for guidance through the storms of life. The poem fuses the secular conventions of the exile's lament with Christian devotion.
works.plot: The speaker, alienated from his earthly lord and wandering in misery, turns to God as his true protector, acknowledging that he has suffered for his sins, and prays for wisdom, steadfastness, and a safe passage through life's sea of troubles to the heavenly home.
works.significance: A major example of the Old English religious lyric's absorption of elegiac conventions, and a witness to the penitential spirituality of late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Standard alliterative long line with the formulaic diction of the elegiac tradition; the poem is textually imperfect, with apparent lacunae.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English religious lyric, where the conventions of heroic exile poetry were appropriated for penitential devotion; comparable to The Wife's Lament in its fusion of personal loss and landscape imagery.
works.structure: A sustained first-person prayer in which the imagery of exile, sea-voyage, and homelessness is progressively reinterpreted as the soul's spiritual condition; some editors detect a break in the middle of the text suggesting an incomplete or composite poem.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The title 'Resignation' is an editorial convenience, not in the manuscript.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Exile and homelessness
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: Resolution and Independence
works.form: Conversation poem and meditative lyric on the model of the earlier dialogue with a rustic; the poem's argument is the recovery of the mind from dejection by the observation of endurance.
works.description: A long narrative-and-mediation lyric recording a meeting with an aged leech-gatherer on a bare Highland moor in the winter of 1802, and the effect of that meeting on a mind troubled by fears of its own destiny. The poem is at once a picture of solitary labour and a debate within the speaker's own breast, in which the old man's uncomplaining endurance becomes a rebuke and a support. It is the clearest example of the conversation poem raised to the length and weight of meditation.
works.plot: The poem opens with weather and with the speaker's own agitated moods: after a storm and a shining morning the poet asks why, if nature's plan for the animal is content, human hope should be tortured by fear of the morrow, and dwells on the sad and anxious thoughts that have followed him from infancy. On the moor he encounters a very old man, bent and blind, who supports himself by gathering leeches from the pools with a staff and a light, labouring day after day without help from man or boy. The speaker addresses him twice, and the old man answers in a plain account of his means and of his patience, repeating the same words in the same manner; the poem ends with the charge to himself to be strong and resolute, and to be warned and healed by the simple sight of that unhelped old man, whom the speaker figures as a type appointed by providence to test and steady the wavering mind.
works.significance: A central poem of the period's account of how another person's plain speech can repair the poet's own mind, and the most discussed instance of the Romantic representation of age, poverty and stoical labour. Later criticism has made it a test case for the questions of whether such a figure is observed or invented, and of what the poem's rhetoric does to the voice of the man it consoles itself with.
works.meter: A long series of short stanzas of mixed four- and three-beat iambic lines with an insistent rhyme pattern, the regularity being used to register the old man's unwavering repetition against the more agitated syntax of the opening meditation.
works.context: Written in January 1802 immediately after a meeting recorded in the same terms in the journal kept by the poet's sister, during a winter of fear for his own future and of anxiety about the fate of the revolutionary hope of his youth; the leech-gatherer's trade reflects the medical demand of the day, and the poem belongs to the group of moor and road encounters made out of the walking tours of the north.
works.characters: The aged leech-gatherer, blind and staff-supported; the solitary poet-speaker who questions him
works.structure: A three-part design: an outdoor prelude of weather and of personal doubt, a central encounter written largely as dialogue and reported speech, and a closing application in which the figure is read as a vision or sent agent. The repetition of the old man's words at two points in the encounter is the structural hinge of the poem.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the companion sonnet addressed to the same encounter is sometimes printed with it.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Respublica
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality play of the commonwealth, written for performance at Christmas 1553 during the first months of Mary I's reign; a sophisticated political allegory of the misgovernment of the 1540s.
works.plot: Respublica, the widowed commonwealth, is robbed by Avarice and his crew — Oppression, Adulation, and Insolence (disguised as Policy, Honesty, and Authority) — who plunder her goods and divide them among themselves; the four sisters People, Verity, Peace, and Justice return, strip the thieves of their disguises, and restore the commonwealth, with Mercy pronouncing judgement and the audience promised amendment under the new queen.
works.significance: The most politically sophisticated of the sixteenth-century moralities: its allegory of the commonwealth, its disguised Vices, and its address to the monarch anticipate the political drama of the Elizabethan stage, and it documents the mid-Tudor crisis of counsel and plunder.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic speeches
works.context: Performed at Christmas 1553, evidently by a company of boys, in the first months of Mary's reign; the play's allegory of the plunder of the commonwealth under Edward VI's ministers (Somerset and Northumberland) and its restoration under the Catholic queen marks a rare moment when the morality tradition served immediate dynastic politics.
works.characters: Respublica; Avarice; Adulation; Oppression; Insolence; People; Verity; Peace; Justice; Mercy; Nemesis
works.structure: Five acts of morality allegory applied to contemporary politics, with the Vice Avarice doubling his disguises and a final scene of restoration and loyal address to Mary I.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named in the manuscript; Nicholas Udall has been proposed by some scholars, but the attribution remains unproven, and the work is treated as anonymous.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: Reuben Sachs: A Sketch
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1888 and the first sustained English novel of Anglo-Jewish middle-class life: a satire of a prosperous London Jewish family and the love story of a clever woman and an ambitious politician.
works.plot: Judith Quixano, educated and passionate, loves Reuben Sachs, a rising Conservative politician determined to marry money and position; the family's marriage market and the pressures of the community defeat them both, and the novel ends with Reuben's engagement to a rich heiress and Judith's retreat into illness and faith.
works.significance: Reuben Sachs is a landmark of English-Jewish literature: the first English novel to describe the Anglo-Jewish middle class from inside, and one of the first to analyse the position of the Jewish woman between community and modernity. Its reception — condemned by the Jewish press as a betrayal — is itself a chapter in the history of English Jewish identity.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is metrical accomplishment in traditional forms (sonnet, ballad, dramatic monologue).
works.context: The 1880s, the Anglo-Jewish gentry of Bayswater and Maida Vale, the debate on assimilation, and the first wave of Jewish immigration from eastern Europe. The record dates the work as composed in 1888 and first published in 1888 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Judith Quixano; Reuben Sachs; Leopold Leuniger; Esther Sachs; Rose Quixano; Bertie Lee-Harrison; the Cohen family
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
Regional identity and the American sectional character
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: Revaluation
works.form: Critical study (the revaluation of the English poets)
works.description: The study that revalued the English poetic tradition from Jonson to the moderns. It is a prose work of 1936 by F. R. Leavis; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Revaluation carries the revaluation across the English poetic tradition - Jonson, Donne and the line of wit, Milton's verse, Pope and the Augustans, Wordsworth, Shelley and Keats - and fixes the canon of the verse in the judgments of the Scrutiny critic.
works.significance: Revaluation fixed the canon of the English verse for the Scrutiny generation: its judgments from Jonson to the moderns made the revaluation the method of the literary history and remain the standard statement of the Leavisite canon.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical sentence of the moral urgency.
works.context: Cambridge in 1936, and the canon of the English verse. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.characters: Ben Jonson; John Donne; Andrew Marvell; John Milton; Alexander Pope; William Wordsworth; Percy Bysshe Shelley; John Keats
works.structure: A study in essays, one poet or one question to an essay. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Revelations of Divine Love
works.description: Julian of Norwich's account of the sixteen revelations ('showings') she received during a grave illness on 8 May 1373, in two versions — the Short Text written soon after, and the Long Text, the fruit of some twenty years of meditation, completed c. 1393. Its theology of divine love — 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — and of Jesus as mother makes it the greatest work of English mysticism and the first book in English known to be by a woman.
works.plot: At the point of death, the thirty-year-old Julian receives a series of visions of Christ's Passion, the Virgin, the world's littleness (the hazelnut), and the Lord's meaning: that love is his meaning; the Long Text unfolds these showings into a theology of sin, suffering, divine motherhood, and the 'great deed' by which all shall be made well.
works.significance: The summit of the English mystical tradition: the first major theological work by an English woman, and a text of the first importance for the history of women's writing and of Christian theology.
works.meter: Plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; homely images (the hazelnut) carrying speculative theology.
works.context: The showings occurred in Norwich on 8 May 1373; Julian became an anchoress at St Julian's church and wrote the Short Text shortly after and the Long Text c. 1393; Margery Kempe visited her c. 1413; the Long Text circulated in manuscript and in the printed editions of Serenus Cressy (1670).
works.characters: Julian (visionary); Christ; the Virgin Mary; the fiend
works.structure: Eighty-six (or more) chapters of vision, exposition, and prayer, organized by the order of the showings and the decades of their meditation.
works.attributionNotes: The author is known only as Julian of Norwich (from her church); her name in the world is unknown.
themes: Consolation and endurance
The Passion of Christ

works.title: Revelations of the Dead-Alive
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: A tale of premature burial published in 1824, in which a man laid out and consigned to the grave returns to life unseen and learns what the living really think of him. The book is a domestic romance of a trading town, and its machinery of the coffin, the vault, and the resumption of identity makes it one of the earliest English prose treatments of the dead-alive subject. Its exposure of the greed that waits on a supposed death gives it a place in the lineage that runs from the Gothic tale to sensation fiction.
works.plot: The hero, a man of substance in an Irish market town, is struck down and pronounced dead, and is laid in his coffin while the household settles into mourning that is mostly calculation. Restored to consciousness and to life within the place of burial, he escapes and keeps himself unknown, watching the conduct of those who had an interest in his death, and hearing their claims, hopes, and exposures. The later developments turn on the discovery of the living man, on the disappointment of the expecting heirs, and on the punishment or confoundment of those who had profited by the funeral. The tale's interest is the disclosure of character by the assurance that a man cannot hear it.
works.significance: Revelations of the Dead-Alive is an early and influential English treatment of the premature-burial terror as a device for social exposure rather than for simple horror, and it anticipates the resurrection plots of later sensation and detective fiction. It also shows the range of an author otherwise classified by his national tales.
works.context: Published between the author's tragedy and his Irish tales, in a decade much exercised by the fear of live burial, by the anatomy and the watch-house, and by the newspaper case of the coffin opened too late; the tale draws on a stock of popular terror already worked in periodical fiction and in the German tale. Its town setting belongs to the provincial Irish life the author was simultaneously putting into the O'Hara tales.
works.characters: the buried man who returns; the household and kinsfolk expecting his estate; the friends and creditors whose conduct the watch exposes; the town officers and undertakers of the funeral
works.structure: A continuous third-person tale of single design, built on the secret survival of the hero and on the successive revelations his observation produces; it closes with the public unmasking that the plot has deferred.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship and undisputed; the volume carries the writer's name and no share has been claimed for his brother or collaborators.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Fortune and mutability
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: Reynard the Fox
altTitles: The History of Reynard the Fox
The Historye of Reynart the Foxe
works.description: William Caxton's translation of the Dutch prose Reinaert de Vos, printed at Westminster in 1481: the beast epic of the fox Reynard, whose crimes are arraigned at the court of King Noble the lion, and whose cunning turns every accusation — and his own execution — into the ruin of his accusers. Caxton's print brought the European Reynard tradition to English readers and printers alike.
works.plot: Summoned to the lion's court to answer the complaints of the wolf Isengrim, the bear Bruin, and the other beasts, Reynard tricks each accuser in turn, confesses to save his neck, and is sent on pilgrimage only to murder his escort; his enemies' heads decorate his house, and the lion makes him his counsellor — the trickster triumphant.
works.significance: The classic English Reynard and the ancestor of the beast satire that runs through Spenser's Mother Hubberds Tale to the seventeenth-century Reynard reprints; a landmark of Caxton's publishing program.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's plain, lively narrative style at its best.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from the Dutch and printed in 1481, in the same year as his Godfrey of Boulogne; it fed a long English print tradition of Reynard editions and the beast satire of the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Reynard the Fox; King Noble the Lion; Isengrim the Wolf; Bruin the Bear; Tibert the Cat; Chanticleer the Cock
works.structure: A beast epic in episodic form: arraignment, defence, confession, and triumph, in the framework of the animals' court.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation documented in his own colophon.
