works.title: Rhymes for the Nursery
works.form: juvenile verse of the nursery rhyme and song
works.description: The successor of the infant poems, and the source of the most sung poem in the English-speaking nursery. It carries the verse for very young children a step further into the sheer fancy and the song, and it contains the little lyric of the wondering child before the distant light which became, set to an older air, the universal rhyme of childhood.
works.plot: The volume is a collection of short rhymes and songs for the nursery, of three kinds: the lyric of wonder and of the fancy, the little narrative of the child and the animal, and the rhyming lesson of the duty and the consequence. Its most famous poem addresses the distant twinkling light with the child's naked question, and passes from the wonder of the thing seen to the comparison of the small lamp of the evening and to the closing reverence of the maker; the pieces about it run through the sports, the pets, the seasons, and the small morals of the nursery day, in the smallest possible measure and with the emphasis always upon the sound and the repetition. The intention throughout is to give the child verse he can learn by ear, and to make the learning of the first words a pleasure rather than a task.
works.significance: It holds the single poem which is known, in some language or another, by more children than any other verse in the world, and it fixed the form of the nursery lyric of wonder, in which the child's question about the sky is asked without explanation; its little rhymes have been the first verse repeated by generation after generation of children, and its place in the history of the reading of the young is quite out of proportion to its size.
works.meter: Short rhymed couplets and stanzas of the song measure, in the trochaic and iambic swing of the rhyme meant to be sung or chanted; the emphasis on the sound, the reduplication, and the easy close.
works.context: Published in the year following the second volume of the infant poems, from the same juvenile trade and by the same two hands, in the season when the picture-book and the song-book for the very young child became a staple of the nursery and of the Sunday school. One of its lyrics was set almost at once to the continental air which has carried it round the world, and it has been translated into a great number of languages.
works.characters: The wondering child; the little creatures and companions of the nursery rhymes; the objects of the evening and of the garden
works.structure: A single volume of independent short rhymes, without argument or sequence of subjects, arranged in no order of matter but in the order of the reciter's pleasure and command of the words.
works.attributionNotes: The volume is the joint work of the two sisters, the greater number of the pieces being by the younger, whose lyrics have since been separated from her sister's by the family editors and by the history of the juvenile trade; the individual attribution of several rhymes has been variously reported in the reprints.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Rhymes of Childhood
works.description: Published in 1890 and the collection containing 'Little Orphant Annie': the classic American poems of childhood. It is a verse work of 1890 by James Whitcomb Riley; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poems present the world of the Indiana child — the orphan girl who tells ghost stories, the boy at the swimming hole, the child at the window on Christmas Eve, the old couple and the grandchild — in dialect narratives that move from comedy to sentiment and back.
works.significance: Rhymes of Childhood contains 'Little Orphant Annie', the most famous American children's poem of the century and a permanent part of American popular culture: the collection made Riley the national poet of childhood, and it is the essential document of the American small-town imagination before the machine.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse with exact phonetic spelling.
works.context: 1885-90: the American small town of the 1880s, the children's market for recitation verse, and the vogue of the dialect poem in the schools. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self

works.title: Richard II
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
works.description: Shakespeare's lyrical tragedy of deposition, opening the second tetralogy: Richard's misgovernment, the quarrel of Bolingbroke and Mowbray, and the king's fall from the throne of England — the first English history play written entirely in verse, culminating in Richard's murder at Pomfret and the new king's guilt.
works.plot: Richard banishes Bolingbroke and seizes his inheritance on Gaunt's death; Bolingbroke returns to claim his own, and the king's support melts away; in the deposition scene Richard unkings himself before Parliament; the plot of Aumerle is discovered, and Exton, reading Henry's wish, kills Richard in prison.
works.significance: The great English meditation on kingship, legitimacy, and the theatre of power — the seed of the Henriad that follows.
works.meter: Entirely in verse, much of it rhymed — Richard's elegiac lyricism is the play's signature music.
works.context: Written 1595 and printed 1597; the deposition scene was omitted from the early quartos for political reasons, and the play was notoriously performed on the eve of Essex's rising in 1601.
works.characters: King Richard II; Henry Bolingbroke; John of Gaunt; the Duke of York; the Duke of Aumerle; Thomas Mowbray; the Queen; Northumberland; the Bishop of Carlisle; Exton; the Gardener
works.structure: A five-act fall of princes, symmetrical in its structure of deposition, prophecy, and fulfilment, with the garden scene as the play's emblem of the commonwealth.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: Richard III
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
works.description: Shakespeare's first great tragedy, completing the first tetralogy: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, murders his way to the crown through his brothers, his nephews (the Princes in the Tower), and his allies, seducing and discarding Lady Anne along the way, until the ghosts of his victims curse him at Bosworth and Richmond's victory ends the Wars of the Roses and plants the Tudor line.
works.plot: Richard announces his villainy in the opening soliloquy, eliminates Clarence, Hastings, Buckingham, Rivers, and the young princes, weds Anne and then plans her death; at Bosworth the procession of ghosts damns him and blesses Richmond, who slays him and marries Elizabeth of York.
works.significance: The first fully achieved Shakespearean tragedy of character, and the role that has defined the tragic actor from Burbage to Olivier.
works.meter: A verse of rhetorical virtuosity — Richard's soliloquies are among the most quoted in the canon — with the stichomythia of the wooing scene.
works.context: Written about 1592–93 from More's History of King Richard III via the chronicles of Hall and Holinshed; the Tudor myth of Richard's monstrosity serves the founding ideology of the Elizabethan state.
works.characters: Richard, Duke of Gloucester (Richard III); the Duke of Buckingham; Lady Anne; Queen Elizabeth; Queen Margaret; the Duke of Clarence; Lord Hastings; King Edward IV; the Duchess of York; Henry, Earl of Richmond; the two young Princes
works.structure: A Senecan revenge-cum-chronicle play driven by Richard's direct address — the audience as confidant — and crowned by the symmetrical dream of ghosts.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Riders to the Sea
works.form: One-act tragedy (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 25 February 1904)
works.description: The perfect one-act tragedy in English: a mother in the Aran Islands loses her last son to the sea. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by J. M. Synge; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Verse Drama and the Poetic Play and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Maurya has lost six sons and her husband to the sea; her last son Bartley insists on taking the horses to the mainland fair. While he is gone, the body of her drowned son Michael is brought in, and Bartley is killed when his horse throws him into the sea; the play ends with Maurya's great lament.
works.significance: Riders to the Sea is the finest one-act tragedy in English: in twenty minutes it achieves the scale of Greek tragedy, its prose is the most musical in modern drama, and its lament is one of the great passages in Irish writing.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is a poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech.
works.context: The Aran Islands and the fishing economy of the Congested Districts; the keening tradition and the ritual lament of the Irish wake. The record dates the work as composed in 1903 and first published in 1904 and first performed in 1904 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; verse drama and the poetic play.
works.characters: Maurya; Bartley; Cathleen; Nora; the young priest; the women at the wake
works.structure: Single act in a cottage kitchen, with the offstage sea as the antagonist. The action is divided into acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edmund John Millington Synge. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Right Ho, Jeeves
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1934
works.description: The greatest Jeeves novel: Gussie Fink-Nottle, the prizes and the midnight in the garden. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by P. G. Wodehouse; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bertie Wooster arrives at Brinkley Court to find his aunt's household in chaos: Gussie Fink-Nottle cannot propose to Madeline Bassett, Tuppy Glossop has quarrelled with Angela, and Bertie's own attempts to help make everything worse until Jeeves, deprived of his fish, saves the day.
works.significance: Right Ho, Jeeves is the greatest of the Jeeves novels and one of the funniest books in English: its construction, its farce and its prose made it the model of the comic novel and the one Wodehouse book that is most often named as his masterpiece.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the elaborate comic plot of farce and coincidence.
works.context: Brinkley Court and the English country house of the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Jeeves; Bertie Wooster; Gussie Fink-Nottle; Madeline Bassett; Tuppy Glossop; Angela Travers; Aunt Dahlia
works.structure: A single comic narrative in the first person, over three days. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Pelham Grenville Wodehouse. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Rights of Man
altTitles: Rights of Man, Part the First and Part the Second
works.form: political pamphlet and treatise; polemic, constitutional scheme, and project of social provision
works.description: The great popular vindication of the French Revolution and of the rights of man, published in two parts, the first as an immediate answer to the counter-Revolutionary Reflections, the second as a systematic theory of government, a constitution for England, and a plan for public provision. It is the most widely read political book of the 1790s and the text that made its author a prosecution target in both countries.
works.plot: Part the first denies that one generation can bind another, holds that a nation has a right to model its constitution at pleasure, and treats the American settlements as proof that society can be rebuilt upon the rights of man; the ancient-constitutional pleading of the Reflections is met with ridicule and with the claim that the Revolution of 1688 was no such inheritance. Part the second sets out first principles: civil government is a delegate of natural rights, none of which are surrendered, and every institution that does not add to the aggregate happiness of the community is an usurpation. It then analyses hereditary government as a civil species of despotism, and proposes annual national parliaments, manhood suffrage on a modest franchise, the abolition of place and monopoly, and a scale of taxation that falls on property in proportion to its excess. The celebrated closing plan is a system of public allowances for every person at every age of life, for education, for the old, and for the young, to be paid by a graduated contribution and by the abolition of aristocratic perquisites, and the book ends with the argument that a government of this kind is a condition of peace among nations as well as of happiness at home.
works.significance: It is the founding text of popular radicalism in the English-speaking world and the strongest statement of natural-rights democracy between the American founding and the reform movement of the next century. Its second part, with its calculation that government is a national establishment for civil purposes and that the poor are creditors rather than objects of charity, shaped the language of welfare argument for a hundred years, and its style became the model of demotic political prose.
works.meter: Plain, direct, conversational prose addressed to the working reader, with sarcastic simplification of an opponent's argument, blunt arithmetic, and an evangelistic optimism of the new era.
works.context: Part the first appeared within weeks of the constitutional polemic it answered and was suppressed within months; part the second, published early in 1792, was followed by a prosecution for seditious writing, by the author's flight and outlawry, and by the arrests of the societies that circulated it. The book supplied the creed of the British radical societies and of the Corresponding Society, and it was answered by a literature of loyalist pamphlets.
works.structure: Two parts of very different scale: the first a brisk occasional reply, the second a systematic treatise of principles, of constitutions, of finance and of social provision in numbered chapters.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to the author of the political writings is secure, but the share taken by one philosophic friend of the author's Paris period in the composition of the first part is a standing question in the biography of the text; the second part is undivided.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

works.title: Rob Roy
altTitles: Rob Roy: A Tale of the Eighteenth Century
works.form: Historical novel and picaresque journey narrative; a commercial and domestic plot set in a time of armed rebellion.
works.description: A tale of the Jacobite rising of 1715 seen from the Lowlands, in which a young Glasgow-Jacobite-Whig merchant's son is drawn into the company of the outlaw chieftain and must repair a commercial fraud committed inside his own family. It is the most autobiographical of the series in its concern with credit, trade and the failure of paper, and the most romantic in its Highland scenery. Its hero-narrator tells his own story in retrospect.
works.plot: Francis Osbaldistone, refused by his father for refusing a counting-house career, is sent to the North to settle affairs with the stubborn tenant Andrew Fairservice, and finds the country in confusion as the Jacobite agents make their preparations. The outlaw Rob Roy, whose wife and children are quartered on the family, dominates the middle of the book; a mysterious player of the violin, in fact a nobleman in disguise, and the beautiful Diana Vernon, betrothed to another, give Francis the passions the plot cannot satisfy. His cousin Rashleigh, who has forged and stolen the title-deeds that ruin the family credit, is defeated at the lodgings in Osbaldistone Hall, the outlaw's justice is procured, the '15 breaks out and is lost, and the narrator is reconciled to trade and to a wife of his own station.
works.significance: Created the enduring image of the Highland outlaw as noble bandit and fixed the narrative of Jacobite Scotland for later fiction. Its pairing of a commercial plot with a romantic one makes it the most explicit treatment in the series of money as moral language. It is also the most quoted of the tales for its scenes of hospitality, cattle-feeding and clan mustering.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Scots Lowland speech for Fairservice and the Glasgow bailie, with Highland song and border ballad quoted in the notes.
works.context: Written in the year of the author's own brush with commercial failure, and much preoccupied with bills, credit and the ruin of a house, which is its real subject. The 1715 rising supplies the political framework, and the Highland-lowland relations of cattle, patronage and law are drawn from the records of the forfeited estates. Its publication at the end of 1817 was timed to the post-war depression that made its anxieties about solvent trading acute.
works.characters: Francis Osbaldistone; Robert 'Rob Roy' MacGregor; Bailie Nicol Jarvey; Diana Vernon; Rashleigh Osbaldistone; Andrew Fairservice; Hildebrand, the disguised fiddler
works.structure: First-person retrospective narrative by the hero, who reports his education and errors; the political rising is approached obliquely through commerce, hospitality and private fraud; explanatory notes and a later editorial preface record the tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; the personal author's name was first prefixed in the 1829-30 collected edition, for which a Memoir and Introduction were written.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Robert Elsmere
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1888
works.description: Published in 1888 and the central English novel of the Victorian crisis of faith: the story of a clergyman who loses his belief and finds a religion of social service. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Mary Augusta Ward; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Robert Elsmere, a young Oxford clergyman of the Broad Church school, falls in love with Catherine Leyburn, a woman of austere Evangelical faith; his reading of the German critics and his visit to the German universities destroy his belief in the resurrection, he resigns his living, and he founds a 'New Brotherhood' of social service in the East End, where he dies of overwork.
works.significance: Robert Elsmere was the most discussed novel of the 1880s and the central literary document of the Victorian religious crisis: it sold in enormous numbers, was preached against from pulpits across Britain and America, and its picture of the passage from faith to social service made it the representative novel of its decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of ideas with a large social canvas.
works.context: 1888: the Broad Church and the Lux Mundi group, the higher criticism of the Bible, the university settlement movement, and the Oxford of T. H. Green and Arnold Toynbee. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Robert Elsmere; Catherine Leyburn; Rose Leyburn; Agnes Leyburn; Squire Roger Wendover; Henry Grey; Edward Langham; Mrs Thornburgh; Hugh Flaxman; Madame de Netteville
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Humphry Ward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Robert Mannyng's Chronicle
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's verse history of England from Noah and the Trojan Brutus to the death of Edward I (1307), completed in 1338: the first part translates Wace's Roman de Brut, the second Peter Langtoft's French chronicle. It is the principal vernacular chronicle in English verse between Layamon and the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The poem narrates British and English history in sequence — Brutus, Arthur, the Saxon kings, the Norman Conquest, and the Plantagenet reigns — with particular fullness on the baronial wars of the thirteenth century.
works.significance: The chief English verse chronicle of the fourteenth century and a key witness to the national, vernacular historical consciousness of the period.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the first part, six-line tail-rhyme stanzas in the second.
works.context: Completed in 1338 by Mannyng, Gilbertine canon of Sempringham, at Sixhills, for the instruction of lay readers in English history; preserved in two manuscripts, BL Harley MS 1317 and Lambeth Palace MS 131.
works.characters: Arthur; the English kings from William I to Edward I; Simon de Montfort
works.structure: A two-part regnal chronicle (Brut section; Langtoft section) with patriotic and didactic digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Mannyng in the poem's own colophon.

works.title: Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner
works.form: novel; prose fiction in the form of a spiritual autobiography and travel relation
works.description: A first-person narrative of a mariner cast away for twenty-eight years on an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco, presented as a true history and a penitential life. It joins an extremely detailed account of material survival - building, planting, pottery, calendaring - to a providential reading of the narrator's own sins and mercies. Published in April 1719 and struck off in several issues that year, it made the individual survivor narrative the central plot of English prose fiction.
works.plot: Against his father's counsel of a middle station the York mariner sails, is taken by Sale pirates, escapes, plants a plantation in Brazil, and is wrecked in a course that leaves him sole survivor on a shore. He salvages the ship, builds a fence and a country house, learns by trial and error to make boards, earthenware, bread and goats' milk, keeps a journal, and reads scripture, gradually interpreting his preservation as conversion. He discovers a footprint, then cannibal feasts, saves a captive whom he names Friday, and with Friday and a Spaniard fights off further visitors. An English ship arriving after a mutiny carries him home by way of Brazil and land travel through hostile country, and the closing narrative reports his plantation wealth and a second, briefly summarised marriage.
works.significance: It established the material-realist individual narrative as the governing model of the rising English novel, and its treatment of labour, property, dominion and providence has made it the founding text for debates about middle-class identity, colonial possession and the philosophy of the isolated mind.
works.meter: Unornamented prose of the low or business style, with periodic sentences, accounting clauses, inventories and repeated temporal markers ('first', 'then', 'about'); the rhythm is documentary rather than rhetorical, and the couple of passages of elevated meditation are marked off by scriptural quotation.
works.context: Written in the spring and summer of 1719 out of real and romanced sources, including the marooned Alexander Selkirk, Spanish-American trade geography and the project-mongering literature of the 1690s, and printed in the same decade as the expansion of the plantation and slave trades. Its title-page assertion that the narrator is the author answered the contemporary vogue for detected 'memoirs'.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; Friday; Xury; the Portuguese captain of the Lisbon trade; the captain of the Brazil plantation; the mutineer mate; the Spaniard
works.structure: Continuous first-person retrospect, with embedded journal entries at the centre and a list-and-inventory mode of description; the frame of an edited 'original' account allows the narrator to comment on his own earlier blindness.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was published without the writer's name, and the two continuations, advertised as by the same hand, establish continuity of authorship.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Sea voyage and seafaring
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The slave trade and abolition
movements: The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: Rodman the Keeper: Southern Sketches
works.description: Woolson's Reconstruction stories: the Union keeper of a Southern cemetery and the ruined South. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Constance Fenimore Woolson; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Woolson's Southern stories — 'Rodman the Keeper', 'King David', 'Sister St Luke', 'The Andros Island' — written after her travels in the Reconstruction South, in which Northerners and Southerners meet in the cemeteries, the missions and the ruined plantations.
works.significance: Rodman the Keeper was the first substantial body of Northern fiction about the Reconstruction South and one of the finest American story collections of the century: its sympathy for the defeated and its refusal of caricature made it a landmark of American regionalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the regional sketch of the Great Lakes and the Sea Islands.
works.context: The Reconstruction South of the 1870s, the national cemeteries and the defeated Southern towns. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; war narrative of the common soldier.

works.structure: A collection of Southern sketches and stories. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Constance F. Woolson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Romeo and Juliet
altTitles: The Most Excellent and Lamentable Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
works.description: Shakespeare's lyric tragedy of young love: the star-crossed children of Verona's feuding houses meet at the Capulet feast, marry in secret, and are destroyed by chance and haste — the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, the exile, the sleeping potion, and the double suicide in the tomb that reconciles the houses too late.
works.plot: Romeo and Juliet fall in love across the family feud; Friar Laurence marries them; the street brawl kills Mercutio and Tybalt and exiles Romeo; the Capulets press Paris's suit; Juliet takes the friar's potion; the undelivered letter dooms the lovers; and the play ends with the discovery in the tomb and the prince's judgment on 'a glooming peace'.
works.significance: The archetype of the love tragedy in world literature — the play that fixed 'star-crossed lovers' in the language and on every subsequent stage and screen.
works.meter: The lovers' first dialogue is a shared sonnet; the play's verse runs from Mercutio's prose fantasia on Queen Mab to Juliet's aubade, with the final couplets of the tomb scene.
works.context: Written about 1595–96 from Arthur Brooke's poem Romeus and Juliet (1562) via continental novella; printed in quarto in 1597 and in a fuller text in 1599.
works.characters: Romeo; Juliet; Friar Laurence; Mercutio; Tybalt; the Nurse; Benvolio; Lord and Lady Capulet; Lord and Lady Montague; Paris; Prince Escalus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of accelerating momentum — comedy in the first two acts, catastrophe in the last — built on the sonnet-form exchanges of the lovers and the antitheses of love and hate.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Romola
works.description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from July 1862 to August 1863 and published in three volumes: Eliot's only historical novel, a study of Florence in the years of Savonarola (1492-98) and the most ambitious attempt by a Victorian novelist to reconstruct the Renaissance mind.
works.plot: Romola de' Bardi, the daughter of a blind classical scholar, marries the Greek adventurer Tito Melema, who betrays her father, her brother and her city; the novel follows her through the expulsion of the Medici, the preaching of Savonarola and the plague, her flight from Florence, and her return to a life of charity in the household of the Platonist Bardo.
works.significance: Romola is the most scholarly of Victorian historical novels and the fullest English attempt to imagine the Renaissance from within its own intellectual life; it is also the key text for the Victorian debate about the relation of art to moral duty, and its heroine is one of the few fully realised women intellectuals in Victorian fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The Florence of Lorenzo de' Medici, the French invasion of 1494, Savonarola's republic and his execution in 1498, and the Victorian vogue for the Italian Renaissance that produced Browning's poems and Ruskin's and Pater's criticism in the same years.
works.characters: Romola de' Bardi; Tito Melema; Savonarola; Bardo de' Bardi; Baldassarre; Tessa; Nello; Piero di Cosimo; Bernardo del Nero; Dino
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Rookwood
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's first novel, a Gothic-Newgate romance centered on the notorious highwayman Dick Turpin, published in parts and immediately popular. It sits at the close of the Romantic period, fusing the Gothic and the Newgate calendar into a new popular mode.
works.plot: The Lorrimer family's country house at Rookwood is haunted by the murder of a child by two of its own sons; the guilt and pursuit of the family interweaves with the legend of Dick Turpin, whose ride to York and capture and execution provide the novel's most famous episodes. Gothic inheritance — haunted chambers, concealed crime, familial sin — merges with the roadster romance of the Newgate tradition, producing the author's characteristic mixture of the topographical, the criminal, and the supernatural.
works.significance: Rookwood fixed the modern legend of Dick Turpin and launched the author's long career as the popular chronicler of London's criminal and historical past; it marks the transition from Romantic Gothic to Victorian popular romance.
works.context: Published in monthly parts from late 1831 to 1832, at the end of the Romantic period and the revival of interest in the Newgate Calendar; its success inaugurated the Victorian romance of real-life crime and the topographical Gothic novel.
works.characters: Dick Turpin; Ralph Lorrimer; Bradfer; Lester; Tom Dapple; King
works.structure: Multi-plot romance: the Lorrimer family Gothic interwoven with the Turpin roadster narrative; serial publication in monthly parts shaped its episodic, cliff-hanger structure.

themes: Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Rosalynde
works.description: Lodge's pastoral romance, the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It: Rosader (Orlando), disinherited by his brother, flees to the forest of Arden, where the banished king, the disguised Rosalynde, and the shepherds' loves play out the courtships, disguises, and recognitions of the greenwood — the whole styled 'Euphues' golden legacy' and salted with eclogues.
works.plot: Saladyne's cruelty drives Rosader to the forest; Rosalynde, banished by the usurper Torismond, walks there disguised as Ganymede; the lovers' meetings in disguise, the lion's attack, the rescue of Saladyne, and the final scene's restorations — the true king, the brothers, and the three marriages — close the romance in Arden's court.
works.significance: The pastoral romance that became one of Shakespeare's greatest comedies — the greenwood's prose and the stage's poetry in one tradition.
works.meter: Euphuistic prose with pastoral verse, in Lodge's sweetest and most musical register.
works.context: Published 1590, at the height of the pastoral vogue; Shakespeare followed its plot closely in As You Like It (1599), keeping the forest, the disguises, and even the names of Phoebe and Adam.
works.characters: Rosader; Rosalynde (Ganymede); Saladyne; Alinda (Aliena); Torismond; Gerismond the exiled king; Phoebe; Montanus; Corydon; Adam Spencer
works.structure: A prose romance of exile and disguise in the pastoral mode, with verse eclogues and the euphuistic style of its subtitle.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Rose Aylmer
works.form: Short elegiac lyric and epitaphic poem of mourning for a private friend; a romantic revival of the simple elegy on the model of the ballad stanza and of Ben Jonson's lyric.
works.description: The author's shortest and most celebrated lyric, a quiet elegy for a girl of his childhood neighbourhood who died abroad. Twenty-four lines of plain, monosyllabic diction recall a shared village schooling and a wood fire seen at a distance, and then pass to the news of her death and to the poet's wakeful remembrance. It is the poem by which its author enters the anthologies, and its extreme spareness is quite unlike the texture of Gebir or the dialogues.
works.plot: The speaker and Rose Aylmer grew up together in the same village, rang the same bell, and learned the same lesson; he saw her mostly at a distance, by the blaze he set in the chinks of the turpentine bark at nightfall, and shouted to her among the birds. Years later they met again, and she sailed away to India, where the poem reports that she died. The closing movement gathers the tokens of her affection - the broken ring, the ring's divided half, the dying gift - and ends by consecrating to her memory a night of recollection and sighs which her living eyes could not be present to.
works.significance: One of the most anthologised short poems of the romantic period and the locus classicus of its author's reputation as a lyricist, its praise of monosyllabic plainness became a touchstone for later arguments about style, memory and the elegy for an ordinary friend.
works.meter: Short accentual lines alternating four-beat and three-beat movement, with an irregular rhyme; the monosyllabic diction and the epigrammatic close give the stanza an epitaphic weight.
works.context: Composed in the later 1790s, when its author was an undergraduate at Oxford and estranged from his family; Rose Aylmer, an Anglo-Indian he had known in childhood, died in India around 1800, and the poem's revised stanzas carry that news. It belongs to the decade's revival of the unadorned elegy.
works.characters: Rose Aylmer; the speaker
works.structure: A single brief lyric moving from the shared childhood scene to the distant fire, to separation and reported death, and closing in an address to the dead; the argument is carried by a sequence of remembered images rather than by events.
works.attributionNotes: The usual dating of composition is the later 1790s, with revision after the news of Rose Aylmer's death abroad, and the poem was first printed some years after it was written; the composition-to-publication gap is long and the earlier versions are known only from manuscript and from later reprint. Scholarly accounts give the first appearance as 1806, but the venue of that first printing is not settled, and the author himself reprinted and revised the poem in later collections.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Early death and the mourning of poets
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind

works.title: Rose of Dutcher's Coolly
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1895
works.description: Published in 1895 and the first American novel of the farm girl who escapes to the city: the education and emancipation of a Wisconsin farmer's daughter. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Hamlin Garland; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Rose Dutcher grows up in the Wisconsin countryside, loses her mother, is sent to the state university by her father, and becomes a poet in Chicago, befriended by the physician Isabel Herrick; she refuses the marriage the coolly expects of her and accepts the journalist Warren Mason only on terms that preserve her freedom to live as an artist.
works.significance: Rose of Dutcher's Coolly is the first American novel of the farm girl's escape and one of the earliest American feminist novels: its refusal of the marriage plot and its insistence on a woman's right to work and to sexual freedom made it a landmark of the American New Woman novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is plain, documentary, unadorned prose.
works.context: 1895: the Wisconsin farm of the 1880s, the state university and the Chicago of the World's Fair, and the American debate on the New Woman. works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: Roughing It

works.description: Published in 1872 and the great American book of the western frontier: Twain's account of his years as a silver prospector and newspaperman in Nevada and California. works.significance: Roughing It is the central American book of the frontier and the finest comic travel narrative in American literature: it records the myth of the West at the moment of its making and it is the source of the cowboy and the mining camp in American popular culture.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is first-person vernacular narration.

works.title: Roughing It in the Bush; or, Life in Canada
works.form: Memoir / series of sketches; local-colour sketch
works.description: Published in 1852 and the classic English memoir of Canadian settlement: thirty sketches of the years the Moodies spent clearing a farm in the backwoods of Upper Canada. It is a prose work of 1852 by Susanna Moodie; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Moodie records the voyage out, the first winter in the bush, the clearing of the land, the births of her children, the drunken neighbours, the fires and illness, and the slow discovery that the gentility she brought from England is useless in the Canadian woods.
works.significance: Roughing It in the Bush is the central text of English-Canadian literature and one of the greatest Victorian accounts of emigration: it created the image of the Canadian backwoods in English writing, and it is a foundational document of the literature of the frontier and of women's settler experience.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is episodic sketch narrative in the manner of the periodical.
works.context: The 1830s-40s, the settlement of Upper Canada, the emigrant trade, and the English middle-class emigration after the Napoleonic wars. works.title: Roxana
altTitles: The Fortunate Mistress: Or, a History of the Life and Most Surprising Adventures of a Lady
works.form: novel; confessional and picaresque prose fiction
works.description: The last and most searching of the great fictional confessions of the 1720s, the career of a woman who converts her own person into an asset and rises from a silk-stockinger's daughter to the mistress of a duke and the envy of the town. It is the most coolly ironic of the series, withholding the penitence its heroine repeatedly promises and making the reader wait for an ending the narrative refuses to supply.
works.plot: Married against her inclination and then abandoned by a husband ruined in trade, she persuades herself that virtue is a word used by the poor to keep them poor, and becomes successively the wife, mistress and pensioner of a series of men in England and on the Continent, accumulating fortunes in Holland and Paris. She returns to London, is courted by a nobleman whom she refuses to marry, discovers that a former husband and her own daughter have tracked her down, and ends in want and remorse, the loss of her child and the collapse of her design being the catastrophe she cannot argument her way out of.
works.significance: It is the most radical study of the marriage market in early fiction and a key text for the debate about whether the eighteenth-century novel could represent female desire without punishing it; its unfinished ending has generated a large critical literature.
works.meter: An elaborate argumentative prose of casuistry, full of self-interrogation, exclamation and the repeated counting of stocks; the colloquy with Amy supplies a dialogue of conscience inside the monologue.
works.context: Published in 1724 in the wake of the South Sea bubble and its aftermath of fortune-hunters and bigamy scandals, and drawing on the continental travel and money-market knowledge of the author's earlier project writing.
works.characters: Roxana; her husband the silk merchant; the Scottish landowner; the Duke of M.; the Dutch merchant; Susan, the lost daughter; Amy, the confidante
works.structure: First-person confessional retrospect with a self-consciously unfinished close; the irony is generated by the gap between the narrator's casuistry and the events she reports, and the Dutch and French sections slow into a series of reckonings.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the name Roxana is the heroine's own assumption in the narrative and the convenient title established by later editors.

works.title: Rupert of Hentzau
works.description: Published in 1898 and the darker sequel to The Prisoner of Zenda: the return of the villain and the death of the hero. It is a prose fiction work of 1898 by Anthony Hope; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.

works.meter: Prose. works.title: Rural Rides
altTitles: Rural Rides, in the years 1821, 1822, &c., with Letters on the Times
works.form: Topographical and travel prose in epistolary form, a pedestrian tour transformed into political economy and social survey.
works.description: The author's pedestrian and hack rides through southern, midland and northern England, and into Wales, written up as letters for the Political Register and gathered into a book in 1830. This record describes the book form of 1830, which reprinted the serial letters and added the Letters on the Times. The rides turn topography into political argument: every hedgerow, turnpike and workhouse is read as evidence of the condition of agriculture and of the labourer.
works.plot: The rides follow roads from Berkshire and Hampshire into Wiltshire, the midland counties, and the north, and from North Wales across the border counties, revisiting places seen decades earlier. At each stage the writer reports fares at public houses, wages, the state of the enclosures, the roads, the tithe, and the aspect of the villages, and compares what he sees with what he remembers. The argument throughout is that the paper system, the taxes, and the corn laws have impoverished a country formerly prosperous, and that the labourer's table is now bare where it once was full. The later letters add a polemic against the clergy, against the poor-law officers, and against the 'distance' and 'fine feelings' of the rich.
works.significance: The founding text of English social survey in literary form, and the witness on which all later accounts of the romantic-era rural labourer depend; it made the road narrative an instrument of class analysis and remains the most quoted prose of English radicalism.
works.meter: Prose, in a colloquial, Anglo-Saxon idiom built on concrete nouns, direct address and invective.
works.context: Conducted and written between post-war depression, the Six Acts, the repeal of the Corn Law agitation and the Reform crisis, with the rides of 1821-22 answering the agricultural distress after 1815 and the later rides answering Catholic emancipation and the vote reform debates.
works.structure: Serial letters of travel, reordered and enlarged in book form; each ride is a self-contained route narrative with appended letters of general argument, and the whole is organised geographically and retrospectively rather than by a single thesis.

Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer

works.title: Rural Walks: In Dialogues
works.form: Juvenile, School and Educational Book; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
works.description: Charlotte Smith's first book for young readers and the first part of a trilogy of educational dialogues continued by Rambles Farther (1796) and Minor Morals (1798). A set of prose dialogues put among walks and conversations in the country, it teaches a girl and her relations to read the landscape, the weather, plants, animals, and social conduct by inquiry rather than by lesson, and it converts the country walk into a method of instruction. Its argumentative, anti-sentimental handling of the child's questions makes it a distinctive contribution to 1790s educational writing.
works.plot: Members of a family and a young female relation talk their way through a series of country excursions, drawing moral, historical, natural-historical, and social instruction from what they see; the dialogues correct vanity, prejudice, and false sensibility, and insist on the education of judgement, on the dignity of labour, and on the duties of the rich towards their poor neighbours.
works.significance: Rural Walks is valued as a serious piece of Romantic-era educational theory in fictional form, and as a feminine antipastoral that refuses to sentimentalize the countryside; it is a standard example in the history of children's literature of the didactic dialogue turned to political and economic instruction.
works.meter: Plain prose dialogue in short conversational turns, with occasional quotations of verse as sententious point; no metrical design proper.
works.context: Written for the expanding market in books for young women at the moment when Smith was supporting her children entirely by her pen, and in the intellectual climate of the 1790s educational dialogue, in which natural history, politics, and moral reasoning were taught conversationally rather than by catechism.
works.characters: the Woodfield family of the dialogues; their young female relation who asks and is corrected; the elder interlocutors who guide the conversation
works.structure: Twelve prose dialogues, each a self-contained walk or conversation with a topic of its own, without continuous plot; instruction is delivered by question and correction rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
Women's education and intellectual friendship
movements: The Bluestockings and Women's Letters

works.title: Ruth
works.form: Novel in three volumes; new woman
works.description: Published in 1853, the year after Cranford, and the most controversial of Gaskell's books: the story of an orphaned milliner's apprentice who is seduced, abandoned and taken in by a Dissenting minister, and who is not punished with the death that the moral convention of the 1850s required.
works.plot: Ruth Hilton, seduced by the wealthy Henry Bellingham, is taken in by the minister Thurstan Benson and his sister Faith, who pass her off as a widow; she becomes a governess and a nurse, refuses Bellingham's later offer of marriage, and dies of fever while nursing the poor of the town, having been publicly exposed by the father of her pupil.
works.significance: Ruth is one of the founding texts of Victorian feminist argument about sexuality and the double standard. Its refusal to treat its heroine as a 'fallen woman' and its attack on the cruelty of respectable opinion gave the 1850s debate over the Contagious Diseases and the Magdalen houses its most widely read fictional argument.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
works.context: The 1830s-50s and the treatment of the 'fallen woman': the milliner's shop, the governess's reference, the Dissenting chapel, and the fever hospital; the novel's refusal of the conventional deathbed of the seduced woman was attacked in reviews and defended by Dickens, who published it.
works.characters: Ruth Hilton; Henry Bellingham; Thurstan Benson; Faith Benson; Mr Benson; Sally; Leonard; Jemima Bradshaw; Mr Bradshaw
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Gaskell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Ruth Hall
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1855
works.description: The first American novel of a woman's professional independence: a widow who writes her way out of poverty. It is a prose fiction work of 1855 by Fanny Fern; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Ruth Hall is widowed with two daughters and no money; her husband's family refuses to help, she is exploited by the editors and mocked by her relatives, and she becomes a successful newspaper writer on her own terms, ending with an independence her family cannot touch.
works.significance: Ruth Hall is the first American novel of a woman's professional independence and the founding text of the woman's career novel: its portrait of the woman writer in the marketplace made it a scandal in 1855 and it remains one of the most important American novels of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the short newspaper sketch in the first person.
works.context: New York and Boston in the 1850s, the new newspaper market and the position of the genteel widow. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Ruth Hall; Hyacinth Hall; Nettie; Daisy; Mr Tibbets; the editors
works.structure: A novel in chapters following the widow's struggle to independence. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Rutherford and Son
works.description: The play of the glassmaster, his children and the stolen design. It is a dramatic work of 1912 by Githa Sowerby; it belongs to Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre and it is catalogued here under Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: John Rutherford, the old glassmaster, holds his family in his tyranny; his son designs the window glass that will free him, but the daughter and the stolen design bring the patriarch and the woman's escape into one of the great plays of the Edwardian stage.
works.significance: Rutherford and Son is Sowerby's play of the glassmaster's tyranny: its patriarch, his children and the woman's escape made it one of the great plays of the Edwardian stage and the recovered classic of the suffrage generation.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain dialogue of the provincial household and the works.
works.context: The north-east of England and the glass trade in 1912. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and first performed in 1912 and the corpus places it within Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre, it is catalogued under suffrage play and the woman's drama; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: John Rutherford; his son; his daughter; the woman of the design
works.structure: Three acts, in the glassmaker's house and its crisis. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Sad Steps
works.description: Sad Steps is a poem by Philip Larkin, completed in April 1968 and collected in High Windows (1974). Its title comes from Sir Philip Sidney's sonnet 'With how sad steps, O Moon, thou climb'st the skies'; Larkin's sad steps are a middle-aged man's on his way back to bed.
works.summary: The speaker's sight of the moon at four in the morning; his mockery of the poetic moon; and his sober recognition of what it reminds him of.
works.plot: Groping back to bed after a piss, the speaker parts the curtains and is startled by the rapid clouds and the moon's cleanliness over the wedge-shadowed gardens. There is something laughable about the moon dashing through cloud, high and preposterous and separate, and he tries out and rejects the romantic apostrophes ('Lozenge of love! Medallion of art!'). Instead he shivers: the hardness, brightness and far-reaching singleness of its stare remind him of the strength and pain of being young, which cannot come again but is for others undiminished somewhere.
works.significance: A much-anthologised example of Larkin's dialogue with the English lyric tradition, here with Sidney's Astrophil and Stella.
works.meter: A crude opening, a parody of high poetic diction in the middle, and a sober, generous close.
works.context: Completed on 24 April 1968, during the years of the poems of ageing and mortality that make up much of High Windows.
works.structure: Eighteen lines in six three-line stanzas, rhymed, turning on the word 'No' from mockery to reflection.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
movements: The Movement

works.title: Saint Joan
works.description: First performed in 1923 and Shaw's greatest tragedy: the trial and execution of Joan of Arc as a conflict between the individual conscience and the institutions of the world. It is a dramatic work of 1923 by George Bernard Shaw; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Joan, a peasant girl, leads the French armies at Orléans, crowns the Dauphin at Reims, and is then captured, tried by the English and the Inquisition for heresy and executed at Rouen; the epilogue shows her return in a dream to the men who condemned her, and her final refusal to accept a world that cannot bear her.
works.significance: Saint Joan is widely regarded as Shaw's masterpiece and the greatest English history play since Shakespeare: its portrait of Joan as a Protestant before the Reformation and a nationalist before nationalism made the play a landmark of the modern stage, and it won Shaw the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1925.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.
works.context: 1923: the canonisation of Joan of Arc in 1920, the aftermath of the First World War, and the debate on nationalism and the individual conscience. The record dates the work as composed in 1923 and first published in 1923 and first performed in 1923 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; victorian verse drama and revived tragedy.
works.characters: Joan; Robert de Baudricourt; the Dauphin, later Charles VII; Dunois; the Earl of Warwick; Bishop Cauchon; the Inquisitor; John de Stogumber; La Hire; the Archbishop of Rheims
works.structure: A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it. A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.

works.title: Saints and Sinners
works.description: First performed in 1884 and the first English play to put a Nonconformist minister on the stage: a clergyman's daughter is seduced and the town's piety is exposed. It is a dramatic work of 1884 by Henry Arthur Jones; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Jacob Fletcher, a popular Dissenting minister, is confronted with the ruin of his daughter Letty by the dashing Captain Fanshawe; the play exposes the hypocrisy of the congregation, the cruelty of the village's moral code, and the minister's own failure of sympathy, and ends with Letty dead and the father broken.
works.significance: Saints and Sinners was the first English play to treat Dissent and provincial respectability seriously and one of the founding works of the English problem drama: it shocked the critics and the clergy, it made the case for a serious drama of contemporary life, and it preceded Pinero's problem plays by a decade.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the strong melodramatic situation with a moral core.
works.context: 1884: the Nonconformist conscience of the English provinces, the Victorian double standard, and the debate on the morality of the stage. The record dates the work as composed in 1884 and first published in 1884 and first performed in 1884 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Jacob Fletcher; Letty Fletcher, his daughter; Captain Fanshawe; George Kingsmill; Samuel Hoggard; Prabble
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: Salar the Salmon
works.form: Nature narrative (the life of a salmon)
works.description: The life of the salmon Salar from the river to the sea and back: the companion to Tarka. It is a prose work of 1935 by Henry Williamson; it is catalogued here under Nature Essay and the Rural Observation; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Salar the Salmon follows the salmon from the parr in the river to the sea and the return of the grilse to the pool and the net, in the prose of the water that made Tarka the standard of the nature narrative.
works.significance: Salar the Salmon is the companion to Tarka and the second of the great nature narratives: its river, its sea and its net carried the prose of the wild creature into the migration and the return.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the wild creature followed hour by hour and season by season.
works.context: The rivers and the sea of the west country in the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1935 and it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Salar; the nets; the river; the sea
works.structure: A nature narrative in chapters of the migration and the return. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.

works.title: Salem Chapel
works.description: Published in 1863 and the most searching of the Carlingford novels: the ministry of a young Dissenting preacher and the ruin of his wife's mind. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Margaret Oliphant; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Serial and Monthly-Part Novel.
works.plot: Arthur Vincent, a gifted young Dissenting minister, comes to Salem Chapel in Carlingford, chafes under the petty tyranny of his shopkeeping deacons, led by the butterman Tozer, and falls hopelessly in love with the beautiful widow Lady Western; the story turns to sensation when his sister Susan is lured away by the mysterious 'Mr Fordham', really Colonel Mildmay, who is shot by his estranged wife, the strange Mrs Hilyard, and Vincent's defence of his family against scandal ends with his leaving the chapel.
works.significance: Salem Chapel is the finest Victorian novel of Dissent and one of the earliest English fictions to treat mental illness in marriage with clinical honesty: its portrait of Adelaide Vincent is a landmark in the Victorian novel of the mind.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1860s: the Dissenting chapels of the English provinces, the tensions of Nonconformist culture, and the Victorian treatment of puerperal insanity. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; serial and monthly-part novel.
works.characters: Arthur Vincent; Mrs Vincent, his mother; Susan Vincent, his sister; Lady Western; Mrs Hilyard (Rachel Mildmay); Colonel Mildmay ('Mr Fordham'); Alice Mildmay; Mr Tozer; Phoebe Tozer; Adelaide Tufton
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume.

works.title: Salmacida Spolia
works.description: The last masque performed at the court of Charles I, presented at Whitehall on 21 January 1640 with designs by Inigo Jones and with the young Prince Charles and his brothers among the masquers.

works.significance: The final Caroline masque and a poignant document of a court culture on the eve of destruction; it also marks Davenant's official succession to Jonson as laureate.

works.context: Presented at Whitehall in January 1640, months before the calling of the Short Parliament and the collapse of Charles's personal rule; Davenant had been made Poet Laureate in 1638 on Jonson's death.
works.characters: Discord; Wisdom; the Genius of Britain; the masquers
works.structure: The standard court masque form: antimasque of discord, main masque of harmony, and the revels.

works.title: Salmagundi
works.form: Periodical essay series in the Spectator and Independent Whig manner, with verse, character writing and burlesque dissertations
works.description: A series of miscellany numbers satirizing the manners, politics, literature and fashions of New York, issued in the Addissonian and Spectator tradition. The voices are those of a fictional club of idlers and observers, including a painter, a critic and a country wit. It created the American sketch-series and the persona of the detached, good-humored observer of civic life.
works.plot: The numbers alternate between essay, character sketch, mock dissertation, song and reported anecdote, all directed at contemporary targets: the passion for improvements, duelling, pedantry, theatrical fashion, the antiquarian pretensions of local societies and the politics of the ruling party. A frame of club meetings and papers left behind by deceased members supplies the miscellaneous principle. The satire is personal rather than doctrinal, ridiculing the pretensions of the emerging literary and political class of New York.
works.significance: It established the American sketch and character-series as a publishable form and introduced the urbane observer-persona that later defined the Knickerbocker school. Its parody of civic improvement set a permanent tone in American urban comedy. It is the earliest of the metropolitan periodicals that made New York a literary capital.
works.meter: Chiefly prose, with interspersed songs and occasional verse in common metres
works.context: Published in New York between January 1807 and February 1808, in a season of fierce party conflict over embargo and the ruling family's New York allies. Its models were British: the Tatler, the Spectator, and the Anti-Jacobin review. The collaboration of three young writers, one of them still an apprentice lawyer, made the series the first American example of a literary enterprise organized on magazine lines.
works.structure: Serial periodical miscellany of twenty numbers, unified by a club frame and by recurring pseudonymous contributors rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Produced collaboratively by three New York writers; the batch records the series under its principal contributor, and the joint authorship was openly advertised in the numbers themselves.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona

works.title: Salomé
works.form: Tragedy in one act (written in French)
works.description: Written in French in 1891 and published in Paris in 1893 with illustrations by Aubrey Beardsley; the English text appeared in 1894 with a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas. Banned from the London stage by the Lord Chamberlain, it was not performed in England until 1931.
works.plot: Salomé, daughter of Herodias, desires the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist), who is imprisoned in Herod's cistern; when he rejects her, she demands his head on a silver charger as the price of dancing the dance of the seven veils, and at the end Herod orders her execution.
works.significance: Salomé is the central English text of dramatic decadence and the most influential one-act tragedy of the 1890s; its fusion of the biblical, the erotic and the aesthetic made it a scandal and a founding work of the modern theatre of cruelty.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the French symbolist theatre, the Decadent movement, and the censorship of the English stage. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1893 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; problem play and well-made drama.

works.structure: The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
works.attributionNotes: Written in French; the English version was a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas revised by Wilde.

works.title: Salt-Water Ballads
works.description: Masefield's first book and the source of 'Sea-Fever': the sailor's ballad and the English sea lyric. It is a verse work of 1902 by John Masefield; it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Sea-Fever', 'A Wanderer's Song', 'Trade Winds', 'The Golden City of St Mary' and the sailor's ballads of the forecastle, the brothel and the voyage.
works.significance: Salt-Water Ballads gave the period its most popular sea poetry: 'Sea-Fever' — 'I must go down to the seas again' — is one of the best-known English poems of the century, and the collection revived the sailor's ballad as a modern form.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the rhymed ballad with a strong driving narrative.
works.context: Masefield's own years at sea, the English merchant marine, and the revival of the ballad in the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
works.structure: Twenty-three ballads and lyrics of the sea. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Edward Masefield. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum
works.description: Aemilia Lanyer's volume of sacred poetry, one of the first books of poems published by an Englishwoman: the long title poem on Christ's Passion — with its celebrated 'Eve's Apology' defending women against the blame of the Fall — framed by the eleven dedicatory poems to the great ladies of the court and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
works.plot: The Passion poem narrates Christ's betrayal, trial, and crucifixion through the eyes of the women who followed him, with Pilate's wife's dream and the 'Eve's Apology' arguing women's innocence and worth; the dedications praise the Queen, the Countess of Pembroke, and the other patronesses; and Cooke-ham celebrates the estate of Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland, in the farewell of its trees and walks.
works.significance: A founding text of English women's poetry — the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and the first country-house poem.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the Passion poem, with the varied stanzas of the dedications and the elegiac couplets of Cooke-ham.
works.context: Published 1611, in the year of the King James Bible, by a woman of the court's margins; its argument for women's learning and worth answered the querelle des femmes with theology, and its Cooke-ham preceded Jonson's 'To Penshurst' in the country-house genre.
works.characters: Christ; Pilate's wife; Eve; the women of Jerusalem; Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland; Anne Clifford; the dedicatees
works.structure: A tripartite volume — dedications, Passion poem, country-house poem — organized as a woman's address to women, the patrons and readers its intended audience.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: The Passion of Christ
Women's experience and the feminine voice
