works.title: Samson Agonistes
works.description: A Greek tragedy in English on the blind Hebrew hero Samson, written to be read rather than performed: imprisoned and blinded by the Philistines, Samson moves from despair to renewed faith and, at the feast of Dagon, pulls down the temple, destroying himself and his enemies in an act of divine vengeance.
works.plot: Samson laments his blindness and capture; he is visited in turn by the Chorus of Danites, his father Manoah, his wife Dalila, and the giant Harapha; summoned to make sport before the Philistine lords at the temple of Dagon, he prays for strength, topples the pillars, and dies triumphantly with his enemies.
works.significance: The greatest English example of classical closet tragedy, it fuses Greek form with Hebrew subject and Milton's own condition, and has generated sustained debate about its violence, its politics, and its catharsis.
works.meter: Blank verse with choruses in varied lyric meters, using the Greek tragic forms of strophe and antistrophe.
works.context: Published with Paradise Regained in 1671; the blinded, politically defeated hero has long been read as a figure of Milton himself after the Restoration, and the play engages the problem of violent divine justice.
works.characters: Samson; the Chorus of Danites; Manoah; Dalila; Harapha; the Philistine Officer; the Messenger
works.structure: A classical drama observing the unities of time and place, with chorus, stichomythia, messenger, and catharsis, modeled on Sophocles and Aeschylus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the title page notes it was 'never intended' for the stage.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Marriage and women's conduct
Penance, confession, and sin
Revenge and justice

works.title: Samuel Johnson
works.description: Published in 1878 in the English Men of Letters series and one of the best short lives of Johnson in the language: a portrait of the writer and the man by a critic in deep sympathy with both. It is a prose work of 1878 by Leslie Stephen; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Stephen follows Johnson from Lichfield and the Grub Street years through the Dictionary, the Rambler and the friendship with Boswell to the last years and the death-bed, and treats the moral writings as the centre of his achievement.
works.significance: Stephen's Johnson is a classic of English biography and a key text in the Victorian making of the English literary canon; it established Johnson as a moralist rather than a talker and shaped the modern reading of the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact critical prose.
works.context: The 1870s, the English Men of Letters series edited by John Morley, and the Victorian interest in the professional writer. The record dates the work as composed in 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Samuel Johnson; James Boswell; Hester Thrale; Tetty, his wife; David Garrick; Joshua Reynolds
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Leslie Stephen. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Sapho and Phao
works.description: Lyly's mythological court comedy: the ferryman Phao, made beautiful by Venus, is loved by the queen Sapho; Venus, jealous of the queen she meant to humble, afflicts Phao with love of herself; and the play resolves through Cupid's arrows and Sybilla's lore into Sapho's triumph over Venus and the renunciation of Phao's love.
works.plot: Venus, angered by Sapho's chastity, arms Cupid against her; the arrows misfire, Phao is loved and Sapho infatuated; the court's debates (between the scholars and the women) anatomize love; Sybilla's counsel and Venus's flight end the play with Sapho restored to rule and Phao banished from desire.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan mythological court play — a genre in which the Queen's own image was negotiated on stage.
works.meter: Prose of Euphuistic balance, with songs and the debate set pieces.
works.context: Performed at court in 1584 and printed the same year; its Sapho is read as a mirror of Elizabeth I, and its love-psychology answers the Alençon courtship debates of the early 1580s.
works.characters: Sapho; Phao; Venus; Cupid; Sybilla; the court ladies; the scholars; the pages
works.structure: A five-act mythological debate-comedy of the Ovidian type, with the low comedy of the pages and servants as counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Sappho and Phaon. In a Series of Legitimate Sonnets, with Other Poems, and a Ballad
works.form: Romantic Sonnet Revival; Sonnet Sequence; Lyric
works.description: Mary Robinson's most important volume of verse and a central book of the 1790s sonnet revival: a series of sonnets cast as the correspondence of Sappho and Phaon, in which the ancient poetess becomes the voice of a woman pleading, loving, and complaining in the first person. With its accompanying shorter poems and a ballad, the volume claims legitimacy for the sonnet as a form of female passion and argument, and it deliberately rewrites the Petrarchan tradition from the side of the mistress rather than the lover.
works.plot: The sonnets dramatize Sappho's love for Phaon, her remonstrance, her jealousy, and her abandonment, and draw the anecdote of the Grecian poetess's leap and death into the sequence; the interwoven miscellaneous poems and the ballad extend the same argument about inconstant love, female reputation, and the poet's power, so that the volume's story is the history of a woman's passion answered by coldness and finally converted into verse.
works.significance: Sappho and Phaon is one of the two or three volumes on which the 1790s revival of the English sonnet rested, and it is the most audacious instance of a woman writer appropriating the Petrarchan sequence for female desire and self-justification; it fixed Robinson's contemporary title of the English Sappho and is now indispensable to any history of the Romantic sonnet.
works.meter: Sonnets of fourteen iambic pentameter lines in the Italian manner, with the volume's own emphasis on legitimate and correctly-modelled sonnet structure; the accompanying lyrics and the ballad use shorter popular stanzas.
works.context: Published in the middle of the extraordinary vogue for the sonnet that Robinson and Charlotte Smith together created, and after the Della Cruscan period of her fame; her use of Sappho as a speaking female poet is a claim of authority made at a time when her own public history as a scandalous woman still governed her reception.
works.characters: Sappho; Phaon; the rival object of Phaon's regard; the Grecian legend of the poetess's leap
works.structure: A sonnet sequence with a loose narrative core - the Sappho and Phaon story - supported by a group of separate lyric and descriptive poems and a closing ballad; the progression is from address and hope through complaint and jealousy to resignation.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Idealized love and the lost beloved

Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: Sartor Resartus: The Life and Opinions of Herr Teufelsdröckh
works.description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34 and published as a book in Boston in 1836 and in London in 1838: a 'clothes philosophy' in the form of an English editor's account of the German professor Diogenes Teufelsdröckh and his book on clothes, which becomes the spiritual autobiography of a modern soul.
works.plot: The editor presents Teufelsdröckh's life and his 'Philosophy of Clothes', the doctrine that all institutions, creeds and customs are garments which time wears out. Teufelsdröckh's own history — the 'Everlasting No' of his despair, the 'Centre of Indifference', and the 'Everlasting Yea' of work and renunciation — is the model of the Victorian conversion narrative.
works.significance: Sartor Resartus introduced German idealism to English readers and invented the modern spiritual autobiography of doubt and recovery; it was the single greatest influence on the Victorian literature of the 'Everlasting No', and Emerson's American edition of 1836 made Carlyle the intellectual hero of New England Transcendentalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: German idealist philosophy (Fichte, Goethe, Kant) and the Scottish Calvinist background; the crisis of faith of the 1820s; and the Fraser's Magazine circle of the 1830s. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1834 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Diogenes Teufelsdröckh; the English editor; Hofrath Heuschrecke; Blumine; Herr Towgood; Gretchen
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Satires
works.description: Donne's five formal verse satires of the 1590s — on the foppish courtier, the corrupt lawyer, religion and the quest for true church, the court, and the suitors and officers of the law — the poems that established the English formal satire and prompted the 1599 ban on satires, with their Juvenalian 'railing' and their portrait of Elizabethan London's vices.
works.plot: Each satire is a walk through a vice — the courtier's affectations, the lawyer's bribes, the sects' errors, the court's vanity, the law's extortion — with the poet as reluctant companion and ironist, and the third satire's 'On a huge hill, / Cragged and steep, Truth stands' as the sequence's moral summit.
works.significance: The foundation of English formal satire — the model for Pope's couplet and for every later poet of the town's vices.
works.meter: Rough, deliberately harsh heroic couplets — 'strong lines' — whose jagged enjambment and parenthesis imitated the speech of the town and the Roman satirists' abruptness.
works.context: Written 1593–98, in the decade that also produced the satires of Hall and Marston; the bishops' ban of 1599, which ordered the burning of satires, answered this vogue directly.
works.characters: the satirist; the fop; the lawyer; the courtier; the officers and suitors
works.structure: Five numbered satires in the formal Roman manner, each a single scene or progress through the city, in the couplet form Donne hardened into an instrument of speech.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Satires of Circumstance, Lyrics and Reveries
works.description: Published in November 1914 and the volume that contains the 'Poems of 1912-13', the greatest English sequence of mourning after In Memoriam: the poems written after Hardy's visit to Cornwall and to Emma's birthplace following her death in 1912.
works.plot: The 'Poems of 1912-13' revisit the places of the early marriage — St Juliot, Boscastle, Beeny Cliff, Pendennis — and record the speaker's grief, guilt and belated recognition of the wife he had neglected; the volume also contains the 'Satires of Circumstance' and the lyrics of the Wessex world.
works.significance: The 'Poems of 1912-13' are the central English elegies of the twentieth century; their honesty about a failed marriage made them the model for the modern confessional elegy and established Hardy as a major poet.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The death of Emma Hardy in November 1912, the visit to Cornwall in March 1913, and the Edwardian and Georgian poetry of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1914 and first published in 1914 and it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Sawles Warde
works.description: An allegorical homily in AB-language prose on the custody of the soul: the house of the body is governed by Wit and Will, guarded by the five senses, threatened by the devil, and comforted by the virtues and the joys of heaven. It adapts Hugh of St Victor's De Anima and is the earliest extended allegory of the inner life in English prose.
works.plot: Wit (reason), with his wife Will, rules the soul's house; the messenger Fear of Death warns of the devil's assaults; the virtues — Prudence, Strength, Moderation, Righteousness — and the vision of the heavenly bliss fortify the household against temptation.
works.significance: A foundation stone of English allegory: its personified psychology anticipates the moralities (The Castle of Perseverance) and the dream allegories of the fourteenth century.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative AB-language prose.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, adapting Hugh of St Victor; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34, BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii, and Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: Wit; Will; Fear of Death; the Virtues; the Devil
works.structure: A continuous allegorical narrative built on the house/castle metaphor, with set-piece descriptions of the pains of hell and the joys of heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)

works.title: Scaramouche
works.form: Novel; historical novel, first issued in 1921
works.description: The greatest swashbuckler: a lawyer becomes an actor and a revolutionary. It is a prose fiction work of 1921 by Rafael Sabatini; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Andre-Louis Moreau, a lawyer in Brittany, is radicalised by the death of his friend at the hands of a nobleman, becomes the actor Scaramouche and then a leader of the Revolution, and discovers the secret of his own birth in a novel of the French Revolution.
works.significance: Scaramouche is the greatest swashbuckling novel ever written, with its famous opening line about birth and death and its actor-hero: it made Sabatini the master of the historical romance and has never been out of print.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the swashbuckling hero and the duel.
works.context: France in the years before and during the Revolution. The record dates the work as composed between 1920 and 1921 and first published in 1921 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Andre-Louis Moreau; Scaramouche; Aline de Kercadiou; the Marquis; Danton; Robespierre
works.structure: A novel in three books, from the law courts to the stage to the Revolution. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rafael Sabatini (Scaramouche). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Scenes of Clerical Life
works.form: Three linked tales (Blackwood's Magazine, 1857); two volumes 1858
works.description: Three tales — 'The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton', 'Mr Gilfil's Love-Story' and 'Janet's Repentance' — published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1857 and collected in 1858: the first fiction of George Eliot, written when she was already the author of translations and the editor of the Westminster Review.
works.plot: 'Amos Barton' follows the failure and death of a dull curate's wife in the parish of Shepperton; 'Mr Gilfil's Love-Story' recovers the tragic past of the old vicar of Knebley; 'Janet's Repentance' traces the conversion of a drunken wife-beating clergyman's wife in the town of Milby through the ministry of the Evangelical Mr Tryan.
works.significance: Scenes of Clerical Life introduced the fictional method that Eliot developed for the next twenty years — the provincial community studied through several ordinary lives, the sympathy that refuses moral simplification, and the narrator who speaks as a member of the community — and it established her as the most serious new novelist of the 1850s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The Warwickshire and Staffordshire of the 1820s-30s, the Evangelical revival inside the Church of England, and the provincial town of the pre-Reform era; the stories were modelled on the recollections of Eliot's aunt, Elizabeth Tomlinson.
works.characters: Amos Barton; Milly Barton; Mr Gilfil; Caterina Sarti; Janet Dempster; Mr Tryan; Mr Dempster
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Science and Poetry
works.form: Critical essay (the poem and the language of science)
works.description: The essay on the poem in the age of science and the fate of the poetic statement. It is a prose work of 1926 by I. A. Richards; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Science and Poetry asks what becomes of the poem when the scientific statement has replaced the poetic, and answers with the doctrine of the pseudo-statement: the poem is the instrument of the attitude rather than of the belief, and survives the death of the cosmology.
works.significance: Science and Poetry is the key essay of the quarrel between the poem and the language of science: its pseudo-statement saved the poem for the scientific century and remains the standard statement of the case.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the analytic prose of the psychologist of reading.
works.context: Cambridge in the mid-1920s, and the quarrel of the two languages. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.title: Science and the Supernatural
works.description: The geneticist's examination of the supernatural claims. It is a prose work of 1927 by J. B. S. Haldane; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Science and the Supernatural examines the claims of the spiritualism, the miracle and the psychical research against the methods of the sciences, and argues the limits of the natural knowledge, in the rigorous plain prose of the scientist who took the supernatural seriously enough to test it.
works.significance: Science and the Supernatural is the scientist's classic of the psychical debate: its examination of the miracle and the séance set the standard of the skeptical inquiry in the decade of the spiritualist revival.

works.title: Scoop
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1938
works.description: The funniest English novel about journalism: a country columnist is sent to Africa as a war correspondent and gets the wrong man. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by Evelyn Waugh; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: William Boot, the author of a nature column in the Daily Beast, is mistaken for the novelist John Boot and sent to the fictional African state of Ishmaelia to cover a war. He stumbles into a scoop, wins the girl and the reputation, and returns to England while the real correspondents fail.
works.significance: Scoop is the funniest English novel about journalism and one of the great comic novels of the century: its portrait of Fleet Street, its African republic and its innocent hero made it the permanent satire of the foreign correspondent.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face.
works.context: Fleet Street in the 1930s, the Abyssinian crisis of 1935 and Waugh's own experience as a correspondent in Ethiopia. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: William Boot; John Boot; Lord Copper; Salter; Mrs Stitch; Katchen; Corker
works.structure: Five books, from London to Ishmaelia and back. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Evelyn St John Waugh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Scots Wha Hae
altTitles: Scots, wha hae wi' Wallace bled
works.form: persona song and war lyric set to a traditional march air, in the national-song mode of the 1790s
works.description: Burns's war-song written in the voice of Bruce addressing his men before Bannockburn, and the most powerful political lyric of the 1790s in Scotland. Under the cover of the fourteenth-century battle it speaks the language of liberty and of servile dependence in the present, and its challenge - who will be a slave, who a freeman - made publishers hesitate to print it anonymously as an old song. It is the classic instance of Burns turning national history into a democratic battle hymn.
works.plot: Bruce calls on the Scots who bled with Wallace to remember the days that made their names, and sets the tyrant's hirelings against the freemen who fight for their own land. The song demands the choice of slavery or liberty in the strictest terms, promises the reward of victory and the shame of the slave, and ends with the call to share the battle and its prize. The historical speaker makes the contemporary application unmistakable without naming it.
works.significance: It became one of the national songs of Scotland and a standard text of the literature of liberty, admired for its concentration and for its way of making medieval history speak to contemporary radicalism. Its use as a battle and commemorative hymn, and its place in the song repertory of the nations, make it a central document of the 1790s bardic revival.
works.meter: Four-beat Scots lines in short stanzas with a strong march rhythm, adapted to the air of Bruce's March; the diction is imperious and monosyllabic, with the refrain-like closing address.
works.context: Composed in the summer of 1793, in the excitement and repression that followed the French Revolution and the trials of the king, when Burns's radical sympathies were constrained by his office in the excise, to which he had been appointed in 1789; it was contributed to Johnson's musical collection as a song of the northern nation, and its publication raised the question of political offence.
works.characters: Robert the Bruce; the Scots host; Edward of England as the tyrant; Wallace as the remembered leader
works.structure: A short strophic song in the persona of Bruce, each stanza advancing the exhortation from memory of Wallace to the present choice, the threat of the tyrant, and the final rally.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Burns's own letter to Johnson in the summer of 1793, and the printing of the song in the musical collection is documented, though the volumes' issue dates have been variously reckoned.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Warfare and battle
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: Sea Garden
works.description: The purest book of Imagism: the sea, the shore, the garden and the mineral world, in the hardest English free verse. It is a verse work of 1916 by H. D. (Hilda Doolittle); it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poems — 'Sea Rose', 'The Helmsman', 'Mid-day', 'Garden', 'Sea Lily', 'The Cliff Temple' — are short, hard, unrhymed lyrics of shells, salt, stone and petals, in which the natural world is presented as a set of exact and severe objects and the speaking voice is barely present.
works.significance: Sea Garden is the founding book of Imagism and the purest body of free verse in English: its crystalline images and refusal of rhetoric made it the model for the modern short poem and established H. D. as the finest poet of the movement.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the single crystalline image.
works.context: The Imagist programme of 1912–14, the Greek lyric (Sappho), and the London little magazines in which the poems first appeared. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.
works.structure: Thirty-eight short poems, mostly of a few lines, in free verse. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hilda Doolittle. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Seasons for Fasting
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Additional MS 43703 (a sixteenth-century transcript by Laurence Nowell of the lost Cotton Otho B.xi)
works.description: A poem of some 230 lines on the proper observance of the Ember fasts, defending the English custom of four seasonal fasts against the laxity of those who fast only once a year, and citing biblical and canonical authority for the practice. The text breaks off imperfectly.
works.plot: The poet rebukes priests who observe the Ember days wrongly, argues from scripture (Moses, Elijah, the Ninevites, Christ's forty days) that fasting is commanded, sets out the correct times of the four seasonal fasts, and attacks drunken priests; the poem ends incomplete amid a catalogue of fasts.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem on a live question of ecclesiastical discipline, valuable for its picture of eleventh-century religious controversy and its fusion of homiletic and satirical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic urgency of Wulfstan's prose; the text is incomplete, and some lines are metrically irregular.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English period's debates over ecclesiastical discipline, contemporary with Wulfstan's legislation on fasting and the reform of the clergy; its strictures on drunken priests echo the reformers' campaigns.
works.structure: An argumentative structure: rebuke, biblical proof-texts, prescription of the fasts, and invective against clerical abuses, in the manner of Wulfstanian homiletic verse.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The poem's Wulfstanian manner has suggested to some scholars an origin in his circle, but no attribution is established.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Sejanus His Fall
works.description: Jonson's Roman tragedy of the favourite's fall: the ambitious Sejanus, minister of Tiberius, destroys the house of Germanicus piece by piece and rises toward the throne itself — until Tiberius's letter from Capri, read in the Senate, turns the city against him, and the mob tears him to pieces in the streets, his children executed, his statues melted down.
works.plot: Sejanus corrupts and removes Drusus, Agrippina, and their sons; the senators' servility and the informers' trade fill the middle acts; the emperor's withdrawal and the counter-plot of Macro prepare the fall; the Senate scene reverses Sejanus's fortunes in a single letter, and the final act follows the executioners through the city's vengeance.
works.significance: The first great English political tragedy of the Jacobean age and the founding text of the Roman play's documentary tradition.
works.meter: A grave, scholarly blank verse with extensive marginal annotation in the printed text — the play as documented history.
works.context: Performed at the Globe in 1603 (with Shakespeare in the cast), then revised for print in 1605, with Jonson's marginal notes citing his classical authorities; it landed him before the Privy Council on charges of 'popery and treason'.
works.characters: Sejanus; Tiberius; Macro; Silius; Arruntius; Agrippina; Drusus; Livia; the Senate; Cordus; Natta; Eudemus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of state built on Tacitus, with the Senate scenes as its rhetorical engine and the messenger's report of the mob's savagery as its climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the original Globe version contained a share by another hand, which Jonson replaced for the printed text.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Courtly service and courtly danger
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Selected Letters of Philip Larkin, 1940-1985
works.description: Selected Letters of Philip Larkin, 1940-1985 is the posthumous selection of the poet's correspondence edited by Anthony Thwaite and published by Faber and Faber in 1992.
works.summary: Letters written over forty-five years to friends, lovers and fellow writers, including his Oxford friend Kingsley Amis and the poet and historian Robert Conquest, tracing his career from undergraduate days to his final illness.
works.plot: The letters show Larkin's wit, his devotion to writing and jazz, and the daily texture of a librarian's life, but they also exposed private attitudes that shocked many readers: obsessive interest in pornography, racist and misogynistic remarks, extreme right-wing political opinions and habitual venom towards colleagues and other writers. Read across the decades, they also form an informal autobiography, documenting his years in Leicester, Belfast and Hull, his working life as a librarian, the composition and reception of his books, and his long relationships.
works.significance: Together with Motion's biography, it transformed Larkin's posthumous reputation and provoked a long debate about the relation between a writer's private views and the value of his work.
works.meter: Comic, profane, intimate and often brutal correspondence, very different from the restraint of the poems.
works.context: Published in 1992, the year before Andrew Motion's biography Philip Larkin: A Writer's Life, at a time of intense debate about political correctness and the literary canon.
works.structure: Letters arranged chronologically from 1940 to 1985, with the editor's explanatory notes.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Love, intimacy and loss

works.title: Self-Control
works.description: the author's first novel, a philosophical Gothic romance set in Scotland and the Canadian wilderness, in which the heroine Juliet must exercise reason and self-command to escape destructive passions. Sir Walter Scott praised it in the Quarterly Review, and it stands as one of the most intellectually ambitious Scottish novels of the 1810s.
works.plot: Juliet, a young Scottish gentlewoman, refuses to marry the dashing but dangerous Lord Montalbert. After she travels to Canada, she is kidnapped by Montalbert in the wilderness, where she endures captivity, pursuit, and attempted forced marriage. She resists not through sensibility but through principled self-discipline. The novel's philosophical argument — that rational self-command protects against passion's destructiveness — is enacted through Gothic suspense; Juliet ultimately marries the steadfast Henry.
works.significance: the author's fusion of Gothic and philosophical modes anticipated the moral seriousness of the later Scottish historical novel; its praise by Scott established the precedent of the novel as a vehicle for moral philosophy.
works.context: Published during the height of the Gothic vogue; the author deliberately reworked Gothic conventions to serve a philosophical argument about rational self-control rooted in Scottish moral philosophy. The Canadian setting drew on contemporary accounts of the fur trade and Loyalist emigration.
works.characters: Juliet; Lord Montalbert; Henry; Ellen; Lady Montalbert
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; episodic movement from Scotland across the Atlantic to the Canadian wilderness; the Gothic captivity plot resolves into moral domestic fiction.
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Sense and Sensibility
works.form: Novel of manners and domestic moral comedy, inheriting the 1790s vogue for the fiction of sensibility while inverting it through irony and conditional endings.
works.description: A social novel of two orphaned sisters, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who illustrate contrasting regimes of feeling and judgement after being displaced from their father's estate. The work grew out of an epistolary juvenile experiment of the late 1790s and was reworked into a third-person narrative of discretion, disappointment and eventual settlement. Its argument is not that sensibility is false but that unexamined feeling needs the discipline of principle.
works.plot: Sir John Dashwood, influenced by his wife Fanny, keeps the promised provision from his stepmother and half-sisters, who remove to a cottage on the estate of a distant relation. Marianne attaches herself passionately to the charming, impecunious John Willoughby, who is recalled to London and marries a rich heiress instead; Elinor quietly endures the secret engagement of her own beloved Edward Ferrars to the artful Lucy Steele. Marianne's exposed grief carries her to illness and near death, while Edward is disinherited for honouring his early pledge and is only freed when Lucy transfers herself to his brother. The novel closes with double marriages, Marianne's cooler second choice of the steady Colonel Brandon, and a modest restoration of family order.
works.significance: The first work of the school of social realism that displaced the romance of sensibility, and the founding text of the novel of manners in the Regency mode. Its treatment of female feeling as both social currency and private suffering set the terms for later women's fiction. Its revision from epistolary draft to narrated tale is a documented case of 1790s experimental form being absorbed into nineteenth-century realism.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; balanced periodic sentences, epigrammatic dialogue, and a famous antithetical title-phrase in iambic rhythm.
works.context: Written through the 1790s controversy over sensibility and the education of women, and revised during the Napoleonic Wars when the commercial and clerical careers open to gentle families were precarious. The novel's entailed estates, half-pay officers and drawing-room politics register the specific economic vulnerability of the landless gentry. It was offered to a London publisher at a moment when the three-volume novel had become a financial as well as a literary form.
works.characters: Elinor Dashwood; Marianne Dashwood; Edward Ferrars; Colonel Brandon; John Willoughby; Mrs. Jennings; Lucy Steele; Fanny Dashwood; Sir John Dashwood; Mrs. Dashwood; Robert Ferrars
works.structure: Third-person narration with sustained free indirect discourse anchored now in Elinor and now in Marianne; linear, episodic plot of removals between Devonshire, Sussex, London and Cleveland; letters and reported conversation carry offstage information.
works.attributionNotes: Published as 'By A Lady'; identification of the author rests on publisher's records and family documentation and is not in dispute.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
The marriage market and the limited estate
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: Sensibility
altTitles: Sensibility. A Poem. In Two Parts
works.description: A moral essay in couplets on the culture of feeling, distinguishing a true from a false sensibility and arguing that tenderness without principle is a form of self-love. It was the first considerable poem of its author and established her reputation in the fashionable literary world.
works.plot: The poet examines the temper of the age, in which the refinement of feeling has been mistaken for virtue, and shows the man of sensibility pursuing his own pleasure under the colour of sympathy. Examples of the false and the real are contrasted - the suffering of the poor, the distress of friendship, the duties that a feeling heart evades. The second part passes to the consolation of religion and to the assertion that sensibility must be governed by duty and by the hope of another world.
works.significance: It is one of the clearest early statements of the case against the ethics of feeling, and it announced a career that was to span the century's passage from fashionable sensibility to evangelical duty.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the Augustan school, with the closed and balanced antithesis of the sententious line and the occasional pathetical pause.
works.context: Published in 1773, in the height of the cult of sensibility and of the first attacks upon it, and written by a young woman of the Bath and London literary circles who was shortly to become a dramatist and a conduct writer.
works.structure: A discursive poem in two parts, opening with a complaint of the manners of the age, passing through instances and characters, and closing in an elevation of principle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in her collected verse.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

works.title: Sensus Communis: An Essay on Wit and Humour
altTitles: Sensus Communis, an Essay on Wit and Humour
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.description: Shaftesbury's essay on wit, written as a friendly critique of Anthony Collins's Essay Concerning the Use of Reason and issued the same year as the Letter Concerning Enthusiasm. It proposes ridicule as the proper test of wit and of whatever claims assent, and distinguishes true raillery, which supports sociability and liberty of thought, from the spleen and ignorance of the mere witling.
works.plot: The essay opens on the character of a book and the conditions of free examination, then passes to an anatomy of wit and humour, classifying wits by their governing humour. Shaftesbury insists that ridicule, like reason, must be exercised freely and without fear, since a doctrine or religion that cannot endure to be ill-used deserves to be. He distinguishes genuine raillery, addressed to opinions and manners, from personal abuse, and traces modern wit to a mixture of the fine and the humorous. The argument closes with a defence of good manners in raillery and an appeal to common sense as the public standard of the ridiculous.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential account of ridicule as a criterion of truth and civility, directly conditioning Addison's papers, Pope's doctrine of wit, and later theories of humour and the comic.
works.meter: Conversational, pointed prose in the manner of a letter to a friend, rich in distinctions, short definitions, and barbed asides; passages of rhythmic tripartite enumeration give it the feel of spoken raillery.
works.context: Printed in 1709 amid the freethinking debates opened by Collins and Toland, and written in dialogue with the author of A Discourse of the Liberty of the Press, whose press Shaftesbury praises while disagreeing with his conclusion. It forms part of what became the Characteristics.
works.structure: A single discursive essay in loose epistolary form, moving from the conditions of free enquiry through a classification of wits to the doctrine of ridicule as test.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: Serious Reflections During the Life and Afflicting Circumstances of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: meditative and didactic prose essays in a fictional persona
works.description: The third Crusoe volume, a collection of meditations, dialogues and practical essays put into the mouth of the retired islander. It abandons narrative for moral reflection on providence, solitude, the fear of man, temperance and the duties of a master, and is organised as a set of numbered serious thoughts.
works.plot: The narrator, now settled and prospering, meditates on the religious meanings of his preservation, debates with imagined interlocutors the questions of conscience and enthusiasm, reflects on the condition of servants, wives and children, and argues that a Christian's true business is the government of his own passions. The volume adds visionary and allegorical papers on the invisible world, including a dialogue with the soul and a description of the world of spirits.
works.significance: It supplies the strongest internal evidence of the moral and religious frame that contemporaries read in the first volume, and its mixed reception marked the boundary between fiction and edification in the early-eighteenth-century book trade.
works.meter: Serious plain prose of the conduct-book manner, with balancing clauses, scriptural tags and the interrogative turn of meditation; the allegorical papers admit a more ornate visionary rhetoric.
works.context: Published in the same year as the second volume and in the wake of controversies over enthusiasm and natural religion, it draws on the Puritan tradition of the serious meditation and on the 1710s vogue for soliloquy on the passions.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the imagined interlocutor; Friday as a figure of natural religion; the narrator's own soul
works.structure: A serial of short reflective papers rather than a continuous plot, with inset dialogues and a few narrative fragments; the Crusoe persona functions as a mask for a moralist.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the volume has conventionally been treated as the weakest of the three; the title-page carries the same fictional persona as its warrant.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Fortune and mutability
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind

works.title: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
altTitles: The Sermon of the Wolf to the English
works.description: Wulfstan's most famous sermon, preached in the crisis year 1014 as the Danish conquest of England was completed: an impassioned jeremiad interpreting the Viking devastation as God's punishment for the nation's sins, culminating in the vision of the enslaved nation — 'an Englishman is not worth more to a Dane than a dog'. The masterpiece of Old English pulpit rhetoric.
works.plot: The sermon catalogues the nation's sins — betrayal of lords, perjury, oppression of the poor, the violation of churches — and reads the tribulations of Æthelred's reign (the treachery of Eadric Streona, the burning, plundering, and enslavement of the people) as the biblical pattern of divine wrath; it calls the nation to repentance before the last things overtake it, in a crescendo of Wulfstan's two-stress rhythms.
works.significance: The greatest Old English sermon and the classic statement of the period's theology of national sin.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical prose: two-stress phrases, alliteration, anaphora, and word-pairs ('byman and bærnan' — burn and ravage).
works.context: Preached in 1014, after the expulsion of Æthelred and before Cnut's final conquest (1016); preserved in five manuscripts, including British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i.
works.characters: Wulfstan (preacher, as 'Lupus'); the English nation
works.structure: A single continuous exhortation built on the antithesis of sin and punishment, with the historical crisis framed as the fulfilment of prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is certain ('Lupus' is his Latin signature).

works.title: Sermon of the Plough
works.description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
works.plot: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
works.significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
works.structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The English Reformation

works.title: Sermons (Hugh Blair)
works.form: published pulpit oratory and practical divinity, in the polite sermon tradition of the eighteenth century
works.description: The collected sermons of Blair, minister of St Giles's in Edinburgh and the most widely read Scottish preacher of his generation, issued from the later 1770s and reprinted across the English-speaking world. They exhibit the temperament of moderated Augustan pulpit oratory: practical, moral, polished, addressed to the feelings and to the conduct of ordinary life rather than to doctrinal controversy. Their success made Blair the standard model of the polite sermon and a central presence in the rhetoric of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.plot: The discourses take up the duties of the Christian life - the government of the passions, the duties of social and family conduct, the improvement of the mind, the conduct of affliction and the hope of a future state - and expound their texts with an orderly argument from observation of human feeling to practical application. Blair's handling of the parables and of the gospel history is narrative and affective, and his perorations press the auditor toward self-examination without invoking terrors.
works.significance: The Sermons were among the most reprinted religious books of the age, admired for their style by Blair's Scottish auditors and by the French and German translators who used them. They supply the practical counterpart to the Lectures on Rhetoric and remain the standard illustration of polite pulpit oratory in the culture of feeling.
works.meter: Prose; the balanced period, the graduated triple, the measured cadence and the clear syllabic emphasis for which Blair's theory of elocution was written into his own practice.
works.context: Preached and collected in the decades of Blair's incumbency at St Giles's and of his Edinburgh professorship of rhetoric and belles lettres, when the moderated Calvinism of the Scottish church and the culture of feeling met in the pulpit, and when the sermon was a literary genre with a substantial print market.
works.structure: A serial volume of separately preached discourses, each a single argument with an opening explication of the text, a progression of reflections and a closing application; the several series were gathered in successive volumes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several series of Blair's Sermons appeared across the later eighteenth century and the volumes are documented by his own publication of them, so the date entered here is that of the first collected series, with the later volumes described in the note.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society

Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
altTitles: Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
Sermons, Founded on Several Occasions, Preached at the Rolls Chapel, in Chancery Lane
works.description: Butler's early sermon sequence on human nature, conscience, and the authority of reflection, preached at the Rolls in the 1720s and published as a philosophical defence of the natural constitution of moral agents. Its central claim, that conscience is by nature authoritative in man, answers Mandeville, Hobbes, and Shaftesbury at once.
works.plot: Butler argues first that human nature is a system, not a heap of instincts, in which self-love and benevolence are naturally implanted and commonly coincide. Against psychological egoism he shows that particular passions have their own objects, and that pursuing them, not self, is the true path to happiness. Reflection or conscience surveys our actions and approves or disapproves with a natural authority that is one of degree as well as strength; to follow it is the case of the whole creature. The later sermons treat self-deception, the pursuit of pleasure, and the respect owing to conscience, grounding religion in the same constitution that grounds morality.
works.significance: The Preface and sermons anticipated the theories of benevolence, conscience, and authority debated by Hume, Reid, and the intuitionists, and remain the most-cited eighteenth-century text in moral philosophy besides the Treatise.
works.meter: The plain, exact, cumulative prose of the pulpit turned to analytic purpose: distinction after distinction, quietly weighted, with an unwonted precision of definition.
works.context: Preached between 1719 and 1725 before a Rolls audience drawn from the chancery bar, amid the Mandeville and Shaftesbury debates on self-love; the sermons were published in 1726 with a Preface that became a locus classicus of moral philosophy.
works.structure: A collected series of fifteen sermons with an analytical Preface, each sermon isolating one branch of the argument from human nature.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.description: The collected sermons of John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1691, published posthumously by his chaplain Ralph Barker; they are the model of latitudinarian preaching and were among the most widely read religious works of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: The sermons expound a rational, moral, and tolerant Christianity: the reasonableness of revelation, the duties of charity and justice, the evil of strife and persecution, and the practical character of true religion.
works.significance: Tillotson's sermons defined latitudinarian prose style and were a principal influence on Addison, Swift's models of plain preaching, and the moral temper of eighteenth-century Anglicanism.
works.meter: Clear, balanced, plain prose that became the standard of English pulpit eloquence.
works.context: Tillotson preached at St Lawrence Jewry and at court through the Restoration and after the Revolution; he was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1691 and died in 1694; the folio of his Works appeared in 1696.
works.structure: A collection of occasional sermons arranged by subject and occasion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Tillotson; the posthumous collection was edited by Ralph Barker.

works.title: Sesame and Lilies
works.description: Two lectures delivered in Manchester and Dublin in 1864 and published in 1865: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' on reading and education, and 'Of Queens' Gardens' on the education of women, the most widely read of all Ruskin's writings.
works.plot: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' argues that true reading is an act of attention and obedience to the author, and that a nation's education consists in its libraries and its reading; 'Of Queens' Gardens' argues that women should be educated to a 'queenly' influence in the home, and its conservative ideal of womanhood provoked a long controversy.
works.significance: Sesame and Lilies was the most widely read of Ruskin's books and the one that made him a public educator; 'Of Queens' Gardens' became a central text in the Victorian debate on women's education, and its ideal of 'queenly' domesticity was the target of the New Woman argument of the 1890s. The essays are the classic English statements of the moral value of reading.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The 1860s, the movement for women's higher education (Girton, 1869; Newnham, 1871), and Ruskin's own lectures at the Working Men's College. The record dates the work as composed in 1864 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Seven for a Secret
works.form: Novel (the seven gypsies and the secret)
works.description: The novel of the seven gypsies and the secret of the hills. It is a prose fiction work of 1922 by Mary Webb; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale.
works.plot: Seven for a Secret brings the seven gypsies and their secret into the Shropshire hills, and the novel follows the quarrel of the old religion and the chapel through the secret they carry.
works.significance: Seven for a Secret is Mary Webb's novel of the old religion of the hills: its seven gypsies and their secret carried the nature romance into the wonder-tale of the county.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather.
works.context: Shropshire in the early 1920s. The record dates the work as composed in 1921 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: the seven gypsies; the keeper of the secret; the chapel folk
works.structure: A novel of the secret in chapters of the hills and the old religion. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary Gladys Meredith. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
works.description: The great English prose epic of the desert war: Lawrence of Arabia and the Arab Revolt. It is a prose work of 1922 by T. E. Lawrence; it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lawrence's memoir of the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire in 1916–18: the campaigns with Feisal and Auda abu Tayi, the raids on Aqaba and the Hejaz railway, the capture of Damascus, and his own self-examination as the leader of other men in a war he has come to doubt.
works.significance: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is the great English prose epic of the desert war and one of the finest memoirs in the language: its prose, its self-scrutiny and its portrait of the Arab revolt made it the permanent literary record of the war in the desert and the founding text of the modern literature of the Middle East.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the memoir written as a confession and a history at once.
works.context: The Arab Revolt of 1916–1918, the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, and the imperial settlement of the Middle East. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: T. E. Lawrence; Prince Feisal; Auda abu Tayi; General Allenby; Ali ibn el Hussein
works.structure: Ten books, from the Arab Revolt's beginning to the capture of Damascus. A memoir in episodic chapters organised by posting or battle, the later self reflecting on the earlier experience. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Edward Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Seven Types of Ambiguity
works.form: Critical study (the analysis of verbal ambiguity)
works.description: The study that made ambiguity the instrument of the close reading. It is a prose work of 1930 by William Empson; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Seven Types of Ambiguity analyses the degrees of verbal ambiguity, from the simple metaphor to the contradiction that opens the whole of the meaning, in readings of Shakespeare, Donne, Herbert, Marvell, Hopkins and the moderns, and makes the unfolding of the senses the method of criticism.
works.significance: Seven Types of Ambiguity is the founding text of the close reading: its seven degrees of ambiguity made the analysis of the word the instrument of criticism and gave the century its most imitated critical method.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the close reading that unfolds every sense of the word.
works.context: Cambridge in 1930, and the founding of the close reading. The record dates the work as composed in 1929 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A study in seven chapters, one degree of ambiguity to a chapter, with the readings. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir William Empson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Seventy-Six
works.form: Historical novel of the Revolutionary period in the comic and popular manner
works.description: A novel of the year of the Declaration of Independence, and one of the earliest American attempts to write the Revolution as popular comedy rather than as civic legend. Its scene is a New England town and its personages a company of ordinary men swept into the war. The book treats patriotism as a matter of temperament and of incident.
works.plot: In a community on the eve of the war, neighbours are divided by interest, habit and fear as the crisis arrives, and the call to arms draws each of them into the contest by a different motive. The narrative follows the enlistments, the quarrels and the comic misadventures of a company raised from the town. Private interest and public duty are played against one another until the war settles the argument. The book ends with the Revolution established and the community transformed by the demands made on it.
works.significance: It is among the first American fictions to make the Revolution available as popular comedy, and it anticipates the later native treatment of the founding as everyday history. Its crowded speech and provincial idiom are an early experiment in American vernacular. It documents the range of the historical novel in the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at New York in 1823, in the efflorescence of centennial and semi-centennial interest in the founding events. Its plebeian treatment of patriotism belongs to the author's quarrel with the dignified historical novel. The book was written when its author was editing a newspaper and preparing his move to English publishing.
works.structure: Third-person popular novel of a community in crisis, episodic and crowded with speech-types, with the historical year imposed as frame and title.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code

works.title: Severe Poems
works.description: Gurney's first collection: the Gloucestershire landscape and the trench side by side. It is a verse work of 1917 by Ivor Gurney; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Georgian Anthology Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection gathers Gurney's early poems — 'Strange Hells', 'The Silent One', 'To His Love', 'The Target', 'De Profundis' — in which the landscape of Gloucestershire and the experience of the trench are held together in a single music.
works.significance: Severe Poems was Gurney's first collection and one of the finest books of the war: its music, its landscape and its unsentimental grief made him the most original English poet of the war after Owen, and it established the poetry that the later collections fulfilled.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact image of the trench and the county.
works.context: Gloucestershire and the Western Front in 1915–17. works.title: Shadow and Act
works.description: Shadow and Act is Ralph Ellison's first collection of essays, published by Random House in 1964: reviews, lectures, interviews and memoirs written over some twenty years on literature, jazz and the blues, and the representation of Black Americans in fiction and film.
works.summary: Three sections: "The Seer and the Seen", on fiction and the writer's craft, including "Twentieth-Century Fiction and the Black Mask of Humanity", "Change the Joke and Slip the Yoke" and "The World and the Jug"; "Sound and the Mainstream", on jazz and the blues, including essays on Charlie Parker, Charlie Christian and Jimmy Rushing; and "The Shadow and the Act", on film and society, including the title essay on Hollywood films about race and "Harlem Is Nowhere".
works.plot: Ellison argues that Black American life is not a mere reaction to oppression but a culture with its own complexity, discipline and joy, and that the Black writer must be judged as an artist rather than as a sociological spokesman. The literary essays attack the reduction of Black characters to stereotypes in American fiction and defend the writer's use of folklore and the vernacular, as in his exchange with Stanley Edgar Hyman over the trickster figure and with Irving Howe over Richard Wright's legacy. The music essays present jazz musicians as models of artistic discipline and improvisation within a tradition, and the closing essays read Hollywood's treatment of race and the psychological cost of life in Harlem as symptoms of a national failure to see Black Americans.
works.significance: It established Ellison as a major American essayist and remains a key statement of the view that African American culture is central to American identity; "The World and the Jug" is a classic document of the debate over protest literature.
works.meter: Lucid, urbane and allusive prose that moves easily from memoir to argument, enlivened by anecdote and by the conversational give-and-take of the interviews.
works.context: The collection appeared in 1964, at the height of the civil rights movement and just before the rise of the Black Arts Movement, when the role of the Black writer was fiercely debated.
works.structure: A personal introduction followed by three thematic sections of essays, interviews and reviews from 1942 to 1964, arranged by subject rather than date.

Nationhood and national identity
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: Shakespear Illustrated
altTitles: Shakespear Illustrated: Containing the Genuine Plot of His Best Plays, Proving That They Are Translations from the Italian, Spanish and French
Shakespear Illustrated, with Essays Proving His Plays Translations
works.form: critical treatise with comparative abstracts of sources
works.description: A critical collection proving from the antecedent tales that the plots of Shakespeare's best plays are borrowed from Italian, Spanish and French originals, each play being faced with an abstract of the source. Its prefatory discourse on the properties of drama is an early statement of neoclassical plot doctrine in English criticism.
works.plot: The work examines a sequence of the plays - among them Othello, Measure for Measure, All's Well That Ends Well, Romeo and Juliet and The Taming of the Shrew - and sets against each the story Shakespeare found. It shows the plot as given, the alterations as made, and argues that the poet's judgement rather than his invention is to be praised or blamed. The prefatory discourse draws the conclusion that fidelity to probability and to the unities is the measure of dramatic merit.
works.significance: It is an important document of source study before scholarship and of the eighteenth-century argument about Shakespeare's obligations to the romance tradition, anticipating later source criticism.
works.meter: Plain argumentative prose of the mid-century critical essay, with the quoted abstracts in a deliberately bald narrative style.
works.context: Published in 1753 in two volumes, in the season of the great editions of Shakespeare and of the quarrel over his regularity, and written by a novelist-critic with access to the Italian and Spanish sources through translation.
works.structure: A series of comparative essays, each pairing an abstract of the source with remarks on the play, framed by a general discourse on the drama; the argument is cumulative and evidential.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though early bibliographers occasionally misassigned it.

works.title: Shakespeare's Plays: The Princess's Theatre Productions
works.description: The antiquarian Shakespeare of the Victorian stage: the researched production and the historical tableau. It is a prose work of 1850 by Charles Kean; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Kean's production records of his Shakespeare revivals at the Princess's Theatre — The Tempest, A Midsummer Night's Dream, Henry VIII, Richard II, King Lear — with the historical research into costume, setting and antiquarian detail that made his productions a new kind of theatre.
works.significance: Kean's production records are the founding documents of the antiquarian Shakespeare and of the modern director's theatre: his historical research made the Victorian Shakespeare a vehicle of historical education and established the production as an interpretation of the play.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian production with its researched setting.
works.context: London in the 1850s, the Victorian Shakespeare and the antiquarian movement of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1859 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Kean; the Princess's company; the designers; the antiquarian advisers
works.structure: Production records and promptbooks of the Shakespeare revivals. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. works.title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
works.description: The 154 sonnets printed in 1609, with the long poem 'A Lover's Complaint' appended: a sequence to a beautiful young man urging him to marry and immortalizing him in verse, shadowed by a rival poet and by the 'dark lady' of the later sonnets — the greatest sonnet collection in the language, and the most argued-over book of poems in English literary history.
works.plot: The first seventeen sonnets press the youth to marry; the middle poems anatomize love, jealousy, absence, and the rival poet; the dark lady sequence (127–152) turns on lust and self-betrayal; and the final poems rework Cupid and the cures of love, closing with 'A Lover's Complaint' spoken by a forsaken maid.
works.significance: The summit of the English sonnet tradition; its identities, erotic shapes, and textual mysteries have made it a permanent site of scholarship and dispute.
works.meter: The Shakespearean sonnet (abab cdcd efef gg) brought to its definitive form, with 'A Lover's Complaint' in rhyme royal.
works.context: Composed across the 1590s and early 1600s, partly circulating in manuscript; printed by Thomas Thorpe in 1609 with the dedication 'To the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets, Mr. W.H.' — the most famous crux in English bibliography.
works.characters: the poet; the young man (Fair Youth); the dark lady; the rival poet; the maid (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of 154 sonnets with a detectable narrative arc — courtship, crisis, self-reproach — followed by the appended complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Shakespeare's; the identities of the Fair Youth, the dark lady, and 'Mr. W.H.' remain unknown.
themes: Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue

works.title: Shamela
works.form: short epistolary burlesque and prose satire
works.description: A short burlesque of the servant-girl novel, published anonymously in the same season as its original, which turns the heroine's letters into the devices of an artful seductress pursuing her aim. It is the earliest and sharpest of the answers to the conduct fiction, arguing from inside the form that its morality was interested.
works.plot: Shamela Andrews, a country servant with an eye on her mistress's estate, writes letters home rehearsing her own arts of attack and defence. She is courted, resisted and finally complied with on her own schedule, her scruples being the scruples of design, and she secures a proposal from the squire while keeping the old woman and the parson in play. The piece ends with her married and in possession, the pretence of virtue having served the whole design.
works.significance: It invented the technique of the ideologically inverted parody and remains the standard instance of the eighteenth-century argument that the novel of moral reward was a fiction of interest; it also led directly to the author's own theory of comic prose.
works.meter: A debased copy of the servant style, with the idiom and misspellings of the original mocked and the candid sentences of the design breaking through the piety.
works.context: Published in April 1741, three months after the conduct novel it answers, in a season crowded with its imitations and abridgements; the pamphlet war over the education of women and the price of virtue formed its immediate context.
works.characters: Shamela Andrews; Squire Booby; Parson Williams; Mrs. Slipslop; the old lady of the family
works.structure: An epistolary burlesque in a single short volume, the letters' dates and self-exposures replacing the original's suspense; the prefatorial apparatus directs the reading as party attack.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long anonymous and established by internal evidence, the contemporary advertisement and later acknowledgment; recorded here as single.
