works.title: She Stoops to Conquer; or, The Mistakes of a Night
works.form: Laughing comedy in five acts, dialogue prose, for the London theatre, printed with prologue and epilogue and with the customary dramatis personae; built on the comic conceits of mistaken place and assumed condition.
works.description: Goldsmith's masterpiece for the stage and one of the two or three comedies that survived continuously in the English repertory from the eighteenth century: a laughing comedy in which a mistake about the identity of a house sets the whole plot going and in which a young woman deliberately 'stoops' in order to win the man she loves. It was written in explicit opposition to the sentimental comedy of distress and was dedicated to Samuel Johnson.
works.plot: Young Marlow, ardent and forward with women of easy reputation but dumb and bashful before a modest woman, is brought by his father's arrangement to the house of the neighbouring Mr Hardcastle, whom he is to marry. The idler Tony Lumpkin, who has no wish to be married himself and delights in mischief, directs the travellers to Hardcastle's house as though it were an inn; Hardcastle, learning of the mistake and determined to cure his son's bashfulness by it, plays the landlord. Marlow therefore behaves with insolent freedom towards the real daughter of the house, whom he takes for a barmaid, and Kate, perceiving what has happened, consents to the deception and 'stoops' to the character in order to be loved for herself. The subplots of Tony's own refused match and of the elopements are gathered into the same night's confusion, and the discovery of the mistake at the end restores order, consent and the couple.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comedy between Congreve and Sheridan, and the practical vindication of Goldsmith's theory that comedy should correct by laughter rather than by distress. Its Tony Lumpkin and its Kate Hardcastle became standards of the repertory, and its plot of the assumed condition remains the best-known illustration of the eighteenth-century effort to reconcile sentiment with mirth.
works.context: It was produced in the season in which the managers were rebuilding the comedy of the London stage and in which Goldsmith's quarrel with the theatre of sentimental distress had been running for years; its success is part of the theatrical regeneration associated with the great players and managers of the 1770s. Its satire upon provincial idleness and upon the fashionable manners of London belongs to the same decade's comedy of national character.
works.characters: Young Marlow; Kate Hardcastle; Mr Hardcastle; Mrs Hardcastle; Tony Lumpkin; Mr Hastings; Constance Neville
works.structure: A five-act comedy of errors and disguised identities with a single night's duration, driven by one sustained mistake and by characters' knowledge of it, and resolved by the discovery scene; the amatory main plot is supported by the comic country plot of the idler and his intended.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's, its production history is documented, and the printed edition carries his name and his dedication. Its relation to the earlier project of 'The Mistakes of a Night' is a matter of editorial chronology rather than of authorship.

works.title: She Would if She Could
works.description: Etherege's second comedy, a brilliant but famously unsuccessful intrigue play in which two rakes, Courtall and Sir Joslin Jolly, pursue two masked beauties through a series of crossed appointments.
works.plot: Courtall and Sir Joslin arrange assignations with Ariana and Gatty; the women appear in disguise, the men are deceived, and a series of farcical failures leads to the marriages the title promises.
works.significance: Now recognised as one of the finest and most formally daring Restoration comedies, its plotless brilliance anticipating Congreve.
works.meter: Sparkling prose throughout.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields on 6 February 1668 and failed with the audience, though Pepys admired it; it was long undervalued before the twentieth-century revival.
works.characters: Courtall; Sir Joslin Jolly; Ariana; Gatty; Lady Cockwood; Rakehell; Mr Trim; Betty
works.structure: Five acts of almost pure intrigue with a single day's action and minimal plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.

works.title: She: A History of Adventure
works.description: Published in 1887 and Haggard's masterpiece: the discovery of the immortal queen Ayesha in a lost city beneath an African volcano. It is a prose fiction work of 1887 by H. Rider Haggard; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation.
works.plot: Leo Vincey and Horace Holly travel to the lost city of Kôr, where Ayesha, who has lived for two thousand years, believes Leo to be the reincarnation of her murdered lover Kallikrates; she bathes him in the flame of life, but the experiment that would make her mortal again destroys her, and the explorers escape the collapsing city.
works.significance: She is one of the foundational books of modern popular fiction: Ayesha became one of the great mythic figures of English literature, the novel invented the lost-world romance that Conan Doyle, Kipling and the cinema would carry into the twentieth century, and it has never been out of print.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person testimony of the practical man.
works.context: 1887: the archaeology of the ancient world, the Victorian interest in spiritualism and immortality, and the imperial exploration of central Africa. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1887 and first published in 1887 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
works.characters: Ludwig Horace Holly (the narrator); Leo Vincey; Ayesha, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'; Job; Ustane; Billali; Kallikrates
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Rider Haggard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Shirley: A Tale
works.description: Published in October 1849, written during the illness and deaths of Emily and Anne, and set in the Luddite Yorkshire of 1811-12: the first English novel to make an industrial dispute its central public subject, and the one in which Brontë tried to write a social novel on the scale of her contemporaries.
works.plot: Robert Gérard Moore, a mill-owner of Belgian descent, attempts to introduce machinery into his mill during the Napoleonic blockade and is attacked by the Luddite frame-breakers; his mill is defended by troops. His cousin Caroline Helstone, neglected by her family, falls ill, and Shirley Keeldar, the heiress who gives the novel its name, takes up Caroline's cause. Shirley at last accepts Robert's brother Louis Moore, the tutor who has loved her in silence, and Caroline, who discovers that the quiet Mrs Pryor is her own mother, is united with Robert when the repeal of the Orders in Council restores the mill's prosperity.
works.significance: Shirley is one of the earliest English novels to give the industrial conflict serious fictional treatment, and its two heroines — the heiress who owns the mill property and the penniless relation who must work — set out the 'woman question' of the 1840s in terms that the 1850s debate over 'surplus women' took up. It is also the only Brontë novel with a sustained comic and social panorama.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
works.context: The Luddite risings of 1811-12 and the Yorkshire frame-breaking, the Napoleonic Orders in Council and the blockade, and the Chartist and 1848 revolutionary year in which Brontë was writing. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1849 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Shirley Keeldar; Caroline Helstone; Robert Gérard Moore; Louis Moore; the Reverend Matthewson Helstone; Mrs Pryor, Caroline's mother; Hortense Moore; Hiram Yorke; Joe Scott; William Farren; the curates Malone, Donne and Sweeting
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Shooting an Elephant and Other Essays
works.description: The first posthumous collection of Orwell's essays, published by Secker and Warburg on 5 October 1950, nine months after his death: eighteen essays written between 1931 and 1949, among them 'Shooting an Elephant', 'A Hanging', 'Politics and the English Language' and 'Reflections on Gandhi', the core of his reputation as an essayist.
works.summary: The essays are 'Shooting an Elephant', 'A Hanging', 'How the Poor Die', 'Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool', 'Politics vs. Literature: An Examination of Gulliver's Travels', 'Politics and the English Language', 'Reflections on Gandhi', 'The Prevention of Literature', 'Second Thoughts on James Burnham', 'Confessions of a Book Reviewer', 'Books v. Cigarettes', 'Good Bad Books', 'Nonsense Poetry', 'Riding Down from Bangor', 'The Sporting Spirit', 'Decline of the English Murder', 'Some Thoughts on the Common Toad' and 'A Good Word for the Vicar of Bray'. The WorldCat contents note also lists an 'I Write As I Please' selection.
works.plot: The book opens with two Burmese pieces. In 'Shooting an Elephant' a young police officer kills an elephant he does not want to kill because the watching crowd expects it, and learns that the imperialist becomes the prisoner of the people he rules; 'A Hanging' recounts an execution at which a condemned man's step aside to avoid a puddle reveals what Orwell calls the unspeakable wrongness of cutting a life short. 'How the Poor Die' recalls a public hospital ward in Paris. The central essays argue about language and literature under political pressure. 'Politics and the English Language' contends that the decay of English and political dishonesty feed each other, that euphemism and dead metaphor make atrocities sayable, and ends with six rules for clear writing. 'The Prevention of Literature' argues that totalitarianism, and the intellectuals' acquiescence in it, destroy the conditions for honest prose. 'Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool' defends King Lear against Tolstoy's attack and reads the attack as the work of a man who renounced the world without renouncing power over others, and 'Politics vs. Literature' examines Swift's misanthropy and asks why Gulliver's Travels can delight readers who reject its politics. 'Reflections on Gandhi' weighs sainthood against the humanist's loyalty to this world. The shorter pieces, most from Tribune, on the common toad in spring, book-reviewing, the cost of reading compared with smoking and the decline of the classic English murder, carry the same concern with truth, decency and ordinary pleasure.
works.significance: The collection contains the most widely read of Orwell's essays: 'Shooting an Elephant' and 'A Hanging' became standard texts on imperialism, and 'Politics and the English Language' became the most influential English statement on plain style and political euphemism, its six rules reprinted and taught for generations. It fixed the image of Orwell as the conscience of plain English prose.
works.meter: The narrative essays use understated first-person testimony in which a single physical detail carries the moral judgement; the argumentative essays proceed by quotation, example and, in the case of the essay on language, numbered rules; the Tribune pieces are conversational and comic. The prose throughout practises what 'Politics and the English Language' prescribes.
works.context: Published nine months after Orwell's death on 21 January 1950, the collection gathers work mostly from 1945-49, the years of Animal Farm's success, of Nineteen Eighty-Four and of the first Cold War quarrels over communism, censorship and the intellectuals; many of the essays had appeared in Horizon, Polemic, Tribune and Partisan Review.
works.structure: Three personal narratives (Burma and the Paris hospital) come first, then six long critical and political essays of 1946-49, then shorter pieces written mostly for Tribune in 1945-46, without section divisions.
themes: Death, illness and mourning
Decolonisation, the end of empire and the new nation
Language, writing and the limits of representation
Power, the state and surveillance

works.title: Shorter Poems
works.description: Published in 1890 and Bridges's finest collection of lyrics: love poems, nature poems and songs of a classical perfection. It is a verse work of 1890 by Robert Bridges; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet.
works.plot: The collection gathers the lyrics of twenty years — 'London Snow', 'A Passer-By', 'Nightingales', 'On a Dead Child' and the songs of the English countryside — in forms of exquisite finish and classical restraint.
works.significance: Shorter Poems is the finest English lyric collection of its decade and the model of classical restraint in Victorian verse: its technical perfection made Bridges the poet's poet of his generation, and it contains some of the most perfect short poems in the language.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is exquisite metrical control in received forms.
works.context: 1873-90: the Oxford of Pater and Hopkins, the English country house, and the reaction against the rhetoric of Tennyson and Swinburne. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Seymour Bridges. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs
works.form: Epic poem in four books, first issued in 1876
works.description: Published in 1876 and Morris's greatest poem: a retelling of the Norse Volsunga saga, the source of the Nibelungenlied and of Wagner's Ring. It is a verse work of 1876 by William Morris; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Sigurd slays the dragon Fafnir, wins the hoard and the ring Andvaranaut, awakens Brynhild on Hindfell, is drugged and marries Gudrun, and is murdered by the Niblungs; the poem ends with Gudrun's revenge and the destruction of the Niblung house.
works.significance: Sigurd the Volsung is the finest English epic poem of the nineteenth century and the central text of the Victorian Norse revival: its influence on Tolkien, on the modern fantasy and on the English idea of the heroic is enormous.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The author's characteristic manner is long, even, unrhymed or heroic-couplet narrative.
works.context: 1876: the Victorian interest in the Norse sagas, the Icelandic scholarship of the period, and Wagner's Ring (first performed complete in 1876). The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.

works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.

works.title: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe
works.form: Novel in one volume; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in one volume in April 1861, Eliot's shortest novel and the one most often read as a parable: the story of a linen-weaver who loses his faith and his gold and is restored by the child who walks into his cottage.
works.plot: Silas Marner, falsely accused of theft by his fellow Dissenters at Lantern Yard, settles in the village of Raveloe, where he hoards his guineas until they are stolen by the squire's son Dunstan Cass. A little girl, Eppie, comes to his fire one winter night, and the novel follows her upbringing and the attempt of her true father Godfrey Cass to reclaim her, which she refuses in favour of the weaver who raised her.
works.significance: Silas Marner is the most formally perfect of Eliot's novels and the one that most clearly states her secular religion of sympathy; it is a permanent school text and the standard English example of the redemptive foundling plot, and its treatment of religious community and of the alienated craftsman anticipates the sociology of the novel in the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The rural Midlands at the turn of the nineteenth century, the Dissenting chapel and the village church, the isolation of the weaver and the new industrial economy, and the paternalism of the squire's family.
works.characters: Silas Marner; Eppie; Godfrey Cass; Dunstan Cass; Nancy Lammeter; Squire Cass; Dolly Winthrop; William Dane; Molly Farren
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Silex Scintillans
altTitles: Silex Scintillans; or, Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
works.description: Henry Vaughan's great collection of mystical religious verse (1650, expanded 1655), whose poems seek God through nature, childhood memory, and visionary longing — 'The Retreat', 'The World', 'Peace', and the 'Rules and Lessons' — earning him the title 'the Silurist' and a place among the metaphysical poets.
works.plot: The poems move between longing for a lost innocence and eternity glimpsed behind the world ('Eternity' in 'The World'), meditations on scripture and the sacraments, elegies, and practical rules for holy living.
works.significance: Once obscure, Silex Scintillans was recovered by the Romantics and Coleridge (whose 'intimation of immortality' echoes 'The Retreat') and is now recognised as major mystical poetry of the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Luminous, musical verse with emblematic structure and a visionary intensity drawn from Herbert but wilder and more personal.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the Civil Wars and Vaughan's royalist seclusion in Breconshire, and deeply influenced by Herbert's Temple; the 1655 edition added secular and satirical pieces.
works.characters: the poet; God; the soul; natural and biblical figures
works.structure: A two-part collection (1650, then 1655 with 'Flamma sine Fumo') of devotional lyrics, translations, and epigrams loosely ordered around themes of nature, eternity, and faith.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under the initials 'H.V.' and the title 'the Silurist'.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Divine love and holy desire
Exile and homelessness
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey

works.title: Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book
works.description: Published in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes: 120 nursery rhymes, riddles, lullabies and poems on natural history written for and about children, and one of the foundation texts of English children's verse.
works.plot: The poems are short lyrics on the moon, the wind, birds, flowers, death and sleep, many of them in question-and-answer form or in dialogue with a child; some are riddles whose answers lie in the natural world.
works.significance: Sing-Song is one of the purest bodies of children's verse in English and a central document in the history of Victorian children's literature. Its frank treatment of death and its formal perfection have made it a permanent text for the study of the Victorian child, and it influenced de la Mare and the children's poets of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
works.context: The 1870s and the new market for illustrated children's books (Caldecott, Crane, Greenaway), the Victorian cult of childhood, and the mortality rates among children that the poems accept without evasion.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christina Georgina Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale
Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
movements: Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature

works.title: Sinister Street
works.description: The great novel of Oxford and London before the war: a young man's education. It is a prose fiction work of 1913 by Compton Mackenzie; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Michael Fane, the illegitimate son of a baronet, grows up in London, goes up to Oxford and comes down into the city, in a long novel of education, class and the passions that became the model for the modern novel of youth.
works.significance: Sinister Street was one of the most influential novels of its age and the founding text of the modern novel of education: its Oxford and its London made it a model for Waugh, Powell and the twentieth-century novel of youth.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the comic novel of the island.
works.context: England in the 1890s and 1900s, from the London streets to Oxford. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1914 and first published in 1913 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Michael Fane; Stella Fane; Lily; Sylvia Scarlett; the Oxford friends
works.structure: A novel in two volumes, from childhood to Oxford and London. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Montague Compton Mackenzie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Sir Degaré
works.description: A Breton lay of the foundling knight: Degaré, son of a fairy knight who ravished his mother, is exposed at birth, raised by a hermit, and wins his spurs through combat with a dragon; his search for his father ends in recognition, reunion, and the marriage of his widowed mother to her long-lost lover. Preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Degaré, given his father's broken sword at birth, defeats the dragon, unhorses the knights of Arthur's court, and proves himself; seeking his father, he jousts with the fairy knight himself, and the two recognize each other; the poem ends with the father's return and the family's reunion.
works.significance: A representative minor lai valuable for the incest-anxieties and recognition patterns of the genre, and a staple of romance anthologies.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, plain and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1325, probably in the south-east; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and later copies including the Percy Folio.
works.characters: Degaré; the fairy knight (his father); his mother; the hermit
works.structure: A foundling-quest in the lai manner, with the father-son combat as its climactic recognition scene.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.description: The supreme masterpiece of the Alliterative Revival and one of the greatest poems of the English Middle Ages: 2,530 lines in alliterative stanzas with the 'bob and wheel' close, recounting Gawain's beheading-game with the Green Knight and his testing in the castle of Sir Bertilak. A romance of courtesy, chastity, and shame, in which the pentangle and the green girdle measure the hero against an ideal he cannot perfectly keep.
works.plot: At Arthur's Christmas court, the Green Knight offers his axe-blow for a return stroke a year hence; Gawain beheads him, and the knight rides off alive. The following winter Gawain journeys to the Green Chapel, is entertained for three days at Hautdesert — where his host's wife tests his chastity with escalating temptations while the host hunts deer, boar, and fox in parallel scenes — and, having accepted the protective green girdle and concealed it, receives at the Chapel a nick on the neck: the girdle's shame is revealed as the whole adventure was Bertilak's design, set on him by Morgan le Fay.
works.significance: The most admired English romance ever written: its fusion of alliterative craft, courtly ideals, and moral seriousness — and its unmatched winter landscapes and temptation scenes — have made it a touchstone of English literature (translated by Tolkien, Armitage, and many others).
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the five-line rhymed 'bob and wheel'.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by an unknown north-west Midlands poet (the 'Gawain-poet'), probably in the household circle of the Cheshire/Staffordshire gentry; preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Nero A.x, with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: Gawain; the Green Knight (Sir Bertilak); Lady Bertilak; Arthur; Guinevere; Morgan le Fay; the guide
works.structure: A two-part structure (the beheading game at Camelot; the journey, temptations, and exchange of winnings at Hautdesert), interlaced by the three parallel hunts and the three bedroom temptations, and closed by Gawain's return and Arthur's court's adoption of the girdle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness to the single 'Gawain-poet' on grounds of style, dialect, and shared manuscript.
themes: Arthurian legend
Chivalry and knighthood
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: Sir Launfal
works.description: Thomas Chestre's late fourteenth-century Breton lay of the fairy mistress: the knight Launfal, impoverished and slighted at Arthur's court, receives boundless wealth and the love of the fairy lady Tryamour on condition of secrecy, and is saved from death by her at his trial. The most accomplished English version of Marie de France's Lanval.
works.plot: Launfal, neglected by Arthur, rides out in despair and meets Tryamour, whose gifts restore his magnificence; his boast of her beauty at court — provoked by the queen's advances — brings trial for treason, but Tryamour appears at the judgement, vindicates him, and carries him to the fairy isle of Olyroun.
works.significance: The finest English fairy-mistress lay and the standard version of the Lanval story in English; a key text for the romance's treatment of women and power.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas of the popular romance kind.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 by Thomas Chestre (who names himself in the poem), reworking the earlier Sir Landevale and Marie de France; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Launfal; Tryamour; Arthur; Guinevere (unnamed queen); the mayor of Caerleon
works.structure: The classic lai structure: courtly exclusion, otherworld encounter, transgression, trial, and translation to the otherworld.
works.attributionNotes: The author names himself 'Thomas Chestre' in the poem's opening lines.
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: Sir Orfeo
works.description: The masterpiece of the English Breton lay: the classical myth of Orpheus and Eurydice retold as a Celtic fairy romance, in which King Orfeo, harper of Winchester, loses his queen Heurodis to the fairy king and wins her back through the power of his music. Some 600 lines of haunting narrative, preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Heurodis is taken by the fairy king from under the ympe-tree; Orfeo abandons his throne to live as a harper in the wilderness, sees his queen among the fairy riders, follows them into their castle, and recovers her by his harping; the poem ends with the steward's loyalty tested and the kingdom restored.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the finest of the Middle English Breton lays and one of the great short narratives of the period; the classical myth's medieval transformation is a touchstone of romance criticism.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lyrical set-pieces; economical and evocative.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in the London area, reworking the Orpheus myth through Celtic fairy-lore and the Breton lai tradition; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and two fifteenth-century copies.
works.characters: Orfeo; Heurodis; the fairy king; the steward
works.structure: A lai of loss, wilderness exile, and recovery, framed by the steward episode; the Otherworld journey is its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
Monsters and the marvellous

works.title: Sir Thomas More; or, Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society
works.form: Humanist dialogue and moral-philosophical prose, a Christian-humanist colloquy of the kind written by More himself, turned to the question of social progress.
works.description: The author's late prose colloquy, long gestating and issued in two volumes, in which the writer converses with the ghost or the spirit of Sir Thomas More about the condition and the future of society. It is the most systematic of his prose works, ranging over education, the press, the working classes, pauperism, Rome, and the colonies in a humanist dialogue form. The book is a storehouse of the period's anxieties about progress, and was later quarried by Marx for its evidence on the manufacturing system.
works.plot: More, learned and sceptical, is made to survey the modern world from the vantage of a man who knew another civilisation before the Reformation and the age of commerce. He questions the writer about the diffusion of knowledge through cheap print, about the education of the poorer classes, and about whether the increase of reading has improved the readers. Other colloquies treat the condition of labour, the growth of the towns, the state of Ireland, Roman Catholic claims, the colonies and slavery, and the prospects of Christianity in an age of machinery and of political change. The argument throughout is conservative in method but genuinely alarmed: material progress is admitted, and then weighed against the moral and religious cost, with More pressing toward a defence of counsel, conscience, and settled order.
works.significance: The most complete statement of its author's social thought and one of the most quoted conservative analyses of the manufacturing age, important both as a document of romantic-era Toryism and as a source of evidence on early industrial conditions later used by writers of the opposite opinion.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Published in the years of post-war depression, of the quarrel over Catholic emancipation, and of the first factory and education legislation; the first volume appeared in 1829, on the eve of the Reform crisis, and the second followed soon after, when the debate about the 'condition of England' was opening.
works.characters: Sir Thomas More; the enquiring writer
works.structure: Series of colloquies in dialogue form between the author and the shade of More, without dramatic setting or plot; each colloquy takes up one subject and is free to digress into report, history, and prophecy.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Order and degree: the body politic
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: Siris
altTitles: Siris: A Chain of Philosophical Inquiries and Speculations concerning the Virtue of Tar-water
Siris: or, the Chain of Philosophy
works.description: Berkeley's strange and late 'chain of philosophical inquiry', occasioned by the vogue of tar-water as a medicine, which rises from remedies and agriculture through electricity, the animal fibre, and the Platonic one to a hymn to light and the divine mind. It is his most explicitly Platonizing and most idiosyncratic published work.
works.plot: Berkeley praises tar-water as a specific for many distempers and derives from its humble origin a chain of enquiry into virtue in physical things, fire, air, and electricity as the universal active medium. He speculates that a far subtler electric or aetherial spirit pervades and quickens nature, the seat of vital motion and of the animal spirits, and that light is the most universal being whose finite emanation binds the world. From physics the chain ascends to Platonic ontology: the one, the good, and intellectual light, closing with an apostrophe to the source of light and truth. The book thus makes medicine the stairway to natural theology.
works.significance: It stands as the century's most curious fusion of empiricist science and Platonist mysticism, and it renewed the ancient doctrine of the one and of vital spirit in a modern scientific vocabulary.
works.meter: A rising, sometimes rapturous prose of questions and responsive speculations, with a long hymnic peroration in rhythmic periods.
works.context: Published in 1744 after Berkeley's return from America and the failure of his Bermuda college scheme, in the season of electrical excitement following Franklin and of popular medical specifics; it was reviewed, mocked, and translated on the continent.
works.structure: A serial chain of short linked enquiries, each section drawing the previous upward, in the manner of a Platonizing rhapsody.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Medicine, healing, and the body
The New Science and experimental philosophy

works.title: Sirius: A Fantasy of Love and Discord
works.form: Novel; scientific romance, first issued in 1944
works.description: Stapledon's finest novel: a dog given human intelligence, and the loneliness of the creature between species. It is a prose fiction work of 1944 by Olaf Stapledon; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Sirius, a puppy of the Great Dane breed, is given human intelligence by a scientist, and grows up between the human and the animal worlds: he loves a woman, plays music, writes a book, and is destroyed by the hatred of the humans who cannot accept him.
works.significance: Sirius is Stapledon's finest novel and the most moving book in the scientific romance: its study of a creature between two species and its treatment of love and loneliness made it the most humane work of his career.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the future history narrated by a species rather than a character.
works.context: North Wales in the 1930s, the biology of the period and the war years. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1944 and first published in 1944 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under scientific romance and the utopian tale.
works.characters: Sirius; Thomas Trelone; Plaxy Trelone; Elizabeth Trelone
works.structure: A biography in fourteen chapters, from puppyhood to death. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Olaf Stapledon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Sister Carrie
works.description: Published in 1900 and the founding American naturalist novel of the city: a country girl's rise in Chicago and New York through the men who desire her. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Theodore Dreiser; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Carrie Meeber comes from a Wisconsin village to Chicago, works in a shoe factory, is taken up by the salesman Drouet and then by the saloon manager Hurstwood; Hurstwood steals money and flees with her to New York, where he declines into poverty and suicide while Carrie becomes a successful actress.
works.significance: Sister Carrie is the founding American naturalist novel and the first great American novel of the city: its refusal to punish Carrie, its sympathy for Hurstwood and its cold analysis of desire made it a scandal in 1900 and the model for the twentieth-century American novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is slow accumulation of documentary detail.
works.context: 1900: the Chicago of the 1890s, the department store and the new consumption, the Broadway theatre, and the American debate on the 'woman adrift'. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Carrie Meeber; Charles Drouet; George Hurstwood; Julia Hurstwood; Minnie Hanson; Robert Ames; Lola Osborne
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: Sister Songs
works.form: Poem in two parts; pastoral elegy
works.description: Published in 1895 and the most personal of Thompson's long poems: a celebration of two sisters, the children of his patrons, and of the love of children as a figure of divine love. It is a verse work of 1895 by Francis Thompson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem.
works.plot: The poet addresses first the younger sister and then the older, and moves from the observation of their play to a meditation on childhood, innocence, the Incarnation and his own unworthiness.
works.significance: Sister Songs is the finest English poem of the love of children after Patmore and one of the great religious poems of the 1890s: its fusion of the domestic and the mystical made it the model for the modern devotional poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is irregular odes with long, hovering lines.
works.context: 1895: the Meynell household, the Victorian poetry of childhood, and the Catholic theology of the child. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Francis Joseph Thompson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Sketches
works.description: The founding American society sketch: London, Paris and the fashionable world in the magazine. It is a prose work of 1835 by Nathaniel Parker Willis; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Willis's sketches collect his letters and impressions from Europe and America: the great house, the dinner party, the actress, the club and the fashionable assembly, in the confiding first-person voice of the magazine correspondent.
works.significance: Sketches was the founding American society sketch and made Willis the most popular magazine writer in the country: it created the personal column and the celebrity profile in American journalism and prepared the way for the mass-market magazine.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is the familiar letter from abroad.
works.context: London and Paris in the 1830s, and the new American magazine market of the Jacksonian period. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1835 and first published in 1835 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Willis as narrator; the actresses; the grandees; the travellers
works.structure: A collection of magazine sketches and letters. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: Sketches by Boz, Illustrative of Every-Day Life and Every-Day People
works.form: Collected periodical sketches in two series
works.description: Dickens's first book: fifty-six sketches, mostly reprinted from the Monthly Magazine, the Morning Chronicle and the Evening Chronicle, issued in two series (first series February 1836, second December 1836) with illustrations by George Cruikshank. The pieces fall into four groups: sketches of London streets, of 'characters', of 'scenes' and of private life, and they invent the method of the later novels — the observing reporter's eye, the comic inventory of metropolitan types, and the sentimental vignette of the poor.
works.plot: There is no continuous narrative. The 'Scenes' section follows a London day from morning to night, the 'Characters' section presents a gallery of types (the beadle, the parish clerk, the hospital patient, the 'gentleman' in reduced circumstances), and the 'Tales' section includes the first version of the story later worked into The Pickwick Papers, 'A Dinner at Poplar Walk'.
works.significance: Sketches by Boz established the pseudonym, the market and the subject of Dickens's whole career, and it is the first sustained attempt in English to write the modern city as a series of close-up notations rather than as a panorama.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The 1830s London of the new police and the new penny press, of coaching inns giving way to the railways, and of a reading public created by the cheap miscellany. Dickens was a parliamentary reporter for the Mirror of Parliament and the True Sun while writing them.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Sketches of Southern Life
works.description: Published in 1872 and Harper's most original contribution to American dialect poetry: the monologues of Aunt Chloe, a freedwoman of the South. It is a verse work of 1872 by Frances E. W. Harper; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Aunt Chloe tells her own story in her own voice — the sale of her children, the war, emancipation, the founding of her school and her church, and her opinions of the Reconstruction politicians — in a series of poems that use dialect as a voice of authority rather than comedy.
works.significance: Sketches of Southern Life is the finest American dialect poetry of the Reconstruction era and the founding text of the black vernacular monologue: its use of Aunt Chloe's voice to record the black experience from inside reversed the minstrel convention and prepared the way for Dunbar and the twentieth-century black poets.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The spelling and syntax carry a spoken dialect. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat.
works.context: 1872: the South during Reconstruction, the freedmen's schools, and the black church. The record dates the work as composed in 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

works.title: Sketches of the History of Mankind
altTitles: Sketches of the History of Man
works.description: Kames's anthropological history of the human species, the richest single compilation of the Scottish Enlightenment's conjectural and ethnographic history. It sketches the progress of mind, language, memory, perception, and the social and moral faculties from savagery to polish, drawing on travellers, antiquaries, and the philosophy of the stages.
works.plot: The Sketches open on the origin and progress of the mental faculties, tracing perception, remembrance, and the growth of general language from the signs of savage passion. They then follow the successive social stages from hunter and shepherd to tiller and citizen, the history of the sexes in marriage and domestic authority across nations, the progress of religion from superstition and idolatry to Christianity, and the development of the moral sense through custom, law, and the arts. Kames weaves ethnography, ancient history, and philosophical conjecture into a single narrative of the species' slow perfection, treating the savage as the living evidence of the primitive mind. The last sketches examine the influence of civil society on the faculties and close on the perfectibility of mankind.
works.significance: It is the sum of eighteenth-century Scottish conjectural history in a single work, a storehouse of Enlightenment anthropology whose method and materials shaped the later human sciences and the century's idea of progress.
works.meter: A brisk, anecdotal, aphoristic prose, travellers' facts and philosophical inference stitched in quick paragraphs.
works.context: Published in 1774 at the high tide of the conjectural history of mankind, when the circumnavigation reports and the ethnography of the north were transforming the subject, and within the circle of Millar, Adam Smith, and Robertson; it was read and translated across Europe.
works.structure: A series of sketches grouped by theme, each a short essay of conjectural history and ethnography, cross-referenced into one history of the species across the four volumes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Snow-Bound: A Winter Idyl
works.description: The great American poem of the rural household: a snowstorm, a family and the fireside. It is a verse work of 1866 by John Greenleaf Whittier; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A snowstorm buries the Whittier farm in Haverhill; the family gathers at the fireside, and the poem recalls the household of the poet's childhood — the father, the mother, the sisters, the hired man and the schoolmaster — in a meditation on the lost home and the dead.
works.significance: Snow-Bound is the great American poem of the rural household and Whittier's masterpiece: it sold in enormous numbers, made the New England fireside into a national symbol, and is the finest pastoral idyll in American poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, ballad-like quatrain and the domestic idyll.
works.context: The New England farm of the early nineteenth century and the disappearance of the rural household after the Civil War. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the father; the mother; the sisters; the hired man; the schoolmaster
works.structure: A pastoral idyll in the blank-verse couplet, framed by the storm. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Society in America
works.description: Published in 1837 after a two-year tour and the most systematic English account of the United States before Tocqueville's English readership: a study of American politics, religion, education, class, family life and slavery.
works.plot: Martineau examines the machinery of American democracy — the constitution, parties, the press, the churches, colleges, commerce — and tests it against the condition of women, the treatment of the black population and the state of the poor, concluding that the country has failed its own principles in each case.
works.significance: Society in America founded the comparative sociology of the United States and is the most important English book about American society between Birkbeck and Bryce; its chapters on the 'non-existence' of women and on slavery were used by the American feminist and abolitionist movements.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
works.context: The 1830s, Jacksonian democracy, the abolitionist movement and the mob violence of 1835, and the 'woman question' in America. The record dates the work as composed between 1834 and 1836 and first published in 1837 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: Sohrab and Rustum
works.description: Published in the 1853 Poems and generally regarded as Arnold's finest narrative poem: a story from the Persian epic the Shahnameh, in which a father unknowingly kills his son in single combat. It is a verse work of 1853 by Matthew Arnold; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Rustum, the Persian hero, has a son Sohrab by the princess Tahminah; Sohrab, seeking his father, joins the Tartar army and challenges the Persian champion, and in the duel Rustum wounds him mortally before discovering the truth. The poem ends with the father's grief on the banks of the Oxus.
works.significance: Sohrab and Rustum is the finest English narrative poem of the 1850s and the work in which Arnold's classical ideal is fully realised: it was written in deliberate imitation of Homer and gave Victorian poetry a model of the objective narrative that the age's criticism demanded.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The Victorian interest in the East (the Shahnameh, the 1850s oriental scholarship), the imperial frontier wars of the period, and Arnold's theory of the permanently interesting subject. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.characters: Rustum; Sohrab; Tahmineh; Peran-Wisa; Ferood; Afrasiab; Gudurz; Zal
works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.

works.title: Solomon and Saturn I and II
altTitles: The Dialogue of Solomon and Saturn
works.description: Two wisdom dialogues in which Solomon, the biblical master of wisdom, contends with Saturn, the legendary Chaldean sage, over questions of fate, prayer, and the powers of the Pater Noster — its letters imagined as armed warriors assailing the devil. The poems are the most extravagant of the Old English wisdom tradition.
works.plot: In Solomon and Saturn II, the sages debate the powers of the Pater Noster: each letter becomes a warrior with a specific weapon against the fiend ('P has a golden rod and fights the devil...'); the poem surveys the poem's battles against evil in a fantasia of personified letters. Solomon and Saturn I concerns the praise of the Pater Noster and the books it governs, with a runic passage on the letter R.
works.significance: The wildest flights of the Old English wisdom tradition; central to the study of Anglo-Saxon learned imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense, sometimes eccentric diction.
works.context: Preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422; the dialogues draw on apocryphal Solomonic and computistical lore.
works.characters: Solomon; Saturn; the personified letters of the Pater Noster
works.structure: Question-and-answer dialogue in the wisdom-contest tradition, elaborated with the allegorical letter-warfare of the Pater Noster passages.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
works.description: A reflective poem on the Preacher's theme, in which the riches, pleasures and honours of the world are weighed against the wisdom that knows their end. It is the most ambitious of its author's serious pieces and the one by which his contemporaries judged him a philosopher as well as a wit.
works.plot: The poet follows the Solomon of Ecclesiastes through the trial of magnificence, building, planting and possessing, and finds the account of all his labour to be vanity. The poem passes over the conditions of the wise man and the fool, the fortune of the wicked and the rewards of the just, and resolves the enquiry into the fear of God and the government of the present heart. The close turns from the world measured to the world renounced.
works.significance: It shows the other face of the most popular light poet between the two greatest of the age, and its manner of argumentative couplet meditation was a school for the younger writers who at once imitated and dismissed him.
works.meter: Stanzaic meditative verse of the ode manner, with a regular rhyme scheme and balanced antithetical lines carrying the moral argument in the Dryden school.
works.context: Written in the later years of a career divided between diplomacy and poetry, when the poet had been disappointed of employment and had turned to the serious essay in verse; it belongs to the company of the century's vanity-of-the-world poems.
works.structure: A sustained meditative poem in the manner of the ode and the essay in verse, the argument advancing by the review of the several species of worldly good and their judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in more than one state and length, and the several issues are dated variously in the catalogues of the trade, so the year given is that of the earliest collected printing and no year of composition is asserted.

works.title: Some Do Not…
works.description: The first volume of the great English war tetralogy: Christopher Tietjens, the last Tory, and the end of Edwardian England. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Christopher Tietjens, a brilliant statistician in the Imperial Department of Statistics, is married to the unfaithful Sylvia and in love with Valentine Wannop, a suffragette. The novel moves between the golf course at Rye, the London of the war office and the trenches of the Western Front in 1917, and ends with Christopher's return to England and the collapse of his marriage.
works.significance: Some Do Not… opens the greatest English war novel: its portrait of Christopher Tietjens as the last English gentleman, its technical brilliance and its picture of a society destroying itself made Parade's End the finest English novel of the war and the transition to modern England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.
works.context: Edwardian England before 1914 and the Western Front of 1917, the suffrage movement and the official class. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Christopher Tietjens; Sylvia Tietjens; Valentine Wannop; Vincent Macmaster; General Campion; Mrs Duchemin
works.structure: Two parts: the pre-war England and the Western Front of 1917. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

works.title: Some Reflections upon Marriage, Occasion'd by the Duke and Duchess of Mazarine's Case
works.description: Astell's second major feminist work, written in response to the scandalous separation of the Duke and Duchess of Mazarin, arguing that the legal subjection of wives is a form of arbitrary power inconsistent with the principles of the Glorious Revolution.
works.plot: Astell asks how it can be that all men are born free, yet every woman is born a slave; she argues that marriage as constituted gives husbands arbitrary power over wives, that women must cultivate their reason, and that a rational education would make better wives and mothers.
works.significance: One of the most powerful early feminist critiques of marriage and of the sexual double standard; its argument that arbitrary power over women is inconsistent with the principles of 1688 has made it a canonical text of political theory.
works.meter: Ironical, pointed prose with a sustained rhetorical question.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1700, with second and third editions in 1703 and 1706; the Mazarin case was a cause célèbre in Restoration and post-Revolution London.
works.characters: the Duchess of Mazarin; Hortense Mancini (alluded to)
works.structure: A continuous argument in three parts with a preface to the third edition of 1706.

works.title: Some Thoughts Concerning Education
works.description: Locke's influential treatise on the education of a young gentleman, which grew out of letters to his friend Edward Clarke and argued for physical hardiness, moral habituation, and a practical curriculum over rote learning.
works.plot: Locke advises on the health of the body, the formation of the mind through habit and example, the teaching of reading, writing, languages, history, geography, arithmetic, and a trade, and the importance of curiosity over coercion.
works.significance: The most influential English work on education of the eighteenth century; it shaped Rousseau's Emile, and its emphasis on habit and on the child's own interest transformed educational theory.
works.meter: Practical, conversational prose.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1693, expanded in the 1695 and 1705 editions; it derived from Locke's letters to Edward Clarke of Chipley concerning Clarke's son.
works.structure: A series of numbered sections following the natural order of education.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship was publicly acknowledged only in the 1705 edition.

works.title: Some Versions of Pastoral
works.form: Critical study (the pastoral as the social irony)
works.description: The study that read the whole range of English literature as versions of the pastoral. It is a prose work of 1935 by William Empson; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Some Versions of Pastoral reads the pastoral - from the proletarian literature and the pastoral of Shakespeare and Donne to Alice in Wonderland and the jazz of the music hall - as the social irony of the degree, in which the simple figure carries the complex mind.
works.significance: Some Versions of Pastoral is the most original critical book of the 1930s: its reading of the pastoral as the social irony of the degree opened the whole range of English literature to the close reading and remains the model of the criticism of the mode.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the close reading that unfolds every sense of the word.
works.context: Cambridge and London in the 1930s, and the pastoral of the depression. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1934 and first published in 1935 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.title: Somebody's Neighbors
works.description: The New England village in its own dialect: the spinster, the hired man and the declining farm. It is a prose fiction work of 1881 by Rose Terry Cooke; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life.

Wilkins Freeman.

The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the dialect story of the Connecticut farm.
works.context: Connecticut in the 1870s and 1880s, and the decline of the New England farm after the Civil War. works.title: Song to David
works.form: Sacred ode or hymn of praise in the English Pindaric tradition as revised in the eighteenth century, with stanzaic response to the order of the subject and with a strongly Hebraic rhetoric of accumulation and parallelism.
works.description: Christopher Smart's great ode, a poem of praise addressed to the psalmist-king and through him to God, and the most extraordinary achievement of English Augustan verse between the odes of Dryden and those of the Romantic period. It passes from the invitation to sing to the works and the names of David, to music, to the beasts and elements attending him, and finally to the typological and prophetic range of the Israelite kingdom. Its stanzas are irregular by design, each shaped to its subject, and its diction, rhyme and vowel-pattern are among the most carefully experimental of the century.
works.plot: The poem is an invitation, a catalogue and a praise. It begins by calling the muse of Israel to her task and then proceeds through the parts of David's story and his attributes, treating the psalmist as the inventor and patron of sacred music and as the type of Christ. The middle movements are a natural history and a physics of praise: harp and organ, the vocal powers of beasts, birds and the elements, and the famous enquiry into the properties of vowels and consonants, in which Smart's theory of the inherent music of language is made the ground of the poem's own practice. The conclusion gathers the typology together, making David's kingdom and the builder of the temple figures of a spiritual and prophetic order. Praise, not narrative, is the argument, and the poem's form is an argument that variety of measure is itself a mode of devotion.
works.significance: It is the supreme religious ode of the mid-eighteenth century and the strongest claim made in the period for poetry as an act of praise rather than of instruction or of taste; its recovery in the twentieth century altered the estimation of Smart and of Augustan verse generally. Samuel Johnson's recorded admiration of parts of it is the beginning of its reputation among the poets of the club.
works.meter: A planned variety of measures: long and short lines, recurring burden-like refrains, dense internal and vowel rhyme, and experiments in the sound of the alphabet itself; the poem is the age's most self-conscious treatment of the relation of phonetic material to devotion.
works.context: It was published in the year of Smart's release from the retirement in which he had been confined, and stands with 'Jubilate Agno' and the other poems of the confinement years at the centre of his work. Its Hebraism belongs to an age of psalm translation, of the debate about 'enthusiasm' and true religious poetry, and of the High-Church and Jacobite sympathies of its author.
works.characters: David, the psalmist and king, addressed and celebrated; the personified muse and music; the created things, animal, vegetable and elemental, that attend the praise
works.structure: A continuous ode in unequal stanzas, moving by association and amplification from invocation through the subjects of David's praise to typological and prophetic conclusion; the stanzaic irregularity is planned, not accidental.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is Smart's and its authorship was never disputed. The year of first printing is recorded, but the venue of the first impression and the stages of composition within the confinement years are matters of editorial detail which are not asserted here.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Divine love and holy desire
Time, death, and immortality through verse
Wisdom and learning
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: Songs and Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
altTitles: The Works of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
works.description: The small but influential body of verse by the Earl of Dorset — courtier, wit, and patron — including the famous sea-song 'To all you ladies now at land', written, according to tradition, the night before the battle of Solebay.
works.plot: The poems are light, graceful lyrics of love and parting, several written on public occasions and to particular women of the court; the sea-song consoles the ladies ashore while the men fight at sea.
works.significance: 'To all you ladies now at land' became one of the best-known songs of the period; Dorset's work is a touchstone for the ideal of effortless courtly wit.
works.meter: Short song stanzas in an easy, colloquial register.
works.context: Dorset's verse circulated in manuscript at the court of Charles II; he was a leading patron of Dryden and Prior and a central figure in Restoration literary society.
works.structure: A short miscellany of songs and occasional verse.
works.attributionNotes: The canon is small and some attributions are uncertain; the sea-song is traditionally ascribed to Dorset.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Sea voyage and seafaring
movements: Cavalier Poetry

works.title: Songs and Sonnets
works.description: The collective title given in the 1633 posthumous Poems to Donne's lyrics of love — 'The Good-Morrow', 'The Sun Rising', 'The Canonization', 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', 'The Ecstasy', 'The Flea', and some fifty more — in which the conventions of Petrarchan love are re-forged by argument, paradox, and the new 'metaphysical' wit.
works.plot: No single plot: the poems dramatize the phases of love — waking, parting, quarrelling, dying, transcending — each lyric a miniature drama of persuasion in which a lover argues a mistress, a rival, the sun, or himself into a truth about love.
works.significance: The founding book of metaphysical poetry — the lyric revolution that Jonson's classicism answered and that the twentieth century would re-canonize.
works.meter: Dramatic, speech-like rhythms within stanza forms of Donne's own devising — the 'strong lines' of the metaphysical manner, with conceits drawn from astronomy, alchemy, law, and cartography.
works.context: Written from the 1590s (the 'Jack Donne' of Lincoln's Inn and the Essex and Ralegh voyages) into his middle years, circulating in manuscript among the wits and Inns of Court; printed only after his death in the 1633 Poems.
works.characters: the poet-lover; the beloved (unnamed); the Sun; Death; God (in the religious lyrics)
works.structure: A group of some fifty-five lyrics gathered posthumously under a title Donne never gave them, arranged in the 1633 edition as a loose anthology of the love poems.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the group's composition dates span at least two decades, and individual datings are widely disputed.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: Metaphysical Poetry
