works.title: Songs before Sunrise
works.description: Published in 1871 and Swinburne's political masterpiece: the poems of liberty written for the Italian risorgimento, the Irish cause and the republican movement in Europe. It is a verse work of 1871 by Algernon Charles Swinburne; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume contains 'Hertha', 'The Emancipation of the World', 'Before a Crucifix', 'A Song of Italy' and 'Ode on the Proclamation of the French Republic', in which the poet calls for the overthrow of kings and priests in the name of liberty.
works.significance: Songs before Sunrise is the finest body of political poetry in Victorian English and the central text of the republican tradition: its poems on Italy and on liberty made Swinburne the poet of European revolution and influenced the radical poetry of the next generation.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is incantatory anapaestic and trochaic metres.
works.context: 1867-71: the Italian risorgimento, the Paris Commune and the fall of the Second Empire, and the Fenian movement in Ireland. The record dates the work as composed between 1868 and 1870 and first published in 1871 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.structure: A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as A. C. Swinburne. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause
themes: Democracy, individualism, and the American experiment
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: Songs from the Cradle
works.description: Published in 1867 and Skipsey's volume of poems on childhood, the family and the loss of children: simple songs in the manner of the nursery rhyme and the ballad. It is a verse work of 1867 by Joseph Skipsey; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The poems are lullabies, songs of the cradle and elegies for dead children, written in a plain ballad metre and with a directness that owes much to the Border ballads.
works.significance: Songs from the Cradle is a remarkable body of working-class poetry on childhood and bereavement, and a key text in the literature of the nineteenth-century family.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is plain ballad stanzas and simple lyric metres.
works.context: The 1860s, the high infant mortality of the coalfield, and the Victorian poetry of the family. The record dates the work as composed between 1860s and 1867 and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: Songs of a Semite: The Dance to Death and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1882 and the first English book of poetry to treat the Jewish people as a modern nation: poems of the persecutions and the Zionist hope. It is a dramatic work of 1882 by Emma Lazarus; it belongs to The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume contains 'The Dance to Death', a verse tragedy on the massacre of the Jews of Nordhausen in 1349, together with lyrics on the Russian pogroms of 1881, the Jewish exile, and the hope of a return to Palestine.
works.significance: Songs of a Semite is the founding text of American Zionist literature and the first English poetry collection to treat Jewish persecution as a contemporary political subject: its verse tragedy on a medieval massacre made it a landmark, and it prepared the way for 'The New Colossus' and for the literature of American Zionism.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the classical sonnet and the verse drama in a formal, measured style.
works.context: 1880-82: the Russian pogroms of 1881, the beginning of American Zionism, the Jewish immigration to New York, and the English tradition of the verse tragedy. The record dates the work as composed between 1880 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: Süsskind von Orb and his daughter Liebhaid ('The Dance to Death')
works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy

Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction

works.title: Songs of Childhood
works.description: De la Mare's first book: the songs and riddles of the nursery, published under a pseudonym. It is a verse work of 1902 by Walter de la Mare; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale; Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The collection's forty-seven poems, among them 'Tartary', 'The Silver Penny', 'The Pedlar', 'The Ogre', 'Dame Hickory' and 'The Child in the Story Goes to Bed', are the ballads, spells and nursery songs that established his voice — the first appearance of the child's world that Peacock Pie would perfect.
works.significance: Songs of Childhood is the first book of the greatest English writer of children's verse: published under the pseudonym Walter Ramal, it began the body of nursery poetry that Peacock Pie would perfect, and it is one of the permanent children's books in English.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric of the half-heard and the unseen.
works.context: The Edwardian nursery and the golden age of the illustrated children's book. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1901 and first published in 1902 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; georgian anthology lyric.
works.characters: the would-be Lord of Tartary; the Lady Caroline ('Lovelocks'); Marjorie May, Madeleine Rose, Humphrey John and Emmanuel ('O Dear Me!'); the sailorman and Jenny ('The Silver Penny'); the gnomies; the Ogre and the singing mother; Dame Hickory; Captain Lean; the child in the story
works.structure: Some fifty nursery songs and riddles. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Walter John de la Mare. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale

The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road

works.title: Songs of Experience
works.form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the experienced state, in the line of the song and the emblem, designed as a direct reply to the earlier collection and printed with its plates as one book.
works.description: The second and darker of the two illuminated collections, etched and printed by the author in 1794 and issued with the earlier songs under a single title announcing the two contrary states of the human soul. Its lyrics answer, correct and destroy the trust of the first collection: the maker of the lamb is now questioned as the maker also of the tiger, the garden of innocence is planted with a chapel, and the poems of the city expose the institutions, the priests and the kings that keep the soul in bondage.
works.plot: The collection opens with an earth answerable to the eternal, and with the tiger, whose frightful symmetry forces the question of what hand or eye could frame such dread and what exchange of fear was made when it was given life, an answer that reverses the child's trust in the lamb. Songs of the lost childhood follow: the sick rose destroyed by the invisible worm, the sunflower pined out in the marsh, the grey-bearded physician who knows the tree by its leaf and nothing else, and the youth who is told that the garden of love, where his infant joys were planted, is now a chapel, its gates shut against the child and its altar dressed with the thorns and briars of the priest's curse. The later plates turn on London and on the moral state of the kingdom, in which every black'ning church, the palace rebuilt from the blood of the soldier, the marriage hearse and the cries of the chimney-boy are read as a state of bondage, and the poems of the harlot, of the flies of summer and of the little lost one close upon pity for the sinner and the child, so that the contrary state is presented at once as knowledge and as the loss of the power to feel. The last poem figures the bard of a new age who shall restore the departed powers.
works.significance: One of the two collections that define the Romantic reading of innocence and experience as contrary and answering states of the soul, and the source of the most discussed single lyric in English on the problem of the maker of evil. Its plates are the standard evidence of the poet's illuminated method, and its London poems are a permanent part of the literature of the city and of the critique of institutional religion.
works.meter: Song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with a tightened and more reiterated pattern, the tiger's trochaic four-beat lines and its insistent questions being the most quoted example; the rhythm is deliberately hammer-like where the argument demands it, and the later plates allow longer and more prophetic periods.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in 1794, in the years of the author's most active experiment with illuminated relief-printing and in the decade of the repression of English radical opinion, the wars with France and the trade in wealth of the metropolis, all of which give the city poems their targets; the combined issue of the two collections under one title states the theory of contrary states from which the poems proceed.
works.characters: The tiger and the questioning singer; the rose and the invisible worm; the sun-flower and the lily of the valley; the grey-bearded sage; the child who sees the chapel in the garden of love; the harlot of the city of London; the soldier, the chimney-sweeper and the labouring poor of the London plates; the little lost one; the bard of the new age
works.structure: A plate-for-plate collection answering the earlier songs poem by poem, with a progression from the tiger and the lost garden through the city poems to the harlot and the closing promise of the bard; several pieces exist in two versions in the earlier copy, and the design of the sequence is the collection's argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the existence of earlier drafts of several poems, and the differences between the copies in the order of the plates, are matters of bibliography and of the text's several states.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: Songs of Innocence
altTitles: Songs of Innocence. Written for the Children of the Age to Come
works.form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the innocent state, in the line of the nursery song and the devotional hymn, engraved and designed by the poet as a single art object.
works.description: A short collection of lyrics etched, printed and hand-coloured by the author himself in 1789, and issued as plates with the poems and the designs engraved on the same copper, so that text and image were made as one object. Its voices are those of children, of the piper who is taught by them, of the lamb, the nurse, the chimney-sweeper and the schoolboy, and its subject is a state of the human soul in which protection, joy and trust are still unbroken. It was later combined with a second collection to show the two contrary states of the human soul.
works.plot: The poems present a world of open country and of the city's poor in which innocence is both a fact and a condition exposed to danger. A piper hears a child asking for a song about a lamb, writes it, and rejoices; another song answers the child's question about who made the lamb by tracing the maker's meek and gentle likeness in himself. The lamb, the little black boy, the chimney-sweepers of London, the nurse whose play is over, the schoolboy who watches the winter morning and the evening's returning flock, and the shepherd and the boy who has lost his ball, give a sequence of small states of the soul; two of the poems name the cruelty of the institutions that employ children and one of them sets the child's complaint against the prayer and the doctrine taught him, so that the collection's innocence is figured as a trust that others are ready to betray. The closing poems turn to the grown-ups who have lost that trust, and the little bird, the clod and the pebble give the short lyric argument about the answerable heart.
works.significance: The founding work of the illuminated books and one of the two collections that make up the standard Romantic statement of innocence and experience as contrary states; its songs entered the anthologies of children's verse and its plates are the central example of the poet's method of making text and design one. Its account of protected and betrayed childhood remains a starting point of modern criticism of the lyric of innocence.
works.meter: Short song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with simple recurring rhyme, many of them written as airs to be sung, with repetitions and question-and-answer patterns proper to children's verse; the irregularities are part of the song manner rather than errors of the ear.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in 1789, when the author had developed his method of illuminated relief-printing and was working as an engraver and designer of plates in the City; its concern with children, with the sweeper chimneys of the metropolis and with the teachings of the church belongs to the philanthropic and dissenting writing of that decade.
works.characters: The child who asks the piper to write a song; the lamb and its questioning child; the little black boy; the chimney-sweepers Tom Dacre and his fellow workers; the nurse and the schoolboy; the shepherd, the blossoms and the lost boy; the piper who becomes the writer of the songs
works.structure: A plate-for-plate collection of short lyrics, without a continuous story but designed as a sequence, the order of the illuminated copies varying slightly and the images supplying a running commentary on the texts; the poems answer one another by their repeated figures of the child, the maker and the guardian.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several hand-coloured copies differ in the order of the plates and in the colouring, and the number of copies printed from the copper plates is a matter of bibliography rather than of disputed authorship.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: Songs of Joy and Other Verses
works.description: The collection that carried 'Leisure', the most quoted short lyric of the Georgian anthologies. It is a verse work of 1911 by W. H. Davies; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The volume gathers Davies's lyrics of the roadside, the hedge and the open sky, among them 'Leisure' - 'What is this life if, full of care, we have no time to stand and stare' - in the plain short line that made him a household poet of the Georgian anthologies.
works.significance: Songs of Joy and Other Verses gave the Georgian anthologies their most quoted lyric in 'Leisure' and established Davies as the plain voice of the roadside among the poets of the garden.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain short line and the plain word.

works.title: Songs of the Affections, with Other Poems
works.form: Collected volume of short lyrics and elegies; the governing genre is the affectionate meditative lyric, with the hymn-like stanza and the topical elegy beside it.
works.description: A late collection in which its author's shorter lyric manner is gathered under a title that names its whole repertoire: affection tried by separation, loss and time. It shows the mourning and devotional lyric of her final decade.
works.plot: The poems move through states of attachment - friendship recalled, love unanswered, the dead imagined still present - without forming a sequence with a plot. Several pieces build upon a single emblem, a farewell, a lake image or a link, and develop it as a meditation. A group addresses the consolations of faith, asking whether affection dissolved by death is restored. The remaining poems are descriptive or occasional, on places, on the dead, and on the lot of the poet. The volume's argument is cumulative rather than progressive: feeling is proved durable by the repetition of cases.
works.significance: These songs supplied the idiom that middle-class Victorian mourning and devotional culture later took for granted, and their lines were set to music and reprinted without attribution for decades. The volume is the clearest evidence that the most widely circulated verse of the later Romantic period was affective, occasional and domestic rather than prophetic or rebellious. Its very popularity made it the target of later dismissal.
works.meter: Regular iambic stanzas, largely common and short measure with refrains, built for vocal repetition; occasional anapaestic and mixed measures mark the pieces written to be recited or sung.
works.context: It followed the volume of records and confirmed its author's position as the century's most borrowed poet of affection, at the moment when the literary annual was becoming the chief market for such verse. Her income and fame in these years depended on the annuals and on transatlantic reprints, and the collection gathers what those markets demanded. Its publication year falls between the Catholic Emancipation Act and the Reform crisis, a period of turbulent public verse from which the volume is entirely absent.
works.structure: An unordered company of short lyrics grouped under the affectionate design of the title; the arrangement is by tone and length, and the reading experience is one of recurring situations rather than of sequence.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Early death and the mourning of poets
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
works.description: Forty-four Petrarchan sonnets written in 1845-46 during the courtship and published in 1850, with the pretence of being translated 'from the Portuguese': the greatest English sonnet sequence of the century by a woman, and the founding text of the Victorian love lyric.
works.plot: The sequence moves from the speaker's disbelief that she can be loved, through the growth of love and the fear of losing it, to the marriage and the giving of the child; the central sonnet, 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways', follows 'I never gave a lock of hair away' and precedes the closing sonnets of renewed devotion.
works.significance: Sonnets from the Portuguese gave English poetry its central sequence of reciprocal love and reversed the gender of the Petrarchan tradition: the beloved speaks. 'How do I love thee' is among the most quoted poems in the language, and the sequence is a founding text for the study of Victorian women's writing.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
works.context: The 1845-46 courtship at 50 Wimpole Street, the invalid's seclusion, and the Victorian conventions of the love sonnet, which had been modelled on Petrarch and on the masculine sequence since Wyatt. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Sons and Lovers
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1913
works.description: The first great English novel of working-class childhood: the Morel family, the mining village, and a son torn between his mother and his lovers. It is a prose fiction work of 1913 by D. H. Lawrence; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Gertrude Morel, a cultivated woman, marries a miner and is disillusioned by his drinking and brutality; she turns her love on her sons. Paul, the second son, is bound to her and unable to love either Miriam, the spiritual girl who loves him, or Clara, the married woman who gives him passion; his mother's death at the end frees him into a desolate, unfinished future.
works.significance: Sons and Lovers is the first great English novel of working-class experience and the founding text of Lawrence's art: it made the mining village and the miner's family a subject for serious fiction, and its account of a son's possession by his mother gave psychoanalytic criticism its favourite English novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the loose, repetitive, urgent sentence driven by the rhythm of feeling and breath.
works.context: The Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire coalfield of the 1880s and 1890s: the pit village, the miners' strike, the chapel, and the new educational opportunities that took miners' sons into clerkships and art schools.
works.characters: Paul Morel; Gertrude Morel; Walter Morel; William Morel; Miriam Leivers; Clara Dawes; Baxter Dawes
works.structure: Two-part chronological novel of childhood and youth, with the mother's death as the climax. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Herbert Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Sophonisba
works.description: Thomson's regular tragedy of the Carthaginian princess who chooses death rather than the Roman triumph, written deliberately in the observance of the unities and in the manner of the antique and French classical drama.
works.plot: Sophonisba, taken between the rival African princes and the advancing Rome, is given by the conqueror to the suitor she must not love; she disappoints both by choosing the poison, and the play closes on the spectacle of her constant death.
works.significance: It is the century's most complete English attempt at the classical regular tragedy, and its death scene became a byword for the calculated pathos of the closet and the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse of studied smoothness, with the formal expiring dialogue of the last scene.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the season of Thomson's struggle with the theatres and of the debate over classical regularity, when the Racine model and the unities were being reasserted against the opera and the burletta.
works.characters: Sophonisba; Syphax; Masinissa; Scipio; the attendants of the captive princess
works.structure: Five acts of strict regularity, with the set dying scene as the prepared catastrophe and the political argument of the rival parties supplying the tension.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.description: Lee's early heroic tragedy on the Carthaginian princess Sophonisba, who drinks poison rather than fall into Roman hands, and whose lines 'O happiness! O pleasure!' became proverbial for heroic bombast.

works.title: Sordello
works.form: Long narrative poem in blank verse
works.description: Published in 1840 and the most notoriously difficult poem of the century — Tennyson said he could make nothing of it, and Browning's readers could not follow its syntax: a poem on the thirteenth-century troubadour Sordello and the politics of Lombardy.
works.plot: Sordello, a poet of Mantua, seeks fame and love; he becomes involved in the Guelf-Ghibelline struggle over the succession of the emperor Frederick II, betrays his trust, and dies in obscurity, having learned that the poet's true work is to make the world's will conscious.
works.significance: Sordello is the extreme case of Browning's difficult middle style, and its failure in the market taught him to write for the voice and for the dramatic moment rather than for the reader of narrative. Its theory of the poet's social function is the philosophical key to his later work.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The Italian communes of the thirteenth century, Dante's Purgatorio (where Sordello appears), and the Victorian interest in Italian history and in the poet's political role. The record dates the work as composed between 1839 and 1840 and first published in 1840 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Sordello; Palma (Cunizza); Taurello Salinguerra; Ecelin da Romano; Adelaide; Naddo; Eglamor
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: Soul and Body I and II
altTitles: The Soul's Address to the Body
works.form: religious debate poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A pair of related poems (Vercelli Book I, 166 lines; Exeter Book II, 121 lines) in which the soul, revisiting its decaying body once a week, reproaches it for the sins of the flesh and foretells the torments of judgment. The earliest English body-and-soul debate, ancestor of a long medieval tradition.
works.plot: The damned soul, forced to revisit its corpse, addresses the silent body: 'Where are the riches you gathered? The hall you feasted in?' — enumerating the body's pleasures and their price in hell, the worms and the fire; the Exeter version closes with a brief address to the blessed soul by contrast. The debate's later fortunes run through the Middle English 'Desputisoun bitwen the Bodi and the Soule' to the danse macabre.
works.significance: Inaugurates the body-and-soul debate tradition that runs through Middle English literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 101v-103v) and the Exeter Book (fols. 98a-100a); the genre derives from Latin and homiletic sources.
works.characters: the Soul; the Body; (in II) the blessed soul
works.structure: A monologue of reproach and warning, spoken by the soul to the body at the grave; the two versions differ in length and ending.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology

works.title: Sounding Brass
works.description: The novel of the advertising business that made Mannin's name. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by Ethel Mannin; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Sounding Brass is set in the advertising business of 1920s London and follows the office, the copy and the women of the trade, in the plain fast prose of the working woman's novel that gave Mannin her first commercial success.
works.significance: Sounding Brass made Ethel Mannin's name: its advertising office and its working women began the career of the popular novelist of the working-class woman.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain fast prose of the popular novelist.

works.title: South Riding

works.description: The great English regional novel of the 1930s: a Yorkshire county council and the woman who serves it. works.plot: Sarah Burton, a new headmistress, returns to Yorkshire to take up her post and is drawn into the politics of the county council, the poverty of the South Riding and the lives of its people, in a novel of a whole community and the woman who tries to change it.
works.significance: South Riding is the great English regional novel of the 1930s: its portrait of a Yorkshire county council and its women made local administration into epic, and it is one of the finest English feminist novels of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail of the county council.
works.context: The East Riding of Yorkshire in the early 1930s, and the local government of the Depression. works.title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
works.form: Pamphlet; social inquiry, first issued in 1892
works.description: Published in New York in 1892 after she was driven from Memphis: the first systematic analysis of lynching in the United States. It is a prose work of 1892 by Ida B. works.plot: Wells shows that lynching is not a response to rape but an instrument of economic and political terror; she documents the cases, exposes the newspapers that justify the murders, and calls on black Americans to arm themselves and to leave the South.
works.significance: Southern Horrors is the founding text of the American literature of anti-lynching and the first systematic study of racial terror: it created the documentary method that would be used by the NAACP and the civil rights movement, and it remains one of the most important American political pamphlets.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass.
works.context: 1892: the lynching of her friends in Memphis, the People's Grocery boycott, and the national anti-lynching campaign. works.title: Spanish Testament
works.description: The testimony of the Spanish imprisonment and the party's disillusion. It is a prose work of 1937 by Arthur Koestler; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Spanish Testament tells Koestler's arrest by the Francoists in Málaga, the months in the prison under sentence of death, and the politics of the Popular Front and the party that produced them, in the testimony that made the decade's disillusion a document.
works.significance: Spanish Testament is the testimony of the party's disillusion: its prison, its death sentence and its politics made Koestler the witness of the Popular Front's Spain and prepared the novel of the confession that followed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the argument carried in the cell and the interrogation.

works.title: Specimen Days
works.form: Prose diary and memoir; review essay
works.description: Published in 1882 and Whitman's prose masterpiece: a diary-memoir of the war hospitals, the American landscape and the poet's old age. It is a prose work of 1882 by Walt Whitman; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Whitman records the wounded in the Washington hospitals, the death of Lincoln, his own strokes, the New Jersey countryside and the butterflies and birds of his garden at Camden, in a series of dated notes that build a portrait of a life.
works.significance: Specimen Days is the finest American prose memoir of the century and one of the great works of American nature writing: its war journal is the most truthful record of the Civil War hospitals, and its landscape notes made the American sketch a serious literary form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the dated entry, continuous in its observation. The author's characteristic manner is free verse built on syntactical parallelism and anaphora.
works.context: The years 1862-82, the Civil War hospitals, the Camden years, and the American tradition of the diary and the sketch. The record dates the work as composed between 1876 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Walt Whitman, the narrator; the wounded soldiers of the Washington hospitals; Abraham Lincoln
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.

works.title: Specimens of the British Poets
altTitles: Specimens of the British Poets, with Biographical and Critical Notices, and an Essay on English Poetry
works.form: Anthology and editorial collection with literary biography and prefatory commentary; a work of Romantic-period literary history in the handbook manner.
works.description: A seven-volume anthology of British verse with prefatory biographical and critical notices and a general essay on English poetry, assembled by a living poet rather than by a scholar. It arranges its selections chronologically from the early Tudor and Scottish writers to the poet's own contemporaries, and its notices became a standard source of information and judgement. The series of lives later circulated separately and shaped the nineteenth century's sense of a native poetic tradition.
works.plot: The work's argument is that English poetry can be understood as a continuous national tradition, recoverable through carefully selected passages and through short critical lives attached to each poet. It gives precedence to moral and imaginative seriousness, defends the older writers against neoclassical disparagement, and reserves some of its most discriminating comment for the living Romantic generation. Its selections act as a canon: what is quoted defines what a nineteenth-century reader was likely to know. The prefatory essay generalises this practice into an account of the phases of English poetry and of the conditions of patronage, print and national taste that produced them.
works.significance: For two generations its notices and selections were the ordinary medium through which readers met the earlier English poets, and its judgements on the Romantics entered the standard accounts of the period. It shows how a practising poet's editorial authority could be used to construct a national canon, and it preserves much early scholarship on forgotten writers. Later histories of canon formation cite it as a decisive instance of Romantic anthologising practice.
works.meter: Prose notices and essay framing verse extracts of every prevailing metre from the old ballad stanza to the blank verse and couplets of the eighteenth century.
works.context: It belongs to the post-war boom in national literary history and in the collected-standard-poets trade, when publishers turned poetry into a respectable branch of national education. Its compiler was by then a successful narrative poet and a London literary manager, and his judgements were conditioned by the review culture and by friendships and quarrels within the Romantic generation. The essay on English poetry addresses directly the question, urgent in the 1810s, whether a modern British school existed worthy of the name.
works.structure: A chronological anthology with prefatorial lives and critical notes, opened by a general essay on English poetry; not a narrative but an argument about literary history conducted through selection.
themes: Primitive genius and national poetry
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public
Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: Specimens of the Later English Poets, with Preliminary Notices
altTitles: Specimens of the Later English Poets, in Three Volumes
works.form: Editorial anthology with prefatory critical commentary: a specimens collection in the line of the Reliques and of the earlier English specimens, used as a vehicle for review-style criticism.
works.description: The author's anthology of modern English verse, planned as a companion to the collections of specimens of the earlier English poets and issued in three volumes with substantial preliminary notices on each poet. The selection is wide and deliberate, rescuing minor and forgotten writers while judging the famous, and the notices are essays in criticism rather than mere biography. It is the best document we have of how a laureate-in-waiting read the poetry of the previous half-century.
works.plot: The volumes arrange extracts from poets writing since the middle of the eighteenth century, each preceded by a notice of the writer's life, character, and principal works, and followed by comments on particular poems. The editor praises Cowper's originality and faults his religious melancholy, gives an early and influential estimate of Robert Burns, and appraises the descriptive, topographical, and sentimental schools. He sets the doctrine of a national poetry against mere delicacy, and argues for seriousness of subject, for the dignity of the labouring writer, and for the critic's duty to the reader rather than to the party. The collection also prints much verse otherwise hard to trace, from odes and sonnets to ballads and local poems.
works.significance: A primary source for the period's canon-formation and for the earliest critical estimates of Burns and Cowper, and a document of the transition of the poet into the editor-critic; its notices are still quarried for evidence on eighteenth-century and romantic reputation.
works.meter: Prose notices framing verse extracts of every kind.
works.context: Compiled when the successful sale of earlier specimens collections had made literary antiquarianism a market, and when the review journals were establishing professional criticism; it belongs to the years in which its author was moving from radical verse to editorial and critical authority.
works.structure: Anthology organised by author, each unit consisting of a biographical and critical notice followed by selected extracts; there is no continuous argument across volumes, though the notices accumulate a critical position.

works.title: Speculations
works.description: The founding document of the modern movement: the classical reaction against Romanticism. It is a prose work of 1924 by T. E. Hulme; it belongs to Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution and it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Hulme's essays and notes — on the classical and romantic attitudes, on Bergson, on modern art, on the philosophy of the Renaissance — in which he argues for a new classical, disciplined, anti-Romantic art and for the poetic image.
works.significance: Speculations is the founding document of the modern movement in English poetry: its classical reaction, its theory of the image and its argument against Romanticism shaped Pound, Eliot and the New Criticism, and it remains the central statement of the modernist aesthetic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the image as the unit of poetry.
works.context: London in the 1910s, the Imagist movement and the pre-war avant-garde. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution; Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine, it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Hulme as critic; Bergson; the classical and romantic attitudes; the modern artist
works.structure: A posthumous collection of essays and notes, edited by Herbert Read. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.

works.title: Speke Parrot
works.form: verse satire in Skeltonics with macaronic Latin
works.description: The first of Skelton's great anti-Wolsey satires: a parrot — polyglot, learned, and fearless — speaks the court's dangerous truths in a torrent of macaronic verse, attacking the Cardinal's pride, his monopoly of the king's ear, and the corruption of the church, all under the parrot's traditional licence of the fool.
works.plot: The Parrot complains of his cage and his mistress's neglect, then turns to the abuses of the age: Wolsey's supremacy, clerical greed, and the decay of learning; the poem closes with a prayer for amendment.
works.significance: The founding text of the English tradition of political satire under censorship; its speaking-bird device recurs through the century to Spenser and beyond.
works.meter: Skeltonic lines studded with Latin, Greek, and school tags; the parrot's 'speaking' is a display of learned polyglot wit.
works.context: Written in 1521 as Wolsey's power peaked; the parrot's cage is the poet's own position under surveillance, and the poem circulates the satirical truths the court could not speak.
works.characters: the Parrot; (implicitly) Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: A monologue of the speaking bird in the complaint tradition, shifting between personal grievance and public satire without fixed argument.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: The English vernacular and national letters
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry

works.title: Spreading the News
works.description: The comedy that opened the Abbey Theatre: a rumour in a fair-day village and a magistrate's court in uproar. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by Lady Gregory; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: At the fair in the village of Cloon, a casual remark about a man with a hayfork sets off a rumour of murder that spreads through the whole village and ends in a magistrate's court, with every witness contradicting the last.
works.significance: Spreading the News is the comedy that opened the Abbey Theatre on 27 December 1904 and one of the funniest one-act plays in English: its anatomy of rumour made it Lady Gregory's most performed work.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close.
works.context: The west of Ireland, the petty sessions court and the oral culture of the village. The record dates the work as composed in 1904 and first published in 1904 and first performed in 1904 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.

works.structure: A single act, set at the fair and in the court. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.

works.title: Spring
works.description: The third of Thomson's seasonal poems, on the return of the year and on the love and generation it awakens, closing with the prospect of the human season and the hymn to the creator of the seasons.
works.plot: The opening of the year is described in its birds, its blossoms and its gales, the song of the groves and the courtship of the creation; the poem then turns to the spring of human life, to love and to the education of the mind, and to the moral use of the season.
works.significance: Its account of the returning year and of human youth became the common stock of English descriptive and lyrical writing, and its later state is the chief example of Thomson's revision of his own seasons.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines, with the short spring measures of the bird and flower passages and the stately period of the hymn.
works.context: Published in the year of the quarrel over the opera and of the new topographical vogue, and the part of the sequence most deeply affected by Thomson's later rewriting in the middle of the century.
works.characters: the birds and the groves of the returning year; the friend addressed in the poem's second half; the human lovers of the spring
works.structure: A progressive description of the season's return, with the address to the poet's friend and the reflection on human youth interposed before the closing hymn.

works.title: Spring and All
works.form: Poetry collection with prose (published in Paris by Contact Editions)
works.description: The most radical American book of the period: poems and prose manifestos of the imagination, including 'The Red Wheelbarrow'. It is a verse work of 1923 by William Carlos Williams; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line; Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The book alternates between prose chapters arguing for the primacy of the imagination and short poems that demonstrate it — 'By the road to the contagious hospital', 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'To Elsie', 'Spring and All' — and ends with the declaration that the imagination is the only reality.
works.significance: Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period: its mixture of manifesto and poem, its plain American idiom and its insistence on things made it the founding text of the American objectivist tradition, and 'The Red Wheelbarrow' is the most discussed short poem in American literature.
works.meter: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the line measured by the breath and broken by speech.
works.context: The New Jersey of Williams's medical practice, the Armory Show and the new American art of the 1910s, and the Imagist and Dadaist movements. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric; Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line; modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.characters: Elsie, the girl of 'The pure products of America' ('To Elsie')
works.structure: Twenty-seven sections alternating prose chapters and poems. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.

works.description: The comedy of the spring meeting: the hunt, the house and the season. It is a dramatic work of 1938 by Molly Keane; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.

works.title: St Erkenwald
works.description: An alliterative miracle-legend of 352 lines on the discovery, during the rebuilding of St Paul's, of a pagan judge's incorrupt tomb: the bishop Erkenwald's tearful prayer draws from the corpse the story of his just life and the baptism that, in the moment of his speech, admits the just pagan to heaven. The finest short alliterative poem of the period.
works.plot: Workmen excavating at St Paul's find a tomb whose body lies uncorrupted as in life; none can identify it, until Bishop Erkenwald, summoned to the mystery, speaks to the dead man, who reveals himself as a judge of heathen London, just in all his dealings; at the bishop's words of baptism, the corpse — denied heaven's sight so long — sighs, and crumbles to dust as its soul ascends.
works.significance: The classic Middle English treatment of the salvation of the just pagan (the problem Dante faced with Trajan and Virgil), and one of the most moving poems of the alliterative tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, restrained and solemn.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–1400 in the north-west Midlands, in the circle of the Gawain-poet (many scholars assign it to him), perhaps occasioned by work on St Paul's; preserved uniquely in BL Harley MS 2250 (dated 1477).
works.characters: Erkenwald; the pagan judge; the London crowd
works.structure: A single dramatic episode: discovery, wonder, dialogue, and resolution, in the manner of the alliterative miracle-legend.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed by many scholars to the Gawain-poet.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church

works.title: St. Leon
altTitles: St. Leon: A Tale of the Sixteenth Century
works.form: Philosophical tale and alchemical romance; a gothic-tinged analysis of wealth in the form of a confessional autobiography.
works.description: A tale of the secret of gold, in which an unlucky nobleman receives from a wandering Hebrew the alchemical formula for the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life, and finds that boundless wealth destroys every human tie. It applies the earlier novel's analysis of persecution to a new subject: the moral consequences of economic power without social obligation. Its framing as a sixteenth-century narrative gave the alchemical and wanderer traditions a modern philosophical use.
works.plot: Raymond, count of St. Leon, ruined by his father's losses and by a quarrel with the house of his bride, is thrown upon the road in Germany with his wife and infant son. In a solitary retreat he meets the undying wanderer, who purchases his silence with the secret of transmutation and of the elixir; the gift makes him rich, and wealth makes him a stranger to his family, an object of suspicion to the state and at last a hunted man. Pursued by the agents of a rival claimant and by the creditors of a fabricated prosperity, he assumes other names, loses his son's confidence and his wife's trust, and at length flies to America with a fortune that can buy no repose. The narrative closes on the exhaustion of a man who has outlived every motive by which men are held together.
works.significance: The most complete application of eighteenth-century philosophical fiction to the problem of wealth, and an important source for the nineteenth-century novel of the man who can buy anything. It preserved and reinterpreted the alchemical and wanderer legends for a rational age. Its influence on later treatments of immortality, of the isolated benefactor and of domestic ruin is considerable.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a measured, argumentative first-person style in which the marvellous is related in the tones of evidence.
works.context: Written in the years of the author's own financial desperation and of furious controversy over property, credit and the paper economy. The legends of the Wandering Jew and of the philosopher's stone supplied a familiar machinery which the novel turns to the analysis of money. Its publication coincided with the renewal of the same radical publishing interest that had issued the earlier tales.
works.characters: Raymond, count of St. Leon; the undying wanderer who reveals the secret of gold; his wife; his son; the agents who pursue him
works.structure: First-person confession from a manuscript found and published by an editor; continuous autobiographical narrative with embedded letters and an account of the wanderer's own history.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.

works.title: Star Maker
works.description: The greatest cosmological vision in English fiction: a journey through the inhabited universe to the creator. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by Olaf Stapledon; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.

works.description: Published in January 1886 and written in a few weeks after a dream: the story of a London physician who separates the good and evil elements of his nature by a drug, and of the double who takes his place.

works.title: Strictures on the Modern System of Female Education
altTitles: Strictures on the Modern System of Female Education; in a Series of Letters
works.form: conduct and educational treatise in epistolary form; familiar moral argument
works.description: The most widely read conduct book of the decade, addressed to the education of girls and young women and written against the fashionable seminary system and against the theories of female independence then in circulation. Cast as a series of letters, it argues that accomplishments without principle, and learning without religion, produce not accomplished women but spoiled ones, and that the true end of female education is character.
works.plot: The letters begin with the complaint that the new system has exchanged solidity for show, that the seminary teaches a little of everything and nothing thoroughly, and that the French Revolution, by loosing all authority, has corrupted female manners as it has corrupted public principle. It then examines the accomplishments in detail, music, drawing, French, and the small literature of the closet, and finds that they consume the time and destroy the simplicity which the domestic and religious duties require. Against the popular vindications of female rights it urges that the office of woman is not to contest her station but to fill it well, and that her influence, which is real and great, is lost when it is spent on display. The later letters set out the positive scheme: the formation of habit, the government of the temper, the cultivation of cheerful piety, the training for the trials of life, and the duty of the mother as the first educator; and the whole is closed by an appeal to the Christian standard as the only rule that will hold a woman in the day of temptation and of sorrow.
works.significance: It is the central document of the conservative reply to the women question in the 1790s, and the form in which the arguments from duty, character, and influence were put against the arguments from rights; it shaped the practice of the girls' schools and of the conduct literature of the following generation. As social description it preserves, more vividly than any treatise of the period, the actual accomplishments, reading, and expectations of the educated young woman of the rank it addressed.
works.meter: Brisk, pointed, indignant yet obliging prose, full of antithesis and of the shrewd particular illustration, with a woman writer's command of the domestic detail; the tone of persuasion sharpened by reproach.
works.context: Published in the decade of the controversy over female education opened by the vindications of the rights of women, when the seminaries and the new female literature had become a public question, and when the fear of French principles made the government of the family a subject of national anxiety. Its author was already the most skilful manager of religious publishing in the country, and the book sold in large editions and was answered as well as praised.
works.structure: A series of letters in two volumes, arranged by topics rather than by a narrative: the general charge against the modern system, the criticism of the accomplishments and of the fashionable reading, the vindication of the female office, and the positive scheme of habit, temper, and piety.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose private and public educational work is recorded in the biographical literature.

works.title: Such, Such Were the Joys
works.description: The American collection of Orwell's essays, published by Harcourt, Brace on 26 February 1953 and named after its opening piece, the long memoir of his preparatory school, St Cyprian's in Eastbourne. Its British counterpart, England Your England and Other Essays (Secker and Warburg, 12 November 1953), left the memoir out and substituted two excerpts from The Road to Wigan Pier.
works.summary: Besides the title memoir the collection gathers essays including 'Why I Write', 'Writers and Leviathan', 'Anti-Semitism in Britain', 'Poetry and the Microphone', 'Looking Back on the Spanish War', 'Inside the Whale' and 'England Your England'. The memoir had first appeared in Partisan Review in September-October 1952.
works.plot: 'Such, Such Were the Joys', its title an ironic quotation from Blake's 'The Echoing Green', recalls Orwell's years at St Cyprian's (1911-16) with almost unrelieved bitterness: a school run for profit by a headmaster and his wife, nicknamed Sambo and Flip, who took him at half fees in the expectation that he would win a scholarship, crammed him for the public-school examinations, beat him, and reminded him of his poverty among richer boys. Orwell describes a world of force and fraud and secrecy in which virtue meant winning and the weak deserved to lose, and concludes that for such a child it was not possible to be good; he ends by asking whether children still live amid irrational terrors and lunatic misunderstandings. 'Why I Write' sets out four motives for writing and declares that every line of serious work he had written since 1936 was written against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism. 'Writers and Leviathan' considers the writer's integrity in an age of state control and political loyalties; 'Looking Back on the Spanish War' returns to Spain and to the lies told about it; 'Inside the Whale' (1940) reads Henry Miller as a writer who accepts the world passively in an age of catastrophe; and 'England Your England', from The Lion and the Unicorn (1941), describes the English character under the bombs.
works.significance: The memoir is one of Orwell's most anthologised essays and the central text for his account of how the English class system is learned in childhood; it is also the main source, contested by contemporaries at the school and by biographers, for the image of St Cyprian's. This collection was its first appearance in a book; it was later included in The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters (1968).
works.meter: The memoir joins exact sensory recall (the porridge, the swimming baths, the beatings) to the adult's analytical commentary on what the child could not understand; the essays are in Orwell's plain argumentative manner.
works.context: The memoir was probably drafted in 1939-40, revised in 1945-46 and completed in May or June 1948, and appeared two years after Orwell's death, first in Partisan Review (1952). The collection belongs to the posthumous assembling of Orwell's work in the early 1950s, after Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four had made him famous.
works.structure: The long memoir opens the volume and is followed by shorter essays written between 1940 and 1948, mostly on the writer's relation to politics.

works.title: Summa Logicae
works.description: William of Ockham's systematic treatise on logic, written c. 1323 before his summons to Avignon; in three parts it expounds terms, propositions, and the theory of argument, developing the nominalist ontology — the rejection of universals as real entities — for which Ockham is chiefly remembered.
works.summary: Part I analyses terms and the problem of universals, arguing that only individuals exist and that universal concepts are signs in the mind; Part II treats propositions and the properties of terms; Part III examines syllogistic, demonstrative, and probable argument, including the analysis of fallacies. The work is the vehicle of Ockham's razor in its methodological form: entities are not to be multiplied without necessity.
works.significance: The most influential logic textbook of the later Middle Ages; its nominalism reshaped fourteenth-century philosophy and theology and remains a principal point of reference in the history of logic.
themes: Wisdom and learning

works.title: Summer
works.description: The second of Thomson's seasonal poems, carrying the reader from the morning of the ripening year through the heat, the storm and the evening coolness of summer, with the episode of the rural lovers and the poem on the grove and the hound.
works.plot: The day and the weather of summer are traced from the early morning to the night, the labours of the hay field and the flock, the threat of the tempest and the relief of the cool, while the story of two lovers is interrupted and completed within the season's changes.
works.significance: Its storm passage and its treatment of the growing year are the most influential pieces of weather writing in English, and they established the seasonal structure that the later descriptive and meditative poems adopted.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines, with the long compound period for the advancing weather and the short lyric interlude for the hymn and the tale.
works.context: Issued as a separate poem in the season of Thomson's patronage at Richmond, in the same years in which the natural-history writing and the new landscape taste were making the description of the growing year respectable.
works.characters: the rural lovers of the inset tale; the labourers of the field; the storm and the evening
works.structure: A diurnal and meteorological progression, with the inset tale of the lovers and the hymn and ode passages interposed at the crisis of the storm.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843
works.description: Published in 1844 and Fuller's first book: an account of a journey through the Great Lakes and the prairies, with portraits of the Indians, the settlers and the emigrant women. It is a prose work of 1844 by Margaret Fuller; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Fuller travels from Niagara to Milwaukee and the prairie, and records the scenery, the societies of the frontier towns, the condition of the Native Americans, the lot of the emigrant women and, in a long digression, the story of Mariana, a passionate girl broken by school and marriage.
works.significance: Summer on the Lakes is the finest American travel book by a woman of the 1840s and a founding text of the literature of the American West: its account of the Native Americans and of the emigrant women makes it a key document of the American frontier.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, digressive and allusive prose.
works.context: The year 1843, the westward emigration of the 1840s, the forced removal of the Indians, and the Transcendentalist interest in the West. The record dates the work as composed between 1843 and 1844 and first published in 1844 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Margaret Fuller, the narrator; Mariana; the Seeress of Prevorst
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Summer's Last Will and Testament
works.description: Nashe's one surviving solo play, a summer show performed at Archbishop Whitgift's palace at Croydon: Summer, dying of the plague-year's sickness, makes his will and bequeaths the world to Autumn and Winter, while the seasons, the personified vices, and the jester Will Summer pass in review — the play's songs ('Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss') and its memento mori making it the great plague elegy of the Elizabethan stage.
works.plot: Summer, sick and dying, summons his officers — Ver (Spring), Solstitium, and the rest — to account for the year; the debate of the seasons, the entertainment of the Harvest lord, and the pageant of the vices fill the show; Summer makes his will, bequeathing the world to the colder seasons, and dies, with the songs and the jester's epilogue closing the play on mortality itself.
works.significance: The great plague poem of the English Renaissance and Nashe's masterpiece of the mixed mode — masque, satire, and elegy in one.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the famous lyric 'Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss' ('A Litany in Time of Plague') as its summit.
works.context: Performed at Croydon in the plague summer of 1592 (perhaps September), for the Archbishop of Canterbury's household; printed in 1600.
works.characters: Summer; Autumn; Winter; Ver (Spring); Solstitium; Bacchus; Harvest; Will Summer (the jester); the satyrs; the nymphs; Death (in the songs)
works.structure: A masque-like entertainment of pageants, debates, and songs, loose in structure but unified by the dying Summer's progress to his will and death.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Sunset Song
works.description: The finest Scottish novel of the century: Chris Guthrie, the Mearns farming country, and the destruction of a world by war and the machine. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Lewis Grassic Gibbon; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Chris Guthrie grows up on a croft in the Mearns, is torn between her mother's Scots and her father's English, watches her family break up and her father die, marries the farmer Ewan Tavendale, and loses him to the First World War. The novel ends with the village dead of the war, the farms sold, and Chris leaving for the city.
works.significance: Sunset Song is the finest Scottish novel of the century and one of the great novels of rural dispossession in English: its Scots-inflected prose, its choric parish voice and its elegy for a destroyed world made it a permanent classic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness.
works.context: The farming country of the Mearns between 1911 and 1919, the First World War, and the agricultural depression that emptied the land. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Chris Guthrie; Jean Guthrie; John Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Chae Strachan; Long Rob
works.structure: Four parts (Prelude, The Song, The Woman, Epilude) with choric openings. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Leslie Mitchell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Supernatural Horror in Literature
works.description: The history and theory of the weird tale by its greatest practitioner. It is a prose work of 1927 by H. P. Lovecraft; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Supernatural Horror in Literature traces the weird tradition from the gothic novel through Poe and the ghost story to the cosmic horror of the pulps, and defines the literature of fear as the literature of the unknown, in the scholar's essay of the pulp writer.
works.significance: Supernatural Horror in Literature is the weird tale's own history and manifesto: its definition of the literature of fear framed the tradition that Lovecraft's fiction then fulfilled.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript.
works.context: Providence and the amateur press, 1927. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: the gothic novelists; Poe; the weird tradition
works.structure: A critical essay in the chapters of the tradition. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Howard Phillips Lovecraft. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Critical Essay and the Modern Review
themes: Myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination
