works.title: Surfeit of Lampreys
works.description: Ngaio Marsh's tenth Roderick Alleyn novel, first published in Boston in 1940 as Death of a Peer and in London by the Collins Crime Club in 1941 as Surfeit of Lampreys: a peer is murdered in the lift outside the London flat of his younger brother's spendthrift family, and their friend from New Zealand, Roberta Grey, is drawn into Alleyn's investigation.
works.plot: Roberta Grey comes to London from New Zealand to see the Lampreys, a minor aristocratic family she knew there, whose spendthrift ways have always been rescued by the timely death of a relative. She finds them in the worst trouble yet. Charles Lamprey appeals for money to his elder brother Gabriel, Lord Wutherwood; a charade of Jael and Sisera put on by the children, with a skewer for the tent peg, fails to soften him, and he refuses. Leaving their top-floor flat, he is skewered through the eye in the lift and dies soon afterwards. Chief Inspector Alleyn and Inspector Fox find the Lampreys the obvious suspects, since the death ends their money troubles and makes Charles heir to the title; the family try to steer suspicion towards Gabriel's eccentric wife Violet, and Roberta lies to Alleyn on their behalf. After Gabriel's chauffeur Giggle is found with his throat cut, Alleyn shows that Violet's maid Tinkerton had manipulated Giggle into killing his employer, so that he would inherit a valuable parcel of land that she hoped to secure for herself. She had sent the lift down to him and back up again to make it seem that both of them were already on the stairs, persuaded Violet into acts, such as cutting off her dead husband's hand, that made her look guilty, and killed Giggle when his conscience began to trouble him.
works.significance: Erik Routley, in The Puritan Pleasures of the Detective Story (1972), found Marsh here 'at the top of her form', calling the novel 'her longest and I think her richest story'. The murder of a peer was a subject to which Marsh would return, and the youngest Lamprey, Michael, reappears in the short story 'I Can Find My Way Out' and, as a police constable, in Opening Night (1951). A stage adaptation by Owen Howell, revised by Marsh, was produced in London in 1950 without success.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the theatre and the country house as the setting of murder.
works.context: Marsh, a New Zealander, had arrived in England in the late 1920s; Earl F. Bargainnier, who also identified the real family that inspired the Lampreys, called Roberta Grey 'obviously Marsh's view of herself on her arrival in England in the late 1920s'. The title alludes both to Henry I, said to have died of a surfeit of lampreys, and to the family under suspicion.

works.structure: A detective novel that follows the Lampreys' friend Roberta Grey from her arrival in London through the murder in the lift and Alleyn's investigation to his explanation.

works.title: Surrey's Poems
altTitles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
works.description: The collected shorter poems of the Earl of Surrey — sonnets in the new 'English' form he devised (three quatrains and a couplet), elegies, and lyrics such as 'The soote season', 'Alas, so all things now do hold their peace', and the elegy on Wyatt — printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
works.plot: A courtier's lyric record: love's complaints, the seasons' changes, the deaths of friends, and the poet's imprisonment at Windsor, all in a grave, musical decasyllabic line.
works.significance: With Wyatt, the founder of the English sonnet; Surrey's smoother line and his rhyme scheme became the Elizabethan standard, and Tottel's printing of his verse made him the model of the English courtly poet.
works.meter: The regular iambic pentameter and the English sonnet rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that Surrey perfected and Shakespeare inherited; smooth alternation of the accents.
works.context: Written in the last decade of Surrey's life, under the factional warfare that ended in his execution in 1547; the elegy on Wyatt makes the dead poet a mirror of his own fate.
works.characters: the speaker; the beloved ('Geraldine', Elizabeth Fitzgerald); the court
works.structure: Miscellany of sonnets and lyrics without narrative frame; Tottel's printed canon of forty poems is the principal witness.
works.attributionNotes: The Tottel canon of forty poems is accepted in the main; a few attributions are contested.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry

works.title: Swallowdale
works.description: The second sailing novel: the wreck of the Swallow and the fell country of the dale. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by Arthur Ransome; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The Swallow is wrecked on the rock in the night fog, and the Walkers and the Blacketts turn to the fell country above the dale, where the search for the lost Titty and Roger and the meeting with the sheep-farmer and the charcoal-burner carry the adventure from the water to the high ground.
works.significance: Swallowdale carried the sailing adventure from the water to the fell and proved that the series could change its country without losing its method; its fog, its wreck and its high-ground campaign are among the best chapters Ransome wrote.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, exact, practical prose of the sailor.
works.context: The Lake District fells in the summer of 1930. The record dates the work as composed between 1930 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.structure: A children's novel in chapters, from the wreck to the recovery of the boat. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: Swallows and Amazons
works.description: The founding novel of the sailing adventure: the Walker children, the Blacketts and the war on the lake. works.significance: Swallows and Amazons is the founding novel of the English sailing adventure: its practical exactness, its children's republic and its lake made competence the substance of adventure, and it gave English childhood its classic open-air fiction and its most imitated series.

works.title: Sybil; or, The Two Nations
works.description: Published in 1845 and the most important English novel of the condition of England: the discovery of the two nations, rich and poor. It is a prose fiction work of 1845 by Benjamin Disraeli; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Charles Egremont, a young aristocrat, travels in the industrial north and discovers the misery of the mining and manufacturing districts; he falls in love with Sybil, the daughter of a Chartist leader, follows the Chartist petition and the Plug Plot riots of 1842, and at the end Sybil, whose father is killed in the riots, is revealed as the heiress of the Mowbray estates of which her family had been dispossessed, and is free to marry Egremont.
works.significance: Sybil is the first English novel to make the industrial working class the central subject of national politics: its phrase 'the two nations' entered the language, its documentary account of the mining districts influenced Engels and the whole condition-of-England tradition, and it remains the most important political novel of the 1840s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is epigrammatic dialogue and brilliant repartee.
works.context: 1845: the Chartist petition of 1842, the Plug Plot riots, the reports of the Children's Employment Commission, the Anti-Corn Law agitation, and the Young England movement. The record dates the work as composed in 1845 and first published in 1845 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Charles Egremont; Sybil Gerard; Walter Gerard, her father; Stephen Morley; Lord Marney; Baptist Hatton; Bishop Hatton; Dandy Mick; Devilsdust; Lord Mowbray; Lady Joan and Lady Maud Fitz-Warene
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees and the Propagation of Timber
works.description: Evelyn's treatise on trees and timber, written at the request of the Royal Society and the first book it published, which urged the planting of oaks and other timber for the navy and became a classic of forestry.
works.plot: Evelyn describes the principal forest trees of England, their uses, propagation, and management, and argues that the nation's naval strength depends on the systematic planting of timber.
works.significance: The founding text of English forestry and an important document of the new scientific culture; its practical influence on tree-planting was immediate and long-lasting.
works.meter: Learned but readable prose, with verse quotations and classical allusion.
works.context: Published in 1664 as the first book issued by the Royal Society; four editions appeared in Evelyn's lifetime.
works.structure: Four books, each treating a group of trees, with appended treatises on fruit trees and on the propagation of timber.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Evelyn; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Sylvie and Bruno
works.form: Fantasy novel (with illustrations by Harry Furniss)
works.description: Published in 1889 and the strangest of Carroll's books: a double narrative that alternates between the fairy world of Elfland, ruled by the Warden and the Chancellor, and the Victorian country house of the real world.
works.plot: The narrator moves between the fairy kingdom of Sylvie and Bruno and the English world of Lady Muriel and Arthur Forester; the fairy plot turns on the Warden's abdication and the usurping Chancellor, the real plot on a love affair and a death, and the two are linked by the narrator's trances.
works.significance: Sylvie and Bruno is the most ambitious and least successful of Carroll's fantasies, but it is a key text for the late-Victorian fairy revival and for the study of the double narrative in children's fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The author's characteristic manner is logical paradox, pun and wordplay.
works.context: The 1880s, Carroll's later interest in logic, spiritualism and social reform, and the Victorian fairy painting of Richard Dadd and Joseph Noel Paton. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.title: Table Talk
works.form: discursive essay in verse on taste and society, in the line of the Augustan art-poem renewed by Thomson
works.description: Cowper's discursive blank-verse poem on society, reading and taste, published with the Task in 1785 and much admired by Hazlitt. Its subject is the talk of the table itself - the pleasures of conversation, the choice of books, the study of one's own company and the criticism of the literature of the day - treated with an ease that had been Thomson's before him. The poem is the most explicit statement of Cowper's beliefs about taste, retirement and the uses of letters.
works.plot: The poem opens on the advantages of social intercourse and of the well-ordered table, then turns to the love of reading, the choice of the old writers against the modern scramble for novelty, and the necessity of solitude within company. Its central argument is that a man should think for himself at the table as in the study, that friendship and domestic happiness refine rather than dull the mind, and that the critic's first duty is to the plain honest sense of the writer he reads.
works.significance: Later readers, Hazlitt among them, have prized it as the most accomplished of Cowper's shorter poems, and its remarks on reading and originality belong to the century's theory of taste. It also displays the blank-verse style that the romantic poets inherited from Thomson through Cowper.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, the smoothest and most colloquial of Cowper's blank verse, with long sentence-periods and a marked caesural poise.
works.context: Published in 1785 with the Task, in the season of the great vogue of the familiar essay and of the debate about reading, novelty and the book trade; its praise of the older native writers is a protest against the hurry of fashionable taste in the same years as Blair's lectures on rhetoric.
works.characters: The speaking friend at table; the company of readers; the modern writers of the day, unnamed
works.structure: A single continuous meditation in several marked divisions, moving by association from conversation to reading, to retirement and to literary criticism, without narrative incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is not fixed with certainty within the years before publication, and the composition start is therefore left null with the range indicated by the printing date.
themes: Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules
Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: Table Talk (Hazlitt)
altTitles: Table Talk: A Series of Essays
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch, with a share of moral philosophy and of critical review, in the line of the table-talk and of the miscellaneous paper.
works.description: A series of essays on the miscellaneous, published in two volumes in 1821 and 1822 and written for the fireside on the model of the talk of a table rather than of a periodical paper. Its subjects are the pleasures and the opinions of a private reader: the love of the old books, the principles of human action and of taste, the differences of town and country, the pleasures of the imagination, travel, the theatre and its great actors, and the history and the quarrels of the age. It is the completest body of its author's familiar prose and one of the classic books of the English essay.
works.plot: The papers have no single thesis but return constantly to a set of oppositions. Several argue that the imagination and not the understanding governs human conduct and opinion, that we are moved by what we hold as an idea rather than by what we know as a fact, and that self-love, with its hope and its fear, is the root of our moral life; one of the earliest papers states this as a philosophy of action, and others apply it to taste, to the love of the great and to the envy that attends it. A second group is the essay of relish: the town and the country and the character of each, the pleasure of reading the old poets, the sound of a stringed instrument, the theatre, a long absence and a return, the luxury of ease, and the use of a library. A third deals with the persons and the quarrels of contemporary literature and politics, pleading the spirit of the age against the cant of the party journals. The whole is bound by the writer's temper, at once eager and indolent, generous and resentful, and by the constant reference of every subject to the act of thinking and feeling in a private mind.
works.significance: One of the canonical books of the English familiar essay, and the storehouse of its author's most repeated papers on the principles of action, on taste and on the pleasures of reading; its essays on the town and the country, on old books and on the actors have been continuously anthologised. Its philosophical papers are also the plainest accessible statement of the theory of the imagination that underlies his criticism.
works.meter: Prose of remarkable variety, passing from the aphoristic sentence and the sharp paradox to the long and lapping period of the essays on relish, with habitual balance of clause and a frequent use of the negative for emphasis.
works.context: Written and published in London in 1821 and 1822, when its author was at the height of his critical reputation and before the domestic catastrophe that broke his life, and when the essay, the review and the lecture made a single literary market; the title pages advertise his earlier books of criticism, and the papers were among the first fruits of the profession of letters he had chosen.
works.characters: The essayist at his table; the reader and the idler, the man of town and the dweller in the country; the actors and the authors of the old and of the present drama, and the persons of the literary quarrels of the day
works.structure: Two series of short essays, some thirty in all, with no order of matter except the alternation of the philosophical, the descriptive and the critical papers; each piece is a completed meditation, and the unity is that of the voice and of the recurring theory of the imagination.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the bare title is shared with a poem of the same name by a writer of the previous generation and with a later volume of table-talk by a friend and collaborator, and the three are distinguished in libraries by the author's name.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Imagination as a way of knowing
Melancholy and self-analysis
The city and urban life
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: Tales from Shakespeare
altTitles: Tales from Shakespeare. Written for the Young Folks who love their Books, but have not leisure to read all the Plays themselves
works.form: Juvenile retelling of dramatic romance in prose, a children's anthology that adapts the stage for the reading of the young and holds the sentence structure of the original within a plain narrative.
works.description: A collection of prose retellings of twenty of the plays, issued in 1807 in two volumes and written for young readers by two brothers and sisters of one family, with the elder's hand chiefly in the preface and in some of the histories and the younger's in the greater number of the tales. The volume tells the comedies and tragedies as stories, keeping much of the original dialogue in its narrative, and it has been the ordinary introduction to the plays for children in English for two centuries.
works.plot: The tales follow the plays in a single continuous narrative each, abridging the sub-plot and explaining the characters rather than arguing about them. The volumes open with the tale of the storm-raising enchanter and the recovered dukedom, and pass through the comedy of twins separated, the comedies of error and of mistaken identity, the pastoral and romantic comedies, the histories of the English kings, and the great tragedies of revenge, jealousy and ambition, ending with the tale of the tempest, the injured Duke and the renounced magic. Each narrative retains the words of the original wherever they can be given without difficulty, so that the child's first knowledge of the plays is of phrases still belonging to the plays themselves; the moral commentary is light, and the interest is the story, the wonder and the pathos.
works.significance: The most durable children's book of the Romantic period and for most English readers the first entrance into the plays; its retellings fixed a canon of the plays for young readers and are still in print. It is also the most widely read work to which a woman of the period contributed the larger share, and its joint authorship has been a standing case in discussions of collaborative and unattributed women's writing.
works.meter: Prose of great simplicity, in short declarative sentences for the child's ear, with the quoted lines of the plays set in their own rhythm inside the narrative; the style is deliberately free of the moralising manner of much children's book-writing of the day.
works.context: Written and published in London in 1807, in the years when the family of the writers was established in literary work and when the plays were being widely acted and read; it belonged to the growing trade in books for the young, and its companion volume of educational tales by the same household had already made the authors' names familiar to publishers.
works.characters: The figures of the plays retold in prose, including the twins of the comedy of errors, the merchant and the heiress of the comedy, the star-crossed children of the tragedy of Verona, the Scottish thane and his wife, the wronged Duke of the melancholy comedy, and the injured Duke of the last romance with his spirit and his abjured art
works.structure: Twenty independent prose tales, one to each play, arranged in two volumes with no continuous frame; the method is a plain narrative voice, with dialogue transcribed or paraphrased, and with the supernatural and the comic elements preserved in their original strangeness.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly written, with the division of labour variously reported; the customary account assigns the greater part of the tales to the younger member of the household and a smaller share, with the preface, to the elder, and the evidence is the family correspondence and the later statements of the survivors rather than any contemporaneous record of the partition.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Childhood, innocence, and education
Marriage and women's conduct
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: Tales of a Traveller
altTitles: Tales of a Traveller, by Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
works.form: Sketch series and supernatural romance in three parts, closing in essayistic satire on speculation
works.description: A second miscellany of tales and essays, framed as the papers of a Travelling Bachelor and organized into three self-conscious divisions: German tales of the supernatural, sketches of Italy, and a burlesque third part on money and speculative schemes. It shows the sketch turning deliberately toward romance and satire. Its essay on the love of riches has been read as the first American meditation on speculation as a national pathology.
works.plot: The German tales, translated from alleged source papers, give ghost, portrait and metamorphic stories in a schoolroom frame, including a bridegroom undone by an archbishop's curse and a painter whose portrait destroys his happiness. The Italian sketches pass from the Coliseum and the Catacombs to the robber stories of the Papal territory, where romance and banditry meet. The concluding division, a wallet of a late Travelling Bachelor, turns to the pursuit of money in a series of essays and projected schemes. Its unfinished shape, part legend and part satire, makes the book a laboratory for later romance.
works.significance: It carried the German supernatural tale into American letters and supplied the model for the native ghost story of the 1830s and 1840s. Its essay on money is an early and searching critique of speculation as a national mood. Its unevenness is itself evidence of the sketch-book's limits as a form.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1824, when its author was resident in Europe and the American market for metropolitan sketch-books was at its height. Its Italian material belongs to the post-Napoleonic tourist literature of the peninsula. The third part responds to the boom in banks, canals and paper schemes that prefigured the speculative manias of the 1830s.
works.characters: Geoffrey Crayon; the Travelling Bachelor; the young editor and his schoolmaster
works.structure: Three-part miscellany with an overarching persona; internal frames include a schoolmaster's translation of German manuscripts and the papers of a deceased bachelor.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; like the first miscellany it appears under the Crayon persona.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
movements: The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch

works.title: Tales of Mean Streets
works.form: Collection of short stories; local-colour sketch
works.description: Published in 1894 and Morrison's first book: fifteen sketches and stories of the East End, written in a hard, laconic prose and without a trace of charity or sentiment. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: The stories move from the comic ('The Red Cow Group', a pub circle of would-be revolutionaries) to the terrible ('On the Stairs', a mother saving for her dying son's funeral; 'Lizerunt', the destruction of a woman by her husband), and the volume ends with 'To Bow Bridge', a walk taken after a funeral.
works.significance: Tales of Mean Streets is the finest English collection of slum stories and a founding text of the modern English short story: Kipling, Conrad and Wells all admired it, and its refusal of pity and moral commentary was a decisive break with Dickensian philanthropy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
works.context: The 1890s, the East End, the new journalism and the 'cosmopolitan' short story, and the debate on the authenticity of slum writing. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Lizerunt, Billy Chope and Sam Cardew ('Lizerunt'); Mrs Curtis and her dying son ('On the Stairs')
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Tales of Men and Ghosts
works.description: Published in 1910 and the best of Wharton's supernatural collections: ten stories of the uncanny set in the drawing rooms of the New York and European upper class. It is a prose fiction work of 1910 by Edith Wharton; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The ghost stories 'Afterward' and 'The Eyes', set beside psychological tales such as 'The Bolted Door' and 'The Letters', present hauntings that are always also moral facts: a husband who vanishes with a visitor his wife will recognise as a ghost only afterward, and a pair of hideous eyes that reveal to a man the cruelty hidden in his own kindnesses.
works.significance: Tales of Men and Ghosts contains the finest American ghost stories after Henry James: 'Afterward' and 'The Eyes' are permanent classics of the form, and Wharton's treatment of the supernatural as a moral and psychological fact rather than a sensation made her the most sophisticated American writer of ghost stories in the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is precise, ironic exposition of a social world.
works.context: 1898-1910: the American vogue for the ghost story after James and Bierce, the country houses of New England and Europe, and the new psychology of the unconscious. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1910 and first published in 1910 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Mary and Ned Boyne ('Afterward'); Andrew Culwin ('The Eyes'); Hubert Granice ('The Bolted Door'); Lizzie West and Vincent Deering ('The Letters')
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edith Newbold Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil

works.title: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians
works.form: Short-story collection; war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: Published in 1891 and the greatest American collection of Civil War stories: the war as a series of private encounters with death and illusion. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by Ambrose Bierce; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge', in which a planter is hanged and his escape occurs only in the instant before death, 'Chickamauga', in which a deaf child wanders through a battlefield, and 'A Horseman in the Sky', in which a sentry shoots his own father, among other stories of soldiers and civilians caught by the war.
works.significance: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians is the greatest American book about the Civil War after Crane: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' invented the modern ironic short story, and Bierce's cold technique — the delayed revelation, the reversed ending — made the collection a founding text of the modern American short story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the common soldier: the plain first-person account, the exact vocabulary of the trench, the ration, the march and the casualty, and the understatement that carries the horror. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short, precisely engineered story with a reversed or delayed ending.
works.context: 1861-65 and 1891: the Civil War, the American cult of the veteran, the new magazine fiction of the 1880s, and the American reception of Poe. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Peyton Farquhar ('An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge'); the deaf-mute child ('Chickamauga'); Carter Druse and his father ('A Horseman in the Sky'); Jerome Searing ('One of the Missing'); Captain Downing Madwell and Sergeant Halcrow ('The Coup de Grâce')
works.structure: A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ambrose Gwinnett Bierce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Talking in Bed
works.description: Talking in Bed is a short poem by Philip Larkin, completed in August 1960 and collected in The Whitsun Weddings (1964), about a couple for whom talk in bed, which ought to be easiest, has become difficult.
works.summary: A couple lying together in silence; the wind, clouds and dark towns outside; and the closing difficulty of finding words at once true and kind.
works.plot: Talking in bed ought to be easiest, the speaker begins, since lying together is an emblem of two people being honest; yet more and more time passes in silence. Outside the wind builds and disperses clouds and dark towns heap up on the horizon, and none of it cares for the couple. Nothing explains why, at this unique distance from isolation, it becomes still harder to find words at once true and kind, or not untrue and not unkind.
works.significance: Frequently anthologised and taught; its last lines are among Larkin's most quoted.
works.meter: Plain statement, a single image of wind and towns, and a final litotes ('not untrue and not unkind') that enacts the hesitation it describes.
works.context: One of the poems of love and marriage in The Whitsun Weddings, written in the year of 'MCMXIV'.
works.structure: Twelve lines in four three-line stanzas, loosely rhymed, ending on a self-correcting double negative.
themes: Language, writing and the limits of representation
Love, intimacy and loss
movements: The Movement

works.title: Tam o' Shanter
works.form: comic-gothic tale poem in the Scottish vernacular, written to illustrate an antiquarian drawing of Alloway
works.description: Burns's narrative masterpiece, a tale of the farmer Tam who, leaving a fair at Alloway after drink, sees the witches and warlocks dancing by the haunted kirk and is pursued across the Auld Brig by the ghastly band, losing his mare's tail at the keystone. Written in 1790 to accompany a drawing of Alloway Kirk for Grose's antiquarian series, it moves from tavern realism to supernatural panic and back to homely commentary in a single sweep. It is the most perfectly timed comic poem in Scottish verse.
works.plot: Tam's day of market, his supper with friends and his drunken ride home at moonlight are set at length, with the county's characters and pleasures named. At the kirk he watches the dance of the witches and of the Devil with his tarred tail, and, crying out in admiration at the sight, is discovered; the horde pursue him, and he escapes across the Auld Brig because a witch has no power over running water. The poem ends with the loss of Meg's tail, with Tam's shrift before his wife, and with the poet's own homely closing commentary, which deflates the horror he has just raised.
works.significance: It is generally held to be the greatest Scottish narrative poem and the supreme example of Burns's command of dialect, of tonal switch and of the antic machinery of belief. Its mixture of gothic terror and homely comedy makes it a central text for the literature of the supernatural in the 1790s, and its stanzaic and couplet technique was widely imitated in vernacular verse.
works.meter: Octosyllabic heroic couplets in Scots, broken at the crisis into triplets of fourteen-syllable alexandrine lines for the dance and the pursuit, the formal swell carrying the poem's terror and its comedy.
works.context: Composed in 1790 at Burns's own request to supply a poem to Francis Grose's engraved series of Scottish antiquities, and thus directly tied to the antiquarian interest in kirk, brigs and witch-traditions; the witchlore of Ayrshire, the Kirk sessions' records and the popular belief in second sight supply its matter, and the poem quickly entered both printed and sung tradition.
works.characters: Tam o' Shanter; Kate, his wife; Souter Johnnie; Nansie, Johnnie's wife; the Devil and the witch band; Meg the grey mare
works.structure: A single continuous narrative in four recognisable movements - the market and tavern scene, the ride and the vision at the kirk, the pursuit, and the closing commentary - with the tonal registers of realism, terror and comedy sharply opposed.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the circumstances of commission are documented by Burns's letters and by the account of his friendship with Grose, and the poem's text was revised by him in later printings.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Monsters and the marvellous

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 1
works.description: Marlowe's first play and the manifesto of Elizabethan blank verse drama: the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine rises by conquest to overthrow kings, takes the Egyptian princess Zenocrate, defeats the Persian Cosroe, and tramples the Turkish emperor Bajazeth in his cage — the play closing with Tamburlaine's marriage and his vow of further conquests, 'still climbing after knowledge infinite'.
works.plot: Tamburlaine, armed with eloquence and terror, wins Zenocrate, deposes Mycetes, and crowns himself after Cosroe's fall; Bajazeth and Zabina are caged and mocked; Damascus is sacked for its defiance, Zenocrate's father pardoned for her sake; the play ends with the betrothal and the tyrant's speech of unappeasable aspiration.
works.significance: The first great English blank-verse tragedy and the fountainhead of Elizabethan heroic drama; its hero became the type of the Renaissance overreacher.
works.meter: The 'mighty line' — Marlowe's blank verse of sweeping hyperbole and classical allusion, which transformed the English stage.
works.context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1587, the Armada year; its prologue's defiance of 'jigging veins of rhyming mother-wits' announced the new poetics that Shakespeare's generation inherited.
works.characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Bajazeth; Zabina; Mycetes; Cosroe; Theridamas; Techelles; Usumcasane; Agydas; the Soldan of Egypt
works.structure: A two-part rise structured as a chain of conquests and debates, with the great set speeches — 'Is it not passing brave to be a king' — as its pillars.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Fortune and mutability
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 2
works.description: The sequel Marlowe was pressed to write after Part 1's success: Tamburlaine's further conquests — the slaughter of the virgins of Damascus, the bridling of the conquered kings who draw his chariot, his burning of the Koran at Babylon — until the death of Zenocrate breaks him, his own sickness follows, and the 'scourge of God' dies in his camp, his empire uncompleted.
works.plot: Tamburlaine defeats the Christian Sigismund's treachery, kills his coward son Calyphas, humbles the Turkish and Egyptian powers, and burns the Koran in defiance; Zenocrate's death opens the way to his own — the physician's verdict, the self-anatomy in the mirror, and the dying survey of the map of the world he could not finish conquering.
works.significance: The completion of the first great two-part epic of the English stage and the template for the overreacher's fall.
works.meter: The mighty line at its most sustained, with the dying speeches of Zenocrate and Tamburlaine as its elegiac close.
works.context: Written immediately after Part 1 and printed with it in 1590; its burnings and blasphemies made Marlowe's name feared as well as famous.
works.characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Calyphas; Amyras; Celebinus; Orcanes; Sigismund; Callapine; the Turkish Concubines; the Physician
works.structure: A series of conquests and defiances culminating in the two deaths, with the chariot scene and the burning of the books as the peaks of its provocation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Fortune and mutability

works.title: Tamerlane and Other Poems
works.form: Romantic narrative poem and lyric collection in the Byronic manner; confession in verse
works.description: A slim first pamphlet of romantic verse, issued in Boston without the author's name and now one of the rarest books in American literature. Its title poem is a long confession of a wanderer who has forfeited love by ambition, and the accompanying pieces treat loss and solitude in the manner of the younger romantic poetry. The volume is the starting point of the author's career and of his lifelong quarrel with the hack writers.
works.plot: In the title poem a solitary wanderer recalls a love withdrawn from him and a destiny of exile that he has chosen for himself, and he recounts a life of conquest abandoned for remorse. The shorter poems dwell on bereavement, on the memory of the dead and on the consolation or the emptiness of the natural world. The volume's movement is from the expansive romance of the long poem to the compressed elegy. Its speaker is a creature of will and of guilt rather than of observation.
works.significance: It is the rarest and most quoted of American poetry pamphlets and the document from which the author's career is dated. Its Byronic confession supplies the native origin of the poetry of guilt and exile. It is the starting point of the American strand's closing phase in this installment.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter and mixed stanzas, with a dominant blank-verse recitative
works.context: Published in Boston in 1827 while its author was a student in the city, in a small run of which very few copies survive. Its manner imitates the available romantic models, and its appearance preceded by two years the metropolitan review war over American letters. It belongs to the first generation of American poets writing after the British romantic example had become unavoidable.
works.characters: The wanderer of the title poem; the lost beloved
works.structure: Pamphlet collection: one long narrative-confessional poem followed by shorter lyrics and an address to a patron of the imagination.
works.attributionNotes: Issued anonymously, the title-page naming only the city of the author; attribution rests on the author's later acknowledgement and on the bibliographical census of the pamphlet.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt
The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Tancred; or, The New Crusade
works.description: Published in 1847 and the strangest of the Young England trilogy: a young English aristocrat goes to Jerusalem and the Sinai to discover the meaning of faith. It is a prose fiction work of 1847 by Benjamin Disraeli; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Tancred, Lord Montacute, heir to the Duke of Bellamont, refuses a political career and, armed with introductions from the financier Sidonia, makes a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, where he meets the beautiful Jewess Eva and the scheming young emir Fakredeen, seeks a revelation on Mount Sinai, and is drawn into a desert intrigue to found a new empire; the novel breaks off in Jerusalem as he declares his love for Eva and his parents, the Duke and Duchess of Bellamont, arrive to reclaim him.
works.significance: Tancred is the most ambitious and most prophetic of Disraeli's novels: its portrait of Sidonia, its vision of a Jewish national destiny in Palestine, and its argument that the English aristocracy needs a spiritual mission made it a founding text of the Zionist imagination and one of the most extraordinary political romances of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is epigrammatic dialogue and brilliant repartee.
works.context: 1847: the Eastern question, the beginnings of Zionism, the Victorian enthusiasm for the Holy Land, and the religious crisis of the 1840s. The record dates the work as composed in 1847 and first published in 1847 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Tancred, Lord Montacute; Eva Besso; Fakredeen, Emir of Canobia; Sidonia; the Duke and Duchess of Bellamont; Baroni; Lady Bertie and Bellair; Queen Astarte
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Benjamin D'Israeli. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Tarka the Otter
works.form: Nature narrative (the life of an otter)
works.description: The life of the otter Tarka from the cub to the hound's tooth: the epic of a single animal. It is a prose work of 1927 by Henry Williamson; it is catalogued here under Nature Essay and the Rural Observation; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tarka the Otter follows the otter from the cub in the holt on the two rivers to the hunted dog-otter of the last chapter, hour by hour and season by season, in the prose of the naturalist's exactness charged with the elegiac.
works.significance: Tarka the Otter is the greatest of the English nature narratives: its life of a single animal, followed hour by hour and season by season, made the wild creature the matter of the epic and remains the standard of the prose of the water.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the wild creature followed hour by hour and season by season.
works.context: The rivers of Devon and Somerset in the years of the writing. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Tarka; the hounds; the otter-hunters; the two rivers
works.structure: A nature narrative in chapters of the seasons, from the cub to the hunt. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry William Williamson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Taxation Tyrannical; or, The Colonies and Britain Compared
altTitles: Taxation Tyrannical: or, The Colonies and Britain Compared, in Answer to a Pamphlet entitled Taxation No Tyranny
works.form: political pamphlet and polemical answer in the Augustan tractate manner
works.description: Johnson's last and fiercest political pamphlet, written at the crisis of the American dispute as a reply to the anonymous Taxation no Tyranny and to the colonial claim that representation is necessary to lawful taxation. It argues that authority rather than consent is the ground of government, that the colonies are subordinate parts of an empire maintained at the cost of the whole, and that the language of liberty used by the planters covers the interest of slavers. Its invective against the slave trade is the most quoted passage in the pamphlet and among the strongest in Johnson's prose.
works.plot: Johnson denies the doctrine that taxation without representation is tyranny, urging that no part of a community can be exempt from the burdens of the whole and that the ties of empire are not dissolved by distance. He compares the condition of the colonists with that of Britain, insists on the expense and risk incurred for the colonies, and predicts that a claimed independence would produce only a republic of planters and a new scene of revolt. Against the colonial assertion of the rights of Englishmen he sets the treatment of their own slaves, asking why the loudest yelps for liberty should come from the drivers of negroes, and closes with an unapologetic defence of the authority of the mother country.
works.significance: The pamphlet is the classic tory answer to the American case, and its exposure of the hypocrisy of slaveholding revolutionaries made it a durable text in the literature of abolition as well as in the history of political argument. It closes Johnson's career as a public writer and remains a touchstone in debates about authority, consent and empire.
works.meter: Prose; rapid and indignant, heavy with rhetorical question, amplification and stark antithesis, the style of the late political tractates rather than of the periodical essays.
works.context: Written after the destruction of the tea at Boston and before the outbreak of war, when Johnson, aged and ill, took the ministerial side in a cause many of his friends favoured, in a pamphlet war that included repeated colonial declarations and Burke's conciliatory policy. His protest against the slave trade belongs to a longer engagement with slavery that includes the arguments with Boswell.
works.characters: The anonymous author of Taxation no Tyranny (conventionally identified as Josiah Tucker, Dean of Gloucester); the American assemblies and their leaders; the planter and his slaves
works.structure: A short polemic in continuous argument: statement of the question, refutation of the doctrine of representation, comparison of colonies and mother country, and a peroration of indignation against colonial inconsistency.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship is documented by his correspondence and by Boswell, while the authorship of the pamphlet answered rests on a conjecture long current among bibliographers.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
The slave trade and abolition
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: Temora
works.form: Restored ancient epic in books, with argument, dissertation and explanatory notes, and with an apparatus of translated Irish and Highland remains attached to support the claim of source.
works.description: Macpherson's second and longer Ossianic epic, offered as a translation of ancient poems on the war for the Irish throne and on the hill and hall of Temora. It carries a more elaborate scholarly apparatus than 'Fingal', including an introductory dissertation and translations of shorter Irish remains, and it presses further after a regular heroic structure.
works.plot: The action concerns the invasion of Ireland and the contest between an expelled family and an usurping line, with Fingal again the arbiter of the north whose arms decide the quarrel. The poem's real subject, as its contemporaries saw, is the moral cost of war: its chiefs are magnanimous, wounded and funereal, and its interest is concentrated on combats, deaths and laments rather than on the mechanics of plot. Love and friendship run through the action in the persons of the young heroes and their mistresses, and the machinery is provided by the spirits and the reciting bards of the earlier poem. The design is closer to the classical epic than 'Fingal', and its ambition is explicitly to restore the 'epopoeia' of the ancient northern nations.
works.significance: It completed the Ossianic corpus as an epic system and fixed the European image of the ancient northern world as a scene of gloomy sublimity, generous enmity and funerary tenderness. Its reception, from German poets and painters to English reviewers, is one of the largest episodes in the history of literary forgery and of the primitive-genius doctrine.
works.meter: The ossianic cadence continued: unrhymed, heavily accented and inverted periods of long decasyllabic and alexandrine-like measure, with sustained apostrophe and epithet; the rhythm is the poem's principal claim to authenticity and to sublimity.
works.context: It followed 'Fingal' within a year, at the high point of Macpherson's credit, and appeared amid a swelling controversy over the manuscripts, in which Highland gentlemen and Irish scholars were invited to verify what he had transcribed. Its Irish setting drew upon the antiquarian knowledge of the Gaelic nations then being assembled by writers such as Charles O'Conor, whose attacks on the forgeries came soon after.
works.characters: Fingal and his sons; the competing Irish chiefs of the war for Temora; the young lovers of the episode; the spirits and bards
works.structure: An epic in books with a continuous central action, framed by an introductory dissertation, and reinforced by the shorter poems and the prose fragments appended; internal recitation and prophecy still interrupt the sequence.
works.attributionNotes: As with the other Ossianic publications the ancient authorship is disputed: Macpherson offered the work as a translation from Gaelic originals of the heroic era, and the charge that he composed them, on slight foundation, has never been fully withdrawn. The record assigns the printed text to Macpherson and marks the claimed ancient source as contested.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Warfare and battle
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: Tender Buttons
works.description: The most radical book of the period: objects, food and rooms, in a prose that abolishes the noun's ordinary work. It is a verse work of 1914 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The three sections — 'Objects', 'Food' and 'Rooms' — are sequences of short prose portraits of a carafe, a chair, a plate, a room, in which Stein repeats and displaces words until the object appears as a pattern of language rather than a description.
works.significance: Tender Buttons is the most radical book of the period and the founding text of literary Cubism: it dissolved the descriptive sentence into pattern and repetition, and it remains the extreme limit of what prose poetry can do.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
works.context: The Paris of the 1910s, the Cubist painting of Picasso and Braque that Stein was collecting, and the new avant-garde little magazines. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.structure: Three sections of short prose pieces, arranged as a cubist still life. A single poem, read as one continuous whole from its opening to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

The suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity

works.title: Tender Is the Night
works.form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1934
works.description: Fitzgerald's most ambitious novel: the Divers on the Riviera, and the destruction of a marriage by money and illness. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by F. Scott Fitzgerald; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Dick Diver, a brilliant young psychiatrist, marries his patient Nicole Warren, whose family's wealth has bought her cure; the novel follows their marriage across the Riviera, Paris and Zurich, Dick's decline into drink and obscurity, his affair with the young actress Rosemary Hoyt, and Nicole's recovery and departure.
works.significance: Tender Is the Night is Fitzgerald's most ambitious novel and one of the great American studies of marriage and money: its portrait of the destruction of a gifted man by the wealth that cured his wife is unmatched in American fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the romantic lyric sentence held in tight structure.
works.context: The American expatriate Riviera of the 1920s, the psychiatric clinic, and the Wall Street crash that ended the party. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1933 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under jazz-age novel and the expatriate romance; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Dick Diver; Nicole Warren Diver; Rosemary Hoyt; Tommy Barban; Baby Warren; Abe North
works.structure: Originally in three books, with a flashback structure; Fitzgerald reordered it in 1951. A novel in chapters of the pleasure and the retrospect, the party scene and the elegiac judgement held in the same short paragraphs. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented
works.description: Published in 1891 with the subtitle 'A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented' and the most controversial of Hardy's novels: the story of Tess Durbeyfield, seduced by Alec d'Urberville, married and abandoned by Angel Clare, and destroyed by the double standard of her society.
works.plot: Tess Durbeyfield, whose family believes itself descended from the Norman d'Urbervilles, is sent to claim kin and is seduced by Alec; she bears a child who dies, works at the dairy at Talbothays, marries Angel Clare, confesses her past on the wedding night, is abandoned by him, is driven back to Alec, and when Angel returns she kills Alec and is arrested at Stonehenge and executed at Wintoncester.
works.significance: Tess is the central English novel of the sexual double standard and one of the great novels of the nineteenth century: its defence of Tess as 'a pure woman' made it the founding text of the novel of social justice for women and a permanent point of reference for feminist criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, the decline of the rural labourer, the evangelical revival, the Victorian sexual double standard, and the publication history of the novel. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Tess Durbeyfield; Alec d'Urberville; Angel Clare; Joan Durbeyfield; John Durbeyfield; Marian; Retty Priddle; Izz Huett; Liza-Lu; Sorrow
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: First published in a censored serial version in the Graphic (1891) and then in three volumes with the full text restored; the standard text is the Wessex Edition of 1912.

works.title: Testament of Love
works.description: Thomas Usk's allegorical prose apologia, written in the Tower of London before his execution in 1388: the imprisoned author, in Boethian dialogue with Love and her company, defends his political career, expounds free will and grace, and seeks the 'Margaret' of his devotion. For three centuries it was printed and read as Chaucer's.
works.plot: The narrator, cast down by fortune and imprisoned, laments until the lady Love appears with her sisters; in three books she teaches him the nature of love and virtue, vindicates his service and his betrayals, and leads him through the doctrine of predestination and free will to the vision of the pearl of perfect bliss.
works.significance: The first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of the political prisoner's consolation; its false attribution shaped the early reception of Chaucer himself.
works.meter: Prose, richly Chaucerian in vocabulary and cadence.
works.context: Composed 1384–88 in prison, in the factional struggles of Richard II's London (Usk had betrayed John of Northampton to Nicholas Brembre); the author's identity was recovered from the acrostic, overturning the Chaucerian attribution, only in the nineteenth century.
works.characters: the Narrator (Usk); Love; Margaret (the pearl); Fortune; the Virtues
works.structure: Three books of Boethian consolation, with the acrostic of the opening chapters spelling the author's name and his lady's — 'MARGARETE OF VIRTW HAVE MERCI ON THIN USK'.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Usk secure from the acrostic and the records of his trial; previously attributed to Chaucer.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Fortune and mutability

works.title: Testament of Youth
works.form: Prose (memoir); war memoir, first issued in 1933
works.description: The greatest English memoir of the First World War: a young woman, her generation and its loss. It is a prose work of 1933 by Vera Brittain; it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Brittain records her provincial childhood, her fight to go to Oxford, her engagement to Roland Leighton, her service as a VAD nurse in London, Malta and France, and the deaths of Roland, her brother Edward and her friends Victor and Geoffrey, ending with the peace and her own survival.
works.significance: Testament of Youth is the greatest English memoir of the First World War and the central woman's record of the conflict: it made the experience of the war generation of women visible, and it founded the modern literature of grief, pacifism and feminist witness.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the memoir built from letters and diaries.
works.context: England, Malta and France in 1914–18, and the postwar world of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1933 and first published in 1933 and it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Vera Brittain; Roland Leighton; Edward Brittain; Victor Richardson; Geoffrey Thurlow; Winifred Holtby
works.structure: A memoir in twelve chapters, from the provincial childhood to the postwar world. A memoir in episodic chapters organised by posting or battle, the later self reflecting on the earlier experience. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Vera Mary Brittain. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Thalaba the Destroyer
works.form: Metrical tale and Oriental romance in verse, a philosophical tale of providence and temptation constructed on the machinery of Eastern narrative as then known to English readers.
works.description: An Oriental romance in verse, published in 1801 and described by its author as a tale of the East, in which a young man of the race of the destroyer of magic goes in quest of his betrothed through a desert peopled by genii, sorcerers and the relics of an old superstition. Its plan was to build an English poem on the machinery of Eastern romance and on the single providence of a faith without idols, and its experiments in a new prosody were among the most discussed versification projects of the decade.
works.plot: Thalaba, son of the line whose office is to destroy the hosts of magic, is bound by a vow of chastity and obedience to a pilgrimage that shall lead him to the promised bride, and the poem follows his way through desert, cavern and enchanted city, with the powers of the old superstition pressing on him and the guardian spirit of his race failing at intervals to direct him. The beloved of the hero is preserved through captivity and rites of fire, and the episodes of the journey - the magicians, the sepulchres, the hollow music of the enchanted halls, the trials of thirst and the victories over the servants of the evil law - carry the poem's religion of trust in one invisible God. The argument ends with the destruction of the hosts of the sorcerers, the final abandonment of the guardian spirit, who is withheld from Thalaba at the last because the hero must learn to depend on Providence alone, and the accomplishment of the vow.
works.significance: The boldest of the Romantic experiments in a new English prosody and the earliest serious English poem to take its machinery wholly from Eastern tale; the preface on accentual measurement is a document of the period's versification debates. Its reputation has declined, but it remains the standard instance of the quest poem built on providence rather than on chivalry.
works.meter: A deliberately experimental accentual prosody, in which the lines are measured by the number of accents rather than by syllables, and the stanzaic pattern is varied with the scene, sometimes in long flowing periods and sometimes in short and reiterated lines; the poet's own preface defended this treatment at length.
works.context: Composed in the years of the author's retirement in the west and of his marriage, and published in 1801 with a preface on the principles of English prosody; its Eastern machinery drew on the translations of Arabian and Persian tales then current, and its monotheism was written as an answer to the idolatrous apparatus of the fashionable romance.
works.characters: Thalaba, the destroyer of magic; his betrothed and beloved; the guardian spirit of his ancestors; the sorcerers and the hosts of the evil law; the hermit and the companions of the desert
works.structure: A romantic quest in twelve books, organised as a string of episodes of trial and deliverance in a desert landscape, with the machinery of Eastern tale and a prophetic and guardian spirit whose intermittent absence is itself the poem's moral instrument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse

Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Thanatopsis
works.form: Philosophical lyric meditation in the graveyard tradition, cast as a conversation poem addressed to nature
works.description: A meditation on death and the common receptacle of the earth, and the poem that announced the American nature lyric. Its argument is consolation without revelation: the dead are not lost but deposited in the same ground that holds all generations. The title, a view of death, names its method, and its blank verse gave American poetry its first authoritative meditative voice.
works.plot: The poem opens by inviting the reader to attend to the voices of nature, which speak of mortality from the wood, the grove and the mountain. It then describes death as an inevitable and shared condition, in which every generation of humankind lies down in the earth together. The speaker consoles the mourner by making the grave a brotherhood rather than a solitary pit, and by describing the endless procession of the dead beneath the surface. The conclusion presents the earth as one great tomb in which the reader shall fall on and be at rest.
works.significance: It made the author the first American poet taken seriously in Britain and fixed the native meditative lyric on death and nature. Its blank verse set the standard for American philosophical poetry for fifty years. It remains the most anthologized American poem written before 1830.
works.meter: Blank verse, iambic pentameter with irregular feminine endings and a suspended syntax
works.context: First printed in a Boston review in 1811 in an imperfect text, and enlarged in the collected volume of 1821; the story of its publication by a parent without the young author's knowledge became part of its legend. Its stoical consolation belongs to the post-Calvinist religious climate of New England. The poem was read in Britain as evidence that American letters could rival the Lake poets.
works.structure: Continuous lyric meditation in three movements, addressed to a generic reader and moving from observation of nature to the doctrine of the common grave and to consolation.
works.attributionNotes: The circumstances of the first printing, and the share of the father's revision in the text, have been long debated; the authorship of the poem is not in doubt.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
movements: Bryant and the American Nature Lyric

works.title: The Absentees
works.form: Prose fiction; novel of manners and political tale of the union period
works.description: A novel of Ireland immediately after the act of union, whose subject is the withdrawal of the Irish gentry and their dependants from the country to the English metropolis. The book follows a family of the county and its tenants through the miseries produced by absence, by the desire to be received in London, and by the ruinous expense of a fashionable exile. It is the most directly political of the writer's Irish fictions and was read from its first page as a commentary on the union's consequences. The comedy is social and the argument is economic.
works.plot: An Irish county family, its hopes raised and its fortunes unsettled by the union, removes to London to purchase acceptance and to place a daughter in the marriage market, while the estate at home is governed by agents and falls into confusion. A younger relation left behind in Ireland sees the mischiefs of exile and of the borrowed money that maintains it, and the family's pretensions are exposed by a successful rival connection. The tale ends with the recognition that a family and a country are ruined by spending their income elsewhere, and by a settlement which keeps one branch of the house at home.
works.significance: The first sustained novel on absenteeism and the union, and a key text for the study of Irish fiction between the 1800 act and the Famine. It supplies the economic argument that the later Irish novel made its central theme, and it remains a document of Anglo-Irish social history as well as a piece of fiction.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain conversational style with Irish and metropolitan speech used to mark the two economies the book compares
works.context: Published in 1812, a generation after the author's first Irish tale and within a few years of the union, when the departure of the Irish parliament made absenteeism an immediate public question. Its subject matter is the London Irish social season, the agent-governed estate, and the debate in the periodicals over the economic consequences of union. The writer's own position as a celebrated Irish author resident between London and the Longford estate gives the book its double point of view.
works.structure: Third-person social novel in three volumes, alternating an Irish county plot with a London plot; the narration is brisk, illustrative and openly argumentative, with the writer's own political reasoning framed by the story.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

works.title: The Admirable Crichton
works.description: First performed in 1902 and Barrie's most class-conscious comedy: a perfect butler becomes the ruler of a shipwrecked aristocratic family. It is a dramatic work of 1902 by J. M. Barrie; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: The Loam family is wrecked on a desert island with their butler Crichton; on the island, competence makes him the master and the aristocrats his servants, until a rescue returns them to England and to the old hierarchy, where Crichton resumes his place and the secret of the island is never spoken.
works.significance: The Admirable Crichton is the cleverest English comedy of class in the period: its inversion of master and servant is a serious political comedy about the arbitrariness of the social order, and it has remained in repertory as one of the most durable Edwardian plays.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect.
works.context: 1902: the Edwardian class system, the 'servant question', the Boer War, and the debate on the natural aristocracy. The record dates the work as composed in 1902 and first published in 1902 and first performed in 1902 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Crichton; Lord Loam; Lady Mary Lasenby; Lady Catherine; Lady Agatha; Ernest Woolley; the Reverend John Treherne; Tweeny; Lord Brocklehurst
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Matthew Barrie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
