works.title: The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry
works.description: Dennis's first major critical treatise, arguing that modern poetry in the European vernaculars has genuinely advanced upon the ancients, chiefly by the invention of rhyme and by the access a Christian and gallant age gives to terrors and refinements of passion unknown to antiquity. Its second half turns from advancement to reformation, urging that the same gifts have been wasted by a corrupt stage and by a mercenary book trade. The book is the founding document of Dennis's lifelong case for enthusiasm as the life-blood of great writing.
works.plot: Dennis maintains that the rules of the ancients are rules of nature, and that where modern practice satisfies nature more fully than ancient practice it deserves the preference; rhyme is defended not as a barbaric licence but as an artifice that supplies the sound and measure that English verse needs. The greater heights, however, are reached only by poetic enthusiasm, a kind of elevated transport proper to poetry and quite distinct from the reasoning craft of criticism. Against this standard the present age is then arraigned: the stage has debased its patrons' morals, the dunces have debased its praise, and the reform of poetry must therefore be at once technical and moral.
works.significance: It put the defence of rhyme and the theory of poetical enthusiasm on the English agenda a generation before the sublime became common property, and supplied the vocabulary in which Addison, Hughes, Akenside and later the French critics of the genie enthousiaste would conduct their debates.
works.meter: Prose; the style is deliberately emphatical, with long periodic structures, triple weight, and a syntax that strains toward the sublime it theorises.
works.context: Issued in the season still dominated by the stage-morality quarrel opened by Collier in 1698 and by the party and denominational warfare of the last years of William's reign; Dennis wrote as an obscure dependant of patrons and of the theatre he simultaneously defended and attacked.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative treatise in two movements, advancement and reformation, each built from numbered heads and supported by example from the modern poets, with a polemical conclusion addressed to the present state of the drama and of letters.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's authorship is documented by his own subsequent collection of his critical works.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: The Advancement of Learning
altTitles: The Two Books of Francis Bacon of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Human
works.description: Bacon's great survey and defence of knowledge, addressed to James I: the first book vindicates learning against its 'distempers' and detractors; the second maps the whole territory of human knowledge — history, poesy, and philosophy, with their divisions and gaps — in the programme that the Latin De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623) would expand.
works.plot: Book I argues the dignity and utility of learning against the objections of divines, politicians, and the learned themselves; Book II proceeds through the three faculties of memory, imagination, and reason, charting each science, noting its deficiencies, and closing with the practical counsel for the advancement of knowledge in Bacon's own time.
works.significance: The founding charter of English scientific and philosophical prose — the map of knowledge that organized the intellectual world until the Encyclopedists.
works.meter: Prose of sustained periodic power, with the famous catalogue of the impediments to learning.
works.context: Published in 1605, in the first years of James I's reign, as Bacon's bid for the role of philosophical counsellor; it is the seed of the Instauratio Magna and the later Latin works.
works.structure: Two books of systematic argument — apology, then map — in the humanist tradition of the treatise addressed to a prince.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: The English vernacular and national letters
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom
altTitles: The Adventures of Ferdinand, Count Fathom
works.description: The history of a complete villain, a foundling instructed in every cheat who rises by forgery, bigamy, gambling and war into a title and an estate. It was offered in a prefatory advertisement as a defence of the regular novel against the charge of exceeding probability, and it is the most methodically wicked of the century's heroes.
works.plot: Ferdinand, the son of a gypsy and a cheat and educated by a fencing master, is expelled from his patron's house after an intrigue and turns to the gaming and betting stages of Europe. He follows an army in Italy, is made a count by a deception on a noble house, and marries into wealth by the double fraud of two sisters. His crimes prosper almost unchecked until the last pages, when the exposure of his person and history reduces him to penury and a professed repentance.
works.significance: It is the century's most sustained attempt to make a professedly wicked life the subject of regular fiction, and its advertisement stands as an early statement of the theory of the novel as a structure of probable incidents.
works.meter: A hard, latinate and economical prose of the case and the contrivance, without the colloquial warmth of the earlier histories; the irony is reported rather than voiced.
works.context: Published in 1753 after the author's return from France and his editorial labours, in the season of the debate on the novel's morality and of the new attention to the law of fraud and marriage which the plot exploits.
works.characters: Ferdinand Count Fathom; his fencing-master and patron; the dupe noble family of Italy; the two sisters he deceives; the gamblers and camp-followers of his education
works.structure: Continuous third-person narration of a single career in volumes, the episodes organised as the successive schools of villany; the prefatory argument on probability frames the design rather than interrupting it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.

works.title: The Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane
altTitles: The History and Adventures of the Famous Gil Blas of Santillane
works.form: translation of a picaresque romance; prose fiction in books
works.description: A translation of the Spanish picaresque romance of Le Sage, issued in several volumes and carrying the career of a servant of great part from the roads of Spain to the courts of the dukes and the practice of physic. It became the standard English Gil Blas and a school for the translators of the following generation.
works.plot: Gil Blas, a boy of Astorga, runs from his uncles and falls into the company of robbers, from whom he escapes to service in the great houses of Madrid. He passes through the keeping of an archbishop, a nobleman and a physician, is enriched and ruined by his own knaveries and by the examples of his masters, and at last marries and retires to tell his history. The sequence of services forms a continuous satire on the professions and the vanity of the world.
works.significance: It gave English readers their habitual Gil Blas and was a principal channel through which the Spanish picaresque reached the mid-century novelists, the translator's own fiction owing something to its method.
works.meter: A robust and idiomatic English prose rendering of the French original, its sentences adapted to the colloquial energy of the picaresque manner.
works.context: Published in London in 1749 in the season of the great translation enterprises of the hack and the aspirant, the original French having been composed by Le Sage from Spanish materials, and the English market having already tried partial versions.
works.characters: Gil Blas of Santillane; his uncles and the robbers of the road; the successive masters of his service in Madrid; the physicians and the ministers of the interpolated tales; the housekeeper and the wife
works.structure: First-person picaresque autobiography in books, the episodes arranged as successive services and recoveries, with the inserted tales of the patrons carrying the satire.
works.attributionNotes: The translation is uncontroversially the work of the novelist here recorded, though it drew on and superseded earlier English versions; the French original is the work of another hand.

works.title: The Adventures of Master F.J.
altTitles: A Discourse of the Adventures Passed by Master F.J.
works.description: Gascoigne's prose fiction of seduction, printed in A Hundred Sundry Flowers (1573): the gallant F.J., a guest in a northern castle, conducts an affair with the lady Elinor — their letters, verses, and assignations documented in the narrative's self-conscious apparatus — until the affair sours into jealousy, betrayal, and the narrator's moralizing close; the first English novel of intrigue, revised and bowdlerized in The Posies (1575).
works.plot: F.J. arrives at the castle, courts Elinor by letter and verse; the affair progresses through the night meetings and the gift of the sword; the secretary's treachery and Elinor's inconstancy turn love to jealousy; and the narrator's apparatus — the editor's letters and comments — frames the tale as 'translated' from Italian and morally cautioned.
works.significance: The first original English novel of manners — the seed of the English tradition of prose fiction that runs through Deloney and Nashe to Defoe.
works.meter: Prose with interpolated verses, in the manner of the Italian novella and the French Heptameron tradition.
works.context: Printed in 1573 and revised in The Posies (1575) after the scandal of its supposed real-life originals; it anticipated the psychological fiction of the next century by a generation.
works.characters: Master F.J.; Elinor; the secretary; Dame Frances; the narrator-editor (G.T.)
works.structure: A framed novella with the editorial machinery of letters, verses, and marginal commentary — the first English fiction to flaunt its own making.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle
works.description: The history of a young man of fortune from his mischief in a Scottish school through the sea, the tour, the stage and the King's Bench, to a reformation engineered by his faithful friend. It is the most various of the picaresque sequences, containing the century's most famous comic set pieces.
works.plot: Peregrine, the son of a Lancashire family, is bound apprentice to a sea captain, runs away, and passes his youth in mischief and gambling. His guardians plot to ruin him for his estate, but his uncle intercepts their design and secures his estate; he travels in France, is seduced and seduces, keeps a mistress and a house, and turns to politics and the stage. His cruelty to a woman he has wronged and his duelling bring him to the prison and to death-bed penitence, before a final reconciliation and marriage.
works.significance: It fixed the picaresque at its most energetic in English and supplied the age's most quoted comic tableaux; its treatment of the repentant rake made it a station on the road from the amatory to the sentimental novel.
works.meter: A rowdy and various prose of caricature and ventriloquism, from the commodore's nautical thunder to the cant of the convent and the stage; the set pieces are comic declamation.
works.context: Published in 1751 after the success of the first novel and the author's editorial warfare of the late 1740s, in the season of the Jewish Naturalisation bill's street agitation and of the arguments about French and popish customs which the book exploits.
works.characters: Peregrine Pickle; his uncle the commodore; the two designing guardians; the faithful friend of the ship; the French mistress and the injured woman of the London books
works.structure: First-person-adjacent picaresque narration in volumes, the episodes grouped by place - school, ship, house, France, London - with the friend's loyalty supplying the moral continuity; the famous embedded tales interrupt the sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, with later issues revised in the 1760s.

works.title: The Adventures of Quentin Durward, Captain of the Guard of the Scottish Bow
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the French court
works.description: A historical romance of the court of France at the end of the reign of Louis the Eleventh, seen through a young Scottish archer of the king's bodyguard of the Scottish Bow. The book's interest is political: a patient, ironical king who hates the state of his own nobility is opposed to a great vassal of the league of the Public Weal, and the private fortune of the Scottish soldier is entangled in the quarrel over an heiress whom the two princes would each use. The chase, the ambush, the siege of a prince's city and the trial of the injured heiress supply the incident. It is the most completely wrought of the French romances of the series.
works.plot: A young Scottish gentleman of a ruined house obtains a place in the king's archers of the guard and is at once employed in a dangerous private errand. His mistress, an heiress of the borders of France, is courted by a powerful neighbour of her father's blood and threatened by an allied prince, and the Scottish captain's protection of her brings him into the king's policy and into the league's hostility. The king's agents and the prince's soldiers dispute the city, the heiress and the succession, and the archer's fidelity through ambush, imprisonment and siege is rewarded at the close with his mistress's hand and the recovery of his own fortunes.
works.significance: The model example of the court intrigue romance in the series and a standard source for the nineteenth century's idea of a shrewd, ironical king working against feudal privilege. Its treatment of honour and interest through a soldier's loyalty made it a school and library favourite, and it remains the most frequently read of the French tales.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a formal and courtly idiom for the French chapters, with a Scots and border speech for the hero and his countrymen
works.context: Published in 1825, it was written after a journey on the continent which put its author in possession of the French towns, castles and archives used in the tale, and it depends on the histories of the league of the Public Weal and of the king's destruction of great vassal power. Its Scottish bodyguard of the French king reflects the antiquarian knowledge of the Auld Alliance then being recovered by Scottish historians, and its picture of a patient political king answers the statesmanship literature of the post-war decade.
works.characters: Quentin Durward, a Scottish archer of the king's guard; Louis the Eleventh; the great duke of the league; an heiress of high birth and her injured family; a kinsman suitor of power and violence; retainers of the Scottish bow
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, following one hero's advancement through a court and a military quarrel; the political argument is carried in long interviews with the king, and the plot in pursuit, concealment and the defence of a city.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger

works.title: The Adventures of Rivella
altTitles: The Adventures of Rivella: Or, The History of the Author of the New Atalantis. Written, By HERSELF
works.form: fictional autobiography and confession in prose
works.description: An autobiographical romance in which the author of the political secret history appears disguised as Rivella and tells the story of her own literary and amorous career. It is one of the earliest English examples of a writer using fiction to account for her own publication, her prosecution and her reputation.
works.plot: Rivella, a young woman of parts and no fortune, is pressed by need and by the examples of the writers about her into authorship; she composes verses, romances and a political key-history, and moves through a society of courtiers, book publishers and rival wits. She tells how her performances brought her fame, malice and a prosecution, and how she answered her enemies by writing again. The narrative closes with her retired from the town, reflecting on the price paid by a woman who publishes.
works.significance: It is a foundational document of women's literary self-representation and of the professional author's apology, and it remains the principal source for the biography of the early-eighteenth-century woman of letters.
works.meter: Conversational prose of the familiar romantic style, light, ironic and unapologetic, with inserted verses and letter-forms.
works.context: Published in 1714 in the season of the author's last quarrels and the fall of her party, and attached to a volume reissuing her earlier fiction; its defence of a woman's right to write answers the attacks made on her in the theatre and the press.
works.characters: Rivella; her mother and patroness; the book-publishers and duellers of the town; the rival wit of the playhouse quarrel; the companion to whom the paper is addressed

works.title: The Adventures of Roderick Random
works.description: A picaresque novel in two volumes, the history of a disinherited Scottish boy who runs to sea, survives the South Seas station and the West India fleet, and works his way in England and Jamaica to the recovery of his fortune and the discovery of his family. Its note of personal grievance and its command of low life made it an immediate success.
works.plot: Roderick Random, expelled from his grandfather's house and beaten at school, sails as a surgeon's mate in a man-of-war and endures the brutality of the captains, the sickliness of the station and the horrors of a West India voyage. He deserts, fights, is wrecked, and reaches Jamaica, where he accumulates money and connections. In London he is seduced into debt and marriage by a designing woman, but a series of discoveries restores his estate, his father's name and his friend's fortune, and the tale ends in the marriages of the good.
works.significance: It revived the picaresque in English with an unprecedented documentary force and made the Caribbean and the naval service central to the novel's geography; its political and professional satire shaped the later careers of the writer.
works.meter: A vigorous colloquial first-person prose, abundant in cant, Scots and naval vocabulary, with the sustained invective passage as its characteristic unit.
works.context: Published in 1748 after the author's own medical and naval service and his London editorial work, in the season of the close of the war of the Austrian succession and of public inquiry into the sick and wounded seamen; its navy scenes draw on report and experience.
works.characters: Roderick Random; Andrew Strap, his friend; the grandfather and the relations who wrong him; the ship's surgeons, captains and mates of the navy; the designing woman of the London books
works.structure: First-person picaresque in two volumes, a continuous chain of adventures ordered by the hero's progress upward; the sea books are tightly documented and the English books looser and more satirical.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and advertised as the work of the editor of a periodical history.

works.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
works.form: Collection of twelve short stories (Strand Magazine, 1891-92)
works.description: Published in 1892, collecting the twelve stories that appeared in the Strand Magazine from July 1891: the volume that created the modern short detective story and made Holmes a national institution. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by Arthur Conan Doyle; it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The twelve cases include 'A Scandal in Bohemia', in which Irene Adler outwits Holmes; 'The Red-Headed League', a bank robbery disguised as a sinecure; 'The Speckled Band', a murder by snake; 'The Blue Carbuncle', a Christmas goose; and 'The Final Problem', in which Holmes and Moriarty fall at the Reichenbach Falls.
works.significance: The Adventures created the modern short story of detection and the serial character who outlives his author; its formula — a problem, a client, a chain of inference and a final explanation — became the template for the entire genre.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the clue and the deduction.
works.context: The 1890s, the new mass-circulation illustrated magazine, the suburban railway and the telegraph, and the professionalisation of the detective. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.
works.characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Mrs Hudson; Inspector Lestrade; Irene Adler; Professor Moriarty; the King of Bohemia; Helen Stoner
works.structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves
works.form: short comic novel in the Quixote tradition
works.description: A short novel on the Quixote plan, in which an honest country knight of the mid-century, mad on the romances of chivalry, rides out to redress grievances in a Suffolk town. It was published in monthly numbers in a periodical before appearing in book form, and its comedy lies in the collision of an archaic code with a commercial county.
works.plot: Sir Launcelot, having read nothing but romances, arms himself and sallies forth to right the wrongs of the neighbourhood, taking a squire and a doctor with him. He is set upon by creditors, justices and the retainers of a rival family, and his adventures end in beating and confinement rather than in conquest. His cause finally prevails by the intervention of his friends and by the exposure of the combinations that had oppressed the poor, and the book ends with the knight restored to his senses and his estate.
works.significance: It is the subtlest of the century's English Quixotes and an important document of the serialization of fiction in periodicals, anticipating the later short comic novel.
works.meter: A dry and compressed prose of dialogue and report, the chivalric phrases of the hero set against the plain idiom of his attendants.
works.context: Issued in numbers in a monthly magazine between 1760 and 1762, during the author's editorship of periodical work and the war-season enthusiasm and party heat that the book gently satirises; the romantic madness theme answers the Gothic vogue beginning in the same years.
works.characters: Sir Launcelot Greaves; his squire and his physician; the justice and the designing family who oppose him; the creditors and the tenantry of the county
works.structure: A serially published short novel of monthly parts, the episodes arranged as a sequence of mishaps answering the romance structure; the periodical origin makes the numbers tight and the irony economical.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name in the magazine and in the collected edition of his novels.

works.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1876
works.description: Published in 1876 and the most popular boys' book in American literature: the childhood of Tom Sawyer in the Mississippi river town of St Petersburg, and the buried treasure of Injun Joe. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by Mark Twain; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tom plays hooky, whitewashes a fence, attends his own funeral, runs away to Jackson's Island, falls in love with Becky Thatcher, and with Huck witnesses the murder of Dr Robinson in the graveyard; the novel ends with the treasure found and Huck taken into the Widow Douglas's house.
works.significance: Tom Sawyer is the classic American book of boyhood and the fount of the American literature of childhood: it created the image of the river town and made Hannibal a national place, and its portrait of a boy's freedom is one of the permanent American idylls.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is first-person vernacular narration.
works.context: The 1840s: the Mississippi river town of Hannibal, the American Sunday school and the temperance movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1875 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The African Queen
works.form: Novel (the river pursuit); imperial adventure romance
works.description: The novel of the launch, the missionary's sister and the river war. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by C. S. Forester; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The African Queen sets Rose Sayer, the missionary's sister, and Charlie Allnutt, the launch's captain, on the river of the German East Africa at the war's outbreak, and follows the voyage of the crazy launch to the torpedoing of the Königin Luise, in the plain exact prose of the professional river and gun.
works.significance: The African Queen is Forester's most loved novel: its launch, its two civilians and its river pursuit made the small war of the water a classic of the adventure novel, and its film made the story one of the most famous of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact prose of the professional.
works.context: German East Africa at the outbreak of the first war. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Rose Sayer, the missionary's sister; Charlie Allnutt, the captain; the Königin Luise
works.structure: A pursuit novel in the chapters of the river and the voyage. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: The Age of Innocence
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1920 and the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of old New York: a man's love for a woman the society of the 1870s cannot accept. It is a prose fiction work of 1920 by Edith Wharton; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Newland Archer, a young lawyer of old New York, is engaged to May Welland when her cousin the Countess Ellen Olenska returns from Europe, separated from her Polish husband; Newland falls in love with Ellen, and the novel follows his renunciation, his marriage to May and his long life afterwards, ending with his refusal to see Ellen again in Paris.
works.significance: The Age of Innocence is Wharton's masterpiece and the greatest American novel of manners: it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, it is the definitive portrait of old New York, and its analysis of the cost of social conformity made it one of the central American novels of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is precise, ironic exposition of a social world.
works.context: 1920: the New York of the 1870s, the codes of the Knickerbocker aristocracy, the First World War and the vanished world it destroyed. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1920 and first published in 1920 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.

works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Age of Reason
altTitles: The Age of Reason Part the First and Part the Second
works.form: religious polemic and deist treatise; argumentative pamphlet with scriptural criticism
works.description: The most widely circulated deist manifesto of the revolutionary decade, written in parts and published while its author was a prisoner in revolutionary France. Its first part states a creed of rational theism, denounces priestcraft as the corrupter of religion, and rejects the Bible as a collection of human and often obscene writings; the second part pursues the same argument through the Old Testament in detail. It made the case for unbelief in the plain, popular style of the pamphlet trade, and it was prosecuted, pirated, and answered by the whole religious press of two countries.
works.plot: The book opens by professing belief in one God and by refusing the creed of any church, holding the study of the universe through its works to be the only true theology. From this it argues that the religion of revelation rests on hearsay, since no living generation can verify a miracle it has not itself seen, and that the evidence demanded for scripture is of a kind no court of law would receive. It then reads the biblical history as a record of cruelty, obscenity, and imposture, denies the divine origin of the book of Genesis and of the Mosaic law, and treats prophecy as an argument manufactured after the event. The church-and-state polemic follows: revealed religion, once made an establishment, becomes an engine of revenue and of persecution, and the moral character of the deity is impugned by the scriptures that pretend to reveal it. The closing position is the deist alternative: a universal, unclerical religion of creation, of benevolence, and of the rights of conscience, with the duties of man toward his neighbour as the whole of practical religion.
works.significance: It is the textbook of English popular deism and the most durable attack on scriptural authority between the deist controversy of the early eighteenth century and the rationalist theology of the nineteenth; it fixed for radicals the claim that a revealed religion cannot be evidenced, and for its opponents the problem of how to answer a lay reader without scholarship. Its frankness, and the biography of its composition in a prison, made its author a martyr figure for freethought, and its arguments reappear in the sceptical literature of the following century.
works.meter: Plain, contemptuous, colloquial argumentative prose, short sentences, direct address, and the demotic irony of the debating society; the rhetoric of evidence and common sense rather than of learning.
works.context: Part the first was composed during the author's imprisonment in France and issued in the year of his release, in French translation and in London simultaneously; it was prosecuted in England, and the second part, appearing two years later, was answered by a stream of episcopal and evangelical replies. The book belongs to the radical religious culture of the 1790s, where the criticism of scripture followed naturally from the criticism of throne and altar.
works.structure: Two parts of unequal argument: the first a statement of rational theism and of the evidential objection to revelation, the second a running critical examination of the Old Testament writings, each subdivided into short numbered chapters for cheap circulation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a projected further part survives in manuscript and in report, and the editions of the early nineteenth century differ in the material they admit, so the volume of any given issue is not a reliable guide to what its author sanctioned.

Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: The Alchemist
works.description: Jonson's comedy of alchemical confidence tricks: in Lovewit's vacated London house during the plague, Subtle the alchemist, Face the housekeeper, and Doll Common the prostitute run their roaring shop, fleecing the knight Sir Epicure Mammon, the tobacconist Abel Drugger, the Puritan brethren Ananias and Tribulation, and the quarrelling Kastril — until Lovewit's return and the final distribution of the spoils.
works.plot: Each gull arrives with a different dream — the philosopher's stone for Mammon, a lucky shop for Drugger, the widow Pliant for Kastril, the orphans' goods for the Puritans — and each is worked by the 'venture tripartite' of Subtle, Face, and Doll; the quarrels of the conspirators and the return of the master bring the whole house of cards down in the last act's cascade of exposures.
works.significance: Generally reckoned the greatest English comedy after Shakespeare — the most perfect machine of comic construction in the language.
works.meter: Verse for the gulls' fantastic speeches (Mammon's visions of the stone), prose for the roaring shop's business — Jonson's richest mix.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men in 1610 and printed in 1612; its plague setting mirrored the London closures of 1609–10, and its Puritans were recognized at once.
works.characters: Subtle; Face (Jeremy); Doll Common; Sir Epicure Mammon; Surly; Abel Drugger; Ananias; Tribulation Wholesome; Kastril; Dame Pliant; Lovewit; the Neighbours
works.structure: A single-day, single-house intrigue observing the classical unities to the letter, with each act a fresh round of gulling and the final act a tournament of unmaskings.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning

works.title: The Alhambra
works.form: Local guide and topographical prose combined with romantic legend and the familiar essay
works.description: A sketch-book of the Moorish palace at Granada, part guide, part legend and part antiquarian romance, written after the author's residence in Spain. The ruins of the Alhambra supply both scenery and argument: a palace of the imagination that survives its own history. It closes the installment's American strand by turning the native sketch toward European decay.
works.plot: A tourist sojourning in the monument recounts its Muslim history, its Christian occupants and its gradual degradation, then fills the courts and towers with legends of enchantment, treasure and lost beauty. Tales told by his Moslem guide and by the villagers about the palace alternate with essays on the tastes of travellers and on the value of Moorish ornament. The later numbers describe the search for hidden riches in the towers and the visitor's departure, leaving the palace as an emblem of transience.
works.significance: It is the most durable American account of the Alhambra and fixed its legendary reputation for generations of travellers. Its mixture of guide-book and tale anticipated the later gift-book and keepsake miscellany. It completes the development of the American sketch into an archaeology of ruins.
works.meter: Prose, with translated ballads and songs in stanzaic form
works.context: Written after the author's stay at Granada in 1829 and published in 1832, in the season of the romantic recovery of Moorish Spain by British and American travellers and novelists. The monument was then a squatter's ruin as much as a museum. Its antiquarian romance belongs to the European vogue for ruins and for the expelled Islam of the peninsula.
works.structure: Miscellany of sketches, legends and antiquarian essays unified by the setting of the palace and by a travelling narrator's stay there.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence

works.title: The Allegory of Love
works.form: Critical study (the medieval allegory and the doctrine of courtly love)
works.description: The study that founded the modern reading of the medieval allegorical imagination. It is a prose work of 1936 by C. S. Lewis; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Lewis traces the allegorical method from the Psychomachia of Prudentius through the Roman de la Rose to the Faerie Queene, and the doctrine of courtly love from the troubadours to Chaucer, arguing that the allegory is the natural instrument of the medieval mind and that the love religion is its heresy.
works.significance: The Allegory of Love founded the modern study of the medieval allegorical imagination and of the doctrine of courtly love: its two arguments - the allegory as instrument and the love religion as heresy - remain the starting point of the field, and its prose made the scholarship literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer.
works.context: The medieval Latin and vernacular tradition, read from Oxford in the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A critical study in four chapters: the allegory, the religion of love, Chaucer and Spenser. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Clive Hamilton, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to C. S. Lewis is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.description: The founding text of the gentleman thief: A. J. Raffles, the cricketer who burgles the great houses. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by E. W. Hornung; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Bunny Manders, a ruined young man, is rescued by his old school hero A. J. Raffles, who turns out to be a burglar; the stories follow their crimes from London clubs to country houses, always with Raffles's charm and cricket blue in the foreground.

works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrative by the admiring accomplice.
works.context: London and the English country house in the 1890s, and the taste of the fin-de-siecle for the elegant criminal. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: The Amateur Poacher
works.form: Essays; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1879
works.description: Published in 1879 and the finest English book about the countryside from a boy's point of view: the poaching, bird-nesting and observation of a Wiltshire childhood. It is a prose work of 1879 by Richard Jefferies; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Jefferies remembers the farmers, gamekeepers, poachers and labourers of his Wiltshire boyhood, the long days in the fields and woods, the trapping and the bird's-nesting, and the whole rural economy of a countryside in which every creature is either a food or a trespass.
works.significance: The Amateur Poacher is a classic of English country writing and the best book of its kind about the rural world of the labouring poor: its combination of exact natural history, social observation and personal memory made it a model for English nature writing, and it is one of the finest accounts of a Victorian rural childhood.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals.
works.context: 1879: the agricultural depression, the game laws and the poaching wars, the decline of the rural labourer, and the Victorian country book. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Richard Jefferies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Ambassadors
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1903 and generally regarded as James's finest novel: the story of Lambert Strether, sent to Paris to bring back a young American, and of the education that changes his mission. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by Henry James; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Strether is sent by Mrs Newsome to Paris to rescue her son Chad from a presumably disreputable life; he discovers that Chad's attachment to the Countess de Vionnet is a relationship of real value, and he returns to America alone, having 'not, out of the whole affair, got anything for myself'.
works.significance: The Ambassadors is the most perfectly constructed novel in English and the central text of James's late manner: its 'central consciousness' method and its treatment of the American failure to live made it the model for the modern psychological novel, and it is the book in which James's theory of fiction is fully realised.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification.
works.context: The 1900s: the American expatriate in Paris, the international marriage market, and the Puritan inheritance in American culture. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Lambert Strether; Chad Newsome; Madame de Vionnet; Maria Gostrey; Waymarsh; Mrs Newsome; Sarah Pocock; Jim Pocock; Little Bilham
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry James, Jr. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Amber Gods and Other Stories
works.description: The most ornamental American story collection of the century: 'The Amber Gods', 'Circumstance' and the jewelled Gothic tale. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Harriet Prescott Spofford; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale.
works.plot: The collection gathers Spofford's finest magazine stories: the decadent 'The Amber Gods', the terrifying 'Circumstance' in which a woman is carried off by an Indian devil, 'In a Cellar', 'The South Breaker' and the New England ghost stories.
works.significance: The Amber Gods is the most ornamental American story collection of the century and a founding text of the American Gothic tale: 'Circumstance' is one of the great American short stories, and Spofford's prose brought the decadent style into American fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ornate, jewelled prose of the magazine tale.
works.context: New England and the American magazine world of the 1860s, and the taste for the Gothic and the ornate. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: the amber goddess; the narrator of 'Circumstance'; the Indian devil; the villagers
works.structure: A collection of magazine stories, several in framed narratives. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Harriet Elizabeth Prescott Spofford. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Ambitious Stepmother
works.description: Rowe's first tragedy, a play of a Hellenistic court in which an ambitious stepmother's pursuit of her stepson and the struggle for a kingdom destroy one another; it made Rowe's reputation as the successor to the regular tragedy of the Restoration stage.
works.plot: A king's second wife, inflamed with an unlawful passion for the son of his first bed, presses her claim and her desire until the conspiracies, the jealousies and the rival affections of the court end in discovery and death.
works.significance: It established Rowe as the century's chief practitioner of moral and pathetic tragedy and marks the passage from the heroic drama of the 1670s to the regulated, sentimentally serious stage of the Augustans.
works.meter: Blank verse of the post-Dryden regularity, with the set rhetorical complaint and the sententious short line.
works.context: Acted at the opening of the century by the company in which the actors of the Restoration tradition still controlled the patent houses, at the moment when the reformed regularity of French-model tragedy was being pressed against the heroic mode.
works.characters: the ambitious stepmother; the injured prince of the first bed; the king; the heroine of the court
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy of intrigue and recognition, with the passion of the stepmother as the governing mechanism of the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Penance, confession, and sin
Revenge and justice

works.title: The American Crisis
altTitles: Thirteen Papers on the American Crisis
works.description: Paine's series of thirteen wartime papers, begun in December 1776 with the famous opening line on the times that try men's souls and read to Washington's troops in the war's darkest retreat. Written to sustain the cause through the hard years, they are the classic papers of civic nerve in a revolution.
works.plot: The first Crisis rebukes the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot who shrink from serving their country in the hour of trial, insists that the hardness of the conflict is what gives it value, and calls the colonies to hold fast the cause. The following papers argue the American cause against the projects of pacification and Tory reunion, defend it against the charges of ingratitude and rebellion, and analyse the war's prospects and the interest of Europe in it. Paine sets his celebrated dialogue with General Howe, who urged submission, into an early paper, and the series closes on the rewards of perseverance and the dignity of a cause fought out in the open view of the world.
works.significance: It became the war's most quoted prose and a founding text of American civic encouragement, a schoolbook exercise in patriotic rhetoric for generations of readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
works.meter: The short declarative idiom of Common Sense heightened by martial rhythm, anaphora, and the famous opening apostrophe to the trying times.
works.context: Written to the rhythm of the war from the dark days of 1776 through Yorktown, the first paper issued in the season of the retreat across the Delaware and printed in the Pennsylvania Journal; the papers were reprinted and recited throughout the campaigns.
works.characters: the reader-soldier; the summer soldier and sunshine patriot; General Howe as respondent
works.structure: A serial of thirteen numbered papers published in Philadelphia and other presses between 1776 and 1783, each a self-contained exhortation and argument, with the Howe dialogue embedded in an early number.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Warfare and battle
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: The American Universal Geography
altTitles: The American Universal Geography; or, A View of the Present State of All the Empires, Kingdoms, States, and Republics in the Known World
works.form: Didactic and school geography; topographical and statistical survey with religious argument
works.description: A comprehensive geography of the world in American hands, revised and reissued for three decades and used as a school and reference book. It sets the continents, empires and trades against one another and treats the United States as the scene of a new civil and religious society. Its account of the country is bound up with the author's argument for public piety and learning.
works.plot: The work describes the divisions of the earth, the states of Europe and Asia, the commerce of the world, and then passes to the American republics, their boundaries, produce, population and institutions. Statistical accounts of the states, including their inhabitants and their religious divisions, carry its argument that geography is a branch of public morality. Its later issues bring the tables and the histories of the western country up to date. It closes with the duties of a Christian nation placed among the powers of the world.
works.significance: It made the systematic survey of the world available to American schools and helped to found the American trade in geographical textbooks. Its account of the republic's resources and divisions is a document of national self-description. It shows how the didactic geography carried the religious and political argument of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled from the author's earlier geographical work and issued in successive editions through the 1790s and after, when American schools wanted a native textbook instead of British imports. Its tables answer the first federal censuses and the post-Revolution expansion of trade. Its author was a Congregational minister and a publicist who used geography as a vehicle for the cause of religion and learning.
works.structure: Systematic geography in books and chapters, combining cosmographical description, regional accounts, statistical tables and moral and religious reflection.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the several editions differ greatly in extent and in the material they include.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Mission, conversion, and the Church
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature
altTitles: The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed
works.description: Butler's great apologetic treatise, answering deism not by evidences but by analogy: the difficulties of revealed religion are shadowed at every point in the constitution and course of nature, so that a critic of the one must condemn the other. It was dedicated to Lord Chancellor Talbot and at once recognized as the century's most formidable defence.
works.plot: Part I shows that the course of nature, governed by general laws with rewards and penalties attaching to conduct, is exactly the system deists find improbable in religion; the imperfections of human government, the mixture of good and evil, and the unknown ends of providence all reappear in the divine dispensations. Part II argues that Christianity, as a scheme of religious office and authority, answers to the same analogy of nature, and that a presumed a priori standard of what religion should be is self-defeating. A concluding appendix treats the credibility of Moses's history and the Christian dispensation as a scheme progressively developed. The cumulative moral is that the actual world and the actual religion stand or fall together.
works.significance: It changed the terms of natural and revealed religion from evidence to analogy and constitution, dominating Anglican apologetic for a century; Gladstone and Arthur Balfour counted it decisive, and it remains a landmark of philosophy of religion.
works.meter: Massively circumstantial, judicious prose of balance-sheet periods, whose famous obscurity comes from the accumulation of qualifications and analogical correspondences.
works.context: Published in 1736 when the deist controversy had reached its height with Tindal and Morgan, and when Hoadly's latitudinarianism had made the church's authority a practical question; it was the response of a preacher of the Inns of Court and future bishop.
works.structure: Two main parts of argument from analogy, each subdivided into chapters answering one class of objection, followed by appendices against specific critics.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: The Analyst
altTitles: The Analyst; or, A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician
The Analyst: or, A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician
works.description: Berkeley's attack on the foundations of the calculus, aimed at the mathematicians who scoff at the mysteries of religion while accepting infinitesimals and vanishing quantities on faith. It mocks the method of fluxions as 'the ghosts of departed quantities' and presses the analogy between mathematical and divine evidence.
works.plot: Berkeley reviews the algebraists' methods for drawing tangents, quadratures, and cubical determinations, and shows that their mysterious infinitesimal differences and vanishing increments cannot be rigorously explained on their own terms. He distinguishes the sound practical rules from the defective logic of the fluxionary foundations, and charges that mathematicians conceal incoherence under jargon. Since nothing in this world can be understood without faith, he argues that the infidel who cannot believe in the arithmetic of infinities has no standing to deride the Trinity. The discourse ends with the famous query whether mathematical evidence is a better or a worse pattern for religious evidence than the sceptic admits.
works.significance: It exposed genuine foundational weaknesses in the early calculus, helped drive eighteenth-century rigour, and became a classic of the analogy between mathematical and religious evidence; 'ghosts of departed quantities' entered the language.
works.meter: Sardonic, colloquial argumentative prose, the manner of a plain gentleman putting questions to specialists, with technical terms treated as so much mystic jargon.
works.context: Published in 1731 when Berkeley was engaged in his Alciphron campaign against the freethinkers and when the Newtonian calculus was the standard weapon of deistic rationalists like Collins and Morgan; it provoked James Jurin's Reply and a decade of mathematical pamphlets, and eventually guided the foundations debate that reached Maclaurin and beyond.
works.structure: A single polemical discourse, expository first on the mathematicians' procedures, then critical, then theologically applicative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The New Science and experimental philosophy
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
works.description: Robert Burton's encyclopedic treatise-masquerading-as-self-cure, written under the name 'Democritus Junior': the causes, symptoms, and cures of melancholy anatomized across three 'partitions' — its kinds, its cure, and the special melancholies of love and religion — in a prose of endless quotation, digression, and humane wit, expanded by Burton through five editions to 1651.
works.plot: The First Partition defines melancholy, its causes, and symptoms; the Second prescribes the cures — diet, medicine, mirth, and the consolation of philosophy; the Third anatomizes love-melancholy and religious melancholy, with the great final meditation on despair; the whole is a labyrinth of authorities, stories, and self-portraiture.
works.significance: The great English anatomy — the book that taught Sterne, Lamb, and every digressive prose writer since how to wander gloriously.
works.meter: Prose of magnificent copiousness — the style of the study, the pulpit, and the joke fused — with Latin tags and verse interludes.
works.context: Published 1621, with enlargements in 1624, 1628, 1632, 1638, and posthumously 1651; its melancholy was the century's master-disease, and its book the century's master-digression.
works.characters: Democritus Junior (the author's persona); the melancholic patient; the lover; the religious despairer; the quoted authorities
works.structure: Three partitions with their sections, members, and subsections in the scholastic manner, the apparatus of quotation and marginalia making the book a library in itself.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published pseudonymously as Democritus Junior.
themes: Medicine, healing, and the body
Melancholy and self-analysis
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Angel in the House
works.form: Long narrative poem in four parts (The Betrothal 1854, The Espousals 1856, Faithful for Ever 1860, The Victories of Love 1862)
works.description: Published in four instalments between 1854 and 1862 and the most popular long poem of the Victorian age: the courtship and marriage of Felix Vaughan and Honoria Churchill, and the idealisation of the wife as the moral centre of the home.
works.plot: Felix, a young poet, courts Honoria through a long sequence of domestic scenes, wins her, and the poem follows the marriage through its trials; the sequel, The Victories of Love, turns to Honoria's rejected cousin Frederick Graham and his marriage to the humble Jane, and ends with Jane's death and the transfiguration of married love.
works.significance: The Angel in the House gave the Victorian age its name for the ideal wife and is the central poem of Victorian domestic ideology: it is the text against which the whole feminist critique of Victorian marriage was written, and its idealisation of the wife is still the standard image of the Victorian home.
works.meter: Mostly octosyllabic couplets in a plain, conversational narrative style, with lyric interludes.
works.context: The 1850s, the ideal of the companionate marriage, the Oxford Movement, and the Victorian cult of domesticity. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1862 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Felix Vaughan; Honoria Churchill; the Dean, Honoria's father; Honoria's sisters; Frederick Graham, her rejected cousin
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
works.form: history and chronicle (prose with verse insertions)
works.description: A set of interrelated vernacular annals recording English history from the arrival of Julius Caesar to 1154, begun c. 892 (the 'Common Stock') in the circle of King Alfred and continued in centres across England for over two and a half centuries. The earliest continuous vernacular history of any European people and the backbone of the period's historiography.
works.plot: The annals record year by year the wars of the kings of Wessex and England, the Viking invasions, ecclesiastical events, and natural portents; they incorporate poems (The Battle of Brunanburh, The Capture of the Five Boroughs, the deaths of Edgar and Edward), documents, and, in the Peterborough continuation (to 1154), the last original Old English prose composed in England.
works.significance: The foundation of English historical prose; a continuous vernacular record unmatched elsewhere in early medieval Europe.
works.meter: Prose, with alliterative verse poems incorporated at several annal years.
works.context: The Common Stock was compiled c. 892, probably under Alfred's direction, from earlier annals, Bede, and oral tradition; continuations were kept at Winchester, Abingdon, Worcester, Peterborough, and Canterbury.
works.characters: Alfred; Æthelstan; Edgar; Æthelred; Cnut; Edward the Confessor; William the Conqueror; Peterborough continuator
works.structure: Annalistic: brief yearly entries of varying fullness, from single sentences to extended narrative set-pieces; the seven manuscripts (A-G) diverge into regional continuations.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous, corporate authorship; traditionally associated with Alfred's court for the Common Stock.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Mission, conversion, and the Church

movements: Alfredian Renaissance

works.title: The Anniversaries
altTitles: Of the Progress of the Soul
works.description: Donne's two commemorative poems for Elizabeth Drury, the fifteen-year-old daughter of his patron Sir Robert Drury, who died in 1610: 'An Anatomy of the World' (1611) and 'Of the Progress of the Soul' (1612) — cosmic elegies in which the girl's death becomes the death of the world's coherence, her virtue the measure of its decay, and her translation to heaven the poem's only consolation.
works.plot: The First Anniversary anatomizes the world's sickness — 'new philosophy calls all in doubt' — and finds in the dead girl the pattern of lost virtue; the Second follows her soul's progress beyond the corrupt world to the joys of heaven, ending with the praise of the 'she' whose worth the world could not hold.
works.significance: The great English poems of the scientific revolution's first shock — and the most extreme test of the elegy's power to make a private grief cosmic.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of extraordinary intellectual density, with the famous passage on the 'new philosophy' as its centre of gravity.
works.context: Written 1611–12 in the household of Sir Robert Drury, whose patronage they repaid with a hyperbole that scandalized Ben Jonson; the poems register the crisis of cosmology after Copernicus, Kepler, and Galileo.
works.characters: Elizabeth Drury (the subject); the poet as anatomist; the World; the Soul; Death
works.structure: Two linked poems of several hundred couplets each, built as formal 'anatomies' — the dissection of the world, then the itinerary of the soul — with the funerary apparatus of elegies and epitaphs.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)

works.title: The Antipodes
works.form: comedy; masque-comedy; play within a play
works.description: Shirley's fantastic dream comedy in which Peregrine, a man crazed by reading travel books, is carried to an imaginary antipodal world where everything is inverted, and is cured by the dream itself.
works.plot: Peregrine, obsessed with Mandeville's travels, is drugged and conveyed to the Antipodes, a world of reversed customs and reversed theatre; the experience restores him, and the play ends with marriages.
works.significance: Shirley's most formally daring play and an important document of the Caroline fascination with travel, utopia, and the theatre's own conventions.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at Salisbury Court in 1636 and dedicated to the Earl of Newcastle.
works.characters: Peregrine; Lord Letoy; Doctor Hughball; Diana; Martha; Joyce; the Antipodal king
works.structure: Five acts with a large embedded play-within-the-play occupying most of the second half.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

The public theatre and the players' world
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Antiquary
works.form: Comic novel of manners and character, with antiquarian dissertation and dialect scene; a society comedy of the Borders.
works.description: The most purely comic of the early historical novels, built on an old collector of inscriptions, coins and family papers whose zeal for the past is turned to account by an impostor and finally defeated by a beggar. Its subject is the social uses of antiquarian knowledge, and its joke is that the past is a property still in dispute. The author held it the most natural of his own tales.
works.plot: Jonathan Oldbuck, the antiquary of Fairport, takes into his house the young stranger Lovel, whose romantic bearing conceals a claim connected with Oldbuck's own family history. The decayed baronet Sir Arthur Wardour, living on credit and on his daughter Isabella's expectations, is seduced by the pretended second-sight of the German trickster Dousterswivel, who is digging for hidden treasure on Oldbuck's land. A French invasion alarm, a runaway elopement, and a death-bed revelation of an abandoned child expose the fraud and settle the rights of the estate. Oldbuck's youthful passion, never followed up, is recovered in the person of Mrs. Stirling, and the beggar Edie Ochiltree, whose evidence has saved him, is provided for in the churchyard monument he had long designed.
works.significance: The period's richest novel about the appetite for the past, and the founding text of comic antiquarianism in fiction. It supplies one of the great stock figures of Scottish letters, the collector whose learning is also his meanness. Its treatment of a fake, of testimony and of an inheritance makes it a central text for studies of romantic fraud and of historical evidence.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a mixed register of Latin and Scots, burlesque inscription and formal pastiche of the antiquary's own writings.
works.context: Composed in a few months of extreme financial pressure, and written against the background of the invasion scare of the war years, the collapse of provincial credit, and the thriving trade in forged and romanticised antiquities. Its antiquarian apparatus draws on the same body of Border and monastic materials as the author's editorial work. The volunteer associations and the poor-house pensioners it depicts belong to rural Scotland on the eve of agricultural transformation.
works.characters: Jonathan Oldbuck; Edie Ochiltree; Sir Arthur Wardour; Isabella Wardour; Lovel; Herman Dousterswivel; Mrs. Stirling; the Rev. Mr. Balwhiddy; the laird of Dumbiedikes
works.structure: Third-person narration with strongly marked free indirect rendering of the antiquary's own pedantry; a comedy of errors resolved by testimony and revelation; the past is mediated through documents, monuments and tradition rather than narrated directly.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the Author of Waverley; attribution undisputed.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Border, ballad, and national memory
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Aran Islands
works.description: Synge's record of his visits to the Aran Islands: the finest English travel book about Ireland and the source of the language of his plays. It is a prose work of 1907 by J. M. Synge; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Synge describes four visits between 1898 and 1902: the cottages, the kelp-making, the fishing, the wakes, the story-tellers and the old men whose speech he transcribes almost phonetically, and his own slow acceptance by the islanders.
works.significance: The Aran Islands is one of the great English travel books and the laboratory of Synge's art: the speech he recorded there became the language of the plays.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The author's characteristic manner is a poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech.
works.context: The Aran Islands and the Congested Districts Board, the last years of the Irish-speaking peasant culture, and the folklore collecting movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1902 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; nature essay and the rural observation.
works.characters: J. M. Synge, the narrator; old Mourteen, his teacher of Irish; Pat Dirane, the story-teller; Michael, his young guide
works.structure: Four parts corresponding to four visits, in diary and descriptive prose. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edmund John Millington Synge. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Arraignment of Paris
works.description: Peele's pastoral-mythological court play: the shepherd Paris, commanded by the gods, judges the beauty contest of Juno, Pallas, and Venus; he awards the golden apple to Venus, whose bribe is the love of the nymph Oenone, and the play ends — after the goddesses' appeal — with Diana's famous judgment awarding the apple to 'Eliza', the Queen herself, a 'nymph' above all the goddesses.
works.plot: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis, Discord casts the golden apple; Paris, in his pastoral solitude with Oenone, receives the task of judgment; the three goddesses plead their cases in set speeches; Paris judges Venus; the goddesses appeal to the Olympian court; and Diana's final verdict transfers the prize to Eliza, flattering the Queen beyond the myth.
works.significance: The founding text of the Elizabethan court pastoral and of the genre of the Queen's mythological flattery.
works.meter: Mixed verse forms — blank verse, rhyme, and songs — with the pageantry of the goddesses' entries.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel before the Queen about 1581–84 and printed in 1584; its compliment to Elizabeth made Peele's name at court.
works.characters: Paris; Oenone; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Diana; Eliza (Elizabeth I); Colin; Hobbinol; Thenot; the shepherds and nymphs
works.structure: A masque-like pastoral in five acts, built on the judgment set piece and the appeals, with the shepherd scenes of Colin and the nymphs as pastoral interludes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Kingship and good rule
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre
The University Wits

works.title: The Art of Thomas Hardy
works.description: Published in 1894 and the first book-length study of Hardy's fiction: a critical appreciation by a fellow poet, of Hardy's Wessex, his tragic method and his poetry of place. It is a prose work of 1894 by Lionel Johnson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Johnson examines Hardy's novels in turn, and argues that their power lies in the fusion of a Greek sense of fate with a local English landscape and a modern scepticism.
works.significance: The Art of Thomas Hardy is the founding critical study of Hardy and one of the best books of Victorian criticism: it established Hardy as a tragic novelist rather than a regionalist and shaped all later criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is classical and medieval metres handled with learning.
works.context: 1894: the Hardy controversy after Tess, the new criticism of the novel, and the Rhymers' Club. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Lionel Pigot Johnson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Regional identity and the American sectional character
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade
