works.title: The Ascent of Man
works.form: Long poem in blank verse, first issued in 1889
works.description: Published in 1889 and the most ambitious English poem of evolutionary ideas: a blank-verse epic of the ascent of humanity from the primeval slime to the socialist future. It is a verse work of 1889 by Mathilde Blind; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem.
works.plot: The poem moves through the formation of the earth, the emergence of life, the age of the reptiles and mammals, the coming of man, the rise of religion and art, and ends with a vision of a future of human solidarity in which 'the Many' inherit the earth.
works.significance: The Ascent of Man is the only Victorian evolutionary epic written by a woman and one of the most ambitious poems of the century: it brings together Darwin, Shelley and the socialist future in a way no other English poet attempted.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is blank-verse narrative epic.
works.context: The 1880s, Darwinism, the popular evolutionary epic of the period, and the socialist revival of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1888 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mathilde Cohen. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Science, religion, and the question of design
movements: Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature

works.title: The Atheist's Tragedy
works.description: Tourneur's tragedy of providence: the atheist D'Amville murders his brother to advance his house, plots the ruin of his nephew Charlemont and the rape of his niece Castabella, and is finally killed by his own axe — striking his own brains out as he raises it against his son's head — in a play whose argument is the certainty of divine justice, staged against the atheist's every calculation.
works.plot: D'Amville kills Montferrers and blames bandits; Charlemont is sent to the wars and believed dead; the uncle's schemes against Castabella and his own sons proceed; the ghost of Montferrers appears, the counter-plots of the villains fail one by one; and the last act's trial and the accidental suicide of D'Amville ('the justice of God') complete the demonstration, with the lovers' marriage as the play's reward.
works.significance: The great counter-revenge tragedy of the Jacobean stage — the play that turned the genre's own machinery against the atheism it usually indulged.
works.meter: A harsh, emblematic blank verse with the sententious choruses of the play's moral argument.
works.context: Printed in 1611 with a dedication to Sir Walter Chute; it answered the decade's revenge vogue with an anti-revenge tragedy, and its atheist answered the Marlovian overreachers.
works.characters: D'Amville; Charlemont; Castabella; Montferrers (the Ghost); Levidulcia; Sebastian; Rousard; Borachio; Snuffe; the Puritan chaplain Languebeau Snuffe
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of providence built as a counter-argument to the revenge play — the wronged hero refuses revenge, and heaven's engines work without him.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Revenge and justice
movements: Jacobean Tragedy and Revenge Drama

works.title: The Author's Farce
works.form: farce and comic afterpiece, with inserted musical entertainment
works.description: The first of the Haymarket comedies, a farce about a playwright, his patronage and his poverty, in which the author's own career is made the subject and the theatre is satirised from inside. It was performed by a small company of actors at the little theatre in the Haymarket and at once established the writer as a theatrical as well as a literary force.
works.plot: A unsuccessful author of plays is tempted by his family and his friends to abandon the pen, and is courted by a printer and an alderman project who would employ his wit for money. A rival poet and a set of theatrical supernumeraries complicate his chances, and the action passes into a show within the show in which the persons of his own imagination appear and dispute their creation. The author's fortunes are finally settled by the exposure of the projects and by the applause of the audience he has courted.
works.significance: It began the series of plays that made the author a manager-dramatist and supplied the model of the play about authorship and the literary marketplace; its project satire feeds directly into the later comic prose.
works.meter: Brisk prose dialogue with versified songs and the rhymed set pieces of the inserted show; the style is deliberately low and topical.
works.context: Staged in the summer of 1730 at the little Haymarket theatre, in the season of the decay of the patent houses, the vogue for burletta and opera afterpieces, and the writer's own need for theatrical income; it answers the theatrical quarrels of the day and looks forward to the licensing bill of 1737.
works.characters: the author of the title; the printer and the projecting alderman; the rival poet; the family who press him to quit the pen; the actors and supernumeraries of the Haymarket company
works.structure: Two-act farce with an inserted burletta and a battle of the authors on the stage; the plot is a chain of theatrical situations rather than a regular intrigue, and the personation device carries the satire.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name after performance and recorded in the bills of the Haymarket season.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
The public theatre and the players' world
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
The Restoration Theatre

works.title: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp
works.form: Autobiography (the road in England and North America)
works.description: The classic English account of the road: the tramp's life in Wales, England and the American hobo camps. It is a prose work of 1908 by W. H. Davies; it is catalogued here under Autobiography and the Modern Memoir; Memoir and Autobiographical Prose and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Davies recounts his leaving of Newport, his tramping of the English and Welsh roads, his crossing to America and the hobo camps of the freight trains, the loss of his foot under the cars at Renfrew, Ontario, and his return to the English road and the workhouse, in the plain prose of the tramp.
works.significance: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp is the classic English account of the road: its hobo camps, its workhouses and its charity made the tramp's life a literary subject, and George Bernard Shaw's introduction made its author a writer.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of autobiography: the first-person narrative of the life, the set-piece of the formative scene, the quotation from letters and diaries, and the reflection on the formation of a self. The author's characteristic manner is the plain short line and the plain word.
works.context: The roads of Wales, England and North America in the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1907 and first published in 1908 and it is catalogued under autobiography and the modern memoir; memoir and autobiographical prose.
works.characters: the tramp; the hobo kings; the farmers and the charwomen of the road; the surgeon at Renfrew
works.structure: An autobiography in chapters of the road, from Newport to the workhouse and back. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points. A memoir of a life or a period, the remembered scene and the quoted letter carrying the account.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Davies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy

The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road

works.title: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas
works.form: Memoir (written as if by Alice B. Toklas)
works.description: The most entertaining memoir of the period: Stein's own life told in the voice of her companion, and the whole Paris avant-garde. It is a prose work of 1933 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Biography and the Modern Life; Autobiography and the Modern Memoir and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Stein writes her own autobiography in the first person of Alice B. Toklas: the San Francisco childhood, the Paris apartment at 27 rue de Fleurus, the sittings for Picasso, the Saturday evenings with Matisse, Apollinaire, Hemingway, Fitzgerald and the whole of the avant-garde, the war years and the American lecture tour.
works.significance: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is the most entertaining memoir of the period and a landmark of modernist self-fashioning: it made Stein a best-seller at fifty-nine and remains the most vivid record of the Paris avant-garde.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
works.context: The Paris of 1903–32, the avant-garde art world, the First World War, and the American discovery of modernism in the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed in 1932 and first published in 1933 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under biography and the modern life; autobiography and the modern memoir.
works.characters: Gertrude Stein; Alice B. Toklas; Pablo Picasso; Henri Matisse; Ernest Hemingway; F. Scott Fitzgerald; Guillaume Apollinaire
works.structure: A chronological memoir in the voice of Alice B. Toklas, with an epilogue. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man
works.description: The founding novel of the Black American passing narrative: a man who crosses the colour line. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by James Weldon Johnson; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: An unnamed narrator, born in the South to a Black mother and a white father, grows up as a talented musician, travels in Europe, witnesses a lynching in the South, and finally decides to pass as white and live in the North, ending with his regret for the heritage he has abandoned.
works.significance: The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man was the founding novel of the Black American passing narrative and the first novel by a Black American to be published anonymously as a genuine autobiography: its portrait of the colour line made it a central text of American literature and a direct ancestor of Invisible Man.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person passing narrative.
works.context: The United States and Europe in the 1890s and 1900s, and the Black American world of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
works.characters: the unnamed narrator; his mother; his father; the millionaire; the woman in Paris
works.structure: A first-person narrative in eleven chapters, from the South to Europe and the North. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James William Johnson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Autobiography of Margaret Oliphant
works.description: Published in 1899 after her death and one of the greatest of Victorian autobiographies: the record of a life spent supporting a family by writing. It is a prose work of 1899 by Margaret Oliphant; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Oliphant writes of her childhood in Scotland, her marriage and the early death of her husband, the loss of her children, and the unending labour of fiction, criticism and biography by which she kept her household; the book is interrupted by her own outbursts of grief and ends with her unfinished story of the deaths of her sons.
works.significance: The Autobiography is one of the most moving and most valuable documents of Victorian literary life, a frank account of the cost of a woman's writing career that has become a central text in the history of women's authorship.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.
works.context: 1885-97: the professional literary world of Blackwood's and the Victorian periodical, and the economics of women's authorship. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1897 and first published in 1899 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Margaret Oliphant, the narrator; Frank Oliphant, her husband; Maggie, her daughter; Cyril and Francis (Cecco), her sons; her brothers Frank and Willie; John Blackwood
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table
works.description: The founding text of the American familiar essay: the autocrat, his boarding house and the talk of a Boston morning. It is a prose work of 1858 by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Serial and Monthly-Part Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The autocrat of a Boston boarding house holds forth at breakfast on everything — heredity, theology, the weather, the human body, the profession of letters — while the other boarders, the professor, the poet, the schoolmistress and the old gentleman, answer back.
works.significance: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table created the American familiar essay and the style of the Atlantic Monthly: it made the Boston boarding house a literary institution and established the conversational essay as the central form of American prose.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the discursive table-talk of the breakfast room.
works.context: Boston in the 1850s, the boarding house and the Atlantic Monthly circle. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; serial and monthly-part novel.
works.characters: the autocrat; the professor; the poet; the schoolmistress; the old gentleman; the landlady
works.structure: A series of breakfast-table papers with a recurring cast. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oliver Wendell Holmes. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
Science, religion, and the question of design

works.title: The Awakening
works.description: Published in 1899 and the founding American novel of female emancipation: the story of Edna Pontellier's awakening to desire and selfhood in New Orleans and on Grand Isle. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Kate Chopin; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Edna Pontellier, the wife of a New Orleans businessman, learns to swim, falls in love with Robert Lebrun, takes a lover in Alcée Arobin, moves out of her husband's house, and at the end walks into the sea at Grand Isle.
works.significance: The Awakening is the central American novel of female selfhood and one of the founding texts of American feminist criticism: condemned in 1899 and rediscovered in the 1960s, it is now read as the great American novel of a woman's refusal to be defined by marriage and motherhood.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is cool, exact, sensory prose.
works.context: The 1890s: Creole New Orleans, the summer resort of Grand Isle, the marriage law and the position of the married woman, and the American reception of French fiction. The record dates the work as composed in 1898 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Edna Pontellier; Léonce Pontellier; Robert Lebrun; Alcée Arobin; Adèle Ratignolle; Mademoiselle Reisz; Doctor Mandelet; Madame Lebrun; Victor Lebrun
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katherine Chopin. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: The Awntyrs off Arthure
altTitles: The Anturs of Arther at the Tarnewathelan
works.description: An alliterative Arthurian poem of some 700 lines in two adventures: the ghost of Guinevere's mother, risen from a lake in Tarn Wadling to warn of pride and the fall of the Round Table, and the duel in which Gawain and Galeron contest disputed lands before Arthur's judgement. Its spectral first episode is among the most powerful scenes in the alliterative corpus.
works.plot: While hunting at Tarn Wadling, Guinevere and Gawain meet a ghost who prophesies the ruin of Arthur's court and shows the torments of the dead; in the second adventure, Gawain fights the knight Galeron for the lands Arthur has granted him, and Arthur's equitable judgement restores them — with the ghost's warning shadowing the court's splendour.
works.significance: The finest of the northern Gawain romances after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and the classic statement of the ghost-warning topos in Arthurian verse.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, perhaps for a northern gentry audience with an interest in its Cumberland setting; preserved in four manuscripts and printed in the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Gawain; Guinevere; the ghost of Guinevere's mother; Galeron; Arthur
works.structure: A two-part romance (ghostly warning; judicial combat) linked by the theme of land, justice, and mortality.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Arthurian legend
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: The Alliterative Revival
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Ayenbite of Inwyt
works.description: The Kentish translation, completed in 1340 by Dan Michel of Northgate, monk of St Augustine's, Canterbury, of the Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens: a comprehensive prose manual of the vices, virtues, commandments, and the art of holy dying. Its title — 'remorse of conscience' — gives the work its penitential keynote.
works.plot: The treatise anatomizes the deadly sins and their remedies, the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the preparation for death, in a systematic scheme of moral and catechetical instruction.
works.significance: The most extensive Kentish text in Middle English, invaluable to historical linguistics, and a principal document of lay catechesis in the age of the Somme le Roi tradition.
works.meter: Prose; a famously conservative Kentish dialect with heavy French-derived vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1340 at St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, on the eve of the Black Death; preserved in a single autograph manuscript, BL Arundel MS 57.
works.characters: none (doctrinal treatise)
works.structure: A systematic doctrinal handbook following the structure of the French Somme le Roi, with illustrative exempla.
works.attributionNotes: The translator names himself in the colophon: Dan Michel of Northgate.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Penance, confession, and sin
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Ayrshire Legatees; or, The Correspondence of the Pringle Family
works.description: the author's comic epistolary masterpiece, a series of letters from three Ayrshire bailies sent to London on a lawsuit about a burgh's common guilder, as they confront the metropolis with provincial astonishment. It is one of the great picaresque comedies of Scottish letters.
works.plot: Bailie Edmonston, Bailie Burns, and Doctor Law, three worthies of the Ayrshire burgh of Drumlummock, travel to London to plead their claim to a disputed common guilder. Writing letters home to their wives and fellow bailies, they submit London to the most delightful provincial misapprehension — its monuments, theatres, politics, and law courts all misread through Ayrshire categories. As the lawsuit stalls in Chancery their funds and confidence diminish, until they find unexpected patronage and return triumphant and none the wiser.
works.significance: The Ayrshire Legatees established the comedy of provincial innocence in the metropolis and is a central text in Scottish comic fiction; its epistolary irony influenced later Scottish comic writing and remains the author's most widely read novel.
works.context: Published in 1821 alongside Annals of the Parish; the author, himself a failed London businessman with first-hand knowledge of squabbling burgh councils and Chancery delays, satirises both provincial Scotland and metropolitan law with equal affection.
works.characters: Bailie Edmonston; Bailie Burns; Doctor Law; Mrs. Law; the narrator's families in Drumlummock
works.structure: Epistolary comedy in a series of letters to families in Ayrshire; the journey plot provides the sequence; the humour resides entirely in the gap between the narrators' self-satisfied interpretation and the reality they describe.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
The city and urban life
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Bab Ballads
works.form: Comic verse with drawings; nonsense verse
works.description: Published in 1869 and the finest English comic verse of the period after Lear: sixty ballads written for Fun and illustrated by the author. It is a verse work of 1869 by W. S. Gilbert; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The ballads present a gallery of comic unfortunates — the captain of the Pinafore-type ship, the bishop who is eaten by a boa constrictor, the lady who is carried off by a gorilla, the baby farmer, the thwarted lover — each in a narrative that proceeds by impeccable rhyme and impossible logic to a shocking or absurd conclusion.
works.significance: The Bab Ballads are the masterpiece of English comic verse between Lear and Gilbert's own operas: their perfect technique and their savage absurdity made them a permanent classic, and they are the direct source of the Savoy opera plots and of the modern English comic poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is inverted logic carried to absurdity.
works.context: 1861-69: the comic magazine Fun, the burlesque theatre of the 1860s, the Victorian nursery and the illustrated comic book. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Schwenck Gilbert. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule

Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: The Babees Book
works.description: The classic late medieval courtesy book: a poem of instruction for young boys ('babees') entering noble households, teaching them how to stand, dress, serve at table, and speak to their betters, with the companion courtesy poems and John Russell's Boke of Nurture that accompany it in the manuscripts. The standard English manual of the civility that defined the late medieval and early modern gentleman.
works.plot: The poem addresses the boy entering service, prescribing his conduct from rising to bedtime — cleanliness, table manners, deference of speech and gesture — and moralizing the discipline of courtesy as the school of virtue, in the tradition of the medieval courtesy literature descended from the classical 'nurture' of the young.
works.significance: The classic English courtesy book and the ancestor of the early modern conduct tradition (Erasmus, Castiglione's English imitators); its rules of table and speech chart the history of English civility.
works.meter: Couplets and seven-line stanzas, plain and mnemonic.
works.context: Composed c. 1475, when the great households' demand for trained service and the school curriculum of manners converged; preserved in BL Harley MS 5086 and related manuscripts; edited by F. J. Furnivall (1868) in the volumes that founded the study of English manners literature.
works.characters: the 'babee' (addressee); the master
works.structure: A single didactic poem in the courtesy tradition, with the companion poems (Urbanitatis, Stans Puer ad Mensam, Russell's Boke of Nurture) forming a curriculum in the manuscripts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Wisdom and learning
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Backwoodsman
works.form: Didactic and topographical poem in the eighteenth-century manner, with political argument
works.description: A two-canto poem defending the western settler and the plain republican character against the pretensions of landed aristocracy and of borrowed European taste. It is one of the founding texts of Knickerbocker verse and an early statement of the claim to a national literature. Its argument is explicitly political, attacking the old Dutch family pride of the Hudson valley.
works.plot: The first canto sets the backwoodsman's life against the luxury of the refined planter, and describes the log cabin, the clearing and the forest as the school of republican virtue. The second canto turns to the aristocratic pretensions of the eastern families and to the danger that borrowed European manners will corrupt a young country. The poem invokes the western emigrant as the true representative of the nation. It ends with an appeal to letters to be made on native material and by native conditions.
works.significance: It gave the backwoodsman a poetic dignity before the prose romance did so, and it is a document of the Knickerbocker group's formation. Its polemic against cultural dependence states the terms of the transatlantic argument of the 1820s. It helped to establish the western theme in American verse.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter
works.context: Published at New York in 1818, when the western settlement and the old Hudson valley patroonships were live political questions. Its anti-aristocratic polemic belongs to the Democratic-Republican attack on the surviving families of the eastern elite. It appeared in the same season as the first native attempts to make a national poetry out of the forest.
works.structure: Descriptive and didactic poem in two cantos, proceeding by contrast of settings and by invective against social pretension.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the author was later identified with a second, collaboratively written series.
themes: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters
The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch

works.title: The Balade of Charitie
altTitles: A Ballad of Charitie (ascribed to Rowley)
works.form: Ballad in the antique manner with an exemplum structure, printed among the Rowley poems with obsolete spelling and gloss; one of the pieces Chatterton supplied to the fashionable taste for old popular poetry.
works.description: The best-known of Chatterton's short Rowley poems: a religious ballad in praise of Christian charity, put out as the work of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk and dated by its ascription to an earlier century still. It is at once an exemplum of alms-deeds and a piece of invented antiquity, and it has had a longer independent life in anthologies than almost any other of the Rowley poems.
works.plot: The ballad's argument is an encomium of the virtue of charity and a warning against the neglect of it. It opens by invoking charity as a heavenly quality with authority over earthly judgement, and then illustrates its thesis with the fate of a shelterless wanderer turned from the doors she begs at and left unrelieved, so that religious instruction becomes social accusation. The closing movement turns the dead wanderer into a judgement on the uncharitable, and sets the virtue of pity against the pomp of rites and of endowed devotion. It is therefore a poem about the obligations of wealth to visible poverty, framed as an old popular ballad.
works.significance: It gave the Rowley forgeries their most durable lyric, and its standing with later poets is remarkable: Wordsworth defended and quoted it in 'The Prelude' as a specimen of genuine national poetry, which shows how completely the fiction of antiquity could survive the exposure of the fraud. It is a key text for the afterlife of literary forgery in romantic taste.
works.meter: Stanzaic ballad measure in Chatterton's archaising imitation, with echoing rhyme and a weight of obsolete diction; the deliberate uncouthness of sound is the poem's evidence of age.
works.context: It belongs to the Rowley papers and to the mid-1760s rush of enthusiasm for old English poetry, when Walpole, Percy and their readers were collecting and reprinting ballads and when the charity sermon in verse was a living form. Its subject of neglected poverty had immediate force in a culture beginning to debate poor laws, alms and the duties of the rich.
works.characters: Charity personified as the invoked virtue; the unsheltered wanderer; the householders who turn her from their doors
works.structure: A short exemplum-ballad: invocation and doctrinal statement, the narrative instance of the rejected wanderer, and a moral-judgement conclusion, in the order of a preacher's example rather than of a plot.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Chatterton and ascribed to Thomas Rowley, with a fabricated earlier date attached in the manuscripts; the 'antient' authorship is a forgery and is recorded as such, while the poem's own authorship is undisputed. Composition and first-print years are left null because the dating within the Rowley papers is not settled.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Primitive genius and national poetry
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: The Ballad of Reading Gaol
works.form: Ballad in six parts (published under the pseudonym C.3.3.)
works.description: Published anonymously in 1898 under the prison number 'C.3.3.' and Wilde's last work: a ballad on the execution of Charles Thomas Wooldridge at Reading in 1896, and on the pity and horror of the common criminal's fate.
works.plot: The ballad follows the prison routine, the condemned man's last days, the hanging, and the narrator's meditation on the shared guilt of all men; its refrain 'each man kills the thing he loves' made it one of the most quoted poems in English.
works.significance: The Ballad of Reading Gaol is the great English poem of prison reform and the last major Victorian poem; its refrain entered the language and its subject made it a founding text of the literature of incarceration.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the ballad stanza, the four-stress and three-stress lines rhyming on the even lines. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the prison system, the campaign against capital punishment, and Wilde's own experience as prisoner C.3.3. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the narrator; the condemned trooper, 'the man who had to swing'; the warders; the Chaplain; the Governor
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Banished Man
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Historical Novel and Romance
works.description: Charlotte Smith's novel of political exile published between The Old Manor House and her books for young readers, a narrative that interweaves several plots and several countries around characters driven from home by the French Revolution and by aristocratic tyranny. Its subject, announced in its title, is banishment as a condition: the loss of country, property, and protection, and the attempt of generous minds to sustain principle in exile. The book also contains a Gothic romance strand that makes it one of Smith's clearest engagements with the literature of terror.
works.plot: Characters displaced from France and from other European countries pursue, across separate plots, the same conditions of proscription, dependence, and threatened inheritance; a tale of confined and pursued heroine is embedded in the larger narrative of exile, and the novel's resolution depends on the exposure of the interest and tyranny that produced the banishment, rather than on any single hero's education.
works.significance: The Banished Man is important as the most sustained novel of the 1790s to make political exile its governing condition and to combine it with Gothic machinery, and it is now cited in discussions of women's revolutionary fiction and of the migration of Gothic plot into questions of proscription and refuge.
works.meter: Prose romance; the Gothic inset passages are written in the heightened descriptive register of the romance of terror, with verse quotations used as moral comment.
works.context: Written and published in the darkest year of the British debate about the Revolution, when émigré settlement in England was a daily spectacle and when government repression had silenced many of Smith's radical acquaintances; her own dependence on copyright and subscription, and the failure of her hopes of a French restoration, inform the book's treatment of exile and of charity.
works.characters: the banished families and their European hosts; the pursued heroine of the inset Gothic story; the interested kinsmen and patrons who procure the exiles' disinheritance
works.structure: An interlaced multi-plot novel of exile, combining political narrative with an inset Gothic romance; the separate stories are bound together by their shared situation of proscription and dependency rather than by a single point of view.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

Prose Fiction and the Early Novel

Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine

works.title: The Bard
works.description: Gray's Pindaric ode on the British bard and on the curse of the poet's people against an unworthy king, drawing upon the legends of the Welsh bards and on the imagery of the northern poetry.
works.plot: The Muse of Poetry, driven from the courts of the degenerate, warns the people of the island and their bard; the royal house and its favourite are given over to ruin, and the bard's curse and the vanishing of his nation before the conqueror fill the closing strophes.
works.significance: It created the image of the bard as the prophet and arraigner of a nation, and together with the fragments and forgeries of the same decade it formed the mythology of primitive poetry for the romantic period.
works.meter: The Grayian Pindaric measure, with the short opening line, the long swelling strophe and the emphatic epodic close; the stanzaic schemes are imitated from the Norse and Greek models he had studied.
works.context: Written in the years of the antiquarian recovery of the Welsh and northern poetry, of the argument about the barbarous and the polished, and of the fashion for the curse of the poet, when the bard was becoming the figure of national and primitive genius.
works.characters: the British bard; the Muse of Poetry; the unhappy king and his favourites; the people of the island
works.structure: Three parts of paired Pindaric stanzas, moving from the invocation and the warning to the curse and the prophetic conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Battle Day, and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1851 after his release from prison: the collected Chartist poems, including 'The Battle Day', 'The Factory Slave', 'The Prisoner of the Tower' and the elegy on the Chartist dead. It is a verse work of 1851 by Ernest Jones; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The poems range from the songs of the mass meeting to the prison lyric and the elegy for the martyrs of the movement; their subject is the hope of the revolution and the cost of the defeat.
works.significance: The Battle Day is the central collection of Chartist poetry and the finest body of English political verse between Shelley and Morris: it preserves the songs of the movement and records the experience of the political prisoner.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is ballad and song forms with heavy refrain.
works.context: The year 1850, the collapse of the Chartist movement after 1848, and the prison literature of the political detainee. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1851 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ernest Charles Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Battle of Brunanburh
works.form: battle poetry (chronicle poem) in alliterative verse
works.description: A panegyric of 73 lines, entered in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 937, celebrating the crushing victory of King Æthelstan and his brother Edmund over a coalition of Scots, Strathclyde Britons, and Dublin Norsemen led by Constantine and Anlaf (Olaf) Guthfrithson. The greatest of the Chronicle's poems, composed in the full heroic manner.
works.plot: The poem exults in the day-long battle — 'never was greater slaughter in this island' — as the West Saxons and Mercians pursue the fleeing allies; Constantine, his son slain, and Anlaf flee to their ships, and the victors return to Wessex leaving the battlefield to the carrion beasts, the raven, eagle, and wolf.
works.significance: The masterpiece of late heroic panegyric; Tennyson's translation (1880) is a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense use of kennings and the beasts-of-battle formula.
works.context: The battle of Brunanburh (937), the greatest English victory of the tenth century, secured Æthelstan's supremacy in Britain; the poem is preserved in four manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
works.characters: Æthelstan; Edmund; Constantine of Scotland; Anlaf Guthfrithson
works.structure: A compact celebration in the heroic mode: the boast of victory, the pursuit, the flight of the kings, and the 'beasts of battle' topos, with a closing return to the annalistic frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Battle of Hastings
altTitles: A Battle of Hastings (ascribed to Rowley)
works.form: Projected national epic in the Rowley manner, with antiquarian gloss and an analysis of the intended work attached; heroic-length lines rather than the couplet of contemporary epic practice.
works.description: The most considerable of the narrative poems Chatterton attributed to Thomas Rowley: a 'Saxon' account of the Norman conquest of England, planned on an epic scale and written in a heroic measure that Chatterton supposed to be the practice of the fifteenth century. It is at once a battle poem, a patriotic history of the defeated English, and a further stage in the Rowley forgeries.
works.plot: The subject is the crisis of the year 1066 and the subjection of the English to a foreign conqueror, treated with the sympathies firmly on the side of the losing nation. The poem opens by invoking the patron and the muse of the intended work, gathers the Saxon host and its leaders, and passes to the shock of the field and to the lament over what England lost. Chatterton's interest is in the dignity and the misery of a conquered people rather than in a regular epic machinery, and the piece survives as the projected opening of a design that was never finished. Its argument is thus double: a narrative of defeat, and an imitation of an 'ancient' national epic believed capable of arousing patriotic feeling.
works.significance: It is the strongest evidence that the Rowley forgeries were not merely antiquarian hoaxes but an attempt to reconstruct an English epic tradition older than the Norman conquest, and it influenced the later vogue for Saxon and British subjects in poetry and in the novel. It also stands as one of the founding documents of English medievalism and of the romantic cult of unfinished genius.
works.meter: Long decasyllabic and eleven-syllable heroic measure in Chatterton's archaising imitation of early English verse, with heavy sounding of old names and a deliberate roughness contemporaries accepted as antique evidence.
works.context: It stands within the Rowley papers of Chatterton's last Bristol years, and within the wider 1760s revival of the Saxon and 'Gothic' past as a source of native liberty and of poetic sublimity. The conquest theme was a live political myth in Augustan England, and Chatterton turns a schoolroom subject into an imagined national epic.
works.characters: The Saxon leaders and their host; the Norman conqueror; the conquered English people; the framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'
works.structure: An unfinished epic design: invocation and proposition, mustering and battle, lament and prophetic retrospect on English liberty under the conqueror, in the annalistic manner Chatterton assigned to Rowley.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Chatterton and ascribed in the manuscripts and collections to the fictitious Thomas Rowley; no medieval original exists, and the 'ancient' authorship was a forgery discredited by the antiquarian inquiry into the Rowley papers. Composition and first-print dates are left null because the chronology of the surviving papers is debated.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
National identity and Englishness
Primitive genius and national poetry
Warfare and battle
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: The Battle of Hastings; an Epic Poem in Twelve Books
works.form: National epic and didactic poem in the historical manner: an anti-machinal epic which treats chronicle as its authority and the battle piece as its centre.
works.description: The author's only attempt at a full-scale historical epic, twelve books of blank verse on the Norman conquest, published anonymously and almost unnoticed. Its theory of epic is austere and archaeological: the poet is to be a faithful recorder of the event, elevating nothing, inventing little, and trusting the subject itself for its terrors. The result is a strange, concentrated poem, remarkable for its hatred of the machinery of machinery and for its concentration on the physical facts of slaughter.
works.plot: The poem opens with the death of Edward the Confessor and Harold's oath to support William's succession, then follows the Norwegian invasion of Harald Hardrada, Stamford Bridge, and the march south to Hastings. William's claim, the papal sanction, and the crossing are treated as a chain of political and legal acts rather than as providence. The central books give the battle itself in close, almost documentary detail, ending with Harold's death and the rout of the English. The later books show the submission of the English leaders and the partition of the land, closing with the Conqueror's coronation and a mournful retrospect on what England lost.
works.significance: A significant oddity in romantic epic: it anticipates the modernist suspicion of decorative machinery, and its insistence that the poet must subordinate invention to record makes it a document of its author's classicist theory of history in verse.
works.meter: Blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, with a close, elided, sometimes Latinate syntax and frequent enjambment.
works.context: Written during its author's years in Wales and Italy, and published in 1815 at the moment of Waterloo, when national epic again seemed a possible form; its austere theory of historical fidelity is a reply to the machinery of contemporary poem.
works.characters: King Harold; Duke William; King Edward the Confessor; Harald Hardrada; Earl Tostig; Odo of Bayeux
works.structure: Twelve books of continuous narrative with brief prefatory argument and minimal divine machinery; the action is framed by invocation and by the poet's own explicit remarks on the limits of epic invention.
works.attributionNotes: Published without the author's name in 1815; The book was known to its author's circle, and he accepted responsibility for it in later life, and it was admitted to his verse collections after his death.
themes: Kingship and good rule
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
Warfare and battle

works.title: The Battle of Maldon
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 325 lines commemorating the battle of Maldon (10 or 11 August 991), in which Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex and his retinue fought a Viking army at the causeway of the Blackwater and were destroyed; the poem is the last great expression of the heroic code, celebrating loyalty unto death.
works.plot: Byrhtnoth arrays his levies against the Vikings on the tidal causeway of the Pante; he refuses tribute, and when the Vikings ask passage he grants it 'for his ofermod' (overconfidence) — the poem's great crux — drawing up for battle on the shore. After Byrhtnoth falls, a series of retainers make speeches vowing to avenge him or die beside him, and the poem breaks off in the midst of the last stand.
works.significance: The fullest poetic statement of the comitatus ethic of loyalty unto death; Byrhtwold's speech is among the most quoted passages of Old English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of the classical kind, with sustained martial diction.
works.context: The battle is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 991 and in the Vita Oswaldi; the poem survives only in an early eighteenth-century transcript of Cotton MS Otho A.xii, destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731. The tribute of 10,000 pounds paid after the battle began the Danegeld payments.
works.characters: Byrhtnoth; Wulfstan; Ælfhere; Maccus; Offa; Ælfwine; Leofsunu; Dunnere; Byrhtwold; Godric (the betrayer)
works.structure: A single continuous battle-narrative built from speeches: the Viking messenger's demand, Byrhtnoth's reply, the combat, and the laddered sequence of retainers' vows (Ælfwine, Offa, Leofsunu, Dunnere, Byrhtwold — 'will shall be the harder, heart the keener').
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the opening and closing of the poem are lost with the manuscript.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Loyalty and the comitatus bond
Warfare and battle
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Battle of Marathon: A Poem
works.description: Privately printed in 1820 when she was fourteen, and her first published work: a verse narrative of the Athenian victory over the Persians in 490 BC, written in imitation of Pope's Homer and of the Greek historians.
works.plot: The poem narrates the Persian invasion, the Athenian appeal to Sparta, the Marathon campaign and the victory, with speeches of the Athenian generals and a providential interpretation of the Greek success.
works.significance: The Battle of Marathon is a founding document in the history of women's classical scholarship in English: a fourteen-year-old's imitation of the epic mode that shows both the precocity and the excluded ambition later realised in Aurora Leigh.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
works.context: The classical education she had shared with her brother Edward, the 1820s taste for epic narrative in verse, and the Greek War of Independence of that year, which gave the poem its topical interest. The record dates the work as composed between 1819 and 1820 and first published in 1820 and it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.characters: Miltiades; Aristides; Themistocles; Callimachus; Hippias; Datis; Pallas Athene
works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Printed privately in 1820 in an edition of fifty copies for family and friends; the attribution to Elizabeth Barrett Browning is documented by her own references and by the surviving copies.
genres: Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole

works.title: The Battle of the Books
altTitles: The Battle of the Books: A Paper, which was Read in a Great Club
works.description: Swift's short ironic allegory of the quarrel of the ancients and the moderns, in which the spider and the bee dispute over their claims to invention and to the honey of the hive, and the modern critick is defeated in the library of St James's.
works.plot: The narrator enters the court library at the moment when the ancient and modern books fall out; the spider, who spins all things from his own bowels, and the bee, who gathers from abroad and digests what it collects, plead their rival causes, and the battle of the ants, the wasp and the critick ends with the ancient party's discomfiture and a joke at the author's expense.
works.significance: It fixed the image of the two kinds of writer, the spider and the bee, and turned the rules-of-art quarrel into a durable piece of English literary mythology.
works.meter: Plain Swiftian prose of the fable and the character, with the balanced pleading of the two rivals and the abrupt deflating close.
works.context: Written in the season of Wotton's and Bentley's engagement over the quality of modern learning and of Temple's essay on ancient and modern discipline, and printed with the Tale of a Tub in 1704; it is the founding document of the Scribleran war against the modern critick.
works.characters: the spider; the bee; the wasp; the critick; the narrator who reports the scene
works.structure: A brief narrative frame containing an allegorical dispute and a battle piece, closed by an authorial rebuke to the reporter.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the piece was long circulated in manuscript before its 1704 printing.
themes: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Wisdom and learning
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: The Bean Eaters
works.description: The title poem of Gwendolyn Brooks's third collection, The Bean Eaters (1960): an old couple eat their dinner of beans in a rented back room crowded with the keepsakes of their life.
works.summary: An elderly couple at a plain meal; their routine of dressing and tidying; their memories, stirred by the objects that fill their room.
works.plot: 'They eat beans mostly, this old yellow pair.' Dinner is a casual affair of plain chipware, creaking wood and tin flatware. They are two who are 'Mostly Good', two who have lived their day but keep on putting on their clothes and putting things away, and remembering, with twinklings and twinges, as they lean over the beans in their rented back room full of beads and receipts and dolls and cloths, tobacco crumbs, vases and fringes.
works.significance: One of Brooks's most anthologised short poems; Gale's Poetry for Students gives it an entry of its own.
works.meter: Plain description with ironic touches ('Dinner is a casual affair') and the closing list of objects, which holds the couple's past.
works.context: The Bean Eaters (1960) is the collection in which Brooks turned increasingly to the lives of poor Chicagoans and to the public events of the civil rights years.
works.structure: Three brief stanzas of irregular line length and loose rhyme, ending in a long catalogue line.
themes: Class, labour and social mobility
Death, illness and mourning
Family, marriage and domestic life
movements: Postwar African American Writing: Protest and Its Critics

works.title: The Beautiful
works.description: Published in 1913 and Vernon Lee's short, lucid statement of her theory of beauty: an introduction to the psychology of aesthetic experience. It is a prose work of 1913 by Vernon Lee; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The book distinguishes the beautiful from the merely pleasant and the merely interesting, explains beauty as the satisfaction of the mind's demand for unity in variety, and treats the arts as the deliberate organisation of that satisfaction, in a compact argument that draws on her earlier physiological and psychological work.
works.significance: The Beautiful is the clearest English statement of the psychological theory of beauty and the summary of Vernon Lee's lifelong work in aesthetics: written for a general audience, it remains one of the best short introductions to the subject in English.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, analytical prose that moves between description and argument.
works.context: 1913: the new psychology of aesthetics, the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature, and the twentieth-century debate on formalism. The record dates the work as composed in 1913 and first published in 1913 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Violet Paget. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist

works.title: The Beaux' Stratagem
works.description: Farquhar's last and greatest comedy, written on his deathbed, in which the fortune-hunters Archer and Aimwell arrive at Lichfield to repair their ruined estates and encounter the unhappily married Mrs Sullen.
works.plot: Archer and Aimwell take turns posing as lord and servant at Lichfield; Aimwell courts Dorinda, Archer is drawn into the unhappy marriage of Mrs Sullen and Sullen; a highway robbery, a French invasion scare, and the discovery that Aimwell is not the real lord resolve the plot in marriage and reconciliation.
works.significance: The finest comedy of the early eighteenth century and the culmination of the Restoration tradition; its treatment of divorce and of provincial English society was ahead of its time, and it has been continuously revived since.
works.meter: Prose of remarkable richness and speed.
works.context: Performed at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket on 8 March 1707 and published the same year; Farquhar died in March or April 1707, weeks after the first performance.
works.characters: Archer; Aimwell; Mrs Sullen; Sullen; Dorinda; Lady Bountiful; Cherry; Boniface; Gibbet; Count Bellairde; Foigard
works.structure: Five acts with the celebrated bedroom scene (III.iii) in which Archer and Mrs Sullen debate marriage and divorce.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Farquhar; authorship undisputed.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct
The city and urban life
Wit, libertinism, and the rake

works.title: The Beggar's Opera
works.description: Gay's ballad opera, proposed by Pope as a burlesque of the Italian heroic opera, in which the highwayman, the thief-taker and the Newgate clerks are made to sing the airs of the town, and the criminal economy of the city is staged as the mirror of high life.
works.plot: Macheath, the gay highwayman, is betrayed by Peachum to Lockit and to the gallows, having married both Polly and Lucy; the rival fathers scheme, the gang quarrels, and the last-minute reprieve, protested by the Beggar who superintends the piece, exposes the convention by which the hero of quality escapes the rope.
works.significance: It created the ballad opera, made the criminal underworld the true subject of a musical entertainment, and remains the century's most sustained identification of the gallows and the drawing room as one economy.
works.meter: Ballad and song stanzas of the street and the theatre, set to borrowed airs, alternating with prose dialogue; the metres are those of the popular tune rather than of the dramatic blank verse.
works.context: First performed and printed in the season of the London opera companies' triumph with Handel's Italian dramas, and of the South Sea collapse, when the language of credit, the press gang and the property of the stage were all in dispute; the work was licensed without difficulty and became the most pirated text of the decade.
works.characters: Macheath; Peachum; Lockit; Polly Peachum; Lucy Lockit; the gang; the Beggar; the Player
works.structure: An opera in three acts with spoken dialogue between the airs, framed by the Beggar's argument with the poet and the composer about probability and about the fate of the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Gay's, on the plan suggested by Pope; the airs, the tunes and the many pirated keys and continuations are other men's work.

Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

works.title: The Belle's Stratagem
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The most successful comedy by a woman dramatist of the late eighteenth century, in which a young woman determined to be won rather than to win pursues the man she loves through a series of disguises. Its heroine's stratagems make it the most direct descendant on the stage of the amatory fiction of the earlier century.
works.plot: Letitia Hardy, promised to a young man of fortune who does not know her worth, resolves to make him pursue her by assuming a different woman each night, first as a neighbour's daughter and then in other persons of the town. Her friend and the gallants of her father's circle are drawn into the design, and the lovers' fathers make their own plans of marriage. The last stratagem brings the lover to a declaration, and the discoveries justify the heroine's conduct and complete the match.
works.significance: It holds the place of the century's most durable comedy by a woman playwright and is a key text for the history of the female plotter in drama and of the theatrical revival of romantic disguise.
works.meter: A bright prose dialogue of retort and affected persons, with the disguised speeches carrying the satire of fashionable address; the songs and letters serve as set pieces.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1780, in the season in which the woman dramatist became a regular attraction of the theatres and in which the old device of personation was revived for a polite audience.
works.characters: Letitia Hardy; Dorilton, the lover she must win; her friend of the stratagems; the fathers who arrange the matches; the gallants and the imposed-with company
works.structure: Five-act comedy of personation, the successive disguises supplying the movement and the final recognition the close; the heroine's management of the plot is the play's governing interest.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after her first successes, though some of her verse had circulated earlier under a poetic signature.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: The Bestiary
works.description: A Middle English bestiary of 802 lines, probably of East Anglian origin, describing the nature of the lion, eagle, serpent, stag, whale, and other creatures and drawing from each a moral and allegorical lesson, in the tradition of the Physiologus. It is the earliest English bestiary to survive in the vernacular.
works.plot: Each animal's natural history — the lion's sleep with open eyes, the whale luring sailors, the phoenix's rebirth — is expounded as a figure of Christ, the devil, or the Christian soul.
works.significance: The link between the Old English Physiologus poems and the later English bestiary tradition, and a vivid example of medieval allegorical natural history in the vernacular.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets of varying length, with some alliterative ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1250, translated from the Latin Physiologus of Theobaldus; preserved uniquely in BL Arundel MS 292, with Norwich connections.
works.characters: the animals (lion, eagle, serpent, stag, fox, spider, whale, siren, elephant, turtle-dove, panther, dove)
works.structure: A sequence of discrete animal exempla, each divided between natural description (natura) and moralization (significacio).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Typology and biblical interpretation

works.title: The Beth Book
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1897
works.description: Published in 1897 and Grand's finest novel: the growth of a girl of genius into an independent woman against every obstacle of Victorian family life. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by Sarah Grand; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Beth Caldwell grows up in an Irish and English household of careless parents and brutal schooling, marries Dr Dan Maclure, a mercenary, philandering doctor who runs a lock hospital and practises vivisection, and after years of illness and poverty discovers her vocation as a writer and an orator for women's freedom.
works.significance: The Beth Book is the most fully realised of the New Woman novels and one of the first English novels to treat a woman's artistic vocation from childhood to fulfilment: its portrait of a girl of genius has made it a key text in the history of women's writing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays.
works.context: 1896-97: the Irish and English provincial middle class, the Victorian education of girls, and the feminist lecture platform of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Beth Caldwell; Captain Caldwell, her father; her mother; Dr Dan Maclure, her husband; Arthur Brock
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Bible in Spain
works.description: Published in 1843 and Borrow's most popular book: his years as a Bible agent in Spain from 1835 to 1840. It is a prose work of 1843 by George Borrow; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Borrow travels through Spain during the Carlist wars, distributing Protestant scriptures in Madrid, Seville, Cordoba, Galicia and the wilds of the country, and records the smugglers, the priests, the innkeepers, the gypsies and the bandits he meets, together with his arrest and imprisonment at Madrid.
works.significance: The Bible in Spain was one of the most popular travel books of the century and the classic English account of Spain in the 1830s: its portrait of the country and its people, its dialogue and its adventure made it a best-seller on both sides of the Atlantic, and it remains the most vivid English book about Spain of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is picaresque episodic narrative.
works.context: 1835-40: the Carlist wars, the Spanish Inquisition's legacy, the British and Foreign Bible Society, and the English romantic view of Spain. The record dates the work as composed between 1835 and 1840 and first published in 1843 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: George Borrow, the narrator; Antonio Buchini, his Greek servant; Benedict Mol, the treasure-seeker; the gypsies of Madrid and Badajoz; Mr Villiers, the British minister
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The Biglow Papers
works.description: The founding American political satire: a Yankee farmer's letters against the Mexican War. It is a verse work of 1848 by James Russell Lowell; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Hosea Biglow, a Yankee farmer, writes dialect verses against the Mexican War and the slave power, with a preface and notes by the Rev. Homer Wilbur; the poems range from the famous 'Jonathan to John' to the satire of the press and the recruiting sergeant.
works.significance: The Biglow Papers created the American political satire in dialect and made the Yankee farmer a national voice: its anti-war and anti-slavery verse was the most influential political poetry of the 1840s, and it founded the tradition of American dialect satire that Twain inherited.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The spelling and syntax carry a spoken dialect. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Yankee dialect of Hosea Biglow.
works.context: The Mexican War of 1846–48, the abolitionist controversy and the New England anti-slavery movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1846 and 1848 and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Hosea Biglow; the Rev. Homer Wilbur; Birdofredum Sawin; Jonathan
works.structure: Nine papers in dialect verse with prose preface and notes. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. R. Lowell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Bijou: An Annual Remembrancer of Literature and the Fine Arts
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: the miniature gift-book miscellany of occasional lyric and anecdote, designed around a steel-engraved frontispiece.
works.description: A London literary annual of the smallest and most decorative kind, issued for the seasons from 1828, that gathered short poems and tiny prose pieces with engraved plates in a jewel-like pocket volume. It was the most aggressively miniature of the great annuals, bought for the same gift market as the larger keepsakes, and it preserved some of the period's most quoted occasional verse. Its importance lies in the form it carries: the bijou as the annual economy's last reduction of literature into a presentable object.
works.plot: The volumes have no argument; their contents are a sequence of lyrics, sonnets, sentimental tales and plates. One of its distinctions was to print a late meditative lyric by a major poet of the preceding generation, and it drew on the same circle of fashionable contributors as the larger annuals, sometimes competing with them for the same poem.
works.significance: It documents the annual economy at its most commodified and is a standard source for the circulation of Romantic verse into gift-book culture, including a much-anthologised late poem first printed in its pages. Its history illustrates how the period's lyric was paid for, placed and reproduced.
works.meter: Occasional lyric and sonnet in conventional measures, with short hymn-like stanzas; prose in compressed anecdote form.
works.context: Published in the years when the annuals were saturating the Christmas trade, when editors competed directly for contributions and when the same poem might appear in two rival gift books, producing the public quarrels about originality that followed. Its format answers the commercial logic of the keepsake at its most concentrated.
works.structure: Serial annual anthology: plate, then a compact succession of verse and miniature prose, undifferentiated except by contributor.
works.attributionNotes: The volumes were issued without an editor's name on the title and the editorship has been described in trade and biographical sources rather than established by the books themselves; contents are individually attributable.
