works.title: The Black Arrow: A Tale of the Two Roses
works.form: Historical adventure novel (serialised in Young Folks, 1883)
works.description: Published in 1888 though serialised in 1883: a romance of the Wars of the Roses in which Dick Shelton, a young Lancastrian, takes to the greenwood to avenge his father and win the heiress Joanna Sedley.
works.plot: Dick Shelton escapes from the tutelage of his treacherous guardian Sir Daniel Brackley, joins the outlaw band of the Black Arrow, rescues Joanna Sedley from Sir Daniel, and after the battle of Shoreby and the siege of Tunstall Keep wins her hand.
works.significance: The Black Arrow applies the adventure formula of Treasure Island to English history and is one of the earliest and most influential historical novels for boys.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.
works.context: The 1460s, the Wars of the Roses, and the outlaw tradition of the English ballad and the Robin Hood legend. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Richard Shelton; Joanna Sedley; Sir Daniel Brackley; Ellis Duckworth; Bennet Hatch; Lord Shoreby; Clerk of Tunstall
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: The Black Dog and Other Stories
works.description: The collection of the black dog and the omens of the village. It is a prose fiction work of 1923 by A. E. Coppard; it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale.
works.plot: The Black Dog and Other Stories gathers the tales of the omen, the black dog and the funeral of the village, in the manner of the strange in the everyday that made Coppard's name.
works.significance: The Black Dog and Other Stories fixed Coppard's manner of the omen and the black dog: its tales are the standard text of the English wonder-tale of the village between the wars.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the single strange turn in the everyday.
works.context: England in the early 1920s, and the village wonder-tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: the black dog; the villagers; the mourners
works.structure: A collection of short stories of the omen and the strange. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred Edgar Coppard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Black Riders and Other Lines
works.description: Published in 1895 and the most original American poetry collection of the decade: short, harsh free-verse parables about God, nature and the human condition. It is a verse work of 1895 by Stephen Crane; it belongs to The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poems present brief, enigmatic scenes — a man climbing a mountain and finding a bitter fruit, a creature eating its own heart, a god who admits he is a lie — in which the biblical and the ironic are set against one another, and the reader is left to find the meaning.
works.significance: The Black Riders is the most radical American poetry of the 1890s and a forerunner of modern American free verse: its refusal of metre and rhyme, its bitter irony about God and its compressed parables influenced Carl Sandburg, Edgar Lee Masters and the Imagists, and it made Crane the only American poet of his generation to write poetry as modern as his prose.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The line is free verse, cadenced by the phrase and not by a received pattern. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation.
works.context: 1895: the American free-verse experiments of the 1890s, the collapse of the Puritan certainties, and the vogue for the epigram after Whitman and Emily Dickinson. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America; American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stephen Townley Crane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Blacker the Berry: A Novel of Negro Life
altTitles: Blacker the Berry: A Novel of Negro Life
works.description: The first Black novel of colour prejudice within the race: Emma Lou and the shade of her skin. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Wallace Thurman; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Emma Lou Morgan, a dark-skinned Black woman, is rejected by her own family and community for her colour; the novel follows her through college, Harlem and a disastrous marriage in a study of colour prejudice within the Black world.
works.significance: The Blacker the Berry was the first Black American novel to make colour prejudice within the race its subject: its portrait of Emma Lou made the intraracial colour line visible in literature and made Thurman the most daring satirist of the Harlem Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the satire of the movement from inside.
works.context: The United States in the 1920s, and the Black communities of Boise, Los Angeles and Harlem. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Emma Lou Morgan; Alva; the mother; the uncle; the Harlem friends
works.structure: A novel in five parts, from Boise to Los Angeles to Harlem. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Wallace Henry Thurman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Blackstone Rangers
works.description: A poem in three parts by Gwendolyn Brooks on the Blackstone Rangers, a Chicago street gang, published in In the Mecca (1968), the book of her turn towards the Black Arts Movement.
works.summary: The gang as seen by those who would discipline it; its leaders; and a 'Rangerette', one of the gang girls.
works.plot: In 'As Seen by Disciplines' the Rangers are thirty at the corner, black, raw, ready, sores in the city that do not want to heal. 'The Leaders' names Jeff, Gene, Geronimo and Bop, who are hardly the dupes of downtown, hardly Belafonte, King or Malcolm X, and whose country is a nation on no map. 'Gang Girls' follows Mary Ann, a rose in a whiskey glass, whose year passes in the narrow world of the gang, save for her love.
works.significance: A key poem of Brooks's late-1960s transformation and of the Black Arts era's attention to the black city.
works.meter: Compressed, inventive diction and wordplay ('They cancel, cure and curry'), mixing street names and lyrical figures; freer forms than her earlier work.
works.context: In the Mecca (Harper and Row, 1968), Brooks's first new collection in nearly ten years, pairs its long title poem with shorter poems on contemporary figures and events, among them Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, the Chicago Picasso, the Wall mural and the Blackstone Rangers.
works.structure: Three titled sections of different length and manner, moving from the outside view to the leaders and then to a single girl.

works.title: The Blessed Damozel
works.description: Written in 1847, published in the Germ in 1850 and revised for the 1870 Poems: the poem in which the Pre-Raphaelite image of the beloved in heaven was first fully stated, and the text of Rossetti's own painting of 1871-79.
works.plot: The blessed damozel leans out from the bar of heaven and looks down to the earth where her lover still lives; she prays that he may join her, and the poem ends with her tears and with the lover's sense of the distance between them.
works.significance: The Blessed Damozel is the founding poem of Pre-Raphaelite poetry and the work in which the aesthetic movement's image of the woman in heaven was created; it is the source of the pictorial and poetic tradition that runs through Burne-Jones and the 1890s.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound.
works.context: The 1847-50 Pre-Raphaelite movement, the Dantean model of Beatrice in paradise, and the Victorian poetry of the dead beloved. The record dates the work as composed between 1847 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gabriel Charles Dante Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Blithedale Romance
works.description: Published in 1852 and Hawthorne's most directly contemporary novel: a fictional account of the Brook Farm experiment and of the failure of a utopian community. It is a prose fiction work of 1852 by Nathaniel Hawthorne; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Miles Coverdale narrates the life of Blithedale, a socialist community, and the fates of the philanthropist Hollingsworth, the beautiful Zenobia and the mysterious Priscilla; the community fails, Zenobia drowns, and Coverdale confesses at the end that he loved her.
works.significance: The Blithedale Romance is the central American fictional treatment of the utopian community and one of the first American novels about the position of women: Zenobia is the finest portrait of the woman reformer in American fiction, and the novel's analysis of the failure of the Transcendentalist experiment is the most searching of its time.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The years 1841-47, the Brook Farm community and American Fourierism, and the women's rights movement and the woman question. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1852 and first published in 1852 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum; Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.
works.characters: Miles Coverdale (the narrator); Zenobia; Hollingsworth; Priscilla; Old Moodie; Westervelt; Silas Foster
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Blue Fairy Book
works.form: Fairy-tale anthology (with illustrations by H. J. Ford and G. P. Jacomb-Hood)
works.description: Published in 1889 and the first of the twelve 'coloured' fairy books: the volume that gave English children the classic French, German, Norwegian and English tales in a single collection. It is a prose fiction work of 1889 by Andrew Lang; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume contains 'The Bronze Ring', 'East of the Sun and West of the Moon', 'The Yellow Dwarf', 'Little Red Riding-Hood', 'Cinderella', 'Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp', 'The Forty Thieves', 'Beauty and the Beast' and 'The Master Maid', among thirty-seven tales.
works.significance: The Blue Fairy Book created the modern English canon of the fairy tale and was the most important single agency in transmitting the world's folklore to English-speaking children; the twelve books together form the largest fairy-tale collection in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is an anthology, the pieces ordered by the editor. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The author's characteristic manner is easy, witty, allusive journalism.
works.context: The 1880s, the Victorian fairy-tale revival, the folklore scholarship of the Folklore Society, and the golden age of the illustrated gift book. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.title: The Boke Named the Governour
works.description: Elyot's treatise on the education and conduct of the English ruling class, the first major work of English political and educational theory written in the vernacular rather than Latin.
works.plot: The first book prescribes the upbringing of a future governor from infancy — nurses, tutors, the curriculum of classical authors, music, painting, and physical exercise. The second book treats the virtues proper to a ruler: justice, fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and the golden mean. The third discusses the cardinal virtues and their application in counsel and judgement.
works.significance: A founding text of English humanism in the vernacular: it established the ideal of the educated magistrate, coined or first recorded many English words ('education', 'encyclopaedia'), and remained an authority on gentlemanly conduct for two centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1530–31 while Elyot, a diplomat and clerk, was out of royal favour after Wolsey's fall; dedicated to Henry VIII, it drew on Castiglione's Il Cortegiano and Patrizi's De regno, and shaped the humanist programme of gentlemanly education institutionalized in the grammar schools.
works.structure: Three books of systematic exposition, dense with citation of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Plutarch, and illustrated with exemplary stories of classical princes.

movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
altTitles: The First Prayer Book of Edward VI
The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administracion of the Sacramentes
works.description: The first Book of Common Prayer, compiled chiefly by Thomas Cranmer and imposed by the Act of Uniformity of 1549 as the single liturgy of the English church; the foundational text of Anglican worship.
works.plot: The book replaces the medieval service books (missal, breviary, manual, pontifical) with one English liturgy: Morning and Evening Prayer, the collects, the order for Holy Communion, baptism, confirmation, matrimony, visitation of the sick, burial, and the ordination rites, with the psalter and lectionary — retaining much medieval devotion while recasting the eucharist as a communion of all the people in both kinds.
works.significance: The greatest single achievement of English liturgical prose: Cranmer's collects ('whose service is perfect freedom', 'read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest') entered the language itself, and the book's cadences shaped English prose from Hooker to the Authorized Version and beyond.
works.meter: Prose with psalmody
works.context: Drafted in 1548–49 by Cranmer with a committee of bishops and divines, authorized by the first Act of Uniformity (January 1549), and introduced at Whitsun 1549, provoking the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall; the book was revised in 1552 (the Second Prayer Book), restored by Elizabeth in 1559, and its language survives in the 1662 book used for four centuries.
works.structure: A complete liturgical manual arranged by rite, with rubrics, calendar, and lectionary; the prose is Cranmer's — sonorous, cadenced, and scriptural.
works.attributionNotes: The book is the work of Cranmer and his committee; the title page names no author, and the record attributes the compilation to Cranmer as chief author, following universal scholarly usage.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The English Reformation

works.title: The Book of Faith
works.description: Reginald Pecock's vernacular treatise of 1456 on the nature of faith and its relation to reason, written in the last years before his condemnation: faith, he argues, is a species of knowledge grounded in evidence and reason, not mere belief on authority — the doctrine that brought him to trial and abjuration. It survives in the author's own manuscript.
works.plot: Pecock analyzes faith as intellectual assent produced by the 'doom of reason' on credible testimony, distinguishes it from opinion and knowledge, answers the objections of the 'unbilevers', and defends the lay person's right and duty to understand what he believes.
works.significance: The boldest medieval English statement of the rationality of faith, and the terminus of vernacular theology before the Reformation.
works.meter: Argumentative English prose, technical and precise.
works.context: Completed in 1456, a year before Pecock's trial; its rationalism was among the charges against him, and the work survives only in the Trinity College, Cambridge, autograph manuscript (MS B.14.45).
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Two books of philosophical-theological analysis, in the scholastic quaestio manner adapted to English.
works.attributionNotes: Pecock's authorship secure.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Wisdom and learning
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Book of Homilies
altTitles: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed by the King's Majesty to Be Declared and Read
works.description: The first official book of sermons of the Church of England, issued in 1547 under the direction of Thomas Cranmer (who wrote several of the homilies himself) to be read in parish churches; a principal vehicle of Reformation doctrine for the laity.
works.plot: Twelve homilies expound the Protestant faith in plain English: on scripture, the misery of mankind, salvation by faith alone, good works, Christian love, against swearing and perjury, against strife, obedience to rulers, and against whoredom and adultery — each designed to be read from the pulpit by clergy who could not preach.
works.significance: The official voice of the English Reformation for ordinary congregations: the homilies translated Protestant doctrine into a national plain style and remained binding on the church for three centuries, feeding directly into the religious language of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Issued in 1547, the first year of Edward VI, as part of the royal Injunctions requiring the homilies' use; the homily 'Of Good Works' and others are Cranmer's own, and the second book (with the famous homily 'Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion') followed in 1571, making the two books the official theology of the Elizabethan church.
works.structure: Twelve self-contained sermons, each with a scriptural text, exposition, and application, written for oral delivery by non-preaching clergy.
works.attributionNotes: The book is a collaborative production of Cranmer, Thomas Becon, and other reformers; the record attributes it to Cranmer as the supervising compiler, following standard scholarship, while noting the collaboration.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The English Reformation
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

works.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
works.description: The dictated spiritual autobiography of Margery Kempe of King's Lynn (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English: her conversion after childbirth, her marriage and vow of chastity, her uncontrollable weeping at the thought of the Passion, her pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, and her examinations for heresy before the archbishops of Canterbury and York. A unique document of female lay piety and of fifteenth-century English life.
works.plot: Margery recounts her visionary conversations with Christ, her struggle with her husband for chastity, her travels through Europe and the Holy Land, her clashes with hostile clergy and her vindications, her visit to Julian of Norwich, and her old age caring for her ailing husband — the whole narrated in the third person through her scribes.
works.significance: The first autobiography in English and the earliest extended account of a laywoman's religious life; its frankness about body, marriage, and authority has made it a founding text of women's literary history.
works.meter: Direct, colloquial prose, vivid in dialogue and detail, mediated by her scribes.
works.context: Dictated c. 1436–38, with a second book of the 1430s–40s, in the East Anglian culture of orthodox lay devotion shadowed by the Lollard trials; the complete text was lost until the discovery of the manuscript in 1934 (BL Additional MS 61823), and first published in 1936.
works.characters: Margery Kempe; John Kempe (her husband); Julian of Norwich; Christ (in dialogue); the archbishops
works.structure: Two books of episodic autobiography, moving between mystical colloquy and the social world of East Anglian towns, courts, and pilgrim routes.
works.attributionNotes: Margery Kempe's authorship (by dictation to scribes) is recorded within the book itself.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
The Passion of Christ
The contemplative life
movements: The English Mystics

works.title: The Book of Snobs
works.description: A series of sketches published in Punch in 1846-47 and collected in 1848: a taxonomy of English snobbery — the country snob, the city snob, the military snob, the clerical snob, the literary snob — written in the person of a satirical observer who includes himself among the objects of the analysis.
works.plot: The book has no narrative. It proceeds by category and example, with mock-learned definitions and illustrative anecdotes, and it closes with an account of 'the snob royal' and the observation that 'the world is a snobbish world'.
works.significance: The Book of Snobs fixed the word 'snob' in its modern social sense and gave the nineteenth century its most serviceable word for the fear of social inferiority; it is the satirical key to all of Thackeray's fiction, and it anticipates the modern sociology of status.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The 1840s, the decade of the railway and the new money, the club and the dinner party, and the Punch humour of Douglas Jerrold, Lemon and Thackeray himself. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
movements: Arnold and the Criticism of Culture

works.title: The Book of St Albans
altTitles: The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Heraldry
works.form: courtesy book and household manual (verse and prose)
works.description: The gentleman's handbook printed at St Albans in 1486: treatises in verse and prose on hawking, hunting, and heraldry, together with the terms of venery and the 'companies of beasts', traditionally attributed to Dame Juliana Berners, prioress of Sopwell. It is the classic English manual of the gentleman's arts, reprinted and expanded into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: The book instructs the reader in the falconer's and hunter's crafts — the mews, the lure, the chase of the hart, the terms of the hunt — and in the blazoning of arms, closing with the famous catalogues of collective nouns ('a parliament of rooks', 'a murmuration of starlings') that fixed the English vocabulary of the field.
works.significance: The foundational English manual of the gentleman's arts: its venery terms entered the language and its heraldry shaped Tudor and Stuart practice.
works.meter: Mixed: the hawking and hunting treatises in rhyme royal and couplets, the heraldry in prose.
works.context: Printed at the schoolmaster press of St Albans in 1486 (a colophon names 'the schoolmaster of St Albans'), in the post-Caxton provincial print boom; the attribution to Juliana Berners appears in the 1496 de Worde reprint.
works.characters: none (manual)
works.structure: A compilation of distinct treatises (hawking; hunting; arms; blazoning) in the practical-manual tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dame Juliana Berners (prioress of Sopwell) in the 1496 reprint; the attribution is traditional and doubted. authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Wisdom and learning
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Book of the Duchess
altTitles: The Deth of Blaunche the Duchesse
works.description: Chaucer's earliest major poem (1,334 lines in octosyllabic couplets), a dream vision elegy for Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, who died in 1368: the insomniac dreamer overhears a grieving knight in black, whose lament for his lost lady — 'White' — unfolds the ideal of courtly love into a meditation on death and consolation. The poem that founded the English dream-vision tradition.
works.plot: The dreamer, sleepless from an eight-year love-sickness, reads Ovid's tale of Ceyx and Alcyone and falls asleep; in his dream he meets the Man in Black, who tells of his long service to Fortune and of the peerless lady White whom he won and has now lost; only the dreamer's blunt question — 'she is dead?' — breaks the elegy's obliqueness, and the dream ends with the hunting of the hart and the poem's closure on the word 'king'.
works.significance: The first great English dream poem and the foundation of Chaucer's mature art; its fusion of consolation, allegory, and courtly elegy shaped the entire English dream-vision tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of courtly grace, adapted from Machaut and the Roman de la Rose.
works.context: Composed c. 1368–72, commemorating Blanche of Lancaster (d. 12 September 1368), first wife of John of Gaunt, Chaucer's patron; the poem's courtly audience would have recognized the dead duchess in the knight's 'White'.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Man in Black; Lady White; Fortune
works.structure: A double frame (reading; dream) enclosing the knight's elegiac autobiography, in the French dit manner; the wordplay on 'White', 'hart/heart', and 'king' ties consolation to allegory.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the occasional reference to Blanche is universally accepted.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
movements: Ricardian Poetry

works.title: The Book of Urizen
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a book of cosmogony and theodicy written as a scripture of the poet's own invention, with the chapter divisions and the style of a biblical book.
works.description: The first of the great illuminated books of the poet's own myth, etched and printed in 1794 as a cosmogony in nine chapters, giving an account of the creation of the world as a fall. An eternal being of separate reason, who divides himself from the other powers and sets up a law of one, is the maker of a contracted and legal universe; his books, written in the dark proportions of his own solitude, are the law and the religion that bind mankind, and the poem tells of his revolt, his loss of a companion power, and the long age of priesthood and sacrifice that follows.
works.plot: The first chapters describe the self-separation of the fourth power, who becomes a king and a lawgiver in a vacuum, calls his book and his priests into being, and sets the measure of a world in which all things are bounded and weighed. His companion joy, who is cast down from his side in the contest with the other powers, is lost to him, and the birth of the female powers and of the world of nature follows his fall, the creation being an act of division and of grief. In the middle chapters the new created world is given its seasons, its cities and its religions, and the priests of the law of one preach sacrifice and fear; the later chapters bring the revolt of the serpent and of the woman in the garden of the new-created race, the flood of sorrow, and the long dark age of the book and the law, closing with a vision of the day of judgment in which the fabricated universe is shaken and the powers of the dead are broken.
works.significance: The foundation of the poet's private prophecy and one of the most ambitious inventions of English Romantic verse: a creation myth in which reason, law and priesthood make a world of contraction, and in which the universe of single authority is presented as a fall from unity. Its Urizen has become a standard name in literary culture for the reasoning power set against imagination, and the book is central to all accounts of the Romantic myth-making.
works.meter: Short and stern accentual lines of varying beat, mostly in common and ballad measures, with an insistent repetition of words and a harsh monosyllabic music appropriate to its law and its terrors; the several chapters vary their stanzaic pattern.
works.context: Etched and published in London in 1794, in the year in which the poet issued the two books of songs and the European prophecy, and when his myth of a fallen reason was being formed out of his reading of the religious and philosophical systems of the day; its parody of a book of Moses and its attack on a religion of law belong to the same moment of revolutionary dissent.
works.characters: Urizen, the fourth power who becomes king and lawgiver; his lost companion joy, called Ahania; the other eternal powers who contend with him; the priests and the books of the new law; the created female powers and the new-made race of the bounded world
works.structure: A cosmogonic book in nine numbered chapters, proceeding by proclamation and narrative from the prime separation through the making of the bounded world to the age of law and the threatened dissolution; its design answers and parodies the book of Genesis, and the argument is carried in the fall and reign of a single reason-god.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several issues of the book and the plates' arrangement in the surviving copies differ, and the myth's relations to the poet's other books are a matter of interpretation, not of authorship.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: The Bostonians
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1886
works.description: Published in 1886 and the great American novel of the women's movement: the struggle between a southern conservative and a Boston feminist for the soul of a young orator. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by Henry James; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Verena Tarrant, a gifted speaker, is taken up by the Boston reformer Olive Chancellor and groomed for the women's cause; Olive's cousin Basil Ransom, a Mississippi lawyer, falls in love with Verena and persuades her to abandon the platform for marriage, and the novel ends with her escape from the hall on the night of her great speech.
works.significance: The Bostonians is the central American novel of the women's movement and one of the most complex treatments of same-sex attachment in nineteenth-century fiction: its portrait of Olive Chancellor and its analysis of the politics of reform made it a key text of American feminist criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification.
works.context: The 1870s: the Boston women's movement, the American suffrage campaign, and the post-war South. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Olive Chancellor; Verena Tarrant; Basil Ransom; Mrs Luna; Selah Tarrant; Miss Birdseye; Dr Prance
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry James, Jr. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Democracy, individualism, and the American experiment
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
movements: American Realism and the Howells Program
The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel

works.title: The Bothie of Toper-na-Fuosich: A Long-Vacation Pastoral
altTitles: Bothie of Toper-na-Fuosich: A Long-Vacation Pastoral
works.description: Published in 1848 (the title later corrected to Tober-na-Vuolich), a 'long-vacation pastoral' in English hexameters: a party of Oxford undergraduates reading in the Scottish Highlands, and the decision of one of them to marry a Highland girl and emigrate.
works.plot: Philip Hewson, a radical undergraduate, falls in love with the peasant girl Elspie Mackaye and, rejecting the conventional options of the educated man, marries her and emigrates to New Zealand, where the poem's epilogue shows him as a settler and a democrat.
works.significance: The Bothie is the first English poem to use hexameters for a sustained modern narrative and the first Victorian poem to treat marriage across class as a serious democratic choice; it is the crucial link between the Victorian long poem and the modernist verse novel.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The line is the English hexameter, the unrhymed six-stress line of the classical experiment. The author's characteristic manner is hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms.
works.context: The 1848 revolutions, the Oxford of the Tractarian crisis and the undergraduate reading party, the Scottish Highlands after the Clearances, and the emigration schemes of the later 1840s. The record dates the work as composed in 1848 and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Philip Hewson; Elspie Mackaye; David Mackaye, her father; Adam, the tutor; Hobbes; Arthur Audley; Lindsay, 'the Piper'; Airlie; Katie; Lady Maria
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Democracy, individualism, and the American experiment
Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: The Bowge of Courte
works.description: Skelton's first major poem, a dream satire in rhyme royal: the dreamer Drede boards the ship Bowge of Courte, where the personified vices of the court — Flattery, Suspicion, Harvy Hafter, Disdain, Riot, Deceit — successively menace and betray him, until he leaps overboard. It is the founding text of the Tudor court-satire tradition.
works.plot: Drede, standing at the shore, is invited aboard the Bowge of Courte; each passenger woos him and then turns on him, and the poem breaks off as he prepares to leap from the ship to save his life.
works.significance: The first sustained court satire of the English Renaissance, combining the dream vision of Chaucer with the estates satire of the Middle Ages and setting the pattern for the complaint literature of the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Seven-line rhyme royal stanzas, handled with Chaucerian fluency but a distinctly satirical edge.
works.context: Written at the turn of the century, when Skelton was moving from court service to the country living at Diss; its portrait of court corruption anticipates his later anti-Wolsey satires.
works.characters: Drede (the dreamer); Flattery; Suspicion; Harvy Hafter; Disdain; Riot; Deceit
works.structure: Dream vision with prologue; an allegorical sea voyage in which successive encounters with the courtly vices build to a single climactic decision to abandon the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1499.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry

works.title: The Brass Bottle
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1900
works.description: Anstey's comic djinn: an architect's life ruined by the gratitude of an ancient spirit. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by F. Anstey; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
works.plot: Horace Ventimore, a young architect, buys a brass bottle and releases the djinn Fakrash, whose extravagant gratitude — palaces, treasure, flying carpets — wrecks the young man's engagement and his career before everything is resolved.
works.significance: The Brass Bottle gave the modern djinn story its English form and was the most popular comic fantasy of the period, dramatised and filmed repeatedly: its formula of the well-meaning but disastrous magic has become a permanent comic device in English fiction and film.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The author's characteristic manner is the comic premise carried to its logical extreme.
works.context: London in the 1890s and the vogue for the oriental tale and the Arabian Nights. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the new humour; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Horace Ventimore; Fakrash; Sylvia Futvoye; Professor Futvoye; the Jinnee
works.structure: A comic novel in twelve chapters, from the auction room to the palace. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Anstey Guthrie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale
Comic Novel and the New Humour

Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination

works.title: The Bravo
works.form: Historical novel and political romance in the Italian setting; state-fiction of a declining republic
works.description: A historical romance of republican Venice in the decay of its aristocratic power, and the author's most concentrated political novel. Its plot of a rescue from the council of ten exposes the machinery of a state that calls itself free. The book is unusually frank in treating a city as an idea, and its prefatory letter became a cause of controversy with the American press.
works.plot: Two Venetian gentlemen, whose family has been ruined by the council of ten, seek to destroy the state and to free the Dalmatian islanders from Venetian rule. Their design is served by an adopted daughter who is loved by a boatman of the arsenal, and by a Greek captive whose loyalties are divided. The rescue of the conspirators from the prisons and the failed rising give the later books their momentum. The romance ends with the conspirators discovered, the boatman dead, and the republic's patience shown to be only another form of tyranny.
works.significance: It completes the movement of the American romance of forest and sea into the political history of Europe. Its analysis of liberty as an institutional appearance influenced later American republicanism. It is the earliest American novel to treat the state itself as its main character.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1831, the year of the Italian risings and of the author's return from seven years in Europe. Its treatment of aristocratic Venice was read at home as an allegory of American party government. Its preface, discussing the conduct of the American press, provoked a prolonged newspaper war.
works.characters: Jacopo the bravo; the two young Venetians of a proscribed house; the Council of Ten; Venice
works.structure: Third-person historical romance with a tightly limited time and place; political expository dialogue between masked and unmasked citizens carries the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Revenge and justice
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Cooper and the American Romance of Forest and Sea

works.title: The Bravo of Trieste
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's Venetian historical tale, published in his 1812 collection Tales of Wonder, set in the Trieste-Venice border world of the late fifteenth century and featuring a bravo's love for a girl accused of sorcery. It continues his Gothic treatment of Italian tyranny, superstition, and passionate loyalty in a more restrained and romantic mode than The Monk.
works.plot: Jacopo, the bravo of the title, loves Maria, a young woman of Trieste falsely accused of witchcraft by the Inquisitor and the Duke of Venice's agents. As Maria is imprisoned and tortured, Jacopo leads an armed band of bravos against Venetian authority to rescue her; their assault on the prisons becomes a battle between individual loyalty and institutional tyranny. The tale ends in the lovers' escape and a broader reflection on popular revolt against the despotism of the early Renaissance state.
works.significance: The Bravo of Trieste shows the author continuing to develop the historical Gothic after The Monk; its treatment of institutional tyranny and loyal popular revolt prefigures later Romantic historical romance and demonstrates the breadth of his contribution to the genre.
works.context: Published in Tales of Wonder, 1812, a four-volume collection of the author's original prose romances and translations from Schiller; the Italian tyrant tale had renewed currency during the Napoleonic period's engagement with Venice and the Adriatic.
works.characters: Jacopo; Maria; the Inquisitor of Venice; the Duke of Venice; Jacopo's band of bravos
works.structure: Linear prose romance within the collection Tales of Wonder; the captivity and rescue plot draws on the Italian tyrant tale and the witchcraft prosecution as its central dramatic mechanisms.

themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Revenge and justice

works.title: The Bride of Abydos
altTitles: The Bride of Abydos: A Turkish Tale
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the oriental love tale, with the interpolated song and the domestic tragedy of concealed kinship.
works.description: The second oriental tale, set at Abydos on the Hellespont and built on a love between a half-brother and half-sister who do not know their kinship. The girl is promised to the old pasha who holds her father's life in pawn, and the lovers attempt a flight by sea that ends in pursuit and death. The poem is the most lyrical of the tales, rich in song, apostrophe to the nightingale and the rose, and in imagery of the water, the moon and the veil. It was written out of the poet's own domestic crisis, and the theme of forbidden affection is handled with an unusual frankness.
works.plot: The young warrior loves the daughter of the same father by another mother, believing her only his sister in name, and the pasha of Abydos demands her in marriage as the price of her father's safety. The lovers plan escape across the straits; the father discovers the kinship and dies of the shock, and the pasha pursues in the night, finding the two locked together on the shore and killing the youth before the girl dies of grief. The argument turns on the guilt of desire that is innocent of knowledge, on the commerce in women that the eastern court practises, and on the faithless protection of fathers. Lyric interruptions, including the songs of the harem and the apostrophe to the hour of love, slow the plot in favour of mood.
works.significance: It carried the guilty-hero tale into the region of innocent and unknowing transgression, and its lyrics made it one of the most widely set and quoted of the tales, with songs that entered the popular repertoire. Its frank handling of a forbidden affection became a permanent scandal of the poet's reputation and a test case for the argument about the relation of life and work.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter for the narrative, with lyric stanzas of shorter measure for the songs and a marked use of repetition and exclamation in the passages of alarm.
works.context: Published before the end of 1813 and at once attacked by the quarterly press for its treatment of incest and for its oriental licence, the poem belongs to the moment when the exile's private history had become a matter of public speculation and when the Turkish tale was the most saleable verse form in Britain. The second issue of 1814, greatly enlarged, doubled its length and gave the poem its final shape.
works.characters: the youth of Abydos; his half-sister and bride; their father, a lord in the pasha's power; the pasha of Abydos; the slave and confidante of the harem
works.structure: Two short cantos in continuous couplet narrative with embedded songs and dramatic addresses, the exposition compressed and the crisis deferred by lyric reflection.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the 1813 first issue and the much enlarged 1814 second issue are both authorial, and the differences are recorded in the variorum.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Idealized love and the lost beloved
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: The Bride of Lammermoor
altTitles: Tales of My Landlord, Third and Fourth Series
works.form: Historical novel and domestic tragedy; gothic romance of the pursued heroine and of the haunted house in the series' frame.
works.description: The most completely tragic of the historical novels, a story of ruined houses and a forced marriage on the Lammermoor coast, told with the series' antiquarian frame but with none of its reconciliation. The feuds of the assembled families are already dying when the plot begins, and the tragedy arises from the collision between an extinguished honour and a working legal ascendency. Its ending is one of the most quoted in Scottish fiction.
works.plot: Edgar, master of Ravenswood, dispossessed by the new law and the new wealth of Sir William Ashton, is warned by the old presbyterian servant of his house not to seek the family of his ruin, and yet loves Ashton's daughter Lucy. Ashton, scheming to secure his office, contracts a marriage between Lucy and the brutal Master of Bucklaw; Ravenswood appears at the contract, is affectedly entertained, and at the Wolf's Head tavern in Edinburgh writes his vow of revenge with a dagger. The nuptials are celebrated, the bride's mind gives way, and Ravenswood, pursued across the Lammermoor sands, perishes in the quicksand at the place long afterwards called the Wolf's Crag, whence neither horse nor rider was ever drawn; Ashton's house falls with him.
works.significance: Provided the archetypal plot of the forced marriage and the lost heiress, and one of the standard scenes of nineteenth-century melodrama and of later opera. It is the fullest example of the school's tragic mode and of its treatment of property, entail and dispossession. Its frame and title-page matter have made it a central text in the editorial history of the series.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; the high rhetorical cadence of the servant's warnings and of the last scenes, with popular song and prophecy quoted.
works.context: Set in the reign of Queen Anne at the junction of the Scottish feuding order and the Union's legal government, and drawn from an actual East Lothian family tradition. The novel's atmosphere of extinguished aristocracy reflects the condition of the Border gentry after forfeiture and after the collapse of the Jacobite cause. Its composition followed close on the publication of the preceding series and was partly a reply to criticism of the second.
works.characters: Edgar, master of Ravenswood; Lucy Ashton; Sir William Ashton; the Master of Bucklaw; Lady Ashton; the Warden of the Three Towers
works.structure: Framed tale in the same editorial apparatus as the series, with the landlord's letter and preface; third-person interior narrative dominated by set scenes of hospitality, contract and pursuit; the concluding disappearance is reported rather than shown.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; authorship undisputed.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Blood-feud, vengeance, and kinship
Jacobitism, loyalty, and the '45
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Bride's Tragedy
works.description: A blank-verse tragedy of love, duel, and death in an Italian setting, written two years before the author went up to Oxford and published in his nineteenth year. It is constructed self-consciously on the models of the later Elizabethan and Jacobean drama, with short scenes, a heavy use of exclamation, and an ending in which the bridal and the funeral coincide. The volume established its author's reputation among the younger critics and reviewers of the early 1820s.
works.plot: A young man of a great house loves a bride whose kin has been killed by his sword, and the marriage is made against the duty of blood that the widow and the kinsmen insist upon. Honour, jealousy, and the importunity of friends drive the pairs of lovers through a series of confrontations in which the past crime is repeatedly recalled and never forgiven. The closing acts bring the wronged household and the bridal chamber together, and the play ends in death for the lovers, with the funeral taking the place of the wedding it had promised. The interest is rhetorical and funereal rather than dramatic, the situation being explored for its imagery of love and dissolution.
works.significance: The Bride's Tragedy is the earliest and most influential English drama of the Romantic period to be written deliberately in the Jacobean manner, and its reception fixed the reputation of the author as the poet of death. Its treatment of the bride and the tomb as one image has made it a reference point for studies of Gothic and fin-de-siècle sensibility.
works.meter: Blank verse of the old English school, deliberately Websterian and Tourneurian in its exclamation, its compound epithets, and its funeral imagery, with songs and dirges interposed; the line is declamatory and often broken rather than fluently conversational.
works.context: Written in 1819 and printed in 1822, in the first years of the revival of interest in the Jacobeans as models for a poetry of terror and mortality, when the young poets of the London magazines were editing and imitating the old drama. The author's own family connections ran to the Irish and English letters of the period, and the volume was the work of a Charterhouse and Oxford undergraduate.
works.structure: A five-act regular tragedy with an argument, built on rapid scene changes and on repeated confrontation rather than on slow development; the catastrophe unites the marriage plot and the revenge plot in a single death.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship, printed with the author's name; no dispute attends the play, though its early success rested on the praise of a small circle of reviewers.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Revenge and justice

works.title: The Bridge
works.description: The great American epic of the Brooklyn Bridge: the myth of America, the machine and the poetic imagination. It is a verse work of 1930 by Hart Crane; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poem begins with 'Proem: To Brooklyn Bridge' and moves through Columbus, Pocahontas, the subway, the Mississippi riverboat, the tramp, the sailor and the film comedians, ending with 'Atlantis' and a vision of the bridge as the symbol of American possibility and of the poet's own aspiration.
works.significance: The Bridge is the great American epic poem of the period and the most ambitious answer to The Waste Land: it attempted to give America a mythic poem of its own, and its fusion of the machine, the past and the imagination made it the most beautiful long poem of American modernism.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the dense, prophetic, syntactically compressed lyric.
works.context: The Brooklyn Bridge, New York in the 1920s, the American past from Columbus to the frontier, and Crane's reading of Whitman and Eliot. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1929 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
works.characters: Columbus; Pocahontas; Rip Van Winkle; the sailor; the poet
works.structure: Fifteen sections in a symphonic structure, from 'Ave Maria' to 'Atlantis'. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Harold Hart Crane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
works.description: The Pulitzer Prize novel of the five who fell: a bridge in Peru and the meaning of chance. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Thornton Wilder; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In 1714 the bridge of San Luis Rey in Peru collapses and five people fall to their deaths; Brother Juniper investigates their lives to prove the justice of God, and the novel reconstructs the five — the Marquesa, her daughter, Esteban, Uncle Pio and the little Jaime — in a meditation on love and accident.
works.significance: The Bridge of San Luis Rey won the Pulitzer Prize and is one of the great American novels of the century: its structure, its prose and its meditation on chance and love made it the finest American philosophical novel of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the bare stage and the Stage Manager.
works.context: Peru in the early eighteenth century, and the Spanish colonial world. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Brother Juniper; the Marquesa de Montemayor; Dona Clara; Esteban; Uncle Pio; Jaime
works.structure: A novel in five parts, reconstructing the lives of the five who fell. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thornton Niven Wilder. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The British Barbarians
works.description: Published in 1895 and Allen's satirical anthropology of English life: a visitor from the twenty-fifth century observes the barbarism of the Victorian suburb. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Grant Allen; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Bertram Ingledew, a traveller from a future civilisation, arrives in a Surrey suburb and studies its inhabitants as an anthropologist; he records their taboos — the worship of respectability, the ritual of the Sunday, the sacrifice of women to the marriage law, the fetish of property — and finally leaves them to their barbarism.
works.significance: The British Barbarians is the most effective English satirical utopia of the 1890s and the model for the modern anthropological satire of one's own society: its device of the future observer among the suburban Victorians made it a landmark of English social criticism, and it is one of the funniest and most radical books of its decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery.
works.context: 1895: the vogue of the scientific utopia after Bellamy and Morris, the anthropology of the 1890s, and the New Woman debate on marriage and the family. The record dates the work as composed in 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Bertram Ingledew, the visitor from the future; Philip Christy; Frida Monteith, Philip's sister; Robert Monteith, Frida's husband
works.structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.

works.title: The British Recluse
altTitles: The British Recluse: A Pastoral Romance
works.form: pastoral romance in prose with interspersed verse
works.description: A short pastoral romance in which a retired lady and her companion recount the course of their loves in a cultivated English landscape. It is the author's deliberate domestication of the French heroic pastoral into English scenes, with songs and dialogues interspersed among the narrated histories.
works.plot: Two gentlewomen, withdrawn from the town and its disappointments, pass their retirement in a British grove, where they tell and answer one another's histories of service, constancy and betrayal. Their own loves are reported in the manner of pastoral gallantry, trials of fidelity intervene, and the tales close in reconciliation rather than in tragedy. The frame presents retirement itself as the moral condition of the narrative.
works.significance: It shows the persistence of the heroic pastoral mode inside the emerging novel and is a document of the woman writer's control of the romance tradition, later reworked by the same hand in the novel of conduct.
works.meter: Ornamented romantic prose relieved by short lyric songs and dialogues in the conventional pastoral measures of the day.
works.context: Published in 1728 in a volume issued with a comic opera adaptation, in the season of the pastoral revival and of the quarrel over the theatre's licentiousness; its retirement theme answers the town satire of the same years.
works.structure: A framed pastoral with embedded tales and interspersed songs; the dialogue of the two narrators gives the sequence and the recessional structure of the romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the tale was gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction and reissued in the 1730s.

works.title: The Broken Heart
works.description: Ford's stately tragedy set in Sparta, in which the enforced marriage of Penthea to the aged Bassanes destroys her love for Orgilus, and the play ends in a chain of ritual deaths.
works.plot: Orgilus, cheated of his love Penthea by her brother Ithocles' ambition, returns in disguise; Ithocles loves the Spartan princess Calantha, whose father the king dies; Orgilus kills Ithocles, Penthea starves herself, and Calantha dies of a broken heart.
works.significance: Ford's most artistically controlled tragedy and the clearest Caroline example of a tragedy of honour, obligation, and emotional starvation.
works.meter: Blank verse with lyric interludes and songs, of unusually measured and elegiac cadence.
works.context: Published in 1633; probably written for a private playhouse or for court reading, given its restrained action and heavy lyricism.

works.title: The Brother of Daphne
works.description: The funniest comic thriller of the century: the Berry books begin. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by Dornford Yates; it is catalogued here under Novel of Manners and Fashion; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners.
works.plot: Daphne's brother and his friends — Berry, Boy, Jonah and the narrator — fall into a series of comic adventures on the Continent and in the English countryside, in the collection that founded the Berry books and the gentleman-adventurer comedy.
works.significance: The Brother of Daphne founded the Berry books and the comic gentleman-adventurer novel: its dialogue, its farce and its upper-class world made Dornford Yates one of the most popular and funniest writers of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of manners: the dialogue of the social world, the exact vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built on the breach or the observance of a convention. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The author's characteristic manner is the comic dialogue of the gentleman-adventurer.
works.context: England and the Continent before the First World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1914 and first published in 1914 and it is catalogued under novel of manners and fashion; comic novel and the satire of manners.

works.title: The Brothers
works.description: Young's domestic tragedy of two brothers, one of whom is condemned for a capital offence against a family's honour, drawn from the recent criminal case reported in the ordinary accounts of the town.
works.plot: A seduced woman's accusation, a mistaken identity and the pursuit of the brothers through the stages of flight, trial and sentence bring one to the scaffold, while the father's anguish and the brother's devotion fill the play's intervals of pathos.
works.significance: It is the founding example of the English tragedy of the gallows and of the middle-rank family, the dramatic complement to Lillo's London merchant, and it fixed Young's reputation as the poet of mourning.
works.meter: Blank verse deliberately reduced to the nearest speech of grief, with the short exclamatory line and the address to the sufferer.
works.context: Written and acted in the year of the Beggar's Opera's triumph, when the criminal case on the stage and in the ordinary was a popular species and when the controversy over laughing and sentimental comedy was opening.
works.characters: the two brothers; the injured woman; the father; the judges and officers of the law
works.structure: Five acts of domestic calamity in the plainest tragic manner, with the trial and the execution as the two public crises framing the family's private distress.

works.title: The Brownies and Other Tales
works.description: Published in 1870 and Ewing's best-known collection: the story of a boy who dreams himself into a race of helpful brownies, and other tales of childhood, work and kindness. It is a prose fiction work of 1870 by Juliana Horatia Ewing; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
works.plot: 'The Brownies' follows Tommy and his brother Johnnie, the idle sons of a widowed tailor, who learn from the Old Owl that they themselves can be the brownies who do the housework unseen; the volume also includes 'The Land of Lost Toys', 'Three Christmas Trees' and 'An Idyll of the Wood'.
works.significance: The Brownies is a classic of Victorian children's literature and one of the first stories to make work itself a pleasure rather than a duty; its title entered the English language as the name of the junior girl guides.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a child's-eye view.
works.context: The 1860s, the Victorian children's magazine Aunt Judy's, and the folklore of the household spirit. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1870 and first published in 1870 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Tommy and Johnnie, the tailor's sons ('The Brownies'); their father, the tailor; the Old Owl
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Juliana Horatia Gatty. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Brus
works.description: John Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert Bruce and the Scottish wars of independence, completed c. 1375 in some 14,000 octosyllabic lines: the murder of the Red Comyn, the crowning at Scone, the years of guerrilla warfare, and the great victory at Bannockburn (1314), with James Douglas as the poem's second hero. The first great work of Scottish literature and the fountainhead of the nation's heroic self-image.
works.plot: The poem follows Bruce from the killing of Comyn and his coronation through defeat, exile, and the legendary perseverance of the spider episode to the recovery of the kingdom castle by castle, the battle of Bannockburn, the raids of Douglas into England, and the king's death — all framed by the poem's great theme, that 'fredome is a noble thing'.
works.significance: The first great poem in Scots and the founding text of Scottish national literature; Burns's 'Scots Wha Hae' and the whole Bruce tradition descend from it.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of energy and speed, in Older Scots.
works.context: Completed in 1375 by the archdeacon of Aberdeen, in the court of Robert II (Bruce's grandson), when the Stewart dynasty needed a heroic past; preserved in two manuscripts (1487, 1489) and printed in 1571.
works.characters: Robert Bruce; James Douglas; Edward II; Edward Bruce; the Scottish and English armies
works.structure: Twenty books of continuous narrative in the romance-chronicle manner, with set-piece battles and speeches, closed by the king's death and the poet's envoy.
works.attributionNotes: Barbour's authorship secure (named in the text and the royal records).
themes: Fortune and mutability
Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle

works.title: The Brut Chronicle
works.description: The Middle English prose Brut, the most popular secular text in late medieval England: a chronicle of Britain from the Trojan Brutus through the Arthurian kings to the fourteenth century, with continuations carrying the story through the Wars of the Roses. Over 180 manuscripts survive in English — more than any other secular work — and Caxton's print (1480) made it the standard popular history of England.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the legendary British history of the Brut tradition — Brutus, Lear, Arthur — then the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns, with the continuations adding the Lancastrian and Yorkist wars; its plain, annalistic prose made it the layman's history of England.
works.significance: The bestselling secular book of the English Middle Ages: its diffusion defines the popular historical culture out of which Tudor history writing grew.
works.meter: Plain, formulaic prose of the chronicle tradition.
works.context: The earliest version was made in the later fourteenth century, probably in London, from French and Latin sources; it was expanded continuously through the fifteenth century (the 'common version' to 1419, continuations to 1461 and later) and printed by Caxton in 1480.
works.characters: Brutus; Arthur; the kings of England to Edward IV
works.structure: A regnal chronicle in the Brut tradition, open-ended and continuously continued by successive compilers.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous and compilational.
themes: Arthurian legend
National identity and Englishness

works.title: The Buccaneer, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, with lyric and meditative poems; the maritime branch of the American romantic poem
works.description: The first collected volume of the Boston and Cambridge poet who was also the most discerning critic of his generation in America. Its title poem is a narrative of the sea in the romantic manner, and the accompanying pieces treat passion, solitude and the power of scenery. The book introduced to American readers the command of blank verse associated with the review circle of the United States.
works.plot: The title poem tells of a buoyant and lawless sea-rover whose career of plunder ends in remorse and in a death that the ocean itself seems to witness. Its narrative is interrupted by invocations to the sea, to the storm and to the memory of the beloved. The shorter poems pass from love and loss to meditative observation of New England and Italian scenery. The volume's dominant movement is from romantic action to the moral seriousness that its author later brought to criticism.
works.significance: It is one of the ablest American metrical tales of the 1820s and a landmark of the maritime strand in American romantic verse. Its author's criticism made the volume a document of the transatlantic argument about poetry. It supplies the link between the review culture of Boston and the native romance of the sea.
works.meter: Blank verse for the metrical tale, with iambic lyric stanzas for the shorter poems
works.context: Published in 1827, when its author was an editor and critic in Boston and Cambridge and a member of the circle that shaped the American review. Its subject belongs to the New England commerce with the sea and to the Byron-derived romance of the outlaw. The volume's reception was bound up with the quarrels of the native periodicals over the possibility of an American poetry.
works.characters: The buccaneer; the beloved of the meditative pieces
works.structure: Collected volume with one dominant metrical tale of the sea, followed by lyrics and meditative pieces of occasional origin.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; a small number of handbook accounts date the first collection to the late 1820s, and the year here follows the literary histories consulted.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Sea voyage and seafaring
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters
