works.title: The Buke of the Howlat
works.description: Richard Holland's Scottish alliterative beast-allegory of some 1,000 lines, composed c. 1448 for the Douglas family: the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the assembly of birds to the pope and the emperor, each bird vying in flattery, until Dame Nature restores him to his proper worth. A satire of pride, courts, and flattery, and the last major alliterative poem of the tradition.
works.plot: The howlat, complaining of his feathers, is counselled by the peacock to seek redress; the birds assemble in parliament before the pope and emperor, but the debate degenerates into mutual slander and sycophancy, until Nature intervenes, clothes the owl in dignity, and the poem ends with the Douglas heraldry and the family's praise.
works.significance: The last major alliterative poem in the British tradition and a key document of Douglas politics, heraldry, and the Scottish reception of the Alliterative Revival.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1448 by Richard Holland, secretary to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for the Douglas family at a moment of their power; preserved in the Asloan and Bannatyne manuscripts (c. 1515, 1568).
works.characters: the Howlat; the Peacock; the Pope; the Emperor; Dame Nature; the birds of the parliament
works.structure: A beast-parliament in the Chaucerian manner, framed by the owl's complaint and closed by the heraldic celebration of the Douglases.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Holland on the evidence of the poem's colophon and Douglas records.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: The Busie Body
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A city comedy of gossip, project and guardianship, the play that established its author as the most successful woman dramatist of the early eighteenth century. Its busy-bodies, a pair of meddling widows who superintend everyone's affairs, frame a plot of a fortune-hunting colonel, a ward and her several suitors.
works.plot: An amorous colonel arrives in London resolved to make his court to a rich ward, and finds her guarded by two busy-body neighbours who report his designs and arrange her marriage to a fool. His servant and the ward's lovers counterplot, a ball and its gig of the age assemble the company, and the final division of the lady's property among three competitors exposes the arithmetic of the marriage market. The busy-bodies themselves are outwitted and reconciled to the younger pair.
works.significance: It is the central instance of the post-Restoration city comedy rewritten for a Whig commercial audience, and a landmark in the history of women's professional playwriting; its treatment of female guardianship and of the price of an heiress anticipates the comic novel.
works.meter: Brisk prose dialogue with the irregular mixture of verse passes usual in early-eighteenth-century comedy; the scenes run on quick repartee and the interruption of gossip.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1709 and frequently revived; the division-of-property scene was read aloud in the House of Commons in 1719 during the debate on the bill against patent projecting, a mark of how topical its satire on project and gossip had become.
works.characters: the two busy-body neighbours; the fortune-hunting colonel; his witty servant; the wealthy ward; her three competing suitors; the projectors of the age
works.structure: Five-act city comedy in prose and verse with a strictly interlocked main and underplot; the scenes of the busy-bodies' surveillance provide the comic engine and the division-of-property set piece the climax.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and its success was registered in the pirated editions and revivals of the following decades.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Marriage and women's conduct
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
The city and urban life
movements: Comedy of Manners
The Restoration Theatre

works.title: The Butterfly's Ball, and the Grasshopper's Feast
works.form: children's poem of the beast-fable and assembly manner; the nursery party piece
works.description: The most enduring of the poems written for children of the period, a gay assembly of the insects of the garden given as an entertainment for the young, and printed in the smallest of the little volumes which the nursery trade made its own. It is at once a party piece, a natural-history lesson, and a miniature masquerade, and it passed into the nursery language of two continents.
works.plot: The poem invites the company of insects to the ball of the butterfly and the feast of the grasshopper, and musters the guest list of the garden and the hedge, the beetle, the fly, the moth, the bee, and the rest, with their several graces and their several follies. It then describes the company in assembly, the music, the dance, the supper, and the merriment, till the hour and the accident break up the party, and the little readers are left with the joke and the lesson of a pleasure that is over. The charm of the piece is its complete seriousness about a fantastic scene, the manners of a ball-room applied to the creatures of the summer grass, and the courtesy with which the smallest insect is introduced and remembered.
works.significance: It is one of the two or three poems which every generation of English-speaking children has said before it could read, and a landmark in the history of the verse written for the nursery, since with it the assembly of the creatures of the garden became a stock of the children's book. Its influence on the later animal-party poem, and its permanence as a piece of popular recitation, are among the curiouser facts of literary history, and its author is remembered by it rather than by his histories.
works.meter: Brisk rhyming couplets of comic nursery verse, with a triple-time swing and the refrains and catch-phrases of the children's song; the measure of the piece is one of the reasons of its memory.
works.context: Written by a man of letters who was also the historian of the Medici and the abolition poet, and first printed in the small volume of the nursery trade of the years after the turn of the century, when the picture-book and the gift-book for very young children became a distinct branch of publishing; it was reprinted with cuts through the century and crossed to America at once.
works.characters: The butterfly; the grasshopper; the company of the garden insects, the beetle, the moth, the fly, and the bee
works.structure: A single short poem of invitation, muster, entertainment, and breaking-up, in continuous rhymed verse with the list of the company as its central movement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was long circulated also in a prose version and with the added moral of the later nursery editors, and the earliest issues are small and imperfectly recorded.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Natural history, science, and the poetic eye

works.title: The Call of Cthulhu
works.description: The tale that built the Cthulhu Mythos from the three documents. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by H. P. Lovecraft; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Call of Cthulhu assembles the sculptor's bas-relief, the police report of the swamp cult and the sailor's narrative of the risen city to build the sleeping god of R'lyeh, in the documentary structure that makes the mythos - the cult, the book and the buried god - the architecture of the modern weird tale.
works.significance: The Call of Cthulhu is the founding tale of the Cthulhu Mythos: its three documents, its cult and its risen R'lyeh gave the weird tale its shared cosmology and its cosmic horror the form the later century inherited.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript.
works.context: Providence, Louisiana and the Pacific, in the years of the dreaming god. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: the sculptor; Inspector Legrasse; Gustaf Johansen; Cthulhu
works.structure: A weird tale in three documents: the bas-relief, the cult, the risen city. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Howard Phillips Lovecraft. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale
themes: Mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent
Myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination
movements: The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale

works.title: The Call of the Wild
works.description: Published in 1903 and the most widely read American novel of the north: a domestic dog's return to the wild in the Klondike. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by Jack London; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Buck, a huge St Bernard cross, is stolen from a California ranch and sold into the Klondike gold rush; he is beaten into the sled traces, learns the law of the club and the fang, is rescued by John Thornton, and after Thornton's murder by Indians answers the call of the wild and runs with a wolf pack.
works.significance: The Call of the Wild created the modern American myth of the north and remains the most widely read American novel ever published: its animal point of view, its Darwinian allegory and its primitivist ending made it a permanent classic, and it established London as the most popular American writer of his day.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third.
works.context: 1897-1903: the Klondike gold rush, the sled dogs of the Yukon, the Darwinian and Spencerian ideas of the age, and the American market for the adventure story. The record dates the work as composed in 1903 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Buck; John Thornton; François; Perrault; Manuel; Judge Miller; the Yeehats
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Griffith London. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

The American wilderness and the myth of the forest
The closing of the American frontier

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece and the supreme achievement of Middle English literature: a frame-tale collection in which some thirty pilgrims journeying from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury agree to a storytelling contest, the tales ranging from the Knight's romance and the Miller's fabliau to the Wife of Bath's prologue, the Pardoner's sermon, and the Parson's treatise. Begun c. 1387 and left unfinished at Chaucer's death in 1400.
works.plot: In the General Prologue the narrator joins a company of pilgrims — knight, miller, reeve, wife of Bath, pardoner, summoner, nun's priest, and the rest — each vividly portrayed; Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes the tale-telling game, and the tales that follow answer and quarrel with one another across the whole range of medieval genres, from courtly romance (Knight, Squire, Franklin) through fabliau (Miller, Reeve, Shipman, Merchant) and saint's life (Second Nun, Prioress) to sermon (Pardoner), beast fable (Nun's Priest), and the closing penitential treatise of the Parson.
works.significance: The most influential single work of English literature: its pilgrims, its tales, and its frame established the English tradition of comic realism, dramatic monologue, and narrative irony that runs through Shakespeare to the novel.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of unprecedented flexibility, with rhyme royal, tail-rhyme, and prose for special effects; the decasyllabic line perfected.
works.context: Composed c. 1387–1400 in London, drawing on Boccaccio, Ovid, Boethius, and the estates tradition; the pilgrimage to Becket's shrine at Canterbury supplied the frame; circulated in some eighty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1476–78) and his successors, making it the foundation of the English printed canon.
works.characters: the Narrator; the Host (Harry Bailly); the Knight; the Miller; the Reeve; the Wife of Bath; the Pardoner; the Friar; the Summoner; the Nun's Priest; the Parson; and the other pilgrims
works.structure: A frame narrative (the pilgrimage, the Host's game) enclosing twenty-four tales grouped into ten fragments; the links between tales stage the pilgrims' quarrels and judgments, and the work's unfinished state is part of its design.
works.attributionNotes: Uniquely well attested: Chaucer's authorship of the Tales is not in doubt, though the ordering of the fragments and some links are editorial.

Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: The Cantos
works.form: Long poem (A Draft of XVI Cantos, 1925; continued to 1970)
works.description: The modernist epic without an epic: a hundred and seventeen cantos of history, economics, myth and invective. It is a verse work of 1925 by Ezra Pound; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Cantos begin with Odysseus's descent to the underworld and move through the Italian Renaissance, the Chinese ideogram, the American founding fathers, the troubadours, the Confucian order, the usury of the bankers, the Pisan prison camp and the wreck of the poet's own politics — assembling a history of civilisation out of quotation, translation and collage.
works.significance: The Cantos are the great unfinished epic of modernism: they extended the method of The Waste Land to the scale of a civilisation, made the long poem a field rather than a narrative, and are inseparable from the political catastrophe of Pound's fascism — the period's central case of the poet's political failure.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the image as the unit of the poem.
works.context: Western and Chinese history as Pound understood it, the First World War, Italian fascism, the poet's imprisonment at Pisa in 1945, and the economic theories that led him to political catastrophe. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1970 and first published in 1925 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
works.characters: Odysseus; Sigismundo Malatesta; John Adams; Confucius; the poet himself
works.structure: One hundred and seventeen cantos in a collage of quotation, translation and juxtaposition. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ezra Loomis Pound. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Cardinal
works.description: Shirley's last tragedy, written in Ireland and performed at the Cockpit in 1641, in which a scheming cardinal forces a marriage that leads to poisoning, madness, and death.
works.plot: The Cardinal, thwarted in his own designs on the Duchess of Pavia, compels her to marry his protégé Columbo; when she loves the soldier Alvarez instead, Columbo kills him, and the Duchess poisons the Cardinal and herself.
works.significance: A late and vigorous Caroline revenge tragedy, notable for its portrait of ecclesiastical ambition and for closing Shirley's career.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Composed during Shirley's Irish period and revived at the Cockpit in 1641, on the eve of the civil wars; printed in Shirley's Six New Plays of 1653.
works.characters: the Cardinal; the Duchess of Pavia; Columbo; Alvarez; Celinde; Hernando
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a catastrophic denouement.

works.title: The Careless Husband
works.form: Domestic comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for a particular acting company and printed from the theatre's text.
works.description: A comedy brought out by the Drury Lane company at the end of 1704 and printed in the following year, which keeps the machinery of Restoration sexual intrigue but redirects it towards the reformation of a rake and the reconciliation of a married couple. Its central conceit, a woman's virtue tested while she lies unsuspecting and asleep, supplied the eighteenth century's most celebrated showcase for an actress. The play is habitually cited as the hinge between the libertine comedy of the 1690s and the sentimental domestic drama of the following generations.
works.plot: Sir Charles Easy, a hot-tempered and inattentive husband, has come to believe that his wife Lady Easy has countenanced the addresses of Lord Careless, a gay seducer whose boast is that no woman has yet refused him. The jealousy of the husband and the vanity of the rake are answered by a stratagem of the wife's own: she writes the assignation, then contrives that she shall be found asleep in a posture that seems to invite surprise. Lord Careless, admitted to the chamber and discovering the unconscious lady, contends with himself, leaves the written appointment unfilled, and abandons the design. In the underplot the young fop Sir Easy Foppington, lately and unwillingly married, makes a fool of himself in courtship of the housemaid, and the valet Moody is detected in picking his master's pocket. Convinced by these proofs of his wife's constancy, Sir Charles asks her pardon; the reformed rake is reconciled to the family he had traduced, and the comedy closes with forgiveness and marriages.
works.significance: It is the standard example of the century's turn from libertine wit to sentimental proof of female constancy, and it gave the stage a situation, a woman's virtue tested in her own unconsciousness, that novelists of the next generation and later domestic drama exploited. Its mixed inheritance of intrigue and moral seriousness makes it a fixed reference point in accounts of how English comedy changed after 1700.
works.meter: Familiar prose speech with quick re-partee and deliberate pauses, the pauses carrying the moral weight of the sleeping scene; the customary prologue and epilogue spoken to the audience are in closed couplets.
works.context: The manager-actor who wrote it had helped to run the Drury Lane company since the patent lapsed in 1695, and the piece answers the stage-anti-stage campaign of the 1690s by offering a comedy in which seduction is refused and reform is won on the stage. The fop plot continues the city-marriage and chambermaid intrigue that the same management had made its stock in trade. The play held the repertory through the century and remained a trial of skill for leading performers.
works.characters: Sir Charles Easy; Lady Easy; Lord Careless; Sir Easy Foppington; Moody the valet; the chambermaid courted by the young fop
works.structure: Five-act stage comedy with a main plot and a fop underplot tightly linked by their shared subject of tried virtue; the movement runs from suspicion through a single staged trial of a woman's constancy to public vindication and marriage, with the sleeping scene at the centre as the turning-point.

works.title: The Carved Lions
works.description: Published in 1895 and Molesworth's finest late novel: the story of two children sent away to a boarding school, and of the carved lions on the staircase that become their comfort. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Mary Louisa Molesworth; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Geraldine LeMarchant, looking back across fifty years, tells how her father took a post with a bank in South America and her mother went with him, leaving her brother Haddie at a preparatory school for Rugby and Geraldine at Miss Ledbury's boarding school, Green Bank; lonely and misunderstood, she runs away to the furniture shop whose great carved lions she and Haddie had imagined coming alive, and is taken in by kind friends who give her a gentler home.
works.significance: The Carved Lions is one of the most affecting Victorian children's books about loneliness and the consolations of the imagination; it is a key text in the history of the school story and of children's fantasy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unhurried narrative.
works.context: The 1890s, the Victorian boarding school, and the literature of the unhappy child. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Geraldine LeMarchant, the narrator; Haddie, her brother; their parents; Miss Ledbury; Myra
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Molesworth. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Case of Rebellious Susan
works.description: First performed in 1894 and the wittiest English comedy on the double standard: a wife retaliates against her husband's infidelity and finds the retaliation harder than the injury. It is a dramatic work of 1894 by Henry Arthur Jones; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lady Susan Harabin, whose husband has been unfaithful, takes a young admirer to Cairo as a deliberate counter-scandal; the comedy follows her husband's fury, her own disillusion, and the worldly-wise intervention of her older friend Sir Richard, who arranges a reconciliation in which nobody is allowed to be honest.
works.significance: The Case of Rebellious Susan is the most intelligent English comedy on the double standard of the 1890s: its wit and its refusal of either sentimentality or moralising made it the model for the modern comedy of manners, and it is the best of Jones's social plays.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the strong melodramatic situation with a moral core.
works.context: 1894: the New Woman debate, the divorce law and the double standard, the English colony in Cairo, and the West End theatre of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and first performed in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Lady Susan Harabin; Sir Richard Kato; Lucius Harabin; Elaine Shrimpton; Lady Darlington; the Rev. Mr Brabazon
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry A. Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: The Castaway
works.form: meditative lyric on an occurrent disaster, in the graveyard-school manner of gloom and self-analysis
works.description: Cowper's shortest and starkest poem, founded on the wreck of an East Indiaman in which one seaman, described as deranged, was said to have been lost, and turning the incident into a figure of the poet's own spiritual exposure. The speaker watches the thoughtless crew about their business while the abandoned man lies at the mast foot, and the wreck becomes an image of the soul for whom no pity and no hope remain. It is the most intense of the preromantic lyrics of desolation.
works.plot: The poem reports the wreck, the crew's exertions and the fate of the abandoned seaman who, past reason and past hope, was left to the sea. The speaker then draws the moral likeness: he too is exposed without pity, without prayer and without the sympathies that keep others from despair. The closing stanzas refuse consolation, identifying the castaway with a man abandoned both of God and man, and leave the figure of the storming sea as the poem's last image.
works.significance: It is the poem by which Cowper is most often read as a precursor of Romantic despair, and one of the strongest lyrics of abandonment in English. Its identification of a public news-item with private spiritual state makes it a document of the culture of feeling and of the graveyard meditation.
works.meter: Ballad-like stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a solemn rhyme, the measure giving the poem its hymn-like severity.
works.context: Written in January 1785 on the news of the loss of an East Indiaman eastward, in the same months in which Cowper's religious depression was returning; the wreck lies near the centre of the decade's interest in maritime disaster, providence and the limits of sympathy.
works.characters: The lost seaman; the surviving crew; the meditative speaker
works.structure: A brief narrative in short stanzas, passing from the reported wreck to the meditative identification of the speaker with the castaway and ending without consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Cowper's own letter, and the year usually given for the first printing is 1786, a reckoning followed here with the qualification recorded in the bibliographical note.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Evangelical experience and assurance
Melancholy and self-analysis

works.title: The Castle of Health
works.description: Elyot's vernacular treatise on diet and regimen, the first substantial English medical handbook written by a layman for lay readers.
works.plot: The book surveys the four humours and complexions, the properties of foods and drinks, sleep, exercise, and the regimen proper to each age and season, advising the reader how to preserve health through moderation and self-knowledge.
works.significance: A landmark in the vernacularization of medicine and natural knowledge in Tudor England, influential on later dietary literature and a document of humanist attitudes to the body.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the mid-1530s and printed by Thomas Berthelet in 1539 (with editions to 1610); Elyot's attempt to bring learned medicine into English paralleled his linguistic programme in The Governour.
works.structure: Four books of systematic exposition, compiled from Galen, Hippocrates, and the medieval regimen literature.
themes: Medicine, healing, and the body
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The Castle of Indolence
altTitles: The Castle of Indolence: An Allegorical Poem
works.description: Thomson's last and most finished allegorical poem, in the Spenserian measure: a knight is allured into the castle of Indolence, its slumber, its luxury and its self-consuming sweetness, and is delivered by the sight of the wizard's own punishment and of the castle's fall.
works.plot: Two companions, the lover of labour and the lover of ease, come to the enchanted castle; the slumbry of its inhabitants, the pleasures of its gardens and the tales of its enchanter's love hold the indolent guest fast, until the philosophy of the active life and the destruction of the place recover him to virtue.
works.significance: It restored the Spenserian stanza to English verse, and it remains the period's most complete poem on the temptation of ease, answering the season's own moral economy with an allegory of the unspent life.
works.meter: The nine-line Spenserian stanza, revived by Thomson for this poem and used with a sensuous richness of sound that made the measure a permanent option for English allegory.
works.context: Conceived in the early 1730s as a burlesque of the poet's own company and long retouched before its publication in the year of his death, when the Spenserian revival, the poetry of retirement and the moral argument about industry were all active.
works.characters: the two guests of the castle; the enchanter of the place and his fair one; the personified indolence and her crew
works.structure: Two cantos of continuous allegorical narrative, with the inserted tale of the enchanter and his fair one, the personified crew of the castle and the moral conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

works.title: The Castle of Otranto
altTitles: The Castle of Otranto. A Story. Translated by William Marshal, Gent. From the Original Italian of Onuphrio Murelli
works.form: Gothic romance and tale of terror
works.description: A Gothic tale of a tyrant prince of Apulia, his giant helmet, his murdered son and the prophecy that his castle and name would fall to the rightful possessor, published as a translation from an Italian original of the sixteenth century. It founded the romance of terror and supplied the machinery, the castle and the curse that the following generation of writers inherited.
works.plot: Manfred's son Conrad is crushed to death by an enormous helmet on the day of his marriage, and Manfred, needing an heir, designs to divorce his wife and take the young Isabella himself. Isabella flees through the castle's secret passages, and the captive Theodore is discovered and released, Manfred's daughter Matilda being killed by her father's mistake in the dark. The prophecy is fulfilled as the castle falls and the true possession is restored to Theodore, Manfred retiring to a cloister.
works.significance: It is the founding work of the Gothic and the origin of a whole century's popular fiction; its prefatory theory of romance made it also a piece of criticism, and its imitation of the old tales defined the literature of terror.
works.meter: A rapid, dramatic prose of portent and exclamation, modelled on the phraseology of the old translation and the tragedy of the stage; the inserted supernatural actions are reported in a plain chronicle manner.
works.context: Written at Strawberry Hill amid the antiquarian revival and published in 1764, in the season of the debate over the licentiousness of fiction and of the quarrel over the authenticity of the old romances; the second edition's confessions of the trick answered the charge of forgery.
works.characters: Manfred; Hippolita his wife; Matilda his daughter; Conrad and the murdered line; Isabella the escaped bride; Theodore the captive; the hermits and Friar Jerome
works.structure: A short continuous romance in five acts or chapters of the drama-like design, with the supernatural machinery appearing at the decisive moments; the second edition added the author's own preface and defence of romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published as a translation and a reprint from an unseen Italian original, a device withdrawn in the second edition, which acknowledged the modern authorship.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror

themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Kingship and good rule
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: The Castle of Perseverance
works.description: The earliest complete English morality play (c. 1400–25, 3,649 lines): the life of Mankind (Humanum Genus) from birth to judgement, staged on the famous circular 'place' with its central castle and five scaffolds, as the virtues and vices battle for his soul through the Seven Ages. The most ambitious play of the English medieval stage.
works.plot: Mankind, born in sin, is led by his Bad Angel through World, Flesh, and the Devil to the seven deadly sins; rescued by Confession, he is garrisoned in the Castle of Perseverance with the virtues; the sins' siege fails, but Covetousness wins him in old age, until Death strikes and the debate of the four daughters of God — Mercy, Peace, Righteousness, Truth — yields his salvation.
works.significance: The foundational English morality: its stage diagram, its allegorical cast, and its theology of mercy set the pattern for the genre through Everyman to the Elizabethan stage.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanzas (rime couée with wheel), with stage directions prescribing the elaborate fixed staging.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–25 in East Anglia (the manuscript's language is Norfolk), in the milieu of the great fifteenth-century moralities; preserved uniquely in the Macro manuscript (Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354, c. 1440) with Mankind and Wisdom.
works.characters: Mankind (Humanum Genus); the Bad and Good Angels; World, Flesh, and the Devil; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Seven Virtues; Confession; Death; God; the Four Daughters of God
works.structure: A four-scaffold cosmic drama (God; World; Flesh; Devil) around the central castle, with the banns, the siege, the death scene, and the parliament of heaven as its great movements.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: The Castle Spectre
works.form: Gothic drama and musical romance of the patent theatre; tragedy with interpolated song and spectacle.
works.description: A gothic drama of haunted castle, murdered mother and forced marriage, written for a London patent theatre and built around spectacle, songs and the rising of a spectre from her grave. Its plot of a woman compelled to wed the lord of the castle, and of a guilt that walks the vaults at night, made it one of the most acted romantic dramas of the decade. Its machinery was openly criticised by the new review press while its music and its ghost scene held the stage for a generation.
works.plot: Madeline, the ward of the castle, is commanded by its lord, Osbert, to become his bride, while her attachment belongs to another; the confessor Father Dominic, who has designs of his own on the inheritance, counsels compliance. The castle vaults give up their history: the spectre of a lady murdered in an earlier generation appears, and the secrets of the house, including a concealed child and a dead woman's testimony, are disclosed. Osbert, pursued by the apparition and by his own crimes, is brought to a dreadful catastrophe; Madeline is delivered, the hidden kinship is unravelled, and the drama closes with the exposition of the family guilt.
works.significance: One of the most successful and most attacked of the romantic dramas, and a standard reference for the stage history of gothic. Its handling of the haunted vault and of the compelled heroine supplied scenes and plots to later melodrama. Its reception documents the critical reaction against terror machinery at the close of the 1790s.
works.meter: Verse and prose: blank verse five-beat lines for the serious dialogue, with metrical songs and choruses set to music for the stage.
works.context: Produced in the season when gothic spectacle was the stock-in-trade of the great London theatres, and when the restricted patents made such machinery a commercial necessity. Its songs, written to be set, belonged to the long fashion for the ballad opera revival. The reviews of the later 1790s, which attacked the play's improbability, mark the beginning of the campaign against gothic stage machinery.
works.characters: Madeline; Lord Osbert of the castle; Father Dominic; Edmund, the minstrel; Alice, the gipsy; the spectre of the murdered lady
works.structure: Regular five-act drama with songs, chorus and spectacular scenic effects; the supernatural is presented as evidence, and the exposition of the buried history is deferred to the apparition scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Published and performed with the author's name; no dispute.
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Love, constancy, and betrayal
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Caxtons: A Family Picture
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1849 and Bulwer's gentlest and most successful family novel: the education of a young man by his bookish father and his practical uncle. It is a prose fiction work of 1849 by Edward Bulwer-Lytton; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Pisistratus Caxton, the son of a gentle, unworldly scholar, grows up between his father's books and his uncle Roland's soldierly pride; in London he becomes secretary to the politician Trevanion and falls hopelessly in love with his daughter Fanny, the family's money is lost in Uncle Jack's speculations, and he emigrates to Australia with Roland's prodigal son Vivian, returning to restore the family fortunes and marry his cousin Blanche while his father's great history of human error goes forward.
works.significance: The Caxtons was the most popular of Bulwer's domestic novels and one of the finest English family chronicles of the 1840s: its affectionate portrait of a bookish father and its comedy of literary ambition made it a great favourite, and it inaugurated the 'My Novel' series that carried the family story into the 1850s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue.
works.context: 1849: the English country parsonage, the literary market of the 1840s, and the Victorian ideal of the family as a school of character. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1849 and first published in 1849 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Pisistratus Caxton, the narrator; Austin Caxton, his father; Kitty Caxton, his mother; Captain Roland de Caxton, his uncle; Herbert de Caxton (Vivian), Roland's son; Blanche, Roland's daughter; Uncle Jack Tibbets; Albert Trevanion; Fanny Trevanion; Mr Squills
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Cenci
works.form: Revenge tragedy and domestic tragedy in blank verse, without supernatural machinery; the historical crime tragedy of the Italian chronicle tradition turned to a study of violated duty and of state justice.
works.description: A five-act historical tragedy in blank verse, founded on the chronicle of a Roman count who murdered his children's father with the help of his stepmother and was for that crime executed by the papal court. Its preface uses the story to argue for a drama of human passion rather than of allegory, and the tragedy sets a father's violation against a daughter's duty and a state's justice. It is the period's most sustained attempt to write revenge tragedy without its machinery, and the most terrible treatment of tyranny within the family in Romantic drama.
works.plot: A father returning from banishment discovers his estates seized and his wife and daughters ruined by his own expense, and resolves on a vengeance which he conceals from his son and reveals only to God's ministers as a duty. The son is murdered on a mountain pass by the hired ruffians and thrown into a lake, and the father, fearing discovery, violates his daughter, whose long denial and final appeal to the law fail before the corruption of the courts. Her stepmother then persuades the household servants to the murder, the body is carried to the chamber and stabbed in the night, and the trace of the crime is found in the rings that were melted from the fingers. All are tried at the papal court, tortured and condemned, and the daughter, her mother and her brother are executed, while the last act shows the survivors' fate and the poet's own comment on the justice that avenged the first crime.
works.significance: It is the strongest of the period's closet tragedies and a central text in the argument about whether the Romantic drama could be acted at all, its preface supplying the period's sharpest defence of character over allegory. Its treatment of sexual tyranny within the patriarchal house and of the failure of legal remedy anticipated a permanent theme of later literature, and its daughter remains the century's most terrible figure of wronged endurance.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, deliberately plainspoken and close to dialogue, with short stichomythic exchanges in the trial scenes and only a few lyric passages.
works.context: Written at Rome and Naples in 1819, in the year of the poet's permanent settlement in Italy and of the executions and imprisonments that followed the failures of the Italian risings, and published in the same year with a preface on the difference between the ideal and the practical drama. Its matter came from a sixteenth-century Italian chronicle, and its treatment of papal justice and of paternal authority was a direct provocation to the Catholic and Tory reviews. It was read privately to a circle of friends in London in 1821, an event sometimes recorded as its first representation.
works.characters: the Roman count, the father and tyrant of the house; his first wife and her daughter; the stepmother who plans the murder; the elder son and the younger daughter who dies with them; the hired ruffians of the pass; the papal judge and the officer of the law
works.structure: Five acts of continuous tragedy in the classical manner, the violation deferred and reported rather than shown, the murder in the fourth act and the trial and executions in the fifth, with a choral comment carried by the surviving sister.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text was lightly revised in the posthumous collections, and the acting manuscript differs from the printed first edition in passages of the trial.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Revenge and justice
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: The Changeling
works.description: Middleton and Rowley's tragedy of desire and madness: Beatrice-Joanna, betrothed to Alonzo but in love with Alsemero, commissions the ugly servant De Flores to murder her fiancé; his price is her virginity, and the play follows the pair's descent through murder, the bed-trick with the maid Diaphanta, and madness to the final deaths — while the comic sub-plot of the madhouse, where the pretended fools and madmen perform, doubles the theme of 'change'.
works.plot: De Flores kills Alonzo and claims Beatrice-Joanna; the wedding to Alsemero proceeds through the virginity-test and the Diaphanta substitution; the castle catches fire (in the plot), the murders of Diaphanta and the witnesses follow, and the final scene's confessions — Beatrice-Joanna's 'I am that of your blood was taken from you' — end with the lovers' deaths and the madhouse's ironic close.
works.significance: One of the great Jacobean tragedies — the study of complicity and self-loss ('the deed's creature') that T. S. Eliot would single out as the age's masterpiece of moral horror.
works.meter: Middleton's verse in the main plot — swift, ironic, and chilling — against Rowley's prose farce in the madhouse.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men in 1622, at court in 1624, and printed in 1653; based on Reynolds's God's Revenge Against Murder (1621).
works.characters: Beatrice-Joanna; De Flores; Alsemero; Alonzo de Piracquo; Tomazo de Piracquo; Vermandero; Diaphanta; Jasperino; the madhouse crew (Alibius, Lollio, Antonio, Franciscus, Isabella)
works.structure: A two-plot structure unique in the canon: the main tragic plot (by Middleton) and the madhouse comedy (by Rowley) run in deliberate counterpoint, never meeting until the thematic rhyme of the final scene.
works.attributionNotes: Middleton (main plot) and William Rowley (madhouse sub-plot) as stated on the title page; the division is uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Penance, confession, and sin
Women, chastity, and constancy

works.title: The Cheap Repository Tracts
works.form: religious and moral tract; didactic tale and dialogue for the labouring reader
works.description: A series of small religious and moral tracts, sold at the halfpenny and the penny, launched to supply the labouring poor with wholesome reading in place of the chapbook, the penny song, and the political pamphlet. Written mostly by one hand with the help of a few contributors, and paid for by subscription, it is the first organised experiment in the mass religious circulation of cheap print in England.
works.plot: The design is stated in the series' own terms: to imitate the form and the price of the corrupted chapbook while supplying it with Christian matter, so that the reader who would buy the obscene tale or the seditious song may buy instead a story that recommends industry, honesty, sobriety, and the church. The tracts therefore fall into an argument by example: the village tale of the good and bad servant, the dialogue of the ignorant labourer instructed by his superior, the account of a pious parish, and the plain exposition of the catechism and of the Sunday; each insists that religion is a practical rule of life and that the poor man's true comfort is his duty cheerfully done. Alongside the instruction runs a political argument in the same keys, the duty of submission to the established government, the danger of the new philosophy, and the blessing of the country's constitution. The series also carries a case for the religious education of the poor, and for the reading of the scripture in a form that may be trusted.
works.significance: It is the origin of the tract as an instrument of national religious and political circulation, the ancestor of the great tract societies of the nineteenth century, and an epoch in the history of reading among the poor, since it first proposed to reach the labouring reader on his own terms of price, form, and language. It also fixed a permanent stereotype of the didactic tale of the virtuous labourer, and it provoked the first great debate about the effect of cheap print upon the opinions of the people.
works.meter: Deliberately plain, colloquial, and dramatic prose, with the homely proverb, the dialogue of the ignorant and the knowing, and a warm humour of the village; the style of the tract as a designed instrument of persuasion.
works.context: Founded in the spring of 1795 in the heat of the counter-Revolutionary anxiety, when the circulation of cheap political and sceptical print among the labouring classes had become a subject of alarm to the government and to the religious societies, and supported by subscriptions from the nobility and the bishops. Its machinery of circulation, by which the tracts were sent out in astonishing numbers and dispersed through the country by the country subscribers, was the model of the tract society that followed.
works.structure: A continuously issued series of small tracts, generally of a few pages, in prose dialogue, tale, and exposition, each complete in itself and numbered as it appeared; the units were afterwards gathered in collected series.
works.attributionNotes: The series is a joint undertaking in its circulation and in a few of its numbers, but the great majority of the tracts are from one hand; the individual numbers are variously dated and reattributed in the collected series, and the exact contents of any given collected issue vary.

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man
altTitles: A Tragedy or Interlude Manifesting the Chief Promises of God unto Man
works.description: John Bale's interlude of the covenants of God from Adam to Christ, composed c. 1538 and printed at Wesel in 1547; a dramatic sermon on the promises fulfilled in the gospel.
works.plot: God the Father, in seven acts, makes his successive promises to man — to Adam of the woman's seed, to Noah of the rainbow covenant, to Abraham of the blessing of nations, to Moses of the law, to David of the everlasting throne, to Isaiah of the virgin's son, and to John the Baptist of the Lamb of God — each act closing with a prayer or antiphon, the whole demonstrating that the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ.
works.significance: The most accomplished of Bale's biblical interludes and a model of Reformation dramaturgy: its covenant structure turned the mystery-cycle tradition to doctrinal ends and influenced the biblical drama of the Elizabethan church.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages with antiphons
works.context: Written c. 1538 during Bale's service as a Protestant dramatist under Cromwell, and printed at Wesel in 1547 in the collection of Bale's biblical plays; the play embodies the Protestant programme of replacing the old mysteries with doctrinal drama drawn from scripture alone.
works.characters: God the Father (Pater Coelestis); Adam; Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Isaiah; John the Baptist; Baleus Prolocutor
works.structure: Seven acts, each a dialogue between God the Father (as Pater Coelestis) and a biblical figure, framed by a prologue (Bale as Prolocutor) and an epilogue; the play is a doctrinal pageant of the covenants.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture

works.title: The Children of the Night
works.description: Published in 1897 and the book that founded modern American poetry: the first Tilbury Town poems and the lyrics of failure and endurance. It is a verse work of 1897 by Edwin Arlington Robinson; it belongs to The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'Richard Cory', the rich man who goes home and puts a bullet through his head, 'Luke Havergal', the ghost-haunted lover, 'The House on the Hill', the abandoned house, and 'Credo', the poem of a faith that survives doubt, in plain, hard, traditional verse.
works.significance: The Children of the Night is the founding book of modern American poetry: 'Richard Cory' became one of the most anthologised American poems, the Tilbury Town method changed the subject of American verse, and the collection made Robinson the first American poet to write modern poetry in traditional forms.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, colloquial line in traditional metre.
works.context: 1896-97: the depression of 1893-97, the small New England town in decline, the American magazine poetry of the 1890s, and Robinson's own poverty in New York. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Richard Cory; Luke Havergal; John Evereldown; Aaron Stark; Cliff Klingenhagen; Reuben Bright; Fleming Helphenstine
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. A. Robinson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Children of the Poor
works.form: Sonnet sequence (in 'The Womanhood', the last part of Annie Allen)
works.description: A sequence of sonnets by Gwendolyn Brooks that opens 'The Womanhood', the final part of Annie Allen (1949), the book that made her the first African American to win the Pulitzer Prize. A mother asks what she can give her children, who are poor and black, to carry them through the world.
works.summary: A mother's meditation, in sonnets, on what she can give her poor children, on whether to teach them to pray, and on what they must do to survive.
works.plot: The sonnets speak as a mother. In the best-known, she asks what she can give her children, who are poor, 'adjudged the leastwise of the land', her 'sweetest lepers', who demand no luxuries but have begged her for a firm shape, crying that they are unfinished, made by a hand less than sure. Her hand is full of mode, design and device, but she lacks access to her proper stone, and no plan, grief or love will be enough to ratify her little halves as they cross an autumn freezing everywhere. Other sonnets ask whether she should teach them to pray, and urge that they first fight, then fiddle.
works.significance: The sonnets are among Brooks's most admired formal achievements and a key text of mid-century African American poetry; Norton prints the sequence, or part of it, as its representation of Annie Allen.
works.meter: Dense, Latinate diction and inversions ('My hand is stuffed with mode, design, device') set against plain speech; the formal sonnet bent to a mother's anger and tenderness.
works.context: Annie Allen, published by Harper and Brothers on 1 October 1949, follows its heroine from girlhood through the mock epic 'The Anniad' to 'The Womanhood', where she looks at a world she would like to change; it won Poetry's Eunice Tietjens Prize and the 1950 Pulitzer Prize.
works.structure: Petrarchan and Shakespearean sonnets, compressed and syntactically intricate, in the sequence that begins the volume's final part.
themes: Class, labour and social mobility

works.title: The Choice
works.description: The one-act play of the choice and the new drama. It is a dramatic work of 1910 by Allan Monkhouse; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: A young man and the choice between the old and the new; the one-act play that carried Monkhouse's class question into the Manchester repertory.
works.significance: The Choice is Monkhouse's one-act play of the choice: its class question and its woman's question carried him into the Manchester repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the plain dialogue of the servant's hall and the drawing room.
works.context: The Manchester repertory and the Edwardian household in 1910. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1910 and first published in 1910 and first performed in 1910 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.

works.structure: A single act, in the household. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: The Christian
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The religious bestseller of the 1890s: a clergyman, a woman doctor and the slums of London. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by Hall Caine; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: The Reverend John Storm, an ascetic High Church clergyman, loves Glory Quayle, who becomes a doctor and then a music-hall star; his struggle between the world and the cloister ends in renunciation and death in the London slums.
works.significance: The Christian was the greatest bestseller of the 1890s and the first English novel to sell a million copies: it made Caine the most famous novelist in the world and its treatment of the clergyman's vocation and the woman doctor gave the religious novel its modern subject.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the three-decker architecture of climax and reunion.
works.context: London in the 1890s, the High Church movement, the new profession of medicine for women and the music hall. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: John Storm; Glory Quayle; Lord Robert Ure; Polly Love; Brother Paul
works.structure: A novel in eight books, from the London parish to the music hall and the monastery. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Christian and Civic Economy of Large Towns
altTitles: Christian and Civic Economy of Large Towns
works.form: practical and pastoral treatise on social administration; sermon-discourse with a plan of reform
works.description: A series of discourses on the moral government of great cities, written out of the practical work of a Glasgow parish and addressed to the failure of the centralized administration of religion and of relief in the masses. It argues that neither church nor poor-law can reach a population that has no local ties, and that the remedy is territorial: a resident pastorate, a district school, and a face-to-face administration of charity.
works.plot: The discourses begin with the observation that the populous units of a great city are not a society but a multitude, without mutual knowledge, without local attachment, and without the relations in which character is formed; the institutions of the established church and the parish machinery of the poor-law, administered over so wide a field and by agents who never see the persons, therefore miss their mark and may even make matters worse. It then pleads for the division of the town into small districts, each with its own school, its own resident minister or visitor, and its own administration of relief, so that the eye of the governor and the eye of the governed may meet. The argument proceeds to the economy of charity, distinguishing the alms that pamper idleness from the provision that is earned, anticipated, and repaid in character, and it urges the voluntary principle and the cooperation of the subscribed district. It closes with the claim that this territorial religion is the only machinery that can carry Christianity to the mass at all, and that a city so organised would be at once more moral and more cheaply governed.
works.significance: It is the classic statement of the territorial cure for the city, and one of the most influential texts in the history of the district-visiting, the endowed district church and school, and the machinery that preceded the later municipal and welfare administration; its analysis of the multitude without local bonds anticipates a permanent theme of social writing. Its mixture of statistics, sermon, and administrative proposal also makes it a landmark of the new prose on the industrial town.
works.meter: Vivid, urban, statistical prose of the popular pulpit: enumerated masses, the rhetorical question, the homely analogy, and a moral urgency that stops short of invective.
works.context: Written while its author was translating into practice the district schemes he had tried in the poor parishes of a manufacturing city growing with unprecedented speed, and in the years when the town-planted church, the session of the district, and the debate over the poor laws were becoming the great questions of British social policy. The book belongs to the movement that made the moral condition of the towns a national subject.
works.structure: Discourses I and following, published in parts and afterwards gathered into a volume, each part a single sustained argument from the observation of the city to the proposal of the district plan.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the discourses are securely documented among the undisputed writings of their author, and the practical work out of which they grew is recorded in his own accounts and correspondence.

works.title: The Christian Hero
altTitles: The Christian Hero: An Argument, That no Principles can be effectual to encourage Vertue and Goodness, but those of Christianity
works.description: Steele's devotional and moral argument that unassisted virtue is unsustainable and that Christianity supplies the only adequate motive to goodness; a confession of his own past profligacy and the book he feared would be thrown in his teeth.
works.plot: The author proves from experience and from the passions that honour, interest and good nature leave a man unprotected against himself, then argues that the Christian rule alone both forbids and enables, and closes with the picture of the hero of piety.
works.significance: It is the periodical essay's other face, the serious religious self-examination that made Steele's name a byword for professional conscience, and it supplied the model of the reforming tract of the century.
works.meter: Plain, earnest, familiar prose, deliberately free of ornament, with the short imperative sentence and direct address to the reader.
works.context: Written early in Steele's army years and published as his public career made him a target, at the height of the deist and anti-deist controversy and in the year of his quarrel with Addison and of his entry into party politics.
works.characters: the penitent author; the man of the world
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered sections, moving from autobiography and diagnosis through scriptural proof to the exemplary character.

works.title: The Christian Religion, as Professed by a Daughter of the Church of God
works.form: Practical divinity and conduct treatise in prose, a devotional and moral system rather than an occasional controversy.
works.description: The longest and most systematic of her prose works, published in 1705 and reprinted through the century, a practical divinity written in the manner of a moral essay. It argues that Christianity is a reasonable and orderly scheme of duty, and then lays out the devotional, moral and social conduct proper to a churchwoman, with sustained sections on the government of the passions and on the duties of the single and the married state. The title announces the standpoint: an account of religion written from within the communion, and addressed to practice rather than to controversy.
works.plot: The first division establishes the grounds of belief, the evidence of revelation and the authority of the church, and answers the pretences of free enquiry and of latitudinarian moderation which would relax those grounds for the sake of ease or of party. The second division reduces the Christian life to a method: a settled rule of devotion, periodical self-examination, the ordering of the affections towards the love of God, and the practice of charity and of the duties of each station. Along the way she argues that the Passions, esteem, and the love of the world are the real enemies of a devout life, and that the conscience must be disciplined by the church's rule instead of left to its own temper. The whole is intended as a complete guide to conduct for a reader who means to think and to believe consistently.
works.significance: It is her most ambitious prose work and the one by which she was best known to readers who never reached her scheme of female education. Its blending of conduct book, practical divinity and moral philosophy is the fullest evidence of the religious content of her case for women, and the number of its editions measures the reach of a woman's prose theology in the early eighteenth century.
works.context: It appeared in 1705, after the occasional conformity controversies of the last years of the war had sharpened the language of church party, and between her earlier philosophical writings and the high-church polemic of the following decade. Its assertion that Christianity is a reasonable service answers the latitudinarian and deist vocabularies then current, and its tone is that of a woman writing within the communion's discipline for readers of both sexes. The bookseller who issued it had printed her occasional prose, and it passed through many editions without the name of its author on the title page.
works.structure: Treatise in two main divisions, speculative grounds followed by a rule of life in numbered practical sections; the manner is sententious and hortatory, with long periodic sentences and frequent appeal to the reader's own experience.

works.title: The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holidays throughout the Year
altTitles: Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holidays throughout the Year
works.form: Poetry collection (109 poems, one for each Sunday and holy day)
works.description: Published anonymously in 1827 and the most widely read poetry book of the nineteenth century after the Bible and the hymnbook: a lyric for every Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer, written for family devotion.
works.plot: Each poem takes the Gospel or Epistle of its day and turns it into a meditation — on the beauty of nature as a sign of grace, on childhood, on death, on the sacraments, and on the trusting submission of the soul to God; the sequence follows the liturgical year from Advent through Trinity and the saints' days.
works.significance: The Christian Year was the most influential devotional poetry of the Victorian age and gave the Oxford Movement its popular voice; it shaped the spirituality of Newman and Pusey, and its Sunday-by-Sunday structure made it a permanent text of Anglican devotion and a model for later liturgical poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood.
works.context: The 1820s-30s, the High Church devotional tradition, the Oxford of Oriel and the beginnings of the Oxford Movement, and the Victorian culture of family prayer. The record dates the work as composed between 1823 and 1825 and first published in 1827 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Chronicle of the Cid
altTitles: The Chronicle of the Cid, translated from the Spanish
works.form: Translation of an epic chronicle, with critical dissertation; a chivalric and national heroic narrative rendered into English prose.
works.description: The author's prose translation of the medieval Castilian chronicle of Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, made from the Spanish edition of the royal academy and addressed to John Hookham Frere. It is both a scholarly performance, with a long prefatory dissertation on the poem's date, authorship and metrics, and a piece of propaganda for chivalric example in the age of Napoleon. The volume is a landmark of British Hispanism.
works.plot: The chronicle follows the Cid from his banishment from Castile through his campaigns as an independent leader in the marches of al-Andalus to the conquest of Valencia and the famous judicial duel of the Cide's daughters. Its episodes praise loyalty, courage and liberality, and its ending restores the Cid to royal favour through alliance with the houses of Navarre and Barcelona. The translator's dissertation argues for the antiquity and the oral-professional origins of the Castilian epic, and compares it with the French chansons and with the Spanish romances.
works.significance: The first widely read English version of the Castilian national epic, it supplied the Cid legend to the whole nineteenth-century British romance revival, and its dissertation anticipates modern scholarship on the Cantar de mio Cid.
works.meter: Prose, with occasional verse and stanzaic quotations from the Spanish romances.
works.context: Published at the opening of the Peninsular War, when Spain became an object of British popular sympathy; The author's own friendship with Spanish scholars in London and his interest in the Cid as a model of Christian knighthood drove the volume.
works.characters: The Cid (Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar); Ximena; King Alfonso; the Counts of Carrion; King Motamid of Seville
works.structure: Prose translation of a continuous chronicle, preceded by a substantial editorial dissertation; the narrative proceeds in campaign episodes with genealogical and formulaic recurrences.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood

altTitles: The Citizen of the World; or, Letters of a Chinese Philosopher, Respecting His Residence in London
works.form: Periodical essay and spectator paper in epistolary form: short papers of character and custom, mixed with fable, translation and reflection, written for a daily newspaper and reprinted as books.
works.description: Goldsmith's periodical essays cast as the letters of a Chinese philosopher resident in London, first contributed to a daily newspaper and then collected in two volumes. The device of the observing foreigner, familiar from the 'Persian Letters' tradition, is used to make English manners, laws, learning, commerce and show appear strange, and to let a writer of little consequence comment on a great city with the immunity of an outsider.
works.plot: The letters are connected not by plot but by the persona of Lien Chi Altangi, a Chinese merchant-philosopher in London, whose correspondence with friends at home reports and judges everything he meets: the exchange, the playhouse, the auction, the coffee-house and the critics, the luxury of the rich and the misery of the poor, the laws, the duels, the salons and the political factions. His outsider's eye produces the two characteristic effects of the series, an invention of British society as a system of contradictions, and a defence of simple virtue and of the 'mandarins' of his own country against European pretence. As the letters proceed, the philosopher's own family misfortune is woven into the papers, so that the spectators' pleasure is gradually seasoned with sentiment and with a plea for benevolence. Its most quoted material is its account of the 'golden fairies' of British credit, the paper money and the phantom wealth of a commercial nation.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished of the mid-century spectator series and a central text of the literature of politeness, commerce and national self-observation; its letters shaped the essayistic treatment of commercial society for a generation. It also shows the sentiment of the 1760s turning the essay from a machine of wit into a machine of sympathy.
works.context: It appeared in the efflorescence of the English periodical paper after Addison and Steele, when a contributor could supply a newspaper with a series of essays and when the foreign-letter conceit had become a standard means of criticising national manners. Its publication belongs to the years when Goldsmith was moving between the magazines, the book trade and the great houses, dependent on the very world he describes.
works.characters: Lien Chi Altangi, the Chinese philosopher; his correspondent Hoamsy and the family at home; the London citizens, critics, tradesmen and great whom he observes
works.structure: A sequence of independent periodical letters in two collected volumes, unified by the persona of the Chinese correspondent and by the seasonal and topical round of London life, with a few serial threads, chiefly the philosopher's domestic sorrows, running through.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the papers were known to be Goldsmith's and were collected under his name. Some letters appeared in the newspaper press before the collected edition and were revised for it, so the exact order and dating of individual papers is not fixed here.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: The Spectator and Periodical Journalism

works.title: The City Madam
works.description: Massinger's comedy of a citizen's wife, Lady Frugal, whose ambition to be a lady leads her husband to fake a departure for the Indies and to test her virtue and her daughters' constancy.

works.title: The City Mouse and Country Mouse
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd to the Story of the Country Mouse and the City Mouse
works.description: A burlesque of Dryden's The Hind and the Panther (1687) by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu, retelling Dryden's fable of the mice in mock-heroic terms to ridicule his conversion and his religious argument — a celebrated example of Whig literary mockery and Prior's early wit.
works.plot: Following Aesop's fable (used by Dryden), the country mouse visits the city mouse and, after witnessing the dangers and hypocrisies of town and court, returns to the safety of the country, applied as satire on Dryden's religious and political position.
works.significance: A notable Whig burlesque of Dryden and an early showcase for Prior's wit; it reflects the literary politics of James II's reign and the quarrel over Dryden's conversion.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in a witty, parodic mock-heroic register.
works.context: Written in 1687 by the young Prior and Montagu (later Earl of Halifax) against Dryden's Catholic poem, and published anonymously; it launched Prior's reputation.
works.characters: the City Mouse; the Country Mouse
works.structure: A burlesque verse fable in heroic couplets parodying Dryden's poem.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu; Montagu is not in this database, so only Prior is linked.
