works.title: The Cloister and the Hearth: A Tale of the Middle Ages
altTitles: Cloister and the Hearth: A Tale of the Middle Ages
works.description: Published in 1861 and the greatest English historical novel of the Middle Ages: the story of Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou, who travels from Holland to Rome in the fifteenth century in search of the woman he loves, and becomes the father of Erasmus.
works.plot: Gerard, an illuminator's son, loves Margaret Brandt but is driven from home by his father; he travels through Burgundy, France and Italy, is imprisoned, joins a company of soldiers and survives a series of picaresque adventures, while Margaret bears his son and dies before his return; Gerard becomes a priest and the novel ends with the boy Erasmus at the age of reason.
works.significance: The Cloister and the Hearth is the classic English historical novel of the fifteenth century and the one Victorian book that attempts a full material reconstruction of medieval life — food, costume, trade, disease and travel; its portrait of a pre-Reformation world on the edge of change shaped the historical novel for a century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative.
works.context: The 1450s-70s, the Burgundian Netherlands, the eve of the Reformation, and the medieval illuminated manuscript. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1861 and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Gerard Eliassoen; Margaret Brandt; Denys the soldier; Catherine Elias; Elias the printer; Ghysbrecht van Swieten; Cornelis and Sybrandt; Clement the hermit
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Cloud of Unknowing
works.description: The classic English treatise of apophatic contemplation, written in the late fourteenth century by an anonymous master (perhaps a Carthusian or secular priest) for a young disciple: the soul seeking God must enter the 'cloud of unknowing' between itself and God, striking down every thought with the dart of longing love and the 'naked intent' of the single word. The most intellectually rigorous work of the English mystical canon.
works.plot: The author teaches his disciple the work of contemplation: the forgetting of all creatures, the rejection of discursive meditation, the piercing of the darkness with love — and warns throughout against the false mysticism of physical fervour and deluded visions, prescribing the discipline of the single word ('God' or 'love') repeated in the heart.
works.significance: The supreme English expression of the negative way and a work of the first rank in the European contemplative tradition; its psychology of attention and intention has given it a continuing modern readership.
works.meter: Precise, sinewy prose, paradoxically articulate about the ineffable; vivid negative imagery (clouds, darts, nakedness).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, in the orbit of the Carthusian order; it circulated with the author's other works (The Book of Privy Counselling, the translation of pseudo-Dionysius's Mystical Theology) and was read by the English Benedictine revival and by modern contemplatives (Thomas Merton).
works.characters: the author (spiritual director); the young disciple (addressee)
works.structure: Seventy-five short chapters of graduated instruction, in the apophatic tradition of pseudo-Dionysius, with the 'cloud' as its organizing image.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is often identified as a Carthusian on grounds of the work's transmission, but the identification is conjectural.
themes: The contemplative life
movements: The English Mystics
sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Code of the Woosters
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1938
works.description: Wodehouse's own favourite: the cow creamer, the fascist and the heliotrope pyjamas. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by P. G. Wodehouse; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bertie Wooster is sent by his aunt to steal a silver cow creamer from Sir Watkyn Bassett, encounters the fascist Roderick Spode, the engagements of Madeline Bassett and Stiffy Byng, and is saved by Jeeves in a plot of extraordinary complication.
works.significance: The Code of the Woosters was Wodehouse's own favourite among his novels and is the most perfectly constructed of the Jeeves books: its farce, its satire of the fascist and its prose made it the summit of English comic fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the elaborate comic plot of farce and coincidence.
works.context: Totleigh Towers and the English country house of the late 1930s, and the appearance of the domestic fascist. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Jeeves; Bertie Wooster; Roderick Spode; Sir Watkyn Bassett; Madeline Bassett; Stiffy Byng; Gussie Fink-Nottle

works.title: The Collected Essays of Ralph Ellison
works.description: The Collected Essays of Ralph Ellison is a posthumous Modern Library volume (1995), edited by his literary executor John F. Callahan, that gathers Ellison's nonfiction in one book.
works.summary: It reprints Shadow and Act and Going to the Territory together with essays, reviews and addresses not collected in either book.
works.plot: By placing the two published collections beside previously uncollected pieces, the edition presents Ellison's nonfiction as a continuous body of cultural criticism from the 1940s to the 1980s, centred on literature, music and American identity.
works.significance: It made the whole of Ellison's nonfiction available in a standard edition and is the usual text cited for his uncollected essays.
works.meter: An editorial compilation of Ellison's essays, preserving their original texts.
works.context: Published the year after Ellison's death as the first of four volumes edited from his papers between 1995 and 2000.
works.structure: A collected edition: the two essay books in full followed by uncollected material.
themes: Nationhood and national identity
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters of George Orwell
works.form: Collected edition in four volumes (posthumous; edited by Sonia Orwell and Ian Angus)
works.description: The first attempt at a comprehensive collection of Orwell's shorter writings, edited by his widow Sonia Orwell and Ian Angus and published by Secker and Warburg in four chronological volumes: An Age Like This (1920-1940), My Country Right or Left (1940-1943), As I Please (1943-1945) and In Front of Your Nose (1945-1950).
works.summary: Essays, reviews, columns and letters arranged by date of writing, including the essays of the published collections, much uncollected journalism and the memoir 'Such, Such Were the Joys'.
works.plot: Arranged across thirty years, the edition lets the reader follow Orwell's development from the tramping journalism of the early 1930s through the Spanish war, the BBC and Tribune years, to the essays and letters of his last illness, setting the famous essays among the weekly journalism and private correspondence from which they grew.
works.significance: Until the Complete Works it was the fullest printed collection of Orwell's journalism and letters, and the form in which most readers and critics of the 1970s and 1980s met them.
works.meter: The edition preserves the range of Orwell's registers, from the formal essay to the weekly column and the private letter.
works.context: Published eighteen years after Orwell's death, as his reputation was being consolidated in schools and universities; Peter Davison's twenty-volume Complete Works (1986-1998) later superseded it as the standard edition.
works.structure: Four volumes, each covering a span of years, with pieces of every kind interleaved in chronological order.
themes: Language, writing and the limits of representation
Power, the state and surveillance
War, combat and its aftermath

works.title: The Collected Poems of Edward Thomas
works.description: The 140 poems Thomas wrote in three years: the finest English nature poetry of the century and the quietest war poetry. It is a verse work of 1920 by Edward Thomas; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Nature Lyric and Meditation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poems — 'Adlestrop', 'The Owl', 'Rain', 'Old Man', 'Words', 'Lights Out', 'Aspens', 'The Glory', 'February Afternoon' — record the English countryside, the road, the hedge, the bird and the coming of the war, in a plain, unemphatic verse that stops rather than concludes.
works.significance: Thomas's Collected Poems is the finest body of English nature poetry of the century and among the greatest war poetry: in three years he wrote 140 poems, 'Adlestrop' and 'Rain' are permanent, and his prose founded the modern nature essay.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, quiet, unrhymed or loosely rhymed line.
works.context: The English countryside of Kent, Hampshire and Wiltshire; the First World War, which Thomas enlisted in 1915 to escape his own depression, and his death at Arras on 9 April 1917. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1917 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem; nature lyric and meditation.
works.characters: Lob ('Lob'); the child of 'Old Man'
works.structure: One hundred and forty poems in plain rhymed and unrhymed verse. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.

works.structure: Collected poems with a memoir and selections from the letters. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative. works.title: The Colonel's Dream
works.description: Published in 1905 and Chesnutt's most ambitious novel: the return of a southern colonel to rebuild his home town after the Civil War, and the defeat of his plan by the racial order. It is a prose fiction work of 1905 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Colonel French returns to North Carolina with northern capital and the intention of modernising the mills and educating the black workers; he is defeated by the old aristocracy, the convict labour system and the racial hatred of the town, and the novel ends with the deaths of his small son Phil and the old servant Peter, who dies trying to save him, the town's desecration of Peter's grave in the white cemetery, and the Colonel's departure.
works.significance: The Colonel's Dream is the finest American novel of the New South and one of the most radical works of American social criticism of its time: its analysis of the economic interests behind segregation makes it a key text in the literature of American race and capitalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. works.title: The Colour Out of Space

works.significance: The Colour Out of Space is Lovecraft's finest tale by his own judgement: its poisoned farm and its unnameable colour made the cosmic indifference - the horror that has no malice and no meaning - the form of the modern weird tale.

works.form: National epic and didactic poem: a republican epic of discovery, settlement and progress built on a vision-frame, with prose arguments, hymn, eulogy and prophetic address
works.description: Barlow's national epic of the American republic, first published at Philadelphia in 1807 and re-modelled and enlarged in the text he issued in 1809, where the poem runs to ten books each preceded by a prose Argument. It is a recasting of his own earlier Vision of Columbus (1787) - the Preface calls that volume a sketch of the present poem - and it keeps the vision-frame of the older work while making it the vehicle of a far more ambitious historical argument. Christopher Columbus, chained and deserted in a Spanish prison after his final ruin, is visited by Hesper, the guardian genius of the western continent, and carried to a mount of vision above the coast of Spain; from there the poet and his guide survey, in order, the American continent and its peoples, the Inca empire of Capac and Oella, the destruction of Peru, the effect of the discovery upon Europe, the planting of the North American colonies, the war of Independence, and at last the future progress of the arts, of republican government, and of a general congress of nations. The poem is openly didactic: its declared object is to strengthen in the rising generation a sense of the importance of republican institutions, and it invokes Freedom rather than a Muse.
works.plot: The Argument of Book I sets the frame: the condition of Columbus in a Spanish prison, his monologue on the great actions of his life and the manner in which they had been rewarded, the appearance and speech of Hesper, and the ascent of the mount of vision, whence Europe settles from their sight and America is described in its mountains, rivers, lakes, soil and productions. Book II shows the natives of America in vision, discusses the diversity of human beings and the first peopling of the continent, and passes to Mexico and its destruction by Cortez and to Cusco and Quito, with the tradition and the real history of Capac and Oella, founders of the Peruvian empire. Book III is the Inca narrative: the invasion of the mountain savages, the embassy of Rocha, the worshippers of the volcano and of the storm, the chief Zamor, the sacrifice of Rocha's companions and the death song of Azonto, the war dance, the rout of the Peruvians at an eclipse of the sun, and the recovery of Rocha. Book IV foretells the destruction of Peru, consoles Columbus with a vision of future ages, surveys the effect of the discovery on the commerce, government and letters of Europe, with the Jesuits, persecution and the Inquisition, then turns to Raleigh's plan for North America, the formation of the coast by the gulf stream, the first colonial settlements, the arrival of Delaware with settlers for Virginia, and the prophetic speech of Potowmak to the night scene on the Chesapeake. Books V to VII carry the American Revolution in vision: the colonies and their wars with France, Braddock's defeat and Washington, Bunker Hill and the death of Warren, Montgomery before Quebec, the treatment of American prisoners and the prison ship, the recrossing of the Delaware, Burgoyne's advance and the battles of Saratoga with the story of Lucinda, the alliance with France, Monmouth, Wayne's storming of Stonypoint, the fall of Charleston, Greene and Eutaw, the siege of York and Gloster and the capture of Cornwallis. Book VIII opens with a Hymn to Peace and an eulogy on the heroes slain, in which the author names his own brother; Atlas, the guardian genius of Africa, denounces to Hesper the crimes of his people in the slavery of the Africans, and the poet addresses his countrymen on that subject and on the principles of their government before the arts, fisheries, commerce and education of the United States are displayed. Book IX reasons from the progress of the physical world to the progress of the moral, answers Columbus's doubts with the rise of modern science - Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Newton, Bacon, Herschel, the printing press and the magnetic needle - and proposes the federal system extended over the whole earth. Book X resumes the vision over the whole world, foresees the assimilation and final union of languages and closes on a general congress from all nations assembled to establish the political harmony of mankind.
works.significance: The Columbiad is the most ambitious single attempt of the early American Republic to produce a national epic, and the document in which the revolutionary hope of the 1790s is re-stated as a philosophy of historical progress and continental destiny; its ten-book plan makes the discovery of America, the war of Independence and the projected congress of nations a single providence of reason, and its Book VIII puts the denunciation of African slavery into the machinery of the poem itself. Because Barlow revised his own earlier Vision of Columbus into it, the poem is also a case study in the transmission of revolutionary writing into the nineteenth century, and the surrounding pamphlet warfare of 1809-1810 is one of the fullest records of early American poetical criticism. It has long been slighted as the type of the ambitious failure, which is itself part of its significance: later accounts of American verse defined their own modernity against it.
works.meter: Written in heroic couplets of closed decasyllabic rhyming pairs, the diction public, sententious and expository, with the couplet used for maxim and antithesis ("Almighty Freedom! give my venturous song / The force, the charm that to thy voice belong"). The Preface defends the choice of modern rather than classical subject matter and vocabulary, arguing that the names of modern weapons, machines and institutions are at least as poetical as the ancient ones, and expressly declines to prove that he has written an epic poem in the regular form, because the recentness and importance of his events would have debased them in a conventional modelling. The prose Arguments and the substantial prose notes on the historical and scientific passages make the verse part of an explicitly instructional apparatus.
works.context: The poem belongs to the early republic's demand for a national literature and to Barlow's own career as poet, diplomat and republican controversialist: the first edition was published at Philadelphia in 1807, printed - as the Library of Congress catalogue records - at the expense of Robert Fulton, the steamboat engineer whose partner and friend Barlow had become, and with a portrait of the author and plates by Smirke. It grew out of The Vision of Columbus, a poem in nine books printed at Hartford in 1787 for the author, which had already made Columbus the subject of American verse; the 1807 text recast that poem as a national epic and the 1809 text re-modelled it again into ten books. Editions followed immediately in London (R. Phillips, 1809) and Paris (1813, with the last corrections of the author), and a Georgetown edition in 1825. Its publication revived the old quarrel over whether a republic could have an epic: critical observations on the poem were printed at Philadelphia in 1809, the abbé Grégoire addressed a letter to the author on the work, and Barlow's reply and a collected correspondence on the poem appeared in print in 1809 and 1810. A copy belonged to Thomas Jefferson's library, catalogued at Monticello.
works.characters: Christopher Columbus; Hesper, the guardian genius of the western continent; Atlas, the guardian genius of Africa, who denounces the slavery of his people; Freedom, invoked in place of a Muse; Capac and Oella, founders of the Peruvian empire; Rocha, the Inca's son, and Azonto and Zamor of the savage armies; Raleigh and Delaware and the patriarchal settlers of Virginia; the river gods of the Chesapeake and Potowmak; Cortez; Washington, Warren and Montgomery; Lucinda, the heroine of the Saratoga episode
works.structure: A long didactic epic in ten books (in the 1809 recension, each book preceded by a prose Argument that summarises it) and unified not by a single action but by a sustained vision-frame: the dungeon and the mount of vision hold the narrative together while the panorama moves historically from geography to Inca romance to colonial settlement to revolutionary war to philosophical forecast. Time is deliberately manipulated - in Book VIII Hesper reverses the order of time to show the continent again in its savage state and so exhibit the progress of the arts - and the poem's parts are rhetorical set pieces (invocation, hymn, eulogy, denunciation, prophecy) rather than a plot.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship is certain and the title page names the author. The record's bibliographical difficulty is not authorship but recension: the poem exists in materially different states - the Hartford 1787 Vision of Columbus as originally conceived, the 1807 recasting as The Columbiad, and the enlarged and re-modelled ten-book text of 1809, with further authorial correction in the 1813 Paris edition - so description and quotation in this record are tied to the 1809 text, which was consulted directly, while the publication date records the first edition of 1807. The Library of Congress catalogue note describes the 1807 volume as an amplification of the Vision of Columbus and Barlow's own Preface calls the earlier poem a sketch of the present work.

Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world

works.title: The Comedy of Errors
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest play and his only pure farce, built on Plautus's Menaechmi: twin masters and twin servants, both pairs named Antipholus and Dromio, are separated by shipwreck and reunited by coincidence in Ephesus, where the confusions of mistaken identity multiply until the family is restored in the recognition scene before the Abbess.
works.plot: Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio arrive in Ephesus, where their long-lost twins live; the day becomes a cascade of wrong beatings, wrong dinners, and wrong arrests, until the Duke's judgment and the Abbess's revelation untangle the knots and reunite husband, wife, and sons.
works.significance: The most technically perfect of the early comedies and Shakespeare's demonstration that classical comedy could be outdone in English.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the servants' comedy; the play includes the verse 'discourse' scene between Antipholus of Syracuse and Luciana.
works.context: Probably written for Gray's Inn's Christmas revels of 1594; the frame of Egeon's doom under Ephesian law darkens the farce with the threat of execution.
works.characters: Antipholus of Syracuse; Antipholus of Ephesus; Dromio of Syracuse; Dromio of Ephesus; Adriana; Luciana; Egeon; the Abbess (Emilia); the Duke
works.structure: A single-day, single-city action — the closest Shakespeare came to the classical unities — with the errors compounded scene by scene to the recognition finale.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Marriage and women's conduct
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
works.description: George Etherege's first comedy, a witty Restoration intrigue play that alternates heroic verse scenes of courtship with prose scenes of low comedy, and gave the stage its first true Restoration rake in Sir Frederick Frollick.
works.plot: Two brothers love two sisters; Colonel Bruce and the Widow Rich clash in the main plot, while Sir Frederick Frollick pursues the Widow with comic irreverence; all is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: The first of the great Restoration comedies of manners; Sir Frederick Frollick established the type of the gallant-rake that Dorimant would perfect.
works.meter: Rhymed couplets in the high plot and prose in the low comedy.
works.context: Performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1664; it made Etherege's reputation immediately.
works.characters: Sir Frederick Frollick; the Widow Rich; Colonel Bruce; Graciana; Beaufort; Palmer; Dufoy; Mrs Gudgeon
works.structure: Five acts with three parallel plots of differing social register and metre.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: The Coming Race
works.description: Published in 1871 and the first English scientific romance of a superior underground race: the discovery of a subterranean civilisation powered by a mysterious force. It is a prose fiction work of 1871 by Edward Bulwer-Lytton; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: An American mining engineer descends into a vast cavern and finds the Vril-ya, a race of winged superhuman beings who live in a socialist utopia powered by 'vril'; he learns their language and customs, is nearly married to a Vril-ya woman, and escapes back to the surface with a warning about the future of humanity.
works.significance: The Coming Race introduced the word 'vril' and founded the English scientific romance of a hidden superior civilisation: it anticipated H. G. Wells and the whole tradition of the scientific utopia and dystopia, and its vision of a technologically powered master race became one of the founding myths of modern popular fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue.
works.context: 1871: the Darwinian debate, the electrical and galvanic sciences, the utopian fiction of the 1870s, and the fear of a coming master race. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the narrator, an American mining engineer; Zee; Aph-Lin, his host; Taë, Aph-Lin's son; the Tur, chief magistrate of the Vril-ya
works.structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Bulwer-Lytton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Commonwealth of Oceana
works.description: James Harrington's utopian treatise on the ideal commonwealth, in which he argues that political power follows the distribution of landed property and proposes an elaborate republican constitution with a bicameral legislature and rotation of office.
works.plot: The Archon of Oceana, after the dissolution of the old government, establishes a commonwealth founded on an agrarian law limiting landed property, with a Senate proposing, a popular assembly resolving, and a magistracy executing; the model is Venice and ancient republics rather than monarchy.
works.significance: The most original political theory of the Interregnum; its theory that power follows property influenced Marx, and its constitutional model directly shaped the constitutions of the American colonies and of the early United States.
works.meter: A mixture of narrative and constitutional prose.
works.context: Written during the Protectorate and dedicated to Cromwell, who is said to have suppressed it until Harrington's friends obtained its release; published in 1656.
works.characters: the Archon; Olphaus Megaletor; the Council of Legislators; Parthenia
works.structure: A narrative frame of the founding of Oceana followed by the text of the proposed constitution and the Model of the Commonwealth.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Harrington; authorship undisputed.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Kingship and good rule
Order and degree: the body politic
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Commonwealth and Interregnum Literature

works.title: The Commonwealth of Slaves
works.form: Heroic tragedy in five acts, the continuation of an adaptation already recorded, written for the patent house and printed from the acting text.
works.description: The second part of the stage adaptation of the Oroonoko story, brought out for the Drury Lane stage at the turn of the century and printed in 1701. Where the first part had made the African prince's constancy and betrayal the substance of a tearful tragedy, the continuation carries the consequence into rebellion, siege and execution, and keeps the comedy of planter appetite running beneath it. The very title, a commonwealth of slaves, makes the plantation a scene of political danger as well as of pity.
works.plot: Oroonoko, sold into the plantations and still honoured as a prince by those about him, finds that the colony's laws leave him no redress, and combines the captives into an armed community resolved to win its liberty or to die. Imoinda, who has followed him into bondage and bears him a child in the new world, is the occasion both of his tenderness and of his exposure. The English planters conduct the suppression with a cruelty that the play invites its audience to measure against their Christian profession: the widow of fortune who had pursued the slave with her purse, the governor and the trading captain who first cozened him, and the young heiress whose suit is disputed among them, all pursue their several bargains while the revolt is being crushed. The rising is betrayed and put down, Oroonoko is taken, scourged and destroyed, and the subordinate plots close in marriage or in the discomfiture of the greedy. The tragedy is thus carried from the pathos of betrayal to the politics of a slave republic and its suppression.
works.significance: It completes the most influential stage version of the tale and, by converting the first part's pathos into a slave revolt and its suppression, brought the politics of plantation slavery into the tragedy of the patent theatre. Its two-tier handling of African heroism and English avarice became the standard framework for later treatments of the subject, and it remains a fixed reference in the history of the stage Oroonoko.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic five-beat line for the heroic roles, with couplets closing the scenes of the prince's speeches; the planter underplot is in prose, with the song matter of the earlier part reduced.
works.context: The adaptation had held the London stage since the middle of the 1690s and was the most frequently revived treatment on the English theatre of African slavery and of African nobility. The continuation appeared in the years when the royal trade in captives was a matter of charter and of parliamentary dispute, and when the plantations were becoming a visible political question. Its title plays upon the vocabulary of rebellion and of contested government which the previous century had made familiar to every playhouse audience.
works.characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the widow of fortune who designs upon the hero; the governor of the colony; the captain who betrayed him; the planter family about whom the underplot turns; the followers of the slave community
works.structure: Tragedy in five acts with a two-tier design, the heroic line in verse and the plantation underplot in prose; the first part's single movement of betrayal is here expanded into plotting, discovery and military suppression.

works.title: The Complaint, or, Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality
altTitles: The Complaint: or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality
works.description: Young's long meditative poem on the night, death and the immortal life, spoken by a grieving soul under the patronage of the personified Night: the central work of the century's cultivation of melancholy and of the thought of death.
works.plot: Across nine nights the poet addresses Night, the stars, the tomb and his own losses, passes through the tales of the ruined house, the physician and the fallen ambition, and rises from the meditation on mortality to the argument for immortality, the proof of religion and the triumph over the fear of death.
works.significance: It made the gloomy meditative night-piece the most influential English verse form of the later eighteenth century, supplied the imagery of the graveyard and the ruin to the Gothic, and was read across Europe in translation.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of great variety, with the abrupt short line, the capitalised abstraction, the exclamation and the suspended period of the night piece.
works.context: Issued in the season of the century's mourning culture, the burial-ground and the fashionable garden, and in the same years as the debate over enthusiasm, ridicule and the reality of religion; the separate numbers were sold as they appeared and were gathered into a single poem as it grew.
works.characters: the poet; the personified Night and her daughters; the auditor of the tales; the dead whom the poem mourns
works.structure: A serial of nine numbered nights, each a continuous meditation with the inset narrative and the address to an auditor, first issued one by one and afterwards collected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation
works.description: Izaak Walton's pastoral dialogue on fishing, in which the angler Piscator instructs Venator, combining practical lore on the taking of fish with songs, poems, and reflections on the contemplative life; the fifth edition of 1676 added Charles Cotton's second part.
works.plot: Over five days of dialogue, Piscator teaches Venator and Auceps the arts of angling and defends the quiet life of the angler against the pursuits of the hunter and the falconer.
works.significance: One of the most reprinted books in English (over 400 editions), a founding text of the English pastoral tradition, and the standard expression of the ideal of quiet country retirement.
works.meter: Gentle, conversational prose with interpolated songs and verses.
works.context: First published in 1653, in the Commonwealth, when Walton had withdrawn from public life; revised and expanded in five editions to 1676, when Charles Cotton's part on fly-fishing was added.
works.characters: Piscator (the angler); Venator (the huntsman); Auceps (the falconer); Peter Manwood; Piscator's scholar
works.structure: A pastoral dialogue in five chapters or days, interspersed with songs, verse quotations, and digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Parts I-III by Walton; the 1676 edition adds Part II by Charles Cotton (not in this database), who is named on the title page.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
Solitude and the hall community
The contemplative life
movements: Cavalier Poetry

works.title: The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar
altTitles: Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar
works.description: Published in 1913 after his death and the standard collection of Dunbar's verse: the dialect poems, the standard English lyrics and the late poems of love and death. It is a verse work of 1913 by Paul Laurence Dunbar; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume gathers the four major collections and the uncollected poems, and shows the full range of Dunbar's work — the plantation dialect that made him famous, the lyrics of 'The Debt', 'Slow through the Dark' and 'The Haunted Oak', and the poems of his last illness.
works.significance: The Complete Poems is the standard text of the first African-American poet of national reputation and shows the full achievement behind the dialect reputation; it is essential to the history of American poetry and of black literature.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill.
works.context: 1913: the posthumous reputation of Dunbar, the Harlem Renaissance to come, and the American canonisation of black poetry. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1906 and first published in 1913 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance; The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Paul Dunbar. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Complete Short Stories of Saki
works.description: The collected stories of the finest English comic writer of the short story: Clovis, Reginald and the wolves. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Saki (H. H. Munro); it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume gathers Munro's stories — 'Sredni Vashtar', 'The Open Window', 'Tobermory', 'The Interlopers', 'The Schartz-Metterklume Method' — in which children, animals and the Wildean epigram take revenge on the English middle class.
works.significance: The Complete Short Stories of Saki gathers the finest comic short stories in English: Munro's wit, his cruelty and his perfect construction made him the master of the English short story, and his influence on Waugh, Wodehouse and the modern comic story is beyond measure.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story built on a single surprise.
works.context: Edwardian England, the country house, and the years before the First World War in which Munro was killed. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1916 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Clovis Sangrail; Reginald; Vera; Conradin; Tobermory; the Interlopers
works.structure: A collected edition of the stories, with a memoir by Ethel Munro. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hector Hugh Munro. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Conduct of the Allies
altTitles: The Conduct of the Allies: And of the Late Negotiation for a General Peace
works.description: Swift's great party pamphlet against the management of the War of the Spanish Succession, arguing that the confederate allies have made the war a business of conquest and that Britain's blood and treasure have been spent to the profit of the captains and the ministers.
works.plot: The essay reviews the design of the Grand Alliance, the declarations and the campaigns, and shows by the allies' own papers how the nation was drawn into an endless war, before turning on the general and his ministers, whose conduct is figured as the picture of a great white animal of prey.
works.significance: It is the most effective war pamphlet in English and a permanent document of the literature of anti-war argument, influencing the language in which the cost of campaigns and the credibility of ministers were questioned for two centuries.
works.meter: The plain, emphatic prose of Swift's party writing, built from quotation, interrogative rebuke and the closing single sentence.
works.context: Published in the winter of the ministerial change and the negotiation of the peace, at the height of the campaign to discredit the Duke of Marlborough and the Whig management, and repeatedly reprinted within the year as an instrument of the election and the address.
works.characters: the allies and their courts; the captains of the confederacy; the British ministry; the nation as the injured party
works.structure: A sustained historical argument in numbered parts, with the review of documents, the computation of the war's charges and the closing personal portrait.

works.title: The Confederacy
works.form: City comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, spoken from the theatre's own text.
works.description: A city comedy brought out and printed in 1705 which replaces the wits and rakes of the 1690s with two rich, jealous money-scriveners and their confederating wives. The plot is built out of surveillance and counter-plotting: the husbands watch each other and their wives, and the women combine to turn that jealousy against its authors. Long judged the best of its author's later comedies, it depends for its effect on the pressure of two mirrored households set side by side.
works.plot: Gripe and Money-trap, two wealthy City husbands of suspicious and niggardly temper, are each persuaded that the other's wife has designs upon his own affections; Clarissa distrusts Araminta and Money-trap watches Clarissa. Against this surveillance the two wives form the confederacy of the title, with the help of the gossips Mrs. Amlet and Mrs. Cloggit, and lay a scheme in which Dick, a young gamester, serves as the apparent instrument. Their design is to draw the jealous husbands into the outlay and the loss of a considerable sum, and to make their watchfulness the means of their own deception, while the serving-men Brass and Clip carry the messages that keep the two houses in ignorance of each other. The discovery at the last leaves the husbands defrauded of their suspicions together with their money, the wives in quiet possession of the field, and the gamester provided for. The interest of the play is not moral reformation but the mechanics of a trick well done.
works.significance: It is the strongest surviving example of its author's mature comic method and one of the last plays in which the City-household plot of the Restoration stage is rebuilt entirely in terms of female alliance. The confederate wives and the use of jealousy as a mere engine of plot look forward to the domestic intrigue of the following century, and its construction has often been preferred to that of comedies now better known.
works.meter: Brisk prose dialogue with short alternating speeches and soliloquies of suspicion; the addresses to the audience are in closed couplets.
works.context: It was acted and printed in the year following the settlement of the patent theatres into their Drury Lane and Lincoln's Inn Fields rivalries, and its money-scriveners belong to the long stage tradition of the jealous citizen which the comedy of the 1670s and 1690s had exploited. Its author, a gentleman dramatist and officer of arms, wrote here for the City audience of the patent house, and the play's treatment of wedlock, covetousness and female alliance carries the debate about the immorality of the stage into the counting-house.
works.characters: Gripe; Money-trap; Clarissa; Araminta; Dick the gamester; Brass; Clip; Mrs. Amlet; Mrs. Cloggit; Corinna
works.structure: Five acts of prose comedy in which the two households alternate scene by scene; the action is carried by concealed letters, eavesdropping and mistaken jealousy, and resolves by discovery rather than by penitence.

works.title: The Conjure Woman
works.description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's first collection: seven stories told by the old freedman Uncle Julius, in which the conjure tales of slavery turn the plantation tradition against itself. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Uncle Julius tells the northern narrator and his wife about the conjure woman Aunt Peggy and her spells — 'The Goophered Grapevine', 'Po' Sandy', 'Mars Jeems's Nightmare', 'The Conjurer's Revenge', 'Sis' Becky's Pickaninny' — and each tale records the cruelty of slavery under cover of a comic anecdote.
works.significance: The Conjure Woman is the founding work of African-American fiction and a permanent rebuke to the plantation tradition: its frame narrative turns the minstrel tale into a record of slavery's cruelty, and it is one of the most important books in the history of American race and literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.
works.context: The 1890s: the North Carolina plantation country, the American plantation tradition of Harris and Page, and the market for dialect fiction. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charles Waddell Chesnutt. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Conjure-Man Dies: A Mystery Tale of Dark Harlem
altTitles: Conjure-Man Dies: A Mystery Tale of Dark Harlem
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1932
works.description: The first Black detective novel: a Harlem conjure-man, a locked room and a Black detective. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Rudolph Fisher; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Dr Archer, a Harlem physician, and Detective Perry Dart investigate the murder of the conjure-man N'Gana Frimbo, found dead in a locked apartment in Harlem, in the first detective novel by a Black American with Black detectives and a Black setting.
works.significance: The Conjure-Man Dies created the Black detective novel: it was the first detective story by a Black American, with Black detectives and a Black setting, and it founded the tradition of African-American crime fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the comic novel of Harlem.
works.context: Harlem in the early 1930s, and the world of the conjure-man and the Black professional class. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro; The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; ghost story and the modern weird tale.
works.characters: Dr John Archer; Detective Perry Dart; N'Gana Frimbo; Jinx Jenkins; Bubber Brown
works.structure: A locked-room detective novel in the Harlem manner. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.

works.title: The Conquered
works.description: The historical novel of the conquered Gaul. It is a prose fiction work of 1923 by Naomi Mitchison; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance.
works.plot: The Conquered tells the Roman conquest of Gaul from the conquered - the Gallic household, the slave, the woman of the tribe - in the plain anthropological prose of Mitchison's first novel, and sets the conqueror's Rome against the memory of the conquered land.
works.significance: The Conquered made Naomi Mitchison's name as the historical novelist of the defeated: its choice of the conquered side and its plain prose set the manner of her historical novels of the 1920s and 1930s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the historical novel of the ancient world in the anthropologist's eye.
works.context: Gaul under the Roman conquest, written in the years after the first war. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance.

works.title: The Conquest of Granada
altTitles: The Conquest of Granada by the Spaniards
works.description: Dryden's heroic play in two parts on the Christian conquest of Moorish Granada in 1492, whose overweening hero Almanzor became the type of the Restoration hero of honour and love.
works.plot: Almanzor, a free-lance warrior of boundless ambition, serves first the Moors then the Spaniards, loves Almahide, and is torn between love, honour, and freedom until the fall of Granada and the lovers' final recognition.
works.significance: The supreme example of the English heroic drama and the occasion of the most important Restoration quarrel over the form; Almanzor's rhetoric of boundless will anticipates the eighteenth-century sublime.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets at their most sonorous and rhetorical.
works.context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre Royal in December 1670 and January 1671 and dedicated to the Duke of York; it was attacked by Buckingham in The Rehearsal and defended by Dryden in the Defence of the Epilogue.

works.structure: Two parts of five acts each, with a masque and an epilogue; the plot interweaves the historical siege with the love story.

works.title: The Conscious Lovers
works.description: Steele's five-act comedy of sensibility, modelled on Terence and rewritten to substitute tender feeling and generous self-command for the wit and rake of the Restoration stage; the most influential example of the laughing-and-crying reform of English comedy.
works.plot: Young Bevil, torn between duty to his father's choice and love for Indiana, discovers that the girl he has rescued from slavery in Turkey is the daughter of his father's presumed dead friend, so that his benevolence is rewarded by a match both honourable and affectionate; the subplot of Myrtle and the betraying Humphrey secures the second pair.
works.significance: It made the hero of sensibility respectable on the London stage, supplied the pattern of the reformed sentimental comedy for three decades, and gave the century its clearest statement that virtue rewarded by feeling is the proper business of the drama.
works.meter: Prose dialogue of polished conversational ease, interrupted by set speeches of feeling whose periodic rhythm imitates oratory rather than wit.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in the season after Steele's return from Ireland and his quarrel with Addison, and acted in the same years as the dispute over laughter in comedy which culminated in Fielding's defence of humour.
works.characters: Young Bevil; Indiana; Sir John Bevil; Myrtle; Leonora; Isabella; Humphrey; Cimber
works.structure: Regular five-act comedy with a double plot, anagnorisis deferred to the final discovery and a prologue and epilogue framing the moral argument about the theatre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested Steele, though his borrowings from the Andria of Terence and from previous French plots are extensive and were noticed by the reviewers.

works.title: The Consolidator
altTitles: The Consolidator: Or, A Dream of the Court of Great Britain
works.form: political satire; prose dream vision and mock-utopian travel
works.description: A political dream vision in which the narrator is carried to a moon court and given a flying machine, the Consolidator, with which he surveys the British parliament, church and party system. It is the earliest of the great Augustan satiric fictions and a direct attack on the ministry of the day and on the traffic in addresses and votes.
works.plot: Summoned before the emperor of the moon, the narrator receives the Consolidator and a commission to report on the state of Great Britain. He flies over London, watches the Commons sit, and sees the ministers voting Purgatory, the sale of boroughs and the address-makers at work. He is present at the trial of the party leaders before the moon court, where the factions plead their causes, and the dream ends with a sentence upon the nation's corrupt management.
works.significance: It anticipates the machinery of the later Augustan dream satire and stands with the moon-project pamphlets as the founding text of the fiction of political flight; it also evidences the early use of the miscellany press for party work.
works.meter: Spare ironic prose alternating with formally declaimed speeches and inserted verse addresses; the invective passages rise into the periods of pulpit and stage rhetoric for satiric effect.
works.context: Published in 1705 in the heat of the Junto ministry crisis and the debate over the Scottish union, and dedicated into the interest of the Godolphin-Marlborough administration; its imagery draws directly on the party pamphlet war of the season.
works.characters: the narrator-dreamer; the emperor of the moon; the Consolidator machine personified; the party leaders at the bar; the address-makers and the voting politicians
works.structure: A first-person dream vision in the classical manner, framing a series of satirical tableaux and set-piece orations; the moon book supplies the apparatus, the London book the invective, and the trial the formal conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by internal and bibliographical evidence and accepted without serious dispute; the first issue was printed without the writer's name.

works.title: The Constitution Violated: An Essay
works.description: Published in 1871 and the central legal argument of the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts: a demonstration that the Acts violate the constitutional rights of Englishwomen. It is a prose work of 1871 by Josephine Butler; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Butler sets out the Acts clause by clause, shows that they subject any woman suspected of prostitution to examination, registration and imprisonment without trial, and argues that this establishes a legal class of persons outside the protection of the constitution.
works.significance: The Constitution Violated is the classic Victorian argument that the regulation of prostitution is unconstitutional as well as immoral; it framed the repeal campaign as a question of the rights of the subject and is a founding text of English feminist legal argument.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is prophetic, impassioned oratory in print.
works.context: The Contagious Diseases Acts of 1864, 1866 and 1869, the military garrison towns, and the campaign for repeal led by the Ladies' National Association. The record dates the work as composed in 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Josephine Elizabeth Butler. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Contemplative Quarry
works.description: The poetry of female rebellion: marriage, motherhood and the woman's rage. It is a verse work of 1915 by Anna Wickham; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Georgian Anthology Lyric and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Wickham's poems — 'The Affinity', 'Divorce', 'The Garden', 'The Wife', 'Meditation at Kew' — in which marriage, motherhood and the woman's anger are rendered in short, hard, ironic lyrics.
works.significance: The Contemplative Quarry is the first book of English poetry to write the woman's anger without apology: its short, hard lyrics of marriage and motherhood made Wickham the pioneer of the poetry of female rebellion and a direct ancestor of the feminist poetry of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short lyric of the woman's anger.
works.context: London and the suburbs in the 1910s, and the first wave of the women's movement. works.title: The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean
altTitles: Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean
works.description: The founding desert-island adventure for boys: three shipwrecked boys, cannibals and pirates in the Pacific. It is a prose fiction work of 1858 by R. M. Ballantyne; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Ralph Rover, Jack Martin and Peterkin Gay are wrecked on a coral island in the Pacific; they build a life from the wreck, explore the reef, encounter cannibals and pirates, and are rescued after a series of adventures that teach them courage and providence.
works.significance: The Coral Island founded the desert-island adventure for boys and was the book that Stevenson, Haggard and Kipling all read as children: it created the formula of the wreck, the island, the resourceful boy and the encounter with savagery that the whole imperial adventure tradition inherited.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail drawn from first-hand experience.
works.context: The Pacific islands of the 1850s, the missionary and trading frontier, and the British boy's education in the mid-Victorian period. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Ralph Rover; Jack Martin; Peterkin Gay; the pirate chief; the natives
works.structure: A first-person narrative in thirty-six chapters, from the wreck to the rescue. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: The Corn King and the Spring Queen
altTitles: Corn King and the Spring Queen
works.description: The historical novel of the corn king, the spring queen and the ritual year. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by Naomi Mitchison; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Corn King and the Spring Queen is set in the third-century BC world of Sparta, Scythia and the Hellenistic kingdoms, and follows Erif Der, the queen of the year-ritual, and the corn king who must die for the harvest, through the politics of the reforming king and the rites of the year, in the anthropological historical prose that made it Mitchison's masterwork.
works.significance: The Corn King and the Spring Queen is the great historical novel of the ritual imagination: it joined the anthropology of Jane Harrison to the politics of the 1930s and made the dying king and the year's rite a modern novel of the state, the body and the sacrifice.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the historical novel of the ancient world in the anthropologist's eye.
works.context: The Hellenistic world of the third century BC, written in the decade of the thirties. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Erif Der, the spring queen; the corn king; the reforming king of Sparta
works.structure: A long historical novel in the parts of the year's ritual and the politics of the kingdoms. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The Corsair
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the outlaw and sea-romance tale, with the minstrel figure and the scene of pursued concealment.
works.description: The most immediately successful of the verse tales, selling tens of thousands of copies on the day of publication. A pirate chief, famous for a hardness that spares no enemy, discovers that a captive has won his wife's pity, and in a crisis of jealousy commits a private murder on the island of his followers. He then returns to the scene of his youth, is taken by the lord of the island, and perishes in a burning convent whose aisles shelter his bride. The tale turns the outlaw's career into a study of a love that cannot survive knowledge of itself.
works.plot: The pirate is a lord of the archipelago, dreaded and obeyed, whose one tie is to the woman who has softened his ferocity; hearing that she has pitied a prisoner, he steals at night to the cave and kills him. The murdered man's lord pursues him to the isle where he was born, and the pirate is taken and condemned; he escapes by night to the convent where his bride waits, and the building is fired about them, so that they perish together in the aisles while the islanders watch. The argument is that a nature formed for command is destroyed by the one sentiment that makes it human, and that concealment, not guilt, is the outlaw's real condition. The meditations on the sea, the cave and the mind's secret history carry the poem far beyond its plot.
works.significance: It made the outlaw hero the dominant figure of popular European romance, and its combination of crime, conjugal devotion and spectacular burning scene set the pattern for the century's melodrama and its successors. It is also the best document of the relationship between a famous name, a bookseller's market and a reading public, and its pirated theatrical versions became a case in the argument about the property of the drama.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with an interpolated song of the ocean in short lyric measure and a marked use of piling repetition in the passages of terror.
works.context: Published in 1814, in the last months of the Napoleonic war and in a season of popular appetite for romance of the sea and the pirate, the poem was a commercial event, its first issue of many thousands of copies exhausting itself in a day. It was attacked by the reviewers as a corrupting exhibition of guilty greatness, translated at once into the principal languages of Europe, and dramatized and pilfered in print, which led to an unusual public complaint by its author.
works.characters: the corsair; his bride; the captured minstrel; the lord of the isle and his train; the hermit and the convent's inmates
works.structure: Three cantos of compact narrative, opened by a summary of the pirate's history and character, with long reflective set pieces and a rapid, spectacular close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text was revised in the collected editions, and the poem's separate 1816 issue with its tale of the lake survives in differing states.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: The Cotter's Saturday Night
altTitles: The Cotter's Saturday Night. In Imitation of Spence
works.form: descriptive and moral poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the domestic-picture tradition imitated from Spence as the subtitle indicates
works.description: Burns's most cherished poem, a picture of the Sabbath evening of an Ayrshire cottager's family, composed in November 1785 and first printed in the Kilmarnock volume. The scene of family worship, with the father reading and expounding and the mother ordering both the devotions and the supper, is rendered with an accuracy that made the poem the standard image of Scottish domestic Presbyterianism. It closes with addresses to the poet's rustic muse and to his native country that turn the cottage scene into a declaration of poetic and national allegiance.
works.plot: The poem follows the household from the day's work finished to the assembling of the family, the call to worship, the reading of scripture with plain homely expounding, the singing of a paraphrase, the father's discourse on the religion of the heart, and the simple meal. The mother appears as the practical head of the household's piety and economy, the daughters at their work, and the old grandfather remembering the covenanting past. The closing stanzas withdraw from the scene to set the honest poverty of the cotter against the empty splendour of rank, and to ask that Scotland itself be the poet's theme.
works.significance: It became the emblematic poem of Scottish domestic and religious life, among the most reprinted, quoted and illustrated texts in the language, and was taken from Francis Jeffrey onward as the instance of genius nourished by home scenes. Its representation of family worship also makes it a document for the social history of Presbyterianism and for the sentimental celebration of rural poverty.
works.meter: Stanzaic Scots in alternating four- and three-beat lines with a close-running rhyme, in the old Scottish narrative manner inherited from Ramsay and Fergusson; the invocation and the closing addresses use the same measure.
works.context: Written at Mossgiel in the hardest years of Burns's farming, out of a household scene he knew exactly, and shaped by the eighteenth-century cult of honest poverty and domestic piety as well as by Fergusson's dialect pictures of Edinburgh life. Its Presbyterian Sabbath subject matter belonged to a culture of family worship, paraphrase singing and covenanting memory still vivid in Ayrshire.
works.characters: The cottager father; his wife, the mother of the family; the daughters and sons; the grandfather of the former times
works.structure: A continuous descriptive-didactic poem in several grouped stanzas, opening with a short invocation, passing through the hours of the evening in order, and ending in an apostrophe to the muse and to native Scotland.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns recorded the poem in his own memorandum of dates and discussed its dialect and its models in his literary correspondence. The identification of the Spence named in the subtitle remains a matter of comment and is not asserted here.
themes: Evangelical experience and assurance

movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: The Countess Cathleen
works.form: Verse play; verse drama, first issued in 1892
works.description: Yeats's first major verse play and the founding production of the Irish literary theatre. It is a dramatic work of 1892 by W. B. Yeats; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Verse Drama and the Poetic Play; Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: During a famine, the Countess Cathleen sells her lands and finally her soul to the demons who are buying Irish souls for corn; the play ends with her death and her salvation by divine mercy. It opened the Irish Literary Theatre in May 1899 and was attacked from the pulpit for its theology.
works.significance: The Countess Cathleen founded the Irish literary theatre and made the verse play a national form: its opening night in 1899 began the movement that built the Abbey Theatre.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama: the poetic line, blank verse or a regular stanza, carries the dialogue, and the play alternates the verse speech with lyric and choral passages. The author's characteristic manner is the symbolist image and the esoteric system.
works.context: The Irish famine of the 1840s, the folk legends of soul-selling, and the politico-religious controversy of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1892 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under verse drama and the poetic play; peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.
works.characters: Countess Cathleen; Aleel; the two demons; Shemus; Teigue; Oona
works.structure: Four scenes in verse and prose, with songs. A play in acts in verse, the poetic line carrying the dialogue and the lyric and choral passages set apart. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Butler Yeats. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Countess of Montgomery's Urania
works.description: Lady Mary Wroth's prose romance, the first by an Englishwoman and a continuation of her uncle Sidney's Arcadia: the interlaced adventures of Pamphilia, Amphilanthus, Urania, and their knights and ladies through the courts and islands of the romance world, with the sonnet sequence 'Pamphilia to Amphilanthus' appended — the book whose recognizable court portraits caused a scandal at its publication.
works.plot: The romance follows the loves of Pamphilia (constant) and Amphilanthus (inconstant), the wanderings of Urania and the shepherds, and the enchanted palaces and rival queens of the romance geography; the appended sonnet sequence tells the same story of constancy and betrayal from Pamphilia's side.
works.significance: The first English romance and sonnet sequence by a woman — the foundation of the women's fiction tradition, recovered and canonized by modern scholarship.
works.meter: Prose of the Arcadian school, with the appended sonnets in the Sidneyan form of Wroth's inheritance.
works.context: Published 1621, dedicated to Susan Herbert, Countess of Montgomery; Sir Edward Denny's furious response to his alleged portrait in the book and Wroth's reply are the first documented quarrel of an English woman novelist with her public.
works.characters: Pamphilia; Amphilanthus; Urania; Parselius; the romance's queens, shepherds, and enchanters
works.structure: An interlaced prose romance in the Sidneyan manner, with the sonnet sequence as its lyrical mirror and the author's own family history (the Sidney–Herbert circle) thinly veiled in its portraits.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
works.form: Novel in linked sketches; local-colour sketch
works.description: Published in 1896 and the masterpiece of American regionalism: a summer in the Maine coastal village of Dunnet Landing, and the lives of the women who live there. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Sarah Orne Jewett; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: A visiting woman writer lodges with the herbalist Mrs Todd, visits the retired sea captain Littlepage, attends the funeral of the old sailor, goes with Mrs Todd to the reunion on Green Island, and hears the stories of Mrs Fosdick, Mrs Begg and the eccentric Elijah Tilley; the book ends with the departure of the visitor and the closing of the summer.
works.significance: The Country of the Pointed Firs is the finest work of American regionalism and one of the most perfect books in American literature: its structure, its treatment of women's community and its rendering of the speech of the Maine coast made it the model for the American regional novel and a central text of feminist criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is episodic sketch structure held together by a visiting narrator.
works.context: The 1890s: the decayed Maine port towns, the disappearance of the shipping trade, and the world of the unmarried and widowed women who remained. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Mrs Almira Todd; the narrator; Captain Littlepage; Mrs Blackett; William Blackett; Mrs Fosdick; Elijah Tilley; Mrs Begg; Joanna Todd
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Theodora Sarah Orne Jewett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
