works.title: The Country Wife
works.description: Wycherley's most famous comedy, in which Horner, a rake who pretends to have been unmanned by a surgeon, gains access to the wives and mistresses of the jealous town while the innocent country wife Margery is brought to London.
works.plot: Horner's feigned impotence lets him seduce Lady Fidget, Mrs Squeamish, and others; the country wife Margery Pinchwife is kept under lock and key by her jealous husband, but her innocence defeats his vigilance; Horner's trick is nearly exposed and is saved by the women's complicity.
works.significance: The most performed and most discussed Restoration comedy; its savage exposure of jealousy, hypocrisy, and the marriage market makes it the darkest of the comedies of manners.
works.meter: Prose of great energy, with the famous china scene as the height of comic innuendo.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in January 1675 and published in the same year; it drew on Molière's L'École des femmes and L'École des maris.

works.structure: Five acts with two parallel plots — Horner's intrigue and the Pinchwife marriage — and a low comic subplot of Sparkish and Alithea.

works.title: The Courtship of Miles Standish
works.description: The Plymouth colony romance: John Alden, Priscilla Mullins and the captain who sent a rival. It is a verse work of 1858 by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Miles Standish, the captain of the Plymouth colony, sends his young friend John Alden to woo Priscilla Mullins on his behalf; Priscilla famously asks 'Why don't you speak for yourself, John?' and the poem ends with the captain's reconciliation and the marriage of the young couple.
works.significance: The Courtship of Miles Standish was the most popular of Longfellow's narrative poems in his lifetime and it fixed the image of the Pilgrim Fathers in the American imagination: its Mayflower, its captain and its courtship made the founding of New England into a national romance.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The line is the English hexameter, the unrhymed six-stress line of the classical experiment. The author's characteristic manner is the long narrative poem in regular tetrameter.
works.context: The Plymouth colony of 1621, the first years of the Pilgrim settlement and the war with the Indians. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric; Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: Miles Standish; John Alden; Priscilla Mullins; Elder Brewster
works.structure: A narrative poem in nine cantos of hexameter. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.

works.title: The Covent-Garden Tragedy
works.form: burlesque tragedy in two acts, written for the stage
works.description: A two-act burlesque tragedy in which the inhabitants of a house of accommodation talk the language of virtue, tenderness and heroic distress, and the domestic tragedy of the higher classes is inverted into the parlour of the lower. It was played at Drury Lane at the end of the author's first theatrical season.
works.plot: The mistress of the house and her daughter are rivals for the affection of a young gentleman of the town, each insisting on the claims of nature and of merit. The lover is torn between gratitude and passion, the officers of the watch and the creditors press upon the family, and the high tragic style is sustained through the lowest of situations. The piece ends in a catastrophe of tenderness rather than of blood, the moral being the ridiculousness of tragic phrase.
works.significance: It is one of the most sustained English parodies of the diction of tragedy and a necessary link between the theatrical burlesque of the writer's early career and the theory of the ridiculous worked out in the comic prose.
works.meter: Blank verse and the declamatory periods of tragedy used for the lowest subjects, with the couplet sententiae of the tragic closure intact; the effect depends on the discrepancy of style and scene.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in June 1732, in the season of the author's experiments in the little theatre and of the fashionable decline of tragedy, and after the burlesque success of the Tom Thumb piece of the previous year.
works.characters: Mother Punchbowl, the mistress of the house; her daughter, the rival of the same address; Dimple, the young gentleman pursued by both; the watchmen and officers of the garden
works.structure: A two-act farce of tragic form, the scenes arranged as the exchanges of a regular tragedy with their dignity inverted; the parody is continuous and the plot is a thin excuse.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name in the collected dramatick works of the later thirties.

works.title: The Coverdale Bible
altTitles: Biblia: The Bible Faithfully Translated into English
works.description: Miles Coverdale's translation of the whole Bible into English, printed in 1535 (probably at Antwerp); the first complete printed Bible in English.
works.plot: A complete Bible — Old Testament, Apocrypha, and New Testament — translated 'out of Douche and Latyn' (German and Latin versions) as Coverdale's title page honestly states, with Tyndale's New Testament and Pentateuch incorporated; dedicated to Henry VIII, with a preface defending vernacular scripture.
works.significance: The first complete English Bible in print and the bridge from Tyndale to the authorized versions: its psalter became the Prayer Book psalter of 1662, still sung in Anglican worship, and its title page initiated the tradition of the English Bible as a national book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1535, probably at Antwerp (the colophon of some copies points to Cologne); Anne Boleyn's patronage and Cromwell's diplomacy won it royal acceptance, and in 1537 it was licensed for sale in England, making the English Bible legal for the first time.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, chapter summaries, and a dedication to the king.

works.title: The Crater
works.form: Maritime and island romance with a philosophical argument about priestly power; utopian and anti-utopian fiction
works.description: The most speculative of the author's romances, a tale of a volcanic island in the Pacific on which a shipwrecked American sailor founds a theocracy. It joins maritime adventure to a political and religious analysis of a community built from scratch. Its second half, in which the island's priest-king degenerates into persecution, makes it a study of enthusiasm in a state of nature.
works.plot: A New England seaman, passed over for his beloved's hand by a ship's captain, is cast away with a small company on an island newly risen from the sea. He marries the woman he loves, and the little community, cut off from all law, gradually accepts him as its religious leader. He founds a creed, a ritual and a chronology of his own invention, and his authority hardens into tyranny over those who doubt it. The narrative then carries a visiting ship and its passengers into the island's history, and closes with the overthrow of the priestly power and the return of the survivors to the world.
works.significance: It is the strangest and most ambitious of the author's fictions, anticipating later island narratives of conscience and domination. Its analysis of how a religious authority is manufactured from necessity has kept it in view for students of American theocracy. It shows the romance of forest and sea turning inward to political philosophy.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1827, in the decade of American South-Sealing voyages and of the published narratives that made the Pacific a theatre for moral experiments. Its theocratic plot belongs to the American argument about religious enthusiasm and republican government. The geological speculation reflects contemporary interest in volcanic theory.
works.characters: Eric Berg; Martha Boardman; the shipwrecked company; the doubters of the island community
works.structure: Romance in two movements, the founding of an island community and its degeneration into persecution, framed by cosmological and geological disquisition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Sea voyage and seafaring
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: The Creed
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (creedal paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A versification of the Apostles' Creed in 57 lines, expanding each article of the faith — the creation, the Incarnation, the Passion, the harrowing of hell, the Ascension, and the last judgment — into alliterative verse of notable doctrinal clarity.
works.plot: The poem follows the articles of the Creed in order: God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth; Christ's conception, birth, suffering, death, descent into hell, resurrection, and ascension; and the coming judgment of the living and the dead.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English verse rendering of the Apostles' Creed, valuable for its formulation of Christology and eschatology in the native idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the poem's compact clauses follow the Creed article by article.
works.context: The Creed was taught to all Christians as the summary of the faith and recited in the daily offices; its versification belongs to the same vernacular devotional project as the Lord's Prayer poems.
works.structure: A sequential paraphrase of the Creed's articles, each expanded with traditional doctrinal imagery (the descent into hell, the trumpet of judgment).

works.title: The Crime at Black Dudley
works.description: The first Campion novel: a country house, a gang and a dagger. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Margery Allingham; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A weekend party at Black Dudley is interrupted by a gang of criminals searching for a missing treasure, and Albert Campion — the effete, bespectacled guest — quietly takes charge in one of the founding novels of the Golden Age.
works.significance: The Crime at Black Dudley introduced Albert Campion and founded one of the great detective series: its mixture of the country house, the gangster and the comic hero made it a founding novel of the Golden Age and the first appearance of Allingham's great detective.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the comic detective and the grotesque villain.
works.context: An English country house in the late 1920s. works.title: The Critic
works.form: comic rehearsal drama with inserted burlesque tragedy
works.description: A comic rehearsal piece, subtitled a tragedy in the irony of the day, in which the pretences of contemporary tragedy and criticism are exposed by the staging of an absurdly grandiose play within the play. It was the last great success of the eighteenth-century theatre of self-reference.
works.plot: A family of country gentlefolk and their hangers-on go to see a new tragedy, and the business of the pit, the boxes and the green-room is reported before and after the performance. The play itself, a monstrous romance of terror with an old castle and a ghost, is rehearsed and criticised by its authors and by the wits of the town. The exposure of the bombast ends the comedy, the lovers of the frame being united in the last scene.
works.significance: It is the century's sharpest analysis of theatrical taste and of the critic's trade, and its portrait of the self-satisfied dramatist remains the stock image of literary vanity.
works.meter: Prose dialogue for the comedy and an exaggerated blank verse and declamation for the inserted tragedy, the joke lying in the contrast of the two registers.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1781, in the season of the manager's quarrels, the revival of old plays and the persistent debate about tragic declamation; its target includes the contemporary school of domestic terror on the stage.
works.characters: Mr. Puff, the author of the inserted tragedy; his friends the critics and the observers of the pit; the family of the frame and the lovers of the underplot; the players of the burlesque romance
works.structure: Two-act comedy of the rehearsal and the audience, with a running performance of the inserted tragedy; the frame and the inserted piece comment on each other throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the author's share was discussed in the press in relation to an earlier fragment of the same design; published in his name.

works.title: The Cuckoo Clock
works.description: Published in 1877 and the most famous of Molesworth's books: the story of Griselda, sent to live with two old aunts, and of the cuckoo in the clock who takes her into the world of the birds. It is a prose fiction work of 1877 by Mary Louisa Molesworth; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
works.plot: Griselda, lonely and proud, is visited by the cuckoo from the clock in her aunt's hall; he takes her to the country of the nodding mandarins, the land of the butterflies and the other side of the moon, and through him and her new friend Phil she learns to be less selfish and more patient.
works.significance: The Cuckoo Clock is one of the finest Victorian fairy tales and the book that made Molesworth the most popular children's writer of the 1880s; its allegory of time and childhood is a permanent part of the English nursery canon.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unhurried narrative.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian nursery and the fairy tale, and the child's isolation in the house of elderly relatives. The record dates the work as composed between 1876 and 1877 and first published in 1877 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: The Curse of Kehama
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, and an Oriental philosophical poem of the providential type, in which the machinery of a living religion is used as the apparatus of a moral fable.
works.description: An Oriental tale in verse published in 1810, founded on the machinery of the Hindu theology as it was then known in translation, and telling of a sacrilegious Brahmin who dares the powers of heaven and is pursued by a curse. The poem's design was to make an English epic out of an Eastern religion, giving its subordinate spirits, its places of punishment and its hierarchy of gods a continuous narrative function, and its argument is that the defier of the moral order is destroyed while the innocent suffer briefly for his guilt.
works.plot: Kehama, a Brahmin of boundless ambition, obtains by violence the bride of another man and, having set at defiance the powers that govern the world of spirits, is struck by the curse pronounced upon him, which pursues him through the books of the poem. The machinery works continuously: inferior ministers of the divine justice are sent to execute the sentence, and the guilty man's prosperity is made to turn to the ruin of those about him, while a patient and devoted member of his own house, whose life is spent in endurance and devotion, is taken out of suffering rather than preserved to enjoy it. The last books bring the curse to its execution, the destroyer of Kehama's happiness being himself destroyed, and the poem ends with the justification of the moral government of the universe and with the assurance that the obedient and the meek are remembered by the powers they serve.
works.significance: The most elaborate of the Romantic English poems built wholly on Hindu machinery, and a document of the period's appetite for an epic apparatus drawn from the religions of the East; its treatment of the curse as an engine of narrative influenced later Oriental tale in verse, and its theology of patience and punishment is a plain instance of the religious temper of the author's middle years.
works.meter: An accentual versification of the experimental kind already tried in the author's earlier Eastern tale, with lines measured by stress rather than by syllable count and a stanza that varies with the scene, the whole giving a rolling and reiterated effect much remarked on by the reviewers.
works.context: Published in 1810, when translations of Hindu scripture and commentary were supplying English poets with a new apparatus of machinery, and when the author had settled into the Lake community and was moving from the radicalism of the 1790s towards the conservative religious position of his later years; the poem's theodicy belongs to that transition.
works.characters: Kehama, the sacrilegious Brahmin; the bride carried off by his violence and her kindred; the ministers and subordinate spirits of the Hindu theology who execute the curse; a patient and devoted member of the offender's own house
works.structure: A metrical tale in a long series of books, organised as the pursuit of one guilty man by a supernatural sentence, with the action of the machinery intermixed with the domestic calamities of the mortals; the argument is carried by episodes of temptation, punishment and patience rather than by a continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning

works.title: The Custom of the Country
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1913 and the most satirical of Wharton's novels: the rise of a beautiful, ruthless midwestern girl through three marriages. It is a prose fiction work of 1913 by Edith Wharton; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Undine Spragg, a beautiful girl from Apex City, comes to New York determined to have everything; she marries Ralph Marvell for his name, leaves him for a French nobleman, divorces him for a richer man, and finally, with her son lost to her, achieves the marriage she has wanted, only to find that there is nothing left she wants.
works.significance: The Custom of the Country is the greatest American satire of the period and the finest novel of American social climbing: its portrait of Undine Spragg is one of the most complete characters in American fiction, and its analysis of the relation between money, marriage and nationality makes it the central American novel of the new rich.
works.meter: Prose. The author's characteristic manner is precise, ironic exposition of a social world.

works.title: The Daisy Chain
works.form: Novel (first of the 'Chronicles of the May family')
works.description: Published in 1856 and the first of Yonge's family chronicles: the eleven May children of a country doctor grow up through loss, school and vocation. It is a prose fiction work of 1856 by Charlotte M. Yonge; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The May family of Dr May of Stoneborough loses its mother in the first chapter, and the novel follows the children's education, the invalid Margaret's long illness, Ethel's struggles to manage the household and teach the poor, and the founding of the mission school that becomes Cocksmoor.
works.significance: The Daisy Chain is the founding text of the Victorian family chronicle and one of the most complete pictures of ordinary genteel life in English fiction: its large cast and its moral seriousness made 'the May family' a household name and founded the dynasty of chronicles that dominated girls' reading for fifty years.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the large family chronicle with an enormous cast.

works.title: The Damnation of Theron Ware
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The finest American novel of a clergyman's crisis: a Methodist minister in a small town finds the world. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Harold Frederic; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Theron Ware, a young Methodist minister in the small town of Octavius, New York, is flattered by the local Catholic priest, by a cultivated woman of the world and by a scientist, and his faith and his marriage collapse under the intellectual and sexual temptation of the larger world.
works.significance: The Damnation of Theron Ware is one of the finest American novels of the 1890s and the first American novel to treat a clergyman's crisis of faith with full intellectual seriousness: it is a direct ancestor of the modern novel of belief and of the naturalist small-town novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the free indirect style of the provincial mind.

works.description: The long baroque poem of the quick and the dead in the same stanza. It is a verse work of 1935 by Sacheverell Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method.
works.plot: The Dance of the Quick and the Dead gathers the long poems of the baroque manner - the palace, the fountain, the firework and the dance of the quick and the dead - in the loaded line of the mature poet, the fullest statement of the Sitwell sound in the long poem.

works.title: The Dark River
works.form: Play (the Thames backwater); comedy of manners
works.description: The play of the idle household against the Spanish war and the coming fascism. It is a dramatic work of 1937 by Rodney Ackland; it belongs to The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners and it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Dark River sets the household of the Thames backwater - Catherine Lisle, her infantile ex-husband Chris and her politically awake lover Alan - against the Spanish Civil War and the coming war, in the Chekhovian drawing-room play that on its 1984 revival was called the one indisputably great play of the half-century in English.

works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The author's characteristic manner is the drawing-room dialogue of the West End with the politics of the decade beneath it.

works.title: The Daughters of Danaus
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1894
works.description: Published in 1894 and the most intellectually ambitious New Woman novel: the sacrifice of a woman composer to her family and the maternal 'instinct'. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Mona Caird; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Hadria Fullerton, a gifted composer, is urged by her family to marry and to give up her music for husband and children; she marries Hubert Temperley, bears children she cannot love, escapes to Paris to study composition, and is called home by her mother's illness, which her family uses against her; the novel ends not in reconciliation but in defeat, her music abandoned and her revolt absorbed by a duty she cannot refuse.
works.significance: The Daughters of Danaus is the most searching of the New Woman novels and the only one to make a woman artist's vocation its central subject: its refusal of the maternal ideal and its unflinching account of the cost of marriage made it the most radical feminist novel of the 1890s, and it has been recovered as a key text of Victorian feminism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical essay with a plain and logical argument.

works.title: The Day of the Locust
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1939
works.description: The great Hollywood novel: the dream factory and the mob at the end of the world. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by Nathanael West; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tod Hackett, a painter working in the studios, drifts through the Hollywood of the 1930s among failed actors, dwarf cowboys and the beautiful Faye Greener, until the crowd at a premiere turns into a riot and the novel ends in apocalypse.
works.significance: The Day of the Locust is the great Hollywood novel and one of the finest American novels of the 1930s: its portrait of the dream factory and its vision of the mob made it the permanent novel of American mass culture and the ancestor of the modern Hollywood novel.

works.title: The Day They Burned the Books
works.description: A short story by Jean Rhys, set in the Dominica of her childhood around the turn of the twentieth century and told by a white Creole girl who remembers her friend Eddie and the day his mother burned his dead father's books. Rhys wrote it while she was working on Wide Sargasso Sea, and it was published in 1960, six years before the novel; it was collected in Tigers Are Better-Looking (1968).
works.summary: The narrator's friendship with Eddie Sawyer, the son of an Englishman and a coloured wife; Mr Sawyer's room of books from England; his death, and the afternoon when Mrs Sawyer clears the room, sorting the books to be sold or burned; the two children's attempt to save a book each.
works.plot: The narrator, a white Creole girl of twelve on a West Indian island, recalls her friend Eddie, small, consumptive and precocious, the son of Mr Sawyer, an Englishman who works as an agent for a steamship line and has settled on the island for no reason anyone can see. He is not a gentleman by colonial standards, and he treats his pretty, nicely educated coloured wife with insulting contempt. His one passion is the room of books he has had sent out from England, which Eddie calls his own and where the children read; through Eddie the narrator first comes to doubt the England the colonials call home. After Mr Sawyer dies suddenly, Mrs Sawyer and her servant clear the room, sorting the books into those to be sold and those to be burned, and Mrs Sawyer tears and pitches them with evident satisfaction. Eddie protests and rushes at her, and in the confusion the two children each snatch a book and run. Eddie's is Kim, torn; the narrator's turns out to be Maupassant's Fort comme la mort, in French.
works.significance: One of Rhys's most discussed stories and a companion piece to Wide Sargasso Sea, it is a frequently anthologised text of Caribbean and postcolonial writing; Norton prints it with "On Not Shooting Sitting Birds".
works.meter: Plain, exact and economical prose; imagistic detail of heat, light and the room; the child's half-understanding of adult tensions conveyed without commentary.
works.context: Written in the years when Rhys, long out of print and thought by many to be dead, was working on Wide Sargasso Sea, and drawing on her childhood in Dominica, where she was born in 1890; the story looks back to the colonial society of about 1900.
works.structure: A first-person reminiscence told from an unspecified later date but through the child's eyes, as a cluster of vivid memories; brief scenes build to the single afternoon of the burning and end abruptly with the two rescued books.
themes: Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
Decolonisation, the end of empire and the new nation
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
movements: Caribbean Literature in English
Postcolonial Literature

works.title: The Dead Secret
works.description: Serialised in Household Words in 1857 and the first of Collins's novels to show the full sensation method: a deathbed secret hidden in a Cornish house, and the slow uncovering of a substituted identity.
works.plot: Mrs Treverton dictates on her deathbed a confession that Rosamond is not her daughter but the child of her maid, Sarah Leeson, passed off as her own to keep her husband's love; the confession is hidden in the Myrtle Room at Porthgenna Tower, and the novel follows the servant Sarah Leeson's flight, the search for the letter, and Rosamond's marriage and discovery of the truth.
works.significance: The Dead Secret is the technical experiment in which Collins developed the method of The Woman in White — the hidden document, the withheld identity and the domestic secret.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1850s, the Cornish setting and its wrecking economy, the Victorian deathbed and testament, and the Household Words readership. The record dates the work as composed between 1856 and 1857 and first published in 1857 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: Rosamond Frankland (née Treverton); Leonard Frankland, her blind husband; Sarah Leeson; Captain Treverton; Mrs Treverton; Uncle Joseph Buschmann; Andrew Treverton; Shrowl
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Death of the Heart
works.description: Bowen's masterpiece: a young girl in a London household and the betrayal of her love. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by Elizabeth Bowen; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Portia Quayne, sixteen and orphaned, comes to live with her half-brother Thomas and his wife Anna in London; her innocence is exploited by the cad Eddie, and the novel ends with her flight and her refusal of the adult world that has betrayed her.
works.significance: The Death of the Heart is Bowen's masterpiece and one of the finest English novels of the period: its portrait of Portia, its dialogue and its anatomy of adult betrayal made it the great English novel of innocence and one of the central novels of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the image that carries the emotion.
works.context: London and the seaside in the late 1930s, and the English upper middle class between the wars. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Portia Quayne; Anna Quayne; Thomas Quayne; Eddie; St Quentin Miller; Matchett
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the London house to the seaside flight. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Dorothea Cole Bowen. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Deemster
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Caine's first Manx novel and the book that made him famous: a killing on the shore and the doom of two families. It is a prose fiction work of 1887 by Hall Caine; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Dan Mylrea, the deemster's son, and his cousin Ewan love the same woman; Dan kills Ewan in a quarrel on the Manx shore, is transported, returns as a dying preacher, and the novel ends in renunciation and sacrifice.
works.significance: The Deemster was Caine's first Manx novel and the book that made him famous: it put the Isle of Man at the centre of English fiction and its melodrama of crime, exile and renunciation set the pattern for the popular religious novel of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the three-decker architecture of climax and reunion.
works.context: The Isle of Man at the beginning of the nineteenth century, the old Manx deemster court, and the fishing community of the north of the island. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1887 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; sensation novel.
works.characters: Dan Mylrea; Ewan Mylrea; Bessie Collister; the Deemster; Mona
works.structure: A novel in three books, from the Manx shore to the convict settlement and back. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Henry Hall Caine. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems
altTitles: Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems
works.description: Published in 1858 and Morris's first book: a collection of dramatic lyrics of the Arthurian and medieval world, which puzzled the reviewers and later became one of the founding texts of the Pre-Raphaelite movement.
works.plot: The title poem is Guenevere's defence before her accusers; the volume also contains 'King Arthur's Tomb', 'The Haystack in the Floods', 'Concerning Geffray Teste Noire' and the dramatic lyrics of the French and English middle ages.
works.significance: The Defence of Guenevere is the founding book of Pre-Raphaelite poetry and one of the great collections of dramatic lyrics in English: its treatment of Guenevere's desire and its grim realism about violence made it a permanent influence on the twentieth-century Arthurian tradition.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is long, even, unrhymed or heroic-couplet narrative.
works.context: 1850s: the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, the Oxford of Burne-Jones and Rossetti, and the Victorian medieval revival. The record dates the work as composed between 1856 and 1858 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature; The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Guenevere ('The Defence of Guenevere'); Launcelot ('King Arthur's Tomb'); Robert de Marny, Jehane and Godmar ('The Haystack in the Floods'); John of Castel Neuf ('Concerning Geffray Teste Noire'); Sir Galahad ('Sir Galahad, a Christmas Mystery'); Rapunzel
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Morris (designer and poet). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Defence of Poesy
works.description: Sir Philip Sidney's treatise in defence of poetry, written in answer to Stephen Gosson's attack The School of Abuse (1579): poetry is the first light-giver to ignorance, the sweet food of sweetly uttered knowledge, superior to both philosophy and history, and the English tongue is fully capable of the highest poetic kinds.
works.plot: Sidney answers the charges against poetry one by one, derives its antiquity and dignity from the ancients and the Bible, anatomizes the genres (pastoral, elegy, comedy, tragedy, lyric, epic), diagnoses the current poverty of English drama, and closes with the famous mocking peroration on the poet's power to make men 'not only to know, but to do'.
works.significance: The founding document of English literary criticism, from which the tradition runs through Jonson and Dryden to the Romantics.
works.meter: Prose, in the polished periodic style of the humanist oration.
works.context: Written about 1579–82 amid the Puritan attack on the stage; circulated in manuscript and printed posthumously in 1595 in two editions under its two titles.
works.structure: A classical judicial oration: exordium, narration, proof, refutation of objections, and peroration, salted with anecdote and wit.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Time, death, and immortality through verse
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Descent into Hell
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A narrative poem on Christ's descent into hell between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection, his release of the patriarchs and prophets, and the Resurrection itself. It draws on the Gospel of Nicodemus tradition and dramatizes the harrowing as a triumphant act of liberation.
works.plot: Christ descends to hell, breaks its gates, and frees the captive righteous — Adam, the patriarchs, and the prophets — who greet him as their long-awaited redeemer. The poem closes with the women's discovery of the empty tomb and the angel's announcement of the Resurrection.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English poem devoted wholly to the harrowing of hell, and an important witness to the devotional imagination that also produced The Dream of the Rood and Christ III.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with formulaic phrasing; the speeches of the patriarchs are given rhetorical weight through balanced alliterative clauses.
works.context: The harrowing of hell was a central motif of early medieval devotion, represented in art and liturgy as well as poetry; the poem is contemporary with the flourishing of the theme in Anglo-Saxon stone sculpture and homiletic prose.
works.characters: Christ, Adam, the patriarchs and prophets, the women at the tomb
works.structure: A compact narrative in two movements: the harrowing itself (the descent, the breaking of the gates, the speeches of the patriarchs) and the Resurrection morning at the tomb, with typological echoes of the Exodus throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No attribution has been proposed.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

works.title: The Descent of Liberty: A Mask
altTitles: The Descent of Liberty: A Mask; with Poems
works.form: Political allegorical mask in the Romantic reviving of the Spenserian and Miltonic masque, published with accompanying shorter poems
works.description: A political allegorical mask by Leigh Hunt, written to celebrate the peace that followed the fall of Napoleon and first published in 1815 in a volume that also gathered shorter verses. The personified Liberty descends from heaven to a Europe exhausted by war, and the poem passes in vision over the ruined and the recovering lands before turning to hopes for England and to Hunt's own imprisonment for libel. It is a characteristic piece of Hunt's radical-liberal Romanticism, joining the masque allegory of Spenser and Milton to contemporary protest against the Holy Alliance and for national freedom.
works.plot: In an introductoryInvocation the spirit of Liberty is summoned; she descends and surveys a Europe scorched by the long Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, mourning the liberties that have been betrayed by tyrants and restored monarchs. The mask passes in allegorical pageant through the fates of nations, contrasts the promise of freedom with its post-war disappointment, and ends in a brighter vision of liberty's future return and a personal note in which the imprisoned poet claims his suffering for the cause of free speech.
works.significance: The mask is a central document of Hunt's political Romanticism and of the liberal-allegorical current that ran alongside the more Tory or apolitical strand of the period's verse; it shows how the older masque was retooled for contemporary protest, and it shaped the younger Hazlitt, Keats, and Shelley's sense of a poetry of liberty and sensuous fancy.
works.meter: Chiefly Spenserian stanzas and other elaborate rhymed measures in smooth iambic lines, the ornamented stanza forms of the allegorical mask chosen for their musical and decorative effect; Hunt's easy, tuned versification is prominent rather than weighty.
works.context: Written in 1814-15 to greet the peace and published the year of Waterloo and the Congress of Vienna, the mask expresses Hunt's Liberal hope that liberty would triumph over despotism and his fear that the settlement would only enthrone new tyrants. Hunt wrote it in the aftermath of his two-year imprisonment in Dorchester Gaol for libelling the Prince Regent, an experience that made him a byword for the Romantic literary radicalism associated with the Examiner.
works.characters: the personified Liberty; War and its victims; the tyrants and restored kings of the post-war settlement; the poet-spectator who is also the imprisoned Leigh Hunt
works.structure: A dramatic-allegorical mask in rhymed stanzas, framed by an invocation and unfolding as a procession of visions and personified abstractions rather than a plot of individual characters; the movement is from descent and survey through lament to prophetic hope.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; Leigh Hunt's authorship is undisputed.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: The Descent of Odin
altTitles: The Descent of Odin: A Translation from the Norse
works.description: Gray's imitated translation of the northern poem in which Odin raises a dead prophetess from her grave to learn the fate that awaits him, a short dramatic lyric of the nether world.
works.plot: The father of the northern gods descends to the boundaries of the dead and compels the sealed prophetess to speak; her answers tell of a grief among the powers of light and of the doom that is coming upon them, and the vision closes with the dread of the hour.
works.significance: It is the earliest English poem to make the mythology of the Edda a poetic machinery, and it prepared the northern sublime of the following century.
works.meter: The short lines and the alternate rhyme of the reconstructed Norse measure, with the abrupt address and the reiterate question.
works.context: Written with The Fatal Sisters from Gray's antiquarian reading of the Edda in the editions then new to English students, in the decade which made the northern mythology a resource of poetry.
works.characters: Odin; the prophetess raised from the dead; the powers and the doomed of the northern mythology
works.structure: A brief dialogue of the questioner and the raised dead, in the staves of the imitated measure.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, with the same qualification as The Fatal Sisters: the piece is an imitated translation, and the identification of the source poem rests on later scholarship.

works.title: The Description of a New World, Called The Blazing-World
works.form: utopian fiction; prose romance; science fiction; philosophical dialogue
works.description: Margaret Cavendish's fantastical prose fiction, appended to her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, in which a young lady is carried to a parallel world at the North Pole inhabited by hybrid animal-men and rules it as empress.
works.plot: A lady is abducted, carried to the Blazing World, and made empress; she converses with the animal-men and with the soul of the Duchess of Newcastle about natural philosophy, then returns to rescue her native world from invasion.
works.significance: The first science fiction by a woman in English, a pioneering work of utopian and speculative fiction, and a philosophical answer to the experimentalists; it has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing.
works.meter: Vigorous, digressive prose of great imaginative freedom.
works.context: Published in 1666 together with Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, as an appendix; Cavendish was living in exile and later visited the Royal Society in 1667, the first woman to do so.
works.characters: the Empress; the Duchess of Newcastle; the Bear-men; the Bird-men; the Fish-men; the Ape-men; the Satyrs; the Worm-men
works.structure: A two-part narrative of travel and philosophical dialogue, combining utopian fiction, romance, and natural philosophy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cavendish; the title page names her as the Duchess of Newcastle.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Creation and cosmology
Female authorship and the woman writer

works.title: The Deserted Village
works.form: Elegiac and didactic poem in the estate-and-topographical tradition, in heroic couplets, with the personification of luxury and the social portrait borrowed from the descriptive tradition; issued as a separate quarto.
works.description: Goldsmith's most admired poem and one of the canonical complaints of English literature: the elegy of a ruined country village, remembered as the seat of poverty, pleasure and paternal virtue and now deserted through the accumulation of wealth. Its remembered place is Auburn, an imagined Irish village drawn from the scene of the poet's own childhood, and its argument is a moral history of the decay of the countryside.
works.plot: The poem moves from the present desolation of the village to the loving inventory of what has been lost: its sports, its fireside, its church and school, its poor and their pleasures. The portraits that follow, the pedlar, the schoolmistress, the minister and the beggar-woman, are a social survey of a community now scattered, and the poem then turns the survey into an argument about causes. Luxury, the love of gain, the enclosure and the pooling of landed property in great hands, and the pride of the rich are indicted as the forces that have expelled the peasantry, so that the village's desertion becomes the emblem of a national disease in which population and virtue are exchanged for wealth. The emigration of the ruined poor to the colonies supplies the poem's saddest consequence, and the closing movement retires to the poet's own lot, content to have preserved feeling and integrity in an age of opulence.
works.significance: It is the great poem of rural depopulation and of the sentimental critique of commercial society, and it fixed the image of the lost village in English and Irish consciousness. Its influence on later rural poetry, on the literature of the cleared Highlands and of enclosure, and on the language of anti-luxury is considerable, and it established Goldsmith's reputation as the poet of feeling.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in a plain, sententious and affective manner, with the balanced generalisation of the Augustan school used for complaint rather than for wit.
works.context: It appeared in the early 1770s, in the middle of the public debate about depopulation, engrossment and enclosure, and after the famine and emigration which had made Irish decay an English question. Its politics belong with the country-party language of liberty and corruption and with the moral economists' alarm at luxury, and it was attacked at least one reviewer for its doctrine rather than for its verse.
works.characters: The deserted village of Auburn and its scattered poor; the pedlar; the schoolmistress; the minister; the emigrants; the rich and their accumulations
works.structure: A continuous elegiac-complaint poem in the manner of a topographical meditation: present desolation, remembered scenes and characters, analysis of causes, prospect of emigration and moral conclusion in the poet's own retirement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at first but immediately known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and his authorship was never in question. The poem's chronology of composition, which stretched over several years and was revised after publication, is not fixed here.

works.title: The Destruction of Troy
altTitles: The Gest Hystoriale of the Destruction of Troy
works.description: The longest alliterative poem of the revival (over 14,000 lines), translating Guido delle Colonne's Latin Historia destructionis Troiae: the full Trojan story from Jason and the golden fleece to the fall of the city and the homecomings of the Greeks. A work of encyclopedic narrative scope, prized for its battles, storms, and sieges, preserved in a single manuscript.
works.plot: The poem recounts the causes and course of the Trojan war — the Argonauts, the first destruction of Troy, the judgement of Paris and rape of Helen, the ten years' siege with its councils, battles, and single combats, the treachery of the wooden horse, the burning of the city, and the fates of the returning heroes.
works.significance: The fullest Middle English Troy narrative and the summit of alliterative translation; its matter links the revival to Lydgate's Troy Book and the Tudor Troy tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line sustained over an unprecedented length.
works.context: Composed c. 1385–1400 in the north-west Midlands, translating Guido delle Colonne (1287) with additions; preserved uniquely in Glasgow, Hunterian MS V.2.8 (mid-sixteenth century).
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Agamemnon; Ulysses; Troilus
works.structure: A continuous chronicle-romance in the Guido tradition, organized by the war's causes, course, and aftermath, with elaborate set-piece descriptions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Warfare and battle
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: The Devil Rides Out
works.description: The occult thriller of the black mass and the devil's ride. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Dennis Wheatley; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Devil Rides Out sets the Duke de Richleau against the Satanist Mocata for the soul of the young Simon Aron, through the black mass, the ritual circle and the night of the chase, in the occult thriller whose ritual detail made it the classic of the English devil novel.
works.significance: The Devil Rides Out is Wheatley's classic: its black mass, its ritual circle and its Mocata made the occult thriller a national fashion and remain the standard of the English devil novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the thriller's pace and the set piece of the escape.
works.context: England in the mid-1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; detective novel and the golden age mystery.
works.characters: the Duke de Richleau; Mocata, the Satanist; Simon Aron; the rescued
works.structure: An occult thriller in the chapters of the ritual and the chase. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.

works.title: The Devil's Dictionary
works.description: Published as The Cynic's Word Book in 1906 and as The Devil's Dictionary in 1911: the great American work of satire, in the form of a dictionary of cynical definitions. It is a prose work of 1906 by Ambrose Bierce; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The book defines the vocabulary of American public life — politics, religion, law, journalism, marriage, money — in a series of epigrams that reverse the official meanings, so that a 'painting' becomes a way of protecting flat surfaces from the weather and exposing them to the critic.
works.significance: The Devil's Dictionary is the great American work of satire and one of the most quoted books in American literature: it is the source of a large part of the American vocabulary of cynicism, and its definitions of politics, religion and the press remain the permanent American critique of official language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the short, precisely engineered story with a reversed or delayed ending.
works.context: 1881-1911: the American newspaper culture of the Gilded Age, the Hearst press, the satirical tradition of Swift and Voltaire, and the American disbelief of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1906 and first published in 1906 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ambrose Gwinnett Bierce. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Diary of a Nobody
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1892
works.description: The funniest English comic novel of the century: Mr Pooter, the suburb and the dignity of the ordinary man. It is a prose fiction work of 1892 by George Grossmith; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Charles Pooter, a City clerk living in Holloway with his wife Carrie and his worthless son Lupin, records a year of domestic life in his diary: the wallpaper, the dinner parties, the misunderstandings with tradesmen and the rise and fall of his son's fortunes, all in perfect deadpan.
works.significance: The Diary of a Nobody is the funniest English comic novel of the nineteenth century and the founding text of the suburban comedy of manners: it has never been out of print, it made Mr Pooter a permanent English type, and it established the comic suburb in English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the mock diary form with its deadpan self-importance.
works.context: The London suburbs of the 1880s and 1890s, the lower middle class and the new commuter culture. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the new humour; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: A mock diary in weekly entries over fifteen months. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
works.description: Pepys's private shorthand diary, kept from 1 January 1660 to 31 May 1669, the most detailed and most candid account of daily life in Restoration England ever written, recording the Restoration, the coronation, the Plague, and the Fire of London.
works.plot: The diary records Pepys's work at the Navy Board, his amours, his household, the theatre, music, books, politics, and the great public events, with an unflinching self-portrait of ambition, curiosity, and pleasure.
works.significance: The greatest diary in the English language and the single most important source for the social, political, and cultural history of the 1660s; it invented the modern confessional journal and has never been out of print since 1825.
works.meter: Lively, colloquial, and confidential prose, written in Thomas Shelton's tachygraphy (shorthand) and not intended for publication.
works.context: Kept during Pepys's rise in the naval administration and during the two great catastrophes of the Restoration; the diaries passed to Magdalene College, Cambridge, and were first deciphered and published in 1825.
works.characters: Samuel Pepys; Elizabeth Pepys; Sir William Coventry; the Duke of York; Deb Willet; Mary Knep; Nell Gwyn
works.structure: A daily entry over nine and a half years, interrupted only by illness and the strain of failing eyesight.

works.title: The Dictionary
altTitles: The Dictionary of Syr Thomas Eliot Knyght
works.description: Elyot's Latin–English dictionary, the first classical dictionary of the English language and the basis of the later English lexicographical tradition.
works.plot: A reference work with no argument: Latin headwords with English definitions, drawing on Calepino's Dictionarium and enriched by Elyot's own scholarship, published in a revised edition as Bibliotheca Eliotae in 1542 (revised and enlarged by Thomas Cooper, 1548).
works.significance: The founding work of English lexicography: it made classical learning accessible in the vernacular, standardized English equivalents for Latin terms, and served as the model for all subsequent Latin–English dictionaries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled 1536–38 for Thomas Berthelet, with a dedication to Henry VIII; it was the first Latin–English dictionary intended for the study of classical authors rather than the medieval vocabularies, and Cooper's revisions made it the foundation of Renaissance lexicography in England.
works.structure: Alphabetical dictionary entries.

works.title: The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution
works.form: Editorial collection of state papers with commentary; documentary history and letters
works.description: A twelve-volume editorial collection of the letters, instructions and negotiations of the American ministers abroad during the war of independence, printed from the state papers and furnished with biographical and historical notes. It was the first great documentary edition of the founding period and made the diplomacy of the Revolution readable as history. Its editorial method set the standard for the American historical enterprise.
works.plot: The volumes gather the correspondence of the commissioners in France and Spain, the negotiations for the treaties of amity and commerce, the instructions of Congress and the reports of the envoys in the northern courts. Each document is placed in chronological order and accompanied by notes identifying persons, explaining transactions and citing the parallel records. The editor supplies biographical memoirs and historical dissertations that turn the papers into a narrative of the foreign struggle for recognition. The collection closes with the peace and its immediate diplomatic consequences.
works.significance: It founded the scholarly documentary edition in America and created the archival basis on which later histories of the Revolution were written. Its editorial apparatus established the American model of the annotated national papers. It is the touchstone of the era's claim that the republic could preserve and interpret its own records.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at Boston from 1829, with the closing volumes in 1830, in the season of the new American historical societies and of public interest in the founding records. Its editor had just taken charge of a national periodical and was assembling the materials for the biographical works that made him the chief American editor of his generation. The edition answered the British possession of much of the diplomatic record.
works.structure: Multi-volume documentary edition arranged chronologically by correspondent and year, with editorial notes, memoirs and dissertations interposed.
works.attributionNotes: The collection is an editorial compilation of documents written by many hands; the record is assigned in the batch map to the editor who chose, arranged and annotated it.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature

movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana
works.description: Ralegh's report of his 1595 voyage up the Orinoco in search of the fabled golden empire of El Dorado: the rivers, peoples, and wonders of Guiana described with the eyewitness's precision and the courtier's art, the gold of Manoa promised and half-believed, and the whole offered to Elizabeth I as the instrument of Spain's overthrow.
works.plot: The narrative follows the expedition from Trinidad up the Orinoco's mouths; the Indian peoples, the Spanish depredations, the rumours of Manoa's gold, and the hardships of the return fill the account, which closes with Ralegh's arguments for the conquest of Guiana and his answers to the objections of the envious.
works.significance: The classic English narrative of exploration — the book that fixed El Dorado in the European imagination.
works.meter: Prose of grave, plain magnificence — the Elizabethan traveller's style at its finest.
works.context: Published 1596 after the 1595 voyage; its promise of El Dorado underwrote Ralegh's career, his 1617 return voyage, and his death.
works.characters: Sir Walter Ralegh (the narrator); the Indian peoples of the Orinoco; Topiawari (the aged cacique); the Spanish governor Berreo; the expedition's captains
works.structure: A first-person voyage narrative with the apparatus of argument and apology — the explorer's report fused with the promoter's prospectus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Discovery of a World in the Moone; or, A Discourse Tending to Prove That 'Tis Probable There May Be Another Habitable World in That Planet
altTitles: The Discovery of a World in the Moone
works.description: John Wilkins's popular scientific treatise arguing, on Copernican grounds, that the moon is probably a habitable world, with a discussion of the possibility of flight to it; it introduced the new astronomy to a general English readership.
works.plot: Wilkins argues that the earth is a planet, that the moon is an earth, and that it is probable the moon is inhabited; the final proposition considers whether flying to the moon might one day be possible.
works.significance: The first popular English exposition of the plurality of worlds and a major influence on seventeenth-century imaginative literature, including Milton's cosmology and the early science fiction of Cyrano de Bergerac.
works.meter: Clear, persuasive prose for a lay readership.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1638 by the young Wadham College fellow who would become a founder of the Royal Society; it drew on Galileo, Kepler, and Godwin's The Man in the Moone.
works.structure: A series of numbered propositions with arguments and objections answered.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Wilkins's authorship was acknowledged in the third edition of 1684.

works.title: The Distichs of Cato (Old English)
altTitles: The Old English Dicts of Cato
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Trinity College MS R.9.17 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Julius A.ii and Cotton Vespasian D.xiv
works.description: An Old English prose translation of the Disticha Catonis, the late-antique collection of moral distichs that was the standard first reader of the medieval schoolroom. The translation renders Cato's maxims — on wisdom, speech, friendship, thrift, and the conduct of life — into plain vernacular prose for readers without Latin.
works.plot: The text translates the four books of Cato's moral couplets and the prefatory matter: exhortations to wisdom, prudence in speech, care in friendship, moderation in all things, and the fear of God, each maxim expanded into a clear Old English sentence with occasional explanatory glosses.
works.significance: The first English version of the most influential moral textbook of the Middle Ages, linking the Old English wisdom tradition to the classical curriculum inherited by later English literature.
works.context: The Disticha Catonis was the most widely read school text of the Middle Ages; its translation into Old English shows the vernacular classroom tradition of the reform era extending the standard curriculum to those learning through English, in the same spirit as Ælfric's Grammar and Colloquy.
works.structure: A book-by-book, maxim-by-maxim prose translation following the order of the Latin distichs, with each couplet rendered as one or two vernacular sentences.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Doctor's Family
works.description: Published in 1861 and the first of the Carlingford stories: the arrival in the town of the doctor's feckless brother Fred and his family, and the doctor's hopeless love. It is a prose fiction work of 1861 by Margaret Oliphant; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Serial and Monthly-Part Novel.
works.plot: Dr Rider, a hard-working Carlingford physician, is burdened with his worthless brother Fred, returned from Australia, and Fred's helpless family; the story turns on the doctor's love for Nettie Underwood, the capable young sister of Fred's wife, who has taken the whole family on her shoulders, and on the discipline of charity that his profession demands.
works.significance: The Doctor's Family sets the pattern of the Carlingford chronicles and shows Oliphant's characteristic subject at its purest: the ordinary professional life, the burden of dependants, and the hard economy of doing good in a small town.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely chronicle with a large cast.

works.title: The Doctor's Wife
works.description: Published in 1864 and a deliberate English answer to Flaubert's Madame Bovary: the story of a doctor's wife whose reading of novels fills her with romantic expectations her marriage cannot satisfy. It is a prose fiction work of 1864 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Isabel Sleaford marries the good, dull country doctor George Gilbert, drifts into a romantic friendship with the wealthy poet-squire Roland Lansdell and refuses to elope with him; her husband dies of fever, Lansdell is fatally beaten by her father, a returned convict, and Isabel, widowed and left Lansdell's fortune, devotes it to good works.
works.significance: The Doctor's Wife is the most self-conscious English novel about the novel-reading woman: it takes the French realist diagnosis of romantic reading and turns it into a defence of English domestic life, and it is a key text for the history of the woman reader.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.
works.context: The 1860s, the circulating-library novel and its female readers, the medical profession, and the English reception of French realism. The record dates the work as composed in 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce
altTitles: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce: Restor'd to the Good of Both Sexes
works.description: Milton's controversial tract arguing that incompatibility, not merely adultery, is grounds for divorce, prompted by his own unhappy marriage to Mary Powell; it defends companionship and 'meet and happy conversation' as the true end of marriage against a rigid scriptural literalism.
works.plot: Milton argues from scripture, reason, and natural law that marriage exists for mutual help and companionship, and that an uncongenial union frustrates its divine purpose, warranting divorce and remarriage.
works.significance: A landmark in the history of marriage and divorce debate and an important document of Milton's radical Protestant individualism; it also occasioned his defence of unlicensed printing.
works.meter: Dense, passionate argumentative prose, at once learned and personal.
works.context: Written in 1643–44 after Mary Powell left Milton; it scandalised the Presbyterians and led directly to Areopagitica when Milton published without a licence, and to his later tract Tetrachordon (1645).
works.structure: A two-book argumentative treatise in prose, with scriptural exegesis and appeals to reason and natural law.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: The Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity Illustrated
altTitles: The Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity Illustrated: Shewing the Safety and Advantages of That Doctrine
works.description: Priestley's hard determinist treatise, arguing that all events, including the voluntary actions of men, are fixed by the chain of causes and by divine necessity, and that liberty of spontaneous self-determination is an absurdity. It set necessity as the article separating the philosophical Christians from the moralists and the Methodists.
works.plot: Priestley defines necessity as the certain connection of causes and effects and shows that every act of the mind has its efficient cause without which it could not exist, so that liberty of indifference is unintelligible and self-determination a contradiction. He argues from the uniformity of character, the determination of choice by motive, and the witness of experience, then meets the moral objections: praise, blame, law, and even the atonement stand on necessity's own ground, for it is the certainty of consequences that makes motives efficacious. He reads Scripture as a corroborating narrative of foreordination, providence, and grace, and closes by defending the doctrine against its clerical opponents and the Arminian scheme of free will. Hartley's associationism underwrites the whole.
works.significance: It is the century's starkest religious determinism, the classic statement of Hartleyan necessitarian theology, and the standing text for the metaphysics of the radical Unitarians.
works.meter: Plain, blunt, sermon-near prose of a dissenting teacher, syllogistic but warm, determinism delivered as good news.
works.context: Published in 1777 after Priestley's Hartleyan conversion and amid the Birmingham and Leeds controversies with the moralists and the Methodists; it drew the immediate and famous reply from Richard Price, opening a decade of necessitarian polemic.
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered propositions and objections answered, physiological, moral, and scriptural in turn.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
