works.title: The Dolly Dialogues
works.description: Published in 1894 and the wittiest English society dialogue of the decade: a series of conversations between a young man and the woman he does not quite marry. It is a prose work of 1894 by Anthony Hope; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The dialogues follow Sam Carter and the beautiful, imperious Dolly Mickleham through the drawing rooms, racecourses and country houses of the 1890s, in conversations that turn on flirtation, marriage, money and the small absurdities of English society, and that end with Dolly marrying someone else and Sam accepting it gracefully.
works.significance: The Dolly Dialogues is the finest English dialogue sequence of the 1890s and one of the wittiest books of the period: its style and its irony make it the English equivalent of the French maxim, and it is the book by which Hope's contemporaries rated him above the Zenda romances.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is fast-moving adventure narrative with a first-person narrator.
works.context: 1893-94: the London season of the 1890s, the daily press and the dialogue sketch, and the English vogue for the light comedy of manners. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; realist novel of common life.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Hope Hawkins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: The Domestic Affections, and Other Poems
works.form: Collected volume of lyrics, occasional verse and translations; the governing mode is the lyric meditation on feeling, with the song-like imitation and the devotional stanza as secondary genres.
works.description: The first collected volume of verse by a writer who would become the most extensively reprinted woman poet of the nineteenth century. It gathers meditative lyrics, occasional and descriptive pieces, and translations and imitations from Spanish and Italian sources. Its title poem states the volume's programme: affection within the household, and its survival beyond the death of its objects, as the durable ground of happiness.
works.plot: The title poem traces a daughter's grief for her mother and settles the loss within a creed of domestic virtue that outlasts fortune. Shorter poems attach the same argument to landscape and to ruin, to the fireside year, and to the recollection of friends separated by emigration or death. The translations supply romance matter - Moorish halls, prisoners' songs, and constant lovers - in a softened, melodious register. Later pieces widen from private feeling to national and religious subjects, ending toward the prospect of immortality. No single story governs the book; its unity is a declared attitude to experience.
works.significance: The volume sets the repertoire - domestic affection, exile, constancy and the beloved dead - that later made its author a staple of annuals, gift-books and school anthologies. It shows a woman poet entering print by affiliating with sensibility rather than contesting it. Lines from these pages passed into proverb through a century of reprints and school extract collections.
works.meter: Heroic couplets frame the title poem; the shorter pieces use iambic common measure, eight-line stanzas and song refrains, with anapaestic substitution where the imitation of Spanish and Italian measures is audible. The diction keeps a deliberate vocal smoothness adapted to singable stanza forms.
works.context: Published in the eleventh year of the war with Napoleonic France, when the national war-poem and the public occasion dominated the trade, the volume offers instead a withdrawn domestic scene. Its author had been contributing verse to the Monthly Magazine from about 1808, and the book collects that apprenticeship. A separate long patriotic narrative by the same hand appeared in the same year, showing a range the first volume does not display.
works.structure: Arranged by length rather than by chronology or design, with the longest poem at the opening and shorter lyrics, hymn-like pieces and translations following. Several items had already appeared in magazines, so the volume acts as a first stock-taking of a periodical career rather than as a planned sequence.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Dong with a Luminous Nose
works.description: Published in Laughable Lyrics (1877) and the most moving of English nonsense poems: the exile's search for the Jumbly Girl he loved. It is a verse work of 1877 by Edward Lear; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
works.plot: The Dong, a lonely creature of the shore, falls in love with a Jumbly Girl who sails away with her people; he makes himself a luminous nose of bark and wax to light his way, and wanders the cliffs at night, singing a melancholy song of loss, while the Jumblies dance in the moonlight beyond his reach.
works.significance: 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' is the finest of all English nonsense poems and one of the great poems of unrequited love in the language: it demonstrates that nonsense is not the absence of sense but a form that can carry feeling more purely than the conventional lyric, and it is the poem in which Lear's private grief and his comic genius are most completely fused.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity.
works.context: 1877: the children's poetry market of the 1870s, Lear's loneliness in San Remo, and the Victorian taste for comic verse with an undertow of pathos. The record dates the work as composed between 1876 and 1877 and first published in 1877 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Lear's nonsense. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule
themes: Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child

works.title: The Doomed City
works.form: Romantic vision poem and descriptive meditation; the tableau poem of terror
works.description: A vision of a dead city sinking in a strange western sea, published in the collected volume of 1831 under this title and reissued later as The City of Sin and as The City in the Sea. Its image of a town of towers mirrored in still water, watched over by personified Death, is the author's most durable tableau. The record keeps the title the poem actually bore within this installment's period.
works.plot: The poem describes a city of amber towers lying level on a silent sea in a strange western country, where no wind blows and no wave stirs. The towers, the domes and the palaces are reflected in the water, which is a dim mirror of the abyss. Death, as an entity, sits robed and crowned above the town, and the scene is presented as the lake of unmannerly and unquiet things. The closing movement suggests that the waters will at last rise and swallow the city in one consummation.
works.significance: It is the source of one of the most often reproduced images in American verse and a laboratory for the author's later doctrine of the single effect. Its revisions across three titles make it a case study in his practice of recasting. It closes the American lyric strand of this installment at the point where the vision poem and the short effect-poem meet.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter and trimeter stanzas with long reverberant vowels and repeated refrains
works.context: Printed in the 1831 collected volume as a separate poem, at a moment when the author was building his theory of the unity of poetical effect. Its imagery belongs to the repertory of the European picturesque and of the graveyard meditation, transferred to an oceanic scene. The poem's later titles track its repeated revision through the 1830s and 1840s.
works.characters: Personified Death; the doomed city and its towers
works.structure: Continuous descriptive vision in two movements, the tableau of the city and the presence of Death, ending in a prophecy of dissolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the three titles denote successive stages of one poem rather than separate works, and the batch keeps the earliest.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: The Double Dealer
works.description: Congreve's second comedy, a tightly plotted intrigue play built around the double-dealing Maskwell, who betrays his patron, his friends, and his mistresses in pursuit of an heiress.
works.plot: Maskwell, the trusted friend of Mellefont, secretly loves Lady Touchwood and conspires to disinherit Mellefont and win Cynthia; the plot is discovered only at the last moment and the lovers are saved.
works.significance: Congreve's most formally rigorous comedy and one of the most intricate plots in English drama; Maskwell is the finest villain of Restoration comedy.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in November 1693 and published in 1694 with a dedicatory epistle to Charles Montagu, later Earl of Halifax.
works.characters: Maskwell; Mellefont; Lord Touchwood; Lady Touchwood; Cynthia; Lady Froth; Sir Paul Plyant; Careless; Brisk
works.structure: Five acts observing the unities of time and place, a formal experiment in the French manner that made the play less popular than its predecessor.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher

works.title: The Doubt of Future Foes
works.description: Queen Elizabeth I's poem on Mary Queen of Scots and the succession: the 'doubt of future foes' — the captive rival queen and her foreign allies — threatens the realm, but the poet's 'wit' and providence shall cut off the 'tops of hope' before they grow; the most famous of the queen's surviving poems, circulated in manuscript from the early 1570s.
works.plot: The poem moves from the menace of the rival and her 'foreign banished wights' to the queen's resolve: the sword of justice and the pruning of ambitions — a lyric of statecraft in the register of the mirror-for-princes tradition.
works.significance: The queen's own voice in the literature of her reign — the poem through which the sovereign entered the lyric tradition she patronized.
works.meter: Fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets), the form of the queen's Protestant poetics.
works.context: Written about 1571, after the Ridolfi plot, when Mary Stuart's captivity and the Catholic powers' intrigues made the succession the realm's danger; it circulated in manuscript and was printed in Puttenham's Art of English Poesy (1589) as the queen's poem.
works.characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); Mary Queen of Scots (the 'future foe', un-named)
works.structure: A single lyric in two movements — the threat, then the answer — in the courtly plain style of the queen's circle.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Puttenham in 1589 as the Queen's.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Kingship and good rule

works.title: The Dragon and the Raven; or, The Days of King Alfred
altTitles: Dragon and the Raven; or, The Days of King Alfred
works.description: Henty's Saxon novel: a young thane in the wars of Alfred against the Danes. It is a prose fiction work of 1886 by G. A. Henty; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Edmund, a young Saxon thane, is driven from his home by the Danes, joins Alfred's court, and fights through the campaigns of the 870s from Athelney to Edington in a story of the making of England.
works.significance: The Dragon and the Raven was one of Henty's most popular books and the one that taught a generation of boys the story of Alfred and the making of England: its Saxon hero and its Danish wars made the early Middle Ages into a school of Englishness.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the young hero placed at the centre of a real historical campaign.
works.context: England in the 870s, the Danish invasions and the Alfredian revival of learning and law. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; sensation novel.
works.characters: Edmund; King Alfred; Guthrum; Ealdorman Ethelred
works.structure: A historical adventure in twenty-one chapters, from the Danish raid to the peace of Wedmore. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Alfred Henty. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self

works.title: The Drapier's Letters
altTitles: Letters Written by M. B. Drapier to the People of Ireland
works.description: Swift's six letters to the people of Ireland against Wood's patent for a copper coinage, spoken in the plain voice of a wool-draper, and turning a monetary grievance into an argument about the rights of a dependent kingdom.
works.plot: M. B. Drapier explains why the halfpence will ruin the kingdom's trade, answers the government's advocates and the friendly advisers who tell the people to submit, and rises in the later letters to the claim that a nation cheated of its own coin is being made a province of a project.
works.significance: It made the language of liberty and of national resistance available to a dependent kingdom, and it is the century's most powerful instance of pamphlet writing changing the terms of an imperial quarrel.
works.meter: The blunt idiom of the shopkeeper turned to oratory, with the plain short sentence, the repeated address to the people and the closing biblical tags.
works.context: Published in Dublin in the year of Wood's patent, when the Irish currency question became the occasion for the first mass popular mobilisation against the administration, and when Swift's own station as dean of St Patrick's set him against the government his church depended on.
works.characters: M. B. Drapier; William Wood and his patent; the officers of the administration; the shopkeepers and weavers of Dublin
works.structure: A serial of open letters, each answering the previous objection, moving from the arithmetic of the coinage to the constitutional argument and to the invitation to resist.
works.attributionNotes: Swift's authorship, though long disavowed and pursued by the administration with a reward for the writer's discovery, is uncontested; the earlier answers printed against the letters include pieces by Irish writers and by Swift himself in another character.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
National identity and Englishness
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: The Dream of Eugene Aram
altTitles: The Dream of Eugene Aram, the Murderer
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza
works.description: A long ballad-poem on the scholar-murderer of Westmorland legend, first printed in a literary annual and issued as a separate volume with illustrations in 1831. The poem is a dream and self-accusation: Eugene Aram, now a schoolmaster, is discovered by the father of the man he killed for money years before, and the poem tracks the guilty memory to its confession and execution. It was the most widely reprinted serious poem of the author's career and long served as his standard piece in school anthologies.
works.plot: Aram, sitting in his school, is disturbed by a dream of the murder, and the poem opens on the divided consciousness of the man who has lived long with a hidden crime. A wandering father, searching for his dead son, arrives and reads the guilty face; Aram's own speech betrays him, the body is found in the cave where it was flung, and the poem closes with the confession, the condemned cell, and the death. The argument is not the detective plot but the analysis of a mind that has made a philosophy of its own guilt, with the refrain-questioning of a heart that dares not search itself.
works.significance: The Dream of Eugene Aram became the representative Romantic poem of concealed guilt and self-analysis, and its presence in school and family collections through the whole nineteenth century made its author a household name independently of his comedy. It shows the ballad form used for a psychological case, and it is the clearest instance in the author's work of the serious Romantic verse he was known for before the joke-books took over his reputation.
works.meter: A ballad-poem in short rhymed stanzas with exclamatory address and recurring questioning refrains; the rhyme-run is irregular and the effect built on repetition and on broken syntax rather than on a settled stanza, deliberately nearer the broadside and the ordinary ballad report than to meditative blank verse.
works.context: Composed in the later 1820s and first given to the public in the literary annual the author edited from 1829. It was reprinted as a separate volume in 1831 with a series of illustrations, the dedication of the reprint explaining the occasion of the issue. The real Westmorland murder of the 1740s, in which a schoolmaster was hanged for the killing of a friend for money, had already supplied a famous philosophical commentary on guilt. The poem works within that well-known criminal history rather than inventing it.
works.characters: Eugene Aram the schoolmaster and murderer; Daniel, the father of the slain man; the slain friend of Aram's youth; the cave in which the body lies
works.structure: A single continuous ballad narrative in short stanzas with recurrent address and question, its action broken by dream, memory, and self-interrogation; the confession scene forms the structural hinge.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the poem's prior appearance in the annual the author edited is recorded in the reprint's dedication, which states the occasion of the separate issue.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse

works.title: The Dream of Gerontius
altTitles: The Dream of Gerontius: A Poem
works.description: Published in 1865 and set to music by Edward Elgar in 1900: a poem of the soul's journey after death, from the deathbed through judgment to purgatory, and one of the great Victorian poems on death. It is a verse work of 1865 by John Henry Newman; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Gerontius dies, his soul is borne by the guardian angel through the regions of the air, hears the demons and the angelic choirs, is presented to God and, judged, passes to the cleansing fire of purgatory with the angel's song in his ears.
works.significance: The Dream of Gerontius is the finest Victorian poem on death and the basis of Elgar's oratorio (1900), the greatest English choral work of the century; its imagery shaped the English imagination of the afterlife and its verse carries Newman's prose cadence into poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
works.context: The 1860s, the Catholic doctrine of purgatory, the Victorian literature of death and the deathbed, and Newman's own old age. The record dates the work as composed in 1865 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; victorian verse drama and revived tragedy.
works.characters: Gerontius (the Soul); the Guardian Angel; the Priest and the assistants; the demons; the Angel of the Agony; the souls in Purgatory; the choirs of Angelicals
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Dream of the Rood
works.description: The greatest religious poem of the Old English period (156 lines): a dream vision in which the Cross itself speaks, recounting the Crucifixion as a heroic battle in which Christ, the young warrior-king, mounts the cross of his own will. Related texts survive on the eighth-century Ruthwell Cross runic inscription and the Brussels Cross.
works.plot: The dreamer sees a wondrous tree shining with gold and gems, stained with blood, and the Rood tells its story: cut down in the forest, it was made the gallows of the young hero who climbed it willingly; it trembled, dared not bow, and with Christ it was pierced with nails and mocked, then buried and later raised up as the honoured sign of salvation. The poem ends with the dreamer's hope of the heavenly homeland and the injunction to seek the tree of victory.
works.significance: The supreme fusion of Germanic heroic form with Christian content in the period; one of the great medieval dream poems.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, richly figured; the poem's end has been thought to show hypermetric lines.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 104v-106r); the Ruthwell Cross (Dumfriesshire, early eighth century) carries an inscribed extract in runes, and the Brussels Cross (c. 1000) a related couplet, evidence of the poem's early circulation.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Rood (Cross); Christ (the young hero)
works.structure: A frame vision enclosing the Cross's first-person narrative, followed by the dreamer's response and a homiletic conclusion; the Cross is the earliest sustained prosopopoeia in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; early attributions to Cædmon or Cynewulf are not accepted.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Heroism and the heroic code
Typology and biblical interpretation

works.title: The Dreme
altTitles: The Dreme of Schir David Lindsay
works.form: dream vision in couplets and stanzas
works.description: Lindsay's dream vision addressed to the young James V: the poet, transported in sleep to hell, purgatory, and paradise, meets the spirit of the king's ancestors and returns to instruct the king in the duties of rule — an epistle to the sovereign that founds Lindsay's career as the conscience of the Scottish crown.
works.plot: The poet dreams he travels with Dame Remembrance through the three realms, hears the lament of the dead Scots kings over the realm's decay, and wakes to write the 'Exhortation to the King' that closes the poem.
works.significance: The classic Scots poem of princely counsel and the seed of the Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis; its vision of national decay set the tone of the Scottish Reformation's literature.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzaic passages in the Makar tradition; plain, forceful didactic verse.
works.context: Written in 1528 as James V escaped the Douglas faction and took personal rule; Lindsay, his childhood companion, speaks as the king's tutor and conscience.
works.characters: the poet; Dame Remembrance; James V (addressed); the dead kings
works.structure: Dream vision with epilogue; the three-realm journey frames the political exhortation, which is the poem's true centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: The Drinking Gourd
works.description: The Drinking Gourd is a television play about slavery that Lorraine Hansberry wrote in 1960; it was not produced and was published after her death in Les Blancs: The Collected Last Plays (1972). The Gale entry describes it as a Black woman's story of slavery and emancipation.
works.summary: Life on a Southern plantation on the eve of the Civil War, seen through the enslaved woman Rissa and her son Hannibal, the ageing owner Hiram Sweet and his harsher son Everett, introduced by a narrating Union soldier.
works.plot: Hannibal, a young enslaved man, dreams of escaping north by following the Drinking Gourd, the Big Dipper, and secretly learns to read. When this is discovered, Everett, who has taken control of the plantation from his ailing father, has Hannibal blinded as punishment. Rissa, who had trusted in her master's paternalism, abandons her loyalty, steals a gun and helps her son escape north. Through the owner's family and the plantation's poor white overseer, the play shows how slavery degrades everyone bound up in it.
works.significance: An early attempt to present slavery from the perspective of the enslaved in American television drama, unproduced in its time.
works.meter: Historically grounded dialogue and direct narration designed for a mass audience.
works.context: It was commissioned by the producer Dore Schary, who called it a powerful script about the peculiar institution of slavery, for a planned television series marking the centenary of the Civil War; its frank treatment of slavery was considered too controversial and it was never broadcast.
works.characters: Rissa; Hannibal; Hiram Sweet; Everett Sweet; Tommy; the Soldier (narrator)
works.structure: A televisual structure of short, cinematic scenes framed by a narrator's direct commentary.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
Violence, crime and justice

works.title: The Drummer
altTitles: The Drummer; Or, the Haunted House
works.description: The comedy of the haunted house and the alarming drum, printed in 1716 in a text that represents Steele's earlier The Funeral of 1701 heavily revised; it is the published trace of the Addison-Steele partnership working on one play after the rupture of the essay papers.
works.plot: The ghostly apparatus of a haunted house is engineered by a scheming butler and a counterfeit spirit to secure the heroine; a cowardly fife and drum scare, a rival suitor, and the exposure of the trick resolve into the marriage of the man who has shown real courage.
works.significance: It documents the dissolution of the Addison-Steele collaboration in the same medium that had made it famous, and it is the period's clearest instance of a play remade by one partner's hand under another's name.
works.meter: Prose dialogue with the song interpolations characteristic of the early eighteenth-century afterpiece comedy.
works.context: Acted and printed at Drury Lane in 1716, in the settled years after the failure of the Jacobite rising, when the ghost comedy and the operatic machine were competing with reformed moral comedy for the same audience.
works.characters: the heiress and her mother; the two rival suitors; the servants who stage the ghostly fraud; the drummer whose signal frightens the house
works.structure: Regular five-act comedy of intrigue and humours, with the burlesque ghost-plot as the mechanism of discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative and displaced: the ground plot belongs to Steele's The Funeral of 1701, the printed 1716 text was revised and enlarged with new scenes and songs generally assigned to Addison, and prefatory matter has been variously distributed between the two writers; the record is placed with Steele because the design and the earlier version are his.

Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
Warfare and battle

works.title: The Duchess of Malfi
works.description: Webster's tragedy of the widowed Duchess who remarries her steward Antonio against her brothers' will: the 'Aragonian brethren' — the twisted Ferdinand and the corrupt Cardinal — pursue her with spies, imprisonment, and madmen's masques until her murder by strangling; the play then turns to the revenges that destroy the brothers, ending with the famous line, 'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle; she died young'.
works.plot: The Duchess secretly marries Antonio and bears children; Bosola, the malcontent spy, discovers the truth; Ferdinand's fury and the Cardinal's policy drive the persecution — the wax corpses, the madmen, the executioners; the Duchess dies with her dignity ('I am Duchess of Malfi still'); and Bosola's belated revenges kill Ferdinand, the Cardinal, and himself in the final bloodbath.
works.significance: Generally ranked the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage — the supreme study of courage under persecution.
works.meter: The summit of Webster's blank verse — the wooing scene, the prison scene, and the dirges — with the malcontent prose of Bosola as its instrument of irony.
works.context: Based on the story of Giovanna d'Aragona (d. 1510) via Painter's Palace of Pleasure; performed about 1614 by the King's Men at Blackfriars and the Globe; printed in 1623.
works.characters: the Duchess of Malfi; Antonio Bologna; Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria; the Cardinal; Bosola; Delio; Cariola; Julia; Pescara; the Doctor; the madmen
works.structure: A five-act tragedy in two movements — the Duchess's love and martyrdom, then the revengers' self-destruction — with the echo scene and the madmen's masque as its set pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Women, chastity, and constancy

works.title: The Duenna
works.description: A comic opera in three acts, founded on the old Spanish play of the duenna and carried by a score of popular songs, and one of the most successful musical entertainments of the century. It was the joint work of a young playwright and of the composer with whom he was connected by family, and its first run outdid the fashion of the ballad opera.
works.plot: Two lovers are kept apart by a jealous father and his duenna, the elderly Don D. being made to marry the lady's duenna in his own mistake. Isaac the rich Jew is cozened out of his intended bride, and the elopements, disguises and forged letters clear themselves in the last act. The songs interrupt and advance the intrigue, and the comedy ends with the double marriage and the duenna's confusion.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comic opera before the nineteenth century and a decisive step in the revival of musical theatre in London, its songs remaining in the repertory longer than the play.
works.meter: Prose dialogue in the ballad-opera manner, with songs in the common lyric measures of the stage, several of them still sung as independent airs.
works.context: First performed at Covent Garden in November 1775, in the season of the quarrel over the relative merits of opera and comedy and of the manager's own struggles to revive English musical drama; its authorship was debated in the press at the time of its first run.
works.characters: the duenna Donna Rodriguez; the jealous father Don Jerome; Clara his daughter; Isaac Mendosa; Antonio and the lover of the elopement
works.structure: Three-act comic opera of spoken dialogue and set songs, the plot a regular intrigue of mistake with the musical numbers functioning as the sentimental set pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the spoken dialogue and the general design are assigned to the playwright, and the composition to Thomas Linley, whose share was publicly questioned in 1775 and whose family connection with the author complicates the record; only the playwright is named in the relationship map.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct
The public theatre and the players' world
movements: Comedy of Manners

works.title: The Duke's Children
works.form: Novel in monthly parts; three volumes 1880 (Palliser, 6)
works.description: Published in 1879-80, the last of the Palliser novels: the widowed Duke's struggle with his three children, each of whom wishes to marry against his wishes. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Anthony Trollope; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: The Duke of Omnium, now out of office and mourning Glencora, finds that his son and heir Lord Silverbridge wants to marry the American Isabel Boncassen, that his daughter Mary loves the impoverished Frank Tregear, and that the younger son Gerald has been sent down from Cambridge. The novel resolves in the Duke's recognition that his children's choices are worthy of respect.
works.significance: The Duke's Children is the most personal and the most formally elegant of Trollope's political novels, and its study of a father's pride is one of the finest things in Victorian fiction. It closes the Palliser series on a note of reconciliation that the twentieth century found unexpectedly moving, and it is a key text for the study of transatlantic marriage.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The late 1870s and the first appearance of the American heiress in English society, the decline of the landed estate, and the rise of the professional politician. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Plantagenet Palliser; Lord Silverbridge; Lady Mary Palliser; Gerald Palliser; Isabel Boncassen; Frank Tregear; Lady Mabel Grex; Mr Boncassen; Major Tifto
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story

works.title: The Dunciad
altTitles: The Dunciad: A Heroic Poem in Four Books
works.description: Pope's satiric epic of Dulness enthroned in London: a mock-heroic coronation, games of the poetasters and a prophecy of the triumph of ignorance, directed at the trade in bad books, at dull scholarship and at the writer's own enemies.
works.plot: Dulness and her son transfer the seat of their empire to the British capital, where the poetasters and booksellers compete for her prizes; her dominion is extended over the theatre, the presses and the schools of the city and the universities, until the poem closes on the extinction of light and order in an universal sleep of mind.
works.significance: It is the central English poem of cultural despair, transforming personal revenge into a philosophy of the decline of letters, and it fixed the figure of Dulness as the century's image of its own public.
works.meter: Heroic couplet strained to the strongest cadences of English satire, with the heavy monosyllabic line for the progress of Dulness and the rapid couplet for the attack.
works.context: Written in the years after the failure of the Scriblerian papers, the success of the Homer and the quarrels over the Shakespeare edition; the immediate provocation was the hack scholarship and the pirated and hostile publishing to which Pope's name had become a commodity.
works.characters: Dulness; her son; the poet; Lewis Theobald; Edmund Curll; the tribe of poetasters and booksellers
works.structure: Four books of mock-epic action, with invocation, games, prophecy and descent, framing a personal catalogue of the poet's enemies inside a cosmology of cultural decay.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Pope's, though the first edition's title-page carried its jokes about translation and about the author's name; the personae are real contemporary writers and the identification of several remains a bibliographical problem.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Patronage and the literary marketplace
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness

works.title: The Dunciad Variorum
altTitles: The Dunciad in Four Books, with the Notes of the Variorum Editors
works.form: mock-scholarly satire in verse with apparatus
works.description: The 1729 edition of the Dunciad encrusted with a forged critical apparatus: prolegomena, the scholia of ancient and modern commentators, the key, the dedication to a living bookseller and the printed fragments of its enemies' works.
works.plot: The same four books of the Dunciad are presented as an authenticated classic, annotated as if by a succession of editors and illustrated by the reprinted titles and offences of the dulness under attack.
works.significance: Its invention of the hostile editorial apparatus turned scholarship itself into a satiric object and remains the period's most complete exposure of literary authority as a made thing.
works.meter: Heroic couplet for the poem; the prose of the notes imitates the learned commentary, with Latin and Greek tags turned to burlesque.
works.context: Made in the year of the quarrel over Shakespeare, when Theobald's restoration of the text had exposed Pope's own edition, and in the season of the booksellers' counter-publication of keys and replies.
works.characters: Dulness; the poet; the editor-personae of the apparatus; Lewis Theobald; Edmund Curll
works.structure: A satiric text inside a mock-scholarly frame: prolegomena, argument, notes in the manner of the classical editors, and appended documentary specimens of the offenders.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the notes and apparatus are the work of Pope's Scribleran circle, standardly credited in part to Arbuthnot and to other friends, and are spoken in the personae of invented editors rather than in Pope's own name.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: The Durham Proverbs
works.description: A collection of forty-six Old English proverbs, each paired with a Latin version, written into a Durham cathedral manuscript of Ælfric's Grammar. The proverbs are earthy and practical — about friendship, speech, household management, and the follies of men — and descend from a common European proverb tradition.
works.plot: The proverbs counsel prudence in speech and friendship ('a friend in need is a friend indeed'), household thrift, and wariness of fair words, pairing each English saying with its Latin equivalent in the manner of a bilingual schoolbook.
works.significance: The only substantial surviving Old English proverb collection outside the poetic corpus, and evidence of the international proverb lore that fed later English wisdom literature.
works.meter: The Old English proverbs are rhythmical prose, often with alliterative patterning; they are not verse in the strict metrical sense.
works.context: Copied into a manuscript associated with the reform's school curriculum, the collection shows the continuity between vernacular wisdom literature (Maxims, Precepts) and the bilingual classroom tradition of the eleventh century; several proverbs have parallels in Wulfstan's homilies.
works.structure: A numbered list of proverb pairs (Old English with Latin), without framing narrative; the sayings range from two to six lines.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The proverbs are drawn from common tradition; the compiler is unknown.
themes: Solitude and the hall community
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Dutch Courtesan
works.description: Marston's city comedy of appetite and virtue: the young gallant Freevill, about to marry the chaste Beatrice, casts off his mistress, the Dutch courtesan Franceschina, whose jealousy hires the pander Cocledemoy's 'murder' of him; the counterfeit death, the trial of the innocent Malheureux, and the final act's reversals end with the courtesan whipped and the lovers married — virtue triumphant over the city's flesh-markets.
works.plot: Freevill's engagement and Franceschina's fury set the plot; Malheureux, the would-be virtuous friend, is tempted by the courtesan and trapped; the staged murder, the substitute corpse, and the trial scenes complicate the middle acts; and the final scene, with the 'dead' man's return, sentences Franceschina to the cart and the whip and marries the two honest couples.
works.significance: Marston's best comedy — a satire of appetite whose frankness about sex and money tested the private theatre's licence.
works.meter: Prose for the London scenes and verse for the lovers, in Marston's sharpest comic register.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605 and printed the same year; its London scenes answered the city-comedy vogue of 1604–05.
works.characters: Freevill; Malheureux; Franceschina; Beatrice; Crispinella; Cocledemoy; Mulligrub; Mistress Mulligrub; Tysefew; Mary Faugh
works.structure: A five-act comedy of intrigue on the Jonsonian model, with the brothel scenes and the trial as the play's moral poles, and Cocledemoy's prose trickeries as its comic engine.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Marriage and women's conduct
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: The Dutchman's Fireside
works.form: The sketch and character tale in narrative form; pastoral comedy of the old Dutch country
works.description: A tale of the old Dutch settlement on the Hudson, and the most durable of the author's fictions. Its spirited young heroine of the settlement is courted by two very different men, a quiet hunter of the woods and an idle schemer who lives on the neighbourhood's hospitality. The tale is a comic study of industry against idleness and belongs to the Knickerbocker recovery of the Dutch colonial past.
works.plot: An attractive and managing young widow or maid of the settlement is courted by a quiet hunter of the woods and by a scheming idler who lives on the neighbourhood's hospitality. The idler's pretensions, his projects and his imposition on the family are exposed by degrees, while the hunter's worth is proved by service and by knowledge of the country. The tale moves between the fireside of the Dutch household and the woods and hills around it. It ends with the exposure of the idler and the marriage of the heroine to the hunter.
works.significance: It is the best of the Knickerbocker Dutch tales and an important source for the domestic representation of the Hudson valley. Its use of the idler as a social type belongs to the American comic tradition that the sketch series founded. It shows the frontier theme turned to the settled country rather than to the wilderness.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1831, in the last phase of the Knickerbocker interest in the Hudson valley Dutch past and on the edge of this installment's period. Its quarrel between industry and idleness addresses the moral economy of a farming country under pressure from speculation. The date is given by the electronic census of early American fiction; some handbooks place the tale earlier, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved.
works.structure: Third-person comic tale of a settlement, with the domestic fireside as its centre and a chase and exposure plot at its edge.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the first edition names the author as the writer of a prior poem.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
The marriage market and the limited estate
movements: The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch

works.title: The Duties of Women: A Course of Lectures
altTitles: Duties of Women: A Course of Lectures
works.description: Published in 1881 and delivered as a course of lectures: a systematic account of the moral duties of women, understood as the duties of citizens and workers rather than as the duties of wives and mothers alone.
works.plot: The lectures consider women's duties to themselves, to their families, to the poor, to education and to the state, and argue that the vote and the professions are not favours but obligations that the modern woman must claim.
works.significance: The Duties of Women is the fullest Victorian statement of a feminist ethics of obligation: it moves the argument from rights to duties and in doing so gives one of the most coherent accounts of the moral case for women's full citizenship.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
works.context: The 1880s, the campaign for women's suffrage, the girton and newnham colleges, and the debate on women's 'natural' sphere. The record dates the work as composed in 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: Arnold and the Criticism of Culture

works.title: The Dyetary of Health
altTitles: A Compendyous Regyment or a Dyetary of Helth
works.description: Andrew Boorde's vernacular regimen of health, first printed in 1542; a popular handbook of diet, dwelling, and daily conduct for the English householder.
works.plot: The book advises on diet (meats, drinks, bread, and their digestions), on choosing a healthy dwelling site, on sleep and clothing, and on the management of the body's humours, in a plain and often earthy prose salted with proverbs and personal opinion.
works.significance: One of the most popular health manuals of the sixteenth century and a rich source for Tudor domestic life, diet, and popular medicine; Boorde's colloquial style anticipates the plain-speaking of later popular medical writing.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written by Boorde after his return from his European travels and printed in 1542 (with many later editions to 1630); it belongs to the same vernacular medical movement as Elyot's Castle of Health, aimed at readers without Latin.
works.structure: A systematic handbook in short chapters, arranged by topic from dwelling-place to foodstuffs to regimen.
themes: Medicine, healing, and the body
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The Dynasts: An Epic-Drama of the War with Napoleon
altTitles: Dynasts: An Epic-Drama of the War with Napoleon
works.form: Epic-drama in three parts, nineteen acts and 130 scenes
works.description: Published in three parts between 1903 and 1908 and the most ambitious English verse drama of the modern period: an epic of the Napoleonic wars, from Trafalgar to Waterloo, with the 'Phantom Intelligences' of the Immanent Will commenting on the action.
works.plot: The drama follows the campaigns of 1805-1815 across Europe, with Napoleon, Wellington, Nelson, Pitt and the common soldiers of Wessex as its figures; the Spirits watch from above, and the work ends with the retreat from Moscow and the field of Waterloo.
works.significance: The Dynasts is the greatest English verse drama of the twentieth century's beginning and the fullest statement of Hardy's philosophy of the Immanent Will; it is the last English epic.
works.meter: Blank verse for the principal speeches and lyric metres for the choruses, with prose for the domestic scenes.
works.context: The 1890s-1900s, the new imperialism and the Boer War, and the Edwardian taste for the pageant and the historical spectacle. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1908 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Napoleon Bonaparte; Wellington; Nelson; Pitt; the Spirit of the Years; the Spirit of the Pities; the Spirit Ironic; the Spirit Sinister
works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Early Italian Poets
works.description: Published in 1861 as The Early Italian Poets from Ciullo d'Alcamo to Dante Alighieri (1100-1200-1300), and reissued in 1874 as Dante and His Circle: the translations of Dante's Vita Nuova, the poetry of the stilnovisti, and the poems of the contemporary Italian poets, with Rossetti's prefaces.
works.plot: The volume translates the Vita Nuova entire, with its prose narrative of Dante's love for Beatrice, together with poems by Guido Cavalcanti, Cino da Pistoia, Guido Guinicelli and others, and a selection of the poets of Dante's circle.
works.significance: The Early Italian Poets is the finest body of verse translation of the Victorian period and the work that established Dante's Vita Nuova as a central English text; it is the foundation of the modern English reception of the dolce stil novo and the model for Pound's and Eliot's use of medieval Italian poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The author's characteristic manner is rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound.
works.context: The 1850s-60s revival of Dante (the Pre-Raphaelite paintings, the 1862 centenary, the new editions), the Victorian interest in the Italian Middle Ages, and Rossetti's own Italian inheritance. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gabriel Charles Dante Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Earth Compels
works.description: MacNeice's second collection: the title poem, the Thirties and the compulsion of the earth. It is a verse work of 1938 by Louis MacNeice; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Thirties Political Lyric and the Auden Generation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers MacNeice's poems of 1935-38 - 'Carrickfergus', 'The Sunlight on the Garden', 'Bagpipe Music', 'Leaving Barra', 'June Thunder' and the 'Eclogue from Iceland', poems of Ireland, the Hebrides, Iceland and the approaching war - in which the public crisis and the private life are held in the same loose, musical, argumentative line.
works.significance: The Earth Compels is the collection that made MacNeice the second poet of the Auden generation after Auden himself: its title poem, its 'Snow' and its elegiac politics gave the Thirties poem its late and most musical phase, and it is the standard against which the war poetry of the forties is measured.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the long conversational poem in sections.
works.context: England, Ireland and Greece in the late 1930s, and the years before the Second World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under thirties political lyric and the auden generation.
works.characters: John MacDonald, Annie MacDougall, Willie Murray and Mrs Carmichael ('Bagpipe Music'); Craven, Ryan and the ghost of Grettir ('Eclogue from Iceland')
works.structure: A collection of lyrics and the long title poem, in several groups. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Louis MacNeice. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Earthly Paradise
works.description: Published in three volumes between 1868 and 1870 and the most popular long poem of the Victorian age after Idylls of the King: a frame narrative of wanderers in search of a deathless land, and the tales they tell.
works.plot: A company of medieval Norsemen sail west in search of the Earthly Paradise and come instead to an island of Greek descendants, where the two groups exchange stories month by month through the year; the twenty-four tales include 'The Story of Cupid and Psyche', 'Atalanta's Race' and 'The Doom of King Acrisius'.
works.significance: The Earthly Paradise is the central Pre-Raphaelite poem and one of the great narrative works of the century: its tales, its frame and its decorative design made it the model for the Victorian long poem and the direct ancestor of the modern fantasy tradition.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. works.title: The Ebb-Tide: A Trio and Quartette
works.form: Novel (with Lloyd Osbourne; serialised in To-day, 1893)
works.description: Published in 1894 and the grimmest of Stevenson's Pacific works: three beachcombers in Papeete take command of a plague ship carrying champagne, and the story of what they find on the island they sail to.

The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.

works.title: The Eclogues (Barclay)
works.description: Barclay's five eclogues, the first English pastoral poetry: three adapted from Mantuan and two from Aeneas Sylvius's De Curialium Miseriis, in which shepherds debate the miseries of courts and the corruption of the clergy, and the city's poverty is set against the country's sufficiency.
works.plot: Shepherds — Coridon, Cornix, Faustus, Amyntas — meet and debate in turn: the woes of courtiers, the pride of churchmen, the pleasures of the country life, and the duties of the rich toward the poor.
works.significance: The first English pastoral, founding the tradition that runs through Spenser's Shepheardes Calender to the great pastoral of the 1590s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the pastoral dialogue; the smooth didactic verse of the early Tudor humanists.
works.context: Written in the decade when the court satire was becoming the period's dominant mode; the eclogues import the Mantuan model that every Elizabethan grammar school would memorize.
works.characters: Coridon; Cornix; Faustus; Amyntas; Codrus; Minalcas
works.structure: Five discrete eclogues in the Virgilian-Mantuan manner, each a debate between named shepherds with its moral explicit.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the eclogues are adaptations of Mantuan and Aeneas Sylvius.

works.title: The Edinburgh Review
altTitles: The Edinburgh Review, or Critical Journal
works.form: critical review and periodical essay; the unsigned journal as a collective work
works.description: The quarterly journal which made the critical review into a literary and political institution, founded in 1802 by a small group of young Whigs and long identified with the criticism of the age. Its unsigned articles reviewed books as occasions for argument on constitution, finance, education, and taste, and its method, at once liberal in opinion and severe in judgement, gave the review its modern authority and its modern weapons.
works.plot: The enterprise of the journal was to carry into the criticism of books the analytical method of the moral and political sciences, and to treat every considerable publication as evidence upon some question of principle; accordingly its numbers interleave the review of a poem, a history, or a treatise of law with a discussion of the condition of the country, of the administration of the colonies, of the currency, or of the laws for the poor. Its declared rules forbade personal and party invective in form, while its practice made the exposure of an opponent's principles its most relished performance; and its attacks upon the poets and novelists of the day, upon what it took for the egotism of one school and the dullness of another, became the most discussed literary quarrels of the period. In politics it trained a generation to liberal Whiggism, argued for the reform of the criminal law and of representation, and by its treatment of Ireland, of the slave trade, and of the colonies made the review a branch of public business. Its later history, the long editorship, the rejection of contributions for want of space, and the rival quarterlies it provoked, belong to the social no less than to the literary history of the century.
works.significance: It is the founding institution of the modern critical review, the model which the rival quarterlies and the century's magazines copied, and the tribunal before which the literature and the policy of a generation were tried. Its influence upon the practice of the essay, upon the relations of author and public, and upon the diffusion of the liberal creed is larger than that of any single book of the period; and the controversy it raised about the power of criticism over letters is one of the permanent subjects of the literature of the age.
works.meter: The manner of the school of the review: lucid, argumentative, and caustic, passing from the summary of the book to the principle it raises, with the dry parenthesis, the mock concession, and the sententious close; the prose of a tribunal rather than of a chat.
works.context: Founded at Edinburgh in 1802 by four friends, of whom the first two editors were its two most conspicuous critics, printed in Edinburgh and published in London, and sustained at first against the handicaps of a Scotch and Whig undertaking in a loyal and Tory reading public. Its earliest numbers coincided with the war, with the suspension of the habeas corpus, and with the quarrel over the new poetry, and its prosperity made every party found a journal.
works.structure: A continuously issued quarterly of reviews and state papers, each number several hundred pages of independent unsigned articles, with the occasional list of new works at the end; the unit is the article and the series is the work.
works.attributionNotes: The articles were published without the writer's signature, and the attribution of individual numbers to individual hands rests on correspondence, manuscript, and internal evidence and is still revised by the editors of the collected articles; the two founders who served as its editors are recorded here as the authors of the undertaking.
themes: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: The Education of Henry Adams
works.description: Printed privately in 1907 and published in 1918: the greatest American autobiography, and the central American meditation on the modern world. It is a prose work of 1907 by Henry Adams; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Adams tells his own life in the third person as the education of a man who was never educated: Harvard, the London legation during the Civil War, Washington, the writing of history, a silence of twenty years that passes over his wife's suicide, and the discovery — in front of the dynamo at the Paris Exposition of 1900 — that the modern world has replaced the unity of the Virgin with the force of the machine.
works.significance: The Education of Henry Adams is the greatest American autobiography and one of the central texts of modern American thought: its theory of the dynamo and the Virgin, its third-person narrative and its account of the failure of education have made it the essential American meditation on modernity, and it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1919.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the third-person autobiography that treats the self as a scientific case.
works.context: 1838-1905: the American political dynasty of the Adamses, the Civil War, the Gilded Age, the Darwinian revolution, and the technology of the dynamo and the radio. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: The Egoist: A Comedy in Narrative
works.form: Novel in three volumes; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1879 and generally regarded as Meredith's masterpiece: the comedy of Sir Willoughby Patterne, a baronet of perfect self-satisfaction whose engagement to Clara Middleton is gradually destroyed by the revelation of his egoism.
works.plot: Sir Willoughby, having been jilted by Constantia Durham, is engaged to the young and intelligent Clara Middleton, who comes to see that his generosity, his taste and his charm are all functions of his self-love. Her escape is engineered by Vernon Whitford, whom she marries, while Willoughby marries the adoring Laetitia Dale.
works.significance: The Egoist is the great English comedy of the ego: its analysis of a self-love that mistakes itself for generosity is a permanent contribution to the psychology of the English gentleman, and its portrait of Clara Middleton is one of the finest studies of a woman's intellectual coming-to-consciousness in the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
works.context: The 1870s, the position of the educated woman and the marriage market, the English country house, and the Victorian debate on egoism and altruism. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.

works.structure: Single-location comedy of manners with a chorus of house guests and a narrator who comments as the 'comic spirit'.

works.meter: Plain argumentative prose.
works.context: Circulated in manuscript in 1640 during the Short Parliament; Hobbes fled to Paris in November 1640 as the treatise's royalism became dangerous.
works.structure: Two parts, each subdivided into chapters; the 1650 printing divided them into separate books.

works.title: The Elizabethan World Picture
works.form: Critical study (the chain of being and the order)
works.description: The study of the Elizabethan order: the chain of being and the correspondences. It is a prose work of 1943 by E. M. W. Tillyard; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Elizabethan World Picture recovers the common belief of the Elizabethan age - the great chain of being, the correspondences of the macrocosm and the microcosm, the doctrine of order and of degree - from the schoolbooks, the sermons and the popular verse, and makes it the key to the reading of the period.
works.significance: The Elizabethan World Picture gave the twentieth century its key to the Renaissance imagination: its chain of being and its correspondences became the common property of the readers of Shakespeare and Donne and remain the standard introduction to the period.

The author's characteristic manner is the exposition of the doctrine in the plain ordered sentence.

works.title: The Embargo; or, Sketches of the Times
altTitles: The Embargo, or Sketches of the Times
works.form: Political satire and verse invective in the Augustan manner; occasional public poem
works.description: A political satire in heroic couplets directed against the Jeffersonian embargo and against the administration that imposed it, written when the poet was a schoolboy. It is the earliest American poem of consequence to take national policy as its subject and to use the Augustan satiric manner for it. Its animus is Federalist, but its argument about the corruption of republican office looks forward to the author's later moral seriousness.
works.plot: The poem denounces the laying up of ships and the ruin of commerce as the work of men who sacrifice their country's trade to a foreign policy of their own making. It attacks the venality of office-holders, the cowardice of the mercantile interest and the stupidity of a press that praises the measure. A second impression rewrote parts of the satire for a changed political moment. The closing invective promises that the embargo will be remembered as an example of how a free people may be misled.
works.significance: It shows the transplantation of Augustan political verse into American party controversy and supplies the first documented instalment of the poet's career. Its couplet discipline marks the starting point of an American public poetry. It is the standard example of the juvenile political poem.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, closed and antithetical
works.context: Written and printed in 1808, in the season of the Embargo Act, and reissued in revised form in 1809. Its politics are those of New England Federalism, and it was published at a time when a boy's authorship was itself a party argument. It belongs to the long pamphlet and verse war over the embargo and over non-intercourse.
works.structure: Continuous satiric argument in couplets, invective addressed to a party and to its measures, without narrative personages.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established from the author's own later account of the broadside; the revised second issue differs materially from the first.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: The Emigrants, A Poem, in Two Books
works.form: Nature Lyric and Meditation; Meditative Blank Verse; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
works.description: Charlotte Smith's most ambitious poem and the first long blank-verse meditation by a woman poet on the French Revolution as an English coastal spectacle: French refugees, driven out by war and proscription, are watched on the Sussex cliffs and the Downs, and their dispossession becomes the occasion for a national poem about exile, charity, and the failure of revolutionary hope. Written in two books dated November 1792 and April 1793 and offered in the lineage of Cowper's The Task, it converts topographical description into political and moral argument.
works.plot: Book I, set on the Sussex cliffs in November 1792, follows the coming of the émigrés, the suffering of the dispossessed French families, and the poet's own recollection of exile, and turns the landscape of the beach and the channel into a commentary on the Revolution and on the war now beginning between Britain and France. Book II, dated April 1793 and set on the Downs, widens the meditation to the causes and consequences of war, to the fate of the poor at home as well as of the refugees abroad, and to the disappointed expectation of liberty, closing in a mood of resigned charity rather than of prophecy.
works.significance: The Emigrants is a central work of women's political poetry in the 1790s and an important early instance of Romantic coastal topography used to think about revolution, refugee hospitality, and war; it shows the conversation-poem and blank-verse meditation traditions being reshaped by a female professional writer, and it is now read as a necessary precedent for the Lyrical Ballads politics of poverty and landscape.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of self-contained lines and passages, with the suspended syntax, apostrophe, and descriptive enumeration characteristic of blank verse after Cowper and Thomson; the poem's rhetorical cadences carry its political argument.
works.context: Published in the spring of 1793, the month Britain declared war on revolutionary France, when the arrival of émigrés made the Revolution a visible social problem on the south coast, and when Smith, who had spent part of her childhood in France, wrote from her own experience of dispossession and dependence. Its address to Cowper locates it in a tradition of national poetry that was being rapidly politicised by the Revolution controversy.
works.characters: the poet-walker of the Sussex shore; the French émigré families; the labouring and fishing poor of the English coast; the distant actors of the Revolution and of the declared war
works.structure: A poem in two books, each anchored in a dated season and a named stretch of coast and downland; the movement is that of Cowperian conversation poetry, where walking and looking generate reflection, and where the émigrés and the local poor supply the human cases on which the argument turns.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
movements: Topographical and Estate Poetry

works.title: The Emperor Jones
works.description: The expressionist tragedy of the American emperor: Brutus Jones and the forest. It is a dramatic work of 1920 by Eugene O'Neill; it belongs to The American Theatre and the Modern Stage and it is catalogued here under Expressionist and Epic Drama; Domestic and Sentimental Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Brutus Jones, an American Pullman porter who has made himself emperor of a Caribbean island, flees into the forest when his subjects revolt; the play follows him through the night as his past and his racial memory rise up in hallucination until he is killed by the silver bullet he had reserved for himself.
works.significance: The Emperor Jones brought expressionism to the American theatre and made O'Neill famous: its single protagonist, its drumbeat and its hallucinatory scenes made it the first great American expressionist play and a landmark of the modern theatre.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose and verse of the non-realistic stage: the numbered or titled scenes, the chant and the direct address, the split self and the narrating figure who stands outside the action, and the bare platform in place of the furnished room. The author's characteristic manner is the expressionist set and the mask.

works.title: The Enchanted Castle
works.description: Published in 1907 and Nesbit's most inventive fantasy: a magic ring, a castle, a sleeping princess and a very practical dinosaur, in a comedy of wishes gone wrong. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Edith Nesbit; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Gerald, Jimmy and Kathleen discover a castle and a sleeping princess, and a ring that makes its wearer invisible and grants wishes; the ring's magic escalates through a series of transformations until the children must use it to undo everything.
works.significance: The Enchanted Castle is the most formally playful of Nesbit's fantasies and a key text in the development of the modern children's fantasy: its combination of real children, real places and uncontrollable magic is the pattern that Lewis and Rowling would follow.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader.

works.characters: Gerald; Jimmy; Kathleen; Mabel Prowse; Mademoiselle; Lord Yalding; the Ugly-Wuglies
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
