works.title: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Second Part of the Life of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: novel; prose voyage narrative with an inherited fictional persona
works.description: The second of the three Robinson Crusoe volumes, issued in August 1719 after a spurious continuation had appeared in London. It returns the narrator to the island, then carries him through the East Indies, the Cape and across the deserts of Central Asia in a series of voyages that replace settlement with motion.
works.plot: Crusoe revisits his island, now peopled by the mutineers he left there and by newly arrived Englishmen and Spaniards, and settles disputes over worship and government before sailing on. He is attacked off Madagascar, trades and travels through the Malay coast, China and Persia, and after a near-fatal crossing of the Great Tartary desert reaches Moscow and travels overland to England, where he finds himself unexpectedly wealthy. The volume closes with a third voyage contemplated rather than narrated.
works.significance: It fixed the model of the sequel and the return-novel, and its colony-building episode has been much discussed as a fable of plantation government, toleration and colonial ownership.
works.meter: Plainer and more hurried prose than the first volume, dominated by dates, distances and commoditues of trade; the meditative periodic sentence gives way to the listed itinerary.
works.context: Composed within months of the first volume's success, it draws on East India Company and privateering narratives and expressly supersedes the pirating Continuation of the World of Robinson Crusoe published in London in mid-1719.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the island governor; Friday's brother; the Portuguese pilot; the Tartar and Muscovite guides
works.structure: First-person retrospect in an episodic voyage sequence, the island episode framing a picaresque chain of traverses and encounters; less concentrated than the first volume and more dependent on reported incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was advertised as the true second part to displace the anonymously pirated continuation.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Sea voyage and seafaring
The slave trade and abolition
movements: The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: The Fashion in Shrouds
works.description: Margery Allingham's tenth Albert Campion novel, published in 1938 by Heinemann in London and Doubleday in New York: a crime novel set among a London couture house, the theatre and an aircraft factory, in which a series of deaths, apparently the work of 'the hand of fate', always falls out in the interest of the actress Georgia Wells.
works.plot: Campion has found the skeleton of Richard Portland-Smith, a barrister and the former fiance of the actress Georgia Wells, who vanished three years before, and his sister Valentine Ferris, a fashion designer whose best friend and most important client is Georgia, introduces him to her circle: Georgia's husband Raymond Ramillies, governor of an African colony; her manager Ferdie Paul; and Alan Dell, the aircraft designer Val loves, who is drawn to Georgia. Ramillies is found dead in the gold-painted plane that was to fly him back to his colony from Caesar's Court, a luxury resort outside London; suspicion falls on Val, whose painkiller Georgia says she gave him; and the house model Caroline Adamson, who had leaked the design of Georgia's dress and then offered Campion information, is found stabbed. With the help of Lady Amanda Fitton, an engineer at Dell's factory who announces a pretended engagement to him, Campion shows that Caroline and an accomplice had blackmailed Portland-Smith until he killed himself, that Ramillies was given a drug that killed him, and that Caroline was murdered when she tried to blackmail her former accomplice. Ferdie Paul, who committed the crimes for Georgia's sake, tries to kill Campion by staging his suicide in a gas oven and is taken by the police Campion had arranged to follow him; Dell asks Val to marry him, and Campion tells Amanda he will marry her if she wishes.
works.significance: The tenth Campion novel, between Dancers in Mourning and Traitor's Purse, brings back Lady Amanda Fitton from Sweet Danger and sets its crimes among the couture house, the theatre and the aircraft factory; its interest lies as much in the rivalry of Val and Georgia over Alan Dell, and in Campion's relations with his sister and with Amanda, as in the detection.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the comic detective and the grotesque villain.
works.context: London in the late 1930s: the couture house, the West End theatre, the aircraft industry and the colonial service. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery.
works.characters: Albert Campion; Valentine Ferris; Georgia Wells; Raymond Ramillies; Alan Dell; Lady Amanda Fitton; Ferdie Paul; Caroline Adamson; Gaiogi Laminoff; Stanislaus Oates; Magersfontein Lugg
works.structure: A detective novel that moves between the couture house, the theatre, the aircraft factory and Caesar's Court, and closes with Campion's exposure of the murderer and a last attempt on his life.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Margery Louise Allingham. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery
works.description: Thomas Southerne's most successful tragedy, an adaptation of two of Behn's novellas, in which Isabella, believing her husband Alonzo dead, remarries and is destroyed when the first husband returns.
works.plot: Isabella, in poverty, believes Alonzo dead and marries Biron; Alonzo returns; Isabella, unable to bear the guilt, kills Biron's brother and then herself.
works.significance: The most popular she-tragedy of the 1690s and an important adaptation of Behn's prose fiction for the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1694 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's Isabella was one of the great performances of the age, and the play held the stage into the nineteenth century.
works.characters: Isabella; Alonzo; Biron; Baldwin; Carlos; Anne
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a subordinate comic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Southerne; he acknowledges the debt to Behn in the dedication.

works.title: The Fatal Sisters
altTitles: The Fatal Sisters: A Translation from the Norse
works.description: Gray's imitated translation of an old Norse poem of the women of the battle, in which the fatal sisters sing the names of the doomed and the course of the fight while they ply the wound and the hair.
works.plot: The daughters of the whirlwind and the battle chant their terrible weaving of the fates of the warriors, name the king whose hour is come and the land that is to be won, and ride away to the north and to the night after the song.
works.significance: It introduced the imagery and the machinery of the northern mythology into English verse, and it is the most exact of the century's poetic reconstructions of primitive poetry.
works.meter: The short paired lines of the reconstructed northern measure, with the heavy alliteration and the repeated burden.
works.context: Written in the same year as The Bard out of Gray's study of the Danish and Norse poetry in the antiquarian editions, at the moment when the northern and the primitive were being made the models of a new sublimity.
works.characters: the fatal sisters of the battle; the king whose doom is chanted; the warriors of the two hosts
works.structure: A short series of antiphonal stanzas of the imitated Norse measure, with the refrain and the enumeration of the slain.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Gray's, though the piece is an imitation rather than a literal translation and the identification of his Norse original is a matter of the antiquarian scholarship of the following century.

works.title: The Fate of Adelaide
works.form: Collected volume: a long verse romance with shorter lyrics, elegies and descriptive pieces; the governing genres are the metrical tale and the meditative lyric in a woman's voice.
works.description: The first volume of verse from the pen that would become the most cultivated poetess of the annuals, built around a long romance in stanzas and a company of shorter pieces. It introduces the characteristic situations of the whole career: the abandoned woman, the artist's vocation, and mourning figured as a landscape.
works.plot: The title romance tells of a young woman's attachment, desertion and ruin, and frames the story with reflective commentary on the fate such attachments leave behind. Around it the volume gathers lyrics of disappointment, elegies on the dead, and descriptive pieces that make scenery the language of feeling. Several poems already treat the figure of the gifted woman whose art is at once her fame and her exposure. The argument is not a single thesis but a repertoire of postures - constancy, wounded pride, and self-dramatising grief. The book ends with shorter occasional verse rather than with the romance's closure.
works.significance: The book is the starting point of a persona - the gifted, wounded, professional woman poet - that its author's later volumes and her imitators developed into an idiom of the annuals. It documents the economics by which a woman could live by verse in the 1820s, since its reception was managed through review work and periodical payment. Modern editions have restored it to the history of Romantic authorship as a case study in female self-fashioning.
works.meter: The romance runs in regular stanzic iambic verse with a rapid movement of talk and ejaculation; the lyrics use common measure, refrains and triple-metre openings, and the couplet appears in the argumentative passages.
works.context: The volume appeared while its author was still writing for the magazines and the Literary Gazette, and unusually for a woman poet of the moment it was issued under her own name rather than over initials. It was reviewed at once in the very periodical press she was herself supplying. Its register is wholly private at a moment when the book trade was saturated with public, political and scandalous verse.
works.characters: Adelaide, the heroine whose fate the title romance records
works.structure: A long narrative romance in stanzas occupies the centre of the volume, preceded and followed by shorter lyrics, elegies and descriptive pieces; the collection is ordered by length, not by design, and the romance interrupts its own story for moral and personal comment.
works.attributionNotes: The first issue carries the author's own name on the title page; the magazine verse of the same years, much of it identical in subject, was signed with initials.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
works.plot: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
works.significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
works.characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
works.structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Mission, conversion, and the Church

works.title: The Father and Daughter
works.description: the author's first novel, a domestic sentimental tragedy of a father's unconditional love for his seduced daughter, based on the real case of a fallen woman and her broken family. It was an immediate bestseller, admired for its moral seriousness and its refusal to condemn its heroine. Mary Wollstonecraft's principles were cited in defence of the novel when critics attacked its leniency.
works.plot: Clara Franklin, the only daughter of a widowed country gentleman, is seduced by the rake Sir Edward Mordant and elopes with him. When the deception is exposed, she is abandoned; her father, rather than cast her off, takes her back and cares for her in her shame. The novel traces their years of quiet exile, Clara's suffering, and her gradual death, ending with the father's inconsolable grief. The narrative is structured around the unconditional bond between parent and erring child rather than around the seduction itself.
works.significance: The Father and Daughter is the most influential of the Romantic-era seduction novels and a landmark in the compassionate representation of the 'fallen woman'; it connects the sentimental tradition to later Victorian treatments of female vulnerability.
works.context: Published in 1801, during the aftermath of Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman and in the height of the sentimental 'fallen woman' novel; The author, already a celebrity by her novel The Tricks of Fiction, deliberately treats the fallen woman with compassion rather than moral condemnation.
works.characters: Clara Franklin; Mr. Franklin; Sir Edward Mordant; Mrs. Clotilde; Arthur Mordaunt
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; the domestic tragedy is centred on the father-daughter bond; the seduction is treated as an event that precipitates but does not dominate the story of endurance and love.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: The Feast of the Poets; with Notes, and Other Pieces in Verse
works.form: Mock-heroic and critical verse satire in the Augustan tradition, revived in Regency England with a lighter, more sociable manner
works.description: A mock-heroic verse satire by Leigh Hunt, first published in the Reflector in 1811 and issued as a separate poem with notes and other pieces in verse in 1814. The poem imagines a banquet to which the living British and classical poets are summoned, and, in the manner of the Dunciad and of Scottish Burns's 'Epistle to the Old Poets', treats the guest-list of contemporary verse as a comic feast of presences and conspicuous absences. Its courteous wit, its critical as well as playful manner, and its copious annotation made it a widely-quoted document of Regency literary taste.
works.plot: An invitation goes out to a feast of the poets at which the muses and their votaries gather; the poem names, praises, gently derides, or pointedly omits the poets of the day from Wordsworth and Coleridge to Rogers, Moore, and Byron. Classical poets are also invited, and the moderns are contrasted with the ancients in a running comic comparison. The notes expand the poem into a critical gloss on contemporary reputations, and the accompanying pieces in verse extend Hunt's manner into lighter lyrics.
works.significance: The Feast of the Poets is a central document of Regency literary sociology and of the mock-heroic satire's survival into the Romantic period; its catalogue of presences and omissions shaped later nineteenth-century judgments about the literary field, and its blend of courtesy and critical edge typifies Hunt's contribution to Romantic periodical culture.
works.meter: Written chiefly in smooth heroic couplets, following the Pope-Byron line of Augustan satire in a lighter, conversational tempo; the diction is witty and allusive, and the poem's argumentative edge is carried in the couplet as often as in the notes.
works.context: The poem first appeared in the Reflector, the quarterly Hunt edited for his brother John in 1810-11, and was expanded into a separate edition in 1814 as Hunt moved from journalism into open literary controversy. Its satiric guest-list engaged the quarrels over contemporary taste that would soon harden into Blackwood's and Quarterly attacks on Hunt and his circle, and Byron himself noted the poem in conversation.
works.characters: the poet-host who presides at the feast; the invited contemporary poets of Regency England; the classical poets who appear for comparison
works.structure: A single mock-heroic poem in rhymed couplets preceded by a brief epistle-like opening and followed by a set of explanatory notes and shorter verses; the design is episodic, moving through the guest-list of poets, and the prose notes carry much of the critical content.
works.attributionNotes: Published by 'The Editor of the Examiner'; authorship by James Henry Leigh Hunt is established and undisputed.

works.title: The Female Husband
works.form: fictional biography and scandalous tale in prose
works.description: A fictionalised life of the woman who passed as a man and married several women, published on the occasion of her trial at the Bristol court in 1746. It is a short scandalous biography in the Newgate manner, mixing report, invention and moral comment on the boundaries of sex and marriage.
works.plot: A young person of masculine appearance and no fortune takes to the road in male dress, learns the practice of a physic, and courtships and marries women in several counties. The marriages are consummated or refused, the wives complain of deformity and distance, and the pursuit of an affectionate partner leads at last to detection, trial and punishment. The narrative reports the exposure with a mixture of sensational detail and professed moral horror.
works.significance: It is a central text for the history of cross-dressing, gender impersonation and the legal fiction of sexual identity in eighteenth-century print culture, and evidence of the novelist's movement from amatory to documentary material.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose with the abrupt, evidential sentences of the trial report and the raised register of the moral reflection.
works.context: Published in 1746 out of the reports of a real prosecution for bigamy and deceit at the Bristol sessions, and in the same decade as the author's own conduct-oriented fiction; the case touched the law of marriage and the definition of sex.
works.characters: the female husband; the successive brides; the constables and prosecutors; the Bristol court
works.structure: A continuous pseudo-biographical life in two short parts, following the trial report and the confessional narrative conventions of criminal biography; detection serves as the structural hinge.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution generally accepted on stylistic and publishing grounds and recorded as single; the text was published without the writer's name, and its subject is a real person whose own account differs.

works.title: The Female Quixote; or, The Adventures of Arabella
works.form: comic novel; moralities of reading in prose
works.description: The comedy of a young heiress who, having read nothing but romances, governs her conduct by their laws and reads every man as a knight and every civility as a homage. It is the most sustained English treatment of the madwoman of the reading plot and one of the century's central statements about fiction's power over its readers.
works.plot: Arabella, beautiful and rich, insists upon the ceremonious courtship prescribed by the romances and refuses the plain addresses of the man she ought to marry. Her lover and her friend try various devices to cure her, including a counter-romantic treatment which makes her believe herself admired in the old style. The exposure of a designing admirer at last breaks the illusion, and the closing reconciliation is effected by a physician who prescribes history and religion against romance.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential figure of the female reader corrupted by fiction and supplied the model for later treatments of romantic delusion, from its own imitators to the nineteenth-century novel of reading.
works.meter: A clear ironic prose that quotes and parodies the diction of the heroic romance in the heroine's speeches, the comedy lying in the mismatch of registers.
works.context: Published in 1752, in the season of the quarrel over the danger of novel-reading and of the author's own friendship with the leading writers of the day, including the lexicographer who advertised the book; its target includes the surviving vogue of translated romance.
works.characters: Arabella; her lover and friend; the designing admirer who works on her delusion; the physician and the moralist of the conclusion
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes, the plot a single sustained irony maintained by the heroine's misreadings; the episodes are arranged as trials of her interpretive system and resolved by an anti-romance cure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and long, wrongly, credited to another hand by early bibliographers before being firmly reassigned.

works.title: The Female Reader
altTitles: The Female Reader: Pieces, Prose and Verse, Selected from the Most Classick Writers and Calculated as a Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
The Female Reader. A Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
works.form: anthology and critical guide to reading
works.description: An anthology of prose and verse selected for the use of young women and furnished with rules of reading and with the editor's remarks on taste, elocution and the choice of books. It was planned as the practical completion of a female education and issued in several volumes.
works.plot: The collection passes in order through the species of composition - description, argument, narration, the drama, the epic, lyric and the letters of history - each being illustrated by extracted specimens and preceded by directions for reading it well. Remarks on the choice of books, on the cultivation of the ear and on the danger of incorrect reading supply the connective argument. Its design is to make a woman's taste an instrument of judgement rather than of amusement.
works.significance: It is an important document of the pedagogy of taste for women at the end of the century and evidence of the author's methods as a critic and teacher before her political writing.
works.meter: A didactic prose of rule and remark for the connecting matter, the verse extracts being given as specimens of the several measures and the prose as models of style.
works.context: Published in 1789 in the same season as the author's work on the education of women and within the dissenting and Bluestocking projects for female improvement, the anthology genre then being a principal means of literary instruction.
works.structure: A systematic anthology in classes with the editor's dissertations and notes interposed; the order of the species governs the sequence, the extracts supplying the examples.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by the publisher's records and by the correspondence of the period, the work having been issued without the name of the editor; part of the compiling labour has been associated with a sister's hand, and the record is held as partial.

works.title: The Fiddler's House
works.form: Play (one act, the Abbey peasant drama)
works.description: The play of the wandering fiddler and the house left empty. It is a dramatic work of 1907 by Padraic Colum; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement.
works.plot: The farmer's wife leaves the house and the children for the wandering fiddler of the road, and the play follows the empty house, the returned wife and the road that takes the fiddler again, in the spoken Irish idiom of the Abbey stage.
works.significance: The Fiddler's House is the second of Colum's founding peasant plays and the first to put the woman's leaving on the Abbey stage: its road and its empty house made the emigrant and the wanderer the subjects of the revival's drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish idiom carried into English dialogue.
works.context: The Irish west in 1907, and the Abbey peasant play. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and first performed in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.
works.characters: the wife; the fiddler; the farmer; the children; the neighbours
works.structure: A peasant play in one act on the road and the house. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Colum. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Field of Mustard
works.description: The collection of the field of mustard and the country of the stories. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by A. E. Coppard; it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The Field of Mustard gathers the stories of the field, the fair and the funeral of the southern country, in the deadpan of the teller who does not explain.
works.significance: The Field of Mustard is the collection of Coppard's maturity: its field and its fair are the standard text of the English country story of the 1920s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the single strange turn in the everyday.
works.context: England in the mid-1920s, and the country of the short story. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: the field folk; the fair folk; the mourners
works.structure: A collection of country stories in the deadpan manner. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The Financier
works.description: Published in 1912 and the first American novel of the financier: the rise and fall of a Philadelphia street-railway magnate. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by Theodore Dreiser; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Frank Cowperwood, a young Philadelphia broker, makes a fortune in street railways and city finance, is caught in the panic of 1871 and convicted of embezzlement, serves thirteen months in prison and emerges with his ambition intact, while his wife and his mistress wait for him outside.
works.significance: The Financier is the first great American novel of finance and the founding text of the American business novel: its portrait of Cowperwood, based on the street-railway magnate Charles Yerkes, made the amoral financier a central American literary figure, and it is the essential American fiction of the Gilded Age economy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is slow accumulation of documentary detail.
works.context: 1912: the Philadelphia of the 1860s-70s, the panic of 1871 and the great Chicago fire, the corruption of city politics, and the American cult of the 'captain of industry'. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Frank Cowperwood; Lillian Cowperwood; Aileen Butler; Edward Butler; Peter Laughlin; Stener; Harper Steger
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Theodore Dreiser. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Finnsburh Fragment
works.manuscriptDate: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
works.description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
works.plot: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
works.significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
works.context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
works.characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
works.structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Blood-feud, vengeance, and kinship
Loyalty and the comitatus bond

movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The First Settlers of New-England; or, Conquest of the Pequods, Narragansets, and Pokanokets, as Related by a Father to His Children
altTitles: The First Settlers of New England
works.form: Juvenile and educational history in the tales-of-the-settlement mode: a framed narrative of war and planting designed to form national feeling in the young reader.
works.description: A historical narrative for young readers recounting the settlement of New England and the wars with the Pequods, Narragansets and Pokanokets, put into the mouth of a father telling the story to his children. It was written as part of a programme of national education, and it is notable for the way its sympathetic treatment of the conquered combines with an unrepentant account of the settlers' cause. Its frank description of atrocity on both sides makes it one of the more unusual juvenile histories of the period.
works.plot: The narrative begins with the earliest plantings and the first contact between settlers and the Native nations of the region, and moves through the Pequot war, the destruction of the fort at the Mystic, the flight and death of the Narraganset king, and King Philip's war. Each campaign is recounted as an episode of courage and cruelty, with the writer's sympathy frequently diverted from the English to their opponents, whose loss of land and people is lamented plainly. The father's frame supplies the moral instruction: the children are to love the settler's fortitude but to pity the conquered, and the tale closes on the hope that justice might yet be done to the remnant.
works.significance: It is a significant early American book for children and an unusually conflicted piece of national origin-writing, in which the elegy for the conquered sits inside a celebration of the conquest. Its treatment of the Native past anticipates the romantic Indian tale of the following decade and documents the moral ambiguity of Jacksonian-era education.
works.meter: Clear expository prose addressed to children, with occasional apostrophe and lament; no verse.
works.context: Written in the late 1820s for a national audience of children at a moment when American historical writing was being rebuilt as usable origin-myth and when Indian policy was moving toward removal. Its author was by then editing a juvenile periodical in Boston and writing the reform-adjacent fiction and pedagogy that led her, in the following years, to the great abolitionist argument of the 1830s.
works.characters: The narrating father and his listening children; the Pequot and Narraganset chiefs; the confederated king of Pokanoket; the settlers and captains of the United Colonies
works.structure: Framed juvenile history: a father's continuous narrative addressed to his children, divided into episodes of war and settlement in strict chronological sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is established and uncontested; the book was published under the author's own name in her second year of professional writing.

Colonial enterprise and the New World
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal

works.title: The Fleece
works.form: Didactic and topographical poem in the Thomson school, in books, with the technical instruction of a husbandry poem combined with the survey of a trade; issued after subscription proposals and dedications.
works.description: John Dyer's principal poem: a didactic and topographical work on the English wool trade, from the feeding of the sheep and the shearing to the staple, the marketing and the international commerce that carried the fleece to the world's ends. It was published by subscription and carries the name of the clergyman who wrote it. The ambition is at once technical and moral: to make the whole circuit of a national industry the subject of elevated unrhymed verse.
works.plot: The poem moves outward in stages from the pasture to the ocean. Its first care is practical: the breeds, the feeding, the shearing and the management of the flock, with the shepherd and the shepherdess introduced as figures of a vanishing rural order. From the fleece in the fold it passes to the wool in the warehouse and the market, and then to the merchant, the ship and the ports of the Mediterranean and the north, arguing that this single commodity has bound England into the world's trade. A moral anxiety runs under the praise: the growth of wealth threatens to corrupt the labour and the independence that produced it, and the prospect of national fullness is shadowed by the fear of decline. The argument is therefore a sustained piece of political economy in verse, closer to a discourse of the wool trade than to any earlier English poem.
works.significance: It is the most ambitious of the eighteenth-century attempts to put a national industry into elevated verse, and the crucial link between Thomson's meditative topography and Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' in the poetry of rural labour, commerce and depopulation. Samuel Johnson's account of its crabbed sublimity made it the standard example of a poet who mistook harshness for strength, and it remains a primary document of the age's thinking about commerce and its discontents.
works.meter: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of notoriously harsh and laborious texture, with long compounds, stretched and hypermetric lines, and an evident attempt to bend English measure to the weight of Latin and Italian syntax.
works.context: It was written in the decades when the wool and cloth trade was the acknowledged foundation of English national power, and when the staple, the export markets and the growing manufactures were matters of public debate. Dyer, a Welsh-born curate with a small living and large schemes for rural industry, published by subscription after earlier ventures failed, and the poem carries those projects' hopes and disappointments.
works.characters: The shepherd and shepherdess of the English hills; the wool merchant; the mariner; the labouring poor of the staple towns
works.structure: A didactic poem in books, each gathering its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression, apostrophe to the labouring poor, and an ascending sweep from local husbandry to global commerce.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's own name in the collected editions and its composition is documented in Dyer's correspondence with his friends. Precise years of composition for the individual books are not fixed here and are left null.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society

Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village
movements: Topographical and Estate Poetry

works.title: The Fleshly School of Poetry
works.description: The most famous act of literary criticism of the century: the attack on Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites. It is a prose work of 1871 by Robert Buchanan; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Writing as 'Thomas Maitland' in the Contemporary Review, Buchanan attacks Rossetti's Poems of 1870 as the 'fleshly school of poetry' — sensual, obscene, and morally corrupt — and extends the attack to Swinburne and Morris in a pamphlet of 1872.
works.significance: The Fleshly School of Poetry is the most famous act of literary criticism of the nineteenth century: it destroyed Rossetti's health, ended his public career, and defined the Victorian debate over the morality of art, being the central document of the war between the aesthetes and their critics.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The author's characteristic manner is the abusive review and the pamphlet war.
works.context: London in 1871, the Pre-Raphaelite circle at its height and the Victorian controversy over the morality of art. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1872 and first published in 1871 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.characters: Buchanan as 'Thomas Maitland'; Rossetti; Swinburne; Morris
works.structure: A review essay and a pamphlet in the critical war of 1871-72. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Williams Buchanan. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Forest
works.description: Jonson's collection of fifteen poems printed in the 1616 Folio, including the country-house poem 'To Penshurst', the odes 'To Celia' and 'To Heaven', the song 'That Women Are but Men's Shadows', and the epistle 'To Sir Robert Wroth' — the volume that made the estate, the court, and the virtuous life the matter of English lyric.
works.plot: No plot: the poems move from the celebration of Penshurst's hospitality and Sidneyan estate-life, through the songs and odes of love and devotion, to the epistles and epitaphs that map Jonson's moral world of patrons and friends.
works.significance: Home of the English country-house poem and of Jonson's most enduring lyrics — the classical counterweight to the metaphysical fashion.
works.meter: Couplets, odes, and songs of classical restraint, including the famous lyric 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' (a cento from Philostratus).
works.context: Collected for the 1616 Folio; 'To Penshurst' (c. 1612) founded the country-house poem that Lanyer, Carew, and Marvell would continue.

works.structure: A miscellany of fifteen poems organized by theme — place, love, virtue, mortality — with 'To Penshurst' as its opening masterpiece.

works.title: The Forest of Vaud
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's later Gothic novel, set in the Swiss forest of Vaud and the Jura mountains, in which an isolated heroine encounters persecution and the supernatural. It belongs to the author's final phase of Gothic writing, after the great vogue of the 1790s had passed.
works.plot: In the Alpine canton of Vaud, a young woman is confined in a forest hermitage by a guardian whose intentions are sinister; pursuit, supernatural threat, and the wild landscape combine in the Gothic ordeal. The novel's Swiss setting draws on the Rousseauian and Gothic Alpine traditions, and its heroine's endurance under confinement is the novel's central dramatic pattern.
works.significance: The Forest of Vaud extends the author's lifelong Gothic interrogation of female vulnerability and confinement; it illustrates the Gothic mode's endurance into the late Romantic period beyond Scott and the historical novel.
works.context: Published in the mid-1820s, at the twilight of the Gothic novel vogue and at the end of the author's career; the Alpine setting reflects the enduring Romantic fascination with Switzerland and its literature of terror.
works.characters: The heroine of the forest; her persecutor guardian; her protector
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; the Gothic captivity and pursuit plot is set against the Swiss forest landscape; a resolution restores the heroine's rightful position.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror

Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind

works.title: The Forest Sanctuary
works.form: Verse romance and religious narrative poem in six cantos; the metrical tale of providential preservation is the governing genre, with descriptive and meditative lyric passages embedded.
works.description: The longest serious narrative poem in the author's canon, worked out in six cantos around a providential plot of shipwreck, rescue and rearing. It converts an adventure story into a meditation on gratitude, vocation and the claims of a religious house upon a soul preserved by it.
works.plot: An infant's life is saved in a storm at sea, and the child is brought up within a monastic retreat sheltered in a forest, which gives the poem its title and its central image of sanctuary. The middle cantos pass from the discipline and kindness of that training into the world, where the grown hero meets ambition, society and a love that threatens the allegiance formed in the forest. The argument resolves not by dramatic catastrophe but by a returning sense of obligation to Providence and to the retreat that saved the child. Descriptive and reflective passages interrupt and enlarge the story, so that the fable carries a sustained argument about grace and gratitude. The close confirms the sanctuary as a moral as well as a physical place.
works.significance: The poem is the index of a reputation that was drifting toward the sentimental and the occasional; reviewers who had treated the earlier volumes as sweet now had to address a Spenserian romance with a theological argument. Its celebration of the religious house as sanctuary sits oddly with the anti-monastic current of an age formed by Gothic fiction, and that friction is its most interesting feature. Its later eclipse measures how fast the long moral poem passed out of fashion before the 1830s.
works.meter: Written in Spenserian stanzas, a choice that aligns the poem with the romance measures then being revived by the older generation of narrative poets; the stanza's closing alexandrine is used for reflective weight, and the caesura is managed for devotional pause.
works.context: It appeared after a decade in which its author had published lyrics, translations and shorter narratives, and marks her attempt to be read as a poet of sustained moral narrative rather than of occasional feeling. Its providential plot answers the age's taste for Catholic romance while insisting on a plainly Protestant devotional temper. A revised second edition in 1829 shows that the longer poem carried her name into a different critical category.
works.structure: Six continuous cantos, each opening from a different vantage and returning periodically to the sanctuary; the plot of preservation is interwoven with lyric invocation and moral reflection rather than driven by incident.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Forget-Me-Not
altTitles: The Forget Me Not: A Christmas and New Year's Present
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: the miniature lyric and the sentimental prose sketch arranged for gift presentation with engraved plates.
works.description: The first of the English literary annuals proper, a small ornamented gift book issued for the Christmas season of 1823 and continued for some years afterwards. It established the pattern the trade would make famous: a finely bound volume, a plate or plates of the fine arts, and a miscellany of short poems and prose sketches of sentiment, presented as a token of affection to be given rather than bought for reading. It belongs to the moment when the steel engraving and the seasonal gift created a new market for Romantic verse.
works.plot: The volume has no continuous argument; its design is a sequence of lyrical pieces on memory, parting and affection, and of brief prose tales of sentiment and historical colour, each framed to the plate it accompanies. Its titles and its emblematic device announce its subject: remembrance, the transience of feeling and the keeping of tokens between the absent.
works.significance: It is the prototype of the English literary annual, the object that began the gift-book economy through which much Romantic and early-Victorian verse reached its readers, and a necessary starting point for any account of the annual as a form. Its miniature aesthetic, addressed to memory and affection, defines the tone later critics associate with the annuals.
works.meter: Predominantly short lyric in song and sonnet measures, with simple rhyme schemes and a soft meditative register; prose in familiar sentimental style.
works.context: Issued at the opening of the annuals' decade, when improved steel engraving, the book trade's expansion and a new etiquette of gift-giving created demand for seasonally dated volumes. It precedes by five years the foundation of the great commercial annual and shows the form's origins in topographical and decorative publishing rather than in literary editing.
works.structure: Annual anthology miscellany: emblem plate, then an unbroken succession of short poems and prose sketches, without editorial argument.
works.attributionNotes: The volume was issued without a named editor. Its editorship has been popularly assigned to a celebrated poetess of the following decade, but the attribution rests on tradition rather than on documentary evidence and is now generally doubted; the volume is therefore recorded as anonymous.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Forging of the Anchor
altTitles: The Forging of the Anchor: A Legend of the Bay of Carrick
works.form: Ballad and Popular Song; Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza
works.description: A vigorous industrial ballad published in a leading Edinburgh periodical in February 1832, the poem that made its author's reputation as an English verse-writer in Ireland before he was twenty-two. The scene is a forge on the Bay of Carrick, where a huge anchor for a ship of war is welded by a squad of smiths, and the labour of the anvil is joined to a story of love, rivalry, and death. Its bounding measure and its technical vocabulary of work made it at once celebrated and much quoted.
works.plot: The poem opens on the forge-fire and the band of smiths at Carrick, mustered to weld an anchor for the service of the navy, and it follows the labour through its stages of heating, welding, and dipping with an insistent chorus of action. A love-plot runs beneath the industrial frame: the smith's winning of the maiden whose favour is at stake, the rivalry of a proud companion, and the catastrophe which brings the work of the anchor into contact with drowning and with death. The poem's closing movements unite the forged metal and the human fate, the anchor holding where the affections failed. The diction is deliberately muscular and technical, the labour terms and the bay place-names carrying the poem's local pride.
works.significance: The Forging of the Anchor is the founding poem of the Irish academic verse tradition in English and the instance most often cited of a Romantic-period ballad that makes industrial labour itself its subject and its music. It remains a standard anthology piece and a touchstone for the argument that the ballad revival passed into a national poetry of work.
works.meter: A strongly accented, fast-running ballad measure with burdens and refrains, close to the bagatelle and the street stave, and much praised for the way its line mounts the physical work of the hammer; the stanza is regular and the rhyme pressing.
works.context: Published in the period when the Ulster and Dublin magazines were attempting a national poetry in English. A reviewer of the leading Scottish magazine school first noticed the poem and made the author's name. The anchor forged for a ship of war belongs to the working smithing and ship-supply economy of the Irish Sea coast in the 1820s, and the poem's technical pride is of an Ulster artisan world.
works.characters: the foreman smith of the forge; the maiden whose love is contested; the rival smith; the crew and the drowned of the bay legend
works.structure: A single continuous ballad in numbered sections, built on recurrent refrain and on the staged progress of the forging, with the love and rivalry plot interwoven rather than sequentially opposed to it.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship and undisputed; the poem appeared in a periodical, where its author was initially unknown to many readers, and was afterwards collected in his verse volume of the 1860s.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Love, constancy, and betrayal
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Form of Living
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
works.plot: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
works.significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
works.context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); Margaret Kirkby (addressee)
works.structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
The contemplative life
movements: The English Mystics

works.title: The Forme of Cury
works.description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
works.plot: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
works.significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
works.meter: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
works.context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
works.characters: none (recipe collection)
works.structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (compiled by the king's cooks).
themes: Wisdom and learning
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

works.title: The Fortunes of Men
works.description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
works.plot: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
works.significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
works.characters: none
works.structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Wisdom and learning
Wyrd (fate) and providence
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Fortunes of Nigel
altTitles: The Fortunes of Nigel; or, Nigel Olifaunt of that Ilk
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Jacobean metropolis
works.description: A historical romance of the reign of the first British king, in which a poor young laird of a Scottish house goes up to London to prosecute a claim at court and is thrown among the money-lenders, goldsmiths and players of the Jacobean capital. Its subject is the fortune of a dependent and a kingdom: a Scotch estate, a pawned jewel, a court favourite's malice, and the cause of an injured house which the king must finally judge. The romance is the most concentrated study of the new British politics after 1603 that the series contains, and it treats the transaction of land for money as the real event of the age. Its London topography and its portraits of a famous king and a famous goldsmith have been much quoted.
works.plot: A young Scottish laird, sent to London to secure the repayment of a debt owed to his house by the crown, finds his estate threatened by a court favourite, is arrested for debt, and is befriended by a goldsmith of the Exchange whose credit and whose household he endangers. A diamond pledged and lost, a suit of wrong, a duel, and the protection of the king himself carry the cause from the counting-house to the council, and the Scottish claimant is finally preferred while the favourite is discountenanced. The lower world of London law-writers, actors and money-lenders carries on the same argument in the by-plot.
works.significance: The most important of the series' romances of the British union and one of the earliest historical novels to make credit, pawn and legal suit the motive force of its plot. It is a standard document for the study of the representation of London, of Scottish migration to the English capital, and of the fiction of money in the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Scottish speech for the hero and his countrymen, and a city idiom of trade, law and the playhouse for the London chapters
works.context: Published in 1822, it uses the removal of a Scottish court to London after 1603 as a study of the union in practice, of the crown's dependence on merchants' credit, and of the favourites and suits which then determined fortunes. Its treatment of a king famously wrote, argued, and favoured supplies a political anatomy of the early British state, and the tale's money-lending and pawnbroking world reflects contemporary debate about credit, debt and the opening of professions to those formerly restricted.
works.characters: A young laird of a Scottish house; King James; the goldsmith to the Exchange and his household; a favourite of the court who wrongs the Scottish family; a law-writer, actors and money-lenders of London
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with a single hero's cause as its spine and a fully realised urban by-plot; the king's conversations and the goldsmith's house supply the two poles of the design.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
The city and urban life
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Fortunes of Perkin Warbeck: A Romance
works.form: Historical novel and romance; a tragedy of imposture, legitimacy and dynastic extinction.
works.description: A historical romance on the impostor who personated one of the vanished princes of the house of York, and on the fall of that house after Bosworth. The tale treats the pretender as a gentleman bred to a name he never fairly held, and reads the Tudor settlement as the extinction of an aristocratic and romantic order. Its materials are the chronicles, the ballads and the drama that had long handled the same story; its interest is moral rather than evidential.
works.plot: Perkin Warbeck, an unhappy child of a Kentish household, is marked out by a patron of the Yorkist cause, instructed in the part he is to act, and acknowledged as one of the princes believed murdered in the Tower. He is welcomed by the duchess of Burgundy, married to a Scottish gentlewoman while the Scottish king plays the cause for his own advantage, and led through insurrection in Cornwall, through the siege of a northern town and through the mercy of a court he had hoped to inherit. Henry the Seventh's policy narrows about him; he is taken, pardoned, again entrusted and again convicted, and dies at Tyburn, while the romance's closing chapters follow the extinction of the house whose name he wore.
works.significance: An important late instance of the historical romance by a writer whose earlier fiction had reshaped the gothic tale, and a study of identity, adoption and legitimacy conducted through dynastic material. It supplies evidence of how the school of national romance was adapted to a tragic and feminine moral interest. It is now chiefly studied for its treatment of imposture and of the claims of the disinherited.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a formal romantic narrative with quoted ballad and chronicle phrase.
works.context: Written in the later 1820s, when the historical romance of the previous generation had become the dominant model for fiction on national subjects and when the pretender's story had been revived by drama and by ballad editing. The novel's Yorkist sympathy continues a tradition of dynastic romance rather than the new Whig history. It was published in the year of the French revolution that closed the post-war settlement.
works.characters: Perkin Warbeck; Margaret, duchess of Burgundy; Katherine Gordon; James IV of Scotland; Henry VII; the patron who frames his identity
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with ballad and chronicle material absorbed into the narrative and with an epigraphic apparatus; a rise-and-fall structure keyed to the pretender's claims.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the author of an earlier tale; authorship undisputed. Not to be confused with the seventeenth-century chronicle play on the same subject already held in this corpus.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Kingship and good rule
Women, chastity, and constancy
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle
Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Four Elements
altTitles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
works.description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
works.plot: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
works.significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
works.characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
works.structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: The Four Georges
works.description: Four lectures on the Hanoverian kings, delivered in the United States in 1855-56 and in Britain from 1856, and published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 and as a book in 1861: a satire on the House of Hanover that works by the accumulation of trivial detail and by the contrast between the king's private life and the public pageant.
works.plot: Each lecture follows one king — George I, George II, George III, George IV — from accession to death, with anecdotes of mistresses, debts, court ceremonial and the king's tastes, and with Thackeray's commentary on the time's literature and manners.
works.significance: The Four Georges was the most discussed historical writing of its year, and it taught the Victorian lecture audience that history could be written as social comedy; its method descends to Lytton Strachey's Eminent Victorians and to the modern biographical essay.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The Hanoverian succession and the Jacobite risings, the Regency of the future George IV, and the 1850s vogue for historical lecturing that Thackeray shared with Dickens. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
movements: Arnold and the Criticism of Culture

works.title: The Four Just Men
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1905
works.description: The founding thriller: four men who execute the unjust. It is a prose fiction work of 1905 by Edgar Wallace; it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Four mysterious men threaten to kill the British Foreign Secretary unless he withdraws an unjust bill, and the police race to protect him, in the novel that founded the modern thriller and made Wallace famous.
works.significance: The Four Just Men founded the modern thriller and made Edgar Wallace the founder of the British thriller industry: its vigilantes, its race against time and its publicity stunt made it one of the most influential popular novels of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid plot of pursuit and revelation.
works.context: London in the early 1900s. The record dates the work as composed in 1905 and first published in 1905 and it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: the four Just Men; the Foreign Secretary; Superintendent Falmouth; the public
works.structure: A thriller of pursuit and threat in London. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Richard Horatio Edgar Wallace. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Four PP
altTitles: The Play Called the Four PP
works.description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
works.plot: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
works.significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
works.characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
works.structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Early Tudor Drama

works.title: The Fox and the Wolf
works.description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
works.plot: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
works.significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
works.context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
works.characters: the Fox; the Wolf
works.structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: The Freedom of the Press
works.form: Essay (proposed preface to Animal Farm, written 1945; first published posthumously)
works.description: The preface Orwell wrote in 1945 for Animal Farm, which was not printed with the book; it was first published in the Times Literary Supplement on 15 September 1972, with an introduction by Bernard Crick, after Ian Angus found the typescript.
works.summary: Orwell recounts the difficulty of finding a publisher for Animal Farm, quotes a publisher who withdrew after consulting an important official in the Ministry of Information, and generalises from the episode to the self-censorship of the British intelligentsia over the Soviet Union.
works.plot: Orwell says the book was first thought of in 1937 and written down at the end of 1943, and that it was refused by four publishers, only one of them for ideological reasons. The chief danger to free expression in England, he argues, is not official censorship but the voluntary conformity of intellectuals, who accept that some opinions, above all criticism of Stalin during the wartime alliance, are not to be printed; he cites the applause for the purges of 1936-38 and the concealment of famine in Ukraine. He ends: 'If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.'
works.significance: A central document of Orwell's thinking about intellectual freedom, frequently quoted in arguments about free speech, especially for its closing sentence.
works.meter: Direct, combative argument from one documented case, with the publisher's letter quoted verbatim.
works.context: Written in 1945, while Britain was still allied with the Soviet Union and Animal Farm was going the rounds of publishers; it lay unpublished until the typescript was found, in 1971 or 1972 according to different sources.
works.structure: A single continuous essay that moves from the publishing history of Animal Farm to a general argument about liberty and a closing defence of free speech.
themes: History, truth and the uses of the past
Power, the state and surveillance

works.title: The Freedom of the Streets
works.description: The collected essays of the working-class voice of the Adelphi. It is a prose work of 1938 by Jack Common; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Freedom of the Streets gathers Common's essays of the decade - the street, the workshop, the dole, the education of the self-taught man and the freedom of the ordinary life - in the plain northern prose that Orwell praised as the authentic voice of the working man and Pritchett called the most influential book of his life.
works.significance: The Freedom of the Streets is the classic essay book of the working-class voice: its streets, its workshop and its argument made the ordinary working man a literary presence of the thirties, and its influence on Orwell and Pritchett fixed its place in the decade's prose.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain northern prose of the street and the workshop.
works.context: London and Newcastle in the Depression decade. The record dates the work as composed between 1930 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: the working man of the streets; the self-taught reader; the comfortable culture
works.structure: A collection of essays of the street and the workshop. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Jack Common. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Freeholder
altTitles: The Freeholder: a Collection of Papers
works.description: Addison's late political essay paper, written in support of the Hanoverian settlement during the Jacobite rising of 1715 and addressed to the freeholder electorate; it argues the case for limited property-based liberty against both arbitrary power and popular licence.
works.plot: A freeholder addresses his constituents and a succession of imaginary opponents, tracing the constitution from the feudal conquest, defending the settled succession, and warning that a standing army, Jacobite intrigue and the demagogic temper threaten the same liberty from opposite sides.
works.significance: It became a standard textbook of the moderate Whig constitutional argument, reprinted in America through the 1760s and 1770s as an elementary school of British liberty.
works.meter: Clear argumentative prose of the Spectator manner, with heavy use of balanced pairs, historical example and closing sententiae.
works.context: Published during and immediately after the '15 rising, in the season of Whig pamphlet warfare that also produced Swift's and Steele's party papers and Addison's breach with Steele over The Drummer's circle.
works.characters: the freeholder-writer; the party opponent; the Jacobite conspirator
works.structure: A short serial of letter-like papers addressed to a named friend or to the freeholders, each taking up one branch of the argument, with an inserted historical dissertation.
works.attributionNotes: Addison's authorship is uncontested, though the paper was issued without his name; his official connection with the administration has encouraged readers to treat it as ministerial writing.

Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
