works.title: The French Revolution: A History
works.form: Historical prose narrative in three parts
works.description: Published in three volumes in 1837 after the manuscript of the first volume was accidentally burned by John Stuart Mill's housemaid: the greatest work of Victorian historiography and the book that made Carlyle famous.
works.plot: The three parts — 'The Bastille', 'The Constitution', 'The Guillotine' — narrate the French Revolution from the death of Louis XV to the fall of Robespierre, by a method of vivid present-tense scenes, documents, portraits and choric commentary rather than by continuous analysis; the Revolution is presented as a terrible and necessary judgment on a corrupt society.
works.significance: The French Revolution changed the writing of history in English: its present-tense scenes, its documentary collage and its prophetic judgement created the modern literary history. Dickens used it as a source for A Tale of Two Cities, and its account of the Revolution as the work of 'the great dumb deep' shaped the Victorian and modern understanding of revolutionary politics.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
works.context: The 1830s and the memory of 1789 and 1830; Carlyle's reading of the French memoirs and pamphlets; and the British debate on reform that made the French Revolution a living political question. The record dates the work as composed between 1834 and 1837 and first published in 1837 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: Three parts of seven, five and seven books, in a loosely chronological sequence of scenes and portraits rather than an analytical argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Friend
works.form: Periodical essay and moral-critical miscellany in the line of the Spectator papers, transformed by the Romantic habit of self-analysis and by the projector's account of his own enterprise.
works.description: A weekly literary and moral sheet conducted by the author at his own risk between 1809 and 1810, and reissued in an enlarged edition in 1812, in which the essayist addressed a small circle of subscribers on character, ambition, marriage, the duties of the young, the politics of the day and the principles of literature. It grew out of a scheme of public lectures on government and public feeling that had failed, and it carries that origin in its habit of arguing with an imaginary audience of men of business and of men of letters. The numbers mix moral meditation, literary criticism, autobiography and editorial matter, and the enterprise lost its projector money.
works.plot: The essays proceed by proposition and appeal rather than by narrative: the writer states the condition of a private mind in a public age and then examines the resources available to it - habit, principle, the example of the ancients, the discipline of a chosen occupation. Some numbers deal with the conduct of life, warning against ambition without talent and against the love of reputation, and prescribing the economy of a character to be maintained in a world of parties; others comment on the literature and the criticism of the day, on the education of the mind and on the duties of the clergy, and on public affairs, including the conduct of the war and the state of the press. The whole is framed as a manual for a young man of character, and the series ends with the projector's plain account of the failure of the scheme, which became part of the biographical record of the author's life.
works.significance: The chief monument of the author's own attempt to found a moral-literary journal, and a document of the Romantic essayist's quarrel with the market: its numbers on ambition, on the discipline of the mind and on the conduct of a public career are part of the period's preoccupation with character, and its material was later worked up in the literary autobiography of 1817.
works.meter: Prose of a dense and hortatory kind, marked by long sentences, abstract nouns and a repeated appeal to principle, with passages of narrative simplicity in the autobiographical numbers.
works.context: Founded in London in 1809 after the failure of the author's lecture course on the state of public feeling and after the collapse of his domestic and marital prospects, at a time when the weekly literary sheet was being established as a vehicle for criticism and when the author's quarrel with his collaborator's public position was beginning; its financial failure left him dependent on lecture and periodical work for years.
works.characters: The essayist-editor addressing his subscribers; the imagined young man of character for whom the series is a manual; the friends and correspondents whose letters are inserted
works.structure: A serial periodical of weekly numbers, gathered into a volume at the close of the first series and enlarged in the second edition of 1812; the numbers are free-standing, with a continuity of voice and of purpose rather than of argument, and with occasional letters and contributions from correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a few inserted letters and contributions by correspondents are distinguished from the projector's own matter in modern editions.

works.title: The Frozen Deep
works.form: Melodrama in three acts (with Charles Dickens)
works.description: Written with Charles Dickens in 1856 and performed at Tavistock House in January 1857 with Dickens as Richard Wardour: a melodrama of Arctic exploration, self-sacrifice and the discovery of a rival's worth.
works.plot: Two explorers, Richard Wardour and Frank Aldersley, are rivals for the same woman; in the Arctic, Wardour discovers that the man he is about to kill is his rival and instead carries him across the ice to safety, dying in the effort.
works.significance: The Frozen Deep is the most famous collaboration of Dickens and Collins, and it shaped the climax of A Tale of Two Cities; it is a key document in the theatrical culture of the 1850s.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose of the domestic stage: the dialogue of the drawing room and the household, the revelation scene, the timed entrance, and the act ending on a discovery or a suspense. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1850s, the Franklin expedition and the Arctic searches, and the amateur theatricals of the Dickens circle. The record dates the work as composed in 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation drama and the domestic stage; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Richard Wardour; Frank Aldersley; Clara Burnham; Lucy Crayford; Lieutenant Crayford; Nurse Esther
works.structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts, each closing on a discovery or a suspense, with the revelation scene placed at the crisis.
works.attributionNotes: The work is recorded as a joint undertaking with Charles Dickens, the contribution of each being stated in the work-author relationship. Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Fruits of Christianity
works.description: Published in 1876 and one of the most notorious pieces of Victorian freethought: a series of lectures arguing that the historical effects of Christianity have been harmful, delivered on secularist platforms.
works.plot: Besant examines the Christian record on slavery, war, persecution, the treatment of women, science and the arts, and argues that the churches have opposed every movement for human improvement and that morality is independent of Christian belief.
works.significance: The Fruits of Christianity is a central document of Victorian freethought and of the argument over the moral effects of religion; its publication made Besant the most notorious woman speaker in England and it was answered by the leading Anglican apologists of the day.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is direct argument and plain diction.
works.context: The 1870s, the National Secular Society, the prosecution for blasphemy, and the Victorian debate on the social consequences of religion. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: The Fudge Family in Paris
altTitles: The Fudge Family in Paris; and Other Poems
works.form: Comic verse epistle and travel satire, in the tradition of the tourists' letter and of Regency light political verse.
works.description: A verse epistolary comedy in which a middling English family reports its first season in Paris after the peace, published under the same pseudonymous Irish correspondent used for the earlier letter-poems. It reprints and frames letters from the British tourist in Paris, adding an account of the spoliated collections and of the politics of the Restoration city. Its humour depends on the gap between the family's patriotic confidence and what it actually sees.
works.plot: The letters record the family's progress through hotels, shows, sales, prefects' offices and society, each member misinterpreting French manners in a way that exposes English prejudice and greed. The father's commercial curiosity, the daughters' romantic sensibility and the young attachements of the family produce a running comedy of misreading. The volume's most sustained argument concerns the loot of European art held in Paris, and the poet anticipates the demand for its restitution. Later letters extend the satire to the diplomatic congresses and to the trading politics of post-war Britain, so that the tourist narrative becomes a general account of national character and of European reconstruction.
works.significance: It was one of the best-selling comic poems of the period and created the template for the Victorian tourists' satire in verse, remaining in print for generations in expanded editions. Its passages on the spoliation of art entered the debate that led to the restitution of the royal collections. It remains the standard illustration of how high Romantic verse and commercial light verse coexisted in the same publishing house.
works.meter: Predominantly octosyllabic and decasyllabic couplets, iambic, with inserted songs and ballad stanzas.
works.context: Published in the first season of peace travel to the continent, when Paris was crowded with English visitors and when the fate of the spoils of the public collections was a public controversy. Its politics address the restored monarchy, the Allied settlement and the commercial mood of Regency Britain. The pseudonymous Irish voice allowed the poet to satirise both English and French national vanities while his own Irish question remained implicit.
works.characters: The Fudge family; the pseudonymous Irish correspondent who reports the letters; French hosts, cicerones and officials; English tourists and speculators in Paris
works.structure: An epistolary comic sequence, loosely chronological over a single season, with additional letters supplied in later editions; the family letters are interspersed with lyric and with the correspondent's editorial comment.
works.attributionNotes: Issued under the same pseudonymous young Irish correspondent used for the earlier intercepted letter-poems; subsequent editions were enlarged by the same hand.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn

Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence

works.title: The Furys
works.form: Novel; proletarian novel, first issued in 1935
works.description: Hanley's Liverpool family chronicle: a mother, her sons and the return of the sailor. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by James Hanley; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle.
works.plot: Mrs Fury waits in Liverpool for her son Peter to return from the sea, while her other sons and daughters struggle with poverty, religion and the threat of the workhouse; the novel is a great chronicle of a working-class Catholic family in the Depression.
works.significance: The Furys is Hanley's Liverpool family chronicle and the finest of his novels: its portrait of the working-class Catholic family made it one of the great achievements of the thirties' proletarian novel.

works.context: Liverpool in the early 1930s, the Irish Catholic working class and the Depression. works.title: The Future of the American Negro
works.description: Published in 1899 and Washington's fullest statement of his social philosophy: a series of essays on the past, present and future of black Americans. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.

works.title: The Gamester
works.form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
works.description: A domestic tragedy of a gentleman undone by the gaming table, whose weakness is exploited by those about him until he destroys his family and himself. It was one of the most effective and most imitated of the century's moral tragedies and remained a stock piece of the repertory.
works.plot: Beverley, an honest man with a passion for play, is drawn on by a cheating companion and by the artifices of a serving man who wins his own ends by the ruin. His wife's remonstrances and the losses at the table drive him to despair, and he is led by a false report of her infidelity to a fatal act. The discovery of the cheat and of the innocent wife comes too late, and Beverley dies penitent on a bed of straw in the playhouse's most quoted scene of domestic ruin.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the eighteenth-century plays on the ruinous passions of the middle class and a central text of the sentimental theatre, its ending being a byword for the pathos of the domestic catastrophe.
works.meter: A grave and affective blank verse of the middle style, with the homely sentences of the domestic scenes and the long dying periods of the last act.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1753, in the season of the new statutes against gaming and of the vogue for moral domestic tragedy; the writer was a periodical essayist and editor of the same years.
works.characters: Beverley the gamester; his wife; the designing servant; the cheating friend at the table; the family and the creditors of the ruin
works.structure: Five-act regular domestic tragedy, the action contracted about the game and the house, with the villainy of the inferiors supplying the machinery of the fall; the catastrophe is a death-bed discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with a dedication that argues the moral design.

works.title: The Garden
works.description: Marvell's meditation on the pleasures of a garden and the withdrawal from worldly ambition and sensual love into contemplative solitude, culminating in the famous image of the mind as a sea that 'Annihilates all that's made / To a green thought in a green shade'.
works.plot: The poem rejects the vain pursuits of ambition and the grosser pleasures of love for the superior delight of the garden, then rises to a Platonic vision of the soul's meditation and the paradise of the solitary, innocent mind.
works.significance: A central poem of retirement and contemplation in English, admired for its wit, its green imagery, and its metaphysical meditation on the mind.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter quatrains with a serene, meditative wit and paradox.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, published in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it reflects the Neoplatonic and Epicurean ideal of retirement valued by Marvell and his contemporaries.
works.characters: the poet; the soul
works.structure: A nine-stanza lyric meditation moving from satire of worldly pursuits to celebration of the garden to visionary contemplation.

works.title: The Garden of Cyrus
altTitles: The Garden of Cyrus: Discourse on the Quincunx
works.description: The companion piece to Hydriotaphia, a learned and increasingly mystical discourse on the quincunx — the five-point arrangement — as it appears in the gardens of Cyrus, in nature, and in art, and as an emblem of cosmic order.
works.plot: Browne traces the quincunx from the Hanging Gardens of Cyrus through Roman military formations, botanical patterns, and the arrangement of the stars, arguing that the figure reveals a divine geometrical order in creation.
works.significance: A unique experiment in emblematic natural philosophy and one of the strangest and most beautiful works of English prose; it has been a touchstone for critics interested in the seventeenth-century imagination.
works.meter: Dense, incantatory prose; the concluding 'night-piece' is famous for its drowsy cadences.
works.context: Published in 1658 together with Hydriotaphia and dedicated to Nicholas Bacon.
works.structure: Five chapters of accumulating pattern and digression, ending in a nocturnal vision.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Garden of Florence; and Other Poems
altTitles: The Garden of Florence and Other Poems
works.form: Romantic narrative verse in the Italian manner of Hunt's circle, joined to a collection of lyrics and sonnets. The form of the title poem is that of the metrical tale, colloquial, unhurried and devoted to situation and feeling rather than to incident, and it deliberately avoids the machinery and declamation of the Byronic narrative; the shorter poems continue the same interest in tenderness, music and homely detail.
works.description: Reynolds's most serious collection of verse, and the book in which his Italian narrative manner, learned from Hunt and from Boccaccio, was given its fullest scope. Its title poem, which bibliographers and earlier commentators describe as a pair of tales in verse named collectively The Garden of Florence, develops the kind of Boccaccian story that Keats was treating at the same moment in Isabella, and it stands at the head of a volume that also carries shorter poems and sonnets. Contemporary accounts of Reynolds's work single out his command of the tender and musical lyric, and the volume as a whole is the best evidence that the Cockney interest in Italian story was a shared enterprise of the group rather than Keats's possession alone.
works.plot: Scholarly accounts of Reynolds's Italian verse identify the title poem as his version of the seventh tale of the fourth day of Boccaccio's Decameron, and the earlier memorials of Reynolds describe the chief poems of the collection as taken from Boccaccio. The tale as Reynolds retells it concerns an attachment that family and money forbid, the attempt to confine the woman who is loved, and her passage at last to Florence; the interest of the poem, in the manner the Cockney school had learnt from Boccaccio, is laid on feeling, tenderness and situation rather than on incident or moral judgement. The shorter poems that follow are occasional and lyrical, among them a piece on Devon which one modern account reports as Reynolds's most successful poem, and a sonnet which he had sent to Keats before printing it here.
works.significance: The Garden of Florence is the chief witness to Reynolds's attempt to make the Boccaccian tale a serious form within the Cockney school, and it is the standard evidence for the rivalry and partnership between his verse and Keats's. Its title poem and its shorter pieces show how widely the fashion for Italian story had spread by 1821, and its reception, and the survival of single lyrics from it in later anthologies, is part of the history of how that fashion was remembered and then discounted.
works.meter: The narrative is in regular rhymed English verse of the Hunt school, with an easy decasyllabic movement and a diction chosen for plainness and for closeness to speech; the shorter poems use simple lyric stanzas and the sonnet, and Reynolds is often praised for the purity of his musical effects. There is no attempt at the spikenard of the Lake school or at Byron's variety, and the effect of sameness and softness that reviewers noticed is a property of the metre as much as of the subject.
works.context: Published in 1821 by John Warren in London, the volume belongs to the last months of the London group around Hunt and to the years in which Keats's Isabella and Reynolds's own Italian tales were written in conscious emulation of one another; Reynolds alludes to Keats in its preface, and the friendship of the school days had by then become a matter of published record. The book also appears at the point when Hunt himself had left England for Italy, so that the Cockney school it represents was already dissolving.
works.characters: The lovers of the Florentine tale; the speakers of the shorter poems and sonnets
works.structure: A volume, not a single design: the long Florentine narrative occupies the first part of the book and a section of shorter poems follows it, with the title piece itself, according to the older biographical accounts, made up of two poems carried under one collective name. Within the narrative the structure is that of the plain tale in order, without frame or digression, while the minor pieces are discontinuous lyrics, sonnets and sketches whose organising principle is the sensibility of the writer rather than sequence.
works.attributionNotes: There is no doubt of Reynolds's authorship; the volume appeared in his own name and is catalogued among his works, and the only complication is that the title piece is described in the older biographical accounts as two poems published collectively under one name. No part of the book has been claimed for another writer, though the shared habits of Hunt's circle make it difficult to isolate what Reynolds owed to Keats and what Keats's contemporaries thought of as a common manner.

Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics

works.title: The Garden Party and Other Stories
works.description: Mansfield's finest collection: the garden party, the doll's house, the fly and the last stories of loss. It is a prose fiction work of 1922 by Katherine Mansfield; it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The title story sets a wealthy garden party against the death of a carter in the lane below; the collection also contains 'The Doll's House', 'The Fly', 'Her First Ball', 'At the Bay' and 'The Voyage' — stories of childhood, family, marriage and grief.
works.significance: The Garden Party is the summit of Mansfield's art and one of the finest short-story collections in English: 'At the Bay' and 'The Garden Party' changed the form, and the collection's exact surface with its hidden grief is the model for the modern story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the story without a plot: a moment of perception, a family scene, a shift of light.
works.context: The New Zealand of Mansfield's childhood and the England of the war and after, written while she was dying of tuberculosis. The record dates the work as composed between 1921 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: Laura Sheridan; the workmen; Kezia Burnell; the boss; the fly
works.structure: Fifteen stories, several set in the same New Zealand world. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Garden That I Love
works.description: The finest English garden book of the century: a poet's garden through the year. It is a prose work of 1894 by Alfred Austin; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: Austin records the garden he made at Swinford Old Manor in Kent: the roses, the lilies, the planning of the beds and the seasons of the year, in a series of essays that are at once practical, descriptive and personal.
works.significance: The Garden That I Love is among the finest English garden books of the century and the ancestor of the modern garden essay: its prose, its observation and its record of a year in a garden made it a classic of English nature writing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The text is the dated entry, continuous in its observation. The author's characteristic manner is the garden diary of the seasons.
works.context: Kent in the 1890s, and the English garden movement of the late nineteenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture; Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.characters: Austin as narrator; the gardener; the roses; the seasons
works.structure: A garden diary of essays following the year. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred Austin (Poet Laureate). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Garland of Laurel
works.form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
works.description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
works.plot: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
works.significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
works.meter: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
works.context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
works.characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
works.structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.

works.title: The Gates Ajar
works.description: Published in 1868 and the most popular American novel of consolation ever written: the diary of a young woman whose brother has been killed in the Civil War, and the vision of heaven that consoles her.
works.plot: Mary Cabot is left desolate by the death of her brother Roy at Antietam; her aunt Winifred arrives and describes a heaven that is a continuation of earthly life, with houses, families, work and the reunion of the beloved, and Mary moves from grief to a faith that answers the orthodox teaching of her minister.
works.significance: The Gates Ajar is the central American novel of mourning and the founding text of the consolatory literature of the post-war decade: it sold in the hundreds of thousands, was translated into many languages, and gave Victorian Americans a domestic heaven that answered the slaughter of the war.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is domestic detail extended into the afterlife.
works.context: The 1865-68: the American Civil War dead and the mourning of the nation, the New England ministry, and the spiritualist movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under sentimental and domestic novel.
works.characters: Mary Cabot (the diarist); Roy Cabot, her dead brother; Aunt Winifred Forceythe; Faith Forceythe; Deacon Quirk; Dr Bland
works.structure: A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Gay Lord Quex
works.description: First performed in 1899 and Pinero's most elegant comedy of manners: a reformed rake is tested by the manicurist who knows his past. It is a dramatic work of 1899 by Arthur Wing Pinero; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lord Quex, a reformed roué of fifty, is engaged to Muriel Eden, a young woman of strict principles; Sophy Fullgarney, his former mistress and now a fashionable manicurist, sets out to expose him, and the play ends with Sophy's generosity saving the marriage and Quex's real reformation confirmed.
works.significance: The Gay Lord Quex is Pinero's wittiest comedy of manners and one of the most accomplished English plays of the 1890s: its portrait of the reformed rake and the professional woman made it a success, and it is the play in which Pinero's craftsmanship and his social observation are most perfectly united.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion.
works.context: 1899: the fashion for the manicure and the beauty parlour, the Victorian double standard, and the West End theatre of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed in 1899 and first published in 1899 and first performed in 1899 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Lord Quex; Muriel Eden; Sophy Fullgarney; Sir Chichester Frayne; Mrs Eden; Jack Eden; the Duchess of Strood
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Pinero. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Gebir; a Spanish Romance, Poetical, in Four Books
works.form: Romance in verse: an English Spenserian romance that revives allegorical machinery, enchanted guardians and genealogical prophecy from The Faerie Queene while treating the matter as symbolic rather than narrative.
works.description: The author's first published poem, a four-book romance in Spenserian stanzas drawn from a supposed Moorish-Spanish source about an infant heir of Spain. The story mixes dynastic exile, enchanted river-gods, and a quest for water that turns out to be a quest for the poet's own blood. It is at once a late-romantic allegory and a deliberate archaism, and it established the dense, allusive manner kept for the rest of its author's career.
works.plot: Gebir, infant son of the murdered King Alphonso of Spain, is saved from his uncle's slaughter by being laid in a brazen cradle upon the waters and nursed in secret among goatherds. Grown unknown to himself, he loves his sister Gwendolin without knowing her kinship, and marches to war against the giant Dan and the Sorayzan host. A drought afflicts his army, and Gebir descends through caves of the earth to seek water from the river-gods of the Guadalete and the Genal. There he must pass the guard of the serpent Tondalu and is shown, in visionary genealogies of Spain, his own destiny. He learns that the promised stream can flow only from his own wounded heart; he slays Tondalu, is himself destroyed in the effort of the victory, and his life-giving water rises to relieve the host.
works.significance: A landmark of the romancing reaction of the 1790s, and one of the earliest English poems to treat dynastic exile and thirst as a private mythology; Swinburne and later Pre-Raphaelite readers made it the keystone of its author's reputation as a poet rather than as a prose stylist.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine; archaic diction and inverted syntax throughout.
works.context: Written in the first flush of the 1790s romancing reaction and published as its author left Oxford; its withdrawn first issue made it a bibliographical rarity for a generation, and its Jacobean archaism answers the decade's taste for romance and for Spenserian revival.
works.characters: Gebir; Gwendolin; Alphonso; Dan; Tondalu; the river-spirits Guadalete and Genal
works.structure: Continuous four-book narrative romance in Spenserian stanzas, with prophetic visions and set-piece descents interrupting the linear plot; the middle books form a katabasis framed by the two outer war narratives.
works.attributionNotes: Published without the author's name; Its author acknowledged it in later life, and the 1798 date rests on bibliographical evidence rather than a dated title page.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The supernatural ballad and willed belief

works.title: The General

works.title: The Genius of Oblivion and Other Original Poems
works.form: Lyric and meditative collection; personification poem, elegy and occasional verse in the sentimental manner
works.description: A volume of occasional and meditative verse by a widowed mother of five children, published with the help of her late husband's lodge and the author's first book. Its longest poem personifies oblivion as the power that veils the past and finally releases the mourner. The book marks the beginning of the most influential editorial career in American letters.
works.plot: The title poem addresses oblivion as the gentle power that draws a veil over the sorrows and the errors of the past, and asks whether remembrance is a blessing or a burden. Shorter pieces treat death, bereavement, the seasons, the duties of the survivor and the prospects of the republic. Several poems take public occasions and national subjects, and others are elegies on private losses. The volume's movement is from grief toward resignation and then toward useful labour.
works.significance: It is the first monument of a woman of letters who would dictate the taste of American households for half a century. Its treatment of oblivion and remembrance shows the psychology of sentimental verse turned to the service of bereavement. It documents the patronage economy by which women's books were first financed.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter stanzas and heroic couplets, with hymn-like shorter metres
works.context: Published in 1823 after the death of the author's husband left her without means, and supported by subscription and lodge patronage. Its appearance belongs to the first great decade of women's periodical and gift-book writing in America. Its national poems answer the post-1815 demand for a republican verse.
works.structure: Collected volume with one dominant personification poem and a company of shorter occasional pieces; no imposed sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; the authorship was established by her own later account and by the subscription records of the first edition.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Genius of Universal Emancipation
altTitles: The Genius of Universal Emancipation and Colonization Journal
works.form: Reform periodical in the abolitionist mould: the essay-editorial combined with printed testimony, statistical extract and reprint, in a small weekly or monthly sheet.
works.description: An abolitionist monthly, and later weekly, journal begun in 1821 and continued for nearly two decades, the first periodical in the United States devoted entirely to emancipation. Its editor was a Quaker journeying agent who made the paper a clearing-house for facts about slavery: testimony, legislative reports, prices of slaves, extracts from British abolition writing and verse on the subject. Its editorial line combined immediate emancipation with a colonisation scheme, which gave it a double character and made it the school of the movement's later leaders.
works.plot: The journal's persistent argument is that American slavery must end at once and that the slaveholder's claim of property in human beings is void. Its numbers accumulate evidence rather than build a single thesis: accounts of the internal slave trade, sketches of enslaved people's condition, memorials of cruelty, arguments for the moral and economic superiority of free labour, and reports of manumission abroad. Editorially it urged the formation of state societies, the education of the free Black population and a gradual, compensated, colonisation-based plan for emancipation; it later opposed the Texas annexation war as a slaveholding project.
works.significance: It is the founding organ of the American abolitionist press before immediatism, and the best record of how the movement learned to use periodical form as evidence-gathering. Its files preserve a large body of otherwise lost verse and pamphlet matter, and its editor's practice of travelling to collect testimony set the pattern for the movement's literature.
works.meter: Plain earnest prose, with frequent quoted evidence; the journal also printed much occasional abolitionist verse in conventional stanzas.
works.context: Begun in the decade of Missouri statehood controversy, when the American Colonization Society had just been founded and when the British abolition movement supplied American reformers with models of organised publicity. The paper gave the young editor of a later and more famous abolition weekly his first apprenticeship, and its survival into the 1830s documents the transition from gradualist to immediatist argument.
works.structure: Serial monthly and later weekly: editorial essay, documentary extracts, testimony, correspondence and verse, with annual indexes; individual numbers are compilations rather than designs.
works.attributionNotes: Editorial responsibility rests with its founder, an editor who wrote most of its leading matter; the journal's extracts and reprints are of course by other hands.

works.title: The Gentle Craft
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the shoemakers' craft: the legendary origins of the 'gentle craft' in the saints and heroes who took up shoemaking — St Hugh, St Crispin and Crispianus, Sir Simon Eyre the shoemaker Lord Mayor, and the apprentice who married a king's daughter — the book that gave Dekker his Shoemaker's Holiday and the trade its mythology.

works.significance: The classic of the craft romance — the book that made the shoemaker's bench a seat of English legend.
works.meter: Prose of Deloney's popular register, with songs and the frame's festive setting.
works.context: Published about 1597–98; its Eyre story supplied the plot of Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), and its craft-patriotism answered the decade's civic pride.

works.title: The Giaour
altTitles: The Giaour: A Fragment of a Turkish Tale
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the oriental or gothic tale poem, with the interpolated popular song and the supernatural credulity of the ballad tradition.
works.description: The first and shortest of the oriental tale poems, subtitled 'a Fragment of a Turkish Tale' and set in Greece under Turkish rule. A Christian lover has seduced and abandoned the daughter of a Turkish lord, who drowns her in the sea; the lover lives in a monastery under a curse and in terror of the dead woman's coming judgment, and is finally killed by her father in a mountain encounter. The poem establishes the outlaw, the haunted guilty self and the eastern landscape as a theatre of conscience. Its manner is not narrative continuity but a sequence of vivid fragments, songs and interpolated voices.
works.plot: The story is given in pieces and by shifting narrators: an opening description of the evening sea, the drowned girl's funeral and the mourning songs, the father's quest for revenge, and then the long encounter at the hermit's cell in which the outlaw tells his own history of seduction, desertion and the beloved's death. The Turkish lord slays him, and he dies unreconciled under the monk's curse, while the villagers declare that the vampire of the drowned girl haunts the shore. The argument is less a tale than a study of guilt without repentance, of a will that refuses the church's remedy, and of revenge as the only honour left to an eastern lord. The interpolated songs, on the happiness of the fisherman's life and on the roses and nightingales of the east, offer a lyric counterworld to the tragedy.
works.significance: It set the pattern of the verse tale, guilty hero, eastern scene and fragmented narration, that the sequel tales and the whole school of popular romance in verse imitated. It also gave the century its first great study of a conscience that refuses forgiveness, and its vampire and superstition passages fed the gothic imagination of the following decades.
works.meter: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, broken by interpolated songs and lyric stanzas of popular measure, with anapestic variation in the passages of supernatural terror.
works.context: Written and published within two months of the poet's separation from his wife and the public scandal that followed his departure from England, the tale converted the materials of the recent tour into a drama of unpardonable sin. The Greek cause, the Albanian court of a local pasha and the current taste for eastern scenery supplied both its subject and its market, and its success fixed the couplet-tale as the form of popular poetry for a decade. Its treatment of seduction and its hostile portraits of monastic remedy drew moral criticism from the quarterly press.
works.characters: the Giaour; the Turkish lord, father of the drowned girl; the drowned girl; the hermit of the cell; the fisherman and the Greek villagers
works.structure: A deliberately fragmentary sequence of set pieces, told now by a fisherman, now by a monk, now by the Giaour himself, with ballad songs and a concluding apostrophe on the superstitious credulity of the Greek villagers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was revised and enlarged across several issues in the author's lifetime, and the suppressed lines concerning the heroine's fate are recorded in the variorum.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine

The supernatural ballad and willed belief

works.title: The Gifts of Men
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
works.plot: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
works.significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
works.structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays
altTitles: Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays
works.description: Published in 1868 and the book that named the modern young woman: a collection of satirical essays on the fashionable girl, marriage, dress and the woman question. It is a prose work of 1868 by Eliza Lynn Linton; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: The title essay attacks the 'Girl of the Period' — the young woman who paints her face, dresses in the latest fashion, speaks slang and thinks of nothing but pleasure and money — as a false and degraded modern type; the other essays consider the fashionable marriage, the education of girls, the woman of business and the 'shrieking sisterhood' of the feminists.
works.significance: 'The Girl of the Period' was the most discussed magazine essay of the 1860s and it set the terms of the Victorian debate over the modern woman: Linton's attack made the 'Girl of the Period' a national figure and provoked a decade of argument about fashion, work and female independence.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical periodical essay with a strong persona.
works.context: 1865-68: the London periodical press of the 1860s, the controversy over women's dress and employment, and the rise of the woman's movement after the 1867 Reform Act. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.title: The God in the Car
works.description: Published in 1894 and Hope's most serious novel: a financial adventurer builds an African empire and loses the woman he loves. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Anthony Hope; it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Willie Ruston, a ruthless young empire-builder, floats the Omofaga Company to open a great African territory and draws a whole London circle, the cynical Lord Semingham among them, into its toils; Maggie Dennison, the clever, restless wife of the devoted Harry Dennison, is fascinated by his force, and the novel follows the duel between the woman and 'the thing', the enterprise to which Ruston will sacrifice anyone, herself included.
works.significance: The God in the Car is the finest English novel of imperial finance: its portrait of the empire-builder and its analysis of the relation between money, press and politics made it the most serious of Hope's books, and it is a key text of the English literature of the scramble for Africa.

works.description: Written in Tothill Fields prison in 1848-49 and published in 1849: a Chartist romance of the fourteenth and the nineteenth centuries, in which a medieval gold harp passes into the hands of the modern workers.

works.significance: The Gold Harp is the most important Chartist novel and a key text in the history of English working-class fiction: it is the only full-length novel written in prison by a Chartist leader and one of the first to attempt a revolutionary historical narrative.

works.title: The Golden Age
works.description: Published in 1895 and the finest English prose of the aesthetic 1890s on childhood: eight episodes narrated by children who have outgrown the nursery and watch the grown-ups with ironic distance. works.significance: The Golden Age is the central English book of the 1890s on childhood and a key influence on the children's literature of the next century; its ironic children and its nostalgic narrator invented the tone of the modern memoir of childhood.

works.description: The first novel: the Shropshire hills, the fair and the golden arrow. It is a prose fiction work of 1916 by Mary Webb; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The Golden Arrow sets the lovers of the Shropshire hills against the chapel, the fair and the omen of the golden arrow, in the charged prose of the nature romance that made the county a world.
works.significance: The Golden Arrow is Mary Webb's first novel and the founding text of her Shropshire nature romance: its hills, its chapel and its omen made the county a world and announced the prose of Precious Bane.

works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1904 and the last and most difficult of James's novels: the marriage of an American heiress to an Italian prince, and the affair that threatens it. works.plot: Maggie Verver, the daughter of a rich American collector, marries Prince Amerigo, whose former mistress Charlotte Stant then marries Maggie's father; the two resume their affair, and Maggie, by a campaign of silence and generosity, recovers her husband and manipulates the couple back to Europe.
works.significance: The Golden Bowl is the most formally daring of James's novels and the culmination of his late style: its treatment of marriage, adultery and the exercise of power through generosity is one of the great achievements of the modern novel, and it has become central to the criticism of James's ethics.

works.title: The Golden Legend
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
works.plot: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
works.significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar
works.structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.

works.title: The Golden Violet
altTitles: The Golden Violet, with its Tales of Romance and Chivalry, and Other Poems
works.form: Collected volume of metrical romances and lyrics; the governing genres are the short metrical tale of chivalry and the meditative love lyric.
works.description: A volume of short verse romances and lyrics gathered under a title emblem, with tales of chivalry and of the household forming its narrative section. It marks its author's fullest exploitation of the romance material - troubadours, captive nuns, devoted brides - that her readers expected from her.
works.plot: The tales dramatise women placed under a vow, a desertion or an unequal marriage, and resolve them in renunciation rather than in reward. Chivalric settings supply the external order - hall, tournament and cloister - against which feeling is measured. Shorter poems on love, memory and the poet's lot repeat the same situations without narrative. The volume's movement is from impersonal romance to personal address, so that the earlier tales read retrospectively as autobiography. No single argument is advanced; the book works by accumulation of a recognisable set of cases.
works.significance: The volume shows how thoroughly romance had been domesticated for the woman poet's public by the later 1820s, chivalric matter converted into a grammar of feminine feeling. It supplied later annual writers with a set of transferable scenes. Its modern interest lies in the way it makes genre inheritance the model of a women's literary tradition.
works.meter: The tales use stanzic iambic measures with ballad-like refrains and a marked tendency to triple time; the lyrics are in common and short measure, with compressed sonnet-like pieces at intervals.
works.context: It appeared in a year of change in its author's professional arrangements, when her periodical and review work was being attacked in the press, and the volume's retreat into chivalry is partly an occupational move. The annuals were by then the main market for such verse, and several pieces were made for gift-book contexts. Success in the United States, where the book was rapidly reprinted, was by now a substantial part of her income.
works.structure: Two orders of composition: verse tales in romance settings, then a company of shorter lyrics; the sequence runs from the impersonal to the confessional, which is the volume's characteristic shape in place of a plot.

works.title: The Gondoliers; or, The King of Barataria

works.description: First performed in 1889 and the last of the great Savoy operas: two Venetian gondoliers discover that one of them is the king of a foreign country. It is a dramatic work of 1889 by W. S. Gilbert; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Marco and Giuseppe Palmieri, gondoliers of Venice, learn that one of them is the kidnapped heir of Barataria and that both are married to the same woman; the arrival of the Grand Inquisitor and the discovery that the real king is the drummer boy Luiz resolves the plot, and the opera ends with the republican principles of the gondoliers restored.
works.significance: The Gondoliers is the last of the great Gilbert and Sullivan collaborations and their most politically radical opera: its argument for republican equality and its satire of the divine right of kings made it a landmark, and it is generally considered the most musically accomplished of the Savoy operas.
works.meter: Dramatic text. works.title: The Good Soldier: A Tale of Passion
works.description: The most perfect English novel of the period: a study of deception told by a narrator who is himself deceived. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: John Dowell, a wealthy American, recounts the nine years he and his wife Florence spent at Nauheim with their friends Edward and Leonora Ashburnham — the 'good soldier' of the title — and slowly reveals the adulteries, the lies and the cruelties beneath the surface, including his own blindness and Florence's suicide.
works.significance: The Good Soldier is the most perfect English novel of the period and the great novel of unreliable narration: its broken chronology, its narrator's self-deception and its famous opening — 'this is the saddest story I have ever heard' — made it the model for the modern novel of deception.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.

works.title: The Good-Natur'd Man
works.form: Comedy in five acts, in dialogue prose with sententious and tender passages, written for the London stage in the reforming 1760s and prefaced in print by epistle and dramatis personae.
works.description: Oliver Goldsmith's first produced comedy, and the play with which he entered the quarrel about sentimental comedy: an essay in the 'laughing comedy' of which he became the theorist, in which goodness of disposition, not wit or contrivance, is made the subject and the instrument of the plot. Its unhappy first run gave it a place in theatrical history larger than its later performance on the stage would suggest.
works.plot: The comedy is built on a generous young man whose very openness of temper makes him the prey of everyone with a claim upon him, and on the confusions his readiness to oblige produces in his own affairs of the heart. He is in love with a lady under the control of an interested guardian, and the artful about him exploit his good nature in order to advance their own designs, so that the action consists less of a scheme than of a series of impositions. Against these the play sets the worth of uncalculated kindness, and its resolution restores the lovers and exposes the designs. The moral interest is deliberately affective rather than satirical: the audience is asked to laugh with good humour and to approve benevolence, and the antipathy of the malicious and the calculating is what the comedy finally defeats.
works.significance: It is the first of the two plays in which Goldsmith tried to restore mirth and national character to the English stage against the fashion for distress, and its failure and its defence shaped the subsequent history of the sentimental-comedy quarrel. It supplies the practical counterpart to his theoretical case for laughing comedy.
works.context: It belongs to the theatrical controversy of the 1760s between the laughing comedy of manners and feeing and the sentimental comedy of distress, a debate Goldsmith had already entered as a critic and was to state formally in his essay on the theatre, which argued for laughing against sentimental comedy. It was produced in the season when the managers were remaking the repertoire and when the 'sentimental' piece was at its height.
works.characters: The good-natur'd young lover at its centre; the lady he loves and the guardian who controls her; the artful claimants upon his generosity; his friends and dependants
works.structure: A five-act comedy of character and imposition, with a double amatory plot and a succession of deceptions worked upon the protagonist's generosity, resolved by exposure and restitution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's and its production is documented. The dating of the surviving manuscript and the extent of the revisions made after the first run are matters of editorial detail, not of authorship.

works.title: The Goodness of St Rocque and Other Stories
altTitles: Goodness of St Rocque and Other Stories
works.description: Published in 1899 and the first collection of short stories by an African-American woman: Creole New Orleans, the colour line and the lives of women. works.plot: The stories present the Creole and Catholic world of New Orleans: Manuela's appeal to St Rocque to win back Theophile from her rival Claire, the young novice of 'Sister Josepha' who stays in her convent rather than face the world outside, the old musician of 'M'sieu Fortier's Violin', the wronged wife of 'Tony's Wife'; the colour line is left almost wholly unspoken.
works.significance: The Goodness of St Rocque is the first book of short stories by an African-American woman and the finest literary treatment of the Creole colour hierarchy: its analysis of intraracial colour prejudice made it a unique text in the period, and it is a founding document of African-American women's fiction.

works.title: The Governess; or, Little Female Academy
works.form: children's fiction; framed school story with embedded tales
works.description: A story of a boarding school for girls, in which a wise governess governs by letting her pupils tell and judge one another's tales. It is the first English book written deliberately for the entertainment and instruction of girls of that age, and a foundation text of the children's novel.
works.plot: Ten or eleven girls arrive at the academy, each with her own fault of temper, vanity or falsehood, and the governess discovers their characters by observation rather than by rule. The girls are set to tell stories of their own invention - tales of lovers, of servants and of the adventures of the world - and to pass judgement on one another's conduct. The book closes with the reformation of the stubborn and the reward of the modest, the governess's method having turned amusement into moral discipline.
works.significance: It invented the English school story for girls and is a landmark in the history of a literature designed for female childhood, influencing the didactic fiction of the following century.
works.meter: Simple conversational prose suited to young readers, with the inset tales adopting the diction of the popular romance they parody.
works.context: Published in 1749, in the season of new attention to the education of girls and of the didactic tales of the day, and written by an author already associated with conduct-oriented fiction and school teaching.
works.characters: the governess of the academy and her pupils, each standing for a fault or a virtue of temper
works.structure: A framed collection: a continuous school narrative enclosing tales told by the pupils, the frame supplying the judgement and the tales the example; the sequence is orderly and episodic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and with a preface addressed to the parents of the pupils.

works.title: The Grandissimes: A Story of Creole Life
altTitles: Grandissimes: A Story of Creole Life
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1880 and the first great American novel of New Orleans: the feud of two Creole families in the years after the Louisiana Purchase. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by George Washington Cable; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Honoré Grandissime, a young Creole, returns to New Orleans in 1803 and is drawn into the feud between his family and the Fusiliers; he loves Aurora Nancanou, whose family his has ruined, and his half-brother, the free man of colour also called Honoré Grandissime, becomes the novel's moral centre, in a story that ends with renunciation and a divided inheritance.
works.significance: The Grandissimes is the first great American novel of the deep South and the most important American novel about race before Twain: its treatment of the free man of colour, its portrait of a society built on racial hierarchy and its refusal of a sentimental resolution make it a central text of the American literature of race.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. works.title: The Grapes of Wrath
works.form: Novel; proletarian novel, first issued in 1939
works.description: The central American novel of the Depression: the Joads, the road and the promised California. It is a prose fiction work of 1939 by John Steinbeck; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Joad family are driven from their Oklahoma farm by the dust bowl and the banks; they travel Route 66 to California with the migrant poor, endure the hostility of the growers and the death of the grandparents, and end with Tom's vow to be wherever there is injustice.
works.significance: The Grapes of Wrath is the central American novel of the Depression and Steinbeck's masterpiece: it won the Pulitzer Prize, it changed the American debate over poverty, and its intercalary chapters and biblical prose made it the great American social novel of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail of the migrant road.
works.context: The dust bowl and the migrant road from Oklahoma to California in the 1930s, and the labour camps of the period. works.title: The Grave
works.form: Meditative blank-verse poem in the continuation of the 'Night Thoughts' tradition of the 1740s; descriptive and declamatory passages alternate with direct address and apostrophe; passages were afterward used as hymns and as anthology pieces.
works.description: Robert Blair's meditation on death, buried bodies and the resurrection, the poem that gave the graveyard school its name and its characteristic atmosphere. It is written in a heavy, sonorous blank verse and moves through the churchyard, the coffin, the worm and the general dissolution, turning the contemplation of putrefaction into an argument for immortality. It is also a work of the devotional edge of the Augustan age: Blair was a friend and fellow-minister of the evangelical circle around Ralph Cudworth the younger, and the poem's religious weight is not merely decorative.
works.plot: There is no story, only the sustained exercise of a single thought. The speaker first dwells on the physical facts of burial and decay with a candour that the age found almost indecent, and describes the churchyard at night as the place where these facts are most visibly assembled. From the darkness of the grave the poem argues upward: the same dissolution which appals the unbelief of the worldling is for the believer the avenue to a resurrection, and the dead body becomes a 'seed' committed to the ground. The meditations on the last judgment, on the sleep of the dead and on the triumph of the living over the grave are the poem's true conclusion, and they justify its terrible preliminary imagery. Its characteristic mixture of horror and hope is what later readers of the 1740s and 1790s recognised as a new seriousness in English verse.
works.significance: It is the founding text of what later historians have called the Graveyard School, and its title gave the group its name. Its blend of physical realism about death with evangelical hope marks the transition from Augustan meditation to the preromantic taste for terror, and it shaped the devotional and funereal vocabulary of Gray, of Blair's Irish and Scottish successors and of the Gothic romance of the following generation.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of great weight and latinity, with long suspended syntax, repeated keywords and a deliberate harshness of sound which contemporaries admired as sublimity and others censured as inflation.
works.context: It belongs to the religious current running under Augustan neoclassicism: the evangelical revival of the 1730s and 1740s, Blair's friendship with the ministers of the London 'British' Presbyterian meeting, and the vogue for poems upon the last things which produced Parnell's and Young's meditations and Gray's early essays in terror. It was published in the decade of the 'graveyard' imagination and soon associated with an engraving design by William Hogarth.
works.structure: A continuous meditative argument in a single voice, loosely articulated in sections following the progress of thought from the churchyard and the coffin to the resurrection and the last day; no dramatis personae and no narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested: published anonymously or initialed at first and afterward with Blair's name, and edited with a memoir by William Mason in the mid-century editions, which fixed the text and the biography. The years of composition are uncertain and are not asserted.

works.title: The Grave (Hugh Blair)
works.form: published sermon and graveyard meditation, in the solemn descriptive manner of the mid-century
works.description: The sermon on death and the grave that made Blair's reputation while he was still a young minister in Carrick, and one of the most quoted pieces of Scottish pulpit prose of the mid-century. Preached at Colmonell and published at Edinburgh in 1743, it meditates on the burial place, the bodies of the dead and the terrors and consolations of the last hour, and passes from the spectacle of the grave to the hope of the resurrection. It belongs with the graveyard verse of the same decades as an expression of the new taste for solemn meditation.
works.plot: Blair leads his auditors to the graveyard and holds before them the equality of the dead, the silence of the tomb and the uncertainty of the hour of death, pressing each hearer to imagine himself laid there. He then turns the meditation upon the resurrection and the judgment, so that the terrors of the grave are answered by a reasoned hope. The argument moves by description and appeal rather than by doctrine, and its aim is the reformation of present conduct through the continual thought of death.
works.significance: It is the classical prose statement of the graveyard meditation and helped to fix the rhetoric of solemnity in Scottish preaching for a generation. It also supplies the link between sermon and poem in the preromantic interest in death, and its reputation was long maintained by its place in collections of elocution.
works.meter: Prose; deliberately sonorous and cadenced, with the balanced period, the pause and the climax of the elocutionary school that Blair later theorised.
works.context: Preached and issued in the tradition of graveyard meditation opened by Parnell's night piece and by Edward Young's Night Thoughts, and some years before Robert Blair's poem of the same name; it belongs to the religious atmosphere of the Scottish west before the Moderate ascendancy, and its success marked the arrival of a new taste for the awful and the pathetic in Scottish discourse.
works.structure: A single preached discourse moving from the meditation on the grave and the dead, through the contemplation of mortality and judgment, to the consolation of the resurrection and the practical application.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the sermon's publication at Edinburgh in 1743 is given in the usual bibliographical reckoning, and the later enlarged editions are Blair's own revision.

works.title: The Great Bible
works.description: The first authorized English Bible, a revision of Matthew's Bible (itself based on Tyndale and Coverdale) carried out by Miles Coverdale and printed in Paris and London in 1539 under Thomas Cromwell's patronage; the Bible ordered to be set up in every parish church.
works.plot: A complete Bible in large folio format, with the title page by Hans Holbein showing Henry VIII handing the Word to Cranmer and Cromwell; the text revises the Matthew Bible's Old Testament against the Hebrew and Latin, and its 1540 second edition carried Cranmer's preface, giving the book its later name.
works.significance: The Bible that made the English Bible a public institution: chained in the churches, read aloud to the people, it established the vernacular scriptures at the centre of English religious life and supplied the psalter of the Prayer Book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Commissioned by Cromwell and begun in Paris (the French printing was seized by the Inquisition, and the presses moved to London), the Great Bible of 1539 was ordered by the injunctions of 1538 to be placed in every parish church; its psalter entered the Prayer Book tradition, and it remained the standard English Bible until the Bishops' Bible of 1568.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, summaries, and the famous illustrated title page.
works.attributionNotes: The revision is Coverdale's, on the basis of the Matthew Bible (edited by John Rogers from Tyndale and Coverdale); the record attributes the work to Coverdale as revising editor, following standard usage.

works.title: The Great Gatsby
works.form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1925
works.description: The most nearly perfect American novel: Jay Gatsby's dream, Daisy Buchanan and the green light at the end of the dock. It is a prose fiction work of 1925 by F. Scott Fitzgerald; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest, rents a house on Long Island next to the mysterious Jay Gatsby, who gives lavish parties in the hope of attracting Daisy Buchanan, the married woman he loved before the war. The affair, the confrontation in the Plaza Hotel and the death of Myrtle Wilson end in Gatsby's murder and Nick's disillusioned return west.
works.significance: The Great Gatsby is the most nearly perfect American novel and the definitive book of the 1920s: its lyric prose, its structure and its meditation on the American dream made it the great American novel of the century, and its last page is among the most famous in American literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the romantic lyric sentence held in tight structure.
works.context: Long Island and New York in the summer of 1922, the jazz age, Prohibition, the old money of the Buchanans and the new money of the bootlegger.
