works.title: The Great God Pan
works.form: Novella; ghost story, first issued in 1894
works.description: The most influential English horror story of the 1890s: an experiment on the brain that opens the way to the pagan god. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Arthur Machen; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Dr Raymond's experiment on a young woman opens her mind to the god Pan and destroys her; years later her daughter Helen Vaughan spreads corruption and death through London society until she is hunted down and destroyed by her father's friends.
works.significance: The Great God Pan is the most influential English horror story of the 1890s: its theme of the pagan survival and its suggestion of unspeakable horror made it the model for the modern weird tale, and Lovecraft and Stephen King both acknowledge it.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the tale built on an ancient survival beneath the modern town.
works.context: The decadent London of the 1890s, the new psychical research, and the pagan revival of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Dr Raymond; Helen Vaughan; Villiers; Austin; Clarke
works.structure: A novella in eight sections, told through documents and testimony. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The Great Hunger
works.form: Long poem (the clay and the celibate farmer)
works.description: The long poem of the clay, the potato and the celibate farmer of Monaghan. It is a verse work of 1942 by Patrick Kavanagh; it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Great Hunger follows Patrick Maguire, the celibate farmer of the Monaghan clay, through the farming year, the potato and the hunger of the body and of the soul, in the long poem that answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the parish.
works.significance: The Great Hunger is the greatest Irish poem of the twentieth century before the war's end: its Maguire, its clay and its celibacy made the parish the matter of the long poem and answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the field.
works.meter: Verse. works.title: The Grey Coast
works.description: The first novel of the Scottish Renaissance's northern coast. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by Neil Gunn; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle.

works.significance: The Grey Coast is the founding novel of Gunn's north and one of the first novels of the Scottish Renaissance: its coast, its village and its quarrel made the Gaelic north a world of the modern Scottish novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain.
works.context: Caithness and the north of Scotland in the years of the Scottish Renaissance. works.title: The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry
works.description: Dennis's systematic companion to the treatise of 1701, which sets out the foundations of a critical art: poetry is an imitative and designing craft whose ends are to instruct and delight, whose means are the passions, and whose highest achievements depend upon enthusiasm, both ordinary and poetical. The argument grounds the rules in nature and in the reason of things, and then argues from the same premises that the religion of a modern nation is a necessary foundation of its poetry. It is the most rigorous of Dennis's attempts to hold neoclassical rule and Augustan sublimity in one system.
works.plot: Dennis first disposes of the sceptical objection that criticism is a vain art, insisting that as surely as the rules of music produce harmony the rules of poetry, learned from nature and from the ancients, produce pleasure; he then distinguishes the passions that a poet must know from the craft that copies them, and derives from this the doctrine that great poetry requires an enthusiastick elevation which no mere rule-making can supply. He next argues that a religion of terrors and of grandeur such as Christianity provides gives the modern poet materials the pagan epics never possessed, while the machinery of a revealed faith is at once more awful and more instructive than the personifications of the heathens. Finally he tests the moderns against the ancients in the several genres, and finds that the critic's office is to reconcile the love of the ancients with the claims of a more knowing age.
works.significance: It is the chief English link between Renaissance poetics of the rules and the eighteenth-century psychology of enthusiasm, the sublime and genius, and much of what Addison, Hughes, the Blairs and the French theorists said on those subjects was worked out first in these pages.
works.meter: Prose, in the emphatical and heavily coordinated style Dennis associated with grandeur, with long periods, balanced clauses and repeated key terms.
works.context: Published in the last years of the reign of Queen Anne's precedent period of the Whig war and the expedition to the continent, when Dennis, an ardent Williamite, was writing against the Tory revival in letters; it was reprinted after his death, in the age of the Scottish enquiry into taste, because it was one of the few native treatises on enthusiasm available to eighteenth-century readers.
works.structure: A treatise advancing in numbered sections and argumentative heads from first principles to the doctrine of enthusiasm, then to religion as the foundation of modern poetry, then to an evaluation of the modern genres, with a closing defence of the critical enterprise itself.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art

works.title: The Growth of Love
works.description: Published in 1876 and Bridges's first major work: a sonnet sequence on the growth of love in the mind of a young man. It is a verse work of 1876 by Robert Bridges; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: The sequence traces the awakening and the deepening of love in a young man's consciousness, through doubt, absence and the fear of loss, to a settled and mature devotion in which the beloved is seen as the visible form of a universal beauty.
works.significance: The Growth of Love is one of the finest English sonnet sequences after Meredith and Rossetti: its restraint and its Platonic seriousness made it a critical favourite, and it established Bridges as the most technically accomplished of the younger Victorian poets.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The author's characteristic manner is exquisite metrical control in received forms.

works.title: The Guardian Papers
works.description: Steele's thrice-weekly paper of 1713, conducted in the guardian mask and chiefly against the deism of Anthony Collins, the free-thinkers, the pretenders and the married men's project; the most openly party-political of the essay papers and the occasion of the Addison-Steele breach.
works.plot: The guardian reports the transactions of his ward, the public, attacks the trick of ridicule against religion, stages the Married Men's claim to be governed by their wives, and defends the Christian foundation of moral obligation.
works.significance: It documents the moment at which the periodical essay became an instrument of party and of religious polemic, and its controversy with the anti-theatrical and deist press shaped the later eighteenth-century debate on ridicule and morality.
works.meter: Colloquial, urgent argumentative prose with the interrupted sentence and the indignant apostrophe, less periodic than Addison's.
works.context: Published in the months of the Asylum Bill and the fall of the Harley ministry, when Steele turned from the moderate essay to high-church and Whig polemic; the paper's attack on the Married Men drew the rebuttals of the female writers of the period.

works.structure: Serial papers alternating party argument, fictional letter and project, character writing and the dialogue between the guardian and his correspondents.

works.title: The Half Sisters

works.description: The founding novel of the woman's vocation: two sisters and the choice between marriage and work. It is a prose fiction work of 1848 by Geraldine Jewsbury; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.

works.meter: Prose. works.title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
works.description: Published in 1888 and the first of Wilde's two collections of fairy tales: 'The Happy Prince', 'The Nightingale and the Rose', 'The Selfish Giant', 'The Devoted Friend' and 'The Remarkable Rocket'. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Oscar Wilde; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.significance: The Happy Prince is the finest English literary fairy tale of the century and one of the first children's books to make social justice its subject; its fusion of aesthetic beauty and Christian compassion is unique in the period.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: The Harley Lyrics
works.description: A collection of some forty secular and religious lyrics preserved in the Ludlow scribe's anthology, BL Harley MS 2253 (c. 1340), the richest single manuscript of early Middle English lyric: love songs, laments, satires, and devotional poems in French, Latin, and English, including such masterpieces as 'Alysoun', 'Wynter wakeneth al my care', and 'Blow, northerne wynd'.
works.plot: The poems range across the lyric repertoire: the lover's springtime longing and complaint, the satire of corrupt clergy and unjust lords, the meditation on death and the Passion, and the praise of the Virgin.
works.significance: The indispensable witness to the early Middle English lyric tradition at its best, and the principal source of the poems that bridge early and Ricardian poetry.
works.meter: A remarkable variety: tail-rhyme stanzas, alliterative long lines, and French-derived stanza forms, often with refrains.
works.context: Copied c. 1340 by a professional scribe working near Ludlow, Herefordshire, for a gentry household, from materials of the later thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
works.characters: the lovers and speakers of the lyrics
works.structure: An anthology, not a sequence: the manuscript's trilingual arrangement (with English poems often paired with their French and Latin analogues) supplies the order.

works.title: The Hasty-Pudding
altTitles: The Hasty-Pudding: A Poem, in Three Cantos
works.form: Mock-heroic and verse satire in three cantos: a burlesque didactic poem on cookery and national diet built on the machinery of the epic invocation, the origin myth and the art-poem of precepts
works.description: Barlow's mock-heroic poem on a New England dish, three cantos of couplets written in exile at Chambéry in Savoy in January 1793 and first printed in 1796. Its premise is a burlesque of the epic and didactic conventions Barlow himself had used in the Columbiad material: the poet refuses his Alpine and revolutionary subject matter - the audacious Alps that cramp the day, the Gallic flags that bear death to kings and freedom to the world - and chooses instead a virgin theme, unconscious of the Muse, the sweets of Hasty-Pudding. The poem then treats cornmeal pudding with all the apparatus of serious verse: an invocation, a search for the dish's lineage through the wrecks of time, an origin myth in which a nameless Indian squaw, a tawny Ceres, first cracked the dried maize, sifted the golden flour and stirred it in boiling water, and a celebration of the pudding's appearance in the author's path of exile. Behind the joke is a political and cultural argument about diet, plainness and luxury: the Yankee's simple abundant feast that cheers servant and lord alike against the vicious rules of art of the French kitchen, the cities of Europe that exclude maize from their climes, and a footnote, appended to the passage on London lost in smoke and steeped in tea, in which Barlow names a certain king who was publishing proclamations to prevent American principles from being propagated in his country.
works.plot: Canto I is invocation and origin: after rejecting the Alps and the Gallic flags the poet addresses the bowl directly, welcomes the milk smoking from the kine that tempers its heat, and asks what lovely squaw in days of yore first gave the food to the world, crediting some tawny Ceres with the invention of cracking the maize, sifting it through the rough seive and stirring the yellow flour till it swells, thickens, puffs and wallops to its true consistence. He claims the discovery of Oella, the Peruvian heroine of his own earlier poem, for the honour, then greets his long-lost unforgotten friend in Savoy, remembering how vainly he sought it through Paris, where cold Bacchus usurps the morning board, and how London, lost in smoke and steeped in tea, will not let a Yankee lisp the name. Canto II turns from praise to precept and to social comparison: the kitchen Muse framed her book to mix food by vicious rules of art, to sink the stomach and make friends wonder why children die, whereas the Yankee feast, furnished with simples and dressed with plainness, gathers a numerous offspring round the board and cheers servant and lord alike, health attending them from the short repast. The canto describes the morning cauldron, the mother stirring the pudding, the table spread and the bowls prepared, the children fed and combed and sent to school, and then, in the manner of an art of cookery, the exact rules of proportion and manipulation by which the purest of all foods may be made bad, indifferent or good. Canto III moves to the autumn: the days grow short, the corn-house is filled and the harvest home called, and the neighbours assemble for the corn-husking, a frolic scene where work, mirth and play chase the hours away among brown corn-fed nymphs and strong hard-handed beaux ranged in circling rows, the dry husks rustling and the corn-cobs cracking, cider tripping in silence round. The laws of husking are celebrated as the best-kept laws on earth - a kiss for every red ear, a bedaubing for the blackened ones, the favour'd beau who pays the luscious tribute - and the poem closes with mock-geometric precepts on the choice of spoons, the deep-bowl'd Gallic spoon being unfitted for substantial food, the true form being a small section of a goose-egg-shell, and the final advice not to fear to slaver but to suspend the ready napkin like the free Frenchman or poise the bowl upon the knee.
works.significance: The Hasty-Pudding is the finest short American mock-heroic of the revolutionary decade and the one piece of Barlow's verse that has kept a continuous place in later anthologies and reprints. It matters for two reasons. As criticism it exposes, from inside, the conventions of the didactic and national epic that Barlow was himself attempting in the Columbiad material: the humble subject tests whether the machinery of invocation, origin myth and precept can be made to serve a republic of plain food rather than kings. As cultural argument it anticipates a persistent American theme, the moral contrast between European luxury and American plainness, and binds that contrast to a specific defence of indigenous and colonial material culture - the Indian inventor of maize cookery is named as the dish's true foundress, and the poem's English, French and Italian cityscapes are the places where the food cannot be found. Its footnote on royal proclamations against American principles also makes a cookery poem a document of the transatlantic radical publicity of 1792-1793.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout, closed decasyllabic pairs used for antithesis, sententious generalisation and the point of the joke ("Some tawny Ceres, goddess of her days, / First learn'd with stones to crack the well-dry'd maize"). The register shifts deliberately between epic solemnity, homely monosyllables of the cookery terms and mock-technical geometry, and the humour depends on the couplet's capacity to make a maxim out of a spoon. Barlow adds prose apparatus in the manner of the serious didactic poem, including the explanatory footnote on the king's proclamations.
works.context: The poem was written in January 1793 at Chambéry in Savoy, in the year Barlow was travelling and writing on the continent as a republican sympathiser during the French Revolutionary wars, and its earliest printings appeared three years later, in 1796, when he was in Paris: a New Haven edition printed by T. and S. Green for Tiebout and O'Brien, a New York edition printed from the author's manuscript for Fellows and Adams, and a Poughkeepsie re-print, all in three cantos and all carrying the Chambéry date-line on the title page. The paratext of the Newburyport reprint of the companion poem The Conspiracy of Kings advertises its author on the title page as the author of Advice to the privileged orders, which places the pudding poem squarely in the same radical publishing campaign. Through the nineteenth century the poem remained in print, in editions of 1838, of 1847 printed with a memoir on maize or Indian corn by D. J. Browne, and of 1856, so that a Jacobin mock-heroic became a durable item of American domestic literary merchandise.
works.characters: the exiled poet-speaker; the nameless Indian squaw, a tawny Ceres, who first invented the dish; Oella, the Peruvian heroine of the poet's earlier verse, to whom he alternatively ascribes the honour; the Yankee mother, the milk-maid and the children sent off to school; the brown corn-fed nymphs and strong hard-handed beaux of the husking; the free Frenchman with his napkin at his chin; the cook and the kitchen Muse of the vicious rules of art; the unnamed king of the note on proclamations against American principles
works.structure: Three cantos of continuous couplet argument, organised as a mock-epic and mock-didactic sequence rather than a story: invocation and praise in Canto I, social comparison and cookery precept in Canto II, harvest manners and the physiology of eating in Canto III. The single voice of the poet-speaker carries the poem, and its structure imitates the larger didactic epic it parodies, complete with a learned footnote of the author's own.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship is unproblematic: the 1796 editions print the poem by Joel Barlow and state the place and date of composition on the title page, one of them claiming to be printed from the author's manuscript. Bibliographical caution is needed rather than attributional caution, since several 1796 issues were printed from the same manuscript text in different cities and their title pages differ in detail - one reads Written in Germany, in Savoy, January, 1793 and others Written at Chambery, in Savoy - and the earliest surviving printed copy may not be the first appearance. This record's text and quotation are taken from the digitised 1796 New Haven edition in the Eighteenth-Century Poetry Archive (Evans text N22715), which is the source edition used by that archive.

works.title: The Haunted Hotel: A Mystery of Modern Venice
altTitles: Haunted Hotel: A Mystery of Modern Venice
works.form: Novella; ghost story, first issued in 1878
works.description: Published in 1878 and the finest of Collins's shorter sensation works: the story of a Venetian palace, the disappearance of Lord Montbarry, and a dream that reveals a murder to a sleeping woman. It is a prose fiction work of 1878 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Lord Montbarry abandons his fiancée Agnes for the Countess Narona and dies in Venice; the palace he bought becomes a hotel, and the guests are troubled by a smell, a stain and a dream. The Countess's confession reveals that Montbarry was murdered for his money, and the hotel's room yields the evidence.
works.significance: The Haunted Hotel is the most perfect of the English supernatural detective stories and a key text in the literature of the dream as evidence; it was a model for Henry James's later Venetian fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1870s, the Venetian tourist industry, and the Victorian interest in dreams and psychical research. works.title: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
works.form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1940
works.description: The greatest Southern novel of adolescence: a deaf mute in a Georgia mill town and the four people who need him. It is a prose fiction work of 1940 by Carson McCullers; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: John Singer, a deaf mute, is the confidant of four people in a Georgia mill town — Mick Kelly, a young girl who loves music; Jake Blount, a drunken radical; Dr Copeland, a Black physician; and Biff Brannon, the café owner — and when his friend Spiros Antonapoulos dies, Singer kills himself and each of the four is left alone.
works.significance: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter is the greatest Southern novel of adolescence and one of the great American novels of loneliness: written at twenty-three, it made McCullers the youngest of the Southern writers and gave American fiction one of its permanent portraits of isolation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, bare, exactly observed sentence.
works.context: A Georgia mill town in the late 1930s, the Depression, and the isolation of the small Southern town. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: John Singer; Mick Kelly; Jake Blount; Dr Copeland; Biff Brannon; Antonapoulos
works.structure: Three parts following the four characters around Singer. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Heart of Midlothian
altTitles: Tales of My Landlord, Second Series
The Heart of Midlothian: A Tale
works.form: Historical novel and plebeian romance of the pilgrimage; a legal and domestic tragedy of infanticide and mercy.
works.description: The proudest achievement of the series and one of the strongest plots in English fiction: a Scottish plebeian heroine walks to London to save her sister from the gallows. The novel takes the Edinburgh mob, the Tolbooth, the law of infanticide and the royal prerogative of mercy with full seriousness, and its moral argument is carried not by wit but by conscience and a journey. Its title names the Old Tolbooth, 'the Heart of Midlothian'.
works.plot: Effie Deans is condemned to death at Edinburgh for the murder of an infant child, the seducer having concealed his interest and the mother refusing from shame to name him. Her sister Jeanie, holding to the plain rule that a falsehood may not save a life, sets out on foot to London to plead for a reprieve, and on the way is present at the Porteous mob of 1736, when the guard officer who had fired on the crowd is dragged from the Tolbooth and executed on a scaffold reared in the street. Reuben Butler, the presbyterian schoolmaster, follows Jeanie's cause with patience; David Deans, her father, dies of grief and obstinacy. Jeanie's audience with Queen Charlotte, and the intervention of the Duke of Argyll, procure transportation instead of death; the real father, a man of parts and ruin, is exposed, and Jeanie's constancy is rewarded.
works.significance: Widely held to be the finest single achievement of the school, and the period's most admired heroine of the people, whose refusal to lie is treated as an act of intellectual as well as moral courage. It fixed the fictional treatment of the Porteous riots and of infanticide law. Its prefatory essay on the composition of the tale is a primary document of the theory of historical fiction.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Scots vernacular speech carried at length, with popular song and the burial-service cadence quoted in the scenes of Madge Wildfire.
works.context: Set in the 1730s, when the Porteous mob and the law of infanticide were live problems of Edinburgh governance, and the Scottish legal system was still negotiating capital punishment for concealed childbirth. The novel's London chapters record the patronage and the royal household of the early Hanoverian court. It was published at the height of the series' commercial power and of the author's own involvement in Edinburgh publishing.
works.characters: Jeanie Deans; Effie Deans; David Deans; Reuben Butler; Madge Wildfire; George Staunton; the Duke of Argyll; Queen Charlotte; Lady St Ives
works.structure: Third-person narrative divided between the Scottish Lowlands and London, with the journey as its spine; the Porteous riot and the dying mother's story are set pieces; the frame is the fictitious landlord who edits the series, and the tale carries a dedicatory preface and notes.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley in the Tales of My Landlord series; authorship undisputed.

Revenge and justice
Women, chastity, and constancy
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: The Heavenly Twins
works.description: Published in 1893 and the central English New Woman novel: the boy-and-girl twins Angelica and Diavolo, three marriages, and the destruction of women by the sexual double standard. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by Sarah Grand; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Evadne Frayling, learning on her wedding day of her husband Major Colquhoun's dissolute past, refuses to consummate the marriage and lives with him in name only; Angelica Hamilton-Wells, the wilder of the mischievous 'heavenly twins' with her brother Diavolo, proposes to the much older Mr Kilroy and then, disguised as a boy, strikes up a nocturnal friendship with the Tenor, a singer of the cathedral town, who dies after discovering her sex; and Edith Beale, married to the syphilitic Sir Mosley Menteith, dies insane after the birth of a diseased child, which provides the novel's indictment. The last book is narrated by Dr Galbraith, whom Evadne marries after Colquhoun's death.
works.significance: The Heavenly Twins was the most discussed novel of 1893 and it made the New Woman a national figure: its treatment of venereal disease, sexual ignorance and the double standard made it a founding text of the English feminist novel, and Grand's own essay of 1894, 'The New Aspect of the Woman Question', helped put the phrase 'the New Woman' into circulation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays.
works.context: 1890-93: the Contagious Diseases Acts campaign, the sexual ignorance of middle-class girls, the marriage law and the feminist periodicals of the early 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; novel of development and the growth story.

works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Heir of Redclyffe
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1853
works.description: Published in 1853 and the most popular religious novel of the Victorian age: the story of two cousins, one generous and one proud, and the discipline of Christian self-sacrifice. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by Charlotte M. Yonge; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Guy Morville, the heir of Redclyffe, is a high-spirited young man wrongly suspected of pride by his cousin Philip; his courtship of Amy Edmonstone, his illness and death abroad, and Philip's slow repentance form the pattern of a novel that made Guy the model of the Christian gentleman for a generation.
works.significance: The Heir of Redclyffe was the most influential religious novel of its decade and is the central text of the Victorian High Church imagination: it shaped the ideal of the Christian gentleman, it was the favourite book of the officers of the Crimean War, and it made Yonge a national figure.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the large family chronicle with an enormous cast.
works.context: 1853: the Oxford Movement and the High Church revival, the close-knit world of the English county family, and the Crimean War generation that took the novel to its heart. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Sir Guy Morville; Captain Philip Morville; Amabel (Amy) Edmonstone; Laura Edmonstone; Charles Edmonstone; Mr and Mrs Edmonstone; Mary Ross; Mr Ross; Sebastian Dixon
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. works.title: The Hermit
works.description: Parnell's tender narrative tale of a hermit drawn from his cell by a pleasing guide, of a betrayed country maid, and of the care exercised over the tempted soul: one of the most reprinted English short poems of the century.
works.plot: An old hermit, peevish at the world and at his own past, is allured from his cell by a fair guide who leads him through the country night to a cottage, where he learns the story of a maid seduced and lost; the tale turns on the discovery of the guide's errand and on the hermit's humbling.
works.significance: It supplied the century with one of its most quoted examples of pathos and of the supernatural tale, and its reprints, translations and schoolbook presence made it a conduit for the sentimental ballad.
works.meter: Plain couplet and short lyric stanza of the old ballad manner, with the night description in a slower measure.
works.context: Published in the years when the ballad, the romance tale and the tender religious narrative were displacing the heroic manner, and when Pope and the Scriblerans held Parnell's verse to be the model of easy native simplicity.

works.title: The Heroic Slave
works.description: Published in 1853 and the only work of fiction Douglass wrote: a novella based on the revolt led by Madison Washington aboard the slave ship Creole in 1841. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Imperial Adventure Romance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Madison Washington, an enslaved Virginian who has escaped to Canada, returns to rescue his wife and is shipped to New Orleans; he leads the seizure of the Creole and sails the ship to Nassau, where the British free the rebels.
works.significance: The Heroic Slave is the first American work of fiction by a black writer and the founding text of African-American fiction: it invented the black revolutionary hero of American literature and made the slave revolt a subject of the American imagination.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
works.context: The year 1841, the Creole case, the British abolition of slavery in the colonies, and the American debate on the legal status of slave revolt. The record dates the work as composed in 1852 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Madison Washington; Mr Listwell, the Ohio abolitionist; Susan, his wife; Tom Grant, the Creole's first mate
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: The Hill of Dreams
works.description: The finest decadent novel in English: a young writer's ecstasy and destruction in the Welsh hills and London. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Arthur Machen; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lucian Taylor, a Welsh clergyman's son, becomes a writer, escapes to London and lives in poverty and ecstasy, caught between the Roman past of his native hills and the visions of his own imagination, until his mind and body fail.
works.significance: The Hill of Dreams is the finest decadent novel in English and Machen's masterpiece: its prose ecstasies, its Welsh landscape and its portrait of the artist destroyed by his own vision made it one of the great novels of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the tale built on an ancient survival beneath the modern town.
works.context: Wales and London at the end of the nineteenth century, the decadent movement, and the poverty of the literary hack. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Lucian Taylor; Annie Morgan; the rector; the London landlady
works.structure: A novel in five parts, from the Welsh childhood to the London collapse. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The Hind and the Panther
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther: A Poem in Three Parts
works.description: Dryden's great beast-fable of religious controversy, written after his conversion to Roman Catholicism: the milk-white Hind (the Roman Church) is pursued and slandered by the Panther (the Church of England) and the other beasts of the English sects.
works.plot: The Hind, immortal and unafathed, seeks her lost children; she debates authority and interpretation with the Panther, recounts her own conversion, and the poem ends with the fable of the Swallows and the Martins.
works.significance: The longest and most serious of Dryden's poems and the fullest statement of his Catholic apologetic; a masterpiece of sustained argumentative verse that influenced Pope's Essay on Man.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of sustained eloquence, with the most complex syntax of Dryden's verse.
works.context: Published in April 1687 under the Declaration of Indulgence, when James II's policy of toleration for Catholics briefly encouraged open Catholic argument; it was parodied within weeks by Montagu and Prior in The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd.

works.structure: Three parts: the characters of the beasts, the theological debate at the Hind's house, and the concluding fable; framed by an extended address to the poem itself.

works.title: The History and Present State of Electricity
altTitles: The History and Present State of Electricity, with Experiments and Observations
works.description: Joseph Priestley's definitive survey and experimental history of electricity, written with Franklin's encouragement and the Royal Society's papers in hand. It gathered a century of electrical discovery into a single narrative and added Priestley's own experiments, including the charged cylinder that opened the age of large machines.
works.plot: Priestley narrates the history of electricity from Gilbert and the philosophical trials of the seventeenth century through the improvements of his own age, arranging the phenomena, instruments, and controversies into a chronological and analytical account. His inserted experiments establish the inverse-square law of electrical attraction, the conductivity of charcoal, and the identity of lightning with the electrical discharge, and his account of the electrical cylinder records the machine that made experiments on a great scale possible. The history ends with the state of the theory, the sparks, the shocks, and the promised uses of the science. The book is at once a museum of discovery and a programme for the next, its experiments pointing toward the chemistry of gases.
works.significance: It became the standard history of electricity and the model of the scientific survey, and its success funded and framed Priestley's pneumatic chemistry, the empirical foundation of his natural theology and his radicalism.
works.meter: Plain, businesslike experimental prose with a historian's synoptic periods, apparatus described in working detail.
works.context: Written in the wake of the Leyden jar's craze and Franklin's experiments, at Priestley's early Leeds and London period; published 1767 with the Royal Society's encouragement, it made its author a Fellow and the historian of a science whose next chapter he would himself write.
works.structure: A chronological history interleaved with numbered reports of the author's own experiments and theoretical commentary.

works.title: The History of America
works.description: Robertson's history of the Spanish discovery and settlement of America, the standard English account for a century, the first volumes appearing in 1777 and the later books on the other European colonies completed after his death. It turned the conquests and colonial histories into a philosophical narrative of the extension of Europe.
works.plot: The narrative opens with the state of the American nations before 1492, their arts, governments, and religions treated with Robertson's blend of wonder and condescension, then follows Columbus from the enterprise to the governorship, the voyages, and the discovery of the mainland. It chronicles the conquest of Mexico and Peru with Cortes and Pizarro, the establishment of the Spanish colonial system, the treatment of the natives, and the rise of the other European colonies in North America and the West Indies. The closing volumes, completed after his death, carry the history of the British plantations, their constitutions, and the temper of the new societies. The whole reads as a science of colonies: climate, soil, constitution, and commerce explaining the destinies of the European America.
works.significance: It was the received history of America in English well into the nineteenth century, the book through which generations read Columbus and the conquests, and a foundation of the historical geography of the Atlantic world.
works.meter: The capacious balanced periods of late philosophical history, campaign and constitution set in stately alternation with the moralist's clauses of judgment.
works.context: Published from 1777 as the American revolution broke out, drawing on the historians of the Indies and the accumulated voyage literature; it stood at the centre of Robertson's late work as the great historical geographer of the Atlantic.
works.characters: Columbus; Cortes; Pizarro; the American nations; the colonial projectors
works.structure: Volumes published from 1777 with the later books completed after the author's death: the discovery, the Spanish conquests, and the northern colonies forming one history of America under Europe.

works.title: The History of British India
works.form: philosophical and national history; utilitarian history of civilisation with administrative argument
works.description: A three-volume history of India written wholly out of books by a clerk of the governing company, and the most influential and most offensive English history of the subcontinent for a century. It divides Indian history into three civilisations, the Hindu, the Muslim, and the British, and it argues that the Hindu period was one of stationary ignorance and despotism out of which only European science and law could carry the country.
works.plot: The first volumes survey the Hindu state of society: the religion, the mythology, the literature, the sciences, the laws, and the institutions of caste, of all of which the historian judges that they exhibit a people sunk in the lowest depth of intellectual and moral degradation, governed by a priesthood and by a military aristocracy, without accurate knowledge, without useful art, and without a sense of human dignity. It then traces the Muslim conquests and dynasties, whose tyranny and turbulence it holds to have changed nothing essential, and passes to the entrance and progress of the European companies, the wars and policy by which the British power was made paramount, and the administration of the provinces. Throughout, the test applied to every institution is that of utility: whatever promotes knowledge, security, and the interests of the many is approved, and whatever rests upon superstition, upon hereditary rank, or upon the caprice of a ruler is condemned. The closing argument pleads for a government of laws and of education, and for the substitution of a directed administration for the patronage and the commercial interest which had hitherto governed the territories.
works.significance: It is the classic example of the philosophic history written in the study without travel, and the book on which the British governing class in India was educated; its periodisation of Indian history into three epochs and its denial of a civilisation to the Hindu period became the orthodoxy of the administration and, in the following century, the thesis which Indian writers undertook to refute. Its authority and its arrogance together make it one of the most significant and most criticised works of the intellectual history of empire.
works.meter: Bare, dogmatic, generalising prose, contemptuous of ornament and of the picturesque, with the sweeping judgement and the summarising catalogue; the style of a reasoner who measures everything against a single standard.
works.context: Written over more than a decade of leisure hours by a writer of the radical school while the territories of the governing company were administered under the patronage system, and published just before its author took an official charge of the company's education and appointments, from which he was long able to act upon the principles of the book. It supplied the historical teaching of the company's college and of the administration for generations.
works.structure: Three volumes: the first two on the Hindu and Mahometan civilisations, arranged by subject as religion, arts, sciences, and institutions; the third on the British progress and administration, arranged as a narrative of events with the closing analysis of the company's affairs.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the share of the author's son in the later editions, and of several specialist writers in the notes on the law and sciences of the country, are recorded in the history of the editions, and the book is properly cited by edition.
themes: Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The History of England
altTitles: History of England, from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688
works.description: Hume's six-volume history of England, written backwards from the Stuarts to Caesar and the earliest ages, and the most widely read history of the century. It narrates the growth of the constitution, party, and commerce from a philosophical standpoint hostile alike to Whig martyr legends and Tory divine-right tales.
works.plot: The Stuart volumes first show the fatal collision between the prerogative and the commons, the errors of Charles I and of his opponents, and the way enthusiasm and faction made civil war and then commonwealth plausible; the Tudor volumes trace the centralizing monarchy, the reformation, and the rise of the people's claims; the early volumes from the invasion of Caesar through the Plantagenets and the establishment of the commons narrate how law, property, and civility emerged slowly out of conquest, feudal anarchy, and monastic learning. Throughout, Hume explains events by the opposition of authority and liberty, the interests of ranks, and the unnoticed moral effects of commerce and the laws, refusing providential and party readings alike. The volume covering the accession of the house of Stuart to the revolution of 1688 closes his own published series.
works.significance: It was the standard English history for half a century, shaped nineteenth-century historiography and the Whig-Tory synthesis, and is still studied as the monument of history written as the science of human nature applied.
works.meter: The level, capacious, periodic historiographic prose of the philosophical historian, marked by balanced judgment clauses and sardonic character portraits.
works.context: Written while Hume was librarian of the Faculty of Advocates in Edinburgh and supported by copies of records from London, the History drew furious party reviews and episcopal remonstrance, yet made Hume financially independent and a European name.
works.characters: Henry VIII; Elizabeth I; Mary Queen of Scots; James I; Charles I; Cromwell; William III
works.structure: Six volumes issued in reverse chronological order between 1754 and 1762, each a continuous political narrative with inserted constitutional, legal, and economic remarks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
National identity and Englishness
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: The Scottish Enlightenment

works.title: The History of England (Smollett)
altTitles: The History of England, from the First Accession of James the Second to the Treaty of Chatellerault
works.description: A multi-volume narrative history of England from the Revolution of 1688 to the middle of the eighteenth century, undertaken as a commercial compilation and executed with a historian's argument about party, commerce and national character. It was the standard readable English history of the 1760s and 1770s and was several times revised and continued by the writer.
works.plot: The work narrates the reigns and ministries from James II to the peace of 1763, attending to the settlement of the constitution, the wars, the funds and the parties. It judges the Toleration and the Revolution in a Tory-Whig middle register, dwells on the '45 and on the administration of the elder minister, and treats the growth of trade and credit as the true subject of the age. The later volumes and continuations carry the story into the author's own decade.
works.significance: It shows the eighteenth-century novelists' command of the philosophy of history and supplied a generation with its narrative of the recent past; its judgments on liberty, faction and commerce are a document of the Scottish and English historical thought of the mid-century.
works.meter: A sententious and rhetorical historical prose, closer to the manner of the Augustan historians than to the documentary school, with the balanced period of judgment as its characteristic unit.
works.context: Written as a bookseller's speculation out of the earlier histories and the printed sources of the day, and published volume by volume in the years of the Seven Years' War, when the demand for a readable national history was acute and the party press still argued over the Revolution settlement.
works.characters: James II; William III; the ministers and commanders of the wars; the pretender and the '45; the party leaders of the Hanoverian age
works.structure: A regular chronological narrative in volumes with periodic continuations and revised issues; the books are organised by reign and administration, with inserted character sketches and constitutional remarks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though the work was largely composed from earlier histories, a practice then normal and afterwards criticised.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Kingship and good rule
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history

works.title: The History of English Poetry
altTitles: The History of English Poetry, from the Close of the Eleventh Century to the Commencement of the Eighteenth Century
works.form: literary history and critical scholarship, in the new historical method of letters
works.description: Warton's great unfinished scholarly history, the first attempt to trace the whole course of English poetry from the medieval minstrels to the Augustan age and to explain it by the manners, learning and opinions of each period. Its four volumes set the model of historical literary criticism in English and made the romance, the chivalric lays and the early drama part of a continuous national story. The work is at once a history of letters and an argument for the imaginative tradition that the age of rule had disparaged.
works.plot: The history follows the poets in their social and intellectual conditions, beginning with the remains of ancient poetry and the minstrel and romantic lays, and moving through the allegorical and chivalric tradition, the rise of the drama, the Spenserians, and the ages of the civil war and of the Restoration. Its great digressions treat the origin and progress of romance and chivalry, the origin of the ancient epick poems, and the rise of the drama, each a piece of general literary history. The method throughout is antiquarian: to recover the documents, the manners and the beliefs from which the poems were made.
works.significance: It founded the historical study of English poetry and supplied the framework within which later romantic and Victorian scholars read their own tradition. Its account of chivalry, allegory and romance made the native medieval past available as literary history, and its method established the digression as a vehicle of general criticism.
works.meter: Prose of the narrative and dissertations, the metrical specimens quoted being the objects of historical and prosodic comment rather than of verse composition.
works.context: Issued volume by volume from 1774 to 1781, in the decades of antiquarian recovery, of the Ossianic debate over primitive poetry and of the growing claim that the imagination, not the rule, was the poetical faculty; it belongs with Percy's and Evans's collections and with the revival of the early drama as a single movement of taste.
works.characters: The medieval minstrels and romancers; Chaucer; Spenser; the Elizabethan dramatists; the poets of the Restoration and of the Augustan age
works.structure: A multi-volume literary history arranged chronologically with long embedded dissertations or digressions on general subjects; the volumes were issued successively and the fourth was published after the earlier three, with materials left imperfect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the successive volumes and their imperfect completion are documented in Warton's own correspondence and in the later biographies, and the volume sequence is recorded in the note below.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Primitive genius and national poetry
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The English vernacular and national letters
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The History of Henry Esmond, Esq., a Colonel in the Service of Her Majesty Queen Anne. Written by Himself
altTitles: History of Henry Esmond, Esq., a Colonel in the Service of Her Majesty Queen Anne. Written by Himself
works.form: Historical novel in the first person
works.description: Published in three volumes in 1852 and set in the reign of Queen Anne (1702-14): Thackeray's masterly historical novel, written throughout in the idiom of the early eighteenth century, and the only one of his books to sustain a single voice from beginning to end.
works.plot: Henry Esmond, a foundling of the Castlewood family who believes himself to be illegitimate, serves as a soldier under Marlborough in Flanders and as a man of letters in London, falling in love with his cousin Beatrix, who prefers the young Pretender. He marries Rachel, Lady Castlewood, who is in fact the mother of the true heir and whom he has loved since boyhood, and they emigrate to Virginia, where the novel's frame places the aged Esmond and his descendants.
works.significance: Henry Esmond is the finest historical novel of the eighteenth century written in the nineteenth, and its archaised first-person narration — Thackeray's most sustained experiment in style — has been a permanent model for the historical novel in the first person, from Scott's and Thackeray's heirs to the historical fiction of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The War of the Spanish Succession and the campaigns of Queen Anne, the Jacobite succession crisis, the death of Anne and the Hanoverian accession of 1714, and the London of Addison, Steele and Swift. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1852 and first published in 1852 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Henry Esmond; Rachel, Lady Castlewood; Beatrix Esmond; Francis Esmond; the second Viscount Castlewood; Lord Mohun; the Duke of Hamilton; Swift; Steele; Addison; Colonel Esmond
works.structure: A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story

works.title: The History of Joseph
altTitles: The History of Joseph: A Poem
works.description: A narrative poem on the patriarch Joseph, retelling the scriptural history of the dreamer, the sold slave, the tempted servant in Potiphar's house and the exalted minister of Egypt. It is the largest of the author's verse undertakings and one of the most read of the century's scriptural poems.
works.plot: The poem follows the Genesis narrative from the dreams of the boy and the envy of his brethren to their journey into Egypt and the discovery of their guilt. It dwells on the temptation by Potiphar's wife and on Joseph's refusal, on the prison and the interpretation of dreams, and on the final discovery of Joseph to his family. The argument is at once providential and moral, the purity and patience of the hero being held up as an example of the government of the passions.
works.significance: It is a central example of the sacred narrative poem by a woman in the eighteenth century and much of the century's taste for the chaste and pathetic scripture story is formed by it and by its imitators.
works.meter: Narrative verse of the moderate middle style, in the blank verse and the strophic lyric measures proper to the paraphrase tradition of the day, the pathetical scenes being carried in the slower line.
works.context: Published in 1736 by a poet long established as the century's most admired writer of pious verse, in the season of the vogue for the scriptural paraphrase and for the sacred poem as a female preserve.
works.characters: Joseph; his father and his brethren; Potiphar and his wife; the butler and the baker of the prison; Pharaoh
works.structure: A continuous narrative poem in books and divisions following the scriptural sequence, with the lyrical addresses and the moral reflections interposed at the crises of the story.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the collections of her works after her death.

Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey

works.title: The History of King Richard III
altTitles: History of King Richard the Third
works.description: More's unfinished prose history of the rise and fall of Richard III, composed in parallel English and Latin versions; the English text was first printed in a corrupt form in Hardyng's Chronicle (1543) and the definitive version appeared in Rastell's edition of More's English Works (1557).
works.plot: The narrative traces Richard's path to the throne: the death of Edward IV, Richard's seizure of power as Protector, the removal of the princes, Buckingham's rebellion, and Richard's coronation and brief reign, breaking off during Morton's embassy to France. It portrays Richard as a dissembling tyrant whose deformity mirrors his moral deformity.
works.significance: The first great work of English prose history and the fountainhead of the Tudor myth of Richard III; its psychological portraiture and dramatic irony made it a major source for Shakespeare and for sixteenth-century historiography.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written during More's second period of public service, probably 1513–1518, drawing on oral testimony from Morton's household where More was raised; the work circulated in manuscript and shaped the Tudor 'black legend' of Richard III long before Shakespeare used Hall's chronicle (which incorporated More's account) for his play.
works.characters: Richard III; Edward IV; Elizabeth Woodville; Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham; John Morton; Lord Hastings; Edward V; Richard, Duke of York
works.structure: Unfinished chronicle in five books, driven by dramatic set-piece speeches (Buckingham's oration, Elizabeth Woodville's lament) and a Tacitean focus on character and motive rather than providential design.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The History of Little Henry and his Bearer
works.form: juvenile and devotional tale; the domestic narrative with a missionary argument
works.description: The little Indian tale which made its author's fame and which was read as a children's book for three quarters of a century: the story of an English child left in the hands of a native servant in the company's territories, and of the knowledge of the Bible which passed from the child to the man. It is a founding text of the missionary story for children and of the English picture of domestic life in India.
works.plot: The history opens with the little English child placed under the care of his bearer in an Indian station, where the family's own round is broken and the child is left almost wholly with the native servant; and it tells how the child's simple reading of the Bible, his cheerfulness, and his talk about the Saviour, wrought upon the mind of the attendant, who in his turn becomes a student of the scriptures and a secret teacher of his own countrymen. The narrative follows the separations of the child's life, the trials and the sickness of the servant left behind, and the steadfastness of a faith which had been taught without art; the closing pages report the death of the bearer and the account of his hope, and pass into the argument that the religion which had reached one Indian heart by the means of one English child may be trusted for the conversion of the whole country.
works.significance: It is the most influential of the children's tales of the missionary movement, and the book by which generations of English readers first conceived the religious claim upon India; its picture of the child as the teacher and of the servant as the convert supplied the stock pattern of the missionary story, while its representation of the native and of the station has made it, in the modern history of writing about empire, one of the most studied and most criticised of children's books.
works.meter: Plain, tender, earnest narrative prose, with the direct little speech of the child and the elevated close of the devotional appeal; the style of the tract-tale at its most winning.
works.context: Written by a young officer's wife resident in the company's territories, out of the domestic life of the stations and of the evangelical interest in the missions of the war years, and printed first in India and afterward in the metropolis, where it was put out by the religious book-sellers and carried to every nursery. Its subject lay upon the two great public interests of the moment, the missions and the education of the children of the settlement.
works.characters: Little Henry; his bearer; the household and the servants of the Indian station; the narrator and the family at home
works.structure: A single short tale in continuous sequence, framed by the letter and the report of the narrator, with the closing argument upon the field of India added as the moral of the story.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the tale was long reprinted in abridged and in combined issues, sometimes with the sequel and sometimes with the other Indian tales of the same pen, and the first Indian and English impressions are distinguished in the bibliography of the author's works.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Colonial enterprise and the New World
Evangelical experience and assurance
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave. Related by Herself. With a Supplement by the Editor. To which is added, the Narrative of Asa-Asa, a Crowing Negro
works.form: Slave narrative and abolitionist testimony: a related-by-herself life story addressed to a British reading public in the emergency months before emancipation legislation, framed by an editor's supplement and documents.
works.description: The first book-length narrative of an enslaved woman published in Britain, dictated in London by a Bermudian and West Indian slave who had come to England seeking her freedom. It gives in the first person the labour, punishment and sexual vulnerability of enslaved women in salt ponds, on sugar islands and in domestic service, and it was written to support a real legal claim. An editorial supplement and the appended narrative of another formerly enslaved man frame and authenticate her testimony. It is at once evidence, petition and autobiography.
works.plot: The history follows the narrator from an enslaved childhood in Bermuda through service in the Turks Islands, where the hard labour of the salt ponds and the neglect of the enslaved are described in detail, and back to Bermuda and Antigua under masters whose cruelty is named. It records separations from her husband and children, the sale of kin, punishments for refusing submission, and her eventual attempt to rest in England when her owner travelled there. When she refused to return to service abroad she was deserted, advertised for sale and left without wages, and the narrative becomes the public statement of her case. The supplement documents the legal and religious obstacles she met and argues the wider claim that slavery, not the individual, is the criminal institution.
works.significance: It is the central surviving account of enslaved women's labour and discipline in the British Caribbean and a landmark of women's life-writing, and it supplied immediatist agitators with testimony that no gradualist report could match. Its frank account of the sexual danger of the household expands the conventions of the contemporary slave narrative, and it anchors Black Atlantic writing within the Romantic period's reform literature.
works.meter: Vivid vernacular prose, with direct speech, exclamatory appeal and an accumulating list of injuries; no verse.
works.context: Published in London in February 1831 while the British movement for immediate emancipation of the colonial enslaved was pressing the reformed Parliament, and while the test-case of a slave resident in England was being argued. Its editorship and transcription were undertaken by abolitionist supporters who knew the legal risk of publishing such a statement, and its facts were attacked by the planter interest in the press.
works.characters: Mary Prince; her first mistress in Bermuda; the salt-pond overseers; her husband, a free Black mariner; the Antiguan mistress who flogged her; the owner who deserted her in London; Asa-Asa, the African whose appended narrative follows
works.structure: Continuous first-person testimony with a chronology of masters and islands, followed by an editor's supplement of argument and documents and an appended second narrative.
works.attributionNotes: The narrative is related by its subject but was transcribed and edited by an abolitionist writer, and the supplement and documents are editorial; the book is therefore authored collaboratively in its production while the testimony itself is hers.
themes: Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless
altTitles: The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless
works.form: novel; domestic and conduct fiction in prose
works.description: A domestic novel in six volumes on the model of the conduct book, tracing a lively, vain young woman from an unprotected fortune through a bad marriage to a hard-won prudence. It is the author's fullest attempt to convert the amatory plot into a moral education and a deliberate address to the conduct of young women.
works.plot: Betsy, orphaned and left to the guard of uncles and brothers, enjoys the flattery of admirers and the liberties of an unregulated spirit. Her brother's choice of a drunken husband for her proves ruinous; separation, attempted seduction, scandal and the intervention of a steadfast friend expose the danger of a woman's dependence on male protection. She earns at last the right to remarry well, the narrative closing on the lessons her suffering has taught.
works.significance: It is the most complete of the early novels by a woman that reframes the seduction plot as an education in prudence, and an important link between the amatory romance of the 1720s and the later novel of female experience.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose with a strongly intrusive narrator, apostrophes to the female reader and sententious closures; dialogue carries the social comedy.
works.context: Published in 1751 in the season of the novelist's conduct turn and of the rival domestic fictions of the same decade, and drawing on the licensing debate and the new moral seriousness of the mid-century book trade.
works.structure: Continuous third-person narration in six volumes with didactic addresses to the reader; the plot is organised as a progression from thoughtlessness to discretion rather than as an intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and reissued in the following decade.

works.title: The History of Mr Polly
works.description: A small draper burns down his own shop, fakes his death and discovers freedom on the road. It is a prose fiction work of 1910 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Alfred Polly, a quarrelsome, incompetent draper in Fishbourne, is trapped in an unhappy marriage and a failing business. He resolves on suicide, but before he can act the shop catches fire; he takes the opportunity to disappear, is presumed dead, and reinvents himself as an inn-keeper and woodsman, fighting a local bully, finding a companion, and finally returning to visit his widow's new marriage.
works.significance: The History of Mr Polly is the funniest and most humane of Wells's social novels: it is the great English novel of the small tradesman's escape, and its comic invention — the burning shop, the fight at the Potwell Inn, Mr Polly's private vocabulary — has made it a permanent English classic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The Edwardian drapery trade, the small provincial town and the new mobility of the motor road and the bicycle; Wells's own escape from the draper's shop. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1910 and first published in 1910 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Alfred Polly; Miriam Polly; the plump woman; Uncle Jim; Johnson
works.structure: Third-person comic narrative with a mock-heroic fight and a deliberate fairy-tale ending. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The History of Pendennis: His Fortunes and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy
altTitles: History of Pendennis: His Fortunes and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy
works.description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from November 1848 to December 1850, a semi-autobiographical Bildungsroman of a young gentleman of the 1830s-40s and the first of Thackeray's novels to be set in his own century.
works.plot: Arthur Pendennis, the son of a West Country doctor's widow, goes up to Oxbridge, gets into debt, is jilted in his first love for the actress Emily Fotheringay, and comes to London to read for the bar and to write for the press. His uncle Major Pendennis manages his social career and the family's fortune, and after a period of dissipation and a broken engagement to Blanche Amory, he marries his childhood friend Laura Bell and settles into the life of a country gentleman and a successful novelist.
works.significance: Pendennis is the most directly autobiographical of Thackeray's novels and the fullest English account of the making of a gentleman and a professional writer in the 1840s; it established the 'novel of a young man's education' as a vehicle for social criticism that Dickens, Trollope and Meredith all used.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The 1830s-40s: the Regency survivors who manage the young man's career, the press as a profession for gentlemen, the debts and bailiffs of the 'swell', and the literary market that Thackeray himself inhabited.
works.characters: Arthur Pendennis; Helen Pendennis; Major Pendennis; Laura Bell; Emily Fotheringay; Blanche Amory; George Warrington; Harry Foker; Dr Portman; Costigan
works.structure: The work is in 24 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
