works.title: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia
works.form: philosophical tale in the Oriental-fiction manner, drawing on early modern travel narrative
works.description: Johnson's philosophical tale, the briefest and most widely read of his works, in which a prince of Abyssinia escapes from the Happy Valley to try the possible forms of life and finds none sufficient. Its fable of choice - the inspection of marriage, trade, public life, religion, retirement and country solitude - is delivered in a style of proverbial compression. It was composed for a purpose Johnson's friends recorded and was published without his name on the title-page.
works.plot: Rasselas, secured in the Happy Valley among princes kept from the succession, flees with his sister Nekayah and the poet Imlac to see the world. They examine the conditions of happiness in turn - the court and its favours, the town and its commerce, marriage and the family, the country life, the scholar's solitude, the religious house - and each proves disappointed by jealousy, idleness, avarice or sorrow. The closing chapters assemble the travellers to report their conclusions and leave the choice of life undecided, commending instead the inquiry itself and the knowledge of human limits.
works.significance: Rasselas is the classic English example of the experiment-of-life tale and the standard literary statement of Johnson's doctrine that happiness cannot be found by choice alone; its Happy Valley became one of the most allusive places in English letters. Its treatment of religion, of suicide and of the inequality of conditions made it a work on which later readers tested their own opinions.
works.meter: Prose; balanced, abstract and strongly periodic, closer to the Rambler than to the novelistic manner of his contemporaries, with dialogue carried in sententious exchange.
works.context: Composed at the end of the 1750s, when Johnson was occupied with the Dictionary and the Idler papers and had recently suffered his mother's death; the Abyssinian setting draws on travel accounts of Ethiopia current in translation, and the tale's analysis of choice belongs to a decade of speculative fiction from Voltaire to the Scottish moralists.
works.characters: Rasselas; Nekayah; Imlac; the keepers of the Happy Valley; the hermit of the earlier chapters; Pekuah
works.structure: A short tale in 46 brief chapters: the escape from the Happy Valley, a middle sequence of experiments of life, and a closing symposium of reported conclusions, with little incident and much general reflection.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship was known among his friends and asserted in later editions, while the speed and occasion of composition are reported at second hand, so the composition dates here are approximate.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
themes: Fortune and mutability
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
The contemplative life
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: The History of Scotland
altTitles: History of Scotland, During the Reigns of Queen Mary and James VI
works.description: William Robertson's first great history, the narrative of Scotland under Mary and James VI that made its author the historian of the Scottish Enlightenment. Written from the state papers and the early writers, it recast the troubled sixteenth century as a school of constitutional and religious history.
works.plot: Robertson opens with an introduction on the ancient state of Scotland and then narrates the reign of Mary from her return from France: the Rizzio murder, the marriage to Bothwell, the collapse of her cause, and the abdication in favour of her infant son. The regencies and the education of James VI fill the middle books, with the lords, the reformed clergy, and the king's slow mastery of his churches and nobles. The closing volumes trace James's settling of the kirk and state and the succession question on the verge of the English inheritance. Throughout, Robertson's method is source-criticism, character judgment, and the political lesson that order grows out of the ruin of feudal power.
works.significance: It created the scholarly narrative of Mary and the Scottish reformation on which all later debate has worked, and set the style of philosophical history in Britain.
works.meter: The new periodic clarity of the Scottish Enlightenment: balanced paragraphs of fact and reflection, character portraits compressed into judgment-sentences.
works.context: Published in 1759 after years of charter and state-paper research among the Edinburgh literati, it made Robertson's reputation and led to his appointment as Historiographer Royal for Scotland.
works.characters: Mary Queen of Scots; James VI; Bothwell; John Knox; Elizabeth I
works.structure: A continuous political narrative in three volumes with prefatory discourses on the ancient state of Scotland and chronological tables.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The History of Sir Charles Grandison
altTitles: The History of Sir Charles Grandison. Written in a Series of Letters Between Some Respectable Persons
works.description: The third and least-tried epistolary novel of the series, a history of a perfect Christian gentleman and of the woman who might have married him, written partly in answer to the objection that the last hero had been a libertine. Its subject is the regulation of desire by honour within a family and a church.
works.plot: Harriet Byron, an heiress of principled modesty, is pursued by Sir Charles Grandison, whose suit is delayed by an Italian entanglement and the obstinacy of his sister. A rival relation attempts to carry her off and to marry her by surprise, and a bigamous Italian nobleman complicates the design. The several letters of the family and the friends sort out the errors, and the novel ends with Harriet refusing the imperfect suitor and remaining a single exemplar of conduct.
works.significance: It is the most complete attempt of the century to write a novel of positive exemplarity, and its failure to satisfy the readers of Clarissa became a lasting case study in the limits of exemplary fiction; it also transmitted the novelist's method to later domestic fiction.
works.meter: A polished and at times redundant prose of the polite letter, with the formal period and the moral tag; the variety of correspondents is marked by slight differences of idiom.
works.context: Published in 1753 after several years of composition and documentary preparation, in the same parliamentary season as the Jewish Naturalisation bill, whose antisemitic street violence the novelist watched and which the novel's character of the Jewish physician reflects.
works.characters: Sir Charles Grandison; Harriet Byron; the Grandison family; Mrs. Selby and her spying cousin; the Italian nobleman; the friends of the correspondence
works.structure: Epistolary narration by a circle of correspondents, with the heroine's letters framing a society rather than a single suspense; the Italian episodes slow the English plot and the ending is deliberately quiet.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the composition and publication are documented in the author's correspondence of the period.

Marriage and women's conduct
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct

works.title: The History of Sir Richard Calmady
works.description: Published in 1901 and the boldest English novel of heredity and disability: a man born with deformed legs and his fight for the right to love. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Lucas Malet; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Richard Calmady is born with his legs crushed in a hunting accident before his birth, and grows up beautiful, brilliant and mutilated; the novel follows his education, his struggle with his mother's possessive love, his travels, and his love for Honor Middleham, whom he refuses to marry because he believes his deformity makes him unfit for fatherhood, until he finally accepts his own body and his right to happiness.
works.significance: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is a landmark of English fiction about the body and one of the boldest novels of its decade: its frank treatment of disability, sexuality and the right to love made it a scandal and a succès, and it has been recovered as one of the most important English novels about physical difference.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rich, elaborate, slightly archaic prose.
works.context: 1901: the new science of heredity, the Victorian treatment of the disabled, the aesthetic cult of the beautiful body, and the English reception of Nietzsche. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Richard Calmady; Katherine Calmady; Honor Middleham; Julius March; Dr Knott; Lady Louisa; Roger Hensley
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The History of the Adventures of David Simple
works.form: novel; sentimental and exemplary prose fiction
works.description: The history of a young man of good nature who trusts the world to be like himself, written by a novelist who set out to improve the moral fiction of her brother's school by making sensibility the subject rather than the instrument. Its design is to show how an honest and credulous heart is tried by interest and flattery.
works.plot: David Simple, disinherited by a father's second marriage and thrown upon his own fortune, travels and lodges among a succession of friends and impostors, each testing his generosity. He is imposed upon by designing relations, tried by a false friendship and rewarded by a faithful one, and his sister's and his own loves are disentangled by discoveries. The narrative ends with the good established and the worldly exposed, the moral being that benevolence requires judgement.
works.significance: It is an early and influential statement of the cult of good nature in the novel, and one of the first English fictions to make a benevolent man's disappointment in the world its governing interest.
works.meter: An artless and colloquial prose, modelled on conversation and on the plain style, with the didactic summary at the close of the scene.
works.context: Published in 1743 in the season immediately following the comic histories, and written within the author's own family circle; the novel's theory of good nature answers the selfish-system philosophy then under debate.
works.characters: David Simple; his brother and his sister; the false friend and the true; the designing relations and the tried lovers
works.structure: Third-person episodic narration with a strong exemplary frame, the episodes arranged as trials of David's trust; dialogue carries most of the moral argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was published without a name at the first issue but was acknowledged within the family circle and by advertisement.

themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society

works.title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
altTitles: Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
works.description: Gibbon's monumental narrative of more than a thousand years of decay, from the age of the Antonines to the fall of Constantinople, the most famous work of history in English. Its first three volumes appeared in 1776 and the last three across the following twelve years, gathering a vast apparatus of learned annotation around the ironic grand narrative.
works.plot: Gibbon opens at the height of empire under the Antonines and shows the machinery of civilization destroyed by military anarchy, civil war, barbaric pressure, and the settlement of the northern peoples within the frontiers. He traces the triumph of the church and the establishment of Christianity as a historical revolution whose effects, monasticism and episcopal wealth, are recorded with searching irony, then follows the Eastern empire through the age of Justinian, the rise and conquests of Islam, and the long decline to the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453. The narrative alternates set-piece constitutional analysis, campaign history, and cultural description, and the celebrated chapters on the progress of the Christian religion make religion itself a subject of philosophical history. The concluding volumes survey the ruins, the republics of Italy, and the fall of the Greek empire, closing where modern Europe begins.
works.significance: It fixed the modern narrative of Rome's fall, made philosophical history the century's grandest genre, and remains the standard of ironic secular historiography; Gibbon's prose is the most quoted in English historical writing.
works.meter: The most imitated prose in the language: periodic historical sentences of balanced members closing in epigrammatic irony, with a second footnoted voice of learning.
works.context: Conceived among the Roman ruins in the early 1760s and written through the Lausanne and London years, the first volumes appeared in 1776 amid the American crisis; the ecclesiastical chapters, especially that on Julian, drew furious clerical replies and formal condemnations which Gibbon answered with ironical detachment.
works.characters: Marcus Antoninus; Constantine; Julian; Attila; Belisarius; Mahomet; Charlemagne
works.structure: Seventy-one chapters in six volumes, the first three carrying the western fall of 476 and the later three retreating into the eastern and mediaeval prospect, with retrospection and revision across the editions.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

works.title: The History of the Fairchild Family
works.form: juvenile and domestic tale; the religious family history for home instruction
works.description: The most famous and the most feared of the English books for children of the nineteenth century, a history of three children and of the religious discipline of their home, published in parts beginning in 1818 and long read in every family of the middle rank. It puts before the child the whole course of a pious day, the duty, the fault, the punishment, and the forgiveness, and it carries its lesson to the verge of the terrible.
works.plot: The history sets the Fairchild children in their house in the woods, with their father and mother as the governors of a little commonwealth of which the rule is the Bible and the catechism, and it follows their lessons, their work, their play, and their sins. Its central method is the severe object-lesson: the children are taken to the remains of the body of an executed criminal, that they may see what the wages of guilt come to; they are punished with a public severity which the modern reader finds hard, and they are taught to read, to give to the poor, to visit the cottages, and to consider their own hearts. The narrative passes through the illness and the death of one of the children, the trial of the survivors, the gipsy and the beggar episodes, and the steady government of the parents, whose religion is at once tenderness and terror. Later parts carry the family forward to the growth and the trials of the survivors, and the whole book is a manual of the discipline of the soul applied to the very young.
works.significance: It is the type and ancestor of the English religious family book for children, and one of the few children's books that has become a subject of cultural history in itself: its mixture of piety, fear, and the terrible object-lesson has been read ever since as the image of a whole method of governing the young, and its influence on the children's literature of both countries, and upon the nineteenth-century conscience about education, is very great.
works.meter: Plain, urgent, unembellished narrative prose of the devotional teacher, with the direct speech of children, the solemn parental address, and the inserted hymn and scripture; its effect rests on the plainness of the moral said.
works.context: Published from 1818 by the book-seller of the religious and the fashionable trade, in the season of the evangelical family and of the tract for the young, when the religious instruction of children at home was a serious concern of the middling ranks and when the theory of the child's depravity was taught as frankly as the theory of his innocence. Its author, an officer's wife returned from India, had already written the little Indian tale, and the Fairchild books were followed by the third part and by imitations without number.
works.characters: Mr and Mrs Fairchild; Lucy, Emily, and Henry Fairchild; the poor, the gipsy people, and the dependents of the neighbourhood; the survivors of the family in the later parts
works.structure: A continuous family history in numbered chapters, published in parts and in volumes, each part a sequence of the occasions of the home, the lesson, the fault, and the consequence, with the hymns and the readings bound into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single pen is uncontested; the book is nevertheless a long series rather than a fixed text, since the later parts were given out at a great interval after the first, and the many abridgements, the edited and the expurgated issues of the later century alter the text materially, so that the work is cited by part and by edition.

Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: The History of the Peninsular War
altTitles: History of the Peninsular War, which invaded Portugal in 1807
works.form: Military and political history in the narrative manner of the period, combining official-document editing with eyewitness inquiry.
works.description: The author's monumental narrative of the war in Spain and Portugal, written from official despatches, Portuguese and Spanish sources, and the testimony of officers he interviewed at first hand. It is at once a campaign history, a defence of the Spanish and Portuguese peoples, and a partisan account of British conduct of the war. As laureate and as an old Iberian traveller, its author made the subject his own.
works.plot: The work begins with Junot's march into Portugal in 1807 and the convention of Cintra, and follows the war through Moore's retreat, Wellington's campaigns, the Sieges of Badajoz and Ciudad Rodrigo, Salamanca, Vitoria and the Pyrenees. It gives equal space to the guerrilla and to the popular rising of 1808, insisting that the peninsula's own resistance, not British generalship alone, wore the French down. It also weighs the politics of the Cortes of Cadiz, the regency, and the restored Ferdinand VII, whose treatment of his liberators the historian records with bitterness. The final volumes carry the narrative to the close of the war and the French expedition of 1823, with copious notes on sources and on disputed dates.
works.significance: The authoritative English account of the Peninsular War for a generation and a key text of romantic-era nationalism and liberal sympathy for Spain; it also documents how a poet of the 1790s turned the historical method he had learned in Brazil against the diplomacy of the Restoration.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written in the long peace after Waterloo, when the Peninsular War was being absorbed into national memory and into Wellington's monument, and when the Holy Alliance's intervention in Spain in 1823 made the recent past an immediate political issue.
works.structure: Multi-volume chronological campaign history with substantial notes, appendices of despatches and returns, and recurring interpretive chapters on Spanish and Portuguese politics.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Warfare and battle

works.title: The History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
altTitles: The Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
works.description: Ferguson's narrative history of Rome from its agricultural and citizen origins through conquest, civil discord, and the loss of the republic, written by the philosopher of civil society as its practical case study. It showed how the virtues that built Rome, martial spirit and public ambition, dissolved the very constitution they had founded.
works.plot: The history opens on the earliest ages, Rome's peasant militia, patrician families, and kingless commonwealth, and follows the struggle of the orders as the engine of Roman liberty. It narrates the progress of conquest, the agrarian laws, the rise of the commons and their leaders, the civil wars of Marius, Sylla, Pompey, and Caesar, and the final extinction of the republic under Augustus. Ferguson treats the dissolution not as a mere conspiracy of great men but as the structural outcome of empire without civic capacity, the corruption of the people, and the army's transfer of loyalty from the state to its generals, closing with reflections on the fate of free states.
works.significance: It became the standard Scottish reading of Rome's fall as a lesson in the political sociology of liberty, much admired in its day and read by the founders of the American republic as a mirror of corrupt commonwealths.
works.meter: A declamatory, periodic prose in the manner of the classical historians, its judgment-sentences modelled on the moralities of republican rise and decline.
works.context: Published in Edinburgh and London in 1769, a work of Edinburgh lecture culture and of the age's Roman republicanism, written in the same years as the Wilkes and parliamentary debates that made the fate of free states a live British subject.
works.characters: Romulus; the Gracchi; Marius; Sylla; Pompey; Caesar; Cicero; Augustus
works.structure: Four books of continuous narrative from the regal and early republican ages to the establishment of the monarchy under Augustus, with inserted institutional and moral reflections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The History of the Reign of the Emperor Charles V
altTitles: History of the Reign of Charles V
works.description: Robertson's imperial history of Charles V and the European states system, built on the Habsburg archival and printed materials he was among the first English historians to exploit. It made the age of the Reformation and the Habsburg-Valois wars intelligible as the birth of the modern balance of power, and became the most admired British history of the decade in several languages.
works.plot: Robertson narrates the accession and inheritance of Charles, the rivalries with Francis I of France, the Turkish pressure on the empire, and the German religious division from Luther to the Peace of Augsburg, showing how the dream of universal monarchy collapsed against the particular liberties of princes and nations. He treats the Reformation as high politics: the leagues, the diets, the councils, the Schmalkaldic War, and the emperor's eventual weariness and abdication. The narrative constantly weighs the springs of state, the expedients of finance, and the maxims of a balancing Europe, in set-pieces on the constitutions of the continent. The history ends on the divided inheritance and the modern states system it left behind.
works.significance: It defined the age of Charles V for generations of English readers, established the balance-of-power narrative of modern European history, and stood among the most admired works of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.meter: The mature philosophical style: capacious periods, weighty antithesis, and the judgment of cabinets, a prose of authority with a moralist's poise.
works.context: Published in 1769 after Robertson's appointment as Historiographer Royal and years of archival research; it was translated into French, Italian, and German and read as a textbook of statecraft in the Atlantic world.
works.characters: Charles V; Francis I; Henry VIII; Luther; the princes of the Schmalkaldic League; Suleiman the Magnificent
works.structure: A continuous political and military narrative in several volumes, with separate disquisitions on the state of Europe appended in the later editions.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade, by the British Parliament
altTitles: History of the Abolition of the Slave Trade
The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the Slave-Trade
works.form: Abolitionist history and documentary testimony: a large-scale argumentative narrative built from evidence, correspondence and reported examination, in the tradition of the state-of-the-question pamphlet enlarged to history.
works.description: A monumental two-volume documentary history of the British abolition movement, written by its chief investigator and published immediately after the abolition of the trade. It combines personal narrative, evidence gathered from ships' papers and slave testimony, and the argumentative history of a quarter-century of agitation. Its purpose is at once evidential and exemplary: to prove what the trade was, and to show how a moral crusade succeeded through organisation, enquiry and patient publication.
works.plot: The work opens on the geography, commerce and human character of Africa and then documents the mechanism of the trade with an accumulating mass of testimony about the Middle Passage and the West India colonies. It traces the formation of the abolitionist committees, the parallel histories of the movement in the United States and France, the failure of the first parliamentary bills, and the long process by which public opinion, county petitions and seamen's evidence were assembled. The narrative closes with the passing of the abolition act, which the author reads as the accomplishment of a moral revolution carried out by the British people. Throughout, the author's own research interviews and voyages of enquiry function as the movement's first documented fieldwork.
works.significance: It is the foundational documentary history of British abolition and one of the largest works of argumentative prose in Romantic-period reform writing, a model for the movement's later reliance on accumulated testimony. Its evidence remains a standard source for the history of the slave trade and its critique of commercial innocence speaks to Romantic writing about empire, sympathy and the moral economics of consumption.
works.meter: Prose of plain, earnest periodicity, with long quoted evidence passages; no verse.
works.context: Written after twenty years of enquiry, petitions and pamphlet war and published in the year the abolition act took effect, at a moment when the movement needed both a record and a defence against planter counter-argument. It preserves evidence collected earlier and answers sceptics who claimed the trade was humane or economically necessary.
works.structure: Chronological and evidential history in two volumes, with books within volumes: state-of-Africa and state-of-the-trade material first, then the agitational history, then the parliamentary accomplishment; documentation and testimony are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is certain and the work is signed; its factual claims have been tested by later historians, with some corrections to dates and roles, but the work itself is not disputed.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
The slave trade and abolition
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge
works.description: Thomas Sprat's official history of the Royal Society, commissioned by the Society itself, which defends the new experimental philosophy against its critics and sets out the ideal of a plain, unadorned prose suited to the reporting of fact.
works.plot: Part I surveys the history of learning and the corruption of philosophy; part II describes the Society's constitution, methods, and achievements; part III answers the objections of the schools, the wits, and the clergy.
works.significance: The principal source for the early history of the Royal Society and the classic statement of the ideal of plain prose that dominated English non-fiction for a century; it has been a touchstone in the history of scientific writing.
works.meter: Elegant but plain prose; the famous passage on the Society's resolution to reject 'swelling of style' and to use 'a close, naked, natural way of speaking' became the manifesto of the plain style.
works.context: Published in 1667, five years after the Society's charter; Sprat was a chaplain and Fellow who had access to the Society's records and to Evelyn and Wren.
works.characters: Francis Bacon; Charles II; the Fellows of the Royal Society
works.structure: Three parts in a continuous history and defence.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sprat; the work was commissioned and corrected by the Society.

works.title: The History of the World
works.description: Ralegh's great history, written during his imprisonment in the Tower: the story of the world from the Creation to the end of the Macedonian empire, told as the record of God's providence over kingdoms — with the famous preface's meditation on death ('O eloquent, just, and mighty Death!') and the running argument that the wise man serves God, not fortune.
works.plot: The five books move from the Creation and the patriarchs through Egypt, Assyria, and Persia to Greece and Alexander; the rise and fall of each empire demonstrates the providence that raises and casts down; and the closing books and the preface frame the whole as counsel to princes and consolation to the prisoner.
works.significance: The great English history of the Renaissance — the prisoner's summa of providence and power that Milton and Cromwell's generation read as scripture of state.
works.meter: Prose of grave sententiousness — the prison's composure in every period.
works.context: Written 1603–14 in the Tower, dedicated to Prince Henry, and published in 1614; James I is said to have disliked it as 'too saucy in censuring princes', and the book was suppressed after Ralegh's fall.
works.characters: Adam; Noah; Moses; the kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Persia; Alexander the Great; the historical actors of the five books
works.structure: A universal chronicle in the classical and biblical tradition, organized by empire, with the author's moral reflections interlacing the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Kingship and good rule
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)

works.title: The History of the Worthies of England
works.description: Fuller's great county-by-county biographical and antiquarian survey of the notable men and women of England, with descriptions of each county's natural resources, wonders, and families; it was published posthumously in 1662.
works.plot: Each county is treated in a uniform sequence: its natural commodities, manufactures, wonders, battles, families, and memorable persons, with biographical notices of its 'worthies'.
works.significance: A foundational work of English local history and biography, and the source for countless later antiquarians; it remains in use as a biographical reference.
works.meter: Fuller's characteristically digressive, witty, and compressed prose.
works.context: Written during the Commonwealth and published in 1662, after Fuller's death in 1661; it is the first systematic topographical and biographical dictionary of England.
works.structure: An alphabetical arrangement by county with a general introduction.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Fuller; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
works.form: comic novel in prose, in the manner of a comic epic in eighteen books
works.description: The author's masterpiece and the most completely designed English novel of the century, the history of a foundling's education in good-nature and in error, from the country house of his benefactor through the road and the great city to the discovery of his birth. Each of its eighteen books opens with a chapter of critical preface.
works.plot: Tom, an unknown child taken in by the wealthy Allworthy, grows up generous, hot-blooded and imprudent, and is opposed by the artful Blifil and instructed by the tutor Thwackum and Square. His love for Sophia is cross'd by her family's design on her for another; he is expelled, she runs away, and both travel to London by separate adventures. There Tom's errors culminate in an imprisonment and a near-execution, and the discovery that he is Allworthy's own sister's son clears his title to the estate and to Sophia.
works.significance: It is the touchstone of the theory of the novel as a formally ordered art, its design and its analysis of good-nature and prudence setting the terms of discussion from the eighteenth century to modern criticism.
works.meter: A commanding narrative prose of balanced period and pointed irony, capable of the colloquial energy of the road and the oratory of the prefatory essays; dialogue is sharply differentiated by class and profession.
works.context: Composed after the author's marriage and during his essays on administration and society, and published in 1749 in the season of the riotous rejoicing over the peace and of the street disturbances which the novel's London scenes use.
works.characters: Tom Jones; Squire Allworthy; Blifil; Sophia Western; Mrs. Western; Thwackum; Square; Lady Bellaston; Jenny Jones and her husband
works.structure: Eighteen books in three great movements - country, road, London - with a doubled chronology and an elaborate chain of discoveries; the prefatory chapters form a parallel argument on the writing of comic history.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in his correspondence and in the contemporary reviews.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel

Country retirement and the estate poem

Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art

works.title: The Hobbit; or, There and Back Again
altTitles: Hobbit; or, There and Back Again
works.description: Bilbo Baggins, the dwarves and the dragon: the quest of the Lonely Mountain. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by J. R. R. Tolkien; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Bilbo Baggins, the hobbit of Bag End, is taken by Gandalf into the company of thirteen dwarves and the quest of the treasure of the Lonely Mountain; the road carries him through trolls, goblins, Gollum and the riddles in the dark, the elves of Mirkwood and the dragon Smaug, to the Battle of Five Armies and the return to the Shire.
works.significance: The Hobbit is the founding text of the modern high fantasy for children and the door into The Lord of the Rings: its hobbit, its dragon and its riddles in the dark gave the invented world its grammar and made the quest romance the dominant mode of twentieth-century fantasy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it.
works.context: The invented Middle-earth of the Third Age, published in London in 1937. The record dates the work as composed between 1930 and 1936 and first published in 1937 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Bilbo Baggins; Gandalf; Thorin Oakenshield; Smaug; Gollum; Bard; the Elvenking; Balin
works.structure: A quest romance in nineteen chapters, from the unexpected party to the last stage. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Ronald Reuel Tolkien. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale
themes: Childhood, the nursery, and the Edwardian idyll
Myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination
The absurd, the void, and the failure of meaning

works.title: The Hole in the Wall
works.form: Novel; detective story, first issued in 1902
works.description: Published in 1902 and Morrison's best late novel: a crime novel of the Wapping riverside, told by the boy who comes to live at his grandfather's tavern, the Hole in the Wall. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Arthur Morrison; it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Young Stephen Kemp, sent after his mother's death to live with his grandfather Captain Nat, landlord of the Hole in the Wall at Wapping, watches the riverside underworld close around the tavern: Marr, the shipowner whose fraud drowned Stephen's father, absconds with the firm's money and is waylaid by the bully Dan Ogle in a thieves' den; the pocket-book of notes falls into Captain Nat's hands; and Ogle, Musky Mag, the blind fiddler Blind George and Marr's betrayed partner Viney all scheme to recover it, while the old man turns a new bitterness on the men who ruined his son.
works.significance: The Hole in the Wall is one of the finest English novels of the Thames and the docks, and a key example of the child's-eye detective narrative that would be developed by Dickens's and Stevenson's successors.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care.
works.context: The 1900s, the Port of London and its river trades, the London docks and their casual labour, and the child witness in the English courts. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.
works.characters: Stephen Kemp (the narrator); Captain Nat Kemp, his grandfather; Marr; Viney; Dan Ogle; Musky Mag; Blind George
works.structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

themes: Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will

Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations

works.title: The Holy Fair
works.form: comic-descriptive tale-poem with allegorical debate, in the Scottish rambling tradition of Ramsay's Christ's Kirk
works.description: Burns's great comic survey of a Church of Scotland communion preaching in the open air, in which the religious solemnity of the Holy Fair is matched against the thronging, drinking, courting and quarrelling of the field. The poem frames the scene as the vision of a ploughman homeward on a moonlit night, and lets three personae of the fair - religion, interest and fancy - contend for the meaning of what he has seen. It is the most complete poetic record of Scottish communion-season culture and one of the most sustained satires of enthusiasm in the century.
works.plot: The poet, riding homeward at moonlight, recalls the scene of the preaching: the crowd spread over the braes, the preacher working the auditors with the terrors of the law and the glories of the gospel, the professional religionists scanning each other for signs of grace, and the young people making their own business of the day. The allegorical voices of Religion, Interest and Fancy then dispute the event, Religion pleading for the seriousness of the doctrine, Interest for its worldly uses, and Fancy for the human spectacle of appetite and mirth. The poem closes with the ploughman's sober re-entry into common life, leaving the value of the fair undecided.
works.significance: It supplies the classic literary account of the Scottish communion season and remains a primary source for the social history of Scottish popular religion. Its mixture of dialect realism, allegory and comic detachment made it a landmark of the preromantic interest in vernacular popular spectacle, and its portraits of the preacher and of the audit of grace have become standard.
works.meter: Stanzaic Scots in long running measures of four- and three-beat lines with a brisk rhyme and much colloquial idiom, adapted to the tune known as Cherry and Cream; the allegorical sections keep the same narrative pace.
works.context: Rooted in the communion preachings of the Ayrshire and Scottish west, seasonal events that drew thousands to the fields and were notorious for their profane diversions, and in the contemporary debate about enthusiasm, Methodist and evangelical preaching and the suspicion of religious enthusiasm. Burns's own experience of the revival at Kirkoswald and his acquaintance with the lay preaching of the period give the poem its technical accuracy.
works.characters: The ploughman-speaker; the preacher of the sermon; the sitters of the audit; Religion, Interest and Fancy as speaking abstractions; the courting country folk
works.structure: A framed narrative: a moonlit opening scene with the ploughman, the long descriptive middle on the preaching and the crowd, an allegorical tripartite dispute, and a brief closing retirement of the spectator.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns revised the poem across editions and his authorship of the earlier and later states of the text is documented in his correspondence and memoranda. The precise date of first composition is not fixed, and the range entered here follows the usual scholarly reckoning.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

works.title: The Holy Grail and Other Poems
works.form: Arthurian idylls and poems; pastoral elegy
works.description: Published in 1869, containing 'The Holy Grail', 'The Coming of Arthur', 'The Passing of Arthur' and 'Pelleas and Ettarre': the volume in which the Arthurian epic was given its spiritual centre and its frame.
works.plot: 'The Holy Grail' narrates the Grail vision and the quest that breaks the Round Table, told by Percivale to a monk; 'The Coming of Arthur' establishes the founding myth; 'The Passing of Arthur' narrates the last battle and Bedivere's return of Excalibur.
works.significance: 'The Holy Grail' is the supreme Victorian treatment of the Grail legend and the moment at which the Idylls became a sustained critique of spiritual ambition as a force that dissolves human community; it is also the poem in which Tennyson's blank verse reaches its most incantatory.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.
works.context: The 1860s and the Victorian fascination with the Grail (the 1869 volume coincided with the Pre-Raphaelite and Wagnerian treatments), the religious doubt of the period and the poem's answer in the vision granted only to the pure.
works.characters: King Arthur; Guinevere; Sir Percivale and Ambrosius the monk ('The Holy Grail'); Galahad; Lancelot; Bors; Gawain; Percivale's sister, the holy nun; Pelleas and Ettarre; King Leodogran and Bellicent ('The Coming of Arthur'); Sir Bedivere ('The Passing of Arthur')
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alfred, Lord Tennyson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.description: Thomas Fuller's most popular work, a book of 'characters' describing the ideal states of the church, the family, the court, and the commonwealth, followed by the contrary vices of the profane state.

works.context: Published in 1642, on the eve of the civil wars, and dedicated to the Lady Montagu; it was reprinted throughout the century.
works.characters: the good parson; the good husband; the good magistrate; the good soldier; the good merchant; their profane opposites
works.structure: A series of short character-pieces followed by a historical narrative.

works.title: The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World
works.description: Bunyan's second great allegory, a military and spiritual epic of the town of Mansoul, built by Shaddai, captured by Diabolus, and recovered by his son Emmanuel; it is a complex allegory of the soul's fall and redemption.
works.plot: Shaddai builds Mansoul and gives it law; Diabolus besieges and takes it; Emmanuel, Shaddai's son, wages war to recover it, captures and pardons the town, and appoints officers; Diabolus returns by stealth and the town must be continually defended.
works.significance: Bunyan's most ambitious and most learned allegory, and a major work of Puritan theology in narrative form; it has been judged more complex but less popular than The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Plain prose with an elaborate allegorical nomenclature and occasional verses.
works.context: Published in 1682 with a copperplate frontispiece, four years after Part I of The Pilgrim's Progress, and dedicated to the reader in an allegorical address.

works.title: The Honest Whore, Part 1
works.description: Dekker and Middleton's comedy of conversion: the courtesan Bellafront, courted by all Milan, is converted to virtue by the grief of her rejected suitor Hippolito; the madhouse of Bethlehem, where her father Anselmo feigns madness to save her, supplies the play's great scene; and the play ends with her marriage to the patient Matheo — the first part of the diptych continued in Part 2 (c. 1605).
works.plot: Bellafront plies her trade until Hippolito's lament and her father's disguise break her heart; her conversion, the testing of her suitors, and the schemes of the pander and the courtiers follow; the scene in Bedlam, with the madmen's pageant of the city's vices, is the play's moral centre; and the final act restores Bellafront to marriage and her father to peace.
works.significance: The great Elizabethan-Jacobean comedy of conversion — the play that made the 'honest whore' a type of the English stage's moral theatre.
works.meter: Prose and verse in the two authors' distinct registers, with the madmen's speeches as the play's most quoted passages.
works.context: Performed by Prince Henry's Men in 1604 and printed the same year; the Bedlam scene answered the vogue for madhouse shows, and the play's reform of the whore answered the city's moralists.
works.characters: Bellafront; Hippolito; Matheo; Anselmo (disguised as the madman); Candido the linen-draper; the Duke of Milan; Infelice; Fluello; Castruccio; Pioratto; the madmen of Bedlam
works.structure: A five-act comedy of conversion built on the two great set pieces — the madhouse and the conversion — with the Duke's disguised progress through the city as frame.
works.attributionNotes: By Dekker and Middleton jointly, as printed; the division of scenes is debated.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
Women, chastity, and constancy

works.title: The Hopes of the Human Race, Hereafter and Here
altTitles: Hopes of the Human Race, Hereafter and Here
works.description: Published in 1874 and Cobbe's most systematic work of religious speculation: an argument for a moral universe that survives the collapse of orthodox Christian doctrine. It is a prose work of 1874 by Frances Power Cobbe; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Cobbe examines the evidence for immortality, the problem of evil, the future of the human race and the moral argument for a progressive afterlife, and defends a theism grounded in conscience rather than revelation or miracle.
works.significance: The Hopes of the Human Race is a central text of Victorian unorthodox theism and one of the first attempts to construct a post-Christian ethics on evolutionary lines; it shows the intellectual range of the feminist movement and its refusal to accept the simple choice between orthodoxy and unbelief.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the documented essay with statistics and case evidence.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian crisis of faith, the spread of secularism, and the new spiritualism. The record dates the work as composed in 1874 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
works.description: Serialised in the Strand from August 1901 and published in 1902, set before the Reichenbach Falls: the most famous of all detective novels, and the one that fuses the ratiocinative plot with the Gothic horror of the moor.
works.plot: Sir Charles Baskerville dies of fright on the moor, and Holmes sends Watson to Devon with Sir Henry Baskerville; the hound is a painted and phosphorescent animal kept by the naturalist Stapleton, a Baskerville descendant, who hopes to inherit the estate. Holmes arrives, the hound is shot, and Stapleton is lost in the Grimpen Mire.
works.significance: The Hound of the Baskervilles is the most widely read detective novel in English and the great English example of the Gothic detective story; its moor, its hound and its rational explanation of a supernatural legend are the classic statement of the genre's double logic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is the clue and the deduction.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, Dartmoor and its legends, the Victorian folklore of the spectral hound, and the naturalist's collecting culture. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Sir Henry Baskerville; Stapleton; Beryl Stapleton; Dr Mortimer; Laura Lyons; Selden; Sir Charles Baskerville
works.structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Hour and the Man: A Historical Romance
altTitles: Hour and the Man: A Historical Romance
works.description: Published in 1841 and the first English novel to take a black revolutionary as its hero: a fictional life of Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian revolution. It is a prose fiction work of 1841 by Harriet Martineau; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Toussaint, the former slave who becomes the leader of the revolution in Saint-Domingue, is shown in council, in battle and in his household, and the novel follows the uprising, the French expedition of 1802 and Toussaint's betrayal and death in the prison of Fort de Joux.
works.significance: The Hour and the Man is the founding English novel of the Haitian revolution and the first substantial fictional treatment of a black leader in English literature; it was read by abolitionists on both sides of the Atlantic and marks the limit of what a British novelist in 1841 could say about slave revolution.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the exemplary narrative with a documented argument.
works.context: The 1790s, the Haitian revolution, the abolitionist movement of the 1830s-40s, and the British emancipation of 1833. The record dates the work as composed between 1840 and 1841 and first published in 1841 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; social inquiry and the documented survey.

works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: The House Behind the Cedars
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1900
works.description: Published in 1900 and the classic American novel of racial passing: the story of a brother and sister who pass for white in South Carolina and of the catastrophe that follows. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Rena Walden, of mixed race and fair enough to pass, joins her brother John, now the white lawyer John Warwick, in the South Carolina town of Clarence and is courted by the well-born George Tryon; when he discovers her origin he abandons her, and, pursued both by the repentant Tryon and by the predatory Jeff Wain, she flees into the swamp and is carried home by her faithful friend Frank Fowler to die of brain fever.
works.significance: The House Behind the Cedars is the central American novel of passing and a key text in the literature of race: its treatment of the tragedy of racial classification made it the model for the twentieth-century American novel of passing from Larsen to Roth.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.
works.context: 1900: the South Carolina of the 1890s, the one-drop rule and the racial law of the American South. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under sensation novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Rena Walden; John Walden (John Warwick), her brother; Molly Walden, their mother; George Tryon; Frank Fowler; Jeff Wain
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The House by the Churchyard
works.description: Published in 1863 and the strangest of Le Fanu's long novels: a mystery of eighteenth-century Dublin and Chapelizod, built on a buried body, a disputed will and a ghost. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The novel moves between the garrison town of Chapelizod and the Dublin of the 1760s, where the murder of a man in the churchyard, the fate of the beautiful Miss Gertrude Chattesworth and the schemes of the sinister Dangerfield are gradually explained.
works.significance: The House by the Churchyard is Le Fanu's most Irish book and the fullest fictional picture of eighteenth-century Dublin life; it influenced Joyce, who cited it in Finnegans Wake, and it is a key text in the Irish regional novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor.
works.context: The 1760s, the Dublin garrison, the Irish Protestant gentry, and the Irish folklore of the banshee and the haunted churchyard. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: The House in Dorset
works.form: Novel (the Dorset house and the inheritance)
works.description: The novel of the Dorset house: the inheritance, the woman and the land. It is a prose fiction work of 1920 by Mary Webb; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The House in Dorset follows the woman who inherits the Dorset house and the land, and the quarrel of the inheritance with the man and the county, in the charged prose of the nature romance.
works.significance: The House in Dorset carried Mary Webb's nature romance from Shropshire to Dorset: its house and its inheritance are the standard text of her novel of the land and the woman.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather.
works.context: Dorset in the years after the war. The record dates the work as composed in 1919 and first published in 1920 and it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the inheritor; the man; the county; the house
works.structure: A novel of the inheritance in chapters of the house and the land. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The House in Paris
works.description: Bowen's novel of the divided generations: a Paris house, a secret and two children. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Elizabeth Bowen; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Two children meet in a house in Paris in 1934 — Henrietta and Leopold, who is waiting to meet his mother — and the novel goes back to the story of Leopold's parents, Karen and Max, in 1914, in a study of love, betrayal and inheritance.
works.significance: The House in Paris is one of Bowen's finest novels and the great English novel of the divided generations: its structure, its Paris house and its portrait of the illegitimate child made it one of the central novels of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the image that carries the emotion.
works.context: Paris in 1914 and 1934, and the English and French upper classes between the wars. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Henrietta; Leopold; Karen Michaelis; Max Ebhart; Naomi Fisher; Mme Fisher
works.structure: A novel in three parts, moving between 1934 and 1914. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The House of Fame
works.description: Chaucer's comic dream vision of fame and rumour (2,158 lines in octosyllabic couplets, unfinished): the dreamer is carried by a talkative eagle through the heavens to the House of Fame, where the goddess dispenses reputation with sublime arbitrariness, and on to the whirling House of Rumour where every report, true and false, takes wing. A poem about poetry, authority, and the instability of language itself.
works.plot: The dreamer, pondering the causes of dreams and the nature of fame, finds himself in a temple of Venus adorned with the story of the Aeneid; an eagle (comically garrulous, in the Dantean manner) snatches him up and lectures him on sound, air, and the physics of speech; before the House of Fame he sees the petitioners — great and small — receive arbitrary reward or oblivion; and in the twig-built, whirling House of Rumour every tiding breeds and flies; the poem breaks off as 'a man of gret auctorite' appears.
works.significance: The most brilliant medieval English poem about poetry, fame, and the circulation of language; its self-reflexive comedy anticipates the metacritical concerns of modern literature.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with colloquial verve; the eagle's lecture burlesques the didactic mode.
works.context: Composed c. 1378–80, during Chaucer's Italian-inspired middle period, drawing on Dante, Virgil, Ovid, and Boethius; the invocation promises tidings 'of love or such thinges glade' — a tease never fulfilled.
works.characters: the Dreamer (Geffrey); the Eagle; Fame; Aeolus; the suitors of Fame; the 'man of great authority'
works.structure: Three movements (the temple of Venus; the eagle's flight and lecture; the houses of Fame and Rumour), with the Aeneid and the physics of sound as its digressive armature.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure.
themes: Fortune and mutability

works.title: The House of Mirth
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1905 and the novel that made Wharton famous: the destruction of a beautiful woman who cannot bring herself to sell herself in the marriage market. It is a prose fiction work of 1905 by Edith Wharton; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Lily Bart, a beautiful but poor member of old New York society, is caught between the need for a rich husband and her refusal to marry a man she does not love; a series of social mishaps and her own fatal indecision strip her of her position, her friends and her last chances, and she dies alone in a shabby boarding-house, having taken an overdose of sleeping medicine.
works.significance: The House of Mirth is the central American novel of the marriage market and the first great American novel of a woman's social destruction: its portrait of Lily Bart is one of the great American characters, and its analysis of the economics of marriage made it the founding text of the American novel of manners.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is precise, ironic exposition of a social world.
works.context: 1905: the New York of the Knickerbocker aristocracy, the 'dollar princess' marriages to European titles, the new rich of the Gilded Age, and the American debate on women's work. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1905 and first published in 1905 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.

works.title: The House of the Seven Gables
altTitles: The House of the Seven Gables: A Romance
works.description: Published in 1851 and the most formally perfect of Hawthorne's novels: the story of an ancient Salem house, a family curse, and the working out of an ancestral crime in the present. It is a prose fiction work of 1851 by Nathaniel Hawthorne; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Hepzibah Pyncheon, poor and proud, opens a shop in the ancestral house; her brother Clifford returns from thirty years in prison for a murder he did not commit, and the family is haunted by the curse of the wizard Maule and by the greed of the judge who bears the Pyncheon name. The novel ends with the curse lifted and the lovers Phoebe and Holgrave united.
works.significance: The House of the Seven Gables is the great American novel of the ancestral house and of the burden of the past on the present; its combination of Gothic romance and comic realism is unique in American fiction, and its treatment of photography and mesmerism makes it a key text of the nineteenth-century American imagination.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The year 1850, Salem and its decayed gentility, the American belief in progress and the railroad, and the mesmerism and photography of the 1840s. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1851 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

works.title: The House with the Green Shutters
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The novel that ended the kailyard: a small-town tyrant, his broken son, and the ruin of a house. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by George Douglas Brown; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: John Gourlay, the bullying carrier of Barbie, builds a house with green shutters to outface the town; his son is sent to Edinburgh and fails, his business is ruined by a rival, and the novel ends with the destruction of the family in a scene of drunken violence and suicide.
works.significance: The House with the Green Shutters is the most important Scottish novel of the period and the book that ended the kailyard: its unsparing realism, its tragic structure and its refusal of sentiment founded the modern Scottish novel and made it the direct ancestor of Lewis Grassic Gibbon.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the objective, unsentimental narrative.
works.context: A small Ayrshire town at the end of the nineteenth century, and the commercial rivalries of the Scottish provinces. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; naturalist and determinist novel.

works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the building of the house to the family's destruction. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.

works.title: The Housing Lark
works.description: A comic novel of West Indian London, published by MacGibbon & Kee in 1965, in which Battersby and his friends try to pool their savings to buy a house. The Lynne Rienner synopsis calls it Selvon's fifth novel; by the dates of the first editions it is his sixth.
works.summary: A scheme to buy a house together, and the gatherings, outings and quarrels of the West Indians drawn into it.
works.plot: Faced with unscrupulous and racist landlords, Battersby, a West Indian exile in London, and his rakish friends hatch a scheme to pool their money for a place of their own, but it does not go as planned (Caribbean Beat). The search for decent, affordable shelter brings hardships and comic situations and shows the exiles' dealings with English women, with the British in general and with one another (Lynne Rienner synopsis). The Northern Arizona University essay notes that the lark remains a lark to Battersby but becomes a grim commitment for Jean, and that at a community fete the Indo-Trinidadian Syl, asked why he does not go back to India, answers, 'Brit'n is my country'.
works.significance: Selvon's second novel of West Indian London; reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, in 1990.
works.meter: Caribbean Beat calls it a cheeky comedy of a West Indian exile's search for shelter.
works.context: Set in London in the early 1960s, when West Indian migrants met discrimination from landlords; published in 1965.
works.characters: Battersby ('Bat'), who devises the scheme; Syl, an Indo-Trinidadian; Jean
works.structure: An ensemble comedy organised around the house-buying scheme.

works.title: The Hunting of the Snark: An Agony in Eight Fits
altTitles: Hunting of the Snark: An Agony in Eight Fits
works.form: Nonsense poem in eight fits; nonsense verse
works.description: Published in 1876 and the greatest long nonsense poem in English: the voyage of a Bellman, a Baker, a Butcher, a Barrister, a Billiard-marker, a Banker, a Beaver, a Boots and a Bonnet-maker in search of a creature that may not exist.
works.plot: The crew sails with a map that is a blank, a rule that the Snark may be a Boojum, and the Baker's warning that if the Snark is a Boojum he will 'softly and suddenly vanish away'; the Baker finds the Snark, discovers it is a Boojum, and vanishes.
works.significance: The Hunting of the Snark is the most philosophically serious nonsense poem in English: it is at once an allegory of scientific pursuit, of the search for meaning and of the fear of annihilation, and it has never been fully explained, which is its point.
works.meter: Fourteen-line stanzas of anapaestic tetrameter and trimeter with the rhyme-scheme of 'The Lady of Shalott'.
works.context: The 1870s, the Victorian culture of exploration and classification, and the philosophical debate about the reality of the external world. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: The Bellman; the Baker; the Butcher; the Barrister; the Banker; the Beaver; the Billiard-marker; the Boots; the Bonnet-maker
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.

works.title: The Husband's Message
works.description: An elegiac poem of 54 lines in which a wooden rune-stave, carved with a message, speaks on behalf of an exiled lord to the woman he loves, recalling their former vows and summoning her to join him across the sea.
works.plot: The stave tells how its lord was forced into exile by a feud, how he longs for his lady, and how he now sends word that he has wealth and a hall prepared for her; the poem closes with a runic passage (often solved as 'sige', 'rad', and other rune-names) promising their reunion and the renewal of their vows.
works.significance: An early and sophisticated use of the speaking-object device and of runic writing as poetic material.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, following the riddles; often paired with The Wife's Lament as complementary perspectives on exile and separated love.
works.characters: the rune-stave (speaker); the lord; the lady
works.structure: A speaking object (prosopopoeia) delivers the lord's message; the closing runic riddle has prompted attempts to read the poem as part of a composite sequence with the riddles that follow it in the manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Idea of a University
altTitles: The Idea of a University Defined and Illustrated
works.form: Lectures and essays (Dublin, 1852; collected 1873 with the 1858 essays)
works.description: The lectures delivered in Dublin in 1852 as rector of the new Catholic University, revised and collected with additional essays in 1873: the classic English defence of liberal education, and the source of the modern idea of the university.
works.plot: Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, that the university is a place of teaching universal knowledge rather than of research or of professional training, that theology must be included among the sciences, and that the educated gentleman is the product of a liberal education; the later essays add the argument for the study of literature.
works.significance: The Idea of a University is the founding text of the modern debate on the purpose of higher education; its doctrine of knowledge as its own end and its portrait of the gentleman shaped the ideal of liberal education in England and America, and its argument against the purely utilitarian university is still the standard one used against vocational education.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
works.context: The 1850s, the founding of the Catholic University of Ireland (1854) and the Oxford debates on the relation of university to Church, and the Victorian controversy over useful versus liberal knowledge (Huxley's 'Culture and Science' answered it in 1880).
works.structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
