works.title: The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow
altTitles: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow
works.form: Collection of comic essays; review essay
works.description: Published in 1886 and the book that made Jerome famous: a series of comic essays on idleness, love, vanity, memory, babies and the miseries of life. It is a prose work of 1886 by Jerome K. Jerome; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: The essays develop a persona of the amiable idler who reflects on the small absurdities of existence — the undeserved devotion of dogs, the misery of being in love, the vanity of authors, the pleasures of doing nothing — and end with a melancholy meditation on the passage of time.
works.significance: The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow established the modern English comic essay and made Jerome one of the most popular writers of the 1890s: it founded the tradition of the self-deprecating personal essay in English, and its mixture of comedy and melancholy is the source of the tone later perfected by Wodehouse and Milne.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is digressive, anecdotal first-person narration.
works.context: 1886: the London magazine market, the Victorian essay after Lamb, and the comic sketch tradition that ran from Dickens to Wodehouse. The record dates the work as composed in 1886 and first published in 1886 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: The Idler
altTitles: The Idler, by the Author of The Rambler (series title)
works.form: periodical essay and character-writing in the Spectator tradition
works.description: Johnson's second periodical paper, a weekly series of short essays contributed to a London newspaper between 1758 and 1760 and afterwards collected. Its persona - a man who has resolved to do nothing and to write only what comes to him - lets Johnson examine idleness, attention, marriage, reading, hopes and fears with a lighter, more playful touch than the Rambler, while still turning each subject to moral account. The 104 papers include some of his best brief criticism and his wryest analysis of self-deceit.
works.plot: Each paper takes a single topic - the danger of sloth, the pleasure of novel-reading, the conduct of life in easy circumstances, the use of criticism, the fears of the ignorant, the duty of parents and children - and pursues it by definition, example and epigram rather than by sustained argument. The framing personae of the Idler and of his club of loungers supply a comic distance from the matter, and several numbers advertise Johnson's own habits and quarrels. The series repeatedly insists that idleness is itself a labour of the mind and that the unexamined life of ease is the most dangerous of all.
works.significance: The Idler consolidated the essay serial as a vehicle for criticism as well as morals, and the numbers on Shakespeare, on the pleasure of reading and on the vanity of expectations are among the most quoted of Johnson's shorter prose. In a lighter register it carries out the same analysis of dependence and self-knowledge that makes the Rambler serious.
works.meter: Prose; shorter and less Ciceronian periods than the Rambler, with a pointed conversational sententiousness that Johnson himself thought more readable.
works.context: Written in the same years as the Dictionary and the Rambler, for a new newspaper venture that needed established hands; Johnson's authorship was recommended by the reputation of the Rambler and his papers were read as a continuation of the Addison-Steele serial, from which they differ by their scepticism about politeness.
works.characters: The Idler; the members of his club; the correspondents of the occasional papers
works.structure: A serial periodical of 104 weekly papers, first issued from 1758 within a newspaper and later gathered in volumes; the numbers are free-standing, with only a slight continuity of personae.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the Yale edition records the very few papers doubtfully assigned to other hands.

works.title: The Idler in Italy
works.description: The fashionable travel book of the 1830s: Italy, the salons and the English abroad. works.title: The Iliad of Homer
altTitles: The Iliad of Homer Translated from the Greek
works.description: Pope's complete translation of the Iliad, issued in parts by subscription and then in volumes: the most commercially successful and most criticised English Homer, which recast Greek epic as Augustan heroic couplet and as a national monument.
works.plot: The translation follows Homer's argument from the plague and the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon through the great battles, the embassy, the death of Patroclus and the vengeance on Hector, to the ransoming of the body, with the accompanying scholarly notes and the essay on the genius and writings of Homer.
works.significance: For a century it was the English Homer, the book by which the epics were known to readers of verse; at once the monument of Augustan neoclassicism and the translation that later critics, from Blake to the Victorian Hellenists, chose to destroy.
works.meter: Heroic couplet sustained over the longest English poem of the century, with the epic simile compressed into the closed pair and the line-end made the unit of judgment.
works.context: Subscribed for at the height of the war's aftermath and of the classical vogue, it was attacked for its fidelity by Bentley and by the scholars, defended by the fashionable, and made the centre of the quarrel over the study of the ancients; its subscription model also made Pope the century's first profiting English poet.
works.characters: Achilles; Hector; Agamemnon; Patroclus; Priam; Homer as the translated author
works.structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the twenty-four books of the Iliad, published in installments and collected in volumes, each with argument, notes and classical apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Pope's own hand, working with a library of Latin, French and English commentators and with the help of friends on the notes; the verse translation itself is not divided among several writers.

works.description: Published in 1879 and the most widely read English translation of the Iliad of the Victorian period: a plain prose version designed to give the modern reader the effect of the original. works.title: The Image Breakers
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1900
works.description: The socialist feminist novel of the 1890s: a woman's place in the coming commonwealth. It is a prose fiction work of 1900 by Gertrude Dix; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation.
works.plot: A young woman joins a socialist community and falls in love with two men, one a revolutionary and one a reformer; the novel works out the place of women in the socialist future and ends with the woman's own choice of work and love.
works.significance: The Image Breakers is one of the most explicitly socialist New Woman novels of the period: its vision of the socialist future and its argument about women's place in the movement make it a central text of the conjunction of feminism and socialism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the socialist utopia of the future.
works.context: England at the turn of the century, the socialist movement and the women's question within it. works.title: The Imitations of Horace
works.description: Pope's free translations of Horace's satires and familiar epistles, in which the Roman poet's circle becomes the poet's own: a sequence of personated self-defence, retirement and judgment on the age.
works.plot: Taking one Horatian poem after another, the speaker reports his own life among his friends and patrons, answers his enemies, refuses the offers of the great, and turns the ancient dialogue into an account of the modern writer's independence.
works.significance: It redefined imitation as a modern mode of citation and self-portraiture, and it is the century's fullest demonstration that the ancients could be occupied rather than copied.
works.meter: Heroic couplet made colloquial and broken by the dialogue line, the interruption and the narrative aside, in deliberate contrast to the close cadence of the Essay on Criticism.
works.context: Written across the later 1730s, after the failure of the last Scriblerian projects and in the years when the Licensing Act and the defeat of the administration changed the relation of the writer to party and patronage; Horace supplied the model of a private friendship publicly defended.
works.characters: Horace as the personated speaker; Pope; the friend; the patron; the importunate poetaster; the bookseller
works.structure: A serial of separately printed imitations, each a self-contained dialogue or epistle, accumulating by recurrence of persons into an autobiography.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the mask of Horace is a deliberate prosopopoeia and the identification of the speakers with Pope's own circle has encouraged, without proving, division of hands in the earliest pieces.

works.title: The Importance of Being Earnest: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People
works.form: Comedy in three acts; problem play
works.description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 14 February 1895 and the most perfect English comedy of the nineteenth century: the comedy of two young men who both invent a fictitious invalid in order to escape their social duties, and of the women who love them for a name.
works.plot: Algernon Moncrieff invents 'Bunbury', Ernest Worthing invents his invalid brother Ernest; Gwendolen Fairfax and Cecily Cardew both believe they are engaged to a man named Ernest, the engagements collapse on the discovery of the invention, and the play resolves when it appears that Jack was in fact christened Ernest and is Algernon's elder brother.
works.significance: The Importance of Being Earnest is the greatest English stage comedy since the Restoration and the definitive statement of Wilde's comic method: the epigram as a weapon against Victorian earnestness, and the pun on a name as the engine of a plot.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the marriage market, the country-house weekend, and the aesthetic and dandy culture of London. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and first performed in St James's Theatre, London, 14 February 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: The Imported Bridegroom and Other Stories
works.description: Published in 1898 and the best of Cahan's stories: the immigrant generation and its children in the New York ghetto. It is a prose fiction work of 1898 by Abraham Cahan; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.

works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. works.title: The Improvisatrice
works.form: Collected volume dominated by a long narrative lyric romance; the governing genres are the metrical tale and the dramatic lyric of the artist-poet, with the descriptive Italian piece beside them.
works.description: The second volume and the one that fixed its author's fame, named for its long central poem on the woman of genius who sings and loves. It consolidates the persona of the professional poetess and adds the exotic romance and the historical scene to her repertoire.
works.plot: The title poem imagines an Italian singer-poetess whose art and her sex's destinies are set against each other: she is admired, used and finally silenced, while the gift that made her survives in song. The poem moves through performance, patronage, love and renunciation, and closes the biography as a monument. Other pieces record disappointed affection, the death of friends, and the consolation or insufficiency of memory. A group of descriptive lyrics turns Italy and its arts into the scenery of feeling. The volume's argument is that the improvisatrice's gift is both her only inheritance and the cause of her exposure.
works.significance: The Improvisatrice supplied the nineteenth century with its most influential image of the woman poet as popular artist and victim, a figure that later novelists and poets of the annuals reworked without cease. It is the point at which the poetess tradition becomes self-conscious, taking its own situation as its subject. Criticism of women's professional writing now treats the poem as a founding text.
works.meter: The title poem uses a stanzic iambic measure with a rapid declamatory movement and frequent triple-time openings; the lyrics keep refrained common measure and compressed direct address, all tuned for recitation.
works.context: Published by Hurst and Robinson in 1824, the volume appeared in the season when the annual and the keepsake were remaking the market for short verse, and its success made its author the model of the gifted female contributor the annuals required. Contemporary reviews were divided, praising the facility and questioning the propriety of a woman's self-exposure in print. Its fame rested heavily on transatlantic reprinting, which was by then outrunning British copyright.
works.characters: the improvisatrice, the Italian singer-poetess of the title poem, whose career of performance, patronage and renunciation the poem records
works.structure: The long title poem is a continuous biographical romance in verse, told in successive phases of the singer's career; the rest of the volume is an unordered company of lyrics and elegies repeating its situations in shorter measure.
works.attributionNotes: Much of the magazine verse gathered here had appeared over initials, and the volume itself was put out under that signature rather than the full name used for the first collection.

works.title: The Indian Princess; or, La Belle Sauvage
works.form: Musical entertainment and afterpiece: sentimental drama with songs, scene-designs and rescue spectacle, belonging to the popular London stage convention rather than to closet drama.
works.description: A two-act musical entertainment on the Pocahontas story, played in London's theatre of the Regency years and the first American-authored drama to treat a Native American heroine of the Jamestown legend as its central figure. It converts John Smith's narrative and the older stage versions of the tale into a sentimental rescue plot with songs, spectacle and a happy ending. Its interest is double: as a piece of transatlantic popular theatre, and as an early instance of the Pocahontas myth serving a romantic account of settlement and reconciliation.
works.plot: The action follows the capture of the English captain by the Virginian people, the intercession of the chief's daughter, and the reprieve at the place of execution. The heroine, raised in the forest and called La Belle Sauvage by the English, is torn between duty to her father and affection for the captive, and she resolves the conflict by a staged death and restoration that leaves the father humiliated and the lovers free. A romantic subplot between an English soldier and a Native woman doubles the theme of crossing cultural boundaries, and the piece ends in clemency and union rather than in conquest.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the American-literature stage treatment of Pocahontas and a standard example of how Romantic melodrama turned colonial history into a moral spectacle of nature-culture reconciliation. Its design is now read against the history of Indian removal and of the noble-savage tradition, and it marks the beginning of a continuous American dramatic career.
works.meter: Spoken dialogue in prose with lyric songs of conventional stanzaic measure set to the composer's music.
works.context: Written by an American for the London stage at the height of the Regency's taste for spectacle, frontier melodrama and the Indian on the theatre, and produced at a patent theatre in 1808. The Jamestown story was then a live transatlantic property, and the play draws on the same romantic material that made the Pocahontas legend a stock subject of the period.
works.characters: La Belle Sauvage; the Indian chief; the English captain; the English soldier in love with a Native woman; the treacherous attendant who engineers the false death
works.structure: Two-act afterpiece with a linear rescue plot, set pieces of spectacle, and interpolated songs that comment on the action at its emotional turning points.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by the American dramatist is established and was stated on the title page of the printed edition; the music was by the house composer of the theatre.

works.title: The Indicator
works.form: A weekly periodical in the tradition of the Spectator papers and of Hunt's own Examiner, and one of the chief vehicles of the Romantic familiar essay. Its constituent forms are the short critical essay, the literary character sketch, the retold tale, the note on a passage of verse and the occasional poem. The paper is a miscellany rather than a review: it carries no political intelligence and no reports of Parliament, and it subordinates book-notice to the essayist's reflection, which is why it is usually classed with Elia and Table Talk rather than with the Edinburgh Review.
works.description: A weekly literary journal founded, edited and very largely written by Leigh Hunt, issued in London by Joseph Appleyard from 1819 and continued through 1820 and into 1821; its essays were also collected in a two-volume issue dated 1820 to 1821. It was Hunt's attempt to carry the manner of the Examiner into a sheet devoted to poems, tales and short critical essays, and it became one of the founding documents of the familiar Romantic periodical style. Its pages mix definitions of poetry, notices of contemporary verse, reworkings of older stories and sketches of literary character, all in a voice that treats reading as a form of friendship. The Indicator, with The Companion of 1828, is the practical demonstration of the prose Hunt theorised.
works.plot: As a periodical the paper has no argument, but its recurring proposition is that good writing is a kind of conversation and that verse and prose alike should be judged by their humanity and their ease. Numbers carry short essays on poetry and on the poets Hunt admired, reprints and redressings of Italian and English tales, notices of current books and papers of general literary instruction, together with original verse. Its practical polemic is against the hierarchical and personal manner of the great reviews: it proposes instead a criticism of sympathy, addressed to an ordinary reader who buys a penny sheet rather than a quarterly.
works.significance: The Indicator established the model of the personal literary weekly that later Romantic and Victorian periodical writing followed, and it is the place where Hunt's idea of a criticism of humanity, rather of judgement, was worked out in practice. Through it the familiar essay became a Romantic institution, setting the manner that his contemporaries and successors copied in the cheap serial press, and shaping how the generation that included his own later collectors understood the relation of verse and criticism. It also documents the economics of authorship: a poet of real distinction earning his living by a weekly sheet. As criticism it remains a key source for Hunt's judgements, for his accounts of Shakespear, Dante and his own contemporaries, and for the quarrels of the Cockney school controversy.
works.meter: Prose throughout, in Hunt's characteristic familiar manner: short sentences, colloquial vocabulary, first-person speculation and an easy alternation of seriousness and play. Verse appears within the prose in the quoted passages and in the contributed poems, and Hunt's own occasional pieces in the paper are regular in metre, mostly simple lyric or epistle. The prose rhythm is deliberately conversational, closer to spoken ease than to the periodic style of eighteenth-century prose, and it was this quality that later essayists identified as Hunt's contribution.
works.context: The Indicator belongs to the explosion of small cheap periodicals after 1815, when technological and Circulating-library growth made the weekly sheet a livelihood for professional letters, and to the aftermath of the suppression campaigns that had imprisoned Hunt for the Examiner. Its appearance coincides with the height of the Cockney School controversy, and it gave Hunt a steady income from the press and a platform independent of the great reviews that had insulted him. Its contributors and its circle overlapped with Blackwood's and the London literary world of Hazlitt, Shelley and the younger poets, and its career, like his, ended at the point when Hunt left England for Italy in 1821.
works.structure: Discontinuous and miscellany-based: a weekly sequence of short numbers, each containing several self-contained pieces, with no plot and no sustained argument across issues. The organising principle is the persona of the editor, who moves between quotation, exegesis, criticism and remonstrance within a single number. Bound runs therefore read as volumes of essays rather than as a serial narrative, and the paper's unity is one of voice, of subject-matter and of the weekly rhythm of appearance.
works.attributionNotes: The journal was published under Hunt's editorship and reference sources state that he wrote much or most of its content, though the weekly numbers carry no consistent individual attributions and the usual practices of periodical composition of this kind mean that the assistance of his literary friends and family cannot be excluded. Its separate authorial identity is secure, but the share of its copy that is Hunt's own is a matter of scholarly inference rather than of documentation, and its collected reissues carry his name as author. Nothing in the evidence supports the transfer of any specific number to another hand.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: The Inheritance
works.description: the author's second novel, a wider social comedy following the young heir, who unexpectedly inherits a great fortune and is transplanted from humble Scottish origins into English and Scottish high society. The novel examines how sudden wealth corrupts and tests character across two generations of fortune-hunters.
works.plot: Eliot, a young man of modest means, learns that an unexpected inheritance has made him one of the wealthiest commoners in Britain. His sister Julia's prospects transform correspondingly, and the pair are drawn into the worlds of Edinburgh and London society, where they encounter the mercenary calculations of the aristocracy, the manipulative Mrs. St. Clare, and the proud Lady Victoria. the author's education in wealth and Julia's trials in the marriage market trace the novel's central argument that inheritance tests moral nature more severely than poverty.
works.significance: The Inheritance is the author's broadest social canvas and her most sustained analysis of class mobility; it is a key text for the representation of wealth and gentility in Scottish Romantic fiction between Scott and later Victorian social novels.
works.context: Published in 1824, the author's most ambitious novel consolidates the Waverley-era market for Scottish social fiction and responds to the speculative excesses of post-war gentility; it draws on her knowledge of Edinburgh legal and clerical society.
works.characters: Eliot; Julia Eliot; Mrs. St. Clare; Lady Victoria; Fanny Elliot; Colonel Macquarie
works.structure: Linear three-volume narrative; the ascent plot from obscurity to wealth is the organising device; contrast between Scottish and English society structures the satire.
themes: Fortune and mutability
The marriage market and the limited estate
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners

works.title: The Innocence of Father Brown
works.description: The founding text of the metaphysical detective story: the little priest and the impossible crimes. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by G. K. Chesterton; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Twelve stories in which Father Brown, the unobtrusive priest, solves crimes by his knowledge of human sin: 'The Blue Cross', 'The Invisible Man', 'The Queer Feet', 'The Honour of Israel Gow' and 'The Sins of Prince Saradine' among them.
works.significance: The Innocence of Father Brown created the metaphysical detective story and the clerical detective: its twelve stories made Chesterton the rival of Conan Doyle, and the genre of the detective story as a parable of the moral order begins here.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the paradox turned inside out.
works.context: England and France at the turn of the century, and the Golden Age of the detective story. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: Father Brown; Flambeau; Valentin; the criminals
works.structure: Twelve stories with a recurring detective and a friend. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gilbert Keith Chesterton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by Himself
works.form: Autobiographical slave narrative with embedded travel journal and polemic
works.description: The first great slave narrative in English, published in two volumes in 1789 and subscribed by hundreds of readers, including members of the royal family. Equiano tells of his childhood in Africa, his kidnapping and sale, the Middle Passage, twenty years of slavery and service in the Royal Navy and the merchant trade, his purchase of his own freedom, and his conversion and public anti-slavery activism. The narrative combines autobiography, travel writing, commercial detail and protest, and it became the most widely used text of the abolitionist campaign.
works.plot: From an idealised account of Igbo society in what is now Nigeria the narrative moves to the horror of the middle passage, where the close-packing, mortality and torture of the ship are registered with precise numbers. Enslaved in the West Indies and then in England, Equiano serves the Royal Navy officer Michael Henry Pascal, is christened Gustavus Vassa by the Shipley family at Guernsey, works as a domestic servant and ship's crewman, and under the Philadelphia merchant Robert King learns bookkeeping and accumulates enough to buy his freedom in 1766. Later volumes recount his travels in the Arctic, Central America and Jamaica, his evangelical conversion and his circle of Methodist and Calvinistic friends, and a closing appeal to the imagination of British readers, in which the suffering of enslaved people is figured in the language of familial and Christian sympathy.
works.significance: It established the conventions of the English-speaking slave narrative, the testimony of an authenticated self that refutes the theory of African incapacity. Its argument from felt sympathy, commercial evidence and Christian providence made it a decisive instrument of public persuasion and it is now a central text of eighteenth-century studies, of Atlantic history and of life-writing.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, periodically structured narrative style with biblical and sentimental cadences
works.context: Published in the year of the first abolitionist petition to Parliament and of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, it belongs to the evangelical and Quaker anti-slavery movement, to the boom in spiritual autobiography, and to the eighteenth-century literature of travel, commerce and natural history.
works.characters: Michael Henry Pascal; Robert King; Granville Sharp; the Shipley family
works.structure: Two-volume spiritual and commercial autobiography in chronological order, with a frame of providential design and a final section of documents, testimonials and abolitionist argument.
works.attributionNotes: Equiano's own authorship is accepted, though the degree of editorial help from abolitionist friends such as the bookseller and clergyman supporters is debated. Vincent Carretta has argued from contemporary records that Equiano may have been born in the British colonies rather than in Africa, which would make the opening African childhood a persuasive fiction; the narrative's factual status remains contested even where its authorship is not.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Sea voyage and seafaring
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.description: Andrew Boorde's popular geography and travel book of 1547, the first English printed book to describe the nations of Europe in verse and prose for the general reader.

works.title: The Invisible Man: A Grotesque Romance
works.description: Published in 1897: the story of Griffin, a scientist who makes himself invisible and is destroyed by the consequences of his own discovery. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Griffin takes refuge in the village of Iping, robs and terrorises the neighbourhood, takes shelter with Dr Kemp and reveals his plan for a reign of terror, and is hunted and killed by the mob in Port Burdock.
works.significance: The Invisible Man is the classic English fable of the scientist without a moral community: its subject is not invisibility but the isolation and violence it produces, and it founded the modern literature of the dangerous discovery.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The 1890s, the physics of light and refraction, the new research university, and the English fear of the unregulated scientist. works.title: The Iron Heel
works.description: Published in 1908 and the first modern American dystopia: the rise of a fascist oligarchy in the United States and the crushing of the working class. It is a prose fiction work of 1908 by Jack London; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A manuscript of the 1930s, annotated by a scholar of a later socialist era, records the rise of the Iron Heel, the American oligarchy that destroys the socialist movement after 1912, the failed Chicago Commune and the extermination of the revolutionaries, and the long dark age that follows before the final triumph of the brotherhood of man.
works.significance: The Iron Heel is the first modern American dystopia and the founding text of the American political novel of the future: it anticipates Orwell, Huxley and Zamiatin, it invented the fictional future history annotated from a later age, and it is the most radical American novel of the period.

works.title: The Island of Doctor Moreau
works.description: Published in 1896 and the most disturbing of Wells's early romances: the story of a shipwrecked man who finds on a Pacific island a physiologist who turns animals into human beings. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

works.title: The Island Race
works.description: Published in 1898 and Newbolt's most ambitious imperial collection: the English race, the sea and the imperial mission in verse. works.title: The Italian Opera
works.description: Addison's satiric essay on the Italian opera then occupying the London stage, a comic indictment of declamatory singing, castrato heroes, improbable machinery and the abdication of sense before sound.
works.plot: The spectator reports the absurdities of an evening at the Italian opera, where artificial voices command armies and melt away in affected rapture, stage machinery manufactures thunder, and the audience most admires whatever most forbids belief.

works.context: Written while Handel and Handel's rivals were establishing Italian heroica opera at the Queen's Theatre, and while the English opera, the ballad entertainment and the spoken drama were competing for the same audience; the paper belongs to the long quarrel between English spoken theatre and foreign sung drama.
works.characters: Mr. Spectator; the opera singers; the applauding audience
works.structure: A single character paper: expository frame, catalogued instances of abuse, and a closing general reflection on credulity and taste.

works.title: The Italian, or, The Confessional of the Black Penitents. A Romance. In Three Volumes
altTitles: The Confessional of the Black Penitents
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, with the confessional, the robbers' cavern and the Inquisition for its machinery; the last of the mature prose romances Radcliffe published in her lifetime
works.description: The last prose romance of Ann Radcliffe, advertised in the London press in December 1796 and published in three volumes with the imprint of 1797, of which she sold the copyright to Thomas Cadell. Vincentio di Vivaldi, seeing Ellena di Rosalba at church in Naples, loves her at first sight against the pride of his family; Ellena, reared in seclusion on the coast of Sorrento, is carried off on the road by the robbers who own Schedoni for their chief, is driven through the caverns of the banditti and the fortress of the suitorous Duke of Braccivalo, is accused of a murder committed in her chamber by Schedoni's assassin Spalatro, and is pressed by ecclesiastical arts into vows, while the confessional of the black penitents and the Inquisition darken the way. The disclosures at the close unite the houses of Schedoni and Ellena, establish her nobility so that Vivaldi may honourably wed her, and unbind the terrible history of the Schedoni family from which the title-piece takes its name.
works.plot: Ellena, beloved of Vivaldi, is kidnapped on the road to Naples by robbers under Schedoni, protected from harm by his own troubled conscience, and pursued by the suit of the powerful Duke of Braccivalo, whom her pride and her lover's danger oblige her to resist; a murder in her lodging, done by the assassin Spalatro, throws suspicion on herself, and she is driven toward the convent and its arts of the confessional to escape forced marriage. Schedoni's history, of anhouse disowned, a sister lost, and the black-robed penitents of his family's Easter rite, is unfolded till he finds in Ellena a kinswoman, her parentage is cleared, the crimes are brought home to their authors, and her marriage with Vivaldi is made lawful in honour.
works.significance: The Italian is by many judges Radcliffe's most accomplished romance, concentrating her method into a single tragic fable of conscience and persecution; it stood as the school-example of the explained supernatural and of Gothic's anti-clerical machinery through the nineteenth century, was a measure for Scott's and Peacock's accounts of terror, and remains the canonical companion volume to Udolpho in the Gothic syllabus.
works.meter: Prose romance without interspersed verse; the rhythm of the book is that of its tragic scene-setting, the bay of Sorrento, the caverns and the fortress, and its style is nearer to tragedy than to the lyricism of Udolpho.
works.context: Published at the close of the first vogue of the Gothic, when the campaign against the Inquisition and monastic craft was a staple of radical as well as Tory polemic, and when the Directory's wars had made Italy a subject of anxious English attention; its December 1796 press notice and the Cadell copyright mark the height of Radcliffe's fame before her withdrawal from publication.
works.characters: Ellena di Rosalba; Vincentio di Vivaldi; Schedoni, captain of the robbers; Spalatro, his assassin; the Duke of Braccivalo; Vivaldi's mother; Ellena's father; the sister and confessor of the Schedoni house; the Inquisition of Naples
works.structure: A continuous three-volume romance, close-knit and rapid beside its predecessors, moving through abduction, pursuit, accusation and trial toward a single expository revelation that ties the robbers' chief to the heroine's house and resolves the machinery of the confessional and the Inquisition.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the author of The Mysteries of Udolpho on the title page; the newspapers of December 1796 name Ann Radcliffe, and her authorship is undisputed.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Penance, confession, and sin
Religious persecution and martyrdom
Revenge and justice
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror
The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: The Itinerary
works.description: John Leland's topographical survey of England and Wales, the record of his itineraries undertaken with a royal commission from Henry VIII to search the libraries of the monasteries, compiled c. 1535–43 and first printed by Thomas Hearne in 1710–12.
works.plot: The Itinerary is a county-by-county record of Leland's travels: towns, rivers, bridges, castles, churches, and the antiquities of each place, noted in terse first-person entries that document the landscape of England on the eve of the dissolution of the monasteries.
works.significance: The founding text of English antiquarianism and topography; it inaugurated the tradition of the county survey that runs through Camden, Aubrey, and the eighteenth-century antiquaries, and its value as an eyewitness record of pre-dissolution England is irreplaceable.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Leland held a commission from Henry VIII (1533) to search the monastic and collegiate libraries; his itineraries of c. 1535–43 covered most of England and Wales, and his notes preserve records of books, inscriptions, and buildings later destroyed in the dissolution and after.
works.structure: Topographical notes arranged by county, preserved in autograph notebooks; the printed text of 1710–12 follows Hearne's edition of the surviving manuscripts.
themes: National identity and Englishness
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: The Jew of Malta
works.description: Marlowe's black comedy of Machiavellian revenge: the merchant Barabas, his wealth seized to pay Malta's tribute to the Turks, revenges himself on the Christian state by intrigue and poison, betrays the island to the Turks, and is finally caught in his own engine — the cauldron prepared for his enemies — in a play whose prologue is spoken by 'Machevill' himself.
works.plot: Barabas is stripped of his estate; through his daughter Abigail he recovers his hidden gold and buys the deaths of the governor's son and suitor; Abigail's conversion and death, his purchase of the slave Ithamore, and the double poisonings follow; made governor by the Turks, he plots the city's destruction, but the falling floor delivers him to the cauldron and the Christians' triumph.
works.significance: The most corrosive of the Elizabethan revenge plays — a satire of Christian, Jew, and Turk alike that Shakespeare answered in Shylock.
works.meter: Blank verse for Barabas's great soliloquies of gold ('infinite riches in a little room') against the prose of the play's farcical intrigues.
works.context: Performed from 1592, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and the Marrano anxieties of the 1590s; not printed until 1633, when it was revived with prologues by Heywood.
works.characters: Barabas; Abigail; Ithamore; Ferneze, governor of Malta; Lodowick; Mathias; Calymath; Bellamira; Pilia-Borza; the two Friars (Jacomo and Bernardine); Machevill (the Prologue)
works.structure: A five-act intrigue of escalating double-dealing, alternating the prologue's sardonic commentary with farcical villainy, and ending in the spectacular engine of the cauldron.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Ambition and the overreacher
Revenge and justice
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre
The University Wits

works.title: The Jewel of Seven Stars
works.form: Novel; ghost story, first issued in 1903
works.description: Published in 1903 and the most Egyptological of Stoker's novels: the attempt to revive the mummy of the ancient Egyptian queen Tera, and the terror that follows the experiment. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by Bram Stoker; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Margaret Trelawny's father is found in a trance in his study surrounded by Egyptian antiquities; the investigation by Sergeant Daw and the scholar Corbeck reveals that Tera's mummy and jewels have been assembled in England, and the attempt to resurrect her ends in catastrophe.
works.significance: The Jewel of Seven Stars is the central English mummy novel and a key text of the literature of Egyptology and imperial archaeology.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is epistolary and documentary collage.
works.context: The 1890s-1900s, the Egyptian mummy-unwrapping craze, the archaeology of the Valley of the Kings, and the Victorian occult revival. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
works.characters: Malcolm Ross (the narrator); Margaret Trelawny; Abel Trelawny; Eugene Corbeck; Sergeant Daw; Dr Winchester; Queen Tera
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Abraham Stoker. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation
Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: The Judgement Day I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (Judgement Day I); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (Judgement Day II)
works.description: Two independent eschatological poems on the last judgment. Judgement Day I (119 lines) describes the cosmic terrors of doomsday and the soul's reckoning; Judgement Day II (306 lines), based on Bede's De die iudicii, is a sustained meditation on sin, penance, and the judgment, addressed to the individual soul.
works.plot: Judgement Day I depicts the universal conflagration, the trumpets, and the assembly of all souls before the judge, contrasting the fate of the blessed and the damned. Judgement Day II urges the penitent soul to recall its sins now, while confession is still possible, painting the terrors of judgment in images of fire, darkness, and weeping, and closes with hope for those who repent.
works.significance: The fullest Old English verse treatments of the last judgment, and (in Judgement Day II) an important vernacular witness to the reception of Bede's Latin eschatological poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; Judgement Day II's sustained length and homiletic urgency make it the most ambitious of the Exeter/CCCC 201 eschatological poems.
works.context: The judgment was the master-image of Anglo-Saxon homiletics, from the Blickling and Vercelli homilies to Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi; the poems belong to that culture of penitential fear and are the verse counterpart of the homilists' doomsday rhetoric.
works.structure: Both poems move from description of the cosmic catastrophe to exhortation; Judgement Day II is organized as a sequence of meditations on sin, the hour of death, the judgment, and the possibility of mercy through penance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are independent compositions; Judgement Day II is an adaptation of Bede's De die iudicii, not by Bede himself.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition
The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature, 2nd edition

works.title: The Judgment of Paris
works.form: Masque or libretto for sung drama in three acts, composed as a competition text for the music prize of 1701.
works.description: A masque written in 1701 for the musical prize contested by the chief composers of the day, and not seen as a stage entertainment until the Haymarket production of 1712. The classical fable of the apple and the three goddesses is recast as an English pastoral contest, in which the rival claims of power, wisdom and beauty are set out for music rather than for dramatic action. The piece is the only considerable dramatic writing of its author's mature years, and it reads as a study in how a poet may build a text to be set.
works.plot: Celestial machinery opens the fable anew, and the three goddesses descend to the shepherd Paris on Ida that he may judge their appeals as of old. Juno offers power and extended empire, Pallas offers wisdom and renown in arms, and Venus offers beauty and the pleasures of love; each claim is urged in set airs and in recitative addressed to the shepherd's judgment. Paris, who is already beloved by the nymph Oenone, awards the prize to Venus, and the desert of the forsaken nymph supplies the tender undercurrent that keeps the allegory from being merely a programme. The several appeals are commented upon by pastoral attendants and by choruses, so that the moral of the choice is delivered in the alternation of musical effects rather than by argument, and the closing matter commends the triumph of beauty to the audience of the day.
works.significance: It preserves the only masque written by the foremost comedy-writer of his generation and is a document of the English effort to make serious musical drama out of an allegorical fable. Its graded lyric lines, adjusted to the composer's convenience, were long cited as a model of the poet's service to music, and the piece marks the late reach of the masque tradition into the competitive concert and opera life of London.
works.meter: Deliberately varied lyric line-lengths, short song-measures set off against longer declamatory lines for recitative, a prosody designed to give the composer distinct musical occasions; the choral and closing matter is in brisk regular rhyme.
works.context: The libretto was written for the musical contest of the spring and summer of 1701, in which several composers set the same English poem, an episode in the attempt to sustain an English musical drama after the generation of the great court composers. The interval of eleven years between the prize and the full stage production at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket in March 1712 measures the small market for such work before the Italian vogue of the following decade changed conditions. The poet had by then abandoned the public stage for other employments, and this text stands alone among his later writings for the theatre.
works.characters: Jupiter; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Paris the shepherd; Oenone the forsaken nymph; the attendants of the goddesses and the pastoral chorus
works.structure: A masque in three acts for singers, machinery and chorus; the dramatic line is subordinated to a sequence of competitive appeals and their musical answers, with an opening invocation and a celebratory close.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Love, constancy, and betrayal
National identity and Englishness
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules
The Restoration Theatre

works.title: The Jungle
works.description: The most influential American protest novel: the stockyards of Chicago and the immigrant worker. It is a prose fiction work of 1906 by Upton Sinclair; it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant, comes to Chicago with his family to work in the stockyards; the novel follows their destruction by the filth, the speed-up and the corruption of the packing plants, and ends with Jurgis's conversion to socialism.
works.significance: The Jungle is the most influential American protest novel ever written: it led directly to the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act of 1906, founded the American muckraking novel, and made the industrial horror story a permanent American form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary accumulation of the stockyards.
works.context: The Chicago stockyards in the early 1900s, and the immigrant labour of the packing houses. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1906 and first published in 1906 and it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Jurgis Rudkus; Ona Lukoszaite; Teta Elzbieta; Marija Berczynskas; Antanas
works.structure: A novel in thirty-one chapters, from the arrival to the socialist meeting. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Upton Beall Sinclair Jr. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Jungle Book
works.form: Collection of animal stories and poems
works.description: Published in 1894 and one of the most influential books in the world: the stories of Mowgli, the boy raised by the wolves of the Seeonee hills, together with the animal tales of the white seal, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and the elephants' dance.
works.plot: Mowgli is adopted by Mother and Father Wolf and taught the Law of the Jungle by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther; he is hunted by Shere Khan the tiger, taken by the Bandar-log, and finally returns to the man-village, while the other stories follow the white seal's search for a safe island and the mongoose's war on the cobras.
works.significance: The Jungle Book is the greatest English animal story of the century and one of the most influential books of the modern imagination: its Law of the Jungle, its Mowgli and its animal characters shaped the twentieth century's idea of nature and of childhood, and it is read as a parable of empire and of the feral child.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, concrete narrative.
works.context: The 1890s, the forests of the Central Provinces, the lore of the Indian jungle, and the Victorian animal story after Black Beauty. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Mowgli; Father Wolf and Mother Wolf (Raksha); Akela; Baloo; Bagheera; Shere Khan; Tabaqui; Kaa; the Bandar-log; Messua; Kotick, the White Seal; Rikki-Tikki-Tavi; Nag and Nagaina; Little Toomai and Kala Nag
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudyard Kipling. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole

movements: Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire

works.title: The Juvenile Miscellany
works.form: Juvenile and educational periodical: the monthly miscellany of instruction and amusement, with the tale, the dialogue lesson and the recitation poem as its characteristic units.
works.description: The first periodical published in the United States specifically for children, begun in Boston in 1826 and edited there through its earliest years. It appeared monthly in small numbers combining stories, natural history, geography, poetry, puzzles and moral tales, and it was written and compiled with a deliberate educational theory: that the child's imagination should be engaged before the conscience is lectured. Its editorship gives it a place in the reform literature of the period as well as in the history of schooling.
works.plot: As a serial it has no single argument but a programme. Its numbers teach through narrative rather than catechism, offering tales of animals and travel, short biographies of worthies, lessons on the temperance and abolition questions, and verse meant to be repeated aloud. Its editorial voice insists that children are rational beings entitled to interest and delight, and it gradually introduces political and moral subjects, including the condition of the enslaved and of Native Americans, into the child's reading room.
works.significance: It is the founding periodical of American literature for children, and an early demonstration that reform argument could be addressed to the young; its editorial practice shaped the juvenile book trade for a generation. Its history is also the history of its editor's developing politics, since the abolition and Native American questions entered her pages before they entered her books.
works.meter: Chiefly simple prose; its verse is in singable ballad and hymn stanzas written for juvenile recitation.
works.context: Launched in the same years as the American Sunday-School Union's mass juvenile publication and as the great reform agitations were beginning, it belongs to the period's new conviction that the child reader could be addressed directly and seriously. Its Boston origins place it at the centre of the unitarian and abolitionist print culture of the 1820s and 1830s.
works.structure: Serial monthly miscellany: undifferentiated succession of tale, lesson, poem, puzzle and answer, with editor's notes to correspondents and young contributors.
works.attributionNotes: The first years were edited by the woman who founded it, and its leading matter is hers; individual contributions are otherwise anonymous or by correspondents, so the serial is a collaborative print object.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
The education of princes and magistrates
The slave trade and abolition
Women's education and intellectual friendship
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: The Katherine Group
altTitles: The Lives of St Katherine, St Margaret, and St Juliana
works.description: Three prose lives of virgin martyrs — St Katherine of Alexandria, St Margaret of Antioch, and St Juliana of Nicomedia — written in the same West Midlands 'AB language' as Ancrene Wisse for a female religious audience. They are the classic Middle English saints' lives: rhetorically elaborate, vivid in their debates and torments, and fervent in their celebration of virginity.
works.plot: Each saint refuses a pagan suitor and judge, defeats her learned or demonic adversaries in debate, endures spectacular torments, and wins a martyr's crown, with Christ or angels as her comforters.
works.significance: The founding texts of the AB language group and the model for Middle English hagiography in the thirteenth century and after.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose with the characteristic AB-language vocabulary and spelling.
works.context: Composed c. 1190–1225 in the same Herefordshire milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: St Katherine; St Margaret; St Juliana; the tyrant-judges (Maxentius, Olibrius, Eleusius); the demons
works.structure: Conventional martyr-act structure (arraignment, debate, torture, death) enriched by long speeches and prayers; Juliana includes the saint's dialogue with a demon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; grouped with Ancrene Wisse and the Wooing Group by dialect and manuscript kinship.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Mission, conversion, and the Church
The contemplative life
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)

works.title: The Keepsake
altTitles: The Keepsake: An Annual Gift-Book of Poetry, Entertainment, and the Fine Arts
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: a serialized gift-book miscellany of lyrical poems, sentimental tales and engraved plates, sold in decorative bindings at a premium price.
works.description: The first and longest-lived of the fully commercial literary annuals, an embossed and finely bound gift book published each season from 1828 with an engraved steel plate as its centrepiece. It assembled poems, short tales and plates from fashionable contributors and was presented as a New Year's and birthday present. The record covers its foundation volume and the model it established. Together with its competitors it created the gift-book economy that dominated periodical literary production through the 1830s and 1840s.
works.plot: As an anthology it has no plot; its characteristic structure is a frontispiece after a painting, followed by an assortment of occasional verse, prose tales of sentiment and adventure, and contributions of historical or decorative interest. Its editorial programme, announced in its opening numbers, was to combine the fine arts and letters in a form made for giving, so that the plate and the poem were designed as a single presentational unit.
works.significance: It defines the annual as an economic and aesthetic institution: the form that set the price, the plate-and-poem design and the contributor list of Victorian literary culture, and the market in which much of the period's best-known verse by women was published and paid for. Its history is central to accounts of Romantic and early-Victorian authorship, patronage and the literary marketplace.
works.meter: Mixed; its verse is predominantly song-like lyric and short meditative pieces in familiar stanzas and blank verse, written to a small emotional register suited to the plate.
works.context: Founded by an engraver seeking a new market after the boom in illustrated topographical books, and published in London for a seasonally gift-buying readership with money to spend on presents. Its commercial success created a decade of imitation and drove the annuals' characteristic combination of art reproduction and commissioned literary work.
works.structure: Serial annual anthology: undated-in-essence miscellany of verse, prose and engraved plates, each volume built around one or more steel engravings.
works.attributionNotes: Volume editorship changed hands during the long run and the founding volume's editorial responsibility is a matter of scholarly description rather than of single authorship; contents are individually attributed to their contributors.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Patronage and the literary marketplace
The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Kentish Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi, fol. 69 (tenth century)
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A 43-line paraphrase of the Gloria in excelsis in the Kentish dialect, the only substantial Old English poem preserved in that dialect. It praises the Trinity, Christ the Lamb, and the Holy Spirit, and prays for the mercy of the Lord.
works.plot: The poem renders the Greater Doxology clause by clause: praise of God the Father, the Lamb of God who takes away sin, the Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and a closing petition for the Lord's mercy and protection.
works.significance: A rare dialectal witness to Old English religious verse and an early example of the Gloria rendered in English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the Kentish forms of the text are among the few dialectally marked verse survivals outside West Saxon.
works.context: The hymn was added to a manuscript otherwise containing Kentish glosses and documents; it attests the spread of vernacular liturgical paraphrase beyond the West Saxon heartland of the literary standard.
works.structure: A direct liturgical paraphrase following the order of the Gloria; the doxological clauses are expanded with brief devotional glosses.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Mission, conversion, and the Church
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The King of Ireland's Son
works.form: Folk-tale novel for children (the Irish tales retold)
works.description: The retelling of the Irish tales: the king's son, the fedgeder and the enchantments. It is a prose fiction work of 1916 by Padraic Colum; it belongs to The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Historical Novel and Romance.
works.plot: The King of Ireland's Son sets out to find the lost Gilly of the Goatskin and the Fedelma of the mist, and the tale carries him through the enchantments, the giants and the islands of the Irish wonder-tale, retold in the plain narrative sentence of the storyteller.
works.significance: The King of Ireland's Son is the classic retelling of the Irish wonder-tale for children: its fedgeder, its giants and its islands made the Irish tale the property of English-speaking childhood and remain the standard text of the revival's folk-telling.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish idiom carried into English dialogue.
works.context: The Irish wonder-tale retold in 1916, and the children's book of the revival. The record dates the work as composed in 1915 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story; The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; historical novel and romance.
works.characters: the King of Ireland's Son; Gilly of the Goatskin; Fedelma of the mist; the shee; the giants; the king of the lochlanns
works.structure: A folk-tale novel in chapters of the quest, the enchantment and the return. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Colum. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The King of Schnorrers
works.form: Novella; tall tale, first issued in 1894
works.description: Published in 1894 and Zangwill's comic masterpiece: the exploits of Manasseh Bueno Barzillai Azevedo da Costa, the proudest beggar in eighteenth-century London. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Israel Zangwill; it is catalogued here under Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Manasseh, a Sephardi schnorrer of immense dignity, lives by extracting alms from the rich of Bevis Marks; he outwits a wealthy Ashkenazi on the point of honour, tricks a merchant into supporting his daughter's wedding, and defeats every attempt to humiliate him, in a picaresque comedy of the Jewish community of 1780.
works.significance: The King of Schnorrers is a comic classic and the first English book to draw on the Yiddish humour of the immigrant world: its portrait of Manasseh is one of the great comic creations in English fiction and it opened the way for the Jewish-American humour of the next century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the tall tale: the frame of the literate narrator and the vernacular teller, the dialect spelling, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan, and the punch that turns on the outsider's credulity. The author's characteristic manner is dialect speech transcribed with care.
works.context: 1780s: the Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities of London, the Bevis Marks synagogue, and the Yiddish comic tradition of the schlemiel and the schnorrer. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under tall tale and south-western humour sketch; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Manasseh Bueno Barzillai Azevedo da Costa; Joseph Grobstock; Yankele ben Yitzchok; Deborah, Manasseh's daughter
works.structure: A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The King of Spain's Daughter
works.form: Play (one act, the Abbey); peasant play
works.description: The one-act play of Ellie Irwin and the king of Spain's daughter. It is a dramatic work of 1935 by Teresa Deevy; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The King of Spain's Daughter sets Ellie Irwin, the girl of the fantastical dream, among the suitors and the family of the rural Ireland, and closes on the custom's refusal of her escape, in the theatrically flamboyant one act that is Deevy's most revived play.
works.significance: The King of Spain's Daughter is Deevy's classic one-act: its Ellie Irwin, her dream and the unsettled close made the woman's confinement on the Abbey stage into the play that the revival of her work in the late century turned on.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the Abbey dialogue of the rural Ireland with the woman's confinement at its centre.
works.context: The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, April 1935. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1935 and first performed in The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, April 1935 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Ellie Irwin; the suitors; the family of the house
works.structure: A one-act Abbey play of the dream and the refusal. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.

works.title: The Kingis Quair
works.description: The dream vision traditionally attributed to James I of Scotland, written c. 1424 after his eighteen years of captivity in England: the imprisoned narrator, sleepless with love, reads Boethius, sees his lady from the tower window, and is taught by the goddesses of Love, Fortune, and Wisdom in a vision that reconciles him to his fate. The fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition.
works.plot: The sleepless captive, turning the pages of Boethius, hears the bell of matins and falls into a dream; guided by the goddesses, he ascends to the sphere of Venus, where his love for the lady seen from the tower is confirmed and fortune's wheel is explained; waking, a dove brings him the message of hope, and he ends his book in praise of love and his lady.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the makars' tradition: the first great poem in the Scottish Chaucerian line and the model for the royal and courtly poetry of the Stewart century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Chaucerian fluency, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1424, on the eve of James's release, celebrating his love for Joan Beaufort, whom he married in February 1424; preserved uniquely in the Selden manuscript (Bodleian Arch. Selden. B.24, c. 1488).
works.characters: the captive narrator (James I); the lady (Joan Beaufort); Venus; Minerva; Fortune; the dove
works.structure: A single dream vision in the Chaucerian-Boethian manner: reading, waking complaint, dream ascent, counsel of the goddesses, and waking resolution.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution to James I rests on the poem's autobiographical frame and manuscript tradition; it is widely but not universally accepted.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Courtly love and fin'amor
Fortune and mutability
movements: The Scottish Makars

works.plot: The Knight of Cheerful Countenance, the first novel of M. J. Farrell, sets the Anglo-Irish big house and its cheerful knight against the modern world, in the satirical sentence of the insider that made the Farrell manner.
works.significance: The Knight of Cheerful Countenance is the first of the Farrell novels and the founding text of Molly Keane's satire of the big house: its cheerful knight and its house made the class a subject of the comic novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of manners: the dialogue of the social world, the exact vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built on the breach or the observance of a convention. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical sentence of the insider.
works.context: The Anglo-Irish big house in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed in 1925 and first published in 1926 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; novel of manners and fashion.

works.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
works.description: Beaumont's mock-romance of the citizen audience: a grocer and his wife, watching the play 'The London Merchant', demand that their apprentice Rafe act the part of a knight errant; the 'Knight of the Burning Pestle' then rides his adventures through Waltham Forest and the giant Barbaroso's barber shop, while the merchant play and the citizens' interruptions double and parody each other to the final, multiple endings.
works.plot: The Citizen and his Wife interrupt the Prologue and hijack the play; Rafe's quests — the dainty damsel, the giants, the adventure of the barber — alternate with the merchant comedy of Venturewell, Jasper, and Luce; the plots collide at the mock-death of Rafe ('for the honor of Knights') and the play ends with the citizens' epilogue and the players' revenge on their audience.
works.significance: The first great English theatrical burlesque — the ancestor of Sheridan's Critic and of every later play about the audience's power over the stage.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the ballad metres of Rafe's adventures and the songs of old Merrythought ('Nose, nose, jolly red nose') as its parodic instruments.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Revels at Blackfriars about 1607, where it failed; revived by the Queen's Revels boys and printed in 1613; it mocks the citizen taste that The Shoemaker's Holiday had flattered.
works.characters: the Citizen; his Wife; Rafe (the Knight of the Burning Pestle); George (the apprentice); Venturewell; Jasper; Luce; Humphrey; Merrythought; Mistress Merrythought; Barbaroso the barber; the players
works.structure: A play-within-a-play satire in which the audience is on stage from the start — the first burlesque of the English theatre's own conventions, including the romance, the city comedy, and the 'lamentable' death scene.
works.attributionNotes: Generally assigned to Beaumont alone (perhaps with Fletcher's help); the 1613 title page names only Beaumont.
themes: Social satire and estates criticism
The public theatre and the players' world
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.description: The historical novel of the European maid of honour at the Burmese court. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by F. Tennyson Jesse; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance.
works.plot: The Lacquer Lady follows Fanny Moroni, the European maid of honour, through the court of the Konbaung dynasty in the years of the Third Anglo-Burmese War and its defeat, in the historical novel of the empire's Burma that is Jesse's neglected classic.
works.significance: The Lacquer Lady is the neglected classic of the empire's historical novel: its lacquer lady and its fallen court made the Burmese end of the British empire a novel of the woman's rebellion and the cry for freedom.
works.meter: Prose.
