works.title: The Life of Lorenzo de Medici
altTitles: The Life of Lorenzo de' Medici, Called Lorenzo the Magnificent
works.form: prose biography and historical narrative; the life with an introductory survey and scholarly annotation
works.description: The first considerable English history of the Italian Renaissance, built as a life of the Florentine ruler and prefaced by an introductory view of the history of Italy before his age. It rests upon manuscript matter gathered in Italy as well as upon the printed authorities, and it made its author's European reputation with the companion life which followed.
works.plot: The introductory view traces the rise of the communes, the divisions of the guelfs and ghibellines, and the fortune of the house of Medici to the position from which Lorenzo governed; the life then follows his policy, the maintenance of the balance of the Italian states, the league made against the conspiracy of the Pazzi, and the journey to Naples by which, at the height of a crisis, he shifted the fortune of the war by his personal presence and his address. Alongside the narrative runs the history of the revival of letters and of the arts: the Platonist circle, the poetry and the architecture, the collectors and the schools, and the magnificent patronage with which the prince of a republic made Florence the court of Europe. The moral judgement is severe as well as admiring: the genius, the taste, and the political dexterity are allowed their praise, but the corruption of a free constitution under the forms of it, the spending of the public money upon private splendour, and the cultivation of luxury as an instrument of power are handled as the ruin of the country; the book closes with the death of Lorenzo and with the view of the French invasion and of the anarchy that followed his burial.
works.significance: It fixed for English readers the image of the Renaissance and of its most famous patron, and it established the historical method of the English liberal treatment of Italy, the authority against which the later students, from the historians of the age to the travellers of the nineteenth century, measured their own judgments. Its political moral, that a cultivated despotism disguised as a republic destroys the liberty which makes culture possible, was one of the most influential readings of Italian history of the revolutionary decade.
works.meter: Dignified, circumstantial, moralising narrative prose of the Whig historical school, with the full period, the balanced judgement of character, and a constant consciousness of the example to modern times.
works.context: The work of a country-bred lawyer and banker of the great trading community who had retired from practice to letters, made out of years of reading and out of manuscript copies obtained in Italy, and published in the decade in which the French invasion of Italy and the controversy over the French Revolution gave the fall of Italian liberties a direct political bearing. Its author sat afterward for the town of his residence in the short Parliament of the abolition era, and was the centre of a circle of learning and of the arts in the port.
works.characters: Lorenzo de' Medici; Giuliano de' Medici; the conspirators of the Pazzi; the scholars and artists of the Florentine circle; the princes and statesmen of Italy
works.structure: Two parts: the introductory view of Italian history before the age of the Medici, and the life itself in continuous narrative with the historical and literary disquisitions and the notes of the authorities bound in; the whole closes with the fortunes of the immediate successors.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the book's reliance upon the manuscript transcripts obtained from Italian libraries and upon the counsel of an antiquary friend is stated in the work itself and in the correspondence of the author's family.

works.title: The Life of Nelson
altTitles: The Life of Horatio, Viscount Nelson
works.form: Prose biography of the short national type, combining the memoir built on letters with the account of campaigns, and written for a general reader rather than for the navy.
works.description: A short prose biography of Admiral Viscount Nelson, published within months of the subject's death at Trafalgar and written by the poet who had spent the years of the Peninsular War in Portugal and had collected materials there. It was planned as one life in a series of the worthies of the country, and it rapidly became the standard account, passing through many editions and giving the national story of Nelson its permanent shape.
works.plot: The life follows the admiral from his entry as a boy into the service and his apprenticeship in the Arctic and the East Indies, through the losses of his right eye and his right arm, to the Mediterranean command, the battle of the Nile, and the Neapolitan episode, and then to the blockade of Toulon, the pursuit of the enemy fleet across the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and the battle of Trafalgar, in which he was killed at the moment of victory. The narrative is built on the letters and the journals of the subject, quoted at length, and on the documents of the actions described, and it draws from them a portrait of a commander whose prudence, care for his officers and sailors, and religious faith were as remarkable as his daring. The argument is that a rector's son of Norfolk had made himself the instrument of his country's safety by steady attention, humanity and courage, and that his greatest victories were won before the action that killed him.
works.significance: The most durable English biography of Nelson and one of the most reprinted prose works of the period, fixed in the schools and in the gift-book trade of the nineteenth century as the account of the admiral; it is also the document that showed the Lake poet's later career at its most effective, and its method of building a life out of quoted letters was much imitated.
works.meter: Prose of unusual clearness and compression, in plain periods of narrative and quotation, with a habit of pointed summary at the end of the action; the book is commonly cited as a model of English biographical prose.
works.context: Written in 1813, in the middle of the Peninsular War and after the author's residence in Portugal as secretary to the commander-in-chief, when the nation's need of a hero after the death of Nelson and the fame of Trafalgar made the subject a public claim; the life was part of a plan of national biography and appeared in the same years as the author's appointment to the laurelship.
works.characters: Horatio Viscount Nelson; his father, the rector of Burnham Thorpe, and the kindred of his boyhood; his officers and the seamen of his fleet; the adversaries whom he encountered at the Nile and at Trafalgar
works.structure: A continuous prose life in a single volume, chronological and documentary, with the subject's own letters and the official papers of the actions interwoven, and with brief reflective passages on the character and on the use of biography; there is no dramatic partition of the matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
National identity and Englishness
Sea voyage and seafaring
Warfare and battle
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: The Life of our Rev. John Wesley
altTitles: The Life of the Rev. John Wesley
works.form: Prose biography and religious history with documentary appendix, in the evangelical life-writing tradition, turned to a church-political argument.
works.description: The author's two-volume biography of the Methodist founder, compiled largely from Wesley's own journals and letters and from documents supplied to him by the Methodist leadership. It presents Wesley as a providential restorer of vital religion in England while insisting that his connexions were schismatic and should be dissolved. The book was a publishing event and an offence, and the quarrel it provoked with the Methodist preachers occupied its author for several years.
works.plot: The narrative follows Wesley from Epworth and Oxford through the Georgia voyage and the Aldersgate experience to the open-air preaching, the building of the connexional system, and the last years. The biographer stresses Wesley's learning, his industry, and his political quietism, and treats the revival as a divine visitation to a slothful church. At the same time he argues that the Methodist itinerants and their chapels are an illegal and unnecessary separation, and that after Wesley's death union with the established church is the duty of Methodists. The volumes reprint long passages of the Journal, of letters, and of doctrinal tracts, annotated critically, so that Wesley's own voice is permitted to answer his critics.
works.significance: The earliest scholarly biography of Wesley and a primary source for the Methodist journal, whose editorial practice - reprinting and commenting on the subject's own papers - made it a model and a warning for later religious biography; it is essential evidence of the romantic-era relation between revival and established religion.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written when Methodism was negotiating its legal separation from the Church of England and when its author was consolidating his position as a church-and-state writer after the laureateship; it drew replies, pamphlet wars, and a defence in the Quarterly Review, and its text was revised in later editions as the quarrel continued.
works.characters: John Wesley; Charles Wesley; George Whitefield; the Methodist preachers of the connexion
works.structure: Chronological biography interwoven with extensive quotation from the subject's own journals and correspondence, and with argumentative notes and appendices; narrative and polemic alternate by design.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Evangelical experience and assurance
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Life of Samuel Johnson
altTitles: The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D.
works.form: literary biography and memoir, combining chronicle, document transcription and reported conversation
works.description: Boswell's biography of Johnson, the book that fixed the most familiar literary personality in English letters and invented the modern Life as an architecture of documents, conversation and chronology. It gathers letters, notebooks, the recollections of friends and Boswell's own journals into a year-by-year record of Johnson's studies, writings and company. It was advertised by a Prospectus of 1790 and published in 1791, with a revised second edition in 1793.
works.plot: The Life follows Johnson from his birth at Lichfield, through his schooling, marriage, early poverty and labours at the Dictionary, to the years of the Idler, the Tour, the Pension and the last illness, with the conversations of the clubs and the clubs of friends filling the frame. Boswell reports Johnson's arguments on free-will, on death, on Scotland and on the Jacobite past at length, and permits the subject's inconsistencies to stand unharmonised. The result is a biography that is also a record of an age of letters, of the book trade and of opinion.
works.significance: It is the foundational text of modern literary biography and the chief source for Johnson's mind and for the social history of Augustan and late-Augustan letters; its methods of transcription and chronology set the standard for later lives. It also preserves much of the periodical, critical and political writing of the age in a single narrative.
works.meter: Prose; a plain chronological diction framing the reported speech, whose rhythm is carried by Johnson's own sentences as transcribed.
works.context: Composed from materials assembled from Johnson's death in 1784 onward, in the decade when memoir and collected correspondence had become the standard mode of literary monument, and when the Scots and English literary worlds were being renegotiated after the American controversy. The work belongs with the late eighteenth-century efflorescence of biography and of the printed journal.
works.characters: Samuel Johnson; James Boswell; Hester Lynch Thrale; Thomas Tyrwhitt; Joshua Reynolds; the club of the Mitre and the Turk's Head
works.structure: A chronological biography with embedded documents - letters, certificates, earlier journals and the Tour - the largest continuous narrative being the years Boswell knew, and the whole prefaced by a statement of the materials and their provenance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested for the whole, though the Life incorporates the letters and papers of many hands, and the abridgements and re-editings of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have repeatedly altered its state; the modern standard edition restores the several layers of the text.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules
The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More
altTitles: The Lyfe of Sir Thomas Moore, Knighte
works.description: William Roper's intimate biography of his father-in-law Sir Thomas More, written in the 1550s but not printed until 1626; the first biography in English of a private subject written by a close contemporary.
works.plot: Roper recounts More's household and public career from his own memory and family tradition: More's early marriage and life at Chelsea, his rise under Henry VIII, the succession crisis, his resignation of the chancellorship, his imprisonment, trial, and execution, with the celebrated dialogues between More and his wife and daughters and More's reported words to his son-in-law on the king's favour.
works.significance: The founding text of English biographical writing and the principal source for the domestic life of More; its vivid remembered dialogue made it one of the most influential portraits of a Tudor statesman ever written.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1553–58, probably during Mary's reign, by More's son-in-law who had lived in More's household for sixteen years; circulated in manuscript (the 'Harpsfield' manuscript) and first printed at Saint-Omer in 1626, with the first English printing in 1726.
works.characters: Sir Thomas More; William Roper (narrator); Margaret Roper (More's daughter); Alice More; Henry VIII
works.structure: A continuous first-person memoir in chronological order, emphasizing the domestic and moral More, with set-piece conversations and the famous 'King's servant but God's first' speech.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The Life of St Katharine
altTitles: Capgrave's Life of Saint Katharine of Alexandria
works.description: John Capgrave's verse life of St Katharine of Alexandria, composed c. 1445: the learned virgin's conversion, her debate with the fifty philosophers, her refusal of the emperor Maxentius, the wheels of her torture, and her mystical marriage to Christ. The most polished saint's life of the fifteenth century, in rhyme royal with an elaborate prologue.
works.plot: Katharine, the learned princess of Alexandria, is converted by a hermit's vision of the Virgin and wedded to Christ; she confounds the emperor's philosophers in public debate, converts them and the empress, endures the wheels and the prison's angelic visits, and is beheaded — her body borne by angels to Sinai, where the milk, not blood, flows from her severed neck.
works.significance: The most accomplished Middle English life of St Katharine — the patron saint of learning — and the summit of fifteenth-century learned hagiography in verse.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Lydgatean polish, with aureate diction and classical allusion.
works.context: Composed c. 1445 by the Augustinian friar John Capgrave of Lynn, in the learned East Anglian tradition of Lydgate and Bokenham; the prologue places the poem in the line of Chaucer's Legend of Good Women; preserved in Bodleian Rawlinson Poet. 118 and Arundel MS 396.
works.characters: St Katharine; the Emperor Maxentius; the fifty philosophers; the Virgin Mary; the hermit Adrian
works.structure: Five books of hagiographical narrative, from birth and conversion through debate and passion to translation, in the classical five-book scheme.
works.attributionNotes: Capgrave's authorship secure (he names himself in the prologue).
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Wisdom and learning

The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Life of the Fields
works.form: Essays; nature essay, first issued in 1884
works.description: Published in 1884 and Jefferies's finest collection of nature essays: the meadows, woods, birds and weather of the English countryside through the year. It is a prose work of 1884 by Richard Jefferies; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Nature Essay and the Rural Observation; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The essays move through the seasons and the kinds of country — the meadow, the wood, the hedgerow, the brook, the fields after harvest — recording the flowers, the birds, the insects and the farm work with an exactness that turns observation into a kind of prayer, and ending with the great essay on the wind and the sun.
works.significance: The Life of the Fields is the finest single collection of English nature essays of the century: its combination of exact observation and lyrical intensity made it the model for English nature writing, and it is the book in which Jefferies's genius is most consistently displayed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals.
works.context: 1883-84: the English countryside before mechanisation, the agricultural depression, and the golden age of the English nature essay. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.structure: A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Richard Jefferies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
Nature Essay and the Rural Observation
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Science, religion, and the question of design
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature

works.title: The Life of Washington
altTitles: The Life of Washington, with Curious Anecdotes, Equally Honourable to Himself, and Exemplary to His Young Countrymen
works.form: Prose biography for juvenile instruction; exemplary life with anecdotic and moral apparatus
works.description: A biography of Washington written for the young by an itinerant book agent and preaching minister, and the most widely circulated American life of the first president. It established the pattern of the exemplary national life built on anecdote and on the reader's feelings. The cherry-tree story of German honesty, added in a later edition, became the founding fable of American juvenile biography.
works.plot: The narrative follows Washington from the anecdotes of his childhood through the surveying and the French-and-Indian war to the command of the Continental army and the presidency. Each stage is illustrated by short stories of honesty, temperance, courage and courtesy, offered as models for imitation. The book dwells on the death at Mount Vernon and on the national mourning, and it urges the young reader to make private virtue the ground of public service. Its final pages bind the character of the man to the character of the republic he left behind.
works.significance: It is the most influential single book in the American culture of character, and the origin of the anecdote tradition in national biography. Its invention of a private Washington for the classroom defined how generations learned the founding. It is the canonical example of the juvenile and educational book of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published within a year of the death of Washington in 1799, when the national mourning created an immediate market for his life. Its author was a Methodist preacher turned book canvasser who sold subscriptions in the southern and western country. The expansion of the text through the editions of the 1800s answers the new American demand for a usable founding mythology.
works.characters: George Washington; his mother; the planter and surveyor of the northern neck; the slaves and household of Mount Vernon
works.structure: Chronical biography broken into anecdotal episodes, with moral reflection addressed directly to the juvenile reader; the appendix of maxims and sayings grows with each edition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the additions that make the book famous belong to later issues rather than to the first text.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Heroism and the heroic code
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: The Life of William Cowper, Esq.
altTitles: Letters of the Rev. William Cowper
works.form: Prose biography and edited correspondence: a life prefacing collected works, in the evangelical memoir tradition but practised as literary history.
works.description: The author's biography of William Cowper, written as the life prefacing a collected edition of Cowper's works and built on the poet's correspondence and on interviews with survivors. It is a work of editorial as much as of narrative art, and its frank handling of Cowper's madness and of his religious terror made it the most discussed English literary biography of the later 1830s. Its use of private letters also set a precedent, and a warning, for the practice of literary biography.
works.plot: The Life narrates Cowper's school years, his apprenticeship and his first poetry, the friendship with Lady Austen and the years at Olney, the partnership with Mrs. Unwin, and the later settlement at East Dereham and Weston Underwood. It prints and comments on the correspondence with the Rev. Mr. Newton, and gives a clinical and unsentimental account of the poet's depressions, his attempted suicide, and his final evangelical assurance. The biographer draws from the letters a picture of rural and manufacturing England, including Cowper's own condemnation of the way poor parents bound out and ruined their children. The publication of certain letters gave offence to surviving friends and relatives, who objected to what had been made public.
works.significance: The foundation of all later Cowper scholarship and a decisive text in the history of literary biography and of editorial ethics; its documentary passages on eighteenth-century labour and the manufacturing system have been used as social evidence by writers of every politics since.
works.meter: Prose, quoting verse and letters at length.
works.context: Prepared after its author had obtained access to Cowper's papers from the surviving collaterals, and issued in a cheap collected edition of the works in the mid 1830s; the controversy over its use of private letters ran for years and drew replies from those who thought the family betrayed.
works.characters: William Cowper; the Rev. Mr. Newton; Mrs. Unwin; Lady Austen; Mrs. Connard; the curate of Olney
works.structure: Chronological literary biography interwoven with long quoted correspondence and with documentary extract; narrative, letters, and editorial comment alternate, with topographical and social matter folded into the record of the life.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Evangelical experience and assurance
Melancholy and self-analysis

works.title: The Lion and the Unicorn
altTitles: The Lion and the Unicorn: Socialism and the English Genius
works.form: Essay (published as a book, no. 1 of the Searchlight Books)
works.description: Orwell's book-length wartime essay, published by Secker & Warburg on 19 February 1941 as the first of the Searchlight Books, a series edited by T. R. Fyvel and Orwell. It argues that Britain's outdated class system was hampering the war against Nazi Germany, and that only a democratic socialist revolution, at once patriotic and English, could win it.
works.plot: The essay is in three parts: 'England Your England', which opens 'As I write, highly civilized human beings are flying overhead, trying to kill me', 'Shopkeepers at War' and 'The English Revolution'. Orwell argues that the outdated class system is hampering the war effort and that to defeat Nazi Germany Britain needs a socialist revolution, so that being a socialist and a patriot are no longer opposed but complementary. The revolution he proposes would create a democratic 'English Socialism', distinct from the Soviet Communism he regarded as totalitarian, and a new Britishness freed from empire and from the decadent old ruling class; it might keep the royal family as a national symbol while sweeping away the rest of the upper class.
works.significance: The essay states without allegory the democratic socialism and hostility to totalitarianism that shape Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its first part, 'England Your England', is often treated as an essay in its own right; it later gave its title to a posthumous collection. In a speech on Europe in 1993 the Prime Minister John Major quoted its 'old maids bicycling to Holy Communion through the morning mist'.
works.meter: Polemical first-person prose that opens under air attack ('As I write, highly civilized human beings are flying overhead, trying to kill me') and proceeds through three titled parts to a programme for an English socialist revolution.
works.context: Written under air attack, as its opening sentence records, by a writer whose conviction of the dangers of totalitarianism had been formed in the Spanish Civil War. His wife Eileen described its theme as 'how to be a socialist while Tory'.
works.structure: Three parts: 'England Your England', 'Shopkeepers at War' and 'The English Revolution'. Continuous prose in sections or chapters, the argument or the account advanced from its statement to its conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
National identity and Englishness
Totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel

works.title: The Listeners and Other Poems
works.description: The book that made de la Mare famous: 'The Listeners', 'Silver' and the English supernatural lyric. It is a verse work of 1912 by Walter de la Mare; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The title poem, 'The Listeners', is the most famous English ghost poem — the traveller who knocks at the moonlit door and is answered only by silence and the listening phantoms; the collection also contains 'Silver', 'The Song of the Mad Prince', 'Old Susan' and 'The Quince Tree'.
works.significance: The Listeners and Other Poems made de la Mare famous and established the English supernatural lyric as a modern form: 'The Listeners' is the most famous ghost poem in the language and 'Silver' one of the best-loved short poems of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric of the half-heard and the unseen.
works.context: The English countryside and the ghost-story tradition of the period; de la Mare's years as an oil-company clerk writing in the evenings. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
works.characters: The traveller; the listeners; the phantom listeners
works.structure: A collection of lyrics in varied stanza forms, led by the title poem. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Walter John de la Mare. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Literary Souvenir
altTitles: The Literary Souvenir: A Christmas and New Year's Present
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: the miscellany gift-book of lyric, tale and short criticism, formatted for seasonal presentation with steel engraving.
works.description: One of the two great London literary annuals of the later 1820s, first issued for the season dated 1825 and continued annually under a founding editor who was also a poet and man of letters in his own right. It set itself deliberately against the merely decorative keepsake, claiming to offer literature of durable value as well as a gift-book's plates and bindings. Its volumes assembled poems, tales, historical and topographical papers and criticism from the most fashionable contributors of the day. It is the annual that best documents the editorial self-consciousness of the gift-book trade.
works.plot: The volumes have no continuous argument; their design is an assortment of occasional verse, short prose tales, historical sketches and critical papers grouped around engraved plates. Its editor's prefaces do, however, conduct a running argument about the annual's purpose: that a gift book should keep literature in circulation rather than merely ornament a drawing-room, and that the paying of handsome fees to established writers was the way to secure that.
works.significance: It is the most self-consciously literary of the great annuals and a primary vehicle for the transmission of Romantic and early-Victorian verse into middle-class domestic life. Its editorial statements are the best contemporary account of what an annual was for, and its files preserve poems and papers that entered the canon through gift-book circulation.
works.meter: Occasional and reflective verse in conventional stanzas and the sonnet form, with romantic ballad measures; prose in the familiar essay and tale registers.
works.context: Appearing in the years when the annual boom made the gift book the largest single market for verse and short prose, and when editors competed openly for the same contributions, its early volumes record the trade's circulation figures and its editorial quarrels over originality. It belongs to the later phase of Romantic literary commerce, shaped by new engraving technology and by a reading public that bought presents rather than books.
works.structure: Serial annual anthology: frontispiece plate, editor's preface, then a mixed succession of poem, tale, sketch and critical paper.
works.attributionNotes: The volumes were edited throughout by a single named literary editor, but the annual is a collaborative miscellany whose contents are individually attributable; the record is of the serial as a whole.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: The Little Duke
works.form: Children's historical novel; novel of development
works.description: Published in 1854 and Yonge's classic book for boys: the boyhood of Richard the Fearless, Duke of Normandy, in the tenth century. It is a prose fiction work of 1854 by Charlotte M. Yonge; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: The ten-year-old Richard succeeds his murdered father as Duke of Normandy and is carried off by King Louis of France; he escapes, holds his duchy against his enemies, and learns the self-command that makes him a ruler, in a story of courage, loyalty and forgiveness.
works.significance: The Little Duke is one of the great Victorian books for children and a founding text of the historical novel for boys: its picture of a child learning to govern himself has been read by generations and it set the pattern for the moral adventure story of the later century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the large family chronicle with an enormous cast.
works.context: 1854: the Victorian historical novel for children, the vogue for Normandy and the Crusades, and the High Church interest in the medieval past. The record dates the work as composed in 1854 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Richard, Duke of Normandy; Osmond de Centeville; Alberic de Montémar; King Louis IV of France; Queen Gerberge; Prince Carloman; Count Bernard de Harcourt; Hugh of Paris; Harald Bluetooth, King of Denmark
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Mary Yonge. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Little Lame Prince and His Travelling Cloak
altTitles: Little Lame Prince and His Travelling Cloak
works.description: Published in 1875 and one of the best-loved Victorian children's books: a crippled prince who is given a magic cloak that carries him over the world. It is a prose fiction work of 1875 by Dinah Mulock Craik; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Prince Dolor, robbed of his kingdom and lamed by his wicked uncle, is imprisoned in a tower until his fairy godmother brings him a travelling cloak; he flies across the world, learns the wisdom of the kingdoms he sees, and is restored to his throne as a just and gentle ruler.
works.significance: The Little Lame Prince is a permanent children's classic and one of the few Victorian fantasies to make physical disability the centre of its meaning: its image of the boy flying over the world in his cloak has entered the common imaginative inheritance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is plain, warm narrative prose.

works.title: The Little Minister
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1891 and the most popular of the Scottish novels: a young minister in a small town falls in love with a mysterious gypsy girl. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Gavin Dishart, the young minister of Thrums, falls in love with Babbie, who roams Thrums disguised as a gypsy girl but is in fact the ward and intended bride of the old Earl of Rintoul; their forbidden love, the town's scandal, and the heroism of the small minister in a riot make a story that mixes kailyard comedy, romance and a glimpse of the Scottish Chartist troubles.
works.significance: The Little Minister was the best-selling Scottish novel of the 1890s and the book that made Barrie famous: it established the kailyard school of Scottish fiction, it made Thrums a mythical place in the Scottish imagination, and it prepared the way for Peter Pan's combination of sentiment, comedy and childhood.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect.

works.title: The Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
altTitles: The Little Woodman and his Dog Caesar
The History of the Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
works.form: juvenile and devotional tale; the domestic narrative of the injured child with the animal fidelity
works.description: A tale for children, first published in 1818 and reprinted without end through the century, of the youngest child of a poor woodman's family, of the cruelty of his elder brothers, and of the fidelity of the dog Cæsar; one of the most widely read of the English books of the exposed child and of the brute that serves the innocent.
works.plot: The tale opens in the hut of a woodman of the forest country, whose family is poor, whose elder sons are hard and envious, and whose youngest, the little William, is a child of gentleness and of the book. Upon the father's death the burden of the household falls upon the brothers, and the wickedness of the elder sons, prompted by the greed of the portion and by hatred of the piety of the little boy, carries him into the forest and leaves him there to perish by hunger and by the beasts. The dog Cæsar, bound to the child by the tenderness of his rearing, watches over him in the woods, defends him against the wolf that stalks him, and becomes the means of the discovery of the guilt; the cruelty is searched out, the guilty brothers come to ruin, and the preserved child is provided for and brought forward in his little education. The argument of the book is the religious argument of the whole class of these tales: that Providence keeps the innocent, that the sin of the household is found out in its own time, and that the reading of the Bible and the duty of gentleness to the young and to the brute are the whole wisdom of the child.
works.significance: The type of the evangelical tale of the exposed child and of the ministering animal, and one of the most permanently remembered of the books of the English nursery: the figure of the faithful dog and the scene of the forest are among the stock images of juvenile writing, and the tale has been read ever since as the exemplar of the method by which terror, pathos, and providential justice were combined for the moral use of children.
works.meter: Plain, urgent, and affecting prose of the evangelical teacher for the young reader, with the little speech of the child, the terror of the forest scene told in short unadorned sentences, and the solemn tenderness of the moral; the pathos of the brute's fidelity is gained by the restraint of the style.
works.context: Published in 1818, the year which gave the world also the religious family history of the same pen, in the season of the cheap and the Sunday-school book, when the tale of the persecuted child and of the faithful animal was the most powerful instrument of the juvenile trade and when the terror and the tenderness of such stories were held necessary to the formation of the conscience of the labouring and middling ranks. Its author, an officer's wife long resident in the company's territories, had already written the Indian child's tale, and the woodman's story became, with her other little books, a standing possession of the nursery and of the circulating juvenile libraries of both countries.
works.characters: The woodman and his wife; the little William, the youngest of the family; the elder brothers, hard, idle, and envious; the faithful dog Cæsar; the neighbours and the people of the forest country who search out the crime
works.structure: A single continuous tale for the young reader, in short chapters of the plain domestic narrative, moving from the hut and the forest to the exposure, the preservation, the discovery, and the religious close, with the direct address of the moral to the child at the turn of the several parts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the title is variously given at length and at abbreviature in the later issues, the name of the dog and the spelling of the title being altered in the reprints, and the tale was also issued in the combined juvenile volumes and in the abridged cheap series, which do not follow the first text.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Evangelical experience and assurance
Penance, confession, and sin
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: The Lone Swallows

works.plot: The Lone Swallows is Williamson's first book, the memoir of the war in Flanders and of the swallows over the drowned plain, in the prose of the nature writer turned to the battlefield.
works.significance: The Lone Swallows is the first of Williamson's books and the proof that the nature writer's prose could carry the war: its swallows over the drowned plain are the first page of the nature memoir of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the wild creature followed hour by hour and season by season.
works.context: Flanders in the war years, and the first memoirs of the war. The record dates the work as composed in 1921 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; autobiography and the modern memoir.
works.characters: the officer; the swallows; the drowned plain

An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points.

works.title: The Lonely Londoners
works.description: Selvon's third novel, published in London by Allan Wingate in 1956 and in New York by St Martin's Press (142 pages), follows a group of West Indian migrants, 'the boys', through about three years of their lives in post-war London. It has no plot in the usual sense: its episodes are held together by Moses Aloetta, a Trinidadian who has lived in London longer than the others and whose room the newcomers visit every Sunday morning. Its narrator speaks the same creolised English as its characters, a choice Wikipedia calls groundbreaking, and Wikipedia ranks it, with George Lamming's The Emigrants (1954), among the first novels about poor, working-class black migrants after the British Nationality Act of 1948. In 2022 it was one of the seventy books chosen for the BBC's Big Jubilee Read.
works.summary: A sequence of episodes and character sketches rather than a continuous story. It opens on a foggy winter evening as Moses takes the number 46 bus from the corner of Chepstow Road and Westbourne Grove to Waterloo to meet a newcomer off the boat-train, and moves among the men he knows: Galahad, Cap, Bart, Lewis, Big City, Five Past Twelve, Harris and Tolroy's family, with the redoubtable Tanty. About two-thirds of the way through, a long passage without punctuation celebrates summer in the parks; winter and unemployment return, and the book ends with Moses on Chelsea Embankment, looking at the Thames and wondering whether he could write a book.
works.plot:
On a grim winter evening Moses Aloetta, a Trinidadian night worker to whom people at home keep sending newcomers, goes to Waterloo to meet Henry Oliver, just arrived on the boat-train. At the station he finds his Jamaican friend Tolroy waiting for his mother, who arrives with the whole family, including Tolroy's aunt, Tanty Bessy, although he had asked her to come alone; Tanty makes everyone pose for a reporter, and the next day the photograph appears under the headline 'Now Jamaican Families Come to Britain'. Henry steps off the train in light clothes, with no luggage or winter coat and so cheerfully confident that Moses calls him Sir Galahad. Moses feeds him in his room in Bayswater and offers advice; Galahad, an electrician at home, insists on finding work alone, loses his way and his nerve in the street, and is rescued by Moses, who takes him to the employment exchange, where there are no openings but he registers for an insurance card.

The narrative turns to Moses' acquaintances. Cap, a Nigerian sent to London to study law, has spent his parents' money on drink and women, lives on loans he never repays and marries a French woman only to abandon her. Bart, light-skinned, passes himself off as South American and avoids other immigrants; he loses his English girlfriend, Beatrice, and is left searching London for her. Lewis, who works nights in the same factory as Moses, takes Moses' teasing claim that wives receive other men while their husbands are on the night shift as proof against his wife, Agnes, and beats her until she leaves him. Tanty, who never strays from her district, becomes a regular at a local shop that stocks West Indian goods, and makes her first journey alone by train and bus so easily that no one would have guessed it was her first. In summer Galahad, newly dressed in fine clothes, is wounded when a white child remarks on his colour, and alone in his room he addresses his own blackness: 'Colour, is you that causing all this'. Big City, who grew up in an orphanage in Trinidad, flaunts money whose source no one knows, and Harris, who prides himself on English manners, holds a dance at which the boys embarrass him: Tanty sweeps him on to the floor, Five Past Twelve dances close with one of his guests, and the night gets out of hand, ending with a bottle broken over Five's head. A long unpunctuated passage celebrates London in summer, when the boys 'coast a lime' in the parks and the city's sexual traffic between black men and white women runs through the night, until Moses closes it with 'a long sigh like a man who live life and see nothing at all in it'.

Winter brings lay-offs. Hungry and out of work, Galahad catches a pigeon in a park while an old woman threatens to report him, and he and Moses cook it and laugh over stories of home until the talk turns sombre. At one of the Sunday gatherings Moses looks round at the boys with affection, unreliable as some of them are. At the end he stands on Chelsea Embankment, feeling in the river 'a greatness and a vastness', 'like it was something solid after feeling everything else give way'. Remembering Daniel's talk of taxi-drivers, porters and road-sweepers in France who had written best-sellers, he watches a tugboat on the Thames, 'wondering if he could ever write a book like that, what everybody would buy'.
works.significance: South Asian Britain calls it Selvon's most acclaimed and widely known novel. Susheila Nasta's introduction to the Penguin edition describes it as 'a major step forward in the process of linguistic and cultural decolonization', and Wikipedia, citing the British Library, presents it as a precursor of Zadie Smith's White Teeth (2000) and Hanif Kureishi's The Buddha of Suburbia (1990). For Dawes it confirmed that West Indian idiom could carry not only comic character but deep emotion and philosophical introspection. Its success led to two sequels, Moses Ascending (1975) and Moses Migrating (1983), and Selvon adapted its characters for radio in the plays of Eldorado West One (1988).
works.meter: A third-person narrator speaks the creolised English of the characters. Selvon told Michel Fabre that he began with narrative in standard English and dialogue in dialect, could not 'really move', and then wrote both in dialect, after which 'the novel just shot along'. The idiom includes the boys' names for places ('the Water' for Bayswater, 'the Gate' for Notting Hill), 'liming' and 'oldtalk', 'spades' for themselves and a string of slang for white women. Wikipedia links the stream-of-consciousness summer passage to modernism, and Schwarz notes that Selvon confirmed T. S. Eliot's influence, visible in the shared 'unreal' London of The Waste Land; the geography of the city, down to the bus route, is exact.
works.context: Selvon arrived from Trinidad in 1950 and, like his characters, stayed in a hostel near Earl's Court, did menial work and came to know the Bayswater and Harrow Road district, while reading for the BBC's Caribbean Voices. The novel belongs to the first decade of post-war Caribbean migration after the Windrush, when the run-down rooming houses of Notting Hill were packed with migrant tenants by landlords such as Peter Rachman. Two years after publication the area saw the white riots of 1958, and in 1959 the murder of the Antiguan Kelso Cochrane; the first Caribbean carnival in London, held in St Pancras Town Hall in January 1959, was one response (Schwarz).
works.characters: Moses Aloetta, a Trinidadian long settled in London; Henry Oliver, called Sir Galahad, a newcomer from Trinidad; Tolroy, a Jamaican, his mother and his aunt Tanty Bessy; Lewis and his wife Agnes; Cap, a Nigerian who came to study law; Bart and his English girlfriend Beatrice; Big City; Harris; Five Past Twelve; Daniel
works.structure: Episodic and loosely chronological across roughly three years and their seasons, held together by Moses as host, adviser and witness; minor characters receive self-contained sketches. The opening journey to Waterloo and the closing scene on the Embankment frame the book, and Schwarz argues that Moses grows more reflective until he emerges as the author of his own tale. Dawes describes the whole as told like a ballad or calypso, and the summer section is a single stream-of-consciousness passage (pp. 92-102 in the edition Wikipedia cites).

works.title: The Long Ago
works.description: Published in 1881 and the first book of the collaboration: the poems of a shared life, written in the forms of the Elizabethan and Romantic lyric. It is a verse work of 1881 by Michael Field; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume is a sequence of lyrics, each spun from a fragment of Sappho printed in Greek at its head, in which the two poets, writing as one voice, imagine Sappho's loves, for the girls of her circle and for Phaon, and her legendary death at Leucadia.
works.significance: The Long Ago is the founding book of the Michael Field collaboration and one of the earliest sustained bodies of English love poetry written between women: its formal accomplishment and its intimate subject made it a central text for the modern recovery of Victorian women's writing.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric.
works.context: 1881: the Pre-Raphaelite circle, the aesthetic movement, and the Victorian reception of a poetry of female intimacy. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Sappho; Phaon; the girls of her circle
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Lord's Prayer I, II, and III
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (versions I and II); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (version III)
works.form: religious lyric (prayer paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Three independent Old English versifications of the Lord's Prayer. The first (123 lines with its doxology) expands each petition into doctrinal and devotional verse; the second (19 lines) is a close rendering; the third, in a Mercian dialect, survives in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: Each poem paraphrases the petitions of the Pater Noster — the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil — expanding them with commentary on the soul's needs, the devil's snares, and the last judgment.
works.significance: The fullest surviving Old English treatment of the central Christian prayer, showing how poets turned liturgical texts into vernacular verse of considerable doctrinal ambition.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the first version's expansions use formulaic homiletic diction familiar from the Exeter Book religious poems.
works.context: The Lord's Prayer was among the first texts every Christian learned, and Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care singles out prayer as a duty of the learned; vernacular versifications made the prayer available for devotion and meditation in the native idiom.
works.structure: The first version works petition by petition through the prayer, ending with an elaborated doxology; the shorter versions render the prayer more directly with brief homiletic expansions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The three versions are independent texts by different poets, grouped here for convenience as in the standard editions.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, the soul, and the afterlife

works.title: The Lost Saint
works.form: Play in Irish (one act; trans. by Lady Gregory)
works.description: The legend play of the saint who is lost and the village that finds him. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by Douglas Hyde; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Lost Saint brings the Yeatsian legend of the saint who disappears from the village into the one-act play in Irish, played at the Abbey among the early Irish-language nights.
works.significance: The Lost Saint is Hyde's legend play and the proof that the Irish-language drama could carry the wonder-tale as well as the cottage comedy; it remains among the best of the early Abbey plays in Irish.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish of Connacht carried into English by the translation of Lady Gregory.
works.context: The Irish west in 1904, and the legend play of the revival. works.title: The Lost World
works.description: Published in the Strand in 1912 and the founding text of the dinosaur adventure: Professor Challenger's expedition to a South American plateau where the prehistoric world survives. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by Arthur Conan Doyle; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The journalist Edward Malone joins Challenger, Professor Summerlee and Lord John Roxton on an expedition to the Amazonian plateau; they find dinosaurs, ape-men and a lost tribe, escape with a pterodactyl, and Challenger exhibits it at the Zoological Institute.
works.significance: The Lost World founded the lost-world romance and gave the twentieth century its most durable adventure formula; its mixture of scientific speculation and imperial exploration is a key text in the literature of the popular scientific romance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the clue and the deduction.
works.context: The 1910s, the age of polar and Amazonian exploration, and the new palaeontology of the dinosaur. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Professor George Edward Challenger; Edward Malone; Professor Summerlee; Lord John Roxton; Zambo; Gladys Hungerton
works.structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: The Loves of the Angels
works.form: Religious narrative poem in the line of sacred and legendary verse, drawing on apocryphal and patristic matter about the angels who transgressed.
works.description: A devotional narrative poem on the antediluvian legend of the Watchers, telling of pure spirits who love the daughters of men, descend into the world of passion and war, and are reclaimed by penitence. It is written in three parts and is expressly a religious poem, intended to assert the possibility of holiness preserved amid temptation. The volume appeared with other shorter pieces and provoked immediate charges of borrowing.
works.plot: Two angels, bound by a friendship that the poem treats as the type of all holy attachment, are drawn down by love of mortal women into the antediluvian world, where they witness and share its wars, its tyranny and its grief. The narrative moves from their fall-like descent through the history of the race towards the coming Deluge, and then to intercession, repentance and restoration. The poem's argument is doctrinal as well as romantic: it claims that created love, rightly ordered, is the means by which even a fallen spirit may return, and it figures the Deluge as both judgement and cleansing. Its closing movements exchange the narrative for address and prayer, so that the legend becomes an image of the soul's education.
works.significance: It is the clearest statement of the poet's religious imagination and one of the more ambitious attempts of the later Romantic generation to write a doctrinal narrative poem. Contemporary controversy over its sources turned it into a case study in the period's anxieties about plagiarism and influence. Its treatment of spiritual friendship and of redeemable fallenness has drawn renewed critical attention in the study of Romantic religious verse.
works.meter: Varied lyric stanza measures with heavy use of refrain, invocation and apostrophe; blank-verse-like meditative passages are interwoven.
works.context: Published in the early 1820s, when biblical and legendary subjects were being treated by poets of every party and when religious poetry had become a field of controversy between evangelicals, Unitarians and infidels. Its appearance was read as a defence of the poet's own piety against sceptical reputation, and its subject was taken up in the reviews alongside questions of originality and of imitation. The Deluge material was familiar both from Milton and from the popular legendary drama.
works.characters: The two loving angels; the mortal beloveds of the antediluvian world; the patriarchal and warrior figures of the pre-Deluge race
works.structure: A continuous narrative in three parts, rising from the descent of the spirits through human history to deliverance, with meditative and apostrophising passages interrupting the story.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: The Loves of the Plants
works.form: Didactic and descriptive verse in heroic couplets with prose scientific notes
works.description: A didactic poem in four cantos which translates the Linnaean sexual system of botany into a pageant of personified flowers, each plant's reproductive organs rendered as the amours of a nymph and her swain. It first appeared in 1789 and was then issued as the second part of The Botanic Garden in 1791, and its brilliance, obscurity and frank eroticism made it at once a bestseller and a scandal. Erasmus Darwin supplies scientific matter in the accompanying notes, where he argues the vegetable kingdom's real structure.
works.plot: The poem passes in sequence through the classes and orders of the Linnaean system, dramatising each as an allegorical courtship or marriage: the polyandrous female fern, the mutual fidelity of the flax, the violent loves of the poppy, the priestly solemnities of the mosses. Beneath the gallantry runs a serious argument about irritability, the contrivances of pollination, and the vegetable physiology revealed by microscopical enquiry. The closing canto turns from the floral court to the great powers of nature and to a deist hymn to universal benevolence, binding vegetable life into a general economy of heat, light and growth.
works.significance: The most influential English poem on botany, it shaped a generation's reading of Linnaeus and supplied the ornamental scientific vocabulary later parodied and admired. Coleridge and Southey acknowledged its example and Wordsworth's protest against personification is partly aimed at it; its mixture of erotic allegory and apparatus of notes is a distinctive late-Augustan solution to the problem of didactic form.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, variably decorated with lyric intercalations, imitation of air-sounds and insect-music
works.context: Written in the Derby-Lichfield circle of erasmian natural philosophy and popular science, it transmits Linnaeus through translation and the sexual politics of the 1780s, amid the Botanical Society vogue, Erasmus Darwin's own zoonomic researches, and the radical Dissenting enthusiasm for progress and abolition.
works.characters: Venus or the presiding goddess of the garden; personified plant-nymphs; sylphs and gnomes of the floral courts
works.structure: Four cantos of linked ekphrastic episodes arranged by Linnaean class and order, with a scientific apparatus of prose notes appended to each.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Erasmus Darwin is established and undisputed.
themes: Creation and cosmology
The New Science and experimental philosophy
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Sketches
altTitles: Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Sketches
works.description: Published in 1870 and the first collection of Harte's California stories: the volume that made the American West a literary subject. It is a prose fiction work of 1870 by Bret Harte; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Luck of Roaring Camp', 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat', 'Miggles', 'Tennessee's Partner', 'The Idyl of Red Gulch' and 'Brown of Calaveras', and its stories of gamblers, prostitutes and miners fixed the image of the gold rush.
works.significance: The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Sketches is the founding collection of American western fiction and established the local-colour movement in the United States: its stories are the origin of the American literary West.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the single dramatic scene with a surprise ending.
works.context: The 1868-70: the California gold rush remembered, the Overland Monthly, and the eastern market for western writing. The record dates the work as composed between 1868 and 1870 and first published in 1870 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; South-Western Humour and the Tall-Tale Sketch, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.

works.title: The Magistrate
works.description: First performed in 1885 and the most durable English farce of the century: a respectable magistrate is arrested in his own court after a night of mistaken identity. It is a dramatic work of 1885 by Arthur Wing Pinero; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Mr Posket, a London police magistrate, takes his family to a hotel, where his wife's age is misreported and his stepson's gambling leads to a series of mistaken identities; the next morning Posket finds himself on the bench trying his own case, in a farce of escalating confusion resolved only by the discovery that everyone is related.
works.significance: The Magistrate is the finest English farce of the century and one of the most durable comedies in the language: its construction and its dialogue made it the model for the English stage farce, and it established Pinero as the leading comic craftsman of the 1880s.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion.
works.context: 1885: the Victorian police court, the late-Victorian hotel, the farce tradition of the Court Theatre, and the fashion for the 'well-made' comedy of situation. The record dates the work as composed in 1885 and first published in 1885 and first performed in 1885 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Mr Posket; Agatha Posket; Cis Farringdon; Charlotte Verrinder; Colonel Lukyn; Captain Horace Vale; Mr Bullamy
works.structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Pinero. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Magnetic Lady; or, Humours Reconciled
works.description: Jonson's last comedy, in which the learned Lady Loadstone acts as a magnet drawing a set of humours characters together and reconciling them through a marriage plot and a discovered heiress.

works.significance: Jonson's farewell to comedy and a final attempt to reconcile the humours tradition with a romantic plot; its induction is a rare piece of Jonsonian meta-theatrical commentary.

works.title: The Maid of Sker
works.form: Novel; local-colour sketch, first issued in 1872
works.description: Blackmore's favourite among his own books: a Welsh pirate, a foundling and the coast of South Wales. It is a prose fiction work of 1872 by Richard Doddridge Blackmore; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Davy Llewellyn, an old Welsh sailor, tells how he found a child on the sands at Sker and brought her up among the fishermen, in a rambling narrative of wreckers, gentry and the Bristol Channel that is one of the most original novels of the century.
works.significance: The Maid of Sker was Blackmore's own favourite among his novels and is one of the most original first-person narratives in Victorian fiction: its Welsh narrator, its dialect and its rambling structure made it a favourite of later critics and a model for the regional novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person Exmoor narrative in dialect-inflected prose.
works.context: The Glamorgan coast at the beginning of the nineteenth century and the life of the Welsh fishing villages. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; sensation novel.

works.structure: A first-person narrative in three volumes, told in the Welsh sailor's voice. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: The Maid's Tragedy
works.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragedy of honour: Amintor, commanded by the king, breaks his vow to Aspatia and marries Evadne — who is the king's secret mistress; Evadne's repentance, her murder of the king in the bedchamber, and Amintor's and Aspatia's deaths follow, in the play's double catastrophe of the marriage bed and the wedding night turned funeral.
works.plot: The wedding night reveals Evadne's secret; Amintor's honour forbids revenge on the king; Aspatia, disguised as her own brother, takes the duel's death-blow from Amintor; Evadne, converted by her brother Melantius, kills the king; and the last act's cascade — Evadne's rejection, Aspatia's death, Amintor's suicide — empties the court of its lovers.
works.significance: The strongest of the Beaumont–Fletcher tragedies — the play in which the partnership's courtly polish met the Jacobean taste for blood.
works.meter: The fluent tragic verse of the partnership, with Evadne's and Aspatia's great speeches as its heights.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1610–11 and printed in 1619; its king-killing and bedchamber horrors made it the most talked-of tragedy of its decade.
works.characters: Amintor; Evadne; Aspatia; Melantius; the King; Calianax; Lysippus; Diphilus; the Ladies; the masquers
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of honour in the Senecan manner, with the bedchamber murder and the double suicide as its symmetrical climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is debated.

works.title: The Maine Woods
works.description: Published in 1864 after Thoreau's death: accounts of three journeys to the Maine woods in 1846, 1853 and 1857, and the finest American writing on the northern forest. It is a prose work of 1864 by Henry David Thoreau; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Thoreau describes the wilderness of Ktaadn, the moose hunt, the Indian guides, the logging camps of the Allegash and the East Branch, and the meeting of the industrial and the primitive at the edge of the forest.
works.significance: The Maine Woods is the greatest American book of the northern wilderness and one of the first to record the destruction of the North American forest: it is the founding text of the American literature of conservation and a central work of nineteenth-century writing on the Native American.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences.
works.context: The years 1846-57, the Maine lumber industry, the Penobscot and the native communities of the north, and the American debate on the preservation of the forests. The record dates the work as composed between 1846 and 1857 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The Malcontent
works.description: Marston's tragicomedy of the displaced duke: Altofronto, deposed by his usurping brother Pietro, returns to court disguised as the malcontent Malevole, whose bitter truths scour the court of Genoa; through the intrigues of Mendoza, the play's machiavel, the plots double and reverse until the final scene's masque restores the true duke — and with him the play's satirical license.
works.plot: Malevole haunts the usurper's court with truth-telling; Mendoza, the courtier, plots to seize the duchy, poisoning, banishing, and betraying in turn; the counter-plots of Malevole and the banished Pietro (in disguise) entangle the machiavel; and the final masque, with the deaths staged and revealed, restores Altofronto to his throne and pardons the penitent.
works.significance: The play that named the Jacobean malcontent — the great satire of courtly corruption that Shakespeare answered in Measure for Measure.
works.meter: Marston's snarling, paradoxical verse for Malevole's truths, with prose for the court's baseness.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel in 1604 and printed the same year; Webster supplied an induction for the King's Men's revival, and the play's 'malcontent' became the decade's signature type.

works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy built on the disguised-duke device, with the malcontent's satiric set pieces and the final masque of revelations.

works.title: The Maltese Falcon
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1930
works.description: The founding text of the hard-boiled novel: Sam Spade, the falcon and the double cross. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Dashiell Hammett; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Sam Spade, a San Francisco private detective, is drawn into the hunt for a jewelled falcon by the beautiful Brigid O'Shaughnessy, the fat man Casper Gutman and the gunman Wilmer, in a plot of double cross that ends with Spade turning the woman he loves over to the police.

works.meter: Prose. works.title: The Man against the Sky
works.description: Published in 1916 and the collection that established Robinson as a major poet: the title poem on the human figure against the void, and the Tilbury Town portraits. It is a verse work of 1916 by Edwin Arlington Robinson; it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The title poem presents the human being standing against the sky, face to face with the immensity and the indifference of the universe, and asks whether the courage to endure is not itself a kind of answer; the collection also contains 'Ben Jonson Entertains a Man from Stratford', 'Eros Turannos' and 'The Gift of God'.
works.significance: The Man against the Sky made Robinson famous and is the finest single collection of American poetry of the 1910s: its title poem gave the age its image of human courage in an indifferent universe, and it confirmed Robinson's position as the leading American poet of his generation before the modernists.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, colloquial line in traditional metre.

The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
