works.title: The Man in the Queue
works.description: Tey's first novel: a stabbing in the queue at a London theatre. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Josephine Tey; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A man is stabbed in the queue outside a London theatre, and the investigation of the murder takes in the theatre, the West End and the ordinary people in the line; Inspector Grant follows a case in which everyone in the queue had the opportunity and no one the apparent motive.
works.significance: The Man in the Queue is Josephine Tey's first novel and the first appearance of Inspector Alan Grant: its queue, its theatre and its ordinary suspects made the detective novel of the London crowd, and it began the series that ended with The Franchise Affair and The Daughter of Time.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the detective novel as a study of character.
works.context: London in the late 1920s, and the West End theatre. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: Inspector Alan Grant; the man in the queue; the theatre company; the West End witnesses
works.structure: A detective novel of investigation in London. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close.

works.title: The Man of Mode; or, Sir Fopling Flutter
works.description: Etherege's masterpiece, the greatest comedy of manners of the Restoration, in which the rake Dorimant manipulates a whole fashionable society of lovers, fops, and mothers with effortless wit.
works.plot: Dorimant courts the rich heiress Harriet while abandoning Mrs Loveit; the fop Sir Fopling Flutter is mocked throughout; Dorimant wins Harriet by pretending to be a country gentleman, and the play ends with marriage and the rout of the pretenders.
works.significance: The supreme achievement of Restoration social comedy and the model for Congreve, Sheridan, and Wilde; it created the type of the gentleman-rake and the standard of high-comic dialogue in English.
works.meter: Prose of extraordinary rhythmic precision; the dialogue is the model of Restoration wit.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden on 11 March 1676 and dedicated to the Earl of Rochester; Dorimant was widely taken to be Rochester and Sir Fopling to be a caricature of several court fops.
works.characters: Dorimant; Harriet; Mrs Loveit; Bellinda; Sir Fopling Flutter; Young Bellair; Emilia; Lady Woodvill; Medley; Shoat; Orange
works.structure: Five acts of intricate social intrigue with no subplot of consequence, unified by the figure of Dorimant.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal
The city and urban life
Wit, libertinism, and the rake

works.title: The Man of Property
works.description: The first Forsyte novel: Soames Forsyte's possession of his wife Irene becomes a study of property as a whole way of life. It is a prose fiction work of 1906 by John Galsworthy; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Soames Forsyte, a solicitor and art collector, builds a house at Robin Hill for his wife Irene, who does not love him. When Irene falls in love with the architect, young Philip Bosinney, Soames sues him for the cost of the house; the lawsuit destroys Bosinney, and Irene leaves Soames. The novel ends with the family's verdict on a marriage conceived as an investment.
works.significance: The Man of Property is the founding novel of the great English family saga and the finest study in English fiction of the mentality of property: its portrait of Soames — the man who owns his wife — gave the language a new term for the possessive temperament and made Galsworthy the period's leading social novelist.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the leisurely, orderly, ironic family chronicle.
works.context: The London of the propertied upper middle class in the 1880s, the professional classes and their codes of ownership, and the aesthetic movement's effect on the collecting of pictures. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1906 and first published in 1906 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Soames Forsyte; Irene Forsyte; Philip Bosinney; Young Jolyon Forsyte; Old Jolyon Forsyte; June Forsyte
works.structure: Three-part novel with an interlude; dated sections moving chronologically from 1886 to 1887. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Man Who Lost Himself
works.form: Novel (the lost self and the war)
works.description: The novel of the lost self: the soldier who returns from the war as another man. It is a prose fiction work of 1941 by Osbert Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form.
works.plot: The soldier who returns from the war cannot recover the self he lost in the trench, and the novel follows the lost man through the London of the between-wars years, the family that cannot recognise him and the self that will not return, in the satirical prose of the memoirist.
works.significance: The Man Who Lost Himself is Osbert Sitwell's novel of the shell-shocked century: its lost self made the war's damage a subject of the satirical novel and gave the between-wars fiction one of its truest figures of the divided man.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the polished satirical sentence of the man of the world.
works.context: London between the wars, and the shell shock of the lost generation. The record dates the work as composed in 1940 and first published in 1941 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: the man who lost himself; the family; the wife; the doctors of the mind
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the return, the recognition and the refusal of the self. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Osbert Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare
altTitles: Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1908
works.description: The greatest English metaphysical thriller: a poet, an anarchist council and the chase through London. It is a prose fiction work of 1908 by G. K. Chesterton; it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Gabriel Syme, a policeman, infiltrates a council of anarchists who are named after the days of the week; his pursuit of the terrifying Sunday takes him across London and France in a nightmare of disguises and revelations that ends in a garden and the discovery of who Sunday is.
works.significance: The Man Who Was Thursday is the greatest English metaphysical thriller and Chesterton's masterpiece: its nightmare logic, its chase and its final revelation made it a permanent classic of the fantastic and one of the most original novels of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the paradox turned inside out.
works.context: London and France at the turn of the century, and the anarchist scare of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed between 1907 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Gabriel Syme; Sunday; Gregory; Bull; Gogol; the Secretary
works.structure: A novel in fifteen chapters, from the wood to the garden. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The Man with the Blue Guitar
works.form: Poetry collection (long title poem and thirty-three lyrics)
works.description: Stevens's central long poem: the guitar, the blue, and the imagination's argument with reality. It is a verse work of 1937 by Wallace Stevens; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The thirty-three cantos of the title poem take Picasso's painting as the figure of the poet whose instrument transforms the world, and the collection's shorter poems — 'The Idea of Order at Key West', 'A Postcard from the Volcano', 'The Pleasures of Merely Circulating' — extend the argument about imagination and reality.
works.significance: The Man with the Blue Guitar is the central long poem of Stevens's middle period and the fullest statement of his aesthetic: it is the period's great poem about the relation of art to reality, and 'The Idea of Order at Key West' is among the finest American poems of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the exotic and sumptuous vocabulary.
works.context: The Depression and the political pressures of the 1930s, which Stevens answered with a poetry of the imagination rather than of politics. The record dates the work as composed between 1935 and 1936 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.characters: The guitarist; the poet; Ramon Fernandez
works.structure: A long title poem in thirty-three cantos, with a group of shorter lyrics. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture
altTitles: Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture
works.description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's most ambitious work of cultural criticism: an analysis of how the whole of American culture — art, religion, education, law and language — has been shaped by male dominance.
works.plot: Gilman examines the 'androcentric' bias in literature, art, dress, cookery, medicine, education and government, and argues that human culture has been distorted by the exclusion of half of humanity and that the correction of this bias is the great task of the modern age.
works.significance: The Man-Made World is a founding text of feminist cultural criticism and one of the first systematic analyses of what would later be called the social construction of gender.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
works.context: 1910: the suffrage campaign, the new sociology of gender, and the American Progressive era. The record dates the work as composed in 1910 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Perkins Stetson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Manxman
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Caine's greatest success: two foster-brothers, one woman, and the law of the island. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Hall Caine; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Pete Quilliam, a Manx fisherman, and Philip Christian, a young advocate, are foster-brothers; both love Kate Cregeen. Pete goes to sea to make his fortune, Philip betrays him, and the novel works out its tragedy through the Manx divorce court and the conscience of the island.
works.significance: The Manxman was Caine's greatest commercial success and the novel that made him a world figure, selling in the hundreds of thousands and being filmed by Hitchcock in 1929. It is the central text of the Manx regional novel and the most widely read English novel about the island.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the three-decker architecture of climax and reunion.
works.context: The Isle of Man in the 1890s, the Manx courts, the herring fleet and the Methodist community of the island. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Pete Quilliam; Philip Christian; Kate Cregeen; Caesar Cregeen; Auntie Nan
works.structure: A novel in five books, from the herring shore to the divorce court. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Henry Hall Caine. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Marble Faun
works.description: Published in 1860 and the last of Hawthorne's completed romances: the story of four artists in Rome and of a murder that brings the knowledge of evil into paradise. It is a prose fiction work of 1860 by Nathaniel Hawthorne; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Miriam, the mysterious painter, is pursued by a shadowy monk; Donatello, the Italian count who resembles the Faun of Praxiteles, kills the monk for her; the guilt of the pair, and the conversion of Donatello into a moral being through remorse, is the novel's central argument.
works.significance: The Marble Faun is the first American novel of the expatriate artist in Europe and the founding text of the American literature of Italy: its meditation on the fall of man, art and experience makes it the most philosophical of Hawthorne's books and a direct influence on Henry James.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The years 1858-59, the American artists' colony in Rome, the Italian independence movement, and the American expatriate world of the 1850s. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1859 and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Miriam; Donatello, Count of Monte Beni; Kenyon, the sculptor; Hilda; the model, Brother Antonio
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Marriage (Hyde)
works.form: Play in Irish (one act; trans. by Lady Gregory)
works.description: The cottage comedy of the matchmaking and the marriage. It is a dramatic work of 1903 by Douglas Hyde; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Marriage brings the matchmaker, the dowry and the quarrel of the two families into the cottage in the one-act comedy in Irish, played at the Abbey among the first Irish-language nights.
works.significance: The Marriage is among the first Irish-language plays of the Abbey and one of Hyde's best cottage comedies: its matchmaking and its dowry quarrel fixed the subject of the Irish cottage play.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish of Connacht carried into English by the translation of Lady Gregory.
works.context: The Irish west in 1903, and the early Abbey. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and first performed in 1903 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.
works.characters: the matchmaker; the bride; the two families; the priest
works.structure: A cottage comedy in one act, in Irish with Lady Gregory's translation. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name An Craoibhín Aoibhinn, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Douglas Hyde is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
works.form: Illuminated prophetic book and verse-and-prose satire, partly a parody of the devotional table and of the prophetic writing then current, and partly a manifesto of the contrary energies of the soul.
works.description: The most argumentative of the illuminated books, etched and printed by the author in the years following the two collections of songs, and written in a mixed prose and verse manner after the model of a prophetic book and in open parody of the religious tables then current. Its occasion is a memory of a hell where the spirits of the dead are taught by an angel, and its case is that without contraries there is no progression, and that the energies called devilish are the active and creative half of the human soul, while the heaven of patient receiving and the morality of the priesthood are its passive and repressive half.
works.plot: The book opens with the proposition that without contraries there is no progression, and that attraction and repulsion, energy and reason, are necessary to existence, and then reports a memorable fancy in which the author sees in hell an angel sleeping, wakes him, and finds that the angel's religion of patience and of the outward law is undone by the teaching of the place. The voice of the devil follows, arguing that worship is the blessing of the strong to the weak, that the gospel's teacher was a philanthropist and not a priest, and that the true religion is the delight of the senses and the energies of desire. A series of proverbs of Hell then states in short sentences a counter-morality of excess, of the desire that is not executed, of the tigers of wrath being wiser than the horses of instruction, and of the prison and the brothel as built with the stones of law and the bricks of religion. The middle plates give the lights of the six senses, the types of moral character, and a passage on the sacred books of the East, and the book closes with a song of liberty, in which the dragon of the old state is kindled and overthrown and the voices of the morning cry aloud among the nations of the west.
works.significance: The founding text of the poet's own prophetic system and the most widely read of his illuminated books, the source of his most quoted sentences on contraries, on the energies of desire and on the institutions built by the law, and the standing example of the Romantic prose-verse pamphlet. Its closing song of liberty made it a permanent document of revolutionary writing, and its argument supplied the terms in which later readers described the imagination's enmity to the moral system.
works.meter: Chiefly prose of a rapid, gnomic and declamatory kind, with the proverbs in balanced and pointed sentences and the verse passages in short reiterated song lines, the whole varying between the sermon, the aphorism and the air.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in the years immediately after the two collections of songs, in the decade of the English reception of the new religious writings from the Continent and of the controversy about the French Revolution; the book's attack on the priesthood, on the law and on a religion of patience is written out of the radical religious argument of the 1790s.
works.characters: The narrator who records the dream of the sleeping angel; the angel of the book's vision; the voice of the devil, who dictates the book's creed; the daughters of memory and the phantoms of the closed song of liberty
works.structure: A continuous illuminated argument in plates, mixing vision, oration, proverb, catalogue and closing song; the parts are bound by the claim that the book's teaching is the doctrine of contraries, and by the figure of the narrator who reports what the spirits of hell said to him.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of the first issue is fixed by the internal evidence of the plates and by the author's later references rather than by a printed title page.

Imagination as a way of knowing
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: The Marrow of Tradition
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1901
works.description: Published in 1901 and the central American novel of the Wilmington coup of 1898: a fictional account of the white supremacist massacre that destroyed black political power in North Carolina. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The novel interweaves the lives of two families — the white Carters and the black Millers, who are half-sisters — with the political campaign that culminates in the burning of the black newspaper office and the massacre of the black citizens of Wellington.
works.significance: The Marrow of Tradition is the first American novel about the Wilmington massacre and the most important American novel of white supremacist terror: it is the founding text of the African-American political novel and a permanent historical record of a massacre that American history tried to forget.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.
works.context: 1898: the Wilmington coup and massacre, the white supremacy campaigns of the 1890s, and the collapse of black political rights in the South. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.

works.title: The Martian
works.description: Published posthumously in 1897 and du Maurier's last novel: an artist's double life and the visionary guardian he calls the Martian. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by George du Maurier; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Barty Josselin, a brilliant and erratic English artist, is guided through his life by a supernatural presence he calls the Martian, who first appears to him as a child and who dictates his most successful novel; the book follows his loves, his career and his death, in a strange mixture of comic memoir and spiritual fantasy.
works.significance: The Martian is the strangest of du Maurier's books and the last major novel of the aesthetic movement: its fantasy of the guardian spirit and its comic memoir of the artistic life made it a cult novel, and it is the link between Trilby and the twentieth-century fantastic fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is direct, confiding narration with comic digression.
works.context: 1896-97: the aesthetic movement's last years, the Society for Psychical Research, and the Victorian interest in the guardian spirit and the automatic writer. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under sensation novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Barty Josselin; Robert Maurice, the narrator; Martia, the Martian; Leah, Barty's wife

A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Marxist Philosophy and the Sciences
works.description: The Marxist lectures of the geneticist on the philosophy of the sciences. It is a prose work of 1938 by J. B. S. Haldane; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Marxist Philosophy and the Sciences lectures the relation of the dialectical philosophy to the sciences of the genetics, the physics and the biology, in the plain committed prose of the decade's most famous scientist-Communist.
works.significance: The Marxist Philosophy and the Sciences is the thirties left's statement of the science and the dialectics: its lectures by the great geneticist gave the decade's Marxist science its most distinguished name.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The spelling and syntax carry a spoken dialect. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is the essay of the scientist in the plain brilliant prose.
works.context: England in 1938, in the Popular Front's intellectual years. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: the dialectics; the sciences; the Marxist scientist
works.structure: A cycle of lectures on the philosophy and the sciences. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Burdon Sanderson Haldane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Masque of Anarchy
works.form: Political and revolutionary verse; the allegorical pageant poem and public address, in the ballad measure of the periodical and handbill tradition.
works.description: A political poem of ninety stanzas written within days of the cavalry charge on a peaceful reform meeting in a northern city, and withheld from print for more than a decade. Memory, Murder and Fraud ride in a masque with their following of Plagues, Creeds and Laws, and at their head Power, seated on a throne of skulls, announces that whatever is, is right. The poem then turns to an address to the people of England, urging a resistance of folded arms, and it is the first great statement of non-violent mass protest in modern letters.
works.plot: The dreamer sees a pageant marching through the mist of a northern city, a ghost with a mask of gold crying that God and the king and the people are one with its own interest, and behind it Murder with a bald and shining forehead, Fraud holding a blood-besmeared book, and a procession of Plagues, Hypocrisy and Superstition with their laws and creeds. The mask is broken by the appearance of a figure of Liberty who is trampled down, and the poem's second half passes to an exhortation to the thousands who are starving, to rise with their arms folded and let the sabres fall on nothing but the will. The argument is that a people that refuses to strike, and makes the state's violence visible by its own stillness, is the power that cannot be conquered.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the literature of non-violent resistance and its image of the folded arms was taken up by the labour, chartist and later pacifist movements. Its treatment of a state whose allegorical mask is transparent, and its theory that the governed outnumber the governors in will, remain the most influential Romantic account of popular protest.
works.meter: Four-line ballad quatrains of alternating four- and three-beat anapestic lines, rhyming abab, a measure borrowed from the popular and the school of the earlier political song; the repetition of the refrain gives it its force.
works.context: Written at Leghorn in the September of 1819, within a fortnight of the charge of the yeomanry on the reformers' meeting in the northern city and of the prosecutions and suspensions of public meeting that followed, and offered to a liberal editor who judged it unprintable. It was withheld for more than a decade and published only in 1832, the year of the first reform bill's passage, by the same editor who had declined it, with a prefatory account of its suppression; its delayed circulation among friends influenced the radical poetry of the later century.
works.characters: the dreamer-witness of the pageant; the masked Power at the head of the procession; Murder, Fraud and Hypocrisy as the shapes of the state; Liberty, the trampled woman of the crowd; the assembled people of England
works.structure: Two clearly marked parts, the allegorical pageant seen in a dream of the northern city and the direct political exhortation addressed to the crowd; the whole is in a continuous four-line stanza of ballad measure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the manuscript was copied and read in the author's circle, and a version altered for the publisher's fears survives, the full text being established from the holograph.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: The Masque of Blackness
works.description: The first of Jonson's great court masques, designed by Inigo Jones and danced by Queen Anne and her ladies: twelve nymphs of Niger, blackened by the sun, voyage to 'Britannia' in a giant sea-shell seeking the land whose sun (King James) can whiten them — the masque of racial transformation that founded the Stuart court's most spectacular genre.
works.plot: Niger, his daughters, and the moon-goddess Aethiopia arrive in a moving shell drawn by sea-monsters; the songs announce that the nymphs must seek 'a land whose name is Britannia'; they dance, and the final song promises their cleansing by the British sun — a transformation deferred to the sequel, The Masque of Beauty (1608).
works.significance: The inauguration of the Jonson–Jones masque, the Stuart court's supreme art form, and a text now central to studies of race in the Renaissance.
works.meter: Songs in varied lyric forms with the speeches in blank verse, the whole scaled to the banqueting house's acoustics and spectacle.
works.context: Performed at Whitehall on Twelfth Night, 6 January 1605, with the Queen herself blackened in body-paint; the masque's racial and political meanings — union, empire, and whiteness — are now the subject of intense critical debate.
works.characters: Niger; Aethiopia; the twelve nymphs (danced by Queen Anne and her ladies); Oceanus
works.structure: A single masque of arrival and prophecy — antimasque, main masque, and revels — with Jones's machinery (the moving shell, the painted waves) as equal partner to Jonson's verse.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the setting and machines are Inigo Jones's designs.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Massacre at Paris
works.description: Marlowe's late topical tragedy of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572): the Duke of Guise, with the Queen Mother Catherine de Medici, engineers the slaughter of the Huguenots; the Protestant hero Ramus dies; and the play runs through the assassinations of Guise and of Henry III to the accession of the Protestant Henry of Navarre.
works.plot: Guise murders the Huguenot leadership and the scholar Ramus; Navarre escapes the massacre; the Guise's ambition threatens the crown itself until Henry III has him killed; the friar's dagger avenges Guise by killing the king, and the play ends with Navarre's triumph and England's alliance.
works.significance: The first English play of contemporary European politics — Protestant propaganda raised to tragedy, surviving only in mutilated form.
works.meter: Blank verse with the 'mighty line' audible in the surviving fragments, notably Guise's soliloquies of ambition.
works.context: Performed by Strange's Men in January 1593, in the wake of Henri IV's conversion and English fears of the Catholic League; printed in a poor octavo about 1594.
works.characters: the Duke of Guise; Catherine de Medici; Henry III of France; Henry of Navarre; Ramus; the Duke of Anjou; the Cardinal of Lorraine; Mugeroun; the Friar
works.structure: A compressed chronicle of murder and counter-murder — the surviving text (an octavo of about 1,250 lines) is clearly a cut or memorially reconstructed version of a longer play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the text is evidently a damaged report of the original.

works.title: The Master of Ballantrae: A Winter's Tale
works.description: Published in 1889 and the darkest of Stevenson's romances: the story of the two Durie brothers of the 1745 rising, the one who goes out and the one who stays, and of the hatred that survives across the world.
works.plot: James Durie, the Master of Ballantrae, joins the Jacobites while his brother Henry stays at home and marries the woman they both love; James returns from India and France to torment Henry, and the brothers travel to America, where they die in the North Woods, James's body guarded by Henry until both are found.
works.significance: The Master of Ballantrae is Stevenson's most ambitious novel and the finest English treatment of fraternal hatred; its narrators' unreliability and its colonial settings make it a key text for the study of the Scottish novel and empire.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.
works.context: The 1745 rising, the Scottish estates after Culloden, the Atlantic trade and the North American fur trade. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.

works.title: The Mayor of Casterbridge: The Life and Death of a Man of Character
works.form: Novel (Graphic, 1886); realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1886 and generally regarded as the most perfectly constructed of Hardy's novels: the story of Michael Henchard, who sells his wife and daughter at a fair in a drunken impulse and lives to be destroyed by the return of his own past.
works.plot: Henchard sells his wife Susan and baby Elizabeth-Jane at Weydon-Priors fair, swears an oath of temperance for twenty-one years, and becomes mayor of Casterbridge; Susan returns, Henchard's rival Donald Farfrae rises in the town, the wife sale is discovered, and Henchard's fortune, reputation and relationships are progressively destroyed, ending in his death alone in a hut on Egdon Heath.
works.significance: The Mayor of Casterbridge is the classic English novel of character and fate: its wife-sale opening is one of the most famous scenes in English fiction, and its study of a man destroyed by his own past is the purest statement of Hardy's tragic method.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The 1840s, the corn trade and the agricultural depression, the town of Dorchester, and the Victorian debate on character and determinism. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; sensation novel.

works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. works.description: Dryden's angry direct satire, provoked by the Whig medal struck to honour Shaftesbury after his acquittal on the charge of high treason; it abandons allegory for open invective.

works.structure: A three-part invective: the medal and its meaning, the character of the Whig leaders, and the concluding political doctrine.

works.title: The Melting Pot
works.description: First performed in 1908 and the play that gave the language its phrase: the love of a Russian-Jewish immigrant and a Christian girl in New York, and the vision of America as the crucible of the races.
works.plot: David Quixano, a composer who survived the Kishinev pogrom, writes an American symphony in a New York settlement house; he falls in love with Vera, the daughter of the Russian baron who commanded the pogrom, and in the last act the two are united in a vision of the great melting pot in which all races are fused into a new American.
works.significance: The Melting Pot gave the English language its most enduring metaphor for American immigrant assimilation: the play was a sensation in the United States and its title became the standard term for the American fusion of peoples, making Zangwill one of the most influential writers on the idea of America.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is dialect speech transcribed with care.
works.context: 1908: the mass immigration through Ellis Island, the settlement houses of New York, the Kishinev pogrom of 1903, and the American debate on assimilation. The record dates the work as composed in 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; social inquiry and the documented survey.

works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: The Member of the Wedding
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1946
works.description: The great American novel of a girl's growing up: Frankie Addams, her brother's wedding, and the end of childhood. It is a prose fiction work of 1946 by Carson McCullers; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Frankie Addams, twelve, is desperate to belong to her brother Jarvis's wedding and plans to go away with the couple; the wedding comes and goes without her, and the novel ends with her recovered from the crisis, changed and about to move.
works.significance: The Member of the Wedding is one of the great American novels of growing up: its portrait of Frankie, its dialogue and its title have made it a permanent American classic and a landmark of the Southern Renaissance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, bare, exactly observed sentence.
works.context: A Georgia town in the 1940s, the kitchen of the Addams house and the Black servant Berenice's kitchen. The record dates the work as composed between 1944 and 1945 and first published in 1946 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
works.characters: Frankie Addams; Berenice Sadie Brown; John Henry West; Jarvis; Janice
works.structure: Three parts over the days before and after the wedding. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. works.title: The Menologium
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.i (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201), eleventh century
works.description: A metrical calendar of the church year in 231 lines, versifying the fixed feasts and saints' days from Christmas through the year to Advent, with careful attention to the intervals of days between festivals. It is prefixed to the C-text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: The poem proceeds through the liturgical year — Christmas, Epiphany, the spring feasts, Easter's movable cycle, the summer and autumn saints' days, and the return of Advent — computing the days between the major festivals and naming the saints honoured in the English church.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English metrical calendar, and a document of the English church's festal year at the height of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Alliterative long line disciplined to the calendar's enumerative demands; the poet's art lies in varying formulaic phrasing within a rigid frame.
works.context: The poem reflects the English church's calendar as reformed in the tenth century, and its position beside the Chronicle shows the integration of liturgical and historical time in Benedictine Reform culture.
works.structure: A strictly sequential calendar, each feast introduced with its date and interval from the last; the structure is numerical and liturgical rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Merchant of Venice
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of credit, bonds, and mercy: the merchant Antonio pledges a pound of his own flesh to the Jewish moneylender Shylock to fund his friend Bassanio's courtship of the heiress Portia, who — disguised as a lawyer — saves Antonio in the trial scene and turns the bond against its maker.
works.plot: Bassanio wins Portia by choosing the lead casket; Shylock, his daughter Jessica fled with a Christian and his bond forfeited, claims his pound of flesh; Portia's legal trap — the bond allows flesh but not blood — defeats him, and the play ends with the ring trick and the news of Antonio's restored argosies, leaving Shylock's forced conversion and the play's anti-Semitism to shadow the comedy.
works.significance: One of the most performed and most contested plays in the canon — the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech and the quality-of-mercy plea are cornerstones of world drama.
works.meter: Blank verse for the trial and courtship, prose for the Venetian streets, with the lyric interludes of 'Tell me where is fancy bred'.
works.context: Written about 1596–97, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and against the background of the Venetian Ghetto; its Jew is both the period's stock villain and its most human outsider.
works.characters: Antonio; Shylock; Bassanio; Portia; Jessica; Lorenzo; Nerissa; Gratiano; the Duke of Venice; Tubal; Launcelot Gobbo
works.structure: Interlaced Venice and Belmont plots — the bond and the caskets — joined at the trial, with the Jessica–Lorenzo elopement and the ring episode as connecting tissue.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
works.description: Shakespeare's only citizen comedy, traditionally said to have been written because Elizabeth I wished to see Falstaff in love: the fat knight courts the wives Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, who turn the tables on him through the buck-basket, the disguise of the fat woman of Brentford, and the final horns of Herne the Hunter in Windsor Forest.
works.plot: Falstaff sends identical love letters to two wives, who conspire to humiliate him; Ford's jealousy supplies a second plot of disguise and misprision; and the play resolves in the midnight masque of the fairies, where Falstaff is pinched and the eloping Anne Page marries the suitor of her choice against her parents' plots.
works.significance: Shakespeare's only comedy of his own England and time — the ancestor of the English sitcom and the later operatic masterpieces it inspired.
works.meter: Over ninety percent prose — the most prosaic of Shakespeare's plays — with the fairy rhymes of the final scene.
works.context: Dated about 1597, possibly for a Garter feast at Windsor; it transplants Falstaff from the history plays into contemporary Windsor life.
works.characters: Sir John Falstaff; Mistress Ford; Mistress Page; Ford; Page; Anne Page; Fenton; Slender; Doctor Caius; Sir Hugh Evans; Mistress Quickly; Pistol; Nym; the Host
works.structure: A three-humiliation comic structure (basket, beating, forest masque) interwoven with the Anne Page marriage intrigue and the Latin lesson of Sir Hugh Evans and William.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: The Methods of Ethics
works.description: The greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century: the analysis of the methods of ethics. It is a prose work of 1874 by Henry Sidgwick; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Sidgwick examines the three methods by which we reason about conduct — egoism, intuitionism and utilitarianism — and shows that they cannot be reconciled without a further postulate, in an analysis that made him the central moral philosopher of the age.
works.significance: The Methods of Ethics is the greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century and the foundation of modern utilitarian ethics: its rigorous analysis of the conflict between self-interest and the general good made it the central text of Victorian moral philosophy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the analytical survey of the competing methods of ethics.
works.context: Cambridge in the 1870s, the utilitarian tradition and the crisis of Victorian religious belief. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1874 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument.
works.characters: Sidgwick as philosopher; the egoist; the intuitionist; the utilitarian
works.structure: Four books of philosophical analysis. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. Sidgwick. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Metrical Charms
works.description: A group of verse charms against illness, theft, and misfortune, preserved mainly in eleventh-century medical manuscripts (the Lacnunga and related collections). The charms blend Christian prayer with pre-Christian incantation — most famously the Nine Herbs Charm, invoking Woden as the healer of herbs, and Wið færstice, against a sudden stabbing pain caused by a 'mighty woman's' riding.
works.plot: Each charm prescribes words and actions for a specific ill: the Nine Herbs Charm enumerates the nine sacred herbs and their powers against poison and infection, invoking Woden's victory with nine glory-twigs; Wið færstice fights the elf-shot with a spear-image and a boiled herbal drink; others protect bees from swarming, fields from blight, and travellers from harm.
works.significance: The richest vernacular evidence for Anglo-Saxon folk medicine and for the survival of Germanic ritual in a Christian culture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, often irregular; incantatory repetition.
works.context: Preserved in London, British Library, Harley MS 585 (the Lacnunga), the Old English Herbarium manuscripts, and other medical compilations; the pre-Christian elements survived within Christian manuscripts.
works.characters: Woden (in the Nine Herbs Charm); the healer; the malevolent powers
works.structure: Prescriptive lyric sequences: invocation, narrative of the ill or its cure, and ritual instruction, often in verse alternating with prose directions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Christian-pagan synthesis
Mission, conversion, and the Church
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Metrical Psalms of the Paris Psalter
works.description: A verse translation of Psalms 51-150 preserved in the Paris Psalter (Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 8824), accompanying the prose translation of Psalms 1-50. Once attributed to King Alfred, the verse psalms are now regarded as anonymous tenth- or eleventh-century work; they constitute the largest single body of Old English psalmody.
works.plot: The psalms are rendered in fluent alliterative verse, expanding the biblical text with traditional poetic diction; the collection provides the fullest surviving example of Old English liturgical translation in verse.
works.significance: The fullest English verse psalter before the late Middle Ages; important for the study of vernacular liturgy.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of a relatively plain, expository kind.
works.context: Preserved in the Paris Psalter (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS lat. 8824), a mid-eleventh-century manuscript with Latin text and Old English translation in parallel columns; the first fifty psalms are in Alfredian prose.
works.characters: David (as psalmist); God
works.structure: A continuous psalter translation, psalm by psalm, in the versified mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the older attribution to Alfred is not now accepted, though the prose portion may be Alfredian.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Creation and cosmology
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Middle English Lyric
works.description: The corpus of short Middle English lyric poems, secular and religious, composed and copied between c. 1200 and 1500: spring songs, love complaints, carols, lullabies, Passion meditations, and Marian praises, preserved in manuscripts and early printed collections. The most widely practised and most elusive of medieval English genres.
works.plot: The corpus's subjects are love and spring, mortality and judgement, the joys and sorrows of the Virgin, and the Passion; many poems are songs, with refrains and burdens, meant for performance.
works.significance: The lyric is the most continuous English poetic tradition of the period, feeding the courtly song of the Ricardians, the carol, and the Tudor songbooks.
works.meter: Every available stanza form, from the tail-rhyme romance stanza to carol form, rhyme royal, and the macaronic hymn.
works.context: Preserved in preaching manuscripts, commonplace books (Harley 2253; the Vernon manuscript), and, at the end of the period, in the printed collections of Wynkyn de Worde and Richard Pynson; the carol flourishes in the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the lovers, mourners, and devotees who speak the lyrics
works.structure: A corpus rather than a single work; individual lyrics are typically stanzaic, with refrain patterns.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; individual poems occasionally attributable (e.g., to Rolle's circle or to Lydgate).
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition
The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Middle Parts of Fortune: Somme and Ancre, 1916
altTitles: Middle Parts of Fortune: Somme and Ancre, 1916
works.form: Novel; war memoir, first issued in 1929
works.description: The finest novel of the ordinary soldier: the ranks on the Somme, without a hero or a plot. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by Frederic Manning; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Bourne and his comrades in a battalion of the Shropshire Light Infantry endure the mud, the raids, the rum ration and the terror of the Somme in 1916; the novel follows the ranks through an attack and a leave in England, and ends with Bourne's death in a pointless rush.
works.significance: The Middle Parts of Fortune is the finest novel of the ordinary soldier in the First World War: its anonymity, its dialect and its unsparing record of the ranks made it the war's most complete fictional document, admired by Hemingway and T. E. Lawrence and every later writer on the war.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the third-person narrative that stays with the ranks.
works.context: The Somme in 1916, and the ranks of the British infantry. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony.
works.characters: Bourne; Shem; Martlow; Weeper Smart; Captain Malet; the battalion
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the line to the leave and the attack. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederic Norton Manning. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Middleman
works.description: First performed in 1889 and the first English play about industrial capital: a manufacturer and his son-in-law, the middleman, in conflict over a new process. It is a dramatic work of 1889 by Henry Arthur Jones; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cyrus Blenkarn, an old potter and inventor working for the china manufacturer Joseph Chandler, the 'middleman' who grows rich on his genius, learns that Chandler's son Julian has seduced his daughter Mary; ruined and half-mad, he labours alone at his kiln until he rediscovers the lost secret of a famous glaze, and his triumph reverses the fortunes of the two families, in a drama of the ethics of capital.
works.significance: The Middleman was the first English play to put industrial capitalism on the stage and one of the earliest English dramas of ideas: its portrait of the manufacturer and its argument about the ethics of wealth made it a landmark, and it is a key document of the English theatre's turn to social questions.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the strong melodramatic situation with a moral core.
works.context: 1889: the industrial depression of the 1880s, the new capitalism of the Midlands, the labour movement of the 1880s, and the fashion for the drama of ideas after Ibsen. The record dates the work as composed in 1889 and first published in 1889 and first performed in 1889 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Cyrus Blenkarn; Mary Blenkarn; Nancy Blenkarn; Joseph Chandler, the middleman; Julian Chandler, his son
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry A. Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist

works.title: The Mighty Atom
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1896
works.description: Corelli's novel of education and unbelief: a child destroyed by a rationalist schoolmaster. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Marie Corelli; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Lionel Valliscourt, a delicate and imaginative child, is placed in the care of a fanatical schoolmaster who teaches him that the soul does not exist; the boy's mind gives way and the novel ends in tragedy, with the mother's faith vindicated.
works.significance: The Mighty Atom is Corelli's most directly polemical novel and one of the strongest attacks on scientific rationalism in Victorian fiction: its portrait of the child destroyed by unbelief made it a favourite of the religious press and a bestseller of 1896.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the occult machinery of the romance — electricity, reincarnation, the astral body.
works.context: The 1890s, the debate over scientific education and religious instruction, and the cult of the child. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.
works.characters: Lionel Valliscourt; Mrs Valliscourt; Professor Paracelsus; the schoolmaster
works.structure: A novel in three books, from the nursery to the schoolroom and the deathbed. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary Mackay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as minor canon.

works.form: Verse drama (translation of Calderón's El mágico prodigioso)
works.description: FitzGerald's verse translation of Calderón's drama of the magician Cyprian and the martyr Justina, privately printed in 1853 and revised as The Mighty Magician (1865): one of the earliest English translations of Calderón and a key text of the Victorian revival of Spanish drama.
works.plot: Cyprian, a pagan student, sells his soul to the devil for knowledge of Justina; he is converted by her faith and both die as martyrs, and the play enacts the triumph of grace over the magical will.
works.significance: The Mighty Magician is the most important Victorian translation of Calderón and a significant document of the English revival of the Spanish Golden Age; its theme of the magician's bargain links it to Marlowe's Faustus, which FitzGerald and his circle saw as a native counterpart.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).
works.context: The 1840s-50s, the Victorian interest in Spanish drama (Lope de Vega, Calderón), and the Tractarian and Catholic revival of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.

works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.

works.title: The Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu
altTitles: Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu
works.description: First performed in 1885 and the most popular of the Savoy operas: a Japanese town where flirting is a capital offence and every problem is solved by a legal technicality. It is a dramatic work of 1885 by W. S. Gilbert; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Nanki-Poo, the Mikado's son, loves Yum-Yum, who is betrothed to the tailor Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner; Ko-Ko must produce an execution to satisfy the Mikado, and Nanki-Poo agrees to be beheaded after a month of marriage to Yum-Yum, but the discovery that the Mikado's son cannot be executed and the exaggerated report of an execution produce a legal crisis resolved by the Mikado's own arrival.
works.significance: The Mikado is the most performed of all the Savoy operas and one of the most successful theatrical works ever written: its satire of bureaucracy and its comic logic made it a permanent institution in Britain, America and Australia, and its Japanese setting created a vogue that changed English decorative art.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is inverted logic carried to absurdity.
works.context: 1885: the English fascination with Japan after the 1860s, the Gilbertian satire of English bureaucracy, and the Savoy theatre's spectacular production. The record dates the work as composed in 1885 and first published in 1885 and first performed in 1885 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.

works.title: The Milesian Chief: A Romance
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's first novel, a Gothic-Irish romance in which O'Donovan, the exiled Milesian chief, attempts to liberate Ireland from English tyranny but is destroyed by betrayal and his own fatal pride. The novel draws on the tradition of the dispossessed Gaelic aristocracy to create a doomed-hero narrative of colonial resistance.
works.plot: O'Donovan, last of an ancient Irish noble line, is driven by messianic conviction to liberate Ireland from English rule. His love for Rosamond De Lacy, daughter of an English official, becomes entangled with political ambition. Betrayed by allies and pursued by agents of the lord-deputy, his rebellion fails; his final retreat and death enact the impossibility of heroic resistance against the modern colonial state.
works.significance: The first of the author's Gothic novels, establishing his themes of doomed heroism, religious guilt, and political exile; a precursor of the Irish Gothic tradition and a significant contribution to the political novel.
works.context: Published in 1812 amid rising Irish nationalism and the post-1798 disillusionment following the Act of Union. The author, an Anglican clergyman of Huguenot descent, explored the tensions of Irish identity and colonial subjection.
works.characters: O'Donovan; Rosamond De Lacy; Clifford; Lady Melbourne; Sir Edward
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; political intrigue interwoven with romance; a conclusion of failure and exile.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: The Mill on the Floss
works.form: Novel in three volumes; novel of development
works.description: Published in April 1860, the most autobiographical of Eliot's novels and the one that states her central subject: the conflict between a woman's need for intellectual life and the claims of family loyalty, set on the river Floss in the Lincolnshire of the 1820s-30s.
works.plot: Maggie Tulliver, passionate and clever, grows up in the mill of Dorlcote against the preference of her family for her prosaic brother Tom; the family is ruined by the lawsuit of the lawyer Wakem, Maggie meets Wakem's hunchback son Philip in secret, is compromised by her cousin's fiancé Stephen Guest, and is finally reconciled with Tom in the flood that drowns them both in each other's arms.
works.significance: The Mill on the Floss is the great English novel of a girl's education and the fullest early statement of the problem of the intellectual woman; its ending has been the central test case in criticism of Eliot's realism, and it is the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century novel of female development.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
works.context: The 1820s-30s, the mill and the river trade of St Ogg's, the education available to clever girls, and the legal costs of the Chancery suit that ruins the Tullivers. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1860 and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: The Miltonic Setting
works.form: Critical study (Milton and the Puritan imagination)
works.description: The study of the Puritan setting of Paradise Lost. It is a prose work of 1938 by E. M. W. Tillyard; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: The Miltonic Setting recovers the Puritan world of belief - the providence, the fall, the hierarchy - in which Paradise Lost was written, and reads the poem as the poem of that world rather than of the poet's private heresy.
works.significance: The Miltonic Setting is the standard introduction to the Puritan imagination of Paradise Lost: its recovery of the world of belief answered the personal heresy of the Eliot school and fixed the terms of the Milton study.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the exposition of the doctrine in the plain ordered sentence.
works.context: Cambridge in the 1930s, and the Milton controversy. The record dates the work as composed in 1937 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.

works.structure: A study in chapters of the Puritan world, the belief and the poem. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: The Minister's Wooing
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1859 and Stowe's finest novel of New England: a story of Calvinist theology, the sea and a woman's conscience in Newport, Rhode Island. It is a prose fiction work of 1859 by Harriet Beecher Stowe; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Sensation Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mary Scudder, a young woman of Newport, is loved by the minister Dr Hopkins and by the sailor James Marvyn, who is lost at sea; the novel's real subject is the Calvinist doctrine of election and the agony it produces in a devout and loving woman.
works.significance: The Minister's Wooing is the finest American novel of New England religious life and the great Stowe novel of the Calvinist conscience: its portrait of Mary Scudder and its analysis of the doctrine of election are unmatched in American fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is sentimental tableaux designed to produce tears and conversion.
works.context: The 1850s, New England Congregationalism after Edwards, the slave trade in Rhode Island, and the American theological debate on the atonement. works.title: The Minstrel; or, the Progress of Genius
altTitles: The Minstrel, a Poem, in Two Books
works.form: allegorical didactic poem in two books
works.description: Beattie's allegorical poem of the young bard's education, two books of Spenserian stanzas tracing genius from a wild Hebridean childhood through the discipline of taste to the visions of imagination, melancholy, and Fame. It is at once a pre-Romantic cult of genius and a learned Augustan allegory of the poet's progress.
works.plot: Book I follows the infant minstrel through a 'barren rocky island' of storm and solitude, a nursling of genius who, transplanted to the south, awakens to the beauty of landscape, history, and the arts under the eye of instruction. The poet's education proceeds through contemplation, melancholy meditation, and the society of learning, until the summons of active genius. Book II passes from the school of taste into the realms of Imagination, where the minstrel contemplates the grand, the pathetic, and the terrible, the ghost of Fame and the triumph of the poetical genii over time. The allegory closes on the powers of genius sanctified by virtue, the wild native gift disciplined by art, the century's definition of the poet as at once savage and sage.
works.significance: It ranks with Gray's odes and the poems of the primitive bard as a key document of the pre-Romantic imagination, and it shaped the Victorian reading of poetic education; Wordsworth's boyhood of genius is inconceivable without it.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the alexandrine, in a diction deliberately coloured by Akenside, Thomson, and the antique.
works.context: Book I appeared in 1765 amid the prize and blank-verse vogue and the Ossian debate; the completed poem of 1771 belongs to the cult of genius and the primitive-bard fervour of the 1760s-70s, and Beattie's Edinburgh-Aberdeen circle of Smith, Reid, and the Fergusson vogue frames its theory of native genius.
works.characters: the Minstrel; Genius; Melancholy; Contemplation; Fancy; the ghost of Fame
works.structure: Two books of Spenserian stanzas, the first the biography and education of the minstrel, the second a procession of personified powers culminating in the vision of Fame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
