works.title: The Mint
works.description: Lawrence's private record of life as an aircraftman: the making of a soldier in the ranks. It is a prose work of 1955 by T. E. Lawrence; it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book.
works.plot: Written in 1922–23 and published after his death, The Mint records Lawrence's life as an aircraftman in the Royal Air Force: the barrack room, the drill square, the bullies and the camaraderie, and the destruction of the individual in the machine of military training.
works.significance: The Mint is the most pitiless record of military training in English: its prose and its refusal of self-pity made it a radical document of the machine age and the dark companion to Seven Pillars.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the memoir written as a confession and a history at once.
works.context: The Royal Air Force of 1922 and the postwar demobilisation. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1955 and it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Lawrence (as 352087 A/c Ross); the flight sergeant; the recruits
works.structure: Three parts: the Depot, the training and the service. A memoir in episodic chapters organised by posting or battle, the later self reflecting on the earlier experience. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Edward Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ
works.description: Nicholas Love's English translation and adaptation of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi, completed c. 1410: a life of Christ from the Annunciation to Pentecost, written for the 'simple' reader to make the humanity of Jesus present to the imagination, with meditations, prayers, and passages against Lollard positions. The most widely circulated devotional work of fifteenth-century England.
works.plot: Following the gospel narrative day by day, the Mirror unfolds the life, ministry, Passion, and resurrection of Christ in vivid meditative episodes — the nativity, the sermons, the agony, the crucifixion as witnessed by Mary — each closed with moral application, and supplemented by Love's own anti-Wycliffite 'treatise on the sacrament'.
works.significance: The great bestseller of late medieval English devotion: it fixed the affective image of Christ's humanity for a century of English readers and is the key exhibit in the politics of vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions.
works.meter: Plain, warm prose of the Carthusian devotional school.
works.context: Completed c. 1410 by Nicholas Love, Carthusian prior of Mount Grace, with the explicit approval of Archbishop Arundel as an orthodox counter to Lollard vernacular scripture; preserved in more manuscripts than any other Middle English devotional text and printed by Caxton (1484) and his successors.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the disciples
works.structure: A day-by-day meditation on the life of Christ in the Meditationes tradition, with the Passion as its affective centre and devotional prayers appended.
works.attributionNotes: Love's authorship secure (named in the work's memorial note).
themes: The Passion of Christ
The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion

works.title: The Mistress
altTitles: The Mistress; or, Several Copies of Love-Verses
works.description: The long sequence of love poems in Cowley's Poems (1656), a display of metaphysical wit and conceit on an idealised, largely fictitious mistress, which Johnson cited for its 'violence' of conceit but which shows Cowley's command of the amorous lyric.
works.plot: The poems court and lament an unnamed mistress through elaborate conceits of love's pain, hope, and constancy, more an exercise of wit than a record of a real attachment.
works.significance: A representative and influential work of metaphysical love poetry, central to Johnson's definition of the 'metaphysical' wit and to later understanding of the school.
works.meter: Varied lyric meters with dense metaphysical conceits and witty argument.
works.context: Published in Poems (1656); Johnson's Life of Cowley famously quoted it as an example of the metaphysical 'violence' of conceit, by which he meant the yoking of heterogeneous ideas.
works.characters: the poet; the mistress
works.structure: A loose sequence of love lyrics united by the conceit of the unattainable mistress.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the identity of 'the mistress' is thought to be largely fictitious.

works.title: The Monk: A Romance
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's scandalous sensation novel about the Hieronymite monk Ambrosio, whose fall from piety into lust, murder, and damnation made it the most notorious Gothic romance of the 1790s. Published anonymously to immediate sales success and vigorous critical condemnation, it combined religious terror with lurid sexual transgression in ways no English novel had previously attempted. The book's notoriety shaped the commercial possibilities of the Gothic and drew down attacks linking sensational fiction to moral dissolution.
works.plot: Ambrosio, a celebrated preacher in Madrid and prior of the Hieronymites, becomes obsessed with the young novice Antonia, whom he has secretly fathered through his own mother's illicit line. Guided by the demon in the guise of the novice Matilda, he passes through a sequence of escalating transgressions: seduction of the innocent Angela, rape, and murder. Meanwhile the parallel plot of Lorenzo and Marguerite involves the ghostly Bleeding Nun and a false marriage. Matilda reveals her true demonic nature and bargains Ambrosio's soul for escape from the Inquisition. After a final act of blasphemy and fratricide against the hermit Serapio, Ambrosio is delivered to eternal torment. The novel ends with his damnation unmitigated.
works.significance: The Monk established the conventions of the English Gothic in the 1790s: fusion of religious terror with sexual transgression, the supernatural as psychological drama, and the lurid anti-Catholic romance. Its commercial success defined the genre's market and its scandal provoked decades of critical debate about fiction's moral influence.
works.context: Written during the 1790s reaction against French Revolutionary violence and amid public anxiety about Catholicism, religious enthusiasm, and the Inquisition. the author drew on Beckford's Vathek and the German horror tradition; it appeared the same year as Godwin's Things Near as Possible and was immediately recognised as a deliberate competitor to Radcliffe's Gothic.
works.characters: Ambrosio; Matilda; Antonia; Jerome; Lorenzo; Marguerite; the Bleeding Nun; Captain Raymondo; Angela; the Devil
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative with two embedded tales (Lorenzo and Marguerite; the Bleeding Nun) and a frame of Inquisition proceedings; the perspective shifts between multiple characters; the conclusion is unrelieved.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship confirmed within months. A heavily expurgated second edition with an altered ending appeared in 1798.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Monster and Other Stories
works.form: Short-story collection; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1899 and the collection containing 'The Monster', Crane's most disturbing story of race and small-town America. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Stephen Crane; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In the town of Whilomville, a black coachman, Henry Johnson, rescues a doctor's son from a fire and is hideously disfigured; the doctor saves his life, but the town cannot bear to look at him, and the story ends with the doctor ostracised and the monster wandering the woods at night.
works.significance: 'The Monster' is the most radical American story about race published in the 1890s: its portrait of a town that destroys the man who saved a white child, and its refusal to soften the ending, made it a scandal in 1899 and it has since been recognised as one of the great American stories about race.
works.meter: Prose. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation.

works.title: The Moon and Sixpence
works.description: Maugham's novel of the artist: a stockbroker abandons his family for painting and Tahiti. It is a prose fiction work of 1919 by W. Somerset Maugham; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Charles Strickland, a London stockbroker, leaves his wife and children without explanation and goes to Paris to paint; the narrator follows his ruthless career through Paris and Tahiti, where he dies of leprosy after producing the paintings that make him famous.
works.significance: The Moon and Sixpence is Maugham's most famous novel of the artist and the founding text of the modern novel about the painter: its portrait of the ruthless genius and its Tahitian ending made it a permanent study of art against life, and its narrator invented the modern novelistic biography.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrator who listens rather than judges.
works.context: London, Paris and Tahiti in the early twentieth century, and the reception of the post-impressionists. The record dates the work as composed between 1918 and 1919 and first published in 1919 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Charles Strickland; the narrator; Mrs Strickland; Dirk Stroeve; Blanche Stroeve; Ata
works.structure: A first-person biography in chapters, from London to Paris to Tahiti. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Somerset Maugham. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Moonstone
works.description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1868 and described by T. S. Eliot as 'the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels': the theft of a sacred Indian diamond from a Yorkshire country house, told by a succession of witnesses and solved by Sergeant Cuff.
works.plot: The Moonstone, looted from a Hindu temple by a British officer, is left to his niece Rachel Verinder on her birthday and disappears that night; Sergeant Cuff's investigation, the suspicion of the servants, the devotion of the three Indian priests who follow the stone, and the discovery that Franklin Blake took it in an opium-induced trance lead through a London moneylender and a scientific experiment to the stone's return to India.
works.significance: The Moonstone founded the English detective novel and established its conventions: the country-house crime, the closed circle of suspects, the professional detective, the chain of evidence and the final explanation. Its colonial subject makes it a central text of postcolonial criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1860s, the empire and the colonial looting of India, the new detective police, the professionalisation of medicine, and the Victorian country house and its servants. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.

works.title: The Moralists, a Philosophical Rhapsody
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.description: Shaftesbury's platonizing dialogue on natural theology and the happiness of virtue, first printed in the third volume of the Characteristicks and issued separately in the same year. Over a day's walk through the fields near Hampstead, the young Philocles is led by the accomplished Theocles to behold the system of the universe and the interior moral system that mirrors it.
works.plot: Philocles, a youth fresh from reading the moralists, meets Theocles and Crantor in the meadows near Hampstead and asks whether virtue alone is happy. Theocles replies first by an ironical panegyric in the style of the sophists, then seriously, rising through an account of the affections and the moral sense to the 'rhapsody' proper: the visible scene of nature becomes the occasion for the vision of the whole system, its administrative god, and the self-enjoying blessedness of a mind in harmony with it. The dialogue ends with Philocles convinced that virtue, happiness, and the contemplation of the universal system are one.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished piece of Shaftesbury's prose art and a key text of eighteenth-century natural theology and the aesthetics of the sublime system; its rhapsody anticipated the nature-contemplation of Thomson, Akenside, and the Romantic moment.
works.meter: Animated prose dialogue with dramatic description, rising in the closing rhapsody to a deliberately periodic, almost poetic cadence of accumulation and apostrophe.
works.context: Composed in the 1690s from material in Shaftesbury's Journals of the Meridian and printed in 1709, when deistic natural theology was being hotly contested; its vision of the system draws on the Cambridge Platonists and on the new cosmology of the Royal Society age.
works.characters: Philocles; Theocles; Crantor
works.structure: An occasional dialogue framed as a 'rhapsody': reported walk and conversation in a single day, climaxing in an extended inspired passage of natural theology.

works.title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian
works.description: Robert Henryson's cycle of thirteen beast fables (c. 1480s), translating and transforming Aesopian material into the great vernacular fable collection of the British Middle Ages: the cock and the jasper, the two mice, the lion and the mouse, the fox and the wolf, and the parliament of beasts before King Lion. Its moralitates raise the fable to satiric and philosophical art, with a marked sympathy for the poor and the small.
works.plot: The fables move from the country mouse's visit to the town and back, through the fox's adventures with the wolf and the cock's with the fox, to the lion's parliament, where the beasts' complaints against their rulers and their own natures are heard and judged; each fable closes with its moralitas applying the tale to the estates of men.
works.significance: The summit of the medieval European fable tradition in any vernacular: its moralitates are among the finest medieval poems on justice, poverty, and power.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of supple, colloquial power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1480s by the Dunfermline schoolmaster Robert Henryson, in the European fable revival of the fifteenth century (Steinhöwel, Caxton's Aesop of 1484); printed in 1570–71, and preserved in the Bannatyne and other manuscripts.
works.characters: the Cock and the Fox; the Town and Country Mice; the Lion; the Wolf; the Sheep; the Swallow; the Toad
works.structure: A prologue and thirteen fables, each bipartite (taill and moralitas), in the medieval Aesopic tradition raised to a coherent cycle.

works.title: The Morgesons
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1862
works.description: The strangest American novel of the century: a New England heroine who refuses the marriage plot. It is a prose fiction work of 1862 by Elizabeth Stoddard; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cassandra Morgeson grows up in a decaying New England seaport, is sent to school, falls in love with her cousin and then with a wealthy invalid, and marries for money and independence rather than love in a narrative that refuses to explain or justify her.
works.significance: The Morgesons is the strangest and most original American novel of the nineteenth century and a direct ancestor of the modern novel of female desire: its refusal of the marriage plot and its abrupt, dislocated style made it a central text of the American novel rediscovered by feminist criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt, unassimilated scene.
works.context: A New England seaport in the 1840s and 1850s, and the commercial decline of the old port towns. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Cassandra Morgeson; Veronica Morgeson; Charles Morgeson; Desmond; Ben Somers
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the seaport childhood to the marriage. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

works.title: The Mother and Other Poems
works.description: The first collection: the baroque lyric of the mother, the clown and the sun. It is a verse work of 1915 by Edith Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume gathers Edith Sitwell's first lyrics - the mother, the clown, the sun and the harlequinade - in the chanted, consonant-loaded line that set her against the Georgian anthologies from the first book.
works.significance: The Mother and Other Poems is the first book of English modernism by a woman poet: its chanted line and its baroque image announced the poet of Façade and gave the little magazines their most accomplished English contributor.

works.title: The Mourning Bride
works.description: Congreve's only tragedy, a heroic verse play set in a fictionalised Morocco and Granada, which was the most successful tragedy of the 1690s and the source of the proverbial lines on music and on grief.

works.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1926
works.description: The most audacious solution in detective fiction: a murder in a village, and a narrator who is not what he seems. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by Agatha Christie; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Roger Ackroyd is found stabbed in his study in the village of King's Abbot, and Hercule Poirot, retired and growing marrows, is drawn into the case. The solution — that the narrator, Dr Sheppard, is the murderer — is the most famous coup in the genre.
works.significance: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is the most audacious detective novel ever written: its solution changed the rules of the genre, and it remains the most famous example of the unreliable narrator in detective fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play plot with its clues planted in plain sight.
works.context: The English village of the 1920s, the country-house study and the small-town gossip network. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Hercule Poirot; Dr Sheppard; Roger Ackroyd; Caroline Sheppard; Ralph Paton; Flora Ackroyd
works.structure: A first-person narrative by Dr Sheppard, with Poirot's final explanation. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.

works.title: The Mysteries of Udolpho. A Romance; and Interspersed with Some Pieces of Poetry. In Four Volumes
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, the exemplary form of the explained supernatural, with interspersed songs and pastorals
works.description: The fourth novel of Ann Radcliffe, published in four volumes in May 1794 under her own name, and the masterwork of the Gothic romance of terror. Emily St. Aubert, educated in the Languedoc chateau of Le Blanc by a father whose death on a Pyrenean journey is softened by a monastery funeral and the mourned abbey of St. Clare, falls in love with Valancourt against her aunt Madame Cheron's will; her aunt's runaway second marriage to the Italian Signor Montoni carries Emily into the Apennines and into the castle of Udolpho, where Montoni tyrannises over her person and her hopes of an inheritance. A labyrinth of Italian strongholds follows, of subterranean passages and intercepted letters, of the veiled figure that proves a wax image, of the death of the Signora Montoni and the terrors of banditti, until the mysterious papers, the miniature of the Marchioness de Villeroi found in her father's closet, and the confession of a dying nun make known an old tragedy of enforced vows and jealousy; Emily recovers her fortune, and her constancy is rewarded by the reconciliation of Valancourt.
works.plot: Emily's father St. Aubert dies on the way from the Pyrenees; under her aunt Madame Cheron she is forced into the society of the usurping Montoni, who seizes the castle of Udolpho and would coerce her into signing away her hopes and into a match with a wealthy Italian count; her lover Valancourt, already dismissed by St. Aubert for supposed dissipation, is absent and tried by his own errors. Emily escapes through the castle's secret ways, falls among banditti, is befriended by honest Italians and by the family of Villefort, endures the mysteries of the covered figure, the poisoned draughts and the lady of the papers, and hears at last the Marchioness de Villeroi's whole story: Montoni's imprisonment in the Venetian states and his death leave her wealthy, and her tried love is restored.
works.significance: The Mysteries of Udolpho is the most famous and most imitated of English Gothic novels, the book by which the literature of terror became the dominant prose mode of the 1790s: it defined the pursued-heroine plot, castle and convent scenery, and the ethics of terror regulated by explanation; it was read, praised and parodied across the century, with Catherine Morland's raptures in Northanger Abbey measuring Austen's generation against it, and it remained in print into the Oxford World's Classics and Norton Critical editions.
works.meter: Chiefly prose romance; the interspersed poetry is lyric - songs, pastorals and the Castellan's air, Emily's own verses and the monk's hymn - in regular stanzas, with the great descriptive passages of mountain and lake scenery carrying a poetry of the picturesque within the prose.
works.context: Published in 1794, in the war with Revolutionary France and the height of the Italian picturesque bred of travel and of Ann Radcliffe's own tours, and the year of her Lake District journey; issued in four volumes by G.G. and J. Robinson as by Ann Radcliffe, it was the first of her novels to carry her name, and its success made the sale of her next copyright one of the largest paid a woman writer of the age.
works.characters: Emily St. Aubert; St. Aubert, her father; Madame Cheron, her aunt, later Signora Montoni; the Marchioness de Villeroi, lost to the family history; Valancourt, Emily's lover; Signor Montoni; the Signora Montoni; the Count de Villefort and the Marchioness's story in the papers; Madame Montoni's attendant Annette; Sister St. Agnes of the convent; Du Pont and his brother the Abbot of St. Clare
works.structure: A continuous four-volume romance following a single heroine's experience from the Pyrenees to the Apennines and back toward France, sustained by embedded papers, songs and a concluding expository narrative that resolves every appearance of the supernatural into natural and juridical causes.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name, Ann Radcliffe; authorship undisputed. The later prefaces and the Memoir of 1826 document its place as the decisive success of her career.

works.title: The Mysterious Mother
works.form: tragedy in five acts, a closet and private-press drama
works.description: A closet tragedy of a mother's incestuous passion for her son, written for private performance and printed at the author's villa press. It is the most daring of the century's domestic horrors and an experiment in placing an unrepresentable subject at the centre of a regular tragedy.
works.plot: The Countess of Ardenal, whose husband has died and whose son has been kept from her, conceives an unlawful and secret passion for the young count himself. She intercepts his marriage, imprisons his beloved and pursues him with designs that her attendants misread as tenderness. The discoveries arrive too late, the young count learns the truth and kills himself, and the countess's guilt is exposed to the house in a catastrophe of horror rather than of pity.
works.significance: It is the century's most extreme attempt to write the unspeakable family passion as tragedy and a key document of the transmission of Gothic horror from romance into drama.
works.meter: Blank verse of a deliberately old-fashioned and sometimes uneven regularity, with a strong use of the sententious pause and the ominous half-revealed phrase.
works.context: Printed at the villa printing press in 1768 after the author's retirement from active politics, in the season of the domestic tragedy and of the analysis of horror in fiction; its subject was one the public stage could not have carried.
works.characters: the Countess of Ardenal; the young Count her son; his betrothed and her friends; the attendants and officers of the house
works.structure: A regular five-act tragedy of secrets and delayed discovery, with the mother's soliloquies carrying the horror and the final recognition producing the catastrophe; written to be read and privately acted rather than staged.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; printed privately at the author's press with his name withdrawn but never in doubt among his circle.

works.title: The Mystery of Edwin Drood
works.form: Unfinished novel in monthly parts (6 of 12 numbers published)
works.description: Dickens's last novel, of which only six of the twelve projected monthly numbers were published (April-September 1870) before his death on 9 June; the remaining part of the sixth number was in proof. It is the most famous unfinished novel in English, and the central problem of its criticism is the disappearance of Edwin Drood.
works.plot: John Jasper, the choirmaster of Cloisterham, is an opium addict in love with his nephew Edwin Drood's betrothed, Rosa Bud. Edwin disappears on Christmas Eve after a quarrel with Neville Landless; a watch and a scarf-pin are found in the river, and Jasper accuses Neville. The novel's remaining numbers introduce the twin themes of the opium den and the Cathedral close, and Dickens's own notes and the surviving plans have been used ever since to argue whether Jasper murdered Edwin.
works.significance: The Mystery of Edwin Drood inaugurated the Detective Club tradition of the 'unfinished mystery', and it has generated a whole literature of solutions (from Cuming Walters to the modern attribution scholarship). It is also the clearest evidence of the direction Dickens's late art was taking — towards the short, tightly plotted, symbolically dense novel of crime.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The cathedral close of Rochester (Cloisterham), the opium trade and the East India Company's traffic, and the Anglo-Indian characters (Neville and Helena Landless) that Dickens drew from his 1869-70 reading tour and his interest in the colonies.
works.characters: John Jasper; Edwin Drood; Rosa Bud; Neville Landless; Helena Landless; Mr Grewgious; Mr Crisparkle; Durdles; Deputy; the Princess Puffer; Mr Honeythunder; Mr Bazzard
works.structure: Twelve projected monthly numbers of which six survive; the extant text ends mid-number with the discovery of the watch and pin.
works.attributionNotes: Unfinished at the author's death; the surviving text is the first six numbers only. All completions and solutions after 1870 are by other hands.

works.title: The Napoleon of Notting Hill
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1904
works.description: Chesterton's comic prophecy: a future London in which the boroughs go to war. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by G. K. Chesterton; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In a future London of 1984, where nothing ever changes, the new king appoints a joke Lord Provost of Notting Hill; Auberon Quin's joke becomes a real war of the London boroughs, in a comic fantasy of local patriotism and the romance of place.
works.significance: The Napoleon of Notting Hill is Chesterton's comic prophecy and his most original early novel: its vision of the London boroughs at war made a permanent argument for local patriotism and the romance of place, and it is the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century comic dystopia.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the paradox turned inside out.
works.context: London in the future of 1984, and the Edwardian anxiety about the uniformity and dullness of modern life. The record dates the work as composed between 1903 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia, it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; scientific romance and the utopian tale.

works.structure: A comic novel in three books, from the joke to the war. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.

works.title: The Natural Daughter; with Portraits of the Leadenhead Family
works.form: Novel of Manners and Fashion; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
works.description: Mary Robinson's last completed novel, published in two volumes in the same year as her Letter to the Women of England, and the most satirical of her fictions. Its subject is the illegitimate daughter of a man of rank, whose natural claim to consideration is set against the artificial morality of a family portrait gallery of the prosperous and the opinionated, the Leadenheads of the title. The book argues in narrative form the case for women's vulnerability that the Letter had argued in prose.
works.plot: The natural daughter, acknowledged by affection but excluded by law and custom, struggles against the interest, pride, and hypocrisy of the families who protect and dispose of her; the Leadenhead portraits supply a comic exposure of genteel prejudice, mercenary marriage, and social ambition, and the heroine's trial ends only when the calculations that governed her are dismantled and her worth is acknowledged on its own terms.
works.significance: The Natural Daughter is valued as the fiction that completes Robinson's attack on the marriage market and on the legal dependence of women, and as one of the most accomplished satires of prosperous family pretension before the Regency novel; it is now read as an important stage in the development of women's social fiction in the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose narrative with pointed satirical description; verse and letter papers are interspersed, and the portraits are drawn in an epigrammatic manner derived from her periodical writing.
works.context: Written in the last years of Robinson's life, when her novels were being bought by the publisher for sums recorded in his accounts and when her own public history as an acknowledged but unprotected woman made the legal position of illegitimacy and of women her natural subject; the novel's pairing in modern editions with the Letter reflects the continuity of their argument.
works.characters: the natural daughter of the title; the Leadenhead family of the satirical portraits; the man of rank whose acknowledgment the law refuses; the marriage-market interests around the heroine
works.structure: A two-volume novel combining a heroine's tale of exclusion with a satirical series of family portraits; the movement is between sentimental analysis and comic exposure, with letters and papers interspersed.

works.title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne, in the County of Hampshire
works.form: Epistolary natural history and antiquarian survey in familiar letters
works.description: The published form of a long correspondence between the country naturalist Gilbert White and his friends Daines Barrington and Thomas Pennant, The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne records the seasons, weather, birds, mammals, insects and parish antiquities of one Hampshire village. Its method is patient first-hand observation entered in a memoranda book and then shaped into familiar letters. The result is the founding text of English phenomenological nature-writing and a classic of empirical natural history.
works.plot: White surveys the natural history of Selborne parish under a sequence of heads: the zoology of its vertebrates and invertebrates, the periodical return of migrations, the phenomena of hibernation in bats, the structure of swallows' nests, and the monthly calendar of appearance. Interwoven are antiquarian notices of the parish and its manors, and the weather-journal whose measurements anchor the whole. From these particulars he draws general conclusions about instinct, the economy of nature, and the value of quantitative records kept over many years.
works.significance: It has never been out of print and is read both as a scientific classic, for its accurate records and its early treatment of hibernation and migration, and as a literary model of the observed particular. It set the manner of all later English nature-writing from Richard Jefferies to Laurie Lee, and it is a key document of the empirical, descriptive temper that eighteenth-century natural philosophy bequeathed to Romantic-era writing about the external world.
works.meter: Prose only, in an unadorned, precise, quietly humorous plain style
works.context: The book belongs to the late-eighteenth-century vogue for parish-level natural history, for systematic weather observation, and for correspondence networks among gentleman-naturalists; it also reflects the Linnlean and Buffonian taxonomy then current and the antiquarian culture of the Society of Antiquaries.
works.characters: Gilbert White; Daines Barrington; Thomas Pennant
works.structure: Two parts in the form of letters to two correspondents, arranged topically rather than narratively, with the weather journal and observations woven as enumerated particulars.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Gilbert White is established; the letters were edited for the press by his brother Revd Dr Thomas White, whose editorial hand is documented but does not displace Gilbert's authorship.

works.title: The Natural History of Religion
altTitles: Of the Natural History of Religion
works.description: Hume's account of how polytheism arose from human fears and hopes and how the human mind tends, through adulation and complaint, back toward a single supreme being: religion explained as a natural history of the mind rather than a truth discovered. First printed among the Four Dissertations of 1757 and composed by 1751-52.
works.plot: Hume argues that the first ideas of the Deity arose not from contemplation of nature's order but from the anxiety and hopes of ordinary life, which clothed unknown causes with human shapes and interests. Because the motives of polytheism are the ordinary interests of men, its gods are limited, sociable, and ludicrous, and its rituals familiar; monotheism, by contrast, lifts God above human comprehension and so inflames priests and fanatics into a jealousy of divine attribute. Polytheism thus proves more gentle and more favourable to civil liberty, while the road from polytheism to monotheism runs through flattery, and the return to superstition through philosophy is via enthusiasm and the pretended reason of natural theology. The closing pages make the whole history of religion a lesson in the uniform passions of the human species.
works.significance: It founded the natural history and psychological explanation of religion, the ancestor of the scientific study of religion from Spencer to contemporary cognitive accounts of religion, and the most quoted religious writing of the Enlightenment.
works.meter: Ironically courteous expository prose, cool generalizations about 'the religious' set against the heated vocabulary of the priesthoods, with a famous dry closing cadence.
works.context: Conceived in the early 1750s, published in London in 1757 in the volume of Four Dissertations that also contained the Dissertation on the Passions and the two historical dissertations, in the season of the French and Indian War's zealotries and of the Church-of England controversy over enthusiasm.
works.structure: A single dissertation in twenty-eight short sections, moving from origins in fear through polytheism's domestic character to monotheism, superstition, and enthusiasm.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

works.title: The Nebuly Coat
works.form: Novel; detective story, first issued in 1903
works.description: J. Meade Falkner's suspense novel of church architecture and heraldry, published by Edward Arnold in London in 1903, five years after Moonfleet: a young architect sent to restore a provincial minster is drawn into the mystery behind the claim to a peerage.
works.plot: Edward Westray, a young architect, is sent to the remote town of Cullerne to supervise the restoration of Cullerne Minster. Drawn into the life of the town, he hears rumours of a mystery surrounding the claim to the title of Lord Blandamer, whose coat of arms, the nebuly coat of the title, fills the great transept window of the Minster. When the new Lord Blandamer arrives and promises to pay all the costs of the restoration, Westray comes to suspect that he is not what he seems.
works.significance: Reviewed in the Spectator and the Leeds Mercury in November 1903, reprinted by Penguin in 1943 and by Oxford University Press in 1954 and 1988, and adapted for BBC radio in 1965, The Nebuly Coat has been reissued repeatedly; A. N. Wilson, in the Telegraph in 2004, warned that it 'could strike the careless reader as no more than a curiosity, a bit of amateur work. Yet this would be a mistake.'
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person Dorset narrative of the boy smuggler.
works.context: Falkner's own interests in church architecture and heraldry: the Romanesque arches of Cullerne Minster recall those of Durham Cathedral, which he knew as Honorary Librarian to the Dean and Chapter and saw from his house on Palace Green, and Jacques Heyman has suggested that the plot was inspired by the collapse of the central tower of Chichester Cathedral in 1861.
works.characters: Edward Westray; Lord Blandamer; Sharnall; Canon Parkyn; Dr Ennefer; Janaway; Anastasia; Miss Joliffe
works.structure: A suspense novel built around the restoration of Cullerne Minster and the mystery of the Blandamer title.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. Meade Falkner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Necessity of Atheism
works.form: Polemic and pamphlet prose in the dissenting tradition of the freethinking broadside; the juvenile metaphysical essay with its apparatus of propositions and its appeal to the booksellers' conscience.
works.description: The earliest printed work of its author, a short pamphlet of sixteen pages issued at a seaside town in the first months of his undergraduate career and the occasion of his dismissal from the university. It argues that belief in a creator is not a matter of evidence but of habit, that every chain of reasoning must stop at the limits of sensation, and that the hypothesis of a god explains nothing. Its tone is that of the schoolboy metaphysician, aggressive and compressed, but its premises are those the poet was to hold all his life.
works.plot: The pamphlet begins by refusing the burden of proof, since a negative cannot be demonstrated, and then argues that all human knowledge is built on the relation of sensation and idea, so that no evidence of a first cause is accessible. It presses the impossibility of accounting for the existence of matter and the still greater impossibility of an uncaused creator, and closes that a being all-powerful and all-good would be incompatible with the evils of the world. The concluding pages deny that atheism breeds the moral laxity the apologists assume, and insist that inquiry, however unsettling, is the only ground of a reasonable faith. The argument is throughout a train of short propositions with the manner of a college disputation turned against itself.
works.significance: It is the founding document of a lifelong radicalism and the reason its author's university career ended in dismissal, an event that shaped the whole later biography and the poetry of the outlaw intellect. Its epistemology, that the mind can reason only from the data of sensation, reappears in the mature philosophical prose, and the pamphlet remains the standard case in the history of academic discipline and of the English freethinking tract.
works.meter: Prose; the style is sententious and abrupt, with short declarative sentences, rhetorical questioning and the cadence of the abstract printed for discussion.
works.context: Printed at Worthing in 1811 and offered through the Oxford booksellers who sold the author's earlier joint volume of verse, the tract was the ground on which he was summoned before his college and, refusing to disown it, was dismissed in the March of that year. Its appearance falls in the season of the statutes against blasphemous and seditious writing, when unitarian and deist pamphlets were prosecuted, and the incident made an undergraduate's metaphysics a public scandal.
works.structure: A continuous pamphlet argument in numbered propositions, opening with a plea for the freedom of inquiry, passing to the epistemological case, and ending with a challenge to the reader to disprove the conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long contested: the title page carried no name, the author refused to own the tract before his college, and an early biographer and a schoolfellow were credited with a share in it. Modern scholarship accepts the main text as the work of a single undergraduate hand, with the schoolfellow's participation unproven.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: The Negro in the American Rebellion
works.description: Published in 1867 and the first history of African-American service in the Civil War: an account of the black soldier from the Revolution to emancipation. It is a prose work of 1867 by William Wells Brown; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; War Narrative of the Common Soldier.
works.plot: Brown surveys the black soldier in the American Revolution, the War of 1812 and the Civil War, and gives a detailed record of the United States Colored Troops, the battles, the massacres and the treatment of black prisoners.
works.significance: The Negro in the American Rebellion is the first African-American military history and a founding text of the black contribution to American nationhood: it made the case for black citizenship through the record of black service.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is first-person testimony with documentary documents.
works.context: 1867: the Civil War and emancipation, the Reconstruction debates, and the American debate on the black soldier's citizenship. The record dates the work as composed between 1866 and 1867 and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: William Wells Brown, the historian; Crispus Attucks; Denmark Vesey; Nat Turner; Robert Smalls; Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts; the soldiers of the United States Colored Troops
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wells Brown (self-chosen name). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Nether World
works.description: Published in 1889 and the most documentary of Gissing's slum novels: the life of a Clerkenwell family in the 1880s, and the slow destruction of the young by the conditions they live in. It is a prose fiction work of 1889 by George Gissing; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel.
works.plot: In the Clerkenwell of the 1880s old Michael Snowdon plans to make his granddaughter Jane, rescued from drudgery in the Peckover household, the almoner of his fortune among the poor, a plan his worthless son Joseph schemes to defeat; Clara Hewett, the proud daughter of a struggling radical, leaves home for the stage and is disfigured with vitriol by a rival; and Sidney Kirkwood, who loves Jane, marries the ruined Clara out of duty; the 'nether world' of the title is a whole society with its own economy, pleasures and desperations.
works.significance: The Nether World is the finest English novel of the London slum after Morrison and one of the most exact records of the 1880s poor: its refusal to sentimentalise made it a key text of English naturalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1880s, the London slum and the charity organisations, the penny dreadful and the music hall, and the socialist movement of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Sidney Kirkwood; Clara Hewett; Jane Snowdon; Michael Snowdon; Joseph Snowdon; John Hewett; Bob Hewett; Pennyloaf Candy; Clem Peckover; Mrs Peckover; Scawthorne
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.

works.title: The New Aspect of the Woman Question
altTitles: New Aspect of the Woman Question
works.description: Published in March 1894 and the essay that named the movement: Grand's statement of what the New Woman wanted and why. It is a prose work of 1894 by Sarah Grand; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Grand argues that the woman movement is a claim for the 'new aspect' of an old question: women demand education, economic independence and a single moral standard, and they claim the right to be judged as individuals rather than as members of a sex, in an essay that answers the caricatures of the New Woman in the press.
works.significance: 'The New Aspect of the Woman Question' is the manifesto of the New Woman and one of the most influential feminist essays of the century: it defined the movement for its contemporaries, it was reprinted and answered across the English-speaking world, and it remains the clearest statement of what the 1890s meant by the New Woman.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays.
works.context: 1894: the North American Review's symposium on the woman question, the suffrage campaigns, and the height of the New Woman controversy in Britain and America. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The New Atalantis
altTitles: The New Atalantis: A Romance. Designed for a Secret History of the Present Juncto
works.form: political romance and secret history in prose
works.description: A political romance and secret history of the Whig Junto, published in August 1709 and prosecuted for libel in the following November. Under the disguise of an Italianate island court it reports the sexual and fiscal intrigues of the ministers, turning the key of romantic fiction into an instrument of party attack.
works.plot: A company of ladies and gallants recounting the histories of the great are led by the goddess Intrepida through the courts and closets of Atalantis. There they see the ministers intrigue for money and for the persons of their female dependants: the snares laid for the yielding, the bribery of the chamber, the ruin of the too frank and the triumph of the crafty. The tales end in exposure and desertion, and the framing discourse claims that Atalantis is a transparent name for England, so that the reader is invited to apply the key herself.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the early key-writing romances and the text that showed how the amatory plot could be turned to party work; it shaped the later secret history and the scandalous novel of the 1720s.
works.meter: The high romantic prose style of the amatory fiction, with elaborate periods, apostrophe and euphemistic detail of the bed-chamber, used to carry identifiable party scandal.
works.context: Published in the last years of the Godolphin ministry and reprinted several times before the Sacheverell season; its libel prosecution in November 1709 was pressed and then dropped with the change of administration, an event central to the history of the press.
works.characters: Intrepida; Delia; Countess de Verruyse; the Duke of Sidonia; the gallants and the betrayed women of the Atalantis court
works.structure: An embedded-tale romance with a framing dialogue, in which reported histories of seduction are stitched together by allegorical presentation; the key is offered openly in the argument and the prefatorial matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by the contemporary party attacks and by the author's own defence of the design; the first issue was published without the writer's name.

works.title: The New Chronicles of England and France
works.description: Robert Fabyan's chronicle of England and France from Brutus to the reign of Henry VII, compiled from the London chronicles and printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France; the first city chronicle of London to reach print.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the kings of England (with a parallel account of France) reign by reign, drawn from the Brut, the London chronicles, and the work of the French chroniclers, and closes with the accession of Henry VIII; the appended 'Concordance of Histories' aligns the chronicles of England and France.
works.significance: The first printed London chronicle and a major conduit of the English historical tradition from the medieval Brut to the Tudor chroniclers; Shakespeare knew its material (including the story of Lear) through Holinshed and the chronicle tradition.
works.meter: Prose with verse envoys
works.context: Compiled by Fabyan, a London draper and alderman, from the 1490s to c. 1504, with continuations to 1516; printed by Pynson in 1516 and again by William Rastell in 1533, it supplied material to Hall, Holinshed, and the Elizabethan playwrights.
works.structure: Annalistic chronicle in seven parts, each divided by reign; Fabyan's additions include the civic history of London and verse 'Lenvoyes' moralizing each reign.

works.title: The New Law of Righteousness
works.description: Winstanley's principal theological and political manifesto, published in January 1649, which argues that private property is the origin of oppression and that the restoration of the earth as a common treasury is the true law of righteousness.
works.plot: Winstanley identifies the curse of Cain with the enclosure of the earth, argues that Christ's kingdom is a commonwealth of shared labour and property, and calls for the abolition of buying and selling.
works.significance: The founding text of English agrarian communism and an essential document of the radical revolution of 1649.
works.meter: Vigorous, scriptural prose of the radical sects.
works.context: Published in January 1649, days before the execution of Charles I; it prepared the ground for the Digger settlement on St George's Hill in April 1649.
works.structure: A single continuous argument in biblical and prophetic prose.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Winstanley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The New Negro: An Interpretation
works.description: The anthology that defined the Harlem Renaissance: the New Negro and the new art. It is a prose work of 1925 by Alain Locke; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Locke's anthology gathers the fiction, poetry, drama, essays and art of the Harlem Renaissance — Hughes, Cullen, Toomer, McKay, Hurston, Fisher and others — with his own introduction announcing the New Negro and the new Black American art.

works.meter: Prose. The work is an anthology, the pieces ordered by the editor. The author's characteristic manner is the editorial anthology with its manifesto.
works.context: Harlem and the United States in the mid-1920s, and the cultural politics of the Renaissance. works.title: The New Testament (Tyndale's translation)
altTitles: The New Testament Translated by William Tyndale
works.description: William Tyndale's translation of the New Testament from the Greek, the first English New Testament translated directly from the original language and the foundation of all later English Bibles, including the King James Version.
works.plot: A complete translation of the Greek New Testament with prefaces and marginal notes; the Cologne fragment (Matthew 1–22) was interrupted by the authorities in 1525, and the first complete edition appeared at Worms in 1526, followed by Tyndale's thorough revisions of 1534 and 1535.
works.significance: The fountainhead of English Bible translation: Tyndale's phrasing survives in as much as 80–90 per cent of the King James New Testament, and his English — 'the powers that be', 'a law unto themselves', 'the spirit is willing' — permanently shaped the language's biblical register.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale, denied episcopal support in England (the famous rebuke attributed to a Gloucestershire divine — 'we were better to be without God's law than the Pope's'), went to the continent in 1524; the Cologne printing (Quentel, 1525) was raided, and the Worms octavo of 1526 was smuggled into England, where Bishop Tunstall bought up copies for burning. Tyndale's 1534 revision is the text behind the later English versions.
works.structure: Biblical text in the order of the Greek canon, with prologues to the books and expository marginal glosses.

works.title: The New Woman
works.description: The play that named the New Woman: a husband, a wife and the education she wants. It is a dramatic work of 1894 by Elizabeth Robins; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: A husband discovers that his wife has been reading and thinking and wants an education and a life of her own; the short play dramatises the collision between the Victorian husband's assumptions and the woman's new demands.
works.significance: The New Woman gave the movement its name and its first stage embodiment: written with Florence Bell, it is the founding dramatic text of the New Woman controversy and the ancestor of the suffrage play.

The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the suffragist meeting as dramatic scene.
works.context: London in 1894, and the New Woman controversy of the decade. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.

works.structure: A one-act play in a single drawing-room scene. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

works.title: The Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family
altTitles: Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family
works.description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from October 1853 to August 1855, narrated by Arthur Pendennis, and the most encompassing of Thackeray's family chronicles: the history of the Newcome family from the Indian fortune of the 'Campaigner' to the ruin of the banker Barnes Newcome.
works.plot: Clive Newcome, an artist, loves his cousin Ethel Newcome, who is pressed by her family into the marriage market; the novel follows the family's fortunes through the colonial service, the City bank, the influence of the evangelical 'Bungay' faction and the collapse of the bank of Hobson Brothers. Clive marries Rosey Mackenzie and is widowed, and Ethel remains unmarried in a resolution that the narrator leaves deliberately unresolved.
works.significance: The Newcomes is Thackeray's most sympathetic book and the most complete picture of the Victorian family across three generations; its portrait of Ethel Newcome as a woman with no independent income and no independent will is one of the period's sharpest studies of the position of women, and its phrase 'the most respectable family' became a byword for respectable hypocrisy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.

works.title: The Nine Tailors
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1934
works.description: The most perfectly constructed English detective novel: a body in a Fens churchyard and the bells of Fenchurch St Paul. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Dorothy L. Sayers; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lord Peter Wimsey, stranded in the Fenland village of Fenchurch St Paul on New Year's Eve, joins the bell-ringers in a nine-hour peal; a body is later found in a grave, and the solution turns on the ringing of the bells and an old crime of stolen emeralds.
works.significance: The Nine Tailors is the most perfectly constructed English detective novel and Sayers's masterpiece: its use of the bells, its Fenland setting and its final flood made it the finest technical achievement of the Golden Age.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play plot carried by character rather than mechanism.
works.context: The Fenland village of the 1930s, the English campanology tradition, and the flood of the Fens. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.

works.structure: A village investigation structured around the nine-hour peal and the bell-ringing method. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.

works.title: The Non-Juror
works.form: Political comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for the patent theatre and printed close to performance.
works.description: An anti-Jacobite comedy brought out at Drury Lane in the winter of 1717 and printed with a title page dated 1718, which makes a non-juring clergyman the type of political and religious cant. Passive obedience, the oaths, and the converts of the church are laughed out of doors, and a plain British sea-officer is set against the scheming divine as the voice of national good sense. The play is also remembered for a scene that quoted the national dramatist back at itself, a passage its author withdrew when it was thought to do irreverence to the dead poet.
works.plot: Doctor Wolf, a non-juring clergyman, combines disaffection to the settled succession with greed: he designs upon the fortune of a young Protestant heiress, whom he hopes to win both to his own communion and to his suit, and keeps his son in constraint and in debt. Young Wolf, a rake of the town, runs a course of his own, and the plain-spoken British officer who loves the heiress opposes the divine's arts with open national loyalty. The household dependants, whose interests Wolf professes to serve, are the instruments by which his contrivances are carried on and at last discovered; a disputed obligation pressed with a canting plea of mercy exposes the hypocrisy of the claimant. The father's principles are disavowed by the son, the heiress keeps her fortune and her party, and the comedy ends in the exposure of the divine rather than in a reconciliation.
works.significance: It is the most direct instance of a patent-house comedy written as party warfare, and the one play of its era that made the non-juring clergyman a stock stage character. The history of its suppressed Shakespearean scene is a document in the rising reverence for the bard, and its use of hypocrisy for party ends measures how far the comic treatment of cant had moved since the 1690s.
works.meter: Plain prose dialogue with set speeches of some formality for the party argument; the addresses to the audience are in closed couplets, and the quotation that gave offence is taken from the blank verse of the national stage.
works.context: It was written in the temper of the years after the rising of 1715, when non-juring churchmen were a visible and legally precarious class, and it belongs to the flush of anti-Jacobite stage writing that followed the settlement of the succession. The divine supposed to be satirised complained of a libel and proceeded against the publisher, but the complaint did not prosper. The management that staged it had by then made party business of loyalty on the stage.
works.characters: Doctor Wolf, the non-juring clergyman; Young Wolf, his son; the bluff British sea-officer; the rich Protestant heiress whose fortune is designed upon; the dependants of Wolf's household
works.structure: Five acts of prose comedy organised as a double opposition, the designing hypocrite in the house and the plain British officer against him; the plotting moves through forged claims and overheard counsel to a public unmasking in the final act.

works.description: Richard Brome's first comedy, and his most popular, in which a young woman from the north of England, Bess Bridewell, is carried to London, falls among thieves and gulls, and is finally matched with her true love.

works.title: The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith
works.description: First performed in 1895 and the boldest of Pinero's problem plays: a freethinking woman who lives openly with a politician, and her return to the faith of her childhood. It is a dramatic work of 1895 by Arthur Wing Pinero; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Agnes Ebbsmith, a freethinker who has lived with the politician Lucas Cleeve, is confronted with his ambition to marry a rich woman; she destroys his career to save him, and then, in a final act of renunciation, takes up the Bible she had thrown into the fire and returns to the faith of her childhood.
works.significance: The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith was one of the boldest English plays about free union and was attacked by the censors and the press: its portrait of a woman who chooses both intellectual freedom and religious faith made it one of the most interesting problem plays of the decade, and it is the finest of Pinero's serious works after The Second Mrs Tanqueray.
works.meter: Dramatic text. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion.

works.title: The Novel and the People
works.description: The posthumous Marxist case for the novel of the people. It is a prose work of 1937 by Ralph Fox; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review.
works.plot: The Novel and the People argues the case for the novel as the literature of the people - against the dying bourgeois form and for the writer who serves the many - in the plain committed prose of the Communist critic published after his death in Spain.
works.significance: The Novel and the People is the thirties left's statement of the novel's politics: its case for the people's fiction, written by the critic killed in Spain, stands with Caudwell's studies as the Marxist criticism of the decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the plain argumentative prose of the Communist journalist.

works.title: The Obedience of a Christian Man
altTitles: The Obedience of a Christen Man and How Christen Rulers Ought to Governe
works.description: Tyndale's treatise on the obedience owed by Christians to rulers and on the reading of scripture, printed at Antwerp in 1528; the book that, shown to Henry VIII, drew the king's reported remark that 'this is the book for me and all kings to read'.
works.plot: The book argues that every Christian — ploughman, weaver, or king — must obey his temporal rulers, whom God has ordained; it attacks the pope's claim to absolve subjects of allegiance, defends vernacular scripture against the charge that it breeds heresy, and expounds the duties of fathers, husbands, masters, and kings from the New Testament.
works.significance: The most politically consequential English book of the early Reformation: its doctrine of obedience made the English Reformation conceivable as an act of state, and its defence of vernacular scripture became the platform of the English Bible.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed at Antwerp in 1528 (by Hans Luft's press or its associates); Anne Boleyn's copy reached Henry VIII, and the book's doctrine of royal supremacy over the church made it a cornerstone of Henrician propaganda, feeding directly into the Reformation statutes of the 1530s.
works.structure: A continuous treatise divided into topical sections on the estates and their duties, with a famous preface on the reading of scripture.
themes: Kingship and good rule

works.title: The Octopus: A Story of California
works.form: Novel (first of 'The Epic of the Wheat')
works.description: Published in 1901 and the greatest American novel of the railroad: the wheat ranchers of the San Joaquin Valley against the Pacific and South-Western Railroad. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Frank Norris; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The wheat growers of the San Joaquin are ruined by the railroad's freight rates and land claims; Magnus Derrick and his son Lyman are drawn into a bribery scandal, the ranchers' league is broken, and the novel ends with violence at a railroad roundhouse, while the wheat itself flows out of the state to feed the world.
works.significance: The Octopus is the central American novel of the railroad and the greatest American naturalist epic: its portrait of monopoly capital, its documentary account of the wheat country and its attempt to see a whole society in a single story made it the model for the American social novel, and it remains the essential literary record of the Populist revolt.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories.

works.title: The Odd Women
works.description: Published in 1893 and the most important English novel of the 'surplus women' question: the story of three sisters, the plain women who must support themselves, and of two sisters' very different answers to their situation.
works.plot: The Madden sisters, daughters of a ruined doctor, face a choice between genteel poverty and self-support: Alice and Virginia take poorly paid work as governesses and companions, while Monica, the beautiful one, marries the elderly and forbidding Edmund Widdowson and is destroyed by jealousy; the novel ends with Rhoda Nunn, the feminist who trains women for work, engaged to the cynical Everard Barfoot.
works.significance: The Odd Women is the most rigorous English novel on the economic position of unmarried women and a founding text of English feminism: it treats marriage as an economic institution and asks what work and independence might mean, without either sentimentality or a happy ending.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, the 1891 census and the 'surplus' of half a million unmarried women, the expansion of women's clerical work, and the debate over marriage reform. works.title: The Odyssey of Homer
works.description: Pope's translation of the Odyssey, published in volumes with the scholarly apparatus and the essay on Homer's genius, and completed largely by under-writers whose share Pope acknowledged in his advertisement.

works.description: Congreve's first comedy, written while he was still in his early twenties and produced at Drury Lane with a cast that included Betterton and Anne Bracegirdle; it ran for an unprecedented fourteen nights.
