works.title: The Penitential Psalms
works.form: psalm paraphrase in terza rima (prologue) and various stanzas
works.description: Wyatt's paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), framed by a prologue in which David, the royal lover of Bathsheba, is made the type of the penitent courtier. Based on Aretino's I Sette Salmi, the work turns the psalmist's repentance into a sustained meditation on the dangers of the court and the sovereignty of God.
works.plot: The frame narrative follows David from his sin with Bathsheba through the prophet Nathan's parable to his repentance; each psalm is then paraphrased as David's own speech, with Wyatt's added commentary.
works.significance: The major English religious poem of the Reformation's first generation and the ancestor of Sidney's and Milton's psalm paraphrases; its David is the first great self-portrait of the Tudor courtier in verse.
works.meter: Terza rima in the prologue — the first sustained English use of Dante's metre — and ottava rima in the psalm paraphrases.
works.context: Written after Wyatt's imprisonment of 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn; the psalmist's court becomes a mirror of Henry VIII's, and repentance the courtier's only safety.
works.characters: David; Bathsheba; Nathan
works.structure: Prologue narrative (in terza rima) followed by seven paraphrases; each psalm introduced by a stanza of commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: Early Tudor Court Poetry
sources: Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems

works.title: The Pentateuch (Tyndale's translation)
works.description: Tyndale's translation of the first five books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew, printed at Antwerp in 1530; the first English translation of any part of the Hebrew Bible from the original language.
works.plot: A complete translation of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, with prefaces to each book explaining its sense and typological bearing, and a prologue to the whole ('W. T. to the Reader') setting out Tyndale's principles of translation from the Hebrew.
works.significance: The first English translation from the Hebrew and the origin of the English Old Testament's distinctive phrasing ('let there be light', 'the Lord bless thee and keep thee'); it established the principle that the Bible must be rendered from the original tongues.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale learned Hebrew on the continent (probably from Jewish scholars), and the Pentateuch of 1530 was printed by Hans Luft at Antwerp (or Marburg) and smuggled into England; it supplied the Old Testament basis for the Matthew Bible (1537) and, through it, for the Great Bible and the King James Version.
works.structure: Biblical text in the Hebrew order, with per-book prefaces and glosses; Genesis and Numbers were printed separately with their own title pages.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
The English vernacular and national letters
movements: The English Reformation
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature
The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

works.title: The People's Palace
works.description: The first collection: the palace, the fountain and the firework of the baroque lyric. It is a verse work of 1918 by Sacheverell Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom.
works.plot: The People's Palace gathers Sacheverell Sitwell's first lyrics of the palace, the fountain, the firework and the fair, in the long loaded line of the baroque that made him the third poet of the Sitwell family.
works.significance: The People's Palace is the first book of the baroque lyric in English modernism: its palace and its fountain announced the poet of the arts and gave the Sitwell sound its third voice.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the long, loaded, alliterative line of the baroque lyric.
works.context: London at the end of the war, and the baroque revival of the little magazines. The record dates the work as composed between 1917 and 1918 and first published in 1918 and it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.structure: A collection of baroque lyrics in the long loaded line. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Sacheverell Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

The little magazine and the modernist institution

works.title: The Perennial Philosophy
works.description: Huxley's anthology of the mystical tradition: the 'perennial philosophy' common to every religion. It is a prose work of 1945 by Aldous Huxley; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Huxley assembles passages from the Upanishads, the Buddhist scriptures, the Christian mystics, the Sufis and the Taoists, and connects them with a commentary arguing for a single metaphysical truth underlying all religions.
works.significance: The Perennial Philosophy is Huxley's most influential work of ideas and the founding text of the modern comparative mysticism: it made the mystical tradition available to a general readership and shaped the spiritual culture of the postwar decades.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The work is an anthology, the pieces ordered by the editor. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of ideas with a large cast and competing arguments.
works.context: The Second World War, Huxley's years in California, and his study of Vedanta with Gerald Heard and Swami Prabhavananda. The record dates the work as composed in 1944 and first published in 1945 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.structure: An anthology of mystical texts with an extended commentary in chapters. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Aldous Leonard Huxley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey
altTitles: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey
works.description: The founding text of Black nationalism: the speeches and the programme of the UNIA. It is a prose work of 1923 by Marcus Garvey; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Political Treatise and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The two volumes gather Garvey's speeches, editorials and addresses: the case for Black pride, the Universal Negro Improvement Association, the Black Star Line, the return to Africa and the programme of racial self-determination.
works.significance: The Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey is the founding text of Black nationalism in the twentieth century: its speeches and programme made the case for Black self-determination to millions and became the permanent document of the movement and the ancestor of modern Black nationalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is the mass meeting and the oration.
works.context: Harlem and the world of the 1920s, and the Black nationalist movement of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1925 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; political treatise.
works.characters: Garvey as orator; the UNIA; the Black Star Line; the membership
works.structure: Two volumes of speeches, editorials and addresses, edited by Amy Jacques Garvey. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. A treatise in numbered propositions and books, each definition followed by its deduction and by the objection answered.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Marcus Mosiah Garvey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents

works.title: The Philosophy of Rhetoric
works.description: The treatise that made metaphor the instrument of thought. It is a prose work of 1936 by I. A. Richards; it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Philosophy of Rhetoric states the theory of metaphor as the interaction of tenor and vehicle: metaphor is not the ornament of thought but its instrument, and the rhetoric of the poem is the grammar of the mind.
works.significance: The Philosophy of Rhetoric made metaphor the instrument of thought: its tenor and vehicle entered the vocabulary of every criticism of the poem and remain the standard terms of the theory of metaphor.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the analytic prose of the psychologist of reading.
works.context: Cambridge and Harvard in the mid-1930s, and the theory of metaphor. The record dates the work as composed between 1935 and 1936 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A treatise in lectures: the theory of metaphor, the tenor and the vehicle, the rhetoric of thought.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ivor Armstrong Richards. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Science, technology, and the machine age

works.title: The Phoenix
works.form: allegorical religious narrative in alliterative verse
works.description: An allegorical poem of 677 lines on the legend of the phoenix, which burns itself on its nest of spices and rises renewed: a figure, the poem explains, of the resurrection of the body and the Christian's hope of the heavenly homeland. Based on the Carmen de ave phoenice attributed to Lactantius, it contains one of the finest paradise descriptions in Old English.
works.plot: The poem describes the earthly paradise in the east where the phoenix dwells; after a thousand years the bird flies to Syria, builds a nest of spices, is consumed by fire, and after three days revives from the ashes. The second half interprets the legend allegorically: the phoenix is Christ and the blessed soul, the nest the good works, and the renewal the resurrection at the Last Judgment.
works.significance: The fullest Old English allegory of resurrection and the richest nature-description in the corpus.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the poem is notable for its extended descriptive set-pieces.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the Latin source (fourth century, attributed to Lactantius) circulated widely in Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: the Phoenix (as bird and as allegorical figure)
works.structure: A bipartite structure of literal legend followed by sustained allegorical exposition (the latter an original expansion of the Latin source).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Typology and biblical interpretation
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry
The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Phoenix and the Carpet
works.form: Children's fantasy novel; imperial adventure romance
works.description: Published in 1904 and the second Psammead book: the five children find a Persian carpet that flies and a phoenix's egg that hatches into a talking bird. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by Edith Nesbit; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The children buy a second-hand carpet which turns out to be a magic flying carpet, and with the phoenix they travel to a French castle, to a tropical island where the cook stays behind as queen, and to India, with the usual Nesbit consequences.
works.significance: The Phoenix and the Carpet is one of the finest of the Psammead books and a classic of imperial children's fantasy; its chattering phoenix is one of Nesbit's most memorable inventions.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader.
works.context: The 1900s, the Persian rug trade, the British in the Gulf, and the Victorian and Edwardian vogue for the Oriental tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1903 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Cyril; Anthea; Robert; Jane; the Lamb; the Phoenix; the Psammead; the cook
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. Nesbit. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: The Phoenix and the Turtle
works.description: Shakespeare's 67-line metaphysical elegy, printed in Robert Chester's collection Love's Martyr (1601) alongside poems by Jonson, Chapman, and Marston: the funeral of the phoenix and the turtle dove, whose chaste love united them 'in a mutual flame', leaving reason itself to compose the threne over their urn.
works.plot: The birds assemble for the obsequies; the anthem declares the lovers one in essence, 'two distincts, division none'; reason, confounded, speaks the threne; and the poem closes on the paradoxes of truth and beauty buried with them.
works.significance: The strangest and most debated of Shakespeare's poems — the one place where he joins the metaphysical company of Donne.
works.meter: Trochaic tetrameter with the irregular 'threne' in trimeter — the most deliberately 'metaphysical' verse Shakespeare wrote.
works.context: Published in 1601 as an appendix to Chester's Love's Martyr, dedicated to Sir John Salusbury; its allegorical referents (Salusbury's circle, the Earl of Essex, or pure emblem) remain undetermined.
works.characters: the Phoenix; the Turtle; Reason; the assembled birds
works.structure: A tripartite ceremony — summons, anthem, threne — in the form of a compressed metaphysical emblem poem.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: The Piazza Tales
works.form: Collection of six stories; ghost story
works.description: Published in 1856 and the only collection of Melville's stories in his lifetime: 'The Piazza', 'Bartleby', 'Benito Cereno', 'The Lightning-Rod Man', 'The Encantadas' and 'The Bell-Tower'. It is a prose fiction work of 1856 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Imperial Adventure Romance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The volume moves from the domestic comedy of the piazza to the horror of Bartleby, the slave-ship narrative of Benito Cereno, the sketches of the Galápagos, and the fable of the bell-tower and its automaton, a parable of machinery and pride.
works.significance: The Piazza Tales contains the greatest short fiction of the American nineteenth century: 'Bartleby' and 'Benito Cereno' alone would make it a central book, and the volume as a whole is the foundation of the American short story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The years 1853-56, Putnam's Monthly and the American magazine market, the Galápagos voyages, and the American debate on slavery and technology. The record dates the work as composed between 1853 and 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: the narrator and Marianna ('The Piazza'); Bartleby; Benito Cereno, Babo and Amasa Delano; Hunilla, the Chola widow, and the hermit Oberlus ('The Encantadas'); Bannadonna ('The Bell-Tower'); the lightning-rod man
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Herman Melvill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief

works.title: The Pickwick Papers
altTitles: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club
works.form: Comic novel in monthly parts (20 numbers, 1836-37)
works.description: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, published in twenty monthly parts from March 1836 to October 1837, began as a commission to supply letterpress for Robert Seymour's sporting plates and became, after Seymour's suicide in April 1836 and the arrival of 'Phiz' (Hablot K. Browne), the first great popular success of the Victorian serial novel.
works.plot: Mr Samuel Pickwick, founder of the Pickwick Club, sets out with his three fellows — Tracy Tupman, Nathaniel Winkle and Augustus Snodgrass — to travel England and report on their observations. The early chapters are a sequence of comic disasters at the club's expense; the entrance of Sam Weller as Pickwick's servant gives the book its double act, and the plot thickens into the breach-of-promise action brought by Mrs Bardell, Pickwick's landlady, which sends him to the Fleet Prison rather than pay the damages. The interpolated tales (the 'Bagman's Story', 'A Madman's Manuscript') darken the comic surface, and the ending restores Pickwick to Dingley Dell and to a bachelor old age surrounded by his friends.
works.significance: The Pickwick Papers created the Victorian bestseller and the monthly-part system, and with it the idea of a national comic fiction readable aloud in the family. Its sales (40,000 a number at the height of the run) made publishers understand the economics of serialisation for the rest of the century, and Sam Weller's speech became a permanent English idiom.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
works.context: The reforming 1830s: the new poor law of 1834, the reformed Parliament, the coaching inn and the stagecoach at the moment of the railway, and the legal system of the Fleet and the King's Bench prisons. The book's comedy of clubs, elections and litigiousness is also a satire on the unreformed institutions the Reform Act had not touched.
works.characters: Samuel Pickwick; Sam Weller; Tony Weller; Nathaniel Winkle; Tracy Tupman; Augustus Snodgrass; Mrs Bardell; Alfred Jingle; Mr Perker; Serjeant Buzfuz
works.structure: Twenty monthly numbers of loose episodic narrative, unified by the Pickwick Club frame and by the Bardell lawsuit, with interpolated tales inset at intervals.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Regional identity and the American sectional character
The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
movements: Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel

works.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
works.description: Published in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in June 1890 and expanded for book form in 1891: the story of a beautiful young man whose portrait ages and corrupts while he remains untouched, and the central English novel of aestheticism.
works.plot: Lord Henry Wotton persuades Dorian Gray that youth and beauty are the only things worth having; Dorian wishes that the portrait painted by Basil Hallward would age instead of him, and the wish is granted. He lives a life of concealed vice, murders Basil, blackmails Alan Campbell, and finally stabs the portrait, which restores him to his ruined age and kills him.
works.significance: Dorian Gray is the founding novel of English decadence and the most complete statement of the aesthetic doctrine that life should imitate art; its treatment of concealed desire has made it a central text of queer literary history.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
works.context: The 1890s, the aesthetic movement, the trial of the novel in the press, and the Wilde circle of the Rhymers' Club and the Café Royal. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1891 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: Dorian Gray; Lord Henry Wotton; Basil Hallward; Sibyl Vane; James Vane; Alan Campbell; Lady Agatha; Lord Fermor
works.structure: Third-person narrative with interpolated chapters of aphorism and a chapter of Dorian's collection of corrupting books.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin; A Child's Story
altTitles: Pied Piper of Hamelin; A Child's Story
works.description: Written for the son of the actor William Macready in 1842 and published in the Hood's Magazine and in the Bells and Pomegranates series the same year: the best-known English retelling of the medieval legend.
works.plot: The town of Hamelin is infested with rats; a mysterious piper offers to remove them for a reward, does so with his music, and is refused payment; he returns and pipes away the children of the town, all but one lame boy who is left behind.
works.significance: The Pied Piper is one of the founding poems of English children's literature and the version in which most English-speakers know the legend; its moral about the consequences of bad faith gave the story its Victorian currency as a parable of the social contract.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The medieval German legend (attested from the thirteenth century), the Victorian children's book market, and the 1840s interest in folk narrative that produced the Grimms' Tales in translation. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1842 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: the Pied Piper; the Mayor of Hamelin; the Corporation; the lame boy left behind; the children of Hamelin; the rat who survives to tell the tale
works.structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part I)
works.form: allegory; dream vision; prose fiction; spiritual narrative
works.description: Bunyan's allegorical dream-narrative of the journey of Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, begun in his second imprisonment and published in 1678; it is the most popular and most translated work of English prose fiction.
works.plot: Christian, burdened with sin, is directed by Evangelist to the Wicket Gate; he passes through the Slough of Despond, the House of the Interpreter, the Cross where his burden falls, the Hill of Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation where he fights Apollyon, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Vanity Fair where Faithful is martyred, Doubting Castle where he is imprisoned by Giant Despair, and the Delectable Mountains, until he crosses the river into the Celestial City.
works.significance: The supreme English prose allegory and, with Robinson Crusoe, one of the two founding works of the English novel; it has never been out of print, has been translated into more than two hundred languages, and has shaped the imaginative vocabulary of the English-speaking world ('Vanity Fair', 'the Slough of Despond', 'Doubting Castle').
works.meter: Plain, colloquial prose interwoven with biblical phrase and with short verses at intervals.
works.context: Composed during Bunyan's second imprisonment (1675-6) and published in February 1678 by Nathaniel Ponder, whose shop sign gave the book the nickname 'The Pilgrim's Progress from Ponder's'; it went through ten editions in Bunyan's lifetime.
works.characters: Christian; Evangelist; Pliable; Obstinate; Mr Worldly Wiseman; Faithful; Talkative; Hopeful; Apollyon; Giant Despair; Christiana (Part II); Interpreter; Great-heart
works.structure: A framed dream-vision in two stages of journey, with episodic encounters, embedded verses, and the author's Apology as a preface.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Judgment Day and eschatology
Penance, confession, and sin
Social satire and estates criticism
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part II)
works.description: The second part of Bunyan's allegory, in which Christian's wife Christiana, with her four sons and the neighbour Mercy, undertakes the same pilgrimage under the protection of the valiant Great-heart.
works.plot: Christiana repents her earlier harshness to Christian and sets out with Mercy and the children; guided by Great-heart, they pass through the same places Christian knew, overcome Giant Grim and the other giants, and reach the Celestial City.
works.significance: Completes the allegory with a domestic and communal pilgrimage that has been widely read as a feminist counterpart to Part I; it is normally printed with Part I in every edition.
works.meter: Plain prose with interpolated verses, gentler and more social in tone than Part I.
works.context: Published in 1684, six years after Part I, in response to its enormous popularity and to the many spurious continuations that had appeared.
works.characters: Christiana; Mercy; Matthew; Samuel; Joseph; James; Great-heart; Mr Prudence; Mr Piety; Giant Grim; Despondency's daughter Much-afraid
works.structure: A framed dream-vision following Part I's itinerary with a female party and a protective escort.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Pilgrim's Regress
works.form: Allegorical novel (the pilgrimage of the reason to belief)
works.description: The allegory of the reason's pilgrimage from the Puritan town to the island and back. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by C. S. Lewis; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: John, the pilgrim of the Puritan town of Puritania, follows his desire for the sweet desire of the island across the lands of the north and the south - the stoics, the pagans, the philosophers and the fashionable - until the reason and the desire meet at the crossing of the canyon and the island is reached.
works.significance: The Pilgrim's Regress is Lewis's first book and the allegory of his own conversion: its pilgrimage of the reason and the desire stated in narrative the argument the apologetic prose would carry, and it founded the mode of the Christian allegory of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer.
works.context: England between the wars, and the pilgrimage of the converted intellect. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1933 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: John; Vertue; Mr Wisdom; the Steward; Mother Kirk; History; the Shining Man
works.structure: An allegorical novel in ten books, the pilgrimage out and the regress home. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Clive Hamilton, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to C. S. Lewis is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Novel of Development and the Growth Story

works.title: The Pilgrimage
works.form: Devotional-descriptive poem in the Rowley manner, with obsolete diction and gloss; closer to a popular song or carol tradition than to the chronicle-poems of the same series.
works.description: A shorter poem of the Rowley series, in which Chatterton depicts a company of pilgrims making their way to a holy shrine. It belongs to the devotional and descriptive side of the forgeries, and shows Chatterton using the supposed licence of an earlier and simpler age to write religious poetry that no Augustan poet publishing under his own name could have offered.
works.plot: The piece describes the progress of the pilgrimage and the scenes and people it passes: the shrine and its offerings, the devotion of the company, and the rough, homely and unsolemn life of the road. The emphasis falls on the externals of an older popular religion, treated with affection and with a frankness Chatterton thought characteristic of a time before politeness had refined devotion into decorum. There is no dramatic conflict; the interest is pictorial and vocal, sustained by the archaized diction which carries the fiction of date. The underlying argument is that a nation's religion, like its poetry, is most powerful when it is most naive.
works.significance: It is a striking example of the religious imagination available within the forgery: Chatterton invented not only an antique manner but an entire devotional culture, and the poem helped to form the later romantic and antiquarian interest in medieval popular piety. Its frankness about the bodily and homely side of devotion anticipates the romantic recovery of the Middle Ages.
works.meter: Rowley's irregular long measure, with a strong lyric and song-like beat in parts, in deliberately antique spelling; the harshness of the sound is part of the designed effect.
works.context: It is one of the pieces that went out under Rowley's name in the Bristol correspondence of the mid 1760s, at a time when the collecting of old English poetry was becoming a fashionable antiquarian pursuit and when pilgrimage, shrines and popular superstition were being reinterpreted as picturesque national material.
works.characters: The pilgrim company; the shrine and its keepers; the framing poet 'Thomas Rowley'
works.structure: A processional poem: the pilgrimage observed in a sequence of descriptive and apostrophic passages, with invocation and devotional address framing the movement.
works.attributionNotes: Authored by Chatterton though ascribed in the Rowley papers to the fictitious monk; no medieval original exists, and the 'antiquity' of the piece rests on forged manuscripts and glosses. Its place in the series and its date of composition are not fixed with confidence, so the year fields are left null.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian

works.title: The Pioneers
altTitles: The Pioneers; or, The Sources of the Susquehanna
works.form: Frontier romance and novel of settlement; social panorama in the manner of the Scottish historical novel
works.description: The first of the series set in the New York backcountry and the earliest American novel to make settlement, law and the destruction of the forest its subject. A declining frontier county in the 1790s supplies a full social survey: judge, lawyer, doctor, Quaker, settler and Indian. Its portrait of an aging scout who prefers the wilderness to the courthouse remains the type of the American frontiersman.
works.plot: In an outpost town on the sources of the Susquehanna, a family of landed English stock is joined by an heiress, and the neighbouring settlers contest game laws, land titles and the right to punish. An old huntsman, the finest woodsman in the county, is fined by the judge for shooting deer out of season and then dispossessed of his cabin by a legal technicality. A disguised prisoner turns out to be a son of the house, and an attempted marriage to a French count reveals the vulnerability of the heiress. The novel ends with the burning of the Indian winter village, the death of the Englishwoman and the huntsman's departure west to die.
works.significance: It created Natty Bumppo, the first permanently American heroic type, and made the conflict between wilderness and institution the masterplot of American fiction. Its legal and ecological conscience anticipated later environmental narrative. It is the foundation text of the American romance of forest and sea.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in January 1823, drawing on the author's childhood in Cooperstown and on the land law, game law and Indian policy of the trans-Allegheny west. The year of its appearance saw the debate over the Indian removal bill, and the novel's dispossession plot answers that debate. Its topographical details were later supplied in a key by the author's family.
works.characters: Natty Bumppo; Judge Marmaduke Temple; Richard Jones; Elizabeth Temple; Oliver Edwards; Chingachgook
works.structure: Third-person panoramic novel of a community, with a central action of legal dispossession and a subsidiary romance; the description of institutions repeatedly interrupts the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Cooper and the American Romance of Forest and Sea

works.title: The Pit: A Story of Chicago
works.form: Novel (second of 'The Epic of the Wheat')
works.description: Published posthumously in 1903 and the second volume of the wheat epic: the Chicago Board of Trade and the destruction of a speculator by the market. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by Frank Norris; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Curtis Jadwin, a Chicago speculator, attempts to corner the wheat market; his obsession destroys his marriage to Laura, who turns to the artist Sheldon Corthell, and the crash of the corner and Jadwin's ruin end the novel with his wife returning to him and the wheat still moving through the city.
works.significance: The Pit is the finest American novel of speculation and the best literary picture of the Chicago Board of Trade: its treatment of the market as a natural force and its portrait of a man destroyed by his own success completed Norris's plan for the epic of the wheat and made it the central American novel of finance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories.
works.context: 1903: the Chicago Board of Trade, the great wheat corner of 1897-98, the American fear of the trust, and the speculative culture of the Gilded Age city. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Curtis Jadwin; Laura Jadwin; Sheldon Corthell; Gretry; Sam Lewiston; Landry Court
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Benjamin Franklin Norris. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Plain Dealer
works.description: Wycherley's second masterpiece, a bitter comedy of the blunt sea-captain Manly, who believes himself too honest for the world and is betrayed by his mistress, his friend, and his own self-deception.
works.plot: Manly returns from sea to find his mistress Fidelia (disguised as a page) the only faithful soul; his friend Vernish steals his money and his mistress Olivia; Manly's rough justice exposes them and he marries Fidelia.
works.significance: The bleakest and most psychologically complex of the Restoration comedies; Manly's misanthropy made the play a favourite of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and influenced Sheridan and Shaw.
works.meter: Prose, harsher and more rhetorical than in The Country Wife.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal on 11 December 1676 and published in 1677 with a dedication to the Duchess of Cleveland; Charles II is said to have rewarded Wycherley for it.
works.characters: Manly; Fidelia; Vernish; Olivia; Eliza; Jerry Blackacre; the Widow Blackacre; Lord Plausible; Major Oldfox
works.structure: Five acts, closely modelled on Molière's Le Misanthrope, with the low comic plot of Jerry Blackacre and the Widow Blackacre's lawsuit.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Wycherley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Plains of Caroni
works.description: Published by MacGibbon & Kee in London in 1970, the novel grew out of research on Trinidad's sugar industry sponsored by Tate and Lyle, which financed Selvon's return visit in 1969 (Journal of West Indian Literature, citing Michel Fabre). It turns on the trial of a mechanical cane harvester on a sugar estate.
works.summary: An Indo-Trinidadian cane-cutting family and the trial of a mechanical harvester on a fictionalised Caroni estate, ending with an old cutter's fight against the machine.
works.plot: Romesh, a university-educated agricultural scientist working for the management of a fictionalised Caroni Ltd., oversees the testing of a new harvesting machine on the estate where his family cuts cane. The labourers fear, rightly, that it will cost them their jobs, and suspect it of being a 'metal Trojan horse'. The old cutter Balgobin, whose love for Seeta was thwarted by her arranged marriage to his brother, has given his life to the craft of cutting, and he resists the harvester with his cutlass. As he is dying, he is saved from arrest by the revelation that Romesh, raised as his nephew, is his son. Romesh leaves for London with his white girlfriend, while Balgobin is venerated as a hero.
works.significance: Selvon turned it into the radio play Harvest in Wilderness (collected in Highway in the Sun, 1991). works.description: Davenant's comedy of fashionable Neoplatonic love, in which the court of the Duke of Florence practises a chaste 'platonic' devotion until nature and desire assert themselves and the lovers marry.

works.title: The Play of the Weather
altTitles: A New and a Very Mery Enterlude of All Maner Wethers
works.description: John Heywood's interlude in which Jupiter receives petitions for every kind of weather and reconciles them all by leaving the weather as it is; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Jupiter, wishing to settle the world's complaints about the weather, summons the estates of the realm: a gentleman wants fair weather for hunting, a merchant wind for his ships, a ranger frost, a water-miller rain, a laundress sun, a boy snow; each pleads his case, and Jupiter's final decree — that the weather shall continue as it has been — demonstrates the impossibility of pleasing all parties and the wisdom of accepting the established order.
works.significance: The best known of Heywood's interludes and a classic of early Tudor political satire: its survey of competing interests remains the liveliest dramatic picture of the Tudor commonwealth, and Mery Report is a landmark in the development of the stage Vice.
works.meter: Couplets and doggerel, with prose in Mery Report's asides
works.context: Printed by William Rastell in 1533, the year of Henry VIII's divorce crisis and the statute in restraint of appeals; the play's debate on sovereignty and the impossibility of pleasing all suitors has been read as a commentary on royal counsel and the conflicts of the Reformation Parliament.
works.characters: Jupiter; Mery Report (the Vice); The Gentleman; The Merchant; The Ranger; The Water-Miller; The Wind-Miller; The Laundress; The Boy
works.structure: A single continuous action of successive petitions before Jupiter's throne, ending with a report of Jupiter's decree; the comic petitions build a survey of the commonwealth by estates.

works.title: The Playboy of the Western World
works.form: Play in three acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 26 January 1907)
works.description: The greatest Irish comedy: a young man who claims to have killed his father becomes a hero in a Mayo shebeen. It is a dramatic work of 1907 by J. M. Synge; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Christy Mahon arrives at a public house in County Mayo claiming to have killed his father with a spade, and is celebrated by the villagers, the widow Quin and Pegeen Mike; when his father appears alive, the villagers turn on him, and Christy — having lost everything — goes out to meet his fate.
works.significance: The Playboy of the Western World is the greatest Irish play of the century and one of the great comedies in English: its language — Irish English made into poetry — is the finest invention of the revival, and its riot at the Abbey was the period's most famous theatrical scandal.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is a poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech.
works.context: The west of Ireland, the peasant society of the Congested Districts, the oral story-telling tradition, and the nationalist politics of 1907, which made the play a riot on its first production. The record dates the work as composed in 1906 and first published in 1907 and first performed in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Christy Mahon; Old Mahon; Pegeen Mike; Widow Quin; Michael James Flaherty; Shawn Keogh; Sara Tansey
works.structure: Three acts in a single shebeen set, built on the repeated arrival. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edmund John Millington Synge. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Playhouse to Be Let
works.form: burlesque comedy; play within a play
works.description: Davenant's Restoration burlesque comedy in five acts, each a parody of a different dramatic mode — French farce, English history, Spanish intrigue, opera, and the heroic play — with the notable introduction of the first professional actresses on the English public stage.
works.plot: A playhouse is offered to let; each act presents a different burlesque entertainment, including a mock-Cromwellian history, a French farce, a parody of The Siege of Rhodes as 'The Cruelty of the Spaniards in Peru', and a send-up of heroic drama.
works.significance: A valuable theatrical document of the Restoration transition and one of the earliest English stage burlesques.
works.meter: Mixed prose and verse, with songs.
works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in August 1663 by Davenant's company; it records the moment when women first acted on the English public stage.
works.characters: Sir Positive At-All; Caution; Sneaky; the Playhouse Keeper; the actors
works.structure: Five self-contained acts framed by the playhouse-letting plot.

works.title: The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies
altTitles: The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, Hero and Leander, Lycus the Centaur, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Literary Annual and Keepsake Verse
works.description: The author's only collection of serious verse, containing the long fairy poem that gives it its title together with a metrical retelling of Hero and Leander put into the mouth of Lycus the Centaur, a poem on the two peacocks of Benington, and a body of minor lyrics. The volume was the attempt of a periodical writer to be read as a poet of imagination rather than as a maker of jokes. It is a transitional book, eighteenth-century in its measured descriptive line and Romantic in its subject, the plea of a vanishing fairy commonwealth.
works.plot: The Plea is an oration and pleading case for the fairies delivered before the court of their queen, arguing that the fairy belief has been slandered by the age and that the little commonwealth still haunts the fields that enclosure and tillage have improved away. The poem passes through the fairies' history, their relations with mortals, their decay, and their eventual retreat, with set speeches, embedded song, and a large descriptive apparatus of meadow, bank, and brake. Hero and Leander, by Lycus the Centaur, retells the ancient legend of the priestess of Aphrodite and the youth of Abydos as a lament sung by a monstrous bystander, and the minor poems include hymns to the sun and the moon, ballads, fragments, Ruth, and the lyric Remember, I Remember.
works.significance: The book is the serious core of a reputation built on comedy, and its fairy poetry supplied a model for the later Victorian verse of the pre-Raphaelite circle, which admired it. The volume also first collected the lyric Remember, I Remember, one of the most anthologised short poems of the century, and it preserves the metrical retelling of the Hero and Leander legend by a writer of the second generation.
works.meter: Measured rhymed verse in the eighteenth-century descriptive manner, with interposed songs in popular stanzas and a sustained rhetorical line for the set speeches; the closing lyrics use common and long measure. The model is the school of Thomson and the seasons poets rather than Romantic blank verse.
works.context: Published in 1827, printed for a great Paternoster Row house, when the author was earning his living in periodical and annual work and his comic series had just appeared. The fairy subject belonged to a wider revival of popular belief in poetic form, and the volume's plea against improvement speaks directly to the enclosure and landscape-change debates still live in the 1820s.
works.characters: the fairy queen and her court; the poet-orator of the plea; Hero and Leander; Lycus the centaur as narrator; the speaker of the minor lyrics
works.structure: A collection in which the title poem is a continuous rhetorical-descriptive sequence with interposed songs and speeches; Hero and Leander is a single narrative idyll in the voice of a centaur; the minor poems are unordered.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the collaborative burlesque volume of odes issued a few years earlier by the same writer is a separate work and is not included here.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved

works.title: The Pleasures of Hope
altTitles: The Pleasures of Hope; with Other Poems
works.form: National and didactic poem in the 'Pleasures' tradition, combining topographical description, elegy and revolutionary prophecy.
works.description: A didactic poem in two parts which made its author famous within months of publication and at the age of twenty-two. Part I traces the pleasures of hope through the seasons of childhood, the expectations of love and the ambitions of a young poet, and Part II raises the argument to the prospect of human improvement, liberty and moral progress. Its title deliberately answers an earlier generation's 'Pleasures' poems while its politics are unmistakably those of the 1790s.
works.plot: The poem's speaker examines how hope shapes a life, beginning with the natural year and with memories of Scottish landscape, then moving through disappointed attachment to the poet's vocation and to the claims of fame and friendship. The second part turns from individual expectation to universal history, rehearsing the sufferings of war and tyranny and closing on a millennial prospect of liberty, science and human perfectibility. Contemporary events, including the French revolutionary wars and the fate of Poland, are drawn into the argument as tests of hope rather than as decoration. The structure is that of a consecutive meditative argument in two books, sustained by apostrophe and by an optimistic philosophy of expectation.
works.significance: It was one of the few poems of the 1790s to become an immediate bestseller, running through many editions and establishing the model of the Romantic popular didactic poem in couplets. Its fusion of landscape memory, national expectation and humanitarian prophecy made it a reference point for later poets of reform. Modern accounts treat it as evidence that the high style of the eighteenth-century didactic poem survived well into the nineteenth century in the hands of Romantic writers.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with lyric interpolations and occasional ballad stanzas in the enlarged editions.
works.context: Published within a decade of the French Revolution and of the reaction that followed, it belongs to the generation that inherited the early radicalism of the Lake poets and expressed it in the older didactic metres. Its author was a dissenting Scottish family's son, educated in Glasgow, and its celebration of liberty and of Scotland's natural scenery addresses both the British and the Irish debate over national identity. Later editions were enlarged and politically softened, a history that mirrors the wider moderation of Romantic-era radical verse.
works.structure: Two-part didactic meditation in the eighteenth-century 'Pleasures' form: an individual and seasonal movement followed by a historical and prophetic one, unified by a single apostrophising voice.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Pleasures of Imagination
altTitles: The Pleasures of Imagination, a Poem
works.description: Akenside's didactic poem on the imagination, developing Addison's account of the pleasures of the mind into a philosophical and moral system in which the beauties of the senses, of the passions and of virtue are the discipline of an educated soul.
works.plot: The poem traces the workings of the mind in the perception of greatness, novelty and beauty, passes to the pleasures of the passions and of the moral sense, and closes with the cultivation of taste as the preparation for virtue and for the happiness of a well-ordered mind.
works.significance: It is the most ambitious attempt of the mid-century to fuse the theory of taste, the philosophy of mind and the poem of religion, and its blank verse and its vocabulary of the imagination passed to the romantic theorists.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of the Thomson and Milton school, with the long descriptive period and the abstract noun in place of the concrete image.
works.context: Written in the years of the association of ideas, of Hutcheson's moral sense and of the debate over the imagination begun by the Spectator essays, by Akenside's physician and patron circle and by the new metaphysical writing of the Scottish professors.
works.characters: the poet's Muse and the powers of imagination; the mind of the spectator; the personified Beauty and the moral sense
works.structure: A continuous argument in books, first issued in one book and afterwards enlarged, with the philosophical analysis, the illustrative description and the apostrophe interwoven.

works.title: The Pleasures of Memory
altTitles: The Pleasures of Memory. A Novel
works.form: sentimental and domestic novel in the lineage of Richardson and of the conduct tale
works.description: Barbauld's first prose work, a moral tale of sensibility in two volumes which takes its title and its method from the theory of memory as a source of pleasure and of virtue. It follows a young heroine of principle through dependence, courtship and the trials of family interest, and makes the recollection of past affection the ground of her conduct. The book belongs with the domestic and educational fiction of the 1770s and was repeatedly reprinted.
works.plot: The story sets a virtuous young woman against the importunities of interest, flattery and worldly alliance, and resolves the trials of fortune by the constancy of affection and by the moral uses of remembrance. The narrative dwells on home, on the society of good minds and on the pleasures which the memory draws from former scenes of kindness, and it argues that feeling rightly governed is the basis of duty. Its conclusion rewards principle and exposes the claims of rank and money as the false scales of merit.
works.significance: It is the earliest evidence of Barbauld's power to put moral philosophy into narrative and a document of the culture of feeling as practised by women writers of the 1770s. Its concern with memory, affection and education anticipates Lessons for Children and the prose hymns, and its success helped to establish her livelihood by letters.
works.meter: Prose narrative with letters and dialogue; the style is reflective, balanced and addressed to the feelings rather than to incident.
works.context: Published in 1776, in the vogue of the moral and sentimental novel and of the educational tale, and in the same nonconformist intellectual circle that produced her poems and, later, the children's books and the essays written with her brother . Its argument about memory and virtue draws on the associationist psychology then current.
works.structure: A novel of character and sentiment in two volumes, proceeding by domestic episodes and reported conversation, with the moral reflection of the title sustained as the principle of selection and of judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution rests on the standard bibliographies and on her family and biographical record; the novel was published anonymously, and the date of composition is not fixed, so the composition start is left null.

works.title: The Plough and the Stars
works.form: Play in four acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 8 February 1926)
works.description: O'Casey's Easter Rising play: the tenement and the Rising seen from below, and the riot it caused. It is a dramatic work of 1926 by Sean O'Casey; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Verse Drama and the Poetic Play and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: In a Dublin tenement in 1915 and Easter week 1916, the inhabitants — the newly married Nora Clitheroe, her husband Jack, the ex-soldier, the union man and the prostitute Bessie Burgess — are caught up in the Rising. Jack is killed, Nora loses her baby and her mind, and Bessie is shot by a sniper while protecting Nora.
works.significance: The Plough and the Stars is O'Casey's masterpiece: it refused the heroic version of 1916 and showed the Rising from the tenement, and the riots it provoked in 1926 drove O'Casey out of Ireland.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the tragi-comedy that turns from farce to tragedy in a single scene.
works.context: The Easter Rising of 1916, the Irish Citizen Army and the slum tenements of Dublin, and the nationalist sanctification of 1916 that the play attacked. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and first performed in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; verse drama and the poetic play.

works.description: The country novel of the Northamptonshire poacher and the field. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by H. E. Bates; it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: The Poacher follows John Champion, the poacher of the Northamptonshire fields, from the boy's snaring to the man's quarrel with the keepers, the farm and the law, in the prose of the field and the season that made Bates the novelist of the county.

works.title: The Poems of Emma Lazarus
works.description: Published posthumously in 1889 and the collected edition that made Lazarus's reputation: the lyrics, the verse dramas and the poems of the Jewish nation. It is a verse work of 1889 by Emma Lazarus; it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The two volumes gather the whole of her poetry — the early classical lyrics, 'Admetus', 'The Spagnoletto', the Heine translations, 'The Dance to Death', the poems of the pogroms and 'The New Colossus' — with a biographical memoir by her sister.
works.significance: The Poems of Emma Lazarus is the collected edition that established her as the first American poet of the Jewish people and of immigration: it made 'The New Colossus' available to the campaign that inscribed it on the Statue of Liberty, and it is the essential text of her achievement.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is the classical sonnet and the verse drama in a formal, measured style.
works.context: 1889: the year of her death, the American Jewish community of the 1880s, and the posthumous recognition of a poet who had died at thirty-eight. The record dates the work as composed between 1866 and 1887 and first published in 1889 and it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Political History of the Devil
altTitles: The Political History of the Devil, as the Present Governor of the World
works.description: A satirical history of the world written as the biography of the Devil, shown as the true political manager of modern Europe. Its argument is that the powers, churches, courts and trading companies of the world are all in leaguement with the old serpent, and that political Christianity is a mask for interest.
works.plot: The Devil organises the governments of Europe by the machinery of interest, war and party; he plants the church at Rome, presides at the courts of princes, funds the stock-jobbers, and sets the faction of the enthusiasts against the settled clergy. A narrative of his own history, from his first settlement in Britain to the present, is interrupted by political dissertations and by the ironic apologies of the editor. The closing papers judge the nation's management by the standard of diabolical policy and find it creditable.
works.significance: It is the most sustained of the early-eighteenth-century satires that read modern politics as providential machinery inverted, and a central text for the study of the Devil as a figure for commercial and political modernity.
works.meter: Deadpan ironic prose of the historical narrative, with the flat connectives of chronicle used to hold absurd conclusions together; the prefaces heighten the register for satiric effect.
works.context: Published in 1720 during the South Sea explosion and the quarrel over the ministry, in the same season as the author's other diabolical and project histories, and in the tradition of the Devil as political narrator running back to the seventeenth-century diabolica politia.
works.characters: the Devil; his cabinet council; the European princes and politicians as his correspondents; the editor-narrator
works.structure: A mock-history in two main books combining chronicle, dialogue and dissertation, with a heavily ironic prefatorial apparatus; a second part issued some years later repeats the design with more explicit party reference.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume appeared with the same prefatorial persona as the other political histories of the period, and its party allusions are consistent with the author's known positions.

works.title: The Political Register
works.form: Political journal and polemic: weekly report-and-commentary in the tradition of the eighteenth-century newspaper, transformed into an organ of extra-parliamentary agitation.
works.description: The weekly journal founded, edited, and largely written by its author, which was the principal organ of popular radical politics in England from 1802 until his death. Its mixture of report, correspondence, pamphlet-in-serial and abuse created a new kind of political writing addressed explicitly to the mechanic and the agricultural labourer. The Register is also the vehicle in which most of its author's larger prose works, including the Rural Rides letters, first appeared.
works.plot: Each number collects parliamentary and trial report, local intelligence, letters from correspondents, and a running editorial attack on what the editor calls 'the system' - paper money, sinecure, corn-law monopoly and the tax burden. In its first years the paper defended the war against Napoleon and attacked corrupt ministers; after 1812 it turned against the old officers and against Pitt's successors, and after 1815 it took up the cause of the agrarian and industrial poor. It covered Peterloo in detail, prosecuted and was prosecuted for its reports, campaigned against the six Acts, supported agitation for reform, and by the later 1820s had become the most influential single political publication in the country.
works.significance: The single most important work of English radical prose of the Romantic period, and the model of a journalist's power over public opinion; E. P. Thompson made it the central evidence of a self-conscious popular political culture, and its plain idiom shaped all later plebeian journalism.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Founded after its author's return from America and imprisonment at Bench, and stamped by the wartime fiscal state, the Corn Law of 1815, Peterloo and the long struggle over parliamentary reform; the Register survived his prosecution, the six Acts and the collapse of its earliest readership.
works.structure: Serial weekly journalism: a repeating weekly structure of report, correspondence, essay and polemic, with long runs and separate parts (the 'Pole' volumes and occasional halfpenny tax-destroys-trade numbers) gathered from the same series.
works.attributionNotes: Numbers are unsigned or variously signed; the overwhelming majority of the editorial matter is the founder's own, but report and correspondence in any given number may be by other hands.

works.title: The Portion of Labor
works.description: Published in 1901 and Freeman's most ambitious novel: a New England shoe-manufacturing town, a strike and a young woman's choice. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Mary E. Wilkins Freeman; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ellen Brewster, a factory girl of talent, is loved by the mill owner's son and by a young socialist; when the strike comes she must choose between her class and her love, and the novel ends with her refusing the rich marriage and committing herself to the work of the town.
works.significance: The Portion of Labor is Freeman's most ambitious book and one of the first American novels to treat the factory girl as a serious subject: its analysis of class and its refusal of the conventional marriage ending made it a landmark of American industrial fiction and a bridge between the regional story and the American social novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn.
works.context: 1901: the New England shoe industry, the labor wars of the 1890s, the socialist movement of the new century, and the American debate on the 'woman question'. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Ellen Brewster; Andrew Brewster; Fanny Brewster; Cynthia Lennox; Robert Lloyd; Granville Joy
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Portrait of a Lady
works.form: Novel (three volumes); realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1881 and James's first masterpiece: the story of Isabel Archer, an American heiress in Europe, and of the marriage that imprisons her. It is a prose fiction work of 1881 by Henry James; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Isabel Archer comes to England with her aunt, refuses two good offers of marriage, and is persuaded by Madame Merle to marry the aesthete Gilbert Osmond; the discovery that Osmond and Madame Merle have used her for her money is the crisis of the novel, and she returns to Rome at the end, bound by a promise and by her own sense of honour.
works.significance: The Portrait of a Lady is the central American novel of the international theme and one of the great novels of the nineteenth century: its study of a woman's freedom and its anatomy of a bad marriage made it the model for the modern novel of consciousness, and Isabel Archer is the most fully realised American heroine in fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification.
works.context: The 1870s: the American heiress in Europe, the international marriage market, and the position of married women under English law. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; novel of development and the growth story.

works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Practice of Prelates
works.description: Tyndale's polemic against the English bishops and Cardinal Wolsey, published in 1530, arguing that the prelates' craft had corrupted both church and state and broken the king's marriage.
works.plot: The book traces the 'practice' (craft) of the prelates through English history, attacks Wolsey's legatine power and the annulment proceedings, defends the king's cause against the pope's usurped jurisdiction, and argues from scripture that no man may set himself over kings; it closes with the charge that the bishops oppose the vernacular scripture because it exposes their greed.
works.significance: The most aggressive of Tyndale's political works and a landmark in the English tradition of anti-prelatical polemic that runs to Milton; it documents the convergence of Reformation doctrine and Tudor statecraft.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1530 at the height of the king's 'great matter', while Wolsey's fall was fresh (November 1529); Tyndale's attack on the annulment as the prelates' contrivance, and his denial of the pope's dispensing power, aligned him with the Henrician propaganda campaign while going further than the king would allow.
works.structure: A continuous polemic in three movements — historical narrative, political argument, and scriptural proof — addressed to the king, lords, and commons.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The English Reformation

works.title: The Prairie
works.form: Frontier and maritime romance in the plains mode; philosophical tale of the state of nature
works.description: The fourth of the frontier series and the first American novel to take the great plains west of the Missouri as its scene. The aged scout now lives among trapping parties and French settlers on the edge of the unexplored desert, and the plot turns on the chase of fugitives across a country without roads. Its philosophy of the wilderness as the last refuge of independence gives the book its seriousness.
works.plot: A trapping encampment on the prairie is joined by an emigrant family and by a party pursuing two fugitives from the law, one of them an unprincipled man who has wronged his companions. The old scout acts as guide, judge and finally protector, and a midland settlement of French hunters and a hereditary chieftain of the Osage supply a social background to the chase. A fire on the plains, a secret cave used as a stronghold, and a duel before the tribe structure the later books. The novel ends with the death of the scout in the arms of his Mohican brother, the last of the forest men yielding the country to the prairie.
works.significance: It moved the American romance from forest to prairie and made the empty continent a moral problem rather than a scenery. The death of the scout is the founding elegy of the American wilderness tradition. Its prophecy of a settled, commercial plains country is the series most influential passage.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1827, after the first federal surveys of the Louisiana Purchase had begun to make the plains imaginable to eastern readers. Its settlement politics answer the debates over public land and Indian title that led to the removal legislation of the following decade. Its topography was assembled from printed travels and from the author's own knowledge of the western country.
works.characters: Natty Bumppo; Chingachgook; Inez; the trappers and settlers of the encampment
works.structure: Third-person romance in seven parts, with set-piece description of the plains and of the encampment; the pursuing party and the pursued alternate chapter by chapter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Cooper and the American Romance of Forest and Sea
