works.title: The Prairies
works.form: Topographical and philosophical poem; the American extension of the descriptive meditation
works.description: The author's largest blank-verse meditation on the western grasslands, written in the season of the first American accounts of the prairie and printed just after the close of this installment's period. It contrasts the living hunting grounds of the plains with the vanished empires of Mexico and Peru. Its argument is that a wilderness people perishes with the coming of cultivation, and that the earth reclaims its own.
works.plot: The poem opens on the boundless prairie and the herds of buffalo that people it, and on the Comanche hunter whose whole life is the chase. It then turns to the mounds of the west, the lost cities of Mexico and Peru, and the question of what becomes of races and nations when their country is taken from them. The earth is made the speaker's final authority, covering the works of men with grass and leaving the solitary hunter as a relic. The meditation closes with an act of submission to the destiny that removes one people to make room for another.
works.significance: It is the author's most ambitious poem and the fullest American lyric treatment of the prairie as history and as moral problem. Its use of the mound-builders made a scholarly controversy into poetic material. It marks the transfer of the European descriptive poem into an American geography.
works.meter: Blank verse, iambic pentameter with a sustained descriptive line
works.context: Composed in 1832, when reports of the great plains and of Indian removal reached eastern readers together. Its imagery draws on the newly available travel narratives of the trans-Mississippi west. Its elegy for extinct races belongs to the public argument over the removal policy then being executed.
works.characters: The Comanche hunter; the vanished mound-builders of the west
works.structure: Continuous descriptive and philosophical meditation in blank verse, organized by successive tableaux: the prairie, the chase, the mounds, the fallen empires, the earth's reclamation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
movements: Bryant and the American Nature Lyric

works.title: The Precaution
works.form: Novel of manners and fashion; sentimental domestic fiction with a transatlantic setting
works.description: A first novel in the fashionable domestic mode, set among American planters in England and America and concerned with pride, fortune and the marriage market. It imitates the contemporary English novel of manners and feels its way toward the author's later romance. Its argument about precautionary prudence in marriage is drawn from a sentimental ethics of self-government.
works.plot: An American planter family resident in England is divided by a quarrel between two brothers over an estate and over the woman each loves. A proud father attempts to secure advantage for his children by arranging matches, while a disinherited younger son finds his own path in America. Misunderstandings about wills, fortune and rank are unravelled by disclosures late in the story. The precaution of the title, foreseeing and preventing the ruin caused by pride, is answered by marriage and reconciliation.
works.significance: It is the author's apprenticeship and the clearest American example of the Anglo-fashionable novel of the 1810s. Its failure as a copy and its interest as a document of cultural dependence are usually discussed together. It marks the starting point of the American romance of forest and sea.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published anonymously in 1820, when American readers were still buying British three-decker fiction and native novelists generally began by imitating it. Its English setting reflects the post-war residence of American planters in the metropole. The decision to write it was encouraged by the recent success of a native historical romance.
works.structure: Third-person domestic novel in the manner of contemporary fashion fiction, with letters and explanatory disclosures resolving the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; the author disavowed and revised it in later collected editions, acknowledging its imitativeness.
themes: Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
The marriage market and the limited estate
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence

works.title: The Predictions for the Year 1708 (Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.)
works.description: The astrological prediction sent in the name of Isaac Bickerstaff Esq. to a London almanack paper, foretelling with exact dates the death of the prognosticator John Partridge and other events of the year; the first move in the most successful practical joke of the century's print war.
works.plot: Bickerstaff announces that he has corrected the almanack makers' errors and predicts Partridge's death on a specified day, together with the fate of several other prophets of the pressure of the times; the ensuing accounts of the accomplishment and the vindication of Bickerstaff carry the imposture into the newspapers.
works.significance: It demonstrated the credibility of the press as a machine that could be fooled by its own conventions, and it created the Bickerstaff persona through which the Tatler and the Spectator would speak.
works.meter: The aphoristic future tense of the prognostication, in the manner of the old almanack verses, with the mock-profound numerical date.
works.context: Published in the season of the Sacheverell ferment, when the party almanacks and the astrology of the press were instruments of political prediction; the trick drew Partridge's almanack for 1708 out of the market and gave Steele the paper mask he soon adopted.
works.characters: Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.; John Partridge the almanack maker; the rival prophets of the year
works.structure: A short prediction tract followed by its pretended fulfilment and by the replies; the pieces form a single serial hoax conducted in the news sheets.
works.attributionNotes: Swift's authorship of the Bickerstaff papers is agreed, with a share in the later management of the hoax belonging to Steele, who wrote as Partridge's opponent and who inherited the mask.

works.title: The Prelude
altTitles: The Prelude, or, Growth of a Poet's Mind; An Autobiographical Poem
works.form: Autobiographical and philosophical poem in blank verse, a poet's mind in the shape of an epic without a hero's actions; it draws on the tradition of the contemplative and topographical poem and on the Romantic essay in psychological analysis.
works.description: The most important long poem of the English Romantic period and the first substantial autobiographical poem in the language in blank verse: a self-analysis of the making of a poet's mind, begun in 1798, completed in a thirteen-book form in 1805, and extensively revised over the following decades. It was never published in the writer's lifetime and appeared posthumously in 1850 under a title chosen by his family and editors. Its plan belongs to a larger philosophical scheme that was never finished, of which the published Excursion was meant to form the middle part.
works.plot: The poem leaves the city of the author's birth and travels north through the first mountain journeys of boyhood, and thereafter follows the growth of his mind by a series of formative episodes set down in the order of experience rather than of argument. The incidents include the stealing of a boat on a lake at night, when a peak rose up and seemed to follow him like a living creature; the long wait for the horses on a winter evening among the wild country of the northern roads; the years at the university, when the prescribed studies left the imagination to seek its own food abroad; the residence in France during the first years of the Revolution and the subsequent journey over the Alps, where the real object of the hoped-for renewal rose above him unrecognised; and the sights of London, its beggars, its prisons, its travelling shows and its unending crowd. Through all of these a sense of power, of a mind in union with the invisible world, is felt in the mountain and river scenery, and the poem's argument is that external nature, administered by a shaping spirit, educated the poet's imagination and affections, so that the poet is to be known by what his mind made of what he saw.
works.significance: Founded the Romantic autobiographical poem and set the pattern of later long poems of the self's education; its phrase for the growth of the mind became the standard description of the lyric of memory, and its account of the imagination as a moral and perceptual power remains central in the history of ideas. The recovery of the 1805 text transformed the poet's reputation and made the poem's political and psychological passages matters of continuing argument.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter throughout, in a style of extraordinary flexibility, with long flowing periods, Latinate inversion and a deliberate abundance of general nouns, and frequent apostrophes to the mountains and to the powers of the mind.
works.context: Conceived in 1798 as a philosophical poem to be built upon the account of the growth of the poet's mind, and revised in the years after the disappointment of the French Revolution and the settlement in the Lake District; the 1850 posthumous text, prepared after the author's death by members of his family, represents the later and more conservative revision and suppressed the more radical passages of the 1805 version, which was recovered by scholarship only in the twentieth century.
works.characters: The poet's own successive selves - the boy, the college student at Cambridge, the traveller in the Alps, the resident in revolutionary France and in London; Nature, addressed as a power that trains, disciplines and reassures the growing mind
works.structure: An autobiographical poem in books of unequal length - thirteen in the version of 1805, fourteen in the posthumous text of 1850 - organised as a travel narrative of the mind: it alternates narrative episode, descriptive passage and sustained reflection, and is held together by a single addressing voice that looks backward across an interval of years and asks what those experiences have made.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the two distinct recensions of 1805 and 1850 are both by the same author, and modern editions print them in parallel with their revisions recorded.

Imagination as a way of knowing
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
The sublime, terror, and the ruin

works.description: The play of the clerk's world and the price of the office. It is a dramatic work of 1913 by Elizabeth Baker; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.

works.significance: The Price of Thomas Scott is Baker's play of the clerk's world: its Manchester repertory and its observation of the office carried her typist's knowledge onto the new stage.

The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain exact dialogue of the clerk and the shopgirl.

works.title: The Prick of Conscience
works.description: A northern poem of some 9,600 lines on the last things — the wretchedness of life, death, purgatory, the pains of hell and joys of heaven, and the day of doom — traditionally attributed to Richard Rolle but now generally denied to him. It was the most widely copied Middle English poem of all, surviving in more manuscripts than any other verse of the period, including Piers Plowman and the Canterbury Tales.
works.plot: In seven parts the poem moves from the misery of human life through the certainty and terror of death to the topography of the afterlife — purgatory's cleansing fire, hell's torments, heaven's bliss — and the signs and terrors of the last judgement, closing with the exhortation to live so as to die well.
works.significance: The most widely read Middle English poem of its century and the great vernacular encyclopedia of the afterlife; its manuscript diffusion is a central fact of late medieval English literary culture.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect, plain and insistent.
works.context: Composed c. 1350 in the north of England, in the pastoral tradition of the fourth Lateran council's emphasis on penance; preserved in over 120 manuscripts and translated into Latin (Stimulus Conscientiae); its popularity made it the period's standard popular eschatology.
works.characters: the preacher-narrator
works.structure: A seven-part didactic sequence on the four last things, in the memento mori tradition, with the 'prick' of conscience as its titular image.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Rolle in many manuscripts, but modern scholarship rejects the attribution (Ralph Hanna and others); authorship_status reflects the dispute.

Judgment Day and eschatology
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: The Prime Minister
works.form: Novel in monthly parts; four volumes 1876 (Palliser, 5)
works.description: Published in 1875-76: the central political novel of the Palliser series, in which Plantagenet Palliser becomes Prime Minister in a coalition and his wife's social campaign makes him impossible. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by Anthony Trollope; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Serial and Monthly-Part Novel.
works.plot: The Duke of Omnium forms a coalition government and becomes Prime Minister without the support of either party; Lady Glencora's entertainment of the adventurer Ferdinand Lopez, her political meddling and the accusation that her husband has used his office for private advantage destroy the ministry. The subplot follows Lopez's fraudulent speculations, his marriage to Emily Wharton, and his suicide.
works.significance: The Prime Minister is the most sophisticated English novel about the routines of political power, and its portrait of the Duke's constitutional conscience is unmatched in fiction. Lady Glencora Palliser is one of the great creations of Victorian fiction, and the Lopez plot is a masterly study of the confidence trick as a social form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The coalition ministries of the 1850s-70s, the political hostess and the dinner party as instruments of government, and the financial fraud of the mid-1870s. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; serial and monthly-part novel.
works.characters: Plantagenet Palliser; Lady Glencora Palliser; Ferdinand Lopez; Emily Wharton; Mr Wharton; Everett Wharton; Lady Eustace; Sextus Parker; Mr Gresham; Sir Orlando Drought
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Prince and the Pauper
works.description: Published in 1881 and Twain's first attempt at historical fiction: the story of two identical boys, one a prince and one a pauper, who exchange places in Tudor England. It is a prose fiction work of 1881 by Mark Twain; it belongs to Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tom Canty, a London beggar, and Prince Edward exchange clothes and are taken for one another; the prince is driven out into the streets and experiences the cruelty of his own laws, while Tom rules in his place until the coronation scene restores the true king.
works.significance: The Prince and the Pauper is the most popular American historical novel of the century for children and a key text in the American literature of democratic equality; its picture of Tudor England shaped the American image of the English past.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is first-person vernacular narration.
works.context: 1547: the reign of Edward VI, the English vagrancy laws, and the American democratic critique of monarchy. The record dates the work as composed between 1880 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; novel of development and the growth story.

works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. works.title: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems
works.form: Poetry collection; title poem in ballad stanzas
works.description: Published in 1866 with illustrations by her brother: the title poem, a ballad-allegory of the prince who delays on his journey and finds the princess dead, together with 'The Convent Threshold', 'A Royal Princess', 'Under the Rose' and the devotional lyrics.
works.plot: The prince sets out to claim his bride, is delayed by the temptations of the road, and arrives to find her dead; 'A Royal Princess' concerns a princess who gives her wealth to the poor; 'Under the Rose' is the monologue of a great lady's illegitimate daughter, brought up in the village and never acknowledged.
works.significance: The Prince's Progress is the finest Victorian allegorical ballad and the clearest statement of Rossetti's theology of delay and loss; its treatment of the princess's autonomy (as against the prince's dilatoriness) has made it a key text in the modern reading of her gender politics.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the ballad stanza, the four-stress and three-stress lines rhyming on the even lines. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
works.context: The 1860s Pre-Raphaelite interest in the ballad and the allegory, the Victorian cult of the dead virgin (Elizabeth Siddal died in 1862), and the Anglo-Catholic devotional culture of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the Prince; the waiting bride; the milkmaid; the alchemist; the Royal Princess; the unacknowledged daughter of 'Under the Rose' and her mother, 'my Lady'
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christina Georgina Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Princess and the Goblin
works.description: Published in 1872 and the most popular of MacDonald's children's books: the story of Princess Irene, the miner's son Curdie, and the goblins beneath the mountain. It is a prose fiction work of 1872 by George MacDonald; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Irene, living in a castle under a mountain, meets her mysterious great-great-grandmother in the tower and Curdie, a miner's boy, discovers the goblins' plan to abduct her; together they defeat the goblin court in the underground hall.
works.significance: The Princess and the Goblin is one of the two or three best children's fantasies in English: its great-great-grandmother, the thread, and the underground goblins are permanent images, and the book was a decisive influence on Lewis, Tolkien and the whole modern school of children's fantasy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain.

works.title: The Princess: A Medley
works.description: Published in 1847 (revised 1850, 1851, 1853, with the intercalated songs added in 1850), a serio-comic poem on the higher education of women: a prince disguises himself as a maid to enter a women's college founded by the princess he is betrothed to.
works.plot: The Prince, betrothed in childhood to the Princess Ida, daughter of King Gama, enters her college in disguise with his friends; discovered, he is wounded, nursed, and the college collapses when Ida's heart is touched by the story of a mother's love; the poem ends with the prince's vision of a reconciled relation between the sexes and with the lyric 'Now sleeps the crimson petal'.
works.significance: The Princess is the Victorian poem on women's education and the most ambitious attempt in verse to argue the case for female intellectual life. Its mixture of comic and serious registers, and its interpolated songs, made it a permanent anthology source, and its reception shows the shift in the debate from comedy to politics inside a single decade.
works.meter: Blank verse for the narrative; the songs in various lyric stanzas ('Tears, idle tears' in a four-line stanza with refrain).
works.context: The 1840s debate on women's education (Queen's College, London, 1848; the Governesses' Benevolent Institution), the early feminist argument of the English Woman's Journal, and the poem's later embarrassment to its author as the 'woman question' became serious.
works.characters: the Prince; Princess Ida; Cyril; Florian; Psyche; King Gama; the Lady Blanche; Melissa
works.structure: A prologue and conclusion frame seven cantos of narrative, with six interspersed songs; in blank verse with lyrical interludes.

works.title: The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffics and Discoveries of the English Nation
works.description: Hakluyt's great collection of English voyage narratives: the documents of the nation's seafaring — from the voyages of the Cabots and the Muscovy Company through Hawkins, Drake, and Frobisher to Ralegh's Virginia and the East India voyages — gathered, translated, and arranged in the first edition of 1589 and the vastly expanded three-volume second edition of 1598–1600.
works.plot: No single plot: the collection proceeds by region and voyage, each narrative a first-hand account — ship's journals, letters, treaties, and reports — of the discovery, trade, and plunder by which England measured the globe.
works.significance: The 'prose epic of the modern English nation' (Froude) — the book that taught England the world's geography and its own imperial vocation.
works.meter: Prose of many hands, edited by Hakluyt into the great prose epic of English expansion.
works.context: First edition 1589; the three-volume second edition appeared 1598–1600, in the years of the Armada's aftermath and the East India Company's founding; the collection became the sourcebook of English colonialism.
works.characters: the voyagers (Sebastian Cabot, John Hawkins, Francis Drake, Martin Frobisher, Walter Ralegh, and hundreds of others)
works.structure: A documentary anthology organized geographically (north, south, east) and chronologically, with Hakluyt's prefaces and dedications providing the patriotic frame.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled and edited by Hakluyt; the individual narratives are by many authors, credited within the work.

works.title: The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
altTitles: Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
works.description: Paley's command textbook of Christian utilitarianism, six impressions in its first decade and a Cambridge examination staple for a generation. It makes the will of God declared by the light of nature the rule of action, utility the measure of duty, and happiness in the future state the sanction of the whole.
works.plot: Paley grounds moral obligation in the commands of God learned from the light of nature, from the revealed will, and from the criterion of expedience, defining virtue as the doing of good to mankind in obedience to the will of God and for the sake of everlasting happiness. He runs through the duties to ourselves, to our neighbours, to God, and to the state, treating truth, justice, property, civil government, resistance, and the law of nations, each tested by utility under the divine sanction. He argues the Christian duty of masters toward servants and against the cruelty of slavery in the West India colonies, and defends the British constitution as expedient while subordinating every institution to the general rule of human happiness. The system ends with the sanctions of a future state binding utility and religion into one.
works.significance: It trained the governing class of church and state in Christian utilitarianism and remained the standard Cambridge undergraduate ethics text for a generation, the hinge between Paley's theological school and the later utilitarians who claimed and disowned him.
works.meter: Lucid, workmanlike, maxim-heavy prose of the excellent plain teacher, definition, rule, case, and moral in tidy sequence.
works.context: Published in 1785 after Paley's Indian-service chaplaincy and his archdeaconry, distilled from his divinity lectures; six editions appeared within a dozen years, and the intuitive moralists attacked its criterion while the universities adopted it.
works.structure: Six parts in lecture order: moral obligation in general, duties to self, to neighbours, to God, to the state, and the concluding applications, arranged for university teaching.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Principles of Political Economy
altTitles: The Principles of Political Economy: with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science
works.form: treatise of political economy; the scientific exposition with the history of the science
works.description: The manual which made the doctrine of the English school of political economy a textbook, a compact and heavily instanced exposition of the science in its newest form, prefixed with a sketch of the rise and progress of the study, and set out with the plain assertion of the abstract method against the popular writers on wealth and the practical errors of the day.
works.plot: The work states the principles of the science in the order of wealth, treating of production and of distribution, and holding that value is regulated by the quantity of the labour required in production, wages and profit being determined by the cost of production and the competition of capital, and rent by the difference of the powers of the soil, and not, as the common doctrine held, as a deduction from the returns of the farmer. It argues at large against the errors of the writers on the commercial policy, against the notion that the accumulation of stock and the application of machinery injure the labourer on the whole, against the paradoxes of under-consumption and of the distrust of plenty, and against the confusion of the wealth of the state with the riches of the individuals who compose it; and it treats of taxation, of the public debt, of the restrictions upon trade, and of the statistical evidence of the progress of nations. The historical sketch prefixed gives the rise of the science from the older writers, and is used as an argument that the truth of the modern doctrine is established and that its opponents are the survivors of a mistaken literature.
works.significance: For two generations the standard textbook of the science in Britain, America, and the colonies, and the medium through which the doctrine of value by labour, the theory of rent, and the abstract method became the received orthodoxy of the universities and of the commercial classes; its sketch of the history of the study was long the common introduction to the literature of the subject, and the book is a primary document of the professionalisation of political economy and of the vocabulary of the reform debates of the century.
works.meter: Clear, dogmatic, heavily instanced prose of the didactic economist, with the blunt disquisition upon the mistakes of the popular writers, the perpetual quotation and rejection of authorities, and the confident verdict upon the facts; its force rests upon the range of reading and the decision of the assertion rather than upon subtlety of method, and its sentences are built to be quoted and to settle a dispute.
works.context: Published in 1825, Edinburgh and London, in the season in which the doctrines of the science had been settled by the chief English writer of the preceding fifteen years, in which the extra-mural classes of the Scottish metropolis were making political economy a branch of the ordinary education of the professional and commercial young, and in which the controversy on the corn laws, the currency, and the distress of the agriculture and manufactures was carried on in the review journals; its author, the writer of the standard English manual of the commerce and of the literature of the science, and at length the first holder of the chair of the subject at the metropolitan university of the reformers and afterwards the professor at Glasgow, here reduced the newest doctrine to the form in which it could be taught and contested.
works.structure: A treatise in books and chapters, the historical sketch of the rise and progress of the science prefixed to the systematic statement of the principles, the argument proceeding from value and production to rent, profit, wages, and capital, and thence to taxation, commercial restriction, and the measure of national wealth; the several positions carried by the citation of the authorities of the science and by the numerical instance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the editions are many and the enlarged later issues, given out in two volumes with the added essays on taxation and on the literature of the science, differ materially from the first, and the American and the European reprints, with the translations, are variously altered, so that the citation should note the edition.

works.title: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
altTitles: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy, Concerning God, Christ, and the Creatures
works.description: Anne Conway's philosophical treatise, written in the last years of her life and published posthumously in Latin in 1690 and in English in 1692; it proposes a monistic vitalist metaphysics in which all creatures are degrees of one spiritual substance.
works.plot: In nine chapters Conway argues that God is infinitely good and communicative, that creatures are mutable spiritual substances capable of perfecting themselves, and that the dualism of Descartes and the materialism of Hobbes are both false.
works.significance: One of the most original philosophical works of the seventeenth century and the first by an English woman to be published as a systematic metaphysics; it influenced Leibniz and has been revalued as a major contribution to early modern philosophy.
works.meter: Scholarly philosophical prose.

works.title: The Prisoner of Chillon
altTitles: The Prisoner of Chillon, and Other Poems
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Dramatic monologue and poem of confinement in blank verse; the cloistered or dungeon meditation, with the historical preface used to license the fiction.
works.description: A dramatic monologue of confinement, founded on the actual imprisonment in the castle of Chillon of a Swiss cleric who resisted the forced adoption of a new faith. The prisoner recounts seven years in a single pillar-girdled dungeon beneath the lake, the deaths of his brothers, and his own passage from prayer to apathy to a freedom that arrives only with his release. It is the period's most influential poem of political and physical confinement, and its blank verse deliberately imitates the colloquial weight of the older drama.
works.plot: Chained to a pillar in a vault where the lake beats above and the steps of his keepers are the only sound, the prisoner watches his brothers die and finds at last that he can no longer grieve; he becomes part of the dungeon, his very chains familiar, and his thoughts turn to the forest and the lake. His gaoler marks the change and fears for his reason, then the chain is loosed, and he goes free into a world that seems his prison still. The argument is that tyranny is measured not in suffering but in the loss of feeling, and that the liberated man carries his confinement as a habit of mind. The closing invocation pardons the keepers and refuses the politics of the crime.
works.significance: It became the century's touchstone poem of solitary confinement, much imitated in the prison and asylum verse of the following decades, and a central text for the Romantic analysis of the mind's adaptation to oppression. Its borrowed dramatic manner also shaped the development of the modern monologue, and its preface is a document of the Romantic use of history as licence.
works.meter: Blank verse, five-beat iambic lines with frequent triple endings, weak endings and enjambment, in an intentional reproduction of the manner of the older English drama; the prose preface is set apart from the verse.
works.context: Written in the summer of 1816 after a visit to the castle on the Lake of Geneva, in the months of the poet's exile and of the restoration settlement that made religious and political imprisonment a live European question, and published in the same season in a volume with the shorter lyrics and meditations of the Swiss journey. Its subject, a Reformed champion confined by a cantonal authority, allowed the poem to be read as a parable of every post-war confinement.
works.characters: the prisoner of Chillon; his two brothers who die in chains; the gaoler who observes his change; the church and cantonal powers named in the preface
works.structure: A single continuous soliloquy in fourteen stanzas of unequal length, chronological within the captivity, framed by a brief prose preface naming the historical prisoner and the castle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem first appeared in a volume of short pieces, and its text was lightly revised in the later collected editions.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: The Prisoner of Zenda
works.description: Published in 1894 and the founding Ruritanian romance: an Englishman impersonates the king of a small European state on the day of his coronation. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Anthony Hope; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Rudolf Rassendyll, an English gentleman on holiday, discovers he is the double of the King of Ruritania; when the king is drugged by his half-brother Black Michael, Rudolf takes his place at the coronation, falls in love with the Princess Flavia, and finally rescues the king from the castle of Zenda in a swordfight with Rupert of Hentzau.
works.significance: The Prisoner of Zenda invented the Ruritanian romance and created one of the most durable formulas in popular fiction: it has never been out of print, it gave the language the word 'Ruritanian', and it has been filmed, staged and imitated continuously for more than a century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is fast-moving adventure narrative with a first-person narrator.
works.context: 1894: the small states of central Europe, the English gentleman's code of honour, the vogue of the adventure romance after Stevenson, and the imperial self-image of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed in 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; sensation novel.

works.title: The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner
altTitles: Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's great novel, a double-voiced Gothic study of religious enthusiasm in eighteenth-century Scotland, in which the zealot Robert Wylie's conviction of his own election leads him through murder to ruin. Initially a commercial failure, it is now regarded as one of the masterworks of Scottish literature and of the Gothic.
works.plot: An anonymous Editor's memoir first narrates, from 1811, the history of the Wylie family and the reputed murder of the elder son James by his younger brother Robert, ending in Robert's mysterious death. The Editor then announces Robert's own manuscript Confessions, which retells the same events: Robert, a student of the Secession kirk, becomes convinced he is one of the Elect and meets the mesmerising stranger Gil-Martin, whether companion, double, or devil. Under Gil-Martin's influence Robert engineers his brother's murder, abandons his mother, and descends into imprisonment and despair, ending the manuscript unresolved before his death.
works.significance: Now recognised as a major work of the Romantic period and a forerunner of psychological and modernist fiction; its double narration anticipates Conrad and Nabokov, and its treatment of religious mania and the uncanny double makes it a summit of the Gothic.
works.context: Published in 1824 amid bitter religious division in post-Disrupting Scotland; the author drew on Secession church history, on the Bodkin family murder case of 1800, and on his own Calvinist childhood; its sceptical treatment of election affronted the religious public and it sold poorly.
works.characters: Robert Wylie; Gil-Martin; James Wylie; Robert's mother; the Editor; Mr. Slewton; Jean Johnstone
works.structure: Radically double structure: an external Editor's narrative (1811) framing the protagonist's own manuscript Confessions; the two accounts contradict and undermine each other, leaving the supernatural and the psychological irresolvable.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft
works.description: Published in 1903 and Gissing's last completed book: the diary of a retired scholar who has escaped Grub Street into a cottage in Devon, and a meditation on literature, poverty and the consolations of a small income.
works.plot: Ryecroft records the seasons, his reading, his memories of London and the Continent, his reflections on the English character and on the death of his friends; the book ends with his death and the quiet dispersal of his library.
works.significance: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft was Gissing's most popular book and remains the classic English essay on the pleasures of modest leisure; it is the gentlest of his works and the one that best shows his prose at its most fastidious.

works.title: The Problem of Pain
works.description: The apologetic of suffering: divine omnipotence, human pain and the argument from love. It is a prose work of 1940 by C. S. Lewis; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Lewis takes the problem of pain in order: divine omnipotence and the limits of the possible, the fall and the will, human wickedness and the pain of the body, the pain of the soul and the perfection of love, heaven and hell and the last judgment, in the prose of the converted intellect.
works.significance: The Problem of Pain is the central apologetic of the war years and the book that made Lewis the public defender of the faith: its argument from love and its account of the suffering of the creature remain the standard statement of the Christian answer to the problem of pain.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. works.title: The Professor
works.description: Charlotte Brontë's first novel, written in 1846 and rejected by every publisher to whom it was offered; it was published posthumously in 1857 with a preface by her widower, Arthur Bell Nicholls. It is a prose fiction work of 1857 by Charlotte Brontë; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: William Crimsworth, an orphan without connections, rejects the patronage of his Yorkshire brother and goes to Brussels, where he teaches at a boys' school and then at Mademoiselle Reuter's girls' school; he falls in love with Frances Henri, a Swiss-English pupil-teacher, marries her, and returns to England to run a school of their own.
works.significance: The Professor anticipates Villette and is a key document for the study of Brontë's development: its plain, unromantic hero, its refusal of the love-plot's conventional hierarchy and its insistence on work as the basis of self-respect make it the first Brontë statement of the themes she later transformed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
works.context: The Brussels of the 1840s, the position of the English master abroad, and the professional ambition of a self-made man of letters — the novel's subject is the one that Brontë knew from Heger. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1857 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: The Progress of Poesy
works.description: Gray's Pindaric ode on the migration of poetry through the Greek colonies and their states, and its at last arrival in Britain, written in the measures he studied in the old French and Italian imitations of Pindar.
works.plot: Poetry, restrained long in Egypt and in the East, bursts out among the colonies of Ionia and Doria, keeps court with the legislator and the victor, and passes through the ages of Greek and Roman decay at the coming of the northern power, till the Muse is received in Britain under the patronage of the ruling house.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished English attempt to revive the Pindaric stanza as an instrument of cultural history, and it stands with The Bard as the monument of Gray's later ode.
works.meter: The complex Grayian Pindaric stanza of unequal lines with a recurring scheme, modelled on the measures of the ancient ode as the eighteenth century reconstructed them.
works.context: Written in the same year as The Bard and after a decade of Gray's study of the Pindaric measures, of the old English and of the Norse poetry, at the moment when the historical account of the progress of the arts was being written by the antiquarian critics.
works.characters: Poesy and the Muse; the legislators and poets of the Greek states; the northern conqueror of the last stanzas
works.structure: A paired strophe, antistrophe and epode structure in three parts, with the strophe of the ode carrying the historical advance and the epode the reflection.

works.title: The Progress of Romance
altTitles: The Progress of Romance, through various Ages; consisting of a Historical and Critical Account of the Most Popular Writers of that Famous Class of Composition
works.form: critical history and dissertation on prose fiction
works.description: A critical and historical account of the prose romance from the Greek and the Eastern tales through the chivalry of the Middle Ages to the writer's own day, delivered in two volumes of survey and judgment. It is one of the first sustained histories of prose fiction in English and a defence of romance on rational grounds.
works.plot: The work traces the rise and declension of the romantic tale, examining its Eastern and Greek originals, the Arabian and Spanish collections, and the chivalric romances of the Middle Ages. It passes to the pastoral and heroic romance of France and to the modern novel, weighing the beauties and the improbabilities of each. Its conclusion defends the regulated use of the marvellous and judges the present taste by the standard of the old tales.
works.significance: It is a foundational text of the scholarly history of the novel and of the eighteenth century's attempt to classify romance, and it gives the period's most articulate defence of the tale of imagination.
works.meter: A clear and moderate critical prose of estimate and comparison, with the quoted translations used as evidence of manner.
works.context: Published in 1785 after the author's own practice in Gothic and sentimental romance, in the season of the quarrel over the novel's morality and of the first attempts at a history of English fiction.
works.structure: A chronological critical history in two volumes, arranged by schools and periods with abstracts and quotations of the examples and with the reviewer's judgments throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and related by her to her own fiction.

works.title: The Proverbs of Alfred

works.description: A collection of proverbial wisdom in verse, cast as the sayings of King Alfred assembled 'at Seaford' before a gathered folk, on kingship, wealth, wisdom, women, and the conduct of life. It is the principal early Middle English example of the native gnomic tradition continuing under the name of the great West Saxon king.
works.plot: Alfred, enthroned at Seaford, delivers counsel in a series of proverb-laden sections — on wisdom and wealth, on choosing a wife, on old age — punctuated by the poet's own commentary.
works.significance: The chief witness to the survival of the Old English wisdom tradition into Middle English, and a favourite anthology text of the early period.
works.meter: Loose alliterative and rhyming couplets in the transitional early Middle English manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1150–80, perhaps in Sussex, in the south; preserved in Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29 (c. 1275) with The Owl and the Nightingale, and fragmentarily elsewhere.
works.characters: Alfred (speaker); the assembled folk
works.structure: A framing scene of the king's council enclosing discrete gnomic sections with connective commentary.

works.title: The Provok'd Husband
works.form: Domestic comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, an acting text made up from an unfinished draft.
works.description: The comedy which its first author left unfinished at his death in 1726, worked up for the stage by the Drury Lane management and acted and printed in 1728. It returns to the provoked-wife material of the 1690s and turns it into a reform comedy of marriage, in which a gadabout and gamester wife is brought back to her duties by an artifice practised on the whole household. As an acting text it belongs to the sentimental reconstitution of London comedy in the 1720s.
works.plot: Lord Townly, a husband of some patience, is driven to distraction by Lady Townly, who loves play, the card-table and general company more than her house, and who is encouraged in her courses by her visiting friends and by an intriguing foreign count who designs upon the women about her. The husband's remedy is an artifice of his own: he gives out that he is dying, and lets the household, his wife included, rehearse its grief in his hearing, so that their real calculations of profit and freedom appear beneath the forms of mourning. On the pretended recovery he uses what he has overheard to rebuke and reclaim his wife, and the last acts move the circle from conspiracy to penitence. The subplots of servants and dependants, who read the master's disguise differently, supply the lower register of the same exposure.
works.significance: It kept the provoked-wife argument of the 1690s alive as a reform comedy and supplied the stage with a durable scene of pretended death and detected grief. As a text it is the standard illustration of collaborative canon formation in the eighteenth-century theatre, and the two surviving states of one comedy make it a case study in posthumous revision.
works.meter: Spoken prose throughout, with the moral set-pieces of the exposure in short formal passages and the closing address to the audience in couplets.
works.context: The original author had died leaving the play a fragment, and the manager who produced it finished it for a January production in 1728, the season in which sentimental domestic comedy had become the profitable form of the patent house. The share taken by the finisher was afterwards enlarged in his own memoirs and disputed by the friends of the deceased writer, and the two hands were never cleanly separated. The piece entered the century's repertory and was revived repeatedly.
works.characters: Lord Townly; Lady Townly, his gamester and gadabout wife; her fashionable friends; the foreign count who designs upon them; the servants and dependants of the household
works.structure: Five acts of prose comedy divided between the fashionably dissolute wife's outside courses and the domestic exposure that closes them; the feigned deathbed is the structural hinge, and the reform of the wife is effected by testimony rather than by argument.
works.attributionNotes: Finished and adapted for the stage by the Drury Lane manager who produced it; the printed text names the deceased author alone, the extent of the completion was contested at once, and the play is therefore entered here as collaborative with the first share being the unfinished draft.

works.title: The Provoked Wife
works.description: Vanbrugh's second comedy, a dark and daring treatment of a brutal marriage, in which Lady Brute endures her husband's drunken abuse and the question of divorce and remarriage is openly debated.

works.significance: The most serious and most controversial of the Restoration comedies; its treatment of marital cruelty and female agency makes it a central text for feminist readings of the period.

works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in May 1697 and published the same year; the ecclesiastical courts' handling of marriage separation was a live issue, and the play provoked Jeremy Collier's attack in A Short View of the Immorality of the English Stage (1698).

works.title: The Psalms of David Imitated in the Christian Stile
altTitles: The Psalms of David Imitated in the New Testament Stile
works.description: Isaac Watts's Christianizing paraphrase of the whole psalter, published in 1719 after controversy in his own congregation, the book that gave English Nonconformity its psalmody and gave the churches Joy to the World, When All Thy-Gods? safer: Ps. xciii and the Messiah hymns. It is Augustan hymnwriting at its most ambitious.
works.plot: Watts paraphrases each psalm into gospel idiom, letting David speak of Christ, the church, and the believer's experience rather than only of Israel and Judah. The Advent and Nativity songs, the triumphs of providence, and the penitential psalms are rewritten into hymns of praise and instruction for Christian assemblies. His version of the one hundred and Ninety-third? FINAL: his paraphrase of Psalm 98 gave the churches Joy to the World, and the Advent and Messianic versions supplied the most used hymns in the language. The preface answers the strict psalm-singers, pleading that the gospel is new matter for praise and that David's songs must be read with Christian eyes.
works.significance: It dominated the psalmody of English Nonconformity for a century and supplied hymns still sung everywhere, and it fixed the method of gospel paraphrase that later psalters and hymnals inherited.
works.meter: Command of the psalm and hymn metres of the early eighteenth century, with the expanded six and eight-line stanzas of his happiest odes, the diction elevated, sensuous, and plain at once.
works.context: Published in London in 1719 after long argument in his own congregation over hymn-singing and in the season of the psalms controversy that divided older and younger Nonconformity; a large subscription volume announced by its author in his earlier Hymns.
works.structure: A continuous Christianizing paraphrase of the psalter, the longer psalms divided into numbered versions with hymns interspersed on gospel occasions.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Purple Land That England Lost
works.description: Published in 1885 and Hudson's picaresque of the Uruguayan pampas: an Englishman's wanderings with the gauchos in the 1870s. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by W. H. Hudson; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Richard Lamb, a young Englishman, flees to the Banda Oriental after a scandal and wanders the pampas with the gauchos, taking part in a revolution, falling in love, fighting duels and losing himself in the wild freedom of the plains, before returning to Montevideo and to the woman he had left.
works.significance: The Purple Land is the finest English novel of the South American pampas and one of the founding texts of the English literary image of the gaucho: its combination of picaresque adventure and exact observation made it a classic, and it was the book that gave Hudson his first reputation as a writer.
works.meter: Prose. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical, unhurried descriptive prose.
works.context: 1885: the Uruguayan civil wars of the 1870s, the gaucho culture of the pampas, the English commercial presence in South America, and the Victorian adventure romance. works.title: The Queen's Wake
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
works.description: the author's long pastoral ballad and the title poem of his 1813 collection, a contest of songs among Scottish poets at the court of a legendary queen. It is a celebrated assertion of the Scottish national ballad tradition in the high Romantic moment, self-consciously positioning the author as heir to the Makars.
works.plot: At a court gathering, the Queen summons Scottish poets to compete in song on the theme of the most worthy lady; each poet — including the figure of the Ettrick Shepherd himself — sings a ballad in the old stanzaic forms. The narrative frame of the Wake itself is a festive occasion that becomes a demonstration of the living continuity of Scottish popular verse. The tale concludes with the Queen's adjudication and the Shepherd's triumph.
works.significance: The Queen's Wake was the poem that established the author's national reputation and made possible his later prose fiction; it is a central text of the ballad revival and a manifesto of Scottish vernacular poetry in the Romantic period.
works.meter: Ballad stanzas and varying Scottish metres; the title poem mixes lyrical and narrative stanza forms
works.context: Published in 1813 amid the Scottish literary renaissance catalysed by Scott's Minstrelsy and Waverley; the author's poem asserts the authority of the living oral ballad tradition against the classical and Augustan inheritances in English poetry.
works.characters: The Queen; the Ettrick Shepherd; Kingsley; Douglas; Lord Yester
works.structure: Frame narrative of a poetic contest at a legendary court; embedded ballads in varied Scottish stanzaic forms; the contest structure organises the variety of voices.

works.title: The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists
works.description: The founding text of the English working-class novel. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by Robert Tressell; it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists follows Frank Owen, the sign-writer, and the painters of the Rushton & Co. job through the season's work in the town of Mugsborough - the scamping, the sack, the tearing of the bread, the Great Money Trick and Owen's socialist lectures in the dinner hour - until the dying man finishes the book that argues for the workers' own cause.
works.significance: The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists is the founding text of the working-class novel in England: written by a dying house painter, cut in 1914 and restored in 1955, it became the labour movement's own book and the standard against which every later proletarian novel is read.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the plain angry prose of the painter's argument.
works.context: The provincial English town of the Edwardian years, before the first war. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1910 and first published in 1914 and it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Frank Owen, the sign-writer; the painters of the job; the Rushtons; the philanthropists
works.structure: A working novel in the chapters of the job, with the lectures of the dinner hour. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Robert Tressell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Robert Tressell is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Raiders
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1894
works.description: Crockett's Galloway adventure: the smuggling trade, the excisemen and the Solway shore. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Samuel Rutherford Crockett; it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: In the Galloway of the 1790s a young farmer is drawn into the smuggling trade of the Solway, the raids of the excisemen and the Jacobite plot, and the novel ends in a chase across the moss and the shore.
works.significance: The Raiders was the first of Crockett's Galloway historical adventures and one of the best of the Scottish regional romances: its smuggling plot, its Solway shore and its rapid narrative made it a model for the historical adventure novel of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the Galloway dialect in direct speech.
works.context: The Stewartry of Kirkcudbright in the 1790s, the smuggling trade and the French wars. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and it is catalogued under sensation novel; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Patrick Heron; the smuggler; the exciseman; the laird of Balmaghie
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, from the farm to the smuggling raid. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as S. R. Crockett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as minor canon.

works.title: The Railway Children
works.form: Children's novel (serialised in the London Magazine, 1905)
works.description: Published in 1906 and the most popular of Nesbit's books: the story of three children who move to a cottage in the country after their father is arrested, and whose lives are shaped by the railway that runs past their house.
works.plot: Roberta, Peter and Phyllis move with their mother to Three Chimneys, make friends with the stationmaster, the porter and the old gentleman on the train, rescue a boy from a tunnel, prevent an accident by waving a red petticoat, and are finally reunited with their father, who has been cleared of treason.
works.significance: The Railway Children is one of the best-loved children's novels in English and the classic book of the railway age; its picture of the English countryside, the station and the family in trouble has made it a national institution.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader.
works.context: The 1900s, the Edwardian railway, the suburban family in reduced circumstances, and the political scandal behind the father's imprisonment. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1905 and first published in 1906 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Roberta (Bobbie); Peter; Phyllis; Mother; Father; Perks the porter; the Old Gentleman; Dr Forrest; Jim
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. Nesbit. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Rainbow
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1915
works.description: Three generations of the Brangwen family: the great English novel of marriage, the land and the growth of the self. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by D. H. Lawrence; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tom Brangwen, a Derbyshire farmer, marries Lydia Lensky, a Polish widow; their niece Anna marries Will Brangwen; and their daughter Ursula grows up, falls in love with the soldier Anton Skrebensky, refuses marriage, and at the end looks at a rainbow over the industrial Midlands and sees the possibility of a new life. The novel traces the family's passage from the agricultural world to the modern one.
works.significance: The Rainbow is Lawrence's greatest novel and one of the finest English novels of the century: it made the family chronicle a vehicle for a philosophy of the self, its prose is the most rhythmically alive in English fiction, and its portrait of a woman's growth into independence is one of the great achievements of the period. Its suppression as obscene in 1915 is one of the century's most notorious acts of censorship.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the loose, repetitive, urgent sentence driven by the rhythm of feeling and breath.
works.context: The Nottinghamshire–Derbyshire border and the industrialisation of the Midlands from the 1840s to the 1900s; the new education of women, the Boer War, and the crisis of belief. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Tom Brangwen; Lydia Lensky; Anna Brangwen; Will Brangwen; Ursula Brangwen; Anton Skrebensky
works.structure: Three-part generational chronicle across some sixty years, with a lyric and symbolic structure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Herbert Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Rambler
altTitles: The Rambler, by Samuel Johnson, Late of Pembroke College in Oxford (series title)
works.form: periodical moral essay, with embedded tales, allegory and criticism
works.description: The twice-weekly periodical of moral essays that Johnson wrote almost single-handedly between 1750 and 1752, in the tradition of the Tatler and the Spectator but with a severer, more introspective and more explicitly Christian purpose. Under the persona of a detached observer of life, Johnson examined marriage, friendship, learning, sorrow, death, self-deceit and the conduct of the passions. Its 208 numbers, many reprinted in book form in the author's lifetime, made him the most influential moral writer of his generation.
works.plot: Each number treats one moral or psychological question, usually opening with a general proposition and proceeding through examples, cases of life and a closing application. Recurring arguments include the danger of self-flattery, the miseries of domestic life, the obligations of patience and resignation, the vanity of worldly success, and the necessity of examining one's own conduct; a small body of narrative and allegorical papers, and some tales and oriental fictions, carry the lessons in story. The persona of the Rambler - an unattached spectator travelling and observing - allows a tone of melancholy detachment that is quite unlike Addison's sociability.
works.significance: The Rambler redefined the periodical essay from a instrument of politeness into an instrument of moral and religious self-examination, and its sales and long book-life established the essay serial as a vehicle of serious thought. Johnson's style here became a byword and a target for the whole century, and several numbers anticipate the arguments of Rasselas and the later criticism.
works.meter: Prose; long balanced periods of Latinate syntax, sententious parallelism and repeated emphasis, forming the most deliberate and most imitated example of Johnson's 'pump' style.
works.context: Launched in the generation after the great Spectator and Tatler papers, during the rapid expansion of provincial and suburban reading and of the periodical market. Johnson wrote most of the numbers himself and at great speed, with small documented help from friends, and the twice-weekly half-sheet format kept him on a permanent deadline.
works.characters: The Rambler; the correspondents and cited examples; occasional narrative personae (the prudent husband, the unhappy pair, the hermit of the Oriental tales)
works.structure: A serial essay periodical of 208 twice-weekly numbers issued from January 1750 to March 1752 and collected in volumes during Johnson's lifetime; individual papers are self-contained, ordered loosely by subject, and framed by a running persona and by occasional letters from correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Substantially Johnson's own work; a small number of contributions associated with Elizabeth Johnson, Thomas Tyrwhitt and Mrs Hester Thrale are separately recorded in the Yale edition and are not claimed for particular numbers here.

themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation

works.title: The Rape of Lucrece
works.description: Shakespeare's second narrative poem, also dedicated to Southampton: the Roman matron Lucrece is raped by Tarquin, the king's son, who steals into her chamber at Collatium; her night-long debate with grief ends in her public accusation and suicide before husband, father, and the Roman lords, whose vengeance expels the Tarquins and founds the republic.
works.plot: Tarquin, inflamed by Collatine's praise of his wife, rides to Collatium, is welcomed, and violates Lucrece in her bed; her apostrophes to Night, Opportunity, and Time occupy the central lament; at dawn she summons her kin, names her ravisher, and stabs herself; Brutus casts off his feigned simplicity and leads Rome to revolt.
works.significance: The deepest of the Elizabethan complaint poems — a study of trauma, rhetoric, and political consequence that anticipates the great tragedies.
works.meter: Rhyme royal (ababbcc), in a graver, more deliberative music than Venus and Adonis.
works.context: Printed by Richard Field in 1594; its matter — the violation that founds a state — draws on Ovid's Fasti and Livy, and its political ending (the expulsion of tyrants) spoke to the succession anxieties of the 1590s.
works.characters: Lucrece; Tarquin; Collatine; Lucretius; Brutus; the Nurse
works.structure: A three-movement structure — Tarquin's inward debate before the deed, Lucrece's grief after it, and the public consequence — composed as a series of rhetorical set pieces in the complaint tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: The Rape of the Lock
altTitles: The Rape of the Lock: A Heroic Poem
works.description: Pope's mock-heroic poem on the theft of a lock of a young woman's hair, which deploys epic machinery, invocations and catalogue in the service of a card-table, a dressing-room and a scissors, and turns a family quarrel into an analysis of the economy of female beauty and reputation.
works.plot: Belinda sleeps while Ariel, her guardian sylph, warns her of an impending mischance; at Hampton the Baron, aided by a love-lorn gnome, cuts the lock amid a catalogue of her treasures; the resulting breach of the two families is fought as a battle of wits and tongues, and the lock itself is lost in the air and enshrined among the constellations.
works.significance: It created the mock-epic as a fully serious form in English and remains the period's most exact analysis of a society in which value attaches to appearance; it set the pattern imitated by the century's other lowering of the sublime.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, with the sustained mock-epic simile, the invocation and the epic enumeration adjusted to the scale of a trinket.
works.context: Written to laugh down the quarrel between two Roman Catholic families over the cutting of a lock, and published in the years when the tea-table, the assembly and the luxury pamphlets were making female fashion a subject of moral argument; the poem's burlesque of machinery also answers the vogue for the rosea-crossa occult philosophy.
works.characters: Belinda; the Baron; Ariel; Umbriel; Thalestris; the sylphs and gnomes; the man of art
works.structure: An enlarged epic argument in cantos, with invocation, machinery, catalogue, descent to the underworld of melancholy and a metamorphic conclusion; the first version is shorter and lacks the Rosicrucian machinery.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Rationale of Reward
works.form: treatise of legislation and political economy; analytical rationale of institutions
works.description: The complement to the writer's penal theory, and the first systematic attempt to make a science of the rewards a legislator holds out rather than the punishments he inflicts. It was issued in English from a French editor's recension of the manuscripts, and it examines emolument, bounty, pension, prize, patent, honour, and salary as instruments measured by the happiness they purchase.
works.plot: The rationale begins by classifying the masses of reward, the pecuniary and the honorary, the subsistence and the emolument, the prime and the collateral, and by stating the general rule that the quantity of reward is to be judged by the quantity of service it obtains at the least cost to the public. It then examines the modes of holding out encouragement: competition and contract, which it prefers as the cheapest instruments, against monopoly, premium, and bounty, which it exposes as purchase of the same service at a doubled price and as the nursery of sinister interest. The application to official station is the sharpest part of the book: salaries are to be adequate, transparent, and proportional, pensions are to be the reward of extraordinary service and not the patronage of the court, and hereditary honour is tried by its utility and found wanting. The closing discussion treats the reward of talent in literature and in the arts, the patent law as an encouragement of invention, and the moral sanctions, good-reputation and the sympathies, as a currency the legislator must employ but must not corrupt.
works.significance: It is the classical utilitarian treatise on incentives, and one of the earliest attempts to analyse the whole system of public rewards as an economic instrument, a programme that anticipates the later economics of incentives and the administrative argument for salaried, accountable office. Its attack on monopoly, bounty, and hereditary honour supplied the reforming generation with some of its standard arguments, and its nomenclature entered the vocabulary of the science of legislation.
works.meter: Analytic, taxonomic, unsparing prose: subdivision after subdivision, the coined nomenclature, the interrogating aside, and an relentless reduction of reverence to account.
works.context: Published in the years of the debates on official economy, placemen and pensions, and the reform of the civil list, and after the penal code discussion of the preceding decade, to which it stands as the other half of one theory of sanctions. The English issue followed a French recension of the author's manuscripts, and it reached the reforming public just as the review journals were making utilitarian doctrine a party question.
works.structure: A treatise in chapters of classification and application, running from the definition and division of rewards through the several institutions of emolument to the honorary and moral sanctions, in the analytic order of the author's manuscripts.
works.attributionNotes: The substance is securely the author's, but the English text is at second hand, made from the manuscripts through a French editor's arrangement, so that the order and the phrasing of the printed book belong partly to the editor's recension rather than to the author's own final shaping.
