works.title: The Razor's Edge
works.description: Maugham's postwar novel of the spiritual quest: Larry Darrell, America and the search for meaning. It is a prose fiction work of 1944 by W. Somerset Maugham; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Larry Darrell, an American airman traumatised by the First World War, refuses a conventional career and marriage, travels to Paris and India in search of enlightenment, while the narrator follows the fates of the woman who loved him and the friends of their Chicago youth.
works.significance: The Razor's Edge is Maugham's postwar novel of the spiritual quest and his most widely read late work: its portrait of Larry Darrell's search for meaning made the modern novel of the spiritual journey and it remains the century's most popular treatment of the turn to the East.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrator who listens rather than judges.
works.context: Chicago, Paris and India between the wars, and the spiritual ferment of the 1930s and 1940s. The record dates the work as composed between 1943 and 1944 and first published in 1944 and it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Larry Darrell; Isabel Bradley; Elliott Templeton; Gray Maturin; Sophie Macdonald; Suzanne Rouvier
works.structure: A first-person narrative in seven sections, from Chicago to Paris to India. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Somerset Maugham. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Ready and Easy Way to Establish a Free Commonwealth
works.description: Milton's last political tract, published in two editions in the desperate weeks before the Restoration, proposing a perpetual senate and constitutional safeguards to preserve a free republic and avert the return of monarchy, in a tone of prophetic warning and undaunted republican faith.
works.plot: Milton argues for a self-perpetuating ruling council (with local government and a 'grand council'), warns of the dangers and moral degradation of restoring the Stuarts, and urges his countrymen not to throw away the fruits of the Revolution.
works.significance: Milton's final and most poignant republican statement, a constitutional proposal and a testament of unyielding commitment to liberty in the face of imminent defeat.
works.meter: Passionate, prophetic, argumentative prose of a man writing against certain defeat.
works.context: Written in early 1660 as General Monck moved to restore the monarchy; the second edition appeared only weeks before Charles II's return, when publication was an act of considerable personal danger.
works.structure: A political pamphlet in two editions (February and April 1660), combining constitutional proposal with urgent exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name at great personal risk.

works.title: The Reapers
works.description: The first Abbey play of the Waterford playwright. It is a dramatic work of 1930 by Teresa Deevy; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement.
works.plot: The Reapers, Deevy's first produced play, sets the rural household of the Waterford country against the return of the son and the marriage question, in the Abbey dialogue of the peasant play with the woman's confinement already at its centre.
works.significance: The Reapers opened Deevy's Abbey career - the first of the plays that made her the foremost woman dramatist of the Irish stage between the revival and the war.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the Abbey dialogue of the rural Ireland with the woman's confinement at its centre.
works.context: The Abbey Theatre, Dublin, 1930. works.title: The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition
altTitles: Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition
works.form: Pamphlet (issued at the World's Columbian Exposition)
works.description: Published in Chicago in 1893, with Frederick Douglass, Irvine Garland Penn and Ferdinand L. Barnett, and distributed at the World's Columbian Exposition: the pamphlet answer to the exclusion of black Americans from the Fair.
works.plot: The pamphlet sets out the reason for the black boycott of the Fair's official representation - that no African American was admitted to the organising bodies and that the Southern exhibit glorified the slave system - and then documents the condition of black Americans: the convict-lease system, the disenfranchisement, the denial of schooling and the statistics of lynching, with Douglass's preface on the injustice of the Fair.
works.significance: The Reason Why is the central document of the black protest against the World's Columbian Exposition and one of the most widely distributed American pamphlets of the 1890s: it carried Wells's anti-lynching statistics to an international audience and made the Fair itself a stage for the argument about American citizenship.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass.
works.context: 1893: the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, the rise of Jim Crow in the Southern legislatures, and the black boycott campaign led by Wells and Douglass. The record dates the work as composed in 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ida Bell Wells-Barnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Reasonableness of Christianity, as Delivered in the Scriptures
works.description: Locke's anonymously published theological treatise, which argues that the single necessary article of Christian faith is the belief that Jesus is the Messiah, and that reason and Scripture are in harmony.
works.plot: Locke examines the Gospels and Epistles to show that the essential doctrine of Christianity is the messiahship of Jesus, and that this belief is both scripturally grounded and reasonable.
works.significance: A founding text of English rational religion and latitudinarian theology; its influence on the eighteenth-century debate on revelation and reason was profound, and it prepared the way for Deism and for Locke's own reputation as a rational Christian.
works.meter: Plain argumentative prose.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1695, during the Trinitarian controversy, and attacked by John Edwards in Socinianism Unmask'd; Locke replied in Vindication of the Reasonableness of Christianity (1695).
works.structure: A continuous argument following the narrative of the Gospels.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship was widely suspected and acknowledged in the second edition.

works.title: The Rebel of the Family
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1880
works.description: Published in 1880 and Linton's most searching novel of the woman question: a young woman who rebels against her family and finds that freedom has its own price. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Eliza Lynn Linton; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Perdita Winstanley, the plain, bookish 'rebel' among the beautiful daughters of an impoverished and snobbish widow, takes a clerkship in the Post Office Savings Bank, joins a women's rights society led by the masterful Bell Blount, and falls in love with the chemist Leslie Crawford, who proves to be bound to an absent, faithless wife; banished from home after Bell denounces her, she waits until the wife's death frees him, and Leslie's payment of the Winstanleys' debts reconciles her family to the match.
works.significance: The Rebel of the Family is the most interesting of Linton's novels and a key text of the 1880s debate on the New Woman: it takes the feminist case seriously and then tests it against experience, and it is far more ambivalent than the essays for which Linton was notorious.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical periodical essay with a strong persona.
works.context: 1880: the London of the women's colleges and the new professional openings, the feminist debates in the periodical press, and Linton's own complicated position between feminism and anti-feminism. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Perdita Winstanley; Mrs Winstanley; Thomasina and Eva Winstanley; Bell Blount; Connie, her 'little wife'; Leslie Crawford; Mrs Crawford; Florence Crawford; M. Bois-Duval
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Rebels; or, Boston before the Revolution
works.form: Historical novel and romance of the revolutionary generation: domestic plot set against documented popular violence, with local topography, crowd scenes and a forward glance at national independence.
works.description: A historical novel of prerevolutionary Boston, the first published book by a New England woman who was only in her twenties, and an early instance of the American historical tale written before the British model had been fully absorbed. It treats the years of the Stamp Act and the tarring-and-feathering of a hated tax officer as popular insurrection seen from the inside, and it frames that public violence in the domestic trials of two sisters who fall in love with men on the opposing political side. Its sympathy with the crowd is qualified by misgiving about the crowd's temper.
works.plot: The story is set in Boston in the resistance to the tax measures, and opens on a household whose father is a loyalist official while the daughters are drawn into the patriotic cause. The mob that terrorises the obnoxious officer, burns his effigy and forces his resignation is rendered with a mixture of excitement and alarm, and the novel's domestic plot turns on the danger that this public turmoil brings to the sisters' loves and reputations. One sister's attachment to a young man of the popular party and the other's to an officer of the crown divide the family, and scenes of tar-and-feather justice interrupt the courtship design. The conclusion reaches toward the Declaration of Independence, reading the riots of the 1760s as the schooling of a nation, while leaving the writer's ambivalence about mob rule unresolved.
works.significance: It is a significant early American historical novel and the first work of one of the century's most consequential reform writers, and its treatment of revolutionary mob action as both legitimate and frightening makes it a key text for the literature of the early republic's political memory. It also marks the opening of a career in which education, abolition and Native American rights were argued through fiction and periodical form.
works.meter: Prose narrative in the familiar early-American style; colloquial and expository, with occasional interpolated song and period letter.
works.context: Written and published in the middle of the 1820s, when American fiction was newly confident and when the Revolution had become usable as romantic material, and before the historical romance of the British novelist had set the terms for American imitation. Its author was already editing a juvenile periodical in Boston and was absorbed in the question of how a republic should remember its own founding disorder.
works.characters: The two patriot sisters; their loyalist father; the obnoxious tax officer who is tarred and feathered; the young lover of the popular party; the British officer beloved by the other sister; the Boston mob
works.structure: Linear historical novel in three volumes with alternating domestic and public action; chapters of crowd violence and political meeting interleave with the sisters' courtship plot, and the frame looks forward to independence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is established and uncontested; the novel was published at the very start of its author's career, before she was known to the wider public, and was reissued in later editions under her own name.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Warfare and battle

works.title: The Recruiting Officer
works.description: Farquhar's comedy of military recruiting in the provincial town of Shrewsbury, drawn from his own experience as a recruiting officer in Ireland during the War of the Spanish Succession.

works.title: The Red Badge of Courage
altTitles: The Red Badge of Courage: An Episode of the American Civil War
works.form: Novel; war narrative of the common soldier
works.description: Published in 1895 and the greatest American novel of the Civil War: the first battle of a young soldier who fears he will run away. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Stephen Crane; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under War Narrative of the Common Soldier; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Henry Fleming, a young Union volunteer, goes into his first battle terrified that he will prove a coward; he runs, wanders behind the lines among the wounded, is struck on the head by a fleeing soldier, and returns to his regiment in time for the next assault, where he fights with a reckless courage and believes he has become a man.
works.significance: The Red Badge of Courage changed the literature of war: its impressionist rendering of battle from inside a single soldier's consciousness, its irony about courage and its refusal of the heroic made it the first modern war novel, and it has remained the essential American book about the Civil War.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the common soldier: the plain first-person account, the exact vocabulary of the trench, the ration, the march and the casualty, and the understatement that carries the horror. The author's characteristic manner is impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation.
works.context: 1895: the Civil War thirty years on, the American cult of the soldier, the new mass-circulation magazines, and the realism of Howells and Garland. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under war narrative of the common soldier; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Henry Fleming; Wilson; Jim Conklin; the tattered soldier; the lieutenant; the colonel
works.structure: A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stephen Townley Crane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Regiment of Princes
works.form: mirror for princes in rhyme royal
works.description: Thomas Hoccleve's mirror for princes of 5,463 lines in rhyme royal, addressed to the future Henry V and completed in 1411: an adaptation of the pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum Secretorum, Egidius Romanus's De Regimine Principum, and Jacobus de Cessolis's chess moralities, framed by the poet's famous dialogue with a beggar on poverty, patronage, and the life of the London clerk. The classic Lancastrian poem of good governance.
works.plot: The sleepless poet, walking the fields of Westminster, meets an old beggar who catechizes him on the vanity of court service and the miseries of poverty; the dialogue then opens into the treatise proper — justice, mercy, patience, chastity, liberality, and the duties of the prince — closing with the counsel to the young Henry of Monmouth, prince of Wales.
works.significance: The principal English mirror-for-princes of the fifteenth century and a landmark of autobiographical poetry; its beggar dialogue inaugurates the tradition of the poor poet's complaint.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of plain correctness, in Hoccleve's characteristic conversational register.
works.context: Completed in 1411 by the Privy Seal clerk Hoccleve for the prince of Wales, on the eve of Agincourt; its portrait of the poor clerk's London is the most vivid account of bureaucratic life in the period; preserved in forty-three manuscripts.
works.characters: Hoccleve; the Beggar; Henry, Prince of Wales (addressee)
works.structure: A mirror-for-princes in the frame of the poet's own autobiographical dialogue, the first English poem to make the writer's economic anxieties its prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; he names himself throughout.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Marriage and women's conduct
movements: Fifteenth-Century Chaucerians

works.description: Marvell's witty prose satire in two parts (1672–73) answering the intolerant Samuel Parker, Bishop of Oxford's chaplain; defending toleration and mocking Parker's bombast and persecution with sustained, devastating irony, it is a masterpiece of Restoration prose polemic.

works.meter: Ironic, energetic prose of sustained satirical wit, mixing learned argument with humour and burlesque.
works.context: Written during the Restoration persecution of dissenters and the campaign for comprehension and indulgence; it made Marvell famous as a champion of toleration.
works.characters: Andrew Marvell (the author); Samuel Parker; the 'Bayes' figure
works.structure: A two-part prose satire structured as a mock-serious, ironic rebuttal of Parker's argument.

works.title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy
works.description: Reginald Pecock's great vernacular apologia (c. 1449–55), answering the Lollards' eleven 'blamings' of the clergy — against images, pilgrimages, clerical endowments, the pope, and the religious orders — not by authority but by the 'doom of reason'. The most original work of English theology between Wyclif and the Reformation, and the cause of its author's own condemnation.
works.plot: Pecock restates the Lollard objections with scrupulous fairness and answers each by rational argument: faith is grounded in reason, images and pilgrimages serve the memory and the affections, clerical endowment is lawful when used rightly, and the church's hierarchy is the ordinance of God — while insisting, to his ruin, that the clergy must be judged by scripture and reason rather than by bare authority.
works.significance: The supreme monument of fifteenth-century English rational theology and a tragic witness to the church's fear of its own vernacular defenders.
works.meter: Plain English of argument, with an invented philosophical vocabulary ('unbileve', 'moral philosophi').
works.context: Composed c. 1449–55 by the bishop of Chichester, in the controversy over vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions; Pecock's reliance on reason over authority led to his trial (1457), his abjuration at Paul's Cross, and the burning of his books.
works.characters: Pecock (as reasoner); the Lollard interlocutors (implied)
works.structure: Five parts answering the successive Lollard conclusions, in the dialectical form of objection and response.
works.attributionNotes: Pecock's authorship secure.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Wisdom and learning

works.description: Published in 1878 and the most tragic of the early Wessex novels: the story of Eustacia Vye, the passionate and thwarted woman of Egdon Heath, and of her marriage to Clym Yeobright, the native who returns from Paris to teach.

works.title: The Revenge
works.description: Young's first tragedy, a blank-verse drama of jealous error in a Spanish and Moorish setting, in which a husband's belief in his wife's guilt destroys the innocent and himself; the play that introduced the century's high pathos of conjugal jealousy.
works.plot: A Moorish and court intrigue, an intercepted letter and a treacherous third party work upon a husband's jealousy until the accused wife's constancy is proved only by her death, and revenge falls instead upon the author of the slander.
works.significance: It is the earliest considerable English tragedy of suspicion and of injured female constancy, and it carried the pathetic drama of The Fair Penitent into the domestic and conjugal register the century preferred.
works.meter: Blank verse of passionate declamation, with the broken apostrophe, the long simile and the sententious close.
works.context: Brought out on the London stage at the opening of the decade, in the season when the reformed regular tragedy of Rowe and the new musical entertainment competed for the same house; Young had attached himself to the great families of the governing interest, and the play's success began his long dependence on patronage.
works.characters: the jealous husband; the accused and faithful wife; the artificer of the slander; the Moors and courtiers about them
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue with the surprise of the false evidence and the discovery scene, closing on the death of the innocent and the ruin of the jealous.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Revenger's Tragedy
works.description: The great anonymous (formerly Tourneur, now generally Middleton) revenge tragedy: Vindice, whose beloved was poisoned by the old Duke for resisting him, revenges her by the poisoned skull trick — the Duke kissing the painted, poisoned lips of the skull he thinks a country girl — and then by masquerading through the corrupt court to the final masque of revengers, in which the Duke's son and his faction die and Vindice himself, boasting, is condemned by his own confession.
works.plot: Vindice and his brother Hippolito enter the Duke's service to destroy him; the skull of Gloriana, dressed and poisoned, kills the Duke in the 'bony lady' scene; the succession struggle of Lussurioso, Ambitioso, Supervacuo, and Spurio fills the middle acts; the final masque — revengers killing revengers — clears the stage; and Vindice's boast, 'we are ourselves our own revenge', delivers him and his brother to execution.
works.significance: The most extreme and most brilliant of the Jacobean revenge plays — a tragedy of skulls, lust, and self-consuming justice.
works.meter: A verse of savage brilliance — the openings ('Duke, royal lecher!') and the skull scene are its peaks — with the play's memento mori running through every act.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men in 1606 and printed in 1607 without an author's name; attributed to Tourneur from 1656 until the twentieth century's stylistic case transferred it to Middleton.
works.characters: Vindice; Hippolito; the Duke; Lussurioso; Ambitioso; Supervacuo; Spurio; the Duchess; Gratiana; Castiza; Antonio; Piero; the skull of Gloriana
works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy of accelerating symmetries, built on the skull device, the play-within-the-play of the masque, and the choric commentary of Vindice's soliloquies.
works.attributionNotes: Printed anonymously; long attributed to Cyril Tourneur, now generally assigned to Thomas Middleton on stylistic evidence; the question remains open in some scholarship.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Courtly service and courtly danger
Revenge and justice

works.title: The Revolt of Islam
altTitles: Laon and Cythna; or, The Revolt of Islam
works.form: Romantic verse romance and political vision poem in the Spenserian stanza; the revolutionary tale of the school of the earlier long poems, with the hymn and the choral ode inserted.
works.description: The largest of the author's long poems, a revolutionary romance in Spenserian stanzas set in a southern caliphate whose people rise against their priests and kings. Two lovers, a man and a woman of the ruling house, preach reason and liberty from a car of the mind, survive the stakes and the flood, and are destroyed at the moment of the city's deliverance by the armed intervention of a holy confederacy. It appeared first under one title with an argument for free love and was withdrawn and reissued, with the offences expurgated, as the present poem.
works.plot: The poem opens with a dream on a moonlit sea, a vessel, a victory and the death of the tyrant, and passes to the tale of the two lovers, who were taught by a hermit the creed of reason and who, on emerging from a cave of learning, preach a new faith of love and liberty to the multitude. The caliph's priests burn the woman in the market-place and the man is bound to the same pile, but the two are saved by a vision of the world's future; the city rises, the throne of the despot is burned and a free council meets. The lovers at last die of wounds received in the counter-attack of the confederate kings, and the poet awakes on the sea with the vision unfinished. The argument is that the revolution of the mind is stronger than the stake, but that its triumph is always bought with the death of its teachers.
works.significance: It is the most ambitious attempt of the period to fuse a revolutionary argument with the machinery of romance, and its history of withdrawal and expurgation is the best document of the pressure of the blasphemy and libel laws on long verse. Its treatment of the failure of a revolution from within, of the martyrdom of teachers and of the hope that survives it, shaped the later political odes and the drama of the unbinding.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas of nine eleven-syllable lines, ababbcbcc, sustained over a very great length with an increasing freedom of the caesura; the inserted chants pass to shorter lyric measures.
works.context: Written chiefly between the spring and the autumn of 1817, in the years of the continental settlement, of the suspension of the habeas corpus and of the persecutions following the northern march of the reformers, and of the poet's own removal to the seaside and then to London. It was issued late in 1817 over its first title, withdrawn by the publishers within a few weeks on account of its treatment of religion and of sibling love, and reissued in January 1818 with nearly two hundred lines cancelled or altered. Its sales were negligible, and the poet's response was to turn to the shorter and denser forms of the following years.
works.characters: the two lovers of the title, a prince and a maid of the caliph's blood; the hermit teacher of the cave; the priests and the caliph of the city; the Demogorgon of the cavern of human thought; the wingless thing of the vision
works.structure: A dream frame on the ocean, an argument in prose prefaced to the original issue, and twenty-nine cantos of continuous narrative, with inserted hymns, chants of the earth and spirit and a long philosophical speech on the past and future of the world.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the two states of the text, that of 1817 and that of 1818, are both authorial, and the cancelled passages were recovered from the proof sheets and manuscript by modern editors.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: The Rhyming Poem
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A unique experiment in Old English prosody: an elegiac meditation on the fall of a once-powerful lord, written in rhyming couplets with end-rhyme sustained line after line, a technique otherwise foreign to alliterative verse. The speaker remembers his former glory as a generous ruler surrounded by retainers, and contrasts it with his present misery and loss.
works.plot: The speaker recalls his past prosperity as a lord who distributed treasure and ruled a loyal comitatus, then laments the reversal of fortune that has stripped him of wealth, retainers, and honour. The poem moves from remembered joy to the recognition that all earthly glory decays, and closes with reflection on the grave and the soul's fate.
works.significance: The earliest extended rhyming poem in English; evidence that Old English poets could adapt the alliterative line to rhyme, anticipating the rhyming experiments of later medieval English verse.
works.meter: Rhymed couplets with pervasive end-rhyme and internal rhyme over an alliterative base; the poet sustains rhyme through some 87 lines, a virtuoso performance in a language whose native metre is alliterative.
works.context: Composed in the later Old English period, when the heroic conventions of the hall and the comitatus were already literary memory rather than living institutions; the poem shares the vocabulary of exile and transience with The Wanderer and The Seafarer.
works.structure: A single first-person meditation organized around the contrast between past splendour and present ruin, framed by ubi sunt reflection; the paired rhymes and internal rhymes bind short clauses into couplets.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No attribution has ever been proposed.
themes: Exile and homelessness
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
Wyrd (fate) and providence
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Rhythm of Life and Other Essays
altTitles: Rhythm of Life and Other Essays
works.description: Published in 1893 and Meynell's first collection of essays: short meditations on time, childhood, poverty, art and the rhythm of the spiritual life. It is a prose work of 1893 by Alice Meynell; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: The essays take a small subject — a clock, a child's sleep, a beggar at the door, the colour of the sky — and turn it into a meditation on time and eternity; 'The Rhythm of Life' itself argues that the spiritual life has a tempo that the modern world destroys.
works.significance: The Rhythm of Life is one of the finest collections of English essays of the century and established Meynell as the successor of Lamb and Hazlitt in the meditative essay; her prose was admired by Ruskin, Meredith and Wilde.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short lyric metres with a delicate rhythmic suspense.
works.context: The 1890s, the English essay tradition, the Catholic revival, and the aesthetic appreciation of the ordinary. The record dates the work as composed in 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alice Christiana Gertrude Meynell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman

works.title: The Riddle of the Sands
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1903
works.description: The first modern spy novel: two yachtsmen discover a German invasion plan. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by Erskine Childers; it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Memoir and Autobiographical Prose and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Carruthers, a Foreign Office clerk, joins his friend Davies on a yachting holiday in the Frisian Islands and discovers a German plan to invade England; the two amateur spies uncover the secret of the sands and warn the Admiralty.
works.significance: The Riddle of the Sands was the first modern spy novel and the founding text of the genre: its exact seamanship, its German invasion plot and its documentary detail created the espionage novel and made the threat of war the subject of popular fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the yachting narrative and the exact seamanship.
works.context: The Frisian Islands and the German coast in 1902. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; memoir and autobiographical prose.
works.characters: Carruthers; Arthur Davies; Dollmann; the German fleet; the Memmert
works.structure: A first-person narrative of yachting and discovery in the Frisian Islands. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Erskine Childers. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Rights of the Christian Church Asserted
altTitles: The Rights of the Christian Church: with a Civil and Historical Account of the Tithes and Revenue of Priests
works.description: Tindal's Erastian controversy treatise, arguing from scriptural and historical grounds that the primitive church required no endowments, no clergy as a separate order, and no coercion, and that the modern established priesthood had repealed the very religion it professed. It turned the deist critique outward onto the political economy of the church.
works.plot: Tindal first proves from Scripture that the apostles intended no permanent clerical order with temporal power, and that the law of Moses, whose ceremonial was temporary, was the model of a church supported by voluntary maintenance. He then traces the rise of tithes, patronage, and ecclesiastical jurisdiction to human constitutions and imperial policy, showing the clergy's claim of divine right to be historically fraudulent. Argument from the nature of spiritual advantage follows: religion that requires wealth and coercion has repealed its own principles. The conclusion demands a return to the primitive pattern and threatens the temporal basis of the established church.
works.significance: It moved the deist controversy from epistemology to institutional history, became the standard handbook of Erastian and anticlerical argument for decades, and shaped Hume's later church histories.
works.meter: Dense citation-heavy prose, patristic and canon-law authorities stacked in long trains, with a plain republican bluntness of tone.
works.context: Published in the last years of Queen Anne's reign amid the Sacheverell frenzy and high-church assaults on toleration, it went through several rapid editions, was answered by dozens of divines, and was ordered burnt by the Commons in 1715.
works.structure: A controversial treatise in two long parts of cumulative proof: scriptural demonstration, then historical confutation of the clergy's title, with an appendix of authorities.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
altTitles: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
works.form: Lyrical ballad and metrical romance in verse, written in the revived manner of the antique minstrel ballad, with deliberate archaisms, and transformed into a vision of guilt, curse, repentance and the sacredness of created things.
works.description: The long supernatural ballad that opens the anonymous 1798 volume and soon became the most discussed poem of the English Romantic period. A wedding-guest on his way to the feast is stopped by an old seafarer who tells how his ship drove south to the equator and the icy seas, how an albatross that had followed them through the fog was shot with a cross-bow, and how the guilt of that gratuitous act brought death on all hands but his own. The poem is a tale of penance as much as of adventure: the Mariner is condemned to live, to know what he has done, and to tell the story again to each stranger who seems to choose him for his listener.
works.plot: The Mariner's ship is becalmed in a hot and rotting sea after the killing of the bird, and his crew, who first approved the deed and then lament it, are visited by a skeleton hull carrying two passengers, Death and Life-in-Death, who play a game for the ship's company. Two hundred men drop one after another and cannot bury their dead, while the Mariner alone survives, unable to pray and with the dead bird hung about his neck in place of the cross; the charm breaks only when, without meaning to, he blesses the water-snakes that coast the ship, and the albatross falls from his neck. He is then guided homewards by a spirit, and the tale of the killing and of the curse is told again, its moral delivered in the lines that say that he who loves all things that God made and made best prays best. The outer scene closes with the wedding-guest, from whom the Mariner departs, left like a stunned man and, in the poet's phrase, a sadder and a wiser man; the story has taught him to distrust his own joy and to value the created world.
works.significance: The poem that established the Romantic supernatural ballad and made the outcast confessing narrator a permanent figure of modern verse; it supplied the period's most quoted image of unforgiven guilt and of the love owed to all created things. Its critical history, from the reviews of 1798 to the gloss of 1817 and to the poet's own later account of the volume's plan, is a classic case study of Romantic reception.
works.meter: Chiefly the ballad stanza of alternating four-beat and three-beat lines with a leading rhyme, varied by internal rhyme, alliteration, repetition of a single keyword and occasional shorter stanzas, giving an insistent song-like movement; archaic spelling and vocabulary were introduced to strengthen the impression of an old recovered tale.
works.context: Composed principally in the spring and summer of 1798 during the western collaboration, and suggested in part by a shared reading of accounts of southern voyages; its theology of sin, curse and enforced penance belongs to the poem's moral imagination rather than to any single source. Its first readers were divided between admiration for its power and complaints that its diction and machinery were absurd.
works.characters: The Ancient Mariner; the Wedding-Guest; the Pilot and the Pilot's boy; the Hermit; Death and Life-in-Death; the albatross; the dead ship's company
works.structure: A framed oral narrative: an outer scene at the wedding-gate, an inner first-person confession divided into seven parts, and, when the poem was reprinted in 1817, an added marginal gloss in the manner of an old ballad or a commonplace book, which annotates and at times ironically moralises the tale. The frame returns in the closing stanza.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was contributed by the collaborator who later wrote the volume's critical history, was given a head of its own in the second edition, and was placed in a separate section of his collected poems in 1817.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Creation and cosmology
Penance, confession, and sin
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
Sea voyage and seafaring
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: The Ring and the Book
works.form: Epic-length narrative poem in twelve books, in blank verse
works.description: Published in four volumes in 1868-69 and the longest and most ambitious of Browning's poems: the story of a Roman murder trial of 1698, retold twelve times by the different people involved, until the reader has to weigh the versions.
works.plot: Count Guido Franceschini, a poor nobleman of Arezzo, marries Pompilia, the supposed daughter of the Roman couple Pietro and Violante Comparini, and takes her to Arezzo, where she is mistreated and flees towards Rome with the priest Giuseppe Caponsacchi; Guido pursues and murders her and her parents, and is tried and executed. The twelve books give the story in the voices of half Rome, the other half Rome, the tertiary, the murderer, the murdered wife, the young priest, the Pope, and finally the poet's own book.
works.significance: The Ring and the Book is the Victorian age's one true epic and the fullest treatment in English of truth as a product of multiple perspectives; its structure anticipates the modernist impersonal narrative (Eliot, Pound, Joyce) and its dramatic psychology is unmatched in Victorian poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
works.context: The Old Yellow Book, a printed record of the 1698 trial that Browning bought in a Florence market in 1860, the Italian legal system of the seventeenth century, and the Victorian interest in casuistry and in the relativity of evidence.
works.characters: Count Guido Franceschini; Pompilia; Giuseppe Caponsacchi; Pietro and Violante Comparini; Pope Innocent XII; Dominus Hyacinthus de Archangelis; Johannes-Baptista Bottinius; Half-Rome; the Other Half-Rome; Tertium Quid
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.significance: The Ringer is Edgar Wallace's greatest thriller and one of the most famous crime novels of the century: its criminal hero, its pursuit and its twists made it a stage and film classic and the model for the modern thriller.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul
altTitles: The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul, in Two Parts
works.description: Doddridge's classic account of experimental religion in the soul, a series of discourses with letters and meditations, published in 1745 and the most used Protestant guide to conversion, self-examination, and growth in grace between Bunyan and the Victorian evangelicals. Its careful cadence of assurance made it a standard of moderate dissenting piety.
works.plot: The discourses trace the sinner's progress from awakening under the sense of divine justice, through conversion, justification, adoption, and sanctification, to the believer's combat with remaining corruption and the assurance of hope. Doddridge balances the enthusiast's heat and the formalist's cold, prescribing self-examination, the duties of the closet, and the improvement of reason joined to the affections. Interposed letters and meditations carry the same lesson into the hours of the day and the table of the Lord. The whole is a Protestant pilgrimage of the soul in sermon form, its aim, in his phrase, experimental and practical religion.
works.significance: It trained generations of evangelicals, dissenters, and Methodists in the phenomenology of grace, ran through countless editions and translations, and shaped the devotional literature of the English-speaking Protestant world.
works.meter: The balanced, affectionate sermon-cadence of the high dissenting style, periodic sentences of tenderness with psalm quotation and doxology.
works.context: Composed across the Northampton academy years, parts appearing from the later 1730s and the whole published at London in 1745, in the debate over enthusiasm and experimental religion opened by Whitefield and carried on by the moderates.
works.structure: A series of discourses on the stages of salvation in the soul, interspersed with letters, meditations, and prayers for daily use.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Melancholy and self-analysis

works.title: The Rise of David Levinsky
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1917
works.description: Published in 1917 and the greatest American immigrant novel: a Russian yeshiva student becomes a millionaire in the garment trade and finds that success is emptiness. It is a prose fiction work of 1917 by Abraham Cahan; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: David Levinsky arrives in New York in 1882 penniless, works in a sweatshop, studies at night, and rises through the cloak-and-suit trade to become a millionaire manufacturer; at the height of his success he looks back on the faith, the mother and the love he has lost, and finds that he would give it all to be a poor yeshiva student again.
works.significance: The Rise of David Levinsky is the greatest American immigrant novel and one of the central American novels of success: its analysis of the cost of Americanisation, its portrait of the garment trade and its plain, unhurried prose made it the model for the American ethnic novel, and it is the finest fictional record of Jewish immigrant life in America.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is documentary realism with a precise record of work and wages.
works.context: 1882-1917: the Russian pogroms, the Jewish immigration, the garment industry of New York, and the American ideology of the self-made man. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1917 and first published in 1917 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: David Levinsky; Dora; Matilda; Gitelson; Mrs Levinsky; Shiphrah; Meyer Nudelman
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Rise of Silas Lapham
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1885 and the central American novel of business: the story of a self-made paint manufacturer who loses his fortune, and of the moral choice that makes his ruin a rise. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by William Dean Howells; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Silas Lapham, a Vermont farmer's son turned paint magnate, moves to Boston and tries to marry his daughter into the Brahmin class; his speculation in stocks fails, he refuses a fraudulent offer to save himself at the expense of others, and the family returns to Vermont, where Lapham finds his true dignity.
works.significance: The Rise of Silas Lapham is the finest American novel of business and the central text of American realism: its portrait of the self-made man and its argument that moral failure can be worldly success made it the model for the American business novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is plain, unobtrusive narrative prose.
works.context: The 1870s-80s: the American paint and mineral trade, the Boston Brahmins, and the Gilded Age business cycle. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Silas Lapham; Persis Lapham; Irene Lapham; Penelope Lapham; Tom Corey; Bromfield Corey; Anna Corey; Bartley Hubbard; Milton K. Rogers
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Rising of the Moon
works.description: Lady Gregory's most famous one-act play: a policeman, a ballad singer and the choice of loyalty. It is a dramatic work of 1907 by Lady Gregory; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: On a quay in a west of Ireland town, a sergeant of the Royal Irish Constabulary is posted to watch for an escaped rebel; a ragged ballad singer sits down to talk with him, and by the end the sergeant has let the man go, knowing who he is.
works.significance: The Rising of the Moon is Lady Gregory's most famous play and the finest one-act play of the Irish revival: its stagecraft, its dialogue and its quiet treatment of loyalty and nation made it a permanent part of the repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close.
works.context: The west of Ireland at the turn of the century, the Land War's aftermath and the Irish revolutionary movement. The record dates the work as composed in 1906 and first published in 1907 and first performed in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: The Sergeant; the Ragged Man; two policemen
works.structure: A single scene on a quay, in one act. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Isabella Augusta Gregory. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.form: Novel (the rising tide against the big house, as M. J. Farrell)
works.description: The last Farrell novel of the 1930s: the rising tide against the house. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by Molly Keane; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Novel of Manners and Fashion.
works.plot: The Rising Tide sets the rising tide of the new Ireland against the big house and its class, in the satirical sentence of the insider turned elegist.
works.significance: The Rising Tide is the last of the Farrell novels of the 1930s and the elegy of the Ascendancy: its rising tide made the decay of the big house the subject of the comic novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of manners: the dialogue of the social world, the exact vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built on the breach or the observance of a convention. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical sentence of the insider.
works.context: Ireland in the later 1930s, and the decay of the Ascendancy. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1937 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; novel of manners and fashion.

works.title: The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great
works.description: Nathaniel Lee's wildly popular heroic tragedy on the death of Alexander, driven by the rivalry between his two wives, Roxana and Statira; it was the most performed play of the Restoration and a byword for bombast.
works.plot: Alexander returns to Babylon to find Roxana mad with jealousy of Statira; the conspiracy of Cassander, Perdiccas, and others breaks out, Alexander is poisoned, and Roxana kills Statira before being carried off in triumph.
works.significance: The most successful Restoration tragedy after All for Love and the standard example of the excesses of the heroic drama; its 'rival queens' structure influenced the eighteenth-century she-tragedy.
works.meter: Blank verse of extravagant rhetorical height, famously parodying the heroic style.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in March 1677 and published the same year; it held the stage for over a century and was parodied by Fielding and in The Rehearsal tradition.
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Roxana; Statira; Cassander; Perdiccas; Lysimachus; Hephaestion; Thessalus
works.structure: Five acts of high heroic tragedy with two rival women at the centre.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lee; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Rivals
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A comedy of Irish and London gallantry, of fathers' authority and of the mistakes of young lovers, its fame resting on its dialogue, its first act's declaration of war against sentiment on the stage and its creation of the century's most quoted blundering matron.
works.plot: Ferdinand Absolute, reported dead by a feigned letter, is loved in absence by his betrothed, while his father returns from Ireland to marry a young wife and to dispose of the lovers. Julia elopes by mistake with the wrong lover, Lydia Languish is courted by an assumed name, and the Irish captain Sir Lucius is challenged over a letter he does not understand. The several mistakes are cleared at the end, the fathers consent, and the double marriage is prepared.
works.significance: It restored the comedy of humour and intrigue to the London stage after the sentimental fashion and remains a standing repertory piece; its prefatory attack on sentiment on the stage is a document of the century's genre quarrel.
works.meter: Brisk prose dialogue of repartee and malapropism, with the sentimental and the high-flown styles deliberately deflated; the letters and messages read aloud are the comic set pieces.
works.context: First performed at Covent Garden in January 1775, in the season of the quarrel between sentimental and laughing comedy, and of the Irish comedy of the London stage; its author was a young playwright soon to be a theatre manager.
works.characters: Mrs. Malaprop; Sir Anthony Absolute; Captain Absolute; Faulkland; Julia; Lydia Languish; Sir Lucius O'Trigger; Fag and the servants
works.structure: Five-act comedy of erring letters and mistaken persons, with the famous prefacial ploy of the author answering his first-night critics; the plot turns on a chain of written and reported misunderstandings.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the success of the revivals following an uncertain first night.

works.title: The Road to Wigan Pier
works.description: Orwell's report on the industrial North: the coal mine, the dole, the tripe shop and the middle-class socialist. It is a prose work of 1937 by George Orwell; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The first half reports Orwell's investigations in Lancashire and Yorkshire in 1936: the lodgings, the coal face, the unemployment and the means test, the housing and the diet. The second half is a polemic against the English middle-class socialist, whose snobbery stands between the left and the working class.
works.significance: The Road to Wigan Pier is the finest English documentary book of the 1930s: its account of the coal face is one of the great passages of English reportage, and its second half is the period's sharpest critique of the left's own class prejudice.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The author's characteristic manner is the plain declarative English sentence with no ornament.
works.context: The Depression of the 1930s, the means test, the Special Areas, the Jarrow March, and the Left Book Club that commissioned the book. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; critical essay and the modern review.
works.characters: George Orwell, the narrator; Mr and Mrs Brooker, the tripe-shop lodging-house keepers; the miners of Wigan
works.structure: Two parts: a documentary report and a critical essay on socialism and class. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.

works.title: The Robber Bridegroom
works.description: Welty's fairy-tale novel of the Natchez Trace: the bandit, the planter's daughter and the Mississippi. It is a prose fiction work of 1942 by Eudora Welty; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Historical Novel and Romance.
works.plot: In the Mississippi of the 1790s Clement Musgrove, a planter of the Natchez Trace, sets out to find his kidnapped daughter Rosamund, and falls in with Jamie Lockhart, the bandit of the Trace and the robber bridegroom of the title; the novel runs as a fairy tale of disguise, theft and marriage along the Trace, ending with the birth of the child and the closing of the frontier road.
works.significance: The Robber Bridegroom is Welty's fairy-tale novel and one of the most original American novels of the war years: its bandit of the Natchez Trace, its disguises and its ballad logic made the Mississippi frontier into a story-book country and showed that the Southern Renaissance could write comedy and enchantment as well as tragedy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the comic monologue and the first-person eccentric voice.
works.context: The Natchez Trace and the Mississippi frontier in the 1790s, remembered from the 1940s. The record dates the work as composed between 1941 and 1942 and first published in 1942 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Jamie Lockhart; Rosamund Musgrove; Clement Musgrove; Mayor Holston; Little Harp; Salome
works.structure: A fairy-tale novel in chapters along the Natchez Trace. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.

works.title: The Roman Actor
works.description: Massinger's tragedy of the Emperor Domitian, his love for the virtuous Domitia, and the murder of the actor Paris, framed by an elaborate defence of the theatre's moral function.
works.plot: The actors are tried before the Senate on the charge of slandering the state; Paris defends the stage; Domitian, inflamed by desire for Domitia and by jealousy, kills Paris; the tyrant is finally assassinated by the Senate's agents.
works.significance: The most important early modern dramatic treatise on the function of the stage, embedded in a tragedy; it was revived by the King's Company after 1660 and was long Massinger's most admired play.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the inset plays.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1626 and published in 1629; the play's defence of the theatre responds to puritan attack.
works.characters: Domitian; Domitia; Paris; Lamia; Aretinus; Philargus; the Senators

works.title: The Romance of a Shop
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1888
works.description: Published in 1888 and the first English novel about women running a business in the age of the New Woman: four orphaned sisters open a photographic studio in Baker Street. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Amy Levy; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The four Lorimer sisters, left penniless by their father's death, refuse to be scattered among relations and open a photographic studio in Upper Baker Street: Gertrude, the would-be writer, and the practical Lucy run the business, the beautiful Phyllis sits to the painter Sidney Darrell and runs away with him to Italy, and the simple elder half-sister Fanny keeps house; their first commission, a photograph of the dead wife of the scientist Lord Watergate, brings Gertrude the man she will marry, while Lucy marries the artist Frank Jermyn, rescued after an ambush in Africa, and carries on the studio.
works.significance: The Romance of a Shop is the founding English novel of the woman's small business and one of the first to treat women's professional work as a subject rather than a problem; its picture of the 1880s London of shops, studios and lodgings is a key document of the New Woman's world.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is metrical accomplishment in traditional forms (sonnet, ballad, dramatic monologue).
works.context: The 1880s, the first generation of professional women, the new photography trade, and the debate on women's work. The record dates the work as composed in 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. works.title: The Romance of the Forest, Interspersed with Some Pieces of Poetry. In Three Volumes
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror; sentimental fiction of the pursued heroine with interspersed songs and ballads and embedded manuscript narrative
works.description: The third novel of Ann Radcliffe and the first great popular success of the Gothic romance of terror, published anonymously in three volumes on 22 December 1791 as the work of the authoress of A Sicilian Romance. Adeline, an orphaned girl of secretly noble fortune, is handed over by her father's appointment to the guardianship of her unscrupulous kinsman the Marquis de Montalt, who schemes to marry her and seize her inheritance. Driven from her home with the family of Pierre de La Motte, her guardian's steward, she takes refuge in a ruined forest abbey, where she discovers old manuscripts recording a tragic captivity of the seventeenth century, and passes through a series of shelters and imprisonments, at the chateau of La Motte and in the castle of La Valombrosa, before her parentage is cleared, her pursuer defeated, and her hand won by the soldier Theodore. The abbey papers and the slow documentary unveiling set the pattern Radcliffe perfected in The Mysteries of Udolpho, and the interspersed songs and ballads mark the place of her romance in the lyricised Gothic.
works.plot: Adeline, born into wealth but kept by her father's quarrel from her claim, is educated in a convent and placed under the Marquis de Montalt, whose proposals she refuses. The La Motte family, Pierre, his wife Theresa and their children, befriend and shelter her; her flight with them leads to the ruined abbey, where she reads the manuscripts of a hermit's tragic past; she is pursued by Montalt's agents, falls under the power of interested priests at La Valombrosa, and is separated from Theodore, the young officer she loves, who is imprisoned for defending her. Forgeries, murders and a stolen heiress are at last laid open; the family that betrayed her is punished and broken, Adeline is restored to her fortune and rank, and after mourning her father she marries Theodore.
works.significance: The Romance of the Forest made Radcliffe the most read English novelist of the 1790s and fixed the working formula of the Gothic romance: the persecuted heroine, the ruin as refuge, the hidden archive, and detection explained by natural causes. It shaped Gothic fiction through Mary Shelley and the Victorian sensation novel, provoked the parody that Jane Austen gave the genre in Northanger Abbey, and established the model of terror regulated by sensibility and reason.
works.meter: Chiefly prose romance; the interspersed pieces of poetry are short lyric songs and ballads, hymns of the cloister and of the forest hermitage, set into the mouths of characters and subordinate to the prose.
works.context: Published two years after A Sicilian Romance had begun Radcliffe's career and in the first years of the war with Revolutionary France, when debates over tyranny, property and providence made the abused heiress and the crooked guardian powerful political emblems; it appeared in the three-volume duodecimo format of the circulating libraries, at the height of the vogue for monastic ruins and picturesque scenery fostered by Gilpin and by the antiquarian revival of Gothic.
works.characters: Adeline, the orphaned heiress; the Marquis de Montalt, her grasping kinsman; Pierre de La Motte and his wife Theresa; their children; Theodore, the soldier whom Adeline loves; Arnaud La Luc, the exile and his family; Jerome, the forest hermit; Theresa and the abbey manuscripts
works.structure: A continuous prose romance in three volumes centred on Adeline's successive protection and expulsion, punctuated by embedded documents: the abbey manuscripts, recovered papers and a final expository revelation that explains by natural and legal causes what the scenery had clothed in terror.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the authoress of A Sicilian Romance; the authorship of Ann Radcliffe is undisputed, established by the designations of the successive editions and by her husband's memoir of 1826.

works.title: The Romany Rye
works.description: Published in 1857 and the sequel to Lavengro: the scholar's further wanderings and his life with the Roma. It is a prose work of 1857 by George Borrow; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The narrative continues Borrow's wanderings after the departure of Isopel Berners: his stay at the Welsh inn, his journey to the fair at Horncastle, his life with the horse-dealers and the Roma, and his return to the road, with long digressions on language, religion and the character of the English.
works.significance: The Romany Rye completes Lavengro's strange and original project and is the most extended English record of Roma life in the nineteenth century: its horse-fair chapters and its conversations make it a classic of English travel writing, and it is the book in which Borrow's sympathy with the outcast is most fully displayed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is picaresque episodic narrative.
works.context: 1820s-50s: the horse fairs of England, the Roma, the Welsh border country, and the English road before the railway. The record dates the work as composed between 1852 and 1857 and first published in 1857 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; realist novel of common life.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: The Romaunt of the Rose
works.description: A Middle English translation of the Roman de la Rose, surviving in a single manuscript and divided by scholarship into three fragments (A, B, and C), of which only Fragment A is now widely accepted as Chaucer's — and even that attribution is debated. The work is the great conduit by which the French allegory of love entered English, and its early attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
works.plot: The dreamer enters the garden of Mirth, where the god of Love shoots him and he pledges service; the narrative then follows the lover's quest for the Rose through the allegorical figures of the garden — Fair Welcome, Danger, Reason, Shame, Jealousy — in the French poem's anatomy of courtly love.
works.significance: The principal English version of the poem that dominated late medieval literary culture; the attribution question remains a central problem of Chaucerian scholarship.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets.
works.context: Composed in the 1360s–70s (Fragment A possibly c. 1360s), translating Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun; preserved uniquely in the Hunterian manuscript (Glasgow, Hunter 409); the attribution to Chaucer rests on his own mention of a Romaunt translation in the Legend of Good Women prologue and on Thynne's 1532 edition.
works.characters: the Dreamer-Lover; the Rose; the god of Love; Fair Welcome; Danger; Reason; Jealousy; the Old Woman
works.structure: A continuous allegorical dream vision following the French original's sequence of episodes, surviving here in three discontinuous fragments.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship disputed: Fragment A is often accepted as Chaucer's; Fragments B and C are generally rejected; modern editors treat the whole as doubtful. authorship_status reflects this uncertainty.
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor

works.title: The Rose and the Ring; or, The History of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo. A Fire-Side Pantomime for Great and Small Children
altTitles: Rose and the Ring; or, The History of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo. A Fire-Side Pantomime for Great and Small Children
works.description: Published in December 1854 (title page 1855), written for the Christmas pantomime and for the children of the household: a burlesque fairy tale of two rival kingdoms, the magic rose and ring that make their bearers irresistible, and a cast of comic courtiers.
works.plot: Prince Giglio of Paflagonia and Prince Bulbo of Crim Tartary are both endowed with supernatural charms by the fairy Blackstick; their rivalry for the Princess Angelica, the interference of the wicked Countess Gruffanuff, and the eventual pairing of the true lovers produce a plot of transformations and reversals in which nobody is quite what they seem.
works.significance: The Rose and the Ring is one of the two or three founding texts of Victorian children's fantasy and the direct precursor of the comic fairy tale from Thackeray to Nesbit and beyond; its subversive treatment of royal and parental authority is unusual for its decade and it remains one of the funniest children's books of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The Victorian pantomime and the Christmas gift book, the chapbook and fairy-tale revival of the 1840s-50s, and the new market for children's illustrated books that Thackeray, Dickens and Ruskin all entered.
works.characters: Prince Giglio of Paflagonia; Prince Bulbo of Crim Tartary; Princess Angelica; Rosalba, the lost Queen of Crim Tartary (Betsinda); the Fairy Blackstick; Countess Gruffanuff; King Valoroso XXIV; King Padella; Glumboso; Captain Hedzoff
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Rover, Part II
works.description: Behn's sequel, set in London rather than Naples, in which Willmore returns to his roving ways and the same company of cavaliers is caught up in the intrigues of the town.

works.significance: An important sequel that transfers the carnival liberty of Naples to Restoration London and sharpens Behn's satire on the town's treatment of women.

works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1681 and published in the same year; it was less successful than Part I.

works.title: The Rover; or, The Banish'd Cavaliers
works.description: Behn's most famous and most successful comedy, set in Naples at carnival time, in which the libertine Rover Willmore pursues the witty Hellena while her sister Florinda evades a forced marriage.
works.plot: At carnival, Hellena disguises herself to meet Willmore; Florinda loves Belvile but is promised to the aged Vincentio and pursued by her brother's friend; a series of attempted rapes, duels, and disguises ends with the marriages of both sisters and Willmore's abandonment by Hellena.
works.significance: The most performed play of the Restoration after The Way of the World and the greatest comedy by a woman before the twentieth century; its treatment of female sexual agency and of carnival liberty is central to modern feminist criticism.
works.meter: Prose dominant with some verse.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre on 24 March 1677 and dedicated to Charles II's illegitimate son the Earl of Rochester's circle; it derives from Thomas Killigrew's unacted play Thomaso.
