works.title: The Royal Convert
works.description: Rowe's tragedy of religion, conscience and political conversion in an early Northern court, in which a princess's change of faith entangles duty, affection and the succession.
works.plot: A royal convert's new religion divides her family and her lover's allegiance, and the conspiracies raised about the throne, with the treachery of a waiting-woman substituted for the daughter, drive the play to its discoveries and executions.
works.significance: It is the century's earliest considerable tragedy of conscience and conversion, and its substitute-bride intrigue became one of the most imitated devices of the pathetic drama.
works.meter: Blank verse of the regular school, with the argumentative scene of conscience and the declaimed religious debate.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the season of the Occasional Conformity disputes, when the conscience of a convert and the loyalty of a subject were live political questions in England.
works.characters: the royal convert; her lover and rival claimants; the substituted bride; the father of the house
works.structure: Five acts of court intrigue, with the recognition of the substituted woman as the plot's famous mechanism and the religious division as its motive force.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey

works.title: The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia
works.form: Verse translation (75 quatrains in the first edition; 101 in the fourth, 1879)
works.description: Published anonymously in 1859 in a paper wrapper at one shilling and largely ignored until Dante Gabriel Rossetti found it in 1861: the most famous English translation of Persian poetry and one of the most popular poems in the language.
works.plot: The poem is a sequence of quatrains on the vanity of speculation and the urgency of present pleasure: the potter shapes the clay of dead men into pots; the Sultan and the Saint alike go down into dust; the only answer is wine and love 'here underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread — and Thou'.
works.significance: The Rubáiyát is the most popular English poem of the later nineteenth century and the founding text of the vogue for Persian literature; its celebration of the present moment and its scepticism made it the philosophical poem of the 1890s aesthetic movement, and its influence on the modern English quatrain and on the decoration (Rossetti, Morris, and the Kelmscott circle) is direct.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the quatrain. The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).
works.context: The 1850s, the new English Orientalism and the study of Persian (Edward Cowell and the Bodleian manuscript), the Victorian crisis of faith, and the aesthetic movement's cult of melancholy pleasure. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: A free adaptation rather than a literal translation: FitzGerald selected, rearranged and partly invented quatrains from the Persian and constructed a continuous poem. The first edition (1859) has 75 quatrains; the fourth (1879) has 101 and is the text usually reprinted.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist

works.title: The Ruin
works.description: A fragmentary elegy (about 49 lines, damaged by burning of the manuscript leaf) describing the ruins of a great stone city — hot springs, halls, and baths that are almost certainly Roman Bath — and meditating on the fall of its builders.
works.plot: The speaker marvels at 'enta geweorc' (the work of giants): broken walls, fallen roofs, and the hot baths where once many men bathed in comfort; the city's warriors are dead, its halls decayed, and the poem closes with the reflection that a hundred generations have passed since its glory.
works.significance: The earliest ruin-poem in English, anticipating the ruin tradition of the eighteenth century; a haunting witness to Anglo-Saxon wonder at Roman remains.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the text is incomplete through fire damage.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the identification with Roman Bath is standard.
works.characters: none (descriptive speaker)
works.structure: A description of ruins moving from sensory observation to historical meditation, in the ubi sunt mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Ruins of Rome
works.form: Topographical and meditative poem in the manner of the 'ruins' tradition, combining description, historical narration and reflection; a single sustained line of verse addressed to no auditor.
works.description: John Dyer's first poem and one of the most remarkable of Augustan ruin meditations: a topographical and philosophical survey of the fallen city of Rome, written by an English country curate who had made the Grand Tour. It was printed anonymously, and its attribution to Dyer rests on contemporary notice and on the later collection of his verse. The manner is deliberately archaising and sonorous, closer to a Latin or Italian 'grand manner' than to the couplet idioms of his English contemporaries.
works.plot: The poem is a description which becomes a philosophy of history. The traveller moves over the ruins, the aqueducts, the broken statues and the buried bases of the city, and from their mass and fragments draws an argument about the transience of empire and the mortality of glory. Rome is at once a moral spectacle and a Christian one: the pagan capital that conquered the world has been conquered by time, and the modern papal city that sits among the ruins supplies a second lesson on the revolutions of power and on the providential government of nations. The moral energy of the piece is spent on the disproportion between the grandeur of what was and the meanness of what remains.
works.significance: It is the earliest and one of the strangest of the eighteenth-century English poems about imperial decay, and it established the harsh, 'sublime and antique' voice that Johnson, in his life of Dyer, described as a deliberate attempt to naturalise Latin majesty in English measure. It stands between Thomson's meditative topography and the ruin-poetry of the following century, and it is a source text for the age's association of topography with the philosophy of history.
works.meter: Predominantly decasyllabic English heroic measure handled with marked asperity: long Latinate compounds, hypermetric and stretched lines, and a deliberate refusal of couplet neatness, giving the blank-verse-like solemnity Dyer thought proper to his subject.
works.context: It appears in the aftermath of the second decade of Grand Tour travel and of the growing English quarrel about taste, precedent and Gothic versus classical authority, and it takes the ruins of Rome as the emblem of national and imperial decline at a moment when British commerce and empire were beginning to make that emblem urgent. Its classical-subject treatment in unpolished native verse was itself a position in the debate about the reach of English poetry.
works.characters: The surveying traveller-poet; personified Rome and her ruins
works.structure: A continuous descriptivo-philosophical poem following the topography of the ruins, with the traveller's present survey, the recollected history of the republic and empire, and the Christian and modern city interwoven without formal division.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1740; the ascription to Dyer rests on contemporary attribution and on the inclusion of the poem in collections of his work, and it is now universally accepted. Because the first edition was unsigned, the record is entered under 'attributed'.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Topographical and Estate Poetry

works.title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying
works.description: The companion volume to Holy Living, a manual for the dying that instructs the Christian in the preparation for death, with famous meditations on the vanity of the world.

works.significance: One of the most widely read devotional works in English; it shaped the Protestant art of dying and influenced the elegiac and meditative literature of the period.
works.meter: Baroque Anglican prose of great rhetorical power.
works.context: Published in 1651, dedicated to the Countess of Carbery, whose death occasioned the book; it belongs to the long tradition of the ars moriendi.
works.structure: Four books of instruction with prayers.

works.title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living
works.description: Jeremy Taylor's devotional manual of the Christian life, written during the civil wars while Taylor was deprived of his living, and one of the most popular religious books of the seventeenth century.
works.plot: Four chapters treat the universal instrument of holy living: the nature and measures of temperance, of justice, of the Christian religion, and of prayer, with directions for the practice of each virtue.
works.significance: With Holy Dying the most influential Anglican devotional work of the period; it defined the ideal of the holy life for generations and remains a classic of English prose.
works.meter: Oratorical, richly figurative prose of the Anglican baroque; Taylor was called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'.
works.context: Published in 1650, after the execution of Charles I, when Taylor was living in retirement in Wales under the patronage of the Earl of Carbery.
works.structure: Four books of systematic devotional instruction with prayers at the end of each.

works.title: The Rune Poem
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Otho B.x, fol. 165 (destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731; survives in the transcript printed by George Hickes, 1705)
works.form: runic wisdom poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which each of the 29 runes of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc is given a stanza beginning with the rune's name and elaborating its traditional meanings: feoh (wealth), ur (aurochs), thorn, the gods, the horse, the sun, and the rest. The poem fuses native Germanic rune-lore with Christian wisdom.
works.plot: Stanza by stanza, the poem unfolds the lore of each rune — wealth's mutability, the aurochs' ferocity, thorn's sharpness, the sun's blessing to seafarers, the grave's coldness — building a gnomic encyclopaedia of the natural and social world as encoded in the runic alphabet.
works.significance: The principal source for the names and meanings of the Anglo-Saxon runes, and a bridge between Germanic pagan lore and Christian Old English poetry; its loss in the 1731 fire makes Hickes's transcript the only witness.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; each stanza opens with the rune's name, and the verses carry the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition.
works.context: The poem is the fullest surviving statement of the Anglo-Saxon runic tradition, composed when runes were still written for inscriptions and magic while the script's pagan associations were being absorbed into Christian learning; it descends from the same tradition as the Old Norwegian and Old Icelandic rune poems.
works.structure: A catalogue of 29 stanzas, one per rune, in the fixed order of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc; each stanza is a self-contained gnomic meditation introduced by the rune-name.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The prose and verse traditions around the runes descend from a common Germanic inheritance; the Old English poem is an independent composition.
themes: Christian-pagan synthesis
Wisdom and learning
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Rural Muse
works.form: Nature Lyric and Meditation; Romantic Sonnet Revival
works.description: The last volume of verse published by the author before his permanent confinement, a preface admitting that the poems are selected from a great mass of manuscripts. It gathers the mid-series lyrics and a sequence of fourteen or more sonnets on rural scenes, including the poem on the grazing heath most admired by modern readers. The book is the record of a labouring poet writing after his public fame had failed.
works.plot: The volume moves through the seasons in short descriptive numbers, then through churchyard meditation, a sonnet on a fallen continental emperor, bird-nest lyrics, and a closing group of sonnets on rural scenes, water-lilies, the village boy, the sedge-bird's nest, and the shepherd's tree. Its central achievements are the poem on the common grazing cut and spoiled by inclosure and the pieces on small nests and insects, which render the poet's own precarious shelter in the language of natural history. The prefatory complaint about neglect frames the whole as a testament rather than a bid for fame.
works.significance: The volume contains the poems on which the modern revival of the author's reputation mainly rests, and it documents the survival of a labouring poetic outside the patronage and subscription machinery that had launched his career. Its seasonal and nest lyrics have been taken as a counter-model to Wordsworthian meditation, grounded in the eye of a paid hedge-right rather than a retired proprietor.
works.meter: Short lyric stanzas in common and long measure, a group of meditative pentameter pieces, and a numbered sonnet sequence in iambic pentameter; the diction is plainer and more compressed than in the earlier long poems, with fewer rhetorical inversions.
works.context: Published in the year after the author's return from a metropolitan asylum episode and his final settlement in a labourer's cottage, with the volume dedicated by permission to a noble patron of the family that had interest in his parish. Sales were insufficient for his support, though a leading Scottish periodical noticed it favourably, and the copies unsold passed into the hands of a provincial publisher.
works.characters: the poet-speaker; the shepherd boy and the village boy of the sonnets; the nesting birds of the lyric numbers; the dead of the churchyard meditations
works.structure: A collection in loose seasonal and thematic order: an opening address to the muse, descriptive and reflective lyrics, a single-sentence sonnet on the emperor, then a numbered sonnet sequence, with no narrative frame.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the poems are drawn from manuscript volumes of the 1830s, some of which circulated in the asylum years.
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
movements: Labouring-Class and Village Poetry

works.title: The Saint and Mary Kate
works.form: Novel (the young man and the young woman of the republic)
works.description: The novel of the young man and the young woman of the new republic. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Sean O'Faolain; it is catalogued here under Novel of Manners and Fashion; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Saint and Mary Kate follows the young man of the republic and Mary Kate, the woman of the convent school, through the quarrel of the desire and the church in the Dublin of the new state.
works.significance: The Saint and Mary Kate is O'Faolain's novel of the young republic and its censored desire: its quarrel of the desire and the church made the novel of the new state one of the forms of Irish fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of manners: the dialogue of the social world, the exact vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built on the breach or the observance of a convention. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence.
works.context: Dublin in the early 1930s, and the censorship of the republic. The record dates the work as composed in 1931 and first published in 1932 and it is catalogued under novel of manners and fashion; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the saint; Mary Kate; the Dublin of the republic
works.structure: A novel of the quarrel in chapters of the city and the convent. A novel in chapters of the social world, the scenes built on the breach or the observance of a convention. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sean Proinsias O Faolain. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis and Aulus Persius Flaccus

works.description: Dryden's translation of Juvenal's sixteen satires and Persius's six, prefaced by his long Discourse Concerning the Original and Progress of Satire, the foundational English treatise on the genre.
works.plot: The Discourse distinguishes the 'Varronian' Menippean satire from formal verse satire, classifies formal satire into the delicate Horatian, the severe Persian, and the copious Juvenalian modes, and defends the last as suited to a corrupt age.
works.significance: Its preface supplied the vocabulary of eighteenth-century satire criticism and directly shaped Pope's self-understanding; it remains the standard early modern English account of the genre.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Published in 1693, in the Catholic exile of James II's court and at the height of the controversy over the ancients and moderns.
works.structure: A critical preface followed by the translated satires, Juvenal's Satire I and Persius's Satire VI being Dryden's own work and the rest by his sons and collaborators.
works.attributionNotes: Dryden translated Juvenal I, VII-XVI and Persius VI; the remainder by Charles, John, and Henry Dryden and others; the Discourse is entirely Dryden's.

works.title: The Savoy
works.description: Edited by Symons with Aubrey Beardsley in 1896 and the central magazine of the English Decadence: eight numbers that printed the work of Yeats, Dowson, Johnson, Beardsley, Conrad and Shaw. It is a prose work of 1896 by Arthur Symons; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
works.plot: The Savoy published poetry, fiction, criticism and drawings of the Decadent school, defended itself against the charge of obscenity, and printed Conrad's early story 'The Idiots'.
works.significance: The Savoy is the central magazine of the English Decadence and one of the most important little magazines in English literary history: its eight numbers preserve the work of a whole movement and its collapse marks the end of the 1890s aesthetic moment.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the short lyric built on a single mood.
works.context: 1896: the Wilde trials and the collapse of the Decadent market, and the new little magazine culture. works.title: The Scale of Perfection
works.description: Walter Hilton's masterpiece, in two books: the first (c. 1380s) addresses an anchoress on the reformation of the soul in faith and the destruction of the image of sin; the second (c. 1390s), on the reformation of the soul in feeling, expounds the contemplative life and the discernment of true spiritual experience. The most systematic and influential English treatise on contemplation.
works.plot: Book I anatomizes the soul's sinfulness and its reformation through faith, humility, and the practice of prayer, with the famous analysis of the image of sin to be broken down; Book II teaches the higher work of contemplation — the entry into the 'darkness' of unknowing, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the tests by which true spiritual experience may be known from false.
works.significance: The classic systematic treatise of English mysticism: its discrimination of true and false spiritual experience and its doctrine of the image of God shaped English devotional thought for three centuries.
works.meter: Measured, precise prose, plainer than Rolle's and theologically more careful.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–96 by the Augustinian canon Walter Hilton, for a woman recluse and for the devout laity; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1494) and read by the English Benedictine revival of the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Hilton (teacher); the anchoress (addressee)
works.structure: Two books of graduated instruction (the 'scale'), moving from the active to the contemplative life, in the tradition of the spiritual ladder.
works.attributionNotes: Hilton's authorship secure.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
The contemplative life

works.title: The Scarlet Letter
works.form: Novel (romance); realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1850 and the founding novel of American literature: the story of Hester Prynne, condemned to wear the letter A for adultery in Puritan Boston, and of the two men who destroy themselves over her secret.
works.plot: Hester Prynne stands on the scaffold with her infant daughter Pearl and refuses to name the father, the Reverend Arthur Dimmesdale; her husband, the physician Roger Chillingworth, arrives to take revenge on the minister, and the novel ends with Dimmesdale's confession on the scaffold and Hester's return to the letter in old age.
works.significance: The Scarlet Letter is the central American novel and the founding text of the American romance: its treatment of adultery, female independence and secret guilt made it the origin of the American novel of conscience, and its heroine is the first fully realised woman in American fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The years 1642-49, Puritan Boston, the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and the 1850 debate on slavery and the woman question. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; sensation novel.
works.characters: Hester Prynne; Pearl; Arthur Dimmesdale; Roger Chillingworth; Governor Bellingham; Mistress Hibbins; John Wilson
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Scarlet Pimpernel
works.form: Novel; historical novel, first issued in 1905
works.description: The first masked hero: Sir Percy Blakeney and the rescue of the condemned. It is a prose fiction work of 1905 by Baroness Orczy; it is catalogued here under Historical Novel and Romance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Sir Percy Blakeney, a foppish English aristocrat, is secretly the Scarlet Pimpernel, who rescues French aristocrats from the guillotine; his wife Marguerite is blackmailed by the French agent Chauvelin into betraying him, and the novel ends with the rescue and the revelation.
works.significance: The Scarlet Pimpernel created the masked hero and the double identity in modern fiction: its portrait of Sir Percy and Lady Blakeney founded the superhero narrative, the rescue adventure and the secret-identity plot, and it remains one of the most popular historical novels ever written.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the historical novel: the period vocabulary and the studied anachronism avoided, the set-piece of battle, ceremony or trial, and the narrative pitched between the documented public event and the invented private life. The author's characteristic manner is the double-life hero and the secret identity.
works.context: London and revolutionary France in 1792. The record dates the work as composed between 1904 and 1905 and first published in 1905 and it is catalogued under historical novel and romance.
works.characters: Sir Percy Blakeney; Lady Marguerite Blakeney; Chauvelin; Armand St Just; the Prince of Wales
works.structure: A novel of disguise and rescue in England and France. A novel in chapters set in a documented past, the public event and the invented private life carried in the same narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Emma Orczy. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Sceptical Chymist
altTitles: The Sceptical Chymist; or, Chymico-Physical Doubts and Paradoxes
works.description: Robert Boyle's dialogue attacking the Aristotelian and Paracelsian theories of the elements, arguing for a corpuscular (mechanical) account of matter and insisting that chemical claims must be established by experiment.
works.plot: In a dialogue among Carneades, Eleutherius, Philoponus, and Themistius, Boyle argues that neither the four Aristotelian elements nor the three Paracelsian principles can be demonstrated; only experiment can determine the composition of bodies.
works.significance: The work that separated chemistry from alchemy and established it as an experimental science; its sceptical method and its corpuscularianism were decisive for the new philosophy.
works.meter: Argumentative prose with detailed experimental description.
works.context: Published in 1661, a year after the Restoration and the year before the Royal Society's charter; Boyle was a founding fellow and the leading experimental philosopher of the age.
works.characters: Carneades (Boyle's spokesman); Eleutherius; Philoponus; Themistius
works.structure: A dialogue in six parts with an appendix of experiments.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Boyle; authorship undisputed.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
The New Science and experimental philosophy
Wisdom and learning

works.title: The Scholar-Gipsy
works.description: Published in the 1853 Poems and one of the most influential lyrics of the century: the legend of the Oxford student who joined the gipsies to learn their secret, transferred to a meditation on the modern world's 'strange disease of modern life'.
works.plot: The speaker recalls the seventeenth-century scholar who left Oxford for the gipsies and asks whether he still walks the Oxfordshire countryside; the poem turns from the legend to the contrast between the scholar's single-minded quest and the 'sick hurry' of modern life, ending with the wish that the scholar may never be caught by the modern world.
works.significance: The Scholar-Gipsy is the central English poem of the modern intellectual's nostalgia for a unified life, and its closing description of the 'darkling plain' of modern existence (developed in 'Dover Beach') gave the Victorian age its most quoted diagnosis of itself. It is a foundation text for the criticism of modernity.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The Oxfordshire landscape of Arnold's youth, the 1850s railway and the 'strange disease of modern life', and the seventeenth-century source in Glanvill's Vanity of Dogmatizing. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The School for Scandal
altTitles: The School for Scandal: A Comedy
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The greatest comedy of the late eighteenth century, a play about scandal-mongering and hypocritical virtue in which the surface candour of a fashionable society is dissected by a series of eavesdroppings. Its famous fourth-act screen scene gathers the whole design into one tableau.
works.plot: A house of professed candour is divided against itself: the outwardly moral younger brother supplants his frank and spendthrift elder, and a circle of wits live on the malice of the tea-table. Sir Peter Teazle, newly married to a country girl, is set against his wife by the same tribe, and the wife is taught the ways of the town. The discovery of the hypocrite by the try-all brother and the exposure of the school of scandal in the screen scene restore the elder brother and reform the young couple.
works.significance: It is the final masterpiece of the English comedy of manners and the standard instance of the argument that society's conversation is a form of action; it has never left the repertory.
works.meter: A brilliant prose dialogue of epigram, retort and malaprop-free precision, the high style of the moral sententiae being reserved for parody; the speeches are built to be quoted.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in May 1777 after the failure of a rival play on the same design, in the season in which its author became a principal manager of the house; the comedy of sensibility and the comedy of laughter were then openly contending for the stage.
works.characters: Sir Peter Teazle; Lady Teazle; Joseph Surface; Charles Surface; Sir Oliver Surface; Lady Sneerwell; Snake; Maria; the backbiters of the breakfast table
works.structure: Five-act comedy of intrigue and discovery, its turns effected by concealed hearing and the misreport of conversation; the dialogue advances the plot almost entirely by what is overheard.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and recorded in the manager's own accounts of the season.

Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: The School-Master
works.form: pastoral eclogue in three parts, with argument and annotations
works.description: William Shenstone's earliest considerable poem, a pastoral eclogue in three parts which memorialises his old schoolmaster and turns the village school into an Arcadian scene. The poem honors the learned country usher, sketches his poverty and his patience, and asks what returns a nation makes to the men who form its youth. It is at once a tribute, a pastoral of letters, and a complaint about the treatment of the obscure teacher, and it announced the distinctive Shenstonian mixture of tenderness, rural observation and self-conscious antiquarianism.
works.plot: In the first part the scene of the school is drawn in pastoral disguise, the master's patience and cares mustered, and the poet recalls the benefit he personally received; in the second the ageing master's distresses and his dependence upon a generous eye are set out with a melancholy directness; the third part resolves the poem into an address to the patron and to the Muses, asking that the man who taught others to live should not be left to die neglected. The design is thus tripartite in feeling as well as in form: recollection, complaint, and petition.
works.significance: It gave the century one of its most reprinted poems of gratitude and educational piety, helped to fix the image of the poor country schoolmaster in British feeling, and stands with Shenstone's Leasowes writings as a document of the mid-century culture of retirement, sensibility and rural taste.
works.meter: An uneven pastoral stanza of short iambic lines, in the deliberate archaisms and irregularities of the English eclogue tradition inherited from Spenser and from the seventeenth-century school of the shepheardes calendars; Shenstone's own notes on the stanza's antiquity accompany the poem.
works.context: Published in 1742, when the country retired gentleman and the minor poet of the counties were a recognised figure in the literary geography outside London, and when the school-master was a stock of both charity sermon and satire; Shenstone printed and circulated his poems largely through friends and local presses rather than through the great London houses.
works.characters: the schoolmaster; the pupil-poet; the neighbouring rustics and pupils
works.structure: A pastoral eclogue in three parts, framed by an invocation and a dedicatory address, moving from recalled schoolroom scene to present complaint to closing petition, with the shepherd-poet convention carrying the memoir.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Shenstone's authorship is documented by his own circulation of the poem and by the collected editions of his works.

works.title: The Schoolmaster
works.description: Ascham's posthumously published treatise on the education of children, especially the teaching of Latin by double translation, with an autobiographical preface on the occasion of its writing.
works.plot: Book I, framed by the preface recalling a 1563 dinner conversation at Windsor on the flogging of schoolboys, advocates gentleness in teaching, criticizes the harsh grammar-school regime, and sketches the ideal education of a gentleman's son. Book II offers a practical method — the 'double translation' of Latin — by which the student imitates classical models, with detailed advice on style, imitation, and the choice of authors.
works.significance: The classic statement of Elizabethan humanist pedagogy; its doctrine of imitation and its advocacy of the vernacular prose style influenced Sidney, Spenser, and the school curriculum for generations.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Begun c. 1563 after the Windsor dinner with Cecil and Sackville (the latter of whom prompted the book), and left unfinished at Ascham's death in December 1568; published in 1570 by his widow Margaret with a dedication to Cecil. Its composition and publication bridge the early Tudor and Elizabethan periods.
works.characters: Roger Ascham (narrator); Sir William Cecil; Sir Richard Sackville
works.structure: Two books; the first is anecdotal and hortatory, the second a systematic method with specimen exercises.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: The Science of English Verse
works.description: Published in 1880 and the founding work of American prosody: an attempt to reduce English verse to the laws of music. It is a prose work of 1880 by Sidney Lanier; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lanier argues that verse is a form of music: that the rhythms of English poetry can be analysed in musical notation, that stress, quantity and pitch combine in a system of bars and notes, and that the whole history of English verse can be read as a series of musical arrangements of the same materials.
works.significance: The Science of English Verse is the founding work of American prosody and the most original English-language theory of verse of the century: its musical analysis of metre influenced Pound, Eliot and the whole modern study of versification, and it remains the starting point of any serious discussion of English rhythm.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is long, musical, rhythmically inventive lines.
works.context: 1880: the new science of acoustics, the American study of prosody after Lowell, the musical training of the period, and the professionalisation of literary study in the American university. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sidney Clopton Lanier. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Scots Musical Museum
altTitles: The Scots Musical Museum, in Six Volumes
works.form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of Scottish song; ballad and popular song, printed with the airs and a vocal part
works.description: The great serial anthology of Scottish song, projected and published by the Edinburgh music-engraver James Johnson and issued in six volumes between 1787 and 1803. It prints traditional and modern Scots songs with their airs, arranged for the voice with simple instrumental accompaniments, and in its later volumes it became the principal printing ground for the songs of Robert Burns, who from about 1788 was its most active contributor and, in effect, its literary editor. The collection is the single most important body of song into which Burns poured his late labour: he revised old texts, recovered fragments from singers and from the printed repertoire, wrote new verses to familiar airs, and supplied the illustrative notes and the historical and critical remarks that carry the volumes. Its six volumes hold the repertory out of which the modern idea of the Scottish song tradition was made, and they document a collaboration between a music publisher and a poet in which the poet's share came to dominate the series.
works.plot: The volumes are not a narrative but a repertory: each number is a song text printed with its air, arranged so that the words and the tune are presented together, with the older traditional pieces beside new or revised lyrics. The scheme broadens from the opening volume's gathering of favourite Scottish songs toward the later volumes' wider historical and comparative range, which includes early pieces, songs in the Scottish dialect, and illustrative prose notes on the texts and their authorities. Burns's contributions fall chiefly in the volumes issued from about 1790 onwards: songs of love, drinking and friendship, comic and pastoral songs, Jacobite and border pieces, and revised versions of traditional texts whose phrasing he restored or re-made. His own account of the work, in letters of the period, describes his method of collating printed and sung versions, keeping the old words where they were best, and writing new stanzas only when the air required them.
works.significance: The Museum is the repository in which Burns's achievement as a songwriter, the largest and most durable part of his work, was first collected and printed, and it changed the status of song within his canon from occasional verse to serious poetic labour. It also fixes the model of the poet at work on traditional texts, revising, restoring and re-creating rather than inventing, a model that bears directly on later accounts of Romantic authorship, orality and cultural property. Its repertory, edited and largely made by Burns, remains the standard record of late-eighteenth-century Scottish song and a central document of the Romantic construction of national tradition.
works.meter: Strophic song verse written to be sung, not read: the texts run mainly in the ballad and song stanzas of the Scottish repertory, common and short measure with alternating four- and three-beat lines, with refrains, tags and the short-tailed stanza forms Burns adapted to individual airs. Because the air governs the line, the metre is disciplined by musical phrase, syncopation and repeat, and Burns's revisions are often measurable as adjustments of syllable count to the notes. Scots dialect spelling, with its own rhyme and assonance habits, carries much of the series' verbal texture.
works.context: Published at Edinburgh by James Johnson, engraver and music-seller, in the same decade as the Kilmarnock and Edinburgh volumes of Burns's poetry, the Museum belonged to the enthusiastic collecting of national song that followed Percy's Reliques and the ballad revivals of the 1780s, and to Edinburgh's competitive music trade, in which Johnson and his rival George Thomson vied for airs, verses and subscribers. Burns, established as a poet after 1786 and settled at Ellisland and then Dumfries from 1788, took up the collection as the work of his later years, believing that the old Scottish songs were a national inheritance worth preserving against the polite dilution of the English stage. His engagement made the series a partnership of a craftsman publisher and a poet-editor; the sixth volume appeared after his death in 1796.
works.characters: the singer-speakers of the songs; the beloveds and false lovers of the lyric texts; the shepherd, hind and ploughboy of the pastoral and labouring numbers; the drunkards and revellers of the tavern songs; the Highland chiefs, border raiders and Jacobites of the historical pieces; James Johnson as projector and publisher and Robert Burns as contributing editor
works.structure: A serial anthology in six octavo volumes, each a numbered sequence of independent songs rather than an ordered argument; the unity is the repertory and the continuing editorial scheme, which passed in practice from Johnson's musical arrangements to Burns's textual judgement as the series reached its middle volumes. The set was completed only after Burns's death, and he interleaved copies of the earlier volumes with his own notes and corrections.
works.attributionNotes: The volumes are Johnson's publication and a joint undertaking: Johnson chose and engraved the airs, contracted the arrangements and holds the title-page credit, while Burns supplied an immense body of lyrics, revisions and notes without ever appearing as author of the work. Burns is named here as a contributing author only, not as the author of the collection. Estimates of his share run in modern accounts to some two hundred songs, but the figure varies between authorities and the attribution of individual numbers between traditional texts, other contributors and Burns has been actively re-opened by recent scholarship, so the record is left at research_status partial.

works.title: The Screwtape Letters
works.form: Epistolary satire (the letters of the devil to his nephew)
works.description: The satire of the soul in the voice of the devil: Screwtape's letters to Wormwood. It is a prose work of 1942 by C. S. Lewis; it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Screwtape, the senior devil of the Lowerarchy, writes to his nephew Wormwood on the conduct of the patient: the war, the church, the sex, the friends, the reading and the prayers of the Englishman are examined from below, and the satire of the soul is carried in the devil's own administrative prose.
works.significance: The Screwtape Letters is the most original satire of the twentieth century and the most read of Lewis's books: its devil's-eye view of the ordinary soul made the examination of conscience a public art and gave the war years their sharpest religious fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose: the argument or the account is carried in continuous prose, divided into sections or chapters. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is the lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer.
works.context: England in the war years, published first in The Guardian and then in volume in 1942. The record dates the work as composed in 1941 and first published in 1942 and it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire.
works.characters: Screwtape; Wormwood; the Patient; the Patient's mother; 'He' (the Enemy)
works.structure: Thirty-one letters in sequence, the conduct of the patient from the first temptation to the last.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Clive Hamilton, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to C. S. Lewis is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Sea-Wolf
works.description: Published in 1904 and the best of London's sea novels: a literary critic is rescued from a shipwreck by a seal-hunting schooner commanded by a Nietzschean brute. It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by Jack London; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Humphrey Van Weyden, a soft civilised critic, is taken aboard the Ghost by Captain Wolf Larsen, who rules his crew by force and philosophy; Humphrey is toughened by the ship, falls in love with the poet Maud Brewster, and escapes with her to an island where he finally defeats the dying Larsen.
works.significance: The Sea-Wolf is London's most intellectually ambitious novel and the central American fictional treatment of Nietzsche: Larsen is one of the great American characters, and the novel's conflict between the superman's philosophy and the civilised values of Humphrey and Maud is the most direct American response to Nietzsche's ideas in the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third.
works.context: 1904: the American seal-hunting fleet of the Pacific, the vogue of Nietzsche in America, and the debate on individualism and the 'superman'. The record dates the work as composed between 1903 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: Wolf Larsen; Humphrey Van Weyden; Maud Brewster; Mugridge; Johansen; Louis; Death Larsen
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Griffith London. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Seafarer
works.description: An elegy of 124 lines spoken by a veteran seafarer who describes the hardship and the irresistible pull of the sea voyage, then allegorizes it as the soul's pilgrimage away from the world toward its heavenly home.
works.plot: The speaker recounts winters of cold watch on the ice-cold sea, hunger, and isolation, yet declares that the sea calls him again; earthly joys, lords, and kingdoms all pass, and the wise man sets his hope on the eternal home where all things endure — the journey of the seafarer becoming a figure for the Christian's exile in the world.
works.significance: Alongside The Wanderer, the great poem of Old English exile; its seascape and spiritual allegory influenced Pound's 'The Seafarer' and much modern poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; vivid winter seascape imagery rare in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; influenced by the penitential and pilgrimage traditions (the phrase 'dryhtnes dreamas' has suggested the peregrinus ideal of Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasticism).
works.characters: the Seafarer (speaker)
works.structure: Two movements: a first-person account of seafaring hardship and longing, and a homiletic second half that interprets the voyage allegorically (peregrinatio pro amore Dei); the transition between them is a crux of interpretation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

Exile and homelessness
Sea voyage and seafaring

works.title: The Search
works.description: The classic novel of the scientist's vocation and its renunciation. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by C. P. Snow; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Search follows Miles Vane-Merrick, the physicist of the provincial grammar school, through the Cambridge laboratory and the promised discovery to the failure of the result and the renunciation of the research for the public life, in the plain novel of the laboratory that made Snow the scientist-novelist.
works.significance: The Search is the classic novel of the scientific vocation: its laboratory, its failed discovery and its renunciation made the scientist's conscience literary and prepared the institutions of the Strangers and Brothers series.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the plain unadorned prose of the committee room and the laboratory.
works.context: Cambridge and the scientific England of the early 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Miles Vane-Merrick, the physicist; the laboratory; the wife; the public men
works.structure: A vocation novel of the laboratory, the failure and the renunciation. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Second Mrs Tanqueray
works.description: First performed in 1893 and the central English problem play of the 1890s: a woman with a past marries a respectable widower and is destroyed by the double standard. It is a dramatic work of 1893 by Arthur Wing Pinero; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Paula Tanqueray, formerly the mistress of several men, marries Aubrey Tanqueray, a widower, and tries to enter respectable society; her stepdaughter Ellean's engagement is broken off because of Paula's past, and Paula, realising that she can never be accepted, takes her own life, leaving Aubrey and Ellean to the conventional world.
works.significance: The Second Mrs Tanqueray was the most discussed English play of the 1890s and the founding work of the English problem drama: its treatment of the woman with a past, its refusal of a comfortable ending and its exposure of the double standard made it the model for the serious English theatre, and it prepared the way for Shaw and the new drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion.
works.context: 1893: the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, the double standard in Victorian law, the New Woman debate, and the Lord Chamberlain's censorship of the stage. The record dates the work as composed in 1893 and first published in 1893 and first performed in 1893 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Paula Tanqueray; Aubrey Tanqueray; Ellean Tanqueray; Sir George Orreyd; Mrs Cortelyon; Captain Ardale; Dr Wynne; Morse
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Pinero. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1907
works.description: A Soho shopkeeper in the pay of a foreign embassy plots a bomb attack on Greenwich Observatory, and destroys his own family in the process. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Joseph Conrad; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mr Verloc, a lazy Soho shopkeeper who sells pornography and frequents anarchist meetings, is an agent of a foreign embassy. Ordered to stage an outrage against 'the fetish of science', he sends his simple-minded brother-in-law Stevie to carry a bomb to Greenwich; Stevie stumbles and is blown to pieces, and Verloc's wife Winnie, discovering the truth, murders him and is herself destroyed. The novel ends in a fogbound London of police, spies and solitary misery.
works.significance: The Secret Agent is the greatest English novel about terrorism and one of the darkest comedies in the language: it invented the domestic spy novel, has never been equalled in its analysis of the political agent as an ordinary, lazy, frightened man, and the murder of Stevie is one of the most shocking scenes in English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
works.context: The anarchist scare and the spy mania of the 1890s, the Greenwich Observatory bombing of 1894 (an actual attempt by a French anarchist), and the London of Soho, the embassy and the detective police. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Mr Verloc; Winnie Verloc; Stevie; Adolf Verloc's mother; Chief Inspector Heat; the Assistant Commissioner; Vladimir; Ossipon
works.structure: Chronological narrative with a delayed revelation of the murder and a documentary account of London's police and anarchist underworld.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Secret Garden
works.form: Novel; children's fantasy, first issued in 1911
works.description: The most widely read children's book of the period: a sour orphan, a hidden garden and the cure of a house. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Frances Hodgson Burnett; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mary Lennox, orphaned in India and sent to Misselthwaite Manor in Yorkshire, discovers a walled garden that has been locked for ten years; with the gardener's boy Dickon and the hidden invalid Colin she restores the garden and, through it, the health of the household.
works.significance: The Secret Garden is the most widely read children's book of the period after Alice in Wonderland and the finest of Burnett's works: its garden as a place of healing, its portrait of the neglected child and its quiet religious naturalism made it a permanent classic of English childhood.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The author's characteristic manner is the child's-eye view of adult failure.
works.context: Yorkshire in the 1900s, the great house in decline, and the new interest in gardening and in the psychology of the child. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Mary Lennox; Colin Craven; Dickon Sowerby; Martha Sowerby; Ben Weatherstaff; Archibald Craven
works.structure: A novel in twenty-seven chapters, from the Indian childhood to the restored garden. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frances Eliza Hodgson Burnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Semi-Detached House
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: The wittiest English comedy of manners between Austen and Thackeray: two households in one villa. It is a prose fiction work of 1859 by Emily Eden; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: A baronet's family takes one half of a semi-detached villa in the suburbs while a City merchant takes the other; the novel follows the collision of the two households, the courtship of the daughters and the comedy of class and pretension.
works.significance: The Semi-Detached House is one of the wittiest English comedies of manners between Austen and Thackeray: its two households, its class comedy and its epigrams made it a classic of the society novel and the founding text of the suburban comedy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the country house and the suburban villa.
works.context: London and its suburbs in the 1850s, and the new middle-class villa. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Lady Chester; the baronet; the merchant; the daughters; the servants
works.structure: A novel in chapters alternating between the two households. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Seraphim, and Other Poems
works.form: Verse drama and poems; victorian verse drama
works.description: Published in 1838 when she was thirty-two: the title poem is a Greek-style drama on the angels who watch the Crucifixion, together with 'The Romaunt of Margaret', 'The Poet's Vow' and the ballads that show the influence of the Greek dramatists she had studied since childhood.
works.plot: The Seraphim stages the angels who witness the Crucifixion and cannot understand God's purpose; the poem is a chorus-driven drama of grief and prophecy. The shorter poems are ballads, romances and meditations on art and the poet's vocation.
works.significance: The Seraphim made her name and shows the classical and prophetic ambition of her early art; it is the volume in which the woman poet claims the Greek dramatic form, and its critical reception opened the way to her appointment as a leading poet of the 1840s.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is blank verse of sustained narrative drive.
works.context: The 1830s, her reading of Aeschylus and the Greek tragedians, the Italian exile of her father's political sympathies, and the provincial religious culture of Herefordshire. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1838 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: Ador and Zerah, the seraphs ('The Seraphim')
works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Barrett Moulton-Barrett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Series
works.description: Thomas Hoccleve's linked sequence of poems (c. 1419–21), beginning with the Complaint and the Dialogue with a Friend — the first extended account of mental illness in English poetry, describing his 'wylde infirmity' of 1416 — and continuing with the tale of the emperor Jereslaus's wife and the Learn to Die, translated from the Gesta Romanorum and Suso. The founding text of English confessional poetry.
works.plot: The poet, unable to persuade the world of his recovered wits, complains of his illness and its social stigma; a Friend counsels and cajoles him back to writing; the sequence then proceeds through the exemplary tale of the empress and the treatise on dying, the poet's own voice threading the whole.
works.significance: The first extended English poem of mental illness and recovery, and the first secular autobiography in English verse; its frankness has made it a touchstone of disability and confessional studies.
works.meter: Rhyme royal throughout, with the prosimetric flourishes of the translated treatises.
works.context: Composed c. 1419–21, after Hoccleve's breakdown of 1416, for Humphrey Duke of Gloucester among others; preserved in the holograph manuscripts (Durham, Cosin V.iii.9; BL Harley 4866) — the earliest English authorial manuscripts after Orm.
works.characters: Hoccleve; the Friend; the Emperor Jereslaus and his wife (tale)
works.structure: A self-consciously linked series — complaint, dialogue, tale, and treatise — in which the frame of the poet's illness governs the exemplary matter.
works.attributionNotes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; parts survive in his own hand.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Fortune and mutability
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: Fifteenth-Century Chaucerians

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI
altTitles: The Seven Sermons before Edward VI
works.description: Hugh Latimer's seven Lenten sermons preached before King Edward VI in the privy garden at Westminster in 1549 and printed the same year; the fullest surviving example of Latimer's court preaching.
works.plot: Preached weekly in Lent 1549, the sermons press the young king and his court with the duties of the magistrate: Latimer denounces the greed of landlords and enclosers, the plunder of church goods, the oppression of the poor, and the corruption of officials, urging the king to be the father of the commonwealth and warning that England's plagues are God's judgement on its sins.
works.significance: The classic example of court preaching in English and a prime source for the social history of Edwardian England; Latimer's plainspoken rebukes of the powerful made him the archetype of the prophetic preacher.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Westminster in Lent 1549, the year of the First Prayer Book, the rebellions of 1549, and the fall of Protector Somerset; printed by John Day in 1549, the sermons document the preaching office at the summit of the state and the social crisis of the mid-Tudor years.
works.characters: King Edward VI (addressee)
works.structure: Seven self-contained sermons, each on a set text, in Latimer's direct, colloquial, and anecdotal style, with running rebukes of his courtly audience.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Kingship and good rule
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The English Reformation

works.title: The Sermons of Mr. Yorick
altTitles: Sermons, by the Late Mr. Yorick
works.description: A collection of parish sermons published under the name of the fictional clergyman whose life the novels also report, and running to several volumes over the middle years of the decade. They are sermons of the conscience and of the passions, on temperance, on the nature of religious consolation, on the duty of mirth and on the danger of a hard heart.
works.plot: The discourses examine the religious emotions of ordinary people, pressing on their hearers the duty of open-heartedness and the sin of the self-flattering hearer. They treat the love of pleasure, the neglect of the afflicted, the temper of a winter evening and the use of religious melancholy. The argument is not doctrinal but diagnostic, aiming to persuade the conscience by the analysis of its own feelings.
works.significance: It supplies the serious underside of the author's reputation and is evidence of how the culture of feeling was worked through in the established church; several of the discourses were separately reprinted and translated.
works.meter: A spoken prose of the pulpit of the day, with the short sentence of application, the rhetorical question and the tender parenthesis; the cadence is deliberately colloquial and moving.
works.context: Published between 1760 and 1767 by a country clergyman who was simultaneously a fashionable writer, in the season of the sensible sermon and of the argument with enthusiasm, and often sold in numbers of the same bookseller as the fiction.
works.characters: Mr. Yorick as the preaching persona; the parish audience; the afflicted and the self-deceived of the instances
works.structure: A serial collection of printed sermons, each a short regular discourse with text, improvement and application, gathered into volumes with the persona of the preacher supplying the frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volumes carry the pseudonymous preacher's name and are documented in the author's correspondence, though the persona occasionally disguises the hand.

Marriage and women's conduct
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind

works.title: The Seven Lamps of Architecture
works.description: Published in 1849 with Ruskin's own etchings, and the first statement of the moral theory of architecture: the seven lamps of Sacrifice, Truth, Power, Beauty, Life, Memory and Obedience. It is a prose work of 1849 by John Ruskin; it belongs to Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Each lamp is a principle tested against buildings old and new; the lamp of Truth condemns the imitation of materials and the restoration of ancient buildings; the lamp of Memory makes buildings the record of a nation's past; the lamp of Obedience argues for the authority of tradition in architecture.
works.significance: The Seven Lamps founded the moral criticism of architecture and the Victorian Gothic Revival's intellectual programme; its attack on restoration led directly to William Morris's Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (1877), and its seven principles became the vocabulary of the Arts and Crafts movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The Victorian Gothic Revival, the restoration controversies of the 1840s (the 'Anti-Scrape' campaign Ruskin later supported), and the railway and industrial building of the period. The record dates the work as composed in 1848 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

works.title: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Fisher's exposition)
altTitles: This treatise concerninge the fruytfull saynges of Davyd the kynge and prophete in the seven penytencyall psalmes
works.description: John Fisher's devotional exposition of the seven penitential psalms, preached as sermons to Margaret Beaufort and published by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508; the first work of the English Catholic humanist reform tradition.
works.plot: The treatise expounds Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as a programme of penitence — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — applying each psalm to the life of the Christian penitent and to the passion of Christ as the ground of forgiveness.
works.significance: The finest English devotional prose before the Reformation controversy and a witness to the scriptural piety of the pre-Reformation English Church; its emphasis on preaching and scripture anticipates the reform movements on both sides of the sixteenth-century divide.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached as a Lenten course to the household of Lady Margaret Beaufort, the king's mother, whose confessor Fisher was; printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508 and reprinted in 1509 and 1525, it belongs to the devotional revival associated with the Charterhouse and the early humanist circle.
works.characters: David (as penitent)
works.structure: Seven sermon-treatises, one per psalm, each structured by the threefold division of the penitential process, with a preface to Margaret Beaufort.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
The Passion of Christ
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: The Shadow of a Gunman
works.form: Play in two acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 1923)
works.description: The first of O'Casey's Dublin plays: a poet is mistaken for an IRA gunman, with tragic consequences. It is a dramatic work of 1923 by Sean O'Casey; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Donal Davoren, a poet sharing a tenement room with the pedlar Seumas Shields, is assumed by the neighbours to be an IRA man on the run. When a raid comes, the innocent Tommy Owens is killed and Davoren's illusions are exposed, in a play that turns from comedy to tragedy in its last minutes.
works.significance: The Shadow of a Gunman founded O'Casey's Dublin cycle and the modern Irish tragicomedy: it was the Abbey's first great success with a working-class play.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the tragi-comedy that turns from farce to tragedy in a single scene.
works.context: The Irish War of Independence (1919–21) and its aftermath, the Dublin tenements, and the cult of the gunman in nationalist Dublin. The record dates the work as composed in 1922 and first published in 1923 and first performed in 1923 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.

works.title: The Shadow of Ashlydyat
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1863
works.description: Published in 1863 and Wood's best novel after East Lynne: a family curse, a bank failure and the destruction of a household. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Mrs Henry Wood; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Godolphin family of Ashlydyat is haunted by the shadow that appears before a death; the bank fails through the dishonesty of one of the sons, the family is ruined, and the survivors must rebuild their lives, while the shadow appears again before the final catastrophe.
works.significance: The Shadow of Ashlydyat is the finest of Wood's later novels and one of the best English sensation novels of the 1860s: its combination of family curse, commercial disaster and domestic realism made it a favourite, and it shows Wood's characteristic power of making the ordinary household the site of terror.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is direct, urgent narrative address.

works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. works.title: The Shadow of the Rope
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1902
works.description: Hornung's finest novel: a woman acquitted of murder, and the man who married her. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by E. W. Hornung; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Rachel Minchin is tried for the murder of her husband and acquitted; she flees to Australia, marries a stranger who knows her secret, and the novel works out the truth of the killing in a story of guilt, expiation and the colonial return.
works.significance: The Shadow of the Rope is Hornung's finest novel and one of the best sensation novels of the period: its study of a woman under suspicion and its colonial setting made it a critical favourite and a pioneer of the psychological crime novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrative by the admiring accomplice.
works.context: London and Australia at the turn of the century, and the new sensation of the newspaper murder trial.
