works.title: The Shadow over Innsmouth
works.description: The novella of the decayed port and the deep ones. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by H. P. Lovecraft; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Shadow over Innsmouth follows the student's visit to the decayed Massachusetts port of Innsmouth - the fish-like townsfolk, the Marsh family, the order of Dagon and the escape through the hotel - to the revelation of the narrator's own inheritance, in the novella that makes the degenerate town and the sea's gods the mythos's darkest chapter.
works.significance: The Shadow over Innsmouth is the mythos's novel of the blood and the town: its Innsmouth look, its deep ones and its narrator's inheritance made the degenerate port the classic setting of the modern horror.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript.
works.context: The Massachusetts coast of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed in 1931 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale.

works.structure: A novella of the visit, the escape and the inheritance. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.

works.title: The Shape of Things to Come: The Ultimate Revolution
altTitles: The Shape of Things to Come
Shape of Things to Come: The Ultimate Revolution
works.form: Future history (based on the film Things to Come, 1936)
works.description: A history of the next two centuries: the collapse of civilisation in a world war, the rise of a technocratic world state, and the flight to the moon. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale; Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Written as a manuscript by a diplomat of the future, the book narrates a world war beginning in 1940 that destroys civilisation, a plague, a long dark age, the emergence of a technological ruling order, its unification of the world, and the launching of the first lunar expedition — ending with the question of whether humanity will choose the stars or stagnation.
works.significance: The Shape of Things to Come is Wells's last great utopian statement and the most influential future history of the 1930s: it anticipates the world war, the bombing of cities, the plague and the world state, and its images passed directly into the cinema and into the political imagination of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The rise of fascism, the bomber and the fear of total war, the technocratic and utopian movements of the 1930s, and the new medium of the film (Korda's Things to Come, scripted by Wells, appeared in 1936).
works.characters: Dr Philip Raven; the World Council; the Modern State
works.structure: Future history narrated as a recovered manuscript with a framing preface and footnotes. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire.

works.title: The Shaughraun
works.description: The last of the great Irish melodramas: a fugitive, a villain and the Irish rogue. It is a dramatic work of 1874 by Dion Boucicault; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Robert Ffolliott, an Irish gentleman, is hunted by the informer Kinchela and the policeman; the shaughraun Conn, the wandering rogue, saves him through a series of tricks and disguises, and the play ends with the lovers united and the villain defeated.
works.significance: The Shaughraun was the last of the great Irish melodramas and the most popular of Boucicault's Irish plays: its rogue hero made the shaughraun a permanent figure of the Irish stage and it was the greatest Irish theatrical success of the century.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose of the domestic stage: the dialogue of the drawing room and the household, the revelation scene, the timed entrance, and the act ending on a discovery or a suspense. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the sensation scene of the waterfall or the fire.
works.context: Ireland in the 1870s, the Fenian fugitive and the Irish countryside. works.title: The Shaving of Shagpat: An Arabian Entertainment
altTitles: Shaving of Shagpat: An Arabian Entertainment
works.description: Published in 1855 (dated 1856) and praised by George Eliot and the Pre-Raphaelites: an Arabian romance in the manner of the Thousand and One Nights, in which the barber Shibli Bagarag must shave the miraculous hair of the tyrant Shagpat.
works.plot: Shibli Bagarag, a barber of the Persian city, is enlisted by the enchantress Noorna bin Noorka to shave the single hair on the head of the tyrant Shagpat, which makes him invulnerable; the quest takes him through a series of magic kingdoms, and the tale ends with the tyrant's fall and the release of his people.
works.significance: The Shaving of Shagpat is the finest English Oriental prose romance of the century and the work in which Meredith's comic and allegorical gifts first appeared.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
works.context: The 1850s, the Victorian taste for the Oriental tale (Lane's Thousand and One Nights, 1838-40). The record dates the work as composed in 1855 and first published in 1856 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.

works.title: The Shepheardes Calender
works.description: Spenser's first major work, published anonymously under the signature 'Immerito': twelve eclogues, one for each month, in which shepherds debate love, poetry, and religion in a deliberately archaic diction, with a learned commentary by 'E.K.' and woodcuts for each month.
works.plot: Through the revolving year, the shepherd Colin Clout loves the disdainful Rosalind, sings and despairs, while his fellows Hobbinol, Cuddie, Piers, and Palinode dispute the duties of poets and pastors; the sequence closes with December's elegy for the dying year.
works.significance: The manifesto of the new English poetry: it announced Spenser as the heir of Chaucer and Virgil and launched the Elizabethan pastoral tradition.
works.meter: A bravura display of stanza forms and line lengths — from four-stress couplets to sestinas — in a deliberately archaic 'shepherdly' English.
works.context: Published in the year of the proposed Anjou marriage and the height of the Puritan controversy; its ecclesiastical eclogues (May, July, September) engage the debate over the Elizabethan church.
works.characters: Colin Clout; Hobbinol; Rosalind; Cuddie; Piers; Palinode; E.K. (the commentator)
works.structure: A Virgilian eclogue book of twelve parts arranged by month, with framing apparatus (title page, argument, gloss) supplied by the commentator E.K.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by 'Immerito'; the authorship was an open secret and is uncontested.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
The English vernacular and national letters

works.title: The Shepherd's Calendar; with Village Stories, and Other Poems
works.form: Pastoral Poetry; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
works.description: A twelve-part seasonal poem, one number for each calendar month, in which an under-gardener and shepherd's voice records the field labour, weather, birds, and customs of an enclosed midland parish. The month-pieces are followed by village stories and shorter poems. The book is the most sustained attempt in English verse to write the working year itself as a form.
works.plot: Each month presents the tasks pressed upon the labourer at that season, the state of the sky and fields, and the sounds of birds and insects, with an underplot of the shepherd's solitary attendance on the flock. The speaker contrasts the paid day-work of the modern parish with the remembered commons and festivals of his childhood, and moralises on dependence, poverty, and the small economies of the hedge-side. The village stories and accompanying poems extend the same method to incidents of local narrative and to portraits of labouring figures.
works.significance: The work is regarded now as the author's most original achievement, a labouring almanac that anticipates later phenomenologies of seasonal time and that differs from Lake-poet meditation by making paid agricultural work, not retreat, its organising fact. Its publishing history also illustrates how much of the labouring poet's copy was shaped by commercial truncation.
works.meter: The month-pieces run mainly in closed accentual iambic couplets grouped into short stanzas, January for example in tetrameter couplets of six lines, with pentameter and lyric passages among the accompanying village stories; the verse is dense with field, weather, and bird names and avoids rhetorical closure.
works.context: Published after the author's marriage and settlement as an under-gardener in a great park, when his first fame had cooled and his books sold poorly; the volume is dedicated by permission to a noble patron whose family administered the borough and the annuity that supported him. The printed text is shorter than the manuscript, a reduction the author attributed to the publisher's economy.
works.characters: the shepherd-speaker; the flock and its dog; the thatcher, hedge-wright, and day-labourers of the parish; the birds whose note marks each month
works.structure: A cyclical sequence of twelve month-poems in calendar order, without a continuous plot; the unity is the year and the labouring routine, reinforced by framing references to the shepherd's attendance. Later volumes and modern editions restore passages the author complained had been cut by his publishers.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the publisher's abridgement of the manuscript affects length, not authorship.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Natural history, science, and the poetic eye
Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

works.title: The Shepherd's Week
altTitles: The Shepherd's Week, in Seven Days
works.description: Gay's burlesque pastoral of the seven days of a labouring week, in which the lovelorn swains of the conventional eclogue are replaced by clowns, ale, the wake, the farthing spit and the spilling of the dish of milk.
works.plot: Pastoral courtship, complaint and banquet are enacted by village swains in their real occupations, and the week closes with the plainest of love matches; the ancient machinery and the fine phrases of the eclogue are retained only to be laughed at.
works.significance: It broke the genteel pastoral and opened the way for the rustic and labouring representation of country life that the later century inherited, and it supplied the burlesque method Gay himself carried to the stage a dozen years later.
works.meter: Varied stanzaic imitation of the old pastoral and of Spenser, in short lines and plain diction, with the deliberate bathos of the closing couplet.
works.context: Published in the year of the quarrel over pastoral diction, when Pope's Pastorals and Philips's own eclogues had made the representation of real shepherds a critical issue; the volume's prose preface and notes are part of the same argument.
works.characters: the clowns and shepherd swains of the week; the shepherdesses of the courtship plots
works.structure: Seven day-poems, each on one pastoral action, with the introductory preface and the explanatory notes defending the low imitation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Shield of Achilles
works.form: Poem (two alternating stanza forms, one in rhyme royal)
works.description: A poem by W. H. Auden, first published in 1952 and the title poem of his collection The Shield of Achilles (1955), which won the National Book Award for Poetry in 1956. It rewrites Homer's description of the shield of Achilles in the Iliad: Thetis looks for scenes of peace and plenty and finds the barren, impersonal violence of the modern world.
works.summary: Thetis watches Hephaestus making the shield for her son; the scenes she expects and the scenes he makes: a faceless army, an execution watched by a passive crowd, a ragged urchin in a vacant field; her dismay.
works.plot: Thetis looks over Hephaestus's shoulder for vines and olive trees, marble cities and ships on untamed seas, but on the shining metal he has put an artificial wilderness under a sky like lead. An unintelligible multitude, a million eyes and boots in line, waits on a featureless plain while a voice without a face proves by statistics that some cause was just; they march away enduring a belief whose logic brings them somewhere else to grief. She looks for ritual pieties, white flower-garlanded heifers and libation, and sees instead a barbed-wire enclosure where bored officials lounge and sentries sweat, while a crowd of ordinary decent folk watch three pale figures led forth and bound to posts, unable to hope for help. She looks for athletes at their games and dancers moving to music, and sees a weed-choked field where a ragged urchin, aimless and alone, throws a stone at a bird; he takes for granted that girls are raped and that two boys knife a third, and has never heard of any world where promises are kept or one could weep because another wept. The thin-lipped armourer limps away, and Thetis cries out in dismay at what the god has made to please her son, the strong, iron-hearted, man-slaying Achilles, who would not live long.
works.significance: One of Auden's best-known poems and a classic modern ekphrasis, widely anthologised as a poem about war and atrocity; the collection it names won the National Book Award.
works.meter: The lyric, ballad-like short stanzas contrast with the grave, documentary long stanzas; flat, abstract diction for the modern scenes, sensuous imagery for the Homeric ones.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the Second World War, the camps and the show trials, and published in the first years of the Cold War; the 1955 collection gathers poems of about 1951-1954, including the sequences Bucolics and Horae Canonicae.
works.structure: Short-lined eight-line stanzas, giving what Thetis looks for, alternate with seven-line stanzas of longer lines in rhyme royal (ababbcc), describing what Hephaestus makes; a final short-lined stanza gives Thetis's cry.
themes: Power, the state and surveillance
Violence, crime and justice
War, combat and its aftermath

works.title: The Ship of Fools
altTitles: The Shyp of Folys of the Worlde
works.description: Barclay's Englishing of Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin version: a fleet of fools — the bookish fool, the covetous, the gluttonous, the lecherous clergy, the negligent bishops — each shipped aboard the vessel of folly in a comprehensive satire of the estates, printed by Richard Pynson in 1509.
works.plot: The narrator gathers the fools of every estate aboard the Ship of Fools; chapter by chapter, each folly is exhibited and moralized, from the pride of scholars to the corruption of Rome.
works.significance: The channel by which the great European estates satire reached England; its catalogue form and its moralizing woodcuts shaped a century of English satirical writing.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of fluent competence; the moralized catalogue form of the continental Renaissance satire.
works.context: Translated in the years before the Reformation, when anticlerical satire was already a licensed genre; printed by Pynson in December 1509.
works.characters: the narrator; the fools (by estate and vice)
works.structure: A catalogue satire in over a hundred sections, each an emblem of a folly with its moral appended; the ship provides the unifying frame.
works.attributionNotes: Barclay's adaptation of Brant (via Locher) is freely made with English additions; recorded as translation-adaptation.

Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: The Shoemaker's Holiday
works.description: Dekker's comedy of London's craftsmen: the shoemaker Simon Eyre rises from journeyman to Lord Mayor of London, his shop becomes the scene of the play's feasts and jests, and the love-plot of the disguised nobleman Lacy ('Hans the shoemaker') and the Lord Mayor's daughter Rose runs to its happy ending — the play ending with Eyre's feast for all the 'prentices of London and the king's own visit to the shop.
works.plot: Lacy, nephew of the Earl of Lincoln, refuses the arranged marriage and disguises himself as a Dutch shoemaker to serve Eyre and woo Rose; Eyre's fortunes rise through a lucky cargo to the mayoralty; the lovers are discovered and the earl's opposition overcome; and the Shrove Tuesday feast crowns the comedy with the king's blessing on the gentle craft.
works.significance: The classic of the citizen comedy — the play that gave the London trades their theatre, and the ancestor of the sentimental comedy of the next centuries.
works.meter: Prose and blank verse in Dekker's warmest register, with the shoemakers' songs and the feast scenes as its set pieces.
works.context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1599 and printed in 1600; its craftsmen's holiday and its king's visit celebrated the civic culture of London on the eve of the century's turn.
works.characters: Simon Eyre; Margery Eyre; Lacy (Hans); Rose Oatley; Sir Roger Oatley; the Earl of Lincoln; Firk; Hodge; Ralph Damport; Jane; Hammon; the King
works.structure: A five-act citizen comedy in the romantic mode, with the shop as its centre and the rise of Eyre as its civic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: National identity and Englishness
Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
altTitles: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters: Or, Proposals for the Establishment of the Church
works.description: A pamphlet written in the voice of a high-flown Church extremist, proposing that the only safe way with the Dissenters is to repeat the severity of the Counter-Reformation and destroy them root and branch. Its ironical impersonation was widely missed, and its writer was pursued for it some years later.
works.plot: A mock-moderate opening complains that the Church has been tamely forbearing, then argues that the sectaries are the real enemies of the constitution and of the settled clergy. It draws the analogy with popery, demands the closing of the meeting-places and the disabling of dissenters from trade and office, and concludes that if the laws will not do the work the people must burn them out. The appended defence explains the design as satire against the extremists of both sides.
works.significance: It is the classical instance of impersonative satire failing and succeeding simultaneously, the mask worn so exactly that it provoked the prosecution it was designed to discredit, and a case study in the law of seditious libel.
works.meter: Prose of the impassioned party harangue, mimicking the cadences and scriptural tags of the extremist pulpit; the irony is carried by an overwrought syntax of peroration.
works.context: Issued in February 1697/8 in the debate over the standing army, the Triennial Act and the toleration settlement; the writer was arrested in 1703 after a renewed issue, tried for a notorious libel and put in the pillory, an event made memorable in the verse of the day. Recorded here in this installment because it anchors an Augustan career, its date falling on the boundary of the period.
works.characters: the impersonated High Church projector; the dissenting minister; the addressers and the zealots of the Church; the legislator addressed by the pamphlet
works.structure: A short impersonative polemic in a single sustained voice, with a self-explaining apparatus of preface and defence attached at the later issues.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author both acknowledged and defended the design in the follow-up pamphlets, and the prosecution of 1703 establishes responsibility.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
The Spectator and Periodical Journalism

works.title: The Sidney Psalter
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: A complete metrical translation of the 150 Psalms: Psalms 1–43 by Sir Philip Sidney, the remainder by his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, who completed the project after his death — 171 poems in a dazzling variety of stanza forms and meters, the most ambitious poetic translation of the English Renaissance.
works.plot: The psalter follows the biblical sequence, rendering each psalm in a distinct verse form chosen to match its mood — penitential, hymnic, or imprecatory — with Mary Sidney's completion deliberately answering her brother's opening.
works.significance: A landmark of English devotional poetry and of women's literary agency; its formal virtuosity influenced Herbert, Vaughan, and the whole seventeenth-century tradition of sacred verse.
works.meter: An encyclopedia of English verse forms: sonnets, terza rima, sapphics, hexameters, and a vast range of stanza shapes, one per psalm.
works.context: Begun by Sidney in the 1580s, continued by his sister after his death in 1586, and completed about 1599; it circulated in manuscript among the godly aristocracy and was not printed in full until 1823.
works.characters: David (the psalmist); God
works.structure: 150 separate psalm paraphrases arranged in biblical order, with the two translators' portions joined at Psalm 43/44.
works.attributionNotes: The division of the psalms between the two Sidneys is established by the manuscripts and uncontested.
themes: Divine love and holy desire
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: The Siege of Jerusalem
works.description: An alliterative poem of some 1,300 lines on the Roman destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian and Titus, cast as vengeance for the crucifixion: the siege, the famine, the fall of the city, and the punishment of the Jews who bought and tortured Christ. A poem of notorious violence whose anti-Judaism reflects the worst of its age, and a major witness to the romance of Christian vengeance.
works.plot: Titus, healed by the vernicle, vows vengeance on the Jews; the poem narrates the siege and its horrors — the famine, the mother who eats her child, the crucifixions and selling of Jews — and the city's destruction, framed throughout as the working out of Christ's blood-debt.
works.significance: The most widely copied alliterative poem of its theme and a text of central importance — and difficulty — for the study of medieval Christian anti-Judaism in literature.
works.meter: Alliterative long lines in couplets and stanzaic clusters.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 in the north-west Midlands, from the French Vengeance de Nostre Seigneur and related sources; preserved in nine manuscripts, including the Thornton manuscript and Bodleian Laud Misc. 656.
works.characters: Vespasian; Titus; Pilate; Josephus; Caiaphas
works.structure: A single-movement siege narrative built from the French Vengeance tradition, with the torments of the Jews as its repeated set-pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Typology and biblical interpretation
Warfare and battle
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: The Siege of Rhodes
altTitles: The Siege of Rhodes, Made a Representation by the Art of Prospective in Scenes
works.description: Davenant's 'representation by the art of prospective in scenes, and the story sung in recitative music', staged at his house in Rutland during the Commonwealth; it is generally regarded as the first English opera.
works.plot: The Ottoman siege of Rhodes in 1522 is the historical frame; the love story of Alphonso, Ianthe, and Roxolana unfolds across five 'entries' (acts) of sung recitative and spectacular scenery.
works.significance: The first English opera, the first English stage to use painted perspective scenery, the first to employ a professional actress, and the prototype of the Restoration heroic drama.
works.meter: Recitative verse in pentameter couplets and quatrains; the first sustained use of sung drama in English.
works.context: Performed privately at Rutland House in May 1656 and publicly at the Cockpit in 1659, during the Commonwealth ban on public theatres; Davenant's innovations were tolerated because the work was billed as a musical entertainment.
works.characters: Solyman; Alphonso; Ianthe; Roxolana; Mustapha; the Admiral
works.structure: Five entries performed in painted perspective scenes with continuous recitative singing, no spoken dialogue, and a single female performer (Mrs Coleman).
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant; the music was by Matthew Locke, Henry Cooke, Charles Coleman, and George Hudson.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Religious persecution and martyrdom
Warfare and battle
movements: Commonwealth and Interregnum Literature
Heroic Drama
The Caroline Theatre

works.title: The Siege of Thebes
works.form: verse narrative in couplets (framed as Canterbury tale)
works.description: John Lydgate's continuation of the Canterbury Tales (c. 1420–22), presented as the monk of Bury's own tale on the return journey from Canterbury: the story of Thebes from the founding of the city by Cadmus through the tragedy of Oedipus, the war of the Seven, and the deaths of the Theban and Argive heroes. Its frame makes it the first great poem of the Chaucerian succession.
works.plot: Joining the pilgrims at Canterbury, Lydgate's monk tells the Theban story: Oedipus's parricide and incest, the quarrel of his sons Eteocles and Polynices, the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, the duel of the brothers, and the funeral of the heroes — a chain of fortune's falls moralized throughout.
works.significance: The first great act of Chaucerian imitation: by writing himself into the pilgrimage, Lydgate claimed Chaucer's mantle and set the pattern for the fifteenth-century canon of English poetry.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the Lydgate manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1420–22, in direct response to Chaucer's Knight's Tale (the Theban matter of its background), and copied with the Canterbury Tales in many manuscripts; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1497).
works.characters: the Monk of Bury (narrator); Oedipus; Eteocles; Polynices; Tydeus; Adrastus; Creon
works.structure: A Chaucerian frame (the return-journey tale) enclosing the three-part Theban narrative, with the 'tragedy' of Fortune as its moral armature.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Warfare and battle
movements: Fifteenth-Century Chaucerians

works.title: The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window
works.description: The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window is Lorraine Hansberry's second play, staged on Broadway in 1964: a drama of political disillusion and recommitment among the intellectuals of Greenwich Village, where she lived, with a largely white cast and a Jewish protagonist.
works.summary: Sidney Brustein, a restless Greenwich Village intellectual who owns a small newspaper, is drawn into a reform politician's campaign; around him are his wife, Iris, an aspiring actress, her two sisters, a Black friend engaged to one of them, and a gay playwright who lives upstairs.
works.plot: Sidney, cynical about politics after earlier causes, agrees to support Wally O'Hara, a reform candidate for local office, and hangs his campaign sign in the window. His marriage to Iris is failing, as she tires of his idealism and seeks commercial success. Her sister Mavis represents conventional middle-class respectability, and her younger sister Gloria, a call girl, hopes to marry Sidney's friend Alton Scales, a Black activist who rejects her when he learns her history. The reform campaign succeeds, but Wally proves to be controlled by the very machine he opposed. After a degrading night, Gloria kills herself in the Brusteins' apartment. Shattered, Sidney rejects despair and resolves, with Iris, to go on fighting for a better world.
works.significance: Less successful than her first play, it is valued as a rare Broadway drama of ideas about political commitment and as evidence of the range of Hansberry's concerns beyond racial themes.
works.meter: Witty, argumentative dialogue in the manner of a drama of ideas, combining comedy and melodrama.
works.context: Written in the early 1960s during the civil rights movement, while Hansberry was ill with cancer; the play kept running with the support of friends and admirers and closed on 12 January 1965, the day she died.
works.characters: Sidney Brustein; Iris Parodus Brustein; Mavis Parodus Bryson; Gloria Parodus; Alton Scales; David Ragin; Wally O'Hara
works.structure: Three acts in a realistic setting, building from comedy of manners to tragedy and a final affirmation.
themes: Alienation, absurdity and existential freedom
Power, the state and surveillance
Sexuality, desire and the closet

works.title: The Sign of Four
works.description: Published in Lippincott's in 1890 in the same issue as the first version of Dorian Gray: a case that begins with a missing officer, a pearl and a cipher, and ends with the Agra treasure and the Andaman Islander Tonga.
works.plot: Mary Morstan receives pearls from an unknown benefactor and consults Holmes; the investigation leads to the death of Bartholomew Sholto, the one-legged Jonathan Small and his companion Tonga, and the treasure lost in the Thames. Watson marries Mary Morstan.
works.significance: The Sign of Four is the fullest of the early Holmes novels and the most explicitly imperial: its plot turns on the loot of the Mutiny and on the colonial servant's revenge, and its atmosphere of fog, river and labyrinth set the tone of the London detective story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is the clue and the deduction.
works.context: The 1880s-90s, the Indian Mutiny of 1857, the Andaman Islands penal colony, and the opium dens of London. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Mary Morstan; Thaddeus Sholto; Jonathan Small; Tonga; Athelney Jones; Major Sholto
works.structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Detective Story and the Tale of Detection
themes: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
movements: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade

works.title: The Silent Partner
works.description: Published in 1871 and Phelps's industrial novel: the story of a New England mill owner's daughter who inherits the mill and the responsibility for its workers. It is a prose fiction work of 1871 by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Perley Kelso, a Boston merchant's daughter, becomes part owner of a mill at the death of her father and takes an interest in the workers; the novel follows the mill girl Sip Garth and her deaf-mute sister Catty, the death of the child worker Bub Mell, and a threatened strike that Perley's standing among the hands averts, and ends with Perley refusing the junior partner Stephen Garrick to remain a single woman dedicated to her workers, while Sip resolves never to bear children for the mills.
works.significance: The Silent Partner is one of the most important American novels of industrial labour between Davis and the naturalists and a founding text of the American novel of the woman reformer; its treatment of class, philanthropy and the single woman is unmatched in its period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is domestic detail extended into the afterlife.
works.context: The 1870s: the New England textile mills, the first woman's trade unions, and the American debate on industrial paternalism. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Perley Kelso; Sip Garth; Catty Garth, her deaf-mute sister; Stephen Garrick; Maverick Hayle; Mr Hayle, his father; Bub Mell
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Industrial wealth, accumulation, and the gospel of accumulation
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: American Realism and the Howells Program

works.title: The Silent South
works.description: Published in 1885 and the most courageous white southern book of the century on race: essays demanding civil rights and an end to the convict-lease system. It is a prose work of 1885 by George Washington Cable; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Cable argues that the South must accept the black citizen as an equal before the law, attacks the convict-lease system as slavery under another name, defends the public school for both races, and calls on the southern churches to lead the work of reconciliation.
works.significance: The Silent South is the central white southern text of the American struggle for racial justice in the nineteenth century: it cost Cable his southern audience and his livelihood, it was answered by every defender of the New South, and it remains one of the most important American documents of the post-Reconstruction debate on race.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is exact reproduction of Creole and black dialect.
works.context: 1885: the end of Reconstruction, the convict-lease system, the rise of Jim Crow, the Plessy case a decade later, and the northern review culture of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
works.structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George W. Cable. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Silver Darlings
works.description: The epic of the herring fishery and the clearance's son. It is a prose fiction work of 1941 by Neil Gunn; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The Silver Darlings follows Roddie, the boy of the cleared township, from the croft ruin through the herring fishery of the east coast - the drifters, the curing, the boom and the bust - to the mastery of the sea, in the epic prose of Gunn's northern cycle.
works.significance: The Silver Darlings is Gunn's epic of the north: it made the herring fishery the matter of the Scottish novel and its Roddie the classic figure of the cleared people's return to the sea.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain.
works.context: The Caithness and Aberdeen coasts in the great years of the herring fishery. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1941 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: Roddie, the clearance's son; the fisher folk; the curers and the buyers
works.structure: An epic of the fishery in the seasons of the herring and the voyages of the drifter. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Neil Miller Gunn. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle

works.title: The Silver King
works.description: First performed in 1882 and the most successful English melodrama of the decade: a ruined gentleman is accused of murder and redeemed by the love of a good woman. It is a dramatic work of 1882 by Henry Arthur Jones; it is catalogued here under Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Wilfred Denver, a spendthrift, is drunkenly present at a murder and believes himself the killer; he flees to America, becomes a successful prospector, and returns in disguise to clear his name and save his wife and children, in a melodrama of gambling, drink, escape and providential rescue.
works.significance: The Silver King was the most successful English melodrama of its decade and one of the finest examples of the form: its combination of moral seriousness and spectacular stagecraft made it a model for the serious melodrama, and it established Jones as the leading young dramatist of the 1880s.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose of the domestic stage: the dialogue of the drawing room and the household, the revelation scene, the timed entrance, and the act ending on a discovery or a suspense. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the strong melodramatic situation with a moral core.
works.context: 1882: the English melodrama of the 1880s, the gold rush of the American West, the temperance movement, and the Princess's Theatre productions of Wilson Barrett. The record dates the work as composed in 1882 and first published in 1882 and first performed in 1882 and it is catalogued under sensation drama and the domestic stage; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Wilfred Denver; Nellie Denver; Geoffrey Ware; Corkett; Jaikes; Skinner; Brierly
works.structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts, each closing on a discovery or a suspense, with the revelation scene placed at the crisis.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry A. Jones. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
works.form: Sketch and character-tale series with familiar essays and legendary romance; the prose tale of the supernatural is folded into essayistic framing
works.description: A series of essays, sketches and legends by a persona who looks at England and at old New York with the same tender irony. It contains the two tales that became national property, a village schoolmaster and a sleeper who wakes a generation later, together with essays on Christmas, on the antiquities of the Inns of Court and on Westminster Abbey. The volume made the American sketch a transatlantic form.
works.plot: The opening English papers, written in the voice of a retired essayist, meditate on lost friendships, on village churches and on the ceremony of old hospitality. The German and Dutch legends transpose European folk material into American settings: a sleepy hunter returns to find his world changed, and a nervous schoolmaster is undone by a headless horseman. Later English papers describe abbey, gallery and coach-roads as places where the past can still be felt. The concluding letters from an English visitor to his friends at home comment on theatre, society and the scenery of the British countryside.
works.significance: It established the literary sketch in America and made the short tale of willed belief a native form. Its two legends entered the schoolroom and the stage, becoming the most widely read American fiction before 1850. Its transatlantic double publication reshaped the terms of the exchange between American and British letters.
works.meter: Prose, with a few verse addresses and songs in familiar stanzaic metres
works.context: Written partly in England and published simultaneously in New York and London between 1819 and 1820, at a moment when American writers were still dependent on British publishing and British approval. Its English subject-matter answers the claim that the young nation had no picturesque past. Its Dutch-New-York legends were devised to give America an inherited legend of its own.
works.characters: Geoffrey Crayon; Rip Van Winkle; Ichabod Crane; Brom Bones; the headless horseman
works.structure: Loose miscellany of some three dozen papers under a unifying persona, with two internal sequences distinguished by setting: English essays and American or German legends.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; published under the persona rather than the author's own name, with the author identified in the advertisements.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
movements: The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch

works.title: The Slaves of Solitude
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1947
works.description: Hamilton's wartime masterpiece: a boarding house, a bully and the Blitz. It is a prose fiction work of 1947 by Patrick Hamilton; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Miss Roach, a single woman in her thirties, lives in a boarding house in Thames Lockdon during the Second World War; the arrival of the bullying Mr Thwaites and the American lieutenant Dayton makes her life a struggle for dignity in the small world of the boarding house.
works.significance: The Slaves of Solitude is Hamilton's wartime masterpiece and one of the finest English novels of the 1940s: its boarding house, its bully and its portrait of a single woman made it the great English novel of the home front and a central text of the literature of the Second World War.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the pub and the boarding house.
works.context: A London suburb in 1943, and the English boarding house in wartime. The record dates the work as composed between 1946 and 1947 and first published in 1947 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Miss Roach; Mr Thwaites; Lieutenant Dayton; Mrs Payne; Sheila; Vicki Kugelmann
works.structure: A novel in three parts, through a year of the war. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Hamilton (Hangover Square). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Small House at Allington
works.form: Novel in monthly parts (Cornhill); two volumes 1864
works.description: Serialised in the Cornhill in 1862-64 and published in 1864: the Barsetshire novel of the broken engagement, and the book in which Trollope's heroine Lily Dale refuses to marry after being jilted. It is a prose fiction work of 1864 by Anthony Trollope; it belongs to Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lily Dale is engaged to Adolphus Crosbie, who breaks the engagement to marry the daughter of a countess; she refuses the faithful love of Johnny Eames, who has loved her since childhood. The subplot follows the courtship of Crosbie's own unhappy marriage and the ambitions of the de Courcy family.
works.significance: The Small House at Allington is Trollope's deepest study of disappointed love and the most argued-about ending in his work: Lily Dale's refusal to marry has been read both as a failure of the marriage plot and as one of the earliest English novelistic defences of a woman's right to choose singleness.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The 1860s, the season and the marriage market, the position of the unmarried woman, and the world of the minor aristocracy and its hangers-on. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Lily Dale; Johnny Eames; Adolphus Crosbie; Alexandrina de Courcy; Lady Julia de Courcy; the Earl de Courcy; Mrs Dale; Bell Dale; Bernard Dale; Christopher Dale
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Snake's Pass
works.description: Published in 1890 and Stoker's first novel: a romance of the west of Ireland, of a lost treasure, a land dispute and a peasant legend of the Snake's Pass. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Bram Stoker; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Arthur Severn comes to the Mayo coast, falls in love with Norah Joyce, and becomes involved in the struggle over the land and the buried gold of the hill; the villain Murdock is exposed and the legend of the snake is explained.
works.significance: The Snake's Pass is a significant Irish regional novel of the Land War and the earliest evidence of Stoker's interest in folklore and in the power of place.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is epistolary and documentary collage.
works.context: The 1880s, the Irish Land War, the Congested Districts, and the folklore of the west of Ireland. The record dates the work as composed in 1890 and first published in 1890 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: The Snow-Image and Other Twice-Told Tales
works.form: Collection of short stories; children's fantasy
works.description: Published in 1851 and the final collection of Hawthorne's tales: stories of New England, of the artist and of the supernatural, including 'The Snow-Image', 'Ethan Brand' and 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux'.
works.plot: 'The Snow-Image' tells of two children who bring a snow girl to life and lose her to the fire; 'Ethan Brand' is the story of a man who has committed the unpardonable sin by searching for it in his own heart; 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux' is a young man's arrival in colonial Boston and his shaming of his relative.
works.significance: The Snow-Image contains some of Hawthorne's greatest tales, including 'Ethan Brand' and 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux', two founding texts of the American short story and of the American literature of the Puritan past.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The 1840s, the American gift-book market, and the New England historical imagination. The record dates the work as composed between 1840 and 1851 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
works.characters: Violet and Peony Lindsey and the snow-child ('The Snow-Image'); Ernest ('The Great Stone Face'); Ethan Brand; Robin and his kinsman Major Molineux; Richard Digby ('The Man of Adamant')
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.

works.title: The Solitary Man
works.form: Poetry collection (Georgian lyric in the war years)
works.description: The war-years collection: the solitary man and the observed country. It is a verse work of 1941 by Richard Church; it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The Solitary Man gathers the lyrics of the war years, the solitary man of the title poem set against the country and the season, in the plain observed line of the Georgian lyric.
works.significance: The Solitary Man is the war collection of the last Georgian lyricist: its solitary man carried the observed lyric through the second war and fixed Church's place in the lyric of the century.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain observed lyric of the country and the season.
works.context: England in the war years, and the country lyric of 1941. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1941 and first published in 1941 and it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
works.structure: A collection of war-years lyrics, the solitary man as the ordering figure. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.

works.title: The Solitary Reaper
works.form: Nature lyric and song, a lyrical ballad of the later and smoother manner; the poem thematises the relation between untranslated speech, music and memory, and is built as an illustration of the poet's own definition of composition.
works.description: A short lyric of four stanzas, suggested by a scene witnessed during a tour of the Highlands and written in November 1805, in which a peasant girl reaps and sings at the same time in a language the listening speaker cannot understand. The poem's force lies in the withheld meaning: because the sense of the song is unavailable, the speaker invents possible subjects for it, and then surrenders the guess to the sound itself. He carries that sound away as a possession of memory, and the lyric becomes one of the period's plainest demonstrations of what its own theory of recollection claimed for poetry.
works.plot: The speaker tells the valley to be still for one girl's song and watches her single in the field, reaping and singing at once. Since he cannot know what she sings, he asks whether it is some natural sorrow, loss or pain that may be and may be again, or an old, sad and forgotten story of battles long ago, and declares that no nightingale in the forests of the Arabian sand, nor cuckoo-bird in the farthest Hebrides, could have broken the silence of the seas with a happier measure. The girl turns to her labour and the song continues while she binds the sheaves, and the speaker listens motionless until the music stops. In the last stanza he reports that when he had seen and heard no more of it, the music was in his heart and was felt long after it was heard no more, as he lay on a couch in solitude or on a vacant pensive mood - that is, the song is recovered only in memory, and the poem records that recovery.
works.significance: The period's shortest and most quoted illustration of its account of poetry: an uncomprehended sound made permanent by memory, and a demonstration that Romantic lyric can take its subject from a failure of understanding. It was widely imitated and translated in the nineteenth century and remains a standard test case for discussions of lyric address and of the autonomous song.
works.meter: Four quatrains alternating four-beat and three-beat iambic lines with a rhyme scheme that gives the poem an unmistakable song-like regularity; the imperative openings and the repeated question give it the pattern of an air, deliberately unlike the broken stanzaic manner of the 1798 ballads.
works.context: Suggested by an incident on the tour of Scotland taken with his sister in 1803 and composed in November 1805, in the years in which the short lyrics of the 1807 collection were being gathered and the philosophy of the growing mind was being worked out in the long autobiographical poem. The scene of an English listener before a Gaelic song answers the period's vogue for Highland song and its collections of translated airs.
works.characters: The solitary Highland reaper; the travelling listener who remembers her song
works.structure: An occasional lyric moving through a single scene: apostrophe to the landscape, description, a speculative question about the song's meaning, and a retrospective stanza of remembrance, in which the interval between hearing and recalling constitutes the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author's own note identifies the scene as heard among a solitary Highland valley, and no rival claim has been made.

works.title: The Song of Hiawatha
works.description: The great American epic of the Native past: Hiawatha, his bride and the coming of the white man. It is a verse work of 1855 by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; it belongs to The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Hiawatha, the prophet of the Ojibwe, is born of Mudjekeewis and Wenonah, grows up in the care of Nokomis, fasts and wins his name, invents the arts of peace, marries Minnehaha, and at the end of the poem sails west with the prophet of the white man's God.
works.significance: The Song of Hiawatha was the most widely read long poem of the nineteenth century and the first American epic of the Native past: its trochaic tetrameter and its legendary hero gave America a national poem, and its worldwide success made American literature a force in translation.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The author's characteristic manner is the long narrative poem in regular tetrameter.
works.context: The Native American peoples of the Great Lakes before the arrival of the Europeans, and the American antiquarian interest in the Indian of the 1850s. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
works.characters: Hiawatha; Minnehaha; Nokomis; Mudjekeewis; Chibiabos; Pau-Puk-Keewis; the missionary
works.structure: Twenty-two cantos in trochaic tetrameter, from the birth to the departure. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. W. Longfellow. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Sophy
works.description: Denham's tragedy, performed and printed in 1642, set at the Persian court of Shah Abbas, in which court intrigue, jealousy, and the machinations of a favourite lead to the death of the prince and a catastrophe of political and personal ruin.

works.significance: A representative Caroline tragedy of exotic setting and political morality, notable as the dramatic work of the author of Cooper's Hill.
works.meter: Blank verse in a grave, sententious, neoclassical manner.
works.context: Performed in 1642 just before the theatres closed; Waller praised it and it was Denham's early bid for dramatic fame.
works.characters: the Sophy (Shah Abbas); the Prince; Mirza; the courtiers
works.structure: A five-act neoclassical tragedy in blank verse with an exotic Persian setting.

works.title: The Sorrows of Rosalie: A Tale, with Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Literary Annual and Keepsake Verse
works.description: The first volume of a young married woman poet, published in 1829 and containing a long narrative tale of a seduced and abandoned girl together with lyric pieces, translations from the Spanish, and a rendering of the cow-herd's song. The volume announced a feminine Byronic manner, and it was praised in a leading Scottish periodical in the years when that review shaped Romantic taste. Its title poem made the author's reputation and started a connection with the annual and gift-book market that became her livelihood.
works.plot: Rosalie, a poor and beautiful peasant girl, is won and deserted by a man of rank; the poem follows her from the first flattering attention to the loss of her child, the public shame of the village, and the death of her hopes, with the lover's return insufficient to repair what has been done. The tale is told in a continuous meditative address to the sufferer, and the surrounding pieces give the same situation in shorter form, including a fragment on Elvira, the young crusader, Linda Albaya, and the lyric The One you loved the best. Translations and imitations from the Spanish supply the volume's secondary music.
works.significance: The volume is a key document of the woman poet's appropriation of the Byronic tale of outcast guilt for the specifically feminine subject of seduction and deserted motherhood. It established the author as a professional contributor to the annuals and anticipated the protest against the legal disability of married mothers that she later conducted in prose and in the press.
works.meter: The tale runs in measured rhymed stanzas of the popular sentimental line, with frequent apostrophe and refrain; the lyrics use common measure and the song translations keep the stave and burden of the original Spanish and Provençal forms.
works.context: Published in 1829 by a London house then supplying the fashionable annuals, dedicated to a noble patron of letters, at the moment when the gift-book economy was creating paid work for women writers. The author's own position, a marriage already known to be unhappy and a separation shortly to produce a public legal struggle over the custody of a child, gave the seduction subject its biographical edge for later readers.
works.characters: Rosalie; the lover of higher rank who deserts her; her child; the villagers who witness her shame; Elvira; Linda Albaya
works.structure: A single long narrative poem of seduction and death, framed by a section of shorter lyrics and translations, with no organising frame across the volume; the tale moves by stages of feeling rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the volume carries the author's name on the title page and no piece in it has been reassigned.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: The Sorrows of Satan
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1895
works.description: The bestseller that broke every record of the trade: the devil comes to London to test a poor novelist. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Marie Corelli; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Geoffrey Tempest, a starving writer, is offered wealth and fame by a mysterious stranger, Prince Lucio Rimanez, who is Satan; the novel follows Tempest's rise in London society, his love for Sibyl Elton and the destruction of everyone who accepts the devil's bargain.
works.significance: The Sorrows of Satan broke every record of the Victorian book trade, selling in huge numbers on both sides of the Atlantic, and it is the most spectacular English bestseller of the 1890s. Its Satan as a fashionable man about town made the diabolic bargain into a permanent popular subject.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the occult machinery of the romance — electricity, reincarnation, the astral body.
works.context: London in the 1890s, the literary marketplace, the new mass press and fashionable society. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Geoffrey Tempest; Prince Lucio Rimanez; Sibyl Elton; Lady Sybil Elton; Mavis Clare
works.structure: A first-person narrative in five books, from the garret to the great house. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Soul of the Indian
works.description: Published in 1911 and the foundational English account of Dakota religion: an interpretation of Native American spirituality for a white readership. It is a prose work of 1911 by Charles Eastman; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Eastman explains the Dakota belief in the Great Mystery, the practice of prayer and the vision quest, the reverence for the natural world and for the dead, and argues that the Native American religion is a form of natural monotheism closer to the spirit of Christianity than the white man's own conduct.
works.significance: The Soul of the Indian is the foundational English account of Native American religion and one of the most important Native American books of the century: its interpretation of Dakota spirituality shaped the white American understanding of Native religion, and it remains the classic statement of the Native American religious tradition.

works.title: The Souls of Black Folk
works.description: The founding text of modern Black American literature: the colour line and the double consciousness. It is a prose work of 1903 by W. E. B. Du Bois; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Du Bois combines history, sociology, memoir, fiction and the spiritual into fourteen essays that analyse the position of the Black American after emancipation: the Freedmen's Bureau, Booker T. Washington, the Black church, the sorrow songs and the death of his own son.
works.significance: The Souls of Black Folk created the modern literature of the colour line and gave the century its central idea of double consciousness: its essays, its spirituals and its portrait of Black life made it the founding text of Black American literature and one of the great American books.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the essay and the sociological survey side by side.
works.context: The United States after Reconstruction, and the conditions of Black American life in 1903. works.title: The Sound and the Fury
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1929
works.description: Faulkner's masterpiece and one of the most formally daring novels of the century: the fall of the Compson family. It is a prose fiction work of 1929 by William Faulkner; it belongs to The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Compsons of Jefferson, Mississippi — the alcoholic Quentin, the idiot Benjy, the lost Candace (Caddy) and the brutal Jason — decline over thirty years, and the novel tells the same events four times: through Benjy's associative memory, Quentin's suicidal day at Harvard in 1910, Jason's cynical narration, and finally the third-person account of Dilsey, the Black servant who holds the family together.
works.significance: The Sound and the Fury is Faulkner's masterpiece and one of the great novels of the century: its four narratives, its rendering of idiocy and memory, and its portrait of the Compsons gave American literature its most radical experiment in form and its deepest study of the Southern past.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the long retrospective sentence with its parentheses and its piled-up subordinate clauses.
works.context: Jefferson, Mississippi, in 1910 and 1928, the decline of the Southern aristocracy, the Black servant community and the burden of the Southern past. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Benjy Compson; Quentin Compson; Jason Compson; Caddy Compson; Dilsey; Miss Quentin; Herbert Head
works.structure: Four sections: Benjy's, Quentin's, Jason's and a third-person section centred on Dilsey. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Cuthbert Falkner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The South English Legendary
works.description: The earliest great collection of verse saints' lives in Middle English, compiled in the south-west (probably Gloucestershire) c. 1270–85: a cycle of some 300 poems following the church year, from St Michael through the apostles and martyrs to All Souls. Its rollicking couplets and marvel-filled narratives made it the most popular legendary in medieval England.
works.plot: Each entry narrates a saint's life, martyrdom, or feast — with dragons, tortures, and miracles — and draws the moral for the hearers; the collection includes the famous account of St Brendan's voyage and lives of English saints such as Thomas Becket.
works.significance: The foundational text of popular English hagiography and a principal source for Mirk's Festial and the later legendary tradition.
works.meter: Septenary (fourteener) couplets, loose and lively, designed for public reading.
works.context: Compiled in the 1270s–1280s in the diocese of Worcester or Hereford, for parish and household reading; copied and expanded in some sixty manuscripts into the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar (Thomas Becket, Brendan, Edmund, Cecilia, and many others)
works.structure: A calendrical cycle of independent verse legends, ordered by the liturgical year, in a frame of prologue and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; compilational authorship by one or more clerical redactors.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: The Spanish Scene
works.form: Prose of the arts (Spain, the baroque and the eye)
works.description: The book that created the English prose of the arts: Spain seen as a picture. It is a prose work of 1927 by Sacheverell Sitwell; it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Critical Essay and the Modern Review.
works.plot: The Spanish Scene describes Spain - the Escorial, the cathedrals, the Velazquez and the Greco, the bullring and the street - in the cadence of the poem, and created the English prose of the arts as a genre of its own.
works.significance: The Spanish Scene created the English prose of the arts: its Spain seen as a picture made the description of painting and architecture a literary genre and established Sacheverell Sitwell as its master.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The author's characteristic manner is the long, loaded, alliterative line of the baroque lyric.
works.context: Spain in the 1920s, and the baroque revival of the connoisseur. The record dates the work as composed in 1926 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; critical essay and the modern review.
works.structure: A book of the arts in chapters of the scene, from the Escorial to the bullring. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Sir Sacheverell Sitwell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book

works.title: The Spanish Tragedy
works.description: Kyd's revenge tragedy, the most popular play of its generation: the ghost of Don Andrea and the personified Revenge watch from above as Hieronimo, Knight Marshal of Spain, discovers that his son Horatio has been murdered by the prince Balthazar and Lorenzo, and — after his wife Isabella's suicide — avenges him by staging a play in which the murderers die, biting out his own tongue before stabbing himself.
works.plot: Andrea's ghost, slain in battle by Balthazar, returns with Revenge to see justice done; Horatio is hanged in the arbour by Balthazar and Lorenzo; Hieronimo's madness, his laments, and the discovery of the murderers fill the middle acts; the play-within-the-play 'Soliman and Perseda' becomes the engine of revenge, and the survivors' blood ends the tragedy.
works.significance: The fountainhead of Elizabethan revenge tragedy — the play that taught the English stage the ghost, the delay, and the play-within-the-play.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong rhetorical set pieces — Hieronimo's laments and the additions of 1602 (probably by Jonson) — with the famous 'in a word' tableaux.
works.context: Performed from about 1587 and printed in 1592; revived with additions in 1602; it established the revenge formula that Hamlet, Titus Andronicus, and the Jacobean revenge school all answer.
works.characters: Hieronimo; Bel-Imperia; Horatio; Lorenzo; Balthazar; Isabella; the Ghost of Andrea; Revenge; Pedringano; Serberine; the Viceroy of Portugal
works.structure: A revenge tragedy framed by the choric ghost-and-Revenge, built on the discovery-and-delay pattern, and climaxing in the play within the play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Revenge and justice
The public theatre and the players' world
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: The Sparagus Garden
works.description: Brome's comedy of London society set in the fashionable asparagus gardens of Lambeth Marsh, in which two country women come to London to better themselves and are drawn into the intrigues of the city and the garden.
works.plot: Martha and Rebecca travel to London; Martha is seduced into a false marriage by the gallant Touchwood, Rebecca is courted by the honest Striker; the Sparagus Garden provides the social arena where the deceptions are exposed.
works.significance: One of the sharpest Caroline comedies of urban topography and social mobility, and Brome's fullest treatment of the theme of the country woman in the city.
works.meter: Prose dominant with verse.
works.context: Performed at the Salisbury Court Theatre in 1635 and published in 1640; the Lambeth Marsh asparagus gardens were a notorious resort of fashionable London.
works.characters: Martha; Rebecca; Touchwood; Striker; Annabel; Samuel; Lady Annabel; Snoop; the Host
works.structure: Five acts with a strong topographical unity around the garden.
