works.title: The Spectator and Tatler Papers (Addison)
works.description: Addison's contribution to the daily and weekly essay papers he conducted with Steele: the club and character papers, the imagination essays, the Milton criticism, the pastoral series and the oriental tales, which together made the polite essay the century's instrument of everyday moral judgment.
works.plot: Mr. Spectator, who has resolved neither to laugh nor to be serious, presents himself and the club of which he is the silent censor, then reports the speeches, projects and follies of its members and of the citizens, families and readers whose letters arrive at his desk.
works.significance: Addison's papers gave English prose its most widely taught model, invented the character-based periodical essay, and with the imagination and Milton essays installed a criticism of taste and genius inside neoclassical rules.
works.meter: Prose in the balanced middle style Addison theorised, with periodic sentences, tagged couplet quotations from the poets, and the rhythmically clause-balanced close; the papers on verse discuss the couplet and blank verse explicitly.
works.context: The daily Spectator ran from March 1711 to December 1712 and was revived weekly in 1714, exploiting coffee-house and tea-table reading, the provincial postal network and the lapse of the licensing Act; the Addison-Steele partnership divided the papers unevenly and ended in public coolness.
works.characters: Mr. Spectator; Sir Roger de Coverley; Sir Andrew Freeport; Will Honeycomb; Captain Sentry; the club of the Spectator; the letter-writing public
works.structure: A serial miscellany of short unsigned-to-signed papers, framed by a recurring persona and an intermittently advancing club narrative, with inset tales, letters to the editor and critical dissertations.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative by formation: the papers were produced by Addison and Steele together, with contributions from Hughes, Berkeley, Miss Manley and others; individual ascriptions in the early numbers remain partly conjectural, and this record covers the Addisonian share.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: The Spirit of Place and Other Essays
altTitles: Spirit of Place and Other Essays
works.description: Published in 1899 and the second of Meynell's essay collections: studies of landscape, travel and the genius of particular places, from the English downs to Rome. It is a prose work of 1899 by Alice Meynell; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: The essays consider what makes a place speak — the spirit of a river, the atmosphere of a town, the look of a country in a particular light — and argue that the artist's task is to see the place as it is rather than to impose a mood upon it.
works.significance: The Spirit of Place is the classic English collection of topographical essays and a key text in the literature of place; it is the book in which Meynell's prose style reaches its greatest refinement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short lyric metres with a delicate rhythmic suspense.
works.context: The 1890s, the vogue for the topographical essay, the English countryside movement, and the Catholic imagination of place. The record dates the work as composed in 1899 and first published in 1899 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alice Christiana Gertrude Meynell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Regional identity and the American sectional character

works.title: The Spirit of Prayer
altTitles: The Spirit of Prayer, or the Soul rising out of the Vanity of Time
The Spirit of Prayer in Three Parts
works.description: Law's mystical treatise on prayer as the breath of the inward soul, opposing the formal 'prayers of the mouth' to the ceaseless spirit of devotion. Part I appeared in 1733 and Parts II and III followed in 1734, extending the argument into a theology of the believer's constant intercourse with God.
works.plot: Law argues that the Christian life is essentially a spirit and disposition, of which vocal prayers are only the shell; true prayer is the soul's ascending sense of dependence and love. He shows from Scripture and the Lord's Prayer why a form of words is nothing without the wants, humours, and temper it expresses. The later parts work out the practice: the universal, unceasing offering of common life, prayer as the soul rising out of the vanity of time into eternity, and the believer's participation in the intercession of Christ. Formal religion and the love of the world are thus exposed as the same failure of spirit.
works.significance: It transmitted the language of seventeenth-century mysticism into eighteenth-century popular devotion and shaped, among others, the inward-prayer tradition that Methodism and the Oxford Movement both inherited.
works.meter: Incantatory, paratactic prose of long accumulating sentences, borrowing the rhythms of law and the Psalms; the argument advances almost by cadence.
works.context: Written after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment and under the influence of his reading of Jacob Boehme and the German mystical tradition, and published in 1733-34 when the blasphemy and Convocation controversies made inward religion a polemical subject.
works.structure: Three progressive parts, each a devotional argument from Scripture followed by practical direction and spiritual anatomy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Divine love and holy desire
Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
movements: The English Mystics
The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: The Spirit of the Age
altTitles: The Spirit of the Age; or, Contemporary Portraits
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch in the revived Theophrastan manner, combined with critical review and political character-writing.
works.description: A series of contemporary portraits published in 1825 and usually taken to be its author's best book, which gives the name of the age to a collection of critical and political characters. Its plan is to read the mind of the time through a series of individuals, poets, essayists, critics, advocates, statesmen and men of science and of the church, each essay treating its subject as the exponent of a habit of mind rather than as a private person. The book is at once the most acute record of English literature in the 1820s and a specimen of the character-writing revived by the Romantic essayists.
works.plot: The preface argues that a great age of literature may be recognised by its dominant habits of mind, and that the present is an age of discussion, of personality and of transition. The portraits of the poets of the northern lakes, of the poet of abstraction and of the writer of romantic tales are drawn so as to show a poetry of feeling and a poetry of ideas parted from the passion of the public, and the younger and more revolutionary singers are placed under the head of a poetry of motion and of hope. The men of the bar, of the banks, of the church and of the great quarterly journal are given as the characters of an age of enquiry and of party, and the closing papers pass from letters to the arts, with the portrait of the first actor of the London stage and of the one great living painter. Through the whole series the argument is that the age is divided between the spirit of party and the love of the ideal, and that the truest criticism reports the mind of its writer with the same sympathy with which the dramatist reported the minds of his characters.
works.significance: The most quoted book of contemporary portraits in English and the standard account of the literary and intellectual temper of the 1820s, from which most later histories of the period still take their phrases for its poets and its critics. Its method of treating a living writer as the exponent of a habit of mind became the model of the character essay, and its sentences on poetry and on the age are a permanent part of the vocabulary of criticism.
works.meter: Prose of the author's most concentrated kind, built of balanced antithesis, of the short sentence of verdict and of the long period of accumulation, with a constant use of the epigrammatic turn and of the summarising clause.
works.context: Published in London in 1825, several of the papers having appeared during the two preceding years in the magazines, in a season of intellectual and political expectation before the changes in the representation and in the press that followed; the author's own fortunes were at their lowest point, and the portraits of living writers were read as the criticism of a rival and a former friend.
works.characters: The living writers, critics, pleaders, bankers, statesmen and men of the church and of the stage whose portraits make the series; the essayist himself, who comments on the temper of his own age and on the trade of the literary profession
works.structure: A series of some twenty-four independent character-essays, with a general preface on the age and no continuous argument; the unity is that of the method, each paper taking one public figure as the exponent of a habit of mind, and the order being loosely arranged by the divisions of letters, of public affairs and of the arts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a second series of portraits, contributed to another journal, appeared some years later and is printed separately in the collected editions.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The public sphere, print, and the periodical
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review

works.title: The Spleen
works.description: Anne Finch's Pindaric ode on melancholy, depression, and the 'spleen' — a condition she herself suffered — which explores its physical, psychological, and gendered dimensions and defends the imagination and poetry against its deadening effects.
works.plot: The ode describes the many forms and causes of the spleen (vapours, grief, the body's disorder), its particular burden on women, and the consolation of friendship, verse, and faith.
works.significance: An important early poem on depression and on the woman writer's condition, admired for its candour and its Pindaric form, and central to Finch's recovered reputation.
works.meter: The irregular Pindaric form on Cowley's model, with varied and expressive line lengths.
works.context: Written in the 1690s and printed in a 1701 miscellany (attributed to 'Ardelia'); it reflects Finch's own lifelong depression and the period's discourse on the spleen and melancholy.
works.characters: the poet; the Spleen (personified)
works.structure: A Pindaric ode in varied line lengths and stanzas, moving through description, lament, and consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Published under Finch's pastoral name 'Ardelia'; attribution uncontested.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Melancholy and self-analysis

works.title: The Sport of the Gods
works.description: Published in 1902 and Dunbar's finest novel: the destruction of a respectable black family by a false accusation, and their migration to New York. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Paul Laurence Dunbar; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel.
works.plot: Berry Hamilton, a faithful servant, is imprisoned for a theft committed by his employer's brother; his wife and children move to New York, where his daughter falls into the theatre and prostitution and his son into gambling, and the family is destroyed before the truth is discovered.
works.significance: The Sport of the Gods is the first major African-American novel of urban naturalism and one of the founding texts of the literature of the Great Migration: its picture of the city's destruction of a black family is unmatched in its period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The author's characteristic manner is dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill.
works.context: 1902: the black migration to northern cities, the New York of the Tenderloin, and the American naturalist novel. The record dates the work as composed in 1901 and first published in 1902 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
works.characters: Berry Hamilton; Fannie Hamilton; Joe Hamilton; Kitty Hamilton; Maurice Oakley; Francis Oakley; Sadness
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Paul Dunbar. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

The American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy

works.title: The Spy
altTitles: The Spy: A Tale of the Neutral Ground
works.form: Historical novel and romance of the Revolutionary war, with picaresque disguise plot and topographical description
works.description: The first important American historical novel and the book that created a native romance of the Revolution. Set in the neutral ground between the British lines and the American army in Westchester County, it makes espionage, disguise and neighbour-against-neighbour violence the substance of national history. Its pedlar of small wares, who turns out to be a spy of many identities, is the founding American figure of the disguised hero.
works.plot: In the neutral ground of Westchester County, between the British lines in New York and the American army, the daughters of a Loyalist colonel are repeatedly thrown into the power of British officers, partisan leaders and the lawless skinners who infest the border. A pedlar of small wares, treated by both sides now as a simpleton and now as a knave, carries intelligence for the American command under a studied disguise. Hospitality, neutrality and betrayal alternate in a country where neighbour hunts neighbour, and where an old Whig widow's house becomes a refuge. The novel closes with the condemnation of a British officer taken as a spy and with the disclosure of the pedlar's real service to the American cause.
works.significance: It gave American fiction its first historical romance and its first national hero of concealment. Its neutral ground became the model for the American frontier as a moral borderland. It made the historical novel the dominant American narrative form for a generation.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1821-1822 from Westchester tradition, the author's childhood recollections and the histories of the war then current. It appeared in the same season as the Scottish historical romance and adapted its methods to republican material. Its treatment of Tory persecution reflects the nationalist reconciliation of the 1820s.
works.characters: Harvey Birch the pedlar; Colonel Wharton; the Wharton sisters; Sarah the young Quaker; Kirkwood the deserter
works.structure: Third-person historical novel with a choric neutral community at its centre; the plot of espionage is delayed by disguises and revealed at the close, in the manner of a discovered identity romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the author later added a preface and notes defending his use of documentary sources.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
Warfare and battle
movements: Cooper and the American Romance of Forest and Sea

works.title: The Staple of News
works.description: Ben Jonson's late satirical comedy on the new business of news-gathering, in which a 'Staple of News' is established to supply the gulls of London with fabricated intelligence and young Pecunia is courted by fortune hunters.
works.plot: Thomas Barber opens an office that manufactures news for the town; the young heir Pennyboy junior squanders his fortune chasing novelty; the Censure and Prologue figures comment throughout, and the play ends with the Staple's collapse.
works.significance: Jonson's most explicit commentary on the new print culture and journalism, and an important document in the history of the news; it was long considered one of his weaker late plays.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in February 1626 and published in the first folio of Jonson's works in 1631; it attacks the newly emerging news-sheet industry.

works.structure: Five acts with intermeans in which a Censure and a Prologue debate the play's own merits.

works.title: The Steel Glass
works.description: Gascoigne's satirical mirror poem: renouncing the flattering crystal of courtly verse, the poet holds up the 'steel glass' of truth to every estate — kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, and ploughmen — in the first original English poem in blank verse, its plain style answering its plain purpose.
works.plot: The poet's glass shows each estate its vices: the king's flatterers, the soldier's greed, the lawyer's delays, the merchant's falsehood, and the farmer's honest toil praised last and most; the poem ends with the satirist's defence of his plain dealing and his glass's unflattering truth.
works.significance: The first original blank-verse poem in English and the bridge between medieval estates satire and Elizabethan satire proper.
works.meter: Blank verse — the first original English poem in the form — in the plain style its argument demands.
works.context: Published in 1576, in Gascoigne's final year, with the woodcut frontispiece of the author; it answered the court's demand for moral counsel in the decade of the Northern Rebellion's aftermath.
works.characters: the poet; the estates personified (kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, ploughmen)
works.structure: A single continuous satire in the estates tradition, ordered by rank from court to country, with the glass as its governing emblem.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: The Stepmother
works.description: The play of the stepmother and the new domesticity. It is a dramatic work of 1924 by Githa Sowerby; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: A widowed stepmother and her stepchildren in the house of the new domesticity; the play that carried Sowerby's theme of the woman and the household into the post-war period.
works.significance: The Stepmother is Sowerby's play of the stepmother and the new domesticity: its household and its woman's question carried her theme into the post-war period.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain dialogue of the provincial household and the works.
works.context: England in the early 1920s, the new domesticity and the household. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: the stepmother; the stepchildren; the household
works.structure: Three acts, in the house of the new domesticity. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katharine Githa Sowerby. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
The suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity

works.title: The Stickit Minister
works.description: The book that made Crockett famous: Galloway ministers, probationers and the Covenanting past. It is a prose fiction work of 1893 by Samuel Rutherford Crockett; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: A sequence of linked stories of the Galloway parish: the minister who never got a charge, the Cameronian who remembers the persecution, the schoolmaster and the boy, told in the dialect and the sentiment of the south-west.
works.significance: The Stickit Minister was the book that made Crockett famous and the central text of the kailyard school: it created the Galloway parish as a literary country and sold in huge numbers on both sides of the Atlantic.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Galloway dialect in direct speech.
works.context: Galloway in the 1890s and the memory of the Covenanting wars of the seventeenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1893 and first published in 1893 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: the stickit minister; the Cameronian; the schoolmaster; the parish of Barbag
works.structure: A sequence of linked stories with a frame of parish memory. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Still Centre
works.description: Spender's third collection: the still centre, Spain and the coming war. It is a verse work of 1939 by Stephen Spender; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Thirties Political Lyric and the Auden Generation; Trench Lyric and the War Poem.
works.plot: The collection gathers Spender's poems of 1936-39 - 'The Still Centre', 'Spain 1937' revised, 'The pyre', 'Ultima ratio regum', the elegies for the Spanish dead and the poems of the approaching war - in which the political commitment of the Thirties is tested against the private need for a still centre.
works.significance: The Still Centre is Spender's finest collection and the last great book of the Auden generation before the war: its title poem and its Spanish elegies made the argument between political commitment and private integrity the subject of the Thirties poem, and 'Ultima ratio regum' remains one of the most quoted poems of the decade.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric line held in traditional stanza.
works.context: England and Spain in the late 1930s, and the months before the Second World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1939 and first published in 1939 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under thirties political lyric and the auden generation; trench lyric and the war poem.
works.structure: A collection of lyrics, elegies and the long title poem. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stephen Harold Spender. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Stones of Sacrifice
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1915
works.description: Published in 1915 and Caird's last novel: a study of heredity, education and the sacrifice demanded of women by the family. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Mona Caird; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: A young woman of scientific mind is asked to give up her research to nurse the family that has stunted her; the novel examines heredity, the claims of the old and the young, and the ethics of self-sacrifice, and refuses the consolations of conventional piety.
works.significance: The Stones of Sacrifice is Caird's most concentrated late work and shows the continuity of the feminist argument into the twentieth century: it treats heredity and self-sacrifice with a scientific seriousness rare in fiction and it is an important bridge between Victorian and modern feminism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical essay with a plain and logical argument.
works.context: 1913-15: the science of heredity, the suffrage campaign at its height, and the pre-war debate on the family. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Stones of Venice
works.form: Architectural and social criticism in three volumes
works.description: Published in three volumes between 1851 and 1853 and the central work of Ruskin's middle period: a history of Venetian architecture and a moral history of the Venetian republic that becomes, in the chapter 'The Nature of Gothic', a criticism of industrial labour.
works.plot: Volume I treats the foundations and the Byzantine style, Volume II the Gothic palaces and the 'Nature of Gothic' chapter, Volume III the Renaissance and the fall of Venice; the argument is that the decline of Venetian architecture follows the decline of Venetian faith and that the workers of the Gothic cathedral were free men while those of the Renaissance were slaves.
works.significance: The Stones of Venice is the founding text of the social criticism of art: 'The Nature of Gothic' gave Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement their central doctrine that good art depends on the free labour of the craftsman, and through Morris it shaped the socialism of the 1880s and the twentieth-century theory of design.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The 1848 revolutions and the siege of Venice, the Victorian Gothic Revival, and the pre-Raphaelite critique of industrial labour; the book was read by Morris at Oxford in 1853 and changed his life. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1853 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: The Story and the Fable
works.description: One of the finest Scottish autobiographies: Orkney, the ruined family in Glasgow, and the myth of Eden. It is a prose work of 1940 by Edwin Muir; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Autobiography and the Modern Memoir; Biography and the Modern Life.
works.plot: Muir recounts his Orkney childhood on a farm, the family's move to Glasgow and its destruction by poverty and illness, his work in a bone factory and an office, and the slow discovery of his vocation — and interprets it through the myth of the fall and the lost Eden that shapes his poetry.
works.significance: The Story and the Fable is one of the great Scottish autobiographies and the key to Muir's poetry: its account of the fall from Orkney into Glasgow made the myth of Eden the centre of his work, and it is one of the finest autobiographies of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of autobiography: the first-person narrative of the life, the set-piece of the formative scene, the quotation from letters and diaries, and the reflection on the formation of a self. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric.
works.context: The Orkney islands and the Glasgow slums of the 1890s and 1900s, the First World War, and the literary London of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under autobiography and the modern memoir; biography and the modern life.
works.characters: Edwin Muir; his family; Orkney; Glasgow
works.structure: Autobiographical chapters interspersed with the mythic interpretation. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers.

works.title: The Story of a Modern Woman
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1894
works.description: The finest New Woman novel of the 1890s: a woman artist's fight for independence. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by Netta Syrett; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Mary Erle, a young woman artist, must support herself after her father's death; the novel follows her education, her work as an illustrator, her friendships, her love affairs and her refusal of the marriage that would end her independence.
works.significance: The Story of a Modern Woman is one of the most important New Woman novels of the 1890s: its portrait of the woman artist's struggle for independence gave the movement its finest novel of the professional woman and made Syrett a central figure of the fiction of the decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the novel of the woman artist's education.

works.title: The Story of a Short Life
works.description: Published in 1885, the year of her death, and Ewing's most affecting book: the story of a soldier's son, disabled by an accident, who is determined to earn the Victoria Cross. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by Juliana Horatia Ewing; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Leonard, the son of a soldier, is crippled in a fall from a horse; he bears his pain with the code of the army, follows the fortunes of the regiment in Egypt, and dies before he can win the cross, having won the love and admiration of the men.
works.significance: The Story of a Short Life is the classic Victorian children's book about disability and military honour; its portrait of a suffering child and its imperial setting make it a central document of the 1880s and one of the most influential children's books of its decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a child's-eye view.
works.context: The 1880s, the Gordon relief expedition, the Victorian cult of the soldier, and the literature of disabled childhood. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.

works.title: The Story of an African Farm
works.form: Novel (published under the pseudonym Ralph Iron, 1883)
works.description: Published in 1883 under the name Ralph Iron and the first great novel of the South African interior: the childhood and youth of three children on a Karoo farm, and the philosophical argument that is carried inside their story.
works.plot: Waldo, the Boer-woman's son, Em, her daughter, and Lyndall, the orphaned English child, grow up on a sheep farm in the Karoo; the stranger Bonaparte Blenkins cheats the old Dutchwoman Tant' Sannie, the English overseer and the children's lives are shaped by the arrival of the stranger who calls himself the devil, and Lyndall goes away to school, is betrayed by a lover, and dies in a hotel room in Bloemfontein.
works.significance: The Story of an African Farm is the founding novel of South African literature and one of the great English novels of the nineteenth century: it is the first novel to make the South African landscape a spiritual place, its heroine Lyndall is one of the earliest feminists in fiction, and its allegorical 'dream' chapters are among the most original things in Victorian prose.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
works.context: The 1860s-70s, the Karoo, the Boer farm economy, the English immigrants in the Cape, and the Victorian debate on evolution and faith. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1881 and first published in 1883 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.

works.title: The Story of Avis
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1877
works.description: Published in 1877 and the first great American novel of the woman artist: the story of a painter whose marriage destroys her vocation. It is a prose fiction work of 1877 by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Avis Dobell, a gifted painter, marries the physician Philip Ostrander, and the novel follows the slow extinction of her art under the demands of marriage, motherhood and the care of a husband who does not understand her, until her death leaves her work unfinished.
works.significance: The Story of Avis is the founding American novel of the conflict between marriage and artistic vocation and one of the most important feminist novels of the century: its portrait of the slow death of a woman's talent is unmatched in American fiction before Kate Chopin.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. works.title: The Story of My Heart
works.description: Published in 1883 and the central text of English nature mysticism: the record of a soul's search for the meaning of its own existence among the fields and hills. It is a prose work of 1883 by Richard Jefferies; it belongs to Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature and it is catalogued here under Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Jefferies recounts his childhood on the Wiltshire downs, his early sense of the beauty of the earth, his years of illness and poverty, and his conviction — arrived at in the open air — that the human soul is greater than the world and that the world is the visible body of a spiritual power.
works.significance: The Story of My Heart is one of the great English spiritual autobiographies and the central text of English nature mysticism: its prose about the earth and the soul influenced Edward Thomas, Henry Williamson and the whole tradition of English nature writing, and it is the most personal and most radical of Jefferies's books.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals.
works.context: 1883: the Victorian crisis of faith, the Darwinian account of nature, the new interest in spiritual experience, and Jefferies's own tuberculosis. The record dates the work as composed between 1882 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation.
works.structure: A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.

works.description: Published in 1900 and the first of Washington's autobiographies, later revised and expanded as Up from Slavery. It is a prose work of 1900 by Booker T. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Washington tells the story of his birth in slavery, his education at Hampton, the founding of Tuskegee, and his public career, in a version written for a subscription audience and filled with the details of the institution's growth.
works.significance: The Story of My Life and Work is a significant document of black institutional history and the first version of the most important African-American autobiography of the era; it is a necessary comparison text for Up from Slavery.

Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. works.context: 1900: the fund-raising for Tuskegee, and the American autobiography market at the turn of the century. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.

works.title: The Story of Rimini: A Poem
works.form: A narrative or romantic poem in the market for Italian tale-in-verse that Byron's tales had made profitable, but deliberately turned against that fashion's declamation. It is a story poem of ordinary feeling rather than a romance of adventure: no marvels, no contests, no supernatural machinery except the closing Dantean scene. The conventions it works with are those of the colloquial romantic narrative, and its form is that of a plain recital, closer in spirit to a novel reduced to verse than to the epics its reviewers expected of heroic couplets.
works.description: Hunt's only sustained verse narrative, a romantic tale in rhymed couplets that retells and sympathetically modernises the episode of Paolo and Francesca which Dante set in the second circle of Hell in Inferno V. Where Dante judges the lovers, Hunt dwells on the ill-matched marriage, the slow growth of the attachment and the force of circumstance, treating his subject as human rather than exemplary. Published in 1816 and dedicated to Byron, it was the book that brought the full force of the sectional reviewing of the period down on its author, and it remains the central document of what his enemies called the Cockney school of poetry. Its colloquial diction, its homely domestic detail and its insistence that tenderness could be the matter of a serious poem made it a byword and a battleground in Romantic literary politics.
works.plot: The poem takes from Dante its situation and its persons: Francesca, given in marriage to the lord of Rimini for reasons of policy and not of affection, finds in his brother Paolo the companion her marriage has denied her. Hunt builds his argument not on the crime but on the slow preparation for it, on the dulness of the husband, the loneliness of the wife and the civilities of the court in which their friendship grows. The lovers are at last surprised together and slain, and the poem closes on the fate that Dante assigned to them, the pair still bound in the love that was their condemnation. Throughout, Hunt keeps the reader's sympathy with the actors rather than with the moralist, and treats the famous reading of the tale of Lancelot as the decisive incident in two ordinary lives.
works.significance: The Story of Rimini is the fullest statement of Hunt's belief that poetry should be written in the language of felt experience and that a subject once judged damnable might be rendered entirely in terms of human tenderness. It gave the Romantic period its clearest instance of criticism as personal and sectional war, and it helped define the party lines of Regency verse, with the Lakers, the Edinburgh reviewers and the Cockney school each defining themselves against the others. Later readers have valued it as a link between Byron's Italian tales and the sensual narrative impulse of Keats, and as proof that Hunt's theory of familiar verse could carry a subject of real weight.
works.meter: Heroic couplets: rhymed pairs of decasyllabic iambic lines, the ordinary English verse of narrative and of polite speech since Pope, and here used with a studied ease and a run-on syntax that many contemporary reviewers thought a violation of the form. Hunt's couplets are continually enjambed, their diction familiar and their imagery domestic, so that the closed mechanical pair becomes the vehicle of a flowing uncourtly narrative voice. The prosody was the poem's most contested feature: its defenders heard naturalness, its attackers heard the absence of verse at all.
works.context: The poem appeared in the first peace years, when Hunt had just left prison for the sedition committed in the Examiner, when Byron was in exile and when the Edinburgh and Quarterly reviewers were policing the limits of English verse. Its subject belonged to the early nineteenth-century revival of interest in Dante and in Italian story, and its politics belonged to Hunt's liberal London circle, which included Shelley, Keats and Hazlitt. The attacks that followed it in the Edinburgh and Quarterlies, personal as much as literary, were part of the same campaign that degraded Hunt's verse as a Cockney product and made his nose as famous as his poem.
works.characters: Paolo; Francesca; Francesca's husband, the lord of Rimini
works.structure: A single continuous romantic narrative told in order, without frame, allegory or editorial commentary, and organised by the growth of the relationship rather than by incident. Hunt moves slowly through domestic and conversational scenes, so that the poem's action is mostly psychological: the marriage, the acquaintance, the attachment, the discovery and the killing, followed by the brief infernal closing vision taken from Dante. There are no digressive tales within the tale and no competing plots; the machinery of romance is reduced to the few situations needed to make the readers' sympathy inevitable.
works.attributionNotes: The poem is undisputedly Hunt's and appeared with his name on its title page; no part of it has been claimed for another hand and no serious question of apocryphality attaches to it. Complications are bibliographical rather than attributive: the volume was reissued in revised form, later editions were printed for other publishers, and the text is therefore not identical across its first issues. Its dedication to Byron is on the face of the 1816 volume and has been taken as evidence of the friendship the two poets later fell out over, but it raises no question about who wrote the poem.

works.title: The Story of the Treasure Seekers
works.description: Published in 1899 and the book that created the modern children's family story: the Bastable children's attempts to restore the family fortunes, told by one of them who will not say which. works.title: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems
works.description: Published anonymously in 1849 as the work of 'A', and the volume that contains 'The Forsaken Merman', 'Mycerinus', 'The Sick King in Bokhara' and 'Resignation': the poetry of withdrawal, of the classical mask and of resignation before the world.
works.plot: 'The Strayed Reveller' is a dialogue between the young reveller and Circe, in which the poet's vision is purchased by exclusion from action; 'The Forsaken Merman' is a ballad of a sea-creature's wife who leaves him for her church; 'Mycerinus' is the Egyptian king who learns that he has only six years to live and turns them into pleasure.
works.significance: The Strayed Reveller established Arnold's characteristic subject — the modern mind's exile from the world of action and belief — and its title poem is the most complete statement of his theory of the poet's position. The anonymity signalled the volume's difference from the Victorian earnestness of its contemporaries.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
works.context: The 1848 revolutions and the failure of the Oxford hopes, the death of Arnold's father and his own religious crisis, and the classical reading of Balliol. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.

works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: The Subjection of Women
works.description: Published in 1869, written in collaboration with Harriet Taylor and dedicated to her: the most rigorous philosophical argument for the equality of women in the nineteenth century, and the text that the Victorian women's movement took as its manifesto.
works.plot: Mill argues that the subjection of women is a relic of the past preserved by custom, that the evidence of women's inferiority is worthless because it is drawn from a state of constrained development, that the legal ownership of wives under coverture is a form of slavery, that women should be enabled to choose any profession, and that marriage should become a partnership of equals.
works.significance: The Subjection of Women is the founding document of modern liberal feminism and remains the classic philosophical statement of the case: it gave the nineteenth-century women's movement its intellectual authority, and its analysis of the 'custom' and the 'nature' argument is still the core of the modern debate.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
works.context: The 1860s and the campaign for women's suffrage, the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882, and the parliamentary debate on the Second Reform Act in which Mill proposed the inclusion of women.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Published under Mill's name; he states in the Autobiography and in the dedication that the book was an embodiment of his wife's ideas and the result of their collaboration, and modern scholarship (Hayek, Rose, and the Oxford edition) treats Harriet Taylor Mill's share as substantial.

works.title: The Sun Also Rises
works.form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1926
works.description: The definitive novel of the Lost Generation: Paris, Pamplona and Jake Barnes's unhealed wound. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by Ernest Hemingway; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Jake Barnes, an American journalist in Paris left impotent by a war wound, loves Lady Brett Ashley, who loves him but cannot be with him; the novel follows their circle through the Paris cafés to the fiesta at Pamplona, where Brett seduces the young matador Pedro Romero, and ends with Brett's telegram calling Jake back to Madrid.
works.significance: The Sun Also Rises defined the Lost Generation and made Hemingway the voice of his age: its understated prose, its code of grace under pressure and its portrait of a wounded generation made it the decade's definitive novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the short declarative sentence.

works.title: The Supplication of Souls
works.description: More's defence of purgatory, written as the answer of the souls in purgatory to Simon Fish's Supplication for the Beggars (1529), which had demanded the dissolution of the monasteries and denounced purgatory as a clerical fiction.
works.plot: The souls of the dead speak in their own persons, showing from scripture and reason that purgatory exists, that prayers and masses for the dead avail them, and that those who deny purgatory rob both the dead and the living poor who depend on clerical charity.
works.significance: The most rhetorically inventive of More's early controversial works — using the fiction of the speaking dead — and a key document of the pre-Reformation debate on purgatory and monastic wealth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed late in 1529 as a direct reply to Fish's Supplication for the Beggars, which Henry VIII is said to have shown to More; the exchange belongs to the parliamentary debates of the Reformation Parliament and the campaign against church wealth.

works.significance: Mr Tod is the most complex of Potter's books and the one in which her natural history becomes a study of the violence of the wild; it is a key text for the adult reading of Potter and for the environmental reading of children's literature.

works.title: The Tale of Old Mortality
altTitles: Tales of My Landlord, First Series
works.form: Historical novel of religious war and persecution; a tragedy-plot in prose with a framed antiquarian apparatus.
works.description: The first of the Covenanted series, a novel of the Scottish CAMERONIAN persecutions of the 1670s presented as the transcription of an aged tradition-keeper's papers. Its young hero, drawn equally to the disciplined field-preachers of the south-west and to the disciplined cavalry of the Crown, learns that both causes can consume a private conscience. It is the most unsmiling of the series and the one that most openly interrogates fanaticism and its victims.
works.plot: Henry Morton, the son of a deceased Presbyterian minister and a ward of a Jacobite uncle, is apprenticed to a Covenanting elder and becomes entangled in the armed conventions of the south-west. He loves Edith, the sister of the Cavalier Lord Evandale, and is threatened by John Graham of Claverhouse, the dragoon commander who is at once his patron and his enemy; Morton's capture, sentence and reprieve follow the failure of the rising and the murder of Edith's father. Morton finally takes up arms at Bothwell Brig, is condemned, and is saved by an irregular act of the king's soldier, while Evandale falls in the field on the other side. The aged woman of the title, who keeps the memory of the persecuted, supplies the tale's moral register and its material.
works.significance: The period's greatest novel of religious fanaticism and of the violence done in the name of conscience, and the model for later treatments of Scottish covenanting history. Its frame, in which the past is preserved by an old woman and edited by an idler, is a founding statement of the historical novel's theory of evidence. Its portraits of Claverhouse and of the field-preachers entered the permanent debate about the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Covenanting psalm-tags and field-preaching cadences are quoted and parodied; ballad and psalm verse punctuate the narrative.
works.context: Drawn from the Cameronian records of the Killing Time after the Restoration, from the conventions and the battles of 1679-80, and from the family traditions of the author's South-Lowland childhood. The introduction records the pleasure a nineteenth-century reader took in religious controversy now dead. Its publication completed the transition from ballad editorship to prose fiction that the war years had made profitable.
works.characters: Henry Morton; Edith Balfour; Lord Evandale; John Graham of Claverhouse; the Old Mortality; Cuddie Headrigg
works.structure: Framed fiction: the tale is dug out of the papers of an aged traditionary 'Old Mortality' and transcribed by a fictitious idle country gentleman, introduced in a letter from the parish minister; the interior narrative is third-person, with heavy use of sermon, covenant and examination documents.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley, the tale being edited by the fictitious 'Landlord'; authorship undisputed.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.description: Published in 1903 and the second of Potter's little books: the impertinent squirrel who teases the owl Old Brown, and the riddle-rhymes he sings on the way to the island. works.title: The Tales of the O'Hara Family, First Series
altTitles: Tales of the O'Hara Family; by the Author of 'Damon and Pythias'. First Series
works.form: The Sketch and Character Tale; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
works.description: The first series of the national tales of a Kilkenny peasant family, published in 1825 and written in collaboration between two brothers, one of whom supplied the historical and topographical groundwork and both of whom share the narrative voice. The numbers give the cabin, the faction fight, the agrarian combination, and the phantom of the fetch in an Irish speech and at Irish length. The series founded the vogue of the Irish peasant tale and long stood as the standard account of the country people before the Famine.
works.plot: The Fetches tells of the double or phantom seen before a death, of a murdered man whose fetch appears to his kin, and of the country rules by which such an appearance is read, making the supernatural a matter of evidence and of neighbourhood testimony. John Doe; or, The Peep o' Day gives the agrarian war of the secret combinations, the cottier's hatred of the middleman and of the tithe, the midnight burning and the broken contract, and the fate of a family caught in the faction. Crohoore of the Bill-hook follows a woman of the out-lawed countryside who leads the boys in the agrarian rising and is hunted to her end. The series is held together by the O'Hara household and its neighbours, whose talk and genealogy frame the tales.
works.significance: The first series of the O'Hara tales established the Irish peasant narrative as the dominant mode of the 1820s and supplied much of the vocabulary in which the fetch, the combination, and the cottier's grievance were discussed in English. Its collaborative authorship also makes it a standard instance of joint production in the national tale.
works.context: Written in the years after the Act of Union and before the agitation for emancipation reached its crisis, out of the Kilkenny world of the hedge-school, the faction fight, and the agrarian association, and published at the moment when the national tale was the most prestigious form in British fiction. The brothers' earlier training as artists accounts for the series' emphasis on costume, cabin interior, and local scene, and one of them had been a pupil of the national drawing academy.
works.characters: the O'Hara household and its dependants; the murdered man whose fetch is seen; the cottier families of the agrarian combination; Crohoore of the Bill-hook, the woman leader of the boys; the middlemen and the rural police
works.structure: A framed series of independent tales told by and about one family, with a narratorial voice that reports Irish speech and supplies the historical and agrarian explanation inside the story; the series is not a continuous novel.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the two brothers share the series, with one of them understood to have written the woman-led agrarian tale and to have supplied the historical and topographical matter; early reviews and later biographies divided the numbers unequally between them.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

works.title: The Talisman
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Crusades
works.description: A romance of the Third Crusade which sets a fanatical and magnanimous English king beside a generous and sceptical Saradin leader, and makes the mutual respect of the two warriors the moral centre of the book. An English knight of disowned Saxon lineage, whose vows and his mistress's commands bring him to the East, serves unknowingly under the very king who despises him, while a talisman of supposed protection becomes the instrument by which reason and tolerance are shown to work. The book is the most deliberate of its author's apologies for civility across the line of faith. It was published with a companion tale of the same period in one series.
works.plot: A Christian knight of an injured Saxon house, bound by his mistress's command to wear a relic and to forbear battle, attaches himself to the English host in Palestine and is taken into the service of the great commander of the opposite faith. The two chiefs meet, are saved and instruct each other, and are brought into conflict by the jealous ambition of the knight's own patron and by an injured lady's suit for protection. The relic proves in the event to be an innocent object whose supposed virtue worked only by the courage and courtesy it taught, and the tale ends with reconciliation between the enemies and the knight's restoration to his mistress and his line.
works.significance: The clearest statement in the series of the romance of toleration and of the exemplary meeting of enemies, and a much-anthologised source for nineteenth-century ideas of chivalry and of the East. Its treatment of a false relic as an instrument of moral teaching makes it a central text for study of the author's handling of superstition and enlightenment.
works.meter: Prose, no metre, with quoted lyric and dramatic epigraphs in ballad and song measures at the head of chapters
works.context: Published in 1825 with a companion tale of the Crusading period, it belongs to the vogue for Crusade romance revived by the antiquaries and by travelled knowledge of the nearer east. Its plea for courtesy across religious difference reflects the liberal moment of the Catholic and civil-relief controversies then in progress in the British parliament, and the book's oriental chivalry draws on the contemporary translation of Arabic history and poetry.
works.characters: The English king of the Crusade host; the great commander of the Saracen camp; Kenneth, a Saxon knight in disguise; the lady of an English house whose suit he defends; an ambitious courtier patron of the hero
works.structure: Third-person romance in three volumes with a continuous single hero's career, framed by chapter epigraphs from older plays and ballads; the argument is carried by set-piece interviews between the two great captains rather than by intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name now disclosed in the general title of the series; no dispute over authorship.

Warfare and battle

works.title: The Taming of the Shrew
works.description: Shakespeare's farcical comedy of courtship and domestication: the fortune-hunter Petruchio 'tames' the headstrong Katherine of Padua by a regime of contradiction and deprivation, while her sister Bianca is courted by a crowd of disguised suitors — all framed by the Induction, in which the drunken tinker Christopher Sly is tricked into believing himself a lord for whom the play is performed.
works.plot: Sly is gulled into watching a play: Lucentio disguises himself to woo Bianca, his servant Tranio impersonates him, and Petruchio marries Katherine and breaks her will — or teaches her the game — until she delivers the play's closing speech on wives' obedience, its irony a matter of perennial dispute.
works.significance: Shakespeare's most durable farce, endlessly revived and argued over — a test case for every generation's view of marriage, gender, and power.
works.meter: Mostly prose and doggerel in the farcical scenes, with blank verse for the courtship of Kate and Petruchio.
works.context: Written about 1590–92, in dialogue with the anonymous play The Taming of a Shrew (1594); its debate over wifely subjection has made it the most contested of the comedies in modern performance and criticism.
works.characters: Christopher Sly; Petruchio; Katherine; Bianca; Lucentio; Tranio; Baptista Minola; Grumio; Hortensio; Gremio
works.structure: An Induction framing a two-plot comedy (the Bianca courtship intrigue and the Petruchio–Kate duel), in the manner of Italian commedia-derived farce.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the relation to the anonymous A Shrew remains debated.

works.title: The Tapestry Room: A Child's Romance
works.description: Published in 1879 and the best of Molesworth's fairy romances: the story of two children who pass through the tapestry in an old French château into the world it depicts. works.title: The Task: A Poem
works.form: meditative and didactic long poem in blank verse, in the Thomson-Ossian tradition of the reflective essay-poem
works.description: Cowper's principal poem, a blank-verse meditation in six books that begins as an occasional exercise on a sofa and becomes a survey of retirement, of the times, of the world and of the winter year. Its movement from domestic ease to public prophecy, and its account of the Christian's dependence on providence, made it one of the most read long poems of the last third of the century. It contains the century's most quoted plea for solitary escape and some of its earliest verse protest against the slave trade.
works.plot: Book I excuses the trivial occasion of the poem and commences the praise of soft retirement; Book II, the Time-Piece, moralises the hours of the day and the vanity of fashionable occupations; Book III considers the world and its corruption; Book IV the winter evening with its lamp, its tea and its news; Book V the winter morning walk in the country; and Book VI the winter walk at noon, ending in the wish for a lodge in some vast wilderness and in a religious conclusion on the faith that sustains the solitary soul. Throughout, the poem argues that true happiness is found in dependence on providence rather than in the noise of the age.
works.significance: The Task was a bestseller and the model for a generation of reflective and topographical verse, admired by Wordsworth and the younger romantics for its command of blank verse and its treatment of ordinary domestic life. Its abolitionist passage and its 'time and tide' morality made it a site of both moral and literary authority in the 1790s.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of unusual smoothness and variety, with the famous 'O for a lodge in some vast wilderness' lines in a mixed and more prosaic measure; the couplet is used only occasionally and the sentence-periods are long.
works.context: Written at the Olney and Weston Underwood retirements in 1783-84 on a wager or request that he should make a poem in blank verse on an unfashionable subject, and published in 1785; its reflections on the times respond to the American war's aftermath, to enthusiasm in religion, and to the growth of luxury, commerce and colonial exploitation.
works.characters: The retired poet; the friends and patroness of the Unwin household; the world and its votaries; the personified Times and Solitude
works.structure: A long poem in six books of unequal length, each opening with an address and proceeding by reflection, description and digression; the design is associational, with the winter sequence of the last three books giving the strongest local unity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Cowper's own letters and memoranda record the commission and the books' composition, and the several revisions of the text across editions are documented in the standard edition.

works.title: The Tatler Papers
works.description: Richard Steele's three-times-weekly paper, conducted under the mask of Isaac Bickerstaff Esq., which turned the newsbook, the coffee-room gossip and the character sketch into a morally reformed periodical and created the English essay paper.
works.plot: Mr. Speculator and his correspondents report the clubs, the play-house, the opera, the town and the country, alternating manners, marriage and duelling stories with party politics and with praise of Addison's Cato and of private virtue.
works.significance: It made periodical moral commentary a profession and a literary form, and its account of the affective, tearful reform of manners prepared sentimental comedy and the novel of character.
works.meter: A looser, more colloquial and syntactically broken style than Addison's, full of ellipsis, exclamation and half-unfinished sentences, which Steele's imitators took for the natural tone of feeling.
works.context: Launched in April 1709 and running to the beginning of 1711, the Tatler exploited the new cheap journalism after the lapse of licensing, the party pressure of the Sacheverell trial years, and Steele's continuing interest in the reformation of the stage.
works.characters: Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.; the Speculator; cousin Jenny; Will Honeycomb; the Whig and Tory clubs; the readers who write to the editor
works.structure: Serial papers distributed among fixed stations of observation (the coffee-house, the theatre, Kit-Cat, the opera, the country), with a lightly advancing fictional biography of the editor and of his correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Principally Steele's, with a substantial early contribution from Addison and papers from Hughes, Berkeley, Prior and others; the joint numbers are still disputed by bibliographers.

works.title: The Tempest
works.description: Shakespeare's farewell to the stage: Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, has raised the storm that wrecks his enemies on his island; with his spirit Ariel and the enslaved Caliban, he conducts the shipwrecked court through the play's ordeals to repentance, wins the betrothal of his daughter Miranda to Ferdinand, breaks his staff, and sails for Milan — 'our revels now are ended'.
works.plot: The tempest delivers Alonso's court to Prospero's island; Ferdinand and Miranda meet and are tested; Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo plot their drunken coup; Ariel's banquet harrows the 'three men of sin'; and the final scene forgives all — with Caliban left to 'seek for grace' and Prospero to drown his book.
works.significance: Shakespeare's valediction — the play that has served every later age as a fable of art, empire, and forgiveness, and the most reinterpreted text in the canon.
works.meter: The late verse at its most musical — Ariel's songs, the masque, the 'cloud-capped towers' speech — with Caliban's prose and the sailors' comedy as counterpoint.
works.context: Performed at court, 1 November 1611, and for the wedding of Princess Elizabeth in 1613; its New World echoes draw on the Virginia pamphlets and the wreck of the Sea Venture (1609).
works.characters: Prospero; Miranda; Ariel; Caliban; Ferdinand; Alonso; Antonio; Sebastian; Gonzalo; Stephano; Trinculo; Sycorax (reported); Juno, Ceres, and Iris (in the masque)
works.structure: The most classical of the plays — a single island, a single day, a masque at its centre — shaped as Prospero's design from storm to pardon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Tempest; or, The Enchanted Island
altTitles: The Tempest or The Inchanted Island
works.description: The Davenant-Dryden adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest, adding a second island inhabitant, Hippolito, a sister for Miranda, and extensive musical and spectacular material; it held the stage for over a century.
works.plot: Prospero, exiled to the island, raises a tempest that wrecks the Neapolitans; the new plot gives Miranda a sister and adds Hippolito, a young man who has never seen a woman, with whom both sisters fall in love.
works.significance: The dominant version of The Tempest on the English stage from 1667 until the nineteenth century and a crucial document of Restoration Shakespeare adaptation; it inspired Purcell's semi-opera The Fairy-Queen tradition and Shadwell's operatic version of 1674.
works.meter: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
works.context: First performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields on 7 November 1667; Davenant died in 1668 before publication, and Dryden wrote the preface.
works.characters: Prospero; Miranda; Hippolito; Ariel; Ferdinand; Dorinda; Caliban; Trinculo; Stephano; Sycorax
works.structure: Five acts with songs, dances, and machinery; about half Shakespeare's text is retained and the rest newly written.
works.attributionNotes: The 1674 quarto names Davenant and Dryden; the extent of each contribution is disputed, but Dryden's preface claims the greater part of the new material as Davenant's design.

works.title: The Temple
altTitles: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
works.description: George Herbert's posthumous collection of 160 English religious poems, arranged in three parts — 'The Church-Porch', 'The Church', and 'The Church Militant' — which renders the life of the soul and the parish in an extraordinary variety of forms, from pattern poems to hymns and dramatic soliloquies.
works.plot: 'The Church-Porch' gives moral precepts to a young man; 'The Church' traces the soul's struggles with God through poems of sin, affliction, love, and consolation ('The Collar', 'The Pulley', 'Love III'); 'The Church Militant' is a prophetic vision of the church's corruption and the spread of true religion westward.
works.significance: The Temple is the supreme work of English devotional verse, fusing metaphysical wit with Anglican humility; it shaped religious poetry from Vaughan and Crashaw to Coleridge, Eliot, and Heaney.
works.meter: A prodigious variety of stanza forms, shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'), concrete imagery, and colloquial rhythm in the service of devotion.
works.context: Herbert sent the manuscript to Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding shortly before his death in 1633, asking him to publish it if he thought it might 'turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul'; it was printed at Cambridge in 1633 and became a devotional best-seller.
works.characters: the poet-priest; God; the soul; the Church
works.structure: A tripartite collection with the shape of a spiritual autobiography, moving from moral instruction through the drama of devotion to eschatological prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
Divine love and holy desire

works.title: The Temple of Glas
works.description: John Lydgate's early dream vision (1,403 lines in rhyme royal, c. 1400–05): the dreamer, enclosed in a glass temple of Venus, overhears the complaint of a lady bound by an unwanted marriage and the answering lament of her true lover, until the goddess unites them. The most accomplished of Lydgate's courtly poems and the first printed by Caxton.
works.plot: The dreamer finds himself before a temple of glass whose walls depict famous lovers; within, the lady laments her forced betrothal and the knight his despair; Venus, appealed to by both, grants them one another, and the dreamer wakes to write his vision for his own lady.
works.significance: The finest of Lydgate's courtly visions and a key text of the early Chaucerian tradition; its printing history marks the beginning of the English poetry market.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with the early Lydgate line's characteristic fluency.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–05, early in Lydgate's career, perhaps for a marriage occasion; widely copied and printed — it was among the first poems Caxton printed at Westminster (1477).
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Lady; her Lover; Venus
works.structure: A courtly dream vision in the Chaucerian manner (House of Fame, Parliament of Fowls), with the double complaint as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure (named in the envoy).
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
