works.title: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
works.form: Novel in three volumes, epistolary and framed first person
works.description: Published in three volumes in June 1848 under the pseudonym Acton Bell, and the most controversial of the Brontë novels in its own time: the story of a wife who leaves a violent and alcoholic husband and supports herself and her child by her own work, told through letters and a journal.
works.plot: Gilbert Markham, a Yorkshire farmer, falls in love with Helen Graham, a widow newly arrived at Wildfell Hall, and discovers through her journal that she is in fact the wife of Arthur Huntingdon, whom she married against advice and who has become a drunkard and an adulterer. Helen has left him and taken their son; after Huntingdon's death she is free to marry Gilbert, and the novel closes with their union and the recovery of the estate.
works.significance: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall is the first English novel to defend a wife's right to leave an abusive husband, and its unsparing treatment of alcoholism and marital cruelty made it the most attacked book of the Brontës in 1848 and the most valued by modern feminist criticism. Its formal design — a journal inside letters inside a first-person narrative — is the most experimental structure among the Brontë novels.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence.
works.context: The 1820s-30s and the law of coverture, the custody of children as a husband's property, the temperance agitation of the 1830s, and the contemporary debate on the 'social evil' of drink and prostitution.
works.characters: Helen Graham (Helen Huntingdon); Gilbert Markham; Arthur Huntingdon; Frederick Lawrence; Mrs Markham; Rose Markham; Annabella Lowborough; Lord Lowborough; Ralph Hattersley; Milicent Hargrave; Rachel
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the pseudonym Acton Bell; the novel's frankness about marital cruelty drew attacks on the 'coarseness' of the Bell novels, and Charlotte Brontë's 1850 judgement that it was 'hardly ... desirable' shaped its neglect until the twentieth century.
themes: Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict

works.title: The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America
works.description: Anne Bradstreet's first collection, published in London in 1650 without her knowledge by her brother-in-law, containing learned 'quaternions' on the four elements, humours, seasons, and the four monarchies, as well as poems on public events — the first volume of poetry published by a woman in the English colonies.
works.plot: The long poems survey natural philosophy and world history in the Du Bartas tradition, while shorter verses address family, faith, and public events, all framed by prefatory modesty topos.
works.significance: The Tenth Muse is the founding work of American poetry and a landmark of women's writing, documenting Puritan learning and a woman's ambitious but humble voice.
works.meter: Formal verse in the tradition of Du Bartas and Sidney, with learned allusion and occasional homely warmth.
works.context: Written in New England and carried to London by Bradstreet's brother-in-law, who published it in 1650; it made Bradstreet the first American and the first colonial woman to publish a volume of verse.
works.structure: A collection of long didactic 'quaternions' and shorter occasional poems in the Renaissance encyclopaedic manner.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published without Bradstreet's knowledge, signed 'A.B.' in some issues.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World

works.title: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates
altTitles: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates: Proving That It Is Lawful ... to Call to Account a Tyrant, King or Magistrate
works.description: Milton's republican tract, published weeks after the execution of Charles I, arguing that sovereignty originates in the people, that kings are the people's servants, and that it is lawful to depose and execute a tyrant — a defence of regicide and popular sovereignty.
works.plot: Milton argues from scripture, classical authority, and the law of nations that magistrates hold power by the people's trust, that a tyrant forfeits it, and that the people may judge and punish him, defending the Army's act against Presbyterian critics.
works.significance: A foundational text of republican political theory and resistance doctrine, influencing later Whig and revolutionary thought in England and America.
works.meter: Forceful, learned, argumentative prose with a fierce polemical edge.
works.context: Written in February 1649 immediately after Charles I's execution, partly to answer Presbyterians who had supported the war but recoiled from regicide; it secured Milton his post as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth.
works.structure: A polemical prose treatise of sustained argument, moving from political theory to the immediate justification of the regicide.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
Kingship and good rule

works.title: The Terrible Sonnets
works.description: The 'terrible' or 'sonnets of desolation' written in Dublin in 1885-88 — 'Carrion Comfort', 'No worst, there is none', 'To seem the stranger lies my lot', 'I wake and feel the fell of dark, not day', 'Patience, hard thing!', 'My own heart let me more have pity on' — and the most powerful English poems of spiritual desolation.
works.plot: The sonnets record the loss of consolation in prayer: the soul wrestles with a God who seems to withhold grace, the mind is reduced to 'the mind's own self-taste', and the sequence ends in the effort to accept the will of God without the feeling of his presence.
works.significance: The terrible sonnets are the central documents of Victorian religious suffering and the greatest devotional poems in English of the nineteenth century; their analysis of depression has made them permanent texts of the modern literature of mental illness, and their influence on the twentieth-century religious lyric is direct.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
works.context: Hopkins's Dublin years as Professor of Greek at the Royal University, his isolation in Ireland, his failing health and his conflict with the political and religious atmosphere of the country, and the spiritual theology of the dark night.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Testament of a Vivisector
works.description: Published in 1901 and the first of Davidson's 'Testaments': a dramatic monologue in which a vivisectionist defends his work against the claims of pity. It is a verse work of 1901 by John Davidson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: The vivisector argues that knowledge is the highest good and that the suffering of animals is justified by the advance of science, and the poem sets his argument against the moral imagination of the reader in a way that refuses an easy verdict.
works.significance: The Testament of a Vivisector is the most original English poem on the ethics of science and the founding text of the modern poetry of moral argument: its dramatic method of giving the case its strongest voice made it a model for the poetry of debate.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the dramatic monologue.
works.context: 1901: the anti-vivisection movement, the ethics of experimental medicine, and the Nietzschean philosophy of the will. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.characters: the vivisector, the speaker
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.

works.title: The Testament of Beauty
works.description: Published in 1929 and Bridges's last and most ambitious poem: a philosophy of beauty, evolution and the mind of man in a new metre. It is a verse work of 1929 by Robert Bridges; it is catalogued here under Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The poem argues through a series of meditations — on the beauty of the natural world, on the evolution of consciousness, on the difference between the animal and the human, on love, on the State and on the future of civilisation — that beauty is the manifestation of an ordering power in things and that man's task is to cooperate with it.
works.significance: The Testament of Beauty was a best-seller and a public event in 1929 and the last great English philosophical poem: its new metre and its argument for a spiritual reading of evolution made it a landmark of the interwar period, and it is the summation of Bridges's lifelong thinking about beauty and order.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the long poem: blank verse or a sustained narrative measure, the extended simile and the long verse paragraph, carried across books or parts. The author's characteristic manner is exquisite metrical control in received forms.
works.context: 1929: the aftermath of the First World War, the modernism of Eliot and Pound, the new biology, and the public hunger for a philosophy of order. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and it is catalogued under epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.structure: A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Seymour Bridges. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Testament of Cresseid
works.description: Robert Henryson's great continuation of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (616 lines, c. 1475–90): the abandoned Cresseid, stricken with leprosy as judgement on her blasphemy against Venus and Cupid, meets the leper troop at the roadside and is recognized, too late, by Troilus, who cannot name her but casts her alms; she dies repentant, her testament a warning against the falsehood of love and fortune. The most powerful 'continuation' in English literature.
works.plot: The narrator, taking up 'ane uther quair' on the fate of Cresseid, tells how Diomede abandoned her; in her complaint she blasphemes Venus and Cupid, and the planetary court, convened by Saturn and Cynthia, condemns her to leprosy; in the lazar house she meets Troilus, who pities the unknown leper; learning the truth from the leper woman, she makes her testament, dies, and is buried under a tomb inscribed with her tragedy.
works.significance: Universally ranked among the great short tragedies of English literature; its compassion for Cresseid and its cosmic judgement scene make it the supreme Scottish response to Chaucer.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of austere, compassionate power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1475–90 in the Chaucerian tradition of the Scottish makars, answering Chaucer's Troilus with a Scottish judgement on its heroine; printed with Chaucer's works by Thynne (1532), where it long passed as Chaucer's own.
works.characters: Cresseid; Troilus; Diomede; Saturn; Cynthia; Venus; Cupid; the leper woman
works.structure: A five-movement tragedy (abandonment; blasphemy and judgement; leprosy; the roadside meeting; testament and death), closed by the narrator's warning to the women of the audience.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).

works.title: The Testament of the Papyngo
altTitles: The Testament and Complaynt of Our Soverane Lordis Papyngo
works.form: verse satire in the testament tradition
works.description: Lindsay's satire of court and church: the king's parrot, dying after a fall from the palace wall, makes her testament — leaving her heart to the king, her body to the courtiers, and her counsel to the clergy — and delivers a dying bird's-eye satire of the bishops, the court, and the vices of the age.
works.plot: The Papyngo, perched high on the palace wall, falls and dies; before death she disposes of her estate in a testament that satirizes each legatee in turn, closing with an epistle to the bishops on their duties.
works.significance: The wittiest of Lindsay's satires and a classic of the Scots complaint; its parrot looks back to Skelton's Speke Parrot and forward to the beast satires of the later century.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzas; the mock-legal diction of the testament handled with satirical point.
works.context: Written in 1530 as the Scottish church's wealth and the court's corruption became the subjects of Reformation debate; the parrot speaks with the licence of the dying.
works.characters: the Papyngo; James V (legatee); the courtiers; the bishops
works.structure: The testament form — the dying bird's will and last counsel — used as a vehicle for estates satire; mock-legal framework, satirical legacies, and a closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
works.description: Adam Smith's first great work, the fullest elaboration of the moral-sense tradition through the mechanism of sympathy and the impartial spectator. It explains how fellow-feeling, admiration, and the desire for praiseworthiness generate moral judgment, duty, and virtue, and it remains the century's most comprehensive treatise on the social psychology of ethics.
works.plot: Part I shows that we judge the propriety of another's feelings by imagining ourselves in his situation, sympathy being the imaginary transposition of spectator and agent, and that the senses of propriety and justice arise from this exchange of perspectives. Part II traces the feelings of merit and demerit, the rules of justice and beneficence, and the influence of custom and fashion on moral sentiment. Part III introduces the impartial spectator as the internal judge and the desire for praiseworthiness as the mature moral motive. Parts IV and V analyse the corruption of the moral sentiments by the love of riches and rank, and survey the rival systems of ethics from the ancients to the moderns. Part VI completes the taxonomy of the virtues of prudence, justice, beneficence, and self-command. The whole grounds society not on contract but on the mutual mirror of sympathetic sentiments.
works.significance: It supplied the moral psychology for commercial society's self-understanding, is the necessary companion to the Wealth of Nations, and anchors the modern revival of sympathy-based ethics and the study of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.meter: An expansive, illustrative lecture prose dense with social observation, its famous generalizations stated in balanced declaratives, addressed alike to polite and philosophical readers.
works.context: Grown from Smith's Glasgow lectures begun in the early 1750s and published in London in 1759 with Hume's encouragement, it appeared in the season of the Edinburgh and Glasgow debates on scepticism and the French materialists and was revised by Smith through five later editions.
works.structure: Six parts of graduated argument, from the analysis of sympathy through the general rules and the impartial spectator to the history of ethical systems and the taxonomy of the virtues.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct

movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: The Thirty-Nine Steps
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1915
works.description: The first modern chase thriller: Richard Hannay, a dead man and the thirty-nine steps. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by John Buchan; it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Richard Hannay, a South African mining engineer newly arrived in London, finds a dead man in his flat and the notebook of a spy ring; he flees to Scotland, pursued by the police and the conspirators, and deciphers the code of the thirty-nine steps.
works.significance: The Thirty-Nine Steps invented the modern chase thriller and the man-on-the-run novel: its plotting, its landscape and its competent amateur hero founded the twentieth-century political thriller and made Richard Hannay a permanent English figure.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the chase through landscape.
works.context: London and the Scottish borders in the summer of 1914, on the eve of the First World War. The record dates the work as composed in 1915 and first published in 1915 and it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; detective novel and the golden age mystery.
works.characters: Richard Hannay; Franklin P. Scudder; the Black Stone; Sir Harry Bullivant
works.structure: A first-person chase narrative in ten chapters. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.

works.title: The Thorn
works.form: Lyrical ballad and early form of the dramatic monologue; a poem that treats the popular tale as something made by the mind that tells it, and that places the psychology of belief in the foreground.
works.description: The most radical experiment of the anonymous 1798 volume: a long dramatic ballad narrated by a garrulous old man who reports what he thinks he has seen and heard on a hill where a thorn, a heap of moss and a nameless woman in a scarlet hood have gathered a local legend. The poem's interest is not the story but the mind of the teller - his superstition, his vanity, his need for a pathetic tale and his uneasy awareness that the simple truth would not serve him. A prose note explaining the narrator's character was appended in the edition of 1800, and the poem became the test case for the theory of poetic language defended in the Preface.
works.plot: The narrator bids his listener open his eyes wide and observe the thorn, which looks older than it is, and the mound of moss, which looks like a grave though none lies there. He then reports the gossip of the neighbourhood: a woman named Martha Ray met her lover by that thorn, was deserted, and has ever since sat there with her hood about her face, calling on the name Edward in a voice that has frightened those who pass at night. He alternately insists on and disowns the tale, offering natural explanations, then abandoning them for the pleasure of the wonderful, and the poem ends on the repeated cry as it sounds in his own superstitious ear. The subject is thus the growth of a legend and the creative power of an uneducated and sorrowful mind, together with the pleasure a tale of woe can give when it is badly told.
works.significance: Taken by later critics as the clearest demonstration of Romantic interest in the unreliable imaginative narrator and in the psychology of belief, and an ancestor of the Victorian dramatic monologue. It is also the poem against which the co-author of the volume later weighed the success of the Preface's theory, praising in it the power of an excited and credulous voice.
works.meter: A mixture of four- and three-beat ballad lines in stanzas of uneven length, marked by heavy punctuation, exclamatory emphasis and the repetition of words and half-lines, designed to imitate an excited and untrained voice rather than to sound poetical.
works.context: Written in the period of the western collaboration, when the two poets were experimenting with the speech of persons whose language is less refined than that of the class of readers to whom it is addressed. The explanatory prose note of 1800, in which the narrator is accounted for by decayed fortune and superstitious habits rather than by rustic charm, is one of the first applications of the new theory to a particular text.
works.characters: The aged, decayed and superstitious narrator; Martha Ray; the lost lover, Edward; the villagers whose gossip forms the legend
works.structure: A dramatic monologue addressed to an overhearer, in stanzas of unequal length: description of the site, report of the local story, self-correction and protestation of honesty, and a final reversion to the repeated cry. The narrator's unreliability is the structure, since each stanza qualifies the one before it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the prose note of 1800, which explains the character of the speaker, is by the same hand and is printed with the poem in scholarly editions.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Melancholy and self-analysis
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
The supernatural ballad and willed belief
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: The Three Hills and Other Poems
works.description: The first collection: the Georgian lyric of the hills and the landscape. It is a verse work of 1913 by J. C. Squire; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric.
works.plot: The Three Hills and Other Poems gathers Squire's first lyrics of the hills, the landscape and the season, in the polished Georgian line that made him one of the anthologised poets of the 1910s.
works.significance: The Three Hills and Other Poems made Squire one of the anthologised Georgian poets: its landscape lyric is the standard text of the Georgian manner at its most polished.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the polished Georgian lyric of the landscape and the season.
works.context: England in 1913, and the Georgian anthologies. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1913 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
works.structure: A collection of Georgian landscape lyrics. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Solomon Eagle, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to J. C. Squire is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Three Hostages
works.form: Novel; dystopian fiction, first issued in 1924
works.description: The postwar Hannay: a hypnotist, three hostages and the return of the adventure. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by John Buchan; it is catalogued here under Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Richard Hannay, now married and settled, is drawn back into adventure by the disappearance of three hostages; the trail leads to the sinister Dominick Medina, a hypnotist and man of the world who nearly destroys Hannay's mind.
works.significance: The Three Hostages is the finest of the postwar Hannay novels and one of the first English thrillers to use hypnotism and the psychology of the charismatic leader: its portrait of Medina made it a permanent study of the charm of evil.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the chase through landscape.
works.context: England and Scotland in the early 1920s, and the postwar anxiety about the new psychology and the cult of the superman. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Richard Hannay; Dominick Medina; Mary Hannay; Sandy Arbuthnot; the three hostages
works.structure: A first-person thriller in the Hannay manner. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as 1st Baron Tweedsmuir. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Three Midshipmen
works.description: The founding naval adventure for boys: three midshipmen, a frigate and the world. It is a prose fiction work of 1873 by W. H. G. Kingston; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier.
works.plot: Jack Rogers, Terence Adair and Dick Ayliffe join the navy as midshipmen, serve through storms, sea battles and the slave trade on the African coast, and rise to command in a story that made the naval career into a boy's ideal.
works.significance: The Three Midshipmen was the most popular of Kingston's naval stories and the book that fixed the formula of the boys' sea novel: its three heroes, its storms and its sea battles made the Navy into a moral institution for the Victorian boy reader.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the voyage as the organising structure.
works.context: The Royal Navy of the 1830s and 1840s, the anti-slavery patrol and the Mediterranean station. The record dates the work as composed between 1872 and 1873 and first published in 1873 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Jack Rogers; Terence Adair; Dick Ayliffe; Captain Pemberton; Ben Drake
works.structure: A naval chronicle in three parts, from the midshipman's berth to command. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Giles Kingston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Three Miss Kings
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1883
works.description: Published in 1883 and Cambridge's best-known novel: the story of three sisters, newly arrived in Melbourne from the country, who must make their way in the marriage market of the colonial city. It is a prose fiction work of 1883 by Ada Cambridge; it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Elizabeth, Patty and Eleanor King, orphaned and poor, come to Melbourne and are taken up by a wealthy family; each sister faces a choice between an advantageous marriage and her own judgment, and the novel follows them through courtship, disappointment and eventual settlement.
works.significance: The Three Miss Kings is the most accomplished Australian novel of the 1880s and a central text in the history of Australian women's writing: its picture of the marriage market in colonial Melbourne is exact and unsentimental, and its three heroines are among the first fully realised Australian women in fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a strong narrative voice.
works.context: The 1880s, colonial Melbourne, the marriage market of the new city, and the debate on women's education in Australia. The record dates the work as composed between 1882 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Elizabeth, Patty and Eleanor King; Paul Brion; Mrs Duff-Scott
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ada Cross. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Three Perils of Woman; or, Love, Jealousy, and Disobedience of Parents
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's collection of three prose tales warning women against the three perils of romantic love, jealousy, and disobedience to parents, written in the years before his great novel Confessions of a Justified Sinner. It is his most sustained fictional prose before the 1824 novel and combines Gothic, border, and domestic modes.
works.plot: The three tales each demonstrate the ruin that follows one peril: the first, centred on a passionate elopement, shows the disaster of love mistaken for marriage; the second explores a jealous husband's destruction of his innocent wife; the third narrates a daughter's refusal of a suitable match for a dangerous stranger and her consequent suffering. The tales are set variously in Scotland, the Borders, and the Continent, and draw on ballad and Gothic conventions to make their moral case. the author's frame voice is urbane, digressive, and self-aware.
works.significance: The Three Perils of Woman is a major precursor of Confessions of a Justified Sinner and shows the author's development as a prose fiction writer; its Gothic and domestic tales illustrate the range of Scottish fiction in the 1820s.
works.context: Published in 1823, just before the author's masterpiece; the moral framework of the 'three perils' belongs to the conduct tradition, while the settings and plots use Gothic and ballad materials widely popular in the Waverley period.
works.characters: The various heroines of the three tales; their lovers and husbands; the author's frame narrator
works.structure: Three independent tales within a frame; each has its own setting and narrative voice; the moral frame gives coherence to the three very different plots.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Three Taps
works.description: Knox's fair-play classic: a locked room and a gas tap. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Ronald Knox; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Mr Bredon, an insurance investigator, is asked to determine whether the death of a client in a locked hotel room was suicide or murder, and the mystery turns on three gas taps and the exactness of the timetable, in a novel that obeys Knox's own Decalogue.
works.significance: The Three Taps is one of the purest fair-play detective novels ever written and the demonstration of Knox's Decalogue: its locked room, its insurance investigation and its exact logic made it the classical puzzle of the Golden Age.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play puzzle with its rules.
works.context: An English hotel in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery.
works.characters: Mr Bredon; the insurance company; the hotel guests; Inspector Leyland
works.structure: A fair-play detective novel with a map of the hotel and an exact timetable. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ronald Arbuthnott Knox. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Time Machine
works.description: Published in 1895 and the founding work of the modern scientific romance: the journey of an inventor to the year 802,701, where he finds the Eloi and the Morlocks, and to the last days of the earth. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Naturalist and Determinist Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Time Traveller demonstrates his machine, travels to the far future, discovers a pastoral people served by a subterranean race, loses his machine to the Morlocks, escapes to the year thirty million, and returns to tell the tale before vanishing on a second journey.
works.significance: The Time Machine invented the time-travel story and gave the scientific romance its method: the extrapolation of a social and biological idea into a narrative. Its vision of class division becoming speciation is the most powerful single image in Victorian science fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The 1890s, the second law of thermodynamics and the 'heat death' of the universe, the Darwinian and socialist thought of the period, and the class divisions of Victorian London. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; naturalist and determinist novel.
works.characters: The Time Traveller; the Eloi; the Morlocks; Weena; the Medical Man; the Psychologist; the Editor
works.structure: Framed narrative: the Time Traveller's account to a dinner party, with an epilogue by the narrator.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Tinted Venus: A Farcical Romance
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1885
works.description: Anstey's second comic fantasy: a statue of Venus comes to life in a London suburb. It is a prose fiction work of 1885 by F. Anstey; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour and the record grades it as minor canon.
works.plot: Leander Tweddle, a suburban hairdresser, slips a ring on the finger of a statue of Venus and brings the goddess to life; she claims him as her lover, to the despair of his fiancee, until the ring is recovered and the statue is restored.
works.significance: The Tinted Venus was Anstey's second great comic fantasy and one of the funniest novels of the 1880s: its suburban goddess made the classical past into a comic character and founded the modern comedy of the animated statue.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the comic premise carried to its logical extreme.
works.context: London in the 1880s and the classical taste of the Victorian suburb. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under comic novel and the new humour.
works.characters: Leander Tweddle; Venus; Matilda; the Professor
works.structure: A comic novel in twelve chapters, from the studio to the suburban parlour. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Anstey Guthrie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as minor canon.

works.title: The Tomb
works.form: Meditative blank-verse poem, a planned sequel or pendant to 'The Grave', surviving among the manuscripts Blair left and printed posthumously; short in relation to its companion and incomplete in the sense that its author left it.
works.description: Robert Blair's projected companion to 'The Grave', left in manuscript at his death and printed among his posthumous poems. It pursues the same subject in the same measure, but narrows the focus to the sepulchre itself and to the monuments and inscriptions by which the living attempt to keep the dead in mind.
works.plot: Like 'The Grave', the poem is an exercise of thought rather than a narrative. It meditates upon the tomb as a structure, an inscription and a hope: the masonry and the heraldry of memorial are surveyed and found insufficient, while the Christian tomb is read as the pledge of a resurrection. The turn from the vanity of monumental fame to the faith of the buried believer is the argument, and the piece supplies a closing reflection to the open-ended contemplation of its predecessor.
works.significance: It completes the conception of 'The Grave' and shows how far the graveyard meditation had become, in Blair's hands, a structured sequence rather than a single performance. It is a minor but authentic document of the preromantic contemplation of death.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in the same weighty, Latinate manner as 'The Grave'; the diction is funerary and lapidary, with the compressed phrasing of an epitaph.
works.context: It was written in the same period as 'The Grave', when Blair was assembling a sequence of poems on the last things, and it stands within the 1740s fashion for churchyard, tomb and resurrection meditation. Its survival in manuscript and its posthumous printing are part of the history of that fashion, since the editors of Blair's papers were also the editors of his reputation.
works.structure: A continuous meditation addressed to the tomb, in the same sectional, associative movement as 'The Grave', with apostrophe and epitaph-like reflection taking the place of events.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Blair is not contested; the difficulty lies in its publication history. Because it was not printed in the poet's lifetime and because the several posthumous collections and reissues of Blair's poems are differently dated, no first-print year is asserted here and the publication field is left null rather than guessed.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation

works.title: The Tournament
works.form: Antiquarian romance in verse among the Rowley poems; long, irregular and catalogue-driven, in the archaic orthography Chatterton supplied, with glosses of the obsolete words attached in the manuscripts and collections.
works.description: One of the longest and most ambitious of the poems Thomas Chatterton put into the name of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk Thomas Rowley, and a centrepiece of the forgeries he sent to Horace Walpole in 1764. It presents itself as an antiquarian account of a medieval tournament, complete with lists of champions, devices and heraldic blazon, in a deliberately archaized spelling and diction. Its interest is double: as an early achievement of the primitive-genius vogue, and as a document of a Bristol apprentice's furious self-education in the literature of the past.
works.plot: The poem narrates the summoning, the gathering and the running of a great tournament, and dwells on the heraldry, the armour, the ladies' favours and the encounters of the champions with a minuteness meant to look like a period chronicler's rather than a modern poet's imagination. Chivalric honour, religious invocation and the pomp of the field are combined without any neoclassical sense of proportion, so that the piece reads as a series of illuminated tableaux. Its frame is the more important fiction: Rowley is made to be an eyewitness and recorder of the scene, an authority older than any modern antiquary. The result is the most complete of Chatterton's impersonations, in which the medieval is not described from outside but re-enacted in a language the eighteenth century was willing to believe.
works.significance: It is the largest single exercise in the Rowley impersonation and an important text in the history of literary forgery, of medievalism, and of the cult of the primitive genius; its mixture of heraldic learning and genuine imaginative power is what later readers from the Romantics onwards remembered. It also helped to establish the vogue for an invented national antiquity which the same decade received from Macpherson and from Percy.
works.meter: Rowley's supposed measures: long lines with medial caesura and mixed rhyme formations, imitating fifteenth-century verse rather than any Elizabethan or Augustan practice.
works.context: It belongs to the Rowley correspondence of 1764, when Chatterton, a clerk in Bristol, supplied Walpole with parchment 'originals' and letters in a fabricated antiquarian persona, at the moment when the taste for chivalry and for national origins was being formed by Walpole's own circle at Strawberry Hill. The forgery was detected within a few years, but the poems continued to be read as poetry.
works.characters: The framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'; the knights and champions of the listed tournament; the ladies whose favours are proclaimed
works.structure: A chronicle-poem in the supposed voice and hand of Rowley: annalistic opening, catalogue of champions and devices, narrative of the field, and devotional and heraldic digression, without regular stanzaic closure.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship is recorded as single because Chatterton, not any medieval monk, wrote the poem. The ascription in the manuscripts is to 'Thomas Rowley', a fictitious fifteenth-century Bristol priest and chronicler whose parchment 'originals' and glosses Chatterton supplied; the deception imposed upon Walpole and other antiquaries before it was seen through. The year 1764 refers to the Rowley correspondence in which the piece was produced.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
National identity and Englishness
Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales

works.title: The Tower
works.description: The great late collection of Yeats's old age: the tower at Ballylee, the gyres, Byzantium and the rage against mortality. It is a verse work of 1928 by W. B. Yeats; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Irish Revival Lyric and the Celtic Twilight and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection opens with 'Sailing to Byzantium' and 'The Tower' and includes 'Meditations in Time of Civil War', 'Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen', 'Leda and the Swan', 'Among School Children' and 'A Man Young and Old' — poems of the ageing body, the civil war, the mythic vision and the permanence of art.
works.significance: The Tower is Yeats's greatest single collection and the summit of English poetry between The Waste Land and Four Quartets: 'Among School Children', 'Sailing to Byzantium' and 'The Tower' are among the greatest poems in the language.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the symbolist image and the esoteric system.
works.context: The Irish Civil War (1922–23) and the Free State, Yeats's Senatorship, the Nobel Prize of 1923, and his Norman tower at Ballylee. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; irish revival lyric and the celtic twilight.
works.characters: the old man sailing to Byzantium; Mrs French, Mary Hynes, Raftery and Hanrahan ('The Tower'); Leda and the swan; the sixty-year-old smiling public man ('Among School Children')
works.structure: Twenty-five poems in five sections. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Butler Yeats. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great
works.form: burlesque tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A burlesque tragedy on heroic subjects, in which the tiny hero of the old ballad is placed inside an exact parody of heroic verse, with its declamation, its mono-syllabic names and its catastrophes of absurd magnitude. It is the most sustained English exercise in tragicomical burlesque of the century and was revised into a two-act form with a dedication that became a manifesto.
works.plot: Tom Thumb, in miniature and married to the queen, discovers his beloved's intrigue with a courtier and sends his rival on errands that end in death. King Arthur's court supplies the dignity, the giants and the fathers the ceremony, and the accumulating duels and poisonings grow past all probability. The finale buries nearly the whole cast, the survivors being left to moralise on the fragility of heroic design.
works.significance: It is the classic English parody of heroic tragedy and a key document of the quarrel between the legitimate theatre and the little houses; its preface and dedication are primary statements of the comic theory later applied in the novels.
works.meter: Heroic couplets and the inflated blank verse of tragedy used exactly for nonsense, with the famous mono-syllabic names and the tautological similes of the high style.
works.context: First played at the Haymarket in 1731 and revived in altered form at Drury Lane in 1737 with a prose dedication to the reader and a preface critical of contemporary tragedy; the season was one of heroic revival and of managerial dispute.
works.characters: Tom Thumb; King Arthur; Queen Huncamunca; Doodle; Grumio; Glumdalca; Meridanta
works.structure: A regular five-act burlesque tragedy in the heroic manner, reduced later to two acts, with the parody sustained scene by scene against the conventions of tragic structure; the deaths are stacked for cumulative effect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the revised edition of the late 1730s carries the author's name, prefatory matter and a dedication much debated as criticism.
themes: Heroism and the heroic code
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

works.title: The Tragic Mary
works.description: Published in 1890 and the finest of the Michael Field verse plays: a drama of Mary Queen of Scots, her marriages and her imprisonment. It is a dramatic work of 1890 by Michael Field; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
works.plot: The play follows Mary through the crisis of 1566-67, from her estrangement from Darnley and his murder to her marriage with Bothwell and her downfall, and reads her as a figure of tragic passion rather than of political failure.
works.significance: The Tragic Mary is one of the finest English verse dramas of the 1890s and the best of the Michael Field plays: its treatment of a woman's political and sexual destiny made it central to the feminist reading of Victorian historical drama.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric.
works.context: 1890: the Victorian interest in Mary Stuart, the verse drama revival of the 1890s, and the aesthetic reading of history. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Mary, Queen of Scots; Lord Darnley; the Earl of Bothwell
works.structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Traitor
works.description: Shirley's most successful tragedy, a political play on the assassination of the Duke of Florence by his favourite Sciarrha, loosely based on the murder of the Florentine Duke Alessandro de' Medici in 1537.
works.plot: The Duke's favourite Sciarrha, ambitious and jealous, conspires with the Duke's rival to assassinate him; the conspiracy succeeds, but Sciarrha's sister Amidea refuses the Duke and the murder destroys both plotters.
works.significance: The finest Caroline political tragedy and a principal influence on later plays of tyrannicide, including the Restoration heroic drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1631 and read at court by Charles I, who is said to have remarked that it was 'a tragedy'.
works.characters: the Duke of Florence; Sciarrha; Amidea; Cosmo; Lorenzo; Depazzi
works.structure: Five acts following the rise, execution, and ruin of the conspiracy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society
works.form: Philosophical-reflection poem in the tradition of Pope's 'Essay on Man', cast as a verse epistle to a friend and organised as a comparative survey of nations; issued as a separate pamphlet in quarto.
works.description: Goldsmith's first published poem and the work that established him as a poet: a reflection in heroic couplets on the forms of society and on the place each gives to human happiness, written in the manner of the Augustan philosophical essay in verse and addressed to his friend the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds. It takes the traveller's survey of the nations of Europe as the frame for an argument about happiness, government and contentment.
works.plot: The poem opens with the traveller's farewell to his family and his retirement from the world's noise, and proceeds as a survey of the chief states of Europe, each examined for the kind of happiness its institutions secure or refuse. The commercial states of Flanders, the hardy independence of the Swiss cantons, Italy under priestcraft, smiling but servitude-prone Gaul, proud and darkly policed Spain, and England with its liberty, its commerce and its unequal distribution of enjoyments, are each allowed their plea and then judged. The argument is that happiness does not follow from any single form of policy or condition of life, since every state has its own peculiar miseries and every rank its own discontents, and that felicity depends rather on the mind and on the balance of the whole. The close withdraws from the prospect of society to the poet's own retired lot, content to have failed in the world if he has kept his integrity.
works.significance: It made Goldsmith's poetical reputation at the moment when the couplet tradition was beginning to be questioned, and it remains the best example of the Augustan philosophical survey in verse written in the 1760s. Its doctrine that forms of society do not determine happiness, and its portraits of national character, were much quoted, and it prepared the moral manner of 'The Deserted Village'.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in the polished Augustan manner with balanced antithesis, sententious closure and a good deal of the epigrammatic turn Goldsmith took from Pope.
works.context: It was composed largely during a country retirement in the English midlands and published at the height of the debate about commercial society, national character and the comparative history of government, in which the Scottish and English moral philosophers were then engaged. Its survey of Europe drew on the Grand Tour and on the travelling literature of the age, and on the post-war confidence and anxiety about British commerce.
works.characters: The traveller-poet and his own family left behind; the nations of Europe as collectively personified conditions of society
works.structure: A single sustained argument in the epistle-reflection form: opening retirement and apostrophe, a sequence of national portraits each with its own balance sheet of good and evil, general conclusion on the dependence of happiness on the mind, and personal peroration of retirement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published anonymously at first but was known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and its history is documented in his letters and in the contemporary accounts of its subscription publication.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo
altTitles: The Treatise of the Two Married Women and the Widow
works.description: William Dunbar's scandalous Midsummer Eve debate (c. 1500–07, 530 lines): the eavesdropping poet overhears three women — two wives and a widow — exchanging frank confidences on marriage, their husbands' inadequacies, and the arts of deceiving them, in the most sustained exhibition of female licence (and male ventriloquism) in medieval English verse. The most brilliant of Dunbar's alliterative poems.
works.plot: Hidden in the hedge on a June night, the narrator hears the first wife anatomize her husband's age, impotence, and jealousy, the second mock hers as a coward and braggart, and the widow — dismissing both as amateurs — advise on choosing, managing, and surviving husbands, until the dawn and the lark's song end the colloquy.
works.significance: The supreme comic-satiric poem of the Scottish tradition: its frankness and metrical brilliance made it a scandal in its own day and a touchstone of medieval misogyny debate in ours.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in Dunbar's hands — colloquial, obscene, and metrically audacious.
works.context: Composed c. 1500–07 at the court of James IV, in the makars' revival of alliterative verse; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508) and preserved in the Bannatyne manuscript.
works.characters: the narrator (Dunbar); the two married women; the widow
works.structure: A debate-frame of three long monologues, each more outrageous than the last, in the tradition of the débat and the Wife of Bath's prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.
themes: Marriage and women's conduct
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The Scottish Makars

works.title: The Trial: More Links of the Daisy Chain
altTitles: Trial: More Links of the Daisy Chain
works.description: Published in 1864 and the second of the May family chronicles: the trial of a young man for murder and the moral testing of the whole family. It is a prose fiction work of 1864 by Charlotte M. Yonge; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Leonard Ward, a young man of a Stoneborough family close to the Mays, is falsely accused and convicted of murder; the novel follows his imprisonment and his family's ordeal, and an American episode in which Tom May and the Wards seek a new life in an Indiana swamp settlement while the Civil War rages in the distance, until the truth comes out and clears him.
works.significance: The Trial shows Yonge at her most ambitious: it uses the machinery of the sensation novel for a sustained examination of conscience, guilt and religious duty, and it is one of the earliest English novels to dramatise a criminal trial as a test of Christian character.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the large family chronicle with an enormous cast.
works.context: 1864: the Victorian criminal trial and the press, the Oxford Movement's casuistry, and the serial market of the 1860s. The record dates the work as composed between 1863 and 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Leonard Ward; Averil Ward, his sister; Ella Ward; Dr May; Tom May; Ethel May
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Mary Yonge. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The True History of Joshua Davidson
works.description: Published in 1872 and Linton's most original book: the life of a working-class carpenter who tries to live literally by the Sermon on the Mount in modern London. It is a prose fiction work of 1872 by Eliza Lynn Linton; it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: Joshua Davidson, a village carpenter's son from Trevalga in north Cornwall, resolves to live the Gospel literally, is driven from his village, and in London reclaims the prostitute Mary Prinsep and the burglar Joe; his trade unionism leads him to communism, he goes with his friend John, the narrator, to serve the Paris Commune, where Mary is shot as a pétroleuse, and back in England he is killed by a mob inflamed by a clergyman's denunciation, a modern repetition of the life of Christ.
works.significance: The True History of Joshua Davidson is one of the boldest religious novels of the century: its application of the gospel literally to Victorian London anticipated the Christian Socialism of the 1880s, and its scandalous success made Linton a figure of national controversy for the second time.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical periodical essay with a strong persona.
works.context: 1871-72: the Paris Commune, the London of the 1870s, the Christian Socialist movement and the Tichborne case, and the Victorian fascination with the 'historical Jesus'. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Joshua Davidson; John, his friend and the narrator; Mary Prinsep; Joe, the reformed burglar
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eliza Lynn. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
works.description: Ralph Cudworth's massive learned work against atheism, in which he argues that the ancient philosophers were not atheists and that a rational theism is the true intellectual system of the universe.
works.plot: Book I sets out the various forms of atheism and refutes them; the work argues for the existence of plastic natures, for the immateriality of the soul, and for the eternity of moral truths against Hobbesian materialism.
works.significance: The most learned philosophical work of the seventeenth-century English Platonists; its concept of 'plastic nature' influenced Leibniz and later vitalist philosophy, and its refutation of atheism was a standard reference.
works.meter: Dense, heavily cited scholarly prose of the Cambridge Platonists.
works.context: Published in 1678, the year of the Popish Plot, and licensed by Samuel Parker; Cudworth was Master of Christ's College, Cambridge.
works.structure: A single vast treatise in four books (only the first volume was published), with enormous learned apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cudworth; authorship undisputed.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
movements: The Cambridge Platonists

works.title: The Tryal: A Comedy
works.description: The comic play of the first volume of the series delineating the stronger passions, assigned by its author's introductory discourse to the passion of love and laid in the English bathing city of Bath. It is a comedy of mercy and of Scotch-English difference, written in the manner of the older sentimental comedy but built on a hard legal and financial plot. Modern editors have found it the liveliest piece in the volume and the best adjusted for the stage.
works.plot: Withrington, a Scottish officer who has been ruined and imprisoned by the false evidence of the English merchant Harwood, comes to Bath with his daughter Agnes, poor and dependent. Harwood is now prosperous, engaged in a suit of debt in which Withrington, as a witness, holds the power to destroy him, and his son is in love with Agnes. At the trial Withrington withholds the testimony that would have ruined his enemy, and the disclosure of who the injured party has all along been turns the legal victory into forgiveness. The younger lovers are free to marry, and the comedy ends on mercy rather than on punishment, with the passion of love working through a father's power to revenge himself.
works.significance: The Tryal is the clearest illustration in the series of the theory that a comedy may be built on a single passion as rigorously as a tragedy, and its movement from the right to punish to the choice to forgive has made it the most frequently revived of the author's comic numbers. It is now a standard text for the study of women's drama and of the Romantic-period sentimental comedy.
works.meter: Written in dialogue of the closed heroic-couplet school used by the eighteenth-century comedy, with a brisk prosaic interchange in the lower scenes and more sustained rhetorical passages in the scenes of disclosure.
works.context: Published anonymously with the first volume of the series of plays in the last years of the eighteenth century, when the anti-theatrical debate and the licensed patent theatres made a closet series of analytic plays a practical form, and when the union of Scotland and England supplied a stock of national-character comedy. The legal and mercantile business of the plot reflects the small-bath society of the 1790s, where debts, evidence, and imprisonment for debt were familiar.
works.characters: Withrington, the injured Scottish officer; Harwood, the English merchant he could ruin; Agnes, Withrington's daughter; Mariane; Sir Loftus Prettyman; Miss Eston
works.structure: A regular five-act comedy of single design, opening on the master's concealed identity and closing on public disclosure and reconciliation; the courtroom scene forms the structural and moral hinge of the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in the first volume, 1798, and reissued under the author's name in the collected dramas; no dispute attaches to the play.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Revenge and justice
Sensibility, feeling, and its critics

works.title: The Tunning of Elinour Rumming
works.description: Skelton's carnivalesque masterpiece: a Skeltonic account of the alewife Elinour Rumming of Leatherhead and the procession of women who come to drink her noxious ale, a low-life gallery from drunken Alice to the beggarly Maud Ruggy — ugliness, appetite, and disorder rendered with gleeful verbal energy.
works.plot: The poem describes Elinour's brewing and her customers in turn — their poverty, their lechery, their brawling — as the alehouse degenerates into a riot of appetite without plot or moral.
works.significance: The most vivid low-life poem in English before the eighteenth century; its catalogue form and demotic energy made it a model for later satire.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most anarchic — breathless rhymes, macaronic puns, and tavern speech.
works.context: Set at Leatherhead in Surrey; the poem belongs to the alehouse satire of the early sixteenth century and reflects the moralists' anxieties about disorderly women.
works.characters: Elinour Rumming; her customers (drunken Alice, Maud Ruggy, and others)
works.structure: A catalogue or procession of drinkers, framed by the description of the brewing; no plot, but a mounting carnival intensity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Turkish Embassy Letters
altTitles: Letters Written During the Turkish Embassy
works.description: The correspondence of the ambassador's wife at Constantinople and Adrianople, describing the seraglios, the baths, the Greek church and the women's society of the Turkish capital, and reporting the inoculation practice she afterwards brought to England. It is the most vivacious of the century's travel writing and the classic account of the East seen by a woman.
works.plot: The letters follow the party from Vienna through the Hungarian and Bulgarian roads to Adrianople and Constantinople, giving an account of the way of travelling, of the houses and of the ceremonies of the embassy. They describe the women's baths and the seraglio, the Greek ladies and their usages, and the cathedral of the Phanar, with the writer's own freedom of access to a society closed to other travellers. The later letters from the embassy report the smallpox operation, and the correspondence closes with the return into Poland and Germany.
works.significance: It created the literary image of the Turkish women's world for English readers and is a foundational text of the travel letter and of the female account of the East, its evidence on inoculation being of the history of medicine as well as of letters.
works.meter: An animated epistolary prose of the quick phrase, the parenthesis and the indignant comparison, its sentences built on the sudden turn of observation rather than on the balanced period.
works.context: Written during the embassy of 1717-18 at the time of the Turkish war and the settlement of the Passarowitz season, in the current of the correspondence of the diplomatic corps, and returned to by the writer's own account of inoculation in the English medical press.
works.characters: the writing lady of the embassy; the friend at home to whom the letters are addressed; the begum or lady of the seraglio and her attendants; the Greek ladies of Constantinople; the ambassador and his household
works.structure: A continuous family correspondence, chiefly to a single friend, ordered by the route and the stay, and rising to the set descriptions of the baths and the seraglio; there is no plot beyond the journey and the observation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letters remained in manuscript and were given to the press after the writer's death, so that no publication year in her lifetime can be asserted here.

works.title: The Twa Dogs
works.form: beast fable and debate poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the tradition of Ramsay's and Dryden's dialogues of creatures
works.description: Burns's animal fable of the two dogs - Luath the farmer's working stock-dog and Caesar the gentleman's pampered spaniel - who meet at a tavern door and compare the conditions of their lives. Under the covering of the beasts the poem delivers a searching social analysis of rank, idleness, hire and hunger in the agricultural west of Scotland, and one of the sharpest indictments of the privileges of great families in the century. It is among Burns's earliest considerable poems and the first open declaration of his egalitarian creed.
works.plot: Caesar, kept warm and idle by his laird, and Luath, the working dog of a farmer, meet and dispute their respective happiness. Caesar reports the luxuries and the boredom of the hall, the squire's dogs, horses and flatterers, and the uselessness of his own life, while Luath describes the labour, the weather, the hunger and the honest dependence of the poor. The dialogue arrives at the poem's famous conclusion that the rank of the creature makes no difference in its worth, and that the poor dog and the poor man have at least the merit of usefulness.
works.significance: It established Burns's characteristic politics of the worth of the common creature and supplied the imaginative ground of his later songs on rank and equality. As a dialect fable it is the most successful modern descendant of the Scots 'Makkar' tradition of talk between beasts, and it remains a standard text for the literature of the nations and for social analysis in verse.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), four long and two short Scots lines with the a-a-a-b-a-b rhyme, used for sustained dialogue.
works.context: Begun about 1784 and revised for the Kilmarnock volume, in a decade of enclosure, of improving agriculture and of depressed rural wages in Ayrshire; the poem's comparison of the idle and the useful draws on a long native tradition of estates criticism and on the contemporary debate about the condition of the labouring poor.
works.characters: Luath; Caesar; the poor laird; the farmer and his bailiff; the tavern company
works.structure: A framed tavern scene followed by a matched dialogue of the two dogs, each speech elaborating the conditions of its master, closing with the moral of the fable.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns dated the poem in his own memoranda as an early attempt, and the standard editions record his successive revisions of the text.
themes: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

works.title: The Twilight of the Gods and Other Tales
altTitles: Twilight of the Gods and Other Tales
works.description: The finest English collection of fantastic tales of the century: the gods, the philosophers and the impossible. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Richard Garnett; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Garnett's fantastic stories — 'The Twilight of the Gods', 'The Demon Pope', 'The City of the Dead', 'Alexander the Ratcatcher', 'The Potion of Lao-Tsze' — in which the gods of antiquity, the philosophers and the magicians are involved in comic and terrible situations.
works.significance: The Twilight of the Gods is the finest English collection of fantastic tales of the century and the founding text of the modern literary fantasy: its irony, its learning and its invention were admired by Yeats, Wilde and the whole tradition of the English fantastic story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ironic fantasy of the classical and the philosophical.
works.context: The British Museum and the world of Victorian scholarship, and the classical tradition of the fantastic tale. The record dates the work as composed between 1886 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: the gods; the demon pope; Lao-Tsze; Alexander; the philosophers
works.structure: A collection of fantastic tales in the classical and oriental manner. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as R. Garnett. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
