works.title: The Twisting of the Rope
works.form: Play in Irish (one act; trans. by Lady Gregory)
works.description: The first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage: the poet Hanrahan and the twisting of the rope. It is a dramatic work of 1901 by Douglas Hyde; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poet Hanrahan comes to the cottage to claim his bride and is turned from the door by the neighbours' trick of the twisting of the rope, in the one-act comedy in Irish that opened the Irish-language drama of the Abbey.
works.significance: The Twisting of the Rope, played at the Abbey on 21 October 1901, was the first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage: it opened the Irish-language drama of the revival and made the cottage comedy the founding mode of the Abbey.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish of Connacht carried into English by the translation of Lady Gregory.
works.context: The Irish west in 1901, and the Abbey Theatre's first Irish-language night. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and first performed in 1901 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement.
works.characters: Hanrahan the poet; the bride; the neighbours; the rope-twisters
works.structure: A cottage comedy in one act, in Irish with Lady Gregory's translation. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name An Craoibhín Aoibhinn, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Douglas Hyde is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
works.description: Shakespeare's early romantic comedy of friendship and betrayal: Valentine and Proteus, the 'two gentlemen' of Verona, both fall in love with Silvia; Proteus betrays his friend and his own beloved Julia, and the play moves through disguise, forest outlawry, and attempted rape to a reconciliation whose abruptness has troubled audiences ever since.
works.plot: Proteus, sent to Milan, falls in love with Valentine's Silvia and betrays him to the Duke; Valentine joins the outlaws, Silvia flees to the forest, and Proteus's assault on her is stopped by Valentine's intervention, leading to the double reconciliation and the play's famously compressed ending.
works.significance: The first of Shakespeare's romantic comedies and the seedbed of themes — friendship versus love, the heroine in disguise, the green world — he would develop for a decade.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose, with songs; among Shakespeare's earliest surviving verse.
works.context: An early play, probably written about 1590–91 from the Spanish romance Diana Enamorada (via its French and English versions); not printed until the 1623 First Folio.
works.characters: Valentine; Proteus; Silvia; Julia; the Duke of Milan; Launce; Speed; Crab the dog
works.structure: Five acts of alternating Milan and forest scenes, built on the paired lovers plot with the comic servants Speed and Launce (and his dog Crab) as counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Two Noble Kinsmen
works.description: Shakespeare's last play, written with John Fletcher from Chaucer's Knight's Tale: the cousins Palamon and Arcite, kinsmen and friends, both fall in love with Emilia from their prison window; their rivalry is settled by the tournament for her hand — Arcite wins and dies in a riding accident, and Palamon marries her, while the Jailer's Daughter's mad sub-plot runs its course.
works.plot: The cousins swear eternal friendship, then break it over Emilia; Arcite is released, Palamon escapes; the tournament appoints the winner; Arcite's victory is followed by his fatal fall from the horse; the dying Arcite bequeaths Emilia to Palamon; Theseus closes the play on the riddle of fortune, while the Jailer's Daughter is cured by the doctor's masque of her wooer.
works.significance: The closing chord of the Shakespeare canon — a return to Chaucer, and to the question of friendship and love with which his career began.
works.meter: The collaboration's two styles are audibly joined — Shakespeare's ceremonial verse (the prayers at the altars) with Fletcher's supple fluency.
works.context: First performed about 1614, after the Globe fire, probably at Blackfriars; printed in quarto in 1634 as 'by the memorable worthies... Mr John Fletcher and Mr William Shakespeare'; omitted from the First Folio.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emilia; Theseus; Hippolyta; the Jailer; the Jailer's Daughter; the Wooer; Pirithous; the Doctor
works.structure: A tragicomedy of friendship and fortune in five acts, with the Jailer's Daughter's madness as a tragic sub-plot and the Morris dance and tournament as spectacle.
works.attributionNotes: Joint authorship with John Fletcher is established on title-page and stylistic evidence and is universally accepted; the division of scenes is broadly agreed.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: The Two Ways
altTitles: The Boke of the Two Ways
works.description: Sir John Clanvowe's devotional prose tract on the two ways of life and death — the narrow way of virtue and the broad way of the world — a Lollard-leaning meditation written in the circle of the 'Lollard knights' of Richard II's court, probably in 1391. It is the earliest prose work of the English reforming tradition by a lay courtier.
works.plot: The tract expounds Christ's teaching of the two ways, contrasts the few who walk the narrow path with the many on the broad road to perdition, and anatomizes the sins of the world — pride, avarice, gluttony — with a particular Lollard sharpness against clerical wealth and display.
works.significance: A principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite and the earliest lay devotional prose of the Ricardian court.
works.meter: Plain, earnest prose with scriptural quotation.
works.context: Composed c. 1391 by the courtier-knight Clanvowe (d. October 1391), in the company of the Lollard knights at the court of Richard II; preserved in Bodleian MS Eng. th. c. 39 and later copies.
works.characters: the writer (as penitent teacher)
works.structure: A single homiletic meditation organized by the scriptural image of the two ways, with catalogue of sins and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Clanvowe in the manuscripts.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
The contemplative life

Ricardian Poetry

works.title: The Undying One, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Literary Annual and Keepsake Verse
works.description: The second volume of the same hand, built on a long poem in four cantos treating the legend of the Wandering Jew, whom the author calls the Undying One. The poem makes the outcast of Christian legend a figure for the eternally repentant and homeless soul, and the accompanying miscellaneous poems print some of the lyrics most often reprinted in the gift-books of the decade. The book confirmed the author's standing in the annual market.
works.plot: The Undying One passes through four cantos in which the Shoeman of Jerusalem, condemned to walk until the last day, meets at intervals the mortals whose lives his own length makes tragic; his penance, his memory of the crucifixion, and his inability to die form the poem's sustained subject. The miscellaneous section that follows prints short poems on friendship, childhood, the bride, and loss, including The Careless Word, They Loved one Another, My Heart is like a Withered Nut, My Childhood's Home, Old Friends, and The Bride. The volume's argument thus moves from an immortal's guilt to the mortal affections he watches.
works.significance: The poem is the most substantial treatment in English by a woman Romantic poet of the Ahasuerus legend as a figure of unforgiven guilt and homelessness, and its combination of the supernatural tale with short domestic lyric is typical of the keepsake volume at its best. Several of the miscellaneous pieces became standard anthology items and were reprinted in America.
works.meter: The four cantos use a sustained measured rhymed stanza with apostrophe and lament, the notes append ballad and song stanzas, and the miscellaneous poems are in common and long measure with refrain; the whole is rhetorical and vocal rather than narrative in rhythm.
works.context: Published in 1830 by the London firm that issued the fashionable popular books of the season and inscribed by permission to a princess of the blood, at the height of the gift-book economy and of the vogue for legends of penance and exile. The Wandering Jew subject belonged to a stock of continental legends then being rewritten by women poets, and the volume's economics depended on the annuals that bought such pieces.
works.characters: the Undying One, the Wandering Jew; the mortals he successively meets; the speaker of the miscellaneous lyrics; the bride and the old friends of that section
works.structure: A four-canto narrative-lyric in which episodic meetings replace continuous plot, prefaced and followed by notes and by an unordered section of miscellaneous poems.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the volume is signed and dated and the several contents have not been disputed.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: The Unfortunate Traveller
works.description: Nashe's picaresque novel: the page Jack Wilton travels through the wars and cities of Europe — tricking the camp at Tergou, fleeing the sweating sickness and the plague, witnessing the massacre of the Anabaptists at Münster, courting in Italy, and escaping the rape-and-execution plot of the Jew Zadoch and the courtesan Juliana — in the first English novel of adventure and the grotesque.
works.plot: Jack's tricks in the army, his travels with the Earl of Surrey (and the Italian Diamante in boy's disguise), the horrors of Münster and of plague-struck Rome, the anatomies and executions, and the final escape through the villain's own engines carry the narrative to its abrupt, comic close.
works.significance: The first English picaresque novel — the ancestor of Defoe, Smollett, and the English novel's roguish line.
works.meter: Prose of Nashe's most violent invention — the grotesque, the comic, and the lyrical in rapid succession.
works.context: Published 1594; its continental horrors answered the decade's appetite for travel lies and martyrdom pamphlets, and its Italian scenes the anti-Catholic mood.
works.characters: Jack Wilton; the Earl of Surrey; Diamante; Zadoch; Zachary; Juliana; the Pope; Heraclide; the Anabaptists
works.structure: A first-person travel narrative in the manner of Lazarillo de Tormes, episodic and sensational, with the set pieces of horror (the anatomies, the executions) as its climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York
altTitles: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancastre and Yorke
works.description: Edward Hall's chronicle of the Wars of the Roses and the triumph of the house of Tudor, from the deposition of Richard II to the death of Henry VIII; printed posthumously by Richard Grafton in 1548 and continued by Grafton in later editions.
works.plot: Hall narrates the dynastic strife between Lancaster and York as a providential drama culminating in the union of the two houses in Henry VIII, with long set-piece speeches and a moralizing emphasis on the ruin brought by ambition, faction, and rebellion; the reign of Henry VIII occupies the final section ('The Triumphant Reign of King Henry the VIII').
works.significance: The principal source of Shakespeare's English history plays (the second tetralogy follows Hall closely) and the classic statement of the Tudor myth of union and providential kingship; its dramatic speeches made it the most literary of the Tudor chronicles.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled over the 1530s and 1540s by Hall, a lawyer and MP, drawing on More's Richard III, Polydore Vergil, and Fabyan; the 1548 edition was supervised by Grafton, who added continuations in the editions of 1550.
works.characters: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: Chronicle divided by reigns, from Richard II through Henry VIII, framed by a preface on the theme of union and enriched with speeches invented in the manner of classical historiography.

Kingship and good rule
National identity and Englishness
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: The Unknown Eros and Other Odes
works.description: Published in 1877 and Patmore's greatest poetry: a series of odes on divine love, death and the mystical union of the soul with God, written after his conversion to Rome. It is a verse work of 1877 by Coventry Patmore; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric.
works.plot: The odes move from 'Eros' and 'Psyche' through 'The Toys', 'The Azalea', 'Departure' and 'The Unknown Eros' to 'Amelia' and the vision of the love of God; their subject is the continuity of human love and divine love.
works.significance: The Unknown Eros is a landmark of English religious poetry and one of the strangest books of the nineteenth century: its long, unrhymed, free-breathing odes anticipated the rhythms of Hopkins and of modern free verse, and its mystical eroticism is unique in Victorian poetry.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is conversational narrative verse in the plain style.
works.context: The 1870s, the Catholic mystical tradition, the Swedenborgian and Dantean background, and Patmore's own bereavement and conversion. The record dates the work as composed between 1868 and 1877 and first published in 1877 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Unnatural Combat
works.description: Massinger's dark tragedy in which the Marseilles admiral Malefort, under pressure from his son, kills him in single combat, and the son's ghost returns to expose the father's crimes.
works.plot: The young Malefort, corrupted by the villain Beauford junior, demands a combat with his father; the father kills him; the ghost reveals the unnatural deed and the father's earlier crime, and Malefort dies in madness.
works.significance: One of Massinger's most powerful tragedies, notable for its psychological intensity and its treatment of paternal guilt; it was long thought to have influenced later Jacobean and Caroline revenge drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Globe c. 1624-26 and published in 1639.
works.characters: Malefort senior; Malefort junior; Beauford; Theocrine; Montrevile; Rochefort
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a ghost and a catastrophic recognition.

works.title: The Untilled Field
works.description: Published in 1903 and the founding book of the modern Irish short story: fifteen stories of priest-ridden rural Ireland. It is a prose fiction work of 1903 by George Moore; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life.
works.plot: The stories follow the parishioners and priests of a Mayo village through emigration, clerical tyranny, the failure of love and the small cruelties of village life, and end with the departure of the young for America.
works.significance: The Untilled Field invented the modern Irish short story and gave the Irish Revival its most exact prose: its influence on Joyce, O'Connor and the Irish story is direct and acknowledged, and it is the first work in which Moore's Irish subject matter found its proper form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is flaubertian impersonality and exact detail.
works.context: 1899-1902: the Irish Literary Revival, the land agitation and emigration of the 1890s, and the foundation of the Irish Literary Theatre. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1902 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.

works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Augustus Moore. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Vampire; or, The Bride of the Islands
works.form: Drama; Gothic melodrama with songs; supernatural shock-piece
works.description: A two-act Gothic melodrama of the undead which turned a French stage spectre into the most copied English supernatural shock-piece of the 1820s. A ruined bridegroom and his new love are waylaid on a shipwrecked coast by a corpse-bride who kills the men she has already wed, and the play's machinery of moonlit tombs, animated statues and apparitions gave the English stage its standard vampire iconography. Adapted from a French melodrame, it is nonetheless a shaping original performance in its stage business and its ballad and chorus effects. Its success created a decade of vampiric competition on both London patents and the minor theatres.
works.plot: On a Hebridean coast an English nobleman, deserted by the woman who ruined him, loves a Scottish fisher girl and is opposed by her brother. Wrecks, a burial, and the emergence of a pale bride from her family vault disturb the island: the undead woman claims the living bridegroom, vanishing with him to a spectral bridal. A party of rescuers, guided by a hermit's warnings and by the moonlight funeral rites, breaks into the cavern, the vampire is destroyed, and the living pair are freed, with a moral about guilt and the unquiet dead.
works.significance: The play that fixed the vampire on the English stage and created the conventions of stage supernaturalism later developed in the century's sensation drama; it is a central document for study of melodrama, of theatrical piracy and of the Gothic after the 1810s. Its transmission into after-pieces and into continental repertory makes it one of the most influential of Regency popular dramas.
works.meter: Mixed prose and verse, with set songs and choruses in popular ballad and lyrical measures for the supernatural scenes
works.context: First played in the summer of 1820 at a secondary London theatre whose management was then building a specialty in Romantic melodrama, it belongs to the wave of vampire literature that followed a famous unfinished ghost tale of the same season and its printed and staged issue. The piece drew on French melodramatic technique and on the popular antiquarianism of island superstition, and its imitators on the patent houses in the following decade made it a benchmark of the minor theatre's power over London taste.
works.structure: Melodrama in two acts of continuous scene with songs, choruses and stage business; the plot moves by sensational tableau rather than psychological development, and the supernatural machinery is staged as spectacle.
works.attributionNotes: Named on the title page as the adapter's work; the piece is an original English performance founded on a French melodrame and its sources are acknowledged in the attribution rather than disputed. Two rival vampire plays of the same year were separately attributed.

works.title: The Vanity of Dogmatizing; or, Confidence in Philosophy
works.description: Joseph Glanvill's sceptical defence of the new philosophy, which attacks Aristotelian scholastic dogmatism and argues that only experimental enquiry can extend knowledge; it was revised in 1665 as Scepsis Scientifica.
works.plot: Glanvill argues that human understanding is weak and prone to error, that the schools' dogmatism is vain, and that the experimental method of Bacon and the Royal Society offers the only path to reliable knowledge; the work contains the famous witchcraft narrative of the Drummer of Tedworth.
works.significance: The most readable early statement of the case for experimental philosophy in English and a source for the sceptical tradition that influenced Hume; the 1665 revision Scepsis Scientifica was widely read.
works.meter: Elegant, persuasive prose admired by the Royal Society.
works.context: Published in 1661, a year before the Royal Society's charter; Glanvill became a Fellow in 1664 and one of its most eloquent apologists.
works.structure: A series of chapters of sceptical argument with illustrative narratives.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Glanvill; authorship undisputed.
themes: Monsters and the marvellous

The New Science and experimental philosophy

works.title: The Vanity of Human Wishes
altTitles: The Vanity of Human Wishes: The Tenth Satire of Juvenal Imitated
works.form: verse satire and meditative poem in the Juvenalian tradition, with a strong native elegiac and devotional undertone
works.description: Johnson's greatest poem, an imitation of Juvenal's tenth satire on the emptiness of human desire, transposed from Roman invective into a Christian meditation on providence. Its catalogue of disappointed wishes - the scholar, the statesman, the general, the great man, the beauty, the aged - moves from the fall of Sejanus to the quiet exemplary death of the virtuous widow. The poem replaces the satirist's confidence in exposure with the recognition that only prayer and resignation remain.
works.plot: The speaker invites History to reveal the disasters produced by human hope, surveying ambition in learning, in public office, in arms and at court, and showing that each wish, granted or refused, destroys the wisher. The celebrated Sejanus passage enacts the sudden collapse of a favourite's power, and the fall of Wolsey gives the argument a distinctly modern and Christian dimension. The portraits of the beauty and of the aged wretch extend the miseries of the body and of dependence, and the poem ends by surrendering choice to providence in the prayer for wisdom that closes Johnson's verse.
works.significance: It is generally held to be the finest poem Johnson wrote and one of the major moral poems of the century, matching Pope's Essay on Man with a darker and more Scriptural account of desire. Its Sejanus and its closing widow supplied later poets with a model of the meditative satiric couplet, and the poem stands at the centre of the preromantic interest in melancholy, mutability and resignation.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, famously varied by dactylic and trisyllabic substitutions that give the line an unusual weight; the couplet is often enjambed and the antithesis strained to the breaking point.
works.context: Published on 28 January 1749 from Johnson's lodgings in Gough Square in the same season as the opening of his periodical labour; the fate of ministers and favourites was a live topic after the fall of Walpole and the recent rising of '45 made the instability of power and the misery of civil war immediate experience.
works.characters: The speaker; Sejanus; Wolsey; the beauty; the aged wretch; the virtuous widow; History
works.structure: A single invective movement organised as a series of exemplary portraits after the manner of the satire, framed by an invocation and closed by a devotional turn to prayer and wisdom; the examples accumulate rather than develop.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson described the poem in his own correspondence and it was published under his name.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation

works.title: The Venetian Bracelet
works.form: Collected volume with a governing metrical tale; the genres are the romance in verse and the meditative lyric on art and on women's experience.
works.description: The last of its author's verse romances issued before her publisher dropped her, taking Venice and its legends as the scene for a study of jealousy, confinement and betrayed constancy. It gathers the romance with a company of shorter poems on art, exile and women's destinies.
works.plot: The title romance, worked in stanzas, sets a Venetian story of love, suspicion and ruin against the city's ceremonial and domestic life, using the bracelet itself as the token by which attachment and its penalties are read. The shorter poems return repeatedly to the situation of the wronged or patient woman, and to the contrast between public fame and private exposure. Several pieces make painting, music and the poet's craft the medium through which feeling is expressed and misread. The volume ends without resolution, in a register of weariness that its readers took as autobiographical. Its argument is that the symbols by which love is pledged become instruments of its accusation.
works.significance: The book documents a reputation reaching the point at which the poetry of feeling became a public liability for its author. Its treatment of a token - the bracelet - as a figure for pledged and misread meaning is the clearest instance of her emblematic method. Later revision of her work has taken this volume as the turning point at which the persona consumed its creator.
works.meter: The romance is in regular stanzic iambic verse with a talky enjambed movement and refrained closings; the lyrics use short iambic measures, and the triple rhythm of her song manner is frequent.
works.context: Its appearance in 1829 coincided with the end of its author's engagement to the house that had published her earlier volumes, and the book's tone of exposed weariness was read at once as personal history. The annual and keepsake market, on which her income depended, had fully formed the expectation that her verse would be a confession. Venetian and Italian settings remained the standard stock of gift-book romance, and the volume works that stock to its limit.
works.structure: A long romance in stanzas followed by shorter lyrics and descriptive pieces; the Venetian tale governs the volume's imagery, and the later poems are variations upon its situations.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: The Vicar of Wakefield
altTitles: The Vicar of Wakefield: A Tale, Supposed to be Written by Himself
works.form: Sentimental and domestic novel in the picaresque line, in short numbered chapters, with the first-person narrative of an amiable patriarch; mixed comedy and pathos, with inserted songs and moral reflection.
works.description: Goldsmith's novel, and one of the most read and most translated prose fictions of the century: the story of the family of Dr Primrose, a country chaplain, reduced from competence to poverty and tried by a succession of calamities, which it narrates in the first person with an unaffected and comic seriousness. It is the exemplary domestic and sentimental novel of the 1760s, and its fame has rested ever since on the question of whether its virtue is sincere or merely naive.
works.plot: The Primroses, happy and prosperous in their parish, lose their fortune when a trust in which their savings were lodged fails, and they retire to a smaller house where the family's learning, vanity and simplicity are displayed in the father's sermons and in the accomplishments of the daughters. Squire Thornhill, the dissolute nephew of a local great man, seduces and abandons the elder daughter Olivia, while the younger Arabella is courted in turn; the father's resentful attempt at revenge by letter ruins him further, and the family is reduced to a jail in which the father's philosophy, the mother's indignation and the children's several fates are all tested. A disguised benefactor, appearing as the humble Mr Burchell, is revealed at the close as the real power who has been testing them throughout, and the novel ends with restitution, recovered fortune and marriage. The movement is thus from prosperity through a series of calamities to a providential restoration, with patience and benevolence as the family's governing virtues.
works.significance: It is one of the two or three novels that fixed the sentimental domestic form for later generations, and its portrait of family virtue under trial was admired and ridiculed in equal measure, the most durable of the ridicule being Samuel Johnson's objection that its whole design sacrificed probability to affecting circumstance. Its influence on the country-pastoral novel, on the fiction of trials and providential restoration, and on the nineteenth-century reading of Goldsmith as a man of feeling, is considerable.
works.context: It appeared in the decade of the sentimental comedy and of Richardson's moral fiction, when the novel was being taken up as an instrument of instruction and when the 'good-natur'd' philosophy of the moral sense school was a subject of public debate. It was published at a stroke by a writer otherwise known as a poet, essayist and hack, and its scene of rural retirement speaks for an age anxious about the decay of the country and of the paternal clergyman.
works.characters: Dr Primrose, the vicar; his wife; Olivia and Arabella; Moses and Dicky; Squire Thornhill; the disguised benefactor Mr Burchell; the gaoler and the minor friends of the family
works.structure: A picaresque-sentimental novel in fifty-two short chapters, told in the first person by the vicar, with a continuous linear sequence of prosperity, fall, trial and restoration, and with the narrator's own simplicity as the source of the comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the novel was published with Goldsmith's name, and its sale to the trade was famously negotiated for him by Samuel Johnson. Disputed questions concern the order of composition and the extent of revision, not the authorship.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Consolation and endurance
Fortune and mutability
Marriage and women's conduct
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
The Rise of the English Novel

works.title: The Victories of Love
works.description: Published in 1862 and the final part of The Angel in the House: the story of Frederick Graham, Honoria's rejected cousin, and his marriage to the humble Jane, told through a series of verse letters. It is a verse work of 1862 by Coventry Patmore; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The poem follows Frederick Graham, who marries the plain and unlettered Jane on the rebound from his love for Honoria, through the slow growth of love between them and the birth of their children to Jane's early death, and ends with a vision of the union of the lovers in heaven.
works.significance: The Victories of Love completes the great Victorian poem of marriage and makes the case for the ordinary married life as a form of spiritual heroism; with The Angel in the House it gave the age its domestic ideal and provoked much of the later critique of it.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is conversational narrative verse in the plain style.
works.context: The 1860s, the Victorian poetry of marriage and death, and the Tractarian theology of the resurrection of the body. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1861 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Frederick Graham; Jane Graham, his wife; Mrs Graham, his mother; Honoria Vaughan; Felix Vaughan
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
movements: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet

works.title: The Village Minstrel, and Other Poems
altTitles: The Village Minstrel; and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza
works.description: The author's second collection, issued in two volumes, whose title poem is a long Spenserian romance of a peasant boy who becomes a poet. The volume surrounding it collects the village lyrics, ballads, pastoral dialogues, and descriptive pieces written in the years of his first fame. It is the fullest record of labouring-class poetic ambition, uniting a theory of native genius with minute local observation.
works.plot: The Village Minstrel follows Lubin, a peasant boy born to the flail and plough, from childhood winter amusements and fairy tales through May-day, summer insect and bird observation, harvest home, and the village feast and dance. Lubin's sensibility is formed by gleaning women's stories, by ballad-singers, by the greenwood outlaw songs, and by the old castle ruins. The poem's turning point is the enclosure of the village green, its former state contrasted with its present appearance, with the peasantry deprecating inclosure and recalling former pleasures. The closing books leave Lubin in solitude among his recollections, preferring home to all other places, with hopes, fears, and resignation for his future.
works.significance: The volume is the central text of labouring-class poetry, adapting an aristocratic verse form, Spenserian measure, to the biography of a peasant boy, and making enclosure the crisis of its plot. Its mixture of minute natural observation and social complaint complicates the usual account of Romantic nature poetry as a middle-class enterprise.
works.meter: The title poem is written in the nine-line Spenserian stanza (ababbcbcc) in iambic pentameter closing with an alexandrine, stanza I opening 'While learned poets rush to bold extremes'; the accompanying poems use common measure, ballad stanzas, pastoral dialogue, and song refrains.
works.context: Published at the height of the author's first vogue, when a subscription fund and a settled annuity were intended to relieve him from day labour; the volume's dedication and patronage arrangements reflect the machinery of charitable literary publishing in 1821. The poem's enclosure passages belong to the long Northamptonshire agitation over imparking, inclosing, and river cutting.
works.characters: Lubin the village minstrel; his father the hind; the gleaners and old women of the harvest; the poor sailor and the recruiting serjeant; the gipsies of the camp; the dead shepherds of the neighbourhood
works.structure: A long narrative poem in a continuous series of numbered Spenserian stanzas, preceded by a prose Argument summarising the design; the secondary poems and ballads in the two volumes are gathered without an organising frame.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the two-volume collection contains no collaborative pieces.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
movements: Labouring-Class and Village Poetry

works.title: The Virginians: A Tale of the Last Century
altTitles: Virginians: A Tale of the Last Century
works.form: Historical novel in monthly parts (24 numbers)
works.description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from November 1857 to October 1859, the sequel to Henry Esmond and the first English novel to treat the American Revolution from the perspective of a Virginian family divided by it.
works.plot: Henry and George Warrington, grandsons of Henry Esmond, grow up in Virginia; the novel follows Harry's extravagant progress through London society while George is believed killed in Braddock's defeat, George's return from a French prison, the brothers' marriages, and the War of Independence, which divides the brothers between the colonial cause and the Crown. The novel's history is deliberately digressive and its plot subordinate to the panorama of the 1750s-70s.
works.significance: The Virginians is the most substantial English novel of the American Revolution and the fullest picture in Victorian fiction of the transatlantic family; its treatment of the colonial gentleman's divided loyalty is a significant document in the nineteenth-century English imagination of America.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The Seven Years' War, the American Revolution, the London of the 1750s and the literary world of Fielding and Johnson, and the Virginia plantation economy of the eighteenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: George Warrington; Harry Warrington; Rachel Esmond Warrington (Madam Esmond), their mother; Baroness Bernstein (the former Beatrix Esmond); Lady Maria Esmond; General Lambert; Theo Lambert; Hetty Lambert; Fanny Mountain; George Washington
works.structure: The work is in 24 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story

Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
The closing of the American frontier
movements: Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot

works.title: The Virtuoso
works.description: Shadwell's comedy satirising the Royal Society and the new experimental philosophy through the figure of Sir Nicholas Gimcrack, an amateur scientist who wastes his fortune on absurd experiments.
works.plot: Sir Nicholas pursues swimming-lessons for frogs and the extraction of air from cucumbers while his nieces and suitors conduct a normal intrigue; the satire is aimed not at science itself but at its pedantic misuse.
works.significance: The most important dramatic satire on the early Royal Society and a key text in the history of the quarrel between the wits and the philosophers; Gimcrack became a byword for the foolish virtuoso.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in May 1676 and published in the same year; Shadwell claimed to have attended Royal Society meetings for two years to get his material, and the portrait was taken as an attack on the Society's Fellows.
works.characters: Sir Nicholas Gimcrack; Lady Gimcrack; Hazard; Longvil; Clara; Lucia; Mrs Figgup; Snarl; Sneak
works.structure: Five acts with a Jonsonian comic central figure and a conventional love plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shadwell; authorship undisputed.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: The Vision of Judgment
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Augustan verse satire and mock-heroic vision; the dream-vision of judgment turned to political and literary satire, with the Latin and Spanish pretext of the older learned burlesque.
works.description: A satirical dream-vision in sixteen cantos of couplet and stanza, written in answer to the laureate's devotional poem on the death of a late king. The poet dreams the great jury-day at the gate of heaven, where a king's soul is pleaded for by the devil, who is admitted as counsel, and where the assembled saints and worthies, including a Spanish mystic's borrowed vision, decide the case by acclamation. Its target is not the deceased but the machinery of canonization, court poetry and the politics of providence.
works.plot: The dreamer sees the sun put out, the earth wandering dark, and the generation of the dead rising to the judgment; a banner borne by a devil, and a court of heaven crowded with patriarchs, kings and a blackened Spanish friar's procession, precede the trial of a monarch's soul. The accuser's brief is read, the devil's answer is heard and approved, the Virgin intercedes, and the jury of worthies vote the soul to glory by a majority that the dreamer finds unjust. The poem closes with the awakening, a reflection on the value of such visions, and a satire on the poets who sell their measures to the state. The argument is that the machinery by which heaven certifies a king is the same machinery by which the court and the review press certify a reputation.
works.significance: It is the period's boldest satire on the alliance of throne, altar and laureateship, and the work by which the mock-heroic manner of the previous century was revived for Romantic political argument. Its fate, pseudonymous in print and denounced on every hand, became the standard case of prosecution anxieties about blasphemy and libel, and it fixed the poet's reputation as the champion of the irreverent in European politics.
works.meter: A rolling measure of four-line stanzas in the manner of the older romantic burlesque, with anapestic substitution, triple rhymes and a colloquial velocity; passages of couplet and of mock-sublime blank verse are used for irony.
works.context: Written in 1821 in direct reply to the laureate's vision of judgment on the death of the late king in the previous year, at a moment when the regulation of the stage, the prosecution of seditious printing and the patronage of court poetry made the connection of piety and politics a live grievance of the liberal press. The poem first appeared over a Castilian pseudonym in the opening number of the short-lived periodical founded by the poet with a London editor, and unauthorized issues naming its author circulated in the same year.
works.characters: the dreamer-poet; the soul of the departed king; the devil as counsel for the defence; the recorders of the court of heaven; the Virgin as advocate; the Spanish mystic whose vision is the poem's pretext
works.structure: A framed dream vision in a continuous sequence of stanzas, the opening on the cosmos out of joint, the trial in the middle, and the waking commentary and personal digression at the end; the borrowed Spanish vision is cited as the source and then mocked.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously over a pseudonym borrowed from a Spanish satirist; attribution rests on the periodical's own history and on the author's letters, and is uncontested.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Social satire and estates criticism
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Byron and the Byronic Revolt

works.title: The Vision of Leofric
altTitles: The Old English Vision of Leofric, Earl of Mercia
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 367, part II (eleventh century)
works.description: An Old English account of four visions granted to Leofric, earl of Mercia (d. 1057), written soon after his death: a vision of the cross and the hand of God during a mass at St Mary's, a miraculous vision through the mist at Wednesbury, a visit to the shrine of St Peter in Rome, and a vision of the soul's judgment at Christ Church, Canterbury. It is the earliest vernacular prose vision narrative in English.
works.plot: The text narrates Leofric's visionary experiences in order: at mass he sees the cross of light and God's hand blessing the congregation; at Wednesbury the mist parts to reveal the church as God sees it, with Leofric guided by a mysterious companion; in Rome he kneels before St Peter; and at Canterbury he witnesses a dying man's soul weighed in judgment and rescued by the saints through Leofric's intercession.
works.significance: The earliest surviving prose vision narrative in English, anticipating the great medieval genre of Piers Plowman and the Pearl-poet, and a precious first-person witness to eleventh-century English devotional practice.
works.context: Written in the Confessor's reign by a writer close to Leofric's household, the text documents the piety of the last great Old English earl and the penitential spirituality of the eleventh-century church on the eve of the Conquest; it is contemporary with the earliest continental prose visions that shaped later medieval vision literature.
works.characters: Earl Leofric, the mysterious guide, St Peter
works.structure: Four discrete vision episodes in chronological order, each grounded in named places and dates and framed by Leofric's devout response; the Wednesbury and Canterbury visions are developed at length, the others briefly.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author writes from within Leofric's circle and is otherwise unknown.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Judgment Day and eschatology
Monasticism and the religious life

works.title: The Vortex
works.description: The play that made Coward famous: a mother, her lover and her son in a Chelsea flat. It is a dramatic work of 1924 by Noel Coward; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Florence Lancaster, a fashionable woman of forty, takes a young lover; her son Nicky, a composer, returns from Paris with his own secrets, and the two confront each other in a scene of drug-taking and accusation that shocked the West End.
works.significance: The Vortex made Coward famous overnight and changed the English theatre: its treatment of drug addiction and sexual hypocrisy in a drawing-room comedy opened the way for the serious play of modern manners.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the epigram and the witty exchange.
works.context: Chelsea and the London smart set of 1924, and the generation that had come through the war. The record dates the work as composed in 1923 and first published in 1924 and first performed in 1924 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Florence Lancaster; Nicky Lancaster; Tom Veryan; Bunty Mainwaring; Helen Saville; Pauncefort Quentin
works.structure: Three acts, in the Lancester flat and a country house. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Noël Pierce Coward. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
themes: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy
Sexuality, the new psychology, and the Freudian century
The absurd, the void, and the failure of meaning

works.title: The Wages of Sin
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1891 and Malet's most famous novel in her own time: the three generations of a family ruined by the sins of the fathers. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by Lucas Malet; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The artist James Colthurst, who has painted himself and his mistress into the sombre picture he calls 'The Road to Ruin', falls in love with the pure, independent Mary Crookenden while bound by a reluctant sense of duty to Jenny Parris, the fisherman's daughter he seduced, and their child Dot; the novel draws the two women together rather than opposing them, and ends with Colthurst's fall from the cliff where he first seduced Jenny, leaving Mary free to wander the world on her own terms.
works.significance: The Wages of Sin made Malet's name and is one of the most ambitious English heredity novels of the 1890s: its three-generation structure, its religious symbolism and its frank treatment of sexual sin made it the model for the English novel of the decadent family, and it established her as one of the most daring novelists of the decade.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is rich, elaborate, slightly archaic prose.
works.context: 1891: the vogue of the heredity novel after Zola, the Victorian debate on the sins of the fathers, and the aesthetic interest in the decadent family. The record dates the work as composed between 1890 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
works.characters: James Colthurst; Mary Crookenden; Jenny Parris; Dot, their child
works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mary St Leger Kingsley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil

works.title: The Wallace
altTitles: The Acts and Deeds of Sir William Wallace
works.description: Blind Hary's epic life of William Wallace, composed c. 1477 in some 11,800 lines: the hero's outlawry after the killing of Selkirk's sheriff, his battles against the English — Stirling Bridge, the invasion of England, Falkirk — his betrayal and execution at London (1305), and his posthumous vindication. For four centuries it was, after the Bible, the most read book in Scotland, and it fixed Wallace in the national memory.
works.plot: Wallace, driven to outlawry by English oppression, gathers his men, defeats the English at Stirling Bridge, harries England as far as York, and is named guardian of Scotland; betrayed at Falkirk and by the treachery of Menteith, he is taken to London, tried as a traitor to a king he never acknowledged, and executed — his dismembered body displayed, his fame immortal.
works.significance: The great popular epic of Scotland: its Wallace shaped the national hero for five centuries, and its influence on Burns and the romantic revival of Scottish identity is incalculable.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in Older Scots, declamatory and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1477 by Blind Hary, who recited it before James IV for payment, drawing on John Blair's lost Latin life and oral tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (c. 1508) and endlessly reprinted — Burns acknowledged it as his first poetic inspiration.
works.characters: William Wallace; Edward I; Menteith; Graham; Bruce (epilogue)
works.structure: Twelve books of epic narrative, from outlawry through triumph to martyrdom, in the minstrel chronicle manner, with the poet's appeals to his audience throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Blind Hary (Henry the Minstrel) by the poem and the treasurer's accounts.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Warfare and battle
movements: The Scottish Makars

works.title: The Walls of Jericho
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1928
works.description: The first comic novel of Harlem: a Black lawyer, a numbers banker and the colour line. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Rudolph Fisher; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Fred Merrit, a Black lawyer who moves into a white neighbourhood, and Shine, a numbers banker, are drawn into a comedy of Harlem life in which the Black middle class and the Black underworld collide, in the first novel to make Harlem itself the subject.
works.significance: The Walls of Jericho was the first comic novel of Harlem and one of the finest novels of the Renaissance: its portrait of the Black city, its dialogue and its comedy made it the definitive Harlem novel and the model for the fiction of the Black metropolis.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is the comic novel of Harlem.
works.context: Harlem in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
works.characters: Fred Merrit; Shine; Linda; Jinx; Bubber; Miss Cramp
works.structure: A novel in three parts, in the Harlem streets and drawing rooms. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rudolph John Chauncey Fisher. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Wanderer
works.description: An elegy of 115 lines in which a solitary exile, deprived of lord and hall, meditates on the transience of earthly joy and arrives at a hard-won Christian consolation. One of the most admired poems in the Exeter Book and the supreme statement of the Old English ubi sunt theme.
works.plot: The speaker, an 'eardstapa' (earth-stepper) wandering the frozen seas since the death of his lord, remembers the lost joys of the hall and laments the ruin of the world's splendour ('Where is the horse? Where is the young warrior?'); the poem closes with the famous gnomic consolation that a wise man keeps faith and seeks mercy from the Father in heaven, where all stability dwells.
works.significance: The classic Old English elegy; a locus classicus for the ubi sunt topos and for the Christian reframing of the heroic ethos.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with the formulaic diction of the heroic tradition, turned to meditative ends.
works.context: Preserved only in the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 76v-78r), a late tenth-century anthology; the poem's heroic nostalgia is often read against the upheavals of the Viking age, though its date of composition is unknown.
works.characters: the Wanderer (speaker); the lost lord
works.structure: A movement from personal lament through the ubi sunt catalogue of vanished glories to a generalizing wisdom passage and a prayerful conclusion; framed by the figure of the wise man who speaks little and reflects much.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Consolation and endurance
Exile and homelessness
Solitude and the hall community
The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
movements: Anglo-Saxon Heroic Tradition

works.title: The Wanderer; or, Female Diary
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of the pursued heroine; a diary-novel of female dependence and property.
works.description: A dark multi-volume tale kept in the diary of a young woman who arrives with no name, no fortune and no protector, and must make her way by her own skill through a world of contested property, forced attachment and concealed birth. It is the most sustained fiction of female independence in the gothic school, and its heroine's competence - her music, her economy, her self-possession - is set against the laws and customs that deny her an identity. Its French and revolutionary material gives the plot its history of dispossession.
works.plot: A woman, landing without explanation in a French port and afterwards passing into England and Ireland, supports herself by teaching and by her performance, and is alternately protected, claimed and pursued by the men she encounters. The diary records her attempts to establish a legal existence, the interference of a bigoted and a designing relative, an attempted compulsory marriage, and the pursuit of an attachment she does not return. Evidence of a murdered man, of a stolen inheritance and of a concealed parentage accumulates through the volumes; the close discloses her title and her kin, but not in a form that restores her peace.
works.significance: One of the most radical gothic fictions of female self-support, and an important text for the study of women's property, labour and legal invisibility in the period. Its diary form anticipates the later first-person domestic novel of constraint. It is now recovered chiefly by historians of gothic and of women's writing.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; an intense, argumentative first-person style, with documentary inserts and songs performed by the heroine.
works.context: Written in the closing years of the war, when the law of property, the custody of persons and the narrow employments open to unprovided women were frequent subjects of fiction and of pamphlet. Its use of the French revolutionary settlement and of Irish landed society reflects the same post-Union debates that occupied the national tale. Its title has frequently been confused with another contemporary novel on a similar subject.
works.structure: First-person diary in several volumes, with letters, legal documents and inserted narratives; the heroine's own record supplies both the plot and its continuous moral commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. Distinguish carefully from the Old English poem and from another contemporary prose romance of similar title held in this corpus.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
themes: Exile and homelessness
Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Religious persecution and martyrdom
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The War of the Worlds
works.description: Published in 1898 and the most famous of all invasion narratives: the Martian landing in Surrey, the destruction of the Home Counties, and the defeat of the invaders by the bacteria of earth. It is a prose fiction work of 1898 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Imperial Adventure Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Cylinders fall on Horsell Common and the Martians emerge with heat-rays and tripods; the narrator flees through London and Surrey, witnesses the rout of the army, is trapped with the curate, and emerges to find the Martians dead of a bacterial infection.
works.significance: The War of the Worlds is the founding text of the alien-invasion narrative and the great English fable of reverse colonisation; its Darwinian ending is a permanent rebuke to the imperial assumption of moral superiority.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The 1890s, the imperial rivalry of the European powers, the British conquest of Tasmania as a model for extermination, and the new bacteriology of Koch and Pasteur. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: The narrator; the curate; the artilleryman; the Martian fighting-machines; Ogilvy the astronomer; Henderson
works.structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Warden
works.description: Published in 1855, the first of the Barsetshire novels and the book that made Trollope's reputation: the story of a Church of England warden whose income from a medieval charity is attacked in the newspaper press.
works.plot: Septimus Harding, the warden of Hiram's Hospital at Barchester, draws a comfortable income from a bequest intended for twelve poor men; the reformer John Bold brings a suit, and the affair is taken up by the London press and the archdeacon. Harding resigns rather than fight, and the novel ends with his withdrawal to a small curacy and his daughter Eleanor's marriage.
works.significance: The Warden introduced the Barsetshire series and the Trollope method: the moral question examined from every point of view until the reader's sympathy is distributed rather than focused. It is the first English novel to make the newspaper a character and to understand institutional reform as a competition of narratives.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The ecclesiastical commissions and the reform of cathedral and charitable endowments in the 1850s, the new power of the press, and the Oxford Movement's aftermath inside the Church of England. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Septimus Harding; Archdeacon Grantly; Eleanor Harding; John Bold; Dr Grantly; Bishop Grantly; Mr Quiverful; Tom Towers; John Hiram
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Waste Land
works.form: Long poem (five sections; first published in The Criterion, October 1922)
works.description: The central poem of modernism: five sections of fragments, quotation and myth, and the modern world as a waste land. It is a verse work of 1922 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem opens with 'April is the cruellest month' and moves through the burial of the dead, the game of chess, the fire sermon, the death by water and 'What the Thunder Said': a collage of voices — Marie in the Hofgarten, the hyacinth girl, Madame Sosostris, Tiresias, the typist and the young man carbuncular, Phlebas the Phoenician — held together by the myth of the Fisher King and the search for rain.
works.significance: The Waste Land is the central poem of modernism and the most influential poem of the century: its collage of quotation and mythic parallel created the modern long poem, its notes made allusion a public technique, and its vision of a civilisation in fragments defined the period's imagination. Pound's editing of the manuscript is the most famous act of modernist collaboration.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
works.context: Post-war London and Europe after 1918, the collapse of the old order, the Russian Revolution, and the anthropology of Frazer's Golden Bough and Weston's From Ritual to Romance, which Eliot cites in his notes.
works.characters: Tiresias; Madame Sosostris; Marie; the hyacinth girl; the typist; the young man carbuncular; Phlebas
works.structure: Five sections (The Burial of the Dead, A Game of Chess, The Fire Sermon, Death by Water, What the Thunder Said), 433 lines.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Water-Babies: A Fairy Tale for a Land-Baby
altTitles: Water-Babies: A Fairy Tale for a Land-Baby
works.description: Published in 1863 and the strangest children's classic of the century: the story of Tom, a chimney sweep who drowns and becomes a water-baby, and of his moral and evolutionary education in the rivers and the sea.
works.plot: Tom, brutalised by his master Grimes, is drowned in a Yorkshire river and transformed into a water-baby; he travels down the stream to the sea, is taught by the fairies Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid and Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby, searches for Grimes in the Other-end-of-Nowhere, and is finally restored as a man of science.
works.significance: The Water-Babies is the classic English children's book that is also a polemic on sanitation, evolution and education: it is at once a fairy tale, a satire on Victorian science and a plea for the poor child, and it remains one of the most original works of the nineteenth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain.
works.context: The 1860s, the chimney-sweep scandals and the 1864 Act, Darwin's Origin, the sanitary movement, and the Victorian debate on the education of the poor. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature; Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Tom; Mr Grimes; Ellie; Sir John Harthover; Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid; Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby; Mother Carey; Professor Ptthmllnsprts; the Irishwoman
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.

works.title: The Waves
works.form: Novel; experimental novel, first issued in 1931
works.description: Six voices and a seventh, from childhood to death: Woolf's most radical experiment and the most musical of her novels. It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by Virginia Woolf; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Six friends — Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny and Louis — speak in soliloquies that alternate with interludes describing the sea and a house through a single day. Their voices follow them from childhood through school, love, work and age, and the novel ends with Bernard's long final summary of a life, in which the six voices are absorbed into one and the wave breaks on the shore.
works.significance: The Waves is the most radical novel of the period and the summit of Woolf's experimental method: it dispenses with plot, character and narrator in favour of six voices and a lyric structure, and it is the finest English attempt to render consciousness as pure pattern, music and rhythm.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric stream of consciousness and the interior monologue.
works.context: The intellectual world of Cambridge and London in the first decades of the century, and the generation that came of age before and during the First World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Bernard; Susan; Rhoda; Neville; Jinny; Louis; Percival
works.structure: Nine episodes separated by nine prose interludes describing the sea; each episode is a sequence of soliloquies in the six voices.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Adeline Virginia Woolf. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Way of All Flesh
works.description: Written between 1873 and 1884 and published posthumously in 1903: the most complete fictional indictment of the Victorian family, and the novel that made Butler a hero to the generation of Shaw and the Edwardian critics.
works.plot: The novel follows four generations of the Pontifex family, from the tyrannical clergyman Theobald and his son Ernest, through Ernest's miserable childhood, his disastrous marriage to Ellen, his imprisonment for attempted assault, and his eventual inheritance and freedom, to the narrator Overton's amused commentary on the whole.
works.significance: The Way of All Flesh is the central English novel of Victorian family tyranny and one of the founding texts of the modern anti-Victorian reaction; its ironic narrator and its biological view of character influenced the Edwardian novel of the 'new woman' and the twentieth-century family novel, and it is the classic fictional statement of Butler's theory of hereditary habit.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
works.context: The 1830s-50s, the Victorian clergyman's household, the public school and the university, the law and the church as careers, and the social constraints on women and children. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1884 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Ernest Pontifex; Theobald Pontifex; Christina Pontifex; George Pontifex; Alethea Pontifex; Overton; Ellen; Dr Skinner; Towneley
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Published posthumously in 1903, nineteen years after it was written and the year after Butler's death; the text was prepared by R. A. Streatfeild, and Butler had left instructions that it should be published.

works.title: The Way of the World
works.description: Congreve's last and greatest comedy, the supreme achievement of the English comedy of manners, in which Mirabell and Millamant negotiate the famous 'proviso' scene and outwit the jealous Lady Wishfort and the treacherous Fainall.
works.plot: Mirabell needs the consent of Lady Wishfort, whose fortune Millamant depends on, and has pretended to court the old lady; Lady Wishfort is enraged when she learns the truth; the villain Fainall tries to seize the estates, and Mirabell defeats him with the deed of trust.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the greatest comedy of manners in English and one of the supreme achievements of Restoration literature; it was decisively revalued in the twentieth century by T. S. Eliot and Bonamy Dobrée.
works.meter: Prose of the most refined and musical precision; the proviso scene is the high-water mark of English comic dialogue.
works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1700 and published the same year; its relative coolness at first performance ended Congreve's dramatic career at the age of thirty.
works.characters: Mirabell; Millamant; Lady Wishfort; Fainall; Mrs Fainall; Mrs Marwood; Sir Wilfull Witwoud; Petulant; Waitwell; Foible; Witwoud
works.structure: Five acts of intricate intrigue culminating in the proviso scene (IV.i) and the discovery scene (V), each with a formal balance and symmetry unmatched in English comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.
