works.title: The Way We Live Now
works.form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers); two volumes 1875
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from February 1874 to September 1875, and the most savage of Trollope's novels: a study of the financial swindler Augustus Melmotte and of the society that is willing to be swindled by him.
works.plot: Melmotte, a financier of unknown origin, launches the Great South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway in London and is received into the highest society; his daughter Marie's fortune draws suitors, and the collapse of the railway and Melmotte's forgery and suicide destroy the world that had courted him. The novel's second plot follows the ruined squire Roger Carbury and the love of Paul Montague for Hetta Carbury.
works.significance: The Way We Live Now is the great Victorian novel of financial capitalism and of the corruption of the press and politics by money; Trollope's own estimate that it was his best book has been widely accepted since the twentieth century, and its portrait of a society that knows it is being swindled and does not care has kept it the most modern of his novels.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
works.context: The railway speculation of the early 1870s, the failure of the Overend and Gurney bank in 1866 and the memory of the Crédit Mobilier, the London season, and the political corruption of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1875 and first published in 1875 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under sensation novel; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Augustus Melmotte; Marie Melmotte; Sir Felix Carbury; Roger Carbury; Hetta Carbury; Paul Montague; Lady Carbury; Hamilton K. Fisker; Mr Broune; Mr Booker; Lord Nidderdale; Dolly Longestaffe
works.structure: The work is in 20 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Ways of White Folks
works.description: Hughes's finest prose: fourteen stories of the encounters between Black and white America. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Langston Hughes; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The stories — 'Cora Unashamed', 'Slave on the Block', 'Home', 'The Blues I'm Playing', 'Father and Son', 'Red-Headed Baby' — dramatise the encounters of Black servants, artists, musicians and sons with the white world, in a prose of great economy and controlled anger.
works.significance: The Ways of White Folks is the finest prose of the Harlem Renaissance after Cane and Their Eyes Were Watching God: its fourteen stories of race made the short story a political instrument and are among the best American stories of the period.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the blues stanza and the jazz line.

works.title: The Weary Blues
works.description: The first book of the Harlem Renaissance to make the blues a literary form: 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'. It is a verse work of 1926 by Langston Hughes; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'Mother to Son', 'Dream Variation', 'The South' and the poems of Harlem, the cabaret and the Black South, written in the rhythms of the blues and jazz.
works.significance: The Weary Blues put the blues on the printed page and founded the modern African American lyric: 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' and 'The Weary Blues' are permanent poems, and the collection made Hughes the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the blues stanza and the jazz line.
works.context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Great Migration, the blues of Bessie Smith and the cabarets of Lenox Avenue. The record dates the work as composed between 1921 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.
works.characters: the blues pianist ('The Weary Blues'); the mother ('Mother to Son'); the speaker of 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'
works.structure: A collection of blues poems, lyrics and songs. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.

works.title: The Weather in the Streets
works.description: The great English novel of the affair: Olivia Curtis and Rollo Spencer in London. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Rosamond Lehmann; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Olivia Curtis, now married, meets Rollo Spencer again at a party and begins an affair that becomes the centre of her life; the novel follows the lovers through London and the country, through pregnancy and abortion, to the end of the affair.
works.significance: The Weather in the Streets is one of the great English novels of sexual love and its aftermath: its portrait of Olivia and Rollo, its dialogue and its treatment of abortion made it the finest English novel of the affair and a landmark of the literature of women's experience.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the interior monologue of the young woman.
works.context: London in the early 1930s, and the English upper middle class between the wars. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1936 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Olivia Curtis; Rollo Spencer; Marigold; Kate; Etty
works.structure: A novel in three parts, from the party to the end of the affair. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Wedding
works.description: Shirley's first surviving comedy, a witty intrigue play in which the Duchess of Florence tests her suitors by pretending to favour the wrong man, and the various disguises and misunderstandings are resolved in a set of weddings.
works.plot: The Duchess of Florence entertains several suitors, among them the noble Beaufort and the disguised soldier; through feigned favour, a fake death, and a discovered plot, the true lovers are matched and the court is reconciled.
works.significance: Announces Shirley's characteristic mode — elegant, urbane intrigue comedy — and marks the transition from Jacobean to Caroline drama.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the low comic scenes.
works.context: First performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit c. 1626 and published in 1629.
works.characters: the Duchess of Florence; Beaufort; Rawliff; Gratiana; Jane; Annabel; Sir Ambrose Marlove
works.structure: Five acts in the standard Caroline comedy structure of parallel love intrigues converging on a multiple wedding.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley on the 1629 title page; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle
altTitles: The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell
works.description: A fifteenth-century Arthurian romance on the loathly lady theme: to save Arthur's life, Gawain marries the hideous Dame Ragnelle, who holds the answer to the riddle 'what women most desire' — sovereignty — and his courtesy at the wedding night transforms her into a beauty. The wittiest of the Gawain romances and the source of the Wife of Bath's Tale's plot.
works.plot: Arthur, challenged by Sir Gromer Somer Joure, must learn what women most desire; Ragnelle supplies the answer (sovereignty) in exchange for Gawain's hand; Gawain's free gift of choice on the wedding night breaks the enchantment, making Ragnelle fair by day and night, and the two live happily until her death.
works.significance: The most entertaining of the late Gawain romances and the fullest English statement of the 'sovereignty' motif central to late medieval debates on marriage.
works.meter: Six-line tail-rhyme stanzas with comic energy.
works.context: Composed c. 1450 in the East Midlands; preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Rawlinson MS C.86 (c. 1500); the loathly lady plot derives from Irish and English folk tradition (and parallels Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale).
works.characters: Gawain; Dame Ragnelle; Arthur; Sir Gromer Somer Joure
works.structure: A riddle-romance in two movements (the quest for the answer; the marriage and its testing), resolved by the courtesy test.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Arthurian legend
Courtly love and fin'amor

works.title: The Well of Loneliness
works.description: The most important lesbian novel in English: Stephen Gordon and the search for love and justice. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Radclyffe Hall; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Stephen Gordon, born to an English country house and named for a son, grows up knowing herself to be different; the novel follows her through the war, her love for Mary Llewellyn and the persecution she endures, ending with an appeal to God for justice.
works.significance: The Well of Loneliness is the most important lesbian novel in English and one of the most consequential books of the century: its prosecution for obscenity made it a cause celebre, and its portrait of Stephen Gordon gave the lesbian subject its first full novel and founded the modern literature of sexual identity.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the full case history of the lesbian heroine.
works.context: England and Paris in the 1900s and 1920s, and the medical and legal discourse of sexual inversion. works.title: The West-Saxon Gospels
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, University Library Ii.2.11 (c. 1075) and five other copies including Oxford, Bodleian Library, Bodley 441 and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 140
works.description: An anonymous translation of the four gospels into late West Saxon, made in the last decade of the tenth century, probably in the south-west of England. It is the first complete translation of the gospels into English and circulated widely, with six surviving manuscripts and copies reaching into the twelfth century.
works.plot: The translation renders Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John continuously, in a plain, literal but idiomatic Old English prose that follows the Vulgate closely while producing natural vernacular sentences.
works.significance: The first complete English translation of the gospels, the ancestor of the Wycliffite and later English bibles, and a cornerstone of the Old English prose corpus studied by every student of the language.
works.context: Produced in the aftermath of the Benedictine Reform, when vernacular preaching and reading were encouraged; Ælfric's biblical translations belong to the same movement, and the gospels' circulation shows the demand for scripture in English among clergy and laity alike.
works.characters: Christ, the apostles, Mary, John the Baptist, Pilate
works.structure: Four continuous gospel narratives in traditional order, with chapter divisions supplied in the manuscripts; the translation is a continuous prose version without glossing apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No convincing attribution has been proposed; the language is late West Saxon with south-western features.

works.title: The Wet Flanders Plain

works.plot: The Wet Flanders Plain is Williamson's return to the battlefield of the war in 1927: the drowned plain, the cemeteries and the villages of the line are recorded against the memory of the officer who fought there, in the prose of the nature writer.

works.title: The Whale
works.description: A poem of 89 lines on the legend of the whale (Fastitocalon) that lies like an island: sailors moor to it, light fires, and are dragged down when the beast dives. The poem reads it as an allegory of the devil, who lures sinners with the appearance of safety and plunges them into hell.

works.significance: The earliest English version of the whale-island legend, later famous in the Navigatio Sancti Brendani and Mandeville; a vivid allegory of temptation.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Panther and The Partridge.

works.description: Published in 1896 and the most charming of the early Wells novels: the story of a draper's assistant on a bicycling holiday who rescues a young woman from a predatory novelist, and learns that romance belongs to a class he cannot enter.

works.description: Published in 1891 and Doyle's own favourite among his books: a romance of the Hundred Years' War, following the young archer Alleyne Edricson to the wars in France with the free company of Sir Nigel Loring.

works.title: The White Devil
works.description: Webster's first independent tragedy, of the Italian court: Vittoria Corombona, married to Camillo, loves Duke Brachiano, whose wife Isabella is murdered by the lovers' plot; Vittoria's great trial for her husband's death follows, then the revenge of Isabella's brother Francisco — poisoned portrait, masque of murderers, and the final bloodbath in which Brachiano, Vittoria, and her brother Flamineo all die.
works.plot: Flamineo panders his sister to Brachiano; Isabella and Camillo are murdered; Vittoria's arraignment — 'I am summoned to appear before the wolf' — is the play's trial centrepiece; the counterfeit letter and Francisco's disguised revenges pursue the lovers; and the last act's masque of revengers kills Brachiano, with Vittoria and Flamineo dying in the mutual treachery of the close.
works.significance: One of the two masterpieces (with The Duchess of Malfi) of Jacobean tragedy — the play that defined Webster's theatre of corruption and splendour.
works.meter: Webster's dark, emblematic blank verse — the arraignment speeches and the dirges are its heights — with the prose of the panders as counterpoint.
works.context: Based on the historical Vittoria Accoramboni (d. 1585); performed at the Red Bull in 1612 to a hostile audience, as Webster complains in his preface; printed the same year.

works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy of the Italian court, built on the trial scene and the double masque, with the choric comments of the ambassadors and the ghost of Isabella.

works.title: The Whitsun Weddings
works.description: The Whitsun Weddings is Philip Larkin's third mature collection, published by Faber and Faber in 1964, nine years after The Less Deceived. Written mainly in Hull, its poems widen his range to the landscapes, towns, advertising and working lives of post-war England, and its success made him the best-known poet in the country.
works.summary: Lyrics opening with "Here", a panorama of Hull and its surroundings, and closing with "An Arundel Tomb"; among them "Mr Bleaney", "Love Songs in Age", "Faith Healing", "For Sidney Bechet", "Toads Revisited", "Days", "MCMXIV", "Talking in Bed", "A Study of Reading Habits", "Ambulances", "The Importance of Elsewhere", "Sunny Prestatyn", "Dockery and Son", "Afternoons" and the title poem.
works.plot:
"Here" carries the reader by road and rail into Hull, through the crowded shopping streets of the 'cut-price crowd', and out to the empty coast, where existence feels 'unfenced'. Much of the book then observes the lives the poet does not lead. In "Mr Bleaney" a new lodger takes over the bleak rented room of the previous tenant and wonders whether the way a man lives measures what he is. "Afternoons" watches young mothers in a park as their lives begin to be pushed to the side, and "Love Songs in Age" shows a widow finding the sheet music of her youth and realising that love never solved anything. "Dockery and Son" begins with news that a contemporary at Oxford has a son at the college and ends in a meditation on how life is first boredom, then fear, and then age and death.

The title poem describes a slow train journey from Hull to London on the Saturday of a Whitsun holiday. At each station wedding parties crowd the platforms to see off newly married couples, and the poet, at first irritated, gradually recognises the significance of the day for everyone on board. As the train nears London the couples sit together, their lives about to begin, and the poem ends with the image of an arrow-shower sent out of sight, somewhere becoming rain.

History and mortality frame the book. "MCMXIV" looks at a photograph of the long queues of men waiting to enlist in 1914 and ends: 'Never such innocence again.' "Ambulances" shows how an ambulance passing through a street reminds everyone of the solitude of dying. "An Arundel Tomb" closes the collection with a stone effigy of a medieval earl and countess lying hand in hand in Chichester Cathedral; the poet reflects that the gesture may have been the sculptor's convention, yet centuries of visitors have read it as fidelity, and the poem ends with the qualified hope that 'What will survive of us is love.'
works.significance: The Whitsun Weddings made Larkin a widely read public poet; the title poem, "An Arundel Tomb", "MCMXIV" and "Mr Bleaney" became classics of post-war English verse, and the book is often regarded as his finest single collection, the one in which the plain style of the Movement was extended into a panoramic portrait of post-war England.
works.meter: Colloquial, even slangy speech within complex rhyming stanzas; vivid catalogues of modern English life; satire and pathos in close combination; long sentences unfolding across stanza breaks to climactic final images.
works.context: The poems were written between 1955 and 1963, after Larkin's move to Hull, during the years of post-war affluence, consumer advertising and the decline of the British Empire. The book appeared in 1964, when the Movement had been attacked by A. Alvarez's anthology The New Poetry (1962).

works.title: The Widow Ranter; or, The History of Bacon in Virginia
works.description: Behn's last play, produced posthumously, a tragicomedy set in colonial Virginia during Bacon's Rebellion of 1676, combining a love intrigue with an unprecedentedly sympathetic treatment of Native Americans.
works.plot: The wealthy tobacco-planting Widow Ranter loves the dashing Dareing; Bacon leads a rebellion against the colonial government to defend the settlers from Indian attacks; Bacon falls in love with the Indian queen Semernia, kills her accidentally, and dies, while the comic plot resolves in marriage.
works.significance: The first English play set in colonial America and one of the earliest literary treatments of the Atlantic slave economy and of Anglo-Indian relations; it has become central to postcolonial readings of Restoration drama.
works.meter: Prose and verse mixed.
works.context: Written c. 1688-9, produced at the Theatre Royal in November 1689, and published posthumously in 1690 with a preface by an unknown hand.

works.title: The Wife of His Youth and Other Stories of the Color Line

works.description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's second collection: stories of the colour line in the post-Reconstruction North and South, including the famous title story. works.significance: The Wife of His Youth is the finest American short-story collection on the colour line and one of the founding texts of the literature of passing: its treatment of racial loyalty and class among black Americans is unmatched in the period.

works.title: The Wife's Lament
works.description: An elegy of 53 lines, unique in the corpus for its sustained female voice: a woman separated from her lord laments her exile in an earth-cave beneath an oak tree and curses the man responsible for her misery.
works.plot: The speaker tells how her lord departed over the sea, how his kin plotted against them, and how she was banished to a desolate dwelling in the wilderness, where she sits weeping through the long days; she ends by wishing upon her beloved the sorrow of one who sits apart, remembering a happier home.
works.significance: The first sustained female voice in English poetry and a key text for feminist criticism of the period.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; unusually personal and passionate diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the poem has been read as autobiography, as allegory (the Church or the soul lamenting Christ), and as a riddle-like exercise — a famous crux of Old English scholarship.
works.characters: the Wife (speaker); the absent lord
works.structure: A first-person lament moving from past happiness through separation and exile to a bitter wish against the absent beloved; the obscurity of the situation (which lord, which feud) is itself part of the poem's design.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Wild Irish Girl
altTitles: The Wild Irish Girl; a National Tale
works.form: Prose fiction; national tale; epistolary romance of cultural reconciliation
works.description: A national tale in which an English gentleman, sent to take possession of an Irish estate, falls in love with the daughter of a degraded Irish chieftain and is converted to admiration of a vanishing Gaelic culture. The novel opposes ancient Irish hospitality, music and genealogy to the cold improving landlordism of the ascendancy, and makes the heroine's education and her harp the emblem of a nation's injured refinement. Its romantic union of an Englishman and an Irishwoman is the symbolic settlement on which the whole later national-tale genre was built. It was a sensation on publication and gave its author a European reputation.
works.plot: An heir of English family interest in confiscated Irish lands travels to take possession, only to find the old lord of the tribe living in ruined state with his accomplished daughter in a castle on the western coast. The young Englishman is at first contemptuous, then instructed by the girl in the history, music and hospitality of her race, and won over both to her and to her people's claim. A rival connection with an English relation and the pressure of the ascending family's interests obstruct the match, and the tale closes with a union figured as the reconciliation of the two nations and the restoration of the disinherited.
works.significance: The founding national tale and the template for the Irish novel of the Romantic decade, including the historical fictions later written in imitation of it; its marriage plot as an allegory of the two nations is a standard object of postcolonial and Irish-studies analysis. It also established a model of the culturally instructive heroine that shaped European fiction for a generation.
works.meter: Prose narrative containing Irish lyrics and simulated translations from Gaelic verse in short lyric measures
works.context: Published in 1806, in the decade before the act of union had fully changed the politics of Anglo-Irish representation, and amid heated controversy over forfeited estates, the ascendancy's absence and the condition of the Irish poor. Its celebration of Gaelic culture draws on the antiquarian and harp revival of the period and on the travel literature of the western counties. The author came from the Anglo-Irish theatrical and literary world of Dublin and London, and the book was widely reviewed as a political as well as a romantic performance.
works.characters: Horace, an English gentleman with a claim to Irish estates; Glorvina, the wild Irish girl; her father, a chieftain of the old race; an English kinswoman and rival; retainers and harpers of the western castle
works.structure: First-person letters and journals from the English traveller, interrupted by the heroine's own narratives, songs and Gaelic reminiscences; the embedded Irish tales turn the epistolary frame into an argument about who has the right to tell the island's history.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously on its first appearance; the author's identity speedily became known and was acknowledged in later editions. No dispute over authorship.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Marriage and women's conduct
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales

works.title: The Wild Swans at Coole
works.description: The book in which Yeats became a modern poet: the middle style, the public poem and 'Easter 1916'. It is a verse work of 1917 by W. B. Yeats; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom; Irish Revival Lyric and the Celtic Twilight and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The title poem counts fifty-nine swans on the lake at Lady Gregory's Coole Park and measures the nineteen years since the poet first counted them; the collection also contains 'In Memory of Major Robert Gregory', 'An Irish Airman Foresees His Death', 'The Fisherman', 'On Being Asked for a War Poem', 'Ego Dominus Tuus' and 'The Phases of the Moon'; 'Easter 1916' and 'The Rose Tree' followed in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1921).
works.significance: The Wild Swans at Coole is the hinge of Yeats's career: 'Easter 1916' — 'a terrible beauty is born' — is the central Irish political poem of the century, 'In Memory of Major Robert Gregory' is the finest English elegy of the period after 'Lycidas', and the collection marks the moment when the symbolist became the modern poet.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the symbolist image and the esoteric system.
works.context: The First World War, the Easter Rising of 1916, the death of Major Robert Gregory in Italy, and Yeats's marriage in 1917. The record dates the work as composed between 1917 and 1919 and first published in 1917 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; irish revival lyric and the celtic twilight.

works.structure: Thirty-one poems, including a long elegy and a political poem in four-line stanzas. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Butler Yeats. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Willows
works.form: Novella (in The Listener and Other Stories)
works.description: The greatest supernatural story of the outdoors: two men, a canoe, and the willows of the Danube. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Algernon Blackwood; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Two friends canoe down the Danube and camp on a remote island overgrown with willows, where they become aware of a vast, hostile, non-human presence that hunts them through the night and across the river.
works.significance: The Willows is the greatest supernatural story of the outdoors and one of the finest ghost stories in English: its terror comes from the landscape itself, and Lovecraft called it the finest supernatural story in English literature.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the landscape as protagonist.
works.context: The Danube of the 1900s, the river travel of the period, and Blackwood's own canoe trips in Europe. works.characters: The narrator; the Swede; the willows; the unseen presence
works.structure: A first-person narrative of a single night on the river. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.

works.title: The Wind Among the Reeds
works.description: Yeats's finest early collection: the symbols of the wind, the reeds, the cloths and the beloved, and the Celtic twilight at its most musical. It is a verse work of 1899 by W. B. Yeats; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Irish Revival Lyric and the Celtic Twilight; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection's poems — 'The Hosting of the Sidhe', 'The Song of Wandering Aengus', 'The Cap and Bells', 'He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven' — move between the fairy world, the Irish mythic past and the poet's unrequited love for Maud Gonne, and close with 'The Fiddler of Dooney'.
works.significance: The Wind Among the Reeds is the summit of the Celtic Twilight and the last great book of Yeats's early manner: its symbolism — the sidhe, the cloths, the wandering Aengus — gave Irish poetry a mythological vocabulary, and 'He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven' is one of the best-known lyric poems in English.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the symbolist image and the esoteric system.
works.context: The Ireland of the 1890s, the folklore collections of Lady Gregory and Douglas Hyde, the occult societies (the Golden Dawn, the Theosophists) and the poet's hopeless love for Maud Gonne. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under irish revival lyric and the celtic twilight; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.

works.title: The Wind in the Willows
works.description: Published in 1908 and one of the permanent books of English childhood: the river-bank world of Mole, Rat, Badger and Toad, and the comic and terrible adventures of the four friends. It is a prose fiction work of 1908 by Kenneth Grahame; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Mole leaves his burrow for the river and is befriended by Ratty; the two visit Badger and become involved in the wild career of Toad, who is obsessed with motor-cars, steals one, is imprisoned, escapes, and returns to find Toad Hall occupied by the stoats and weasels; the four friends retake the house, and the book ends with the summer on the river.
works.significance: The Wind in the Willows is one of the greatest English books of the twentieth century in any genre: it is at once a children's classic, a pastoral elegy for the Thames landscape, a comedy of English character and a profound meditation on home, friendship and the passing of the world, and it has never been out of print.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is lyrical descriptive prose.
works.context: The 1900s, the Thames at Cookham Dean, the English class structure, and the Edwardian fear of the machine. The record dates the work as composed between 1907 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.

works.title: The Windhover: To Christ Our Lord
works.description: Written on 30 May 1877, the day after his ordination, and the most famous of Hopkins's sonnets: the kestrel's flight read as an image of Christ's mastery and of the beauty that 'buckles' the self. It is a verse work of 1918 by Gerard Manley Hopkins; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The octave watches the kestrel hovering and describes its mastery in compound epithets; the sestet turns from the bird to Christ and to the paradox that the 'sheer plod' of ordinary labour and the 'blue-bleak embers' of a dying fire are more beautiful than the bird's brilliance, because they 'fall, gall themselves, and gash gold-vermilion'.
works.significance: 'The Windhover' is the most anthologised Victorian sonnet after 'God's Grandeur' and the technical showpiece of sprung rhythm; it is the central English poem of the sacramental imagination, and its critical history (from Bridges's puzzlement to the modern readings of Empson and others) is a case study in the reception of difficulty.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
works.context: The 1877 ordination, the Welsh landscape of St Beuno's, and the Ignatian meditation on created things as the 'footprints' of God. The record dates the work as composed in 1877 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: The Wing of Azrael
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1889
works.description: Published in 1889 and the first novel to dramatise Caird's argument against marriage: a wife's revolt against a brutal husband. It is a prose fiction work of 1889 by Mona Caird; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Viola Sedley, persuaded for her parents' sake to marry Philip Dendraith, the cruel heir of Upton Castle, finds herself trapped in a union of legalised cruelty; after her mother's death she resolves to elope with Harry Lancaster, the man she loves, and when her husband tries to stop her she stabs him with the dagger Harry gave her as a wedding present; repelled by Harry's horror, she flees along the shore and throws herself from the cliffs.
works.significance: The Wing of Azrael is the first novel to put Caird's feminist argument into narrative form: its portrait of a wife's psychological destruction by marriage was one of the most shocking books of 1889 and it prepared the way for the New Woman fiction of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the polemical essay with a plain and logical argument.
works.context: 1888-89: the agitation after 'Marriage', the divorce law of 1857, and the Victorian treatment of wives' insanity. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; sensation novel.
works.characters: Viola Sedley; Philip Dendraith; Harry Lancaster; Mr and Mrs Sedley, Viola's parents
works.structure: A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: The Wings of the Dove
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Published in 1902 and the most morally complex of James's late novels: the story of a dying American heiress and the couple who plan to inherit her fortune. It is a prose fiction work of 1902 by Henry James; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Kate Croy and Merton Densher, too poor to marry, scheme to secure the fortune of Milly Theale, a dying American heiress; Densher wins Milly's love, refuses the money after her death, and is left with the knowledge that he has lost both women and the moral ground he thought he had kept.
works.significance: The Wings of the Dove is the finest of James's late novels and the central text of the modern novel of moral ambiguity: its treatment of money, illness and the corruption of love made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of consciousness, and Milly Theale is one of the most memorable heroines in American fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification.
works.context: The 1900s: the London and Venetian society of the international set, and the American fortune in Europe. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1902 and first published in 1902 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.

works.structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: The Winnowing Fan: Poems on the Great War
altTitles: Winnowing Fan: Poems on the Great War
works.description: The first great English poem of the war: 'For the Fallen' and the elegy of the first months. It is a verse work of 1914 by Laurence Binyon; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under Trench Lyric and the War Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection contains 'For the Fallen' — with its fourth stanza 'They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old' — together with the other poems of the first months of the war, written before the scale of the slaughter was known.
works.significance: The Winnowing Fan contains 'For the Fallen', the most famous poem of the First World War and the one read at every Armistice commemoration since: it gave the war its permanent elegy and made Binyon the first poet of the conflict.
works.meter: Verse. Verse of the war poem: the short line and the tight rhyme of the lyric, or the loose blank-verse paragraph, with the colloquial idiom of the ranks set against the elevated diction of the tradition it answers. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ode and the elegy in regular stanzas.
works.context: England in August and September 1914, and the first months of the war. The record dates the work as composed in 1914 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under trench lyric and the war poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: the fallen; the mourners; the poet as celebrant
works.structure: A collection of poems of the first months of the war. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Robert Laurence Binyon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Winslow Boy
works.description: Rattigan's masterpiece: a father's fight to clear his son's name, and the cost to the family. It is a dramatic work of 1946 by Terence Rattigan; it is catalogued here under Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage; Verse Drama and the Poetic Play and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Ronnie Winslow is expelled from the Royal Naval College for stealing a postal order; his father, Arthur Winslow, takes the case to the House of Lords through the barrister Sir Robert Morton, and the family is changed by the struggle — his daughter's engagement broken, his wife's health ruined, and the boy's own innocence consumed.
works.significance: The Winslow Boy is Rattigan's masterpiece and one of the finest English plays of the century: its treatment of justice, family and the price of principle made it a permanent part of the repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Prose of the comedy of manners: the balanced epigrammatic exchange, the social vocabulary of rank, money and reputation, and the scene built as a series of entrances, revelations and exits. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the tight three-act construction with a single set and a small cast.
works.context: England before the First World War, the naval college, and the Edwardian family. The record dates the work as composed between 1945 and 1946 and first published in 1946 and first performed in 1946 and it is catalogued under comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage; verse drama and the poetic play.
works.characters: Arthur Winslow; Ronnie Winslow; Catherine Winslow; Sir Robert Morton; Grace Winslow; Dickie Winslow; Violet; Desmond Curry
works.structure: Four acts, in the Winslows' drawing room. The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A comedy in acts, the scene built as a succession of entrances, revelations and exits, with the social convention breached and restored.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Terence Mervyn Rattigan. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Winter's Tale
works.description: Shakespeare's romance of jealousy and resurrection: Leontes of Sicilia, seized by groundless suspicion, destroys his queen Hermione and orders the exposure of their newborn daughter; the child Perdita grows up a shepherd's daughter in Bohemia; sixteen years later the flight to Sicilia, the revelation of her birth, and the 'statue' scene bring Hermione back to life and the family together again.
works.plot: Leontes' sudden jealousy condemns Hermione; the oracle's verdict comes too late and the prince dies of grief; Perdita is exposed and found; the Bohemian pastoral of the sheep-shearing and the courtship of Florizel occupy the middle acts; the flight to Sicilia unravels Perdita's birth; and Paulina reveals Hermione, preserved in secret, in the play's miraculous final scene.
works.significance: The most moving of the romances — the play of grace, time, and forgiveness that defined the tragicomic art of the late Shakespeare.
works.meter: The late style at its richest — the flower speeches of Perdita, the ballads of Autolycus — with the trial scene's forensic verse as the tragic core.
works.context: Written about 1610–11 from Greene's Pandosto; performed at court in 1611 and at the Globe; the statue scene's art-life paradox crowns Shakespeare's last engagement with Ovid and Pygmalion.
works.characters: Leontes; Hermione; Perdita; Florizel; Polixenes; Paulina; Camillo; Antigonus; Autolycus; the Old Shepherd; the Clown; Time (the Chorus); Mamillius
works.structure: A two-part structure — tragedy in Sicilia, pastoral in Bohemia — bridged by Time the Chorus and resolved in the resurrection ending, with the bear's exit as the most famous stage direction in English.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Penance, confession, and sin
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: The Witch of Edmonton
works.description: Dekker, Ford, and Rowley's tragicomedy of the real Elizabeth Sawyer, hanged as a witch at Edmonton in 1621: the old woman, cursed and beaten by her neighbours, sells herself to the devil in the shape of the black dog Tom; the parallel plot of the bigamist Frank Thorney and his murders runs alongside; and the play ends with Sawyer's execution and Thorney's confession, the village's two sins joined in one scaffold.
works.plot: Old Banks's curses and the villagers' cruelty drive Sawyer to the dog Tom; her witchcraft plagues the village while Frank Thorney, secretly married, stabs his second wife Susan and is pursued by the law; the two plots converge in the final acts, where Sawyer's repentance and execution and Thorney's scaffold confession close the play on the wages of desperation and greed.
works.significance: The most humane of the English witch plays — the first to make the witch's persecution, not her malice, the tragedy.
works.meter: The three authors' mixed verse and prose, with Sawyer's curses and the dog's speeches as the play's remembered scenes.
works.context: Performed at court in December 1621, within months of the real Sawyer's execution in April of that year; printed in 1658; its sympathetic witch answered the decade's pamphlet wars over witchcraft.
works.characters: Elizabeth Sawyer; the Dog (Tom); Frank Thorney; Susan Carter; Winnifred; Old Thorney; Sir Arthur Clarington; Cuddy Banks; Old Carter; Katherine Carter; the Justice
works.structure: A two-plot tragicomedy — the witch and the bigamist — built on the documentary record of the 1621 trial and the pamphlet of Henry Goodcole.
works.attributionNotes: By Dekker, Ford, and Rowley, as stated on the title page; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Jacobean Tragedy and Revenge Drama

works.title: The Witlings
works.description: A five-act comedy of the blue-stockings and the tea-table wits of the town, written for the stage but never performed in the author's lifetime, its rehearsal being stopped by the interference of her father and of the leading players. It survives in manuscript and in modern print as the sharpest contemporary attack on the society of wit.
works.plot: A young lady of the school of the witlings is set by her friends against the plain suitor her family approves, while the club of the blue-stockings, its critics and its authors, divides the conversation of the town between pretension and malice. The several devices of the wits, the verses and the reviews, expose the vanity of the set. The comedy was withdrawn before performance, and its argument about the price of literary reputation was left to be read.
works.significance: It is a primary document of the century's argument about women's literary sociability and of the practical censorship of the stage, and its suppression has become a central case in the history of women's access to publication.
works.meter: A brilliant conversational prose of quotation, review and affected sensibility, the jargon of the witlings being reproduced for exposure.
works.context: Written in 1779 in the season of the quarrel between the author's father and the theatres, and suppressed at the rehearsal stage with the intervention of the leading manager; the Bluestocking society and the review trade supplied its immediate targets.
works.characters: the young lady of the witlings; her mother and the friends of the circle; the plain suitor disapproved by the set; the critics and the authors of the tea-table club
works.structure: A regular five-act comedy of conversation and pretension, the satire concentrated in the scenes of the blue-stocking circle; the text is that of the withdrawn manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the comedy remained in manuscript and in the author's papers, and was not printed until modern times, so that no first edition date is asserted here.

works.title: The Woman in White
altTitles: The Woman in White: A Novel
works.form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1859-60; three volumes 1860)
works.description: Serialised in Dickens's All the Year Round from November 1859 to August 1860 and published in three volumes: the first and greatest English sensation novel, and the book that made the phrase current. It is a prose fiction work of 1860 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Walter Hartright, a drawing master, meets a woman dressed in white on the road to London and learns that she has escaped from an asylum; he goes to Limmeridge House to teach the half-sisters Laura Fairlie and Marian Halcombe, and Laura is married to Sir Percival Glyde, whose secret is an illegitimacy that invalidates his title. Glyde and Count Fosco confine Laura in the asylum in place of Anne Catherick, the woman in white, who has died; Marian and Walter recover Laura's identity through documents, and Glyde's secret is discovered and he dies in the burning church.
works.significance: The Woman in White is the defining sensation novel and one of the founding texts of the English detective story; its multiple narration, its critique of the legal non-existence of wives and its villain Count Fosco made it the model for the whole literature of mystery and testimony.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
works.context: The 1850s, the lunacy laws and the private asylum, the legal position of married women under coverture, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and the Italian political exiles in London. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1860 and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; detective story and the tale of detection.
works.characters: Walter Hartright; Laura Fairlie; Marian Halcombe; Anne Catherick; Sir Percival Glyde; Count Fosco; Countess Fosco; Frederick Fairlie; Mr Gilmore; Mrs Catherick
works.structure: Multiple first-person narration by the witnesses, assembled as evidence in a case. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Woman Who Did
works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1895
works.description: Published in 1895 and the most scandalous New Woman novel of the decade: a woman who refuses marriage and lives openly with the man she loves. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Grant Allen; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Herminia Barton, a Cambridge-educated woman of principle, agrees to live with Alan Merrick without marriage because she believes the marriage law degrades women; after his death she raises their daughter alone, is ostracised by respectable society, and finally takes her own life so that her daughter may marry respectably.
works.significance: The Woman Who Did was the most radical New Woman novel of the century and the most discussed book of 1895: its heroine's refusal of marriage, its frank treatment of unmarried motherhood and its tragic ending made it a national scandal, and it remains the central text of the argument over free union in the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature.
works.context: 1895: the campaign for the reform of marriage law, the feminist circles of the 1890s, the Wilde trials and the moral panic of 1895, and the debate on the 'free union'. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.

A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.

works.title: The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret
altTitles: The Wonder, A Woman Keeps a Secret
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A comic drama of jealousy and female reticence, set in a Spanish-Portuguese court and its island, and the author's most popular play with the following generation of readers and managers. Its title phrase passed into proverb, and its heroine's refusal to explain her secret supplies the plot's mechanism.
works.plot: A jealous governor suspects his sister's conduct and confines her, while a rival lover's designs on an heiress are pursued in the island scheme. The women keep their counsel through apparent betrayals, the men misread every signal, and the discovery of the secret clears the innocent and unites the lovers. The comedy ends with the governor's jealousy turned into an emblem of the sex's power over male inference.
works.significance: It consolidated the comedy of female discretion as a civic virtue and became the stock example of a woman dramatist's command of regular construction; its proverbial title marks its penetration into everyday language.
works.meter: Heroic couplets mixed with prose for the lower scenes, in the post-Dryden comic manner; the repartee depends on balanced half-lines and the interruption of the couplet.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1714 and revived throughout the century, including in the altered version of the 1740s; its Spanish setting belongs to the vogue for Iberian comic scenes inherited from the Restoration.
works.characters: Inez, the wondering woman; her brother the jealous governor; Caesario; Clara; Blazina; the rival gallants
works.structure: Five-act regular comedy in verse and prose, with a tightly interlocked intrigue of jealousy and a delayed revelation; the secret is structurally held until the fifth-act discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and was claimed for her in the biographical prefaces of the collected edition.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Marriage and women's conduct
Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion

works.title: The Wonders of the East
works.form: travel and wonders literature in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English catalogue of the marvels of the East, preserved in the Nowell Codex beside Beowulf and illustrated with vivid drawings: dog-headed men, giants, serpents, the phoenix's nest, the hens that burn men, and the gold-guarding ants of Gorgoneus — the fantastic geography of the age compiled for an English audience.
works.plot: The text proceeds place by place through the wonders of Egypt and the East — the two-headed beasts, the monoculi, the cynocephali, the generous king of the Hostes, the locusts and dragons of the desert — describing each marvel's appearance and habits, with the famous closing account of the gold-digging ants as large as dogs.
works.significance: The fullest English witness to the medieval geography of marvels and to the monstrous races that haunted the period's imagination.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated from a Latin original (itself from the Epistola Alexandri tradition) in the late tenth or early eleventh century; preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv), the Beowulf manuscript, and in Cotton MS Tiberius B.v.
works.characters: the monstrous races and beasts of the East
works.structure: A catalogue of marvels organized by region, each entry a short description.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Woodlanders
works.description: Published in 1887 and Hardy's own favourite among his novels: the story of the woodland economy of Little Hintock and of Grace Melbury, educated above her neighbours and returned to marry the woodlander Giles Winterborne.
works.plot: Grace Melbury, the timber merchant's daughter, is educated and returns engaged to Giles Winterborne; she marries the doctor Edred Fitzpiers instead, is betrayed by his affair with Mrs Charmond, and after Giles's death in a storm and Fitzpiers's reform she returns to her husband.
works.significance: The Woodlanders is the finest English novel of the woodland economy: its treatment of the destruction of a rural trade by the market and the railway is a key text for the ecological criticism of Victorian fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The 1880s, the decline of the woodland trades and the coming of the railway, and the position of the educated woman in a rural community. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1887 and first published in 1887 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.

works.title: The Wooing of Our Lord
altTitles: On Wel Swuðe God Ureisun of God Almihti
works.description: A group of lyrical prose meditations on the love of Christ, in the AB language: the Wooing of Our Lord, On Ureisun of Ure Louerde, On Lofsong of Ure Louerde, and related prayers. Addressed to a female recluse, they figure Christ as a knightly wooer whose love and Passion the anchoress must return, in prose of extraordinary affective intensity.
works.plot: The speaker addresses Christ as lover and spouse, meditating on his beauty, his suffering on the cross, and the soul's answering love, weaving prayer, praise, and erotic-spiritual longing into a single meditation.
works.significance: The earliest English expression of the bride-mysticism and Passion devotion that culminate in Rolle, Julian, and the lyrics; a landmark of affective prose.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative, incantatory prose with lyric repetitions and refrains.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands for a woman recluse, in the same milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in BL Cotton MS Nero A.xiv and Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: Christ as wooer; the anchoress speaker
works.structure: A sequence of meditative addresses, each moving from invocation through Passion meditation to petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Workhouse Ward
works.description: The finest comic one-act play in Irish English: two old men in a workhouse who cannot live together and cannot live apart. It is a dramatic work of 1908 by Lady Gregory; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Two old paupers, Michael Miskell and Mrs Donohue's brother, quarrel endlessly in the workhouse ward; when Michael's sister offers to take him away, he refuses to leave his enemy, and the two settle back into their quarrel.
works.significance: The Workhouse Ward is the finest comic one-act play in Irish English and Lady Gregory's masterpiece: its two old men quarrelling made a permanent comic archetype and the play remains in the Abbey repertory.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close.
works.context: The Irish workhouse at the end of the nineteenth century and the poverty of the rural west. The record dates the work as composed between 1907 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and first performed in 1908 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.
works.characters: Michael Miskell; Mrs Donohue's brother; the Warden; the Matron
works.structure: A single act in the workhouse ward. The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Isabella Augusta Gregory. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus
altTitles: Memoirs of the extraordinary Life, Works, and Discoveries of Martinus Scriblerus
works.form: Collaborative satirical miscellany: mock-biography, mock-didactic essay, eclogue and parodic scholarly apparatus
works.description: The collected issue, in two volumes, of the papers of the Scriblerus club, printed seven years after Arbuthnot's death and four after Swift's and Parnell's. Its centrepiece is the Memoirs of the imaginary pedant Martinus Scriblerus, a burlesque life and catalogue of false discoveries, accompanied by the club's earlier pieces against false learning, bad taste and the abuse of scholarship. The volume is the published monument of the greatest joint satirical project of the Augustan age.
works.plot: The Memoirs recount how Martinus, the posthumous son of a great man, is educated by a circle of projectors who teach him every system of error: false philosophy, obsolete scholarship, the art of digging for hidden treasure, and the machinery of pedantic invention. Thereupon he devotes his vast industry to useless discoveries, among them a treatise on the shadow of a bat and a mechanical device for travelling by pinning the wind, and ends in a universal scheme of knowledge that teaches everything and signifies nothing. The accompanying tracts attack the modern critick, the moneyed interest and the corrupt clergy, converting the club's private jests into a public indictment of learning without sense and of wit in the service of dullness.
works.significance: It fixed the type of the pedant and of organised dullness for two centuries and is the foundational document of Augustan collaboration. Its model of satire as a joint construction of fictitious scholarship runs directly from here through Fielding, Sterne and the nineteenth-century mock-book, and it remains the best evidence of the Scriblerans' theory that ridicule is the test of imposture.
works.meter: Chiefly prose in a parodic latinised period style, with interspersed Hudibrastic and Augustan verse pieces
works.context: Drawn up during the club's Oxford and London meetings of roughly 1710-1714 and assembled for the press in the literary quarrels of the 1730s, the volume reflects the Scribleran campaign against the criticks, the projectors and the Whig learning of the age, and Pope's use of club material in the Dunciad.
works.characters: Martinus Scriblerus; his tutors and projectors; the club's personae of invented editors
works.structure: Miscellany: a Mock-biographical Memoirs in continuous narrative, followed by separately titled essays, eclogues, notes and pieces of club origin, with an apparatus of fabricated scholarship.
works.attributionNotes: Club composition: the shares of John Arbuthnot, Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift and John Gay, with Thomas Parnell and Bishop Atterbury, are much debated and cannot be assigned with confidence; the Memoirs are chiefly Arbuthnot's with Pope's revision, and the 1741 text was prepared with Pope's involvement. Recorded here as a single collaborative volume, with the four principal club members credited in the map.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans

works.title: The Works of Ossian
works.form: Collected translated epic and lyric corpus with editorial dissertation and annotation: the founding edition of the Ossianic canon, and the vehicle for its scholarly defence.
works.description: The collected edition in which Macpherson gathered the fragments and the two epics, with a large scholarly apparatus of dissertations, imitations of ancient poems and a history of the era, and which gave Europe 'Ossian' as a single book. This is the form in which the poems were read, translated, attacked and imitated for the rest of the century, and the volume round which the authentication quarrel hardened.
works.plot: As a collected work it presents a complete imagined literature: the epic actions of Fingal and of his grandson, the shorter poems of lament and of love, and the critical dissertations that supply a chronology, a bardic religion and a theory of ancient heroic poetry. Its argument throughout is that the northern nations possessed, before letters, a poetry of passion and of the moral imagination equal to the classical epic, and that this poetry can be recovered by a modern translator. The shorter pieces add the tender and domestic register: the dead mourned by women, the ghosts of the fallen, the last departures of a failing race. The volume closes the circle by making the reader's own sensibility the proof of the poems' truth.
works.significance: It is one of the most influential books of the second half of the century across Europe, the standard reference for the primitive sublime, for the poetry of melancholy and for the idea of a national bardic literature; its influence is traceable in poetry, in the Gothic, in music and in painting. It is also the most celebrated case in the history of literary forgery or reconstruction, and it forced the age to define the evidence required for a text's antiquity.
works.meter: The uniform cadenced unrhymed measure of the Ossianic books, with the shorter poems in a more purely lyric and elegiacal movement; apostrophe, epithet and inverted syntax carry the rhythm.
works.context: Published in 1765, after the controversy had already become public and political, and at the moment when the Highland Society, Irish antiquaries and English critics were all examining the claims. The edition's apparatus is an answer to that scrutiny, and its confidence provoked the more systematic denials of the later eighteenth century.
works.characters: Ossian as the supposed ancient author and speaker; Fingal; his sons and successors; the bards, spirits and mourning women of the shorter poems
works.structure: A collected two-volume edition: preliminary dissertations on the era and on the heroic poetry of the ancients, the epics, the shorter poems and translations, with arguments and notes; the sequence is encyclopaedic rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: The collection is Macpherson's in every recoverable sense, and the ancient authorship it asserts, that of the bard Ossian, is recorded here as disputed: the claimed Gaelic and Irish originals have never been authenticated, and the case for composition rather than translation was made within a few years of publication and renewed since. The edition's own dissertations are Macpherson's defence.

Primitive genius and national poetry
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules

works.title: The Works of Virgil Translated into English Verse
altTitles: The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Aeneis
works.form: epic translation; pastoral translation; didactic translation
works.description: Dryden's complete translation of Virgil — the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the Aeneid — undertaken over more than a decade and published by subscription in three folio volumes in 1697.
works.plot: A translation of all of Virgil: ten pastoral eclogues, four books of didactic georgic poetry, and the twelve-book epic of Aeneas's journey from Troy to the foundation of the Roman race.
works.significance: The dominant English Virgil for over two centuries and a decisive influence on the Augustan verse style; Johnson judged it 'such a translation as no age or nation could hope to see again'.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout; Dryden's translation method is 'paraphrase' — sense for sense rather than word for word.
works.context: Begun after Dryden lost his laureateship in 1689 and completed as his chief source of income; the subscription edition raised some £1,300, an unprecedented sum for a translation.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Tityrus; Meliboeus; Aristaeus
works.structure: Three sections following Virgil's own tripartite oeuvre; Dryden's prefatory essays on pastoral, georgic, and epic theory accompany each.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Heroism and the heroic code

works.title: The World before the Flood: A Poem, in Ten Cantos
works.form: Biblical and Miltonic narrative poem in rhymed stanzas, treating a scriptural subject as Romantic descriptive epic
works.description: A long narrative and descriptive poem on the antediluvian world before the Deluge, by the Sheffield poet and editor James Montgomery, first published in 1813. The poem peopled the generations from Cain to Noah with the inventions of a Romantic imagination reading Genesis as a lost golden age of giants, agriculture, music, and crime. Its grand sweeps of the primeval earth and its moral of corrupt innocence made it one of the most widely read Biblical poems of its day and the work that established Montgomery's reputation.
works.plot: The poem moves through the ten antediluvian generations. It pictures the descendants of Cain building cities, inventing music, metalwork, and agriculture, and rising into a mighty and beautiful but doomed civilisation, while the sons of Seth remain apart in innocence. A race of giants and kings grows in wealth and in violence; the daughters of men mingle with the fallen ones; and the earth fills with corruption and blood. The poem closes with Noah's warning long rejected, the coming of the flood, and the destruction of the world that had seemed so glorious, leaving the moral that splendour without righteousness perishes.
works.significance: The poem established Montgomery as a poet of popular Religious Narrative Poetry and gave the antediluvian subject its most circulating Romantic treatment; contemporaries ranked its descriptive passages alongside Thomson and it remained a staple of the gift-book and school anthology through the century. It is a key example of how Biblical history was reimagined as a lost age of sublimity and guilt.
works.meter: Written in a sustained stanzaic measure derived from the Spenserian and Thomsonian tradition, in smooth iambic lines with an elaborate rhyme scheme, suited to swelling description and moral reflection rather than to dramatic speech.
works.context: Published in 1813, the poem belongs to the enduring vogue for long Biblical and 'secondary epic' poems and to the taste for the sublime and the primitive that carried over from the late eighteenth century. Montgomery, a Unitarian preacher turned Sheffield editor, had made his name with radical journalism and hymn-writing, and the poem marks his movement into the Romantic descriptive mode on a scriptural subject.
works.characters: the Cainite line of Tubal-cain, Jabal, and the giant kings; Noah the preaching monitor; the sons of Seth and the daughters of men; the fallen watchers; the ruined antediluvian people
works.structure: A continuous narrative in ten cantos, arranged generationally and thematically rather than around a single hero; each canto opens a new phase of the primeval history, and the whole builds from creation of a culture to its catastrophic end, framed by prophecy and warning.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; Montgomery's authorship is undisputed. The poem is a single-author work issued in ten cantos.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Judgment Day and eschatology
Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
