works.title: The World's Desire
works.form: Novel (with Andrew Lang); imperial adventure romance
works.description: Published in 1890 and Haggard's collaboration with Andrew Lang: the wanderings of Odysseus, the last of the heroes, in search of Helen and the world's desire. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by H. Rider Haggard; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Odysseus, returned to Ithaca but unable to forget Helen, sets out again and comes to Egypt, where he meets the Queen Meriamun, who believes him to be her destined lover; he is imprisoned, escapes, and dies at last in the desert, while the gods take Helen away.
works.significance: The World's Desire is one of the most interesting English continuations of Homer and a key text of the Victorian reimagining of the ancient world: its collaboration between a romancer and a scholar produced a strange and haunting book that influenced the later historical fantasy of the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person testimony of the practical man.
works.context: 1889-90: the Victorian Homeric revival, Andrew Lang's anthropology and folklore, and the imperial reading of the Odyssey. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1890 and first published in 1890 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Odysseus, the Wanderer; Helen, the World's Desire; Meriamun, Queen of Egypt; Pharaoh Meneptah; Rei, the old priest; Telegonus
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Rider Haggard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Wouldbegoods
works.description: Published in 1901 and the sequel to The Treasure Seekers: the Bastables attempt to be good, with results far worse than their attempts to be naughty. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Edith Nesbit; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Bastables form the 'Wouldbegoods', a society for being good; their efforts to help the poor, to befriend the villagers and to perform good deeds produce one disaster after another, until they abandon goodness for the summer.
works.significance: The Wouldbegoods is the funniest of the Bastable books and a key text in the modern children's comedy of good intentions; its satire of the Victorian good-deed literature is one of Nesbit's sharpest jokes.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader.
works.context: The 1900s, the Victorian and Edwardian morality of self-improvement, and the holidays of the suburban middle class. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Oswald Bastable, the narrator; Dora; Dicky; Alice; Noël; H. O.; Daisy and Denny Foulkes; Albert's uncle
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. Nesbit. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: The Wreck of the Deutschland
works.description: Written in 1875-76 on the wreck of the Deutschland, which sank in the Thames estuary in December 1875 with five Franciscan nuns among the drowned; offered to the Month and refused, and unpublished until the 1918 edition: the first poem in sprung rhythm.
works.plot: The ode opens with the poet's personal address to God, turns to the shipwreck and to the tall nun's cry 'Christ, King, Head', and ends in a prayer for the conversion of England; the wreck is read as an instance of divine mastery and of the 'harvest' of the tall nun's faith.
works.significance: The Wreck of the Deutschland is the greatest English religious ode of the century and the work in which sprung rhythm was invented; its rejection by the Month kept Hopkins's poetry unpublished in his lifetime and its publication in 1918 changed the technique of English verse.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas.
works.context: The Deutschland disaster of 7 December 1875, the Jesuit province of North Wales where Hopkins was studying, the conversion of England for which the Jesuits prayed, and the Oxford Movement's legacy. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence

works.title: The Wrongs of Africa
altTitles: The Wrongs of Africa, a Poem. Part the First
works.form: abolitionist verse in the descriptive-complaint manner; poem of argument and appeal
works.description: The first of the great abolition poems, written at the request of the committee of the cause and published in two parts, the first in 1787 and the second in the following year. Its subject is the whole progress of the trade, from the coast of Africa through the voyage to the colonies, and its method is the plea of humanity made in the heroic line against the interest of a nation.
works.plot: The first part opens upon Africa in its peace and its innocence, the domestic affections and the simple life of its people, and passes to the arrival of the trading ships and to the arts by which the victims are caught: the treachery of the traffic, the wars raised to procure captives, and the seizure of the husband, the parent, and the child. It then sets before the reader the prison, the march to the shore, and the embarkation, and urges upon Britain the argument from her own love of liberty, from the Christian name, and from the plain justice of the case, that a trade carried on by such means is a national crime for which the country must answer. The second part pursues the subject to the other side of the ocean, the voyage and the treatment in the colonies, and closes with the argument that the abolition is the duty as well as the interest of a trading people, and that the true commerce of Africa is in her freedom and in the produce of cultivated labour.
works.significance: It is the founding poem of the abolitionist agitation and one of the most influential of the poems which forced the slave trade into the literature of the period; it fixed the humanitarian pictorial sequence, the innocent Africa, the treacherous seizure, the broken family, and the appeal to national conscience, which the oratory, the prints, and the novels of the next forty years repeated. Its history is also a chapter in the social history of literature: a trade poem written against the commerce of its author's own community, and welcomed by the committee as the voice of the cause.
works.meter: Blank verse of the heroic line, sustained by apostrophe and invective, with the pathetic domestic picture and the direct national address usual to the poetry of the abolition cause.
works.context: Composed for the movement opened by the committee of the friends of the abolition, in the year of the first petition to Parliament and of the great pamphlet warfare of the trade's defence, and issued by the publisher of the cause with a preface by a friend of the author. Its author, a banker and scholar of the greatest slave-trading port in the kingdom, stood by the trade's victims against the interest of his own town and of his own family.
works.characters: The people of Africa; the captured husband and father; the slave trader and his crew; the planter and the colonists; the people of Britain addressed as the judges of the cause
works.structure: A poem in two parts, each in books of descriptive and invective sequence: the picture of Africa, the seizure and the march, the plea to Britain, then the voyage and the colonies, with the closing argument and the appeal to the conscience of the nation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the two parts were published in successive years and the poem was completed no farther, and the prefatory matter of the first part is from another hand than the poet's own.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
The slave trade and abolition
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: The Yeomen of the Guard; or, The Merryman and His Maid
altTitles: Yeomen of the Guard; or, The Merryman and His Maid
works.form: Comic opera (two acts) with tragic elements
works.description: First performed in 1888 and the darkest of the Savoy operas: a jester's unrequited love in the Tower of London under the Tudors. It is a dramatic work of 1888 by W. S. Gilbert; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Colonel Fairfax, condemned to death as a sorcerer, is secretly married to Elsie Maynard by the jester Jack Point; the marriage saves Fairfax when his reprieve arrives, but Elsie loves Fairfax and Point, who loves Elsie, is left at the end to fall senseless on the stage in one of the darkest endings in Victorian comic opera.
works.significance: The Yeomen of the Guard is the most musically ambitious of the Savoy operas and its most emotionally serious: the character of Jack Point and the refusal of a happy ending made it a critical favourite, and it is the work in which Gilbert's comic and tragic gifts come closest to balance.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is inverted logic carried to absurdity.
works.context: 1888: the Tower of London and the Tudor revival, the Victorian interest in the historical romance, and the Savoy opera's move toward the serious. The record dates the work as composed in 1888 and first published in 1888 and first performed in 1888 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; victorian verse drama and revived tragedy.
works.characters: Jack Point; Elsie Maynard; Colonel Fairfax; Phoebe Meryll; Wilfred Shadbolt; Sergeant Meryll; Sir Richard Cholmondeley
works.structure: The action is divided into two acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Schwenck Gilbert. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: The Young Philosopher
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion
works.description: Charlotte Smith's last novel and the darkest of her political fictions: the story of a generous young man of principle whose idealism is destroyed by the failure of the French Revolution and by the condition of England in the 1790s, and who finally quits Europe for America. Written during her London stays of 1797 and 1798 and published in the summer of 1798, after the collapse of revolutionary expectation and during the war and repression that followed, it converts the history of a decade into the education and undoing of a single mind.
works.plot: The young philosopher is formed by reading, by friendship, and by enthusiasm for liberty; he encounters in England a world of interest, dependence, and enforced idleness, loses the woman he loves to considerations of fortune, and sees the cause he espoused degenerate into tyranny and war; the novel ends with his resolution to seek in America the independence that England refused him, while the women and dependants he leaves behind are provided for by the kindness of those the plot had earlier condemned as vulgar.
works.significance: The Young Philosopher is read as the most explicit record in fiction of the extinction of revolutionary hope in England, and it is a key text for the history of radical sentiment and of the idea of America as a refuge; its ending, which abandons Europe rather than reforming it, marks a decisive stage in the political imagination of the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose narrative containing embedded verse and letter papers; the philosophical argument is delivered in formal set-piece speech as well as in dialogue.
works.context: Conceived and written during Smith's stays in London in the summers of 1797 and 1798, and published in the summer of 1798, when the failure of the French Revolution, the repression that followed the war, and the collapse of radical expectation had made enthusiasm for liberty untenable in England; the suit in Chancery over the inheritance that had engaged her family since the 1770s was still undetermined, and her own sense of a closed future informs the novel's argument that principle cannot be lived under existing English conditions.
works.characters: the young philosopher of the title; the woman he loves and cannot marry; his patron and his rival; the family and dependants left behind
works.structure: A multi-volume novel of the education and failure of an enthusiast, told in the third person with letters and papers interspersed, and organized as a series of disillusionments: philosophical, amatory, political, and finally national, resolved by emigration.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.description: The play of the younger generation against the older in the mill town. It is a dramatic work of 1912 by Stanley Houghton; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.

works.title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
works.form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1937
works.description: The finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance: Janie Crawford's three marriages, and a Black woman's voice at the centre of American fiction. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by Zora Neale Hurston; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Janie Crawford, raised by her grandmother in West Florida, is married off at sixteen to an old farmer, then runs away with the ambitious Joe Starks to Eatonville, becomes the mayor's wife, and after his death falls in love with the young gambler Tea Cake. They go to the Everglades, are caught in the hurricane, and Tea Cake is bitten by a rabid dog and killed by Janie in self-defence; she returns to Eatonville alone.
works.significance: Their Eyes Were Watching God is the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American novels of the century: its free indirect rendering of Black Southern speech, its portrait of a woman's self-making and its hurricane ending made it a permanent classic, recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s and now central to the canon.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension.
works.context: The Black towns of Florida, Eatonville, the Everglades and the migrant labour camps of the 1920s and 1930s, and the folklore that Hurston had collected as an anthropologist. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro; The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Janie Crawford; Tea Cake; Joe Starks; Logan Killicks; Nanny; Pheoby Watson
works.structure: A framed narrative: Janie tells her story to Pheoby on her return to Eatonville. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Zora Hurston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Theron and Aspasio; or, A Scriptural and Critical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians
works.form: Prose devotional and doctrinal treatise in epistolary and dialogic form with embedded biblical commentary
works.description: James Hervey's devotional-argumentative masterpiece, issued in three volumes in 1755, casts the doctrines of grace and the righteousness of faith into a frame of letters, dialogues and a running commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Its ornate, balanced prose was admired across denominational lines even by readers who disliked its Calvinism. The work immediately became the occasion of John Wesley's furious reply, because Wesley read its teaching on justification as antinomian and disparaging of holiness of life.
works.plot: The letters and dialogues between Aspasio, a Christian nobleman, and his friend Theron trace the grounds of natural religion, the corruption of human nature, and the necessity of an imputed righteousness. Hervey then appends a scriptural and critical commentary on Galatians, arguing that the epistle establishes justification by faith alone and excludes all human boasting. The intermediate dialogues dramatise the contrast between a moralist religion of self-effort and a gospel religion of reliance on Christ, and press home the practical duties of the regenerate life. The whole is designed to be at once devotional reading, doctrinal instruction, and exegetical argument, and to show that profound Calvinism can be spoken in the most polished and affecting English.
works.significance: For a century Theron and Aspasio was quoted as a model of English religious prose, and Samuel Johnson and Robert Hall admired its eloquence. Its publication provoked one of the most energetic pamphlet exchanges of the century, Wesley's Defense of his own letter and the long controversy with the label "Calvinism" attached to it. The book remains the clearest instance of how evangelical doctrine could be accommodated to polite Augustan diction.
works.meter: Prose only, in a highly wrought periodic style of balanced clauses and cadenced rhythm
works.context: Published in the middle of the Calvinistic-Arminian revival controversies, the book belongs to the effusive piety associated with the Countess of Huntingdon's connection and to Hervey's own late meditations at Weston underoclic. It also belongs to the broader eighteenth-century fashion for ornamental religious prose and to the growing use of dialogue and epistle as vehicles for theological argument.
works.characters: Aspasio; Theron
works.structure: Three volumes arranged as a sequence of letters and dialogues framing a verse-by-verse commentary on Galatians, so that meditation, conversation and exegesis alternate throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by James Hervey is established and undisputed.
themes: Conscience and moral self-examination
Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Penance, confession, and sin
Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
movements: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing

works.title: These Sad but Glorious Days: Dispatches from Europe
works.description: Written for the New-York Tribune between 1846 and 1850 and collected posthumously, in full only in 'These Sad but Glorious Days': Dispatches from Europe, 1846-1850, edited by Larry J. Reynolds and Susan Belasco Smith (Yale University Press, 1991): Fuller's letters from England, France and Italy, above all her dispatches from Italy during the revolutions of 1848-49 and the siege of Rome.
works.plot: The letters begin as travel sketches of England, France and Italy and become an account of the revolutionary upheaval of 1848: from her apartment in Rome Fuller sees the attack on the Quirinal Palace in November 1848 that drove the Pope from the city and led to the Roman Republic headed by her friend Giuseppe Mazzini, and she reports the siege and bombardment of Rome by the French army sent to restore the Pope in June 1849, in which she served as a hospital director.
works.significance: Fuller's Roman dispatches are among the finest American war correspondence of the century: they are a central document of the 1848 revolutions and of the American engagement with European democracy.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is conversational, digressive and allusive prose.
works.context: The years 1846-50, the Italian revolutions, the Roman Republic, and the American reception of European radicalism. The record dates the work as composed between 1846 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A first-person narrative of service, organised by the stages of the campaign and told in the plain idiom of the ranks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: They Were Sisters
works.form: Novel; realist novel of common life
works.description: Whipple's finest novel: three sisters, three marriages and the ordinary English household. It is a prose fiction work of 1943 by Dorothy Whipple; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Lucy, Anne and Charlotte Ashenden grow up in a comfortable English household and make three very different marriages: Lucy to a kind but colourless man, Anne to a charming and cruel one, Charlotte to a man who will not marry her; the novel follows each marriage to its catastrophe, and ends with Anne destroyed by the husband who has driven her to drink.
works.significance: They Were Sisters is Dorothy Whipple's finest novel and one of the great English domestic novels of the century: its three marriages, its exact household detail and its account of cruelty inside a respectable home made it the central novel of the English marriage question in the 1940s and the book that established Whipple's reputation beyond the bestseller lists.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is the domestic detail of the middle-class household.
works.context: England from the Edwardian years to the 1930s, and the middle-class household of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1941 and 1943 and first published in 1943 and it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Lucy; Anne; Charlotte; Geoffrey Purdon; William; Brian
works.structure: A novel in three parts, one for each sister's marriage. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

works.title: Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams
works.form: Philosophical and anarchist fiction; picaresque pursuit novel and domestic gothic of lawless power.
works.description: The founding novel of philosophical anarchy and of the pursuit plot, written to dramatise the argument that private virtue is destroyed by law, rank and the arbitrary power of a benefactor. Its hero, a curious clerk who forces out of his patron the secret of an old murder, becomes the victim of an inexorable persecution that carries him from a country house to a London prison. The novel's machinery of spies, forgery, false arrest and flight supplied the gothic and sensation plotting of the next half-century.
works.plot: Caleb Williams, the son of an old dependant of the country gentleman Falkland, is educated, made secretary and admired, and by an unlucky question extracts from his benefactor the confession that years before he killed a low and malignant rival in the fight over an estate. Falkland's pride turns to alarm and then to systematic persecution: Caleb is dismissed, falsely suspected of theft, pursued through the country and driven to London, where, poor and unknown, he is befriended by an alderman and by a man of ruined reputation, and is at last trapped by an artifice of friendship into a spunging-house and a marshal's custody. Escape, disguise and a project of revenge put weapons in his hands; he returns to England, extorts from Falkland a public confession, and stands by while his persecutor is prosecuted, convicted and sent into exile, where he dies. Caleb, the victor, has spent his patron's fortune and ruined his own prospects, and the tale closes with the writing of his confession.
works.significance: The most influential English novel of persecution and of the psychology of a tyrant and his victim, and the work that gave the pursued-hero plot its secular, legal form. Its treatment of class power, of the spectacle of punishment and of the failure of revenge makes it a founding text of political fiction. Later gothic, sensation and detective fiction inherited its apparatus of spies, forgeries and prisons.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; rapid first-person argumentative narrative with long analytical passages and colloquial dialogue of clubs, prisons and the road.
works.context: Written in the train of a systematic treatise on justice published the year before, and in the atmosphere of the 1790s controversies over law, aristocratic privilege and the efficacy of punishment. Its legal machinery reflects the actual procedures of civil arrest, spunging-houses and criminal trial at the close of the century. Its publication was followed by denunciation in the ministerial press as a school of Jacobinism, and a table of the contents of the argument was prefixed to the first edition.
works.characters: Caleb Williams; Falkland, the patron who becomes his persecutor; Mr. Bailey, the London alderman who befriends him; Julian, the friend who is ruined by his kindness to the hero
works.structure: First-person confession written by the hero and addressed to the public; three volumes of continuous pursuit, with an inserted narrative told by another sufferer; a conclusion that reports the deaths of both principals.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. Early copies are dated 1793 or 1794 according to the issue of the last volume.

themes: Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero

works.title: Thirty Years in Australia
works.form: Memoir; review essay, first issued in 1903
works.description: Published in 1903 and Cambridge's memoir of her life as a clergy wife in colonial Victoria: a central record of the woman settler's experience of Australia. works.significance: Thirty Years in Australia is one of the finest memoirs of Empire by a woman and a key text in the history of Australian settlement: it is the fullest account we have of the daily life of an English parsonage family in colonial Victoria.

works.title: This Be The Verse
works.description: This Be The Verse is a poem by Philip Larkin, first published in the August 1971 issue of New Humanist and collected in High Windows (1974). Its profane first line about parents and its advice not to have children have made it one of the most quoted English poems of the century.
works.summary: The claim that parents pass on their faults to their children; the observation that their own parents did the same; and the conclusion that misery is handed down and the only escape is to have no children.
works.plot: Your parents mess you up, the speaker says in far blunter words: they do not mean to, but they fill you with their faults and add some extra just for you. They were messed up in their turn by fools in old-style hats and coats, who were half the time soppy-stern and half at one another's throats. Man hands on misery to man; it deepens like a coastal shelf. Get out as early as you can, the poem ends, and don't have any kids yourself: the only way to stop the inheritance is to refuse to pass it on.
works.significance: Larkin's most quoted poem, endlessly cited and parodied; Wikipedia, citing the Oxford Companion to Modern Poetry, notes its dark humour, directness and taboo-breaking language.
works.meter: Shocking colloquial obscenity in a strict, light-verse form; the title parodies Robert Louis Stevenson's 'Requiem' ('This be the verse you grave for me').
works.context: Completed in April 1971 and first printed in New Humanist, the journal of the Rationalist Press Association, in August 1971.
works.structure: Three four-line stanzas of rhymed iambic tetrameter, the neat form of a hymn or epitaph.
themes: Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
Family, marriage and domestic life

works.title: Those Who Eat the Cascadura
works.description: Published in London by Davis Poynter in 1972, a novel of interracial love on a Trinidad plantation, framed by an obeahman's prophecy.
works.summary: An Englishman's stay on a friend's Trinidad estate, his love for a young Indian woman and the prophecy of the village obeahman.
works.plot: Manko, the village obeahman, predicts trouble when an Englishman, Garry, comes to stay, and the prophecy is fulfilled when Garry falls in love with a local Indian woman, Sarojini (Caribbean Beat; Northern Arizona University essay). The essay reads the outcome as racism proving stronger than love, since Garry feels she cannot be transplanted from the world that made her, and notes the discovery that Roger Franklin, the plantation owner, secretly visits Indian women at night and is probably Sarojini's father.
works.significance: At his death Selvon was negotiating a film adaptation (Dawes).
works.meter: Caribbean Beat calls it a story of interracial romance and the chaos it creates in a village; the essay sees the distant thunder of I Hear Thunder grown into a hurricane threatening the whole society.
works.context: Published in London in 1972, six years before Selvon left Britain; it was reissued in Toronto by TSAR in 1988.

works.title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Justice of Great Britain by the Africans
altTitles: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery
works.form: Polemical essay in natural-law, scriptural and legal argument
works.description: An abolitionist polemic by Ottobah Cugoano, a Fante man kidnapped and sold in 1769, who by the 1780s was a literate servant in the London household of the artist Richard Cosway. The book argues from natural law, scripture and British law that the slave trade and West Indian slavery are crimes against God and humanity, and it demands immediate remedy rather than gradual relief. A short abridgement for wider circulation followed in the same year, and a second edition with an appendix on the slave insurrection in Jamaica appeared in 1788.
works.plot: Cugoano first states the natural right of every human being to liberty, so that enslavement is a violation of the law of God written on the conscience. He then examines the scriptural evidence and shows that neither Hebraic servitude nor the New Testament's household codes sanction the modern traffic, and he presses the legal argument that a Christian cannot lawfully hold a fellow Christian in perpetual slavery. Turning to practice, he denounces the planters' plea of necessity and property, refutes the political arithmetic that counts colonial wealth as national strength, and proposes remedies: the recall of British subjects from the colonies, the education of the enslaved, and the establishment of lawful commerce in Africa in place of the trade in persons. The conclusion warns that Britain's national guilt for the trade will draw national judgment.
works.significance: It is the first published abolitionist argument written by an African in England to confront the slave trade as a national crime and to claim the authority of reason and scripture against the planters' case. Its insistence that liberty is a divine and natural right, and its refusal of gradualist compromise, make it a foundational text of black Atlantic political writing and a necessary companion to Equiano's narrative.
works.meter: Prose only, in an urgent, latinate, sermon-like style marked by biblical cadence
works.context: Written between the Somersett decision of 1772 and the first parliamentary abolitionist campaign of 1788, it joins the printed output of the Committee for Abolishing the Slave Trade and the black London community of Equiano, Sharp and Ramsay, and reflects the evangelical moral-language of natural rights then current.
works.structure: Continuous argumentative treatise in short numbered sections, moving from first principles to scriptural, legal and commercial refutation and then to proposals for remedy.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Cugoano is accepted; the extent of assistance from friends and patrons in a household of artists and literati is discussed but does not displace his authorship, which the text signs as an African speaking for Africans.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing

works.title: Thoughts on African Slave-Trade
works.form: Polemic and pamphlet; applied moral and political philosophy addressed to a public question
works.description: A short polemic against the slave trade and against the argument that commerce in human beings can be regulated or excused. Its reasoning is applied philosophy rather than feeling: the trade is shown to rest on the same violation of private judgement and of person which the writer's political theory had condemned, and the pleas of property, of climate and of gradual amendment are answered one by one. It belongs to the renewed abolition campaign of the 1820s and is the writer's most direct intervention in a live parliamentary question. The pamphlet is argumentative, lucid and unhedged in its conclusion.
works.plot: The trade in enslaved people is examined as a system of law and interest rather than as a scene of private cruelty, and the writer contends that no regulation can alter the nature of a claim to property in a person. The apologies offered for the trade - that it is sanctioned by long usage, that the condition of the enslaved is improved by service, that abolition would ruin commerce and endanger the colonies - are each tested against the principle that judgement and the person are not transferable. The argument closes with the claim that emancipation, not amendment, is the only consequence consistent with the principles of justice, and with an appeal to the public and to the legislature to act on that principle.
works.significance: A significant document of the abolition campaign of the 1820s and of the application of philosophical anarchism to a live political question. It is read now as part of the literature of slavery and emancipation, and as the late political writing of the circle out of which the period's radical fiction came.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain, closely argued style of the philosophical pamphlet, free of invective
works.context: Published in 1823, when the renewed abolition movement was pressing the question of the colonial slave populations before parliament and when the writer's own political reputation had lasted a generation. It answers the amelioration argument of the period's colonial writing and draws on the reports and speeches of the renewed campaign. It belongs to the literature of emancipation between the abolition of the trade and the acts of the 1830s.
works.structure: Continuous short argument in a single pamphlet compass: statement of the question, examination of the defences offered for the trade, and a positive conclusion addressed to the legislature and the public.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of a named author of the philosophy of political justice, whose identity was indicated on the title page; the attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
altTitles: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, in the Early Part of Life
Thoughts on the Education of Daughters. In the Early Part of Life; with Remarks on the Management of Children, from Birth to the Age of Ten Years
works.form: conduct and educational treatise in prose
works.description: A conduct and educational treatise for the management of girls from earliest childhood, drawn from the author's experience as a governess and a schoolmistress. It argues for the cultivation of reason, truthfulness and independence in girls, and for the reform of the needlework and accomplishments curriculum of the day.
works.plot: The work sets out the duties of the mother and the governess in the first years of a girl's life, treating the government of the temper, the formation of habits of veracity and the dangers of false modesty. It criticises the female academies and their round of accomplishments, recommends the study of religion and of reason, and gives directions on health, amusement and the choice of company. Its conclusion is that a woman's virtue depends on her understanding being taught to act for itself.
works.significance: It is the first published work of the century's most influential advocate of women's rational education and supplies the practical ground of the later argument about the rights and the cultivation of women's minds.
works.meter: A clear, earnest and direct prose of instruction, with the occasional apostrophe to mothers and the sententious summation of the section.
works.context: Published in 1787 after the author's keeping of a school for girls and her service as a governess, in the season of the public debate on female academies and on women's rational education, the same debate that occupied the Bluestocking writers of the day.
works.structure: A continuous didactic essay in numbered heads and reflections, with the instance and the practical direction alternating; the argument is orderly rather than systematic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was issued without the writer's name in the first edition, its authorship being established by her correspondence and by the later issues.

Marriage and women's conduct
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Women's education and intellectual friendship

works.title: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
altTitles: Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Three Parts
works.description: Berkeley's immaterialism restated in dialogue form, his most readable and most-quoted philosophical performance. Over three consecutive conversations on a walk, the sceptical materialist Hylas is led to concede that matter is unintelligible and that only spirits and their ideas exist, to the vindication of common sense and religion.
works.plot: In the first dialogue Philonous drives Hylas from the dispute about secondary qualities to the concession that no sensible thing can exist unperceived. In the second, the doctrines of absolute space, time, and motion, and of matter as an inert occasion or unknown cause of ideas, are dismantled, and the real is redefined as what is perceived by minds. The third dialogue answers the charge that immaterialism breeds scepticism, solipsism, and atheism: the stability of things is secured by the divine perception, the senses give real knowledge of a world, and God is nearer to us than matter ever was. Hylas ends convinced, Philonous having shown that the paradox destroys only a philosophical fiction and leaves the garden, the table, and the body exactly as they were.
works.significance: It supplied the century's model of dialogue as philosophical argument and remains the standard entry to immaterialism; its Hylas-Philonous exchange shaped later philosophical dialogues from Hume to the Victorians.
works.meter: Lucid dramatic prose of question and retort, with the courtesy, warmth, and scene-painting of the Platonizing dialogue tradition.
works.context: Published in London in 1713 as a popular companion and corrective to the difficult Treatise of 1710, after the furor over the Principles had made Berkeley a marked man in Dublin and London intellectual society.
works.characters: Hylas; Philonous
works.structure: Three consecutive dialogues framed by a brief narrative introduction of the speakers and their walk, rising from sensation to substance to theology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy

works.title: Three Lives
works.description: Stein's first major work: three working-class women of Baltimore, and a prose that dismantles the nineteenth-century sentence. It is a prose fiction work of 1909 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The three lives — 'The Good Anna', 'Melanctha' and 'The Gentle Lena' — are those of a German servant, a Black woman and a German immigrant girl in the small town of Bridgepoint, told in a prose of repetition, present tense and simple declarative sentences that refuses the conventions of the Victorian novel.
works.significance: Three Lives is the first work of literary modernism in English by an American and the foundation of Stein's experimental prose: its repetition, its present tense and its refusal of plot made it the model for Hemingway's sentences and for a whole century of American prose.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
works.context: The Baltimore of Stein's childhood, the working-class immigrant and Black communities, and the new psychology of William James that Stein had studied at Radcliffe. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1908 and first published in 1909 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; modern short story and the magazine tale.
works.characters: Anna; Melanctha Herbert; Lena; Jeff Campbell; Dr Jeff Campbell
works.structure: Three separate lives, each in its own section, in a prose of repetition and continuous present.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog)
works.description: Published in 1889 and the most durable English comic book of the century: three young men and a dog take a boat up the Thames and fail at everything. It is a prose work of 1889 by Jerome K. Jerome; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour.
works.plot: J., George and Harris decide to take a fortnight's boating holiday up the Thames to cure their imaginary illnesses; the boat is packed with excessive luggage, the tent collapses, the food is inedible and the three men are entirely incompetent, and the narrative digresses into anecdotes about the uncle, the maze at Hampton Court and the cheese that smelled like a dead body.
works.significance: Three Men in a Boat is one of the small number of English comic classics: it has never been out of print, it made the comic travel book a genre, and its deadpan narrative and escalating lists are the foundation of English comic writing in the twentieth century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose: the argument or the account is carried in continuous prose, divided into sections or chapters. The author's characteristic manner is digressive, anecdotal first-person narration.
works.context: 1889: the Thames excursion vogue, the Victorian cult of the holiday, the suburban clerk's fortnight off, and the comic book market of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the new humour.
works.structure: Continuous prose in sections or chapters, the argument or the account advanced from its statement to its conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Jerome Klapka Jerome. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Three Soldiers
works.form: Novel; war memoir, first issued in 1921
works.description: One of the first great American novels of the First World War: three soldiers, the army machine and the failure of escape. It is a prose fiction work of 1921 by John Dos Passos; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Three American soldiers — Dan Fuselli, an Italian-American from San Francisco; Chrisfield, an Indiana farm boy; and John Andrews, a Harvard-trained composer — are ground down by the army and the war; Andrews deserts to Paris and is arrested, and the novel ends with his unfinished music and his imprisonment.
works.significance: Three Soldiers was one of the first great American novels of the First World War and the founding work of the American anti-war novel: its naturalism and its anger changed the American treatment of the war, and it made Dos Passos the most promising young novelist of his generation.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the collage of narrative, newspaper headline (Newsreel), autobiographical prose poem (Camera Eye) and biography.
works.context: The American army in the First World War, the camps and the front, the military machine that destroys its soldiers, and the post-war disillusion of the American intellectual. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1920 and first published in 1921 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; proletarian novel and the working-class fiction.
works.characters: Dan Fuselli; Chrisfield; John Andrews
works.structure: Three parallel lives in the army, in a naturalist narrative. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Roderigo Dos Passos. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Three Years in Europe
works.description: Published in London in 1852 and the first travel book by an African-American: Brown's letters from Britain during his abolitionist tour of 1849-54. It is a prose work of 1852 by William Wells Brown; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Brown describes the voyage, the Great Exhibition of 1851, the English countryside, the London of the abolitionists, and his visits to Paris and the Continent, with reflections on the condition of the black American abroad and the difference of English racial attitudes.
works.significance: Three Years in Europe is the first African-American travel book and a founding text of the black Atlantic tradition: its comparison of British and American race relations made it a central document of nineteenth-century black internationalism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is first-person testimony with documentary documents.
works.context: The 1849-54: the Great Exhibition, the British abolitionist movement, and the American fugitive slave in Europe. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1852 and first published in 1852 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: William Wells Brown, the narrator; Victor Hugo, at the Paris Peace Congress; William and Ellen Craft
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wells Brown (self-chosen name). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait

works.title: Threnodia Augustalis
works.description: Dryden's funeral ode on the death of Charles II in February 1685, a public lament that mourns the king and welcomes the accession of James II.
works.plot: The poem opens with an ominous vision of a bleeding comet, narrates the king's last illness and death, laments the nation's loss, and turns to consolation in the new reign.
works.significance: A significant example of the Restoration public ode and of Dryden's adaptation of Cowley's Pindaric form to serious occasion.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas with varying line lengths and rhyme schemes.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's death on 6 February 1685 and printed in the same year.
works.characters: Charles II; James II; the mourning nation
works.structure: A Pindaric sequence of irregular stanzas moving from omen through narrative to consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife

works.title: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There
works.form: Children's fantasy novel (with illustrations by John Tenniel)
works.description: Published in 1871 and generally thought the finer of the two Alice books: the mirror-world of chess, with its reversible logic, its chessboard landscape and its great inventions Tweedledum and Tweedledee and the Jabberwock.
works.plot: Alice climbs through the drawing-room mirror into a country laid out as a chessboard and plays her way from pawn to queen; she meets the Red Queen, Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Humpty Dumpty, the White Knight, and wakes as she takes the Red Queen's crown.
works.significance: Through the Looking-Glass is the most formally perfect children's book in English: its chess structure, its mirror logic and its invented vocabulary ('Jabberwocky', 'chortle', 'galumphing') gave the language new words and the modern literature of the absurd its method.
works.meter: Prose narrative interspersed with parodic verse ('Jabberwocky', 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', 'A-Sitting on a Gate').
works.context: The 1860s-70s, the game of chess and the algebra of symbols, and the Victorian interest in mirror imagery and reversibility. The record dates the work as composed between 1869 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
works.characters: Alice; the Red Queen; the White Queen; Humpty Dumpty; Tweedledum; Tweedledee; the White Knight; the Jabberwock; Haigha; Hatta
works.structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Time and the Conways
works.description: Priestley's finest play: a family in 1919, in 1937 and again in 1919, and the failure of the future to arrive. It is a dramatic work of 1937 by John Boynton Priestley; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: At a birthday party in 1919 the Conway family are full of promise; in act two, set in 1937, the promise has collapsed into failure and bitterness; act three returns to 1919, when the young Kay sees what is coming.
works.significance: Time and the Conways is Priestley's finest play and the clearest statement of his theory of time: its structure and its portrait of a family's disappointment made it one of the great English plays of the decade.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the symmetrical three-act play with a single set and a small cast.
works.context: The English middle class between the wars, the slump and the lost generation of the twenties. The record dates the work as composed in 1937 and first published in 1937 and first performed in 1937 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
works.characters: Kay Conway; Mrs Conway; Alan Conway; Hazel Conway; Madge Conway; Robin Conway; Carol Conway; Joan Helford; Ernest Beevers
works.structure: Three acts, 1919, 1937 and 1919 again. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. B. Priestley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Timon of Athens
works.description: Shakespeare's (with Thomas Middleton's) unfinished-seeming tragedy of misanthropy: the prodigal Timon of Athens bankrupts himself in bounty, is abandoned by his flatterers, and retires to the woods to curse Athens and mankind — digging for roots and finding gold, which he flings to the whores, thieves, and the general Alcibiades, whose sack of Athens the play leaves hanging.
works.plot: Timon's feasts and gifts draw the parasites; his creditors call; his friends refuse him; at his last banquet he serves them warm water and curses them; in the woods his gold draws a new parade of leeches; Alcibiades marches on Athens; and the play ends with Timon's epitaph and the city's submission, its loose ends never fully tied.
works.significance: The most extreme of the tragedies — a play of pure negation that has found its moment in every age of financial crisis.
works.meter: A verse of savage curses — Timon's tirades against gold and mankind are its glory — with the prose of the flatterers' scenes.
works.context: Probably written about 1605–08, in the phase of Lear and Coriolanus; its satire of the Jacobean credit economy has made it a favourite of economic criticism.
works.characters: Timon; Flavius; Apemantus; Alcibiades; the Poet; the Painter; Lucullus; Lucius; Sempronius; Phrynia; Timandra; the Fool
works.structure: A two-movement structure — Athens and the woods — with the masque of the false banquet as hinge; the play's rough edges suggest an abandoned draft revised for the press.
works.attributionNotes: Thomas Middleton's share (the banquet scene and parts of the middle acts) is generally accepted on stylistic evidence.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Social satire and estates criticism

works.title: Tirocinium
altTitles: Tirocinium; or, Advice to Parents on the Point of Sending Their Sons to Public Schools
works.form: didactic poem and conduct piece in blank verse, belonging to the century's writing on education and domestic duty
works.description: Cowper's poem of advice to parents on the education of their children, urging home and day-school teaching against the boarding public school. It sets the school-boy's loneliness, the tyranny of his seniors and the hardness of classical drudgery against the supervision of a father and the example of a Christian household, and extends its argument to the education of daughters. The poem is the most vigorous poetical statement of the eighteenth-century attack on the boarding-school.
works.plot: The speaker urges parents to keep their sons at home, arguing that the public boarding school exposes childhood to fear, vice and an idle learning of words rather than of sense. He describes the boy's first day at school, the austerities of the seminary, the return home with its spoiled affections, and the mischief of friendships formed under such confinement. The close passes to the education of girls and to the plea that the domestic and religious instruction of the family is the true seminary of the mind.
works.significance: It is the strongest poetical intervention in the eighteenth-century quarrel over boarding, and its appeal to the domestic and imaginative life of childhood belongs with the growing cult of the child that leads to the Romantic poets. Its influence on later conduct and educational writing was considerable, and it remains a primary document for the social history of schooling.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the Task's school, more abrupt and hortatory than Cowper's meditative verse, with pointed sententious closures.
works.context: Written in 1784, when the boarding public school was already a target of moral and educational writers and when the debate over classical curriculum, parental authority and the religious training of children was active in Evangelical and dissenting households; Cowper's own schooling and its hardships lie behind the picture.
works.characters: The advising speaker; the parent addressed; the school-boy of the description; the masters and ushers of the seminary
works.structure: A continuous didactic argument in several thematic sections, opening with the direct advice to parents, proceeding through the picture of school life, and closing with the extension to female education and the commendation of home.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is given in Cowper's own account, while the year of first separate impression has been variously reported, so publication_date is left null with the uncertainty stated.
themes: Childhood, innocence, and education
Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Women's education and intellectual friendship
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: Titus Andronicus
works.description: Shakespeare's first tragedy, written in collaboration with George Peele: the Roman general Titus returns from the Goths with the captive queen Tamora, whose revenge — the rape and mutilation of Titus's daughter Lavinia, the deaths of his sons — drives the play to its banquet of horrors, where Titus serves Tamora her own sons baked in a pie.
works.plot: Titus sacrifices Tamora's son and refuses the empire; Tamora, empress through Saturninus, avenges herself through her lover Aaron and her sons Chiron and Demetrius; Titus feigns madness, discovers the rapists, and executes his revenge in the cannibal banquet that ends the play.
works.significance: The most performed of the early tragedies and a laboratory of Shakespeare's tragic art — revenge, madness, and the stage as charnel house.
works.meter: Early verse of rhetorical set pieces — Lavinia's mute testimony, Titus's mad wordplay — with Ovid's Metamorphoses as the play's internal book of horrors.
works.context: Performed from 1594 and printed the same year; its extreme violence answered the vogue for Senecan blood inaugurated by Kyd's Spanish Tragedy.
works.characters: Titus Andronicus; Tamora; Aaron the Moor; Lavinia; Saturninus; Bassianus; Marcus Andronicus; Lucius; Chiron; Demetrius; young Lucius
works.structure: A Senecan revenge tragedy of symmetrical atrocity and counter-atrocity, with Aaron the Moor as its gleeful vice-figure.
works.attributionNotes: George Peele's co-authorship of Act 1 (and possibly other scenes) is now widely accepted on stylistic evidence.
themes: Blood-feud, vengeance, and kinship
Revenge and justice

works.title: To a Mouse
altTitles: To a Mouse, On Turning Her up in Her Nest with the Plough, November, 1785
works.form: occasional meditative lyric and address, in the tradition of the 'To a' poems of the Scottish vernacular
works.description: The shortest and most quoted of Burns's ploughman poems, addressed to a field mouse whose nest has been laid bare by the poet's plough in November 1785. Pity for the small creature turns into a meditation on provision, fear and the human lot, since the mouse at least lives in the present while mankind is tormented by memory and forecast. It is the classic lyric instance of the eighteenth-century cult of sympathy extended to the lower creation.
works.plot: The speaker apologises to the frightened mouse for the destruction of its winter house, and reflects that its pains in storing for the winter have been laid aside by an accident it could not foresee. He then envies it, because its troubles are but of the moment, whereas man looks backward and forward and is wretched. The poem ends in a prayer that the mouse may be spared the cruel human remembrances, and that its fate may teach the poet himself to bear his own disappointments of hope.
works.significance: Its lines on the best laid schemes of mice and men passing often ago became among the most familiar proverbs in English, and the poem is a standard example of the preromantic lyric that reasons outward from a small accident of feeling. It also fixed the figure of the thinking ploughman as a poet of sensibility and of providential anxiety.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie): four four-beat Scots lines and two short trimming lines, with the rhyming pattern a-a-a-b-a-b and an insistent colloquial rhythm.
works.context: Written at Mossgiel in the autumn of 1785, when Burns's farming prospects were failing and his poems were being prepared for the press; the mood of disappointed hope and of dependence on the weather of a small farm belongs exactly to that season, and the poem's ethic of pity for animals draws on the contemporary debate about sympathy and the moral sense.
works.characters: The mouse; the ploughman-speaker
works.structure: Six short stanzas moving from the immediate incident to apology, comparison and general conclusion, the argument of the meditation rising steadily out of a single act of ploughing.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is Burns's own, entered in his memorandum of the poem, and the printed title carries that date.
themes: Fortune and mutability
Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling

works.title: To a Skylark
works.form: Romantic ode and elemental hymn; the invisible-voice lyric of the school of the greater odes, with the simile catalogue of the devotional hymn.
works.description: The period's most quoted hymn to an invisible bird, addressed to a skylark rising out of the English meadow into the unfelt air and singing as it ascends. The poem reasons from the bird's joy to the condition of the human mind, which can only imagine pleasure it cannot feel and which forebodes pain even in its mirth. Its structure of twenty-one stanzas with a recurring short closing line gives it the character of an incantation, and it was written, by the poet's own account, from a walk on the shore near the Tuscan city where he then lived.
works.plot: The bird, hailed as a spirit rather than a bird, hides in the blue deep of the sky and is known only by the sound that falls like hail, like moonlight, like a glow-worm in the grass. The poem then runs through a series of comparisons, a poet new to his thoughts, a noble damsel in a palace of hushed sorrow, a glow-worm, a rose hidden by its own leaves, rain waking the flowers, and every sweet and joyful sight, before granting that no simile reaches the bird's happiness. The human condition is then set against it, we look before and after and mourn before our mirth is gone, and the poem ends with the prayer that if the bird's spirit were known, the poet's words would not fall dead upon the world. The argument is that the unembodied song measures the distance between nature's joy and human self-consciousness.
works.significance: It is the best-known of the period's lyrics and became a schoolroom and anthological test of pure rapture in verse, much imitated in the short measures of the later nineteenth century. Its analysis of human consciousness as a creature that looks before and after gave the century one of its most portable definitions of melancholy, and the stanza's structure has been much discussed as a model of the lyric line's upward figure.
works.meter: Stanzas of four iambic pentameter lines followed by a single trimmed tetrameter line, rhyming ababb with the short fifth line repeated as a refrain; the abbreviations of the measure, all but two lines being of fewer syllables, give the stanza its upward momentum.
works.context: Written in the summer of 1820, in the season the poet spent on the coast of Tuscany after the birth of a son and in the months of the Neapolitan and Piedmontese risings and their suppression, and published in the London volume of that year's shorter poems. Its companion volume of the same season contained the titan drama and the wind ode, and its treatment of inspiration as something granted rather than achieved answered the era's account of the poet's faculty.
works.characters: the skylark, addressed as a star of heaven and as a spirit of joy; the poet who would be taught the measure of its thoughts
works.structure: Twenty-one stanzas of continuous address, moving from the ascent to the catalogue of similes, to the reflection on human sorrow and to the closing prayer; there is no story but a single sustained act of attention.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; an early prose note on the circumstances of composition was written out by the poet, and the text varies only in small readings between the first issue and the posthumous collections.
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
movements: Shelley and Radical Romanticism

works.title: To a Waterfowl
works.form: Nature lyric and conversation poem addressed to a bird
works.description: The shortest and best-known of the author's nature lyrics, in which a single bird flying across an evening sky becomes a lesson in providential guidance. The poem's argument is that the same power which directs the bird also orders the wanderer's steps. It is the central text of the American conversation with nature.
works.plot: The speaker watches a waterfowl flying alone across the twilight, seeking its resting place on the marsh or the lake. He asks what guide directs the bird over pathless waters, and answers that no eye watches it in vain. The second movement draws the moral: the same power that teaches the bird his way will teach the poet, wandering alone, his path too. The poem closes with an act of trust, committing the wanderer's steps to that guidance.
works.significance: It is the model of the American lyric of single perception and moral inference, imitated for a generation. Its trust in a guidance revealed by nature rather than by scripture defines the author's religious imagination. It is the poem most often cited as the native counterpart of Wordsworth's shorter lyrics.
works.meter: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter in the common-metre hymn stanza, with regular rhyme
works.context: Composed in 1811 on a solitary ride and long kept among the author's papers before appearing in print; the collected volume of 1821 gave it its permanent text. Its providential consolation belongs to the decline of Calvinist election in New England. The poem's currency in school recitation made it a national property by mid-century.
works.structure: Two-stanza lyric of observation and application, the first stanza picturing the flight, the second drawing the consoling inference.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the date of the poem's first periodical appearance is reported differently in the biographical literature and is not asserted here.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
movements: Bryant and the American Nature Lyric

works.title: To Autumn
works.form: Romantic ode and nature lyric of the school of the great odes; the seasonal meditation and the hymn of the year's departure, in the most concentrated form the period reached.
works.description: The last of the great short poems and the closing piece of the volume of 1820, a lyric of three eleven-line stanzas which presents the season not as the prelude to death but as a condition of ripeness and of its own music. It personifies autumn as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the harvester resting by the half-reaped furrow and as the gatherer of the last gleanings, and answers the questions of the spring with the sounds of the day of departure. Its stillness, its freedom from argument and its handling of the transience of the year have made it the most admired short poem of the period.
works.plot: The first stanza presents autumn as the neighbour of the sun that ripens the fruit and fills the gourd and the hazel shells with kernel, and as the season that makes the swags bulge and the cyder press drop the last oozings. The second finds the season itself at rest, sitting on a half-reaped furrow, winnowing on the floor, and sleeping by the harvest cider-house while the last gleanings cross the brook, and the third asks where are the songs of spring, and answers that the listener has his own music in the wailful choir of the small gnats, the bleating lambs, the crickets and the swallow. The argument is that the season of decay has its own completeness and that the music of departure is not an absence but an instrument.
works.significance: It is the most complete and most quoted of the period's short poems, and the standing example of a lyric that presents a process without a moral and a death without lamentation. Its handling of the personified season gave the later nature lyric one of its permanent registers, and the sequence of the three odes and this poem forms the schoolroom definition of the Romantic lyric at its limit.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in three stanzas of eleven lines, the rhyme abab and the remainder varied, with the closing line of each stanza used as a caesura of rest; the poem is almost free of metaphor of the violent kind and depends on the verb and on the article of detail.
works.context: Composed on a Sunday in the September of 1819, on a walk in the fields near the town where the poet was staying with a friend, in the season of his last effort at the titan poem and of the beginning of his illness, and printed in the volume of July 1820 as one of the closing pieces. Its date, after the abandonment of the larger work, made it the symbol in later biography of a short career's harvest, and its freedom from the argument of the greater odes was widely imitated in the seasonal lyric of the later century.
works.characters: autumn personified as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the reaper, the winnower and the gleaner, and as the hearer of the season's own choir
works.structure: Three stanzas of eleven lines, the first of ripening, the second of the season at rest in the harvest field, the third of the sounds of the evening of the year; there is no development but a change of aspect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is in the transcript of the volume and is dated by the poet's own letters of the season.
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
Time, death, and immortality through verse
movements: Keats and the Sensuous Ode

works.title: To Be Young, Gifted and Black
works.form: Dramatic and autobiographical compilation (posthumous, adapted by Robert Nemiroff)
works.description: To Be Young, Gifted and Black is a portrait of Lorraine Hansberry in her own words, adapted by Robert Nemiroff from her plays, letters, journals, speeches and essays. It was staged in New York in 1969 and published in book form with an introduction by James Baldwin.
works.summary: A collage of passages from Hansberry's writings, including her childhood memories of Chicago, letters, diary entries, speeches on the Black writer and scenes from her plays, arranged to tell the story of her life and thought.
works.plot: The work traces Hansberry's growth from a Chicago childhood marked by segregation, through her political education in New York and the success of A Raisin in the Sun, to her final illness, letting her voice speak through her writings. Its title comes from a speech Hansberry gave in May 1964 to the young winners of a creative-writing competition sponsored by the United Negro College Fund; it also became the title of Nina Simone's 1969 civil rights song.
works.significance: It spread Hansberry's reputation beyond A Raisin in the Sun, introduced her essays and letters to a wide audience, and has been frequently revived.
works.meter: Hansberry's own varied voices, from intimate diary to public oratory, assembled by an editor.
works.context: Prepared by Nemiroff, her former husband and literary executor, at the height of the Black Power era, it introduced Hansberry to a new generation.
works.structure: An episodic montage of scenes and monologues drawn from texts of different kinds.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
