works.title: To Helen
works.form: Romantic lyric of idealized beauty; address-poem in the Horatian and classical manner
works.description: A short lyric of classical beauty addressed to a woman whose loveliness is figured as a ship arriving from a warm sea into a harbour of the soul. It is the poem that made beauty, and not desire, the author's enduring subject. Its three stanzas move from simile to arrival to a scene of the beloved as a torch-bearer of the antique world.
works.plot: The beloved's beauty is compared to the barks that, wind-laid upon a perfumed sea, bear weary wayfarers to their native country. The poem then asks what the tired wanderer would give to reach the casements of that shore and the Niche where the Faun stands, half-embowered in the fragrant lilies of the stream. In the last stanza the beloved comes across the night with shining feet, and the region of the poem is disclosed as a home to which the wanderer belongs.
works.significance: It is the earliest of the author's lyrics to enter the permanent anthologies and the source of his reputation for the poetry of beauty. Its treatment of the beloved as a vessel of homecoming set a pattern for later American lyric addresses. It marks the moment at which his verse left cosmological ambition for the short perfect form.
works.meter: Iambic trimeter and tetrameter stanzas of nine lines with an intricate rhyme scheme
works.context: First printed in the collected volume of 1831, where it stands among the poems the author's later editors classed with his verse of youth. Its classical furniture belongs to the schoolroom Hellenism of American colleges in the 1820s. The lyric was revised and reissued through the following decade.
works.characters: Helen; the weary wayfarer
works.structure: Three-stanza lyric, each stanza developing one figure: the arriving ship, the shore and its shrine, the beloved's approach by night.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the title under which the poem is known was settled in the author's lifetime.
themes: Idealized love and the lost beloved
Imagination as a way of knowing
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: To His Coy Mistress
works.description: Marvell's most famous lyric, a carpe diem argument to a reluctant mistress: had we world enough and time, coyness were no crime, but time's winged chariot hurries near, so let us rather devour time than languish — a brilliant fusion of logic, wit, and urgency.
works.plot: A three-part syllogistic argument ('Had we but world enough and time ... But at my back I always hear / Time's winged chariot ... Therefore ...'), urging physical love against the pressure of mortality.
works.significance: One of the most anthologised and admired English lyrics, a supreme example of metaphysical wit applied to the carpe diem theme.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter couplets with metaphysical conceits and a witty, urgent tone.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, unpublished in Marvell's lifetime and printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it draws on the classical carpe diem tradition of Horace and Ovid.
works.characters: the speaker; his coy mistress
works.structure: A dramatic monologue structured as a logical argument in three movements, in iambic tetrameter couplets.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
Love, constancy, and betrayal
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: To the Diaspora
works.description: A poem by Gwendolyn Brooks in To Disembark (1981), published by Third World Press, subtitled 'you did not know you were Afrika': an address to black people of the diaspora on a journey towards Africa that turns out to be a journey into themselves.
works.summary: An address to 'you', who set out for Africa without knowing that the black continent to be reached was yourself; the speaker's earlier, disbelieved prophecy; a call to the hard work still to be done.
works.plot: When you set out for Afrika, the speaker tells the diaspora, you did not know you were going, because you did not know you were Afrika, that the black continent that had to be reached was you. The speaker could not have told you then that some sun would come, evoking the diamonds of you; you would not have believed it, and when told you smiled and thanked her but hardly believed. Here is some sun, the poem says, and now off into the places rough to reach: your work, that was done, to be done to be done to be done.
works.significance: A representative late poem of Brooks's Black Arts commitment, and the latest of her poems that Norton prints.
works.meter: Direct address, the spelling 'Afrika', repetition and incantation in the closing line.
works.context: After 1967 Brooks left Harper and published with black presses such as Broadside Press and Third World Press; To Disembark gathers poems of this period.
works.structure: Free-verse paragraphs addressed to 'you', moving from the journey to the speaker's prophecy and to the repeated, open-ended last line.
themes: Identity, authenticity and the divided self
Migration, exile and diaspora
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights
movements: Black Arts Movement

works.title: To the Ladies
works.form: ironic address in verse; poem of the women question
works.description: A short ironic poem addressed to women, remonstrating against the conditions of marriage and against the education that makes a wife a dependent. It is one of the most anthologised lyrics of the debate about women, and its couplets turn the commonplaces of gallantry against the law and custom that they conceal.
works.plot: The poet addresses her sex with a complaint of their treatment, showing that they are educated only to please and are then governed by the men they have pleased. Marriage is represented as a condition in which the wife's person and estate pass into another's keeping, and the language of superiority used against women is turned back upon it. The poem closes on the advice that the ladies improve their minds and their use of them.
works.significance: It is a landmark of early feminist verse and one of the most quoted of the period's poems on marriage and women's condition, much used in the modern recovery of the writing of women before the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the plain Augustan manner, the point of the argument closing on the rhyme; the idiom is that of the conversation poem of the debate about the sexes.
works.context: Written in the circles of learned women of the south-west in the last years of the seventeenth century, circulating in manuscript, and appearing in print among her poems in 1703, in the season of the pamphlet and stage war about women's abilities that produced the essays and the verse poems of the question.
works.structure: A single continuous address in closed couplets, moving from complaint to argument to counsel; there is no narrative, the argument being carried by the sequence of the retorts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to the poet is settled by the manuscript tradition and by the printed collections that carry her name; the poem existed in more than one state, so the year recorded here is that of the printed collection and not of composition.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
Marriage and women's conduct
Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
Women's education and intellectual friendship
Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: To the Lighthouse
works.description: Two days ten years apart at a Hebridean holiday house: the Ramsay family, the artist Lily Briscoe, and the war in between. It is a prose fiction work of 1927 by Virginia Woolf; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The Ramsay family is on holiday on the Isle of Skye before the war: Mr Ramsay, the philosopher, tyrannises over his family with his need for sympathy; Mrs Ramsay holds them together; Lily Briscoe paints; James longs to go to the lighthouse. The second part, 'Time Passes', records the war and the deaths of Mrs Ramsay, Andrew and Prue in a few pages, and the house's decay. The third returns ten years later, with Lily completing her painting and the surviving Ramsays finally reaching the lighthouse.
works.significance: To the Lighthouse is Woolf's most perfectly achieved novel and one of the great English novels of the century: its three-part structure, its rendering of the passage of time and of a mother's presence, and Lily Briscoe's painting — the female artist's struggle to make form — are among the finest things in modern fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric stream of consciousness and the interior monologue.
works.context: The pre-war world of the Cambridge philosopher and the summer house; the First World War as an absence; the changes in women's lives and the death of the Victorian family. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Mr Ramsay; Mrs Ramsay; James Ramsay; Cam Ramsay; Lily Briscoe; Charles Tansley; Augustus Carmichael; Minta Doyle; Paul Rayley
works.structure: Three parts (The Window, Time Passes, The Lighthouse); a single day, a ten-year interval, and a single morning.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Adeline Virginia Woolf. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: To the Memory of Mr. Oldham
works.description: Dryden's elegy for the young satirist John Oldham, who died of smallpox in December 1683; a short masterpiece of restrained praise that compares Oldham's early death to that of Marcellus and Nisus.
works.plot: The poem laments the loss of a kindred wit, concedes the difference in style between the two poets, and consoles with the thought that Oldham's early death spared him the decay of age and dulness.
works.significance: Often judged the finest short elegy in English between Lycidas and In Memoriam, and a canonical instance of Dryden's capacity for personal warmth.
works.meter: Heroic couplets with frequent enjambment and a deliberately unpolished, masculine roughness suited to the subject.
works.context: Written in the winter of 1683-4 and prefixed to the 1684 edition of Oldham's Works.
works.characters: John Oldham; the speaker; Marcellus (alluded to)
works.structure: A single continuous elegiac meditation of twenty-seven lines.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.
themes: Patronage and the literary marketplace
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Tono-Bungay
works.description: The rise and fall of a patent-medicine fortune and a portrait of England from the 1870s to the 1900s — Wells's finest novel. It is a prose fiction work of 1909 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: George Ponderevo, nephew of the fraudulent chemist Edward Ponderevo, recounts his uncle's rise from provincial pharmacist to the owner of the Tono-Bungay patent medicine empire, the family's ascent into the wealthy classes, and its collapse. George's other life as an aeronautical engineer and his flight over Africa give the novel its images of the modern age; the book ends with the uncle ruined and dying and England seen as a system of shams.
works.significance: Tono-Bungay is Wells's masterpiece and one of the great Edwardian condition-of-England novels: it invented the novel of advertising, and its portrait of the sham empire of commerce — the patent medicine as a metaphor for the whole society — is the finest thing Wells wrote.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
works.context: The patent-medicine boom and the advertising culture of the 1890s, the new wealth of the Edwardian middle class, the failure of English institutions, and the beginnings of aviation. The record dates the work as composed between 1908 and 1909 and first published in 1909 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: George Ponderevo; Edward Ponderevo; Susan Ponderevo; Marion Ramboat; Beatrice Normandy
works.structure: First-person retrospective with a large cast and a documentary survey of English society. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Tottel's Miscellany
altTitles: Songes and Sonettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward late Earle of Surrey, and other
works.form: anthology of sonnets, lyrics, and epigrams
works.description: The first great printed anthology of English poetry: 271 poems by Surrey, Wyatt, Nicholas Grimald, and other courtly poets, published by Richard Tottel on 5 June 1557 under the title Songes and Sonettes. It fixed the public canon of the Henrician lyric and went through nine editions by 1587.
works.plot: An anthology without narrative frame: sonnets, songs, elegies, and epigrams arranged by author, beginning with Surrey, whose name gave the volume its selling title.
works.significance: The founding anthology of English poetry: it created the reading public for the lyric, fixed the reputations of Wyatt and Surrey, and supplied the Elizabethan poets with their metre and manner.
works.meter: The full range of the early Tudor lyric: sonnets, poulter's measure, short-line songs; the anthology standardized the decasyllabic line for a public audience.
works.context: Printed two years after the Marian restoration began; the miscellany carried the Henrician court's poetry into the Elizabethan age and made the court lyric a national possession.
works.characters: the courtly poets (Surrey, Wyatt, Grimald, and others)
works.structure: Miscellany organized by poet, with the Earl of Surrey's poems first; the arrangement itself constitutes the first printed history of the English lyric.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled by Richard Tottel (publisher); the authorship of the 'uncertain authors' poems remains largely unknown. Recorded as collaborative with no author links, per the validator's anonymity rule.
themes: Courtly service and courtly danger
Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Towneley Plays
works.description: The Towneley (Wakefield) cycle of thirty-two plays, from the Creation to the Last Judgement, preserved in the Towneley manuscript (c. 1500) and long associated with Wakefield: famous above all for the six plays in the nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' attributed to the Wakefield Master — including the Second Shepherds' Play, the comic masterpiece of the English cycles, with its sheep-stealing Mak and its nativity of the stolen lamb.
works.plot: The cycle retells salvation history from Lucifer's fall through the patriarchs to Christ's Passion and the Judgement; the Master's plays — Noah and his scolding wife, the two Shepherds' plays, Herod, and the Buffeting — transform the biblical matter with a vernacular comedy of Yorkshire shepherds, shrews, and ranting tyrants unmatched in the other cycles.
works.significance: The Second Shepherds' Play is the most famous English medieval drama: the cycle's blend of farce and nativity embodies the mystery tradition at its theatrical summit.
works.meter: The unique nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' (aabcccbddb with internal rhyme) in the Master's plays; thirteen-line stanza and couplets elsewhere.
works.context: Composed and compiled c. 1400–1500, probably at Wakefield, where the plays were performed on Corpus Christi day; the manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 1) belonged to the Towneley family of Lancashire, from which the cycle takes its name.
works.characters: Mak the sheep-stealer; Gill; the shepherds (Coll, Gib, Daw); Noah and his wife; Herod; Christ; Pilate
works.structure: A pageant cycle of thirty-two plays, partially dependent on York but transformed by the Wakefield Master's comic and homiletic genius.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the 'Wakefield Master' is a scholarly construct for the author of the six stanza-linked plays.
themes: The Passion of Christ
Typology and biblical interpretation
movements: Vernacular Religious Drama

works.title: Toxophilus
works.description: Ascham's dialogue on the art of archery, presented to Henry VIII as both a practical treatise and a model of English prose style — the first book on a sport written in the English language.
works.plot: Two speakers, Toxophilus ('lover of the bow') and Philologus ('lover of learning'), debate whether study or shooting better befits a gentleman; Toxophilus vindicates archery as recreation, describes the bow, its parts, and the craft of shooting, and argues for the health and military value of the sport, while the dialogue itself demonstrates the eloquence the English tongue can achieve.
works.significance: The first English treatise on a sport and a deliberate demonstration of the capacities of English prose for learned subjects; together with The Schoolmaster it established Ascham's reputation as a stylist and educational theorist.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1544–45 when Ascham was reader in Greek at St John's College, Cambridge, and presented to Henry VIII in 1545 in the royal library at Westminster, for which Ascham received a pension; archery's military role had been reaffirmed by statute in 1541.
works.characters: Toxophilus; Philologus
works.structure: Two-book dialogue framed by a preface to 'all gentle men and yeomen of England', with a systematic technical exposition embedded in the conversational form.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
Wisdom and learning
movements: English Renaissance Humanism

works.title: Trading Twelves: The Selected Letters of Ralph Ellison and Albert Murray
works.description: Trading Twelves is the correspondence between Ralph Ellison and Albert Murray, published by the Modern Library in 2000 and edited by Murray and John F. Callahan, Ellison's literary executor. The title borrows the jazz term for musicians trading twelve-bar choruses.
works.summary: Letters exchanged by the two friends from Tuskegee in the 1950s, while Ellison was writing and then promoting Invisible Man and living in Rome, and while Murray was serving as an Air Force officer and beginning to write.
works.plot: The letters discuss jazz, literature and politics with intimacy and wit: the reception of Invisible Man and Ellison's struggles with his second novel, Murray's ambitions as a writer, their admiration for Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Count Basie, their reading of Hemingway, Faulkner, Malraux and Mann, and their shared conviction that African American culture is central to American culture. The exchange reads as a sustained improvisation between two minds working out the ideas they later published.
works.significance: It documents the origins of the aesthetic Ellison and Murray shared and is a major source for the history of postwar African American intellectual life.
works.meter: Playful, allusive and often vernacular epistolary prose, rich in jazz idiom and private jokes.
works.context: Published six years after Ellison's death, during a period of renewed interest in his unfinished novel, a year after the edited Juneteenth.
works.structure: Chronologically arranged letters from both correspondents, with editorial notes identifying people and events.
themes: Art, the artist and the creative life
Nationhood and national identity
Race, racism and the struggle for civil rights

works.title: Translation of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (Hutchinson)
works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's complete verse translation of Lucretius's De Rerum Natura, the first ever into English, undertaken in the 1650s and dedicated to the Earl of Anglesey; she later wrote a preface condemning the Epicurean philosophy she had so brilliantly rendered.
works.plot: The translation renders all six books of Lucretius's didactic epic on Epicurean physics, the nature of the soul, the origin of society, and the fear of death.
works.significance: A landmark of Restoration translation and of women's classical learning; its preface is a striking document of a devout Puritan woman negotiating with Epicurean materialism.
works.meter: Heroic couplets; Hutchinson's version is the first complete English Lucretius.
works.context: Composed in the 1650s and revised up to the 1670s; the manuscript was dedicated to Arthur Annesley, Earl of Anglesey, and remained unpublished until 1996.
works.characters: Venus; Epicurus (alluded to); Memmius
works.structure: Six books in heroic couplets, following Lucretius's own structure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand with her prefatory address to the Earl of Anglesey.
themes: Creation and cosmology
Death, the soul, and the afterlife
Female authorship and the woman writer
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: Translations of the Letters of a Hindoo Rajah
works.form: Prose fiction; epistolary and travel satire with an oriental framing device; fiction of the India question
works.description: A satirical epistolary fiction presented as the letters of an Indian envoy and his attendants, translated by their interpreter, observing English society, its politics, its literature and its religions on a tour from Bengal through London and Scotland. The oriental point of view exposes the arrogance, inconstancy and self-interest of the British in India, and the ridicule of Anglo-Indian nabob wealth and of fashionable exotic taste is double-edged, since the observer's own superstition is also laid bare. The book was an immediate success and established the writer's reputation. It is the most accomplished of the 1790s vogue of oriental-mirror satire.
works.plot: A Hindoo rajah's embassy, accompanied by his interpreter and his family, travels to England on the business of a disputed succession and a claim for redress against company officials. In letters home the party describes the English constitution, its parties and its pulpit, its theatres, its manners and its treatment of women, while the interpreter's own narrative of an injury in India reveals the mechanism of corruption and ruined families behind the civilising spectacle. The succession claim miscarries, the embassy disperses, and the closing letters report the observer's return and his confirmed contempt for a nation that talks of liberty while oppressing dependants.
works.significance: The ablest of the woman-written oriental satires of the 1790s and an important text for study of British writing about India before and after the impeachment, of the epistolary travel-satire tradition, and of the conservative answer to philosophical fiction. Its framing of translation and interpretation has made it a frequent object of later critical attention.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; the style imitates formal translated correspondence, with sententious moral reflection and sustained ironic understatement
works.context: Published in 1796, after the India debates, the impeachment trial of a company governor-general and the regency settlement had made oriental dependency a subject of daily parliamentary and print controversy. The book also answers the decade's fashion for pretend oriental tales and for imitations of a famous Persian translation, and its Edinburgh and London scenes draw on the debate over Jacobin novels and political enthusiasm after the French Revolution.
works.characters: The interpreter-narrator and his family; a young rajah and his counsellors; English acquaintances in London and Edinburgh, including a man of letters and a political orator; a nabob's family in Bengal
works.structure: Epistolary satire in two volumes with an embedded narrative by the interpreter; the letters progress from description to argument and are framed by a translator's preface and notes, which allow the joke to be sustained at several levels of narration.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name, with the translation device as a fictional persona; no dispute over authorship.
themes: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review
The Bluestockings and Women's Letters

works.title: Travels in New-England and New-York
works.form: Travel narrative and local guide; topographical and statistical survey with moral argument
works.description: A survey of the country and the people of the northern states, written from journal matter and printed after the author's death. It combines topographical description, agricultural observation, statistical tables and moral and religious argument. It is the fullest early American example of the traveller's national survey.
works.plot: The narrative moves through Connecticut, Massachusetts and the eastern and western parts of New York, describing towns, soils, manufactures, schools and churches as it goes. It reports conversations with farmers, clergymen and lawyers, and it argues that the prosperity of the country depends on its religious and educational institutions. Its accounts of the Dutch settlements and of the western districts give a picture of a nation in motion. The work closes with reflections on the destiny of a Christian and lettered commonwealth.
works.significance: It is the most systematic American portrait of the northern states before Tocqueville and a central document of the clerical survey of the republic. Its fusion of topographical detail with religious argument shows the didactic descriptive tradition continuing into the 1820s. It supplies the social map against which the native fiction of the same decade was written.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published from the author's papers in 1821, with an enlarged four-volume issue shortly afterwards, and composed from tours taken in the last years of the eighteenth century and after the peace of 1815. Its attention to canals, schools and denominations reflects the internal-improvement moment of the era. Its author had been president of Yale since 1795.
works.structure: Travels arranged by route and district, with journal narrative, descriptive survey, tables of numbers and inserted disquisition; posthumously edited from memoranda.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the volume was edited and issued after the author's death from his journals.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Treasure Island
altTitles: Treasure Island; or, The Mutiny of the Hispaniola
works.form: Adventure novel (serialised as The Sea-Cook in Young Folks, 1881-82)
works.description: Serialised as The Sea-Cook in Young Folks in 1881-82 and published in 1883: the founding modern adventure novel, and the book that fixed the image of the treasure map, the one-legged pirate and the boy hero for all later fiction.
works.plot: Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map in the sea chest of the dead Billy Bones, sails on the Hispaniola with Squire Trelawney and Dr Livesey, discovers that the crew has been recruited by the mutineer Long John Silver, survives the mutiny and the island, and returns with the treasure.
works.significance: Treasure Island is the origin of the modern adventure novel and of the pirate of popular culture; it established the narrative grammar of the boys' adventure story and made the romance respectable again in English fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.
works.context: The 1880s, the revival of the romance after the realist dominance of the 1860s-70s, the Stevenson family's lighthouse engineering and the Pacific voyages of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Jim Hawkins; Long John Silver; Squire Trelawney; Dr Livesey; Captain Smollett; Billy Bones; Ben Gunn; Israel Hands; Blind Pew
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as R. L. S. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Treatise on the Astrolabe
works.description: Chaucer's prose treatise on the construction and use of the astrolabe, written in 1391 for his ten-year-old son Lewis: the first technical treatise in English prose, and the earliest English work on a scientific instrument. Its precision, clarity, and fatherly address make it unique in the medieval English canon.
works.plot: In five planned parts — of which the first two and a supplement survive — the treatise describes the astrolabe and its parts, teaches the child to take altitudes and tell the time, and promises the tables and theories that would complete the work; the famous prologue addresses 'Lyte Lowys my sone' with pedagogical tenderness.
works.significance: The first scientific prose in English and the classic of its kind: the treatise's plain style is a landmark in the development of English as a language of learning.
works.meter: Prose: plain, exact, and carefully ordered, in the tradition of the practical manual.
works.context: Dated 1391 in the prologue, written for Lewis Chaucer, then about ten years old, in London; it draws on the Latin tradition of Messahala and the practical astronomy of the universities; preserved in some thirty manuscripts.
works.characters: the author (as father-teacher); Lewis (addressee)
works.structure: A didactic treatise of definitions, propositions, and conclusions, each numbered for the child's use, with worked examples from the Oxford latitude.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the prologue).
themes: Creation and cosmology
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Trelawny of the 'Wells'
works.description: First performed in 1898 and Pinero's warmest comedy: an actress of the old Sadler's Wells school tries to enter respectable society and returns to the stage. It is a dramatic work of 1898 by Arthur Wing Pinero; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Rose Trelawny, the leading lady of the theatre company at the Sadler's Wells in the 1860s, becomes engaged to Arthur Gower, a young gentleman, and tries to live with his family; she cannot bear the drawing room, returns to the theatre, and is finally reunited with Arthur when he becomes an actor himself.
works.significance: Trelawny of the 'Wells' is the finest English theatrical comedy of the century and a loving memorial to the world of the old stock companies: its portrait of the Victorian stage made it a permanent classic, and it is the play in which Pinero's craftsmanship serves pure affection.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion.
works.context: 1898: the Victorian theatre of the 1860s, the passing of the old stock companies, the social stigma of the actress, and the new respectability of the stage. The record dates the work as composed in 1898 and first published in 1898 and first performed in 1898 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Rose Trelawny; Arthur Gower; Sir William Gower; Vice-Chancellor Sir William; Miss Trafalgar Gower; Tom Wrench; Avonia Bunn; Mr Balfour
works.structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Arthur Pinero. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Trilby
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1894
works.description: Published in 1894 and the most popular novel of the decade: a tone-deaf artists' model becomes a great singer under the hypnotic power of Svengali. It is a prose fiction work of 1894 by George du Maurier; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Trilby O'Ferrall, an Irish artists' model in the Latin Quarter, is loved by three English art students; the sinister musician Svengali hypnotises her and makes her a famous singer, she collapses when he dies, and she dies herself soon after, while the pathetic and comic details of bohemian Paris fill the novel.
works.significance: Trilby was the most popular novel of the 1890s and one of the first modern best-sellers: it created Svengali and the word 'Svengali', it made the artists' model and bohemian Paris into a popular mythology, and 'Trilby' gave the world the trilby hat, the most successful merchandising event in nineteenth-century publishing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is direct, confiding narration with comic digression.
works.context: 1894: the Paris of the Latin Quarter in the 1850s, the vogue of hypnotism and Mesmerism, the English art student abroad, and the new mass market for the illustrated novel. The record dates the work as composed between 1893 and 1894 and first published in 1894 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under sensation novel; early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
works.characters: Trilby O'Ferrall; Svengali; Little Billee; Taffy Wynne; the Laird; Madame Vinard; Gecko; Zouzou
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Trilogy
works.description: The great poem of the London Blitz and one of the major long poems of the century: war, resurrection, the female divine and the making of a poet out of the ruins. It is a verse work of 1946 by H. D. (Hilda Doolittle); it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The three books — 'The Walls Do Not Fall' (1944), 'Tribute to the Angels' (1945) and 'The Flowering of the Rod' (1946) — begin among the ruins of London under bombardment and move through a meditation on the poet's craft, a vision of the angels and the Lady, and the legend of Mary Magdalene and the alabaster jar, arriving at a vision of resurrection.
works.significance: Trilogy is one of the great long poems of the period and the founding work of the modernist woman's epic: it turned the Blitz into a vision of resurrection and made the female divine the centre of a modernist poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the single crystalline image.
works.context: The London Blitz of 1940–41, the Second World War, H. D.'s analysis with Freud, and her study of the Gnostic and Hermetic traditions. The record dates the work as composed between 1942 and 1944 and first published in 1946 and it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
works.characters: The poet; the angels; the Lady; Mary Magdalene
works.structure: Three books of three parts each, in free verse and short lyrics. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Hilda Doolittle. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Tristram
works.description: Published in 1927 and the Pulitzer Prize-winning climax of Robinson's Arthurian trilogy: the tragedy of Tristram and Isolt. It is a verse work of 1927 by Edwin Arlington Robinson; it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Epic and the Long Philosophical Poem and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tristram, married without love to Isolt of the white hands in Brittany, returns to Isolt of Ireland, King Mark's queen; after a summer together at Lancelot's castle of Joyous Gard she is taken back to Cornwall, and when Tristram comes to her there the jealous Andred stabs him to death as she lies dying, while the poem ends, as it began, with Isolt of Brittany gazing at the empty sea, in a retelling that strips the legend of its magic and leaves only the human cost.
works.significance: Tristram won the Pulitzer Prize in 1928 and is the finest American narrative poem of the century: its treatment of the Tristan legend as a study of human failure and its blank-verse music made it a landmark, and it completes the Arthurian trilogy that is Robinson's most ambitious work.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The dialogue or narrative runs in blank verse, the unrhymed iambic pentameter. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, colloquial line in traditional metre.
works.context: 1925-27: the American Arthurian revival of the 1920s, the aftermath of the First World War, and the modern scepticism about romantic love. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; epic and the long philosophical poem.
works.characters: Tristram; Isolt of Ireland; Isolt of Brittany; King Mark; Andred; Gawaine; Brangwaine; Queen Morgan; Lancelot and Guinevere
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A long poem in books or parts, its narrative or its argument carried continuously from the statement of its subject to its close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. A. Robinson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Tristram of Lyonesse
works.description: Published in 1882 and the finest of Swinburne's long poems: a version of the Tristan and Iseult legend in rhymed verse of extraordinary music. It is a verse work of 1882 by Algernon Charles Swinburne; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The poem follows Tristan from his voyage to Ireland and the killing of the dragon, through the love potion and the years of the lovers' secrecy, to the final voyage and Iseult's arrival too late, and ends with the deaths of the lovers and their burial.
works.significance: Tristram of Lyonesse is the great English poem of adulterous love and one of the finest narrative poems of the century: its treatment of desire and death made it a central text for the Decadent reading of the Arthurian legend.
works.meter: Verse. Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The author's characteristic manner is incantatory anapaestic and trochaic metres.
works.context: 1882: the Victorian Arthurian revival after Tennyson, the Pre-Raphaelite painting of the legend, and the Tristan cult of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.characters: Tristram; Iseult of Ireland; King Mark; Iseult of the White Hands; Brangwain; Palamede; Ganhardine; Morold
works.structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as A. C. Swinburne. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Trivia
altTitles: Trivia; or, the Art of Walking the Streets of London
works.description: Gay's mock-didactic guide to the sights, shows, coaches, clothes and night entertainments of London, written as an art of town-walking in the manner of the classical didactic poem.
works.plot: The Muse of Trivia instructs the citizen and the country visitor where to look and how to dress, what to see by day in the parks, the exchange and the shops, and what to seek by night in the tavern, the box at the theatre and the masquerade, with an antiquarian appendix on the town's own history.
works.significance: It is the century's most charming urban descriptive poem and the complement to the country prospect of Windsor-Forest, preserving the topology of Augustan London for later readers.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of easy narrative breadth, with the rapid list and the colloquial tag.
works.context: Published in the season of the Spectator's town-painting essays and of the new London guide books, when the coach, the pawn and the opera made the street a subject of moral and commercial description.
works.characters: the poet and his Muse of Trivia; the town of London and its shows
works.structure: Three books of didactic argument after the manner of the art poem, with the catalogue of places and the closing historical inquiry.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the poem appeared among the pieces of a periodical miscellany conducted by Gay and his friends, which has encouraged occasional mis-division of the volume's parts.

Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct

works.title: Troilus and Cressida
works.description: Shakespeare's bitter anatomy of the Trojan War: the lovers Troilus and Cressida are separated by her exchange to the Greeks, and her infidelity with Diomedes poisons their romance, while the Greek camp degenerates into a satire of its own heroes — Achilles sulking, Ajax a blockhead, and the cynical Thersites commentating on the whole — and Hector's chivalry dies under Achilles' Myrmidons.
works.plot: The war stalls; Cressida is traded for a Trojan prisoner and betrays Troilus with Diomedes before his eyes; the debate over Helen, Ulysses' speech on degree, the gulling of Ajax, and the duel of Hector and Ajax fill the middle acts; the play ends with Hector's murder and Pandarus's epilogue bequeathing the audience his diseases.
works.significance: The great Elizabethan debunking of the heroic ideal — the play in which the Renaissance turned its scepticism on its own founding myth.
works.meter: A harsh, debate-driven verse, with Thersites' prose invective as the play's running commentary.
works.context: Written about 1602, in the wake of the 'war of the theatres' and Essex's fall; printed in 1609 with an epistle hailing it as a play never clapper-clawed by the vulgar.
works.characters: Troilus; Cressida; Pandarus; Hector; Achilles; Ulysses; Agamemnon; Nestor; Ajax; Diomedes; Thersites; Helen; Priam; Cassandra
works.structure: A double plot — the love story and the war council — that refuses tragic or comic closure, ending in anti-climax and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Warfare and battle
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Troilus and Criseyde
works.description: Chaucer's great poem of love and loss, some 8,200 lines in rhyme royal, translating and transforming Boccaccio's Il Filostrato: the Trojan prince Troilus, aided by Pandarus, wins the love of Criseyde, loses her to the Greek camp in an exchange of prisoners, and learns of her betrayal with Diomede before his death in battle — all concluded by the narrator's Boethian repudiation of worldly love. The greatest love poem in Middle English.
works.plot: Troilus, scorning love, is struck by Criseyde's beauty in the temple; his friend and uncle Pandarus engineers their union through letters and stratagems, and the lovers enjoy a secret happiness — until Criseyde is exchanged for the prisoner Antenor and sent to the Greek camp, where Diomede courts her and she yields; Troilus, after ominous dreams and the sight of the brooch he gave her on Diomede's armour, seeks death in battle, and his soul ascends to the eighth sphere, laughing at the woe of the world below.
works.significance: The greatest narrative poem of the English Middle Ages after the Canterbury Tales; its psychological depth and tragic irony made it the model for Henryson's Testament of Cresseid and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas (seven-line, ababbcc) handled with supreme flexibility; the first sustained masterpiece of the English decasyllabic line.
works.context: Composed c. 1382–86 in London, after Chaucer's Italian journeys, adapting Boccaccio's Filostrato with additions from Boethius, Dante, and the Trojan romances; dedicated to 'moral Gower and philosophical Strode'; preserved in sixteen manuscripts and printed by Caxton (c. 1483).
works.characters: Troilus; Criseyde; Pandarus; Diomede; Hector; the Narrator
works.structure: Five books moving from courtship through consummation to betrayal and death, framed by the narrator's ironic service to the servants of love and closed by the palinode commending the love of God.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the work is the first he names in the Retraction.
themes: Courtly love and fin'amor
Fortune and mutability
Wyrd (fate) and providence
movements: Ricardian Poetry

works.title: Trooper Peter Halket of Mashonaland
works.description: Published in 1897 and the most direct English protest against the imperial conquest of southern Africa: the story of a trooper of the Chartered Company alone in the veld, and the stranger who comes to him.
works.plot: Peter Halket, a trooper in Rhodes's Mashonaland, sits by his fire in the veld and is joined by a stranger who shows him the reality of what he has done in the name of empire, and of the hanging of a native chief; the trooper's conscience is awakened and the story ends with his death.
works.significance: Trooper Peter Halket is the most important English literary protest against imperialism in the 1890s and a founding text of the anti-colonial novel: it was suppressed by the circulating libraries and it marks the beginning of the literary critique of empire from within English writing.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary.
works.context: The years 1896-97, the Jameson Raid, the Matabele and Mashona risings, and the English debate on the Chartered Company's conduct. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance.
works.characters: Peter Halket; the stranger; the captive Mashona man; the Captain
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
movements: Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire

works.title: Troy Book
works.description: John Lydgate's vast verse translation (over 30,000 lines) of Guido delle Colonne's Historia destructionis Troiae, commissioned by Henry V in 1412 and completed in 1420: the full Trojan story retold as a mirror of chivalry, kingship, and tragedy. The most ambitious poem of the fifteenth century and the foundation of Lydgate's fame.
works.plot: From Jason and the golden fleece through the rape of Helen and the ten years' war to the fall of Troy and the wanderings of the Greeks, the poem recounts the Trojan matter at length, moralizing throughout on pride, treason, and the fickleness of fortune, with Hector as its pattern of knighthood.
works.significance: The fullest English Troy narrative and the great monument of Lancastrian literary patronage; it made Lydgate the laureate of the fifteenth century and fed the Tudor cult of Troy.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the 'Lydgate line', frequently headless, with aureate diction.
works.context: Commissioned by Henry, Prince of Wales, in 1412, completed in 1420, and dedicated to the king after Agincourt; its Troy matter spoke to Lancastrian imperial ambition; printed by Pynson (1513) and widely read into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Troilus; Ulysses; Agamemnon
works.structure: Five books following Guido's divisions, with prologue and envoy to Henry V; set-piece descriptions, speeches, and moral digressions throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.
themes: Fortune and mutability
National identity and Englishness
Warfare and battle
movements: Fifteenth-Century Chaucerians

works.title: Tulips and Chimneys
works.description: Cummings's first collection: the typographic lyric, the love poem and the satire of the modern state. It is a verse work of 1923 by e e cummings; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom.
works.plot: The collection contains 'in Just-spring', 'the Cambridge ladies who live in furnished souls', 'Thy fingers make early flowers of', 'Buffalo Bill's defunct' and 'next to of course god america i' — love lyrics, satires and the first full display of Cummings's typographic method.
works.significance: Tulips and Chimneys introduced the typographic poem to English and established Cummings as the most popular experimental poet of the century: its lowercase 'i', its broken words and its parenthesis made the printed page part of the poem.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the typographic page as a compositional unit.
works.context: The Cambridge and Greenwich Village of the 1910s, the First World War, and the new art movements of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
works.structure: Seventy-three poems, including sonnets, songs and typographic experiments. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Estlin Cummings. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Turn Again Tiger
works.description: The sequel to A Brighter Sun, published by MacGibbon & Kee in London in 1958 (1959 in Wikipedia's list and Caribbean Beat), takes Tiger back to the sugar-cane country of his childhood for a year. Britannica calls it perhaps Selvon's best novel and singles out its extensive and striking use of dialect.
works.summary: Tiger's year in the cane-growing village of Five Rivers, where his father lives, among the cane workers and the white overseer's household.
works.plot: Tiger leaves Barataria to return for a year to the sugar-cane country of his childhood and help his father, and after several misadventures learns more about life and himself (Caribbean Beat). At Five Rivers he is ashamed of his sexual response to Mrs Robinson, a white woman of the estate, but is saved, in the reading of the Northern Arizona University essay, by his peasant values; after the Robinsons have left, a cane worker tells him, 'You is one of we, Tiger', though near the end another reproaches him for boasting that he could read and write while helping nobody. In the radio play Selvon made from the novel, Tiger learns that he cannot turn his back on his Indian past if he is to lay its ghosts to rest and face the future whole (Peepal Tree).
works.significance: Britannica's 'perhaps his best'. Reissued by Heinemann in 1979 with an introduction and study questions by Sandra Pouchet Paquet, and adapted by Selvon for the BBC as one of the plays later collected in Highway in the Sun (1991).
works.meter: Britannica singles out its extensive and striking use of dialect.
works.context: Published two years after The Lonely Londoners, it returns to the Indo-Trinidadian countryside; South Asian Britain groups it with A Brighter Sun and The Plains of Caroni as Selvon's fiction of South Asian life in Trinidad.
works.characters: Tiger; Urmilla; Tiger's father; Mr and Mrs Robinson, a white couple on the estate; cane workers of Five Rivers
works.structure: Organised around a single year's stay in the cane country, continuing the protagonist of A Brighter Sun.

works.title: Twelfth Night
altTitles: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of disguise and desire: Viola, shipwrecked in Illyria, serves Duke Orsino disguised as the boy Cesario and carries his love-suit to Olivia — who falls in love with Cesario — while the Puritan steward Malvolio is gulled into yellow stockings by the forged letter, and the revels of Sir Toby and the clown roll on to the reunion of the twins.
works.plot: Orsino loves Olivia; Olivia loves Cesario (Viola); Viola loves Orsino; the triangle dissolves when Sebastian, Viola's twin, appears and marries Olivia; Malvolio's humiliation darkens the last scene with his promise of revenge — 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you'.
works.significance: The crowning achievement of Shakespearean comedy — the subtlest study of erotic fluidity before modern drama — and the seed of a thousand later plots.
works.meter: A flexible mix of blank verse, prose, and song, with Feste's 'Come away, come away, death' and the closing rain-song.
works.context: Performed 1601–02 (the Middle Temple performance of 2 February 1602 is recorded); the title marks the Feast of Epiphany and the licence of holiday misrule.
works.characters: Viola (Cesario); Orsino; Olivia; Sebastian; Malvolio; Sir Toby Belch; Sir Andrew Aguecheek; Maria; Feste; Antonio; Fabian
works.structure: Two households — Orsino's and Olivia's — with the sub-plot of Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, Maria, and Feste against Malvolio, all resolved by the twins' reunion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Love, constancy, and betrayal
movements: The Elizabethan Public Theatre

works.title: Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards
works.description: The Lollard manifesto of 1395, presented to parliament and nailed to the doors of Westminster Hall and St Paul's during its session: twelve conclusions denouncing the church's temporal lordship, clerical celibacy, transubstantiation, blessing of material things, clerical exemption, and the wars, crafts, and oaths by which the clergy sustain their power. The most famous document of English medieval dissent.
works.plot: The conclusions move from the church's worldly dominion and the clergy's unworthy estate through the 'false miracle of the sacrament' to the 'unnecessary trades' (goldsmiths, armourers) that serve the church's pride, closing with the demand for a poor, preaching clergy and the renunciation of war and oaths.
works.significance: The founding manifesto of English religious dissent: its arguments against images, pilgrimage, and transubstantiation anticipate the Reformation by a century and a quarter.
works.meter: Plain, forceful English with Latin tags, in the Lollard plain style.
works.context: Presented to parliament and posted at Westminster and St Paul's in 1395, in the political crisis of Richard II's reign; it provoked the orthodox counter-writings of Roger Dymmok and others and fixed the public image of Lollardy.
works.characters: none (collective manifesto)
works.structure: Twelve numbered propositions, each with its brief scriptural and logical support, in the petitionary form of a parliamentary bill.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (collective authorship in the Wycliffite movement).
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Lollardy and religious dissent
movements: Lollardy

works.title: Twice-Told Tales
works.form: Collection of short stories; ghost story
works.description: Published in 1837 and Hawthorne's first collection: eighteen tales and sketches, mostly of the Puritan past, that established the American short story as a serious form. It is a prose fiction work of 1837 by Nathaniel Hawthorne; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection contains 'The Minister's Black Veil', 'The May-Pole of Merry Mount', 'The Grey Champion', 'Wakefield', 'The Great Carbuncle' and 'The Prophetic Pictures', each a study of a single moral emblem in a New England setting.
works.significance: Twice-Told Tales created the American short story and made the Puritan past the central subject of American fiction: 'The Minister's Black Veil' is the founding American tale of secret sin, and the collection established the method that Hawthorne would develop in the novels.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is allegory with psychological depth.
works.context: The 1830s, the New England historical revival, the Unitarian and Transcendentalist ferment, and the American gift-book market. The record dates the work as composed between 1830 and 1837 and first published in 1837 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Mr Hooper ('The Minister's Black Veil'); Edith and Edgar ('The May-Pole of Merry Mount'); Wakefield; the Gray Champion; Dr Heidegger and his friends ('Dr Heidegger's Experiment'); Walter and Elinor Ludlow ('The Prophetic Pictures')
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait

works.title: Two Old Men's Tales
works.description: The Evangelical frame narrative: two old men and the sins of their youth. It is a prose fiction work of 1834 by Anne Marsh; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Two old men, one a clergyman and one a man of the world, each tell the story of his youth: the one of a seduction and a deathbed repentance, the other of duelling and the ruin of a family, in a pair of tales that made Marsh's name.
works.significance: Two Old Men's Tales made Anne Marsh's name and is the central text of the Evangelical novel of the 1830s: its frame of the two old men and its tales of seduction and repentance gave the religious novel its most effective form.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the Evangelical plot of conversion and death.
works.context: England in the 1830s and the Evangelical revival of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1834 and first published in 1834 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under sensation novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the two old men; the seducer; the duellist; the dying penitent
works.structure: Two tales framed by the conversation of two old men. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anne Caldwell Marsh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Two Treatises of Government
altTitles: Two Treatises of Government: In the Latter, the False Principles and Foundation of Sir Robert Filmer and His Followers are Detected and Overthrown
works.description: Locke's classic of liberal political theory, published anonymously in 1689, which refutes Filmer's divine-right absolutism and sets out a theory of government founded on natural rights, consent, property, and the right of resistance.
works.plot: The First Treatise demolishes Filmer's Patriarcha chapter by chapter; the Second Treatise argues that political power derives from the consent of free and equal individuals who form a society to protect their natural rights to life, liberty, and estate.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern liberalism and of the theory of limited constitutional government; it directly influenced the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man.
works.meter: Vigorous argumentative prose with biblical and legal citation.
works.context: Composed during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679-81, revised in Holland, and published anonymously in December 1689 (dated 1690) as a justification of the Revolution that brought William and Mary to the throne; Locke never acknowledged authorship.
works.structure: Two treatises: the first a detailed refutation, the second a positive theory in 19 chapters.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Locke's authorship was not publicly acknowledged in his lifetime but is established from his correspondence and papers.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Order and degree: the body politic
Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life
works.form: Narrative of travel (novel); imperial adventure romance
works.description: Published in 1846 and Melville's first book: an account, partly fictional, of four weeks among the Typee of the Marquesas after deserting the whaler Acushnet. It is a prose fiction work of 1846 by Herman Melville; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Tommo and Toby desert the whaler and flee inland, are taken in by the Typee, and Tommo lives among them, learns their language, observes their customs, and fears their cannibalism until he escapes on a boat.
works.significance: Typee is the first great American book of the Pacific and the founding text of the American literature of the South Seas: it made the Polynesian idyll a permanent American literary myth and established the genre of the Pacific travel narrative that would produce Melville's own later work.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is encyclopaedic digression and catalogue.
works.context: The year 1842, the Marquesas, the Pacific whaling trade, and the American and European debate on the noble savage. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1846 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Tommo, the narrator; Toby; Fayaway; Kory-Kory; Mehevi; Marheyo; Tinor; Marnoo
works.structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: U.S.A.
works.description: The most ambitious American novel of the period: the history of America from 1900 to 1930 through twelve lives, newsreels and biographies. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by John Dos Passos; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The trilogy — The 42nd Parallel (1930), Nineteen Nineteen (1932) and The Big Money (1936) — follows twelve Americans from the 1900s to the Wall Street crash, interrupted by the Newsreel (headlines and songs), the Camera Eye (the author's autobiographical prose poems) and the biographies of public figures from Eugene Debs to Woodrow Wilson.
works.significance: U.S.A. is the most ambitious American novel of the period and the founding work of the collective documentary novel: its four-strand technique invented a form for writing the history of a nation in fiction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the collage of narrative, newspaper headline (Newsreel), autobiographical prose poem (Camera Eye) and biography.
works.context: America from 1900 to 1930: the labour movement, the First World War, the Red Scare, Prohibition, the boom and the crash. works.description: Rowe's last completed tragedy, taking the return of Ulysses to a court and a household invaded by suitors, and making the trial of recognition and of constancy the moral centre of the play.

works.title: Ulysses (Joyce, 1922)
works.description: The greatest novel of the century: a single Dublin day, every style at once, and the modern city rendered completely. It is a prose fiction work of 1922 by James Joyce; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Leopold Bloom, a Jewish advertising canvasser, spends 16 June 1904 in Dublin: he makes breakfast, attends a funeral, works, lunches, is insulted by the Citizen in a pub, and returns home to his wife Molly, who has been unfaithful with Blazes Boylan. works.meter: Prose. works.title: Uncle Silas: A Tale of Bartram-Haugh
works.description: Published in 1864 and the finest of Le Fanu's novels: the story of a young heiress left in the power of her sinister uncle in a remote Derbyshire house. works.plot: Maud Ruthyn, whose father has made her uncle Silas her guardian, goes to Bartram-Haugh, where Silas — a ruined gambler suspected of the murder of a moneylender — and his governess Madame de la Rougierre conspire to marry her to Silas's son Dudley and, when that fails, to murder her; she escapes with the help of her cousin Monica and the servant Mary Quince.
works.significance: Uncle Silas is the greatest English novel of suspense before the 1890s and the finest single achievement of the Irish Gothic: its portrait of a charming, hypocritical villain and of a young woman's isolation is unmatched in Victorian fiction, and it was a model for Henry James and for the modern thriller.

works.description: Serialised in the National Era from June 1851 and published in two volumes in March 1852: the most influential novel ever published in the United States. works.significance: Uncle Tom's Cabin is the central American novel of slavery and the most politically effective novel ever written: it converted hundreds of thousands to abolitionism, made Uncle Tom and Simon Legree permanent figures of the language, and is the founding text of the American literature of human rights.

works.title: Under Western Eyes
works.description: The political novel of Russian autocracy and exile: a student informer in St Petersburg and Geneva, and the impossibility of innocence under a police state. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Joseph Conrad; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Razumov, a St Petersburg student, is approached by a fellow student, Haldin, who has just assassinated a government minister and asks for help; Razumov betrays him to the police and is set to spy on the revolutionary exiles in Geneva. There he falls in love with Haldin's sister Nathalie and is slowly destroyed by guilt, finally confessing to the revolutionaries and being deafened and crippled by their vengeance.
works.significance: Under Western Eyes is the finest English novel about the police state and the moral condition of the informer: it is the direct ancestor of Koestler's Darkness at Noon and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its portrait of Razumov is one of the great studies of betrayal and self-knowledge in the language.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. works.title: Under Which Lord?
works.description: Published in 1879 and Linton's most ambitious social novel: the conflict between a High Church squire and the Radical workman he has made his son-in-law. It is a prose fiction work of 1879 by Eliza Lynn Linton; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: A freethinking landowner who settles with his devout wife Hermione at the Abbey finds his household and his standing in the parish undermined by the new ritualist vicar, Mr Lascelles, who wins Hermione through the confessional and the cult of the High Church; written from Linton's agnostic standpoint, the novel follows the struggle between husband and priest for the wife's obedience, the 'which lord' of the title, and the social ostracism the husband's opinions bring on the family.
works.significance: Under Which Lord? is one of the strongest English novels of class and religion in the 1870s: its portrait of a working-class intellectual and its analysis of the alliance between radicalism and unbelief make it a serious contribution to the condition-of-England tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical periodical essay with a strong persona.
works.context: 1878-79: the ritualist controversy in the Church of England, the agricultural labourers' unions, and the Radical press of the 1870s. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Hermione; her freethinking husband; Mr Lascelles, the ritualist vicar; Mrs Nesbitt; Beatrice
works.structure: A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
