works.title: Underneath the Bough
works.description: Published in 1893 and the most beautiful of the Michael Field collections: a book of lyrics on love, art and the natural world, arranged as a garland of songs. It is a verse work of 1893 by Michael Field; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume, a book of songs, contains 'A Girl' and 'It was deep April, and the morn', in which the two women vow 'against the world, to be / Poets and lovers evermore', among songs of the shared garden and the shared life in which the classical and the English pastoral are fused.
works.significance: Underneath the Bough is the finest single collection of the Michael Field partnership and one of the great English volumes of the 1890s: its lyrics of a shared love made it a key text of the literature of female intimacy.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric.
works.context: 1893: the aesthetic movement, the English classical revival, and the lives of the two poets at Reigate and Richmond. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1893 and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Undertones of War
works.form: War memoir (with a section of poems)
works.description: The most lyrical prose memoir of the First World War: the Western Front seen by a country poet. It is a prose work of 1928 by Edmund Blunden; it belongs to Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Blunden records his service in the Royal Sussex Regiment from 1916 to 1918 — the Somme, Ypres, Passchendaele — in prose that moves like a country walk, noting the weather, the birds, the ruined villages and the dead, without protest and with an unbroken attention to the visible world.
works.significance: Undertones of War is the most beautiful prose memoir of the First World War: its pastoral attention and its refusal of rhetoric make it the perfect counterweight to Good-bye to All That, and its poems are among the finest of the war.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the war memoir: the first-person retrospective, the episodic chapter organised by posting or battle, the transcribed speech of the ranks, and the judgement passed by the later self on the earlier. The author's characteristic manner is the pastoral lyric in traditional measure.
works.context: The First World War and the English countryside from which Blunden came, and the war books boom of 1928–29 in which it appeared. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; nature essay and the rural observation.
works.characters: Blunden; his battalion; the ruined villages; the landscapes of the Somme and Ypres
works.structure: Prose memoir in chapters, followed by a section of thirty-two war poems. A memoir in episodic chapters organised by posting or battle, the later self reflecting on the earlier experience. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.

works.title: Unitarian Christianity
works.form: Homily or sermon with polemical argument; the party sermon of a religious movement
works.description: The sermon that gave American Unitarianism its public statement of faith and its reply to the charge of unbelief. It distinguishes the doctrinal and practical articles of the Unitarians, claims the authority of reason in religion, and refuses to make the creeds of other parties its own. Its plain, deliberate style became the manner of a movement.
works.plot: The sermon first separates the doctrines on which its party is defined from the practices for which it is censured, and grants that some charges are just. It then states the Unitarian belief in one God and in the moral authority of Christ, and argues that a unitarian creed is simpler and therefore more fit for a reasonable creature. It answers the accusation that its party denies the scriptural scheme of atonement and of innate depravity. It closes by commending charity of judgment and by claiming for the conscience the duty of thinking.
works.significance: It is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a self-conscious party and one of the most influential religious statements of the early republic. Its defence of reason in religion shaped the preaching, the criticism and the social reform of the next generation. It supplies the intellectual context for the religious conscience of the literature of New England in this period.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Baltimore in May 1819, at the moment when the Unitarian controversy had divided the standing congregations of eastern Massachusetts and when the party was organizing its churches, its periodicals and its divinity school. The occasion was an ordination service, and the sermon was soon read as the public statement of a body of ministers who had not yet taken an institutional name. Its plain rhetoric was itself a claim about the relation of reason to faith in a republican country.
works.structure: Occasional sermon in the discursive New England manner, divided between statement of doctrine, answer to objections and practical application.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the sermon was printed from the pulpit notes and reissued in the author's collected discourses.
themes: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: Unspoken Sermons
works.form: Three series of sermons; review essay
works.description: Published in three series between 1867 and 1889 and MacDonald's most direct theological writing: sermons on the Fatherhood of God, the will, death and the redemption of all things. It is a prose work of 1867 by George MacDonald; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
works.plot: The sermons argue that God is a father who will not rest until every child is saved, that hell is a purifying rather than an eternal state, and that obedience to the conscience is the beginning of faith.
works.significance: Unspoken Sermons is the most important English statement of universalist theology in the nineteenth century: it influenced Lewis, Chesterton and Barth, and it made MacDonald one of the most original religious thinkers of the Victorian age.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered.
works.context: The 1860s-80s, the Victorian debate on eternal punishment, and the Broad Church movement. works.title: Unto This Last: Four Essays on the First Principles of Political Economy
works.description: Four essays published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 under the title 'Unto This Last' (the parable of the labourers in the vineyard) and collected as a book in 1862: the most influential attack on classical political economy in English.
works.plot: Ruskin argues that the 'economic man' of Ricardo and Mill is a fiction, that wealth is not the accumulation of commodities but the possession of 'things that are useful and life-giving', that the 'illth' produced by commerce is a real cost, and that the just wage and the responsibility of the employer are moral duties. He proposes a guild of labourers and an education for the poor.
works.significance: Unto This Last is the most influential English work of moral economics: Gandhi read it in 1904 and said it 'captured' him and led him to the doctrine of the 'welfare of all'; Attlee and the founders of the British Labour Party took their moral vocabulary from it, and it is the founding text of the twentieth-century critique of economics as a value-free science.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
works.context: The 1860 Cornhill controversy (Thackeray, the editor, stopped the series after the fourth essay), the Lancashire cotton famine of 1861-65, and the socialist and Christian-socialist movements of the 1880s.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.

works.title: Up from Slavery
works.form: Autobiography; review essay, first issued in 1901
works.description: Published in 1901 and one of the great American autobiographies: the account of a life from slavery in Virginia to the founding of Tuskegee Institute. It is a prose work of 1901 by Booker T. works.significance: Up from Slavery is the central African-American autobiography of the post-Reconstruction era and one of the classic American narratives of self-making: it made Washington the most powerful black man in America and defined the politics of uplift for a generation.
works.meter: Prose. works.title: Upon Appleton House
altTitles: Upon Appleton House, to My Lord Fairfax
works.description: Marvell's long country-house poem written while he was tutor to Mary Fairfax at Nun Appleton during the Civil Wars: a topographical and meditative tour of the estate that allegorises the Fairfax family's retirement, the turmoil of the times, and the ideal of a well-ordered natural and social world.
works.plot: The poem moves through the house, gardens, meadows, river, and woods of the estate, reflecting on the modest architecture against the vanity of great buildings, on Fairfax's withdrawal from public life, and on the mowing of the meadows as an emblem of the Civil Wars, before turning to the young Mary Fairfax as the estate's hope.
works.significance: The great English country-house poem, it combines topography, politics, natural history, and allegory and has been central to modern readings of Marvell, of landscape poetry, and of the literature of the Interregnum.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with a witty, glancing, associative movement.
works.context: Written c. 1651 during Fairfax's retirement from Parliament's command, amid the Civil Wars and the Scottish campaign; it is the fullest English estate poem and a subtle reflection on the political moment.
works.characters: Lord Fairfax; the poet; Mary Fairfax; the estate
works.structure: A country-house poem in octosyllabic couplets, structured as a progress through the landscape with meditative digressions.

works.title: Utilitarianism
works.description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and published in 1863: the classic statement of the utilitarian ethics of the greatest happiness principle, with the influential distinction between higher and lower pleasures.
works.plot: The five chapters treat the question of utility, the 'proof' of the principle (that the only evidence of desirability is actual desire), the ultimate sanction of the principle in the social feelings, the proof of the principle, and the connection between justice and utility.
works.significance: Utilitarianism is the definitive formulation of the ethics that the Victorian age inherited from Bentham and Mill's father, and the higher/lower pleasures distinction gave modern moral philosophy one of its central arguments; the justice chapter is still the starting point for the modern debate on punishment and rights.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
works.context: The 1860s, the critique of utilitarianism by Whewell, Hamilton and Carlyle, and the social reform movements that Mill hoped to ground in a philosophical ethics. works.title: Utopia
altTitles: Libellus vere aureus, nec minus salutaris quam festivus, de optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia
works.description: A humanist dialogue in two books describing the imaginary island commonwealth of Utopia, where property is held in common, religious toleration prevails, and the social and economic abuses of early sixteenth-century Europe are criticized by contrast.
works.plot: Book I frames the work as a report of a conversation in Antwerp among More himself, his friend Peter Giles, and the fictional traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who denounces the social evils of Europe — enclosure, penal severity, court flattery — and debates whether a philosopher should serve princes. Book II contains Hythlodaeus's full description of Utopia: its geography, magistrates, working day, communal property, marriage customs, education, religion, and warfare.
works.significance: The founding text of the utopian genre and one of the masterpieces of northern humanism; its punning title (ou-topia 'no place' / eu-topia 'good place') and its fusion of satire, political theory, and fiction made it the most influential secular prose work of the English Renaissance, directly shaping works from Bacon's New Atlantis to modern dystopian fiction.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Composed in 1515–16 during More's embassy to the Netherlands for the wool trade negotiations, at the height of his humanist circle's activities; printed at Louvain by Thierry Martens under the supervision of Erasmus, Giles, and others, and translated into English by Ralph Robinson in 1551.
works.characters: Thomas More; Peter Giles; Raphael Hythlodaeus; Cardinal John Morton (recalled in the dialogue)
works.structure: Two-part dialogue framed by a prefatory letter to Peter Giles and paratexts (maps, Utopian alphabet and quatrain); Book I is a debate on counsel, Book II a systematic description of the island, with the whole enclosed in the fiction of Hythlodaeus's eyewitness report.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth

works.title: Vainglory
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A moralizing poem of 84 lines contrasting the boastful man, puffed up with wine and pride in the hall, with the wise man who walks humbly before God. The poem analyses the psychology of vainglory and warns that pride corrupts the soul and courts the devil.
works.plot: The poet describes the vainglorious man at the feast, eloquent in self-praise but hollow within, deceived by the devil's arrows of pride; against him is set the wise man of measured speech and right counsel, whom God rewards. The poem closes with the warning that the proud man's fall is certain.
works.significance: A penetrating psychological study of pride that fuses the wisdom and homiletic traditions, and a vivid picture of the moral dangers of the Anglo-Saxon feast-hall.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic diction of the Exeter religious poems; the hall setting is evoked in the heroic vocabulary of feasting and treasure.
works.context: Pride was the sin of the heroic hall culture, and the poem turns the imagery of the feast and the boast against its own social setting, in the manner of the homilists' attacks on drunkenness and vainglory.
works.structure: A diptych structure: parallel portraits of the proud man and the wise man, developed through antithesis, followed by a homiletic conclusion on the wages of pride.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Judgment Day and eschatology
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Vancenza; or, The Dangers of Credulity
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Epistolary Fiction
works.description: Mary Robinson's first novel, a two-volume gothic romance written in letters and published by subscription the year after her first volume of poetry. Its heroine, Vancenza, is a girl formed by the extravagant reading of romance and of the marvellous, and the plot subjects her credulity to real persecution, so that the book at once exploits and criticizes the machinery of the novel of terror. Its large subscription list shows how quickly Robinson translated poetical fame into novel-reading capital.
works.plot: Vancenza, an imaginative young woman brought up on tales of the marvellous and persuaded of preternatural intimations, is drawn into a succession of real dangers engineered by interested and tyrannical men; the narrative of her trials, told in letters, converts the expectations formed by romance into evidence of the vulnerability of women left uninstructed, and resolves her sufferings by the exposure of the fraud and violence that produced them.
works.significance: Vancenza is an early and instructive instance of a woman writer using gothic machinery to argue against the credulity that gothic feeds, and it marks the start of Robinson's remarkable sequence of eight novels, of which Walsingham and The Natural Daughter are the most considered; its subscription success is a fact of the first importance for the economic history of women's writing in the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose correspondence; the novel's heightened situations are phrased in the diction of Robinson's descriptive and elegiac verse, and verse is quoted as sententious comment on the action.
works.context: Published in the same years as the most productive phase of the English gothic, and immediately after Robinson had begun her public career as a poet and performer dependent on subscriptions and on her own credit; its title-page promise of a moral against credulity belongs to the 1790s debate about the dangers of novel-reading, in which women's fiction was simultaneously a commercial and an educational risk.
works.characters: Vancenza; the tyrannical and interested men who persecute her; the female companions and protectors to whom she writes
works.structure: An epistolary gothic novel in two volumes, the story delivered in letters from the heroine and her companions, with romance-style suspense and explanation used in the service of an argument about reading and belief.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Vandover and the Brute
works.description: Written in 1895 and published posthumously in 1914: the best American novel of the descent of a civilised man into the brute. It is a prose fiction work of 1914 by Frank Norris; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Naturalist and Determinist Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Vandover, a rich and cultivated young San Francisco art student, drifts into dissipation, seduces Ida Wade, a girl of his set, who kills herself, is cheated out of his property by his friend Charlie Geary, and gradually loses his will, his work and his self-respect; the novel follows his alcoholism, his hallucinations and his final collapse into the animal condition that the title names.
works.significance: Vandover and the Brute is the most rigorous American naturalist novel and the best American treatment of the theme of degeneration: its analysis of a man's loss of will and its Darwinian conclusion make it the darkest and most theoretically consistent of Norris's books, and it has been recognised as one of the most important American novels of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories.
works.context: 1895: the San Francisco of the 1890s, the American reception of degeneration theory and Lombroso, and the debate on heredity and environment. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1902 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Vandover; Charlie Geary; Ida Wade; Turner Ravis; Dolly Haight; Flossie; Vandover's father
works.structure: A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Benjamin Franklin Norris. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vanity Fair: A Novel without a Hero
works.form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers, 1847-48); one volume 1848
works.description: Published in twenty monthly parts from January 1847 to July 1848, with Thackeray's own illustrations, and subtitled 'A Novel without a Hero': the great English novel of the 1810s-20s seen from the vantage of the 1840s, and the book that fixed the word 'snob' and the phrase 'vanity fair' in the language.
works.plot: The novel follows two schoolfellows from Miss Pinkerton's academy: Amelia Sedley, the sentimental and self-deceiving daughter of a rich City merchant, and Becky Sharp, the penniless governess who determines to make her fortune. Amelia marries George Osborne, who is killed at Waterloo, and later the faithful, self-sacrificing William Dobbin; Becky marries Rawdon Crawley, becomes the favourite of the jealous Miss Crawley, is received into the highest society and then ruined by her intrigue with Lord Steyne, and ends as a respectable pensioner of Jos Sedley. The Waterloo section, the Brussels chapters, and the final fair scenes are the novel's set pieces.
works.significance: Vanity Fair is the central English novel of social satire in the nineteenth century and the definitive portrait of the adventuress. Becky Sharp is the first great female anti-heroine in English fiction, and the novel's refusal of a moralising ending made it a permanent point of reference for the ironic novel from Meredith to Thackeray's modernist readers.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
works.context: The Regency and the Napoleonic wars, the Battle of Waterloo, the City bankruptcy of 1815-16, the marriage market of the gentry, and the India service and the colonial fortune; the novel is also a satire on the 1840s readership that consumed it.
works.characters: Becky Sharp; Amelia Sedley; George Osborne; William Dobbin; Rawdon Crawley; Miss Crawley; Lord Steyne; Jos Sedley; Mr Sedley; Sir Pitt Crawley; Miss Briggs
works.structure: Panoramic third-person narrative in twenty monthly parts, with a narrator who comments from the vantage of 1848 on the events of 1813-30, and a 'before and after the curtain' frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vathek
altTitles: The History of the Caliph Vathek
works.description: An Arabian tale of a curious and voluptuous caliph who pursues knowledge and power until he is carried down into the palace of Eblis. It was composed in French by its author and issued in English in 1786, and its magnificence of description and its philosophy of despair made it at once notorious and influential.
works.plot: Vathek, caliph of Samarah, abandons the duties and the pleasures of his throne for the search after intellectual power, and is tempted by a sorcerer's project of an underground palace. He abandons the worship of his fathers for the star-worship of his cousin Carathis, and with her and the genii penetrates the cavernous halls of Eblis. He is sealed there in the company of the Petrified Worshippers of the Stars, doomed to an eternity of unsatisfied desire, while the tale reports his former splendour and his mother's prophecy.
works.significance: It is the most splendid of the century's literary arabesques and a central text of the Gothic-Oriental imagination, its palace of Eblis being one of the great visions of despair in English prose.
works.meter: A prose of superb and accumulated description, translated and revised from the author's French, with the long period of the catalogue and the terrible closure of the sentence as its characteristic effects.
works.context: Composed in French during the author's villa years in the early 1780s and published in English translation in 1786, with the French original printed soon afterwards; it stands in the line of the Arabian tales and of the Gothic romance of the same decade.
works.characters: Vathek the caliph of Samarah; Carathis his cousin and temptress; the old sorcerer Holgher; the rebellious genii and the prince of the palace of Eblis; the mother and the prophetess of the opening
works.structure: A single continuous oriental tale with the frame of prophecy and the descent as its climax, arranged as a sequence of spectacular tableaux; the interpolated stories of the palace of Eblis are set within the last movement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution of the design uncontested, the English first edition being a translation from the author's French manuscript made with his knowledge and revised by him, the translator's share being traditionally assigned to a scholar of the day; the record is here held under the author's name alone.

Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

The sublime, terror, and the ruin
Wisdom and learning

works.title: Venice Preserv'd; or, A Plot Discover'd
works.description: Otway's masterpiece and the greatest tragedy of the Restoration, in which the young Venetian Jaffeir joins a conspiracy against the Senate to relieve his poverty and is destroyed between his oath to his friends and his love for Belvidera.
works.plot: Jaffeir, disinherited for marrying Belvidera, swears to the conspirators led by Pierre; Belvidera persuades him to betray the plot; the conspirators are condemned, Pierre accuses Jaffeir of treachery, and the two friends die together, Belvidera going mad and dying of grief.
works.significance: The most performed tragedy between Shakespeare's revival and the nineteenth century, and a canonical work of political and emotional tragedy; it profoundly influenced the Romantic poets and remained in repertory until the 1880s.
works.meter: Blank verse; the Pierre-Jaffeir friendship scenes are among the most eloquent in Restoration drama.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre on 9 February 1682, dedicated to the Duchess of Portsmouth, and read as a Tory attack on Shaftesbury and the Whigs after the Rye House Plot; Antonio caricatures the Whig Earl of Shaftesbury.
works.characters: Jaffeir; Belvidera; Pierre; the Senator Antonio; Priuli; Renault; Spinosa; Theodore; Nadan
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a single tragic action of extraordinary intensity and a large role for the hero's female victim.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Otway; authorship undisputed.

Marriage and women's conduct

works.title: Venus and Adonis
works.description: Shakespeare's first published work, a 1,194-line Ovidian epyllion dedicated to the Earl of Southampton: the goddess Venus courts the boy Adonis, who scorns her for the hunt; her warnings of the boar come true, and the poem ends with the flower sprung from his blood and Venus's prophecy of love's future sorrows.
works.plot: Venus plucks Adonis from his horse and pleads her love through the day's rhetoric of desire; he resists, breaks away at dawn, and is killed by the boar; Venus finds the body, curses love, and transforms the youth into the purple flower she plucks and cradles.
works.significance: The founding text of the English Ovidian vogue of the 1590s and the first of the two narrative poems on which Shakespeare staked his poetic fame.
works.meter: Six-line stanzas (ababcc) of iambic pentameter — the 'Venus and Adonis stanza' — of unexampled sensuous polish.
works.context: Printed by Richard Field in 1593, during the plague closure of the theatres; it was Shakespeare's best-seller, reprinted some fifteen times by 1636, and advertised by Francis Meres in 1598 as proof of 'sugared' Shakespeare's wit.
works.characters: Venus; Adonis; the boar
works.structure: A single erotic episode expanded by debate, digression, and the two great set pieces of the horse and the hunted hare, framed by the myth's metamorphosis.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published with Shakespeare's name on the title page.
themes: Love, constancy, and betrayal
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Vercelli Homilies
works.description: A collection of twenty-three anonymous Old English homilies and six poems (including The Dream of the Rood, Andreas, Elene) preserved in the Vercelli Book: the largest body of anonymous late tenth-century vernacular preaching, notable for its intense eschatological themes, penitential fervour, and vivid accounts of judgment and the afterlife.
works.plot: The homilies treat repentance, judgment, and the last things — the coming of Antichrist, the signs before doomsday, the fate of the soul, the joys of heaven and the torments of hell — together with Rogationtide sermons, expositions of the Creed and Lord's Prayer, and saints' day pieces, several drawing on the same apocryphal sources as the Blickling collection.
works.significance: A central witness to the anonymous homiletic tradition of the Benedictine Reform era.
works.meter: Old English prose of the late tenth-century homiletic register.
works.context: Copied in the late tenth century, probably in the south-east; the manuscript's presence at Vercelli (northern Italy) is usually attributed to pilgrims on the Rome road.
works.characters: Christ the Judge; the penitent; the blessed and the damned
works.structure: Twenty-three independent homilies of varying length, interspersed with the six poems of the manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife

works.title: Verses
works.description: Privately printed in 1893 for the Society of the Sacred Cross and reprinted in 1896 as New Poems: the devotional verse and prose of her last years, including 'The World', 'A Better Resurrection' and the poems on the Eucharist.
works.plot: The poems are devotional lyrics on the sacraments, the saints, the love of God and the preparation for death, with a number of paraphrases and hymns.
works.significance: Verses is the late devotional testament of the century's finest religious poet, and it shows the continuity of the Tractarian tradition in English poetry at the very end of the period; its recovery in the twentieth century completed the modern edition of Rossetti's work.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
works.context: The 1890s, her final illness and the Anglo-Catholic devotional revival of the period, and the private circulation of devotional literature among religious communities. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1893 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christina Georgina Rossetti. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence
themes: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief

works.title: Verses (1896)
works.description: Published in 1896 and Dowson's first collection: the lyrics of renunciation, wine and hopeless love that made him the most admired poet of his generation. It is a verse work of 1896 by Ernest Dowson; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume contains 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae', 'Nuns of the Perpetual Adoration', 'Villanelle of Sunset', 'To One in Bedlam', 'The Three Witches', 'Spleen', 'Extreme Unction' and 'Vain Resolves', and its subject is the exhaustion of desire in the shadow of death.
works.significance: Verses contains the purest body of English Decadent lyric poetry: its perfection of form and its absolute refusal of consolation made Dowson the poet's poet of the 1890s and an influence on Yeats and Eliot.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is short lyric metres of great smoothness.
works.context: 1896: the English Decadence at its height, the Rhymers' Club, and Dowson's own poverty and illness. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Verses on the Death of Dr. Swift
altTitles: Verses Written at the Approach of His Death
works.form: satiric verse meditation on the self
works.description: Swift's poem on his own approaching death, written a decade before it and spoken from the sick chamber: a satiric inventory of the mourners, the friends, the flatterers and the enemies who will attend the funeral of the Dean of St Patrick's.
works.plot: The dying speaker asks his friends to stop lamenting and permits the poem to rehearse the company of the wake, the visitors who will come to see the great man's end, the enemies who will rejoice, and the character of the Irish who have profited by him; it closes with the epitaph of the stern resting place.
works.significance: It is the century's hardest poem about dying and about the use of a reputation, the counterweight to the century's own cult of the funeral and the mourning poem.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of the plainest Swiftian hardness, with the run-over line and the abrupt maxim, deliberately unsentimental.
works.context: Written in the year of the Dean's serious illness and of the Drapier triumph, when Swift's fame in Ireland was at its height and his English reputation had long been attached to the fallen ministry.
works.characters: the dying Dean; his friends and visitors; his flatterers and his enemies; the people of Ireland
works.structure: A single first-person meditation and catalogue, with the imagined future scenes of the mourning and the character of the nation interposed before the epitaph.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the poem circulated in manuscript among Swift's friends before printing, and the copies differ in the order of the passages.

works.title: Verses to the Memory of an Unfortunate Lady
altTitles: An Epistle to an Unfortunate Lady
works.description: Pope's blank-verse monologue of a banished woman dying abroad, who charges her friends not to mourn her and asks only that her urn be carried home; an early English example of the rhetoric of obscurity, exile and unremembered death.
works.plot: The speaker, an outcast from her own country and betrayed by the man she loved, dictates from her deathbed the terms of her burial, refuses the pomp of mourning, and reflects on the fate of women whose passion has destroyed their reputation.
works.significance: It is the earliest English poem to make the un mourned dead woman a subject of sustained blank-verse reflection, and it prepares the path from the couplet public to the meditative lyric of the mid-century.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the elevated Miltonic manner, with strong enjambment and Latinate inversion.
works.context: Printed among the poems collected in 1717, in the years when the Catholic exile and the concealed nunnery were live political subjects and when the graveyard meditation was beginning to form as a mode.
works.characters: the unfortunate lady; the absent friend addressed; the unworthy lover
works.structure: A single continuous apostrophic address, moving from the charge to the friends, through the memory of the betrayal, to the prophecy of an unknown grave.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Vice Versa; or, A Lesson to Fathers
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1882
works.description: The founding comic body-swap novel: a father and son exchange lives. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by F. Anstey; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Paul Bultitude, a pompous City merchant, and his son Dick exchange bodies through the magic of a stone from the East; the father is sent back to school, the son runs the business into ruin, and both are restored with their characters corrected.
works.significance: Vice Versa invented the comic body-swap novel in English and was a bestseller on both sides of the Atlantic: its school, its City office and its satire of the Victorian father founded a comic formula that has never gone out of use.
works.meter: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The author's characteristic manner is the comic premise carried to its logical extreme.
works.context: London and a Victorian boarding school in the 1880s, and the commercial middle class of the City. The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the new humour; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
works.characters: Paul Bultitude; Dick Bultitude; Dr Grimstone; Marmaduke Paradine; Dulcie
works.structure: A novel in twelve chapters, from the City to the school and back. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Anstey Guthrie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vienna
works.description: Spender's poem of the Austrian crisis: the failure of the left and the coming of fascism. It is a verse work of 1934 by Stephen Spender; it belongs to The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem and it is catalogued here under Thirties Political Lyric and the Auden Generation; Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book.
works.plot: The sequence records the Austrian civil war of February 1934 and the defeat of the Social Democrats in Vienna, in verse and prose, as the first defeat of the European left before fascism.
works.significance: Vienna is the most politically direct poem of the Auden generation: its account of the defeat of the Viennese left made it the period's clearest statement about the failure of the European left before fascism.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric line held in traditional stanza.
works.context: The Austrian civil war of February 1934, the rise of Dollfuss and the fascist movements of central Europe. The record dates the work as composed in 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under thirties political lyric and the auden generation; documentary prose and the reportage book.
works.characters: Engelbert Dollfuss; Major Emil Fey; Koloman Wallisch, the executed socialist leader
works.structure: A sequence of poems and prose passages. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stephen Harold Spender. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Vile Bodies
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1930
works.description: The definitive novel of the Bright Young Things: a comic whirl of parties, gossip columns and the coming war. It is a prose fiction work of 1930 by Evelyn Waugh; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Adam Fenwick-Symes loses his manuscript at customs, wins and loses a fortune on a horse, and drifts through the parties of the Bright Young Things — Nina Blount, Agatha Runcible, Miles Malpractice — in a novel that ends with a battlefield of the next war and the famous last line 'Oh, Nina, what a lot of parties'.
works.significance: Vile Bodies is the definitive novel of the Bright Young Things: its speed, its jokes and its sudden ending made it the most brilliant English comic novel of the twenties.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face.
works.context: London in the late 1920s, the gossip columns, the Bright Young Things, the crash of 1929, and the new mass culture of the cinema and the tabloid. The record dates the work as composed in 1929 and first published in 1930 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; jazz-age novel and the expatriate romance.
works.characters: Adam Fenwick-Symes; Nina Blount; Agatha Runcible; Miles Malpractice; Lottie Crump; Colonel Blount
works.structure: A rapid episodic narrative with a race, a party and a battlefield ending. A novel in chapters of the pleasure and the retrospect, the party scene and the elegiac judgement held in the same short paragraphs.

works.title: Villette
works.form: Novel in three volumes, first person
works.description: Published in three volumes in January 1853, and the most inward and formally controlled of Charlotte Brontë's novels: the story of Lucy Snowe in a French-speaking girls' school in the invented city of Villette, drawn from the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels.
works.plot: Lucy Snowe, without family or money, goes to Villette as a teacher and then as a schoolmistress, loves the autocratic Paul Emanuel, and is separated from him by his voyage to the West Indies; the novel also contains the ghostly visit of the nun and the subplot of the heiress Polly Home and Dr John Bretton. The ending leaves Paul's fate uncertain, with a report of a storm and a shipwreck.
works.significance: Villette is now generally read as Brontë's finest novel and one of the great novels of interiority in English; its refusal of a closed happy ending and its study of repression and vocation made it central to twentieth-century feminist criticism, and its analysis of a woman's professional identity anticipates the New Woman fiction of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
works.context: The Brussels pensionnat, the English governess abroad, the Catholic-Protestant antagonism of continental and English manners, and the debate over women's employment that followed the 1851 census. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Lucy Snowe (the narrator); M. Paul Emanuel; Dr John Graham Bretton; Paulina Mary Home de Bassompierre (Polly); Ginevra Fanshawe; Madame Beck; Mrs Bretton; Count de Hamal; Miss Marchmont
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
genres: Novel of Development and the Growth Story

works.title: Vindiciae Gallicae
altTitles: Vindiciae Gallicae: A Defence of the French Revolution and its English Admirers
A Defence of the French Revolution
works.form: political pamphlet and philosophical vindication; argumentative defence in sections
works.description: The most learned and most generous of the replies to the counter-Revolutionary constitutional argument, written in a few months of furious work by a young Scottish lawyer and published in the spring of 1791. It accepts the issue of abstract right which the counter-Revolutionary book had refused, and answers the historical pleading with a philosophy of rights, of progress, and of the perfectibility of institutions.
works.plot: The defence begins by denying that the age of a constitution is an argument for its excellence, and by asserting the right of every generation to choose its own government; prescription, it urges, is the sophistry of interest, and the true lesson of history is that institutions resting on force and on superstition must be expected to fall. It then examines the state of France before the Revolution, and argues that the burthens of the people, the privileges of the few, and the anarchy of the law made some great change not an evil but a duty; the horrors of the contest are met with the parallel horrors of every successful reformation, and the argument from the licence of a people newly freed is answered by the mischief of a people never trusted. The constitution of the following year is then defended as a settled and temperate scheme of representative government, and the English admirers of the Revolution are vindicated from the charge of disaffection. The closing pages turn upon the influence of the new principles upon the future improvement of the world, and the whole is animated by the belief that the Revolution is the beginning of a moral and intellectual emancipation of the species.
works.significance: It is the ablest philosophical defence of the Revolution in English, and the text which the counter-Revolutionary argument most feared; it supplied the radical tradition with its answer to prescription, and its argument on the right of innovation, on representation, and on the education of a people to freedom passed into the reform literature of the next century. Its author's own later reservations, and the pamphlet's fate as the credential of a career that ended on the bench and in the service of the state, make it one of the most quoted cases of the change of opinion in a revolutionary generation.
works.meter: Diffusive, earnest, learned prose of the philosophical jurist: the long period, the historical illustration, the sympathetic abstraction, and a moral fervour which its author afterwards qualified.
works.context: Composed rapidly in London in the winter of 1790-91 at the instance of a publisher who wanted an immediate answer to the constitutional writings of the season, and published in the year in which the first French constitution was completed and the party rupture opened in England. Its author, a physician's son of Glasgow who had taken a Scottish medical degree and turned to law and to letters, wrote as a friend of the American and French principles alike, and the book made his name at once.
works.structure: A single continuous argument in numbered sections, opening with the statement of the two rival theories of the state, proceeding through the history and condition of the old government, the criticism of the objections, and the defence of the new constitution, and closing on the prospects of the species.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose later qualifications of its doctrines are recorded in his own correspondence and in the biographical memoir of his son.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
movements: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle

works.title: Violets and Other Tales
works.description: Published in 1895 and the first book by an African-American woman from the deep South: stories, sketches and poems of Creole New Orleans. It is a prose fiction work of 1895 by Alice Dunbar-Nelson; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The volume mixes short stories of New Orleans life with lyrics on love, death and the poet's vocation, and closes with an essay on the position of women, presenting a Creole world in which race, class and desire are entangled.
works.significance: Violets and Other Tales is the first book by an African-American woman of the deep South and a founding text of African-American women's literature: its portraits of Creole life and its lyrics on love and ambition made Dunbar-Nelson one of the most important black writers of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is dialect and French-inflected Creole speech.
works.context: 1895: the Creole society of New Orleans, the emergence of the black woman writer, and the literary culture of the black press of the 1890s. The record dates the work as composed in 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Alice Ruth Moore. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vision and Design
works.description: The book that brought modern art into English criticism: the formalist essay and the case for Post-Impressionism. It is a prose work of 1920 by Roger Fry; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Critical Essay and the Modern Review.
works.plot: The essays — 'An Essay in Aesthetics', 'Art and Socialism', 'The Art of the Bushmen', 'Negro Sculpture', 'Giotto', 'The French Post-Impressionists' — argue for the primacy of form over subject and defend the art that Fry had exhibited in 1910 and 1912.
works.significance: Vision and Design made modern art intelligible to English readers: its formalism gave English criticism a method, its defence of Post-Impressionism changed the taste of a generation, and it is the founding book of modern English art criticism.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the formalist description of a picture — line, mass, colour and the organisation of the surface.
works.context: The Post-Impressionist exhibitions of 1910 and 1912, the Bloomsbury art world, and the English resistance to modern art. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1919 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review.
works.structure: Twenty-five essays written over twenty years, arranged thematically. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Roger Eliot Fry. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist

works.title: Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland
works.description: The great collection of Irish folk belief: the fairies, the dead and the second sight, recorded from the mouths of the people. It is a prose work of 1920 by Lady Gregory; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Lady Gregory records, in the words of the country people of Galway and Clare, their beliefs about the fairies, the banshee, the dead, the evil eye and the second sight, with notes on the survival of paganism in the Irish countryside.
works.significance: Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland is the great collection of Irish folk belief and the finest work of folklore to come out of the Irish revival: its fidelity to the spoken word made it a primary source for Yeats, for Synge and for every later student of Irish tradition.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close.
works.context: The west of Ireland at the turn of the century, the oral tradition, and the folklore movement of the revival. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1920 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; nature essay and the rural observation.
works.characters: The people of Galway and Clare; Lady Gregory as collector
works.structure: Two volumes of recorded testimony with notes and commentary. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Isabella Augusta Gregory. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Visions of the Daughters of Albion
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a tract of liberty written in the manner of the prophetic book and drawing its situation from the contemporary controversy over slavery and over the rights of desire.
works.description: An illuminated verse tract etched and printed by the author in 1793, written as a vision addressed to the daughters of a benighted island, and built on a single situation of violated love and disputed possession. A planter of the western colonies takes a bound girl by force while her lover, a pale youth of speculative sorrow, does nothing to save her, and the poem argues from that situation that desire denied, jealousy brooding in the mind, and the law of another's property in a human body are all one tyranny.
works.plot: The poem is framed as an address to the daughters of Albion, who sit in a rockbound shore and are bidden to awake and see what the senses of the Slaves of America have endured. Oothoon, the bound girl, goes to the grove with her flowers and is taken by Bromion, the thunder-footed planter of the West Indies, who brands her as his possession and boasts of the rape to Theotormon, the jealous and contemplative youth who loved her. Oothoon pleads that her soul is free and that no clod of a body can bind the daughter of the morning, and she calls on the slaves of the east and the west to rise; Theotormon, unable to answer her, sits in the cave and questions the winds, the beasts and the star of the morning, tortured by a jealousy he cannot name and by a religion that forbids him to pity. The poem closes with the awakening of the daughters and the declaration that where there is no desire there is no virtue, and that the state of the slave and the state of the inhibited lover are one state.
works.significance: The most sustained Romantic poem on the identity of sexual and civil bondage, and one of the earliest English works to make the enslaved woman's own speech the vehicle of an argument for liberty; it is central to modern readings of the poet's myth of desire and jealousy, and its situation has been a standing example in the criticism of abolitionist and feminist reading of the 1790s.
works.meter: Blank verse of an irregular and vehement kind, with long overrunning periods, apostrophes and reiterated questions, and a few short lyrical interpolations; the lines vary in beat and are printed as part of the illuminated design.
works.context: Etched and published in London in 1793, the year of the controversy over the slave trade and of the poet's most active sympathy with the revolutions of France and America; its plea for the slave and its attack on a law that makes a body property belong to the radical religious writing of that decade, and its title names the island whose daughters are asleep.
works.characters: Oothoon, the bound girl of the plantations; Bromion, the thunder-footed planter of the West Indies; Theotormon, her lover, a youth of jealous speculation; the daughters of Albion, addressed as a chorus; the slaves of the east and the west invoked in her plea
works.structure: A visionary tract in long blank-verse lines, framed as an address to a chorus of daughters and organised as a single situation reported in three voices, with the pleading of the injured girl, the boasts of the planter and the questioning solitude of the lover alternating; the poem's argument is carried by the speeches rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Exile and homelessness
Idealized love and the lost beloved
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy

works.title: Vita Sancti Cuthberti (metrical and prose lives)
works.form: hagiography (saint's life) in Latin verse and prose
works.description: Bede's two lives of St Cuthbert: a metrical life (c. 705) and a prose life (c. 721), the latter revised and expanded from the earlier anonymous Life by a monk of Lindisfarne. They are the fullest early accounts of the great Northumbrian hermit-bishop of Lindisfarne and a classic of insular hagiography.
works.plot: The lives trace Cuthbert's youth, his vision of the soul of Aidan, his years as prior of Melrose and Lindisfarne, his eremitic retreat on Farne, and his reluctant episcopate, with the famous miracle stories (the otters who warmed his feet, the sea that served him food) and the account of his incorrupt body at the translation of 698.
works.significance: The canonical life of the Northumbrian church's greatest saint; a model for later insular hagiography.
works.meter: The metrical life is in Latin hexameters; the prose life in Bede's clear narrative Latin.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow for the community of Lindisfarne; the prose life was written after the translation of Cuthbert's relics in 698.
works.characters: Cuthbert; Aidan; Boisil; Æthelthryth; King Ecgfrith; the monks of Lindisfarne
works.structure: Biographical narrative ordered by the saint's successive vocations, with miracle collections attached to each phase; the prose life adds chapters on posthumous miracles at the shrine.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Solitude and the hall community
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Vita Sancti Gregorii
altTitles: The Earliest Life of St Gregory the Great
The Whitby Life of Gregory the Great
works.description: The earliest life of Pope Gregory the Great, written at Whitby in the early eighth century by an anonymous monk of the double house, and a principal source for the story of Gregory's encounter with the Anglian slave-boys in the Roman market — 'not Angles but angels' — that led to the mission of Augustine to England in 597.
works.plot: The Life recounts Gregory's Roman background, his election to the papacy against his will, the providential encounter with the English boys that inspired the English mission, the sending of Augustine and his companions, and the miracles that confirmed the mission's success; it closes with Gregory's death and the vindication of his authority.
works.significance: The earliest biography of the pope who sent the mission that converted the English, the source of the 'non Angli sed angeli' story that became part of English national legend, and a witness to the piety of the Whitby community of the early eighth century.
works.context: Written at Whitby under Abbess Ælfflæd, the text defends the Roman and Gregorian foundations of the English church at a time when the authority of Rome was disputed in Northumbria; it preserves traditions of the conversion not found in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica.
works.characters: Gregory the Great, the Anglian slave-boys, Augustine of Canterbury, King Edwin of Northumbria
works.structure: A loosely organized collection of episodes rather than a strictly chronological biography, mingling Roman history, English conversion narrative, and edifying miracles, written in the unpolished Latin of a remote Northumbrian house.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is conventionally called the Anonymous of Whitby. No author record is created for this work, per the database's policy that anonymous works carry no author links.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Wisdom and learning
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Vita Sancti Guthlaci
works.description: Felix of Crowland's prose life of Guthlac, the Mercian warrior turned hermit of the fens, composed at the request of King Ælfwald of East Anglia. The first Latin saint's life written in England for an English saint, and the source of the Old English poems Guthlac A and B and of the later vernacular lives.
works.plot: The life narrates Guthlac's youth in the Mercian warband, his conversion after nine years of warfare, his two years at Repton, and his retreat to the island of Crowland in the fens, where he fought with demons, was consoled by the apostle Bartholomew, and died in 714; the second book records posthumous miracles, including the healing of King Æthelbald.
works.significance: The foundational text of the Guthlac tradition and a major witness to eighth-century monastic culture.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Written c. 730-740, within a generation of Guthlac's death (714), for the East Anglian court; the cult centred on Crowland Abbey, refounded in the tenth century.
works.characters: Guthlac; Bartholomew; Æthelbald; Ælfwald; Beccel; Pega; the fen demons
works.structure: Two books — the saint's life and his posthumous miracles — in the pattern of the Antonine and Martinian lives.
works.attributionNotes: Felix's authorship is stated in the prologue.
themes: Mission, conversion, and the Church
Solitude and the hall community
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Vita Sancti Wilfridi
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi (ninth century, with later additions)
works.description: The earliest surviving biography written in England of a contemporary English churchman: a partisan life of Bishop Wilfrid of York (c. 634-709) by Stephen of Ripon, a priest of Wilfrid's household, written at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. It defends Wilfrid's career — his appeals to Rome, his quarrels with kings and bishops, and his missionary work — against his detractors.
works.plot: The Life follows Wilfrid from his education at Lindisfarne and his journeys to Rome and Gaul, through his consecration and his building of the stone churches of Ripon and Hexham, to his repeated exiles, his missionary work among the South Saxons and Frisians, his vindication at Rome, and his death at Oundle in 709, with posthumous miracles at Ripon.
works.significance: A principal source for the seventh-century Northumbrian church and for the career of its most controversial bishop; with the anonymous life of Cuthbert it inaugurates the English tradition of the contemporary saint's life that culminates in Bede's hagiography.
works.context: Written within a decade of Wilfrid's death amid continuing controversy over his legacy; the Life is a contribution to that controversy, answering the charges of Wilfrid's enemies and presenting him as a persecuted saint in the manner of the confessors of the early church.
works.characters: Wilfrid of York, King Ecgfrith, King Aldfrith, Archbishop Theodore, Acca of Hexham
works.structure: A chronological vita in the hagiographic manner, interweaving documented events (the synods, the appeals to Rome) with miracle stories; the narrative is punctuated by set-piece scenes — the shipwreck of Wilfrid's party on the Sussex coast, his baptisms, and his deathbed settlement of his affairs.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Stephen of Ripon (Eddius Stephanus), who names himself; his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' is traditional but unproven.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Mission, conversion, and the Church
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age

works.title: Voices of Freedom
works.description: The collected abolitionist verse of the American poet who was mobbed for the cause. It is a verse work of 1846 by John Greenleaf Whittier; it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The collection gathers Whittier's anti-slavery poems of the previous decade: 'The Hunters of Men', 'The Farewell', 'Song of the Negro Boatmen', 'Massachusetts to Virginia' and the ballads of the fugitive and the auction block.
works.significance: Voices of Freedom was the central collection of American abolitionist poetry and the book that made Whittier the poet of the cause: its ballads and songs were sung at abolitionist meetings and it gave the movement its hymns.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, ballad-like quatrain and the domestic idyll.
works.context: The abolitionist movement of the 1830s and 1840s, the mob violence against abolitionists and the Underground Railroad. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1846 and first published in 1846 and it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the slave; the fugitive; the abolitionist; the master
works.structure: A collection of abolitionist poems and ballads. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. G. Whittier. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
genres: Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause
themes: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
Race, voice, and the dialect of freedom
Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction

works.title: Voices of Freedom (Massey, 1850)
works.description: The finest Chartist poetry: the poor, the worker and the coming republic. It is a verse work of 1850 by Gerald Massey; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause.
works.plot: The collection gathers Massey's Chartist poems — 'The People's Advent', 'The Red Banner', 'The Voice of the Master', 'The Slave' — in which the working class, the fallen woman and the revolutionary future are rendered in simple, singing verse.
works.significance: Voices of Freedom gave the Chartist movement its finest verse and made Massey the most popular working-class poet of the 1850s: it is the central document of Chartist poetry and the finest English political poetry of the poor before Morris.
works.meter: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Chartist lyric of liberty and the poor.
works.context: England in 1848-50, the Chartist movement and the European revolutions. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1850 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under political verse and the poem of public cause.
works.characters: the worker; the slave; the fallen woman; the poet as prophet
works.structure: A collection of Chartist lyrics and songs. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Gerald Massey (poet). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Volpone
works.description: Jonson's greatest comedy, a beast fable of greed: the magnifico Volpone, the Fox, feigns death to draw gifts from the legacy hunters Voltore (the vulture), Corbaccio (the raven), and Corvino (the crow); with his parasite Mosca, the Fly, he escalates the game to Corvino's offer of his own wife Celia — until the dupes, double-crossed, drag the plot into the Venetian courts and the final, ferocious sentences.
works.plot: The suitors heap gold on the 'dying' Volpone; Corbaccio disinherits his son, Corvino prostitutes Celia; Volpone's attempted rape of Celia is exposed in the trial scenes, where Mosca's perjury and Volpone's disguises nearly win; the trickster's final mock-death turns Mosca to his own advantage, and the double betrayal brings everything before the Avocatori, who strip, sentence, and exile them all.
works.significance: The most perfectly constructed comedy in English — a moral anatomy of greed that has never lost its bite.
works.meter: Blank verse of a muscular, satirical energy, with the mountebank's prose sales pitch and the songs of the deformed fools.
works.context: Performed at the Globe and both universities in 1606; its Venice is a mirror of Jacobean London's gold-rush, and its Epistle and prologue announce Jonson's classical ambitions.
works.characters: Volpone; Mosca; Voltore; Corbaccio; Corvino; Celia; Bonario; Sir Politic Would-Be; Lady Would-Be; Peregrine; Nano; Castrone; Androgyno; the Avocatori
works.structure: A five-act intrigue in the classical manner, with the sub-plot of Sir Politic Would-Be's English follies (a Lady Would-be's parrot) as satirical counterpoint, and the mountebank scene as its comic summit.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Appearance, dissembling, and self-fashioning
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Jacobean City Comedy

works.title: Volume the Last
altTitles: The History of the Adventures of David Simple. Volume the Last
works.form: novel; sentimental fiction in twelve books
works.description: The continuation and reversal of the first history of David Simple, in which the exemplary reward given to good nature in the earlier volume is withdrawn and the world's punishment of it is shown in earnest. It is a darker and more experimental book, much praised by later readers for its honesty about disappointment.
works.plot: David, now settled in a family and a fortune of his own, is successively stripped of what he loved: his wife dies, his children are taken or lost, and his property is engrossed by a fraudulent relation. The friends who were promised by the first volume fail him, and the closing books report his decline into poverty and death. The tale ends with an address on the condition of the good in a world governed by interest.
works.significance: It is an early and striking instance of the anti-exemplary novel, its reversal of the rewards of virtue being read as a critique of the sentimental plot and of the conduct tradition.
works.meter: A plainer and more compressed prose than the first volume, with the pathos carried by short report and by the narrator's restrained comment.
works.context: Published in 1747 after some years of retirement from print, in the season of the author's own editorial and translation work and of the mid-century debate about the instruction of novels.
works.characters: David Simple; his wife and children; the fraudulent relation and the law officers; the failing friends of the first volume
works.structure: A continuous third-person narrative in twelve books, structured as a progressive bereavement rather than an intrigue; the ending refuses closure and turns to direct moral address.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, established by the family circle's records and by the continuity of person and design with the earlier volume.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Marriage and women's conduct
Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
