works.title: Votes for Women
works.description: The first full-length suffrage play on the London stage: a politician's wife joins the campaign. It is a dramatic work of 1907 by Elizabeth Robins; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Vida Levering, the wife of a Conservative MP, is drawn into the suffrage campaign by her sister-in-law; the play follows the meeting, the heckling, the imprisonment and the conversion, ending with the women's demonstration outside the House.
works.significance: Votes for Women was the first full-length suffrage play on the London stage and the central dramatic text of the campaign: its meeting scene and its portrait of the converted woman made it the most effective piece of suffrage theatre ever written.
works.meter: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the suffragist meeting as dramatic scene.
works.context: London in 1907 at the height of the militant suffrage campaign, and the West End theatre of the new drama. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
works.characters: Vida Levering; the MP; the sister-in-law; the campaigners; the police
works.structure: Three acts, from the drawing room to the demonstration. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Elizabeth Robins (actress). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vox Clamantis
works.description: John Gower's Latin poem of some 10,000 elegiac couplets: an estates satire and dream vision in which the poet, during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, sees the commons transformed into beasts and the social order inverted, then hears the estates — clergy, knights, peasants, merchants, lawyers — arraigned for their corruption. The great Latin poem of Ricardian England.
works.plot: The first book (the Visio) allegorizes the 1381 rising as a bestial horde under Wat Tyler and Jack Straw ravaging the land; the remaining books survey each estate in turn, condemning clerical greed, knightly violence, peasant envy, and mercantile fraud, and close with a vision of the king (Richard II) as the realm's hope.
works.significance: The most substantial Latin poem of fourteenth-century England and the classic estates satire of the Ricardian period; its account of the revolt is the age's defining literary image of 1381.
works.meter: Ovidian elegiac couplets, sustained with remarkable facility.
works.context: Composed 1377–81, with the Visio added after the revolt of June 1381 (which Gower probably witnessed in London); revised in the 1390s; preserved in ten manuscripts, several with Gower's own annotations.
works.characters: the Poet; the rebels (as beasts); the estates of society; Richard II
works.structure: Seven books: a dream-vision prologue on the revolt, then a systematic estates satire with the poet's own voice as its moral centre.
works.attributionNotes: Gower's authorship secure.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: Ricardian Poetry

works.title: Voyage in the Dark
works.description: Rhys's London novel: a young Caribbean girl alone in the city and the money economy of sex. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Jean Rhys; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Anna Morgan, a nineteen-year-old girl from the West Indies, is left penniless in London and drifts into the world of older men and their money, in a first-person narrative that moves between the cold English streets and the remembered warmth of the Caribbean.
works.significance: Voyage in the Dark is one of Rhys's finest novels and the great English novel of the woman without money: its first-person narrative and its colonial memory made the modern novel of exploitation and founded the literature of the Caribbean woman in England.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrative of the woman without money.
works.context: London in 1913–14, and the Caribbean colony of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
works.characters: Anna Morgan; Walter Jeffries; Hester; Vincent; Maudie
works.structure: A first-person narrative in four parts, between London and the remembered Caribbean. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ella Gwendolen Rees Williams. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Vulgaria
works.description: Robert Whittington's collection of everyday sentences in English with their Latin renderings, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1520; the most celebrated of the Tudor vulgaria used to teach Latin composition by translation.
works.plot: The book presents model English sentences — the talk of the schoolroom, the market, and the household — each with its idiomatic Latin equivalent, arranged to drill the schoolboy in the idiom of daily speech turned into classical Latin.
works.significance: The finest surviving example of the Tudor vulgarium and a vivid record of early sixteenth-century English speech and schoolroom practice; it documents the humanist method of teaching Latin through the vernacular.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1520 at the height of the grammar-school humanist reform; Whittington, a prolific grammarian and laureate of Oxford, was among the schoolmasters who replaced the medieval grammars with humanist vulgaria, and his book was reprinted through the 1520s.
works.structure: A collection of sentence-pairs grouped by topic, prefaced by Whittington's remarks on teaching method.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
movements: English Renaissance Humanism
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: Waiting for Aunty to Cough
works.description: Waiting for Aunty to Cough is a comic story by Samuel Selvon about Brackley, a young West Indian in London, and his English girlfriend Beatrice. It appeared in the Evening Standard on 1 April 1957 and was collected the same year in the London part of Ways of Sunlight.
works.summary: Brackley's nightly journeys to see Beatrice home to the far suburbs; a night when she has forgotten her key and they wait outside for her aunt to cough; his violent solution at dawn; and the joke the boys make of it.
works.plot: Brackley, who has taken up with a girl living far from central London, must see Beatrice home every night and make his way back late, missing buses and trains. One night she has forgotten her door key, and rather than rouse the household they wait in the cold outside the house in the early hours, hoping to hear Aunty cough. Beatrice dozes on his arm while Brackley, folded into the small doorway, cramped and frozen, waits through the night. Between five and half past he thinks he hears Aunty cough and, to Beatrice's amazement and horror, pelts the house with a stone. Word gets round, and the boys never let him forget it, hailing him with 'Brackley! You still waiting for Aunty to cough?'
works.significance: A frequently anthologised example of Selvon's comic London writing and of his use of Caribbean speech in narration.
works.meter: Selvon's creolised narrative voice, with Trinidadian syntax and idiom carrying the comedy.
works.context: One of the London stories of Ways of Sunlight (1957), written in the years of The Lonely Londoners and of the Windrush migration; Selvon's papers at the University of the West Indies hold its manuscript and the Evening Standard clipping.
works.structure: An anecdote framed as a story told among 'the boys', ending on their catch-phrase.
themes: Love, intimacy and loss
Migration, exile and diaspora
The city, the suburb and modern space
movements: Black British Writing and the Windrush Generation

works.title: Waiting for Godot
works.form: Play (tragicomedy in two acts; the author's English version of En attendant Godot)
works.description: Samuel Beckett's tragicomedy in two acts, in which two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait by a leafless tree on a country road for a Mr Godot, who never comes. Beckett wrote it in French between October 1948 and January 1949; En attendant Godot was published in 1952 and first performed in Paris in January 1953, and his own English version, recorded here because it is the text Norton prints, was published in 1954 and first staged in London in 1955. It is his best-known work and one of the most influential plays of the century.
works.summary: Two acts on two successive evenings, each with the same shape: Vladimir and Estragon pass the time waiting for Godot; the master Pozzo and his servant Lucky pass by; a boy brings word that Godot will not come today but surely tomorrow; the two decide to go and do not move. Between the acts Pozzo has gone blind and Lucky dumb, and the tree has put out a few leaves.
works.plot:
Act I. On a country road by a bare tree, in the evening, Estragon struggles to pull off his boot and tells Vladimir that he spent the night in a ditch and was beaten. They talk at length, about the two thieves crucified with Christ and why only one gospel says one was saved, about hanging themselves from the tree, and about the man they are waiting for, Godot, though they are not sure they have ever met him, whether this is the right place or the right day, or what they asked him for. Pozzo arrives, driving Lucky before him on a rope and laden with his bags. Pozzo eats chicken while Estragon begs for the bones, lectures on the twilight, and says he is taking Lucky to the fair to sell him. At Pozzo's order Lucky dances and then, told to think, pours out a torrent of broken academic and theological speech about a personal God and a shrinking, petrifying humanity, which ends only when the others seize his hat. Pozzo and Lucky leave. A boy comes with a message from Mr Godot: he will not come this evening but surely tomorrow. The boy minds the goats; his brother, who minds the sheep, is beaten. Night falls and the moon rises. 'Well, shall we go?' 'Yes, let's go.' They do not move.

Act II. The next day, the same time and place; the tree has a few leaves. Vladimir sings a circular song about a dog; Estragon has been beaten again and remembers little of yesterday. To pass the time they abuse each other, make up, exercise, play at being Pozzo and Lucky and juggle hats, including the one Lucky left behind. Pozzo and Lucky return: Pozzo is now blind and Lucky dumb, and they fall in a heap from which Vladimir and Estragon, after much delay, raise them. Pozzo remembers nothing of the day before and, asked when his blindness came, rages that one day is like any other: they give birth astride of a grave, the light gleams an instant, then it is night once more. When they have gone Vladimir, watching Estragon sleep, wonders whether he too is asleep and what he will remember of today. The boy returns, or another like him, says he did not come yesterday and repeats the message: Mr Godot will not come this evening but tomorrow. Godot, the boy says, does nothing, and his beard is white. The two try to hang themselves with the cord that holds up Estragon's trousers, which breaks, and the trousers fall. They will hang themselves tomorrow, unless Godot comes; then they will be saved. 'Well? Shall we go?' 'Yes, let's go.' They do not move.
works.significance: Voted the most significant English-language play of the twentieth century in a 1998 poll by the Royal National Theatre, the play transformed modern drama in Britain, Ireland, Europe and America, freeing the stage from plot and psychological realism and influencing Pinter, Stoppard and generations of dramatists. It made Beckett famous and was central to the case for his Nobel Prize in Literature (1969). It is constantly revived, adapted and studied, and Norton prints it entire.
works.meter: Spare, rhythmic dialogue built from short exchanges, repetitions and echoes; the comedy of the music hall, the circus and silent film (hats, boots, falling trousers) set against lyrical and philosophical passages; an English version that keeps the French text's plainness while adding its own idiom.
works.context: Beckett, an Irish writer living in Paris, turned to writing in French after the Second World War, in which he had served in the Resistance; he wrote the play between his novels Malone meurt and L'Innommable. Roger Blin directed the premiere at the Théâtre de Babylone in January 1953. Martin Esslin later placed it at the head of what he called the Theatre of the Absurd.
works.characters: Vladimir (Didi); Estragon (Gogo); Pozzo; Lucky; a Boy
works.structure: Two acts of nearly identical design, the second a variation of the first with the decline of Pozzo and Lucky; a single setting (a country road, a tree, evening); cross-talk, repetition, routines, pauses and silences; Lucky's monologue as the one unbroken torrent of speech; each act ends with an exchange contradicted by the stage direction 'They do not move'.
themes: Alienation, absurdity and existential freedom
Death, illness and mourning
Faith, doubt and the sacred
movements: Theatre of the Absurd

works.title: Waiting for the Verdict
works.form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1868
works.description: Published in 1868 and Davis's novel of the Civil War and its racial aftermath: the story of a black surgeon and the family that passes for white. It is a prose fiction work of 1868 by Rebecca Harding Davis; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Dr John Broderip, an eminent Philadelphia surgeon who has passed as white, loves the Southern-bred Margaret Conrad, who cannot love him once he reveals his African descent; Garrick Randolph, heir of a Southern family, moulds the illegitimate and impoverished Ross into his ideal and then recoils from her birth; the war and the sale of an old slave down the river test both stories, and the novel ends with the nation's verdict on what it owes the freed people still awaited.
works.significance: Waiting for the Verdict is one of the first American novels to treat a black professional as its hero and the first substantial American novel of the Civil War from a woman's perspective; it is a key text in the literature of race and Reconstruction.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary detail of mill work and company housing.
works.context: The 1863-68: the Civil War, the hospital and the field, emancipation, and the American debate on racial equality. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Dr John Broderip; Margaret Conrad; Garrick Randolph; Ross, the girl Garrick moulds; Broderip's brother
works.structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rebecca Blaine Harding. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
works.description: Published in 1854 after nine years of revision and the central text of American nature writing: the account of two years, two months and two days in a cabin at Walden Pond, and of an experiment in living deliberately.
works.plot: Thoreau describes the building of the house, the economy of his life, the reading of the classics, the sounds and visitors of the woods, the bean field, the pond, the animals, the seasons and the spring thaw, and ends with the parable of the artist of Kouroo.
works.significance: Walden is the founding text of American nature writing and one of the great works of American prose: it is at once a manual of economy, a naturalist's journal, a spiritual autobiography and a political argument, and it has shaped the modern environmental movement more than any other book.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is concrete, comma-heavy cumulative sentences.
works.context: The years 1845-47, Concord and the Transcendentalist circle, the Mexican War and the market revolution, and the American debate on labour and simplicity. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1854 and first published in 1854 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.characters: Henry David Thoreau, the narrator; Alek Therien, the woodchopper; John Field, the Irish labourer
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Henry Thoreau. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Waldere
works.description: Two fragments (about 63 lines) of an Old English heroic poem on Walter of Aquitaine, the legend known fully from the tenth-century Latin Waltharius: the hostage Walter, escaped with his beloved Hildegyth, is overtaken by the Burgundian king Guthhere (Gunther) and refuses to surrender his treasure and his bride.
works.plot: In the first fragment, Hildegyth urges Walter to fight, praising his sword Mimming and the treasures of the world's kings; in the second, a warrior (perhaps Guthhere or Hagen) taunts Walter over the shield and byrnie taken from Weland's workshop, and Walter answers boastfully that the man who comes for the gold shall have battle. The fragments preserve the defiant speech-exchange before the single combats of the fuller legend.
works.significance: The English witness to one of the great heroic legends of the Middle Ages, bridging the worlds of Beowulf and the continental epics.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: The legend of Walter of Aquitaine, rooted in fifth-century events, circulated across the Germanic world (Waltharius, the Nibelung tradition); the English fragments were discovered in 1860 in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, used as binding material.
works.characters: Waldere (Walter); Hildegyth; Guthhere; Hagen (in the underlying legend); Weland (as maker of the arms)
works.structure: A dialogue of challenge and defiance between two (or three) warriors, in the heroic flyting mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

Treasure, gift-giving, and reciprocity

works.title: Walker's Appeal, in Four Articles; Together with a Preamble, to the Coloured Citizens of the World, but in Particular, and Very Expressly, to Those of the United States of America
altTitles: An Appeal, in Four Articles, to the Coloured Citizens of the World
works.form: Political and religious polemic in the pamphlet tradition: an open address to a named public, organised in articles, with sustained use of quotation, amplified capitals and italics for emphasis, and an apocalyptic prophetic register borrowed from the jeremiad.
works.description: A 78-page polemic pamphlet addressed directly to free and enslaved Black Americans, and secondarily to the white slaveholders who read it over their shoulders. It mixes indictment, scriptural exegesis, historical example and statistical citation from American encyclopaedias and slave codes. Its four articles move from a general statement of the condition of coloured people to a denunciation of slavery, a rebuttal of racist pseudo-science, and an appeal to the diaspora to organise and educate itself. It is the most uncompromising American abolitionist pamphlet of the Romantic generation and the first to be written by a Black American for publication at his own risk.
works.plot: The preamble declares that the oppression of coloured people is unprecedented in history and that the work's plain speaking is therefore excused. Article the First addresses the colouring of the American promise of liberty, quoting the Declaration of Independence against the practice of slavery. Article the Second, the longest, indicts American slavery itself, citing the cruelty of the slave codes, the separation of families and the horrors of the Middle Passage, and warns that a God of justice will not tolerate it forever. Article the Third attacks the prejudices of white Americans and the claim that Black people are naturally inferior, turning the argument back on the Christian churches that licensed the system. Article the Fourth urges education, moral reform, economic self-help and, if necessary, resistance, and includes an address to the slaves that counsels submission only as a temporary discipline while demanding improvement of condition. The conclusion prophesies racial reckoning, with the language of Exodus and of divine vengeance.
works.significance: It marks the moment when American abolitionist writing turned from gradualist appeal to immediate, unconditional demand, and from white benevolence to self-assertion by the oppressed. Its use of scripture, of American founding documents and of the slaves' own experience created a rhetorical model later developed in the great slave narratives and speeches of the 1840s and 1850s. Scholars treat it as a founding text of African American literature as well as of radical political writing.
works.meter: Powerful prose; rhythmic emphasis achieved through repetition, amplification, italics and capitalized nouns rather than metre.
works.context: Published in Boston on the eve of the American immediatist surge, when colonisation societies were proposing to remove free Black people to Africa and when Black Bostonians had built a vigorous institutional and print culture of their own. Its author ran a clothing business and was active in Black civic and mutual-aid circles, which supplied both its audience and its distribution network. Southern legislatures responded with stricter penalties for circulating such literature, and it was read widely enough to make slaveholding authorities treat Black literacy itself as a danger.
works.structure: A preamble followed by four numbered articles of unequal length, plus a closing address to the slaves and an appended circular letter to agents; the argument is cumulative rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship is certain; the pamphlet was published under the author's own name and dated by him at Boston on 28 September 1829.
themes: Religious persecution and martyrdom
Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
The slave trade and abolition
Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing
The Early American Republic and Its Letters

works.title: Waller's Poems
altTitles: The English Poems of Edmund Waller
works.description: The collected poems of Edmund Waller, first gathered in 1645 and revised across his long life, containing the smooth, melodious Cavalier lyrics and panegyrics — 'Go, Lovely Rose', 'On a Girdle', the poems to 'Sacharissa', and panegyrics to Cromwell and Charles II — that made him the model of polished Restoration verse.
works.plot: The poems address love and courtly compliment ('Sacharissa'), offer panegyric to public figures across the political changes, and reflect on time, old age, and the value of verse.
works.significance: Waller's technical polish of the couplet directly shaped Denham, Dryden, and the Augustan line; he was long regarded as the father of smooth English verse.
works.meter: The smooth, closed heroic couplet and melodious song forms that Dryden credited with perfecting English 'numbers'.
works.context: First collected in 1645 and revised to 1686; Waller wrote panegyrics to Cromwell (1655) and to Charles II (1660), embodying the court poet's adaptability.
works.characters: the poet; Sacharissa (Lady Dorothy Sidney); Cromwell; Charles II
works.structure: A collected volume of lyrics, panegyrics, and occasional verse, revised over many editions.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
Time, death, and immortality through verse

works.title: Walsingham; or, The Pupil of Nature. A Domestic Story
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Novel of Manners and Fashion
works.description: Mary Robinson's most ambitious novel and, by general consent, her best: a domestic story in four volumes which combines the friendship of a young writer for a generous and eccentric man with the ruin of a seduced and abandoned heroine, and which satirizes the literary, philosophical, and fashionable circles of the 1790s with a roman à clef sharpness. Its treatment of female vulnerability and its exposure of philosophical cant make it a decisive novel of the decade.
works.plot: The young poet narrates his education by Walsingham, a man of principle and fortune whose benevolence is exploited by the world, and his witnessing of the trial of Isabella, a woman seduced, cast off, and driven to destitution; the two histories are interrupted by satirical portraits of the literary and philosophical society of the day, and the novel ends in the failure of virtue to be protected by law or custom.
works.significance: Walsingham is the novel that shows Robinson's full command of the 1790s domestic fiction of seduction, and is valued as a satirical record of the literary field of the decade and as one of the strongest feminist analyses of seduction before the nineteenth century; its recovery has made it a standard text in the study of women's fiction of the Revolutionary era.
works.meter: Prose narrative with embedded verse and letter papers; the satirical portraits are handled in a pointed, epigrammatic style continuous with her journalistic writing.
works.context: Written in the years when Robinson's intimacy with the radical literary world, her dependence on Longman and other publishers, and her own history as a public mistress made her simultaneously an insider and an object of libel; the novel's attacks on philosophical pretence and on the sexual double standard were read by contemporaries as portraits of identifiable persons, and its finances were settled with the publisher in a payment recorded for the first edition.
works.characters: Walsingham; Isabella; the young poet-pupil who narrates; the profligate seducer; the satirical portraits of literary and philosophical society
works.structure: A four-volume novel with a framing first-person narrator and a plotted inset of Isabella's ruin, interlacing domestic narrative, satire of contemporary literary society, and moral argument; the tone alternates between tenderness and public accusation.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed, and the identification of individual satirical portraits remains a matter of scholarly argument.

Prose Fiction and the Early Novel

Female authorship and the woman writer
Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Patronage and the literary marketplace

works.title: Walt Whitman: A Study
works.description: Published in 1893, the year of Symonds's death, and the first book-length English study of Whitman: an argument for Whitman as the poet of democratic comradeship and of the modern self. It is a prose work of 1893 by John Addington Symonds; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
works.plot: Symonds reads Leaves of Grass as the epic of democracy and of 'adhesiveness' — the love of comrades — and defends Whitman against the charge of indecency by placing the 'Calamus' poems in the tradition of Greek friendship.
works.significance: Symonds's Whitman is the founding English study of the poet and the book through which Whitman entered the English literary tradition as a thinker of democracy and of same-sex love.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is historical narrative on a large scale.
works.context: The 1890s, the English reception of Whitman, the Wilde–Whitman meeting of 1882, and the debate on democracy and literature. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1892 and first published in 1893 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. A. Symonds. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
themes: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
Democracy, individualism, and the American experiment
Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil

works.title: War Is Kind
works.description: Published in 1899 and Crane's second collection: bitterly ironic poems on war, death and the consolations offered to the bereaved. It is a verse work of 1899 by Stephen Crane; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: The title poem sets the rhetoric of national glory — 'Do not weep, maiden, for war is kind' — against the bodies of the dead, and the book's other poems present monologues of suffering, of the dying soldier, of the woman abandoned and of the universe's indifference.
works.significance: 'War Is Kind' is one of the great American anti-war poems and the collection defines the irony of the 1890s: its title became a permanent phrase for the hypocrisy of martial rhetoric, and its free-verse monologues anticipate the war poetry of 1914-18.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The line is free verse, cadenced by the phrase and not by a received pattern. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation.
works.context: 1898-99: the Spanish-American War, the imperial rhetoric of 1898, and Crane's own experience as a war correspondent in Cuba and Greece. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Stephen Townley Crane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole

works.title: Wat Tyler
works.form: Closet drama and dramatic poem on a popular rising, in the line of the republican historical plays of the revolutionary decade, with the choruses and the debates of the commons taking the place of the stage machinery.
works.description: A dramatic poem on the rising of 1381, written in the summer of 1794 in the heat of the author's republican enthusiasm and kept from print until 1817, when it was issued with two other plays. It is a political closet drama in which the peasants of Kent and Essex, provoked by the poll-tax and by the cruelty of the tax-gatherers, march on London under the leader whose name gives the poem its title, and where the demands of the rebels are argued at length by a preaching priest of the insurrection. Its publication in 1817, in a season of domestic repression, gave offence and brought the printer into trouble for the politics it contained.
works.plot: The poem begins with the insult offered to a peasant's daughter by an officer of the excise and with the summary killing that lights the country fire; the rustics of Kent and Essex gather, choose their leader, and are heartened by the itinerant preacher who argues that all men were born free and that the bondage of the poor is the work of the covetous and of their laws. The rebels come to London, are received with promises by the young king, and obtain a charter, after which the leader is treacherously summoned to a conference, struck down before the lord mayor and beheaded, the insurrection ending in the revoked promises and in the executed peasant. The argument is an open plea for the rights of the oppressed, in which the dialogue of the commons, the priest and the leader states the case for resistance and the closing scene states the price of defeat.
works.significance: The most direct English drama of the 1790s to make a medieval peasant rising the figure of contemporary revolutionary argument, and one of the documents by which the later reputation of the Lake school was contested: its appearance in print long after composition forced readers to reconsider the relation between the radical writings of the period and the conservatism of their authors. It remains a standard text for the literature of the poll-tax rising and for the Romantic drama of revolt.
works.meter: Blank verse of a plain and declamatory kind, with short speech-lines and a share of rhymed and song-like passage for the commons, deliberately free of the polish of the fashionable drama of the 1790s.
works.context: Composed in 1794, the year of the repression of the English radical societies, of the Treason trials and of the author's own communitarian hopes, in company with a friend and fellow-planter of the same schemes; withheld from press for more than twenty years, it appeared in 1817 amid the prosecutions for libel and sedition that followed the peace, and its publication was used against the author's politics in the reviews of the later 1820s and 1830s.
works.characters: Wat Tyler, the leader of the commons; the itinerant priest who preaches the equality of mankind; the chiefs of the Kentish and Essex rebels; King Richard the Second and his council; the officers of the tax and the lord mayor of London
works.structure: A dramatic poem in several acts, written for the reader rather than for the stage, moving from the single provoking insult to the mustering of the counties, the march and the parley with the king, and the betrayal and execution; the political case is carried in set speeches and in the debate between the preacher and the peasant leader.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the circumstances of its joint composition and its long suppression are documented in the author's correspondence and in the memoir written by his successor.
themes: Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
Social satire and estates criticism
Tyranny and the abuse of power
Warfare and battle
movements: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets

works.title: Waverley; or, 'Tis Sixty Years Since
works.form: Historical novel and romance of civil war; a society-novel of manners transplanted into the recent past, with ballad and antiquarian apparatus.
works.description: The first historical novel in English, presented as a recovered memoir of the previous century and prefaced by an advertisement on the art of fabricating such a tale. Its young English officer hero, caught between the rival claims of Hanover and Jacobite Scotland during the '45, becomes the model for the neutral witness who moves between two worlds and two codes of honour. The book's anonymous appearance, and the pseudonymous 'Author of Waverley' it created, made publishing history.
works.plot: Edward Waverley, a sentimental young Englishman attached to his Tory cousin the Baron of Bradwardine, is sent to a Border castle, is captured on suspicion, and falls under the spell of the Highland chieftain Fergus Mac-Ivor and his sister Flora. He joins the rising, is trusted by Prince Charles, and duels his patron's kinsman; meanwhile the Baron's estates are sequestrated and Bradwardine's chivalric logic collapses before the fact of defeat. Waverley's English protector Colonel Talbot obtains his pardon; he visits Edinburgh and London, refuses preferment, and marries the Baron's daughter Rose, while the concluding chapters and notes record the extinguishing of the patriarchal law of the Highlands.
works.significance: Founded the historical novel as a major European form and set the template of the neutral hero who mediates between opposed cultures and epochs. Its mixture of romance, ballad, footnote and sociological explanation defined the mode later writers imitated and criticised. The commercial and pseudonymous history of the book changed the economics and the authorship conventions of the nineteenth-century novel.
works.meter: Prose, no metre, with inserted verse, song fragments and quoted ballad and Latin tags.
works.context: Begun during the Napoleonic Wars and completed while the British state was mobilising against France, it revisits the last civil war on British soil at the exact moment when Highland and Border cultures were being documented, enclosed and recruited. Publication was delayed by the author's fear of being identified as a poet, and the novel appeared anonymously when paper and copyright conditions favoured the triple-decker. Its dialect, law and theology are drawn from the antiquarian collection work of the preceding decade.
works.characters: Edward Waverley; the Baron of Bradwardine; Rose Bradwardine; Fergus Mac-Ivor; Flora Mac-Ivor; Davie Gellatley; Colonel Talbot; Donald Bean Lean
works.structure: First-person framed memoir in fifty chapters with an 'Introductory Chapter' on the principles of romance and a postscript of explanatory notes; the narrator's hindsight, classical allusion and marginal learning constitute the historical perspective.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; the author's identity was public within months and was formally acknowledged in the 1829-30 collected edition, for which a first-person Memoir and Introduction were prefixed.
themes: Border, ballad, and national memory
Jacobitism, loyalty, and the '45
The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel

works.title: Ways of Sunlight
works.description: Selvon's only collection of short stories, published by MacGibbon & Kee in London in 1957 (1958 in Britannica), sets stories of rural Trinidad beside stories of hard times among West Indians in London.
works.summary: Short stories of village life in Trinidad, with its washerwomen, cane-cutters and the superstitious Ma Procop, and of West Indians in the cold basements of London.
works.plot: In the Trinidad stories, according to the publisher's synopsis, village washerwomen gossip and quarrel, cane-cutters toil for a meagre harvest, and old Ma Procop protects the fruit of her mango tree with magic. The London stories turn to the depression of hard times in the city, where people live in cold, damp basements and hustle for survival. Dawes finds in the collection Selvon's wit, his trickery as a writer and his poetic sensibility.
works.significance: Reissued by Longman in 1987 with a critical introduction by Jane Grant; Britannica lists it among Selvon's later works.
works.meter: Dawes stresses wit, trickery and poetic sensibility, and Selvon's complete immersion in telling a story for its entertainment.
works.context: Published the year after The Lonely Londoners; South Asian Britain counts it, with The Housing Lark, as an extension of Selvon's writing on migrant life in Britain.
works.structure: Separate stories set in Trinidad and in London; the number and order of the stories were not checked.

Land, place and regional belonging
Migration, exile and diaspora

works.title: We Have Been Warned
works.description: The socialist novel of the family and the politics of the decade. It is a prose fiction work of 1935 by Naomi Mitchison; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama.
works.plot: We Have Been Warned follows Dora, the doctor's wife, and her family through the politics of the 1930s - the election, the hunger march, the rise of the European dictatorships and the biology of the clinic - in the documentary prose of Mitchison's committed decade.
works.significance: We Have Been Warned is Mitchison's socialist novel of the thirties: it carried the family, the clinic and the election into the novel of the decade's politics and was refused by publishers for its frankness before it appeared.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the historical novel of the ancient world in the anthropologist's eye.
works.context: London and Europe in the mid-1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
works.characters: Dora, the doctor's wife; the family; the political comrades
works.structure: A socialist novel in the parts of the election, the family and the continent. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Naomi Mary Margaret Haldane. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: We Real Cool
works.description: A poem by Gwendolyn Brooks, written in 1959 and published in her third collection, The Bean Eaters (1960). In eight short lines, seven young pool players boast of the life they lead and arrive at its end, 'We / Die soon.' It is one of the most famous and most taught American poems of the century.
works.summary: Under the heading 'The Pool Players. / Seven at the Golden Shovel', the players list what they do: leave school, lurk late, strike straight, sing sin, thin gin, jazz June, and die soon.
works.plot: The poem is spoken by seven pool players at a hall called the Golden Shovel. 'We real cool,' they begin, and in short boasts they say what they do: they left school, they lurk late, they strike straight, they sing sin and thin gin, they jazz June. Each line ends on 'We', so that every boast is carried over into the next line, until the last, which has no 'We' after it: 'We / Die soon.' The swagger collapses into the knowledge, or the fate, the boasting has concealed.
works.significance: Cited as one of the most celebrated examples of jazz poetry, it has been printed on broadsides, reprinted in textbooks, banned in places for 'jazz', and answered by later writers; Terrance Hayes's 'golden shovel' form takes its name from it.
works.meter: Monosyllabic, vernacular speech with the syncopation of jazz; alliteration ('strike straight', 'sing sin') and the dropped copula of Black English.
works.context: Brooks said the poem came from passing a pool hall full of boys in her Chicago neighbourhood and wondering how they felt about themselves. The Bean Eaters (1960) takes many of its subjects from the news of the civil rights years.
works.structure: Four couplets of three-word lines (after the two-line heading), with internal and end rhyme and the pronoun 'We' placed at the end of each line but the last, so that the enjambment enacts the players' hesitation.
themes: Childhood, adolescence and coming of age
Counterculture, drugs and rebellion
Death, illness and mourning

works.form: Novel; new woman, first issued in 1884
works.description: Lyall's suffrage novel: a woman's education and the campaign for the vote. It is a prose fiction work of 1884 by Edna Lyall; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The heroine, brought up to think for herself, campaigns for women's suffrage and falls in love with a man who opposes it; the novel follows her education, her public work and the reconciliation of love and principle.
works.significance: We Two was one of the most popular suffrage novels of the 1880s and the first bestseller to make the women's vote its central subject: it gave the campaign a mass readership and made Lyall a heroine of the movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The author's characteristic manner is the problem novel of doubt and conscience.
works.context: England in the 1880s and the first phase of the women's suffrage campaign. The record dates the work as composed between 1883 and 1884 and first published in 1884 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: the heroine; the anti-suffrage lover; the campaigners; the family
works.structure: A novel in three volumes, from the education to the campaign. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ada Ellen Bayly. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Weird Stories
works.description: The finest Victorian ghost stories of the haunted house: 'The Open Door', 'The Old House in Vauxhall Walk'. It is a prose fiction work of 1882 by Charlotte Riddell; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Sensation Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Riddell's ghost stories — 'The Open Door', 'The Old House in Vauxhall Walk', 'Walnut-Tree House', 'The Last of Squire Ennismore' — in which the haunting has a legal or financial cause and the ghost is a wronged party.
works.significance: Weird Stories contains some of the best ghost stories in English: 'The Open Door' and 'The Old House in Vauxhall Walk' are among the finest Victorian supernatural tales, and Riddell's device of the legal ghost made her the central woman writer of the English ghost story.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the documentary detail of the counting-house and the ledger.
works.context: London and the English country house in the 1870s and 1880s, and the Victorian taste for the Christmas ghost story. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1882 and first published in 1882 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; sensation novel.
works.characters: the haunted house; the ghost; the lawyer; the heir
works.structure: A collection of ghost stories, several with a legal frame. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Eliza Lawson Riddell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Wessex Poems and Other Verses
works.form: Poetry collection (with the author's own drawings)
works.description: Published in 1898, Hardy's first collection of verse after thirty years of novel-writing, with his own illustrations: poems of Wessex landscape, of the dead, of the Napoleonic wars and of the ironies of circumstance.
works.plot: The collection ranges from the ballad-like 'The Dance at the Phoenix' and the Napoleonic 'The Sergeant's Song' to the elegiac 'Friends Beyond' and the sardonic 'Nature's Questioning'.
works.significance: Wessex Poems began Hardy's career as a major poet and set the tone of his verse; it is the volume from which the twentieth-century revival of Hardy's poetry dates.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
works.context: The 1890s, Hardy's return to the poetry he had written since the 1860s, and the decline of the rural community. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1896 and first published in 1898 and it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Westward Ho!
works.description: Published in 1855 and the founding novel of English imperial adventure: the story of Amyas Leigh of Devon in the age of Elizabeth, the Armada and the Spanish Main. It is a prose fiction work of 1855 by Charles Kingsley; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; War Narrative of the Common Soldier and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Amyas Leigh sails with Drake and Frobisher against the Spaniards, pursues the murderer of his brother across the Atlantic, and is blinded and broken by the vengeance, learning in the end that the destruction of the Spanish empire was the work of God rather than of man.
works.significance: Westward Ho! created the English adventure novel of empire: it was the model for Henty, Ballantyne and the whole schoolboy literature of the imperial age, and it made the Elizabethan seaman the central hero of Victorian popular culture.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1570s-88, the Elizabethan sea-dogs, the Armada of 1588, the Spanish colonies, and the 1850s revival of interest in the Elizabethan age. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; war narrative of the common soldier.
works.characters: Amyas Leigh; Frank Leigh; Rose Salterne; Don Guzman de Soto; Salvation Yeo; Eustace Leigh; Ayacanora; Sir Richard Grenville; Sir Walter Raleigh; Sir Francis Drake; Mrs Leigh
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

works.title: What D'Ye Call It
altTitles: What D'Ye Call It: A Comedy
works.description: Gay's comic burlesque of the modern drama, which plays heroic tragedy, the sentimental plot and the new French manner against one another and asks the audience by what name the stage-piece is to be called.
works.plot: A country family and a pair of lovers are involved in an outrageously regular tragedy of captive princes, recognition and virtue rewarded, until the housemaid's dream and the exposures of the plot turn the whole into farce; the play ends by denying that it belongs to any known species.
works.significance: It is one of the founding pieces of English dramatic burlesque and a direct preparation for the Beggar's Opera, and it records the century's argument about genre in the comic register.
works.meter: Prose dialogue interrupted by heroic-couplet and blank-verse tragedy, the shift of metre carrying the satire.
works.context: First acted in the season after the death of the queen and the change of ministry, when the pastiche of operatic and tragic convention was a competitive theatrical genre and when the theatre managers were anxious over the vogue for the old and the new. It answered the running of Addison's and Rowe's tragedies in the same houses.
works.characters: the lovers of the burlesqued tragic plot; the country family; the dreaming housemaid; the critic of the audience
works.structure: Five acts of prose comedy with inserted scenes of rhymed heroic tragedy and a dream piece, the forms being parodied against each other.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
themes: Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
Seduction and the betrayed heroine
Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
The public theatre and the players' world

works.title: What Maisie Knew
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1897
works.description: Published in 1897 and the most daring of James's experiments in point of view: the story of a child's view of her parents' divorce and remarriage, told entirely through what she can understand. It is a prose fiction work of 1897 by Henry James; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Sensation Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Maisie is the pawn in the divorce of her parents, who each remarry and use her as a cover for their affairs; she is cared for by her step-parents, Sir Claude and Miss Overmore, and the novel ends with her choice to leave them and go home with her governess Mrs Wix.
works.significance: What Maisie Knew is the central novel of the child's consciousness in English and a founding text of the modern novel of point of view: its method of showing only what a child can see made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of the limited perspective.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification.
works.context: The 1890s: the English divorce law, the American expatriate world, and the Victorian and Edwardian literature of childhood. The record dates the work as composed between 1896 and 1897 and first published in 1897 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; sensation novel.
works.characters: Maisie Farange; Beale Farange; Ida Farange; Miss Overmore (later Mrs Beale); Sir Claude; Mrs Wix
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.

works.title: What Use Are Flowers?
works.description: What Use Are Flowers? is a short play for television by Lorraine Hansberry, published after her death in Les Blancs: The Collected Last Plays (1972), described by the Gale entry as a fable about an ageing hermit who tries to pass on his memories of a lost civilisation to children in a ravaged world.
works.summary: A hermit, a group of children who have grown up without language after a catastrophe, and his attempt to hand on the knowledge and values of the vanished world.
works.plot: A hermit who withdrew from society returns to find civilisation destroyed and a band of wild children with no language or culture. He tries to teach them speech, skills and the idea of beauty, symbolised by flowers, so that something of human culture may survive him.
works.significance: A minor play that shows Hansberry's interest in philosophical fable beyond realism.
works.meter: Spare, allegorical dialogue in which the hermit's eloquence contrasts with the children's wordlessness.
works.context: Written in the early 1960s, amid fears of nuclear war; Leonard R. N. Ashley describes it as an optimistic view of the aftermath of nuclear war, and it is often read as Hansberry's affirmative reply to the despair of the Theatre of the Absurd.
works.structure: A single short act of brief, fable-like scenes written for the television screen.
themes: Education, institutions and the academy
The Cold War, nuclear threat and the bomb
Utopia, dystopia and imagined futures

works.title: While the Billy Boils
works.description: Published in 1896 and the founding book of Australian literature: sixty-two short pieces, most of them written in or after the year Lawson spent in the drought country around Bourke. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Henry Lawson; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Tall Tale and South-Western Humour Sketch and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories give the bush in brief, hard anecdotes: the swagman and the squatter, the shearer and the cook, the mother and the lost child, the man who dies of thirst in the tank, the union men and the non-union men on the track.
works.significance: While the Billy Boils created the Australian short story and made the bush the national place: its plain speech, its laconic narrator and its refusal of sentiment shaped Australian literature for the next century, and it is the first book in which Australian English is written as it is spoken.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is terse, laconic, anecdotal prose.
works.context: The 1890s, the Australian shearers' strikes, the drought of 1891-95, the Bulletin school, and the federation movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; tall tale and south-western humour sketch.
works.characters: the drover's wife; the bush undertaker; Mitchell, the swagman; Steelman; Arvie Aspinall
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A framed sketch: the literate narrator, the vernacular teller, the escalating impossibility delivered deadpan and the punch that turns on the outsider.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Archibald Hertzberg Lawson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Whims and Oddities
works.form: Mock-Heroic and Verse Satire; The Sketch and Character Tale
works.description: The first series of comic prose sketches, vers de société, punning songs, and parodies by a writer who had passed from parliamentary reportage and magazine sub-editorship to full-time literary work. The numbers treat the trivia of Regency and post-Regency urban life, from bathing and hair to tailors and the opera, with a relentless play of homonym and refrain. A second series followed in 1827, and the book established the author's popular reputation independent of his serious verse.
works.plot: There is no continuous argument; the series is a succession of short pieces in which a stated commonplace is driven through every possible pun until it collapses, as in the song on a washed-out face or the sketch in which a list of complaints turns on a single monosyllable. Several numbers develop a ridiculous conceit with mock-earnest rhetoric, others parody the sentimental annual verse and the fashionable poetaster. The cumulative effect is a comic anatomy of metropolitan literary and leisure life, and of the small miseries of the writer whose bread depends on it.
works.significance: The series is the founding text of Victorian comic verse, the source of the punning and self-parodying manner later inherited by comic song and the joke-book, and it documents how a Romantic-period man of letters made a living when serious poetry would not pay. It also preserves the parodic relationship of the generation after the review era to annual and fashionable verse.
works.meter: An explosive mixture of forms: songs in common and double-measure with refrains, parodies of well-known lyrics in their original stanzas, rhymed epigrams, and prose rhythms built to a pun; the metre is subordinate to wordplay, and the serious blank verse of the same writer's longer poems is wholly absent.
works.context: Produced in the crowded annual and periodical market of the later 1820s by a contributor to the great quarterlies and to the magazine circle that had published the Lake and second-generation Romantic writers; the author had edited foreign papers and worked as an assistant at a leading literary magazine before marriage and the need for regular income forced comic hack-work. The volumes were followed in 1830 by a Comic Annual that ran for over a decade.
works.characters: the comic persona of the sketch writer; the battered dandy, the bill-disdains-the-payee tradesman, the opera audience, the bashful lover of the parodied songs
works.structure: An anthology of unsigned-to-signed short comic pieces, prose sketches and lyrics, arranged without narrative order; each item is self-contained and closes on its verbal payoff.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the collaborative volume of burlesque odes issued earlier by the same writer is a separate book and is not included here.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public

works.title: Whisky Galore
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1947
works.description: The funniest Scottish novel: an island and a shipwreck full of whisky. It is a prose fiction work of 1947 by Compton Mackenzie; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: When the SS Cabinet Minister runs aground off the Hebridean island of Todday with 50,000 cases of whisky aboard, the islanders — deprived of whisky by wartime rationing — salvage the cargo against the efforts of the authorities, in a comedy of island life.
works.significance: Whisky Galore is the funniest Scottish novel ever written: its island, its wreck and its whisky made it a permanent comic classic, and its portrait of the Hebrides made Compton Mackenzie one of the great Scottish novelists of the century.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the comic novel of the island.
works.context: The Hebrides during the Second World War. The record dates the work as composed between 1946 and 1947 and first published in 1947 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
works.characters: the islanders of Todday; Captain Waggett; Joseph Macroon; the Sergeant; the SS Cabinet Minister
works.structure: A comic novel of an island and a shipwreck. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Edward Montague Compton Mackenzie. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: White Fang
works.description: Published in 1906 and the companion to The Call of the Wild: the taming of a wolf-dog in the Yukon by a gentle master. It is a prose fiction work of 1906 by Jack London; it belongs to American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: White Fang, a wolf-dog born in the wild, is captured by Indians, trained as a sled dog and a fighting dog, and nearly ruined by a brutal owner; he is rescued by the mining engineer Weedon Scott, taken to California and slowly domesticated through kindness, ending as a devoted guardian of the family.
works.significance: White Fang is the great American novel of domestication and the mirror image of The Call of the Wild: its reversal of the earlier book's direction — from wild to tame rather than from tame to wild — shows London's Darwinian imagination from the other side, and it is one of the most popular animal novels in the world.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third.
works.context: 1906: the Klondike, the American fashion for the animal story, and the debate on heredity and environment in the new century. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1906 and first published in 1906 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; novel of development and the growth story.

works.title: Whose Body?
works.form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1923
works.description: The first Lord Peter Wimsey novel: a naked body in a Battersea bathroom and a missing financier. It is a prose fiction work of 1923 by Dorothy L. Sayers; it belongs to The Golden Age of Detective Fiction and it is catalogued here under Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery; Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: A naked man's body is found in the bath of a Battersea architect, and Lord Peter Wimsey, the aristocratic amateur detective, investigates alongside Inspector Sugg and his manservant Bunter; the case turns on a missing financier, Sir Reuben Levy, and a substitution of bodies.
works.significance: Whose Body? introduced Lord Peter Wimsey and founded the English detective novel of character: its wit, its aristocratic detective and its fair-play plot made Sayers the finest writer of the Golden Age after Christie.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the fair-play plot carried by character rather than mechanism.
works.context: London in the early 1920s, the City and the art trade, and the postwar world of the aristocratic amateur. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; comic novel and the satire of manners.
works.characters: Lord Peter Wimsey; Bunter; Inspector Sugg; Sir Reuben Levy; Mr Thipps; Mr Parker
works.structure: An investigation in London, with Wimsey's reconstruction at the close. A novel in chapters: the crime is stated early, the investigation proceeds by interview and document, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation before the close.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dorothy Leigh Sayers. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Why Come Ye Nat to Courte?
works.description: Skelton's most direct assault on Cardinal Wolsey: taking up the courtiers' question of the title, the poet answers that the court is barred to all but Wolsey's creatures, and proceeds to a full-scale attack on the Cardinal's arrogance, his building, his rule of the king, and the degradation of the realm under his hand.
works.plot: The poem opens with the question of why honest men shun the court, answers that Wolsey has shut the king away from his subjects, and develops into a sustained invective against the Cardinal's person and policy, closing with a warning to the king.
works.significance: The most fearless political satire of the early Tudor period and the classic of the English anti-court diatribe.
works.meter: Skeltonics of unusual venom and speed; the metre's rattle becomes a weapon.
works.context: Written when Wolsey's power was absolute and Skelton had taken sanctuary at Westminster (1523) to escape the Cardinal's anger; the poem circulated in manuscript before printing.
works.characters: the poet (speaker); Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: A satirical diatribe organized as an answer to a question; cumulative invective rising to direct warning.

works.title: Why I Am a Socialist
works.description: Published in 1886 at the moment of Besant's conversion to socialism: a short and forceful argument that the private ownership of land and capital is the cause of the poverty she had seen in the East End.
works.plot: Besant recounts the matchgirls' strike, the unemployment demonstrations of 1886 and the condition of the dock labourers, and argues for the collective ownership of the means of production as the only remedy.
works.significance: Why I Am a Socialist is a central document of the making of British socialism and of the transition of the 1880s radical movement from freethought to economics.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is direct argument and plain diction.
works.context: The 1880s, the Great Depression in trade, the foundation of the Social Democratic Federation and the Fabian Society, and the London unemployed riots of February 1886. The record dates the work as composed in 1886 and first published in 1886 and it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; social inquiry and the documented survey.

A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: Widdershins
works.description: The greatest English ghost story collection of the century: 'The Beckoning Fair One' and the haunted artist. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Oliver Onions; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The collection gathers Onions's supernatural stories — 'The Beckoning Fair One', 'Rooum', 'The Accident', 'The Cigarette Case', 'Benlian' — in which artists, inventors and solitary men are destroyed by the presence they have admitted into their lives.
works.significance: Widdershins contains 'The Beckoning Fair One', the greatest English ghost story of the century: the collection is the central text of the modern psychological ghost story and stands with M. R. James and Blackwood at the summit of the English weird tale.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the psychological ghost story of the obsessive.
works.context: London and the English provinces in the 1900s, and the world of the artist and the inventor. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; modern short story and the magazine tale.

works.structure: A collection of supernatural stories, several of them novellas. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.

works.title: Widsith
works.description: A catalogue-poem of 143 lines spoken by the scop Widsith, who boasts of the lands, kings, and tribes he has visited — a thula (name-list) that preserves the oldest stratum of Germanic heroic legend in English, from Eormanric the Goth to Hrothgar of the Danes.
works.plot: Widsith introduces himself as a poet of the Myrgings, recounts the lords he has served (Eormanric, Eadgils, Ælfwine, Hrothgar and Hrothwulf among dozens), and ends with a professional credo on the value of the scop, who wanders among peoples earning praise and treasure with his songs.
works.significance: The earliest map of Germanic heroic geography in English; a key text for the prehistory of Beowulf's world.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of the older, stichic kind.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its name-lists reach back to the fourth-century Gothic world and have been central to reconstructing Germanic heroic legend.
works.characters: Widsith (speaker); Eormanric; Hrothgar; Hrothwulf; Eadgils; Ælfwine; Offa; Ealhhild
works.structure: Three thulas (catalogues of kings, tribes, and personal patrons) framed by first-person narrative and a gnomic coda on the poet's craft.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
