works.title: Wieland; or, The Transformation
works.form: Gothic novel of terror in the self-described precarious-narrative mode, blending domestic romance, religious memoir and detective plot
works.description: A tale of religious fanaticism and mysterious voices in the Pennsylvania backcountry, and one of the first American novels to make psychological terror its subject. The book is narrated by a young woman who recounts the destruction of her family as a precarious narrative meant to instruct a listener. Its machinery of disembodied speech, inherited enthusiasm and suspected possession gave the American Gothic its first fully developed plot.
works.plot: Clara Wieland recalls how her father, a German emigrant preacher, burned himself to death in his barn after mistaking his own zeal for a divine command. Years later her brother Theodore, raised in the same creed of feeling, is driven to murder his children and then himself by voices that seem to come from his father and from Clara herself. An itinerant pedlar named Carwin is discovered to possess an unusual power of duplicating voices without moving his lips, and the family friend who loves Clara suspects him of the trick. The novel closes with a search for Carwin in the city that leaves the deepest motive unexplained, so that reader and narrator alike must decide whether the agency was human or diabolical.
works.significance: It founded the American Gothic by relocating terror from castles to sects, barns and wooden backcountry houses. Its treatment of enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination made it a source for later American fictions of interior voices. It is the earliest American novel routinely studied as a work of the first rank rather than as a curiosity.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the late 1790s in Philadelphia, a city then arguing over sectarian enthusiasm, Deism and the legacy of the Revolutionary rejection of authority. The novel transposes the British Godwinian enquiry into a dissenting sect led by a zealot father. Its anxiety about voices without bodies belongs to a decade of pamphlet wars about religious credulity and rational belief.
works.characters: Clara Wieland; Theodore Wieland; the elder Wieland; Carwin
works.structure: Retrospective first-person narrative cast as a framed confession to a silent auditor; a second book introduces an independent narrator and shifts the investigation to the city, producing a deliberately uneven, two-part design.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the author announced the work in his own publishing imprint and defended it in a prefatory letter.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
movements: Charles Brockden Brown and the American Gothic

works.title: Wild Earth
works.form: Poetry collection (the Irish lyric of the road)
works.description: The collection of the Irish lyric: the road, the fair and the leaving. It is a verse work of 1907 by Padraic Colum; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Irish Revival Lyric and the Celtic Twilight; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance.
works.plot: Wild Earth gathers Colum's lyrics of the Irish road, the fair, the emigrant ship and the west, among them 'The Strolling Player' and 'The Old Woman of the Roads', in the spoken idiom of the revival's lyric.
works.significance: Wild Earth is the collection that made Colum the lyric poet of the revival beside Yeats and Synge: its road, its fair and its leaving are among the best lyrics of the Irish revival.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the spoken Irish idiom carried into English dialogue.

works.title: Wild Honey from Various Thyme
works.description: Published in 1908 and the last collection of the collaboration, containing the poems written after the turn of the century and the beginning of the two poets' turn to Catholicism. It is a verse work of 1908 by Michael Field; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Dramatic Monologue and Masked Lyric; Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence.
works.plot: The volume gathers the secular lyrics of the partners' maturity, nature poems, classical pieces, love poems and songs of the shared garden, written before their conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1907, and stands as the last major book of their pagan phase before the devotional Poems of Adoration (1912).
works.significance: Wild Honey from Various Thyme is the final testament of one of the most remarkable literary partnerships in English and a key text in the history of Victorian women's writing and of the aesthetic movement.
works.meter: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric.
works.context: 1908: the end of the Decadent decade, the Catholic revival, and the last years of the partnership at Richmond. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
works.structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

works.title: Wild Wales: Its People, Language and Scenery
works.description: Published in 1862 and Borrow's great book on Wales: an Englishman's walking tour through a country he loves and whose language he has learned. It is a prose work of 1862 by George Borrow; it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Borrow walks through north and south Wales in 1854, visiting the inns, the chapels, the castles and the mountains, and records the conversations of the Welsh people, the poetry and the language, the history of the Welsh princes, and his own fierce advocacy of Welsh culture against English contempt.
works.significance: Wild Wales is the finest English book about Wales and one of the great books of the nineteenth century on a Celtic language and people: its record of the Welsh language and culture at a moment of crisis made it a founding text of Welsh cultural history, and it is Borrow's most affectionate and most generous book.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is picaresque episodic narrative.
works.context: 1854 and 1862: the Welsh language in the nineteenth century, the temperance and chapel culture, the antiquarian revival of Wales, and the English romanticism of the Celtic past. works.title: Windsor-Forest
works.description: Pope's topographical poem from the view over Windsor and the Thames, which reads a surveyed landscape as the evidence of a harmonious order in nature, in the British past and in the commercial present, and closes in a prophecy of national peace and plenty.
works.plot: The poet surveys the prospect from the forest, descends to the Thames and its fishing and trading, reviews the violent history of Britain from the conquest and the civil wars, and resolves the spectacle into a providential harmony of the elements and of the realm.
works.significance: It renewed Denham's Cooper's Hill for the eighteenth century and made the surveyed landscape the occasion for a national argument about order, commerce and providence; its river and forest writing is the direct precedent of Thomson.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of ceremonious regularity, with the long descriptive passage, the apostrophe and the closing epilogic couplet.
works.context: Published in the closing months of the negotiation of the peace that ended the War of the Spanish Succession, and addressed in its first state to the peace and to the royal seat; the poem's Whig language of liberty, trade and improved property belongs to the estate-poetry vogue of these years.
works.characters: the poet; the Thames; the genius of the place; the bird and beast inhabitants of the forest
works.structure: A single topographical sweep from prospect to river to history to prophecy, held together by the couplet's reflective transitions rather than by action.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Winesburg, Ohio
works.description: The founding book of the modern American short story: the small town as a place of hidden loneliness. It is a prose fiction work of 1919 by Sherwood Anderson; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The stories follow George Willard, a young reporter on the Winesburg Eagle, through the town's inhabitants — the 'grotesques' whose lives have been twisted by an untold truth — and end with George's departure for the city.
works.significance: Winesburg, Ohio is the founding book of the modern American short story: it made the small town a place of hidden lives, invented the linked story cycle as an American form, and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner and Carver.

works.context: The small town of Clyde, Ohio, of Anderson's childhood, and the American small town at the moment of industrialisation. works.title: Winner and Waster
works.description: The earliest datable poem of the Alliterative Revival (c. 1352): a debate dream vision in which Winner (the thrifty, hoarding merchant) and Waster (the lavish, spending lord) plead their cases before the king, who assigns each his proper sphere. Its satire of Edward III's economic policies — and its superb description of the armies — make it a key document of mid-century social thought.
works.plot: The dreamer sees two armies drawn up in a land divided between wealth and want; Winner and Waster, their champions, dispute before the king: Winner attacks Waster's reckless feasting and ruinous retinues, Waster defends liberality as the lifeblood of the realm; the king's judgement — sending Winner to the papal court and the friars, Waster to London and the magnates — restores each to his proper economy.
works.significance: The earliest witness to the alliterative revival's social satire and the direct ancestor of Piers Plowman's field of folk; its economic debate has made it a touchstone for medieval political thought.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, early and vigorous.
works.context: Composed c. 1352, referencing the Order of the Garter (1348), the Statute of Treasons (1352), and the king's household; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 (mid-fifteenth century), with a line lost to damage.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Winner; Waster; the king (Edward III)
works.structure: A debate vision framed by the arming of the two hosts, in the tradition of the altercatio; the poem breaks off, unfinished, in the king's judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Kingship and good rule
Social satire and estates criticism
movements: The Alliterative Revival

works.title: Winter
works.description: The first of Thomson's seasonal poems: a description of the closing year, the frost, the snow and the thaw, in which the rigour of the weather tries the labouring poor and the mind of the spectator together.
works.plot: The poem passes from the early frost and the wild fowl of the fen through the deep snow, the cottage fire-side, the sports of the frozen field and the house of labour, to the thaw and the drowning of the country, closing on the contemplation of death and of the season of the soul.
works.significance: It renewed English descriptive verse by making weather and labour rather than estate and prospect the subject, and it gave the century the diction of natural observation that Cowper, Crabbe and Wordsworth later absorbed.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of great period-length, with the suspended syntax, the accumulation of adjective and participle and the onomatopoeic weather passage.
works.context: Published in the year after Thomson's arrival in London from the north, in the season when the lapse of licensing, the new topographical taste and the debate over the merits of blank verse made a long descriptive poem on the weather a commercial and critical event.
works.characters: the personified musing of the opening invocation; the peasant and the shepherd of the frozen country; the wild fowl of the fen; the hare, the stag and the huntsmen
works.structure: A continuous descriptive progression through the phases of one season, animated by inset tales, the apostrophe to the personified mood of the opening, and the reflection addressed to the spectator.

works.title: Winter Holiday
works.description: The frozen lake and the voyage to the North Pole of the winter of 1931. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by Arthur Ransome; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
works.plot: Quarantined by diphtheria at Beckfoot, Nancy and Peggy join the Walkers and the Dorotheas on the frozen lake, where the iceboat, the signalling and the voyage to the North Pole - the houseboat in the snow - carry the winter campaign of the two crews.

works.title: Winter in Moscow
works.description: Muggeridge's satire of the Soviet Union and of its Western admirers, drawn from his time in Moscow as the Manchester Guardian's stand-in correspondent in 1932-33: it describes conditions in the 'socialist utopia' and satirises Western journalists' uncritical view of the Soviet regime.
works.plot: Drawing on what Muggeridge saw in Moscow and on his journey to the famine regions, the book describes conditions in the Soviet 'socialist utopia' and satirises the Western journalists whose reports of the regime were uncritical.
works.significance: The book turned to satire the experience behind Muggeridge's famine reports, which with those of Gareth Jones helped to confirm the extent of the famine; he later called Duranty 'the greatest liar I have met in journalism'. It marks the point at which his politics began to move from an independent socialism towards the conservative religious position of his later career.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical sentence of the journalist with the moralist's edge.
works.context: Muggeridge went to Moscow in 1932, initially attracted by communism, to stand in for the Manchester Guardian's correspondent William Henry Chamberlin. Travelling to Ukraine and the Caucasus without the permission of the Soviet authorities, he reported the famine in despatches sent in the diplomatic bag; those that were printed, on 25, 27 and 28 March 1933, appeared without his name, while Walter Duranty of the New York Times denied that any famine existed. After this conflict with British newspapers' policy of not provoking the Soviet authorities, Muggeridge returned to novel writing.

works.title: Wisdom
works.description: The most learned and musical of the English moralities (c. 1460–70): the play of the soul — Mind, Will, and Understanding — wedded to Wisdom (Christ), corrupted by Lucifer into a life of lechery and law, and reclaimed through penance. Its elaborate costumes, dances, and liturgical music suggest performance by a learned monastic or clerical household.
works.plot: Wisdom (Christ) espouses the soul with her powers Mind, Will, and Understanding; Lucifer tempts them to abandon contemplation for the world, and the soul falls into lechery, maintenance of law, and perjury; Wisdom returns, and the powers, moved by his speeches, do penance and are restored to grace.
works.significance: The most theologically sophisticated English morality: its fusion of mystical doctrine, music, and dance makes it a summit of the genre's learned tradition.
works.meter: Stanza forms with Latin liturgical texts and music cues, the most literate of the moralities.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–70, probably for an East Anglian monastic or noble household with trained singers; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354) and Bodleian Digby MS 133.
works.characters: Wisdom (Christ); Anima (the Soul); Mind; Will; Understanding; Lucifer; the Seven Deadly Sins
works.structure: A two-movement morality (union with Wisdom; fall and restoration), with the masque-like dances and the court of Lucifer as its theatrical centre.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Wit and Science
altTitles: The Play of Wit and Science
works.description: John Redford's morality play of the courtship of Wit and Science, the masterpiece of the educational interludes written for the choirboys of St Paul's; surviving in a single manuscript and first printed in 1848.
works.plot: Wit, son of Nature, sets out to win the lady Science, daughter of Reason; beguiled by Idleness he falls asleep and is transformed by the enchantment of Ignorance into the fool Ingenio; Shame and Reason restore him, Instruction and Study arm him anew, and he defeats the giant Tediousness, winning Science in a dance of reconciliation. The play celebrates the humanist programme of learning through labour.
works.significance: The finest of the school interludes and the purest dramatic expression of Tudor humanist pedagogy; its allegory of the arduous courtship of learning shaped the later academic plays and the tradition of the children's companies.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1530–47 by Redford, choirmaster of St Paul's, for performance by the cathedral choirboys; the play belongs to the humanist transformation of the morality tradition into a vehicle for the new learning, and its songs survive with music by Redford himself.
works.characters: Wit; Science; Reason; Nature; Idleness; Ignorance; Shame; Instruction; Study; Diligence; Tediousness; Honest Recreation
works.structure: A two-part morality play of quest, fall, and restoration, with songs, dances, and stage spectacle; the action alternates between Wit's education and the comic threats of Tediousness and Idleness.

works.title: With Clive in India; or, The Beginnings of an Empire
works.description: Henty's Indian novel: a young clerk in the wars that founded the British Empire in India. It is a prose fiction work of 1884 by G. A. Henty; it belongs to Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire and it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Sensation Novel.
works.plot: Charlie Marryat, a young English clerk, serves under Clive at the siege of Arcot and the battle of Plassey, survives captivity in the Black Hole, and returns to England with a fortune from the beginnings of the empire in India.
works.significance: With Clive in India was Henty's great Indian novel and the most influential of his imperial books: it taught a generation of English boys the founding of British India and its mixture of adventure, plunder and moral confidence is the central document of the imperial adventure for boys.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the young hero placed at the centre of a real historical campaign.
works.context: India in the 1750s, the Carnatic wars and the foundation of British rule in Bengal. works.title: With the Wild Geese
works.description: The great Irish historical poem sequence: the Wild Geese, the Jacobite wars and the exile. It is a verse work of 1902 by Emily Lawless; it is catalogued here under Political Verse and the Poem of Public Cause.
works.plot: The poems follow the Irish soldiers who left Ireland after the Treaty of Limerick to serve the kings of France — the Wild Geese — through the battles of the eighteenth century and into the exile, in lyrics of defeat, loyalty and the memory of home.

works.title: Witty and Witless
altTitles: A Dialogue on Wit and Folly
works.description: John Heywood's debate dialogue on the relative happiness of the witty man and the witless, surviving in a single manuscript; first printed in 1846 by the Percy Society.
works.plot: James and John dispute whether it is better to be witty or witless: James argues that wit brings care and envy, John that witlessness is mere animal contentment; each supports his case with proverbs, exempla, and the testimony of fools, until the conclusion grants each condition its proper happiness.
works.significance: A minor but revealing document of the Erasmian debate on wisdom and folly in the English household; its survival in manuscript shows the interlude circulating beyond print.
works.meter: Couplets with proverb-dense argument
works.context: Written c. 1525–33, probably for a household audience; the debate on wit and folly belongs to the Erasmian praise-of-folly tradition, and the play's proverb lore links it to Heywood's collection of proverbs and epigrams.
works.characters: James; John
works.structure: A continuous debate in alternating speeches, without action, in the manner of the scholastic disputation turned to moral entertainment.
works.attributionNotes: The manuscript ascribes the work to John Heywood; the attribution is accepted in modern scholarship.

works.title: Wives and Daughters: An Every-Day Story
works.form: Novel in monthly parts (Cornhill Magazine); two volumes 1866
works.description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866, unfinished at Gaskell's sudden death in November 1865 and published with the editor's note that the last chapter was wanting; the most mature of her novels.
works.plot: Molly Gibson, the motherless daughter of a country doctor, is given a stepmother in the scheming and charming Hyacinth Clare, and a stepsister in Cynthia Kirkpatrick, whose beauty and improvidence complicate Molly's love for the naturalist Roger Hamley. The novel's interests are inheritance, professional vocation, the provincial town and its gossip; the last chapter was to have married Molly to Roger.
works.significance: Wives and Daughters is generally regarded as Gaskell's masterpiece and the most satisfying English novel of provincial life after Middlemarch; its unfinished condition has made it a permanent case in the study of the Victorian novel's endings, and its portrait of the stepmother is one of the period's most subtle studies of feminine performance.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
works.context: The 1820s-30s in the fictional county of Hollingford, the professional middle class of the country doctor and the landowning gentry of the Hall and the Towers, and the scientific natural history of the 1830s.
works.characters: Molly Gibson; Mr Gibson; Hyacinth Clare; Cynthia Kirkpatrick; Roger Hamley; Osborne Hamley; Squire Hamley; Lady Harriet Cumnor; Lord Cumnor; Lady Cumnor; Mr Coxe; Mrs Goodenough
works.structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Unfinished at the author's death on 12 November 1865; the Cornhill serial and the 1866 volume text break off before the final chapter, and the intended ending is known only from Gaskell's correspondence and the editor's note.

works.title: Woman and Labour
works.description: Published in 1911 and the most systematic work of feminist theory by a nineteenth-century English writer: a history and analysis of women's labour, and an argument for women's economic independence. It is a prose work of 1911 by Olive Schreiner; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Schreiner argues that women have been historically the producers of the means of subsistence, that the industrial revolution destroyed their economic function, and that the claim for the vote and for work is a demand for the restoration of an ancient position rather than for a new privilege.
works.significance: Woman and Labour is a founding text of English feminist theory and the most important work of its kind between Wollstonecraft and Woolf: its argument about the economic function of women shaped the suffrage campaign and the twentieth-century analysis of women's work.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. works.title: Woman in the Nineteenth Century
works.description: Published in 1845 and the first major American feminist book: an expanded version of the Dial essay 'The Great Lawsuit' and the foundation of the American women's movement. It is a prose work of 1845 by Margaret Fuller; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Fuller argues that the soul has no sex, that the woman question is the question of whether every human being is allowed to grow according to her own nature, and that the separation of men's and women's spheres has mutilated both; she surveys the history of women and calls for their full participation in the life of the mind and of the state.
works.significance: Woman in the Nineteenth Century is the founding text of American feminism and the most important American book on women before The Second Sex: it established the demand for women's intellectual and political independence as a matter of principle, and it shaped the Seneca Falls Declaration of 1848.

works.title: Women
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's third novel, a Gothic romance of obsessive love and self-destruction published between his first novel The Milesian Chief (1812) and his masterwork Melmoth (1820). It explores the destructive power of passion through a narrative of a man whose love becomes a kind of spiritual damnation.
works.plot: The narrator recalls his early passion for a mysterious woman, whose identity and intentions remain partly hidden. His obsessive attachment leads him into a sequence of Gothic crises — pursuit, entrapment, and despair — as the woman's own secrets unfold. The novel prefigures Melmoth's theological treatment of inescapable guilt and the soul pursued by its own desire.
works.significance: Women marks the intermediate stage in the author's development toward the great theological Gothic of Melmoth; its treatment of obsessive love as damnation is a significant contribution to the Gothic tradition in the 1810s.
works.context: Published in 1817, during the author's most productive period as a Gothic novelist; it continues the treatment of passion as spiritual ordeal begun in his first novel and looks forward to Melmoth (1820).
works.characters: The narrator; the woman; her hidden family history
works.structure: First-person retrospective narrative with embedded disclosures of the beloved's history; a linear sequence of escalating crises; the unresolved revelation anticipates Melmoth's later frame techniques.

works.title: Women and Economics
works.description: Published in 1898 and the most systematic American feminist book of the century: an economic analysis of women's dependency and a programme for their emancipation through work. works.title: Women Beware Women
works.description: Middleton's tragedy of Florence: Bianca, married in flight to the merchant's factor Leantio, is seduced by the Duke — Leantio watching from the balcony in the play's most infamous scene — while the parallel plot of Isabella and the incestuous Hippolito (her uncle) runs alongside; the play ends in the masque of revenges in which the Duke, Bianca, and the whole company die by poison, trap, and sword.
works.plot: Bianca's elopement, the Duke's lust, and Livia's pandering destroy the Leantio household; Hippolito's incestuous love and Livia's matchmaking destroy the Ward's marriage-plot; the final masque — prepared as entertainment — becomes the engine of mutual revenge, killing the Duke, Bianca, Hippolito, Livia, and the rest in a cascade of 'justice' that spares no one.
works.significance: Middleton's tragic masterpiece — the darkest anatomy of marriage, lust, and commodified womanhood on the Jacobean stage.
works.meter: Blank verse of Middleton's most controlled bitterness, with the masque's spectacle and the chess scene as its formal coups.
works.context: Based loosely on the Bianca Cappello story via Malespini; written about 1621 and printed only in 1657; its chess scene is the most famous stage metaphor of Jacobean seduction.
works.characters: Bianca; Leantio; the Duke of Florence; Livia; Hippolito; Isabella; the Ward; Guardiano; Fabritio; the Cardinal; the Mother
works.structure: A double plot of seduction and revenge converging in the masque of Act 5, with Livia's chess game — the moves paralleling the seduction — as the play's most celebrated device.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

Women, chastity, and constancy

works.title: Women in Love
works.form: Novel (privately printed in New York, 1920; London 1921)
works.description: Two sisters, two men and the search for a complete relationship, set against the industrial Midlands and the Alps. It is a prose fiction work of 1920 by D. H. Lawrence; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Ursula Brangwen and her sister Gudrun are schoolteachers in the Midlands. Ursula falls in love with Rupert Birkin, a school inspector, and Gudrun with Gerald Crich, the industrialist's son. Their relationships work themselves out through a series of set pieces — the wedding, the boating party, the water-party drowning, the sculpture of the horse, the snow in the Alps — and end with Gerald's death in the snow and Birkin's insistence that he needs another man's love as well as a woman's.
works.significance: Women in Love is the finest English novel of the period after Ulysses and Woolf's major work: it is the great novel of sexual love in English, its set pieces are among the most memorable in modern fiction, and its analysis of industrial civilisation and the will to power has never been surpassed.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the loose, repetitive, urgent sentence driven by the rhythm of feeling and breath.
works.context: The industrial Midlands before the First World War, the colliery and the mine-owner, the artistic colony of London, and the Alps of the end — Lawrence's own years in England, Germany and Switzerland. The record dates the work as composed between 1916 and 1917 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Ursula Brangwen; Gudrun Brangwen; Rupert Birkin; Gerald Crich; Hermione Roddice; Loerke; Thomas Crich
works.structure: Thirty-one chapters in a loose episodic structure, with symbolic set pieces and a tragic conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as David Herbert Lawrence. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands
works.description: Published in 1857 with a preface by W. H. Russell of The Times and one of the great Victorian autobiographies: the life of a Jamaican-Scottish woman who nursed through the Crimean War as an independent businesswoman.
works.plot: Seacole recounts her childhood in Kingston, her travels to England, Cuba and Panama, her nursing during the cholera epidemic in Jamaica and Panama, her journey to the Crimea after the official nursing service refused her, her British Hotel at Balaklava and her work under fire at Sevastopol.
works.significance: Wonderful Adventures is the founding text of black British autobiography and one of the most important first-hand accounts of the Crimean War: it records a black woman's professional life in the British Empire with humour and authority, and it is now central to the study of race, nursing and empire in Victorian Britain.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is first-person comic narrative with direct address to the reader.
works.context: The 1850s, the Crimean War, the nursing reform of Florence Nightingale, the colonial colour line in Britain, and the abolition of slavery in the British Empire (1833). The record dates the work as composed between 1856 and 1857 and first published in 1857 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; imperial adventure romance.

works.title: Work: A Story of Experience
works.form: Novel; novel of development, first issued in 1873
works.description: Published in 1873 and Alcott's most directly feminist novel: the story of a New England girl who must earn her own living and tries a series of occupations. It is a prose fiction work of 1873 by Louisa May Alcott; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
works.plot: Christie Devon works as a servant, an actress, a seamstress, a governess and a companion, marries the reformer David Sterling, is widowed, and finally finds her vocation as a nurse and a woman of independent judgment.
works.significance: Work is the founding American novel of women's employment and one of the most important feminist novels of the nineteenth century: its survey of the occupations open to women and its insistence on economic independence made it a key text of the American women's movement.
works.meter: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is domestic realism with a strong narrative voice.
works.context: The 1870s: the new women's occupations, the American labour question, and the debate on women's work. The record dates the work as composed between 1872 and 1873 and first published in 1873 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; new woman and marriage-question novel.
works.characters: Christie Devon; David Sterling; Mrs Sterling; Rachel (Letty Sterling); Philip Fletcher; Mrs Wilkins; Uncle Enos; Helena Carrol
works.structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as A. M. Barnard. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Working with the Hands
works.description: Published in 1904 and Washington's fullest account of the Tuskegee method: a book on the dignity of manual labour and the teaching of trades. It is a prose work of 1904 by Booker T. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
works.plot: Washington describes the teaching of agriculture, carpentry, brickmaking, dressmaking and housekeeping at Tuskegee, and argues that the education of the hand is the education of the whole person and the foundation of black economic independence.
works.significance: Working with the Hands is the classic American statement of industrial education and a key text in the history of American education and of black self-help.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of struggle and institutional building.
works.context: The 1900s: the industrial education movement, the Tuskegee curriculum, and the American debate on vocational training. The record dates the work as composed between 1903 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.

works.title: Works and Days: From the Journal of Michael Field
works.description: Published in 1933 from the 9,000-page journal kept by the two poets from 1884 to 1914: the most extraordinary diary of the aesthetic movement. It is a prose work of 1933 by Michael Field; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: The journal records the meetings with Browning, Ruskin, Pater and Wilde, the composition of the poems, the two women's travel in Italy and France, their reading, their quarrels and their love, and the conversion and deaths at the end.
works.significance: The Michael Field journal is one of the great English diaries and the central document of the aesthetic movement's daily life: its publication made the two women central figures in the history of Victorian sexuality, of women's writing and of the literary culture of the 1890s.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The text is the dated entry, continuous in its observation. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric.
works.context: 1884-1914: the aesthetic movement, the English literary world of the 1890s, and two women living and working as one author. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1914 and first published in 1933 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
works.characters: Katharine Bradley ('Michael'); Edith Cooper ('Henry'); Robert Browning; Walter Pater; Oscar Wilde; George Meredith; Bernard Berenson; Charles Ricketts and Charles Shannon; Whym Chow, their dog
works.structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.

works.title: Written in the Eleventh Century
works.description: Shenstone's late meditative poem, which situates its speaker by conceit in the eleventh century and so makes the present a remote antiquity. The resulting double perspective - an early age contemplating its own ruins, and a modern reader discovering his own remoteness - is the poem's machinery, and it turns the graveyard meditation outward upon history. It is Shenstone's most purely philosophical verse and one of the neatly depressing classics of preromantic reflection.
works.plot: The speaker, casting thought back into a millennium already gone, surveys what the vanished centuries had built and what time had spared, and finds that the proudest works of men stand in the same relation to the future as the ruins he contemplates to the past; the poem therefore proceeds by a chain of retrospection and anticipation, in which nations, foundations, learns and families alike are made to look forward to their own oblivion. It closes not in despair but in the tempered resignation proper to the moralised melancholy of the age, the reader being left to imagine his own century as the eleventh.
works.significance: It carries the graveyard meditation from the churchyard into historical time, anticipating the philosophy of ruin and of the distant century that would occupy the preromantic and romantic generations, and it long remained the standard anthology instance of Shenstone as a thinker rather than merely a poet of gardens.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the mid-century reflective school, with a slow, suspended syntax, frequent apostrophe and a marked fondness for the balanced pair of past and future.
works.context: Published in 1759, the year that also brought the first collected reputation of Young's meditations, the vogue of the graveyard, and the first great quarrel over the authenticity of ancient native poetry; Shenstone was then at the Leasowes, writing and planting, and the poem's temper of retired retrospect belongs to that scene.
works.characters: the meditating antiquary-speaker; the vanished ages and their founders
works.structure: A continuous meditative poem, moving by association through a sequence of historical retrospect and prospective fancy, without dramatic or argumentative division; the conceit of the dating is itself the organising principle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
The sublime, terror, and the ruin
movements: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation

works.title: Wulf and Eadwacer
works.form: elegiac dramatic monologue in alliterative verse
works.description: A famously enigmatic poem of 19 lines in which a woman cries out against the separation of 'Wulf' from herself and 'Eadwacer', their child; its refrain — 'Ungelice is us' ('It is different for us') — and its riddling situation have made it the most debated short poem in Old English.
works.plot: The speaker laments that her people will take Wulf if he comes to them ('they will receive him if he comes in a band'), that their child is being carried off to the woods, and that the embrace she once knew is gone; the poem closes on the refrain and the image of Wulf carrying their whelp to the wood.
works.significance: The most mysterious and most modern-sounding of the Exeter Book poems; a touchstone for theories of the Old English lyric.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with a refrain; the irregular lineation has suggested an underlying strophic form.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; interpretations range from heroic legend to riddle to Christian allegory.
works.characters: the speaker; Wulf; Eadwacer (their child)
works.structure: A compressed dramatic monologue of seven half-stanzas bound by a refrain, preserving an otherwise lost story (perhaps from the cycle of Wulf and Eadwacer, or a riddle, or an allegory).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)
altTitles: Wulfstan's Homilies on the Last Things
works.description: Wulfstan's corpus of sermons on the end times and the faith: the coming of Antichrist and the signs of the end, the true God and the false gods (De falsis deis), baptism and the duties of Christians. These homilies, saturated with the belief that the world was in its last age, formed the moral engine of Wulfstan's preaching and lawgiving.
works.plot: De Antichristo narrates the rise of the deceiver in the last days, the persecution of the faithful, and the judgment; De falsis deis traces the history of idolatry from the pagan gods of the classical pantheon (Saturn, Jove, Mercury — euhemerized as wicked men) to the Danish idols, and urges the English to hold to the one God; the related sermons expound the Creed and the duties of the baptized.
works.significance: The classic vernacular statement of early medieval eschatology and the theology of the one true God against the gods.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1000-1023, in the atmosphere of millennial expectation surrounding the year 1000 and the Danish conquest; preserved in manuscripts of Wulfstan's 'commonplace book' (e.g. British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i).
works.characters: Antichrist; the false gods; the faithful
works.structure: Independent homilies on eschatological and catechetical themes, each a self-contained exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
themes: Christian-pagan synthesis
Judgment Day and eschatology

works.title: Wuthering Heights
works.form: Novel in three volumes (with Agnes Grey), framed narrative
works.description: Published in December 1847 in three volumes together with Anne Brontë's Agnes Grey, under the pseudonym Ellis Bell, and the one Victorian novel that has never been domesticated into the conventions of its decade: a chronicle of two families on the Yorkshire moors, told by two partial narrators, in which the passion between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff exceeds every social and religious form available to it.
works.plot: Mr Lockwood, the tenant of Thrushcross Grange, visits his landlord Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights and is told the history of the house by the servant Nelly Dean. The foundling Heathcliff, brought home from Liverpool by Mr Earnshaw, and Catherine Earnshaw grow up inseparable on the moors; Catherine marries Edgar Linton for social position, Heathcliff returns wealthy and embittered, and the second half of the novel follows his revenge on the next generation — Hindley's son Hareton, and Catherine's daughter Cathy, whom he forces to marry his dying son Linton — until his own death releases the pair into their marriage and the ghosts of the first Catherine and Heathcliff are reported on the moor.
works.significance: Wuthering Heights is the most radical novel of the Victorian period and the only one that has resisted every attempt to place it in a history of the novel's development: its double narration, its two-generation structure and its unassimilable passion made it a permanent test case for criticism (from Charlotte Brontë's 1850 preface to Kermode, Miller, Gilbert and Gubar, and the postcolonial reading of Heathcliff's racial origin). Its influence runs through the modern Gothic, the novel of the moors, and the fiction of the American South.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is a frame-within-a-frame narrative with two partial and unreliable narrators.
works.context: The West Riding of Yorkshire in the 1770s-1802, the yeoman and gentry economy of the moorland farms, the Liverpool of the slave trade and the Irish famine emigration (the source of Heathcliff's origin, which the novel leaves unexplained), and the Calvinist and Methodist religious culture of the Brontë household.
works.characters: Heathcliff; Catherine Earnshaw; Catherine Linton; Edgar Linton; Isabella Linton; Hindley Earnshaw; Hareton Earnshaw; Cathy Linton; Linton Heathcliff; Nelly Dean; Joseph; Mr Lockwood; Mr Earnshaw; Zillah
works.structure: Two framed narratives (Lockwood's outer frame and Nelly Dean's inner chronicle) covering two generations over some thirty years, with a symmetrical doubling of the first and second pairs of lovers.
works.attributionNotes: It was published under the name Ellis Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Emily Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: Wyatt's Poems
altTitles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Sir Thomas Wyatt
works.description: The collected shorter poems of Sir Thomas Wyatt — sonnets translated and imitated from Petrarch, rondeaux, epigrams, and songs — including the masterpieces 'Whoso list to hunt', 'They flee from me', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness', and 'Blame not my lute'. They circulated in court manuscript during his life; ninety-six were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
works.plot: A lyric sequence without narrative frame: the poems trace the courtly lover's service, betrayal, and disenchantment, and the courtier's peril under the prince's eye.
works.significance: The foundation of the English lyric: Wyatt brought the Petrarchan sonnet and the courtly song into English, and his 'difficult' style set the standard of authenticity the Elizabethans imitated.
works.meter: The first English sonnets, in deliberately rough iambic pentameter with enjambment against rhyme; songs in short lines built for music.
works.context: Written across Wyatt's diplomatic career and his two imprisonments (1536, 1541); the poems encode the dangers of Henrician court life in the idiom of Petrarchan love.
works.characters: the speaker; the beloved (variously identified); the court
works.structure: Manuscript miscellany; the Egerton MS (with Wyatt's own revisions) is the principal witness, supplemented by Tottel's printed text.
works.attributionNotes: The canon rests on the Egerton MS and Tottel; a few poems printed under Wyatt's name in 1557 are of uncertain authorship.

Love, constancy, and betrayal

works.title: Wyatt's Satires
works.description: Three verse epistles — 'Mine own John Poins', 'My mother's maids', and 'A spending hand' — written from Wyatt's Kentish retirement after his 1536 imprisonment: adaptations of Horace and Alamanni in which the speaker rejects the court's falseness and the town's corruption for the honest poverty of the country life.
works.plot: Each epistle weighs the court against the country: to Poins, the speaker explains why he cannot flatter; to the courtiers, why he will not hunt with them into the wind; to Bryan, why honesty is the only policy he can keep.
works.significance: The first English satires in the classical manner and the models for the Elizabethan verse epistle and satire (Donne, Hall, Marston); their country-house ideal anticipates the seventeenth-century poems of retirement.
works.meter: Terza rima throughout — the metre of the Penitential Psalms prologue — giving the epistles a grave, conversational movement.
works.context: Written at Allington after Wyatt's release from the Tower in 1536; the satires voice the disillusion of the courtier who has survived the fall of Anne Boleyn.
works.characters: the speaker; John Poins; Francis Bryan
works.structure: Three independent verse epistles in the Horatian manner, linked by their common theme of withdrawal from the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Wycliffite Bible
works.description: The first complete translation of the Bible into English, produced in the circle of John Wyclif at Oxford and Lutterworth: the literal Early Version (c. 1382), associated with Nicholas of Hereford, and the idiomatic Later Version (c. 1388–95), associated with John Purvey. Banned by Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions (1409) but copied throughout the fifteenth century, it is the greatest monument of Lollard vernacular theology.
works.plot: The translation renders the whole Vulgate — Old and New Testaments, with the apocrypha — into English, the Early Version word-for-word after the Latin, the Later Version in fluent, idiomatic prose, with prologues defending vernacular scripture and a general prologue expounding the Lollard program of 'poor priests' and scriptural preaching.
works.significance: The foundational text of the English Bible: its phrasing passed into the sixteenth-century translations and into the common language of English devotion, and its very existence redefined the politics of vernacular religion.
works.meter: Prose: the Later Version in particular is a landmark of plain, idiomatic English style.
works.context: Made c. 1382–95 in Wyclif's circle, condemned by the Blackfriars council (1382) and by Arundel's Constitutions (1409), which forbade unlicensed vernacular scripture; despite the ban, some 250 manuscripts survive, and the translation fed the English biblical tradition through Tyndale to the King James Version.
works.characters: none (scriptural translation)
works.structure: The complete biblical canon in translation, with the characteristic Lollard prologues and glosses (in some manuscripts) as its apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally called the 'Wycliffe Bible', but modern scholarship dissents from Wyclif's personal authorship; the translation is the work of his circle (Hereford, Purvey, and others). authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.
themes: Ecclesiastical reform and criticism
Lollardy and religious dissent
movements: Lollardy

works.title: XX Poems
works.description: XX Poems is a pamphlet of twenty poems that Larkin had privately printed in Belfast in 1951, in an edition of only one hundred copies, after his manuscript had been rejected by publishers.
works.summary: Twenty short lyrics from the years after The North Ship, several of which reappeared four years later in The Less Deceived.
works.plot: The pamphlet gathers the short lyrics of Larkin's first years in Belfast and Leicester, in which he moved away from the Yeatsian manner of The North Ship towards the plain, ironic voice of his maturity; several of the poems reappeared in The Less Deceived.
works.significance: The least noticed of Larkin's books, it is important as the bridge between The North Ship and The Less Deceived.
works.meter: Increasingly colloquial, compressed verse that already shows Larkin's mature balance of irony and feeling.
works.context: Most of the copies were posted to critics and literary figures, but with too little postage after a rise in rates, so that many never arrived.
works.structure: Twenty short lyrics, most of them in rhymed stanzas, gathered in a slim privately printed pamphlet.

works.title: Yeast: A Problem
works.description: Published in Fraser's Magazine in 1848 and in book form in 1851: the story of a young aristocrat's education, and the most direct English novel of the religious and social crisis of 1848. It is a prose fiction work of 1851 by Charles Kingsley; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Lancelot Smith, a young gentleman, is drawn between the world of the country house and the world of the farm labourer, and between the agonies of doubt and the claims of faith; his friendship with the Cornish gamekeeper Tregarva, who opens his eyes to the misery of the labourers, and his love for the squire's daughter Argemone Lavington, who dies of a fever caught among the poor, lead him through doubt to the mysterious Prophet who points him towards a Christian socialism.
works.significance: Yeast is the central English novel of the religious crisis of the 1840s and the first to make a young man's intellectual doubt the subject of a novel; its comic and satirical scenes were admired by Carlyle, and its picture of rural poverty shaped the social-problem novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
works.context: The 1840s, the agricultural depression and Irish famine, the Oxford Movement, and the Christian Socialist experiment of the 1848 revolution. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1850 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Lancelot Smith; Argemone Lavington; Honoria Lavington; Squire Lavington; Tregarva, the gamekeeper; Colonel Bracebridge; Luke Smith, Lancelot's cousin; the Prophet Barnakill
works.structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto
works.description: Published in 1896 and the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant: a Russian Jew's Americanisation and the wife he has left behind. It is a prose fiction work of 1896 by Abraham Cahan; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
works.plot: Yekl, a young Russian Jew, has become 'Jake' in the New York ghetto, with American clothes, American manners and an American girl; when his wife Gitl arrives from Russia with their son, he is ashamed of her old-world appearance, and the novella ends with the divorce, Gitl free to marry the scholarly boarder Bernstein and Jake riding off, already uneasy, to marry the dance-hall girl Mamie.
works.significance: Yekl is the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant and the founding text of the Jewish-American novel: its portrait of the immigrant who is ashamed of his own wife, and its recording of the mixed English of the ghetto, made it the model for the American immigrant novel, and Howells praised it as the finest American story of the year.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The author's characteristic manner is documentary realism with a precise record of work and wages.
works.context: 1896: the mass immigration of Russian Jews, the Lower East Side ghetto, the sweatshop, and the American debate on assimilation. The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
works.characters: Yekl (Jake); Gitl, his wife; Yossele (Joey), their son; Mamie Fein; Bernstein, the boarder; Mrs Kavarsky
works.structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Avrom Cahan. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

works.title: York Play
works.description: The York Corpus Christi cycle: forty-eight (originally more) pageants dramatizing sacred history from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed annually by the city's craft guilds on wagons through the streets of York from the late fourteenth century to 1569. The longest and most complete surviving mystery cycle, registered in the great civic manuscript of 1463–77.
works.plot: The cycle moves from the creation and fall of the angels, through the Old Testament pageants (Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses), to the life of Christ — the Annunciation, Nativity, ministry, the great Passion sequence (the Crucifixion and the death of Christ are its summit), the Harrowing of Hell, and the Resurrection — and closes with the Last Judgement.
works.significance: The greatest surviving English mystery cycle: its Passion sequence is among the most powerful religious writing of the Middle Ages, and its civic organization is the fullest expression of medieval urban piety.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanza and couplet forms, with the alliterative 'York realism' of the Passion pageants.
works.context: The play is first mentioned in 1376, and the surviving register (BL Additional MS 35290) was compiled 1463–77; performances continued until suppressed in 1569, the cycle's long life making York the best-documented of the English civic dramas.
works.characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah; Abraham; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Pilate; Herod; the soldiers of the Crucifixion
works.structure: A sequential pageant cycle performed on Corpus Christi day, each play assigned to a guild (the Shipwrights' Noah, the Pinners' Crucifixion), the whole forming a civic salvation history.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (many guild poets, revised over generations); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.
themes: The Passion of Christ
The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion

works.title: Ywain and Gawain
works.description: The northern English adaptation of Chrétien de Troyes's Yvain: the knight Ywain wins Laudine by slaying her husband at the magic fountain, loses her by overstaying his leave, and regains her through madness, penance, and a career of championing the oppressed, with his lion as companion. The most accomplished English Arthurian romance after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
works.plot: Ywain kills the fountain's defender and marries the widow Laudine through her maid Lunet's advocacy; forgetting his year's leave, he is rejected, goes mad, and is healed; as the Knight of the Lion he rights a succession of wrongs (the giant Harpin, the sisters' inheritance), and by keeping faith at last wins back Laudine.
works.significance: The chief English witness to the French Arthurian romance's central themes of love, honour, and self-knowledge, and a bridge between continental romance and Malory.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect.
works.context: Composed c. 1325–50 in the north of England from Chrétien's Yvain (with an intermediary version); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Galba E.ix (c. 1400).
works.characters: Ywain; Laudine; Lunet; Gawain; the lion; the giant Harpin
works.structure: A quest-sequence of episodes bound by the fountain, the lion, and the promises made and broken, in the interlaced manner of French romance simplified for English taste.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Chivalry and knighthood
Courtly love and fin'amor
Penance, confession, and sin

works.title: Zanoni
works.description: Published in 1842 and the founding English occult novel: the love of an immortal Rosicrucian for a young singer, and the price of immortality. It is a prose fiction work of 1842 by Edward Bulwer-Lytton; it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
works.plot: Zanoni, a Rosicrucian brother who has conquered death, loves Viola, a young opera singer; he must choose between his immortal wisdom and mortal love, and his pupil Glyndon is tempted by the powers that Zanoni renounces, in a novel that moves from Naples to Paris during the Revolution.
works.significance: Zanoni founded the English occult novel and the modern literature of the immortal adept: its combination of Rosicrucian lore, mesmerism and revolutionary history influenced Bulwer's friend Dickens, the theosophists, and the whole tradition of occult fiction from Rider Haggard to Dion Fortune.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue.
works.context: 1842: the Rosicrucian revival, the Mesmerist and Swedenborgian circles of the 1840s, and the Victorian fascination with the occult. The record dates the work as composed between 1841 and 1842 and first published in 1842 and it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; novel of development and the growth story.
works.characters: Zanoni; Viola Pisani; Clarence Glyndon; Mejnour; Jean Nicot; Fillide; Robespierre; the Dweller of the Threshold
works.structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Bulwer-Lytton. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

works.title: Zofloisca; or, The Rose of Fantasy: A Romance
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's prose romance exploring the dangerous power of imagination and delusion, in which an enchanted rose induces fantasies that dissolve the boundary between reality and dream. Published in the same year as her more famous Zofloya; or, The Moor, it represents her earlier and more lyrical engagement with Gothic fantasy.
works.plot: The narrative alternates between a realistic frame and an embedded fairy-tale sequence about Zofloisca and the enchanted Rose of Fantasy. Characters in the realistic tale become entrapped by fantasies induced by the rose; the story-within-a-story structure enacts the novel's central theme of imagination as both enchantment and danger. The boundary between fairy-tale and waking life dissolves as passion overrides reason.
works.significance: the author's use of the embedded fairy tale anticipates later Romantic experiments in narrative frame; the novel's theme of dangerous imagination connects it to the broader Gothic preoccupation with the divided mind.
works.context: Published during the author's most productive Gothic period (1804–1811) and alongside Zofloya; it interrogates the cult of sensibility in the post-Wollstonecraft moment and draws on the fairy-tale tradition of the 1790s.
works.characters: Zofloisca; Rosalie; De Montfort; the Genius of Fantasy
works.structure: Frame narrative with an embedded fairy-tale sequence; the story-within-a-story enacts the novel's argument about the seductions of fantasy.

works.title: Zuleika Dobson; or, An Oxford Love Story
works.form: Novel; comic novel, first issued in 1911
works.description: The only great English comic novel about Oxford: the beautiful Zuleika and the drowning of the undergraduates. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Max Beerbohm; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the Satire of Manners; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
works.plot: Zuleika Dobson, a beautiful and heartless conjurer, visits her grandfather, the Warden of Judas College, and every undergraduate in Oxford falls in love with her; when she tells them she can never love a man who has not done something great, the whole university drowns itself in the Isis for her.
works.significance: Zuleika Dobson is the only great English comic novel about Oxford and Beerbohm's masterpiece: its prose, its fantasy and its satire of the university made it one of the finest comic novels of the century and the permanent Oxford novel.
works.meter: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the parody that catches the style exactly.
works.context: Oxford in the Edwardian period, and the aesthetic and undergraduate culture of the university. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under comic novel and the satire of manners; experimental novel and the modernist form.
works.characters: Zuleika Dobson; the Duke of Dorset; the Warden; Noaks; the undergraduates of Judas
works.structure: A comic novel in the essayist's narrator's voice. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry Maximilian Beerbohm. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
